Lessons learned: UNICEF's joint interventions with the Department of Vocational and Adult Education have highlighted the importance of integrating transferable skills into the TVET system and shifting to competency-oriented assessments in the context of the historical highest youth unemployment rates. 

Future outlook: continued prioritization of vocational education reforms, fostering youth entrepreneurship, and enhancing STEM, digital, and green skills. Policy advocacy will focus on including ECD services in the national basic public service package. Continued support for policy and system strengthening to shift the inclusive education paradigm,  ensuring  all children, including children with disabilities and special learning needs, have equal learning opportunities.

Child Protection

Challenges: the ministries' understanding of "child protection" is linked to the broader "protection of minors" as outlined in the Law on the Protection of Minors, rather than a specialized response. Additionally, more progress needs to be made in terms of wider implementation of child justice principles across the board. 

Lessons learned: UNICEF has a crucial role in advocating for a specialized definition of child protection at both national and local levels. Furthermore, for policy, direct engagement with academia and influential experts is essential to influence sensitive agendas and shape strategic policy papers. Successful engagement with private companies, especially tech companies, has advanced child online protection through documenting good practices on safety by design and responsible innovation.

Future outlook: Provide technical assistance for scaling up of existing models, such as ICPM and one stop centers tapping on recent policy developments. Expanding the pool of experts and formalizing partnerships with universities will be critical for high-level policy exchanges. There is a strong interest in international cooperation to exchange good practices and lessons learned. Addressing issues like child sexual abuse and exploitation online through a global challenge-global solution approach has been effective and will continue to be a focus.

Social Policy

Challenges: addressing multi-dimensional child poverty remains a challenge,  as the national focus has hitherto been on extreme poverty which now stands eradicated. Economic recovery post-COVID-19 has constrained government fiscal space, particularly at the local level, affecting the graduation and sustainability of UNICEF's pilot projects.  Under PFM, limited availability of programmatic data in each social sector level constraints  identifying PF4C gaps.

Lessons learned: strengthening partnerships with key stakeholders like IPRCC, MCA, and NDRC has enabled UNICEF to undertake more comprehensive work linked to challenges addressing child poverty. The need for innovative financing mechanisms and improved public finance management is crucial as part of UNICEF’s technical assistance. Balancing the selection of research partners and enhancing policy influence through strategic research are essential for effective project implementation.

Future outlook: continued advocacy for the acceptance of the FFP concept by line ministries, which includes inclusive ECC services, ECD, child allowances, and employment policies. The organization will focus on optimizing fiscal employment policies to benefit children and seek synergies with other UN agencies.

Partnerships & Engagement

Lessons learned: the importance of increased political trust and willingness from Chinese government partners, which can align UNICEF's objectives with China's global development goals through collaboration. Strengthened alliances with public and private sectors can fuel innovation and scalable solutions. The establishment of a dedicated social and behavioral change function has also been crucial.

Future outlook: focusing on climate and digital learning as new priority areas for collaboration. There are opportunities to advance child-focused ESG and financial initiatives by enhancing awareness and engagement with Chinese financial institutions. The UNICEF-MEE partnership on South-South cooperation on climate change has been strengthened, and sustainable energy for children in Africa has been identified as an emerging area. Additionally, a single advocacy campaign on climate change will be prioritized, culminating in a World Children’s Day event aligned with COP30.

PSFR

Significant progress was made with the private sector, securing long-term funding. However, challenges persist in the grey area of fundraising operations. Negotiations with the Government of China (GoC) will require changes in the current fundraising format for the next CPD. The future outlook for current fundraising methods is uncertain, but the team is ready to explore alternative strategies.

Key lessons include aligning with UNICEF mandates through Family Friendly Policies and ESG initiatives. Despite slow progress, efforts to promote human rights and business with government ministries like SASAC continue. 

Looking ahead, the opportunities to partner with the private sector in China are immense.  Enhanced communication support is needed to expand partner reach and promote partnerships. Better alignment between the PI team and communications is essential for digital space efficiency.

The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is a low-income country with a population of 26.4 million people, including 1.7 million children under the age of five years. Following periods of economic contractions during COVID-19 pandemic, the centrally planned economy has experienced modest growth again in 2023 and 2024.  




The modest economic growth has been made possible by a gradual and selective opening of the country in 2024. In line with this, some diplomatic missions returned to Pyongyang and selected DPRK officials resumed overseas missions. On the other hand, the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) and its international staff were not granted permission to return to the country or to carry out an exploratory mission. As a result, UN international staff remain based outside of the country and there is no concrete timeline for a return. The continued physical absence of international staff severely hampers programmatic activities of the UNCT.  




The year 2024 has also shown that the development trajectory of the country is increasingly shaped by a complex array of global and regional dynamics, both geopolitical and economic. This became all the more apparent as the country recalibrated its external relationships in response to unfolding world events and evolving national priorities, while gradually reemerging from COVID-19 isolation. It also saw a realignment of the country’s alliances, with the Russian Federation emerging as the DPRK’s closest partner. In March 2024, Russia vetoed a resolution to renew the mandate to the Panel of Experts supporting the Security Council Committee established pursuant to Resolution 1718, effectively hampering international oversight over the implementation of sanctions on the DPRK.  




In line with previous years, the availability of data about children and women remained constrained in 2024. The 2017 DPRK Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey Findings Report thus remains a key source of information for women and children. UNICEF maintains a remote monitoring system in close collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health. These systems have been useful to inform UNICEF on the quality of services provided at these health facilities, monitoring of distribution and utilization of supplies procured by UNICEF and identify areas to be improved. The information collected from these remote monitoring visits are triangulated with another set of data, collected by the Child Data Monitoring Unit of the Central Bureau of Statistics with UNICEF support, to understand overall coverage levels of key interventions.   




Despite prevailing data gaps, available systems are clearly able to demonstrate challenges faced by the national immunization program. That is, before the COVID-19 pandemic, immunization coverage in DPRK was over 96 percent for all routine vaccines. However, vaccines could not be delivered to DPRK in 2020 because of border closures, so that vaccine stockouts occurred by late 2021 and vaccination activities ceased in 2022. In 2023, UNICEF was able to restart the delivery limited quantities of vaccines to DPRK, and the year 2024 saw a significant breakthrough with the delivery of 7.2 million doses of vaccines to DPRK and the subsequent conduct of a national vaccination campaign and restart of the routine immunization programme. Coverage gaps remain in other areas, however. To illustrate, in 2024, only one in three children undergoing medical treatment for diarrhea received oral rehydration salts.  




In the area of nutrition, the DPRK saw substantial progress between the years 2000 and 2017 towards reducing stunting and wasting among children under 5 years of age, which in 2017 affected 19.1% and 2.5% of children, respectively. However, no updated data has become available on overall child nutrition status.  Agricultural outputs are an important underlying determinant of child nutritional status. Supported by overall favorable meteorological conditions, the country reportedly recorded improved harvests in 2023 and 2024. It is unclear, however, how these improved harvests affected the prevalence of undernourishment (defined as the percentage of the population whose habitual food consumption is insufficient to provide the dietary energy levels that are required to maintain a normal active and healthy life), estimated to be 45.5% from 2020-2022 according to latest available estimates. The lack of recent data and information thus limits assessments of food security and nutrition in the DPRK. 




The provision of safe water and sanitation (WASH) is one of the DPRK’s greatest developmental challenges. MICS survey in 2017 indicates 93.7% of the population used improved drinking water sources but only 66.4% of the population used a safely managed drinking water source that combines with water availability, accessibility, and safety. It is further evident by the disparities between provinces within the country. Similarly, 15.3% of the population lack access to basic sanitation facilities. As a result, one household in three still relies on contaminated water as their source of drinking water and 3 in 20 people live in unhealthy environments due to the unsafe disposal of human waste and the lack of access to improved sanitation facilities. However, in 2024, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Urban Management (MOUM) in completing twelve community-focused water programmes, that were carried over from 2020.  




In 2024, the global community continued to focus on human rights in the DPRK. The DPRK government addressed various issues, particularly during its active participation in the UN Human Rights Council’s universal periodic review in November 2024, where it initially accepted over 200 recommendations. However, the Secretary General expressed serious concerns about the right to food, freedom of expression and information, the use of the death penalty, fre12 edom of movement, the situation of overseas workers, and the overall lack of accountability for violations. These concerns were echoed by the Special Rapporteur on human rights in the DPRK and the Third Committee of the General Assembly, which adopted a resolution by consensus in November 2024

Despite the continued absence of its international staff from the country, UNICEF continued to provide life-saving interventions across the health, nutrition, and water, sanitation and hygiene sectors to women and children in DPRK in 2024. UNICEF’s ability to transport essential supplies continued to improve compared to previous years. In total, as of early December 2024, UNICEF successfully transported US$ 8.97 million worth of supplies to DPRK during the year.  

 
Health 

UNICEF arranged five chartered flights to ship the vaccines in the pipeline since 2021 and ensured the provision of essential vaccines during 2024, significant progress was made in reducing the number of children who had missed routine vaccinations since 2022.  With UNICEF support, the DPRK Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) organized a national multiantigen catch-up campaign and restored the routine immunization. These concerted efforts ensured that large numbers of children were following vaccinated. Specifically, 369,404 children received the required single dose of BCG vaccine and 23,145 and 443,606 children the required single doses of Hep B and inactivated polio virus vaccines, respectively. Furthermore, 457,617 children received the required two doses of with measles-rubella vaccine and 164,374 pregnant women two doses of tetanus-diphteria vaccine. In addition, UNICEF’s support to the government helped reduce the proportion of zero-dose children (children who missed the 1st dose of Pentavalent vaccine) from 40% in 2023 to 32.5% in 2024 by vaccinating 274,120 children with the 1st dose of the Pentavalent vaccine. 

 

As other areas of support to the national vaccination programme, UNICEF procured 217 pieces of cold chain equipment (CCEs), five cooling units for 40 m3 walk-in cold chain rooms and seven cooling units for 10 m3 walk-in cold chain rooms and delivered to DPRK as a continuous effort to strengthen the cold chain system and to increase the cold chain capacity for storing the vaccines at central, provincial, and country levels. These CCEs were distributed and installed in 217 sites across 13 provinces by national technicians, a good approach for capacity building of the human resources in the system. The upgraded system benefited more than a million children and women in the country by ensuring access to safely stored effective vaccines. 

 

Lastly, UNICEF supported the MoPH with the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for effective vaccine management (EVM). Recommended by a previous EVM assessment for DPRK, the SOPs cover the areas of vaccine arrival, temperature monitoring, storage capacity, maintenance of equipment and transportation, stock control, distribution, vaccine management, and overall program management. The SOPs represent a significant step forward towards strengthening national vaccine management, especially with regard to sustainability, resilience and quality of immunization services. Additionally, UNICEF played a crucial role in identifying and equipping national trainers who effectively trained immunization focal persons at the provincial, county, and village levels.   

 

In addition to its support to the national vaccination programme, UNICEF also supported the effective delivery of other essential health interventions. In the area of the integrated management of newborn and childhood illnesses (IMNCI), UNICEF led the update of national IMNCI guidelines for children under two months. The guidelines were endorsed by the DPRK government in 2024 and disseminated to service providers. Beyond this guideline work, UNICEF also procured and delivered a large quantity of essential medicine including antibiotics, antipyretics, ORS, ORS and zinc kits, zinc tablets, antiseptics, analgesics, and commodities to DPRK. These essential drugs and commodities items were distributed to more than 1,850 health facilities in 50 UNICEF priority counties. These supplies are sufficient to benefit over 5 million people, including more than 600,000 children under five years of age. 

 

When it comes to coverage of maternal and child health interventions, more than 429,000 children with diarrhoea received medical attention in 2024. However, only 32.3 per cent (123,698) received oral rehydration salt (ORS). In the 50 UNICEF focus counties, 123,696 children with diarrhoea received medical attention but only 40.3 per cent (50,015 children) received oral rehydration salt (ORS). The low coverage of ORS is due to the shortage of ORS in the first half of 2024. A total of 40,247 children with pneumonia received care and 97 per cent of them received antibiotics.  

 

Based on the recommendations of a 2023 needs assessment carried out in 250 hospitals, UNICEF worked to improve the availability of hospital equipment and continuous stocks of essential drugs and commodities to provide quality Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmONC) and Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (CEmONC) services. Specifically, UNICEF procured and delivered life-saving drugs including antibiotics, antipyretics, analgesics, antiseptics, and essential supplies such as cannula, sutures, gloves, and bandages to DPRK to support maternal and newborn services. UNICEF also provided hospital equipment including weighing machines for adults, children and newborns, portable pulse oximeters, infusion stands, vacuum extractors, suction pumps, resuscitation sets for adult/child/newborn, delivery sets, sterilization kits, stethoscopes, blood pressure machines,  penguin suctions for newborns, midwifery kits, suction pumps, patient monitors, phototherapy units, infusion pumps, defibrillators, electrical cardiography machines, incubators,  monitors, operation theatre lights, ultrasound scanners, instrument mayo tables, suture sets, abdominal surgery sets, abdominal examination sets, and cervical tear repair sets. In all, 10 hospitals with CEmONC services and 252 hospitals with BEmONC services in 50 priority counties received the hospital equipment. The items provided were vital to upgrade the BEmONC and CEmONC sites, to improve the quality of care and reduce preventable deaths and morbidities among pregnant women and their newborns. In all, over 78,000 pregnant postpartum mothers and their newborn infants benefitted from the items provided in 2024. 

 
Nutrition  

Annually, an estimated 95,000 children with wasting (42,000 severely wasted and 53,000 moderately wasted children) were targeted for treatment. A total of 39,778 children with wasting (42 per cent of the annual target) were identified and treated in 189 Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) sites. Given the severe constraints on the availability of resources, only 17,133 (41 per cent) children with severe form of wasting were identified and received treatment, while a total of 22,560 (43 per cent) with moderate form of wasting and concurrent illnesses were identified and treated as per the CMAM protocol. Significant progress in identifying and treating moderate form of wasting cases is largely attributed to UNICEF's first-ever procurement and delivery of Ready-to-Use Supplementary Food (RUSF) in DPRK, sufficient to manage approximately 35,000 children with MAM and associated medical complications. This effort helped prevent the progression of moderate form of wasting cases to severe form of wasting and reduced mortality among severe form of wasting cases. It is worth noting that children with moderate form of wasting did not receive critical malnutrition treatment services from 2020 to 2022 due to resource constraints. However, in 2023 and 2024, a significant number of children with moderate form of wasting with complications received treatment. 

 

As part of the Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) guidelines for wasting management, children with severe forms of wasting and underlying medical complications are admitted to hospitals or in-patient treatment/stabilization centres. The children receive specialized care under 24-hour medical supervision. In 2024, 7,045 children under five in DPR Korea with severe form of wasting with medical complications were admitted in the 189 CMAC sites. This is a critical treatment period, ranging from 5 to 15 days, when specialized therapeutic milk (F75) was used for stabilizing malnourished children. When these children were stabilized, they were discharged and referred to outpatient nutrition rehabilitation programs, where they continued treatment for two to three months with F-100 therapeutic milk or Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) to ensure full recovery and prevent relapse. 

 

In 2024, in addition to improvements in the treatment of wasting, significant progress was made in micronutrient supplementation among children under five. Through the Child Health Days (CHD), 1,094,020 children aged 6-59 months (81 per cent of target) received the required two doses of vitamin A.  A total of 56,616 children aged 6-23 months received multiple micronutrient powders (MNPs) during the May 2024 CHD to enrich their home foods with essential vitamins and minerals. Coverage was limited because of limited funding to procure MNPs. In all, 132,895 (44 per cent) of the targeted 300,000 pregnant and lactating women received multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS), while approximately 74,500 women of childbearing age received Iron Folic Acid (IFA). Funding constraints also limited the coverage of these interventions.   

 
WASH 

In 2024, UNICEF in collaboration with the Ministry of Urban Management (MOUM), completed nine community water supply projects and three water supply projects in health facilities in nine counties of seven provinces benefitting 227,677 people (109,091 men and 118,586 women) through clean and safe water. Similarly, 18 schools and 16 health facilities in the catchment areas of the completed water supply projects were connected to the piped water system.  

 

To strengthen the capacity of local people’s committee members and lower-level government technicians, UNICEF organized operation and maintenance training with support from MOUM’s engineers. The training was attended by 69 participants (58 men and 11 women) and was focused on building the capacity of the water supply service personnel at the lower levels – county and village levels, to enhance the knowledge of the participants on the importance of O&M, develop essential skill and learn from others’ experiences. 

 

In close collaboration with UNICEF, the MOUM successfully delivered pre-positioned WASH supplies including 100 pcs of water filters, 17,470 water buckets, 260,000 handwashing soaps, 1,000 set of hygiene kits, 120 rolls of tarpaulin, and 500 drums of 45 kg calcium hypochlorite. These supplies were distributed across 23 counties in 8 provinces and Nampo City, benefiting 26,000 people in need. 

 

Additionally, UNICEF successfully advocated for the inclusion of WASH activities in Child Health Days (CHD) and distributed 100,000 soap bars and 5,000 towels to over 7,000 children. This initiative aimed to promote safe hygiene practices and handwashing as part of a preventive cross-sectoral intervention alongside health and nutrition programs in seven counties of seven provinces. 

 

UNICEF continued to lead the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector together with the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), World Vision, and Concern Worldwide, amongst others. Nine virtual WASH sector coordination meetings were organized in 2024 and attended by UN, donors and CSOs namely IFRC, WVI, Concern Worldwide, MCC and Triangle. In the absence of international professionals in the country, WASH partners are also working remotely outside the DPRK and have not been able to implement any activities since 2020.  

 
Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation 

In the absence of international professionals in-country, the remote monitoring of the programme started in December 2021 and has continued with the support of MOUM engineers throughout 2024 in line with agreed guidelines. To date, the monitoring teams have been able to conduct monitoring visits to all water supply projects using an agreed checklist and template. The remote monitoring guidelines represent a temporary mechanism for programme assurance and quality oversight in the absence of international staff presence in the country, whereby teams of engineers from the MoUM visit project locations and provide technical on-site training to People’s Committees to complete the construction of the projects. Government engineers and the UNICEF national officer completed the monitoring of the projects in 17 counties in 8 provinces.  

 

UNICEF continued its efforts to implement remote programme monitoring of the Health and Nutrition program. Teams from Government ministries and UNICEF national seconded staff visited 85 village and neighborhood facilities in 20 counties of six provinces for the Health and Nutrition Programme. Key information was obtained from these visits, including noting good practices, stocks of supplies of medicines, drugs, vaccines and medical consumables at the facility level, and knowledge and capacity of the gap among service providers.   

 

UNICEF supported the Child Data Management Unit within the Central Bureau of Statistics in the collection and processing of data, resulting in an expansion of information received through quarterly data sets. This practice enables better triangulation of data between county-level distribution plans and the number of children receiving UNICEF services, to support improved programme assurance in the absence of international staff field visits, as well as monitor how resource allocations and programmes are impacting on key child rights indicators.  

 

Based on these results, a Power BI dashboard was launched, including information on population, births, children under 5, children above 5, adolescents, and population per age band, disaggregated by year and province. It also includes data on fund analysis, immunization, MCH, and nutrition. The Power BI dashboard is expected to be updated regularly as monitoring data becomes available. However, its potential to generate evidence-based programme decisions is limited by the lack of disaggregated data in gender and other areas. 

 

In 2024, the DPRK team continued to make substantial progress in implementing the Management Response to the Country Programme Evaluation. The country team has carried out all activities that can be done while the international team remains outside the country. Once the team returns, the remaining three recommendations, which focus on the next country programme, will be implemented

Despite the continued remote working modality of international staff from Bangkok, partnerships remained important for UNICEF’s work to drive results for children. 

 

Throughout its team of national staff in Pyongyang, and remote support from its Bangkok-based staff, UNICEF maintained productive working relations with the Government of DPRK that were guided by signed annual work plans. In 2024, the Country Programme was extended with the approval of the UNICEF Executive Board for a further 12 months, until 31 December 2025. 

 

UNICEF supported the Ministry of Public Health on the immunization and other health programmes, as well as key nutrition responses. UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Urban Management on WASH responses, and the Central Bureau of Statistics to monitor and collate data on both the status of children, to the extent possible, and the implementation of the Country Programme.  

 

UNICEF was an active member of the UN Country Team (UNCT), providing input to regular UNCT meetings and initiatives led by the Resident Coordinator’s office. Among the different UN partners, UNICEF worked especially closely with the World Health Organization (WHO) to ensure alignment of approaches in the fields of immunization.  

 

Among UNICEF’s resource partners, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, provided crucial resource support for health system strengthening, ensuring the availability of supplies, human resources and enabling environment. Gavi funds made it possible to ensure availability of vaccines and its delivery to DPRK, procurement of cold-chain equipment, nutrition therapeutic supplies and intervention to improve WASH facilities in health facilities. Throughout the year, UNICEF greatly appreciated Gavi’s unwavering support to the DPRK immunization programme despite a challenging operating environment
