The major challenge of the country programme is the continued inability of international staff to return to the country. This continued absence limits UNICEF’s ability to raise funds and implement and monitor programmes, UNICEF has therefore implemented a programme criticality phase in which the recruitment of positions has been frozen and programmatic activities prioritize lifesaving interventions.   

 

The continued hybrid approach to programme management, with international staff based in Bangkok, Thailand, and the seconded national team in Pyongyang, requires careful coordination and planning to ensure both programme and financial assurance controls were in place and implemented effectively. The approach showed that major results for women and children can be achieved through the current approach.  

 

With the continued absence of international staff from the country, the Country Office’s remote monitoring systems remained highly relevant. The systems were based on a combination of field visits by national staff field and consultants from the Ministry of Public Health and the Ministry of Urban Management using a monitoring checklist and sharing of trip reports with international staff outside the country for review and feedback. Despite prevailing limitations, the system helped to assess quality of care, competency of service providers, project completion rates, and the overall availability and utilization of supplies and commodities. 

 

The year 2024 marked a period of gradual and selective opening of the DPRK to the international community. Despite continued optimism that the opening of the country will continue in 2025, there is currently no concrete information on a potential return of international UN staff to the country. Furthermore, the geopolitical landscape has become more complex. UNICEF is therefore planning on continuing to implement a hybrid approach through international staff based in Bangkok and national staff based in Pyongyang. UNICEF is ready, however, for its international staff to return to the country should relevant approvals be obtained

The East Asia and Pacific region, home to a quarter of the world’s population of children, or 552 million children under 18 years of age and about 458 million young persons (10-24), is undergoing significant demographic shifts. Rapid population growth in countries like Indonesia, the Philippines, and Viet Nam has increased demand for quality education, health care, and other services for children while in aging societies like China, Thailand, Malaysia and several Pacific Islands resources invested in social services for children are diverted to cater for the increasingly elderly population. Urbanization in the region is accelerating, increasing pressure on urban education and health care systems.

In 2024 most Southeast Asian economies experienced economic growth, with countries like Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines exceeding 5 per cent GDP growth. However, rising debt levels and tightening fiscal space for social sectors are impacting public finances including for social sectors.

Technology and internet access expansion was accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. As of 2022, 73 per cent of the region’s 15–24 years old are online. Digital education has surged, and digital health initiatives have improved health outcomes. Social media has changed the way people interact, with users in East Asia spending an average of 3.5 hours per day online. The rise of gaming culture and digital communication has brought opportunities for participation and communication, as well as challenges like cyberbullying and mental health struggles. The digital divide has become a new face of inequality, prompting the need to reduce socio-economic and gender disparities in access to technology. Private sector-led research in 2022 found that among the region’s underserved and marginalized youth, 47.8% struggled with essential proficiency in basic workplace software and a staggering 72.2% possessed minimal to no advanced digital skills.

The East Asia and Pacific region is considered one of the most disaster-prone regions globally. Climate hazards (typhoons, heavy rain, floods, landslides), disrupted access to clean water, health care, food, and shelter, and interrupted the education of some 50 million children in 2024. Typhoon Yagi and subsequent flooding affected over 5.6 million people, including 1.6 million children, in Lao PDR, Myanmar, Thailand and Viet Nam, while six typhoons hit the Philippines in a single month. El Niño-driven heatwaves and drought triggered severe water shortages in Cambodia, Viet Nam, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands, while Mongolia endured its harshest dzud in 50 years. Public health emergencies included outbreaks of polio in Indonesia, measles in Mongolia and the Philippines, and cholera cases in Myanmar and Thailand. Volcanic eruptions in 2024 impacted Indonesia, the Philippines, Tonga, and Vanuatu. While recovering from cyclone Lola, Vanuatu experienced a 7.3-magnitude earthquake, affecting more than 80,000 people and leaving 12,655 school children without a learning space. The political crisis in Myanmar, resulted in an estimated 6 million children requiring humanitarian assistance and displaced a record number of 3.5 million people.

Progress on achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the region remains uneven. According to SDG data analysis, all children in the region live in a country where the goals will not be achieved by 2030. 16 million children aged 3-5 years (19% of the region’s 84.2 million children in that age group) are not enrolled in any early childhood care and education programme. Early childhood education teaching conditions vary, with half of the region’s countries not meeting international benchmarks and 78% of the region’s countries have not met the international benchmark of allocating at least 10% of government education expenditure or at least 1% of GDP to early childhood development. One in three children under 5 years (over 40.5 million), are at risk of not reaching their developmental potential due to extreme poverty and stunting.

The region has had some of the fastest increases of overweight and obesity: 22% of all children aged 5–19 years – and in some countries more than two out of three children – are overweight. Greater efforts are needed to protect and promote diets, services, and practices to prevent malnutrition in all its forms across the life cycle.

Although access to education has improved, learning outcomes remain problematic. An estimated 45% of children, approximately 67 million, in the region are unable to read and understand a simple sentence by the age of 10 years, an increase from 35 % in pre-COVID-19 times. The latest regional figures indicate that an estimated 32.3 million children and adolescents are out of school.

Children with disabilities, children from lower socio-economic backgrounds, and children from linguistic minority groups continue to be disadvantaged. Many of the region’s estimated 43 million children with disabilities have limited access to basic services. The out-of-school rate in low-income countries was 33% in 2023, about 11 times higher than that in high-income countries (at 3%). Around 37% of children in the region are estimated to be learning in a language they do not understand.

Despite major gains in increasing access to and completion of education in the region, there is a gap between the skills taught in schools and those needed to obtain decent work. Despite the rapid growth in green jobs, girls remained underrepresented in STEM fields and green skills training. Additionally, 160 million youth are not in employment, education, or training with nearly three-quarters of them being girls and young women.

The region continues to have some of the world’s highest rates of violence against children. With 75 million, East and Southeast Asia had the second-highest number of women and girls impacted by contact sexual violence before the age of 18 years. While Pacific countries have the lowest absolute number (6 million) it represents that one in three women reported sexual violence before the age of 18 years – the highest rate in the world. Between 1 and 20% of children in Southeast Asia reported experiencing online sexual abuse. Across the region, 49–92% of children aged 1–14 years reported experiencing violent discipline on a regular basis; up to 84% of them experienced bullying; and up to 26% of girls experienced intimate partner violence.
In a region where civic spaces have been shrinking, adolescent girls and boys are struggling to raise their voices, inform policies and decisions affecting their lives, and be changemakers. Girls and young women continue to be disproportionately affected and have even less space than their male counterparts to realize the changes they aim to achieve.

The UNICEF East Asia and the Pacific Regional Office (EAPRO) provides policy advice, technical advice, oversight, knowledge brokering and partnership cultivation that supports UNICEF country programmes to achieve results for children.

Outcome 1: Health and nutrition
In East Asia and the Pacific curative or treatment options for most diseases are available but not accessible to all. To address this challenge and enable UNICEF country programmes to reach universal coverage in public health care, EAPRO had invested in systems strengthening and generated evidence for enhanced programming. Multi-country research identified options and strategies for countries to work towards universal access to quality primary health care. A landscape analysis of primary health care in all 14 countries of the region led to a series of webinar events promulgating evidence and options for strengthening health systems and to advance primary health care. With the increased uncertainty of health-related official development assistance and possible reductions in donor funding, sustainable domestic health financing and health system strengthening have become increasingly critical. EAPRO collected evidence and generated analysis on the economic case for investing in community-based primary health care and supported an innovative pilot of subnational financing of community health worker roles in Cambodia.

To close the gap of 2.5 million zero-dose children in the region, UNICEF helped strengthen the immunization system in seven countries. This included organizing a capacity-building Vaccine Procurement Forum to analyse the barriers to such procurement and potential solutions, including how to stimulate domestic financing and using technology that creates access to reliable data that then allows governments and partners to identify the children who have been missed. UNICEF has been supporting the scaling up of digital health solutions, such as real-time vaccination monitoring and analysis, to help governments to better plan, implement and evaluate immunization campaigns. 

EAPRO consolidated efforts to enhanced capacities at country office level to prevent and treat malnutrition in both humanitarian and development settings. Strategies entailed systems-strengthening, building up the evidence and brokering knowledge on a wide platform. With the ASEAN Secretariat and partners, EAPRO produced minimum standards on nutrition priorities and six nutrition guidelines for the region to strengthen nutrition governance and capacities. Through technical advice and financial support, EAPRO helped with transitions to improved maternal nutrition services, including the shift to promoting multiple micronutrient supplements during pregnancy and improved policies and standards for commercial complementary foods (for which EAPRO developed new manufacturing guidelines). EAPRO provided evidence to encourage policies that curb overweight and obesity, including nutrient profile models, analysis of sugar-sweetened beverage taxes, marketing restrictions for unhealthy foods and research on how to improve retail food environments. To improve wasting programmes, support was provided to update national wasting guidelines and treatment programmes, including in emergency settings. EAPRO reviewed the nutrition relevance of public financial management systems in eight countries that led to more versatile recommendations and support for country offices on addressing the challenges. EAPRO leveraged the Child Nutrition Fund to increase the availability of supplies and financial resources in eligible countries. The delivery of health and nutrition action at the community level was strengthened in selected countries and the development of an action agenda on climate change and nutrition was supported.

Outcome 2: Education and early childhood development
With a persistent learning crisis in the region, EAPRO continued to support countries to improve capacities for and commitment to ensuring that children and young people have improved access to inclusive and equitable education, learning and skills. Strategies concentrated on systems-strengthening, evidence generation and convening regional partnerships. In early childhood development, an EAPRO initiated regional Parenting Mapping Study led to a policy brief which provided guidance on the inclusion of parenting in national budgets and programmes across the East Asia and Pacific and South Asia regions. The study which aimed to make early childhood development policies and programmes more sustainable was cited by regional partners, as critically invaluable.

In 2024, EAPRO and the Southeast Asia Ministers of Education Organization co-led the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) assessment at the Grade 5 level in seven countries, which helped education ministries improve their capacity to produce and analyse learning data. The partnership also leveraged increased resources from the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea for assessments and foundational learning. In addition to the essential evidence it generates, this support increased national expertise and regional collaboration in large-scale assessments and evidence-based decision-making targeting the learning crisis.

The Empowered and Equal Futures for Adolescent Girls programme advanced gender-transformative education in the target countries of Cambodia and Viet Nam and paved the way for an enabling environment for gender-transformative education at the regional level through increased commitments to such education. Amongst those commitments is the outcome statement of the sixth Asia–Pacific Meeting on Education 2030 to accelerate learning in the region and ensure the achievement of SDG 4 by 2030 and to the UN Girls’ Education Initiative’s Regional Declaration for Gender-Transformative Education.

Advocacy and the development of technical guidelines, including on assessing multilingual learners, the multilingual education agenda across the region advance the importance of language of instruction. The inclusive education action planning promoted in Cambodia and China led to systematic shifts towards disability-inclusive education models.
Leveraging its position as a regional oversight practitioner, EAPRO secured nearly US$5 million for climate-smart education initiatives in seven countries. A regional report on teachers’ digital literacy filled evidence gaps and helped to inform policies in several countries, such as the Digital and AI Competency Framework in Viet Nam.

Outcome 3: Child protection
To ensure that children and adolescents are better protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and unnecessary family separation, EAPRO supported UNICEF country offices to strengthen inclusive and gender sensitive child protection, care and justice systems and prevention programming at scale. Key strategies included system strengthening, regional standard settings and convening, and innovation.

UNICEF in Timor Leste and Myanmar reported an overall increase in their national child protection systems’ maturity and Primero (a child protection information management system) went live in three additional countries (China, Timor-Leste, the Philippines). Endorsement of ASEAN Guidelines on the role of the social service workforce in the Education Sector was a major milestone for intersectoral collaboration for child protection.

EAPRO led the way in positioning child protection on the climate agenda and providing pragmatic guidance to UNICEF country offices, developing the first framework for ensuring climate resilience of child protection systems strengthening, and the first Primero climate marker - an innovative initiative to track the impact of climate on child protection risks. Supported by EAPRO, Regional Guidance for ASEAN Member States on the Role of Social Workers and the Wider Social Service Workforce in Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Resilience was endorsed – the first regional framework of its kind. EAPRO’s innovative technical mentoring scheme led to the strengthening of emergency preparedness capacities for child protection in 11 countries.

To accelerate action on violence prevention, EAPRO helped 10 countries prepare for their engagement in the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. With UN Women and UNFPA, EAPRO supported the development of ASEAN Guidance on “Empowering Women and Children: Delivering Quality Social Work Services for Those at Risk of or Affected by Violence”, which was launched on ASEAN Social Work Day. EAPRO supported the 3rd ASEAN ICT Forum on Child Online Protection, which was hosted by the Government of Indonesia, at which government officials, industry experts and young people explored how to effectively future proof tech against evolving online harms. EAPRO supported the contextualization of Laaha, a virtual safe space for women and girls to access gender-based violence information and services, for Myanmar.

With EAPRO support, by the end of 2024, 37,484,405 children and adults across 15 countries had access to safe and accessible reporting channels for cases of sexual exploitation and abuse, a 35% increase from 2023.

To advance programming on mental health, EAPRO jointly with UNESCO developed a tool to assess mental health and psychosocial support readiness in schools. Further with WHO under the Joint Programme on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Malaysia and Papua New Guinea, EAPRO strengthened systems, supported policy development, and capacity-building of front-line workers.

Outcome 4: Water, sanitation, hygiene and climate
EAPRO continued to support countries across the region on strengthening their capacities for, and commitment to ensuring that more children and adolescents have access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services and live in a safe and sustainable environment. Strategies included technical advisory, oversight, evidence generation, capacity-building and convening regional partners and resource mobilization, all of which resulted in securing resources for a multi-country climate programme.

All 14 UNICEF country offices and their partners received high-quality technical support and capacity-building from EAPRO on the circular economy, solar-powered water systems and the human right to safe water and sanitation, including in health care facilities. This included mobilizing resources and coordinating seven WASH-related proposals and concept notes on behalf of country offices.

UNICEF’s sector leadership role was reinforced through the engagement in the World Water Forum, which the Government of Indonesia hosted. EAPRO conducted studies and guidance on climate-resilient WASH and on community resilience.

EAPRO provided technical support on climate programme preparation to 10 country offices; this included inception reports and country missions in Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, Vanuatu and Viet Nam. EAPRO also drafted Climate Smart Programme Guidance for East Asia and the Pacific and developed a Climate Smart Regional Results Framework.

In 2024, EAPRO established new partnerships and mobilized resources for a multi-country climate programme (covering Cambodia, the Lao PDR, Malaysia and Thailand: The Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) committed US$29 million in grants and the KAKAO Bank (through the Korea National Committee) provided nearly US$1 million. EAPRO worked with UNICEF headquarters on Green Climate Fund accreditation and advanced partnership-building on climate programming with the governments of Australia and Japan, international financial institutions and private sector companies. EAPRO also launched Solar Hub 2.0 to provide training on solar energy applications for health, education and youth skills. For instance, trainings in Fiji covered WASH, health and education; a multicountry online training covered solar WASH; trainings in the Lao PDR and Viet Nam and a training in Mongolia focused on youth skills.

Outcome 5: Social policy
EAPRO supported countries across the region in strengthening their capacities and commitment so that more children have equitable access to inclusive social protection and benefits from inclusive policies to live free from poverty. Strategies included systems-strengthening, evidence-generating, resource-mobilizing and convening regional partners. Achievements included increased commitment and interest from governments to invest in child-friendly cities and countries better engaged in public finance management aimed at leveraging more resources for children.

In 2024, EAPRO continued to enhance social protection systems across the region, focusing on child-sensitive and gender-responsive measures and improving national capacities to handle shocks and climate change. This involved evidence generation, capacity building and technical assistance for emergency implementation. The newly introduced ‘Scaling Up Anticipatory Action and Shock Responsive Social Protection in ASEAN’ project, equips countries with evidence, guidelines and technical knowledge to manage climate shocks and disasters through their social protection system. EAPRO’s Gender-Responsive Social Protection Programme conducted landscape mapping and political economy analyses to generate insights on gender-related impacts and to build up country office capacity for gender-responsive social protection. The Viet Nam Country Office was supported to operationalize its Social Protection in Emergencies programming and assisted with cash transfers in its response to typhoon Yagi.

EAPRO’s second Regional Meeting on Child-Friendly Cities conducted in Jinan, China attracted more than 300 representatives from national and local governments, UNICEF and partners. There is growing interest in child-friendly city action, with rapid scaling up in China and Malaysia and interest from Cambodia, the Lao PDR, Thailand and Timor-Leste.

The second phase of EAPRO’s Public Finance Facility in South and South-East Asia was negotiated and concluded for 2024–2028, with 3 million euros mobilized for eight countries in two regions.
EAPRO’s first South–South exchange on Prioritizing Tomorrow: Strategic Spending for Children's Rights and Resilience in Asia brought together finance ministry officials from nine countries in South and South-East Asia, along with officials from the International Monetary Fund, the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and resulted in the elevation of the social sector spending agenda within governments.

Thought leadership on the impact of climate risks on social sector spending included working papers that EAPRO generated on the governance of climate finance. This led to enhanced leadership on finance for children by programme sectors and updated regional budget analysis for social sectors.

Outcome 6: Protection and realization of children's rights
EAPRO supported countries in the region to improve their capacity and commitment to promote normative frameworks, equity and empowerment for the protection and realization of children’s rights, with a focus on the most marginalized children. EAPRO continued its strategic involvement in enhancing capacities on child rights-based approaches and programming with a focus on office that were developing country programmes in 2024. The integration of businesses’ adherence to children’s rights continues to be a relevant cross-sectoral approach for programming in the region. The Disability Regional Action Plan was finalized based on consultations with EAPRO and country offices. EAPRO launched its Skilled, Employed and Empowered Girl and Youth Force vision for the region. Programming and advocacy to address harmful practices against adolescent girls through the scaling up of interventions and the development of regional accountability frameworks continued to be strengthened in 2024. Investments in data, such as through the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, generated the required evidence to promote equity and children’s rights in the region.

Outcome 7: Private sector fundraising
During the year, all country offices with structured fundraising successfully implemented the 2022–2025 Private Sector Plan. The Regional Support Centre helped country offices raise US$184 million in private sector revenue, including US$173 million from individual donors – a 7 per cent increase from 2023. The Regional Support Centre enabled US$16.7 million in fundraising investments across five countries and secured US$1.4 million to establish UNICEF’s first Asia-focused R&D Fund to accelerate innovation in individual giving. New market investments were also mobilized for Viet Nam and the South Asia Cluster, thus expanding private sector fundraising capabilities.

The Regional Support Centre delivered robust strategic, technical and operational support throughout the year, including advanced negotiation and foundational training for more than 60 staff persons, strategic planning and financial guidance to country offices and quarterly performance reviews aligned with real-time forecasting. Individual giving remained the dominant revenue stream, with more than 500,000 new pledge donors acquired. In addition, EAPRO launched fundraising campaigns in India and Thailand and continued its growth in dialogue channels, such as face to face and telemarketing.

The Regional Support Centre helped to secure or renewed 15 corporate partnerships and facilitated US$12 million in revenue, including major contributions from the private sector in China, Philippines, Thailand and Viet Nam. Major philanthropic contributions from regional foundations and individuals included a US$2 million donation from the Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation (Singapore) and US$225,000 from the Temasek Foundation in response to emergencies. EAPRO’s capacity-building and due diligence efforts scaled up significantly, with 731 cases completed (a 38 per cent increase from 2023) and 14 region-wide learning sessions delivered to enhance staff capabilities and deepen engagement with high-value partners.

Outcome 8: Management
During the year, two Regional Management Team network meetings took place. The management teams engaged on the latest developments at the global and regional levels in digital transformation, children’s rights, partnerships with academia and innovative financing. Based on foresight analysis a 2040 Vision for the UNICEF region, which will influence strategic shifts for the new Regional Office Management Plan and new country programmes was agreed upon identifying key megatrends for the region.

Country offices benefited from increased high-quality technical support and guidance for management, operations, logistics, human resources, ICT and security that strengthened internal systems, governance mechanisms and capacities for the effective delivery of programmes. Efforts to improve staff engagement, staff well-being and the workplace culture contributed to better organizational performance and achieving the strategic objectives, thus better performance towards achieving the SDGs.

Supply and Logistics team management was enhanced through emphasis on regional supply priorities. They included the strengthening of regional emergency preparedness capacity through the stockpiling of programme supplies managed at the regional level; support to country offices to leverage well-established entry points, such as UNICEF Procurement Services, and financing solutions to strengthen national supply systems for primary health care; and further developing the supply community in the region, with concentration on upskilling and facilitating information-sharing within the different communities of practice.

The security section empowered security culture, mainstreamed across country offices. In Myanmar, the deteriorating security situation, intercommunal conflict, elections, crime and civil unrest continued to shape the security environment. Programme implementation, however, continued at an acceptable level of security risk.

Outcome 9: Development effectiveness
EAPRO provided technical assistance and guidance to country offices in designing, implementing, monitoring and evaluating their country programmes, in alignment with the UNICEF Strategic Plan and procedures. EAPRO also supported country offices in scaling up results for children through the effective use of change strategies in their programmes and to ensure that the programmes were gender-focused, risk-informed and harnessed the potential of digital transformation. EAPRO made foresight analysis of the megatrends affecting children in the region to shape reflections around the upcoming drafting of the Regional Office Management Plan and its strategies. This was followed with a vision exercise involving the Regional Office and country offices to determine how best EAPRO could channel its support towards the countries, in line with its accountabilities. EAPRO also ensured continued support to countries undergoing humanitarian, disaster and crisis situations (such as in Myanmar and Papua New Guinea).

An increased focus on high-value audiences – corporations, foundations and major donors led to the establishment or renewal of 15 partnerships and generated significant funding for programmes across the region. Highlights included US$750,000 from Transsion Holdings (China) to support learning in Nigeria; US$500,000 from BJC Big C Foundation (Thailand) for early childhood development; and the renewal of the Change for Good partnership with CEBU Air (Philippines), valued at US$1.5 million over five years. The first-ever regional field visit for private sector donors, hosted in Cambodia, brought together 13 donors from five countries to witness UNICEF’s work firsthand. This experience, along with strategic engagements during the Philanthropy Asia Summit and visits by UNICEF’s Deputy Executive Director for Partnerships, helped deepen relationships and attract new prospects.

Two new UNICEF International Council members from Asia were welcomed, including Hannah Nguyen, with a US$1 million donation for adolescent girls and women in Viet Nam. Internal enablers for engagement with high-value audiences were advanced, supporting more than 730 due-diligence cases and leading tailored research, including the China for the World report that maps 256 companies with potential to support programming globally.

EAPRO supported country offices’ resource mobilization efforts with strengthened and expanded collaboration with governments, international finance institutions, multilateral development banks and regional bodies (ASEAN and the Public Investment Fund). Public partnerships were strengthened by aligning with United Nations sister entities via the Regional Collaborative Platform, such as co-chairing with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) the Issue-Based Coalition on Inclusive Economic Growth and Recovery and co-chairing several working groups. EAPRO engaged frequently with international financial institutions, connecting programme teams to explore new modalities of engagement with country offices on innovative finance to unlock, accelerate and amplify resources and impact to support children's needs.

Children’s Rights and Business Principles: EAPRO’s partnership with the Global Alliance for Care was formalized during the 2024 Asia–Pacific Care Forum in Bangkok, in which the visibility of children’s rights in the context of ‘caring cities’ was promoted informing subnational strategies on inclusive care and support systems, including family-friendly policies. EAPRO established a new partnerships Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on disaster management to strengthen business participation in regional disaster risk management mechanisms. This included the Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation (to strategize business resilience and humanitarian action in the Philippines) and the World Benchmark Alliances (to improve corporate accountability on child nutrition).

EAPRO strengthened strategic education partnerships with organizations like SEAMEO, ASEAN, the Asia–Pacific Regional Network for Early Childhood (ARNEC), the World Bank, the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), UNESCO and Save the Children to enhance advocacy, capacity-building and evidence generation. With ARNEC EAPRO worked on climate-resilient early childhood development, finalizing an advocacy tool kit and co-designing the 2024 ARNEC Conference. The Learning and Education 2030+ Networking Group collaboration was advanced through EAPRO’s close engagements with UNESCO Bangkok, the UNICEF Regional Office for South Asia (ROSA) and the UNICEF Europe and Central Asia Office and with the sixth Asia–Pacific Meeting on Education 2030, which focused on equity, climate-smart education, digital education, gender-transformative education and foundational learning. EAPRO also strengthened its partnership with DFAT to support gender-transformative education in South-East Asia. The partnership with the Asia Philanthropy Circle for the Philanthropy Asia Summit in Singapore highlighted the role of philanthropy in supporting education and early childhood development.

Together with UNICEF ROSA and the International Labour Organization, EAPRO revitalized the Technical Working Group on Adolescent Skills. This multi stakeholder group brings United Nations agencies, the private sector, NGOs and youth networks together as a platform for learning, collaborating and scaling up skills development programmes.

The ASEAN Secretariat remained a key partner on the child protection agenda. New frameworks which included the role of the social service workforce in climate resilience and in education were adopted. Engagement continued with the private sector on online safety and well-being through the convening of the ASEAN Industry Working Group, which comprises 12 industry actors, and the 2024 ASEAN ICT Forum on Child Online Protection, which brokers dialogue between governments and industry. In this process, EAPRO secured partnerships with DFAT, the Australia eSafety Commissioner, the Australian Attorney Generals Department, ECPAT, Down to Zero and ChildFund.

EAPRO continued to partner with the World Health Organization (WHO) under the Joint Programme on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Malaysia and Papua New Guinea to include system-strengthening, support to policy development and capacity-building of front-line workers in health, child protection and education.

EAPRO’s continued partnership with UNICEF Australia National Committee enabled further strengthening of systems for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse and safeguarding across the region.

To reduce maternal and child mortality, partnerships with the WHO South-East Asia and Western Pacific regional offices were strengthened, through which EAPRO applied data and digital transformation assistance to improve evidence-based strategies. EAPRO’s work with the WHO and UNAIDS on the Elimination of Mother-to-Child Transmission of HIV continued: A long-term agreement was established with the Asia eHealth Information Network, the Pacific Health Information Network and the Mahidol and Oxford consortium to provide technical support to countries. Additional partnerships were forged with the private sector, focusing on accessible and green technologies.

Under the European Union and UNICEF Public Financing Facility, EAPRO and ROSA worked with the European Union on partnerships for innovations for social sector budgeting across Asia. With UNDP the impact of climate risks on social sector spending in Cambodia and the Philippines was assessed and with the OECD, EAPRO assessed the potential for partnerships in public finance across Asia, especially for monitoring public expenditures regarding green, gender-based and children’s initiatives.

In the Pacific, EAPRO partnered with the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR) to implement the subnational climate and disaster risk assessment model, thereby tapping into existing databases as well as established collaboration with government counterparts, especially for exposure to hazards. The partnership allows EAPRO to benefit from UNITAR's strong technical expertise, especially in data management, geospatial mapping and risk analytics.

In efforts to create healthier retail food environments in the region a partnership with the Deakin University (in Australia) in the context of the RESHAPE initiative as maintained.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, EAPRO identified several key lessons emphasizing the importance of integrated approaches, digital solutions, capacity building, strong partnerships and use of foresight to achieve objectives and improve outcomes for children in the region.


Integrated Fundraising Approaches: Combining corporate and philanthropy teams has proven effective in securing significant funding. For instance, the Thailand Country Office successfully secured $1 million for early childhood development through a combined approach involving both corporate and major donor strategies. This integrated method ensures shared recognition and maximizes funding opportunities.
Digital and Dialogue Fundraising: While digital fundraising is crucial, traditional methods like face-to-face and telemarketing remain effective. These traditional channels contributed significantly to new donor acquisition in countries such as Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines, highlighting the need for a balanced approach in fundraising strategies.
Digital Health Solutions: Expanding digital health solutions, such as mobile health applications and electronic immunization records, has significantly improved data reach and robustness. These digital tools have been instrumental in informing communities, enhancing data systems, and improving health outcomes across ten countries in the Asia Pacific region.
Nutrition Governance: Strengthening regional nutrition governance and integrating nutrition into pre-service education for health professionals have been pivotal. These efforts have addressed malnutrition, scaled up treatment services, and developed nutrition agendas on climate change and public finance for children, leading to improved maternal and child health outcomes.
Early Childhood Development (ECD): Advocacy and policy briefs have been instrumental in securing government commitments to ECD. For example, the Policy Brief on the ASEAN Declaration for Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) led to increased funding and program inclusion, ensuring better access to inclusive and high-quality ECCE.
Foundational Learning: The Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) program has strengthened national and regional expertise in data collection, analysis, and utilization. This program has improved foundational learning outcomes by leveraging financial and technical resources and fostering evidence-based policy making.
Climate Resilience Child Protection Systems: Developing frameworks for climate adaptations in child protection systems has been crucial. These frameworks address vulnerabilities exacerbated by climate change, ensuring that child protection systems are resilient and adaptive to environmental changes.
Social Service Workforce: Strengthening the social service workforce through regional frameworks and technical support has led to significant improvements in child protection systems. This includes the endorsement of ASEAN Guidelines on the role of the social service workforce in disaster risk reduction and climate resilience.
Public Finance Management: Effective allocation of resources to social sectors like education and healthcare is essential for safeguarding vulnerable populations and promoting inclusive growth. Public finance management initiatives have ensured that resources are directed towards critical social services, directly impacting children's well-being.
Digital Transformation: Implementing digital tools and governance mechanisms has improved efficiency and effectiveness in program management and operations. Digital transformation initiatives have streamlined processes, enhanced data management, and supported better decision-making.
Gender Equality: Advancing gender equality and adolescent girls’ empowerment through policy shifts and programmatic interventions has led to significant progress. Efforts to address harmful practices and promote gender-responsive services have been successful, with over 10,000 adolescents accessing support and 1.5 million people engaged in awareness efforts.
Data and Evidence: Investing in data generation and enhancing capacities around data use is crucial for maintaining UNICEF’s leadership in child-related data. Improved data availability and utilization have supported evidence-based decision-making, ensuring that programs are effective and responsive to the needs of children.
Combining lessons learnt with foresight for strategic visioning: In a changing regional and global context, UNICEF EAPRO used foresight methodology to ensure the work in the region remains fit for purpose. The office therefore conducted a strategic visioning exercise which allowed the Regional Management Team to reflect on past achievements, lessons learnt and agree on a 2040 vision for the region. Critical inputs for this exercise were provide by country offices and were based on regional trends and views from a diverse range of stakeholders (including government, NGO and private sector partners, adolescents and representatives from academia).
While there has been immense improvement for children in this region, the following lessons were learnt across the region: UNICEF has to 

be bold and courageous in the advocacy for children’s rights, especially political rights, and building alliances with key influencers. 
understand the digital world that children and young people live in and accelerate engagement in this space 
be more relevant to and creative in addressing the climate crisis and its impact on children. 
be a more collaborative partner of civil society organizations.
accompany children and their parents in building a wholesome society, where young people can access opportunities and have a prosperous life within communities or environments in which people care for each other. 
invest in genuine partnerships with private sector allies, not just for funding but by recognizing the influence of partners. Give them voice and foster trust and empowerment with humility. 
continue the good work on changing social norms and expand across areas for programming priorities. 
The following key trends that are and will impact the region and its children have been identified:
Increasing investments in children and young people; harnessing the power of the digital world that children live in; addressing crises (especially climate and learning) and their consequences; adapting to the effects of demographic transitions; and effectively advocating for the realization of children’s rights.
Bringing together lessons learnt and foresight, the regional management team agreed that UNICEF in East Asia and the Pacific in 2040, will be a visionary force and champion for all children, known for catalysing change and results at scale, by being an evidence-driven thought leader that effectively builds and convenes alliance.
These lessons underscore the importance of integrated approaches, digital solutions, the need for data, and foresight and strong partnerships in achieving results for children in the East Asia and Pacific region. By leveraging these insights and strengthen programming around identified trends, UNICEF can continue to enhance its impact and support the well-being of children across the region.

Efforts in health systems-strengthening and evidence generation led to improved access to primary health care and immunization. Multi-country research and landscape analysis informed strategies for universal health coverage. Initiatives like subnational financing of community health workers in Cambodia, and digital health solutions, (real-time vaccination monitoring and analysis), enhanced health system efficiency. Collaboration with the ASEAN Secretariat produced minimum standards and guidelines that improved maternal nutrition services and policies on commercial complementary foods. Efforts to curb overweight and obesity included nutrient profile models and sugar-sweetened beverage taxes. Support for wasting programmes and public financial management systems strengthened national capacities.

Initiatives in education focused on systems-strengthening, evidence generation and regional partnerships. The Multiregional Parenting Mapping Study influenced ECD policies and budgets. The SEA-PLM assessment improved learning data analysis in seven countries, leveraging additional financial resources. Gender-transformative education programmes in Cambodia and Viet Nam led to regional commitments and policy changes. Advocacy for multilingual education and inclusive education models in Cambodia and China resulted in systematic shifts. Climate-smart education initiatives secured nearly US$5 million, enhancing digital literacy and foundational learning.

EAPRO supported inclusive and gender-sensitive child protection systems, integrating climate resilience and child protection. The Primero climate marker initiative and regional guidance on social service workforce in disaster risk reduction were significant milestones. Technical mentoring schemes and emergency preparedness capacities strengthened child protection systems in Myanmar and Timor-Leste. Engagement in global ministerial conferences and regional forums raised awareness and commitments to ending violence against children. The launch of Laaha in Myanmar provided a virtual safe space for girls and women to access gender-based violence information and services.

Technical support and capacity-building efforts in WASH and climate resilience led to increased access to safe water and sanitation services. Partnerships with the ASEAN Secretariat, multilateral development banks and humanitarian agencies reinforced sector leadership. Climate programme preparation in 10 countries included inception reports and missions, while Solar Hub 2.0 provided training on solar energy applications. Resource mobilization efforts secured US$29 million from KOICA and nearly US$1 million from KAKAO Bank, advancing climate programming and Green Climate Fund accreditation.

The Scaling Up Anticipatory Action and Shock-Responsive Social Protection in ASEAN project equipped countries with evidence and guidelines. Gender-responsive social protection programmes generated insights and built capacities. Support for child-friendly cities and public finance management mobilized resources and increased commitments. Regional meetings and South–South exchanges elevated social sector spending agendas and informed policies on climate finance governance.

15 high-value partnerships that generated significant funding were established or renewed: Transsion Holdings contributed to learning initiatives, BJC Big C Foundation to ECD and CEBU Air to the Change for Good partnership. Strategic engagements, such as the Philanthropy Asia Summit, and the first regional field visit for private sector donors in Cambodia, deepened relationships and attracted new prospects. EAPRO strengthened public partnerships by collaborating with governments, international finance institutions, multilateral development banks and regional bodies. Initiatives included co-chairing the Issue-Based Coalition on Inclusive Economic Growth and Recovery with UNDP and engaging with international financial institutions to explore innovative finance modalities. EAPRO also aligned with United Nations sister to enhance resource mobilization and advocacy strategies.

In 2024, UNICEF continued its multi-country programme across 14 Pacific Island Countries and Territories (PICTs) for the second year. The year was characterized by challenges including slowed economic growth, government changes due to elections and a series of natural disasters. In parallel, high-level visits from the UNICEF Executive Director and the UN Secretary-General, the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and the 4th International Conference on Small Island Developing States also provided opportunities for advocacy on child rights.
 
The Pacific region continued to face geopolitical tensions and socio-economic challenges from post-pandemic recovery[1] as well as from the impact of climate change. Costs related to climate disasters in the region have increased by eight times over the past decade amounting to a loss of approximately US$ 4.5 billion with a 700 per cent rise in the number of people affected[2].  Economic growth across the Pacific was forecasted at 3.6 per cent in 2024, down from 5.8 per cent in 2023. The World Bank suggests that the Pacific will continue to face weaker investment, increasing climate risks, and structural challenges. 
 
According to the Inter-Agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation, more than half of the PICTS have already or partially achieved the SDG target on newborn and child mortality.  However, the annual rate of mortality reduction since 1990 in all 14 PICTs is below the global and regional average and progress has stagnated recently. At 56 and 23 per 1,000 live births, Kiribati has the highest under-five and neonatal mortality rates, respectively, among 14 PICTs. Fiji has shown a constant increase in mortality since 2013 and is now off track[3]. In Fiji, the surge of HIV cases (260 per cent increase since 2010) fueled the concerns related to an increase in injecting drug use, unprotected sex, a general lack of HIV awareness, family violence, abuse and mental health issues, and gaps in health services. [4]
 
The latest WHO and UNICEF estimates[5] of national immunization coverage showed a mixed picture of the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. While most countries except for Vanuatu, Solomon, and Kiribati reached or surpassed the pre-pandemic level for DTP (diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis) third dose coverage, there remains a concern for suboptimal measles vaccine coverage. Low Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine coverage was observed in almost all PICTs. This reflects persistent low acceptance of HPV vaccines among the population and health system challenges to reach school-aged children and adolescent girls.    
 
According to the newly released Vanuatu MICS (Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey), the nutrition situation is deteriorating with almost a third of children under-five stunted, which is the highest prevalence among the 14 PICTs. Child wasting increased from four per cent in 2013 to eight per cent in 2023. Overweight and obesity among children under-five doubled from five per cent to 10 per cent in the past decade. The most recent MICS for Nauru shows a similar trend, with a stunting rate of 16 per cent and overweight of eight per cent.
 
Significant disparities remain within Pacific countries regarding access to early childhood education, ranging from 93 per cent in Fiji to 38 per cent in Samoa. Latest regional learning outcome data showed a concern: in year four of school, 33 per cent of children cannot do basic mathematical problems while almost 60 per cent cannot read and understand a simple story (PILNA, 2021). Overall, girls outperformed boys particularly in reading. The results also highlighted challenges in critical thinking skills, one of the non-cognitive skills identified as important for children to reach their full potential. 

The Pacific is facing increased rates of family violence, child abuse and neglect due to climate and economic mobility, with reduced levels of care and supervision as extended family care systems are stretched to cope.  Child marriage, with a 25 per cent prevalence rate in Oceania, remains common throughout the region, with related effects on high incidences of teenage pregnancy[6]. A rapid increase in online presence is increasing risks for children, especially teenagers who are subject to bullying and associated mental health issues, as well as the transmission of harmful gender norms.  Rates of violence against children continue to be extremely high, in turn driving violence against women as children model violent behaviour.  The prevalence of gender-based violence remains endemic, with nearly two out of three women subjected to physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime, with adolescent girls presenting unique vulnerabilities – some with long term consequences[7]. Services to remote island communities are limited or nonexistent, with efforts underway to link community and faith-based mechanisms with the formal system.
 
Reforms have been made in child protection legislation across Pacific Island Countries (PICTs), particularly in Fiji with the Child Justice Act 2024, and Childcare and Protection Act 2024.   Similar reforms in Samoa and the Solomon Islands signal progress in strengthening legal frameworks for children's rights. The Fiji Child Justice Act notably raises the minimum age of criminal responsibility to 14 years, making Fiji the first country in the Pacific to adhere to internationally recommended standards based on medical evidence regarding adolescent brain development and the effectiveness of rehabilitative approaches in preventing re-offending. Both Tonga and Samoa introduced their respective Social Protection Policies to help set their guiding frameworks. While most PICTs are up to date with their CRC reporting obligations, implementation of recommendations requires systematic monitoring. According to recent Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS), Vanuatu and Nauru show concerning trends in child wellbeing indicators, with data highlighting significant disparities in access to services and child protection concerns. Furthermore, women’s livelihood vulnerabilities due to climate change are exacerbated due to gender inequalities and harmful norms. In particular, inequalities around access to resources, care responsibilities, and lower levels of education and decision-making disproportionately affect women during climate events. [8]

Although the PICTs were spared major cyclones this year, countries were still recovering from several cyclones in late 2023 and were hit by other disasters. The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) and the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI) experienced severe droughts, affecting 25 per cent and 35 per cent of their populations, respectively. UNICEF's response focused on Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), education, child protection, health, and nutrition. On December 17th a 7.3 magnitude earthquake struck near Vanuatu. The Government estimated that over 80,000 people were affected, with more than 1,450 displaced. A state of emergency was declared, and UNICEF's Vanuatu team were among the first responders, addressing immediate needs across all sectors.

Improving and sustaining health and nutrition services 
 
UNICEF continued to support immunization programmes through intensified outreach campaigns to increase demand, which improved vaccination coverage. For example, Kiribati introduced HPV vaccine and reached 82 per cent coverage. Following completion of effective vaccine management assessment (EVMA) in all 14 PICTs, UNICEF partnered with Fiji National University for the first-ever regional cold chain equipment management training workshop to narrow gaps in cold chain maintenance. The plan is to establish the Pacific Regional Centre of Excellence for cold chain and immunization supply chain management, modeled after the East African example. UNICEF-supported immunization training efforts reached health workers and managers in seven PICTs with improved knowledge on immunization practice, programme management / supportive supervision tools, micro-planning, and EVMA.

Through the Vaccine Independence Initiative (VII) mechanism, 11 types of routine immunization vaccines and related supplies valued at US$ 3.94 million were procured for 13 PICTs using pooled procurement via the regional vaccine warehouse. Five PICTs successfully increased the VII ceiling to accommodate the cost of newly introduced vaccines such as HPV, which affirms the government commitment to immunization programmes. VII and UNICEF procurement service (PS) contributed to vaccine security and other health emergency preparedness and response measures. Notably, Tuvalu’s Ministry of Health commissioned a solar-powered Oxygen Plant procured under UNICEF PS modality with DFAT funding at the country’s only hospital. UNICEF’s time-sensitive procurement enabled typhoid vaccination campaigns in Tuvalu and Kiribati in response to suspected or confirmed outbreaks. When Kiribati faced a stockout of essential medicines due to national tender failures, UNICEF rapidly delivered emergency supplies to fill these critical gaps. At the annual Pacific Heads of Health Meeting, discussions focused on the importance of a strong supply chain system for PHC resiliency and the potential of leveraging VII’s success to find regional solutions to supply chain challenges in the Pacific. 
 
To build a stronger and more resilient PHC system, UNICEF continued to provide on-the-ground technical assistance to strengthen institutional capacity and health system accountability at sub-national level in three PICTs. Improved sub-national health coordination, better understanding of stakeholder roles and responsibility, improved monitoring and documentation of partner activities, and standardization of procedures such as integrated supportive supervision, annual planning, budgeting, and reporting were some of the common achievements.  For building climate resilience, solar electrification of 40 health facilities across five PICTs is underway, following the training of 25 biomedical and health infrastructure engineers. 
 
While demand for nutrition service is increasing in the face of the Non-Communicable Disease (NCD) crisis, UNICEF supported health system strengthening to deliver high impact nutrition services including during climate-induced emergency through training, quality assurance, and community engagement. Promoting breastfeeding through strengthening implementation of Baby Friendly Hospital Initiative (BHFI) with links to community-based services is among such support. Beyond the health sector, strong momentum was created for multi-system engagement for nutrition with the government approval of National Food Security, Food Safety and Nutrition Policy in the Solomon Islands and a Multisectoral Plan of Action for Nutrition in FSM. Multi-sectoral stakeholder workshops were convened in Fiji, RMI and FSM, with immediate priority actions defined. Key progress was made in support of the legal analysis of introducing front of pack nutrition labelling (FOPNL) in Fiji, and a dietary intake assessment and food system mapping to develop context-specific, climate-smart food-based recommendations was completed in multiple PICTs. 
 
Across these achievements, the cross-cutting strategy was to enhance integrated services for children, as demonstrated in UNICEF’s coordinated health, education, child protection and communication support in response to HIV and drug use surge in Fiji.

Expanding access to quality education 
 
UNICEF Pacific contributed to building resilience of the education system and building the capacity of the Ministries of Education and teachers on evidence-based inclusive practices. To generate evidence on the effects of climate change in education in the region, a Climate Change in Education study was carried out across five countries ensuring that adolescent boys' and girls’ voices were included throughout the study through digital technologies. The study results will further inform the education sector to integrate components of climate change in the programme for the following years to strengthen resilience in the education sector.  UNICEF further provided support in the development of resources and capacity building on School Based Disaster Risk Reduction and Education in Emergency initiatives in Fiji, Vanuatu, and the Solomon Islands to strengthen their response to any upcoming natural disasters.
 
Under the “leave no child behind” agenda, UNICEF has significantly contributed to building the capacity for PICTs to deliver Inclusive Education. This includes technical support to review and update the inclusive education policies for Vanuatu and Tonga, as well as capacity building for master trainers, school principals and teachers in Solomon Islands. In Tonga, community awareness was raised through focus group discussions to understand the perceptions of parents and community members on inclusion and to identify opportunities for partnerships between schools and communities to support the learning of children with disabilities. To ensure all children have access to learning even during disasters, Tonga identified that learning for children in Early Childhood Education (ECE) as well as children with disabilities were the most effected in school disruptions due to natural disasters. UNICEF supported the development of culturally relevant inclusive storybooks written in the mother tongue which included tips on inclusion for teachers and parents. Audio visual versions of the books, incorporating sign language, were also developed and will be uploaded in the national e-learning platform to ensure continuity of learning. Additionally, 100 per cent of ECE teachers were trained in inclusive principles and practical strategies to promote inclusion in their classrooms. 
 
UNICEF supported ECE through the development and dissemination of culturally relevant and inclusive storybooks across four countries including teacher capacity building on utilization of the storybooks with culturally sensitive and inclusive methods. Furthermore, UNICEF supported the development and training on the ECE curriculum in two countries, pre- and in-service ECE teacher training across the region ensuring the use of the mother tongue and contextualization of the curriculum and teaching methods to the respective countries. 
 
To ensure that all girls and boys have access to quality early childhood development and care, UNICEF provided support for the development of multisectoral national ECD policies and inclusive, costed action plans in countries such as the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), Tokelau, and Samoa. In Fiji, the Cabinet endorsed the ECD Policy, and UNICEF supported its official national launch in December 2024. UNICEF also continued to support the implementation of ECD initiatives, including promoting effective parenting practices during early childhood. As the secretariat for the Pacific Regional Council for Early Childhood Development (PRC4ECD), UNICEF has initiated preparations for the 2025 Regional ECD Forum to be held in Samoa. The forum will explore the theme, “The Role of ECD in Nurturing and Preserving Culture Across the Pacific.” UNICEF is a core partner in other Pacific regional initiatives (see partnership section below for details).
 
Five Pacific countries defined education transformation agendas with UNICEF support, largely focused on foundational learning. Selected themes include: improving gender equality and inclusion in pedagogy, strengthening early childhood and early grade learning, and improving learning outcomes through mainstreaming indigenous knowledge and skills in education. 
 
UNICEF contributed to generating evidence and supporting data-driven planning, including the analysis of education data from MICS in seven countries and this helped address data gaps on out-of-school children, ECE attendance as well as disability and other data related to learning and equity. The Giga initiative in Fiji resulted in nationwide real-time connectivity data that will be used to identify opportunities to strengthen connectivity. A climate change in education study was completed in Fiji, Vanuatu, Kiribati, FSM and Solomon Islands, while Kiribati, Fiji, Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, Samoa and RMI engaged in education sector analysis and planning processes.  
 
UNICEF is the grant agent for seven Global Partnership for Education (GPE) System Capacity Grants and six System Transformation Grants, leveraging local presence and knowledge to support global efforts to increase education system capacity.

Strengthening Climate-Resilient WASH Services Across the Pacific
UNICEF strengthened delivery of climate resilient WASH services supporting Pacific governments and communities with a focus on systems strengthening and delivery of climate resilient WASH services. With support from the EAPRO regional solar power hub, Water Mission, and International Water Centre, 34 engineers and technicians from Fiji, FSM, Kiribati, Vanuatu, and Solomon Island were trained in the design and implementation of solar powered water supply systems to support climate resilient water supplies. This initiative is reinforcing the Pacific region’s capacity to deliver resilient water solutions. 

UNICEF constructed climate-resilient WASH infrastructure in 117 schools and 17 health facilities across six countries. In Fiji in collaboration with the Department of Water and Sewerage, UNICEF initiated a costed rural water and sanitation master plan with annual targets for universal climate-resilient WASH coverage. In partnership with the DWS and Water Authority for Fiji, training for 425 water committee members in 110 communities was conducted to improve rural water supply management, with plans for scaling based on results. In the Solomon Islands, UNICEF supported water governance through the finalization of draft instructions for the water resources bill and the development of a WASH climate rationale. Efforts to end open defecation transitioned from operational implementation to scaling up through national systems strengthening. Provincial Open Defecation Free (ODF) plans were developed for Malaita while sub-national provincial CLTS coordinators and 60 new communities achieved ODF status reaching 8,000 people with basic sanitation services. In Vanuatu, UNICEF strengthened partnerships with the Department of Water Resources (DoWR), updated the DWSSP database, and improved monitoring systems. Through the MFAT-funded Water Sector Partnership, 1,023 people gained access to climate-resilient water services, and 90 technicians, including women and people with disabilities, received Level II Plumbing Certification. In Kiribati, UNICEF supported improved coordination in the WASH sector and assessed water infrastructure in outer islands. Efforts are ongoing to reach all 2,400 people from 600 households without improved toilets with an aim to transform Kiritimati into an open defecation free island. In FSM, UNICEF is finalizing an implementation plan for climate-resilient sanitation access. Awareness campaigns on safe drinking water reached 2,000 people in Kosrae State.

Significant advancements in schools and healthcare facilities (HCFs) have been made across the Pacific. In Vanuatu, a WASH in school policy was endorsed by MOET in October complemented with training of all school principals and chairpersons of school committee associations in Malampa on 3- star monitoring, WASH in schools Improvement Plan development, WASH clubs and facilities guide.  UNICEF supported a five-year WinHCF provincial implementation plan in Torba, Penama, Tafea, and Shefa. Infection prevention training also reached 85 healthcare workers. In Fiji, UNICEF supported the strengthening of investments through a national baseline assessment on WASH in HCF, the development of standards, guidelines, and an engineering assessment for 49 HCFs in the Western Division. Improvements were made in nine climate-resilient WASH HCFs in Raki Raki that will benefit 32,400 people (9,100 children) while upgrades in six Northern Division facilities and 27 in the Eastern Division, including rainwater systems and cyclone preparedness, reached 55,884 people. Operation and maintenance training was provided, and the WASH in Schools program was revived with the 3-Star Approach in 14 pilot schools. 

In the Solomon Islands, a national WinS policy was developed, a survey assessed 1,021 schools, and enhanced WASH services in 12 healthcare facilities were completed benefitting 26,000 people. Over 4,500 children and 679 teachers received WASH and menstrual health training. In Kiribati, WASH facilities were built in two schools and one healthcare facility on Kiritimati Island, ensuring improved sanitation and hygiene for students and patients. This intervention directly benefited girls and women by addressing their menstrual health dignity and enhancing WASH services in the healthcare facility, particularly for safe and dignified childbirth. Additionally, 350 girls and women from three schools and two women's groups were trained on menstrual health and hygiene on Kiritimati. Across the Gilbert Islands, UNICEF, and the Ministry of Education (MoE) kicked off a three-year WASH in schools programme assessing 119 schools, training 680 teachers on the Three-Star approach, and reaching 19 islands.  In FSM WASH infrastructure was strengthened in 20 schools, benefitting 6,184 students, and 24 schools were trained in water testing and hygiene. Rehabilitation efforts of WASH facilities are underway at Yap State Hospital. In Samoa and Tuvalu, UNICEF improved WASH in 83 per cent of Samoa’s HCFs and surveyed plans for new infrastructure in Tuvalu's Motofoua High School. Tonga completed a WASH FIT baseline for all 19 HCFs, enabling scalable improvements.

UNICEF also supported emergency preparedness, response, and resilience across PICTS through coordination, anticipatory action, and pre-positioning of supplies at strategic locations. Partnering with IFRC, UNICEF trained over 18 national Red Cross societies and government staff on emergency preparedness. Supplies are pre-positioned in key locations, including Brisbane, Fiji, and Samoa. These supplies provided major support for the Vanuatu WASH Cluster during Tropical Cyclone Lola, providing sanitation to 15,712 people and safe water to 23,037 individuals; also, essential WASH supplies were distributed to 5,225 people in FSM and water tanks in RMI. UNICEF support also reached almost 1,000 residents and over 2,000 visitors during the Micronesia Games. In Kiribati, UNICEF in partnership with the University of Technology is finalizing the Kiribati WASH Climate Rationale. UNICEF supplied five portable solar desalination units to outer islands, addressing drought-related water challenges.

UNICEF integrated climate resilience into water safety planning and school reconstruction in Vanuatu and finalized the Kiribati and Solomon Islands WASH Climate Rationale. The focus includes addressing risks such as cyclones, droughts, saline intrusion, and rising sea levels.

Protection and prevention of violence against children (VAC) 
 
As part of a shift toward partners with closer proximity to children, UNICEF is increasingly collaborating with local actors such as faith-based organizations and civil society. A more coherent and comprehensive approach is being put in place by linking non - governmental organizations with government as part of a coordinated approach. An example of this is the technical assistance to develop a combined action plan for street children in Fiji – promoting family based non-institutional approaches wherever possible. 
 
Consistent with a systems-based approach there has been noteworthy progress in cross sectoral engagement. This has included a leadership role in developing technical guidance for climate induced relocation in Fiji, as well as MHPSS multi sectoral action planning with governments in Tonga (Health, Education-plus). UNICEF also has made significant efforts to promote climate justice through engagement with Pacific governments on ensuring young people’s voices are heard and arguments related to children’s rights are at the centre of climate change policy and advocacy. 
 
UNICEF has made a sustained effort to promote a whole-of-government approach to improving children’s access to justice across the Pacific. In addition to the landmark Childcare and Protection and Child Justice legislation passed in Fiji, legislative reform efforts moved forward in Vanuatu, Samoa, Kiribati, and the Solomon Islands. Based on comprehensive national reviews of child justice systems, UNICEF also embarked on a renewed partnership with the police in Fiji, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, FSM, and Kiribati. This has combined skills transfer for child sensitive investigations and greater use of diversion in policing. 
 
Deepening prevention efforts have included community-based co-design processes on violence prevention to tailor each approach to the cultural contexts. In recognition of the power of religion in the Pacific in shaping an enabling or harmful environment, UNICEF has developed technical material for church-based enablers as well as curriculum for leaders on child protection. UNICEF has also increasingly focused on engaging men and boys, including conducting a consultation with adolescent boys across seven countries. The consultation shed light on Pacific boys’ attitudes regarding masculinity, gender socialization, and the construct of ‘manhood.’  Boys reference groups will now be formed to inform ongoing engagement and provide a platform for the co-creation of gender-transformative programming.
 
Advocacy has been strengthened by building an evidence base on the current landscape and child protection challenges. Notably, research was conducted on labour mobility with findings generating a set of recommendations at an inter-governmental level. This study was launched and discussed with stakeholders during the visit of UNICEF’s Executive Director in July 2024. Economic research has provided advocacy material for governments on the cost of violence with modelling studies completed in the Solomon Islands and Fiji. Both governments were supported to develop pledges ahead of their attendance at the Global Ministerial VAC conference in November in Bogota, Colombia.

Improving evidence on child rights and promoting social protection for children 
 
In 2024, PICTs made significant progress in enhancing data availability on the status of children and women. This included the completion and official launch of Vanuatu and Nauru’s Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), ongoing MICS in Tonga and FSM, and the real-time monitoring surveys (MICS Plus) in Fiji and Samoa. Advocacy and preparatory activities for MICS in RMI and Samoa also started and will be completed in 2025. 
 
The enabling environment was strengthened through improved advocacy for investments in children. A high-level side event on investing in children was organized during the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Leaders Meeting which the UN Secretary General attended for the first time. This brought together high-level representatives from governments, development partners and CSOs to share evidence of the high return on investment in children and experiences in high-return interventions in early years and significantly improved the awareness of the needs and urgency for appropriate investments in children. UNICEF continued to engage the annual PIF Forum Economic Ministers Meeting (FEMM) and provided another information paper on financing ECD in the Pacific, further improving the awareness of Economic and Finance Ministers for improved ECD investment.

UNICEF spearheaded significant disability inclusion initiatives across the Pacific region through multiple strategic programs.  A cornerstone initiative is the UNPRPD project, which spans ten PICTs including FSM, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Nauru, Palau, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu.  Launched in 2024, this project encompasses comprehensive capacity building, development of situational reports, and fully developed proposals specifically for Kiribati and Vanuatu. Complementing this work, UNICEF is conducting extensive landscape assessments for Assistive Technology (AT) across ten Pacific nations, providing crucial baseline data for future interventions. Mental health and psychosocial support services were redesigned to be disability-inclusive, creating sustainable support systems that respect children's right to access quality healthcare regardless of ability.
 
In addition, UNICEF completed multi-dimensional child poverty analyses in Fiji, Kiribati, Samoa, Tonga, and Tuvalu. The analyses will inform child-centered national policies, programmes, plans, and budgets. In particular, the child poverty data will significantly contribute to the advocacy around child-sensitive and shock-responsive social protection. This is also planned for Vanuatu and Nauru in 2025.
 
The first-ever training on child-sensitive social protection was delivered in the Solomon Islands, with around 60 participants strengthening their understanding of how to design and implement policies that address the needs of children. The training brought together senior government officials, provincial governments, development partners, CSOs, NGOs, and faith-based organizations (FBOs). Participants gained critical insights into the economic, social, and political impacts of social protection in small island states, while advocating for increased investment in child-sensitive social protection. 
 
UNICEF also implemented a joint programme with UNDP and the Government of the Solomon Islands, funded by the European Union (EU), to support strengthening provincial governance for service delivery. This initiative aims to strengthen decentralization efforts and improve social sector service delivery systems. The national decentralization assessment and provincial financing analysis are on-going and were complimented by capacity building on social service delivery. The evidence generated will form the basis to support evidence based provincial and national dialogues.
 
Social Behaviour Change (SBC) has strengthened its cross-sectoral interventions by improving social data collection and utilization and building relevant skills and mindsets across UNICEF sectors and partners. By identifying key social drivers SBC developed evidence-based interventions to address diverse health challenges and behaviors. Insights from the Behavioural Insights on Routine Immunization (RI) study and formative research have been pivotal in shaping and testing targeted SBC strategies in the Pacific. Social research findings have also informed the development of the SBC Communication Strategy for the Marshall Islands, focusing on improving demand for essential Early Childhood Development services.
