In response to rising HIV rates and substance abuse among Fijian youth, SBC partnered with the Ministry of Health to enhance knowledge and promote preventive behaviors, further demonstrating its commitment to addressing pressing social and health issues through collaborative, data-driven approaches.

UNICEF entered a formal partnership with the Pacific Island Forum Secretariat (PIFS) with the signing of an MOU. Building on past collaboration, the formalization of this partnership will further expand cooperation with this important regional body in areas including health, education, WASH, child protection and social protection. This is a major breakthrough as PIFS is the overall coordinating body in the Pacific.  
 
UNICEF continued its partnership with the Governments of Australia (DFAT), New Zealand (MFAT), Japan, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), GAVI and COVAX for sustaining COVID-19 vaccination and rebuilding stronger immunization systems in the PICTs. For new vaccine introduction, UNICEF collaborated with ADB. The partnership with Japan on digital health continued. In the Solomon Islands, GAVI’s support for immunization and health system strengthening was significant. UNICEF ensured close technical collaboration with WHO in all areas.
 
With Joint SDG fund support, UNICEF’s collaboration with FAO and other UN agencies continued to expand nutrition interventions in select PICTs. UNICEF built a new partnership with the Latter-day Saints (LDS) Church in scaling up high impact nutrition interventions. UNICEF collaborated with World Bank on the dietary intake assessment, with close cooperation with UNFPA and WFP in ensuring coordinated support in reproductive and maternal health and food systems, respectively. 
 
UNICEF actively contributed to sub-regional platforms such as the Pacific Heads of Health Meeting and the Pacific Ending Childhood Obesity (ECHO) network, working closely with the Pacific Community (SPC) and WHO. UNICEF played an active role in emergency coordination platforms, including the health cluster (as a co-chair for nutrition sub-cluster) and Pacific Joint Incident Management Team.

UNICEF is also a core partner in multiple Pacific regional education sector initiatives, including the Pacific Regional Education Framework (PacREF), the Pacific Regional Inclusive Education Taskforce (PRIET), the Pacific Regional Early Childhood Education Taskforce (PRECET) and the Pacific Regional Council for Early Childhood Development (PRC4ECD). Of these, UNICEF serves as secretariat to PRIET, PRECET and PRC4ECD, with both PRIET and PRC4ECD holding Ministerial-level representation. Through these bodies, UNICEF partners closely with the Pacific Community (SPC), the University of the South Pacific (USP), the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS), the Pacific Disability Forum (PDF), United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and others in support of 15 Pacific Island countries, representing the 14 covered by UNICEF Pacific, plus Papua New Guinea. UNICEF is actively engaged in the regional education architecture through the Conference of Pacific Education Ministers (CPEM), Pacific Heads of Education (PHES), and Forum Economic Ministers Meeting (FEMM) and provides technical and advocacy support to these bodies as relevant in education and ECD.

UNICEF is active in country led education partner groups and clusters where they exist and coordinates actively with Australia, New Zealand, the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the U.S. Office of Insular Affairs, Save the Children, and others around specific initiatives in Pacific countries. UNICEF is the grant agent for seven Global Partnership for Education (GPE) System Capacity Grants and six System Transformation Grants, leveraging local presence and knowledge to support global efforts to increase education system capacity. For the Regional Inclusive Education Taskforce and the Pacific ECE Taskforce and the Pacific Regional Council for Early Childhood Development (PRC4ECD), UNICEF also takes the role of the Secretariat partnering with nominated Ministers and senior officials to ensure that these bodies represent the region and can provide technical advice and guidance to leaders. In addition, a specific partnership with USP, Institute of Education and UNESCO is strengthening capacity and networking of educational planners across the region.
 
Other partnerships with Pacific institutions were strengthened including the Pacific Conference of Churches to significantly increase the reach of behavior change strategies.  Local civil society partners supported assessment and response efforts on issues for street children, for example in Fiji.  As the key regional academic institution, the University of the South Pacific was a key partner in conducting research and ensuring evidence-based advocacy for children left behind due to labor mobility, making use of Pacific regional academics with strong cultural links to target countries such as Samoa.  

UNICEF Pacific, in partnership with the Fiji Council of Social Services (FCOSS), is implementing the project "Supporting Community Preparedness and Resilience to Future Climate-Related Shocks" in Fiji. This initiative emphasizes Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), ensuring that communities play a central role in identifying their needs and priorities. In Vanuatu, UNICEF partnered with Wan Smolbag theatre group to generate the demand for HPV vaccines. Using drama and performances, the group was able to effectively engage with communities. In Samoa, UNICEF partnered with the Samoa Red Cross Society to generate evidence on immunization and engage with communities to increase the uptake of immunization. In the Solomon Islands, UNICEF has partnered with ADRA to strengthen community networks and community engagement for family care practices such as immunization, hygiene and accessing services for health and nutrition.
 
UNICEF Pacific continued to partner with the UN system playing a lead role in the UN Strategic Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) for the Pacific. UNICEF colleagues co-chair the UN Programme Management Team, the UN results group on people, the UN working group on adolescents and youth, plays a lead role in the UN PSEA efforts, and other colleagues are active participants in various UN structures.   Joint reviews of UN country implementation plans (CIPs) for 2023 to 2024 were undertaken during the year with the support of UNICEF colleagues.  These reviews will inform the development of new CIPs in early 2025. 
 
UNICEF co-chairs the UN interagency working group on Adolescents and Youth ensuring this important group is well reflected in UN guidance and programs across all agencies and within regional bodies.  This support included engagement of youth from 14 PICTs via the Pacific Community (SPC) and the Pacific Youth Council (PYC) to inform the new Pacific Youth Development Framework (PYDF) which was an outcome of the annual Pacific Minister for Youth meeting in September. The PYDF demonstrates how youth-led advocacy and participation contribute to regional development. A total of 21 PICTs Ministers of Youth met and committed to allocating more resources for youth development priorities over the next decade as part of the 2050 Strategy for Blue Pacific.  Ahead of the 4th Conference on the Small Islands Developing States (SIDS4) in Antigua and Barbuda, UNICEF supported a series of consultations and U report polls reaching a diverse group of young people across eight Pacific countries.   UNICEF supported five youth delegates to attend the SIDS4, with a focus on elevating young people’s voices on the unique and complex challenges faced by SIDS.  This resulted in a Youth Action Summit where over 90 young people from 35 SIDS engaged with leaders on specific actions going forward after SIDS4 including the establishment of a SIDS Centre of Excellence with the integration of youth within the centre. Pacific youth were instrumental in securing a legitimate space with government with the support of the UN to engage to address the disproportionate impact of climate change on SIDS and advance climate justice.  UNICEF also supported the collaboration of youth in the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting hosted by Samoa including preparations for the Commonwealth Youth Forum which held youth-led sessions on climate resilience and mental health that culminated into a youth declaration for the next two years. 

As the lead agency for the UNPRPD project across 10 PICTs, UNICEF collaborates with the Pacific Disability Forum to implement disability-inclusive systems, with support from DFAT.  The partnership with the Pacific Community (SPC) focused on improving disability data collection and statistics for evidence-based programming. Collaboration with the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat (PIFS) enabled high-level policy engagement on disability rights with Pacific member states.  

UNICEF Pacific partnered with the ministries responsible for climate change in Fiji, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands and Kiribati to advance building climate resilience in social services. In Fiji, UNICEF is working with the Fijian Taskforce for Relocation and Displacement to ensure that the rights of children are being protected and fulfilled before, during and after a climate induced planned relocation. UNICEF Pacific has also partnered regionally with youth organizations such as the Pacific Islands Students Fighting Climate Change (PISFCC) to champion climate justice for children and future generations, amplifying Pacific youth voices in national, regional, and international high-level fora.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
With a small number of health workers posted in each facility, high staff turnover and logistical challenges in remote islands, the one-size-fits-all “workshop model” is not the most cost-effective approach to capacity building in the Pacific.   Workshops in the Pacific have a high unit cost and reach low numbers.  Based on this lesson, UNICEF is working with health partners to work differently by: i) strengthening mentoring programmes as part of supportive supervision to allow the simultaneous practical learning and service continuity, ii) institutionalizing the essential trainings in existing educational institutions (rather than one off events), and iii) updating the pre-service curriculum for frontline workers. 

Fiji’s surge in HIV and drug use cases highlighted the need for age-specific investment throughout the 8,000 days of childhood and adolescence. A generation unaware of the threat of HIV can underestimate the risk as seen in the fast spread of this outbreak.  Similarly, the nutrition and food system studies highlighted the unhealthy food environment in and around schools contributing to rising childhood overweight and obesity across PICTs. While vaccine hesitancy is an important issue to tackle, the lack of quality school health outreach services also underlies the consistently sub-optimal HPV coverage. Moving forward, UNICEF will expand its support in improving capacity to provide standardized school-based health and nutrition services and creating a school environment conducive to students’ health, nutrition, and wellbeing, while strengthening school health and nutrition data management.    
 
Addressing complex public health challenges requires culturally tailored approaches, innovative tools, and collaborative partnerships. Efforts to improve HPV vaccine uptake highlighted the importance of combating stigma, misinformation, and barriers to reliable information through culturally sensitive strategies. In Vanuatu, UNICEF partnered with Wan Smolbag Theatre to use storytelling and community dialogue to dispel myths and build trust, while in Samoa, SBC, and Technology for Development (T4D) teams enhanced dengue outbreak monitoring by integrating digital tools like Ona to support the Ministry of Health. In the Cook Islands, the Ministry of Health, SBC, and T4D strengthened capacity in Human-Centered Design, engaging seven ministries and eight influential church groups to cascade training and foster sustainable, community-driven solutions. These initiatives demonstrate the transformative power of combining cultural sensitivity, innovation, and partnership to advance public health outcomes.
 
Improving coordination efforts across government remains critical, given limited resources, geographical challenges, and the intersectionality of child protection.  Whole of government approaches across education, justice and health are needed to deliver on services.  Similarly, greater investment is needed to bring faith-based organizations together with government to ensure coherence and reach, for prevention and early intervention programs.  
 
Building on our disability-inclusive programming achievements in 2023, UNICEF Pacific's leadership of the UNPRPD project demonstrated effective multi-partner coordination. While successful in establishing key regional partnerships with PDF, SPC, and PIFS, gaps remain in reaching children with disabilities in remote areas. Moving forward, we will strengthen data systems for disability statistics, expand Assistive Technology access, and deepen engagement with organizations of persons with disabilities to ensure no child is left behind across the Pacific.
 
UNICEF has introduced Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) approaches across Pacific countries. In Fiji, a digital Community Feedback Mechanism (CFM) is being implemented to ensure that the voices of disaster-affected communities are heard and acted upon during emergency responses. This initiative empowers local communities by facilitating their feedback on services, thereby fostering resilience and supporting community-driven responses.

The Fiji MICS-LINK programme faced significant delays due to limitations in capacity as well as competing priorities at the Ministry of Education. This highlights the importance of strengthening technical capacity to effectively use data in education planning and monitoring as well as ensuring full ownership of the Ministry of Education at the design of any programme.

Working with small, capacity-constrained education systems underscores the need to focus on fewer, high-priority interventions to ensure quality and impact. Further attention needs to be paid to establishing comprehensive and strong monitoring and evaluation frameworks ahead of any programme intervention to assess the extent of impact.

An operational challenge across all sectors continues to be the complex government financial systems across the 14 PICTs (with five different fiscal year calendars) as well as within PICTs as they decentralize and delegate more to sub-national levels of government (provinces, districts, etc.).  This has meant UNICEF funding at times moves slowly through these systems resulting in bottlenecks during implementation and reporting.  A better understanding of these flows of funds is needed to improve efficiency and effectiveness. 

Future Outlook
The Pacific Regional Education Framework (PacREF) is transitioning into its second phase, with significant work focused on securing funding and coordinating efforts to deliver regional public goods for education. However, the uncertainty of funding for this phase poses challenges for UNICEF’s 2025 workplan and beyond.

Education has been established as a standing agenda item at the Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting (PILM) from 2024 onward. This provides a strategic opportunity for UNICEF to engage in direct advocacy, influence regional policy, and contribute to drafting key papers to shape education priorities across the Pacific. 
 
UNICEF procedures on the Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) will be revised to better cope with the complexities of financial flows across the PICTs as part of fine tuning of decentralization efforts.  These will include timing of transfers that make sense within each of the five different fiscal year calendars across the 14 PICTs as well as closer monitoring of the release and uptake of funds through frequent follow up with partners to ensure notification of funds release and commencement of planned activities.  New UNICEF tools in EZ HACT will enable this follow up as they move away from paper notifications to electronic platforms. Efforts will also be made to rationalize funds flows across a range of partners ensuring the right balance between funds to government partners, CSOs and institutional contracts.

UNICEF Pacific is adopting a convergent approach to design its climate-resilient programme, integrating efforts across sectors to strengthen the resilience of social services against climate challenges. As part of this effort, UNICEF is implementing a US$ seven million KOICA-funded climate programme in the Solomon Islands and advancing the preparation of a Green Climate Fund (GCF) multi-country programme across four Pacific nations. This emphasis on convergence enables UNICEF to maximize impact, minimize duplication, and establish a unified foundation for child-responsive climate-resilient programming in the region.

Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country, had an estimated population of approximately 281.6 million in 2024, with children aged 0 to 17 accounting for 30 per cent (84 million) and adolescents aged 10 to 19 constituting 15.6 per cent (44.1 million) of the overall population. The country is undergoing transformative changes, guided by its National Long-Term Development Plan (RPJPN) 2025-2045, adopted by Parliament under Law No. 59 of 2024. This plan aims to achieve the "Golden Indonesia 2045" vision, focusing on sustainable economic growth, social welfare, and environmental sustainability. By 2045, Indonesia aspires to achieve a high-income country status, with targets including a six-fold increase in GDP per capita and significant poverty reduction. Indonesia’s economy has performed well in recent years, achieving a GDP growth of 5.05 per cent in 2023 and 4.95 per cent in the third quarter of 2024, while inflation has remained low at 1.55 per cent as of November 2024. However, funding for the social sector continues to face challenges. Education, legally mandated to receive 20 per cent of the national budget, has averaged only at 16.4 per cent of actual spending between 2021 and 2024. In 2024, health spending accounted for 5.8 per cent and social protection for 13.6 per cent of national expenditure. 
Political developments in 2024 shaped policy directions moving forward, with a focus on promoting children’s rights and accelerating progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A significant milestone in 2024 was the election of Indonesia’s new President, His Excellency Pak Prabowo Subianto. The new administration, established on 20 October 2024, introduced the Asta Cita framework, a strategic blueprint aimed at achieving the “Golden Indonesia 2045” vision. The administration prioritised early ‘quick win’ programmes for immediate implementation, emphasising human-capital development, particularly in areas such as nutrition, agricultural productivity, health, sanitation, education, social protection, eliminating extreme poverty, and ensuring well supported civil servants. Among these initiatives is the Free Nutritious Meals programme which targets pregnant women, children under five, and school age children. These Government’s efforts are underpinned by ambitious fiscal goals, with tax revenue projected to increase to 16–20 per cent of GDP by 2045. 
 
The Government of Indonesia continues to prioritize protection and fulfilment of child rights as evidenced in national development plans. In 2024, the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child examined the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child in Indonesia based on the country report as well as alternative reports received from civil society organizations (CSOs). UNICEF remained engaged with the Government of Indonesia, the Committee and all key actors on this on-going dialogue. 
 
Indonesia has made progress toward achieving the SDGs with indicators for education, health insurance and child marriage on track. However, indicators for nutrition, climate change, and water and sanitation require accelerated efforts. Indonesia faces a triple burden of malnutrition, 21.5 per cent of children under five (5 million) were stunted, 8.5 per cent (2 million) wasted, and 4.2 per cent (1 million) overweight as of 2023. Anaemia affects 23.6 per cent (5 million) of children and 27.7 per cent of pregnant women. Chronic energy deficiency impacts 16.9 per cent of pregnant women, while food insecurity persists, affecting 4.5 per cent of households nationally. Climate change continues to exacerbate the risks faced by children, including those from natural disasters, air pollution, and waterborne diseases. By December 2024, 1,918 disasters had affected an estimated 5.55 million people, including 1.67 million children. The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in Indonesia showed that approximately 45 million children live in earthquake-prone areas, 1.5 million in tsunami-prone zones, 400,000 in regions vulnerable to volcanic eruptions, and 21 million in flood-prone areas. In response, Indonesia has pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 32 per cent by 2030 (or 43 per cent with international assistance), focusing on renewable energy, land-use improvements, and climate resilience. Regarding safely managed water and sanitation, Indonesia is yet to make significant progress on this SDG. The country achieved 11.8 per cent of safely managed drinking water and 10.25 per cent of safely managed sanitation. The National SDG Roadmap estimates that financing requirements for all SDGs by 2030 stand at around USD 8.7 trillion, currently with a gap of USD 1.7 trillion.
 
Advancements in digital transformation are reshaping economies and societies, fostering growth and innovation through improved governance, education, healthcare, and financial inclusion. Initiatives such as "Making Indonesia 4.0," the National Digital Literacy Movement, and the adoption of ASIK (a digital health platform) for health systems demonstrate a commitment to inclusive development. 
 
The Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection (MOWECP) and the Ministry of Communication and Informatics hosted the ASEAN ICT Forum on Child Protection in 2024. The forum, supported by the ASEAN Commission on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Women and Children, brought over 200 representatives from ASEAN countries, ICT companies and the UNICEF regional and Indonesia offices. The forum emphasized the need to keep children safe online including safeguarding against risks including cyberbullying, online exploitation, and misinformation. UNICEF Indonesia will continue to collaborate with the Government on its digital transformation agenda and its implications on children. 
 
Indonesia’s demographic profile presents a unique opportunity to drive social and economic growth by investing in adolescents and young people. Recognizing this, UNICEF collaborates with the government and young people to equip them with the skills, opportunities, and platforms needed to contribute meaningfully to society. The UNICEF Indonesia Adolescent Strategy, developed with adolescents, provides a roadmap for a multi-sectoral approach to their development and transition into adulthood. UNICEF supports the government in elevating youth voices, including through MoWECP’s Monitoring Information System. The Youth-Led Action Initiative has demonstrated models for meaningful youth partnerships on mental health and violence prevention, fostering youth leadership and advocacy for policies that shape their futures.
Additionally, inclusive education is a government priority, with efforts to reach the 36% of children with disabilities who are out of school. UNICEF is supporting the expansion of Disability Service Units to benefit children with disabilities’ learning opportunities.

Under the leadership of the Ministry of National Development Planning (BAPPENAS), UNICEF and the Government of Indonesia (GOI) have started the process of developing the next programme of cooperation for the period 2026-2030. The consultative process engaged a wide group of stakeholders, including working group (POKJA) coordinators, representatives of line ministries, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), the State Secretariat, Civil Society Organisations, the private sector and donors. UNICEF consulted with over 13,100 adolescents and young people including through U-report (UNICEF's digital community for young people) to gain insights into their lived realities to identify priorities for the next Country Programme. Under the leadership of the Ministry of Home Affairs, consultations were extended to 13 sub-national provinces, during the National Management Coordination Meeting (RAKORMAN) in November 2024. As part of the process, UNICEF and GOI commissioned an evaluation for the 2021–2025 Country Programme. The evaluation report was validated by the Evaluation Reference Group and found that UNICEF field presence and investments both at the sub-national and national level constitute the strength of the organization and its comparative advantage in Indonesia. The evaluation also found that UNICEF leveraged innovation and digital transformation to support the Government’s efforts to scale up results for children in different sectors. Also in 2024, a Gender Programmatic Review (GPR) was conducted to assess progress under the 2021–2025 Country Programme and to identify priorities for the 2026–2030 cycle. The GPR found that UNICEF Indonesia made significant progress in promoting gender equality and empowering adolescent girls in Indonesia. However, there is need to further strengthen the transformative impact of UNICEF-supported programmes. 
 
UNICEF continues to support Indonesia’s health transformation agenda, prioritizing maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health. Key contributions include advancing under-five and neonatal mortality reduction through initiatives such as the development of a presidential decree on maternal and infant mortality reduction, updating maternal and child health guidelines, and the creation of the Childhood TB Case Management Guidelines and the Malaria Elimination Roadmap (2025–2045). Other efforts include piloting and rolling out the Quality Improvement Guidelines for Health Facilities, updating the Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) guidelines to include under-five mortality reviews, and introducing four lifesaving vaccines: pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus, Japanese encephalitis, and HPV vaccines. As a result, 14 million children were vaccinated against preventable diseases. In addition, UNICEF supported interventions reached 570,410 adolescents, including students in Islamic boarding schools, through digital campaigns addressing non-communicable diseases, mental health, substance abuse, and HPV vaccination for adolescent girls. Collaborative efforts also led to the elimination of malaria in 14 additional districts, bringing the total number of malaria-free districts to 394 (77 per cent of all districts in Indonesia). 
 
To address immunization gaps, UNICEF supported catch-up immunisation efforts, outbreak responses for measles and diphtheria, gender analysis of barriers to immunisation, vaccine management assessments, and the digitalisation of the electronic immunization registry (ASIK). Additional efforts focused on addressing vaccine hesitancy, improving supply chain logistics, and developing digital training modules for health workers.
 
In partnership with BAPPENAS and the Ministry of Health (MOH), UNICEF contributed to public health policies, including subnational human capital index estimation, improving healthcare in underserved areas, and mapping healthcare accessibility. UNICEF also supported strategic planning for community health workers and the implementation of government health strategies, including MOH’s 2024–2029 Strategic Plan, to ensure equitable access to quality healthcare across Indonesia. UNICEF collaborated with partners to develop and test several Social Behaviour Change (SBC) immunization modules for newly married couples, teachers, healthcare workers, community leaders and young people. These modules were later institutionalised as part of the SBC systems strengthening programme.
 
In collaboration with MOH and local CSOs, over 75 000 people, including frontline workers, enhanced their knowledge on routine immunisation through education sessions and community engagement. Additionally, interpersonal communication modules for training of trainers and communicators, developed with UNICEF’s support on nutrition and immunization, have been standardized and streamlined into government systems for broader reach. 
 
UNICEF, in collaboration with BAPPENAS, launched a formative evaluation of the National Strategy to Accelerate Stunting Prevention. Key findings emphasized the importance of leadership, cross-sector collaboration, and behaviour change as critical factors for sustainable stunting reduction. These insights are shaping the next National Strategy 2025-2029 and informing the forthcoming presidential regulation on sustainable stunting reduction. UNICEF and the Government successfully launched the Landscape Analysis of Large-Scale Food Fortification, which identified an increasing demand for fortified salt, wheat flour, and palm cooking oil driven by population growth, alongside a decline in rice consumption as diets become more diverse. In partnership with MOH, UNICEF has also made significant strides in strengthening the nutrition data and information system at the national and sub-national levels. This includes capacity building for data management on infant and young child feeding indicators to improve national surveys and surveillance systems. Additionally, UNICEF launched a digital campaign promoting key practices to prevent stunting, which reached over 18 million people. 
 
The Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition programme was expanded to 48 additional districts, bringing the total to 175 out of 223 districts in UNICEF’s focus provinces. This expansion included integrating MUAC measurements into primary and community healthcare services. As a result, approximately 7.7 million children under five were screened for wasting and 36,514 severely wasted children received lifesaving treatment. UNICEF also played a pivotal role in finalising the national standards on therapeutic foods for treating severely wasted children, ensuring alignment with global standards and supported the government’s adoption of the 2023 WHO guidelines on child wasting.  Based on global evidence, UNICEF supported the Government in transitioning from iron folic acid supplementation to multiple micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women, aiming to reduce micronutrient deficiencies and low birth weight. Additionally, UNICEF played a key role in supporting preparations for one of the new President’s flagship programmes: the provision of free, nutritious meals to schoolchildren, expectant mothers, and children under five. In close collaboration with BAPPENAS and the newly established National Nutrition Agency, UNICEF provided technical assistance for the design of a comprehensive set of guidelines and standards for the programme. 
 
UNICEF worked closely with national and sub-national government partners to expand the Out of School Children (OOSC) interventions to 14 districts in Central Java, resulting in the programme being scaled-up to 56 districts. With UNICEF’s technical support in implementing gender-responsive planning and budgeting systems, local governments developed tailored programmes to address the unique barriers faced by both girls and boys. This expansion of interventions for OOSC successfully prevented approximately 176,000 children from dropping out of school and enabled 71,300 OOSC to return to learning. Life skills education and 21st-century skills programmes reached over 19,000 girls, fostering leadership, decision-making, and critical-thinking abilities. Despite these achievements, challenges remain as nearly to 3.9 million children in Indonesia are out of school, representing 7.26 per cent of the child and adolescent population aged 7 to 18 years. 
 
The Early Childhood Development Indicator (ECDI) 2030 is now integrated into the national Family Data Collection (Pendataan Keluarga) initiative, led by the Ministry of Population and Family Development (BKKBN) with support from the Ministry of National Development Planning (BAPPENAS) and the National Statistical Bureau (BPS), helping monitor progress towards early childhood development-related SDGs. UNICEF contributed to the replication and expansion of quality early childhood education services, reaching nine additional districts, bringing the total to 33 out of 34 targeted districts. By November 2024, 18,652 children benefited from improved learning and development outcomes. A policy discussion is underway in Indonesia regarding the possibility for the Government adopting one compulsory year of pre-primary education. The Early Grade Learning (EGL) programme was expanded to five new districts, reaching 34 out of 37 targeted districts. 
 
UNICEF contributed significantly to strengthening the legal and policy frameworks for the protection of children and women in Indonesia. This included successfully advocating for the adoption of three derivative regulations for the 2022 Law on Crimes of Sexual Violence: Regulation No. 9/2024 on Integrated Training for Law Enforcement Officers and Service Providers, Presidential Regulation No. 55/2024 on Integrated Service Hubs, and Government Regulation No. 27/2024 on Coordination and Monitoring of Prevention and Victim Response. In collaboration with MOHA and the Ministry of Villages (MOV), UNICEF supported the development of guidelines for sustainable planning and budgeting of child protection at sub-national level, as well as guidelines for the allocation of village funds to community-based child protection activities. UNICEF also ensured the inclusion of key child protection indicators in the 2024-2029 National Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN).  
 
UNICEF continued supporting MOWECP to enhance the accessibility and quality of integrated protection services for women and children (UPTDPPA). In 2024, a total of 117 districts established UPTDPPA, bringing the total number to 333 of 514 districts/ and 34 out of 38 provinces. Among these, 276 districts received a special allocation fund (DAK) from MOWECP, totalling IDR 132 billion (approximately USD 8.5 million), to support their operations. 
 
Through UNICEF support, 22,622 children (14,598 girls and 8,024 boys) and 14,603 parents/caregivers (8,798 women, 5,805 men) were reached through community-based mental health and psychosocial interventions. Parenting interventions, which focused on child online safety, family planning, appropriate care, protection from child marriage and violence prevention reached approximately 63,000 parents and caregivers (55 per cent women) in the provinces of Aceh, Central Java, and East Java. UNICEF facilitated memorandums of understanding (MOUs) between regional health offices and civil registration offices in Papua, Aceh and East Java, enabling the provision of birth-registration services at health facilities. 
 
As part of the team assisting Indonesia in organising the 2023 UN Water Conference and successfully hosting the 2024 World Water Forum, UNICEF reinforced the Government of Indonesia’s global leadership in the water and sanitation agenda. UNICEF also supported the Government in launching new policies, including roadmaps on safe drinking water and sanitation, which aim to provide 60 million Indonesians with safely managed sanitation and 100 million with safely managed water services by 2030.  
 
By December 2024, 195 out of the 514 districts (38 per cent) were declared Open Defecation Free (ODF). UNICEF and the Government of Indonesia implemented a pilot programme in 37 districts since 2021, benefiting 33 million people who now live in a clean environment. This represents 59 per cent of the total ODF beneficiaries in Indonesia. Lessons learned and good practices from the pilot programme have been documented and are now being used by provincial administrations to scale up ODF interventions across other districts. 
 
UNICEF supported the provision of climate-resilient WASH facilities in 182 healthcare facilities in 2024, benefiting over 6.1 million people. UNICEF teams at the national and sub-national levels continue to use evidence and engage the Ministry of Health, provincial and district authorities to address the WASH services in the health sector. The promotion of the Oky App has empowered an additional 156,000 girls with accurate menstrual health and hygiene information.
With catalytic funding, UNICEF supported efforts to improve water quality at the subnational level. This includes strengthening the capacity of provincial governments to monitor water supplies and facilitating the development of water-safety plans in Banten and Aceh. The plans by Government of Indonesia to further invest in housing as part of the national priorities offer a new opportunity for the Indonesia to accelerate achievement of SDG 6 on WASH. 
 
UNICEF achieved significant milestones in advancing child rights in Indonesia through evidence-based advocacy, data-driven research, and multi-stakeholder partnerships. UNICEF played a pivotal role in shaping the draft RPJMN (2025-2029), by enhancing the child rights focus of the medium development plan. UNICEF supported the BAPPENAS to enhance social protection system by launching   the national integrated socioeconomic registration system aimed at making the system more inclusive, effective, and efficient. With UNICEF technical support, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) engaged 18,700 young people in policy discussions and learning journey on budget formulation processes during sub-national and national competitions. UNICEF also worked with MoF to conduct budget analysis as well as budget tagging to generate baseline on planning and budgeting for children by provincial and district governments. The evidence is used for dialogue and advocacy on improving sectoral allocations and spending to accelerate child related SDGs. 
 
UNICEF continued to invest in innovative financing, including leveraging Islamic finance with local government institutions. In Aceh, UNICEF supported Baitul Mal Aceh in mobilizing USD 13.8 million from the Zakat and Infak to date. Through these funds, more than 84,000 individuals, including children, gained access to essential services in addition to other support provided by local government programmes. UNICEF’s support included technical assistance on guideline development, institutional capacity building, implementation of ISO standards to enhance transparency and fund management and facilitating collaboration with government social assistance programmes through data integration and beneficiary synchronization. Given the potential of Islamic finance in Indonesia, UNICEF will continue to work with Government actors, academia and UN agencies on a broader innovative financing strategy to accelerate progress towards the SDGs. 
 
UNICEF accelerated efforts to strengthen cross-sectoral, integrated programming on climate change and environmental action to build more climate and disaster-resilient child-critical social services. These efforts focused on ensuring that climate policies are inclusive of all children and young people as stakeholders and drivers of change. In collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (MoEF), UNICEF launched and disseminated the ‘Climate Landscape Analysis for Children’ report and commissioned the development of national guidance to support the integration of climate, environment, and energy considerations into sectoral policies and plans. UNICEF also facilitated the meaningful engagement of youth in climate and environment action, enabling them to share their experiences and innovations for addressing climate-change at national and regional levels.  UNICEF also advocated for more child-sensitive Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) led by MoEF, providing evidence on the impacts of climate change on children and offering key considerations and recommendations for more child-sensitive climate policies. 
 
Additionally, UNICEF supported a young climate advocate to participate in COP 29 and contribute to a side event at the Indonesia Pavilion, where she shared her experiences and key messages on the role of children as changemakers in the climate space, emphasising the need for climate justice and policy recommendations to promote child inclusive NDCs.
UNICEF also continued its groundwork to support the development of the Children’s Climate and Disaster Risk Index at national and sub-national levels in collaboration with key government stakeholders and partners. Furthermore, UNICEF supported capacity development for provincial and district government representatives, CSOs, academia, and youth networks in Aceh province. UNICEF also advocated for the development of child-centred contingency plans, ensuring the meaningful engagement of adolescents and young people, in close collaboration with the National Disaster Management Agency.
 
UNICEF Indonesia continued its strategic advocacy with key stakeholders before and after the national elections held in February 2024 to promote child rights and ensure they remain a top priority on the new government’s agenda. The advocacy strategy included public outreach, engagement around child rights, direct advocacy and alliance building. Ahead of the elections, UNICEF presented seven programmatic and advocacy priorities to all political parties in the form of policy briefs under the banner '7 Asks for the 8th President of Indonesia’. These priorities covered health, nutrition, WASH, child protection, education, social protection, and climate change, and were accompanied by tangible recommendations to accelerate progress for children across the country. UNICEF welcomed the inclusion of child rights as a top priority for the new government. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF successfully reached over 88.7 million social media users and achieved 27.6 million engagements by sharing meaningful and informative content on critical child rights issues. These included topics such as routine immunization, tackling polio, addressing childhood malnutrition, early childhood development, and child rights in general. To date, UNICEF Indonesia’s digital platforms now engage over 2.7 million followers on child rights issues. The #SetiapAnakBerhak initiative, a child-rights public advocacy campaign launched in late 2023, directly reached over 20 million people, with an additional 3 million reached indirectly through influencer collaborations. UNICEF Indonesia also saw a substantial increase in media coverage, with 3,400 articles published featuring or quoting UNICEF’s work – nearly double the figure from 2023. UNICEF Indonesia gained almost 100,000 new U-Reporters (young people aged 15 to 24) in 2024, bringing the total number to approximately 1.1 million. Throughout the year, U-Reporters actively participated in various campaigns and provided valuable insights to the UN Common Country Assessment (CCA) and UNICEF Country Programme Evaluation (CPE).
 
Throughout 2024, the Operations section of UNICEF Indonesia maintained its role as a pivotal business partner, facilitating the effective implementation of the country programme. Key operational and management services, including financial, administrative, human resources, information and communications technology (ICT), supply and logistics, and security, were delivered efficiently through well-established governance mechanisms and teams. These efforts were guided by the Annual Management Plan (AMP) and overseen by the Country Management Team (CMT) and senior management. Internal control frameworks were strengthened through comprehensive self-assessments, resulting in improved risk mitigation measures and adherence to UNICEF policies. The successful rollout of EZHACT 2.0 improved process efficiency and strengthened collaboration between programme and operations staff through targeted training sessions. As a result, the office achieved 100% completion of assurance activities such as programme monitoring visits (PMVs) and financial assurance activities such as spot-checks. 
 
The office actively participated in the UN inter-agency Operations Management Team, chairing the administration working group and contributing to the UN common back-office analysis. This involvement facilitated the sharing of best practices and the alignment of operational strategies across agencies, enhancing overall efficiency and effectiveness. UNICEF Indonesia led the UN Digital Transformation working group alongside UNESCO. The office also worked closely with the Government of Indonesia to facilitate the donation of 10 million doses of polio vaccines to Afghanistan, demonstrating the power of international collaboration in addressing global health challenges. 
Further, workplace culture, staff wellbeing, and professional development, implementing initiatives to enhance staff support and growth were prioritised. Key achievements included launching an on-demand wellbeing and counselling programme for all staff, publishing a directory of local mental health resources, and developing a progressive workplace culture action plan. ICO’s telecommuting guidelines were also updated to better support flexible working arrangements. To strengthen staff wellbeing, the team actively engaged in the Joint-Consultative Committee and the ICO’s Advisory Committee on Workplace Culture.

UNICEF Indonesia continued to establish and maintain partnerships with a wide range of stakeholders, including government, academia, local and international non-governmental and CSOs, professional associations and faith-based organisations, for the realization of children’s rights. UNICEF Indonesia signed programme documents with 17 line ministries, coordinated by BAPPENAS and MOHA for decentralised implementation in 13 focus provinces. UNICEF Indonesia assessed 38 (100 per cent) of CSOs on the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) using UN-wide standards to ensure safer environments for vulnerable populations. 
 
Partnerships with private sector offered opportunities not only to mobilize resources, but also to collaborate on the child rights agenda in Indonesia. Private sector fundraising grew during the reporting period with an income steadily increasing. Over 70,000 individual donors contributed monthly donations, collectively providing more than IDR 9 billion per month. Efforts to refine the Salesforce system and related processes continued, resulting in greater efficiencies. In collaboration with businesses and foundations, partnerships were sustained and further developed with key partners such as the Tanoto Foundation, Wings Group, Prudential Indonesia, and CIMB Niaga. New initiatives were launched with In Journey Aviation Services, while partnerships with DBS Indonesia and National Football Association (PSSI) were formed at year-end. UNICEF Indonesia continued to work with businesses to advance the Children’s Rights and Business Principles framework in partnership with the Ministry for Law and Human Rights.
 
UNICEF also engaged public sector actors as key partners throughout 2024. New partnerships were established with the Government of the Republic of Korea and Global Affairs Canada to support initiatives including improving immunization coverage, WASH in health facilities, evidence-based planning for budgeting and governance at health facilities, budget tagging of health budgets at the district level, and improving birth and death registration services in health facilities. 
 
UNICEF’s partnership with USAID continued to support efforts to eliminate childhood tuberculosis, particularly in Papua, while funding from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria (GFATM) focused on accelerating malaria elimination in Eastern Indonesia. UNICEF’s health programme also collaborated with other UN agencies, including WHO, UNFPA, UNDP and UNEP to strengthen health systems. Additionally, UNICEF worked closely with professional associations to gather technical input aimed at improving the quality of health services.
 
UNICEF signed an MOU with the Ministry of Religious Affairs (MORA) to promote child rights across the faith sector and communities. This collaboration paved the way for stronger engagement with religious leaders nationwide, supporting the dissemination of 500 copies of the book Islam and Child Rights and 10,000 calendars featuring key child rights messages to mosques and religious schools across Indonesia. The MoU also served as foundation for convening a multi-stakeholder workshop, during which an action plan was developed to strengthen the knowledge and involvement of religious leaders in promoting child rights. 
 
UNICEF Indonesia continued its role as a key convener within the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement, serving as the lead for the Donor and UN Country Nutrition Network (DUNCNN). Under UNICEF’s leadership, the DUNCNN analysed nutrition related policies, shared knowledge on best practices and provided technical assistance to various line ministries. UNICEF partnered with the SUN Business Network to support the local production of therapeutic foods, including ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF). As a result, the Ministry of Health issued Ministerial Decree no HK 01.07-MENKES1-1341-2024 approving the production of RUTF for the treatment of malnourished children. UNICEF Indonesia worked with national higher education institutions to establish Centres of Excellence aimed at improving the quality of Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) services nationwide. 
 
UNICEF continued its role as a key convenor supporting government and CSO coordination mechanisms in the education sector. As the grant agent for the GPE System Capacity Grant Part 1, UNICEF worked with 17 members of the Local Education Group to finalise Indonesia’s Partnership Compact. The compact aims to harmonise interventions from government and non-government partners to enhance learning quality. Under its framework, USD 24 million was mobilised to support this effort.
 
In the social media space, UNICEF Indonesia partnered with 35 high-profile public figures to support its campaigns, content, and events in 2024. These collaborations enabled UNICEF to reach nearly 30 million people through celebrities’ social media channels alone.  Additionally, a week-long World Children’s Day campaign in November engaged approximately 24 million users via celebrity partner channels, highlighting the strategic value of influencer partnerships. UNICEF’s online child protection campaign benefited from a partnership with META (global), which extended the campaign’s reach to over 50 million internet users. 
 
A pro bono partnership with an out-of-home advertising agency allowed UNICEF to further amplify its message, reaching more than 12 million people through outdoor screens, banners, and billboards in busy commercial areas. These messages focused on child rights, immunisation, and fundraising campaigns for World Children’s Day and Independence Day.
 
UNICEF Indonesia actively supported the Government of Indonesia’s foreign policy on South-South cooperation. In 2024, UNICEF Indonesia and the Ministry of Finance (MoF) participated in a South-South exchange initiative led by EAPRO on strategic spending on child rights. MoF shared its experiences with countries such as Viet Nam, Thailand, the Philippines, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal, showcasing innovative approaches to child-responsive planning, budgeting, monitoring, budget tagging, and the development of a child-spending dashboard. In the area of child protection, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection and BAPPENAS to share experiences in strengthening child protection systems. These insights were shared with 15 countries from Latin America, the Caribbean, Europe and Central Asia. UNICEF Indonesia also facilitated the participation of Surabaya City’s local government authorities in a global forum on Child-Friendly Cities organised by the Regional Office in China. Surabaya representatives showcased their achievements in promoting and implementing child-friendly policies and service delivery. 
 
Finally, UNICEF Indonesia facilitated a youth climate resilient learning exchange for students from the Philippines who were interested in learning about WASH innovations and Indonesia’s experiences in this area.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF Indonesia’s lessons learned in 2024 will inform the planning and implementation of its programme for 2025 and beyond. High level and sustained advocacy with political platforms, while leveraging national expertise and strategic partnerships, was key to advancing the child rights agenda during politically charged processes such as general elections. The implementation of an agile programme enabled UNICEF to be flexible and adaptive to the changing operating environment. For instance, UNICEF repurposed existing resources to swiftly respond to the new Government’s request for technical support and policy advice on nutritious meals programme.  This support led to the National Nutrition Agency and BAPPENAS adopting national standards and guidelines for the implementation of the free nutritious programme nationwide. Leveraging innovation and technology in the health sector allowed UNICEF to support the Ministry of Health at both national and subnational levels to accelerate the digitalization of the immunization system in Indonesia. At the subnational level, sustained advocacy with provinces, beyond district-level engagement, created opportunities for UNICEF to influence development planning and unlock local government resources to scale up quality services for children. Looking ahead, UNICEF will continue to advocate for a balanced role between provincial and district governments focusing on leveraging decentralized entities for child-centred planning and budgeting.
 
The implementation of the 2024 country programme faced several challenges. Despite progress in the digitalization of various services, its potential remains limited in geographically remote areas, reflecting economic disparities between provinces. The Government’s prioritization of digital transformation as a key enabler in long-term development plans, including the President’s Quick Wins programme, is expected to address this challenge and ensure last mile service delivery across different sectors. UNICEF will continue to drive inclusive digital transformation, advocating for equitable access and ensuring technological advancements enhance service delivery and positively benefit children. Provincial governments play a crucial role in bridging national policies with district-level implementation. They have the capacity to leverage regional budgets and mobilize resources to scale up interventions for children. However, programme replication at the district level often encounters challenges, as governments responsible for implementation often face resource constraints—both financial and human—limiting their ability to deliver at scale.
 
Delivering communication and advocacy objectives through social media also presented challenges in 2024. Platforms increasingly prioritised paid content while reducing unpaid organic reach (e.g. removing users' ability to follow hashtags). This ecosystem trend, coupled with tightened UNICEF Indonesia’s digital advertising budgets, led to reduced social media engagements compared to 2023. UNICEF Indonesia navigated these challenges by building and strengthening relationships with key media professionals, staying updated on industry trends, and producing engaging content supported by credible spokespersons. Media visits with top-tier outlets were a key strategy for generating quality coverage on priority topics.
 
Interpersonal communication training conducted by UNICEF Indonesia in collaboration with the government enhanced the capacity of health cadres and volunteers in community engagement. This training improved the delivery and outreach of child-rights messages to communities.

The year 2024 marked a critical juncture for Lao PDR.

On the one hand, the country as the ASEAN Chair successfully led the 44th and 45th ASEAN Summits under the theme "ASEAN: Enhancing Connectivity and Resilience." The summits stressed priorities such as regional integration, digital transformation, climate resilience, and health systems strengthening. ASEAN leaders commended Lao PDR's contributions to regional prosperity, peace, and stability, particularly through the Five-Point Consensus on Myanmar.

On the other hand, in the context of post-COVID recovery and global challenges, Lao PDR continued facing critical domestic socio-economic challenges that directly impact child rights. Macroeconomic instability, high inflation, and slow GDP growth hinder the country's recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. Public debt remains a concern, with the debt-to-GDP ratio reaching 108% by 2023. GDP growth was projected at 4% in 2024—still below pre-pandemic levels—while inflation reached 18.32% as of November 2024, a decrease from 31.23% in 2023 attributable to sound government efforts, including tightening monetary policy and issuing government securities. However, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) climbed to 246 from 189 in 2023, signaling continued pressure on household budgets. Rising costs for healthcare, food, and fuel particularly burden rural families, impacting children's access to essential services. Government spending on education and health remains below regional averages, at 1.2% and 1.5% of GDP respectively. Despite improved tax policies and ongoing fiscal reforms, tax revenues remain among the region’s lowest at 11.3% of GDP in 2022, further limiting government spending on education, health, and social protection. 

In addition, severe floods and landslides in 2024 further exacerbated vulnerabilities: over 255,000 people across 16 provinces were affected, including more than 48,500 children. Tropical cyclones and prolonged rainfall caused agricultural losses, infrastructure damage to schools and health facilities, damage to water and sanitation facilities and can have an impact on the nutritional situation of children. Lao PDR is also prone to droughts, heatwaves and air quality issues, increasing children exposure to diseases such as malaria, dengue fever and respiratory problems, exacerbating food insecurity, and eventually impacting cognitive development and overall physical growth. These threats highlight the need for a sound strategy to address climate change and environmental degradation.

Lao PDR's Human Development Index (HDI) scored 0.620 in 2022, placing the country 139th out of 193 featured in the index. Lao PDR ranks 119th out of 166 countries on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) Index, with a score of 62.95. Moderate progress has been made on goals such as No Poverty (SDG 1), Gender Equality (SDG 5), Clean Water and Sanitation (SDG 6), Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 7), and Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure (SDG 9). However, progress on other goals has stagnated. Quality Education (SDG 4) faces challenges due to a reduced net primary enrollment rate and lower secondary completion rates. Similarly, Good Health and Well-being (SDG 3) shows declines in key indicators. In its third Voluntary National Review (VNR) in 2024, Lao PDR acknowledged progress but stressed persistent gaps in poverty, education, and health, calling for stronger partnerships and targeted efforts to reduce inequities.

Achieving universal health coverage remains a significant challenge, particularly for children and adolescents. According to the Lao Social Indicator Survey (LSIS III, 2023), more than half of children aged 12-23 months do not receive all basic immunizations, increasing their risk of preventable diseases. 64.5% of children under five and 69.9% of children aged 5-17 are not covered by any health insurance, leaving most children vulnerable to out-of-pocket healthcare expenses. Despite these challenges, there is a positive trend in child survival, with under-5 mortality declining from 46 per 1,000 live births in 2017 to 28 in 2023, and neonatal mortality dropping from 18 to 12 during the same period.

Malnutrition and food insecurity represent pressing issues. Stunting affects one-third of children under five, while 10.7% suffer from wasting in 2023 (LSIS III). A slightly positive trend in exclusive breastfeeding shows about 6% increase, with 50.6% of infants under 6 months exclusively breastfed in 2023, up from 44.9% in 2017. Nutrition surveillance indicates that 65% of children aged 6-23 months did not receive a diverse diet in 2024, and three-quarters (75%) did not receive a minimum acceptable diet during the lean season, putting them at risk of poor physical and cognitive development.

Learning outcomes remain low; 81.4% of Grade 2/3-aged children do not achieve foundational reading skills and 77.4% do not achieve numeracy skills (LSIS III). The country struggles with decreasing participation in Early Childhood Education (ECE), with attendance dropping from 32.1% in 2017 (LSIS II) to 26.9% in 2023, (29% for females and 24.9% for males, LSIS III), along with rising numbers of out-of-school children. One in ten primary-aged children, three in ten lower secondary-aged children, and six in ten upper-secondary-aged children are not attending school (LSIS III). Household poverty and rising living costs have contributed to a nearly 30% increase in upper secondary dropout rates between 2021-2022 and 2023-2024 (LESMIS, 2024).

Child marriage and adolescent pregnancies pose serious risks to children's health and development. Three in ten women are married before the age of 18 – the highest percentage in the region – and the adolescent birth rate stands at 89 births to women aged 15-19, per 1,000 women in that age group (LSIS III). 23.1% of children aged 5-17 are involved in child labour, including paid and unpaid economic activities, despite existing laws prohibiting employment under the age of 14. The Government of Lao PDR had the honour to become the first ASEAN Member State to ban corporal punishment, and monitoring mechanisms are being developed to address violence against children, which remains prevalent (62.3% of children experiencing violent discipline at home). Additionally, birth registration for children under age 5 dropped from 73% in 2017 to 65% in 2023, posing challenges to appropriate child protection.

Significant progress has been made in improving access to Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services. Efforts continued with the implementation of the National Sanitation Roadmap to Reach Open-Defecation Free (ODF) status by 2025, with initiatives led by the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment on regulations, guidelines, and the monitoring and evaluation system. As of October 2024, 97.5% of villages were declared ODF, a significant increase from 86% in November 2023. Over 90% of households report having an accessible water source. However, 72.3% of the households still have E. coli contamination in their drinking water (LSIS III). More than 85% have improved sanitation facilities. Additionally, nearly 84% of women aged 15-49 have access to hygiene materials and private spaces for washing, which marks critical progress in public health, gender equality, and dignity for women and girls in Lao PDR.

Social protection systems in Lao PDR remain underdeveloped, with only 23.8% of children living in households that receive any type of social transfer. Expanding cash transfer programmes and improving targeting mechanisms could help reduce household poverty and prevent children from dropping out of school or engaging in child labour. The new minimum wage policy implemented in October 2024 is a positive step towards reducing economic vulnerabilities, but additional measures are needed to strengthen social safety nets and ensure child well-being during economic shocks. A 2022 by UNDP Digital Maturity Assessment categorized Lao PDR as ‘Digitally Nascent,’ the lowest level of digital readiness. In response, the Government of Lao PDR has committed to a Digital Transformation agenda across three key areas: Digital Economy, Digital Government, and Digital Society. 

Combining child rights deprivations and exposure to climate-related hazards, UNICEF in Lao PDR produced the Equity Analysis, a child rights-focused statistical tool to identify and measure inequities across geographic areas and population groups. This tool allows UNICEF to gain a deeper understanding of the performance of progress on child rights, to promote evidence-based adaptive programming, and to improve targeting of interventions. Preliminary findings of the Equity Analysis highlight that the provinces most prone to high levels of children vulnerabilities are Oudomxay, Savannakhet, and Salavan, followed by Luang Prabang, Attapeu, and Sekong. The analysis also highlighted opportunities for targeted support to different population groups, based on ethnicity, age and sex. It also identified a clear correlation between deprivation index and hazard index, showing that provinces most prone to hazards also have the highest child rights deprivations, highlighting the need for a stronger commitment to climate action.

In 2024, UNICEF Lao  PDR made significant strides across all programmes, contributing to improved  outcomes for children and promoting systemic changes. Key achievements and  contributions are highlighted below:
  
Goal Area 1: Every  Child Survives and Thrives
  
In the area of health,  the year marked a transformative step with the endorsement and implementation  of the Primary Health Care (PHC) Law, creating an enabling environment for primary  health system strengthening and establishing a strong foundation for  achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC).
  
According to the Laos Social Indicator Survey (LSIS III),  under-five mortality declined from 46 per 1,000 live births in 2017 to 28 in  2023, while neonatal mortality dropped from 22 to 12 during the same period. Integrated  Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) initiatives have  significantly helped to improve the situation, addressing key drivers of  under-five mortality such as diarrhea and pneumonia. 536 health workers from  285 health facilities were trained on IMNCI. In addition, the  development and scaling up of VHV toolkits supported the engagement of 1002 Village  Health Volunteers (VHV) at the community level, enhancing their capacity to  address community needs aligned with their role in primary health care  delivery. These efforts align with global  guidelines, contributing to healthier childhood outcomes.
  
The  first National Immunization Strategy (NIS) is in the process of finalization with  UNICEF’s support, fostering a country-led, partnership-driven, and  community-focused approach to ensure a sustainable and impactful immunization  programme over the next 5–7 years. Immunization Supply Chain has been  strengthened through significant enhancements in cold chain infrastructure  and temperature monitoring systems. The Electronic Immunization Registry  (EIR) initiative, promoted by UNICEF, registered 99.7% of children under one  year, enabling real-time data visualization and informed decision-making at  all levels of the health system. An innovative eLearning platform on cold  chain and vaccine management was launched –a key success in capacity building.  Based on a Gender analysis of routine immunization, HPV and COVID-19  vaccination programs, the Gender roadmap for Lao PDR has been drafted and is  currently under review and is expected to be endorsed by Government of Lao  PDR in Q1 2025

Data from the Ministry  of Health (MoH) reveals that the coverage of routine immunization increased  compared to previous years, with the Pentavalent vaccine dose 3 coverage  reaching 86.3% (+2% from 2023). UNICEF provided technical assistance for the  nationwide Measles-Rubella (MR) vaccination campaign, which immunized 633,831  children aged 9–59 months. The Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination  campaign supported by UNICEF achieved over 102% coverage of its target  population, vaccinating approximately 127,586 girls aged 10–13 years.
  
In the area of  nutrition, the capacity of the Government has been reinforced on the  management of the National Nutrition Information System. Over 400 government  staff received training on data collection and evidence generation. The  Nutrition Information Platform for Nutrition (NIPN) and regular monitoring  through multisectoral nutrition dashboards improved strategic planning and  evidence-based policy-making.
  
Government capacity  has also been strengthened in implementing both preventative and curative  nutrition interventions. Training was provided to 392 health  workers to deliver quality Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM)  services, and to 48 healthcare workers as breastfeeding counselors. IMAM  outpatient department (OPD) sites were scaled up from 50 to 205, and all 18  provinces were supplied with Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) enabling 2,521  children with severe acute malnutrition to access live-saving treatment.  Meanwhile preventive interventions such as Vitamin A and Iron Folate  supplementation reached over 115,000 children and 110,000 pregnant women  respectively.
  
Compliance with the  Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes (BMS) Decree has been strengthened  through monitoring at retail points across 10 provinces and in 7 provincial  and 14 district hospitals. An innovative AI-based tool was also developed and  tested to monitoring the promotion of BMS across digital platforms. Government  leadership to improve nutrition behaviors of women and children has been  enhanced through the establishment of a "National Technical Social  Behavior Change (SBC) Team," that developed an SBC for Nutrition  training package at the subnational level which has already been rolled out in  3 provinces.
  
The government elevated  the prioritization of the nutrition sector through publicly committing,  during the Human Capital Summit on Nutrition, for its inclusion in the 10th  National Socioeconomic Development Plan (NSEDP) and to ensuring line  ministries focus on evidence-based and cost-effective nutrition  interventions. This high-level commitment was bolstered by UNICEF advocacy  efforts through the national nutrition forum, research conference and  high-level meetings. The government’s commitment to the nutrition sector will  underpin and enhance the nutrition interventions to ensure less children are  malnourished. 
  
Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns
  
In 2024, UNICEF continued its efforts to address the learning crisis in Lao PDR through evidence-based policy advocacy, and initiatives focused on system strengthening. UNICEF played a key role in the implementation of the 9th Education and  Sports Sector Development Plan (ESSDP) and the development of the 10th  ESSDP, advocating for foundational learning, addressing key equity  bottlenecks, and promoting the use of formative assessments and remedial  education. The Assessment of Student Learning Outcome (ASLO) Grade 5 findings  and Positive Deviance School Study provided crucial data to inform ESSDP,  ensuring evidence-based policymaking. UNICEF continued to improve and  strengthen education data systems, most notably through support to the Lao  Education and Sports Management Information System (LESMIS) and the roll-out  of the Fundamental Quality Standards (FQS) for school improvement. The FQS  were implemented in 30 districts across five provinces, with plans for  nationwide scaling in 2025.
  
A significant  achievement was the endorsement of Lao PDR's first national ECE Decree,  renewing commitment to investment in Early Childhood Care and Education  (ECCE). The ASEAN Education Minister's Forum on ECCE, hosted by Lao PDR,  culminated in an ASEAN Ministerial Statement on ECCE and Climate, addressing  the impacts of climate change on children's learning. In the nationwide  rollout of the new pre-primary curriculum, 228 pre-primary teachers, 257  school principals, and 258 Grade 1 teachers were trained, improving early  learning environments for over 229,000 children. Additionally, 136 village  facilitators and 1,080 parenting group members were trained on school  readiness, to support child's social-emotional, cognitive, and physical  development to prepare her for entering primary school.
  
Digital innovations  remained a priority, with the Khang Panya Lao (KPY) platform registering  18,343 new users (50% girls) in 2024. The platform now hosts STEM videos and  a Gender Empowerment Package. Training on digital literacy for 1,298 teachers  and principals in 650 schools benefited approximately 130,000 students. A  sector-wide Digital Education Strategy was endorsed, paving the way for more  inclusive access to digital learning for over 2.5 million children and adolescents  in Laos. This strategy is expected to guide future investments in educational  technology and digital literacy.
  
In response to the challenges  in enrolment rates, a year-long back-to-school campaign promoted student  re-enrollment and retention nationwide. STEM4Girls boot camps reached 992  adolescents, primarily girls, equipping them with science, technology,  engineering, and mathematics (STEM) skills, digital literacy, and career  guidance. UNICEF also partnered with Lao Youth Union and became the 56th  country to launch UPSHIFT, the social innovator for young people to create  new learning pathways, as well as roll out of the youth action guide, a yearlong  youth-led action initiative reaching over 200 youths (70% girls) and delivering  over 6,000 learning hours in total with a focus on issues such as child  marriage, climate change, entrepreneurship, among others. 
  
UNICEF also played a crucial role in coordinating  development partners’ response to severe flooding which damaged schools in  September 2024 and provided learning materials to primary schools and Early  Childhood Education (ECE) toolkits and teacher guidebooks for ECE centers in  Luang Namtha to enable the continuity of learning for 1,600 children.

  
Goal  3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation
  
In 2024, UNICEF  continued supporting the government's implementation of its 5-year National  Plan of Action for Child Protection Systems Strengthening (2022-2026). This  involved strengthening the enabling environment, workforce capacities, and  protective services available for children and adolescents. 
  
Building on the 2023  legal breakthrough of banning corporal punishment in all settings, UNICEF  supported the government with the dissemination of key provisions of the  Amended Law on the Protection of the Rights and Interests of the Child. This  effort aimed to raise awareness and promote compliance with the new law,  contributing to a reduction in violence against children from 69% in 2017 to  63% in 2023, according to LSIS III. Another significant development was the continued  work on the draft of the Law on Social Work with UNICEF's support. This law,  to be submitted to the National Assembly for consideration in June 2025, will  be pivotal for professionalizing and strengthening the social service  workforce in the country.
  
Child Protection  Systems are being modeled in Xiengkhouang province. Guidelines on legal  proceedings and investigation-interrogation for police officials were  developed to ensure timelier and child-friendly services. 169 (F50, M119)  police, judges, prosecutors, lawyers, and village authorities have now  capacities in legal aid and community-based diversion. As a result, 9,851  children (F4,301, M5,550) received legal aid and advice, including 968  children who committed minor offenses and were able to go through the  mediation process – used as a means to divert children from a formal justice  system. Furthermore, the manual (Trainers' Guide) and Participants' Handbook  for the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) on Child Protection Case  Management were developed. 
  
To address social and  gender norms that contribute to protection risks, UNICEF engaged a wide range  of duty-bearers including parents, families, teachers, and communities  through community platforms. A Joint Programme with UNFPA led by the Ministry  of Labor and Social Welfare (MOLSW) has been designed to address child  marriage in the provinces most prone to social and gender norms that  contribute to protection risks, including Xiengkhouang, Luang Prabang, Luang  Namtha, Bokeo, and Phongsaly. 12,487 (F6,094 M6,393) social service workforce  (SSW), including para-social workers (Child Protection Networks), are now  equipped with knowledge and skills to provide quality services ranging from  case management, counseling, and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS).  A total of 5,447 (F3,227 M2,220) adults, adolescents, and children were  reached through awareness-raising campaigns on key child protection and  gender issues, through newly developed communication assets, such as an  innovative edutainment board game “Choose My Way,” and a short film, “The  Story of Three Girls,”, broadcasted in Hmong, Khmu, and Akha languages. All these  engagements involved reflective dialogue aimed at eliminating discriminatory  social and gender norms and harmful practices.
  
In response to the  flood emergency caused by Typhoon Yagi, 841 affected children and parents  were reached with psychosocial support. UNICEF, working with various  ministries and the Lao Women's Union, established Child Friendly Spaces (CFS)  in four affected villages.

  
Goal Area 4: Every  Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment
  
In 2024, Lao PDR  continued to make progress in improving access to safe water and sanitation.  According to LSIS III, the population with access to at least a basic  drinking water service increased to 86% in 2023, while coverage with basic  sanitation services increased to 84%. UNICEF bolstered the government's  capacity to plan, coordinate, and allocate resources for rural WASH services  through climate risk assessments, life cycle cost and affordability analysis  of community-managed water supply systems, and trialing climate-resilient  water safety planning.
  
Through nationwide  support for Community Approaches to Total Sanitation (CATS) and following the  adoption of the 2023 Sanitation Roadmap to eliminate open defecation, provinces,  districts and development partners supported the so-called “last mile  households” including low-income and vulnerable households, and households  with persons with disabilities who are unable to cover the investment needed  to improve their sanitation. As a result of these collective efforts, 17 provinces  achieved Open Defecation Free (ODF) status as of 2024 with Lao PDR on track  to achieve nationwide ODF status by 2025.
