An additional 200,000 people are  now living in ODF-declared communities since the launch of the Sanitation  Roadmap and an innovative mobile phone-based CATS tracking application is  being trialed to support the Government and partners to improve progress monitoring,  and minimize the risk of slippage.  
  
Through the  establishment of community-managed, metered, and reticulated water supply  schemes benefitting 3,000 people, climate-resilient water safety planning,  and innovative flood-resilient designs for WASH in institutions, UNICEF  provided replicable models for rural WASH service provision and fostered  learning exchanges through the WASH Sector Development Partners Coordination Group.  
  
UNICEF supported  systems strengthening for WASH in Schools and Health Care Facilities, leading  to enhanced monitoring of WASH services with a focus on equity-based and  gender-sensitive indicators. The integration of these indicators into  national systems (LESMIS and DHIS) was a key achievement. UNICEF, in  collaboration with the Provincial Education and Sports departments in five  provinces of Phongsaly, Houaphanh, Xiengkhouang, Savannakhet, and Saravane,  supported 54 schools with WASH facilities and water filters, benefiting 6,126  children (including 3,037 girls) with a safer school environment. 
  
In collaboration with  the Disability Management Advisory Services, disability-inclusive WASH  facilities were constructed to improve accessibility at a rehabilitation  center in Xiengkhouang. The Provincial Health Departments of Phongsaly,  Houaphanh, Xiengkhouang, and UNICEF completed improvements in 7 health  centers including water supplies and disability-friendly and flood-resilient  toilets, serving more than 14,335 people, including 6,697 females living in  55 satellite villages.   
  
Following the launch  of a climate risk assessment for children, a climate strategy is being  implemented with development partners using innovative and risk-informed  approaches including the development of a sub-national children and climate  index, using machine learning for air quality monitoring and development of  green- and eco-school concepts. Youth engagement and child-sensitive national  climate policies and strategies aim to secure increased attention to, and  financing for, climate adaptation in social services. As part of the Lao PDR  Inter-Agency Contingency Plan, UNICEF coordinated humanitarian relief efforts  for WASH Cluster members for the Typhoon Yagi response.

  
Goal Area 5: Every  Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life
  
UNICEF deployed its  technical expertise to support the generation and availability of  high-quality and reliable data. The successful completion of the third round  of the Lao Social Indicator Survey (LSIS III) was a major achievement in  2024, providing valuable insights into key social indicators in the country.  The LSIS III Key Indicator Report was released in January 2024, including 164  internationally standard indicators about children and women. As part of this  initiative, nine statisticians from the Lao Statistics Bureau and 10  technical staff from the Ministry of Education and Sport, and Ministry of  Health received training in data compilation and report writing.
  
In the area of “Public  Finance for Children”, UNICEF continued its advocacy for increased investments  in education, engaging with the National Assembly and conducting field  monitoring across seven provinces to discuss about major bottlenecks with  local education authorities, school personnel and parents. The results were  presented during the 8th Ordinary Session, requesting the Government to  implement more concrete actions, including an increase of the investment in  education to 18% of the national budget. 
  
In addition, data  collection from constituencies was incorporated into budget discussions  during the Ordinary Sessions of the National Assembly, influencing  discussions on social sector spending to mitigate the impact of macroeconomic  and inflation challenges on poor households.
  
The Government of Lao  PDR through the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, in partnership with  UNICEF, has made significant strides in advancing disability inclusion. A key  initiative, the pilot Disability Grant Plus programme, was implemented in  Xiangkhouang Province, where 496 Children with Disabilities (236 girls and  260 boys) benefited from monthly unconditional cash transfers, 239 children  received assistive devices, 233 families received training on caring for  children with disabilities, sign language financial literacy and, to enhance  children’s independence, mobility, and community connection. To build  national and sub-national capacity in disability-inclusive social protection,  UNICEF supported a training programme for 44 government officials (23 females  and 21 males), CSOs, and UN agencies. This training series explored pathways  and strategy options to enhance social protection for persons with  disabilities and highlighted the need for a Disability Management Information  System (DMIS). With UNICEF's support, the roadmap for DMIS development was  drafted and discussed among government counterparts, development partners,  and INGOs involved in disability programmes in the country.

In 2024, UNICEF continued to leverage strategic partnerships and mobilize support for the ongoing Country Programme, 2022-2026. Throughout the year, UNICEF regularly engaged with a range of development partners, including public sector partners with whom UNICEF has existing partnerships in Lao PDR (such as Australia, Canada, China, the European Union, France, Japan, Luxembourg, the Republic of Korea, the United States, and USAID, among others) while exploring collaboration opportunities with new partners. 
In addition, UNICEF continued to work closely with several National Committees for UNICEF, particularly those from Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea, the United Kingdom, and the United States. During the year, new partnerships were launched with UNICEF Australia, UNICEF China, the Korean Committee for UNICEF, United States Fund for UNICEF, and United Kingdom Committee for UNICEF. 
UNICEF is deeply grateful for the invaluable support of development partners and the National Committees for UNICEF which was instrumental in driving the results highlighted in this report.
Key milestones, such as the bilateral engagements between the outgoing UNICEF Representative and the newly appointed Representative, as well as the Country Programme Mid-Term Review consultations with development partner, provided opportunities to reinforce partnerships with existing and potential partners, while raising awareness on the situation of children in Lao PDR. 
Partnering and building alliances with a variety of stakeholders has also been key to promoting child rights throughout the year. Some examples below: 
-          In health, strategic partnerships across ministries, UN agencies, and development partners significantly strengthened the health system in Lao PDR. UNICEF, with support from USAID and WHO, provided critical support to the development of the Primary Health Care Law, a transformative milestone, involving extensive consultations with diverse stakeholders led by the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Justice. Members from the National Assembly, Prime Minister’s Office, and key ministries are part of the Primary Health Care committees from national to village levels. UNICEF’s collaboration with WHO, the World Bank (HANSA project), and John Snow Inc. facilitated the scaling up of critical interventions, including Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses, Essential Early Newborn Care, and Kangaroo Mother Care. With support from USAID and Luxembourg, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of Village Health Volunteers. These partnerships advanced health outcomes and progress toward Universal Health Coverage and the Sustainable Development Goals. The partnership with Luxembourg has been key to advancing Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health in Lao PDR, through a Joint programme in collaboration with UNFPA and WHO.
 
-          In nutrition, UNICEF's partnership with Alive & Thrive led to the development of an AI tool to monitor the violations of the Breastmilk Substitute Code on social media, enhancing breastfeeding practices and data-driven decision-making. Collaborating with the World Bank and the Ministry of Health, UNICEF continued the advocacy for transitioning from iron and folic acid to multi-micronutrient supplements to improve maternal health in Lao PDR. UNICEF also partnered with the World Bank on the Human Capital Summit, securing commitments for better nutrition governance and capacity building. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with the Center for Health Statistics and Information to organize subnational trainings and technical support on Social and Behavior Change for nutrition. Regional collaborations and thematic funds have further bolstered UNICEF's role in nutrition and emergency preparedness. Thematic funds have been essential in allowing UNICEF to co-lead initiatives like the Human Capital Summit and have reinforced UNICEF's position as a key partner and technical leader in nutrition within the country. In addition, the regional pooled funds have enabled improved emergency preparedness.  
 
-          On education, UNICEF collaborated with key partners to advance education system strengthening and inclusive learning in Lao PDR. UNICEF worked closely with the EU, Australia and USAID, and as Co-Coordinating Agency for the Global Partnership for Education-III grant, facilitated strategic initiatives with the World Bank. UNICEF also enhanced digital learning initiatives and maintained coordination with 15 development partners contributing to the Khang Panya Lao platform. UNICEF’s collaboration with the National University of Laos built Information and Communication Technology capacity within the Ministry of Education and Sports. Regional engagement was strengthened through the ASEAN Early Childhood Care and Education Forum, as well as the ongoing collaboration on the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics, positioning Lao PDR as a regional leader in early childhood care and education. UNICEF’s efforts in 2024 also included significant advancements in digital learning and early childhood education. UNICEF thematic funding also helped in support to mitigate school drop-out through back-to-school campaign and remedial learning programmes. It also enabled capacity building of teachers on digital literacy.
 
-          In child protection, UNICEF continued to collaborate with multiple partners, including civil society organizations, UN agencies, and government agencies, to address diverse child protection issues through a system approach. Strong partnerships with the Government of Lao PDR, including the Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare, and the Lao Women’s Union, led to significant progress in strengthening the legal framework, responsive and preventive services, and positive behavior change. Partnership with UNFPA has provided the ground for a long-term work to eliminate child marriage. UNICEF partnered with the National University of Laos to upgrade the Bachelor of Arts Programme in Social Work Curriculum. Collaboration with the business sector, such as Lao Telecom, amplified UNICEF’s efforts in supporting the government reaching youth from ethnolinguistic communities in all areas to better access essential counselling through a free SMS notification and calling services. 
 
-          In WASH, UNICEF supported the government in implementing WASH and climate resilience policies through evidence generation, capacity-building, and system strengthening. Partnerships with the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, Global Green Growth Institute, JICA, and NGO partners supported sector coordination and planning. Collaboration with national and international universities strengthened sector research capacity and knowledge management. UNICEF fostered collaboration with development partners to leverage WASH sector investments for major infrastructure and coordinated urban sanitation efforts. Inter-UN collaboration was actively pursued for various initiatives, including WASH in health care facilities and schools, disaster preparedness, and the climate agenda.
 
-          Finally, in social policy, partnerships with the National Assembly played an important role in positioning children's rights on the policy agenda. With UNICEF’s Thematic Funding, the Social and Cultural Affairs Committee undertook a comprehensive review of human capital development and education reform. UNICEF remained a key partner in promoting inclusive social protection programmes and influencing policy in collaboration with the Government and the National Assembly.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
During 2024, UNICEF Lao PDR completed a comprehensive review of its Country Programme, 2022-2026. This Mid-Term Review (MTR) was undertaken against the backdrop of significant changes in Lao PDR's socioeconomic landscape, particularly in the aftermath of COVID-19 and amid growing economic difficulties, and served as a key reflection to define the way forward.
The review revealed a complex picture of both progress and persistent obstacles. While Lao PDR has made strides in some areas of child rights, the country continues to face substantial challenges. To mention a few: 
·         Economic Pressures and Budget Constraints: The persistent macroeconomic challenges in Lao PDR have had far-reaching effects across all sectors. Limited government budget allocations, exacerbated by high inflation, have constrained the sustainability and scalability of various programmes. This has led to shortages in essential resources, from nutrition commodities to education personnel, hampering service delivery and widening disparities in access to critical services for children.
·         Systemic Capacity Limitations: Across sectors, limited capacities, community-based structures, and cross-sectoral committees have posed significant challenges. Competing priorities and high staff turnover rates have led to delays and inefficiencies in programme implementation, affecting areas from health service delivery to child protection initiatives.
·         Environmental and Climate-related Disruptions: Severe flooding in 2024 highlighted the vulnerability of infrastructure and services to climate-related events. This affected multiple sectors, disrupting education, damaging WASH facilities, and exacerbating existing challenges in service delivery. This reaffirmed the need for a coherent children and climate action.
·         Social and Cultural Barriers: Engaging certain demographics, such as fathers and male caregivers in parenting programmes, has remained a persistent challenge. Cultural norms and practices have also influenced the uptake of various services, from nutrition interventions to child protection measures.
Thanks to the results of the Equity Analysis, the MTR highlighted how these challenges are particularly acute in certain population groups - such as those living in the rural areas, and certain ethnolinguistic communities, where access to quality services remains limited.
The lessons emerged during the review have allowed UNICEF to finetune its approach in several important ways. The most important are as follows: 
·         Increased focus on complementing policy and upstream work with service delivery and community engagement: UNICEF recognizes the need to prioritize support for service delivery in communities, acknowledging Lao PDR's limited capacity to implement multiple strategies simultaneously given its economic and financial context. While continuing to advocate for public finance for children, there has been an increased focus on practical aspects of policy and strategy implementation, strengthening duty bearers' capacities in complying with their mandate. 
·         Enhance Inclusion Efforts: Recognizing Lao PDR's diversity, UNICEF is tailoring responses to the specific needs of each ethnolinguistic family, as well as children with disabilities. This approach ensures that interventions are inclusive and effective in reaching all children, leaving no one behind. 
·         Better integrate Social and Behavior Change (SBC) as a Change Strategy: UNICEF aims to provide better technical support, leadership, and coordination for SBC initiatives within each sector. This will improve the measurement of impact and differentiation between communication/advocacy and community-based SBC strategies. 
·         Diversify Programme Implementation and Partnerships: Expanding collaborations with non-governmental actors such as Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), private sector, and academia is helping leverage specific technical knowledge, capacity on emerging topics, and local networks. This approach will enhance UNICEF's ability to address complex challenges and reach communities more effectively.
Based on the analysis of cross-sectoral issues, UNICEF Lao PDR has identified several sectoral priorities that will feed the 2025-2026 Work Plans (WPs) with the line ministries and partners. Four key cross-sectoral priorities that will be mainstreamed into those WPs are as follows:


Promote Gender Transformative Programming: UNICEF will focus on eliminating child marriage and other forms of gender-based violence, promoting adolescent girls' nutrition and     health, advancing girls' education and skills development, and integrating gender-responsive strategies across all programmes. This approach aims to transform gender power relations and build an enabling environment for gender equality. 
Support Digital Transformation: Recognizing Lao PDR as a 'digitally nascent' country, UNICEF will focus on creating opportunities for children to positively engage with digital     systems while avoiding negative consequences. This includes addressing policy gaps, improving data collection and monitoring systems, and enhancing digital service delivery across sectors. 
Mainstream Climate: UNICEF Lao PDR's Climate Strategy, 2024-2026 focuses on integrating climate considerations across all programming areas. This strategy emphasizes data-driven climate-responsive programming, prioritizes youth skills development and empowerment, promotes child-sensitive, gender-responsive, and risk-informed programmes to build resilience among communities. Additionally, UNICEF Lao PDR commits to "walking the talk" by     implementing Environmental and Social Safeguards alongside various greening initiatives in its own operations. 
Foster Youth Engagement: UNICEF Lao PDR will implement a comprehensive Youth Engagement Strategy focusing on empowering young people as agents of change. Through initiatives like Project Sinxay that supports 1000 Volunteer Advocates, UNICEF aims to integrate various youth engagement efforts, mobilizing youth across Lao PDR to engage in climate action, gender equality, and child rights advocacy. This approach will foster a new generation of leaders equipped to drive sustainable and equitable change in Lao PDR, placing youth engagement at the core of UNICEF's advocacy, programming, campaigning, and communication strategies.
 
This comprehensive outlook reflects UNICEF's commitment to continuous improvement, innovation, and responsiveness to the evolving context. What has made this review particularly significant was its timing — coming at a point when Lao PDR faces multiple challenges but also opportunities for transformation. The insights gained have helped shape UNICEF's 2025-2026 Rolling Work Plans, ensuring that its work remains relevant and effective in improving the lives of children across Lao PDR, and set the basis for the next Country Programme. By adopting this analytical and evidence-based approach, UNICEF Lao PDR demonstrates its added value to more effectively support duty bearers in addressing the complex, interrelated challenges facing children in the country.

Malaysia is today an upper-middle-income country with a per capita GDP of US$ 11,379.10 (2023).[1] Its impressive economic growth since independence has been accompanied by substantial development benefiting its population of 34.1 million (including 9.14 million children).[2] In 2024, political stability and a stronger fiscal outlook led to higher-than-expected economic growth, estimated at 4.9 per cent, and the ringgit appreciated by 14.9 per cent against the US dollar in the third quarter of 2024.[3] 
Malaysia has shown encouraging progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); however persistent inequities remain, affecting the country’s commitment to leave no child behind. Income inequality (GINI coefficient: 0.404 in 2022),[4] low female labour force participation (56.2 per cent, compared to 82.3 per cent for men),[5] and limited decision-making opportunities persist. Fluctuating oil prices and global inflationary pressures also contribute to these inequities. 
Hardcore poverty (SDG1), defined as households with monthly income less than RM1,169, has been virtually eliminated, and absolute poverty stands at 6.2 per cent (2022). However, poverty among households with children is estimated to be higher, at 8.7 per cent [6]. Moreover, Bumiputera and indigenous peoples in East Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak states) have higher poverty rates  at 8.0 per cent (SDG10), compared to other ethnic groups.
While overall child and infant mortality rates (SDG3) are almost at par with those in developed countries, and 95 per cent of households (SDG6) have access to electricity, water and sanitation, marginalized children (such as indigenous peoples of Peninsular Malaysia, known as Orang Asli, and those affected by migration) experience substantial disparities. Similarly, while primary and secondary school enrolment rates are nearly 100 per cent and 90 per cent respectively (SDG4), disparities remain. About 6.3 per cent of primary-age children in Sabah do not attend school, while only 42.3 per cent of Orang Asli children complete upper-secondary school.[7] Learning outcomes are poor: 42 per cent of  11-year-olds, and 61 per cent of children in the poorest quintile, lack proficiency in reading.[8] Although over 152,000 children were recorded in the government disability registration system in 2022, only a quarter of primary schools have adapted infrastructure.
Government efforts to ensure well-being, stability, and inclusion are guided by the Twelfth Malaysia Plan (12MP) and the Madani Economy Framework. The current administration has launched a series of reforms, including rationalization of subsidies, the launch of an integrated socioeconomic data hub, and legislative review of 3,000 outdated laws. 
Malaysia’s spending on the social sectors amounted to 32 per cent of government expenditure in 2023, and is expected to reach 7.8 per cent of GDP by 2025. [9] In 2025, approximately 8.9 per cent of the federal government budget is allocated to subsidies and cash assistance. The diesel subsidy rationalization in 2024 demonstrated a commitment to shifting from broad-based subsidies, with savings repurposed towards social protection. 
The social service sector is beset with challenges around data and fragmented programmes, resulting in gaps in coverage and poor alignment with lifecycle needs. Only 29 per cent of the population is served by a social protection floor, and under two per cent of children receive social assistance.[10] Undocumented people, including refugees, are excluded from social protection. Children affected by migration have limited access to basic services, including education and health, and are excluded from child protection services. As of September 2024, 2092 children were held in immigration depots nationwide.
Violence against children persists. According to the Department of Statistics, reports of sexual assault against children rose to 1,389 cases in 2023, an increase of 21.1 per cent from 1,147 in 2022.[2] One in every 25 children aged 12–17 years is subjected to online sexual exploitation and abuse annually.[11] In September 2024, shocking cases of abuse and exploitation of over 600 children in care institutions associated with Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings highlighted the urgent need for care reform, including a professional and well-supported social service workforce. At least 1,500 children, the overwhelming majority of them girls, are recorded as entering child marriage every year, although the actual figure is likely higher.[12]  
Malaysian children bear the triple burden of malnutrition (SDG2), with high rates of stunting (21.2 per cent) and anaemia (46.5 per cent) among children under five, and overweight and obesity (30.5 per cent) among adolescents aged 13–17. Six of ten Malaysians aged 15–40 experience depressive symptoms (SDG3). Symptoms are most prevalent amongst girls and indigenous people in Sabah.[13]
While Malaysia is considered relatively less vulnerable to climate change (ranking 52 out of 182 countries in terms of vulnerability and 54 out of 192 in terms of readiness),[14] flooding and heatwaves have become more frequent and intense. Data on children and climate are not systematically collected, but studies suggest that marginalized children, including undocumented and indigenous children, those with disabilities and those belonging to the poorest families are most vulnerable to climate shocks and environmental hazards.[15]

In 2024, UNICEF marked its 70th year of support for the rights of children in Malaysia. During the year, this longstanding partnership between UNICEF and the Government bore significant results, achieved through policy change, evidence generation as well as piloting and modelling innovative interventions to address the specific needs of children, particularly the most marginalized.
Strengthening policy frameworks and advocating for children and families
In 2024, UNICEF drew on robust evidence, provided technical support rooted in global expertise, amplified the voices of rights-holders, advocated with government and the public and strengthened systems to ensure no child is left behind.
In 2024, the Ministry of Women, Family, and Community Development (MWFCD) launched the National Child Policy, developed with UNICEF support in 2023. The policy aims to protect children from violence, exploitation and neglect; ensure holistic development and foster meaningful participation. The MWFCD is now drafting the costed National Plan of Action to implement the policy and its monitoring and evaluation framework with support from UNICEF.
UNICEF played a crucial role in supporting the implementation and reporting of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in Malaysia. Following on the government’s submission of the second report to the CRC Committee (combined 2nd–5th Periodic Report) in 2021, and in preparation for government participation in the Session with the Committee in 2025, UNICEF provided training and technical support to 32 civil society organizations (CSOs). This ensured that the CSO and children’s reports complemented the state report, highlighted areas where significant legal and policy reforms are needed and offered a more complete picture of the CRC’s implementation.
With UNICEF’s technical support, the Legal Affairs Division substantially amended the Evidence of Child Witness Act, which aims to reduce the trauma experienced by child victims and witnesses in court by ensuring that their evidence is treated on par with that of adults and that they are presumed competent to testify. This was an important step in implementing the recommendations of the Parliamentary Special Select Committee on Women, Children and Community Development around creating child-friendly judicial processes.
Building on the success of the 2023 Heroes Amongst Us campaign in enhancing public and parliamentarian awareness of the need to enact the Social Work Profession Bill, UNICEF supported a knowledge-sharing visit to the Philippines by government and CSO partners. The officials then jointly prepared policy briefs advocating for the professionalization of the social service workforce and informing the development of the bill. In partnership with the Malaysian Association of Social Workers (MASW), UNICEF also supported capacity development for the Children’s Development Department and continued to advocate for the enactment of the draft social work profession bill, which is expected to be tabled in 2025. UNICEF developed and facilitated the finalization of a foundational training curriculum for the Child Protection Officers in the Children’s Development Department in preparation for the passage of the bill.
As a key partner of the Ministry of Health (MOH) in addressing nutrition challenges, UNICEF supported the initiation of a comprehensive evaluation of the National Plan of Action for Nutrition by the MOH and ensured the plan’s strategies and outcomes were vigorously assessed. The evaluation will result in evidence-based recommendations to inform the next plan, strengthen policy frameworks to promote healthier food environments, and identify promising areas of collaboration in UNICEF’s new country programme. 
A series of legal analyses, desk reviews, and cost-benefit analyses, supported by UNICEF informed the framework of a Nutrition Bill, which was explicated in a cabinet paper tabled by the MOH at the end of 2024. UNICEF provided technical inputs for advocacy to incorporate obesity prevention in primary schools, prohibit unethical marketing of breastmilk substitutes, and introduce Nutri-grade labelling. 
UNICEF built capacity and developed systems to incorporate the needs and perspectives of children and young people at every stage of development, implementation and evaluation of policies and programmes affecting them. As Malaysia began developing its first National Adaptation Plan (MyNAP) and updated its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 to climate change action, UNICEF ensured that these were child-sensitive and responded to the voices of young people. UNICEF also successfully advocated for the establishment of a Youth Cluster within the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability (MNRES) and supported training of trainers on child-sensitive climate policies. A total of 361 children and youth participated in 15 focus group discussions nationwide, while 172 youth leaders engaged in high-level discussions with policymakers, including the MNRES minister, at the Youth Climate Adaptation Forum.
Building upon legislative amendments enacted in December 2023, which empowered the Office of the Children’s Commissioner (OCC) to address child rights, complaints, and develop effective child participation mechanisms, UNICEF, the OCC and the Social Welfare Department supported 55 adolescents (51 per cent girls) to participate in a Symposium to Empower Children’s Commissions and thus inform the OCC’s reform agenda.
The National Baseline Assessment on Business and Human Rights, supported by UNICEF to uphold children’s rights in the context of labour, environment, and governance, and submitted to the Government in 2023, was signed off and released by the Law Minister in 2024 after a full government review. The assessment provides recommendations for a National Action Plan on Business and Human Rights, to be adopted in 2025. UNICEF trained 14 labour regulators on family-friendly policies as part of advocacy efforts to foster support for the adaption of the plan.
UNICEF contributed to the joint UN consultation on the inclusion of business and human rights as a UN priority in cooperation with the federal government. With UNICEF support, two Malaysian youth advocates attended the UN Forum on Business and Human Rights in Geneva and articulated youth perspectives on climate, just transition, and access to justice, helping shape the CRC’s General Comment No. 27. 
Building evidence on the situation of children 
The office employed evidence generation as a core change strategy, contributing to significant progress towards results in 2024. Using internally generated evidence pieces, UNICEF advanced the basis to support the children’s agenda. For example, an evaluation of the country programme based on extensive consultations with government, CSOs, children and young people found that UNICEF’s work was highly relevant and effective in meeting children’s needs, particularly on policy and legislative changes, but pointed to the need to ensure sustainability of interventions. This evaluation drew out rich lessons learned to inform the development of the new CPD. In addition, UNICEF developed five thematic briefs and evidence syntheses for 17 child rights sub-dimensions to aid in prioritization during the development of the new CPD. 
In 2024, UNICEF used evidence generated in-house for effective policy advocacy leading to change. The office commissioned the 2024 Living on the Edge study which provided evidence on the vulnerabilities experienced by children living in urban poverty in the capital, Kuala Lumpur (KL), particularly those with intersecting forms of marginalization, such as living in households headed by women or persons with disabilities. The advocacy and communication campaign accompanying this ground-breaking study received wide media and online coverage (over 100 articles and TV/radio spots; 3.3 million TikTok views), and questions were raised in Parliament regarding its findings on nutrition. UNICEF seized this opportunity to organize the Second Regional Social Policy Forum in Sarawak, bringing over 250 participants from 14 countries to discuss best practices in inclusive, shock-responsive social protection systems. 
As a result of UNICEF’s advocacy, the Ministry of Finance allocated 5 million ringgit (US$ 1.12 million) in the 2025 budget towards a Cash-Plus pilot for urban families in KL low-income housing to tackle poverty and malnutrition. Additionally, two models focusing on the first 1,000 days and adolescence were co-designed with the Sarawak Ministry of Women. The three models will be rolled out in 2025, with options for national scale-up. 
The office also enhanced its capacity to analyse and engage with public budgets to better advocate for social services for children. In 2024, this led to a fiscal space analysis for a social protection floor for children, enabling this key policy recommendation to be costed. UNICEF prepared the first budget briefs for Malaysia, focusing on education and the social sector, yielding clear findings on the adequacy and efficiency of spending to guide advocacy in the coming years.
UNICEF commissioned a joint study with the Legal Affairs Division of the Prime Minister’s Department on the challenges faced by children subject to sexual abuse when navigating the justice system. The report informed the Evidence of Child Witness Act to enable a child-sensitive system for children. To improve equitable learning outcomes, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MOE) in implementing the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEAPLM) survey involving 4,574 students, 1,944 teachers and 40 MOE officials, enhancing longitudinal understanding of learning loss and recovery efforts. 
Modelling innovation to advance the rights of children
In 2024, UNICEF conducted innovative pilots, with robust monitoring and evaluation, to provide evidence-based measures to advance children’s rights to health, nutrition, and learning, including for children with disabilities and those from indigenous communities. 
The Child-Friendly City Initiative (CFCI) model amplifies the voices of children in local decision-making and increases focus on children in local policy frameworks and budgeting. Building on Petaling Jaya as the regional pioneer of CFCI, in 2024 UNICEF generated evidence to underpin an action plan for a localized Malaysian CFCI model. Eight cities signed memoranda of understanding to become child-friendly cities, with 20 more expressing interest. The seven cities in Sarawak that signed memoranda of understanding conducted situation analyses to provide evidence on the situation of urban children. With UNICEF support, children in Sarawak participated in workshops on using photography to amplify their messages, received training on interviewing, and engaged in a media takeover on World Children’s Day, interviewing policymakers on state priorities for children. This empowered children to meaningfully partake in decision-making, while strengthening local authorities’ capacity and motivation to include children in decision-making processes. As a result, four children’s councils were established, with selection mechanisms that ensured inclusion and diversity. 
MOH child growth initiatives saw important advances as UNICEF designed and implemented pilots that measurably improved children’s nutrition and growth outcomes. These included Cara Hidup Anda Terbaik (C-HAT), a school-based obesity intervention piloted by the MOH in partnership with UNICEF. C-HAT integrated health education and lifestyle promotion into the primary school curriculum in 49 schools, equipping 2,346 children aged 10–12 years with high BMI with lifelong habits to combat obesity and overweight. Of these children, 65.8 per cent achieved their weight status targets within six months, and depression, stress and anxiety levels also declined. This provided the evidence for UNICEF advocacy with the MOH and MOE to integrate the programme into the national programme (known as 3K) to improve the cleanliness, health and safety of school environments.
UNICEF continued to leverage its commitment to equity and intersectionality and enhanced the MOE’s DELIMa learning platform through Future Skills for All (FS4A), an inclusive approach to teaching digital skills. In 2024, UNICEF built on its prior support for the design of online and offline FS4A materials to scale it up in Sarawak and north and east Peninsular Malaysia. A total of 43,838 children (57 per cent girls) and 3,721 teachers gained programming skills through online FS4A courses with sign-language and accessibility features, in-person workshops and gamified offline kits. Additionally, 84 teachers from the MOE Special Education Division were trained to support 3,879 children with disabilities, and to create communities of practice in their schools to cascade their learning. FS4A also facilitated 316 indigenous schoolchildren aged 13–15 years in Sarawak to implement 79 projects fostering creativity, agency, and alignment with the SDGs and the state’s Post-COVID Development Strategy. Following an impact analysis showing significant improvements in digital literacy, this evidence formed the basis of a strategic partnership with Google, CelcomDigi, MDEC, Arus and the MOE to bring FS4A to low-income communities in Selangor state, and train teachers to equip 61,000 children with future skills. To date, the FS4A portal has acquired over 1.67 million page-views (350,000 in 2024 alone) and 223,598 unique users. 
UNICEF also introduced and strengthened digital tools and localized global toolkits to support children and adolescents in learning, receiving psychosocial support and essential life skills. With UNICEF support, the MOE further integrated AI into its early warning system for school dropouts using data for 2016–2023. This enabled the MOE to use machine learning to conduct multi-year predictive analyses that strengthened its ability to assess drop-out risks for Malaysia’s 5 million schoolchildren, and to identify interventions for schools with high drop-out rates. Through strategic collaboration with the MOE and the Ministry of Finance, and equity-focused evidence-based advocacy, the early-warning approach was integrated into the national Anak Kita programme, which was allocated RM 30 million (US$ 6.72 million) in the 2025 budget. It was also designated a key pillar of regional education programmes during Malaysia’s chairmanship of ASEAN in 2025.
Over 10,000 schoolchildren enhanced their resilience to disaster through a pilot of disaster risk reduction (DRR) in schools led by UNICEF, in collaboration with the MOE and the National Disaster Management Agency. UNICEF developed interactive educational materials, including activity booklets, board games and toolkits, to strengthen children’s understanding of DRR and trained 120 teachers and 70 state and district education officials to support the rollout of this intervention. With UNICEF, Malaysia showcased its commitment to empowering children as agents of change for DRR at the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on DRR.
In partnership with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF supported the translation and localization of Helping Adolescents Thrive tools, in consultation with 40 mental health experts from government, CSOs and 23 adolescents representing urban, rural, and disability groups. A teachers’ guide to provide adolescents with mental health and psychosocial support was launched, using the contextualised characters of Mei and Friends on World Mental Health Day in partnership with the National Centre of Excellence for Mental Health (NCEMH). With the rollout of the tools in 2025, about 300 student teachers  in-training will be  capacitated and close to 10,000 adolescents will have improved access to psychosocial support at school.
Key enablers and fundraising
In 2024, UNICEF operations were strengthened to enable accountable, transparent and efficient programming through agile systems that respond effectively to change. These included embedding sustainability requirements into procurement, and investments in training for supervisors to develop a dynamic and inclusive organizational culture. Trainings on the Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT) were provided to all government and CSO implementing partners, mitigating financial risks. UNICEF reviewed its technology for development initiatives to ensure that they comply with its information management policies, with a particular focus on protecting children's data.
UNICEF increased its brand audience by 41 per cent in 2024 – an important achievement in a self-funded office. A strategic decision to launch the office on LinkedIn expanded its reach with 1,211 new followers. Leveraging growing interest in local youth-centred content, UNICEF increased website engagement by 32 per cent, which was driven by youth takeovers that amplified children’s voices through dynamic reels, articles and videos featuring UNICEF national ambassador Lisa Surihani, UNICEF staff and key supporters. These broadened UNICEF’s digital footprint and increased awareness of child rights.
UNICEF Malaysia is a unique hybrid programme/fundraising office, ranking second in fundraising globally. In 2024 it took steps to diversify its face-to-face (F2F) fundraising operations by appointing two new F2F agencies. In 2024, the office raised 101.4 million ringgit (US$ 22.2 million), a 5.5 per cent growth compared to 2023. All funding for the country programme comes from generous donations from Malaysians. This unique funding model provides UNICEF Malaysia with flexibility and enables a swift and responsive approach to addressing the evolving needs of children across the country.

Multi-stakeholder partnerships with the government, CSOs, private sector, and young people were the foundation of results achieved in 2024. As UNICEF sets the direction of its cooperation with the Government of Malaysia, partnerships remain critical to envisioning and realizing a better future for children. 
UNICEF entered partnerships with United Nations agencies which drew on the competitive advantages of individual agencies to amplify results. Working with UNHCR, IOM, OCC, and civil society partners, UNICEF advocated for protection of children affected by migration, coordinated a working group to advocate for community-based alternatives to immigration detention for children, and arranged a South-South study visit to observe successful models in Thailand. Through a joint programme with WHO, UNICEF supported NCEMH in localizing the Helping Adolescents Thrive tools and developed a monitoring and evaluation framework for a data-driven approach to youth mental health, aligned with the National Strategic Plan for Mental Health 2020–2025. Over 8,900 youth benefited from the UNDP-UNICEF Youth Environment Living Labs partnership, which provided seed funding for eight climate change projects, developed 17 innovative tools, and showcased young climate champions at COP29.
As a member of the UN team in Malaysia, UNICEF supported the development of the new UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Leading the Inclusive Social Development and Wellbeing pillar, UNICEF kept children at the heart of UN action and advocacy in Malaysia.
UNICEF’s close partnerships with government bodies enabled successful evidence generation and advocacy and built technical capacity. These partnerships empowered key ministries, such as the MWFCD, to build policy frameworks, make services more equitable and to work towards systemic change. Major partnerships in implementation throughout the year led to enhanced programme coordination and evidence generation with key line ministries at the national level and local government partners in Sarawak and Sabah (EPU and UPEN respectively). 
As a trusted partner and thought leader, UNICEF was invited to join, contribute and technically assist the steering committee on the National Strategic Plan in Handling the Causes of Child Marriage 2021–2025 and contribute to its mid-term review. UNICEF was also invited to provide technical assistance to the National Strategic Dialogue on SDG4 (education). UNICEF participated in high-level consultations for the Malaysia Education Blueprint 2026–2035 and successfully argued for incorporating pre-primary education into compulsory education requirement; investments in foundational learning, system resilience and future skills; and ensuring young people’s voices are considered in education sector plans. 
Using its convening power UNICEF brought young people into partnerships with decision-makers, ensured their voices were heard, and empowered them to solve issues that matter to them. For example, UNICEF strengthened climate action by youth groups and Youth Cluster members, providing seed grants and capacity-building. Nearly 17,000 children and youth (56 per cent girls) engaged in climate and environmental action, while 92 participated in city decision-making through children’s councils. 
Sub-national governments in Sabah and Sarawak partnered in strengthening systems locally, such as the rollout of CFCI and expanding the reach of FS4A to indigenous schoolchildren in Sarawak and Sabah, UNICEF collaborated with the Resident Coordinator’s Office to generate evidence on education in the context of migration. This resulted in a series of papers on education for undocumented children and strategic engagements with 80 government stakeholders, SUHAKAM and CSO partners. UNICEF also partnered with ILO, European Union, and Project Liber8 to address child labour on Sabah oil palm plantations and co-designed a media fellowship programme to increase public awareness of child rights (to be launched in 2025). UNICEF and the Sabah Jurisdictional Approach for Sustainable Palm Oil convened grassroots actors (farmers, palm oil companies, CSOs) to build their capacity to address root causes and devise solutions for a roadmap towards eradicating child labour.
UNICEF empowered and capacitated CSOs to advocate effectively and complement government services for children. In 2024 UNICEF conducted a workshop to build capacity on strategic advocacy of organizations led by women and girls and persons with disabilities, as well as UNFPA and UNHCR. The organizations used this training to develop collaborative advocacy strategies and advocate effectively for addressing child marriage and strengthening early intervention for children with disabilities. For example, Sabah authorities tabled a paper on a minimum age of child marriage in customary law, largely through CSO-led advocacy.
Partnerships with the Childline Foundation supported young people to participate meaningfully in upholding child rights by developing the CRC children’s report and participating in the Young Persons’ Advisory Group. Through collaboration with Project ID, the Kita Connect programme capacitated 1,906 young people (56 per cent girls) to lead civic engagement on the SDGs. 
Its partnerships with CSOs were critical for UNICEF to address the exclusion of marginalized groups. For example, UNICEF collaborated with the Malaysian Federation of the Deaf to develop learning materials with sign language interpretation so children with hearing impairments could access digital training through FS4A. Through its partnership with HOST International, UNICEF supported 115 children affected by migration (63 per cent girls) to access case management services. UNICEF also worked with Justice for Wildlife Malaysia to develop content in support of environmental journalism.
UNICEF seized the opportunity of its 70th year in Malaysia to enhance public support for child rights through the Bersama Malaysia communication campaign. On World Children’s Day, UNICEF convened over 200 high-level representatives (government, business, diplomats) and 108 children, and engaged them in dialogue on digital transformation. Positioning this discussion at a major media event solidified existing partnerships, amplified children’s voices and enhanced UNICEF’s position as a brand leader advocating for children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
As the office approached the end of its CPD (2022–2025), preparations accelerated for an equity-focused and inclusive successor programme that leverages UNICEF’s competitive advantages and close collaboration with government to uphold children’s rights. This entailed a thorough external evaluation of the current CPD to identify successes and strategic-level course corrections, and stakeholder consultations with government partners, CSOs, business representatives, the media and 43 children and young people from diverse backgrounds.
The reflective process pointed to a need for UNICEF to shift from a traditional role as implementer towards becoming a thought and knowledge leader on children’s rights. This requires expertise in evidence generation and child rights monitoring, strategic partnership development, and an effective advocacy strategy to influence decision-makers. UNICEF results in 2024 confirm the validity of this approach. For example, the Living on the Edge report created momentum for UNICEF advocacy for a universal child grant and its findings were cited in the 2025 Budget speech. 
Advocacy, evidence-generation, and high-level engagement for the enactment of the Social Work Profession Bill have led to the bill being expected to be tabled in 2025. Going forward, UNICEF will develop an evidence-based investment case and resource mobilization plan to continue advocating for sustainable social sector workforce reforms.
Close partnerships with the government have been vital for advancing child rights, with UNICEF and the Ministry of Economy enhancing coordination through annual reviews and quarterly meetings to improve alignment, accountability, and timely resolution of bottlenecks. Building on this approach, UNICEF will strengthen its collaboration with the Ministry of Finance in 2025 through quarterly technical meetings on Public Finance for Children.
A key strategic shift was to increase complementarity with the 12MP and to shift programmatic focus towards East Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak) – where poverty is higher than in Peninsular Malaysia – to address regional disparities and for subsequent nationwide uptake. While initiated in 2023, collaborations with national and state-level actors led to key results in 2024, such as the government’s decision to fund and launch a pilot social protection programme in Sarawak. This demonstrated that productive partnerships focusing on specific states can lead to rapid systems strengthening and address geographical disparities. 
To take systems strengthening forward in Sabah, UNICEF will complete the Sabah Child Well Being Index and implement the inaugural 2024–2025 Sabah Action Plan (co-developed with state ministries) to strategically coordinate programming for children. 
The introduction and rapid expansion of CFCI increased focus on children in local-level policy frameworks and budgets, especially when supported by capacity development on engaging children in decision-making... This is particularly crucial given the high degree of urbanization – and urban deprivation – experienced by children in Malaysia. Going forward, UNICEF will take this as an opportunity to create safe, stimulating environments that meet diverse needs among large and concentrated populations.
The success of CFCI and the culture change it catalysed in local-level decision-making has validated UNICEF’s approach to supporting children and young people to voice their concerns, make decisions and act on the issues that concern them and their future. This was underscored in 2024 when children and youth who developed an alternative report to the CRC recommended that UNICEF foster positive behavioural change that values children’s opinions, ensure children’s voices are represented in legislative processes, provide child rights education for all age groups, allocate resources for youth participation in government programmes and create inclusive platforms where children can speak out. Moving forward, UNICEF will continue to fulfil young people’s demands, advocate for their rights and ensure they are empowered in decisions about their needs.
In 2024, UNICEF laid the groundwork for the introduction and regional scale-up of the Healthy Centralized Kitchen (HCK) pilot to improve nutrition and promote healthy nutritional habits. The pilot is scheduled to launch in 2025 targeting children aged 2–4 years within the childcare system. 
Through benchmarking with other countries and enabling policymakers to draw insights and best practices, UNICEF showcased international comparators and created opportunities to promote understanding of child rights issues. UNICEF support for study tours and attendance at forums in China (on CFCI), Japan (on HCK), the Philippines (DRR and social work professionalization), Thailand (shock-responsive social protection and alternatives to detention) and Finland (education innovation), and hosting the Regional Social Protection Forum in Sarawak, were key to building policymaker awareness and ownership of evidence-based solutions. As Malaysia takes up its role as ASEAN Chair in 2025, UNICEF will support continued international learning to advance child rights, within the country and regionally.
Key aspects of UNICEF’s approach to inclusion were validated in 2024. First, grouping elements of social inclusion for adolescents (gender, disability, mental health) into a cluster enhanced recognition of the salience of these issues among duty-bearers. Second, the twin-track approach of building inclusive policy frameworks benefiting all children, while developing tailored interventions targeting specific groups, was validated by take-up of CFCI in Sarawak and capacity development for children to participate in decision-making. 
In 2025, Malaysia’s ASEAN chairmanship, the 100th CRC session, and the development of the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan (13MP) offer opportunities for UNICEF to build on progress in 2024 to accelerate results. In particular, 13MP offers significant opportunities due to its focus on driving economic and industrial growth, closing regional development gaps, and fulfilling citizen welfare aspirations, in order to ensure well-being, stability, and inclusion. Moreover, the theme of “Inclusivity and Sustainability” for the ASEAN chairmanship, and the commitment to work towards narrowing development gaps and inequalities, improving living standards and mitigating climate change impacts, offer opportunities in Malaysia and the broader region.
UNICEF will seize these opportunities in the final year of the current CPD, and moving forward into its successor agreement, by continuing to generate rigorous evidence, monitor child rights, convene stakeholders, amplify youth voices, and vigorously advocate to support Malaysia in achieving its development goals and realizing the rights of all children.

Mongolia’s economic growth has elevated the country to upper-middle-income status in 2024. This transition marks a significant milestone, with GDP reaching 70.4 trillion MNT (20.6 billion USD) in 2023—a 30.8 per cent increase from the previous year[1]. Economic growth slowed to 5.3 per cent in 2024 due to reduced global demand for coal and slower mining output[2]. Human development progress has partly been enabled through economic growth. Between 2009 and 2023, GDP per capita rose from $1,718 to $4,040. The country’s Human Development Index (HDI) stood at 0.741 (2022), one of the highest in the region, but persistent inequalities in access to social services and regional disparities remain critical challenges[3]. These are compounded by vulnerabilities to external shocks and climate change.
As of 2023, Mongolia’s population was 3.504 million, including 1.282 million children, nearly half of whom reside in Ulaanbaatar[4]. Poverty remains entrenched, with 27.1 per cent of the population living below the poverty line and 41.2 per cent at rural areas in the countryside compared to 21.6 per cent in Ulaanbaatar[5].
The political landscape in 2024 was marked by heightened tensions surrounding the electoral cycle and the implementation of constitutional reform in 2023. Parliamentary elections held in June 2024, coinciding with increasing public demand for political accountability and transparency. The constitutional reforms, introducing a mixed electoral system and gender quotas, increased inclusiveness in governance, resulting in 32 women being elected to the 126 members at the Parliament, raising female representation to 22 per cent[6]. 
The fiscal framework has undergone significant changes in 2024. The government implemented measures to support the social sector. Total current expenditures reached 22.4 trillion MNT in 2024, marking a 29.9 per cent increase over the previous year. Key allocations included salary increments for public sector employees and social welfare allowances ranging from 10 per cent to 40 per cent and pension increases of 100,000 MNT starting April 2024 (Ministry of Finance, 2024 Budget Execution Report). However, with increased demand of budget accountability among Parliamentarians, the President put embargo on the expansionary 2025 approved budget that pressured Parliament to amend  budget without a deficit. The revised 2025 budget constraining resources for social sectors, placing strain on increasing cost of social service and adequacy. 
The 2023 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS)[7], launched in 2024 shed light on disparities affecting children. Malnutrition among children under five has worsened, with wasting tripling to 2.7 per cent since 2018, while early childhood development indicators declined, particularly in rural areas. Educational disparities are stark, with one-third of children failing to meet minimum proficiency in reading and mathematics. Violence against children is pervasive, affecting 44.2 per cent of the population under 18. Environmental challenges further exacerbate vulnerabilities. Only 30.6 per cent of the population has access to safely managed drinking water, and dzud conditions during the winter of 2023-2024 impacted 150,500 people, including 62,500 children[8].
Challenges in the education sector persist, with 6 per cent of upper secondary school-age children out of school and 17.6 per cent of youth neither in education nor employment[9].
Healthcare remains inequitable, particularly in rural where 36.5 per cent of residents lack health insurance[10] . Rising costs for medicine and limited social protection exacerbate these inequalities. While healthcare reforms have shifted to output-based financing, urban hospitals are overburdened and rural facilities remain under pressure of resources[11]. Efforts to increase coverage and address accessibilities are in high pressure.
Air pollution remains a critical concern, especially in Ulaanbaatar, where levels far exceed safe thresholds, posing significant health risks to children[12]. Poorly planned urban areas are increasingly vulnerable to floods and other climate shocks.
Following the 2024 elections, the Government of Mongolia has prioritized a family-centred approach as a cornerstone of its 2024–2028 Action Plan, reflected in the renaming of the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection to the Ministry of Family, Labour, and Social Protection. This strategic shift aligns with UNICEF's emphasis on enhancing equity for children through integrated social protection systems that address socio-economic and geographic disparities, thereby advancing child rights and well-being. Social spending remains a priority, with pensions, allowances, and subsidies comprising 59.4 per cent of total current expenditures in 2024, according to the 2024 Budget Execution Report. These allocations highlight efforts to stabilize household incomes and expand access to essential services. In line with its "Vision-2050" and "New Revival Policy," the government has declared 2024 as the "Year of Regional Development Support," aiming to promote balanced urban and rural growth, which could positively impact children by addressing regional disparities and improving access to essential services in underserved areas. Mongolia is advancing and set objectives on digital governance[1] by streamlining services and digitalizing public services for improved citizen access and engagement which implicating on data and evidence as well as transparent social services.
Despite these measures, fiscal pressures remain a concern. Inflation is projected to exceed 6.5 per cent in 2024, while public debt limits fiscal space for additional social sector investments[13]. UNICEF emphasizes the need for improved public finance for children, advocating for better planning and accountability in budget allocations to track. Investments in early childhood development and early childhood education, nutrition programs, child and social protection systems remain crucial to addressing disparities and safeguarding children’s rights.
UNICEF’s engagement in Mongolia remains focused on evidence-based advocacy and capacity-building. MICS 2023 data underpins its efforts to address malnutrition, education gaps, and violence against children through targeted policy reforms. UNICEF started working with each Local governor’s offices to enhance service delivery in rural areas, leveraging interventions to reduce rural-urban disparities reaching every child furthest behind.
Mongolia’s transition to upper-middle-income status brings opportunities for sustainable development but also highlights persistent inequalities and challenges. UNICEF’s strategic focus on reducing disparities, enhancing resilience, and advocating for equitable policies aligns with Mongolia’s commitment to leaving no child behind.
