Guided by the principles of equity, gender equality, resilience and sustainability, in 2024, UNICEF Mongolia Country office has contributed to the Mongolia Vision 2050 policy in meeting its commitment to respect, protect and fulfil children’s rights in line with the national and international obligations. 

2024 is the second year of the  Country Programme. The Office continued to focus on the five outcome areas of  the UNICEF Strategic Plan, supported by a Programme and Operations  Effectiveness outcomes. 
  
In 2024, the programme was  able to operate nationwide with shift from a geographically focused approach  to a universal one by implementing workplans with all 21 provincial  Governments and Ulaanbaatar city Mayor’s Office to tackle geographic  disparities on the ground and leveraging local human and financial resources  as well as provincial alliances to scale up results.
  
Outcome 1: Health,  nutrition, and development (HND)
  
HND outcome made strides  towards strengthened systems, through integration of more numbers of  age-appropriate, gender-sensitive services to meet diverse needs of  population groups. Highlights include school-based HPV vaccination reached 10,904  girls and 9,531 boys that constitute 25 per cent of the eligible age children  as of 13th January, 2025 since its launch, health monitoring &  nutrition services, and community-based development screening, with digitally  enabled referral and treatment services. The revised Maternal and Child  Health book readily available at primary health centres (PHC), as the  community-based record with references to PHC services, has now expanded in  its scope with more aspects of child health, nutrition and development, and  it further expanded in its usability with cross-sector references,  facilitated through a whole ecosystem of interoperable apps and digital  services. UNICEF bridged the gap between Ministry of Health and Digital  development and communication by including E-Health in E-Mongolia system  which is one stop data shop for the 3,5 million people.  
  
The second main strategy to  achieve high coverage with maximum efficiency is to offer health promotion,  health monitoring and referral services at schools, considering its high  attendance rates. School-based services offer good continuum of care, following  community and PHC based services for 0–5-year-old children, covering  6–18-year-old children with broad spectrum of health, nutrition and  development services, such as school-based Td and HPV vaccination for 7, 11,  15-year-old, and health monitoring for 6, 10, 14 year-old, and school lunch  programme for 6-11 year old. Age-appropriate services of oral hygiene,  nutritional counselling, promotion of physical activity and life skills based  SRH education services offered for the respective grades. UNICEF advocacy led  to the 66 per cent increase in school meal program budgetc.
  
Further to improve healthcare  efficiency and to prevent service disruptions, IPC breach, UNICEF has  supported solar electrification of health facilities (10), introduction and  integration of green technologies of healthcare waste management (51) and  completed medical gas piping and construction of oxygen plant houses (5).
  
Outcome 2: Education
  
UNICEF's digitally integrated  alternative pre-primary and primary education initiatives provided over  80,000 children with education, enhancing foundational skills. Advocacy  expanded public-private partnerships, boosting resource mobilization and  cost-sharing. Evidence-based policymaking was further supported through  studies on critical educational topics, strengthening responses to key  challenges in the sector.
  
UNICEF has played a pivotal  role in fostering partnerships between educational institutions and  governments, expanding access to quality Early Childhood Education (ECE)  across remote regions. Notable initiatives include the "Teacher with a  Tablet" program, which provides digital ECE services to children aged  2-5 in 192 rural communities, benefiting over 5,400 children and training  preschool teachers in tablet-assisted learning, promoting innovative, and  home-based education.
  
Training initiatives such as  "ECE Accelerator Toolkits" and "Efficient Implementation of  Child Protection Policy" have equipped 815 practitioners and 4,385  parents, fostering child-friendly environments and nutritious meals in 109  kindergartens. These programs, driven by multi-sectoral partnerships, have  reached 22,740 children, including children with disabilities.
  
UNICEF supported the revision  of the national pre-primary and primary curriculum, aligning it with  contemporary challenges such as climate change and digital transformation.  This updated curriculum emphasizes foundational learning, holistic  development, and the preparation of children for lifelong learning, ensuring  they acquire the necessary skills, values, and knowledge to thrive in an  evolving world. The national curriculum revision addressed key contemporary  educational challenges such as digital transformation, inclusive practices  for diverse learners, education for sustainability and climate change,  tackling educational disparities, promoting student mental health, and reducing  school-based violence.
  
UNICEF's "Let's Learn  Together" initiative benefited over 2,476 children in grades 3-5,  including those in remote and disadvantaged communities, improving reading  skills from 64 per cent to 81 per cent. The initiative was implemented during  the 2023-2024 academic year and as part of a Summer Education program.
  
UNICEF contributed to  generating data on critical educational topics, such as emergency  preparedness in the education sector, to ensure evidence-based policymaking,  particularly regarding continuity of learning during harsh winters and  students' learning recovery after prolonged absences. Furthermore, 1,422  children benefited from improved, inclusive, and safe learning environments  through the renovation of damaged outdoor areas.
  
UNICEF has significantly  advanced digital learning in Mongolia’s primary education sector, creating 25  interactive Mathematics content for grades 1-2, now publicly available on  Medle.mn. These resources have attracted 70,000 users and generated 312,000 engagements.  With this, all curricula content for 1st and 2nd grades' Mathematics and  Mongolian language have now been converted into interactive lessons, marking  a significant milestone in providing comprehensive digital resource. To  address challenges faced by remote herder families during harsh winters,  UNICEF distributed 2,200 custom audio players with educational content to  children across nine provinces. A new initiative, "Girls Code"  summer bootcamp, has been piloted for potential scale up supporting 30 girls  with coding, STEM, and English skills. A Digital Community Information  Workers (DCIWs) initiative was launched, training 80 teachers and public  officials to troubleshoot connectivity issues and teach digital skills. As a  result, 757 schools, as compared to 670 schools in early 2024, were supported  with improved connectivity, through the Daily Check App, covering 89 per cent  of schools nationwide.
  
Outcome 3: Child  protection
  
UNICEF continued to support  the stakeholders in strengthening the child protection system by focusing on  specific system components and addressing barriers and bottleneck that  include insufficient resource allocation for prevention and response  services, lack of means to ensure public expenditure tracking for child  protection, and unavailability of independent oversight mechanism, lack of  data to inform policy and public investment. 
  
Based on UNICEF previous  evaluation, supports and advocacy, a new child protection law was developed  and approved in January 2024.
  
UNICEF and Government joint  efforts resulted in improved policy framework, increased public financing for  services, in independent oversight mechanism and in strengthened admin data  for child protection. Accordingly, Mongolia has reached the stage of system  integration from system enhancement as scored by  UNICEF’s maturity assessment for a country  child protection system. 
  
Major amendments were approved  in the Law on Child Protection in January 2024 where the child protection  system, its key elements and links to other systems including health,  justice, and education ¿are clearly defined. UNICEF further supported  development of 13 SOPs and standards for different types of child protection  services for enforcement of this Law including national standards of response  and rehabilitation services for child victims of sexual abuse..  
  
Joint UNICEF and Government  efforts resulted in an increase of budget allocation for child protection  services for 2025, from MNT14.0 bln (USD 4.1 mln) in 2024 to MNT20.9 bln (USD  5.5mln). From 2025, 833 additional social workers will be recruited by the  Government - 1 social worker focused on child protection and families for  every soum and khoroo. This significant expansion of the workforce follows  the 2024 revision of the Law supported by UNICEF.  
  
UNICEF advocated for a  performance audit with purpose to establish an independent oversight  mechanism and a quality assurance process to improve practice and the quality  of the service provided to children in need of care and protection.  Accordingly, an independent review was undertaken by the National Audit  Office (NAO) to oversee implementation of the laws and policies by assessing  operations of relevant government agencies with roles for child protection,  and service providers for adherence to child protection minimum standards.  This is the first ever national audit on child protection by an independent  body like the NAO. The report was submitted to the relevant Parliamentary  Standing Committees. Its findings will help the parliament hold the  government accountable for its use of public resources and for policy  changes. 
  
UNICEF also advocated for  strengthening the social service workforce for child protection by addressing  some of the bottlenecks including absence of normative framework for social  work. UNICEF supported the development of a draft Law on Social Work -d with  aims to establish the legal basis for the social work practice system and its  function, legal status of, professional ethics of, and professional liability  system for social workers, and licensure for practice.
  
Over 11,529  children *4,620 boys and 6,909 girls) who  have experienced violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect have been reached  by health, social work and justice/law enforcement services through UNICEF  supported programmes including trainings of senior social workers from all  provinces who are mandated to provide professional guidance and supervision  to social workers of 725 community multidisciplinary teams and staff of  protection shelters. 
  
Outcome 4: Water,  sanitation, hygiene and climate change 
  
The Cooking, Heating,  and Insulation Product innovation that was developed to reduce indoor air  pollution received the Golden Rose award 2024 "Distinction from Young  environmental group"
  
The WASH sector coordination  and financing mechanisms, including the emergency preparedness and response  system, are strengthened through the provision of essential WASH facilities  and supplies to the national and sub-national authorities with UNICEF’s technical  support. Within the framework of Mongolia’s 3rd Nationally Determined  Contribution, UNICEF is collaborating with the MoECC on mainstreaming Climate  Smart Social Services into it.
  
Water safety plans was  implemented in three provinces. UNICEF cooperated with national and local  authorities, NGOs, and the private sector to increase access to safe drinking  water (30,910 people), sanitation (111,688 people), and hygiene (35,803  people) services. Nine schools were supported to improve their WASH  facilities by providing drinking water dispensers, renovating toilets and  handwashing rooms, and establishing Girl's Corners to promote menstrual  health and hygiene, benefiting 60,525 children. In addition, UNICEF supported  24 hospitals to improve medical waste treatment facilities and 3 family  health centres to improve wastewater treatment practices by installing  container-based wastewater treatment systems. An innovative, energy efficient  and climate resilient school is being constructed to introduce green school  concept to the government. Furthermore, liquid waste management that is  introduced in the school is operable at negative 50 degrees and fully functioning.
  
41,800 people have been  supported through the National Emergency Management Agency to provide  essential tools and WASH facilities (high-capacity water pumps, mobile  toilets, wastewater treatment systems, etc.). 
  
Within the framework of  Mongolia’s 3rd Nationally determined contribution (NDC 3.0) UNICEF Mongolia  has collaborated with the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change on  mainstreaming Climate Smart Social Services into NDC3.0. Furthermore, the  Country Office has been jointly implementing the project “Acceleration of  just energy transition”, in particular, energy transition in the education  and health sectors. In addition, as a result of UNICEF Advocacy action,  Government of Mongolia has committed to accelerate inclusive, child and  youth-centered climate policies and action at national and global levels by  signing Intergovernmental Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate  Action. 
  
Outcome 5: Social  inclusion and evidence
  
 UNICEF advocated for increased investments  in children and local governance,securing    50 million USD budget increase and approval from 2024 to 2025,  enhancing child-sensitive fiscal frameworks and ensuring children benefit  from inclusive social policies and interventions bringing children into  prioritization in all streams of governance and mechanisms with more solid  evidence.
  
UNICEF made significant  strides in enhancing Mongolia’s social protection system, ensuring children  benefit from inclusive, evidence-based, and child-sensitive policies. Aligned  with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan and Outcome 5 of the Theory of Change, these efforts  aimed to address systemic bottlenecks, particularly those affecting  children’s access to robust social safety nets and poverty alleviation  strategies.
  
A key achievement in 2024 was  the strengthening of Mongolia’s financial and governance frameworks for  child-sensitive budgeting. Through close collaboration with national  stakeholders, including the Ministry of Finance (MoF), Cabinet Secretariat,  and provincial governor offices, UNICEF identified gaps in policy  implementation and aligned national systems with local governance frameworks.  The Provincial Workshop held on November 19-20, 2024, was instrumental in  laying the groundwork for improved local government policies and planning for  2025 and beyond. By engaging with all 21 aimags and Ulaanbaatar city, UNICEF  ensured that local governments implemented child-sensitive fiscal reforms and  governance structures, fostering stronger linkages between national policy  goals and local governance priorities. UNICEF leveraged around4 million USD  from 21 local governments as programme matching fund to support the joint  programmes.
  
UNICEF’s efforts led to  significant budget increases focused on child protection and social welfare.  In 2024, evidence-based advocacy resulted in a 1.5-fold increase in the child  protection program budget under the MFLSP Portfolio, rising from MNT 14  billion to MNT 20.8 billion in 2025. Additionally, investments of 9.7 billion  tugrug were made to the Development Center for Children with Disabilities,  alongside increased subsistence allowances (11.8 billion tugrug) and hygiene  consumables (1.7 billion tugrug) for children with severe disabilities. These  targeted financial allocations have been critical in promoting equity in  social protection.
  
UNICEF also focused on  sustaining child money programs, ensuring that 1.33 million children received  child money allowances in 2025, up from 1.30 million in 2024. The budget  increased from 1,540.9 million tugrug to 1,580.2 million tugrug,  demonstrating a commitment to supporting marginalized families and ensuring  financial resilience amidst inflation.
  
To address chronic  underfunding and improve child nutrition at schools and dormitories, UNICEF  facilitated a costing analysis of meal programs. As a result, 125 billion MNT  was allocated to finance the raw materials required to prepare  meals for over 700,000 children. These  efforts align stakeholders on minimum cost standards for child nutrition,  improving health outcomes and ensuring sustained access to nutritious food. 

Outcome on Programme effectiveness:
  
To overcome the identified  barriers, the programme has employed cross-cutting strategies that include  generating evidence for advocacy to achieve positive changes in policy and  practices; expanding strategic partnerships and youth engagement; harnessing and  leveraging the power of the private sector; and social and behaviour change  to promote positive norms. 
  
Private sector engagement had  significantly increased in 2024, with 8 MOUs signed to collaborate in areas such  as CRBP, fundraising campaigns, customer engagement, and awareness raising.  UNICEF partnered with leading organizations such as Nomin Holding, one of the  largest supermarket chains, and Shoppy, a prominent online shopping and  ticketing platform that have committed to implementing CRBP. Given the size  of these companies, the partnership opens up significant opportunities to  advocate for children’s rights on a large scale. The total amount generated  through local campaigns to support CHIP and Teacher with tablet reached 97,000  USD in 2024 and an addition USD 33,800 in donation. 
  
Beyond working with the  private sector, UNICEF has actively advocated for policy changes that support  CSR and CRBP. UNICEF promoted a new change in the corporate tax law, which  offers companies the opportunity to tax deduction of up to 1 per cent of  their imposed tax if they spent from the taxable revenue on CSR projects. In  2025, UNICEF Mongolia will explore opportunities under this amendment to  mobilize systematic and accountable private sector contributions through  initiatives such as the One Percent Club for Children, focusing on improving  the lives of children and addressing critical social issues. In collaboration  with Khan Bank, UNICEF Mongolia brought together representatives from the top  100 companies to showcase UNICEF’s programs while providing information about  potential collaboration opportunities. As a result, companies learned about  the opportunity to implement CSR projects while benefiting from it  financially and agreeing on future partnerships. 
  
In partnership with government  and NGOs, UNICEF increased youth participation in decision making through  promoting skills development and youth-led advocacy projects. A specific  focus was on the development of policy documents on healthy and safe schools,  standards for child development services and costing guidance. 7,374 (65 %  girls) youth were consulted through 28 activities, covering areas of young  people’s skills on advocacy, education, nutrition, climate change and green  skills, renewable energy, WASH and STEM, and youth engagement in local  governance involving youth nationwide.
  
UNICEF delivered humanitarian  assistance to 17 out of 21 provinces of Mongolia, assisting 27,840 children  affected by dzud. UNICEF assistance covered underfunded priority areas of the  Dzud Inter-Agency Early Action and Response plan, covering urgent needs in  nutrition, child protection, education, WASH, and health sectors. UNICEF’s  role as lead for sectors and sub-sectors strengthened through provision of  continuous coordination, technical and fundraising support. 1,05 million USD  was mobilized from various funding sources including CERF, UNICEF  Humanitarian Thematic Funding and through local fundraising campaigns. The  office effectively coordinated with UNRC office, FAO and UNFPA to deliver  holistic, multi-sectoral response to the urgent needs created by the dzud,  filling critical gaps in Mongolia’s traditional siloed humanitarian approach.  This approach included the distribution of multipurpose cash assistance (by  FAO), enabling children to continue their education, combating malnutrition  risk among pregnant, lactating mothers and children, and ensuring women’s  specific needs.
  
UNICEF played an instrumental  role in providing the technical, financial and managerial support in the  operations of the country's largest household survey process - the Social  Indicator Sample Survey. The results derive over 150 development indicators related  to children's outcomes and impact including 40 SDG indicators with high  disaggregation potentials. It has employed technological innovations such as  new tools for monitoring of operations leading to more effective utilization  of resources as well as data collection quality assurance allowing nearly  real time detection of inaccuracies and inconsistencies.
  
The office has generated  behaviour related evidence in the areas of parenting, immunization,  nutrition, adolescent health to support development of SBC strategies and  interventions for the programmes.  Based on the evidence, the office  supported communication and demand creation component of Measles  Supplementary Immunization Campaign and the ongoing HPV Vaccination roll out  nationwide. Numerous communication materials were developed and disseminated  on respiratory infections, Rheumatic Heart Disease, nutrition, dental health,  household injury reduction which were disseminated to parents during  community engagement activities and parenting  trainings.

The Country Office maintained  effective and efficient operations in support to achievement of programme and  management priorities throughout the year. In terms of programme delivery,  during 2024 the office transferred a total of $3.7 million in Cash transfers  to implementing partners which represents 33 per cent of the total throughout  as well as delivered additional $3.6 million in programme supplies and  services.

Mongolia office highlights the following initiatives targeting the most vulnerable. “Teacher with Tablet” reaches the remote rural herder children with the early childhood education services resulting in improvement in literacy and numeracy development domain which has been behind for the last two decades. Furthermore, this has been important for the parents’ engagement and participation, contributing to the family-based service provision concept promoted by the Government. “Let’s learn together” initiative is an important contribution to enforcement of the inclusive, quality educational services articulated in the new package of Education Laws reducing the implication of COVID on learning achievement. With the Ministry of Education UNICEF has initiated the ONE SCHOOL ONE BAGH with the aim to keep children close to their parents. This initiative will mature in 2025

Additionally, expansion of the primary health services introducing community-based records with more health, nutrition and development aspects contribute extensively to capturing the reach out of the primary services supporting both the universality (leave no one behind) of the access and integrity of the services with cross-sector references, facilitated through a whole ecosystem of interoperable apps and digital services. The digital ecosystem further strengthens the continuity of the services from birth to and through school-age by offering the health promotion, health monitoring and referral services at Schools. Combination of multiple strategies and approaches including the universal geographical approach, multiplies the effect on advancing the reach out the most marginalized with integrity and reveal their visibility and voices. Expansion of the partnership with the Cabinet Secretariat and local Governments, using the momentum of local elections, culminated in a joint regional workshop which played an important role to bring children in the focus of the local and regional development.  
UNICEF I-CHECK innovation has been expanded and use in different public settings. This innovation is fundamental to ensure that basic physical health checks are conducted close to home and referal to neary family health centers.

The HPV introduction remain a challenge as its introduction encountered some difficulties including accepting and anti-vax movement. The office is working with partners on the best ways to communicate and improve HPV acceptance.

Furthermore, public finances for children work made possible an increase of the budget allocation through the processes that advance conceptual partnership and collaboration of the line ministries with the finance ministry, building mutual understanding on development gaps and priorities making the budgets equity focused and evidence based.  
 
However, further enforcement of the laws and policies through effective and efficient operationalization and implementation is needed. Grounding the policy work into practice in timely and effective manner requires further strategizing and stronger advocacy and partnership, especially in introducing new development concepts, operations of the new guidance and provisions.

Major challenges remain as sustainability, timeliness, and risk management. Parliament and local elections affect the development processes as the major partners and stakeholders are engaged in these processes throughout the year initially as preparations and effect further continues with re-structuring and re-staffing of the Government which require additional resources especially time to retain the interest, commitment, and continuity of the programme. Furthermore, the processes affect the Government priorities as well. Relatively weak national monitoring systems and capacities further challenge the operation and implementation of the development programmes leading to poor management of data and maximization of data and evidence utility for effective decision making as well as effective accountability systems. Mongolia Country Office will further address the challenges and the opportunities by strengthening the evidence and knowledge generation and utilization especially in area of energy transition, green sustainable growth, digital transformation and financing. Multi-faceted partnership for development and financing will be further strengthened to build common ground and understanding on new emerging concerns including climate change, vaccine hesitance, financing and other issues to maintain the achievement for children and realization of their rights. Capacity building for Mongolia Country Office to shift from post disaster response to anticipatory humanitarian action, and agile local fundraising system will also be among priorities.

Throughout 2024, Myanmar's humanitarian situation deteriorated sharply amid escalating armed conflict and insecurity, with children bearing the brunt of mass displacement, grave violations, and disruptions to essential health and education services. The crisis was further compounded by economic decline and climate shocks, including monsoon floods and the remnants of Typhoon Yagi, which devastated communities across nine states and regions in central and southern Myanmar.


The intensifying conflict across the country triggered a massive surge in displacement, climbing to a record nearly 3.5 million[1] people—an increase of over 30 per cent from the 2.6 million displaced at the end of 2023. Nearly 40 per cent of the displaced population were children. 


At least 650 children were killed or maimed in violence across Myanmar in 2024. Children also made up 32 per cent of civilian casualties from landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW) in 2024. The increasing use of deadly weapons, including airstrikes and landmines, in civilian areas—hitting homes, hospitals, and schools—further diminished the already limited safe spaces for children. All states and regions of Myanmar—outside Naypyitaw—are now contaminated with landmines, placing Myanmar among the most heavily landmine-contaminated countries in the world.


Myanmar's economy continued to decline throughout the year, with socio-economic shocks, conflict, and insecurity drastically reducing livelihood opportunities for families, leaving nearly 55 per cent of children living in poverty. This crisis was further exacerbated by monsoon floods that devastated farming communities, particularly in northern and central Myanmar. 


High food inflation and declining household incomes severely affected dietary quality, leaving over 40 per cent of children aged 6 to 23 months[2] unable to access the diverse and nutritious meals essential for their survival, growth, and development. Displaced households were among the worst affected - approximately 85 per cent of internally displaced households faced unmet needs, with one in four resorting to emergency or crisis strategies to cope with food and income shortages.[3]


Critical services, including health systems, continued to struggle and faced near-collapse in some areas due to ongoing conflict and the large-scale departure of health workers as part of the civil disobedience movement following the 2021 military takeover. Conflict-affected and vulnerable children and pregnant women struggled to obtain basic healthcare amid violence and logistical challenges.


Myanmar was one of the countries with the highest number of zero-dose children, with over 1 million children missing out on critical immunizations, increasing their vulnerability to vaccine-preventable diseases.  The under-five mortality rate remained concerningly high, at 40 per 1,000 live births[4] —the highest in Southeast Asia.


Nearly one-third of school-age children remained out of school due to the ongoing and protracted crisis,[5] with seasonal disasters such as monsoon floods further exacerbating disruptions to education and safe learning environments. The limited access to education not only increased protection risks but also threatened to create a lost generation of children.


In 2024, escalating violence and armed clashes further exacerbated the plight of children and families across Myanmar, as humanitarian access faced increasing threats and disruptions. Road closures, checkpoints, and movement restrictions across key locations and major supply routes impeded access to vulnerable and conflict-affected areas. These barriers not only hindered humanitarian operations but also disrupted civilian movements, leaving families stranded and struggling to access essential services.


The disruptions and impediments to life-saving assistance intensified the suffering of displaced children and families, already grappling with the trauma of conflict and displacement. Damaged infrastructure and restricted movement compounded their hardship, leaving families struggling to access basic necessities such as food, clean water, and healthcare. 


Despite increasingly challenging and complex operating conditions, UNICEF maintained a strong programmatic presence with seven field offices, ensuring coverage across the country, including in conflict-affected and hard-to-reach areas. In partnership with local and community-based actors, and through a range of modalities, including cash assistance, direct deliveries, cross-border support, and low-profile mechanisms, UNICEF delivered essential, integrated services in nutrition, child protection, health, and water, sanitation, and hygiene to some of the most affected and vulnerable children and families.


A pilot catch-up immunization campaign began across Yangon, Naypyidaw, and Mandalay, with plans to extend to hard-to-reach areas using multiple modalities and access options. UNICEF facilitated a robust response to the outbreak of acute watery diarrhea and cholera in Yangon, Chin, and Rakhine, delivering oral vaccines and other vital supplies. Additionally, UNICEF prioritized disability inclusion, providing cash assistance to families and specialized support, including assistive devices, to children living with disabilities, ensuring they received the care and resources needed to thrive.

[3] UNICEF analysis of Myanmar’s 2024 Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA)

Overall


Since the military takeover in February 2021 and ensuing conflict, Myanmar has experienced an unprecedented political, socioeconomic, human rights and humanitarian crisis. Armed conflict has escalated and continues to spread to new areas of the country; the economy has taken a severe hit, impacting families and livelihoods; and the overall humanitarian and development situation has deteriorated significantly. Up through 2024, little progress has been made to resolve the conflict driving most of the humanitarian need and the context of high uncertainty, political polarization and shifting areas of control has had a significant impact on UNICEF programming and on its partners.


Throughout 2024, Myanmar remained one of the most access-constrained countries, making humanitarian assistance delivery highly challenging. The ongoing conflict has displaced over 3.3 million people (October 2024), with 18.6 million in need of assistance (HNRP, 2024). UNICEF has continued to adapt its operations and programmes to meet these challenges, focusing on delivering principled and needs-based humanitarian assistance across the country in high-priority programme areas that directly benefit children and local communities. Overall, UNICEF has focused on ensuring continuity of critical services, while promoting long-lasting, durable community-based systems and solutions for children’s survival, growth, and development, through local partners and civil society organizations, including community-based organisations, and the private sector.

The Transitional Cooperation Framework (TCF), finalized in 2024, provides a planning framework both from an operational perspective and as a way of engaging with donors and partners. This has helped to strengthen the discussion around the humanitarian–development-peace nexus, with more of a focus on the sub-national, decentralized level, which is an important step towards ensuring impact on the ground for communities.

While previous years saw an overwhelming focus on the humanitarian response, in 2024 we saw in increased recognition from donors and partners that the protracted nature of the crisis requires engagement with all actors and an investment in building systems, resilience and community structures – and an increased appetite to support this work. 


Field offices began an analysis in 2024 on the operating environment and where there are opportunities to strengthen service delivery and how to align programme implementation strategies in a dynamic and volatile environment.The year also saw increased collaboration across the country office when access and security pose difficulties – ‘piggy backing’ on delivery mechanisms across programme areas. Systematic and routine consultation and close coordination and collaboration between programme and field offices took place on how to strengthen our integrated delivery – critical in the volatile and dynamic environment currently seen across Myanmar. 


In the area of health and nutrition, Myanmar's health system continued to be severely impacted by the crisis in 2024, as significant numbers of health workers remained out of the public system and their replacement requires further capacity building, otherwise it will weaken the system's capacity to provide essential services. Other challenges such as inaccessibility of services; shortage of medicines, vaccines and essential supplies; declining public confidences in the services, mass population displacements and limited funds to support awareness-raising activities also prevailed.


Throughout 2024, UNICEF focused on delivering essential and life-saving primary health care services focusing on immunization, maternal, newborn and child health (focusing on child survival); providing essential medicines and health kits, including amoxicillin, oral rehydration salts, zinc tabs, clean delivery kit, community newborn kits, and first aid kits; and ensuring essential nutrition services, including screening, treatment for severe acute malnutrition, IYCF counselling and promotion, micronutrient supplementation. Major achievements were achieved in the area of immunization, where 65 per cent of targeted children (600,000) were vaccinated against measles, and primary healthcare provision, where more than 95 per cent of the HAC 2024 target was reached (400,000 children and women accessing primary health care in UNICEF target areas). More than 2,500 children with acute malnutrition were treated out of about 525,000 children screened for wasting. Campaigns for vitamin A supplementation and de-worming were undertaken through the public system and reached more than 2 million children 6-59 months.


In the area of water, sanitation and hygiene, 2024 saw a continued decline in WASH services due to limited investment and ongoing displacement. Natural disasters and severe floods worsened the situation, affecting nearly one million people in 2024 alone. Public health emergencies like acute watery diarrhoea (AWD)/Cholera outbreaks and related deaths were reported in Yangon and other parts of the country. In view of the rapidly escalating conflict and displacement, UNICEF’s WASH response necessarily prioritized scaling up lifesaving humanitarian responses, while substantially scaling down WASH service delivery in communities and public institutions (schools and healthcare facilities). This shift was supported by on-ground team presence, strong procurement and warehousing capacity, and active WASH cluster coordination.


Priorities included emergency lifesaving WASH response for conflict-affected populations (distribution of critical WASH supplies, emergency water supply, emergency latrines, and hygiene promotion); implementing durable WASH solutions (rehabilitation/ new construction of water systems, sanitation facilities, community empowerment, and promotion of improved hygiene behaviours); and community resilience-building (climate-resilient water supply and sanitation services, sanitation marketing, improvement of WASH services in schools, community empowerment, and SBCC in communities and institutions). Major WASH results in 2024 include more than 662,000 people reached with critical WASH supplies, more than 129,000 people accessing appropriate sanitation services, and about 598,000 people accessing a sufficient quantity and quality of water for drinking and domestic needs.  


In the area of child protection, the collapse of the nascent child protection system meant that community-based protection systems continued to be a key approach to building a protective environment for children in 2024, while maintaining the central social welfare system at the sub-national level. In addition, parents and caregivers were supported to increasingly play a key role in ensuring children can access the support they need. With a key strategy of ‘localization’, service delivery of the Child Protection in Emergency (CPiE) minimum package through existing community structures was the key driver for addressing the critical needs of children. The package includes case management, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), and specialized services, such as support to GBV survivors, victim assistance to explosive ordinance/mine affected, legal advice for children in contact with the law, and services for unaccompanied and separated children. Emphasis was also made on building the fundamental capacity of frontline workers and community volunteers to expand existing social service workforces, especially the community workforce. 


In 2024, UNICEF also scaled up children and armed conflict programming and Mine Action and continued to co-lead the UN Country Task Force for Monitoring and Reporting (CTFMR) at both technical and principal levels and generate the evidence to inform advocacy and action to prevent the six grave violations against children. Printing of IEC materials for the prevention of grave violations is ongoing, expected to be delivered in early 2025. UNICEF reached almost 150,000 children and parents/caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support, and 43,000 women, girls and boys accessing gender-based violence risk mitigation, prevention and/or response interventions. More than 70,000 people were given access to a safe and accessible channel to report sexual exploitation and abuse by aid workers, and 430,000 children in areas affected by landmines and other explosive weapons provided with relevant prevention and/or survivor-assistance interventions.


In 2024, in education, UNICEF focused on ensuring the continuity of learning amid the severe disruptions to education caused by the ongoing conflict following the 2021 military takeover and the destruction by typhoon Yagi. This was achieved by engaging and re-engaging children through safe, inclusive, and quality learning opportunities, providing a range of flexible and diverse educational pathways. These pathways included Education in Emergencies and Supplementary Learning programmes, offering early learning, reading enhancement, alternative basic education, non-formal education, social emotional learning/mental health and psychosocial support, and skills development. A central focus was on reaching the most marginalized children, including IDPs, host communities, conflict-affected children, out of school children, girls, children with disabilities, and ethnic minorities. 


Significant achievements in 2024 included reaching 1,017,437 children (512,817 girls) with learning opportunities and the distribution of teaching and learning materials. Additionally, 2,000 Community Education Committees were supported, and partnerships were maintained with 22 partners, half of which were national. A strong emphasis on quality learning was prioritized through the deployment of the adapted Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) tool and Southeast Asian Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) to assess the foundational literacy and numeracy proficiency levels of over 9,000 children nationwide. In addition, the completion of a Rapid Gender Analysis, carried out in collaboration with a couple of International NGOs, identified critical barriers to education for girls in crisis contexts and proposed practical solutions, alongside targeted advocacy, to ensure their continued access to education. These efforts were instrumental in addressing gender disparities and strengthening the inclusivity and resilience of the education system. The resilience of the education system was further reinforced by a community-led approach and the strengthening of the Education Cluster, which expanded to over 80 members and seven full-time staff. Moreover, US$ 70 million was secured for the 2022-2026 period, ensuring vital resources to sustain and enhance learning opportunities for children.


In the area of social policy, UNICEF worked to expand the coverage of humanitarian and social cash transfers to ensure vulnerable families can meet essential needs and strengthen community systems and capacities to enhance access to disability-inclusive and gender-responsive care and support services for cash beneficiaries. UNICEF developed a robust foundation of data and evidence on child poverty, vulnerability, and the impact of social interventions to support programming and resource mobilisation.


Major achievements included 47,500 children and adults screened and registered in UNICEF’s Disability Management Information system (DMIS) to support access to disability benefits and specialised support services; and 223,000 people reached with UNICEF-funded cash transfers, through maternal and child cash transfers during the first 1,000 days of life, cash assistance for children with disabilities, and multi-purpose cash for internally displaced and other conflict-affected families. Furthermore, UNICEF’s Child Well-Being Panel Survey provided the most thorough overview of children's conditions in Myanmar since the onset of the crisis in 2021 and thematic studies on child well-beings, gender and disability contributed crucial insights for targeted interventions.


Social and Behavioral Change (SBC) focused on fostering community-driven engagement for adoption of essential childcare practices across UNICEF programmes and building community resilience to withstand emergencies. SBC is custodian of Accountability to Affected Population (AAP), which ensures communities have channels to voice their concerns, access information, and provide feedback on the humanitarian assistance and services. 


Major achievements in 2024 included: About 4.7 million people were reached surpassing the target of 3 million people through scaling-up of multi-media messaging on promotion of critical hygiene behaviours; reducing AWD and cholera risks in vulnerable areas; and increasing demand for routine immunization and nationwide immunization campaigns on Human papillomavirus (HPV), Diphtheria Tetanus (DT), catch-up andOral Cholera Vaccine (OCV). Successful social media campaigns provided preventive health, nutrition, hygiene and protection advice to wide audiences, especially during disease outbreaks, emergencies and vaccinations and addressed myths and corrected misinformation. In addition, on-ground interpersonal community engagement reached 312,014 (M-96,350, F-215,664) beyond the target of 150,000 people with integrated packages of childcare family practices, behaviour practices to contain community transmission of AWD/Cholera with a focus on hard-to-reach areas.  


Through AAP feedback mechanisms, programmes improved transparency and accountability, helping communities feel more empowered - especially women - and engaged in programme implementation. A total of 55,869 (M-20,918, F-34,951) provided feedback or concerns and were engaged through satisfaction surveys. The indicator is below the target of 359,529 due to changes in means of verification which indicates people utilizing the CFM and not accessing it. SBC has localized the AAP training, which enabled training of community leaders and volunteers in health, education, community mobilization and community feedback mechanisms. The trained cadre are trusted sources of information in their communities, extending the reach of public health messaging and contributing to a more resilient community-based public infrastructure.


Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) is central to UNICEF’s mandate, underscored by a strict zero-tolerance policy for any SEA committed by UNICEF staff or partners, ensuring full accountability to the communities served. In 2023, UNICEF Myanmar accelerated its PSEA initiatives by increasing technical capacity to scale up the PSEA Action Plan. Their focus is on strengthening safe, accessible SEA reporting systems, providing survivor-centered support, and maintaining accountability across all humanitarian efforts.


Key structural changes were introduced to drive these outcomes, including forming an internal PSEA Taskforce, securing senior leadership buy-in, developing an organization-wide Accountability Framework defining staff roles and responsibilities, and activating PSEA Focal Points across all UNICEF units and sections. Additionally, UNICEF Myanmar was selected as co-chair of the Inter-Agency PSEA Network, a collaborative platform essential for aligning on priority outcomes. In 2024, with EPF funding, UNICEF Myanmar made significant investments to bolster the capacities of both UNICEF staff and high-risk Implementing Partners, while improving SEA reporting mechanisms within communities and IDP camps. This funding also supported several major Inter-Agency PSEA Network projects, such as the SEA Risk Assessment and training of local partners’ investigators.


Despite these advancements, challenges persist, including cultural norms around sexual conduct, limited trust in reporting systems, and inadequate victim assistance through existing reporting and referral mechanisms. In 2025, UNICEF Myanmar will seek further funding to consolidate recent progress and embed a zero-tolerance culture toward SEA. From 2026 onwards, sustainable funding will be crucial to maintain a dedicated PSEA team in Myanmar.


In the area of Operations, the ongoing crisis and restrictions on access to deliver supplies in hard-to-reach areas coupled with floods have severely impacted the supply chains across the country. The logistics function is facing unprecedented challenges in moving supplies from Yangon warehouse to many field locations, with cases of supplies being confiscated at checkpoints or trucks denied entry to some areas. An increased number of checkpoints managed by different armed groups and restrictions in delivering some selected items is a key factor. Another major challenge is related to the importation of supplies, especially health and nutrition supplies.


Despite these challenges, there have been achievements - UNICEF Myanmar maintained optimal stock levels and continued to replenish stocks from offshore and local markets to ensure the availability of supplies in all warehouses across the country. MCO also explored the possibility of local procurement of various health and nutrition supplies. MCO also received an Local Procurement Authorisation (LPA) for pharmaceuticals and is expecting to receive LPAs for nutrition supplies test kits soon. With support from EAPRO and COs in neighbouring countries, MCO also explored alternative channels to bring supplies to hard-to-reach areas, and pilot activities are ongoing under Health and Nutrition programmes.


UNICEF Myanmar made significant strides in maintaining operational continuity and efficiency amidst the complex political, economic, and security landscape in Myanmar. Key achievements in 2024 included streamlining visa processing for staff, thereby reducing delays and improving coordination with immigration authorities; improving field office communications with IT equipment installations across field locations; numerous initiatives for staff well-being; and the integration of sustainability initiatives through the Greening Committee and partnerships, including launching disability-friendly services such as a canteen run by Myanmar Deaf Chefs and wheelchair accessibility enhancements.


On the security side, due to the absence of hardening measures, the security team focused on strengthening emergency preparedness and response mechanisms through tabletop exercises, creation of tailored SOPs, providing training (SSAFE and IFAK) and through the application of the SRM process to enable programmes and movement of personnel.


In the area of advocacy and communications, UNICEF Myanmar remained the leading advocate for children throughout 2024 in a complex and volatile political landscape. Advocacy and communication efforts showcased UNICEF’s critical work on the ground, supporting vulnerable children and their families in challenging operational contexts. The organization consistently spotlighted rights violations through its social media platforms, as well as through Regional Office and HQ channels. 


Digital engagement steadily increased, and new partnerships were explored throughout 2024. UNICEF Myanmar’s social media engagement grew steadily in 2024, despite the highly politicized operating context impacting perception, sentiments, and the public engagement landscape. UNICEF’s X page (formerly Twitter) grew to over 7,100 followers, creating a dynamic space to engage directly with donors, influencers, the Myanmar diaspora, and the media. At the same time, more than 156,000 people visited the UNICEF Myanmar website – up from about 141,000 in 2023 - demonstrating the growing interest in our work and impact for children. UNICEF Myanmar Facebook followers grew to 1,045,193 followers, with 7,500 new followers gained in 2024. These platforms have become powerful tools to rally support, share stories, and inspire action for the most vulnerable children in Myanmar. 


In 2024, UNICEF Myanmar used digital platforms to champion the rights and safety of children and families through 22 impactful campaigns. From #ListenToTheFuture on World Children’s Day, amplifying children’s voices and dreams; to #IMAD2024 on Mine Awareness Day, calling for protection from landmines; each campaign highlighted urgent issues. #GirlGoals celebrated girls’ potential on International Day of the Girl, while #EarlyMomentsMatter during Parenting Month emphasized the importance of nurturing care. On Menstrual Hygiene Day, #PeriodFriendlyWorld advocated for dignity and opportunity for every girl. Together, these campaigns united audiences to protect children from harm and create a world where they can thrive in safety and dignity. 


As the protracted crisis continued in Myanmar, young people faced increasing challenges to share and access information. To help combat these challenges, UNICEF engaged young people, including through the U-Report programme, providing advocacy skills and child rights training to youth networks to equip them with skills and tools to advocate on child rights issues and be UNICEF advocacy allies and influencers.Despite connectivity and other challenges, U-Report Myanmar maintained the highest average poll response rate in Southeast Asia, at around 95 per cent and co-created content plans and content with young volunteers. U-Report Myanmar Facebook had 135,000 followers - the second highest out of 95 U-Report countries globally - and achieved nearly 9,000 YouTube subscribers (almost a 50 per cent increase over 2023) - the second highest globally. A female U-Reporter was chosen as a UNICEF Innocenti Youth Foresight Fellowship along with 11 from other countries across the globe. In 2024, 350 youth volunteers across the country were empowered with different skills and information such as MHPSS, PSEA, video content creation, vlogging and creative writing skills. UNICEF Myanmar continued to mobilize and empower its network of young volunteers across the country as agents of change and champions for child rights.  


Advocacy efforts continued at the international, regional, and national levels, with UNICEF Myanmar issuing statements calling for the protection of children’s rights, adherence to international humanitarian law, and an end to grave violations, particularly following the spike in conflict and attacks targeting or affecting children and other civilians. In addition, UNICEF actively contributed to inter-agency advocacy efforts, addressing incidents and ongoing child rights concerns. Joint statements on Myanmar were released and amplified by partner agencies, Regional Offices, and HQs, further strengthening the advocacy impact. UNICEF Myanmar’s public advocacy not only raised awareness of the dire situation facing children but also generated public demand for access to essential services. 


UNICEF’s June 2024-June 2025 Advocacy Strategic Framework prioritizes the following three targeted and specific areas: (1) Access, (2) Children and Armed Conflict, specifically landmines and forced recruitment, and (3) Immunization, andhave been operationalized across the office.   


In 2024, UNICEF led a joint advocacy strategy development initiative to address the immunization crisis for children and pregnant women. Together with in-country donors, development partners, WHO and GAVI, UNICEF began the process to develop a joint advocacy strategy towards ensuring that all children and pregnant women have access to routine immunization and are protected from vaccine-preventable diseases. The strategy will be rolled out by WHO, UNICEF, GAVI, in-country donors and development partners and other key stakeholders as a joint effort in 2025. 


UNICEF continued to produce materials that highlighted its critical role and impact in responding to the humanitarian and development crisis. Regular situation reports, a quarterly newsletter, and thematic briefings kept partners informed of achievements, challenges, needs and opportunities for collaboration and joint advocacy. Additionally, UNICEF leveraged social media to recognize donor support—when appropriate, given security and other considerations—to encourage their continued commitment to children, particularly during key advocacy moments and significant occasions. 


Regarding resource mobilization, UNICEF re-doubled its efforts to build trust with partners and donors in its ability to deliver in a highly conflicted, constrained, complex and politicised environment, and demonstrate its critical role in responding to the humanitarian crisis – while also stressing the need to invest in safeguarding systems and building resilience (‘the nexus’). The volatility of the Myanmar operating environment makes flexible, predictable, sufficient and timely funding critical for delivering for millions of children across the country, including those living with disabilities or separated from their families, facing an uncertain future. 


Regular donor briefings, bilateral meetings and donor project site visits were organized to showcase UNICEF’s work in these and programme areas, with a view to encouraging funding support. These efforts paid off following major flooding, and the cholera and AWD crisis, with several donors, including Japan, Korea, ECHO, BHA and CERF, contributing to the response to these challenges. Our close engagement also enabled us to mobilize significant contributions this year from BHA (US$8 million), Japan (US$5.6 million), CERF (US$ 3.7 million), ECHO (US$3.2 million), Korea (US$ 2.5 million), France (US$ 2.2 million) and Myanmar Humanitarian Fund (US$ 2 million). 


It's worth noting the contributions from new or returning donors, such as Korea and France, on top of those from key existing donors like BHA, Japan and ECHO, to support critical efforts. MCO has been expanding its donor base for humanitarian funding, which includes Norway and Thailand, along with the Hong Kong National Committee and Australia National Committee. 


In the coming year, priority areas for donor diversification will focus on engaging the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), China, Germany, the UK and International Financial Institutions (IFIs) such as the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, as well as the private sector, with support from UNICEF National Committees. Some of these donors have already pledged or are expected to pledge support in 2025. 


As part of its private sector engagement, UNICEF, in partnership with Rakuten Viber, reached communities in Myanmar with life-saving messages through the ‘Knowledge Talk’ Viber channel. An extension and expansion of this partnership will be discussed, along with further private sector engagement to strengthen support for both humanitarian and development efforts.

UNICEF continued to scale up partnerships with local actors (including community- and faith-based organizations) to expand localization and reach in hard-to-reach areas, and to conflict-affected and otherwise vulnerable populations, including those displaced.


In doing this, UNICEF explored diverse and flexible modalities to facilitate implementation and to reach children in the challenging environment. This required consultant consultations with local actors and partners, advocacy with stakeholders, and support from UNICEF Regional Office, other Country Offices and Headquarters. These efforts enabled UNICEF to apply direct implementation methods through communities, contractors, volunteers and UNICEF staff, in addition to partnerships with national and international non-governmental and civil society organizations. Key to this approach was the continued capacity development of local actors in relevant technical areas, as well as financial and risk management, and dedicated, set aside funds in partnership to promote localization. Through its extensive field presence, UNICEF ensured monitoring of its implementation throughout the year, despite access challenges.  


Partnerships with sister agencies also yielded results, including working with WFP to maximize their community platforms (school committees), bringing in UNICEF programming areas beyond education – including WASH and nutrition. Collaboration with WHO, UNOPS brought health sector partners together for joint planning and discussion with donors, including the World Bank, regarding implementation modalities and pathways to delivering assistance.  We worked closely with WHO to respond quickly to outbreaks of AWD/cholera in urban and peri-urban areas that are not part of the HNRP, bringing in critical supplies to help stop the spread of the outbreak. 


A workshop on immunization advocacy with WHO, UNOPS, the World Bank and donors, set the stage for joint planning and advocacy in 2025 to ensure that we can increase the reach of our immunization efforts in hard-to-reach areas, speaking with one voice to increase access.  UNICEF, as chair of the re-established Social Protection Sector Coordination Group, also coordinated with WFP and development partners to strengthen programming across the humanitarian-development nexus. 


Opportunities include identifying a growing number of donors (DFAT, GAVI, and the World Bank) that wish to work with UNICEF in hard-to-reach/ conflict-affected areas. In 2024, MCO received US$5 million (Procurement Service) from DFAT to provide an integrated package of immunization, health and nutrition services in hard-to-reach/conflict-affected areas. A two-year joint proposal with UNOPS and WHO is currently in the final stages of approval by Gavi to expand the DFAT-supported initiative. Similarly, the World Bank plans to provide US$15 million for the next two years to scale up the delivery of a package of essential health and nutrition interventions at the primary and referral levels.


UN inter-agency collaboration continued to be critical in the face of the ongoing crisis in Myanmar, including increasing access constraints, banking constraints and volatility and security risks. UNICEF actively participated in cross-agency efforts to find common solutions to these challenges, including in the UN Country Team (UNCT), the Operations Management Team (OMT), the Security Management Team (SMT) and the Humanitarian Country Team (HCT). 


The support of the Operations Management Team to the UNCT has been instrumental in many areas, encompassing staff concerns and well-being to UN’s operating environment in the areas of finance, logistics, joint procurement, telecommunications bottlenecks, and UN common premises in the various locations around the country. 


Relocations due to insecurity during 2024 affected UNICEF. The SMT, with advice from the Security Cell, supported the staff and eligible family members’ safety and security to reach safe havens. In addition, the OMT supported with guidance on securing assets and support to affected staff. Measures to enhance the living conditions of national staff were considered, such as during the fuel crisis, as well as in considering extension of the flexible working arrangements. The OMT contributed to the process for the Place-to-Place survey and the comprehensive salary survey for national staff. The functioning of the UN clinic was regularly reviewed, and necessary extension of services were proposed, as in the situation of AWD and cholera, where information sessions were organized. Furthermore, given the current situation in Myanmar, recommendations for mental health support were provided. Difficulties faced by staff with regards to fund transfers were managed with UNFCU, as well as the exchange of information between respective UN entities, which helped in providing solutions for all staff.


UNICEF contributed to regular discussions about logistics challenges faced by UN entities and possible solutions. Through the OMT, UNICEF prepared recommendations for the visit of the Under-Secretary-General for Safety and Security in May 2024. Regular discussions were held, and best practices exchanged, with regards to telecommunication facilities and Internet availability. The BOS annual review and the calculation of cost avoidance, leading to overall reduction of costs for UN entities, also constituted an important part of the tasks of the OMT. Ensuring that common facilities and services in the various locations are being provided efficiently and effectively was also part of the regular agenda. Given the complex banking situation of the country, the analysis, review, and recommendations to UN entities contributed to ensuring that they could operate optimally.


In 2024, UNICEF conducted ongoing capacity building support including through Emergency Preparedness and Response (EPR) trainings targeting emergency focal points within the office to strengthen their knowledge and operational capacities to implement UNICEF’s preparedness and humanitarian response, including for natural disasters such as floods. 


UNICEF continued its strong partnership and collaboration by serving as Cluster Lead Agency in four clusters/areas of responsibility (Nutrition, WASH, Child Protection and Mine Action) and co-led the Education cluster. The WASH Cluster coordinated a multi-layered response to meet critical water, sanitation, and hygiene needs, focusing on vulnerable populations affected by conflict and natural disasters. Operating through national and sub-national platforms, the cluster leveraged a network of over 50 partners. In collaboration with the Health Cluster, targeted prevention and response activities for water-borne diseases were implemented in affected areas. The Nutrition cluster continued its efforts achieve its targets for the treatment of severe acute malnutrition, moderate acute malnutrition, other preventive measures, including provision of multiple micronutrients and micronutrient supplementation. The education cluster continued to build on efforts towards localization and building capacity of local partners – enabling their effective and active participation in the response, leveraging their unique delivery abilities at field level. To date, 252 staff of partner agencies have benefitted from trainings on issues like PSEA, Gender, Child Protection, and M&E, strengthening partners’ capacity to enable them to deliver a safe, timely and quality response. The Child Protection Area of Responsibility (AoR) is working towards delivering quality life-saving child protection services and is projected to reach over 900,000 children and caregivers in 2024. The AoR supports with coordination, capacity building of protection and non-protection actors as well as key resources. The Mine Action AoR has advanced efforts this year to address explosive ordnance risks by mobilizing resources, integrating Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) into wider humanitarian activities. 


UNICEF Security Section advocated for and represented UNICEF’s interests in the Security Cell, ensuring all Security Risk Management (SRM) documents help ensure UNICEF programmes are enabled. UNICEF actively contributed and supported the efforts of the inter-agency Security Cell to support the safety and security of staff and eligible family members. This included adapting the Area Security Risk Management documents to reflect the current context and the corresponding Areas Security Plans; the risk assessment, planning and operational implementation enabling a total of six relocations in 2024; and contingency plans for areas at increased risk. UNICEF chaired and co-chaired two Security Cell Working Groups.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
There were several external challenges that required innovative solutions in order to ensure that UNICEF could continue to deliver effectively for children in Myanmar throughout 2024. These included escalating armed conflict that limited humanitarian access; natural and manmade emergencies increasing demand for services; CSO registration and conscription laws affecting partners’ staff and community volunteers, leading to project area withdrawals; safety and security risks for UNICEF and partner staff hindering programming and monitoring visits; operational challenges, including commodity price escalation and communication issues, such as internet and phone service blackouts; high inflation and cash withdrawal difficulties impacting transactions with partners; and supply movement restrictions, especially in Rakhine (since Nov 2023) and Kachin (since Mar 2024), reducing contingency stocks and limiting the ability to respond. Also, comprehensive monitoring of the situation of children was challenging due to the suspension of major household survey programmes, the politicisation of data, capacity constraints, and weak inter-agency coordination on data collection and analysis. Political instability, security concerns and the movement of people made it challenging to engage communities consistently with behaviour change interventions, and the huge linguistic and cultural diversity required localized and often multilingual programme development.


There were also internal challenges, such as reduced funding, despite increasing needs; high human resource costs for partners, especially INGOs; short grant durations (6-12 months); onerous and complex financial management and internal procedures complicating partners’ understanding of systems; and siloed programme approaches within UNICEF as a whole.


These challenges required UNICEF Myanmar to exercise extreme flexibility in programme implementation across different modalities, and to keep pushing for increased integration across programme areas, when it comes to delivering a package of services to communities. It also required requests for increased flexibility from HQ when it comes to internal processes and procedures and increased advocacy with donors regarding donor conditionalities that hamper support for the delivery of critical assistance in areas without (I)NGO partners. It also required us to find innovative solutions such as local procurement of essential goods; increased cash assistance - providing dignity and flexibility to families to meet their needs amidst supply chain and access challenges (Myanmar’s Inter-Cluster Coordination Group and Cash Working Group endorsed a new Multi-Purpose Cash Strategy in 2024); and for UNICEF to develop and implement its own Child Well-Being Panel Survey to provide an overview of children's conditions in Myanmar since the onset of the crisis in 2021 to address the lack of data. 


Disease outbreaks in areas that were not part of the Humanitarian Needs Response Plan (HNRP) and where we do not have local implementing partners required us to take alternative approaches to delivering and stretched our regular resources at a time of funding crisis. 


To enable the movement of personnel in such a highly volatile and fluid environment requires a high degree of agility and flexibility, with UNICEF increasingly needing to alternate between relocation, sheltering in place (or forced to when roads are closed) and then taking advantage of short windows of opportunity when fighting temporarily ceases and access is possible. However, in the absence of hardening measures (no PPE, armored vehicles, bunkers, satellite phones, earth-filled gabions, etc.) the UN is largely reliant on preventative security measures such as training, liaison and information collection, analysis, advice, and coordination, security assessment missions and participation of security staff on programme missions – all of which is human resource intensive and requires professional security capacity. The number of relocation procedures have increased since the beginning of the year, with six relocations in the past six months (compared to none in 2022 and 2023) and we are forecasting further relocations will be very likely in the coming year. The risk management processes to support these programme activities in this environment, and also the work to return and resume operations, takes significant security support.


In the area of programming, we learned that we will need to take advantage of rising digital access, particularly through mobile devices, as avenues for SBC messaging and interactive AAP platforms. We will look towards increasing collaboration with grassroots ethnic organizations, local influencers and community-based media to extend reach and amplify social and behaviour change impact. In the area of education, we will explore the potential of cash voucher assistance to improve educational outcomes, with a particular emphasis on increasing the retention of girls and marginalized children. We will also work to identify and implement community-driven strategies that enhance the resilience of the education system, while effectively addressing its challenges and complexities. We will ensure close alignment with CP AoR to strengthen the social service workforce at the community level to maximize existing community structures for agile and timely case management support and work to simplify child protection case management processes. We will also look at increasing engagement with all parties to the conflict to advocate for the rights of children, especially on the six grave violations and to further discuss prevention and response to these violations.


We also learned that the specialized skills we have in climate-resilient services, solar-powered gravity water supply, sanitation marketing, WASH in institutions, and emergency response - with a strong understanding of local contexts – will allow us to scale-up our work in these areas, especially with a view to climate mitigation and resilience building.  We also learned that current social enterprises focused on clean and affordable water kiosks in peri-urban Yangon can be scaled up to improve water access in other under-served urban areas – and that private sector engagement in sanitation businesses can attract investment, foster innovation, and enhance sanitation services.


Through our work we learned that opportunities exist to integrate WASH with nutrition, gender-based violence (GBV), and cash transfer programmes, which will provide holistic support for vulnerable populations as we take this work forward – and that active coordination mechanisms for the WASH cluster enhance collaboration and effectiveness.


We will also engage international financial institutions, particularly the World Bank and Asia Development Bank, to attract multi-year predictable investments to strengthen community resilience.

Papua New Guinea (PNG), a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) in the Pacific, is characterised by significant natural resources and extensive cultural and linguistic diversity. Demographic pattern indicates that nearly 87 per cent of the estimated population of 11.7 million reside in peri-urban, rural, or remote areas, with 80 per cent relying on subsistence activities such as fishing, hunting, gathering, and horticulture for their livelihoods[1].
PNG faces significant challenges with frequent disasters and other crises. In January 2024, nearly nationwide unrests erupted in response to public sector pay cuts and proposed tax reforms, resulting in at least 20 deaths and numerous injuries. In February, tribal conflicts in the Highlands region escalated, with violent clashes in Enga Province displacing almost 20,000 individuals (10,200 females) and a conflict violence in Angoram District, East Sepik, affected 400 people, including 223 children. In addition, the country faced several natural disasters: severe flooding and a 6.9-magnitude earthquake in East Sepik destroyed nearly 1,000 homes; a landslide in Enga in May buried an entire village, affecting an estimated 7,849 people (1,427 households) including 3,360 children; prolonged flooding in Western Province from March to July disrupted the lives of 55,000 people and displaced 1,261; and floods and landslides in the Southern Highlands displaced 2,000 people and affected 14,000 others. These disasters severely impacted children, exposing them to violence, displacement, and trauma. Education was disrupted, leaving thousands without learning opportunities, while healthcare access declined, worsening health outcomes. Weak law enforcement and impunity further heightened risks of abuse and violence.
According to the 2025 INFORM Risk Index, PNG is classified as “high risk,” ranking 29th out of 191 countries worldwide and the highest risk country in the Pacific region. Environmental challenges, including climate change and biodiversity loss, pose significant threats to livelihoods in PNG and directly affect the health and prospects of children. While the government has demonstrated its commitment to sustainable development through the National Adaptation Plan (NAP), the National Disaster Risk Reduction Plan 2017-2030 and participation in international agreements, effective implementation of these initiatives remains an ongoing challenge. 
In 2024, PNG’s critically under-resourced health system further worsened children's access to essential services. The COVID-19 pandemic had already exposed weaknesses, and ongoing shortages of health workers and resources, especially in rural areas, deepened the crisis. Maternal and child mortality rates remain high: under-five mortality is 41 per 1,000 live births, neonatal and infant mortality are 21 and 33 per 1,000, respectively, and maternal mortality stands at 192 per 100,000. PNG is the only country in the region yet to achieve the Maternal Neonatal Tetanus Elimination (MNTE) target. Pentavalent vaccine coverage has remained below 50% over the past decade (2015–2024). Many women give birth at home due to understaffed facilities, lack of basic amenities like running water and electricity, and financial barriers such as healthcare and transportation costs. 
Child malnutrition is a pervasive issue, with PNG recording the fourth highest stunting rate globally. Approximately 48.2 per cent of children under five are stunted. Stunting is most prevalent among the poorest households (55 per cent) but remains significant even among the wealthiest quintile (36 per cent). This condition severely impacts children’s physical and cognitive development, leading to poor educational outcomes, reduced productivity, lower lifetime earnings, and long-term health challenges.
Educational outcomes reveal significant disparities and systemic challenges. Primary school completion rates are critically low, with only 62.8 per cent of students (Female: 69.59) completing primary education. In rural areas, the rate drops further to 27 per cent. Approximately 23 per cent of children aged 6 to 18 are out of school, with girls disproportionately affected (25 per cent in 2024). Transition rates from primary to secondary education have also declined sharply (64 per cent in 2019). In 2024, net enrolment rates are not available, however, enrolment rates in 2019 was 58 per cent at the primary level and 20 per cent at the secondary level. Compounding these issues, many schools lack essential infrastructure, including clean water, functional toilets, and adequate classroom space.
Access to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in PNG is among the lowest in the Pacific region.
