According to the 2019 Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) update, only 41 per cent of the population has access to safe drinking water, and just 13 per cent has access to improved sanitation facilities. Approximately half of all households rely on unimproved water sources, such as surface water, dug wells, or springs, which are often contaminated. More than 80 per cent of the population lacks access to basic sanitation, resulting in widespread open defecation and heightened vulnerability to waterborne diseases, including diarrhea.
Violence against children is pervasive, with 75 per cent of children experiencing physical violence and 85 per cent of fathers admitting to hitting their children (DHS 2016–2018). Furthermore, recent data shows that in Oceania 34 per cent of women reported experienced sexual violence in their childhood. The absence of robust birth registration systems further complicates child protection efforts, with only 13 per cent of children under the age of five registered at birth. This lack of documentation undermines their access to essential services and legal protections. Protection systems and services for children and vulnerable populations are severely constrained in PNG due to limited financial and human resources and weak coordination mechanisms. Access to preventive and responsive services is inadequate, and reliable data on child protection issues is scarce. 
The National Policy on Social Protection (NPSP) 2015-2020 introduced contributory schemes, including the Government Tuition Fee Subsidy Policy to provide social insurance for old age, work accidents, sickness, and maternity. However, these initiatives mainly benefit those in formal employment, leaving much of the population without essential safety nets. Approximately 57 per cent of Papua New Guineans live in multidimensional poverty, which often contributes negatively to existing problem of malnutrition, inadequate health care, and limited access to education.

The new country programme cycle (2024-2028) commenced in 2024, focused on three overarching priorities: (i) Improving the quality and accessibility of basic social services to build public confidence and encourage their use; (ii) Building resilience and reducing risks to children, families, and services in the face of disasters and crises; and (iii) Reducing violence, abuse and exploitation of children and women. During the first year, UNICEF PNG achieved significant results in these priority areas.
 
Strengthening quality social services and fostering demand generation: 
UNICEF focused on strengthening of social services with a view to enhancing the well-being of children and families. This is being achieved primarily through support to improve policies and guidelines, including the Infant and Young Child Feeding (Control) Act and the Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) Guideline. Evidence is being generated, such as the Education Sector Analysis, to improve service delivery systems and mechanisms. This is combined with capacity building of social service workers.
The health system’s capacity to deliver quality immunisation services increased significantly. In 2024, cold chain functionality reached 92 per cent, stock reporting reached 80 per cent (compared to 90 per cent and 50 per cent respectively in 2023), and there were no national vaccine stockouts. Following UNICEF’s advocacy, the government allocated US$2,897,706 for vaccine funding, covering 39 per cent of the annual requirement. In addition, the Government’s budget committee approved a budget allocation of 18.966 million PGK (approx. US$4.75 million) for 2025 compared to 3.466 million PGK (approx. US$0.87 million) in 2024, more than five times increase.  
In 2024, facility-based deliveries increased to 37 per cent (one per cent increase from 2023), and pentavalent vaccine coverage reached 43 per cent (three per cent increase from 2023). More than 70,629 pregnant women received four antenatal care visits, an increase of 7 per cent from 2023. In addition, 93,447 women (37 per cent of estimated pregnant women) delivered in health facilities, a significant increase of 32 per cent from 70,892 women in 2022. 90,692 newborns were delivered alive in health facilities and received postnatal care within two days of discharge, a slight increase of 0.7 per cent from 2023 and 31.4 per cent from 2022. Early essential newborn care (EENC) services were provided to 63,090 newborns, an increase of 11 per cent from 2023. 
With UNICEF’s advocacy effort and technical assistance, the MNTE action plan (2024-2027) was revised and adopted by NDOH. Going forward, UNICEF will collaborate with NDOH, WHO and partners to support the implementation of the action plan. 
Through UNICEF’s technical support, the government introduced Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) Guidelines in January 2024, which contributed to improved management of acute malnutrition. A total of 18,413 children aged 6-59 months with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) were treated, reaching more than three times the annual target. This achievement was made possible by the contribution of the new community nutrition model which has enabled early screening, identification and treatment of children at home. 
With UNICEF’s support, the drafting of regulations for the Infant and Young Children’s Food Supply (Control) Act was completed, providing a framework for implementing the act adopted by Parliament in 2023. Additionally, 170,184 mothers—surpassing the target of 100,000—received counselling on maternal, infant, and young child feeding (MIYCF). Recognizing UNICEF’s expertise, the Government has contracted us to provide technical support for the rollout of the Child Nutrition and Social Protection (CNSP) project, reinforcing UNICEF’s leadership in this area.
UNICEF supported the government in conducting a long-awaited Education Sector Analysis (ESA) in 2024, enhancing the evidence base for education planning. The ESA utilized EMIS data from 2021 and 2019, along with partner-produced data. At the sub-national level, UNICEF introduced micro-planning and school clustering in 46 districts across 11 provinces, training 238 officials and supporting the ongoing 1-6-6 restructuring reform. 
In 2024, UNICEF made huge strides in Early Childhood Education (ECE) and the overall efficiency of the education system in PNG. A governance model for ECE was set up, the ECE school registration framework was piloted, and 11 schools were approved for registration following the assessment of 84 schools in five provinces. In 2025, the National Department of Education (NDoE) will launch the ECE implementation, including the presentation of ECE schools that have registered and the dissemination of the registration process for ECE centres. 
The ECE governance planning in the Bogia and Nawaeb districts is now established in their district development plans, and the ECE curriculum package has been finalised, paving the way for the NDoE to introduce ECE in early 2025.
The partnership with SILAG marks an important milestone in developing PNG's first-ever Child Protection Social Service Workforce curriculum. This groundbreaking initiative will be scaled up through a strategic rollout of certified training programmes (CERT2 and CERT3) in 2025 in five provinces. The expansion includes promising partnerships with academic institutions in Goroka and Madang, further strengthening the foundation for a professional child protection workforce.  
The 2024 UNICEF supported the access to birth registration services through innovative deployment of 44 mobile registration kits and strategic capacity building, birth registration services surged by 145%, processing 63,662 certificates compared to 26,000 in 2023.
The Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) initiative in Papua New Guinea, a collaboration between UNICEF and the PNG Government, is contributing to improve demands for sanitation and hygiene in rural and underserved communities. The programme has reduced open defecation and improved health outcomes by empowering 1,887 people from 14 Open Defecation Free (ODF) communities. 
 
Building resilience and reducing risks to children and families: 
UNICEF continued to work closely with the government and its partners to build resilience and reduce the risk of disasters to children and their families.  This is being achieved by integrating resilience building, climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction into all programme areas.  UNICEF focused on building resilient, cost-effective and safe water and sanitation solutions tailored to isolated and underserved communities, including informal urban settlements in 2024. 
With UNICEF’s support, the PNG Government developed and adopted the WASH Climate Rationale, a critical milestone to ensuring that climate change considerations are integrated into national WASH programme planning. As a prerequisite for applications for climate change funding, the Climate Rationale provides a comprehensive framework for integrating climate change considerations into national development plans and strategies. Government and its partners are applying for climate fund for WASH Sector programmes. 
In the area of institutional WASH, UNICEF has initiated an innovative climate-resilient, multi-purpose, solar-powered borehole water supply systems in three health centres and solar-powered water systems in three schools. These pilots will not only ensure sustainable and reliable access to safe water, especially in rural and vulnerable communities, but also will serve as a model to replicate in other locations. 
UNICEF also tailored support to ensure sustainable energy solutions, capacity building and improving local preparedness for public health emergencies: conducted energy needs assessments for 20 health facilities, including nine provincial vaccine stores and 11 health centres, and designed solar power systems with capacities of 5 KVA, 10 KVA and 15 KVA to ensure continuity of health services to children. 
In addition, UNICEF has developed in partnership with the National Office of Child and Family Service a toolkit for Child Friendly Spaces (CFS) and implemented technical training programmes to improve the skills of thirty CFS volunteers in health and hygiene promotion during Mulitaka humanitarian response. 
UNICEF launched Climate Resilience and Peacebuilding in Education Programme in Morobe province to strengthen school resilience. Twenty target schools (10 in each district) will benefit from this programme, which aims to create resilient educational environments, minimise disruptions to learning and improve the overall safety and preparedness of schools in the face of climate-related and humanitarian challenges. Going forward, UNICEF intends to broaden its scope by undertaking a review of the Education in Emergency (EiE) policy, with a focus on climate and resilience enhancement.
Reducing violence, abuse and exploitation of children and women:
At the 1st Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children (EVAC) in Bogota in November 2024, PNG marked a significant milestone as the 33rd Pathfinder Member country through a comprehensive pledge delivered by the Ministry for Community Development, Youth and Religion. The pledge outlined key commitments, focusing on developing evidence-based action plans to EVAC, reviewing child protection laws, allocating dedicated budgets for child protection services, implementing positive parenting programmes. Through this commitment, PNG demonstrated its dedication to collaborating with Civil Society Organizations and government institutions to enhance the protection and wellbeing of all children in the country. To implement these commitments, UNICEF with child protection stakeholders will work closely with the PNG government to develop and implement a comprehensive implementation plan and advocacy strategy at both national and subnational levels to EVAC. This includes establishing robust coordination mechanisms, developing action plan to end violence against children, advocating for the institutionalization of the Parenting for Child Development (P4CD) programme, and supporting the creation of a dedicated parliamentary committee to EVAC.  
UNICEF continued its efforts to understand violence in all its types along with the root causes of conflict among communities and tribes through various studies and research. The study “Understanding barriers to gender equality in the WASH sector” found that less females (18 per cent) work in the WASH sector and the barriers to women’s entry, retention, and career progression in WASH sector include a lack of information and awareness, behavior and perception at individual, family social levels. UNICEF supported the set-up of a professional WASH women network, which is a platform for information sharing and will contribute to advocate and influence gender equality in the sector. Insight from “Addressing conflict and climate risks to WASH services in Papua New Guinea” provided recommendations for assessing, identifying and designing conflict informed and peacebuilding solutions for climate resilience WASH. 
In addition, the deep-dive diversion study on Diversion and Alternative Sentencing for adolescents in conflict with the law established the new pathways for children in conflict with the law, providing critical recommendations: that included increasing access to gender responsive and disability inclusive justice and child protection services for boys and girls in conflict with the law in urban and rural settings; developing linkages with the information justice mechanisms such as the Village Courts; developing clear referral pathways for  diversion for children in conflict with the law; capacity building of actors including in data and knowledge management; and strengthening coordination mechanisms. Furthermore, on November 2024 PNG National Parliament passed the new low on Civil Identity and Vital Statistics, a milestone for the country to provide children with universal access to birth registration
UNICEF worked strongly in violence prevention interventions, alongside the National Office of Child and Family Services (NOCFS) and local level organizations, advancing the implementation of the P4CD programme, which reached over 5303 (2941 females)  parents and caregivers across six provinces. The institutionalization process of the P4CD programme gained significant momentum through the national P4CD network, bringing together National and Provincial government representatives, academia, CSOs, and FBOs. The second annual network meeting in 2024 convened 43 participants, including 22 females, from 17 partner organizations, facilitating the sharing of good practices and establishing a roadmap for scaling up and institutionalizing the P4CD programme at the subnational level.
The programme's integration into government structures at both national and provincial levels, particularly through NOCFS and the FBO Evangelical Lutheran Church, has gained high-level support, exemplified by the Governor of Morobe Province's pledge to allocate budget for P4CD implementation, pending approval in February 2025.
The PNG Teen Entrepreneur pilot programme reached 1,307 Year-6 students (629 girls) in seven target schools since 2023, including 678 students (323 girls) in 2024. The programme develops entrepreneurial knowledge and skills, empowering students to lead productive lives and fostering an entrepreneurial mindset. Students have been involved in projects such as crop farming, handicraft design and poultry rearing, generating small incomes, and learning how to start small businesses. This initiative helps students develop key skills such as innovation, problem solving, creativity, financial literacy, teamwork, and self-confidence. An independent review of the project will be conducted in mid-2025 for possible expansion to other provinces.
 
Humanitarian response:
In 2024, UNICEF focused on improving preparedness through better planning, prepositioning of supplies and coordination among partners. UNICEF signed important long-term agreements (LTAs) with local suppliers to make sure that supplies and emergency stocks were delivered quickly to disaster hit areas.  Capacity building training provided to Health Project Promotion Officers, who are part of provincial health authorities, has been effective in providing technical assistance to provincial administrations during emergencies. 
In 2024, UNICEF provided essential life-saving supplies and support to 72,360 people, including 46,112 children. Pre-positioned supplies facilitated quick and timely response. In Enga Province, 34 inter-agency health kits were distributed for the landslide response, and maternal, newborn and child health services were provided in care centres through PHA during the Angoram violence. UNICEF health consultants supported the Provincial Health Authorities to conduct rapid assessment, planning, partners coordination, supplies distribution, tracking and response activities for Enga and East Sepik’s emergencies.   
In the conflict-affected Highland provinces, UNICEF provided essential nutrition supplies to treat 2,916 children (1,398 girls and 1,518 boys) aged 6–59 months for severe acute malnutrition. To ensure high-quality nutrition services, UNICEF trained 85 healthcare workers (44 women and 41 men) and 130 village health assistants (72 women and 58 men). Additionally, 25,551 children aged 6–59 months (12,264 girls and 13,287 boys) received Vitamin A supplementation, while 38,071 children aged 12–59 months (18,274 girls and 19,767 boys) received deworming tablets to support their growth and development. Counselling to improve maternal, infant, and young child feeding and care practices reached 59,023 primary caregivers of children aged 0–23 months through healthcare facilities and village health assistants.
The Child Protection in Emergency response to the Enga landslide and Angoram violence outbreak showcased UNICEF’s operational excellence, reaching 5,820 children, of whom 2,924 were females, through CFS and providing psychosocial support to 988 children, including 471 females, and 79 children with 43 being female were referred to other services, and engaged 20,400 people, through community awareness initiatives and Child Protection messaging. Seven CFS were established and equipped with 30 recreation kits, where 38 CFS facilitators were recruited to provide support. In addition, 30 children with disabilities were reached through tailored child protection interventions.
UNICEF’s Child Protection in emergency preparedness and response leadership demonstrated exceptional agility in addressing natural disasters and tribal conflicts. As co-chair of the Child Protection Sub-Sector, UNICEF orchestrated a coordinated response of 37 organisations, facilitating 12 strategic meetings throughout the year and trained 371 individuals, including 261 females, on child protection in emergency response, gender-based violence prevention, mental health, and psychosocial support, and psychological first aid. 
Emergency education activities included the assessment and provision of essential supplies to 14 affected schools in East Sepik. In Enga and Morobe Provinces, temporary learning spaces were established benefiting 5064 learners. During the response to the Angoram violence, educational and recreational kits were provided, and a safe temporary learning space was established, allowing 155 children to continue their education. 
 
Key enablers for results:
UNICEF achieved significant results in establishing comprehensive PSEA systems for staff and implementing partners, including community-based orientation and reporting mechanisms. Through targeted capacity building efforts, UNICEF trained 321 individuals (176 female) from implementing partners and staff, with 130 participants (77 female) representing government sectors. The program's reach extended to 13,947 people who received essential safeguarding information. Working in collaboration with other UN agencies through the Inter-Agency PSEA network, UNICEF strengthened safeguarding expertise, conducted systematic risk assessments, and helped establish robust complaint handling procedures. The collaboration with UN agencies led to the creation of confidential reporting channels, while ensuring 100 percent compliance with SEA standards among UNICEF's CSO Implementing Partners.
UNICEF engaged community-based structures, including ward committees, community influencers and health authorities to improve their understanding and build capacity on demand promotion for immunization and health services. This increased ownership, participation, and sustainability of the desired behaviors. To achieve this goal, UNICEF deployed nine provincial technical consultants, conducted Behavioural and Social Drivers (BeSD) study on immunization, health and nutrition to inform SBC interventions and concluded partnerships with two the CSO to promote demand for immunization in the six zero dose provinces. UNICEF also delivered all tools for improved demand promotion, including Child Health Record Book and the Routine Immunization Toolkit. 
UNICEF demonstrated an exemplary crisis communication in response to the Enga Province landslide in May and the East Sepik Province violence in August 2024. These efforts garnered widespread media attention, amplifying UNICEF’s voice during critical moments, and reinforcing its role as a trusted communicator in times of crisis.  Similarly, a significant stride has also been made in digital communication. The launch of a LinkedIn page for UNICEF Papua New Guinea marked a milestone, drawing thousands of followers within months. Digital engagement through platforms such as the website, social networks, and mobile initiatives has skyrocketed, reaching 727,508 people in 2024, a remarkable increase compared to 81,444 in 2023.  
UNICEF PNG particularly excelled at emergency contingency planning and staff awareness, prepositioning of emergency supplies, and signing key LTAs with local vendors to secure maximally short timing for supplies delivery. Prepositioning of emergency supplies facilitated a quick and timely response to various emergencies addressing the immediate lifesaving needs of children in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. 
UNICEF developed a resource mobilization strategy in early 2024 to ensure sustainable funding and resources for effective program implementation and disaster response. UNICEF PNG’s financial performance in 2024 was strong, achieving 115% of its annual ORR ceiling of US$16,740,000. This success was largely driven by substantial funding for health sector initiatives, particularly GAVI-funded vaccination programs, which significantly improved immunization coverage and health outcomes for children. However, there remains significant underfunding in key sectors such as WASH, and cross-sector initiatives, with a limited funding pipeline across all sectors that needs urgent attention.

UNICEF established strong partnerships with government, civil society, WB, the UN, and other organizations to effectively leverage resources for programme implementation. In collaboration with development partners such as GAVI and the World Bank, UNICEF exemplified joint advocacy efforts to secure government support for increased funding allocations. Engagement with the Global Partnership for Education brought together partners to support the government's 1-6-6 restructuring scale-up plan, with a commitment from all partners to pool resources for scale-up nationwide.
Engagement with the Government
·         UNICEF strategically positioned itself in the last couple of years by supporting the Government in the design of the WB supported CNSP. In 2024, UNICEF has signed a contract with the Government to provide technical support in the implementation of this critical intervention. 
·         A notable advancement was the new partnership with the National Capital District Commission (NCDC), which led to the plan to establish of PNG’s first Child Protection Centre, marking a significant milestone in local child protection infrastructure. The partnership with Department of Justice and Attorney General yielded substantial results through comprehensive legal framework review on juvenile justice, capacity building and comprehensive studies on diversion and alternative sentencing for children in conflict with the law that provides new pathways for children’s access to Justice. Simultaneously, collaboration with Somare Institute for Leadership and Governance to strengthen the Social Service Workforce, resulted in the development of crucial consultation to develop assessment guidelines and certified learning offers for Child Protection. 
·         In 2024, UNICEF expanded engagement with National Department of Health, including Environmental Health, ICT Branch, Medical Supply Procurement and Distribution Brach, Performance Monitoring and Research Branch, Health Facility Standard Branch to implement new areas such as healthcare waste management, health facility solarisation, Digital Health Strategy development and implementation, digital literacy promotion, and digital health solutions.
·         UNICEF reinforced its engagement with the Climate Change and Development Authority  in 2024 and provided technical support for the design and implementation of new WASH programme strategy, which is focused on climate resilience.
·         UNICEF strategically engaged all Divisions of the National Department of Education, Office of Library and Archives , the Teaching Service Commission and sub-national education offices to collaborate various aspects of the implementation of multiyear work plan, particularly during the Education Sector Analysis and Joint Sector Review. 
Engagement with UN agencies 
·         UNICEF partnered with the WB in supporting the Government roll out the USD 80 m CNSP project in two provinces. This is a nutrition sensitive, the first of its kind, social protection project in the country.
·         UNICEF has worked closely with UN partners in PNG in 2024, mainly through the UNSDCF. UNICEF co-leads the human development outcome with WHO. 
·         During 2024, UNICEF worked closely with UNAIDS, UN Women, the National AIDS Council Secretariat and UNFPA to strengthen the response to HIV/AIDS in Eastern Highlands Province. This joint effort focused on reducing the transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis and ensuring that comprehensive health services were accessible to those in need.
·         UNICEF’s collaboration with UNAIDS, UN Women, National AIDS Secretariat and UNFPA remained crucial to leverage the resource and expertise to respond to the HIV/AIDS epidemic and drastically reduce the rate of vertical transmission of HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis in Eastern Highland Province. The UNICEF-IOM joint protection programme strengthened protection mechanisms for vulnerable populations, particularly women, children, and migrants. 
·         UNICEF worked in partnership with WHO to develop and implement the MHPSS joint programme to strengthen the Heath and Child Protection systems and provide MHPSS services, including in emergency settings.
·         UNICEF and IOM continued to implement the joint and multi country programme: Addressing Protection Risks in Humanitarian Settings in Timor-Leste and Papua New Guinea, successfully delivered in its second year of implementation in the emergency response in Enga and East Sepik. 
Engagement with Development partners: 
·         One of the milestones in 2024 was that UNICEF PNG was selected as a Grant Agent (GA) for the GPE’s System Transformation Grant (STG – US$14.91million) and remaining SCG (US$1.9 million), while finalising the GPE Partnership Compact in PNG. Furthermore, the new partnership proposal with the Government of Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for the duration of the new UNICEF PNG Country Programme 2024-2028 has been finalized with an initial funding scope of AU$30 million, pending final approval. 
·         UNICEF PNG has been the GA for the Global Partnership for Education - System Capacity Grant (SCG)’s initial US$700,000 while receiving funds through the Asia Development Bank for the implementation of the Pacific Regional Education Framework. 
·         UNICEF’s efforts were further supported by several donors, including DFAT Australia, MFAT, the Government of Japan, and the World Bank, KOICA, and the Australian High Commission and the world Bank. Alliances with organisations such as GAVI and professional associations such as the PNG Paediatric Society and the PNG O&G Society played a critical role in advancing health initiatives. Nutrition efforts received significant support from donors such as USAID, UNICEF Australia, the Eleva Foundation, and the UK National Committee. 
Sector leadership and humanitarian coordination.
·         Through its role as sector lead agency for Education, Nutrition and Child Protection, UNICEF played a key role in coordinating humanitarian actors during various emergencies. As part of the Health Cluster, UNICEF played a key role in managing maternal and child health work.
Engagement with CSOs
In 2024, strategic partnerships with civil society organisations remained critical to leverage resources and maximise impact on results for children, both in terms of regular development work and humanitarian response. UNICEF partnered with Catholic Church Health Services in the implementation of nutrition services in health facilities, communities and schools. UNICEF collaborated with Touching the Untouchables for the Hygiene and CLTS component of the Klinpela Banz projek, and CARE International for the Climate Resilient WASH as a Catalyst for Peace project and the emergency response landslide project; with CARE and ChildFund for child protection in emergency response, MHPSS and community based child protection; with ADRA and CARE International to ensure a multisectoral response that encompassed the domains of education, water, health, and child protection.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Limited Resource and Capacity
Resource limitations are a significant challenge across key sectors. In health, many facilities are understaffed and under-resourced, which affects the ability to provide consistent, high-quality care. Similarly, the education sector faces staff shortages and high turnover, which undermine the quality of educational services. In the WASH sector, planning, implementation, and monitoring are continually impacted by limited financial, logistical, and human resources at the national, provincial, and district levels.
The establishment of the child protection center showed promise but struggled with sustained government funding and staffing in 2024. This experience underscored the need for long-term resource allocation and workforce development beyond initial setup support. In 2025, efforts will focus on advocacy to secure government and partner commitment to key funding priorities. This will involve shared ownership among stakeholders, including the private sector, and improved tools to strengthen the social service workforce.
Data and Evidence
The challenge of updated data availability in PNG is significant. The national EMIS remains outdated, with critical components lacking, and data analysis capacity at the DoEs is rudimentary. The absence of geolocation data for schools is also a concern. The lack of accurate population data undermines planning and resource allocation. The nutrition sector grapples with outdated data, with the last national survey conducted in 2005 and recent data from 2009/2010. The absence of real-time, reliable data on the status of WASH services in the country persists, despite the efforts of the DNPM in developing the mWater MIS system, which requires further expansion and enhanced accessibility for users. 
In 2025, an evaluation of the Convergence Programme will be conducted to assess its relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, coherence, and sustainability. This evaluation will generate evidence on the programme's impact across all five converging sectors of UNICEF programming: Health and Nutrition, Education, WASH, Child Protection, and Social Policy. The findings will inform future refinements to the programme's design and approach. Additionally, support for the National Nutrition Survey is expected to address the current data gap in the Nutrition Programme. UNICEF will continue to advocate for and support the functionality of the Education Management Information System (EMIS).
Policy and Plans:
There is currently no government implementation plan for the National WASH Policy 2015 - 2030. Formation of the NWASHA (National WASH Authority) with the mandate to implement the policy has not yet materialised after almost 10 years of the policy. The lack of clearly defined responsibilities for the delivery of WASH services contributes to an uncoordinated WASH Sector with no systematic plan nor funding to achieve WASH Policy targets. Consequently, the delivery of WASH services in rural areas continues to be disorganised and fragmented. 
UNICEF will continue to provide support to the WASH Programme Management Unit (PMU) to strengthening coordination within the WASH sector and to improve collaboration among stakeholders, streamline efforts and ensure more effective delivery of water, sanitation and hygiene services.
Cultural Beliefs and Practices:
Cultural beliefs and practices often have a significant influence on health-seeking behaviour in PNG. Some communities still prefer traditional birth attendants to skilled healthcare workers. In Angoram, cultural resistance initially hampered the establishment of child-friendly spaces, demonstrating how local traditions and community perspectives can significantly influence programme implementation. The successful resolution of cultural barriers in Angoram provided particularly valuable insights. By engaging local leaders, acknowledging community concerns, and adapting activities to align with local traditions, the program eventually gained community acceptance. This experience underscored the importance of flexible, culturally sensitive implementation strategies. Building on these lessons, UNICEF plans to continue its engagement with local level organizations, community leaders, and faith-based organizations, ensuring that activities are adapted through community consultation. Furthermore, UNICEF will document this experience to strengthen and inform future community-based interventions, creating a knowledge base of effective cultural engagement strategies.
Coordination: 
Close collaboration with sub-national actors is vital. This strategy was particularly effective in modelling ECE schools and governance, as well as in 1-6-6 school clustering micro-planning. While dedicated budgets and labour-intensive technical assistance and capacity building at provincial and district levels were essential, these efforts yielded immediate results, contributing to the realisation of key policies and reform initiatives.
The timely coordination and engagement with the regional office in related areas enabled the Office to be better equipped with resources and available expertise, identified solutions to challenges and enabled risk-informed decision-making. It also contributed to learning from practices within the region and beyond. Efficiency and coherence were secured through regular catch-up discussions, joint monitoring, shared accountability and agreed adjustments following any change developments. 
The Enga province landslide crisis exposed gaps in coordinating responses across government agencies, non-governmental organisations, and community groups. UNICEF has been working closely with UN agencies in Papua New Guinea to support the development and implementation of the Mulitaka Disaster Recovery Plan (MDRA). A key focus of the MDRA is to strengthen coordination among stakeholders. The Steering Committee provides overall leadership by bringing together government and development partners, including donors, UN agencies, and major NGOs, on a quarterly basis to coordinate efforts, provide advisory support, and review the implementation of the recovery plan. 
Partnerships & Resource Mobilization: 
In 2025, UNICEF PNG will strengthen its resource mobilization strategy to better align with its partnership objectives and funding priorities. Efforts will focus on securing both immediate and long-term funding through direct donor engagement, strategic positioning, leveraging private sector partnerships and stronger relations, particularly with key financial institutions. Addressing underfunding in critical sectors such as WASH, Nutrition and cross-sector initiatives remains a priority, alongside expanding the funding pipeline.

In 2024, poverty in the Philippines dropped. August figures show the number of families that stayed poor1 lowered to 10.9 per cent in 2023 from 13.2 per cent in 2021. In the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region of Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), the most impoverished region, the proportion of poor families fell to 23.5 per cent from 28 per cent.  
 
The economy was stable, with gross domestic product (GDP) growing by 5.6 per cent in 2024. It is projected to expand 6.2 per cent in 20252, positioning the country for upper middle-income status and achieving the Philippine Development Plan's social and economic transformation objectives. The Philippines has one of the highest Gini coefficient (39.09) in the region. With inequalities persisting, greater investment in social protection is crucial in a country that allots 2.6 per cent of its GDP to social protection expenditure, significantly below the Asia Pacific average of 7.5 per cent.3  
  
The release of the 2023 National Nutrition Survey (NNS) showed child stunting fell to 23.6 per cent from 26.7 per cent in 2018-2019, putting the country on track to meet Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, wasting (5.6 per cent) and anemia among pregnant women (21.7 per cent) and children aged 6-23 months (25.3 per cent) remain concerns. Overweight and obesity are increasing at an alarming rate among 5-10-year-olds (12.9 per cent) and 10-19-year-olds (12.5 per cent). Stunting in BARMM declined slightly to 34.4 per cent in 2023 from 36.0 per cent in 2018–2019 and 2021, though it remains alarmingly high. Meanwhile, wasting increased marginally, from 6.8 per cent in 2018–2019 and 2021 to 6.9 per cent in 2023.  
 
Philippines no longer ranks among the top five countries with the most unvaccinated children. WHO and UNICEF reported in 2024 that only 163,000 children had zero dose of vaccination in 2023 compared to 637,000 in 2022. The measles outbreak (declared in March) drove the BARMM government to address the low vaccination rates – 61 per cent of Bangsamoro children remained unvaccinated and only 18 per cent were fully vaccinated4. UNICEF-supported campaign saw 1.19 million children inoculated by May 2024. 
 
Adolescent pregnancy dropped to 5.4 per cent in 2022 from 8.6 per cent in 2017 but the percentage of women aged 15-49 who received antenatal care at least four times after giving birth to live babies fell to 76.68 per cent in 2023 from 87.81 per cent in 2019. As of September 2024, 1,643 new HIV cases were reported among individuals aged 10-19 years, underscoring the need for targeted prevention and care. 
 
Six tropical cyclones entered the country in a span of 26 days in October and November, affecting 13 million people – many repeatedly – in 17 out of 18 regions. Floods, landslides, and winds destroyed homes, schools, health facilities and impacted 23,224 children under 5; 4,354 pregnant women; and 4,354 breastfeeding mothers. Some 20.9 million learners were forced to stop learning. Several regions suspended classes as temperatures soared to above 50 degrees Celsius, exacerbated by El Nino in the second quarter, and affecting 3.6 million students.  
 
The learning crisis persists. Data from the 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment released in 2024 revealed that the Philippines ranks last in the regional and global assessment of 15-year-old students.  In 2022, only 19.5 per cent of 3-4-year-olds were enrolled in early childhood education, 20.3 per cent among girls and 18.7 per cent among boys. In 2023, one in four children did not enroll in compulsory kindergarten classes on time. Nine out of 10 fifth grade children cannot read at their expected level; fourth grade students in BARMM lag behind their peers by two years. Seven per cent of adolescents aged 16 and 17 nationally and 18 per cent in BARMM are not in school in 2022, due to the need to work, lack of personal interest, marriage, among other reasons, with higher percentage among boys. 
 
Shifts in the leadership at the Department of Education (DepEd) in June introduced legislative changes by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). New regulations include laws institutionalizing comprehensive mental health initiatives in basic education; and the implementing rules for the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning Law, supporting struggling learners. Their implementation will be key to addressing the learning crisis. At the same time, a new law was passed to discontinue the use of mother tongue, both as a medium of instruction and subject, in multi-lingual classes from kindergarten to Grade 3 which may hinder effective learning of children with various mother tongues other than Filipino and English.  
  
The Philippines struggles to meet SDG targets for water and sanitation, with progress among the poorest 20 per cent falling short. Some 3.4 million people practice open defecation daily, including 1.3 million children. Five regions, including BARMM had less than 80 per cent of their population with access to basic sanitation. Basic drinking water coverage is high (at 97 per cent) but disparities persist, particularly on access to premises, needing equitable and targeted interventions.

The year marked the official start of the 9th Country Programme for Children (CPC9) in the Philippines after approval by the UNICEF Executive Board in February 2024 and the signing of the Country Programme Action Plan by the government in March. 
 
Following extensive consultations with all relevant national and sub-national agencies, work plans were signed with 35 national agencies and BARMM entities. The National Steering Committee meeting that took place in August was an opportunity to discuss government priorities for children as well as UNICEF modelling approach and climate action for children. 
 
Building on key programmatic shifts, UNICEF further developed programmatic strategies, including those for social behaviour change, public finance management, child rights and business, and knowledge management. The country office also developed a modelling guide that provides a framework and tools for designing scalable, replicable, and sustainable models.  
 
UNICEF in collaboration with the Council for the Welfare of Children (CWC), the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) launched the virtual Situation Analysis (SitAn) of Children (www.situationofchildren.org/PH) to promote evidence-based decision-making. The site provides access to data on over 100 indicators and analysis on six dimensions and 25 subdimensions of children’s rights. The virtual SitAn is envisaged to serve as a primary source of knowledge on children; guide strategic and technical partnerships; and inform statistical development plans.
 
UNICEF supported Philippines Statistics Authority (PSA) in developing the Philippine SDG data platform, which automates data collection, validation, and consolidation. This platform aids in the regular updating and publication of the Philippines’ SDG Watch, supporting SDG monitoring relevant to child rights. UNICEF also assisted in finalizing data assessment results to inform the statistical framework on children, paving the way for smart data production. 
 
Following the severe weather disturbances that hit the country in the final months of 2024, UNICEF provided WASH, social protection and education response. With the Department of Welfare and Social Development (DSWD), UNICEF distributed multipurpose humanitarian cash assistance to 9,000 vulnerable households with 0–5-year-old children, which are part of the Pantawid Pamilya Pilipino Program (4Ps). Vulnerable families were given Php6,700 through the cash transfer programme to help with their expenses. Cash transfers empower families to make their own choices, restore dignity, stimulate local economies, and provide flexible, cost-effective aid that helps families recover faster in a manner of their own choosing. 
 
Health and Nutrition
UNICEF provided strategic support to the Department of Health (DOH) for the reinstatement of the national immunization programme – a long-term policy bottleneck. The reinstatement led to the establishment of the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group and the reactivation of the National Immunization Committee and Maternal and Newborn Health Technical Working Group. 
 
Responding to the measles outbreak in BARMM, UNICEF supported the region in vaccinating 87 per cent of its target population. By the third quarter, 50 per cent of the children in the region were fully immunized, from 43.8 per cent in 2023. UNICEF mobilized health workers and religious leaders who promoted vaccine use through fatwas; and it strengthened the Ministry of Health capacity by enhancing human resources, cold chain management, and monitoring systems. 
 
UNICEF’s technical and financial support empowered 275 local governments to implement a strategy called ‘Reaching Every Purok’ (subdivision of a village), a crucial component for improving immunization. UNICEF also financed and technically facilitated a gender study on immunization that will provide inputs to shaping the upcoming national immunization strategy. 
  
UNICEF successfully advocated and provided technical support for the approval of the first PhilHealth Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) Benefit Package that will give more than 100,000 children access to treatment without financial burden. This marks the world’s first primary care social health financing package for SAM. Through the benefit package, families with children suffering from SAM will receive treatment services worth ¿7,500 (approximately US$125) for children 0-6 months old and ¿17,000 (US$280) for children 6-60 months old. This financial support helps relieve families from the burden of added treatment costs. The treatment package provides medical care and ready-to-use therapeutic foods, which help restore weight and treat the underlying infections affecting children with severe acute malnutrition. Families are also supported with ongoing counseling from health professionals, who guide them in proper infant and young child feeding and hygiene practices to prevent the recurrence of malnutrition. 
 
As the key partner to DOH and World Bank for the Philippine Multisectoral Nutrition Project (PMNP), a US$178 million government loan agreement with the World Bank to address stunting in 235 high-prevalence municipalities, UNICEF led the development of evidence-based nutrition SBC prototype interventions focusing on antenatal care, breastfeeding, complementary feeding, food production and WASH. Moreover, UNICEF led capacity building efforts for 1,782 health providers in growth monitoring, MIYCN, Philippine Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition, and nutrition in emergencies. Technical support also enhanced 4Ps Social Welfare and Development Indicator monitoring tool, and revitalized salt iodization efforts. Based on implementation research and advocacy supported by UNICEF, Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS) was recommended by the Health Technology Assessment Council for inclusion in the essential medicines list. This will improve access for pregnant women and contribute to addressing anemia and other micronutrient deficiencies. As a result, UNICEF contributed to delivery of essential nutrition services to 980,168 children (503,709 boys and 476,459 girls) aged 0–5 years and 86,249 pregnant women.      
 
UNICEF supported the development of the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition Operational Plan, which includes nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions. In partnership with EDCOM II, UNICEF assisted in the planning and development of a nutrition investment plan that aims to address the triple burden of undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and overnutrition. To prevent overweight and obesity, UNICEF advocated for legislation that aims to establish front-of-pack nutrition labelling and regulate the marketing of unhealthy food to children. Additionally, a school nutrition assessment tool was tested in selected schools, identifying opportunities to strengthen school nutrition programmes.
 
BARMM saw a reduction stunting, falling to 34.3 per cent in 2023 from 36 per cent in 2018-2019 & 2021 while wasting increased marginally to 6.9 per cent.  UNICEF continued to support efforts to strengthen local systems, including the adoption and implementation of the Bangsamoro Regional Plan of Action for Nutrition 2023-2028. Through the growth monitoring programme, 233,196 children were screened, achieving 90 per cent coverage across programme sites, while 320 children were admitted to the Management of Acute Malnutrition programme. UNICEF’s impact extended to over 414,000 people, 52 per cent of whom were 0-18 years old.
 
Learning and Skills
To improve the quality of early learning, UNICEF supported the government in implementing reforms in the early childhood education system. Early learning and development standards were updated, a new kindergarten curriculum was rolled out, and training guidelines for child development workers were created. UNICEF also supported the Early Childhood Care and Development Strategic Plan 2030 and introduced a budgeting tool for early childhood education programmes.
 
New models initiated by UNICEF with governments bolstered efforts to tackle the learning crisis. A modelling initiative on early childhood education to primary education named “LINK” commenced in Regions 8 and 9 to facilitate smooth transition from early childhood to basic education for better learning outcomes and wellbeing of children. A model on multigrade schools that has a digital learning component is also being tested in one region. UNICEF’s inclusive child-centred disaster risk reduction and management model promoted effective implementation of disaster risk reduction management policies in schools and communities.
 
Taking a system strengthening approach to tackle the learning crisis, UNICEF in partnership with DepEd strengthened national and subnational capacity through training education officials in planning and monitoring, developing Division Education Development Plans and the finalization of the costed Bangsamoro Education Reform Development Plan 2035. Technical assistance was provided to key reform initiatives including a revised curriculum for grades 1–3 with digital resources for literacy and numeracy, a grade 5 regional learning assessment (SEA-PLM 2024), and tools for socio-emotional learning. Strategic roadmaps for learner support, teacher excellence, and inclusive education were created, alongside research on learning loss, education financing, and teacher hardship to inform policy and programs.
 
The finalization of the Bangsamoro Education Reform Plan 2035 was one of the key measures supported by UNICEF to address the severe learning crisis in the region, uncovered financing gaps that require collaborative effort to address. Plugging the gaps is crucial to ensure that no child is left behind in Muslim Mindanao. 
 
Child Protection
The visibility of, and commitment to, strengthening child protection systems increased in 2024, indicating that advocacy efforts are paying off. UNICEF marked a milestone with the endorsement of the 4th National Plan of Action for Children (NPAC). Developed by UNICEF with DSWD and CWC, the NPAC includes a chapter dedicated to child protection that takes on a holistic view on child safety as opposed to treating issues that harm children in a fragmented manner. It focuses on systems strengthening at the national and sub-national levels. 
 
UNICEF also partnered with the Office of the Undersecretary for Attached Agencies and International Affairs and contributed to planning and delivery of key commitments at the 1st Global Ministerial Conference on EVAC, including a commitment to allocate 3 per cent of government funding to child protection.
 
Using catalytic funds, UNICEF is supporting DSWD efforts to include child protection systems in its modelling process, a move that may result in the institutionalization of the systems within government. The model will also be implemented in BARMM, where achievements in strengthening child protection systems include the establishment of women and children protection units, capacity building of the social service workforce, and strengthening justice for children initiatives. The child protection systems model will be the first of its kind and will showcase the functionality of critical components in a system at local level. The model is anticipated to scale up once proven successful. 
 
In BARMM, with technical support of UNICEF, the Ministry of Social Services and Development (MSSD) and partners finalized the roadmap on child protection system strengthening, which addresses gaps in legal frameworks, human resources, budgeting, governance, programmes, and community engagement. It provides a costed, comprehensive plan for MSSD to improve and monitor child protection services. A visit by members of the Committee on the Rights of the Child visit further boosted visibility and government commitment to reforms in child protection, child marriage, birth registration, and other child rights.
 
Through UNFPA and UNICEF technical and financial support, the national strategy to eliminate child marriages was drafted. UNICEF also enhanced its partnership with UNHCR to increase birth registration in BARMM. As secretariat and co-chair of the Country Task Force on Monitoring and Reporting, UNICEF worked with the UN and civil society organizations to extend the Strategic Plan with the Armed Forces of the Philippines to protect children in situations of armed conflict.
 
Child-Sensitive Public Policy 
Given the government’s prioritization of work on inadequacies in social sector financing and public finance inefficiencies, UNICEF focused on strengthening child-responsive public finance systems and improving social sector allocations in education, health and nutrition, and social protection at national and sub-national levels through evidenced-based policy advocacy. UNICEF facilitated the Philippines' participation in the Regional EU-UNICEF South Asia and Southeast Asia Public Finance Facility and supported evidence generation in Public Expenditure and Financial Accountability (PEFA) gender and child-responsive assessments, regional child poverty and public finance patterns. 
 
UNICEF supported updating the 4Ps tool for monitoring household beneficiaries' status in income, health, nutrition, and education of their children to optimize social protection coverage[1]. The initiative also addresses challenges in adopting child multi-dimensional poverty measures that hinder the development of policies and programmes that reflect children's changing needs. 
 
UNICEF's advocacy and technical support increased national level financial commitment in the 2025 Budget for integrating nutrition and health services for the first 1,000 days of children and pregnant mothers. Technical support was also provided for developing a model to design disability-inclusive social protection interventions planned for 2025 scale up. 
 
UNICEF invested in building new partnerships and advocacy with government agencies to influence regulations across various business sectors, provided guidance on child rights and business practices in ESG reporting reforms for public companies and promoted family friendly policies with corporate partners and the Department of Labor and Employment's family welfare programme.
 
Climate, Environment and Resilience
In 2024, UNICEF established strong partnerships with government entities, particularly in support to the implementation of the national action plans and nationally determined contributions. UNICEF's advocacy contributed to the prioritization of child and youth dimensions within disaster resilience frameworks, notably at the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction, which included the Local Conference of Youth 2024. The statement, which advocates stronger youth participation in disaster risk reduction, was also presented at the 29th Conference of the Parties for the United Nations Climate Change Conference. 
 
Through U-Report platform, UNICEF also empowered children and the youth to play an active role in shaping climate and disaster risk reduction programmes and policies. UNICEF’s partnership with the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) and National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council contributed to the development of the local disaster risk management and management formulation guidelines, ensuring children and youth perspectives are included in local disaster resilience planning.
 
UNICEF developed a toolkit for children and youth climate action and disaster resilience developed offers practical strategies for fostering long-term behavioural changes in households, schools, and communities. It also created a training to equip Sangguniang Kabataan officers with the knowledge and skills to address climate challenges in their communities and enable them to integrate climate action and disaster resilience into local planning processes. Championing child and youth engagement in designing sustainable solutions, UNICEF harnessed partnerships with government agencies and youth networks to mobilize nearly 3,000 children and young people in climate and disaster resilience initiatives. 
 
UNICEF developed and launched together with the Department of Education and CSO partners the use of Oky app that enhanced culturally sensitive menstrual health awareness and digital literacy for 46,386 adolescents, particularly girls. Further opportunities include integrating the app into the school curriculum and exploring cross-sectoral links with health and child protection programs.
 
Key interventions targeted the 3 per cent of the population still practicing open defecation. Collaborative efforts resulted in the development of an aide-mémoire, presented by DENR to the board of the Infrastructure and Utilities Development Committee of NEDA. It underscored the need for integrated, sustainable solutions and resource mobilization. UNICEF's technical contributions reinforced the alignment of national climate and WASH priorities with resilience frameworks, enhancing the capacity for effective implementation and ensuring long-term, scalable impact. This led to the development of a consolidated action plan and the achievement of key milestones ahead of the formal approval of the Integrated Water Resources Management Plan by NEDA in February 2024. 
 
UNICEF helped to expand financing options and strengthen accountability of 75 local governments that received Php1 billion funding for WASH using the Results-Based Monitoring and Evaluation framework. Supporting DOH, UNICEF finalized the WASH in Emergencies Manual of Operations, which standardized emergency response protocols. To address planning gaps and align local actions with national priorities, the WASH in Healthcare Facilities Roadmap was also developed.  
 
In BARMM, UNICEF addressed key WASH bottlenecks such as limited local governance capacity and inadequate sanitation access. This impacted 414,000 people in the region, including approximately 52 per cent of children. Among others, UNICEF's supported zero open defecation communities and established iWASH Councils to integrate WASH planning into local governance structures; conducting emergency preparedness and response training to strengthen disaster resilience for 41 local government units in Lanao del Sur and equipping participants with critical disaster risk reduction skills; and holding 140 community dialogues across 44 local governments to engage diverse sectors, including children, youth, and women, to develop inclusive disaster risk reduction plans.

UNICEF continues to establish and strengthen its partnerships with a wide range of actors in support of the realization of children's rights. In 2024, UNICEF particularly strengthened its partnership with national agencies for modelling and scaling up innovative approaches. A list of 20 models with key partner national agency committing to take part and scale up the initiative was successfully approved by the National Steering Committee of the country programme co-chaired by NEDA. One notable partnership is with DSWD’s Social Technology Bureau which will operationalize both the model of the child protection systems model as well as Project CHERISH, which is a community-based programme that provides holistic care and support to Children with Disability (CWD) and their families to address substantial unmet needs and provide comprehensive social services.
 
UNICEF also established a Memorandum of Understanding with EDCOM II to contribute to the education reform in the Philippines. UNICEF will particularly contribute through evidence generation and key area of collaboration include the development of early childhood care and development-early childhood education and nutrition investment plans to ensure that the sector is appropriately funded.
 
UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with international financial institutions. UNICEF collaborate with the World Bank and DOH for the enhancement of multisectoral nutrition programming through the PMNP, particularly leading on the components of social behavior change, capacity building for frontline workers and local leaders, performance-based grants to local governments, and project evaluation. The collaboration also advocated for the institutionalization of a nutrition resource tracking framework that UNICEF developed in partnership with the Philippine Institute of Development Studies. UNICEF provided technical assistance in the development and testing of a household convergence scorecard to ensure comprehensive, multisectoral nutrition services and interventions reach targeted women, children in households. UNICEF also contributed to the Philippines Economic Update, which highlighted the need for investments in the early years for building human capital and driving economic growth.  
 
Other examples include UNICEF, partnership with the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and the Australian Government, to support various reform interventions across three bureaus of the DSWD and with the Ministry of Social Services and Development in BARMM. 
 
UNICEF and the European Union successfully advocated for the Philippines’ inclusion into the Public Finance Facility, an initiative that supports the best use of the public budget. The facility seeks to alleviate the lives of the most vulnerable children with efficient and effective management of public finance system at national and subnational levels. 
 
Due to the fragmented accountability of climate action for children, UNICEF dedicated time to explore and broker new partnerships for climate change, a priority in the new country programme. This included the establishment of the Inter-Agency Working Group for Children and Youth Participation in Climate Action and Disaster Resilience, which counts as members DENR, OCD, CWC, DepEd, the Climate Change Commission, and the National Youth Commission. UNICEF supported the drafting of its terms of reference and aligned its structure with national priorities. This ensures children and youth are integrated into policymaking processes and institutionalizes their leadership in the climate and disaster risk reduction agenda. 
 
Partnerships were formalized with regulatory agencies in Labor, Trade and Investment, and the Securities and Exchange Commission to consult and set the engagement strategy to support progressive universal social protection coverage and set the momentum for human and child rights business operations for the country. UNICEF will prioritize establishing its credibility as a leading technical advisor to support impactful child-sensitive public policy development and implementation through robust and quality policy tools, high caliber evidence and advocacy efforts to mobilize human and financial resources of local government units through models for scalability and replicability.
 
UNICEF Philippines continues to partner with a wide range of stakeholders to mobilize resources to improve the lives of children and adolescents in the country and support them during emergencies. For instance, UNICEF worked with 100 organizations and engaged 3,211 individuals to form multisectoral immunization coalitions in two regions and 42 localities. Advocacy efforts helped pass 167 policies supporting an Php11.11 million initiative to provide universal immunization services, including to marginalized populations. 
 
Philippine corporate and philanthropic donors continued to support health, nutrition, education and emergency relief services for children and adolescents across the country, as well as advocacy and communications efforts. These include Cebu Pacific through its in-flight fundraising programme Change for Good, SM Prime,  J. Amado Araneta Foundation, Universal Storefront Services Corporation, GoRewards, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, For in-kind contribution HCG Philippines provided water closets and a promotional grant to support WASH programmes, while Cebu Pacific contributed to freight services for emergency supplies.
 
Individual donors remained a significant source of unrestricted funding used by UNICEF to support children’s needs, accounting for Php 250.137 million last year. Donations were made through e-wallets and payment service providers GCash and Maya, e-commerce channels Shopee, Lazada, and Grab, and venues for face-to-face giving like SM malls and St Luke’s Medical Center.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
The need for stronger coordination and alignment of priorities across various government agencies and stakeholders remains. Issues-based laws in child protection led to fragmented strategies at the sub-national level. The newly created Presidential Office for Child Protection’s mandate also overlaps with other government agencies. Continuously reinforcing a child protection system approach and streamlining child protection issue-based policies, especially at the national level, is necessary. Similarly, coordination of efforts on climate action for children is a challenge due to the fragmented accountability across national and subnational agencies.

Establishing new partnerships required extensive relationship-building, which took time. In climate action and disaster resilience, aligning partners’ goals to integrate child-sensitive approaches into frameworks was a complex process. Efforts to develop the Climate Landscape for Children highlighted a wide range of stakeholders involved in climate with fragmented accountabilities.
 
Changes in leadership and restructuring within government, for example in DepEd, resulted in changing priorities and necessitated a period of re-establishing relations and clarifying expectations. The upcoming 2025 elections may exacerbate this but also provide opportunities with the leadership turnover particularly for child protection in BARMM and across the country. 
 
Limited and uneven capacity for Social Behavior Change (SBC) across levels of government continues to hinder efforts to effectively address behavioral issues and harmful social norms. Many interventions still rely on communication strategies alone to influence behaviors. While communication remains a critical component of SBC, it is insufficient to drive meaningful change in behaviors. As UNICEF continues to provide technical support to government in addressing behavioral issues and harmful social norms, there is a need to strengthen systems for social and behavioral data collection, community engagement platforms, human resources, and capacities. This will ensure quality programming for SBC, which promotes positive behaviors and norms, improved community engagement and participation, and demand for quality services. 
 
Lessons learned 
Building on the lessons from the previous country programme, where UNICEF pilots have not always been scaled consistently or sustainability, UNICEF Philippines reflected on the characteristics and lifecycle of interventions in order to ensure that they are scalable, replicable and sustainable at both local and national level. This led to the development of a modelling guide. 
 
UNICEF defined models as illustrations of how a set of interventions work in an integrated way at local level to create change with the intent of replicating that approach on a large scale and a strategy for scaling up impact. The stages of the modelling approach were defined as model selection, concept development, prototyping, scale-up testing and finally, full scale up. The modelling guide developed identified the key elements to support the design and implementation of this modelling approach considering elements such as the core concept (including the scaling up approach), ecosystem, finance and lifecycle. In the context of CPC9, UNICEF identified 20 models across various sectors which were presented and approved by the National Steering Committee of the country programme.
 
The first year of the country programme for PCO prioritized a more intensified approach across all programme sectors to apply public finance management (PFM) for children to move away from “projectizing” interventions to more at-scale results for the most vulnerable. To ensure programme sectors’ effective coordination and optimal strategic partnership with government, an office PFM strategy was developed paired with internal training and workshops that laid out clear directions towards a collective upstream engagement for child-sensitive public policy. The strategy combined with the roadmap for each sector prioritized existing interventions for scalability with a PFM lens; identified gaps in data, frameworks and partners; and set the vision in motion to establish UNICEF PCO as a main actor in the PFM space.   
 
The evaluation of UNICEF Philippines’ adolescent programming found distinguishing the strategy as a flexible policy framework that guides comprehensive adolescent programming rather than limiting it to specific outputs ensures adaptability to national and local contexts. The evaluation underscores its alignment with the “second decade of life” approach and enables targeted interventions to address childhood deficits and support vulnerable adolescents.

The evaluation highlighted the importance of inter-sectoral collaboration, emphasizing the need for clear leadership, defined roles, and accountability to optimize coordination and results. The adolescent task force played a relevant role in fostering collaboration across UNICEF sections. However, its efficiency and effectiveness could have been enhanced with clearer terms of reference, stronger accountability for collaborative outcomes, and the designation of a dedicated unit or focal person. While the taskforce demonstrated fair alignment with UNICEF's internal sections and programme modalities, it fell short of engaging external stakeholders comprehensively or encompassing all aspects of adolescent programming as initially envisioned. 
 
Gender analysis and equity considerations are critical at all stages of adolescent development and participation programming to ensure inclusivity and responsiveness to vulnerabilities. Strengthening systems for collecting disaggregated data by gender, geography, and other factors will enable evidence-based planning and targeted interventions.

Sustainability emerged as a central lesson, with findings underscoring the need for early engagement with government counterparts, clear exit strategies, and capacity-building for local stakeholders. Institutionalizing successful initiatives, such as the Oky period tracker app, within government systems demonstrates the potential for long-term impact. Risk management, including emergency preparedness strategies, must be integrated into programme designs to ensure continuity during crises.

Strengthening governance platforms, scaling successful pilots, and leveraging national frameworks like the hharmonized gender and development guidelines will ensure that programming remains inclusive, sustainable, and impactful.
 
The evaluation recommends refining the theory of change for adolescent programming, integrating a unified results framework with clear indicators and process metrics.
 
Outlook
In 2025, key milestones will include the mid-term review of the Philippine Development Plan – where it is anticipated that the NEDA request for the inclusion of child protection will be discussed – and the Philippines conducting the next round of Voluntary National Review. Both processes will be opportunities to take stock of progress towards inclusive and transformative development and facilitate the sharing of experiences in accelerating the implementation of the 2030 agenda. New evidence will be available in measuring progress against child outcome, with the government conducting major surveys such as the Demographic and Health Survey, and results of the census and other key social sector surveys being made available.
 
IN BARMM, election in May 2025 may change the political landscape as well as increase possible violence between competing political parties and fractions. While the parliamentary elections to determine the new Bangsamaro autonomous government are possibly postponed to 2026, local elections in BARMM will take place in 2025 and may lead to localized tensions and confrontations. This in turn is likely to disrupt service delivery of social programmes for children, at least temporarily.

Thailand’s economy demonstrated resilience amidst global uncertainties, steadily recovering from the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2024, Thailand ranked third in GDP among ASEAN nations and fourth in GDP per capita, with economic growth of 2.4% fueled by private consumption and tourism. Despite these achievements, structural challenges, such as high household debt and competitiveness issues among small businesses, continued to hinder economic performance. Socio-economic disparities remain entrenched and disproportionally impact children, as evidenced by a 21.5% national incidence rate of multidimensional poverty.
The political landscape in 2024 also witnessed significant shifts, with Paetongtarn Shinawatra selected as the new Prime Minister in a parliamentary vote following the dismissal of Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin by the Constitutional Court. The new administration continued to prioritize economic growth through initiatives like the flagship digital wallet scheme, designed to boost household purchasing power and stimulate the economy, especially among low-income earners.  
Thailand’s demographic transition has far-reaching implications for its economic and social trajectory. By 2050, children are projected to comprise only 16% of Thailand’s population, down from 21% in 2023. This trend places immense pressure on social welfare systems, with fewer working-age individuals supporting an ageing population. Without transformative investments in human capital, this demographic shift risks translating into higher taxes, reduced public spending on education and early childhood development, and prolonged economic stagnation.
The total national budget increased from 3.185 trillion baht ($95.55 billion) in 2023 to 3.48 trillion baht ($104.4 billion) in 2024, representing a 9.3% rise. In 2024, budget increases were observed across key social sectors, aligning with Thailand’s broader social and human development goals under its 20-Year National Strategy, related Master Plans, and the 13th National Economic and Social Development Plan. Specifically, the education budget allocation increased by 0.8%, health by 7.0%, and social protection by 6.5%. However, as a percentage of the total sectoral budget allocation, the combined share for the social sectors slightly declined from 34.48% in 2023 to 33.65 in 2024.
Meanwhile, environmental challenges exacerbated vulnerabilities in 2024, with intensified flooding in northern Thailand that affected 64,000 children, highlighting the urgency of building climate resilience. Vulnerable communities bear the brunt of these crises, further underscoring the importance of inclusive policies that prioritize the well-being of children and future generations. Thailand is ranked as the 9th most vulnerable country in the world as per the Global Climate Risk Index. 
While economic policies address some immediate needs, these trends underscore the critical need to strengthen human capital development and ensure equitable access to quality services from birth and is crucial for Thailand to achieve its aspiration to become a high-income country and an OECD member.
Thailand’s 2020 Human Capital Index of 0.61 underscores this urgency, indicating that a child born today will achieve only 61% of their potential productivity due to gaps in education and health. Although the country’s universal health care programme is a notable achievement, persistent weaknesses in the quality of public education demonstrated by declining trends in education outcomes and fragmented service delivery across sectors threaten long-term human development. The ‘Thailand Zero Dropout’ (TZD) initiative, launched in 2024, aims to reintegrate over 1 million out-of-school children into school or work within five years. This initiative represents a unique and timely opportunity to reimagine secondary education as a system of multiple pathways while addressing systemic barriers that push children out of school. 
In parallel, Thailand’s election in 2024 to the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) marked a critical moment in its global standing and its domestic commitment to human rights. This achievement reflects the country’s progress in aligning with international human rights standards, with significant implications for the well-being and future of children in Thailand. Legal and policy reforms brought domestic legislation closer to principles enshrined in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The passing of the Marriage Equality Act, which affirmed the rights of LGBTQ+ individuals and also harmonized the legal age of marriage to 18, was a groundbreaking achievement. This reform directly protects children from the risks of early and forced marriages, promoting their right to education, health, and development.
Additionally, amendments to the Civil and Commercial Code banning corporal punishment by parents and guardians represent a transformative step in protecting children from violence in a context where more than half of children aged 1-14 have experienced violent discipline. This legal shift underscores Thailand’s commitment to fostering a safe and nurturing environment for all children, promoting non-violent discipline and positive parenting practices.
