Further progress includes the proposed amendments to the Criminal Code to explicitly criminalize online child sexual exploitation, which are currently under public review. The submission of a revamped Child Protection Act to the Cabinet highlights the government’s proactive approach to addressing emerging threats to child welfare and enhancing protective frameworks.
Thailand’s withdrawal of its reservation on CRC Article 22 – focused on the rights of refugee children – was a landmark decision with profound implications. We can imagine a girl like 10-year-old Nadi, born in rural northern Thailand. Her family fled for their lives more than a decade ago, escaping armed conflict and instability in Myanmar’s Karen state. Not far from the border, the typical community where she is growing up is home to a mix of refugees, migrants, and Thai families. 
For Nadi and 30,000 other refugee and asylum-seeking children like her, Thailand’s decision fulfils their right to nationality or permanent residency and removes barriers to quality education, health care, and social participation. By addressing the vulnerabilities of displaced children, Thailand reinforced its commitment to inclusive and equitable child rights. Moreover, the government accelerated pathways to permanent residency or citizenship for 483,000 stateless individuals, including 142,000 children, covering over 80% of the total registered child stateless population. The move aligns with Thailand’s obligations under the CRC and strengthens the country’s social fabric by promoting integration and equity.

CROSS-CUTTING AND SYSTEMS-LEVEL APPROACHES
UNICEF Thailand’s achievements in 2024 reflect its commitment to the Country Programme strategic priorities, which highlight evidence generation, policy analysis, scalable programming, and high-level technical support. Programme efforts also focused on fostering partnerships and mobilizing diverse stakeholders, including the private sector, to protect and advance children’s rights.  
A partnership with the National Statistical Office advanced data quality through workshops on geospatial and survey methodologies, culminating in the public release of GIS data from the 2022 MICS survey. The dissemination of MICS data through provincial reports and national briefings contributed to informing policy discussions on child welfare. UNICEF’s flagship report, Addressing the Gaps: Ensuring every child has an equal chance to thrive, provided actionable recommendations for addressing inequalities. An analytical brief helped shed light on the challenges faced by children with disabilities and will further support UNICEF programming in this area.
UNICEF partnered with the World Bank and Thailand Development Research Institute to advocate for revisions to Thailand’s poverty line, leading to the first update in over a decade. UNICEF supported the Equity Education Fund in piloting an equity-based school funding formula in 180 small, remote schools, addressing disparities linked to geography, poverty, and disability. Preliminary findings revealed gaps in understanding equity budgeting, prompting further capacity-building with partners. 
UNICEF, in collaboration with government partners, is addressing the challenges in child protection planning and budgeting in 2024 by conducting an analysis of child protection funding in Thailand. This effort aims to provide evidence to combat the inadequate allocation of funds that could benefit 120,000 children currently in institutional care and approximately 300,000 children who are in lower income quantiles and not living with their parents who currently do not receive any alternative care funding. Based on the evidence from 2024, alternative care will be an advocacy priority for 2025.
Public financing for children (PF4C) was central to UNICEF’s 2024 strategy, leveraging the Royal Thai Government’s commitment to human capital development. Building on its earlier engagements and advocacy on “sustainable financing of social sectors”, in 2024, UNICEF partnered with the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC) to conduct a cross-sectoral analysis identifying gaps and priority investments in human capital. Partnerships with the Budget Bureau and NESDC influenced Thailand’s FY2026 Budget Allocation Strategy, focusing on early childhood development, education, youth, and social protection. UNICEF supported line ministries in translating these priorities into project proposals for submission to the Budget Bureau and will continue engaging and monitoring future budget allocations. To further support continued investment in social services for children, UNICEF updated its fiscal space analysis, projecting public investment capacity over 20 years, and put forth a technical note on priority revenue reform options for sustainable social sector funding. 
EARLY CHILDHOOD (0-5 YEARS)
The universalition of the Child Support Grant (CSG) (currently focusing on families with children 0-6 years old with an annual income of less than 100,000 baht, approximately USD 3,000) remained a priority throughout the year. After years of UNICEF technical assistance and high-level advocacy, the Ministry of Social Development and Human Security (MSDSH) presented a proposal for the expansion of the CSG to all families with children 0-6 years old to the Cabinet. Follow-up on the endorsement by the Cabinet will remain a UNICEF priority in 2025. 
UNICEF spotlighted the importance of parenting support and early childhood education (ECD) by linking these issues with declining birth rates, childcare, family-friendly policies, and human capital development. Flagship research on childcare services provided critical insights into parental demand and service gaps, including costed policy options for care services for children under 3, and was validated by inter-ministerial stakeholders. This was complemented with a rapid assessment of paid parental leave benefits in Thailand, capturing the experiences of 10 Thai companies. Findings were disseminated to businesses and policymakers at an event co-hosted by the Global Compact Network Thailand and the Swedish Embassy in Bangkok. 
Promoting positive parenting and gender equity in family roles and shared responsibilities was at the heart of UNICEF‘s research on gender dynamics in parenting and child socialization. Findings revealed persistent norms casting mothers as caregivers and fathers as breadwinners. Recommendations include media engagement, professional training on gender equity, and programs encouraging shared caregiving roles. These findings will inform UNICEF’s 2025–2026 advocacy for universal ECD parenting programs in partnership with WHO, civil society, and the government. 
To grow and develop optimally, children need adequate nutrition, good health, safety and security and opportunities for learning and stimulation. These are all the components of the Nurturing Care (NC) framework that UNICEF is prioritizing to integrate into child-focused services. A cross-sectoral assessment highlighted gaps in early stimulation, safety, and responsive caregiving despite universal access to health, nutrition, and early learning services. UNICEF supported the Department of Health to enhance its Parent Schools programme in 20 hospitals across six provinces, incorporating gender-responsive training and parental engagement tools. Sixty frontline workers developed action plans to expand PS coverage, and online NC training reached 1,442 health personnel. The Early Moments Matter on Mobile (EMMM) platform gained 39,360 new subscribers before transitioning to a public-private partnership, ensuring sustainability. UNICEF also revised the caregiver curriculum for children under 3, strengthening NC, gender, and inclusion elements.
UNICEF collaborated with the Department of Local Administration (DLA) and Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) to strengthen ECD centres through early reading, science-based learning, and peer-teacher networks benefitting 2,984 children. Earlier support to 270 BMA centres for early reading was consolidated, with 70 centres active in peer networks. Ongoing discussions aim to institutionalize this approach across all BMA centres. At the policy level, UNICEF partnered with the National ECD Policy Committee and its Secretariat, the Office of the Education Council (OEC), to strengthen governance and leadership. In August, UNICEF organized the third National ECD Forum on the importance of play in early childhood, attended by 500 participants from ministries, academia, NGOs, teachers, and caregivers. Advocacy with OEC leadership led to plans for an evidence-based ECD assessment to guide national policy, improve monitoring frameworks, and address sectoral silos.
Findings on malnutrition drivers among children under 5 emphasize the need to strengthen antenatal and childcare services, target stunting interventions, and train community workers, shaping UNICEF’s 2025–2026 nutrition priorities. In collaboration with the Bureau of Nutrition (BoN), UNICEF launched new food-based dietary guidelines featuring responsive feeding practices. Training reached 3,700 staff from 2,000 hospitals, with 27,000 accessing recorded sessions, while social media campaigns, supported by six influencers, garnered over 400,000 views. Further, research on Thai-specific weight gain standards for pregnant women to address stunting risks was completed and to be launched in early 2025.
MIDDLE CHILDHOOD (6-11 YEARS)
To address the Thai government’s overreliance on institutional care as an alternative for children without parental care and the presence of numerous unregistered residential care facilities, UNICEF published two studies focusing on Thai and non-Thai children in the southern and northwestern border provinces. These efforts are part of the ongoing implementation of the National Roadmap on Alternative Care.
Justice reforms continue to focus on reducing juvenile detention. In 2024, 71% of children in conflict with the law benefited from diversion orders or non-custodial measures, contributing to a drop in juvenile offenders to under 13,000, compared to 17,500 in 2020 (92% boys). UNICEF revised standard operating procedures for the Alternatives to Detention programme and developed case management guidelines for Rohingya children. Advocacy for children’s rights to peaceful assembly included training law enforcement and releasing guidelines on safe protests in partnership with the National Human Rights Commission.
UNICEF enhanced services at Provincial Shelters for Children and Families by developing gender-responsive standards. These shelters now provide improved care and case management frameworks, supporting over 13,000 children and women annually. 
Efforts to end violence against children (EVAC) in 2024 demonstrated its transformative potential to accelerate development across sectors, from improving economic productivity to enhancing learning outcomes and strengthening social protection. UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Education to address violence in school settings. This collaborative effort began with a consultative process alongside the Education Safety Centre to lay the foundation for the roadmap and culminated in a technical workshop where existing policies and prevention and response mechanisms were benchmarked to inform the development of the national “Safe to Learn” roadmap. Additionally, through UNICEF-supported programmes, over 17,000 children (44% girls) accessed social welfare and justice services, benefiting from strengthened systems and targeted interventions. 
UNICEF co-hosted the second National Conference on Children in the Digital Age, promoting ASEAN guidelines to address online child sexual exploitation. The conference fostered actionable strategies to protect children in digital space. UNICEF also supported efforts to strengthen referral processes for online sexual exploitation and abuse and child trafficking cases. These efforts ensure online risks and child protection issues are included in the UNICEF-supported comprehensive mapping of referral pathways and contribute to the national digital well-being guidelines. 
In education, UNICEF reached over 1,500 marginalized children, primarily from linguistic minority and migrant communities. Nationally, UNICEF co-founded the Mother Tongue-Based Multilingual Education (MTB-MLE) Action Network and advanced recommendations for integrating migrant children into public schools through the Thai Border Affairs working group. UNICEF initiated research with the Equitable Education Fund (EEF) on out-of-school children, spotlighting disparities tied to wealth, gender, location, and language. Findings were shared during technical forums, reinforcing the role of data in policy development including the role of household survey data in equitable policy-making. 
UNICEF made significant strides in foundational learning, digital education, and STEM for lower-secondary girls and boys. The ‘A Book a Week’ campaign under the Every Child Can Read initiative reached over 102,000 students (50% girls) in 200 schools, while virtual training on assessment data usage benefited 13,000 teachers. Mobile libraries in five border provinces supported 81 teachers (90% female) and 14,279 children (48% girls) in remote areas. A learning loss pilot in Samut Sakorn trained 1,200 teachers (75% female) in 120 schools, impacting 20,000 children. The One Teacher Thailand network reached over 200,000 peers nationwide, improving digital competencies and classroom management.
Disability inclusion remained a priority. UNICEF collaborated with the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPD) to harmonize disability determination systems, drawing on global best practices and a bio-social approach. Exchanges and discussions around data integration among disability services saw a breakthrough in October when the Cabinet announced a decision to integrate all disability data into one information system, assigning the DEPD as the coordinator. A study on cash and in-kind benefits for children with disabilities recommended a multi-tiered system tailored to individual needs. UNICEF also supported a model for integrated services for children with disabilities, including protocols and a monitoring framework, slated for piloting in 2025. 
UNICEF supported the 2024 UN Migration Report by highlighting barriers for migrant children in accessing basic services and facilitated a cross-border memorandum of understanding between Thailand and Cambodia to strengthen child protection services. Inclusion and identity initiatives supported stateless children, with over 4,200 undocumented children gaining legal identity and 176 achieving Thai nationality. UNICEF and UNHCR developed an e-course, ‘Ending Childhood Statelessness,’ to enhance service providers’ capacity to assist stateless individuals. 
ADOLESCENCE AND YOUNG PEOPLE (12-24 YEARS)
Mental health and psychosocial services (MHPSS) initiatives featured prominently. UNICEF supported the Department of Mental Health in launching the Integrated MHPSS Action Plan (2023–2027) and piloted integrated services in four provinces, training over 1,000 providers and screening 146,270 children. Despite improvements in intersectoral coordination, gaps in system readiness underscored the need for stronger national leadership. UNICEF enhanced digital health services for adolescents by developing an e-learning programme for service providers, with over 1,000 participants registered. This initiative aligns with efforts to integrate digital health into Thailand’s universal health coverage framework.
Around 2.5 million children, about 1 in 10, are now affected by overweight or obesity in Thailand. Among older children, being overweight is the dominant form of malnutrition. UNICEF developed an operational nutrition plan that integrates life-cycle interventions across sectors. To promote healthier diets, UNICEF supported draft legislation restricting the marketing of high-fat, high-sugar, and high-sodium products to children. Contributions included a regulatory impact assessment, nutrient profiling, and consultations with stakeholders, including 250 parents and civil society members. Approved by the Permanent Secretary of Health, the draft awaits ministerial endorsement.  
In the southern border provinces, UNICEF partnered with the Kenan Foundation to promote healthy lifestyles. Sixty youth health champions (55% female) and 12 teachers were trained to lead school and community activities, prioritizing gender equity and addressing adolescent health needs. The project aims to reach 2,000 young people in person and 35,000 online by 2025.
UNICEF and the Institute for the Promotion of Teaching Science and Technology (IPST) supported 20 universities to host environmental science camps for 7,105 students (59% girls) and 1,716 teachers (76% female) from 171 lower secondary schools. These camps generated 200 student-led projects showcased at a national symposium. UNICEF advocated for competency-based education (CBE), conducting an assessment in 163 sandbox schools, identifying successful integration despite limited teacher support. An OECD-UNICEF workshop explored scaling CBE, while a virtual exchange reached 13,000 teachers (75% female) to promote awareness. Vocational education expanded transferable skills training to 79 institutions, benefiting 300 teachers who incorporated social innovation into learning.   
UNICEF expanded youth employability systems to provide second-chance opportunities for young people not in employment, education, or training (NEET) in collaboration with the NESDC and the Ministry of Labour. Pilots in six provinces engaged 10,200 youth, identifying 2,417 NEET (35% female), of whom 1,827 received tailored assistance. In Udon Thani, 96% of participants reintegrated into education, employment or training, earning national recognition and funding for expansion to 11 additional sub-districts by 2025.
UNICEF also refined the E-Workforce Ecosystem platform with the Thailand Professional Qualification Institute, incorporating career guidance tools. To further support employability, UNICEF trained 705 service providers and developed national occupational standards for youth workers. Plans underway for 2025 include expanding private sector engagement to motivate and retain workforce entrants.
CLIMATE CHANGE and ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION 
UNICEF is developing a consolidated climate strategy and will continue to strengthen its position within the climate-smart social services niche, working with the Ministry of Education and Department of Climate Change and Environment to support the development of an equitable and climate-smart school education system, including a focus on mainstreaming of climate resilient and crisis sensitive planning approaches. 
Taking steps towards this goal, UNICEF partnered with communities in Pattani to strengthen disaster preparedness, conducting two training sessions and developing prevention and mitigation plans for high-risk areas. A landscape analysis of climate-smart education identified gaps in policy, curriculum, infrastructure, and data systems, while climate-mapped education risk heat maps highlighted flood-prone schools. 
UNICEF collaborated with the OEC to enhance evidence generation in the education sector and hosted national forums engaging 300 policymakers and experts alongside young people on climate-smart education, competitiveness, and decentralization. In partnership with the EEF and UNESCO, UNICEF co-hosted the Lifelong Learning conference for youth and adults, fostering dialogue on education policies among governments and other stakeholders to plan and implement youth responsive policies aligned with the sustainable development goals.  
CHILDREN AND YOUNG PEOPLE’S PARTICIPATION
At the national level, UNICEF supported the Children and Youth Council of Thailand (CYCT) in developing a 10-year strategy using foresight, also informed by a nationwide survey of 30,121 young people. The CYCT National Assembly translated these insights into actionable recommendations. 
UNICEF and DLA launched the CYCT Registration and Monitoring System, registering 19,774 young people and 603 local administrative organizations. This platform provides real-time data to identify gaps in youth inclusion and leadership. UNICEF trained 300 local authorities to implement the system effectively. 
A pilot project with Raks Thai Foundation engaged 1,188 student leaders and 194 teachers in youth-led initiatives on mental health, anti-bullying, and environmental sustainability, benefiting 8,629 students. Student confidence in influencing school decisions increased from 70% to 82%, shaping future interventions under the Safe to Learn initiative. 
The Youth-Led Action (YAG) initiative empowered 1,225 young people to tackle issues like education equity, gender equality, and disability inclusion. At Ubon Ratchathani University, 169 students developed solutions to local environmental challenges, including a flood vulnerability assessment adopted by local authorities. With UNICEF’s support, the university aims to become a regional hub for youth participation in climate governance and sustainable development across northeastern Thailand. 
UNICEF actively engaged 2,907 children and adolescents (51% girls) in violence prevention, online safety, and migration-related initiatives. Through partnerships with the CYCT, the Department of Children and Youth, and the National Human Rights Commission of Thailand, UNICEF ensured inclusive representation across gender, ethnic, and religious groups. 
Ninety-nine young people aged 13–24 provided input that helped UNICEF adjust its strategies to address the evolving needs of children and adolescents as part of the mid-term review process. UNICEF’s Young People Advisory Board (YPAB), comprising 51 members, contributed to 33 consultations and events, ensuring youth voices informed key policies on issues of pressing concern. 
BORDER AREA PROGRAMME
In response to ongoing instability in Myanmar and increased numbers of children on the move, UNICEF and Save the Children co-led the education response under the Inter-Sector Working Group, delivering home-based learning kits to 7,556 children (52% girls) in Mae Hong Son, Tak, and Kanchanaburi provinces. Sixty-five community volunteers (65% female) received training on education in emergencies, child protection, and mental health support to address critical needs. UNICEF supported 192 unaccompanied and separated children (65% boys, 35% girls) with case management services and reached over 3,600 children and caregivers with mental health and psychosocial support, primarily along the Myanmar-Thailand border. These efforts expanded the reach of essential services to ensure children and families in vulnerable situations receive the support they need. UNICEF in partnership with Help Without Frontier also supported communities impacted by displacement across the border with durable sanitation and drinking water services, supporting up to 11,703 people with access. A further 10,907 people affected by flooding in Mae Hong Son and Tak provinces received critical WASH items as part of the emergency response, including essential hygiene supplies.

Expanded partnerships
Building on previous efforts, UNICEF fostered strategic engagement with Parliament and its standing committees to advocate for children’s rights to remain a priority in national agendas. UNICEF partnered with the Parliamentary Budget Office to present the situation of children in Thailand and held a panel discussion featuring youth leaders and dialogue with parliamentarians, child-related committees, and civil society. UNICEF’s collaboration with the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Rights, Justice, and Law Reforms achieved significant legal milestones, including amendments to the Criminal Code to criminalize online child sexual exploitation and align domestic laws with the CRC. Additionally, UNICEF served as a technical advisor to the Standing Committee on Social Welfare, contributing to a comprehensive report on ECD policies, which was later presented to the House of Representatives.
A newly launched collaboration with the Thai Media Fund identified common priority areas in ECD, education, and online child protection. It holds significant potential to advance outcomes for children by promoting media and content that prioritizes their rights, education, and well-being. 
The first partnership of its kind was formalized with the Southern Border Provinces Administrative Centre to promote the well-being of children in a region where children face heightened vulnerabilities, with an initial focus on child protection. 
Cooperation with other UN agencies continued. UNICEF, working with UNHCR, contributed technical input and advocacy to support efforts led by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the National Security Council to address barriers to legal identity, helping to expedite permanent residency and citizenship procedures for stateless children. Cooperation continued with the OHCHR on the civic space for freedom of expression, UNESCO on education and UNDP on climate change and young people.
In ECD, UNICEF partnered with the Department of Health, Mahidol University, and Kasetsart University to revise caregiver curricula for children under 3, integrating nurturing care principles. 
UNICEF reinforced its partnerships with key national agencies within the Ministry of Education. The Office of the Permanent Secretary focused on digital learning and coordination, and the Office of Basic Education supported foundational reading and math, competency-based education, and the Safe to Learn initiative. The Office of Vocational Education and Training promoted transferable skills and social innovation. Collaboration with IPST introduced a focus on equitable and gender-responsive science-based education – from the early years to secondary education – to increase awareness and quality of instruction.
Internationally, partnerships with UNESCO, OECD, and EdTech Hub enabled UNICEF to act as a knowledge broker, aligning global good practices with Thailand’s education needs.  
UNICEF Thailand’s partnership with the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs also resulted in more financial resources (US$ 35,800) being leveraged for children. UNICEF Thailand also facilitated South-South learning and exchanges by sharing Thailand’s best practices related to children with other countries, i.e. Malaysia, Nepal, Uzbekistan and China. 
Partnerships at the community level
UNICEF worked with grassroots organizations to drive impactful change at the community level. Civil society partners, including the Legal Status Network, Help Without Frontiers, World Vision, and Save the Children, were instrumental in answering the needs of children in emergencies. Partnerships with the Thailand Development Research Institute, Mahidol, Chiang Mai and Huachiew Chalermprakiet universities generated critical evidence on social protection, alternative care, family-based care and youth work, which informed UNICEF’s advocacy and policy strategies.
At the community level, collaborations with the Foundation for Applied Linguistics localized education strategies like the MTB-MLE programme, improving learning outcomes for linguistic minority children. In ECD, UNICEF began engaging the Thai Health Promotion Foundation, EEF, and the Dek Noi Pattana Foundation to streamline teacher training and parenting initiatives. Partnerships with the Raks Thai Foundation and Kenan Foundation mentored youth-led organizations in healthy lifestyles, and youth participation. Ubon Ratchathani University also tested methodologies for youth participation in climate governance to promote leadership in environmental decision-making.
Significant partnerships with the private sector
UNICEF leveraged private sector collaborations to mobilize resources, promote innovation, and enhance program sustainability. Prudential Thailand disseminated nurturing care messages to parents and caregivers through corporate networks, including storybooks designed for children. The EMMM platform transitioned into a public-private partnership with a digital health company, ensuring its long-term sustainability. A shared-value collaboration with BJC Big-C launched flagship childcare centres and child-friendly retail spaces and also supported the establishment of healthy checkout lanes to encourage better dietary habits. The partnership with Baan Dek Foundation engaging the construction sector to improve the living conditions of children living in construction site camps expanded to 24 member companies benefiting 13,603 workers and children. 
Public engagement and audience-focused partnerships
In 2024, UNICEF Thailand focused on expanding its public engagement and enhancing brand perception, achieving strong results across multiple communication channels with content creation and partnerships key to success. By November 2024, total followers reached 937,870 - an increase of 99,297 since 2023. Facebook saw substantial growth, reaching 816,953 followers. LinkedIn also emerged as a key platform, with followers increasing by 56.52%, reflecting a greater strategic focus on business-to-business communications. 
UNICEF amplified public awareness through campaigns and collaborations. The #CountMeIn youth-centric campaign reached 19.4 million people. The campaign showcased real-life stories of children affected by climate change and further elevated the voices of young people, including those who participated in the Thai COP29 delegation. 
‘Better Tomorrow Today’ was an integrated fundraising campaign reaching 2.1 million people in its first month. As part of the campaign, UNICEF launched the ‘Train to the Future’, which showcased artwork from 25 children from diverse backgrounds. Their creations were displayed on Bangkok subway lines serving 720,000 daily commuters. The campaign culminated on World Children’s Day with the illumination of Thailand’s Wat Arun, a powerful symbol of collective commitment to children’s rights. Partnerships and celebrity participation were pivotal to the campaign’s success. 
Partnerships with Prudential Thailand extended parenting messages through corporate networks, while BJC Big-C’s family-friendly workplace initiatives highlighted the private sector’s role in advancing ECD.
Youth-led networks, such as the CYCT, Student Reflect, and YoungRise Thailand, provided platforms for amplifying young people’s voices. Meaningful participation was complemented by capacity-building initiatives led by civil society and academic partners.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
Thailand continues to face political and governance issues, including frequent cabinet reshuffles, political instability, and overlapping responsibilities between national and local governments. Slow decentralization, excessive bureaucracy, and fragmented structures hinder evidence-based reforms. Recent government changes have required renewed advocacy to align priorities. 
Demographic and societal pressures exacerbate challenges. Thailand’s ageing population places economic burdens on younger generations, shifting priorities toward elderly care and reducing resources for children. Family-friendly policies and investments in support of human capital development, such as the NEET pilot or gender-responsive approaches to STEM education, remain critical to addressing inequities and improving outcomes for disadvantaged children.  
Environmental challenges, including frequent natural disasters, rising greenhouse gas emissions, and regional inequalities, threaten economic stability. National climate strategies often overlook children’s participation, excluding their perspectives and needs. Digital transformation may expose users to misinformation, repression, and online exploitation, while education systems lag in integrating technology learning improvements.
UNICEF programming faces resource and systemic challenges. Overlapping national and local government responsibilities often hinder policy implementation and service delivery. For example, overreliance on institutional care and unregistered facilities weakens child protection, compounded by workforce shortages and unclear ministry roles. MHPSS pilots exposed gaps in coordination and training, while preventive and family-based services remain underfunded, with weak enforcement of child protection laws.
Significant social and economic inequality results in very uneven access to quality education, job opportunities, and economic mobility for youth from poorer or ethnic backgrounds. The fear of reporting due to stigmatization and discrimination continued to be a barrier, particularly in cases of online child sexual exploitation and abuse. 
Lessons learned
Strong partnerships and collaboration were pivotal to success. Joint advocacy with UNHCR to end childhood statelessness underscored the value of leveraging partnerships. Similarly, the Udon Thani NEET youth project showed how localized approaches and strong leadership can achieve meaningful results. Cross-sectoral collaboration, as demonstrated by the Safe Toto Learn national roadmap, integrated sectoral expertise in child protection, education, and young people’s participation to ensure students are safe and actively engaged in learning at school. 
Tested solutions, such as e-learning for digital health services for adolescents and justice system professionals and hybrid STEM training models, highlighted the need for localized adaptation and continuous support. Scaling such initiatives will require robust technical backing, sustained advocacy, and funding. 
Policy advocacy and systemic reforms were critical. Leveraging Thailand’s OECD membership ambitions, UNICEF supported ongoing curriculum reforms and teacher development. In collaboration with the EEF, UNICEF designed research on out-of-school children and youth to align with the national ‘Thailand Zero Dropout’ (TZD) policy. The study, scheduled for 2025, will analyze dropout risks, including among children with disabilities, using global frameworks for education exclusion. This research will inform work in priority provinces under TZD and strengthen school-based early warning systems for at-risk students.  
To enhance the integration and coordination of social protection schemes, UNICEF has initiated technical assistance to support MSDHS in connecting its MIS (MSO Logbook) with other databases, such as those for CSG beneficiaries and children with disabilities. These efforts aim to establish a single registry for social protection and lay the foundation for a sector-wide management information system.
Meaningful youth participation is essential. The CYCT emerged as a vital platform for fostering youth participation in decision-making processes. However, sustaining impact will require deeper investments in mentorship, leadership development, and institutional support to strengthen youth-led advocacy. Enhancing foresight capacity within the CYCT will also be critical to enabling long-term planning and strategic engagement by young leaders.
The private sector’s evolving relationship with UNICEF reflects a growing shift from simply offering financial contributions to a desire to co-develop solutions to development issues that affect children. Businesses increasingly recognize corporate social responsibility and Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG) as a way to extend beyond philanthropy to create meaningful, sustainable impact, which also strengthens their brand image and public trust. However, active fundraising can generate tension with programmatic objectives, particularly in industries like food and nutrition. By aligning fundraising with programmatic goals and fostering responsible practices, UNICEF can transform potential conflicts into collaborations that support children’s well-being and advance its mission.
Way forward
Thailand’s aspiration to become a high-income country by 2037, its strategic geopolitical position within ASEAN, and its ambition to join the OECD, and Free Trade Agreement negotiations with the EU present opportunities to advance reforms and invest in children. Thailand’s commitment to human capital development, aimed at boosting workforce productivity and addressing the challenges of an ageing society, positions UNICEF to advocate strongly for greater investment in children.  
While challenges persist, Thailand’s established technocratic governance system provides a strong foundation for policy implementation. The country’s financial and human resources, coupled with its track record of fiscal discipline, position it well to prioritize long-term investments in child welfare. Therefore, UNICEF’s success hinges upon leveraging resources and generating and operationalizing political will that employs a long-term horizon view.
UNICEF will continue its technical and advocacy role to ensure children are prioritized in domestic budgets, strengthen the CSG and social protection schemes, and lobby for legislation embedding child rights in the national legal framework. UNICEF will provide critical advocacy tools while holding the government accountable, evolving into a more strategic political actor, and forming alliances with key decision-makers while maintaining neutrality and impartiality.   
With Thailand’s growing national institutional capacity, UNICEF will focus on providing specialized expertise to guide the government in strengthening service delivery systems and improving the quality and scope of services. Evidence-based approaches and multi-stakeholder engagement will be central to regaining momentum and building consensus. 
UNICEF will adopt a business model tailored to Thailand’s upper middle-income and high-income context and contribute to the organizational thinking on the new business models. This model will focus on upstream policy work, leveraging domestic resources, and mobilizing highly specialized technical expertise. Advocacy efforts will include building coalitions with civil society and private sector partners and influencing political priorities.

Driven by expansionary fiscal policy coupled with increased capital investment and steady consumption, Timor-Leste’s growth output is expected to improve in 2024 and is anticipated to maintain its momentum into 2025. During the Prime Minister’s state budget speech in December 2024, the Government announced non-oil real GDP growth for 2024 at 3.7%. After peaking in 2023, inflation has fallen sharply and is projected to continue easing, thanks to the moderation of global food prices. Despite the public finance reforms, government budget execution was relatively moderate during the year's first half, estimated at around only 63% by October, with an expected increase by the end of the year. 
In December 2024, the Government finalized the 2025 budget, focusing on “Investment in Strategic Infrastructure, Economic Strengthening, and Enhancing Citizen Well-being", with a proposed budget of US$2.62 billion. This is significantly higher than the 2024 budget of US$1.95 billion. The 2025 budget includes a necessary increase in spending for capital projects, health, and education; however, it also features a rise in recurrent expenditures. Fiscal deficits will likely persist as spending remains high, resulting in significant withdrawals from the Petroleum Fund.
In 2024, Timor-Leste formalized its accession to the World Trade Organization, and in 2025, it is expected to become a member of ASEAN, with several supporting preparatory activities undertaken during 2024. Both memberships open new markets and opportunities for the country. Timor-Leste, however, must swiftly fulfil all the criteria set out in the roadmap for full membership in ASEAN.
Timor-Leste marked in August 25 years since the Popular Consultation or “The Referendum” when it voted for its independence. The Secretary-General of the United Nations, António Guterres, attended the event in person. In September, Pope Francis visited the country and addressed the nation, signifying profound cultural and religious issues and highlighting the need to invest in the children. Timor-Leste also received significant global attention, with several Head of States visits.
In mid-2024, Timor-Leste launched the first "Timor-Leste South Submarine Cable" installation at Dili, which connects Timor-Leste to Australia. While the high-speed internet is expected to help accelerate economic development and quality of life, it is only likely to become functional in the second quarter of 2025.  
The year 2024 also marked the initiation of the process to develop the next UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the UNICEF Country Programme Document (CPD) 2026-2030. The UN system and UNICEF undertook their country programme evaluations and developed situation analyses, including initial consultations with the government and key stakeholders to agree on the priorities and programme areas. The UNSDCF and UNICEF CPD will be finalised in 2025.
In 2024, Timor-Leste did not encounter any significant disasters. The anticipated food and water shortages caused by El Nino remained the key focus of emergency preparedness and response, making the usual preparedness for floods a secondary priority. Three UN agencies, WFP, UNICEF, and FAO supported the government in providing humanitarian responses to drought with food and water supplies, nutrition screening, and improved agricultural capacity for three months to the most vulnerable pockets of four municipalities.
During the year, the country focused on the rollout of the Law on Protection of Child and Youth in Danger (2023), led by the Ministry of Social Solidarity and Inclusion (MSSI), and improving access to birth registration, led by the Ministry of Justice (MoJ).A high-level political commitment to ending violence against children (EVAC) was secured through pledges at the First Global Ministerial Conference on EVAC in Bogota, Colombia, attended by Timor-Leste, which will contribute significantly to address high prevalence of violence against children.   59% of women in Timor-Leste aged between 15-49 experienced violence in their lifetime, with the rate higher for women with low education and from the poorest households. Women aged 20-24 years married by 18 years is currently 15%. 
In 2024, the national recurrent budget allocation to Ministry of Health was cut down, which directly impacted the procurement of essential drugs and medical supplies, operational costs and procurement of spare parts. Stockout of essential drugs was recorded throughout 2024.  
The recent data from the Population and Housing Census 2022 highlights participation rates in organized learning (one year before the official primary entry), which is low at 38.2 per cent.  The country has achieved near-universal net enrolment of 91.7 per cent at the primary level, with more girls in school. However, in secondary education, enrolment drops to 47.7 per cent (EMIS,2022) and is significantly lower for boys (41.50 per cent) than girls (54.31 per cent). Despite high levels of youth literacy, 88.3 per cent, the proportion of youth (aged 15–24 years) not in education, employment or training is 29.3 per cent, an increase of 10 per cent from 2015 (PHC, 2022). The Labour Force Survey highlights that the unemployment rate for young people aged 15-24 is 10 per cent, higher than the national average of 5 per cent.  The country’s education budget falls significantly short of the international benchmark (15-20 per cent), limiting investments in quality education and highlighting the need for continued donor support to the sector.

Health
UNICEF supported scaling up of routine immunization coverage and the introduction of a new vaccine, Human Papillomavirus (HPV), in 2024, targeting 11-year-old girls and adding a catch-up campaign to reach 12-14-year-old girls with single doses. UNICEF procured the HPV vaccine and further provided operational costs to the Ministry of Health to roll out the HPV vaccine efficiently. The HPV vaccination coverage reached over 95% of its target (1442 in total). In 2024, more than 10 municipalities reached 95% coverage with a second dose of measles-rubella vaccination. Additionally, UNICEF installed solar refrigerators in 105 health facilities to ensure the vaccines are stored safely. UNICEF continued to support the national warehouse in monitoring temperature of the vaccine cold chain across the country and addressed all issues raised, particularly at the sub-national level. UNICEF scaled up investment in digital health to record all immunization data from 73 fully functional community health centers (CHC) into the national health database providing ICT equipment to each municipality and community health center with in-service data recording, analysis and reporting training. Furthermore, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health in conducting an effective vaccine management (EVM) 2.0 assessment which indicated that the Timor-Leste score has improved to 63 from 40 since the last EVM assessment. The improvement in cold chain systems across the country is attributed to sustained investment made at the national / regional / municipal / health facility level with new cold chain equipment, spare parts, training of health workers and operational costs. UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Health in conducting the national expanded programme on immunization (EPI) review, which will pave the path for developing a national immunization strategy. 
In 2024, 11,181 live births were recorded in the community health centres supported by UNICEF across the country.  At the government request, UNICEF expanded its assistance to two additional municipalities, Los Palos and Aileu. UNICEF equipped five community health centers in each municipality and one health post; in total 11 health facilities are equipped with medical equipment to enhance quality of maternal and newborn care. In 2024, in collaboration with WHO and UNFPA, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health in launching one Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmoNC) facility in Oeussi. This is the sixth BEmoNC facility established by MoH with the UN agency's support since 2022. UNICEF continues to provide technical support to revise and update the national Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) strategy. To enhance the quality of care, UNICEF expanded the continuous quality improvement (CQI) initiative into an additional 21 health facilities.
UNICEF initiated the installation of an oxygen plant in the box (PiB) at the Baucau referral hospital and introduced green technology healthcare waste management equipment at the national hospital and five referral hospitals. These activities are expected to be completed by the first quarter of 2025. The oxygen plant, with dual capacity and function, can provide oxygen through the hospital pipeline and can fill oxygen cylinders that other health facilities can use.
Nutrition
 
In 2024, the Ministry of Health (MOH), with  UNICEF, made significant progress in improving child nutrition services across the country. With support from UNICEF, the total number of children who received Vit A was 94,961, with 45% coverage. For Deworming tablet, total children aged 12-59 months received deworming tablet was 110,719, with 58% coverage. Also, 4,349 (2,477 girls;1,872 boys) children suffering from Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) were reached with treatment services, with a 94.6% cure rate.  UNICEF also supported the distribution of multiple micronutrient powders (MNP) to 89% (47,902 out of a target of 53,971) children aged 6-23 months across all 13 municipalities.
To enhance the quality of diets for children aged 6-23 months, UNICEF collaborated with the Interministerial Task Force on Social Affairs and CONSSAN-TL to conduct food system dialogues. These discussions focused on creating sustainable food systems that would improve child nutrition. Formative research in partnership with Sydney University helped identify key factors for improving dietary quality for this age group.
UNICEF worked alongside the MOH to implement the National Health Sector Nutrition Strategy (NHSNSP), which included finalizing its costing and conducting a bottleneck analysis in all 13 municipalities. This analysis helped identify challenges in delivering the NHSNSP at primary health care facilities and informed the 2025 planning and budgeting processes for the National Directorate of Nutrition (NDN) and Municipality Health Services.
A significant milestone was the digitalization of nutrition data, linking it to the District Health Information Software (DHIS2) for real-time reporting. This system, implemented in all 13 municipalities, enables timely access to nutrition data, improving decision-making and planning.
In partnership with the National Committee for Control of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (NCCIDD) and JUS Legal Firm, UNICEF helped develop a sustainable, climate-friendly salt iodization program. This included drafting standard operating procedures and capacity-building support to ensure effective salt iodization.
UNICEF also continued its work on adolescent nutrition, reaching 40,000 girls aged 12-16 with micronutrient supplementation out of a target of 77,770. The "Fix my Food" regional initiative educated over 500 adolescents on nutrition. Furthermore, UNICEF, together with local NGOs like Alola Foundation and HIM, mentored 6,100 members of Mother Support Groups (MSG) to deliver community nutrition interventions.
UNICEF, the National University of Timor-Leste (UNTL), the Instituto Nacional de Saúde de Timor-Leste (INS-TL), and the MoH, are collaborating on research on a simplified approach for treating wasting in children. This approach streamlines protocols using MUAC and edema assessments to enhance accessibility in resource-limited settings. INS-TL leads health worker training, while MoH provides facility-based support. The partnership combines local expertise, training capacity, and global guidance to improve treatment coverage and outcomes, advancing child health in Timor-Leste
WASH
With UNICEF’s facilitation, chemists of the national laboratory of the National Directorate for Water and Sanitation  trained 26 health staff (16 males, 10 females) from all 13 municipalities on testing key water quality parameters using UNICEF-supplied mobile laboratory equipment. Following the training, health authorities of 8 municipalities, Bobonaro, Baucau, Manatuto, Covalima, Lautem, Ainaro, Viqueque and Manufahi commenced testing the water quality of random sources thus contributing to develop a database.
14 out of 31 previously triggered Sucos (villages) in Dili were declared Open Defecation Free (ODF). Moreover, four out of seven sub-districts (admin posts) in Covalima, initiated in 2019, were also declared ODF.
Continuing the extended COVID-19 recovery and nutrition improvements, UNICEF was able to upgrade WASH facilities in 18 additional Community Health Centers (CHCs) in four municipalities: Ainaro, Aileu, Oecusse and Lautem. Moreover, WASH infection prevention and control supply packages were distributed to 24 Community Health Centers in 5 municipalities, Oecusse, Lautem, Bobonaro, Liquica and Manufahi, as well as 20 Health Posts in 5 other municipalities, Baucau, Manatuto, Dili, Ermera and Covalima. WASH upgrades in the remaining CHCs and health posts are still in progress, with the target completion date for the first quarter of 2025. Accordingly, UNICEF will complete upgrading WASH in all the CHCs in the country. To support this long-awaited investment, UNICEF also facilitated an awareness workshop for 75 health and administrative officials of all 13 municipalities focusing on operation, maintenance and leveraging recovery budgets and supply chains. 
In partnership with Bee Timor-Leste (BTL), UNICEF contributed to the joint UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) response to anticipated food and water scarcity triggered by El-Nino. Accordingly, over three months, humanitarian water supply was provided to 29,236 vulnerable persons (14,120 males and 15,116 females) belonging to 49 sub-villages (aldeias) in Bobonaro, Covalima, and Lautem municipalities. 
 
Education
UNICEF continued to lead the education sector coordination of the Açao Conjunta para Educaçao Timor-Leste (ACETL- Local Education Group (LEG)) and co-chairs it with the Ministry of Education (MoE). The LEG comprises bilateral and multilateral donors and civil society organizations (CSOs). A notable achievement was the initiation of the first-ever Joint Education Sector Review for the Education Strategic Plan 2020-2024 to review the progress. The findings will also inform the Education Sector Plan (ESP) 2025-2030 development, coinciding with the last six years of the SDGs. Another noteworthy progress was the finalization of the evidenced-based Education Compact under the leadership of the MoE, which identified inclusive and equitable education as the key priority reform for the country. This Compact secured a USD 5 million System Transformation Grant (STG) from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE).
A significant milestone was Timor-Leste’s participation in the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics (SEA-PLM) survey for the first time with technical and financial support from the UNICEF Regional and Country Office. A nationally representative sample of 7,376 grade 5 students and 176 teachers participated in the survey on literacy, numeracy, and teacher-related questions. CARE facilitated the availability of 35 test administrators to support the process. Moving forward the availability of SEA-PLM data will facilitate in strengthening teaching and learning practices, actionable insights to promote learning outcomes, and foster peer learning mechanisms with the countries in the region.  
 
In 2024, UNICEF supported 5,976 children (2,966 girls and 3,010 boys) in 87 Community-based Pre-schools (CBPS) and through the School readiness Programme (SRP) in 71 Primary schools in Ermera and Viqueque municipalities. CBPS is a community-led initiative to ensure access to early childhood education in rural, remote areas where public preschools do not exist. Complementing early childhood education, a parenting programme was rolled out for parents of children 0-8 years of age in the communities where CBPS are functional. The programme emphasises the role of fathers and mothers in child development. This program aimed to raise awareness among parents and caregivers about the importance of early learning and play-based education and how they could support their children at home and in the community. 1,076 parents (F:648, M:428) now know about activities to support children at home. UNICEF collaborated with the Centre for Research in Early Childhood Education at Macquarie University, Australia, on evidence generation on the effectiveness of SRP. 
Building upon the success of the Eskola ba Uma Timor-Leste Learning Passport Platform (TL-LPP), UNICEF, in collaboration with the Instituto Nacional de Formação de Docentes e Profissionais da Educação (INFORDEPE—teacher training institution), is building teachers' capacity to integrate ICT. 154 school leaders (M:95 F:59) and teachers were trained. 
UNICEF also collaborated with Organizations of People with Disabilities (OPDs), such as Asosiasaun Halibur Defisiénsia Matan iha Timor-Leste (AHDMTL) and ALMA Sisters, to advocate for disability inclusion education.  In collaboration with INFORDEPE, training of 89 school coordinators (Male 55, Female 34) was completed to equip them with knowledge and skills to prevent violence against children (VAC) in schools. 
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education's annual media campaign to promote school enrolment. This campaign targeted parents of preschool and basic education students, focusing on the importance of enrolling children at the correct age, re-registering older students, and encouraging them to complete their education.
Child Protection
UNICEF strengthened the child protection system through improved policies, coordination, political commitment to ending violence against children, enhanced capacity of the social service workforce, including during emergencies, digitization of case management (Primero) and community empowerment. Almost 11,000 children were reached with preventive and response services (37 times more than in 2023), and almost 3% of the population was reached through various outreach interventions in different areas of child protection. As per maturity benchmarking, the child protection system improved from 47 to 49 points and remains in the integration stage. 
In the area of child enabling environment, the rollout of the newly enacted law on the protection of children and youth in danger (2023) continued, with dissemination to all key stakeholders at the national and municipality level, reaching 2,202 people, including 840 children. To further operationalize the law, the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) for child and youth protection case management for all kinds of violence was also endorsed and is being rolled out. The SOP will be further built upon to enhance the country's preparedness capacity for emergencies, including climate shocks. To increase access to birth registration, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to MoJ to conduct mobile birth registration.  As a result, 7,563 children (48% female) 0-5 years old were registered and issued with a birth certificate in five municipalities with the lowest coverage. Mobile birth registration modality was found effective for hard-to-reach communities in line with the principle of ‘leave no one behind’. The campaign was also successful in creating a national impact, with more than 15,000 children being registered and receiving birth certificates nationwide. This was part of a package of comprehensive reforms that in addition also included the strengthening of the demographic management information system, training of relevant officers and local authorities who provide birth registration service, as well as policy reform. 
 
Coordination mechanisms also improved, establishing an informal donor and development partners coordination group at the national level and training the Child Protection Networks in two municipalities. A high-level political commitment to ending violence against children (EVAC) was secured through pledges made in the First Ministerial Conference on EVAC in Bogota, Colombia and subsequently through request to be part of the Pathfinding countries, the process for which has started. This will bring the overshadowed area of violence against children in the country to the forefront. 
The professionalization and capacity strengthening of the social service workforce continued, focusing on training the social service workforce on the child protection Law, SOP, Primero case management, birth registration, child online protection and how to mainstream child protection in humanitarian settings. A total of 377 (36% female) workforce were reached. Recognizing that multiple service providers are involved in implementation, the training includes participation from across sectors such as Social Affairs, Health, Education, Justice and the Police. Mainly, the area of child online protection was new for the country, and the first participation in the regional ASEAN ICT Forum enabled the country’s cross-sectoral inter-ministerial members to understand the country's issues while providing possible options to tackle the situation. 
The strengthened social service workforce improved quality services to children and families, reaching 10,958 (51% female) children (including in emergencies), of which 345 children have been registered in Primero. In line with the newly enacted child protection Law, registration of children living in residential care started, with 1,985 children (58 % female) registered in 47 residential care institutions.  
The household and community capacity to protect children was also enhanced, reaching approximately 43,000 members of the community.  
 
 
Social policy and evidence generation
UNICEF ensured the inclusion of child-related indicators in Timor-Leste’s Living Standard and demographic health surveys, focusing on functional limitations, violence, nutrition, and child labour. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with partners, including UN Partnership on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to develop a situation report on persons with disabilities. In collaboration with the Ministry of Finance and the Institute of Statistics, UNICEF shared census data at the village level to assist in preparing the 2025 Annual Plan and promoting evidence-based budgeting for equitable social services. 
UNICEF developed a policy brief on social protection that emphasizes cash transfers during a child's first 1,000 days to improve nutrition, health, and early learning by highlighting different costing models.  The policy brief was shared with the Ministry of Health. UNICEF’s involvement in shock-responsive and climate-smart social protection included collaboration with the Minister of Social Solidarity and Inclusion (MSSI) and initial discussions with development partners. The note is anticipated to be finalized next year.
UNICEF supported the government in visiting China to understand the Child-Friendly Cities Initiative. This was followed by developing an advocacy note highlighting the importance of focusing on children in urban settings. The advocacy note for the child-friendly village initiative was also presented to the Ministry of Rural Development.
By providing training on child markers, and its applicability, UNICEF assisted the Ministry of Finance and INDDICA, the Child rights institute, using the Child Marker within the national budget to monitor funding for children's rights, enhancing transparency in the 2024 budget. 
UNICEF engaged with the Ministry of Youths, Sports, Art, and Culture to develop an analytical report on social innovations and entrepreneurial ecosystems to help promote innovations in skilling and employability. The report's recommendations will be implemented in 2025.
With IOM, UNICEF conducted a study to assess Vulnerabilities and Resilience in Border Communities through the Human Security Approach during COVID-19 by applying a cross-sectoral human security assessment across three border municipalities. The report, along with a policy brief, was finalized and disseminated.
Sustained advocacy with the government led to approval for initiating the process of developing a National Action Plan on the Rights of the Child. The government agreed upon the roadmap, and the inception report was finalized and will be developed during early 2025. 
UNICEF has evaluated the current Country Programme (CP) to inform the new CP (2026–2030). It has undertaken an equity analysis by examining indicators, budget allocations, and performance of programmes implemented. It has also undertaken an evidence synthesis by analyzing child-related indicators and bottlenecks. The findings will be incorporated into the new CP.
 
Climate Change
UNICEF finalized the planning of the first climate-smart social services project in Timor-Leste with funding from KOICA across six social sectors: Health, Nutrition, WASH, Education, Child Protection and Social Protection. Extending the same concept, UNICEF undertook a desk review and partner consultation across the same six sectors to expand multi-sector climate financing by tapping into major global climate resources. 
Addressing persistent climate-induced water shortage, UNICEF continued to support the scaling up of community-based water catchment management through nature-based solutions in 35 more sub-villages in the two municipalities Ainaro and Viqueque. Implementation was done by 70 community members trained, together with nearly 350 other community members, including women and youth. As a result, 532 nature-based infrastructures were built (45 retention ponds, 313 terraces and 174 natural check dams), thus creating added capacity to retain and conserve at least 12,567 cubic meters of rainwater in one rainfall event. This is expected to replenish the neighboring natural water pathways increasing their yield and availability during the dry season. Moreover, UNICEF partnered with the University of Technology of Sydney to develop a monitoring framework for tracking long-term community resilience, which is expected under this program model.
UNICEF also participated in advocacy and financial support in representing Timor-Leste in COP29. Accordingly, UNICEF facilitated the participation of the President of the National Designated Authority (NDA) for the Green Climate Fund (GCF) in the conference, and the country delegates were updated on reflecting youth engagement in climate action.
Youth and adolescent empowerment
UNICEF has collaborated with the Ministry of Youth, Sports, Art, and Culture (MoYSAC) to enhance the civic participation of adolescents and youth. UNICEF and MoYSAC conducted a capacity assessment involving 34 youth groups across three municipalities. Following this assessment, 15 youth groups were selected to participate in a one-year Mentorship Programme facilitated by the NGO Ba Futuru. The Programme aims to equip these youth groups with the knowledge and skills to enhance their decision-making abilities. To date, around 110 members from the youth groups and 60 elected youth leaders have participated in training sessions in three municipalities. The 15 youth groups are registering to obtain legal status as CSOs, providing them with institutional capacity.
UNICEF, MoYSAC and the Ministry of State Administration (MSA) officially launched the Adolescent Civic Participation campaign. This campaign aims to promote civic participation and change public perceptions of adolescents’ abilities and contributions, including girls and adolescents with disabilities. The sensitization sessions of the campaigns were implemented in 10 administrative posts in Dili, Ermera and Bobonaro municipalities and have reached more than 500 adolescents, young people, local authorities, decision-makers, parents, teachers, and people with disability.  In addition, more than 20,000 people have accessed the videos, radio dramas, posters shared through social media platforms, and local television and community radio. 
The Operational Guidance on Integrating Girls’ Empowerment in Activities with Adolescents was launched in 2024. The event, chaired by the Minister of Youth, Sports, Art and Culture, was attended by 100 participants from local and international NGOs, UN agencies, students and teachers. This document serves as tool for more appropriate intervention for the newly elected youth representatives and to guide the government and other implementing partners in promoting gender equality in their programs. 
UNICEF celebrated the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, which included workshops, training, and a strong social media campaign to promote awareness and engagement in disability inclusion. One hundred participants attended the event. UNICEF worked with the Timor-Leste National Disability Association to enhance the capabilities of youth centres, OPDs, and young people with disabilities and raise awareness about their rights.

During 2024, UNICEF Timor-Leste further deepened its partnerships with the Government, other UN agencies, development partners and CSOs.
UNICEF signed rolling work plans with 14 key government counterparts and ministries. Furthermore, UNICEF supported the Government in coordinating Early Childhood Development (ECD) through technical support to the Interministerial Working Group on ECD, which has drafted a work plan providing coordinated interventions for children 0 to 8 years old. Supporting cross-sectional work across Ministries, UNICEF has strengthened the capacity of the Government on the concept of Child-friendly cities, supported the Child Rights Institute in developing the next Action Plan for Children, provided technical assistance to the development of a multisectoral national nutrition action plan to combat stunting and engaged with eight Ministries and institutions on Child Online Protection, among other initiatives. Financial support from the Government of Japan, CIFF, and FCDO enabled UNICEF to partner with the MOH at all levels to strengthen the capacity of the Primary Health Care (PHC) network. The support also facilitated the development of a multisectoral national nutrition action plan to combat stunting, signed by the two Vice-Prime Ministers and 12 ministers, underscoring the government’s strong commitment to addressing nutrition challenges.
UNICEF, as the Coordinating Agency, co-chairs the Local Education Group (LEG) with the Ministry of Education (MoE). The LEG is a critical platform that brings the education development partners (bilateral and multilateral) and civil society organizations together to align resources and support to MoE. Partnerships with Organizations of People with Disabilities (OPDs) such as Asosiasaun Halibur Defisiénsia Matan iha Timor-Leste (AHDMTL) and ALMA Sisters continue to be central for advocacy on disability inclusion in education.
Within the UN system:
·       UNICEF concluded its partnership with WHO and World Vision International to provide efficient and effective support to the Government’s response to COVID-19, through a joint programme funded by the Australian Government. 
·       Partnering with the ILO and WFP, UNICEF concluded negotiations with the European Union on a new joint programme on nutrition-sensitive social protection, which was approved to start in early 2025.
·       Together with FAO and UNEP, UNICEF has developed a proposal to strengthen food systems to be funded by the Joint SDG Fund on Food Systems Transformation, that is being assessed for funding. 
·       With funding from USAID (Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance), UNICEF continued implementing a joint programme with IOM to support child protection in emergencies.
·       Partnering with OHCHR and UN WOMEN, UNICEF is jointly implementing capacity-building activities on the rights of people with disabilities and enhancing data through research and analysis, exploring gaps and barriers to collecting accurate disability data.
·       In response to the drought caused by El Nino and funded by OCHA, UNICEF partnered with WFP and FAO to provide food, water and tools for agriculture to affected communities.
·       With UN Women, UNICEF has collaborated on establishing an integrated hotline for violence against children and violence against women
·       In the area of Protection from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation (PSEA), UNICEF joined forces with other UN agencies to train partners and relevant staff on the new UN common PSEA assessment tool. 
·       In planning for the upcoming Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), UNICEF partnered with other UN Agencies to provide joint technical and financial support to the conduction of the survey in 2026.
·       UNICEF partnered with the World Bank, and other key development partners like Australia, on technical collaboration, promoting sector coordination and high-level advocacy, in several areas including education, performance-based financing of community health workers, and social protection.
·       Together with all other UN agencies, UNICEF contributed to updating the Common Country Assessment and to the strategic thinking around the new UNSDCF that will start in January 2026.
·       UNICEF also continued to strengthen joint results and interventions of the UN system as: Chair of the UN Communications Group, Chair of the UNSDCF Results Group on Education, Co-Chair of the Results Group on Nutrition and Food Security, Chair of the UN Programme Management Team, Chair of the UN Operations Management Team, Co-Chair of the UN Youth Results Group and Member of the Joint UN Humanitarian Cash Group
 
UNICEF continued advocacy with development partners to drive support, visibility and funding for child rights. This included broadening the partnership base by adding new donors, such as the Government of China through its South-South Cooperation Fund.
UNICEF partnered with CSOs, including academic institutions, youth-led organizations, UNICEF national committees and national and international NGOs to build evidence, working hand-in-hand with families, community decision-makers and service providers to deliver education, health and protection services, mobilizing public opinion and building momentum for positive change. With the in-kind support from the private sector, Timor Plaza mall, the World Children’s Day was organized to provide a platform for advocacy and to empower youth in photography, organizing an exhibition of photographs where they expressed their dreams, but also challenges they encounter in their daily life. Ongoing engagement and partnerships with the local media (radio, television, and print) supported UNICEF’s child rights advocacy and helped bring to public attention priority issues, including ECD, climate change, malnutrition and implementing the Protection Law for Children and Youth in Danger.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
In the health sector, 3,000 health staff were suspended from their duties resulting in nearly 60% of health posts and a few community health centres either partially or fully closed in quarter one of 2024. New replacement recruits were fresh university/college graduates who needed preservice and in-service training to record, analyze and report health data. This posed a critical problem of capacity gaps in health services both at national and decentralized levels. These changes come as reforms and restructuring undertaken in 2024 by the Government elected in 2023.
Certification and official declaration of Open Defecation Free (ODF) status in 4 previously supported municipalities by UNICEF was not completed in 2024 due to the lack of resources of the Ministry of Health. Following the Ministry of Public Works restructuring, the new WASH sector lead National Directorate for Water and Sanitation (DNRAS) could not recommence national WASH coordination. As a result, the national consultation for developing a climate rationale for the WASH sector was compromised. While the donor interest in community-managed water conservation was on the rise, the proposed standardization and improvements of the program model and its scaling up have been compromised due to the limited capacity of the local stakeholders. 
The availability of reliable data and evidence, including a robust Education Management Information System (EMIS), is a persistent challenge in the Education sector. The national education budget has significant shortfalls against the international benchmark (15-20 per cent). The inadequate provision of preschool education leaves most children in rural and remote areas without school readiness for primary education. The education system’s capacity to withstand climate-induced disasters and ensure learning continuity is significantly lacking. The capacities at decentralized levels for planning, budgeting, and monitoring the education sector, including accountability at the school level, continue to be a challenge and impact the ownership, implementation and accountability of the Education Sector Plan (ESP).
The government’s budget process overlooks poverty and equity, despite the Sustainable Development Program's (SDP) goal to eliminate poverty by 2030. Funding for the social sector is insufficient, budgets are blocked, and there are delays and inflexible regulations. Recently, the government decided to close a social protection program due to fiscal constraints. This decision will directly and negatively affect children and families who depend on financial assistance to meet basic needs. 
UNICEF needs to continue making substantial efforts to gather and build reliable evidence that can be used to support the case for increasing investments in social protection programs that specifically focus on the needs of children. At the same time, it is crucial to ensure these programs are climate-smart and gender-responsive, paying special attention to the unique needs and challenges faced by children, in different social and environmental settings. 
The government’s Disability Subsidy program is only available to persons with disabilities aged 18 and above and for children who are in school, leaving younger individuals who are not in schools with disabilities without financial support. This creates a significant gap in assistance for children and adolescents with disabilities, who often require early interventions, education, and specialized care. 
The Disability Markers are set to be developed as a critical tool for evaluating the effects of policies and budgets on Persons with Disabilities. These markers will help identify gaps, ensure equitable resource allocation, and promote accountability by aligning initiatives with principles of inclusion and equity. Additionally, integrating the Child Functioning Module into the 2025 Demographic and Health Survey aims to collect reliable data on children with disabilities to support evidence-based policymaking.
The digitalisation of nutrition data, linking it to the District Health Information Software (DHIS2) enhanced real-time reporting and data visualisation. Hence, it facilitated supportive supervision, problem-solving, and reporting. As future strategies, UNICEF will work on the food systems agenda – consolidating food system dialogue findings and a study on identifying key factors to improving diet for children 6-23 months and supporting the development of the plan and finalizing operational research on acute malnutrition management. It will also scale up Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) counseling, adolescent nutrition interventions, scale-up individual digitalized data entry. 
The LEG provides the forum for ensuring alignment and collaboration of education donors and partners around priority reforms, including overcoming challenges with resources, data, and evidence. This is evidenced in the collaborative advocacy on SEA-PLM, EMIS and disability inclusion and alignment on the education sector priority reform of the Education Compact. Systematic capacity building at decentralized levels will be crucial for improving learning outcomes. A climate-smart and resilient education system will be possible through the systematic capacity building of education personnel, the integration of low- and high-technology solutions, and the creation of multiple ways of learning. 
In the medium term, the strategic priorities include using SEA-PLM results to inform the strategic intervention for improving literacy and numeracy, such as classroom-based support for teachers and strengthened monitoring of learning. With promising developments in internet connectivity, UNICEF plans to convene MoE on school connectivity through GIGA.

2024 was marked by leadership transitions and institutional reforms, continued stability and economic growth, along with accelerated environmental/climate challenges impacting the realization of children’s rights. 
  
A major leadership transition took place in August when H. E. Tô Lâm became General Secretary of the Party in Viet Nam, with a vision for a ‘new era of the nation’s rise’ – calling for major reforms for Viet Nam to become a middle-income country by 2030 and high-income country by 2045.
