The Government’s investing priorities are in areas such as green energy, digital transformation, science and technology and human capital development to ensure continued economic growth. The largest-ever institutional reform was launched to improve efficiency and effectiveness, which will lead to significant organizational and personnel changes at national and provincial levels and may delay programme implementation in 2025. Viet Nam’s regional and global positioning continued with strong multilateral cooperation (e.g. the President’s attendance at the United Nations (UN) Summit of the Future and meetings with the UN Secretary-General and UNICEF Executive Director).  
  
Viet Nam is one of the fastest growing economies in the region and globally. Economic growth continued at 7.09 per cent in 2024; the Government target for 2025 is 8 per cent.  Inflation was below 4 per cent and public debt under 50 per cent. However, challenges remain to ensure sustainable, inclusive growth. Industrialization led Viet Nam to experience the 2nd highest air pollution in the region and 22nd highest globally. National poverty rates continue to decline (5.71 per cent multi-dimensional poverty in 2023), but disparities remain. Around 2.1 million children (8.6 per cent) experience multidimensional poverty and 5.1 per cent live in households earning below the international poverty line (US$3.65/day). 
  
The annual population growth rate has declined to 0.68 per cent. Viet Nam has one of the most rapidly aging populations globally: 14.3 per cent of Vietnamese are over age 60, a figure projected to reach 26.5 per cent by 2050. Viet Nam is on course to become an ‘aged society’ by 2034 – which calls for strategic investment in children and younger generations to secure a quality workforce for continued growth and development. 
  
Viet Nam remains highly exposed to climate risks. Typhoon Yagi—the most powerful in 70 years—hit Viet  Nam in September 2024, resulting in 320 deaths, 25 missing, 978 injured and  an estimated total economic cost of more than US$3 billion, particularly in  vulnerable communities in northern Viet Nam where many thousands of children  lost access to safe drinking water, nearly 1 million students lost 60-120 hours of learning and were put at enhanced risk of malnutrition,  neglect and violence. 
  
During 2024 children’s rights were significantly impacted in multiple dimensions, including:
  
Health - Children from marginalized groups (those with disabilities or living in rural, poor or ethnic minority communities) continued to face higher health risks due to limited access to quality healthcare and preventive services. By November 2023  procurement delays had caused a drop in the full immunization rate for infants under one year to 77.1 per cent—from 98 per cent in 2016—contributing  to an alarming measles outbreak in almost all provinces in late 2024.
  
Nutrition: Two regions exceeded the national stunting prevalence of 19.2 per cent: Northern Midlands (25.3 per cent) and Central Highlands (27 per cent). Treatment for the over 200,000 annual cases of acute malnutrition is not covered by health insurance. Meanwhile, childhood obesity rates are rising; 1.9 million children are projected to be obese by 2030. 
  
Education: Viet Nam continues to increase access to education across all levels. Challenges remain regarding quality, equity and retention, especially for preschool, lower secondary and upper-secondary school. Disparities exist along geographic, gender and regional lines; the Highlands and Mekong Delta regions have lower enrolment rates. Public spending on education and training declined from 3.5 per cent to 2.9 per cent of GDP in recent years. 
  
Water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH): Although access to drinking water through a centralized water supply system has increased from 86.7 to 94.2 per cent, only 57.9 per cent of Vietnamese use safely managed water and 43.9 per cent use safely managed sanitation facilities. Rural and remote communities generally have lower levels of access and quality, due to limited public investment. 
  
Social protection: Despite a relatively advanced system, fragmented design and policy implementation leave many children from marginalized and low-income households behind. Social protection programmes are not sufficiently shock-responsive and are unable to support poor and near-poor households, resulting in limited safety nets during disasters. 
  
Child protection: UNICEF support contributed to improving the legal framework for children through the first ever Juvenile Justice law, adopted in 2024. Violent discipline remains a key concern – together with gaps in service provision and limited human resource capacities that hamper systemic child protection responses. 
  
Gender: Viet Nam has achieved gender equity in school enrolment and attainment, with only a modest gender wage gap. However, ongoing concerns include sex selection (increased male ratio at birth due to son preferences); increased early marriage, especially for girls (before 18 years at 9.1 per cent); and gender-based violence (GBV)—21.8 per cent of women and girls experienced partner violence. 
  
Disability, ethnic minority or migrant status: Children with disabilities continue to be excluded from many areas of society and basic services, including education and health. Sharp disparities remain, ethnic minorities generally experience worse social and economic outcomes than the majority population. Children are heavily impacted by both internal and international migration, especially regarding access to services.  
  
Climate: The 2020 Global Climate Risk Index ranked Viet Nam as the 13th most-affected country by climate variability and extreme weather events between 2000-2019. Children are disproportionately affected: 99.5 per cent of Viet Nam’s 26.2 million children face three or more types of climate shocks, well above the 73 per cent globally and 89 per cent in the region. 
  
Digitalization: Despite the potential of digital transformation to accelerate children’s learning and wellbeing, significant remaining challenges include unequal access to digital services, limited digital literacy and significant online safety risks.

In 2024 UNICEF convened national and subnational partners from the public, private and civil society sectors to advocate for child rights; provided technical assistance to advance the legislative and policy framework; developed models to strengthen social services for children and promoted innovation for and with children and youth.
  
Health
  
Due to UNICEF’s efforts to strengthen primary health care, especially for ethnic minorities, through capacity building, provision of essential equipment and vaccines, outreach, digital innovations and campaigns, 61,241 pregnant women attended four antenatal visits, 81,217 mothers received care from skilled birth attendants and 74,557 newborns received early essential care. UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Health (MoH) on a Directive to strengthen child healthcare and reduce child mortality and updated guidelines on maternal and child health; capacity building of healthcare workers; supply of medical equipment; organization of advocacy events and media campaigns. To enable a rapid response to a measles outbreak, UNICEF and WHO assisted the Ministry of Education and Training (MoET) to develop communication materials and guidance for schools and communities.
  
The network of 1,203 village midwives was strengthened and made sustainable through UNICEF support for strengthened capacities in skilled birth attendance and newborn care. The amended social health insurance law now includes health insurance for mid-wives and monthly allowances for village health care workers from local governments. These frontline workers reached 18,630 pregnant women, aided childbirth for 2,740 mothers and made postnatal visits to 9,472. 
  
With UNICEF support, the MoH successfully launched the digital ‘Maternal and Child Health, Reproductive Health Information System’ (e-MCH), facilitating interoperability between e-MCH and existing health information systems. This will improve planning, monitoring and decision-making for health managers. 
  
Viet Nam’s commitment to children’s environmental health was strengthened through key initiatives, e.g., the Global Partnership for a Lead-Free-Future. With UNICEF technical assistance, the MoH (i) developed the first report on children’s environmental health as part of the 2024-2030 Green Growth strategy and action plan; (ii) organized a regional conference on climate change, health and green health systems; and (iii) built health worker knowledge about climate change, air pollution and climate-smart health systems. 
  
Nutrition
  
Targeted UNICEF  advocacy and technical support contributed to the inclusion of  sugar-sweetened beverages (SSB) in draft amendments to the excise tax law. A  UNICEF-supported study on SSB consumption habits, knowledge and perceptions  among Vietnamese aged 11 to 25, together with other evidence, informed  discussions at three advocacy meetings with 200 participants from the  National Assembly and relevant ministries. The new law taxing SSB is expected  to be adopted in 2025. 
  
Following UNICEF advocacy, in 2024 the MoH issued Circular 30, which  provides guidelines for implementation and funding for community-based health  and nutrition benefit packages for children suffering from severe acute  malnutrition (SAM). This represents significant progress toward large-scale SAM  prevention and treatment, which is not covered by health insurance. 
   
UNICEF supported nutrition interventions under three national targeted  programmes to improve socio-economic development in ethnic minority and  mountainous areas. It assisted the MoH to organize three regional workshops,  attended by 300 officials from provincial Centres for Disease Control across  all 63 provinces, to review and plan these interventions. UNICEF’s  high-impact nutrition interventions are being scaled up by Dien Bien and Gia  Lai provinces: Dien Bien expanded Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition  interventions in all 93 poor communes in seven districts and Gia Lai in 112  communes across 17 districts. Combined, the interventions benefited 9,764  pregnant women with micronutrient supplements and 5,600 children aged 6–23  months with micronutrient powder and treated 524 severely malnourished  children with UNICEF-supplied ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF). With  UNICEF's support, 700 health workers in Gia Lai were trained on SAM detection  and treatment. Outreach efforts screened 1,800 children under age five,  leading to the identification and treatment of over 400 SAM cases with 5 tons  of RUTF supplied by UNICEF. This support will allow detection and treatment  of seriously malnourished children to expand throughout the Central Highland  region.
  
WASH
  
UNICEF supported strategic WASH policies and guidelines to increase access to water services for vulnerable children and women through national and provincial dialogues on WASH financing with the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) and National Women’s Union. Advocacy messages on private-public partnerships, priorities for ethnic minorities and financing were included in MARD's directives to all provinces. At an international scientific conference on climate change and health UNICEF advocated for including sanitation in the next phase (2026–2030) of a national programme targeting ethnic minorities. 
  
UNICEF support allowed over  140,651 people, 36 schools, 12 healthcare facilities and 89,236 children (around  50 per cent girls) to benefit from increased access to WASH services using  climate-resilient technologies (e.g., climate-resilient sanitation models,  rainwater harvesting and treatment systems for schools and communities). More  than 3,351 WASH officers and schoolteachers participated in capacity-building  programmes for climate-resilient WASH in schools, social and behaviour change  (SBC) communication, renewable energy and energy efficiency, climate risk  assessments and water safety planning. These initiatives led to the approval  of water safety plans for multiple water schemes and SBC strategies to  encourage healthy practices, as well as tools to strengthen investment,  operation and maintenance of WASH facilities. 
  
UNICEF promoted innovative, climate-resilient technologies in 2024 – including through a human-centred design project to address WASH challenges faced by isolated populations in the Mekong River Delta and Central Highlands. The project developed user-centric latrine products and service packages that are affordable, sustainable and tailored to local contexts, including areas prone to flooding, salinity and water scarcity. It fostered close collaboration with local private stakeholders and communes, resulting in three climate-resilient sanitation pilots endorsed for widespread replication by the MoH. 
  
UNICEF supported the Women’s Union and Da Nang City to design and implement a menstrual hygiene health communication campaign to provide knowledge and skills and create an enabling environment for adolescents. A national hybrid event on Global Menstrual Hygiene Day was held in 63 provinces/cities, raising hygiene awareness among more than 30,000 children. 
  
Child protection
  
UNICEF supported improvements in the legal and policy framework on social work, child protection and child justice. The new social work decree is expected to enhance social work professionalization and improve protection services for vulnerable children and women. Building on UNICEF advocacy for establishing school counsellor positions in all schools in 2023, MoET promulgated professional standards for school counsellors – expected to ensure quality mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) for students across the country. Approval of the Law on Justice for Minors in November 2024 marked a milestone, introducing a specialized approach to access to justice by children in contact with the criminal justice system. UNICEF provided technical advice on Decree 76/2024, increasing the level of cash support for vulnerable children. Viet Nam participated and endorsed the Outcome Document of the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. 
  
UNICEF, in collaboration with relevant ministries and universities, strengthened the child protection workforce and services by training 100 trainers who will cascade their knowledge to frontline child protection staff. To address trauma experienced by abused children, in cooperation with the MoH, Ministry of Labour, Invalid and Social Affairs (MOLISA) and public universities, UNICEF supported trauma therapy training for 40 trainers and key child protection staff from the National Child Protection Helpline and other institutions. UNICEF also supported training on child online protection, reaching 24,000 child protection staff to better safeguard children in the digital space. These training programmes will be integrated into the pre-service social work curriculum at key universities. Guidelines on the provision of integrated child protection services were developed and rolled out in selected provinces, including through government funding. A plan was developed to pilot the ‘Primero’ digital case management system in 2025. 
  
UNICEF introduced the concept of multidisciplinary child protection services in hospitals and helped to launch the first Child Protection Committee at the National Children's Hospital, informing a national guideline on integrated services for abused children. UNICEF supported training on child-friendly, gender-sensitive forensics with abused children for 180 forensic experts (most of whom are male), obstetricians and pediatricians.  
  
In schools, UNICEF supported the provision of social work, child protection and MHPSS that allowed 150 school managers and counsellors to receive training in these skills. Ten schools received support to pilot social work and counselling models to provide evidence for national scale-up. 
   
With support from the Netherlands Government, UNICEF partnered with MoET, local child protection staff and civil society organizations (CSOs) to train teachers, administrators, business owners and parents on the importance of preventing child labour, ensuring children’s education, protection and compliance with child labour laws. To prevent at-risk children from engaging in child labour UNICEF reached 10 million students with awareness-raising activities. 
  
To improve handling of child justice cases and foster a more child- and gender-sensitive justice system UNICEF helped to strengthen capacities of 2,252 justice and law enforcement officers (1,037 women) via partnerships with top law institutes, law enforcement and justice agencies. Another milestone was replication of the Police ‘Child-Friendly Investigation Room’ model across all provinces; over 20 new rooms were established in 2024.
  
The integrated early childhood development parenting programme reached over 12,000 parents and caregivers in seven provinces, equipping participants with critical knowledge and skills for nurturing care and protecting children from violence and abuse, indirectly benefiting over 24,000 children under eight years of age. Local child protection systems in six focus provinces were further strengthened to provide protection and support for 15,123 vulnerable child victims and those at risk of abuse, child labour and exploitation.
  
Education
  
UNICEF continues to co-lead the Education Sector Group, together with the MoET. UNICEF supported early learning and development standards and a national resolution to mobilize resources for implementation of the new early childhood education (ECE) curriculum. Based on the successful ECE universalization for five-year-old children, UNICEF continued advocacy for ECE universalization for children from three-to-five-years-old.   
   
Social  emotional learning (SEL) is now a national and subnational government priority and was included in the new ECE curriculum; capacity-building is taking place nationwide. With UNICEF support, guidelines, training materials and sample videos developed by MoET and the National College of Education assist localities with implementation. 
  
UNICEF also supported  enhanced digital literacy for teachers and marginalized students—especially to empower girls—through implementation of the digital literacy and transferable skills framework and innovation spaces. UNICEF supported MoET to  develop the first national digital competency framework for teachers and educators and the national artificial intelligence (AI) competency framework  for students. Several pilots using digital innovations for learning and inclusion have matured and are under discussion for scaling-up.  
  
A national data-management system received UNICEF support to build capacity for data analysis, ensuring more informed and equity-focused planning and decision-making, as well as teacher training on the Southeast Asia Primary Learning Metrics. 
  
UNICEF promoted the inclusion of gender equality, diversity and inclusion in school settings through awareness-raising and capacity-building activities for teachers and education managers in several provinces. In collaboration with authorities in Lao Cai, An Giang and Dong Thap provinces, UNICEF undertook action research on gender inclusion, using guidelines and training materials that UNICEF helped to develop, to inform national and sub-national strategies. 
  
UNICEF collaborated with MARD and MoET to offer training on integrating disaster-risk management, climate change adaptation and mitigation into regular curricular activities,  reaching 160 educational managers and teachers (43 females) nationwide who  will cascade the training. Guidelines for integrating DRR and climate change into upper secondary, lower secondary and Pedagogical University subjects were also developed.
  
Social  policy and governance
  
In close collaboration with the International Labour Organization and UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UNICEF provided technical support to MoLISA to review implementation of Decree 20, to improve effectiveness and relevance of social assistance in Viet Nam. This effort resulted in a new Decree (76/2024) that increases the level of cash support to regular social assistance  beneficiaries. The Decree also encourages provinces to expand social  assistance coverage to more vulnerable people and raise support levels above the national standard. 
  
UNICEF developed a strategic paper on comprehensive child development to contribute to the  Government’s Viet Nam 2045 report and the 2026–2030 Socio-Economic Development Plan. The paper recommends policies that place children at the centre of Viet Nam’s development policies, including human capital development, to inform the 14th Communist Party Congress in early 2026, which will approve the new socio-economic development plan and strategy beyond 2030.
  
Cross-cutting
  
UNICEF contributed to national efforts to accelerate monitoring, reporting  and implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In collaboration with the Ministry of Planning and Investment and the General  Statistics Office (GSO), UNICEF supported a mid-term review of  the SDG National Action Plan, focusing on children and women. UNICEF also  provided technical support to the GSO for updating Viet Nam’s SDG indicators. The GSO is considering recommendations and solutions for standardizing important SDG indicators on education completion, WASH, child labour and multi-dimensional  child poverty and/or adding new ones; e.g., on early childhood development, foundational learning skills, damage to schools and health facilities, exclusive breastfeeding and handwashing with water and soap.
  
Communication, public advocacy and behaviour change activities reached 88.6 million people in 2024 (30.3 per cent increase), with stronger outreach to young audiences on key priorities, such as climate. The Typhoon Yagi response increased UNICEF’s visibility in both traditional and digital media. The emergency—in  addition to key events and campaigns (World Children’s Day, International Day of Play, Fix My Food, Child Labor)—contributed to sharp increases in social  media engagement (78.2 per cent) with significant impact among followers younger than 24 years (26.6 per cent increase). U-Report results also showed  increased interest and engagement by young people in UNICEF's work, reflected in the 34.7 per cent rise in registered U-Reporters during 2024. 
  
Disaster-risk reduction, emergency preparedness  
  
UNICEF support to MARD’s Viet Nam Dyke and Disaster Management Agency (VDDMA) led to enhanced government focus on disaster-risk reduction (DRR) and emergency response capacities, particularly building resilience among children and communities. UNICEF support included technical assistance to (1) assess implementation and propose changes to two decrees related to  disaster prevention and managing international emergency aid for disaster recovery and relief), (2) policy recommendations for improving evacuation centres and warehouses in  emergencies; (3) data collection and visualization of child vulnerability in Viet Nam’s Disaster Monitoring System and (4) enhanced capacity of provincial disaster-prevention and control officials (26 per cent female) from 13 Mekong Delta provinces to meet international standards on DRR, emergency preparedness and response.
  
Adolescent and youth engagement and participation
  
A total of 488,006 adolescents and young people (aged 10-24) participated in or led civic engagement initiatives through UNICEF-supported programmes. Creative communication activities supported by UNICEF empowered children and young people to advocate for and contribute to climate action, encouraging them to share their perspectives and propose solutions to reduce disaster impacts and mitigate and adapt to climate change. Online competitions such as a national contest on disaster prevention and climate change adaptation and the ‘One Day as a Child Reporter’ video challenge attracted over 16,000 participants. 
  
In collaboration with the Youth Climate Action Network, UNICEF supported the 2024 Local Conference of Vietnamese Youth, a platform that attracted over 500 young people and stakeholders to discuss actionable adolescent and youth-led solutions. This led to development of the ‘Vietnam Youth Statement on Climate’ and attendance of two young leaders at the 29th UN  Climate Change Conference in Baku, amplifying Vietnamese youth voices on a global stage. In addition, a child-friendly Vietnam Nationally Determined Contributions document was developed and being implemented following broad consultation with children. 
  
Vietnamese adolescents and youth were empowered to affect societal change through advocacy and action. Over 180 young people aged 18–24 were trained on UNICEF’s Young Action Guide, resulting in implementation of seven youth-led projects on mental health and psychosocial support that reached 5,000 adolescents and youth across the country, including the most vulnerable.   
  
Humanitarian response and recovery
  
UNICEF responded to two climate-induced emergencies in 2024—a drought and saltwater intrusion in the Mekong Delta and major flooding and destruction following Typhoon Yagi in northern Viet Nam. UNICEF was among the first agencies to mobilize action on Yagi, including more than US$4 million. UNICEF concluded partnerships with MARD and four heavily affected provinces with pre-existing  vulnerabilities to deliver immediate humanitarian assistance and recovery support to the most vulnerable families. A post-disaster Viet Nam Multisectoral Assessment was conducted in December with UN partners, the European Union (EU) and the Government. Guided by the assessment, UNICEF is supporting recovery efforts in WASH, nutrition, education, humanitarian cash transfers, child  protection and resilience-building. UNICEF leads the WASH and nutrition sectors and  co-leads the education (with Save the Children) and child protection sectors –  together with relevant government agencies.
  
Key results include:
  
-           WASH, health and nutrition:  Over 53,000 people (3,900 people in the Mekong River Delta affected by drought and 49,300 people in eight provinces affected by Yagi) received critical WASH supplies. UNICEF supported health workers to screen for malnutrition, reaching more  than 100,000 children under five years in 582 communes of six provinces, resulting  in referrals to health centres for 601 children with SAM and 4,750 with  moderate acute malnutrition. 
  
-           Education and child protection:  UNICEF provided essential teaching and learning  materials and school supplies to ensure continued learning by 22,000 children; 11,000 child protection and learning kits were provided to children and families in eight heavily affected provinces; 68,000 children, parents and caregivers were reached with messages on mental health and psychological support, prevention of GBV and child abuse; and approximately 11,400  parents/caregivers were reached with messages on preventing sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA).
  
-           Humanitarian cash transfers:  UNICEF delivered multi-purpose cash to 1,200 families affected by Yagi (5,000 people) in Lao Cai. To ensure accountability to affected populations (AAP),  NICEF operates a toll-free hotline number to address questions or complaints  and a third-party monitoring firm began conducting a baseline survey, payment verification and post-distribution monitoring. 
  
 
  
Key cross-cutting priorities such as PSEA, AAP and GBV are integrated into all humanitarian activities; GBV risk-mitigation guidance was included in all training activities and materials for implementing partners.

UNICEF deepened its engagement with government authorities and other partners at all levels to mobilize action and resources for children. Through its sector leadership role in the areas of education, WASH, nutrition and child protection, UNICEF convened key partners to help advance child rights. UNICEF Viet Nam’s emergency responses provided opportunities for deepening engagement with government and UN agencies and developing new partnerships with the public and private sectors.  
  
Support from the Government of Japan allowed UNICEF to work with MARD on strengthening child-focused DRR and ensuring that children are placed at the heart of climate resilience strategies, as well as to support MoH development of the first maternal and child e-health system. The Australian Government supported UNICEF’s work with the MoH on strengthening health system capacity for immunization and primary health care. 
   
Partnerships on child protection with key national agencies (e.g., Ministry of Justice,  MoLISA, Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuracy) and sister UN agencies were further strengthened in 2024. UNICEF continued to implement three UN Joint  Programmes: to improve access to justice (with UNDP, support from the EU); on human trafficking and child justice (with IOM, support from the U.S. Government); and to eliminate violence against women and children (with UNFPA and UN Women, support from the Australian Government). With support from the Netherlands Government, UNICEF completed an important initiative to end child  labour.  
   
UNICEF expanded partnerships to foster more inclusive and higher-quality learning environments for all children. In addition to strong collaboration with MoET and MoLISA, UNICEF enhanced partnerships with provincial education authorities to ensure a comprehensive approach to delivering learning opportunities to children, especially the most vulnerable (ethnic minorities and children with disabilities). UNICEF also supported a five-year cooperation framework between MARD and MoET to integrate knowledge on natural disaster prevention, control and mitigation into the education and training sector. With support from UNICEF National Committees (Natcoms)  in Finland, Netherlands, New Zealand, South Korea and Switzerland UNICEF supported various initiatives on inclusive quality education. To advance children’s digital learning and skills development—especially for ethnic minority students and children with disabilities—and to promote STEAM education, UNICEF partnered with the Office of Innovation, international and national EdTech companies, Steam for Vietnam Foundation, national mobile network operators and others.  
  
UNICEF and the EU launched a new partnership to address public financing bottlenecks to shock-responsive social protection. UNICEF participates in the UN Joint Programme on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. UNICEF also continued successful partnerships to co-create ‘healthy cities for adolescents and youth’ in Danang, with support from the Botnar Foundation, through the Swiss Natcom.
  
To advance climate action and community resilience, UNICEF and the Viet Nam Development Bank (VDB) forged a strategic, long-term partnership with a strong focus on children. Accredited by the Green Climate Fund as the national implementing agency, VDB is collaborating with UNICEF to propose a large-scale ‘net-zero climate resilience for children’ programme to support Viet Nam’s net-zero ambition, prioritizing child-centred adaptation and mitigation efforts.  
 
  
UNICEF also expanded public-private partnerships on water and sanitation with the Gravity Water company, which delivers low-cost, green and innovative common public goods using renewable energy and local materials for WASH facilities. UNICEF leveraged partnerships with foundations and NGOs (e.g. Health Bridge and GHAI) to advocate for the production of sugar-free drinks. 
  
In 2024 UNICEF achieved significant milestones in private sector partnerships and resource mobilization, driving transformative impact for children and vulnerable communities. It expanded its major donor partnerships and welcomed its second International Council member – making Viet Nam one of the Asian countries with the strongest presence in the UNICEF philanthropy network. Recurring donations grew substantially through the expansion of the ‘Champion for Children’ campaign and a new ‘Nutrition for Children’ campaign launched in collaboration with Thanh Nien newspaper, which raised public awareness about childhood malnutrition and mobilized resources for life-saving nutritional support.
  
UNICEF engaged with 215 companies to incorporate the Children’s Rights and Business Principles framework (CRBP)—focused on child protection and family-friendly workplace policies—into their operations. UNICEF convened ‘Bridging The Gap: Business and Social Impact Forum 2024’ to raise awareness on child rights and business sustainability with foreign chambers of commerce including European, Belgium-Luxembourg, Korean, American and Indian chambers of commerce. UNICEF worked with the Vietnam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) to promote CRBP, the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour to prevent child labour and the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association on child-responsive ESG guidelines. UNICEF also worked with the Vietnam Human Resources Association to promote family-friendly policies among Vietnamese enterprises. 
  
UNICEF also partnered with mass organizations (e.g., Viet Nam Women’s Union), universities and local and international NGOs (e.g., Viet Nam Association for Protection of Children’s Rights), Thao Dan, World Vision, Save the Children, Plan and Y-Net. UNICEF reconnected with a wide range of CSOs and plans to expand partnerships with organizations of persons with disabilities and  youth-led organizations. Several campaigns and visibility events were held in collaboration with other UN agencies, government counterparts and bilateral donors, including the International Day of Play (government partners and LEGO Foundation), World Children’s Day (multiple partners) and the ‘Ending Violence Against Women’ campaign (with UN agencies and the governments of Viet Nam and Australia).
  
UNICEF’s longstanding  partnership with MARD and the VDDMA was significantly strengthened in 2024  through  fruitful cooperation on two emergencies, and four new partnerships were developed with provinces (Lao  Cai, Dien Bien, Cao Bang and Yen Bai) affected by Typhoon Yagi. UNICEF’s Yagi  emergency response was facilitated by generous contributions from the  Governments of Japan, United Kingdom, Ireland and New Zealand; from UNICEF Natcoms in Germany, South Korea, Switzerland and USA, as well as an innovative initiative with the Embassy of Canada. UNICEF demonstrated agility in its first-ever emergency resource mobilization efforts with the private  sector: two creative emergency campaigns supported life-saving aid for  crisis-affected regions, resulting in support from private sector partners. Investments in effective emergency communication provided strong visibility for UNICEF’s humanitarian and recovery activities.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
  
Developments during 2024 revealed that along with continued inequities such as inter-generational poverty and exclusion, Vietnamese children are deeply affected by three megatrends highlighted in UNICEF’s 2024 State of the World’s Children report: climate and environmental crises, significant demographic transitions and frontier technologies. Typhoon Yagi both revealed the country’s exposure to climate risks and reinforced existing inequities, as it predominantly affected already marginalized communities. This confluence points to the importance of UNICEF investment in more shock-responsive, climate-resilient systems and adaptive and innovative programming approaches, including climate-smart solutions. Similarly, meeting the needs of a rapidly aging society reduces public funding available to invest in children and youth, which is required to build the human capital for continued socio-economic growth. This highlights the need for UNICEF to continue making the case for investing in children, including through universal child grants. Lastly, frontier technologies, including AI, are opening up huge opportunities for learning and empowerment for children and young people, while at the same time posing immense risks for child protection and wellbeing, all of which will require action by the government and partners. 
  
As in previous years, in 2024 UNICEF faced delays in programme implementation, including the emergency response, due to lengthy programme approval processes and complex operational requirements. As part of the UN and Development Partners’ Task Force, UNICEF advocated with the government for simplified procedures and accelerated approval processes. Despite senior-level commitment to addressing bottlenecks for ODA implementation, ongoing institutional reforms may further slow decision-making in the coming period. UNICEF has had to be more adaptive and agile to deliver on the country programme in a timely and effective manner, including by broadening partnerships and direct implementation of activities. 
  
Despite some successful resource mobilization efforts, in 2024 UNICEF faced resource constraints due to: (1) a reduction in flexible core resources, (2) decreased public sector funding for development activities (tied to Viet Nam’s middle-income status) and (3) the funding crunch for humanitarian aid caused by increasing global crises and stagnant funding. In addition, some donors prioritized restricted funding tied to specific projects, limiting UNICEF’s operational adaptability and capacity to address urgent, unforeseen needs. Nonetheless, in addition to growing engagement with the private sector, space remains for UNICEF to strengthen cooperation with international and national corporate partners, major donors and through individual giving. 
  
Additional challenges and opportunities appeared in some cross-cutting areas: data privacy and protection requirements hindered data generation and sharing, creating delays for the introduction of some innovative technologies.  Advancing gender equality and ensuring child protection requires profound changes to social norms, calling for investment in long-term social and behaviour change (SBC) communication and advocacy, including engagement with parents and teachers on topics such as early marriage and child sex selection. Increased need for effective SBC was also highlighted by the government decree on solarization—a good entry point for movement on renewables—as a vehicle for advocacy for green behaviours and habits, especially among children and youth. More work is needed on environmental protection, including air pollution, to raise awareness and mobilize action. 
  
Lessons learned 
  
Many challenges, opportunities and emerging trends were captured in an internal visioning exercise undertaken by UNICEF Viet Nam to inform the ongoing mid-term strategic reflection on progress achieved and lessons learned to date. 
  
The complex reality of persistent inequities overlapping with and reinforcing new megatrends demand that UNICEF and partners redouble efforts to ensure that children will thrive, be prepared to cope with new threats and to seize emerging opportunities. Strategic and early investment in key cross-cutting programming areas (e.g., climate change, digital transformation, demographic shifts, mental health) is needed to ensure that UNICEF is well-positioned to support government efforts to ensure sustainable, inclusive economic growth. This will require shaper prioritization based on child rights, enhancing internal capacity and expertise in these areas and broader partnerships and alliances.  
  
Key lessons include the need for UNICEF to strengthen its convening power, thought leadership and influence to keep the child rights agenda at the very heart of national and international partners’ priorities, as well as to invest in efforts to deepen and diversify public and private partnerships for scaling up innovative programming, financing and resource mobilization for children. Investing in public awareness campaigns and broad-based alliances on child rights remains essential to mobilizing broader support, in particular with children and youth themselves. Moving forward, UNICEF will focus on expanding its audience and partner base—particularly among younger, tech-savvy groups—while fostering long-term partnerships with governments, public sector partners and corporations to drive systemic change for the most vulnerable children. 
  
To address the constrained operational environment UNICEF will continue to advocate for simplified procedures and accelerated approval processes with national government partners, while also exploring expanded partnerships at the subnational level and with CSOs. UNICEF hopes to remain at the forefront of large-scale alliances on key cross-sectoral priorities (environmental protection and climate change, green and digital transformation, human capital development and protecting women and children from violence and exploitation) through ever-stronger partnerships with UN agencies, national and international non-governmental organizations and academia.
  
Future Outlook   
  
In past decades Viet Nam achieved impressive results for children as part of its remarkable socio-economic development. While this positive trend continued in 2024, children's rights and futures are at a critical point due to rapid demographic, economic, technological, environmental and societal changes. In 2025 UNICEF and partners will mark the 50-year anniversary of the UNICEF-Viet Nam partnership for child rights and the 35th anniversary of Viet Nam’s ratification of the Convention of the Rights of the Child – key opportunities to mobilize action for advancing child rights. UNICEF is well-placed to, and will further invest in, supporting the Government and partners to ensure that children can thrive and be protected, are well equipped to face new challenges, can participate fully in society and contribute positively to Viet Nam’s continued socio-economic development.

In October 2024, the Government of Albania (GoA) formally opened accession negotiations with the European Union (EU), with fundamentals (Cluster 1), including child rights. Concurrently, the European Commission endorsed Albania's Reform Agenda and its multiannual work programme (2024–2027) under the Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans. While the agenda includes reforms in (i) the business environment, (ii) human capital, (iii) digitalization, (iv) energy and the green transition, and (v) fundamental rights and the rule of law, it prioritizes economic growth over investments in human capital. Albania, an elected member of the Human Rights Council for 2024-2026, commemorated the 75th anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, pledging its commitment to improve its justice system, particularly juvenile-friendly justice, enhance protection of the rights of persons with disabilities, and improve women’s participation in the workforce.
Released in 2024, the Global Sustainable Development Report propelled Albania to 42nd place, marking a significant leap of 12 positions from 2023 and reflecting steady progress in recent years. To respond to challenges, the State Agency for Strategic Development Aid Coordination, in collaboration with line ministries, prepared the roadmap for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
 
Albania’s Corruption Perceptions Index 2023 ranking of 98/180, together with illicit finance flows and money laundering concerns, represented a serious challenge. In response, a new major reform process on ‘good governance, rule of law and anti-corruption for Albania 2030’ was launched by parliament, at the behest of the Prime Minister.
 
The World Bankprojected 3.3 per cent growth of Albania’s economy in 2024 is expected through 2025–2029, according to the World BankInternational Monetary Fund. However, gross domestic product (GDP) per capita remained the lowest in the Western Balkans, with consumption 36 per cent of the European averageEuropean average. Demonstrating a decreasing trend in recent years, the proportion of the population at risk of poverty in 2023 was 19.7 per; 26.5 per cent for children; and 23.9 per cent for households with dependent children.[1] In response, GoA approved the National Strategy on Social Protection (2024–2030), which adopts a life-cycle approach and underscores its commitment to the Child Guarantee Action Plan.
 
According to the Census, Albania’s population dwindled to 2.4 million in 2023, against the 3.2 million recorded in 1991. The number of children under 18 years of age represents 19 per cent of the population, decreasing by 38.7 per cent compared to 2011. The average age was 42.5 years, compared to 35.2 in 2011, indicating an ageing population, largely due to emigration and low fertility. Emigration continued at pace with 46,460 leaving in 2022,[2] shifting from unskilled workers to well-educated professionals, straining pensions, social security, and increasing the likelihood for those left behind not to have children.[3] According to the World Bank index, Albanians born today will only achieve 63 per cent of their human capital potential than if they enjoyed complete access to education and health services. This value is lower than the regional average human capital index and is higher for girls (66 per cent) than boys (61 per cent).[4]  
 
Despite the welcome return to normal parliamentary functioning in March 2024, political polarization remained high in the lead-up to the May 2025 general elections. Parliament was unable to appoint a new Ombudsperson or Commissioner against Discrimination, leading to an extension of their terms beyond the intended mandate.[5]  
 
The education system suffered from low public spending (2.1 per cent of GDP in 2023[6], below the regional (4.6 per cent) and EU (4.7 per cent) averages) [7] and inefficient resource allocation, alongside shortages of qualified teachers in small municipalities and limited career growth opportunities. Albania's 2022 low PISA scores highlight deficiencies in education quality, with youth aged 15 years performing below the OECD average in key subjects, especially those coming from a lower social-economic status. Poor educational outcomes create skills gaps, limiting opportunities for youth, disadvantaged groups, and women. This exacerbates unpaid caregiving and informal work among women (over 50 per cent), and high youth not in employment, education or training rates (25 per cent for those aged 15–29). Additionally, poor labour force quality stems from limited education investment, challenging transition to work, skills mismatch, slow economic growth, fiscal pressures, climate risks, and inadequate revenue for social protection and human capital.[8] To mitigate these issues, GoA assessed implementation of the Education Strategy (2021-2026) and the Youth Strategy, with their respective Action Plans (2022-2029) to refine priorities and enhance progress.   
 
One in four Albanian adults commonly report violence against children (in any form).[9] The November 2024 stabbing of a 14-year-old student sparked public calls for stricter school safety and online protection, prompting the government to launch the National Action Plan on School Safety.  
 
Afghan evacuees continued to arrive in Albana with approximately 4,500 individuals (57 per cent children, 48 per cent women) passing through and receiving comprehensive immediate support, during their average one-month stay. In 2024 alone, border and migration police intercepted 98 unaccompanied and/or separated children (UASC), although this figure only accounts for those who reached official border points and underwent screening. The true number remains unknown, as many evade detection, for whom no data is available. In February 2024, the Government of Italy finalized a deal with GoA to transfer up to 36,000 asylum seekers annually, excluding children, pregnant women and other vulnerable individuals, to detention centres in Albania each year until resolution of their case. 
 
UNICEF is committed to continuing the monitoring of children’s rights in Albania, in support of GoA, to match efforts with the EU accession process, building overall resilience, and protecting every child's right, safety, well-being, and dignity, including in prevention and emergency response.

Every child survives and thrives
The Ministry of Health and Social Protection (MoHSP), with UNICEF assistance, positioned universal progressive home visiting (UPHV) as a central and integrated intervention to deliver primary health care (PHC), reaching the most vulnerable children and families. As a result, 4,360 children under five (2,076 girls), out of whom 773 were Roma and Egyptian children (368 girls) were reached by health personnel who conducted 13,802 home visits in seven counties (Tirana, Korçë, Vlore, Elbasan, Lezha, Kukes, Berat). Around 80 professionals improved their skills in child growth and development monitoring, vision and hearing screening, supporting parenting skills, early identification and referral of postpartum depression, positive gender socialization, identification of early signs of gender-based violence, child protection against discrimination and stigma. Overall, 84 cases of children at risk were identified during home visits, benefiting from early intervention services. 
 
With UNICEF support, 120 health professionals across nine maternity hospitals (covering 80 per cent of births) enhanced care quality through training, supervision, and coaching, addressing concerns related to newborn health and developmental challenges in premature and at-risk newborns. UNICEF supported the development and dissemination of national guidelines and standards in areas of newborn care.  
 
Following a 2024 measles outbreak, 3,080 under-vaccinated children and their families received the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. In coordination with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF supported the Institute of Public Health (IPH) by training 205 health professionals in Tirana, Durres, and Fier on vaccine administration and communication skills. A national campaign addressed vaccine hesitancy, reaching over 8,000 parents, community members, and religious leaders, with an additional 188,446 engaged online.
As part of efforts to implement the National Mental Health Plan (2023–2026), the UNICEF-WHO Joint Programme on Mental Health advanced the advocacy agenda using newly released evidence[1] and strengthened the capacities of health professionals to support the Operator of Health Services and IPH. In Lezha, Elbasan, Berat, and Tirana, 424 health professionals (356 women) participated in accredited training for early identification, support, and referral of mental health issues in children and adolescents. The online platform, IfightDepression was promoted among adolescents and providers as a source of relevant information on available services and support. In collaboration with IPH and local health and education authorities, 1,207 children and adolescents (645 girls) in five counties participated in informative sessions on mental health and well-being, advocating for access to quality, child-centered mental health and psychosocial services.

Aligned with the priorities of MoHSP for early childhood interventions, UNICEF supported the technical working group established to prepare a mapping of services, resources and normative framework targeting children with autism spectrum disorders, developmental delays and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Discussion of diverse options of service delivery models is expected to contribute to improved early identification and access to early interventions for children in this target group.

Every child learns
Early childhood education represents a critical investment in Albania's future, with evidence showing significant returns in terms of school readiness and long-term educational outcomes. 
Under the leadership of the Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES) and UNICEF support, Albania’s early childhood education and care (ECEC) policies were aligned to EU standards; the monitoring and evaluation framework was approved, and a roadmap to reform ECEC for children aged 0–6 years was developed. Leveraging evidence was a useful advocacy tool in 2024, with UNICEF using a recent study “Policy options for Early Childhood Education Financing" in Albania ” and the policy paper on human capital to draw the attention of key stakeholders (including the World Bank, EU, municipalities, and the government) to underbudgeted areas such as early childhood development and social protection. 

Over 550 preschool teachers (all women) and directors received training and coaching on the latest curricula, including Reggio Emilia and Universal Design for Learning approaches, with a focus on child-centred, project-based learning and fostering community involvement, particularly through the collaboration of fathers in education. UNICEF promoted digital tools like the Akademi.al platform for interactive learning for children aged five years through a series of 136 videos and interactive lessons aligned with preschool curricula.
GIS-driven school infrastructure planning improved learning environments and governance across 100 schools in six municipalities. By identifying resource gaps, prioritizing investments, and enhancing access for marginalized children, GIS helped boost attendance and reduce dropouts. Engaging communities, donors, and government agencies, it fostered collaboration and accountability while supporting long-term education goals.

Reaching 15,908 parents (2,098 fathers), the Bebbo application was promoted in preschools delivering skills to caregivers and professionals on how to monitor the development of children and engage them in appropriate play activities.  

UNICEF supported the midterm review of the National Education Strategy, prioritizing actions to build inclusive, skills-based, and innovative school environments. The PISA 2022 secondary analysis and a review of second-chance education highlighted low-quality outcomes and the need for updated curricula. UNICEF then implemented a programme to enhance blended learning skills, training and mentoring for 600 teachers.

MoES developed a roadmap with UNICEF support identifying how improved legal framework can be translated into actions and measures to transform special schools in Albania. To date, 418 assistive and classroom teachers have been trained in inclusive education.
A cross-sectoral action plan against school violence was launched by MoES with technical assistance from UNICEF, using a holistic approach to address the entire ecosystem surrounding violence prevention in schools. The plan is based on improving capacities of professionals, linking education with the protection and referral system, and ensuring the efficient response of school security in risky situations. By fostering an inclusive and supportive school setting, the aim is to encourage an environment where children can learn and thrive in safety. 
UNICEF leveraged government funding for scholarships, benefiting 3,804 out-of-school or at-risk students under the leave no child behind agenda. With UNICEF support, MoES enhanced dropout prevention by developing a monitoring guideline for scholarship recipients and an investment case to expand scholarships to upper secondary education. The early warning system (EWS) supported 17,261 students in 14 vocational education training (VET) and 84 secondary schools, with 400 adolescents (260 boys, 140 girls) supported through individual dropout prevention plans. The EWS framework is now accredited by the National Agency for Employment and Skills for VET schools and by MoES for secondary schools.
 
UNICEF-supported periodic monitoring of the Youth Strategy and Action Plan revealed a critical need to revise the ‘youth’ law. Recognizing that young voices must be at the heart of this change, UNICEF worked alongside the Minister of State for Youth and Children (MoSYC) to bring 360 young people (216 girls) from Youth Municipal Councils across 12 municipalities into the conversation. Together, they shared their perspectives, shaping proposed amendments that reflect their aspirations and needs.
 
In collaboration with MoSYC, UNICEF empowered local youth councils in three municipalities (Shkodër, Vlorë, and Korçë) and supported 300 youth activists with training in project management, career guidance, and youth engagement. Youth play a pivotal role in Albania’s society and its transition to a green and digital economy, highlighting the need for comprehensive skills development. Through MoES and the Redebate programme with MoYSC, 1,675 youth (1,034 girls) received soft skills and media literacy training, while 30,000 youth (60 per cent girls) were reached via social media, promoting 21st century skills, advocacy, and entrepreneurship, with a focus on NEET youth.
 
Further skills building in foundational and socio-emotional learning were boosted for 400 low-achieving VET students aged 15–18 years (100 girls) in collaboration with the Ministry of Economy, Innovation and Culture, focusing on mathematics, information technology, communication, and personal development with positive impacts on attendance and retention rates in VET schools.

The National Agency for Skills and Employment, in partnership with UNICEF, introduced 10,000 at-risk youth to generative technologies via Albania’s employment portal, improving job search capabilities. Approximately 5,870 VET students benefited from hackathons, business mentorship, and skills-building workshops through the AFPro network, connecting education with the private sector. Additionally, 1,200 career guidance teachers participated in the Pick a Skill campaign with MoES, an integrated, multi-stakeholder approach that holistically advanced youth capacities.

Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
By the end of 2024, UNICEF successfully handed over to MoHSP the management of two one-stop centres (Barnahaus model) in Shkodër and Fier that assist victims and witnesses of domestic violence and sexual abuse. In 2024, 40 children (21 girls; 19 boys) and nine caregivers benefitted from services linked to family crisis management and counselling.
 
Under the framework of the National Action Plan on Fight against Trafficking in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior, UNICEF continued its partnership with three anti-trafficking shelters. Child potential victims/victims of trafficking (8 boys; 14 girls) aged 0-17 years, and 23 dependents (10 boys; 13 girls) benefitted from reintegration services and 48 families in Bulqizë and administrative units at risk of trafficking benefited from integrated services at community.
 
The National Authority on Cyber Security addressed online safety, reaching 1,200 children and generating 210 cyberbullying reports through 27 activities in nine municipalities with UNICEF support. UNICEF partnered with Meta on a campaign targeting adolescents (aged 13–19 years), addressing cyberbullying, exploitation, misuse of data, and harmful content, particularly for children on the move, while engaging parents and caregivers. The campaign provided practical online safety guidance and encouraged reporting. Under the Bibliotech approach, UNICEF trained 99 participants (64 female) in Tirana and Shkodër, enhancing digital literacy among children, young adults, and teachers.
 
UNICEF support to state police ensured that 563 children in conflict/contact with the law (110 girls) received specialized child protection support and immediate counseling at police stations. This group included 224 children in conflict with the law, 139 children who were witnesses to various forms of abuse, and 200 children who were survivors of violence.  

In close collaboration with the State Agency for Child Rights and Protection, 280 children identified as being at medium to high risk of abuse were referred to appropriate child protection units, with 34 of these children (total of 95) receiving individual case management support. Concurrently, 76 child protection workers benefited from on-the-job coaching and capacity building in case management referral pathways, provided through UNICEF support. 
Justice and law enforcement stakeholders continued to receive UNICEF support in the implementation of the Criminal Justice for Children Code and the Child Rights and Protection Law, through dedicated technical assistance to the Juvenile Criminality Prevention Centre in the use of the online integrated data system for justice for children (63 professionals (46 female) trained and mentored), increased skills to conduct child-friendly, victim-centred and trauma-informed interviews with victims of crime, including gender-responsive interviewing witnesses and alleged offenders (over 150 police officers (41 women) trained; strengthened knowledge and practice in intersectoral case management).

The multi-disciplinary approach to child justice engaged 24 local businesses from the private sector in Shkodra and Lezha to provide employment and on-the-job training for juveniles in conflict with the law, strengthening ties with public authorities for socio-economic reintegration. In 2024, 45 children (10 girls) accessed services like restorative justice, mediation, psychological support, legal aid, and mentoring. Additionally, 282 students (21 Roma, 147 boys) gained conflict resolution skills through workshops, and 151 children (16 Egyptian, 78 boys) participated in education and recreational peer-to-peer activities using artistic methods. Representatives from 15 public agencies in Shkodra reaffirmed their commitment by re-signing a memorandum with UNICEF and a civil society organization.
As part of a series of workshops with parents on positive parenting/positive disciplining, with gender equality lenses, 182 parents (24 men, 21 Afghan) obtained professional advice and knowledge regarding healthy family relations, domestic violence, parent-child (in conflict/ contact with the law) interaction, and how the new penal code for children is protecting juveniles and families.

Every child lives in a safe and clean environment  
UNICEF worked with the government and civil society organizations to prepare the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, to explore, in a holistic manner, the implication of climate, environment, energy, and disasters on the well-being and development of Albania’s boys and girls and provide recommendations for action to UNICEF.
 
Focusing on increasing awareness on climate change risks for children UNICEF reached around 35,182 individuals (Meta), 6,057 individuals (Instagram), 527 (twitter/X) in 2024. Through community engagement around 451 professionals and community members (310 women), of which 166 were from rural areas and 285 from urban areas, in seven districts, were reached, bringing together public health experts and local government representatives, to discuss socioeconomic and health consequences of climate change, reflect on community-driven adaptation strategies, and emergency preparedness in the face of climate change.  
 
Guidelines on water, sanitation and hygiene in the context of climate change, developed with UNICEF’s assistance to IPH, oriented the training of around 58 professionals from local health care units, state health inspectorate and water supply organizations from Tirana, Korçë, Elbasan and Vlora where topics such as managing the quality and safety of drinking water, addressing the challenges of climate change, and other risks to public health were discussed. Moreover, UNICEF partnered with USAID to advocate with MoHSP for actions in the framework of ‘Lead free future for children’, with the vision for a world in which all children grow up free from lead exposure.

UNICEF advanced youth-led social and environmental actions on air quality and climate, focusing on girls. Under the National Action Plan for Youth Guarantee 2024-2026, 305 school staff and leaders were trained in clean air and environmental experiential learning and in February 2024, Youth4AirQuality members formally submitted air quality demands for action to Tirana municipality. Under the Youth for Air and Climate initiative, youth addressed traffic issues in Korçë, modeling sustainable urban living. UNICEF also supported two Albanian youth representatives at COP29, where they advocated for child-friendly nationally determined contributions to national and global leaders.

Every child has an equitable chance in life  
With UNICEF support, the National Strategy on Social Protection (2024–2030) was approved, emphasizing a life-cycle approach, integrating shock-responsive measures, mainstreaming gender, and advancing the decentralization of social care and deinstitutionalization of residential care for children and adults.
To increase quality, efficiency and transparency of the social protection system, UNICEF continued to support the management information system (MIS) by engaging in policy dialogue with MoHSP on reinforcing its use and initiating discussions with the World Bank on the integration of three existing MIS systems to enhance cash assistance, disability allowances, and social care.  
 
To advance the deinstitutionalization (De-I) plan, residential care facilities in Vlorë and Korçë were transformed into family-based and community services using a scalable UNICEF-developed methodology, approved by the National De-I Steering Committee. In Shkodër, Tirana, and Durrës, efforts to prevent family separation and support reunification were strengthened, with the social workforce providing dedicated support to 83 at-risk children and their families through home visits, parenting classes, and psychological counseling. Additionally, 160 professionals across five municipalities received training on De-I reform and child support services using UNICEF-developed modules. 
 
UNICEF partnered with the Order of Social Workers to enhance its licensing mandate and contribute to professionalization of the workforce, adding 97 social workers (totaling 597 nationwide). It also supported the University of Tirana's Department of Social Work in strengthening curricula and launching a new master’s programme on social policy and sustainable development.

UNICEF worked with social welfare services and cross-sectoral professionals in four counties (Kamëz, Bulqizë, Puka, Kukës) to enhance capacities, gender awareness, and responsiveness. This initiative established an outreach model, supporting social welfare staff with case management to assist 10,000 families as part of the economic aid scheme, including 1,300 families with more than three children.
 
MoHSP rolled out, with UNICEF support, the national bio psychosocial assessment-disability reform, and trained 124 representatives of local health and social welfare authorities. A dedicated module, developed with UNICEF's technical assistance, provided child-friendly guidance for assessing children with disabilities and is included in the accredited training manual for multidisciplinary disability assessment commissions.
 
UNICEF invested heavily in strengthening the human rights framework in Albania in 2024, particularly in relation to children’s rights. Not only did UNICEF technical assistance advance Albania’s progress toward EU integration for Chapter 19 of the Acquis on Social Policy and Employment, but continued support to MoHSP also led to the preparation of a positioning paper and a draft roadmap for Chapter 19 (social policy) and Chapter 23 (child-related aspects). As a result, the EU common position document on Cluster 1: Fundamentals sets as interim benchmark for the accession the completion of transition of children without parental care from residential care towards community based care. 

In response to the 2023 Committee on the Rights of the Child Concluding Observations, UNICEF supported MoHSP / State Agency for Child Rights and Protection in developing an action plan with around 300 targeted actions aligned with policy commitments and EU-acquis chapters. Endorsed by the National Council of Child Rights and Protection, its implementation monitoring will begin in 2025. UNICEF also guided INSTAT and ministries on completing a Data Gap Assessment for the multiple indicator cluster survey (MICS) 2025 to identify priority child and youth well-being indicators. Governance mechanisms for the implementation of MICS 2025 were established to ensure stakeholder collaboration.
 
Humanitarian
The increasing complexity of migration means that emergency settings present multiple challenges that impact children's rights, protection, and well-being. For the third year, UNICEF continued to provide support to Afghan families and strengthen the capacities of government stakeholders to respond to emergencies through integrated and holistic approaches. The country office, building on the experience of Afghan support, further strengthened its emergency preparedness and response capacity and contributed to increasing resilience and shock responsiveness of the national system. 

In 2024, UNICEF and partners provided coordinated health and nutrition, early childhood and education, child protection, multipurpose cash and care services to a total of 4,500 Afghan evacuees, of whom 54 per cent were children, and 48 per cent women.   
Multipurpose cash assistance reached approximately 1,157 Afghan households, including about 3,174 children under 18 years of age (1,561 girls; 1,613 boys). This initiative, alongside technical assistance on shock-responsive programming, advocated for expanding cash transfers and integrating a shock-responsive model into the national social protection system. UNICEF's cash-plus support for Afghan refugees in Albania could serve as a replicable model for other emergencies.

[1] Namely: 1. Secondary analysis on mental health from 2023 Healthy behavior of school-aged children; 2. Study on policy options to finance mental health services.

In 2024, UNICEF prioritized partnerships and leveraged public and private sectors to amplify support for children, strengthening its position in Albania and the region.
As part of the UN Resident Coordinator (UNRC)-led EU-UN collaboration, a dynamic policy dialogue on human capital development was initiated, steered by UNICEF, with co-leadership of EU and World Bank. A paper on human capital and a series of deep dives were developed to: (i) leverage global policy priorities to advance joint impact and results in Albania to accelerate the SDGs and EU accession, and (ii) establish a space for joint sectoral dialogue on specific topics of common interest and/or emerging trends, such as early childhood learning and development.
 
UNICEF leveraged the EU accession process to prioritize child rights in policy and programming, through implementation of two EU-funded programmes: EU4Social Care in partnership with World Vision Albania to enhance municipal social services; and EU4Youth with UNDP to make education, training, and employment more accessible for NEET youth under the Youth Guarantee initiative.
 
UNICEF advocated with the EU delegation and government to extend the European Child Guarantee (ECG) to Albania, emphasizing the importance of early childhood education; and with MoHSP for the integration of the ECG in the new social protection strategy. The government has requested support for ECG through the Instrument for Pre-accession Assistance 2025-2027 indicating UNICEF as partner of choice. 
 
As a leading agency in Albania's One UN approach, UNICEF spearheaded Outcome 1 on human capital under the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2022–2026. UNICEF coordinated the UN Youth Task Force (UN YTF), which contributed to the National Youth Strategy and Social Protection Strategy (2024–2030). Following participation in the 2024 Summit for the Future, UN YTF promoted youth engagement in peacebuilding, AI-driven digital expansion, and sustainable finance.
 
UNICEF, UNDP, UNWomen and ILO partnered on the joint SDG Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection initiative, leading to Albania being selected globally as one of the 14 countries that will be engaged in this initiative. 
 
UNICEF strengthened cooperation with UN agencies through joint programmes like EU4Youth and LEAP-SDG Accelerator support. A joint action plan and signed MoU with UNHCR addressed the needs of refugees, stateless individuals, and UASC, while UNICEF worked with IOM on protection, outreach, and psychological first aid to combat trafficking, smuggling, and exploitation risks.
 
UNICEF and UN agencies advocated for child provisions in the Gender Equality and Sexual Reproductive Health Laws under parliamentary review. As co-chair of the UN-People’s Advocate Coordination Group with UNRC, UNWomen, UN Population Fund and UNDP, UNICEF contributed to the global UN Toolkit for Collaboration with National Human Rights Institutions through an Albanian case study.
 
Proactive steps were taken to map out the private sector landscape and identify areas of mutual interest. UNICEF engaged with eight prominent CEOs from Albanian businesses, exposing UNICEF's mission and priorities to new audiences, leading to the creation of the first Business Advisory Board. 
 
Collaboration with CREDINS Bank resulted in a US$100,000 contribution for Every Child Alive programme. Building on this, UNICEF is exploring strategic partnerships with the private sector that harness the potential of youth. UNICEF collaboration with Tirana Business University provided internships encouraging young people to pursue their studies in Albania and access meaningful job opportunities.
 
UNICEF mobilized the private sector for UPSHIFT, supporting 429 youth (252 girls) directly and 5,410 indirectly, funding 31 projects, 100 young innovators (40 girls), and 20 start-ups. 
Through non-traditional partnerships like Meta, UNICEF expanded its reach via an online campaign that raised awareness on cyberbullying, sexual exploitation, data misuse, and harmful content—especially for children on the move, offering safety guidance through interactive content. Targeting adolescents (13-19 years) and caregivers, it promoted reporting and normalized discussions on digital risks.
 
UNICEF and the Albanian Football Federation leveraged football's popularity to promote child rights, engage communities, create safe spaces, and provide training on child rights and protection for coaches, parents, and children. 
 
UNICEF supported the National Agency for Scientific Research and Innovation in its dialogue with the European Commission on Chapter 25 (science and research). This led to 13 per cent (US$277,097) of the National Scientific Research Programme budget being allocated to research on vulnerable groups. Law 109/2024, On Science and Scientific Research in the Republic of Albania, mandates the development and approval of an Ethical Code for Research (Article 30), a measure UNICEF strongly advocated for, during the past two years.
 
UNICEF’s Albania Advisory Board (AAB) influenced key initiatives, including the Learning for Careers report in Brussels, eco-literacy curricula advocacy, and Youth Guarantee expansion. AAB prioritized climate action, air quality, and contributed to the Young People’s Guide to Climate Change and Children’s Health. Members shaped the policy on child rights, mental health, education, and migration at major events, promoted youth programmes like U-Report and UPSHIFT, and participated in the global Leading Minds Conference on Climate Action.
 
With UNICEF support, the National Agency for Employment and Skills launched an AI-powered tool for the National Employment Office portal to help young and vulnerable individuals apply for and access jobs. The initiative empowers youth, with UNICEF advancing in 2025 UPSHIFT efforts through private sector partnerships and crowdfunding.
 
By appointing Alban Skenderaj as Albania’s first national ambassador for children, UNICEF positioned itself as a contemporary partner with a powerful and visible voice. Alban engaged with children and young people through UNICEF programmes both in the field and at public events like World Children’s Day when he delivered awareness messaging at the national football stadium and advocacy messages in a special session with the Speaker of Parliament. 
 
UNICEF engaged with influencers as an innovative way to reach more audiences. The Ministry of Interior, with UNICEF support, launched the E VERTETA N’DRIT anti-trafficking campaign, partnering with influencers to raise awareness and prevent human trafficking. Influencers amplified key messages and engaged at municipal level, fostering grassroots community resilience.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
