The evaluation of the country office’s work on justice for children’s case management at the subnational level provided critical insights to guide future strategies. It underscored the need for UNICEF to invest in understanding the full cost of services and explore sustainable financial models that gradually transition funding and human resources from donors to national and local stakeholders. In response, in 2024, UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with municipalities through the EU4SC initiative, focusing on building staff capacity over the coming years to refine social plans and budgets.
 
Another key lesson from the evaluation emphasized the importance of a holistic approach that addresses the full spectrum of children’s legal and non-legal needs. This insight was integrated into the Extended Programme Review (EPR) exercise, ultimately strengthening linkages between justice, protection, education, and social protection interventions. This integration is crucial for advancing holistic case management and ensuring that children in contact or conflict with the law are seamlessly included in comprehensive support systems.
 
The 2024 evaluation of ‘Earthquake response efforts provided by the UN in Albania 2020-2024’ identified efforts taken forward by UNICEF in education and child protection sectors, as highly relevant to the needs of the country and well anchored in the country programme document (CPD). Its recommendations brought to attention the importance of establishing the relevant technical and oversight mechanisms in the event of national disasters. These mechanisms are expected to have an impact on coordinated and effective responses, reducing the fragmentation of efforts. UN agencies were also made aware that the alignment and synchronization of monitoring and evaluation tools and efforts should be considered in such coordinated responses. The evaluation brought to the attention of UN Agencies, including UNICEF, how continuous investment in enhancing disaster preparedness and risk reduction governance and the capacities of relevant institutions is essential for the long-term sustainability of any response. In response to these insights, UNICEF improved its internal planning for emergency response scenarios, whilst recognizing the response to children on the move as flagship area as a result of the EPR. 
 
The 2024 evaluation of the UN joint programme Leave No One Behind, in which UNICEF plays a key role, highlighted that advancing social inclusion and protection requires systemic, coordinated, and sustained efforts. A comprehensive approach that addresses both demand (empowering vulnerable groups) and supply (building service providers’ capacity) was found to be essential for meaningful change and should be replicated in similar large-scale programmes. Sustained capacity building for social workers and local government staff proved crucial to addressing high turnover and skill gaps. Effective coordination among UN agencies, government, and civil society organizations was identified as a key factor, with strong partnerships and joint ownership facilitating smoother reforms. Persistent, evidence-based advocacy with policymakers—supported by clear communication and data—was effective in advancing social care reforms. Proactive alliances with international and civil society stakeholders further drove progress by leveraging data and emphasizing the links between social inclusion and human capital development. The evaluation also underscored the importance of cross-sectoral collaboration in education, health, social protection, and employment to deliver integrated services, particularly for vulnerable groups, including children.
 
In response to these findings, UNICEF, in collaboration with other UN agencies and government partners, has begun designing follow-up actions to implement the evaluation’s recommendations. Looking ahead, UNICEF plans to align its 2025 social inclusion strategies with the broader EU accession reforms.
 
With the CPD in its third year of implementation, EPR provided an opportunity to sharpen programming, evaluate progress and identify challenges as UNICEF adapts to a shifting environment.The exercise was fully inclusive with participation from all staff members, the regional office and AAB, which fostered a collaborative and stimulating process. Based on a robust methodology and guiding criteria, EPR received strong engagement and support from the staff association. Staff actively contributed to and became familiar with the evidence produced,[1] recognized as pivotal in shaping and guiding the programmatic and operational changes introduced through the EPR process.
 
As part of EPR, UNICEF documented key lessons learned from programme implementation, including the office’s siloed approach to working across programmes, limited coordination/convergence at municipality level, weak capacity for change and innovation, and for engaging with new partners. Providing more opportunities for staff to grow beyond sectorial areas and embarking on new models of operation, were identified as ways to improve an office-wide perspective and increase collective ownership. 
 
A key outcome of EPR has been the programmatic sharpening achieved by reducing from 60 to 30 the number of key interventions. Furthermore, three programmatic flagships were identified, prompting a reorganization of human resources to align with them. For the remaining country programme period 2025-2026, this means that UNICEF will focus on: 1. The promise for every child-safe start in life and a nurturing family environment (child guarantee); 2. Pathways to potential: Quality education, skills building and transition to employment (youth guarantee); and 3. Building resilience and protection for every child (emergency response). Given that UNICEF, both globally and regionally, is re-considering its business model to address the unprecedented challenges it faces, it was also agreed that the changes introduced through EPR are fully aligned with these strategic approaches. These changes are expected to be critical, and compelling to position UNICEF as strategic government partner, and of other key stakeholders like EU, and increase its chances to leverage resources and results for children.
 
UNICEF remains committed to driving results for children through policy development, advocacy, and evidence generation. In 2025, it will expand partnerships beyond traditional allies, adapt its structure for greater agility, and introduce innovative solutions to navigate a shifting financial landscape. New financing mechanisms will also be explored to support Albania’s Growth Plan and help the government accelerate reforms to build and protect human capital, shaping the next CPD.

Armenia experienced significant challenges in 2024, following a large-scale influx of ethnic Armenian refugees in late 2023. The overall geopolitical situation and outlook remained uncertain. Armenia and Azerbaijan made some progress in their peace process during 2024 but a final agreement remains elusive so far.
In late September 2023, over 115,000 refugees, including 36,000 children fled into the country, or were escorted through the Lachin corridor between December 2022 and September 2023, joining 26,700 people displaced since the 2020 conflict. The integration of refugees became a key priority, requiring additional resources and support systems while straining the country's social services and infrastructure. The Multi-Sector Needs Assessment by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MLSA) and UNICEF revealed that refugee families in Yerevan have better living conditions than those in rural areas. Families with children are twice as likely to share housing with other families compared to childless households. Among refugee families with preschool-age children, 42% reported having a child not attending kindergarten, with half never having attended. Refugee adolescents face higher dropout risks due also to differences in mandatory schooling requirements between education systems. Mental health concerns are prevalent, with 26% of surveyed households reporting at least one emotionally unstable member. While significant in itself, it is assumed that this is still an underestimation given the stigma associated with mental health. Barriers to seeking mental health support include lack of information, financial constraints, mobility issues, and limited services in communities.
Armenia's implementation of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was reviewed at the Committee's 97th session in September 2024, following a February pre-session with participation of children from Child and youth council of the Human Rights Defender’s Office (HRDO), Armenia’s HRD, UNICEF and representatives of civil society. The Committee’s concluding observations acknowledged progress in realization of certain rights, like children's survival and education, while recommending increased funding for reforms across all social sectors, swift passage of pending child rights legislation, more efforts for improving child care and justice systems, enhanced coordination and monitoring mechanisms, and stronger public awareness campaigns and mechanisms to combat discrimination and violence against children.
Despite the refugee crisis, the economic growth continued though at a slower pace, with the World Bank (WB) estimating 5.5% GDP growth for 2024. While lower than in 2023 (8.3%), it remains higher than the average in the Europe and Central Asia (ECA) region at 3.2%. As reported by the Central Bank of Armenia (CBA), the remittances continued to decline in 2024, while labor market data presented mixed signals. Household survey data indicated a 2-percentage-point rise in unemployment, whereas State Revenue Committee data showed an increase in registered employees during the same period, possibly reflecting a shift from informal to formal employment. Unemployment rate has improved to 12.4% compared to 13.5% in 2022 and is higher among women (13.2%) and youth (27.2% among 15–29-year-olds). Armenia's NEET (youth not in education, employment, or training) rate decreased slightly from 25.9% to 24.4%, with improvements particularly among females (down 3.5 percentage points to 33.3%) and youth aged 15–24 (down 2.1 percentage points to 16.9%). However, females continue to have significantly higher NEET rates than males, highlighting persistent gender inequality. NEET rate among youngest age group (15-19) continued rising slowly, increasing from 8% to 8.4%.
Consumer price inflation remained low at 1.4% in November 2024, influenced by external deflationary pressures and weakening demand for certain domestic services. The increase in international food prices has not been yet fully transmitted into domestic prices.
As reported by ArmStat, poverty rates generally continued to decline, except for the upper poverty line rate, which increased by 1.3 percentage points to 42.6%. The average poverty line rate fell by 1.1 percentage points to 23.7%, and multi-dimensional poverty dropped significantly to 17.3%, down from 20.7% in 2022 and below the 2021 rate of 18.7. The lower poverty line rate decreased by 1.9 percentage points to 9.7%, with extreme poverty remaining stable at 1.1%. Child poverty also showed slight improvement, decreasing by 0.6 percentage points to 31.6%, with children's share in multi-dimensional poverty remaining relatively stable at 27.6%.
Sex ratio at birth, though still skewed, shows slight improvement in 2023 at 1.11 (111 boys per 100 girls), compared to 1.12 (112 boys per 100 girls) in 2022. 
Public expenditure on social sectors has improved with exception of the health sector, where budget nominally did not change significantly, but decreased to 1.5% of GDP (from 1.7% in 2022). Public spending on education and social protection increased to 2.5% and 7.5% of GDP accordingly, from 2.3% and 7.3% in 2022. With the focus on the refugee crisis and their integration, over 58.5 billion AMD (USD145mln) was provided in financial assistance to the refugees and a new housing programme was launched in 2024.
Armenian 4th graders’ Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) results showed mixed performance: math scores improved to 513 from 498 in 2019, surpassing the median score for the first time, with 72% reaching a minimum proficiency level in mathematics (up from 64% in 2019), while science scores declined to 457 from 466 in 2019, with intermediate benchmark achievement dropping to 40% from 47%, despite slight improvement in minimum benchmark attainment (82% vs 80%). According to annual national assessment, functional literacy has improved among 10-year-olds, with the number of underperforming students decreasing by approximately 20% and more than half of students achieving 64.3% performance. An evaluation of the curriculum reform pilot in STEM in one region concluded that the reform had a positive and sizeable impact on student achievement in math and science, equivalent to an additional six months of learning over the two years of implementation. In 2024 investments continued also in the school infrastructure with focus on safety and improved equipment for teaching STEM, as well as in teacher support and development, aiming at improving incentives for teachers and gender balance. The gross preschool enrollment rate for children aged 3-5 reached 68.6%, a 5% increase from 2022. Improvement in preschool infrastructure across the country continued with 195 facilities completed in 2024.
The number of children in residential care institutions continued to decrease (from 937 to 905 in state residential care) despite the refugee crisis, which can be attributed mostly to increased placement in foster care and enhancement of case management with more family reunification outcomes. Nevertheless, many of those in residential care are children with disabilities. The regulation on transition of special schools to resource centers was approved to advance deinstitutionalization of children with disabilities. Personal assistant services for select groups of children with disabilities have been scaled up nationwide through new policy provisions and dedicated state funding. A pilot program providing disability services through vouchers continues, with the service package under review for finalization and approval in 2025. The assessment shows monthly expenses for a child with disability exceed the current disability benefit by 1.5 times, varying by location (capital, urban, or rural areas) and disability type and severity. The existing benefit is primarily used for necessities like food, medication, clothing, and transportation.
The focus of the healthcare system in 2024 was on the launch of the universal health insurance system, which, however was delayed. There is no improvement in child mortality numbers, with neonatal mortality still accounting for 75% of cases of infant mortality. Vaccination coverage improved reaching overall 92.9% for 1-year-olds, 92.6% for 2-year-olds, and 93.1% for 6-year-olds. Double burden of malnutrition remains an issue. WHO estimates 22% of Armenian adolescents are overweight (26% boys, 17% girls), while HBSC data shows the country leads 50 nations in teen sweet consumption, with 64% of girls and 56% of boys (age 15) eating sweets multiple times daily.
In justice system, the work focused on developing mechanisms for ensuring independence of the court system and anti-corruption measures, as well as improving infrastructure within penitentiary and probation services, including making required adaptations and creating mechanisms for accessibility for persons with disabilities, and a maternity ward was established in one of the facilities. Certification system for forensic psychologists was improved and more psychologists were certified, bringing the pool of available psychologists to 51 and allowing to include them on mandatory basis into all investigative actions involving children across the country.
In 2024, Armenia advanced several key legislative initiatives. Two important laws – the Law on State Benefits and the Law on Social Assistance with respective legal documents package – were adopted by the Parliament in 2024 thus, commencing a new chapter for social services and rolling out new vulnerability assessment system based on hybrid means testing to address poverty and improve targeting and adequacy of social assistance programmes. The first ever draft Youth Policy Law (defining youth as ages 13-35) underwent its initial parliamentary review. A comprehensive child rights package, including updates to the Family Code and the Child Rights and Child protection Law, awaits Cabinet review before heading to parliament in 2025. While drafts of the Equality and Anti-Discrimination Law and National Minorities Law were circulated for public comment as part of the Human Rights Action Plan, they remain unfinalized. Two key strategies were adopted: Armenia’s Demographic Strategy, aiming to enhance family well-being, reduce mortality risk factors, ensure dignified aging, and address migration causes, and the Employment Strategy, focusing on job creation, poverty reduction, and sustainable economic growth.
The draft Comprehensive Programme on Protection of Child Rights 2025-2029 was developed by MLSA, following consultations with children and a collaborative process involving national institutions, civil society and partners and incorporating the CRC concluding observations, where possible. It is submitted to the Government for review.

In 2024, UNICEF Armenia continued to respond to the emergency that unfolded in September 2023 and maintained a balance between addressing the specific and urgent needs of refugee children and working to uphold the rights of all vulnerable children in the country. More specifically, UNICEF Armenia continued to contribute to national efforts to address the evolving needs of an estimated total of 46,000 ethnic Armenian refugee children and their families displaced between 2020 and 2023 as well as children affected by a flooding in the north of the country in May 2024, combining humanitarian response strategies and system strengthening approaches along the humanitarian-development nexus.  In parallel, it continued to further strengthen the capacity of national stakeholders to address the child rights issues affecting the most vulnerable children and to accelerate progress towards the expected results of the 2021-2025 Country Programme Document (CPD) and United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).  These combined efforts proved to be consistent with the needs of children in Armenia as depicted in the latest Concluding Observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) on Armenia issued in September and the findings of the 2024 Voluntary National Report on Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) implementation in Armenia. 
UNICEF’s humanitarian response built on the actions spearheaded during the initial phase in late 2023, with UNICEF playing a key role in coordination of Refugee Response Plan (RRP) partners, particularly for the Education, Child Protection and Cash Sector Groups. Several interventions soon evolved from a humanitarian approach to a combination of system strengthening and service delivery strategies, as also the Government’s approach moved quickly  towards integrating refugees in national systems. Considering this, in April 2024, UNICEF Armenia amended the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal launched in October 2023, and integrated emergency response activities in the consolidated Multi-Year Work Plan 2024-2025 signed with the Government of Armenia and the UNSDCF Joint Work Plans. 
In this spirit, UNICEF Armenia continued to work along the humanitarian development nexus. Investments made as part of the development agenda in strengthening shock-responsiveness of national systems prior to the emergency continued to pay off by accelerating and maintaining results at scale for the emergency response. UNICEF’s constant dialogue with relevant Ministries and Government agencies and its convening role in enabling dialogue with and within civil society actors allowed timely adjustments to response modalities as needs of refugee and host community children evolved. The only comprehensive Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) of refugee families undertaken for this emergency was co-led by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MLSA) and UNICEF using a tool that had been tested prior to the start of the crisis. MSNA findings highlighted needs in terms of housing, employment, access to services, especially specialized ones, as well as the need for mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) and were used by Government, RRP partners and other stakeholders for medium-term planning.  
The effectiveness of consistent and coordinated investments in emergency preparedness in earlier years was reconfirmed this year. At the February 2024 UNICEF Executive Board meeting, UNICEF Deputy Executive Director Ted Chaiban referred to UNICEF Armenia as a positive example of strategic investment in emergency preparedness that lately enabled effective and efficient response during the refugee influx. A similar conclusion was drawn in the UNICEF global evaluation on emergency preparedness conducted in the last quarter of 2024, whose preliminary findings highlight: “Interagency partnerships and proactive co-leadership with the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs have established UNICEF’s role in cash response, child protection and education working and sub-working groups, ultimately leading to widespread and timely refugee response […]. This has been anchored in contingency partnerships, piggybacking on systems used in development programming”. It also flags that “UNICEF’s work exemplifies the importance of recognizing the value of supporting these systems. UNICEF is well placed to listen to government and civil society partners, to inject contextual awareness into international discussions, and to anchor emergency preparedness in joint efforts”.
Direct service delivery through implementing partners allowed UNICEF to cover a wide range of needs of refugee and host community children and to expand its reach to a significant number of them. Refugee children from 11,335 households, representing all refugee children under ten years of age, benefitted from UNICEF-supported multipurpose vouchers for clothing and pharmacy cards. Among these households, also all refugee pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers (506 and 1,507 respectively) received vouchers to address healthcare and nutritional needs. Since the beginning of the emergency, 37,453 children and caregivers accessed safe spaces, child protection support and protection hubs (19,044 in 2024). 34,712 children, adolescents and caregivers (18,150 in 2024) received MHPSS. 6,701 children (3,982 in 2024) benefitted from individual case management along with correlated support to their families, including facilitated access to essential healthcare and education services for over 1,000 families as well as specialized services through speech therapists, special pedagogues, psychologists, legal advisors and others. Over 300 refugee children with disabilities received needs-based and specialized support, developmental and rehabilitation services, MHPSS and assistive technologies. The number of refugee children provided with learning materials, early childhood and remedial education and MHPSS in educational institutions raised to 20,036 (11,964 in 2024).  In parallel, the number of adolescents and young people benefitting from age-specific psychological first aid and MHPSS programs and materials increased to 2,800 in 2024. By the end of 2024, the number of children receiving health and nutrition services through primary health care (PHC) and specialized mobile pediatric units raised to 9,543 (4,911 in 2024), those diagnosed with some health or nutrition issue were referred to the national health system when relevant. The number of caregivers receiving age-specific coun
selling on health and nutrition-related childcare practices increased to 5,886 (1,180 in 2024).  Since the beginning of the emergency, 36,684 women, girls and boys had access to gender-based violence (GBV) risk mitigation, prevention and/or response interventions (22,546 in 2024).
The scope and scale of these results was possible thanks to UNICEF’s co-leadership of RRP sector groups with MLSA and the Ministry of Education Science Culture and Sports (MoESCS) and connected coordination mechanisms. As a result, duplication of efforts was reduced and referrals between the different government and non-government stakeholders to manage cases of families with multiple vulnerabilities became more effective.  This approach emerged from the lessons learnt from the 2020 emergency and illustrates how effective risk-informed programming can generate positive and mutually reinforcing outcomes along the humanitarian-development nexus. In this spirit, in 2024 UNICEF also supported relevant partners in testing and learning new lessons from this emergency to inform new directions. An example is the rollout of the e-wallet cash-based programme for refugees, which involved UNICEF, MLSA, Unified Social Service (USS), Nork Technology Center, CSOs and a financial service provider, which has good potential for scale-up as part of the national social protection system. Another example is the joint effort of UNICEF, MLSA, USS, local authorities and Armenian Association of Social Workers to test community outreach mechanisms and to promote coordination between USS and community social workers for case management, which anticipates provisions included in the upcoming reforms in social assistance and the child protection system. 
UNICEF Armenia adjusted its programme to continue responding to the emergency while also advancing the longer-term development agenda. Good progress was made towards country programme outcomes since 2021. Despite intensifying anti-vaccination messaging in the society, immunization coverage was sustained at over 90% for all antigens as a result of continued joint efforts with the Ministry of Health (MOH) in strengthening immunization services and communication strategies.  The number of children in residential care continued to decrease, despite the existence of factors usually contributing to placement into residential care, including the refugee inflow. The number of placements into foster care increased by 70%, as a result of continuous partnership with MLSA and other state and non-state actors to advance alternative care. Enrolment of children under 5 years of age in preschools increased to 36.2% in the 2023-2024 academic year compared to 32.3% in 2021-2022, as a result of continued efforts, also supported by UNICEF, to invest and prioritize early childhood education. Child poverty was reduced mainly due to economic growth and the effects of the rollout of universal childcare benefits for all parents until the age of 2 started in 2023 with UNICEF’s support.
Most of these outcome-level results can be at least partially attributed to UNICEF Armenia’s support, building on its longstanding engagement and reputation as a reliable and knowledgeable partner for national stakeholders. In 2024, UNICEF Armenia continued positioning itself as a partner of choice and effective convener in key social sectors related to children and youth, and actively contributed to advancing the ongoing comprehensive national social reform agenda, a unique opportunity to address key systemic bottlenecks hindering the realization of child rights. In this context, good progress was made this year in developing or reviewing several legislative frameworks. The new edition of the Law on Social Assistance was approved in November, setting the legal foundations to transforming social assistance provision for families, including incorporation of notions on resilience-building and shock-responsiveness, effective governance, quality standards for service provision, and professionalization of social work. The Law on State Benefits was amended to change the targeting method for the family living standards enhancement programme. The legislative package including the new Law on Child Rights and Child Protection System and the amendments to the Family Code and other legislative acts are awaiting Parliament’s approval and envisage provisions to strengthen child protection mechanism at local level, prohibition of corporal punishment in all settings, and additional guarantees to prevent unnecessary separation of children from families prioritizing family-based alternative care. The first ever draft Law on Youth Policy is also awaiting Parliament’s approval and envisages lowering the minimum age for accessing youth programs, enabling more systematic provision of youth services through a nationwide network of youth houses and by formalizing the professional profile of youth workers. Overall, UNICEF efforts also aimed at ensuring that these new provisions are responsi
ve to gender considerations, climate change effects on children and to the needs of children with disabilities.
Substantial progress was made towards operationalizing policies and legislative provisions and strengthening systems at central and local levels to ensure upgraded, more integrated, and inclusive services for children and families. After the law on the Rights of the Child was amended in 2023 to reinforce the role of the Commission on the Rights of the Child and mandate it with the development of a multi-year comprehensive national programme on child rights, in 2024, the Comprehensive Programme on Child Rights was drafted under the coordination of MLSA and with UNICEF technical assistance, which enabled alignment with international standards and treaty bodies’ requirements as well as a participatory engagement of multiple stakeholders across sectors, including children. Members of the Adolescent and Youth Council adjacent to the Human Rights Defenders Office (HRDO) along with HRDO and civil society actors prepared and presented their alternative report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child at its pre-session on Armenia. The Concluding Observations of the CRC issued in September reflect the importance of accelerating legislative changes, including those mentioned above, and of operationalization of reforms that have been initiated, confirming that the current collaboration between the Government of Armenia and UNICEF focuses on the most critical concerns on child rights realization identified by the Committee.  
In the framework of the ongoing education reform, the MoESCS embarked in the mid-term revision of the Action Plan adjacent to the State Program for Development of Education until 2030 (ESP) and initiated planning for the next implementation phase. UNICEF’s technical assistance contributed to strengthening coordination of the reform process, as well as enhanced monitoring, accountability and budgeting, through costing exercises, improvement of financial and non-financial indicators, a joint education sector review, and the establishment of a new mechanism for education policy dialogue co-chaired by MoESCS, the European Union (EU) and UNICEF. As a key component to accelerate progress on the ESP, the national system for teachers' professional development under the National Center for Educational Development and Innovation (NCEDI) and MoESCS was further strengthened with UNICEF technical assistance which this year focused particularly on enhancing teacher attestation preparatory courses, aiming at greater efficiency, standardization, and accessibility while maintaining high-quality standards. Rollout of the new curriculum also continued, and 79,000 schoolchildren of 5th and 7th grades of all schools used the new Healthy Lifestyle curriculum supported by UNICEF, UNFPA and UNESCO.
Operationalization of the Law on Preschool Education continued, also through UNICEF-supported improvements in personnel management and infrastructure. The second National Conference on Preschool Education consolidated a practice that provides a comprehensive and regular platform for preschool practitioners to discuss new developments, bottlenecks, and ways forward, and serves as mechanism for more systematic monitoring. Further investment in infrastructure to expand preschool service supply remained a priority and, as a result of collaboration between UNICEF, MoESCS, Ministry of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure (MOTAI) and local authorities, 5,685 children (47% girls, 4% refugees) aged 2-5 benefitted from the services of 50 kindergartens and 37 alternative preschool education facilities refurbished and equipped. 
In the framework of the disability reform, amendments to the regulations on the provision of Personal Assistant Services and to the Regulation of Day Care Centers formulated with UNICEF’s technical assistance were approved, enabling children with disabilities to receive tailored support that helps them function optimally in daily life, enhancing their ability to participate in educational and social activities. In parallel, the findings of a UNICEF-commissioned study assessing the extra costs sustained by families with children with disabilities complemented by an analysis on overall spending on disability from the state budget in compliance with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) triggered important policy dialogue and informed the design of new programmes and service packages for persons and children with disabilities. 
As part of the ongoing de-institutionalization reform, several policy documents, guidelines, standard operational procedures on matching, support, transition to independent leaving were developed and are awaiting Government approval. Two key Government decrees were developed and are awaiting approval. They regulate child daycare, night care, and crisis care, and related standards to ensure residential care is used as last resort and to strengthen the alternative care services overall. A new awareness-raising programme on foster care to attract more candidate foster parents, with a focus on emergency foster care, was developed and launched in 2025. 
In the framework of the PHC system reform, the upcoming introduction of Universal Health Insurance (UHI) schemes and other ongoing system strengthening initiatives within health and nutrition services, UNICEF initiated the adaptation of WHO PHC Pocketbook for children, to be further introduced in the PHC system as mandatory standard within the UHI.  The quality of services provided to children at PHC level was enhanced by updating current guidelines on integrated management of childhood illnesses and training over 1,700 PHC providers.  To ensure continuity of neonatal and paediatric services at regional level, 150 neonatologists and paediatricians working in regional hospitals and maternities were trained on first aid and resuscitation.  
Child nutrition and immunization remained key priorities for the health sector. Functional effectiveness of the e-based child nutrition surveillance system developed by UNICEF and the National Institute of Health (NIH) was enhanced, ensuring that up-to-date and standardized data on child malnutrition for each PHC facility are presented in NIH’s online data platforms and subsequently analysed and used for decision-making and monitoring purposes.  A new technical expert group on child nutrition was established and its operational capacity ensured, thus enabling the development of nutrition standards for children of different age groups and of mechanisms for their implementation at educational facilities. The first-ever National Immunization Social and Behaviour Change Strategy was developed with UNICEF support to ensure coordinated interventions in addressing immunization bottlenecks and misinformation. Evidence-based behaviour insights interventions resulted in positive trends in Measles Mums Rubella vaccination uptake.  Almost 95% of the vaccine managers in the higher risk regions for the measles outbreak that started this year were trained on catch-up vaccination.  
As part of the process of operationalizing child-friendly provisions in the Criminal Procedure Code enacted in 2022, the pool of certified child forensic psychologists was expanded three-fold compared to 2023 with UNICEF’s support, thus enhancing the quality of child-sensitive investigative processes across the country. A dedicated department responsible for children in the justice process was established in the Legal Education and Rehabilitation Programme Implementation Centre of the Ministry of Justice (MoJ), expanding the institutional capacity of the Council of Justice for Children, a critical mechanism for inter-sectoral coordination. Training of professionals in the justice and law enforcement sectors led to improved responses to cases of violence against children (VAC). More cases were reported and investigated, signaling a shift in professional attitudes toward child protection. Expanding the national agenda to counter VAC, cybersecurity and online safety as well as explosive ordnance risk education became more prominent topics, with over 500 adolescents and 1,670 children and teachers trained respectively, in a first phase this year.
In parallel to the development of the draft Law on Youth, UNICEF continued its technical assistance and dialogue with MoESCS anticipating some of the actions required to operationalize it once approved. UNICEF’s efforts to establish youth houses/centers over the past years, alongside skill-building initiatives in local communities showcased effective modalities to expand skills, engagement, and empowerment of adolescents and young people, also highlighting the importance of approaches that are gender-responsive and consider emerging needs, including climate change, use of technology and innovation. In view of the operationalization phase of the upcoming law, UNICEF brought this wealth of experience at the discussion table to ensure that these youth aggregation mechanisms and educational and engagement opportunities could serve as a model once designing youth-related services as part of the reform process. In 2024, UNICEF continued to test modalities of community engagement and non-formal education reaching over 1,000 young people as change agents within their communities. 
In the framework of the county’s Nationally Determined Contributions and its commitments under the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action that Armenia signed in 2023, the decision to establish a Youth Advisory Board adjacent to the Ministry of Environment was reached and criteria for establishing this Board were developed with UNICEF’s support. This platform is expected to advance inclusive climate policies with integration of young people’s views in decision-making. This year, the number of settlements completing Climate Risk assessments reached 364 in seven regions. Based on the findings of these assessments, relevant climate risk mitigation and adaptation measures will be integrated into local development plans, which should also attract resources to invest in community resilience.
UNICEF continued to accelerate advocacy and technical support to promote the MHPSS agenda in the country and strengthen capacity to deliver MHPSS for children. The ongoing emergency also contributed to scaling up delivery and diversifying services using different channels, including the healthcare system, community-based social services, and schools. Mental health services for children were mapped in four more regions to enable capacity building and referrals in almost the entire country. Initial steps were taken to introduce advanced principles of child/adolescent MHPSS into the pre-service curriculum of the Pedagogical University. To expand the overstretched capacity of MHPSS professionals responding to the emergency, UNICEF supported the activation of a network of specialized MHPSS professionals trained during the 2020 crisis that supported pro-bono a group of 343 professionals with ‘help the helpers support’, professional development trainings as well as individual and group supervision. In parallel, the profile of peer support volunteers was introduced in 6 regions and trained on basic psychological first aid and referral pathways to be able to guide parents of adolescents in need to reach specialized support. The Republican Pedagogical-Psychological Support Center introduced a new training programme on MHPSS in schools developed with UNICEF support, which aims at expanding school-based capacity to deliver social-emotional learning, psycho-social resilience building, and creating a safe environment for children to learn.
UNICEF continued to engage with various stakeholders to tackle negative parenting practices as one of the key concerns in childcare. Social listening on digital platforms was used to identify information gaps and areas of interest for caregivers, and this evidence informed the design of two seasons of “Parent’s Meeting” TV show with national coverage during prime time, resulting from the partnership between UNICEF and Public TV. Topics covered include newborn care, breastfeeding and healthy nutrition, immunization, emergency preparedness, MHPSS, positive parenting, parenting of adolescents. Subsequent dissemination through UNICEF’s platforms and social media brought 3,535,455 views.
Gender-transformative programming was further advanced by UNICEF with focus on policy and legal framework development, capacity strengthening of frontline workers on gender roles and empowering adolescent girls with leadership and tech skills to shift gender norms and stereotypes. Moreover, women-led and youth-led organizations were engaged in program design, delivery, and monitoring, with a particular focus on the MSNA that included gender-sensitive tools and GBV risk prevention mechanisms and identified gender-specific risks and vulnerabilities faced by refugee women and girls.
In 2024, the Country Programme and the emergency response were implemented with a financial expenditure of USD10.3 million, an overall 20% increase compared to 2023 and 45% compared to 2022. The modest and slow uptake of Armenia’s HAC appeal, due to several complex emergencies unfolding in last 2023 and 2024 around the world, created challenges in ensuring continuity of support to the refugee population. Nevertheless, UNICEF was able to maximize its response and remain relevant after having effectively positioned itself with a timely and efficient response at the onset thanks to preparedness investments. Global Humanitarian Thematic funds were instrumental. Besides, UNICEF Armenia expanded the range of partners by engaging with diaspora organizations for humanitarian response for the first time. As a result, Armenia’s HAC was 81% funded by end of 2024, for a total of USD11.6mln. Effective implementation of the programme, including the emergency response, was possible thanks to the coordinated efforts of the programmes, operations, communications and monitoring and evaluation teams based in the Yerevan Country Office and the Goris Field Office.

In 2024, UNICEF successfully partnered with a range of line Ministries  and other parts of the Government of Armenia, including Ministry of Education,  Science, Culture and Sports (MOESCS), Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs (MOLSA),  Ministry of Health (MOH), Ministry of Justice (MOJ), Ministry of Environment (MOE),  Ministry of Interior Affairs (MOIA),  and  Ministry of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure (MOTAI) to achieve shared  results for children, while also contributing to cross-sectoral cooperation for  children. 
  
Two milestones in the process of development of an extensive reform  package on child rights and child protection system were achieved in 2024. UNICEF  provided MOLSA with technical expertise for the finalized draft, which received  positive feedback from two relevant parliamentary standing committees and was  supported by the Human Rights Defender of Armenia (HRDO) and MOTAI. UNICEF further  supported MOLSA to include develop the Comprehensive Programme of Child Rights  and its costed Action Plan, which is meant to also serve as a monitoring  mechanism for child rights, which was submitted for Government review. 

UNICEF’s partnership and strong engagement with MOLSA led to the approval  of the new edition of the Law on Social Assistance with amendments to 15 other  legal documents in November 2024. The Law aims to transform social assistance  provision for families and children in Armenia, including incorporation of notions  on resilience-building and shock-responsiveness, effective governance with clear  roles and responsibilities between national, regional and local actors. UNICEF  partnered with MOLSA, providing technical expertise and public communication support  for the launch of the new household vulnerability assessment system, advocating  for the integration of a child poverty angle in overall reform communication,  as well as in preparation of the launch of needs-based cash assistance for displaced  and host community families through electronic payment system.
  
UNICEF continued advocacy and support on strengthening the shock-responsiveness  of the social protection system, including through inter-agency cash coordination  efforts. Close to US$ 9.8mln was mobilized by partners in support of Government-led  cash schemes along the humanitarian-development nexus for at least 30,000 refugees  due to UNICEF’s co-leadership with MOLSA and UNHCR of the Cash working group.
  
Following Armenia’s signature of the Declaration on Children, Youth  and Climate Action, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Environment to launch  an open call for establishing a youth advisory board adjunct to the Minister and  provided child-friendly inputs to the draft Law on Climate.
  
Advocacy efforts with the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture  and Sports resulted in acknowledgement of UNICEF role in ongoing reforms on a  number of occasions throughout 2024 and consistent joint communication on results  and reform processes. With the financial assistance from EU, UNICEF supported  the Ministry to jointly organise a first in a decade three-day media briefing  on general education reforms, feeding into further plans for regular engagement  with the media.
  
2024 was an important milestone as the country reached the midpoint  of the Education State Programme's 2023-2026 Action Plan. UNICEF’s analytical  work, field-level engagement, and capacity development initiatives built a strong  foundation that contributed to education and youth reforms, demonstrating incremental  improvement in access and quality of education at all levels and in youth policy  framework. UNICEF partnered with MOESCS to embark on mid-term revision of the  action plan for evidence-based planning for the next implementation period of  the strategy. In addition, UNICEF facilitated policy dialogue and youth engagement  to support the national youth agenda and drafting of the Law on Youth Policy.
  
UNICEF also partnered with the HRDO to enable children and adolescents,  including children with disabilities, to attend the hearings of Armenia’s combined  fifth and sixth periodic reports on the Convention on the Rights of the Child.  The CO supported the process additionally through a shadow report and technical  assistance to the Government in the process of reporting. UNICEF further supported  the Human Rights Defender’s Office to induct the new members of its Council on  Protection of Child Rights, also marking the achievements documented by the outgoing  members of the Council in the last two years. 
  
Active collaboration with IFIs continued, including with the World  Bank, ADB and IMF, and was critical in terms of joint advocacy for more effective  and inclusive social protection programmes in Armenia. The partnership with ADB  focused on national policies and regulations on WASH in schools. Engagement with  the EU continued to evolve from a donor-type partnership to joint advocacy especially  in relation to the education sector reform, a partnership strategy that was further  consolidated with the establishment of a new platform for education sector policy  dialogue co-led by UNICEF, the EU and the Ministry of Education.
  
UNICEF expanded the range of cooperation with implementing partners  and the number of civil society implementing partners continued to increase especially  for the emergency response. The Country Programme and the emergency response  were implemented with a financial expenditure of USD10.3 million, an overall  20% increase compared to 2023 and 45% compared to 2022. Average cash transfers  per partner increased by 45 percent, thus increasing efficiency in programme delivery.
  
In 2024, UNICEF also expanded the range of partnerships in support  of both the humanitarian response and the country programme by targeting new public  donors, engaging with diaspora organizations as well as initiating small  scale local fundraising for humanitarian response for the first time. UNICEF  was able to manage the impact of the initially slow uptake of Armenia’s HAC  appeal, due to several complex emergencies unfolding in last 2023 and 2024  around the world, thanks to the Global Humanitarian Thematic funds allocated  to the CO which played a critical role in ensuring flexibility and allowing the  CO to address transitional gaps until additional funding came in. Proactive  engagement with a wide range of partners enabled the CO to mobilize 81% of the  HAC by end of 2024, a total of USD11.6mln. In addition, UNICEF continued  strategic engagement with development partners which leveraged about USD6  million of Other Resources (non-emergency). This represents an 8-fold  increase since 2022, the first full year of the Country Programme, without  considering funds raised for the emergency response.
  
UNICEF continued its 2023 partnership with the Armenian State Symphony  Orchestra. Through a series of concerts, the Orchestra, together with National  Ambassador and Orchestra Conductor Sergey Smbatyan, donated raised funds in 2024  to UNICEF, expanding UNICEF’s humanitarian cash support programme in support of  children with disabilities.
  
The office was able to further capitalise on private sector engagement,  successfully positioning with diaspora organisations and individual donors from  Argentina, the United States, and Europe. An 18-months partnership was launched  with Afeyan Foundation together with the US Fund for UNICEF in support of mental  health and psychosocial services and adolescent development programmes.
  
UNICEF started a successful joint advocacy partnership with the Public  Television of Armenia, co-producing two seasons of a new show, entitled Parents’  Meeting, and securing commitment for the third season in 2025. The show set a  new benchmark for broadcast content for parents, raising awareness about nurturing  care, incorporating insights from social listening to address caregivers’ most  pressing questions and positioning UNICEF as a trusted expert in the field with.  Aired nationally during prime time, the show reached impressive 3,535,455 views  for the first season and 2,037,000 for the second. 
  
With the support of France, UNICEF partnership with the Ministry of  Labor and Social Affairs and the Enterprise Incubator Foundation led to an innovative  approach to ensuring feedback loop and access to information on services for vulnerable  groups. In July 2024, partners developed a mobile chatbot, based on Telegram.  The chatbot supports refugees to navigate social protection programmes by simplifying  complex processes, significantly reducing wait times and easing the strain on  the main hotline. In its first five months, the chatbot gained over 5,400 users,  enabling them to access vital information more efficiently.
  
UNICEF continued to play its convening role for UNSDCF Outcome Groups  on Education and Social Protection as well as for the Cash, Education and Child  Protection groups under the Refugee Response Plan. In this framework, UNICEF coordinated  the RRP in-depth needs assessment on behalf of the UN and in partnership with  MLSA engaging whole-of-government, UN, all RRP partners, and donor community,  IFIs, academia and other stakeholders. UNICEF contributed to a number of joint  UN endeavors, including the UN country team Plan of Action on countering and addressing  hate speech in Armenia and the UN Day event at Yerevan State University on Youth  and Climate Change. The event, attended by Deputy Prime Minister and other high-level  representatives of the Government, aimed to explore the critical role of youth  in addressing climate change and highlighted the work and advocacy of young people  that have repeatedly worked with UNICEF on climate action.
