In 2024, UNICEF Armenia continued to demonstrate flexibility and adaptability in supporting the country considering evolving circumstances. The emergency unfolded in September 2023 that saw a sudden and large influx of refugees for the size of the country (62 refugee children per every 1,000 children) overstretched key services for children and families.  In parallel, multiple comprehensive social reforms continued, targeting most of these services. In this context, UNICEF Armenia’s approach focused on combining humanitarian response strategies and system strengthening approaches along the humanitarian-development nexus.
Investments made as part of the development agenda in strengthening shock-responsiveness of national systems prior to the emergency continued to pay off. UNICEF’s constant dialogue with relevant Ministries and Government agencies and its convening role in enabling dialogue with and within civil society actors allowed timely adjustments to response modalities as needs of refugee and host community children evolved. The effectiveness of consistent and coordinated investments in emergency preparedness in earlier years was reconfirmed this year. At the February 2024 UNICEF Executive Board meeting, UNICEF Deputy Executive Director Ted Chaiban referred to UNICEF Armenia as a positive example of strategic investment in emergency preparedness that lately enabled effective and efficient response during the 2023 refugee influx. A similar conclusion was drawn in the UNICEF global evaluation on emergency preparedness conducted in the last quarter of 2024, whose preliminary findings highlight: “Interagency partnerships and proactive co-leadership with the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs have established UNICEF’s role in cash response, child protection and education working and sub-working groups, ultimately leading to widespread and timely refugee response […]. This has been anchored in contingency partnerships, piggybacking on systems used in development programming”. It also flags that “UNICEF’s work exemplifies the importance of recognizing the value of supporting these systems. UNICEF is well placed to listen to government and civil society partners, to inject contextual awareness into international discussions, and to anchor emergency preparedness in joint efforts”.
With this experience, UNICEF Armenia consolidated the practice of meaningfully mainstreaming emergency preparedness in its regular programming. This also allowed for explicit reflection on lessons learnt from this emergency to inform ongoing work on longer-term priorities, including policy reforms and other efforts to expand the shock-responsiveness of national systems, including through testing of new and innovative approaches relevant for both emergency and non-emergency situations. An example is the rollout of the e-wallet cash-based programme for refugees, which involved UNICEF, MLSA, Unified Social Service (USS), Nork Technology Center, CSOs and a financial service provider, and which has good potential for scale-up as part of the national social protection system.In connection to that, UNICEF and MLSA also developed an innovative Telegram ChatBot to support refugees navigating social protection programs. As the experience showed positive results in terms of simplification of complex processes and reduction of waiting times easing the strain on hotlines, it will be further improved for replication. 
Another example is the joint effort of UNICEF, MLSA, USS, local authorities and Armenian Association of Social Workers to test community outreach mechanisms and to further coordination between USS and community social workers for case management, which anticipates provisions included in the upcoming reforms in social assistance and the child protection system. In addition, in collaboration with the State Rescue Service, UNICEF supported the testing of Disaster Risk Management plans in two locations considering different priority scenarios. Child-centered drills involved multiple stakeholders, including children from schools, and revealed gaps and needs in schools' emergency response procedures that will be addressed based on an agreed plan.
This combined approach – mainstreaming emergency preparedness and risk-informed programming to strengthen the shock-responsiveness of national systems – will continue to be applied in the remainder of this programme cycle and will be embedded in the new Country Programme Document, thus ensuring positive and mutually reinforcing outcomes along the humanitarian-development nexus.
The preliminary findings of the Country Programme Evaluation (CPE) analysed the correspondence between UNICEF Armenia’s ongoing priorities to implement the current CPD and the key concerns highlighted in the Concluding Observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child. The large overlap between the two confirmed the relevance of UNICEF Armenia’s work to advance the agenda for children in the country.  The Concluding Observations also highlighted the importance of accelerating legislative changes and initiating related reforms, particularly in relation to the revision of the Family Code and the adoption of the Law on Child Rights and Child Protection Systems, which would address many child rights issues in the country. Building on the longstanding and comprehensive policy dialogue UNICEF Armenia has had during the preparation of these legislative pieces, advocacy will be further intensified in multiple directions.
With regards to effectiveness of the CPD’s implementation, the preliminary findings of the CPE highlighted that key informants generally recognized UNICEF Armenia’s comparative advantage in the following elements: “strong mandate”; “strong reputation (e.g. child rights and technical expertise it offers)”; ability to be “flexible and adaptable”; “strong institutional expertise and experience (both at the Country Office level and corporately)”; “access to deep institutional knowledge, best practices and innovations”; and the fact that “UNICEF corporately approaches solutions holistically”.  As the Country Office is in the initial phase of development of the new CPD and contributing to the preparation of the new UNSDCF, greater awareness of the key recognized contributions of UNICEF in Armenia is very relevant information to inform the design of the priorities and strategies for the next programme cycle.  In parallel, the preliminary findings of the same evaluation as well as the Gender Programme Review also conducted in 2024 highlighted that gender discrimination remains comparatively unaddressed and therefore recommended to better streamline UNICEF Armenia’s programming on gender, with more targeted and intentional prioritization of key needs. This important finding is also already being taken into account to inform future programming for the short and long-term.

Azerbaijan is an upper middle-income country with an ambitious programme of economic diversification and has subsequently reported continued economic growth, including an increase in gross domestic product (GDP) by 4,9 per cent in 2024 compared to 2023 according to the State Statistical Committee.  Azerbaijan has made signi¿cant strides in its economic journey, marked not only by robust GDP growth but positive social indicators despite facing global challenges. Azerbaijan has committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), incorporating them into its national development agenda. The country also made notable progress in various areas aligned with the SDGs, such as reducing under-five child mortality.

Since the economy is driven by revenues from energy exports, global energy market instability and rising food prices created significant challenges, like inflationary pressures, particularly on food and essential commodities, which disproportionately affected low-income families, aggravating vulnerabilities among children. Although the government continued to mitigate these impacts through social spending and targeted support for vulnerable populations, additional measures are needed to address the socio-economic disparities affecting children and families. UNICEF will continue advocating for increasing government investments in social services, strengthening multisectoral partnerships, and leveraging additional resources to ensure the sustainability of programmes for children and adolescents. By aligning these efforts with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the principle of “leaving no child behind,” the county will create an enabling environment for every child to thrive.

In 2024, UNICEF Country Office in Azerbaijan (CO) continued to focus its efforts on advancing children’s access to essential health, nutrition, education, child protection, adolescent development and social protection services and fostering equitable results for children across the country. The significant work of UNICEF included a strong focus on children and adolescents during the UN Climate Change Conference (UNFCCC COP 29), the finalization of the report of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in close cooperation with the Government of Azerbaijan and initiating the development of the new five-year programme of cooperation. 

COP29 marked a significant milestone in global climate action and finance. The two-week high-level conference highlighted the urgent need for integrated climate responses and clear actions to decrease the impacts of climate change on vulnerable populations, including children. It emphasized the importance of climate finance, climate education, health, social protection, and resilience-building measures. A key achievement was the establishment of the Baku Finance Goal, setting a core target for developed countries to mobilize at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. Additionally, COP29 saw a historic decision to ensure the full operationalization of the Loss and Damage Fund, a long-awaited initiative for developing countries, including small island states, least-developed countries, and African nations. COP29 was also pivotal for children and youth's meaningful participation and engagement. Children participated in the Youth-led Climate Forum Dialogue on Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)|UNFCCC. UNICEF co-created this forum with the UNFCCC and COP29 Presidency and supported children in taking an active part. Adopting the Baku Guiding Principles on Human Development for Climate Resilience, aimed to address intersectoral synergies and complementarities between greening education, health, social protection, decent jobs, and skills, highlighted the importance of investing in child-responsive policies. 

Approving the MICS survey report by the Cabinet of Ministers of the Republic of Azerbaijan in 2024 was a critical milestone, considering that the last MICS was conducted in 2000. The MICS is the largest source of statistically sound and internationally comparable data on children and women worldwide. It provided comprehensive, reliable, and disaggregated data on the well-being of children and women in the country, including data for 21 SDG indicators, of which 13 are national priorities. The MICS findings demonstrate significant improvement 
in certain child rights areas such as under-five child mortality rate, stunting among children, antenatal care coverage and others.  However, the prevalence of violence against children, early marriages, immunization, exclusive breastfeeding, and adolescent birth rate underscores the need for accelerating the efforts to improve child protection, nutrition, health, early childhood development (ECD), and social services, particularly for the most vulnerable, such as girls and boys with disabilities and those living in remote rural areas.

As the current Country Programme (CP) of UNICEF and the Government of Azerbaijan ends in 2025, the CO focused on the preparation of the new programme, including the evaluation of the current, conducting Situation Analysis of Children, holding consultations with national partners and conducting internal prioritization discussions. 

UNICEF’s work in 2024 continued to align with the global 2022-2025 Strategic Plan and regional flagship areas, focusing on advancing equitable access to health, nutrition, education, child protection, adolescent development services and enhancing their quality. Disruption in routine immunization coverage interrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in rural areas, resulted in a measles outbreak. In collaboration with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF responded to the measles outbreak, including a catch-up immunization campaign in Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic (NAR), Gobustan, Mingachevir, and Yevlakh public awareness initiatives, and capacity-building for healthcare workers, which were instrumental in addressing the situation. The outbreak underscored the urgent need to strengthen routine immunization services and enhance public trust in vaccination programmes to prevent future outbreaks and prevent children's fatal illnesses. 

Despite substantial investments in the education system, students miss foundational skills and competencies, impeding their academic progress and future opportunities. The 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results released in 2024 indicated a notable decline in Azerbaijan's educational outcomes in mathematics, reading, and science compared to 2018.

Azerbaijan ranks moderately on the Gender Inequality Index of 0.294 and a Global Gender Gap Index rank of 101 out of 146 countries, showing progress in education and health; and room for improvement in political representation and labour market participation.

The government continues the recovery efforts in the Karabakh region, including resettling more internally displaced families in the region which requires significant logistical and operational work. Additionally, landmines and unexploded ordnance continued to pose serious risks to children and their families. Thus, UNICEF prioritized its Explosive Ordnance Risk Education programmes, working closely with government and affected communities to enhance awareness and safety measures.

Every child survives and thrives 
After successfully testing the 2021–2022 Universal-progressive Home Visiting (UPHV) model, UNICEF supported the government in scaling it up. By 2024, UPHV was fully integrated into the Administration of the Regional Medical Divisions’ (TABIB) primary healthcare package and insurance benefits for pregnant women and young children. In collaboration with ECARO and the Ministry of Health (MoH), CO organized a Regional Training of Trainers on UPHV in Baku, involving 35 local and international educators and participants from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, fostering South-South cooperation.

UNICEF assisted medical training institutions in updating curricula and integrating new modules of UPHV and ECD. In 2024, 1,028 nurses and 2,462 students were trained in ECD and UPHV. An online course at www.eudi.az (ECD Resource Hub), available to all ECD sectors, was completed by 8,480 professionals, and five new online modules were produced. In partnership with MoH, UNICEF expanded the UPHV model to the Nakhchivan AR and is supporting the Maturity Model Assessment of UPHV to enhance the quality and accessibility of the service.

UNICEF supported the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative, expanding it to the Nakhchivan AR, with 15 maternity wards supporting 19,000 births, earning the "baby-friendly" status. 

In 2024, UNICEF and WHO supported the development of national immunization guidance endorsed by the MoH. A Coverage and Equity Analysis, supported by UNICEF’s Europe and Central Asia Regional Office (ECARO), in four low-coverage regions (Mingachevir, Gobustan, Khachmaz, Baku) uncovered barriers, leading to the development of action plans addressing vaccine safety, data gaps, and healthcare provider knowledge. UNICEF-led immunization campaign delivered catch-up vaccines to 5,283 children across four regions, trained 427 healthcare workers on immunization guidance and interpersonal communication for vaccination, and hosted Q&A sessions for caregivers. Online vaccine safety campaign reached 40,000 parents.

A new national guidance from 2024, introduced Measles, Mumps and Rubella job aids developed by ECARO and helped address knowledge gaps among healthcare workers. An immunization training module for home visitors on www.eudi.az  complemented these efforts. UNICEF also supported a global exercise on Cold Chain Equipment gap analysis, vaccine forecasting and procurement.
UNICEF supported the MoH and Azerbaijan Food Safety Agency (AFSA) in implementing the International Code for Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes, and the MoH established a multi-stakeholder working group to align national legislation with the Code. 
UNICEF partnered with the Food Fortification Initiative to provide technical guidance to AFSA in wheat flour fortification, including developing national guidelines for the milling industry and training. 

Every child learns 
The number of inclusive schools in Azerbaijan increased from 40 to 67 across 22 regions, enabling over 350 children with disabilities (168 girls) to access formal education. Over 4,600 children with and without disabilities in primary and secondary classes of inclusive schools benefitted from enhanced teaching and learning practices in an inclusive environment.
Approximately 1,400 educators, school leaders, psychologists, and special educators, received advanced training significantly enhancing their ability to deliver inclusive education. Social and Behaviour Change initiatives reached over 5,000 individuals, including children, parents, and community members, fostering positive attitudes and reducing stigma and disability-related stereotypes. 

The community-based Early Childhood Education (ECE) model expanded to over 18,000 children aged 3-4 (9,360 boys and 8,640 girls). With UNICEF’s advocacy and technical assistance, a comprehensive ECE Financing Study provided a high-level roadmap for expanding ECE access to 50 per cent by 2026 and 75 per cent by 2030, in line with the national targets. 

In alignment with COP29 priorities, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Science and Education (MoSE) to launch transformative climate education initiatives. The Green Skills through STEM programme equipped over 500 students aged 12–16 in 8 regions with expertise in green energy and technologies, fostering innovation and empowering students to develop solutions to climate challenges. Additionally, the Green Garden Initiative, piloted in 2024, provided climate education to over 1,300 preschool-age children. This initiative strengthened the capacities of preschools and early childhood educators.

With national partners, UNICEF equipped more than 10,000 adolescents and youth with socio-emotional, digital and transferable skills in 2024. Career counselling and work preparedness services were introduced in 60 per cent of Youth Houses, prioritizing NEET youth and girls, benefiting 596 participants (56 per cent girls, 44 per cent boys). 

To support young people with disabilities, UNICEF partnered with the Agency for Sustainable and Operative Social Provision (DOST), State Employment Agency and the business sector to launch a career acceleration programme, reaching 70 adolescents and young people with disabilities (26 girls, 44 boys) in 2024. It focused on building job readiness and transition skills, facilitating internships, and fostering inclusive workplaces while addressing stereotypes.
To address post-pandemic mental health challenges, UNICEF supported the Youth Foundation and the Prosecutor General’s Office in conducting a survey on youth and adolescent mental well-being, engaging 1,200 young people. The findings will inform future interventions for strengthening socio-emotional resilience of young people.

Young people from Internally Displaced People (IDP) families and return volunteers (55 per cent girls, 45 per cent boys) received training in life skills, career development, digital literacy, EORE, and community building to support sustainable communities and actively engage youth in development processes in Karabakh.

UNICEF's adolescent and youth participation programme, implemented with the Ministry of Youth and Sports, prioritized climate action, empowering 600 youth (58 per cent girls, 42 per cent boys) through the Youth Climate Envoys to advocate for child-sensitive policies and youth-led solutions for sustainable development, including during the COP29. 

To identify challenges and opportunities for transitioning to the labour market, including gender-equality, UNICEF engaged 315 young people (48 per cent boys, 52 per cent girls) from six regions. Key solutions they proposed included improving access to quality education, career guidance, and entrepreneurship opportunities while addressing gender biases through awareness campaigns and enhancing digital and soft skills to support equal employment opportunities. The recommendations are used in developing the new country programme of UNICEF.
   
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation 
In 2024, UNICEF sustained investment in strengthening systems for effective prevention of and response to violence against children (VAC), including gender-based violence (GBV), through technical assistance, advocacy, awareness-raising, and service provision. Applying the Child Safeguarding mechanism in 101 schools in Baku, Lenkeran, Ganja, Agjabadi, Zengilan, and Nakhchivan AR covered more than 109,000 children. Over 1050 child safeguarding cases were identified and addressed accordingly. One of positive outcomes of the model is improved cooperation and referrals between education and social service providers. In partnership with the Azerbaijan Young Teachers Association, more than 10,200 teachers (8435 women) completed the training on the prevention, identification, reporting and responding to VAC. UNICEF and national partners, continued  implementing  the programme “Strengthening the Child Protection and Social Protection Systems”, targeting the  national and district level systems to prevent, identify, and respond to VAC. Almost 1600 children, including 295 (87 per cent boys, 13 per cent girls), in conflict with the law benefitted from high-quality social services in Baku, Ganja, Lenkeran, Absheron, and Agjabadi.  Promoting National Child Helpline services strengthened the awareness of children and families on violence, the culture of reporting violence and receiving professional support. A special edition of the Public Television “Sabaha Saxlamayaq” was dedicated to the International Day of Child Helpline resulting in high visibility. 

One of the key highlights of the child protection programme was extending the work in the Nakhchivan AR. Key child protection partners from the State Committee on Family, Woman, and Child Affairs (SCFWCA), local commissions on minors’ affairs, justice professionals, and school psychologists were trained on child rights, international standards on juvenile justice, child-friendly communication in justice, child-friendly legal aid, and psychological support. UNICEF also modelled child safeguarding in all schools in the capital city-Nakhchivan covering 15,405 children (48 per cent girls, 52 per cent boys).

Key recommendations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (2023) were discussed in different events with the SCFWCA and specific actions were identified to address the recommendations.

Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE)
UNICEF focused on awareness-raising in addressing the dangers of landmines and Explosive Remnants of War (ERW) through EORE. These initiatives uniquely leveraged the power of football as a platform to engage children, families, and communities in conflict-affected districts and IDP settlements, making risk education both accessible and impactful.

In collaboration with the MoSE, the Mine Action Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan (ANAMA), and the Football Development Foundation, awareness-raising initiatives leveraged the power of football in promoting EORE. These efforts targeted children, families, and communities in conflict-affected districts and IDP, disseminating critical information about the dangers of explosive ordnance. As a result, over 300 children actively participated in engaging and impactful EORE interpersonal activities, while over 10,000 children benefited through learning materials. 

Children directly participated in interpersonal EORE sessions, engaging in practical, age-appropriate activities aimed at building their knowledge and safe behaviours in areas contaminated by mines and ERW. The sessions emphasized life-saving strategies, fostering a culture of safety and awareness among the most vulnerable populations.

In addition to direct engagement, the communication campaign reached a broader audience in villages and rural areas delivering key messages on EORE to over 10,000 children and their families, broadening the impact of the initiative.

Recognizing the critical role of youth in spreading awareness, UNICEF supported over 100 young people (64 girls, 36 boys) from IDP families to facilitate EORE sessions for local populations in mine-infested areas and to act as community facilitators on EORE.  This peer-to-peer approach amplified the reach of EORE and empowered young people to take an active role in protecting their communities from the dangers of explosive ordnance.

By combining innovative approaches, such as leveraging football with community-driven strategies, these initiatives helped equip children, families, and communities to better navigate the risks posed by landmines and ERW.

Every child lives in a safe and clean environment 
In 2024, the MICS provided extensive evidence collected from approximately 2,570 household samples nationwide by assessing drinking water quality via biological and chemical analyses.
Also, findings from the UNICEF-supported children’s environmental health assessment were presented in 2024 at the Baku Youth Climate Negotiations Forum and the Green World and Health Symposium. These findings guided capacity-building and awareness initiatives with the government.

An assessment of healthcare workers’ knowledge of pollution and climate change supported UNICEF’s advocacy to revise medical curricula. Consequently, 14 WHO-UNICEF training modules on children’s vulnerabilities, water safety, pollution, and climate change were translated and adapted, including a "B.E.A.T. the Heat" module on protecting children from heat stress.
With UNICEF support, the MoH joined the global Children’s Environmental Health Collaborative    making climate change and environmental health topics mandatory in medical training programmes for doctors and nurses. This change will equip 6,910 healthcare professionals in the current academic year. The relevant training of trainers’ programme was developed and implemented across 13 regions of Azerbaijan with 685 professionals trained in 2024. 

To extend outreach, UNICEF is localizing an Agora-based E-course on children’s environmental health. In collaboration with the Public Health and Reform Centre, community sessions in schools engaged parents and caregivers, to raise awareness about environmental health and climate change.

UNICEF CO’s engagement at COP29 included a series of high-level initiatives aimed at placing children and youth at the heart of climate action. These included close cooperation with the COP29 Presidency, particularly the Youth Climate Champion, to ensure child-focused priorities were integrated into key climate discussions. Engagements included organizing the “Baku Initiative on Human Development for Climate Resilience,” hosting a roundtable on climate action for children at the United Nations General Assembly, facilitating a high-level meeting on advancing climate action for children, and contributing to discussions on the global framework for children, youth, peace, and climate security. UNICEF CO also played a central role in organizing events on the health climate action and integrating children’s perspectives into the UNFCCC process, including a side event with the government, ECARO and World Bank on climate finance and social protection. These efforts ensured that children’s rights and climate resilience were highlighted across COP29.

One of the key achievements was the signing of the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action during COP29, confirming the government’s commitment to placing children at the centre of climate policies.  

Before and during COP29, UNICEF helped empower the Youth Climate Envoys to address climate challenges with innovative solutions and community engagement. Youth advocates emphasized child-sensitive climate policies and the impact of climate change on children at local, national, and international levels. Their recommendations were submitted to the national working group developing Nationally Determined Contributions, ensuring youth voices inform inclusive climate solutions. Both ahead and during the COP29, young envoys championed inclusive policies, showcased solutions on global platforms, presented youth-led recommendations and underscored the importance of child-sensitive approaches in climate action. To ensure a safe environment for children’s participation, UNICEF organized a safeguarding awareness sessions.  
Every child has an equitable chance in life 
UNICEF and the Ministry of Finance initiated the child rights budgeting exercise to introduce child-friendly budgeting within the Mid-Term Expenditure Framework. The primary goal   is to support the measurement of public expenditures targeted at children, ensuring alignment with current government policies to optimize budget contributions towards child-specific objectives. 

The Country Office continued its engagement in implementing the policy options outlined in the comprehensive research on Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) financing completed last year to expand preschool education to 50 per cent by 2026. The study provided a clear, comprehensive roadmap with practical and feasible policy options and solutions for financing the expansion of preschool education. As a result, the ministry prepared legal provisions for ECEC, including family-based ECEC, mobile services, and financing models such as public-private partnerships and vouchers. A pilot of these provisions is scheduled for 2025.

Furthermore, the government approved a 25 per cent increase in the Early Childhood Education (ECE) budget within the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework for 2024-2027, equating to an additional US$77 million investment in ECE over the next three years. This funding increase is expected to extend coverage to an additional 80,000 children by 2027.

UNICEF made significant strides in 2024 in advancing shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) measures in Azerbaijan, reinforcing its role as a key technical partner. UNICEF's proactive engagement and technical support have been pivotal in integrating SRSP measures into national policies.  International experts conducted specialized workshops on simulation instruments for social protection in emergencies. Later, a national-level workshop focused on identifying shock impacts and SRSP targeting criteria, while a thematic seminar brought together key ministries and local authorities to discuss resilience-building, using the Interactive Social Policy Simulator and exploring pre-arranged financing instruments for shock, including climate-related hazards. Approximately 40 participants from central and local government, including those from the Shamakhi and Sabirabad regions, benefited from the capacity-building. 
As a key milestone, UNICEF submitted the draft SRSP Intervention Framework, Legal Analysis and Framework, and Financial Strategy to the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of Population (MLSPP). These documents are essential in guiding the implementation of SRSP in Azerbaijan, providing a strong foundation for the government’s commitment to integrate SRSP measures within its national framework by 2026.

Gender equality
With the support of ECARO, a Gender Programme Review was conducted to support the CO in strengthening the gender responsiveness of the current and new Country Programmes.  The CO continued implementation of the Gender Action Plan 2023-2025, focusing on identified key gender actions and benchmarks in relevant areas of UNICEF work.

Considering the gender transformative role of education and in support of the advocacy for climate change education on the way to COP29, with the Ministry of Science and Education, UNICEF introduced Green Skills through STEM education. About 500 adolescents (240 girls) from eight regions advanced their skills in green technologies.

Home visiting services for pregnant women and young children continued to have a gender-transformative impact by engaging fathers in childcare and ECD. Gender-transformative ECD was also prioritized in developing of ECD Roadmap and Action Plan by UNICEF and a multi-sectoral Working Group. Additionally, UNICEF advocated for and technically supported the integration of multi-micronutrient supplements into the health insurance benefit package for pregnant women to combat high anaemia rates and meet their nutritional needs.

In collaboration with national partners, UNICEF facilitated discussions with young people to better understand their needs and opportunities for transitioning to the labour market, with particular attention to the challenges faced by girls. Around 315 young people (48 per cent boys, 52 per cent girls) from six regions highlighted key challenges, including limited opportunities for social engagement, educational barriers due to financial constraints or lack of access to professional training, and gender-based discrimination, all of which hinder equal employment opportunities.

UNICEF continued supporting informal national platforms to equip adolescents and youth with socio-emotional, transferable, and soft skills through the Basic Life Skills programme. It integrated a gender equality module piloted in several Youth Houses, with plans for expansion in 2025. 

Partnership with the National Child Helpline, expanding the coverage of child safeguarding in education to more than 109,000 children, and MHPSS for 3,573 children in the Karabakh region increased access to safe channels for reporting and responding to violence against children, including gender-based violence. Information sessions involved 9,392 adolescent girls on the prevention of violence and harmful practices and the role of reproductive health. Awareness-raising activities addressed key child rights issues, such as gender-based discrimination and violence, early marriage and other harmful practices in six districts covering 2,698 persons.

Expanded communication and advocacy efforts have significantly improved UNICEF's overall visibility and positioning in Azerbaijan, enhancing relationships and reputation with key government partners and reinforcing UNICEF’s role as a strategic partner of choice. With COP29 being a priority, UNICEF focused its communication and outreach efforts on bringing children and youth at the centre of climate policy by working closely with COP29 Presidency, arranging a series of advocacy events, and engaging youth advocates and volunteers. 

UNICEF scaled up its media outreach with 1,600 mentions in publications in the local press.  Social media engagement across the platforms, reached over 4 million people online. Thanks to digital campaigns on immunization, online safety, youth climate engagement, the overall social media followership of UNICEF accounts increased by 15 per cent in 2024, with website visitors growing to 30 per cent.

UNICEF Country Office is committed to strengthening partnerships with key stakeholders, including government institutions, UN organizations and civil society, to expand the reach and impact of its programmes for the most vulnerable children and adolescents through regular and innovative interventions. 

One such example in 2024 is the work on Explosive Ordnance Risk Education. By collaborating with the MoSE, the ANAMA, UNHCR, and directly involving adolescents, youth and the Football Development Foundation, UNICEF helped create innovative, inclusive, and community-driven approaches to raising awareness about the dangers of landmines and ERW. This work leveraged local expertise, resources, and networks to build safer, more resilient communities and IDP settlements. 

In 2024, UNICEF Azerbaijan and the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Azerbaijan initiated a child rights budgeting exercise, the first of such kind in the country. Its results and recommendations will help integrate child-friendly budgeting practices into national financial frameworks, ensuring a more strategic focus on child-specific priorities. The partnership sets a solid foundation for continued collaboration to enhance policy and budget alignment, with promising prospects for advancing child rights in Azerbaijan and alignment with the UN CRC recommendations.

Technical assistance to the State Committee on Family, Woman, and Child Affairs focused on updating the Law on Child Rights, aiming to include key definitions, concepts and guidance for prevention, identification, reporting and responding to all forms of discrimination and violence against children, meanwhile highlighting the role of child safeguarding mechanisms in all spheres to ensure the protection of children’s rights. 

UNICEF cooperated with numerous national institutions and the UN family to advance climate action for children and adolescents and support their meaningful involvement in COP29. The CO sustained its successful collaboration with the COP29 Presidency Youth Climate Champion, facilitating multisectoral partnerships in adolescent and youth engagement in climate action involving the Ministry of Youth and Sports and the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. A successful collaboration has been established with the UN Country Team in Azerbaijan and the UN Secretary-General's Office to amplify the voices of young people from Azerbaijan through meetings and discussions with high-level officials on topics like youth participation in climate action, child sensitive climate policies, adaptation and mitigation strategies, renewable energy solutions and climate finance. In alignment with COP29 priorities, UNICEF also expanded the scope of the existing partnership with Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education to launch transformative climate education initiatives in 2024. UNICEF secured additional funding for the new initiative on Strengthening Climate Change Education and Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems in Azerbaijan that will be catalytic in strengthening and expanding the scope of UNICEF’s programming in climate change education to prepare Azerbaijan's children and youth for the challenges of a changing climate while positioning the education system as a pivotal driver of sustainable development and climate resilience.

UNICEF CO successfully partnered with UNEP in the development of the programme "Strengthening Climate Information and Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems for Increased Resilience in Azerbaijan", securing approval from the Green Climate Fund (GCF) in 2024. This collaboration highlighted UNICEF’s role as a technical partner, contributing expertise across education, health, adolescent participation, social protection, and emergency. The partnership involved close coordination and months of joint planning, proposal refinement, and addressing feedback from GCF committees, showcasing the strong collaboration between UNEP and UNICEF in advancing the climate agenda from 2025 to 2029. UNICEF CO mobilized close to USD 3 million for the implementation of the cross-sectoral programme to begin in 2025.To ensure the sustainability of human development initiatives and encourage meaningful participation of adolescents and young people in community processes that affect their lives, UNICEF engaged private sector stakeholders to foster a culture of partnership in both the capital city and the regions. A key achievement has been private sector engagement in building the capacities of vulnerable groups, particularly young people with disabilities. This has resulted in a new joint programme with the Agency for Sustainable and Operative Social Provision (DOST) and State Employment Agency to support young people’s career preparedness and smooth transitions into the workforce.

Partnerships with civil society organizations were further extended to create new partnerships and reach vulnerable children and adolescents. Thus, the cooperation with the National Olympic Committee is focused on developing child safeguarding mechanisms in sports federations based on UNICEF’s experience and guidance.  UNICEF’s work on the prevention of all forms of violence against children was presented in II Safe Sports Forum. The joint work will enhance cooperation between sports federations and UNICEF-supported social services, including Azerbaijan Child Helpline. Additionally, UNICEF has initiated partnerships with the Youth Foundation and the Prosecutor General’s Office to do an assessment of the mental well-being of adolescents and young people. Based on the findings, plans are underway to develop targeted interventions.

Partnership with the research community extends beyond knowledge generation, supporting also evidence-based policies, modelling programmes/interventions, and enhancing professionals’ capacities. Through the MICS process, UNICEF CO successfully cooperated with the State Statistical Committee (SSC) and 17 Steering and Technical Committee members from ministries and government agencies. Though design of questionnaires, training on complex MICS questionnaires, developing data collection application, Computer-Assisted Personal Interviews (CAPI), based on Census and Survey Processing System (CSPro) software, data editing, preparing and developing infographics (snapshots) with the support and guidance from UNICEF county, regional and global experts, relevant SSC staff acquired new skills and further built capacities for other large surveys. In 2025, UNICEF and SSC will continue its joint work for further MICS visualization, including data visualization competition, workshops on data for kids, additional analysis of MICS data, and monitoring of MICS data usage in strategies and policies.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Due to the limited availability of donor funding in Azerbaijan, which constrains the impact that core funding of UNICEF could have, UNICEF prioritized mapping of the traditional and emerging donors as well as areas for the significant leveraging of resources by government and other partners to inform further design of its programme, including partnership and fundraising strategy. Additionally, UNICEF is working to engage the private sector as an important partner in implementing the child rights agenda in Azerbaijan. By building partnerships with businesses and leveraging the resources and expertise of both the public and private sectors, UNICEF aims to expand the scale of programmes for children and adolescents and ensure their sustainability.

The small number and insufficient capacities of civil society organizations (CSOs), coupled with challenges in grant registration, hindered UNICEF’s ability to diversify established partnerships across sectors. These limitations affected the scale and outreach of ongoing programmes in early childhood development, health and nutrition, education, adolescent development, and child protection to reach more vulnerable families, children, and youth. UNICEF will work closely with the government to address this issue as it creates difficulties in establishing sustainable mechanisms for advancing child rights, provision of services to children at local levels and developing the capacities of CSOs.

Reducing the number of children in institutions and placing more children in family-based alternative care remains one of the priority areas of UNICEF in close cooperation with numerous national partners. UNICEF will work more closely with key policymakers and service providers in child and social protection, including the National Commission on Minors’ Affairs and Protection of their Rights, to provide technical expertise in different cross-sectoral commissions and working groups on child protection. 

The implementation of Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) initiatives faced delays due to some procedural challenges and limited access to certain conflict-affected areas and IDP settlements, which hindered direct engagement with at-risk populations and constrained optimization of funding. The integration of creative platforms like football proved highly effective in engaging children and families, underscoring the importance of leveraging culturally relevant tools for greater impact. Additionally, the peer-to-peer model, where trained adolescents led EORE sessions, highlighted the potential of youth as catalysts for change within their communities. Flexibility and adaptability in programme implementation emerged as critical for overcoming logistical and procedural barriers.

Moving forward, the focus will be on scaling up community- and school-based EORE interventions by fostering stronger partnerships with the government and civil society while expanding reach to populations and building the capacity of teachers and youth facilitators, ensuring the sustainability of EORE awareness-raising results. UNICEF will also expand the use of digital platforms and innovative communication strategies to broaden the dissemination of life-saving messages, contributing to safer communities and long-term resilience. Additionally, UNICEF will advocate for and support the MoSE in integrating EORE into school curricula, enabling the expansion of EORE interventions through the education system.

UNICEF actively promotes youth engagement by involving young people in decisions that affect their lives. Lessons learned from the Youth Advisory Councils in eight regions, which faced challenges in sustainability, budgeting and management guided the development of a new approach. Building on consultations with partners and youth institutions, UNICEF will launch a new youth-led mechanism to enhance young people's participation and create a robust network of youth initiatives across the regions.

Strengthening the youth development agenda requires increased support, including improved incentives and salaries for youth workers, to reduce high staff turnover and ensure continuity in programmes. Institutionalizing youth participation and engaging young people in decision-making processes can help align youth programmes with the needs and expectations of adolescents and young people. Focus on leveraging government funds to advance the youth development agenda will enhance the impact and sustainability of relevant initiatives. Stronger private sector partnerships will also play a vital role by providing technologies, expertise, and internships to support young people’s transition from learning to earning. 

Scaling up youth development and participation platforms will positively impact the engagement of adolescent and youth in decision-making concerning their lives. Strengthening public healthcare facilities for adolescents' mental health services and the establishment of online digital platforms to provide qualified mental health services for adolescents will be another priority. 

State Programme on Inclusive Education 2018–2024 reflects the political commitment of the national government and the MoSE to expanding access to quality inclusive education for children with disabilities who remain out of school. However, as of 2024, the progress achieved has been modest. Insufficient public funding for the programme’s implementation, coupled with the limited financial resources of UNICEF, constrained the scale of inclusive education initiatives, hindering its rollout across more regions and schools. UNICEF will work with the MSE to enable access to inclusive preschool education and advocate for stronger inter-ministerial coordination for better availability of affordable, high-quality social protection and community-based support services, such as rehabilitation. These measures will increase the effectiveness of inclusive education efforts.

Overall, the systemic barriers to effective coordination among multiple sectors inhibit the timely progress and scale-up of the achieved results. Moreover, the insufficient national capacity in the areas of evidence generation and cross-sectoral cooperation and the use of innovative tools delay effective implementation. Engaging highly qualified international and local experts in technical assistance to the government proves to be vital in further capacity development of national institutions and advancing the agenda for shock-responsive social protection. The successful work on ECE financing showed the value of evidence-based advocacy. In addition, integrating legal expertise with technical assistance, especially in developing policies, is useful to the government and ensures faster adoption and implementation of revised and new policies. 

UNICEF will continue to prioritize multi-stakeholder coordination and building the capacity of all partners. Furthermore, UNICEF plans to intensify data-driven innovative solutions and maximize its efforts to tailor these solutions to local needs and contexts.

In 2024, Belarus maintained its progress in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and has been ranked 30th out of 167 countries (with 78.6 points out of 100) in the Sustainable Development Report 2024. The country’s position in the UNDP Human Development report 2023/2024 remained high: Belarus was 69th among 193 countries in the Global Human Development Index. The Social Progress Index 2024 rated Belarus 61st among 170 countries.

The child population of Belarus decreased by 26,338 compared to 2022, reaching 1,801,380 at the end of 2023.[1] The Government of Belarus (GOB) takes steps to enhance demographic security by increasing support to families with children.

Belarus experienced relative economic stability, with a 4.2% GDP increase[2] in January-October 2024. The International Monetary Fund assessed the GDP growth rate for Belarus at 3.6% in 2024 ranking it third in Europe[3]. In January-November 2024, real wages increased by 12.9%[4] with the inflation rate at 5.5%[5]. In 2023, the national poverty rate slightly declined to 3.6%[6] from 3.9%[7] in 2022. The child poverty rate remained significantly higher at 8.3%[8] although it had decreased from 8.9%[9] in 2022. Despite stable economic performance, Belarus development continued to be impacted by the geo-political situation in the region affecting families’ and children’s well-being.

Belarus maintained a robust system of social benefits and support to vulnerable families, families with many children and other categories in need. In 2024, public welfare payments covered around 366,000 children, representing each fifth child in the country and nearly all children 0-3 years old (198,400)[10].

In 2023, the number of children with disabilities (CWD) increased by 1,492 to 38,749[11]. In 2024, Belarus presented its report on the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities to the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Committee stressed the need for deinstitutionalization as a result of a declaration of legal incapacity or on the grounds of a person’s impairment.

Belarus remains committed to ensuring social protection and support to CWD, their families and caregivers. In 2024, a new law amending public welfare benefits for families with CWD was passed. The law introduced the right for a family with a child with severe disability to receive children’s allowance for other children aged 3-18 years after their CWD turns 18 years but still requires care. The improvement will benefit around 2,000 families[12]. Other amendments improve access to welfare benefits related to sick leave and medical services provided to a CWD, improving the situation for families with two or more CWD. The law came into effect on 1st January 2025.

The Ministry of Education (MoE) invests in further enhancing accessibility and inclusiveness of education. The number of CWD in pre-school and general secondary education increased from 27,772 in 2022 to 32,057 in 2023 or by 15%[13]. According to the MoE, there were 181,000 children with special educational needs in Belarus, 99.9% of them received education with 70% in inclusive education[14]. Despite these numbers, more efforts are required to ensure full-scale inclusion, as currently many CWD receive education outside general educational establishments and lack access to assistive technologies to support their integration.

Belarus has achieved and maintains strong progress on health-related SDGs. There were 58 early childhood intervention (ECI) centers with four newly opened in 2024. The Ministry of Health (MOH) reported a 27% increase in ECI service provision in the first half of 2024[15]. The MOH continued to support 58 Youth-Friendly Health Centers reporting an increase in number of provided consultations by 3.4% in the first half of 2024[16]. Among health issues high on the agenda of the MOH is obesity among children and youth reaching up to 20% of the child population[17].

In December 2024, the GOB passed an order on Coordination Councils on State Protection of Children and an order on Recognizing Children in Social Danger and in Need of State Protection. The order on coordination councils provides for councils to be established in all regions and in Minsk to enhance coordination between different agencies engaged in child protection. The order on children in social danger streamlines the grounds and procedures for recognizing children to be in social danger and in need of state protection regulating the removal of children from families.

Belarus is committed to preventing, identifying, and protecting child victims of sexual exploitation and abuse. While there is a lack of public statistics on violence against children, including sexual violence, the topic remains high on the agenda with individual cases covered by the national media as part of prevention activities. Overall, the number of children victims of different crimes increased from 2,500 in 2022 to 3,050 in 2023[18].

The situation with migrants and refugees remained challenging with arrivals surpassing departures starting October 2023. According to the State Border Committee in 2024, 144,093 entries and 119,440 departures of Ukranian refugees were registered (in 2023 - 78,625 entries and 72,853 departures). The number of entries/exits through the border with the Russian Federation is unknown due to absence of border control there. 45,390 Ukrainians were officially registered in Belarus by December 2024, according to the Department for citizenship and migration, with UNHCR estimating 37% of them to be children. The Government continued to provide comprehensive assistance to Ukrainian refugees. In 2024, 38 unaccompanied minors and separated children were identified. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs engaged with the UN in Belarus to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the child protection system for refugee and migrant children entering Belarus. 

Belarus continued to implement the National Action Plan for Gender Equality in Belarus for 2021-2025 engaging UNICEF and other UN agencies as partners. In 2024, the GOB developed and piloted a mechanism of gender expertise of draft laws with UNDP and UNFPA support. The results were presented during a meeting of the National Council on Gender Policies in December 2024.
