Over 2024, UNICEF continued to support Belarus in achieving its priorities on child related SDGs. The Country Office (CO) contributed to attaining UNICEF’s five global strategic goals for 2022-2025. Working in an upper-middle country, the CO focused on strengthening systems for the most vulnerable children promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The CO built on the humanitarian-development nexus further promoting interagency collaboration and cooperation between regions to enhance the national preparedness capacities and to respond to protection needs of the most vulnerable children including refugees and migrants. 
 
Goal 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives 
Nurturing Parenting Environments: 
Nurturing parenting environment in the early years is foundational for children’s health and development.

The CO continued to partner with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the Republican Practical Research Center “Mother and Child” to promote best breastfeeding practices and improve nutrition and feeding for the most vulnerable children with disabilities in residential institutions.

Under the baby-friendly hospital initiative, the MoH, in partnership with UNICEF, supported the certification of 14 hospitals providing specific services for childbirth preparation and breastfeeding. The MoH updated the reporting form on breastfeeding to include an indicator on the percentage of exclusively breastfed children reporting 62.7% rate in 2024.

With UNICEF support, individual nutrition and feeding needs assessment of 108 children on palliative care and children with severe disabilities were conducted in nine residential institutions. The results informed individual nutrition and feeding plans. The professional competencies of 196 employees working with children with special nutrition and feeding needs were enhanced through tailored training strengthening the capacities of the system to better assist the most vulnerable children. To ensure sustainability of good care practices, the manual "Improving nutrition and feeding practices of children with special needs" was developed and published to be used in residential institutions.

A new Center of Inclusive Nutrition in the Minsk City Medical Rehabilitation Center was established and equipped with UNICEF support. The order of the Minsk City Health Committee on screening of nutritional disorders and feeding difficulties in young children was approved. The screening is now routinely used in the medical rehabilitation center and early childhood intervention (ECI) centers in Minsk.

The CO promoted and updated its Bebbo application as a reliable comprehensive online resource supporting responsible nurturing parenting with 42,635 registered users. 
The Ministry of Labor and Social Protection continued to partner with UNICEF to promote responsible fatherhood and Family-Friendly Policies (FFPs). This collaboration resulted in a social campaign on television and radio and a dedicated photo exhibition. A national-level event "Fatherhood and Career: How to Successfully Balance Both" was organized and served as a dialogue platform bringing together representatives from private and state businesses with large numbers of employees to discuss best practices in FFPs.

Strengthening Systems for Inclusive Early Child Development: 
Early childhood intervention (ECI) is a social model that involves an intersectoral response across education, healthcare, and social protection, supporting families with children (0-3 years) who are at-risk of or have developmental delays, disabilities and behavioral or mental health needs.

Partnering with the MoH the CO built on previous years’ achievements and continued to strengthen the national ECI system focusing on accessibility and sustainability of services. 
To promote the sustainability of ECI centers, UNICEF in partnership with the Belarusian Center for Technologies and Information conducted an ECI costing which assessed the regulatory framework, eligibility criteria for ECI services, and the adequacy of budgetary allocations. The costing included a sample of 20 ECI centers in the Brest and Mogilev regions and in Minsk. Key recommendations included updating ECI standards, eligibility criteria, and a formula for assessing the number of children per region in need of ECI services annually. The package of ECI services was also reviewed, and the amount of required annual financing was estimated. A simulation tool for budgeting was tested by pilot financial departments of the regional health committees. The revised normative package for the ECI system will be submitted to the MoH for approval in 2025. If approved, the proposed changes will enhance the sustainability of public funding and improve access to ECI services, expanding eligibility for different groups of vulnerable children.

Advancing Adolescents’ Health and Well-Being: 
Recognizing adolescence as one of the most challenging periods in a child’s life with multiple changes increasing vulnerabilities in health and psychological well-being, the CO continued to partner with the MoH and the Ministry of Education (MoE) to enhance the quality and access to youth friendly services.

The methodological basis of the extra-curricular course “My psychological well-being and peer support in crisis” introduced in 498 schools across Belarus was enhanced. Over 200 graduate students from the Belarusian State Pedagogical University (BSPU) were trained and conducted lessons under expert mentorship of the Institute of Psychology.

Methodological guidelines were developed for integrating the UPSHIFT methodology in schools for adolescents to develop project related to metal health. One hundred adolescents engaged in UPSHIFT training developed 20 mini-projects on mental health with 7 funded by UNICEF. These projects were implemented in schools, promoted through peers and social networks, and reached over 10,000 adolescents.

In partnership with the Republican Centre of Psychological Assistance the CO further improved the quality of online psychological assistance for adolescents through its Talk2ok online counselling platform with 671 phone and 339 online consultations provided. In view of the platform’s sustainability and expansion, UNICEF supported training resulted in expanding the cohort of Talk2ok consultants to 54 registered psychologists and 18 peer support volunteers to increase access to age-appropriate services.

A series of "Let’s Be Friends! How to Feel Confident in Any Group" workshops were organized at 9 Youth-Friendly Health Centres to enhance social integration and emotional well-being of 229 adolescents.

A social behavior change (SBC) campaign was implemented in partnership with the MoE. It promoted mental health and psychosocial support reaching 305,638 people with 80% estimated to be adolescents. Engaging messages on normalizing conversations around mental health, seeking psychological support and emphasizing its importance were delivered through over 170 publications, 4 radio and 9 TV broadcasts.

Jointly with UNFPA, WHO and UNDP the CO continued to support the MoH to ensure the sustainability of the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and congenital syphilis. UNICEF contributed by guiding national specialists in developing the EMTCT re-validation report as recommended by the Global Validation Advisory Committee. The report will be submitted to the Commitee in the first quarter of 2025. 
 
Goal 2: Every Child Learns and Acquires Skills 
Accessing Quality & Inclusive Learning Opportunities: 
The MoE, in partnership with UNICEF, strengthened the national educational system to include children with disabilities and with special educational needs into quality pre-school and secondary education through a multi-year Inclusive education project.

The CO supported in-service teacher capacity development, needs assessment in assistive equipment, accessibility assessment of educational establishments, and an SBC campaign. Around 4,500 teachers were trained to work with children with disabilities and with special educational needs; more than 350 children with disabilities in 118 pilot educational establishments were provided assistive devices to improve their access and participation in learning and out-of-school activities; over 363,000 people were exposed to messages emphasizing the importance and benefits of inclusive education for the society at large through targeted media interventions.

In November, a National Inclusive Education Forum was conducted jointly by the MoE and UNICEF. Over 1,300 education specialists, scientists, and governmental officials from Belarus and Russia shared of the Inclusive education project’s achievements, exchanged experience, and fostered their cooperation. The Forum contributed to promoting the implementation of the National Strategy of Inclusive Education, implementation of the inclusion principles in the National Strategy of Training Teachers and the Concept of Special Education.

Advancing Skills, Participation & Engagement: 
Fast-paced digitalization, spread of technologies and artificial intelligence, and changing labor markets require the education systems to emphasize providing adolescents and youth skills beyond traditional academic and professional knowledge. In partnership with the MoE the CO focused on developing social-emotional skills (SES) in children and adolescents to enhance their resilience to evolving changes and equip them with key social competences.

With UNICEF support, the Academy of Education successfully piloted SES elective courses for 3-4th and 6-7th grade students in 23 schools of the Brest and Gomel regions. The results of piloting will be assessed and disseminated in early 2025.

In March, a national round table on SES organized jointly by the MoE and UNICEF provided 40 education professionals and adolescents an opportunity to present the major achievements, challenges and lessons learned on SES integration in general secondary and technical vocational education (TVE). The round table highlighted the high interest for further development of SES in Belarus and defined priorities and ways forward. This included further piloting SES courses and incorporating them into secondary education and in-service training for teachers.

With UNICEF contribution, the MoE disseminated a Methodological Letter on introducing SES in the TVE system for the 2024-2025 academic year. This guiding document for educational establishments creates a framework and new opportunities for further developing and institutionalizing SES training for TVE students providing the most vulnerable adolescents an opportunity to learn essential soft skills for success in life.

Youth engagement was enhanced in partnership with the MoE through different channels. Youth SDG Ambassadors engaged adolescents and youth around SDGs. Child- and Adolescent-Friendly Cities (CAFC) continued to be one of the major platforms to promote youth engagement, including through youth parliaments. Currently, 32 cities from different regions participate in the initiative with 24 awarded the CAFC title. As of December, there were 47 children and adolescent parliaments engaging over 600 children and adolescents in the decision-making process.

Volunteers continued to shape and get involved in UNICEF programming, through a network of 333 registered volunteers. They engaged in developing courses on SDGs and on Interacting with People with Disabilities for the u-platform with 2,791 registered users. Over the year 603 courses were completed by adolescents and youth through the u-platform. 
 
Goal 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation 
System Strengthening for Family-based Care: 
The CO continued to strengthen deinstitutionalization mechanisms under its flagship initiative “Family for Every Child” piloted in the Vitebsk region. The project promotes advanced social work tools based on case management to prevent placement of children under four and children with disabilities into residential facilities and reunify children in institutions with their biological or foster families. Over 200 specialists were provided knowledge and skills on social work using case-management, communication with vulnerable families, intersectoral work, and social patronage. Following the needs assessment of 700 families in social risk conducted by UNICEF and its partners, a set of comprehensive measures to address them was developed and 104 children were reunified or obtained a new family in 2024. A Road Map for Deinstitutionalizing Children from all four residential institutions in the Vitebsk region is planned to be introduced in 2025.

The “Family for Every Child” initiative became a platform for scaling up best practices across other regions of Belarus. The Brest Region Social Pedagogical Center, jointly with UNICEF, used the social risk prevention mechanisms piloted in the Vitebsk region. This resulted in preventing 101 children from placement in residential facilities by using the advanced needs assessment tool in selected communities. Case management and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services proved to be an effective prevention intervention for vulnerable families. The services reduced instances of neglect and abuse and prevented institutionalization of children in 70% of cases. The Brest Region Executive Committee committed to scale up this practice in all its districts in 2025.

Building System Responses for Prevention of Violence: 
Recognizing prevention of bullying as critical for children, the MoE with UNICEF continued to scale up the Safe and Enabling Environment in Schools (SEES) programme. SEES engaged 43 schools, reaching approximately 25,000 children across of Belarus. The Belarusian State Pedagogical University with UNICEF proposed a cluster model to scale up the services and introduce SEES model in different communities. Under this cluster model, schools most experienced in anti-bullying will promote SEES and serve as resource centers and mentors for other actors and new schools.

The School as a Space of Trust project, certified as a pilot by the MoE in 2023, was implemented in 11 schools in 3 regions and created MHPSS-informed environment for 8,076 children and adolescents. Based on the positive outcomes of the initial pilot, the MoE approved a follow-up project to explore opportunities for scaling up.

The CO continued to raise awareness on cyberbullying prevention. A one-hour elective class plan to raise children's awareness on cyber safety was developed and presented to the MoE in the framework of the #InternetWithoutBullying project, in partnership with MTS, one of the major network providers. In 2025, the guidance will be piloted in the 43 SEES schools.

Further enhancing the humanitarian-development nexus, the Republican Center for Psychological Assistance, jointly with UNICEF built the capacity of 50 crisis psychologists across Belarus in suicide prevention, violence against children (VAC), and gender-based violence response. Over 2,000 refugees including 440 children and over 800 representatives of local communities including 600 children were assisted through UNICEF supported MHPSS services.

The CO continued to monitor, assess, and provide assistance to Ukrainian refugees under the emergency response. With UNICEF support 368 Ukrainian refugee families including 318 children and 38 unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) received individual case management; 613 families with children were provided consultations on child protection, social protection, and psychosocial support; and 596 children and 302 caregivers received MHPSS services.

The CO used cooperation and advocated with the government and local administrations within the refugee response to facilitate a high-level dialogue on strengthening the national system for the protection of refugee and migrant children with a special focus on unaccompanied minors and separated children (UAMSC). The Ministry of Foreign Affairs requested the UN Belarus to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the child protection system for refugee children and migrants entering Belarus.

Enhancing Restorative Practices: 
The CO in partnership with the MoE and local authorities of the Brest and Gomel regions integrated restorative services based on case management for children in conflict with the law into the work of social pedagogical centers. Eighty pedagogues and psychologists learned about multiple dimensions of providing support to juveniles. These specialists, thus equipped, supported 52 children at risk of placement into closed-type institutions, resulting in 90% of these children getting out of the risk zone. To strengthen gatekeeping mechanisms preventing institutionalization of children despite their vulnerabilities, the CO in cooperation with the regional Education Development Institutes built the capacities of 65 decision-makers from the Juvenile Affairs Commissions, police juvenile inspections, education departments, and school administrations. The specialists are now able to apply the best interests of the child principle in making decisions affecting the most important rights of the child: family separation, placement in closed-type institutions or residential facilities, deprivation of parental rights.

CO’s programming in the Brest and Gomel regions on strengthening the regions’ capacity in restorative practices resulted in a 50% decrease of recidivism among minors under preventive control from the piloting communities.

Based on achieved results, the Brest Regional Executive Committee and the regional Department of Education jointly with the Regional Juvenile Affairs Commission made a strong commitment to scale up the results by developing a normative framework in 2025. 
 
Goal 4: Every Child lives in a Safe and Sustainable Climate & Environment 
Adolescent Voices for Climate Change: 
Recognizing the importance of sustainable climate and environment for every child development and future, the CO conducted the first Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) in Belarus to capture climate risks to children, examine gaps and opportunities related to their rights and child-sensitive approaches. Children, adolescents, and youth provided their opinion: 133 adolescents and youth shared their views during regional consultations; 7,679 children and youth participated in an online poll on climate change; two focus group discussions were conducted with 8-10 adolescents each. The report, once finalized in early 2025, will inform the CO’s Climate, Energy and Environment programming. 
 
Goal 5: Every Child has Access to Inclusive Social Protection & Lives Free from Poverty 
Budgets for Children & Reducing Child Poverty: 
The CO built on last year’s achievements to further enhance social protection and mainstream the integration of public finance for children (PF4C) in social and health care services. 
The CO continued to focus its PF4C efforts in the areas of health, in particular ECI. In November, 35 representatives of the ministries of health, finance and economy, local authorities, and research institutions participated in a three-day national training on PF4C for Health focused on ECI for children with developmental difficulties, organized by the CO jointly with UNICEF Regional Office for Europe and Central Asia (ECARO). Inter-ministerial teams developed and presented projects to improve PF4C for health, which could inform UNICEF future programming. The workshop also contributed to expanding space for CO’s PF4C advocacy efforts and facilitating inter-ministerial dialogue.

Access to Inclusive Social Protection: 
In the Brest and Gomel regions and in Minsk, UNICEF partnered with local authorities to enhance access of low-income families to targeted social assistance (TSA) by providing information support and enhanced communication.

The CO continued the humanitarian cash support programme providing direct financial assistance throughout the year to 737 Ukrainian refugee families, including 1,103 children, for the total amount of over 1.2 million Belarusian rubles (approximately USD 365,000). In addition, cash certificates were issued to 123 newly arrived Ukrainian families with children, including those transiting through the territory Belarus.

The CO maintained a structured multi-channeled approach to collecting feedback from affected populations, with a total of 8,132 feedback forms collected. The feedback was used to better understand the current needs of Ukrainian refugees, improve services and identify most effective communication channels.

A resource center for social service excellence and capacity building was established in the Brest region with UNICEF support to provide training and information resources to social services workforce.

The CO piloted 7 training modules for social service providers with 600 specialists from the Gomel region trained. The specialists are now equipped to provide better quality social services, including through improved communications and outreach to the most vulnerable groups throughout the region with a population of over 1.3 million.

In 2024, the office remained proactive in building partnerships at all levels to leverage resources and deliver results for children. Partnerships with the key ministries allowed to achieve meaningful progress in all areas of UNICEF programming contributing to Belarus’ priorities.

Partnership with key ministries and regional administrations remained essential for effectively responding to the refugee and migrant crisis and expanding the humanitarian-development nexus. Collaboration with the Department on Citizenship and Migration of the MoIA and the State Border Committee improved the CO’s access to critical statistics on the number of refugees arriving and residing in Belarus, allowing for tailored adjustments in the programming. Engagement with regional authorities ensured progress in enhancing the capacities of the social workforce with 600 professionals trained in the Gomel region to assist the most vulnerable children; Additionally, promising models on restorative justice were developed, resulting in a 50% decrease in recidivism among minors under preventive control in the piloting communities of the Brest and Gomel regions, among others.

The CO continued to engage with non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to deliver essential programming for children including the most vulnerable groups such as refugees. The CO partnered with Belarusian Movement of Medical Workers, Belarusian Association of Social Workers and Belarusian Children Fund to deliver information, child protection and MHPSS services to refugee children, their families and caregivers. The NGO “World without borders” trained 40 specialists as master-trainers to disseminate knowledge and best practices on restorative approaches among other specialists. Belarusian Association of UNESCO clubs, with UNICEF support, contributed to engagement of women living with HIV in ensuring sustainability of EMTCT.

Non-financial partnerships were vital in raising child rights awareness and support, opening business networks, and creating growth opportunities. Promoting Family-Friendly Policies through the HR-Brand Award and collaborating on responsible fathering with the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection and UNFPA extended outreach to both private and state businesses. Advocacy on internet safety and digital child rights engaged partners like MTS, Life, Rakuten Viber, and Kaspersky. This topic was the focus for Open Consultations between adolescents and businesses on World Children’s Day, with over 180 participants.

The CO promoted its Sports for Development programming. A memorandum of understanding was signed with the Football Federation. UNICEF partnered with the Minsk City Executive Committee, the Belarusian Cycling Federation and the Minsk Cycling Club to support the third season of the children's cycling competition Pershy Rovar ("My First Bike"). The CO used the competition to raise awareness of children and parents on road safety and trauma prevention, printing 4,150 information booklets. Both partnerships contributed to promoting child rights, responsible parenting and inclusion.

Partnership engagements were initiated with several UNICEF public donors, and the donor landscape was expanded to include Southern donors such as India and China. Understanding the donor landscape through donor mapping was instrumental in identifying key donors and priority areas and reinitiating engagement with partners. This year, the CO’s efforts focused on continuing dialogue with traditional donors, such as the UK Embassy and the Russian Federation, and new partnerships with the India-UN Development Partnership Fund. These efforts resulted in a small grant allocation from the UK Embassy and a proposal submitted to the India-UN Development Partnership Fund to support UNICEF’s efforts to prevent violence against children in Belarus. The CO continued to explore opportunities with BRICS countries, including China and Turkey, and initiated discussions with UNICEF Beijing for China to support the government of Belarus in modernizing health services for the most vulnerable children under five and adolescents. Public sector engagement is still in its initial stages and will take time to cultivate relationships for potential funding.

Fundraising income was increased through corporate channels by developing customer fundraising modalities and organizing dedicated offline campaigns. Support for children with disabilities remained the key topic for offline fundraising campaigns, such as the Minsk Half-Marathon and a new employee engagement campaign with BelVEB Bank. Private sector financial contributions increased by 65,870.5 USD (212,986.08 BYN) (33%) compared to 2023. Individual Giving and corporate channels generated USD 197,207.78 (BYN 637,563), including USD 60,731.49 (BYN 195,990.1) from businesses. New partnerships were established with BelVEB, HAB-Invest, Kaspersky, and Rakuten Viber, and the financial partnership with Priorbank was extended for another year.

Coordination efforts with the United Nation Country Team (UNCT) in Belarus focused on developing the new UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the Country Programme for 2026-2030 (CPD), to align strategic priorities and processes and external consultations. The CO prioritized engagement in developing the new UNSDCF, contributing to the evaluation of the current UNSDCF and the new Country Context Analysis, to ensure the proper inclusion of the child rights agenda into these key strategic documents. UNICEF participated in the UNSDCF prioritization workshop to shape the initial outcomes to be further approved by the Government of Belarus. Regular coordination was maintained through working groups and task forces, UNCT and UNICEF’s contribution to the UN Info planning and reporting. The joint UN programme to enhance Belarus SDG architecture was successfully implemented with the Steering Committee and Russian Federation requesting the UN in Belarus to launch the development of the follow-on programme.

Since its establishment, the national Sustainable Development Council has been supported by the UN in Belarus. Over the last two years the work of the Council has been facilitated through the joint UN project to support Belarus in achieving and reporting SDGs where UNICEF is among the most active partners. This strategic partnership resulted in the Government of Belarus assigning the Council to serve as a dialogue platform for developing the UNSDCF and country programmes of UNICEF, UNDP and UNFPA. This approach allows for enhanced coordination between the RCO, UN agencies and key national partners while providing clear mechanisms and a dialogue platform for receiving feedback and approving the UNSDCF and the CPD.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, the CO continued building on the successful strategies identified in the previous years of the programme cycle while continuously exploring opportunities to facilitate and expand its programming by enhancing existing and new partnerships and engaging with the new donors.

UNICEF further enhanced its positioning with the national partners, donors and business community, and the society at large through different channels. UNICEF positioning as a reliable, independent, and impartial partner of choice for delivering results for children of Belarus and supporting the country in achieving its priorities related to children was mainstreamed through its programming and communications.

In the programming area, the CO shaped ongoing activities and identified future opportunities in close cooperation with the national partners often serving as a conveyor between different governmental agencies, regional and national authorities. Contributing to the national programmes, such as the National Programme on the Health of the Nation and Demographic Security, remained a strong pathway to confirm UNICEF’s commitment to achieving priority results for Belarus.

Communications and advocacy efforts were focused on enhancing direct and open communication channels between UNICEF and governmental agencies, promoting UNICEF recognition among the population, and delivering a clear message on its impartiality, independence, and commitment to children of Belarus. The Representative led direct engagement with the key senior decision makers at the level of ministers and heads of organizations strengthening their understanding and support to UNICEF programming. At the technical level regular working contacts and groups were maintained by the CO’s sections with respective ministerial departments, governmental establishments, NGOs and public organizations. As many sections work with the same key ministries on multiple activities, the CO enhanced its internal coordination through weekly staff meetings with colleagues sharing regular updates and raising challenges to develop a coordinated response.

The CO closely collaborated with the key ministries to jointly promote UNICEF programmes through joint publications and activities significantly expanding the scale of initiatives and increasing the audience of UNICEF social channels by 25%. Joint activities allowed to promote the ownership of the national partners while increasing trust in UNICEF among different targeted audiences by highlighting benefits of cooperation. National conferences, such as the National Inclusive Education Forum, organized in partnership with respective ministries with UNICEF support also contributed to this priority.

CO’s closer partnership with press secretaries from ministries and other organizations enabled it to effectively engage with the media at the regional level and nationwide. This strategy building on the successes of 2023 yielded strong results with approximately 150 articles with UNICEF Belarus mentions published surpassing last year’s output by 25%.

Strengthening partnerships with existing and exploring opportunities to engage with the new donors remained one of the major UNICEF priorities. Although most of traditional donors ceased their support to Belarus, the CO continued to maintain contacts with bilaterals staying in the country, such as the United Kingdom, to keep the dialogue going, advocate for resuming support and partner to implement small-scale initiatives. While Belarus had been expanding its partnerships with BRICS and the far arc countries, UNICEF also prioritized exploring new opportunities resulting in progress achieved with the India-UN Development Partnership Fund and the China International Development Cooperation Agency. Engaging with the new donors requires investment in sensitizing them on UNICEF agenda and key principles, including impartiality, gender mainstreaming, and no child left behind. Among other benefits partnering with donors from the countries of interest for Belarus allows for better engagement with the national partners to develop coordinated proposals with them prioritizing and committing to implement planned activities. The Russian Federation (RF) continues to be the major Belarus’ political and economic partner with the Union State between the two countries steadily evolving. In 2024, the CO has started to explore opportunities for leveraging and programming support through the Union State social programmes.

Belarus continues to register technical and humanitarian assistance funds requiring substantial packages of documents to be submitted to authorized governmental agencies, requiring time for preparation and approval. The CO improved registration time of projects by closely engaging with the Department for Humanitarian Assistance of the Presidential Administration to deliver training on registering funds to the CO’s staff and partners including from the regions. Support and training from the Department resulted in alleviating partners’ concerns and better prepared documents facilitating the registration process.

UNICEF’s consistent positioning and advocacy efforts resulted in several major achievements. The Ministry of Health referred to UNICEF for assistance with procuring critical supply of bandages for “butterfly children” and signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) paving the way for further cooperation in procuring critical medical supplies for the most vulnerable children. Another MoU was signed with the State Border Committee allowing UNICEF access to a border unit and detention facility for irregular migrants including families with children. The MoU opened the way to developing a cooperation plan with the Committee to enhance child protection for migrant children and child-rights training. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs reached out to the UN in Belarus to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the child protection system for refugee children and migrants entering Belarus. 

Over the last years, UNICEF has been constantly adjusting its strategy to the evolving changes in the operating environment to achieve Country Programme priorities and the best results for children. Most of its strategic efforts have been long-term with cumulative effect reached over time. Lessons learned will be used to inform the development of the new Country Programme for 2026-2030 started in the last year and better shape UNICEF programming in the next cycle balancing ambitious goals with available resources, potential risks, existing opportunities and Belarus’ priorities for the next five years.

In 2024, Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH), an upper-middle-income country, has experienced both progress and challenges in various sectors, influencing the situation of 561,217 children (52 per cent boys, 48 per cent girls).[1] 


Bosnia and Herzegovina is facing significant socio-economic challenges exacerbated by external shocks such as the war in Ukraine and rising global inflation, which have increased living costs and strained economic stability. Despite a 4.2 per cent GDP growth in 2022, the economy slowed considerably in 2023, with growth dropping to 1.7 per cent.[2] These challenges have deepened socio-economic inequalities, disproportionately affecting low-income and rural communities who are more vulnerable to price increases and economic instability. In response, the European Commission launched a €6 billion Growth Plan for the Western Balkans in November 2023, aimed at accelerating socio-economic convergence with the EU. However, BiH has yet to submit its Reform Agenda, a prerequisite for accessing this funding, due to ongoing disagreements among the country's authorities. A critical issue for the country is the misalignment of public expenditure with SDG priorities. While public budgets accounted for 42.7 per cent of GDP in 2023,[3] resource allocation remains inefficient. The country’s fiscal policies, heavily reliant on indirect taxes like VAT, place an undue burden on lower-income households. Additionally, insufficient investments in education and healthcare hinder long-term growth and fail to address pressing social needs. Fragmented budget allocations further complicate fiscal coordination, reducing the effectiveness of public spending and undermining efforts to alleviate poverty and social exclusion.


Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Universal Periodic Review (UPR) report, adopted by the BiH Council of Ministers on 19 December 2024[4], provides a comprehensive overview of the country's progress and gaps in protecting and promoting children’s rights. The report underscores significant advancements, such as preparatory work for the 2025–2029 Action Plan for Children, legislative reforms aligning with the Lanzarote Convention, strengthened protocols for child witness protection, and progress in inclusive education through the introduction of educational assistants and tailored approaches for children with disabilities.  Despite progress in inclusive education and anti-discrimination efforts, challenges remain in addressing segregation, implementing protection protocols, and ensuring equitable access for marginalized groups, particularly Roma children and children with disabilities. Gaps in social protection, child welfare, and juvenile justice systems remain significant barriers to safeguarding children’s rights.


The recent measles outbreak in BiH, with over 7,000 reported cases and two deaths registered among adolescents[5], highlighted critical gaps in immunization system, especially in areas with low vaccination coverage like Tuzla Canton and Bijeljina. The rise in cases, primarily among children, emphasizes the risks of vaccine-preventable diseases. Challenges such as vaccine hesitancy, misinformation, and socio-economic barriers, particularly in marginalized communities like the Roma population, further worsened the situation. In response, UNICEF supported the Ministries of Health, local authorities, and NGOs with vaccination campaigns, vaccine distribution, and addressing hesitancy, aiming to strengthen the immunization system and protect vulnerable children. 


In October 2024, Bosnia and Herzegovina experienced severe flooding, particularly affecting the Herzegovina-Neretva and Central Bosnia canton. The floods displaced families, damaged homes, and disrupted education. The Multi-Cluster Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA), conducted by the United Nations, shows that over 1,000 households were affected, with 322 individuals requiring evacuation[6]. In a joint Programme with Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Policy, UNICEF provided financial assistance to support affected households and through collaboration with UNESCO donated laptops, headphones, as well as 4G-enabled SIM cards to schools in the impacted regions ensuring educational continuity. 


Central Bosnia Canton has finalized its Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) Strategy for 2024–2030, marking the first cantonal-level DRR strategy in BiH.[7] Serving as a model for localized resilience planning, it addresses climate risks such as floods and landslides, focusing on protecting vulnerable groups and aligning with the Sendai Framework and UN Sustainable Development Goals. The strategy awaits final approval by the Cantonal Government.


Mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) became a critical focus due to socio-economic challenges, limited mental health services, and the impact of natural disasters. UNICEF supported efforts to address urgent mental health and psychosocial needs caused by the 2024 floods, collaborating with BiH and local partners to provide targeted support for children and families, ensuring their recovery from the trauma. 


In education, 2023 ICILS results revealed that eighth-grade students in BiH scored below the international average in computer and information literacy (CIL), highlighting significant gaps in digital competencies. Conducted in 105 schools, the assessment found socio-economic disparities and limited classroom digital integration as key challenges. Girls outperformed boys in overall scores, yet systemic barriers, including inequitable access to digital resources and outdated teaching practices, remain. The findings call for enhanced teacher training, updated curricula, and targeted policies to bridge the digital divide.[8]


Over 25,000 migrants and asylum seekers transited through BiH in 2024. Fifteen per cent of migrants accommodated in Temporary Reception Centers (TRCs) were children, comprising 6 per cent children in a family and 9 per cent unaccompanied or separated children (UASC). UNICEF continued to provide critical services to children on the move and families. Simultaneously, continuous efforts were made to support the transition of services to BiH institutions and the increase of government ownership with a focus on child-centred migration.


Important initial steps were taken toward strengthening child rights through plans to develop a comprehensive Toolkit for Monitoring and Reporting on Human Rights, supported by UNICEF in partnership with the Ministry of Human Rights and Refugees (MoHRR) and OHCHR. This initiative, funded under the IPA 2020 program, aims to enhance the country’s capacity for monitoring and reporting on human rights, with a focus on addressing the needs of vulnerable groups, including children.

1. Every child survives and thrives


In 2024, UNICEF played a pivotal role in advancing systemic change in health, nutrition, and early childhood development (ECD) in BiH, contributing to transformative improvements that prioritize equity and inclusion. These evidence-based efforts foster long-term resilience by ensuring that vulnerable children and families can access quality services.


Progress toward better protection from vaccine preventable diseases through expanding routine immunization programs was a pivotal achievement. UNICEF supported Public Health Institutes (PHIs) to develop comprehensive plans for the introduction of the pneumococcal vaccine (PCV) into mandatory immunization schedules. UNICEF’s advocacy led the FBiH government to allocate the required budget for incorporating PCV into its immunization programe, marking a milestone in aligning government priorities with global health goals.


PHIs further enhanced Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) through UNICEF-supported establishment of EVM Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for FBiH, RS and Brcko District, along with trainings for 300 health professionals in vaccine management. SOPs are a crucial tool for improving vaccine handling and cold chain integrity, ensuring standardized safety in immunization. With UNICEF support, PHIs and primary healthcare facilities improved immunization systems by procuring WHO-prequalified cold chain equipment and IT infrastructure, upgrading vaccine storage, monitoring, and digital immunization management for better data-driven decision-making. Additionally, healthcare waste management improvement plans, including for immunization waste, were developed and adopted for FBiH and RS, aligning with global standards and environmental health requirements.


UNICEF partnered with local NGOs to improve immunization rates among underserved Roma children, vaccinating 41.7 per cent of those reached by joint interventions (271 boys, 212 girls).  Mobile teams of mediators and nurses, supported by UNICEF, conducted door-to-door outreach to promote immunization and address barriers. Public health campaigns, including during European Immunization Week, addressed vaccine hesitancy, thereby contributing to a more resilient immunization system.


Advancements in early childhood development (ECD) further highlight UNICEF’s transformative role. In collaboration with the Federal and Canton Sarajevo Ministries of Health, two new ECD/ECI centers opened in Sarajevo Canton, providing 14,902 children with access to integrated services. This progress marks a shift to a multisectoral approach, with health, education, and social welfare systems collaborating under a new SOP and Action Plan, developed with UNICEF's technical support, to ensure sustainable, high-quality support for young children and families. Additionally, the designation of PHI FBiH as an official ECD/ECI training institution marked a milestone in capacity-building, with the first cohort of 10 professionals completing Continuous Professional Development (CPD) training.


In nutrition, systemic changes aligned with global standards improved the inclusivity and quality of services. Two UNICEF-supported comprehensive analyses conducted by PHI in RS informed the adoption of improved regulatory frameworks and the introduction of “Nutrition-Friendly Kindergartens/Schools,” expanding coverage to 75 per cent of RS municipalities. 


Evidence generation for nutrition initiatives took a gender-transformative approach, strengthened by the UNICEF-initiated Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices study on nutrition, integrating gender lenses to identify disparities and needs, promote equality in health outcomes and ensure the diverse needs of all children were met. Collaboration with the RS Medical Students Association educated 271 girls and 114 boys, tackling gender-specific barriers and empowering both girls and boys to adopt better nutrition practices. 


To integrate mental health support into broader health and social systems and at community level, UNICEF partnered with civil society organizations (CSOs) to reach over 5,000 children, adolescents, and caregivers with evidence-based interventions, including capacity building for school pedagogues in Una-Sana Canton and strengthening the skills and knowledge of children and families,  to foster resilience and promote help-seeking behaviors, with stronger focus on adolescent girls.


PHI RS, with UNICEF support, piloted a study on indoor air quality in 10 kindergartens, generating evidence for systemic change. Using WHO-aligned monitoring methods and building PHI RS capacity for air quality interventions laid the groundwork for sustainable improvements in preschool and school environments, addressing long-term risks to children's health and learning.




2. Every child learns


UNICEF has made significant strides in strengthening education systems in Bosnia and Herzegovina by leading efforts to support all 12 administrative units to draft evidence-based 10-year education sector action plans for each level of education.  


To drive digital transformation, UNICEF transferred ownership of the Giga initiative to the BiH government, enabling real-time school connectivity monitoring and establishing the first government-led Advisory Body for Digital Transformation in Education. UNICEF expanded the Akelius Digital Language Programme to two schools in Tuzla Canton, benefitting 460 students—30 per cent of whom are Roma. This builds on ongoing implementation in Sarajevo and Una-Sana Cantons, where 3,850 children (1,217 girls), including 2,446 children on the move (356 girls), strengthened their digital and language skills. Additionally, UNICEF trained 112 teachers in blended teaching approaches, enhancing digital competencies and Akelius Digital Language Programme delivery. UNICEF also partnered with the University of Sarajevo to develop an online course on air pollution and climate change and a training module on assistive technologies in education. 


Furthering inclusive education, in Republika Srpska (RS), UNICEF supported education authorities to enhance inclusive early childhood education and care (ECEC). Achievements included the rollout of a child development tracking system in preschools and a multi-sector protocol to protect children from violence, abuse, and neglect, with integrated school violence reporting in the Education Management Information System (EMIS). In Sarajevo Canton, UNICEF provided technical assistance to develop a roadmap for optimization of special schools’ resourcing, including personnel, facility and operational costs, supporting the inclusion of children with disabilities into mainstream education. 


In partnership with the Cantonal Ministries of Education and Department of Education in Brcko District, UNICEF expanded its gender transformative flagship IT Girls programme, reaching one in three secondary schools in BiH. In 2024, UNICEF empowered 1,479 girls and 512 boys with digital skills, tackling the STEM gender gap and promoting girls’ leadership. UNICEF established 36 IT Girls clubs across 141 schools in FBiH and Brcko District, provided Arduino kits, and trained 211 teachers in programming, robotics, and electronics. Through system strengthening and partnerships with youth- and women-led CSOs, UNICEF further localized the Adolescent Girls Agenda, focusing on violence prevention, addressing harmful social norms, mental, and skills development. These efforts earned UNICEF recognition as one of six global leaders for the Adolescent Girls Strategy. 


Through community engagement programmes, including UPSHIFT and green skills programs, UNICEF empowered 430 adolescents (302 girls) to advocate for climate policy, resulting in the governmental Air Quality Action Plan in Tuzla Canton, one of BiH's most polluted regions. These effort engaged 664 high school students, 433 primary school students, and 41 teachers, showcasing the power of youth-led climate action. UNICEF also engaged a record 730 new U-Reporters and supported 60 young activists in shaping recommendations for COP29.


Through sustained advocacy, UNICEF positioned ECEC and digital transformation as priorities in the EU Growth Plan, thus preparing the ground for significant resources for BiH governments over the next three years. By using compelling evidence from ECD Investment Cases, UNICEF influenced political discourse on ECD and ensured continued strategic engagement with BiH parliaments. 


 


3. Every child is protected


Governments and ministries in BiH, with UNICEF’s support, made substantial progress in strengthening child protection and justice systems in 2024. These efforts were anchored in strengthening family-based care, enhancing legal frameworks, and building the capacity of social and justice professionals to address the diverse needs of children and families.


The endorsement of the Road Map for Deinstitutionalization of Children, coupled with a new EU IPA-funded programme, marked a significant milestone. This initiative prioritized family support services and prevention of family separation, focusing on foster care over institutionalization and transforming residential institutions into community-based support centers. The FBiH Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare initiated revision of foster care legislation to improve accessibility and affordability for families. Participation of the BiH delegation in CARE 2024 conference, supported by UNICEF, aided in advancing BiH's capacity to strengthen protection and support systems for children, youth, and families by integrating the latest knowledge and best practices from across Europe.


To ensure sustainable improvements, UNICEF facilitated capacity-building initiatives for the social service workforce. The official curriculum for supervision training, developed with UNICEF’s support, was endorsed by RS and FBiH line ministries, and efforts to integrate supervision into master’s programs began at the universities of Banja Luka and Sarajevo. These initiatives aimed to embed quality assurance mechanisms within child protection systems. Professional associations, such as the Association of Social Workers and Psychologists, played a pivotal role in delivering inclusive, quality services.


 


UNICEF also supported justice systems to increase access for children, addressing gender-specific needs and vulnerabilities. Key efforts included capacity-building for justice professionals, inclusion of children and justice in EU funding priorities, and coordination through the Justice for Children Forum. In the RS, the Ministry of Justice strengthened the protection of child victims and witnesses, while in FBiH, preparatory analyses and work for a new family law laid the groundwork for more inclusive policies. The adoption of the Barnahus model, an internationally recognized approach to protecting child victims and witnesses, in Sarajevo, demonstrated a significant step forward in ensuring child-sensitive justice.


Adolescent girls programming focused on empowering youth through strengthening MPHSS systems, addressing harmful social norms, and preventing gender-based violence. Small grants to youth- and women-led CSOs enabled outreach to vulnerable girls, raising awareness about GBV and available support services. Expanding these efforts could amplify their impact on girls and boys alike, fostering more inclusive and gender-equitable outcomes.


In flood-affected areas near Jablanica and Fojnica, UNICEF, in partnership with local authorities and the Association of Psychologists of FBiH, delivered urgent mental health and psychosocial support through 133 interventions conducted by 14 psychologists, reaching 196 individuals. Of these, 80 received individual support (30 men, 51 women, 7 minors), and 127 joined group sessions. In close collaboration with the CSW Jablanica, these interventions aimed to prevent long-term psychological impacts, reflecting a commitment to inclusive and trauma-sensitive care for affected families.


 


4. Every child has a fair chance in life


In 2024, Bosnia and Herzegovina made significant progress in strengthening social protection and inclusion systems, reflecting collaborative efforts by the government, civil society, and UNICEF. UNICEF’s technical expertise, resource mobilization, and convening power were instrumental in these advancements.


One major milestone was the reform of the Federal Law on Support to Families and Children, which expanded child benefits to children with disabilities and severe illnesses, regardless of family income. UNICEF provided technical guidance to ensure the law addressed vulnerable populations and promoted equity in access to social protection.


Another key development was the Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Policy's Draft Law on Social Services, now under parliamentary review. UNICEF supported this initiative by providing technical inputs to standardize service delivery across the Federation of BiH (FBiH) and prepare the ground for licensing and provision.


UNICEF supported the Feasibility Study for the FBiH Family Fund, setting the stage for its establishment. The examined child support payments for single mothers will feed into the Family Fund provisions and inform unified family and child benefits across all 10 Cantons in FBiH in 2025. 


In close partnership with the Federal Ministry of Labor and Social Policy, RS Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, FBiH Administration of Civil Protection and Civil Protection Administration of RS, UNICEF’s leadership extended to integrating Shock-Responsive Social Protection (SRSP) systems into systems’ strategic and financial frameworks. Conducting BiH’s first SRSP Feasibility Assessments and introducing innovative crisis poverty costing simulation models, UNICEF provided policymakers with evidence-based tools for enhancing fiscal preparedness in social protection. Financial modeling for disaster risk financing further equipped decision-makers to optimize social protection crisis preparedness.


Through UNICEF’s advocacy and collaboration, the City of Bihac allocated $50,000 for a pioneering local SRSP initiative, providing emergency cash support to benefit 5,000 to 8,000 vulnerable individuals. During the 2024 floods, UNICEF provided $54,000 in funding which complemented government investments of $270,000, aiding 694 affected households and demonstrating SRSP scalability.


UNICEF played a transformative role in advancing disability-inclusive reforms, by expanding child disability assessment and referral reforms to additional Cantons and Republika Srpska entity.  Over 600 children with disabilities in only two Cantons of FBiH have been included into the new functional assessment process. Feedback from parents of children with disabilities from Herzegovina Neretva Canton was collected and presented at the Federal Conference in December 2024, underscoring the need for a harmonized country wide approach.


UNICEF facilitated the integration of social protection and inclusion into development plans in eight municipalities. In partnership with UNDP and through collaboration with local governments, social welfare centers, and civil society organizations, these initiatives directly benefited over 3,000 individuals and indirectly impacted 43,000 more. Peer-to-peer exchanges and professional networks fostered long-term collaboration and replication of successful models.




5. Supporting children on the move


A holistic response to the refugee/migrant crisis continued, with close collaboration among the Child Protection, Health, and Education sectors and partners.  At the same time, UNICEF further invested in enhancing government ownership and capacity to take over service provision for children on the move, aiming for a sustainable and gradual transition of the response starting in 2025. As an integral component of the emergency response, the office has further advanced in bolstering Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) mechanisms, including through the EMOPS UNICARE project which will ensure that UNICEF BiH has a fit-for-purpose solution for AAP.


The adoption of the Migration Management Transition Plan by the BiH Council of Ministers represents a significant milestone towards transitioning the management of temporary reception centers and services from international organizations to national institutions. However, challenges such as unclear mandates and the absence of a Child Protection Transition Working Group slowed progress. Therefore, UNICEF’s ongoing advocacy, in collaboration with IOM, remains key to advancing this transition in 2025. 


To strengthen ownership and ensure sustainability of the transition, UNICEF, alongside UNHCR and IOM, trained 28 professionals from social welfare institutions and line ministries, equipping them to integrate children on the move into the national child protection system. Police officers in five locations and service providers in reception centers also received training on child safeguarding, ensuring better protective measures for vulnerable children. 


UNICEF prioritized the protection and resilience of children on the move through tailored interventions. Two child-friendly spaces in TRCs Ušivak and Borici provided safe, gender-sensitive environments for 1,186 children (426 girls and 760 boys), combining protection, learning, and psychosocial support. Despite these efforts, 495 children reported violence or abuse, with actual numbers likely higher due to underreporting. To address these issues, UNICEF supported 520 women, girls, and boys through gender-based violence (GBV) risk mitigation, prevention, and response programs, emphasizing the protection of girls and young women. Additional advocacy efforts emphasized resilience-building for girls on the move, strengthening protective factors, and enhancing psychosocial support.


UNICEF provided non-formal education, including catch-up classes and language learning, in two reception centers. Through collaboration with schools and education authorities, 263 children (54 girls) were integrated into formal education and vocational training programmes across two administrative units and are now nearly fully funded by the governments.


Essential nutrition services, implemented through partnerships with World Vision and NGO Fenix, reached 650 children (322 girls, 328 boys, including 5 children with disabilities), along with 526 mothers, 356 fathers, and 51 pregnant women from refugee and migrant communities nutrition services, implemented through partnerships with World Vision and NGO Fenix, reached 650 children (322 girls, 328 boys, including 5 children with disabilities), along with 526 mothers, 356 fathers, and 51 pregnant women from refugee and migrant communities.




6. Cross-cutting


UNICEF advanced child rights monitoring in BiH by supporting the contextualization of the National Human Rights Database (NRTD), in collaboration with the Ministry of Human Rights and Refugees. This digital platform, aligned with international standards, aims to enhance planning, monitoring and reporting to global human rights mechanisms, including the Committee on the Rights of the Child. UNICEF’s advocacy secured commitments to develop a state-level Action Plan for Children, providing a strategic framework to guide child-centered policies across the country.


To address critical data gaps, UNICEF advocated for the next round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), and led on high-quality evidence generation, including through the Situational Analysis for Children and the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). Addressing data gaps on Roma student enrolment, UNICEF collaborated with Giga to create a mapping tool revealing which revealed that only 7.6 per cent transition to secondary education, underscoring the need for focused action. In partnership with governments and CSOs, UNICEF empowered adolescents with 21st-century skills, prioritizing digital, green, and entrepreneurial competencies. These programs emphasized gender equity and social inclusion, ensuring that girls, boys, and marginalized youth had equal opportunities to participate and thrive.


UNICEF’s gender-transformative efforts included securing funding from Sida and the EU for a joint program to combat gender-based violence (GBV). This initiative strengthens systems for prevention and response while addressing the specific needs of women and girls. 


In response to the 2024 floods, UNICEF supported 1,500 families with cash transfers, bridging critical gaps in government funding and demonstrating the scalability of shock-responsive social protection (SRSP). Investments in Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) strengthened government capacities to mitigate risks and enhance community resilience in disaster-prone areas.


By developing and leading the implementation of innovative advocacy and communication strategies, UNICEF significantly bolstered external relations, enhanced visibility and engaged a broader audience, resulting in an increased number of advocates for UNICEF's mission and work.


Collaborations with high-level supporters, including Olympic swimmer Lana Pudar and influencers such as Edin and Amra Džeko, amplified UNICEF’s advocacy on social media and digital platforms. The introduction of TikTok and LinkedIn channels expanded UNICEF’s online reach, by leveraging diverse and creative content formats, such as interactive posts and impactful visuals, UNICEF has successfully captured the attention of its audience, resulting in increased engagement and visibility. A partnership with Mtel led to an online violence prevention campaign, generating over 200 media reports and reaching diverse audiences through cost-free media coverage.

In 2024, UNICEF’s partnerships in BiH delivered transformative results for children and families. Partnerships with CSOs extended UNICEF’s reach to marginalized populations and delivered tailored interventions. UNICEF’s partnerships with World Vision and NGO Fenix provided essential nutrition services to refugee and migrant children, pregnant women, and caregivers, ensuring no one was left behind.

When severe flooding disrupted education in central and southern BiH, UNICEF responded rapidly through innovative partnerships with UNDP and UNESCO. Donor contributions were pivotal in driving UNICEF’s success.
