Regional Trends and Impact on the Programming Environment (2024)
In 2024, 76 million children across Europe and Central Asia (ECAR) face challenges shaped by socio-economic and geopolitical pressures. The region includes four high-income countries with UNICEF programmes (Croatia, Greece, Bulgaria, and Romania), 15 upper-middle-income countries, and three lower-middle-income economies (Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan).
Despite a projected GDP growth of 2% over the next five years, 19.8 million children live below the poverty line. Refugees, migrants, children with disabilities, those in rural areas, and marginalized communities are especially vulnerable. Over a third of ECAR countries experience double-digit inflation—Türkiye's stands at 60%. Fertility rates average below replacement level at 1.9 (except in Türkiye and Uzbekistan), with migration adding demographic complexity.
The war in Ukraine, now in its third year, continues to affect 1.5 million children in frontline areas. Over 3.2 million are internally displaced and 6.1 million refugees have fled to other parts of Europe. The war has severely impacted children’s mental health, disrupted education, and strained social services. Even high-income countries struggle to absorb the surge of refugees, complicating access to education and health services.
Migration flows from conflicts and instability have overwhelmed countries along the Mediterranean and Balkan routes. In 2024 alone, nearly 173,000 refugees arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, Italy, and Serbia. Armenia hosts over 142,000 refugees, while Türkiye shelters more than 3 million Syrians. Vulnerable groups—especially women, girls, and unaccompanied children—face increased risks of exploitation, violence, and lack of access to services. Rising xenophobia, limited protection systems, and inadequate support structures further endanger these populations.
The multiple crises call for stronger sub-regional capacities for preparedness, response, and resilience. Investments in disaster risk management and national systems are essential to manage complex emergencies.
On the health front, ECAR countries have achieved over 90% coverage for at least one childhood vaccine. However, immunization progress is reversing, with over 108,200 measles cases reported in 2024—a doubling from 2023 and the highest since 1997. Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Romania, and Bosnia and Herzegovina are among the hardest hit. Vaccine hesitancy and underfunded healthcare systems hinder progress.
There are over 20 million children under five in ECAR, with 6 million babies born each year. Despite policy improvements, around 3.2 million young children (about 25%) are not developmentally on track, which threatens their future well-being and potential.
While most ECAR countries are near universal primary education coverage, significant disparities persist. Children with disabilities, Roma children, and children on the move face major barriers due to negative societal attitudes. Preschool attendance averages 63% but is particularly low in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Tajikistan. The 2022 PISA report showed that 40% of 15-year-olds fail to meet minimum standards in reading and math. Challenges remain in learning quality, upper-secondary retention, and educational inclusion.
Adolescents face rising mental health challenges and poor job preparedness. One in three report frequent nervousness, and one in four struggle with sleep. The region has the world’s highest adolescent suicide rate, with over 1,300 deaths annually among 15–19-year-olds. About 20% of youth (7.2 million) are neither in education nor employment (NEET), with young women twice as affected. Gender stereotypes restrict girls’ participation in STEM, affecting their future opportunities and reinforcing employment segregation.
Violence and abuse remain widespread. Over 60% of children in some countries experience violent discipline at home, and 37 million women and girls have suffered contact sexual violence during childhood. Children from minority groups, migrant families, and conflict-affected areas are especially vulnerable. Mental health services and protective measures remain insufficient.
Although institutionalization has declined in many countries, around 456,000 children still live in residential care, with ECAR’s rate (232 per 100,000) double the global average. Children with disabilities are disproportionately institutionalized.
Social protection has weakened. In 2024, 1.6 million households—mainly in Central Asia—lost access to family and child benefits, contrasting with 2023 when 76% of children received such benefits. Fiscal tightening and market-based growth policies have deprioritized child poverty reduction. The EU has seen a shift away from social investment toward economic returns. Budget cuts and reduced development assistance further strain services for children. Aging populations and migration trends may reduce tax bases, shifting spending toward older adults and away from child-focused investments.

In 2024, ECARO set the stage for the next cycle of programming, marking a transition year that built on its 2023 Mid-Term Review re-alignments to enhance its programmatic effectiveness and operational efficiencies.  12 country offices began developing new country programmes, while three more underwent programme reviews. Country programme evaluations were conducted for Turkmenistan and Turkiye, while system-level evaluations for regional flagship results included de-institutionalization in eight COs and immunization in five COs. These processes steered all country offices towards a coherent and structured approach to programming aligned with the key principles of the new Strategic Plan and fully adjusted to the diverse contexts within the region. ECARO laid the foundation for its Business Model Initiative in 2024, focusing on programmatic engagement models designed to ensure CO capacity to leverage resources, pursuing operational efficiencies, and establishing innovative technical assistance modalities in priority areas for the region.
Thriving
ECARO has been achieving notable progress to improve child health and development across the region. Partnering with organizations such as WHO and the EU has been crucial for amplifying its impact. For example, in partnership with DG Health, EUR 2 million was raised to support child health initiatives, including for early childhood development, immunization, nutrition, and mental health. UNICEF's role in shaping overweight and obesity prevention policies has strengthened through partnerships with the European Commission and Global Thematic Fund for Nutrition, supported by the Regional Nutrition Partnership Platform in Central Asia and the Caucasus.
In maternal and newborn health, ECARO provided technical assistance to strengthen healthcare systems and services, including enhancing neonatal care quality in the Western Balkans and improvement of service provision in 230 perinatal care centres in Uzbekistan, benefiting 928,578 newborns. Through leveraging a partnership with Latter-day Saint Charities (LDSC), UNICEF addressed critical gaps in respiratory support for preterm and low-birth-weight newborns in perinatal care centres in six key cities in Uzbekistan. Home visiting has been an effective strategy for improving reach across the region, with investments made to train nurses in antenatal and postnatal care for premature and sick newborns. In Ukraine, the universal home visiting programme expanded in 2024 to 15 oblasts (provinces) and Kyiv. UNICEF advocated for the inclusion of the UPHV model in key national frameworks, the National "Better Care Strategy" (2024-2028), and the National Health Strategy 2030. Through this initiative, home-visiting nurses conducted more than 20,000 visits, supporting 29,680 children and caregivers, including those in remote and conflict-affected areas.
ECARO made notable achievements in effectively handling disease outbreaks. Mobilizing USD13 million for immunization, it supported 15 countries, including for response to measles and pertussis outbreaks. Over 3.1 million children were vaccinated against measles through UNICEF-supported programmes in 15 countries, while more than 20,000 healthcare workers in 16 countries-built capacity on immunization skills. Over a million parents and caregivers were reached with immunization messages in 12 countries.
ECARO has played a key role in advancing mental health and psychosocial support programmes across the region, collaborating with WHO in Serbia, Albania, and North Macedonia to strengthen inter-ministerial cooperation and develop national mental health strategies. In Italy, ECARO supported the integration of mental health services into the broader healthcare system, improving accessibility. Additionally, the innovative e-mental health platform, uSupport, expanded across the region, with Kazakhstan officially adopting it in the national health strategy and Poland joining as a key partner. In Greece, UNICEF leveraged $35 million in EU-RRF funding with the Ministry of Health to implement a mental health programme focusing on strengthening the system early detection, destigmatization, and tailored services for youth with non-suicidal self-injury. This provides a foundation for the development of a regional MHPSS hub in Greece as part of the ECAR business model initiative.
In nutrition, 11 countries with ECARO support, established legislation, policy actions and programmes to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. In Central Asia, along with the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine, government capacity for monitoring and enforcing national laws has been strengthened, and advocacy for food systems transformation has led to several countries committing to evidence-based policies for preventing childhood overweight and obesity. For example, Kazakhstan government agreed to develop fiscal policies and legislation related to sugar sweetened beverages, as an outcome of strong regional and country office advocacy efforts.
ECARO has made significant progress in early childhood development (ECD) by implementing initiatives that monitor children's development and support parents. It has boosted technical capacity and strategic advocacy for ECD in the health sector, while enhancing coordination at the country office level. Through collaboration with health systems, ECD is increasingly integrated into facility-based and home visiting services. In 20 countries, these initiatives have exceeded 2024 targets, improving parental counselling, developmental monitoring, early identification, and early childhood intervention. This comprehensive approach ensures children receive the care they need for healthy growth and development UNICEF has reached 10,000 professionals through the Regional Health Systems for ECD Initiative and established an early childhood intervention regional network across 23 countries with 140 members.  Throughout the year, partnerships were deepened with private sector and framework was developed for engaging with businesses in the area of parenting and ECD.
Learning
In 2024, ECAR advanced inclusive education through technical support that enabled substantial reforms across the region. With ECARO support, Armenia and Albania advanced on the transformation of special schools, the Republic of Moldova strengthened its inclusive education by expanding teacher training and introducing assistive technology, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Ukraine strengthened their inclusive education strategies and North Macedonia improved legislation on enrolment of children with severe disabilities in mainstream schools. Serbia enhanced national systems for teacher professional development reaching 4,150 teachers and financing of inclusive education, while Slovakia and Romania, through Technical Support Instruments, launched national level support for education desegregation of Roma children and safe and supportive schools for wellbeing and mental health. Introduction of innovative tools, including the draft Teacher Development Portal, a professional development platform with online self-learning pathways being initiated in Poland, including an online course on accessibility and assistive technology already piloted in the country. Uzbekistan, with funding from the Islamic Development Bank, launched a nationwide inclusive education initiative, including use of assistive technology.
ECARO provided hands-on assistance to 14 countries to expand Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) coverage, improve planning and financing, and enhance service quality. Peer learning exchanges and study visits—among countries such as the Czech Republic, Romania, and Bulgaria—facilitated the sharing of best practices across the 0–6 continuum. The successful completion of two TSI projects (Austria and Cyprus), the ongoing Czech Republic project, and three new TSI projects (Germany/Lower Saxony, Bulgaria, Portugal) collectively advanced innovation, system quality, and cross-country collaboration. ECARO also launched two regional data publications on Expanding ECEC services through flexible provisions and on status of services for children aged 0–3, reinforcing its thought leadership in this area.
ECARO supported the acceleration of digital transformation of education through technical assistance to six country offices and accompanied by a Digital Learning Community of Practice to share best practices across the region. ECARO also developed school guidance on data protection and privacy, aligned with General Data Protection Regulation standards, addressing critical concerns about student data security in digital learning environments.
ECARO's analysis of PISA 2022 data significantly enhanced the evidence base for education policy and programming, with comprehensive reports and digital storyboards available for nine countries. Technical support to Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan strengthened learning assessment systems and education management information systems (EMIS), while a major EMIS restructuring was supported in Moldova, improving data management and monitoring of educational outcomes.
Climate change education gained momentum with ECARO's technical support to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, North Macedonia, Kosovo, and Croatia, with technical guidance developed with Country Offices. The Comprehensive Safe School Framework Ministerial Meeting in Central Asia resulted in commitments from Ministries of Education to integrate climate change adaptation and disaster risk reduction into education planning.
Significant outcomes in education were achieved through collaborations with the EU, FCDO, World Bank, and OECD, including securing $1.2 million from FCDO for learning assessments in Central Asia, and expanding digital education initiatives with the World Bank.
Protecting
In 2024, ECARO made significant strides in promoting family environments for children. More governments committed to accelerating deinstitutionalization, recognizing UNICEF as a regional leader in this area. Two high-level Child Care Conferences were organized, advancing reforms and responding to growing government demands. UNICEF continued advocating investments in family support, foster care, and social service workforce strengthening, developing tools to accelerate reforms. ECARO worked on two new papers on statutory family support and mental health of children in care, set for launch in early 2025. 
At the Bogotá Violence Against Children Global Conference, ECARO ensured participation from 11 governments, resulting in 15 pledges for child protection system strengthening. Successful projects through the European Commission Technical Support Instrument, for example in Slovakia in assessing the inclusion of children with disabilities in the context of de-institutionalization, led to new initiatives in Spain/Andalusia, Portugal, and Ireland. UNICEF secured EUR 9 million from Sweden for care reforms in Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova, and deepened collaboration with the World Bank to improve child and family services in Uzbekistan and North Macedonia.
ECARO also worked to advance child-friendly justice across the region. By providing technical assistance and expertise, ECARO helped shape national justice reforms, positioning child-friendly justice as a key policy priority. In Poland, Bulgaria, and Ukraine, ECARO's support led to the implementation of child-friendly legal aid training, ensuring better legal support for children. In Czechia and Kazakhstan, ECARO assisted in designing responses for children at risk of offending and those with complex behavioural needs. Additionally, ECARO's advocacy efforts resulted in the development of integrated services for child victims and witnesses of crime in Montenegro, and the creation of a national plan to prevent sexual violence in Kazakhstan.

Including
In 2024, ECARO significantly enhanced country office capacity to address child poverty and deprivation through technical assistance, capacity development, and partnerships. As a result, seven countries improved their Humanitarian Cash Transfer responses, distributing USD 66 million to over 170,000 households. 14 countries enhanced their preparedness for shock-responsive social protection. In Kyrgyzstan, regulations and standard operating procedures for using cash in emergencies were approved, while Uzbekistan piloted an emergency management information system for cash transfers, reaching 1.2 million households. Kazakhstan extended national cash transfers to 3,600 families affected by severe flooding, and Bosnia and Herzegovina established a contingency fund for scaling up cash transfers. These efforts integrated social protection into climate strategies, ensuring a child-focused lens in addressing climate change challenges. Disability-inclusive social protection work also expanded across the region, through collaboration between UNICEF and the World Bank.
Additionally, ECARO focused on public finance for children (PF4C). In Azerbaijan, UNICEF support led to an additional USD 70 million allocation to the multi-year Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) budget. Family-friendly policies gained prominence, with a joint publication with UNFPA highlighting the economic and developmental benefits of such policies.
ECARO’s advocacy has significantly advanced data and statistics on children in the region. Through the European Commission TSI, UNICEF supported Luxembourg’s Department of Children’s Rights to enhance data-driven policy planning, monitoring and evaluation to strengthen child rights, with a focus on child poverty and social exclusion. Key milestones include advocacy and convening role of UNICEF at country, regional and inter-governmental levels leading to the establishment of the Steering Group on Statistics on Children under the Conference of European Statisticians, focusing on children with disabilities, violence against children, and children in alternative care.
Connecting and participating
In 2024, ECARO widened its youth programming to address ongoing crises, socio-economic instability, and climate-related disasters affecting adolescents and youth in the region. Collaborating with COs and Refugee Response Offices (RROs), ECARO focused on supporting successful transitions to adulthood by ensuring youth participation in policy design, skilling, mental health, and green and digital transitions. ECARO strengthened the capacity of COs and RROs in four priority areas: learning-to-earning transitions, adolescent mental health, youth engagement through wraparound services, and youth-led climate action.
As a result, 965,304 young people participated in or led civic engagement initiatives supported by UNICEF COs in ECA. Additionally, 8,336 Ukrainian children and young people were supported through youth engagement mechanisms in the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Slovakia, and Romania in partnerships with Junior Achievement Europe and the Duke of Edinburgh’s International Award Foundation. Communication actions reached an estimated 237,897 individuals across various partner platforms. UNICEF's role in the learning-to-earning initiative aimed to make learning more career-relevant and aligned with the world of work. Partnering with the European Training Foundation (ETF) for the fourth consecutive year, UNICEF launched a joint career guidance study, contributing to system reforms in 11 countries and supporting the Ukraine Recovery Conference and Youth Guarantee.
ECARO also strengthened efforts to integrate young people's participation in sector policy design and implementation. Significant progress was achieved within the TSI framework with DG/SG REFORM in Cyprus, resulting in the National Mental Health Strategy and the Cyprus National Youth Strategy being informed by youth voices.  Over 50,000 new users joined U-Report, a digital platform for youth engagement, with significant contributions from Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Serbia, and Uzbekistan. These efforts highlight ECARO's commitment to bridging the gap between youth and policymakers, ensuring that young people's voices are heard and acted upon.
Gender
UNICEF conducted Gender Programmatic Reviews in 12 countries and supported all 22 Country Offices in developing Gender Profiles and technical guidance to enhance gender equality, gender analysis, and adherence to GAP Standards. Over 65 gender focal points in the ECAR region received support in developing gender action plans at the Country Office level. Gender-focused spending increased from 5% in 2023 to 42% in 2024 in the region.
The region led the development of gender-responsive strategies, including integration in humanitarian efforts and family-friendly policies, in collaboration Social Policy and ECD. Over 15 countries focused on strengthening girls' STEM and digital skills, partnering with UNDP on STEM4ALL and organizing a cross-regional Green Skills Girls Summit. A regional flagship report, In Focus: Striving for Gender Equality, was also published in collaboration with Communication and Advocacy.

Climate Action
In 2024, efforts to influence national climate frameworks, particularly Nationally Determined Contributions 3.0, have progressed through UNICEF's involvement in national and UN-led initiatives, with key commitments on child-sensitive NDC made by Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Türkiye, and Moldova at COP29 held in Baku, Azerbaijan. 14 countries in ECAR are now implementing child-sensitive, multi-sectoral programmes to enhance children's resilience to climate and disasters, reduce environmental degradation, and promote sustainability. Climate change education is becoming increasingly central to country programming alongside environmental health and climate change adaptation as well as shock-responsive social protection.
Humanitarian Response
UNICEF provided emergency preparedness and response support for crises in Ukraine, Türkiye, and Armenia, enhancing resource mobilization and country preparedness across 17 countries. Preparedness and response focused on scaled up support for sudden and slow-onset emergencies, including migration, natural and climate-induced hazards, conflicts, displacements, and disease outbreaks. Training and simulations for emergency preparedness and response took place in Croatia, Romania and Montenegro, and at the regional level, with Belarus, Bulgaria, Georgia, Greece, Moldova and Türkiye. UNICEF partnered with the Red Cross movement to strengthen emergency preparedness, disaster and climate resilience capacities and national DRR efforts in all five Central Asian countries.
In Italy, UNICEF's adolescent development and participation programme combined humanitarian response with systems strengthening to support unaccompanied minors and disadvantaged youth. 4,000 unaccompanied minors and 500 educators were reached in 2024. UReport on the Move registered 5,000 new U-Reporters, reaching 400,514 young refugees, migrants, and caregivers with vital information. 
In Poland, UNICEF prioritized inclusive education, integrating 150,000 refugee children into schools, expanding early childhood education, and enhancing skills building, career guidance, and psychosocial support. Collaborating with partners, UNICEF supported over 700 evacuated Ukrainian children in care facilities. The Akelius app helped 22,304 Ukrainian students learn Polish, while the Learning Passport trained 4,626 teachers to provide mental health support, cross-cultural education, and inclusive pedagogy to 101,772 children.
In in the Czech Republic,  177,000 refugee children, youth, and caregivers were reached with vital social services. UNICEF strengthened healthcare access for refugees, ensuring over 7,100 children and women received primary care and vaccinations. In collaboration with a network of outpatient centres, accreditation were provided to 800 Ukrainian health professionals, while community-based health interventions reached over 1,800 refugees and Roma community members. Additionally, UNICEF supported 198,000 people with safe spaces, protection services, and mental health support, while enhancing the Czech education system to support over 68,000 Ukrainian refugee children.
In Slovakia, UNICEF provided cash assistance to 1,353 vulnerable refugee households, reaching 3,822 people, including 1900 of them children.  6,753 households continued to receive support through the national social protection system. UNICEF supported integration of Ukrainian paediatricians into Slovakia’s healthcare system, enhancing primary healthcare for refugee and host communities. Over 28,000 medical services were provided to Ukrainian children, complemented by the support provided through Bebbo parenting app and developmental monitoring initiatives. UNICEF's campaigns on mental health, social cohesion, GBV, immunization, and parenting reached over 1.2 million people.
In Hungary, UNICEF concluded its operations in 2024, successfully transitioning key services to local authorities. Over 12,000 refugees, including children and caregivers, received multi-sectoral support. Additionally, nearly 22,000 MHPSS consultations were provided, with individualized case management for 3,600 children. More than 5,400 children benefited from formal and non-formal education programs, language support, and psychosocial learning environments that fostered inclusion and resilience; while 3,000 health consultations reached 1,400 women and children. Additionally, the Humanitarian Cash Transfer programme supported 1,823 households, including 3,283 children and 48 pregnant women.
Communication and Advocacy
In 2024, ECARO focused on high-quality content and targeted growth, enhancing advocacy and engagement. Social media engagements surged by 445 per cent to 45.8 million, driven by Meta campaigns on child protection and rights. Organic engagement grew by 17 per cent, despite a 12 per cent decline in total reach. The ECARO website saw a 29 per cent user increase, with content in Russian for parents performing best. Google Ads amplified key messages with 96,000 impressions. Ten high-impact multimedia pieces and 16 communication packages were produced. UNICEF ECARO also launched its first AI-driven campaign for World Children’s Day, setting the stage for future innovations in advocacy.
People and Culture
In 2024, ECARO's People and Culture completed 417 recruitments with an average time-to-recruit of 40 days and issuing 166 consultancy contracts. A revised ECAR learning strategy was launched, while a career transition initiative was introduced for 78 staff members affected by rightsizing, and a Buddy system was established for new Representatives and Deputy Representatives. Additionally, a revised Regional Response Mechanism was launched, and lessons learned from Ukraine were shared to enhance preparedness. The P&C team engaged in a wide consultative process to review and repurpose a new business model and accountability framework, ensuring greater realignment in client services to the evolving context of the RO and Region.
Operational Efficiency
In 2024, ECARO provided oversight, technical guidance, and quality assurance across  audit, administration, finance, emergency preparedness, ICT, security, and supply, ensuring cost-effectiveness and optimized work processes in 22 countries across the region.  Systems and processes were continually adapted to ensure efficient management of the five Regional Office locations as well as four outposts (Italy, Slovakia, Czech Republic, and Hungary).
Governance mechanisms and internal controls were maintained, adapting to the evolving context and scale of budget throughput, with fraud risk assessment, enhanced PSEA capacity and peer reviews, ensuring all country offices met key performance indicators on partnership risk management. Efficient resource management led to consistent performance in budget and finance indicators, with a 2024 throughput of $711 million. Regional ICT strengthened improved cybersecurity resilience, and supported emergency responses, while Regional Security provided operational support across multiple countries, achieving high compliance rates and enhancing security systems.

Partnership Highlights in 2024: ECARO’s Strategic Collaborations
In 2024, UNICEF’s Europe and Central Asia Regional Office (ECARO) forged impactful partnerships with key stakeholders, including United Nations and other international organizations, governments, donors, academia, media, and civil society organizations, to address critical issues in the region. These collective efforts underscore ECARO’s commitment to improving outcomes for children across the region.
Strengthening Donor and Multilateral Engagement
ECARO deepened its partnerships with donors and multilateral organizations in 2024. Despite shrinking fiscal space, ECARO's targeted engagement and innovative strategies continued to drive progress and leverage partnerships and resources.
In 2024, ECAR continued to significantly invest in strengthening its partnership with the EU at the policy, technical, advocacy, and resource mobilization levels. UNICEF strategically utilized the EU accession process to spearhead child-focused policy development, aligning strategies with EU standards, particularly the European Child Guarantee, which offers opportunities to prioritize children politically and financially.
In collaboration with the Directorate-General for Employment, Social Affairs, and Inclusion, ECARO pioneered the implementation of the European Child Guarantee in both programme and non-programme EU countries. Member States and candidate countries can now access EU funding streams, particularly the European Social Fund (ESF), to finance Child Guarantee initiatives. ECARO signed 14 agreements with the EU totaling EUR 69 million, a 23.8% increase from 2023.
UNICEF and the Council of Europe renewed their partnership, reaffirming their shared commitment to protecting and promoting children's rights. This collaboration focuses on preventing all forms of violence against children, including online, and supporting child-friendly justice systems and safe use of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence.

Leveraging the Private Sector
ECARO is deepening its partnerships with the private sector. The Bebbo parenting programme expanded within and outside ECA through strategic partnerships with telecom operators, tech companies, and national television stations in Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and other countries.
A value proposition and blueprint for engaging the private sector in early years programs was developed and tested. ECARO has also explored partnerships and funding opportunities for e-Mental Health with private sector partners, ensuring the sustainability of uSupport and broader system reform for adolescent and youth mental health services.
ECAR continued expanding its strategic dialogue with International Financial Institutions (IFIs), including the Council of Europe Development Bank, World Bank, and Asian Development Bank. UNICEF has been recognized by the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB) as a preferred partner for education in Central Asia.
In 2024, ECARO’s funding pipeline with IFIs grew by 21.5%, reaching USD 55.4 million. A USD 35.7 million pipeline was secured with the IsDB for 2024–2025 across Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. ECARO and the IsDB Regional Hub for Central Asia initiated discussions on integrating climate change education and green skills into programs. ECARO also engaged the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development, unlocking significant opportunities for UNICEF Country Offices in areas including data, immunization, and health system strengthening.
ECARO received its first voluntary annual contribution of USD 3 million from the Russian Federation, through close collaboration with PPD and the legal team. This regular contribution supports projects focused on humanitarian assistance in Africa, and knowledge and technical collaboration across Africa, Asia, and the ECA region.
Advancing Joint Action with UN Agencies
ECARO strengthened collaboration with UN agencies in 2024 to advance regional health, education, and social protection agendas. UNICEF launched a joint regional child and adolescent health strategy with WHO, set for endorsement by member states. ECARO and WHO RO produced 11 fact sheets on key topics, including mortality, ECD, nutrition, adolescents, refugees, immunization, and mental health, providing evidence-based tools for regional strategies.
ECARO and WHO EURO also strengthened their partnership on HIV, immunizations, and ECD, leading to joint advocacy, fundraising, and planning. Engagement with UNESCO included participation in the Asia-Pacific Meeting on Education and collaboration on the Comprehensive Safe Schools Framework Ministerial events.
Meanwhile, ECARO worked with UNDP on a regional initiative to improve social protection systems in Central Asia and with UNFPA to enhance maternal and newborn health services in Eastern Europe, co-authoring a report on the cost of not having family-friendly policies. UNICEF engaged in the ECA Regional Issue-based Coalition on Gender, producing joint knowledge products with UNFPA and UN Women, including studies on gender-responsive family-friendly policies and gender equality backlash.
Strengthening National Government Collaboration
UNICEF continued fostering strong partnerships with national governments. At COP29, UNICEF and the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of Azerbaijan co-organized the “Safeguarding Human Development: Mobilizing Climate Finance for Social Protection” event, which brought together over 145 climate finance and social protection experts to discuss Adaptive Social Protection.
In Slovakia, partnerships with the Ministry of Education, Research, Development, and Youth and the National Institute for Education and Youth were crucial for integrating Ukrainian refugee children into schools and advocating compulsory education. In Italy, collaborations with the Ministry of Labour and Social Policies, the Ministry of Education, and the Asylum and Reception System were pivotal in building school and reception center capacities and ensuring sustainable educational models.
Supporting Evidence and Knowledge Generation
ECARO actively collaborated with research and academic institutions. A capstone project at the London School of Economics (LSE) analyzed the inclusion of social protection within climate policies across ECAR, producing guidance for improved integration. Another LSE project examined demographic decline in the Western Balkans.
A technical note on engaging hard-to-reach populations in evaluations will be published in 2025. Work on mental health and big data/AI was finalized with the University of Edinburgh in October 2024. In Czechia, PAQ Research worked with UNICEF to produce the “Voice of Ukrainians” surveys, providing insights into refugee children’s school participation, language proficiency, and integration challenges.
Civil Society and Community Partnerships
ECARO expanded its partnerships with civil society. Collaborative efforts with the International Step by Step Association included developing a home visiting training package and hosting an Early Childhood Development Conference in Bulgaria, showcasing best practices and political engagement.
Through the Centre for Research on Ethnicity and Culture, municipalities in Slovakia developed local integration strategies for refugee and migrant children. Additionally, ECARO partnered with the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies to deploy a Cashcap interagency partner in Central Asia, producing a scoping study and mainstreaming shock-responsive social protection coordination in interagency plans.
Leveraging the Private Sector
ECARO is deepening its partnerships with the private sector. The Bebbo parenting programme expanded within and outside ECA through strategic partnerships with telecom operators, tech companies, and national television stations in Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and other countries.
A value proposition and blueprint for engaging the private sector in early years programs was developed and tested. ECARO has also explored partnerships and funding opportunities for e-Mental Health with private sector partners, ensuring the sustainability of uSupport and broader system reform for adolescent and youth mental health services.

Cross-sectoral collaboration
The year 2024 has reinforced the importance of cross-sectoral collaboration for ECARO. For example, effective HIV services require collaboration with other sectors to ensure high standards of health for children and adolescents, including prevention and treatment of comorbidities and coinfections. People living with and at risk of HIV need accessible, equitable, affordable, and quality health care throughout their lives. Similarly, to ensure that ECD priorities are addressed requires health, education, social policy and child protection teams regionally and in countries working together to define accelerate results. The development of a regional Early Years Vision and Strategy marks a major milestone in this respect—establishing a coherent way of working across health, education, and social welfare sectors, and setting forth a roadmap for the region with clear programmatic priorities, strategic actions, and measurable targets to guide regional and country-level efforts. To improve immunization outcomes for children, multisectoral strategies must be enhanced, leveraging knowledge and resources to reach zero-dose and under-vaccinated children. This requires strong commitment from partners and governments, built through continuous engagement and joint planning. Additionally, the emergence of mental health and violence prevention concerns in education settings underscores the need for integrated, cross-sectoral approaches that address both immediate needs and systemic factors, especially in post-COVID and crisis-affected contexts. These issues require holistic strategies that bridge education with health and protection priorities.
The importance of youth programming
The recent and ongoing crises in the region have disproportionately impacted youth, highlighting the importance of systematically engaging them in issues affecting their lives, building their skills, and strengthening their mental health and wellbeing to prepare them for a smooth transition to productive adulthood. Recognising youth as leaders, influencers, motivators, peer educators, and young experts is crucial. Sustainable mechanisms for youth engagement and consultations remain essential. Both government and multilateral partners of UNICEF have acknowledged the power of engaging with youth as partners. This unique position allows youth to foster cross-country connections and inter-generational relationships, contributing to more cohesive communities, countries, and the region. This context, combined with the political and socio-economic challenges faced by the region and the world, provides UNICEF with critical opportunities to strengthen its focus on youth programming. Aligning the commitment to engage, connect, and empower young people with the European Union’s agendas (EU Youth Strategy 2019-2027, European Youth Goals, Growth Plans, Union of Skills, Youth Guarantee) is essential. Strong continued partnership with ETF and DG/SG REFORM strengthens UNICEF’s position as the partner of choice for the EU in preparing youth for the Youth Guarantee and integrating youth participation in national sector policies. Revamped partnership with GenU to unlock regional and sub-regional opportunities for L2E transitions will support alignment with the new Strategic Plan. UNICEF should leverage these opportunities to boost investments in youth policies and programming, strengthen partnerships, and enhance visibility around youth advocacy and practical approaches for co-creating with youth.
Digital innovations
UNICEF in ECAR, with RO support, has been leveraging technology to improve learning outcomes and strengthen digital education systems across several countries. In Uzbekistan, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Preschool and School Education in piloting Eduten, an AI-based digital math platform integrated into the national curriculum. The pilot demonstrated a 16.9 percent average improvement in math skills, with better outcomes for users. In Ukraine, 88 digital learning centers in frontline regions facilitated continued and catch-up learning for children unable to access in-person education. Bebbo, a free app developed by UNICEF and partners to support parenting, has been scaled to 15 countries in the region and is ready for global scale up as a global digital public good. Experience with digital innovations like Bebbo, has highlighted important lessons for other initiatives, including business model strengthening, programme integration, and global uptake of regional innovations. Ongoing discussions on digital products and shared lessons are critical to ensure these tools remain aligned with evolving policies and effectively complement on-ground interventions. ECARO is recognized as a leading region for expertise in digital mental health, including approach, safeguarding, and network development. Documenting the implementation outcomes of uSupport and scaling it up, along with establishing new partnerships with public and private stakeholders, the Mental Health Learning Lab, and third-party vendors, is crucial. This approach will ensure a stronger sustainability model, unlocking funding opportunities to support the regional roll-out and scale-up of the initiative.
Machine learning and AI methodologies tailored for UMICs and HICs have been introduced for evaluations, including for country programme evaluations for extracting data from UNICEF databases, including vision, HR database, and e-tools to gain efficiency, while AI for impact evaluation has been explored through causal machine learning, with a significant milestone achieved with the Ministry of Digitalization and Innovation in Kazakhstan, paving a way for innovative methodologies to be further scaled up.
Strategic engagement
In addition to supporting country offices directly, ECARO continued to deliver techncial support directly in high income countries without a country office. Technical support projects (resourced through DG REFORM) were completed in Slovakia and Luxembourg, with positive feedback from EC for high quality results. In 2024, new projects have been initiated in Andalusia, Portugal, and Ireland on childcare reforms. In partnership with DG EMPL and DG ENEST, the implementation of the European Child Guarantee (ECG) in EU countries were accelerated, and promoted ECG adoption as part of EU accession.
In 2024, through the Skills Alliance for Ukraine—an initiative focused on empowering young people to tackle the human capital challenges in Ukraine—ECARO supported the development of the national Youth Policy Concept for 2025-2030. This concept is pivotal in shaping state-funded skills programs for youth. Additionally, a collaborative Youth Investment Case, conducted by UNICEF in partnership with the Ukrainian government, provided valuable insights that informed the national Working Group tasked with developing a EU Youth Guarantee policy for Ukraine.

With the flexible funds provided by GRP-RR, ECARO was able to support to legal reform, policy advice, strengthening evidence generation across programme areas. The utilization of the GRP funds has predominantly supported securing technical expertise and support, as well as in-country support aimed at fostering capacity-building and knowledge-sharing, building global technical partnerships and promoting policy dialogue.
Priority in 2024 encompassed RO support for the development of 12 new country programmes as well as programme reviews, for which GRP was crucial for enabling regional advisers’ travel to country offices to provide tailored and focused support. SBC operational model was developed to support strategic integration of SBC into country programmes, including identification of social and behavioural bottlenecks into analyses. GRP also enabled ECARO to effectively provide strategic advocacy support throughout 2024 through advocacy capacity building and by initiating discussions with Country Offices on strategic integration of advocacy into Country Programmes as part of CPD development process.
GRP enabled the development of the regional DIPAS action plan, supporting its region-wide implementation. GRP was also used to develop four country case studies documenting successful practices in inclusive education systemic reforms, complementing the regional Inclusive Education Policy and Programme Guidance.
Crucial funding gaps were filled, such as for the development of school guidance on data protection and privacy, aligned with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) standards, addressing critical concerns about student data security in digital learning environments.
GRP enabled ECARO to invest in preparedness and resilience support to country offices, which proved to be critical for children in the region.

Contextual Update
 
Georgia is undergoing significant political changes. Earlier constitutional amendments shifted the country to a fully proportional electoral system and appointment of a President by an electoral college, effective as of the elections held in October 2024. Since then, there have been accusations of electoral fraud, widespread protests, and concerns raised about the unnecessary and disproportionate use of force against demonstrators. The European Parliament condemned the political developments in Georgia and called for the European Union (EU) to limit formal EU-level contacts with the Georgian Government. Thereafter, the Prime Minister of Georgia announced that the Government would not pursue negotiations with the EU on candidacy and budgetary grants until the end of 2028, a significant change since the granting of candidacy status in December 2023.
 
Situation of children in Georgia 
 
The share of the population living under the absolute poverty line decreased from 17.5% (2021) to 11.8% (2023), with the share of children decreasing from 22.7% (2021) to 16.0% (2023).[1] Although absolute poverty declined, 43.0% children face either absolute poverty and/or material deprivation.[2] Social protection measures have expanded but remain insufficient to cover all children facing poverty and/or material deprivation, with the child benefit covering 230,995 children (28%) under the age of 16.[3]
 
Women spend 17.8% of their time on unpaid domestic and caregiving work, as compared to 3.7% spent by men, affecting women’s labour market participation rates (64% men; 43% females). Options for childcare are limited, with almost no early child education and care services for children under two years of age and limited preschool access, especially for children living in rural areas. Barriers to preschool affect 12.4% of rural children compared to 1.5% of urban children; and 8.5% of girls compared to 4.3% of boys.[4]
 
While access to primary education is nearly universal, disparities in attendance widen by gender and ethnicity at the secondary education level. The net attendance rate (NAR) at the secondary level was 15 percentage points lower for Azeri children than that of Georgian or Armenian children, and a significant gender gap is evident in the NAR of Azeri girls (68.2%) than Azeri boys (77.7%). Delayed transition to secondary education is also evident with 16.7% of secondary-school aged Azeri girls still attending primary school.[5] 
 
During the academic year of 2024-2025, the recorded enrolment of children with special education needs and disabilities (SEND) reached 14,080, a significant increase from the 160 children with SEND enrolled in 2009. 
 
Many students drop out of school after ninth grade, the end of compulsory education. The number of students abandoning studies increased from the 2019-2020 school year (8,247 students; 41% girls and 59% boys) to the 20223-2024 school year (11,264 students; 42% girls and 58% boys).[6] The highest rate of drop out was in Grade 10, with 22% boys and 11% girls abandoning studies. 
 
A study to map the skills and assess the competencies essential for transitions in education and society of university students between 18-20 years of age showed:

· one-quarter of respondents struggled to articulate their ideas or express their thoughts fully; 
· a third had difficulty providing reasoned arguments showing a lack of experience in critical thinking; 
· writing skills were poor, especially among ethnic minorities, who struggled with Georgian language proficiency;
· understanding of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) remains limited, and application of STEM skills weak; 
· financial literacy was seen as irrelevant and there were gaps in entrepreneurial skills; and
· although there were good digital and technological skills, there are challenges with cybersecurity, social media literacy, and understanding digital threats.
 
Almost a quarter of youth (26.9% of 15–29-year-olds) are not in education, employment, or training (NEET), with large disparities by gender (30.9% female; 23.2% male). Most NEET females fall into the category of inactive (i.e. not in the labour market), while most NEET men fall into the category of unemployed.[7] 
 
The number of births among young women (15-19 years) has declined rapidly since 1995, with the age-specific fertility rate for girls aged 15-19 falling from 65.7 births per 1,000 girls in 1995 to 20.2 in 2023, indicating a shift towards childbearing at later ages.[8]
 
COVID-19 impacted maternal mortality, with a spike in the maternal mortality rate to 71.8 per 100,000 live births in 2021 which has since decreased to 22.4 in 2023. However, the maternal mortality rate is double that of European rates. The use of Caesarean sections has increased dramatically over the past 20 years, increasing almost five times from 9.0% in 2000 to 42.8% in 2021.[9]
 
According to 2023 WHO data, 40% of 15 years old girls received the recommended doses of the HPV vaccine.[10]
 
A study by UN Women and GeoStat (2023) indicates that every second woman (50.1 per cent) aged 15–69 has experienced at least one form of violence in her lifetime, with 19.7% reporting physical and/or emotional abuse before the age of 18 and 8.5% reporting sexual abuse as a child.[11] 
 
According to the 2023 administrative data from the State Care Agency, there were a total of 1,564 cases of child abuse reported (979 girls; 585 boys). The child hotline (111) responded to 2,316 calls.
 
Georgia submitted the combined fifth and sixth periodic reports on the Implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocols to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in June 2023. Concluding observations on Georgia’s combined fifth and sixth periodic reports were issued in June 2024.[12]
