2.1 Cross-sectoral results
 
Initiation of Child Rights Impact Assessments 
UNICEF is leveraging various international experiences and standards to support the pioneering of the Child Rights Impact Assessments (CRIA) in Georgia, in line with the concluding observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. CRIA aims to prioritize children’s best interests and improve the realization of children’s right in Georgia. This initiative seeks to engage various stakeholders including legislative and executive branches of Government, local government, independent monitoring institutions and academia. 

First Child Wellbeing Scorecard published
UNICEF supported GeoStat in publishing Georgia’s first Child Wellbeing Scorecard. The Scorecard consolidates key data on children, with a total of 65 indicators including those from the SDGs and Child Rights Monitoring Framework (CRMF). Additionally, UNICEF facilitated the enhancement of GeoStat’s web-portal for child and youth statistics, including integration of SDG, CRMF, and other relevant indicators into the portal, along with the provision of methodological guidance. The web-portal serves as a centralized resource for disaggregated statistical data on children and youth. It categorizes data into three age groups: children (0–17), youth (15–24, per UN definition), and youth (15–29, per Georgia’s definition). The portal supports policy makers, academia and professionals by facilitating comprehensive data access and evidence-based decision-making. 
 
One million people reached monthly with key messages 
UNICEF’s communication and advocacy efforts reached around one million people with evidence-based messages through media, digital channels, and campaigns. Multimedia stories, comprising compelling photo, text, and video content, were centred on the transformative journeys of children, young people, educators, parents, individuals with disabilities, and professionals dedicated to child wellbeing. In addition, UNICEF continued acting as a key player in promoting media literacy with up to 700 schools teaching media literacy. On World Children’s Day, UNICEF engaged National Ambassadors, children and young people through #KidsTakeOver campaign and discussions on Skills for Future, reaching 20,000 people.
 
Private sector partnership empowered 60 vulnerable children 
UNICEF, in partnership with the Business and Technology University (BTU), empowered 60 vulnerable youth (35 boys and 25 girls) in Tbilisi and Batumi with digital and entrepreneurship skills through an eight-month training programme, including trainings and career bootcamps. Most of the young people were from socially vulnerable families; under state care and were selected by the State Care Agency; or selected by the Probation Department of the Ministry of Justice. 
 
 
2.2 Every child survives and thrives 
 
50 primary healthcare clinics piloting telemedicine services
UNICEF collaborated with 63 doctors in 50 rural PHC clinics across the country to provide perinatal and primary health care services in remote and hard-to-reach areas. Doctors were trained in the provision of remote health services (telemedicine), provided with supportive supervision, and an electronic system for monitoring was installed in all clinics. With telemedicine, parents can consult with a family doctor remotely; to connect at the PHC with early child development specialists based in urban centres; and/or to participate in interactive online health promotion activities. In 2024, over 800 visits were recorded, reaching 380 girls and 420 boys with health services. In addition, 63 remote educational sessions for parents of children were held, reaching over 2,000 beneficiaries.
 
Recommendations for triple EMTCT of HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis B agreed
UNICEF is supporting the Government in the process to validate the triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B. Advocacy contributed to an agreement to strengthen the surveillance system for syphilis and congenital syphilis; update the national surveillance guidelines; revise case reporting forms in the Electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance System; and build the capacity of relevant health professionals. These interventions aim to help the country progress toward validation of EMTCT.
 
Interpersonal communication course on immunization integrated into continuous medical education
UNICEF supported academia to strengthen the skills of medical personnel when interacting with children, adolescents, parents and communities. With the aim to improve immunization rates, including HPV, a continuous medical education training programme was developed and accredited with UNICEF support. In 2024, 84 training sessions were held throughout the country, in which 2,080 medical personnel, including 1,440 PHC doctors (100% of rural PHC doctors; 46% of general practitioners in Georgia), participated. Building capacities of health personnel on communication between doctor and patient/caregiver contributes to better quality of health care, which improves health outcomes, especially for vulnerable populations including adolescent girls. 
 
Mental health for children, adolescents and youth elevated
With mental health, including depression and behavioural problems, estimated to be increasing among adolescents, UNICEF supported the mapping of child, adolescent, and youth mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS) in Georgia. UNICEF also initiated the development of a model for MHPSS and a strategy for strengthening Georgia’s child, adolescent, and youth MHPSS system.
 
 
2.3 Every child learns
 
Strengthening inclusive, bilingual early education and care (ECEC)
UNICEF Georgia supported the Government in strengthening pre-service training for educators, including training of 30 ECEC Bachelor of Arts (BA) students on inclusive early education. In partnership with the Estonian Center for International Development (ESTDEV), UNICEF supported the Government to develop recommendations and an action plan to improve bilingual early education for ethnic minority children, and built the capacity of around 200 specialists, including teachers and representatives from kindergarten agencies of municipalities on early bilingual education. In addition, UNICEF continues to raise awareness on diversified ECEC models.
 
Support for implementing the new inclusive education support system
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education, Science and Youth (MoESY) to initiate implementation of the inclusive education support system, which was approved by Parliament in 2023. This year, UNICEF supported MoESY to: (1) capacitate 70 inclusive education specialists and (2) develop (and revise) different normative documents, tools and protocols to be applied in the system to provide quality and customized services for each child, and for communication and cooperation between different actors (special teacher, parents and etc).
 
Partnerships with academia are expanding pre-service training of professionals
UNICEF, in collaboration with the Government of France, is supporting a consortium of three state universities in the development of Georgia’s first Master of Arts Programme in Child Rights. UNICEF participated in the development of the university-level Subject Benchmark document on early and preschool education for higher education institutions to support quality assurance of Bachelor of Arts programmes in early childhood education and care. In addition, a new Child Rights Center was opened at the Ivane Javakhishvili Tbilisi State University which will serve as a hub for education, research, and public awareness on child rights. The Child Rights Academic Network of Georgia (CRANG) has been established to strengthen cooperation, knowledge creation and research around topics of child rights.
 
Mapping of skills of young people
UNICEF, with the support of the Embassy of France and in partnership with Child Rights Centers of nine universities, conducted a skills mapping of youth to analyse life-long learning competencies and skills needed to thrive in a complex, interconnected, and technology-driven environment. The mapping exercise covered ten competencies including literacy; multilingualism; science, technology, engineering and math (STEM); interpersonal skills, entrepreneurship, citizenship, digital skills, cultural awareness, green skills and mental health. The report outlines the main findings on areas where further interventions are needed to support adolescents to develop skills for learning, employment, personal and social development and active participation in the society.
 
 
2.4 Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
 
Integrated service for child victims of sexual violence strengthened 
The Center for Psychological and Social Services for Child Victims of Sexual Violence (Barnahus), a one stop shop for services developed in collaboration with multi-sectoral stakeholders (State Care Agency (SCA), Ministry of Internal Affairs, Prosecution Service, Legal Aid, and Forensic Bureau), was strengthened, with the support of ESTDEV, through the capacity building of 6 psychologists in evidence-based rehabilitation; improved sound-proofing of interview/examination rooms; development of child-friendly informational materials in Georgian, Armenian, and Azerbaijani languages to raise awareness of the service; and involved agencies were supported to identify indicators for quality assurance mechanism. The Barnahus center became a member of the PROMISE Barnahus Network, which expands opportunities to further enhance operationalization of the service. 
 
Municipal social work conceptualized and strengthened 
UNICEF conducted an analysis of municipal social work and provided an overview of the social service workforce in 10 targeted municipalities. The key findings of the analysis were used to support the development of a shared policy vision. In addition, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of the municipal social service workforce in supporting various groups of parents and enhancing their parenting skills. A comprehensive programme manual was developed and the capacity of 37 professionals was strengthened to apply approaches offered by the programme. 
 
Reinforcement of the best interests of the child in cases of child separation
UNICEF supported the capacity-building of 60 justice and child welfare professionals in improving child-sensitive approaches and strengthening knowledge and skills for handling separation cases. In addition, the initiative resulted in a comprehensive analysis of the legal framework; development of a handbook for professionals; and a policy document with specific recommendations for policy, legal and practice-related reforms. 
 
Supporting children and youth to access justice and child protection mechanisms 
UNICEF, in cooperation with the Public Defender of Georgia (PDO), developed child-friendly materials in Georgian, Armenian and Azerbaijani languages to support children and youth to exercise their rights and access child protection and justice mechanisms. The materials include a set of brochures, infographics, video animation and posters for children above 12 years of age on topics such as children’s rights, the right to appeal to Court, child-friendly justice, the right to education, and child labour rights. These materials were distributed via social media and through face-to-face meetings reaching around 33,00 children and youth including children in state care.
 
 
2.5 Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
 
Lead levels in pregnant women in Adjara fell by 59%
A study reveals that between 2020 and 2023, average blood lead levels in over 9,000 pregnant women across Georgia’s Adjara region fell by 59%, with rates =5 µg/dL dropping from 73.5% in 2020 to 20.4% in 2023. UNICEF contributed to this success by supporting the Government to upgrade its institutional capabilities, laboratory and surveillance capacity, frontline services, regulatory action, enforcement and accountability mechanisms, as well as work to identify the sources of lead exposure. 
 
Access to water, sanitation and hygiene improved for over 1,474 children in 2024
With support from the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, UNICEF improved water, sanitation and hygiene facilities in 17 schools (15 rural, 2 urban) in the Abkhazia region, benefiting 1,474 children (745 girls and 729 boys). In addition, 460 adolescent girls were sensitized on menstrual hygiene management. Since 2022, UNICEF has improved water, sanitation and hygiene facilities in 65 out of 152 (43%) schools in the region, benefiting 10,495 children (5,221 girls, 5,274 boys), and 5,155 adolescent girls were sensitized on menstrual hygiene management.
 
Initiated development of an electronic WASH monitoring system in health facilities and schools
UNICEF, in collaboration with Government, developed and piloted a WASH e-monitoring system for real-time data collection in rural PHC clinics, which will contribute to improving infection prevention and control (IPC) measures. UNICEF adapted the WASH FIT/IPC training package and trained 10 master trainers, who then trained 2,617 rural health care personnel. The WASH FIT/IPC curriculum was integrated into the continuing medical education (CME) courses. Additionally, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education, Science and Youth in developing an electronic system to monitor real-time WASH conditions. The system was piloted in 10 schools, and relevant staff were trained.
 
2.6 Every child has an equitable chance in life
 
Evidence generation informs social programming
UNICEF completed three studies to inform social protection programming:


Social Protection of Children in Georgia: Proposed actionable recommendations to enhance the system’s ability to respond to shocks and address children’s needs effectively. 
Defining the Spending of Child Grants within Targeted Social Assistance: Explored household spending patterns of child benefits, providing evidence on their impact on child welfare and development, and informed discussions on optimizing resource allocation. 
Assessment of Potential Impact of Social Protection Measures on Child Poverty and Deprivation: Evaluated different cash transfer scenarios on their effectiveness in alleviating child poverty and multidimensional deprivation. 

Fourteen municipalities engaged in needs-based social programming
UNICEF initiated comprehensive needs assessments across 4 municipalities (in addition to 10 in 2023) to identify gaps in social services. Over 500 municipal workers in the targeted 14 municipalities received training on needs-based programming, budgeting, and data-driven decision-making. Coaching sessions supported municipalities in translating assessments into actionable programmes. As a result, new programmes like Zugdidi’s cochlear implant maintenance initiative and Dusheti’s transportation service for people with disabilities were developed, reflecting a shift toward data-informed, responsive governance.

Accelerating SDG localization through child-friendly budgeting
UNICEF initiated a new programme with municipalities which aims at accelerating SDG localization to enhance support systems for children and families, ensuring local social service provision is child-centered, needs based, and adequately financed. UNICEF is developing a methodology and piloting a child-friendly budget analysis in two municipalities. This initiative aims to assess spending on children and identify areas for resource allocation to social programmes benefiting children and families, with plans for scaling up to all municipalities and central budget analysis.

Linking biopsychosocial assessment of children with disabilities to targeted support packages
UNICEF continues to support the implementation of a three-year Transformation Action Plan aimed at establishing a biopsychosocial (BPS) framework for assessing and supporting the inclusion of persons with disabilities. The ongoing state reform seeks to diversify support measures for children with disabilities. With the support of UNICEF and its partner MAC Georgia, the results of BPS assessments have been linked to tailored support services, and concept and models of targeted assistance packages have been developed for needs-based assistance for every child. Support packages were comprehensively revised to address diverse disability needs, and multidisciplinary teams received training to translate BPS assessment findings into actionable, child-centered support.

UNICEF continues to engage different actors including Government, civil society organizations, academia, religious leaders, business, community groups, media, schools, professionals, parents and children, on protecting and promoting child rights. UNICEF aims to unite all actors around one core vision with children at its centre to deliver holistic and sustainable impacts for children. 
 
UNICEF collaborated with various Parliamentary Committees including the Health and Social Issues Committee, Education and Youth Committee and Agrarian Issues Committee, as well the Inter-Agency Commission on the Implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. 
 
UNICEF strengthened and expanded partnerships with municipalities to develop social programmes tailored to the needs of the children and families, in collaboration with the Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure and the Ministry of Internally Displaced Persons from the Occupied Territories, Labour, Health and Social Affairs. Mayors, deputy mayors, and respective staff of municipalities have been actively involved. 
 
Partnerships continued with universities (eight state and one private) to strengthen their Child Rights Centres which are moving the child rights agenda forward in academia and professional groups, and empowering communities and children. In addition, UNICEF is supporting academia to develop the first Master of Arts programme in child rights in Georgia. UNICEF also partnered with Batumi State University to host the Third International Conference on Early Childhood Education.
 
UNICEF engaged with independent state agencies, such as GeoStat and the Public Defender’s Office to support data collection and analysis on children and the system of independent monitoring of child rights. In addition, UNICEF closely cooperates with the Public Defender’s Office to improve children’s access to justice.
 
Partnerships with business sector has been strengthened through the Business Advisory Council for Children. Key partnerships were forged with Business and Technology University (BTU) and other companies mobilized by Business and Technology University (BTU) around Junior Tech Initiative, which engaged 60 vulnerable youth in academic programming. An initiative to integrate Child Rights and Business Principles into business practice and regulation to prevent and mitigate adverse business impact was launched by UNICEF, in partnership with the UN Global Compact Network Georgia.

UNICEF began the process for introducing Child Rights Impact Assessments (CRIA) in Georgia, building on various international experiences and standards, and in line with the concluding observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. This initiative seeks to engage various stakeholders including legislative and executive branches of Government, local government, independent monitoring institutions and academia. 

UNICEF expanded its partnerships with the European Union to strengthen child protection, social programming and health services; and with the Government of Sweden to strengthen and expand social services for vulnerable children in Abkhazia, Georgia. Moreover, partnerships were continued with the Governments of Bulgaria, Estonia, France, Switzerland, and United States, as well as with Clarios Foundation. 
 
Coordination amongst UN agencies is conducted through the UN Country Team and its various working groups. UNICEF works with other UN agencies through the development of joint programmes and monitoring, including UN Women to develop a new partnership to address VAW/G and expand access to early childhood education to facilitate economic empowerment of women. Moreover, UNICEF participates in several national coordination groups, led by various Government ministries, departments and agencies.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges:

Political instability affected programming, with delayed decision-making during the pre-election period, uncertainty around the operations of civil society organizations, retracted donor financing, and post-election turbulence which affected all aspects of     programming. 
Some donors added new restrictions on financing and/or withdrew financing completely. This  created several challenges and shifts in programming.  
Inefficient coordination between the central and local government, and among government and civil society actors hindered progress.
 
Lessons learned:    

In a highly polarized political environment, heightened by the Parliamentary elections, political sensitivity is especially important. UNICEF continues to work with all stakeholders, regardless of political or religious affiliation as a trusted and impartial partner, enabling UNICEF to convene and facilitate constructive dialogue between parties. 
Political sensitivity is important in the design, implementation and monitoring of     projects.  
The best interests of the child need to be aligned with the intentions of the Convention on the Rights of the Child.  
Enhanced accountability framework provides clarity on roles and responsibilities to be able to better deliver for children across Georgia.  
Advocacy and dialogue with diverse partners enable buy-in for transformative reforms. 
Generating robust data provides essential evidence for advocacy and programme design. 
Municipal needs assessments and local partnerships fostered scalable and impactful     solutions.
Raising awareness of children on their rights is needed to empower them to exercise their rights effectively.
Child-friendly materials focused on rights and protection mechanisms need to be based on     international and national standards and adapted to local context with the active participation of children from diverse age groups, backgrounds, and regions across Georgia.  
Ethnic minority children and children with special needs and disabilities need specific interventions to address the barriers they face in accessing services and education.   
Pilot programming continues to allow for review of initial models to enable gaps and challenges to be addressed that would hinder quality implementation. 
While significant progress has been made in deinstitutionalization, a comprehensive vision for safeguarding a child's right to a family has been lacking as efforts have primarily focused on closing large-scale institutions. There needs to be a corresponding focus on preventing family separation and supporting quality reintegration of children into family environments.
Long-term financing is critical for supporting the Government to implement complex initiatives from beginning to end without interruption, otherwise it may threaten the     ability to achieve results for children.    
The comprehensive approach to municipal budget analysis through the lens of child rights requires additional refinement, including thorough conceptualization, extensive consultations with municipalities and various stakeholders, and subsequent adaptation for broader application in the analysis of sectoral and/or central budgets.
Empowering municipal authorities through decentralized processes is vital for fostering their active participation in social protection initiatives, promoting autonomy, and enhancing effectiveness.
Mainstreaming training courses into the undergraduate curriculum of medical schools and/or integrating the course into the continuous medical education programme presents sustainable opportunities for ongoing support for medical professionals. 
Connecting with international networks such as PROMISE, Child Rights European Academic Network (CREAN) and various networks on CRIA provide opportunities for learning and collaboration. 
Partnerships with international universities have enabled the analysis of scores of data generated in the Birth Registry and provided critical evidence on levels of lead in the blood of pregnant women. 

Future Outlook:

Scale up CRIA adoption to institutionalize child rights accountability.
Expand the municipal needs assessment methodology to all regions and municipalities, expanding inclusive service delivery.
Advocate for systemic reforms in social protection, including gradual movement towards universal child cash benefits and shock-responsive mechanisms.
Strengthen partnerships with academia and private sectors to institutionalize child rights education and foster sustainable progress.
Support adolescents to acquire competencies and skills.
Capacitate professionals to deliver quality services for children, especially for most vulnerable.
Advocate for primary health care reforms, including information management systems to support decision-making.
Support efforts to strengthen the surveillance system for syphilis and congenital syphilis; and revise case reporting forms in the Electronic Integrated Disease Surveillance System to help the country progress toward validation of EMTCT.
Support the finalization of a model for MHPSS and a strategy for strengthening Georgia’s child, adolescent, and youth MHPSS system.

There are 1,735,061 children in  Greece  (51.5% boys and 48.5% girls), accounting for 16.6 per cent of the total  population, according to the Hellenic Statistical Agency (ELSTAT) report  produced with the support of UNICEF. This indicates a decrease  of 5.3  per cent in the child population in the country compared to the previous  census. Among  the total number of households with children, 517,111 are  with one child, 424,259 with two , 82,415 with three  and 23,097  households with four or more. The majority live with both their parents under  the same roof (83.9%),  13 per cent live with one of their parents,  while 3,1 per cent do not live with their parents. 
  
  
  
Although a high-income country  and  Member State of the European Union (EU), Greece falls short in  realizing  several aspects of children’s rights. Similarly to 2022, the share of  children at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2023 stood at 28.1%  (29.1% male, 27% female)[1]. While the Government  has recognized  deinstitutionalization as a priority, achieving the ambitious  goal of  zero children in institutions by 2030 necessitates the comprehensive   reform of the child protection system. This particularly relates to the  2,582  children in residential care, including 1,206 children in  institutions under  the supervision of the Ministry of Social Cohesion  and Family (MoSCFA)[2] and 1,376 unaccompanied  children in shelters  under the Ministry of Migration and Asylum (MoMA) [3]. The percentage of  young  people (15-29) neither in Employment, nor in Education and  Training (NEET)  remains concerning with a rate of 15.9 per cent (14.6%  male, 17.2% female)  compared to the 11.2% EU average[4]. 
  
  
  
The prevalence of overweight and   obesity among children is also a concerning trend. The recently released  data  from the World Health Organization (WHO) highlights the highest  prevalence of  overweight and obesity in young boys and girls in  southern European  countries, such as Greece[5]. Greece ranks third  with  the highest overweight prevalence rate (37%) and second  with the  highest obesity prevalence rate (18%) among boys and  girls aged 7-9  years old. Results by sex showed a higher prevalence of  overweight (including  obesity) among boys (41%) compared to girls  (33%). Compared with the previous  round of data collection in 2019, a  decline was observed, with  girls noting a difference of six points and  boys 2.9 points.
  
  
  
The national report of the Health Behaviour  in School-age Children  survey released in 2024 provides some evidence  regarding peer violence among adolescents  of 11, 13 and 15 years  old[6]. The  report finds that one third (30,7%) of adolescents in  Greece report having  been involved in a physical fight, while 12,1 per  cent of adolescents report  having participated in a bullying incident  of a peer/schoolmate. In addition,  22.1 per cent of adolescents have  been bullied at school, while 9.5% have  experienced cyberbullying.  Spreading rumors and lies, social exclusion, and  offensive or degrading  jokes, comments, or gestures of a sexual nature are  among the most  frequently reported types of bullying. Less frequently  reported is  victimization through physical violence or through the use of   derogatory terms based on nationality or religion. Boys and girls seem to  be  equally likely to experience bullying, but more boys than girls seem  to engage  in physical fights and cyberbullying. The issue of bullying  was brought also  at the epicentre of public and political debate with  the Prime Minister  establishing a Scientific Committee to develop a  National Strategy to Prevent  and Address School Violence, while in  December 2024 a National Strategy for  the Protection of Minors from  Internet Addiction was presented.
  
  
  
Another type of violence, namely gender-based  violence (GBV) against women and girls, has also been at the forefront of  public attention with extended  media reporting. The Committee on the  Elimination of Discrimination against  Women (CEDAW) highlights the  prevalence of gender-based violence against women and girls, including sexual  and intimate partner violence and insufficient support services,  trafficking  and exploitation of prostitution of women and girls,  especially among vulnerable groups, while also recognizing the progress and  measures taken by Greece in the last decade [7]. The Committee expresses  concerns on the lack of disaggregated data on GBV, trafficking, access to  education and socioeconomic status of women and recommends the promotion and  strengthening of statistical data collection to inform tailored and  gender-responsive legislation, policies, programmes and budgets. Greece   scored 59.3 out of 100 in the Gender Equality Index, ranking 25th in the EU  for  2024 [8]. 
  
  
  
Refugee and migrant issues remained high in  the political agenda. Since  January, 51,620 refugees and migrants had  reached Greece, most by sea (44,498)[9]. Children account for 30.4 per   cent of the total sea arrivals in 2024 – an increase compared to 2022 (22%)  [10]. Shipwrecks in the Aegean Sea continued to claim the lives of children  (1, 2, 3).As of June 2024, 27,500 refugee and migrant children (41% girls,  59% boys) lived in Greece, including 7,444 from Ukraine; of those, 21,790  estimated to be of school age [11]. Some 16,200 (56%  boys, 44% girls)  refugee and migrant children were enrolled in schools [12]. After years of  standstill, the guardianship scheme for unaccompanied children started,  marking a positive development in  the protection of the 2,414   unaccompanied and separated children (89% boys, 11% girls). However, those  arriving have few options but to stay for lengthy periods in inadequate  conditions in reception centres waiting for their placement in a   shelter. In addition, the lack of specialized child protection services  for  all children hinders appropriate safeguarding of their needs  despite progress made in recent years.
  
  
  
Finally, 2024  marked the warmest year  on record since 1890 according to the National Observatory of Athens. Several  incidents  were reported related to water shortages across the Greek  islands, with 25 Municipalities  declaring a state of emergency due to  high water stress, imposing  transitional measures for water use  reduction.

[4] ELSTAT, 2023.

By galvanizing the allocation of domestic  resources based on evidence-based planning and policies, UNICEF focused on  system strengthening and the sustainability of services for children.  Moreover, UNICEF aimed to address specific structural deficiencies in the  country’s governance and public administration system, including coordination  issues at various governance levels, with the aim to drive the child rights  agenda and deliver results at scale for children.
  
 
  
The first ever mapping of child-focused data  and coordination processes among entities at local and central level was  concluded during the year with UNICEF’s technical expertise to the Ministry  of Social Cohesion and Family Affairs (MoSCFA) for the operationalization   of a comprehensive monitoring and governance framework for the Child  Guarantee National Action Plan in a more efficient, data-driven way. This was  made possible through the Technical Support Instrument of the European  Commission’s Directorate General REFORM. Part of the programme also includes  an action plan to address obesity focusing on the most vulnerable children.  The project brought together EU member States to exchange good practices that  could be adopted in the Greek context, draft recommendations were provided  and will enable the Government to provide targeted support to children at  risk of poverty and exclusion and address their needs, including effective  access to services. These concerted efforts will indirectly contribute to the  efficient allocation of European funds, responding to the requirement to  mobilize at least 5 per cent of resources from the EU’s European Social Fund  Plus (ESF+) to tackle child poverty. In addition, producing valuable insights  and contributing towards closing another data gap, the Hellenic Statistical  Authority produced for the first time a joint publication with UNICEF on the  profile of children in Greece based on the 2022 national census.
  
 
  
UNICEF strived to strengthen the child  protection system, both top down and bottom up, focusing on Violence against  Children (VAC) – an issue of expressed concern for the Government and where  data gaps persist. At the central level, UNICEF advocated for policy change  to the authorities by completing research on VAC administrative data and  presenting it in a high-level cross-ministerial roundtable. The research –  which provided insights into data collection practices – will be used to  garner government support for evidence-based policy decisions and  recommendations for harmonizing data collection practices. At the local  level, UNICEF strategically partnered with the Municipality of Athens – the  largest in the country hosting 93,000 children – to develop a child  protection social service model focused on child-centered risk assessments,  case management, and data collection. The model has the potential to be  replicated in other municipalities of the country. 
  
Furthermore, UNICEF partnered with various  professional groups who are directly or indirectly involved in child  protection cases with potential for country-wide scale up: a) the judiciary  for the development of standardized tools that can help them in their daily  work, while also safeguarding children’s rights; b) social workers through a  partnership with the Hellenic Association of Social Workers to build the  capacity of its 9,600 members countrywide for the delivery of child-centered  services; c) journalists to promote ethical, informed media coverage that  supports child protection through a gender and child-sensitive lens.
  
 
  
To enhance child-friendliness in shelters for  GBV survivors, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Cohesion and Family  Affairs in the development of an action plan, which builds on UNICEF’s  previous assessment on the child friendliness of shelters for women  conducted. Resources for the activities included in the action plan have been  identified, yet remain to be mobilized, under ESF+ and UNICEF will sustain  advocacy to this end.
  
 
  
As part of the State’s effort to address  obesity in children, UNICEF and the Ministry of Health continued the  implementation of the National Action against Childhood Obesity, with a  strong focus on system strengthening. Key highlights in 2024 included: expert  support towards the improvement of the legal and institutional framework; the  establishment of the European Centre for Combating Obesity in the Harokopeio  University to promote evidence generation, knowledge exchange and digital  tools; the launch of activities and awareness campaigns countrywide to  promote healthy eating habits and physical activity, informed by young  people’s views through the U-report platform and focus group discussions. So  far, over 26,000 children have indirectly benefited from toolboxes platforms  consisting of educational, experiential, interactive and informative material  for educators aimed at encouraging students' healthy eating and physical  activity habits. In addition, more than 16,800 children have participated in  workshops aiming to sensitize them on optimal nutrition and food waste  management. Ultimately, this multi-sectoral national programme – being one of  the first globally of its kind – aims to make a positive impact on 800,000  children in the country.
  
 
  
By the end of 2024, seven Child Rights  Centres had been established in collaboration with academia with the vision  to establish Centres in all 23 public universities of the 13 regions of  Greece. The Child Rights Centres model builds upon the “whole-of-society’’  approach and has three key interlinked functions: a) promoting child rights  with a focus on schools, Municipalities and community leaders; b) generating  evidence-based knowledge on children; and c) incorporating child rights into  university curricula. Professors and scientific staff of three out of seven  universities had the opportunity to become acquainted with child rightsby  following a two-day seminar on the CRC. A professional development programme  for professors who wish to become specialists in child rights and, thus, to  teach child rights in their respective universities is planned. 
  
 
  
To enhance the child protection system for  refugee and migrant children, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of key  Ministries with responsibilities on refugee education and protection with a  focus on data collection, monitoring and evaluation. More specifically,  UNICEF seconded an expert to MoMA for the support and monitoring of the  implementation of the guardianship scheme for unaccompanied children. This  has been crucial in finding out what works well and what should be adjusted  to better cater the needs of the children, including through the organization  of focus group discussions with boys and girls enhancing child participation,  accountability, transparency and trust. In addition, through an expert  seconded to the Reception and Identification Service (RIS), UNICEF supported  the development of a training package for staff working in 32 refugee sites  to help them incorporate harmonized child protection standards in their  everyday work and to the benefit of over 7,300 children living across  reception and accommodation sites in the country. The training material will  be incorporated in the official training package of RIS for professionals  working with children as well as general staff. Finally, UNICEF’s seconded  expert to MoERAS facilitated evidence generation on the effectiveness and  staffing challenges of reception classes. The expert’s analysis identified  key operational gaps, producing actionable recommendations that resulted in  the timely placement of educators at the start of the 2024-2025 school year.
  
 
  
The All Children in Education (ACE) programme  concluded in June 2024, marking the end of the largest refugee education  initiative in Greece - an initiative of MoMA, co-funded by the European Union  and implemented by UNICEF in cooperation with a number of NGOs and academic  partners, as well as MoERAS. Over three years, the programme supported 26,164  refugee and migrant children (15,792 boys and 10,372 girls) by providing  access to non-formal education, preparation for formal school enrollment,  homework assistance, accelerated learning, and psychosocial support. Within  this framework, a harmonized and flexible approach to refugee education was  applied, establishing operational and quality standards for content,  methodologies, staff, and procedures. It contributed to the professional  development of approximately 5,000 teachers and school leaders through a 400h  professional training programme, coupled with an online platform for an  asynchronous training course tailored to meet the needs of newly recruited  teachers. Both tools strengthened the gender dimension through its horizontal  integration across all thematic areas, promoting gender equality and  inclusivity in education. A campaign on the right to education and the need  of refugee children aimed to sensitized the public attracting with a series  of three episodes (1, 2, 3), more than 1.3 M unique users (reach). A team of  independent experts carried out the evaluation of the programme (per the  costed evaluation plan) which demonstrated relevance and effectiveness in  producing tangible results for the access to education of refugee and migrant  children, including girls. The evaluation also highlighted lessons learned  with regards to achieving greater efficiency and highlighted the importance  of sustainability and complexity of transitioning the programme to the  authorities. To further advance the quality, inclusive education agenda,  UNICEF equipped in 2024 2,886 refugee and migrant children in
 both formal and  non-formal education with critical linguistic and digital skills through the  Akelius Digital Language Learning Course. 
  
 
  
To empower greater youth engagement, UNICEF  engaged with, prepared and aided adolescents and youth to participate  meaningfully in high-level international fora and raise issues of their  concern to policy-makers through various means, namely: a) at COP29 for the  first time two UNICEF-supported young people joined Greece’s national  delegation as contributors to the discussions; b) the first Child and Youth  Advisory Board was established, comprised of 28 representatives (11 boys and  17 girls) with the vision to ensure that UNICEF programmes and interventions  take into consideration and respond to the real needs and priorities of  children and youth in Greece; c) over 5,200 U-reporters participated in  various polls, including on AI, cybersecurity, and climate change; d) 1,196  adolescents and young people expanded their life and green skills through  workshops and trainings on FunDoo and GreenPal.  
  
 
  
UNICEF worked on two levels to promote  environmental justice. At the national level, by conducting the first Climate  Landscape Analysis for Children in Greece which includes a comprehensive  review of the legal framework and climate strategies, a child vulnerability  mapping, and recommendations to relevant Ministries and local authorities on  child-sensitive Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Risk Reduction in  order to adopt specific measures addressing the needs of children. At the  local level, UNICEF - in coordination with the Ministry of Social Cohesion  and Family Affairs – supported Roma communities in the regions of Thessaly  and Central Macedonia where a large number of vulnerable and risk-exposed  families living in deprived conditions (type I – shacks, type II - mixed). In  2024, 1,185 children and women in seven Roma settlements were reached with  trainings in schools on hygiene issues, public health and environmental  justice. Learnings from this programme will be used in recommendations for  the authorities to consider similar interventions for the estimated 20,000  Roma of the country that reside in type I and type II settlements facing  deprivations, including lack of safe access to water for some.

In 2024, the Greece Office secured through  public and private partnerships a total of 35,6 million USD (including  contributions carried forward from 2023), of which 97 per cent from the  public sector (97%).
  
 
  
Public sector funding derived mainly from  partnerships with the Greek State and the European Commission, in particular  DG HOME for the largest refugee education programme and DG REFORM on the  first Technical Support Instrument. In August 2024, the ongoing partnership  with the Ministry of Health was enlarged with a programme on Family and Child  Health Promotion (36 million USD) with implementation starting at the end of  2024 The programme includes three pillars: (1) identification of behavioural  disorders among caregivers and developmental disorders among children and  referral to mental health services through primary paediatric care (2)  destigmatization of menstruation (3) prevention and addressing youth  self-harm incl. through the establishment of a model centre. The conclusion  of this second programme with the Ministry of Health reinforces UNICEF as a  partner of choice for children’s well-being. While sizeable and predictable,  public sector funding is tightly earmarked leaving little flexibility in programme  implementation with efforts to diversify resources continued. 
  
 
  
Alongside public sector resource  mobilization, the gross revenue generated by the private sector stood at USD  641.772. UNICEF and Lidl Hellas renewed their commitment for another two  years to support the child protection system strengthening through enabling  an innovative model pilot with the Athens Municipality, while the partnership  with Piraeus Bank was solidified to advance work on violence against children  in Greece through the country’s Prosecutors. In addition, targeted  engagements with leading private sector organizations and business  associations were organized to leverage the potential of the private sector  in support of UNICEF’s mission in Greece. On the occasion of the Regional  Director’s visit to Greece in December 2024, UNICEF convened for the first  time leading businesses based in Greece in an event to discuss the critical  role of private sector investment in shaping a brighter future for children  in Greece and worldwide. Representatives of at least 20 leading corporates  and business associations attended, expressing their interest in  collaborating with UNICEF to advocate for the rights of children. In June  2024, the Representative addressed, with a video message, the 4th Athens  Environmental, Social and Governance Forum, the flagship event on  sustainability bringing together top Greek companies.
  
 
  
UNICEF also concentrated efforts on forging  stronger and more systematic partnerships with academia, the Hellenic  Parliament, and International Financial Institutions, taking a  whole-of-society approach and following the spirit of the SDGs. In June 2024,  UNICEF co-organized with the Ministry of Education, Religious Affairs and  Sports (MoERAS), the first International Conference on Inclusive Education  and Children’s Rights. The event brought together 98 speakers from 12  countries and over 200 in-person participants and covered a variety of  issues, including current policies and reforms on inclusive education, formal  and non-formal quality education, professional development for teachers, as  well as the role of schools and Child Rights Centres in partnership with  universities in promoting inclusive education. In April 2024, UNICEF  facilitated an international partnership between the University of Patras,  Greece and the Akaki Tsereteli State University of Georgia, for the promotion  and protection of children's rights, through the strengthening of their  respective Child Rights Centers  launching step for the ongoing  cooperation of the two entities in the creation and dissemination of  knowledge on children's rights and inclusive education. As a highlight of  UNICEF’s engagement with the Hellenic Parliament, the Regional Director for  Europe and Central Asia and the Representative in Greece addressed the  Committee on Equality, Youth, and Human Rights on Human Rights Day. The  engaging discussion with parliamentarians from different political parties  reaffirmed the critical role Parliaments play in realizing children’s rights.  To build engagement with International Financial Institutions, UNICEF  initiated a dialogue with the European Investment Bank and Council of Europe  Development Bank to identify opportunities to leverage resources for children  and discuss how to make resources considerate of children’s unique  needs. 
  
 
  
As there is no  United Nations Country  Team in Greece, coordination takes place through interagency national and  local working groups, including with Heads of Agencies. To foster coherence  in action among the largest UN agencies, regular Programme Management Team  meetings were held with the participation of UNHCR, IOM, and the ad hoc  inclusion of WHO, to facilitate  exchange of information, good practices  and advocacy amongst senior management. In parallel, within the framework of  the refugee and migrant response, UNICEF spearheaded the coordination of the  national Education Sector Working Group, co-chaired the PSEA working group  and participated in the Child Protection and GBV sub-working groups.
