Greece has the opportunity to capitalize on the achievements of the Child Guarantee and the availability of EU funds (under ESF+) to move forward with the scale up hand in hand with the – much necessary – reform of the child protection system. However, a year after the 2023 national elections which brought about the establishment of the Ministry of Social Cohesion and Family Affairs, tangible progress in moving forward critical issues of child protection and inclusion has been slow. Since then, the Ministry’s capacity has not been fully solidified, while delays in processes, operational challenges and limited human resources persist.
 
As such, achieving the ambitious goal of zero children in institutions by 2030 necessitates redoubled efforts at national and municipal level. To address this, UNICEF sustained its advocacy towards the Ministry, including for the mobilization of available resources through ESF+, while simultaneously working with Municipalities to build bottom-up a more resilient child protection system; in the future, redoubled efforts will be needed in order to bridge the fragmentation between central and local levels. One such initiative has been the successful partnership between UNICEF, the Municipality of Iraklion, the department of social work of the Hellenic Mediterranean University and the Hellenic Association of Social Workers which exemplified the need and positive impact that such synergies may have in strengthening the capacity of social work at local level. In 2025, UNICEF will aim to facilitate similar initiatives in other social work departments of municipalities as well, including Thrace and Athens who have already expressed interest. 
 
In line with its transition plan, the ACE programme was handed over to the Greek authorities in June 2024. However, this process is currently stalled, as the necessary steps to resume implementation have not been launched yet despite expressed political commitment. As a result, thousands of refugee children in reception centres, accommodation sites and shelters are left with limited language and homework support, which may impact school enrolment and attendance. UNICEF has and remains committed to sustaining a strategic collaboration with MoERAS and MoMA to assume an advisory role on inclusive education that can also help accelerate efforts on refugee education and has provided technical assistance to this end.
 
The above finds UNICEF at the mid-point of implementation of the country programme as agreed with the Greek Government. As such and to leverage domestic and international resources and achieve results at scale, UNICEF will focus on providing the highest-calibre technical assistance to accelerate the SDGs and address the recommendations of the CRC Concluding Observations for Greece. In the immediate future, UNICEF will scale up partnerships with the private sector and with line ministries in leveraging EU/structural funds for scaling up results for children. With the end of the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility eligibility period in December 2025, significant efforts by UNICEF will be required for the smooth implementation of the two large-scale programmes implemented jointly with the Ministry of Health. Emphasis will also be placed on driving progress on system strengthening in inclusive and quality education, including anti-bullying, childcare reform, mental health and child rights monitoring, coupled with initiatives that reinforce youth engagement and promote the climate change agenda. 
 
UNICEF currently delivers its work through 65 personnel (45 female, 20 male), including seconded experts to Ministries to strengthen their capacity. To carry forward its programmatic priorities, UNICEF will adopt a lean, agile business model that concentrates on the need to increase the capacity of the State to deliver results for children, reconnecting its resources to system over service delivery. With Greece having been elected as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for the 2025-2026 term and a candidate member of the UN Human Rights Council for the period 2028-2030, UNICEF will work with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to contribute to the child rights agenda a global level. Operational efficiency will be at the core of the endeavour, with financial sustainability prioritized in line with an enhanced focus on system strengthening. This will be realized through optimized resource allocation, flexible contract modalities, robust resource oversight and risk management, cost-efficiency, and strategic partnerships.

In 2024, Kazakhstan marked the 30th anniversary of ratifying the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

Kazakhstan has registered over the past decade a significant demographic shift. Children (aged 0-17) currently represent 33.4% of the population and youth (aged 14-35) 28.4%. This increase is particularly notable in the southern and western regions, as well as major cities like Astana, Almaty, and Shymkent, driven by high birth rates in rural areas and urbanization. In contrast, the northern and eastern regions registered a decline. 

The country is transitioning to high-income status with ongoing actions to diversify its economy beyond its traditional reliance on oil and extractive industries.

Despite a GDP growth of 4.4% in 2024, the real per capita incomes in October 2024 declined by 6% compared to October 2023, with significant disparities between regions. Regions with the lowest per capita income are also the ones with the most significant child rights deprivations.
Poverty slightly reduced in 2024 compared to 2023 but has not returned to 2022 levels: 5.4% of the population was living below the minimum subsistence level in late 2024, against 5.6% in 2023 and 5.3% in 2022. Though the situation improved, children continue to be more vulnerable to poverty, with 7.8% of them living below the poverty line in 2023 compared to 9.1% in 2022. Children living in rural areas are more affected by poverty (10%) than those living in urban areas (6.4%). Children represented 40% of the poor in 2023 against 47% in 2021. 

The government pursued the digital transformation of its social protection system to improve accessibility, transparency, and efficiency of social services for the population. Notably, the introduction of the Digital Family Card (DFC) in 2023 facilitated proactive public service delivery in 2024, with 263,000 people accessing benefits or payments without the need for formal applications. More needs to be done to ensure that every vulnerable child accesses the social protection needed. Around 525,000 children were living below the poverty line in 2023, only 52% accessed targeted social assistance in 2024. Acceleration in the use of the DFC to proactively reach out to vulnerable families, along with planned social welfare reform implementation should expand children’s access to social assistance.

In the spring of 2024, Kazakhstan faced unprecedented flooding across ten regions, marking the worst disaster in terms of scale and consequences over the past 80 years. A local state of emergency was declared in ten regions, and more than 119,000 people, including over 45,000 children were rescued and placed in temporary accommodation centers, including schools. The flooding disrupted education leading to a shift to online education in the affected areas. The Government led the flood response through civil protection services. In addition to rebuilding and repairing infrastructure and social facilities, it supported the affected population with one one-time cash benefits for 36,455 families, property damage compensation for 21,876 families, and waivers for unconditional TSA payments for the third quarter of the year, benefiting 3,600 families.

As part of the national commitments to achieve carbon neutrality, Kazakhstan made significant amendments to the Concept of Green Economy Transition. The "Taza Kazakhstan" campaign aimed at fostering a culture of nature conservation mobilized 6.2 million people who collected 1.1 million tons of waste and planted approximately 1.6 million trees. 

With five years remaining, the country is working to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals’ (SDGs) achievement by 2030. Out of the 45 child-related SDG indicators, 20% were achieved (9), 22% could be achieved with low or very low effort (10), 15% could be achieved with a high or very high degree of effort (7), 35% have no data (11) or no data trends (5). While 80% of the SDG indicators were integrated into national/strategic plans, less than 30% were integrated into regional development plans. 

In 2024, Kazakhstan endorsed the 2029 National Development Plan (NDP). The Plan aims to foster sustainable and inclusive growth, accelerate SDG achievement, and leave no one behind. It focuses on human capital development, economic diversification, productivity and innovation, and regional development.

Two million schoolchildren in primary and secondary education face learning challenges that require attention especially in rural areas. To strengthen the measures taken by the government earlier in addressing this gap, the complementary program to the State Program of Education Development until 2025 was initiated in 2024 called “Rural School – A Quality Platform,” which aims to equip rural multigrade schools with digital technologies and STEM education. The number of children in residential care facilities in the country reduced by 11%, from 12,651 in 2022 to 11,281 in 2023.

Kazakhstan adopted landmark laws introducing professional foster care and strengthening the custodian and guardianship authorities with UNICEF support. These measures create a more robust social infrastructure to protect children against violence and reduce placement in residential care. Vaccine hesitancy more than doubled since 2022, remains one of the key factors leading to outbreaks. Kazakhstan registered 15,111 measles cases in 2023. The Government introduced vaccination to children aged 6-10 months and is revaccinating children aged 2-4 years.

Kazakhstan made significant progress in tackling adolescent suicide. In 2024, the suicide rate among adolescents aged 15 to 19 was 2.9 per 100,000 against 11.3 in 2016. Nevertheless, self-harm remains the leading cause of death among adolescents, with higher rates in rural areas. The government rolled out Psychological Support Centres countrywide and launched a multisectoral programme on adolescent’s suicides prevention under the leadership of Vice-Prime Minister. The Ministry of Healthcare started developing a national Concept on Mental Health with UNICEF and WHO support.

In 2024, Kazakhstan adopted the 2030 Concept of Inclusive Policy, developed with UNICEF and other UN agencies’ support, building on the concluding observations of the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on the country’s implementation of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. 

In 2024, Kazakhstan adopted and launched a 2024-2029 AI development plan and started developing a Law on the Artificial Intelligence (AI), aiming at promoting local technology solutions, protecting personal data, and ensuring national independence.

Every child thrives 

Health
In 2024, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Healthcare (MOH) in improving children's health, development, and well-being at both national and regional levels. This was achieved by generating evidence, advocating for policy and legal framework adjustments, building service provider capacity, and fostering intersectoral collaboration.
Recognizing the importance of primary health care in ensuring universal access to health services, including detecting and mitigating risks, the MOH with UNICEF support, continued improving the universal progressive home visiting system for pregnant women and children under five. Building on the 2023 UNICEF-supported assessment, the patronage nurses’ training programme was entirely revised, optimized, and integrated with environmental health and zoonotic infections, and is now available in Kazak and Russian languages.
The MOH updated the pediatric standards based on recommendations developed with UNICEF support. The standards clearly define patronage nurses’ functional responsibilities and introduce new tools, such as a checklist for risk identification. The standards also strengthen the primary responsibilities in early interventions and organize data sharing on child health and development with other sectors. Once approved, they will improve multisectoral coordination for case management.

With UNICEF-supported social media campaigns “Vaccination Story” and “Parent Messengers,” overall, 4.6 million people, including 3.1million women and 1.5 million men, accessed fact-based scientific information on immunization in a clear and compelling way. Women were more active than men in watching the campaign and responding with their intention to vaccinate their children.

In support of strengthening global health security, UNICEF launched the first information and education campaign “Sau Bol” to raise public awareness of potential public health emergencies and future pandemics. 

Around two million parents/caregivers gained knowledge and skills to promote personal health responsibility and protective health behaviors within their communities through social media, media projects, and offline workshops in selected regions. Around 500,000 people accessed communication materials in medical facilities in six regions.
“Sau Bol” posters on global health security were also placed at 11 airports in Kazakhstan, with an annual traffic of fifteen million passengers.

Nutrition 
In 2024, UNICEF continued its support to the government    in addressing the triple issue of overweight, obesity and micronutrient deficiency among children, with a particular focus on improving the quality of school meals within the framework of the national free school meals programme benefiting 1.7 million children in primary schools. 
The Ministry of Healthcare and Ministry of Education officially adopted the national nutrition standard for educational organizations, both schools and kindergartens, developed jointly with the Kazakh Academy of Nutrition and UNICEF support. The standard sets precise criteria and rules for balanced and diverse nutrition in preschool and school menus, as well as restrictions on sugar, salt, and saturated fats to prevent childhood obesity. It also restricts the sale of unhealthy food and beverages in schools.

To ensure the continuity and sustainability of efforts to meet national nutrient intake requirements in school menus, the National Center for Public Health, with UNICEF support in 2024, trained 2,000 school health workers on the standard's basic principles. Additionally, they were trained on the use of a jointly developed online application for assessing the macro and micronutrient composition of school meals. The  application is free and open source for everyone to check and monitor the quality of the meals both at schools and at home.

Mental Health
Youth Health Centres (YHCs) now provide adolescents and young adults with mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services, which are supported by nearly 50% [1]of the budget allocated to the YHCs (around 2.2 million USD). With UNICEF support, the MoH developed national guidelines for mental health services provision by the YHCs. 

With the aim to further strengthen access and quality of MHPSS services, the Ministry initiated the development of a National Concept on Mental Health for 2025-2029 involving key stakeholders, with UNICEF and WHO technical support.

As part of the 2023-2025 Comprehensive Plan on Child Protection against Violence, Adolescents’ Suicide Prevention, Promotion of Children’s Rights and Well-Being, developed with UNICEF support, the Ministry of Education created the Psychological Support Centres, expected to support the national network of school psychologists and the multisectoral coordination for case management, connecting general practitioners, YHCs, and schools.

UNICEF co-hosted a Subregional Conference to improve access to mental health support by reducing stigma through language. Delegations from six countries discussed mental health stigma and adopted a statement committing to accessible, equitable, and timely support systems for children and adolescents.

Every child learns

In 2024, with UNICEF’s advocacy, the Ministry of Education (MoE) initiated law revisions on inclusive education to enhance access, equity, and quality to children with special education needs. According to the MoE, 90% of the country's schools have created conditions for inclusive education. The MoE reviewed the draft concept on inclusive education, based on international approaches and the 2024 UNCRPD concluding observations, identifying gaps in national laws. The government    integrated UNICEF’s recommended action package for children with autism into the new National Roadmap for 2025–2027.Following regional trends, the MoE improved financing and access to early childhood education and care (ECEC) services by introducing a voucher system, accrediting preschools, and improving local waiting lists. Out of 11,104 preschool organizations, 48% are private. UNICEF-supported knowledge exchange on ECEC services diversification and parenting led the MoE to seek more guidance and capacity development for ECEC diversification and equitable financing.

Building on evidence generated by UNICEF, the government    reiterated commitments for early childhood development (ECD) and ECE as part of the National Development Plan. In 2024, over 74,000 parents accessed information on developmental milestones and play activities through UNICEF’s social media channels. The Kazakh Government    joined the Belgrade Call to Action on ECD and committed to adopting guides for parents and training modules for health and preschool education frontline workers.

In 2024, Kazakhstan had 406,000 teachers, including 8,000 [2]new ones. UNICEF supported the national in-service teachers training institute in reviewing the curriculum on innovative blended teaching and online safety. New developments in education, such as edtech, online safety, AI, and climate education, highlight the need to strengthen education curricula and teachers’ training.

Preliminary results of the global ICILS 2023 for Kazakhstan identified persisting digital gaps, particularly affecting boys, rural schools, and households with lower socio-economic status. UNICEF continued to support the Government    by introducing new tools to enhance internet quality in schools and provided technical support to review legislation relevant to children’s rights and digital technologies. The Ministry of Digital Development (MDD) launched the Accessible Internet Programme, connecting 1,861 schools to satellite-based solutions and rolling out a new standard on school connectivity developed with UNICEF support.
The Internet Speed Monitoring Daily Check App, introduced by UNICEF, now covers 6,916 state schools, increasing the national average internet speed in schools from 13 to 17 Mbps for uploads. UNICEF also assessed the market for satellite-based solutions to connect remote rural schools to broadband internet. 

The MDD, with UNICEF support, developed a draft national Roadmap for promoting and supporting Digital Public Goods creation, to accelerate progress on child-related SDGs. Despite these advancements, there is currently no overarching vision or national policy for digital integration in the education sector. 

In 2025, UNICEF will continue supporting the Government    with policy advice and technical support to ensure a coordinated and systemic approach to digital education.

Skills
In 2024, with UNICEF support, nearly 23,000 youth (50.7% girls) enhanced Science, Technology, Engineering, Maths (STEM), civic engagement and/or employability skills. 
Following the integration by the Government    of the socioemotional learning Helping Adolescents Thrive package for schools aimed at promoting and protecting adolescent mental health into the 2023-2025 Comprehensive Plan on Protection of Children from Violence, Suicide Prevention and Ensuring Their Rights and Well-Being, UNICEF supported the adaptation of the new version of the package targeting 10-13 yo. adolescents for national roll out in 2025-2026 school year. 

In 2024, KCO integrated climate change, environment, energy, and disaster risk reduction topics into skills building online content. The number of users of supported by Learning Passport based Samgau Digital platform increased by 21.7% since 2023 with more than 10,000 participants. In partnership with the Aerospace Committee of the Ministry of Digital Development and Kazakh National University over 7,000 adolescent girls were empowered and mentored on career for ecology and space through series of on-line webinars. 

Over 1,600 adolescents from 167 educational organizations engaged in Samgau-CCA-DRR with support of trained school staff, adolescents identify problems and develop sustainable solutions for schools and communities.

Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
Important social welfare and child protection system reforms took place in Kazakhstan in 2024, with Commissioner for Child’s Rights and UNICEF’s joint advocacy and technical support. 
Legislation was revised to further strengthen the Guardianship and Custody Statutory Bodies with the establishment of minimum staffing ratio of one specialist per 5,000 children. This measure enhances oversight and ensures that vulnerable children receive appropriate support. The new amendment is expected to bring on board about 1,000 new child protection specialists at the local level.  

The new law on protecting women and children against violence, which criminalizes domestic violence and bullying (including online), and tightens penalties for sexual violence and child murder, reflecting long standing recommendations to address violence against children, was enacted in December 2024.

The government    rolled-out the newly established Family Support Centers in the regions, with UNICEF supporting the development of operational guidelines, protocols and tools for child and gender sensitive integrated service provision to families and individuals at risk. 
UNICEF contributed to the development of assistance programs for children affected by violence, ensuring integrated, gender-sensitive, child-sensitive services that address the specific needs of both victims and witnesses. 

To foster safer educational environments, the government   -initiated testing bullying prevention programs, such as KIVA, originating from Finland, and the locally developed awareness raising program “DOSBOLLike”, alongside safety lessons in schools. These initiatives build on UNICEF’s prior research and recommendations to prevent violence against and among children. Additionally, the government    has rolled out nationally the Program of Pedagogical Support to Parents as well as Centers of Psychological Support to Children.
Around 900,000 accessed information on Child online safety the ‘CyberTumar’ child online safety campaign supported the Ministry of Education, UNICEF and European delegation in Kazakhstan.
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
 
In 2024, thanks to UNICEF advocacy and support, the government    further engaged on children’s rights and climate change (CC) agenda. The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources contributed to the Expert Dialogue on the disproportionate impacts of Climate Change on children and policy solutions in Bonn, June 2024, and officially committed to integrate children and youth in the NDC 3.0, with UNICEF support.

The Ministry of Healthcare initiated the development of a road map to strengthen environmental monitoring in the sanitary and epidemiological monitoring system (SEM), aligning with international standards based on UNICEF supported assessment of the national SEM. The Ministry committed to enhance the hygienic standards for average annual concentrations of air pollutants critical for children’s health, reviewing the methodology for air quality data collection and dissemination, including with Kazhyrdomet and among population and healthcare system. UNICEF assisted in training of staff from all departments of the Committee of the Sanitary and Epidemiological Control in regions on air quality data collection and analysis in line with WHO air quality standards.

UNICEF supported youth voices and participation in the development of national, subregional and regional climate action plans and call for action on youth environment initiatives. Over 35,000 young people took part in opinion pool and focus group discussions to understand how green skills and green competencies are integrated in learning and education environments in Kazakhstan. 

With UNICEF support, more than 130 young climate activists strengthened their climate negotiation skills and engaged in key national, regional and international platforms and initiatives. This included co-facilitation of the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), the Regional Comprehensive School Safety Conference, Kazakhstan Youth Session at the COP-29, and mobilizing young people for various climate actions such as tree planting, air quality assessment in schools, and promoting eco-friendly culture development.

These efforts not only amplified youth voices in climate discussions, but also inspired future youth engagement in advocacy and leadership roles. 

The UNICEF supported Volunteers4Climate program strengthened the green skills of over six thousand school children. This will ensure that young people are integral to shaping a sustainable and equitable future for Kazakhstan.

Every child has an equitable chance in life
 
The newly adopted NDP introduces the multidimensional poverty index, reflecting UNICEF’s long-standing advocacy, thus expanding poverty measurement beyond income to include access to education, healthcare, and social protection.

To further advocate for other key priorities outlined in the NDP, UNICEF enhanced its collaboration with the Ministry of National Economy. This initiative aimed to enhance the expertise of national and subnational authorities in monitoring and assessing spending for child outcomes. More effective tracking of expenditures that directly and indirectly benefit children and youth at a more granular level (rayon) will inform budget planning and strategic resource allocation and help prioritize key investments for children in each region. 
 
Fiscal reforms, with the development of new Budget and Tax Codes, were accompanied by UNICEF’s promotion and use of the KAZAMOD tax-benefit model, which helped in adopting a progressive personal income tax. 

The government    adopted the median income to define, starting from 2025, the poverty line which determines eligibility criterion for Targeted Social Assistance (TSA). UNICEF provided technical support, leveraging methodologies from OECD and EU countries for calculating the median income criteria with the Bureau of National Statistics.
 
The government    adopted the Concept of Inclusive Policy for 2025–2030 developed with UNICEF support. This policy aims to promote equality, inclusion, resilience, and full societal participation of persons with disabilities. It ambitions to improve early diagnosis, prevention practices, and expanded medical services in rural areas and introduces a national model for continuous inclusive education and innovative teacher training. The policy addresses climate change risks, ensuring tailored safety measures for persons with disabilities during emergencies. 
 
Cross-cutting 
 
Evidence generation, knowledge management and evaluation
In 2024, the National Agency of Strategic Planning (ASPIR) and the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS), with joint support from UNICEF, UNFPA and ADB successfully designed and rolled out the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), covering 24,000 households for data analysis disaggregated for each of the 20 regions, with a 96.4% response rate. The MICS findings will allow assessing the country’s progress on 26 SDG indicators and overall situation of children, women, men since 2015 MICS, but also supporting child-related SDGs localization to accelerate progress towards achievement.
 
UNICEF, conducted jointly with ASPIR and BNS, conducted a Situation Analysis of children and adolescents in the country, in consultation with adolescents, line ministries, and NGOs, highlighting the most pressing issues facing children in Kazakhstan. This year, significant legislative changes and amendments were adopted to enhance data governance and quality. 
 
In 2024, the BNS received new authority to assess the quality of administrative data produced by national and subnational government   al bodies. It is a critical step toward ensuring data quality and improving its comparability and accessibility. The Bureau continued, with UNICEF support, to lead the national working group on child data, with priority focus on the development and testing of a minimum set of indicators on violence against children, alternative care, and children with disabilities, ii) the alignment between the Child Rights Monitoring framework and the national monitoring system; iii) the annual Statistic Yearbook on children and TransMonEE reporting.
 
It also joined the Steering Group on Statistics on Children led by UNICEF and UNECE with the commitment to strengthen the methodological work and contribute to exchange of experience among other countries.  
 
UNICEF played an active role in the development of 2026-2030 UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework with the Government, contributing to the Common Country Assessment (CCA), UNSDCF evaluation, multilateral consultations including with youth.
 
Communication and advocacy 
In 2024, UNICEF celebrated with the government    the 30th anniversary of Kazakhstan's ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

In raising awareness on child rights, UNICEF achieved a 22% share of voice in media, 926,000 people visited the UNICEF website, and 115,786 people followed UNICEF on social media, with an 8% increase in followers compared to 2023. 

The Government    jointly with UNICEF celebrated the 30th anniversary of Kazakhstan's ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child with series of high-level events highlighting progress achieved by the country and addressing critical challenges. The Senate organized with the Commissioner for Child’s Rights and UNICEF a national conference on child protection with emphasis on online safety and cyberbullying. The event, in presence of senior level government    officials, senators and experts served as a key dialogue platform for consensus-building on modernizing the child protection system. It underscored the importance of legislative advancements, multi-sectoral efforts to safeguard children, comprehensive approach to addressing mental health and preventing violence against children in the country. A commemorative stamp, issued with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and KazPost in the presence of the foreign diplomatic community, symbolized Kazakhstan’s enduring commitment to child rights. In partnership with the Ministry of Education and the Ombudsperson for Children's Rights, UNICEF engaged 50 child ombudspersons to discuss pressing issues such as cyberbullying and environmental challenges. Held on World Children’s Day, the event reinforced the importance of youth participation in shaping policies that impact their lives.

As the official non-profit partner of the 5th World Nomad Games, UNICEF leveraged this global platform to promote child rights and inclusivity. The UNICEF Yurt in the Ethno-village provided inclusive workshops, traditional games, and interactive activities for hundreds of children and families. Over 150 UNICEF volunteers supported the initiative which generated 333,000 social media impressions.

In 2024, UNICEF launched the U-Report Kazakhstan dual-language platform, empowering youth to voice their opinions and influence decision-making. Since its launch in August 2024, U-Report attracted over 6,000 U-Reporters through digital campaigns. The volunteers’ education campaign in December 2024 established a foundation for a U-Reporters community nationwide in 2025.

In 2024, UNICEF Kazakhstan made significant strides in advancing the rights and well-being of children in the country thanks to strong partnerships with the Ministries of Foreign Affairs; Healthcare; Education; Labor and Social Protection; Information and Culture; Digital Development, Innovations and Aerospace; Ecology; Emergency Situations; the Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms (ASPIR); the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS); the Child Rights Protection Committee (KOPD); and the National Commission on Women and Family Demographic Affairs. UNICEF effectively works across a large variety of stakeholders across sectors. 
The Child Rights Commissioner, the Constitutional Court, and the Senate played an important role in UNICEF’s advocacy for strengthening national commitments to children’s rights and accelerating child-specific reforms, including violence protection and prevention childcare reform.

UNICEF jointly with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs established a Joint Steering Committee for developing the next Country Programme of Cooperation 2026-2030. Co-chaired by the Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs and the UNICEF Representative, the Committee ensured the engagement of 14 ministries, Senate members, and strategic agencies to define the joint priorities and strengthen cross-sector collaboration.

In 2024, UNICEF engaged in United Nations collaborative mechanisms to operationalize the UNSDCF 2021–2025 through joint advocacy, technical coordination, and programming, and to formulate the new UNSDCF 2026-2030 in consultation with the government, civil society, and youth. UNICEF played a key role in setting up the UN Youth Advisory Board. 

UNICEF collaborated with UNFPA on MICS and parenting; WHO on children's health, especially immunization, early childhood development, early interventions, mental health, global health security, and nutrition; and with UN-Women on family support center reforms and gender-based violence prevention, and UNESCO on the comprehensive school safety framework. A Letter of Understanding was signed with UNHCR for strengthened cooperation on refugee and statelessness women and children. UNICEF co-organized events with UN agencies for the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence and World Food Day.

UNICEF strengthened its partnership with USAID to advance global health security in the country. The Asian Development Bank engaged with UNICEF to support the implementation of the MICS 2024 with the Bureau of National Statistics. The partnership with the EU was reinforced to further protect the rights of returnee children and children affected by migration through the child protection system strengthening, and to promote child online safety and digital skills with the 'CyberTumar' campaign run jointly with the government    and business.

UNICEF rallied diplomatic missions and international organizations for the 16 Days of Activism. Close cooperation with the French Embassy contributed to strengthening the capacities of frontline workers on child abuse prevention and response.

UNICEF continued leveraging its strong corporate partnerships in Kazakhstan to advance children’s rights in the country. The Business Advisory Council (BAC) provided a platform for BAC members to discuss the critical role of business in supporting early childhood development, positive parenting, and family well-being, and exchange on the various approaches, based on the findings of the 2023 Family Friendly Policies Assessment undertaken jointly with Atameken National Chamber of Commerce. 

UNICEF extended its partnership with businesses to promote child rights, inclusivity, and healthy nutrition and successfully mobilized business engagement and support for UNICEF’s first-ever fundraising Gala in Kazakhstan for children with special needs and digital education. UNICEF established cooperation with the YPO (Young Presidents’ Organization) Kazakhstan, a global leadership business community, for joint advocacy and programming for children, leveraging business’s assets, technologies, and resources. 

Civil society organizations and academia helped accelerate progress towards achieving results for children in the following areas: nutrition, immunization, schools’ connectivity, learning loss, girls in STEAM, early childhood development, early and inclusive education, parenting, child online safety, child protection, gender equality, youth skills, and volunteering. These partnerships underscore UNICEF's commitment to advancing the rights and well-being of children in Kazakhstan through collaborative efforts and innovative solutions.

UNICEF continued its partnership with the Ministry of Emergency Situations on Emergencies and Disaster Risk Reduction to enhance child-focused and gender-responsive national and local emergency preparedness systems. This collaboration supported the humanitarian response to the floods and initiated the rollout of the sub-national Children’s Climate Risks Index. The joint work with the Red Crescent Society was crucial during the flood response, providing timely family hygiene kits to affected families with children in the Aktobe region.

Strengthening emergency preparedness and response to climate change related risks

In response to the unprecedented floods in 2024, the Government, along with local authorities and civil protection services, demonstrated strong coordination and responsive support mechanisms for immediate assistance to the affected population and recovery. 

Although the government did not officially request assistance from the UN, UNICEF and the UN Country Team closely monitored the situation and maintained dialogue with authorities, ready to provide support as needed. The national emergency response could build on continued UNICEF-supported investments to strengthen, in partnership with the Center on Emergency Situations and Disaster Risk Reduction (CESDRR), Kazakhstan's child-focused emergency preparedness and response systems, with child and gender-sensitive national and local contingency plans and strengthened local authorities' and frontline workers’ capacities on the Core Commitments for Children in humanitarian action, gender in emergencies, multisectoral coordination, and accountability to affected populations. The Red Crescent Society undertook rapid needs assessments in all affected regions using UNICEF’s methodology. Psychologists in affected areas were provided with UNICEF-recommended guidance and tools for adapted psychosocial support to children in emergency shelters.

UNICEF directly complemented the national emergency response with the distribution of prepositioned family emergency kits by the Red Crescent and the CESDRR, benefiting 982 affected persons in the Aktobe region. Additionally, risk communication on child safety, well-being, and hygiene was disseminated through social media, mobilizing influencers, goodwill ambassadors, and volunteers.

The government provided a one-time cash benefit of 369,200 KZT (786 USD) to 36,455 affected families and based on UNICEF study recommendations, waived requirements for the Targeted Social Assistance (TSA) payments in the third quarter of 2024 for 3,600 affected families. While these measures provided vital assistance to affected populations, they did not allow more flexible access to social assistance for non-TSA beneficiary vulnerable families.

The 2024 floods and the national response demonstrated the tremendous added value of investing in national emergency preparedness systems with a child rights lens. However, it also highlighted areas for improvement related to a responsive social protection system based on UNICEF-supported assessments, family rescue operations, education continuity, and multisectoral government    coordination with the private sector and international partners. It also provided opportunities to further strengthen dialogue and cooperation with the government    on the growing and disproportionate impact of climate change on children and accelerated efforts for rolling out the sub-national Children’s Climate Risk Index for Kazakhstan, the comprehensive school safety framework, and climate education.

The first-ever fundraising Gala Dinner in Kazakhstan opens new private partnerships streams.
In 2024, UNICEF held its first-ever fundraising Gala Dinner in Kazakhstan, raising $184,000 through ticket sales and an auction for children with special educational needs. The Gala enhanced brand visibility and laid the foundation for future partnerships with businesses and philanthropists who attended the event.

Lessons learned from the event underscored the importance of implementing a comprehensive marketing strategy, with specialized expertise in organizing large-scale charitable events playing a significant role in the success of the Gala. Extended communication, including digital campaigns, high-visibility locations, influencer collaborations, and partnerships with businesses, significantly boosted awareness of the Gala as a major event, transitioning from a global tradition to a local one, and enhanced the UNICEF brand, reaching around 1.5 million social media users.

The involvement of high-profile celebrities, including those with strong regional recognition, proved particularly effective in drawing public interest and increasing engagement. Among the influencers involved, Dinara Satzhan, a renowned Kazakh TV presenter, journalist, and public figure, played an instrumental role in supporting and hosting the Gala and officially became the first member of the “Friends of UNICEF” community.

Aligning fundraising goals with UNICEF’s key programme goals, such as promoting digital inclusion for children with special education needs, also helped attract a wide range of supporters.

The success of the Gala sets a precedent for becoming a UNICEF tradition with the private sector, building on the country's strong culture of philanthropy.

In 2024, Kosovo[1] faced both progress and challenges impacting the lives of over 423,400 children. 

Politically, Kosovo, driven by its commitment to European Union (EU) accession, adopted a reform agenda on the rule of law, governance, public finance, green and digital transitions, human capital, and aligning with EU standards[2]. 2024 was also marked by ongoing EU-facilitated dialogue with Serbia and continued measures halting Kosovo’s cooperation with the EU.

Kosovo's economy demonstrated resilience and growth, with real GDP to expand by 3.8%, up from 3.3% in 2023. This growth was driven by increased private consumption, rising incomes, credit availability, and public infrastructure investments[3]. Inflation decelerated, averaging 2.1% between January and August. Minimum wages increased alongside the monthly child universal benefit for 407,000 children under 16, improving household stability. The poverty rate decreased slightly from 21.4% in 2023 to an estimated 19.2% in 2024.[4] 

The 2024 Population Census was completed. The total population is 1.6 million, showing an 8.8% decline, due to emigration among young people. One in five Kosovo citizens lives abroad.[5] The average age of the population increased by five years compared to 2011, reaching 35 years. However, Kosovo continues to have the youngest population in Europe. 

While Kosovo strengthened children’s rights this year, significant gaps remain. In health, the finalization of the Health Sector Strategy 2025–2030 prioritized maternal and child health, and public health investment increased by 15% compared to 2023. Kosovo also committed to a fivefold budget increase in immunization, allocated €1.5 million for Early Childhood Interventions, and continued funding for the Home Visiting programme, marking significant advancements in preventive healthcare toward SDG3. However, health expenditure remains very low for the region (3.8% of GDP), and public finance management lacks efficiency, resulting in high out-of-pocket payments (38% of healthcare costs). Social and gender norms and other barriers impact access to services for girls and women, rural, and minority communities.[6] Disparities persist in under-five mortality rates, antenatal care, and immunization coverage between the majority and Roma, Ashkali and Egyptian communities. Moreover, Kosovo’s air quality is among the worst in Europe, with daily PM2.5 levels reaching up to more than 25 times the WHO’s safe limit for children. Coupled with soil and water pollution risks, this impacts mortality risks for children[7], as evidenced by the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children launched jointly by UNICEF and the President of Kosovo in 2024. 

Kosovo consolidated its commitment to Early Childhood Education (ECE) by increasing funding (9.3% of education budget) and expanding preschool infrastructure. Pre-primary education for five-year-olds was made mandatory from the 2024/2025 school year, ensuring universal access to school readiness. However, ECE enrollment remains alarmingly low (36.8% of children), due to unequal geographical distribution of facilities, ineffective local budget planning, pending by-laws, and a fragmented quality development and assurance system.

Kosovo advanced on the right of children to inclusive education with budget allocations for teacher assistants, progress on the digitalization in education, and a better inspectorate. However, socio-economic inequities impact education access for children with disabilities, children from low-income households, from rural areas, and from non-majority or communities. Structural issues related to teacher management and system oversight affect quality and learning outcomes. Not only has student performance declined according to PISA 2022, but the vast majority of 15 years-old do not demonstrate basic proficiency in reading (85%), math (83%) and science (79%). Institutionalizing reforms require continued advocacy and capacity-building, while curbing inequalities necessitates targeted interventions and equity measures. 

2024 marked a conducive environment for youth empowerment. The Law on Youth was operationalized with by-laws to advance youth participation and improve life and socio-economic outcomes. However, the rate of young people not in employment, education, or training is on the rise reaching 33.4% in 2023. 

This year, the government showed commitment in enhancing the enabling environment for child protection with the approval of all 17 sub-legal acts for the Child Protection Law and strengthened sector capacity development. Kosovo also took steps towards cross-sector coordination for the prevention of child marriage and launched a National Action Plan for the Identification and Treatment of Children in Street Situations, informed by a UNICEF study. Ten municipal Child Rights Teams kept on strengthening local accountability for children’s rights and sectoral coordination.

The social protection budget is historically high (EUR 854.6 million, increasing by 3% from 2023), reaching records in terms of share of government spending (26%) and of GDP (8%), although this remains half of the average spending in Europe and Central Asia. Outdated data on poverty hampers financing gap estimates for universal coverage of vulnerable groups, particularly children and system bottlenecks persist, including limited multi-annual funding, limited municipal capacity for services planning, delivery and data monitoring, and low salaries for social workers.[8]  Despite a broad political consensus to amend the Constitution to include the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, an amendment failed to pass in Parliament for lack of quorum. UNICEF and sister agencies conducted a situation analysis of persons with disability to enhance advocacy efforts.

Lastly, limited availability and quality of monitoring data on children’s rights and SDG indicators overall hinders strategic policy planning. However, Kosovo published new census data in 2024, strengthened its child rights monitoring system, and prepared for the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey, laying the foundations for improved policy planning. 
Following a renewed commitment to the SDGs in 2023, Kosovo is however unlikely to fully achieve the 2030 targets as systemic challenges and political tensions threaten progress toward SDG1, SDG3, SDG4, SDG5, SDG8 and SDG10.[9]

In 2024, UNICEF Kosovo amplified its work in response to complex and overlapping social, economic, and environmental vulnerabilities, addressing critical systemic gaps regarding normative frameworks, supply and capacity development, demand, and the quality of services across health, education, child protection, and social protection. This contributed to Kosovo’s progress towards the SDGs in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), towards EU accession, and accelerated the realization of children’s rights in line with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan while consolidating national and local authorities’ accountability for achieving equitable outcomes for all children.

Additionally, UNICEF enhanced its gender-transformative programming to accelerate results through reaching girls with HPV vaccine, involving fathers in parenting, Kosovo’s first gender-responsive ECE curriculum, and adolescent girls’ empowerment and skills building.
 
Young children and their parents
In 2024, UNICEF’s strategic interventions in health and ECE delivered measurable progress, advancing Kosovo’s priorities while contributing to global development goals. Firmly aligned with Kosovo’s development strategies, UNICEF focused on improving access, quality, and equity, while strengthening gender responsive and transformative approaches across interventions—laying a solid foundation for sustainable change. UNICEF made meaningful contributions to SDG3, SDG4, SDG5 and SDG10.

In health, UNICEF supported significant progress toward establishing Kosovo’s first Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) system, a critical step toward addressing the needs of young children with disabilities. The Ministry of Health (MoH), with technical support from UNICEF, developed the first ECI Strategy and allocated €1.5 million to its implementation in 2025. A major achievement was also the introduction of developmental monitoring into the Home Visiting programme, with technical support from UNICEF, enabling early identification and referrals for children with developmental delays, while emphasizing the importance of father’s involvement in child development. During 2024, 16% of fathers actively participated in home visits and 18% of children benefited from early stimulation activities involving fathers, which also contributes to challenging gender norms around parental roles.

The Home Visiting programme reached 76% of newborns in 2024, providing essential services to over 19,200 families, including one in six from vulnerable and marginalized groups, through UNICEF’s technical support and advocacy. The programme addresses equity gaps and overlapping inequalities and barriers to access to health for women and children in Primary Health Care (PHC), leading to improved maternal and child health outcomes. Complementing these efforts, UNICEF supported the development of evidence-based Clinical Guidelines for Antenatal and Postnatal Care and trained around 500 healthcare providers, seeking to enhance the quality of care for mothers and children and provide guidance for the identification and referral of mental health concerns and gender-based violence. 

To further strengthen parenting support, UNICEF, in partnership with the MoH, standardized and revitalized resource rooms in PHC centers for the first time ever. This initiative aims to empower parents with knowledge and skills for early stimulation, responsive caregiving, and early childhood development at home. Moreover, parental engagement was bolstered by the continued promotion of the Foleja app, which provided parenting resources on early childhood to over 19,100 parents (17.5% male). Additionally, 228 parents received hands-on support in positive and gender-responsive parenting and early stimulation, fostering improved nurturing home environments for optimal early development.

Kosovo introduced three high-impact vaccines - Human papillomavirus (HPV), pneumococcal vaccine (PCV), and Rotavirus – as a result of a strategic collaboration between the MoH, the National Institute of Public Health (NIPH), UNICEF, and WHO. Initial uptake rates were remarkable, exceeding 90% for PCV and Rotavirus and 84% for HPV[1] among girls in grade VI, which consolidated the prevention of vaccine-preventable diseases for girls and women. With about 10,000 girls directly impacted, this is one of the gender-transformative results facilitated by UNICEF in 2024. This success was made possible by a fivefold increase in the MoH’s immunization budget, coupled with UNICEF’s efforts to address vaccine hesitancy, particularly in marginalized communities. The integration of the vaccines into Kosovo’s Health Information System, allowed the MoH and NIPH to monitor vaccine uptake in real time. UNICEF continued to support the MoH through vaccine procurement services, amounting to US$ 1.5 million, ensuring the vaccination of approximately 100,000 children in 2024.

In early childhood education, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MESTI) in developing by-laws under the Law on ECE to ensure equitable enrollment for children aged 0–6. These promote diverse service models, such as community-based and public-private partnerships, tailored to meet the needs of children and families. UNICEF, in partnership with MESTI, piloted Kosovo’s first competence-based, child-centered, and gender-responsive ECE curriculum for children aged 0–6 in 10 municipalities, across diverse forms of ECE provision. The curriculum yielded positive outcomes, including enhanced learning experiences, improved professional capacities for over 230 educators, and increased parental engagement. The finalized curriculum will serve as a foundation for systemic reform in ECE quality. Strong partnerships with ministries, the World Bank, and local stakeholders enabled UNICEF to leverage financial and technical resources. The World Bank loan on Early Childhood Development (ECD) and grant for ECE, as well as increased public budgets for health and education highlight the impact of collaborative efforts targeting critical interventions in support of child development.
 
Skills development and empowerment of adolescents and young people
System reforms in 2024 led to notable changes in inclusive and equitable learning opportunities for children. UNICEF leveraged strategic partnerships, advocacy, and capacity-building, and harnessed the potential of innovation to contribute to systemic changes, improved social cohesion, and results for girls, boys, and adolescents, especially the most vulnerable.
UNICEF pursued its efforts toward advancing the digital education reform. Innovative learning resources and interactive courses were developed in collaboration with teachers and made accessible through the learning platform shkollat.org to over 220,000 students (75% of the student population). UNICEF piloted a blended learning initiative in Prishtina, modeling an approach combining capacity building of teachers and students, mentoring, and student technicians’ clubs, benefiting over 2,500 students (1,800 girls) and 176 teachers. Student technicians’ clubs, co-led by the ICT teacher and students, support schools in using technology more effectively in the learning process and in maintaining and troubleshooting ICT equipment. In line with the Education Strategy, UNICEF supported MESTI with an initial assessment of teachers’ professional development needs, a critical step towards enhancing teaching quality, in line with SDG4.

In inclusive education, UNICEF and partners accelerated access and participation for children with disabilities, deploying 25 teacher assistants in five municipalities. These posts were institutionalized, as municipalities integrated qualified teachers into staff payroll. Following sustained advocacy efforts, the government secured a €2.3 million budget and employed 330 teacher assistants Kosovo-wide, with plans to increase their number to 500. This enabled children with disabilities to enhance their participation in the learning process and improve their right to education. Additionally, UNICEF established 15 resource classrooms in mainstream schools, providing educational services and targeted support for over 196 children with disabilities. 

UNICEF supported the capacity building of 249 Prevention and Response Teams against Abandonment and Non-Enrollment (PRTANs) at the school level and 15 teams at the municipal level (40% municipality coverage), on the Early Warning System, case management and referral mechanisms for dropout and at-risk students. As a result, over 78% of children (70% boys and 85% of girls) identified as dropouts or at risk of dropping out were successfully reintegrated into school, ensuring that no child was left behind. To sustain practices and results, UNICEF supported 8 municipalities to adopt gender-responsive Local Dropout Prevention Plans coming with over €350,000 of public funding allocations, and address the gender differentiated dropout risks, and response needs of female and male students. 

To improve the school climate, UNICEF supported initiatives promoting tolerance, conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue, and fighting gender and ethnic stereotypes. Through peer mediation, conflict resolution and critical thinking development, peacebuilding and diversity promotion and the establishment of student councils, the programme reached 1,607 students (889 girls) and 249 teachers (153 women). 

UNICEF supported the advancement of youth policies, including the adoption of a new Law on Youth and the development of sub-legal acts on voluntarism, youth work, central and local youth councils, and non-formal education, aimed at empowering young people. Over 3,210 adolescents (1,972 girls) participated and benefitted from skills-building and 104 youth-led initiatives addressing societal challenges through advocacy and social entrepreneurship. Furthermore, 444 youth volunteers were engaged in air quality monitoring and environmental campaigns, efforts that prepared children to address environmental challenges while promoting sustainability. A youth from Kosovo, with 30 peers from Europe and Central Asia, co-developed the Children and Youth Declaration for Road to Resilience, which was adopted into the EFDRR Roadmap 2021–2030. To enhance employability and support transition to labour market, the Kosovo Generation Unlimited Internship Programme (KGenU) placed 977 youth, including from marginalized communities in public and private sector companies. Moreover, the partnership expanded from 744 to 950 hosting public and private sector entities. A public-private-youth partnership model remains at the core of K-GenU, and UNICEF managed to leverage funds from government and private sector to equally contribute to the implementation of the initiative.

Lastly, UNICEF launched "The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children" (CLAC) with participation of the President of Kosovo, presenting the latest evidence on climate and environment-related hazards, developed in collaboration with the Government, local partners, and most importantly, with children and young people themselves.  Additionally, the finalization of the assessment of the integration of green skills in the pre-university curricula paved the way for developing teacher training modules to equip primary and secondary students with knowledge on climate change and air quality.

UNICEF’s work in 2024, in line with SDG4, SDG5, SDG8, SDG10 and SDG 13, underscores its commitment to creating a transformative, inclusive, and sustainable education system. From multi-level support for inclusive education to climate-resilient education and youth empowerment and the promotion of gender equality, UNICEF’s efforts have laid the foundation for lasting positive change, ensuring that every child and adolescent in Kosovo can thrive in a rapidly evolving world. UNICEF also strengthened its strategic position on youth and climate issues. Dedicated thematic gender sessions took place under UPSHIFT, PODIUM, PONDER and Youth4CleanAir interventions and several youth-led projects addressed gender inequalities in their communities. Under KGenU, 60% of beneficiaries were adolescent girls and young women, and the programme continued to focus on the provision of internship opportunities for girls and women in male dominated sectors. 

Social inclusion and child rights monitoring
In 2024, significant changes occurred in child and social protection. UNICEF strategically supported the enabling environment, addressed supply issues, contributed to the enhanced quality of services, and tackled demand issues to address negative social norms and practices. All normative documents were reviewed from a gender perspective, strengthening gender mainstreaming system capacities.

UNICEF placed a strong emphasis on strengthening the integrated child protection system. Key achievements included the finalization of strategic frameworks for child protection, the expansion of services for children with disabilities, and successful advocacy for increased funding for social protection. A cornerstone of these efforts was UNICEF's support in completing all secondary legislation under the Law on Child Protection, ensuring a robust legal foundation for protecting children's rights and well-being. 

UNICEF supported the development of Minimum Functional and Structural Standards and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for Child Protection Houses. The government has also approved the sub-legal act on Work Procedures in Multidisciplinary Roundtables for Assistance in Case Management (CMR). UNICEF developed the CMR Protocol and trained almost 50% of social workers in its application. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Justice in drafting the sub-legal act on Foster Care Services and trained 103 child protection frontline workers in the Parent Resources for Information, Development, and Education (PRIDE Model of Practice) methodology, and 100% of foster care parents improved their competences for specialized care for children with disabilities and trauma. Additionally, shaped by recommendations from a UNICEF study, the National Action Plan for the Identification and Treatment of Children in Street Situations was approved. UNICEF also supported two day-care centres serving children and parents in street situations. 

2024 marked a renewed commitment to advancing the rights of persons with disabilities, with the draft Law on Evaluation, Status Recognition, Benefits, and Services for Persons with Disabilities being reinstated in Kosovo's legislative agenda. A dedicated Working Group was re-established to advance the legislative process. UNICEF provided technical expertise to finalize the draft law and supported high-level advocacy efforts led by the Kosovo Disability Forum, engaging key government officials, including the Deputy Prime Minister, to advance the finalization of the law. Moreover, UNICEF’s advocacy led to a €3.7 million commitment for disability services across five municipalities.

About 3,800 (40% girls) children in vulnerable situations benefited from UNICEF-supported quality social services, including children with disabilities, children in street situations and out of school, children at risk of violence, children without parental care, and children in conflict with the law. For example, UNICEF supported vocational training and life skills programs to foster the reintegration and enhance the job readiness of juveniles in conflict with the law. All juveniles from the Correctional Education Centre with educational measures benefited from practical training courses supported by newly procured resources. Complementing these efforts, UNICEF tackled demand-side issues by reaching 850,000 people through social media campaigns, delivering key messages on the inclusion of children with disabilities to promote awareness and foster support for vulnerable children. Additionally, over one million viewers were engaged through various communication channels, amplifying efforts to raise awareness about ending violence against children.

In the area of social protection, in line with SDG1, UNICEF interventions focused on evidence generation for strategic advocacy. UNICEF leveraged an analysis of government social protection expenditures to advocate for increased investments in children, which contributed to a notable achievement: a €1 million increase in 2025 funding for social services delivered by licensed NGOs, raising the allocation from €1.5 million in 2024 to €2.5 million. UNICEF’s Budget Brief on Social Protection, nonetheless, noted that despite a boost from the introduction of Child Benefits under the Economic Recovery Package as a post -COVID measure, child-focused spending is less than a quarter of social protection government spending while children make up for 30% of the population. While beneficiary children of social protection programmes have more than doubled between 2021 and 2023, Social Assistance Scheme coverage for poor and vulnerable children has plummeted. Social services, which continue to be minimally funded, have seen their allocation shrink as a share of total sector spending from 1.8% in 2021 to 1.6% in 2023. Joining efforts with the World Bank, the EU, and UN agencies, UNICEF continues to advocate for the reprioritization of social protection spending towards children to ensure sustainable investments in poverty reduction, vulnerability mitigation, and essential social services for children.

Additionally, advocacy efforts for system changes were amplified by UNICEF’s Social Protection System Readiness Assessment, which investigated Kosovo’s readiness to deliver cash-based assistance during shocks and disasters. The assessment identified opportunities for the integration of a “cash plus” approach to ensure more effective responses during crises. It also outlined UNICEF’s role in enhancing the resilience and responsiveness of Kosovo’s social protection system in times of need.

UNICEF enhanced the child rights monitoring’s enabling environment, contributing to improved data systems for better policy making. With support from UNICEF, Kosovo reached a significant milestone in data systems in service of policy making when establishing the Child Rights Monitoring Platform. Coordinated by the Office for Good Governance (OGG) and the Child Rights Council and hosted on the Prime Minister’s Office web page, the platform offers comprehensive information on the progress made by Kosovo’s institutions in advancing child rights and key disaggregated data on child-related indicators, with a view to enhancing transparency and accountability. The Interministerial Committee for Child Rights led by the Prime Minister convened twice in 2024 to discuss child rights situation and hear children’s opinions. At the municipal level, UNICEF continued to support the Child Rights Teams in four selected municipalities to strengthen local accountability for children and ensure coherence and sectoral coordination in advancing child rights. This included monitoring the Teams’ 2024-2026 work plans and enhancing municipal coordination to prioritize and advance child rights, thereby improving implementation and fostering accountability.

In support of improved quality and availability of data on children, UNICEF partnered with the Kosovo Agency of Statistics to prepare for the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS). The Prime Minister reaffirmed the importance of the survey during the MICS donor meeting in September 2024, confirming a €300,000 government funding commitment for its implementation. Two sample frames were defined for both the general population and the Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian communities. Data collection is planned for spring 2025, with results anticipated by year-end.
UNICEF complemented its efforts for enhancing evidence-based policy planning in Kosovo by generating high-quality evidence through five major endeavours: (i) a formative evaluation of UNICEF’s Kosovo Programme strategy on the municipal integrated approach, Leave No One Behind, which assessed progress and provided actionable recommendations to guide future programme design with a focus on reaching the most vulnerable children; (ii) a multi-country regional evaluation inclusive of Kosovo’s immunization programme, which highlighted strengths and challenges in immunization coverage and offered insights for system improvements; (iii) the above-mentioned Climate Landscape Analysis for Children; (iv) a Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents in Kosovo, which identified key bottlenecks affecting child rights to inform UNICEF’s next programme cycle (final report expected in January 2025); and, (v) a Situation Analysis on Persons with Disabilities, conducted in partnership with UNFPA, UN Women, and UNDCO, presenting barriers, challenges, opportunities, and gaps in services for children with disabilities, and outlining ways forward aligned with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) and the SDGs. 

By aligning its strategies with the SDGs and Kosovo’s priorities focusing on inclusive policies, legislation implementation, capacity-building and advocacy, UNICEF remains pivotal in Kosovo’s journey toward achieving the 2030 Agenda and its ability to drive systemic changes that leave no child behind.

UNICEF leveraged partnerships to deliver results in health and ECE. The partnership with the Grand Dutchy of Luxembourg, extended until December 2025, was transformative for ECD services in Kosovo. This collaboration introduced groundbreaking initiatives, including Kosovo’s first gender-responsive ECE curriculum for children aged 0–6, the first parenting support program integrated into Primary Health Care, and the first developmental monitoring instrument. 

In support of MoH and NIPH, UNICEF’s partnership with the GAVI Alliance has been pivotal in ensuring the effective rollout of new vaccines—HPV, PCV, and Rotavirus. In 2024, UNICEF and WHO collaborated to achieve key public health objectives, including the rollout of the new vaccines and the implementation of an Immunization Behavioral Insights Study to address vaccine hesitancy. This joint effort strengthened demand generation, system capacity, and public trust in vaccination.

UNICEF maintained its strategic partnership with the World Bank, supporting technical discussions with the MESTI towards ratifying a US$20 million ECD financing package. Additionally, a US$2 million grant was approved for a voucher system aims to increase ECE access for vulnerable groups. Ongoing advocacy with the EU focused on ECE prioritization within the upcoming Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance (IPA) project and Kosovo’s Reform Agenda – Growth Plan.

Overall, collaboration with the MoH, MESTI, NIPH, PHC institutions, municipal health and education directorates, and partners such as WHO, UNOPS, and Save the Children has fostered a coordinated approach aligned with national priorities and UNICEF’s child rights agenda. Varied partnerships with civil society organizations amplified results at the grassroots level. 

UNICEF enhanced alliances to improve inclusive education, empower youth, and foster social cohesion. At the central level, collaboration with MESTI, the Ministry of Culture, Youth and Sports, and the Ministry of Finance, Labour, and Transfers (MFLT) was strengthened. Under MFLT’s leadership and supported by the Austrian Development Agency, the Kosovo Generation Unlimited initiative expanded partnerships to 950 private and public enterprises, including in Serb-majority municipalities, creating internship opportunities for marginalized youth. Locally, UNICEF maintained partnerships with the municipalities of Dragash, Gjakova, Lipjan, Zubin Potok, and Prishtina, and extended its collaboration to other municipalities to improve coordination and scale up specific interventions.

Under the Joint SDG Fund, UNICEF collaborated with UNDP and FAO on Kosovo's Digital Transformation, supporting legal frameworks to integrate digital technology in education. Together with IOM, UNICEF launched the Peacebuilding Fund-supported project "Youth Empowered through Inclusive Schools and Societies (YESS)," promoting tolerance and social cohesion. This UN strategic partnership approach resulted from UNICEF’s continuous engagement with the United Nations Kosovo Team, contributing to young people’s resilience by supporting their engagement in diversity promotion and combating hate speech. Additionally, for the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence Campaign, UNICEF collaborated with UN Women to raise awareness about gender-based violence.

Notable partnerships included academia and civil society, including collaboration with the Faculty of Education at the University of Prishtina, to draft Kosovo’s first comprehensive analysis of in-service teacher professional development needs, supporting the systemic improvement of teaching quality.

To advance child rights protection and monitoring, UNICEF strengthened collaboration with the Office for Good Governance helping with implementation of the Law on Child Protection and launched a national inclusion campaign with the EU Office. With the Ministry of Justice, UNICEF supported the development of sub-legal acts for the Laws on Child Protection and Social Services, SOPs for Child Protection Houses, and enhanced foster care services through the PRIDE Model of Practice. UNICEF also partnered with the Kosovo Justice Academy to enhance the capacities of justice professionals and ensure dignified handling of child cases. The joint EU, OGG, and UNICEF online campaign to combat violence against children focused on cyberbullying and reached over 300,000 viewers in two months. Additionally, with MESTI, UNICEF developed guidelines for safe internet usage and promoted peer mediation to prevent violence, fostering safer, inclusive schools.

Through the UN Partnership on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, UNICEF, together with UNFPA and UN Women, conducted a Situation Analysis on Disability Rights, identifying barriers and informing policies. Partnership with civil society and the Kosovo Disability Forum played a key role in advocating for disability rights.

This year, a new partnership with academia enhanced evidence generation. Implemented with the Institute of Psychology at the University of Prishtina, the partnership led to the development of situation analyses, studies, and evaluations, which informed UNICEF’s 2026-2030 programme cycle. Additionally, an online evaluation training opportunity was offered to academia, the Strategic Planning Office, and the OGG, fostering a culture of continuous professional development. 

In 2024, UNICEF’s strategic engagement with the private sector continued to yield significant results in skills building for transiting to work for youth. In addition, the negotiation with Devolli Corporation for establishing two ECD centers in a rural area and its evolution into a two-year cause-related marketing partnership is ongoing.
 
Lastly, shared value partnerships flourished in 2024, with private sector entities and media influencers amplifying UNICEF’s public advocacy. The Foleja parenting application gained momentum, reaching over 19,100 downloads with support from influencers and local organizations. Additionally, a joint campaign between UNICEF, the EU and the OGG promoted the inclusion of children with disabilities, resulting in over 700 requests signed and delivered to decision-makers. Consequently, four municipalities increased financial support for disability services.

Flexible funding facilitated major achievements this year. Core UNICEF resources supported parenting interventions, the enhancement of the Foleja digital parenting app in collaboration with UNICEF Regional Office for Europe and Central Asia, and the strengthening of the Home Visiting programme. These funds also facilitated the equipping of community based ECE centers in rural areas, the scale up of UNICEF’s technical support in education and the engagement with the Faculty of Education. The implementation of the Child Protection programme was primarily enabled by donor funds, including EU, UN Trust Funds, and UNICEF funds (Set Aside and Thematic Fund). Set Aside funding supported the capacity development of the recently established Child Rights Teams in municipalities for improved coordination and monitoring of their three-year work plans and the production of the Budget Brief on Social Protection.
