In 2024, UNICEF observed significant progress in Kosovo’s commitment to maternal and child health, particularly in advancing Early Childhood Intervention services for children under six. To leverage the resources for scale up and sustainability, UNICEF advocated with the MoH and other stakeholders resulting in the allocation of €2.1 million for the Home Visiting Programme and €1.5 million committed for ECI system planning starting in 2025. However, challenges remain, as limited capacity to manage and utilize these enhanced budgets has hindered the effective implementation of programmes and restricted the delivery of equitable, high-quality services. Addressing these gaps will require focused capacity-building and sustained operational support from UNICEF.

The Health Information System (HIS) remains a significant challenge. Despite previous investments in technical support, ICT infrastructure, and the development of service modules for immunization, home visiting, and developmental monitoring, progress has been modest. Delays in fully operationalizing the HIS constrain evidence-based decision-making and undermine reporting on maternal and child health services. UNICEF will maintain its support for the MoH, advocating for clear accountability and expedited timelines to ensure the HIS becomes fully functional.

In ECE, increased budget allocations represent an important step toward meeting the EU and SDG targets for enrollment of children aged between 3 and 5 years old, and reforming early learning policy. However, effective budget utilization at the municipal and institutional levels remains a challenge. Limited planning capacity has delayed the operationalization of new ECE facilities and alternative financing models, disproportionately impacting vulnerable children. Additionally, the absence of comprehensive data on ECE enrollment hinders effective planning and monitoring, further stalling efforts to expand access to quality ECE services. The lack of a robust quality framework and limited capacity for monitoring ECE services exacerbate these challenges. Inadequate coordination between central and local authorities, combined with competing priorities, has delayed key initiatives, including capacity-building for financial planning. 

In education, delays in approving MESTI's ICT Department and its structure have significantly hindered the implementation of activities under the Education Strategy. This has affected UNICEF’s planned initiatives to develop a legislative framework for integrating digital technology and creating digital learning materials. 

Regarding youth participation, key challenges in inclusive outreach for young people from non-majority communities were overcome through collaboration with partners at both central and local levels. This strengthened the support network and improved programme access for marginalized populations. It also emphasized the need for targeted approaches jointly undertaken with community-based centers, youth centers, and local organizations directly supporting non-majority groups. 

In the child protection and social protection domains, despite significant advancements, there are pressing challenges in implementing the newly sub-legal acts of the Law on Child Protection and the new Law on Social and Family Services effectively. These challenges include the absence of specific funding allocations for social services, delays in the approval of the Law on Local Government Finance, and insufficient capacity within the social service workforce. These impediments significantly hinder the accessibility and quality of protection services available to children in need. The approval of the Law on Evaluation, Status Recognition, Benefits, and Services for Persons with Disabilities by the government and ensuring sustainability of quality community-based rehabilitation services for children with disabilities remain essential for realizing the rights of children with disabilities, requiring ongoing advocacy, technical and financial support. 

Due to delays in the approval of the Sub-legal Acts and the subsequent establishment of the Child Protection Houses, and challenges faced by the OGG in establishing the Child Helpline, it is essential to extend technical and financial support in this area. One of the critical bottlenecks within the juvenile justice system is the inadequate implementation of diversion measures for juveniles in conflict with the law, compounded by the lack of aftercare services for those released from the Education and Correctional Centre. This gap impedes their successful reintegration into families and communities and heightens the risk of recidivism. This necessitates ongoing support for juveniles transitioning back into their communities and rigorous monitoring of the implementation of diversion measures by child justice professionals. Moving forward, sustainable financing for social services, a strengthened social service workforce, and prevention of violence against children including gender-based violence are imperative. 

Despite efforts to improve data reporting systems for advancing child rights, significant challenges persist, including the lack of disaggregated data for the most vulnerable populations. Administrative data systems often fail to collect relevant information, and the quality of reported data remains poor. 

Looking ahead, UNICEF will adapt its programme strategies, strengthen stakeholder coordination, and explore innovative solutions. Priorities include advocating for stronger accountability frameworks for health and ECE, building technical and planning capacities at municipality level, and accelerating the approval of critical legislative initiatives such as disability inclusion law, the law on social assistance, ECE and Youth by-laws, the ECI Strategy, mental health strategy and new Child Rights Strategy. 

In education, UNICEF will prioritize active engagement with government officials to operationalize the ICT Department through dedicated working groups for advancing the legal framework.

To accelerate the empowerment of all young people, UNICEF will strengthen partnerships with grassroots organizations and community leaders, ensuring that interventions address specific needs and foster greater inclusion. These efforts will target young people from non-majority communities, enabling their meaningful participation in UNICEF’s programmes. 
UNICEF will pursue its multi-level and multi-stakeholder partnerships with central and local stakeholders, communities, parents and children to advance the child protection system, and accelerate advocacy efforts for increased and more targeted social protection spending for children. UNICEF will also improve its integrated approach and support to multisectoral planning at municipal level based on the results of the evaluation of its municipal approach. 
Lastly, to address data shortages and improve policy decision making across social sectors, UNICEF and the Kosovo Agency for Statistics will conduct a new round of the MICS in 2025, providing approximately 100 social indicators on the situation of children and their families. A separate sample for the MICS will focus on the Roma, Ashkali, and Egyptian communities, enabling the monitoring of progress since the 2020 MICS for this specific group.

Moldova is an Upper Middle-Income country that opened EU accession negotiations in 2024, while simultaneously facing economic, energy and humanitarian crises. It continues to host over 110,000 Ukrainian refugees (45 per cent children). While the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection (MLSP) continues to make significant progress in strengthening childcare services and integrating refugee children into the national child protection system, this system remains fragile and is under pressure due to limited financial and human resources and an increasing number of Moldovan and refugee children at risk, such as unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) or children with disabilities (28,343 children[1]). The overall poverty rate continues to increase from 25.2% in 2019 to 31.6% in 2023, and the child poverty rate increased from 24.4% to 30.2%, with stark urban-rural disparities (44.6% in rural areas compared to 14.4% for urban areas)[2]. The social consequences of the downturn have directly affected children and their caregivers, predominantly women, which are listed below. 

Amidst these multiple crises in Moldova, social protection could play a crucial role in mitigating the effects of inflation and preventing children from falling into extreme poverty. Although significant anti-poverty measures were supported and adopted by Parliament, they have not been effective in preventing children from entering absolute poverty. While child poverty increased in comparison with previous years, it could have reached higher rates if not for UNICEF support; for example, national social protection programmes such as family support, disability, and childcare benefits, which were supported by UNICEF, contributed to decreasing poverty rates among children by 3.4%[3].

Children continue to be exposed to many risks in significant numbers. Annually, over 1,000 children are victims of crimes and violence, including sexual violence. Prevalence of gender-based violence, including intimate partner violence, remains high with 40 per cent of women and girls being subjected to physical or sexual violence since the age of 15[4] . A significant 76.5% of the offenses committed against children are violent crimes, compared to 59% in 2022. Of these, 37.8% (336 children) are sexual offenses. As for the gender of the victims, 24 are boys and 315 are girls, predominantly aged between 13 and 15 years[5]. 

In 2023, 1120 children (510 girls), were victims of violence and received assistance, and 26,475 children (12,637 girls) were victims of neglect. 403 children (193 girls) were taken from their parents due to imminent danger to their life and health. There is also an upward trend in the number of separated children, from about 12,500 children in 2017 to 28,343 children (13,465 girls) in 2023, of which 338 are children with disabilities. Important improvements have been noted in deinstitutionalization, yet 676 children (320 girls) remain in residential care, of which 112 are children with disabilities[6]. The number of children involved in criminal offenses stood at 735 (684 boys) in 2023, a much improved 36% decrease from 2022. 
 
Meanwhile, and despite ongoing efforts, important child protection needs of refugees persist; for those living in Refugee Accommodation Centres (RACs), for Roma population, refugee children with disabilities, and out of school children.  
 
Health indicators have been a mixed bag. In 2023, the Infant mortality rate increased to 10.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, up from 9.2 in 2022. Similarly, the Under-5 mortality rate rose to 11.2 deaths per 1,000 live births, compared to 10.5[7] in the previous year, becoming three times higher than the EU average. Conversely, the Maternal Mortality Ratio declined significantly in 2023, dropping to 16.6 deaths per 100,000 live births from a high of 59.2 in 2022[8]. 

Mandatory immunization remains a priority, with some improvements noted. The MMR coverage in 2023 increased by a mere 0.5 percentage points, to 85%., while coverage of tuberculosis vaccination remains highest (96.2 %), and HPV vaccine coverage increased with 13.8 percentage points, reaching 60% of girls aged 10[9].

UNICEF continued supporting Moldova and established four additional Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) centres to increase access to ECI for children with developmental delays and disabilities, reaching a total of 15 ECI centres nationwide. 

Despite certain improvements, the quality of general education still lags behind. Moldovan students score consistently lower than the OECD averages[10]. It is alarming that the share of students who do not reach the minimum level of competencies remains significant, ranging from 40-50%. A critical factor contributing to these poor outcomes is the weak and understaffed teaching cadres, and the outdated curriculum.  

Quality education is being promoted through the digital transformation of education. However, many foundational steps are required that promote student accessibility and engagement, teachers’ skills and capacities, to ensure the effective integration of technology in education.

Due to the lack of inclusive education services in the early years, access to early education remains limited. Only 1,494 children with Special Educational Needs (SEN) and 197 children with disabilities are enrolled in pre-primary educational institutions. In primary and secondary education, 8,521 children with SEN and 1,897 children with disabilities were enrolled in 2023/2024 school year, 4% more than the previous year. As such, the need for sustained and improved education support services for inclusion is increasingly evident. 

Even though the National Strategy for the Development of the Youth Sector is being implemented and some progress has been made in upholding adolescents' rights, reduced funding for the Strategy’s implementation challenges the expected results. Gender inequality and age-related biases remain critical issues, including persisting disparities between girls and boys, rural and urban in education outcomes, employability and participation.

About 29% of young people do not follow any form of education or professional training and are not even employed, higher than the average for EU countries (17.9%). Overall, about two thirds of young people are economically inactive.

UNICEF continues to prioritize these challenges in collaboration with both governmental and non-governmental partners in its country programme.

Building on progress made in 2023, UNICEF continued its investments in flagship governmental reforms – most notably in the social services (RESTART) and education sectors – strengthening systems to better reach and serve vulnerable children and their families.
 
Child Protection & Social Policy
The most substantial investment was in the RESTART reform. In 2024, the reform was effectively rolled out, and work focused on enhancing the administration and institutional capacity of the social protection system while also expanding coverage by reaching more children and vulnerable families. 

MLSP leveraged approximately USD 3.7 million of government funds to enhance social assistance services. This funding enabled the expansion of several social assistance programmes, including the Mobile Team for Children with Disabilities, which was extended nationwide, increasing coverage from 18 to 33 rayons and benefiting a total of 863 individuals (629 children with disabilities). Out of this sum, USD 2.7 million were invested in 136 centre-based specialized social services, now reaching 2,400 beneficiaries (adults and children). Additionally, in collaboration with the National House of Social Insurance and with technical support from UNICEF, the MLSP expanded the social protection package for refugees. This included the introduction of new programmes, such as family support and energy compensation programmes, reaching 10,000 individuals, including refugees. 

The key restructuring under RESTART involved the creation of 10 new territorial social assistance agencies and a central department on social services, shifting and aligning the administrative social protection system, which positively impacted child-related policies and brought services closer to children, especially in rural areas. UNICEF was proud to support the MLSP in this process, as well as in developing an electronic single window platform for the social protection system, and redesigning human resources and finance frameworks to ensure families with children have better access to social protection services. 

With UNICEF’s technical assistance, MLSP also improved the cost-efficiency and service delivery of 14 public social institutions (such as day care centres and temporary placement centres for children with disabilities) under the Agency for Management of Highly Specialized Social Services. This optimized resource allocation and financial management, directly impacting social service delivery for children. 

UNICEF was also a key child protection partner supporting the RESTART reform to enhance the governance, quality, and access to social and child protection services, including family-centred social welfare and childcare services. UNICEF supported the recruitment and training of 150 new child protection specialist, and invested in capacity building of social service workforce and frontline workers, including 3,910 members of multidisciplinary teams (90% women) trained on child protection case management and intersectoral collaboration.  Additionally, the training package “Building Competencies of the Social Service Workforce in Europe and Central Asia”, developed by UNICEF and Columbia University, was rolled out through the organization of a ToT gathering 30 specialists, academics and social workers from Moldova and Ukraine. 

Similarly, UNICEF continued its investment in the implementation of social and child protection assistance for refugees within the Temporary Protection framework. The minimum package of services for children was strengthened including family support, family type care, personal assistance for children with disabilities and others, benefiting 48,417 vulnerable children and their caregivers, including 11,606 refugees, (60% women and girls). Through the network of 4 Blue Dots and fixed and mobile child friendly spaces, 52,637 Ukrainian and Moldovan children and their caregivers accessed MHPSS services. More than 2,000 caregivers (95% women) were reached with various specialised parenting programmes. A module on gender-transformative parenting approaches was integrated into the PEACE Parenting Programme and rolled out. UNICEF also developed a parenting curriculum[1] aimed at empowering parents and caregivers of children with disabilities to mitigate the possibility of institutionalization.

UNICEF organized an important national conference to review violence against children (VAC) response and prevention programmes in partnership with the MLSP, WHO and USAID. During the event, a consensus was reached among participants on key areas of progress and main challenges as well as defining priorities to expand interventions to support achieving the objectives by 2026. In follow up, the government of Moldova committed to significant investments in human, financial and infrastructure resources, and continuum of services during the first ‘Global ministerial conference on combatting violence and abuse against children’ in Bogota, Columbia. At the same event, government approved the framework of action on ending VAC launched at the national conference.

UNICEF continued to scale up its GBV programmes with varied partners: 56,444 women, girls, and boys (50% girls, 40% women, 10% boys) were reached with GBV risk mitigation, prevention and response activities. UNICEF enjoyed impactful partnerships with girl- and women-led associations, where 1,407 adolescents, including 865 girls became better aware of gender discriminatory social roles, gender stereotypes, consent, and healthy relationships through peer-to-peer programmes. Additionally, 17 community engagement support groups, including community-level groups and safe spaces for women and girls, and refugees, were also set up. To complement, UNICEF adapted and launched the Laaha platform [2] in Romanian and Russian. Additionally, behavioural insights research informed the design of a one-month test campaign on Instagram that reached a total of 45,041 unique users, all between 13 and 18 years old (58% female and 42% male).  71 journalists (66 women and 5 men) were also trained on ethical reporting of VAC and GBV cases and developed media material encouraging reporting. A total of 98 child victims were assisted (90% girls), with a constant increase of the number of cases reported; 10,711 pieces of material with child sexual abuse were removed from the digital space, and 20,556 young internet users benefitted from training and awareness raising on online safety.

UNICEF has been at the forefront of the paradigm shift of addressing the intersection between violence against girls, boys and women and became an accelerator country for the implementation of the related programme. A forum on intersections on VAC and violence against women (VAW) was organized under the leadership of the National Agency Against Domestic Violence, a UNICEF partner and cross-sectoral coordination body. 115 Child Protection and GBV specialists enhanced their capacities to respond more effectively to VAC and VAW through a series of events, and based on the forum’s recommendation, a strategy on VAC and VAW was developed with a specific focus on social and behavioural change (SBC), to be led by UNICEF. 

In the field of Justice for Children, UNICEF continues strengthening the restorative justice system and procedures for children in conflict with the law and children in detention, through promoting frameworks for mediation, diversifying and promoting probation, enhancing skills of judges, prosecutors and all other types of specialists working with children to implement specialized child-friendly and gender-sensitive justice for both child victims/ witnesses of crimes and child offenders. In 2024, 1068 justice sector professional (512 women and 556 men) were trained, 156 boys participated in probation programmes developed or adapted with UNICEF support, and 812 children in contact and in conflict with the law received protection assistance. 656 children (65% girls) who were victims or witnesses of crime received appropriate assistance and benefited from child-friendly interviews, which aim to reduce trauma and provide a safe and supportive environment during the investigative process.
 
231 police officers across 12 regions were trained on child friendly interviewing, and 179 (22 women and 157 men) police officers were trained on protecting children in risk situation. 44 probation counsellors from territorial probation bureaus were trained on applying evaluation instruments for assessing the impact of probation programs on children, 22 mediators enhanced their knowledge and skills in mediation for criminal cases, focusing on aspects involving children in conflict with the law. 

Consolidating the cash plus care approach, UNICEF also worked with ministries to improve public finance allocations to services that would effectively mitigate vulnerabilities for children. With UNICEF support, the MER designed and piloted a new per-child funding formula for preschool services, aiming to ensure equitable resource distribution across regions. Several policy dialogues were also carried out on fiscal space analysis for RESTART reform, and cost-efficiency of social assistance. Overall, these efforts ensured more effective use of funds, by enhancing access to services for children, and exploring fiscal opportunities within the state budget.

In September 2024, the MLSP, MER and MoH engaged with UNICEF in an exercise to alleviate child poverty and vulnerabilities by juxtaposing the ongoing reforms against the framework of the European Child Guarantee (ECG), to thread an impactful national action plan, using ECG tools to monitor progress and eventually ringfence public fiscal space to sustain essential services. Conference participation was secured from the highest level of line ministries, the EU Commission, development partners as well as UNICEF Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece and ECARO. The conference resulted in written commitments and a joint declaration by MLSP, MER, MoH and UNICEF adopting a roadmap for the development of a national action plan for Moldova, modelled after the ECG. 

ECED
Contributing to the best start in life and enhancing the early detection of any developmental delays or disabilities, UNICEF trained 1,000 frontline workers in applying the Guidelines for Monitoring Child Development, benefiting 13,500 young children. Following that up with providing suitable intervention services, UNICEF provided technical and financial support for the implementation of the National Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) Roadmap and Action Plan. With UNICEF’s support, four additional ECI Centres and 10 Child Development Offices were established and equipped in rural areas. 220 health specialists and social assistants improved their knowledge on ensuring quality screening, referral, and service provision, and high-quality, transdisciplinary support was provided to 1,533 families with children with disabilities. 109 ECI specialists were trained and certified in family-centred approach, and UNICEF supported the development of a Master’s Program in ECI, together with the Medical and Pharmaceutical University “N. Testemitanu” and Medical School Hamburg launched in September 2024, promoting a shift from a child-centred to family-centred approach.

Universal audiological screening for newborns was established with UNICEF support. Audiological screening was conducted on 14,289 out of 15,149 newborns in 2024, and hearing issues were identified in 18 children, allowing for critical early intervention. 
  
Parents and caregivers were trained on child development through 12 interactive “Ask the Professional” sessions, reaching 172 parents/caregivers. Furthermore, the Bebbo digital platform reached over 20,000 downloads, including 500 refugee caregivers, providing expert advice on child health and development, and helped parents track vaccinations, Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF), and development milestones.

In collaboration with MER, 150 ECE Resource Centres were created and equipped, and over 4,860 educators were trained on playful learning, MHPSS and social and emotional learning, benefiting 29,000 children. Partnership with Lego Foundation enabled around 3K young refugee children to have access to non-formal early learning opportunities, MHPSS and social integration with host communities. 482 preschools teachers were trained in experiential and project-based learning, directly impacting 10,048 children, including through implementing robotics programmes for 1000 children.

The Interregional Conference: Building Bright Futures Across Borders: Investing in ECEC, brought together ministries from Moldova, Romania, and Ukraine, as well as development partners, to discuss equitable access to quality education for refugee children, with the Lego Foundation's support.
 
Health
UNICEF strengthened child development services in 10 localities in Cahul and Ungheni through mentorship and home visits provided jointly by health and social workers. A Guide for Preschool Healthcare on child growth, development, and nutrition was developed and distributed to 2,000 professionals.

Additionally, perinatal care was strengthened by enhancing the skills of 1,755 health workers, including those from the Left Bank, in emergency obstetric and neonatal care, infection prevention, etc. With the support of UNICEF, the MoH adjusted and approved the evaluation and accreditation standards for perinatal centres, with specific criteria on Baby Friendly Health Initiative. 

2,000 pregnant women and parents/caregivers from 11 districts, including the Left Bank and refugee populations, enhanced their IYCF knowledge through seminars. UNICEF also supported the development of nutrition standards and menu adjustments for preschools and schools.  
In UNICEF’s continued efforts to improve routine immunization rates, it enhanced the skills of 620 medical staff (OBGYN, family doctors, pediatricians, and allergologists) in routine vaccination for pregnant and breastfeeding women, including refugees. UNICEF also supported the integration of the “Interpersonal Communication for Immunization Module” into national in-service and pre-service curricula across 10 disciplines at Medical Colleges and 9 disciplines at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy.
 
UNICEF conducted a Behavioral Insights Study to understand factors influencing immunization practices, the findings informed the development of the national SBC in Immunization Strategy 2027. SBC activities in 10 districts and 14 suburbs of Chi¿inau reached 2,412 parents/caregivers (including 2,619 refugees), 1,639 health workers, 6,701 teachers, 22,269 school children (aged 10-15), and 718 representatives of LPAs. As a result, MMR vaccination rates increased by 3% to 5% in some districts, and HPV vaccine coverage for 15-year-olds rose by 40% in certain suburbs. To address vaccination concerns, an online campaign reached 397,000 parents with targeted messages promoting immunization. The SBC interventions in immunization were gender-responsive, successfully engaging fathers and male caregivers alongside mothers. This approach fostered shared decision-making, resulting in increased awareness and collective responsibility, ultimately contributing to improved immunization rates.
 
UNICEF continued to support youth clinics in strengthening capacities in MHPSS and addressing GBV among adolescents. 83 youth clinics health workers and 230 volunteers were trained on these topics, benefiting more than 16,000 adolescents. An SOP on how to identify and address GBV cases was also developed to ensure uniform and quality practice across all youth clinics.

UNICEF continued to support the 24/7 Youth Health Help Line that provided MHPSS and referral to 12,000 adolescent boys and girls, effectively addressing mental health concerns. To improve access of adolescents from rural areas to health services, two additional mobile clinics were procured, bringing the total to five mobile clinics nationwide (four procured by UNICEF). Around 5,000 boys and girls were counselled by Mobile Youth Friendly Health Clinics professionals, while 16,000 young people improved their knowledge and skills on health-related topics through individual and group counselling sessions.
 
Education
UNICEF maintained its focus on strategically designed interventions aimed at enhancing access to quality inclusive education for all children, through enhancing teacher capacities, providing critical technologies, and regularising the path to digitalising education.
Studies on the inclusion of children with SEN, and Gap Analysis on provision of assistive technologies (AT) in education were conducted to reveal trends and design new interventions. Accordingly, UNICEF procured and distributed AT for educational purposes for around 300 children with hearing and visual impairments and equipment for children with intellectual disabilities, and Education Resource Centres in 57 schools is underway.
 
The "Learning Together" campaign was implemented to combat stigma and discrimination against children with disabilities and SEN, refugees and ethnic minorities, promoting their right to quality education.  Key activities (SBC communication, community engagement and social mobilization) reached 1,800 community members (local authorities, professionals, parents) from 10 districts and 300,000 children from 1,204 schools. The media campaign reached over 285,871 people, online and offline. The interventions led to increased inclusive knowledge, practices, and positive attitudes. Post-events surveys showed 96.7% of adults and 97.4% of children support inclusion in mainstream schools.

3,314 refugee children, including 853 in preschools, were successfully enrolled in Moldovan public schools, thanks to MER's efforts and UNICEF's Back-to-School campaign. EDUTech Labs and Play and Learning Hubs provided additional educational support, fostering integration and psychosocial well-being. A comprehensive roadmap has been developed with MER to ensure the integration of refugee children into the education system.
 
Digitalization of education has been advancing through the development of key foundational policies, including the Roadmap for the Digitalization of the Education Sector 2024-2027; Minimum Standards for the Endowment of General Education Institutions with ICT and Internet Connection; Digital Technologies Curriculum; and Methodology for the Assessment of Teachers’ Digital Competencies. In order for schools to join this digitalisation journey, 350 All-in-One PC and 350 Interactive Panels were procured to equip 70 schools. 

The education sector reform has prioritised strengthening teaching cadres. To that end, UNICEF supported the newly created National Institute for Education and Leadership by developing its normative framework and conducting the mentorship training programme for 90 national and 920 institutional mentors. Guides were also developed on student wellbeing and career counselling/ management services, and training is being rolled out for relevant school staff at all 1201 public schools. Local solutions were implemented for future scalability, including training 103 teachers from 12 schools in Cahul and Ungheni in digital tools and STEAM-based project learning, benefiting 2,127 students. An e-Learning course was developed, covering student-centred learning and STEAM education, now accessible to all teachers in Moldova.  The local network of 24 mentors in formative assessment was capacitated and 164 teachers and managers were trained in applying these practices, impacting 18,686 children. 

WASH & CEED
The WASH agenda and Green Education has advanced, by establishing and co-chairing the WASH in Schools Sector Coordination Council, leading a national-level assessment of WASH facilities and services in schools, conducting a KAP study on WASH in schools, initiating WASH infrastructure projects in 124 schools, and finalizing improvements in 8 schools. 

Green skills development was introduced in 20 schools, where managers and young activists were supported to develop and implement school initiatives linked to the promotion of environmental practices in schools and communities. Additionally, in collaboration with the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, UNICEF successfully engaged 1,140 students in the National Security School competition, focusing on the critical theme of Climate Change: Heatwaves and Wildfires, emphasizing the importance of preparedness skills in facing these pressing challenges. Moldova was represented in the Children and Youth Call to Action within the ECA Regional Platform for DRR.
 
ADAP
UNICEF continued to strengthen the meaningful engagement and participation of adolescents and youth. Integrating the UPSHIFT methodology was into the National Programme on Pupils Councils, was approved by MER, along with dedicated public funding. Councils from 100 schools were trained on CRC and child participation in decision-making processes. This training was informed by newly approved guidelines for pupils’ councils, developed collaboratively by UNICEF and MER.
Diversification of adolescents learning opportunities and skills development was implemented through the GirlsGoIT and STEAM on Wheels programmes reaching 10,000 adolescents, particularly vulnerable ones. The UPSHIFT programme engaged 15,000 adolescents and youth, and civic initiatives of up to 43 startups. 

Youth sector analyses were conducted for Cahul and Ungheni, leading to the development of Local Youth Strategies. These strategies were approved by LPAs and the institutional capacities of 10 youth organizations/structures in both regions were strengthened with 163 young people empowered in planning and implementing local youth engagement initiatives.

Partnerships with the government, local authorities, development partners, civil society actors and the private sector remain at the core of how UNICEF works in Moldova. 
 
Since the start of the Country Programme 2023-2027, UNICEF discussed and signed Rolling Workplans with the Ministries of Culture, Education & Research (MER), Health (MoH), Infrastructure & Regional Development (MIRD), Internal Affairs, Justice, and Labour & Social Protection (MLSP), as well as with the Child Rights Ombudsperson, the National Agency for Prevention and Combating Violence against Women and Domestic Violence, and the National Bureau of Statistics. MoU’s were also signed with the Municipalities of Chisinau, Palanca and Otaci to localise interventions for vulnerable populations. 
 
The most ambitious partnership has been with MLSP in supporting the RESTART reform, with more than USD 16 million invested (direct budget and technical support) since 2022. It bridges the continued need for humanitarian interventions with longer-term development of a shock-responsive social protection system to mitigate child poverty, targeting both refugee and vulnerable Moldovan communities to ensure no one is left behind, and to promote social cohesion. Strategic partnerships have been built with key donors (mainly ECHO, FCDO, SDC, Sweden) in this vein, as well as to fund better care reform and innovative initiatives to address violence against girls, boys and women. This partnership with MLSP has already led to absorbing some social protection services into the national budget, including personal assistance to children with disabilities.
 
Partnerships with CSO’s sought to standardise good child protection practices and create synergies between CSO and public sector capacities. Additionally, in combatting gender-based violence, partnerships were signed with women- and girl-led associations, that also worked to strengthen such organisations to gradually play bigger roles in the sector.
 
In 2024, UNICEF intensified its partnerships with the governmental and international financial institutions, organising and participating in inclusive policy dialogues with the Ministry of Finance (MoF), World Bank, International Monetary Fund and others. This has laid the groundwork for advancements in public financing for children and contributed to initiating a consultation with MoF to establish a Rolling Workplan regarding child-sensitive policies.
 
The partnership with the MoH has been effective in strengthening the national health system in the areas of immunization, maternal- and child- care, adolescent health, early childhood intervention, nutrition and HIV prevention. Working with a wide range of actors, from national stakeholders to grassroots organizations, allowed UNICEF to have a holistic approach in its work of system strengthening and to provide high quality health services to the most vulnerable children. UNICEF continued partnerships with the National Agency of Public Health, National Health Insurance Company (CNAM), Institute of Mother and Child (IMC), health care facilities, the State University for Medicine and Pharmacy, School of Public Health Management, Medical Professional Associations, and CSOs. UNICEF has supported MoH and reimbursed through CNAM the costs of health services to refugee children since June 2022. In accordance with the Temporary Protection Governmental Decision, UNICEF has been continuing to support CNAM to reimburse costs for health services for refugee children with Temporary Protection.  In July 2024 a UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund was established and signed by IOM, UNICEF, WHO and UNFPA aiming to provide support to CNAM in covering the budget gap in the provision of health services to the refugees in line with the health-benefit package. Additionally, to ensure the access of refugee children without Temporary Protection, who CNAM cannot cover, UNICEF developed a new partnership with the IMC to reimburse the costs of specialised and hospital care. 

Efficient collaboration with the national authorities had a determining role in achieving the education objectives in 2024. The partnership with MER, the Republican Centre for Pedagogical Assistance and the National Institute for Education and Leadership was instrumental in advancing the inclusive education and digitalization priorities, teacher training, improving the education infrastructure, and implementing SBC interventions aimed at enhancing inclusion. These efforts are supported by the GPE programme and EU partnerships. UNICEF had the unique opportunity to contribute to the creation of the network of 35 model schools in Moldova, thanks to the reliable and productive partnership with the EU Delegation and UNDP.

Regarding the educational inclusion of refugee children, the partnership with MER, UNHCR, the National Congress of Ukrainians in Moldova, and members of the Refugee Education Working Group increased the impact of interventions to reach and serve more refugee children. The grants received from FCDO, BPRM, Lego Foundation, etc. made a real difference in refugees’ access to education.

With MIRD, UNICEF was able to revive the national WASH Sectoral Council and established a multisectoral WASH in Schools Committee within MER. This initiative brought together a diverse array of stakeholders from various sectors, fostering collaboration and dialogue on WASH-related challenges. The concerted efforts in enhancing water and sanitation services underscored the critical necessity of forming a strategic partnership with the Ministry of Infrastructure and Regional Development. This collaboration is designed to enhance coordination within the water and sanitation sector while jointly steering the Water and Sanitation Coordination Council. The overarching aim of these partnerships and coordination efforts is to expedite the realization of Sustainable Development Goal 6, which focuses on ensuring availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all, particularly for children throughout the country.
 
UNICEF also continues to co-chair a number of coordination groups at the UNCT level, within the refugee response framework and beyond, supporting and guiding collective action of sister UN agencies, INGOs, CSOs and government entities towards global good practice standards for children in adolescents and youth programming, child protection, disability inclusion, education, social protection and WASH.

As for the private sector, UNICEF Moldova prioritized private-sector partnerships in 2024, raising USD50,000 from Orange Foundation to support 600 adolescents at Summer Camps. Another key milestone was signing an MoU with TVR Moldova, launching advocacy campaigns to promote the CRC Convention, achieving impactful results in advancing child rights through broad-reaching public engagement. Lastly, a consultation meeting was held with business associations as an exploratory step towards establishing a UNICEF Moldova Business Advisory Board, which was met with enthusiasm.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, there were a few instances when UNICEF Moldova had to seek out alternative solutions to ensure essential services were reaching children in need. We share here four such instances and lessons.


 


With the extension of the Temporary Protection (TP) measures in 2024, UNICEF continued to lobby the National Health Insurance Company (CNAM) to allow for coverage of refugee children who did not yet have TP, as we had done in the previous years. Unfortunately, the updated directive was clear and binding – CNAM could only cover TP holders. While UNICEF continued to lobby CNAM with other partners, it also sought and found an alternative pathway through the Institute of Mother & Child, signing an agreement to directly reimburse services to Ukrainian refugees without TP. Though its location in Chisinau favoured those who could reach it for primary health purposes, as the only tertiary maternal and paediatric hospital in the country, it ensured that any mother or child in need of emergency or specialised medical care would be able to obtain it free of charge. The numbers recorded in the months of implementing the agreement pointed to its success.


 


Another persistent challenge in programming for Ukrainian refugees is around education. The enrolment rate in public schools increased from 2023/24 to the 2024/25 school year by around 1,000 students, but remained low. The increase is credited to the many steps undertaken to promote enrolment – working with the Ministry to eliminate any barriers to registration, implementing an extensive ‘back to school’ campaign, establishing over 100 EduTech labs (81 by UNICEF) across the country to encourage children to study in a school environment, and gradually enrol in school. So, while it is clear that these efforts must continue, we have learned that there needs to be more intensive engagement with parents to address their hesitancy for sending children to school, together with an intensification of Romanian language classes to facilitate and promote enrolment as well as social integration, for both children and parents, beyond Russian-speaking neighbourhoods. These are core parts of the Roadmap for Inclusion of Refugees developed together with UNHCR and MER, with a clear costing exercise to support its implementation.


 


One true example of having to pivot and reprogramme was the Barnahus to be established on the left bank (Transnistrian region). As part of an ongoing justice for children project on the left bank, UNICEF had discussed with partners the possibility of establishing integrated services for child victims and witnesses of crimes (Barnahus-type services). Despite initial indications of approval, and several meetings between UNICEF’s technical team and the de facto structures, the de facto structures continued to hold up establishing the Barnahus. As this was part of an ongoing project with a set timeline, UNICEF Moldova had to make the difficult decision of pivoting away from the Barnahus in Tiraspol, working instead to amp up some of relevant services within existing programmes on the left bank, where possible, and shifting the funding and the project to the right bank to look into constructing a the service in central Moldova instead.


 


Lastly, the political situation in 2024, marked by presidential elections and the EU accession referendum vote passing with a narrow margin, has raised uncertainties impacting the financial planning process and implementation of public policies. Despite UNICEF's technical assistance being effective in terms of leveraging and mobilizing funds, social protection and education are not prioritised by the country's top decision makers. In its path to EU accession, the government has focused instead on infrastructure investment, economic and regional development, and the justice sector. Investments in inclusive quality education and inclusive social protection and services did not figure into the government’s agenda at the Moldova Partnership Platform, nor in negotiations of the EU Growth Plan. To bring attention to ways in which the EU Accession path and instruments can align with education and social protection investments, UNICEF Moldova organised the Moldova EU Child Guarantee (ECG) conference in September 2024 described earlier in this report, highlighting the EU tools and examples that work towards alleviating child poverty as part of becoming/being an EU country. Studies will follow in 2025 that show the impact of such investments on national economic development, and advocating for the practice of the ECG to ringfence public financing for essential services for children.


 


In closing, one must note that a constant challenge to UNICEF is that its work in all areas is highly dependent on donor funding. Although there is an increasing awareness among donors about the importance of nexus programming, donor funding is frequently earmarked and short to medium term, which is inadequate for the necessary system strengthening interventions. UNICEF Moldova has developed tools and resources to support its fundraising efforts locally and advocate for greater and more flexible, long-term funding. These need to continue.

I.  Political and socio-economic landscape 
GDP Growth and Unemployment. GDP growth is expected to be 2.1% in 2024 [1], similar to 2023 and lowest among the Western Balkan countries. Unemployment declined slightly from 12.9% to 12.5%, however the rate among 15- to 29-year-olds remains at 23.6% [2]. Similar to 2023, the budget deficit is estimated to be 4.7% of GDP in 2024 [3]. The increase in public sector wages during the year and the continuing increase in public debt are likely to create long-term pressures on the country’s public expenditures.
Elections with a shifting orientation. North Macedonia elected its first female Head of state – Gordana Siljanovska Davkova. After seven years in opposition, the conservative centre-right coalition won the parliamentary elections in May 2024. The Ministry of Social Policy was restructured with new mandates on demographics and youth, and the Minister without portfolio in charge of Roma inclusion reinstituted. 
EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans. The Plan, approved by the EU Commission in October 2024 aims to boost socio-economic growth and convergence by enhancing economic integration and accelerating fundamental reforms during 2024-2027. €750.4 million in non-repayable grants and favorable loans will be available to North Macedonia when it meets the conditions defined in its own Reform Agenda. [4].  
National Development Strategy (NDS) 2024-2044. With close alignment to the Sustainable Development Goals, the six strategic areas of the NDS are: a sustainable, innovative, and competitive economy; sustainable local and regional development that ensures cohesion, demographic revitalization; social and cultural development; a secure, safe, and resilient society; green transformation; the rule of law and good governance. The NDS Implementation Programme 2024-2028 also adopted by the Parliament envisions one year of mandatory preschool education to be introduced in 2028.
Universal Periodic Review (UPR) of human rights. In response to the 2024 UPR, North Macedonia accepted recommendations related to violence against children, inclusive education for vulnerable children particularly Roma and children with disabilities, and efforts for inclusion and non-discrimination of Roma, while recommendations related to gender identity were noted. 

II.  Current status of child rights in the country
Child poverty persists (SDG1). The latest data on monetary poverty published this year indicate that 32.7% of children were living below the national poverty line in 2021, up from 29.3% in 2020. This made children one of the most vulnerable groups in society. In addition, 53% of households with three or more dependent children and 50% of single parents with children were at risk of poverty [2] Roma children were disproportionately affected by poverty: 79% live below the poverty line [5]. Poverty data for the past three years is yet to be released by the State Statistical Office.
Health indicators improve (SDG3). The neonatal mortality rate continued to improve, dropping from 5.2 per 1,000 live births in 2016 to 1.8 in 2023. Similarly, the under-five mortality rate dropped from 9.9 per 1,000 live births in 2017 to 2.4 per 1,000 in 2023, which is below the regional and EU average. Vaccination rates show slow recovery post-COVID. The low vaccine coverage contributed to pertussis outbreak at the beginning of 2024. The coverage of the HPV vaccine also increased from 52% in 2022 to 56% in 2023. Additionally, in 2023 the country introduced HPV-9 valent vaccine, including for boys [6]. 
Violence against children continues to be a concern, including online (SDG16). The Ministry of Interior recorded a 41% increase in child victims of crime, with 740 cases (412 boys, 312 girls) in 2023 compared to 524 in 2022. However, the centres for social work reported only 212 in 2023 (128 boys, 84 girls), which is significantly lower. This discrepancy is concerning as social workers must be involved in all cases involving child victims of crime to ensure their protection during justice processes and support their rehabilitation. Reports of sharing photos and videos depicting sexual abuse of children have doubled, from 6,045 in 2021 to 12,310 in 2023, according to CyberTipline Data [7].
Child Care reform sustained. No children are in large-scale residential care institutions, with 524 (257 girls and 267 boys) in family-based care, including 111 children with disabilities (60 girls and 51 boys). Three foster care support centres continue to support foster families. Small group homes still accommodate 99 children (55 girls and 44 boys), including 32 children with disabilities (18 girls and 14 boys) [8]. 
A lasting learning crisis (SDG4). The latest OECD PISA results (2022) indicate over two-thirds of 15-year-old students do not meet basic proficiency in reading, mathematics, and science.  Results from TIMSS (Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study) released in December 2024 continue to demonstrate the urgent need for accelerating education system reforms to improve the quality of learning. Students from North Macedonia are ranked 44 in Mathematics and 47 in science out of 58 countries.[9] 
The impact of air pollution on children (SDG13). In North Macedonia, infant deaths linked to air pollution accounted for 11.6 per cent or 1 in 9 of all deaths of children under one year. In winter months Skopje is frequently ranking among the ten most polluted cities in the world. New data also shows that air pollution causes more healthy years of life lost than any other single environmental factor [10]. 
Hurdles for children with disabilities (CWD). In the 2023/2024 school year, the number of students with disabilities in mainstream schools doubled, increasing from an average of four in 2019/2020 to nine students per school. However, revisions to the Primary Education Law, approved by the Parliament in December 2024, risk reversing North Macedonia’s impressive progress in inclusive education by allowing parents to enrol children with complex disabilities in resource centres (former special schools).

The adoption of the National Action Plan for the Mental Health and Wellbeing of Children and Adolescents in North Macedonia 2024-2030 was a key cross-sectoral result for children this year, integrating efforts across health, education, and protection sectors. The Action Plan outlines specific steps to enhance mental health care for children and adolescents and provides a comprehensive framework for a holistic, preventive mental health system that prioritizes the individual. The Plan focuses on prevention, promotion, care and treatment and mainstreams functional intersectoral cooperation. Working in close partnership with WHO, UNICEF supported the Steering Committee coordinated by the University Clinic for Psychiatry. This included: facilitating inter-sectoral coordination and involving key stakeholders, including the civil society; supporting the assessment and analysis of capacities and gaps in the education and social/child protection sectors; and facilitating the consultation with children and adolescents to strengthen age-appropriate, child and gender-sensitive approaches. 
 
UNICEF also supported concurrent efforts to strengthen the mental health capacities of front-line workers, in the health, education and child protection sectors. In the health sector, UNICEF supported capacity development of all (200) patronage nurses (home visiting) and master trainers to provide basic mental health and psycho-social counselling to the most vulnerable pregnant women, mothers with newborns and members of their families. With over 20,000 visits to pregnant women and infants completed annually, the counselling and referrals offered through the home visiting service is a critical entry point for early recognition of mental health conditions. In the education sector, with UNICEF support, approximately 30% of the school support staff including pedagogues, psychologists, and special educators, upgraded their skills to support students’ wellbeing, early identification of mental health conditions, and training materials were shared with schools countrywide to facilitate organizations of workshops with children and adolescents. UNICEF supported the development of gender-responsive training module on mental health and psychosocial support, designed to equip education staff to address culture and norms related to sexual/reproductive health, gender roles, partner relations, and domestic and gender-based violence. In the child protection sector, half of caregivers from all four small group homes for children in conflict with the law and at risk, professionals from Centres for Social Work and the education sector were provided with tools and knowledge to support children develop positive self-image, build interpersonal relationships, and resolve conflict effectively. Tailored individual plans were developed for children in conflict with the law residing in small group homes, with a strong emphasis on mental health support. Coinciding with the adoption of the National Action Plan, UNICEF launched a social media campaign to break the stigma surrounding mental health and promote practical tips to reduce stress and anxiety, resulting in 285,000 video views and over 15,000 website page visits.   
 
Continued focus on strengthening immunization and delivery of primary health care services. Despite slow post-COVID recovery, vaccination rates continued to show some positive trends in 2024. In close coordination with WHO, UNICEF continued to support the Ministry of Health in demand generation including supporting a national campaign reaching 5.6 million on national television, social mobilization of parents during the pertussis outbreak and support for the organization of the European immunization week. UNICEF also supported policy analysis and advocacy to adjust resources, including human resources and outreach, to address current demographic shifts; and partnered with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine to adapt inter-personal communication skills on immunization modules for pre- and in-service training of health professionals. Positive developments in the digital health system capitalised on the investments supported by UNICEF in previous years: the Moj Termin system now includes indicators to measure quality of management of the five most common conditions in children and during pregnancy (pneumonia, anaemia, diabetes type 1, gestational diabetes and vaccination) and at least 1/3 of the health personnel acquired skills to use the module effectively thanks to UNICEF support in 2024. The dashboard allows health professionals at primary healthcare (PHC) level to monitor patients in their catchment area and receive feedback about their performance, to proactively plan activities based on morbidity data; and enables health authorities to review and plan health services according to results in lower levels of the system.

The programme continued support for addressing different forms of child malnutrition, including the remaining pockets of stunting, very low breastfeeding rates and increasing childhood obesity and overweight, supported by evidence generated with UNICEF support on the behavioral drivers and economic costs. In 2024 UNICEF supported consultations with over 30 national stakeholders in the health, education, social protection and communication sectors, leading to the development of a systems map that has identified paths accelerating social change. UNICEF also supported capacity building of front-line workers, reaching approximately 250 family doctors and patronage nurses in the health sector (10% and 50% of the workforce respectively), and over 3,000 preschool professionals (62% of the workforce) on developing healthy nutrition habits from an early age.

Advances in the enabling environment for justice for children. A significant achievement was the adoption of the Law on Justice for Children and the Law on Execution of Sanctions by the Parliament in March 2024. These laws, aligned with international standards, CRC and EU directives, were adopted following rigorous advocacy and technical support provided by UNICEF since 2019. These laws strengthen protection of the rights and interests of children in contact and in conflict with the law, and incorporate a restorative justice approach, ensuring that a child’s right to be heard is actively implemented and rehabilitation and reintegration are promoted. UNICEF continued working closely with the Ministry of Justice to ensure the next cycle of EU Instrument of Pre-Accession (IPA) funding, starting 2026, prioritizes capacity building for the effective implementation of the revised legislative framework.

Continued progress in mainstreaming environmental and climate change education across the education system, and beyond. In 2024, some 160,000 primary school pupils benefited from revised curricula that incorporate climate change and environmental sustainability across multiple disciplines: a result of three years of UNICEF support to the revision of 27 primary curricula. The Experiential Learning Network (ELN), established in 2023 by six science institutions across the country with UNICEF support, expanded with a new institution joining (BioTechnology Laboratory) and the development of new activities on air quality. Some 3,400 primary school children (53% girls), mostly from rural communities, participated in the ELN practical workshops on environment and climate change. Furthermore, practical experiment scenarios and learning materials developed with UNICEF support were implemented in over 190 schools across the country, reaching at least 50,000 or 1 in 5 school children in 2024. In secondary education, UNICEF supported the revision (“greening”) of vocational curricula and learning materials in ten vocational training (VET) profiles and supported capacity development of 25% of vocational teaching staff. UNICEF continued to support adolescent’s and youth green skills, and youth climate advocacy and action, partnering with the National Fund for Innovation and Technological Development, civil society-organizations, and municipal councils to showcase the tremendous potential of adolescents in creating solutions to address air pollution, environmental sustainability, and climate change in their communities. Over 500 youth (327 girls, 222 boys) led the development and implementation of social and technical innovations with tangible results, such as reducing air pollution in 10 secondary schools, developing a mobile app for the Botanical Garden in Skopje and wind/solar-powered educational installations for the Education Center Negrevo. Gender equality and empowerment of girls w
as central in these initiatives, with female role models in sciences and female mentors involved as co-leads, resulting in mobilization of an increased number of adolescent girls. 

In response to a request from the Ministry of Education and Science (MOES), UNICEF supported the development of SOPs for Heat Waves for Schools - adopted for use by schools country-wide -, and the drafting of recommendations for schools in cases of air pollution, addressing the two largest environmental health risks for children in the country. Youth also contributed to the Children and Youth Call to Action within the ECA Regional Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction. The ongoing advocacy, including public advocacy on climate and environmental health risks and on the impact of air quality, contributed to these developments, and a historical decision by the Supreme Court which adopted a principled position that "the state is obliged to provide a healthy living environment, including the right to clean air, as an individual right of citizens". During the country’s official address at the Conference of Parties (COP29) in Baku, the President of North Macedonia specifically referred to the disproportionate vulnerability of children to climate change, and the need to prioritize mitigation and adaptation affecting the most vulnerable populations, including children. Building on these developments, UNICEF will expand its advocacy and support to ensure the government’s green transition and adaptation measures prioritize critical services for children across the health, education, child and social protection sectors particularly in the 2025 review of the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0.

Primary school network optimization and education funding reform are prioritized in the EU reform agenda, ensuring greater leverage and support for accelerated implementation. The country’s EU-endorsed reform agenda, which lays out the priority government reforms until 2027, includes the school network optimization and education funding reform. The associated 750 million EUR financial assistance package is conditional, among other things, on the adoption of the funding formulas for primary and secondary education transfers to municipalities – by the end of 2025 and 2026 respectively. This reform, led by MoES, is critical to strengthen the country’s human capital development and economic competitiveness. It will address the mismatch between allocation of education sector resources– both human and financial – and demographic realities, which is strongly connected to the current learning crisis. Nationwide, 90% of students learn in just 30% of schools, resulting in over-crowded classrooms, less instruction time, and limited opportunities for extra-curricular activities. The child population, on the other side, is rapidly shrinking and, in remote areas, almost half of students learn in extremely small or combined classes of different grades, often poorly equipped, with an adverse impact on learning and socialization. In 2024, the national methodology for primary education transfers to municipalities was developed to enhance the quality of education, support inclusion and equity. This work, supported by UNICEF in partnership with the World Bank, was incorporated by the Ministry of Finance in the updated Mid-Term Fiscal Strategy of the Government, envisaging a 38 per cent increase in funding over a five-year period (by $90 million). Based on consultations with local stakeholders, including students, UNICEF supported municipalities to develop detailed plans to adjust the primary school network, better allocate the school workforce and create modern conditions for learning.Previously developed plans for 10 municipalities were updated with new data, and consultations started on plans for an additional 24 municipalities. Work is expected to accelerate in 2025, considering the ambitious government targets.

Addressing increased vulnerabilities of children (equity, poverty, and exclusion) as a key advocacy priority. In 2024, the Ministry of Social Policy, Demography and Youth led the development of a draft costed National Action Plan (NAP) on Child Rights and an analysis, consultations, and recommendations on the implementation of the European Child Guarantee in North Macedonia, with the involvement of all relevant stakeholders and UNICEF technical support. The Plan incorporates policy measures to reduce child poverty and improve access to basic social services to reach most vulnerable children and envisages a 15% increase in the cash benefits for children. The government has indicated it will utilise EU pre-accession funds to pilot select services for children at risk of poverty and social exclusion under the framework of the Child Guarantee and UNICEF will continue providing technical assistance. In 2024, UNICEF undertook a situation analysis of children and adolescents (SitAn), with participation of key stakeholders and consultations with vulnerable children. The SitAn was an opportunity to reflect on the country’s progress towards realizing child rights, with six years remaining to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Key progress for children over the past period includes a reduced child and maternal mortality (SDG3); strong progress in de-institutionalization and inclusive education; and positive reforms of the legislative framework and social protection sector. Structural challenges were also highlighted, with deepening and persistent child poverty (SDG1); a concerning learning crisis (SDG4); and increasing vulnerability of children to climate change and environmental degradation (SDG13). These challenges are exacerbated by sweeping demographic changes in the country not yet translated into adjusted social services. Findings from the SitAn are critical in shaping UNICEF advocacy, influencing decisions-makers and leveraging resources and results fo
r children. 

Countrywide operationalisation of the human rights-based disability assessment of children. With the establishment and capacity development of two new regional disability assessment bodies in 2024, thanks to UNICEF support, the country has now expanded human rights-based disability assessment of children countrywide, reaching a milestone from the National Disability Strategy 2023-2030 and addressing a key recommendation from the 2022 Concluding Observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child. The system, now operated and funded by the Government, provides more than 2,700 children with assessments annually, enabling each child access to support services and programmes in health, education, social and child protection. The UNICEF-supported electronic register for children and youth with disabilities that have undergone assessment will improve the planning, delivery and monitoring of support services. 

Increased programme and operational effectiveness. The office focused on simplification and efficiencies across programmes and operations, resulting in enhanced focus on accountabilities, managing for results and efficiency. Work plans with government partners, for instance were ready for review or signed by end of 2024, months earlier than in previous years. Special consideration was given to advancing an ethical and positive workplace culture in a year of management transition, with a newly elected Country Office Staff Association (COSA), incoming Representative and Deputy Representative. These efforts showed promising results as the 2024 Global Staff Survey indicated significant improvements. Fundraising efforts resulted in 3.1 million USD of new funding mobilized, more than tripling results of the previous year. Additionally, in close partnership with the government, World Bank and European Union, the office maintained a strong focus on leveraging partnerships to achieve results for children in several areas (education; disability; social services for children) resulting in child-related priorities and funding featuring clearly in grants and loans to the country, including the recently approved Growth Plan for the Western Balkans. 

UN cooperation was strengthened. Key initiatives completed as part of UN coordination groups included, among others: the establishment of long-term arrangements for the provision of internet and transportation services as part of the Business Operations Strategy; capacity building with 19 civil society partners, conducted jointly with UNFPA, on operationalizing the UN Protocol on Allegations of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) involving Implementing Partners; the development of a common framework to support the Government in developing the new NDC 3.0; the development of several joint proposals, for instance on addressing poverty and exclusion as key drivers of irregular migration and child trafficking; and the realization of the Country Assessment, with a focus on leaving no-one behind in preparation for the upcoming UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2025-2029. UNICEF supported youth consultations as part of this process, through the UN Youth Consultative Board, and the use of U-Report.

The office capitalized on the mid-year opportunity of a newly elected government coming into office and the timely arrival of a new UNICEF Representative. UNICEF engaged in dialogue with the new leadership of over a dozen line ministries and government agencies to identify shared goals and priorities for children's rights in the new political agenda. UNICEF reinforced its positioning with the new government by securing the Prime Minister’s commitment to organize a “Kids Takeover the Government,” to mark the 2024 World Children’s Day. 54 adolescents from across the country (38 girls, 16 boys) took over the Government Office and engaged in a dialogue with the Prime Minister and nine Ministers, sharing their views, concerns and policy recommendations on key issues impacting their lives, such as climate, advanced technologies, and demographic change. 

Partnership with the World Bank (WB) continued to be central to leveraging resources for children in North Macedonia. In education, the WB and UNICEF jointly supported the ongoing school optimization process and education funding formula reviews, which form the cornerstone of public sector reform in education, led by the Ministry of Education and Science. UNICEF and the WB undertook joint advocacy and technical support, while ensuring strong coordination with all relevant stakeholders in the education sector, including development partners (USAID, the Swiss Embassy, European Union); the Association of Local Self-Government (ZELS) and national think tanks. In the child and social protection sector, UNICEF drew on its model of human rights-based child disability assessment to leverage significant WB investment in expanding the system to become universal – for all people with disability – under the leadership of the Ministry of Social Policy, Demography and Youth (MoSPDY). The UNICEF-WB partnership on early childhood education and care was further strengthened, with effective coordination between the WB programme on expansion of pre-school services and UNICEF’s support to curriculum reform -- both critical, considering only 46% of children 3 to 5 years are currently enrolled in pre-school. Looking forward, UNICEF and the WB are coordinating efforts on the functional review and strengthening of Centres of Social Work, supporting analysis on reorganization, better integration of case management, and ensuring child protection is adequately resourced, as part of broader social protection reform.

The European Union Delegation (EUD) was critical partner on advocacy for children’s rights. UNICEF contributions to the Annual EU Progress Report were well reflected and ensured a strong focus on the need to address violence against children and social exclusion, child marriage, inclusive quality education, and justice for children. The office maintained ongoing dialogue with the EU Ambassador and technical EUD counterparts, particularly in the areas of education and child protection. Timely, high-level advocacy with the EU Ambassador and his team on the risk of the country backsliding on inclusive education and gender equality resulted in strong alignment and common messaging towards the Government. Work to advance analysis and planning for the introduction of the European Child Guarantee was closely coordinated with the EUD and the relevant departments for EU integration and programmes in Government.

In the health and nutrition sector, the main partnerships included those with the Ministry of Health, the Institute of Public Health, the University Clinic for Psychiatry and WHO to advance programme priorities on primary health care, immunization, mental health of children and adolescents and addressing an increasing trend in child overweight as a key contributor to non-communicable diseases. UNICEF continued to partner with the professional associations of doctors and nurses to mobilize professionals and ensure large reach of the primary health care professionals – family doctors and patronage nurses in particular.

A wide range of partnerships were critical to achieving results and leveraging resources for children in the education sector. Positive results on climate change education and youth engagement on environmental pollution enabled UNICEF to mobilize an additional $1.9 million from the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA), including a second phase of the regional SIDA programme on air quality. UNICEF collaborated closely with Helvetas, a Swiss government-funded organization and initiated a new sub-regional partnership with a private company, NELT, to jointly support greening of VET curricula and dual education. UNICEF coordinated with GIZ contributions to the National Action Plan for Integration of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) and Climate Change Education (CCE) which sets the basis for Global Climate Fund applications; and with[LM1]  UN agencies (UNDP, UNOPS, IOM, FAO and ILO) to define joint support to the Government in the review of the NDC 3.0; municipal councils and civil society organizations leading adolescents and youth engagement on climate action at local level.

Long-standing cross-sectoral partnerships with the Ministries of Justice, Interior and Social Policy, Demography and Youth continued in the area of child protection. UNICEF quickly built a partnership with the newly established Ministry of Digital Transformation, with ongoing engagement on the integration of healthy digital behaviours and child protection in the national cybersecurity framework and addressing online child sexual abuse and exploitation. UNICEF continued to partner with civil society organisations which play a critical role mobilising children and communities and providing services at local level. Building on several years of successful partnership, UNICEF and the Foundation Telekom for Macedonia finalized an agreement for a child-led anti-bullying programme and digital campaign, which will be implemented in 2025. At inter-agency level, UNICEF coordinated with UNFPA, UNODC, IOM and UNHCR to jointly advocate and resource mobilisation efforts for key child protection issues, including child marriage, children in the streets and ending statelessness through free, universal birth registration.
