The year was marked by the Presidential and Parliamentary campaign, elections, and transition resulting in new leadership and a restructuring of key institutions. The prolonged election period, including three months of a caretaker government beforehand and the transition to a new Government, slowed down key developments and programme implementation across several sectors. For example, youth engagement on municipal air quality plans and environmental action was suspended at the beginning of the year due to restrictions on activities in the pre-electoral period. The Agency of Youth and Sports, responsible for the programme, was later dismantled by the new government, with youth responsibilities transferred to the Ministry of Social Policy, Demography and Youth (MoSPDY). As this transition is still ongoing, planned interventions could not be implemented in 2024, however UNICEF is working closely with MoSPDY to resolve this and move forward with the programme in 2025.  
At the same time, the elections also provided opportunities to put children’s rights more squarely on the Government’s agenda and in some cases to accelerate the reform direction. The development of school optimization plans and a revised funding formula for primary education, supported by UNICEF and the World Bank, received stronger attention from key decision makers. This enabled UNICEF to elevate dialogue with the Minster of Education and the Prime Minister within their first two months in office. This commitment was translated into concrete terms by inclusion of these areas in the government Reform Agenda of the EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans. Ensuring adequate additional funding for the implementation of optimization plans and leveraging partnership with the EU, development partners and international financial institutions will be critical to the success of the reform, considering the constrained budget environment. More broadly, UNICEF’s engagement with all political parties, including through its partnership the Parliament positioned it well to quickly establish positive collaboration with the incoming coalition government.

While the number of children with disabilities enrolled in mainstream schools has doubled over the past four years, there was some backsliding on inclusive education. UNICEF continued strong advocacy and technical support to sustain groundbreaking changes introduced by the 2019 Primary Education Law, which transformed special schools into resource centres and mandated the enrolment of children with disabilities in mainstream primary schools. In response to vocal pushback by some teachers and parents on these provisions in 2024, UNICEF facilitated technical consultations with parents of children with disabilities, teachers, education assistants, academics, and civil society. These informed a policy brief highlighting progress, challenges, and recommendations for implementation of inclusive education which was used for public and bilateral advocacy to retain the strong inclusive provisions of the law. This included high-level advocacy towards the Minister of Education; the Parliament Speaker and Ombudsman; the Parliamentary Committee on Education, and key Ambassadors. Despite these efforts, Parliament approved amendments to the Primary Education Law allowing enrolment or transfer of children learning on a modified programme to resource centers. Going forward UNICEF will continue to support system strengthening for inclusive education, including focusing on teacher core competencies to support inclusive classrooms and support mechanisms; and engaging teachers, parents, and communities to address attitudinal barriers and stigma towards disability.

Thanks to the successful fundraising efforts in 2024, the year 2025 will be pivotal in consolidating key results for children prioritized in the current country programme. This includes enhancing primary health care, strengthening the childcare system, and promoting equitable and quality education. Additionally, the findings from the 2024 SitAn and recent developments related to the EU enlargement agenda present opportunities to scale up results with a forward-looking perspective, in line with leadership areas defined for the upcoming programming cycle: optimizing social services, addressing poverty and exclusion—particularly for Roma children and children with disabilities—and prioritizing green skills and services.

Poland is a European Member State situated in Central Europe, bordering Ukraine and six other countries, including the Russian Federation and Belarus. As such, the country is on the frontline of the Ukrainian refugee crisis. Given the uncertainty and unpredictability of the war in Ukraine, throughout 2024, Poland continued playing a vital role in hosting Ukrainian refugees, with over 7.57 million crossing its borders during the year.[1] On 1 July – in response to the increasingly protracted nature of the crisis – the Government of Poland extended the period in which refugees from Ukraine are allowed to stay in the country until September 2025. As of December, 987,781 Ukrainian refugees remained in Poland, of whom 37 per cent were children, 60 per cent women and girls, and 7 per cent elderly persons.[2] Changes to policies supporting refugees – such as mandatory co-payments for collective shelter accommodation – were intended to balance support and resource sustainability but may have increased vulnerability among marginalized groups. 

More than 200,000 children and adolescents from Ukraine are learning in Polish schools. From September 2024, enrolment at school was made mandatory for Ukrainian children in Poland. Previously, these children did not have to attend Polish schools if they were enrolled in the Ukrainian education system online. Importantly, payment of the “800+” benefit – the monthly child allowance of PLN 800 (about EUR 186) – has been made conditional on the attendance of Ukrainian children in Polish schools.[3] Since the introduction of compulsory education in September 2024 more than 18,000 new students are in the Polish Education system. This is a much smaller increase (13,5 percent increase) than the number of potential new enrolments forecast by the Ministry of Education.[4]

The new policy of mandatory school attendance brings specific challenges and additional support needs for students, families and the education system. Key challenges include a shortage of qualified teachers, limited availability of support for Polish as a second language, and gaps in mental health and social integration assistance for students adapting to a new educational system. Adolescents and children who have been out of formal education for extended periods require tailored and bespoken support aiming at ensuring retention in the Polish education system. An Education Sector survey conducted before the start of the school year highlighted barriers to adolescents accessing education, including differences between the Polish and Ukrainian systems, lack of knowledge of Polish language, and bullying from peers[5]. Without targeted interventions, mandatory schooling may place significant additional strain on local education infrastructure, teachers, and social support services, potentially affecting the quality of education for both refugee and host community students and increase levels of dropout. 

Child protection monitoring highlights the persistent risks faced by refugee children and adolescents, including discrimination, bullying, and increased exposure to psychological violence. According to the Socio-Economic Insight Survey (SEIS) 2024, 39% of refugees experienced hostile behaviours or negative attitudes from local population (mainly verbal aggression), a 7% increase from 2023. Psychological violence in the community remained the top risk faced by refugee children, with a significant increase for girls by 11% in 2024[6].  Beyond these risks, gaps in alternative care systems are increasing protection concerns for Ukrainian refugee children.  Ukrainian children evacuated from alternative care facilities to Poland remain outside the Polish alternative care system. Poland has 964.97 per 100,000 children in alternative care[7] - one of the highest rates in Europe - and has been facing increasing rates of family separation and placement in care in the last years¿[8]. The system faces capacity gaps which are being exacerbated by the increasing presence of refugee and migrant children in the system, with more than 1,000 court decisions for placement  remaining non-executed annually.[9]

At the beginning of 2024, nearly 1,500 children evacuated from institutions in Ukraine in 2022 were still accommodated in 24 facilities across Poland, with 4 such facilities hosting over 100 children each. While the number of children has fallen to 900 by the end of the year due to cross-border returns, placements in Ukrainian foster families, resumed adoption procedures in Ukraine, and aging out, care, support and advocacy for this particularly vulnerable group of children continued to be a priority for UNICEF. 

As of June 2024, 44,501 children from Ukraine in total had temporary guardians appointed in Poland since the onset of the full-scale war in Ukraine. However, it remains unclear how many of these children are still in Poland. According to estimates based on data received in November 2024 from the Social Insurance Institutions, 9,100 children with temporary guardians – including children evacuated from institutions in Ukraine – remain in Poland.

Collective accommodation centres remained a critical element of Poland’s refugee response. By the end of the year, there were 939 active centres housing around 29,000 individuals, mainly in Mazowieckie, Dolnoslaskie, and Malopolskie voivodeships. These centres primarily provided basic shelter and meals but lacked adequate support services, such as mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), legal aid, and integration activities. Vulnerable groups – including children, single mothers, people with disabilities, and Ukrainian Roma families – were disproportionately affected by these gaps. Changes to the Special Act on accommodation support (which limit the centres that can receive support, reduce the types of support available, and make contributions from residents necessary after 120 days if residents receive 800+ benefit) further increased the risk of homelessness for residents, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address these challenges.

Poland faced ongoing mixed migration pressures at the Polish Belarusian border alongside the influx from Ukraine. Between January and December 2024, 30,400[10] attempted irregular entries were recorded, a 17% increase from the previous year[11]. Most of the individuals originated from Somalia, the Syrian Arab Republic, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Afghanistan, Yemen, and India. Compared to 2023, there has also been a significant increase in the number of foreigners detained or identified at the Belarus-Poland border—nearly three times more. As of December 2024, 4,247 individuals were detained or identified, compared to 1,920 in 2023, including 69 children held across detention facilities.

In October, Poland adopted its new 2025–2030 Migration Strategy with the main aim to “restore control and ensure security”. The Strategy is intended to introduce new measures to regulate migration and stresses the importance of integration policies and programmes. It outlined the Government of Poland’s plan to introduce legal amendments allowing temporary suspension of asylum procedures, as well as new rules for granting rights to study, reside and work in Poland.

In December, in an expedited procedure, the Government of Poland adopted a proposal to amend the Act on Granting Protection to Foreigners in the Territory of the Republic of Poland, which introduces the possibility of imposing temporary and territorial limitations of the right to apply for international protection.  While the amendment outlines exemptions for certain groups, including unaccompanied children, pregnant women, and individuals requiring special treatment due to age or health, these limitations could significantly restrict access to asylum procedures, increase the risk of refoulement, and undermine the fundamental right to seek protection. Additionally, the proposed restrictions may lead to heightened risks of family separation, particularly for individuals seeking reunification with relatives already in Poland, contrary to international refugee protection standards. It is also feared that the amendment may lead to increased detention of children and denial of access to territory. As per UNHCR[12], the amendment could create legal and practical barriers for asylum seekers, limiting Poland’s ability to uphold its obligations under international and EU law. The proposed amendment is currently pending approval in the Polish Parliament. 

In the final quarter, contingency planning intensified in anticipation of potential winter-related refugee inflows due to geopolitical developments, the sustained impact of the war on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, and escalation of Russian attacks. Increased border crossings by men (over 8,500 newly registered men between October and December and a total of 34,208 newly registered men in 2024)[13]reflect shifting displacement dynamics. UNICEF and partners enhanced preparedness efforts, ensuring resources and response plans were ready to support the most vulnerable populations in case of new mass arrivals into Poland.

In 2024, Poland remained the second largest refugee hosting country in Europe. With a sustained focus on children’s rights and well-being, UNICEF Refugee Response Office (RRO) Poland collaborated with central and local government institutions and civil society organizations to respond to persistent humanitarian needs, promote community engagement, and strengthen education, health and child protection systems to ensure systematic inclusion of refugee children and families. By prioritizing equity, preparedness, and sustainable capacity-building, UNICEF’s efforts not only met urgent humanitarian needs but also contributed to long-term improvements in national systems and infrastructure. This dual approach ensured that Poland’s institutions became more resilient and better equipped to support vulnerable children both now and in the future.

Education
In 2024, UNICEF prioritized inclusive education access, supporting the integration of 150,000 refugeechildren into primary and secondary education, expanding early childhood education, and enhancing skills building, career guidance, and psychosocial support through the education systems for adolescents and youth.

Building teacher capacities 
UNICEF’s Accessible School for All (ASA) project, implemented in partnership with Poland’s Ministry of National Education, the Educational Research Institute (IBE), universities, and NGOs, marked a milestone in inclusive education. In 2024, the project focused on strengthening the competencies of specialist teachers in Polish schools – including educationalists, psychologists, and speech therapists – to provide tailored support for refugee children that are in the Polish education system, parents and educators.
 
A total of 1,139 kindergarten teachers (92 per cent female, 8 per cent male) from 500 institutions were trained, directly benefiting 28,000 children (50 per cent female, 50 per cent male). Simultaneously, 1,127 learning accessibility counsellors (92 per cent female, 8 per cent male) gained skills to identify barriers to learning and inclusion of migrants and refugees in school environment, such as language difficulties, special educational needs, and psychosocial challenges and coordinate support activities, reaching 31,000 children (50 per cent female, 50 per cent male) to foster inclusion of all children in school settings.  
 
The programme adopted an innovative model to make the entire school community responsible for the inclusion of all children. Key components of the programme included the introduction of a the role of Learning Accessibility Counsellor to systematize support; piloting a unique collaboration framework uniting UNICEF, government bodies, academia, and NGOs working with migrant and refugee children; prioritizing practical, in-service training focused on "learning by doing" rather than theoretical instruction; and embedding equity-driven practices to ensure schools address diverse needs of children holistically.
 
Back to learning 
To support successful implementation of the new policy of mandatory schooling for refugee children in Poland, UNICEF and the Ministry of National Education launched the Back to Learning campaign, which harnessed social media to reach 2 million views and drive the enrolment of around 18,000 new Ukrainian children into formal education. Complementing this, a nationwide outreach campaign in December 2024 disseminated information to over 50,000 educational institutions via Poland’s National System of Educational Information. This multi-pronged approach—combining policy reform, teacher capacity-building, and targeted outreach—advanced education access for the most vulnerable children while strengthening systemic resilience for future crises. 

Intercultural assistants 
UNICEF, together with nine municipalities and four civil society partners, deployed 412 intercultural assistants (93 per cent female, 7 per cent male) in schools across nine municipalities to help refugee children overcome language and cultural barriers. These professionals played a key role in overcoming language barriers between Ukrainian families and Polish educators, explaining educational regulations, and clarifying cultural differences. In this way they supported enrolment and retention of refugee students, and improved children's social integration. The employment of intercultural assistants also helped prevent potential conflicts between students or between refugee and host community families, creating a more supportive atmosphere in schools. 

Digital learning 
In 2024, UNICEF collaborated closely with Poland’s Ministry of National Education, particularly its Department of Innovation and Development, to leverage digital tools in addressing educational disparities for refugee children. Flagship initiatives like the Akelius language-learning app and Learning Passport platform played a transformative role in bridging gaps. The Akelius app supported 22,304 Ukrainian students in acquiring Polish language skills, while the Learning Passport trained 4,626 teachers to deliver mental health support, cross-cultural education, and inclusive pedagogy to 101,772 children. These efforts aimed to strengthen refugee children’s adaptation to Polish schools and foster supportive learning environments. 
UNICEF also contributed to shaping the Policy of Digital Transformation of Education, ensuring its alignment with equity, inclusion, and the unique needs of refugee children. Partnering with the EdTech Hub, UNICEF integrated priorities such as media literacy, cybersecurity, digital competencies for students with special needs, and innovative teaching methods into the policy framework. Technical support was prioritized for areas critical to refugee integration, including the development of teacher training modules on modern technologies. 

Building local capacity for integration 
In mid-2024, UNICEF and the European Commission launched two Technical Support Instruments (TSI) projects in Poland, each designed to move the refugee response beyond emergency approaches. Recognizing the urgent need to enhance the inclusivity and resilience of municipal systems, both initiatives are intended to build local capacities to ensure that refugee and migrant children receive sustained, equitable access to quality education and other social services. The first project, “Development of a Framework for Long-Term and Sustainable Inclusion of Migrant and Refugee Children in Education”, was developed in in the first half of the year in close consultation with the cities of Wroclaw and Katowice, and the European Commission DG REFORM. A kickoff meeting in Katowice in September 2024 launched the project officially and by the end of 2024, an inception report and a clearly defined methodological approach were completed. This methodology is designed to systematically identify and address gaps in educational support for refugee and migrant students, providing a roadmap for more inclusive, effective, and sustainable integration measures within Polish schools. The second project, “Supporting Municipalities in Improving Access to Quality and Inclusive Services for Children and Caregivers with Refugee and Migrant Backgrounds: Moving Forward from an Emergency Approach to Long-Term Inclusion Strategies”, is a multi-country project spanning six municipalities across Poland, Romania, and Slovakia. In Poland, UNICEF partners with the cities of Lublin and Bialystok. The project was developed in the first half of 2024 and launched officially in Lublin in October 2024. Project implementation is ongoing, with national consultations and stakeholder mapping already completed. 
 
Enhancing Youth Engagement and Skills Development
UNICEF expanded youth engagement in Poland through U-Report Europe, now its largest community with 4,716 U-Reporters (65% girls). In 2024, 1,400 new users joined via outreach events and co-creation sessions. Ten polls on refugee needs, mental health, bullying, misinformation, education, and green skills gathered nearly 2,000 responses. These insights led to program adjustments, including better targeting and the development of new educational resources.  With a focus on helping Ukrainian refugee adolescents (10-19) develop 21st century skills, UNICEF piloted UPSHIFT in four cities (Warsaw, Wroclaw, Lódz, Katowice) within both formal and non-formal education. 114 teachers and youth workers (51% Ukrainian, 49% Polish) were trained, leading workshops that launched 50 youth-led projects benefiting over 5,000 community members. Through a partnership with Pro Futuro Foundation partnership, 4,400 Ukrainian youth (48% female, 52% male), including out-of-school and at-risk youth, accessed non-formal education through digital means (online courses and webinars), focused on topics related to career orientation and planning as well as entrepreneurship and financial literacy.

Child protection 
In 2024, UNICEF continued working with national and local partners to strengthen Poland's child protection system for the inclusion of refugee children and families. Key efforts included alternative care, social inclusion, prevention of violence against children (VAC), and enhancing access to justice. 

Alternative care and foster family support 
UNICEF collaborated with partners to support over 700 children evacuated from Ukrainian institutions across Poland who remain in care facilities outside the national system. UNICEF provided support to increase supervision, relocate children to care homes in line with the national standards and ensure access to services as per the needs of children. UNICEF supported partners for direct provision of services for these children, including psychosocial support, medical consultations, needs assessments, and creating Child-Friendly Spaces and Adolescent Clubs. With UNICEF support nearly 200 children from Ukrainian institutional care system were relocated to 17 group homes in Poland.  Individual assessments were conducted for 740 children evacuated to 4 locations in Poland by Ukrainian and Polish authorities to inform the long-term planning for all evacuated children. 
UNICEF’s efforts focused on supporting Ukrainian foster families and establishing new foster families under Polish law. UNICEF supported mapping of 174 Ukrainian foster families and 13 Ukrainian foster houses evacuated to Poland caring for 499 children. UNICEF modelled the Lighthouse Centre offering comprehensive support to foster families with the aim to integrate Ukrainian foster families into Poland’s foster care community, offering psychological support, physiotherapy, sensory therapy, and speech therapy. 17 new foster families were recruited in Lódz. UNICEF supported provision of housing, psychological support, and cultural orientation to foster parents, alongside awareness campaigns to increase the availability of foster care services reaching 8,245 people. 

Spilno Hubs and integrated services 
Six multi-sectoral family support centers, or “Spilno Hubs” in cities like Lublin and Kraków offered comprehensive support, including mental health services, legal aid, and Polish language courses. These hubs reached 23,631 individuals, 47 per cent of whom were children. Partnerships with the VELA Foundation extended psychosocial support to 980 vulnerable refugee children and 1,732 caregivers in collective accommodations. 

Justice system reforms 
UNICEF worked with Ministry of Justice to enhance the capacity and adapt the national mechanisms to ensure access to child-friendly justice to refugee children and handle the increasing number of refugee children in contact with the justice system (children vicitms of violence and crime, children in conflict with the law and children in family proceedings). UNICEF supported the National School of Judiciary and Public Prosecution to train justice professionals to handle sexual abuse and domestic violence cases, and to communicate with children in a sensitive manner. With the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), UNICEF organized two training events on alternatives to detention for migration reasons, for nearly 70 judges ruling in detention cases. Thanks to these efforts, 8,559 child victims and witnesses of crime gained access to more child-sensitive justice processes. With ECARO and Poland’s Ministry of Justice, UNICEF rolled out a training of trainers’ module on child-friendly legal services: nine trainers received certificates and will conduct training in this area in the future. 
  
UNICEF contributed to developing national templates for child safeguarding standards in collective reception centres and juvenile facilities, which were adopted by the Ministry of Justice. Moreover, UNICEF partnered with the Institute of Forensic Research to create four sets of guidelines for interviewing children in various procedures and two sets of guidelines for developing expert opinions in criminal and family matters. 
 
On request of the Ministry of Justice, in response to the needs for development of the model of multidisciplinary response to violence against children, UNICEF in co-operation with the European Commission is implementing the project funded by the European Union via the Technical Support Instrument “Strengthening the response to violence against children through better informed policies and enhanced institutional capacity”. Within this multi-country Polish-Romanian project UNICEF RRO in Poland will conduct the mapping of existing support services, including a review the Polish legal framework and a capacity assessment of professionals working on violence against children, which will be the basis for the other project activities, such as developing the standards for Barnahus centres in Poland and for the training and capacity building interventions, as well as developing recommendations and roadmaps. 
 
Community Engagement and Social and Behavior Change
Continuing to deliver on its commitments to ensure accountability to affected populations, UNICEF maintained two-way communication channels and involved refugees in programme design, using platforms like SpilnoinPL to provide trusted information on access to health, education, and other social services and collect regular feedback. In 2024 the platform reached 313,000 new users, and its social media channels engaged over 34,000 followers. This dynamic engagement improved access to public services and fostered community participation.
 
Behavioural research and awareness campaigns 
Collaborative studies with academic institutions informed Poland’s first behavioural interventions to address vaccine hesitancy and mental health stigma among refugees. The “Trust Vaccinations” campaign combined community events engaging 600 participants. Additionally, behaviourally informed research involving 700 Ukrainian adolescents highlighted stigma as a significant barrier to mental health and support and contributed to improvements in the design of MHPSS programs to increase service uptake, especially among young males. A separate study involving 1,673 Ukrainian caregivers explored attitudes toward parenting practices, revealing psychosocial needs and informing interventions to support children aged 3–16. 

PSEA and Safeguarding 
During 2024, UNICEF applied a collaborative approach between AAP and PSEA, which significantly enhanced the safeguarding of refugees and vulnerable communities. This approach focused on strengthening trust and credibility among stakeholders, optimizing feedback and complaint mechanisms, improving PSEA reporting channels, and conducting joint capacity-building. UNICEF delivered a training session for 40 municipal and civil society partners to strengthen PSEA reporting channels and protocols. In 2024, over 64,000 people (34,817 girls and women) shared their concerns and asked questions through variety of feedback mechanisms managed by UNICEF and its partners, including social media channels, hotlines, suggestion boxes and feedback forms. Technical support was provided to partners to develop child safeguarding and PSEA policies and action plans. By December, all CSO partners in Poland demonstrated full or medium PSEA capacity, and over 99,560 beneficiaries, including over 40,000 women and girls, had access to safe channels to report SEA by aid workers through UNICEF-supported programmes. 

Health: vaccination drives and health equity 
During European Immunization Week, UNICEF RRO partnered with Poland’s Ministry of Health (MoH), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the Institute of Mother and Child Foundation (IMCF) to address disparities in vaccine access. Targeted campaigns prioritized refugee children and marginalized Polish communities, combining mobile clinics with multilingual outreach to counter misinformation. These efforts to increase immunization coverage will reduce risks of measles, polio, and other vaccine-preventable diseases. 
To move towards universal health coverage, UNICEF trained 86 nursery nurses in trauma-informed care and early childhood development. This initiative enhanced their ability to support families, particularly those affected by displacement, while also promoting inclusive practices for children with disabilities. 

Emergency preparedness and response 
UNICEF’s proactive approach to crisis management was evident during the September 2024 floods in southwestern Poland. Rapid distribution of 32 institutional hygiene kits and 974 emergency kits to Wroclaw municipality ensured access to clean water and sanitation for thousands. Over the course of the year, partnerships with NGOs such as VELA and municipal authorities facilitated the use of 1,913 hygiene kits in collective shelters, benefiting refugees and vulnerable host community members. 

Conclusion 
UNICEF’s 2024 initiatives in Poland demonstrated the impact of working at the humanitarian-development nexus to address complex and persistent humanitarian challenges. By integrating refugee needs into national systems – from health care and education to child protection – UNICEF ensured that over 250,000 Ukrainian children and adults accessed vital services while building national and local capacity for long-term resilience. Partnerships with government bodies, NGOs, and international agencies laid the groundwork for sustainable progress, aligning with Poland’s commitment to the SDGs.

UNICEF Refugee Response Office in Poland leveraged its partnerships with national, regional, and local governmental bodies and technical institutions and strengthened engagement with civil society to increase its impact via system strengthening and policy level support while continuing to provide essential assistance to Ukrainian refugee families.

The RRO partnered with four government line ministries in 2024: with the Ministry of Education to enhance access to education at all levels, with the Ministry of Justice on child-friendly legal services and prevention of violence against children, the Ministry of Family and Social Affairs on care and protection of children evacuated from Ukrainian alternative care to Poland and enhancing the national alternative care system, and with the Institute of Mother and Child, under the Ministry of Health, improve adolescent mental health and well-being. UNICEF has also provided coordinated support to the governments of Ukraine and Poland to ensure an improved protective environment for the 740 children evacuated from institutions in Ukraine remaining in Poland.

UNICEF also worked at the subnational level in Poland, with an increasing focus on building capacity to provide services at local level in addition to service delivery. UNICEF continued implementation of programs through joint workplans with 11 municipalities, including Gdansk, Gdynia, Sopot, Bialystok, Warsaw, Wroclaw, Katowice, Krakow, Lodz, Kazimierza Wielka and Lublin, as well as the locality of Powiat Slupski, localities which cover an estimated 75 per cent of the refugee population. The increased focus on capacity-strengthening was reflected through two new EU-supported projects that began in 2024: “Supporting Municipalities in Improving Access to Quality and Inclusive Services for Children and Caregivers with Refugee and Migrant Backgrounds” in Lublin and Bialystok, and “Development of a Framework for Long-Term and Sustainable Inclusion of Migrant and Refugee Children in Education” in Wroclaw and Katowice. A new agreement with the Union of Voivodship Marshals of Poland, which unites all 16 voivodship marshals across the country was signed, aiming to promote support solutions for teachers, particularly in their daily work with refuge and migrant children, including refugees from Ukraine.

UNICEF also remained actively involved at the interagency level. In the field, particularly in Lubelskie, Malopolskie, and Podkarpackie, UNICEF continued its active participation in humanitarian coordination platforms. In 2024, UNICEF led the Education Sector Working Group (EWG), uniting 32 member organizations to advocate inclusive education for Ukrainian refugee children. UNICEF provided significant support and leadership in the Inter-Agency PSEA Network in Poland, strengthening efforts to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse. In collaboration with UNHCR and a local CSO partner, UNICEF co-led the Child Protection Sub-Working Group, which was integrated into the Protection Cluster Working Group in 2024 and continued to engage as part of the Information Management Working Group, MHPSS and AAP Working Groups.

Partnership with local civil society organizations remained a key strategy in 2024, working with 14 civil society partners. A new agreement with the Ombudsperson’s Office will ensure the rights of refugee children in Poland are protected, support monitoring of the situation of refugee children, strengthen the engagement and participation of refugee children in Poland. UNICEF is also expanding its engagement with academic institutions, working with SPWS University, the leading psychology academic institution in Poland, to address mental health issues faced by adolescents and refugee children and families and partnering with the University of Warsaw and the Foundation for Child Development to co-host the EARLI 2024 conference, promoting refugee inclusion, empathy and creativity in early childhood education.

The Training of Trainers (ToT) program, organized by UNICEF and SWPS Innovations (SWPS University), ran from September to December 2024, equipping 75 experts from government ministries, NGOs, universities, municipalities, UN agencies, and international organizations with practical skills in applying behavioral interventions to public policies.
UNICEF is also contributing to the future reconstruction of Ukraine through a new focus on public-private partnerships for the upskilling of refugee adolescents and youth. Together with CARE and the Tent Partnership for Refugees, CARE and UNICEF is co-leading the Skills Alliance platform in Poland, which was founded following the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Berlin in mid-2024, and connects public and private sectors, donors, and NGOs to help displaced Ukrainians in Poland find employment and access upskilling opportunities, including through multiple learning pathways and work experience for youth, to better equip them to participate in the rebuilding of post-war Ukraine.

Initial engagement with the Ministry of Interior and the Border Guard focused on enhancing monitoring of Unaccompanied and Separated Children (USAC) movements at the border and strengthening oversight of collective shelters to ensure their safety and well-being in 2025.

Indicator_Status3:
Transition from delivering services to Strengthening Municipal Systems
UNICEF’s programming in Poland in 2024 faced several challenges, necessitating adaptation. The 2024 Humanitarian Performance Monitoring framework (HPM) reflected challenges in achieving initially ambitious targets while highlighting the need to adapt to evolving circumstances and priorities. Key factors contributing to the underachievement of targets, such as rightsizing, knowledge transition and gradual capacity building of staff, as well as programme’s focus on vulnerability instead of previous years' large-scale service delivery (the transition from Blue Dots, which delivered immediate aid to over 840,000 refugees in 2023, to Spilno Hubs was intended to provide tailored, multidisciplinary services for immediate, medium-, and long-term needs), have shaped plans for a more refined and effective approach in 2025.

Increased involvement of municipalities influenced results. While UNICEF focused on fostering sustainability through increased collaboration with and financial contribution to joint work plans by municipality partners, there was a lack of clear methodology to distinguish results achieved through partner contributions. UNICEF ORE primarily supported refugee populations, while municipal contributions often addressed the needs of vulnerable communities, including host population (such as providing MHPSS for children with disabilities). This more systems strengthening approach, while increasing ownership and potential sustainability of the interventions, led to a higher than anticipated proportion of host community beneficiaries in many programs.

Despite these challenges, valuable lessons were learned. The greater focus on strengthening municipal-level government systems and increased financing by municipal governments led to more host community recipients of support, particularly for mental health programmes. This shift underscored the importance of adapting targets and strategies to evolving needs and ensuring continuous capacity building to address operational challenges effectively.

In 2025, the RRO will refine its approach by introducing a clearer methodology to account for indirect beneficiaries and distinguish municipal and UNICEF contributions. Targets will be more focused and aligned with the RRO’s revised value proposition, prioritizing sustainable, high-impact interventions and multi-sectoral support for the most vulnerable groups in the refugee population. This change is intended to provide a more accurate reflection of programme reach and effectiveness, while addressing humanitarian needs using a systems-strengthening approach.

Driving Innovation for Inclusive and Digital Education
Hosting nearly one million refugees, including almost 400,000 children, has strained education resources and infrastructure in Poland. Polish schools have struggled with the diverse educational backgrounds, cultural differences, and language barriers of Ukrainian children, many of whom have faced severe psychosocial distress due to war, displacement, and separation from family and friends, complicating their integration into Poland’s education system. Initial attempts to support learners, such as text-to-speech audio files, encountered technical issues like pronunciation errors, requiring revisions. Additionally, lack of adequate ICT capacity in schools and the need for teacher training in digital tools further compounded these challenges.
The response to the crisis has provided valuable insights. Collaboration between international organizations, governments, and civil society has been crucial in addressing complex educational and psychosocial needs. Initiatives like the Learning Passport, developed by UNICEF and Microsoft, have highlighted the importance of providing teachers with accessible resources and training to support both learning and mental health. The Akelius e-teacher training modules demonstrated the effectiveness of bite-sized, flexible training courses tailored to teachers’ busy schedules. The Pi-station programme has emphasized the value of aligning educational content with refugees’ home curricula to ease transitions and improve retention. Empowering school leaders to drive digital innovation and ensuring strong ICT management systems at school level are critical for sustainable progress. Continuous feedback and adaptation, as seen in the reworking of text-to-speech audio files, are essential to meet learners’ needs effectively.
The rolling out of the fully accredited online teacher training course for Polish as a second language in September 2024 was a significant step toward equipping educators with the skills needed to support refugee children. The expansion of digital learning tools, such as the Learning Passport and Pi-station, will continue to provide flexible and accessible education for Ukrainian students. Strengthening ICT infrastructure and digital learning management systems in schools will remain a priority to ensure long-term sustainability. Additionally, focus on cross-cultural communication and mental health support will be crucial for fostering inclusive and supportive learning environments.

Strengthening Child-Sensitive Justice Systems
Poland faces several challenges in ensuring justice for children, particularly refugee and migrant children. The diverse legal needs of these children, coupled with their experiences of trauma and displacement, complicate their access to justice. The lack of adequate training for justice professionals in child-sensitive procedures and the need for robust legal frameworks further hinder effective support. Additionally, the integration of child safeguarding standards in shelters and juvenile centres remains a significant challenge.

The collaboration between UNICEF and the Ministry of Justice has highlighted the importance of strengthening legal frameworks and building the capacity of justice professionals to enhance access to justice for children, especially refugees and migrants. Key achievements include developing safeguarding standards for shelters and juvenile centres, training over 5,000 justice professionals in child-friendly procedures, and addressing vulnerabilities specific to refugee children. The partnership has also emphasized the need for continuous adaptation and feedback, as seen in the development of methodologies for interviewing children and issuing guidelines for expert witnesses, ensuring a child-sensitive approach in legal proceedings.
In 2025, UNICEF and the Ministry of Justice, with the National School of Judiciary and Public Prosecution and the Institute of Forensic Research, will focus on enhancing child-sensitive justice for refugee and migrant children in Poland. Key initiatives include strengthening legal frameworks, building the capacity of justice professionals, and implementing child safeguarding standards. The partnership is intended to improve local cooperation in child abuse cases, advance serious case review processes, and expand training programmes for justice professionals. Additionally, innovative projects like a multidisciplinary model for children who have survived violence will be launched, ensuring a safer, more inclusive environment for all children.

Conclusion
Strategic humanitarian investments, such as intercultural assistants and justice system reforms, were scaled by the government, ensuring broader impact and sustainability. Initiatives like digital education and policy reforms extended beyond refugees to benefit host communities UNICEF’s adaptive shift from direct service delivery to capacity building and system strengthening has driven government-led scaling, broader impact, and long-term sustainability, ensuring both immediate humanitarian support and lasting structural improvements.

The year 2024 was a prosperous year for Uzbekistan despite the numerous global challenges. The country successfully organized parliamentary elections which took place amidst reforms continuing since 2017, including on socio-economic development, public administration, the judiciary, and respect for fundamental freedoms and human rights provisions in the 2023 Constitutional reforms. Significantly the gender quota for women has been increased from 30% to 40%. Women held 47 of the 150 seats in the outgoing Legislative Chamber and comprised 45% of candidates. Furthermore, the Speaker of the Senate, one of seven Deputy Speakers of the Legislative Chamber, and one of four Deputy Prime Ministers are women. 
 
In 2024, Uzbekistan experienced a robust economic growth at an average of 6.5% of GDP. This expansion was supported by increased remittance inflows, which rose to 14% of GDP in the first half of 2024, up from 13% in 2023. Despite this economic progress, the budget deficit widened slightly to 5.9% of GDP in the first half of 2024, compared to 5.7% in the same period of 2023. This fiscal gap may constrain the government's capacity to allocate additional resources to social sectors, including those directly affecting child well-being.  

The year 2024 marked a significant decrease in poverty rates among the general population and children, with child poverty declining from 21.5% in 2021 to 13.7% in 2023, and overall population poverty dropping to 11%. Social benefits played a key role in this achievement, as UNICEF studies revealed that without social transfers, child poverty would have risen to 15.5% and the overall poverty rate would have increased from 11% to 20.8%. It also showed that 40% of households from the bottom income quintile received social assistance while 60% of the benefits were directed to the lowest and second lowest income quintiles. However, UNICEF raised concerns over tightened eligibility criteria, reducing the number of beneficiary children from 4.4 million in January to 2.5 million in October 2024.  

In November 2024, Uzbekistan took a significant step forward in child protection with the enactment of the Law on the Protection of Children from All Forms of Violence. This landmark legislation aligns the national child protection framework with international standards, institutionalizing robust mechanisms to prevent and respond to violence, abuse, neglect, and exploitation. Its adoption followed extensive evidence-based advocacy and multi-stakeholder engagement, reflecting the government’s commitment to safeguarding children’s rights to protection.  
 
With support from MoPSE, Ministry of Ecology, Youth Affairs Agency, and Zamin Foundation, UNICEF expanded opportunities for children and youth to engage in climate action and advocacy. Participation in the International Youth Eco Camp, capacity-building for Young Climate Champions, and the National Delegation to COP-29 enhanced adolescents' understanding of UNFCCC processes and climate governance. 
 
In 2024, Uzbekistan made significant strides to improve public health and well-being, with a strong focus on delivering tangible results for children. Resolution No. PP-38 introduced key reforms to enhance the quality of medical services in line with international standards. At the same time, Resolution No. PP-311 laid the groundwork for a national health insurance system, ensuring affordable healthcare. The "From Poverty to Wellbeing" program, outlined in Resolution No. PP-330, focused on improving infrastructure and addressing health disparities.  

Mitigation and adaptation to climate change remain key priorities of the Government of Uzbekistan. In his address at COP29, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev highlighted climate change as a significant global challenge, particularly for Central Asia. He emphasized Uzbekistan’s commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing green energy, and collaborating regionally. He proposed several initiatives, including establishing an International Centre for Climate Loss and Damage, improving biodiversity, and launching a Regional Genetic Resources Bank. He also invited international participation to the Global Youth Festival of Digital Green Initiatives to be held in May 2025 in the Aral Sea region. 

During his visit to Tashkent in 2024, UN Secretary-General António Guterres commended Uzbekistan’s dedication to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly in sectors crucial for children’s well-being. He highlighted progress in improving early childhood education, expanding access to healthcare, and addressing climate challenges to secure a better future for vulnerable populations. The visit reinforced the importance of continued investment in these sectors to provide children in Uzbekistan with healthier lives, quality education, and opportunities for sustainable growth. 

In November 2024, Uzbekistan committed at the Arab-Islamic Summit to provide free medical care to war-affected Palestinian children and women. This was fulfilled in December through collaboration with Egypt, transporting 100 women and children from Gaza for treatment in Uzbekistan. Additionally, Uzbekistan supported humanitarian efforts in Afghanistan by sending 28 doctors aboard a Health Train, treating 1,300 earthquake-affected residents in Balk province. UNICEF Uzbekistan, with UNICEF Afghanistan, supported operations through a logistics hub in Termez, ensuring critical supplies reached Afghanistan. However, programming for Afghans in Uzbekistan faced challenges due to limited donor funding and alignment with government priorities. 

Uzbekistan achieved historic success at the Paris 2024 Olympics, securing 13 medals: 8 gold, 2 silver, and 3 bronze, placing 13th globally. This success positioned Uzbekistan as a leading sports nation in Central Asia and the CIS. The achievement is a testament to strategic investments in youth sports programs, fostering national pride, social cohesion and motivation for children and young people to engage in sporting activities. This momentum could drive further government and private sector investments in sporting infrastructure and youth engagement.  

The year 2024 marked the 30th anniversary of UNICEF's presence in Uzbekistan, reflecting three decades of progress for children’s rights. Annual results highlighted advances in maternal and child health, education, child protection, water and sanitation, disability inclusion, and social protection, alongside improvements in policy and regulatory frameworks that promote a child-friendly environment. The 2024 Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents, conducted by UNICEF, captured these achievements and were integrated into the Common Country Analysis to inform the planning of the next country program document (CPD) and the United Nations Cooperation Framework for 2026-2030.

Goal area 1. Every Child Survives and Thrives   
 
In 2024, UNICEF achieved significant progress in advancing maternal, newborn, and child health in Uzbekistan through targeted partnerships, system strengthening, and evidence-based programming. These results align with national priorities within the Uzbekistan 2030 National Development Plan and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. 
  
Neonatal mortality remains a critical concern, with 16 newborns dying daily1. Addressing this challenge, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Health (MOH), WHO, and UNFPA through the Vision 2030 Joint United Nations Programme to standardize service delivery for maternal and newborn care.  Six newborn care guidelines and national service quality standards, including supportive supervision protocols, were revised and adopted with support from UNICEF and MOHF and MOH. These efforts resulted in overall newborn survival improving. Survival rates for newborns weighing between 500 and 1500 grams increased from 70% in 2022 to 75% in 2024. Similarly, for newborns weighing between 1500 and 2000 grams, survival rates rose from 80% in 2022 to 82%.  
  
UNICEF focused on strengthening primary health care (PHC) to improve equitable access to services. Through the assessment of the Universal Progressive Home Visiting Programme, gaps in service delivery were identified, leading to actionable insights for sustainable funding and better resource allocation. To operationalize these findings, 356 master trainers were equipped to deliver high-quality services, paving the way for capacity-building in 2025. These efforts aim to enhance community-based services, strengthen links between facilities and communities, and ensure underserved populations, particularly mothers and children, receive essential care. 
 
Elimination of mother-to-child transmission (eMTCT) of HIV and syphilis remains a government priority. Despite high service coverage, inequities in delivery and gaps in evidence-based programming persist. UNICEF supported the MOH in developing a roadmap for eMTCT, which was approved in April 2024. This roadmap addresses challenges identified in the 2022 pre-validation report and focuses on enhancing service quality for 900,000 pregnant women annually. By paving the way for eMTCT certification, this initiative represents a significant step toward safeguarding maternal and child health rights in Uzbekistan. 
  
UNICEF's technical assistance, in collaboration with GAVI, WHO, and USAID, significantly enhanced immun ization services and infrastructure, benefiting 3.5 million children (96%) through the National Immunization Programme. UNICEF and WHO collaborated with national health authorities to address gaps in vaccine supply chain management. Findings from the 2023 Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) Assessment highlighted critical areas for improvement, from procurement to delivery. UNICEF supported the development of a comprehensive EVM Country Improvement Plan, which will be implemented in 2025. This plan is expected to reduce vaccine-preventable diseases and ensure that every child in Uzbekistan has access to life-saving vaccines.  
  
UNICEF also prioritized breastfeeding, recognizing that exclusive breastfeeding rates remain alarmingly low, with only 1 in 4 children under six months exclusively breastfed2. UNICEF supported the Government of Uzbekistan in developing a comprehensive State Program to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding. This included developing breastfeeding guidelines and revising the national law on breastmilk substitutes to align with the International Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes. These efforts aim to create an enabling environment for breastfeeding, ensuring optimal nutrition for infants and young children. 
 
  
Goal area 2. Every Child Learns 
 
During the reporting period, UNICEF achieved significant progress in enhancing quality and inclusive education through its strategic role as the coordinating agency of the Local Education Working Group within the National Country Platform. 
 
To address key challenges in quality education, with nearly 80% of students not meeting required standards in reading, mathematics, and science, UNICEF supported the operationalization of the Partnership Compact for Education Reform (2023-2026). This initiative leveraged over $600 million in Development Partners’ financial commitments, driving advancements in EdTech, policy development, and competency-based curriculum standards. 
 
At the pre-school level, UNICEF facilitated the development of an integrated professional development system for early childhood educators. The first cohort of 6,500 preschool teachers and managers benefited from a newly developed in-service training curriculum. By 2029, over 119,000 educators are expected to complete this reformed training, consisting of a 100-hour in-person program focusing on child-centered learning and classroom management, complemented by a 72-hour online course. Additionally, over 25,700 teachers accessed preschool professional development through the Learning Passport platform. Pre-service teacher training reform was supported through the National Teacher Training Curriculum Framework (NTTCF), defining essential teacher competencies. 
 
UNICEF addressed competency-based learning challenges by developing new Education Curriculum Standards. These standards, approved in March 2024, emphasize 21st-century skills, gender-responsive education, and life skills integration. A new FCDO-funded regional project was launched to revise the national assessment framework by 2025. 
 
UNICEF promoted innovation and digital learning with Eduten, an AI-driven gamified math platform for fifth-grade students, showing a 16% improvement in math skills. Uzbekistan was selected as a Global Learning Pioneer Country, accelerating digital learning through the GIGA Initiative. A nationwide digital readiness assessment was launched in 2024, involving 17,201 stakeholders, with findings to inform policies on sustainable, inclusive learning environments. National guidelines on device maintenance, usage, and scalability for digital learning and assistive technology are also under development. 
 
To advance inclusive education, the first-ever Programmatic Framework for Inclusive Education was launched, ensuring no child is left behind. This framework fostered collaboration among UNICEF, partners, the Ministry of Education, and parents of children with disabilities. A pilot inclusive school in Tashkent set new standards for accessible school construction, benefiting 950 schools and over 2,000 children with disabilities. UNICEF also launched regional inclusive school models to establish 50 model schools, supporting over 50,000 students, including 300 with disabilities by 2025. In 2024, the first school-based assessments using ICF standards were developed to guide assistive device procurement and upgrades. 
 
In advancing skills development, 1,787,814 young people (894,053 girls and 893,761 boys) gained socio-emotional, green, advocacy, entrepreneurship, and other transferable skills. This resulted from the integration of socio-emotional skills development into the school curriculum for grades 7-9 and extra-curricular opportunities through the FunDoo digital platform, benefiting 991 girls and 718 boys. 
 
To promote youth participation and climate action, the first national Young Climate Champions network was established, raising climate change awareness and mobilizing over 6,400 peers with support from school administrations, the Ministry of Ecology, and local governments. Additionally, the International Youth Eco Camp in Uzbekistan hosted 31 Uzbek youth and 25 participants from Central Asia, Türkiye, Azerbaijan, and Hungary. The Youth Statement advocating for environmental education, green skills, and youth participation in the climate agenda was presented at a COP-29 side event, where Uzbek youth actively participated as part of the national delegation. 
 
Goal area 3. Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation  

In 2024, UNICEF Uzbekistan achieved significant strides in advancing child protection. These milestones reflect UNICEF’s commitment to fostering a gender-responsive, inclusive, and functional child protection system, showcasing its positioning as a trusted partner for impactful reforms. 
 
A landmark achievement was the Presidential signing of the Law on the Protection of Children from All Forms of Violence in November 2024. This comprehensive legislation aligns Uzbekistan’s child protection framework with international standards, institutionalizing mechanisms to prevent and respond to violence, abuse, neglect, and exploitation. UNICEF played a crucial role in the development of this law, leveraging evidence-based advocacy, policy dialogue, and multi-stakeholder engagement. The law’s adoption establishes a strong legal foundation for safeguarding children’s rights to protection and catalyzes ongoing work on regulatory frameworks, including inter-agency SOPs, sector-specific procedures, and a multi-sectoral strategy to address violence against children. 
 
UNICEF’s support to NASP in 2024 resulted in significant progress in social service workforce development and the rollout of the Family Strengthening and Support Programme (FSS). Over 1,770 district and community social service professionals enhanced their capacity in case management, family support, child protection support, and community-based mental health and psychosocial support services (MHPSS). Among others, these efforts directly benefited more than 18,000 individuals, including 3,000 children, addressing complex child and family needs. UNICEF also supported the creation of 15 e-learning modules for NASP’s training centre, with 412 specialists completing foundational courses. These investments in workforce capacity align with global best practices and ensure sustainable improvements in service delivery. 
 
UNICEF reinvigorated juvenile justice reforms, resulting in increased commitment from key government stakeholders, including the National Agency for Social Protection, the Supreme Court, and the Prosecutor General’s Office, to explore and advance diversion mechanisms and alternative measures for children in conflict with the law. In collaboration with the National Human Rights Centre and the Office of the Ombudsperson for Children, UNICEF organized a high-level roundtable showcasing global best practices in child-friendly justice. Concurrently, UNICEF supported the finalization of the Strategy on Children’s Access to Justice and its roadmap, while 517 justice professionals strengthened their capacity in child-sensitive procedures for effectively handling cases involving children. 
 
NASP’s comprehensive alternative care regulations, developed with UNICEF’s support, marked a major milestone in Uzbekistan’s deinstitutionalization agenda. These regulations emphasize family-based care, gatekeeping, and reintegration, embedding international guidelines into national practices. The rollout of the family strengthening and support programme in Andijan, Tashkent region, and Tashkent city laid the groundwork for supporting vulnerable families. 
 
The establishment of the Uzbekistan-Columbia Centre for Advancing Community Strengths and Social Wellbeing in September 2024 represents a significant innovation in professional development and research. This collaboration between UNICEF, NASP, and Columbia University is anticipated to advance community-based solutions for child protection, gender-based violence, and mental health challenges.  
 
Goal area 4. Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment  
 
In 2024, UNICEF made significant progress in advancing climate-resilient and gender responsive Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services in schools, healthcare facilities, and communities across Uzbekistan, addressing critical gaps in infrastructure, knowledge, and behavior change. 
  
With only 70% of schools having access to basic drinking water, UNICEF supported the government in developing Climate-Resilient WASH in Schools Guidelines, promoting the WASH 3-Star Approach to improve school environments. To operationalize this, UNICEF equipped 24 facilitators in the Republic of Karakalpakstan to pilot the approach in 20 schools across four districts. 200 teachers, 100 parents, and 4,000 students benefitted from capacity building on climate-resilient WASH, nutrition, and climate adaptation, while community WASH training reached over 300 individuals. Social and behavior change campaigns on climate-resilient WASH were conducted in 10 communities, reaching over 15,000 people. 
  
UNICEF prioritized healthcare settings, implementing climate-resilient WASH services in three districts of Karakalpakstan, covering three district hospitals and 12 primary healthcare facilities (45% coverage). To strengthen infection prevention and control, 300 healthcare workers enhanced their capacity to prevent nosocomial infections and manage waterborne diseases.  
 
Additionally, eight million people, including three million children in Surkhandarya, benefitted from improved air quality through modern healthcare waste management technologies.  
 
UNICEF’s WASH improvements in Karakalpakstan directly benefitted 320,289 people, including 5,000 children, ensuring sustainable access to safe water and sanitation while building resilience against climate-related challenges.  
 
UNICEF conducted the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) of Uzbekistan assessing the impacts of climate change and environmental degradation on children. The analysis highlighted vulnerabilities such as extreme temperatures and pollution. This analysis will inform policymakers and guide interventions to protect children's rights to a healthy environment.  UNICEF also specifically looked into the impact of heatwaves on the children of Uzbekistan and examined the potential role of social protection in preparing and responding to heatwaves.  
   
UNICEF supported road to resilience event in Montengro, resulting in the adoption of the “Children and Youth Declaration for the Road to Resilience".  Key results include a commitment for governments to allocate 10% of national DRR budgets to youth-led projects by 2026, the establishment of advisory councils to ensure youth involvement in decision-making and the integration of DRR education in schools. This initiative empowers young leaders to drive a climate resilience agenda, aligned with the priorities of the Sendai Framework and calls for urgent action.   
   
UNICEF supported the Central Asia Ministerial Meeting in Almaty resulted in the adoption of the "Ministerial Pledge on Comprehensive School Safety" by education ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. The pledge commits to protecting educational environments from natural and human-made hazards, including climate change. The pledge also calls for policies for comprehensive school safety, promotion of inclusive education, enhancement of educational facility resilience, and the establishment of cross-sectoral partnerships and sustained international support to ensure safe, equitable, and quality education for all children in the region.   
 
UNICEF CO also worked on increasing awareness of adolescents and youth on climate change, mitigation and adaptation measures and their right on healthy environment in line with the CRC General Comment #26. Two chapters of the Young Climate Activists Toolkit, FunDoo GreenPal modules were contextualized and translated to the local languages. Fifty adolescents (24 girls, 26 boys) from 20 schools form all regions of Uzbekistan were equipped with the thematic and climate advocacy knowledge and skills. As a result, they are leading awareness-raising and eco initiatives in their communities. For the last three months, the adolescents mobilized over 6,400 young people in their communities.  
 
Goal area 5. Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life  
 
Recently, poverty rates significantly decreased, with child poverty dropping from 21.5% in 2021 to 13.7% in 2023, and overall population poverty falling to 11% by the end of 2023. According to the Ministry of Poverty Reduction and Employment, the poverty rate in Uzbekistan continued to decrease in 2024 and reached 8.9%. Social benefits played a crucial role, as UNICEF studies showed that without transfers, child poverty would have risen to 15.5% and overall poverty to 20.8%. The study also revealed that 40% of households in the lowest income quintile received social assistance. However, UNICEF raised concerns over stricter eligibility criteria, reducing the number of beneficiary children from 4.4 million to 2.5 million, with the 2025 budget proposing further cuts, risking recent progress. 
 
Luckily, UNICEF succeeded in advocating for the inclusion of multidimensional child poverty indicators in the national data collection system: the Presidential Administration formally tasked respective institutions to regularly collect the data to be used in national policymaking.   

UNICEF’s technical support to the National Agency for Social Protection (NASP) advanced digital transformation, operationalizing the Single Registry module for cash compensations, benefiting 1.2 million vulnerable households impacted by energy tariff hikes. Additionally, UNICEF facilitated Uzbekistan’s national roadmap under the Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection for Just Transitions (GA). UNICEF partnered with ILO, UNDP, UN Women, and the World Bank to mobilize funds for joint programs focusing on social protection and economic inclusion. 

During the year, through strategic bilateral and multilateral engagements, UNICEF’s position was strengthened as a credible advocate for child-focused budgeting within the improved PFM system and budgetary frameworks of Uzbekistan. UNICEF supported the adoption of the resolution by the cabinet of ministers on result-based budgeting implementation. This contributed to the strengthening of the PFM system and equipped the government with tools and processes to plan, budget, and monitor public resources more efficiently, transparently, and equitably, prioritizing the needs of vulnerable groups, including children.   
  
UNICEF expanded efforts to address bottlenecks in local governance to advance the rights of children, youth, and families. The new program focuses on inclusive policies enabling local governments to manage resources for children and youth, improve coordination, strengthen capacities of governance bodies to deliver equitable services, and enhance participation of vulnerable groups in decision-making. UNICEF facilitated Uzbek officials' participation in the October 2024 Regional Forum on Financial Resilience and Risk Reduction in Central Asia, co-organized by the World Bank and UNICEF in Almaty. 
 
Gender Equality and Social Inclusion  

In 2024, UNICEF Uzbekistan made significant progress in advancing disability inclusion, focusing on empowering girls with disabilities, improving services, and addressing stigma. A key milestone was the enactment of President’s Decree ¿ PP-257 in July, transitioning from a medical to a human rights-based disability assessment model. This shift, advocated by UNICEF, emphasizes functional abilities and participation in daily life, aiming to streamline assessments and create personalized rehabilitation and social support plans. Additionally, the Cabinet of Ministers’ Decree ¿ 123 in March outlined procedures for creating individualized social service plans, improving identification and ongoing support for people with disabilities. 

UNICEF secured funds for the second cycle of the UN Joint Programme (UNJP) on the rights of people with disabilities, in collaboration with UNFPA and UNDP. This phase focuses on improving social services and equipping professionals with tools to provide accessible care, including transforming a residential care facility for children with disabilities. Additionally, a study with the Institute for Development of Social Protection on Goods and Services Required (GSR) for inclusion of children with disabilities involved 17 experts and caregivers. The study examined the costs of essential services like assistive technology, healthcare, and education, providing evidence for better community-based support services. 

UNICEF also worked to combat stigma and promote inclusion through partnerships, such as with the International Inclusive Hub, which trained over 33 educators on creating inclusive learning environments for children with disabilities. UNICEF also supported 30 young people with disabilities in developing employability skills. In 2024 four self-initiative parent groups were registered as NGOs with UNICEF’s support, helping to strengthen civil society. UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Preschool and School Education to model an inclusive school, assessing the infrastructure to meet the needs of children with various disabilities. 

Uzbekistan made significant strides in gender equality in 2024. The country improved its position in the Gender Equality Index, rising from 103rd place in 2022 to 52nd in 2024. This reflects progress in women's representation in leadership roles, equal access to education, and stronger enforcement of laws against domestic violence. Legal reforms, including amendments to the Criminal Code introduced in 2023, have established criminal penalties for domestic violence, ensuring better protection for women’s rights and safety.  Gender-transformative approaches were integrated across all Goal Areas, focusing on girls' leadership, challenging harmful gender norms, and addressing gender-based violence (GBV).  

UNICEF also enhanced systems and services related to adolescent girls' nutrition, gender-responsive education, and social protection.  137 national and regional emergency partners received training on gender in emergencies, strengthening UNICEF’s commitment to delivering inclusive and gender-responsive emergency response strategies. These efforts align with UNICEF's Global Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy and UNICEF’s Gender Action Plan, continuing to advocate for the rights women and inclusion of children and adults with disabilities in Uzbekistan, and fostering a more inclusive and equitable future for all.

The 2024 demonstrated UNICEF’s capacity to harness partnerships to bring results for children and young people across Uzbekistan. Partnerships with government, civil society, UN agencies, private sector, and academia played a critical role in advancing outcomes for children.

UNICEF collaborated in the design of the Asian Development Bank $100 million education project focused on STEM and digital learning, aligning its interventions to the Partnership Compact and developing the curriculum framework.
