UNICEF is collaborating with USAID on the Global Health Securities Fund for health in emergencies. In education, the All Children Succeeding Project was launched in 2024. UNICEF also helped establish an inclusive education sub-working group within the Ministry of Pre-school and School Education, in partnership with JICA, and facilitated policy dialogue with Finland following the launch of the Finnish-Inspired Education System with Nordic University in Tashkent. 
 
UNICEF and Special Olympics of Uzbekistan (SOU) engaged the Ministry of Sports, Ministry of Preschool and School Education, Child Ombudsman, and Korzinka to hold a joint marathon to reiterate the Inclusion Agenda. The run, with 110 children, including 60 with disabilities, was an important platform for ending stigma and discrimination. 
 
Partnerships enhanced health outcomes for children, through collaboration with Latter-day Saint Charities (LDSC) equipping six facilities in regions with 20 bubble Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (bCPAP) devices to improve newborn survival rates. Building on this, the Vision 2030 implemented with UNFPA and WHO, continued to improve maternal and newborn care under a $43.5 million initiative. UNICEF also partnered with WHO and national authorities to develop the Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) Country Improvement Plan. 
 
UNICEF joined forces with UNECE and the Ministry of Internal Affairs to launch the Road Safety Performance Review, which identified practical steps to improve road safety and reduce preventable injuries among children. 
 
In WASH, UNICEF brought together key ministries, including Construction, Health, and Preschool and School Education, to share best practices and develop technical solutions to improve school sanitation. Collaborations with the Delivery Unit under the President’s Office and the Zamin Foundation contributed to revising WASH standards and strengthening the Ministry of Preschool and School Education’s capacity.  
 
The Uzbekistan-Columbia Centre for Advancing Community Strengths and Social Wellbeing, a joint initiative of NASP, Columbia University, and UNICEF, launched to support professional development, research, and interventions in child protection, mental health, and gender-based violence. UNICEF strengthened the Institute for Development of Social Protection's capacity to implement behaviourally informed programs. With Johns Hopkins University, it trained health workers for emergency community engagement. Partnerships with local think tanks established child poverty data and assessed disability inclusion costs.
 
The UN Joint Programme on Inclusive Transformation for Youth and Child-Friendly Local Governance was launched with UNDP, Yuksalish, and the Swiss Government, securing USD 1.2 million. UNICEF collaborated with UNDP, SDC, the World Bank, USAID, and Central Asian countries on youth governance, shock-responsive social protection, and climate change. It also secured funding for the second cycle of the UNJP on the rights of people with disabilities with UNFPA and UNDP.

UNICEF Country Office, in partnership with the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Institute of Civil Protection and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, is enhancing disaster preparedness in Uzbekistan.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
SitAn 2024 highlighted disparities, including better services in cities versus rural areas, challenges in inclusive education for children with disabilities, poor education quality shown by below-average PISA-2022 rankings, lack of interagency collaboration (SOPs) in child and social protection, and fiscal constraints limiting social protection expansion. It also identified a 44.7% child multidimensional poverty rate and significant regional disparities. 
 
Recommendations included evidence-based policymaking, better data quality with real-time, disaggregated data, comprehensive child protection policies with cross-sectoral coordination, tackling stigma around disabilities, mental health, and HIV through education and campaigns, and strengthening social protection with child allowances and region-specific poverty strategies. 

UNICEF’s faced critical challenges across sectors in accelerating results at scale. In the legal and institutional domain, while key stakeholders demonstrated increased commitment, translating this into actionable reforms remained challenging. Specifically, in the area of diversion and alternative measures stakeholders have emphasized the need to build capacities and establish robust systems before these measures can be fully integrated into the legal framework.  To address this, advocacy efforts will focus on initiating the drafting of legal amendments alongside capacity-building activities, with a potential government resolution serving as a legal basis for piloting these measures in selected regions during the interim. 

Social and structural issues posed additional challenges. The process of transitioning to the new human rights-based disability assessment system, overcoming stigma, and ensuring resource allocation for adequate social services is complex. Harmful social norms and cultural practices also obstructed progress in areas such as exclusive breastfeeding, early childhood nutrition, and access to services for adolescent girls. These challenges revealed gaps in our Theory of Change, particularly in addressing behavioural and demand-side barriers that impede systemic progress. UNICEF aims to expand inclusive education, strengthen social services provision, and reinforce legal reforms in tandem with enhancement of gender-responsive programming, addressing gender-based violence, and promoting the full inclusion of persons with disabilities in all sectors of society. 

Systemic inefficiencies in health, education and child and social protection also emerged as significant obstacles. Weak governance, fragmented policies, and inadequate data systems undermined health outcomes, particularly in primary health care and school-based interventions and limited the ability to prevent and respond to violence, abuse, and exploitation of children. Limited coordination among stakeholders, especially within and among ministries, hindered alignment and accountability, particularly in primary health care (PHC), school-based interventions and child protection services. Weak health service delivery at the PHC level, compounded by insufficient workforce capacity and resource gaps, slowed efforts to strengthen maternal and child health outcomes. In schools, inadequate infrastructure and operational gaps limited the scale-up of WASH interventions. Similarly, the nascent social service workforce, composed primarily of paraprofessionals, lacks sufficient training, supervision, and institutional support to effectively respond to child protection concerns, while limited coordination between social services, health, education and justice sectors further exacerbates gaps in service delivery and accountability. 

The education sector faced institutional disruptions, with government restructuring delaying pre-school education reforms.  Significant government changes occurred during the reporting period with the dismantling of the National Agency for Pre-school Education and the establishment of new rules and mandates on teacher professional development. Addressing this challenge, UNICEF team prioritized institutional ownership and co-creation of national frameworks and standards to be endorsed by the Local Education Group. Facilitating continuous policy dialogue among national stakeholders within the education sector ensured intervention continuity and ownership. Challenges in digital transformation, including the absence of national standards and fragmented pilot initiatives, further constrained progress. In 2024, UNICEF expanded its partnerships with the International Financial Institutions, in order to scale up successful digital learning models such as Eduten. Furthermore, supporting concrete education technology solutions including assistive technology and inclusive education was prioritized by launching large-scale school-based modeling at national level under Vision 2030 fund. 

Moving forward, UNICEF will enhance capacity-building efforts, strengthen multi-sectoral coordination, and prioritize behavioral change strategies to complement systemic interventions. Additional resources will be required to address data gaps, scale evidence-based innovations, and sustain advocacy for governance reforms to ensure long-term systemic impact. 
Challenges faced by UNICEF were related to limited fiscal space and weak public finance institutions, a shift in the paradigm to more poverty-targeted programs, and new players in the social protection area with different views on the aims of social protection as well as frequent change of roles and responsibilities of national partners and public sector reorganization.  

Limited access to critical data, such as household budget surveys and quality of data adds challenge to evidence-based policy making. Weak institutions at the local level, as well as an influx of new human resources by the government with no clear KPIs, responsibilities, and feedback mechanisms, create additional complications within the system.  

Climate change poses unique challenges for children. Many local governments lack resources and frameworks to implement national pledges, while insufficient climate data hinders effective planning. Exclusion of children and marginalized groups weakens policy inclusivity. Limited fiscal space, weak public finance systems, and shifting roles among national partners further complicate governance and resource mobilization. UNICEF aims to improve strategies and collaboration by leveraging past insights. Key actions include strengthening data systems, developing localized action plans to prioritize vulnerable children, and enhancing capacity building to foster community ownership of climate resilience efforts. 

By reflecting on these challenges and lessons, UNICEF is refining its approaches to better serve the most vulnerable groups of children. Future strategies will focus on scaling evidence-based innovations, fostering collaboration, and ensuring that children’s voices are integral to all interventions. These efforts will drive systemic change, resilience, and inclusive progress across all sectors.

Kyrgyzstan’s gross domestic product grew by 8.1 per cent in real terms in 2024, driven by consumption, exports, and investment (48 per cent) and construction and services (7.7 per cent). Inflation remains concerning, with the Consumer Price Index increasing for non-food items and for services by 8 per cent. Fuel prices rose 13 per cent, driving up transportation costs and eroding purchasing power, particularly for vulnerable populations. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts 4 per cent medium-term growth in output, with inflation expected to decline to mid-single digits. Tax revenue mobilization improved, and public debt declined. The IMF noted that public debt remained contained and should stay manageable in the medium term. International institutions emphasize Kyrgyzstan’s vulnerability to external shocks, particularly due to reliance on remittances from workers abroad, especially Russia. Fluctuations in Russia’s economy and changes in its migration policies affect this income source. In the first nine months of 2024, remittances from Russia increased by 17 per cent, but the number of migrant workers from Kyrgyzstan in Russia fell by 40 per cent, reflecting the sector’s volatility. Over 50 per cent of public expenditure is allocated to social sector spending (education, health care, social protection (including pensions), and culture). Strong performance in each of these sectors is essential for economic growth and human development, including child outcomes.  
National social sector priorities are underpinned by Kyrgyzstan’s commitments from the SDG Summit and the National Development Forum to reduce poverty and inequality in 2023 and the National Development Forum on Human Capital and Sustainable Development, in 2024. The 2024 Forum facilitated the exchange of international and local experience, best practices, and innovative approaches. It emphasized the critical importance of investment in social sectors from the youngest years for future returns for achieving human capital development and upper-middle income status. 
Several significant legislative and policy efforts also took central stage in 2024. Politically, three were crucial. First, in April, the President approved amendments to the Law “On Non-Commercial Organizations”. This law mandates that non-commercial organizations receiving foreign funding and engaging in broadly defined ‘political activities’ must register as ‘foreign representatives’. This may force some civil society organizations (CSOs) to abandon foreign financing and rely on limited national funding for support, while others may lack resources to meet the Law’s burdensome requirements, such as annual independent audits, leading them to cease operations. While implications for the CSO landscape are not currently clear, the Law’s stringent requirements may leave a vacuum in Kyrgyzstan’s vibrant civil society of recent decades. Second, in June, the Parliament approved a law reducing the number of administrative units from 484 (32 urban, 452 rural) to 264 (33 urban, 231 rural). This was achieved by enlarging city administrative boundaries and merging village administrations nationwide. While the reform’s effects are not visible yet, its stated objective is to make public service delivery more rational and effective and reduce the number of local civil servants (accompanied by digitalization). This could improve access to local services and reduce corruption. Consolidating smaller administrative units into fewer, larger ones could, however, affect vulnerable groups, as citizens from remote areas may need to travel further to access public services. 
With regards to policy reforms affecting children directly, following approval of the new Education Law in 2023, the government launched the highly ambitious Altyn Kazyk (‘Polar Star’) initiative for education transformation in March. The components of this initiative include: i) transition to a 12-year education system, ii) modernizing pedagogies and textbooks, iii) optimizing district education offices, iv) digital transformation, and v) expanding national preschool coverage. This will require strong government commitment, costed and detailed planning, substantial resources, and sector coordination for harmonization.
Third, in August the Criminal Code, Code of Offences and Law on Domestic Violence were amended to increase fines and prison terms for domestic violence crimes, increase access to free legal aid and psychological support for survivors of domestic violence and increase the duration of temporary protection orders from 3 to 30 days. Additional preventive measures were introduced to prevent recidivism, including mandatory participation of perpetrators in rehabilitation programmes. However, gaps persist, as domestic violence remains only partially criminalized, and some amendments conflict with international standards and fail to meet United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women requirements. Meanwhile, at the 2024’s Global Ministerial Conference in Bogotá, Colombia the government committed to eliminating all forms of corporal punishment against children in all settings.
With regard to emergencies, in 2024 the scale and frequency of mudflows in Kyrgyzstan increased due to heavy rainfall. In July, severe mudflows struck Osh province, leading to a state of emergency. According to the Ministry of Emergency Situations (MES), Kyrgyzstan has experienced over 331 mudflows during the year, resulting in the loss of 22 lives, including 14 children, and causing extensive damage to housing, social facilities, and infrastructure. These events have placed additional strain on the population, particularly those living in or near the poverty line, and urgent action is needed to protect children and women from natural disasters, particularly those linked to climate change.
The government effectively promoted the Mountain Agenda at the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP29). Kyrgyzstan launched revision of the current Nationally Determined Contributions document, focusing on enhanced climate adaptation and funding for regional projects, especially for mountain ecosystem protection. Additionally, Kyrgyzstan emphasized gender equality in climate agendas, highlighting women’s roles in climate adaptation and decision-making. Active participation at COP29 showcased Kyrgyzstan’s leadership in addressing climate challenges and promoting sustainable development.

In 2024, UNICEF celebrated two key milestones: the thirtieth anniversary of Kyrgyzstan's ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and three decades of UNICEF's operations in the country. These anniversaries served as powerful platforms to renew commitments to child rights, spotlight achievements, and address ongoing challenges. 
Year-long programmatic, advocacy and communication efforts culminated in a statement by President Sadyr Japarov on World Children’s Day, celebrating the thirtieth anniversary of CRC ratification. He reflected on the progress and challenges, and made commitments in the field of education, allocating funds for the preschool education of children living in mountainous and remote areas, children with disabilities, and those from low-income families. 
In order to implement the 146 new recommendations from the Committee on the Rights of the Child, following the latest State Party Report of the Kyrgyz Republic, the Child Rights Commissioner’s role in leading the development of the Action Plan was strengthened. The Commissioner designed the process to develop the action plan, including through face-to-face consultations with line ministries, children's consultations and a two-day workshop to consolidate all inputs.
Specific efforts were made to engage children not normally involved in this kind of initiatives to feed back on the CRC recommendations, children’s priorities and points of view. A key finding was that children do not fully understand child rights but, on the other hand, are clear on their responsibilities. During the consultations, one key area identified by children was the importance of schools being a safe space for them, because of aggressive behaviours by teachers, who sometimes humiliate them, and bullying by peers. Adolescent girls mentioned being told to marry early instead of continuing their education, and not feeling safe in public spaces because of inappropriate stares and touches from men and boys. The next step, in 2025, will be to provide feedback to the children consulted on the outcome of their inputs to the development of the action plan.
The Child Rights Commissioner planned and coordinated the final two-day workshop, involving all key ministries, civil society, and the expert community. Participants were grateful for the opportunity to discuss child rights, as this process had not been conducted previously. They particularly appreciated the presentation of children’s opinions. The Action Plan is currently pending approval by the Cabinet of Ministers. Once approved, biannual updates on its implementation will be provided to a national-level Council on Family Issues, Gender Development, Social Protection and Protection of Child Rights under the Cabinet of Ministers, which the Cabinet plans to convene, for the first time, in early January 2025. Additionally, a monitoring framework and dashboard will be developed to monitor implementation of the Action Plan, ensuring transparency and accountability.
Another key achievement of UNICEF Kyrgyzstan in 2024 was the launch of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS). The survey collected reliable and internationally comparable data for 177 indicators – including 31 Sustainable Development Goals indicators – from 7,200 households. These indicators comprehensively define the situation of women and children in Kyrgyzstan and can be disaggregated by gender, province, wealth status, ethnicity, residence, age of respondent, mother’s educational attainment, and disability status. In general, Kyrgyzstan has achieved progress in several areas, such as reduction in violence against children, non-acceptance of domestic violence, and falling under-five and infant mortality rates. Outstanding concerns, however, include declining routine immunization rates, continued high rates of stunting and stagnating breastfeeding practices. In partnership with the National Statistical Committee, UNICEF conducted secondary analysis of the 2023 MICS results, focusing on provincial and equity gaps in child health, education, child protection, and adolescent experiences. This equity analysis also enabled the Country Office to re-align its priorities for the remainder of the Country Programme and focus on targeted interventions to address identified equity gaps and contribute to moving the needle in these areas. A correlation analysis highlighted a strong link between violent discipline in households and lower learning outcomes for children. Further analysis of MICS data by province provided an opportunity to engage with provincial governors on the situation of children in their provinces. Two presentations were conducted with the governors of Osh and Jalalabad provinces, who expressed significant interest in using this data to inform provincial planning and collaboration with UNICEF. The identification of key child rights issues provides opportunities for the field office in the south to strengthen its partnership with governors and address th
em. Meetings in other provinces are planned for 2025.
UNICEF played a technical leadership role in advancing progress of the government’s ambitious educational reform known as Altyn Kazyk (Polar Star) to transform the system to 12 years of education from the current 11. This transition is accompanied by reforming the curriculum to focus on competences rather than subject knowledge (replacing Soviet-inherited old textbooks with modern textbooks and pedagogies, mainly from Singapore), as well as increasing national preschool coverage through deregulation and privatization. These reforms are intended to ensure that all 1.4 million students are equipped with appropriate skills, competences and knowledge to ensure Kyrgyzstan’s social and economic development in the twenty-first century. 
In this context, in coordination with the Ministry of Education and Science (MOES), the Kyrgyz Academy for Education (KAE) and other stakeholders. UNICEF organized several technical forums on curricular reform, which enabled over 50 key government officials and development partners to better understand global best practices, lessons learned, and potential risks associated with education reforms. While presenting past reform examples of Mongolia, Turkey and other countries, UNICEF explained that curriculum reforms require long periods of time (usually more than10 years) and that a roadmap is required to identify which outcomes are to be achieved; who should be involved; when the work will be undertaken and completed; and how it will be organized, including who will lead it. With these forums, UNICEF was instrumental in enabling MOES and KAE to develop a comprehensive, risk-informed roadmap for the transition to a 12-year schooling system. The roadmap was subsequently approved by Prime Ministerial Decree.
The MOES, KAE and UNICEF also jointly reviewed and enhanced state educational standards (the curricular framework) for preschools, primary and secondary schools in Kyrgyzstan. These improvements emphasized competency-based education and principles of gender equality, inclusiveness and climate resilience. It is envisaged that once the revised standards are approved by the Prime Minister’s Office in 2025, they will guide the overall curricula reforms. UNICEF provided technical assistance to ensure that the philosophy and values for the curriculum were inclusive, prioritizing equity and gender equality. This support is intended to foster deep understanding of fairness, non-discrimination and respect for diversity among learners in teaching and learning. UNICEF made the state standard texts more gender sensitive, helping the MOES and KAE to use the plural forms of words to include both girls and boys and address the inherent gender bias in singular forms like ‘child’, which are often perceived as masculine. The principle of inclusiveness was stressed to address different learning needs of each child, taking account of language, ethnicity and disability. Climate change education was explicitly highlighted as cross-curricular (across different subjects), experiential and participatory learning from primary to secondary education. Furthermore, teacher roles and competencies were reviewed to promote gender-responsive and inclusive pedagogy in lesson planning, teaching methods, classroom management and assessment practices. These standards were improved to make education more equitable and sensitive to the diverse needs of all students, including those with disabilities and from disadvantaged communities. 
Since Altyn Kazyk was launched, UNICEF has made high-level advocacy efforts for meaningful involvement of policy-makers, teachers, parents, young people and students in planning, design, preparation and implementation of the reform. In August, MOES and UNICEF jointly initiated interactive consultations with 2,000 local municipality officers, principals, and teachers in Bishkek and all regions. Despite advocacy and consultations, UNICEF acknowledges that public understanding of curriculum reforms remains limited. MOES and UNICEF will therefore continue working together to accelerate stakeholder consultations with teachers, parents and young people in 2025.
Based on the request of the presidential administration, UNICEF developed detailed social sector financing analyses to strengthen social sector aspects in national socio-economic planning. UNICEF engaged high-level expertise to rapidly develop detailed sector financing analyses in health, education and social protection, also with contributions from UN agencies such as WHO and WFP. This provided a detailed look at ways in which sector outcomes could be improved via strengthened efficiency and equity of social sector spending. This analysis was presented to the Chairman of the Cabinet of Minister, line ministries and at the National Development Forum in November. Based on this, the government committed to include a chapter on social sector priorities in the National Development Strategy 2030, something which was not initially planned. UNICEF plans to deepen this engagement in 2025 to provide detailed recommendations on ways to improve the efficiency and equity of spending in these three sectors, and provide technical assistance to support this. 
In 2024, the second phase of the Enhancing the Resilience of Children to Climate and Disaster Risks in the Kyrgyz Republic project was completed, in collaboration with the MES and MOES. UNICEF leveraged 600 local volunteers from the Red Crescent Society of Kyrgyzstan (RCSK) and UNICEF youth groups, benefiting over 974,500 school children in Grades 1-11 (55 per cent girls) through emergency simulation drills. These drills, held at 1,996 schools, included 1,242 children with disabilities (65 per cent girls) and were led mostly by female volunteers (56 per cent), promoting girls’ leadership. The drills covered locally relevant disaster risks, fostering a culture of disaster risk reduction (DRR) and preparedness.
UNICEF emphasized local ownership and sustainability, ensuring that training and simulations were designed for durability and replicability. The project-end assessment indicated that DRR drills are now regularly conducted in schools, with children reporting these taking place at least twice or three times every academic year, suggesting the project’s success in embedding DRR competences in local schools.
Additionally, the project-end assessment revealed a shift in mindset towards remaining calm during emergencies, with students sharing safety protocols with their families, extending the training’s impact beyond schools. The sustainability of UNICEF’s school-based DRR project is evident from the consistent training practices maintained by local authorities and actors, indicating a positive shift in emergency response capabilities and preparedness, contributing to the program’s long-term impact.
UNICEF continues to play the leading role in supporting the reintegration of children and women from Kyrgyzstan repatriated from conflict zones to the country. In 2024 it supported the government to repatriate 123 children and women from Iraq and Syria, and assisted the government to reintegrate 462 children and women (145 women, 156 girls and 161 boys) repatriated in 2023. UNICEF Kyrgyzstan invested in strengthening the working relationship with the inter-ministerial coordination body, in which UNICEF remains the only outside-of-government actor.  
UNICEF contributed to the development of the new five-year repatriation and reintegration action plan which will strengthen government coordination on this particular issue, particularly important in a context with many new implementing partners. UNICEF is prioritizing efforts to ensure MLSWM takes the lead and uses this opportunity to strengthen the overall child protection system, rather than using a project mindset. This approach is appreciated by donors who, with limited resources, want to support this important work but also need to see how the government’s capacity to take over all the work is strengthened.  
UNICEF supported a government delegation from the Kyrgyz Republic to participate in the first ever ministerial conference on violence against children (VAC). This included supporting the establishment of a multisectoral working group to develop pledges to address VAC. The government pledged to ban corporal punishment in all settings, and to develop a multi-sectoral action plan to address violence against children. The working group met following the return of the delegation to put a roadmap in place on how to implement the pledges made.
UNICEF played a crucial role in controlling a large-scale measles outbreak in the country. Despite an initial outbreak response immunization (ORI) campaign in September 2023, which covered 85 per cent of the target in four areas, measles cases continued to rise in 2024. In February, the highest number of weekly cases reached 670, totalling 2,827 cases for the month, with 12 deaths. UNICEF advocated a nationwide measles campaign and a comprehensive action plan. In February 2024, these efforts led to the development of a comprehensive national action plan to combat the outbreak, including strategies to reduce hospital infections. Consequently, the government funded 294,500 ORI doses in Jalal-Abad oblast, achieving 88 per cent coverage in March. UNICEF also provided support through the Measles Rubella Partnership, the World Health Organization, and Gavi leading to a second ORI phase in June-August with 79 per cent coverage: this included training for 1,182 health workers, and mobile teams, which administered 14,624 vaccinations, including 9,850 measles and rubella (MR) vaccinations. In total, 818,939 children aged 9-84 months were vaccinated, achieving 84 per cent nationwide coverage. By the end of November, monthly measles cases had dropped to 152, with no new deaths reported. 
Since October the Kyrgyz Republic has launched a Supplementary Immunization Activity (SIA) targeting children who missed previous vaccinations, contacts of new measles cases, health and education workers, and other susceptible groups. As of December, 74 per cent of the target group had been vaccinated. UNICEF procured 1,881,500 MR vaccine doses for all ORIs and the SIA, funded by Gavi, the Measles Rubella Partnership, and the government.
Given the challenges related to vaccination and recognizing the importance of public discourse on immunization and its influence in the choices of parents, messages on the importance of immunization and debunking of myths reached three million users through UNICEF-supported media and social media channels throughout 2024. Specifically, during the campaigns, these efforts increased public awareness, reaching 400,500 parents through social mobilization and 850,000 through social media. Targeted communication addressed vaccine hesitancy, reaching 81,000 parents, and multimedia materials debunking myths about childhood immunization reached 1.6 million people.
To better understand the barriers for segmented groups of populations in the areas of nutrition, immunization, and mental health, and to inform the development of targeted, scalable solutions, three behavioural insights (BI) initiatives were undertaken during the year. In the immunization area these focused on developing solutions to address the hesitancy of fathers and lessen the motivational barriers for mothers living without partners. The study found that hesitant fathers are less receptive to information from medical sources, and tend to rely on what they hear from like-minded friends and religious leaders. Barriers identified for mothers living without partners include a lack of health literacy, fears regarding vaccination and its side effects, and negative feelings caused by previous unpleasant experiences. Lack of trust in the health-care system is compounded by perceived low accessibility to expert advice when it is needed. Mothers’ fears are increased by the perception that the burden of the decision to vaccinate rests solely on their shoulders: they are afraid that vaccinating may be the wrong decision and that they are alone if something negative happens to their children following vaccination. In the first quarter of 2025, the proposed solutions will be tested and offered for scaling up.

In 2024, UNICEF, the Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision (MNRETS), the Ministry of Culture, Information, Sports, and Youth Policy (MCISYP), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and civil society collaborated to critically enhance youth participation, particularly on climate policy multi-stakeholder dialogue. After the Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate Action was signed in 2023, UNICEF co-organized a follow-up Regional Conference of Youth on Climate Change (RCOY) with MNRETS in Bishkek, gathering 253 participants from Central Asia and Afghanistan, including 178 girls and 75 boys, International development partners – the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), GIZ, the European Union Delegation, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the United Kingdom Embassy – actively participated alongside local youth organizations and environmental CSOs. The wide group of partners and experts enriched the discussions, which centred on youth empowerment, gender equality, water diplomacy, sustainable mountain development, and climate justice, underscoring the importance of collaboration and expertise to address pressing environmental challenges.
A conference highlight was the leadership of adolescent girls from the Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics for Girls (STEM4Girls) project, who amplified youth voices in climate decision-making. The event’s outcomes, including the Regional Youth Statement, were incorporated into the Global Youth Statement, reflecting a unified youth vision for climate action. To further advocate youth participation, UNICEF and the MCISYP hosted the Youth and Children in Global Climate Processes: Promoting Sustainable Development in Mountain Regions side event at COP29 in Baku, enabling young regional delegates to present their recommendations and advocate greater youth engagement in global climate efforts. Through these initiatives and strong partnerships with governments, CSOs and international organizations, UNICEF continues to champion youth-driven approaches to climate action and sustainable development. 
Through various iterations, the joint Enhancing Equitable and Inclusive Health Coverage by Bridging the Digital Divide project was launched, and saw close collaboration between UNICEF and three other United Nations organizations – UNDP, the World Health Organization (WHO), and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) – each providing its knowledge, expertise and comparative advantage to quickly improve maternal and child health using improved information exchange and specific and tailored referrals, digitalization and use of telemedicine. In this partnership, UNICEF will lead the component on strengthening and scaling up the innovative approach to reach remote and underserved populations on newborn health applying telemedicine and other digital solutions, something which UNICEF has already helped initiate in parts of 3 Oblasts since 2022. UNFPA will complement with a maternal health component. Meanwhile, WHO and UNDP will provide support on overall standards for digitalization and inter-operability of various information management systems used in the health sector. By combining expertise, the agencies address specific health challenges, to ensure that even the most marginalized communities have access to essential health services. The principle of ‘leave no one behind’ is central to this, ensuring that digital health initiatives are inclusive and equitable.
UNICEF, UNDP, and UNFPA continued their partnership to support children with disabilities through the joint Advancing the Rights of People with Disabilities in Kyrgyzstan project. UNICEF successfully advocated the creation of a working group on children with disabilities within the Disability Council, chaired by the Prime Minister. This initiative established a multi-stakeholder partnership, bringing together various stakeholders, including organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) and national and regional institutions. Key results include: (a) the strengthening the capacity of the working group on children with disabilities, based on the principles of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; and (b) Enhanced participation of organizations of people with disabilities in strengthening the two legal and policy frameworks 
In addition, during 2024, UNICEF successfully brought together government decision-makers, facility managers, and experts from the health and social sectors to address service provision for children with disabilities. Agreeing on simple actions – such as jointly defining a referral algorithm, developing a standard template for medical certification, and providing mentorship for regional experts by senior professionals remotely using telemedicine – removes both time and monetary burdens on families. This demonstrates that resolving interministerial bottlenecks can sometimes be more effectively achieved by bringing together key experts and decision-makers, rather than navigating lengthy bureaucratic processes.
At local level, UNICEF’s efforts to model integrated services for families with children with disabilities were enhanced through the partnership with a local CSO in Jalalabad city, leveraging community and peer support. Eight hundred parents and caregivers were accompanied through their transformational journey to deal with the challenges, stress and societal stigma of having children with disabilities: by uniting in self-help groups, they harnessed their skills and confidence to overcome stress, developed their own solutions, broadened their aspirations, and together advocated the reopening of a day-care centre within their community and other support from local authorities. CSOs are crucial in this kind of work, to ensure peer support, sharing of information and positive and constructive dialogue with local authorities and social services. Governmental services alone cannot respond to all the multiple and complex needs of children with disabilities and their families, therefore constructive and positive partnership among families, CSOs, local governments and social services is crucial to ensure children’s rights are fulfilled. 
Resource Transdisciplinary Teams (TDT) were established in four municipalities in partnership with Suzak local administration. TDT members expressed high satisfaction with the transdisciplinary teamwork, and highlighted the importance of involving families as equal partners. They displayed strong commitment to implementing the transdisciplinary approach in their daily work to support children with developmental delays/disabilities and their families. The Mayor of Jalal-Abad and the Suzak district administration approved the four TDTs and appointed team curators. Ongoing supervision support is being provided to the TDTs in Suzak district and Jalal-Abad city to review Individual Family and Child Support Plans for 36 children identified with developmental delays and disabilities. As a result, eight children received diagnoses and disability benefits, two were referred for treatment in Bishkek, five began receiving services from speech therapists and psychologists, and one was enrolled in kindergarten.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

The year began with great parliamentary interest in the topic of children in institutions. This materialized through two roundtables and a dedicated Parliamentary Council for Women’s and Children’s Rights and Gender Equality session. Regrettably, despite strong advocacy and engagement, no further action occurred in 2024. Some high-ranking government officials continue promoting children’s institutions because of their own personal experience in elite sports boarding academies. A UNICEF Regional Office policy brief received negative feedback from the government because of lack of nuance and challenges tempering language to different contexts. The Kyrgyz Republic’s participation in a UNICEF Uzbekistan and Regional Office forum in Tashkent to promote child, youth, and family well-being through social work and services may have provided further confirmation on how to move forward. The forum focused on social workers’ essential child and family support role to keep families together. This is important for Kyrgyzstan as the President had committed to 550 additional parasocial worker positions, with the new Prime Minister confirming this in late 2025. UNICEF will support the training of these new professionals in 2025 to address violence, keep families together and monitor foster parents.  
In February there was high concern over the spike in measles cases, which had reached a monthly total of 2,827, with 12 deaths, primarily among children with disabilities and malnourished children. Strong UNICEF advocacy led to government action, including allocating funds for the Jalalabad response in March. UNICEF also mobilized other funding and resources, which curbed the number of cases by December. Despite this, the response lacked comprehensive measures to improve hospital triage and case management, increase home isolation and treatment, provide Vitamin A supplementation, and strengthen infection prevention and control in health-care facilities. UNICEF advocated a comprehensive response plan to address these issues, aligned with WHO’s root cause analysis. Although the government approved a comprehensive action plan in February it did not fully incorporate all the recommended actions. In particular, the lack of a national guideline hindered Vitamin A supplementation. Currently, UNICEF is assisting the MoH to develop this critical guideline. Further support will be provided to curtailing measles’ spread in hospitals, seemingly the cause of the (lower) number of cases registered in late 2024.
In 2024, UNICEF Kyrgyzstan implemented a localization pilot for an upcoming United Nations Peacebuilding Fund project. This experience – the first in the region and the second globally – enabled UNICEF to engage with the planned beneficiaries, to ensure their interests and needs are central to UNICEF’s and other partners’ decision-making. This important piece of work, which gave rights holders the chance to express their opinions and participate in designing the initiative, gave voice to adolescents and young people in four locations across Kyrgyzstan. Consultations, focus group discussions and key informant interviews also enabled parents, community members and leaders to actively participate, fostering local ownership and strengthening local capacities. Over 200 people engaged in this participatory planning, and the results were validated locally and presented at a national workshop attended by high-level government officials, national CSOs, municipalities, and other stakeholders. This experience of active beneficiary participation in planned interventions was an important exercise for UNICEF Kyrgyzstan and partners, and led to reflection on the importance of beneficiary opinions, views and insights being integrated into all phases of planning and implementation of initiatives. Thanks to this experience, UNICEF Kyrgyzstan programming has gained strength and increased local government ownership of upcoming interventions in the remainder of the Country Programme. 
Behavioural insights (BI) studies conducted in 2024 built strong foundations for effective interventions for the remainder of the Country Programme. In particular, the BI on dietary diversity for children aged 6-24 months found that families lack practical knowledge about how to diversify family diets with locally available products. Mothers are culturally expected to heed guidance from fathers and older family members, and health workers seldom advise on child nutrition, focusing mostly on troubleshooting. Beside behavioural insights, UNICEF tested solutions and found that directly targeting the behaviours of grandparents and how they think about infant nutrition can enable further changes in nutrition among grandchildren in their households. A solution for mothers also proved effective in changing mothers’ attitudes towards children’s nutrition. Mothers’ understanding of the importance of a varied and healthy diet increased, and changes in behaviour followed. However, it was not possible to test another solution: addressing the unpaid care work borne by women that prevents healthier nutrition practices. The results were presented to partners and laid the groundwork for the MoH to develop a Social Behavioral Change Communications Strategy.
In addition, the study on stigma related to mental health and the language of psychosocial well-being revealed growing societal desire – especially among younger generations and urban residents – to talk openly about mental health. However, stereotypes and prejudices remain strong. In more traditional and rural communities, mental health is still taboo. Mental illnesses are often perceived as weaknesses or even curses, meaning many prefer to avoid such discussions and consider them a private matter. Derogatory terms are frequently used to describe those suffering from mental illnesses, stigmatizing individuals and creating barriers to open discussion and acceptance of mental health issues. Fear of judgment prevents people with mental conditions from seeking help and integrating into society. Key partners in Kyrgyzstan increasingly recognize the importance of UNICEF-led BIs for deeply analysing barriers to service uptake and practice of positive behaviours. There is also growing capacity among the local research community to leverage behavioural science, and wide use of participatory methods under UNICEF guidance.
These – and other lessons learned, in addition to new data from MICS and the shrinking funding landscape – guided an internal programmatic re-alignment exercise in the second half of 2024 to address programmatic environmental changes in Kyrgyzstan in the last three years. The re-alignment exercise, undertaken with the technical support from the Regional Office, was intended to strengthen the programmatic focus and rationalize the planned interventions and programmatic structure to reach the most vulnerable children, together with a scaling up approach to ensure sustainability and sector reforms.

Montenegro is an  upper-middle-income country in the Western Balkans with a developed legal and  institutional framework and is an EU candidate country. Montenegro’s  population of 623,633[1] is  declining rapidly. The 2023 Census data, published on 15 October 2024,  highlights three trends, all of which present challenges for Montenegro.  Firstly, an ageing population, especially in the northern and central  regions, with the percentage of children decreasing from 23.4% in 2011 to  21.7% in 2023. Secondly, the depopulation of the northern region and the urbanization  of Podgorica and the coastal region. And finally, what appears to be strong  inward migration of Russian, Ukrainian and Turkish citizens, coupled with  outward migration of young Montenegrin citizens. Of the total number of  children aged 0–17 (134,420), 1.13% (a total of 1,527) have at least one  difficulty/limitation in performing their daily activities. However, these  numbers seem underestimated, having in mind the global average of children  with disabilities. As for the Roma population, according to  self-identification in the Census, there are 2,757 Roma children (1,355 girls  and 1,402 boys) and 812 Egyptian children (399 girls and 413 boys). 
  
With the Human  Development Index value of 0.844, Montenegro ranks 50th out of 193 countries  and territories.[2]  The 2023 Gender Equality Index stood at 59.3, below the EU average of 68.6.
  
The proper functioning  of institutions was affected by political volatility and changes in the government  structure, with a government reshuffle taking place on 23 July 2024 based on  a coalition agreement, thus causing new institutional reorganizations,  stalling decision-making processes and delaying the implementation of reforms.  Challenges remain over the effective implementation of the Convention on the  Rights of the Child (CRC), primarily due to a weak accountability framework,  lack of systematic monitoring of existing laws and strategies, and  insufficient technical capacities and funding to ensure the enforcement of  children’s rights.  
  
The EU accession  agenda remains a core priority, with reportedly over 80% of the population  supporting the endeavor. In this regard, Montenegro has achieved a favourable  assessment as part of the EU’s Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR),  reflecting improvements in governance, fulfilment of the interim benchmarks  and the receiving of the final benchmarks for Chapters 23 (Judiciary and  Fundamental Rights) and 24 (Justice, Freedom and Security). Montenegro will  meet the benchmark for EU negotiation chapter 23 once it, inter alia,  implements a de-institutionalization strategy for persons with disabilities,  as well as a strong child protection system grounded in community-based care,  with the best interest of the child as the guiding principle, including as  regards children deprived of parental care or with disabilities.
  
As per the World  Bank’s projections, Montenegro’s economy is expected to grow by 3.4% in  2024. Growth is projected to be moderate but remain solid at 3.5% in 2025,  boosted by wage increases. Fiscal challenges persist as the government  reduces pension contributions, likely increasing the deficit to 4.1% of GDP  in 2025. Public debt is expected to rise to an estimated 64.5% of GDP by  2026. Maintaining fiscal sustainability will require disciplined policies  amid high external financing costs and geopolitical uncertainty. As per  MONSTAT data, inflation has come down from its 2022 peak of 13%, slowing down  to 3.3% in 2024 from 8.6% a year earlier. However, upside risks persist over  the medium term, and this may put additional pressure on the most vulnerable  families. Youth unemployment is a major structural challenge, standing at  27.9% for the population aged 15–24 as per the latest ILO data. 
  
Goal area 1 - Survive and  Thrive :   
  
Child and maternal  mortality rates in Montenegro have shown significant improvement over the  years. As of 2025, the infant mortality rate in Montenegro is estimated at  2.21 deaths per 1,000 live births,[3]  which is lower than the 2024 EU average of 3.3 deaths per 1,000 live births.[4] The  maternal mortality rate in Montenegro is 6.0 deaths per 100,000 live births,[5]  which is aligned with the 2020 EU average.[6]  These figures indicate that Montenegro has made substantial progress in  reducing both child and maternal mortality, bringing its rates in line with  or even better than the EU averages. This positive trend reflects  improvements in healthcare services, maternal care and child health  initiatives in the country. But certain important gaps, such as immunization  coverage rates, remain a burning issue and an indicator of the suboptimal  performance of the health sector, especially at the primary level.
  
The  low immunization coverage rate is still a cause of concern, as the timely  coverage rate achieved with the first dose of the measles, mumps and rubella  (MMR1) vaccine during 2024 still remains very low at 24.3% for the last  cohort of eligible children born in 2023,[7]  placing Montenegro among the 10 countries with the lowest MMR1 coverages  globally. Also,  according to the same source maintained by the Institute of Public Health  (IJZCG), the overall[8]  MMR1 coverage is currently (as of 10 January 2025) at 82.9%, but still  significantly below the target of 95%.  Although not as pronounced as MMR1, timely coverage with other routine  childhood immunizations is also below the optimal level of 95%, with the DTP1-DTP3  dropout rate being around 12%, indicating a low ability of the immunization  programme to ensure that children are fully vaccinated against vaccine-preventable  diseases.
  
 
  
A comprehensive analysis of the  available human resources in the primary healthcare system, prepared by  UNICEF and Montenegro’s health authorities, with financial support from the  Republic of Korea, shows significant regional  inequalities in the health workforce for maternal and child health (MCH),  affecting the accessibility, availability and quality of services, especially  in underserved areas. There is a deficit of at least 24 patronage nurses (nurses  providing home-based care), stressing the need for an increase of almost a  third to the currently available number of nurses,  and 4to 13 paediatric teams being needed to meet the national standards,  suggesting a need for an increase of up to 20% to the existing capacities.  Many paediatricians are at their patient registration quota limits, resulting  in adult doctors treating more children, which leads to a suboptimal quality  of care at the primary level. An ageing workforce compounds the issue, with  11% of the 81 paediatricians at the primary healthcare level already over the  retirement age. Currently, the system is relying on extending the retirement  age of health workers, with a projected shortage of at least 20 paediatricians  by 2028 if no new specialists are recruited.
  
The 2022 Montenegro  Nutrition Survey (MONS) showed that more than 25% of non-pregnant women are  anaemic, denoting a “moderate” public health problem, according to the WHO  criteria. Nearly 60% of non-pregnant women are iron-deficient. The combined  vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency affects 43 per cent of all women, with  the highest prevalence found in breastfeeding women (58%). Anaemia is found  in 13% of children aged 6–59 months, while more than 40% of children are  iron-deficient. Conservative estimates of the Situation Analysis of Early  Childhood Intervention (ECI) in Montenegro show that, between 10% (3,700) and  15% (5,550) of children from 0 to 6 years require ECI services annually,  among which only every third to second child (from 31% to 46%) has been  identified and served. 
  
Adolescents have  insufficient access to mental health services while reporting an  increased need for support. Young people aged 18 and over, in case of a need  for psychiatric treatment, report to the outpatient service of the Clinic for  Psychiatry of the Clinical Centre of Montenegro where, however, all the practising  psychiatrists are specialists in adult psychiatry. Capacity for the hospital  treatment of children and young people does not exist, but all children and  adolescents who need hospital treatment are referred for treatment in  institutions in the surrounding area. There is a clear need for specialists  in child and adolescent psychiatry and psychology, as well as the need to  establish capacities for the hospital treatment of children and young people  with mental health disorders.[9]   
  
Recent data at the  European level shows that girls, older adolescents and those growing up in  low income households, report the worst mental health, whilst half of mental  health disorders have their onset before or during adolescence. As stated in  the UNICEF–WHO report in 2024, mental illness can lead to worse educational  outcomes, increased substance use and higher rates of unemployment, debt and  social exclusion in adulthood, and although the data for Montenegro has not,  unfortunately, been collected, this is also the case with neighbouring  countries with a similar socio-economic and political landscape. [10]
  
 Goal area 2 -  Learn:   
  
The education system is responsible for over  122,000 pupils (pre-primary, primary and secondary levels).  
  
The percentage of children enrolled in preschool  education increased by 3.4% in comparison to 2023, with the coverage rate of  3–6-year-old children currently standing at 79.6%. However, for Roma  children, we see only 291 (155 boys and 136 girls) enrolled in preschool, out  of a total 1,091 as per the Census data, hence representing only 22.7%. The  number of children with disabilities in preschools increased by as much as  27% when compared to the previous school year with a total of 204 children enrolled,  while for primary education the number increased by 15% to a total of 1,335  children. However, the number of Roma children in primary schools decreased  by 7%, and in secondary schools by 16% in comparison to the previous school  year. One of the most complex issues that the education system is facing is  how to accommodate and provide quality support to the increasing number of  foreign (primarily Russian, Ukrainian and Turkish) children, who constitute,  on average, 7% of the children, while in several municipalities the  proportion reaches almost 30% in primary schools.
  
Fourth-grade pupils from Montenegro, at the  international TIMSS test in mathematics and natural sciences, achieved 477  and 461 points, respectively, which is a significantly better result compared  to the previous cycle of TIMSS 2019 (453 points in both mathematics and  natural sciences), but is still statistically lower compared to the TIMSS  average, which is 500 points. The percentages of pupils achieving the  advanced level in mathematics and natural sciences were 2% and 1%,  respectively, while 84% and 80% achieved the basic level in the respective  subjects. However, 16% and 20% of pupils, respectively, did not achieve even  the basic level in mathematics and natural sciences.
  
Montenegro performed worse than most OECD  countries across subjects in the 2023 PISA assessment. Pupils performance  dropped between 2018 and 2022 in the context of COVID-19-induced disruptions  to schooling. A high proportion of pupils are not achieving even basic  proficiency in the core subjects (in mathematics % of scoring below proficiency  is 60% vs 31% OECD; in reading 53% vs 23% OECD). Advantaged pupils significantly  outperformed their disadvantaged peers.[11] On  average across the region, the performance gap between advantaged and  disadvantaged pupils was equivalent to more than three years of schooling in  OECD member states. This inequality extends beyond academic performance:  advantaged pupils report a greater sense of belonging in school and were more  likely than their disadvantaged peers to report that they expect to complete  tertiary education.
  
 As per latest data, the share of young  people not in education, employment or training stands  declined to  20.3% in 2023 from 23.2 % in 2022.
  
 Goal area 3 - Protection from Violence  and Exploitation:   
  
The number of children  in residential care remained the same as in 2023. Although deinstitutionalization  had slowed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, still the number of children in residential  care had decreased by 29% since 2020. The share of children with disabilities  in residential care has increased, making up 47% of the total number (in  2023, 41% of the total number of children in residential care were children  with disabilities). A significant number of children with disabilities in  residential care are children in Resource Centres, i.e. 19% of the total  number, due to the insufficient availability of inclusive education in the  municipalities of their origin. The number of children with disabilities in  foster care has slightly increased, while the overall number of children in  foster care decreased by 7% compared to 2023 (the decrease is in the number  of children in kinship care, while the number of children in non-kinship care  remained the same). 
  
Several consecutive EU  Reports for Montenegro emphasized that gender-based violence and violence  against children are issues of concern, with an overall weak institutional  response and availability of services. In August, Montenegro established a  register for persons convicted of crimes against sexual freedom committed  against minors, with currently 98 registered individuals. Montenegro has not  yet acted on recommendations by UN monitoring bodies to raise the minimum age  for marriage. The practice of arranged child marriages in Roma communities  remains a concern (32.5% of girls aged 15–19 and 15.8% of boys are currently  married or in a union). Peer violence at school and outside of school appears  to be a growing trend. In Montenegro, 43% of school children witnessed  violence in their school, 17% claimed to have been victims of violence, and  6.7% admitted that they had been violent towards other children during the  2022/2023 school year, according to a 2023 Bureau for Education study  involving over 12,000 pupils. Children’s increased reliance on digital  solutions highlighted the need for strengthened online protection. 
  
 Goal area 4- Safe and clean environment:   
  
Assessment of the  Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) status in healthcare facilities  and Roma and Egyptian communities showed concerning results, as data indicates  that, out of a total of 120 analysed water samples in Roma settlements,  almost 16% of households live with defective water; in almost half of the Roma  settlements, there are no containers for communal waste disposal, with  recorded evidence of missing sanitation, and even open defecation in some of  the settlements. Among the 31 health institutions included in the research,  19 of them (62%) have an estimated level of risk from medical waste  management as insignificant or low, while in eight institutions (25%) the  estimated level of risk was high or critical. Air pollution represents a  health risk for children and adults, especially in urban areas. The impacts  of air pollution and climate change-related events pose a serious threat to  children’s physical and mental health. As per European Environment Agency  data, the mortality rate from fine-particle air pollution PM2.5 in Montenegro  is one of the highest in Europe, where the premature death rate (174 deaths  per 100,000 population) is more than three times the EU average.
  
 Goal area 5- Equitable Chance in Life:   
  
The latest Population Census from 2024 shows that there are 134,420 children (aged 0–17) in  Montenegro, while the data received from the Ministry of Finance shows that  130,685 children in Montenegro receive universal child allowance (UCA), which means that 97% of the  Montenegrin children are UCA beneficiaries. The total funds presently  allocated for UCA are 10 times higher than they were a decade ago (approx. €50  million).
  
In terms of monetary  poverty, the World Bank Report shows that, in Montenegro, 4.1% of children  live in extreme child poverty ($2.15/day), 9.5% subsist on less than $3.65 a  day, while 27.2% live below the higher international poverty line of $6.85  per day.
  
The expansion of child  allowance to all children up to the age of 18 has contributed to a decrease  in child poverty, as the 2023 Survey on Income and Living Conditions (SILC)  data showed that at-risk-of-poverty rate for children declined from 28.4% in  2022 to 27.3% in 2023 – but still the fifth highest among Europe-area  countries. However, as the coverage and quality of services are not at an  adequate level, the EU SILC multidimensional poverty indicator, which  measures the percentage of children at risk of poverty and social exclusion,  is still at a concerning 38.2%. Children with disabilities and Roma children  continue to face significant barriers and inequalities in their access to  basic services, such as health care and nutrition, education and housing.  According to the Multidimensional Child Poverty in Montenegro Analysis  (2021), 96% of Roma children experience deprivations in at least one domain  of their wellbeing, and 65% of children under two years of age experience  simultaneous deprivations for nutrition, ECD and housing. The same analysis points  to the fact that the stigma regarding poverty is often compounded with the stigma  regarding disability or ethnic affiliation (e.g. Roma), and that parents of  children with disabilities often rely only on themselves to cope with  problems. Montenegro still lacks a focused poverty reduction strategy. 
  
The World Bank notes  that “the overall pace of poverty reduction is forecast to slow down from  over 3 percentage points annually pre-pandemic to roughly 1 percentage point  annually between 2022 and 2025, the forecast period, “due to decelerating  growth in the region, to the sharp increases in the prices of food and energy  during 2022 2023, which strained households’ purchasing power, and to the  decline in real wages in 2022”. The cumulative effects of inflation are  expected to pose a challenge, especially for lower-income households. The WB  also warns that “the level of vulnerability to income shocks remains high  despite progress on poverty reduction”, which is confirmed by the SILC data  from 2023, which states that almost 50% of Montenegrin families cannot cope  with unexpected financial expenses. Because the universal child allowance is  allocated at a fixed rate of €30 (with the exception of the UCA for children  with disabilities and those from families receiving family material support),  which is not regularly adjusted to rising incomes and living costs, it is  expected that inflationary pressures will have an adverse effect on the  adequacy of UCA.

Goal area 1 - Survive  and Thrive:  
  
 During 2024, a  cross-sector working group led by the Ministry of Health oversaw and  monitored the implementation of Montenegro's first national cross-sector  Early Childhood Development (ECD) Strategy (2023–2027). The Strategy follows  the global Nurturing Care Framework (NCF) with activities in the domains of  health, nutrition, early learning, parenting, and security and safety. Over €1  million was allocated by the government for implementation of the Strategy’s  first Action Plan in 2024. Activities were related to the capacity building  of those professionals providing Early Childhood Development services,  development of professional guidelines, improvement of the Health Information  System, promotion of services and improvement of infrastructure in primary  healthcare centres. The Government of Montenegro proposed to allocate almost  half a million euros for the 2025 Action Plan.
  
The number of parents  benefitting from parenting support, using Bebbo mobile app or the  face-to-face programme “Caring Families” (known internationally as “Parenting  for Lifelong Health for Young Children”) continued to grow. The total number  of users of the Bebbo app, managed jointly by the Institute of Public Health  of Montenegro and UNICEF, has exceeded 14,000 people (fathers account for 15%  of all users). During 2024, 523 caregivers (11% of them fathers) were  recruited into the face-to-face “Caring Families” programme, predominantly  delivered by preschools, primary healthcare centres and non-governmental  organizations. During 2024, the emphasis was placed on reaching vulnerable  and hard-to-reach populations. Parents’ satisfaction with both programmes  remains very high. Furthermore, a group of home-visiting nurses was supported  in the delivery of UNICEF’s international “Caring for the Caregiver”  programme, which focuses on caregivers’ mental health, benefitting nearly 200  families. 
  
With the support of  the Republic of Korea through ACT-A investments, Montenegro conducted its  first country-wide comprehensive analysis of human resources at the primary  healthcare (PHC) level and a gap analysis, as well an analysis of public  funding in Montenegro’s health system, with a focus on PHC spending. The  Ministry of Health will use this analysis for the ongoing development of the  Strategy of Human Resources in the Health Sector.
  
The Institute for  Public Health of Montenegro was supported in strengthening the knowledge of  preschool teachers, educators and nurses working in preschool institutions  and educational facilities managers on immunization. More than 800 employees  were educated but, unfortunately, the coverage rate with the first dose of  the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in 2024 remained low and way below the  optimal levels for herd immunity of 95% children vaccinated. Focus of the training has been first to advocate among the educators and kindergarten nurses for immunizations and its promotion in nurseries and preschool facilities, and then to enable them to serve as advocates themselves among parents in order to improve the adherence to the proposed national immunization schedule. Also, one of the goals has been in leveraging them as the first line responders to questions, queries and concerns of parents related not only to immunizations but also vaccine preventable diseases and legal requirements for enrolment in schools and preschools that are in connection with child immunization status. UNICEF is  working with the Ministry of Health to have a dedicated Routine Immunization  Coordinator (national EPI Manager), to finalize a National Immunization  Strategy (NIS) and on updating the relevant social and behavioural change  measures. Based on UNICEF advocacy, development of the NIS has been included  in the EU Commission’s recommendations in the Montenegro 2024 Report.
  
In 2024, the Ministry  of Health and UNICEF launched an assessment of the quality of maternal and  neonatal services in health facilities in Montenegro (maternity wards, the Centre  for Neonatology and primary healthcare centres providing emergency obstetric  care), which was conducted in 2023 using WHO EURO methodology. The report recommends, among other things,  institutionalizing statistical data collection and analysis, rolling out evidence based clinical protocols and guidelines including policies to reduce the likelihood of caesarean sections, building capacity of staff on management of normal labour and delivery, on managing labour complications, and on neonatal resuscitation. Following the launch, in collaboration  with Latter-Day Saint Charities (LDS Charities), a training on neonatal  resuscitation was held and the Clinical Centre of Montenegro was supported to  roll out training in 100% maternity facilities. 
  
Contemporary  transdisciplinary, family-centred early intervention, introduced in 2023 in  two pilot municipalities, with oversight by the Ministry of Health, Ministry  of Education, Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare and with UNICEF and EU  support, continued to be provided in 2024. One municipality discontinued the  pilot, but another institution in the capital city joined the pilot instead.  In total, 634 children (361 boys and 273 girls) benefitted from contemporary  screening and early intervention methods. Contemporary transdisciplinary,  family-centred early intervention is an approach designed to support young  children with disabilities or developmental delays and their families. This  model emphasizes transdisciplinary collaboration between professionals from  various areas, such as healthcare, education and social services, to create a  comprehensive and cohesive support system for the child and family. At the  same time, the family’s needs, preferences and goals are at the heart of the  intervention process. Families are actively involved in decision making and  planning, ensuring that the services provided are tailored to their unique  circumstances with interventions that are integrated into the family’s daily  routines and activities. This approach helps the child practise and develop  functional skills in a natural context, making the learning process more  effective and meaningful.
  
    Goal  area 2 - Learn:   
  
 In 2024, Montenegro  grappled with political and institutional instability, which inevitably  impacted the pace of programme implementation in the areas of education and  adolescent empowerment. The country continued to face a profound learning  crisis, mainly related to low-quality teaching, limited access to education  for children from vulnerable groups, and inadequate school infrastructure.  Adolescents had scarce opportunities for developing their employability  skills and for meaningful engagement. Support services for the mental health  of adolescents are also very limited. 
  
However, due to  successful resource mobilization, UNICEF had a most intensive year  implementing – with the support of the EU, SIDA, Montenegro SDG Acceleration  Fund, TUI Care Foundation, Peacebuilding Fund, UNICEF Learning Innovation Hub  and the Micro:bit Education Foundation – several large-scale initiatives in  formal and non-formal education, reaching almost 70,000 children and  adolescents across Montenegro.
  
A first-ever  comprehensive reform of the education system was initiated, culminating in the  draft Education Strategy 2025–2035 document. This new, long-term strategy,  arranged on four pillars (quality and equity, support to teachers, governance  and financing, and school infrastructure) encompasses several shifts from  past approaches, namely a focus on development of ‘future-proof’ key skills  and competencies, reforms of the initial and in-service training of teachers,  enhancing the overall governance and resilience of the education system and  ensuring sustained financing of reforms, and large-scale investment in  improving school infrastructure in such a way that it creates an adequate,  climate-resilient, inclusive and learning-conducive environment for all  children. To ensure that all voices were integrated in the new Strategy, a  broad process of consultations was conducted, including over 1,100 students –  including those affected by poverty, Roma students and students with  disabilities, over 2,800 teachers and 5,500 parents, 84% of whom were  mothers/female guardians. 
  
The national Digital  School Platform (based on the Learning Passport) has 27,918 active users,  with 53 new courses developed in 2024. Furthermore, UNICEF supported the  Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation to establish EdTech hubs and a related  programme across 12 primary and secondary schools in the north of the  country, reaching 6,000 pupils. Over 500 children were supported to develop  digital, critical thinking and problem-solving skills in 12 primary schools,  as well as an additional 1,120 through UNICEF-supported workshops at the  national Days of Science Festival. 
  
The social and  emotional learning programme was further expanded to 121 primary and  secondary schools, reaching almost 46,000 children.
  
Following long and  intensive advocacy, regulations were changed to increase the number of Roma  mediators in schools and preschools from one for every 70 pupils to one for  every 35) and the issue of school transportation for Roma children was  addressed in a timely way for the start of the school year. In addition, 60  preschool staff in the 12 municipalities with the largest Roma population  were trained to provide quality support to Roma children.
  
Children with  disabilities in preschool education and first cycle of education were  supported through multiple initiatives: the Special Olympics programme “Young  Athletes”, intended to encourage inclusion through sport, was expanded to 17  (out of 21) preschool institutions in Montenegro; all preschools in  Montenegro were equipped with tablets, with over 204 children with  disabilities (135 boys, 69 girls) as well as other children benefitting from  the use of the C-board application.
  
Adolescents and young  people continue to face obstacles regarding access to mental health services,  employability and career guidance, as well as opportunities for civic  engagement. Despite these hurdles, the UNICEF Country Office (CO) achieved  notable progress through its key initiatives:
Across all three  regions of Montenegro, 1,650 adolescents (511 males and 1,139 females)  received career guidance and job training through the “Prilike” programme,  which is recognized as a precursor to the EU Youth Guarantee scheme,  integrating private-sector partnerships and civil society collaboration to  support adolescents in acquiring labour market-relevant skills.
  
With UNICEF support, the Ministry of Sports and Youth  developed the new Strategy for Sports, with a strong focus on school sports,  inclusion and new programmes for children with disabilities. The Strategy was  adopted by the government in August. 
  
As part of the new joint UN programme on social  cohesion, supported by PBF, UNICEF launched activities focusing on  capacitating adolescents and young people for civic engagement and  participation – including the launch of child parliaments in five cities in  all three regions. The socio-emotional skills programme was adapted to have a  stronger focus on social cohesion, and multiple programmes were implemented  focusing on violence prevention and conflict resolution.  

Goal area 3 - Protection  from Violence and Exploitation:   
  
In 2024, the Country  Office (CO) continued its extensive support to the government through high-level  technical expertise, guidance and advocacy, which contribute to realizing  Montenegro’s 2024–2027 accession programme to the European Union. UNICEF  intensively supported the government, under the lead of the Ministry of  Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography (MSWFCD) in the design and  adoption of the Strategy for the Development of Social and Childcare System  2025–2028 with the Action Plan for 2025.
