The strategic framework relies on  the Roadmap of Social and Child Protection Reforms from 2022, developed by  UNICEF and recommended by the EU as a key document in the path to reforms.  UNICEF continued to support deinstitutionalization, including through finalization  and adoption of the first national Strategy on Deinstitutionalization  2025–2028 and Action Plan for 2025. The CO continued providing expertise in  establishing the first Centre for Foster Care and Adoption. A Roadmap for  establishing the Centre for Foster Care and Adoption and strengthening foster  care was developed and endorsed by the MSWFCD. Implementation of the Roadmap  could be slowed down due to development of the new Law on Social and Child  Protection to be adopted by the end of the second quarter of 2025. In  addition, the commitment to accelerate DI is not strong enough at the highest  level of the government. In 2024, within the initiative funded by the EU on  Violence Against Children (VAC), the CO provided technical support to the  Government of Montenegro in the finalizing and adoption of the Strategy for  the Protection of Children from and Prevention of Violence 2025–2029 and  Action Plan for 2025 and supported the meaningful participation of children  and young people in the process of its development. The CSO Union of High  School Pupils organized a discussion with 348 high school pupils (110 boys  and 238 girls) that proposed concrete measures and recommendations for the  S
trategy on VAC. The Union of High School Pupils developed a Call to Action to  the Government to take active action in the field of the suppression and  prevention of violence, which was submitted to the Council of Child Rights.  Based on all the inputs, the Strategy envisages responsibilities for all  sectors, improving the normative frameworks for addressing issues of violence  and child protection, enhancing the capacities of professionals and  institutions for prevention, but also the reporting mechanisms and support  services to respond to violence in all sectors, such as establishing the  Barnahus-model service for child victims of severe forms of violence.
  
The CO intensified  communication with the Delegation of the European Union and MSWFCD to improve  coordination for the design and implementation of the European Child  Guarantee (ECG), as a key mechanism for operationalization of the above  mentioned three comprehensive child protection and social protection  strategies. Steps have been undertaken by the CO towards supporting the  drafting of the national Action Plan for the ECG and the exchanging of  experiences with countries that have successfully implemented ECG pilot  projects.
  
The CO, together with the  UNICEF Regional Office and in partnership with the Council of Europe and the  EU, organized a high-level advocacy event – an international conference on the  Barnahus service (a one-stop-shop service) for child victims of violence and  exploitation hosted by the Government of Montenegro. The conference gathered  more than 200 participants and 20 government delegations from ECAR; this  resulted in the government committing itself to establishing the Barnahus-model  service in line with the best EU practices. A multisectoral Technical Group  for establishing Barnahus was established as a follow-up to the conference.
  
The capacities of 176  professionals were strengthened in the areas of: case management in cases of  children exposed to violence and exploitation; child-friendly justice  principles to guide work with child victims of violence; identification,  referral, victim support and forensic interviews of children. Of the total  number of case managers in Centres for Social Work, 85% attended accredited  training sessions and strengthened their capacities for working with child  victims of violence.
  
Support was provided  to the CSOs, the Centre for Roma Initiatives and Defendologija, to provide  comprehensive assistance from their field of expertise for children at risk  of child marriage, including an intensive six-month engagement on the empowerment  of 35 Roma and Egyptian girls and boys and their families (20 fathers, 20  mothers and 60 other family members) through learning support, psychosocial  support, individual and group work and work with families, and to the Centre  for Child Rights which provided intensive support to 74 children with  challenging behaviour (42 boys and 32 girls) and 76 parents (56 mothers, 20  fathers).  
  
A state-led Child  Helpline (111 116) was supported in establishing a new modality for providing  advice to children and young people, i.e. the “CHAT OPTION”. The skills of  90% of the professionals working on the Child Helpline on how to provide  support to children through the chat option were strengthened.  
  
The CO, together with the  UNICEF Innocenti Research Centre, INTERPOL and ECPAT International, led the  process of a large-scale research project entitled “Disrupting Harm”. The  analysis will present unique insights on digital harm and threats to children  and young people, and will provide a tailored roadmap for key actors to act  across sectors; it is scheduled to be published in early 2025. 
  
Goal area 4- Safe and  clean environment:   
  
Assessment of the  Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) status and adaptation of global  protocols by UNICEF and WHO for cleaning facilities, staff training and for  improving the knowledge and practices of employees in this area based on the Water  Supply and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) were  conducted in primary healthcare centres in cooperation with the Institute of  Public Health of Montenegro, and with the financial support of the Government  of the Republic of Korea. By adapting the “WASH FIT” guidelines, Montenegro  became part of a group of selected countries that are leading and proactively  contributing to implementation of the Global Framework for Action on universal  water, sanitation, hygiene, waste and electricity services in all healthcare  facilities. Trainings on the guidelines have been organized across all health  institutions in the country. Qualitative and quantitative research on the  state and quality of water, sanitation and hygiene services in Roma and  Egyptian settlements, with the component of awareness raising of the  population through work with Roma collaborators in social inclusion  (mediators) and the staff of the Institute for Public Health, has been  implemented. In total, 14 municipalities with Roma settlements were covered. Thirty-five  Roma communities with 210 Roma families were reached through integrated  social and behavioural change interventions and community engagement.
  
With UNICEF support,  the Government of Montenegro joined more than 40 countries globally in  signing the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action during an event  in Podgorica attended by the UNICEF regional director. In signing the  Declaration, Montenegro has committed itself to working with children and  young people to identify and take actions that provide future generations  with a clean, healthy and sustainable environment. In 2024, more than 3,000  adolescents played an active role in learning more on air quality and climate  change, as well as designing and implementing community initiatives on air  quality. A project to measure indoor air quality in schools was launched,  which will be followed up by recommendations for safer and healthier school  environments. 
  
The  CO contributed to the successful organization of and participation at the  Europe and Central Asia Regional Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction from 6 to  8 November 2024 with a strong youth presence that led to the Call to Action  on Children and Youth. Emerging from the “Road to Resilience for Europe and Central  Asia’s Children and Youth Forum”, this call emphasizes the crucial role of  young people in disaster risk reduction and their call for greater inclusion  in the decision-making processes. Based on UNICEF’s advocacy, child-focused  interventions were included in the national DRR Strategy 2025–2030. 
  
Goal area 5- Equitable  Chance in Life:   
  
UNICEF provided  technical expertise to the Government of Montenegro in the overall social and  child protection (SCP) strategic framework reform in the country. The  Strategy for the Development of the SCP System 2025–2028 and Action Plan for 2025,  as set forth in the 2022 Roadmap of SCP Reforms, were drafted and adopted  under the lead of the Ministry of Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography  (MSWFCD). One of the key elements of the reform proposed in the Strategy,  resulting from UNICEF’s efforts and continued advocacy, is improvement of the  coverage and adequacy of material allowances targeted at the poor. The  proposed strategic measure encompasses relaxation of the strict eligibility  criteria for the family support allowance, as well as an increase of the  amount for each family member. The ongoing reform of the strategic and  legislative framework is aligned with Montenegro’s EU accession priorities  outlined in the EC 2024 Montenegro Report and Reform Agenda. UNICEF initiated  intensive communication with the Delegation of the European Union (DEU) and the  MSWFCD to improve coordination for the implementation of the European Child  Guarantee (ECG) that is planned for Montenegro. Steps have been undertaken by  UNICEF toward resource mobilization for the initial activities targeted at  ECG design – drafting of the national Action Plan for ECG and the exchanging  of experiences with countries that have successfully implemented ECG pilot  projects, such as Croatia and Romania. UNICEF proposed to the MSWFCD to  include shock-responsive social protection elements in the new Strategy on  SCP 2025–2028, which was accepted by the ministry and is an important step  forward with regards to future activities. Since UNICEF guided the process of  finalizing the strategic framework and since its implementation will further  rely on the Reform Agenda, the plan is to contribute to this process through  active advocacy for and design of the ECG. 
  
UNICEF intensified  cooperation at the local level, which resulted in the signing of an MoU with  the Union of Municipalities of Montenegro (UoM). In addition, support to the  UoM was defined through the implementation of a project for support to  children without parental care once they leave the Children’s Home in Bijela,  having in mind that a support mechanism for their successful integration into  society and the conducting of daily duties is currently missing across  municipalities. 
  
Throughout the year,  UNICEF conducted advocacy activities about the harmful effects of child  poverty at both the global and national levels. Montenegro’s successful  example of child-sensitive social protection and of leveraging funds for  poverty reduction was featured in a global knowledge-sharing event organized  by the UNICEF Evaluation Office NY and the Economic Policy Research  Institute. UNICEF participated in two sideline events on leveraging funds for  poverty reduction dedicated to high-level donors in Europe and Central Asia on  the margins of the UN Summit for the Future. In terms of significant  knowledge products and cooperation with other UN agencies in this area, a  Policy Brief on Poverty was published with the UN Resident Coordinator  Office, featuring UNICEF’s significant contribution to this joint  publication.  
  
Child rights  monitoring   
  
With the CO’s advocacy  and technical support, child rights have been set higher on the country’s  political agenda. The Child Rights Council, a high-level child rights  governance/coordination body, has been progressively improving its work by  addressing child rights priorities and reforms through the six thematic  sessions held in 2024, which resulted in the fostering of cross-sector  cooperation, improved child rights monitoring, accountability for results,  and the acceleration of sectoral reforms in health, social welfare,  education, work on MIC7, Child Guarantee, Child Rights Budgeting, etc. 
  
The high-level  conference “Children’s Rights at the Heart of the EU Accession Process and  the 2030 Agenda”, co-organized by the government, the Delegation of the  European Union to Montenegro and UNICEF, proclaimed a Pledge/Call to Action  for Children, later presented to the Council on the Rights of the Child for  submission to the government for adoption. The Pledge calls for: the mainstreaming  of child rights in all the government’s strategies, policies and reforms  pertaining to the European Union accession and the 2030 Agenda; the recognition  of children and young people as holders of rights and critical agents of  change; implementation and co-funding of the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster  Survey (MICS); making data on children publicly available on the website of  the Council on Child Rights; investing in child rights through Child Rights  Budgeting; and implementation of programmes, such as the EU Child Guarantee  to address challenges such as poverty and inequality. 
  
Close to 70 government  staff from the General Secretariat of the Government, the Office for  Coordination of IPA Assistance, the Office for Sustainable Development,  sectoral IPA Units, line ministries and the judiciary were educated on  international instruments on Child Rights and on mainstreaming Child Rights  in the EU accession process. 
  
The CO advocated for and  supported the Ministry of Finance and line ministries to prioritize  children’s rights in the state budget, which is a key funding source for  children in an EU pre-accession country, such as Montenegro. The CO supported  the strengthening of the MoF’s counterparts on UNICEF’s PF4C for Health and  Immunization, and improvements to communication between the MoF and line  ministries which lead on budget preparations for the financing of social  sectors. To leverage resources for children, two strategic partnerships with  non-traditional partners, including the private sector, were successfully  managed to achieve results for children at scale. 
  
The government’s Office  for Sustainable Development was supported to integrate child rights-related  SDGs indicators into the newly created database for monitoring implementation  of the national Strategy for Sustainable Development. There is an ongoing  discussion on establishment of a child rights dashboard on the website of the  Council on the Rights of the Child, which will serve for improved monitoring  of the CRC’s Concluding Observations for Montenegro and the child rights  situation in the country. 
  
With CO support, the  National Statistics Office (MONSTAT), has been preparing the next round of the  Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey, i.e. MICS7, the country’s second-largest  survey, following the population census. With the advocacy efforts of the CO  and MONSTAT, the government has allocated €300,000 from the 2025 State Budget  for the implementation of MICS7. 
  
With CO support, the government  completed the Country-led Independent External Evaluation of the Strategy on  Exercise of Child Rights 2019–2023, as a crucial foundation for the next  evidence-based, cross-sector strategic policy document on child rights. Also,  the Independent Evaluation of the EU supported the Early Childhood  Development Initiative, and the Joint UN Project on Accelerating Inclusion of  Persons with Disabilities (Phase I), funded by UNPRPD, were completed. The country-based  evaluation, as part of a multi-country evaluation of Childcare System Reform  from 2023, was assessed as exceptional by GEROS in 2024. 
  
Extensive support was  provided to the Parliament of Montenegro to bring the child rights agenda to the  core of the work of the Parliamentary committees. Three thematic sessions  were held on the reform of social and child protection, the situation of the Roma  and Egyptian communities, and children with disabilities and their families.  Meaningful child participation has been strengthened under the umbrella of the  Joint UN Peacebuilding project, implemented by UNDP, UNESCO and UNICEF.  Excellent cooperation with the Women’s Club of the Parliament has been  further cultivated. With the CO’s persistent advocacy and technical  assistance, the Institution of the Ombudsperson increased its capacities to  exercise quality monitoring of child rights. As a result of the CO’s advocacy  efforts, the function of Deputy Ombudsperson for Children has been explicitly  defined in the Draft Law on the Ombudsperson. 
  
Gender equality     
  
The Country Office  Gender Action Plan that is under implementation is aligned with UNICEF’s  Gender Action Plan and Gender Policy, as well as with the recommendations from  the Gender Programme Review. A strong partnership was developed with the  Parliamentary Women’s Club, focused on entry points for gender mainstreaming  across sectors and priority areas for improving children’s and women’s  wellbeing. A Contribution Agreement was signed with the International  Women’s Club of Montenegro as a result of a successful fundraising  initiative, which was conducted in partnership between the Women’s  Parliamentary Club, International Women’s Club and UNICEF, with €167,000  raised to support the procurement of equipment for all Day-Care Centres for  girls and boys with disabilities across the country. 
  
The number of parents benefiting  from gender responsive parenting support, using Bebbo mobile app or the  face-to-face programme Caring Families continued to grow. The total number of  users of the Bebbo app, managed jointly by the Institute of Public Health of  Montenegro and UNICEF, has exceeded 14,000 people (fathers account for 15% of  all users). During 2024, 523 caregivers (11% fathers) were recruited into the  face-to-face Caring Families programme, predominantly delivered by  preschools, primary health care centres and non-governmental organizations.  During 2024, emphasis was placed on reaching vulnerable and hard to reach  populations such as Roma families. Parental satisfaction with both programmes  remains very high. Furthermore, a group of home visiting nurses was supported  in the delivery of UNICEF’s international Caring for the Caregiver programme,  which focuses on caregiver’s mental health, benefitting nearly 200  families.  
  
UNICEF supported a consortium  of two CSOs, i.e. the Centre for Roma Initiatives and Defendologija, which worked  closely on a six-month empowerment of 20 Roma and Egyptian girls and 15 boys  and their families (20 fathers, 20 mothers and 60 other family members) to  tackle issues and harmful practices, such as social exclusion, violent  discipline, child marriages and school dropout. The support to girls and boys  and their families includes both individual and group work, learning and  psychosocial support. Special attention was given to the presence of fathers  and brothers during family visits and workshops, which is of great importance  for the prevention of child marriages. 
  
Compliant with the  assumed obligations from the National Gender Equality Strategy 2021–2025,  UNICEF joined the OSCE to support the Ministry of Education, Science and  Innovation in carrying out an analysis of subject curricula and textbooks in  primary education to assess the extent to which they perpetuate gender  stereotypes, and to formulate recommendations towards mainstreaming gender  equality in the curricula and textbooks which are included in the draft  Education Reform Strategy 2025–2035.
  
In cooperation with  the Institute of Public Health of Montenegro, and with the support of UNICEF  and the Government of the Republic of Korea, good practices and education  were promoted for WASH among Roma and Egyptians to adapt, adopt and maintain  desirable behaviour related to issues of hygiene, menstrual health, water  shortages and adaptation to climate change. The intervention had a specific  gender component related to menstrual hygiene, that is often taboo in the general  population but especially among Roma families.

UNICEF continued to  play a key role in the UN Country Team and has been leading discussions and  coordination of the Human Capital Development Results Group. During 2024,  critical steps were taken towards the implementation of the United Nations  Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework Joint Work Plan 2023–2024 with a  focus on aligning the UN programmes with the government’s needs deriving from  the EU accession process.
  
Furthermore, UNICEF  guided a discussion on joint programming at the UNCT Retreat, noting the  value of joining forces either through the context of the Montenegro  Acceleration Fund (MAF) or outside of it. After successfully implemented the first  phase of the UN joint Programme on Disability Inclusion, funded by UNPRPD,  adding value to system-strengthening efforts in implementing the CPRPD, the  second phase was approved by the same donor with the amount of US$300,000. UNICEF,  together with UNDP and UNESCO, is also implementing a comprehensive joint  programme “Enhancing citizens’ trust in institutions and building resilient  communities”, with the amount of US$2.5 million, supported by the UN  Peacebuilding Fund and the Government of Montenegro. The joint programme is  focused on social cohesion and targeting interventions across the sectors of child  rights monitoring and participation, education, child protection, young  people and adolescents. 
  
UNICEF participated in  the operationalization of the UN MAF – a pooled funding mechanism that aims  to accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development  and the imminent achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in  Montenegro. Under this mechanism, UNICEF’s joint initiative with UNESCO and the  ILO on quality and inclusive digital learning for children and teachers has  been supported, resulting in capacity building for school staff in the area  of digital education, as well as the establishment of EdTech hubs and a related  programme across the north of Montenegro, resulting in matched investment by  the Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation to expand the EdTech  initiative under the EU Growth Plan. 
  
UNICEF also cooperated  with UNHCR in concluding a memorandum of understanding aimed at strengthening  cooperation on education and protection of refugee and asylum-seeking  children and their families. 
  
As a result of  multiple strategies applied through a broad partnership with the line  ministries, the National IPA Coordinator office, the EU Commission and the EU  Delegation to Montenegro, major child rights commitments, such as the Child  and Youth Guarantees, have been integrated into the key EU accession  documents, such as the Reform Agenda EU Growth Plan for the Western Balkans,  as well as the 2024 EU Enlargement Report and the EU’s closing benchmarks for  Chapter 23.   
  
The bilateral  partnership with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) has been further strengthened  through joint work on child budgeting, capacity building of the MoF’s  counterparts on UNICEF’s Public Financing for Children (PF4C) for Health and  Immunization (training organized in Istanbul by the UNICEF Regional Office)  and improvements of communication between the MoF and line ministries which  lead on budget preparations for the financing of social sectors. At the sector  level, in terms of influencing the state budget, PF4C support was provided to  the education programme for development of a costed Action Plan for the  Education Strategy Reform (funded by the EU), which embeds the key elements  of the EU Growth Plan for Education. In terms of evidence generation, PF4C  support was provided for development of the Budget Analysis and Investment  Case for Primary Healthcare in Montenegro. 

An MoU was signed  between UNICEF, the Ministry of Health, Bijelo Polje Hospital and the HEMIIAS  Foundation with the objective of improving maternal and newborn healthcare in  the Municipality of Bijelo Polje through reconstruction of the maternity  ward, procurement of new equipment and capacity building of healthcare  professionals. The estimated funds for implementation, €1.2 million, will be  secured through a combination of private-sector funding, the state budget and  other donations (i.e. from embassies). UNICEF’s key roles in this partnership  are to: 1) provide advice to align the construction plans with international  standards; 2) conduct training for medical staff; 3) support the Ministry of  Health and the hospital to secure one portion of the funding through the state  budget (PF4C support). 

A Contribution  Agreement was signed with the International Women’s Club of Montenegro, as a  result of the successful fundraising initiative, which was conducted in  partnership between the Women’s Parliamentary Club, the International Women’s  Club and UNICEF. Through the event €167,000 was raised to support procurement  of equipment for all Day-Care Centres for children with disabilities across  the country. UNICEF’s key roles in this partnership were to: 1) support  development of partnership between the Women’s Parliamentary Club, the International  Women’s Club and UNICEF’s Business Council members; 2) support the development  of key advocacy messages to support services for children with disabilities  in Montenegro; and 3) procure equipment with the funds raised through the  event. 

The CO cultivated successful cooperation with  academia, with the aim of intensifying cooperation in 2025 through the exchange  of knowledge, information, offering UNICEF knowhow and initiating  multi-sector initiatives at the University of Montenegro to bring added value  to the ongoing reforms. 

Public  communication    
  
UNICEF remains the strongest UN brand in the  country – 96 percent of citizens have heard of it and 80 percent have a  positive opinion about it. In 2024, 1,699 media reports mentioning UNICEF  were generated. Articles on child poverty, violence, health and education  were published on the front pages of daily newspapers 25 times, and these  articles all mentioned UNICEF. The number of UNICEF Montenegro social media  followers (Facebook, IG, X, LinkedIn, TikTok and YouTube) increased by 2%  from 126,013 to 128,312, which represents 23% of the country’s population  online (560 200 internet users out of 633 158 total population). In 2024, UNICEF  Montenegro’s website continued with its trilingual edition – in Montenegrin,  English and Albanian – and gained 179,000 new users.  
  
One of the key highlights of UNICEF’s public advocacy  and comms, led by an inclusive group of UNICEF Montenegro’s young reporters,  was related to the municipal elections in the capital. During the two weeks  before the elections, media release and social media videos with the voices  of young people concerning things that girls and boys want from the new local  government were published on UNICEF’s social media with the aim of focusing  the pre-election public debate on the best ways for the local government to  support the quality of life of all children and families in the capital. 1 in  4 citizens aged 18 and above noticed UNICEF young reporters in 2024, while  this percentage increases to 1 in 3 among citizens aged 18-29. 8 out of 10  citizens consider them a good role model for youth in the country.
  
A visit by the Regional Director, the Barnahus regional  conference and meetings with the President, Prime Minister, Ministers, Mayors  and other decision-makers and partners were used as opportunities for publicly  communicating the key priorities and requests for children. 
  
Safer Internet Day, International Education Day,  International Day of the Girl Child, International Day of Persons with  Disabilities, World Children’s Day (WCD), World Parents’ Day, World Teachers’  Day, World Poverty Day, World Breastfeeding Week, World & European  Immunization Week and others were celebrated, as well as COP29. “Child Rights  at the Heart of the EU accession process and the 2030 Agenda” conference was  organized by UNICEF in cooperation with the Government of Montenegro and the  EU, and with support from the Peace Building Fund, on the occasion of the  35th anniversary of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. It ended  with a call to action to the government to keep child rights at the heart of  the EU accession process by implementing the MICS survey in 2025, developing  the new Strategy on Child Rights, investing sufficient funds for quality  services for children and families, and applying for the EU Child Guarantee  to obtain additional resources for reforms for children. It created significant  social and traditional media coverage.
  
Nationally representative research from 2024 shows  that there is significant public support for prioritizing child rights  issues: 
  
8 out of 10 citizens support inclusive education  and t fostering and adoption instead of placing children without parental  care in an institution; two thirds (66%) think corporal punishment is  unacceptable: 6 out of 10 limit time and media content that the children  follow and talk to children about this; 63 percent say to check information  from media that sound suspicious to them by looking it up in other sources,  talking to experts, friends, etc.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The government’s predominant focus, in the light of the ultimate goal of EU accession, has been primarily on political dynamics and economic issues/infrastructure modernization, while social issues and the situation of the most disadvantaged groups have been less seen as relevant to that agenda. Such a situation has determined some disagreements on leadership and accountability for child rights, limited capacities for child rights, data generation and budgeting for children. Therefore, UNICEF actions must be strategic in bringing child rights to the core of EU integration, rooted in international standards and very much focused on the capacity building of partners, given the fact that there is global pushback on human rights and, consequently, on child rights. The country has been struggling with accountability mechanisms for the effective implementation of laws and policies, and international commitments. Capacities in child rights, data generation, monitoring and evaluation are to be improved, and the existing budgeting process is to be linked with evidence, law and policy formulation. Significant support should be invested in building capacities across the sectors and different branches of power, so that the capacity for child rights realization, monitoring and budgeting is advanced. Political and technical consensus should be built around priority issues for the most vulnerable children and families. Child Rights Monitoring and Public Finance for Children, being cross-sector areas of engagement, require strong coordination, but also the involvement of all sectors. A lack of a holistic approach and equal participation of all sectors in high-level, evidence-based policymaking, coordination, monitoring and budgeting for children needs to be addressed as a matter of priority, and sustainable strategies carefully sought to ensure sustainable reforms. Also, there is a pressing need to improve the capacities of line ministries in budgeting and leveraging resources for 
children, given the fact that the state budget is the biggest provider of funds, including the EU Growth Plan, and child rights actions should be rooted in it. 
In the atmosphere of increased political and societal polarization, the implementation of the Joint UN initiative on Accelerating Social Cohesion and building trust in institutions, implemented by the national and local authorities, the Parliament, the Women’s Club of the Parliament, the Ombudsperson’s Institution, CSOs, children, adolescents and women, proved to be instrumental in working for the common good and a shared vision, regardless of political belief or any other characteristic. The same goes for innovative and promising approaches, such as the multi-stakeholder Platform for Independent Monitoring of the CRPD, established by the Institution of the Ombudsperson in cooperation with/with the meaningful participation of 10 disability rights organizations,  supported by UNICEF. Such initiatives should be further supported and scaled up. Multisectoral education on child rights and civic education proved to be much needed and should continue as a matter of priority. 
Consultations with children and young people were at the core of UNICEF’s planning and provided valuable insights, an example of which was the process of meaningful participation of children and young people in the process of development of the Strategy on the Protection of Children from and Prevention of Violence 2025–2029, with 348 high school pupils (110 boys and 238 girls) proposing concrete measures and recommendations to the government to take active action in the field of suppression and prevention of violence, that were submitted to the Council on Child Rights. To ensure that all voices were integrated into the new Education Strategy, a broad process of consultations was conducted, including over 1,100 pupils – including those affected by poverty, Roma pupils and pupils with disabilities – over 2,800 teachers and 5,500 parents, 84% of whom were mothers/female guardians. Innovative engagement during the municipal elections in the capital city was an opportunity for highlighting child rights issues and promoting political participation of young people. Together with the civil sector and young people, UNICEF is able to maintain its politically neutral role, while giving a platform for young people to have a dialogue with all politicians about key child rights issues. During the two weeks before the elections, media releases and social media videos with the voices of young people talking about the things that girls and boys want from the new local government were published on UNICEF’s social media, with the aim of focusing the pre-election public debate on the best ways for the local government to support the quality of life of all children and families in the capital. UNICEF will continue to ensure the availability of “de-politicized” platforms for the engagement of children and young people in strategic plans and child rights issues. 
Cross-sector cooperation proved to be challenging in many domains and remains a priority to be strengthened through policy dialogue, policy briefs, platforms for multisectoral work and financing. UNICEF and other national and international partners were focused on vulnerable groups of children, who are experiencing inequalities and are not counted in the national averages, as well as on the barriers and bottlenecks that are preventing them from enjoying their rights. Important lessons were also learned during the consultation process for the new DRR Strategy regarding the design of humanitarian responses, emergency preparedness and the overall planning and monitoring systems in emergencies. UNICEF continues to leverage its neutrality to mobilize the private sector, government and wider community to develop new initiatives and build alliances for children.  
Overall, the second year of the 2023–2027 Country Programme successfully contributed to an increased national commitment and awareness of children’s and adolescents’ rights in Montenegro. This was reflected through the adoption or development of a set of strategies and plans in education, social and child protection, youth and child rights monitoring, as well as through the government’s adoption of the Pledge on Child Rights. The next period needs to focus on supporting the country in allocating sufficient technical capacities and budgets for implementing these commitments for all children, particularly the most vulnerable children and adolescents, ethnic minorities and children with disabilities.

Despite progress across sectors, child rights  challenges persist in Romania. Poverty risks remain high, particularly in  rural areas where over 49% of children live. One in five children (22.6%,  Eurostat, 2023) faces severe material and social deprivation, nearly three  times the EU average (8.4%).
  
Political Environment:
  
In 2024, Romania had four rounds  of elections (i.e., local, parliamentary, presidential and European  Parliament), resulting in an unpredictable political landscape. Election  agendas paid attention to critical outcomes for children such as education,  substance abuse, healthcare, and poverty, while deprioritized others like  public health interventions, gender equality, and diversity. A new coalition  Government was formed in December 2024, with new presidential elections  scheduled in May 2025.
  
Economic Context:  
  
Romania’s GDP for the first half  of 2024 decreased by 0.7% as compared to 2023, and the country’s estimated  deficit reached 8% of GDP, being significantly higher than in 2023 (6.5%).  Romania has one of the lowest fiscal revenues in the EU (approximately 26-27%  of GDP), being insufficient given pressures from crisis situations and the  need for greater investments in the education and health sectors. Experiences  from the 2008 economic crisis underscored the importance to maintain social  service resources during fiscal austerity periods, as children’s and  families’ needs increase with reduced funding.
  
According to the National  Institute of Statistics, Romania’s inflation rate in August 2024 was 5.1%,  double the EU rate of 2.4%. The National Bank of Romania revised its  inflation forecast upward to 4.9% for end-2024 and 3.4% by end-2025. Over  this period, Romania experienced a 4.25% increase in food prices, 4.35% in  non-food items, and 8.60% in services. Maintaining the annual indexing policy  of social benefits is critical to support families’ purchasing power and  subsequently adequate living standards. 
  
Romania’s medium-term growth  depends on its ability to absorb EU funds. The country is eligible for up to  €77 billion by 2030, including €28.5 billion in grants and loans from the  'Next Generation EU’ fund through the 2021-2026 National Recovery and  Resilience Plan (NRRP). Additionally, the Romanian Government is implementing  the European Child Guarantee (€19 billion until 2030) to improve access to  basic services for children and families. 
  
Child Rights Status:
  
In December 2023, the Ministry  of Health declared a national measles epidemic setting a political priority  to vaccinate children 9 to 11 months, ensuring recovery of those unvaccinated  (78% MMR1 coverage, 2023). From January 2023 to September 2024, the National  Institute of Public Health reported 23,972 measles cases with 21 deaths.  While the epidemic was closed in September 2024, these developments  underscore the need to accelerate children’s vaccination. Public attention  was also directed in 2024 towards children’s mental healthcare and well-being.  The current provision of mental healthcare remains hospital-centric, but  on-going planning strives to develop community-based services.
  
In April 2024, Law 100/2024 was  approved, comprising a package of amendments to several social assistance  laws. The specific amendments addressed improvements in planning,  organization, functioning, financing, monitoring and evaluation of social  services at the local level. For effective implementation of these new  provisions, secondary legislation (e.g., standards, methodologies,  guidelines) needs to be developed. 
  
In June 2024, 84,577 children  were registered with disabilities, yet the real number is likely higher with  many children unidentified and lacking access to essential services.  Likewise, the National Authority for the Protection of Child Rights and  Adoption (NAPCRA) registered 10,617 cases of child abuse, neglect, and  exploitation as of June 2024. Many cases remain unreported to child  protection authorities.
  
Under the Ministry of  Education’s leadership, the 2024-2030 National Strategy for Parents’ Support  was adopted, providing a wide range of services across sectors, including  parenting education, counselling, and awareness raising activities for  parents. The Strategy's universal support measures for parents established a  solid equity and gender dimension, prioritizing interventions for the most  vulnerable parents and specifically targeting fathers. 
  
A law declaring 2025 as “Year of  the Child” created child rights awareness raising opportunities. Amendments  to Law 272/2004 on the protection and promotion of children's rights  institutionalized child participation at all levels of public administration,  making Romania the first EU country to systematize child participation.
  
Emergency Preparedness & Response: 
  
In 2024, the Government shifted  its response for Ukrainian refugees to stronger social inclusion strategies  and system strengthening. As of December 2024, over 175,000 Ukrainians  obtained temporary protection permits in Romania, of which 52,015 were children  and 8,728 were unaccompanied or separated. In June, emergency ordinance  96/2024 established the legal framework for refugees to access state  services: education, special protection, and health. New provisions extended  temporary protection measures until mid-2026 and granted special protection  to unaccompanied and separated children under Law 272/2004. While these steps  are important advancements for refugees, effective implementation requires  secondary legislation and enforcement instructions.
  
Romania is also prone to natural  hazards, and in September 2024 Galati and Vaslui counties experienced severe  flooding with over 6,115 households affected (approximately 12,234 people  including over 6,000 children). This event underscored the importance for  emergency preparedness, where Government, civil society, business and UN  agencies including UNICEF collaborated to respond to children’s urgent  needs.   
  
Romania’s International Obligations:
  
Implementing the European Child  Guarantee, Romania was one of the first countries to submit a biennial  progress report to the European Commission. The Commission’s feedback  included appreciation but also highlighted the need for further actions for  children in rural areas. The Government also submitted its 6th and 7th  periodic report to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child to the  Committee on the Rights of the Child, where the dialogue with the Committee  will happen in May 2025. In November 2024, the Government participated in the  Global Ministerial Conference on Ending VAC in Bogotá, Columbia, being a  "pathway” country with commitment to end VAC.

While the Sustainable  Development Department with the National Institute of Statistics developed a  national SDG monitoring framework, there are few child-focused indicators.  Romania has made progress towards SDG 1, with a 2.5% poverty decrease to 39%  in 2023. The severe material and social deprivation rate also decreased by  8.2% to 22.6% in 2023. At the same time, SDG 3 on health and SDG 4 on  education failed to progress, with a backsliding immunization rate and  downward trends in school enrolments at 83.5% for lower secondary education  and 79.8% for upper secondary education in the 2022-2023 academic year. For  SDG 5, Romania ranks last within the 2024 EU Gender Equality Index at 57.5  versus the EU average at 71.0, as gender stereotypes continue to  prevail and a strong backlash against gender equality can be noticed in  public discourse.

In the second year of the Country Programme, UNICEF’s programming advanced protective and inclusive environments, contributing to the 2030 SDG Agenda. UNICEF partnered with the Government to leverage the European Commission’s Child Guarantee, serving as a strategic framework for multi-sectoral collaboration that advances access to essential services to break the cycle of poverty for children. With Romania’s graduation to high-income country, UNICEF’s role grew as a technical assistance partner to the Government on key child rights issues, contributing to three state projects supported through the European Commission’s Technical Support Instruments (TSIs). In addition, partnerships were strengthened with civil society organizations (CSOs) and international finance institutions, including with the World Bank.

  
For more than two years, UNICEF has advocated and supported Ukrainian children and families’ integration into national social assistance and service delivery systems, aligning with  country programme objectives and the humanitarian-development nexus. Responding to emerging data and demands from children and adolescents, UNICEF embraced new programme areas, integrating interventions in mental health, social protection and climate change.
  
Goal 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives
  
System Strengthening in Immunization & Primary Healthcare 
  
Contributing to the 2023 National Health & Immunization Strategy, UNICEF partnered with the  Ministry of Health (MOH), the National Public Health Institute, the World  Health Organization and subnational healthcare institutions to strengthen  children’s immunization and primary healthcare (PHC) through capacity  development, evidence generation for decision-making, and development of  guidelines targeting efficiency and effectiveness in service delivery.
  
With immunization backsliding,  measles outbreaks, and difficulties in reaching zero-dose children, UNICEF in  collaboration with the National Centre for Surveillance and Control of  Communicable Diseases conducted a policy analysis targeted at enhancing vaccination  workflows and adapting the National Vaccination Programme to PHC system  developments. Complementing this work, UNICEF generated new evidence with  qualitative research on vaccination non-attendance in 2 counties with high  zero-dose cases to inform communication outreach for increased vaccination  demand. At the same time, 437 health vaccinators gained skills on using the  National Electronic Register for Vaccination, improving system monitoring  through increased quality of registration and data input. 
  
Addressing maternal and child  health, UNICEF enhanced the skills of 590 PHC providers and hospital teams in  prenatal care, immunization, and nutrition education. With the MOH, UNICEF  developed standard operating procedures to register uninsured pregnant women  and improve their access to antenatal services. UNICEF also supported the  national roll-out of the community health nurse application, enabling better  service coordination for vulnerable groups.
  
Integrating Ukrainian Refugees into Healthcare  System Responses
  
Based on evidence from feedback  mechanisms and social media insights, UNICEF advocated for integration of  Ukrainians into Romania’s healthcare system, focusing on barriers to access  such as registration with general practitioners, timely reimbursement for  preventive services and support of translation services. To address system  bottlenecks, 532 health professionals from PHC facilities and hospitals in 8  counties gained skills to better address refugees' needs in perinatal care,  immunization, interpersonal communication, and gender-based violence.  Capacity-building programmes also nurtured connections between protection  services, mental health, reproductive health, and maternity care for  individuals from conflict zones, resulting in enhanced access to services.  
  
Facilitating healthcare access  to the most vulnerable, 27,399 Ukrainians of which 2,335 children, received  essential information on how to access healthcare services in Romania,  vaccination guidance and health promotion messages. Together with Regina Maria  Foundation and Association of Independent Midwives, 4,349 Ukrainians, of  which 1,006 children, received PHC services and 142 children were vaccinated  against measles, polio and other antigens. Through PHC services, 1,793  Ukrainian caregivers’ parenting skills were increased with counselling on  infant and young child feeding practices and development milestones. 
  
Enhancing Access to Integrated Basic &  Specialized Services
  
Recognizing the importance for  integrated services to meet children’s needs, UNICEF partnered with national  and local authorities to develop models that advanced a continuum of support  for children and their families.
  
In 2024, UNICEF contributed to  the operationalization of 200 Integrated Community Centres (ICCs) approved in  Romania's National Recovery and Resilience Plan, leveraging its expertise to  design sustainable multi-sectoral service hubs for basic and specialized  services (e.g., kineto-therapy, psychological counseling, speech therapy).  Under an EEA Norway grant, UNICEF supported five pilot ICCs that provided  health, education, and psycho-social services to 7,785 children and  caregivers across 18 communities. Results of these critical services to  vulnerable children, including those with disabilities and mental health  conditions in underserved communities, were shown through improved school  attendance, better parent-child relationships, and enhanced social skills of  children. Some ICCs also proved instrumental in promotion of girls’  empowerment and prevention of teenage pregnancies. 
  
Partnering with Bucharest  municipality’s health, education and child protection sectors, UNICEF also  defined and tested referral and service pathways to support children’s mental  health and psychological well-being. Innovation was  central to UNICEF’s mental health and psycho-social support (MHPSS)  initiatives, using virtual reality tools to improve service delivery,  creating an MHPSS app for adolescents, and adapting the "On My  Mind" podcast for Romanian youth. Through the Youth-for-Youth (Y4Y)  programme, 8,535 adolescents were also reached nationwide with  socio-emotional skills programmes, including 715 Ukrainians. The program  trained 395 teachers and medical staff on health promotion and distributed  10,760 learning materials.
  
In partnership with the  Government, UNICEF launched a national campaign on parent-child relationships  that were broadcasted across 21 TV stations. Developed  modules targeted caregivers, emphasizing the importance of their engagement  in children's lives. In the campaign’s first three months (September to  November 2024), 2.9 million people from households with children were reached. With  the parent app, Bebbo, approximately 17,000 Romanian parents and caregivers of  young children (0 to 6 years) gained knowledge on parenting skills, monitoring  of child development milestones, vaccination schedules, and suggestions for  creative games.
  
At  the same time, UNICEF co-organized a national conference on child mental  health in partnership with professional health associations and academia; as  well as a national conference on child health with the Prime Minister’s  Office, bringing together over 150 national stakeholders in an  inter-institutional dialogue and advocacy to increase commitment and  investments in child mental health.
  
Goal 2: Every Child Learns and Acquires  Skills 
  
Over 2024, UNICEF partnered with  the Ministry of Education (MOE) in policy development, as well as system  strengthening in early childhood education and care (ECEC) services and  integration of Ukrainian refugees.
  
Advancing Policy Frameworks
  
UNICEF's collaboration with the  MOE was pivotal in the development and adoption of several policies and  national strategies targeted at improving the quality of education and early  childhood development. Key results included adoption of the National Strategy  on Parents’ Support; a new legal framework on school desegregation; MOE Order  3945/2024 on the distribution of children in groups or classrooms; MOE Order  5726/2024 on the framework regulation for school units in pre-university  education (ROFUIP 2024); an update of early learning and development  standards; and Government Decision 1065/2024 for the National Plan for  Combatting Violence in Schools.
  
UNICEF continued to partner with  the MOE in tackling school segregation. The MOE, with technical support from  UNICEF and funding from the EU DG REFORM’s TSI, developed a comprehensive  legal and policy framework addressing five protected criteria: ethnicity,  disability/special education needs, socio-economic status, academic  performance, and residential area. This framework represents a significant  step toward equity in education.  
  
Strengthening System Responses
  
A second EU DG REFORM TSI  project, ‘Safe Schools,’ launched in July 2024 will develop a policy  framework ensuring that all lower secondary schools foster healthy  environments where social and emotional learning, psycho-social support,  well-being, and mental health are integral to a whole-school approach.  Complementing this work, formative research by UNICEF, the Romanian Angel  Appeal and the Institute for Trauma revealed school anxiety as one of the  biggest drivers affecting children’s mental health. Consequently, UNICEF  engaged in testing and refining a capacity building programme focused on  improving the school environment where more than 200 teachers gained access  to essential MHPSS tools, including an early identification tool, a referral  pathway for children facing mental health risks, and a compendium of  non-formal educational activities promoting adolescents' well-being. 
  
The ECEC system was strengthened  through capacity building of personnel from the national education system and  educational hubs, delivering quality education services on early learning,  play, and parenting. UNICEF continued to provide ECEC and education services  for refugee children. While the main priority was inclusion of Ukrainian  children into the national education system, educational hubs especially  targeted for children aged 0-3 years where needed, given the overall scarcity  of pre-school services. These ECEC options enhanced caregivers' opportunities  to pursue employment and learn Romanian, enabling greater integration into  society and improving their livelihoods in Romania. UNICEF also conducted a  costing exercise on these Education Hubs' ECEC services to provide the  evidence base to advocate to the MOE for the opportunity to establish and  fund such complementary ECEC services for the whole community. This work  reflects the synergies gained in leveraging emergency resources for systemic  changes.
  
Although more than 50,000  Ukrainian children were enrolled as full-time students or 'auditors,'  challenges such as low attendance rates and high dropout levels underscored  the need for complementary learning pathways and language support. Through  strategic partnerships with eight CSOs, UNICEF enabled 1,052 Ukrainian  individuals to attend language courses and 2,392 Ukrainian children with  access to quality education services in education hubs. Additionally, these  partnerships strengthened teachers’ capacities in trauma-sensitive teaching;  teaching of Romanian as a second language instruction; and interventions addressing  bullying and gender-based violence. These steps ensured more inclusive and  supportive learning environments for all students. 
  
Goal 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence,  Abuse and Exploitation
  
With the Ministry of Labour and  Social Solidarity (MLSS – currently in 2025, the Ministry of Labour, Family,  Youth and Social Solidarity), the Ministry of Family, Youth and Equality of  Opportunities (MFYEO), the National Agency for Protection of Child Rights and  Adoption (NAPCRA) and other counterparts, UNICEF catalyzed results by  addressing key protection issues for children living in poverty, in state  care, children facing abuse, neglect, and exploitation, and children affected  by the war in Ukraine. 
  
Enhancing Integrated Community Services &  Social Work
  
Supporting implementation of  Romania’s National Strategy for Children’s Rights and the Child Guarantee  National Action Plan (CG-NAP), UNICEF with the National College for Social  Workers (NCSW) and the National Association of Communes (AoC) enhanced capacities  of local authorities from 2,000 rural communities throughout Romania to  conduct social diagnoses of children’s needs, service planning, and  leveraging of resources (including European Social Funds). These steps  ensured local municipalities’ preparedness for MLSS’s nationwide scale-up of  integrated community services (ICS). Recognized internationally, the ICS  model advances equitable access to social services for the most vulnerable  children. In its convening role, UNICEF created forums with national stakeholders  to share the model's lessons learned among several EU countries.
  
Joint advocacy with the MLSS and  the NCSW resulted in the passing of a package of legislative provisions that  enhance access and quality of social assistance, ensuring greater  coordination of services and benefits for children. Research on the status of  social workers’ capacities equipped the MLSS, the MFYEO, the NCSW, and other  key partners to develop needs-based policies on workforce distribution. With  the NCSW, UNICEF also increased social workers’ capacities through new supervision  tools and evidence-based social work frameworks, including an e-learning  platform and package of needs-based resources for planning services.
  
UNICEF transferred the PRIMERO  child protection information and monitoring system to the NAPCRA, supporting  case management of Ukrainian children entering Romania with registration of  4,594 vulnerable children, including 1,499 unaccompanied and separated  children (UASC). Continuous monitoring of UASC by the national care system  enhanced quality and sustainability of services. Furthermore, communication  and coordination between Romanian and Ukrainian authorities facilitated integration  of UASC into Romania’s national child protection system, fostering increased  ownership among local authorities. 
  
UNICEF continued its transition  from humanitarian responses to system strengthening approaches that enhanced  access to services, tackled vulnerabilities and supported social inclusion  both for refugee children and vulnerable child groups from host communities.  A local governance model for refugee children, the “Blue Grid,” was promoted  among local authorities to ensure refugee and vulnerable children with access  to referral pathways and a minimum set of protection services.
  
Addressing Violence against Children (VAC) 
  
With civil society, UNICEF  contributed to the Government’s prioritization of prevention and combatting  VAC, with Romania’s pledge for systemic and sustainable results during the  Global Ministerial Conference on Ending VAC held in Bogotá, Columbia. In December  2024, the national launch by the NAPCRA and the Prime Minister’s Office of  the EU DG REFORM’S TSI on VAC, with technical assistance by UNICEF, also  exhibited the country's heightened commitment to strengthening VAC responses.
  
UNICEF’s work on protection of  Ukrainian refugees from violence continued in 2024, with more than 18,500  caregivers and children gaining access to reporting channels and mitigation  interventions to address gender-based violence. Responding to children’s  increased risks of trafficking, exploitation, and abuse, UNICEF with partners  across the country provided 29,059 Ukrainians, of which 6,123 children, with  access to safe spaces and support hubs. UNICEF also worked with government  authorities to integrate child protection interventions into national and  subnational responses. This work enhanced early detection of child  trafficking, exploitation, and abuse cases, as well as responding service  delivery.
  
 Goal 4: Every Child lives in a Safe and  Sustainable Climate & Environment
  
With evidence generation from  the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, UNICEF reaffirmed its commitment  to integrate climate change and sustainability efforts across programmes.  This research marked a significant milestone, enabling systematic inclusion  of Climate, Environment, Energy, and Disaster Risk Reduction (CEED) in 2025  programme planning to protect and promote a safe, sustainable environment for  children in Romania. 
  
Climate and environment issues  continued to be critical entry points for child participation. Advocating for  child participation, together with the Prime Minister’s Team and the Ministry  of Environment, Forests and Water, UNICEF empowered Romanian children by  fostering their active participation in high-level national and international  events and processes. Resulting from UNICEF’s advocacy, two children  officially participated for the first time in Romania’s national COP29  delegation, enabling their advocacy at this policy-making climate forum.  Through consultative structures including the Romanian Children’s Board, the  National Students Council, and Child-Friendly Cities' Local Children’s  Councils, adolescent members gained skills on climate action that enabled  them to claim and exercise their rights effectively when meeting local and  national decision-makers and in numerous media interventions. UNICEF also  nurtured child- and youth-led climate activism locally with capacity  building and Romania's Local Conference of Youth conducted from July through  October 2024. Among the 60 local and high-level events where UNICEF amplified  children’s voices, 1,000 children were engaged advancing child participation  as a key component of national and regional policy dialogues.
  
In collaboration with the  Ministry of Interior’s Department for Emergency Situations (DSU), UNICEF  supported integration of child-friendly principles into the updated National  Disaster Risk Reduction Framework, which was tested successfully in several  high-risk counties. Following this process, UNICEF initiated with DSU a joint  modeling and testing of the current emergency response system. Resulting  operational strategies will contribute to a more child-sensitive national  emergency response system that increase protection for children during  emergencies. 
  
Goal 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in  Life    
  
Leveraging Resources to Reduce Child Poverty - EU  Child Guarantee
  
While Romania has made progress  in reducing child poverty and social exclusion, its child poverty rate  remains highest in Europe. The European Commission’s Child Guarantee  establishes resources for programmes to prevent and combat poverty and social  exclusion by ensuring access to essential services, including education and  early care, healthcare, nutrition, and housing where vulnerable child groups  are targeted. UNICEF has supported Romania in leveraging these resources for  children, where the NAPCRA led the development of new tools and mechanisms  for monitoring and evaluating the country’s National Action Plan for the  Child Guarantee (CG-NAP) and for budget planning and expenditure monitoring.  As a result, all relevant ministries for the CG-NAP started collaborating  with the NAPCRA in the revision and strengthening of the CG-NAP Monitoring  and Evaluation Framework. ¿ 
  
Advocating for Child Rights and Children’s Voices  High on the Agenda
  
Through UNICEF’s strategic  partnerships with the Government, Parliament and the President’s Office,  child rights were integrated into the political agenda and platforms. With  government and CSO partners, UNICEF significantly advanced adolescent  participation through advocacy, capacity building, and consultations,  contributing to systemic changes in how children’s voices influence  governance and policymaking. UNICEF amplified more than 900 children’s  voices, participating in local and high-level events where they contributed  meaningfully to decision-making processes. Promoting gender equality, UNICEF  engaged adolescent girls in several national and international communications  and advocacy campaigns, such as UNICEF #GirlGoals that highlighted the  importance of empowering girls in society.
  
A major milestone was the  approval of amendments to Law 272/2004 which mandates central and local  public institutions to organize at least one consultation session with  children per year. The law emphasizes accessible communication by publishing  child-friendly information about their activities and objectives, as well as  ensures active involvement of children in decisions that affect them. At the  same time, a new law establishing 2025 as “Year of the Child” creates  opportunities to raise awareness on child rights at national level. 
  
Enhancing Investments for Children
  
With the Ministry of Finance and  the World Bank, UNICEF advanced public financing for children through  technical support to the Government’s public spending reviews, embedding a  child-focused analysis into the reviews' methodology. This partnership resulted  in development of a roadmap on public finance for children which was agreed  by key stakeholders to ensure close coordination as well as foster a dialogue  on public finances for children among all the ministries.  
  
In 2024, UNICEF advocated with  the Government to build a social protection system that was shock-resistant  and agile to respond to developing needs of vulnerable groups. Partnering  with the Chancellery of the Prime Minister’s Office, the Department on  Emergency Situations and the Ministry of Labor and Social Solidarity, UNICEF  conducted a cost analysis of refugee enrollment into the national social  protection system which contributed to the evidence base for the Government’s  decision to enroll Ukrainian refugees in the social protection system from  July 2024. To complement this advocacy for refugees’ integration into the  social protection system, UNICEF conducted an information campaign reaching  more than 70,000 refugees with messages on access to social benefits,  temporary protection and other information that promoted better integration  into national systems. As a result, over 1,800 Ukrainian children accessed  the state allowance for children.

In 2024, UNICEF applied a “whole society” approach in Romania, enhancing its long-term partnerships and building new alliances across sectors. 
  
Long-standing and close partnerships with line ministries, the Parliament, the Presidency, national and local authorities, private sector and civil society enabled UNICEF to strengthen system responses by advancing child-centered policies and  services, including in emergencies. By expanding the partnership with the  Chancellery of the Prime Minister’s Office, key child rights issues such as  child participation, mental health, protection of Ukrainian refugees and  climate change were all placed high on the political agenda. UNICEF also  signed 4 new memoranda of understanding with governmental counterparts,  including the National Agency for Equal Opportunities between Women and Men  with the commitment for greater engagement in gender transformative  initiatives in Romania.
  
Together with national partners, UNICEF scaled up flagship interventions such as integrated community services (ICS), while promoting internationally lessons learned from the models. New  and intensified strategic partnerships on public finance for children with  ¿the Ministry of Finance and the World Bank resulted in establishment of a  roadmap that will enhance partners’ capacities and coordination to maximize  investments for children. UNICEF's new partnership with the Ministry of  Environment, Waters and Forests enabled children to advocate for climate  action and financing at the COP29 climate forum.   
  
The existing partnership with  the Ministry of Family, Youth and Equal Opportunities and the NAPCRA  comprised technical assistance for the implementation of the Child Guarantee,  as well as high-level national and international events with sharing of best practices.  Likewise, the partnership with the Ministry of Education continued to focus  on strategic policy support to establish secondary legislation following  adoption of the 2023 education law. 
  
Parliament continued to be a key  partner for children, raising awareness of UNICEF's interventions and the  challenges faced by vulnerable children and adopting innovative legislation  on child participation (i.e. amendments to Law 272/2004). To enhance awareness  on child rights and place children as a government priority, Parliament  declared 2025 as the Year of the Child.  
  
To bridge the gap between the  evolving legal framework and local institutional practices, UNICEF played a  pivotal role to ensure informed policymaking and implementation of  contextualized solutions. For example, to strengthen links between national  and local protection systems, UNICEF with the national partner, the National  College of Social Workers, prepared 2,000 rural communities with tools on  social diagnosis and on leveraging resources that set the ground for the  MLSS’s upcoming scale-up of the ICS model. UNICEF also worked with national  and local authorities to develop a concept for localization of the EU Child  Guarantee. Leveraging new partnerships at the local level with the National  Union of the County Counsellors, the Association of Municipalities, and the  Association of Communes enabled UNICEF to channel information and increase  engagement with local administrations on key child rights issues. With other  partnerships, UNICEF has also tested and implemented at-scale interventions  in emerging areas such as mental health, climate change and public finance  for children. ¿
  
Building on lessons from the  Ukraine refugee response, UNICEF with national partners and civil society  organizations advanced inclusive systems responses through the  humanitarian-development nexus. Partnerships with CSOs active in education,  such as Step-by-Step, FITT, JRS, PATRIR and Sus Inima, provided  complementary, quality education pathways for over 2,000 Ukrainian children.  To formalize its work in refugee response and emergency preparedness, UNICEF  entered 33 memoranda of understanding with local authorities in 21 counties.  Partnerships with the Chancellery of the Prime Minister’s Office, Ministry of  Interior’s Department on Emergency Situations and the Ministry of Labour and  Social Solidarity resulted in shock-responsive social protection with the  state decision to enroll Ukrainian refugees in the national social protection  system. Likewise, UNICEF initiated an emergency preparedness exercise with  leadership of the Chancellery of the Prime Minister’s Office and the  Department on Emergency Situations to enhance systems’ plans and resilience  to crises. 
  
Over the year, UNICEF also  strengthened its long-term partnerships with child-led groups at different  levels, including the Romanian Children’s Board, the National Students  Council and local children’s councils and youth constituencies from seven  communities. Advocacy initiatives to amplify children’s voices were pursued  across the Prime Minister’s Office, line ministries, and Parliament, as well  as local authorities. 
  
UNICEF collaborated closely with  other UN agencies present in Romania (UNHCR, WHO, IOM) as well as IFIs such  as the World Bank to build stronger systems for children and their families,  including within the on-going refugee response. UNICEF nurtured its partnership  role as a technical assistance provider and in broader advocacy,  collaborating with multiple embassies, the EU, UNICEF National Committees and  the private sector to leverage resources and raise awareness around the  rights of vulnerable children and families in Romania. UNICEF also continued  to partner closely with media, collaborating with top TV stations through  information campaigns to raise awareness about and funds for vulnerable  children, including those in emergencies such as children and families  affected by the floods in Romania.
  
Flexible funding is vital for  fostering innovative programming and testing evidence-based interventions,  such as the ICS model. This funding also provides the agility to respond  quickly with partners on emerging policy and programme issues, as seen by the  advocacy on child participation. In 2024, such funding also facilitated  generation of quality data on mental health, co-design and continuous  refinement of interventions, as well as providing seed funds to leverage  larger investments for children, enhancing UNICEF programmes' effectiveness  and relevance in an ever-evolving environment.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
While UNICEF-Romania had  multiple lessons over 2024, one cross-cutting experience was that establishment  of strong inclusive, protective systems for children and families calls for  integrated collaboration across different levels from national to local  government bodies.
  
Nurturing coherence among national and local work  
  
UNICEF’s work in several  interventions underscored the importance of a vision focused on system change  where local stakeholders co-participate in policy-making, leveraging  opportunities, investing in quality capacity building and supervision  programmes for professionals delivering services. 
  
For example, effective planning  of the integrated community service scale-up nationwide required preparing  local authorities to support the process, building a common understanding  between government agencies at national and local levels about the services  and tools, such as the national case management tool, Child Observatory.  Likewise, with the EU structural funding mechanism, the EU Child Guarantee  (ECG), national partners have an important role to inform municipalities  about the mechanism and to support municipalities’ development of a  monitoring and evaluation framework. With the National College for Social  Workers and National Association of Communes, 2,000 rural municipalities  enhanced their capacities and readiness to develop minimum package of  services. Localization of the ECG has served as a pathfinding model for  evidence-based policy planning and local governance for children. 
  
The importance of coordinated  efforts across national and local partners was also exhibited in UNICEF’s  work with state partners on emergency preparedness. While a contingency plan  was led at the central level by the Department on Emergency Situations, it  was critical that the plan was discussed and agreed for preparedness among  the local communities where specific responses were implemented. Having a  mutual understanding across the partners at the different levels guaranteed  greater coordination and ability to respond timely.
  
Experiences from the Ukrainian  refugee response underscore the importance for the country to maintain work  in the humanitarian-development nexus over the longer term to ensure full  social inclusion of refugee children.
  
Strengthening multi-sectoral partnerships focused  on systemic changes  
  
Coordination with partners, such  as the National Union of the County Counsellors, the Association of  Municipalities, and the Association of Communes created a bridge for local  and national dialogue on social work responses. Leveraging of these  local-based networks enabled UNICEF to channel information, increase  engagement with local administrations on key issues, and advance the  protection of child rights issues. Coordinating with these networks, the  National Agency for Protection of Child Rights and Adoption (NAPCRA) is  co-developing a concept and framework for localization of the EU Child  Guarantee with national and local authorities.
  
The benefits of establishing  platforms among national and local agencies to nurture effective and  inclusive services was also exhibited through the experiences of integrated  community centres (ICC). Under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan  (NRRP), the Ministry of Health (MOH) planned to scale the ICC model to 200  municipalities across the country. Initially, municipalities were not clear  on the process for applying or the requirements for service delivery. To  foster a common understanding, the MOH developed guidelines for  municipalities on the ICC model. Facilitated through information exchanges,  MOH colleagues met with 200 teams of mayors, legal teams, public health  directorates, and other community members to explain the process for  application to the NRRP, leveraging available resources for children to the  local level.
  
Experiences underscored not only  the importance for linkages among national and local colleagues, but also  interaction across sectors at the different levels. For example, the NAPCRA’s  leadership in the coordination, localization, implementation and monitoring  of the National Action Plan for the Child Guarantee (CG-NAP) resulted in  relevant ministries collaborating with the NAPCRA in revising and  strengthening the CG-NAP’s Monitoring and Evaluation Framework. In this  context, integrated services are possible because each sector holds the same  vision and understanding about the programme.
  
Building capacities at all levels on child rights principles  
  
In advancing coordination for  child rights across sectors and different levels of government, greater  efforts are required to expand key stakeholders’ capacities on child rights  principles and system responses.  
  
Implementation of key child  rights principles, such as child participation (article 12 of the Convention  on the Rights of the Child), requires capacity building to establish common  understandings and agreements on how to apply these principles in policies  and services. For example, for systemic inclusion of children’s inputs and  perspectives into policies or processes affecting their lives, there is a  lengthy preparation time in which the young people need to fully understand  the issues and to feel comfortable to contribute with their perspectives in a  meaningful and comprehensive manner. Likewise, colleagues from the national  and local authorities need first to build a common understanding on system  responses, such as planning, budgeting and monitoring and evaluating  interventions to ensure efficient implementation and coordination of efforts  among stakeholders.
  
Being able to contribute in a  meaningful way and to provide information through a child rights ‘lens’ is  not a given; it does require resources, tools and understanding to further  incorporate purposefully a child rights perspective in policy-making, programming  and budgeting. UNICEF has taken significant steps to build partners’ capacities at different levels to establish evidence-based monitoring  frameworks for key child rights interventions in Romania. At the same time,  UNICEF with the Ministry of Finance plans to work together on public finance  for children training sessions, to nurture a common understanding on how to  make investments to maximize the results for children. These tools and  interventions are critical in fostering effective collaboration for child  rights among sectors as well as across different levels of governance.

In 2024, Serbia maintained macroeconomic stability and accelerated economic growth, with GDP growth projected at 3.8%, up from 2.5% in 2023. The unemployment rate declined to 8.1% in Q3 2024, while the employment rate rose to 51.9%, a 1.5% increase compared to the same period in 2023. However, gender disparities in labour participation persist, with women’s participation at 49.1% compared to 62.5% for men.
