Informal employment remained significant at 12.3%, reaching 52.7% in agriculture. The not in education and not in training (NEET) rate for youth aged 15–25 was 13.1%, and 15% for those aged 15–29.1 
Medium-term economic growth is expected to average around 4%, and this continued economic growth has brought about a decline in the population at risk of poverty. However, the remaining poor are concentrated among pensioners and the long-term unemployed, including families with children. Targeted social assistance will therefore become essential to continue poverty reduction. In 2024 the Government increased spending on birth grants, this non-targeted pro-natality measure has been absorbing an increasing share of social assistance envelope, in comparison to the two national pro-poverty programmes: financial social assistance and child allowance. 
The Growth Plan for the Western Balkans, approved in 2024, offers Serbia an opportunity for reforms and potential funding of up to €1.7 billion under the European Commission’s Reform and Growth Facility. Investments in human capital would help increase productivity, which remains low. Women, youth, and ethnic minorities are population groups that could boost future supply of the labour market. Despite progress, Serbia remains one of Europe’s poorest countries, with a GDP per capita of $29,622 (USD PPP) in 2023.2 
Government spending is currently burdened by transport infrastructure investments, military expenditures, and ambitious initiatives under ‘Leap into the Future – Serbia 2027’, including hosting EXPO 2027, building a national football stadium, etc. Many of these large-scale projects are exempt from standard regulations, raising transparency concerns. 
Serbia’s reliance on fossil fuels continues to contribute to environmental pollution, and it remains vulnerable to extreme weather events. Energy security has improved through diversified gas imports, but sanctions on the Serbian NIS oil company with majority Russian ownership could impact growth. The energy sector remained under strain this year, as seen in the electricity producer EPS’s financial challenges due to drought-related imports and high summer consumption. Climate change and extreme weather events threaten agricultural output and economic activity. Many households living in poverty are losing out on the significant energy efficiency investments being made through loans and public subsidies. Children are particularly exposed to environmental hazards (e.g., outdoor and indoor air pollution, heatwaves, water pollution, exposure to heavy metals), especially children 0–5, those in poor households, in Roma settlements, etc., which has adverse health and development effects on them, although this is not always recognized in environmental policies and measures. 
In 2024, women and children transiting through the Western Balkans faced high protection risks, including violent pushbacks by regional authorities. Ukrainian refugees constitute a small portion of Serbia’s migratory population. Concerns remain over safeguards for children on the move. 
Serbia’s European Union (EU) accession negotiations are moderately advanced but in stagnation, putting the likelihood of EU membership in the near future in question. Its lack of progress can be attributed in part to the disputed independence of the territory of Kosovo (as understood under UNSCR 1244), and non-aligning the foreign policy with EU regarding sanctions against Russa. Interethnic tensions in northern Kosovo (under UNSCR 1244) continued in 2024.  
Policy development and coordination are regulated but not systematically enforced. A system for sound policymaking is in place with a clear set of regulations embedded primarily in the Law on the planning system. Enforcement of the regulatory framework lags behind the legal deadlines. Public consultations were carried out in 2023 on 53% of draft laws and 31% of draft regulations, which remains insufficient. The link between the strategic priorities and budget programmes is insufficient, and ad hoc priorities frequently crowd out resource allocation. Serbia still lacks a roadmap for developing child-focused budgeting.  
In late 2024, public protests erupted following the collapse of a train station roof in Novi Sad, killing 15 people. Widespread allegations of corruption and poor construction practices fuelled demands for accountability. These protests, led by students, including from high schools, have continued into 2025. 
Serbia has made limited progress in reducing perinatal mortality, which decreased marginally from 9 in 2010 to 7.5 in 2022, with dominant stillbirths. Maternal mortality ratio remains high at 11.2 per 100,000 live births in 2022, nearly double the EU average (6). Subregional disparities highlight weaknesses in maternal and neonatal care, with Roma communities still experiencing significantly higher infant and under-five mortality rates. Although all pregnant women have at least four prenatal visits, maternity care in hospitals requires improvement. 
Social norms perpetuating violence and discrimination remain prevalent. Children face violence at home, school, online and in communities, with 19% of girls and 17% of boys reporting being victims of bullying in 2022. An increasing number of schoolchildren, including girls, admit to perpetrating peer violence. 
While Serbia’s economy showed resilience and growth in 2024, child-focused policies remain on the margins of government priorities. Vulnerable populations, including children, the poor, and marginalized groups, continue to face significant risks of social exclusion. Targeted measures and investments in human capital and governance reforms will continue to be essential in achieving inclusive and sustainable progress.

USING THE POWER OF EVIDENCE TO DRIVE CHANGE FOR CHILDREN 
In 2024, UNICEF strengthened the evidence base on the rights of children through the publication of a situation analysis (SitAn) on the rights and well-being of children and adolescents, conducted through a widely consultative process with Government, academia, and civil society organizations (CSOs) to provide the Government and other duty bearers with an independent analysis of the situation of children in Serbia. The SitAn highlighted socio-economic inequalities, urban/rural and locational disparities, and the needs of the least visible and the most marginalized children. It will inform the national development agenda, the efforts towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the implementation of the concluding observations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC).  
UNICEF participated in the global evaluation on early childhood development (ECD), providing a solid knowledge base to support organizational learning for ECD work from 2018 to 2023. The findings of this evaluation are expected to offer new pathways for an improved multisectoral government response on ECD. The preliminary findings of the report assess that UNICEF leadership and comparative advantage have contributed to notable advancements in the integrated ECD approach in Serbia, including increased access to holistic services for children with disabilities.  
UNICEF continued to use the findings of its Formative and Summative Evaluation of the Childcare and Deinstitutionalization Reforms in the Republic of Serbia that looked into the national childcare reforms undertaken in Serbia between 2009 and 2022, to support its advocacy and programmes in relation to children with disabilities and other ‘hard-to-place’ children, with a focus on deinstitutionalization.  
UNICEF also continued to use the recommendations of the Formative Evaluation on Preschool Education Reform, commissioned by UNICEF and the Ministry of Education (MoE) and completed in 2023, which scrutinized Serbia’s preschool education reforms from 2012 to 2022, focusing on three fundamental aspects: coverage, quality and equity.  
UNICEF continued to support the monitoring of indicators on the implementation of CRC recommendations that will be reported on in the next session of the UN Child Rights Committee of the State Party in 2026 (with a pre-session scheduled for April 2025). 
PROGRAMMING AT-SCALE RESULTS FOR CHILDREN 
Health & Early Childhood Development 
In 2024, UNICEF played a critical role in advocacy and system-strengthening efforts to advance the quality of maternal and neonatal care and increase national and local attention to backsliding immunization coverage. The integration of ECD service models into primary health care (PHC) reached a pivotal stage for full scale-up, leveraging public financing and gaining higher national and local commitment, along with increased regional and global visibility. 
UNICEF’s successful advocacy resulted in increased investments in maternal, neonatal and child health institutions by the Government of Serbia and the Ministry of Health (MoH). In addition to increasing budget allocations for health infrastructure, MoH provided equipment and initiated dialogues to improve respectful care. Maternal and child health indicators improved at the national level. Neonatal mortality declined from 3.78 in 2020 to 3.06 in 2023 nationally.  
UNICEF continued to play a key role in improving PHC capacities. The paediatric e-health record was enhanced with a digital module to monitor child growth and development, improving data analysis at individual, municipal, district and national levels, and informing medical decisions and policies. Digital social and behaviour change (SBC)-informed solutions to enable PHC centres to automatically generate lists of unvaccinated children by age, improving catch-up immunization efficiency, were piloted and will be deployed across 107 health centres, covering 70% of the country. 
In response to outbreaks of measles and pertussis, UNICEF and WHO intensified their joint advocacy at the highest levels to strengthen the national coordinated response. UNICEF targeted SBC-informed efforts in Novi Pazar, the area with the lowest MMR coverage and the most affected by the measles outbreak. Over the past 12 months, effective community coordination, led by the Public Health Institute of Novi Pazar with UNICEF support, increased the timely MMR1 vaccination rate from 8.3% to 58%, while overall MMR coverage, including missed ages, rose from 57.35% to 67.3%. 
In 2024, Serbia was recognized regionally and globally as a model for integrating ECD and family-centred early childhood interventions (FECI) into PHC, including gender-transformative parenting services through home visits, paediatric care and multidisciplinary developmental counselling for vulnerable children. The Regional Conference Ensuring the Best Start in Life for Children: The Power of Parenting, organized by UNICEF Serbia under the patronage of MoH, hosted 300 participants from 19 countries and was viewed by over 81,670 online, and resulted in the launch of the Belgrade Early Years Call to Action, providing a roadmap for cross-sectoral coordination of parenting programmes. Additionally, five ministries reaffirmed their commitment to the National ECD Call to Action (2018) and decided to develop a National ECD Action Plan for 2025–2026. 
The coverage of the advanced quality home-visiting programme, integrating support for responsive, gender-balanced parenting and parental well-being, reached nearly 50% of municipalities and is at a pivotal stage for full national scale-up. The Home Visiting Maturity Model assessment and costing exercise, set for completion in 2025, will guide the optimization of services to ensure high-quality care for all, including vulnerable children and families. FECI coverage also increased from 60% to 84% of districts, initiating inter-municipal cooperation and greater local self-government (LSG) engagement in service development.  
A major progress was achieved with the increased investment of LSGs in ECD and parenting programmes. Over US$3 million was leveraged through partnerships with LSGs and the Ministry of Family Welfare and Demography to support ECD initiatives, including 100 new local measures integrating ECD and parenting support into strategic local plans, mobile parenting schools, reading corners and early intervention programmes. To ensure the sustainability of local ECD, a comprehensive Guidebook for LSGs on Planning, Programming and Budgeting for Child Rights was published and widely promoted across Serbia and included in the learning materials for the National Academy of Public Administration-accredited course on Child Rights.  
In addition to these results at national scale, another significant achievement in 2024 was the endorsement of by-laws stipulating all FECI components within PHC services and defining the Institute for ECD and Inclusion within the health institutions’ network. 
UNICEF also played a major convening role for the promotion of accessible and quality mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services across the country. Following the signature of a Memorandum of Understanding between 6 ministries around Mental Health in 2023, an Action Plan  mobilizing $1 million of public financing for mental health was developed to support the promotion of information on self-care,  community-based mental health systems,  accessibility to services, to enhance the regulatory framework, foster cooperation among education, social protection and healthcare sectors, and focus on prevention, early identification, and referral protocols. The action plan was launched during the Third International Conference on Mental Health and Well-being of Children and Youth in Serbia, organized by UNICEF and the MoH, Together – On the Same Side, which gathered more than 300 participants. The SveJeOK platform, recognized by the Government as an innovative platform providing MHPSS, expanded its online services, offering educational resources, interactive activities and real-time counselling for young people aged 13–24. In 2024 the platform was visited by 50,000 users. 
Education 
UNICEF continued to support national-scale reforms in preschool education, systemic reforms in inclusive education (IE), and to improve the quality of education through the significant support to professional development of educators, the promotion of digital technologies and the promotion and support to children’s learning and well-being, thus making a major contribution to system strengthening for inclusive quality pre-university education. 
The preschool reform, led by the Ministry of Education (MoE) with a WB loan and the technical support from UNICEF, had a major impact on the preschool levels of enrolment, learning and completion: more than 234,000 children in Serbia are now participating in early childhood education (ECE) through the innovative ‘Years of Ascent’ preschool curriculum approach, which promotes children-led and play-based learning, fostering key skills like confidence and curiosity, and boosting innovation and creativity. More than 95% of all preschool professionals were trained for implementation of the new pedagogic approach. All public preschools benefited from comprehensive six-month-long support that included trainings, hands-on support and mentoring, and communities of practice and were capacitated to assess the level of inclusion in their preschool, plan preschool policies and improve access and participation of children from vulnerable groups. To complement MoE’s efforts on increasing access to early childhood education and care (ECEC), UNICEF focused on increasing the capacities of Inclusive Education teams in all preschool institutions in Serbia.  
UNICEF’s technical assistance also played a pivotal role in strengthening the institutional, legal and policy framework for Inclusive Education (IE) at national and local levels. These efforts aimed at increasing equity, accessibility, gender equality, openness, and inclusion in pre-university education. With EU support and UNICEF technical assistance, MoE established 12 resource centres (RCs), an innovative mechanism aimed at equitable provision of additional support and assistive technologies (AT), to build an accessible learning environment. Professionals in education, social welfare, and healthcare, working in all municipalities across Serbia received systematic support to improve the quality of the assessment and provision of additional support for children in need. 
The Conference on Inclusive Education, We Learn Together, organized by the MoE and UNICEF in partnership with the EU, highlighted 15 years of progress in implementation of IE, showed by the tripling of  the number of students receiving support in regular education from around 8,000 (2014) to 20,200 (2024), and a significant decrease in students in special schools from 7,453 (2013/14) to 4,735 (2023/24). The conference called for greater commitment to further developing IE through transformation of special schools, reform of initial teacher training, intersectoral cooperation and reform of IE financing. 
Digitalization of education is a priority for Serbia, and UNICEF supported the development of digital content for online and distance learning, the National Education Platform adapted from the Learning Passport, an innovative approach initiated and technically supported by UNICEF. The National Education Platform is the main hub for teacher trainings and capacity building, used by approximately 60% of all teachers, and is now managed by the Institute for Improvement of Education (IIE). Over the past 5 years, more than 400,000 teachers attended hybrid or self-paced trainings using this platform. UNICEF and EdTech–World Bank co-organized the annual Digital Education Conference, where 20 experts from 6 countries shared their knowledge with 4,250 participants (both live and online).. 
Child Protection 
In 2024, Serbia’s child protection system witnessed significant advancements to ensure continuous services for the most vulnerable children. Supporting the Government’s efforts towards deinstitutionalization, UNICEF supported the conceptualization of Centres for Children, Youth and Families, thus leveraging EU resources programmed for transformation of four residential institution in 2025–2027, making a significant contribution to the implementation of the Deinstitutionalization Strategy of the Republic of Serbia.  
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Labour, Employment, Veteran and Social Affairs (MoLEVSA) in developing the Rulebook on Conditions and Standards for Providing Intensive Support Services to Families in Crisis, which defines standards and conditions for the licensing of service providers. UNICEF worked on enhancing access to and the quality of foster-care services in 18 local governments through local campaigns for recruitment of new foster families (82 new families recruited), the development and accreditation of an innovative training programme for standard foster care, and the strengthening of knowledge and skills of social protection professionals on standard, specialized, urgent and respite foster care. 
In the area of prevention and response to violence against children (VAC), UNICEF supported MoLEVSA in developing an innovative Special VAC Protocol for the Social Welfare System, which for the first time expanded its scope to all social welfare actors, thus strengthening the overall accountability in the sector.  
UNICEF provided direct support to the National Coalition to End Child Marriage, established in 2019, leading to a stronger government commitment to eliminate this harmful practice. With UNICEF support, the Coalition advocated for regulatory changes, to secure adequate sanctioning of perpetrators by amending the Criminal Code. UNICEF also directly supported Roma girls’ and women’s leadership through capacity building for Roma women human rights activists and an intergenerational mentorship programme. 
UNICEF continued to support the protection and promotion of the rights of children in contact with the law, whether as offenders, victims/witnesses, or participants in civil proceedings. Advocacy for a strategic, equitable and coordinated approach to advancing the Justice for Children agenda resulted in the Ministry of Justice’s reconfirmed full commitment to reforming the justice for children system (visible through inclusion of the topic in the Government’s Reform Agenda, which is an integral part of the EU Growth Plan for the West Balkans), with further elaboration planned for 2025. 
Climate & Environment 
In 2024, UNICEF provided significant input on the drafts of the Environmental Protection Strategy, the National DRR Strategy, and the Air Protection Act proposal, laying the groundwork for policies that recognize and address the specific vulnerabilities of children in the context of climate and environmental challenges. Notably, the draft Air Protection Act for the first time recognizes children as a particularly vulnerable group, a development that can partly be attributed to UNICEF’s advocacy efforts over the years. 
As a result of advocacy efforts and strengthened relations with the Ministry of Environmental Protection, UNICEF has been granted observer status in the working group responsible for developing national reports requested by the UNFCCC, including the Biennial Transparency Report and the National Communication. 
Ongoing efforts for child-sensitive climate policies are focusing on promoting the adoption of Child-Sensitive NDC 3.0, recently introduced to the Government. We now hope for further concrete inclusion of these child-sensitive considerations in future climate policies. 
UNICEF has supported the implementation of National Adaptation Plan (NAP) goals through activities in education, environmental health and youth mobilization. In collaboration with the Ministry of Environmental Protection, UNICEF organized a learning and participation opportunity on the topic of the NAP in Serbia. This created a space for young people and the Ministry to engage in dialogue, where youth presented their recommendations for the NAP, and the Ministry informed them about opportunities for involvement in the process. 
For the third consecutive year, UNICEF has conducted its summer campaign on heatwaves, aimed at protecting children’s environmental health and raising awareness among parents and caregivers about the impact of high temperatures on children’s health and the importance of protective measures. 
Young People 
UNICEF successfully provided technical assistance to the Government of Serbia and civil society for the implementation of the National Youth Strategy by promoting and supporting youth participation and civic engagement, by supporting the network of youth centres and clubs, the provision of quality non-formal education, and by modelling digital learning and career guidance tools.  
UNICEF partnered throughout the year with the Ministry of Tourism and Youth, the Prime Minister’s Office, the German International Cooperation Organization, National Association of Youth Workers, Serbian Association of Youth, National Association of Coordinators of Youth Offices, the implementing partner OPENS and other CSOs, for the establishment of youth centres in Serbia. 
UNICEF leveraged its Regular Resources to foster stronger public investment by the Government in youth centres, amounting to $1.7 million. By supporting the design and implementation of specialized training for youth workers, in partnership with OPENS, the Centre for Youth Work and the National Association of Youth Workers, UNICEF equipped all future centres with skilled professionals who can effectively outreach and engage and support young people from diverse backgrounds. UNICEF also contributed to the selection of eight new cities for the establishment of youth centres.  
By supporting the Government in strengthening career guidance systems, particularly for vulnerable groups like Roma youth, UNICEF developed outreach models, addressing critical needs in underserved communities, and fostering more equitable opportunities for all youth in Serbia. UNICEF provided technical assistance for the pilot phase of the Youth Guarantee, designing outreach models for improved support and services to young people who are NEET, such as Roma youth from waste-picker communities.  
In cooperation with the Ministry of Tourism and Youth, local governments, and youth organizations, UNICEF contributed to the creation and equipment of Innovation Clubs and Corners that enable growth and skill enhancement of young people, through non-formal education, skill-building and active community engagement.  
UNICEF successfully implemented the Girls in ICT initiative, empowering adolescent girls from disadvantaged communities, including Roma youth and those with disabilities, through ICT skills development. The programme helped bridge the digital and gender gaps, nurturing self-confidence and providing practical training, to nearly 350 girls across 3 cities and is ready for scaling. 
UNICEF focused on ensuring that young people can engage meaningfully in decision-making processes, aligning with both the EU Youth Strategy (2019–2027) and the National Youth Strategy (2023–2030), with the objective to help address the low youth participation in Serbia. UNICEF has strengthened mechanisms to amplify youth voices, particularly through platforms like U-Report gathering 17,000 U-reporters and the Volunteer Programme platform, that supported volunteering activities of more than 2,800 young people, thus strengthening volunteer systems at national and local levels. 
UNICEF Youth Advisory Board, comprising 18 members aged 15–26 from across Serbia, has been crucial in advancing youth advocacy. Youth Board represented Serbian youth at 22 national and international events, discussing key issues such as mental health, youth participation, the green agenda, air quality and human rights. 
To further enhance youth participation, UNICEF partnered with the Westminster Foundation for Democracy, empowering the UNICEF Youth Advisory Board to advocate for policies in the Serbian National Assembly. The ‘Parliamentorship’ initiative aimed to institutionalize youth involvement in national legislation, focusing on child rights and youth inclusion. This initiative promoted joint work of Members of Parliament (MPs) on issues like violence prevention and IE, ensuring meaningful change through amendments or new laws. 
Social Policy 
In 2024, UNICEF led efforts to promote child-sensitive budgeting in Serbia by fostering a high-level coalition, drafting a comprehensive training manual for MPs, and prioritizing equity in public finance, laying foundations for transformative systemic change, advancing child-focused SDG targets, and ensuring no child is left behind. 
UNICEF’s interventions targeted systemic bottlenecks in Serbia’s public finance system, advancing transformative progress in the realization of children’s rights. UNICEF prioritized legislative capacity-building and advocacy to address long-standing gaps in transparency and equity in budgeting processes. These efforts directly contributed to a shift in parliamentary discourse, with child-sensitive budgetary considerations gaining visibility and acknowledgement among key stakeholders.  
UNICEF made significant strides towards achieving transformative outcomes for children in Serbia by advancing child-sensitive budgeting practices within the country’s legislature. A key accomplishment was the establishment of a high-level coalition to address persistent challenges in public finance for children, including insufficient transparency and limited legislative capacity to prioritize investments in children’s rights. This coalition brought together Serbia’s National Assembly, international expertise (Center of Excellence in Finance – CEF) and local civil society (Belgrade Fund for Political Excellence) to promote open and child-centred budgetary processes.  
The coalition’s efforts seek to tackle entrenched inequalities in public finance for children by enabling MPs to evaluate budget allocations through a child rights perspective. Targeted advocacy has aimed to integrate child-related SDG targets into legislative budget reviews, laying the groundwork for transformative outcomes for children, especially those at risk of being left behind. 
UNICEF facilitated the development of an advanced draft of a comprehensive training manual on public finance for children. The manual aims to equip MPs with the knowledge and skills needed to advocate for children’s rights in budgetary debates and decisions. While still under development, this resource underscores UNICEF’s essential role in addressing knowledge gaps and embedding child-sensitive approaches into the legislative framework. 
ADVOCACY AND PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT 
In 2024, advocacy efforts played a vital role in advancing the realization of child rights and supporting the sustained impact of national reforms led by the Government of Serbia, with UNICEF technical assistance. Three high-level conferences, organized by UNICEF in partnership with the Government of Serbia, involved six ministries (Health; Education; Tourism and Youth; Labour, Employment, Veteran and Social Affairs; Human and Minority Rights and Social Dialogue; Family Welfare and Demography),  fostering cross-ministerial collaboration, by taking stock of progress, and jointly identifying systemic level changes needed in the area of ECD, IE and Mental Health and psychological wellbeing of children and young people: 

Ensuring the Best Start in Life for Children: The Power of Parenting, under the patronage of MoH and attended by 300 participants from 19 countries and viewed by over 81,670 online, launched the the Belgrade Early Years Call to Action, stressing the importance of investing in parenting programmes. Five ministries reaffirmed their commitment to the National ECD Call to Action (2018) and decided to develop a National ECD Action Plan for 2025–2026. 
Together – On the Same Side, the Third International Conference on Mental Health and Well-being of Children and Youth in Serbia, marked a significant milestone since the signing of the MoU on MHPSS for Children and Youth by six ministries, reasserting their commitment to enhance the provision of MHPSS services for children, adolescents and youth through a costed Action Plan.  
We Learn Together, an international conference organized with the EU and MoE, welcomed 250 attendees and highlighted 15 years of progress in implementation of IE and envisioning the next steps of IE in Serbia. The conference called for greater commitment to further developing IE through transformation of special schools, reform of initial teacher training, intersectoral cooperation and reform of IE financing. 
Through advocacy and strategic communication, UNICEF Serbia championed children’s rights, amplifying its voice through media partnerships and storytelling. Its strong advocacy led Serbia’s Press Council to amend guidelines for reporting on mass shootings, driving meaningful change on ethical reporting on child rights issues. 
UNICEF continued its support to independent institutions and CSOs for children in advocating around the most pressing issues children face in Serbia, particularly around equity and discrimination, as well as around problems that affect the achievement of child rights and equity over the long term.  
UNICEF communication and advocacy efforts resulted in increased advancing of advocacy, programmatic and fundraising goals, reinforcing its position as a leading voice for children in Serbia. The public communication campaigns highlighted UNICEF’s results and impact on children, inspiring greater commitment of the private sector. Through strategic storytelling and strengthened media partnerships, the team expanded the organisation’s reach and impact, cementing its role as a trusted advocate for children.  
UNICEF won the Grand Prix award at the 2024 Campaigns with Purpose festival in the Social Campaign category for the intensified efforts to raise awareness and reduce stigma and discrimination surrounding mental health through educational campaigns targeting youth, parents, professionals and decision makers.

UNITED NATIONS WORKING TOGETHER 
UNICEF maintained high-level quality cooperation with UN sister agencies, co-chairing the interagency-level Result Working Group 2 (RG2) and Monitoring and Evaluation Group and fostering a fruitful Policy Dialogue on Human Capital between the UN RG2 and EU Delegation. 
Four UN agencies (UNICEF, IOM, UNHCR, UNDP) continued the successful implementation of the two-year project ‘Promoting evidence-based migration governance for maximizing development potential of migration’, which aims to promote a data- and evidence-driven migration policy and planning process in Serbia. 
With SDC support, four agencies (UNICEF, UNOPS, UNFPA, UNEP) successfully implemented the joint four-year project ‘PRO – Local Governance for People and Nature’, advancing the capacities of local governments to develop local social protection policies and services to improve the well-being of vulnerable groups. 
UNICEF, together with UNDP, UN Women and UNFPA, started to implement a three-year project ‘Empowering change, ending violence’ in close coordination with the Government’s coordination body for gender equality. The project is supported by SIDA and will foster non-violent and gender-responsive positive parenting, advocacy for the elimination of child marriage, and support leadership of young Roma women and girls. 
In partnership with UNDP, FAO and the Office for IT and e-Government, UNICEF joined a three-year Joint UN Programme on Digital Transformation funded by the SDG Fund to provide a use-case for citizen-centred services in the social protection sector. The Joint Programme, called ‘’Clicking Together with Citizens’’ is designed to assist the Government in achieving its strategic goal of enhancing public services for all, with a focus on the most vulnerable, and to fast-track the achievement of SDGs by transitioning from an institution-centric to a people-centric approach in public service design.  
Following the signature of a Letter of Understanding, UNHCR and UNICEF solidified their collaboration working closely with IOM to advance joint advocacy efforts on child protection in migration.  
UNICEF and UNDP reinforced their collaboration through a joint planning workshop, identifying areas of joint work and advocacy, and paving the way for the strategic reflections on the next UNSDCF 2026–2030.  
UNICEF WORKING WITH IFIs 
Partnership with the World Bank remained instrumental to support the reform process of the ECEC subsystem in all five areas of system strengthening: policy, regulation and planning, financing, workforce development, data and quality assurance, and partnerships.  
Dialogue and collaboration were successfully strengthened with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the European Investment Bank (EIB) and the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB) around digital education, digital skills, child, and maternal health. UNICEF collaborated with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to design and deliver joint evidence-based advocacy on the importance, benefits, and efficiency of two national pro-poverty programmes: financial social assistance and child allowance. 
OTHER PARTNERSHIPS 
In 2024 UNICEF as the co-chair of the UN RG 2 played a pivotal role in initiating a policy dialogue and strengthened collaboration of UN agencies with the EU Delegation to Serbia, particularly in the domain of social policies, including health, education, and skills-building.  
UNICEF’s cooperation with the EU was also continued in IE and further digital education.  
UNICEF continued to nurture its partnerships with data and evidence institutions, including the Statistical Office of the Republic of Serbia, the Republic Institute for Social Protection, think tanks, CSOs and academia. 
In public finance, key partners included International Monetary Fund, Fiscal Council, Serbia’s National Assembly, the Center of Excellence in Finance, and the Belgrade Fund for Political Excellence. A partnership with the Westminster Foundation for Democracy was also established to advance UNICEF’s collaboration with the National Assembly. 
The Standing Conference of Towns and Municipalities (SCTM) remained a major partner for UNICEF’s engagement with LSGs around the provision of local services for the most vulnerable children.  
UNICEF continued to support CSOs and independent institutions active on advocating for child rights across different sectors.  
HARNESSING THE POWER OF BUSINESSES 
In 2024, UNICEF expanded its collaboration with the business sector in Serbia, harnessing its power through financial support, technical knowledge and expertise, in-kind contribution, communication and advocacy to contribute to the programme goals. 
With the support of business networks and associations, UNICEF accelerated its leading position among international agencies and local charities in Serbia, reaching the top position of the most trusted organizations according to the strategic comparator analysis conducted in 2024. This enabled UNICEF to secure high-value corporate partnerships and to influence responsible business practices that have an impact on children, focusing on family-friendly policies, which were promoted with the Chamber of Commerce of Serbia and other business associations, during Parenting Month and around the regional ECD conference organized by UNICEF in Belgrade. 
UNICEF further strengthened its position as a knowledge leader for integration of children’s rights into responsible business practices and industry standards.  
UNICEF’s leading position with the business sector in Serbia enabled the country office to engage businesses to contribute significant resources, core knowledge and improved business practices in favour of children in Serbia. Gross income from the business sector reached $1,748,000, a 123% increase compared to 2023.  
The major increase in corporate income was primarily due to the successful engagement of high-value, multi-country support by Nelt Group, which committed $1.3 million for Serbia, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Angola. This three-year partnership will ensure that children and youth in these countries gain skills and knowledge needed to thrive in a complex digitalized world.  
A new partnership was established with a leading company in the IT industry – Comtrade Distribution, Tesla electronics brand – in support of increased digital skills for the most vulnerable youth in Serbia. A strategic partnership began with the newly established Intesa Foundation, in support of Inclusive Education.  
UNICEF maintained regular communication with the members of the Business Advisory Board, thus fostering resource mobilization and joint advocacy with the business sector for child rights. Advocacy activities focused on family-friendly policies within the business sector, investment in IE and enhanced digital skills of children and youth.  
UNICEF’s participation as the keynote speaker or moderator at business round-table discussions and panels enabled UNICEF to motivate the business sector to review their business practices and their impact on children. The major events included the CSR Serbia Conference 2024, The World in 2025, Kopaonik Business Forum, SPLET 2024, GamesCon 2024. 
In collaboration with the Association of Economists of Serbia, UNICEF participated in the Kopaonik Business Forum, with the UNICEF Representative as a keynote speaker (Strong collaboration is needed for the benefit of children) and through the Youth Call for Action panel.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The dynamic and evolving political and institutional environment emphasizes the need for adaptive strategies that can sustain momentum for advancing child rights despite changes in political and institutional environment.  
UNICEF made significant strides towards achieving transformative outcomes for children in Serbia by advancing child-sensitive budgeting practices within the country’s legislature. A key accomplishment was the establishment of a high-level coalition, composed of Serbia’s National Assembly, international public finance experts, and local civil society, to address persistent challenges in public finance for children, including insufficient transparency and limited legislative capacity to prioritize investments in children’s rights. The combination of advocacy, evidence-generation, partnerships and engagement with civil society and international experts, and capacity building of local and national decision makers, started to yield positive results and increased awareness of child-sensitive budgeting, and inclusive public finance mechanisms.  
By prioritizing the most vulnerable children and embedding systemic solutions into the legislative process, UNICEF has laid the groundwork for sustainable progress in aligning national budgets with child rights and welfare. UNICEF employed multiple implementing strategies, including research, advocacy, and capacity building, to address systemic bottlenecks. Advocacy efforts highlighted the critical need for open budget processes, while collaboration with international partners provided MPs with comparative insights into successful models, and knowledge management integrated best practices into training material, further enhancing MP’s ability to champion children’s rights. 
These integrated approaches have advanced the outcome-level goal of ensuring that no child is left behind in public finance decisions. However, the progress achieved in 2024 also highlighted areas requiring further engagement with child-sensitive budgeting initiatives: fostering collaboration with executive stakeholders, such as the Ministry of Finance, and generating disaggregated data on child-related expenditures to support evidence-based advocacy and policymaking. In 2025, expanded advocacy efforts will focus on establishing improved cooperation with executive bodies and addressing data gaps.  
By building on its achievements and refining its strategies, moving forward, UNICEF will aim to foster a more transparent and equitable public finance environment that prioritizes the rights and welfare of all children. Adaptive strategies and continuous advocacy will be essential for translating the positive shifts observed at the legislative level into tangible improvements in children’s lives.  
Regular Resources (RR) funding played a pivotal role in enabling UNICEF to lead advocacy and public finance initiatives, and to broker new partnerships with the public and private sectors for results at scale for children. The flexible nature of RR funding allowed for swift action in coalition-building, capacity development and advocacy efforts. These resources facilitated progress in Serbia and reinforced UNICEF’s position as a thought leader, convener, and child rights advocate.  
Through successful partnerships with state ministries, EU and IFIs,  UNICEF was able to leverage RR and funds from bilateral donors into major investments jointly made by the Government of Serbia, World Bank, EU and other partners, allowing for a full scaling-up and nationwide implementation of the two major reforms of preschool and inclusive education, triggering transformative changes for the access, quality and learning outcomes of children in Serbia. This model resulted in remarkable returns in investment that benefited the preschool national reform in Serbia. The initial investment of approximately $2 million (2012–2019, thematic, bilateral) triggered a return investment in the ECE sector of around $52 million through the World Bank loan and EU pre-accession funds and was considered as a model of successful cooperation between MoE, World Bank and UNICEF ($4 million, 2019–2024). This highly successful leveraging effort resulted in a major progress on the SDG indicators related to preschool enrolment: the number of children attending preschool programme increased from 52% (2015) to 68% (2023/24), a major result at national scale.  
Following the signature of a Memorandum of Understanding between six ministries around Mental Health in 2023, UNICEF leveraged its Regular Resources, and private funding from Serbian companies and individual givers, to further engage on this topic, provide technical support to all line ministries for the design of an Action Plan mobilizing $1 million of public financing for mental health. The Action Plan supports community-based mental health systems, accessibility to services, improved regulatory framework, cross-sectoral coordination, and represents an excellent example of how UNICEF can leverage RR to trigger the further mobilization of private and public finance for the advancement of child rights and well-being.  
Another major achievement was reached through the successful leveraging of regular resources, private funding (LEGO Foundation), and private and individual giving fundraised by PSFR team, to support the adoption of ECD and parenting measures in approximately 20% of all LSGs in Serbia. This initial investment triggered the allocation of additional funds by municipalities specifically for early development and parental support, showcasing a direct financial commitment towards enhancing ECD services. As a direct result of UNICEF’s approach – community engagement, capacity building and technical assistance and advocacy – approximately $1 million of LSG funds was leveraged in 2023 to improve ECD in Serbia. In 2024, an additional milestone was reached with the increased investment of LSGs in ECD and parenting programmes. Over $3 million was leveraged through partnerships with LSGs and the Ministry of Family Welfare and Demography to support ECD initiatives, including 100 new local measures integrating ECD and parenting support into strategic local plans, mobile parenting schools, reading corners and early intervention programmes. FECI coverage also increased from 60% to 84% of districts, initiating inter-municipal cooperation and greater LSG engagement in service development, resulting in a major improvement of the accessibility and access of ECD services at national scale, and at local level.  
This mobilization of public, private resources was accompanied by a major high-level advocacy and capacity-building effort, conducted at both national and local levels. The approach included capacity building of relevant frontline workers, managers of local services and institutions, as well relevant stakeholders at both the local and national levels. This resulted in MoH endorsing of the national guidance for the ECD frontline workers, which encompasses all components of the global Nurturing Care Framework (developed by WHO, World Bank and UNICEF).To ensure the sustainability of local ECD, a comprehensive Guidebook for LSGs on Planning, Programming and Budgeting for Child Rights was published and widely promoted across Serbia and included in the learning materials for the National Academy of Public Administration-accredited course on Child Rights.  
As a result, in 2024, Serbia was recognized regionally and globally as a model for integrating ECD and family-centred early childhood interventions (FECI) into PHC, including gender-transformative parenting services through home visits, paediatric care and multidisciplinary developmental counselling for vulnerable children. The Regional Conference Ensuring the Best Start in Life for Children: The Power of Parenting, organized by UNICEF Serbia under the patronage of MoH, hosted 300 participants from 19 countries, was viewed by over 81,670 online, and resulted in the launch of the Belgrade Early Years Call to Action, providing a roadmap for cross-sectoral coordination of parenting programmes. Additionally, five ministries reaffirmed their commitment to the National ECD Call to Action (2018) and decided to develop a National ECD Action Plan for 2025–2026. 
UNICEF’s work with LSGs resulted in major improvement of access to ECD, parenting support, IE, and child welfare measures for vulnerable families in more than half of the municipalities of Serbia, triggering transformative and sustainable changes in the access to local services for the most vulnerable children. The partnership with LSGs and the establishment of intersectoral committees at the municipal/city level have been major enablers for inclusive support to children and families to access early childhood development, education, and care in every municipality of Serbia. Moving forward in 2025, UNICEF aims to strengthen collaboration with LSGs to scale up child-friendly measures and improve the sustainable financing of local services for vulnerable children, laying the ground for a possible adaptation of the EU Child Guarantee model to Serbia. By anchoring local spending priorities in sustainable development and child well-being, UNICEF will ensure that local governance continues to deliver meaningful results for children and communities alike. 
The collaboration with the business sector provides UNICEF in Serbia with a unique opportunity to leverage its role in working with IFIs and the public sector, and to engage the business sector in development of innovative solutions and deliver scaled and sustainable impact. The engagement of the business sector to invest its financial and core resources is a testimony to UNICEF’s capacity to leverage public and private resources to accelerate and amplify solutions for children. The partnership fostered between the private sector and the state institutions and line ministries – notably in the sector of Digital Education and STEM learning – secured UNICEF’s brokering role to ensure programme implementation and access to funding for UNICEF’s priority programmes. Private partnerships were built to sustain the impact and results of programmes previously implemented with EU funding, in close collaboration with state ministries, to increase access and learning outcomes for the most vulnerable children in rural areas of Serbia. With these public and private partnerships, UNICEF enabled an innovative model of public and private investment for sustainable outcomes for the most vulnerable children. These successful models pave the way for future collaboration between UNICEF, IFIs, public and private sector to leverage resources for children in 2025.  
Serbia CO successfully piloted core components of new business models consisting in leveraging Regular Resources, Private Fundraising led by PSFR team, partnerships with EU and IFIs, to trigger and leverage sustainable and systemic changes in public financing for children.  
The combination of technical expertise, high-level advocacy, technical assistance and policy advice, capacity building of social sectors professionals, engagement with local authorities, and public campaigns targeting social and behavioural changes, resulted in system level changes and tangible improvements of the lives of children in Serbia in the areas of ECD, ECE and mental health. Serbia CO thus illustrated the power of evidence-based advocacy, policy advice and partnerships to leverage systemic changes in social policies and finance for children.  
In 2025 and beyond, UNICEF Serbia will aim at piloting new models of resource leveraging and partnerships and at scaling up successful approaches nationally and to other sectors.

Tajikistan has been a lower middle-income country since January 2023, the second smallest country in Central Asia ranked by 2023 GDP. In 2023 the GNI per capita (Atlas method) was reported at US$ 1,440 and the GDP per capita was US$ 1,189. Tajikistan has the youngest population in the Europe and Central Asia region, with 36 per cent of its population under 15 years of age, 19 per cent of adolescents aged 10-19 years, and 29 per cent of youth population aged 14-30 years. As of January 2024, the population is 10.3 million, including 4.2 million children, with 71 per cent living in rural areas. This demographic landscape offers both an opportunity for economic growth through human capital development investment, but also a substantive risk regarding government under-investments in the key social sectors. 
 
The completion of the Roghun Dam, originally anticipated by 2027, offers Tajikistan a critical opportunity to enhance fiscal sustainability and address the needs of its population, especially children. With construction funding pressures alleviated and substantial revenues expected from electricity production and exports, the government will gain significant fiscal space to reduce public debt—projected to drop from 43.8 per cent of GDP in 2020 to 31 per cent by 2027 (IMF 2023 Article IV Consultation, baseline scenario).  According to the World Bank however, the project is due to be operational by 2033.
 
In his address to Parliament in December 2024, the President of Tajikistan, among other priorities and challenges facing the nation, referenced high external migration and dependency on remittances, quality of education, lack of access to education for girls, the potential for a green economy, accelerating the economy’s digitization, and developing human resources. This year has been particularly challenging for Tajik labor migrants in Russia with Tajikistan’s economy dependent by over 30 per cent of GDP on remittances, according to the World Bank. The return of many labor migrants from Russia, due to restrictive migration policies there, has posed significant challenges. The returnees have reduced vital remittances, overwhelming local job markets and social services, and potentially deepening poverty and social tensions. Over the long term, this situation could push Tajikistan to diversify its economy, but could destabilize the country if reintegration efforts fail. The President also addressed the critical issue of education, particularly the lack of learning spaces. Currently, 73,000 students lack access to education, and the number is growing each year. The government has pledged to build over 400 new schools annually to meet this demand. In 2024, the government amended the law on education, making secondary education through grade 11 mandatory, including for girls. This policy aims to reduce the dropout rate among girls after grade 9 and encourage participation in technical and vocational training.
 
Despite prioritizing digitalization in education, progress has been slow, with only 16 per cent of schools connected to the internet in 2023. Rural areas face additional challenges, with electricity available for only 5-6 hours per day. Tajikistan has made strides in child health, with the under-5 mortality rate dropping from 43 to 24 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2012 and 2023. Neonatal mortality also decreased from 19 to 10 deaths per 1,000 live births during the same period. Wasting, a life-threatening form of malnutrition, declined from 10 per cent in 2012 to 6 per cent in 2023. However, regional variations persist, with higher rates of wasting in rural areas, especially in Khatlon, where 11 per cent of children are affected.
 
Over 431,000 children under five in Tajikistan are facing severe food poverty, increasing their vulnerability to wasting. In 2020, the government banned palm oil imports, which inadvertently included ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) products and therapeutic milk, creating a shortage of essential nutrition for children with severe acute malnutrition in 2023 and 2024. Following intervention from UNICEF and other partners, the government amended the decree in 2024 to allow the import of RUTF and therapeutic milk. This change will help provide life-saving nutrition to up to 42,000 children annually.
 
Preschool enrollment has improved from 12.3 per cent in 2015 to around 20 per cent in 2024, but this remains far below the national target of 50 per cent. Gender disparities are also evident in education, with only 74 per cent of girls compared to 87 per cent of boys attending upper secondary school. The transition rate from lower to upper secondary education is 63 per cent for girls and 69 per cent for boys. The new education law mandating 11 years of schooling is expected to positively impact these transition rates.
 
Women represent 25 per cent of civil servants, with nearly 20 per cent at senior management levels. Between 2010 and 2020, the number of women in parliament increased from 19 per cent to 24 per cent, and the proportion of women working in national and local government rose to 31 per cent. However, gender disparities remain, particularly in youth employment. Around 90 per cent of youth aged 15-24 who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET) are female, representing approximately 49 per cent of the total female population in this age group. Additionally, the number of women with vocational education has slightly decreased from 114 out of 1,000 women in 2010 to 108.3 out of 1,000 women in 2020.
 
Tajikistan has become the 67th country to ban all forms of violence, including corporal punishment, a significant step for child protection and children's rights. The country has also removed fees for late birth registration through the new Law on Civil Status Acts and the Law on the Upbringing and Education of Children. At the first Global Ministerial Conference on Violence against Children in Bogotá on November 7-8, 2024, Tajikistan committed to comprehensive child protection reforms and improved school reporting mechanisms. Additionally, the Government approved the second National Programme for the Prevention of Domestic Violence (2025–2030) to ensure children grow up in a violence-free environment. These changes strengthen the child protection system and initiate the development of a National Programme for Child Protection System Reform.
  
Tajikistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, which exacerbates the frequency and intensity of natural disasters like floods, landslides, and earthquakes. In 2024, about 74 per cent of children were exposed to heat stress, 68 per cent of children are exposed to water scarcity, 14 per cent to riverine flood risks, and 39 per cent to earthquake hazards. Additionally, 98 per cent of children are exposed to ambient air pollution with PM2.5 levels equal to or exceeding 25 µg/m³, posing serious health risks.  The country’s vulnerability is expected to increase due to rising temperatures and changing precipitation patterns, with projections suggesting that the annual mean temperature could rise by up to 6.3°C by 2080. These changes will intensify droughts and floods, leaving children even more vulnerable to climate-related risks. 
 
In 2024, Tajikistan signed the Ministerial Declaration on Comprehensive School Safety in Central Asia, committing to ensure safe, resilient schools amidst increasing climate-related hazards. The government has also committed to addressing water scarcity, climate change adaptation, and glacier conservation. National policies, such as the 2040 Water Sector Strategy, aim to improve access to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, particularly in communities, schools, and healthcare facilities. These policies reflect the government's commitment to ensuring equitable access to these vital services.
 
Youth engagement is also a priority in Tajikistan, with initiatives like the Youth for Water and Climate Network, which was established in 2024 with UNICEF’s support and in collaboration with the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources, the Committee for Environmental Protection, and the Committee of Youth and Sports. The Network drafted an Action Plan, to be endorsed by the Government, to advance child-centered climate resilience in Tajikistan.
 
Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan recently resolved long-standing border disputes, which had previously impeded the delivery of essential services in border areas. This resolution promotes stability and cooperation between the two countries, ensuring that children and families in these regions have better access to services. Strengthening trust and cooperation along the border will foster a safer and more inclusive environment for children and families, improving access to education, health, nutrition, and child protection services.

Surviving and Thriving
Improving Maternal and Newborn Health
UNICEF’s efforts to enhance maternal and newborn health include improving timely planning and referral to maternal and newborn health support services. In three districts, an electronic perinatal registry was implemented, registering 8,107 pregnant women, a 40.5 per cent increase from 2023. This innovation improved data collection, referral tracking, and analyses, benefiting 3,075 women with timely planning and referral, and 353 women with severe complications were urgently referred to higher-level facilities. The Ministry of Health and Social Protection of the Population (MoHSPP) plans to expand this system. Additionally, UNICEF supported the update of Immunization and Growth Monitoring modules, now serving as a digital Child Health Record Book.
 
Health System Strengthening
The healthcare system was strengthened through improved workforce capacity and infrastructure. Essential medical equipment was installed in 750 primary health care (PHC) facilities and 22 hospitals across 33 districts. Six operational oxygen systems benefited 3,954 patients, including 1,012 children under five. Nationwide, 252,405 children received essential Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) medicines, reducing treatment gaps of common childhood illnesses.
 
In Khatlon and Sughd regions, multidisciplinary groups supported antiretroviral treatment adherence. 166 adolescents living with HIV engaged in education sessions and received psychological support. Trained peers reached 396 adolescents through awareness-raising interventions on HIV and SRHR in schools and universities.
 
A total of 2,521 health workers were trained to deliver quality integrated Maternal, Newborn, and Child Health (MNCH) services. Training focused on the use of ventilators and Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machines, including a new Bubble CPAP. About 10,690 students at the Republican Medical College, including 9,800 female trainees, received trainings equipping the next generation of health professionals with vital skills to improve newborn health.
 
UNICEF supported vaccine availability, including a successful application for new vaccines (HPV) with a rollout planned for September 2025. Immunization coverage in 2024 for MCV1 and DTP3 was 97 per cent and 96 per cent, respectively. An evaluation of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) highlighted support in vaccine coverage, system strengthening, and addressing inequities. Recommendations included enhancing data quality, addressing barriers to vaccine uptake, and ensuring long-term sustainability through increased investments. Vaccine storage capacity was improved through repairs and maintenance of vaccine refrigerators, cold rooms, refrigerated vehicles, diesel generators, stabilizers, and the installation of solar-powered refrigerators in remote areas.
 
Improving Nutrition and Breastfeeding
UNICEF trained 600 healthcare workers in maternity and pediatric units to improve breastfeeding practices, supporting the revitalization of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI). Efforts included adapting guidelines, coaching, and integrating breastfeeding standards into hospital accreditation processes. An additional 300 healthcare workers were trained in maternal nutrition, breastfeeding, and complementary feeding counseling, reaching 278,203 pregnant women and caregivers with essential nutrition messages.
 
UNICEF’s supply of micronutrient supplementation and anthropometric equipment enabled 2,027 pregnant women to receive iron and folic acid supplements, and 1,117,644 children received vitamin A capsules. The Government amended the existing decree to exclude the import of therapeutic milk and ready-to-use therapeutic food from a decree banning the import of children’s food products containing palm oil, allowing access to these life-saving nutrition commodities for up to 42,000 children with severe wasting.
 
UNICEF supported the costing of the Multisectoral Action Plan on Nutrition, showing that the government needs to increase investments in nutrition programmes to 15.2 billion Tajik somoni (TJS), between 2024 -2030 to achieve national nutrition priorities. UNICEF will continue advocacy and provide technical assistance to realize programme-based budgeting, including a nutrition budget line in the national budget.
 
Improving Early Childhood Development
UNICEF, in collaboration with the World Bank and the Government of Tajikistan, co-organized an ECD session at the International Human Capital Forum in May 2024, in Dushanbe. Here, UNICEF advocated for the inclusion of ECD in the national agenda and advocated for increased investments in ECD to support critical lifelong learning and enhanced development outcomes for children. 
 
Around 6,500 children with developmental delays and disabilities received Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) services in 2024. UNICEF provided technical support to establish a Technical Reference Working Group to conduct a situational analysis of existing local ECI services. UNICEF revitalized the Early Start Network, a network of 40 CSOs working in ECD and with children with developmental delays/disabilities and their families.
 
UNICEF supported training and supervision for 1,700 family doctors and nurses to improve home visiting practices in 41 districts, reaching approximately 900,000 children under five, with improved facility-based counseling and home visiting services.
 
Improving Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH)
WASH services in Tajikistan advanced significantly with UNICEF support. National policies were developed and endorsed, including the 2040 Water Sector Strategy, and the 2030 WASH in Health Care Facilities (WinHCFs) Investment Case. Access to WASH facilities expanded, benefiting 50,232 people across 12 social institutions and over 1 million people with hygiene promotion services. Menstrual Health Hygiene (MHH) needs of 3,631 women and girls were addressed during emergency response, and 73,026 women and girls were covered through WASH interventions.
 
UNICEF advocated for increased WASH sector financing, highlighting the need for US$ 213 million annually to reach SDG 6.1 and 6.2 by 2030. Investment cases were developed for other WASH priorities, including US$ 360 million for WinHCFs, US$ 405.1 million for WASH in Schools, and US$ 72.7 million for hand hygiene initiatives by 2030.
 
Youth engagement was prioritized through the Youth 4 Water and Climate (Y4WC) initiative launched at the 3rd Dushanbe Water Action Decade Conference in June 2024, empowering young people to participate in decision-making processes. UNICEF organized a Pre-COP event for the Y4WC network, enabling youth to play an active role in climate and WASH policy dialogue. The youth network has now developed the Youth 4 Water and Climate Action Plan, which lays out tangible results for policy makers, youth, civil society, academia and development partners to achieve, and which has been submitted to the government for endorsement.
 
Learning and Skills
Advancing Safe and Climate-Adaptive Learning Environments
UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Education and Science (MoES) in developing the Medium-Term Action Plan (MTAP) 2024-2026, integrating disaster risk reduction (DRR), WASH, and inclusive learning environments. which defines activities to be achieved over the next three years, links to reform priorities outlined in the NSED, and states the implementation period, funding sources, and responsible agencies. UNICEF and partners ensured the MTAP promotes inclusivity and gender sensitivities across all levels and areas of education, including digitalization, curriculum reform, DRR, WASH, TLM development and teacher professional development. UNICEF supported the development of a national strategic action plan for climate-adaptive WASH in schools, with approval expected in 2025 by the MoES. DRR and climate change adaptation activities expanded to 16 schools, benefiting 5,372 students, 565 teachers, 7,500 community members, and 350 volunteers.
 
Enhancing Inclusive Education and Pre-primary Development
A Joint Sector Review (JSR) was conducted, presenting an Action Plan for a phased introduction of one-year pre-primary education starting in 2025. UNICEF contributed to improving access to inclusive pre-primary education through policy advocacy and targeted interventions. A landscape analysis revealed that only 49.8 per cent of girls aged 3-6 attend UNICEF-supported Early Childhood Education (ECE) centers. A Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) analysis identified gaps and proposed strategies for gender-responsive interventions.
 
Boosting Digital Education and EMIS Modernization
UNICEF facilitated partnerships through the UNICEF-International Telecommunication Union (ITU) GIGA Initiative, resulting in the establishment of an inter-ministerial Task Force to drive school connectivity. UNICEF supported the MoES in shaping the vision for modernizing the Education Management Information System (EMIS). As a result, a three-year EMIS Implementation Plan was developed, complemented by revisions of key performance indicators and enhanced access to education data.
 
As part of the sustainability agenda, UNICEF equipped the Republican Centre for Information Technology and Communication (RCITC) with a solar panel system and other ICT equipment to support digital platforms for education. UNICEF developed a gender-sensitive career guidance programme, endorsed by the MoES, and trained over 20 ICT specialists in digital content creation.
 
Promoting Learning-to-Earning Pathway and Employability Skills
UNICEF advanced the Learning-to-Earning pathway to address education gaps and enhance adolescent employability. The full handover of 67 Adolescent Innovation Labs to the Centre for Additional Education (CAE) marked a significant step toward national ownership and sustainability. UNICEF promoted the Impact Source model, linking graduates with local and remote employers through a National Digital Portal and five operational Impact Source Hubs. UNICEF advanced competency-based education reforms, including the Adolescent Competency Framework (ACF) for 21st-century skills. Evidence-based advocacy led to the MoES’ decision to scale up revised Teaching and Learning Materials (TLMs) for Math and Tajik nationwide.
 
Advocating Youth Participation and Civic Engagement
UNICEF ensured young people were actively engaged in shaping its initiatives, including participation in key national and international events. UNICEF supported the establishment of the National Youth for Water and Climate Network, giving young people a voice in environmental decision-making. Eco Clubs were launched in 22 schools, engaging 5,500 students. The Adolescent Participation Model, engaging 15,470 adolescents (8,750 female), expanded to 15 districts, integrating youth-raised priorities into District Development Plans.
 
Child Protection 
Strengthening Legal Framework for Child Protection
UNICEF advanced legislative reforms to bolster child protection. Tajikistan became the 67th country to prohibit all forms of corporal punishment. Another significant reform was the removal of fees and penalties for late birth registration, empowering children to lodge complaints independently.
 
National Commitment to Child Protection System Reform
The Government of Tajikistan has demonstrated its commitment to child protection through the announcement of a comprehensive National Programme for Child Protection System Reform to strengthen child protection systems nationwide. This initiative was formally introduced by the Deputy Prime Minister during the National Conference on Preventing Violence Against Children, and first Global Ministerial Conference on ending violence against children, held in Bogota, Colombia in November 2024, as well at the 2nd Child Rights Commissions Forum held in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, further reaffirming the government’s dedication to safeguarding children.
 
Advancing School Safety and Violence Prevention
In 2024, the Ministry of Education and Science (MoES) expanded the school-based Violence Against Children (VAC) reporting mechanism by 9 per cent, increasing coverage from 347 schools in 2023 to 377 in 2024. UNICEF enhanced the capacity of 600 student council members to identify, report, and refer cases of violence, empowering students to create safer schools.
 
Capacity-building interventions reached over 600 professionals from justice and social sectors, focusing on child protection, case management, family-based care, social work, justice for children, prevention of violence against children, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). These training courses were institutionalized, resulting in the adoption of training programmes by training institutions within the justice and social protection systems. Additionally, 1,454 individuals, including children, parents, caregivers, and teachers, enhanced their knowledge of their rights, marking progress in social and behavioural change.
 
Strengthening Social Service Delivery and Case Management
UNICEF ensured systematic and standardized social work practices through revised case management instruments and standard operating procedures (SOPs) for child protection, approved by MoHSPP. A mapping of the social service workforce for child protection was submitted to the Government for review, with recommendations aimed at strengthening the social service workforce.
 
UNICEF provided social reintegration services to children and mothers repatriated from conflict zones. Currently, 333 children, 91 mothers, and 31 extended family members receive reintegration support through case management services. By providing targeted case management services, UNICEF facilitated the successful social reintegration of these vulnerable people populations. In 2024, 45 women repatriated in 2023 successfully gained employment, and 355 children participated in educational programmes to catch up with their schooling.
 
 Deinstitutionalization and Policy Support for Reform
UNICEF conducted a multi-country evaluation on deinstitutionalization, which has revealed revealing a 35 per cent reduction in children in residential care from 10,146 in 2009 to 6,409 in 2024. A 3 per cent reduction in children in residential care was achieved decreasing from 6,616 to 6,409, with the rate of 151 children per 100,000 child population in institutions in the country in 2024. Recommendations included prioritizing deinstitutionalization within overall childcare reforms, strengthening the social service workforce, and expanding social change interventions. This led to a broader reform agenda by the National Commission on Child Rights, incorporating deinstitutionalization and alternative family-based care. UNICEF supported the capacity building of 81 staff members across four Family and Child Support Centres, assisting children at risk of being placed in residential care.
 
Inter-Agency Cooperation for Preventing Child Offenses
In collaboration with the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MIA), UNICEF developed SOPs for inter-agency cooperation in preventing child offenses and supporting children in conflict with the law. These SOPs are under review by MIA and aim to establish a coordinated approach to preventing child offenses at the local level.
 
UNICEF supported the Academy of Public Administration under the President of Tajikistan (APA) in advancing child rights in a gender-responsive manner among public servants. Advocacy, capacity-building events, and training modules focused on alternative care, inclusion, and violence prevention, equipping public servants to better address child rights.
 
Tackling Child Labour and Supporting Disability Inclusion
UNICEF contributed to the elimination of child labour by supporting the development of the National Programme on the Elimination of the Worst Forms of Child Labour 2024–2028, approved by the government. A coordination mechanism was established to oversee its implementation.
 
UNICEF supported MoHSPP in analyzing the roadmap for the ratification of the U.N Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). Advocacy efforts led to agreed actions by the government toward ratification. Discussions focused on transitioning from the biopsychosocial model to the International Classification for Functioning (ICF), with the Ministry committing to piloting this model in targeted districts.
 
Governance and Inclusion
Advancing Social Protection and Child Rights Monitoring in Tajikistan
In 2024, UNICEF strengthened Tajikistan’s Social Protection Strategy, public finance for children, and child rights monitoring. Through strategic partnerships, evidence-based advocacy, and technical assistance, UNICEF helped the government develop inclusive, child-sensitive, and shock-responsive measures.
 
Social Protection
Tajikistan’s social protection system became more inclusive, gender-transformative, and adaptive, strengthening resilience for vulnerable children and families. UNICEF supported the development and adoption of a three-year Action Plan (2024–2026), a shock-responsive social protection framework, and enhanced stakeholder coordination. A significant milestone was the development and launch of a simulation model in November 2024 to assess the potential of cash transfers in mitigating poverty impacts caused by natural and climate hazards. Built on data from national household surveys, the model provides evidence and insights for advocating cash transfers as an effective policy instrument. Tajikistan. It includes the cost of inaction, projecting potential increases in child poverty levels without cash support, and serves as a decision-making tool for policymakers, particularly for MoHSPP, CoES, CoEP and MoF. The simulation supports the design of appropriate cash transfer programmes, enabling evaluation of trade-offs and an estimation of required budget allocations for Adaptive and Shock-Responsive Social Protection (ASRSP). By offering critical insights, UNICEF support has informed the development of contingency actions within ASRSP, underscoring the impact of hazards on child poverty and guiding strategies to enhance resilience and reduce vulnerabilities.
 
The investment in ASRSP agenda facilitated greater coordination between the social protection and disaster risk management sectors, highlighting the essential role of social protection in advancing climate action through inclusive adaptation, mitigation, and responses to loss and damage. An analysis of pre-agreed financing options for ASRSP was carried out in alignment with Disaster Risk Financing tools. This analysis evaluated existing and potential pre-arranged financing mechanisms and provided the government and development partners with actionable recommendations to enhance preparedness for pre-financed contingency actions. The findings further aim to facilitate the establishment of mechanisms for rapidly scaling up cash assistance during climate-induced and other emergencies, ensuring timely and large-scale support for vulnerable children and their families.
 
Broader Contributions to Development
UNICEF convened the DCC Social Protection Working Group and co-led the Interagency Cash Working Group (ICWG), enhancing emergency preparedness and effective cash transfers.
