UNICEF launched a joint SDG project with UN Women, the Ministry of Economic Development and Trade, and the Ministry of Finance to strengthen child and gender-responsive budgeting in local planning.
 
Strengthening Public Finance for Children (PF4C)
UNICEF’s partnership with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) led to the publication of the 2024 Citizens’ Budget, promoting transparency. An orientation workshop introduced child-responsive budgeting to key government counterparts. UNICEF developed a methodological note for monetary child poverty measurement, endorsed by the Council for Poverty and Middle-Class Measurement.
 
UNICEF Tajikistan invested heavily in generating evidence on child poverty through a partnership with the World Bank (WB). This collaboration involved the "Listening to Tajikistan" initiative, a real-time data collection effort involving 4,000 households that included child-related questions and new questionnaires focused on nutrition and breastfeeding, education and early childhood development (ECD), and the impacts of heatwaves to address the critical data gaps on wellbeing of children. A comprehensive analysis of child poverty and the climate change risks and impacts were conducted that highlighted the need for urgent policy actions in social protection, agriculture, water and sanitation to reduce climate and poverty risks for families with children and the findings were regularly shared with stakeholders.  
 
Enhancing Child Rights Monitoring
UNICEF continued strengthening Child Rights Monitoring (CRM), guiding the implementation of 2017 CRC recommendations and developing a training module on CRM. Partnering with Tajstat, UNICEF worked to unify child data systems, laying the foundation for a digital child data platform. UNICEF supported CSO engagement in CRC reporting and initiated an e-SitAn to inform strategic priorities ahead of the 2025 CRC pre-session.
 
Programme Effectiveness
In 2024 UNICEF Tajikistan enhanced programme effectiveness by accelerating cross-/multi-sectoral programmes and advocacy (climate action, early childhood development, gender-responsive programming) and scaling up proven sectoral interventions (mother and child health, nutrition, education, WASH, child protection, social protection, adolescent skills development/employability). This strengthened UNICEF's position as a key partner in policy dialogue and reforms related to children.
 
In 2024, significant progress was made in emergency preparedness, disaster risk reduction, and climate resilience, benefiting 8,690 individuals, including 5,464 children, through emergency distributions of hygiene kits and water purification tablets.
 
To support gender norms and Social and Behavioural Change (SBC) strategies, UNICEF established partnerships with key committees including Committee on Religious Affairs, Committee on Women & Family Affairs, and the Strategic Research Center. This partnership aims to institutionalize behavioral evidence generation, SBC strategy development, and community engagement. UNICEF also established an SBC Community of Practice to share best practices and completed studies on gender barriers and health workers' attitudes towards immunization. These findings will inform SBC strategies for immunization, MNCH, parenting, and child protection. Demand promotion strategies were developed to address misinformation, increase vaccine uptake, and promote healthy diets and physical activity, guiding social and behavior change interventions and serving as advocacy tools for public finance allocation.
 
At the mid-term point, an extended programme review identified key shifts: concrete results for CEED (Climate, Environment, Energy, and Disaster Risk Reduction) across sectors, integration of WASH and Water Resource Management, robust gender-transformative interventions, and a U.N-wide strategy to address harmful gender norms.
 
UNICEF's communication, advocacy, and partnerships efforts reached over 916,904 people through 107 events and 7 campaigns, mobilizing close to US$ 9 million for programmes and leveraging public finance from international institutions. Governance and management systems effectively utilized 100 per cent of the programme funds (US$ 30.3 million) in 2024.
 
Operational Effectiveness
UNICEF Tajikistan enhanced accessibility at UN House, implementing over 40 per cent of recommended improvements and achieving Accessibility Level 2. It also became the first building in Tajikistan to receive the EDGE Green Building Certification, demonstrating significant energy, water, and carbon savings.
 
In 2024, UNICEF streamlined work processes and strengthened oversight to mitigate risks like fraud and financial loss. Key tools adopted included eTools, Procurement Case Manager, and Mobile Warehouse and Inventory Management Solution (mWIMS). Efforts to reinforce Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) for staff and partners continued. Security compliance improved, reaching 97.16 per cent global compliance and 100 per cent SRM Matrix implementation.
 
A cybersecurity assessment strengthened ICT infrastructure, ensuring data integrity. As a leader in the U.N Operations Management Team (OMT), UNICEF chaired key working groups on Administration, Finance, and HACT, advancing the U.N Efficiency Agenda.
 
The finance team processed over 1,540 cases, reducing invoice rejection rates and ensuring timely disbursements. UNICEF prepared 42 donor reports, disbursed US$ 4.03 million to implementing partners, and procured US$ 6.62 million in supplies, covering 97 per cent of children with vaccines. The full US$ 30.87 million budget was utilized across key programmatic areas, including health and WASH.
 
Financial assurance activities included 25 spot checks, 7 micro-assessments, and 1 audit. The integration of eTools into Fiori (eZHACT) improved efficiency, and all implementing partners were assessed for PSEA compliance.
 
On human resources, UNICEF recruited 7 staff, finalized 67 consultancy cases, and hired 9 young professionals, ensuring diversity. Two individuals with disabilities were also contracted. HR initiatives included developing "Golden Rules" for staff well-being and organizing two retreats on stress management.
 
Cost-saving efforts led to a 10 per cent rent reduction, saving US$ 35,585 annually. UNICEF also secured 442 square meters of additional office space at no cost, optimizing resources in alignment with the U.N Efficiency Agenda.

In 2024, UNICEF Tajikistan strengthened engagements with existing and new partners, including government, civil society and academic institutions, UN agencies, private sector, and other stakeholders in achieving the results for children.  Ongoing negotiations with International Financial Institutions (IFIs) aim to leverage financing for children's climate initiatives, education programmes including ECE, and strengthening social protection and child protection systems.

Government of Tajikistan
New partnerships were cultivated in 2024 around climate, which will be the basis of leveraging bigger investments and financing for children in 2025 onward. These include the partnership with the Committee on Environment Protection (COEP), the Hydro-metrology under the COEP, Center for Implementation of Investment Projects (CIIP) under the COEP, and the Green Climate Fund. Specifically, a milestone agreement was also reached between UNICEF and the national designated authority of the Green Climate Fund (CIIP) to initiate the concept note and proposal development of the GCF, which is a significant step in potentially securing a large climate finance that dedicated to strengthening climate resiliency and energy efficiency for educational facilities in Tajikistan. 

In 2024, in partnership with the Ministry of Health and Social Protection of the Population, UNICEF Tajikistan worked on strengthening health and WASH systems, improving services for children and women. Pregnant women benefited from improved referral systems, while many others with severe complications received specialized care. Children receive essential medicines and Vitamin A supplements, contributing to better overall health. Key achievements included establishing newborn health standards, developing a digital child health record, and supporting the adoption of the Water Sector Strategy. UNICEF also remains the key partner for the Ministry of Health and Social Protection of the Population (MoHSPP) and the Ministry of Education and Science (MoES) in developing Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) services for children with developmental delays and disabilities. A situational analysis is underway to lay the foundation for a national ECI programme.  

The partnership with MOES and COES was increasingly strengthened, particularly around the signing of the Ministerial Declaration on Comprehensive School Safety in Central Asia, committing to ensure safe, resilient schools. Overall, the partnership with MOES remains key in achieving education reforms, including but not limited to achieving curricula reform for Competency Based Education, safe learning environment including quality WASH services, digital education, 21st Century skills building, and climate education.  

Collaboration with the Academy of Public Administration integrated child protection into public servant education. UNICEF also engaged the Committee on Religious Affairs and religious leaders to challenge gender norms and stereotypes. Ongoing consultations with Parliamentarians and academic institutions continue to build a broad alliance of child rights advocates.

UN Collaboration 
In 2024 UNICEF continued to co-chairing the UNSDCF Outcome 1, “Inclusive Human Development”, leading 3 out of 5 sub-groups and advanced progress on priorities including WASH, social protection, education and health. As a leader in the Interagency Cash Working Group, UNICEF strengthened emergency cash transfer systems using innovative payment mechanisms. Additional funding mobilized through U.N. agencies and the international community supported environmental sustainability and emergency preparedness. 

UNICEF partnered with UNDP and UNHCR to improve civil and birth registration processes, contributing to revisions in the draft Law on State Registration of Civil Status Acts. In 2024, a Letter of Understanding (LoU) with UNHCR reinforced joint efforts to support refugees and stateless persons.

Under the leadership of UNRCO, UNICEF together with FAO, WFP and WHO has initiated the joint programme, which aims to enhance institutional capacities and promote innovative solutions to improve food systems for better nutritional outcomes, including for children and adolescents, in Tajikistan by creating greater demand for healthy and nutritious food through improved policies, financial leveraging, behavioural change, and adoption of better practices in locally sourced food production. 

UNICEF played a key role in the Rapid Emergency Assessment and Coordination Team (REACT), chairing the Education, WASH, Nutrition, and Child Protection subsectors. Collaboration with the Committee of Emergency Situations (CoES), U.N. agencies, NGOs, and development partners reinforced disaster risk reduction, early warning systems, and emergency response coordination. A joint U.N. workshop on the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) enhanced implementing partners' understanding of PSEA standards and policies.

Collaboration with Development Partners
In 2024, UNICEF Tajikistan cultivated partnerships with a wide range of stakeholders including the ADB, ISDB, WB, FCDO, EU, USA, USAID, Korea, KOICA, Japan, JICA, SDC, the UN SDG Fund, the Al Abdulla Family of UAE, and the GPE. New and exploratory discussions with new and emerging partners such as the AT Scale, Andrey Rublev Foundation, Dubai Cares, EBRD, EIB, EFSD, the Russian Federation, Qatar Foundation, LDS Church, and the Government of India were pursued.

In cooperation with the World Bank, UNICEF Tajikistan successfully elevated the investment case on early childhood development (ECD) in the Human Capital Forum organized in May, presenting robust evidence of the economic benefits and human capital accumulation based on investment in the early years. With strong recognition by the Government of Tajikistan as partner of choice on ECD, UNICEF was invited to participate in the National ECD Council and continues to provide technical capacity building of the Council members and line ministries on the multi-sectoral interventions needed for a comprehensive ECD.

Another strategic partnership with the World Bank positioned Tajikistan as a pilot country for social service workforce development. This collaboration also facilitated an assessment of the social protection system using the Interagency Core Diagnostics (CODI) tool and supported the development of a poverty measurement methodology.

As one of the conveners of the Development Coordination Council (DCC) Social Protection Working Group, UNICEF advanced child-sensitive, gender-transformative, and shock-responsive social protection measures. Efforts to improve data availability led to the integration of child-related modules into the DHS and advocacy for enhanced national administrative systems.

UNICEF Tajikistan successfully leveraged essential financial resources and initiated new partnerships with partners such as the Swiss Development Cooperation on the Justice for Children programme, with the Islamic Development Bank on the project on Improving the Quality and Efficiency of Education Services, and with UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) as part of a regional programme on Accelerating Education Attainment in Central Asia for Resilience (AEAR-CA), with the Red Crescent Society of Tajikistan on providing life-saving assistance to affected households, including children.

Private Sector Partnerships
UNICEF fostered public-private collaborations to develop social protection programmes for vulnerable populations. Of special mention is UNICEF Tajikistan’s first ever partnership agreement with a local private sector company – Tcell, one of the leading telecommunications companies in Tajikistan. Acknowledging UNICEF’s value-add in making positive impact on the lives of children and families in Tajikistan through programmes such as early childhood development (ECD) and adolescent skills development programme, Tcell signed an MoU with UNICEF. This partnership focuses on promoting positive parenting by pushing UNICEF and MOHSP-developed Bebbo application to all TCell users and on enhancing adolescent skills by supporting youth employment initiatives and Impact Sourcing Hubs – a remote job sourcing model.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges

Digital Connectivity & Education Reform: Poor internet connectivity continues to hinder digital education and digital skills development. UNICEF, together with ITU, is supporting the Government on the GIGA Initiative, aiming to address the connectivity issues so that all schools will be connected to internet. Competency-Based Education (CBE) reform faces challenges due to fragmented implementation, requiring a unified national roadmap.
Skills & Employment Gaps: The gap between the education and skills opportunity provided to children and the market demand remains. UNICEF continues to support the Government to align education with labor market needs through tailored courses and skill-building programmes, including Adolescent Innovation Labs (AILs), which require sustained funding.
Health Services Funding: The majority (97%) of the immunization budget is allocated to vaccine procurement, leaving essential health services underfunded. Stronger advocacy with the Ministry of Finance, MoHSPP, and Parliament is needed to secure sustainable funding.
Nutrition Policy Implementation: Institutionalizing initiatives like the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative remains slow due to a lack of government funding for nutrition programmes and essential commodities.
Changes in the aid policy of a key development partner and donor will likely have a profound impact on the development and humanitarian work in Tajikistan (across sectors and implementing partners), including some level of impact on UNICEF’s operation. 

Lessons Learned

Collective advocacy proved to be effective in overcoming policy decisions, such as revising the decree on Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF). Partnerships and collective action are crucial for advancing policy and legislative reforms. Driving legislative processes and securing commitments through conferences, public awareness campaigns, and high-level dialogues also proved to be effective. Finally, identifying and engaging key government players, who can champion the agenda is crucial. Investing in their capacity advances UNICEF initiatives and fosters ownership of reforms.
Overcoming vaccine hesitancy among zero-dose and under-vaccinated children requires culturally sensitive strategies, community engagement, and evidence-based advocacy.
Integrating climate considerations into sectoral policies, plans and programmes is critical given Tajikistan’s disaster profile. This approach will shape future strategies for reaching vulnerable children.
Systematizing adolescent involvement in decision-making requires a comprehensive approach by the central government. Shifting perceptions and institutionalizing mechanisms for sustainability are key steps.

Future Outlook 

Looking ahead, UNICEF Tajikistan will continue integrating climate and sustainability dimensions into planning, programming and implementation of key priorities under the CPD considering the challenges and risks created by the climate change for Tajikistan. This includes work on Child-Sensitive NDC 3.0 and finance action plan, Adaptive and Shock-responsive Social Protection (ASRSP), Comprehensive School Safety Framework (CSSF) 2022–2030, Climate resilient social services including WASH and Green Skills among others. 
 
UNICEF Tajikistan will analyse demographic trends and implications for ensuring necessary investments in core sector and services for children i.e. child protection, health, WASH, nutrition, immunization, parenting, education, skills, social protection etc.  to leverage the demographic potential of the country. This analysis will be part of the multi-country report planned for 2025 on ‘Generation 2050: Central Asia’ and will identify and provide policy recommendations to overcome key contextual challenges (such as climate change) that may dampen the impact of these investments. 
 
Given the changing context and constrained resources, UNICEF Tajikistan will continue its efforts to diversify and expand its funding to mobilize the necessary resources. This will include an emphasis on leveraging national resources for children, forming partnerships with IFIs, and engaging with non-traditional donors to operationalize key priorities under the CPD.

Türkiye continues to host over 2.9 million Syrians under temporary protection1, of whom 51.4% (1.5 million) are estimated to be in the 0-18 age group. Addressing the needs and vulnerabilities of this sizeable refugee population continued to be a priority in 2024. The recent political developments in Syria and the till now modest number of returnees to Syria, underscore the need to ensure the safety and services for Syrian and other refugees in Türkiye, while facilitating their voluntary, safe and dignified return.    

The impacts of the catastrophic earthquakes of 2023 which displaced around 3.3 million people, of which 2 million sought shelter in tents and containers2; still present significant challenges with regards to reconstructing lives and homes. The crisis highly impacted the most vulnerable children and people, including the refugees living in Southeastern Türkiye. Protracted displacement, overstretched social services and difficult socioeconomic conditions triggered by inflation have compounded the vulnerability of affected children and families, posing risks to their wellbeing. Adequate shelter, heightened risk of violence, abuse and exploitation, and limited access to water and sanitation facilities, especially hygiene items for women and girls, remain major issues in  informal temporary settlements. As of Feb 2024, there were around 675,000 individuals in formal container sites in 11 provinces3.  
 
Economic indicators reveal a mixed picture. Following global trends GDP growth slowed in 2024, with year-on-year increases of 5.3%, 2.4%, and 2.1% in the first three quarters, respectively, compared to 5.5% in 2022 and 5.1% in 20234. Unemployment rates saw improvements, with an overall rate of 8.8% in Q3 20245, down from 9.4% in 20236. Youth unemployment also decreased slightly to 17.4% in Q3 20247. However, a significant gender gap persists in unemployment rates, with women consistently facing higher unemployment than men. 

High inflation remains a significant challenge, reaching 47.09% annually as of November 20248. The consumer price increase was particularly steep in education (92.49%), housing (74.45%), and food (48.57%), impacting household purchasing power, especially for vulnerable groups. The Gini coefficient, measuring income inequality, rose to 0.413 in 20249, indicating increased inequality. Monetary poverty continues to impact children significantly. The child poverty rate, increased slightly to 31.9% in 2024 (30.9% for boys, 32.9% for girls), compared to 31.3% in 202310. In numerical terms, this translates to 7.039 million children experiencing poverty, up from 7.034 million11 in 2023. 

With its sizeable child population (22.21 million, or 26% of the total population)12; children in Türkiye continue to benefit from progress whilst also facing vulnerabilities and inequities. In education, pre-school enrollment (for 3-5 age group) increased to 51.89% (2023/24 school year)13 as did primary and lower secondary school enrollment. Yet, upper secondary school enrollment decreased, and 16.2% of 15–19-year-olds were neither in employment nor in education or training in 202314 - pointing to continued challenges in ensuring a learning to earning continuum.   

Türkiye has made progress in promoting alternative care for its children: the number of children in foster care rose to 9,806, compared to 9,011 in 2022—a rise of 8.8%15. By the end of 2023, 19,584 children were in adoption, up from 18,947 in 2022, marking a 3.4% increase. Yet, a total of 14,405 children were in residential care (2023), a slight increase from 14,141 (2022).  

Data from the UNICEF-initiated ‘Türkiye Child Survey 2022’ reveals that 10.6% of children had functional difficulties, and that a significant proportion of children face challenges related to bullying, and violent discipline16. In 2022, the percentage of children who indicated being exposed to any violent discipline method including psychological aggression or physical punishment was 54.1%17. The survey further indicates that bullying of children with functional difficulties is much higher than the rest.  
Officially registered marriages for the 16-17 age group have decreased significantly, and yet, significant gender disparities persist - 10,471 for girls and 706 for boys (2023)18. While the incidents of children being placed in security units dropped by 10.7% in 2023 (to 537,583, down from 601,754 in 2022)19- a large proportion (45.2%) of these incidents involved children as victims20. Furthermore, the number of children taken to court for alleged crimes increased from 76,463 (2022)21 to 78,173 (2023)22.  

All this points to the need for continued efforts to target vulnerable children and family and ensure they have the adequate and equitable access to services and support.

Together with partners, UNICEF Türkiye helped advance vulnerable children, women and families’ access to quality and equitable services and the realization of their rights. This was done through a combination of strengthening government systems to be able to reach the unreached with quality services; further improve the legislative and operational environment to facilitate coordinated, integrated service delivery; generate awareness and demand for services; and use disaggregated data and evidence to identify, target and reach the most vulnerable.  
To ensure every child survives and thrives, UNICEF advanced the Early Childhood Development (ECD) agenda by strengthening inter-ministerial collaboration and supporting targeted interventions. UNICEF played a key role in fostering partnerships between the Presidency of Strategy and Budget (PSB), Ministry of Health (MoH), Ministry of Family and Social Services (MoFSS), Ministry of National Education (MoNE) and the municipalities, including through the national, inter-ministerial ECD Task Force. While awaiting official endorsement, the national ECD Strategy is being implemented within the framework of the 12th National Development Plan (NDP) and through joint work plans with Ministries. The modeling of how to deliver integrated ECD services is underway with UNICEF support in Ankara, Mersin, Bursa, and Kahramanmaras provinces, with efforts to promote this in Gaziantep, Hatay, Istanbul, and Izmir through partnership with municipalities. 
UNICEF provided technical guidance to the development of standards on Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) services and regulations for ECD centers, and these are currently under government review. Four ECD centers have been established, with plans for seven more in 2025. Capacity building and supportive supervision for 1,062 professionals in developmental monitoring, early identification of delays/disabilities, and parental counseling was also supported. As part of ongoing efforts to address residual recovery needs arising from the disruption and devastation caused by the earthquakes, UNICEF-supported immunization activities reached 244,423 children and 58,423 parents, while also ensuring access to primary health services for 140,000 people. 
Given the criticality of parenting skills to ensuring children achieve their developmental potential in equitable and inclusive care environments; UNICEF supported the development of a parenting package that includes enhanced content for a skilled workforce (so that they in turn are better able to support parents), and the introduction of the BebboApp, localized as ‘Merhaba Bebek’, a pioneering evidence-based parenting app for parents of children aged 0-6. Additionally, through a social behaviour change approach, a disability-inclusive parenting programme addresses stigma and discrimination against families with children with disabilities (CWDs) to foster a more inclusive family and community environment. This year, it raised awareness, educated parents, and fostered community support, leading to a notable increase (from 15% to 35% in five provinces) in parents advocating for shared play spaces for CWDs. Parents are now actively promoting social inclusion for CWDs, challenging discriminatory social norms, and fostering a more inclusive and supportive community environment. A gender-transformative fathers’ programme in Gaziantep, Adiyaman, Kahramanmaras, Mardin, and Hatay promoted active caregiving roles for men, resulting in a 15% increase in male participation in childcare. This shift challenges traditional gender roles, promotes shared responsibility, reduces the burden on women, and fosters a more equitable and inclusive family environment. 
To improve the quality of Early Childhood Education (ECE), UNICEF supported MoNE revise the preschool curriculum, which was approved and implemented nationwide, with the help of 4,972 trained education personnel. More than 62,355 young children enjoyed improved early learning services in non-formal settings with municipality and NGO partners, and formal settings with MoNE. 
UNICEF also supported improvements to Türkiye's education system, benefiting 10.5 million students, including 682,385 Syrian refugees. This included enhancing assessment skills for 14,851 teachers, impacting 292,020 students in grades 1-4, and ensuring access to formal or non-formal education, including early learning, for 419,791 children. 
In the post-earthquake recovery phase, UNICEF helped address the academic and psychosocial needs of children in affected areas by strengthening the capacities of 995 teachers on learning recovery which benefitted 172,338 children, including 20,284 Syrian refugees. Additionally, 41,942 school counselors were trained in psychosocial support interventions, reaching approximately 1.5 million students, including 384,209 refugee children. The construction of three prefabricated schools and four earthquake-resilient schools provided safe learning environments for 3,043 students (61% refugees); while school cash grants facilitated the rehabilitation of 80 earthquake-damaged schools, benefiting an estimated 30,303 students (45% girls). 
UNICEF's expanded Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) response in earthquake-affected provinces provided safe water, improved sanitation, and hygiene supplies to 2,850,497 beneficiaries. Support included repair and rehabilitation of water and sanitation systems, procurement of chlorine and chemicals, and water quality testing equipment to restore interrupted services, and providing drinking water and water for basic needs for inhabitants of temporary settlements (formal, informal, and container cities). UNICEF's leadership in WASH sector coordination helped ensure coordinated efforts by different partners.   
To ensure children are protected from violence, UNICEF technically supported MoFSS strengthening its alternative care system so that all children without parental care are provided with family-based care. As a result, UNICEF assisted 229 evacuated Ukrainian children (92 girls, 137 boys) in Türkiye with child protection services; and 48 unaccompanied and separated children (21 girls, 27 boys) were supported through alternative care services.  In parallel, UNICEF supported the national care reform by expanding family-based care options so that more children benefitted from foster care services. In particular, 2,000 children aged 0–6 from residential care were prioritised into foster care; detailed assessments of 47 children, across 30 provinces led to the urgent placement of 14 children with foster families in Adana and Mersin; and a new foster care model for temporary and short-term placements was introduced, with 11 prospective families identified as temporary foster carers.   
UNICEF successfully collaborated with CSOs, local authorities, and Municipalities, to enhance community-based Child Protection (CP) and Gender-based Violence (GBV) prevention and response services.  3,632,728 women, girls and boys were reached through GBV risk mitigation interventions and information. Capacities of service providers were enhanced to deliver quality community-based CP and GBV services reaching 178,592 individuals (99,484 female, 78,811 male, 297 non-binary), including 131,407 children and adolescents (67,590 girls, 63,805 boys, 12 non-binary). Of these, 83,937 at risk children (42,328 girls, 41,593 boys, 16 non-binary) were assessed for protection needs, 22,043 children (10,396 girls, 11,641 boys, 6 non-binary) referred to specialized services; 23,798 children (12,188 girls, 11,610 boys) received structured Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), and 57,651 caregivers (42,671 female, 14,980 male) benefited from a gender-transformative parenting programme under the VAGBaW agenda to promote violence prevention through gender-transformative parenting programs that has been implemented with municipalities and NGOs as part of the system strengthening efforts. Notably, 68% of these children and adolescents who benefited from structured MHPSS activities, reported enhanced self-confidence, stress management and future aspiration.    
Working with government ministries, 31 staff at Child Monitoring Centers and multidisciplinary facilities were trained to improve care and protection services for 57,000 child survivors of violence. In partnership with the Union of Turkish Bar Associations, UNICEF expanded the Legal Empowerment, Aid, and Protection (LEAP) programme that empowers children and caregivers while strengthening the child justice sector, including establishing Child Rights Legal Centers within the Bar Association. This provided free legal aid to 865 children, including refugee children, and on-site legal counselling to 1,260 individuals affected by the earthquake.  
UNICEF also supported improvements to Türkiye's national social protection systems. By reviewing gaps in poverty mitigation, UNICEF helped improve targeting mechanisms, leading to more inclusive enrollment and retention of vulnerable families in social protection programmes. Additionally, performance monitoring tools were implemented to assess local service delivery, enhancing the public capacity to serve disadvantaged children, children with disabilities, refugees, and earthquake-affected populations. 
UNICEF promoted learning, skills development and participation of vulnerable and at-risk children, adolescents and youth, particularly refugees and those with disabilities, in partnership with MoNE, Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS), and civil society organizations. Efforts focused on reintegrating vulnerable refugee children into the formal education system, while also facilitating their access to learning and skills in non-formal settings.  
Together with CSO partners, 85,808 out-of-school refugee children (47% girls) were screened and identified; and personalized counseling led to 62,601 of these children (48% girls) being referred to age-appropriate educational opportunities, resulting in the enrollment of 42,424 children (49% girls). To address dropout rates, UNICEF together with MoNE, municipalities, and CSO partners provided access to and retention in formal education for 65,482 vulnerable children and adolescents (55% female, 68% refugees) across 18 provinces. Additionally, 6,226 children and adolescents received academic and homework support, catch-up assistance, and Turkish language skills development in non-formal education settings. 
UNICEF supported the establishment of a robust monitoring framework (the ‘Inter-institutional Schooling Programme’), implemented in collaboration with MoNE and the Ministry of Family and Social Services (MoFSS). This will improve school retention rates by identifying and supporting children who are at risk of dropping out. As many of the reasons for drop out or non-attendance are non-educational, effective inter-ministerial coordination is key to addressing these issues. 
This year, education and learning for children with disabilities had a strong focus. To enhance equitable access to education for students with disabilities in mainstream schools, UNICEF and MoNE developed a comprehensive teacher resource pack. Containing 11 guidebooks on differentiated teaching, inclusive classroom practices, and strategies for social acceptance, this resource, benefitted over 72,788 upper-secondary students (48% girls). The "Secondary Education Parent Guide" provides guidance to the parents of 4.5 million upper-secondary students, addressing adolescents' physiological and academic needs and promoting their overall well-being. To improve employment prospects for students with special needs, 300 teachers had their capacities built on inclusive education. Furthermore, the finalization of six vocational qualifications, benefited over 14,000 students with special needs (38% girls) by enhancing their employment preparedness and workplace-based learning opportunities. 
UNICEF, in partnership with ministries, municipalities, universities, and NGOs, reached over 395,715 adolescents and youth (206,967 female) through adolescent participation and empowerment programmes. Young people engaged in skills building and empowerment activities, including in Vision Clubs and as Climate Volunteers, at MoYS youth centers. Building on the successful "Mahalle Support Mechanism" in 25 provinces, Mahalle (community) youth volunteers conducted outreach, reaching 42,000 people who were helped to identify challenges and connected with government and NGO services. Building on this success, MoYS scaled up this activity in 49 provinces. UNICEF and its partners also supported youth empowerment and participation in earthquake-affected provinces to build the resilience of young people. Over 10,000 adolescents and youth were reached through skills building, empowerment, and civic engagement activities in 14 "Genc Alan" (Youth Hub) and youth centers. 
UNICEF collaborated with the private sector (Confederation of Tradesmen and Craftsmen- TESK) to conduct over 5,000 workplace visits across 11 provinces, identifying 5,500 children (700 girls and 1,000 refugees) at risk of child labour and referring them to public services. UNICEF supported 500 adolescents in acquiring digital and occupational skills, and 520 apprentices with psychosocial support. 
The National Child Forum and Provincial Child Rights Committees reached 545,293 young people through peer-to-peer training, events, campaigns, and community initiatives. UNICEF and the Ministry of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change (MoEUCC) successfully engaged youth in climate policy discussions through the Youth Climate Envoys platform, comprised of youth representatives from each of Türkiye’s 208 universities. The Youth Climate Envoys are recognized in Türkiye’s Long-term Climate Strategy and Updated Nationally Determined Contribution as a milestone of inclusive climate policy development. UNICEF also engaged 117,218 people in reflective discourse through community platforms, promoting positive behaviors and the abandonment of harmful social norms related to child rights, violence prevention, child protection, and gender-based violence response services. 
To give children an equitable chance in life and safeguard them against multi-dimensional poverty, UNICEF invested efforts in building the capacities of civil society organisations, strengthening partnerships with key institutions, and promoting a robust data and evidence agenda. A key achievement in 2024 was conducting a capacity analysis of CSOs across Türkiye, followed by targeted capacity building on child rights and protection, including independent child rights monitoring. Through consultations, workshops, and training programmes, UNICEF bolstered the capacity of five CSOs and networks, which in turn contributed to the Universal Periodic Review mechanism on child rights. 
Collaboration with the Ombudsperson Institution (OI) and the Human Rights and Equality Institution (HREI) further strengthened child rights mechanisms. UNICEF supported OI's outreach, raising awareness on child rights and redress mechanisms; and its technical support to HREI resulted in the launch of a child-focused website and revamped complaint handling procedures. The revision of OI's Child Rights Strategy document, expected to be endorsed in early 2025, further solidifies this commitment. 
UNICEF continued to advance the child-focused data and evidence agenda. In an effort to initiate CPD 2026-203 development process, the Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents (Sitan) was conducted to provide a comprehensive assessment of child rights progress, challenges, and opportunities in Türkiye. Developed with technical support from various ministries, including TurkStat, the SitAn serves as a vital evidence-based advocacy tool and vital analysis for CPD development process. Consultations with children and adolescents were also organized both at national and sub-national level to discuss issues which impacted their wellbeing. The outcomes fed into the Sitan study, and the children presented their views to the Child Intersectoral Board (CIB) members in June this year. UNICEF had organized this yearly meeting during which outcome of Sitan was shared, together broad CPD 2026-2030 strategic programme components which were approved by the members with some feedback. The CPD development process was also supported with exercises such evidence synthesis, causality analysis, Gender Programme Review and theory of change which helped outline key programmatic priorities based on UNICEF’s comparative advantage and emerging contextual issues. As part of the wider UN family – UNICEF played a lead role in the development of the UNSDCF, leading various working groups and extensively supporting the results structure development, resulting in the endorsement of this by the Government. 
In a landmark achievement, Türkiye became one of the few pilot countries to launch the International Classification of Violence Against Children (ICVAC), a standardized framework for identifying and classifying violence cases. Supported by UNICEF, TurkStat and the MoFSS – this will enhance both the collection, quality and use of data on violence against children.  
UNICEF’s collaboration with MoFSS on the "Further Analysis of Türkiye Child Survey" report, has enriched the country’s evidence base by providing in-depth insights into child rights and well-being, and barriers therein. The report's findings and policy recommendations will inform policy decisions.  
UNICEF's advocacy for improved data systems led to TurkStat's role in conducting a "Data Landscape Analysis in Türkiye." This ongoing analysis will map existing child-related data, identify gaps, and recommend improvements to the data ecosystem, ultimately strengthening evidence-based policies and programmes for children. 
UNICEF's media presence surged this year, with 62,200 mentions and 827 million impressions nationally, a 70% increase from last year. Video production nearly doubled, and press materials amplified child rights visibility. All of these results were made possible by strong financial management to ensure maximum efficiency, strengthened monitoring and evaluation to learn from what worked and what did not, and using this learning to inform current programme strategies, as well UNICEF’s next 2026-20230 country programme of cooperation and the United Nations Sustainable Development Framework (UNSDCF).   
Strengthening capacities in financial management helped enhance funds stewardship and accountabilities, including through Harmonised Approach to Cash Transfer trainings for both UNICEF staff and partners.  The Monitoring and Knowledge Management Working Group helped facilitate stronger monitoring mechanisms thereby strengthening programme effectiveness. The roll out of Accountability to Affected People (AAP) prioritised the voices of vulnerable children and women. Safeguarding, Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) and AAP processes were institutionalized to collect beneficiary feedback, inform programme design, support referral and guide course corrections.  
Six evaluations were initiated and four completed, including a Country Programme Evaluation that has informed the 2026-2030 Country Programme development; and the L3 Earthquake Response evaluation that confirmed UNICEF's prompt and relevant actions. These, together with an internal audit, have been seminal in informing and improving UNICEF’s programme and operational strategies.

Partnerships are core to UNICEF being able to deliver results for children. UNICEF used its convening role to expand and strengthen partnerships to support children and families. Key partnerships with government (PSB, MoNE, MoFSS, MoYSD, MoH, MoEUCC, Ministry of Labour, Ministry of Justice, Justice Academy, Ombudsman, Union of Municipalities, various municipalities, PMM, water management entities, Union of Bar Associations, TESK, TURKSTAT) made improved access and quality of services for the most vulnerable a reality; enabled by a strengthened legislative and regulatory framework.  Some illustrative examples are outlined below.  
To strengthen local governance, UNICEF continued its efforts on integrating child-related priorities into municipalities’ five-year strategic plans and Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) action plans. Capacities of nearly 200 staff from 34 municipalities were strengthened on child-focused strategy development. UNICEF also leveraged its partnership with the Union of Municipalities, to create and track municipality child-focused budgets.  
Promoting the ECD agenda was made possible through collaboration between MoH, MoFSS, MoNE and PSB in terms of the development of the ECD strategy, standards of care for children aged 0-3 and piloting of ECD services in select locations. To strengthen this coalition by bringing in CSOs, UNICEF partnered with the national ECD Platform, a coalition of 22 CSOs and an inaugural ECD Symposium was held to highlight the significance of the first 1,000 days and the role of CSOs in empowering parents. 
UNICEF worked with MoNE to address the educational needs of vulnerable children and adolescents. Efforts included tackling dropout rates among out-of-school children and ensuring quality education for those in open schools, promoting skills development and inclusive education for children with disabilities, and expansion of ECE services.  
UNICEF supported MoFSS renewing its 2025–2027 NGO Vision Paper, establishing the Social Partners Cooperation Board which promotes collaboration between the Ministry and CSOs, universities, international organizations, and the private sector. UNICEF also facilitated strategic collaborations between NGOs, MoFSS, the Presidency of Migration Management (PMM), the Ministry of Youth and Sports, and municipalities to improve child protection services for refugees and host communities. Playing its convening role, UNICEF expanded its partnership with MoFSS to include the Inter-Institutional Schooling Programme, identifyin/supporting at-risk students, especially those at risk of dropping out, fostering MoFSS-MoNE linkages.  Partnership with PMM continues to be critical to support child-sensitive migration management, social cohesion, and community engagement. Partnership with the Ministry of Justice, Union of Turkish Bar Associations (UTBA), and the Justice Academy of Turkey continued to be critical to advance the ‘justice for children’ agenda. 
Through UNICEF’s partnerships with MoYS, MoFSS, MoEUCC, municipalities, universities and NGOs; adolescents and youth were reached with skills development, participation and empowerment initiatives; and engaged on key climate policy discussions. As part of the UN system, UNICEF also leveraged its partnerships with government, CSOs, municipalities, and UN agencies to advance gender equality through the joint UN Youth for Gender initiative to bring youth perspectives in policy level discussions and gender advocacy.   
UNICEF plays key role within the Supply Division’s localization agenda. In 2024 UNICEF hosted a Joint Forum for Pharmaceutical Manufacturers, to explore opportunities to source pharmaceuticals from Türkiye to reach children globally and the collaboration possibilities.  This forum contributes to localization agenda to increase availability, reduce lead times, ensure quicker access to pharmaceutical supplies and expand network of pharmaceutical suppliers. To make this sustainable UNICEF works with the MoH, Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency, and vendors. 
Partnerships with PSB, TurkStat, and the MoFSS were key to advancing evidence generation and data TurkStat and MoFSS contributed to child-focused data initiatives, including analyses of the Türkiye Child Survey and the adaptation of the ICVAC. The academia played an important role in providing technical expertise for evidence generation, as evidenced by the partnership with Koç University that helped strengthen evaluation capacities within key ministries. Joint efforts with PSB enhanced coordination among public partners, fostering a coherent approach to evidence generation, especially in relation to National Evaluation Capacity Development.  
Under PSB-UNICEF partnership, a “child tag” has been incorporated into government’s investment budget monitoring system, allowing to analyze child-related investments in the national budget and developing national strategies accordingly.  
In the past year, UNICEF has reinforced partnerships with key institutions to advance child rights and enhance monitoring efforts, which continued this year. Collaborations with the OI and the HREI focused on implementing child-friendly procedures and raising awareness of child rights. Notably, UNICEF provided technical support for the development of the OI’s new Child Rights Strategy and facilitated the launch of HREI's child-focused website, enabling children to submit complaints. 
2024 has been a transition year from EQ response/humanitarian programmes to regular recovery and development programmes in terms of partnerships with CSOs as implementing partners. The office accomplished results through efficient partnerships with 49 active IPs, consisting of 13 CSOs and 36 government partners. These partnerships were key to delivering services in container cities and camps - as well as community outreach and referral to government services.  
UNICEF’s Business Advisory Board (BAB) continued to serve as an effective engagement platform and mobilised support to advance the agenda for children and young people. By the end of the year, the private sector had contributed close to US$11.8 million in financial and non-financial resources to UNICEF. 
UNICEF continued to nurture existing and forge new relationships to expand and diversify donor base.  In 2024, approximately US$ 132 million was mobilised in total from public and private donors. The public sector donors accounted for 88% of funds, with the rest being mobilized through a combination of other sources including the private sector, UNICEF’s core resources and UNICEF thematic funds. By the end of 2024, the total amount raised against the earthquake response against the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) reached US$ 14.1 million with an additional US$ 53.4 million that was carried forward from 2023 funds, leaving the funding gap at 42%. For the Syrian Refugee HAC, the overall funding gap stood at 54% of the required US$ 85.8 million.  
UNICEF continued exploring new partnerships to leverage resources for children through discussion with various partners including IFIs.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Social norms and gender stereotypes continued to marginalize adolescent girls, children with disabilities and burden women with sole caregiving responsibilities. Addressing these challenges requires scalable, gender-responsive strategies, including engaging fathers in caregiving and community involvement to reduce stigma. In response, UNICEF rolled out the gender transformative parenting programme using a social behaviour change approach, which includes strengthened engagement with men, boys (fathers). This will also be a key focus in UNICEF's Country Programme for 2026-2030, emphasizing ongoing efforts to drive evidence-based, gender-transformative behaviour change and challenge social norms. Additionally, UNICEF’s efforts to engage fathers in ECE through role modeling, home visits, and educational sessions were constrained by the fact that community support for inclusive early education declined from 69% to 61% across five provinces (Gaziantep, Adiyaman, Kahramanmaras, Mardin, and Hatay). This decrease signifies ongoing resistance to changing deeply ingrained social norms around fathers’ involvement in ECE and parenting.  Similarly, overcoming cultural barriers limiting adolescent girls' participation in safe spaces and empowerment programmes remains a challenge. To address this, community engagement, culturally sensitive awareness campaigns, and collaboration with ministries, municipalities, and NGOs will continue to be key areas of focus and investment for UNICEF. 
In the education sector, vulnerable children and adolescents, including refugees, continue to face educational barriers due to economic hardship, and discrimination. While rapid school reconstruction post-earthquake, agile coordination and psychosocial support for the affected population addressed some challenges, teacher development and supportive networks proved essential for fostering resilient learning environments. The transition to a new K12 curriculum presented both opportunities and implementation challenges, including teacher capacity, skills focused learning and the inclusion of children with disabilities. Key lessons learned highlighted the importance of investing in a holistic system strengthening approach for more sustained results. Decreasing funding further necessitates stronger partnerships with government, private sector, and other actors to enhance quality inclusive education services.  
UNICEF's LEAP Programme proved to be critical in addressing the increased need for legal services in the South-East region after the earthquakes, focusing on vulnerable populations. The programme faced several challenges in ensuring that legal services were timely and accessible to those affected by the earthquake. In response to these challenges and lessons learned, several key improvements were made to enhance programme effectiveness. Firstly, the complexity of the application process was addressed by simplifying the procedure, making it more accessible to those in need. Further streamlining is expected with the upcoming launch of the TBBApp. Outreach efforts were also strengthened to ensure that hard of reach populations could access legal services. Information sessions were conducted, and coordination with local Bar Associations was intensified to reach those in remote areas. In addition, the mobile unit "YASA-LAW" was established to provide on-site legal aid, distributed materials, engaged local actors, and utilized mosque announcements to raise awareness, overcoming logistical barriers to service delivery. Supplementary training sessions were added, informed by rapid assessments, which identified capacity gaps amongst local lawyers. These sessions covered topics such as expropriation, property law, PSEA, and GBV, ensuring that legal practitioners were better equipped to address the complex issues faced by affected populations. Looking ahead, future priorities for the LEAP program include faster case processing, expanded outreach to remote areas, training non-legal staff for referrals and support, and enhancing ownership and sustainability by UTBA. By addressing these challenges and integrating lessons learned, the LEAP Programme has made significant strides in providing critical legal services to earthquake-affected populations, with a focus on sustainability and continuous improvement. 
As part of UNICEF’s convening role to bring government and civil society partners together in addressing child rights; building the capacities of CSOs on has been an area of focus for UNICEF, a CSO mapping study completed in 2024 helped shed light on the kinds of barriers CSOs face; for example - financial sustainability challenges, including limited funding, fundraising capacity, staff turnovers, and difficulties in engaging with government institutions. This study will inform efforts to specifically address these capacity gaps in CSOs going forward. The study also highlighted the need for stronger dialogue and collaboration between CSOs and national human rights institutions. To bridge this gap, UNICEF organized workshops and training programmes for CSOs, fostering engagement with the OI and facilitating valuable exchanges on child rights violations and complaint procedures. This led to increased complaints to the OI and more recommendations issued. UNICEF plans to replicate this approach with the HREI and strengthen its partnership with the OI to improve child rights monitoring and advocacy. 
Bringing diverse CSOs together for consultation and cooperation, particularly with experienced CSOs, proved beneficial, enhancing their knowledge and international practice experience. Involvement in alternative report submissions and engagement with treaty bodies, including collaboration with the Human Rights Joint Platform on training and mentoring for Türkiye’s Universal Periodic Review cycle, served as a model for future initiatives. 
Prioritizing a "people first" approach, UNICEF institutionalized AAP processes to gather beneficiary feedback and inform programme design. AAP integration was enhanced through its inclusion as an indicator across UNICEF’s partnerships and capacity-building initiatives.  UNICEF’s AAP intervention continues to enhance safe, inclusive, child-friendly, and effective community feedback management.  Further, this has amplified the voices of vulnerable people and children, ensuring their concerns were heard and addressed across the country. However, a key challenge identified through child-friendly feedback mechanisms was declining trust in adults among children aged 4-17. In response, age-appropriate feedback mechanisms were developed to create safe spaces, build trust, and promote responsiveness, aligning services with young people's needs while challenging harmful norms.

Turkmenistan, an upper-middle-income country, derives significant revenue from hydrocarbon exports, which accounted for 89% of total exports in 2023, including 68% from natural gas. While official statistics indicates a GDP growth of 6.3% in 2024, IMF estimates the economic growth at 2.3%. Despite global and regional crises, Turkmenistan remained relatively insulated due to its firm neutrality policy, emphasizing dialogue and good neighborly relations.
The Government allocated 67% of its 2023 budget to social needs; however, public spending as a per cent of GDP on health (1.6%), education (4.7%) and social protection (4.3%) remains low by international standards, with a focus on infrastructure investments. Rising food prices have strained vulnerable households, discussions are ongoing to improve monitoring of household well-being, introduce national poverty measurements, and review social safety net programs.
Turkmenistan has made significant strides in addressing data gaps, aligning with SDG 17 on partnerships for the goals. In December 2024, the State Statistics Committee released (first in 30 years) disaggregated results from the 2022 census, revealing a population of 7,057,841, with 34.9% children. The 2024 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey indicates early childhood education participation among 3–5-year-olds increased to 45% (from 41% in 2019), however, the level of participation in organized learning one year before the official primary entry age (SDG target 4.2.2) has dropped to 44%. Wider use of positive behavior management methods is needed to curb the practice of violent disciplining of children, which continues to be high at 67%.
The establishment of a high-level body, Strategic Advisory Board, in March 2024 has strengthened collaboration between the Government and the UN, advancing discussions on the United Nations Cooperation Framework, joint programming financing, and SDG reporting. UNICEF played a key role in enhancing data availability and aligning initiatives with the 2030 Agenda.
The education system has seen reforms, including the introduction of 12 years of compulsory education, curriculum enhancements, and improved school infrastructure. These efforts align with SDG 4 on quality education. However, challenges persist in expanding pre-primary education for 5-year-olds to improve primary education preparedness, integrating children with disabilities in mainstream schools, and addressing gender norms that limit girls’ access to higher education and STEM fields. Turkmenistan reported 5,997 children in residential care in 2024, of whom 5,200 have disabilities, underscoring the urgent need for reform. Ministry of Education initiation of model inclusive schools in 2024 indicates strong commitment to disability inclusive education.
Child protection systems require further development to ensure a rights-based, community-centered approach. Family-based care options are limited, with most state support focused on institutional care for children with disabilities. The 2023-2028 National Action Plan for the Realization of Children’s Rights aims to transform the system, promoting preventive and community-based solutions. 
Turkmenistan is highly vulnerable to climate change, with 80% of its territory a desert and a medium-high ranking on Children’s Climate Risk Index. Rising temperatures, prolonged heatwaves, and worsening droughts threaten water availability, food security, and children’s well-being. The continuing building of Qosh Tepa canal in neighboring Afghanistan poses a significant risk by diverting water from the Amu Darya River, potentially exacerbating water shortages in Lebap and Mary regions. Support for households affected by emergency situations is an area that requires strengthening within the current social protection system which is being addressed with UNICEF support.
2024 National Micronutrient Survey among women and children indicates that anaemia among reproductive age women reduced from 57% to 36% and among children (6-59 months old) from 44% to 31%, between 2011 and 2024, which is largely attributed to wide access of the population to adequately fortified wheat flour. Still, malnutrition in children 0-5 years remains a concern, as stunting, wasting and overweight prevalence stagnate at 9, 3 and 5 per cent, respectively.
While improvements have been made in access to primary healthcare services, significant barriers remain, particularly in addressing child mortality. Although efforts are made to enhance the capacity of health workers to manage childhood illnesses and advance adequate nutrition for infants and young children, achieving improvements at scale requires a comprehensive approach and sustained investments. Advocacy for increased public financing for child health, strengthening quality of medical education and continuous professional development for health workers, and data generation and use are essential next steps.
In 2024, the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child issued 104 recommendations for Turkmenistan, focusing on areas such as special protection measures, education, health, and children with disabilities. UNICEF has supported the Government in aligning these recommendations with the National Action Plan for Children’s Rights and developing monitoring tools to track progress. Turkmenistan also received 228 recommendations from the 4th cycle of the Universal Periodic Review. These were discussed by the Interdepartmental Commission on Human Rights outlining the next steps for implementing national human rights plans, and UNICEF has been a key partner in advancing disability inclusion and child protection rights.
In 2024, the evaluation of 2021-2025 Country Programme (CP) has been conducted to assess progress, enhance accountability, and inform the design of the 2026-2030 CP and UNSDCF. The evaluation highlighted good practices and lessons learned, emphasizing the need to scale up successful pilots nationally and to reach the most vulnerable children. The new CP have these as key strategies and a stronger focus on early age, disability inclusion and care, climate change and youth engagement. 
While Turkmenistan is making progress on key child rights and SDGs,  challenges remain. Strengthening education systems and primary health care, expanding social workforce and integrating community-based child protection services, addressing climate risks, and improving social safety nets are critical for ensuring no child is left behind. The SDG gap analysis conducted by the UN jointly with the Ministry of Finance and Economy and State Statistics Committee estimates that reaching the SDG transformation targets recommended in the National Commitments to accelerate progress during 2026-2030, additional government funding in the amount of 46.1 billion manats (13 billion USD) will be required. This translates to 2.8% of GDP annually to achieve the national SDG targets by 2030.
Sustained collaboration with UNICEF will be essential for achieving the child-related SDGs.

Every child counts
In 2024, UNICEF made significant progress in advancing data collection and analysis to monitor and support implementation of Turkmenistan’s commitments to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the SDGs. A major achievement was the successful implementation of the MICS survey, which provided crucial insights in areas of progress and persistent challenges.  Turkmenistan also piloted a new MICS module on Violence Against Women, contributing to global methodology refinement and improving referral and support mechanisms for GBV survivors. These findings are informing the development of the 2026-2030 Country Programme Document (CPD) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).

UNICEF successfully contributed to the joint UN advocacy for the release of Census 2022 data, which marked a significant step toward data transparency. The census, published for the first time since 1995, provides essential disaggregated population data on age, sex, education, employment, migration, and other factors essential for UNICEF programming. In addition, Turkmenistan expanded its participation in the TransMonEE regional initiative, enhancing data collection on youth and vulnerable children, including those in institutional care. A new statistical form was introduced for collecting administrative data on children in family-based forms of alternative care (guardianship and trusteeship), which meet the requirements of TransMonEE, and will support the monitoring of the National Concept on Alternative Care and its implementation roadmap.

In 2024, with the support of MoLSP and social work specialists in Dashoguz region, UNICEF conducted the first assessment of multidimensional child deprivation in the Aral Sea region. The report recommendations suggest identification of the national wellbeing line, development of the shock responsive social protection (SRSP) interventions related to climate risks, as well considering innovative contingency financing options.
The findings of the Turkmenistan National Micronutrient Survey (TNMS) among women and children were published with UNICEF support in 2024 and provide insights essential for creating effective evidence-based nutrition policies and strategies to combat micronutrient deficiencies in the country.

Building on the new MICS experience and the growing demand for SDG data, Turkmenistan decided to conduct a MICS Plus survey in 2025, demonstrating a shift toward increased data collection and transparent data practices. This and other evidence generating initiatives of Turkmenistan, coupled with UNICEF technical and advocacy support, underscores a growing national commitment to evidence-based policies, and monitoring of child rights and sustainable development in Turkmenistan.

UNICEF continued to strengthen its longstanding partnership with the Ombudsperson's Office, prioritizing efforts to build institutional capacity and enhance its ability to address child rights effectively. Over years of consistent advocacy, UNICEF has played a pivotal role in supporting the establishment of a specialized department within the Ombudsperson's Office dedicated to children and women rights. The creation of this department ensures that child rights issues receive focused attention and specialized expertise, enabling the Ombudsperson's Office to address challenges more comprehensively and advocate for meaningful change at both policy and community levels. 

Every child survives and thrives
In 2024, UNICEF CO continued to prioritize efforts to reduce preventable maternal, newborn, and child deaths by scaling up essential care, sustaining immunization programs, and supporting services for management of common childhood illnesses. With technical assistance of UNICEF, the Ministry of Health and Medical Industry (MoHMI) developed 12 treatment protocols for childhood illnesses, capacity building of 22 national and regional IMCI trainers continued, and 10 family doctors were trained through postgraduate training program at the State Medical University in 2024. Drafting of comprehensive Order on nationwide rollout of IMCI programme is underway, and its implementation will be highly prioritized by MoHMI in 2025. 

WHO and UNICEF collaborated on adaptation of the "Pocketbook of Primary Health Care for Children and Adolescents: Guidelines for Health Promotion, Disease Prevention, and Management from the Newborn Period to Adolescence." The adapted version of the Pocketbook is being translated in Turkmen language. The Ministry of Health acknowledges the importance of this resource, prioritizing its implementation in 2025. The Pocketbook will serve as a policy framework to ensure a continuum of care from pregnancy through childhood.

Capitalizing on the efforts to ensure healthy and safe childhood, UNICEF CO has put together a parenting program with actions and measures in line with SBC principles to promote age-appropriate nutrition and healthy lifestyles, violence free disciplining and positive parenting. The program foresees development of a series of initiatives in 2025 that would foster change in social norms coupled with analysis of the current barriers, stigmatizing factors and behavior trends that jeopardize child rights and prevent social inclusion. 

Ensuring better emergency care for newborns and young children saw renewed collaboration of UNICEF and MoHMI in 2024 and is an essential component of the healthcare system. Both hands-on training for technicians of the health facilities in operating and maintaining the oxygen systems, and enhancement of the healthcare professionals’ skills in managing neonatal and pediatric emergencies, were the focus, which are crucial for providing life-saving care to children. Professionals at the national and regional levels were trained on emergency care for newborns in the delivery room, identifying treatment for urgent conditions in intensive care units and prescribe the appropriate oxygen therapy to children. Technicians from the health facilities received hands-on experience in operations, maintenance, and monitoring to ensure long-term sustainability of oxygen equipment and patient safety.  

Turkmenistan continues to be self-sufficient in vaccine procurement and maintains an immunization coverage rate over 95%. In collaboration with WHO, UNICEF has helped develop the new National Immunization Programme for 2024–2028. The programme was endorsed in October 2024. Focused on sustainability and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, it aims at maintaining high vaccine coverage and preventing vaccine hesitancy. UNICEF has delivered the first batch of the hexavalent vaccine to support its smooth introduction in the national immunization schedule in 2025. In addition to the switch to the digital Vaccine Arrival Report (e-VAR) for vaccines, the MoHMI transitioned from the traditional Excel-based immunization forecasting tool to a digital one. This marks a step forward in digitalizing the process and significantly improves collaboration between UNICEF Supply Division, the UNICEF Country Office, and Government on the forecast.

MoHMI and UNICEF expanded infant and young child feeding (IYCF) and Baby Friendly Hospital (BFHI) initiatives in 2024. Over 1,000 primary health workers across regions have stronger breastfeeding and complementary feeding knowledge. Notably, Dashoguz's House of Health #1 achieved certification as “Baby-Friendly Facility,” reflecting progress in breastfeeding support. A key milestone in promoting breastfeeding was the initiation of a review of the National Law on Breastfeeding, with a designated Task Force beginning its work. This will ensure full implementation of the International Code of Marketing of Breast Milk Substitutes and relevant World Health Assembly resolutions. UNICEF has also planned a factor analysis on the existing barriers to breastfeeding that going forward will help develop programming in the field. 

To combat malnutrition, UNICEF continued its support for national salt iodization and wheat flour fortification programs, including premix procurement and quality monitoring. Field visits across Ashgabat and all velayats assessed production, storage, and usage practices, ensuring compliance with standards and identifying opportunities to refine fortification formulas in 2025. Capacity-building efforts reached 163 health professionals, enhancing their skills to deliver effective nutrition counseling.

Significant progress was also achieved in scaling up Early Childhood Development (ECD) services in 2024, with developmental monitoring provided by ECD demonstration facilities in all regions of the country and over 130 health professionals trained in ECD and early identification of developmental delays. As a result, 32,516 children benefited from a developmental monitoring program, leading to early intervention for 4,182 identified with delays. Of these, 3,469 received targeted early intervention support, leading to 574 children achieving developmental milestones. This success was further bolstered by training more medical professionals, ensuring future expertise in early childhood development.

Significant strides were made in 2024 in establishing a normative framework for Early Childhood Intervention (ECI) services, with successful advocacy on adoption of the Joint Regulation on provision of Early Childhood Intervention services by key government ministries. Parents played a central role in the child-centered ECI program, participating in assessments and implementing tailored interventions in natural environments. The inter-ministerial ECD Working Group, supported with technical expertise from the St. Petersburg Early Interventions Institute and UNICEF, advanced the social inclusion of children with disabilities and developmental delays, fostering a coordinated and impactful approach to ECD at the national level.

Every child is protected from violence and is socially included
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support the Government to advance the agenda for strengthening child protection systems in line with CRC Concluding Observations to Turkmenistan and UNICEF’s Strategic Plan to fulfil the rights of the most vulnerable families and children.

UNICEF actively promoted the policy of family-based care for children who cannot live with their parents for various reasons and are working with the government to strengthen the country's child protection system and to revise the outdated legal framework of gatekeeping and referral bodies in line with international standards. Regular engagement with the social and justice sector ministries led to the finalization of draft regulations on strengthening the child protection architecture in Turkmenistan, enhancing the functions of the Commission on Minors and the Guardianship and Trusteeship Bodies to closely align with the social services system and to introduce a coordination mechanism at national and subnational levels.
The strong partnership established with law enforcement agencies from the start of the 2021-2025 CPD enabled the advancement of the child justice agenda in the country, by strengthening protection measures for children in conflict with the law, as well as child victims and witnesses of crime, including the introduction of child-friendly procedures, processes and practices. In 2024, UNICEF continued to support the Government in integrating child-friendly procedures for child victims and witnesses of crime into the work of police investigators and prosecutors by developing a special course and training instructors on a child-friendly approach to investigating crimes against children or involving children. As a result, 17 trainers were trained from among police and prosecutor investigators, police detectives, teachers of the Institute of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (MoI) and psychology experts from Ashgabat and the regions. The positive feedback has created a platform to discuss the incorporation of the special course content in the curriculum at the MoI Institute and to rollout regular trainings for investigators, police detectives and other law enforcement practitioners from 2025.

Along with initiatives to introduce procedures to protect child victims and witnesses, enhancing the practice of diversion measures was also a focus of the government’s attention in 2024. With UNICEF support, the MoI, Prosecutor General’s Office and the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection launched a pilot in one of Ashgabat’s districts to improve diversion practices with restorative justice in Turkmenistan, which is the first project of its kind, involving the social work specialists to collaborate with the inspection of minors of police offices and provide social services to children who have committed crimes. The results of the pilot will serve as a model for discussing the introduction of diversion, rehabilitation, and reintegration services for children in conflict with the law throughout the country. It responds to an important recommendation of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child to the Government of Turkmenistan to promote non-judicial measures, such as diversion and mediation.

In 2024, UNICEF continued strategic high-level advocacy for the country-wide scale up of social services to every community. The Law on Social Services that was adopted in 2021, and has been  implemented in 18 out of 52 districts of the country. Since 2022, MoLSP has been annually supporting over 1,000 families with 45 social work specialists in the country. Every year, around 40% of the cases are related to families with people or children with disabilities - this is a good entry point for the discussion of monetary and multidimensional deprivations of the most vulnerable in the country. In addition, policy briefs on structural changes, financing gap analysis with financing options, intersectoral task force meetings and high-level meetings at the level of Secretary General and Country leadership pitched the transformational value of investing in the reform in order to accelerate SGD achievement by 2030. 

In 2024, UNICEF supported the setup of the National Task force with a dedicated subgroup on Cash in Emergency that initiated the development of a National Action Plan to strengthen Shock Responsive Social Protection, with key stakeholders' engagement in hands-on exercises to create contingency actions for natural hazards and discuss crisis financing options. Members of the Cash in Emergency Task force subgroup joined the UNICEF-World Bank subregional Forum on Adaptive Social Protection and Sustainable Financing where representatives from all Central Asian countries shared experience on the latest developments and the lessons learnt. 

Every child learns
In 2024 the education sector commitment and capacity were strengthened on implementation of quality early learning and pre-primary preparation, delivering competency-based, gender-responsive and climate-change education, while the disability inclusive support was significantly increased. Established in 2020 by a joint letter of three Ministers, the inter-ministerial Working Group on ECD consisting of Ministry of Education, Ministry of Health and Medical Industry, and Ministry of Labour and Social Protection, and facilitated by UNICEF, proved useful for coordination in the cross-sectoral area of ECD, and advocacy on diversifying early learning to increase pre-primary preparation coverage.
