The WG served as a platform for achieving stronger capacity of national partners to initiate cross-sectoral parenting support interventions in 2025.

Establishment of a model robotics club in a mainstream secondary school with a set of training materials serves a platform for the Ministry of Education to promote competency-based teaching and learning across formal curriculum with focus on STEAM subjects. The training programme on information, communication, technology (ICT) skills, tested with the graduates of the orphanages in Ashgabat and Balkanabat cities, is a tool for the education sector to further use for implementing competency-based education and empowerment of youth in mainstream education.
UNICEF consistent technical support to the National Institute of Education resulted in finalization and publishing of three manuals on gender-responsive education for teachers, students, and parents. These interactive and user-friendly materials will not only serve as a major training resource for the planned capacity development nation-wide but will also provide a foundation for further integration of gender responsive education in the existing pre- and in-service education curricula and strengthen the overall institutional capacity of the education sector across all levels of education.

UNICEF reinforced the MoE commitment for inclusive education for children with disabilities through a consistent support for piloting inclusive education (IE) principles in 2 selected mainstream kindergartens and 2 secondary schools. The piloting, guided by the principles of the national concept of inclusive education, took a systemic approach to promoting inclusive education with the MoE lead and cross-sectoral commitment of the health and social protection partners. This approach has helped to secure the understanding and commitment of all partners for continuous support services for children with disabilities to promote their inclusive pathways and further mainstreaming. An Action Plan sets to build an inclusive environment for children with disabilities in the selected facilities inlcuding building capacity of pedagogical staff and multi-disciplinary professionals for inclusive teaching, learning and supporting the students with disabilities, providing assistive devices for  children, improving physical infrastructure for accessibility and supportive environment. The program also foresees engagement of parents and the local community into promotion of the inclusive education and reduction of the stigmatizing factors, such as inappropriate language. 

As part of the piloting process UNICEF enhanced capacity of the rehabilitation centers under the Ministry of Education and Ministry of Health and Medical Industry for providing cross-sectoral disability inclusive services with focus on early childhood interventions and addressing autistic spectrum disorders, all in support of inclusive pathways and inclusive education for the target children with disabilities. This approach not only aims to shape the role of the rehabilitation centers as resource centers to promote inclusive education in the target facilities but also aims to empower the children with disabilities and their families to prevent their further institutionalization.

Triggered by the drop of participation rate in organized learning one year prior to official primary school age, a series of analysis and programme discussions were conducted with the Ministry of Education, National Institute of Education and Ministry of Finance to address issues related to capacity building of education sector on planning, implementing, and monitoring the half-day quality one-year pre-primary education programme (PPP) to ensure that Turkmenistan meets its target of 90% participation by 2028 as per NAP on Realization of Children’s Rights 2023-2028. As a result, the Ministry of Education identified a number of regular schools to pilot half-day PPP paving way for discussions and planning among national partners that the country can only reach the SDG 4.2. target with diversification of pre-primary education programmes.

UNICEF provided continuous support to the Ministry of Education on integration of climate change adaptation (CCA) and disaster risk reduction (DRR) across the education system, with efforts in 2024 focused on finalizing the CCA and DRR curriculum and methodological materials for the pre-schools and drafting the relevant curriculum and materials for the higher education institutions. Having integrated the climate change and environment topics in the primary and secondary education levels during 2022-2023, the latest work targeting pre-primary and higher education levels, will complete the climate change education mainstreaming across all school levels, and show case that climate change education is childhood-long development, from early age to adulthood.

During the reporting period UNICEF jointly with Ministry of Education and National Red Crescent Society of Turkmenistan (NRCST) significantly contributed to strengthening capacities of children, youth, adolescents, teachers, and local authorities in emergency preparedness and DRR. Over 2,500 schoolchildren, 700 education personnel and officials, and 300 staff and volunteers of NRCST took an active part in the training sessions, practical exercises and simulations to introduce and enhance the knowledge and skills in comprehensive school safety, emergency preparedness, gender and WASH in school emergency, Early warning systems, Evacuation skills, First Aid support and climate change adaptation with the focus on the rights and needs of children and youth. 

Every child participates
In 2024, UNICEF Turkmenistan has continued to prioritize child and youth participation, ensuring that their voices are heard, and their perspectives are considered in programme development processes. Through various consultations, workshops, and events, UNICEF has created platforms that enable young people to express their views on issues that directly affect them.
As part of development of the new Country Programme Document, UNICEF Turkmenistan organized youth and children’s consultations in Ashgabat and in summer camps, convening 50 young representatives from diverse backgrounds and regions of Turkmenistan. The participants, varying in age and experience, engaged in discussions on issues of importance to their community and the nation. The insights and recommendations from children and youth formed priority areas for consideration in the next Country Programme. One of such initiatives included consultations in focus group format on the mental health and wellbeing. Young people provided insights into the language and practices that stigmatize people with mental health issues. The results of this study have been used to form a glossary on the mental health and other disability types in Turkmen language and shape information materials used throughout various programs.

Leveraging the long-standing partnership with the Government
2024 marked 32 years of UNICEF presence in Turkmenistan, a long-standing partnership that goes back to the early years of independence. Over the past three decades, UNICEF has accompanied Turkmenistan on its development journey, continuously being a partner of choice on issues related to children. 
Given Turkmenistan’s firm neutrality policy, the country cooperation with United Nations is a priority, and UNICEF continued to leverage this opportunity to deepen its partnerships and deliver impactful results for children.  UNICEF’s role is particularly significant given the limited presence of NGOs and development partners in the country. In this context, UNICEF has been supporting the implementation of initiatives and programs in addition to its normative role and technical expertise. This provides UNICEF with the opportunity to ensure quality implementation, interact directly with beneficiaries and achieve meaningful and sustainable outcomes for children.
Recognizing Turkmenistan’s upper-middle-income status, UNICEF continues to explore resource mobilization opportunities, including for Government cost-sharing of child-related development programs and policies. In 2024, UNICEF and the Government developed a Contribution Agreement, which is expected to be signed in 2025. This approach is designed to deliver greater results for children while further strengthening the long-standing partnership between Turkmenistan and UNICEF. 
The establishment of a high-level body, Strategic Advisory Board (SAB) in March 2024 has reconfirmed the strategic importance of the collaboration between the Government and the UN, advancing discussions on the United Nations Cooperation Framework, joint programming financing, and SDG reporting. UNICEF played a key role in enhancing data availability and aligning initiatives with the 2030 Agenda.
Strategic partnership with USAID BHA, IFRC and NRCS on Disaster Risk Reduction 
A key partnership of UNICEF Turkmenistan in 2024 was in the framework of the tripartite agreement between UNICEF Europe and Central Asia Regional Office, USAID Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance for Central Asia, and International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies Central Asia. The year marked the conclusion of the second phase of the programme in the Central Asia subregion.  
Focused on strengthening the emergency preparedness, Climate Change Adaptation and DRR capacities of the children and youth of Turkmenistan, the programme enabled to conduct capacity development sessions, simulations, practical exercises and risks mapping, engaging over 3,282 participants represented by the administrative and teaching personnel and schoolchildren of 18 target schools, staff and volunteers of the NRCST and the local authorities.
This partnership is significant as it is the single investment source in disaster risk reduction area with a strong focus on youth, school, and community engagement. Implemented in several phases, the programme allowed for continuity and sustainability of results for children that often require longer term engagement and support. Moreover, it provided UNICEF the opportunity to further scale up the ongoing strategic partnership with the National Red Crescent Society in Turkmenistan – which is the first responder with capacity to operate at local level in the event of emergency. The subregional nature of the programme enabled the countries to exchange knowledge and learn from the experience across countries in Central Asia.
Initiating new collaborations for future partnerships
In 2024, UNICEF Turkmenistan placed a strong emphasis on exploring new partnerships and strengthening existing ones to expand their reach and impact in the future. For the first time, UNICEF CO established a partnership with the EU Delegation for Central Asia, launching a new phase in our developing bilateral cooperation aimed at strengthening national child rights monitoring and evidence-generation capacities, including the new round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS). This partnership provided a platform for regular communication and UNICEF will leverage this opportunity to deepen and expand the collaboration.
On International Day for Child Protection, UNICEF partnered with Turkmenistan Airlines to introduce children from the Palace of Orphans to STEM professions, by taking them on a tour of Ashgabat International Airport and engaging in simulation activities at the School of Aviation. This initiative not only inspired children but also strengthened the partnership between UNICEF and the Ministry of Education while re-establishing collaboration with Turkmenistan Airlines. 
In the realm of environmental sustainability, UNICEF partnered with Bouygues Turkmen and Yash Tebigatchy NGO to conduct a Youth Environmental Leadership Camp. This program empowered 24 young activists with the knowledge and skills needed to address climate change and sustainable development challenges. In 2024, UNICEF collaboration with Bouygues Turkmen private company matured, while established with Yash Tebigatchy, which is an important avenue to strengthen the capacities of the NGOs in Turkmenistan.    
UNICEF also explored new cultural collaborations, partnering with the French Institute in Turkmenistan during the Francophonie competitions. Youth participants wrote essays on topics such as climate change, disability inclusion, raising awareness on these critical issues. This initiative leveraged the mutual interest in expanding collaboration on strengthening capacities of youth establishing a UNV and internship opportunity funded by the French Government.
Working with the State Committee for TV, Radio Broadcasting and Cinematography yielded results which UNICEF is yet to measure. During the past year, UNICEF and the Committee developed an animation promoting children’s rights which will be released in 2025. This initiative has laid the ground for further expansion of collaboration with the national television to actively tackle social norms.

Promoting Joint Programmes to achieve common results
Building on the positive experience with the implementation of Joint Programmes (JP) and achieving common results during 2020-2023, in 2024 UNICEF continued to play an active role in supporting UN efforts on developing Joint Programmes and promoting Government co-financing.
The flagship UN joint programme on introduction of inclusive community-based social services, led by UNICEF together with the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection of the Population (MoLSP) and implemented during 2020-2023 in collaboration with UNFPA, UNDP, and UNODC, served as a success story of UN joint efforts and inspired the development of new JPs.
The evaluation of UN Cooperation Framework conducted in 2024, has also recognized the benefits of joint planning and programming in driving progress and greater alignment within UN Country Team, and recommended to continue to pursue JPs as a means to achieve common results and programme coherence.
During the UNCT retreat in May 2024, 10 areas of joint collaborations were identified together with the Government, out of which 4 JPs were prioritized for further development with national counterparts. UNICEF participates in two of the four prioritized programmes: i) youth, peace and security, and ii) digital governance.
The Strategic Advisory Board, established in March 2024, has been used as the platform for high-level discussion and validation of identified Joint Programmes for further review and submission for Government cost-sharing and are expected to be confirmed in 2025.
The process of co-creation of the Joint Programmes was the first-time developing JPs for Government contribution, which was a useful experience for all UN and Government entities involved and led to better understanding of the Government budgetary cycle and requirements, which UNICEF and other UN agencies have learned and will use in the future resource mobilization efforts for joint programmes.
Role of Procurement Services in advancing results for children
Procurement Services play a crucial role in UNICEF partnership with the Government of Turkmenistan and is an integral component of the country programme of cooperation. Established in 2006, the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on procurement of vaccines, and in 2008 the MOU on procurement of premix for flour fortification not only contributed to ensuring that the country has the necessary supplies to support immunization and nutrition programmes, it also provided an excellent platform to shape and strengthen the services over the past two decades.
Firstly, UNICEF procurement services to the Government continues to ensure delivery of the best quality vaccines at the lowest prices on the market. As part of the procurement engagement, UNICEF advocacy led to new vaccines added by the Ministry of Health and Medical Industry (MoHMI) to the immunization schedule in 2007 (MMR), 2010 (Hib), 2016 (HPV, IPV), 2019 (PCV, rotavirus, hepatitis A), and in 2024 UNICEF procured the hexavalent vaccine for its introduction in 2025. Children in Turkmenistan are now protected from 14 preventable diseases. Similarly on flour fortification, UNICEF ensures the programme is monitored regularly, micronutrient survey is conducted, evidence is used for continuous quality assurance of flour fortification process, and new developments such as new fortification formula is being explored for introduction in the future.
UNICEF procurement services also help the country to better plan the supply needs, select quality products and equipment, and ensure goods are delivered on time. The success comes from working closely with the partners and UNICEF Supply Division, ensuring constant trilateral communication and transparent procurement processes, and managing forecasting, procurement transactions and funds effectively.
As a result, virtually all children of Turkmenistan have access to free of charge lifesaving vaccination, and the country maintains above 98% immunization coverage and flour fortification over the last decade. In addition to high vaccination rates, the partnership on Procurement Services helped to respond to emerging threats and prevent outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases including during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In Turkmenistan, Procurement Services demonstrated to be an entry point for strengthening government supply chains, scale-up innovative solutions, and increase quality and reach of respective programme interventions. The game changing strategy was the systems strengthening and sustainability approach including: i) Government self-financing, ii) leveraging procurement services to expand partnership beyond supplies, and iv) consistently seeking innovations to enhance service delivery for children.

The escalation of the war in Ukraine passed its 1,000-day mark in November 2024, with more than a decade of conflict across the east, having an ever-worsening impact on the lives of children and their families. As of December 2024, at least 2,502 children have been killed or injured. Humanitarian needs continued to be extensive, with 2.9 million children, including 1.5 million girls, among the 14.6 million people in need of humanitarian assistance in the country (OCHA).  
The war has resulted in internal displacement for over 3.6 million people (IDPs), of which 57 per cent female and 24 per cent children. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) reports more than 6.78 million refugees, with over 6.2 million recorded in Europe. 90 per cent of Ukrainian refugees in Europe are women and children.  
The ongoing war has caused a rise in extreme poverty, with the greatest consequences for households with children (UNECE). An estimated 65 per cent of children live in poverty (2023) and 1 in 5 children face monetary, deprivation, and consumption poverty simultaneously (UNICEF, 2024). Social sector spending remains heavily dependent on international aid and borrowing, as around 95 per cent of nominal domestic state budget revenues are allocated to defense and security. Local Governments have been particularly affected by the reduced allocation to non-defense sectors, centralization of personal income tax (PIT), delayed fiscal transfers, inflation and currency depreciation as well as staff outflow. Social services are 90 per cent financed by local budgets, meeting only 7 per cent of the required funding.  
Children and their families continue to have limited access to essential social services. With 1,614 educational institutions damaged or destroyed since the start of the war, the Ministry of Education and Science estimates that 4.6 million children face barriers to education. Approximately two-thirds of children in frontline regions, including Kharkiv, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia, rely solely on remote learning due to the dangers of in-person schooling, with 79% experiencing poor internet connection, 42% lacking necessary electronic devices, and 40% facing frequent electricity shortages (Save the Children, 2024). The combination of school disruptions, lower quality instruction and stress on students and education staff contribute to substantial learning losses for Ukrainian students. A 2022 Programme International Student Assessment (PISA) highlights the deterioration in Ukrainian 15-year-olds’ learning acquisition since 2018, equivalent to almost two years in mathematics, reading, and science with significant gender, socio-economic and rural/urban inequities. The accumulation of learning losses since February 2022 is estimated to amount to US$7.8 billion (RDNA 4).  
744 health facilities have been destroyed or damaged, limiting access of women and children to primary health care. Restricted access to maternal care has increased the risk of mortality for pregnant and lactating women and their newborns. The latest available data on maternal mortality ratio and neonatal mortality rate in Ukraine show a slightly higher prevalence than that of Europe, with an estimated 14 deaths per 100,000 live births (2022) and 5 per 1000 live births (2021). The war has severely impacted children and young people’s mental health and well-being, with cumulative stress also impacting the capacity of social service professionals to provide effective assistance (HIAS 2023). 32 per cent of households report children displaying signs of psychosocial distress (IMPACT, 2024).  
Access to clean water faces unprecedented challenges across the country, bringing the total recovery needs for the water sector to 11.2 billion USD.  The destruction of infrastructure has interrupted water services causing 1.7 million children to lack access to safe water, and 2.5 million children have no access to proper wastewater treatment services (UNICEF). The war has generated large scale contamination of the environment, particularly water resources. Up to 90 per cent of water facilities have reached or exceeded their intended lifespan, with 40 per cent of water networks in critical condition. The ongoing conflict has pushed this fragile system toward potential collapse. A recent assessment indicates that only 15 per cent of the 37 largest water supply companies, which collectively serve 15 million people, are currently equipped to handle power blackouts.  
Children across Ukraine are at risk due to the use of explosive weapons in populated areas, with over 600 child casualties in 2024 alone. Prior to 2022, eastern Ukraine was known as one of the most mine-contaminated areas in the world. The Government estimates that up to 30 per cent of Ukraine may be contaminated with mines or unexploded ordnance (UXO). Over 100 children are reported to have been killed or injured by mines or UXOs since the escalation of the war (Department of Mine Action).  
Women in Ukraine have been disproportionally affected by the war, with over 4.6 million women and 1.5 million girls in need (OCHA). An estimated 2.5 million IDPs, returnees, and non-displaced people – the majority of whom are women and girls – are at high risk of gender-based violence (GBV). The reported prevalence of gender-based violence in Ukraine was high before the escalation of the war (7 out of 10 women having experienced GBV), and Government-reported rates of sexual violence and domestic violence affecting children increased significantly between 2022 and 2023 (Office of Prosecutor General). The vulnerability faced by women and girls increases with the intersection with other factors such as age, disability, or displacement status. Households with people with disabilities present higher humanitarian needs, with nearly a third of households that include people with disabilities facing food security gaps. People with disabilities also face limited access to shelters which are often inaccessible for them. (RDNA3) 
The European Union (EU) accession process fostered the initiation of key child-related reforms in 2024. With the first intergovernmental conference on accession negotiations held in June 2024, there has been increased momentum to place child rights at the core of humanitarian, recovery, reconstruction, and reform efforts. This is evidenced through key childhood and family care legislative and policy reforms undertaken by the Government of Ukraine in 2024. As part of the EU accession process, the Ukraine Facility was established in June 2024 as a financing instrument to support the recovery, reconstruction, and modernization of the country (EU Ukraine Factsheet 2024). The EU facility provides an opportunity to drive a child and youth centred recovery and sustainable development agenda for Ukraine.

Humanitarian Action for Children 
In 2024, 9.8 million people including 2.5 million children, were reached by UNICEF’s timely and scaled-up humanitarian response with life-saving support and essential services.   
Children and families living within 30km of the frontline areas were among those most severely affected, facing shelling, missile strikes, displacement and deprivation of basic services. In this frontline corridor, UNICEF worked with local authorities and civil society organizations (CSOs) to meet the life-saving needs of children through adapted modalities which considered the safety of both children and humanitarian workers. These modalities included online education and psychosocial support; mobile child protection and health teams; and the delivery of cash assistance and supplies. In the most insecure and inaccessible communities, UNICEF and its partners participated in 45 inter-agency convoys, providing bottled water, hygiene kits and other critical supplies for over 77,000 people.  
Detailed contingency planning and preparedness efforts, including cash registration of families in frontline areas, contingency agreements within implementing partnerships and supply prepositioning in UNICEF and partner warehouses, allowed UNICEF to respond swiftly to newly arising emergency situations. This included the displacement of over 90,000 people from Pokrovsk district; evacuations from frontline areas of Sumy region; and mass energy infrastructure strikes which resulted in nationwide blackouts in both the summer and winter seasons. UNICEF also supported children affected by an attack on the ‘Okhmatdyt’ National Specialized Children’s Hospital in July 2024, providing health, WASH and recreation supplies along with MHPSS and multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) to a total of 430 households.  
When new evacuations were announced, UNICEF was able to immediately transfer multipurpose cash to affected families with children; 23,314 households with children were reached with multipurpose cash in 2024, covering 76,501 people including 39,025 children. Mobile teams provided child protection and education services as well as supplies to newly displaced families in transit centres, humanitarian hubs and collective centres. A unique partnership was developed with Ukrainian Railways, allowing distribution of supplies and child protection services to be extended to scheduled evacuation trains. This was complemented in the central and the western parts of the country with support for newly displaced families, providing 395 children with case management, psychosocial support, winter supplies and referrals to services.   
UNICEF undertook a comprehensive 2024-2025 winter response, providing cash-for-winterization to 165,753 people including 78,371 children in frontline areas or in alternative care; 16,787 people including 7,182 children received solid fuel briquettes; 29,645 children received warm winter clothes and 417,000 children in 700 schools were supported with school winter grants. UNICEF established a dedicated heating emergency cell under the WASH cluster, coordinating the humanitarian response nationwide, and delivered modular boilers and cogeneration units to strengthen district heating systems in vulnerable communities.  In total, 616,671 people benefitted from UNICEF’s investments in repaired district heating systems. Work is on-going to reach over 1.5 million people by the end of the winter season.  
Mental health and psychosocial support provided by UNICEF reached 757,807 children, caregivers and frontline workers through direct services, capacity building of Government social service providers and outreach to strengthen individual and community resilience.  UNICEF reached a total of 62,091 children with individualized support through child protection case management, which included Mental Health and Psychosocial support, gender-based violence risk mitigation, prevention and response interventions, basic needs support, emergency supplies, and safe referrals to specialized services. 
 
In 2024, substantive results were achieved in the repair and rehabilitation of critical services for children and families. 5.8 million people (including 958,000 children) were provided with improved access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene services through UNICEF’s emergency response. UNICEF's direct assistance to 114 water utilities with emergency repairs and the provision of critical equipment and water treatment chemicals had a significant impact on improving the availability of safe drinking water. This is exemplified in Kryvyi Rih city, where the rehabilitation of water distribution networks increased water uptake by 10 per cent, securing safe drinking water for over 500,000 people. Through repairing and equipping shelters in 128 kindergartens and General Secondary Schools, 18,472 children were able to attend in-person learning with more child-friendly and functional safe shelter spaces. UNICEF also contributed to addressing national immunization needs, delivering over 1.8 million vaccines to prevent stock-outs, and ensuring the continuity of vaccination services. 
UNICEF improved communities’ access to life-saving and essential information through innovative behavior change interventions and community engagement that reached 13.2 million people, with 1.2 million participating in engagement actions across Ukraine. Interpersonal sessions on Explosive Ordinance Risk Education were conducted for 1,080,012 children and 200,325 caregivers by mobile teams of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, though schools and community centres. 
 
Child and Youth-Centred Recovery  
While continuing to address urgent humanitarian needs in frontline areas, UNICEF’s efforts in 2024 focused increasingly on advancing child and youth-centered recovery and development goals at national and sub-national levels. Given the significant Government capacity in frontline municipalities, UNICEF’s recovery response included strengthening local capacities to respond to humanitarian needs. This nexus approach of addressing short-term humanitarian needs through a system-strengthening response has contributed to the longer-term recovery agenda of building the capacities of Government to deliver services effectively and efficiently for children and young people.  Informed by a Situation Analysis of Children in Ukraine (2024), the UNICEF recovery programming priorities aligned directly with the new Country Programme 2025-2029 leadership areas namely: 1) Better Start to Life, 2) Better Learning and Skills, and 3) Better Care: A Family for Every Child; as well as advancing Ukraine’s climate resilience WASH agenda. Throughout these areas of leadership is a commitment to equity and participation ensuring that no children are left behind in Ukraine’s recovery journey.  
 
At the national level, significant efforts were made in advocacy and data generation to support ongoing reforms in line with Ukraine’s recovery and EU accession agenda across all flagship areas as outlined below. Powerful and engaging digital content helped drive humanitarian and recovery-related child rights advocacy and influenced online discourse. UNICEF’s digital reach was impressive, with more than 8,000 types of content produced, reaching some 35 million people and engaging 8.1 million. National media continued to cover UNICEF and child rights issues extensively and UNICEF increased its voice through other partners, such as local authorities, when speaking with media. Two impactful Investment Case analytical products, on Early Childhood and on Youth, were undertaken jointly with the Government and findings used to inform UNICEF’s advocacy on the relevance of the EU Child and Youth Guarantee mechanisms for Ukraine.  
 
At the sub-national level, within the framework of Ukraine’s decentralization efforts and UNICEF’s support to Ukraine’s EU accession agenda, UNICEF enhanced its engagement and made significant efforts to strengthen partnerships with local Government and non-government partners. UNICEF partnered with 47 districts covering a population of 9.8 million people, to support communities to plan, budget and implement integrated social services for children and young people. The partnership included the design and initiation of models of decentralized services in education, child protection, health, and water sectors to inform the national recovery agenda. In order to ensure that sub-national recovery processes are grounded in evidence, UNICEF conducted a large household survey across 73 districts in mid-2024 covering over 14,000 households with children. The survey provided district-level representative data on key social service needs and gaps to inform local budgets, plans and programmes. The data has been made available through a user-friendly English and Ukrainian language online dashboard to wider national and international recovery partners in support of leveraging investments towards vulnerable children and their families. In collaboration with the Kyiv School of Economics and the Ministry of Finance, UNICEF delivered training programmes on ‘Child-Centered, Gender Responsive Public Financial Management and its Role for Local Recovery’ for 44 districts and corresponding regional authorities. This was complemented by dedicated capacity building of local authorities and social service frontline workers on gender-responsive and transformative programming, which reached over 34,000 individuals in 2024.  
 
Better Start to Life 
UNICEF Ukraine initiated the development and implementation of an integrated early childhood development (ECD) strategy in 2024 aligned with Government efforts to strengthen access to quality early childhood care and education (ECCE) and advance sector reforms to address intergenerational poverty. An ‘ECD Case for Investment’ analysis provided the basis for defining a multi-sectoral package of interventions, which will be modeled in 47 districts through the new UNICEF Country Programme (2025-29). 
 
UNICEF provided technical assistance and direct support in the development of multiple national ECD policies and legislative reforms in 2024. Taken together, they constitute a core framework to support young children aged 0-6 and their families. In November 2024 a Preschool Law was passed by parliament, outlining a multi-sectoral approach to early childhood care and education services, and a key deliverable under the Ukraine Plan. Other related policies and strategies included a Decree to institutionalize Universal-Progressive Home Visiting (UPHV) and Ukraine’s National Strategy of Demographic Development by 2040. At the request of the Ministry of Social Policy, UNICEF partnered with the Kyiv School of Economics to conduct an analysis of the national state budget for social support to children and families- which allowed for the first time an analysis of the budget by 0-3 and 3-6 age categories. 
 
The Universal Progressive Home Visiting (UPHV) model expanded significantly with UNICEF support in 2024, reaching 29,680 children in 15 oblasts and in Kyiv city. This model, providing vaccination guidance, breastfeeding support and psychosocial services, is being integrated into the health system to promote the long-term health and development of children in Ukraine. The establishment of 12 training resource centers for health care workers allowed for than 900 health care workers to increase their knowledge in early childhood care and the delivery of parenting education. UNICEF provided technical assistance in the drafting of a Positive Parenting package which was included within a costed Better Care Minimum Package.  
 
With UNICEF support, the Ministry of Education and Science (MoES) initiated the piloting of 18 diversified models of ECCE in an effort to develop more relevant and cost-effective early childhood care and education services.  National Early Learning and Preschool Standards (ELPS) were drafted with UNICEF’s technical support, drawing on international best practices and integrating gender considerations, and will serve as the foundation for a review of the National ECE Curricula Framework planned in 2025. 10,000 preschool teachers were trained in delivering social and emotional learning curricula and informed on referral pathways to protection and health services for young children. Numo, an online platform for young children and their parents, reached 131,549 children with updated materials in support of socio-emotional learning competencies.  
 
Better Learning and Skills  
In 2024, UNICEF Ukraine advanced its mission to rebuild and transform the education system amidst ongoing challenges, improving equitable access to quality learning for over 470,000 children and youth, particularly the most vulnerable. Under the auspices of a regional Skills Alliance for Ukraine, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS) in the development of a national Youth Policy Concept (2025-2030) shaping state-financed skills programmes for youth. A Youth Investment Case undertaken jointly by UNICEF with Government, helped inform a national Working Group developing a Youth Guarantee policy for Ukraine. With UNICEF’s assistance, an updated national assessment framework for the evaluation of learning outcomes in adapted and modified educational programmes was completed.  
 
UNICEF supported a third annual learning assessment exercise for sixth and eighth grade students, as a means of identifying trends in student performance in Ukrainian language and Mathematics. This data provided evidence required to design policy actions and to refine a national Learning Recovery strategy which had been drafted with UNICEF’s support in 2023. Results also informed UNICEF’s engagement with 15 districts where dedicated learning recovery plans were developed for 2024/25.  
 
In recognition of the significant proportion of children studying through online modalities, UNICEF continued its provision of assistance to the All-Ukrainian School Online platform, expanding content linked to the curriculum areas in which students were experiencing most significant learning loss. Through this support 884 digitalised lessons were developed, and which benefited 245,576 children (49 per cent girls). 300 catch up centres were established in 2024, providing individual and small group remedial education interventions to over 110,000 children. This was complemented by capacity development for 7,983 General Secondary School teachers who gained skills in remote teaching methods and fostering interactive learning experiences. An innovative model of mentorship by university students for General Secondary Students was further expanded with UNICEF support in 2024.  
 
Through 12 ‘Ko_laba’ spaces established with UNICEF support in 9 districts, 6,000 adolescents participated in science, technology, and entrepreneurial skills-building programmes. These centers have become a model for district authorities and as result, 35 districts are allocating additional funding for municipal youth skills-building programmes.  
 
Better Care: A Family for Every Child  
In the framework of the EU accession agenda, UNICEF supported key reforms in line with Ukraine national Plan and recovery agenda, advocating for the right of every child to grow up in a safe and nurturing family environment. One of these reforms is the Better Care Reform, to which UNICEF’s support contributed to the finalization and endorsement of the National Strategy on Ensuring the Right of Every Child in Ukraine to Grow Up in a Family Environment and a National Action Plan. In addition to this reform, UNICEF supported the Judicial System Reform by drafting of amendments to the Law of Ukraine “On the Judicial System and Status of Judges” to introduce specialized judges for civil cases involving children’s rights and interests, which are currently under review. With technical assistance from UNICEF, the Ministry of Education and Science (MoES) approved an Inclusive Education Strategic Action Plan by 2027, establishing the foundation for systemic inclusion of children with disabilities in the General Secondary School system and therein supporting community-based mechanisms for children’s care. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF aligned its programmatic response with the Better Care Reform to support the Government in strengthening access to social services and support at community level. A key initiative has been the rollout of patronage care, an emergency foster care model designed to provide immediate support to children separated from their families. In 2024, this initiative led to the creation of 397 patronage families across 22 regions, offering a safe and nurturing environment to 790 children.  
 
In coordination with the Office of the President and the Ministry of Social Policy (MoSP), UNICEF designed an integrated social services and benefits package (ISSB) grounded in Ukraine’s Law on Social Services. The package of services aims to address the urgent humanitarian needs of Ukraine’s citizens while helping strengthen provision of basic social services in line with the national recovery agenda. Further, UNICEF supported the monitoring of 5,442 children in alternative care settings, ensuring their safety and well-being by the Ombudsman’s Office and National Social Service.  
 
In addition, UNICEF provided support by ensuring conditions of stay are care for 1,240 children evacuated from institutions abroad who benefitted from child rights monitoring missions to Türkiye, Poland, Italy, Romania and Switzerland. To enhance this work, Ukraine's Cabinet of Ministers endorsed in 2024 the Decree 1026, which adds individual assessments before the return of children evacuated to alternative care settings abroad. In collaboration with the Child Rights Protection Center and Coordination Center, UNICEF and partners provided to a total of 208 children (98 girls, 3 with disabilities) who returned from the Russia Federation, Belarus and Occupied Territories and their 169 parents/caregivers (134 women) with case management, psychosocial support, essential supplies, and referral to relevant services. 
 
In 2024 a pilot was initiated in ten regions aimed at demonstrating services to improve access to safe and nurturing family environments. UNICEF supported the ten regions with guidance and tools to develop regional action plans aligned with the National Strategy for Ensuring Every Child’s Right to a Family Environment (2024–2026). 
The transformation of baby homes was initiated at decentralized level, upon the request of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine and four regional State Administrations. UNICEF, in collaboration with the Coordination Center and the State Services for Children, initiated the process aiming to benefit 250 babies currently in institutions.   

Climate Responsive Water and Sanitation Systems 
To drive sector-wide reform in the Water and Sanitation sector, UNICEF commissioned strategic studies on utility cost recovery and water quality monitoring aligned with EU standards. Early success is evidenced by the National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission's implementation of increased business consumer tariffs, achieving a 5 per cent improvement in cost recovery across 37 major utilities. This was complemented by the implementation of a comprehensive 14-month development programme delivered in partnership with RedR UK for water supply companies. This initiative, launched in July 2024, aims to train 750 water utility staff while institutionalizing capacity development across Government systems. 
UNICEF strengthened environmental and social safeguards across its infrastructural investments, with risk assessments and Environmental and Social Management Plans completed for 281 construction projects of which 114 in the water and sanitation sector, ensuring adherence to standards for environmental protection. This work complements broader climate action initiatives, including Ukraine's signing of the Declaration on Children, Youth, and Climate Action at COP28, facilitated through UNICEF's advocacy.

In 2024, UNICEF expanded its collaboration with international and regional partners to leverage resources and support for ensuring the rights of children in Ukraine. In support of the European Union accession process, UNICEF and the Government of Ukraine jointly convened the international community to align efforts for implementation of a framework on childcare reform- entitled Better Care Reform. As a result of this partnership, the National Strategy on Ensuring the Right of Every Child in Ukraine to Grow Up in a Family Environment, accompanied by a comprehensive National Action Plan, were approved in November 2024. UNICEF also joined efforts alongside development partners in contributing to the annual European Union report on EU enlargement for Ukraine and partnered with Government as they opened accession negotiations on judiciary and fundamental rights.   
UNICEF expanded its engagement within national coordination structures, contributing to national programmes for broader results for children. This was exemplified in UNICEF’s partnership with the national Mental Health Coordination Centre as well as with the First Lady’s Office on a national barrier free initiative and school nutrition reform.  
UNICEF played a leading role in sector coordination in the humanitarian sphere (co)-leading the education, WASH and Child Protection Areas of Responsibilities clusters as well as within the Ukraine Donor Platform in education (led by Ministry of Education and Science and co-led with the Embassy of Finland) and social protection (led by the Ministry of Social Policy and co-led with the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office) sectors. In addition, UNICEF served a critical role in gathering partners, particularly International Financial Institutions, in the Water Supply and Sanitation (WSS) recovery group, with critical participation of the Ministry for Communities and Territories Development.  
UNICEF undertook dedicated efforts in 2024 to strengthen its partnership with the Ministry of Finance as a means of strengthening child-rights budgeting at local and national levels and safeguarding social sector financing for children. These efforts contributed to increases in government budget allocation for key child-related sectors in 2025, with an increase of 40% from the state budget to the education sector and an increase of 45% to the reconstruction of water systems. 
At the decentralized level, UNICEF made significant efforts to strengthen partnerships with districts to ensure sustainable programme investments and leverage greater resources for children’s services. An example of the impact of this partnership is that of the collaboration with local authorities in Poltava region, where local authorities initiated co-funding of an early intervention service for children with developmental disabilities. In Kharkiv city, UNICEF worked with local authorities and the Government of Germany to jointly finance a school in the Maselskogo metro station, which allowed children to attend in-person schooling. 
Partners were consulted during the launch of the 2025-2029 Country Programme Document (CPD) and provided critical assistance, particularly for winter-related needs. In 2024, public sector partners - including Governments and International Financial Institutions (IFIs) - supported UNICEF’s programmes by providing essential financial resources and political backing for children’s initiatives. Around 20 public partners as well as the UNICEF family of National Committees – fundraising through individuals, companies, foundations - renewed or established support for both humanitarian action and development programming for a direct country-level contribution of 329 million USD. Beyond financial contributions, public partners acted as principled advocates for children’s rights, advocating for ensuring the best interests of children in return and reintegration efforts. UNICEF influenced non-financial commitments, notably advocating for a focus on human capital in bilateral engagements. This included the Ukraine Recovery Conference in Germany, which prioritized education and social inclusion, and the Ukraine Mine Action Conference in Switzerland, which highlighted the soft elements of mine action. Further, UNICEF National Committees facilitated awareness and advocacy by engaging Members of Parliament and securing news media coverage.  
 
Additional partnership forums through which UNICEF planned and implemented humanitarian action in 2024 included the Access Working Group and the Humanitarian Operations Planning Cell (HOPC) – the latter of which allowed UN agencies to organize and execute interagency convoys to the most hard-to-reach, insecure locations. Within the UN Transition Framework for Ukraine coordination structure, UNICEF co-chaired the Human Capital Working Group and a Data Taskforce in support of more integrated and coherent UN programming.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges 
UNICEF’s programmatic response in Ukraine in 2024 encountered significant challenges. With a reduced allocation of funding for the social sectors and a high dependency of social sector financing at state level from international aid and loans, the sustainability of national recovery efforts has been affected.  
The institutional capacities of national partners have been further stretched, particularly in service delivery at decentralized levels, with limited numbers and inequitable allocations of staff across the social service workforce. This has been further exacerbated by the fast pace of ongoing reforms recommended by the EU accession process. Despite the importance of responding to multi-dimensional deprivations faced by children, efforts to invest in long-term initiatives have been hampered by the limited scope of interventions funded under humanitarian response programmes. In spite of advocacy efforts from across the United Nations agencies, UNICEF was not able to respond in occupied areas of Ukraine through crossline modalities.   

Lessons Learned  
To respond to these challenges UNICEF’s response has addressed humanitarian and recovery needs through strengthening national systems, which has been proven to be effective under UNICEF’ initiatives at the decentralized level but also with key initiatives at the national level. As part of UNICEF’s recovery response at the decentralized level, diverse models of service provision have been rolled up for a future scale-up to inform the national agenda. One key example has been the case of the collaboration with the Ministry of Social Policy of Ukraine and the Coordination Center of Family Upbringing and Child Care Development in promoting and strengthening family-based care forms as one of the key priorities under the Better Care Reform agenda.  
Another lesson learned has been the importance of generating and utilizing robust data to inform rapidly evolving humanitarian and recovery interventions. In 2024, UNICEF's programmatic response continued to be data-driven with additional analysis to better understand children and community vulnerabilities. UNICEF supported a large-scale household survey conducted across 73 nexus and recovery districts, providing representative data on gaps and needs in key services for children and their families. This was complemented by a detailed mapping of social services across prioritised districts. In addition, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Policy to undertake a national survey on the ‘Perception and Awareness of Social Policy in Ukraine’ which provided insights into public opinion regarding the effectiveness of Ukraine's social protection schemes. UNICEF's ability to respond swiftly to emergency situations was enabled by contingency planning and preparedness measures. These included cash registration for families in frontline areas, contingency allocations integrated into implementing partnerships, and the strategic prepositioning of essential stocks. Digital and cash-based solutions also proved effective in enhancing service delivery and reaching children in need.  Further, UNICEF's pre-established partnerships with utility bodies and streamlined procurement systems enabled rapid repairs of energy systems while building longer-term resilience. The establishment of dedicated coordination cells proved highly effective in mobilizing partners to respond to the emergency brought on by damage to the heating infrastructure, offering a model for other sectors.  
Strengthening the capacity of national and local authorities in child-responsive public financial management has been essential to ensure the sustainability of UNICEF-supported interventions and services. By involving authorities in developing child- and youth-centered budgets, UNICEF has enabling sustained impact, strengthening the ability of authorities to secure external funding by demonstrating their commitment to prioritizing children and youth.     

Future Outlook  
UNICEF will continue contributing to the child and youth-centered recovery efforts in Ukraine. In the framework of the new Country Programme Document (CPD), UNICEF will build sustainable partnerships with the Government of Ukraine at national and decentralized levels and advocate for gender responsive and child-centred resource allocations across government systems.   
In response to the demographic crisis caused by a significant population decline of over 10 million people in the past 10 years, a low birth rate, and an aging population, the Government has developed a national strategy for demographic development until 2040. The strategy provides key entry points to continue promoting children’s rights in the country, which includes actions to improve reproductive health, overcome negative stereotypes about parenthood, and provide comprehensive social protection support for families. 
Based on the positive results achieved by UNICEF in 2024, work on humanitarian preparedness will be enhanced, particularly through a robust monitoring system to better track and respond to emerging needs. An evaluability assessment will be completed, aiming at identifying areas for reinforcing and adjusting UNICEF’s monitoring and evaluation system, intervention logic and approach to scale up and replication, and fostering accountability and results ownership among key programme stakeholders. The results of this assessment are expected to enhance and further refine UNICEF’s programme priorities in 2025. 
Looking ahead, while immediate humanitarian needs remain acute with continuous attacks on critical infrastructure, UNICEF will continue to invest in strengthening the resilience of social sectors. With recovery needs estimated at USD 11.1 billion for 2024-2033, the risk of system collapse could multiply manyfold, requiring sustained support to maintain essential services while advancing critical reforms. UNICEF will accelerate support for critical reforms across social sectors, with a particular focus on the child-related programmes and targets articulated within Ukraine’s plan for EU accession.

The Angolan economy showed signs of recovery in 2024, with four per cent expected growth, marking the strongest annual expansion in many years. While in 2023 the national currency saw a rapid depreciation of 40 per cent, the exchange rate market stabilised in 2024 with a gradual depreciation.  However, this increased the debt burden in Angola, a sizeable part of which is denominated in foreign currency. In 2024, some 59 per cent of the State Budget was allocated to service the debt, constraining Government investments in key services for children. State budget allocations for education and health at 6.4 and 5.5 per cent respectively, are well below internationally agreed targets. Moreover, the budget’s execution rates for the social sectors remain low.
  
Rising global food prices, a weaker Kwanza, and reduction of fuel subsidies have kept inflation at around 30 per cent, eroding household purchasing power. Additionally, Angola was added to the inter-governmental Financial Action Task Force's "grey list" in 2024, which means that the country is considered to have strategic deficiencies, which could lead to a higher cost of living, job losses, and even reduced access to services due to the potential impact on Angola’s international trade and finance obligations. 
  
UNICEF supported the National Institute of Statistics (INE) to collect updated data on children by providing technical assistance to the 2023-2024 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and the 2024 Census. This provides the Government with recent data to better plan and budget services that are focused on child rights. The DHS included key modules on children, and both the DHS and the 2024 Census included questions on disabilities, using the Washington Group question sets for the first time. 
 
Vulnerable families were supported through the approval of a second phase of the national cash transfer programme called Kwenda, which now includes a component on human capital with a focus on early childhood and nutrition. With $320 million in funding from the World Bank and an additional $100 million from the Angolan Government, Kwenda is designed to mitigate a situation where 40 per cent of Angolans live below the national monetary poverty line through supporting 1.6 million vulnerable households.
  
The 2024 DHS Key Indicators Report reveals several notable positive  trends including the decline in under-five mortality from 68 per thousand live births in the 2016 DHS to 52; a similar decline in the neonatal  mortality from 24 to 16; the fertility rate has fallen from 6.2 children per woman of reproductive age to 4.8; pregnancy-related mortality reduced from 239 to 185 deaths  per 100,000 live births; and  a 15 percentage point increase in children under five years of age with  symptoms of acute respiratory infection who received advice or treatment in a  health facility or by a health professional. However, the percentage of fully vaccinated children aged 12 to 23 months fell slightly from 31 to 29 per cent; chronic malnutrition in children under-five increased from 38 to 40 per cent; and there was a decline from 38 to 33 per cent in children under six months exclusively fed with breast milk.
  
The Government continues making efforts to strengthen the health workforce, including through a US$200 million World Bank-supported programme to train over 30,000 professionals. However, while a policy has been drafted, efforts to institutionalise Community Health Workers within Angola’s health system have not progressed as needed. On the other hand, Angola joined the G20 Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty, committing to targeted actions to combat malnutrition, showing high-level commitment to early childhood development (ECD) and nutrition. 
  
In January, a case of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 prompted an urgent and successful response of polio vaccination campaigns, reaching over six million children. However, this public health emergency constrained progress on routine immunization and was a key factor in postponing the introduction of the HPV to the first quarter of 2025. Angola was also impacted by the El Niño climate event, exacerbating persistent drought conditions particularly in the southern provinces.
  
High learning poverty and an estimated out-of-school population of 3.8 million are persistent challenges for the education sector. In 2024, the Government published the National Learning Assessment 2022-2023 in the context of adopting public policies aimed at improving the overall quality of education. This assessment highlighted concerning statistics: only 37 per cent of Grade 4 students could locate explicit text information, and 14 per cent of Grade 6 students could perform metric conversions. The Ministry of Education (MED) pledged to address these issues by publishing learning outcome data and focusing on the quality of foundational learning.  Angola established a Local Education Group (LEG) to enhance sector coordination and foster dialogue among government, development partners, and non-governmental organizations. 
   
Access to basic drinking water and basic sanitation remain low at 58 and 52 per cent respectively, with marked disparities between rural and urban populations. The financial sustainability of water and sanitation service providers is undermined by outdated tariffs, dependency on imported materials, and inadequate government funding. In January 2024, the  operationalisation of the National Forum of Water and Sanitation (FONAS) marked a significant milestone in national sector coordination. However, the absence of approved budgets and implementation plans for strategies like climate change adaptation and Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) continues to hinder progress. 
  
The Government aims to issue 20 million identity cards by 2026. While decentralising document production could ease registration bottlenecks in Luanda, the decision to replace birth certificates with identity cards for voter eligibility raises concerns about birth registration for children under-five.
  
One in ten girls aged 20-24 experienced sexual violence, while 26 per cent of girls between 15-19 have experienced physical violence. High-level commitments were made by the government at the Global Conference on Ending Violence against Children held in Colombia to address violence against children (VAC) and women in 2024. Furthermore, the First Lady launched the "We Are All Equal" campaign to combat gender-based violence and promote gender equality, particularly protecting children.

UNICEF focused on system strengthening for improved child and adolescent health, nutrition, immunization, newborn care, mental health and prevention of vertical transmission of HIV. This work contributed to reduced child mortality, increased vaccination numbers, and enhanced nutrition while supporting efforts to overcome supply bottlenecks and promoting equitable access to essential services. UNICEF contributed to improving service delivery by supporting the collection of disaggregated data to identify gaps. The data, combined with monitoring and evaluation, guided strategic decisions to scale up integrated management of childhood illness services and expand access to adolescent sexual and reproductive health services and HIV prevention.
   
UNICEF's advocacy and technical assistance advanced Angola's health system policy framework through updated policies such as the Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health Strategy, the National Immunization Strategy, and the National Food Security and Nutrition Strategy. The finalised Community Health Strategic Plan, for which UNICEF  provided critical technical leadership and support, represents a key milestone, setting the stage for equitable health service delivery in underserved areas. Furthermore, UNICEF’s advocacy successfully influenced a significant increase in the 2025 State Budget for community health programmes, enabling a greater focus on primary health care.
  
UNICEF scaled up efforts to combat malnutrition through humanitarian action, screening more than one million children under-five and treating over 91,000 of these children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM). A cure rate of 82 per cent and a mortality rate reduced from a high of over 10 per cent in 2019 to one per cent this year was achieved through community-driven  solutions, such as the expansion of mother-to-mother and father-to-father  support groups. These facilitated SAM screenings and reinforced positive nutrition practices. A gender barrier analysis for Vitamin A supplementation, is being used to inform the development of national immunization and  nutrition strategies. 
  
UNICEF played a pivotal role in supporting the Ministry of Health (MINSA) in planning and implementing three rounds of polio campaigns, in response to vaccine-derived polio outbreaks.  High coverage was achieved with more than six million children reached; 162 out of 164 municipalities achieved over 95 per cent coverage, marking a substantial improvement from 2023. Additionally, UNICEF provided technical assistance and support to other multiple public health emergencies including maternal and neonatal tetanus, Mpox, and measles outbreaks. 
  
UNICEF continued to make strides toward universal immunization  with strong support from Gavi to strengthen the planning and implementation of routine immunisation and supplementary immunisation activities. Consequently, the number of zero-dose children receiving their first dose of the pentavalent vaccine surged by 198 per cent compared to 2023, with 248,133 children vaccinated. Coverage for the third dose of pentavalent vaccine (Penta 3) rose to 70 per cent (660,275 children), while coverage for the first dose reached 86 per cent (772,320 children), demonstrating steady progress toward improving vaccination coverage. However, equity gaps  persisted in routine immunization, with fewer municipalities meeting coverage  targets, which will require innovative delivery models to address disparities.  
  
Supervision visits were conducted across five provinces to assess  retention on antiretroviral therapy and service quality in 131 health facilities, with 39,526 records reviewed to strengthen data collection and  monitoring. A UN Joint advocacy mission promoted the Global Alliance to End  Paediatric AIDS, effectively mobilising local resources. Additionally, the  reactivation of a People Living with HIV network enhanced community leadership and representation in Angola’s HIV response.   
  
UNICEF’s efforts to support education in Angola prioritised addressing bottlenecks in sector coordination and  education financing as critical for education reforms in Angola. Through  UNICEF’s leadership, the LEG expanded to 23 active members and held regular  meetings to drive policy dialogue and resource mobilisation. A key achievement in this regard was UNICEF’s coordination of a US$50 million grant  application to strengthen teacher capacity that has been secured and assigned to the World Bank. Additionally, UNICEF led the drafting of a system capacity grant application that will fund strategic deliverables in 2025 including comprehensive sector analysis and sector planning.   
  
Throughout 2024, UNICEF provided  embedded technical assistance to MED through the LEG Secretariat. UNICEF’s efforts in leading and coordinating policy dialogue for systems change  resulted in finalising the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) Compact and an action plan to address recommendations from the independent GPE assessment. 
  
Advocacy efforts led by UNICEF, together with other partners such as the Association for the Development of Education in Africa and the Southern Africa Community for Development, in the context of the African Union Year of Education, elevated  foundational learning as a national priority. This is reflected in the development of the National Plan for the Improvement of Learning Outcomes 2024-2027 (PNA), which integrates UNICEF’s remedial education programme based on the Teaching at the Right Level approach.
  
UNICEF initiated the rollout of the Aprendizagem na Idade Certa (AIC, ‘Learning at the right time’) pilot remedial  education programme during the 2024-2025 academic year, benefiting 36,574 students (18,838 girls) across seven municipalities in four provinces. A total of 662 teachers and pedagogical directors (528 women) received training in delivering remedial education in the Portuguese language and mathematics to Grade 3-5 students. There are strong signs of increased buy-in from MED for the gradual scaling up of the programme, by including it as a key PNA intervention. Additionally, UNICEF contributed directly to improving access to quality education for 59,789 children (30,250 girls) and fostering skills development for 848 youth (398 girls).    
  
UNICEF promoted youth engagement in decision-making in collaboration with the EU, the Netherlands embassy, the Ministry of Youth and Sports, and the Ministry of Planning (MINPLAN). Two provincial Youth Forums gathered 119 young people (47 young women) and local  decision-makers to promote the importance of involving young voices in shaping policies and systems that directly impact their learning and development. UNICEF launched Angola’s first Youth Challenge, attracting 171 teams (including 248 young women) in developing innovative solutions to  community challenges. The initiative culminated in a Youth Fair attended by  300 participants. The concurrent launch of a youth landscape analysis, produced by UNICEF, provided a clear roadmap for the implementation of Generation Unlimited as a strategic tool to align stakeholders around a shared youth agenda.
  
Programmes focused on the protection of children continued  throughout 2024, with Angola joining the Global Alliance on Violence Against Children (VAC) and making a firm commitment to combat VAC while attending the inter-ministerial Conference held in Colombia. Three high-level commitments were made: the legal review and strengthening of the criminalization of violence against  children, especially sexual violence; improving coordination mechanisms between child protection actors and services; and an overall increase in the  budget allocations for child protection by 2027. The Special Representative to the Secretary General (SRSG) on VAC was invited by the Government to visit Angola in June 2025 to witness Angola’s efforts to address VAC.
  
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Social Action, Family, and Women’s Promotion (MASFAMU) in the public consultation processes for the revision of the Law on Domestic Violence (Lei n.º 25/12) in five provinces (Malanje, Lunda Norte, Lunda Sul, Uije and Cuanza Norte). UNICEF advocated for an expansion of the concept of domestic violence to include key issues such as VAC, tackling the legal  gap attached to a minimum age for sexual consent, prohibition of child  marriage, corporal punishment, and witchcraft accusations.
  
UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Justice and  Human Rights (MINJUSDH) on  a comprehensive assessment of the civil registration and vital statistics  system in Angola to identify key bottlenecks and make recommendations for an operational plan. The assessment gathered 80 participants from MINJUSDH in all provinces, MINSA (Directors of Statistics and of Public Health) and MINPLAN to co-create interventions that are to be urgently put in place to scale up civil registration, particularly birth registration.
  
Child marriage is widespread in Angola with one in three girls being married before the age of 18 but there is limited information on the underlying causes. So, an ethnographic study on child marriage was conducted jointly with MASFAMU in provinces with high incidence in northern Angola (Malanje and Lunda Norte provinces). Preliminary findings revealed critical information such as peer  pressure to get married, and pregnancy being used by girls to get married and  leave their parents’ homes. This evidence will inform the design of targeted interventions in 2025. In parallel, a guide on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) integrating mental  health components  was finalised and will be the foundation for a new programme aiming for the  prevention of teenage pregnancy,  Minha Kamba, a girl-to-girl approach for peer dissemination of information and support.   
  
UNICEF’s work in WASH and Climate, Environment, Energy, and Disaster Risk  Reduction (CEED) led to the operationalisation of FONAS in  January 2024. The first joint sector review, co-led by UNICEF, took place in  October 2024, involving 32 entities (ministries, water utilities, civil  society, and the private sector) and 57 officials. UNICEF published  the WASH sector budget brief and advocated for more investment in the WASH sector. These actions resulted in an increase in the 2025 State Budget for water (39 per cent) and sanitation (63 per cent).
  
UNICEF continued to implement three projects focusing on ensuring access to WASH for vulnerable groups: the CLTS pilot project was concluded this year, while the ‘More Water More Life’ regional initiative on deep groundwater mapping and simplified sanitation for peri-urban areas will be finalised in 2025. UNICEF’s direct efforts in community engagement and social and behaviour change resulted in 25,069  people (6,299 women, 5,512 men, 7,200 girls, 6,085 boys, including 277 persons with disabilities) using at least basic sanitation and handwashing  facilities, of which 12,474 people now live in communities free of open defecation. Through humanitarian response to drought (supported by the Central Emergency Response Fund), UNICEF  rehabilitated 33 water solar systems in the municipalities of Lubango, Chibia  and Humpata, reaching a total of 68,183 people (16,281 men, 19,010 women, 14,826 boys, 18,066 girls, including 759 persons with disabilities) with safe water.
  
To strengthen evidence-based decision making around climate issues, UNICEF completed a comprehensive assessment of quantitative datasets and analysis of the biophysical climate indicators to identify the bottlenecks that prevent national stakeholders from making data-driven  decisions. The results were grouped into two categories: hazard exposure and child vulnerability, replicating the Children’s Climate Risk Index and will feed into the planned Digital Public Good Integrated Information Management System to support data-driven decision making for WASH and climate sectors.  
  
Following the first National Youth and Climate Forum held in October 2023, UNICEF  co-designed with the Ministry of Environment (MINAMB) the “Youth and Climate Action Plan 2025-2026”. The Action Plan defines three main objectives: (1) Strengthen youth capacity building to create meaningful environmental education  opportunities for young people to learn about climate change; (2) Promote youth civic engagement through volunteering and supporting the "Environment Volunteer Programme"; and (3) Empower youth advocacy for change. This is a milestone step demonstrating commitment from MINAMB to engage with UNICEF to improve youth participation in the climate and environment area.
  
As part of a South-South cooperation initiative on simplified  sanitation systems, two important booklets were developed: one on social  mobilisation for simplified sanitation; the other on technical guidance for designing simplified sewage collection systems. These technical guides orient  government entities and builders on contextualising simplified sanitation in Africa. They are already being used by other actors in Angola, as simplified sanitation is planned for dense, low-income settlements in many cities across the country. The guides have  been translated into English and are now being utilised by Eswatini, which is planning to initiate simplified sanitation projects through South-South cooperation. 
  
UNICEF’s engagement in social policy and social protection led to increased resources for children, improved data on children and child poverty, and a more child-sensitive  social protection system, contributing to Angola's broader development goals. UNICEF's technical assistance to INE supported generation of high-quality  data on children, including on children with disabilities, particularly through the 2023-2024 DHS and the 2024 Census. Training of INE statisticians contributed to the analyses and preparation of the survey reports, ensuring that child indicators were accurately represented. 
  
UNICEF is supporting the update of Angola's Multidimensional  Poverty Index (MPI) to include measures on child and women’s poverty. Through building capacity and convening key stakeholders, in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Multidimensional Poverty Initiative, UNICEF is contributing to the update of Angola's MPI to provide a clearer understanding of the causes, patterns, and  locations of child poverty. These efforts led to UNICEF's involvement in a task force to redesign the country’s Poverty Reduction Programme and contributed to successful advocacy for Angola to join the G20 Global Alliance against Hunger and Poverty. 
  
To enhance the effectiveness of poverty-reduction policies in addressing child poverty, UNICEF provided technical assistance and led advocacy that influenced the design of the second phase of Angola’s flagship cash transfers programme, Kwenda. These efforts resulted in the integration of a dedicated human capital component focusing on young children’s  vulnerabilities, including ECD, nutrition, and birth registration, with a budget of US$60 million. This represents a significant step forward in mainstreaming child-focused  solutions into national social protection systems.   
  
UNICEF generated high-quality evidence that advanced advocacy efforts with key stakeholders at all levels, including the Ministry of Finance (MINFIN), MINPLAN and Parliament, resulting in significant nominal budget increases for several key social sectors vis-à-vis 2024, Education (43 per cent), Health (46 per  cent), Sanitation (54 per cent), and Social Protection (62 per cent), as well  as disability inclusion (200 per cent). UNICEF produced eight comprehensive budget briefs on the 2024 State Budget, analysing prioritisation, equity, and efficiency across social sectors. In addition, three new budget briefs on Gender, Disability and Inclusion, and  Child Protection were introduced, which fuelled advocacy throughout the year, driving strategic engagement including with the Minister of Finance.  
  
Two high-level Roundtables organized with MINFIN, one on Sanitation  and another on Education Financing, boosted advocacy for increased allocations. UNICEF produced an analysis of the State Budget Proposal and presented it to key Commissions in Parliament during the debate period, which positively influenced final allocations to the social sectors for 2025, with further  increases in allocation for health (2.1 per cent), notably a doubling of the allocation to the Community Health Workforce; education (one per cent), with greater transparency on  the pre-primary allocation; and social protection (2.3 per cent). UNICEF continued to provide technical assistance to MINFIN to increase budget transparency and participation, which led to the production and dissemination of a Citizens Budget, the timely publishing of key budget documents, a more detailed State Budget Proposal document, including disability-related lines, the reinstatement of gender markers in the 2025 State Budget, and consultation with civil society organizations, including Organizations of Persons with Disabilities. 
  
UNICEF focused on promoting evidence generation, capacity  development and mainstreaming the Social and Behaviour Change (SBC)  approach in national and subnational government departments.
