To fill data gaps in demand promotion, the first rapid assessment of polio was implemented in 16 provinces. A Huila pilot for community mapping  of zero-dose children identified 80,000 zero-dose children and a health promotion skill assessment is being implemented to better understand the capacity of health promotion among health personnel.
  
UNICEF and the World Bank strengthened SBC capacity through training of health staff in all provinces on interpersonal communication, evidence generation, and community engagement during the National Ecosystem of Health Promotion Week Workshop, resulting in provinces developing draft proposals of health promotion action plans. 
  
UNICEF supported the National Directorate of Public Health to develop an immunization strategy with a strong SBC focus and is supporting  the drafting of the first National Health Promotion Strategy, which includes a routine immunization advocacy plan focused on media and community  engagement. Recognising the importance of social norms to promote positive practices, UNICEF supported the Provincial Government of Luanda to establish the Alliance of Religious Leaders for Health, including diverse representatives from different religions.   
  
UNICEF is mainstreaming gender and disability across all programmes and implementing targeted actions to ensure UNICEF works as a champion for inclusion of girls and for children  with disabilities. To support this, a series of capacity-building sessions on  gender, advocacy, and communication with women and youth-led organizations  were organized. Three major gender-focused projects are being implemented in partnership with the Government to address gender and social norms: the Vitamin A Supplementation in a New Age project; the HPV+ initiative; and the  teenage pregnancy prevention project. Multiple advocacy events, such as Zero Discrimination Day, International Women’s Day, and International Day of the  Girl, were supported to reach approximately 1,500 people. The first Gender  Budget Brief was produced, leading to the reintroduction of gender markers in the 2025 State Budget.
  
UNICEF aimed to address key programme gaps and building service capacities for disability inclusion. This took the form of advocacy for broader disability data in the 2024 Census, ensuring the collection of critical data for better planning and budgeting for children with disabilities. UNICEF also conducted its first analysis of the State Budget through a disability and  inclusion lens, revealing that only 0.12 per cent of the 2024 Budget was  allocated to disability-related programmes. This insight facilitated high-level engagement with MINFIN and parliamentarians that resulted in a 200 per cent increase in allocation for disability-related programmes in the 2025  Budget. Furthermore, children with disabilities were at the centre of  the agenda in the event to celebrate the 35th Anniversary of the  Convention on the Rights of the Child at Parliament, resulting in lawmakers committing to advocacy and better implementation of children's rights.
  
While transitioning to a more upstream programming approach, fully recognising the importance of evaluations for accountability and learning, UNICEF actively engaged government partners and other stakeholders in the two strategic costed evaluations (the AIC pilot remedial education  programme and the National Immunization Programme) initiated in 2024. UNICEF also supported national evaluation capacity development through promoting evaluation champions in the key government ministry, MINPLAN, sponsoring them to attend the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders and organizing introductory hybrid evaluation training for over 100 participants from the Departments of Studies, Planning and Statistics of 25 ministries. These efforts laid a good foundation for continued engagement with key government personnel to establish an evaluation culture in Angola.

UNICEF’s partnership with the Government successfully advanced national priorities toward the realisation of children’s rights in 2024. Importantly, the Parliament sought closer collaboration with UNICEF, demonstrating the value of UNICEF’s evidence-based analysis on public finance, as well as on key issues such as malnutrition and food insecurity. The status of the rights of children and persons with disabilities were discussed with parliamentarians at high-level events hosted by the Parliament. UNICEF’s technical expertise was also sought for nutrition, and this was effective in advocating for children’s rights in crucial parliamentary debates, including on the State Budget proposal. 
 
Working closely with MINSA, UNICEF strengthened Angola’s immunisation programme by supporting three rounds of polio vaccination campaigns. In its education work, UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with ministries such as the Ministries of Planning, Youth and Sports, Public Administration, Labour and Social Security, as well as MED. These partnerships focused on critical areas such as the school-to-work transition, youth participation in local governance, and inclusive development, ensuring alignment with Angola’s National Development Plan (2023-2027) and the Ministry of Youth and Sport’s Strategic Youth Development Plan (2023-2027). 
 
UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with MASFAMU and with MINJUSDH through joint field missions, international missions, and weekly engagement on joint interventions. This built trust and fostered closer relationships with these key government actors for child protection, laying groundwork for their uptake of a systems approach going forward.
 
UNICEF established a new partnership with the Ministry of Interior through initiating the review of the current law enforcement system in relation to violence against children and women, bringing in the Institute of Legal Medicine as a key player within the child protection system. UNICEF engaged with the Office of the Attorney General to strengthen coordination mechanisms on ending VAC and worked with judges, including the Chief Judge of Luanda, to elevate the issue of child justice to the Supreme Court in 2025.
 
The operationalisation of FONAS is a major achievement for partnership and collaboration within the WASH sector in 2024 under the leadership of the Ministry of Energy and Water (MINEA). Alliances around FONAS were further strengthened with the support of the Sanitation and Water for All global partnership. 
 
Through continuous interaction with key institutions such as INE and the Institute of Local Governance, at both technical and management levels, UNICEF has been part of strategic decision-making within these institutions and influenced key areas of their work. Specifically, UNICEF provided technical input and engagement in key government initiatives including the Census, DHS, the second phase of Kwenda, the revision of the National Poverty Reduction Strategy and international opportunities such as the Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty.
 
Civil society organization (CSO) partners, such as People in Need, PanAfricare and World Vision, were among the key partners on the ground, to deliver essential social services for targeted populations in drought-affected and disaster-prone areas. Enhancing water security, the key aim of the More Water More Life initiative (supported by Thematic Funding Pools), benefited from partnership with the private sector, institutes such as the Geological Institute of Angola, and the University of Agostinho Neto. A women-led CSO, Mwana Pwo, was engaged to support a girl-to-girl approach to increase girls’ knowledge on sexual and reproductive health and rights, prevent teenage pregnancy and HPV and address harmful social and gender norms. UNICEF’s work with the Angolan Paediatric Society continued in 2024, expanding advocacy work on the integrated management of acute malnutrition. 
 
UNICEF’s partnership with UNDP, with technical assistance from the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, was successful in advancing the multidimensional poverty agenda supporting INE to measure multidimensional poverty at the national, municipal, child and women’s levels.
 
UNICEF worked with the World Health Organization, World Food Programme (WFP), the Food and Agriculture Organization and the UN Refugee’s Agency (UNHCR) to prepare the National Action Plan on Wasting. Once approved, this will enable the Government to continue to access the Child Nutrition Fund for procuring essential nutrition supplies. UNICEF also collaborated with these same agencies and the EU-funded resilience programme, FRESAN, on food security and nutrition data collection to support an Integrated Phase Classification analysis. 
 
Collaboration with UN agencies, such as UNHCR, the United Nations Population Fund, UNDP and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS, was critical in strengthening the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse agenda. This included providing training to the Government and civil society partners, advocacy on gender inequality, and violence against women and girls as part of efforts to bring the Spotlight Initiative to Angola and strengthening inter-agency collaboration on human right violations in general, particularly under the coordination of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.
 
UNICEF worked closely with WFP and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs to mobilise funds and implement a humanitarian response to communities impacted by El Niño drought and flood conditions.
 
The European Investment Bank provided financial resources to conduct national polio campaigns; while the U.S. Agency for International Development supported cold chain strengthening in Angola through funding the procurement and installation of 280 solar-powered refrigerators. The Government of Korea also supported interventions to reach zero-dose children and a piloting simulation laboratory in Huila to improve newborn care, ensuring that the most vulnerable populations have access to life-saving services. Long-standing support from UNICEF National Committees from the USA and Japan, was broadened with new engagement with the National Committee of Finland.
 
The Banco de Fomento Angola continued to make financial contributions to support UNICEF’s efforts of retaining children in schools and addressing malnutrition in vulnerable communities. The partnership with UNITEL provided free SMS for U-Report in Angola and free internet for the Internet of Good Things. 
 
Other stakeholders including the International Monetary Fund, World Bank, and other international financial institutions such as the African Development Bank were important partners in 2024 and sought UNICEF’s technical expertise on child and disability-sensitive social protection, data collection, and on the public finance for children and budget analysis of social sectors in Angola, including during Article IV missions.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF’s work in 2024 demonstrated the importance of inter-sectoral coordination but also revealed challenges in initiating, sustaining and strengthening effective collaboration among key actors. In the WASH sector for example, UNICEF’s dedicated technical support and advocacy to MINEA led to the operationalisation of FONAS after 14 years and the first joint sector review with several other ministries. However, external support for coordination is anticipated to continue, reflecting the reality that there are not enough human resources in key ministries with both adequate coordination skills and dedicated time for inter-sectoral collaboration. In the education sector, considering the complexity of out-of-school children issue, cross-sectoral coordination is key to strengthen the availability, quality and accountability of data on out-of-school children, to accelerate efforts in addressing school exclusion and improving access to quality education. UNICEF will continue to offer technical assistance and play a convening role in the Inter-Ministry Coordination Group to keep children in school or provide viable alternative pathways for education and skills development. 
 
Similarly, UNICEF faced challenges to increase child protection services due to limited intersectoral commitment among key sector actors to addressing VAC, despite laws and standard operating procedures having been put in place. This led to cases not being referred to relevant services and data not being aggregated to provide an accurate picture of the situation. However, the involvement of MASFAMU in the Global Ministerial Meeting on Ending VAC in Colombia and the preparatory work with the SRSG on VAC, has been critical in raising this issue and positioning it as one of the Government’s key commitments. A goal has been established to strengthen intersectoral collaboration on ending VAC, ahead of the planned visit of the SRSG in 2025.
 
Disparities in health service access and quality across provinces remained a pressing concern. Despite notable successes, persistent equity gaps, particularly in marginalised and remote areas, continued to be a challenge in 2024. Angola’s immunization programme is an example. The decline in the number of provinces achieving Penta coverage of 80 per cent or more, fell from 69 out of 164 municipalities in 2023 to just 50 in 2024. This indicates that, while success was seen in polio vaccination campaigns, routine immunization services struggled to reach certain populations, especially in hard-to-reach provinces. 
 
Looking ahead, UNICEF will focus on advocacy and technical support for scaling up integrated health services through primary health care, prioritising underserved and marginalised populations to ensure equitable access. Advocacy for increased investments in cold chain infrastructure, timely vaccine procurement, and the approval of the Community Health Strategic Plan will remain a priority. 
 
UNICEF also encountered challenges in human resources and institutional capacity. For example, in education, the roll-out of the AIC pilot programme revealed challenges, including weak supervision systems and significant gaps in teacher capacity, which may impact programme implementation. In the future, UNICEF’s technical support to ensure the link between policy systems and the classroom will be critical to assess the effectiveness and viability of this innovative model to address the learning crisis in Angola. Likewise, overlapping health priorities, such as multiple rounds of polio vaccination campaigns, stretched the already at-capacity human resources and institutional resources, preventing MINSA from investing more on maternal and newborn health initiatives and nutrition. UNICEF’s technical assistance and policy advocacy will continue to play a vital role in supporting MINSA to address these systemic bottlenecks.
 
There are relatively few CSO partners with experience of implementing interventions on gender-related issues in Angola. UNICEF intensified efforts in 2024 to identify more local partners, i.e. youth and women-led organizations, to engage on gender equality and supporting vulnerable adolescent girls. However, the capacity of these organizations was found to be limited, so UNICEF organized a series of capacity-building sessions on gender, human rights, and communication skills. Moving ahead, hand-holding support and technical assistance will be provided to build local capacity in gender-transformative programming and ensuring the realisation of vulnerable adolescent girls’ rights.
 
The limited fiscal space in Angola posed a challenge for translating key recommendations and action points of UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy into concrete policies and implementation of child-sensitive data collection, social protection and public finance actions. This challenge is further accentuated by the high debt-servicing burden, as well as the size of the informal economy. The demographic reality of 1.3 million children born each year is often cited as another constraint to expanding social services at the necessary rate and in line with international targets for investments and budgets for the sectors. 
 
Insufficient budget allocation to address health and nutrition challenges is an example of the struggle. Despite positive advocacy results obtained in 2024, witnessing increased budgets for key programmes such as National Programme for Immunization and for Community Health, the prevalence of stunting remains very high. Addressing stunting requires high-level, multi-sector commitment and coordination. UNICEF can support provincial level structures to generate evidence for children and review public finance budgeting and expenditure for health and nutrition to support informed decisions and investments, but significant investment from the Government of Angola and prioritisation is required.
 
Looking ahead, with UNICEF’s established technical expertise, there is a clear need for closer and broad-based stakeholder engagement to build capacity in planning and budgeting. This includes deeper exploration into key areas such as financing for education and WASH and aligning the nutrition and ECD components of the social protection programme with UNICEF global best practices. Furthermore, recognising the vulnerability of Angola to climate shocks, UNICEF will support the Government to implement climate adaptation and disaster risk reduction measures to address water and food insecurity.

Socio-economic outlook 


Botswana conducted general elections on 30th October 2024 with the opposition taking power in a peaceful transition for the first time since independence in 1966. The complete transition is expected to stretch into early 2025, including policy shifts which may have an impact on children. The new administration has established a Ministry of Child Welfare and Basic Education, signaling a high level of commitment for children's issues.


 


Botswana’s economy has successfully recovered from the effects of COVID-19, but has experienced sluggish economic growth in recent years, dropping from 6.7 per cent recorded in 2022 to 3.3 per cent in 2023.  The International Monetary Fund (IMF) conducted its 2024 Article IV consultation in July 2024, revealing a sharp decline in the country’s economic performance, from 5.5 per cent in 2022 to 2.7 per cent in 2023, driven primarily by reduced demand for diamonds, a key sector for Botswana’s economy. The current economic growth path remains insufficient to attain the policy targets of Vision 2036 (requiring a minimum of 5.7 per cent growth per annum), including making a significant impact on poverty reduction, addressing youth unemployment and attainment of a high-income country status [1]. 


 


Despite Botswana’s history of fiscal prudence, public finances have experienced significant pressures due to the sluggish global diamond market. The budget deficit is expected to deteriorate to 6per cent of GDP in 2024/25, sharply draining government reserves which may result in increased borrowing or expenditure cuts in the forthcoming fiscal years as the government attempts to close the gaps. This will inevitably impact provision of critical services to children.


 


Key issues and challenges 


Botswana’s population continues to grow, albeit at a decreasing rate with a current child population of 36 per cent. The share of the population living in extreme poverty stands at 13.5 per cent and is over four times higher than predicted by Botswana’s GDP per capita [2]. The pace of poverty reduction has stagnated in recent years and Botswana’s is one of the most unequal countries in the world, with a Gini coefficient of 0.53. The country faces high unemployment, especially among youth (25.9per cent overall, 34.4per cent for youth, (as of Q3 2023) [2]. Of greatest concern is the high unemployment rate among youth who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET) – up to 34per cent. The increase in the frequency and magnitude of climate change-related events (including the ongoing El Nino induced drought), especially higher temperatures have increasingly disrupted agricultural output and threatened livelihoods. 


 


Children continue to experience deprivations resulting in mortality and morbidity primarily driven by limited access to health services during the first decade of life. According to the 2023 Inter-agency Group for Mortality Estimation (IGME), infant and child mortality stood at 31 and 39 per 1,000/live births respectively, indicating limited progress in recent years.[3]The maternal mortality ratio has fluctuated in recent years, ranging from 127/ 100,000 live birth100,000 live births in 2015, to 240/ 100,000 live births 100,000 live births in 2021 and 89/100,000 live births in 2022.[4] Full routine immunization coverage rates for children aged 0-12 months have remained below pre-COVID-19 levels, with only 79 per cent of children receiving measles-rubella and only 75 per cent obtaining three doses of Diphtheria-Polio-Tetanus vaccine in 2024 (administrative data). 


With 5,100 children aged 0 to 14 years living with HIV, Botswana continued to implement recommendations in support of its ambition to reach gold tier status on the path to elimination of mother to child transmission, following the achievement of silver tier status in 2021. 


 


While Botswana lacks recent nationally representative data on malnutrition rates for children under five, figures on underweight prevalence from the 2024 Drought and Household Vulnerability Assessment indicate an increase from 3.7 per cent, 4.4 per cent, and 4.9 per cent between 2022 and 2024. It is to be expected that the prevalence of wasting and stunting in children under five (recorded at 5.1 per cent, 19.8 per cent and 3.5 per cent, respectively, for wasting, stunting and underweight based on 2016 data) may also be on the increase due to food insecurity linked to the ongoing drought.


 


While Botswana has achieved high levels of primary school enrolment (96.4 per cent in 2018), enrolment in pre-school for children 3 – 5 years old remains low at 49.5 per cent and is concentrated in urban areas with high levels of private sector provision. 


 


Adolescents aged 10 to 19 continue to experience deprivations related to their physical health, including HIV infection, early unintended pregnancy; exposure to violence; mental health; poor learning outcomes and unemployment, with adolescent girls remaining particularly vulnerable. 


 


In 2024, the Botswana Police Service reported 2,337 rape and defilement cases among girls. While there is no recent survey data on violence against children, this indicates that cases of violence against children (VAC) in Botswana remain high, as per the VAC survey which showed that 46 per cent of boys and 28 per cent of girls experienced physical violence. Sexual violence experienced by girls before the age of 18 stood at 9 per cent [5]. 


While data show that Botswana is on track to reach epidemic control for HIV in the general population over the next 2-3 years, adolescents and young people (AYP) are lagging. For example, 84.5 per cent of AYP are aware of their HIV status (compared to 95.1 per cent for adults), 98.5 per cent on ART (compared to 98 per cent for adults) and 77.1 per cent with viral load suppression (compared to 91.8 per cent for adults) [5]. Overall, only 58 per cent of children aged 0-14 are accessing treatment. 


 


The quality of education at secondary level remains a concern and adds to challenges faced by adolescents. Transition rates from lower secondary to upper secondary have dropped from 70.6 per cent in 2014 with fluctuations between 2018 and 2022, ranging from 56.7 per cent to 59.6 per cent. 


Credit pass rates for the Junior Secondary Certificate are as low as 35 per cent and 13 per cent for senior secondary and the curriculum is outdated and not responsive to the requirements of the labour market in the 21st century.

[2] IMF Country Report No.24/286


[3] IGME (2023): Levels and trends in child mortality. 2023 Report.


[4] Statistics Botswana (2022): Botswana maternal mortality ratio 2022.


[5] Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, 2018, Botswana Violence Against Children Survey

1. First Decade: 0 – 9 years
a. Every child survives and thrives
Following the occurrence of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases in 2023 and low immunization coverage (less than 50per cent children at 1 year are fully immunized), UNICEF Botswana focused its efforts in 2024 towards supporting the Ministry of Health in strategic planning, system strengthening and risk communication and community engagement to strengthen routine immunization and increase coverage. 
 
To set priorities for routine immunization and ensure that services are targeted and evidence-based, UNICEF in collaboration with WHO supported the development and finalization of the costed National Immunization Strategy (NIS) in 2024. The strategy is also expected to inform resource allocation and facilitate annual budgeting of routine immunization up to 2029. In tandem, UNICEF also supported the integration of COVID-19 into routine immunization and other primary health care services, through the development of a costed COVID-19 integration plan, thereby also strengthening emergency preparedness. 
 
Furthermore, UNICEF supported institutionalization of social listening and infodemic management within Ministry of Health, which was achieved through adoption of two social and community listening tools (Talkwalker and Africa Misinformation Portal (AMP)) and training of national and district focal persons on the tools. The establishment of a national infodemic management team within Ministry of Health following joint advocacy by UNICEF and WHO, is a sign of government commitment and ownership of social listening. UNICEF further supported immunization catch-up in 2 districts, Kweneng East and Kweneng West, which had coverage rate of about 40 per cent, reflecting challenges related to social norms and distance to health facilities. Through the intervention, more than 29,000 caregivers were reached with behavior change messaging at community level and more than 1,000 children per month were vaccinated. Additionally, over 100,000 parents and caregivers were reached with messaging on child health through other channels of communication such as Interactive Voice Response (IVR) and national print media. 
Finally, UNICEF continued to support the Government of Botswana to maintain silver-tier status on the path of elimination of mother to child transmission of HIV (eMTCT) through technical assistance to the implementation of the Global Validation Advisory Committee (GVAC) recommendations.
 
b. Every child learns
UNICEF's support in 2024 was aligned with the priorities of the African Union Year of Education (AU YoE) agenda by focusing on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN), enhancing systemic capacity, promoting early childhood development, and encouraging inclusive teaching practices, UNICEF has played a crucial role in advancing equitable access to quality education for all children in Botswana, especially the most vulnerable. In 2024, UNICEF reaffirmed its commitment to improving FLN efforts in Botswana through the piloting of remediation and enrichment programs in over 100 schools nationwide, thereby addressing critical learning gaps, skilling teachers and providing alternative methods of teaching and learning. Building on the groundwork laid in 2023 with the development of the National Literacy and Numeracy Strategy (NLSS) and Early Learning Development Standards (ELDS), UNICEF collaborated with the government in 2024 to further strengthen the education system through training of 60 ministry officers on implementation and monitoring of learner support services, such as guidance, counselling, and assistance for students with special educational needs. In partnership with the Ministry of Education, preschool teachers and ECD officers received training in the use of ELDS, which enabled them to deliver high-quality early education programs. Furthermore, UNICEF continued to support the government in advancing Early Childhood Development (ECD), ensuring the sustainability and scalability of these services. UNICEF's advocacy and technical support also addressed challenges related to teacher allocation through the "Teachers for All" study, contributing to discussions on the link between teacher allocation and learning outcomes.
 
2. Second decade: 10 – 24 years
a. Every child survives and thrives
In 2024, UNICEF built on progress made during previous years and launched “Operation Triple Zero” (OTZ), an adolescent-focused service delivery model, aiming for “zero viral load, zero missed appointments, and zero missed doses”. OTZ provides innovative health service delivery options for children and adolescents living with HIV, including weekend services, monthly peer support group sessions, integrated sexual and reproductive health services, HIV status disclosure counselling, and high viral load management. A total of 27 youth clubs were activated, signifying an increase of 6 new youth clubs from the previous year. Through these youth clubs, 1,781 adolescents and children received a suite of interventions, including mental health support, tutoring for children in school and economic empowerment. 
 
OTZ recognizes the importance of supporting adolescents beyond just their treatment, thereby a critical component on economic empowerment was introduced during this implementation period. Over 400 adolescents were reached with “Ready to Work” training, with some adolescents having been employed, others admitted at schools, and others assisted with Curriculum Vitae (CV) writing and opening of bank accounts.
 
Overall, the programme recorded impressive results, with 96per cent of the adolescents and children attending the youth clubs reported to be virally suppressed. Those that experienced continued adherence challenges were supported by peers through an adherence buddy program. Among those that presented viremia at baseline, 84per cent were virally suppressed at endline, clearly exemplifying the impact of the youth clubs in bridging the treatment gap.
 
b. Every child learns  
In 2024, UNICEF, in collaboration with GIGA and other partners, made significant progress in advancing digital learning, youth empowerment, and digital safety in Botswana. These efforts contributed to equitable access to quality education, enhanced youth employability, and supported the nation's digital transformation goals. With UNICEF's support, Botswana successfully connected 100 schools in marginalized communities, reaching 21,600 learners in public schools. Furthermore, UNICEF, in partnership with the Ministry of Education and Skills Development (MESD), launched the Learning Passport. So far, 2,868 users have been registered, including 1,548 students, supported by in-person training for 600 senior secondary teachers to help them integrate digital tools into classroom teaching. This initiative improved teaching practices and increased students' access to engaging digital resources. The Learning Passport is also accessible to learners with disabilities. The launch of the Setswana version of Text to Speech (TTS) technology will further enhance learning access for learners with visual impairments. 
 
Additionally, in collaboration with the government, UNICEF trained over 780 students in safe online practices through in-person sessions, while thousands more were reached via social media, television, and online courses. These efforts enhanced digital literacy among students, parents, and educators, creating a safer online environment and empowering stakeholders to navigate digital spaces responsibly. Furthermore, UNICEF facilitated consultation of over 2000 children to share ideas and possible solutions to address challenges affecting the education sector. The consultations were done with members of the National Children’s Consultative Forum (NCCF), children with disabilities and secondary school students. Their views formed part of the regional call to action presented by children to Heads of State from Botswana and Zimbabwe at the sub-regional commemoration of World Children’s Day held in Zimbabwe. The NCCF is an equivalent forum to a Children’s Parliament in the Botswana context.
 
UNICEF and its partners, including the Ministries of Labour, Home Affairs, Entrepreneurship, and Youth, Gender, Sport, and Culture, trained over 4,000 youth in employability, entrepreneurship, and digital skills. Additional virtual sessions extended these opportunities to thousands more, equipping young people with the necessary tools to succeed in the job market and for fostering innovation. Employability sessions were delivered in both urban and rural communities, bridging gaps in access to skills development opportunities and contributing to national economic growth.
 
c. Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
Given high levels of violence against women and children in Botswana, UNICEF continued to strengthen capacity of government to implement laws and policies to effectively prevent and respond to violence, exploitation, and abuse of children. Government of Botswana’s commitment to improving access to children friendly justice was demonstrated through the completion and launch of the “Roadmap to Child Friendly Justice” in February 2024, paving the way for increased capacity to deliver services to children.  In all 73 participants (32 M and 41F) attended the launch from the key ministries. Furthermore, quality child friendly justice services will be ensured through the development of standard operating procedures intended to standardise services in Botswana to completed in June 2025. UNICEF supported the training of key stakeholders from judiciary, public prosecution, social work, police, and civil society organisations to strengthen their capacity in providing quality child friendly justice services (27M and 58F). The training has facilitated increased coordination between stakeholders. The National Guidelines for the Prevention and Response to Violence Against Children are being developed to strengthen systems in responding to VAC in schools. To strengthen senior government engagement in the movement to end VAC, UNICEF together with WHO held three (3) dialogues with stakeholders between August and October 2024 which resulted in a statement of commitment to ending VAC by 2030.
 
 
3. Every child has an equitable chance in life 
UNICEF policy advisory, technical support and evidence-based advocacy contributed to the Government of Botswana’s expansion of inclusive and shock-responsive social protection system as well as decisions to enhance allocative efficiency, effectiveness and reach with increased transparency of social sector budgets and meaningful participation of children and adolescents. To support the social protection systems, strengthen work, UNICEF secured dedicated support to conduct a Gender Transformative Assessment of Botswana’s Social Protection System. This assessment will generate critical evidence and insights for enhancing the system’s gender responsiveness and expanding its efficiency. In addition, UNICEF established key partnerships with the IMF and the Botswana Institute for Policy Development and Analysis (BIDPA). These new alliances fostered constituencies for child-focused advocacy and evidence-based decision-making. In collaboration with BIDPA, UNICEF generated and disseminated insights on child multidimensional poverty and disability, including among UN agencies, thus addressing a critical data gap and informing future programming for children with disabilities.  
 
On the public finance for children front, the Government of Botswana made progressive efforts to improve capacity and evidence to plan, implement and monitor public budget effectively and transparently for social sectors with meaningful participation of children and adolescents in policymaking. Through UNICEF’s participation in Botswana’s National Development Plan (NDP) 12 formulation, mechanisms for youth participation in policy planning were adopted. UNICEF developed budget and policy briefs, linking budget allocations to child outcomes, especially in child protection and education. On account of UNICEF advocacy and technical support, the Government expanded public engagement platforms in budgeting, including youth-focused consultative sessions and timely publication of citizen-oriented budget documents. These contributions have resulted in the Government’s continued demonstration of commitment to sustain and increase social sector spending, key to attaining child rights. UNICEF’s policy analysis of the 2024/25 budget revealed that the Ministry of Education and Skills Development accounts for the highest share of total ministerial budget allocation at 17.1per cent, while the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development and the Ministry of Health rank 3rd and 4th, accounting for 13.2per cent and 10.7per cent respectively. On budget transparency, Botswana’s open budget score witnessed a marginal improvement from 34/100 in 2021 to 39/100 in 2023 Open Budget Survey. This still falls short of the sufficient score of 61/100.
UNICEF BCO supported children and youth engagement on climate change through the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), and subsequently, the development and handover of the position paper by children and youth focused on climate change, for incorporation into Botswana`s COP29 position paper on climate change. The children and youth position paper is further expected to be instrumental in the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) process to highlight children and youth’s unique vulnerabilities to climate change for inclusive and child sensitive solutions.  UNICEF has also partnered with a youth led organization (Botswana Climate Change Network) to create a network of climate change champions in key districts as part of climate change governance and sustainable engagement of children and youth on sustainability and climate action.
Furthermore, the country office’s two-year advocacy strategy helped the country office to galvanize support from government and partners around three priority areas, early childhood education, child justice system, and financing for immunization. As part of the strategy, UNICEF continued engagement with the private sector through Chief Executive Officers Council For Children’s rights, and this resulted in Mascom, a local MNO with the largest market share, contributing ending violence against children’s by raising awareness on online safety during their annual Batanani Walk. The initiative highlighted the importance of building systems to protect children from online harm. The walk brought together children, community leaders, the First Lady to unpack potential risks faced by children. The walk raised over $30 000 which will be used to roll out an online safety campaign in selected school across the country. To leverage Air Botswana’s reach and potential financial resources from its ticket sales, the country office engaged with the airline’s leadership to establish a formal partnership to support Early Childhood Development. The fundraising partnership will allow Air Botswana to request customers to donate a fixed amount that will be added to the ticket at the point of purchase or pledge to donate a set amount per ticket sale. The partnership is expected to be finalized and launched in 2025.

Operation Triple Zero (OTZ) programme achieved impactful results thanks to strategic partnerships with Centres for Disease Control, as the primary donor. At community level, Baylor & Sentebale translated programme goals into tangible results with oversight and strategic guidance from UNICEF. UNICEF collaborated with the MOH and NAHPA (National AIDS and Health Promotion Agency) to deliver positive health outcomes for adolescents living with HIV in the national HIV response. Through the rolling workplan signed with UNICEF, MOH provided in-kind contributions, by availing healthcare workers to deliver quality and client-centred services to adolescent living with HIV.
 
UNICEF collaborated with UNDP to develop a programme document on Children and Youth Engagement in Sustainability and Climate Action. This led to a partnership corporation agreement with Botswana Climate Change Network to host Botswana`s second local conference of youth (LCOY) and develop children and youth position. UNICEF further collaborated with UNDP and UNIDO on joint proposal to SDG Funds and secured funding related to the ‘Just Energy Transition’ initiative. Other partnerships included Botswana Red Cross Society for implementation of Immunization Catch Up campaign in Kweneng East and West districts.
 
Additionally, UNICEF in partnership with WHO developed and costed the National Immunization Strategy (NIS) which covers the period 2024- 2029. The significance of this NIS is that it reinforces Governments continued efforts towards universal access to holistic and quality health care for all, while underscoring the importance of equity and accessibility.
Strategic partnerships were instrumental in achieving UNICEF’s 2024 objectives. Partnering with the UN Resident Coordinator’s Office and other UN Agencies contributed to a joint advocacy to meaningful engagement of adolescents and young people in NDP 12 as well as the Establishment of the Youth-Led and Data-Driven Accountability Mechanism for Botswana's national policies and development plans. Engagement with the IMF’s Article IV Country Mission, collaboration with BIDPA, and coordinated advocacy with UN agencies underscore UNICEF’s commitment to integrating child welfare priorities across Botswana’s fiscal, social, and health policies. These partnerships ensure sustainability, enabling long-term impact on child-focused outcomes post-UNICEF support. 
 
UNICEF partnered closely with the private sector to successfully implement the GenU Employability Training and Tour, creating pathways for young people to access employment and entrepreneurship opportunities. This collaboration utilized the expertise, networks, and resources of private sector partners to connect youth with real-world opportunities and foster long-term impact. In 2024, additional partners such as Kromberg and Schubert, Hilton Garden Inn, Human Resource Development Committee, ABSA and FNB banks, joined the initiative, enriching it with their diverse experiences and contributions. Their involvement not only expanded the program's reach but also strengthened its sustainability, ensuring ongoing progress in youth development and empowerment. This partnership model highlights the transformative potential of private sector engagement in creating a brighter future for young people in Botswana.
The focus on 3 advocacy priorities across the office helped to strengthen focus on the most critical issues (early childhood education, child justice system, and financing for immunization) for Government and partners to galvanize support on.  Strengthened partnerships with media, children and young people and programme partners was instrumental in enhancing UNICEF’s visibility and reach among advocacy key audiences. UNICEF partnered with Ministry of Education and Skills Development (MESD) as well as Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development, to support engagement of children in development of regional call to action in education. The call to action has been presented to the President and is expected to contribute to prioritization of key areas on improving learning in Botswana. Additionally, UNICEF, MESD and the Disability Coordination Office facilitated engagement of adolescent girls with disability to share insights on strengthening inclusive education in Botswana.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The election of a new government and a new ruling party (for the first time since independence) at the end of October 2024 presents opportunities for UNICEF to influence the policy agenda for child rights. While the establishment of a Ministry of Child Welfare and Basic Education signals a commitment of the Government towards elevating child rights, the restructuring of ministerial portfolios and associated accountabilities is likely to take some time and to be associated with a period of uncertainty. 
Under the Operation Triple Zero (OTZ) interventions, the cohort aged 20-24 form the largest group in the empowerment clubs. However, reaching this group remains challenging due to their high mobility which leads to vulnerable young people moving out of the catchment area of the empowerment clubs. To address this, OTZ introduced virtual clubs, enrolling 80 young people who currently benefit from flexible, remote engagement. Moving forward, the establishment of the Network of Young People Living with HIV presents an additional opportunity to further support this demographic. As the network formalizes, it can mobilize resources to expand support for this target group, helping them stay connected despite their mobility. OTZ is yet to adequately target adolescents and young people with disabilities living with HIV. With this recognition, in the next implementation year, the program will strengthen the delivery of the program and disaggregation of data to identify and provide targeted services to adolescents with disabilities.
An impactful program relies on the capacities of implementers to deliver the program effectively and timely, under this reporting period, there were delays in disbursement of funds to partners, thereby greatly reducing the implementation period. Fast tracking onboarding of implementation will be the focus for the next implementation period to ensure partners have adequate time. Overall close oversight and technical support to partners ensured that all prioritized activities were completed as planned.
To consolidate and standardize meaningful engagement of adolescents and young people (AYP) by UNICEF Botswana, the country office undertook a consultative consensus building process to map out AYP engagement platforms and modalities. The process resulted in a guide which sets standards for engagement, ensures safeguarding and enables meaningful engagement and avoidance of tokenistic actions. This guidance will result in strengthened mechanisms for oversight of adolescent engagement for UNICEF Botswana. 
The achievements notwithstanding, monitoring progress and transformative nature of the social protection programme is a challenge due to outdated data on poverty developments in the country. There has not been any recent representative household survey since 2015/16 to assess the extent and contribution of poverty reduction in children and young people’s lives during the reporting period. In addition, the electoral period presented peculiar challenges for the office. Key among the challenges included slowed down pace in the responsiveness of key technical counterparts, hesitancy to work on bold interventions that would have been seen as major policy shifts thereby slowing implementation. However, the transition to a new Government usher in new opportunities to advance bold policy changes on child rights.  
Regarding digital connectivity, persistent challenges like ministry personnel turnover, budget constraints, and insufficient, or poor-quality devices hindered scaling digital learning and youth initiatives. These issues limited access for many teachers and learners and limited GIGA’s products to be scaled. Close collaboration between ministries is a strong necessity to coordinate digital transformation however this was not always assured. UNICEF leveraged social media to expand access to the Learning Passport, providing students and educators with quality digital resources. Online platforms scaled GenU employability and entrepreneurship trainings, reaching youth in remote areas. Collaboration with private sector partners injected expertise and resources, enhancing the programmes’ reach and sustainability. It is evident therefore, that the importance of creative solutions and partnerships in overcoming systemic barriers, enabling inclusive, impactful digital education and youth empowerment in Botswana is important. The introduction of Talkwalker and AMP as social and community listening tools demonstrates innovative approaches that enhance community feedback for rapid response to misinformation and disinformation as well as response to emerging issues in communities. A key lesson learned on the institutionalizing social listening and infodemic management is that it needs stronger coordination both within the Ministry of Health as the   Infodemic Management Team comprises of officers from 4 different units and UNICEF and WHO as technical partners especially on the tools being utilized by MoH.

With a population of 13.3 million (46 per cent children), Burundi is one of the most densely populated countries.[1] It is also one of the poorest with around 62 per cent of the population living below the poverty line.[2] The per capita gross domestic product (GDP) was US$321 in 2024, and the needs of the people remained largely unmet.[3] Although social sector funding rose 17.4 per cent in 2024/2025, the budget share dropped from 50.6 per cent to 24.1 per cent in 2024/2025. The education allocation fell from 20.6 per cent to 14.6 per cent; the health share declined from 13.4 per cent to 5.2 per cent.

Poverty heightened the vulnerability of children and women and restricted their access to essential services. The multidimensional poverty rate was 53.1 per cent.[4] Among children, 64.0 per cent suffered three or more deprivations in food, health care, water, sanitation, housing, education, and child protection.[5] Children with disabilities faced numerous barriers to social services including stigma, discrimination, lack of accessible infrastructure, and skilled professionals.

El Niño intensified the impact of climate change. Rain devastated crops, homes, schools, and infrastructure. Around 298,222 people were affected. Flooding and landslides forced 47,915 to flee their homes.

Children were affected by outbreaks of cholera (848 cases; 12 deaths), measles (15,050 suspected cases; 149 deaths, all among children) and malaria (4.1 million cases; 741 deaths, all among children).[6] The Government declared the Mpox outbreak in July 2024, and UNICEF activated a level 3 corporate emergency in August 2024. More than 37.8 per cent of the 2,975 cases in December 2024 involved children under age 15.[7]

Early childhood

The two million children ages 0–5 accounted for 15 per cent of the population.[8] Neonatal mortality fell from 22.5 to 19.8 per 1,000 live births in 2017–2022.[9] The infant mortality rate declined from 42.5 to 36.4 per 1,000 live births. The under-5 mortality rate was 50.5 per 1,000 live births.[10] Preterm birth complications were the leading cause of death among children under age 5, followed by acute respiratory infections, malaria, birth trauma, and diarrhœa. Among pregnant women living with HIV, 97 percent had lifelong access to antiretroviral therapy.

Among children under age 5, stunting prevalence was 52.8 per cent, the highest rate in the world.[11] Global acute malnutrition was 8.0 per cent, up from 4.8 per cent in 2022.[12] A slight improvement of feeding practices was reported with 18 per cent of children ages 6 to 23 months receiving a minimum acceptable diet compared to 13 per cent in 2022 and 28 per cent received a diversified diet up from 21 per cent in 2022.[13] Almost 80 percent of children under age 5 are living in child food poverty (eating two to four food groups).[14]

The main determinants included food insecurity, childhood illness, and poor feeding practices. Price rises for essential goods, disruptions in production associated with climate variability, low household incomes and limited access to agricultural inputs and land affected food accessibility.

Only 62 per cent of the population had access to basic drinking water; only 46 per cent had improved sanitation facilities, and only 6 per cent had access to basic hygiene.[15]

Three in 10 children did not have birth certificates because of the short legal delay for registration, the cost, the distance to registration centres, or loss.[16] Among children, 83 per cent did not have access to early learning.[17]

Children ages 6–13 years

In 2022–2023, the net primary enrolment rate was 87 per cent.[18] Of 2.8 million primary schoolchildren, 9,930 had disabilities, representing 0.3 per cent of students, far below the 10.0 per cent child disability regional prevalence.[19]

The pupil-to-classroom ratio was 75.[20] Around 45 per cent of schools had basic drinking water and basic sanitation.[21] Primary-school completion, at 52.3 per cent, was a pressing issue. The disparity was significant between rural (35 per cent) and urban (60 per cent) areas.[22] The primary repetition rate was 29 per cent. The drop-out rate was 10.7 per cent.[23]

Violence and exploitation were experienced by 90 per cent of children ages 1–14. One in three were engaged in child labour.[24]

Adolescents

Pregnancies among schoolgirls dropped from 1,019 to 879 in 2021/2023.[25] Adolescent pregnancy was associated with sexual violence, exploitation and lack of knowledge or access to reproductive health services. Among girls ages 15–19, more than 10 per cent had experienced sexual violence.[26] The prevalence of HIV was higher among women (1.2 per cent) than men (0.7 per cent). Adolescents ages 15–19 accounted for 29 per cent of the 2,043 new infections in 2021.[27] Two in five adolescent girls (39.4 per cent) aged 15 to 19 suffer from anaemia.[28] 

The gross upper secondary enrolment rate among adolescents ages 16–18 was 29.2 per cent (26.0 per cent in rural areas, 53.0 per cent in urban areas).[29] The chances of completing upper secondary education were higher among boys (21 per cent) than girls (15 per cent).[30] The mismatch between vocational training and labour market needs meant that many young people contributed little to the economy.[31]
