Early childhood development

UNICEF-Burundi elevated early childhood development (ECD) as a priority in the country through advocacy. The High-Level Forum for Women Leaders, organized in October 2024 under the leadership of the First Lady and the patronage of the President of Burundi, advocated for investment in ECD to build human capital and strengthened collaboration with the Government on an operational plan for a national ECD strategy. The plan included the launch of a multisectoral pilot ECD project focusing on the critical first 1,000 days of life in Kayanza health district. To support impact evaluation and guide programme scale-up, baseline data collection and analysis were completed.

UNICEF-Burundi advocacy was successful in the adoption of a ministerial decree on interoperability between health and civil registration services to enhance birth registration. The share of births registered within the legal time limit following birth in the pilot province of Kirundo rose 37 per cent. With UNICEF-Burundi support, the interoperability approach was expanded from 25 to 52 pilot health centres in Kirundo Province. Including through birth registration campaigns, 256,021 births were registered (132,418 girls), and 251,676 birth certificates were issued (130,079 girls) across the country. UNICEF-Burundi is to support the Government in establishing a steering committee to oversee a nationwide scale-up.

Following a literature review and sectoral and ministerial consultations and in collaboration with the Ministry of Communication, UNICEF-Burundi revised the package of family practices to focus on the critical first 1,000 days of life. With its partners, it promoted these practices in communities and reached more than 150,000 people.

Emergency obstetric and neonatal care kits and training benefited 431,811 newborns. The Kira Mama Project, using RapidSMS to monitor pregnant women and newborns, along with pulse oximeters, enabled timely referrals by community health workers (CHWs). The support for the neonatal unit at Gitega Hospital included a unit promoting Kangaroo mother care, a type of care that involves skin-to-skin contact between the newborn and a mother or other caregiver and exclusive breastfeeding among preterm and low birthweight babies. Early stimulation, interventions in favour of at-risk children, and screening services were delivered in Gitega and Ngozi health districts. In the targeted areas, neonatal health indicators improved through reductions in cases of low birthweight, hypothermia, and fœtal distress.

The quality of health care was enhanced in Cibitoke, Karusi, Kirundo, Rutana, and Ruyigi provinces through the connection of 10 health facilities to water networks. This enhanced access to clean water in maternity and pædiatric wards. UNICEF-Burundi helped repair four medical oxygen plants and, with World Bank funding, supported the construction of six additional plants. It collaborated with the United Nations Environment Programme’s Carbon Credit Mechanism to solarize these plants, thereby reducing air pollution and refining sustainability and cost-effectiveness.

UNICEF-Burundi assisted in coordination, vaccination, case management and infection prevention and control. It supported the national measles campaign, reaching more than 2.1 million children ages 6–59 months (92 per cent). This established a positive trend, from a generalized measles epidemic in 2023 to outbreaks in only four health districts in 2024. UNICEF-Burundi supplied emergency kits used to treat 14,965 children with measles and 795 cholera patients. In response to the Mpox outbreak, it supported capacity-building among health professionals and the installation of three isolation units in hot spots, where 1,547 cases (52 per cent of the caseload) had been treated by 31 December 2024.

In UNICEF-Burundi convergence zones, the share of integrated pædiatric HIV care sites rose from 63 per cent to 100 percent.[1] Early infant diagnosis helped screen 1,094 children at risk of HIV. Antiretroviral therapy reached 2,155 children ages 0–14 living with HIV, for a 62.0 per cent rate (33.6 per cent in 2023). Through UNICEF-Burundi capacity-building, 111 community leaders and individuals living with HIV in Gitega and Kirundo provinces were trained in community response and appropriate actions to eliminate mother-to-child transmission. Among pregnant and lactating women, 1,117 received long-term antiretroviral therapy in the two provinces, exceeding the target of 957.

UNICEF-Burundi collaborated with the Ministry of Health to manage severe acute malnutrition across all 49 health districts. Over 1.7 million children under age 5 were screened quarterly for acute malnutrition, including 56,000 internally displaced children in flood-affected provinces. Among these children, 131,027 and 50,000 respectively with moderate and severe wasting were successfully rehabilitated and treated. 
 
To prevent micronutrient deficiency, two annual doses of vitamin A supplementation were provided to over 1.7 million children ages 6–59 months and deworming tablets to 1.5 million children ages 12–59 months, MNP to 254,000 children ages 6–23 months and IFA to respectively 385,000 pregnant women and 25,000 adolescent girls.

To strengthen community capacity in the promotion of improved feeding practices, early stimulation and positive parenting, UNICEF-Burundi supported the training of 7,000 CHWs and 3,700 Light Mothers for supporting the implementation of a minimum community-based nutrition package across 54 communes in 11 provinces through 2,200 established mother support groups linked with village savings and loan associations and 276 ECD spaces. This has allowed to reach 848,000 caregivers with counselling and appropriate messages. 
 
To improve children’s diets UNICEF-Burundi supported capacity building of 633 agricultural monitors resulting to the establishment of 23,000 demonstration kitchen gardens and supported social marketing campaigns to enhance the consumption of locally available nutritious diets including animal source protein reaching 105,500 people. 

UNICEF-Burundi supported an analysis of the management of nutritionally at-risk infants under age 6 months and their mothers. The analysis found that the delivery of nutrition and health services was inadequate and demonstrated the need for an action plan, including the revision of protocols and strategies, to improve these services.

As part of the integrated approach to ECD and malnutrition, UNICEF-Burundi and its partners constructed nine gravity-fed, climate-resilient water supply networks across Cibitoke, Karusi, Kirundo, Rutana and Ruyigi provinces. These networks provided sustainable access to enhanced water services for 81,717 people (22,087 women, 19,587 girls). UNICEF-Burundi supplied kits and supported capacity-building in the maintenance of water infrastructure among 269 local water management committee members (155 women) in three communes.

UNICEF-Burundi enhanced access to hygiene and sanitation, promoting safely managed services. The community-led total sanitation strategy was revised to include training among masons in constructing sustainable latrines, as well as income-generating activities among youth and women, such as the production of soap and sanitary pads to improve product accessibility and affordability in rural areas. As a result, 310 communities were declared open defecation free, benefiting 339,090 people, while 411,800 people (111,309 women, 98,708 girls) gained access to at least basic sanitation, and 17,244 to safely managed services.

As part of its emergency response, UNICEF-Burundi rehabilitated and expanded water supply systems and constructed latrines, providing 202,658 people (57,879 girls, 45,477 women) with safe drinking water and 10,890 people with improved sanitation. Hygiene kits were distributed to 3,465 households, benefiting 20,790 individuals, while 4,965 women and girls received dignity kits for menstrual health. Hygiene and disease prevention messaging (handwashing, safe water management, and cholera and Mpox prevention) reached 355,872 people (101,637 girls, 79,858 women).

Preschool enrolment rose from 15 per cent to 17.1 per cent in 2021/2023. UNICEF-Burundi’s targeted advocacy and community engagement fostered behavioural change and underscored the importance of early childhood education. UNICEF-Burundi distributed learning tools, such as Kerebuka booklets and play kits to 165,791 children (49 per cent girls).

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened the capacities of 162 local authorities (66 women, 102 men) in education, health care, child protection, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) in three municipalities (Kabarore, Kayanza and Muruta) and in the integration of ECD in local planning and budgeting in three communes in the convergence zones.

As part of shock-responsive social protection efforts, UNICEF-Burundi provided technical and financial support to savings groups in sites hosting internally displaced persons, benefiting 1,198 households (885 women) and 4,776 children. It strengthened government capacity in implementing humanitarian cash transfers.

Children ages 6–13

A national stakeholder consultation on the protection of children against violence was organized under the leadership of the Ministry of National Solidarity with the support of UNICEF-Burundi and in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO). As a result, at the First Global Ministerial Conference on the Elimination of Violence against Children, in Colombia, the Government of Burundi pledged to revise the national legal framework to prohibit corporal punishment in all settings, criminalize all forms of sexual violence, abuse and exploitation of children, create an interministerial committee on the protection of children from violence, develop a national strategy on the protection of children from violence, and provide parenting support.

UNICEF-Burundi helped provide 1,575 children victims of violence, abuse and exploitation (876 girls, 699 boys) with at least one service (health care, legal aid, psychosocial support, or alternative care). Of the total, 779 children were affected by humanitarian situations, and 59 were children with disabilities.

UNICEF-Burundi investments in school infrastructure improved the learning environment for 12,000 public school pupils (51 per cent girls). This included the construction or rehabilitation of 168 accessible classrooms, which were equipped with desks. Among these classrooms, 16 were dedicated to preschool children, and 35 were temporary classrooms set up as part of the El Niño emergency response. Another 200 damaged schools were repaired, enabling about 18,000 children to continue in school.

School supplies were provided to 218,952 children (49 per cent girls), including 53,161 children affected by floods, returnee children, indigenous Batwa children, refugee children, and other children impacted by emergencies, including 1,049 children with disabilities. 

UNICEF-Burundi supported inclusive education among 107 children (55 girls) with visual impairments in 16 pilot schools using LEGO Braille Bricks for playful learning. A total of 1,288 LEGO Braille Brick sets were donated. In the last quarter of 2024, 45 educational professionals (58 per cent women), including 35 teacher trainers and 10 teachers at the Reference Centre for Inclusive Education, in Bujumbura, were trained in inclusive education, with a focus on using LEGO Braille Bricks in Braille instruction.

In the convergence zones, 6,316 teachers (49 per cent women), including 944 new primary school teachers (53 per cent women), were trained in new curricula and gained enhanced knowledge of subject content, classroom practices and assessment methods. This accounted for 9.2 per cent of the total teaching workforce in Burundi. Pre- and post-training evaluations showed a 64.8 per cent improvement. Training in psychosocial support and mental health was supplied to 1,844 teachers (43 per cent women), who, along with 250 community focal points, identified children in need and provided psychosocial care.

In Cibitoke, Karusi, Kirundo, Rutana and Ruyigi provinces, 29 schools were connected to water networks, benefiting 17,356 children (9,009 girls). In Cibitoke, Kayanza, Kirundo and Makamba provinces, 41 schools with 28,700 students (14,063 girls, 130 children with disabilities) were equipped with inclusive gender-sensitive latrines.

Adolescents

UNICEF-Burundi supported 12 youth-friendly health centres in Kirundo Province through sexual and reproductive health supplies. It trained 64 nurses and 95 other staff on sexual and reproductive health and service provision among young people. As a result, 13,936 adolescents and young women received services.

Training in sexual and reproductive health was supplied to 3,484 teachers (51 per cent women) who now supervise 1,742 UNICEF-Burundi–supported school health clubs that promote peer education and health awareness. UNICEF-Burundi supported media campaigns on menstrual hygiene management through 17 community and national radio stations reaching an estimated 2.2 million adolescent girls and women, among whom 24,358 were sensitized through the Oky app, a digital platform that has enabled a multisectoral approach through its content covering sexual and reproductive health, mental health, gender relations, family planning, childhood  development, the prevention of gender-based violence, and protection.

UNICEF-Burundi promoted gender-responsive education, including the distribution of sanitary pad hygiene kits in 121 schools to help reduce absenteeism, particularly during menstruation, and foster an inclusive learning environment. Six youth and women associations in Kayanza, Kirundo and Muyinga provinces were supported in producing menstrual hygiene pads to facilitate affordable long-term access to sanitary pads among 98,787 women and adolescents.

Skills4Girls, a UNICEF-Burundi flagship programme, empowered 1,100 adolescents and youth leaders (826 girls) following its launch in 2022. In 2024, 181 young people (129 girls) in Kirundo Province participated in microtraining focused on science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) and aimed at addressing local challenges, such as electricity shortages and income-generating opportunities. As a result, 37 solar kiosks were organized by solidarity groups to provide services powered by renewable energy, including sewing, phone charging, and haircuts.

UNICEF-Burundi collaborated with the Economic Empowerment and Youth Employment Programme (Programme d'Autonomisation Economique et d'Emploi des Jeunes, PAEEJ) to enhance youth entrepreneurship through the PAEEJ Academy. This platform offered microcredentials in transferable skills and STEM, benefiting over 5,000 adolescents (2,651 girls). By overcoming digital access barriers through the provision of modules in Kirundi and radio broadcasts on the PAEEJ Academy platform, UNICEF-Burundi advocacy and communication efforts ensured the inclusion of vulnerable rural youth. Through PAEEJ, 1,350 members of solidarity groups (810 girls) benefited from loans that facilitated the expansion of income-generating activities and promoted self-employment. In collaboration with the UNICEF Office of Innovation and BX Smart Labs, UNICEF-Burundi piloted an innovative data app to ensure more reliable tamper-proof financial records, ease access to loans and promote financial inclusion.

As part of efforts to facilitate access to justice for children in contact with the law, a mobile court was organized with the support of UNICEF-Burundi and partners. This led to the release of 44 children from pretrial detention. UNICEF-Burundi supported the provision of legal aid and closer coordination among relevant actors, resulting in the release of 275 children from police cells through 96 joint monitoring missions to detention facilities. Overall, 464 children in contact with the law (including 65 girls) received legal aid.
UNICEF-Burundi supported the Ministry of Health in developing the 2024–2028 national strategy for the prevention of micronutrient deficiency that, for the first time, included adolescent girls.

Gender, climate change, social and behaviour change and inclusion of children with disabilities

UNICEF-Burundi promoted disability inclusion through a two-year multisectoral work plan, advocacy for inclusive policies, and the implementation of community-based programmes. It completed the Situation Analysis (SitAn) on children with disabilities, trained more than 200 civil society organization (CSO) and government partners on disability inclusion, developed a checklist to improve school accessibility and strengthened the capacity of construction companies. With support from 7 per cent set-aside funds, it launched a project on the community integration of children with disabilities in Muyinga Commune. This included training local authorities and leaders, raising community awareness through parent role models of children with disabilities and promoting inclusive education by supplying kits to 124 children with disabilities. Through the same fund and Regular Resources, 60 children benefited from assistive devices and reasonable accommodation in school. Pilot and satellite schools in Muyinga, accommodating over 40 children with physical disabilities, were rehabilitated to improve accessibility, including the construction of toilets. UNICEF-Burundi worked to improve data availability on children with disabilities in nutrition programmes.

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened gender mainstreaming and the integration of gender transformative approaches across programmes and projects. It collaborated with the Ministry of Solidarity to map women’s organizations in convergence zones. With the Ministry of Health, it conducted a community gender analysis to identify sociocultural access barriers in primary health care, including immunization. This led to the development of a training module on gender mainstreaming in primary care services that was used to train 384 Ministry of Health gender focal points, health district managers, medical staff, and CHWs. Building on the study, UNICEF-Burundi worked with religious and women's organizations to implement community engagement programmes promoting positive gender norms with 270 community leaders, 150 model couples and 280 young champions (50 per cent girls) in Bubanza, Cankuzo, Karusi, Kayanza, Kirundo and Rutana provinces and a media campaign involving six media outlets with more than 3,000 participants and reaching more than 10,000 people.

In partnership with the Burundian Agency for Rural Water Supply and Sanitation and the Women Engineers Association, UNICEF-Burundi implemented a gender-transformative programme to empower rural women in WASH professions. The initiative trained 50 women, organized into four associations, to maintain hydraulic infrastructure, produce soap, and install and market solar kits in Marangara Commune. As part of the Mpox response, gender-based violence (GBV) safety audits were conducted in three treatment centres, thus enhancing measures to mitigate GBV risks and opening opportunities to reinforce gender and GBV considerations across health centres.

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened young people’s awareness of the impact of climate change on children and supported the Government and youth representation at the 29th Conference of the Parties of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP29). It worked on a climate landscape analysis for children to integrate youth priorities in national policies and developed a training module on the pillars of climate action. To empower children, adolescents, and young people to advocate for climate action, 50 were trained on climate change, unsustainable energy use and environmental degradation. 

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened climate-resilient water networks (benefiting 81,717 people) and the establishment of biodigesters in hospitals to promote sustainability and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. As part of a multiyear resilience programme, it supported the revitalization of 81 school environmental clubs across Makamba Province, which established nurseries and planted trees to contribute to environmental protection.

UNICEF-Burundi strengthened social and behaviour change capacities among partners. Following a training of trainers exercise, cascade training will be ensured among partners by 32 trainers in 2025. UNICEF-Burundi supported the participation in the Regional Office’s Social and Behaviour Change and Academia Consortium by two Burundian universities, which committed to supporting relevant coursework and programmes. In partnership with the Essential Programme on Immunization (EPI), it conducted training among 357 health promotion coordinators, health promotion technicians and providers. It strengthened EPI capacity in crisis communication; measles, malaria, and hexavalent vaccines, and the national vaccination strategy. It helped create a CSO platform for immunization funding.

UNICEF-Burundi risk communication and community engagement activities reached six million people through mass communication and 19,407 people through flood, cholera and Mpox response. It relied on mass communication and community engagement to educate and engage communities in disease prevention and services. It worked with the Ministry of Health’s Emergency Operations Centre on coordination, planning and a national plan for the Mpox response.

[1] Following an analysis to identify the most vulnerable communes and provinces, three provinces were designated as geographic and programmatic convergence zones for interventions under the UNICEF-Burundi Country Programme (2024–2027). The provinces are Kirundo, Muyinga and Ngozi.

In 2024, UNICEF-Burundi launched the Country Programme 2024–2027. Effective coordination with the Government resulted in the endorsement of the 2024–2026 rolling work plan and the activation of the e-workplan. After contributing to the 2023 annual reporting exercise, UNICEF-Burundi worked with United Nations agencies to develop a 2025–2027 work plan. As lead of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework outcome in social services, it contributed to the technical joint committee along with key government representatives.

UNICEF-Burundi mobilized US$83.5 million, a 65.6 per cent increase over 2023. Public sector contributions accounted for 90 per cent of total allotments. Emergency response – Mpox, other epidemics and natural disasters – represented 10 per cent of allotments. Funds supported critical sectors, including health care, nutrition, education, child protection and WASH, and were showcased through tailored donor visibility initiatives that emphasized the potential transformative impact on children’s lives. Contributors to the Country Programme included the African Development Bank, the Central Emergency Response Fund, Education Cannot Wait, the European Union, Gavi, the Global Partnership for Education, the governments of Austria, Belgium, Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, and Switzerland, KfW, Mastercard Foundation, Nutrition International, the UNICEF National Committees of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States, the United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, and the World Bank–WHO Pandemic Fund. Donor visits were organized for the UNICEF National Committees of Germany, Spain, Switzerland, and the United States and for other donors, including the Government of Japan, KfW, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, and USAID.

UNICEF-Burundi collaborated with United Nations agencies and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in joint programmes, such as a programme funded by the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (Fondation Stamm, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, UNICEF, and World Food Programme [WFP]), the United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund Joint Programme on Human Rights (alongside Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, United Nations Development Programme, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, and UN Women), a KfW-funded project (Concern Worldwide, UNICEF, WeWorld and Gruppo di Volontariato Civile, and WFP), and a French embassy–funded project (Caritas Burundi, UNICEF, UN Women, and WFP).

In the initial days following the declaration of the Mpox epidemic, UNICEF-Burundi, with support from the UNICEF Regional Office and Headquarters, engaged in high-level advocacy with the Government and the First Lady. This effort emphasized the importance of national mobilization and effective coordination to break the chain of transmission and contain the disease swiftly.

UNICEF-Burundi continued implementing a partnership strategy aimed at strengthening collaboration and capacity-building in key areas, such as accountability to affected populations, disability inclusion, fraud, and the harmonized approach to cash transfers, and to improve the quality of joint and collaborative interventions. Quality assurance in partnership management processes was strengthened through the partnership review committee mechanism. As the new Country Programme was undertaken in 2024, 39 partnership cooperation agreements were signed. Among these, 12 – the Association of Repatriated Women of Burundi, the Global Development Community of Burundi, Help a Child, Irivuga, Radio-Television Isanganiro, Jijuka, Les Vaillantes, RCBF, Ripple Effect, Safe Inclusion, Spring Communities, and Street Child – were new partners, and 27 were existing partners. UNICEF-Burundi partnered with civil society through the development of 49 programme documents, 16 of which focused on humanitarian response (Mpox, cholera, floods, and so on). A pool of partners was identified for the implementation of a multisectoral ECD package through the new Country Programme.

To support partnerships with CSOs and the Government, training sessions among 180 participants were organized on the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse and the harmonized approach to cash transfers. The training covered various topics, including programme document development, reporting and the use of the United Nations partner portal. As a result of the training, all partners were able to submit online reports. Ongoing capacity-building efforts were maintained to ensure accurate reporting, a crucial component of UNICEF-Burundi's monitoring system.

To enhance accountability to affected populations and protection against sexual exploitation and abuse, community engagement and feedback mechanisms were strengthened, particularly in the Mpox response.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In the integration of ECD initiatives in local planning and budgeting, the capacity-building programme on public finance at the local level represented an entry point for UNICEF-Burundi in the effort to strengthen the capacity of municipalities in Kayanza Province and in three municipalities (Kabarore, Muruta and Kayanza) in the convergence zones. This enabled UNICEF-Burundi to increase its visibility in public finance, child poverty and social protection and to influence and guide strategies, programmes and budgets.

Social protection in Burundi faces significant challenges, including increased vulnerability and poverty worsened by recurrent climatic shocks and the prevailing weak economic conditions. The scope of social safety nets remains limited, targeting only 250,000 households, which is insufficient for the largely rural and impoverished population, among which 51.4 per cent are living below the national poverty line. Key issues include weak coordination across social protection interventions, the absence of a unified national social registry and universal health coverage, and insufficient resource allocation and mobilization in social protection programmes.

The lack of adequate emergency preparedness highlighted significant gaps in the ability to respond to public health emergencies in 2024. The availability of the pandemic fund represented an opportunity to address these shortcomings by strengthening the health system across facilities and communities, which should improve preparedness and response in future public health emergencies.

The shocks that Burundi faced in 2024, including population displacements following floods and landslides and public health emergencies, exerted additional pressure on an already fragile child protection system that is insufficiently funded and depends on an under-resourced workforce. The humanitarian response and the child protection response to the Mpox outbreak offered opportunities for system strengthening by building on initiatives already undertaken. The strengthening of child protection committees, which began in 2023 and continued in 2024, was instrumental in ensuring community-based mental health and psychosocial support and individual case management among affected children and households. Providers in the child protection case management system were able immediately to draw on lessons learned from the Mpox response, especially in filling capacity gaps among social workers. The evaluation of the social service workforce in child protection, planned for 2025, will help address the challenges. These efforts will ensure that the child protection system is improved and becomes more inclusive, including in the case of vulnerable groups, such as street children. This is important given the worsening economic situation and the rising number of children living and working on the streets. The results of research on social norms related to sexual violence, expected in the first half of 2025, will help accelerate UNICEF-Burundi work on the prevention of violence, notably sexual violence, against children.

Inclusive education was underserved because of inadequate funding and prioritization among national actors. UNICEF-Burundi supported the Ministry of Education in the development of a national strategy on inclusive education and accompanying action plans aimed at improving access among children with diverse needs, but the plans were largely unrealized. Rising education costs driven by inflation exacerbated the problem and contributed to an increase in the share of out-of-school children because of higher drop-out rates. These challenges negatively affected school completion rates, despite the concerted effort of UNICEF-Burundi and other partners to keep children in school. Insufficient community effort was evident in the identification of children with disabilities, raising awareness on disability inclusion and supporting the parents of children with disabilities. Addressing these shortcomings represented a substantial challenge to the progress towards inclusive and equitable education for all.

A persistent care quality shortfall was associated with 2,439 perinatal deaths and 574 neonatal deaths. UNICEF-Burundi supported neonatology services in Gitega Province, the use of RapidSMS for community health follow-up, and the provision of health facility training. Neonatology interventions were scaled up in selected provinces. Within two days of birth, 79,768 newborns (60 per cent) received postnatal care. The emergency obstetric and neonatal care coverage rate rose from 22 per cent to 50 per cent, and the share of newborns benefiting from essential care increased by 8 per cent, from 400,164 to 431,811. UNICEF-Burundi provided support for the digitization of seven health facilities using Open Clinic software. This initiative successfully reduced the use of paper-based tools to zero and enhanced the information management system.

UNICEF-Burundi remains the principal provider of ready-to-use therapeutic food. Inflation drove up staple food prices, affecting child nutritional status. The 2024 SMART survey results, though technically validated, have yet to be endorsed by the authorities. This has contributed to the postponement of key planned activities, such as the first food consultations with the Government and stakeholders. The establishment of village savings and loan associations, which support women’s access to financial resources and household income generation, was delayed because of new regulations of the Bank of the Republic of Burundi, thereby affecting children’s diets. With one of the highest child stunting rates in the world, Burundi also has an extremely high level of child food poverty with over 80 per cent of children under age 5 affected. Among them, 18 per cent live in severe child food poverty, while 64 per cent experience moderate child food poverty.[1] The coverage of preventive interventions was sparse because of limited funding. Weaknesses in national reporting systems impeded routine nutrition data analysis.

Access to WASH services has not kept pace with demographic growth and rapid urbanization, leading to inequalities, particularly in schools and health care facilities. This has increased demand for sector governance and reform. Climate change has amplified humanitarian needs, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations. As a result, UNICEF-Burundi allocated more financial and human resources to humanitarian response than planned, compromising other activities. Involving local administrations and communities in the planning of infrastructure projects to ensure local ownership and sustainability is critical. This approach has improved WASH infrastructure management and maintenance. Rural women played a vital role in maintaining hydraulic infrastructure and renewable energy systems, fostering empowerment and local development.

UNICEF-Burundi has been organizing multisectoral monitoring missions with the Government for years to strengthen collaboration across ministries. However, the implementation of the resulting recommendations has been limited because of the frequent turnover among ministry focal points and the partly associated lack of adequate follow-up. To address this issue, UNICEF-Burundi plans to organize sector-specific missions conducted prior to annual sectoral reviews. Involving a broader range of stakeholders within a ministry is expected to increase ownership and ensure the more effective realization of recommendations.

[1] UNICEF, Child Food Poverty - Nutrition deprivation in early childhood, 2024.

The Union of the Comoros, a Small Island Developing  State (SIDS) and a Least Developed Country (LDC), is a cluster of four  islands in the Indian Ocean: Grande Comore, Moheli, Anjouan and Mayotte, but  this last island has remained under French administration since the country’s  independence. Forty-four per cent of the estimated 889,676 population in 2024  is poor, and 65 per cent live in rural areas. Children (under the age of 18)  account for 43 per cent of the population. As a fragile State, the Comoros is  highly vulnerable to shocks, including climate change. The country scored 20  out of 100 (162 out of 180 countries) on the Transparency International 2023  Corruption Perception Index.
  
In 2024, the Comorian economy grew by an estimated  3.5 per cent, according to the International Monetary Fund. While inflation  decreased slightly, consumer prices remained high, undermining living  conditions, particularly for the most vulnerable, who were also most affected  by the continued severe disruptions in electricity and water supply, and by  the national waste management crisis resulting in an unsafe land and ocean  environment. 

The political situation remained tense throughout  the year. In January 2024, Comoros held presidential elections that resulted  in the re-election of President Azali Assoumani. Allegations of electoral  fraud sparked violent protests, and the unrest saw the arrest of numerous  minors and youth, further exacerbating the situation. In September 2024, the  President was physically attacked during a public event. His 24-year-old  attacker was quickly apprehended but was later found dead in his cell under  mysterious circumstances. The run-up to legislative and municipal elections  in early 2025, and the continued shrinking of civic space, including a de  facto ban on peaceful demonstrations, have further exacerbated tensions.
  
In 2024, Comoros faced significant humanitarian  crises, including a cholera outbreak and floods. The cholera epidemic,  declared in February, marked the first since 2008, with over 10,540 cases and  152 fatalities as of 13 October 2024 (last available data) – a high toll  relative to population size, partly due to the politicization, and widespread  denial, of the disease, as well as to the weak health system and to  persisting gaps in water, hygiene and sanitation. Sporadic suspect cases  continued to be recorded in the last quarter of 2024. In May and June, heavy  rains from a cyclone that bypassed Comoros caused severe flooding in a few  locations, affecting an estimated 60,000 people. Cyclone Chido, in December,  also brought limited damage to Anjouan and Moheli islands.
  
Comoros continued to be a significant point on the  migration route to Mayotte, for those traveling from mainland Africa (mainly  the Great Lakes region) and to a lesser extent Madagascar, with the lack of  national legislation to protect refugees and asylum seekers exacerbating  their vulnerability. Migrants, including women and children, usually faced  short-term detention upon arrival in Comoros, before making their way to  Mayotte. In addition, French authorities continued to expel from Mayotte  Comorian people deemed irregular migrants, including vulnerable adolescents  and youth. While some of these youth may have extended family in Comoros,  many struggle to integrate into Comorian society due to cultural differences,  and some live in extremely vulnerable situations, until they manage to make  their way back to Mayotte.

In 2024, UNICEF Comoros contributed to significant progress for children across various sectors. The cholera response was a major focus, with essential supplies provided, treatment units established, and community-level interventions reaching over 294.000 people. The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) provided critical data enabling measurement of child-related Sustainable Development Goal indicators, highlighting progress in reducing maternal and child mortality and stunting, while also identifying gaps in learning outcomes and water, hygiene, and sanitation. UNICEF’s continued support to the Government-run care centers for victims of violence helped assist 722 victims countrywide, and its partnership with the Ministry of Education enhanced the capacity of education personnel on inclusive education.  Additionally, UNICEF supported the Government in developing and costing a comprehensive Community Health Strategy, introducing a dedicated budget line for nutrition in the State budget, and promoting improved sanitation through the introduction of an innovative latrine model. Additionally, the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) offered a thorough examination of how climate change impacts children in Comoros, guiding future climate action. 

These achievements, detailed further below, underscore UNICEF's comprehensive approach to enhancing the well-being of children and communities in Comoros. These advancements in realizing children's rights were made possible through the dedication of government and non-governmental partners, resource partners, and the communities, adolescents and children themselves. UNICEF Comoros extends its heartfelt gratitude to all contributors for their unwavering commitment and support.

In 2024, the response to the intense cholera  epidemic was a major priority and mobilized substantial effort and  resources of UNICEF Comoros team for a large part of the year. Working in  close collaboration with the Ministry of Health and its regional  directorates, as well as with key partners such as the Comorian Red Crescent,  Médecins sans Frontières, the International Federation of the Red Cross and  the World Health Organization, UNICEF provided multisectoral technical and  financial assistance. This lifesaving response to cholera was made possible  by the strong commitment of various resource partners, including ECHO,  UNOCHA, JICA, USAID, and France, whom UNICEF Comoros would like to  thank. 

UNICEF provided essential supplies for cholera  treatment and for infection prevention and control in health facilities, and  worked closely with partners to set up cholera treatment units and oral rehydration  points. Case-area targeted interventions (CATI) helped curb infections at  community level, with mixed response team disinfecting over 53,000 households  and providing them with ‘stop cholera’ kits with water treatment and other  items, and sensitizing over 294.000 people to cholera risks and prevention  methods through face-to-face or small group interaction. Post intervention  monitoring of 581 households showed that 93 per cent used the distributed  home water treatment products, and 85 per cent used the bucket with lid and  tap for safe water storage, which were observed to be covered (95 per cent)  and clean (93 per cent).

This community-based response also included public  places such as schools, madrassas and mosques. In addition, 150 schools  hosting more than 52,000 students received hygiene kits, and UNICEF supported  the Ministry of Education to mobilize school councils around preventive  measures for safe schooling in the context of cholera. Recognizing the impact  of the cholera epidemic on mental health, UNICEF recruited three  psychologists who provided psychosocial support to 827 affected individuals  (454 women and girls, and 373 men and boys) on the three islands, including  212 children. Health personnel and other frontline responders, who were  significantly impacted by the crisis, were also among those who received  assistance.
 
Together with the Ministry of Health, UNICEF  co-leads a subcommittee of Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE).  As part of this engagement, to help address cholera denial, UNICEF conducted  two behavioral surveys using Behavioral and Social Drivers approaches, which  helped adapt communication tools, and set up a social listening and community  feedback mechanism, for early identification and demystification of rumors,  utilizing online data collection, national health hotline, and field agents.  Collaboration with 2,000 members of adolescent clubs, 55 community  associations, 37 community media outlets, and 10 influencers was key to  reaching more than 580,000 people with information on preventive measures. By  June 2024, 95 per cent of the population believed in the disease's  existence. 
 
Politicization of the disease was a key challenge  throughout the year. It first led to widespread denial of the disease, then  to the delaying and sub-optimal organization of the oral cholera vaccination  campaign. As a result, only 65 per cent of the population were vaccinated while  the country had received doses for the whole population in a context of  global shortage. Another negative effect, toward the end of the year and in  the context of travel and trade restrictions by other countries, was the  discontinuation of the Ministry of Health’s situation reports, the official data  source guiding the response to the epidemic. The cholera response was also  hindered by important logistical barriers, due to the small market size, the  long lead times to import lifesaving supply to Comoros, and the limited  inter-island connectivity.   While UNICEF addressed these  challenges to the best of its ability—such as working with trusted  community-based associations to combat disease denial, and partnering with  the Ministry of Health and Médecins sans Frontières to facilitate  inter-island supply shipments—the additional time and effort required  impacted the overall efficiency of the response.

UNICEF prioritized a nexus approach in the cholera  response, opting for sustainable solutions whenever possible. This included  setting up decentralized oral rehydration points throughout the country, with  tents and equipment that can be reused in the event of other, future public  health emergencies, as well as increasing the water storage and sanitation  capacity of the main Anjouan hospital, which hosted the island’s cholera  treatment centre. Similarly, the cholera epidemic has helped bring to light  some long-standing issues with water quality. After much UNICEF advocacy, preliminary  steps such as training and community sensitization were carried out in  Anjouan to enable chlorination of water networks in priority sites in 2025,  with the intent to emulate a similar approach in the other islands. This will  be critical, as the country still faced sporadic suspected cases of cholera  at the end of 2024.

In addition to the emergency response, UNICEF  Comoros also supported the Government to implement the national development  plan, the Emerging Comoros Plan 2020-2030, with efforts focusing on evidence  generation and on technical and financial assistance aimed at building  national strengthening systems in key social sectors. 

Recognizing the power of data to spur  progress for children, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Information, Gender,  and Solidarity to measure child poverty through a re-analysis of the 2020  survey on household living conditions. This revealed a concerning increase in  monetary poverty in children, from 42 per cent in 2012/2014 to 46 per cent in  2020, coupled with a significant decrease in multidimensional poverty, from  60 per cent in 2012 to 34 per cent in 2020. 
  
This decrease in deprivations is confirmed by the  results of the 2022 MICS survey, launched in May 2024, which provided  much-needed, reliable data on key child indicators and highlighted clear  areas of progress, including a reduction in maternal mortality, child  mortality and stunting, and an increase in birth registration and school  enrollment. Areas of concern included educational outcomes, water hygiene and  sanitation, as well as strong inequities across indicators based on income  level. UNICEF disseminated both of these reports to decision-makers, encouraging  sectoral ministries to use the data for State programme and budget planning.
  
In child protection, the Ministry of  Interior, the French Embassy and UNICEF Comoros pursued their tripartite  partnership to modernize civil registration, with an independent evaluation  of efforts so far and the start of a second phase project. The Government  signaled its continued commitment by validating the 2024-2028 strategic plan  for the modernization of civil registration, and allocating in the 2025 State  budget a contribution of USD 429,000 toward implementation, out of the  estimated total cost of USD 8.7 million over 5 years.
  
UNICEF continued to support expansion of State-run  care centres for victims of violence, with the opening of a new centre in  Pomoni, Anjouan, located in the health centre to facilitate victim anonymity  and access to health care. In 2024, the country’s 9 care centers recorded 722  cases of violence (compared with 769 in 2023), 82 per cent against women and  girls. Sexual violence was the most reported type of violence, and adolescent  girls were the most affected. While victims accessed much-needed medical, judicial,  and psychological help, and for young victims having given birth, a  socio-economic reintegration programme, the sustainability and quality of  these crucial services remain fragile, as large-scale support from the Korean  International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) ended in December 2024 and the State  budget provides very limited support toward prevention and response to  violence. 
  
It will also be critical to sustain the 195  adolescent clubs created and trained as part of these programmes. Their 3900  members have played an important role in violence prevention and in raising  awareness on other topics important for children’s rights.  Their  community-based activities, including theatre to raise awareness on violence,  and peer information on the cholera epidemic, reached 12,000 people in 2024.  They have also displayed a keen interest in climate change, which provides  further opportunities for them to be agents of change at community level.
  
An important milestone, in 2024, was the adoption  of guidelines for establishing temporary foster families – a critical need,  in a country that does not have an official social worker workforce, nor  shelters for vulnerable children and persons, and where needs are answered at  community level through informal, individual arrangements. 258 potential  temporary foster families that meet set criteria have been identified. It  will be important for UNICEF to continue to support the Ministry of  Information, Solidarity and Gender in 2025 to ensure adequate training and  rigorous monitoring of foster families.
  
There were also some advances in the education sector.  In 2024, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Education to advance  digital learning, with a national workshop including the private sector, to  build interest and capacity to develop a national digital learning strategy,  and by forging a tripartite collaboration with the Ministry and the National  Digital Development Agency (ANADEN), focused on digitizing textbooks and  creating tools to strengthen education sector governance. In addition, with  UNICEF support, the Ministry of Education relaunched efforts to promote  inclusive education for children with disabilities, with training workshops  for 56 educational trainers and supervisors, focusing on supporting teachers  to detect, refer, and support children with disabilities, including the  management of learning disabilities.
  
In the health sector, UNICEF supported the  Ministry of Health in the development of the new Community Health Strategy  2024-2028, which provides a clear vision for a harmonized, integrated package  of interventions to be carried out by the country’s community health workers  (840 currently, with a planned increase to 870 as per the new strategy), to  support both routine health interventions and surveillance and response to  public health emergencies. This support included the development of  operational plans for each island, the costing of the strategy, estimated at  USD 44.6 million over 5 years, and an investment case to support resource  mobilization. 
  
However, two critical areas saw limited progress.  Amidst leadership changes and shifting national priorities, and despite  efforts as part of the Big Catch Up to reach zero-dose and under-immunized  children, immunization coverage continued to lag. As of the end of November  2024, 78 per cent of children under one year old had received three doses of  the Pentavalent vaccine, with inequities among health districts. In addition,  despite sustained advocacy on the part of UNICEF and its partner Gavi, it  proved particularly arduous to ensure the timely disbursement of State funds  for the purchase of vaccines. A payment order was signed on 2 January 2025  for the 2024 vaccines. Similarly, the construction of an oxygen plant in each  of the three islands, started in 2022, could not be completed in 2024 due to  ongoing challenges with construction and electrical components. 
  
In the nutrition sector, a key achievement  was the creation of a dedicated budget line for nutrition in the 2025 State  budget. This resulted from the participation of officials from the Ministry  of Health, Ministry of Finance, and UNICEF Comoros, in a training on public  finance for nutrition co-organized by UNICEF and the Southern African  Development Community (SADC) Secretariat in Senegal, followed by continued  support and advocacy from UNICEF Comoros. 
  
In addition, UNICEF supported the Ministry of  Health to conduct a national digital campaign that reached over 100,000  caregivers on social media and 400,000 through SMS about optimal child  feeding practices. A national vitamin A and deworming campaign reached more  than 120,000 under-five children. Malnutrition screening, undertaken through  the campaign, in health centres, or by parents at home through the Mother  MUAC initiative, resulted in 1058 children admitted to the national treatment  programme for severe acute malnutrition. These actions were supported by the  Japanese International Cooperation Agency (JICA), which has supported the  sector for several years but whose funding ended in December 2024. In  anticipation, UNICEF invested in national capacity building and advocacy for  increased national funding toward nutrition. 
  
In the water, sanitation and hygiene sector,  in addition to the significant support in the response to cholera, UNICEF  collaborated with the Regional Directorates of Water and Energy to train  local authorities and community leaders on best practices in sanitation and  hygiene. The training aimed to raise awareness about the dangers of fecal  contamination. Participants were introduced to the innovative Sato toilet  pan, an affordable, water-efficient and easy-to-install option with a  self-closing ‘trap door’. 122 local artisans then received practical training  on installing improved toilets. There has been an enthusiastic response so  far, and it will be important, in 2025, to bring in the private sector and  co-create a sustainable, market-based system for improved sanitation in  households and institutions.
  
Another important step forward, in 2024, was the  development of the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in Comoros. This  multisectoral analysis of how climate change affects children in  Comoros, and what action is needed in each sector, was developed in close  consultation with key stakeholders including adolescents from the three  islands. This report, expected to be validated nationally in early 2025, is  the first comprehensive analysis linking children and climate change in  Comoros, and as such is a critical step toward guiding UNICEF Comoros and  partners toward climate action for children, in a country where the negative  impact of climate change is already felt, and will only increase.
  
The growing realization of the interconnected  challenges that climate change poses in all social sectors calls for a strategic  shift on the part of UNICEF Comoros. To rise to this pressing challenge,  which affects both development work and preparedness and response to  emergencies, the team must first believe that they must, and can, take action  and be a climate leader in their respective sector. Yet, in a small country  office, where the limited personnel already shoulder several thematic  responsibilities, the question of how to effectively mainstream climate  action is not easily answered. It will be necessary to break silos and find  new ways of working toward common goals. The availability of dedicated  funding for climate change programming, from both KOICA and UNICEF internal  resources, are particularly welcome in this context and will play an  important role in building a collective momentum toward a multisectoral,  coherent climate vision. 
  
A second lesson, brought by the year 2024, is that  emergencies, while disruptive for programme implementation and exhausting for  staff, also bring opportunities. The cholera epidemic has not only  provided an opportunity for the country office to expand its partnerships and  collaboration with civil society organizations and new resource partners, and  to make progress in politically sensitive areas such as water quality. Emergency  response also added significant external support to the team, through UNICEF  surge personnel, standby partner deployees or international consultants.  These brought along their passion, good practices from elsewhere, new  networks and specialized technical capacity, which has significantly boosted  capacity within the office. This increased diversity has also helped broaden  the team’s understanding of the realm of possibilities with regards to human  resources. This is particularly important, in a lower middle-income country  that attracts limited donor interest, yet where much more progress is needed  on children’s rights, as well as particularly timely, as UNICEF is actively rethinking  its business model, including in Comoros.
  
Finally, it is important to recognize that weak governance  is a structural constraint that hinders progress in all sectors and  diminishes the impact of all the initiatives underway. UNICEF Comoros has  experimented on a small scale, for instance with support to the Regional  Directorates for Child Protection to develop their own Standard Operating  Procedures to guide human resource management, processes for purchase of  goods and services, or with mobilizing members of school councils for greater  oversight of school management, including issues such as teacher absenteeism.  However, such approaches are limited. More could be achieved through close  collaboration with other UN agencies to tackle a few, well-chosen priorities.  UNICEF has initiated such discussions within the UN Country Team, and  practical initiatives, such as switching to mobile payment for per diem to  partners, will be explored further in 2025.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

Eritrea has an estimated population of 3,535,603 [1]. About 45 per cent of the population is under 18 years of age [2], while 47 per cent of households are female-headed. Eritrea’s gross domestic product (GDP) growth is projected to increase modestly to 2.8 per cent in 2024 and 3.0 per cent in 2025, driven by the mining sector and domestic demand. Inflation is expected to decrease to 5.1 per cent in 2024 due to lower global food prices [3].
The country’s under-five mortality rate has decreased substantially, dropping from 85.5 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2000 to 38.1 in 2021, to 36.6 in 2022 [4] – below the world average of 37.1 deaths per 1,000 live births. Eritrea continues to make steady progress, and current trends project the under-five mortality rate to drop to 27.9 deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030, though this falls short of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of 25 deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030. Eritrea is projected to achieve this target in 2034 instead.
The ongoing conflict in Sudan has displaced millions of people, with significant flows entering Eritrea (including returnees to the country), particularly through the Gash-Barka and Anseba regions. By the end of 2024, the number of people from Sudan entering Eritrea is expected to surpass 100,000 [5], with the majority of them women and children. This influx has increased the pressure on Eritrea’s health and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, and education systems. In response, UNICEF has actively engaged with partners to leverage resources for children, scaling up provision of social services for displaced populations from Sudan and for Eritrea’s host community. This approach successfully mobilized US$2.5 million from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) for UNICEF, enabling provision of holistic social services to more than 178,000 people, including over 87,000 children (of which about 39,000 were girls) and 46,000 women, building on the existing community-based service delivery structure.
The national malnutrition burden persists, with the prevalence of stunting and wasting in children under 5 years of age still high, at 50 per cent and 15 per cent respectively. Although a population-based standard survey has not been conducted since 2010, mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) screening proxy estimation done in 2023 shows that 14.3 per cent of children under 5 years are wasted. Micronutrient deficiencies continue to be reported in children and women across all Eritrean regions, with the highest rates in the Northern and Southern Red Sea regions.
Eighty-six per cent of health facilities have improved water sources. Yet only 52 per cent of the population uses basic drinking water services, with significant disparities between urban and rural areas (90 per cent vs 28 per cent coverage) [6].
The 2024 Community Mapping Study on Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) [7] found that 5.3 per cent of the 53,000 interviewed households had had at least one female child under 15 years of age circumcised. The practice is most prevalent in the Gash-Barka region, particularly in Shambuqo (32.0 per cent prevalence), and least prevalent in the Anseba region, especially in Elabered (0.2 per cent). The study highlights significant regional disparities in FGM prevalence and in readiness to abandon the practice, necessitating tailored efforts to increase awareness and support to end FGM.
Eritrea is heavily affected by climate change, with average temperatures rising by 1.7°C since 1960 and more frequent and severe droughts leading to significant water insecurity and malnutrition [8]. Additionally, high rainfall intensity combined with sparse vegetation cover results in excessive runoff, high evaporation rates and reduced recharge of underground aquifers. The 2024 Climate Landscape Analysis for Children highlights several risks for children in Eritrea across major social services sectors. Climate change has altered the distribution of vector-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis, increasing their incidence in previously unaffected areas, like Gash-Barka, Northern Red Sea and Southern Red Sea. Also, in these drought-affected regions, nomadic lifestyles contribute to increased school absenteeism and dropout rates.
In 2024, Eritrea made significant progress in addressing climate issues, despite contributing only 0.01 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Following approval of US$9.8 million in climate adaptation funding from the African Development Bank (AfDB) Climate Action Window, strategic missions by AfDB and the UNICEF Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office recommended concrete priority actions. These actions seek to strengthen infrastructure, enhance coordination, increase community engagement, integrate health and education, incorporate aquifer recharge mechanisms and leverage funding to address climate change-related challenges affecting children in Eritrea. UNICEF Eritrea will apply these actions to enhance climate-smart programming.
Eritrea’s re-engagement with the international community in 2024 reflects a strategic effort to strengthen regional cooperation, secure investment for development projects and navigate complex geopolitical dynamics. This re-engagement is expected to reduce external arrears and provide financing. For example, Eritrea has secured investment for key infrastructure projects, including a US$49.9 million facility from AfDB to build a 30-megawatt solar photovoltaic power plant in Dekemhare, Debub, scheduled for completion in 2027.
The government presented the second Voluntary National Review (VNR) report, highlighting progress on SDGs 4 (Quality education), 5 (Gender equality) and 6 (Clean water and sanitation), and reaffirming its commitment to achieving these goals by 2030. Following the 2022 VNR of SDGs 3 (Good health and well-being) and 13 (Climate action), a noticeable data gap was identified, meaning that implementation of the Eritrea Population and Health Survey (EPHS) in 2025 is highly anticipated. EPHS 2025 has begun with the preparation of the sample design and draft questionnaires, which have been reviewed by UNICEF and other data users. Data collection is planned to start in the first quarter of 2025.
The government’s commitment to SDG 4 has led to the approval of US$14 million from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to support the Inclusive and Transformative Reform Agenda for Quality Learning for All Girls and Boys in Eritrea.
The Eritrean Ministry of Finance and National Development (MOFND) has begun reflecting on the National Development Plan 2026–2030 and its accompanying monitoring and evaluation policy. During the annual government–United Nations Joint Performance Review, concrete recommendations were made to strengthen the joint monitoring mechanism of implementation. This includes establishing a Directorate of Monitoring and Evaluation within MOFND. This is a major step towards effective public sector management and evidence-based decision-making.
