Through the joint support of UNICEF, the World Health Organization (WHO) and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, 98.9 per cent of children under 2 years of age in Eritrea were immunized with three doses of the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis/pentavalent vaccine in 2024 [1]. The government’s commitment to mitigating death and illness from vaccine-preventable diseases is evident through its annual 20 per cent domestic contribution towards the cost of vaccines.
UNICEF played a crucial role in supporting the measles-rubella vaccination and vitamin A supplementation campaign, providing technical and logistical assistance from initial planning to final analysis and reporting. UNICEF also supported the preparation and submission to Gavi of a proposal to introduce the hepatitis B birth dose in Eritrea, now approved for introduction in 2025. This milestone is expected to accelerate the reduction in newborn mortality. Additionally, UNICEF provided ongoing support in analysing routine Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) and stock management data, enabling the Ministry of Health (MOH) to monitor immunization services and make timely, informed decisions.
UNICEF Eritrea, in collaboration with UNICEF Supply Division, facilitated procurement of 2,899,650 doses of vaccines across 13 antigens, ensuring availability for 2024 and the first quarter of 2025. For the Gavi Cold Chain Equipment Optimization Platform (CCEOP) project, UNICEF coordinated procurement and customs clearance of 70 items of cold chain equipment for installation in 2025.
To reduce under-five mortality from common illnesses such as diarrhoea, pneumonia and malaria, MOH reached 251,238 children under 5 years (target: 200,000) using the WHO protocol for integrated management of newborn and childhood illnesses (IMNCI). As 30 per cent of the population resides in distant and hard-to-reach areas, UNICEF provided transportation support to ensure access to primary health care services in 19 remote districts, reaching about 9,500 children under 5 years and pregnant women through integrated mobile clinics. These clinics provided services to zero-dose and partially immunized children, as well as antenatal care, vitamin A supplementation, health education, and HIV testing and counselling.
Relatedly, in health care capacity-building, UNICEF provided financial and technical assistance to enhance basic clinical care for common childhood illnesses by training 41 health professionals in IMNCI. Additionally, skilled delivery services were improved by training 33 health workers on life-saving skills and emergency care for pregnant women and newborns. To strengthen national capacities in forecasting and quantification, and cold chain systems, UNICEF supported training for MOH staff on electronic tools, including the electronic vaccine arrival report (e-VAR) and vaccine forecasting tools, and solar direct drive (SDD) equipment installation and maintenance. This ensured timely submissions of e-VARs and forecasts, and quality maintenance of Eritrea’s climate-resilient SDD cold chain equipment.
High-quality promotive, preventive and curative nutrition services reached over 1.2 million people in 2024, including children, adolescents and pregnant and breastfeeding women – an increase of 100,000 people from 2023. These services were also provided to vulnerable communities facing multiple shocks, including drought, and to the influx of populations fleeing the conflict in Sudan. MUAC screening was provided to 366,700 children under 5 years, and adequate treatment given to 37,060 malnourished children, with UNICEF support. Vitamin A supplements were provided to 643,547 children aged 6–59 months (target: 770,000) and iron-folic acid tablets to 101,320 pregnant women (target: 180,000), contributing to improved maternal nutrition and positive birth outcomes.
To support delivery of nutrition services, UNICEF procured and ensured distribution of essential nutrition supplies, including ready-to-use therapeutic food, therapeutic formula milk (F-100, F-75) and ReSoMal for the management of acute malnutrition, as well as vitamin A capsules and iron-folic acid tablets for micronutrient supplementation. This ensured the delivery of quality prevention and treatment services to children and women. UNICEF also supported the capacity development of 102 programme officers and health workers by providing technical assistance and funding for government training programmes.
Supporting the intensified focus on preventive nutrition, UNICEF provided technical leadership in the design and implementation of the First Foods Initiative (DMK+ approach), including the development of guidelines and communication materials to improve complementary feeding practices and the quality of young children’s diets. Further, UNICEF strengthened partnerships with United Nations agencies (WHO, United Nations Population Fund [UNFPA], Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations [FAO] and International Fund for Agricultural Development), resulting in the establishment of the UN Nutrition Technical Working Group (UN-NTWG). UN-NTWG co-developed the operational road map for Eritrea’s adoption as a Global Action Plan country, enabling Eritrea to potentially benefit from the global Child Nutrition Fund. With the engagement of the UNICEF Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office team, foundational work was undertaken to formulate strategies on climate-smart nutrition programming, further strengthening resource mobilization capacities for climate financing for nutrition.
Mitigating the harmful effects of unsafe sanitation practices on health and nutrition, about 93 per cent of Eritrea’s 2,779 villages have been declared and certified open defecation-free as of 2024, a significant increase from 32 per cent in 2015. This achievement also restores dignity.
Access to climate-resilient safe water supply has expanded, with 507 of Eritrea’s 890 water supply systems now solar-powered. This initiative benefits rural and drought-impacted communities by mitigating water stress and carbon emissions and reducing running costs while also restoring dignity and building resilience. With UNICEF support, the Ministry of Land, Water and Environment (MOLWE) Water Resources Department rehabilitated and upgraded 15 climate-resilient water supply systems in 2024, securing access to basic water services for over 35,000 people (target: 60,000) – more than 18,000 females and over 17,000 males. Additionally, to significantly scale up safe water access for communities hosting people escaping from the conflict in Sudan, the drilling of 20 boreholes in Anseba, Gash-Barka and Maekel was completed in 2024.
A key factor in improving water supply systems is grassroots collaboration by local government, to foster strong community engagement in implementing water supply projects and ensuring community involvement throughout the project cycle. Major challenges were experienced in the procurement process and implementation, and in liquidation of direct cash transfers (DCTs) to MOH and MOLWE. Long delays were prevalent due to centralized, multi-layered government processes and obsolete banking systems. To mitigate this, UNICEF remained closely engaged, facilitating the processes. Community-led total sanitation to reach additional people (target:50,000) in villages practicing open defecation and safely managed sanitation are both crucial for addressing gaps that hinder progress beyond the current 93% open defecation-free status and for achieving the targets of SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation). Further, UNICEF supported transportation costs to implement community dialogues, enabling about 15,300 people to be reached with key sanitation and hygiene messages.
UNICEF has been working to address the significant resource gap in WASH programming, achieving the milestone success of securing US$9.8 million in WASH climate financing from AfDB. This underscores UNICEF’s vital role in providing financial support and advancing collaboration with government entities and international financial institutions to improve water accessibility and strengthen climate adaptation efforts. Additionally, UNICEF financial, technical and logistical support, including to procure tablets, computers and other essential accessories, was instrumental in facilitating data collection for the national WASH assessment.
Significant strides towards achieving SDG 4 (Quality education) have been made by the Ministry of Education (MOE), with UNICEF support. In addition to expanding access to education services, efforts to improve learners' outcomes have been successful. According to MOE's 'Essential Education Indicators 2022/23 Report,' the gross enrollment rate (GER) for primary schools increased from 87.7% (M: 92.7% and F: 82.2%) in 2021/2022 to 94.1% (M: 100.2% and F: 87.4%) in 2022/2023. Similarly, the GER for middle schools improved from 87.7% (M: 92.7% and F: 82.2%) to 94.1% (M: 100.2% and F: 87.4%). To strengthen evidence-based planning and data systems related to educational quality, a fifth round of the Measuring Learning Achievement (MLA V) assessment was conducted, after a five-year gap. Covering 83 schools and 4,797 students in Grades 3 and 5, the assessment shows encouraging improvements from MLA IV in combined mean scores for mother tongue, English and mathematics. From 2019 to 2024, the mean score for Grade 3 increased from 46.1 to 54.2; for Grade 5, it rose from 37.6 to 54.3.
Over the same five-year period, the survival rate to Grade 5 improved from 83.7 to 85 per cent, surpassing the 2024 target of 80 per cent, with the survival rate for girls (87.8 per cent) exceeding that of boys (82.7 per cent). Nevertheless, regional disparities remain, with the survival rate in Gash-Barka standing at 78.9 per cent versus 95.7 per cent in Maekel. The increase in survival rates, especially among girls, underscores the effectiveness of targeted interventions aimed at reducing school dropout and ensuring that more students complete primary education.
The positive developments in survival rates and retention are largely attributed to MOE’s targeted interventions, coupled with its several initiatives, particularly enrolment of out-of-school children in complementary elementary education centres, and cash incentives to support 4,500 girls transitioning to secondary school. Most cash transfer recipients are from nomadic communities and sub-zobas (subregions) with low retention and transition rates among girls.
Conversely, the out-of-school rate for primary education increased from 2021/22 to 2022/23 – from 15.43 to 17.7 per cent. Similarly, the middle school out-of-school rate increased from 15.4 to 16.9 per cent over the same period (Education Management Information System [EMIS 2022/23]). Concerted efforts to enhance access to education at all levels are, however, reflected in the notable improvements in the adjusted net enrolment rate (ANER) from the baseline in 2020 (EMIS 2018/19) [2] to the status in 2024 (EMIS 2022/23). At the pre-primary level (ages 4–5 years), the ANER increased from 17.4 to 21.1 per cent. At the primary level (6–10 years), there was a slight decrease, from 84.1 to 82.3 per cent. At the middle level (11–13 years), however, the ANER saw a substantial increase, from 65 to 83.2 per cent, and at the secondary level (14–17 years), it rose from 46.7 to 50.6 per cent.
Pre-primary enrolment increased slightly from 2021/22 to 2022/23, with the gross enrolment rate (GER) for pre-primary level rising from 22.4 to 22.8 per cent (22.0 to 22.4 per cent among girls). Over the same period, the net enrolment rate (NER) rose from 19.9 to 21.1 per cent (19.6 to 20.8 per cent among girls) but remains below the 2024 target of 26 per cent.
Despite this progress, 77.2 per cent of children aged 4–5 years, or 191,311 children (93,943 girls), still lack access to early learning opportunities, with significant regional disparities. For instance, Maekel has the highest regional enrolment rate at pre-primary level, at 40.4 per cent (although still below the national target of 50 per cent), while enrolment in Gash-Barka is only 13.6 per cent (EMIS 2022/23). To tackle low enrolment and address the widespread need to improve school readiness, the MOE Gash-Barka regional office, in collaboration with the community, enabled access to a summer school readiness programme for children aged 6–7 years, benefiting 4,635 out-of-school children (2,105 girls). This new alternative strategy aims to overcome the challenges of limited physical facilities and human resources to improve school readiness nationwide; the programme’s effectiveness will be assessed as part of the continuing partnership with GPE.
Ongoing challenges in education are revealed in the MLA V report: only half of learners in Grades 3 and 5 meet the expected reading proficiency and just 1 in 10 learners meet the desired proficiency in mathematics. Contributing factors include inadequate curriculum implementation, limited resources, and cultural norms that exclude disadvantaged children. In response, a sector-wide remedial learning programme on foundational literacy and numeracy has been designed with technical assistance from Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) Africa. Additionally, UNICEF continued to contribute to MOE’s vision of increasing the textbook-to-student ratio by providing textbooks to primary and middle school students. Over a million textbooks have been distributed in support of improving learning outcomes. In four regions, however, it is a challenge to find qualified mother-tongue teachers for Grades 1–5, and suspension of a teacher training programme has worsened this issue.
UNICEF contributed financial and technical support for expansion of learning spaces and equitable, quality early learning by equipping pre-primary classrooms with furniture and play-based teaching and learning materials, benefiting about 3,000 pre-primary-age children. UNICEF also provided logistical and professional support for capacity-building of 67 MOE personnel.
To further support equitable access to quality education and promote climate resilience, 12 schools in four remote zobas (regions) were each equipped with 14 solar panels, 8 batteries and 15 desktop computers. These renewable energy resources not only provide reliable power but also ensure environmental sustainability of the support. Approximately 6,500 students benefit from these resources, particularly in enhancing their digital skills starting from Grade 8. This initiative is a critical step in bridging the digital divide in underserved and climate-affected areas of Gash-Barka.
Messages about the importance of education reached 1.3 million caregivers in Anseba, Debub, Maekel and Northern Red Sea through the MOE’s media education programme, activated with UNICEF support, which aired 157 education programmes on radio in the Tigre and Tigrigna languages. Additionally, social and behaviour change (SBC) was integrated into the early childhood care and education curriculum to strengthen teachers’ capacity to engage with communities. UNICEF also enhanced the awareness of 45 staff members focusing on holistic child development, including cognitive, social and emotional development, as part of parenting education.
In 2023, MOE, with UNICEF support, began implementing the Eritrea Partnership Compact, which outlines a road map for transforming the education sector. This initiative secured over US$14 million from GPE to fund sector reforms in 2024.
With UNICEF technical and financial support, modest progress has been made towards generating timely and quality EMIS data. The findings will provide the evidence base needed to guide the transformation of the education sector and improve learning outcomes. The 2022–2023 EMIS statistical yearbook was finalized and published in November 2024. This was achieved through capacity-building of relevant MOE staff from all zobas in data collection, entry and analysis, and provision of relevant infrastructure and equipment. UNICEF distributed 80 laptops and 94 desktop computers to the six zobas (and 58 sub-zobas) to improve data management.
A 2024 study led by the Ministry of Labor and Social Welfare (MOLSW) in partnership with UNFPA and UNICEF revealed that the prevalence of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) is 2.3 per cent among girls under 5 years of age and 4.4 per cent among girls under 15 years in 20 sub-zobas across five zobas (excluding Southern Red Sea). Although these study data are not nationally representative and not directly comparable with EPHS findings, they suggest an improvement since EPHS 2010, which recorded national prevalence rates of 12 per cent among girls under 5 years and 33 per cent among girls under 15 years. In Eritrea, 12 out of 67 sub-zobas are now FGM-free, meaning that about 346,102 girls under 15 years (about 55 per cent of this population) have been spared from FGM. Eritrea enforces a law banning FGM, the Female Circumcision Abolition Proclamation No. 158/2007.
Of the 1,086 villages surveyed for the 2024 study, 689 villages (63.4 per cent) reported that no girls under 15 years had been circumcised. Additionally, in 922 out of the 1,081 studied villages (85.3 per cent) with at least one female child under 5 years of age, none of the daughters under 5 years had undergone FGM. This success is attributed to UNICEF-supported mapping programmes, the community-based SBC approach, community mobilization and dialogues, and the airing of preventive messages against violence, including harmful practices such as FGM and child marriage.
In some surveyed sub-zobas, such as Adi Kuala, Areza, and Segeneyti in Debub; Lalay Gash, Mensura, and Shambuqo in Gash-Barka; and Massawa and Qarura in the Northern Red Sea region, most of the studied communities were not yet ready to publicly declare the abandonment of the practice of FGM. The prevalence of FGM is particularly high in certain sub-zobas among girls under 15 years and under 5 years: Shambuqo (29.3 and 23.4 per cent respectively), Mensura (18.3 and 4.4 per cent), Qarura (15.8 and 4.0 per cent), Lalay Gash (13.9 and 5.9 per cent) and Segeneyti (8.3 and 2.9 per cent).
The government cash-transfer programme (Martyrs Trust Fund) benefited an estimated 240,000 individuals, including 93,600 children (45,613 girls, 47,987 boys). This initiative illustrates the government’s dedication to the well-being of society and demonstrates a positive direction in its policies. With such measures, a rise in government spending is expected, emphasizing continuous support and commitment to these families through the provision of needed social protection services. In addition, UNICEF, in partnership with MOLSW, reached a total of 77,053 vulnerable children (48 per cent girls), including 23,883 children with disabilities living in 19,263 households. These children were provided with integrated community-based social protection support, psychosocial support, and cash transfers that improved access to social services, enhancing school enrolment and retention.
UNICEF supported MOLSW in developing an integrated child protection manual to strengthen the capacity of community-based social service workforces, which include social workers, para social workers and community members. This improved the delivery of services for vulnerable children and families. As a result, 87,678 women, girls and boys (including about 60,000 women and adolescent girls) were reached with information and services on accessing gender-based violence risk mitigation, prevention and response interventions. This approach ensured comprehensive support for the most vulnerable children and families, addressing their unique needs and promoting their inclusion in society.
A significant breakthrough was achieved with the government’s endorsement of the establishment of an integrated child and social protection information management system (CSPIMS). An inception report on the assessment of the child and social protection case management system in Eritrea was also endorsed, paving the way for enhanced case management and improved responses to child abuse and exploitation. The rigorous process of elaborating the inception report involved comprehensive data collection for integrated case management, capacity gap assessment, identification of essential data requirements, and the drafting of a strategic action plan for deploying the CSPIMS.
Last but not least, UNICEF facilitated logistical arrangements for government partners to conduct joint field visits. This collaboration allowed for direct observation of both progress and challenges in actual implementation of programmes, advancing a close partnership with the government. It also enabled UNICEF to work closely with government partners in addressing challenges and incorporating lessons learned into the design of new programme interventions.

Strong partnerships between UNICEF, various ministries – including Health; Land, Water and Environment; Education; Labour and Social Welfare, and Finance and National Development – zoba administrations and local communities have been vital in improving outcomes for children and their families in 2024.
Under the Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework between the Government of the State of Eritrea and the United Nations 2022–2026 and the 2024–2026 Joint Triennial Work Plan, UNICEF partnered with MOH to deliver essential health services. This partnership enabled malnutrition prevention and treatment services to reach more than 809,000 people (target: 1.2 million), including children under 5 years of age, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers.
Through this framework, MOH and UNICEF provided high-impact health services, including antenatal, delivery, postnatal and newborn care, immunization, and management of childhood illnesses to 248,572 children and women. Additionally, sanitation and hygiene education aimed at eliminating trachoma and preventing other diseases reached 15,300 people. Opportunities exist to strengthen linkages in 2025 between MOH and other critical ministries such as MOE, for early childhood development; MOLWE, for climate-resilient WASH in health facilities; and MOLSW, for protecting vulnerable children and women through national health service delivery platforms.
The Infant and Young Child Feeding Technical Working Group, led by MOH with representatives from the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Marine Resources, FAO and UNICEF, played a pivotal role in advancing the food systems transformation agenda. The establishment of UN-NTWG strengthened the multisectoral nutrition response and resource mobilization. Within UNICEF, collaboration on nutrition was enhanced across sectors such as WASH, social protection, health, education, and social and behaviour change communication. Integration with health during the measles-rubella vaccination campaign helped the nutrition programme achieve over 90 per cent coverage for vitamin A supplementation.
UNICEF collaboration with the Ministry of Land Water and Environment and other partners have provided safe drinking water to communities and promoted sanitation and hygiene practices, significantly contributing to the nationwide campaign to eliminate trachoma.
UNICEF partnered with UNFPA, MOH and MOLSW, and the National Union of Eritrean Women, which are vital partners in the fight against FGM and child marriage and in strengthening the CSPIMS. The ongoing partnership with the European Union is also critical to expanding coverage to hard-to-reach and resistant communities. For clear and internationally recognized up-to-date data on child protection, specifically for ending FGM and child marriage, it is critical to conduct EPHS 2025 – which UNICEF advocates for and supports.
UNICEF has worked to transform the education sector through a sustained partnership with GPE. As the grant agent for the current Education Sector Plan Implementation Grant (ESPIG), UNICEF supported the implementation of GPE-funded education projects. UNICEF led the technical design and development of a country programme, now supported by the System Transformation Grant and System Capacity Grant from GPE. With support from the UNICEF regional office, UNICEF Eritrea contracted TaRL Africa to assist MOE in designing and rolling out a sector-wide remedial learning programme based on the proven TaRL approach to improve foundational literacy and numeracy skills among primary-level learners.
In 2024, UNICEF forged impactful partnerships to advance education in Eritrea. By hosting a joint mission with the GPE team and UNICEF Deputy Regional Director, high-level meetings, technical sessions and the launch of the new GPE-supported country programme were facilitated. These efforts promoted a collaborative understanding of the education sector’s complexities and successfully accelerated the implementation of the ESPIG for school construction projects.
In addition to UNICEF core resources for results (Regular Resources), crucial support received from funding partners such as the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, Government of Ireland (Irish Aid), CERF and Fred Hollows Foundation was instrumental in achieving results. The integrated implementation of this funding addressed both development and humanitarian needs, including responding to the influx of people displaced by the conflict in Sudan (including returnees to Eritrea), underscoring the humanitarian-development-peace nexus programming approach suited to the Eritrean context. A substantial new partnership with AfDB is also under way, with US$9.8 million in funding secured for a WASH climate adaptation project in Eritrea, co-financed with an additional US$3 million from UNICEF.
UNICEF effectively leveraged South-South partnerships in 2024. With support from UNICEF, WHO and Gavi, five cold chain technicians gained hands-on experience with solar-driven cold chain equipment at an accredited training institution in Malawi. They learned to install cold chain equipment, conduct preventive maintenance and perform repairs. Meanwhile, an EPI manager from MOH travelled to South Africa to share Eritrea’s EPI successes and learn best practices from other countries.
Additionally, a maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) team from MOH, along with WHO and UNICEF representatives, attended a workshop in Zambia focused on reducing newborn and maternal mortality. Further, UNICEF and MOE participated in an early childhood development workshop in the United Republic of Tanzania. Partnerships were also formed between the ministries of education in Eritrea and Zambia, as well as with TaRL Africa.
High-level meetings included MOE participation in the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange in Kigali, Rwanda, and the Knowledge Information Exchange Continental Research Symposium in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, which focused on educational research. Further, the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders (ExCEL) Cohorts Reunion, organized by the UNICEF regional office Evaluation team with cohort countries such as Eswatini, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi and Somalia, allowed Eritrea’s MOFND colleagues and UNICEF to learn from other countries and share the status of each country’s ExCEL Action Plan implementation on evaluation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The efforts in Eritrea encountered some challenges and led to solutions to overcome them, as well as several key lessons learned, particularly in cost savings, enhancing behavioural change, improving service delivery and addressing violence against children. These lessons are crucial in informing future strategies and programmes aimed at improving the lives of children and women.
Challenges: Continuous efforts were made to liquidate outstanding direct cash transfers (DCTs) to partners. The amount of outstanding DCTs over nine months increased, however, from US$2,600,666 (December 2023) to US$3,218,995 (December 2024); over the same period, DCTs totalling US$6.2 million were liquidated. To address this, continuous dialogue was held through tripartite meetings with MOFND, the line ministry and UNICEF. The effort to liquidate the outstanding DCTs was affected by delays and lengthy procurement processes through a centralized government agency, along with time-consuming transfers to the national and subnational levels owing to limited subnational banking facilities.
Extended delays in procurement through the central procurement agency, Red Sea Trading Corporation, significantly affected the construction of schools and the rehabilitation of WASH facilities in 2024. UNICEF has regularly advocated for streamlined procurement processes through tripartite meetings with MOFND and line ministries, and closely followed up to facilitate the process. These delays have resulted in the stagnation of open defecation-free results and the necessary extension of GPE grants. To address these issues, UNICEF advocated for the establishment of a joint procurement taskforce by the government and United Nations agencies, which was agreed upon at the joint annual performance review. This taskforce aims to identify bottlenecks across both parties, reduce challenges and find common solutions.
Key lessons learned in 2024 are as follows:

Cost savings: A proactive approach to financial resource management throughout 2024 resulted in substantial cost savings while maintaining high operational performance. By enhancing budget planning, streamlining administrative and operational processes, and implementing innovative solutions, significant efficiencies were achieved across key areas. Notably, internet communication and connectivity costs were reduced by 90 per cent through optimized service plans, cost-sharing with other United Nations agencies and better contract negotiations. Additionally, United Nations common services benefited from cost reductions through more balanced and efficient cost-sharing mechanisms, streamlined operations and improved resource utilization across agencies. These efforts have strengthened organizational efficiency and enabled the strategic reallocation of resources, ensuring greater impact for children and enhanced value for money.
Participatory approaches for inclusive programming: The light mid-term review (MTR) process highlighted the significance of a participatory approach, ensuring comprehensive consultation with staff associations, sections and units to gather proposals and shape communication strategies. The process started with a pre-process survey that informed the communication strategies. Novel change proposals originated from sections and were discussed with all staff, adhering to the bottom-up principles of the MTR. Discussions on the funding landscape and budget realities facilitated a common understanding, emphasizing that without proposals from sections and subsequent discussions, reaching consensus on changes would have been more challenging. This inclusive approach fosters ownership and accountability among stakeholders, leading to more effective and sustainable programmes.
Community engagement and ownership: In Debub, Gash-Barka and Southern Red Sea, some communities remain hesitant to abandon FGM. Continuous engagement, dialogue and joint efforts have demonstrated that FGM can only be eradicated if the communities unite, agree and build collective determination. This collective approach ensures that no one faces social consequences for not participating in FGM. To achieve this, it is crucial to bring these communities together in a forum where they can collectively agree to stop FGM. UNICEF has provided DCTs to partners to facilitate these dialogue sessions. Additionally, a social norms approach was facilitated, highlighting that harmful practices like FGM are best addressed through collective consensus. This approach has helped the communities understand that changing social norms is key to ending FGM. The effectiveness of this approach has been confirmed by reports from partners and UNICEF field visits to Gash-Barka and by feedback from the Chairperson of the Gash-Barka Zonal Technical Committee.
Integrated child protection and education programmes: Including capacity-building to enable teachers and other school staff to recognize signs of abuse, trauma or neglect and respond appropriately allows a large number of students to be reached. This is an important step in addressing violence against children in schools, creating a safer and more supportive learning environment.
Strategic partnerships for improved service delivery: Leveraging existing programmes, such as EPI, can facilitate the delivery of essential MNCH services, especially in areas with limited funding and strict government policies. By piggybacking on EPI, a well-funded and high-priority initiative, MNCH services can reach a greater number of vulnerable populations, improving health outcomes for more women and children.
Technology for development and awareness: Offline app technology can be exploited to increase awareness, as with the nutrition app that demonstrated the importance of complementary feeding (DMK+ approach) nationwide. This innovative approach has shown that novel technology can be a transformative implementation tool, particularly in settings with low internet access.
Nexus programming for climate resilience: UNICEF’s comparative advantage in humanitarian-development-peace nexus programming and community-based service delivery systems facilitated strategic applications for climate funding, addressing government priorities on SDGs 6 (Clean water and sanitation) and 13 (Climate action). By integrating climate resilience into existing programmes, UNICEF can help vulnerable populations adapt to climate change impacts, reducing the risks of displacement, hunger and disease.
Efficient office management for accelerated results: The audit conducted in the last quarter of 2024 helped the country office identify areas for improvement and address residual risks. This learning experience has paved the way for more efficient and effective office management, accelerating the delivery of results for children in Eritrea. By streamlining processes, reducing bottlenecks, and enhancing accountability, UNICEF strives to maximize its impact, reaching more children and women with essential services and support.
The lessons learned in Eritrea offer valuable insights into enhancing behavioural change, addressing violence against children and improving service delivery. By embracing community-led approaches, integrated programming, strategic partnerships, technology for development, participatory approaches, nexus programming and efficient office management, UNICEF is accelerating its impact, creating a brighter future for children and women in Eritrea.

This section presents the socioeconomic and child rights landscape in 2024 across the 21 countries covered by UNICEF’s Eastern and Southern Africa Office (ESARO).

Eastern and Southern Africa is home to 280 million children, many of whom experience multiple deprivations of their rights. While significant strides have been made toward the child-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), more dedicated investment and prioritized action are needed to prevent the loss of prior gains in a context characterized by frequent climate shocks, conflict, emergencies and large-scale population movements. UNICEF’s Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office (ESARO), which is based in Nairobi, Kenya, supports 21 UNICEF country offices that work in very diverse contexts. This annual report describes ESARO’s achievements and contributions – as well as challenges and lessons – in 2024 in terms of the accountabilities and functions of UNICEF regional offices.

ESARO recognizes that child poverty rates in Eastern and Southern Africa Region (ESAR) have declined in recent years in terms of extreme monetary poverty – from 45 per cent in 2013 to 40 per cent in 2023. The region's growing young population represents a large potential demographic dividend if matched with robust human capital investments, particularly in the early and adolescent years of today’s children, to ensure their rights as per the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC).

However, there are many challenges. The pace of poverty reduction is slowing, food prices remain high, and country debt is a major structural concern. Weak governance is perpetuating inequities and inefficiencies in national spending, resulting in the wastage of about 2.5 per cent of regional GDP, thus limiting poverty reduction and directly impacting children’s access to an adequate standard of living.

The region was affected by serious humanitarian crises in 2024 set against the backdrop of the reduced funding for responses for the region’s children as conflicts elsewhere diverted resources and attention away from the region. At least 74 million people in the region, including 45 million children, needed humanitarian support in 2024. UNICEF Level 2 corporate emergency procedures were put into effect for the northern Ethiopia conflict, while Level 3 procedures were activated in Burundi, Rwanda, Kenya and Uganda to tackle the mpox outbreak. In sum, this year’s humanitarian situation was dominated by numerous public health emergencies (including Ebola, Marburg, cholera, mpox, measles and polio outbreaks), extreme drought and crop failures in southern Africa, and severe floods in eastern Africa, alongside the intensifying impacts of climate change; while several countries grappled with civil unrest, conflict, economic deterioration and population displacement.

The ESAR region has the second highest child mortality rate in the world with all 21 countries off-track for achieving the SDG’s under-five mortality target. Most of them are facing health emergencies and six high priority countries[1] have 9.1 million children with zero-dose immunization. Enhancing the community-based primary health care (PHC) approach for multisectoral system strengthening remained key to fulfilling children’s rights to access essential health services in the region.

Large-scale nutrition deprivation persisted in the region with almost 4 million children suffering from wasting, 26 million from stunting, and 67 million living in food poverty, while over 20 million 5–19-year-olds are overweight. The escalating climate crisis, food insecurity and persistently high rates of malnutrition underline the importance of addressing all forms of malnutrition by programming through multiple systems, and especially the food, social protection and health systems, including with a climate lens.

The Eastern and Southern Africa region still has two-thirds of all AIDS cases worldwide in spite of the remarkable progress made, including the 70 per cent reduction in new infections of children since 2010. Efforts to achieve the ‘triple elimination’ of the transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B from mothers to babies at pregnancy, delivery, and breastfeeding, are gaining traction. But the region is off-track for the SDG targets as half a million affected children and adolescents are not on life-saving treatment, and adolescent girls and young women experience the high rates of HIV, early pregnancy and violence that are driven by poverty, gender inequality, and inadequate health systems.

The ESAR countries are off track to achieve the SDG targets for universal access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), with only 63 per cent of households having access to safe water and 28 per cent to safely managed sanitation. The increased incidence and severity of climate change-exacerbated droughts and floods, and the increased food insecurity and public health emergencies in the region underscore the critical need to increase investments in the WASH sector.

There is significant underinvestment in early childhood development (ECD). Only 24 per cent of the region’s 3 to 5-year-olds have access to early learning, while only 40 per cent of 24 to 59-month-old children receive responsive care while 26 million 0–5-year-olds are growth stunted. Alarmingly, 74 per cent of 1 to 4-year-olds are subject to harsh disciplinary practices.

Forty-seven million of the rapidly growing child and youth population are out-of-school with large disparities affecting the most vulnerable. Nine in ten of the region’s children are unable to read a simple text by age 10. Education spending is low and uneven while the allocation of public resources favours children from wealthier households. Climate shocks, crises, and teacher shortages further strain education systems, while 20 per cent of 15–24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training.

Ongoing crises are worsening violence against girls, boys and women and exacerbating displacement and mental health risks. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest number of victims of sexual violence worldwide with 79 million girls affected before they turn eighteen. Poverty and inadequate fiscal resources are weakening child protection systems, limiting social service workforce investments and deepening service gaps. Finally, the region has the lowest rate of birth registration globally with only 48 per cent of under-fives having such registration for ensuring their identity and access to services.

The region’s women and girls are heavily burdened with unpaid care and domestic duties, are much less employed in formal jobs than their male peers, and are less able to influence government policies. Many adolescent girls face child marriage, pregnancy and gender-based violence, and face a disproportionate risk of HIV transmission and of dropping out of school. The removal of gender barriers requires all programming to be more gender intentional to address girls’ different needs.

The situation of the nearly 29 million children with disabilities in the region remains challenging. Many of them face large barriers to accessing essential services such as education, healthcare, and social protection, while frequently being the victims of harmful traditional practices.

The above-mentioned challenges, as grave as they are, mask the fact that many countries in the Eastern and Southern Africa region have made some of the strongest recent progress globally, particularly on the child-related SDG indicators. Ethiopia, Rwanda, Mozambique, Uganda, and Tanzania are among the top 20 countries in the world that have recorded strong progress across multiple outcome areas for children.[2] ESARO’s support to its 21 countries rests on the recognition of the region’s past achievements and the future potential for attaining the child-related SDGs.

[1] Angola, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Madagascar, Tanzania and Somalia
[2] Progress on Children’s Well-Being: Centring Child Rights in the 2030 Agenda, UNICEF https://data.unicef.org/resources/sdg-report-2023/

This section presents ESARO’s key programme and operations results in 2024, showcasing its accountability to support the region’s 21 countries (country offices), while adding value at the regional level. The specific outcomes of UNICEF's interventions on improving children's lives are detailed in the annual reports of the individual country offices.

Highlights of programme results
Social policy – Public finance work in UNICEF ESAR has shifted towards efficiency, effectiveness and equity of national spending, while UNICEF’s lead on national social protection systems and cash assistance programming continued to grow. ESARO’s specific contributions included the following:

There was a visible shift in UNICEF’s approach to child poverty work in 2024 as its country offices committed to identifying policy reform priorities. Its public finance work put a greater emphasis on gathering targeted, timely and quality evidence to drive improvements in national budgets.
In collaboration with UNICEF WCARO and MENARO, ESARO highlighted the inequity of national spending by age across Africa by producing new evidence, which was shared globally on traditional and social media. The findings revealed that spending in Africa is heavily prioritised toward older children. The research resulted in the development of an Africa-wide advocacy plan on investing in human capital, in partnership with the World Bank and the African Economic Research Centre.
ESARO maintained engagement with international financial institutions, including partnerships with the World Bank on poverty reduction and human capital investment. As a result, UNICEF has become a partner for the Bank in implementing its upcoming human capital plans, is co-launching evidence on poverty and inequality in Africa and has expanded collaboration with the International Monetary Fund.
UNICEF’s leadership in strengthening enhancing national social protection systems contributed to the expansion of social assistance to 30.5 million households across 20 countries in the region. This also included the scaling up of efforts on cash-plus social protection financing and climate initiatives.

Humanitarian response – 20 of the region’s 21 countries faced crises and humanitarian situations in 2024, testing the region’s resilience, preparedness, funding and response capacities. The region sustained effective emergency responses with ESARO’s specific contributions including the following:

ESARO supported ongoing emergency responses in 14 of its countries, while all 21 were supported to strengthen emergency preparedness and timely responses, including the improved reporting on children affected by the numerous crises. Simulation exercises supported in South Sudan, Uganda and Eritrea helped strengthen preparedness capacities.
ESARO supported the South Sudan Country Office to deliver life-saving assistance and protection to South Sudanese returnees and Sudanese refugees.
ESARO supported the scaling-up of multi-sectoral responses to cholera and polio outbreaks in 13 of the region’s countries, and the strengthening of public health responses to mpox outbreaks in Burundi, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda, and a Marburg outbreak in Rwanda.

Climate, energy and environment – In 2024, UNICEF ESARO ramped up its support for climate advocacy, partnerships, resource mobilization, evidence-generation and programming for climate-smart social services for children, including the following contributions:

In partnership with the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) and the World Resources Institute (WRI), ESARO led an Africa-wide event at COP29 to promote the inclusion of child-focused actions in nationally determined contributions (NDCs). Ahead of COP29, ESARO supported 11 country offices to prepare governments’ participation in expert dialogues on climate and children for the sixtieth session of the Subsidiary Body for Implementation (SBI) under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).
All 21 country offices were supported on climate policy making, targeted climate finance capacity-building and climate-smart programming on sustainable energy for education, health, WASH and other subjects.
ESARO engaged more than 66,000 youth (55% female) across the region in climate initiatives towards implementing UNICEF’s Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan 2023-2030 (SCAP).

Health – ESARO focused its 2024 efforts on scaling up and enhancing the quality of primary health care, reaching zero dose communities with immunization and essential services, and responding to public health emergencies. Technical assistance to countries facing public health emergencies dominated ESARO efforts in 2024, while cross-border transmission remained a constant threat. Its specific contributions included the following:

ESARO’s support for developing national community health strategies (NCHSs), establishing national community health worker (CHW) registries and conducting joint country missions with the Africa CDC (Centres for Disease Control and Prevention) contributed towards the number of trained CHWs in the region’s health systems reaching 690,000 or 66 per cent of the regional target.
ESARO supported the ‘Big Catch-Up’ (BCU) initiative, which to the end of 2024 has reached 31 per cent of the targeted 9.1 million zero-dose children in the six high-priority countries in the region. This support has evolved around the high-level task force and regional working groups supporting national plans and multi-partner coordination. These and other efforts to reach zero dose children with routine vaccination, and polio vaccination campaigns led to the number of polio cases decreasing from 208 cases in 13 countries in 2023 to only 76 in 8 countries in 2024.
With ESARO support, human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination coverage increased from 49% of targeted children in the region in 2022 to 58% of them in 2024. The effort included mobilising partners, coordinated technical support to countries and advocacy at high-level meetings.
ESARO supported the introduction and scaling of malaria vaccination in several countries in the region, helping countries with application for GAVI support and organizing peer learning workshops with WHO’s Regional Office for Africa (AFRO).

Nutrition – 2024 saw significant progress on implementing UNICEF’s Transforming Food Systems for Children agenda, while system strengthening continued on nutrition. ESARO’s specific contributions included the following:

A sub-regional undertaking was initiated around food systems for children focusing on sharing technical resources across six country offices, ESARO and UNICEF HQ, as part of UNICEF’s global Business Model Initiative.
UNICEF’s First Foods Africa programme was launched focusing on the local production and consumption of nutritious, safe, and affordable ‘first’ foods.
Fourteen countries were supported to enhance social protection and nutrition synergies, 12 countries to improve nutrition for school children and adolescents, 12 countries to strengthen nutrition information systems, and 13 countries to strengthen the food environment policies.
ESARO continued to support 10 countries to develop new wasting guidelines, 7 countries to transition from iron-folic acid to multiple micronutrient supplementation, including the elaboration of transitioning plans through high-level advocacy in 4 countries, and review nutrition and ECD counselling services in 15 countries.
Regional workshops were provided to build the capacity of all 21 countries on public finance for nutrition, while matching funds from UNICEF’s Child Nutrition Fund continued to double investments for child nutrition interventions.

HIV/AIDS and sexual and reproductive health and rights – ESARO accelerated efforts on improving the HIV indicators for children and strengthening adolescent girls’ sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR):

Its multisectoral work with young people, especially adolescent girls, continued to help prevent HIV and improve sexual and reproductive health including through its allocation of $4.8 million to eight countries to accelerate HIV prevention among adolescent girls and young women.
The outcomes of ESARO–Global Fund work were leveraged in five countries to nationalize assessment and referral mechanisms to improve support for the most at-risk adolescent girls and young women.
With ESARO support, the UNITED! HIV and SRHR movement grew across many countries in the region with the connected young advocates working to improve health outcomes.
ESARO led knowledge management and learning around peer providers for eliminating the vertical transmission of HIV. This and other UNICEF support contributed to Namibia being certified by WHO as on the path to eliminating mother-to-child transmission.
The innovative dissemination of evidence through listening parties and country exchanges helped convert evidence to action to improve the well-being of adolescents and persons with HIV. The supported 2gether 4 SRHR knowledge hub programme provided an important resource for this work.

WASH – With the mounting pressure of health outbreaks, including cholera, in 2024 UNICEF ESARO accelerated efforts to strengthen partnerships, innovation and expand WASH services:

ESARO strengthened its cooperation with international financial institutions and regional bodies including the World Bank, AfDB, SADC and IGAD, and other partners including KfW, SDC, AMCOW and academia through initiatives to enhance climate resilient WASH services and groundwater management that covered 17 countries9.
Several regional programmes, in partnership with UNHCR, UNDP and UNESCO, including the Regional Open WASH programme for Displaced and Host Communities (R-WASH), generated evidence and tested innovative approaches in the WASH sector.
Significant progress was made on innovative groundwater mapping and the drilling of some of the deepest wells in Ethiopia, Kenya, Angola and Somalia for enhancing water security, climate resilience and sustainable water supplies particularly in the Horn of Africa.
The rollout of the WASH FIT management tool for health facility improvements in 8 countries10 made a large contribution to public health emergency responses.

Early childhood development – UNICEF ESARO continued to leverage the momentum of the 2023 Africa Human Capital Heads of State Summit (held in Tanzania) to anchor early childhood development (ECD) as the cornerstone of human development. ESARO’s specific contributions included the following:

ECD capacity building support reached over 3,000 government officials across the region, including in partnership with the African ECD Network and the African Union.
ESARO continued to influence government budget allocations for young children's welfare with per capita public spending by the region’s governments on ECD increasing by 2 per cent annually. Seventeen ESAR countries have adopted ECD policies with priority actions spanning health, nutrition, early learning, and responsive caregiving.
Health systems in 10 countries were strengthened to provide comprehensive support to young children, with most ESAR countries scaling up accelerated school readiness interventions.
ESARO-supported parenting programmes had reached over six million parents across the region by the end of 2024.

Education – UNICEF ESARO’s support made a large contribution to the considerable progress made in the region to address the learning crisis and skills gap during the African Union’s Year of Education (2024). It drove transformative education results during 2024 by maximizing the impetus provided by the continental platform:

ESARO supported the strengthening of foundational learning in 16 sixteen countries by expanding remedial and digital learning and scaling-up Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL).
High-level engagement, strategic partnerships, improved data systems and 20 new knowledge products supported advocacy, and programme and policy decision making on learning outcomes in all 21 countries.
Twelve countries were supported on youth skill development through innovative learning-to-earning pathways; while technical assistance reinforced inclusive, gender-responsive education systems.
ESARO supported continuity of learning in countries affected by public health emergencies such as cholera, Mpox and Marburg by providing guidance for prevention in schools. Similarly, ESARO provided technical assistance to guide safe return to schools in countries affected by climate-related crises that disrupted learning.
ESARO supported eligible GPE (Global Partnership Education) countries across the region to develop expressions of interest and programme documents for System Transformation Grants (STG), Girls’ Education Accelerator (GEA) and multiplier grants with successful results in Eritrea, Madagascar, South Sudan, Burundi, and Lesotho.
ESARO co-convened in partnership with the AU and the GPE a continental thought leadership webinar on innovative financing for education to explore alternative mechanisms to close gaps in education financing.
In partnership with the World Bank, the Association for the Development of Education in Africa (ADEA), and the Hempel Foundation, ESARO supported the Government of Rwanda during the hosting of the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange (FLEX) in November 2024. During this event, Ministers of Education and other high-level officials from 36 countries gathered and pledged to ending learning poverty by 2035. ESARO and several UNICEF country offices facilitated the participation of Ministers or their representatives and played a pivotal role in drafting the declaration and facilitating a Ministerial dialogue.

Child protection, PSEA and MHPSS – UNICEF ESARO leveraged the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, Bogotá, as a milestone to establish governments’ commitments to child rights:

ESARO supported 19 government delegations from the region to participate in the Bogota conference, where they committed to universal parenting programmes, safe school environments, and more support for high-risk children.
It continued to strengthen partnerships with women-led organizations in the region as countries advanced their localization and gender equality priorities on preventing violence.
System-strengthening support continued, including for establishing a regional platform for learning about childcare reforms and a framework on civil registration and vital statistics, and technical support to producing investment cases in Kenya and Zambia that highlighted the economic impacts of violence against children.
Anchored in support for implementing the regional cross-sectoral workplan for Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), a youth-led social media campaign reached 14,000 people, while MHPSS training took place successfully in Ethiopia and South Sudan.
UNICEF’s global children on the move agenda were strengthened in the region through the production of a joint workplan with IOM, UNHCR, and Save the Children, while the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) was integrated into responses to public health emergencies during the year.

Gender and adolescent development and participation – ESARO pursued gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls with strengthening partnerships with women-led organizations (WLOs) as a key strategy to address issues affecting women and girls and in line with the localization agenda:

ESARO advocated for sustained financing on equitable access to quality education for girls and women at the first Pan-African Conference on Girls and Women’s Education in July 2024 (African Union).
Two gender programmatic reviews were supported that informed new country programmes, while the identification of gender barriers to health and nutrition programming were supported in 10 countries.
The integration of gender issues in emergency preparedness was strengthened by investing in national coalitions of women and girls’ organizations, particularly in Malawi and Zambia, which faced major health emergencies. In these countries, Malawi's coalition includes 63 organizations covering 28 districts, while Zambia's coalition comprises 111 organizations across 10 provinces and 68 districts, all contributing to respond to major health crises.
Women and girls were positioned as crucial actors for addressing climate and water management issues in an inter-agency evidence product, while a regional partnership with the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts was pursued on girl-led climate action.
ESARO expanded UNICEF’s global Youth-led Action Initiative in the region, from the earlier focus on youth advocacy training to a solution-oriented model where young people are increasingly involved in civic initiatives that address various issues in their communities ranging from mental health to climate change. Through cascade training programmes, trained youth advocates from 12 countries13 have reached and empowered close to 2,000 young people across the region with skills to lead change and make their voices heard. For example, read "My Story as a Young Changemaker. Making change for nutrition in Rwanda".

Social and behaviour change – UNICEF ESARO made good progress on driving evidence-based social and behaviour change (SBC) as a core change strategy of country programmes:

Major risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) achievements included enhancing behavioural data collection, social and community listening, and community feedback during public health emergencies.
ESARO and Africa CDC led immunization demand-creation efforts under the global immunization agenda 2030 (IA2030) and RCCE cross-border readiness across seven countries.
ESARO helped establish accountability to affected people (AAP) plans in 14 of its countries as part of country office programming, and toolkits for more child-friendly reporting by countries.
ESARO established a regional academia consortium for ‘thought leadership’ for institutionalized capacity development and evidence generation covering 15 universities across 14 countries, while partnering with Cape Town University to map out social norms and related programmes in the region.

Disability inclusion – ESARO continued advocacy and programming on disability inclusion against the backdrop of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Africa coming into force in nine ESAR countries after its ratification in 2024:

ESARO supported the first continental conference of the African Disability Forum on redefining inclusive development and the humanitarian agenda in Africa, which brought together 500 policy makers and representatives from organizations of persons with disabilities. ESARO organized panels on children with disabilities that engaged other actors from the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child.
ESARO developed a technical note to guide disability inclusive public financing, which was subsequently used by Namibia, Angola and other UNICEF country offices to advocate for increased government spending on persons with disabilities including children.

Evidence and thought leadership – UNICEF ESARO continued to strengthen its position as an expert institution on child-related evidence, including on statistics, evaluation and research, while enhancing efforts to disseminate evidence:

ESARO contributed to UNICEF’s ‘Africa Strategy’ by supporting the establishment of the Expert Group on Child and Adolescent Statistics under the Africa Statistical Commission. This group provides strategic high-level access to national statistics offices and helps position child rights as a priority of African development agendas.
The updated Regional Evaluation Framework (2024) and the accompanying ESARO guidance note on conducting evaluations helped ensure the high quality and usefulness of the 23 evaluations completed across the region in 2024. In particular, the findings from strategic, regional evaluations of gender-transformative programming, children in migration, and Level 2 emergencies, were disseminated through social media, online events, and sharing sessions.
Support was extended across the region to enhance national evaluation capacities, including through training programmes that foster demand for evaluation among senior leaders and decision-makers, and that build evaluation skills among mid-level government staff in key ministries and in UN country teams across the continent.
ESARO expanded its standard operating procedures on research on child rights to include efforts to help quality assurance and enhance research impacts in given countries.
UNICEF ESARO’s Regional Evidence Committee (REC) continued to provide oversight and facilitated prioritization on ESARO’s evidence generation and use in line with regional advocacy opportunities.

Communication and advocacy – UNICEF ESARO sustained leadership and advocacy efforts across media, digital platforms, and high-level policy forums, amplifying its voice on critical issues for children:

ESARO increased the visibility of its emergency and advocacy efforts through enhanced strategic planning and its mapping of policy contexts, including for education, polio responses and climate plans on countries’ Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
ESARO leveraged the African Union Summit and Future Leaders Exchange (FLEX), 2024 to advocate on early childhood education, and the Global Polio Eradication (GPEI) principals’ visit to Madagascar to push the polio agenda.
The extent of ESARO’s digital media engagement on its programmes doubled in 2024 as it reached 42 million people through its supported campaigns. Media coverage amplified UNICEF's voice, as ESARO generated almost 200 media clips on the impact of public health emergencies, climate change and protection threats on children.
ESARO worked with more than 18 country offices on strategic advocacy and communication plans, including on humanitarian contexts and in support of partner visibility.

Supplies and procurement – ESARO sustained its efforts to increase the utilization of procurement services, improve adaptability to supply chain systems, and advance localization initiatives. These efforts improved access to essential supplies and services, fostered emergency responsiveness, and addressed recommendations related to post-aid diversion. UNICEF ESAR mobilized and delivered $1.196 billion worth of supplies for child-related programming in the region. Key contributions included:

Through accelerated collaboration, advocacy, guidance, and stakeholder engagement, ESARO supported 20 countries in increasing the utilization of procurement services for health systems transformation, oxygen production, immunization, and other programmes. Technical support was provided to at least 18 countries to enhance emergency preparedness through supply prepositioning, robust collaboration, and strategic deployment of logistics staff, ensuring timely and effective responses to regional emergencies.
In collaboration with stakeholders, ESARO strengthened supply chain systems across 14 countries by conducting maturity model assessments, advocating for roadmap ownership, and supported implementation of digital and other monitoring tools, which increased visibility and accountability of UNICEF supplies. ESARO supported and promoted the localization agenda to enhance the availability and access to supplies and services for effective programmatic results. This included contributing to the Localization Strategy for Africa, mapping local production initiatives in the region, engaging a private company to assess local food manufacturers in 14 countries, supporting the First Foods Africa initiative, and coordinating with key stakeholders on various projects such as egg powder manufacturing in Uganda and Ethiopia, local production and procurement of WASH supplies in Public Health Emergencies-affected countries, and RUTF (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food) manufacturing.

Highlights of operations results

The ICT and innovation team continued to support countries to adopt more digital solutions to programming, including the digital engagement of young people through the use of U-Report tools and the Internet of Good Things (IoGT), chatbots for community workers working on MHPSS and sexual and reproductive health (SRH); and continued partnering with Airtel Africa on connecting schools to the internet.
The operations team focused on bringing enhanced operational efficiency in UNICEF’s work in the region, including peer reviews that strengthened country offices’ oversight and internal controls, and enhanced the cost analysis of staff travel for saving costs. Standardized affordability analyses helped improved country programme management planning and programme budget reviews.
The security team focused on improving the links between the analysis of security situations and programme operations. Stronger context analysis and forecasting for countries and the region led to more effective and efficient security risk management and more dialogue with countries on the substance of programme design and implementation.
The people and culture team implemented a range of learning initiatives (including the Child Rights Learning Initiative webinar series and the mentorship programme for all staff in the region; the coaching of high performing staff in the region; and the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion introduction for ESARO staff), streamlined the human resources processes of the regional and country offices, and strengthened the human resources business partner model. The team enhanced collaboration and capacity among the members of the region’s human resources network using knowledge tools, best practice sharing, and interactions. In 2024, the team reviewed 295 recruitment cases and provided efficient emergency preparedness and response support.

The following writeups provide an overview of the main partnerships that ESARO engaged in 2024.

Public-private partnerships
While large amounts of development and humanitarian aid were being diverted to crises elsewhere in the world, ESARO successfully mobilized US$ 1.1 billion in direct donor contributions (14% less than in 2023), comprising US$ 965 million from the public sector and US$ 97 million from the private sector. A range of strategies were employed, and promising results attained by ESARO for income and influence despite the very challenging funding trends faced in the year.

Global and continental forums were leveraged to position priority child rights issues, including the 29th United Nations Climate Change Conference, the Africa Venture Philanthropy Alliance, the Hamburg Sustainability Conference, and events with public sector partners on trade and aid approaches to addressing child rights issues in global supply chains. ESARO hosted the annual Nextgen Summit in Kenya, which was participated in by philanthropists and partners from nine countries, who were encouraged to engage with and support UNICEF’s life-saving work.

Amidst the competitive fundraising landscape and the shrinking flexibility, quality and predictability of funding, in 2024 ESARO continued to seek and deepen diverse sources of funding. The enhanced efforts to increase corporate fundraising led to the forging of stronger ties with major foundations including the Gates, Latter-day Saints Charities (LDSC) and MasterCard foundations. Platforms such as the Health X Climate donor coordination groups, and SEforAll (Sustainable Energy for All) provided stronger engagement opportunities with partners, while new engagement discussions were pursued with CIFF Africa and Elma Philanthropies. And ESARO launched its first digital fundraising campaign in South Africa in December 2024 through its new digital fundraising system.

UNICEF Africa’s partnership with the telecom company Airtel Africa has connected more than 1,800 schools to the internet and reached over 5 million learners through free-to-access platforms across 13 countries in ESAR and WCAR.

In sum, ESARO sustained close monitoring of the worrisome global aid trends while continuing to support countries in the region by forging stronger partnership ties with traditional donors and international financial institutions, while strengthening its engagement with established and emerging private sector partners.

Partnerships with regional entities
ESARO sustained its participation and contributions to the United Nations reform agenda at the regional level, including through the regional director’s participation at the meetings and annual retreat of the Africa Regional Coordination Platform (RCP), focusing on the United Nation’s value offer in Africa’s transitional pathways towards the SDGs and the African Union’s Agenda for 2063. In particular, the launch of UNICEF’s ‘Africa Strategy’ in 2024 gave a large momentum for ESARO to position child rights in the continental platforms offered by UNECA and the African Union. Where convened, ESARO contributed to the Opportunity and Issue-Based Coalitions (OIBC) under the Regional Coordination Platform mechanism, particularly on strengthening integrated data and statistical systems.

Partnerships were strengthened with the region’s economic communities, including the Southern African Development Community (SADC) and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). ESARO’s collaboration with SADC saw significant developments in 2024. Shortly after SADC’s Extraordinary Summit on the El Nino-induced drought, ESARO’s regional director participated in a donor round table meeting on the resulting drought crisis in southern Africa and issued a regional call-to-action for children in affected countries, including a request for funding for SADC’s regional coordination, data analysis, and oversight functions. Separately, SADC’s Directorate of Social and Human Development joined UNICEF representatives of SADC member states on the margins of the UNICEF Regional Management Team meeting that strengthened mutual understanding of the respective entities’ priorities and shared expectations on the UNICEF-SADC relationship.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In conclusion this section presents the lessons learned in achieving, sustaining and accelerating results by ESARO overall. It presents some forward-looking observations, including how the office intends to use the insights gained during 2024 to adjust strategies, inform future actions and explore new opportunities for collaboration.

Lessons learned in 2024
As of the end of 2024, the importance of leveraging national resources loomed ever larger across all programmes as development and humanitarian aid continued to shrink. For example, to sustain child poverty reduction, UNICEF needs to continue to pivot toward identifying and supporting critical policy reforms and analysing and addressing inequities and inefficiencies in national finances, recognizing the challenges in supporting enhanced social protection as donors scale back funding.

ESARO’s literacy on domestic and innovative financing needs to be enhanced across all sectors, including the ability to save costs while expanding services, to place it as a leader in the region on scaling up system strengthening in the changing aid environment. In 2024, ESARO witnessed the cost inflation of WASH investments and how financial constraints hindered the continental ambition of the learning agenda, among the many challenges to its programming.
ESARO’s teams affirm the fundamental importance of the multisectoral approach and collaboration for their work. For example, the community-based primary health care approach is essentially about more multisectoral collaboration and integrated programming. Barriers to nutrition outcomes must be addressed through the multi-systems approach, while ending AIDS among children and adolescents requires integrated and multisectoral programming to address the drivers of the epidemic.

While ESARO’s research portfolio has evolved significantly in the past couple of years, implementation delays, governance gaps and limited dissemination continue to hinder the progress of thought leadership initiatives.

The fast-changing realities of digital transformation in the world call on ESARO to expedite actions on digital literacy and capacity building within programmes, including improved capabilities on data resilience, AI, and cybersecurity. The appropriate use of digital technologies, including AI, in evaluation, security threat analysis and other applications should improve the efficiency of ESARO’s work processes and products.

The aid diversion that caused major stakeholder concerns in 2023 has led to concerted efforts to enhance accountability in ESARO by conducting assessments, developing new and innovative tools for monitoring and distribution, and establishing better processes to track, manage and mitigate aid diversion cases. A regional Aid Diversion Task Force was established in 2024 led by ESARO and participated in by the most affected country offices, with the carrying out of a proactive in-depth review under development for four of these country offices.

Looking towards 2025
The implementation of UNICEF’s Africa Strategy will be central to both ESARO’s work and informing country programmes in 2025. The implementation of the Africa Strategy’s three pillars of (i) human capital development, (ii) resilience, humanitarian and climate action and (iii) intensified action on child rights, should anchor ESARO’s efforts to strengthen its multisectoral approach to scaling up results for children. Enhanced multisectoral programming will be a key focus of ESARO programming in 2025.

The research focus in 2025 will include updating standard operating procedures, enhancing research quality benchmarks and scaling knowledge management for evidence uptake. Digital literacy and integrating artificial intelligence into evidence work will be important agendas. For example, the use of AI technology will be pursued as a cost-effective and faster way to synthesize evidence from multiple evaluations.

Intensifying its efforts to diversify resources, ESARO will seek relationships with non-traditional partners, explore private sector fundraising in emerging markets, further strengthen high-impact partnerships with international financial institutions and regional development banks, and seek more localization of resource mobilization through self-sustaining and self-financing systems. It will also build stronger narratives and pilot new fundraising approaches to seize donor attention and access funding.

ESARO will lead by example to foster a supportive, inclusive, and empowering workplace culture in its country offices, recognizing that staff well-being directly impacts the quality of results to enhance children’s lives. Ensuring the safety of staff in countries affected by conflict and unrest will continue to be ESARO’s highest priority.

The preparation of the Regional Office Management Plan (ROMP) for 2026–2029 will be a key ESARO undertaking in 2025. A child rights-based approach will be at the core of the plan so that the best interests of children are prioritized in all programmes designs and resource allocations. And ESARO will engage closely with UNICEF HQ to ensure that its plan is aligned with the new UNICEF Strategic Plan for 2026–2029, while ensuring that the regional plan is fit-for-purpose for the region’s children and affordable.

Within the full scope of ESARO’s technical assistance to county offices (COs) and generation of regional public goods, GRP-RR filled a few areas of critical funding gaps not met by OR. For example, it allowed ESARO Early Childhood Development and Social Policy advisors to participate in the global network meetings held in the headquarters (HQ), strengthening the alignment between the HQ and Regional Office (RO) around prevailing policy, strategy and technical standards. It allowed the Social Policy advisor to attend the global UNICEF Child Poverty Working Group in Brussels where ESARO contributed to drafting UNICEF's first child poverty advocacy strategy. It also enabled ESARO gender specialist to join WCARO colleagues to develop the youth action plan ahead of the AU Education summit 2024.

The GRP-RR also supplemented some unmet funding needs required to provide ESARO’s technical assistance to COs around gender and PSEA, help organize the Youth connect Africa Summit and establish the regional social media listen-in strategy. A part of the GRP-RR also supported general operating costs of ESARO.

Please reference the ESARO Achievements and Contributions of 2024 to fully contextualize the value offered by the GRP-RR.
