Eswatini is a landlocked, lower middle-income country with a gross national income per capita of USD 3,860[1] and an estimated Gini Index of 54.6[2], placing it among the five most unequal countries in the world. According to the latest data, 65.3 per cent of Children in Eswatini live below the international poverty line of USD 3.65 per day and 40.6 per cent are in extreme poverty[3]. In non-monetary terms, 46.6 per cent of children are deprived in at least three domains of multidimensional child poverty[4].
 
Due to these high levels of deprivations, monetary poverty, and inequalities Eswatini’s social indicators demonstrate peculiar irregularities and lag behind those of other lower middle-income countries. Deprivations and lack of access to services are striking when one examines the national budget. In the latest fiscal year, the country allocated almost 40 per cent of its budget to social sectors with health and education receiving approximately 10 per cent and 17 per cent, respectively. Progress in many of the child-related indicators are not proportionate to the levels of government investment in social sectors. With this understanding, in 2024 UNICEF Eswatini, relying on its internal capacity, used the evidence generated by the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2021-2022[5] and engaged with the Cabinet at the level of Principal Secretaries to bring to light child deprivations and influence budget allocatons in line with rights of children, and ensure sustainability of UNICEF-supported programmes. This attempt resulted in inclusion of new budget entries for establishment of birth registration services in maternities (See below for details on birth registration), setting aside allocations for vaccine procurement (See below for details on immunization), allocations for implementation of the plan of action for prevention of violence against children, allocation of  SZL 20 million to rural water projects, SZL 10 million to online learning, SZL 6 million to early learning, SZL 11 million to education management information system, SZL 3 million to care and support to teaching and learning programme, and SZL 2 million to inclusive education[6] in the 2025 budget.
 
As mentioned earlier, children in Eswatini experience exceptionally high levels of deprivations and considerable inequalities in access to services. To ensure prioritization of children’s issues in government programmes and promote evidence-based programming for children, UNICEF supported a multidimensional overlapping deprivation analysis study based on the MICS 2021-2022 data which provided government with important information on the main areas of deprivations and how they are affecting different groups of children. The findings of the study are used for the development of the first-ever Child Poverty Reduction Action Plan by the Ministry of Economic Planning and Development (MOEPD) that will be released in 2025. An important feature of this programme component was that the initiative was mostly led by MOEPD and financed by the national financial resources and UNICEF contribution focused solely on technical support. 
 
Eswatini’s performance in education sector is lower than the average of other lower middle-income countries with similar levels of investment in the sector. The relatively high participation of children in primary education (91 per cent enrolment rate) does not result in effective learning, increasing risk of drop out. At grade two and three, only 16 per cent of children demonstrate foundational literacy skills and only eight per cent possess foundational numeracy skills; at grade seven, namely the end of primary education, 20 per cent still lack foundational literacy and 44 per cent do not have foundational numeracy[7]. This low level of learning achievement is resulting in high repetition and dropout rates, very low transition to secondary education, tertiary education, and to work. In line with the priorities of the African Union Year of Education, to address this challenge, UNICEF Country Office conducted a thorough analysis to determine root causes of the problem and identify solutions. The findings revealed that the major bottleneck is very low school readiness caused by low attendance rate of only nine per cent in the costly and inaccessible early childhood education programmes. Introduction of free and accessible pre-primary education services with additional funding lacks feasibility given the Government’s average spending of 5.7 per cent of GDP on education, which is way higher than middle-income countries’ average. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education and Training (MOET) to develop a financing solution to introduce a one-year, free pre-primary education programme to all children with a minimal initial investment. The financing solution focuses on reducing the high per capita cost of education at primary level caused by very high levels of repetition. UNICEF advocated for this proposal at the highest level of Government and Parliament and at this stage, based on UNICEF recommendation the Cabinet has established an Expert Committee on Education Reform
 to support quality improvement. In addition, a Grade Zero[8] cabinet paper was developed and included in the agenda of the Cabinet for endorsement in 2025. Reliance on the Country Office in-house capacity, using available data for evidence-based advocacy and leveraging national financial resources have been the main features of this important initiative.
 
According to MICS 2021-2022, only 77 per cent of children have received basic immunization and only 66 per cent are fully immunized. This is mainly caused by recurrent stock-out of vaccines and suspension of outreach programmes since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. UNICEF analysis showed the stock-outs do not occur because of shortage of funding. The major challenges identified were capacity gaps in cold chain management, vaccine forecasting and inter-ministerial coordination for vaccine supply chain management. UNICEF Eswatini supported the Ministry of Health (MOH) in improving the cold chain management and developing the required tools and processes for timely management of the vaccine supply chain. UNICEF also used its convening power to bring together decision makers from MOH, Ministry of Finance and the Treasury to agree on procedures for management and coordination of the process. As a result, vaccine stock-out was so minimized that in 2024, for the first time, immunization coverage was not affected. At the time of reporting, Eswatini has completed the 2025 vaccine procurement process and vaccines for eight months are available in stock. To address the second cause of low immunization coverage, that is, suspension of outreaches, UNICEF supported a costing exercise that compared outreach programmes and immunization campaigns. The analysis revealed the  relatively higher cost of campaigns. Additionally, considering that outreaches integrate a wide range of health and nutrition services, they help improve other health outcomes. UNICEF advocacy resulted in the reinstatement of outreach programmes in the new health strategy of the country. Avoiding stock-out will eliminate the need for immunization campaigns and thus reduce cost ofthe programme. The above-mentioned improvements will help the country to effectively reach zero-dose children and communities. The programme strategy in this area emphasized utilization of UNICEF internal capacity to engage in evi
dence-based advocacy and capacity development for optimization of the existing national financial resources.
 
High rate of child mortality is a challenge that Eswatini has been facing for some time. While according to MICS 2021-2022, seventy-four per cent of pregnant women use antenatal care services and 79 per cent of them deliver in facilities, indicating acceptable access and availability of services, maternal, newborn, and infant mortality rates are as high as 240 (in 100,000), 21 (in 1,000) and 35 (in 1000), respectively. UNICEF analysis shows that challenges with quality of care are major contributors to these high levels of mortality. Therefore, UNICEF supported MOH to establish a maternal and perinatal death surveillance and response system in maternities in the country. At the time of reporting, 16 out of 19 maternities are using the system to scrutinize every death case to identify and address all bottlenecks with quality of care. One part of the system is an electronic dashboard that enables decision makers at facility, regional and national levels to monitor all cases in real time. It is expected that in the next reporting period actions prompted by the system will result in 30 per cent reduction of mortality at facility level.
 
Strengthening the community-based healthcare system is another approach supported by UNICEF to improve health outcomes. Eswatini uses Rural Health Motivators (RHM) to provide community-based healthcare. An evaluation supported by UNICEF shows that the RHM system faces systematic and structural challenges including financing, continuity of service, and individual and institutional capacity gaps. To improve quality of health service for mothers and children, UNICEF supported MOH with developing a strategy for community-based healthcare services. In line with this, UNICEF supported exchange of experience between Eswatini and Malawi as a South-South Cooperation initiative. Additionally, in collaboration with a local NGO, UNICEF developed and implemented a project for community-based healthcare to demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency of interventions at community level. In its short lifetime, the programme demonstrated a 15 per cent increase in immunization rate in the target communities and 90 per cent improvement in overall health and weights of children who were identified to be malnourished.
 
With 27 per cent, Eswatini has the highest HIV prevalence in the world. New incidences of HIV are mainly among girls aged 15 to 24, and according to MICS 2021-2022, teenage pregnancy is as high as 12 per cent. This high prevalence rate and high rate of teenage pregnancy increases the risk of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV. Building on the findings of the UNICEF-supported study on final transmission rates UNICEF Eswatini, with support from UNICEF Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office, and in collaboration with country and regional offices of the World Health Organization, conducted an assessment of Eswatini’s programme for prevention of MTCT and helped develop the capacity of the National Validation Committee for the application process for certification of elimination of MTCT (EMTCT). With the strengthened institutional capacity, and the evidence generated indicating reduction of MTCT to below five per cent, Eswatini is on the path for EMTCT certification.
 
The high incidence rate of HIV among adolescent and youth, especially girls, requires regular monitoring and improvement of the sexual and reproductive health services in a way that they are accessible, free from stigma and of good quality. UNICEF in collaboration with a local NGO and MOH, supported development and launch of a youth-friendly service provision accountability model that consists of live reporting by clients in a mobile application platform, data analysis and delivery of recommendations to service providers for quality assurance and improvement. In 2024, a total of 1,744 young clients produced 2,875 recommendations. A 55 per cent resolution rate indicates a considerable success in increasing capacity for evidence-based decision making at local level and improvement of accountabilities to affected population in UNICEF-supported programmes.
 
MICS 2021-2022 shows that 34 per cent of children under the age of five do not have birth certificates. While birth registration services are free, challenges with accessibility and lack of awareness result in the low performance of the country in this area. Considering that 79 per cent of deliveries take place in maternities, with the aim of bringing services closer to families, UNICEF supported integration of birth registration services in maternities. Initial reports indicate that newborns are now leaving facilities with their birth registered, promising a considerable increase in birth registration rate in coming years.
 
In the reporting period, UNICEF cooperation programme with the Government of Eswatini witnessed a stronger focus on food systems for children. UNICEF engaged with the cabinet at the level of Principal Secretaries to advocate for programmes aimed at reduction of child food poverty. In 2024, interactions were mostly focused on raising awareness of decision makers to challenges of malnutrition and obesity among poorer children, and capacity development for a comprehensive and well-funded nutrition programme. As a result of these efforts, MOH has now developed a specific nutrition programme that is presented for inclusion in the 2025 budget. 
 
As demonstrated above, in 2024 UNICEF Eswatini placed a strong focus on a few important strategies that proved to be effective. Firstly, the Office maximized the use of its internal technical capacity to offer working solutions to challenges faced; analysis of bottlenecks in quality education, the child poverty assessment, cold and supply chain management improvement are just a few examples of such efforts. Secondly, in addition to engagement with partners in capacity development at technical level, use of evidence for policy advocacy at high levels was intensified in the reporting period. Financing solution for early learning, advocacy for reinstatement of outreach programme, and advocacy for specific and increased budget allocations to child-focused programmes are some instances of this effort. As it is evident from the earlier sections of this report, leveraging domestic financing for children’s rights has been the underlying theme of most of the UNICEF programmmes in 2024 which not only increases ownership and sustainability, but also helps transform the UNICEF programme delivery from providing service to providing solutions. This approach to programming has also resulted in increased trust in technical capacity of UNICEF and has guaranteed the office a seat around the high-level decision-making tables. Moreover, the effort has also provided the Country Office with the opportunity to move beyond delivery of outputs to achieving outcome-level results. Additionally, while at national level focus has been on policy advocacy and promotion of child-focused programming, at community level the programme emphasized empowering for local-level, decentralized decision making; maternal and perinatal death surveillance and response system, promotion of a well-structured community-based health care system and youth-friendly SRH services are examples of this approach. Observing the level of success despite diminishing resources, UNICEF Eswatini will continue with the same appr
oach to programming in 2025 and will adopt these strategies in designing its 2026-2030 Country Programme to increase efficiency and remain fit for its purpose in Eswatini.

Ethiopia continued to grapple with polycrisis throughout 2024, including armed conflict, intercommunal violence, climate-related hazards, disease outbreaks, food insecurity, and socio-economic challenges. An estimated 21.4 million people across the country, including 12 million children, required urgent humanitarian assistance in health, nutrition, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), education, child protection, and social protection. 
 
In Amhara region, ongoing conflict between federal forces and the Fano militia caused displacement, infrastructure destruction, gender-based violence (GBV), restricted access to basic services, and disrupted livelihoods.In Tigray region, despite improvements following the peace agreement, approximately 1 million people were internally displaced, with significant food insecurity. The need for mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) was high, particularly among GBV survivors including women and girls. In Oromia region, armed and intercommunal conflicts damaged health facilities, severely compromised basic services, with nearly 1 million people displaced. 
 
Somali and Afar regions were the most affected by climate change. Prolonged droughts led to crop failures and loss of income for farming households, and livestock was devastated by water and pasture shortages. These challenges deepened poverty, and families struggled to meet their basic needs. UNICEF focused on establishing durable WASH structures, as well as rehabilitating and upgrading water systems. Ethiopia also experienced multiple public health emergencies, including cholera, measles, malaria, and dengue fever. The measles outbreak in Amhara, Gambella, Oromia, and South Ethiopia regions worsened due to low immunization coverage and poor awareness among caregivers. The situation was further exacerbated by population displacement and access constraints.
 
SMART surveys and rapid nutrition assessments conducted across eight regions (including Afar, Somali, Tigray, Amhara, Oromia, and Benishangul-Gumuz) revealed critical, serious, or poor global acute malnutrition rates across all livelihood zones and woredas surveyed. This demonstrated that infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices were suboptimal, and child food poverty posed nutritional risk for populations dealing with multiple shocks. The nutritional status of women was a critical concern in northern Ethiopia, with 60 per cent of pregnant and lactating women requiring nutritional support.
 
Approximately 9 million children are out-of-school, due to multiple reasons, including natural disasters, displacement, violence among others. Over 9,000 schools (or 20% of schools) were damaged by conflict and climate shocks. The situation was particularly dire in conflict-affected areas, where children faced additional risks such as child labor, early marriage, and exploitation. As the number of children affected by armed conflict increased, child protection services were vital to support vulnerable children and women.
 
The prevalence of child poverty remained significant. According to the 2024 Multidimensional Child Poverty study conducted by UNICEF, the American Institute for Research (AIR), and the Policy Studies Institute (PSI), child poverty declined from 88 per cent in 2016 to 78.8 per cent in 2024. Younger children were more likely to experience deprivations in nutrition and health, while older children had higher deprivations in leisure, information, and participation. Children in rural areas were more likely to be multidimensionally deprived (84.8%) than those in urban areas (55.2%). Somali (88.2%), Afar (87.9%), Tigray (86.1%), and the regions previously known as Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples (86.4%) had the highest levels of multidimensional deprivations. 
 
While responding to humanitarian needs, UNICEF made significant progress in investing in the Humanitarian-Development-Peace Nexus and resilience building, and promoted gender equality and disability inclusion in line with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. UNICEF also prioritized disability- and gender-responsive programming, focusing on the most vulnerable populations. It conducted the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), which comprehensively examined the interconnectedness between the impacts of climate, energy, environment, and disaster (CEED) on the country’s socio-economic development and Ethiopian children. The key findings highlighted that children are largely overlooked in the Government of Ethiopia (GOE)’s CEED policies, strategies and data. More than 95 per cent of children were exposed to harmful indoor air pollution due to reliance on biomass, which severely impacted the health of millions of children. Building upon the CLAC’s multisectoral and holistic recommendations, UNICEF will support the GOE to ensure its Nationally Determined Contributions are child-sensitive.
 
Ethiopia continued to face macroeconomic challenges including inflation, foreign exchange shortages, and a high debt burden. Inflation continued to soar (26.9% in 2023/24), with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projection for 2024/25 at 30.1 per cent, further compromising public investments for children. The Ethiopian Birr (ETB) depreciated by more than 100 per cent to the US dollar. Ethiopia’s external position remained vulnerable, and the GOE is struggling to reach an agreement with its Eurobond holders regarding debt restructuring. 
 
The GOE implemented tighter monetary policies since July 2024, including an extended credit facility programme with the IMF to support ongoing home-grown economic reform. As a result, the currency depreciation and inflation remained high, particularly affecting vulnerable populations. However, the GOE was able to expand fiscal space for social sectors, increasing the budget for the social safety net programme by ETB 60 billion (USD 472.5 million). 
 
The total approved federal budget for the 2023/24 fiscal year was ETB 801.7 billion (USD 6.3 billion), a 1.9 per cent increase from the previous year. However, due to high inflation, the real value of the budget declined by 17.8 per cent. Approximately 45 per cent of the budget was allocated to priority sectors such as education, health, road construction, water, and agriculture. This allocation was lower than the previous year (47%) and the historical average over the past decade (60%). The fiscal deficit was projected to be ETB 281 billion (USD 2.2 billion), or 2.48 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product. The budget was financed through domestic revenue (59.8%), domestic borrowing (30.2%), and external sources (10%).
 
In the new country programme, UNICEF will focus on assisting vulnerable women, children, and youth in the hardest-to-reach areas of Ethiopia. By promoting localized innovations and multisectoral approaches, UNICEF aims to save lives, reduce household poverty, maintain dignity, and safeguard rights. Immediate lifesaving efforts will be coupled with building resilient communities and adopting climate-adaptive practices.

Every child survives and thrives 
 
Maternal and child health (MCH) services showed remarkable progress. Antenatal care coverage increased to 78 per cent (43% in 2019, and skilled birth attendance increased to 74 per cent (50% in 2019). The coverage of early postnatal visits reached 89 per cent, and coverage of pneumonia treatment was 81 per cent. UNICEF contributed to the improvements by delivering essential health supplies, supporting the scale-up of neonatal intensive care units (NICU), kangaroo mother care, integrated community case management, and integrated management of newborn and childhood illnesses, as well as renovating 26 maternity waiting homes.
 
UNICEF played a critical role in the GOE’s efforts to support zero-dose and under-vaccinated children in hard-to-reach communities, and 635,110 zero-dose children received essential vaccinations. Over 3.5 million children were vaccinated with the third dose of pentavalent vaccine, over 7.1 million children under-five were vaccinated for polio, and over 1 million people received the COVID-19 vaccination. 
 
UNICEF facilitated access to primary health care (PHC) for over 2.8 million people in humanitarian contexts, including more than 1.7 million children vaccinated against measles. It also supported the renovation of 76 health facilities in conflict-affected regions. Emergency supplies were delivered to establish 200 cholera treatment centers, distribute 749 emergency drug kits, and vaccinate nearly 12 million people with the oral cholera vaccine.
 
The mobile health and nutrition teams (MHNTs) were endorsed by the Ministry of Health (MOH) and regional health bureaus of Afar and Somali to deliver routine services for nomadic populations and in emergency settings, an important achievement for resilience building. UNICEF delivered gender-integrated capacity building to 261 front line healthcare workers (151 women) on MCH, GBV, and MHPSS. 60 MHNTs were trained to support GBV survivors. Accordingly, 299 GBV survivors received counselling and referral services. 
 
UNICEF supported the expansion of community-based health insurance (CBHI) from 1,010 woredas in 2023 to 1,052 in 2024, and birth notification at health facilities increased from 75 per cent to 90 per cent at the national level. UNICEF-supported social and behavior change (SBC) interventions reached over 57 million people with messages on immunization, MCH, and communicable disease prevention.
 
UNICEF renewed focus on local food solutions to address nutrition challenges. In Tigray region, hydroponics technology ensured year-round vegetable production, with plans to scale to 9,000 households. In Amhara region, UNICEF supported the establishment of aquaponics fishponds for 90,000 households. UNICEF also supported the adoption of climate-smart approaches for nutritious food with the Ministry of Agriculture, benefitting over 4,000 households across six regions. The scale-up of egg powder production is currently underway, with procurement of full-solution equipment (170,000 eggs per day capacity) worth USD 1.7 million expected to arrive in mid-2025. Moreover, technology transfer was initiated for production of alternative formulations of ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) using local ingredients.
 
With UNICEF support, nutrition indicators were integrated into Ethiopia's Ten-Year National Development Plan, and the Ethiopian Food and Nutrition Information Platform was established with performance indicators. UNICEF bolstered GOE’s efforts on nutrition system strengthening, including the scale-up of the enhanced community-based nutrition (eCBN) approach. Over 3.4 million children under-two received monthly growth monitoring and IYCF counselling. UNICEF and partners supported the treatment of over 614,000 children with severe acute malnutrition, Vitamin A supplementation of 12 million children, deworming of 8.9 million children, and iron-folic acid supplementation of over 3 million women. Integrated immunization, nutrition, and birth registration services were delivered to zero-dose communities, ensuring children received comprehensive care and services. Integrated services including micronutrient supplementation, deworming, and menstrual hygiene were implemented in 3,000 schools across 100 woredas, reaching over 5.2 million children and adolescents. 
 
UNICEF launched a nationwide campaign to end child food poverty. Through the eCBN platform and the Seqota program, UNICEF supported the production of nutrient-dense foods in 320 woredas targeting 1.9 million children. The enforcement of the National Baby Food Control Directive and the establishment of an online platform for monitoring and reporting violations protected over 1.9 million infants from malnutrition and death associated with breast milk substitutes. UNICEF enhanced aid diversion prevention on RUTF by recruiting third party monitors, and submitting monthly reports on the mitigation and corrective actions to donors. To enhance implementation of the Food and Nutrition Strategy and public financing, UNICEF supported a national nutrition budget tagging and tracking system. UNICEF also implemented SBC campaigns leveraging religious leaders, and reached over 4.5 million people.
 
Every child learns
 
To accelerate equitable and inclusive access to quality education for all school-age children, UNICEF continued its strategic investment in supporting the Ministry of Education (MOE) and regional education bureaus (REBs). With UNICEF support, the Early Childhood Development and Education Policy Framework was finalized and disseminated, ensuring that its operational and strategic implementation plans were inclusive and participatory. To sustain achieved results, UNICEF supported community engagement to promote early childhood education through positive parenting training for 51,208 parents and caregivers (42% women), highlighting play-based learning.
 
Over 89,329 pre-primary students (48% girls) in development and humanitarian settings, and more than 231,464 out-of-school primary school children (50% girls) in humanitarian situations accessed equitable, inclusive, and quality education with UNICEF support. Notably, 99 per cent of out-of-school children aged 10-14 who completed accelerated education transitioned to regular primary education. This is a successful nexus approach that moved from humanitarian to resilience building to development.
 
Rehabilitation and reconstruction of damaged schools are underway, including classrooms, gender-segregated latrines, and menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) facilities in Amhara, Afar, Oromia, Gambella, Tigray, Sidama, Benishangul-Gumuz, and South Ethiopia regions. As a result, 42,036 out-of-school refugee and internally displaced children (48% girls) accessed quality education through receiving education supplies, including 192,226 school bags and 2,625 recreation kits. UNICEF enhanced its inclusive education programme in targeted schools, benefiting 12,167 children with disabilities through educational interventions and assistive devices such as eyeglasses, crutches, orthotic devices, hearing aids, and Orbit Readers.
 
In partnership with the MOE, a revised general education curriculum that integrates skill development was available nationwide. The updated Life Skills module, which includes MHPSS, socio-emotional learning, and peace education, was translated into Amharic to facilitate broader adoption. UNICEF also supported the capacity development of teachers and leaders to implement the revised curriculum. With funding from the Government of Norway, UNICEF provided the ongoing support to teachers and leaders in Afar, Gambella, South Ethiopia, Southwest Ethiopia, and Oromia regions.
 
A total of 1,086 participants (65% women and girls), including school leadership, gender club coordinators, and other stakeholders were trained to prevent school related gender-based violence (SRGBV). They will further train teachers, learners, parents, local government structures, and parent-teacher associations to reduce SRGBV and improve student attendance and learning. Gender clubs were strengthened across the country, with boys and girls learning about their bodies, gender power dynamics, and life skills.
 
UNICEF, as the grant agent for the USD 132.59 million Global Partnership for Education (GPE) Systems Transformation and Girls Education Accelerator fund, collaborated with the MOE and REBs to enhance education outcomes. This initiative focuses on empowering teachers and school leaders, improving girls' access to quality education, and strengthening the education system's ability to overcome barriers. Implemented in 150 woredas, the programme includes school rehabilitation, leadership training, and accelerated learning, with a component on girls’ education. A work plan was developed with government partners, and implementation is underway.
 
The MOE completed the 2023/24 annual education abstract, currently awaiting approval. This document is crucial for decision-making, planning, monitoring, and evaluation. UNICEF provided technical and financial support for its development and assisted with data collection in several regions. As part of this, 218 education management information system experts (12% women) were trained in data collection and indicator analysis.
 
Every child protected from violence and exploitation
 
Constant adaptation of protection approaches was necessitated to ensure service delivery to children and women along the humanitarian, peace, and development nexus. Between January and November 2024, with UNICEF support, 42,221 children (18,501 boys and 23,720 girls) who were victims of violence, abuse, exploitation, or neglect received protection services including health, legal aid, social welfare, and psychosocial support. 
 
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Women and Social Affairs (MOWSA) and civil society organizations (CSOs) to strengthen child protection services and data management systems. In June, the national child protection information management system (CPIMS+) was launched, a use-friendly digital service platform that enables data analysis, reporting, and accountability. 
 
UNICEF positioned mental health as a cross-sectoral issue and identified sector-specific MHPSS accountabilities. Cross-sectoral staff were trained on the MHPSS minimum service package, with training packages updated to streamline MHPSS among social service workers in child protection, education and other programs.  
 
Advocacy to accelerate violence against children (VAC) prevention and response gained momentum at the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Bogota, Columbia. Significantly, Ethiopia adopted the global Framework for Action on Child Protection Systems Strengthening at the conference, and made dedicated national pledges towards ending VAC through the roll-out of CPIMS+, the Nurturing Care Framework, and budget tracking to end child marriage (CM).  
 
Through tailored interventions to end CM and female genital mutilation (FGM), UNICEF and partners helped shift attitudes, influence norms, and reduce the number of incidents. In total, 6,078 girls at risk of CM and FGM received protection and care services, including 5,693 girls at risk of CM and 385 girls at risk of FGM. Active reporting led to the cancellation of 1,868 CM cases, and prevention of 238 FGM cases. Women’s development groups, anti-harmful traditional practices committees, and girls/gender clubs played a critical role in tracking and identification. The data underscored the critical impact of UNICEF’s interventions and the importance of addressing FGM and CM within the broader response of Child Protection in Emergencies and Gender Based Violence in Emergencies (GBViE). To address gender inequality and harmful masculinity, capacity building for 31,489 men and boys was conducted using the Male Engagement Manual, and relevant interventions of the humanitarian cash transfer programmes were expanded in Amhara and Oromia regions. 
 
UNICEF co-chaired regional prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) networks in Tigray, Somali, Sidama, Central Ethiopia, South Ethiopia, and South West Ethiopia. It conducted 16 PSEA trainings to increase awareness and identify responsibilities for 446 implementing partners, government actors, and UNICEF staff. Moreover, 41 PSEA assessments with implementing partners were completed to strengthen safeguarding measures. 
 
The under-one birth registration rate was 40 per cent (over 1.04 million children) in 2024. UNICEF played a pivotal role in advocating for the revision of the civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) proclamation to address barriers, including the integration of national e-ID management and civil registration, and delegation of registration to other government organs. The revision allowed birth registration by one parent and in their place of residence, a critical change for internally displaced populations. Once approved by the Parliament, the revised legal framework will facilitate acceleration of birth registration.   
 
UNICEF reconfirmed its role as a trusted technical partner with UN agencies and the government on disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration (DDR), providing technical assistance and contributing to a joint UN package of support. Key cross-sectoral platforms were leveraged to improve protection outcomes for children, young people and women, including on DDR, PHC for zero-dose communities, access to GBViE in stabilization centers and via mobile health and nutrition teams, and the inter-operability between national identification and CRVS. 
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
 
UNICEF support resulted in more than 13.8 million people gaining access to safe water, over 5.1 million people receiving sanitation services, and 2,016 communities (or 11.2 million people) living in an Open Defecation Free environment in 2024. Furthermore, 729 schools received MHH services, reaching 99,120 adolescent girls and boys. 
 
UNICEF prioritized technical areas to strengthen the WASH sector and ensure sustainable access to water and sanitation services, including:
·        hydrogeological mapping to identify and manage groundwater resources completed in 119 woredas, and underway in an additional 30 woredas;
·        capacity building of water utilities to enhance operational capacity, which improved service delivery through efficient asset and financial management, and robust operation and maintenance;
·        promotion of solar power as a sustainable and innovative solution for water supply, particularly in remote and underserved areas. These efforts reduced carbon emissions and addressed power shortages across eight regions, ensuring long-term sustainability of WASH investments;
·        advocacy for improved WASH policies and frameworks to boost service delivery, including the establishment of a regulatory body for renewable energy to ensure effective implementation and oversight;
·        investment in developing climate-resilient WASH infrastructure, such as sand dams and shallow wells, to build community resilience against drought and flood, benefitting 843,233 people with water supply, and 672,354 people with sanitation services. 
 
In collaboration with the MOH, UNICEF supported the Total Sanitation to End open Defecation and Urination in Ethiopia (TSEDU-Ethiopia) 2030 programme to eliminate open defecations and improve hygiene as part of its rural WASH initiative. SBC strategies and market-based sanitation approaches were prioritized across 10 woredas in five regions. To enhance scalability and sustainability, comprehensive micro-plans with targeted budgets were developed. Additionally, UNICEF is supporting the Prime Minister’s TSEDU cities initiative in Addis Ababa by constructing public toilets and implementing TSEDU in healthcare facilities through the WASH Facility Improvement Tool initiative. With UNICEF support, the guideline for gender representation in media, the national guideline for gender- and disability-inclusive WASH programming, and the national MHH facilitators’ guideline for schools were developed. 
 
UNICEF played a crucial role in supporting the Ministry of Water and Energy (MOWE). Notably, it deployed technical experts to enhance MOWE’s project management, thereby improving its effectiveness in overseeing water and energy projects. Moreover, UNICEF contributed to strengthening the capacity and efficiency of water utilities by improving governance frameworks, institutional capacity, and operational enhancements. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF contributed USD 1 million (Regular Resources) to the ONE WASH National Programme (OWNP) Pool Fund, and led the evaluation of the effectiveness of Phase II interventions. The review assessed achievements, challenges, and lessons learned to refine and expand the OWNP into Phase III, building on past successes while addressing challenges.
 
As part of UNICEF’s support to the humanitarian response, water supply interventions focused on rehabilitating and upgrading diesel-powered systems to solar-powered ones. The shift to local chlorine procurement facilitated timely assistance to vulnerable populations, particularly during cholera outbreaks, by reducing shipping and customs delays. However, securing the second round of Local Procurement Authorization was challenging. Market inflation also created difficulties, leading to frequent price revisions of WASH non-food items and delayed procurement. To mitigate delays, UNICEF collaborated with a limited number of domestic and international suppliers of solar pumping systems to ensure the timely provision of WASH supplies.
 
UNICEF implemented risk-informed programming that integrated humanitarian and development efforts, focusing on sustainable solutions. For example, UNICEF’s work on climate-resilient deep boreholes powered by solar energy ensured  uninterrupted water supply during droughts. To promote positive community behaviors, UNICEF engaged in advocacy, communication, and SBC initiatives. 
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life 
 
UNICEF strengthened the available evidence and data in Ethiopia by supporting the first child poverty analysis since 2016 in partnership with PSI and AIR. UNICEF also supported the design and implementation of the first-ever National Disability Survey, and provided technical and financial support to the fifth Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey. Moreover, capacity building to enhance understanding and expertise in evaluation was supported by UNICEF, contributing to more effective evaluation practices. 
 
To foster a collaborative approach to social inclusion and gender equality, UNICEF supported MOWSA with drafting the Accountability Directive on Gender and Child Rights, and strengthening the National Gender Information System to enhance accountability across sectors. In collaboration with the World Bank, UNICEF and MOWSA also conducted a review of the 2014 National Social Protection Policy to gain insights on design and implementation gaps to evaluate its ability to support populations in need and their emerging vulnerabilities.
 
UNICEF contributed to systems strengthening through adaptive social protection. More than 2.6 million households were covered by cash transfer programmes, including the Productive Safety Net Programme (PSNP). In collaboration with MOWSA and regional bureaus, UNICEF delivered shock-responsive cash transfers (SRCT) to conflict- and climate-affected populations, and reached 31,249 households (estimated 156,245 people) in Afar, Amhara, Benishangul-Gumuz, Gambella, Oromia, Tigray and Somali regions. Over 2,285 people with disabilities received one-time cash transfer top-ups for disability-specific costs. Community service workers linked over 32,246 SRCT beneficiaries to social services, including male engagement SBC sessions for women’s empowerment, and cholera prevention for flood-affected households. 
 
The child grant pilot covered households with pregnant women and children under-one in Addis Ababa, Amhara, Sidama and Somali regions, reaching 6,083 households with bi-monthly cash transfers for 12-18 months. Following the holistic Cash Plus approach, beneficiaries were linked to essential nutrition and health services. In Sidama and Amhara regions, 2,885 households were linked to SBC nutrition sessions, 1,131 children received birth certificates, 1,803 children received growth monitoring, 1,805 children were immunized, and 943 pregnant women accessed antenatal care. UNICEF implemented the SRCT Plus in Oromia region, and 2,214 households received training on financial literacy and life skills to support income generation and resilience building. UNICEF supported the finalization of the PSNP gender-responsive and age-sensitive social protection analysis, providing evidence on the implementation of gender provisions and the political economy of gender institutionalization in the PSNP design. It also supported two evaluations on the Integrated Safety Net Programme in Amhara region and Addis Ababa on the effectiveness of linking PSNP beneficiaries to essential services and CBHI through the social service workforce.
 
UNICEF provided 100 biometric kits for the Fayda Identification programme to provide digital registration for all residents. This innovation facilitated access to social and financial services for vulnerable populations. U-Report was launched as a digital platform for youth engagement with support of MOWSA, Ministry of Innovation, and youth organizations. It registered over 19,000 youths in 2024, with 11 polls and four chatbots implemented. 
 
In 2024, 78 per cent of UNICEF Ethiopia staff were trained on disability inclusion programming. The disability, social norms, and gender study was finalized with MOWSA along with the disability-inclusive SBC strategy. UNICEF delivered basic diagnostic services, a minimum rehabilitation package, assistive devices, case management support, psychosocial support, and financial resources to 250 children and adults with disabilities.

UNICEF maintained, developed, and expanded various strategic and meaningful partnerships in Ethiopia throughout 2024. 
 
UNICEF partnered with government ministries, institutions, and development partners to accelerate health program implementation. It engaged through coordination platforms like the Health Population and Nutrition donors’ platform and various technical working groups to safeguard and uphold the rights of children and women. Partnerships with universities and professional associations were established to assess SBC drivers of maternal, newborn and child health, and inform tailored interventions. Collaborations with donors including GAVI, United States, United Kingdom, and Germany helped reach over 3.5 million children and mothers with essential immunization and health services. USD 5.8 million (Regular Resources) was put towards supporting vaccination, medical consultations, and skilled births attendance, significantly strengthening health services during crises. 
 
UNICEF worked with various partners to strengthen youth engagement and empowerment. Notably, it mobilized USD 39.9 million from the Mastercard Foundation for a three-year programme to support 120,000 young people in conflict-affected areas of Northern Ethiopia to access continued education and employment. UNICEF also signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Rotary Ethiopia to strengthen joint efforts in empowering young people and families to bring positive change in their communities. It partnered with mobile network operator Safaricom to reach millions of young people on the U-Report platform through the provision of free Short Message Service. This will help reach youth with basic phones, ensuring inclusion in UNICEF’s programs and emergency response.  
 
UNICEF partnered with various organizations to address child wasting and nutrition. Significantly, it supported the development of national guidelines and strategic approaches with the MOH and World Food Programme (WFP). UNICEF also collaborated with the World Health Organization and WFP on a Joint UN Program on prevention intervention and evidence generation, and coordinated the Global Action Plan for Child Wasting. In Addis Ababa, UNICEF launched the Adolescent-led Food Urbanism Initiative, aligned with global strategies on active youth participation. With support from UNICEF, the GOE led and coordinated nutrition interventions across sectors, with nine ministers implementing the Food and Nutrition Strategy. 
 
UNICEF partnered with government and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) to resume education for children in crisis-affected regions. Key partners included the MOE, REBs, and NGOs like Save the Children and World Vision. For example, UNICEF expanded the Photovoice project in Afar region, and organized youth-led peer-to-peer network meetings that benefitted 263 participants (65% girls).
 
In partnership with the MOWE and the Ministry of Finance and Economic Cooperation, UNICEF facilitated the import of tax-exempt WASH items for emergency-affected populations, especially those internally displaced. It also supported local utility mentorship to strengthen utility systems and leverage public funding for urban water projects. UNICEF conducted a groundwater drilling analysis with MOWE, and collaborated with various NGOs and private organizations to support humanitarian responses. Significantly, UNICEF supported the development of a protocol for safely managed sanitation with WaterAid and the MOH, and contributed to the Consolidated WASH Account for the OWNP.
 
Building on previous partnerships, the GOE selected UNICEF as a technical partner for the World Bank-funded Response, Recovery & Resilience program for conflict-affected communities. UNICEF will help develop a GBV prevention model by mid-2025, and supported MOWSA in updating MHPSS training manuals this year. UNICEF continued to respond to development and humanitarian needs, prioritizing community-based structures. In 2025, UNICEF will build social workers' capacity for MHPSS interventions. Moreover, collaboration with the International Organization for Migration and Save the Children helped improve cross-border migration management. In addition, UNICEF adopted a PHC approach to enhance child protection services and expanded partnerships with local women led organizations and UN partners for comprehensive child protection, as well as comprehensive services to prevent and address GBV during emergencies.
 
UNICEF prioritized strengthening public finance management (PFM) partnerships in 2024, leveraging collaborations with the World Bank, European Union (EU), and the Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office of the United Kingdom to implement a costed PFM reform strategy. Funding from regular resources supported UNICEF’s public finance for children initiatives. Key achievements in 2024 included the child poverty analysis, support to the Ethiopian Demographic and Health Survey, and a disability-focused national survey. UNICEF built strategic partnerships for evaluation and promoted gender and child rights with various ministries and organizations. Collaborations with the World Bank, International Labour Organization, and others enhance social protection systems in Ethiopia. UNICEF also supported the National Identification Program, and partners with the private sector to improve financial access and resilience for vulnerable households.
 
UNICEF received funding from global organizations in 2024, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Mastercard Foundation, Lego Foundation, EU, KFW (Germany’s credit institute for reconstruction), Education Cannot Wait, the GPE, and the World Bank. Notably, the partnership with the Mastercard Foundation is one of the largest contracts secured from a single private sector entity. It also expanded partnerships with CSOs on SBC interventions, leading to the creation of the SBC curricula and the centers of excellence at Bahir Dar and Jijiga universities. UNICEF established a long-term partnership with Ethiopian Airlines, aligning business and philanthropic goals to improve children's lives. These strategic collaborations drove tangible results through targeted programs, advocacy, and operational initiatives, will continue into 2025 to realize shared goals and objectives for children and women.
 
UN agencies in Ethiopia worked collaboratively to prepare the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025-2030. As a key player, UNICEF significantly contributed to the review and update of the common country analysis and participated in strategic prioritization discussions. UNICEF continued to co-chair the United Nations Programme Management Team, and led the development of the results framework for the social development pillar and provided inputs to the results framework of other pillars. This strategic collaboration with the Resident Coordinator Office and sister agencies was essential to position priorities for children in the inter-agency cooperation framework in Ethiopia and ensure alignment with UNICEF’s Country Programme Document 2025-2030. The preparation of the new UNSDCF was informed by an evaluation of the current UNSDCF and a joint UN peace and conflict analysis, to which UNICEF provided both technical and financial support.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The GOE introduced macroeconomic reforms in 2024, which impacted UNICEF’s programming for children and women across all sectors. Internal conflict and protracted emergencies challenged service delivery, infrastructure improvements, and essential supply provision, and threatened the gains achieved in previous years. Security issues in some regions restricted access for UNICEF staff and implementing partners, causing delays in programme implementation and monitoring. The increased frequency and severity of climate-related shocks continued to exacerbate existing vulnerabilities. While remarkable support was given in 2024 to the GOE, much more needs to be done to reach all children and leave no one behind.
 
In health, programmatic visits and mentorship programs revealed shortages of NICU equipment spare parts, consumables, and reagents. UNICEF accordingly collaborated with the MOH and development partners to increase critical supply availability. Data-related challenges hindered service delivery, including poor reporting of district health information systems, shortages of data tools, and limited reporting from private health facilities. Consequently, UNICEF, MOH, and development partners jointly organized training for private and public health facilities to improve data quality. Conducting situational assessments, engaging communities to identify challenges, and designing tailored interventions proved effective in reaching zero-dose and under-immunized children. Preparedness interventions based on historical trends ensured timely emergency response. Scaling up CBHI and PHC schemes improved service quality, reduced debt, and empowered women and children to leverage community engagement systems. Cross-sectoral collaboration and early stakeholder buy-in were vital for sustainable and efficient implementation of initiatives like the Directly delivering Routine Immunization Vaccines for Equity (DRIVE) and health facility solar electrification.
 
In nutrition, underlying food insecurity and child food poverty reached dire levels, with 92 per cent of children not meeting the recommended dietary intake. The primary healthcare system was suboptimal in improving the coverage of preventive services. In addition, weak cross-sectoral linkages and accountability, poor governance, and lack of community financing for food and nutrition hindered the implementation of the Food and Nutrition Strategy. There was also limited policy implementation to ensure healthy food and nutrition environments and practices. To effectively combat malnutrition, UNICEF is supporting a paradigm shift in programming, with a focus on transforming food systems, enhancing household food production and consumption behavior of nutrient-dense foods, and scaling up system linkages with social protection, health, and WASH. Strengthening public-private partnerships to improve local production of nutrition commodities is essential. UNICEF continued to monitor the distribution of food commodities through health facilities to ensure they reached children and provided thorough follow-up on any issues.
 
In education, negotiating humanitarian access and advocating with key stakeholders was vital for safeguarding the continuation of education during conflicts. This involves working with local authorities, community leaders, and international organizations to secure safe passage for educational materials and personnel, and establishing temporary learning spaces. By fostering relationships, stakeholders created a supportive environment that prioritized education even amidst turmoil. Adoption of cluster approaches and organization of consultative meetings were effective strategies for addressing programme challenges. Cluster approaches brought together various stakeholders to collaborate and share resources, including government agencies, non-governmental organizations, and community groups. Consultative meetings provide a platform for stakeholders to discuss issues, share insights, and develop coordinated responses. This collaborative effort enhanced understanding of the challenges and contributed to more effective solutions. As a result, more children had access to continuous and quality education.
 
In child protection, UNICEF partnered with nine women-led organizations in Somali, Oromia, and South Ethiopia regions to provide life-saving support to women and girls affected by GBV. These partnerships enabled UNICEF to reach communities with culturally sensitive and effective solutions, while building leadership capacities to enable and sustain community-driven efforts to combat GBV. Close collaboration with UNICEF’s Social Policy programme ensured integration of key messaging on the importance of birth registration into humanitarian cash transfer (HCT) programming and the design of the child grant. Early data from the vital events registration agencies in South Ethiopia, Amhara, and Oromia regions indicated that children growing up in families benefiting from cash transfers were more likely to have their births registered due to the integrated programming. UNICEF continued to deliver cash top-ups pegged to the value of dignity kits for female HCT beneficiaries, coupled with social work home visits for case management in new conflict-affected areas. Key lessons were learned about the importance of the health sector in promoting birth registration. By conducting registration services in health facilities and during outreach drives for health and immunizations services, civil registration authorities significantly improved uptake.
 
In WASH, despite challenges, the achievement of the planned results for the UNICEF WASH programme were mostly on track. The process of transitioning from NGO-led to utilities-led operations and maintenance of water systems helped enhanced service sustainability in Kebribeyah, Aw Barre, and Sheder of Somali region and Itang of Gambella region. To bolster the capacity of the water utilities, UNICEF helped establish a national mentor-mentee model, which proved to be both cost-effective and sustainable. In addition, UNICEF’s ongoing partnership with the private sector for monitoring groundwater aquifers has shown positive impacts. Notably, Xylem provided in-kind and technical support, enhancing the effectiveness of monitoring efforts. Hardware support coupled with innovation and strategies like SBC and gender inclusion proved effective. 
 
In social policy, UNICEF continued providing technical assistance and engaged in policy advocacy to safeguard child-focused social sector spending, with the aim to enhance the revenue capacity of the regional governments. The existence of multiple cash transfer programmes using different targeting approaches necessitated sensitization and capacity building of all stakeholders. This made it more difficult to create an enabling environment anchored on a rights-based approach. Several key lessons were highlighted in 2024: programme harmonization and integration is vital, particularly to ensure the GOE’s safety net programmes are more shock-responsive; a dedicated frontline workforce is key to implement integrated social protection services that include linkages to child-specific services; and cash transfer interventions that aimed to support women’s empowerment also required dedicated SBC and male engagement activities in influencing intra-household dynamics in decision-making.

Kenya's population stands at 51.5 million, growing by 2.2 per cent since 2009 (Kenya National Bureau of Statistics [KNBS], 2022). Children aged 0-17 years make up 41.8 per cent of the population, with 11,040,661 girls (50.5 per cent) and 10,847,905 boys (49.5 per cent). Adolescents - ages 10-19 years - account for 11.6 million (22.2 per cent) of the total population, while youth 19-34 years are at 16.49 million (31.4 per cent). People with disabilities account for 2.2 per cent of the population (over 1 million people, of which an estimated 420,000 are children, KNBS 2019 Census). Additionally, Kenya shelters 823,932 registered refugees and asylum seekers in the Dadaab and Kakuma camps, and the Kalobeyei Settlement (UNHCR, 2024).
 
In 2024, inflation dropped from 6.9 per cent in January to 2.8 per cent in November. The Kenyan shilling stabilized after appreciating by nearly 20 per cent earlier in the year. However, Kenya's gross domestic product only grew by 5 per cent in the first quarter and 4.6 per cent in the second quarter, compared to 5.6 per cent for 2023. Severe floods, reduced public spending and ongoing fiscal consolidation affected growth and impacted budgetary allocations for social services. Positively, the government marginally increased national spending in social sectors from 42.8 per cent in 2023 to 43.7 per cent in 2024. However, county budget allocation decreased from 43.7 per cent to 41.7 per cent. The health sector saw a 1 per cent increase to 6.8 per cent, while the education and water sectors increased by 0.8 per cent to 26.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent, respectively. The social protection sector declined by 0.4 per cent to 3.1 per cent (though expected to increase next year), while the child protection sub-sector received an increased budget allocation of 3.7 per cent per year.
 
In the political sphere, the country experienced some civil unrest including the Generation-Z protests, contributing to the rejection of the 2024 Financial Bill and affecting the political environment, including change of senior officials in Government. 
 
Kenya is ranked 152 out of 191 countries on the Human Development Index. Two out of every five Kenyans live in monetary poverty. Additionally, half of the population (26.2 million people, including 10.9 million children) are multi-dimensionally poor, lacking access to basic services. In 2024, child monetary poverty was 42.4 per cent, while multidimensional poverty was 47.7 per cent. 
 
Kenya has advanced gender equality, including the adoption of policy and legal measures on gender-based violence (GBV) and female genital mutilation (FGM), and enhancing women’s leadership representation. As per the World Economic Forum's 2024 Global Gender Gap Index, Kenya is ranked 75th out of 146 countries, improving from 95th in 2021. Yet challenges persist: the country has seen a recent spate of femicides making global news, prompting the President to set aside funds for this issue. Women and girls continue to experience discrimination, exclusion, sexual exploitation and abuse, GBV, teenage pregnancy, higher rates of HIV and child marriage.  
 
Adolescents aged 10-19 years face significant challenges: 44.3 per cent of adolescents aged 10-17 exhibit mental health problems. In 2024, an estimated 2100 new HIV infections were among adolescents 10-19, with AIDS one of the highest cause of adolescent mortality. Data indicates that 16 per cent of adolescent girls aged 15-19 have experienced physical violence and 3.7 per cent have faced sexual violence (Situation of Adolescents in Kenya Report 2024, Government of Kenya, UNICEF and UNFPA).
 
Kenya's health sector faces persistent challenges. Neonatal mortality remains at 21 deaths per 1,000 live births (KDHS 2022), while adult HIV prevalence is 4 per cent and 71,433 children 0-14 years old live with HIV (National Aids Control Council, estimates 2024). Disparities persist, with skilled birth attendance significantly lower in some Arid and Semi-arid Land (ASAL) counties (e.g., Wajir 54 per cent, Mandera 56 per cent) compared to the national average of 89 per cent. Multiple emergencies, including floods and disease outbreaks (polio, measles, Mpox, Marburg), strained resources. Public fatigue with repeated vaccination campaigns and a doctor's strike has further hampered service delivery. Public perception of risk affected routine immunization coverage, leaving many zero-dose children unprotected. Budget cuts and delays in releasing funds from national to county level led to shortages of vaccines and essential commodities, including for HIV diagnostics. The rollout of a new Government social health insurance also disrupted access to care.
 
Despite reduction in stunting prevalence from 26 per cent in 2014 to 18 per cent in 2022 (KDHS), there remains a disparity between counties (Kilifi, West Pokot and Samburu counties reporting over 30 per cent). Only 31 per cent of children 6 to 23 months receive a diet of the right quality and quantity¿. According to the 2024 UNICEF Child Food Poverty report, 6 out of every 10 children are experiencing child food poverty, with rates of over 90 per cent in Turkana and Samburu. ¿Bottlenecks include limited dietary diversity/availability of nutritious foods, high food prices, frequent and recurrent multiple shocks¿, inadequate nutrition knowledge, inadequate financing, and sub-optimal coverage of multi-sectoral services. 
 
About 63 per cent of the population has access to basic water services, and 6.5 per cent practice open defecation (OD), KDHS 2022. However, 19.1 per cent still use surface water as the primary source of drinking water, 63.5 per cent still lack basic sanitation facilities, and 3.5 million people still practice OD (JMP, 2023). Issues include: low coverage of regulated water services in ASAL counties; lack of operations and maintenance sustainability; inadequate monitoring systems; delayed disbursement by the national government to counties; increased urbanization, straining existing limited services; and recurring climate shocks.
 
Data in the education sector remains a significant challenge; based on 2022 data, primary level enrolment declined between 2019 to 2022 (from 92.5 to 78.1 per cent) and stayed similar for secondary level (from 53.3 to 54.1 per cent). The percentage of learners in grade 3 reaching minimum proficiency in numeracy in 2022 dropped compared to 2019 from 68.83 to 54.2. The literacy indicator improved for English but not Kiswahili ¿(Ministry of Education, 2022). The decline in enrolment relates to decreasing budget for education, climate induced emergencies, lack of recognized alternative pathways for education, high rates of teenage pregnancy among school-going girls, and insecurity in some Northern counties.

Positively, prevalence of FGM reduced to 15 per cent in 2022 from 21 per cent in 2014; the UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of FGM has contributed to this; however, there are several high-prevalence counties at above 80 per cent (KDHS, 2022). Media and partner reports late in 2024 indicated increased FGM cases following school closures in certain counties such as Migori. A recent assessment conducted by the Directorate of Children’s Service under the Ministry of Labour Social Protection, found 44,070 children live in 902 institutional care facilities, and 2,056 children with disabilities. ¿Limited financing of the sector and human resources are key bottlenecks.

The UNICEF Kenya Country Programme (CP) 2022-2026 is aligned to the Government of Kenya’s VISION 2030 and contributes towards the Kenya United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF 2022-2026) and UNICEF Global Strategic Plan (2022–2025). In 2024, under the newly signed UNICEF CP financing agreement with the government, UNICEF supported key results, combining support to the Government to achieve large service delivery results – linked in large part to the floods and resilience building work – with strengthening social service systems to enable sustainability of delivery moving forward. 
 
Social Policy  
UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy contributed to budget allocation for children’s priorities. National allocation increased from 42 per cent in 2023 to 43.7 per cent in 2024 (target 44 per cent); however, counties’ budget allocation decreased from 43.7 per cent to 41.7 per cent. The overall decrease is due to huge debt burden at national level (67 per cent of debt to GDP) and public service administration costs at county level crowding out social sector investments. Nevertheless, UNICEF’s advocacy influenced the National Assembly and National Treasury to re-instate KES 6 billion (US$46 million) for social sectors that had been cut following the withdrawal of the Finance Bill for Fiscal year 2024/2025. 
 
Promoting child-related priorities, UNICEF advocated for the inclusion of children’s priorities in the County Annual Development Plans (ADPs), County Fiscal Strategy Papers and programme-based budgets in 19 counties (advocating with county assemblies and executive) and nationally in the budget policy statement. UNICEF supported the development of the Public Finance Management Reform Strategy (PFMR 2023-2028), to strengthen national and devolved service delivery in key social sectors. UNICEF provided technical support for publication of citizens budgets, which enables wider access of budget information, published in 23 counties in 2024 (from 18 in 2023) and one at national level with the county budget transparency score improving to 56 in 2023 from 41 in 2022. 
 
UNICEF contributed to social protection expansion, leading to coverage rising from 1.028 million to 1.703 million households enrolled for national cash transfer (surpassing the target). UNICEF provided technical assistance in the revision of the eligibility criteria for the Cash Transfer for Orphans and Vulnerable Children programme to consider additional vulnerabilities, increasing the number of child beneficiaries. UNICEF continued to partner with the World Bank, Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), and the Kenyan Government to advance the Nutrition Improvement through Cash and Health Education (NICHE) programme, expanding it to six additional counties in 2024, with 63,450 beneficiaries reached in 2024 with cash and services, up from the 32,879 in 2023. UNICEF with stakeholders supported the development of the Kenya Social Protection Policy 2023, launched in 2024, which serves as a landmark and critical tool for the government in advancing the economic and social rights of Kenyans. UNICEF also supported the development of social protection policies in Garissa and Turkana counties, working with county assemblies to ensure these are passed and enacted.  
 
Health 
In 2024, UNICEF contributed to the Government of Kenya’s vision for Universal Health Care, focusing on reducing inequalities, sustaining coverage and bolstering quality of essential services. UNICEF supported immunization to ensure that 1.14 million children (82 per cent coverage, target: 93 per cent) received 3 doses of pentavalent vaccine - a marginal decline from 2023 (85 per cent). Further, 1,123,205 (82 per cent coverage, target: 90 per cent) children received at least one dose of Measles-Rubella vaccine. UNICEF supported three rounds of polio campaigns in twelve high risk counties reaching 8.3 million children. UNICEF supported system strengthening by enhancing the skills of 8,876 health workers and through distribution and installation of 2,060 units of specialized cold chain equipment to health facilities.  
 
UNICEF contributed to improved maternal and newborn health (MNH) service delivery, with nearly 70 per cent of newborns (target 72 per cent) receiving a post-natal check within two days of birth. UNICEF supported 2 counties to set up learning hubs for MNH skills enhancement and newborn care units for inpatient care of small and sick new-born babies, to strengthen quality interventions for mothers and newborns. 
 
To strengthen the health system in a potentially transformative manner, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Quality of Care assessment of health care facilities, led by the Ministry of Health (MOH), implemented in all counties. UNICEF supported the establishment of 25 primary health care networks in eight counties, to help address bottlenecks around demand for services. Further, 2,740 community health promoters (CHPs) were trained to provide household service delivery, creating access to community services for over 1.3 million people; 6,048 had their skills enhanced on the electronic community health information system to strengthen reporting, and 269 were trained in integrated community case management to provide life-saving services in underserved ASAL counties.
 
To support Government efforts, UNICEF implemented the 100-day Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission (PMTCT) approach and Children and Adolescents Living with HIV Rapid Results Initiative (RRI) to address gaps in PMTCT and Pediatric AIDS cascades, reaching 8,265 children. To date, 74 per cent of children (target 85 per cent) received anti-retroviral drugs, with constraints due to the erratic supply chain and ongoing stigma in ASAL counties.  Empowering adolescents and young people, UNICEF supported the national Children and Adolescents Living with HIV Leadership Summit, with representation from all 47 counties.
 
For the flood response, UNICEF supported the government to reach 306,986 men, women, boys, and girls (95 per cent of the target) with uninterrupted essential health services, saving lives and supporting early recovery.  
 
Nutrition 
UNICEF in 2024 supported the Government to address malnutrition and promote adoption of positive nutrition practices by enhancing governance and systems capacity. UNICEF procured doses of vitamin A reaching over 5.3 million children 6-59 months (target of 6.4 million). With partners, UNICEF supported the government to procure and distribute life-saving nutrition commodities, including therapeutic milk and Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF). This effort kept RUTF stockouts below 5 per cent and provided severe acute malnutrition treatment services to 134,164 children aged 6 to 59 months (51.3 per cent girls), achieving 65 per cent against the target of 51 per cent, and a cure rate of 80.5 per cent. Through UNICEF support, the Family Mid-Upper Arm Circumference approach - empowering caregivers to monitor their children’s nutrition status - was scaled up to 13 counties while 76 per cent (742) of health facilities in 10 arid counties implemented the integrated management of acute malnutrition (IMAM) surge approach. UNICEF supported the MOH in adoption and adaptation of WHO 2023 recommendations on prevention and management of child wasting.
 
At national level, minimum diversity of diet as per 2022 KDHS is at 37 per cent against the target of 46 per cent. Under the NICHE programme, UNICEF supported capacity building of 1,886 health workers (755 men, 1,131 women, including 2 with disabilities, exceeding the target of 1,000), contributing to over 1.8 million primary caregivers receiving infant and young child feeding counselling (achieving the target), improving household knowledge and practices.  Over 5 million radio and television listeners (26 per cent of the population in target counties) received nutrition messaging with an additional 624,230 (53 per cent female and 47 per cent males) reached through a digital platform. 
 
As part of the systems approach to preventing malnutrition, UNICEF is developing a strategic roadmap outlining priorities and actions for 2025-2027. With partners, UNICEF’s Food Systems For Children (FS4C) agenda will support the Government to develop a suite of food policies and regulations to protect and promote healthy diets for children and adolescents, while simultaneously scoping food products and producers for the First Foods Africa initiative that will launch next year to combat child food poverty.
 
UNICEF significantly contributed to monitoring and evidence generation, supporting performance reviews, national situation analysis, seasonal assessments, SMART surveys, nutrition knowledge and attitudes surveys, and the use of the National Information Platform for Nutrition to improve access to information for decision-making. These efforts have been crucial for assessing progress, identifying gaps, and guiding emergency preparedness and response in 23 ASAL counties.
 
WASH 
Contributing to sanitation service coverage, UNICEF supported the MOH and Ministry of Water, Sanitation, and Irrigation in developing the Guidelines for Scaling Up Safely Managed On-Site Sanitation Services, guiding county staff and frontline workers in implementing scalable, context-specific sanitation solutions, and enhancing monitoring . These efforts resulted in the launch of real-time monitoring and sanitation hubs across all 47 counties, allowing for frequent programme tracking and adjustment and enhancing accountability.
 
UNICEF supported 10 counties in enabling 2,019 villages to be open defecation free, benefiting 764,504 people (101 per cent of target), using the Community-led Total Sanitation approach. Additionally, 677,060 people gained access to hand hygiene facilities through UNICEF support. Partnerships with private actors upgraded 13,431 toilets, benefiting 67,042 people. In informal settlements, 209,484 people accessed safely managed sanitation. Emergency responses reached 719,698 people with cholera prevention messages, while 53,473 gained improved emergency sanitation services. 
 
During 2024, UNICEF reached 375,103 additional people with basic access to safe water (target of 600,000) through the construction and rehabilitation of water sources of which 365,139 people are served from 75 solarized, drought resilient, sustainably managed and protected boreholes. As part of climate adaptation for building community resilience, drilling for three deep boreholes was completed in Samburu, Garissa and Wajir, providing long-term water solutions to those facing water scarcity challenges.  These boreholes provided water to 3,600 people in 2024 (in Samburu), including 1010 children in three schools and one health care facility, with potential to expand reach through further investment in water provision infrastructure. 
 
In support of WASH in institutions – enhancing health and education outcomes – with MOH, UNICEF capacitated health care workers on WASH in health care facilities, reaching 38 counties out of 47. UNICEF provided access to WASH services in 100 healthcare facilities, and 547 schools (target of 100), reaching 196,805 children. UNICEF’s multi-sectoral interventions across health, nutrition, and WASH have contributed to a decline in stunting among children under five (26 per cent in 2014 to 18 per cent in 2022) and diarrhea prevalence (from 15 per cent to 14 per cent in eight years).
 
Under the UNSDCF, UNICEF leads the Sustainable Water Joint Programme (JP), bringing together 10 UN agencies to harness resources to address the water crisis in ASALs.  The UN JP is an ambitious initiative: the overall budget is US$560 million for 10 years and US$168 million for the first 3 years; US$65 million is available currently from JP partners. UNICEF led the development of resource mobilization strategy and has engaged development banks and donor governments, while exploring opportunities from Climate Funds. 
 
Education
UNICEF collaborates with the Ministry of Education (MOE) to strengthen the education system and support out-of-school children (OOSC). UNICEF’s Country Programme aims to reach 320,000 children with education. In 2024, UNICEF’s interventions including community mobilization and engagement, and advocacy campaigns helped the MOE re-enroll 66,142 children in schools, totaling 317,644 children since mid-2022 (99.3% of the target).
 
To strengthen the system, UNICEF enhanced information management, supporting development of education and WASH in school modules in the national school census 2024, covering around 119,000 schools, including for the first time camp schools. This support will fill data gaps on key education indicators including net enrolment rate, which is not available beyond 2022. UNICEF worked with MOE to ensure the inclusion of pre-primary data into the Kenya Education Management Information System to support informed decisions, policies, and financing on early learning.
