Pre-primary education is the only devolved function in education, and is significantly underfunded at around 2 per cent against the recommended 10 per cent; to address this challenge, UNICEF, the Council of Governors (CoG), ministries and CSOs supported the finalization of the National Integrated Early Childhood Development policy, which should increase the level of investment for early learning. 
 
To improve child learning in schools, UNICEF and UN partner advocacy supported the Government to restore the KES 3.5 billion budget for school meals. UNICEF with partners provided technical support for the Community Service Learning curriculum re-design to align with the Competency Based Curriculum. UNICEF enhanced online access and learning for 389,869 children (43.3 per cent girls) through training of 7,647 teachers (56 per cent female) on ICT integration in Education and connecting nationwide 600 schools cumulatively to the internet. UNICEF supported 36,259 children (14,313 girls) with skills development, surpassing the target.  
 
In counties impacted by emergencies, UNICEF supported evidence generation, advocacy, resource mobilization and coordination. These efforts helped 159,030 children (43 per cent female, 73 per cent refugees) in Garissa and Turkana to access formal or nonformal education. For children affected by climate-induced emergencies, 42,376 children (47 per cent girls) in 11 counties (13 per cent of the children impacted) were supported by UNICEF with access to safe water at in schools, remedial and alternative education classes, teaching and learning materials, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Further, 12 counties were supported with education preparedness and response plans, increasing the resilience of the education system in these counties.
 
Child protection 
With UNICEF’s advocacy, the budget of the Directorate of Children’s Service was maintained during 2024 at KES 250 million (US$1.9 million), despite the challenging circumstances around the 2024 Finance Bill and youth demonstrations. At county level, seven County Governments created a budget line dedicated for child protection for the first time, which will expand services for children. For Garissa, Isiolo, Marsabit and Wajir counties, a budget line was included for the provision of GBV clinical services in the health sector budget as a part of the USAID-funded health project.
 
As a result of UNICEF’s advocacy last year, 50 Children’s Officers (government child protection case workers) were recruited. This year, UNICEF developed a workforce investment case and successfully advocated for more equitable deployment of officers to remote Northern Kenya, including Turkana; though the overall numbers are insufficient to provide quality service, at least one officer per sub-county was secured. The workforce ratio in Baringo, West Pokot and Samburu has also improved. 
 
Despite funding constraints, overall, UNICEF supported 45,781 children experiencing violence with protection and care services (surpassing the target). UNICEF supported 712 unaccompanied and separated children in Busia, Homabay, Kisumu and Garissa with services. To support refugee camps/host communities, 27,800 (16,185 female; 11,615 male) children and caregivers received MHPSS; 18,538 (9,730 girls, 8,808 boys) children were reached through help desks and radio programmes on child protection prevention and response; and 4,979 (3,389 female, 590 male) children and caregivers received GBV risk mitigation services. UNICEF reached 150,000 people with key messages addressing child protection and GBV risks in emergencies including harmful cultural practices
 
UNICEF provided intensive support to the Kenyan Government (GOK) for their engagement in the Global Ministerial Conference on ending Violence against Children in Bogota including the national consultation process. Positively, the GOK has made a progressive pledge with    concrete amount of financial commitment over 19 areas of work. These include scaling up of the parent programme and NICHE, establishment of a fund to advance the care reform; supporting safe and enabling schools; enhancing protection response services in health and justice sectors; and strengthening positive norms and values to end harmful practices. UNICEF will support this work moving forward.  
 
After the successful pilot in Kilifi in 2022-2023, UNICEF has contributed to position the National Positive Parenting programme within the NICHE programme in the second phase of World Bank and FCDO-funded Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project. This gives the parenting programme a precious opportunity for integrated delivery, scaling up to eight counties, and a robust evidence generation in the coming five years. 
 
Through the Global UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), UNICEF reached 6,322 children in school with life skills opportunities, girls’ agency, and peer to peer support for FGM prevention. Further, 48,502 people were reached (double the target) with tailored FGM prevention and response messaging and interventions through community engagement forums to shift deeply rooted social norms in 11 high FGM prevalence counties.
 
Cross-cutting areas & Programme Effectiveness 
In 2024, UNICEF’s humanitarian response reached over one million people affected by floods and health emergencies (78.5 per cent of the 2024 programme target, with 65 per cent of the funding received). At the county level, UNICEF supported development of Disaster Risk Management policies, helping to secure commitments of county development budgets to disaster preparedness. 
 
UNICEF supported prevention of Marburg Virus Disease and responded to cholera, polio, and Monkey Pox (Mpox) emergencies. UNICEF supported development of National Mpox Response Plan and National Mpox Risk Communication and Community Engagement Strategy, also collecting behaviour assessment data, training health workers and social mobilizers and undertaking monitoring of the infodemic. UNICEF reached 4.6 million people with public health messages, and organized community dialogues with over 6,000 people. Promoting accountability to affected populations, UNICEF collected and responded to 3,000 concerns / questions through established community feedback mechanisms. UNICEF also received the Golden Anthem Award 2024 for the “Kits that Fit” Project”, collecting and using behavioral insights to share with suppliers to innovate and improve WASH and dignity kits for drought-affected communities.
 
Through Generation Unlimited (GenU), 310,000 children and young people engaged in UNICEF-supported initiatives, such as U-Report, climate action, and civic engagement programmes, with over 28,000 actively participating in community activities. UNICEF’s GenU initiative also introduced a green entrepreneurship curriculum, with over 700 youth completing business training. The Engaging Kenyan Youth in Agriculture and Nutrition (EKYAN) programme supported youth livelihoods by integrating agriculture and nutrition, establishing 14 centers of excellence in public schools to promote climate-smart agriculture and sustainable nutrition practices. 
 
UNICEF’s focus on disability inclusion contributed to the formulation of the National Disability Policy and the expansion of social assistance programs for children with disabilities. Other notable successes include the provision of assistive technologies to 590 children with disabilities and enrollment of 438 out-of-school children with disabilities into primary schools. UNICEF Kenya also initiated dissemination of Kenya Disability Landscape Analysis Report, conducted by USAID Kenya. 
 
On adolescent programming, UNICEF supported the Government in development of a Situation of Adolescent Report, two policies (the National Adolescents and Young People Reproductive Health Policy and Adolescent Policy), three strategies (Adolescent strategy, National Social Behavior Change Strategy for Adolescents and Young People for their Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH), and National Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics Policy and Strategy for Secondary Schools), and five guidelines.
 
On climate change, UNICEF undertook the development of the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children¿, to highlight children’s issues for policymakers and guide UNICEF programming. The Children’s Climate and Disaster Risk Model (CCDRM) analytical report was successfully launched by the Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, which will support decision-making and resource allocation for climate mitigation and responsive programming. 

To commemorate the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and World Children’s Day (WCD), UNICEF developed a timeline exhibit of milestones and achievements in realizing child rights since the Government ratified the CRC in 1990, attended by the Chief Justice of the Supreme court. UNICEF supported a townhall conversation on child rights, broadcast live on Citizen TV to 2.3 million viewers, featuring panelists from Government, CSOs, parents, teachers and children. For WCD, UNICEF worked with the private sector and diplomatic community to Go Blue for children (lighting buildings in blue and wearing blue), and hosting children to ‘takeover’ or shadow top executives for the day, with 18 entities participating in the events, from private sector, Government CSOs and UN. Finally, UNICEF developed 11 advocacy briefs on key issues for children to influence key Government and development partner stakeholders.
 
Strengthening Protection of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) oversight, UNICEF established an office PSEA Task Team, chaired by the Representative. UNICEF trained around 70 partner staff and all suppliers with access to children and conducted PSEA capacity assessments for all 34 CSO partners. Further, 217 UNICEF personnel received face to face training. An internal SEA reporting mechanism was provided to personnel and disseminated among CSO partners. UNICEF, with IOM, co-chaired the Inter-agency PSEA Network, contributing to UN-wide PSEA efforts.
 
In 2024, UNICEF’s expenditure was US$82.6 million. Assurance activities were at 100 per cent for programmatic visits and spot checks. UNICEF finalized two evaluations and implemented all management response activities. UNICEF procured goods and services worth US$12.6 million, distributing 51.6 million vaccine doses (up from 40 million in 2023). The office completed recruitment of 31 staff to support programmes. The UN Country team in Kenya launched the first-ever UN Common Back Office initiative: as a service provider, UNICEF now supports UNDP and UN Women with HACT-related services (financial assurance, knowledge management, and capacity-building activities). As a client, UNICEF receives ICT, administration, and medical services from the UN.

In 2024, UNICEF worked strategically with the Government to enhance results for children and adolescents. Collaborative efforts with national and county governments – including the Ministries of Health and Education, the Kenya National Examination Council (KNEC) and the Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development (KICD) helped to institute policies, strategies, and funding for health and education programmes. UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection to enhance social protection and child protection results, including the expansion of social protection initiatives. Under the leadership of Representative, UNICEF launched the 11 Advocacy briefs outlining key concerns on child rights, and followed up with the National Parliament, National Treasury and Council of Governors (COG) to protect social sector budgets and positively shift resources for children. UNICEF engaged with the COG, Kenya Public Policy Research and Analysis and Kenya National Bureau of Statistics to support policy, data and monitoring and evaluation efforts. UNICEF also strengthened its partnership around climate change with the Ministry of Environment, which led to the integration of children and young people’s issues in the National Climate Change Adaptation Plan. 
 
In working with counties (county assemblies and executive), UNICEF supported development of National Facility Improvement Financing (FIF) Act and its regulations. UNICEF supported five counties (Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Isiolo and West Pokot) to domesticate the FIF Act and develop regulations, helping to ringfence revenue collected at health facility level for re-investment. UNICEF engaged 8 county assemblies (Garissa, Isiolo, Wajir, Mandera, Turkana, Baringo, West Pokot and Samburu) to build capacity for child-sensitive budgeting, with the county assemblies approving social sector budget increases totaling KES 1.78 billion (US$13.69 million). 
 
At UN level, UNICEF is well regarded in its support for the Resident Coordinator’s Office in scaling up work under the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, including as part of the implementation of the UN Joint Programmes (JPs) and pool funds under the Sustainable Development Goal platform. UNICEF leads the Joint Programmes in Nutrition and Integrated Water Resources Management and contributes to others, including on health, devolution, social and child protection and youth. Under UNICEF’s leadership, the UN JP for Nutrition worked to address malnutrition, including during emergencies. UNICEF collaborated with ILO, WFP, and others to design inclusive programmes and conduct gender assessments, addressing unpaid caregiving work and integrating displaced populations into county policies. UNICEF also engaged with UN agencies (e.g., WHO, UNFPA) in health and HIV programmes. The UN Joint Programme in Water, led by UNICEF, unites 10 UN agencies to address water scarcity in ASAL regions. Collaboration includes developing a joint climate adaptation proposal with government departments, targeting sustainable integrated water management. Inter-agency collaboration has also been bolstered through the launch of the Kenya UN Common Back Office, where UNICEF plays dual roles as both a service provider and recipient. 
 
Collaborations with Fresh Life scaled access to safely managed sanitation for 209,484 people in two informal settlements in Nairobi (approximately 29% of total population) and LIXIL for market-based sanitation solutions in rural areas have fostered innovation across the sanitation service chain, supporting safely managed sanitation levels. UNICEF Kenya was recognized and awarded by Brand Africa as the Most Admired NGO/UN entity Doing Good for Society, Environment, and People in Kenya. UNICEF collaborated with Kenya Society for the Blind, Getway prosthetics, Incursear and Association for Physically Disabled of Kenya to provide assistive technologies for children with disabilities in humanitarian situations and design an innovative financing model.  The private sector played a significant role in UNICEF’s nutrition programming through a strategic partnership with the Kenya Private Sector Alliance (KEPSA). This collaboration aimed to enhance maternal, infant, and young child nutrition by directly reaching 1 million people and engaging 200 private companies, 30 women’s groups and 50 youth groups.
 
UNICEF’s collaboration with donors contributed to key programme results, including UNICEF’s programming for refugees and host communities, under the PROSPECTS program (supported by the Government of Netherlands), integrating WASH, education, and child protection and delivering social services, while improving government systems to support refugees. UNICEF supported the Government’s scaling up of the NICHE programme, combining nutrition, child protection and social protection interventions, funded by the World Bank and FCDO. This is in support to the Government’s Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project funded by World Bank, of which NICHE is part, creating opportunities to expand social safety net programming. USAID provided resources to UNICEF to scale up Reproductive Maternal Newborn Child Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and Nutrition programming in eight counties, also strengthening GBV prevention and response services.  Moreover, UNICEF and UNFPA collaborated on designing of a GBV/Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse prevention project, setting a foundation for further global collaboration between the International Financial Cooperation and UNICEF in the next few years. 
 
UNICEF collaborated with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) like Kenya Red Cross Society and PATH to enhance health and HIV initiatives. UNICEF partnered with universities and CSOs (e.g., Bajeti Hub) for enhanced budget transparency and budget advocacy. UNICEF collaborated with Organizations of Persons with Disabilities to increase the inclusion of persons living with disabilities in workforces. Partnership with the Inter-Religious Council of Kenya (IRCK) enabled Social Intelligence Reports (eSIR) to be launched in Kilifi and Turkana counties. The reports described the gaps in basic social services identified by communities and attracted partners’ attention, leading to expansion of eSIR reporting and building two new primary schools.
 
UNICEF partnered with universities (Turkana University and Garissa University) on research and policy, promoting children’s interests at county level, while providing opportunity for youth (including refugees and host community) to engage.¿ The two universities commenced research on mapping the comprehensive financing from all sources available in the respective counties, producing recommendations for how funding can be better utilized to provide services for all. The information will also inform county policies for optimal use of resources. 
 
Top donors included the Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, USAID, US Fund for UNICEF, GAVI, Governments of Netherlands, Japan, Kenya (with World Bank), Ireland, France, Norway, Qatar and the United Kingdom, the German, UK and Canadian National Committees for UNICEF, Swedish Development Cooperation Agency, European Commission and Education Cannot Wait.
 
Despite funding cuts in 2024 in some areas, regular resources funding enabled UNICEF to address gaps in key areas, for instance supporting pre-primary education and out-of-school children programmes while maintaining policy influence and strategic positioning.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Lessons learnt - Strategic use of data for informing programme shifts.
UNICEF undertook the mid-point strategic review (MPSR) of its Country Programme (CP) in 2024, providing a critical juncture to re-assess the programme. The UN has prioritized the ASAL counties as part of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), based on the data available at the time demonstrating these were the counties most deprived in terms of socio-economic indicators and home to the most vulnerable groups. It was also believed that Western Kenya, particularly the lake economic region, was performing better in terms of social indicators compared to other parts of Kenya. However, as the 2022 KDHS data findings emerged and were further analysed, it became evident that there were areas within Western Kenya that required attention, with significant numbers of women and children affected by key deprivations. Thus, UNICEF has adopted a responsive approach, re-focusing and ensuring that efforts remain relevant and impactful in the face of emerging data and challenges. Six specific target counties in Western Kenya – those with the most pressing overlapping deprivations for children as per KDHS 2022 data – have been identified for programme focus for the remainder of the CP cycle, especially to tackle triple threat, VAC issues and poor indicators for children overlapping across nutrition, WASH, education and health sectors. UNICEF’s comparative advantage remains on supporting policy and the enabling environment. Mobilizing resources and enhancing field office responsibilities for effective programme execution in the region will be a key part of the approach moving forward. 
 
Lessons learnt - Climate change mainstreaming and positioning  
During the MPSR, UNICEF developed an issue paper drawing upon the Children’s Climate and Disaster Risk Model (CCDRM) to determine that the CP did not sufficiently align with UNICEF's global climate ambitions, specifically, the new Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan (SCAP), nor address the government's climate priorities and recurring climate driven emergencies. Consequently, further climate interventions have been included in 2025-2027 work plans with the government, including: shock responsive social protection; integrating climate concerns in county budget briefs; strengthening youth engagement in green entrepreneurship and climate policy processes; disaster risk reduction policy development at different levels; climate resilient WASH interventions such as innovative groundwater exploration methods; research on linkages between climate and harmful practices; and mainstreaming climate change into the school curriculum. The issue paper and focus on climate during the MPSR provided evidence and momentum to promote sectoral climate programming. The reflection and evidence gathering also helped UNICEF increase its engagement with the Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Forestry (MECCF); while the climate space is competitive in Kenya, with many development partners keen on collaborating with the ministry, UNICEF has been able to position itself through data and evidence as a knowledge broker when it comes to climate issues and children, exemplified through the launch of the CCDRM analytical report gathering multiple stakeholders together around data and evidence. Moving forward, UNICEF is finalizing a Climate Landscape Analysis for Children, which will provide a detailed assessment and recommendations for the office and policy makers to enhance the position of children in a changing climate. 
 
Lessons learnt – multi-sectoral programming 
As per the independent evaluation undertaken in 2024 on the NICHE programme, one of the key characteristics is the interconnectedness between social protection, nutrition and child protection services, which has played a major role in the programme’s relevance, efficiency and sustainability. The programme fills an important space in the existing government strategy for the provision of integrated services to vulnerable households with multi-sectoral needs. Moreover, the strong integration of NICHE components in existing systems increases its efficiency and sustainability. NICHE has contributed to strengthening systems through coverage of hard-to-reach populations and enhancing multisectoral collaborations. UNICEF scaled up its nutrition programmes, distributing ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) to malnourished children and providing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services to mitigate the impact of the drought. Additionally, UNICEF leveraged its partnerships with local NGOs and community-based organizations to ensure that aid reached the most vulnerable populations, including children with disabilities and those living in remote areas. 



Challenges in Early Childhood Development (ECD): Despite ongoing efforts to improve access to early childhood education (ECD) UNICEF faced challenges related to low enrolment rates and inadequate infrastructure in 2024.



Coordination and Alignment Among Partners: Coordination among UNICEF’s numerous stakeholders, including the government, NGOs, UN agencies, and donors, remained a challenge in 2024. While partnerships were crucial for achieving UNICEF’s objectives, differences in priorities, approaches, and timelines sometimes led to inefficiencies and duplication of efforts. 
 
Lessons Learned


The Importance of Community Engagement A significant lesson learned in 2024 was the importance of community engagement. UNICEF’s partnership with local community leaders, volunteers, and community-based organizations allowed it to overcome logistical and cultural barriers in remote areas. These partnerships ensured that immunization campaigns, nutrition interventions, and child protection programmes were well-received and effectively implemented. Engaging local communities helped build trust, ensuring that interventions were culturally relevant and more likely to be accepted by the population.



Leveraging Digital Tools for Outreach: UNICEF also learned the value of digital tools in expanding outreach and improving programme effectiveness. Through platforms such as social media, U-Report, and mobile-based campaigns.



Unlocking the Potential of Private Sector Partnerships: One of the key lessons learned in 2024 was the importance of unlocking the potential of private sector partnerships. Collaborating with private sector entities, particularly in the education sector, proved to be a game-changer for UNICEF Lesotho. Through partnerships with telecommunication companies and corporate sponsors, UNICEF was able to introduce digital learning tools and mobile-based education programmes, reaching underserved communities and enhancing the quality of early education. These private sector collaborations also helped mobilize additional funding, resources, and expertise, accelerating the implementation of UNICEF’s programmes in key areas like education.



Evidence-Based Advocacy for Policy Change: The importance of evidence-based advocacy was another key lesson from 2024. Through initiatives like the KAP study on violence against children, UNICEF generated valuable data that informed campaign strategies and contributed to policy change. The use of evidence not only strengthened advocacy efforts but also helped design more targeted, effective interventions. Moving forward, UNICEF will prioritise data generation and use, ensuring that future programmes are grounded in solid research and data-driven decision-making.



Adaptability in Crisis Situations: The drought emergency in 2024 highlighted the need for adaptability in programme implementation. UNICEF had to adjust its activities quickly to respond to the evolving crisis, ensuring that children’s basic needs were met in the face of food insecurity and limited access to clean water. By leveraging its existing partnerships and quickly mobilizing resources, UNICEF was able to deliver timely, life-saving support to those most affected. This experience reinforced the importance of flexibility in programme planning and crisis response.
 
Future Outlook
Looking ahead, UNICEF Lesotho is optimistic about continuing to improve the lives of children, despite the challenges faced in 2024. The foundation laid in areas such as immunization, early childhood education, and social protection provides a strong base for future progress.
 
In the coming years, UNICEF will focus on expanding access to quality education, especially through digital learning tools and private sector partnerships, to address gaps in ECD and secondary education. The lessons learned from the drought emergency will guide future interventions aimed at building climate resilience, with an emphasis on integrating climate-smart education into school curricula and ensuring children’s access to climate adaptation programmes.
 
Additionally, UNICEF will continue to prioritise community engagement, evidence-based advocacy, and digital transformation to drive sustainable change and achieve lasting impact. The experience gained from the challenges of 2024 will serve as a springboard for more effective, inclusive, and resilient programmes in the years to come.

After enduring numerous droughts in recent years, Madagascar saw an improvement in food security in the Great South in 2024, However, the situation in the drought-prone southern regions remained fragile, with 900,000 reached with humanitarian assistance [1]. The country was also severely affected by Tropical Storm Alvaro and Cyclone Gamane, which caused widespread flooding, displaced and left nearly 1.1 million people, including 950,000 children, in need of humanitarian support. Additionally, bushfires in November and December 2024 burned 765 hectares of land, including iconic Ramonafana national park, further impacting the local population and exacerbating existing vulnerabilities and land degradation.
 
On the political front, the year was marked by two key electoral processes. First, the parliamentary elections held on May 29 elected 163 National Assembly members, and second, municipal elections held on December 11, after a year-long delay, elected municipal assemblies and mayors across 1,695 communes. Both elections were won by the presidential majority party. These elections slowed down UNICEF programme implementation, mainly due to a void within the government pending cabinet and ministerial appointments. Diplomatically, 2024 has been a vibrant year for the country, as Madagascar took on the leadership of two major bodies, the general secretariat of the Indian Ocean Commission (IOC) in July, and the chairmanship of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), which will be effective in August 2025.
 
Madagascar maintained a stable economic growth in 2024, projected by the World Bank at 4.5%, higher than in 2023 (3.8%). Inflation was contained throughout the year below 8% but soaring prices of basic primary commodities including rice and cooking oil towards the end of the year, created social difficulties for vulnerable households. In public finance, the general state budget was significantly reduced, with a cut of 20.5% implemented in the amending law. This impacted several social sectors disproportionately, including education, health, social protection water, sanitation, and hygiene. Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) was the most affected sector, with a 57.5% decrease in budget. In the health sector, delays in the payment of vaccines resulted in stockouts in health centres. Despite GDP growth, the country still ranks 177th of 193 on the 2023-2024 Human Development Index, the same as in 2022, Additionally, 80.3% of the population lives below the $2.15 purchasing power parities (PPPs) poverty line, highlighting the persistence of widespread poverty.
 
In June 2024, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) Executive Board approved a Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangement of US$321 million for Madagascar, including reforms to strengthen adaptation to climate change and resilience against natural disasters as well as support to climate change mitigation efforts. The Resilience and Sustainability Facility complements the Extended Credit Facility, bringing the total IMF support envelope to USD 628 million for a 36-month period. However, during the last quarter of 2024, the Government could not secure the disbursement of financial support totalling USD 270 million [2], from the three main international financial institutions (World Bank, IMF and AfDB) mainly due to the non-implementation of stipulated macroeconomic reforms. The national energy company is the largest single beneficiary of government subsidies, and its reform is one of the pillars [3] of public finance consolidation requested by the IMF. Since September 2024, the country has faced disruptions in the delivery of public services in energy and water aggravated by water scarcity due to the late rainy season and deteriorating infrastructure. Antananarivo, the capital, and major cities experienced prolonged power cuts and water supply shortages that affected the population and economic activities and created social unrest. 
 
Meanwhile, a lack of adequate investment in key social sectors, high environmental vulnerabilities, and unfavourable social norms continue to hinder Malagasy children from reaching their full potential. This situation is compounded by persistent gender and urban-rural inequalities which remain a major obstacle to human development. Nearly 44% of children drop out of primary school[4], and only 3 in 10 progresses to secondary school. Violence against children remains prevalent, with 20% of girls aged 15-19 reporting that they have experienced physical violence, and 39% of women aged 20-24 having married or in a union before the age of 18 years. In 2024, children with albinism continued to face extreme vulnerability due to violence, multiple cases of kidnappings, mutilation and killing of children were reported throughout the year, particularly in Vatovavy, Atsimo Atsinanana and Amoron’i Mania regions. Madagascar saw an exponential surge in malaria cases by 262% over seven years, from 795,527 in 2017 to 2,879,747 in 2024, affecting nearly 10% of the national population. On a positive note, no polio cases have been reported since September 2023, reflecting the success of vaccination campaigns in 2023 and 2024. Finally, recent estimates by the National Statistics Institute show that 83.3 % of children (59.2% urban and 88.5% rural) lived under the national poverty line in 2021, compared to 77%[5] in the whole population, yet only 6% of poor children are covered by a regular and predictable social protection programme. The September 2024 Nutrition Smart survey data show a slight reduction in child wasting in the Great South at 7.8 percent in 2024 compared to 12.7 percent a year before. However, the child wasting situation did not improve in the South-East.

In February 2024, UNICEF Madagascar new Country Programme document was approved by the Executive board. The year 2024 therefore marked the start of new five-year programme cycle. The Office increased its field presence with the establishment of a fifth Field Office, the confirmation of an outpost and a shift of the staff posted in the field from 21 percent to 36 percent of the total workforce. During the year, a total budget of USD 66.3 million was utilized for programme implementation and support operations. 

Despite persistent challenges in accessing quality healthcare services, 2024 witnessed significant progress in Madagascar's health sector. Through combined efforts from UNICEF, WHO and the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, three rounds of national campaigns for immunization against poliomyelitis were conducted, over 26.4 million children under the age of 15 years (cumulative number) were vaccinated stopping the circulation of the polio virus. During the October measles campaign, 4,597,573 children under 5 were vaccinated to prevent a potential epidemic. Remarkably, 59.1% of initial vaccination refusals were resolved through targeted interventions. 

The Big Catch-Up Initiative launched in April 2024 by the President of the Republic and the First Lady, supported by UNICEF, WHO, and Gavi Alliance, resulted in the vaccination of 426,000 children that had never been reached by routine immunization services (zero-dose). The annual target of 428,400 children was almost met, while another 798,000 zero-dose children will need to be reached in 2025. UNICEF played a pivotal role in the implementation of the new operational model for community health, adopted in 2023 by the Ministry, working across two regions and five health districts. In the targeted region of Betsiboka, a total of 7,370 community health workers, trained in the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses (IMCI), treated 30,000 children for either malaria, diarrhoea, or acute respiratory infections. 

UNICEF continued to respond to the large burden of malnutrition in Madagascar by playing a critical role in supporting responses to nutrition emergencies and scaling up UNICEF engagement in food systems to improve child diets. Over the course of the year, UNICEF enhanced the emergency preparedness and response skills of over 3,700 frontline workers and 848 health workers (100% of the annual target) in the 22 most vulnerable districts in the south and south-east regions, on forecasting and procurement of essential nutrition supplies, strengthening delivery of nutrition services and information systems. As a result, 75,547 children suffering from severe wasting, a life threating condition, received treatment while an additional 4,196,795 children benefited from other high impact nutrition services through UNICEF support. This marked a 39% increase over the previous year, demonstrating a significant expansion in the reach and impact of UNICEF’s interventions. 
 
Additionally, in collaboration with UNICEF’s Regional Office, UNICEF Madagascar began integrating innovative solutions through climate smart nutrition programming to improve the quality and sustainability of children's diets and well as delivery of nutrition services in the face of climate change. On upstream policy work with the government, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health to roll out a new maternal nutrition package addressing the critical need for improved nutrition among pregnant and breastfeeding women. As well as the development of the first-ever national Early Childhood Development strategy for Madagascar, establishing a foundation for access to quality early childhood development programmes.

UNICEF improved access to resilient water services for over 118,085 people through the installation and rehabilitation of 134 water points, which includes 70 Multiple-Use Water Systems (MUS)[1] and 24 water distribution systems. Among the new water points, 31 out of the 134 water points were achieved through the drilling of new boreholes in both communities and schools. Life-saving emergency interventions reached 102,758 people with safe water, 15,678 with sanitation, and 82,609 with hygiene services. Three sand dams were designed and completed to provide a long-term, climate-resilient water supply. In the Androy region, UNICEF addressed water quality issues caused by saline intrusion through water desalination systems. This approach ensured access to fresh water, increased daily capacity usage, and reduced long-term maintenance of water infrastructure costs. UNICEF supported 721,523 people, included 394 041 children (194 698 girls and 199 343 boys) to access improved sanitation solutions and services, which included household latrines, community sanitary blocks, and facilities for schools and health centres. This includes the construction of 72,518 rural latrines, through the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach. UNICEF also prototyped the new eco-friendly latrine ‘Aborloo’ as part of the Sanitation Marketing Programme. 

Madagascar’s education sector is grappling with significant challenges, including gaps in basic literacy and numeracy among students as well as a shortage of qualified teachers and inadequate infrastructures. In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in improving education for 1,233,185 primary and secondary school children (53% girls) across eight regions, using strategic advocacy, community engagement and gender-transformative programming. 1,456 school principals (30% women) and 6,481 primary school teachers (49% women) were trained on the Teaching at the Right Level-structured pedagogy and benefited from post-training follow-up to improve learning quality. UNICEF also supported the provision of school kits to 275,283 students through the Back to School and Learning strategy, to increase access to education for the most vulnerable children. 

At the secondary school level, 1,593 teachers (72% women) acquired skills in effective approaches to teach scientific subjects and promote interest in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), especially among girls. UNICEF rehabilitated and built 18 classrooms across 3 junior secondary schools, including multi-purpose rooms for science teaching. This action was combined the provision of ICT equipment (158 computers) and internet connection, which increased access to digital learning platforms, benefiting 127,386 learners, through a tripartite partnership with Airtel and the Ministry of Education. Additionally, UNICEF empowered 30 district-based committees in 8 regions on Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Action contributing to adequate and timely responses to natural disasters and allowing 125,610 students (51% girls) to continue their learning during humanitarian challenges.

UNICEF provided 85 (50 girls) out-of-school adolescents with entrepreneurship and 21st-century skills, through the UPSHIFT initiative, testing this new approach to give a second chance to adolescents. In addition, UNICEF played a major role in strengthening school governance, focusing on community engagement and using social and behaviour change approaches. In partnership with Japan International Cooperation Agency, UNICEF trained 3,782 members of School Management Committees (24% women) from 1,267 schools, equipping them with the skills to more effectively carry out their responsibilities.
 
In collaboration with the French Development Agency (AFD) and the World Bank, UNICEF was selected as one of the grant agents of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) System Transformation Grant (STG) to address Madagascar’s learning crisis. UNICEF will receive USD25 million out of the USD 89.4 million STG to support the government. To enhance the efficiency of funds disbursements to the decentralized level, UNICEF continued to work with AFD to operationalize the Education Pooled Fund (FCE). This collaboration resulted in the transfer of USD300,000 for school grants to 1,939 Lower Secondary Schools across 18 regions, directly impacting learning for 489,064 students. Additional funds from the European Union and the GPE have been obtained for the pooled fund, demonstrating the added value of this funding mechanism for the sector.
 
Significant progress was made in supporting the government to strengthen the child protection system. The effort involved close collaboration with the Ministry of Population and Solidarities, UN agencies and other key stakeholders to define a strategic vision for child protection. This was reinforced by the official pledge made by the Minister of Population at the first Global Ministerial Conference on Violence Against Children in November 2024 in Colombia, committing to implement key actions to eliminate violence against children. A key milestone was the reactivation of the National Child Protection Committee (CNPE), which had been inactive for 5 years. With support from UNICEF, the Committee convened twice to strengthen understanding and coordination on child protection issues. To enhance child protection programming in relation to climate change, a study was initiated on the impact of climate change on violence, child marriage, child labour and family separation. The first National Conference of Magistrates, held in June 2024, led to the creation of a roadmap to improve child justice over the coming years. As a result of advocacy efforts, the number of children in detention was reduced by 17% in 2024 compared to 2023, with 854 children in detention as of December 2024.
 
UNICEF created safer school environments and provided care for over 14,000 child victims of violence, and more than 11,000 adolescents including those affected by humanitarian crises. These children received individual care through home visits, psychosocial support for children and their families and referrals to medical and legal services. Further, approximately 3,500 child victims of sexual violence, including 73% of adolescent girls received care through partners including in the UNICEF-supported one-stop Vonjy Centres where integrated services are provided to children. Additionally, 97,253 children in humanitarian situations received mental health and psychosocial support through a range of community-based approaches. UNICEF continued to work with the Catholic Relief Services in ensuring the coordination of Protection Sector interventions in humanitarian response, such as the joint conduct of needs assessment in the North of Madagascar, following cyclone Gamane. Further, an analysis of the humanitarian child protection coordination mechanisms was conducted, which was utilized to improve coordination of the child protection in emergency response while training of key actors at national level on these topics strengthened capacities.
 
UNICEF continued to work with the government and its partners to generate quality, disaggregated evidence on monetary and multidimensional poverty, in alignment with the National Strategy for Statistics Development. Seven years after the release of the previous Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS), UNICEF started the data collection for MICS7 that will allow the monitoring of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) while providing crucial data on children, adolescents, and their families, and informing policy, planning, and programming for children in Madagascar. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF increased its focus on public budget execution through its budget analyses. All social sectors were covered, but specific attention was paid to the Water/Sanitation/Hygiene (WASH) sector, which showed reduced allocations and a lower budget execution, with both WASH and health sectors facing budget reductions of 17.1% and 5.3%, respectively, between 2023 and 2024. Alongside these budget analyses, UNICEF also increased advocacy efforts to raise the government’s awareness on the need to secure domestic resources to fund vaccines. UNICEF collaborated with the IMF to produce a thematic paper as part of Article IV consultations to address the specific challenges of teacher training, which is a major impediment to quality education.
 
The coverage of UNICEF-supported social protection programme Zara Mira expanded with a 45% increase in the number of beneficiaries, from 55,354 (27,403 girls and 27,951 boys) in 2023 to 79,867 children (40,197 girls). These children and their families received bimonthly transfers and accompanying measures such as productive and financial inclusion, educational sessions on various themes such as positive parenting, essential family practices, prevention of early marriage and early pregnancy or attitudes towards persons with disability. Accompanying measures are harmonized with those delivered within the World Bank-funded social safety net programmes, which covers 528,216 children. Preparatory work progressed well to expand UNICEF-supported Zara Mira programme into an additional region, with more than 46,000 children identified and their families enrolled in the social registry. The delivery of cash transfers supported by UNICEF is part of a wider strategy to strengthen social protection system in Madagascar and enhance risk-informed humanitarian and development nexus programming. In this regard, UNICEF, in collaboration with the World Bank and WFP, assisted the government in developing its national social protection strategy, covering both contributive and non-contributive aspects. 
 
Addressing the impact of climate change on children has been identified as a cross-sectoral priority in the new Country Programme. UNICEF conducted the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) set for publication in 2025. The CLAC will inform multiple national strategies, including the revision of the National Determined Contributions (NDC) and the climate finance strategy, which UNICEF supports in close collaboration with the Global Centre on Adaptation (GCA), the World Bank, the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Finance. Additionally, the visit of UNICEF Executive Board to Madagascar recognised Madagascar Country Office leadership around climate change programming. During the special session of the Executive Board dedicated to climate change in September, the Minister of Environment and Sustainable Development delivered a speech highlighting the exemplary work implemented in collaboration with UNICEF. At the same event, the Minister signed the Declaration on Children and Youth in Climate Action, reaffirming Madagascar's commitment to youth-led and child-focused climate solutions.
 
UNICEF initiated a child-sensitive risk analysis at sub-national level together with the Office for Humanitarian affairs (Bureau National de Gestion des Risques et des Catastrophes) and UNDP, using the Index for Risk Management model (INFORM)[2]to ensure children’s needs and risk-informed planning are central to climate and humanitarian efforts. Through the UNICEF “Today and Tomorrow” initiative, UNICEF was able to get funding to respond to cyclones and to implement anticipatory actions strengthening the resilience and preparedness of children, communities and infrastructure.
 
UNICEF supported Madagascar’s participation in global climate forums that elevated Madagascar at these global gatherings. At the at the SB60 Expert Dialogue on Children and Climate Change in Bonn, under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Madagascar presented the first-ever submission for consideration and adoption on the impact of climate change on children. Young people played a key role as policy trackers, following live drafting of international Agreements and informing government decisions in the formulation of these policy proceedings, at UN Climate Change Conference COP 29, the Convention on Biological Diversity Sixteenth meeting (CBD COP16), and the sixteenth session of the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD). 
 
UNICEF expanded its climate change Ecovillage Programme, serving a total of 14,420 people (7021 females) in the initial 10 eco-villages. The climate-resilient infrastructures built include multi-usage water infrastructure, solar-powered systems in schools, health centres, and public spaces. Communities in the ecovillages participated in local dialogues on environmental issues and were involved in tree planting, permaculture, production of reusable sanitary pads, latrine slab production and eco-friendly charcoal initiatives to promote sustainability and community well-being. Through these activities 2,500 youth and 4,000 women benefited from green livelihood initiatives. Additionally, the office made progress on integrating Environmental and Social Standards (ESS) into programmes to ensure sustainability and alignment with international standards. 
 
On social and behaviour change (SBC), more than 200 polio and routine immunization vaccine demand and uptake plans were developed and implemented for each of the national polio campaign. Furthermore, UNICEF supported risk communication, community engagement, and was accountable to affected populations during preparedness, response, and post-emergency phases. Over 11,159 frontline workers, skilled in Social and Behavior Change, Human-Centered Design, and Accountability to Affected Populations, provided key messages and critical communications to affected people. Young people’s voices were heard and amplified through opinion polls conducted using U-report. These polls focused on Gender-Based Violence (GBV), girls’ rights and gender equity, online exploitation and abuse. Through U-report, the Malagasy youth were consulted on the UN Summit of the Future themes. This consultation resulted in a Youth Declaration which was officially handed over to the Minister of Youth ahead of the Summit. Additionally, over 63,000 young people, including 57% girls, were engaged in climate change interventions through various campaigns and initiatives. 

In 2024, gender inequalities across the country continued to be a major constraint on poverty reduction and growth. UNICEF completed a gender review of all its programmes and drew up key recommendations for the programme cycle. Since adolescent girls are a strategic priority in the new Country Programme, a strategy for and with adolescent girls was completed, alongside an investment case. A diversity strategy for emergencies was developed- focusing on gender and disability- to be rolled out in 2025. Additionally, UNICEF and partners supported the development of a national strategic plan for adolescent and youth health (2025-2030) and contributed to updating the Reproductive Health Standards and Procedures, paving the way for concerted actions for adolescent girls.
 
Across sectors, UNICEF Madagascar and its partners achieved an impressive range of gender results, with a strong focus on adolescent girls. Highlights include a life skills programme which reached over 54,000 adolescents aged 10-17, including 57% girls, prioritizing those out of school; advocacy to ensure a violence-free environment in secondary schools, engaging pupils, teachers, administrative staff, school management committees, reaching 460,000 women, men, girls and boys; support to 11,886 adolescent girls recovering from violence, receiving care tailored to their individual needs. Training on Gender Based Violence (GBV) was delivered to national trainers and support provided to update the national strategy on GBV. Prevention messages on GBV were delivered to over 565,000 girls, boys, mothers and fathers to protect girls from all forms of violence, including child marriage; and a draft module on positive masculinities was tested in six regions. Over 200,000 adolescent girls and boys (123,700 girls) were treated in youth-friendly centres with 81 new centres opened and 75 centres equipped to provide enhanced treatment for GBV.
 
UNICEF Madagascar initiated dialogue on Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) with key ministries, including Health, Education, Population and Solidarity, Labour and Employment. Gender modules were developed and delivered to 316 UNICEF staff members, alongside a comprehensive training on Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA).  
 
Adolescent girls were a core focus of UNICEF’s WASH programme, with the design of a new Menstrual Hygiene Management-friendly infrastructure for schools that provides privacy and dignity for girls while supporting school attendance. Overall, just under 289,000 women and girls were reached with menstrual hygiene interventions. Likewise, UNICEF empowered young leaders through the ‘Girl Power Nutrition’ initiative, training over 1,000 girls and using a peer-to-peer approach with the Girl Scouts, engaging 91,022 girls in the promotion of good nutrition.  

On the disability inclusion front, a total of 850 children with disabilities received cash through the Zara Mira cash transfer programme. Additionally, through the Lego braille programme, children learned inclusive ways to communicate with each other in school settings, benefiting 7,403 students, including 279 with visual impairment. UNICEF also supported the government to develop the National Policy for Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, which will be launched in 2025, providing a framework for government and stakeholders to deliver disability inclusion.

Beyond the government, UNICEF engaged in various partnerships with UN agencies, donors – including Germany (BMZ/KfW), Norway and Japan (including with JICA) - and civil society organizations leading to greater complementarity and synergy, and joint programming.  With the European Union, two new agreements were signed to strengthen the health system and expand social protection and child protection programmes. The EU also funded a UN joint programme, aiming at building community resilience in response to the consequences of extreme weather conditions and climate change on local populations, including children and women. This  programme will complement other joint initiatives funded by Germany and Norway, supporting the humanitarian-development nexus programming. Using the results of robust analytical work on access to water in the Great South of Madagascar, UNICEF reinforced its partnership with the World Bank (WB) and the Malagasy Government, implementing an ambitious water project under the WB-funded  Mionjo programme.

In total, UNICEF pursued four joint programming with other UN Agencies. These joint programs included (1) a grant  from the Peace Building Fund for conflict prevention, social cohesion and  peacebuilding with UNDP and UNFPA, (2) a KfW/BMZ funded grant for building  Resilience for Food and Nutrition Security, implemented with WFP, (3) a  Norway government funded grant to Build Resilience for Climate Change  Adaptation and Combat Hunger in Southeast Madagascar with WFP, and (4) the  European Union funded “Pacte Vert” mentioned above implemented with UNDP, FAO  and WFP. Alongside IOM and UNESCO, UNICEF was successful in obtaining funding from the Peace Building Fund for the implementation of a new project on Climate Security in the Atsimo Andrefana region.

UNICEF grew its partnership with  the US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) and the EU ECHO/DG-INTPA, in  emergency programming for Nutrition and Child Protection, which benefitted  communities affected by droughts and cyclones in the southern and south-eastern  districts of Madagascar. Around the emergency response, reinforced engagement  with Japan led to the implementation of interventions targeting protracted  emergencies, such as those affecting the south-eastern districts of  Madagascar.

UNICEF maintained private sector  partnership with AIRTEL Madagascar contributing to the digital transformation  agenda in Education and engaged the AXIAN Foundation to explore potential  partnerships around education, nutrition, Prevention of Sexual Exploitation  and Abuse. A collaboration with We Light, a subsidiary of the Axian Group, is  also being discussed to ensure synergy of both organizations’ interventions  with a focus on local access to renewable energies as well as provision of essential  services.  A Memorandum of  Understanding was signed between UNICEF and the Private Sector Humanitarian  Platform to work hand in hand in humanitarian  action.

Despite multiple and competing  crisis, UNICEF Madagascar succeeded in maintaining a very good level of  resources to support programme implementation, securing USD134 million for  the new Country Programme by December 2024 in flexible ORR funding (Other Resources),  representing 55.8 percent of the total ORR funding needed for the country  programme cycle and USD 21 million for emergency ORE funding.

Under the health component, UNICEF  established a productive working relationship with the First Lady and her  office, who dedicated time and efforts to support immunization, and the  office of the President, which resulted in him declaring 2024 the “Year of  Immunization”. Through the Nutrition Cluster and the Scale-Up Nutrition  Network (SUN), a close partnership and continuous dialogue was maintained  with other UN agencies, governmental and non-governmental organizations  working in emergencies and multi-sector programming for nutrition. UNICEF  advanced nutrition resilience building through the two key joint UNICEF and  WFP projects funded by BMZ/KFW and Norway, and a wasting management and  prevention programme, funded by BHA/USAID. These joint partnerships are  instrumental to deliver results for the most vulnerable children across  multiple systems – food, health, water and sanitation, education, and social  protection.

In the area of WASH, engagement with the private sector was pivotal in scaling up sustainable sanitation services through market-based solutions and improving the management of multi-use water systems (MUS) to address the specific needs of communities and ensure sustainability. UNICEF’s partnership with the University of Antananarivo increased the Government’s capacity on groundwater data collection, borehole log classification, and pump test supervision to address bottlenecks on ground water drilling. The strategic engagement with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) enhanced the analysis and revision of water codes on the WASH Climate Change Platform. On climate change, a new partnership was established with the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, and UNICEF became the co-lead of the Partners’ Coordination Platform for Environment.

UNICEF actively worked with its dynamic network of youth ambassadors and advocates to raise the voices of Malagasy children and youth beyond the country. A new youth advocate for inclusion and people with albinism, Tianarivelo Gilardy Totozandry, was appointed; he made a statement during UNICEF Executive Board meeting in February and has been involved in other advocacy events. Others attended the UNGA and UNGA side-event with UNICEF Deputy Executive Director, Ted Chaiban, COP29 in Azerbaijan, and the African Unions Conference on Education held in Mauritania, among many other national and international initiatives. Media partnerships were sustained, including through training for journalists on various children-related topics. Under the agreement with the national broadcaster ORTM, 25 radio and two television  programmes on children’s rights were produced and aired.

UNICEF engagements with the Malagasy Catholic University, Youth groups and association such as AIKA, the Malagasy Scouts movements, the TAFAVORI youth platform allowed UNICEF to strengthen Social and Behaviour Change mechanisms and raise awareness on climate change actions.

The Today and Tomorrow Initiative (TTI), the world’s first integrated climate and disaster risk finance mechanism, gained national recognition in Madagascar through close collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD) and the National Office for Disaster Risk Management (BNGRC). At COP-29, the Minister of Environment co-hosted a high-profile event with UNICEF’s Deputy Executive Director, showcasing this innovative financing model. The government’s strong commitment to the twin-track approach was further championed through media engagements, international panel discussions, and global donor platforms like the UNICEF Next Gen Global Summit, enhancing visibility and attracting donor interest. In 2024, Today and Tomorrow Initiative delivered significant results in Madagascar, including $1.6 million in rapid payouts through the Tomorrow Component for cyclone response, supporting life-saving interventions like clean water restoration and school rehabilitations. As part of the Today component, Youth-led Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) clubs empowered 1,200 adolescents to lead preparedness efforts. Pre-positioned supplies and training enhanced community resilience and investments in disaster-resilient infrastructures.

Key lessons related to the Today and Tomorrow Initiative highlight the importance of flexible funding to shift from traditional emergency responses toward anticipatory actions, early recovery, and climate-resilient rehabilitation. Prioritizing integration of anticipatory measures into multi-sectoral frameworks and aligning efforts with national policies like Madagascar’s National Adaptation Plans further amplified the benefits of recovery. However, challenges such as limited funding for the Today Component restricting the scale of climate resilience and adaptation activities and the parametric insurance model focuses on cyclone, overlooking vulnerabilities to other hazards, such as severe droughts in the South and frequent flash floods linked to El Niño persists. Addressing multi-hazard risks, scaling youth-led resilience initiatives, and tackling systemic vulnerabilities are critical to fully realizing TTI’s potential.

In the area of social protection, a key lesson is the synergic effect of developing a joint work plan between the government on the one hand and key stakeholders, namely the Ministry of Population and Solidarity, the World Bank and WFP on the other hand, to ensure that partners activities are coordinated, avoid duplication, and are aligned to government social protection strategy. This has proved instrumental for securing long-term, scalable outcomes from UNICEF's investments. It ensures that actions initially implemented on a small scale, starting as a proof of concept, are eventually expanded at the national level by the Government, with support from the World Bank. This is especially the case for the social window which was initially piloted by UNICEF as a decentralized service of the Ministry of Population and Solidarity, and which is now the key entry point of the Unified Social Registry (USR) at the community level. The social window started as a proof of concept in UNICEF-targeted communes, the structure of which has been fully approved by the Government and integrated into the new National Social Protection Strategy (2024-2030) and is now being scaled up nationally.

The most significant innovation of the Management Information System (MIS) within the social window is its capacity to identify vulnerabilities and address them by facilitating referrals to social services. However, several challenges persist that require attention, such as the availability of social services at the community level and the interoperability with other sectoral MIS. Therefore, the next steps involve finalizing work on the interoperability between the social window information system and the nutrition MIS, as well as initiating this interoperability with the education MIS. Without these protocols, the effectiveness of the social registry in addressing vulnerabilities will not be fully maximized.

In 2024, Malawi faced significant challenges in realizing children’s rights despite modest progress toward the goals outlined in the Malawi National Development Plan, Vision 2063. Persistent poverty, climate vulnerabilities, and economic instability exacerbated existing inequalities, leaving children – especially those in rural and marginalized communities – disproportionately affected by malnutrition, limited access to education and inadequate health care. Malawi’s progress toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals was uneven in 2024. Significant gaps persisted in key areas such as SDG 2 (zero hunger), SDG 3 (good health and well-being) and SDG 4 (quality education). 

Malawi remains one of the poorest nations in the world, with poverty deeply entrenched in both urban and rural areas. According to the National Statistical Office, 51.7 per cent of the population lives below the poverty line, while 20.5 per cent live in extreme poverty. This stark reality is particularly severe for children (0-17 years), 70 per cent of whom experience multidimensional poverty. Malawi’s Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) stands at 0.316, with the average poor Malawian enduring more than half of the weighted deprivations assessed by the MPI. The Gini coefficient of 0.39 highlights persistent income inequality, with the wealthiest 20 per cent of households consuming nearly half of the country’s total resources. These disparities perpetuate cycles of deprivation and inequality, leaving children in the most vulnerable households at a significant disadvantage by comparison with other children.
Malawi’s health sector saw mixed progress in 2024. Efforts to improve maternal and child health services contributed to a modest decline in the under-five mortality rate. However, malnutrition has persisted as a critical issue, with approximately 35 per cent of children under the age of 5 years affected by stunting attributable to poor diets and 83 per cent of children under 5 years old consuming foods in fewer than the four recommended food groups per day. The level of wasting has doubled in 2024 compared to 2020, and admissions for treatment of severe wasting increased by 21 per cent in November 2024 compared to November 2023. These trends reflect the compounded impacts of poverty, food insecurity and limited access to quality health services. Public health emergencies further strained the healthcare system. A cholera outbreak affected 15 districts, with 452 cases and 14 deaths reported in 2024. Concurrently, Malawi faced rising measles cases, highlighting gaps in immunization coverage and disease surveillance. Disruptions in vaccine and essential medicine supply chains, driven by economic instability and global shortages, exacerbated these challenges.

Education continued to face challenges despite improvements in primary school enrolment. Retention rates, particularly among adolescent girls, remained low due to early pregnancies and child marriages, both exacerbated by economic hardships. In 2024, 42 per cent of girls aged 15-19 years were married, and 29 per cent had experienced early pregnancies, leading to high rates of school dropout. Educational quality was affected by overcrowded classrooms, insufficient teaching materials and a severe shortage of trained teachers, particularly in rural areas, where pupil-to-teacher ratios often exceeded 120:1. These barriers limited children’s potential and perpetuated cycles of poverty and inequality.

Violence against children remained a pressing issue, with high rates of violence and exploitation reported across the country. Over 140,000 of children reported to have experienced violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect from 19 districts of Malawi in 2024. Economic pressures led to increased incidences of child labour, particularly in rural areas, where children were often engaged in agriculture or informal sectors. Efforts to strengthen child protection systems showed promise but lacked the scale and resources necessary to meet the growing demand for support and services.

The El Niño weather pattern in 2023-2024 had profound implications for Malawi, compounding food insecurity and economic instability. Prolonged droughts disrupted agricultural production, resulting in a 15 per cent reduction in crop yields in 2024 compared to 2023. Over 5.7 million people faced acute food insecurity and required humanitarian assistance. These adverse conditions not only widened existing nutrition gaps but also disproportionately affected individuals with chronic illnesses such as HIV and tuberculosis, whose dietary needs were often unmet. The effects of El Niño underscored the urgent need to integrate climate resilience into Malawi’s development agenda.

Malawi’s economy faced significant challenges in 2024, marked by high inflation, currency depreciation and rising public debt. In December, the Ministry of Finance revised downward the country’s projected economic growth projection to 1.8 per cent from an earlier estimate of 2.3 per cent, reflecting the combined effects of erratic weather patterns, reduced agricultural output, and spillovers of this to other sectors. Inflation averaged 35.4 per cent in 2024, up from 33.3 per cent in 2023, mainly driven by soaring food prices. The Malawi kwacha (MWK) depreciation further eroded purchasing power, while foreign exchange shortages disrupted the availability of essential commodities such as fuel. Public debt rose by 15.9 per cent, reaching MWK 15.2 trillion (81 per cent of GDP) by mid-2024. The Government’s fiscal capacity was constrained by domestic revenue that was 8.2 per cent lower than expected in 2024; this limited social sector investments, affecting programmes addressing child rights and welfare.
The effects of climate change continued to strain Malawi’s social and economic systems. In 2024, the country experienced one of its worst droughts in a decade, significantly reducing food production and increasing reliance on humanitarian aid. Efforts to integrate climate resilience into national policies showed promise, emphasizing safeguarding children’s rights in the face of environmental challenges. However, implementation gaps persisted, limiting the effectiveness of these measures.

Despite these challenges, Malawi’s political environment remained relatively stable. The Government was committed to prioritizing child rights in policy discussions, but weak institutional capacity and governance challenges hindered further progress. Greater investment in systems strengthening and accountability is essential to bridge the gap between policy aspirations and on-the-ground realities.

In summary, 2024 was marked by deepening inequalities and persistent health, education, and child welfare challenges, compounded by climate shocks and economic instability. Some progress was achieved, but the scale of need remains substantial, which underscores the urgency of coordinated and sustained action to realize children’s rights and improve their well-being in Malawi.

Sustained progress was made towards achieving systematic and transformative health outcomes for children and women, ensuring no one is left behind. Notably, the proportion of children vaccinated with three doses of DTP-containing vaccines reached 91 per cent. This reflects progress in addressing bottlenecks related to vaccine access and availability. UNICEF contributions resulted in a 23 per cent increase in cold chain storage capacity – from 116,336 in 2023 to 141,271 litres in 2024. Routine immunization services were integrated into six rounds of polio supplementary immunization activities, while targeted, periodic intensification of routine immunization campaigns was conducted in low-performing areas. UNICEF provided logistical support to outreach teams serving 200 hard-to-reach communities, thus helping reduce inequities in immunization access. 

The percentage of HIV-exposed infants below the age of 2 months receiving virological tests increased from 79 per cent in 2023 to 93 per cent in 2024. This reflects tangible progress in reducing deprivations in early HIV diagnosis and treatment. UNICEF had a role in these achievements through its sustained advocacy for Malawi's triple elimination agenda (HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B), the capacity building for 29 district PMTCT focal points, and assistance in efforts to strengthen PMTCT data management through a mentorship programme in three districts that have a high HIV burden and are prone to emergencies. The proportion of women completing four or more antenatal care visits at clinics increased from 51 per cent in 2023 to 61 per cent in 2024, demonstrating progress in addressing maternal and newborn health bottlenecks.  

A SMART nutrition survey conducted in March 2024 revealed a doubling of children affected by wasting, from 2.2 per cent in 2020 to 4.4 per cent in 2024. Although this prevalence is still below the World Health Assembly target of keeping child wasting to less than 5 per cent, it represents a worrisome reversal of trends. UNICEF supported the screening of over 1.5 million children under the age of 5 years for wasting and nutrition oedema, resulting in the identification of 40,811 children (21,222 girls) with severe wasting. The children were admitted for treatment, representing 65 per cent coverage against an annual caseload of 62,567 children (32,535 girls). Performance management indicators for severe wasting and nutrition oedema were all within acceptable levels: 93 per cent of admitted children were cured (indicator: >75 per cent), 3.2 per cent defaulted on the treatment (indicator: <15 per cent), and 1.7 per cent did not survive (indicator: <15 per cent). Remarkable achievements were made in reducing the number of children with zero-dose immunization, resulting in a 52 per cent reduction; similar efforts are required to reduce the number of children with zero doses of vitamin A supplementation. In 2024, 44 per cent of children under the age of 5 (465,999 children, including 232,220 girls) received two vitamin A supplements.

Climate-resilient, solar-powered systems provided safe water to 197,000 people (including 51,220 women and 100,470 children), with 48,000 people reached through regular programming and 149,000 reached in emergencies. To help ensure the sustainability of water systems, UNICEF supported the training of 700 water point committee members. Community-led total sanitation has been a key strategy for WASH programming; 217 villages were declared open defecation-free in 2024, benefiting 54,250 people (including 14,105 women and 27,667 children). A total of 110,274 individuals gained access to basic sanitation through latrine upgrades, pit emptying and improved toilets, while 94,542 individuals gained access to handwashing facilities. UNICEF assisted in developing climate-resilient standards for WASH in schools, ensuring that WASH facilities are gender-segregated and disability-inclusive. Solar-powered reticulated water systems were installed in 69 rural healthcare facilities. UNICEF supported WASH cluster coordination to ensure effective action by government and non-governmental partners in emergencies. Some 1.41 million people were reached with emergency water supply through the distribution of chlorine and water purification chemicals and the construction of boreholes and solar-powered systems, while 551,489 individuals were engaged through emergency sanitation and hygiene promotion activities.

Despite limited fiscal space – compounded by emergencies and Malawi's weak institutional and systemic capacities – UNICEF contributed to substantial progress in children's learning, skills development, and protection in 2024. A key achievement was the primary-to-lower secondary school transition rate improvement, from 45.4 per cent in 2023 to 49.7 per cent in 2024. The gender parity index (GPI) for secondary education has also improved, from 0.97 in 2023 to 0.99 in 2024. This improved GPI is partly attributed to the scholarship programme for disadvantaged girls supported by UNICEF. The programme assisted some 9,293 girls across 276 secondary schools in 11 districts in the 2024/25 academic year, making UNICEF one of the largest scholarship providers in the country. It is complemented by UNICEF’s sector-wide support of girls’ education, including developing the National Girls' Education Strategy to be completed in 2025.

To address poor learning outcomes in the country, UNICEF made substantial investments in teacher training and support. These investments included the development of a national teacher mentorship programme that will now be brought to scale by the Ministry of Education in collaboration with all 11 teacher training colleges in the country and the strengthening of an electronic continuing professional development (e-CPD) platform, which is complementary to the mentorship programme and enables teachers to access learning materials and training remotely. E-CPD is part of Malawi's digital literacy agenda; as of 2024, nearly 50 per cent of primary school teachers had access to the platform, and 70 district and zonal education officials were trained to manage and support it. In addition, UNICEF provided schools with teaching and learning resources, including education kits, desks, other school furniture, and school bags for students. A total of 105 primary schools were fully furnished with desks, including 20,329 double-seater desks, which directly impacted the education of 81,316 learners (40,658 girls). Priority was given to schools serving as national Standard 8 examination centres and schools newly built after Cyclone Freddy (2023). Providing these resources helps create a more conducive teaching and learning environment, critical for improving student performance.  
 
The Government has committed to ensuring school readiness for every young child in Malawi by introducing pre-primary classes in all public primary schools by 2025. UNICEF contributed to the effort through its support for the Ministry of Education capacity-strengthening activities, planning and preparatory activities, including nationwide consultations and school mapping exercises, and developing a comprehensive pre-primary curriculum. UNICEF also supported an early childhood education (ECE) costing and financing study to determine the financial requirements for the pre-primary classes in public primary schools.
