To ensure continuity in early learning, UNICEF is fostering coordination between the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Gender, Community Development and Social Welfare and supporting improvements in Community-Based Childcare Centres to facilitate children's transition from non-formal early learning to formal schooling. From 2023 to 2024, Malawi recorded an 11 per cent increase in enrolment of children with special needs, reaching 215,224 learners (104,206 girls) in primary schools. UNICEF, working together with the Government and partners, drove this progress; UNICEF supported efforts to train 4,165 teachers (1,697 female) in inclusive teaching, enabling them to support diverse learners effectively and to screen children for special needs. Some 859 students (347 girls) were screened and provided assistive devices like hearing aids and wheelchairs; complex cases were referred for further assessment. UNICEF, jointly with the Ministry of Education, has supported the development of the Malawi Partnership Compact (2023-2027) through a Global Partnership for Education (GPE) system capacity grant. The compact was completed in 2024. It aims to enhance quality foundational teaching and learning for all girls and boys through three key outcomes: (1) improved inclusive school readiness, (2) inclusive foundational learning, and (3) stronger education system capaci
ty, governance, and accountability. 

UNICEF’s advocacy and support were instrumental in establishing the National Children’s Commission (NCC) and operationalizing its Secretariat. UNICEF supported the development of the NCC structure; assisted the Secretariat with its job description and provided office equipment; oriented commissioners and supported their oath-taking; helped develop the annual workplan; and raised awareness of the NCC nationwide. The NCC is a key milestone for child rights protection in Malawi. As a state party to the CRC, its establishment came shortly after the Malawi government submitted its periodical report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child in September 2024. UNICEF’s consistent efforts to raise awareness of the impact of violence and other harmful practices on children and women and of existing channels that people can use to report such violence has contributed to a threefold increase in the number of cases of violence against children reported through the child protection case-management model: 148,664 cases reported in 2024 vs. 49,900 in 2023. Efforts also revealed the need for a better coordinated and comprehensive child protection system in the country. The Malawi Government attended the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children in Bogotá, Colombia, during which it pledged to lead and support a periodic survey on violence against children that will bring new evidence on the magnitude of the issue and subsequently inform the development of the new National Child Protection Strategy in 2025-2028. UNICEF support to 3,519 Children’s Corners nationwide has allowed more than 1.5 million children aged 6 to 18 years to receive psychosocial support and other child protection services in 2024, an 82 per cent increase compared to 2023.

The Government approved a new National Social Protection Policy, which includes nutrition-sensitive and shock-sensitive approaches as priority components. Despite a constrained fiscal environment, the Social Cash Transfer Programme (SCTP) increased from 303,800 households in 2023 to 381,735 households in 2024 (reaching 1,717,807 people, including 738,657 children). It increased additional cash transfer support to 293,631 households impacted by economic and climate shocks (reaching 637,830 people, including 293,631 children). UNICEF influenced an increase of 59 per cent in the value of SCTP cash transfers. UNICEF advocacy and assistance also contributed to adopting a more inclusive, child-sensitive targeting approach to social protection and expanding gender-sensitive resilience activities from 2 to 10 districts, reaching 25,840 people in 2024.

UNICEF’s strategic budget advocacy, in collaboration with CSOs and Parliamentarians, has contributed to an increase in the proportion of total government spending on essential services from 29.3 per cent in 2023-2024 to 31.0 per cent in 2024-2025. Government spending on health, including WASH, increased from 10 per cent to 12.6 per cent, social protection spending increased from 3 per cent to 3.7 per cent, but education spending decreased from 15.9 per cent to 14.7 per cent. Furthermore, UNICEF successfully contributed to designing and launching the National Decentralization Policy to assist local government authorities and actors in better understanding child rights issues and translating knowledge into practice towards effective programmatic outcomes for children. UNICEF has also moved from generating evidence on child poverty to actively leveraging such evidence to shape national perspectives on child-inclusive programming (CIP) that holistically addresses children's multifaceted deprivations. This shift is cultivating a CIP mindset among ministries, departments and agencies while ensuring the integration of child poverty more broadly into public finance management and decentralized policies (district development plans and district implementation plans).

UNICEF’s emergency response in Malawi reached 5.7 million with integrated life-saving services. The beneficiaries include 2.8 million children below the age of 5 years, 66,054 primary-school-aged children, 67,000 adolescents, 340,048 pregnant and breastfeeding women. Strategic efforts bolstered preparedness through enhanced emergency systems, raised US$10 million for humanitarian action, and improved readiness among UNICEF staff for deployment in a crisis. The multi-year transformative partnership with the Malawi Red Cross Society is enhancing its ability to serve as a front-line emergency responder, equipping it with the tools, skills and structures needed to respond effectively to emergencies, deliver life-saving support on time, and improve its operations. By building strong skills and systems, this initiative shows how local organizations can be empowered to take the lead during crises. UNICEF had a key role in inter-agency emergency preparedness and response coordination; in 2024, it led WASH, nutrition, child protection and education cluster efforts and supported the Government’s El Niño Flash Appeal, which mobilized approximately US$24 million.

UNICEF has significantly contributed to operationalizing gender-transformative approaches to programming by both the Government and CSOs. UNICEF worked in partnership with the Ministry of Gender to develop strategic policy frameworks concerning gender, including the National Strategy on Ending Child Marriage, to bring a gender lens to review and planning meetings and conduct gender analyses in four targeted districts (Chikwawa, Nsanje, Mzimba North and Mzimba South) under the Social Protection for Gender Empowerment and Resilience (SP-GEAR) programme; to build Ministry staff capacity; and to create awareness of critical issues like gender-based violence, and in advocacy for gender equality. UNICEF partnered with the NGO Gender Coordination Network to increase awareness of gender-based violence (GBV) and sexual exploitation and abuse and to facilitate gender-transformative approaches in both general and emergency programming. UNICEF supported 30 women-led organizations (WLOs) in their gender-transformative programming and emergency response work, and 20 WLOs in resource mobilization and partnership strengthening. In collaboration with other United Nations agencies, UNICEF contributed to the production of key strategic documents, including a gender scorecard and an inter-agency plan for the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA). A total of 1,491,199 individuals (1,118,399 female) were trained in PSEA, GBV and risk mitigation, including 1,100,000 individuals trained through women’s guide gatherings, 390,218 front-line and community workers, 97 UNICEF staff and 330 implementing partner staff. UNICEF supported the work of five implementing partners in developing PSEA policies and designing PSEA information, education, and communication materials. UNICEF also developed a Gender Action Plan (2024-2028), established internal workflows for effective gender integration, reviewed gender mainstreaming guidelines for partnership agreements, and identified 1,457 gend
er champions who will work to address discriminatory norms and drive change at the community level. UNICEF also contributed to efforts to generate evidence on gender barriers to access to health and nutrition services as part of a gender bottleneck analysis informing gender-transformative programming. 

Over 10 million people were reached through community-based social and behaviour change (SBC) interventions in girls' education, nutrition, hygiene promotion, and immunization. SBC approaches and planning were based on evidence gathered at national and subnational levels, and the interventions themselves were contextualized and tailored for purpose, with the local engagement of school-based networks, care groups and community volunteers. Increased demand for measles and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine services, improved infant and young child feeding, and greater uptake of cholera prevention practices were observed. UNICEF supported coordination at district and national levels and capacity development on community engagement standards and interpersonal communication for district-based partners. This resulted in significant improvements in the quality of SBC interventions. A community engagement toolkit for front-line workers is now ready for field testing; the toolkit is a significant resource for promoting positive care practices at individual, family, and community levels. 
UNICEF established a solid foundation for scaling up innovation and digital transformation initiatives through strategy development, evidence generation and capacity building. The country office adopted its first Innovation and Technology for Development (T4D) strategy with a governance framework, finalized an evaluation of the Youth-led Innovation initiative (on the African Drone and Data Academy) for use in evidence-based programming, and supported government counterparts in system strengthening, through the development and implementation of national strategies and policies (e.g., National Digital Health Strategy and National Science and Technology Innovation Policy) and capacity building of government officials to accelerate digital innovation. UNICEF supported 11 innovation and digitalization initiatives, benefiting over 385,011 children. A key milestone was the institutionalization and scale-up of unmanned aerial vehicles for health supply chain strengthening, now operating in nine hard-to-reach districts of southern Malawi. The Ministry of Education accelerated its school digitalization initiative, benefiting a cumulative total of 18,400 students across 18 districts, with the support of Airtel Malawi, and sought innovative financing solutions for school connectivity with the Association of Internet Service Providers and the Universal Service Fund, through the GIGA initiative. In collaboration with the UNICEF Adolescent Advisory Board, a new youth-led innovation initiative focusing on climate education and green entrepreneurship was launched, benefiting marginalized children from six flood-prone districts. 

Malawi’s development agenda is driven by Malawi 2063, a vision for the future that is being implemented in phases, beginning with the Malawi Implementation Plan for 2021-2030 (MIP-1). UNICEF played a crucial role in engaging children in this vision by supporting the Malawi 2063 comic books initiative, launched in September 2024. The comic books were developed in six local languages and, to date, have reached 96,000 children (49,920 girls), enhancing their understanding and involvement in the national development plan. UNICEF participated with United Nations agencies in joint work planning under the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), the Common Budgetary Framework (CBF), and the Results Framework for 2024 and the entire UNSDCF period (2024-2028). UNICEF used guidance from the United Nations Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning Group to ensure that these frameworks supported UNICEF's new country programme in Malawi (2024-2028) and that collective efforts by the United Nations system in Malawi aligned with national efforts to achieve Malawi 2063, MIP-1, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the African Union's Agenda 2063. UNICEF leads UNSDCF Strategic Priority Area 3 – on ensuring sustainable investments and outcomes in human capital development – and, by doing so, is helping to ensure that interventions promoting the realization of child rights and child-related outcomes are integrated across all strategic priorities. 

UNICEF contributed to strengthening national evaluation systems and building a culture of evaluation in Malawi through its support of the capacity building of 28 government M&E officials, the launch of a new M&E policy, and the development of a national evaluation plan. The M&E policy advocates for more systematic evaluations of the Malawi public-sector programmes and policies, including those directly affecting children's well-being. The national evaluation plan, therefore, covers several programmes and projects: the Malawi Education Reform Project, the School Feeding Programme, the Investing in Early Years for Growth and Productivity Project, the Social Cash Transfer Programme, the Health Systems Immunization Strengthening Grant, and the Cold Chain Equipment Optimization Programme. The planned evaluations will provide learning on how these programmes and projects have addressed the multiple deprivations facing children throughout the life cycle, from childhood to youth, and will help establish accountabilities. Also, UNICEF empowered young researchers from the Malawi University of Science and Technology to design evidence-based solutions to common challenges. The intervention enhanced the researchers' critical thinking and problem-solving skills and abilities, equipping them to address such pressing issues as menstrual hygiene management and sanitation. As a result, 14 innovative, research-based proposals were developed involving 48 participants.
  
UNICEF has strategically deepened partnerships with key stakeholders to drive impactful outcomes for children in Malawi. UNICEF organized six field missions for donors and potential donors, providing them with first-hand insights into the tangible results of their contributions. UNICEF also convened a high-level roundtable with national representatives to examine the challenges facing children in Malawi within the broader global context. UNICEF enhanced its communication strategy to amplify its influence, adopting a more targeted approach to engage diverse audiences effectively.

In 2024, UNICEF made strides in advancing key developmental goals through strategic partnerships, government leadership and multisectoral collaboration. A key success was the Government’s leadership in adapting and endorsing the latest WHO guidelines on preventing and managing wasting. A robust nutrition workforce supported by UNICEF, consisting of a senior nutrition officer in each of the 28 districts, supported by three officers per district, leads the implementation of nutrition interventions per the country’s minimal staffing requirement. Academia contributed significant evidence of the nutrition situation, with Lilongwe University of Agriculture and Natural Resources and UNICEF conducting the eighth round of nutrition SMART surveys in March 2024. Financial support from UNICEF, the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), the United Nations Office for the Coordination for Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the World Food Programme (WFP) further strengthened these efforts. CSOs, including the Farmers Union of Malawi and The Hunger Project, played pivotal roles in programme implementation, reflecting a unified approach to combating malnutrition.

In the health sector, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Health, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the World Health Organization (WHO) and local organizations to improve access to HIV prevention services for adolescent girls and young women. The partnership also supported enhanced virological testing for HIV-exposed infants. The experience of scaling up maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) initiatives in 60 health facilities across six districts demonstrated the impact of multi-stakeholder engagement in addressing health disparities. Resilient WASH programmes benefited from strengthened partnerships with FCDO, USAID and others. Climate risk analyses produced in collaboration with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) have enabled targeted responses to climate-related challenges. CSOs such as Canadian Physicians for Aid and Relief (CPAR), Oxfam and Self-Help Africa were instrumental in implementing emergency WASH interventions. Supply contributions from the Government of Canada supported emergency responses, reaching over two million people. Partnerships with private-sector entities advanced safe water access and improved faecal sludge management, enhancing overall programme efficiency and sustainability.
To improve learning outcomes, UNICEF fostered partnerships under the Ministry of Education’s leadership. The Partnership Compact on Foundational Learning secured nearly US$100 million in Global Partnership for Education (GPE) funding, aligning stakeholders around a common agenda. As the 2024 Education Development Partners Group (EDPG) chair and Coordinating Agent for GPE programmes, UNICEF played a central role in strengthening education systems. Digital learning initiatives, such as the Connect-a-School programme with Airtel Malawi, connected nine additional schools to the internet in 2024, benefiting 6,715 learners (49 per cent girls) and 268 teachers (35 per cent female). With 18 schools connected since 2023, the initiative has had a cumulative reach of 15,500 learners and 503 teachers, promoting equitable access to digital education.

UNICEF's partnership with the National Children’s Commission reinforced institutional oversight for advancing child rights in Malawi. Collaborations with the Ministry of Gender, the Malawi Police Service, and the judiciary expanded child protection services, especially for children affected by emergencies. Post-Cyclone Freddy and El Niño interventions, backed by donors like the Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance and UNICEF Swedish and Spanish National Committees, reached 600,000 children and caregivers with mental health support, case management, and community policing services.

On social protection, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Gender to enhance the Social Cash Transfer Programme (SCTP). Financial support from the European Union and the Government of Ireland under the Social Protection for Gender Empowerment and Resilience (SP-GEAR) programme addressed humanitarian needs during the lean season. KfW (the German Development Bank) funded SCTP evaluations. At the same time, GIZ (the German Development Agency) collaborated with UNICEF to strengthen institutional capacity within the Ministry of Finance’s Poverty Reduction and Social Protection Department. These initiatives underscored UNICEF’s role as a technical and strategic leader in the social protection space.

Emergency preparedness was bolstered through partnerships with the Department of Disaster Management Affairs (DoDMA), the Malawi Red Cross Society and United Nations agencies, including OCHA and WFP. UNICEF helped ensure rapid and scalable disaster responses by signing 12 new contingency programme documents in 2024. Also, UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Health and CSOs to design community engagement toolkits for health workers, enhancing immunization outreach in hard-to-reach areas. Collaborative efforts with John Snow, Inc (JSI), Program for Appropriate Technology in Health (PATH) and WHO supported risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) responses to cholera and measles outbreaks.

UNICEF also prioritized innovation and digitalization activities. Collaboration with the Ministry of Education and internet service providers piloted a connectivity credit mechanism to expand school connectivity. The Rapid Drone Response Unit, developed with DoDMA and the Malawi University of Science and Technology, institutionalized disaster response mechanisms, highlighting the integration of technology into emergency preparedness.

Efforts to strengthen evidence generation saw continued partnerships with the National Statistical Office, the National Planning Commission, and the University of Malawi. UNICEF supported the implementation of key surveys, including the Malawi Demographic Health Survey (M-DHS) and nutrition SMART surveys, ensuring data availability to inform child-centred policies. High-level engagement with the Ministry of Finance advanced child-sensitive budgeting, safeguarding social sector investments despite fiscal challenges. The dissemination of findings from an analysis of child poverty and vulnerability highlighted areas for targeted intervention, reaffirming government ownership of these initiatives.

Strategic partnerships with media, content creators and development partners amplified UNICEF’s impact. Collaboration with academia fostered capacity building, while new partnerships with civil society groups utilized human-centred design approaches to address behavioural and social drivers in hard-to-reach communities. These efforts contributed to a stronger enabling environment for evidence-based decision-making and resource mobilization.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Coordinating Malawi's nutrition sector entails persistent challenges due to its multisectoral nature and diverse delivery platforms. Forums such as the school health and feeding coordination groups are active, but discussions often focus narrowly on school feeding rather than on nutrition initiatives more comprehensively. Other coordination bodies, like those addressing maternal, infant, and young child nutrition and micronutrients, convene infrequently. Food insecurity remains a significant barrier to children’s attendance at Community-Based Childcare Centres (CBCCs). UNICEF works with partners to link CBCCs with care groups for integrated household farming and livelihood initiatives, building community resilience. Despite these efforts, challenges persist with inadequate infrastructure, insufficient caregiver capacity and limited access to play materials at the centres, demanding collective solutions. A comprehensive CBCC assessment commissioned in December 2024 aims to identify systemic gaps and strengthen early childhood development (ECD) services.
Limited availability and misaligned priorities hinder stakeholder engagement in health service delivery. District-level planning is complicated by partner representatives’ lack of decision-making authority, requiring national-level approval. Collaboration among partners on the triple elimination agenda has contributed to improved coverage of early infant diagnosis (EID), but funding constraints threaten progress toward ending HIV by 2030. Adolescent health investments remain insufficient, contributing to high rates of adolescent pregnancy and maternal and neonatal mortality. Addressing these issues requires a holistic approach, including health systems strengthening and cross-sector linkages. UNICEF has supported high-level dialogues, operationalized technical working groups and scaled up primary healthcare programmes targeting adolescents with tailored interventions.

In 2024, WASH construction projects in emergencies faced delays due to short timeframes, underscoring the need for streamlined processes. Implementing climate-resilient solar water systems revealed the importance of integrating climate considerations into infrastructure design. A comprehensive WASH climate rationale was developed to identify vulnerabilities, assess risks, and propose mitigation strategies. These findings are now integrated into WASH interventions to ensure climate resilience. However, capacity gaps at the district level hinder effective WASH project management. UNICEF is enhancing district personnel’s technical supervision and monitoring capabilities, supporting the development of district WASH investment plans, and addressing groundwater risks through advanced data analysis. Innovative approaches, such as 'pay-as-you-fetch' water systems and partnerships with insurance companies for maintenance, are being explored to ensure cost-effective service delivery.

Education sector funding has grown significantly over the past decade, with the budget increasing from MWK 92.4 billion in 2012-2013 to MWK 548.7 billion in 2022-2023. However, funding gaps persist, particularly in non-salary recurrent expenditures vital for quality improvements, such as teacher training and infrastructure development. Internal inefficiencies in fund utilization remain a concern. To address these issues, UNICEF supports cost-benefit analyses, resource optimization, evidence-based advocacy for increased domestic funding, and strengthened budget tracking. Despite a revised coordination structure, there is a need for better alignment of education financing, including foreign aid. Participation in the Education Services Joint Fund (ESJF) has declined, prompting an independent review to enhance its effectiveness. Efforts are underway to attract additional development partners to the funding platform, while the GPE-Malawi Partnership Compact, prioritizing inclusive foundational learning, has mobilized US$100 million to address learning poverty.

Violence against children persists despite ongoing efforts to prevent it. Many children face multiple violations, necessitating a multidimensional response. Holistic, child-centred case management systems and stronger coordination among social welfare, health, education, and law enforcement sectors are critical. Investment in mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) must be prioritized. The social service workforce is overstretched, with increasing case backlogs. Scaling up the number of trained and certified social workers, leveraging community-based volunteers and strengthening support mechanisms are essential to meet the growing demand for social services. Community policing structures have proven effective in addressing violence against children and should be integrated into national child protection frameworks.
Barriers to birth registration include fees and a lack of clarity about the role of health workers. Eliminating registration fees and embedding responsibilities within health worker job descriptions can significantly improve registration rates. Strengthening digital civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems and linking birth registration to social protection benefits can further enhance access. District-level CRVS coordination mechanisms have proven effective, facilitating collaboration among health, education, and social welfare departments.

Malawi’s macro-fiscal challenges – including unsustainable debt, foreign exchange shortages and inflation – threaten social-sector investments. General elections upcoming in September 2025 could exacerbate these issues by diverting funds. UNICEF’s advocacy efforts focus on protecting social-sector spending and mobilizing resources. Strategic partnerships with the Government and CSOs have driven reforms and secured funding for inclusive social protection systems. Evaluations of programmes like the SCTP have led to improved designs and expanded coverage for vulnerable populations.

Humanitarian response effectiveness is hampered by suboptimal data reporting on cross-cutting issues such as sexual exploitation and abuse, and disability. Weak data collection mechanisms at the district level hinder real-time programme adjustments. Delays in fund transfers for contingency programme documents have exposed gaps in activation processes. UNICEF has invested in training district-level disaster management staff and is addressing inconsistencies in content delivery and participant engagement. Plans for 2025 include streamlining activation procedures and enhancing reporting capacity to improve emergency response efficiency. 
Emergency preparedness in Malawi is limited, leaving communities vulnerable during crises. Therefore, it is essential to develop school, community, and district-level emergency plans, pre-position supplies, and train stakeholders in disaster risk reduction. UNICEF’s initiatives in the Chikwawa, Mulanje, Nkhotakota, and Nsanje districts have produced emergency preparedness plans, but these efforts need to be brought to a national scale. Strengthening coordination and knowledge-sharing across districts can foster cohesive disaster management strategies and ensure equitable responses.

Malawi lacks a national innovation policy, leading to fragmented efforts and hindering digitalization initiatives. UNICEF supports the Government in developing such a policy and strengthening systemwide approaches to innovation. Capacity building for government officials and the creation of child-focused strategies are key priorities.
Deficiencies in SBC strategic capacity among partners affect the quality and pace of interventions. UNICEF’s investment in SBC training has enhanced behaviour analysis and programming, emphasizing tailored responses based on evidence. Social listening through community volunteers and online platforms has effectively monitored misinformation and gathered feedback on key issues like Mpox, HPV and PSEA.

The high cost of media monitoring limits the evaluation of communication campaigns' reach. UNICEF will address this challenge by exploring collaborative solutions with other organizations. Additionally, delays in materials production due to a limited number of local suppliers offering good quality work must be mitigated to ensure timely dissemination of communication resources.

Namibia, an upper-middle-income country, is characterized by a predominantly youthful population, with 55% under the age of 25 and 43% under 18. However, this demographic advantage is overshadowed by significant challenges. Namibia ranks as the second most unequal country globally, following South Africa. Over 63% of children experience multidimensional poverty, while youth unemployment remains alarmingly high, reaching up to 50% in some regions. Many adolescents are left without access to education, training, or employment opportunities. Young girls face disproportionately high rates of new HIV infections, reflecting serious public health concerns.
Sanitation access is inadequate, with 46% of households lacking proper toilets, which increases health risks. The ongoing drought in Southern Africa has worsened malnutrition and food insecurity, with 30% of children affected by stunting due to poor feeding practices, as highlighted by SMART surveys. Neonatal mortality rates remain a concern, at 20 per 1,000 live births, underscoring the pressing need for improved health interventions.
The economic outlook presents mixed trends. GDP growth slowed to 3.5% in 2024, down from 4.2% in 2023, largely due to subdued global demand and drought conditions. However, growth is expected to rebound to 4.0% in 2025, supported by improved global conditions, domestic policy measures, and better agricultural output following increased rainfall. Despite these projections, economic growth remains below pre-2016 levels and National Development Plan (NDP) 5 targets, falling short of recovering fully from the COVID-19 pandemic or achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for children. Inflation, however, declined to 4.3% in 2024, improving household purchasing power and contributing to better outcomes for children.
Government revenue performance improved by 11.5% in 2024/25, reaching an average of 29.9% of GDP over the medium term. This growth supports sustained investments in child-related social sectors. Nevertheless, budgetary constraints continue to limit progress for the most vulnerable children.
In this challenging environment, UNICEF Namibia Country Office (NCO) worked to ensure that every child thrives, learns, and participates meaningfully in society, aligning its efforts with global and national priorities. Significant achievements in 2024 included a school enrollment rate of 97.8% for Grades 1–10, an increase in vaccination coverage from below 50% to 62% during a measles outbreak, improved hospital quality scores rising from 56% in 2022 to 74% in 2024, and over 80% birth registration rates. Consistent with UNICEF’s advocacy to protect social sector spending, the government allocated 50.7% of the 2024/25 budget to social sectors, including 23% for education, 14% for health, and 12% for social protection.
Namibia played a critical role on the global stage as a co-facilitator of the United Nations Summit of the Future in 2024, alongside Germany. The summit aimed to address pressing global challenges such as climate change, inequality, and sustainable development, culminating in the adoption of the "Pact for the Future," an action-oriented agreement with chapters on sustainable development, international peace and security, science and technology, youth and future generations, and transforming global governance. 
Namibia's active involvement reinforced its commitment to international cooperation and sustainable solutions.
Adding to this, the UN Assistant Secretary-General visited Namibia in July 2024 to assess the impact of the worsening drought, a direct consequence of climate change. During her visit to the Omaheke region, a malnutrition hotspot, she observed firsthand the severe implications of prolonged droughts on the country's children, including increased malnutrition, disrupted education, and heightened vulnerability to diseases. UN ASG emphasized the urgent need for immediate aid, stating, "Aid must be scaled up immediately." This high-level visit underscored the necessity for global and regional collaboration to address the climate crisis, particularly its disproportionate effects on children and marginalized communities. Recommendations stemming from the visit emphasized enhanced climate-resilient policies, investments in water and food security, and targeted interventions to protect children from the cascading effects of environmental shocks. 
Despite these accomplishments and Namibia's role on the international stage, challenges remain in public financial management and translation of policies to practice for children. Key sectors such as nutrition, Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), Early Childhood Development (ECD), and pre-primary education continue to be underfunded. Public debt, which reached N$165.8 billion (60.1% of GDP) in 2024, far exceeds the government’s 35% debt sustainability threshold. Debt servicing, totaling N$12.8 billion in 2024/25, surpassed the N$10 billion allocated to the Ministry of Health and Social Services, limiting essential social investments.
Namibia maintained political stability throughout 2024, with peaceful elections resulting in the historic election of the country’s first female president. This milestone reflects progress toward gender equality and presents new opportunities to advance child-centered development initiatives.
While Namibia has made significant strides in child development, learning, and youth participation, addressing persistent inequalities, improving health outcomes, and promoting inclusive growth remain critical. Sustained investments, targeted policy reforms, and accelerated efforts are essential to build a resilient, equitable, and child-focused future, ensuring no child is left behind.

UNICEF’s strategic support to the Government of Namibia delivered tangible results in health, education, evidence generation, monitoring and evaluations and public financial management, driving impactful reforms to improve outcomes for children. UNICEF Namibia Country Office (NCO) has played a pivotal role in strengthening Namibia’s statistical and evaluation systems through financial and technical support. A key achievement was the publication of Namibia’s 4th Population and Housing Census, incorporating advanced methodologies to improve the measurement of functional disabilities and provide insights into youth engagement. This milestone addressed critical data gaps, strengthening Namibia’s ability to monitor and evaluate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals. Namibia’s 4th Voluntary National Report further exemplified its commitment to regular monitoring of key development indicators. Through partnerships with line ministries, NCO supported the production of critical statistical reports through administrative system such as Education Management Information System and enhanced national capacities for effective evaluation planning in the National Development Plan (NDP6). In addition, timely evaluations such as the UPSHIFT and Early Childhood Development programs paved the way for improved programmatic outcomes especially in new Country Programme 2025-2029, which was approved in September 2024. 
UNICEF’s advocacy in public financial management has yielded significant outcomes. Namibia’s Budget Transparency score improved markedly from 42 in 2021 to 54 in 2023, while citizen participation in budgeting increased from zero to 20 out of 100. reflecting a move toward inclusivity and accountability in budgeting processes. NCO’s sustained efforts also led to prioritizing social sector spending, resulting in substantial investments in school infrastructure (N$790 million). resulting in the construction of approximately 1,552 fully furnished classrooms. and significantly enhancing access to quality education, particularly in underserved areas.
In the health sector, UNICEF supported reforms in health procurement that achieved efficiency savings of N$135 million, enabling reinvestments to expand healthcare access and improve service quality for children and families. At full implementation, the reforms are projected to generate over N$3 billion in savings over three years, accelerating progress toward Universal Health Coverage. By the end of 2024, Namibia was on track to meet the Abuja Declaration target of allocating 15% of the national budget to health. Capacity-building initiatives in partnership with Namibia University enhanced service delivery in maternal, newborn, and child health, nutrition, HIV/AIDS, and WASH, while partnerships with academic institutions strengthened professional training in critical areas. While gaps in HIV data collection remain, progress is evident. Approximately 8,060 children received critical services such as nevirapine prophylaxis and cotrimoxazole, achieving 85% coverage among children aged 6 to 8 weeks. HIV testing compliance reached 92.1%, demonstrating strong adherence to protocols. Notably, the targeted reduction in HIV positivity rates among exposed newborns from 2.5% to 1% was achieved. However, recent data indicates a rise in positivity rates from 2.38% to 3.2%, prompting a pause in publishing PMTCT data due to concerns about data quality.
NCO’s efforts in climate and gender sensitive WASH have led to notable progress. The implementation of the Community-Led Total Sanitation program reduced open defecation from 52% in 2019 to 40% in 2024. In response to a prolonged drought, UNICEF mobilized substantial funding for water purification and infrastructure upgrades, benefiting thousands of residents. Additional funding supported health and nutrition interventions in drought-affected regions, while partnerships with bilateral donors emphasized resilience-building and sustainable development. To address under-five mortality linked to unsafe water and sanitation, NCO partnered with the Namibia University of Science and Technology (NUST) and the Ministry of Environment, Tourism, and Forestry to develop a climate change strategy. This new initiative integrates the voices of vulnerable populations into national climate dialogues, aligning with UNICEF’s commitment to sustainable development and resilience building while engaging with young people from NUST to ensure voices and perspectives of children are reflected throughout the process. 
Given high malnutrition rates of children in Namibia, it is critical for NCO to enhance national capacity to improve food systems for children (FS4C) built on evidence, research, advocacy, and partnership. Throughout 2024, NCO worked closely with the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) and MHSS in the development of national SBC strategy for nutrition to improve the quality of children’s food and practices. Namibia is in the process of approving the Food Safety Bill by the parliament. The bill provides the establishment of a food safety council that will be an accountability structure for food system in the country and embraces the multisystem approach for nutrition, where NCO will continuously support national efforts. 
Education remains a cornerstone of Namibia’s development agenda, with 23% of the national budget consistently allocated to basic education since independence. However, challenges persist in achieving desired learning outcomes. UNICEF has supported the government in increasing the budget allocation to pre-primary education, reaching 4.4% and advancing foundational learning initiatives. Budget increase demonstrates a strengthened commitment to early childhood education, with a target to achieve 10% by 2030. NCO worked in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, Arts, and Culture (MEAC) to host Namibia’s first national Foundational Learning stakeholder workshop, scaling literacy programs, and mapping schools for digital connectivity. Additionally, the Jolly Phonics literacy program was scaled nationwide, benefiting Grade 1 and Grade 2 learners, and marking a critical milestone in advancing early literacy. Through the GiGa project, all schools in Namibia were mapped for connectivity, paving the way for integrating digital technology into education by 2025, in alignment with national digital education goals. Consultations on the Professional Teachers Bill and Disability Costing were also successfully concluded, focusing on professionalizing the teaching workforce and adopting a needs-based approach to disability social protection.
Significant progress was made in child protection with the approval of the Child Justice Bill and the government’s commitment to legislation combating Sexual Exploitation and Abuse, providing comprehensive protections for children online and offline. Namibia reaffirmed its global commitments to child protection by signing the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange Declaration for Action and pledging to end violence against children at international summits. In 2024, the Mass Registration Campaign resulted in 31,135 additional birth registrations nationwide, enhancing children’s access to legal identity. NCO also strengthened the availability of child protection data by building the capacity of Lifeline ChildLine and the Ministry of Gender Equality, Poverty Eradication, and Social Welfare (MGEPESW) to produce draft administrative data reports. NCO deepened its partnership with the Ministry of Sports, Youth, and National Service, prioritizing systems-level support for adolescent development. The Skills4Girls initiative played a pivotal role, targeting vulnerable adolescents—90% of whom were out-of-school, pregnant, breastfeeding, or parenting. The program equipped participants with life skills, digital and financial literacy, and HIV knowledge, with 83% demonstrating improved competencies and 93% gaining a stronger understanding of HIV prevention. The rollout of the Adolescent and Young People Meaningful Participation Toolkit across four regions further institutionalized adolescent participation. Additionally, the launch of the Namibia Learning Passport provided young people with online skills development opportunities, fostering greater accessibility and inclusivity in learning.
UNICEF’s multi-faceted interventions across health, education, WASH, child protection, and adolescent development have underscored its commitment to creating an inclusive and empowered future for Namibia’s children and young people. By addressing systemic challenges and fostering innovative partnerships, these efforts contribute significantly to the nation’s progress toward sustainable development goals.

As outlined in the Strategic Plan, NCO places strong emphasize on   fostering shared value partnerships with government, civil societies, the UN, development partners, the private sectors, academia, among others. At the national level, NCO is a trusted partner of the government and able to influence the agenda.  At the same time NCO is working closely with local government and NGOs to model various proof of concept, designed to address and showcase successes through seed funding. Where these local initiatives and approaches prove to be successful, NCO provides technical support to accompany the government in rolling out these interventions and approaches to a national scale. 
Within the UN family, NCO is uniquely positioned to provide strategic technical input, leading Social Transformation Pillar as a Chair, advancing the SDG agenda and in implementing the United Nations Partnership Framework (UNPAF) through the UN Country Team, as well as contributing to the successful elaboration of United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025-2029. To mitigate climate change effects on the child rights agenda and greater efficiency for the use of resources, NCO also made the necessary adjustments to Programme through more joint programming and collaborations with other UN agencies for better coordination and synergies as required in operation modalities in an upper-middle income context.
Promoting the South -South Corporation, the 2024 World Children’s Day regional event in Zimbabwe, was held from 15-17 November, bringing together over 500 children from seven countries, including Namibia, for a powerful celebration of inclusive education and child rights. The highlight and the outcome of the event is the “Call of Action”, presented by the children to their governments, underscoring barriers to learning while pledging to be active participants in driving changes by taking their ownership. The gathering concluded with Botswana committing to host the event in 2025.
Throughout the year 2024, the NCO extended its partnerships by engaging the academia, creating opportunities to use data and evidence to address widening inequities and climate change challenges. These efforts resulted in a tripartite partnership with the MGEPECW and the University of Namibia (UNAM) that created a Joint Child Research Initiative and Training Hub situated in UNAM, as well as partnership with relevant departments to train health care providers, and climate change action with NUST.
The on-going strong partnership between NCO and National Assembly led to the hosting of the 6th Session of the Children’s Parliament, under the theme “Transforming Education in Namibia” from the 12-19 July 2024.   Sixty-four (64) members, representing all 14 regions of Namibia, including six indigenous minorities and children with disabilities, participated successfully.  During the session, 33 motions were tabled, with 30 adopted. Through these motions, children prioritized Violence Against Children (VAC) and climate change, calling for the country to declare a state of emergency on VAC, and ensure transparency and accountability in drought relief efforts to benefit the most vulnerable members of the society.
Laying the foundation for a longer-term approach to ensuring children's rights, the NCO supported the MGEPESW to conduct and submit the Country Report on the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). The report highlighted Namibia’s progress and challenges in implementing the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which provides opportunities for NCO in 2025 and beyond through policy advocacy and legislative support, data-driven interventions, climate and disaster resilience, inclusive social sectors and services, participation and empowerment of young people including children. By addressing these opportunities built on enhanced partnership with a wide range of stakeholders, NCO can continue to play a pivotal role in advancing child rights, improving service delivery, and ensuring no child is left behind.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Throughout the year, the Namibia Country Office (NCO) faced significant challenges that influenced program delivery and outcomes. Apart from on-going drought, one major issue was the frequent changes in technical staff within key institutions. These transitions, coupled with ineffective handover processes, a limited number of personnel, and competing national priorities, delayed implementation timelines and resource utilization. The impact of national elections further added to these delays, complicating the operational environment.
Another pressing concern was the unpredictability of sustained funding, which created barriers to planning and scaling long-term projects. Even initiatives with proven success were affected, highlighting the need for more stable financing mechanisms to support sustained impact. Additionally, systemic challenges such as high education dropout rates, violence against children, and alarmingly high youth unemployment contributed to a fragmented ecosystem, leaving many vulnerable children and youth without adequate opportunities.
The recurring droughts and lack of comprehensive resilience-building strategies exacerbated the situation. These environmental and social shocks limited the effectiveness of child-focused interventions, underscoring the necessity for a proactive and coordinated approach to crisis preparedness.
Despite these challenges, valuable lessons were learned during the year. An innovative brokering approach introduced to strengthen procurement efficiency between the Ministry of Finance and the MHSS proved highly effective. This model emphasized co-creation and ownership, supported by the placement of a dedicated project manager (long-term international consultant) within the ministries to ensure timely access to critical information and agile decision-making. The success of this approach has inspired the government to explore its application in other sector where day-to-day technical support are required to driver policy changes and support translation of the policy into actual practices and impact for the children. 
Partnerships with academic institutions also demonstrated their importance, through UNAM and NUST, across the areas of Child Protection, Climate Change, Public Health, among others. For example, capacity-building workshops equipped nearly 300 final-year nursing and midwifery students with life-saving skills, fostering greater ownership within the education system and enhancing program delivery. 
Looking forward, the NCO aims to integrate resilience-building strategies into its upcoming Country Programme (2025–2029). This will focus on enhancing preparedness for crises, emergencies, and disasters to ensure the sustainability of child rights advancements. Efforts will also be directed at addressing funding unpredictability through diversified partnerships and innovative financing mechanisms, while scaling successful initiatives, such as procurement reforms and newborn care training, to a national level.
Effective communication and advocacy for children’s rights require substantial investments of time, financial, and human resources. The limited availability of these resources has hindered the NCO’s ability to expand its outreach, monitor changing environments, and adjust strategies accordingly. However, the upcoming Country Programme (2025–2029) presents an opportunity to implement integrated programming and strengthen advocacy efforts to address these challenges effectively. Collaborations with stakeholders to advance climate adaptation strategies will also be essential, ensuring that programs are adaptable to environmental changes and resilient to future shocks.
By leveraging these insights and lessons learned, NCO is committed to achieving impactful and sustainable outcomes for the country’s most marginalized children together with a wide range of stakeholders within and outside of the country.

The situation for children in Mozambique deteriorated in 2024, exacerbated by multiple and simultaneous crises, including drought, cyclones, conflict in the north, disease outbreaks, displacement, political unrest and the effects of the 2022 fiscal shock. Despite fiscal consolidation efforts, nearly 90 per cent of tax revenues over 2021-2023 were consumed by the wage bill, debt service and pensions. In 2024, the growing wage bill and public debt risks further strained the government’s finances, leading to increased borrowing costs and significant arrears. This fiscal crisis compounds the effects of a decade of various shocks, including the ongoing conflict in Cabo Delgado province. 
 
Between 2015 and 2020, national monetary poverty increased from 48 to 63 per cent, and multidimensional poverty increased from 71 to 78 per cent, according to the latest available data. Poverty remains concentrated in the northern provinces, including Nampula, Cabo Delgado and Zambezia, which account for 60 per cent of the country's poor population. Poverty was primarily driven by the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, the hidden debt crisis, and inflation due to the devaluation of the metical. 
 
The political environment has changed since the general elections in October 2024. The subsequent period was marked by unprecedented and increasingly tense civil unrest across the country, as anti-government demonstrators protested against the election results and subsequent violence and looting in many parts of the country continued through the end of the year and into January 2025.
 
In 2024, an estimated 4.8 million people, including 3.4 million children, needed humanitarian assistance and protection. Mozambique remains highly vulnerable and inadequately prepared to adapt to climate risks which are projected to become increasingly severe. In 2024, Mozambique faced the devastating impacts of Tropical Storm Filipo, Cyclone Chido, and damaging storms whose strong winds and heavy rains affected 604,389 people, and destroyed or damaged 104,403 homes, 537 schools and 127 health facilities. Furthermore, the 2023-2024 El Niño conditions brought erratic and sporadic rainfall, severely impacting local crop yields. This, combined with inadequate sanitation and hygiene, has left children particularly susceptible to malnutrition and disease. The anticipated La Niña weather pattern is expected to bring further heavy rains in early 2025.
 
In addition, the humanitarian situation in northern Mozambique remains complex and challenging. The ongoing armed insurgency periodically triggers mass population displacements, as in Chiure and Macomia, and limits the coverage of humanitarian and development interventions. In Cabo Delgado, more than 1.3 million people, including 676,000 children, required assistance, including 412,288 internally displaced people (IDPs), 411,730 returnees and 481,012 non-displaced conflict-affected people. The conflict disproportionally affects women and children, who constitute the majority of displaced, non-displaced and returnees (approximately 75 per cent).

Impact on Children and Adolescents
 
Children and adolescents in Mozambique face limited access to social services, exposure to violence and exploitation, and rising poverty, all of which severely impact their physical and psychological well-being. Mozambique’s progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) remains constrained:
 
SDG 2 - Ending all forms of malnutrition: Food insecurity and malnutrition continue to remain of great concern, particularly in the north. Mozambique has one of the highest child malnutrition rates globally, driven by insufficient food consumption, poor sanitation and hygiene, infectious diseases, natural disasters and conflict. According to the 2022-2023 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS), 37 per cent of children under five are stunted (have chronic malnutrition) and 13 per cent are severely stunted, while 4 per cent are wasted (acute malnutrition), and 15 per cent are underweight. 
 
SDG 3 - Ensure healthy lives and well-being for all: The 2022-2023 DHS showed Mozambique’s neonatal mortality rate to be 24 deaths per 1,000 live births (21 for girls and 28 for boys), the infant mortality rate 39 per 1,000 live births (33 for girls and 45 for boys) and the under-five mortality rate 60 per 1,000 live births (54 for girls and 65 for boys). WUENIC reported a post-Covid immunization coverage recovery of 72% (up from 50% in 2021, versus 38% for DHS (per-Covid data) and 112% for administrative coverage. UNAIDS reported 140,000 children living with HIV in 2023, and 12,000 new infections registered. The country continues to suffer from regular outbreaks of cholera, measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. 
 
SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education: Mozambique’s overall literacy rate remains low, with female literacy (47 per cent) lagging behind that of males (69 per cent). The DHS revealed that 35 percent of children of primary school age were not attending any level of education. In Cabo Delgado, the conflict continued to disrupt education, with about 15 percent of schools closed in 2024 until the end of the school year.
 
SDG 5 - Gender: Mozambique currently ranks 118 of 189 countries in the Gender Inequality Index. According to the 2022-2023 DHS, 26 per cent of women aged 15-49 have suffered from physical violence, while 8 per cent were victims of sexual violence. Furthermore, 36 per cent of women aged 15-19 have already been pregnant, while 49 per cent of young women got married before 18. 
 
SDG 6 - Water and sanitation for all: DHS data show that 47 per cent of the population has access to basic services of drinking water, while 9 per cent has access to limited services. Only 36 per cent of households have access to improved sanitation infrastructure and 27 per cent of households practice open defecation. Limited access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) is associated with diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Inadequate access to soap and other hygiene items combined compounds the risk of disease. 
 
SDG Target 16.2 Ending abuse, exploitation, trafficking and all forms of violence against and torture of children: The humanitarian crisis in Mozambique has significantly heightened the risks of abuse, exploitation, violence, and psychosocial distress for children, adolescents, persons with disabilities, and women. According to the DHS, an alarming 55 per cent of children between 1 and 14 years reported experiencing violent discipline. Negative coping mechanisms are increasingly prevalent, with over 540,000 children in Cabo Delgado in urgent need of child protection services.

In 2024, thanks to UNICEF’s donor partners across the humanitarian-development-peace (HDP) nexus, UNICEF Mozambique mobilised USD 72 million (across 16 grants), in addition to funds carried over from 2023. The total actual expenditure for 2024 was over USD 119 million. Despite this support, the resources mobilised for the 2024 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal amounted to about USD 22 million (including USD 15 million in new funding), only 19 percent of the appeal target of USD 114 million.  
 
Highlighted below are the key results achieved during 2024, the third year of the 2022-2026 UNICEF Country Programme, prepared in consultation with national authorities in Mozambique, and fully aligned to the 2022-2026 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF). In addition to providing the necessary practical assistance to children, adolescents and their families through a broad range of partners in many sectors, UNICEF also actively supported the development and implementation of national sector strategies and action plans.
 
Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives 

In 2024, UNICEF facilitated a 105 per cent administrative coverage rate for fully immunized children as 1,202,519 children received life-saving vaccines via UNICEF-supported programmes throughout Mozambique. UNICEF also supported the provision of early post-natal care (PNC) to 1,227,312 mothers and newborns (74 per cent of the target), and together with implementing partners Vitamin A supplementation was provided to 3,749,292 children aged 6-59 months (89 per cent of the annual target). 
 
In 2024, UNICEF’s advocacy work for the institutionalization of community health led to the legalization of the status of the community health worker, while renumeration discussions are ongoing. This has expanded access to Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and addressed bottlenecks in healthcare delivery. UNICEF supported the implementation of the Community Health Sub-System Strategy (CHSS) in all 28 districts (100 per cent) of UNICEF’s 4 priority provinces. Furthermore, USD 11 million was mobilised for community health programmes and training 280 (75 per cent of the 2024 target) community health workers (CHWs) to improve healthcare access in remote areas. 
 
The digital health platform upSCALE was expanded to include over 5,500 users, integrating nutrition and HIV services for improved real-time monitoring and delivery efficiency. Additionally, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health (MISAU) with integrated district health planning, aligning resources with local health priorities. The strategic distribution of USD 88.5 million worth of health and nutrition supplies across 10 provinces, while providing support for the maturity model and expanded warehouse capacity and temperature-controlled storage units, further strengthened service delivery¿.
 
UNICEF played a pivotal role in improving maternal, neonatal, and child health outcomes, reducing neonatal mortality from 30 to 24 per 1,000 live births between 2011 and 2023. Over 20,986 newborns received specialized care through strengthened neonatal units and Essential Newborn Care (ENC) protocols. A total of 777 frontline health workers were trained in newborn and maternal care, and 158 health facilities were equipped with critical supplies¿. Over 3,000 adolescents, pregnant women and exposed children benefitted from HIV prevention and treatment services through adolescent-friendly health care initiatives. Additionally, as part of the triple elimination plan for HIV, syphilis and Hepatitis B, UNICEF provided Hepatitis B vaccines birth doses to 43,000 newborns in 9 pilot centres, while 97 per cent of UNICEF-supported facilities provided paediatric HIV services in 2024. Mobile health platforms helped 1,439 people living with HIV, with 899 returning to care and treatment. Furthermore, UNICEF supported the national global alliance plan and triple elimination efforts, increasing early infant diagnosis and viral load testing by 49 per cent.
 
UNICEF supported the Government of Mozambique (GoM) in achieving significant milestones in immunization: 1,222,569 children under one (111 per cent of the target) received three doses of DTP-containing vaccines. The national Big Catch-Up campaigns, reached 524,383 zero-dose children and 861,173 under-immunized children, removing Mozambique from the global list of top 10 zero-dose countries¿. Vitamin A supplementation benefitted 3.7 million children (70 per cent of the target), and HPV vaccination campaigns reached 583,416 adolescents¿. UNICEF also contributed to emergency responses by vaccinating about 4.1 million children against measles and treating 44,182 cholera cases, achieving a reported fatality rate of 0.1 per cent.    
 
Regarding nutrition, UNICEF supported the treatment of over 53,000 (117 per cent of the target) children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), achieving an 80 per cent cure rate¿. Community-based approaches, including Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) interventions, reached 61,484 children via the Integrated Nutrition Package¿. Nutrient-dense dietary solutions validated through community trials addressed moderate acute malnutrition, while advocacy led to the endorsement of the Food Security and Nutrition Policy.
 
UNICEF integrated Early Childhood Development (ECD) services into health care platforms, reaching 18,966 caregivers with ECD messages¿. A total of 431 health workers (78 per cent of the target) were trained on the Malawi Development Assessment Tool (MDAT), enabling early detection and intervention for developmental delays¿. Community engagement initiatives trained 750 community health committee members and produced 72 radio programmes to promote good ECD practices. 
 
UNICEF delivered integrated health and nutrition services during several crises, including El Niño-induced droughts, cyclones, and disease outbreaks. About 4.1 million children were treated for measles and cholera¿ (target: 833,649). Emergency supplies, including 148 health kits and 3,261 community health kits, were pre-positioned to support a rapid response.
 
Goal Area 2: Every child learns  

Education progress continued with primary completion rates improving from 56 per cent in 2021 to 66 per cent in 2024. Despite this progress, learning outcomes remain low: the preliminary 2024 learning assessment suggests only 20 per cent of children in grade 4 can read and understand a simple text, compared to 6 per cent in 2016.
 
Gender parity improved from 0.94 (2021) to 0.97 (2024) in primary and 0.93 (2021) to 0.95 (2024) in lower secondary education. Admission rates to lower secondary education rose from 36 to 56 per cent with slightly better results for girls. Preliminary national assessment results suggest enhanced reading abilities in early grades.
 
Progress result from sector-level interventions targeting school level performance. UNICEF contributes to improving school readiness, teacher capacities, school environment – free of violence and abuse, and enhancing school management.
 
To improve teaching quality and school management, UNICEF trained a total of 488 teachers reaching 98 per cent of the target for the year and 360 School Managers (56 per cent of the annual target). A performance assessment revealed positive impacts on school director performance, though gaps remain in pedagogical management. New tools, including manuals and online platforms, for district level supervision were developed aimed at measuring school performance, and a total of 48 district supervisors were trained in Nampula, Zambezia, and Sofala (about 50 per cent of the target) with expansion planned for Cabo Delgado in 2025. 
 
UNICEF enhanced access to equitable education through enhancing school readiness, creating safe learning environments, and inclusive education for vulnerable children. Out of the 19,000 planned, the Accelerated School Readiness (ASR) Programme reached 16,995 children (90 per cent) under six (including 50 per cent girls) and their parents across four provinces, ensuring a 100 per cent enrolment rate in Grade 1 in supported schools. The Inclusive Education Strategy is being rolled out and efforts to improve transitioning to secondary school included the acquisition of 510 bicycles, as planned, and the introduction of peer mentoring programmes, aimed at reaching 54,100 students and addressing challenges like menstrual hygiene management and violence prevention mechanisms in 2025.
 
UNICEF’s interventions are evidence-based: Evaluations of school council training programmes and school clubs revealed their critical role in reducing absenteeism, promoting accountability, and improving community engagement in education management. An Out-of-School Study was initiated to inform future programming for adolescents and youth. Although the primary completion rate is improving, the education system has failed many children over the years. In 2024, UNICEF stepped up its interventions targeting adolescents with alternative pathways (accelerated learning) and imitated the development of a ‘Learning to Earning ecosystem’ aimed at equipping adolescents and young people in Mozambique with the skills, knowledge, and opportunities needed to transition from education to meaningful employment and economic independence. 
 
In humanitarian settings, UNICEF ensured continued learning for children affected by crises, reaching 60 per cent of the children in need as calculated by the Education cluster through temporary learning spaces, basic learning materials, catch-up classes, psychosocial support, and teacher-in-crisis training. In total, 353,362 children received learning materials and improved learning spaces, exceeding the initial target by 41 per cent (250,000 children). UNICEF played a key role in education cluster coordination, ensuring rapid responses to crisis-affected regions and minimizing disruptions to learning. Several back-to-school campaigns were launched together with MINEDH to encourage school attendance after disruptions. 
 
Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation 

In 2024, UNICEF strengthened legal and policy frameworks to create a more robust child protection system. The National Plan of Action for Children (PNAC III) was finalized, aligning Mozambique’s efforts with international child rights standards. UNICEF supported reviewing progress on the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) recommendations, initiated the next United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) State Party Report, and contributed to consultations on General Comment No. 27. Additionally, UNICEF supported the establishment of an Interministerial Committee on Human Rights, enhancing coordination and accountability across sectors.
 
UNICEF strengthened justice systems as well as civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) mechanisms, enhancing access to rights-based juvenile justice services and legal identity registration. Over 3,000 justice personnel were trained in child-centred practices, and four victim-friendly spaces were established within SERNIC facilities in Cabo Delgado, Nampula, Sofala and Manica provinces. Through the mobile courts pilot initiative, 35 Violence Against Children (VAC) cases were processed, reducing the financial and logistical burden on affected families. Plans to establish three specialized victim-friendly courts advanced, drawing lessons from exchange visits with Zimbabwe. 
 
UNICEF also operationalized four new health-based birth registration post, bringing the total to 156 nationwide, and facilitated 828,949 new birth registrations, improving children’s access to legal identity and essential services. The national birth registration rate for under-fives stands at 32 per cent according to the 2022-2023 DHS. The Child Protection Information Management System, set to launch in 2025, will improve data collection, accountability, and evidence-based planning. 
 
Children’s access to social services improved significantly through capacity-building initiatives and the Cash and Care Programme. Over 153 social workers received training to address VAC, including child marriages, while 7,000 young caregivers affected by early pregnancy and child marriage received financial and psychosocial support. UNICEF promoted positive social norms to prevent child marriage and VAC, using community engagement, peer-to-peer education, and social mobilization campaigns. In 2024, 89,039 adolescent girls received prevention and care interventions, while over 724,000 individuals were reached through community dialogues and awareness programmes. These efforts led to 110 areas declaring themselves child marriage-free zones and 2,725 community action plans being developed. Community-based structures, including 65 Child Protection Community Committees, were reactivated, referring 5,447 cases of VAC and child marriage to formal services. Initiatives such as capoeira sessions benefitted 914 children, fostering healing through physical activity and social inclusion, while 259 children were reintegrated into schools with appropriate support.
 
UNICEF facilitated the reunification of 710 children with their families, surpassing targets by 4 per cent, and reinstated 585 child marriage survivors back to school, promoting gender equity in education. Through the Joint UNICEF/WHO Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) Programme, 4,702 children, including survivors of violence, received support services. Additionally, 33 social workers were mentored to deliver MHPSS services, benefiting over 12,020 vulnerable children. In response to conflict and natural disasters, UNICEF provided holistic protection services to 366,023 children, against the target of 233,952.  
 
Multi-Purpose Centres (MPCs) delivered MHPSS, health, nutrition, WASH, and informal education services. UNICEF improved family tracing and reunification for 65 per cent of unaccompanied and separated children (UASC), with alternative care provided for those unable to reunite with families. Additionally, 649 children associated with armed forces and armed groups (CAAFAG) received reintegration services, including psychosocial support and education. UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Defense (MoD), training 1,200 soldiers on preventing grave violations and protecting children’s rights during military operations.
 
UNICEF also amplified its advocacy efforts through global media partnerships with El País and The Telegraph, raising awareness on child marriage and VAC challenges. Participation in the Ministerial Conference on VAC in Bogotá strengthened Mozambique’s global commitments to child rights. During the conference the Government of Mozambique committed to strengthen parent and caregiver support, the national normative legal and policy framework, as well as response and support services, while also committing more human, financial and infrastructure resources to address VAC. National campaigns, including animated videos on child marriage, reached over 3 million views, empowering adolescents with referral information. 
 
Goal Area 4: Every child lives in a safe and clean environment 

In 2024, UNICEF's WASH programme achieved 80 per cent of the annual target at both upstream and downstream level. Climate-resilient and sustainable water services were provided to 151,588 people, while 476,527 individuals benefited from improved sanitation services. However, despite these achievements, the 2022-2023 DHS highlights the ongoing challenges and limited progress toward achieving universal coverage.
 
In 2024, UNICEF played a critical role in advancing system strengthening and policy advocacy within the WASH sector in Mozambique. UNICEF supported drafting the new Water and Sanitation Law and operationalising the National Sanitation Roadmap, laying a foundation for sustainable WASH governance. Monitoring systems were reinforced through participatory reviews of the National Water and Sanitation Information System (SINAS), integration with health and nutrition indicators, and enhanced data collection tools across WASH programming. These initiatives enhanced transparency, accountability, and data-driven decision-making. Additionally, UNICEF trained over 1,000 government and NGO staff in critical technical areas, addressing sector-wide capacity gaps and improving institutional effectiveness. Further training efforts included risk-informed programming and cross-sectoral workshops integrating WASH with health and humanitarian preparedness strategies.
 
UNICEF integrated climate resilience into WASH programming, supporting studies on child-centred risk assessments, participatory climate risk analysis, and the cost of inaction in WASH. Climate resilience strategies were embedded into district-level WASH plans, supported by evidence-based analysis and community engagement tools. Mozambique’s national delegation to COP29 in Baku included youth representatives, ensuring children’s voices were central to global climate discussions. These initiatives strengthened Mozambique's positioning in international climate dialogues and enhanced evidence-based advocacy for child-centred climate resilience strategies.
 
UNICEF facilitated access to durable and resilient water services for 151,588 people, exceeding the 2024 target by 168 per cent. Overall, 87 per cent of beneficiaries received rural hygiene services (244 per cent of the annual target). In rural areas, solar-powered water systems and borehole installations reached over 71,000 people, while in urban areas, household connections through revolving fund mechanisms extended safe water access to additional communities. Enhanced supply chain management and warehouse investments ensured consistent water supply availability during emergencies. Hydrogeological studies improved planning and drilling accuracy. Furthermore, 40 technicians benefitted from training in borehole installation and maintenance with improved inspection tools and water quality kits.
 
UNICEF's sanitation and hygiene interventions benefited 476,527 people with at least ‘basic’ level sanitation. Over 1,315 communities achieved Open Defecation Free (ODF) status, including one district and eight administrative posts. These achievements were driven by area-wide approaches and community engagement models. In partnership with PSI, UNICEF conducted climate risk assessments to ensure sanitation infrastructure is resilient to extreme weather events. UNICEF also advanced climate-resilient sanitation solutions through risk assessments and private sector partnerships, ensuring sustainable sanitation infrastructure. Participation in the Global SMS Summit and the National Workshop on Safely Managed Sanitation aligned national strategies with global best practices.
 
Integrated planning plays a critical role in maximizing the impact of WASH interventions by ensuring alignment across health, education, and nutrition sectors. In 2024, UNICEF focused on coordinated strategies to address systemic gaps, fostering cross-sectoral collaboration, and driving evidence-based improvements. In health care facilities, UNICEF upgraded WASH services in 32 facilities, benefiting 37,000 maternity inpatients. An additional 29 facilities received emergency WASH services. In schools, 84 institutions improved their WASH infrastructure, benefiting 45,900 children. Capacity-building initiatives included WASH Facility Improvement Tool (FIT) training for healthcare workers, establishment of water committees in schools, and on-the-job technical support. Integration of hygiene promotion into nutrition interventions ensured more comprehensive community outreach. At the policy level, UNICEF contributed to developing a costed national roadmap for WASH in Schools, providing a strategic plan for harmonized implementation across the education sector.
 
UNICEF responded to multiple crises, including cholera outbreaks, El Niño-induced droughts, and the humanitarian crisis in Cabo Delgado. Emergency water services reached 446,470 people, while 47,950 people gained access to sanitation services.
