Hygiene promotion activities impacted 712,845 people, and 29 healthcare facilities and 12 schools received emergency WASH services. Preparedness efforts included pre-positioning WASH supplies in strategic locations and enhancing cholera response capacity through cluster coordination and government collaboration, ensuring rapid response capabilities.
 
Goal Area 5: Every child has an equitable chance in life
 
Significant strides to increase equitable access were made with public finance reform activation and child poverty data availability that is applicable at sub-national level. In addition to national social assistance programme expansion targets exceeded and extended to shock-responsive iteration of implementation in 2024, UNICEF supported the government in advancing the implementation of the Child Grant Expansion Plan (2022-2026), benefitting 48,668 children aged 0-2 years in Nampula and conflict-affected Cabo Delgado, which was 105 per cent of the annual target. This initiative provided financial support during children’s first 1,000 days, while over 7,600 caregivers accessed case management services. Efforts linked beneficiaries with health, nutrition, civil registration, and gender-transformative initiatives, enhancing social protection as a platform for integrated interventions. UNICEF played a pivotal role in digitalising cash transfers by improving e-payment systems for transparency, efficiency, and responsiveness during humanitarian crises. Additionally, UNICEF supported anticipatory action on drought, benefiting 5,000 individuals with mobile money transfers, and strengthened MIS to improve shock-responsive social protection mechanisms. 
 
Amidst Mozambique’s ongoing fiscal crisis, UNICEF advocated for Public Financial Management (PFM) reforms to safeguard social service investments for children. Collaborating with the World Bank (WB), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the European Union (EU), UNICEF contributed to finalizing the National PFM Strategy and operationalizing short-term reforms to maximize fiscal space. These measures improved the Ministry of Economy and Finance’s (MEF) planning and budgeting capacity. UNICEF also secured EUR 4 million from the EU to strengthen planning and budgeting systems for sustainable child-focused investments and mitigation of service delivery disruptions. 
 
UNICEF advanced evidence-based advocacy by collaborating with the National Institute of Statistics (INE) and the MEF. Support included developing a Child Poverty Report, analysing both monetary and multidimensional child poverty, and producing a series of thematic and provincial briefs using data from the 2022-2023 DHS. UNICEF also led the preparation of a Data Action Plan, to improve data quality, accessibility and evidence utilization. Through its new Integrated Data, Evidence and Advocacy Committee (IDEAcom), UNICEF ensured that evidence informed political platforms during Mozambique’s election campaign. 
 
UNICEF supported integration of shock-responsive mechanisms into Mozambique’s social protection systems. The roll-out of e-payment systems reduced delays, improved transparency, and enabled scalable cash transfers during crises. In collaboration with WFP and the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), UNICEF enhanced national emergency preparedness and response systems and invested in anticipatory action protocols, enabling pre-emptive cash transfers to vulnerable households ahead of natural disasters. 
 
Change Strategies

In 2024, UNICEF advocated for Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) to drive improvements in the health, nutrition, education, protection and WASH sectors. Through community engagement platforms, mass media campaigns, and U-Report, UNICEF surpassed the target of 4.7 million by reaching 5.4 million people with messages promoting immunization, cholera prevention, nutrition and hygiene. Digital tools enhanced monitoring and adaptability of SBC strategies. Training programmes equipped frontline workers and community influencers to certify 29,832 new model families in priority districts in four provinces. These efforts contributed to a higher vaccine uptake, improved hygiene practices, better maternal and child nutrition, and stronger community resilience in Mozambique. Furthermore, 4,231 adolescents and youth were engaged, reaching over 6 million people, additionally 7,796 adolescents were engaged in peace clubs, and 4,153 used the Talent Biz platform to build 21st century skills.

In 2024, UNICEF prioritized Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) by placing community voices and feedback at the centre of programme design, implementation, and evaluation. Two-way communication mechanisms gathered real-time feedback, ensuring interventions reflected local needs and cultural contexts. Capacity-building initiatives strengthened partners’ abilities to apply AAP principles, improving trust, collaboration, accountability, and inclusivity, ensuring children and families received effective and dignified support.
 
UNICEF strengthened Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) systems to prevent, detect, and respond to abuse. Training initiatives equipped 3,863 staff, partners, contractors, and community focal points with knowledge of PSEA policies and survivor-centred response protocols. Clear reporting channels, including anonymous feedback mechanisms, ensured safe avenues for raising concerns. Community awareness campaigns promoted an understanding of rights and reporting pathways. Risk assessments and safeguards were integrated into health, nutrition, and humanitarian programs. These measures reinforced accountability, survivor protection, and a zero-tolerance approach across all UNICEF-supported interventions in Mozambique. As a result of these improvements, UNICEF scored strongly (13 out of 16) on the PSEA systems quality assessment. The number of children and young people reached through awareness activities and UNICEF-supported community interventions on PSEA in 2024 was estimated at 600,530.

During 2024 UNICEF Mozambique maintained strong partnerships with key government ministries at central, provincial and district level, including MISAU, MINEDH, MGCAS, MEF and the Ministry of Land and Environment (MTA), to drive results across the health, nutrition, education, WASH, child protection and social protection sectors. UNICEF played a pivotal role in social protection by co-chairing the Social Action Working Group (SAWG) and contributing to the Adaptive Social Protection Working Group, aligning humanitarian and development efforts to build resilient systems¿. 
 
At the policy level, UNICEF co-led strategic platforms such as the Education Sector Group, Health Sector Planning and Financing Working Group (PFSI), and the WASH and Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) Working Group, ensuring cross-sectoral coordination, improved accountability and policy alignment¿. UNICEF collaborated with the Technical Secretariat for Food Security and Nutrition (SETSAN) to advance stunting prevention, food fortification and salt iodisation, as well as advocate for increased financing for child nutrition and health programmes. 
 
Strategic partnerships with international humanitarian and development partners, including the European Union, Sweden, the Netherlands, Norway, Canada, Ireland, the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan, Germany (including through KfW Development Bank), the Republic of Korea, Global Funds, and the World Bank., played a critical role in advancing child-focused outcomes in Mozambique. Multi-year funding agreements and collaboration through technical working groups and partner forums facilitated the delivery of sustainable services in health, education and WASH. Engagement with global platforms such as the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement, the Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunization (GAVI), the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), and the Global Partnership for Ending Child Marriage (GPECM) enabled UNICEF to align programming with international best practices, advocate for systemic policy changes, and mobilize resources. 
 
UNICEF actively collaborated with other UN agencies through several Joint Programmes and Joint Initiatives, including the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Food Programme (WFP), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS),  the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), and the UN University - World Institute for Development Economics Research (UNU-WIDER).
 
UNICEF partnered with 46 civil society organizations (CSOs), local and international non-governmental organisations (NGOs) for a wide range of activities from national advocacy to delivering community-based services. These partnerships enabled the provision of integrated mobile health brigades, nutrition interventions, and life-saving WASH services to vulnerable and hard-to-reach populations¿. In 2025, UNICEF will develop its localization strategy to continue strengthening its strategic partnerships with local CSOs. Additionally, partnerships with academic institutions, such as the Eduardo Mondlane University, supported research, evidence generation, and capacity-building initiatives, including the deployment of the MDAT for early childhood development¿.
 
UNICEF strengthened private sector partnerships to drive innovation and sustainability in programming. Collaboration with Vodacom facilitated zero-rated mobile services for reporting gender-based violence (GBV) and accessing critical child protection services¿. Partnership with LIXIL expanded access to climate-resilient sanitation solutions, while engagement with business associations and chambers of commerce advanced initiatives on salt iodization, food fortification, and child-friendly business practices¿. UNICEF worked closely with private foundations, such as the Gates Foundation and Hilton Foundation, to support community health systems and immunization efforts. The EDGE Advanced Certification underscored UNICEF’s commitment to sustainability through partnerships supporting energy efficiency, digital innovation, and environmental responsibility. These partnerships emphasized UNICEF’s commitment to leveraging private sector resources and expertise for child-focused outcomes.
 
UNICEF played a leadership role in humanitarian response coordination, co-leading the WASH, Nutrition, and Education clusters and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility (AoR). Partnerships with humanitarian organizations, including OCHA, WFP, and WHO, aligned technical and financial resources with national priorities and enabled coordinated responses to disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and conflict-related displacements¿. Contingency partnerships with 23 humanitarian organizations ensured rapid responses during crises¿. Regular Resources (RR) provided critical flexibility, enabling UNICEF to address emerging challenges, reaching districts not covered by project interventions, and sustain long-term goals, linking experiences gained through specific project interventions with policy change and programme strengthening. 
 
Flexible humanitarian funding remains a challenge and has increasingly declined globally. New humanitarian funding for UNICEF Mozambique decreased by 34 per cent in 2024 compared to 2023. This was partially due to a calmer cyclone season in early 2024. Nevertheless, humanitarian needs remained substantial due to the El-Niño-induced drought, Cyclone Chido, cholera and measles outbreaks, and the conflict in the north. UNICEF worked closely with major humanitarian partners in 2024, including ECHO, the United States Agency for International Development/Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (USAID/BHA), Ireland, Canada, and the UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). 
 
The flexibility and timeliness of the Global Humanitarian Thematic funds with support from public and private donors, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Canada and New Zealand, the Today and Tomorrow Initiative with direct support from the United Kingdom and Germany and other private contributors, and UNICEF National Committees, has been pivotal to support UNICEF’s emergency response during 2024. Additionally, emergency response mechanisms in development and humanitarian agreements, such as in the European Union and ECHO funding, have been critical to allow immediate lifesaving response during emergencies in 2024, enabling UNICEF Mozambique to further operationalise the humanitarian-development nexus. 
 
UNICEF also prioritized cross-sectoral integration across its programming in 2024, fostering synergies between social protection, education, health, nutrition, child protection, WASH, and humanitarian responses to address the multidimensional needs of children and their families. Social protection systems were linked with health, nutrition, and civil registration services, ensuring comprehensive support for vulnerable households. In health and nutrition, UNICEF combined immunization, maternal health, and SAM treatment with community health platforms and mobile health brigades. ECD initiatives bridged nutrition, education, and health services, promoting child stimulation alongside breastfeeding and maternal care¿. Cross-sectoral integration was further enhanced through multi-sectoral platforms, such as the Nutrition Partners Forum and the Social Action Working Group, fostering collaborative planning, implementation, and monitoring across sectors¿.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
A key challenge across UNICEF Mozambique's programming in 2024 was the government’s fragile institutional capacity, overlapping mandates, and political instability, particularly during the electoral period, which disrupted coordination mechanisms. Strengthening multi-sectoral platforms, such as the Nutrition Partners Forum and the SAWG, was instrumental in aligning priorities and reducing duplication of efforts of cross-sectoral programming. 
 
Additionally, explicit integration of programme interventions, as outlined in the 2022-2026 Country Programme, maximized quality results for children. Moving forward, UNICEF will reinforce integrated planning processes with district-level convergence models and robust monitoring systems to ensure accountability and evidence-driven decision-making.
 
The ongoing fiscal crisis in Mozambique constrained government spending and the continued population growth negatively affects access to and the quality of education, health and social protection service delivery. Delayed disbursement and liquidation of funds, bureaucratic bottlenecks, and Value-Added Tax (VAT) reimbursement delays created delays in the implementation of UNICEF-supported programmes. Continued support to structural reforms, combined with partnerships with the World Bank, the IMF and the EU, are critical to safeguarding child-focused services. Moving forward, UNICEF will continue advocating for systemic budget reforms and leveraging flexible funding mechanisms to sustain critical services.
 
Mozambique faced multiple humanitarian crises, including Cyclone Chido, outbreaks, El Niño-induced drought, and ongoing conflict in Cabo Delgado. These compounded shocks disrupted health, education, and nutrition services, stretching fragile systems. Limited access to conflict-affected areas and inadequate preparedness measures slowed responses across sectors. UNICEF learned that integrated mobile brigades, combining health, nutrition, and WASH services, were highly effective in reaching remote and conflict-affected communities. In addition, pre-positioning emergency supplies, adoption of anticipatory action protocols, and the ‘Today and Tomorrow Initiative’ emerged as essential tools for improving preparedness and resilience. 
 
Fragmented data systems and inconsistent evidence use created challenges. Furthermore, limited interoperability between sectoral databases, delays in reporting, and data gaps sometimes hindered evidence-based planning. Investing in interoperable digital platforms, building data literacy, and developing clear data sharing protocols are critical for improving decision-making. Platforms like upSCALE mHealth and Kobo-based data collection tools streamlined real-time data analysis, enhancing responsiveness and transparency. Moving forward, UNICEF will prioritize the Data & Capacity Action Plan and scale up digital tools for real-time monitoring.
 
Human resource capacity gaps within government institutions and among frontline workers remained a significant barrier. Limited numbers of trained social workers, healthcare professionals, and teachers, paired with high turnover rates, low payment and inadequate training opportunities, further weakened service delivery. Capacity-building initiatives, paired with retention strategies like incentives and mentorship, are essential for sustainability. Digital training platforms and virtual mentorship programs emerged as scalable, cost-effective solutions. Moving forward, UNICEF will focus on retention strategies, digital training platforms, and advocate the use of incentives to ensure sustained workforce capacity.
 
Inadequate infrastructure, particularly in rural and conflict-affected areas, continued to hinder progress in WASH, education, and healthcare. Poor water and sanitation infrastructure in schools and healthcare facilities exacerbated disease outbreaks and undermined learning outcomes. UNICEF learned that resilient, community-owned infrastructure investments, such as solar-powered water systems, are crucial for sustainability. Hydrogeological studies and financial viability assessments also demonstrated success in improving water system sustainability. Moving forward, UNICEF will intensify investments in climate-resilient infrastructure and prioritize maintenance frameworks for long-term sustainability.
 
In social protection, fiscal constraints weakened social safety nets. Linking social protection programmes with health and education interventions expanded their impact. In child protection, conflict increased risks of violence and exploitation. Digital case management systems and mobile child protection units proved effective in improving service delivery. In nutrition, misinformation and cultural barriers hindered SBC interventions. Community engagement platforms, partnerships with community radio stations, and digital campaigns such as U-Report were effective in addressing these barriers.
 
In education, persistent connectivity gaps limited access to digital tools, while foundational literacy skills remained a challenge. The GIGA initiative, involving a mapping of schools’ connectivity, and the development of digital ecosystems for adolescent engagement and learning, emerged as promising solutions. 
 
As UNICEF Mozambique moves into 2025, the organization will refine multi-sectoral integration strategies, strengthen governance and data systems, and scale climate-resilient infrastructure investments. Lessons from 2024 emphasized the importance of agility, evidence-based planning, and community-centred approaches. Scaling integrated digital platforms like upSCALE and real-time monitoring dashboards will remain a priority. Resilience-building will focus on disaster preparedness, risk-informed programming, and sustainable financing mechanisms. By leveraging insights from 2024, UNICEF will continue to adapt its strategies to Mozambique's evolving context, ensuring every child has the opportunity to survive, thrive, learn and be protected.

Rwanda conducted the general elections in 2024, with President Paul Kagame re-elected to a fourth term. Political stability has been maintained, enabling the government to develop the second National Strategy for Transformation (NST2) for 2024–2029. Building on the achievements of NST1, NST2 focuses on delivering long-term success and a positive impact on the lives of Rwanda citizens by prioritizing sustainable development and climate resilience, development of domestic manufacturing industries to reduce the trade deficit, creation of sustainable and decent jobs, improving the quality and relevance of education, enhancing nutrition and early childhood development to reduce stunting, improving the quality of service delivery while strengthening citizen engagement and participation.  

Rwanda's economy continues to recover, growing by 8.2 per cent in 2023, and is projected to grow by 6 per cent between 2024-2026. While high, an annual average growth rate of 12 per cent is required for Rwanda to attain its stated goal of reaching middle-income status by 2035. Inflation decreased from a peak of 14 percent in 2022 to 5 percent by the end of 2024. Fiscal sustainability remains a concern, with Rwanda’s debt projected to stay below 70% of GDP by 2026/2027 through reduced expenditure and increased revenue. While the national budget has grown to FRW 5,690 billion (USD 4.09 billion) in 2024/25, allocations to social sectors have declined—education dropped to 13.9 per cent of the budget, below UNESCO’s recommended 15–20 per cent, while health stands at 6.6 per cent, well under the Abuja Declaration’s 15 per cent benchmark. The social protection sector saw a 2per cent reduction, leaving many poor families inadequately supported. 
 
In 2024, Rwanda experienced two public health emergencies—mpox and Marburg Virus Disease (MVD). The mpox outbreak affected 74 individuals out of 5,364 suspected cases, with no fatalities, while the MVD outbreak resulted in 66 confirmed cases and 15 deaths, achieving a notably low case fatality rate of 22.7 per cent. Strong government leadership and partnerships ensured rapid containment. The government declared the end of the MVD outbreak on 20th December 2024, reflecting the country’s robust health system response capabilities. 
 
Rwanda made notable progress in Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) despite facing health emergencies. Maternal and child mortality rates have improved, with perinatal mortality (including stillbirths and newborn deaths through 7 days) on a consistent downward trend since 2019/2020 when it stood at 26 per 1,000 births, now at 20.6 per 1,000 births. However, these figures remain significant concerns requiring strengthened health systems. The Health Sector Strategic Plan V (HSSP-V)  was finalized, emphasizing equity, quality, and accountability in healthcare delivery.  
 
Efforts to address adolescent mental health were bolstered by the 2024 Adolescent Mental Health Survey (unpublished), which revealed significant mental health challenges among adolescents, and older, female adolescents disproportionately affected.  
 
While Rwanda sustained its global 95-95-95 HIV targets, only 71 per cent of children accessed treatment compared to 96 per cent of adults. Vertical transmission rates of HIV remain a priority area, with UNICEF, WHO, and UNAIDS supporting Rwanda’s elimination efforts through operational planning and targeted interventions. 
 
A major policy achievement in 2024 was the approval of the National Family and Nutrition Policy, supported by three national guidelines. This policy aims to reduce stunting and malnutrition, aligning with NST2 priorities. A Two-Year Nutrition Acceleration Action Plan and the National Guidelines for District Plans for the Elimination of Malnutrition (DPEM) were developed, which integrates Early Childhood Development (ECD) and nutrition initiatives. 
 
To improve coordination and resource allocation, Rwanda launched a digital ECD mapping platform with the support of UNICEF and other development partners. This platform—which has mapped 31,182 ECD centres and 1,093,012 children thus far— enables data collection and analysis to ensure equitable access to high-quality ECD services. By facilitating evidence-based decision-making, the initiative prioritizes children’s well-being, supporting their healthy development and enhancing program impact at scale. 
 
Rwanda’s education sector has focused on foundational learning, yielding improvements in enrollment and learning outcomes. The pre-primary gross enrollment rate (GER) rose to 53 per cent in 2024, up from 33 per cent the previous year, while the net intake rate for primary education increased from 39 per cent to 45.7 per cent. Learning assessments show significant gains in English and Kinyarwanda proficiency among primary three (P3) students, with 38 per cent achieving English proficiency benchmarks in 2023 compared to 10 per cent in 2021, and 83 per cent meeting Kinyarwanda reading benchmarks, up from 68 per cent in 2021. 
 
Despite these gains, challenges persist. Repetition rates in primary education remain high at 30 per cent, and the transition to secondary education is constrained, with a net enrollment rate of just 2 per cent. Over one million secondary-age children remain in primary school. The Ministry of Education approved a national strategy for foundational learning to address gaps comprehensively and issued a special statute to improve teacher career pathways and working conditions, enhancing the attractiveness of the teaching profession. 
 
The approval of the Family and Nutrition Policy in 2024 marked a significant milestone for child protection. Complementing the Family Law of 2016, the policy emphasizes parenting support, reducing sexual and gender-based violence, and promoting family-based alternative care, including for children with disabilities. Cross-sectoral coordination between the protection and justice sectors improved, with new mechanisms to support children in contact with the law through child protection case management. The ongoing revision of the child protection law aims to formalize the role of child protection workers in statutory services, including alternative care placements and social inquiry reports for courts. 
 
Rwanda’s Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services continue to face challenges despite progress. The 2019-2020 Demographic Health Survey shows 55 per cent of the population had access to basic drinking water services, 61 per cent to basic sanitation facilities, and 25 per cent to basic handwashing facilities. The government increased WASH sector budgetary allocations from FRW 101 billion (USD 72 million) in 2022/23 to 111 billion (USD 880 million) in 2023/24. The new WASH Sector Strategic Plan for 2024–2029 and NST2 underscore WASH as a priority for achieving national and Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets.  
 
In 2024, the government launched the National Climate and Nature Finance Strategy (2024–2030) and began preparing the third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC-3). Climate change adaptation was prioritized in NST2, identifying resilience-building as a key pillar of economic transformation.

Goal 1: Health and Nutrition  

UNICEF collaborated with key partners in 2024 to advance Rwanda’s health systems, delivering strategic results aligned with national priorities and the UNICEF Strategic Plan. Evidence-generation initiatives such as vaccine management assessments, gender barriers to immunization, and adolescent mental health studies informed adaptive health programming. A Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment in Health was launched to guide climate-resilient health systems, while a study on the early identification of children with disabilities laid the groundwork for scaling best practices. UNICEF supported the development of transformative national health strategies, including the Health Sector Strategic Plan V and operational plans for adolescent health and HIV response. Integration of RapidSMS into the community electronic medical records (cEMR) system in five districts enhanced real-time case management. Over 91,000 households were registered, and 1,000 personnel were trained in digital tools to strengthen service delivery. 
The distribution of life-saving oxygen equipment to all 562 health facilities improved equitable access to critical care. Immunization services expanded by implementing e-Tracker and eVLMS systems across 46 hospitals, 514 health centers, and 95 health posts, ensuring robust data management. These efforts achieved high immunization coverage: DPT3 at 97.3 per cent and MCV1 at 98 per cent, with a notable reduction in zero-dose children.  

Rwanda made strides in assistive technology for children with disabilities. Ear and Hearing Care services were scaled to nine districts, and a disability services model was piloted in two districts. Over 900 health providers were trained, identifying 2,393 children with hearing impairments, assessing 1,387, and providing 493 (252 males, 225 females) children with digital hearing aids. This initiative supported to bridge the gap for children with hearing impairments, enabling them to access education, overcome challenges, and pursue their dreams. Plans to expand support to visual disabilities are underway.  
 
UNICEF advanced adolescent health through comprehensive education packages on mental health, sexual and reproductive health, and Gender-Based Violence (GBV). Over 1,000 personnel were trained, and 11,000 adolescents reached through peer support networks. The YAHealth digital platform was upgraded with disability-friendly features, adding 4,413 new users and reaching over 410,000 adolescents through targeted campaigns. 
 
UNICEF played a vital role in responding to public health emergencies, with mpox and MVD outbreaks both declared in 2024. Mobilizing $4.5 million in resources, UNICEF ensured the distribution of Personal Prevention Equipment (PPE) kits, surveillance and diagnostic tools, and training for more than 60,000 health workers in case surveillance and response activities. 
 
UNICEF supported the development of the National Family and Nutrition Policy, enhancing cross-sectoral coordination through initiatives like the National Two-Year Nutrition Acceleration Action Plan and District Plans for the Elimination of Malnutrition. These efforts integrate nutrition and ECD services. UNICEF's technical input contributed to continuously prioritizing stunting reduction and ECD in NST2. 
 
The launch of Multiple Micronutrient Supplementation (MMS) for pregnant women marked a significant shift from iron-folic acid supplementation, benefiting 65,000 women in seven districts. A new partnership was established with the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, aiming to scale MMS nationally in the coming years. 
 
The #OneEggPerChildEveryDay campaign reached over 9 million people, boosting egg consumption among children aged 6–24 months. Nutrition-sensitive interventions, such as small livestock distribution and kitchen gardening, benefited 60,000 Voluntary Saving and Loan Association (VSLA) members in 14 high-burden stunting districts. 
 
UNICEF’s community engagement models for maternal and child nutrition were nationally adopted. Since 2018, over 20,000 ECD settings have been established, including employer-supported centers in sectors like tea farming, banking, mining, and rice farming. ECD achievements were showcased at regional conferences, highlighting Rwanda’s leadership. The digitization of ECD mapping platform improved planning and monitoring, ensuring sustainable progress.  
 
Goal 2: Education  

In 2024, UNICEF supported the Government of Rwanda in successfully convening the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange (FLEX) Summit, attracting leaders and practitioners from 34 countries, including 20 Ministers of Education. The key outcome of the Summit was a joint declaration to eliminate learning poverty in Africa by 2035. Following the FLEX, the President of Rwanda and the Minister of Education attended the Africa Union Continental Education Conference in Mauritania, demonstrating clearly to peers at the continental level Rwanda’s commitment to education, especially foundational learning, at the highest level. 
 
UNICEF contributed to advancing governance, access, quality, and equity in education, directly contributing to improved learning outcomes for 2.2 million children. Through governance, UNICEF supported the integration of the education management information system (EMIS), notably the school data and teacher management information systems, with the national financial and payroll management systems. This innovation streamlined capitation grant disbursements and ensured payroll accuracy by aligning teacher records with active school staff, reducing risks of discrepancies. The digital teacher management system further transformed workforce management by optimizing teacher recruitment, placement, and equitable distribution. 

UNICEF’s advocacy successfully prioritized universal pre-primary education for five-year-olds and alternative education pathways for out-of-school children in NST2 and the Education Sector Strategic Plan. Advocacy further influenced the government's rollout of remedial learning intervention over the summer holiday. As a result, 64 per cent of over 360,000 learners who participated achieved grade-level competencies required for promotion, reducing the repetition rate in lower primary grades by more than 50 per cent. 

To foster inclusivity, harmonized guidelines for identifying and supporting children with disabilities were introduced, equipping teachers with essential skills. Ten inclusive schools were equipped with adapted materials, benefiting 314 children with disabilities while serving as hubs for specialized support to neighboring schools, including assistive devices and psychosocial services. 

UNICEF supported enhancing the capacities of 53,019 teachers in play-based and learner-centered pedagogies, promoting holistic child development and benefiting over 2.2 million primary school children. Pre-primary curricula were aligned with teacher guides, embedding play-based strategies and fostering enriched learning environments. Gender equity was advanced through community engagement addressing harmful norms and equipping 3,662 youth with upskilling opportunities, with 1,870 completing job-relevant courses to prepare for meaningful careers. 

Under the Generation Unlimited initiative, UNICEF, in partnership with the Ministry of Youth and Arts and the Ministry of Public Work and Labour, launched the Passport to Earning platform (Ingazi in local language - https://www.ingazi.rw), a digital learning resource aimed at facilitating youth transitions from education to employment. The platform currently features 132 job-relevant upskilling courses, with 3,662 young people already registered and 1,870 courses successfully completed. Beyond upskilling, the Ingazi platform also includes a “Career Hub” that offers job links, career pathways, and professional development opportunities. An AI-powered career hub, currently under development, will deliver personalized guidance on career and growth pathways, addressing employment barriers and equipping youth with the skills needed for long-term success. Through Ingazi, UNICEF has significantly contributed to the government’s priority of youth employment by preparing a skilled workforce ready to meet labor market demands. 
 
Goals 3: Child protection  

In 2024, UNICEF successfully facilitated the integration of child protection priorities into NST2. In the absence of a dedicated child protection sector, UNICEF influenced the inclusion of critical targets within sectors like social protection (family care, street children, and parenting) and justice (social work reports, diversion, violence against children, and gender-based violence). These efforts ensure that key drivers of child protection results are prioritized over the next five years. 

In collaboration with UNDP, UNICEF supported a capacity assessment by the Ministry of Justice, leading to an agreement to pilot a diversion and probation programme in 2025. This initiative will integrate child protection services into the justice system and progressively reduce child detention. UNICEF also continued its support for a postgraduate diploma in child justice, with the first cohort graduating in December 2024. These graduates, including senior officials, will play a pivotal role in embedding juvenile justice priorities into the justice sector strategic plan for 2024–2029. 
 
UNICEF advanced efforts to prevent family separation and promote psychosocial well-being across development and humanitarian settings. Through family visitation programs led by volunteer child protection workers, over 160,000 families, comprising 670,000 members, benefited from prevention support to address potential stressors that could lead to conflict and psychosocial distress at the family level to provide a safe family environment for children. 

During the mpox and MVD public health emergencies, UNICEF integrated the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Harassment (PSEA) into all emergency response pillars. Over 53,000 frontline workers, including 270 government GBV focal persons, were trained in Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), GBV, and PSEA. UNICEF co-chaired the MHPSS pillar, supporting the government partners in delivering interventions to affected families, including recreational supplies for children affected by MVD. 

Goal 4: WASH  

In 2024, UNICEF played a pivotal role in advancing climate-resilient and inclusive WASH services in Rwanda. Key contributions included supporting the development of the Strategy and Action Plan for Climate-Resilient WASH Services, the Implementation Plan for the WASH Sector Financing Strategy, and the Standards and Guidelines for WASH in Healthcare Facilities (HCF). UNICEF also assisted in drafting the National Roadmap for Universal Access to WASH in HCF, conducting a WASH Sector Situation Analysis, and a national assessment of WASH and infection prevention control in healthcare facilities. 

UNICEF provided critical technical support to mobilize resources for the WASH sector. A funding concept note for a USD 15 million project to strengthen the climate resilience of water supply systems was submitted to the African Development Bank Climate Adaptation Window (AfDB CAW) and shortlisted for funding allocation. Another concept note for a climate-smart wastewater treatment system was accepted for appraisal by the Asian Infrastructure and Investment Bank (AIIB). To promote commercial financing, UNICEF facilitated an investor landscape study, initiating discussions with local banks to launch loan products for the WASH sector. 

In 2024, approximately 17,000 people gained access to basic water supplies, while 51 learning centers were equipped with disability-sensitive sanitation facilities with UNICEF support. During the mpox and Marburg virus disease outbreaks, UNICEF supported WASH emergency responses by installing handwashing stations at high-traffic border points (serving 5,000 people daily) and seconding three infection prevention and control (IPC) experts to the Ministry of Health. UNICEF developed technical guidelines and training materials and supervised IPC measures in healthcare facilities while providing essential supplies for the response. 

Goal 5: Social Protection  

UNICEF has been at the forefront in advancing policy and strategy development, integrating disability into social protection, and building the administrative capacity of Rwanda’s social protection sector. As a result of UNICEF’s support, 842 households with children with disabilities in the districts of Bugesera and Huye benefited from a newly piloted child disability grant. Additionally, UNICEF led the creation of a comprehensive training curriculum for parasocial workers—frontline social welfare volunteers—and trained master trainers to roll out nationwide training for all parasocial workers. This initiative provided the government with a more holistic understanding of the roles and responsibilities of parasocial workers and enabled the development of a cohesive set of guidelines and training materials aimed at enhancing frontline service delivery. 
 
UNICEF has continued to engage with the Government to ensure the needs of the children are incorporated in their articulated national vision and direction for the period 2024-2029. UNICEF provided technical expertise and collaborative support, in the development of Rwanda's Public Financial Management (PFM) Strategic Plan. Through advocacy and strategic collaboration, a social inclusion pillar was established as a standalone priority within the PFM sector. The cost analysis of repetition and dropout in Rwanda’s basic education informed the national priority of preprimary education in the NST to support school readiness, reducing repetitions and improving learning outcomes. It strengthened the capacity of the National Institute of Statistics and Research (NISR) to complete the 7th Integrated Living Condition Survey (ECIV7), a critical data source for measuring the country's progress on poverty reduction, including multiple dimensional of child poverty estimation. UNICEF continued its advocacy on child-focused budgeting through continued analysis and dissemination of national budget briefs and other diagnostic work. 
 
In response to the Marburg outbreak in late 2024, UNICEF provided financial support to 470 MVD-affected households through the shock-responsive cash transfer programme, implemented by the Local Administrative Entities Development Agency (LODA). The lessons learned during this emergency response will contribute to strengthening the social protection system’s ability to respond to future shocks, ensuring it is more resilient and adaptable to the needs of vulnerable populations. 
 
Cross-Sectoral 

In 2024, the UN in Rwanda prepared the new UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF 2025-2029) to align with the government NST2’s priorities and lay out the foreseen contribution of the national efforts in the economic transformation, social transformation, and transformative governance. UNICEF and the Government of Rwanda also finalized the Country-Programme Document (CPD, 2025-2029), set for endorsement by the UNICEF Executive Board by February 2025.  

UNICEF supported the government with inclusive, evidence-based Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) strategies, innovative capacity development, and two-way community engagement models. These efforts focused on national priorities, including Risk communication & Community Engagement (RCCE), the End Stunting and Hehe n’Igwingira (#OneEggPerChildEveryDay campaign) campaign, and education with a focus on responsive parenting and disability inclusion. SBC initiatives expanded to include 10 ministries and 80 partners, empowering over 50,000 functionaries, inter-faith leaders, and volunteers. Digital innovations, including mobile-based training, resulted in significant engagement, with the highest uptake in food and feeding (25 per cent) and antenatal care (17 per cent). UNICEF’s support for parenting education reached one million parents through platforms like ITETERO radio, TV and social media channels. 
Climate change is an increasing priority for UNICEF’s programme in Rwanda, driving efforts across multiple sectors to ensure climate-resilient systems and inclusive action. 

In 2024, UNICEF initiated the Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment, which will guide the health sector in addressing climate-related challenges and fostering sustainable, adaptive health systems. Additionally, UNICEF supported the development of the Strategy and Action Plan for Climate-Resilient WASH Services, emphasizing the education sector’s need to innovate and adapt to the impacts of climate change and other emerging challenges. 
 
In collaboration with Save the Children, the Ministry of Environment, and the Environment Management Agency, UNICEF supported children in drafting an advocacy statement on the impact of climate change on children’s rights. This statement was incorporated into Rwanda’s submissions at COP29, amplifying children’s voices in global climate discourse. 
 
UNICEF’s #GreenRisingRwanda initiative engaged over 182,000 youth in community-driven environmental projects. As part of this effort, over 11,000 young people participated in the “Special Umuganda Day for Youth,” planting 47,000 trees in their communities. The initiative generated over 2.6 million impressions on social media and was featured in the RwandAir inflight magazine. Additionally, UNICEF enhanced the environmental skills of 2,200 students in 10 schools and supported the planting of 42,852 trees on school groundsand in neibouring communities. 
 
UNICEF also implemented the recommendations from the Gender Programme Review, ensuring gender-transformative results were prioritized in the new CPD. Gender barriers analysis, employing Human-Centered Design, was conducted in key areas such as zero-dose vaccination and girls' education, resulting in tailored solutions and enhanced community and youth involvement. 
In the area of data and evidence generation, UNICEF supported the National Institute of Statistics in preparing the upcoming Demographic and Health Survey (DHS-7), with additional support for analyzing EICV-7 household survey data and the new MODA analysis planned for 2025. In 2024, UNICEF supported NISR in developing the new National Statistics Development Strategy (NSDS4) with the pilot of using Child Rights Toolkits, ensuring child rights indicators were integrated and prioritized in the NSDS4.  

Operations collaborate effectively with the Programme to contribute to delivering results for children. This close collaboration enabled the office to provide rapid and crucial emergency response to Marburg and Mpox response during the L3 emergency period, mainly in the areas of procurement of vital health and IPC/WASH supplies, recruitment of staff for the emergencies, and strengthening Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) capacities. The business process simplification initiative from 2023 continues to play a major role during the year as the office continues to identify effective ways to achieve results. The simplified procedures were strengthened during the L3 emergency period, contributing to a faster approach to delivering results. 

The Rwanda Country Office successfully completed a collaborative Country Programme Management Planning process in line with the new Country Programme development, focused on staff development, emergency response, and workforce planning as well as the promotion of a conducive work environment. Key achievements include strategic office restructuring and supporting staff through financial wellness sessions and post-abolished post support. The Country Office successfully responded to the Marburg emergency and implemented a comprehensive workforce plan, resulting in the recruitment of 25 surge support staff, 11 UNVs, and 3 interns. The office also prioritized diversity and inclusion, offering training, mentoring programs, and leadership development. The office promoted work-life balance, improved staff wellbeing through flexible arrangements, and strengthened collaboration with Section Chiefs on people and culture matters.

In 2024, UNICEF Rwanda showcased the transformative power of partnerships in advancing children’s rights and supporting national priorities. Through collaborations with government agencies, civil society organizations (CSOs), the private sector, UN entities, and other development partners, UNICEF reinforced its commitment to creating lasting, positive change for children. These partnerships encompassed 19 government agencies, 23 CSOs, and two academic institutions, underscoring the vital role of multi-sectoral cooperation. 
 
UNICEF’s engagement with government entities centered on evidence-based policy advocacy and system strengthening for broader and more sustainable impact. Support to the Ministry of Health on assistive technology for Ear and Hearing Care elevated the importance of inclusive health services for people with disabilities, integrating early detection, prevention, rehabilitation, and treatment into the national health strategy. Public health emergency response efforts strengthened government commitments to resilient primary healthcare systems. The Ministry of Education committed to the foundational learning agenda and hosted the African Foundational Learning Exchange (FLEX) conference. Meanwhile, UNICEF’s partnership with the National Child Development Agency advanced integrated approaches to early childhood development (ECD), nutrition and stunting reduction, and child protection. In child justice, the Ministry of Justice and justice sector institutions increasingly recognized UNICEF as a primary partner, engaging the organization in all strategic events and sectoral dialogues. A particularly transformative partnership with the Water and Sanitation Corporation (WASAC) shifted from constructing or rehabilitating WASH facilities to innovative financing. With UNICEF’s support, WASAC secured financial resources from international financial institutions (IFIs) and global climate financing initiatives, exemplifying a catalytic shift toward sustainable development. 
 
CSOs remained vital partners in delivering services to vulnerable children and families. In 2024, UNICEF significantly scaled up support for youth-led organizations. The establishment of the Youth Advocate Network, complete with elected leadership and comprehensive training on leadership, communication, and public speaking, empowered young advocates to amplify their voices. Additionally, Four Rwandan youth leaders were selected as the third cohort of the Global Young People’s Action team (YPAT) of Generation Unlimited, furthering global youth engagement. 
 
Under the UN Resident Coordinator’s leadership, UNICEF contributed to developing the new UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025-2029, ensuring alignment with NST2. UNICEF continues to take part in the UN joint programmes such as Nutrition (WFP and WHO), HIV/AIDS (WHO and USAID), and Youth (UNDP, UNFPA, UN Women, etc.). Enhanced collaboration in the health sector was realized through a successful application for the World Bank’s Pandemic Fund (with WHO and FAO) and an award for a joint programme on Health4Life (with WHO). UNICEF worked closely with UNFPA, WHO, and UNAIDS to advocate for multi-sectoral coordination on adolescent and youth health services. Through UNOPS, the partnership with At Scale in assistive technology was expanded from Ear and Hear Care to Vision Care. UNICEF continued to work with UNHCR in supporting refugee children and asylum seekers. The partnership with UNDP was further strengthened through quarterly coordination meetings and support for the 2024 Africa YouthConnekt Summit, the development of the justice sector strategy, and the national climate change agenda. 
Collaboration with development partners in 2024 was pivotal in supporting the Rwandan government’s efforts in developing the NST2 and responding to public health emergencies. UNICEF played a leading role in sectoral working groups, including education, WASH, and others. Key partnerships with USAID (in health, nutrition, and child protection) and FCDO (in education) continued to be crucial in supporting sectoral policy development and system improvements. New partnerships with the World Bank (pandemic fund), the International Development Research Centre (IDRC/KIX), and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (MMS) opened new avenues for addressing both local and global emerging challenges. 
Transformative private sector engagement mobilized significant resources and advanced child-friendly business practices. Through the CEO Forum for Children, UNICEF advocated for Child Rights and Business (CRB) principles, Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices, and nutrition initiatives, collectively engaging 80 companies, mobilizing USD 5 million, and impacting 48,000 children. 
 
The private sector invested in implementing family-friendly workplace policies, establishing ECD and Education centers, and expanded internet connectivity for enhanced access to digital education. Partnerships with Airtel and MTN enabled zero-rating for eight educational platforms, granting free digital learning access to students and teachers. Collaborations with Equity Bank, Inkomoko, and SONARWA LIFE upskilled 3,662 youth, facilitating smoother school-to-work transitions.  
 
In 2024, the UNICEF Rwanda Country Office won the UNICEF Global Inspire Award under the multi-stakeholder platform category, recognizing our good work with the private and public sectors toward child rights. 

Renowned Rwandan musician and songwriter, Andy Bumuntu was signed as the third UNICEF Champion for Children, to influence and amplify advocacy for the children. Andy’s launched song “Bahige” seeks to engage girls and children with disabilities instilling self-belief and confidence to fulfil their potential. 
 
Rwandan Government’s commitment and innovative engagement in hosting regional and global big events offered opportunities for UNICEF to promote child rights agenda. In 2024, UNICEF actively participated in 14 international and many regional, and national events taking place in Rwanda, with more than 20 speaking engagements, multiple presentations, and diverse session moderations. Some standout events like the African Evaluation Conference in March, the 2025 Africa YouthConnekt Summit in October, and the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange (FLEX) Conference in November 2024, facilitated meaningful engagement and interaction with over 40,000 delegates who are predominantly trendsetters and leaders in their respective fields of expertise. Across those events, UNICEF sponsored various participants including UNICEF staff, partners, and youth.  
 
In 2024, the Rwanda country office mobilized around USD 50 million, including USD 31 million from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), which was instrumental in funding initiatives aligned with Rwanda’s Education Sector Strategic Plan (ESSP). Some USD 4.5 million was mobilized for the Marburg and mpox emergency responses, including a USD 2.2 million loan from the UNICEF Emergency Programme Fund (EPF) that ensured UNICEF’s timely responses. UNICEF Rwanda continued to receive contributions from public and private partners, such as the Government of Japan, FCDO, USAID, GAVI, the Hempel and Mastercard Foundations, and the US, Danish, Swiss and Canadian National Committees for UNICEF, showing a strong continuity and satisfaction of the donors regarding the results achieved. A new partnership was established with the Government of China supporting the ECD programme and South-South Cooperation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The Power of Strategic Partnerships. Strategic partnerships have been instrumental in supporting UNICEF's advocacy for child rights and ensuring the prioritization of children in NST2 and UNSDCF. Through active participation in the Development Partners Retreat and Sectoral Working Groups, alongside key partners such as USAID, FCDO, and the World Bank, UNICEF helped emphasize critical targets in NST2, including health workforce development, stunting reduction, and ECD and pre-primary education, and linking them with the quality of education. These collaborations have not only strengthened sectoral efforts but also highlighted the value of coordinated action to achieve sustainable results.

Cross-sectoral collaboration remains pivotal for addressing interconnected challenges affecting children. Breaking down silos among education, health, child protection, and social protection sectors enabled UNICEF to adopt a more holistic approach. In 2024, significant strides were made in developing an integrated adolescent programme. This initiative addressed sexual and reproductive health, HIV, mental health, and gender-based violence (GBV) through close partnerships across health, education, child protection, and social behavior change sectors. Similarly, the FCDO-supported Girls in Rwanda Learning (GIRL) programme extended beyond education to create a supportive learning environment by promoting good health and nutrition, protection from violence, and positive social norms on gender. Additionally, a pilot integrated disability support programme in two districts further demonstrated the effectiveness of multi-sectoral coordination, strengthening district-level systems to serve children with disabilities.

Addressing Systemic Challenges in Human Capital Development. While Rwanda has achieved significant progress in social development in the past decades, the stunting rate is still high. Education quality is now the key barrier to the country’s human capital development. Systemic barriers hinder equity and quality across social services. For instance, the health and nutrition sectors revealed gaps in inclusive service delivery and the effective use of data to inform decisions. The education system grapples with low progression rates, significant dropout, and high repetition, reflecting deeper issues of inadequate foundational learning, strained infrastructure, and insufficient teacher capacity.  Child protection remains a pressing issue, with limited understanding and prioritization among stakeholders impeding resource mobilization. The WASH sector faced significant challenges, particularly in sanitation, where funding constraints and weak capacity slowed progress toward achieving SDGs. 

Advancing Digitalization and Innovation offer critical opportunities to accelerate human capital development in Rwanda. Rwanda’s VISION 2050 and NST2 provide a framework for expanding digital tools to enhance service accessibility and inclusivity, particularly for marginalized groups. Addressing financial gaps will require innovative financing mechanisms, leveraging non-traditional avenues such as climate financing, commercial instruments, and private-sector engagement. Partnerships with International Finance Institutions and national banking systems will be key to sustaining quality and inclusive services. 

Resilience in Emergency Preparedness.  UNICEF's role in emergency preparedness was exemplified through its contributions to the MVD and mpox response programmes. Spanning 11 pillars, UNICEF played a convening role in Infection Prevention and Control (IPC), Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), and the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). Significant support was provided to supplies and capacity building in health surveillance and case management, as well as the continuity of essential services in nutrition, education, and social and child protection. The response was enriched by partnerships with national champions, faith-based organizations, NGOs, academic institutions, and private-sector actors, which helped address stigma, enhance service delivery, and improve social norms and behaviors. Moving forward, UNICEF’s strategies are focused on building shock-responsive resilience in systems by strengthening policies, training personnel, and increasing community engagement and feedback mechanisms. These efforts are designed to have a lasting impact in both humanitarian and development contexts. With climate change, disaster risk reduction, and public health emergencies emerging as priority areas, strong cross-sectoral coordination and innovative intervention strategies will be essential.
 
Strategic Vision for 2025-2029. In 2024, UNICEF finalized its new Country Programme Document (CPD) for 2025–2029 through a highly consultative process. A joint dissemination event with development partners highlighted the "One UN" approach and aligned UNICEF's strategic priorities with Rwanda’s NST2. The new CPD represents a shift toward more catalytic programming, aiming at achieving large-scale results and sustainable impacts. UNICEF’s programmes will increasingly engage adolescents and youth not only as beneficiaries but also as agents of change for children and future parents. This Country Programme will support Rwanda’s progress toward achieving the SDGs and its vision of transitioning to middle-income status by 2035.

In 2024, Somalia was elected as non-permanent member of the UN Security Council. Having the decades long arms embargo lifted in December 2023 and push forward to liberate areas controlled by non –state armed groups, the country negotiated the orderly process of withdrawing and closing the UN and African Union peacekeeping operations. Overlapping security challenges coupled with critical transitions, including the shift from the African Union Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission (AUSSOM), the transition from the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) to the United Nations Assistance Transition Mission (UNATMIS) and the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) significantly impacted humanitarian operations, particularly UNICEF’s ability to deliver services in hard-to-reach (H2R) areas. The drawdown of ATMIS forces and the subsequent transition to AUSSOM reduced the availability of armed escorts for humanitarian convoys, compelling UNICEF, and other actors to explore alternative security solutions, such as community-based approaches and partnerships with private security providers. 

During 2024, government, private sector, civil society, academia, and development partners engaged on the preparations of the NTP, which aims at delivering measurable impact to citizens fostering growth through accountability and public-private collaborations. The NTP aims to produce a quantum leap from current development trajectory to achieve growth rates of 6-8 per cent and reach a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of US$22.1 billion in 2029 from US$12.8 billion in 2024 and a Gross National Income (GNI) per capital of US$981 from US$667. Having received US$4.5 billion debt relief from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank (WB) and other creditors, the country leadership pushed forward in 2024 a comprehensive long-term vision and medium-term development plan with the goal to change the course of Somalia.  
Approximately 53 per cent of Somalia's population is under 18 years old, which is both an opportunity for economic development and a challenge for provision of social services. The nation ranks low on the international Human Development Index. In 2024, UNICEF provided support to the Somalia National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS) to conduct the most recent analysis of multidimensional child poverty using the 2022 integrated household budget survey data. The preliminary analysis indicates an anticipated rise in multidimensional child poverty from 82.2 per cent in 2022. Much remains unknown about Somalia’s progress towards the 48 child-related Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets and the latest (2022) Voluntary National Review report suggests weak SDG progress coordination has challenged measurement of 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development advancement. UNICEF is supporting the Government to implement a Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) that will contribute 40 per cent of SDG indicator data, covering six key child rights sectors and other cross-cutting areas, and provide baselines for the National Transformation Plan, United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the next UNICEF Country Programme (2026-2030). 

The humanitarian situation in Somalia in 2024 continued being highly complex and challenging, driven by multiple, overlapping crises, including armed conflict, extreme weather shocks, and disease outbreaks. Earlier in the year, the El Niño-induced floods severely impacted 2.4 million people, including 1.5 million children, leading to massive displacement, and exacerbating already high levels of acute malnutrition and overwhelming fragile healthcare systems. Compounding the crisis, persistent drought conditions due to La Niña, coupled with anticipated failed Deyr rains in late 2024, are forecasted to continue into 2025, further heightening food insecurity and water scarcity especially in the Central and Southern regions. 
Armed conflicts and military operations, particularly against the non-state armed groups, led to significant displacement, damage to critical infrastructure, consequently causing among others, outbreaks of disease such as cholera, which infected around 19,000 people in 2024. Clan disputes and localized violence, particularly in south-central Somalia (Galmudug, Hirshabelle, Southwest State, Jubaland, and Banadir), further exacerbated humanitarian needs. Furthermore, conflict and political instability in contested regions like Sool, Sanaag, and Cayn (SSC-Khatumo), continued to fuel displacement and restrict humanitarian access, leaving vulnerable populations without essential services. 

The under-five mortality rate stands at 106 deaths per 1,000 live births (UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality 2023), with 1.3 million zero-dose children lacking vaccination, with 16,927 Cholera cases and 136 deaths across 30 districts by mid-August 2024, with children under five comprising 59 per cent of cases, representing a 50 per cent increase in case load from 2023 (DHIS-2). Nutritional issues are prevalent, with 18 per cent of children under five stunted (Joint Child Malnutrition Estimate 2023) and 11.7 percent wasted (IPC Post-Deyr analysis 2024). There has been notable progress on access to basic water services as access increased from a mere 30 per cent (JMP) in 2004 to 71 per cent (UNICEF WASH Needs Assessment) in 2024. However, only 39 per cent of the population have access to basic sanitation facilities, a decline from previous years. There is a need to cross ‘the last mile’ and reach the 29 per cent of the population that still does not have access, most notably in rural areas. Successes in basic water coverage can now be translated into elaborating and implementing a safely managed water service strategy, the last step of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) water ladder. 

In terms of sanitation, progress has been made in the elimination of open defecation as national rates have decreased from 51 per cent in 2004 to 16 per cent in 2024. Improvements in basic sanitation have however been only marginal as coverage only increased from 23 per cent in 2004 to 39 per cent in 2024. It also seems that coverage stagnated from 38 per cent in 2020 to 39 per cent in 2024, which indicates that gains in sanitation are generally offset by population growth. These numbers generally mean that communities are halting the harmful practice of open defecation but are not ‘moving up’ the sanitation ladder to basic access. There is therefore a need to design and scale up a workable model for basic sanitation, most notably in rural areas. Progress during 2024, albeit partial, continues to be visible.  
The primary gross enrollment rate (GER) is only 33.8 per cent while the secondary GER is 26 per cent, and this means over 66 per cent of children aged 6 to 13 are out of primary education systems (FGS Statistical Yearbook 2023). Children with disabilities face greater education barriers, such as community misconceptions, insufficient teacher capacity and inaccessible infrastructure. Child protection issues are critical, including child marriage, gender- based violence and the need to develop juvenile justice systems and birth registration. Between January and September 2024, according to the Country Task Force on Monitoring and Reporting co-chaired by UNICEF and the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM), 1,946 grave violations against children were documented, impacting 1,478 children (1,057 boys 421 girls), This includes recruitment and use, sexual violence, abduction, killing and maiming, attacks on schools and hospitals and denial of humanitarian access. Ninety-nine per cent of girls and women aged 15–49 years have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM), while 34 per cent of females are married by age 18 (SHDS 2020). 

Sixty per cent of children may experience multidimensional poverty, and only 11 per cent have access to a social protection programme (Somali National Bureau of Statistics MODA Report 2022). The Gender Inequality Index is notably high at 0.776, while 11.7 per cent of the adult population live with disabilities. Somalia ranks near the top of most at-risk countries (4 /163) on the Children’s Climate Risk Index. The situation underscores the urgent need for comprehensive interventions to address these multifaceted challenges and improve the rights and well-being of Somali children.

In support of SDG and 2030 Agenda progress, UNICEF contributions to results for children in 2024 were guided by the UNICEF Somalia Country Programme (2021–2025) and fully aligned with the Somalia UNSDCF (2021–2025) and national priorities, including the Somalia National Development Plan 9 (2020–2024).  

Goal 1: Survive and Thrive 
Through comprehensive efforts, UNICEF made substantial progress in improving health outcomes for vulnerable communities in Somalia, particularly for mothers and children, despite the challenging context. In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in maternal and child survival, focusing on advocacy, strategy development, service delivery, and strengthening resilient health systems. 
Advocacy and strategy efforts were ramped up, with UNICEF and WHO leading initiatives such as the launch of the Immunization and Polio Eradication Taskforce and the high-level forum on Child Survival. The Prime Minister’s involvement was pivotal, launching the Immunization and Polio Eradication Taskforce and the high-level Forum on Child Survival, which focused on reducing child mortality. 
For maternal health, the proportion of pregnant women delivering with skilled birth attendance slightly increased from 46 per cent in 2023 to 49.69 per cent in 2024.  Antenatal care improved significantly, from 82 per cent in 2023 to 92 per cent of pregnant women receiving at least one antenatal care service in 2024. The proportion of pregnant women completing four recommended visits slightly increased from 31 per cent to 32 per cent. In terms of child health and immunization, coverage for the third dose of DTP vaccines rose to 92 per cent in 2024 from 81 per cent in 2023. Measles vaccination increased to 90 per cent by November 2024 from 75 per cent in 2023. The introduction of PCV-13 and Rotavirus vaccines is expected to significantly reduce under-5 mortality. 
UNICEF supported the expansion of the Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS) to 200 facilities, with 78 per cent offering nutrition services. Approximately 7.5 per cent of outpatient consultations reported in the District Health Information System (DHIS2) were in UNICEF-supported facilities.  
In 2024, UNICEF contributed to notable improvements in malaria and HIV support. Malaria treatment coverage marginally increased, with 92 per cent of cases receiving first-line treatment in 2024, up from 91 per cent in 2023 (DHIS2). HIV services were integrated into 100 facilities, though the proportion of pregnant women living with HIV receiving ART decreased from 37 per cent in 2023 to 32 per cent in 2024 based on program data collected from the health facilities providing PMTCT services. 
UNICEF also supported the development of the Social and Behavior Change Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn Child and Adolescent Health strategy, linked to the RMNCAH strategy launched in 2024. These strategies aim to expand access to quality RMNCAH services and promote key health behaviors. 
In response to emergencies, UNICEF provided lifesaving services to nearly one million people, including over 430,000 children, and enhanced emergency preparedness to strengthen health system resilience. Support for the DHIS-2 system and the development of an electronic logistics information system helped improve supply management. 
UNICEF focused on system strengthening and continued improving healthcare infrastructure in Somalia. UNICEF equipped three newly constructed District Hospitals in Puntland, serving 1.5 million people, and installed eight oxygen plants across Somalia greatly enhancing capacity to provide critical care and support for children and communities in need, ensuring better access to essential medical services. Furthermore, UNICEF installed 379 Solar Direct Drive units increasing functional cold chain-equipped facilities from 959 in 2023 to 1,117 in 2024. UNICEF’s capacity injection supported a total of 2,198 health staff, enhancing health information management, supply chain systems, vaccine management, and health service delivery in the ministries of health and public health facilities. 
To address gender barriers in immunization, as part of the Gender Programme Review, UNICEF conducted an immunization gender barrier analysis to understand the influence of social norms and power dynamics on vaccination patterns. This evidence is guiding the redesign of gender responsive immunization interventions in the country. 
High prevalence malnutrition among young children, pregnant and lactating mothers remains a public health issue in Somalia. UNICEF continues to enhance the enabling environment for large-scale implementation of high-impact nutrition interventions, facilitate service delivery and coordinate the nutrition sector. UNICEF’s support to delivery of various nutrition services contributed to reducing wasting among under five years’ old children, from 12.3 per cent in 2023 to 11.7 per cent in 2024. However, wasting among young children remains above the World Health Organization emergency threshold (15 per cent) in 29 of the 74 districts.  
To protect and promote optimum breastfeeding, UNICEF supported the revision of the Code for Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes, including its translation in Somali language, making it ready for endorsement by the Parliament.  
Working with 39 implementing partners, UNICEF contributed to providing quality treatment to 481,423 children aged 6-59 months (51 per cent girls) for severe wasting through a network of 700 treatment sites, thanks to existing mechanisms to ensure early case detection and referrals, timely treatment, uninterrupted availability of supplies, well-trained and well-supervised workforce. In 2024, UNICEF supported human capital development of 900 health and nutrition workers and 3,000 community health workers to deliver quality Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) services.  Nutrition service delivery points in Somalia emerged as trusted platforms for delivery of integrated Health, Nutrition, WASH and Child Protection services. 
UNICEF contributed to enhance the knowledge of 1,862,262 caretakers of children aged 6 to 23 months (146 per cent) on appropriate Infant and Young Child Feeding and care practices along with hygiene and sanitation, through a network of 3,000 skilled counsellors. Young children’s resistance to infections was enhanced through a vitamin A supplementation campaign, reaching 3,589,888 (106 per cent) children 6-59 months (51 per cent girls) in 70 out of the 74 districts. Likewise, 1,882,970 children aged 12 to 59 months (960,314 girls) were treated for worms’ infestations in 60 out of the 74 districts and 460,253 pregnant and breastfeeding women (51 per cent of target) received multiple micronutrients supplement (MMS). The implementation of the maternal nutrition acceleration plan will contribute to further increase MMS coverage. In Gedo region, 22,780 young children (38 per cent of target), were reached with micronutrients powder supplementation to enhance their micronutrient status. UNICEF is supporting on a modest scale (200 households) the promotion of one egg per child per day in addition to the promotion of kitchen garden. A formative study to understand the diet related social norms and behaviors of adolescent girls is ongoing in three districts, to inform the design of Social and Behavior Change actions plan, linking with weekly Iron Folate supplementation and gender-based violence prevention among the adolescent girls in 2025.  
To mitigate aid diversion and its impact, UNICEF is championing the digitization of nutrition registers, to address inefficiencies, improve treatment quality, and link nutrition information to the Health Information System. In addition, UNICEF is spearheading the Last Mile Supply Monitoring (LMSM), another digital solution to enhance management of nutrition supplies. Thanks to UNICEF’s advocacy and support, government issued regulations criminalizing aid diversion across the country, and implementing partners demonstrated notable advancements in strengthening enabling environments to counter aid diversion risks, with 100 per cent of partners having anti-fraud and anti-corruption policies, and 50 per cent adopting specific aid diversion protocols. 

Goal 2: Learns 
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in improving access to quality pre-primary and primary education across Somalia, especially for children from marginalized and crisis-affected communities. Through a combination of targeted interventions, UNICEF tackled critical bottlenecks, expanded educational opportunities, and improved learning outcomes, focusing on systemic barriers that hindered educational access and equity. 
UNICEF contributed to the increase in the national primary education enrollment rate. The gross enrollment rate (GER) for the Federal Government of Somalia rose from 31 per cent in 2023 to 33.8 per cent in 2024. Enrollment in Somaliland and Puntland increased to 39.3 per cent and 33 per cent, in 2024, respectively. In addition, strengthening the Education Management Information Systems (EMIS) enabled a decentralized evidence-based decision-making, empowering regional offices to collect and input data, thus improving accuracy, and ensuring that local decision-makers had the information they needed to plan equitably. 
Part of its convening role, UNICEF co-chairing the sector coordination at Federal and Somaliland governments, and led the humanitarian cluster, gender equality and children with disabilities were enhanced in these fora and interconnected with the Education Donor Group. 
Results were achieved in access to education, particularly for children in remote areas and conflict zones. 365 primary classrooms across Somalia were rehabilitated creating safer and more conducive learning environments for 18,250 school going children, mostly those out-of-school children (OOSC) in crisis-affected communities. Social media was utilized in Puntland, engaging graphics, videos, testimonials, hashtags like #GoBackToSchool and #EducationMatters sparked widespread community interest and participation, and encouraged parents. 
Improving educational opportunities for young children focused on supporting Early Childhood Education (ECE) at Federal Government level through the finalization of teaching and learning material development. Also, 12 new ECE centers in Galmudug and 24 in Puntland were established benefiting thousands of young learners, aiming at girls. In Puntland, ECE programs were integrated into 12 primary schools across five districts reaching 3,342 children. These initiatives made it easier for preschool-aged children to attend school in their communities where the capacity of 84 Community Education Committee (CEC) members and 120 stakeholders engaged to increase community awareness emphasized on the importance of early learning. 
Improving the quality of education was central to UNICEF’s work in Somalia.
