UNICEF trained 4,006 primary teachers (1,015 women) focused on child-centered pedagogy, inclusive practices for children with disabilities, and classroom management in crisis-affected areas. An additional 66 teachers were trained, and the Girls' Education Forum was piloted in 30 schools, creating supportive environments to encourage girls’ participation in education. 44 master trainers and 795 teachers were trained as part of the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) pilot.  
Inclusivity in education was another major focus for UNICEF. The establishment of a Children with Disabilities advisory board in all states contributed to the development of an education roadmap aiming at integrating children with disabilities into the education system.  
On learning outcomes, UNICEF conducted Measuring Learning Assessments (MLA) in Puntland, focusing on literacy and numeracy in Grades 3 and 7. Valuable data on the effectiveness of educational interventions will contribute to shaping future programming. The TaRL approach for literacy and numeracy skills for children who were at risk of falling behind saw 18,919 (8,993 girls) children successfully completing the pilot.  
Crisis resilience remained a priority for UNICEF to ensure education continued for 68,676 (31,775 girls) vulnerable children in crisis-affected areas. UNICEF helped education officials in Somalia by building their capacity to monitor out-of-school children and maintain education services during emergencies.  The integrated approach—focused on data generation, human capacity development and inclusive education made substantial contributions to addressing educational barriers, increasing enrollment, and improving learning outcomes.  

Goal 3: Protection 
With UNICEF support, in September 2024, the Somalia Government launched the National Plan of Action (NPA) for Children 2024 to 2029, prioritizing the domestication of the Convention of the Rights of the Child (CRC) and application of 2022 CRC Committee recommendations to Somalia. The Government pledged the implementation of the NPA, to ratify the African Charter for the Rights and the Welfare of the Child and the enactment of the Child Rights Bill on November 8, 2024, at the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children. To reinforce Somalia’s adherence to international conventions, UNICEF supported Somalia’s participation at the March 2024 Human Rights Committee (HRC) on the report of Somalia on the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The HRC review focused on issues including access to justice, women and girl’s rights, the rights of persons with disabilities, and the impact of conflict on human rights.   
On 30 March 2024, Somalia's Federal Parliament adopted amendments to the Provisional Constitution on the prohibition of all types of female genital mutilation (FGM) and the definition of a child as a person under 18 years, preventing potential child rights abuses and adherence to international human rights standards.  
The country has seen other positive developments in protecting girls and women from FGM with Galmudug State enacting their own FGM Bill in February 2024 and therefore setting an example and pathway for other Federal Member States (FMS) to follow. Draft anti-FGM laws are under consultation in all other FMS while an anti-FGM policy was adopted in Somaliland. FMS are reviewing draft Child Rights Bills while Federal level Government is planning to resubmit their draft Child Rights Bill. UNICEF provided technical and financial support for the review of key child rights draft legislations as well as for consultations while sustaining advocacy at technical and principal levels for adherence to the CRC.   
UNICEF supported evidence generation to improve understanding of child protection sector needs including a study on Children in Conflict with Law carried out by UNICEF and the Federal Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs (MoJCA) to assess the situation of children in detention, the procedures for criminal cases involving children, and resource and capacity gaps. An assessment on UNICEF Somalia’s UPSHIFT program effectiveness showed that female led businesses exhibited higher profitability and higher business survival rate than male led businesses. A mapping of Quranic schools and their child safe-guarding policies in place was conducted with the Ministry of Endowment and Religious Affairs. Less than 2 per cent of the schools reviewed had safeguarding procedures in place signaling the need for oversight and establishing protocols.    
To address grave violations against children, UNICEF implemented the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanisms (MRM) in line with Security Council Resolution (SCR) 1612. Between January and September 2024, 1,946 grave violations against children were documented, impacting 1,478 children (1,057 boys 421 girls). This includes recruitment and use, sexual violence, abduction, killing and maiming, attacks on schools and hospitals and denial of humanitarian access. UNICEF worked with civil society partners to facilitate child victims' access to services and with the Government to increase accountability mechanisms and improve protective environment through stronger policy.   
To support children impacted by humanitarian crisis including displacement because of climate induced emergencies or conflict, UNICEF is supporting a large network of civil society organizations to implement child protection and gender-based violence prevention and response programming across the country. 

Goal 4: Safe and Clean Environment 
Somalia has made tremendous progress in terms of improving access to basic water services as access increased from a mere 30 per cent (JMP) in 2004 to 71 per cent (UNICEF Needs Assessment) in 2024.  As access to basic water services increased drastically, there is a need to cross ‘the last mile’ and reach the 29 per cent of the population that still does not have access, most notably in rural areas. Successes in basic water coverage can now be translated into elaborating and implementing a safely managed water service strategy, the last step of the SDG water ladder. 
In terms of sanitation, progress has been made in the elimination of open defecation as national rates have decreased from 51 per cent in 2004 to 16 per cent in 2024. Improvements in basic sanitation have however been only marginal as coverage only increased from 23 per cent in 2004 to 39 per cent in 2024. These numbers generally mean that communities are halting the harmful practice of open defecation but are not ‘moving up’ the sanitation ladder to basic access. There is therefore a need to design and scale up a workable model for basic sanitation, most notably in rural areas.  
In 2024, UNICEF played a crucial role in contributing to the above results by strengthening the enabling environment for the sector, delivering WASH services to communities and institutions, as well as providing humanitarian WASH support.  
UNICEF provided both technical and financial support to federal and state-level Ministries of Energy and Water Resources to develop various strategies, Policies and Plans. Through this support, the Ministry of Energy and Water Resources at the federal level has strengthened the Water Sector Coordination Facility (WSCF) to improve sector governance, facilitate alignment of sector programs, and coordinate interventions. In 2024, UNICEF also supported a Nationwide WASH Needs Assessment to measure current WASH access as per the SDG 6 ladder at national level with a disaggregation at District level. In addition, at member state level, UNICEF supported the elaboration of the Somaliland National WASH Strategic Plan (2025-2029), the Puntland Public Private Partnership Policy and the first ever sustainability check in Somalia (conducted in Puntland). 
To improve WASH in communities, 29 new boreholes were drilled, and 62 existing boreholes were rehabilitated and upgraded with solar power pumping systems to reduce GHG emissions and lower operation and maintenance costs, while 200 shallow wells in rural areas were rehabilitated and disinfected. UNICEF has undertaken innovative new approaches to groundwater mapping, utilizing remote sensing to develop a sustainable groundwater map, which has supported exploratory drilling of the deepest well in Somalia, with positive results found at depths greater than 700 meters.  
The UNICEF WASH programme continued to provide critical life-saving humanitarian interventions throughout the year 2024, through the provision of safe drinking water, adequate sanitation and the promotion of appropriate hygiene practices. UNICEF supported 915,722 people with means to practice safe hygiene and household water treatment through the distribution of Hygiene kits and hygiene promotion messaging.  

Goal 5: Equitable Chance in Life  
The year was marked by the development of the National Transformation Plan 2025–2029 (NTP). UNICEF through its partnerships with the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) provided critical technical and financial support for these initiatives. UNICEF also worked with the Somalia National Bureau of Statistics to generate child-sensitive indicators data on results of the National Development Plan (NDP-9). Despite these efforts, funding gaps delayed the completion of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), limiting further influence on planning processes. Pending the first draft of NTP, investments in maternal health, nutrition, education, WASH, and social protection are likely to be central to government in the next five-year plan. 
The federal budget continued to increase allocations to social sectors, particularly social protection, health, and education. UNICEF’s budget briefs and bottleneck analyses for government programmes provided evidence of the role of these initiatives in enhancing social expenditure for children. The fiscal space created by Somalia’s 2023 debt relief holds potential for improving children’s well-being, provided that the execution of externally funded social sector projects improves. UNICEF has offered actionable measures to support progress. 
UNICEF’s Child Sensitive Social Protection Programme (CSSP-I) phase I accelerated in 2024 and reached 27,700 pregnant and lactating mothers and phase-II made progress on expanding to an additional 13,500 in early 2025. Children’s access to social services delivered by local governments was impacted by the transition, between the UN Joint Programme in Local Governance and Decentralized Service Delivery, which ended in September 2023, and the new UN Joint Programme Dowlad-Kaab, which began in October 2024. It is notable that this period marked the first instance of district-level provision of basic social services using local resources after the cessation of UN support. UNICEF played a key role in influencing the design of Dowlad-Kaab and supporting MoIFAR’s engagement with development partners. MoIFAR acknowledged UNICEF’s leadership in ensuring the continuity of UN support to building local government capacity.  

Programme and Operational Effectiveness 
In 2024, as part of Aid Diversion risk mitigation measures and the realization of UNICEF ‘s Global strategy on digitalization, UNICEF Somalia in collaboration with UNICEF Supply Division and the Office of Innovation rolled out the Last Mile Supply Monitoring Module (LMSM), a supply tracking and monitoring system that will revolutionize the logistics management of supplies in Somalia. Digitalization will ensure efficiency in tracking supplies reaching children in the most remote areas of the country. The increased visibility in the supply chain will contribute to mitigate aid diversions by making it easier to identify potential red flags and to address them at the earliest. As part of human capital development efforts, UNICEF successfully built capacity of 890 users from 54 implementing partners on LMSM, including government representatives spread across Banadir Administrative Area, Southwest, Hirshabelle, Jubaland, Galmudug, Puntland and Somaliland.  
In 2024, UNICEF services reached over two million women, men and children that faced multiple shocks and hazards, working with humanitarian clusters of WASH, Nutrition, Education and Child Protection to collectively respond to the Cholera outbreak, El-Nino flooding, displacement, and conflict and ensure children were kept alive, thrived, safe and were learning. UNICEF reached 9,256,447 people with timely life-saving information engaging 1,500,000 people through community-based platforms. A total of 4,4847,681 people utilized safe and trusted feedback mechanisms while 141,000 users signed up for the U-Report platform. UNICEF co-led inter-agency coordination platforms for Risk Communication and Community Engagement and Accountability to Affected Populations. UNICEF reached 3 million people with key messages through social media platforms, engaged high level political leaders on immunization and child survival, and contributed to parliament’s adoption of the Disability Bill.  
UNICEF Somalia conducted a comprehensive Gender Programme Review (GPR) which revealed that partners had positive experiences with UNICEF, aligning well with national gender priorities. The findings from the GPR will be used for enhancing gender responsive programming in Somalia and meeting the priorities of the Gender Action Plan (GAP).  
Through a partnership with the Ministry of Planning, Investment & Economic Development (MOPIED), UNICEF Somalia proactively spearheaded support towards enhancing the public sector evaluation policy framework through the development of the federal level Evaluation Guidelines. The evaluation guidelines will assist the Somalia Federal government to conduct quality evaluations based on valid and reliable empirical evidence, ultimately contributing to improved decision making and accountability to not only the donors but also its citizenry. UNICEF supported the development of the evaluation curriculum which will support evaluative skills enhancement in the public sector.  This is relevant to the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the national development plans as assessing their progress draws significant attention to availability of evaluative evidence. Furthermore, UNICEF supported MoPIED to convene the first ever National Conference on Monitoring and Evaluation bringing together stakeholders from the government, development sector, academia, and the UN. 
UNICEF Somalia commissioned a Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) Joint Risk Assessment (JRA) in Somalia to establish a national SEA risk baseline, assess intervention needs, and evaluate the capacities of national and international actors in mitigating SEA risks. The assessment, covering key regions across Somalia, provided crucial insights into SEA dynamics in humanitarian and development contexts. Findings will be presented to the UN Humanitarian Country Team in January 2025, by the UN Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary General (DSRSG) in Somalia.

In 2024, UNICEF leveraged a wide range of external resources and partnerships with Government at all levels, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), CSOs, the United Nations system, international financial institutions, and other public and private partners. Flexible funding enabled UNICEF to programme quickly and effectively, while strong collaboration contributed to critical joint advocacy and strategic steer. 
Federal, state, and sub-state Government cooperation was key in furthering the child rights agenda across sectors, including close collaboration with the Office of the Prime Minister and line ministries, departments, and agencies and Parliament. For example, in 2024, UNICEF collaborated with Parliament and signed a work plan, to ensure an enabling environment is created to accelerate scaling up of basic social services required for the child to survive, grow, thrive, and learn. In, 2024, UNICEF and WHO ramped up advocacy for Child Survival and Immunization in Somalia. The Prime Minister’s launch of the Immunization and Polio Eradication Taskforce and the high-level Forum on Child Survival marked a pivotal step towards reducing child mortality. UNICEF and WHO supported the Federal Ministry of Health (FMOH) in reviewing the World Health Assembly resolution to accelerate progress on maternal, newborn, and child health SDG targets. These efforts will have a substantial impact on improving health outcomes of children in Somalia. 
As a key partner in the Global Polio Eradication Initiative, UNICEF, alongside WHO, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the US Centre for Disease Control (CDC), bolsters Somalia's efforts to enhance routine immunization and manage the polio outbreak. A task force, chaired by the Prime Minister, was established, with UNICEF leading state-level advocacy. The first round of the "Big Catch Up" campaign was launched in all six states by their respective presidents, with strong support from professional associations and Islamic religious networks. UNICEF's collaboration with other UN agencies, including WHO and UNFPA, has been vital in developing key Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health policies and strategies. 
UNICEF collaboration with sister UN agencies has been pivotal in advancing resource mobilization through developing joint advocacy documents, such as the La Niña preparedness plan, which successfully secured $2 million in emergency funding for UNICEF's WASH initiatives. Coordinating joint UN proposals throughout the year, fostering greater technical understanding among respective agencies, identifying complementary areas, and enabling more strategic resource mobilization and engagement. UNICEF is also in the process of securing its first ever African Development Bank Funding for an urban WASH program and has been working with the United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) on the design of a blended financing facility for the WASH sector. 
UNICEF participated in numerous programme and operations coordination platforms in Somalia, including holding several leadership roles, such as co-chairing the United Nations Country Task Force on Monitoring and Reporting with UNSOM. The Task Force operationalizes the monitoring and reporting mechanism on grave violations to contribute to making Somalia a safer environment for children by documenting grave violations, including information to enable responsive action by the relevant parties that can range from informing advocacy to guiding programme scope.  
UNICEF’s partnership with the Global Partnership for Education was key to strengthening education systems in Puntland and improved student retention and learning outcomes. Germany’s KfW Development Bank collaboration enabled education as a platform to achieve multi-sector resilience results in Jubaland, and the successful scale-up of the programme in Galkayo through the UN Joint Resilience Programme. The Partnership with Global Affairs Canada supported progress on education outcomes for adolescent girls and children with disabilities. Another critical UNICEF partnership was with Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) Africa and the Africa Educational Trust, which began providing multi-year technical support to Government counterparts and civil society partners to introduce TaRL as a pedagogical package in internally displaced persons sites, and several districts in Somaliland. UNICEF, the Government of Finland, and KfW Development Bank contributed to programme. 
Collaboration with partners through the humanitarian cluster mechanism supported the delivery of quality programme results at scale for children affected by emergencies.  In 2024, UNICEF co-led the Nutrition Cluster with WFP, the WASH Cluster with Polish Humanitarian Action and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility and the Education Cluster with Save the Children International. In addition to coordination, UNICEF’s cluster-dedicated staff support quality information management to support evidence-based response. UNICEF also participated in additional clusters and sub-clusters, adding value by contributing strategic advice, convening support and technical assistance. This participation included Logistics Cluster engagement that helped to achieve results such as identifying solutions to support local procurement and supply transportation for emergency response. 
Working with coalitions of partners, including international and local NGOs; community-based organizations; and civil society, including affected populations, was particularly important to ensure implementation of UNICEF programming. For example, these partnerships were critical in furthering the localization agenda, with UNICEF collaborating to build the capacity of national and subnational partners.  They were also essential in responding to public health emergencies in 2024, Communities impacted by emergencies and recipients of UNICEF support provided crucial input via feedback mechanisms to improve programming and service delivery.   
UNICEF collaborated with other United Nations agencies on UNSDCF implementation, including participating in the United Nations Country Team and joint initiatives.  These included the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), International Labour Organization (ILO), IOM, UNFPA, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat), United Nations Multi-Partner Trust Fund Office, UNSOM, WFP and WHO. Implementation of the WFP–UNICEF joint nutrition action plan addressed wasting and other nutrition needs, such as by strengthening referrals to care for children in hard-to-reach districts; the UNICEF–UNSOM Joint Programme on Human Rights Phase 2 reinforced actions on child protection, supporting Somalia's commitments to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. The Joint Programme on the Elimination of FGM and joint programming on community-based reintegration for displaced people also supported results for children. UNICEF partnered with UNDP, UN-Habitat, on the United Nations Joint Programme on new Local Governance Programme, the revamped Dowlad-Kaab initiative to strengthen community resilience through economic development and improved government operations. The KfW-supported Joint Resilience Programme Phase II in Puntland and South-Central and Somalia with FAO and WFP delivered important integrated multi-sectoral results for children in 2024. 
United Nations system partnerships were also critical for facilitation of humanitarian assessments, response, monitoring, reporting and evaluations. This collaboration, as well as engagement with affected populations, was key to reducing the risk of and addressing aid diversion in 2024, while UNICEF’s regular dialogue on aid diversion with Government officials and donors was key to addressing its systematic drivers.  
UNICEF results  were supported by bilateral, multilateral and private sector donors,  including the Directorate-General for European Civil Protection and  Humanitarian Aid Operations; European Union; Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance; Germany’s GIZ and KfW Development Bank; the Global  Partnership for Education; the Governments of Canada, Denmark, Finland, Japan, Norway and Sweden; Kingdom of  Saudi Arabia; the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development  Office; the World Bank; and the United States  Agency for International  Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance.  UNICEF National Committees also contributed to child protection, education, nutrition, social protection, and WASH programming results, while a variety of funds enabled scaled-up efforts, including the Central Emergency Response Fund; Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; Somali Joint Fund; U.S. Fund for UNICEF; and United Nations Peacebuilding Fund. 
UNICEF engaged donors to gain firsthand experience by facilitating field visits, accompanying them, and maintaining a robust, consistent, and prompt communication channel and through in-person interactions to reinforce transparency. In 2024 UNICEF engaged donors through roundtable meetings with participation from key donor partners. These events were instrumental in addressing concerns about aid diversion while fostering open, transparent, and constructive dialogues with donors.

The year 2024 was marked by a series of critical geopolitical shifts and rising economic pressures that had an impact on UNICEF’s ability to deliver on its mission, including in Somalia. Global challenges, from increased nationalism and populism to economic turbulence and emerging conflicts, are reshaping the funding landscape. As donor priorities continue to shift, funding levels and flexibility are decreasing, with many countries repurposing Official Development Assistance (ODA) toward defense and domestic priorities and decreasing funding for programming. This anticipated reduced funding landscape shaped UNICEF’s donor engagement and resource mobilization efforts. 

The environment in which the UNICEF programme is being implemented is constrained by several challenges affecting service availability, access and its uptake, quality of care at facility, community or at household level. These include insecurity, ongoing conflicts, violence and instability; acceleration of climate change, resulting in repeated droughts and floods that negatively impact on disease pattern, diets and feeding practices, especially among the most vulnerable young children; population displacement; large scale humanitarian aid diversion; frequent disease outbreaks; limited government capacity to lead and coordinate programmes; fragmented enabling environment to scale up high impact cost-effective nutrition interventions; inadequate budget and capacity to scale up interventions.  

Furthermore, lack of up-to-date population-based data which informs measurement of programme results from surveys such as the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) which has significantly delayed due to resource constraints, has limited assessment of key outcome and impact indicators making it difficult to assess progress against the implementation National Development Plans and SDG targets. To address the challenges of population-based data to measure progress at impact level, UNICEF will prioritize supporting the Somali National Bureau of Statistics to complete the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7).  
The nutrition sector in Somalia faces challenges with large-scale RUTF leakage and misuse, despite efforts to address aid diversion. Continued efforts, agile programming, innovations, and strong government-led frameworks are needed to mitigate these issues. However, the slow evolution of institutional frameworks hampers sustainable outcomes. Advocacy and technical support to develop government capacity to mitigate aid diversion remain priorities. To reduce malnutrition among young children, UNICEF will adjust its strategy to ensure the availability of and access to nutritious food. Somalia will adopt the First Food Africa concept, promoting context-specific nutritious foods. UNICEF's internal strategy focuses on positive messaging to combat donor fatigue and address aid diversion concerns. A significant achievement in rebuilding donor trust was UNICEF Somalia's milestone in digitalization, supported by donors like BHA. 

In 2024, significant progress was made at the national level to address maternal and child mortality in Somalia. The expansion of the Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS) accelerated, with UNICEF's Better Lives Project playing a crucial role. However, delays in the Damaal Caafimad Project hindered progress in immunization coverage, antenatal care, and skilled birth attendance. The donor-dependent fiscal space limits the scale and equity of health service delivery, especially in newly accessible areas. High level joint advocacy will be required for domestic resource allocation to enhance coverage of MNCH interventions. By implementing a district-level health and nutrition service delivery model, UNICEF achieved cost savings of 22 per cent in health and 12 per cent in nutrition, enabling broader coverage with available resources. The high number of "zero-dose" children remains a significant challenge. A cross-sectoral approach, leveraging nutrition treatment sites for vaccination and strengthened partnerships with WHO and other INGOs, has shown promising initial results. However, reaching children in remote areas requires innovative access and monitoring strategies. Lack of updated catchment population compounded with weak data and oversight in these areas continue to impede targeted initiative. Collaboration with key health sector partners, including UN agencies and donors, has aligned resources around priority actions. Strengthened subnational coordination structures are critical for effective implementation.
  
UNICEF has expanded its presence at the state level in Somalia, improving oversight and support to state ministries. This has enhanced resource alignment and laid the groundwork for stronger systems. High-level advocacy, particularly in immunization and Polio Eradication, has provided momentum for broader child survival initiatives, focusing on primary health care, nutrition, WASH, and health promotion. The private sector's role in delivering services like immunization is being integrated into broader health sector planning. Justice for children in Somalia remains underfunded. Despite UNICEF's advocacy, the Puntland Government executed four young people arrested as children for crimes allegedly committed as children in August 2024. UNICEF expressed concern and advocated for preventing similar executions in the future. UNICEF is also advocating for children associated with armed forces to be treated as victims needing care and support rather than detention. With only three percent of children registered at birth and significant displacement due to conflict and climate emergencies, it is crucial for children to have identity documents, especially birth certificates, to protect them from rights violations. UNICEF uses Regular Resources to support child protection system strengthening, including birth registration, but additional donor resources are needed to make lasting changes. 
 
In 2024, the Education Sector faced significant challenges due to reduced resources, ongoing conflict, and seasonal rainfall, which disrupted the delivery of critical education programs, especially in remote and underserved regions. Limited capacity for school supervision led to gaps in data on enrollment and attendance, and the implementation of the federal teacher policy was weak, particularly in attracting and distributing female teachers to remote areas. UNICEF's future approach will focus on resilience-building in response to climate change. This includes increasing engagement with Ministries of Education to expand access to education for marginalized groups, such as girls and children with disabilities. Efforts will involve scaling up Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) and inclusive education initiatives, providing targeted support to ensure these children are not left behind.  
 
Supported by HQ Innovation Fund, UNICEF Somalia completed a groundwater mapping study in Somaliland and Puntland, identifying potential climate-resilient aquifers. A test borehole in Qarxis, Puntland, is the deepest ever drilled in Somalia at 750 meters. Additional boreholes are planned for 2025, potentially providing high-quality, resilient water sources for these communities. 
Successes in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) utility management models in urban water supply, combined with a strong private sector and willingness to pay for water, make Somalia's water sector ripe for blended financing. UNICEF is working with the UNCDF to design a facility to de-risk investments and encourage financial flows from the private sector and lending institutions. There is also potential for PPPs in rural water management, which UNICEF will explore further. Progress in basic sanitation has been slow, prompting a re-examination of current approaches. UNICEF will explore new options like City-Wide Inclusive Sanitation and improved Community Approaches to Total Sanitation, supported by sanitation marketing strategies and menstrual hygiene management approaches.  
 
Social protection efforts faced setbacks in 2024. Since its inception in 2019, the Baxnaano programme, which UNICEF and WFP supports, has provided regular cash transfers to 200,000 households, with last payment completed in June 2024. The Ministry of Labor and Social Services was to pilot new initiatives using government delivery systems supported by UNICEF, and World Bank investments were to be informed by these pilots but did not materialize in 2024. In a context like Somalia, where most services depend heavily on external funding, programme transitions pose a significant risk to achieving results for children. Nevertheless, the efforts to build state capabilities and deliver services through government structures, despite short-term gaps and challenges, represent a sustainable pathway to improving children’s lives in the medium and long term. Continued support for capacity building and investments in human capital will be essential to achieving lasting progress for Somali children.  

With 2024 marking the fourth year of the current five-year UNICEF Somalia Country Programme, UNICEF engaged relevant stakeholders including children and communities in consultations at Federal and Member State levels to develop the theory of change for the next country programme (2026-2030) and subsequently convened a national Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR) in October 2024 with key Government partners, other UN agencies, donors, non-governmental partners at which UNICEF and partners agreed on priority programme areas to focus on, in the next country programme to adequately instigate systemic change. Looking ahead to 2025 and beyond, UNICEF plans to apply the insights gained throughout 2024 from the SMR and the 2024 Annual Review by scaling up multi sectoral programme integration to increase the reach and scope of social services, especially prioritizing underserved communities while continuing strengthening subnational capacities, including human capital development to ensure equity and resilience are at the center of programming to realize results for children. In 2025, UNICEF in collaboration with Government and partners, will finalise the next Country Programme (2026-2030) in alignment with the forthcoming National Transformation Plan (2025-2029) priorities, the Somalia UNSDCF (2026–2030) and the Africa Strategy (Agenda 2063).

In 2024, South Africa marked 30 years of democracy with the country having undergone significant political, economic, and social transformations, while still facing numerous challenges including economic inequality, youth unemployment, poor service delivery, and political disenchantment. 

According to the Sustainable Development Goals Country Report 2023, South Africa has made significant progress in education, healthcare, water, sanitation, electricity, and gender equality. However, it continues to face substantial difficulties in addressing poverty, inequality, and unemployment. To achieve the SDGs, South Africa urgently needs to focus on high-impact interventions to reduce inequalities, such as upskilling the workforce with a focus on youth, and monitoring and advocating for allocation and efficient utilization of resources in the social sectors -all crucial to support the acceleration of progress towards 20230 targets. 

The National election was held on 29 May 2024 and for the first time since 1994, the African National Congress (ANC) lost its parliamentary majority, and this has reconfigured the country’s political architecture with the forming of a coalition Government of National Unity. The impact that this will have on the child rights agenda in the country has yet to be seen. 
South Africa continued to play an active role within the BRICS bloc in 2024, positioning itself as a representative of the Global South in economic and political discussions, including an influential role in the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its stance on Palestine. On 1 December 2024, South Africa assumed the G20 Presidency – the first African nation ever to do so - presenting an opportunity to influence global discussions on a wide range of issues that are important to the SADC region, the African continent, and the Global South. The G20 provides a strategic opportunity for UNICEF to advance the child rights agenda as reflected in the “UNICEF contribution to Africa’s development agendas, recently adopted by the Executive Board of UNICEF (E/ICEF/2024/32). 

In 2024, South Africa witnessed an ongoing reduction in government revenues (Rand 22.3 billion less than predicted by Budget 2024), high national debt servicing costs, (roughly 21% of every Rand collected), and stubborn unemployment levels. A contraction in GDP over the year some 1.3% economic growth predicted by Budget 2024 versus the 1.1% projected in the MTBPS 2024, has forced households to reduce their spending on items such as transport, recreation, and housing utilities[1]. In addition, the unemployment rate remains one of the highest in the world, with the youth unemployment rate reaching alarming levels at just over 45%[2]. 
Child poverty remained high, with 33% of children living below the extreme food poverty line and nearly half of all children below the ‘Lower Bound Poverty Line’. In addition, inequality levels hit a record Gini Per Capita Income Index high of 0.67, a rise of three points since the official 2015 estimates.[3]

Inequality varies widely among provinces and population groups with larger-sized, female-headed, and households headed by younger persons, as well as household heads with low levels of education being much poorer in comparison to others. These are also households with the largest percentage of children.

The latest 2022 Census released in November 2023, revealed a population increase of roughly 1.6 percent on average for the last twelve years, raising the overall population from 52 million to 62 million individuals. Of this population, two cohorts of children, particularly those living in ‘at-risk’ areas and homes, continued to be of particular concern. This includes children starting on their first 1,000 days of life, and adolescents, aged 10-19 years. These two groups – children and adolescents aged 0 – 19 -represent 34.4 percent of the population.[4]

Health System Strain: South Africa's public healthcare system continued to face challenges in 2024, exacerbated by funding constraints, health workforce shortages, and inequalities in healthcare access between urban and rural areas. The COVID-19 pandemic revealed deep flaws in the system, and while there were efforts to improve the quality of care, especially for the poor, the system remained overburdened.
Under-five mortality rates increased in recent years, reaching 40 per 1,000 live births in 2022, which is concerning as nearly a decade of progress has been lost. In addition, a sharp rise in zero-dose children suggests that a significant proportion of the under-1-year population is vulnerable to vaccine-preventable diseases, although the country has successfully introduced the measles and rubella, tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis, and birth-dose Hepatitis B vaccines in 2024[5].

Over 1,7 million children are stunted (meaning 3 out of 10 children are short for their age) and though rates have remained largely consistent for the past 30 years, there was a slight increase from 27% in 2016 to 29% in 2024[6]. The prevalence of wasting in children has however doubled from 2.5% in 2016 to 5%6 in 2024 with 219,200 children wasted according to the Joint Malnutrition Estimates (2023). South Africa is amongst the top ten countries globally with the highest number of children under 5 affected by severe wasting. In addition, overweight and obesity levels have nearly doubled in children under the age of five, from 13% in 2016 to 23% in 2024 while exclusive breastfeeding decreased from 32% to 22%[7].

Impact of Climate Change on Children: Climate change continued to affect South Africa with rising temperatures and increasingly erratic weather patterns. South Africa is at medium to high risk of climate and environmental shocks and childhood vulnerability ranking 72nd among nations in terms of risk, with water scarcity, soil, and water pollution. In South Africa, more than 27 per cent of children under five years of age are already stunted, further underlining the importance of protecting water resources. South Africa is also a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution affects the health and development of children. Toxic air can lead to premature birth and can trigger asthma, childhood cancer and may also increase the risk of chronic diseases later in life.

Despite improvements in access to water, communities, and institutions (schools in particular) struggle with climate-related challenges including droughts and water scarcity as well as poorly maintained WASH infrastructure, leaving many children, especially in rural areas, in unsafe conditions. Poor sanitation leads to high school absenteeism, particularly among girls hence urgent improvements in WASH services are needed to protect children's health and well-being.

Challenges in Education: The education sector continued to face significant challenges in 2024. Of particular concern is that 81% of Grade 4 children cannot read for meaning.[8] In addition, despite the approval of the National Coding & Robotics Curriculum in 2024, shortages of resources and qualified teachers are hindering the rollout, also considering that half of existing teachers will retire by 2030.

Public schools, particularly in rural areas, struggled with overcrowded classrooms, inadequate facilities, and a lack of qualified teachers. Quality early childhood development is still limited, yet access to education up to lower-secondary level, including one year before primary, remains high. About 37.7 per cent of children aged birth-to-4 years attended an ECD programme (i.e., ECD centres, and child minders / day mothers). Recognizing the need for greater coordination around ECD, the DBE announced South Africa’s 2030 Strategy for Early Childhood Development Programmes as to fully integrate early learning (ECD) within the basic education system. The education system is marked by inequity and remains affected by one’s circumstances at birth and socio-economic status with learners from poor households dependent on Government grants for school completion. More investment and upgrading of the education system including narrowing the digital divide and strong partnerships with the private sector is required to improve learner outcomes. 

Gender-based Violence and Persistent Crime Rates: Gender-based violence continued to plague South Africa in 2024. According to the latest Crime Statistics, children account for 40% of total sexual offences reported in the fiscal year 2022/2023. Rape is the highest reported crime against children (38%), followed by common assault (25.8%) in 2022/2023. While child abuse affects children below 3 years most, sexual offences, murder, assaults, and kidnapping mostly affect adolescent children [9].

The prevalence of women who experience any physical and sexual intimate partner violence (IPV) in their lifetime is 23.9 %, which represents 3.4 million women in the country. Childhood trauma is also a critical factor associated with both survivors and perpetuators of IPVs, including exposures to violence at home. [10] 
Despite difficulties faced in 2024, there is a sense of hope among many South Africans that the country can overcome its challenges. South Africa’s success will depend on how it addresses its ongoing inequalities, builds more inclusive economic opportunities, and strengthens democratic institutions.

In 2024, results for children in South Africa continued to be anchored in the child rights agenda and were achieved through strong partnerships with Government, civil society, academia, and the private sector, including engagement with children and young people.  
Every child, including adolescents, access inclusive social protection and lives free from poverty.
 
UNICEF continued to support in sustaining and increasing the coverage of social protection services for children through evidence generation to close the exclusion error for children who are eligible to receive child support grants, as well as the promotion of a decent standard of living, and raising awareness - through research - on the impact of the cost of basic goods and services on the standard of living for poor households. By the end of October 2024, 13.6 million children, or nearly 66% received the Child Support Grant. UNICEF supported the policy development process and implementation modalities on integrating child grants with other services such as school nutrition and access to basic education. 
 
Results for children continued to be anchored in the child rights agenda through strong partnerships with Government (via convening stakeholders), civil society (capacity development and partnerships), government at sub-national level (strategic advice), academia (evidence generation), and the private sector, including direct engagement and capacity building for children and young people in budget analysis.
 
In 2024, UNICEF engaged in high-level advocacy for children via formal submissions to Parliament and active use of electronic media platforms through UNICEF op-eds. This included the production and dissemination of Budget Briefs on Equity for Children at the local government level and WASH in public schools. These briefs utilized modern research methods such as multiple imputations and marginal benefit incidence analysis to provide an up-to-date statement on equity for children, especially the poorest and most marginalized. The budget briefs formed the backbone of an oral submission that was made to the National Assembly’s Appropriations Committee at the end of the year and will also be disseminated to a wide range of stakeholders in the first quarter of 2025. 
 
Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives in a safe and clean environment.
UNICEF supported the finalization of the National Immunization Strategy that addresses barriers faced by zero-dose children and under-immunized communities. To support the implementation of the strategy, UNICEF worked alongside district administrations to develop project plans, ensuring activities were tailored to each district's specific needs. This led to a 21% reduction in zero-dose children in three districts after 6 months of implementation. UNICEF also contributed to the redefining of the scope of community health workers, including monitoring and evaluation plans.

UNICEF is a member of the National Food System Coordinating Committee that aims to establish an inclusive food system for the country - one that ensures just and equitable livelihoods and provides nutritious food for all while preserving biodiversity and the environment. As part of this area of work, UNICEF supported the National Department of Health with the finalization of the regulations relating to the labelling and advertising of foodstuffs in South Africa, which includes front-of-pack labelling and restrictions of marketing of unhealthy foods to children. National and provincial nutrition managers were capacitated on wasting caseload determination and forecasting of supplies. This will enable provinces to allocate sufficient budget for the continuous availability of nutrition commodities in 2025. 

UNICEF successfully advocated for the inclusion of at least one indicator, namely the early identification of vulnerable children with malnutrition by community health workers, in the District Health Information Systems with advocacy for an indicator on iron and folic acid supplementation for pregnant women still under discussion. 

Over 1.8 million young people were reached with key nutrition messages and 50 empowered to advocate for a healthier food environment using their personal stories which has facilitated direct engagement between youth and policymakers, supporting regulations to prevent obesity. The school food environment was strengthened through modeling evidence-based interventions to improve the school food environment. UNICEF also supported an economic assessment of the national school nutrition programme. 

Based on the assessment, UNICEF supported the Integrated School Health Programme (ISHP), which consolidates nutrition, SRH, maternal health, and parenting services into national service packages. This will be integrated into the responsibilities of community health workers, thereby enhancing comprehensive care and support for young mothers through integrated services.
UNICEF in collaboration with the South African National AIDS Council (SANAC), UNAIDS, WHO, and other partners have successfully institutionalized the Global Alliance (GA) to end AIDS in children by 2030 as one of key achievements of the UN working together in South Africa.  Through the national chapter alliance, there is an increased focus on pediatric HIV with a breakthrough being the inclusion of pediatric HIV in the global fund GC7 application which will see more funding and support to improve pediatric HIV services. In addition, a GA monitoring and evaluation dashboard was developed in 2025, that draws data from the DOH and the National Health Laboratory Services and allows SANAC to track child-specific AIDS indicators at national, provincial and district levels which is critical for planning, reporting and measuring progress.

UNICEF supported the development of a climate-resilient WASH framework and formulation of norms and standards for direct purchasing of climate-resilient WASH and energy facilities and in partnership with the Clinton Health Access Initiative commenced modeling of climate-resilient WASH in 3 schools, contributing to the development of national technical guidelines. 
The Green Rising initiative engaged nearly 1,000 children and youth (10-24 years) in environmental conservation and waste management, empowering them to become environmental champions, benefiting 60 schools and 7 universities in three provinces (Gauteng. Northwest and KwaZulu Natal). 

UNICEF contributed to the standardization of WASH indicators for schools, and gender-based indicators for SDG 6.2 target and established a cross-sectoral collaboration with relevant government departments and civil society to develop a subnational Children’s Climate Risk Index (CCRI) for South Africa. 

UNICEF, in partnership with World Vision South Africa, distributed 90 hygiene kits and 220 dignity kits to 12,218 people in Limpopo, KZN, and the Eastern Cape while the Rapid Integrated Emergency Assessment tool, and hosted on U-Report, enhanced emergency response by streamlining WASH data collection.

Every child, including adolescents, learns.
In 2024, UNICEF focused on assisting the Government's effort to enhance access and quality of education in Early Learning and Basic Education reaching more than 5.3 million learners evenly split by gender.  UNICEF contributed to the implementation of the National Curriculum Framework for Children from Birth to Four Years Framework prioritizing young children with disabilities and those facing abuse and neglect. In 2024, UNICEF finalized the Learning-and-Teaching-Support-Materials based on play-based pedagogies. This achievement will shift the needle on the quality of ECD teaching and learning environments and impact children's early learning and stimulation outcomes. 

UNICEF capacitated 13,349 parents with information on the importance of parental involvement, an additional 163,127 practitioners and parents, and 10,712 School Governing Bodies on play-based learning that indirectly impacted more than 2.5 million young children. The ECD Info Hub for South Africa was also established in partnership with the Department of Basic Education (DBE) to trigger further cross-departments/organizations collaboration. 
UNICEF supported the DBE’s Curriculum Enhancement Initiative and developed a pilot measurement tool that measures selected ‘competencies’ under the South African Core Competency Framework. The tool was tested among 400 learners. This encourages learners to learn and complete schooling and honing the ‘transferrable skills’ from a young age that are critically needed among young people for their future opportunities. This contribution will inform the upcoming National Curriculum Review Process Policy. 

Responding directly to learning poverty, UNICEF supported the successful implementation of the  National Early Grade Reading Programme (EGRP) second phase as a scale-up of phase one that focuses on the mother tongue and multi-grade classrooms in the Northern Cape with the training of 635 teachers benefitting 21,945 learners. Concurrently, the EGRP Phase One entailed capacity building of 735 teachers that benefited approximately 25,400 learners. Another achievement is the piloting of the National Reading Survey to establish foundational reading benchmarks in all languages which is expected to contribute widely to evidence-based foundational literacy improvement efforts.

Following UNICEF’s direct support in developing the National Coding & Robotics Curriculum since 2021, the Curriculum was approved by Umalusi – the quality control counsel responsible for setting standards and quality assuring qualification for general and further education and training. This made a significant shift towards embracing technology and preparing young people for the challenges of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. 
As part of the government’s rollout of the national curriculum, UNICEF capacitated 1,032 educators and reached 62,515 learners with quality classroom delivery of lessons in 1,011 schools nationwide. 

Under Generation Unlimited, the GIGA global initiative that aims to connect all schools mapped all schools (except Western Cape) on the status of school connectivity nationwide. In addition, UNICEF supported the Siyavula online (math and science) to reach an additional 1,527,498 learners, and Junior Tukkies online with an additional 654,368 learners to empower and strengthen their learning. In the context of high youth unemployment UNICEF in partnership with PWC and the University of Pretoria trained 884 young entrepreneurs for self-employment.

Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence and exploitation.
UNICEF continued to advocate for the inclusion of a separate (7th) pillar for children in the National Strategic Plan for Gender-Based Violence and Femicide (NSP-GBVF) and supported the launch of a Children’s Consultation Report (co-hosted by the Department of Social Development – DSD). The launch was followed by a high-level advocacy event co-hosted by the DSD, UNICEF, UNWOMEN, UNFPA, EU and the United Kingdom’s FCDO to advocate for the importance of the intersection between violence against children (VAC) and violence against women (VAW). UNICEF supported the government in preparing a Country Pledge at the first Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children in Bogota, which consists of seven key areas: Parent and caregiver support; Safe environment; Response and care; Norms and values; Child participation; Collaboration and coordination with SADC and Income and economic strengthening.  Support to the implementation of the pledge will be reflected in UNICEF Country Programme (2026-2030).

Parenting programme reached over 25,000 parents and caregivers both face-to-face and online, through Parent Text. South Africa was included in a global Advocacy Partnership on Parenting funded by LEGO Foundation as one of five ‘trailblazer’ countries and launched the Parenting Support Policy Benchmarking Assessment in coordination with three national departments (DSD, DBE, and Department of Health) as well as CSOs and academia. 
UNICEF seconded a trainer to roll out DSD’s Risiha (Resilience) programme which is implemented in the drop-in-centers (DICs) across the country. With technical support offered and direct assistance through implementing partners, over 425,000 children have been reached with social and other essential services. 

UNICEF has led child online safety initiatives including a social media campaign supported by Meta that has reached more than 11.4 million individuals and has contributed to the Model of National Response to address Online Child Sexual Exploitation and Abuse, led by DSD.  
In coordination with Google and DBE, the online safety curriculum for Grades 8-12 has been rolled out to two provinces (Northwest and Northern Cape) with over 180 educators, school governing body members, and principals trained.  UNICEF convened quarterly roundtable discussions among the tech companies including Meta, Google, TikTok, MTN, and Vodacom alongside the Film and Publication Board to share information about child online safety best practice and create common priorities.

The cabinet approval of the much-debated White Paper on Citizenship, Immigration, and Refugee Protection posed significant concern among United Nations and CSOs, as it was proposing to withdraw from the 1951 Refugee Convention and 1969 Organization of African Unity (OAU) Convention on the Specific Aspects of refugee problems in Africa. UNICEF along with UNHCR, OHCHR, and IOM has submitted feedback to the Department of Home Affairs to reconsider the withdrawal and offered technical support for better management of mixed migration flows.  
UNICEF and UNHCR in coordination with International Social Service (ISS) USA, developed a generic training package that equips social and para-social workers with the necessary skills to recognize and address the unique challenges faced by Children on the Move. UNICEF South Africa in coordination with DSD piloted the training package in February 2024. Despite the challenges in resource mobilization, UNICEF reached 1,600 children on the move with essential services.

Cross Cutting Change Strategies

Communications and Advocacy 
 In 2024, Communications and Advocacy enhanced the media profile of UNICEF South Africa with 140 media interviews and expanded social media presence. LinkedIn showed the fastest growth while TikTok continued to rise as well. Most encouragingly, website views doubled between 2023 and 2024, from 548,643 to 1,336,439.

Successful digital advocacy campaigns in 2024 were aligned with the programmatic priorities including parenting, mental health, climate change, and transforming education.  World Children's Day generated considerable media attention (12 interviews) and was coupled with the SitAn soft launch. Donor visibility remained a priority in 2024 with documentation visits (and content produced) in the Eastern Cape (WASH), KZN (Nutrition), Northern Cape (Early Grade Reading), and North-West (Quality Education).  The communications team also supported the GenU Launch, Green Rising programmes, Be Green Launch, BMW Critical Thinking Forum, and Fix My Food initiatives among others with media engagement and social media outreach. 
The Volunteer Programme, under a new lead in 2024, enhanced its reach with 14 university campus clubs now established up from 10 in 2023. A total 5,200 UNICEF Volunteers are active members all of whom are young people attending university. An estimated 42,000 people, covering a span of 52,500 hours benefitted from the activations of the Volunteers who this year focused on nutrition, climate change and mental health.
 
Social Behaviour Change (SBC)
SBC contributed to reducing the number of zero-dose children in targeted districts by 21%, by integrating social and behavioural data points into formative research on barriers to uptake, and building capacity to integrate SBC approaches e.g., journey mapping, into existing community engagement planning, related to the National Immunisation Strategy.  SBC was integral in designing and coordinating the parenting advocacy strategy, strengthening cross-sectoral partnerships with Government and other stakeholders, and increasing reach and engagement of collaborative campaigns promoting access to parenting support.  Joint digital campaigns with DSD, DBE and SAPPIN helped grow online engagement in parenting conversations by 1300% to 3.6 million. The “Power of Play” campaign tripled targets to reach 6 million caregivers, of which 1.7 million were in areas with limited access to ECD facilities. SBC input in the design and coordination of the Meta Brandlift study on online safety contributed to reaching 11.4 million people.

Fundraising and Partnerships 
SACO’s partnership and fundraising efforts in 2024 have been successful, with overall income growing by roughly 50% from 2023. SACO’s demonstrated growth in income from local corporates and foundations continues to make the case for the potential that exists for local fundraising efforts.
 
In 2024 SACO’s local fundraising successfully drew in over $1.1 million, exceeding the annual target by 6%. National Committee funding grew by 59% in 2024, to $6 million. The combined income from National Committees and local PSFR amount to roughly two thirds of SACO’s ORR in 2024. 
 
Notable income for SACO also included securing the office’s first major gift from a local foundation- Zenex Foundation. In addition, the partnership with Accenture has committed $300,000 a year over three years to UNICEF SACO to support green jobs and the economy. 
 
Partnership between UNICEF, WHO, FAO and other key stakeholders of the One Health approach, resulted in a $25 million pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response grant from the World Bank to support strengthening of local health systems, working in direct collaboration with the National Treasury, the National Department of Health, and other relevant departments. UNICEF received $3 million of the total grant. 
 
In 2024 the local individual giving programme had 1,675 donors, made up of mostly pledged donors that collectively contributed roughly USD $140,000 in revenue. At the end of 2024, SACO launched the first ESAR digital fundraising channel for individual donors, effectively diversifying SACO’s individual giving offering and increasing the ease of giving. 
 
The value of the funds leveraged by the office in 2024 from the private sector is estimated at circa, $250,000, driven largely by the social media credits received from META and funds that SACO redirected to government and local partners. 
 
While income from public partners made up 18% of SACO’s income in 2023, proportionally the contribution of public funds to SACO’s total income continues to decline, with public funds drawing in only 7% of income in 2024. In addition, ORE also continues to decrease as the number of SACO’s emergency grants has steadily declined since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2024 SACO received one emergency grant from the Government of Japan (circa $650,000) for climate and environmental WASH programming and system strengthening in South Africa. 
 
Innovations
In 2024, the innovation portfolio focused on testing some new pilots, sustaining key projects, scaling up best practices, and providing opportunities for young people in the green economy. In support of the government’s ongoing efforts to address the 45.5% youth unemployment rate in the country, UNICEF, the United Nations Resident Coordinator and PwC launched Generation Unlimited (GenU) in August 2024, attended by more than 150 stakeholders and young people. GenU is a global partnership that supports youth in their journey from education to learning and training and employment. 

UNICEF hosted a three-day ‘BeGreen’ workshop where 60 green entrepreneurs pitched their innovative solutions to a panel of experts. Support to the Recycling Champions (ReCha) project resulted in the collection of more than 652,000 kgs of recyclable waste materials, and the establishment of 30 ReCha centres in the Western Cape Province. The Youth Agency Marketplace (YOMA), with its digitally enabled ecosystem approach strengthened the Enviro-Champs initiative, empowering more than 2,300 marginalized youth to work on water-related projects including water monitoring and river clean-up activities. This initiative was co-funded by the Presidential Social Employment Fund and overall, some 1,000 participants gained paid employment over an eight-month period. This work forms part of a larger operational research piece, co-led by Rhodes University, which is supporting the development of accredited and certified green Learning to Earning Pathways

The ‘Fundoo’ skilling app piloted together with the Youth Agency Marketplace (YOMA) supported at least 10,000 young people in their search for employment. Moreover, YOMA supported the piloting of an impact marketplace, with three government funded youth organisations, which, through Web3.0 technology and using innovative finance modalities, allows for the measurement, verification tokenization of social impact activities performed by youth and for children. 
 
Planning, Monitoring and Evidence Generation
2024 laid out the roadmap for the new country programme for 2026-2030. Key milestones achieved include a) An updated and rights-based situation analysis of children and young people in the country; b) UNICEF Country programme evaluation; c) Staff trained on the new UNICEF Global Rights and Results Programming module; d) Evidence Synthesis conducted; and e) Strategic Moment of Reflection held, which culminated in a Strategic Intent Note highlighting the programmatic rationale and strategic shifts expected.  

The inception phase for developing a youth, gender and disability monitoring and reporting system for the Department of Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities was completed in April 2024.  In addition, a business case for the use of drone technology to strengthen data collection to support disaster preparedness and a response approach was finalized and shared with stakeholders working in disaster management including the South African Disaster Management Centre. A ‘data for children’ dashboard pulling together data sets nationally was launched, and conversations are on-going with the Presidency under the National Strategy to accelerate action for child and Statistics South Africa to house the product. 

In 2024, UNICEF continued to enhance national evaluation capacity, particularly through the Young & Emerging Evaluators Programme. Collaborating with SAMEA, CLEAR-AA, and WFP, UNICEF supported 31 emerging evaluators with 7 out of 8 participants in full time work immersing securing employment and 1 returning to school. These efforts are building a future cadre of evaluation professionals, strengthening South Africa’s evaluation capacity.
UNICEF also commissioned an impact evaluation of the Early Grade Reading Programme within the education sector. The evaluation is in its initial stages, with major data collection scheduled for the following year. Additionally, two Evaluation Management Response phases concluded for the Child Protection Online Safety Evaluation and the HIV evaluation of adolescent girls and young women. Over two years, the structured management response process ensured actionable recommendations were implemented, thereby strengthening programme delivery.

Operations
The Operations team, consisting of ICT, Supply, Admin, Quality Assurance and People and Culture, was a key enabler and support function for programme sections to achieve results for children this year. Continued efforts were made to improve Efficiency and Effectiveness through dedicated meetings with programme sections with a focus on supply and procurement. The Operations staffing has remained constant and capacity gaps in the Administration section were addressed, particularly to better support the PSB and travel processes.  Repurposing the receptionist post to assign the internal travel portfolio to the existing incumbent presented challenges, and this has adversely impacted some Key Performance Indicators, such as timely issuance and closing of TAs, and possible missed opportunities to save costs. The launch of the Fiori Travel App and a new workflow, including decentralization of aspects of the travel process, should address the shortcomings.
 
Despite an increase in funding received in 2024, SACO expenditure decreased from USD 21m in 2023 to USD 13.7m in 2024.  The main reason is a sharp decrease in short-duration emergency funding for the country from USD 6.8m in 2023 to USD 1.2m in 2024. It can also be partly attributed to funding received up-front in 2024 for multi-year Grants (primarily BMW and World Bank), resulting in funding being rephased to 2025.  
 
A total of 19 partnership documents were quality-assured and signed in 2024, a reduction from 44 in 2023. Issuance of institutional contracts also decreased in 2024 to 55 having been 88 in 2023.  There were 20 individual consultancy contracts raised for SACO and 11 Medevacs to South Africa from countries such as Burkina Faso, CAR, and DRC, supported by People & Culture.
 
In 2024, the SACO Operations Team provided procurement support to the East and Southern Africa regional office, Namibia, Lesotho and eSwatini country offices. A total number of 72 institutional contracts were raised of which 60 were for South Africa and 12 for the other offices. The value of the procurement for South Africa was $4.8 million and $531,000 for the Supported Offices. A market survey is near finalization and long-term agreements with service providers that have been signed will be for use not only in SACO but in the Region, which should help speed up procurement.

A PSEA Investigation training workshop was organized, led by SACO, in partnership with UNODC and UNHCR over 5 days for NGO Partners and 35 organizations attended. ICT worked closely with Innovations and T4D on an advisory capacity, engaging at a greater percentage with the Programme sections.

UNICEF renewed and established partnerships with the newly elected government through high-level meetings and technical discussions to prioritise the child rights agenda with focus a on health, nutrition, education, child protection and social protection. The Manifesto for Every Child in South Africa 2024 was released by UNICEF during the national election campaign. 
 
UNICEF continued to play an important and leading role in UN coordination structures. These included the UN results and theme groups, where UNICEF co-led the Human Capital and Social Transformation pillar and related sub-groups for Education and Violence, as well as co-leading the M&E theme group. In addition, UNICEF played a key role in the UN Communications Group, UN Operations Management Team, Protection Group, and Social Protection, as well as Gender and Youth Theme Groups. UNICEF's engagement in these UN coordination structures was critical for positioning children’s issues in the overall UN agenda and as part of the ongoing implementation of the UNSDCF. Under the patronage of the UN Resident Coordinator, Generation Unlimited (GenU SA), a public-private partnership platform focused on young people was launched in August 2024 at PWC attended by the private sector, UN and civil society partners together with young people. The Resident Coordinator and CEO of PWC were in attendance to provide the steer and make it a UN-wide priority in South Africa. This partnership platform aims to skill and connect South Africa’s youth to opportunities for employment, entrepreneurship, and social impact. 

UNICEF continued its partnership with the Department of Health at the National, provincial, and District levels, the South Africa Vaccination and Immunization Center, WHO, and other national immunization stakeholders to improve immunization and reduce zero-dose children with funding support from ELMA.
 
UNICEF collaborated with the SANAC, Departments of Health, Social Development, Basic Education, UNAIDS, and the Presidency and to support the development of the national multisectoral Global Alliance plan and convene technical working group meetings. Through the partnership and funding from US CDC South Africa, UNICEF has scaled up the adolescent girls and young women peer mentor programme and supported the implementation of the GA plan to ending AIDS in children.
 
In the area of climate risk, UNICEF partnered with the Department of Fishing, Forest and Environment, the National Disaster Management Center, and other line departments, various CSOs, including Save The Children, One World, as well as the World Bank to develop the subnational child climate risk. UNICEF also partnered with the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) to model climate-resilient WASH.  
 
 
UNICEF strengthened its partnerships on public financing for children with key policy making institutions including the National Treasury, National Planning Commission (NPC), National Economic and Development Labour Council (NEDLAC), Parliamentary Appropriations Committee and other stakeholders. 
 
In partnership with the Treasury, UNICEF led the discussions through public webinars on gender responsive budgeting and Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement in 2024 and responding to the 2023 Open Budget Survey findings and recommendations.  Through the partnership with the NPC provided support on the research on the impact of the cost of basic goods and services on the cost of living for poor and working poor households. 
 
Within government, active collaboration with the Western Cape Children’s Commissioner provided further impetus to focused technical assistance and partnership with that office and its direct line of communications with the Premier, social sector departments, and the provincial legislature. A new partnership was initiated with the provincial legislature in the Gauteng Province, not only to build capacity on basic budget analysis for politicians, but to also facilitate children’s participation in provincial budget consultation processes.
 
UNICEF to continue to advocate for progressively higher resources allocations for children, and for an expanded social protection system for children. This advocacy is done with both national and provincial legislatures, the South African media, and directly with government. Furthermore, UNICEF facilitated CSOs to access the National Economic Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) which is the vehicle by which Government, labour, business and community organisations seek to cooperate, through problem-solving and negotiation, on economic, labour and development issues and related challenges facing the country. This unique and strategic position allows partners to advocate together for progressive income support policies.
 
Within the education sector, there is strong sub-sector coordination and partnerships in the foundational Literacy and Numeracy (FLN) area, with both implementing partners and donors. The partners coordinate works and funding, leading to UNICEF receiving funds from the Zenex Foundation in 2024. LEGO Foundation is involved in both the FLN and ECD sub-sectors, including financial contributions to both sub-sectors through UNICEF. This created an opportunity for UNICEF to serve as a trusted link between the two sub-sectors to enable a smooth transition between the Early Learning and the Foundational Phase.
 
UNICEF partnered with national and provincial stakeholders, including government departments, private sectors, academia, and CSOs to advance child protection across South Africa. UNICEF jointly plans with the Department of Social Development as well as the School Safety Unit of the Department of Basic Education. In 2024, UNICEF started the roundtable with tech companies such as Google, Meta, TikTok, MTN, and Vodacom to leverage support for online child safety in the country.  For the parenting policy benchmarking assessment, UNICEF engaged three relevant government departments (DSD, DBE, and DoH), as well as academia and South Africa Parenting Programme Implementors’ Network (SAPPIN). UNICEF continues to receive local corporates’ support in prevention and early intervention programme, providing necessary services through Drop-in Centers.  UNICEF is an active member of the Protection Working Group, contributing to the protection of children on the move, collaborating with UNHCR, IOM and OHCHR and CSO partners.
 
In terms of private sector engagement, SACO has continued to use the CEO Network as a way of reaching private sector companies in South Africa with knowledge and advocacy messages for child rights. This year’s meetings focused on parenting and protection from violence, and health and immunization. The third and last meeting of the year was jointly convened by the Chair of the CEO Network and the UN’s Partnership and Resource Mobilization Group and focused on the role of the private sector in accelerating the implementation of agenda 2020. Organizing the consultation was UNICEF’s contribution to e development of the 2026 – 2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for South Africa.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The national election in the country and the formation of the new government slowed down the implication of the implementation of the programme during the first of the year. However, the partnerships with the private sector and CSOs facilitated to continue to implement the key interventions. 
 
One of the biggest challenges in 2024 was the reduction in the overall fiscal space (R6.1 billion less non-interest expenditure than similar expenditures in 2023) and the resulting backward slide and constrained delivery of key programmes in basic education, health, and other services that are vital for children’s overall well-being. Departmental fiscal baselines have been continually adjusted downwards over the last few years, thus requiring dexterity from sector departments on how to fulfil their mandates in a shrinking expenditure environment. 
 
Following the Concluding Observations issued by the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in February 2024, the Government of South Africa started the drafting process of both the National Strategy for Accelerated Action for Children (NSAAC) overseen by the Presidency, as well as the 5th National Plan of Action for Children (NPAC 5) under the Department of Social Development, which houses the Office of the Rights of the Child.
 
Recognizing the institutional divergences between these two processes and coordination challenges, UNICEF SA contributed to aligning them through a two-day Children’s Sector Consultation on the NSAAC. This event gathered diverse voices to guide the refinement of the strategy, with a final draft to that was to be presented to the Cabinet for approval in early December 2024, but was postponed due to other pressing political priorities.  The allocation of 7 percent set-aside funding for child rights came at a pivotal time, as the country celebrated 30 years of democracy and UNICEF South Africa was striving to strengthen the children’s rights agenda through greater child participation, focused strategic partnerships, and data-driven and evidence-based initiatives.
