The capacity constraints with the Department of Basic Education for the implementation of commitments towards early learning programmes, impact on timely execution of activities, impacting on some deliverables. In Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) education, teachers' rigid attitudes toward STEM requires additional time and effort for capacitating the teaching cohort. The lack of equipment and infrastructure adds an extra hurdle to deliver STEM education in lower quintile schools. Tracking the long-term impact of the STEM mentorship programme is deemed challenging due to the Protection of Personal Information Act and the change of partnerships.
 
Future Outlook: 
 
Strengthening partnership with the new Government to place child rights at the center of the national agenda: The efforts will continue to leverage and strengthen the partnership with the related ministries and departments to place child rights at the center of the national agenda.  The advocacy will focus on prioritizing efficiency in the use of social sector budgets and safeguarding budgets for children, ending gender-based violence and violence against children, increasing the coverage of child support grants and reducing inequality.  UNICEF SACO will continue to support the Office of the Rights of the Child and the Presidency in consulting with children in each province for the design of the NPAC 5 by the end of 2024. Through these initiatives, UNICEF SACO reaffirms its commitment to a focused, data-driven, and evidence- and rights-based children's sector in South Africa.
 
 
Leveraging the G20 Presidency of South Africa as a strategy to advance the child rights agenda: Building on previous engagements with the G20, and working closely with the UNCT in SA, UNICEF can be the partner of choice for South Africa to identify strategic opportunities and shape the outcome of South Africa’s Presidency for children including in relation to implementation of the UNICEF Africa Strategy. UNICEF’s effective contributions (direct or indirect) to the various tracks, engagement groups, working groups and Task Force documents should lead to influencing the final outcome/declaration of the 2025 G20.   Following the handover meeting with the UNICEF Brazil Office held in December and building on some of organizational experience, established practices and lessons learned, UNICEF South Africa will work closely with all levels of the organization (HQ-ROs-CO) to ensure there is a connecting thread and focused outcomes to the engagement.
 
Harnessing the Power of Private Sector for better Results for Children: UNICEF successfully engaged tech companies to collectively promote child online safety through a business for human rights approach, however, the roll-out of evidence-based parenting programmes with the CEO network did not see significant uptake of the services among the participating corporate members. A more targeted strategy is required for engaging private corporate sectors for leveraging and influencing. An integrated programme approach can open better entry points to offer universal social services in 2025. This includes support for DBE in rolling out the Online Safety curriculum with Google SA and linking birth registration with immunization programmes. Regional collaboration with the Southern African Development Community (SADC) is another opportunity and is needed to address issues facing children on the move, as national cross-border discussions often face challenges.
 
 
Shifting knowledge, attitudes, and practices to support positive child rights outcomes anchored in a solid monitoring system continues to be a long-term priority. Shifting parenting practices across the life course and online, to address violence and promote positive parenting requires further strengthened coordination around a common vision of desired behavioural changes and clear indicators to measure success. Continued strengthening of youth engagement through U-Report, The Girls and Boys Education Movement (GBEM) Clubs and UNICEF Volunteers, will increase child participation and ensure that child and youth voices are included in programmes. 
 
Accelerating the implementation of key interventions and prioritization of issues affecting children to inform the new country programme 2026-2030: The year 2025 will be the fifth and last year of the Country Programme Document and efforts will be made to accelerate the implementation of key interventions to achieve remaining results with work planning adjustments for the year considering   the updated Situation Analysis, evidence synthesis and ToC processes. The preparation for the new Country Programme Document will start in 2025 in alignment with South Africa’s medium term development framework 2025 – 2029 priorities as well as the   new UNIICEF Strategic Plan (2026-2030), UNICEF Africa Strategy, the pact of the future, and Sustainable Development Goals.

The situation of Children in South Sudan remained dire in 2024 as the country continued to experience deepening of the economic crisis with immediate knock on all essential services for children.  This was further compounded by overlapping poly crises ranging from almost five disease outbreaks (cholera, measles, polio, yellow fever, Hepatitis B), flooding that impacted on 1.4 million people and unprecedented influx of refugees and returnees from the widening Sudan conflict. About 9.4 million people, including 5 million children, 2.3 million women and 1.4 million people with disabilities needed assistance in 2024.
 
Political and Security Situation: Though agreement to the revitalized peace agreement continues to hold countrywide with no systemic conflict, South Sudan has continued to witness political and security instability due to lack of clarity on the political transition process with elections now postponed from December 2024 to December 2026, open and violent manoeuvring around presidential succession at the core coupled with continued localized intercommunal violence at the periphery i.e. sub-national level. The unstable political situation has resulted into lack of prioritization of investment in essential services for children, while localized intra and inter-tribal violence has led to disruption of services.  
 
Economic Situation: South Sudan’s economy is plummeting as families grapple with hyperinflation and extreme currency depreciation, driven in part by a rupture in the country’s main oil export pipeline that runs through Sudan. Oil is the main source of revenue for South Sudan. The country’s currency rate against the American dollar shot to SSP5,000 compared to SSP1,050 in 2023 in the parallel, informal market. This has not only eroded the citizen’s purchasing power for goods and services but also increased the cost of operation for humanitarian agencies including UNICEF.
 
Globally, South Sudan is ranked second to last in the Human Development Index, with a deteriorating trend from 0.385 in 2023 to 0.381 this year. Of the population, 67.3 per cent live below the international poverty line (US$2.15) according to the Sida’s poverty analysis for 2024, while 91.9 per cent live in multidimensional poverty according to the Multidimensional Poverty Indicator for April 2024. Several families are unable to send their children to school resulting to a projected increase in the number of out-of-school from 2.8 million children in 2023 to 3.5 million in 2024 according to the National Bureau of Statistics population estimates. Food insecurity among households has worsen and 650,000 children are expected to be severely malnourished in 2025. Poverty has also impacted access to essential services including health and child protection. According to Sida multidimensional poverty analysis conducted in 2024, only 49 per cent of the population are estimated to live within one hour away of health facilities and 66 per cent have difficulty accessing health services. Children remain vulnerable to all forms of violence as some families resort to unfavourable coping mechanisms including child and forced marriages where they exchange their girls for wealth. According to UNFPA report on child marriage, two young girls in Unity State were reported to have died in 2024 due to actions related to forced marriages. 
 
South Sudan’s gross domestic product (GDP) experienced a 5 per cent contraction because of consecutive years of severe flooding and prolonged droughts in parts of the country, as well as the conflict in Sudan that led to the damage to the Dar Blend oil pipeline and its subsequent shutdown. The country’s oil and gas sector saw a 70 per cent reduction in the last quarter of FY2023/2024, resulting in an estimated decline of 105,000 barrels per day, and cited the continued disruption in crude oil production and export as a national security matter. This hinders government’s investment on social sectors and create over reliance on humanitarian assistance. 
 
Humanitarian Situation: The Sudan crisis continues to increase the number of returnees and refugees to South Sudan. As of 5 December 2024, 890,884 individuals, including 447,830 children, were registered as either refugees or returnees in South Sudan following the eruption of conflict in Sudan. Half of these numbers arrived in 2024. As of 13 December, a cumulative total of 4,793 suspected and confirmed cholera cases, including 47 deaths (case fatality rate: 1 per cent), were reported from 22 counties across six states of South Sudan. Of the affected counties, Rubkona county accounted for 30.6 per cent (n = 1,465) of all cases, followed by Juba (26.7 per cent; n=1,278), and Malakal (19.5 per cent; n=932). According to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report, September–November 2024, the acute food insecurity and malnutrition situation in South Sudan is deteriorating because of the economic crisis and repeated climatic shocks, primarily widespread flooding, and conflict and insecurity. Severe and moderate acute malnutrition has deteriorated from 1.65 million in 2023 to 2.1 million children in 2024. About 650,000 children are projected to have severe acute malnutrition in 2025, a 35 per cent increase from 2023. The humanitarian situation this year was further exacerbated by flooding which impacted on 1.4 million people across 43 counties out of the 80 counties in South Sudan. 
 
Despite these dire social development indicators, the Government of South Sudan only allocated 11.2 per cent of its SSP4.2 trillion (about US$1.4 billion) budget FY2024/2025 to health, education and the social and humanitarian pillars. Education fell from 8.3 per cent in 2023 to 5.4 per cent, and Health fell from 2.1 per cent to 1.3 per cent, while the social and humanitarian affairs allocations increased from 0.4 per cent in 2023 to 4.5 per cent in 2024. The humanitarian funding trend continues to decline. In 2022, the funding gap was 25.7 per cent, 2023 was 49.8 per cent and in 2024, the gap is 66 per cent, limiting UNICEF’s ability to reach individuals with life-saving assistance.
 
The Government of South Sudan imposed a series of new taxes and charges on goods imported for humanitarian activities in the country. These measures impacted humanitarian operations, increasing the cost of business, and compromised the ability to timely deliver assistance to people in need.
 
The situation in South Sudan remains grim and none of the key five Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) linked to UNICEF programming will be met. Worrying, some gains were reversed following the COVID-19 pandemic.
 
SDG target 2(2) End all forms of malnutrition: About 2.1 million children under five years are expected to suffer from wasting (IPC report, 2024). Exclusive breastfeeding for infants below 6 months is at 73.3 per cent, and only 16.5 per cent of 6–23-month-olds receive minimum dietary diversity. 

SDG 3 Healthy lives and well-being for all: The United Nations’ world population prospects indicators show that the infant mortality rate for South Sudan in 2024 is 57 deaths per 1000 live births, a 1.56 per cent decline from 2023. Malaria is the leading cause of mortality, followed by pneumonia and diarrhoea. The maternal mortality rate is 1,223 per 100,000, the highest in the world, characterized by a high rate of home deliveries and less than 20 per cent of births attended by skilled health personnel.
 
SDG target 4(1) Ensure free, equitable and quality education: South Sudan still faces an exceptionally low gross enrolment rate (GER) for pre-primary education at 11 per cent, primary education at 74 per cent and secondary education at 7 per cent (Education School Census Report, 2023). With the increasing number of out-of-school children, which significantly exceeds the number of in-school children, access to equitable education remains off track to achieve SDG4. Additionally, the quality of education is low due to the limited availability of qualified teachers, with 61 per cent of teachers having only a secondary education certificate (not sufficiently qualified). Also, less than 20 per cent of teachers are female, and the ratio of learners to qualified teachers is 77 to 1 (Education School Census Report, 2023). 
 
SDG 6 Water and sanitation for all: The proportion of the population in South Sudan that has access to basic-level drinking water remained at 41.2 per cent as in 2022, and 24.8 per cent had access to improved sanitation facilities. Open defecation remains a big challenge (about 60 per cent) in the country, with only 17 communities declared open defecation free (Joint Monitoring Programme, 2023). 
 
SDG target 16(2) End all forms of violence against children: Violence against children is widespread in South Sudan because of the persistent conflict, recurrent climatic and economic shocks, poverty and harmful social norms, though reliable prevalence data are missing.

Goal 1: Every child survives and thrives 
UNICEF, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, World Health Organization (WHO) and other partners, delivered impactful health interventions in 2024, contributing to improvements in health and nutrition outcomes for children. 

In 2024, access to malaria diagnostics was increased with 4.5 million people (2,165,364 children under five) getting tested, of which 2.4 million tested positive for malaria. Of the 2.4 million with confirmed positive malaria diagnosis, 2.1 million people (87.5 per cent) were treated using first-line antimalarials.  To curb the burden of incidence of malaria, an additional 579,975 long-lasting insecticidal nets benefiting over 1.1 million people were distributed in 2024, contributing to an overall net coverage of 93 per cent.  With UNICEF’s technical and financial support on vaccine logistics and social mobilization, a new malaria vaccine was introduced in 28 counties, achieving a 75 per cent coverage of the first dose benefiting 58,522 children. 
 
On immunization, 80 per cent of children 0–11 months received the third dose of the pentavalent vaccine and 65 per cent of children under 1 year received the measles-containing vaccine. Cold chain capacity of health facilities was also improved from 52 per cent in 2023 to 62 per cent (against a target of 70 per cent) in 2024, with the procurement and installation of 396 solar direct drive refrigerators enhancing vaccine storage. Efforts to reach unvaccinated (zero-dose) children included integrated outreach services in 80 counties, immunizing 165,657 children aged under 1 year with the Penta 3 vaccine and 146,363 children aged under 1 year with the measles vaccine. Vaccination campaigns, such as the polio response, exceeded targets, reaching over 3 million children in each of the two rounds (102 per cent first round and 117 per cent second round) while a UNICEF/WHO-supported measles campaign reached 692,199 children (91 per cent of the target). UNICEF also supported the capacity building of vaccinators on Immunization in Practice guidelines, enabling them to better manage and deliver vaccination services to children. 
 
UNICEF’s health initiatives also worked on improving maternal, newborn and child health (MNCH) and expanding access to primary health care. To increase the population’s access to primary health care services, the Health Sector Transformation Project – a government-led, multi-donor initiative – was launched in July 2024 to expand access to the basic health package. UNICEF partnered with 28 implementing agencies across all 10 states and three administrative areas, distributing medicines and supplies worth US$ 24.2 million to 816 facilities and paying incentives amounting to approximately US$ 16 million to 24,379 health workers. To enhance MNCH services, UNICEF provided mentorship for 3,626 health workers (101 per cent of target), supplied equipment to 280 targeted health facilities in three states and promoted community mobilization through 892 (30 per cent women) Boma health workers who reached 46,700 (52 per cent female) people with health messages. However, maternal and newborn service uptake remained low, with only 19 per cent of pregnant women attending four antenatal visits and 17 per cent (declined from 25 per cent in 2023) receiving skilled birth attendance due to cultural beliefs, limited access, long distances to health facilities, and flood impacts.
 
In 2024, over 2.4 million (87 per cent of the targeted 2,844,362) children aged 6–59 months and 1,526,001 (84 per cent of targeted 1,811,338) women benefited from malnutrition prevention and treatment services. The Government also endorsed the first ever national nutrition policy (which focuses on ensuring that all people have optimal nutrition at all stages of life, enabling them to be productive and contribute to the economic growth of the country), and a preservice curriculum for nutrition  (which guides that all preservice training programs for health and nutrition care providers includes a comprehensive curriculum on nutrition), creating an enabling environment for nutrition programming and reinforcing systems strengthening. In addition, to enhance governance and analysis of nutrition information systems, UNICEF, World Food Programme (WFP) and FAO supported the effective implementation of the FSNMS 2024 data collection, IPC-AMN analysis, and the first phase of the joint NuVAC (Nutrition Vulnerabilities Assessment in Crisis) initiative.
 
The complex drivers of malnutrition were addressed through a multisectoral approach, integrating gender-based violence (GBV) prevention and referrals in over 1,200 nutrition sites, with 94 per cent of sites having water access. Additionally, over 80 per cent of nutrition services were integrated into health facilities, and nutrition-social protection integrated services benefited 1,626 pregnant and breastfeeding women. As the Nutrition cluster lead, UNICEF coordinated over 80 agencies and partners and supported the shaping of the national work plan for Scaling Up Nutrition. Collaborating with WFP, UNICEF implemented strategies to prevent and address aid diversion of nutrition supplies, resulting in the timely reporting of supply losses and six states enacting laws to prevent such diversions.
 
UNICEF also supported influential policy actions, such as the initiation of the adoption of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes, the development of strategies for anaemia prevention and salt iodization, and the creation of a national roadmap for implementing WHO guidelines on wasting prevention and treatment. Operational achievements included reaching over 2.4 million (87 per cent) children aged 6–59 months with vitamin A supplementation, deworming 2.1 million (82 per cent) children aged 12–59 months and providing lifesaving treatment to 293,011 (99 per cent) children with severe acute malnutrition.
 
UNICEF played a pivotal advocacy role in making food systems work for children, supporting six initiatives to improve diets with local foods like peanut butter and fortified blended flour. Through a network of over 10,000 mother-to-mother support groups and 6,931 community nutrition volunteers, UNICEF promoted exclusive breastfeeding among infants under 6 months, promoted optimal breastfeeding for children 2 years and beyond, established kitchen gardens and hosted cooking demonstrations to scale up food access for young children. Several mother-to-mother support groups engaged in village savings and loans associations, and 1,613 pregnant and lactating women received cash transfers and nutrition services, increasing their incomes and ability to improve the dietary diversity and uptake of health and protection services of their young children. 
 
Evidence generation remained central to UNICEF’s Nutrition programme, with significant studies and assessments conducted in partnership with stakeholders, including food and nutrition surveys and an ethnographic study on child feeding behaviours. To enhance efficiency and transparency, UNICEF digitalized the nutrition information system dashboard and introduced online supply incident reporting.
 
UNICEF’s persistent advocacy led to progress in integrating nutrition into South Sudan’s national development agenda. Key achievements include the endorsement of the first national nutrition policy, the adoption of a preservice curriculum for nutrition, the inclusion of nutrition staff cadres at various health system levels and the harmonization of their incentives with other government staff.
 
Goal 2: Every child learns, from early childhood to adolescence 
 UNICEF contributed to increasing equitable access and improving the quality of education in South Sudan. UNICEF provided access to formal and non-formal education for 743,344 children in humanitarian and non-humanitarian settings (446,006 boys and 297,338 girls). In humanitarian settings specifically, UNICEF supported 392,315 children (207,261 boys, 185,054 girls), representing 148 per cent of the targeted 265,000 children in realizing their right to education. UNICEF also enabled 97,244 out-of-school children (55,325 boys and 41,919 girls) to access education through evidence-based community mobilization and sensitization campaigns. These efforts targeted access barriers to education and learning faced by out-of-school children, particularly vulnerable girls and marginalized groups, in a challenging programming environment.  Thirteen 'Back to Learning' campaign and four community dialogue sessions focused on addressing key issues on girls’ access to education such as child marriage and child labour in 10 States and three administrative areas. As a  result of these dialogues around barriers to girls’ education, the Ministry of General Education and Instruction (MoGEI) in partnership with UNICEF, local authorities, and partners in targeted locations developed communiques highlighting the key barriers to girls’ education and provided recommendations in addressing them.  UNICEF will continue partnering with MoGEI, partners and local authorities to enable the implementation of these recommendations.
 
 To address the gross enrolment rate for pre-primary education of just 11 per cent, early childhood education (ECE) was advanced by annexing 113 early childhood education (ECE) classes into 85 primary schools, integrating 28 community-based centres into nutrition sites and building capacities of 406 ECE teachers (65 per cent women). 
 
Additionally, UNICEF improved teacher quality, training 6,169 (30 per cent women) unqualified primary school teachers (4,318 men and 1,851 women) through an in-service programme against a target of 6,080 teachers. This initiative covered professional studies and emphasized gender-sensitive and disability-inclusive teaching approaches, laying the groundwork for achieving qualified teacher status. UNICEF improved capacities of 630 headteachers (63 women), inspectors and supervisors to enhance the quality assurance of teaching and learning, and enabled capacity enhancement of 977 parent-teacher associations and school management committees in strengthening school governance and accountability across 78 counties in 10 states and three Administrative Areas. 78 Education Transfer Monitoring Committees (ETMC) were supported at the national and state levels to aid and strengthen the education transfer management systems by developing state and county education transfer guidelines, and training ETMC members on meeting conduct, coordination, monitoring, accountability and reporting. These systems ensured accountability, transparency and efficient monitoring of an estimated US$ 2,430,740 capitation grant and US$ 2.7 million teachers incentives fund transfers, including domestic and donor funds like the muti-donor-funded Girls’ Education South Sudan capitation grants and European Union-supported teacher incentives for 8,328 teachers (887 women) working in hard-to-reach areas.
 
To improve the Education Management Information System (EMIS) for enhanced monitoring, evaluation and education sector data management, UNICEF, in partnership with MOGEI and the World Bank, collaborated on the development of the diagnostic assessment of EMIS and will continue to partner with MOGEI and the World Bank in 2025 in strengthening the EMIS based on the business plan developed by the World Bank. MOGEI’s EMIS team also worked closely with a consultant funded by UNICEF to ensure the transfer of knowledge and skills in data analysis, and three staff members gained skills (the deputy director, senior inspector and inspector) for data and statistics.
 
Goal 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation 
UNICEF provided Child Protection services, including case management, family tracing and reunification, mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), explosive ordnance risk education, and gender-based violence (GBV) to 494,488 people including 163,359 boys, 170,335 girls, 119,697 women and 41,097 men (193 per cent of 2024 target of 255,000). 
 
In 2024, partnerships expanded from 23 to 29 non-governmental organizations (NGOs), including six women-led organizations, 17 national NGOs and six international NGOs operating in 43 counties across 10 states and three administrative areas. During 2024, UNICEF continued to expand the Child Protection programme through an ambitious localisation strategy designed to establish a sustainable child protection and GBV system to meet long-term needs and quick-onset emergency priorities. This made substantial contributions towards building a network of local child protection and GBV partners with multiyear partnerships that allowed for the professional development of a workforce capable of meeting the child protection, GBV and MHPSS needs of women, children, youth and vulnerable populations. The partnerships developed with the six international NGOs supported the Child Protection programme delivery: three responding to the Sudan Crisis (three), and the remaining providing 1) technical support on Child Protection Information Management System (CPIMS+) to strengthen case management services; 2) specialized care for high-risk GBV cases; and 3) disability-inclusion programming. 
 
UNICEF invested heavily in developing the capacities of social workers by giving each social worker a career path with clearly assigned simple and progressive duties and responsibilities in the identification of children in need, case management, care, referral and advocacy. In mid-2024, UNICEF launched the Social Work Certificate Programme in partnership with Juba University. To date, 139 social workers (83 per cent women) are enrolled out of planned 360 social workers (12 cohorts of 30 participants) to be targeted by early 2025 to professionalize the social service workforce. 
 
Structured and non-structured MHPSS services reached 217,980 people (110,384 boys, 96,196 girls, 5,703 men and 5,697 women), while explosive ordnance risk education reached nearly 48,000 individuals (119 per cent of the 40,000 target). Case management services assisted 7,193 children, including 577 who were reunified with families or placed in alternative care. UNICEF also technically and financially supported six youth centres that implemented the innovative 'Take 5' methodology of five pillars: adult caring and peer relationships; mental, physical and emotionally safe spaces; skill mastery; pro-social behaviours; and opportunities that served 2,123 individuals, with plans to expand this approach with child protection partners across the country. Within youth centres, transformative peer- and mentor-based reintegration and well-being programmes target adolescents and youth in dangerous circumstances including youth and adolescents in gangs, living on the street, in conflict with the law and associated with armed forces and groups.
 
UNICEF collaborated with 12 partners, including six women-led organizations, to increase the availability of GBV services in 16 counties including areas impacted by the Sudan crises. GBV prevention, response and risk mitigation programming reached 220,855 people (28,684 boys, 52,999 girls, 30,838 men and 108,334 women), nearly three times the planned target of 80,000 people. In September 2024, UNICEF successfully validated findings from the multiyear research on ‘Understanding and Measuring the Effectiveness of GBV Risk Mitigation in Emergencies’ that focused on a) proactively identifying and mitigating GBV-related risk in nutrition programming and b) measuring corresponding changes in the safety, accessibility and efficacy of nutrition services. Learnings from the operational research demonstrated increased disclosures of GBV, improved reporting and two-way referrals between nutrition and GBV services and enhanced decision-making power for women and mothers at the household level. UNICEF is currently rolling out the GBV/Nutrition programmatic package developed during this study and trained 200 partners on the package across five states. 
 
Goal 4: Every child lives in a safe and clean environment 
In 2024, South Sudan made some progress in the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector becoming the first country on the continent to sign a national WASH compact - the President of South Sudan signed the WASH Compact, committing to end open defecation by 2030. As part of the sanitation drive to eliminate open defecation, UNICEF supported the rollout of the community-led total sanitation (CLTS) approach and integration of climate-resilient infrastructure into WASH programme that led to 83 communities achieving open defecation-free status and close to 74,500 people gaining access to improved sanitation facilities. 
 
Additionally, 49 health-care facilities (196 per cent of the target) and 124 schools (165 per cent of the target) were supported with WASH facilities. Those health care facilities and schools benefited either from a component or full packages of WASH interventions depending on the needs. 
 
UNICEF also played a pivotal role in strengthening coordination in the WASH sector by engaging the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation and enhancing state-level collaboration. The coordination efforts at all levels and UNICEF’s support in convening high level engagements (e.g. Joint sector review meeting and strategic development partners meetings) bridged humanitarian and development processes, fostering a unified approach. The National WASH Joint Sector Review meeting brought together key stakeholders, including the private sector, civil society, the Government and donors, reinforcing the importance of strategic planning and partnerships for sustainable WASH sector development. It  cemented the need for a more robust, sustainable and long-term developmental framework and revamping the SDG commitment, as well as integrating climate resilience approach in the sector. Through this engagement, the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation took the lead in integrating climate action into WASH by collaborating with key development partners and amplifying the climate agenda in the sector. As part of the climate resilient WASH and strategic shift, 37 water points were upgraded with solar-powered systems, resulting in more resilient and sustainable water supplies, which benefitted 92,500 individuals. The use of a solar-powered system, as opposed to fuel-powered generators, contributed to a cleaner and safer environment by reducing carbon emissions. 
 
On a more global scale, UNICEF supported the Government’s participation in the Stockholm World Water Week, where the WASH compact was presented, and in the delegation to the 29th Climate Change Conference of the Parties (COP29) in Baku. These platforms presented an exceptional opportunity for Government officials to engage alongside UNICEF in advocacy with donors and international financial institutions such as the World Bank, African Development Bank, Green Climate Fund etc., to leverage much-needed investment for the WASH sector. Domestically, UNICEF strengthened the management capacity of urban water utilities through on job trainings on tools and management practices, enabling them to effectively operate and manage urban water supply systems in Bor, Juba (Lologo) and Torit. The urban water infrastructure and system improvement in Bor town is at final stage of completion and would provide more than 70,000 people with safe drinking water. 
 
Despite challenges such as flooding, cholera outbreaks and the continued Sudan crisis, UNICEF, as the WASH strategic player in humanitarian response, provided more than 659,800 (30 per cent of cluster target) people with temporary safe water and over 140,700 (22.6 per cent of cluster target) people with improved sanitation facilities. In late September 2024, South Sudan also experienced a cholera outbreak. As WASH cluster lead, UNICEF played indispensable role in developing a response plan for an estimated 300,000 affected people (50,000 households), based on the Ministry of Health projection of anticipated spread of the cholera. 
 
UNICEF supported the WASH Cluster to effectively coordinate the WASH response to ensure agile responses to the affected people in need and training of partners on identified capacity gaps. 
 
To improve the management of the WASH core pipeline, a voucher system for the delivery of critical WASH non-food items (NFIs) was piloted in Renk county. This provided an alternative to the core pipeline supply system, which faces challenges such as accessibility issues, inefficiencies in data management, and high warehouse management costs. Through the voucher system, the local private sector was engaged to deliver NFIs to the affected populations and receive direct payment for their services. The pilot was successful, and UNICEF plans to scale it up in the coming year, building on the lessons learned and addressing the challenges in core pipeline management.
 
Goal 5: Equitable chance in life 
In partnership with the Ministry of Gender, Child and Social Welfare, UNICEF contributed to social protection interventions in 2024. UNICEF launched three cash transfer programmes benefiting 14,926 mothers against a target of 14,936 mothers. The main cash transfer project - the nationwide Shock-Responsive Cash Transfer initiative targeted 12,109 breastfeeding women and caregivers of children under 2 years old, while the Young Child Support grants in a stable (Aweil) and remote area (Ruweng) targeted approximately 2,000 beneficiaries. These unconditional cash transfers were implemented alongside nutrition, health, and protection services, with the latter focusing on gender-based violence. Further, UNICEF partnered with United Nations Office for Project Services, WFP, and World Bank to revise the National Social Protection Policy Framework (NSPPF) by advancing MIS development, coordinated social protection actors, fostered technical collaboration and enhanced technical capacities through trainings and facilitated workshops.
 
UNICEF also provided subnational public financial management (PFM) support and produced key advocacy and evidence-based documents, including national and subnational budget briefs and an investment case for the education sector. The budget briefs demonstrated the low budget scores for the sector, and possibly contributed to the exceptionally high Social Protection budget allocation of US$63 million (4.5 per cent) in FY2024/2025 from just 0.4 per cent in FY2023/2024.  Additionally, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Finance and Planning and the Government of Abyei special administrative area to enhance PFM in Abyei. With UNICEF’s technical, financial and logistical support to the Intergovernmental Fiscal Relations (IGFR) unit of the Budget and Revenue Directorate of the Ministry of Finance and Planning, dedicated PFM packages on planning, reporting and budget oversight were delivered to the ministries of education and finance in Abyei. Equipped with knowledge and skills, the subnational authorities, together with Parliament, partners and CSOs would advocate for budget reforms and improved social sector allocations. 
 
UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) through a memorandum of understanding for the implementation of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7), positioning South Sudan to generate data on 170 indicators, including 38 SGD and 25 child-focused indicators, that are essential for planning interventions in the health, nutrition, education, WASH, and child protection sectors. Through a systems’ strengthening capacity-building strategy, UNICEF supported the NBS to implement the MICS7, through two international technical assistance (TA) embedded in the NBS workforce. These TAs facilitated the development and approval of the MICS7 memorandum of understanding, the formation of the MICS7 technical and steering committees, development of the MICS7 budget, MICS7 survey plan, sample design and creation of critical tools and systems including the Computer Assisted Personal Interview (CAPI) application, and conduct of pre-enumeration activities (household mapping, listing and pre-testing). 
 
Humanitarian action and other emergencies 
In 2024, South Sudan faced a compounded humanitarian crisis driven by public health emergencies, flooding, currency depreciation, and the influx of refugees from Sudan, with 9 million people in need of assistance, 54 per cent of whom were children. UNICEF responded swiftly through its six field offices, establishing a new satellite office in Renk to scale up the Sudan crisis response. Of the 9 million people needing humanitarian assistance, UNICEF met the needs of 3,648,098 people (2,527,359 children), 70 per cent of the total target. 
Key efforts included risk-informed interventions, localization, and gender- and disability-sensitive programming, with a focus on community-driven accountability. UNICEF actively engaged in the development of a subnational risk assessment model, engaging 17 United Nations agencies and non-governmental organizations. Despite challenges in data-sharing, UNICEF aims to launch the model in early 2025 to improve risk management and decision-making.
 
Programme and Operational Effectiveness 
In 2024, UNICEF successfully rolled out the Health Sector Transformation Project and enhanced community engagement and partnerships, facilitating widespread awareness, vaccination campaigns and vitamin A supplementation for populations in need. Effective financial management resulted in 100 per cent budget utilization for Regular Resources, 99 per cent for Other Resources and a refund of a balance of US$3 million working capital loan ecured in 2021. Partnerships were strengthened, fostering local leadership and sustainability. UNICEF supported multiple evaluations, such as the finalization of the joint UNICEF-WFP resilience project evaluation, the first-ever Country Programme Evaluation and regional evaluations, including UNICEF’s localization approach and climate action.

Social and Behavioural Change (SBC) was advanced through evidence-based strategies addressing health and social barriers. Key outcomes included 91 per cent measles vaccine coverage, vitamin A supplementation for 2.48 million children, and engagement of over 3.5 million people via community radio platforms. These initiatives supported school enrolment for 373,285 children, vaccination of over 3.3 million children against polio (95 per cent target), a reduction in immunization dropout rates from 14 per cent to 11 per cent and increased first antenatal care visits from 54 per cent to 57 per cent.

The integration of community networks under the Boma Health Initiative in Lakes state provided scalable insights, while digital platforms like the Internet of Good Things and community feedback mechanisms enhanced youth engagement. UNICEF's advocacy efforts were amplified through media coverage, social media engagement, and a newly launched WhatsApp channel with over 15,000 followers. Campaigns on malnutrition, child marriage, and youth empowerment gained prominence, while the Young Reporters Programme engaged over 300 youth in advocacy efforts. A new 2024–2025 advocacy plan was also launched, addressing food security, climate protection and youth empowerment.

In 2024, UNICEF hosted its first joint programme review and work plan development workshop with the Government, aligning strategic priorities. A monitoring and evaluation framework was operationalized to improve results-based reporting through training. As co-leader in United Nations coordination groups, UNICEF provided strategic leadership for social service interventions and facilitated the timely submission of the 2025 Humanitarian Action for Children Appeal, requesting US$278.2 to target 5.7 million people, including 3.6 million children. 

Strengthening donor partnerships, UNICEF secured multi-year funding for child protection, WASH, and GBV initiatives while building trust in its financial systems, attracting new donors like the United Arab Emirates and Latter-Day Saints Foundation. 

UNICEF South Sudan Country Office kept all five mandatory office committees operational, conducted strategic programme reviews and introduced the Digital Operating Platform to improve process efficiency. Eight of nine audit recommendations were closed, reflecting enhanced governance. 

The Risk Control Matrix was also updated to tackle emerging challenges, and the Business Continuity Plan was maintained with regular simulations to ensure preparedness. Financial controls were enhanced through biometric systems for incentive payments under the Health Sector Transformation Project. Emphasis on decentralization enabled the effective delegation of VISION roles to field officers, improving accountability at the field level and enhancing efficiency in partner transactions. 

UNICEF also ensured that governance frameworks aligned with organizational goals. Efforts focused on strengthening partnerships, promoting informed risk-taking, and prioritizing localization and multi-year financing to enhance sustainable and resilient programming.

In 2024, UNICEF South Sudan achieved considerable progress across key sectors by leveraging strategic partnerships with Government, United Nations agencies, civil society, donors and private sector. 
 
Flexible, Global Thematic Funds enabled the immediate scale up of the Sudan Crisis response and the response to public health emergencies including Yellow Fever, Mpox, Measles, Polio, and a national Cholera outbreak. Further, thematic funds enabled us to secure technical staff required to support preparedness and response activities. Funds were used to initiate activities, and leverage additional resources through the documentation of results achieved with the initial contributions. Half of our humanitarian results this year can be attributed to the contribution of Global Thematic funds. 

UNICEF expanded partnerships with private sector including MTN telecommunications and Stanbic Bank and civil society organizations, promoting community engagement and gender-transformative approaches in health, nutrition, education and child protection. Initiatives such as vaccination campaigns, malnutrition prevention, GBV and climate-resilient water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) programmes were implemented alongside advocacy events like World Children’s Day, World Breastfeeding Day, Day of the Girl Child etc., that brought all stakeholders together, fostering strategic partnerships and collaboration. 
 
Collaborations with donors and United Nations agencies, including the World Food Programme (WFP), World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank, the African Development Bank, Global Fund, Gavi, the Global Partnership for Education, the European Union, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), the Korea International Cooperation Agency, Norway and Germany supported systemic reforms, programme alignment and evidence-based advocacy. 
 
Inter-agency cooperation, such as with the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, the WFP and the International Organization for Migration, on solarization of United Nations compounds, and logistics management, highlighted the power of joint action in benefiting from economy of scale in doing business, avoiding duplication and waste of resources.  

Through these partnerships, UNICEF delivered impactful results, including improved service delivery, strengthened coordination mechanisms, and enhanced institutional capacities.
 
Health: significant progress in maternal, newborn and child health programmes was achieved through strategic partnerships with key donors and organizations, including Canada; the European Union; FCDO; the Global Fund; the United States Agency for International Development (USAID); the World Bank and WHO, among others. Together, they launched the Health Sector Transformation Project, supported by 28 implementing partners nationwide. In response to disease outbreaks, UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with WHO and national stakeholders to enhance campaign planning and delivery. Collaboration with the Global Fund enabled nationwide access to malaria prevention and treatments, and the Against Malaria Foundation supported the distribution of long-lasting insecticidal nets.
 
Nutrition: In partnership with 30 non-governmental organizations and donors such as the Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations and FCDO, UNICEF delivered nutrition services at over 1,200 sites, led the Nutrition cluster and coordinated over 80 agencies, to streamline service delivery and reduce treatment costs for severe acute malnutrition. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), WFP, WHO and civil society organizations (CSOs) to assist the Ministry of Health in roadmap development and funding for new WHO guidelines implementation on wasting prevention and treatment, making South Sudan a pioneer in its adoption. Partnerships with FAO and WFP contributed to enhanced governance and analysis of nutrition information systems, through the effective implementation of the FSNMS 2024 data collection, IPC-AMN analysis, and the first phase of the joint NuVAC (Nutrition Vulnerabilities Assessment in Crisis) initiative.
 
WASH: UNICEF collaborated with the South Sudan Urban Water Cooperation to improve the management of urban water utilities and strengthen sector governance in major towns. WASH’s Joint Sector Review with strategic partners led to a comprehensive status assessment and helped refine future priorities. UNICEF’s partnership renewal with USAID enabled implementation of climate resilience and sustainable WASH interventions in three states. 
 
Education: Varying collaborations with the WFP and the International Organization for Migration supported resilience-building and integrated programmes, enhancement of education access and livelihood and community reintegration in areas affected by displacement. Collaborations with the Global Partnership for Education, Norwegian Refugee Council, Save the Children International and the World Bank promoted informed policy dialogue, programme alignment and joint advocacy.

Child Protection: UNICEF partnered with 29 NGOs, including six women-led organizations, 17 national NGOs and six international NGOs, to provide Child Protection and GBV services. UNICEF collaborated closely with the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Interior on civil registration and vital statistics (on birth notification); the Ministry of Gender, Child and Social Welfare (MoGCSW), Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation on the child protection system; the National Disarmament Demobilization and Reintegration Commission and United Nations Mission in South Sudan on the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism and Children Affected by Armed Conflict agenda; and the National Mine Action Authority on explosive ordnance risk education. UNICEF is also partnering with Juba University and MoGCSW to deliver the Social Work Certificate Programme.

Social Policy: UNICEF partnered with the International Budget Partnership and local entities, such as Samahi Research Limited to advance work on public financial management.
 
SBC: Social and Behavioural Change forged new alliances with private-sector companies like Mobile Telecommunication Network (MTN) and academic institutions like the University of Juba, enhancing community engagement and institutional capacity. Partnerships with civil society and media organizations, including women-led groups like the Women Empowerment Centre of South Sudan and the United Network for Health, promoted gender-transformative approaches and scaled up community engagement.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
The programming environment was challenged by the unprecedented flooding preventing access, public health emergencies including yellow fever, Mpox and cholera, economic crisis, currency depreciation, subnational conflict and an influx of returnees and refugees from the Sudan crisis, all putting a further strain on the fragile social service system, coupled with scare resources.  
 
Economic crisis: The economic crisis coupled with the currency depreciation negatively impacted UNICEF programming, leading to increased costs of doing business, particularly, operational costs that are generally poorly funded by donors. Anticipated public sector capital investment in social sectors and programmes such as education (early childhood education and alternative and flexible learning opportunities), social protection (Young Child Support Grant) was constrained, not meeting expected targets. Delayed salaries for civil servants, particularly, teachers have demotivated key frontline workers, resulting in high absenteeism, and consequentially, slow and delayed implementation of programmes, especially in education and health. Currency depreciation also exponentially impacted the cost of locally procured materials. This particularly impacted WASH operations and maintenance of WASH waterpoints and water treatment facilities. 
 
Sudan Crisis: Meeting the needs of the 900,000 South Sudanese and refugees fleeing the Sudan conflict further strained the existing fragile systems - health, nutrition, WASH, education and child protection - and challenged the humanitarian community to respond with limited resources. It also further required the reprioritization of the limited humanitarian resources to respond. Essentially, UNICEF was able to only respond to humanitarian needs in six of ten states. 
 
Flooding: Programme delivery was challenged due to inaccessibility of vulnerable communities due to flooding.  For example, school closures due to the flooding severely impacted access to quality education for over 184,000 learners, and relocation of vaccine storage facilities affected health service delivery. In the coming year, the office will ensure timely dry season prepositioning to avert supply stock outs during the rainy season of June to November. 
 
Limited and delayed funding: Limited funding for WASH, child protection, and education in emergencies challenged programme delivery in these sectors. The launch of the Health Sector Transformation Project (HSTP) increased demands on UNICEF, while the funding release from the World Bank was greatly delayed by completion of agreements. This affected service delivery and posed a reputational risk for UNICEF. Pre-financing for supplies and a Working Capital Loan for incentive payments were key mitigation strategies employed.
 
Security challenges: Insecurity in some parts of the country and internal conflicts leading to inaccessibility of communities affected delivery of some programme interventions such as the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) household listing. Theft, aid diversion and intimidation of United Nations staff have remained constant throughout the year frustrating programme implementation and affecting staff welfare.

Government capacity challenges: Limited government investment in malnutrition prevention, with complete reliance on non-governmental organizations for nutrition service provision remains a challenge to nutrition programming.  

Levying of taxes: The imposition of taxes and levies on imported supplies, and delays in customs clearance culminated in delays in the delivery of programme supplies and posed a reputational risk to UNICEF. This heavily impacted on WASH, health, HSTP and nutrition supplies. 

Lessons Learned
Prepositioning supplies and stronger logistics networks: Prepositioning supplies and strengthening logistics networks improves emergency response times. This approach helps address accessibility challenges caused by unforeseen events like flooding while also reducing distribution costs and ensuring timely supply delivery. However, limited resources for pre-emptive supply procurement is a challenge. 

Government ownership and leadership: The active involvement and ownership of the Government at the national and state levels are pivotal in ensuring harmonized programme implementation and streamlined operations. The strong leadership shown in coordinating and monitoring WASH programmes demonstrates the importance of Government-driven accountability, resource allocation and policy support in achieving sustained sector improvements. 

Multisectoral integration: Addressing malnutrition requires a systems approach that leverages food, health, WASH, education and social protection systems to tackle key drivers and prevent all forms of malnutrition. UNICEF must also build, document and advocate investment in successful cross-programme integrations that have yielded results to improve services and outcomes and bring them to scale. 

Streamlining partnerships for greater impact - the Country Office leveraged many implementing partners to implement key interventions. However, an analysis revealed that 94 per cent of the active partnerships operate as standalone agreements, with some duplication involving the same partners within and across sectors. This fragmentation limits programmatic synergy and increases administrative cost and workload. To address this, the office is focusing on integrating and harmonizing partnerships to achieve programme convergence and complementarity, enhancing impact while reducing administrative burdens. Moving forward, this approach will align partnerships more closely with programme priorities, fostering collaboration and sustainable results.

Cluster advocacy: UNICEF's leadership in three clusters and the Child Protection Area of Responsibility demonstrated the effectiveness of clusters as platforms for evidence collection and consensus building around key advocacy messages. Through the Nutrition cluster, UNICEF successfully raised awareness of the critical nutrition needs of children, mobilizing resources to secure the nutrition pipeline until mid-2025.

Funding advocacy: Multiyear, flexible funding is important to resilience and multisystem programming. Increasing humanitarian needs and a challenging economic environment underscore the necessity for predictable, sustained funding with integrated resilience objectives. 

Innovation and adaptability: Using artificial intelligence (AI) in automating data management processes significantly enhanced efficiency, saving time and improving report clarity, and could extend to areas like longitudinal report analysis. The need to address persistent insecurity also emphasized the value of flexible, conflict-sensitive programming and adaptive strategies to ensure programme continuity in volatile contexts and effective responses.

Capacity building and local empowerment: Sustainable education requires addressing structural challenges, such as teacher salary delays and infrastructure gaps, through evidence-based advocacy. In child protection, capacity building for case management including supervision is critical and remains a priority.  

Future Outlook
For health, UNICEF will build on the Ministry of Health’s leadership and commitment to the HSTP, ensuring strong government ownership and stewardship in the country.

For nutrition, UNICEF aims to transition service provision from partners to the government and communities. This involves advocating for increased government investment, building the operational capacity and leveraging the HSTP to increase the nutrition workforce on the Government payroll. To improve the quality of young children’s diets, UNICEF will make the social protection and food systems work for children. 

In WASH, UNICEF plans to support the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation in reviewing water policies to include climate considerations, passing the water bill and strengthening state-level coordination mechanisms.

For education, UNICEF is preparing to support the roll-out of the Global Partnership for Education System Transformation Grant. Foundational literacy and numeracy will be central, early childhood education will be expanded and alternative, non-formal and distance learning will be prioritized. The Education in Emergency strategy will be implemented to ensure rapid responses and education continuity during crises.

In child protection, UNICEF will continue to invest in professionalising the social service workforce to meet the needs of children, adolescents and women requiring case management and MHPSS services. 

In social policy, UNICEF will explore innovative fundraising opportunities in 2025, to expand social protection interventions, and pursue service integration and sectoral collaboration for greater impact. 

For operational and programme effectiveness, focus will be put on greater decentralization and localization through strengthening the technical and operational capacity of both local civil society and state governments. Investments would be made in partner capacity building and risk management to strengthen partnerships and reduce capacity gaps. Long-term resource mobilization strategies will be developed to address broader infrastructure needs. Focus will also be placed on establishing contingency plans and expanding partnerships to ensure operational resilience in emergencies.

In 2024, Uganda's socio-economic situation remained stable, with gross domestic product (GDP) growth estimated at 6 per cent, up from an average of 4.1 per cent between 2019 and 2023. The economy grew from US$48.8 billion in fiscal year (FY) 2022/23 to US$53.2 billion in FY 2023/24, indicating strong path of recovery. Uganda met the Least Developed Country graduation criteria, aiming for middle-income status by 2029/30. Meanwhile, inflation was managed at 3.3 per cent, below the central bank target of 5 per cent, significantly improving from 8.8 per cent in 2022/23. While government spending more than doubled from US$9.6 billion in 2019/20 to US$20 billion in 2024/25, a substantial portion was allocated to debt amortization, which constituted 34 per cent of the total national spending. Similarly, while inflation in food decreased to -0.4 per cent, sectors like education, health, and housing experienced significant increases in inflation. The price increase had a detrimental impact on households and jeopardized the access to basic services and education, especially for the many children already living in high poverty.  Social sector spendings decreased as well, with the budget on education going from 8.4 per cent (FY 2023/24) to 7 per cent (FY 2024/25) of the national budget despite an increase in per capita spending from US$51 to US$56. The health spending dropped from 7.7 per cent to 5.5 per cent with per capita spending steady at US$23, and the child protection and WASH expenditures reduced from 0.6 per cent to 0.5 per cent and 2 per cent to 1.4 per cent, respectively. Yet social protection spending remained unchanged at 0.6 per cent.

In 2024, Uganda achieved improvements in maternal and child health, with the institutional maternal mortality ratio declining from 90.3 in FY 2022/23 to 82.6 per 100,000 deliveries in FY 2023/24, and institutional perinatal deaths decreased from 17.8 in FY 2022/23 to 16.5 per 1,000 births in FY 2023/24. The maternal mortality ratio fell by 44 per cent (from 336 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2016 to 189 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2022). Neonatal mortality decreased by 19 per cent and infant mortality by 16 per cent (with the rates dropping from 27 to 22 deaths and from 43 to 36 deaths per 1,000 live births respectively; between 2016 and 2022). Under-five mortality rate saw a 19 per cent reduction (from 64 to 52 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2016 and 2022) (Uganda Demographic and Health Survey – UDHS 2022). The proportion of zero-dose children (5 per cent, 102,260) in FY 2023/24, compared to 6 per cent (138,424 children) in FY 2022/23 and the prevalence of teenage pregnancy (24 per cent overall, 21 per cent in urban and 25 per cent in rural areas) declined slightly in 2024 from 25 per cent in 2016 (Ministry of Health, Annual Health Sector Performance Report 2023/24). 

Uganda's new HIV infections in 2024 dropped to 1.23 per 1,000 susceptible population, compared to 1.3 in 2020, well below the projected 2.5 per 1,000, signaling effective intervention. However, knowledge of HIV prevention remains low at 56 per cent for men and 54 per cent for women aged 15–24 years. The initiation of antiretrovirals (ARVs) for elimination of mother-to-child transmission slightly increased while early Deoxyribonucleic Acid/Polymerase Chain Reaction (DNA/PCR) testing for HIV-exposed infants declined from 91 per cent to 81 per cent, between FY 2022/23 and FY 2023/24 and ART coverage for all ages slightly decreased from 98 per cent to 96.8 per cent between April and June 2024, but remaining above the target of 95 per cent.

Nutrition indicators showed both progress and ongoing concerns. Stunting among children aged under 5 decreased from 29 per cent in 2016 to 26 per cent in 2022, wasting levels remained around 4 per cent, and exclusive breastfeeding increased from 66 per cent to 94 per cent in 2022 (UDHS 2016; UDHS 2022). However, dietary diversity for children aged 6 to 23 months reduced dramatically from 30 per cent in 2016 to 10 per cent in 2022 (UDHS 2016; UDHS 2022), and anaemia levels remain stagnant, affecting 53 per cent of children aged under 5, 30 per cent of adolescent girls, 32 per cent of women of reproductive age, and 38 per cent of pregnant women (UDHS 2016). Only 23 per cent of the severely wasted children received treatment, reflecting the need for better access to nutrition interventions.
In 2024, clean water supply coverage remained stagnant with rural areas at 67 per cent and urban areas at 72.8 per cent. Access to basic sanitation showed an improvement of 2.5 per centage from 27 per cent to 29.5 per cent, while urban areas saw open defecation decrease from 6.4 per cent to 6.2 per cent. Handwashing practices in rural areas remained nearly stagnant, at 36 per cent, highlighting the importance of establishing robust social norms for better sanitation and hygiene. (Ministry of Water and Environment Programme Report 2024)
 
Access to quality education continued to present challenges. The national average pass rate for the Primary Leaving Examination dropped from 88.6 per cent in 2022 to 78.6 per cent in 2023, despite the higher pass rate in 2022 being largely due to the record number of 811,810 learners who took the exam post-COVID, compared to 734,788 in 2020 and 749,379 in 2023. As per the most recent data available (Uganda Bureau of Statistics, 2021), only 9 per cent of children were enrolled in licensed and registered early childhood development (ECD) centres in Uganda. According to UDHS 2022, 55.8 per cent of children aged 24–59 months are developmentally on track in literacy-numeracy, physical, social-emotional, and learning domains, with younger children (24–35 months) more likely to be on track than their older counterparts, indicating potential developmental regression as children age toward school entry. Furthermore, literacy rates have deteriorated by 11 per cent since 2018, with 47 per cent of Primary 3 (P3) children and 68 per cent of P6 children lacking proficiency in literacy. Likewise, numeracy skills are concerning, with 57 per cent of P3 children and 42 per cent of P6 children failing to reach proficiency. Only 34 per cent of children completed the primary education cycle, which coupled with education system’s inability to keep up with the knowledge and skills demands of the rapidly changing labour market, led to a significant number of adolescents and young people categorized as not in employment, education, or training (NEET).

Despite efforts to raise awareness on child rights, substantial challenges persist, with violence and harmful practices still prevalent. Statistics reveal that 76 per cent of children aged 1–14 years have experienced violent discipline, 1 in 2 girls aged 15–19 and 64 per cent of women aged 20–24 faced sexual abuse as children (before age 15), 39.5 per cent of children aged 5–17 are involved in harmful child labour, and 44.3 per cent of human trafficking cases involve children. Additionally, child marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM) remain significant concerns, with 42 per cent of women aged 25–49 married before 18 and FGM rates exceeding 50 per cent in certain districts, while mental health issues affect children severely, with 22.2 per cent experiencing depression and 14.4 per cent anxiety. Birth registration for children under 5 remains low in Uganda, with only 32 per cent registered (UDHS 2016) and 30 per cent holding certificates according to the 2014 census, resulting in nearly 60 per cent lacking legal identity.

Poverty in Uganda is persistently high, with the national monetary poverty rate at 20.3 in 2019/20, although exhibiting a decrease from 21.4 per cent in 2016/17. However, multidimensional poverty rates paint a grimmer picture, at a national average of 44 per cent. Sub-regional data show higher deprivations, with Karamoja at 84.9 per cent and Acholi at 63.6 per cent, respectively. 

Uganda faced multiple humanitarian challenges in 2024, with approximately 2.4 million people in need of humanitarian assistance, including 1.6 million children. The country is host to over 1.8 million refugees and asylum-seekers. Additionally, the Mpox epidemic affected 1,415 individuals, with 44 per cent being women and girls, and 20 per cent children under 18. In Karamoja, the global acute malnutrition rate increased from 11 per cent in 2023 to 12.2 per cent in 2024, surpassing the emergency threshold, while 112,270 children and 8,980 pregnant or breastfeeding women were estimated to require treatment for acute malnutrition (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, June 2024). Additionally, from January to May 2024, natural disasters, including floods and droughts, impacted 100,302 individuals and exacerbated food insecurity and disruptions to essential services.

Every child survives, thrives, and lives in a safe and clean environment.
In  2024, UNICEF Uganda’s integrated approach to primary health care (PHC)  service delivery demonstrated significant progress, achieving a 69 per cent  institutional delivery rate in UNICEF Uganda-supported districts and strengthening  newborn care and prevention of mother-to-child transmission through joint  work plans and joint field evaluations with partners. The mentorship in early  essential newborn care benefited 908 health care providers across 186 health  facilities in 24 districts, contributing to a 90 per cent safe delivery rate  and a 75 per cent Kangaroo Mother Care provision. Children and women’s  survival rate was notable, with 97 per cent of 13,669 pregnant women in High  Dependency Units and 99 per cent of 10,894 sick newborns in special care  units recovering following treatment in the West Nile Region. These key  lessons learned will be disseminated and support will be scaled up nationwide.

In  October 2024, UNICEF Uganda supported the Ministry of Health (MoH) in disseminating  the National Community Health Services guidelines in all 146 districts, with  all partners committing to aligning their programmes with this harmonized  approach by January 2025. This initiative enhances the well-being of children  and women by ensuring uniformly high-quality community-based health care  services across the country, reducing fragmentation, improving access to  services, and ultimately strengthening the resilience and responsiveness of  the primary health system.

With support from UNICEF Uganda, the electronic  Community Health Information System was effectively implemented in 21 out of  146 districts, involving 18,454 community health extension workers (CHEWs)  and village health teams (VHTs). The rollout resulted in a 40 per cent  improvement in reporting rates through the District Health Information  Software 2 (DHIS2) from 2022 to 2024, vital for identifying and monitoring  zero-dose and under-immunized children, and addressing access to basic  sanitation and nutrition services. 

UNICEF  Uganda made significant efforts to deliver the first and second rounds of the  polio campaign across 49 districts in close partnerships with the Uganda  National Expanded Programme on Immunization (UNEPI), District Local  Governments, and the World Health Organization (WHO). Vital contributions were  made by health workers and community health workers who played a crucial role  in enhancing vaccine awareness and disseminate accurate information.

Collaborative efforts between UNICEF Uganda, the  United Nation’s AIDS Programme (UNAIDS) and the United Nations Population  Fund (UNFPA) helped develop and implement a comprehensive national action  plan towards ending paediatric AIDS and strengthening the capacities of  various stakeholders in the paediatric HIV response. In the 29 focus  districts supported by UNICEF Uganda, 568 facilities provided antiretroviral therapy  (ART) to 7,358 children and 19,000 adolescents living with HIV, exceeding the  national annual target. Notably, 88 per cent of children and 90 per cent of  adolescents on ART achieved viral suppression, nearing the national goal of  90 per cent for both treatment and viral suppression.

UNICEF Uganda prioritized the development of the  Food and Nutrition Policy (not yet finalized) in collaboration with the  Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industry and Fisheries and the implementation  of the third National Nutrition Forum, emphasizing the importance of  nutrition for the country’s economic growth. With UNICEF Uganda’s technical  and financial assistance, the MoH reached over 5.1 million mothers and  caregivers with infant and young child feeding counselling, surpassing the  original target of 828,121. Furthermore, UNICEF Uganda through the donation  of the Canadian Government and Nutrition International (NI) contributed to  the supplementation of 9.7 million children 6-59 months with Vitamin A  capsules, achieving 96 percent coverage of the target, with 2.5 million of  the children in Karamoja and refugee hosting-districts Across Uganda.  Additionally, 783,331 adolescents received nutrition messages, with UNICEF  support. To increase access to quality diets, UNICEF Uganda engaged with the  private sector to produce egg powder for children and carried out a scoping  exercise for ‘early foods’ for children. 

To  increase access to quality diets, UNICEF Uganda engaged with the private  sector (Pristine Foods Limited) to produce egg powder for children aged 6–23  months in Tooro sub-region in western Uganda as part of broader efforts to  combat stunting. Relatedly, working  with Taylor Foods and the UNICEF East and Southern Africa Regional Office (ESARO),  UNICEF Uganda also conducted a scoping exercise to identify the most suitable  ‘early foods’ for children 6–23 months. Using this evidence, UNICEF Uganda will support the private  sector and government to increase production and demand for quality foods.

UNICEF Uganda supported Community-Led Total Sanitation  and Market-based Sanitation initiatives to drive demand for sanitation services,  promoting a private sector-driven approach to open defecation-free communities,  which resulted in 121,875 people (24,375 households) gaining access to basic  sanitation services in 2024. UNICEF Uganda also supported the installation of durable, solar-powered  water systems and sanitation facilities in five health care facilities in  Terego and Adjumani districts. In preparation for the Conference of Parties (COP29),  the Ministry of Water and Environment (MoWE) committed to child-centred  climate action and endorsed a Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate  Action. 

During the year, UNICEF Uganda continued to invest in  upstream work,  enhancing normative guidance for the operation  and maintenance of water infrastructure. This led to the establishment of management  structures for rural water systems in 15 districts.  Additionally, groundwater resources were  assessed to support improved and  sustainable access to safe drinking water for children and families. Reduced  investments in water infrastructure and a growing population raise concerns  about equitable access to safe drinking water, with the maintenance of  existing infrastructure being particularly challenging. 

Every child and adolescent learn and acquires skills  for the future.
UNICEF Uganda continued to collaborate with the  Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES) in delivering quality education for  all children. MoES was nominated to be the anchor of the Human Capital  Development programme of the National Development Plan IV (NDP-IV, 2026–2030),  seeking to enhance human capital development throughout the life cycle and emphasizing  access, relevance, equity, and quality of education, alongside  industry-driven skilling and training. 

A result of UNICEF’s Uganda advocacy, in May 2024, the  cabinet approved the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) policy  establishing a vital framework for enhancing ECD services in Uganda. UNICEF  Uganda supported the development of a National Integrated ECD Costed  Strategy, designed to strengthen coordination of ECD efforts, and the formulation  of Basic Requirements and Minimum Standards for pre-primary education,  ensuring that early learning is standardized and quality driven. It is  expected that these initiatives will significantly improve the quality and  reach of ECCE nationwide. MoES and UNICEF Uganda celebrated the first National  Play Day in 2024 in partnership with Education Cannot Wait and the LEGO  Foundation. Some 4.5 million people were reached with messages about the  importance of play in enhancing children’s learning and growth. At district level, UNICEF Uganda supported  52,365 children through 645 ECD centres, offering integrated WASH, nutrition,  and health services. 
 
A  total of 605 teachers were trained in competence-based learning achievement assessment,  including disability, thus improving assessment practices for children with  disabilities. To establish  baseline data on students' reading comprehension and numerical abilities, an  assessment was conducted at the classroom level for 116,880 learners,  comprising 57,208 boys and 59,672 girls. This evaluation focused on the  students' capabilities to read and understand a passage by the age of 10, as  well as their proficiency in counting from 1 to 10 and then from 1 to 100  effectively. To  address low learning outcomes, UNICEF Uganda and the Belgian NGO Education  for Development (VVOB) piloted the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL)  methodology, which was subsequently adopted and will be scaled up nationwide by  MoES under the U-Catch Up programme. 

UNICEF Uganda continued to support government priorities  in unlocking the potential of young people outlined in NDP-IV  (2026–2030) and Uganda’s Joint Adolescent and Youth Programme (2023–2025) by incorporating market-relevant skills  into formal and non-formal education. In 2024, 126,836  adolescents and young people, including refugees, vulnerable girls, NEET  youth, adolescents with disabilities, and those in conflict with the law,  gained 21st century skills, such as problem solving, critical  thinking, creativity, innovation and effective communication, among others, through UNICEF Uganda-supported programmes  and 12 per cent of all government schools integrated  holistic life-skills education. 

With  funding from Swedish International Development Cooperation (Sida), UNICEF  Uganda supported the government in launching the National Digital Agenda  Strategy and the Digital Skills Framework for the education sector. These  initiatives define national priorities for leveraging digital transformation  to enhance digital education, expand learning opportunities, and improve  skills training. Leveraging UNICEF Uganda’s partnership with Airtel, 139  schools were connected to free internet expanding access to digital learning  to more than 45,000 learners. A digital skills training toolkit was  successfully piloted by MoES in secondary schools and ICT centres and  recommended for further integration in the education system institutions. 

Every child and adolescent is protected from  violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices. 
In 2024, UNICEF Uganda continued to work on enhanced  resilience of Uganda’s child protection system. UNICEF Uganda advocacy led to  a government decision to waive birth certificate fees for children registered  within six months of birth, and designating remand homes as Magistrates'  Courts to expedite juvenile justice cases, thus improving children’s access  to legal identity rights and justice services.

Child Wellbeing Committees (CWCs) flourished in 32  out of 34 UNICEF Uganda-supported districts, promoting collaboration among  judiciary, health, education, and community services, as well as the police  and civil society. The priorities set out by CWCs led to enhanced accountability  and contributed to resource allocations. As such, Karamoja’s Abim District  provided transport to boost child protection responses, and Kaabong District  allocated UGX 3 million for child protection in the fiscal year 2024/2025. Throughout  the year, UNICEF Uganda continued to emphasize at national and sub-national  level the need for a gradual increase in domestic financing of child  protection services, decreasing reliance on donor funding and ensuring more  sustainable support for these services.
