To address fragmented data collection systems, the  Ministry of Gender, Labour, and Social Development (MGLSD), with support from  UNICEF Uganda and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID),  developed standardized tools and indicators for a unified Child Wellbeing  Management Information System (CBMIS). The procurement process for an  ICT-based system was initiated, while platforms, like SAUTI 116 helpline,  continued offering real-time data on abuse and to amplify children's voices  as well as support for those affected.

UNICEF Uganda supported initiatives  to empower communities and families and create  safer environments for children. In 2024, nearly 50,000 caregivers  participated in evidence-based parenting programmes, and 3,060 children  acquired life skills to identify and report violence. Social and behaviour  change (SBC) interventions reached 321,930 people, challenging harmful norms  and promoting gender equality. Community influencers led dialogues to address  child marriage and FGM, with 126,159 people gaining knowledge and skills to  prevent gender-based violence (GBV). Additionally, 59,727 individuals,  including children, learned about safe reporting channels for sexual  exploitation and abuse. The National Parenting Manual rollout further  supported families in adopting positive practices.

Through Sida  funding, over 540,000  children gained their right to identity through birth registration, and birth registration services at decentralized health  facilities were strengthened to enable timely realization of children’s right  to identity. A total of 112,465  individuals received mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) through  innovative mechanisms such as the MHPSS chatbot integrated into case  management. Justice services reached over 10,300 children in contact with the  law, and more than 1,500 were successfully reintegrated back into their  communities. The SAUTI 116 helpline supported 7,341 children experiencing  violence with tailored responses and referrals.

The government's approval of the National  Operational Framework for Social Care and Support System and the National  Strategy for Strengthening the Social Service Workforce marked an important  step in providing quality multi-sectoral services. UNICEF Uganda trained  1,182 para-social workers and 200 police and health officers in child  protection case management, enhancing responses to violence against children.

Amid climate shocks, refugee influxes, and public  health emergencies, UNICEF Uganda scaled up protection services in  refugee-affected districts, including training para-social workers,  strengthening government coordination, and integrating MHPSS into child  protection services. During the Mpox outbreak, UNICEF Uganda mobilized  support to enhance community-based services and reinforce social service  workforce participation in government-led coordination. This effort ensured  strong case management and the provision of MHPSS to 6,686 children and  placed 85 unaccompanied and separated children in alternative care,  significantly improving child protection outcomes.
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life.
In 2024, UNICEF Uganda made significant progress in  ensuring child poverty was routinely measured and used for policy and  programming decisions. Through UNICEF Uganda advocacy, child rights  indicators were incorporated into the 2024 Population and Housing Census and  the 2023/24 Uganda National Household Survey, providing comprehensive and  systematic data to compute monetary and multidimensional child poverty. 

MGLSD and UNICEF Uganda successfully launched a  National Chapter of the Global Coalition to End Child Poverty in Uganda,  co-chaired by UNICEF Uganda and Save the Children. This is a major milestone  towards collective advocacy and action to end child poverty in Uganda. UNICEF  Uganda continued its partnership with the Kampala Capital  City Authority in implementing the Girls Empowering Girls programme for vulnerable  adolescent girls. In 2024, the programme provided support to 3,435 adolescent  girls, including peer mentoring, access to youth-friendly services, and cash transfers. 

UNICEF Uganda developed an Investment Case for  Social Protection and conducting disability-focused studies to support the establishment  of a child disability grant in Uganda. UNICEF Uganda also supported the finalization  of the National Social Protection Strategy (2025–2029) and made preparatory  steps to create a Single Social Registry.

In 2024, UNICEF Uganda continued to strengthen the  capacity of national and sub-national government counterparts for effective  and efficient use of public resources, aiming to improve child-related  spending. UNICEF Uganda supported five local governments on local revenue mobilization,  with one district ringfencing 30 per cent of local revenue for social spending,  while others ringfenced various proportions for education, health and  nutrition. Critical budget analytics contributed to increased per capita  spending in education from US$50.5 in 2023/24 to US$55.9 in 2024/25. However,  despite an increase in the national budget from UGX 54.74 trillion to UGX  72.14 trillion, the proportion allocated to education and health declined as  the sector budget did not increase by the same proportion as the national  budget. The huge increase did not filter to social sectors as it related to  the recapitalization of the Central Bank as a once-off payment, with the  total national budget expected to normalise in trend starting 2025/26.

UNICEF Uganda policy analysis and advocacy on public  finance for children led to enhanced budget transparency, with Uganda's  oversight score in the Open Budget Survey improving from 56/100 in 2021 to 67/100 in 2023.  Disability-inclusive budgeting was promoted through capacity building and the  production of the audio-visual versions of the citizen budget, to compliment  the braille version that was launched in 2023.

UNICEF Uganda continued to enhance the quality of  the Equity Atlas, an online portal that connects budgetary data with  development outcomes across all districts in Uganda, through the addition of  lower-level government disaggregated data. The data from the portal has been  used in five local governments where UNICEF has successfully supported  enhancement of local level for social spending. In Kyegegwa and Adjumani, for  example, increased resources were earmarked to support education spending.  Lamwo ringfenced 30 per cent of total local revenue for social spending. As  part of a South-South cooperation, the tool was shared with other countries  in the East and Southern Africa Region. 

In support of the national planning process, UNICEF  Uganda successfully supported the design of the Human Capital Development  Programme of NDP-IV and supported related district development planning in 34  districts. This ensured that the process reflected the social needs, with  specific strategies to tackle challenges in the social sector. 

Programme  effectiveness
In 2024, UNICEF Uganda effectively used multimedia  campaigns to promote SBC, awareness and uptake of health and education  services, including promoting Integrated Child Health Days, routine  immunizations, handwashing, yellow fever vaccination, Mpox prevention, and  the development of 21st-century skills. Using radio and TV broadcasts, the  campaigns disseminated essential health, education, and protection messages,  reaching an audience exceeding 26.7 million people. U-Report chatbots exemplified  the use of technology to engage young audiences and facilitated conversations  with over 73,400 young individuals and community members on 21st-century  skills, job readiness, human papilloma virus (HPV) vaccination, Mpox  prevention, violence against children, nutrition, HIV/AIDS, online child  exploitation and abuse, and healthy relationships. The U-Report Communities  of Action, a youth-led initiative, successfully mobilized over 143,00  community members during the polio house-to-house campaign across 49  districts, highlighting the power of youth participation.

As  part of Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), over 30,000 responses  to complaints, concerns and questions were provided to users through the  U-Report live chats/U-Partners platform with the support of trained partners  such as MoH’s call centre, SAUTI 116 help line counsellors and KCCA social  workers.

In 2024, UNICEF Uganda submitted a written complementary report on the implementation of the  Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in Uganda. The report analyses  the current legislative and policy developments, provides the CRC Committee  with critical information to assess the State Party’s compliance and progress  in implementing the 2005 CRC Committee Concluding Observations. It  complements the State Party combined third to fifth periodic Report  (submitted in May 2021) and offers insights into achievements and ongoing  challenges in implementing the Convention. UNICEF also provided technical  support to Uganda Child Rights NGO Network to prepare alternative reports for  civil society and children, which were submitted to the CRC Committee.

UNICEF Uganda actively engaged in the Comprehensive  Refugee Response Framework (CRRF) Development Partner Group and interagency  coordination to ensure child-sensitive refugee response strategies. In  partnership with the United Nation’s High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR),  UNICEF Uganda contributed to the achievement of the key operational goals of the  CRRF National Plan, successfully reaching approximately 90,000 refugee and  host population children with a crucial multi-sectoral package of humanitarian  interventions in refugee-hosting districts[1].  

Communications,  advocacy and partnerships
UNICEF Uganda strategic media efforts led to 623  mentions in the media and a rise in online followers to over 5.3 million,  underscoring the importance of digital communication. Two media field visits to showcase the  positive impacts and value of UNICEF maternal and newborn health, nutrition  and WASH programmes funded by the Swedish and UK governments in southwestern  (Mbarara, Isingiro and Kamwenge) and northern Uganda (Arua, Adjumani and  Koboko) were organized. UNICEF Uganda produced  3,252 advocacy materials on education, social protection, health, ECD, and  nutrition to promote children's rights. UNICEF Uganda created a simplified  version of the 2024 report on Multi-Dimensional Child Poverty in Uganda for  young readers, which was shared at the launch of the National Coalition to  End Child Poverty. To celebrate the World Children’s Day and the 35th  anniversary of the CRC, UNICEF Uganda partnered with the Uganda  Communications Commission for a live broadcast showcasing children’s  technology skills. Under the Business for Results (B4R) framework, UNICEF  Uganda engaged 26 businesses, securing US$417,085 in support for youth  skilling and digital learning. Internships for 50 youths in digital  skills programmes were facilitated as well. The continuous partnership with Airtel Uganda  provided 45,150 students and 1,935 teachers with digital learning access  through 111,600 gigabytes of data at 1,270 schools.

In 2024, UNICEF Uganda played an important role in advocating for policy decisions reinforcing Uganda’s primary health care system through active engagement with key government and development partners across platforms such as the Mother and Child Health Technical Working Group (TWG), the Health Development Partner Group, and the Community Health TWG. Collaborations with Ministries, Departments, and Agencies (MDAs), including MoWE, National Medical Stores, Uganda Bureau of Statistics (UBOS), MGLSD, Uganda AIDS Commission, the National Drug Authority (NDA), and regional referral hospitals, facilitated improvements in health service delivery as described under the results above. 

At the district level, partnerships with District Local Governments and other stakeholders, including international NGOs, national NGOs, community-based organizations and academic institutions like Makerere University, helped to enhance health interventions at the sub-national level. Public-private partnerships were also key. Collaborating with Genome and Crown Health Care, UNICEF Uganda facilitated critical infrastructure improvements such as installing oxygen plants in regional hospitals. UNICEF Uganda, alongside MoH, UNEPI, and WHO, successfully conducted polio vaccination campaign in 49 districts and worked with partners to ensure equitable vaccine distribution. 

In nutrition, UNICEF's Uganda leadership in TWGs, together with the World Food Programme (WFP), WHO, and USAID, addressed critical issues like the Karamoja nutrition crisis. UNICEF Uganda collaborated with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) to provide WASH climate resilience training for 25 staff and partnered with Water Aid Uganda to enhance coordination and harmonization in the water and sanitation sector.

UNICEF Uganda reinforced commitment towards advancing the ECD agenda through strategic alliances with governmental partners, civil society organizations, and faith-based organizations. This was crucial for successfully implementing and scaling ECD initiatives and contributing to the adoption of the ECCE policy, the development of pre-primary education standards, and the celebration of Uganda's first National Play Day that highlighted the educational value of play. 

At the sub-national level, partnerships with Core Primary Teachers' Colleges enabled professional development training for caregivers and teachers. Innovative approaches, such as mobile ECD centres developed with Finn Church Aid, brought services to remote areas. Partnerships with academia, including Makerere University and the University of the Witwatersrand, helped improve caregiver well-being through interventions like Caring for the Caregiver. UNICEF Uganda also played a prominent role as Chair of the Education Development Partners Group, working closely with the World Bank, the Embassy of Ireland, USAID, the United Kingdom government, the European Union, United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and UNHCR, to leverage support for transforming the education sector. 

UNICEF Uganda partnered with the Moroto Teacher Training Institute and the Embassy of Ireland to train primary teachers and implement competence-based assessments. Enhanced alliances within the Netherlands-funded PROSPECTS partnership, implemented jointly by UNICEF Uganda, UNHCR, International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Bank, and the International Finance Cooperation, as well as KfW, Enabel, and the European Union through the Gender for Development Uganda (G4DU) programme, focused on girls' empowerment and education. UNICEF Uganda strengthened its collaboration with the Generation Unlimited (GenU) team by joining the Green Rising Initiative and collaborating on imaGen Ventures solutions.

In partnering with the Lutheran World Federation, UNICEF facilitated child protection services for Sudanese refugee children in Kiryandongo and co-chaired the Child Protection Sub-Working Technical Committee with UNHCR to coordinate responses and integrate refugee data into the CWBMIS. In collaboration with USAID, UNICEF Uganda mobilized funds through the Social Care and Support TWG to enhance the alternative care framework, ensure the safe closure of unregistered children’s homes, advance justice for children, and develop the national CWBMIS further. UNICEF Uganda also worked with Makerere University to include child protection in social work and MHPSS curricula. 

During the Mpox response, UNICEF Uganda worked with MoH to enhance the coordinated delivery of MHPSS services at both national and district levels. This included offering technical support for coordination meetings and deploying 12 animators to create child-friendly spaces in partnership with World Vision International, ensuring MHPSS services were available in communities. In collaboration with MGLSD, para-social workers received training in key areas such MHPSS, child protection, first aid, and identification of mental health concerns. Enhanced coordination between social welfare services and MHPSS teams reinforced an integrated, multi-sectoral response, ensuring a holistic approach to child protection and violence prevention. This partnership was key in addressing vulnerabilities and safeguarding children during public health emergencies.

UNICEF Uganda’s Mpox risk communication and community engagement interventions reached 7,326,464 people with life-saving information. The multimedia campaign reached 5,895,718 individuals (3,124,731 males and 2,770,987 females) and targeted communication efforts, in partnership with Solutions for People (S4P) and Uganda Red Cross Society (URCS), saw 147,856 people engaged in Kampala and Wakiso districts (67,279 males and 80,577 females), and 1,282,890 people reached in nine districts in cities, towns, municipalities, and peri- urban areas (630,749 males and 652,126 females), including 15 male persons with disabilities. UNICEF supported MoH to deploy film and audio-visual vans to support social mobilization efforts in Nakasongola, Mayuge, Wakiso, and Luweero districts, reaching over 300,000 individuals with prevention messages on Mpox. 

Through partnerships with S4P, URCS, and district-specific community engagement interventions, 103,140 key influencers (54,819 males and 48,212 females) were engaged, including boda boda riders who formed the largest group, accounting for 92 per cent of the total with 95,042 participants. Key influencers and local leaders were well-represented, including 2,123 private sector leaders, 1,106 VHTs, 611 health workers, and 332 Local Council members. Additionally, specialized outreach reached 1,987 truck and bus drivers, 891 sex workers, and 392 law enforcement officers, all informed on Mpox prevention. Efforts were also directed towards vulnerable populations, engaging 329 refugee leaders. Political and traditional leadership figures were included, with 196 leaders and 13 traditional healers participating. Finally, 118 division leaders supported community outreach efforts effectively.

With support from UNICEF Uganda, S4P launched the Safe Text initiative to promote safe communication through a digital platform. This innovative approach encouraged individuals to engage in safer communication practices by pledging to send messages to the designated number, 8500, thus creating a support network for those in need. The Text Safe campaign, integrated with social media texting and a WhatsApp chatbot under the U-Report, successfully reached 20,407 participants (11,468 males and 8,939 females) in Kampala and Wakiso. This robust level of engagement underscores the initiative's success and highlights the growing community awareness about the importance of safe and effective communication. Qualitative community feedback revealed several key issues regarding Mpox. Firstly, knowledge gaps were significant, with many people unaware of Mpox, its transmission, severity, and prevention methods. Secondly, there was considerable fear and stigma, with concerns about contracting Mpox and potential stigmatization being prevalent. Thirdly, economic concerns were notable, with significant anxieties about potential lockdowns and their economic impact. Lastly, questions arose about the health care system’s capacity to manage an outbreak effectively.

UNICEF Uganda partnered with UBOS, MGLSD, and Ministry of Finance Planning and Economic Development, among others, to deliver several child-focused outcomes. Partnerships with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), UNWOMEN, and UNFPA enhanced coordinated efforts in national development planning, data collection, and resource mobilization. In partnering with Makerere University and the Economic Policy Research Centre, UNICEF Uganda provided evidence-based advocacy in support of the NDP IV development process, as well as setting of targets for the Programme Implementation Action Plans (PIAPs). Partnerships with the Trailblazers Mentoring Foundation and Uganda Youth Development Link have strengthened grassroots outreach, promoting the expansion of social protection for adolescent girls. Additionally, media partnerships have been enhanced to provide editorial coverage and live broadcasts of key UNICEF events and milestones. These partnerships also included participation in eight national and regional Mpox training sessions, equipping journalists with comprehensive insights on the disease and improving their ability to report on outbreaks in detail beyond just numbers. These engagements amplified the impact of UNICEF Uganda’s programme work by reaching out to affected and at-risk communities through a wide range of national and local media. This included newspapers such as the Daily Monitor, The New Vision, The Observer, and Bukedde; television channels like NTV, UBC TV, NBS TV, and Bukedde TV; and 46 different radio stations.

Partnering with MoH and OPM, UNICEF Uganda enhanced advocacy and communication for the ‘No Time to Waste – Let us reduce stunting today’ campaign. UNICEF Uganda also supported journalist training in the Tooro region to and the development of the Uganda Nutrition Advocacy and Communication strategy, its implementation plan, and a national campaign concept. Utilizing the B4R framework, UNICEF Uganda collaborated with 26 businesses (including StartHub Africa, Standard Chartered Bank, Stanbic Business Incubator, Airtel Uganda, MTN Uganda, and its foundation) for in-kind, financial, and advocacy support for youth skilling and digital learning. This included engagement with 22 private sector companies to support the ‘Learning to Earning’ initiative for NEET youth and advancing digital skills training for 40,000 adolescents and young people and professional internships. Additionally, through the European Union-funded Ending Child Labor in Coffee Supply Chain pilot project, UNICEF and the ILO trained 11 coffee companies and three associations in child labour monitoring and prevention. This initiative, in collaboration with Kalungu District CWC, is benefitting nearly 1,700 children.

The Skill and Transform Resilient Youth to Invest in the Development of Early Childhood (STRYIDE) Initiative, co-developed with United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF), involved continuous collaboration to advance ECD financing solutions with pro-bono experts, UNICEF Canada, and the Helsinki Hub’s Innovative Finance team. UNICEF Uganda collaborated with 14 Programme Cooperation Agreement partners (VSO and World Vision were the largest partnerships), other United Nations agencies, and governmental bodies, including the OPM, MoFPED, and the National Planning Authority, to prepare the One UN report, work plans, and a multi-year funding framework for the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF).

Flexible funding mechanisms, including Regular Resources and thematic funds, enabled UNICEF Uganda to introduce innovate solutions amplifying results for children. These resources allowed for responsive and targeted interventions, such as the introduction of Oxygen-as-a-Service model at the primary health care level, the development of the mobile ECD centres, and the deployment of MHPSS services during public health emergencies such as Mpox.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Child Survival  and Development identified the growing need to address health disparities in  urban settings, including a more integrated approach in urban health care and  private health facilities, improving services for zero-dose children, meeting  the high demands for safe delivery and neonatal care, and focusing on urban  sanitation for vulnerable populations such as refugees and slum dwellers.  Strong partnerships and integrated services have been vital, particularly in  resource-constrained areas, to leverage local maternity and neonatal systems  effectively through training programmes like Essential Training in Operations  and Obstetrics and emergency obstetric care mentorships. Digital health  integration remains a barrier, requiring enhanced interoperability of health  management information systems, combining various digital health tools and  platforms in the health sector and other relevant sectors. Resource  constraints in regions like the West Nile necessitate efficient leveraging of  existing partnerships and forging new partnerships with entities supporting  service delivery to support essential training and health care delivery. 
  
Going forward,  strong government leadership will be crucial. The government's unprecedented  political commitment, exemplified by setting a deadline for aligning partners  with designated cadres like CHEWs and VHTs, marks a significant step towards  a more organized and effective community health system. Deliberate efforts to  integrate climate change resilience into WASH and PHC services are also in  progress through situation analyses and the development of national  strategies and programming that advocate for child-sensitive and  climate-resilient initiatives aligned with the Nationally Determined  Contributions and National Adaptation Plans.   
  
Integrating  nutrition assessment, Vitamin A supplementation and deworming services is key  to address the diverse needs of children in ECD centres and promote their  overall well-being and readiness for formal education. Innovative solutions,  such as the prototype disability-inclusive ECD kit used in emergencies and  the Caring for Caregivers package that enhances the mental and emotional  health of caregivers, have yielded significant positive outcomes and present  opportunities for broader applications in various emergency and non-emergency  contexts. Community-based ECD centres, particularly in remote areas and those  supported by grassroots organizations, alongside mobile ECD centres, have  effectively improved access to early education for underserved populations.  The scale up of these models is key to promote inclusive education.
  
UNICEF Uganda  is a key player in adolescent and youth skills development. To expand impact,  UNICEF Uganda should continue to utilize its technical expertise to enhance  and expand the institutionalization of several 21st-century skills  training programmes within educational systems, focusing on resilience,  employability, and preparedness for adulthood while targeting the most  vulnerable group of young people, including refugee adolescents and youth.  Strengthening national programmes with market-driven skills training through  an ecosystem approach is also vital. This approach entails high-level  advocacy, including the annual celebration of World Skills Day with focus on  21st-century skills, development of the National Skills Framework  with focus on future-jobs-ready skills, incorporating relevant components  into ongoing TVET reform showcasing successful practices, partnering with the  private sector to assess labour market needs, providing post-training  transition pathways, leveraging technology, and involving adolescents as key  stakeholders. 
  
Furthermore,  Uganda’s Continuous Professional Teacher Development model, which trains Core  Primary Teacher College Centre Tutors on life skills and provides ongoing  mentorship and support to other teachers, has proven to be effective and  sustainable and is recommended for full integration in the curricular of  pre-service and in-service trainings of Primary Teacher Colleges. This model  attracts more educators to life skills education, ensuring broader  dissemination and implementation of these essential skills within the  educational system.
  
Uganda  has launched the Operational Framework for the Social Care and Support System  and the National Strategy for Strengthening the Social Service Workforce at  the end of 2024. Translating this framework into tangible implementation is  critical, as is investing in cross-sectoral collaboration with justice,  health, education, and social protection sectors. This will enhance resource  mobilization and accountability for the delivery of integrated services to  address violence against children, GBV, and other vulnerabilities affecting  families.
  
Community-based  response mechanisms, coupled with improved linkages to essential services,  have significantly strengthened the case management process. Investing in the  capacity of Local Council Courts will be pivotal in expanding community  access to justice. Additionally, leveraging innovative case management  solutions—such as the SAUTI/Child Helpline and the MHPSS Chatbot – has  improved access to MHPSS services while ensuring privacy, anonymity, and cost  efficiency.
  
Moving forward,  continued high-level advocacy with the MGLSD and development partners will be  a priority to secure sustainable budget allocations for the SAUTI helpline  and other critical justice mechanisms. This includes the deployment of  Justice for Children Coordinators in High Courts to ensure timely and  effective access to justice for children in contact with the law.
  
Securing legal  identity for children is fundamental for accessing health care, education,  and social protection. The gazetting of courts within remand  homes is a transformative step in strengthening Uganda’s juvenile justice  system. It enhances access to child-friendly legal proceedings, reduces case  delays, and minimizes logistical challenges like transportation to district  courts. This approach aligns with global best practices, ensuring cases are  handled swiftly by trained judicial officers while fostering collaboration  between justice, social welfare, and rehabilitation services for better care  and reintegration of juveniles. Through Sida funding, support is being  provided to finalize the Child Justice Strategy, a key framework for  strengthening Uganda’s justice system to protect children's rights. This  strategy will institutionalize child-friendly legal procedures, ensuring  inclusivity, non-discrimination, and meaningful child participation. By  embedding child-sensitive approaches, it will enhance access to justice for  vulnerable children, and drive accountability for timely, equitable legal redress.  
  
The completion  of CWBMIS – designed to be interoperable and integrated with health,  education, and justice management systems – will be a game-changer for  evidence-based planning and service delivery. By leveraging data innovations  at both village and national levels, Uganda can enhance real-time monitoring,  improve case management, and strengthen responses to violence against  children and GBV. At the national and sub-national levels, these data-driven  approaches will enable more targeted interventions, optimize resource  allocation, and improve accountability in service delivery. The integration  of digital solutions will not only enhance coordination across sectors but  also make child protection and social welfare responses more agile,  cost-effective, and impactful.
  
Despite progress,  challenges remain in community engagement and the adoption of  gender-transformative approaches across contexts. Emphasizing cross-sectoral  collaboration and mixed implementation approaches (government and civil  society) will help tailor solutions to local needs and enhance  sustainability. To strengthen child protection services, district and  sub-county CWCs need broader mandates to encompass more protection issues,  while local funding is required to guarantee long-term programme sustainability.  Ongoing capacity building and mentorship for local officials are also  essential for sustainable and coordinated responses.

In humanitarian  crises, combining clinical care with strong community engagement is  essential. Psychosocial support is also vital for bridging hospital and  community settings, helping to alleviate fear, anxiety, stigma, and  discrimination. Collaboration among mental health workers, VHTs, para-social  workers, and community development officers is fundamental to fostering  community engagement and trust, key to managing epidemics effectively.  Additionally, integrating school-based programmes into epidemic response  plans ensures timely and appropriate support for children, among the most  vulnerable during outbreaks.
  
Following the  2024 Violence Against Children Global Ministerial Conference, the Government  of Uganda reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening the child protection  system. Key priorities include enhancing support for caregivers, ensuring  safer learning environments, expanding access to quality child protection  services, and fully implementing the National Child Policy. These efforts aim  to create a more resilient and responsive system that safeguards children  from violence and promotes their well-being.   Moving  forward, UNICEF Uganda will focus on innovative partnerships with NGOs,  financial institutions, and cultural institutions to challenge entrenched  social norms and ensure cohesive collaboration with existing partners, while  advocating for sustainable child protection financing through targeted  engagement with parliamentary committees and the Ministry of Finance.
  
Several  challenges were encountered in Social Protection. The Population and Housing  Census experienced significant delays due to insufficient funding.  Additionally, the questionnaire was overloaded with multiple issues, reducing  the usefulness of the results. These delays impacted the development of new  multidimensional child poverty and census reports. The overall budget  increased by 37 per cent, from UGX 52.74 trillion in 2023/24 to UGX 72.14  trillion in 2024/25. As social sector budgets changed by a smaller proportion  (health by 14 per cent, social protection 22 per cent, while WASH and education  declined by 6.1 per cent and 0.94 per cent, respectively) than the increase  in the total national budget, the proportion of the sector budgets showed significant  decline, taking the country off the track to meet international targets. Limited  financial resources also hampered several planned activities for UNICEF  Uganda, including reduced support for local revenue enhancement in districts.  In total, only five districts were able to be supported  to a limited scale, despite the huge  potential to achieve better results at scale. 
  
From these  challenges, several lessons were identified. First, surveys should not be  overloaded with too many questions in order to maintain their efficacy and  integrity. Second, not all indicators can be collected from any survey, and  thus it is critical to ensure that indicators are only included in surveys  whose design can facilitate objective response and ensure data quality. Third,  leveraging partnerships and co-creation is vital for achieving better results  for children. For example, UNICEF Uganda collaborated with key partners to  launch the National Coalition to End Child Poverty and supported Uganda’s  development planning with other United Nations agencies and the National Planning  Authority (NPA). This facilitated the inclusion of evidence-based priorities  and PIAP indicators in the NDP-IV, which is expected to allow for better  focus and measurement of progress towards 2030. 
  
Looking ahead,  a partnership with UBOS will enable the production of new monetary and  multidimensional child poverty statistics and a child census report in 2025,  along with a functional difficulties survey. Additionally, advocacy under the  National Coalition to End Child Poverty, humanitarian cash transfers for the  Mpox health emergency, policy updates, budget analytics, and a peer review of  district development plans will be pursued in collaboration with MGLSD,  UNICEF Uganda, and other partners.

Tanzania experienced robust economic growth in 2024 and the International Monetary Fund and the Africa Development Bank both forecasted a real growth in gross domestic product (GDP) of over 5% for 2024, with projections of an increase in 2025. Still, poverty reduction has progressed more slowly than anticipated (from 26.5% to 26.2% based on the national poverty line); the poverty rate, based on the international poverty line, is projected to decrease from 43.0% in 2024 to 41.7% by 2026[1]

A nominal annual increase is noted in relevant government’s budgets apportionment for the social sector; for example, the education budget grew by 3.4% and the health budget by 4.3% compared to the previous fiscal year. Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding inefficiencies and inequities in overall resource allocation and utilization. To tackle these challenges, UNICEF Tanzania is working with the government to formulate policies and guidelines geared towards increased budgets and spending in the social sector.    

Tanzania embarked on the elaboration of Vision 20/50; a key planning futuristic document that will guide policies, both medium and long term. UNICEF and other Development partners had opportunity to contribute. The Vision 20/50 takes cognizant of the significant mega trends, such as demographic shifts, with about half of Tanzania's 62 million people being young people under the age of 18 years, and increase in urbanization3, and climate change, present real challenges in the programming environment.  Tanzania, like other countries in the region, is highly vulnerable to climate change, ranking 47th globally in susceptibility and 150th in readiness to cope. Climate change erodes household livelihoods, reduces access to education and essential services, and heightens poverty and vulnerability. These factors compound existing challenges, making it imperative to prioritize child-centered policies and interventions that address both current needs and future risks.   

Between January to May 2024, floods caused by the El Niño phenomenon and Cyclone Hidaya impacted over 200,000 people in eight regions in Tanzania; 212 people were injured and 177 lost lives. UNICEF was quick to provide support to government ensuring over 2,000 individuals received mental health and psychosocial support services: over 2,000 school children with temporary learning spaces and educational supplies. including science kits and early child development (ECD) kits to ensure continuation of learning. Child-friendly spaces and play materials were provided to secure a safe environment where children can learn and play.  
 
In the reporting year, UNICEF provided support to 232,728 families (1,168,451 people) affected by cholera across the 23 regions in mainland and three regions in Zanzibar.   The Second Vice President’s Office-Disaster Management Commissioner (Zanzibar) and the Prime Minister’s Office-Disaster Management Department (Mainland Tanzania) have integrated disaster risk reduction into sector development plans and set up a Disaster Management Information System resulting in better information sharing and decision-making. In addition, the Prime Minister’s Office with UNICEF support has now developed guidelines for Humanitarian Cash Transfers (HCTs) to ensure efficient, transparent, and accountable distribution of cash assistance during emergencies.  
   
UNICEF Tanzania continues to place emphasis on addressing various challenges faced by children and while progress has been made, a lot remains to be done. Under-five mortality has significantly declined, from 67 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2015/16 to 43 in 2022, while neonatal mortality remains unchanged at 24 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022, compared to 25 deaths in 2015/16. The proportion of children under five whose births have been registered has risen substantially, from 26% in 2015/16 to 68% in 2022; Access to basic drinking water and sanitation services has improved, with 64% of the population having access to (at least) basic drinking water services, up from 49% in 2015/16. However, open defecation remains a concern, with only a slight reduction from 16% in 2010 to 10% in 2022. Although efforts in the education sector have increased, 1 in 5 primary-school-aged children and 2 in 5 lower-secondary school aged children are out of school. The prevalence of stunting among children under five has decreased from 31.8% in 2015/16 to 30% in 2022.  There has only been a slight decline in the prevalence of female genital mutilation (FGM), with 8% of women aged 15-49 and 4% of adolescent girls aged 15-19 having undergone FGM in 2022, a decrease from 10% and 5%, respectively, in 2015/16. The percentage of adolescent girls aged 15-19 who have experienced physical violence since the age of 15 has decreased from 22% in 2015/16 to 8% in 2022. Similarly, the incidence of sexual violence decreased from 11% in 2015/16 to 9% in 2022. The percentage of adolescents who have had a child or are pregnant has seen a slight decrease, from 26.7% in 2004-2005 to 22% in 2022 against a government target of 5% by 2022.[2]   
 
Going forward, in 2025, UNICEF Tanzania will support key policy shifts as well as change strategies that will foster bigger results for children in Tanzania. This includes support to reforms in the Education Sector, National ECD strategies focusing on the first 1000 days. As well as parenting and the adolescent agenda. In 2024, UNICEF supported the Minister of State, President’s Office Regional Administration and Local Government (PORALG) in co-designing Early Childhood Development (ECD) center models for creches (for children under 2 years), day care and community centers. The Government will use these architectural designs to build ECD centers.

ECD:
To enhance access to integrated services for young children, UNICEF supported the government of Tanzania to identify contextually relevant ECD centre models for scaling up. This effort included a South-to-South learning visit of a multi-ministerial delegation from Tanzania (Mainland and Zanzibar) to Rwanda, followed by co-designing initiatives with ECD stakeholders under the leadership of the government. As a result, for the first time, children-centred architectural plans have been created to implement the national standards for establishing creches, daycares, and community-based centres to expand access to quality childcare and holistic child development. The government has committed to operationalizing and scaling the ECD centre model, highlighting the political will to advance the ECD agenda. 

In Zanzibar, UNICEF is supporting the government in implementing an integrated ECD service delivery model through community-based early childhood education centres (TuTu Centres) dedicated to holistic development and school-readiness for young children. This is done through engaging in play-based activities and comprehensive ECD programmes. This support has benefitted 1,047 children aged 3 – 5 years old (570 girls and 477 boys) and their parents/caregivers, providing nurturing care services to enhance their comprehensive growth and development. 

As part of creating an enabling environment to advance the ECD agenda in Zanzibar UNICEF supported the government to conduct a comprehensive situation analysis of young children to inform the development of a multisectoral ECD strategy. This support also contributed to establishing an ECD multisectoral coordination mechanism within the Zanzibar President’s Office to oversee all ECD initiatives. Also, UNICEF supported Tanzania in organizing the high-level Eastern African Regional ECD Conference, which brought together over 1,600 ECD professionals and partners. The conference advanced ECD advocacy and highlighted the importance of investing in the early years for building human capital along the life course. Additionally, UNICEF facilitated the dissemination of ECDI2030 data at both national and subnational levels (11 regions) to inform government and ECD stakeholders about young children for policy decision- making and effective programming.

Adolescents:
UNICEF facilitated cross-sectoral programming for adolescents to address teenage pregnancy and child marriage by promoting gender transformative approaches. The 5-year joint initiative with UNFPA called Girls’ Reproductive Health, Rights and Empowerment Accelerated in Tanzania (GRREAT) aimed at improving sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and wellbeing among vulnerable adolescent girls in Mbeya and Songwe regions and Zanzibar was successfully concluded in 2024. A significant increase in the Girls’ Empowerment Index (GEI) scores in the targeted regions indicates that the initiative was successful in empowering girls across different domains. A high number of adolescent girls and boys benefitted from quality information and services on SRH through different platforms such as schools, communities, and radio, along with frontline providers who benefitted from capacity strengthening interventions to deliver adolescent-friendly and gender responsive services to adolescents. Community engagement and positive parenting were crucial in addressing harmful social norms affecting adolescents. The initiative promoted meaningful adolescent engagement and participation and supported the development of key policies, strategies, and guidelines. The successful completion of the initiative resulted in the donor, Global Affairs Canada, extending support for another five years.

Another cross-sectoral programme for adolescent girls’ empowerment using child marriage as an entry point was implemented in Songwe region. Tanzania was among 11 countries globally and the only country from East and Southern Africa region selected to receive financial support from HQ for implementing UNICEF’s global Adolescent Girls’ Strategy. This programme focused on strengthening the policy environment to prevent child marriage and other deprivations faced by girls; supporting families, communities, traditional and religious leaders, and other community influencers to challenge harmful social norms and practices; and providing adolescent girls with opportunities for skills development and economic empowerment, including life skills and vocational skills, to address gender-based violence such as child marriage. Targeted geographical convergence facilitated different sectors to build synergies for adolescent girls’ empowerment which was measured through the GEI. This initiative has generated significant learning for modeling cross-sectoral programming for adolescent girls. Furthermore, UNICEF continued to support the government with the coordination of the National Accelerated Action and Investment Agenda for Adolescent Health and Wellbeing (NAIA-AHW) 2021/22-2024/25, including the NAIA-AHW Forum organized in October 2024.

Every Child Survives and Thrives:
UNICEF supported the government to increase access to quality health, nutrition and HIV/AIDS services through Primary Health Care (PHC) delivery platforms. These efforts led to 21% increase in the number of zero dose children vaccinated, from 759,083 in 2023 to 967,948 in 2024, reaching 96% coverage.  During the multi-cohort HPV campaign, 4,866,200 (96%) girls aged 9 to14 years were vaccinated.  Through the Measles Rubella catch-up campaign, 10,164,868 (114%) children under five years were vaccinated. Anti-retroviral treatment coverage for pregnant women was  almost universal at 98% through implementation of the national plan for elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, supported by UNICEF and partners. 

UNICEF contributed to increased utilization of quality nutrition services, resulting in 9,664,897 (98%) children aged 6-59 months receiving vitamin A supplementation between January and June 2024 and 1,023 children 0-59 months receiving lifesaving treatment for severe wasting. In Zanzibar, UNICEF reached 36,359 (100%) adolescent girls, while 67,000 children from 72 secondary schools also benefitted from school vegetables and fruit gardening, giving them better diets and life skills.
   
In 2024, UNICEF led health system strengthening efforts on leadership, governance and policy, health information and evidence generation, health workforce, supply chain, financing and service delivery. Operational guidelines were revised for Community Health Workers’ (CHW) selection and training, operational modalities, and scope of services.  In total, 9,560 CHWs from 10 mainland regions and Zanzibar were recruited and 44% commenced training. UNICEF strengthened multisectoral nutrition governance through the design of evidence-informed nutrition policies and strategies including the new National Nutrition Policy Implementation Strategy. UNICEF supported an assessment of private sector food companies for developing nutrient-dense complementary foods, with a potential to reach 3,369,498 children aged 6 to 23 months.

With UNICEF support, the community health digital platform, Unified Community Solutions (UCS), was updated to enable interoperability with the Government of Tanzania’s Health Operation Management Information System (GoTHOMIS) and digital client feedback, Afya Yetu (formerly Mama na Mwana).  The CHW register records client and service information including HIV, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health. This has strengthened referrals to formal health services, information for decision making and follow-up care.
  
In collaboration with regional authorities in Songwe, Kigoma, Mtwara and Lindi, UNICEF modeled the operationalization of the Ministry of Health (MoH) outreach guidelines. Targeting hard-to-reach communities, 240,977 beneficiaries received integrated services; of these, 83,910 immunization doses were administered of which 26% were first dose. 14,865 people were tested for HIV. Iron Folate was provided to 18,384 with two thirds being antenatal women, 39,117 received vitamin A, 43,582 children were screened for malnutrition, and 41,868 received education on GBV. 

In collaboration with Mbeya region, UNICEF modelled the Family Centred Approach that led to increased case detection for children with HIV achieving a 14% positivity rate which is higher than other HIV testing models. The model which promoted referral and integration with other child health and survival interventions is now planned for scale up using Global Fund resources. UNICEF supported implementation research in Mbeya to improve maternal nutrition during pregnancy and piloted the introduction of multiple micronutrient supplements which will be scaled up.

UNICEF ensured that child health and survival remained integral to government and partner agendas. UNICEF’s financial contribution in Tanzania Mainland leveraged eight development partners (Canada, Switzerland, Ireland, KOICA, Denmark, UK FCDO, World Bank, UNFPA) in a health basket fund totaling USD 59.9 million in 2024, an increase of USD 5.8 million, which directly benefited all 6,798 public PHC facilities. UNICEF partnered with UNAIDS and the MoH to strengthen governance and implementation of the national action plan for the Global Alliance to end AIDS in children, leveraging Global Fund investments. At sub national level, UNICEF partnered with the Regional Commissioner of Njombe to develop an acceleration plan to reduce childhood stunting in a region with one of the highest stunting burdens.

Every Child Learns:
In 2024, more than 154,000 vulnerable children and adolescents (51% of whom were girls) participated in UNICEF-supported learning and skills development programmes, to reduce disparities and inequities in education, particularly for marginalized populations. The provision of cash incentives by UNICEF was one of the ways employed to facilitate adolescent participation in skills development opportunities. Some of the programmes used to achieve this were IPOSA in Mainland Tanzania and ZIPOSA in Zanzibar. These programmes continue to address critical challenges such as limited access to quality education, gender inequality, and inadequate infrastructure. UNICEF continued to support the strengthening of non-formal education and alternative delivery models and by promoting gender equality and empowering adolescents, contributed to building resilient and sustainable education systems.

To foster full participation and promote gender equality in innovation and development, 103,000 secondary school students (52% girls) benefitted from improved teaching and learning methodologies designed to enhance science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) outcomes with support from UNICEF. Incorporating innovative practices in effective STEM teaching strategies, gender-responsive pedagogy, climate change, and integration of ICT as a pedagogical tool in the teaching and learning process, quality learning materials, and teacher training, these efforts ensured inclusive STEM education, equipping students with critical skills for future careers, fostering innovation, and preparing them to contribute to sustainable development.

To equip children and adolescents with essential skills for their future, UNICEF supported 1.44 million children and adolescents with digital learning opportunities, bridging the digital divide in line with global education goals to provide equitable access to technology. Additionally, an integrated climate change curriculum benefited 4.43 million primary and 1.9 million secondary students. This curriculum raised environmental awareness, fostered personal empowerment, and nurtured entrepreneurial skills, preparing young people to tackle global challenges and drive sustainable solutions in their communities.

By championing policy changes, UNICEF eliminated systemic barriers to education, supporting the global goal to promote education access for marginalized groups. Efforts included assessing the re-entry policy for reintegrating pregnant and married girls into the education system. These actions illustrated how strategic advocacy and evidence-based interventions challenge societal norms, promote gender equality, and empower vulnerable adolescents to reclaim educational opportunities and shape their futures.

Every Child is Protected from Violence, Abuse and Exploitation:
In May 2024, UNICEF, alongside other UN agencies and development partners, supported the launch of Tanzania's second National Plan of Action to End Violence Against Women and Children (NPA-VAWC II). UNICEF continued its support for the Social Norms, Strengthening Families, and Response Pillars of NPA-VAWC II, providing technical guidance to enhance government interventions. Over 200,000 children, parents, and community members benefited from face-to-face, radio, and online content designed to transform gender norms and parenting approaches across Tanzania. Additionally, more than 15,000 children, at risk of or victims of violence, exploitation, and abuse, gained better access to quality child protection services.

In 2024, UNICEF spearheaded two major initiatives to strengthen coordination in gender equality and violence research. One initiative, funded by Ireland, involves a joint programme with UNFPA and UN Women, aimed at harmonizing the work of UN agencies on gender equality, VAWC prevention and response, and Women’s Peace and Security. Additionally, UNICEF led the Multi-Sectoral Taskforce for the second Violence Against Children and Youth survey, funded by CDC, beginning the process of analyzing and interpreting results.

UNICEF remained one of the few development partners supporting Alternative Care and Justice Sector reforms. Alternative Care involved developing family-based options and conducting an assessment of Tanzania's Alternative Care system, both institutional and family-based. This work will inform a new Alternative Care Strategy in 2025. Tanzania was as a case study country in the global evaluation of justice for children, as part of the second Five-Year Strategy for Progressive Child Justice Reform (2020/21 – 2024/25). Key achievements included integrating child justice activities into sector plans and budgets, which improved access to justice services for children and raised awareness of children’s rights among stakeholders.

In 2024, the final report on the Canada-funded birth registration programme, which ran for over a decade, showed remarkable progress. The birth registration rate for children under five rose significantly, from just 12% in 2013 to 68% in 2022. By January 2024, the simplified birth registration system was being implemented in all 184 district councils in Mainland Tanzania, reaching over 10.3 million children.

Every child has access to water, and lives in a safe and clean environment:
UNICEF was pivotal in improving Tanzania’s Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) sector, supporting the ministries of water and health in enhancing sector coordination, creating a roadmap for service delivery models, and developing a Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan. UNICEF worked closely with the National Bureau of Statistics to strengthen WASH data systems, contributing to evidence-based interventions, resource allocation, and monitoring systems. UNICEF also supported climate adaptation in the sector, assisted with updates to the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), and played a role in Tanzania’s participation in COP29 to address climate-related challenges.

UNICEF’s direct contributions reached over 1.4 million people, focusing on sanitation and water access. Key achievements included declaring Iringa the first Open Defecation Free region in Tanzania, providing 558,637 people with access to basic sanitation and helping 427,077 individuals access basic hand hygiene services. It also launched the second phase of the National Sanitation Campaign to achieve universal basic sanitation by 2025. In response to public health emergencies like cholera and El Nino, UNICEF provided essential supplies, trained local teams, and ensured timely interventions, helping 930,369 people in Mainland Tanzania and 378,884 in Zanzibar.

In Zanzibar, UNICEF trained Environmental Health Officers, contributed to national health contingency plans, and supported the review of Zanzibar's water policy, which will be launched in 2025. It also improved water quality monitoring through collaboration with the Zanzibar Water Authority. 

In addition, UNICEF worked on WASH in institutions, improving facilities in 25 schools and 13 healthcare facilities, reaching 162,860 people, including 85,755 schoolchildren, and trained 436 WASH and health professionals across 14 regions, strengthening infection prevention practices. UNICEF co-hosted the African WASH in Schools International Learning Exchange Conference in Zanzibar, bringing together 18 African countries to share best practices.
UNICEF’s social and behavior change (SBC) initiatives reached 8 million people across nine regions, focusing on children's health, hygiene, and climate action. 1,463 community mobilisers were trained, and 634 influencers were engaged in SBC activities. UNICEF also supported the MoH in finalizing the National Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHH) Guidelines and supported 851 youth in climate action, providing technical assistance for child-friendly climate policies. In Songwe and Mbeya, UNICEF empowered youth to create social enterprises addressing MHH and WASH challenges, generating livelihoods and promoting hygiene.

Every child has an equitable chance in life:
UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) to conduct a comprehensive budget analysis across social, economic, and infrastructure sectors. Key recommendations were incorporated into the FY2025/26 Budget Guidelines. UNICEF also supported the development and implementation a national budget transparency roadmap which contributed to Tanzania’s Open Budget Score doubling from 21 to 41 between 2021 and 2023. The Minister of Finance acknowledged UNICEF’s technical support and committed to further improving the score to above 60 by 2025.

In Zanzibar, UNICEF supported the President’s Office of Finance and Planning (POFP) in producing fiscal reports, including the Citizens Budget, and refining budget projections for FY2024/25 with a focus on social sector allocations. UNICEF enhanced budget monitoring and expenditure tracking in six social sectors, linking resources to measurable outcomes. A transformative gender and equity budgeting initiative resulted in a $22 million allocation for gender and equity across these sectors. To maximize the use of evidence, UNICEF further facilitated a strategic partnership between the Presidential Delivery Bureau (PDB) and MoF. The analytical results were presented to the President of Zanzibar.

UNICEF engaged Members of Parliament in high-level budget dialogues for FY2024/25, raising awareness of public financial management (PFM) challenges and advocating for increased financial commitments to Early Childhood Development (ECD). UNICEF further supported PFM capacity-building in ECD, nutrition, WASH, and education financing.

In Tanzania Mainland, UNICEF assisted the Prime Minister’s Office’s Department of Disaster Management in developing national guidelines to integrate humanitarian cash transfer in the national emergency response toolkit. Through support to the Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN II) programme, 2.7 million children benefited from conditional cash transfers for education and health; 394,000 households exited extreme poverty. Notably, UNICEF’s Stawisha Maisha “cash plus” programme, which aims to prevent stunting among children under five, has been successfully integrated in the national social protection architecture through PSSN.
 
UNICEF also supported the Ministry of Community Development in developing the ZSPP 2024–2029 implementation plan and reactivating its Steering and Technical Committees.
Finally, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to integrate a child multidimensional poverty module into the 2025 Household Budget Survey and organized an international conference on child wellbeing in Zanzibar.

Management:
In 2024, the Tanzania country office conducted a series of internal strategic reflections to look at the cross-sectoral work, change strategies and programme performance to ensure that the programme is on track to achieve the results expected by 2027. A reflection on the changing donor context, the nature of technical assistance in a lower middle-income country and opportunities to shift programming to urban locations was also undertaken.

Throughout 2024, UNICEF strengthened existing and expanded new partnerships to benefit children. Two agreements with the World Bank and the Government of Zanzibar were initiated with UNICEF providing technical assistance. UNICEF continued to partner with the Korean International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) on maternal and newborn health and education with USD 5.8 million mobilized to implement the IPOSA programme in six additional regions. With the Netherlands, UNICEF inaugurated school WASH (SWASH) facilities in Iringa.
 
UNICEF was able to mobilize additional resources for children in Tanzania from longstanding partners such as Educate-A-Child (EAC) and Global Affairs Canada (GAC) and from new partners such as the Church of Latter-Day Saints. This support helped UNICEF and the government to improve equitable access to quality education and retention for out-of-school children (EAC) and access to learning and skills development for adolescent girls (GAC) in Kigoma, Tabora and Songwe regions and Zanzibar.

With an additional five years funding support from GAC, UNICEF and UNFPA continued to improve equitable access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) in Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, building from a previous partnership which saw a significant increase in the Girls’ Empowerment Index (GEI) scores across different domains.

UNICEF also continued to collaborate with other UN agencies, including through the Kigoma Joint Programme. This addressed the people outcome and focused on violence against women and children (VAWC), education, WASH, health and nutrition in addition to governance and natural resource management under the enabling environment and planet outcomes. Through the Kigoma Joint Programme, UNICEF created synergies with other development partners to amplify the impact of investment, noting strong collaboration with government as the co-lead in implementation and monitoring. 

Continued cooperation with relevant development partners, particularly the Governments of Netherlands, Republic of Korea, along with private partners, notably with LIXIL, and philanthropic engagement with Grundfos Foundation, resulted in increased funding for basic and safely managed WASH services. The ongoing collaboration with CDC helped to strengthen government efforts in Zanzibar for cholera elimination interventions. 
On data and evidence for WASH, the collaboration between UNICEF, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) and Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) was instrumental in supporting the Ministry of Water to undertake the first ever Sector-wide Sustainability Check in Tanzania, helping to generate data on the functionality of WASH systems in communities and institutions. Similarly, UNICEF together with WHO supported the government to implement the UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-water (GLAAS).

UNICEF continued to play an active role in all development partners groups – in many serving as chair or co-chair. For instance, UNICEF worked closely with development partners through the Education Development Partners Group and CSOs to implement the Global Partnership for Education (GPE)’s—System Capacity Grant. UNICEF Tanzania's partnership with tGPE also played a crucial role in strengthening the country’s education system.

UNICEF continued its engagements with the private sector and advocated for child rights among corporates. UNICEF’s partnership with Airtel was instrumental in expanding digital access to education, particularly in underserved areas. By leveraging Airtel’s extensive mobile network, UNICEF helped connect 250 schools to the internet, enabling students and teachers to access online learning resources and educational tools through the SmartWasomi project. Through this partnership, Airtel and UNICEF aim enhance digital literacy, and contribute to achieving inclusive and quality education for all, particularly in communities facing infrastructure challenges.

UNICEF continued to engage with national level private sector partners such as National Microfinance Bank (NMB) and Cooperative Rural Development Bank (CRDB) foundations. Partnership with academia, Tanzania Interfaith, and Girl Effect has optimized resources and timely programme implementation, while effectively enlisting young people’s voice in leading social and behaviour change, community engagement, and evidence-based outcomes. AMREF and UNICEF partnered on the LEAP mobile learning platform, to provide accessible and scalable training, equipping CHWs with interpersonal and effective communication skills. This approach demonstrates the potential for innovative, cost-effective, and sustainable solutions. 

In 2024, UNICEF hosted a delegation of global child protection development partners from Sweden, Belgium and the Children's Investment Fund Foundation (CIFF) in Tanzania which highlighted the crucial role of flexible funding for protecting children from violence and abuse and ensuring their right to a legal identity. The Canada-Africa Parliamentary Association and the USAID monitoring mission, Canada and the USA featured UNICEF’s work with adolescents. UNICEF also hosted members of the UNICEF NextGen programme - foundation and philanthropist partners from different parts of the world - to generate investment for children.

UNICEF collaborated with IMF (AFRITAC) to conduct a gender and equity budgeting assessment in Zanzibar which led to a roadmap to implement further actions. UNICEF has begun actively exploring partnership opportunities with the private sector and CSOs to enhance ECD service delivery across Tanzania to create a foundation for sustainable, scalable improvements in ECD service delivery.

UNICEF collaborated with the World Bank on a study for the social protection financing strategy. UNICEF further collaborated with World Food Programme on different social protection adaptative initiatives including training. UNICEF supported UN DESA in its initial country workshop on strengthening National Social Protection Policies and Capacities to Respond to the Triple Crisis in Africa and Asia and the Pacific.

In Research and Evaluation, UNICEF built authentic partnerships with our government counterparts notably the Zanzibar Planning Commission Department of Research (ZPC), National Planning Commission, National Statistical Office (NBS and OCGS), and PMO PMED. 

For emergency preparedness, 
In 2024, UNICEF Tanzania continued to respond to multiple emergencies including public health emergencies (Cholera, Acute Watery Diarrhea and Measles), climate related shocks (floods induced by El Nino and cyclone “Hidaya”), and the protracted caseloads of refugees from Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo. UNICEF Tanzania regularly participated in the bi-monthly interpillar and emergency partners coordination mechanisms on public health emergencies which included UN agencies, development partners and I/NGOs. Quarterly WFP-led UN Emergency Coordination Group meetings discussed ongoing emergency preparedness and response interventions. In both Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, UNICEF and the MoH co-led the water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) pillar as well the risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) pillar. UNICEF Tanzania worked closely with the Government at national and sub national level to support the response to localized floods and mudslides by participating in the rapid needs assessment of affected areas and through the provision of multi-sector emergency supplies and basic services for WASH, education, child protection, mental health and psychological support (MHPSS) and non-food items. UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Home Affairs-Refugees Service Department and UNHCR for refugee response specifically on policy and planning. At the regional level, UNICEF supported the Kigoma Regional Government and MOHA-Regional Refugee Liaison Office to coordinate the response. UNICEF Tanzania participated in the weekly inter-agency coordination forum in the field as well as sector meetings taking place regularly.

For the emergency preparedness and response in 2024, UNICEF collaborated with government MDAs and non-government organizations including the WHO, WFP, UNHCR, Danish Refugee Council (DRC), Tanzania Interfaith Partnership (TIP), Tanzania Development Information Organization (TADIO), Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) – Radio Kwizera, ONA Foundation and Tanzania Red Cross Society (TRCS)

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The systematic involvement of community-based actors and networks such as Community Health Workers (CHWs), and religious leaders effectively reduced vaccine hesitancy and identified unvaccinated children in urban slums. The "Ilala Model" used human-centered design to create tailored strategies like household visits and influencer collaborations, boosting vaccine awareness and uptake, especially among people with disabilities.

Innovative integrated outreach campaigns, during the Africa Cup of Nations, engaged over 500,000 people, promoting male involvement in parenting, HPV vaccination, and cervical cancer prevention. Similarly, the endline survey of the Safari-Ya-Malezi parenting programme reported significant improvements in male engagement and child-care outcomes, emphasizing the importance of community-based approaches. In total, 3.7 million people were reached through these initiatives, highlighting the effectiveness of local involvement and tailored social and behaviour change strategies.

Digital tools like the Internet of Good Things (IoGT) and Talkwalker countered misinformation, reaching 15.4 million people. Social listening tools provided real-time insights for social and behaviour change strategies, particularly during outbreaks. UNICEF partnered with community radio stations to reach over 42 million listeners, and strategic collaborations with government and community leaders ensured the sustainability of these efforts. These initiatives highlight the importance of community trust, digital innovation, and cross-sector collaboration in driving social and behavioral change.

Prolonged floods induced by El-Nino and cyclone Hidaya stretched the human resources in the Prime Minister’s Office resulting in inadequate implementation of agreed activities during the year. Possible solutions to this include exploration by government of the feasibility of increasing human resources and strengthening coordination and partnerships.  

The UNICEF country office internal series of programmatic reflections at mid-term highlighted the need for synergistic and collaborative programming. To do this, UNICEF Tanzania will have to ensure pillar cross sectoral programmes, ECD and Adolescents, are modelled and implemented in a synergistic way during the next two and a half years. Good examples of synergistic programming exist, such as the Girls Reproductive Health, Rights and Empowerment Accelerated in Tanzania (GRREAT) programme in Songwe. The key strategies such as system strengthening, advocacy, social and behaviour change, gender, innovation anchored in the two cross sectoral pillars of ECD and Adolescent programming will be key to implementation in the second half of the country programme. 

Despite the results reached at scale, the success of adolescent learning and skills programming, particularly for girls, continues to face challenges, including the limited engagement of men and boys. This disengagement not only affects the effectiveness of initiatives but also perpetuates gender inequalities within communities. In response, UNICEF is working closely with government and CSOs to address these barriers by fostering greater and more deliberate involvement of men and boys in adolescent learning and skills programmes from the design phase. 

Furthermore, a deep dive into the attitudes of men and boys regarding gender equality in their communities is underway to identify and address underlying biases. UNICEF is also assessing the reasons behind boys dropping out of school in certain regions, to develop targeted interventions to ensure equitable access to education and skills development for all adolescents.

UNICEF played a crucial role in developing Tanzania's Digital Education Strategy, emphasizing the need for a holistic and inclusive digital transformation. The strategy addressed systemic challenges in digital learning and highlighted the benefits of balanced investments and partnerships with mobile network operators. This approach led to a robust digital education ecosystem. Through UNICEF's support, 1.44 million children gained essential future-ready skills, demonstrating the significant impact of targeted digital education initiatives. 
Moving forwards, UNICEF will amplify resource mobilization (GPE especially) as education lead in Tanzania, enhance public-private partnerships (e.g., internships, mentorships, apprenticeships in the Learning to Earning Agenda), and engage with children and young people, especially girls, systematically and in an age-appropriate manner, from programme design stage.

UNICEF's Improving Maternal Nutrition (IMAN) model in Mbeya region highlighted the importance of government leadership for sustainable and scalable nutrition programmes. The model will expand to ten regions, integrating into the health system with increased government involvement.

Challenges continue to include social norms and the limited capacity of frontline workers. UNICEF will empower caregivers, parents of young children on integrated nurturing care, for the early years through social and behaviour change. UNICEF will also continue to advocate and strengthen multiple systems to be more accountable. 

Despite efforts, children's diets have not improved significantly, and unhealthy foods are prevalent. UNICEF will support the government in improving access to nutritious foods and addressing malnutrition, focusing on regions with high stunting rates. Limited resources hinder treatment of children with severe wasting. UNICEF will continue to advocate for increased domestic investment in nutrition through the development of nutrition investment cases with government.

The launch of Tanzania's second National Plan of Action to End Violence Against Women and Children (VAWC II) was significant, but implementation faced challenges. Delays in setting up thematic groups and coordinating large donor contributions are key issues. Effective coordination is needed in areas like economic empowerment, social norms, parenting, social welfare, and justice.

Despite collaboration on amending the Law of the Child Act and Cybercrimes Act, many proposed changes were diluted. UNICEF and CSOs will continue advocating for further amendments, especially regarding the age of marriage, corporal punishment, and online child offenses.
For birth registration, integrating the simplified system into local budgets and addressing the registration backlog and interoperability with the National ID system are priorities. Funding for child protection work is challenging, with limited resources for violence prevention, justice reform, and birth registration. Donors are focusing more on gender equality and climate change while the funding pots available for joint programming are reducing each year.
 
The community WASH programme faced several challenges in the first half of the year, including funding shortages, bureaucratic delays, and technical capacity issues. Poor groundwater potential and lack of transparency in disease outbreak reporting also hindered progress. Excessive rainfall further affected project implementation. Key lessons learned include the importance of community empowerment, high-level government engagement, and private sector involvement. Innovations like pre-paid water dispensing machines and remote water supply monitoring have shown positive results. Looking ahead, the focus will be on strengthening government and CSO capacities, improving policies, and promoting gender-transformative WASH practices. Emphasis will also be placed on innovation in climate, water quality, and financing.

In 2024, Zambia faced numerous adversities that  severely impacted its socio-economic conditions, including the worst drought  in decades caused by the El Niño weather phenomenon, which crippled the  country's power-generation capacity. On February 29, 2024, the President of  Zambia declared the drought a National Disaster and Emergency, affecting over  50 per cent of the country (84 out of 116 districts) and 9.8 million people.  Among those affected, 6.6 million require humanitarian assistance, including  1.4 million children under the age of five.
  
Evidence from the Standardized Monitoring and  Assessment of Relief and Transitions (SMART) survey conducted in May 2024  indicated that without timely preventive actions, Zambia risked facing a  severe nutrition crisis. Despite being the harvest season, more than half of  the households in six of the seven surveyed provinces experienced moderate to  severe hunger. Western Province had the highest hunger levels, with 88.6 per  cent of households affected, followed by North-Western (84.3 per cent) and Southern  Provinces (73.2 per cent).
