Compounding the drought and energy situation, the  country also experienced one of the worst cholera outbreaks in its history  between October 2023 and June 2024, recording 23,378 cumulative cholera cases  with 740 deaths and a case fatality rate of 3.17 per cent. The cholera  outbreak affected 72 out of the 116 districts across all the 10 provinces of  Zambia.[1] 
  
Due to contractions in economic sectors resulting from  effects of the drought and energy crisis, the 2024 GDP growth was at 1.2 per cent, a  significant reduction from 5.4 per cent in 2023. The country’s monthly inflation  increased monthly from 13.2 per cent in January 2024 to 16.7 per cent in  December 2024,[2]  resulting in sustained increase in the general level of prices  for goods, services, and food. 
  
Despite facing  numerous challenges, Zambia has made some notable strides. The focus on  political and fiscal decentralisation has advanced, marked by an 18 per cent increase  in Constituency Development Fund (CDF) allocations, the introduction of a new  CDF Act, and updated guidelines with support from UNICEF.
  
The 2024 National  Budget allocated ZMW60 billion to the social sectors (34 per cent of the total  budget) which include Education, Health, Social Protection, and Water,  Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), representing roughly a third of the total  budget. This allocation represents an 18 per cent nominal increase and a 3.8 per cent increase in real terms from the previous year's ZMW51 billion. Breaking  it down by sector, the education sector was allocated ZMW27.4 billion, or  15.4 per cent of the total budget. This is an 18 per cent increase in nominal  terms and a 4 per cent increase in real terms compared to 2023. 
  
The health budget for  2024 increased to ZMW20.9 billion from ZMW17.4 billion in 2023, reflecting a  20.2 per cent nominal increase and a 6 per cent real increase. Despite this  rise, the allocation remains below the Abuja Declaration target of 15 per  cent of the national budget, as it constitutes only 11.8 per cent of the  total budget, affecting the quality of health care. 
  
Social protection  allocations have seen a substantial increase. The allocation has risen by 19 per  cent, from ZMW8.1 billion in 2023 to ZMW9.7 billion in 2024, boosting its  share of the total budget from 4.9 per cent to 5.4 per cent. In real terms,  however, the increase was 11 per cent. The Social Cash Transfer (SCT)  programme’s funding increased by 10.7 per cent, and the Food Security Pack  (FSP) saw an increase from ZMW1.2 billion in 2023 to ZMW1.3 billion in 2024.  Notably, the rise in the allocation to the SCT corresponds with an increase  in targeted beneficiaries, from 1,374,000 in 2023 to 1,413,237 in 2024.  Despite this, the value of the SCT transfer remains at ZMW200 per month,  which is insufficient to meet basic nutritional needs. 
  
In contrast, the WASH  sector budget was reduced from ZMW2.3 billion (1.4 per cent of the total  national budget) in 2023 to ZMW1.9 billion (1.2 per cent of the total  national budget) in 2024. This continues a downward trend that began in 2020  when the sector's allocation represented 2.5 per cent of the total budget.  This decrease is concerning, as it threatens the sector’s ability to address  the urgent water and sanitation needs of communities, and more especially  with the ongoing drought situation and the recurrent disease outbreaks. 
  
Despite concurrent  public health emergencies in the year, with responses to Mpox, polio, measles  and cholera, the continuity of essential health services was maintained with  less than 3 per cent coverage disruption in essential Reproductive, Maternal,  Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAHN) services across  the continuum. Zambia recorded improvements in selected health outcomes.  Newborn deaths (neonatal mortality) have dropped from 27 to 17 out of every  1,000 births, and infant deaths (infant mortality) have fallen from 42 to 29  out of every 1,000 births, from 2018 to 2024.[3] 
  
Zambia  is off track to meet the global target of reducing stunting to 25 per cent by  2025 but is on track to achieve exclusive breastfeeding,  wasting reduction and halting overweight in children under age 5 years. ZDHS 2024 reported a modest decline in  stunting from 35 per cent to 32 per cent. However, wasting among children under  5 years of age reduced from 6 per cent in 2013 to 4 per cent in 2018, then to  3 per cent in 2024. The minimum dietary diversity for children aged 6-23  months remained almost unchanged, at 22 per  cent in 2024, also indicating that Zambia is not on track to meet the global  target of improving dietary diversity.  
  
In a landmark event  for Zambia’s education system, the country, in the reporting year, launched  the new Education Curriculum Framework, which will be implemented in a phased  approach in 2025. The framework introduces several progressive reforms aimed  at streamlining the education system and aligning it with international  standards.  
   

[1] Zambia National Public Health Institute (ZNPHI) Cholera situation report, June 2024.
[2] Zambia Statistics Agency (ZamStats)-December 2024 Vol.
[3] Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS), 2024

In 2024, UNICEF  supported maternal, newborn, child, adolescent health, and HIV/AIDS programmes  for strengthened policies, high-level advocacy, institutional capacity  building, and emergency response. Key achievements included reduced maternal,  neonatal and child mortality, improved community health systems, and enhanced  epidemic preparedness, addressing cholera outbreaks, drought, and  immunization gains protecting vulnerable populations.
  
Resulting from these  efforts, significant progress in Zambia’s Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child,  and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) and HIV/AIDS programmes was achieved. Skilled  birth attendance reached 93 per cent, and 85 per cent of women received early  postnatal care, although challenges persisted, with only 65 per cent of  children fully completing vaccinations and 38 per cent receiving diarrhea  treatment with Oral Rehydration Salt (ORS) and Zinc. Supported by UNICEF, the  first Maternal and Newborn Health (MNH) Summit and Community Health Symposium  was held, encouraging collaboration, institutionalising Community Health  Workers (CHW) and enhancing private-sector financing for Maternal, Neonatal,  and Child Health (MNCH), and community health. Normative advances included Standard  Operating Procedures (SOPs) for newborn care, Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC), CHW  supervision, and launching the Zambia Pediatric AIDS Action Plan. Centres of  Excellence (COEs) trained 310 professionals and mentored 880 healthcare  workers, benefiting more than 10,000 sick newborns (1,867 resuscitated and  461 supported through KMC). 
  
During the period  under review, UNICEF addressed multiple cholera outbreaks, vaccinating 1.88  million people (99.2 per cent coverage), and enhancing surveillance via the Electronic  Integrated disease surveillance and Response (eIDSR) platform. 
  
UNICEF proactively supported  the Ministry of Health to deliver routine and supplemental immunization  services through vaccine forecasting, supply planning, vaccines stock  management and monitoring, cold-chain inventory assessments, regular review  and increase of cold-chain capacity at all levels. Support also included  procurement of high-quality cold chain equipment, review and updating of the  effective vaccine management comprehensive improvement plan. As a result, 4.1  million children were vaccinated with measles vaccine in the year, surpassing  the target of 2.8 million.  
  
Over the past few  years, Zambia's maternal and child nutrition has shown progress with  reductions in stunting (35 per cent to 32 per cent) and anemia among women  (31 per cent to 21.2 per cent) according to the Zambia Demographic Health  Survey (ZDHS), 2024. Despite gains in wasting management and micronutrient  supplementation, challenges persist with dietary diversity, low exclusive  breastfeeding rates, and food insecurity, exacerbated by poverty, inflation,  and the worst drought in 40 years. 
  
Infant and Young Child  Feeding (IYCF) counselling reached an unprecedented number of caregivers.  With UNICEF support, coverage of micronutrient deficiency reduction  interventions increased with a total of 197,162 pregnant women receiving iron  supplementation (117 per cent of the target), while 214,570 (127 per cent of  the target) benefiting from folic acid supplementation, ensuring essential  micronutrient support. Through Child Health Weeks support, 947,369 children  aged 6-59 months were reached with Vitamin A supplementation and 844,973  children aged 12-59 months with deworming (94 per cent coverage,  respectively). UNICEF efforts also contributed to improved coverage of feeding  practices; dietary diversity interventions for children 6-23 months continued  in 17 SUN-II districts (74 per cent of the target 23 districts), while 2,623  health facilities provided IYCF counselling services (118 per cent facilities  target), reaching 3,032,286 primary caregiver sessions for children aged 0-23  months against a target of 1,030,900. UNICEF directly contributed 1,542,768  to the national IYCF counselling reach (51 per cent). 
  
During the period  under review, UNICEF enhanced the National Nutrition Cluster's capacity and  expanded it to 20 districts. Severe wasting treatment improved from 15,551  cases in 2023 to 24,277 in 2024, covering 45 per cent of the national  caseload. However, low active case-finding and last mile distribution  challenges persist, limiting treatment coverage in under-resourced districts.  
  
Beyond cholera, UNICEF  supported the development of the Nutrition Drought Response Plan and built  capacities of Cluster members for coordination, cascaded down to establish  clusters in 20 districts. The Nutrition Cluster was one of the most  functional under the Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU). Within  the period under review, UNICEF supported SMART surveys across six provinces,  guiding the prioritisation of drought response efforts to the most affected  areas-Western, Southern, Central, and Northwestern. For Integrated  Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM), UNICEF provided support to the  Ministry of Health to adapt the IMAM guidelines for the drought emergency.  These guidelines enabled the training of 763 health workers and orientation  of 4,175 Community Based Volunteers (CBVs) in IMAM. This significantly  expanded health facilities providing IMAM services, reaching 1,208  facilities, just short of the target of 1,210. UNICEF supported and  complemented the Government in supplies procurement and distribution to  district level for all drought-affected districts. Nationally, 24,277  children were admitted for Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) treatment, an  increase from 15,551 in 2023 though still falling short of the target of  34,661. This coverage represents 45 per cent of the estimated national  caseload. A comprehensive Nutrition in Emergencies service delivery package  in 26 districts was also supported. The estimated SAM caseload in these  districts is 5,177, and at the time of reporting, a total of 5,226 cases had been  treated representing 101 per cent.
  
UNICEF also supported  the Ministry of Finance and National Planning to estimate nutrition budget  needs and equipped them for advocacy, helping mobilise resources from  domestic and partner contributions. Using a match-funding facility, the  Government allocated US$1,326,881 for Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF),  resulting in the procurement of 54,138 cartons, the highest quantity procured  by the Government to-date. The joint funding of supplies by UNICEF and the  Government resulted in adequate availability of therapeutic feeds for all  districts for the duration of the current response plan. However, low active  case-finding and last-mile distribution challenges in districts without  partner support remain critical challenges. In total, UNICEF raised 60 per cent  of the HAC appeal for the Nutrition Cluster.
  
In 2024, the  UNICEF-supported Food Consumption and Micronutrient Deficiency Survey report  was released and is informing strategies to reduce micronutrient deficiencies  among women, children, and adolescent girls. UNICEF expanded capacity for  Public Finance for Nutrition across key government ministries and partners  and is supporting revision of the National Food and Nutrition Policy. Capacities  of key ministries and the Parliamentary Budget Office on Public Finance for  Nutrition were built resulting in UNICEF invitation to comment on the 2024 Budget  to the Health and Social Services Parliamentary Committee providing an  advocacy opportunity for nutrition and other child rights priorities. UNICEF  continues to support the on-going revision of the National Food and Nutrition  Policy
  
Zambia's Education for  All policy has enhanced access to education and ECE enrollment. However,  challenges in secondary education transition persist. Improving learning  outcomes remains a priority, requiring close monitoring as the new curriculum  framework is implemented in 2025.
  
The signing of the UNICEF  and EU’s $48.2 million multisectoral and multiyear human development programme  will lead to scaling up of community based integrated ECD. As part of the  programme, 3 Early Childhood Education (ECE) hubs and 35 ECE satellite  centres will be constructed, with a provision of integrated services in the  provinces of Luapula and Northwestern. 
  
The development of the  draft national multisectoral ECD Policy and the launch of key ECE documents  has further contributed to a more enabling environment for ECD. In 2024, the  programme reached 31,205 children 0-8 years with essential Early Childhood  Development Education (ECDE) services, including capacity building and equipping  the centres. Additionally, 53,156 caregivers were reached with key messages  about nurturing care through home visits, a new group counselling delivery  method at health facilities and other community settings, as well as through  outreach during Child Health week. Some hubs are now receiving ECE grants and  have been integrated into the home-grown school feeding programme thus  increasing ECE enrollment at the ECD hubs and ensure sustainability of the  ECDE programme.  UNICEF supported the  launch of the country’s 5th Annual National Playful parenting  campaign, as well as a newly developed social and behavioral change package—Tikonde  Bana, both enabling mass dissemination of key messages around responsive  caregiving, including on the importance of play to support child development.  
  
The Catch-Up programme,  which is based on the Teaching at the Right Level approach with support from  UNICEF reached over 122,000 learners in grades 3-5 (against a target of 87,080)  and improved students' foundational literacy and numeracy skills. The Ministry  of Education, with support from UNICEF and partners, developed an investment  case to scale the Catch-Up programme. Remedial learning guidelines were also  developed to institutionalise the programme and ensure its sustainability. 
  
Efforts are being made  to integrate the Teaching at the Right Level approach into both in-service  and pre-service teacher training. Strengthening the Catch-Up Coordinating  Committee, which provides strategic oversight is ongoing, including efforts  to track learning outcomes at the national level beyond the project-level  approach. Key studies were completed to improve evidence-based decision  making, and national dialogue and coordination structures were strengthened,  ensuring better education outcomes and continuity. Studies on language of  instruction, Education for All, Positive Deviance, and Teacher Allocation  have provided valuable insights and evidence for decision making.
  
With UNICEF's support,  40,153 learners, against a target of 32,400 participated in skills  development programme, gaining career guidance, mentorship, and employability  skills. The Career Education Framework aimed at providing comprehensive  guidance on career education and skills development interventions for both  in-school and out-of-school adolescents was reviewed, 25 STEM clubs were established  to address gender barriers impeding girls from pursuing male dominated fields  in STEM and support interactive peer to peer learning and collaborative  teaching in STEM, 578 teachers were trained, and Learning Passport users  increased to 8,272 (4,376 males; 3,896 females) by December 2024, compared to  just 100 in 2022. 
  
To ensure protection  services are taken to scale for children and their families, UNICEF supported  the Ministry of Community Development and Social services with partners in  finalising a Minimum Package of Child Protection Services. Efforts have been  made to develop child protection information management systems used for case  management. With UNICEF support, Zambia’s Cabinet approved key amendments,  including three optional protocols to the United Nations Convention on the  Rights of the Child (UNCRC), Marriage Act to align to the Children’s  Code Act, voiding marriage before age 18 years. Statutory instruments for the  operationalisation of the Children’s Code and Social Workers Association Acts  await cabinet approval. 
  
During the period  under review, UNICEF collaborated with the First Lady, leveraging her  influence to advocate against child marriage and profiling visibility on Violence and harmful practices against children. Following this, the government has pledged to develop a parenting and caregiver package to reach 2 million caregivers and implement child safeguarding guidelines for safe school environment. The SRSG-Violence Against  Children (VAC) high-level advocacy meetings with the President, Vice  President, Finance Minister, Speaker, and stakeholders renewed Government and  partners commitment to prevent VAC. Trained Community Welfare Assistance  Committee (CWAC) members facilitated dialogues on ending child marriage,  resulting in 531 adolescents (501 girls and 30 boys) out of 988 adolescents  (683 girls and 295 boys) who had dropped out of school due to marriage and/or  pregnancy re-enrolling, representing 54 per cent re-entry. Additionally,  94,822 (61,662 women and 33,160 men) out of a target of 70,000 people  participated in dialogues on transformative norms shift. CWAC members also  reached 20,576 children (11,306 girls and 9,270 boys) at risk of violence and  assisted them to access protection services, including 2,240 children (1,135  girls and 1,105 boys) who were supported to access educational support  through CDF. A total of 1,071 chiefs, headmen, and traditional councils (291  women and 780 men) championed advocacy against child marriage in their  chiefdoms. 
  
A minimum package of  services for children was integrated into the National Guidelines for  Intensive Family Support Services and implemented in all the 20 pilot  districts. Capacities of 114 Community Development Assistants (39 men and 75  women), 912 CWAC members (310 men and 602 women), and 150 Civil Society  Organisation (CSO) representatives on the provision of integrated family  support services was strengthened. Subsequently, 12,500 community members  were reached with messages on family-based care and 7,009 children (3,173  boys and 3,836 girls) were prevented from family separation.          
  
Eighty-five per cent  (17 of the 20 target districts) applied case management, reaching 23,565  children (12,558 boys, 11,007 girls) at district and community levels. UNICEF  and partners continued to support the Government in advancing childcare  reforms, mentoring four residential care facilities, and strengthening  family-based programmes including training of 60 emergency foster parents.  These efforts resulted in 1,021 children (347 boys, 674 girls) including 22  children with disabilities transitioning from institutional care to family  and community-based care. 
  
 In 2024, 92,738 children between 0 and 5  years of age were registered and 27,035 between the same age category  received birth certificates. This increase was notable in six  UNICEF-supported districts, which reached 50,155 children through integration  in immunization, ECD, and SCT 1000 days programmes. 
  
The social service  workforce investment case study supported by UNICEF spurred interest of  Government, providing evidence to recruit 1,700 social welfare officers in  2025 and led to the restructuring of the Ministry of Community Development  and Social Services. During the ministerial conference on Violence Against  Children (VAC) in November 2024, the Government pledged increased child  protection funding and implementing a continuum of age-specific and  gender-responsive services. The Government also pledged recruitment of 5,000  social workers by 2027   as well as supporting parenting and caregiver  package reaching 2 million parents. Additionally, the Government pledged to  strengthen Child Safeguarding to ensure safe and enabling school environment  free from violence targeting 4 million children by 2027¿. 
  
During the period  under review, UNICEF supported the Government to finalise the Social Behaviour  Change plan prioritising ending violence against children, promoting birth  registration and family-based care and Advocacy Plan to end children  marriage. 
  
Awareness on  Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) was scaled up to mitigate  risks due to drought emergency in 84 out of 116 districts, reaching a total  of 95,946 (55,649 female and 40,297 male) children and adults. Use of the Child  Helpline 116, Gender Based Violence (GBV) Helpline 933 and DMMU Hotline 909  for PSEA reporting was popularized. PSEA materials were translated into local  language and distributed to communities. 
  
As part of emergencies  response, UNICEF increased access to essential hygiene, sanitation, and  drinking water services, providing 3.6 million people (against a target of 2.1  million) with basic drinking water and 2.8 million people (against a target  of 2.1 million) with WASH and IPC supplies, during the cholera emergency.
  
UNICEF’s direct  service delivery included the successful drilling of over 164 new boreholes  and the rehabilitation of 481 existing ones. In educational and healthcare  facilities, UNICEF constructed or rehabilitated 107 water facilities in  schools and 96 in health centres.  To  support the sustainability of this work, a total of 442 Village Water  Sanitation and Hygiene (V-WASHE) committees, 218 Area Pump Minders (APMs) and  117 Environmental Health Technicians (EHTs) across eight provinces were  trained.  Behaviour change activities  resulted in over 150,000 people building handwashing and sanitation  facilities in their homes and 37,018 people now living in newly certified  Open Defecation Free (ODF) communities. Overall, 3.6 million people impacted  by the cholera outbreak and drought crises benefitted from boreholes, the  distribution of WASH Kits, and the promotion of sanitation and hygiene interventions.  A draft Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) in Zambia is  under development and set to enhance climate change policies and programming.  
  
On WASH systems  strengthening, UNICEF focused on enhancing the long-term sustainability of  WASH interventions. Collaborative efforts with multiple ministries and  regulatory bodies resulted in improved delivery and management of WASH  services. Notable achievements included the development of draft sustainable  water treatment chemical strategies applicable to all 11 Commercial Utilities  (CUs) in the country, the submission of the UN-Water Global  Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking Water Report, and  an assessment of data systems aimed at ensuring safely managed  sanitation. Additionally, UNICEF developed an SMS system strengthening  framework to monitor progress in this sector.  
  
UNICEF’s support in  emergency response has been pivotal for improving coordination within the  WASH sector, particularly during rapid assessments in times of cholera and  drought-related emergencies. Furthermore, UNICEF's commitment to knowledge management was  exemplified through leadership in numerous learning events, including the  12th Zambia Water Forum and Exhibition (ZAWAFE), the 9th Africa Water Week,  and the 1st Zambia Community Health Symposium. These platforms facilitated  knowledge sharing, networking, and collaborative strategies among  stakeholders in the WASH sector.
                           
  
In 2024, the SCT programme reached  1,311,101 households nationally plus 952,570 households with drought  emergency cash transfers. The 1000 days in SCT pilot continued, with five  cycles completed, reaching 12,904 households. SCT guidelines and manual were  approved, and operationalization of its M&E framework continued. The  National Social Protection Policy was approved. In response to the drought,  the Government approved a supplementary ZMW5.2 billion budget for the SCT  programme. Decentralisation progressed with an 18 per cent increase in CDF  allocations. A new CDF Act, and updated guidelines to guide CDF  implementation was supported by UNICEF.  However, economic growth remains constrained at 1.2 per cent, with social  budgets stagnant at 34 per cent. National surveys were disseminated  (LCMS, DHS, Child Poverty, Census), providing an updated evidence base, with  new child-specific statistics available. Social protection evidence was  expanded, as the gender and nutrition sensitive pilot study showed positive  outcomes. The research repository platform is being  piloted, led by the Ministry of Finance and National Planning.
  
To strengthen advocacy  and public engagement, the country office delivered high-impact multimedia  campaigns and advocacy initiatives, reaching communities, adolescents, the media,  and stakeholders with messages on child rights, health, nutrition, education,  and protection. These efforts contributed to increased public awareness and  policy shifts in priority areas, such as expanding school enrolment,  addressing malnutrition, and improving access to essential social  services. Additionally, through strategic collaboration with the  Government, adolescents and young people, the media, private sector, and  civil society actors, resources were mobilised, and multi-sectoral coalitions  strengthened to support critical interventions nationwide. These partnerships  enabled the amplification of policies targeting the most vulnerable children  and communities. To bolster Social Behaviour Change (SBC), robust IEC  materials and behaviour change campaigns tailored to local contexts were  deployed, fostering community ownership and action in areas such as  immunization uptake during Child Health Week, WASH practices during the  cholera outbreaks, and adolescent mental health support.

In 2024, UNICEF  continued to play a leadership role in the United Nations Joint Programme on  Social Protection (Phase II), collaborating alongside the International  Labour Organization (ILO), World Food Programme (WFP), and United Nations  Development Programme (UNDP). This programme is supported by Irish Aid,  Swedish International Development Cooperation (SIDA), Swiss Development  Cooperation (SDC), and the United Kingdom Foreign, Commonwealth, and  Development Office (FCDO). To advance the rights of persons with  disabilities, UNICEF continued to lead the United Nations Partnership for the  Rights of Persons with Disabilities Programme, collaborating with ILO, UNDP,  and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). With the aim to reduce  adolescent pregnancies and new HIV infections in targeted districts, UNICEF  worked with the World Health Organization (WHO), UNFPA, and other United  Nations agencies under the UN Joint Programme on reducing adolescent  pregnancies and HIV amongst adolescent girls and young women. During the  period under review, UNICEF and WHO continued implementation of the Nutrition  Information System funded through a global grant by the European Commission,  through which the Ministry of Health was supported to improve data quality  and completeness focusing on the drought-affected districts.
  
At the national level,  UNICEF continued to build strong partnerships with key government ministries.  Notably, collaboration with the Ministry of Finance and National Planning and  the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development has been crucial in  strengthening Public Financial Management systems. Close collaboration with  the Ministry of Health was critical in strengthening health policies,  enhancing epidemic preparedness, and scaling up community health systems. Further,  UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Health and PATH to scale up the  CHiP, and to digitize community health systems. 
  
UNICEF continued as a  lead agency for the SUN-II partnership under the NFNC-led 1000 days Most  Critical Days Programme (MCDP-II). The SUN-II platforms bring together 21  different organisations/institutions including seven government ministries,  four United Nations agencies, five international NGOs and five bilateral  donors, with UNICEF managing the partnership, overall strategic direction,  and administrative leadership of the compendium. 
  
With regards to Child  Protection, UNICEF continued actively to collaborate with the ministries of  Community Development and Social Services, Justice, Home Affairs and Internal  Security, and Gender Division including CSOs and community structures. These collaborative  efforts enhanced child welfare and justice services, collectively resulting  in outcomes such as; legal drafting and finalisation of Statutory Instruments  for Cabinet approval, implementation of prevention services through CWAC members,  implementation of  the national  alternative care framework in selected districts, transitioning children from  institutional to family-based care, revised National Diversion Framework and  development of guidelines for police on managing children in the criminal  justice system, and integration of birth registration into health services,  particularly immunization and education, and leveraging of the SCT programme  to address the backlog of children needing birth registration services.  UNICEF also worked closely with the Parliamentary Budget Office,  strengthening parliamentary capacity to make informed fiscal decisions. The  Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities, Disability Rights Watch, and the  Zambia Federation of Disability Organizations were partnerships engaged to  plan, coordinate, and review disability inclusion interventions across the  country. 
  
The Ministry of  Education continued to be UNICEF’s primary partner, supporting work from  early learning to secondary education. The ministries of Health and Community  Development and Social Services were instrumental in advancing work around  integrated ECD. Relationships with the Ministry of Science and Technology and  the Ministry of Youth were fostered to advance work related to Digital  Learning and Adolescent and Youth Engagement.    To  advance WASH outcomes, UNICEF continued to nurture partnerships with the  Ministry of Green Economy and Environment, Ministry of Water Development and  Sanitation, Ministry of Health, Ministry of Education including WASH  regulators such as Water Resources Management Authority (WARMA) and National  Water Supply and Sanitation Council (NWASCO)
  
International  partnerships have continued to be essential with GIZ, USAID, and the World  Bank playing significant roles in supporting Zambia’s decentralization  efforts. These partnerships have contributed to the development of local  governance and sustainable development initiatives. In 2024, the Gavi  Alliance played key roles in delivering vaccines and improving health systems  through equity-focused programming in 23 low-performing districts. 
  
UNICEF's response to  the cholera and drought emergencies led to the establishment of several  critical partnerships aimed at addressing urgent public health challenges and  improving water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) conditions. Key partnerships  included the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the European Civil  Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), the Government of Japan,  and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 
  
$31.9 million (out of  the target of $25million) was mobilized as other resources for the country  programme in 2024. This included two flagship agreements signed in the year  with the EU; the $10 million Nexus Energy Water Zambia Programme, which  includes a 1:1 matching contribution to be implemented in 6 provinces and the  EU Human Development Programme, a multi-donor and multiyear agreement between  UNICEF and the EU, worth $48.2m. This is a multisectoral programme for early  childhood and development and adolescents, to be implemented in Lupula and  Northwestern provinces.
  
UNICEF in 2024  partnered with several CSOs in its development work and in response to emergencies.  These included the Civil Society for Poverty Reduction, Jesuit Centre for  Theological Reflection, Disability Rights Watch, Vision Africa Regional  Network, Rise Community Aid Programme, Lions Aid Zambia, Red Cross, Plan  International, Catholic Relief Services, CARE, Save the Children, Population  in Need, VVOB, VAREN. As part of evidence generation, UNICEF partnered with  academic institutions, such as University of Zambia and Zambia Institute for  Policy Analysis.
   
In 2024, the Country Office mobilized $565,962 from private sector; and out of the pipeline to be mobilized by 2027, which stands at $1,5 million, $191,822 were allocated in 2024. The key highlight was the launch of the partnership with Airtel resulting in 100  schools being connected to internet.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenge 1: Climate induced emergencies are on the rise and impacted the implementation of UNICEF programme in the year, the provision of services and gains made in realizing children's rights. In 2024 alone, Zambia had Cholera, flash floods, Measles, Mpox, Polio and drought. Over 3,000,000 children under 18 and 1,200,000 children under 5 years were impacted by the drought alone in the year. In addition, global emergencies (natural and manmade) are increasingly having an impact on development funding as developed countries are looking more inwardly. This is affecting the resources available for both development programmes and for organisations such as UNICEF. 
Lessons learnt and future outlook for challenge 1.
Climate change induced emergencies are here to stay, and for a long time. UNICEF ZCO programming needs to reinforce the humanitarian-development nexus, building resilience, sustainability of interventions and continuity of routine services whilst responding to emergencies. Furthermore, UNICEF programmes need to be more agile in responding with speed to rapidly emerging public emergencies.

Challenge 2: Too many pressing needs, within constrained capacity and resources: The Whole of Society approach underscores the need for clarity in UNICEF's role, given our comparative advantage, mandate and the role of other stakeholders including other UN agencies. 
Lesson learnt and future outlook for challenge 2.
It is crucial to differentiate between activities that UNICEF should directly undertake, those it should implement through other actors, and those that are outside of UNICEF’s scope. This distinction will help ZCO focus its resources on the most impactful actions.
ZCO needs to position itself in line with the global shift in the new UNICEF strategic Plan concept, as ‘thought leaders’ and the ‘go to Agency’ on highlighting child rights deprivations and issues, with evidence from data (quantitative and qualitative- rapid assessments, etc.).

Challenge 3: Increase in poverty levels due to the slowdown in economic growth affecting provision of social services and worsening household poverty.  60 percent of the people in Zambia are below the poverty line, up from 54.4 percent in 2015; LCMS 2022. 
Lessons leant and future outlook for challenge 3
Social Protection interventions remain critical to cushion the impact of economic shocks on the most vulnerable populations. The UN Joint Programe on Social Protection remains a vital mechanism to support the government in its efforts to manage and sustain the Social Protection programme.

Challenge 4: Quality and access to social services remains an issue. This is both a demand and supply issue, with demand for services, capacity of providers and infrastructure needing improvement.
Lessons leant and future outlook for challenge 4
Systems strengthening remains key. UNICEF needs to continue building the capacity of government to provide services and for communities to demand services. UNICEF also needs to continually strengthen internal capacity of  staff to engage and influence at policy and systems level.
 
Challenge 5: Inadequate coordination between national and subnational levels, ensuring timely delivery of services to beneficiaries, especially during humanitarian response.
Lessons leant and future outlook for challenge 5.
Decentralisation is key to improving service delivery. Decentralisation brings services and decisions closer to the population for whom these services are intended. This presents opportunities to enhance social accountability, make decisions more transparent, reduce turnaround time for feedback, and use resources more efficiently and effectively. 
Frontline workers are essential to the delivery of services and community engagement in UNICEF programs, yet several challenges persist, including the voluntary nature of these roles, lack of sustainability, unstandardized service packages, and weak institutionalization undermine their effectiveness. UNICEF must rethink how to support and strengthen the role of frontline workers, considering their strategic importance across sectors.

The year 2024, was both challenging and transformative for the children of Zimbabwe. As the country experienced the worst drought in 40 years, children were disproportionately affected as food insecurity and economic hardship impacted their access to adequate nutrition, led families to adopt negative coping mechanisms, such as taking children out of school to work or having them care for family members, as parents sought economic opportunities elsewhere. Despite these hardships, efforts were made by the Government, and local and international partners to improve access to essential services, and to include children and young people, in the development of the national strategies and policies. 
 
Zimbabwe has a population of 15.2 million inhabitants (52 per cent female) with an annual growth rate of 1.5 per cent. Currently, 47 per cent of the population are under the age of 18 and 61.4 per cent live in rural areas (Zimbabwe 2022 Population and Housing Census report). Ranking 159 out of 191 countries on the Human Development Index, 61 per cent of children experience multidimensional poverty, that is most acute in rural areas, high-density and peri-urban informal settlements, and for those with disabilities.
 
In 2024, Zimbabwe experienced the worst drought in 40 years, exacerbating its fragility as it grappled with public health emergencies (cholera, polio and measles). As a response, the Government issued an El Niño Appeal estimated at US$3.9 billion in May 2024, the first appeal of its kind by Government. Subsequently, the United Nations and humanitarian partners also launched an inter-agency Flash Appeal for US$443m, which received only 32.4 per cent funding. The El Niño induced drought resulted in massive crop failure and depletion of water resources. An estimated 50 per cent of the population (7.6 million people) were affected, including 3.5 million children. Reduced water levels at Lake Kariba, limited hydropower production and exacerbated already strained energy supplies, leading to frequent power outages, disrupting livelihoods, education, and access to essential services. The impacts on food security and malnutrition are expected to be felt up until early 2025.
 
The National Development Strategy 2 (2026-2030) geared towards achieving middle-income country status by 2030, underpinned by inclusive governance through devolution and decentralized service delivery is being prepared in a context of significant macroeconomic challenges, including, high inflation, exchange rate volatility, limited foreign exchange and energy concerns. The economy slowed from a Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth rate of 5.3 per cent in 2023 to an estimated 2 per cent in 2024 largely on account of the El Niño induced drought. In 2025, growth is expected to rebound to 6 per cent, driven by improved agriculture and easing commodity prices. 
 
In 2024, social sectors received 29 per cent of the total actual government expenditures. Wages and salaries accounted for over 80 per cent of allocations. In 2025, overall Government projected spending on the social sector is at 35 per cent of the national budget (7 per cent of GDP). The health sector allocation is 10 per cent, whilst education was allocated 17 per cent. Water, hygiene and sanitation (WASH) received 1 per cent, and social protection was allocated 7 per cent of the national budget. Low disbursements against these allocations impede implementation of programmes.
 
Zimbabwe has a public debt of US$21.1 billion, with US$12.3 billion in external debt (59 per cent). This includes US$7.1 billion in arrears and penalties, while domestic debt accounts for US$8.7 billion (41 per cent). Limited access to international financing since 2000 and rising debt service costs—7 per cent of the 2025 national budget—have constrained social spending. The ongoing Structured Dialogue process with donors, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, and European Union, focused on governance and economic reforms, as well as compensation for former farm owners, intends to improve access of Zimbabwe to international financing and loans. This dialogue presents an opportunity to rebuild trust and unlock development support and is in line with the government’s request for an IMF Staff Monitored Programme (SMP) to support macroeconomic reforms. 
 
Whilst Zimbabwe’s political situation in 2024 was largely calm following a series of by-elections triggered by recalls of opposition legislators after the August 2023 general elections, persistent calls for the extension of the presidential mandate and possible constitutional amendment will require close monitoring. 
 
Zimbabwe is currently serving a one-year tenure as chair of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) since August 2024. Under Zimbabwe’s leadership, SADC’s strategic focus includes economic development, regional integration, climate resilience, youth empowerment, gender equality, and regional food security. As such, Zimbabwe hosted key regional meetings, including the SADC Disaster Management Meeting to discuss El Niño-induced drought impacts, disaster preparedness, and climate resilience; and the SADC Health Ministers Meeting which discussed Mpox and cholera outbreaks, focusing on regional health system strengthening. Zimbabwe’s leadership of SADC offers an avenue for collaboration in influencing the regional agenda for children.
 
Zimbabwe has made progress in several SDGs, especially in education and gender equality. However, more remains to be done particularly in health and water and sanitation. HIV, malaria, tuberculosis, are still of concern, aggravated by public health emergencies. The country continues to confront multiple health system challenges mainly: dwindling financing, obsolete or inadequate equipment, increasing stockouts, as well as insufficient health workforce which negatively affects service delivery. As a result, women and children face challenges in accessing quality maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) services and this has translated to increasing neonatal and child mortality rates as reflected in the ZDHS 2024 preliminary results. Under-five mortality rate declined from 73 to 69 deaths per 1,000 live births, whilst the neo-natal mortality and infant mortality rate increased from 31 to 37 and 53 to 56 deaths per 1,000 live births, respectively (ZDHA, 2024). The 2022 Census estimates maternal mortality ratio at 363 per 100,000 live births. 
 
Malnutrition remains a key cause of the health burden in Zimbabwe. Though Zimbabwe is on track to meet the global nutrition target for wasting at 2 per cent for children 0-5 years, stunting has increased from 23.5 to 27 per cent and the percentage of those overweight has increased from 2.5 (MICS 2019) to 4 per cent (ZDHS 2024). Furthermore, exclusive breastfeeding for children 0-5 months is at 42 per cent, making Zimbabwe among the lowest in the Eastern and Southern Africa region. These numbers are also in line with the trends found in the 2024 Zimbabwe Livelihoods Assessment Committee. To ensure that Zimbabwe meets the SDG targets, efforts to address childhood undernutrition, micronutrient deficiencies, and overweight, need to be part of an integrated package implemented through the through the health, food, education, social protection and WASH systems.
 
Although Zimbabwe has surpassed the 95:95:95 UNAIDS targets with 97 per cent of people living with HIV knowing their status, over 95 per cent of these being on anti-retroviral therapy (ART), and 96 per cent on ART being virally suppressed, children, adolescents, and pregnant women are being left behind. According to Zimbabwe’s DHIS2 system, ART coverage amongst children 0-14 years is lagging at 73 per cent, a slight increase from 69 per cent in 2023. Coverage amongst pregnant women living with HIV has increased from 89 per cent in 2023 to 93 per cent in 2024 (DHIS2 2024). Adolescent pregnancy is high at 22 per cent and new HIV infections are threefold higher in adolescent girls and young women. In Zimbabwe, 48 per cent of adolescents and youth are neither in education, employment or training (NEET), with unemployment at 41 per cent (Labour Force Survey, ZIMSTATS, 2024). Drug and substance use are on the rise amongst youth, whilst only 47 per cent of young people participate in government decision making processes for development (NDS1 Mid-Term Review).
 
Progress on meeting SDG targets on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene remain stagnant in part due to ongoing deterioration of water infrastructure across the country and the failure to rehabilitate these systems, stemming from inadequate investments in operational maintenance. Access to basic drinking water services is at 64 per cent since 2020 and the percentage of people using basic sanitation remains constrained, at 36 per cent. The national hygiene coverage has remained at 42 per cent. Disparities in hygiene access are notable between rural (36 per cent) and urban (56 per cent) areas, highlighting the need for targeted hygiene promotion and educational programmes for vulnerable rural populations (WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for WASH).
 
Net enrolment for pre-primary education remained practically unchanged from 42.7 in 2023 to 42.91 in 2024; the transition rate from Grade 7 to Form 1 declined slightly from 82 to 79.53 per cent between 2023 and 2024 indicating systemic pressures. Girls had a higher transition rate than boys at 81.14 per cent versus 77.87 per cent. The survival rate from Form 1 to Form 4 increased to 80.58 per cent in 2024, from 76.4 per cent in 2023, though still below the target of 85 per cent. Boys had better survival rates than girls, reflected in a gender parity index of 0.95. Additionally, survival rates from Form 1 to Form 6 improved from 12.37 per cent in 2023 to 13.89 per cent in 2024, with girls surpassing boys at 14.03 per cent compared to 13.89 per cent).
 
Child marriage rate remains high at 21.2 per cent for adolescent girls aged 15-18 (MICS 2019), driven largely by poverty and social norms. Birth registration coverage is relatively low still at 51 per cent (Secondary Analysis of Census 2022). Violence against children remains a concern with 64 per cent of children experiencing violent discipline (MICS 2019) and 35 per cent of children between the ages of 5-17 years are involved in some forms of child labour, whilst 26 per cent work in hazardous situations in agriculture, artisanal mining and waste management sectors (Labour Force and Child Labour Survey, ZIMSTAT 2020). Progress is constrained by limited resources for child protection services and a shortage of social workers.
 
A 2024 UNICEF study of Children on the Move indicated that there are three distinct categories of CoTM in Zimbabwe: i) children migrating to rural and urban centres such as Harare or Bulawayo in search of better socio-economic conditions and many end up living on the streets; ii) children who establish somewhat permanent residence in the border areas between Zimbabwe and South Africa with frequent movements between the two countries for informal business activities; and iii) children crossing into South Africa who face various and risks such as sexual exploitation, and a lack of access to education and healthcare.

In 2024, UNICEF completed a Mid-Term Review of the UNICEF Zimbabwe Country Programme (2022–2026) with Government leading to programmatic shifts and priorities, which equally aligned with the outcome of the Mid-Term Review of the National Development Strategy (NDS1) (2021–2025). These will support the acceleration of results for children for the remainder of the implementation period. Furthermore, the Country Programme contributes towards the Zimbabwe United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (2022–2026) and UNICEF Global Strategic Plan (2022–2025). Strong Government ownership, leadership, partnership, and collaboration were drivers that enabled the delivery of results in 2024.
 
Social Policy
 
UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy efforts through budget briefs and quarterly economic bulletins, which analyzed socio-economic trends and their effects on the most vulnerable children, contributed to the increased share of government investment in social sectors, enabling these sectors to deliver improved services for children. National budgetary allocations to health, education, WASH, and social protection rose from 30.6 per cent in 2024 to 35.2 per cent in the 2025 budget, with non-contributory social protection programmes increasing from 4.5 to 6.9 per cent. 
 
Despite this, actual disbursements for social sectors in 2024 remained low. As of 30 September 2024, budget utilization stood at 68 per cent for Education, 53 per cent for Health, and only 18 per cent for Social Protection. This was largely due to fiscal space constraints, delayed releases, procurement bottlenecks, and macroeconomic instability in Q1 2024. In addition to UNICEF’s advocacy for timely disbursements, the organization is working with ministries to strengthen their capacity in budget planning, utilization, and monitoring. For the Education sector specifically, this is being implemented under the Building Public Finance Capabilities for Improved Social Services for Children (BPFCC) program, in collaboration with the Collaborative Africa Budget Reform Initiative (CABRI) and the MoFED&IP. UNICEF is supporting the institutional strengthening of the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (MoPSE)
 
UNICEF continued to technically and financially support the identification and implementation of budget transparency reforms in collaboration with Government and other stakeholders during the Open Budget Survey (OBS) process. As a result, as announced in May 2024, Zimbabwe had an improved score of 63 (out of 100 and surpassing the budget transparency sufficiency threshold of 61), in 2023 compared to 59 in 2021, 49 in 2019, and 23 in 2017, placing it 30th globally and third in Sub-Saharan Africa. The consistent improvement since 2017 highlights Zimbabwe’s commitment to transparency and is also a result of UNICEF supported capacity building efforts for improved planning and service delivery. 
 
As co-leader of the Social Protection Sector alongside the Ministry of Public Service, Labour, and Social Welfare (MoPSLSW), UNICEF continued to strengthen social protection systems, and ensure vulnerable households are resilient to shocks through the Emergency Social Cash Transfer Programme (ESCT) Programme, which reached, 19,489 households (115,774 individuals, including 65,917 children) across six districts. UNICEF also supported the School Feeding Programme, in collaboration with MoPSE which benefited 36,724 children in 123 targeted schools. Funds were transferred to school accounts, enabling the procurement of food items, which has contributed to reducing absenteeism and dropout rates.
 
UNICEF's collaboration with key ministries, the Zimbabwe Statistics Agency (ZIMSTAT) and Parliament has reinforced its role as a trusted partner in addressing issues affecting children, adolescents, and women. During the year, UNICEF in partnership with ZIMSTAT developed and launched Provincial and District Profiles based on the 2022 Population and Housing Census, providing vital data for policymakers which are serving the in the implementation of government’s devolution agenda. 
 
Preparations for Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS 7) are underway, with UNICEF supporting government-led efforts, including signing a memorandum of understanding (MOU) and conducting a questionnaire design workshop. This survey will offer essential data on the well-being of children and women, serving as a baseline for measuring progress toward Vision 2030 and the 2030 Agenda. Funding mobilization efforts are underway with US$1.145 million out of the US$2.3 million required for MICS mobilized. The significant funding gap will impact the timely implementation of the survey, that is still very much needed to guide a broad range of programmes related to child well-being. The MICS will complement the Zimbabwe Demographic Health Survey (ZDHS) 2023-2024 whose results are expected in the first half of 2025. 
 
Health
 
In 2024, UNICEF support to strengthening health systems bolstered the implementation of the Ministry of Health and Child Care (MoHCC)’s 2020-2025 National Health Strategy. Under the Health Resilience Fund (HRF) Programme, UNICEF procured US$6.375 million worth of health commodities contributing to 63 per cent of primary and secondary health care facilities being adequately stocked with essential medicines. In addition, UNICEF procured and distributed medical equipment to 55 districts to support the establishment of neonatal units, leading to 100 per cent of designated Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EmONC) facilities operating 24 hours a day and 7 days a week.
 
The revision and simplification of the Results-Based Financing (RBF) model enabled the resumption of subsidy disbursements to 1,498 health facilities to improve availability of their operational funds for improved service delivery. Furthermore, to address the critical human resources issue in the health sector, UNICEF trained 23,864 village health workers (VHWs) to provide integrated community case management (iCCM) and interpersonal communications. Additionally, 1,714 health care workers were trained to implement the integrated management of newborn and childhood illnesses (IMNCI) protocol resulting in 83 per cent of children aged 0-59 months with diarrhoea receiving appropriate treatment using oral rehydration solution (ORS) and zinc (target: 85 per cent).
 
Within the health sector, UNICEF has supported the Government in health promotion by implementing intensive social and behaviour change (SBC) initiatives, which led to high vaccination coverages for measles and rubella (MR). Notably, 371,536 children (90 per cent of the target population), received the MR1 vaccine whilst 323,252 children (78 per cent of the target population) received the MR2 vaccine as of October 2024. Additionally, 94 per cent of children (388,859) were reached with diphtheria tetanus toxoid and pertussis (DTP3) vaccine, surpassing the target of 93 per cent. The number of girls receiving the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine has seen a significant increase, with 181,148 girls receiving their first dose, compared to 20,879 girls during the same reporting period in 2023, this is largely attributable to UNICEF’s support on integrated facility-based outreach services. These numbers demonstrate the effectiveness of a multi-faceted approach that combines SBC and outreach services to promote vaccine uptake and protect children against vaccine preventable diseases.
 
Regarding public health emergencies, UNICEF actively supported the cholera, Mpox and polio responses guided by the national preparedness and response plans. This involved providing technical and financial support for response coordination, vaccine management, surveillance, case management, infection prevention and control (IPC), risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) and provision of the oral cholera vaccine (OCV). This resulted in 2,285,237 people vaccinated against cholera in targeted hotspots and 4,265,483 children under 10 years vaccinated against polio.
 
HIV and Adolescent Participation
 
UNICEF’s technical support to the Government enabled the successful roll out of the 2023-2026 Triple Elimination of Mother-to-Child Transmission (EMTCT) of HIV, Syphilis and Hepatitis B Plan. This support contributed to the review of the 2024 Country Plan on the Global Alliance to End AIDS in Children, the development of the National Adolescent and Youth Health Implementation Plan (AHIP), the 2024-2030 Multi-Sectoral Framework for Prevention and Management of Adolescent Pregnancies, and Part A of the National HIV Response Sustainability Roadmap. As a result, hepatitis B testing and treatment have been integrated into antenatal care (ANC) services at high-volume sites, and data collection tools have been revised to accurately monitor service utilization.
 
UNICEF’s technical and advocacy efforts towards closing the paediatric HIV treatment gap contributed to an increase in adolescents from 10-19 years living with HIV receiving ART from 73.4 per cent in 2023 to 82 per cent in 2024 (DHIS2 2024), surpassing the target of 80 per cent. Continuity of treatment in pregnant and breastfeeding girls and women living with HIV increased from 88 per cent in 2023 to 93 per cent in 2024 (DHIS2 2024), surpassing the annual target of 90 per cent. This was achieved through the integration of prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT)-Immunization-Nutrition services through the primary health care (PHC) platform and the capacity strengthening of 24 health care workers (14 female and 10 male) and 98 young mentor mothers (YMMs), who were equipped with new knowledge and tools to implement the triple elimination plan addressing HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B. 
 
With regards adolescent engagement and participation, UNICEF continued to enhance programming for, and with adolescents in a systematic manner, including enabling 63,010 adolescents and youth (33,353 female and 29,657 male) to meaningfully participate in civic engagement and decision making on multiple platforms including the Child Parliament, Junior Council, and Advisory Committee for Adolescents and Youth for UNICEF (AYAC), and U-Report. These young people influenced priorities in education, health, child protection, and climate change. The results from the U-Report climate change poll informed a report which was presented at the Expert Dialogue on Children and Climate Change during the Bonn Climate Change Conference. 
 
Nutrition
 
UNICEF championed integrated multi-sectoral actions aimed at preventing all forms of malnutrition with technical and financial support provided to the MoHCC and the Food and Nutrition Council (FNC). As such, national legislation on the marketing of breastmilk substitutes (SI-46) was reviewed, approved and came into effect on 1 Jan 2025. 
 
The policy environment for the optimal nutrition of children, adolescents, and women was supported by UNICEF with technical and financial support to ten evidence generation activities throughout the year. In this regard, i) an Overweight and Obesity Landscape Analysis, ii) a Packaged Food Survey, iii) stakeholder engagement on food systems, iv) a Social Media and Market Analysis (to quantify the level of inappropriate marketing of foods that is targeted to children), v-vi) two Zimbabwe Livelihoods Assessment Committee (ZimLAC) surveys, vii) a survey to estimate the coverage and quality of services for treatment of severe wasting, viii) a trend analysis of MICS data estimating the impact of climate change on child food poverty and malnutrition, ix) a child food insecurity experience assessment, and x) an advocacy brief on the new Statutory Instrument for protection of breastfeeding will be used to inform quality improvements, policy and legislative interventions for optimal nutrition for children, adolescents and women.
 
UNICEF continued to implement a multi-systems approach to enhance the delivery of nutrition services, with 36,724 school-aged children (18,663 girls and 18,601 boys) receiving nutritionally balanced school meals in 123 schools across five districts, as part of integrated nutrition, education and social protection services to vulnerable children through the ESCT programme. A total of 1,200 health and education frontline workers were trained on school nutrition interventions, resulting in 127,480 adolescents (66,645 girls and 60,835 boys), surpassing the target of 100,000 who received iron-folate supplementation and nutrition education aimed at preventing anemia, improving learning outcomes and improving nutrition knowledge among adolescent girls and boys. 
 
UNICEF technical support to the Multi-sectoral Community Based Model (MCBM) programme resulted in over 12,417 functioning Care Groups across 30 districts and functioning Food and Nutrition Security Committees (DFNSCs) in all 60 rural districts. The Care Groups provide peer-to-peer learning, early childhood development (ECD) counselling, social behaviour change and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counselling for caregivers of infants and young children, as well as for pregnant and lactating mothers. Through the Care Groups and facility based IYCF, 811,403 caregivers of children aged 0-23 months were reached with counselling on optimal feeding and care practices, surpassing the target of 750,000.
 
Effective nutrition cluster coordination with leadership from UNICEF and the MoHCC has allowed tracking and coordination of response activities. UNICEF’s El Niño response included intensified community-based screening in 29 high-priority districts. In total over 1.9 million children were screened using mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) and 12,786 children (7,078 girls and 5,708 boys) treated for severe wasting and achieving a 79 per cent cure rate, exceeding the global target of 75 per cent.
 
ECD
 
UNICEF in collaboration with the FNC rolled out training on ECD for MCBM structures, including District Food and Nutrition Security Committees (DFNSCs) and Care Groups, with 21 DFNSCs trained in September 2024. 
 
UNICEF renewed its partnership with the Zimbabwe Civil Society Organizations Scaling Up Nutrition Alliance (ZCSOSUNA) to engage parliamentarians on nutrition and ECD, aiming to increase their understanding of key nutrition and child development issues to influence and improve key legislation, and identify champions of nutrition and child development legislation. In terms of ECD outcome data, the Early Childhood Development Index 2030 (ECDI2030) indicator set will be included in the MICS7, scheduled to start in 2025. This will provide an updated and robust measure of ECD among children aged 24 to 59 months in Zimbabwe and enable the country to report on the SDG indicator for ECD.
 
Climate-Resilient WASH
 
UNICEF continues to collaborate with the Government of Zimbabwe to enhance access to water services, especially in the vulnerable rural areas as well as urban centers affected by the cholera outbreak. UNICEF's engagement in the WASH sector in 2024, which included both development programming and emergency relief efforts, reached an additional 574,060 individuals and 156 schools with access to at basic water services. These improvements have been made through various initiatives, such as rehabilitating boreholes, chlorinating existing water points, constructing piped water schemes, and establishing water kiosks. Improved access to basic water services is especially beneficial to women and girls as it reduces the burden of fetching water, increasing time available for women and girls to engage in other productive and/or social endeavors.
 
Despite these efforts, national indicators on access to basic water services remain stagnant. This is primarily attributed to the ongoing deterioration of water infrastructure across the country, stemming from inadequate investments in operational maintenance. Furthermore, rapid urbanization and population growth have exceeded the pace of infrastructure development, leading to increased demand for water services. Consequently, current investments are failing to keep pace with this growth, resulting in a lack of significant improvement in service access.
 
In 2024, UNICEF supported the Government of Zimbabwe in improving sanitation access by facilitating the development and approval of the Sanitation and Hygiene Policy. This policy is designed to promote sanitation through self-sponsored latrines, with UNICEF facilitating implementation in six districts and reaching 31,899 beneficiaries with basic sanitation services; additionally, 17 villages in Matabeleland South province were declared open defecation free. However, the construction of latrines remained low, as communities prioritized food security over infrastructure development due to drought conditions induced by El Niño. 
 
Mainstreaming climate, environment and energy remained critical to WASH programming to enhance the sustainability, resilience, and effectiveness of such initiatives, ultimately leading to better health outcomes and improved quality of life for children and their communities. UNICEF made significant strides in integrating child sensitivity into climate and environment policies, evidenced by the development and enhancement of two key strategies. The National Adaptation Plan (NAP) was submitted to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and reflects a commitment to prioritizing children's needs within national climate strategies. Additionally, UNICEF is actively involved in the ongoing consultations regarding the Climate Change Management Bill, ensuring child sensitivity is integrated into the framework for climate adaptation and mitigation in Zimbabwe.
 
UNICEF's engagement also extended to influencing the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) Implementation Plan. This involvement ensures that critical services for children in sectors such as WASH and Health are prioritized, alongside the promotion of age and gender responsive indicators. As UNICEF prepares to support the development of the NDC 3.0 for UNFCCC submission in 2025, all elements will be aligned with UNICEF’s criteria for child sensitivity, further solidifying the integration of children’s rights in climate strategies.
 
To promote child-sensitive climate vulnerability assessments, prior to COP29, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Wildlife, and the Ministry of Youth Empowerment Development and Vocational Training to conduct child-led consultations on climate change impacts on child health. A total of 1,000 children provided inputs into the Climate Change Impacts on Child Health report, which was presented at the 60th Subsidiary Body sessions of UNFCCC in Bonn, Germany. This effort highlighted the disproportionate effects of climate change on children and informed strong recommendations for advancing children's rights at COP29. Additionally, UNICEF empowered young advocates and facilitated comprehensive assessments of climate vulnerabilities. Incorporating children's needs into national climate frameworks represents a transformative approach to climate action, which prioritizes the rights and input of the youngest stakeholders. 
 
Education 
 
UNICEF supported MoPSE to implement priorities outlined in the 2021-2025 Education Sector Strategic Plan. The “My Dream School” back-to-school campaign, complemented by advocacy and community outreach efforts contributed to an increase in pupils’ enrollment with 4,735,506 in 2024 compared to 4,750,441 in 2023. UNICEF supported the distribution of storybooks to 50,594 infant learners (25,331 girls and 25,263 boys) in six underperforming districts, which served as age-appropriate teaching and learning materials at the foundational learning level to foster reading.
 
An Early Warning System (EWS) to prevent dropouts was piloted in 103 out of 100 targeted schools, with 76 per cent reporting improved enrolment and retention. By the end of the pilot of the EWS in July 2024, there was an overall enrolment of 24,307, reflecting an increase of 1,347 (including 788 girls) from the baseline of 22,960, representing a 5.9 per cent increase since the EWS implementation in January 2024. 
 
Due to economic challenges that have persisted over the last two decades, UNICEF continued to implement interventions to mitigate barriers, including the provision of school improvement grants (SIG) that kept 2,799 disadvantaged primary and secondary schools operational. This benefited 893,784 learners (445,340 girls and 448,444 boys) enabling them to access inclusive and quality education. UNICEF supported the sector with other SIGs for WASH and school feeding contributing to improved school environments and retention of learners.
 
Through its solarization project, UNICEF supported 154 schools with improved teaching and learning environments through solar energy systems, benefiting a total of 62,487 learners (30,883 girls and 31,604 boys) and 1,710 teachers. UNICEF also equipped schools with offline learning passport servers to enhance blended learning. This has contributed to positive working environment for teachers thereby reducing teacher attrition and has also providing a conducive environment for blended learning.
 
Child Protection
 
UNICEF’s strategic advocacy and technical assistance resulted in an improved and strengthened legislative framework in Zimbabwe for child protection. Eight laws and policies were enacted to strengthen child protection safeguards and improve access to justice, including the Children’s Amendment Act, the Child Justice Bill, and the Legal Aid Amendment Bill, which aligned with cabinet-approved principles, aiming to improve access to justice for children, persons with disabilities, and women in civil cases.
 
With technical and financial support from UNICEF, a total of 27,134 children (16,552 girls and 10,582 boys), benefited from child protection services delivered through the National Case Management System (NCMS). Additionally, a total of 117,588 children and adolescents in humanitarian situations benefited from community-based mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). 
 
Through the sectoral integration of child protection in education, a total of 106,090 learners (58,350 female and 47,740 male) benefited from the Safe to Learn Programme contributing to reducing violence against children in school environments and strengthening referrals. In addition, UNICEF piloted a localized community-based advocacy intervention against child marriages that enabled a total of 10,116 adolescent girls in the remote and hard to reach areas (Buhera, Chipinge, Chimanimani and Chiredzi) to access prevention and care services.
 
Through UNICEF’s advocacy, the Civil Registry Department in charge of births acknowledges the strategic role of traditional leaders in activation notification of community births and deaths and this is now institutionalized and legally established in Zimbabwe. A total of 5,700 traditional leaders comprising village heads, headmen and chiefs were trained on active notification of community births and deaths. Their role is now institutionalized and legally established in Zimbabwe and3,070 children (1,608 girls and 1,642 boys) had their births notified by traditional leaders.
 
UNICEF contributed to the successful implementation of the disability inclusive parenting initiative in five districts in collaboration with Zimbabwe Parents of Handicapped Children Association (ZPHCA) that resulted in 1,090 parents and caregivers (864 female and 226 male) equipped with information, knowledge and skills on positive parenting and disability management. A total of 272 support group leaders were equipped with special skills in advocacy and they have become community-based advocates for the provision of disability services and positive parenting for children with disabilities in their communities. 
 
In humanitarian situations, 93,474 people (54,500 female and 38,974 male) had access to a safe and accessible channel to report sexual exploitation and abuse. UNICEF also implemented prevention and risk mitigation activities related to gender-based violence in emergencies (GBViE), reaching 28,918 people (21,110 female and 7,808 male). Of these, 7,183 individuals (863 female and 320 male) received GBV response services, including medical care, psychosocial support, and legal aid to help survivors seek justice and hold perpetrators accountable. 
 
UNICEF established child protection surveillance and enhanced case management for children on the move (CoTM). In Beitbridge, 1,658 migrants (1,223 women and girls, 435 boys) in informal settlements received psychosocial support and health services and 174 women and girls received menstrual hygiene management kits. A total of 362 children on the move (170 girls and 192 boys) were also identified, with 47 per cent successfully reunified.
 
Emergency and Resilience
 
UNICEF mobilized US$10.5 million (37 per cent) of the 2024 Humanitarian Appeal for Children (HAC) for the cholera and drought responses.[1] This included reprogramming of development funds amounting to US$1 million from the Health Resilience Fund towards the cholera multi-response across the health, WASH, and the SBC sectors resulting in the management of 34,550 cholera cases. UNICEF’s cluster leadership in Education, Nutrition, WASH and Child Protection, in partnership with the Government and civil society organization (CSOs) successfully delivered humanitarian assistance to 2.5 million children, with over 6.5 million people, reached with key messages in response to climate induced and public health emergencies.
 
Enablers
 
In 2024, partnerships and resource mobilization efforts resulted in US$42 million in new funding mobilized, bringing the total funds raised for the Country Programme (2022-2026) to US$304 million (47 per cent of the planned budget). In support of programme delivery, over 8.5 million people were reached with campaigns through digital communication, media outreach and social media, including 308 mentions of UNICEF Zimbabwe on local, regional, and global media.
 
In addition to its support to Government, UNICEF worked with 80 implementing partners throughout the year. As part of risk management and oversight, the office implemented assurance activities, achieving 100 per cent of programmatic visits, 110 per cent of spot checks, and 100 per cent of audits conducted. 
 
To strengthen partner planning, effective implementation and reporting, the Country Office trained 61 UNICEF staff and 88 individuals from 32 CSO partners on eTools, UNICEF’s corporate software to facilitate partner reporting and adherence to policy requirements, PSEA, HACT, fraud awareness, and budget management. Internal processes were streamlined using Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), enhancing risk management and segregation of duties. The Country Office launched a digital petty cash request system integrated with a dashboard for real-time tracking, while the invoice processing dashboard facilitated timely monitoring and processing of payments, improving operational efficiency. The Procurement Case Management (PCM) roll-out in 2025 will enhance oversight, streamline procurement processes, and reduce risks, ensuring adherence to Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
 
UNICEF strengthened implementing partners' capacity to prevent and respond to SEA by providing guidance, trainings and reviewing their PSEA self-assessments. As a result, the percentage of partners with a low or moderate SEA risk rating increased from 76 per cent in 2023 to 100 per cent in 2024.
 
UNICEF maintained robust operations management and oversight in response to Zimbabwe's dynamic and complex operating environment. UNICEF disbursed US$ 34.7 million to implementing partners and US$8.6 million through bulk payments directly to beneficiaries under the Emergency Social Cash Transfer Programme and programmes in Health, WASH, Child Protection, and Education. Additionally, the Country Office met the bank optimization target of 25 per cent in ten out of twelve months, ensuring adherence to UNICEF standards.
 
Furthermore, to enhance system strengthening and the implementation of gender sensitive emergency programming, UNICEF conducted joint trainings for GBV and PSEA in emergencies with the Resident Coordinator’s Office and WHO. A total of 136 Government and CSO stakeholders (65 female and 71 male) were equipped with knowledge and skills to effectively prevent and respond to GBV and SEA during emergencies. Furthermore, it strengthened inter-agency collaboration and coordination, enabling a more effective and efficient response to GBV and SEA incidents, ultimately leading to better protection and support for vulnerable populations, including women, girls, boys, and men, during emergencies.
 
During the year, UNICEF maintained logistics operations targets in 2024, with zero per cent of non-emergency stock exceeding 24 months. Inventory levels stood at US$1.5 million, while Goods in Transit (GIT) were valued at US$1.4 million. To support programme results, UNICEF procured supplies and services worth US$15.7 million, including US$20,544,295 through Procurement Services and over US$9,353,319 in local procurement. Offshore purchases totaled US$6,352,326, and more than US$5,561,913.25 was allocated to institutional services contracting. Furthermore, the office developed a sustainability-focused supplier database, prioritizing environmentally friendly procurement practices. This initiative facilitated market engagement through supplier forums and significantly influenced procurement policies within Zimbabwe. Four supply end-user monitoring (SEUM) visits ensured the effective utilization of programme supplies, preventing aid diversion, while also providing recommendations to strengthen the supply chain system.
 
To improve efficiency and value for money, UNICEF expanded the use of corporate pre-paid cards, reducing the payment processing time. Additionally, UNICEF achieved significant cost savings by utilizing solar energy to lower electricity expenses, reducing costs by an average of at least US$2,000 per month. Similarly, reviewing cleaning contracts for the Country Office and warehouse reduced costs by 38 per cent, in preparation for the relocation to new premises.
