These savings are being reinvested to optimize office and warehouse space requirements, ensuring a smooth transition and efficient use of resources.

UNICEF continues to collaborate with UN sister agencies and leverages its wide and strategic network of partnerships with the Government of Zimbabwe and stakeholders to advance the rights of children.
 
A highlight of the year was UNICEF’s support to the Government of Zimbabwe in hosting the 2024 Regional World Children’s Day in Victoria Falls, with participation from seven SADC member states. The event provided children a vital platform to advocate for child-friendly policies directly to Heads of State. A total of 8,290 children across seven countries made a unified Call-for-Action that “all children have the right to a quality education, to grow up in a safe and secure environment and to be protected from harm,” which aligned with the event’s theme of "Educate and Skill the African Child for Posterity".
 
As part of coordination through the UN Country Team, UNICEF led the UN inter-agency Operations Management Team and the Procurement Working Group, while actively participating in the UN Programme Management Team for enhanced inter-agency collaboration. UNICEF also served in various Results Groups and technical working groups of the Zimbabwe United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (ZUNSDCF) and served as the Pillar 1—‘People Pillar’ lead. These coordination mechanisms enabled numerous synergies and efficiencies in the delivery of the ZUNSDCF. 
 
Serving as Fund Administrator, UNICEF collaborated with the MoHCC, UN Population Fund (UNFPA), World Health Organization (WHO) and development partners, Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), European Union (EU), the Embassy of Ireland and Gavi to deliver critical health services through the Health Resilience Fund (HRF) Project. In addition, collaborative efforts with United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), GAVI, WHO, UNFPA, the World Bank, the Global Financing Facility (GFF), and World Vision, Youth Advocates, CHAI, SoliderMed, Welt Hunger Hilfe, Oxfam, Christian Care, Africa Ahead, International Medical Corps-UK and Mercy Corps, as well as regional stakeholders like Africa CDC, SADC and private sector strengthened multi-sectoral coordination for primary health care (PHC) and facilitated an integrated response to public health emergencies.
 
To continue improving the sexual and reproductive health rights of adolescents and young people, UNICEF in collaboration with UNAIDS, UNFPA, and WHO implemented the 2gether 4 SRHR programme funded by the Government of Sweden. UNICEF in partnership The Global Fund focused on adolescent girls and young women to advance HIV prevention.
 
UNICEF has partnered with the Ministry of Youth Empowerment, Development and Vocational Training and the Zimbabwe Youth Council to develop the National Advocacy and Communication Youth Strategy, a National Drug and Substance Use Harm Reduction Strategy, and Child Parliament evaluation, along with consultations with children and young people on climate and education. UNICEF also continued to directly forge stronger partnerships with adolescents and young people through AYAC. AYAC members were trained as young advocates equipping them with skills to advance the child rights agenda in various thematic areas including SRHR, GBV, child marriage, climate action, nutrition and education. UNICEF also partnered with Boost Fellowship and Youth Advocates, two youth led NGOs to advance innovation and strengthen skills for young people.
 
UNICEF worked closely with the MoHCC and the FNC to implement nutrition activities including in emergencies. Other key implementing partners have been World Vision Zimbabwe and Nutrition Action Zimbabwe for anticipatory action and emergency response interventions to reduce the impact of the El Niño induced drought and rising levels of food insecurity on child nutrition. In addition, UNICEF has continued to partner with the Paediatric Association of Zimbabwe for quality improvement of in-patient care for children with severe wasting with complications, including disability. 
 
In an effort to improve WASH infrastructure and access to services, UNICEF has continued its collaboration with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), UNOPS, and UNDP, as well as the African Development Bank (AfDB), European Union (EU), Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), alongside multiple NGOs. In partnership with the WHO, UNICEF is conducting the 2024-2025 Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking Water (GLAAS) survey in Zimbabwe, which evaluates global WASH system status. UNICEF also collaborated with Vitens Evides International (VEI) for urban WASH resilience interventions demonstrating a successful public/private partnership. The partnership with VEI allowed UNICEF to interact with Harare City Council in new ways, including the secondment of individuals to sit within and strategically support city council structures and understand what needs to be done for urban resilience. UNICEF channelled resources to boost chlorination at reservoir tanks in Harare, and in the process boosted service delivery to more people than just focusing on point water sources in urban areas. 
 
As co-chair of the Water and Sanitation Working Group, UNICEF collaborated closely with the Department of National WASH Coordination Unit within the Ministry of Lands, Agriculture, Fisheries, Water, and Rural Development (MoLAFWRD), the secretariat of the National Action Committee for the WASH Sector. UNICEF conducted bilateral meetings with senior officials in various ministries to advocate for the approval of the National Sanitation and Hygiene Policy.
 
In the context of climate, environment, and energy (CEE), UNICEF partnered with UNDP, UN Environment Programme (UNEP), and FAO to host World Environment Day in June 2024 and collaborated with UNDP and the Resident Coordinator's Office during the Climate Change and Development Conference and Local Conference of Youth 2024. 
 
UNICEF continues to strengthen its partnership with the Ministry of Environment, Climate, and Water (MoECW), on critical climate and environment initiatives. This includes support for consultations on the Climate Management Bill, the Nationally Determined Contribution Investment Plan, and the launch of the National Adaptation Plan, all of which are designed to be child and gender sensitive. Furthermore, UNICEF has enhanced collaboration with MoPSE in climate education, including the development of an infant climate education module. 
 
UNICEF also serves as the Grant Agent for the Global Partnership for Education System Transformation and System Capacity Grants in collaboration with FCDO (Coordination Agent), Save the Children, World Vision, and The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). 
 
To advocate for increased financing to the education sector MoPSE and UNICEF collaborated with MoFED&IP, to develop the School Financing Policy. Furthermore, UNICEF partnered with Education Coalition of Zimbabwe (ECOZI), which represents civil society organizations in the education sector, to address education financing issues.
 
UNICEF worked with the CSOs, Forum for African Women Educationalists (FAWEZI) and Youth Advocates Zimbabwe (YAZ) to implement girls’ education projects in peri-urban areas of Harare, as well as CARITAS in on foundational learning focusing on parental involvement using story books in ECD.
 
Partnerships with the MoPSLSW, MoHCC, MoPSE, and Ministry of Justice have led to the development of robust child protection systems, policies, and service delivery for child protection. Efforts such as integrating child protection in health and education programmes and supporting the Victim Friendly Court have made significant progress in safeguarding children. Collaboration with NGO partners, Family Support Trust (FST), Regional Psychosocial Support Initiative (REPSSI), Justice for Children Trust (JCT) and Zimbabwe Parents of Handicapped Children Association (ZPHCA) complemented Government’s direct child protection service delivery and to prevent and respond to abuse, exploitation and violence against children in communities. 
 
UNICEF is implementing the third phase of the Child Protection Fund, which is now solely funded by Sweden and aims to support national capacity in strengthening the National Case Management System. In addition, UNICEF is collaborating with WHO and UNHCR on civil registration systems strengthening work. 
 
UNICEF has also collaborated with Zimbabwe Parents of Children with Disabilities (ZPHCA), Terre Des Hommes Italy and Family Support Trust to address child protection issues, including child marriages and gender-based violence (GBV). Such partnerships have expanded the reach of child protection services, particularly in marginalized communities. 
 
The increase in public investments and budget transparency has been facilitated by strategic partnerships with MoPSLSW, Ministry of Local Government, Public Works and National Housing (MoLGPW), Parliament, MoFED&IP, and ZIMSTAT.
 
UNICEF also engaged in partnerships with NGOs (World Vision and Goal), and the mobile payment service provider, Mukuru for delivering cash transfers to targeted beneficiaries under the Emergency Social Cash Transfer programme. In addition, UNICEF received the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) funding to support its emergency response efforts in addressing cholera and drought crises. The funding enabled UNICEF to provide critical assistance, including access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene, as well as nutrition support to affected communities.
 
The GIGA/Reimagine Education Initiative brought together key stakeholders, including the Ministry of Information Communication Technology, MoPSE, the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe (POTRAZ), and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), to advance school internet connectivity. A total of 7,913 out of 11,371 targeted schools were mapped, revealing that only 2,800 schools were connected to the internet, while 75 per cent of mapped schools still lack connectivity. To leverage the Government’s adoption of Starlink, UNICEF in collaboration with ITU is advocating for Starlink to be recognized as a Digital Public Good (DPG), a crucial step in promoting equitable access to internet connectivity for schools and health centres.
 
UNICEF strengthened efforts in private sector engagement with ten private sector partnerships and collaborations were secured—locally with Fastjet, Wild Horizons, JC Decaux, Alliance Media, the Chamber of Chinese Enterprises in Zimbabwe and Lithium Prospect, as well as through UNICEF National Committees (NatComs) with TUI Care Foundation, Gilgan Foundation, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and a high-net-worth individual (HNWI) from the Zimbabwe diaspora, exceeding the target of four. 
 
The partnership with Fastjet, the first of its kind, is expected to reach an average of 300,000 customers annually with child rights awareness campaigns. The FairChance Initiative in partnership with Goodwall, Wild Horizons and SPAR reached over 500,000 marginalized girls while, 35 nine young women secured paid internships, advancing youth development and economic empowerment for marginalized girls through partnerships and innovative digital approaches in Zimbabwe. 
 
Regular Resources (RR) funding was instrumental in advancing key achievements in 2024 and allowed UNICEF to leverage development partner funds already received to enhance programme coordination, implementation, and support staffing costs. This includes the implementation of key strategic shifts from the Mid-Term Review, which positioned UNICEF as a key player in upstream technical conversations, notably in the recent National Health Financing Dialogue. UNICEF has also used funding to conduct webinars and develop critical data sets. These estimates were used to model the impact on maternal, newborn, child, and nutrition interventions in support of resource mobilization. UNICEF participated in ZIMSTAT technical meetings and supported the secondary analysis of the 2022 Population and Housing Census, resulting in 92 district profiles and 10 provincial profiles used for equitable policymaking.
 
UNICEF also used RR funding to provide high level technical and strategic support on policy and programme planning and implementation in HIV/AIDS, adolescent development and participation, and emergency preparedness and support. Specifically, the resources were used to generate new evidence on the functioning of the Child Parliament through an evaluation and supported the implementation of skills building Generation Unlimited activities for the renovation of the Ruwa Social Innovation Hub. This has led to high visibility, promotion of children’s rights especially on HIV/SRHR outcomes and active engagement of adolescents and youth. 
 
Additionally, RR funding supported the national coordination for the scaling up nutrition (SUN) which has contributed to the active SUN networks (in particular civil society, academic and UN) in Zimbabwe. UNICEF provided critical support for technical meetings related to the Open Budget Survey with RR funding and actively participated in budget advocacy forums that influenced increased public investment in social sectors. 
 
Moreover, UNICEF Thematic Funds have facilitated inclusion of ECD in the national Care Group approach, including training of mid-level coordination structures (the DFNSCs) on ECD and inclusion of ECD in all the national care group materials. In addition, thematic funds have supported the evidence generation around Zimbabwe's food systems, which has resulted in a Government-led national action plan for food systems engagement with the aim of prevention of overweight and obesity, in line with the regional SADC overweight prevention strategy. Thematic Emergency Funding also supported preparation and response for the potential impact of returning Zimbabweans, including children on the move, from South Africa, following the planned termination of Zimbabwean Exemption Permit (ZEP) holders.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF’s third year of implementing the Country Programme (2022–2026) produced lessons learned and approaches to accelerate results at scale going forward.
 
Challenges
 
The macroeconomic challenges faced by the country have resulted in inadequate financing for social services across sectors. This has impacted the implementation of programmes, including an increasing number in stockouts of health commodities; demotivated and insufficient number of health and social service workers due to staff attrition; and aging infrastructure impacting to the provision of adequate and quality service delivery.
 
To bring attention to these issues, UNICEF has leveraged its position as an advocate for children’s rights to convene and collaborate with stakeholders. To address overall funding reductions, UNICEF continued to strengthen advocacy efforts through the Health Resilience Fund (HRF) Policy Forum, Parliamentary Portfolio Committee, engagements with MoFED&IP and hosting a Health Financing Dialogue to advocate for increased domestic funding for health. As a result, MoHCC, procured approximately US$15 million worth of essential medicines from government resources in 2024 (MoHCC Finance Reports), and the budget allocation for the health sector increased to 13.01 per cent for 2025 compared to 9.8 per cent for 2024
 
With limited funding for specific nutrition activities and to tackle staff attrition and lack of human resources for nutrition both at national and sub-national levels. UNICEF has adopted a mid-stream approach, to build capacity of the network of nutritionists already in place at district and provincial level across the country and empower them to coordinate and implement all key nutrition activities in their respective districts and provinces. As a priority, UNICEF will continue to model interventions while conducting high-level advocacy and policy engagement including increased public financing for nutrition and child development programming.
 
Specific issues for child protection are districts facing constraints that include underfunded social workers with high caseloads, limited mobility to reach vulnerable children, and insufficient financial and administrative support for comprehensive case management. In response, UNICEF is supporting the Government in decentralizing case management to community levels by placing social workers at the ward level, following a multisectoral district child protection workplan approach.
 
UNICEF’s implementation of multi-sectoral and integrated approaches has yielded mixed results depending on the sector. In WASH, while these approaches can offer cost-efficient solutions, as evidenced during the cholera emergency response, they require substantial investment in coordinated planning, capacity building, and monitoring from the outset. 
 
Another challenge has been the low uptake/use of digital learning platforms, including the Learning Passport. While this platform has the potential to enhance blended learning and teacher capacity building, its adoption remains limited mainly because of lack of ICT devices but above all because no communication has been made since COVID-19 crisis on it while returning to face-to-face academic schooling. MoPSE and education stakeholders plan to promote its use more effectively. UNICEF has also procured electronic devices for the 154 schools that have undergone solarization, facilitating the implementation of blended learning approaches that can serve as a model for others.
 
Challenges in youth engagement and participation include limited coordination within the youth sector, lack of a robust information management system, few public-private-youth partnerships (PPYPs), and limited opportunities for systematic youth participation. UNICEF is supporting the Ministry to develop a Strategy which will outline coordination mechanisms and information management system framework. Furthermore, UNICEF will support convening of key stakeholders on adolescents and youth to enhance collaboration.
 
Moreover, the challenges faced in the social sectors are further hindered by gaps in data availability, quality, and management which limited the ability to generate robust evidence for decision-making, monitor progress, and adapt interventions effectively. Efforts to strengthen data systems require greater investment and coordination.
 
Lessons Learned
 
Reinforcement of Multi-Sectoral Integrated Programming, Community Engagement, and Community Capacity Strengthening are Vital to Resilience-Building and Scaling-Results
 
As a response to the challenges, efforts have been made to leverage the resources and foster closer inter-sectoral collaboration. For example, the nutrition programme, working together with the food and agriculture sector and the social welfare sector, has supported evidence generation on the state of food environments in Zimbabwe. Synergies are being built between nutrition and social welfare by linking Care Groups with activities such as food and cash distributions, on the ground and policy level engagements. A high-level inter-ministerial meeting led by the FNC was held with MoPSLSW and MoHCC resulting in recommendations on the way forward for closer integrated programming.
 
In order to sustainably influence the primary health care agenda (PHC) in Zimbabwe, UNICEF recognized the necessity of further streamlining processes through the development of an Integrated PHC toolkit and service package. This optimization freed up frontline workers’ time while enhancing their competencies for integrated services. The application of behavioural science, particularly through the behavioural and social drivers of vaccination framework, provided valuable data to tackle localized challenges effectively. This is a multi-faceted approach to child health that integrates newborn care, Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), and non-communicable disease (NCD) management and is essential for improving overall health outcomes.
 
UNICEF also introduced innovative strategies for integrating health services, such as combining COVID-19, HPV vaccinations, and adolescent sexual reproductive health services in the "One-Stop Approach" And integrated campaigns to ensure scale up of vaccine uptake. This model allowed clients to receive comprehensive healthcare within a single visit. Furthermore, telemedicine facilitated remote consultations and education for families in underserved areas, overcoming barriers to access. Empowering community health workers with essential equipment and tools, improved early detection of health care issues and referral to service delivery points. Microplanning training for polio mop-up campaigns in Harare City enhanced local health workers' ability to identify zero-dose children and communities in need. This initiative strengthened community linkages and built trust, promoting a culture of quality improvement in immunization efforts. 
 
Integrated HIV services and approaches are essential for enhancing the identification of HIV positive children. High-impact integrated models that demonstrate positive outcomes include combinations such as PMTCT-Immunization-Nutrition and HIV/SRHR-GBV-HPV-Mental Health. Increased investments in these areas are necessary to support programme expansion and enhance identification of HIV positive children for timely treatment and care. In addition, Zimbabwe's innovative Zvandiri model for peer support has proven to effectively enhance HIV treatment adherence and viral suppression among HIV-positive children and adolescents. 
 
Capacity-building initiatives focused on risk-informed programming have strengthened WASH governance across community, district, and provincial levels, leading to better planning, monitoring, and reporting of WASH interventions. Successful integrated approaches combining WASH, nutrition, and agriculture have demonstrated effectiveness in resilience-building and community ownership, particularly in the Matabeleland South region. Regular collaboration with partners is essential for achieving programme objectives, as it increases alignment and effectiveness in service delivery. Inadequate coordination underscores the critical need for a more structured, systems-based approach to planning, implementation, and stakeholder engagement. Moving forward, the focus will be on strengthening institutional accountabilities, coordination mechanisms and advocacy for climate resilient WASH services at national and sub-national levels, fostering multi-sectoral collaboration, and ensuring that WASH interventions are integrated across social sectors primarily in health, education and agriculture, and also into broader development frameworks as Zimbabwe envisions the NDS2. 
 
At the community level, UNICEF’s pilot with the Zimbabwe Parents of Handicapped Children Association (ZPHCA) demonstrated the power of collective action by uniting and empowering community members with shared interests in advocating for improved child services.
 
In conclusion, systems strengthening through multi-sectoral integrated programming, community engagement, and community capacity strengthening is vital to achieving sustainable, long-term development results. For the children of Zimbabwe, these strategies foster resilience, empower communities, and create the conditions necessary to scale-up successful interventions in a sustainable manner, that reach the most vulnerable and towards attainment of the SDGS.
 
Reinforcing Young People’s Role as Champions of Change is Key in Implementing Sustainable Programmes
 
Engaging adolescents and young people is critical for successful programme implementation and necessitates flexibility, mindset shift, and simplifying communication. Young people are eager to engage in humanitarian responses, provided they acquire necessary knowledge and skills as demonstrated by the success of youth advocates in promoting HPV vaccination, illustrating the effectiveness of empowering young people to lead health campaigns. This strategy enhances messaging and increases community engagement as by integrating youth into programme design and implementation, interventions become more relevant and resonate authentically with young audiences. 
 
Another example is in response to the cholera and drought induced El Niño emergencies. UNICEF successfully integrated adolescents and youth interventions into the humanitarian response. Through technical and advocacy support, 40 U-Report Champions in Emergencies (24 female and 16 male) from the ten provinces of Zimbabwe were equipped with skills in social mobilization through training. These champions shared vital information on the impact of emergencies and promoting preparedness and mitigating measures with 500 peers contributing to increase in awareness and knowledge on emergences.
 
To foster youth innovation and participation, strengthening collaboration between the Ministry of Youth Empowerment, Development, and Vocational Training (MoYEDVT) and MoPSE is vital.
 
Future Outlook
 
Financing, Policy, and Infrastructure for Effective Service Delivery
 
UNICEF will intensify advocacy efforts to support increased public investments and budgetary allocations to social sectors, promoting resource efficiency and effectiveness, expanding the coverage of social protection programs, and improving data related to children. Strategic engagements with Government and other stakeholders will emphasize the long-term benefits of investing in child-centered policies. Partnerships with academia will also be leveraged to provide technical assistance, training, and research support.
 
Strengthening partnerships with local CSOs will be vital for localized programming efforts, and UNICEF plans to enhance evidence-based programming through the use of the UNICEF maturity assessment model to improve the country’s procurement and supply chain management systems.
 
Furthermore, UNICEF seeks to stimulate the development of policy and strategy documents focusing on maternal and newborn health, and to expand the use of behavioural science in health programmes, with a target of formulating a comprehensive Health Promotion Policy and National Strategy by 2025, including extending the life of the National Community Health Strategy to 2030 with key components on universal health coverage (UHC) and acceleration of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets.
 
Moving forward, it is essential to prioritize government budgeting for the operations and maintenance of WASH infrastructure and strengthen local government capacities to deliver quality interventions. Addressing underfunding in sanitation and hygiene will be crucial to advancing towards open defecation-free communities and ensuring the long-term success of WASH initiatives in Zimbabwe.
 
Other priorities for 2025 include scaling up integrated PMTCT-Immunization-Nutrition interventions, adapting the Zvandiri young mentor mothers (YMM) model for HIV negative pregnant and breastfeeding adolescent girls and young women, continued roll out of the Triple Elimination Plan and the implementation of the Global Alliance Country Plan to end AIDS in children and disseminate the HIV response sustainability Part A while developing Part B. 
 
UNICEF will focus on the strengthening of the youth sector, in particular the coordination and implementation of recommendations from the evaluation of the Child Parliament, the launching of social innovation hubs, and strengthening systematic engagement and participation of adolescents and young people on key national, regional and global activities. The expansion of U-Report coverage, and capacity building of youth led networks will also be pursued.
 
Due to the rising rates of wasting and setbacks in stunting reduction progress, reprioritizing triple-duty multi-sectoral systems strengthening will be essential to building nutrition resilience and protecting vulnerable populations from climate-related shocks and disease outbreaks. Key strategies involve engaging at the sub-national level and capacity development of food and nutrition security committees at the district and ward levels. Additionally, investing in pre-service nutrition training for frontline health workers will help systematically build capacity and ensure sustainability amid ongoing funding constraints.
 
In 2025, UNICEF will continue efforts to support inclusive learning opportunities, including collaborating with MoPSE on the Learning Pioneer Initiative to pilot and accelerate digital learning tools to address the learning crisis and shape the future of learning. Zimbabwe is one of six countries that includes Egypt, Ghana, Malaysia, Rwanda, Uzbekistan selected for the initiative through UNICEF’s Office of Innovation and plans to pilot an EdTech solution to address gaps related to inclusive foundational learning.
 
Recognizing the lack of a unified national framework for disability identification and access to social protection, UNICEF has begun a harmonization process. This initiative aims to eliminate barriers, redundant assessments, and simplify access to essential services, potentially improving the lives of individuals with disabilities in Zimbabwe by mid-2025.
 
Data and MICS
 
Data generation remains vital for programming and advocacy across all sectors. UNICEF aims to increase investment in robust data management systems to enable real-time tracking of integrated health initiatives, while also leveraging artificial intelligence tools to create cohesive care models that enhance telemedicine integration with local health services. UNICEF will also support coordination between childhood NCDs and other public health interventions building on existing risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) strategies like infodemic rumour management, behavioural advocacy, and community engagement to better involve vulnerable populations. 
 
To address data-related constraints, investments will be made in improving data systems to enhance availability, quality, and analysis. This includes supporting the government to embark on the MICS through allocation of domestic resources and resource mobilization, which would enable the MICS to generate reliable evidence for policymaking as well as providing essential data for a solid analysis to inform the next UNICEF country program cycle. 
 
Evidence generation for child protection advocacy and legislative reform is also essential. UNICEF has initiated documentation of programme interventions and will support studies on thematic areas like child labour and service mapping at the district level.

Argentina is an upper middle-income country with a Gross National Income (GNI) per capita of USD 12,520 in 2023[1]. Argentina's economy has been stagnant for over a decade. The average annual GDP growth rate was -0.3 per cent between 2012 and 2019, dropped to -9.9 per cent in 2020 due to the pandemic, rebounded to an average of 7.9 per cent in 2021-2022, and fell again by -1.6 per cent in 2023. This performance has been linked to the accumulation of imbalances in the fiscal and external sectors: between 2012 and 2023, primary fiscal deficit averaged 2.7 per cent of GDP, and overall deficit averaged 4.6 per cent. On the other hand, balance of payments’ current account deficit averaged 2 per cent of GDP during this period. These imbalances resulted in successive currency devaluations, rising inflation, and the decline in real household incomes. 

In 2023, USD appreciated 356 per cent against the Argentinian peso, and inflation, measured by Consumer Price Index, reached 211% in December 2023 compared to December 2022. National Government’s Gross public debt reached USD 442.515 billion in June 2024, equivalent to 110.5% of GDP. For 2024, private analysts and international organizations project a contraction of GDP between -3.5% and -3.6% as a result of measures taken to restore macroeconomic balances, including a 211% devaluation of the peso at the beginning of the new administration and a 5-GDP-point fiscal adjustment to achieve fiscal balance in 2024. Inflation rate closed 2024 at 117,8% on a year-over-year basis compared to 2023.

During the first semester of 2024, 67.1 per cent of children lived in monetary poverty, showing an interannual increase of 10 percentage points. Food security continued to be a significant challenge: 27.3 per cent of children experienced extreme poverty. 52 per cent of households with children reported that they stopped buying certain food items due to income constraints, and around 30 per cent stated they had incurred debt to purchase food. Preliminary information for second semester shows a poverty rate decrease, which could return to end of 2023 levels.  

In 2024, social protection system maintained an elevated coverage, reaching 95 per cent of children, with a persisting challenge of approximately 650,000 children that remain outside the system. It is worth highlighting that the Prestación Alimentar program was expanded to include adolescents aged 15 to 17, who were previously excluded. Furthermore, the mechanism for updating the amount of cash transfers and family allowances was modified, leading to a recovery of the purchasing power of main income protection policies addressed to children, reaching pre-pandemic levels. This helped to reduce the effects on children of current macroeconomic adjustment and marked a priority set on children in a context of national budget reductions. Nevertheless, Prestación Alimentar still lacks an automatic updating mechanism.

Early Childhood Development (ECD) services show varying attendance rates according to age. In 2022, only 20 per cent of children aged 0–2 accessed childcare and education services, while it rose to 64 per cent for 3-year-olds. Attendance was nearly universal among 5-year-olds and exceeded 93 per cent for 4-year-olds. These rates vary across regions and socioeconomic groups, largely due to disparities in service availability. Also, there is limited coordination among early childhood institutions, which hinder the delivery of quality services across sectors and regions.

Primary school attendance is virtually universal. At secondary level, while attendance rates remain high (92.3 per cent), almost 300,000 adolescents were out of school (2022 Census).

In terms of learning achievements, 34 per cent of primary school students did not achieve satisfactory levels in language, and 48.6 per cent fell short in mathematics in 2023. Learning achievements in secondary schools have deteriorated: the percentage of students not reaching satisfactory levels increased from 38 in 2019 to 43 in 2022 in language, and from 71 to 82 in mathematics.

In 2022, the infant mortality rate was 8.4 per 1,000 live births, reflecting a slight increase from 2021 (8.0 per 1,000 live births). Maternal mortality rose to 7.4 deaths per 10,000 live births in 2021 but decreased to 3.4 in 2022, though it remained above pre-pandemic levels. Adolescent mortality rate in 2022 was 4.2 per 10,000, unchanged from 2021. The adolescent fertility rate in 2022 was 12,7 per 1.000 adolescent females, a 50% decrease compared to 2018. Significant disparities in these indicators persist among provinces.

Regarding nutrition, overweight remains the most prevalent form of malnutrition: 13.6 per cent of children under 5 years old and 41 per cent of school-aged children and adolescents. 

Between 2009 and 2019, national vaccination coverage declined by an average of 10 percentage points, with an additional 10-point drop in 2020. Although there was some recovery in 2021-2022, vaccination rates declined again in 2023.

Violence remains the primary reason for separating children from their families. In 2020, approximately 6,400 children were in the care of extended families, while 9,154 were in residential care facilities.

Despite 97.4 per cent of parents believing that children should not be physically punished, 59% of children under 15 experienced violent parenting practices. 11% of women aged 18–49 reported experiencing sexual abuse during childhood. 

National juvenile justice system remains inconsistent with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, allowing judicial discretion. In 2023, 4,156 adolescents and young adults who committed offenses as minors were held in penal facilities. Among them, 1,971 were under 18 years old, including 44 under the age of 16.

Adolescents aged 16–17 have the right to vote since 2012. In 2023, 93 per cent were aware of this right, however 30 per cent did not meet all the formal requirements to vote.

Migrants represents 4.2% of the total population, but this proportion drops to 1.5% among children. Migrant population faces worse living conditions: 12% experience unmet basic needs compared to 9 per cent among native population. Migrant children have lower school attendance rates: while 4 per cent of children aged 10–14 overall is out of school, this figure more than doubles to 9 per cent among migrant children.

[1] This report uses the latest available information.

In 2024, significant progress was made in addressing barriers to child well-being in Argentina, driving systemic changes to improve outcomes for children and adolescents. Efforts to promote informed advocacy highlighted key challenges such as child poverty and inequities in social protection systems. This supported the implementation of targeted public policy interventions. Research efforts, including reports on child poverty, cash transfer programs, and the national budget, provided critical insights. These insights supported adjustments like the expansion of the Alimentar Card to benefit adolescents and the adaptation of transfer amounts to address inflation’s impact.
 
Data on public finance included three analyses of the national budget with a focus on children, based on official public information from a long-standing cooperation with the Ministry of Economy. Policy dialogue actions included participation in an informative session of the National Lower House’s Commission of Social Security in April and the 2025 budget informative session in the Lower House’s Commission of Family, Childhood, and Youth in October. Despite fiscal challenges, significant investments in child-focused governmental programs were preserved, particularly through increased budget allocations for social protection programs benefiting children and their families nationwide.
 
Technical assistance led to the development of tools like the Child-Care Basket in Buenos Aires province and Buenos Aires City. This tool generates concrete evidence to inform judicial decisions on child-support –when there are unmet child-support obligations that lead to legal proceedings- and policy decisions regarding income security for female single-headed households.
 
Efforts prioritized reaching vulnerable and marginalized communities in four provinces, addressing food insecurity and enhancing access to essential resources through partnerships with community-based organizations Monte Adentro and Food Bank Network. Initiatives provided nutritional support, healthy food kits, and capacity-building workshops for families, promoting long-term development opportunities for these communities. Additionally, local governments received technical support and capacity-building training to strengthen planning processes, fostering the development of inclusive policies prioritizing the rights of children with disabilities.
 
The Municipality United for Childhood and Adolescence (MUNA) initiative expanded its scope, engaging a new province and 46 new municipalities, totaling 138, representing over half of the child population in participating provinces and near 40 per cent of total children in the country. Municipal teams developed strategic action plans, enhancing their ability to design, implement, and monitor policies focused on child and adolescent well-being. Forty new municipalities were certified as “Municipality Committed to Children and Adolescents,” totaling 86 with this status. Collaboration between local and provincial governments facilitated cohesive planning and resource allocation processes aligned with child-rights priorities. Training sessions and thematic workshops empowered municipal teams to adopt evidence-based approaches. New MUNA models are being designed to achieve scale and sustainability for the initiative during 2025, with intense support from provincial governments.
 
At the subnational level, innovative budgetary frameworks were incorporated into planning processes in two provinces, ensuring sustained resource allocation for children’s priorities. Agreements are being signed to scale up this initiative to other provinces in 2025. Twelve local governments advanced their public financing strategies by improving budget management, adopting participatory approaches to budgeting, and addressing disparities in access to essential services. These initiatives demonstrated the tangible benefits of enhanced governance and inclusive development practices and are expected to be scaled up in 2025 as part of the new MUNA models.
 
To promote the well-being of children from 0 to 6 years of age and reduce social and territorial disparities, UNICEF carried out technical assistance at different government levels. 
 
At the national level, the emergence of a Human Capital Ministry with responsibilities over Education, Social Development, and Labor posed new opportunities for developing comprehensive childhood policies. UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Under Secretary of Family Policies in defining the Federal Early Childhood Strategy for 2025.
 
At the provincial level, UNICEF's continued technical assistance to implementing and monitoring Comprehensive Provincial Early Childhood Strategies in four provinces. Actions included updating comprehensive analysis to inform public policy priorities and intersectoral plans for the year. The Ministries of Human Development and Health of Entre Ríos, Jujuy, and Salta implemented a community-based ECD program for vulnerable families, emphasizing play and responsive care.
 
At the local level, the improvement of government capacities to design, implement, and monitor comprehensive early childhood policies continued as part of the MUNA initiative in 51 municipalities. UNICEF provided technical support and capacity building for local public officials to design and implement action plans in early childhood, including interventions on health, nutrition, education, and care and protection.
 
UNICEF contributed to the Federal Literacy Plan, working with the Ministry of Education in Salta to ensure foundational learning by implementing an early literacy program with an intercultural perspective in two prioritized vulnerable and indigenous localities. This reached 139 teachers and 9,400 pre-school and primary school children. UNICEF also provided technical assistance to establish a Monitoring Taskforce led by the Ministry of Education to manage a provincial literacy plan for enhancing the teaching skills of 192 community educators, benefiting 1,300 children.
 
To promote the right to health, UNICEF contributed to strengthening perinatal health services in rural areas with indigenous populations by focusing on the quality of perinatal care, women need, and equality with an intercultural approach. Strategies implemented in 15 maternity hospitals across four provinces helped reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity, benefiting more than 20,000 mothers and newborns. Additionally, UNICEF supported the provincial implementation of the Healthy School Environment component of the Promotion of Healthy Eating Act by conducting studies to measuring public awareness and school-based barriers to improve nutritional quality. Evidence on digital Breast Milk Substitutes (BMS) marketing was published, an AI system to document non-compliances on the International Code on Breast Milk Substitutes (ICBMS) was developed, and 300 health professionals were trained on breastfeeding across four provinces. During World Breastfeeding Week, UNICEF contributed to certify public and private spaces as breastfeeding-friendly and also ran a communication campaign on breastfeeding. These efforts included raising awareness and training "breastfeeding counselors" in hospitals, health centers, educational spaces, and industrial parks, where a large number of women work. This initiative significantly improved support for breastfeeding mothers in these areas. 
 
UNICEF strengthened the response to the health emergency in Salta, addressing acute malnutrition through technical support to the Ministry of Health and procurement of RUFT and therapeutic formula for 600 children. Also contributed to improve food security among vulnerable families, training 190 indigenous women in culinary and healthy eating skills.
 
Adolescents in Argentina face several problems, including a learning crisis, limited access to quality health services, and insufficient opportunities for meaningful participation. To address these challenges, UNICEF focused on a multidimensional approach fostering intersectoral programming. UNICEF made significant strides in advancing adolescents' rights by implementing key strategies such as system strengthening, advocacy and communications, community engagement, social and behavior change, research and evaluation, digital transformation, and gender-transformative programming. UNICEF directly impacted over 152,000 adolescents and indirectly benefited 1.5 million more through initiatives to ensure the expansion of quality educational opportunities, formal participation, and access to adolescent-oriented health services in priority provinces.
 
To tackle the adolescent learning crisis, UNICEF contributed with the education sector to enhance foundational learning, promote out-of-school adolescents’ inclusion, and foster secondary school transformation. The PLaNEA program implemented in Tucuman and Cordoba benefited 35,500 students and improved the skills of 7,247 teachers and principals. Additionally, a new annual training program to transform secondary education reached 5,440 teachers and principals in 7 provinces (Jujuy, Santiago del Estero, Mendoza, Cordoba, Tucuman, Misiones, Salta y Mendoza), impacting 900,000 students. The Unique Opportunities-APP initiative, supported by 10 business partners and 35 local governments, trained 2,800 adolescents in digital and transferable skills.
 
Efforts to reduce out-of-school adolescents included strengthening 60 local governments to ensure school attendance for 3,000 adolescents and scaling Technology-rural-based-secondary-schools by 32%, reaching 177 communities. The intervention comprised installing Starlink Satellite connectivity in 100 isolated rural schools and provide literature books through a key private sector alliance.
 
In the health sector, UNICEF expanded technical assistance and capacity development to enhance adolescents' access to quality health services, focusing on adolescent girls. This included supporting 14 local governments in developing epidemiological monitoring systems and training health professionals to address pregnancies in girls under 15. Moreover, to foster adolescents’ mental health support, UNICEF scaled a pilot innovative peer-to-peer support initiative, Listening Centers, in three priority provinces, and trained primary health care workers in comprehensive adolescents’ health, impacting near 72,000 adolescents.
 
UNICEF also strengthened adolescent participation by creating institutionalized spaces and providing technical assistance to create local participation strategies with 40 municipalities through the MUNA initiative. The PLAN A annual meeting, held with UNFPA and civil society organizations (Asociación Conciencia and Centro Ana Frank) promoted intergenerational dialogues with adolescents from different provinces. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with 11 leading youth organizations to change social norms, develop platforms for adolescents to share their experiences, and propose solutions to stakeholders on issues that concerned them.

In 2024, ACO made significant technical contributions to improve parenting skills and prevent all forms of violence at national level and local levels. The launch of a new parenting portal proved both necessary and highly successful, garnering over 100,000 online visits in less than a year. The portal's publications, videos, and podcasts in addition will also be utilized in a pilot parenting program, designed in collaboration with the Province of Salta, to bring the online content closer to local communities. Provincial authorities praised this intersectoral approach for its effectiveness in enhancing caregivers parenting skills with a transformative perspective about fatherhood. They also highlighted the positive impact on children through the reinforcement of municipal initiatives that promote positive child-rearing environments. This pilot program will provide essential insights and lessons for scaling the initiative to other provinces across the country.

ACO's efforts yielded significant results through a study providing recommendations and lessons learned on specialized protection responses for victims of violence against children (VAC) in the context of domestic violence and other forms of violence across Buenos Aires, Chaco, Jujuy, Salta, Tucumán, and Santa Fe. Furthermore, to promote the participation of children and adolescents in defining violence prevention policies and eliminating adult-centric biases, the project “Corners, Rounds, and Playgrounds” was successfully conducted in the provinces of Salta and Santa Fe, engaging numerous local stakeholders in the process. This initiative engaged over 500 children and adolescents, local grassroots organizations, and municipal authorities, fostering collaboration and dialogue. Based on the guidelines provided by the INSPIRE initiative for ending VAC, this project strengthened community involvement and awareness, paving the way for more effective and inclusive violence prevention strategies. The findings and impact of this initiative are detailed in the publication “Rincones, rondas y patios” (2024).
 
As part of an improvement plan to prevent the institutionalization of children without parental care, UNICEF, in collaboration with RELAF (Red Latinoamericana de Acogimiento Familiar), provided technical support to local governments. This initiative aimed to enhance and expand foster family programs in Buenos Aires, Salta, Jujuy, and Santa Fe. Through this partnership, provincial authorities received resources and guidance to strengthen their foster care systems, ensuring better care and support for children. ACO and RELAF also developed evidence and tools for case management and supported technical teams in their implementation, leading to improved interventions that prioritized alternatives to institutionalization in residential care.
 
Significant progress was made because of these efforts. In Buenos Aires, the children's agency agreed to strengthen the implementation of foster care programs, and provincial authorities committed to further improving the alternative care system. In Santa Fe, a governmental decree establishing procedures for foster care modalities is under development, alongside a bill proposal aimed at providing better legislative support for foster care programs. In Jujuy, a bill for family foster care is under legislative review; if approved, it will offer formal and budgetary support to foster care programs. In Salta, dialogue, training, and advocacy efforts with authorities led to the reinstatement of the family foster care program after a period of inactivity, successfully preventing further admissions of children under three to the Casa Cuna (residential care).
 
ACO also made significant advances in enhancing the judiciary's management of cases involving children and their access to justice. By partnering with provincial supreme courts and the Federal Board of Courts (JUFEJUS), ACO developed comprehensive data collection tools for child protection and juvenile justice, resulting in a nationwide data map. This tool was validated at the 7th annual meeting of the "Network of Judges Committed to the Rights of Children and Adolescents" in Buenos Aires, attended by top authorities from all 24 provincial courts and technical teams. Bilateral agreements with several provincial courts have been crucial in bolstering the judiciary's capacity to handle cases of child violence and abuse more effectively.
 
UNICEF also played an important role in the legislative reform discussion of the juvenile criminal system by providing key evidence to inform public and legislative discussions. Works included the meticulous collection and analysis of data, which was then disseminated publicly and shared with key authorities and parliamentary committees. This evidence was also presented at a high-level roundtable organized in UNICEF's offices, ensuring that the insights reached influential stakeholders and contributed effectively to the legislative process.
 
To enhance migrant children's rights, CAREF, supported by UNICEF, conducted a study in Jujuy and Misiones, focusing on birth registration in border areas. This initiative addressed the unique challenges in these regions that affect children's right to identity and access to other rights. By collaborating with local authorities, the study aimed to develop robust solutions and provide recommendations to improve birth registration processes for migrant children at high-transit land borders. This effort will strengthen the protection and recognition of migrant children's identities and rights.
 
UNICEF took a proactive role in following up on the Committee on the Rights of the Child's recommendations made to Argentina in its ninety-seventh session in Geneva from 26 August to 13 September 2024. By providing technical assistance, facilitating consultations, and supporting the development of policies and programs at the national and local levels, UNICEF aimed to help Argentina meet its obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child. This collaboration ensures that the Committee's recommendations are translated into concrete actions that improve the lives of children across the country.
 
UNICEF actively participated in consultations for the Committee on the Rights of the Child's General Comment 27, which focuses on children's rights to access to justice and effective remedies. Working with partners, UNICEF consulted with children to gather their views on matters related to the general comment, and the participation of an adolescent from Argentina in a meeting organized by UNICEF in Panama, ensuring that children's voices are represented and heard in these crucial discussions.
 
Argentine society knows, supports, and trusts UNICEF’s work. In 2024, the country office reinforced its positive image, achieving 90% awareness according to the latest brand barometer. The 2024 activities and iconic events like Un Sol para los Chicos, the Festival for Children, and the UNICEF Run for Education, informed and nurtured the largest donor base in the region, exceeding 240,000 people about UNICEF’s work. UNICEF Argentina garnered 97% positive media mentions and 1,847,255 social media followers. Economic and Social Situation of the Eastern Caribbean 
In 2024, the Eastern Caribbean subregion faced a complex socio-economic landscape, marked by modest economic growth, persistent social challenges, and environmental vulnerabilities.  Growth decelerated to 4.8 per cent in 2024, down from 6.3 per cent in 2022 and public debt remains above the 60 per cent debt-to-GDP target, underscoring the need for fiscal reforms and sustainable debt management strategies. 
   
In July 2024, Hurricane Beryl, the earliest Atlantic storm to intensify to a Category 5 level, caused extensive damage across Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, affecting 200,000 people, particularly in Grenada’s Carriacou and Petite Martinique and Union Island in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines - where some 95 per cent of buildings were damaged or destroyed.  The hurricane resulted in at least six fatalities and left thousands needing humanitarian assistance. 
   
The devastation brought by Hurricane Beryl prompted discussions on innovative financial instruments to enhance resilience. The Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF) provided prompt payouts totaling approximately US$44 million to Grenada, marking its largest single payout. Grenada became the first nation to activate a ‘hurricane clause' in its Government bonds. This was a significant application of flexible financial instruments to manage the economic impacts of climate-related disasters. Discussions at COP29 also emphasized innovative debt solutions, with some Caribbean nations securing partial debt write-offs tied to commitments to climate resilience investments. 
   
Youth unemployment remains a critical issue, averaging 24 per cent and exceeding 40 per cent in some countries, nearly triple the adult rate. A quarter of the youths in several countries live below the poverty line. Food insecurity affects approximately 3.7 million people - about 50 per cent of the population in the English-speaking Caribbean.  
   
Rising crime and violence continue to threaten social and economic progress. Countries in the Eastern Caribbean have among the highest rates of homicide globally, namely the Bahamas (29.2/100,000), Saint Kitts and Nevis (29.4), Saint Lucia (39), Saint Vincent and the Grenadines (30.7) and Trinidad and Tobago (29.4) (UN Office on Drugs and Crime - UNODC - Homicide Report, 2023). Marginalized youth are disproportionately affected, with many becoming involved in criminal activities. The economic cost of crime is estimated at 3.7 per cent of GDP, reflecting its significant burden on regional development.  

 

  
Situation of Children in the Eastern Caribbean Area (ECA) 

Education inequities have worsened due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Findings from the 2022 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in Trinidad and Tobago highlighted persistent disparities: for example, 97 per cent of children living in wealthier households completed secondary school, compared to only 70 per cent of their peers living in less wealthy households. According to 2023 data from the World Bank, three Caribbean countries had more than 20 per cent of youth not in education, employment, or training (NEET): Barbados (28 per cent), Saint Lucia (34 per cent), and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines (27 per cent). 

Harmful child discipline practices remain widespread. The 2022 Trinidad and Tobago MICS revealed that 60 per cent of three- to four-year-olds experienced severe physical punishment, while 65 per cent aged five to nine was subjected to psychological aggression. Mental health has emerged as a critical issue for youth in the post-pandemic era. According to the 2024 Child and Youth Mental Health Study conducted by the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) and UNICEF, more than half of the respondents reported experiencing anxiety. 

The subregion is facing growing humanitarian challenges due to the influx of refugees and migrants, particularly from Venezuela, driven by economic and political crises. Venezuelan children and adolescents encounter significant barriers to accessing protection, health, adequate nutrition, psychosocial support and education, with an alarming 96 per cent outside of the formal education system. Despite the Government’s 2023 commitment to integrate Venezuelan children registered under the 2019 Migrant Registration Framework (MRF) into public schools, only 60 out of over 4,500 school-aged children were registered in formal schools in 2023-2024. Legal and administrative obstacles continue to block most of the school-aged children from enrollment. The main cause is the Government policy that prevents Venezuelan children who were not registered in 2019 from attending school. Additionally, there is no formalized pathway for unregistered children to enroll, and administrative delays further hinder the process. 


  
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Regional Trends 
  
There are significant challenges in achieving child-related SDGs. Approximately one in three children live in poverty (SDG 1). In Trinidad and Tobago, home to over 60 per cent of the children in the Eastern Caribbean, a 2024 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index revealed that about 36 per cent of children under 17 are affected by multidimensional poverty. Dominica, Grenada, and Saint Lucia are among the most vulnerable nations. 

In health (SDG 3), issues such as low immunization coverage and comparatively high under-five mortality rates in some countries undermine progress.  Dominica, for example, has a rate of 32 per 1,000 live births - more than double the regional average of 13.26.  

Education (SDG  4) presents a mixed picture, with relatively high primary and secondary enrollment rates but ongoing disparities in attendance and learning outcomes. Data from the 2022 MICS revealed that in Trinidad and Tobago attendance rates at the lower- secondary level differed by over 20 per cent between the wealthiest and poorest households. Furthermore, the Education Statistical Digest (2022-2023) of the Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States (OECS) highlighted that there were significant differences in pass rates across subjects in the CSEC examination. English A recorded a high pass rate of 78.3 per cent, while Mathematics had a considerably lower pass rate of 38.2 per cent. Additionally, female students outperformed male students in English A and B, whereas the gender gap in Mathematics was minimal. 

Gender equality (SDG 5) remains a significant challenge, particularly in addressing gender-based violence (GBV) and disparities in educational and economic opportunities. For the Caribbean in general, GBV is one of the most widespread forms of violence, directly impacting citizen security, including the stability and health of families and communities. While some countries have enacted laws criminalizing domestic violence and child marriage, enforcement is inconsistent. For instance, the Domestic Violence Act in Trinidad and Tobago has been revised, but its implementation is hindered by inconsistent police responses and limited support services for survivors. A 2018 UN Women report highlights significant variability in police handling of domestic violence cases, with some victims facing delays in obtaining legal protection. Additionally, sexual violence remains a serious concern. According to UNODC data, in 2020 Trinidad and Tobago recorded 680 cases of sexual violence, corresponding to a rate of 44.79 per 100,000 people. 

The 2022 MICS further reported an adolescent birth rate of 22 per 1,000 adolescent women, underscoring the challenges of early pregnancies and their impact on young women's education and economic opportunities. Addressing these disparities is crucial for promoting gender equality and ensuring inclusive development.

In the area of protection (SDG 16), violent discipline remains widespread. No Caribbean country has fully prohibited corporal punishment in homes, and few have limited the practice in day care and alternative care settings. Only Anguilla, Saint Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago have implemented bans in schools. Additionally, the Caribbean region faces significant challenges related to child protection, including the high prevalence of sexual violence against children and, as suggested, some of the highest homicide rates in the world. In 2024 alone, Trinidad and Tobago recorded 623 homicides, marking the highest number ever in a country with a population of approximately 1.5 million. In response, the Government declared a state of emergency, as the surge in violence has been linked to the influx of firearms from the United States. Addressing these issues is crucial for achieving SDG 16. 

In the face of these challenges, the UNICEF Office for the Eastern Caribbean Area has taken a leadership role in advocating for children and youth through initiatives such as the Children and Youth Action Summit and the Small Island Developing State (SIDS) process. Ahead of the 4th International SIDS Conference (SIDS4) in Antigua and Barbuda, UNICEF ECA supported the development of position papers, briefs, and other advocacy materials to amplify the voices of children and youth. By focusing on key issues like climate resilience, equitable education, and child protection, UNICEF has ensured that youth priorities are embedded in regional development agendas. These efforts underscore the agency’s commitment to advancing child rights and fostering sustainable development across the Eastern Caribbean.

Goal Area 2: Education

UNICEF ECA’s education initiatives delivered measurable results, positively impacting 138,375 children across the region. Programmes focused on early childhood development (ECD), inclusive education, access to digital resources, disaster preparedness, emergency response, advocacy, and capacity building.
 
Efforts to enhance ECD prioritized building the skills of parents, teachers, and caregivers - particularly adolescent mothers - in creating safe, inclusive learning environments. Professional development sessions improved curriculum delivery, technology integration, and support for children with developmental challenges, benefiting 1,525 stakeholders and 13,375 children across Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, Montserrat, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and Trinidad and Tobago.
 
In Grenada, UNICEF partnered with the Caribbean Centre for Child Neurodevelopment to produce an integrated ECD strategy, policy, and implementation plan. This initiative, informed by contributions from over 200 stakeholders through workshops and focus groups, integrated health, nutrition, protection, responsive parenting, and early learning to improve developmental outcomes for children aged 0-8.
 
Advocacy efforts strengthened nurturing care for young children. Grenada’s Ministry of Education produced the advocacy video ‘A Day in the Life of a Preschooler,’ highlighting the importance of structured play and positive adult-child interactions. Similarly, Saint Lucia’s ‘Bonding’ parenting series reached over 10,000 viewers, addressing behaviour management and promoting child-centred practices. In Barbados, the Early Childhood Symposium empowered 350 stakeholders to foster inclusive environments, benefiting over 6,000 children.


UNICEF’s education recovery efforts in emergency contexts ensured continuity of learning. Following Hurricane Beryl, mental health interventions and psychosocial support for early-grade teachers in Grenada were complemented by the distribution of ECD and recreational kits to 351 children and their teachers. Additionally, 180 children in Carriacou and Petite Martinique received home learning packages. In Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, 103 children in private ECD centres accessed safe and well-equipped learning environments.
 
UNICEF’s partnerships with the OECS Commission, the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), and CARICOM strengthened regional education systems. Initiatives such as the 9th Annual Statisticians Meeting advanced data-driven policymaking and monitoring, benefiting over 125,000 children in pre-primary, primary, and secondary education. A Commitment to Action for Foundational Learning was established across OECS countries, marking a significant milestone in improving literacy and numeracy outcomes.
 
Key regional events, such as the OECS Youth and Sports meeting, the Education Meeting, and the Digital Curriculum Hackathon, engaged hundreds of participants and informed education policies. These efforts extended to the United Kingdom Overseas Territories - Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat, and Turks and Caicos Islands - through research and consultations following the 2022 Transforming Education Summit.

UNICEF’s collaboration with Trinidad and Tobago’s Ministry of Education facilitated the integration of Venezuelan migrant children into public schools, enabling 60 children to access 22 schools. Enrolment efforts continue and will be further supported with community outreach strategies, but access for the more than 4,000 children not registered under the 2019 Migrant Registration Framework is hindered by the legislative framework. Support is extended to 1,500 out-of-school children through child-friendly spaces (CFS) and the online secondary education programme, DAWERE, with up to 231 children (130 girls, 101 boys) enrolled. Additionally, UNICEF provided eye screening and glasses for students in need, improving their readiness for learning.
 
Disaster preparedness initiatives under the Caribbean Safe School Initiative (CSSI) yielded significant results. Six countries (Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Dominica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines) approved the CSSI policy, and training in disaster risk management equipped educators to benefit over 5,000 students and 3,950 parents. Concurrently, efforts to migrate over 9,000 curriculum-based digital content items to ministry platforms progressed, with completion expected by 2025.
 
The GIGA initiative improved access to quality online resources by building regional capacity to manage connectivity and finance digital inclusion. Workshops for senior officials from eight governments strengthened strategic approaches, ensuring children’s equitable access to digital learning opportunities.
 
These achievements reflect UNICEF ECA’s commitment to measurable, impactful interventions that transform education systems and build resilience for children and families in the Eastern Caribbean.

Goal Area 3: Child Protection

UNICEF ECA achieved significant progress in strengthening child protection systems in 2024 by addressing critical bottlenecks such as legislative gaps, harmful social norms, fragmented protection frameworks, and barriers to migrant children’s inclusion. Through targeted advocacy, partnerships, innovative solutions, and systemic reforms, UNICEF enhanced child safety, access to mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS), justice systems, and digital innovations to protect children effectively.
 
UNICEF supported the drafting of Grenada’s Child Justice Bill and Probation of Offenders Act, laying the foundation for a Family Court and fostering gender-transformative, restorative justice practices. These efforts advanced child-friendly legal systems and enabled stronger protection for vulnerable children. A multi-sectoral assessment facilitated the development of a regional roadmap addressing online child sexual exploitation and abuse in five countries, achieving buy-in for a regional child policy for the OECS. In Trinidad and Tobago, the Primero Child Protection Information Management System enhanced case management, coordination, and service delivery across sectors, ensuring timely support for children.

UNICEF’s launch of the Caribbean’s first online youth mental health hub, www.youngcaribbeanminds.com, which reached 92,645 individuals across 12 countries, expanded access to critical MHPSS resources. The U-Matter text line pilot in Trinidad and Tobago resulted in the capacity building of 66 volunteers. The chatline is poised for subregional expansion in 2025. Additionally, 2,681 frontline workers received psychological first aid training, and 159 workers were trained in the Return to Happiness programme, ensuring responsive care to 1,901 children, particularly following Hurricane Beryl. Finally, in response to alarming mental health statistics, members of the Caribbean Mental Health Focal Point Network spanning 17 countries created youth-led MHPSS solutions that were integrated into national, regional and government systems.
 
UNICEF’s social and behaviour change (SBC) initiatives reached 230,000 individuals in four countries through campaigns, public surveys, and focus groups addressing corporal punishment, sexual abuse, and juvenile offending. These efforts contributed to a shift in attitudes, promoting positive caregiving and discipline practices, directly strengthening child protection outcomes.

Violence against children remains a critical concern in the Eastern Caribbean, with significant implications for their mental, physical, and social well-being. Social norms and structural gaps perpetuate cycles of violence, including corporal punishment and sexual abuse, often exacerbated by economic vulnerabilities and migration pressures. UNICEF’s targeted interventions prioritized the prevention and response to violence through integrated programming. Public campaigns and community outreach initiatives raised awareness among approximately 230,000 persons and shifted harmful attitudes, creating a foundation for more supportive environments for children. UNICEF’s efforts contributed to strengthening referral pathways and expanding access to protective services, ensuring that children affected by violence received timely and effective support. Partnerships with USAID, the University of the West Indies (the UWI), the International Organization for Migration, the United Nations Population Fund, the Pan American Health Organization, the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA), and the OECS Commission strengthened cross-sectoral responses to violence against children and gender-based violence. These collaborations enhanced service coordination and delivery, fostering a unified regional approach to child protection challenges. Representatives from 6 of the 12 countries attended the 1st Global Conference on Violence against Children with Dominica and Trinidad and Tobago making pledges to enhance parenting support, promote safe school environments and strengthen response services to address this issue. In 2025 UNICEF will be supporting these countries in the realization of these pledges. 
 
Evidence giving insight into public and key stakeholders’ perceptions, attitudes, and knowledge on various key issues was generated. A social survey/public opinion poll on sexual abuse, corporal punishment and on justice for children carried out among 5,000 people across the subregion produced evidence that will be used to enhance an SBC violence prevention strategy. Focus groups and U-Report polls were conducted among parents and children to influence parenting interventions to prevent abuse and to engender behaviours that positively support children’s mental health. In addition, SBC evidence generation is being supported in Grenada to inform the introduction of new vaccines for under-fives in 2025.

As a result of UNICEF’s SBC advocacy for human-centred approaches in programme design, there was also enhanced reflection and co-creation processes with parents and caregivers in the design of the content for parenting sessions. This approach was seen in the capacity-building sessions for parents across three ECA countries where the knowledge and skills of some 1,380 parents/caregivers on how to implement positive caregiving, including positive discipline, were enhanced. 

In 2024, 295,000 people were reached with messages on positive parental practices, supporting children’s mental health and protecting them from online violence and sexual and emotional abuse via traditional and social media across four countries - Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Dominica, and Grenada.  
 
Following UNICEF’s advocacy, partners are recognizing the importance of institutionalizing training in child protection. For example, this year the Ministry of Youth, Sports and Community Empowerment in Barbados committed to institutionalizing such training for anyone working with children and youth under its programmes.   

Risk-informed humanitarian and development programming safeguarded displaced and vulnerable children by increasing birth registrations for 127 children of migrant parents, mitigating gender-based violence risks for 2,937 persons, and providing family reunification services and alternative care for 88 unaccompanied and separated children in Trinidad and Tobago. Following Hurricane Beryl, UNICEF’s integrated response ensured that affected children received essential protection and psychosocial services.
 
UNICEF’s results-driven initiatives in 2024 reflect its commitment to creating safer, more inclusive environments for children, embedding protection across systems, and fostering resilience for the most vulnerable populations in the Eastern Caribbean.




Goal Area 4: Climate Change and Resilience  

Significant strides were made in strengthening governments and regional institutions to implement risk-informed, resilient, and child-sensitive climate policies through the active participation of children, young people, and communities, promoting climate action and resilience including in emergency contexts. Progress was evident in embedding child-sensitive approaches in climate policies, interventions, and humanitarian responses, particularly in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH). This underscores UNICEF's unique ability to mesh technical expertise, evidence generation, and stakeholder engagement into effective policy action.

The agency provided technical assistance and, where applicable, financial support to ministries responsible for climate and education, as well as national disaster offices. This support facilitated capacity strengthening, policy development, and implementation of child- and youth-sensitive climate resilience measures. By engaging directly with governments, UNICEF played a pivotal role in advancing systemic change at regional and national levels, ensuring that climate resilience policies prioritize children’s needs.

UNICEF ECA enhanced the participation of children and youth in climate change and resilience through advocacy, and technical and financial support to governments. UNICEF-led youth advocacy training empowered young people to identify issues and develop campaigns, increasing their capacities and contributing to a growing movement of young climate leaders shaping policies and solutions.

UNICEF directly supported eight governments in developing, financing, and implementing child-sensitive climate policies and programmes, strengthening climate and disaster resilience for children. In Saint Kitts and Nevis, the Children’s Climate Index-Disaster Risk Model (CCRI-DRM) was instrumental in bridging data gaps, informing policy decisions, and engaging communities in risk reduction. At the Caribbean Conference on Comprehensive Disaster Management (CDM) 2024, UNICEF highlighted how the tool enhances early warning systems, school safety planning, and disaster preparedness by integrating child-focused risk assessments. By working with government agencies, schools, and local organizations, UNICEF ensures community-driven resilience measures that address children's vulnerabilities. The success of this initiative led to five countries committing to embedding child-sensitive approaches in their National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
