There was a significant increase in children and young people engaged in climate action and advocacy, driven by UNICEF ECA’s targeted initiatives, including youth climate and disaster risk reduction training, climate education workshops, and school-based disaster risk reduction programmes. These efforts improved climate literacy and disaster preparedness by equipping young people with the skills to identify local climate risks and engage with policymakers. Through the Climate Fundoo platform, U-Report polls, and national youth dialogues, UNICEF created platforms for young people to voice their concerns and propose solutions. Additionally, teacher training programmes on climate and disaster resilience helped integrate climate education into school curricula, strengthening the ability of schools and communities to respond to environmental and climate-related shocks. As a result, youth networks expanded, and more young people participated in national climate discussions, influencing policy decisions at both the regional and country levels. In 2024, UNICEF contributed to a multi-hazard gap analysis and supported the UN Secretary-General's Early Warnings for All (EW4ALL) implementation plan for Antigua and Barbuda and Barbados, focusing on communication, data collection, and early warning systems tailored to children's needs.

UNICEF continued to lead or co-lead national WASH sectoral coordination mechanisms, strengthening public and private sector capacities to prepare for, and respond to, climate-related shocks. In 2024, three countries increased their national monitoring system capacities through WASH coordination groups and e-coordination platforms. A Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Caribbean Chambers of Commerce was signed, enhancing collaboration with the private sector in resilience building and in support of the regional response mechanism.  This is in alignment with the recent MOU signed between UNICEF and CDEMA where the agencies aim to work collaboratively with the private sector to identify and overcome communication, operational and coordination gaps in disaster management.


Goal Area 5: Child poverty (Shock-Responsive Social Protection)

In 2024, UNICEF ECA significantly strengthened social protection frameworks, focusing on resilient, child-sensitive policies and legislation. In the British Virgin Islands, UNICEF's support led to the Cabinet's approval of a social protection policy and the drafting of a new bill. UNICEF ECA also prioritized the digitalization of social protection delivery systems. Management information systems were implemented in Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, and Saint Kitts and Nevis, enabling streamlined, data-driven integration of social services. In Saint Kitts and Nevis, UNICEF's technical assistance to the ‘LIFT’ programme, a cash-plus model, helped address multidimensional poverty by combining financial assistance with essential services.
 
A pioneering multidimensional child poverty analysis in Trinidad and Tobago provided new insights and guided Government policy. Additionally, UNICEF provided rapid assistance to 794 households in Grenada in response to Hurricane Beryl, highlighting the role of adaptive social protection systems in crisis management.
 
In Trinidad and Tobago, the TEEN programme expanded, offering cash support to 279 households to help children access online education. UNICEF's collaboration with the British Red Cross in the UK Overseas Territories institutionalized shock-responsive social protection, combining cash support with psychosocial services. UNICEF ECA’s Public Finance for Children (PF4C) initiatives emphasized budget analysis and fiscal space assessments in Antigua and Barbados, the British Virgin Islands, Dominica, and Trinidad and Tobago. The agency also advocated climate-sensitive social protection, linking climate adaptation with social policies. A workshop co-hosted with the Food and Agriculture Organization in May explored integrating social protection into Nationally Determined Contributions, fostering resilient systems to protect children against climate and economic shocks.

These comprehensive efforts by UNICEF ECA in 2024 underscore its commitment to enhancing the well-being of children and families in the Eastern Caribbean through innovative and sustainable social protection measures. 

Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) 
 
UNICEF ECA began sensitizing partners on the relatively new concept of AAP and how to integrate its principles into development and emergency programming. The three AAP principles of focus were: establishment of complaints and feedback mechanisms (CFMs) participation by key stakeholders, especially in the design and monitoring of interventions; and information and communication to ensure that participants receive pertinent information through culturally relevant, age-appropriate channels. The knowledge and skills of approximately 40 stakeholders from key WASH and environment sectors in Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago on integrating AAP principles into their programmes were enhanced. Complaints and feedback mechanisms were successfully implemented by partners in the social protection sector in relation to cash transfers for migrants in Trinidad and Tobago, as well as for people affected by Hurricane Beryl in Grenada. UNICEF supported partners in obtaining input and feedback from the target groups in the development and design of programmes. This was done by the ECD sector in Grenada, the education sector in Antigua and Barbuda and by child protection partners in Dominica and Grenada.
 
Finally, the integration of AAP principles into new donor proposals as a result of UNICEF’s advocacy was another achievement. Partners from the ministries of health in Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines included CFMs in their new 2025 donor proposals to GAVI, the vaccine alliance. AAP was also integrated into proposals to receive funding for the Hurricane Beryl response and partners were supported to integrate CFM into their existing mechanisms.

Child and Youth Participation
 
UNICEF provided several platforms and capacity-building engagements for children and young people to amplify their voices and to meaningfully participate in, and influence, policy at all levels. The signature event was the Global Child and Youth Action   Summit, a precursor to the 4th International Small Island Developing States Conference (SIDS4) in Antigua and Barbuda, which successfully convened over 90 delegates, aged 15-29, from the three SIDS regions across the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the Atlantic, Indian Ocean and South China Sea. Key outcomes included the integration of child- and youth-led solutions into the official SIDS4 Outcome Document and the establishment of the Alliance of Small Island States Youth Council.
 
The Summit generated a Youth Commitment to Action outlining priorities for safe societies, resilient economies, sustainable futures, and environmental integrity over the next decade. The creation of a SIDS Centre of Excellence in Antigua and Barbuda is flagged to oversee and advance these commitments, ensuring ongoing youth participation and advocacy. 
 
Building on 2023’s youth advocacy training, continued capacity building and opportunities were offered through the Let’s Unpack It and UNICEF Caribbean Mental Health Focal Point Network. Additionally, a 17-year-old graduate from Saint Vincent and the Grenadines was facilitated to address the UNICEF Board on the personal and societal impact of climate change.  The observation of the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) was also employed as a key moment to engage children and youth to advocate the realization of their rights through a series of events where 1,100 children in Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Lucia, and Trinidad and Tobago were empowered to speak out. Additionally, 100 children in Barbados urged rights holders to commit to a ‘Wall of Promises’, while another 80 were facilitated to engage seven members of the Cabinet in a children’s rights dialogue. Some 120 children also engaged in an interactive exploration of their rights at the 19th Annual Child Research Conference and 116 were involved in written submissions on progress - or otherwise - in the 35 years of the Convention.    

Further growth was achieved in the Child Rights Ambassador programme, which was extended to Antigua and Barbuda, where 25 ambassadors were trained, and to Barbados where the programme was launched as part of CRC35 activities. Additionally, UNICEF ECA supported growth in the Trinidad and Tobago programme which caters to over 300 children. 
 
The U-Report platform, which crossed the 20,000 barriers in the reporting year, continued to be a key facet of the Office’s youth engagement portfolio, providing opportunities for over 10,000 youth to share their opinions, while 5,324 young people used the FunDoo skills development platform to complete modules on topics ranging from preparing for the job market to climate action.

Child Rights Mmonitoring
 
The status of the Convention on the Rights of the Child highlights both progress and challenges. While all countries have ratified the Convention, reporting remains inconsistent, with Dominica, for example, not having reported since 2004. The ratification of the optional protocols relating to children in armed conflict and child prostitution and pornography varies greatly across the region.  
  
Significant efforts have been made to address these gaps. Under the leadership of the Resident Coordinator’s Multi-Country Office, a confidential report on the CRC situation in Saint Kitts and Nevis was produced and shared with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, offering valuable insights. Additionally, in Dominica, targeted contributions to the Universal Periodic Review of Human Rights included specific recommendations on children's rights. 
  
UNICEF ECA has continued advocacy for child rights through supporting the Government of Barbados in its Child Protection Bill (that became an Act in 2024) for which UNICEF received notable praise from leaders.   


Response to Hurricane Beryl
 
UNICEF ECA has been instrumental in providing humanitarian and recovery support to children and families affected by Hurricane Beryl in Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Collaborating with partners, the agency swiftly helped improve access to clean water for the most affected islands and co-led weekly WASH coordination meetings. Over 1,400 hygiene and dignity kits, along with collapsible water containers, were distributed, benefiting 4,524 people. Additionally, a partnership with Water Mission and collaboration with the Central Water Authority, Ministry of Health, and Ministry of Education ensured that 2,000 people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines - including 1,000 children - now have access to safe drinking water. Two 4,000-litre water storage tanks were installed, providing reliable decentralized access points. With UNICEF’s support, the ministries of health in both countries developed messages promoting good hygiene practices which reached approximately 1,000 people in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, including children, and around 6,000 people in Grenada through loudspeaker broadcasts, due to the absence of media outlets. 
 
Stakeholders received vital training in psychological first aid, child-friendly spaces, gender-based violence risk mitigation, and the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse. The Return to Happiness MHPSS programme was also implemented with psychological first aid, resulting in support for 1,906 children and the distribution of 800 child mental health workbooks and 1,000 MHPSS service directories.
 
UNICEF ECA conducted consultations with the ministries of education in both countries and co-chaired an emergency group to develop an integrated education response plan. Materials to support the resumption of educational activities, including recreational kits, ECD kits, and high-performance tents (to facilitate the Return to Happiness programme) were supplied. 

In Grenada, UNICEF supported the provision of multipurpose cash for the most vulnerable households through the expansion of the Support for Education, Empowerment, and Development (SEED) programme. A total of 794 households (2,779 persons) received a payment of XCD330.00 (US$122.22) to aid in their recovery. Messaging for parents on the prevention of child abuse and safe relocation of children after an emergency was disseminated. Approximately 480 parents were reached through face-to-face sessions, and, again, around 6,000 were reached via loudspeaker.

UNICEF works through partnerships with governments, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and the private sector to advance children's rights and well-being globally. By collaborating with local and international partners, UNICEF amplifies its impact through partnerships enabling UNICEF to leverage expertise, resources, and networks, ensuring that interventions are contextually relevant, scalable, and sustainable. 
 
Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency 

Significant progress was made in enhancing disaster preparedness and response across the Caribbean, with a strong focus on child-centred interventions. Emphasis was placed on the education system having a more resilient learning environment through the implementation of the UNICEF- and CDEMA-supported Caribbean Safe School Recognition Programme in Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Dominica, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, ensuring that schools are better equipped to handle emergencies. 

Anguilla has increased its capacity to adapt and implement sustainable shock-responsive social protection systems by conducting a simulation exercise in the country involving key national counterparts. Advancement was made to strengthening institutions to prevent and effectively respond to violence, abuse, and exploitation and provide psychosocial support to children through the integration of child protection in deployment teams based on hazard response, aimed at coordinating services during disasters. In response to strengthening communication and advocacy strategies, a concept note was produced to guide the implementation of child-led development of disaster preparedness messages, within the framework of the CSSI. These initiatives collectively contribute to a more resilient and prepared region, prioritizing the safety and well-being of children and adolescents. Additionally, there was an integration of child protection concerns into CDEMA training and preparation of deployment teams, including Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse.

Hurricane Beryl resulted in the activation of the thematic working groups of the Education Emergency Group in Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. UNICEF ECA and CDEMA coordinated more than 25 development partners, NGOs, civil society organizations, and international financial institutions to provide support in MPHSS, education recovery, school supplies, and technical assistance in the reopening of schools. A Caribbean Psychosocial Support Interagency Consortium was also established to guide MHPSS support during emergencies and disasters.

The agency signed a regional MOU with CDEMA at the 13th Comprehensive Disaster Management Conference in Saint Kitts and Nevis in December. This partnership will focus on collaborating to promote synergies and coordination to reinforce shock-responsiveness for enhanced child-centred disaster risk management. 
 
Organization of Eastern Caribbean States 

UNICEF ECA worked with the OECS Commission to advance the youth engagement agenda in the subregion through the expansion of U-Report which registered 6,500 sign-ups and the skills-building platform, FunDoo, which provided a space for 4,320 young people from the nine member states to complete their chosen modules. 
 
The agency advocated the adoption of the Commitment of Action for Transforming Education and for Foundational Learning. These were unanimously adopted with countries actively developing work plans for 2025 implementation. This is a first for UNICEF ECA, with country and intergovernmental adoption of a global declaration focused on addressing inequalities in education for some of the most vulnerable populations. UNICEF’s efforts to secure the adoption of the Commitment of Action for Transforming Education and Foundational Learning mark a significant step in ensuring equitable access to quality education. This initiative directly benefits children by prioritizing foundational literacy and numeracy skills, which are essential for lifelong learning, skills development and personal growth. By addressing inequalities in education, the framework enables vulnerable populations, including children with disabilities, Indigenous groups and those in marginalized communities, to overcome systemic barriers. With active work plans underway for 2025 implementation, the initiative fosters inclusive policies and practices, empowering children to reach their full potential and contributing to the broader goal of sustainable human development.

Caribbean Community 
 
UNICEF ECA leveraged CARICOM’s Council for Human and Social Development (Education) for advocacy around a regional all-of-education workstream to prevent violence against women and children. Ministers of education universally adopted the programme with the adaptation that special consideration for boys should be a focus. The council acknowledged the work of UNICEF ECA in supporting marginalized groups across the region. 
 
The Education Council also endorsed the Transforming Education Task Team to provide regional coordination and technical assistance to support countries in ensuring all students have equitable access to education. This will see UNICEF ECA implement a Business Model Initiative approach to a Caribbean-wide intervention in 19 countries, bringing support to approximately nine million children across varying jurisdictions with priority given to teaching, quality education, special education services, and systems transformation to include digitalization of education. 
 
This approach enables UNICEF ECA to make impactful, large-scale interventions across the Caribbean, addressing the diverse educational needs of approximately nine million children. By prioritizing equitable access, quality education, and digital transformation, the initiative creates a cohesive framework that empowers children, especially those in marginalized and underserved communities, to thrive academically and socially across 19 countries.

UN-to-UN Collaboration
 
In 2024, a core group of UN bodies, including the Office of the Resident Coordinator, the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), UNICEF, and the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), initiated a collaborative effort to develop a comprehensive cooperation framework. This initiative, which began in the second quarter of 2024, aimed to enhance data sharing and integration across agencies, identify and address data gaps, and explore opportunities for joint capacity-building initiatives in statistical and other government departments. UNICEF played a pivotal role in this collaboration, contributing significantly to a concept note on a UN Committee of Practice, Data. This concept note has been endorsed by several UN Agencies serving Barbados and the Eastern Caribbean.
 
UNICEF also spearheaded the implementation of the SDG Resilient Caribbean Joint Programme in partnership with the World Food Programme, the International Labour Organization and UNESCO. Concluded in June 2024, it achieved substantial progress in institutionalization, digitalization, capacity building and programme design. A lesson learned document highlighted that the structures established during the intervention were effectively utilized in subsequent projects and programmes.

ECLAC and UNICEF entered into a UN-to-UN agreement to provide essential WASH goods and services in response to Hurricane Beryl in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with the UN Development Programme to produce the WASH sector report for post-disaster needs assessments in Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. UNICEF and UNFPA also signed a UN-to-UN agreement to facilitate youth participation in the Global Children and Youth Action Summit, enabling 90 participants from all SIDS regions to influence the outcomes of the 4th Small Islands Developing States Conference. ECA was successful in two further joint programmes for 2025 applications: Localization of the Caribbean Safe School Initiative and Energy Transition of Education Systems.

UNICEF co-led the United Nations Emergency Technical Team, providing technical coordination of UN agencies to facilitate thematic working group plan enhancement. In the aftermath of Hurricane Beryl, UNICEF played a pivotal role in coordinating the efforts of the UN agencies ensuring an effective response in support of the Regional Response Mechanism.  This included effective and timely coordination with CDEMA relating to the deployment of teams and supplies.  This coordinated response not only maximized the impact of humanitarian aid but also reinforced the importance of a unified approach in addressing the complex challenges faced by affected communities.

Migrant Response 
 
In February 2024, Trinidad and Tobago amended its Immigration Act granting Venezuelans registered under the Migrant Registration Framework access to primary and secondary education. To date, the school registration exercise that commenced in June 2024, placed 60 of at least 111 accepted applicants across 22 public schools (20 primary and two secondary). However, this facility is only accessible to an estimated 2,400 registered Venezuelan children. A further 4,500 not registered under the MRF cannot yet access education. UNICEF ECA continued to address this gap by assisting close to 1,800 children across 18 child-friendly schools - which offer informal education, protection and support - and online programmes run by eight community-based organisations. UNICEF continues to collaborate with key stakeholders to address the migrant response through participation in multiple working groups on education, child protection and social protection. A key UN-to-UN partnership between UNICEF and UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, was renewed to support access to online, accredited secondary education for Spanish-speaking children on the move in Trinidad and Tobago via the DAWERE programme. Since 2021, 140 children have graduated with secondary school diplomas (27 in 2024). As of July 2024, up to 525 children were registered.   

South-South Cooperation 
 
In July 2024, UNICEF ECA collaborated with UNICEF’s Latin America and Caribbean Office, UNICEF Headquarters and the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore - with support from the Sagicor Cave Hill School of Business and Management at the UWI - and hosted a wide-ranging two-week leadership-building event for public sector chiefs: the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders (ExCEL).

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
 
In 2024, UNICEF ECA faced multiple challenges that highlighted the complexities of working in high- and upper-middle-income countries with diverse socio-economic and climatic vulnerabilities. A significant challenge was the limited availability of sustainable funding. Many donor partners perceive such countries as less in need of development assistance, leading to reduced financial commitments. This reliance on short-term funding constrained UNICEF’s ability to scale up interventions and address emerging needs, particularly in disaster preparedness and social protection.
 
The increased frequency and intensity of climate events further stressed already stretched resources. Hurricane Beryl underscored gaps in integrated multi-sectoral preparedness and response strategies within national systems. As climate resilience becomes a growing priority, the need for enhanced financing mechanisms to support multi-country emergency preparedness and responses remains critical.
 
Commitments by the Government of Trinidad and Tobago to integrate migrant children into the national education system have not been fully realized. Persistent barriers, including insufficient resources and administrative challenges, have delayed progress. Advocacy and partnerships remain essential to bridge educational gaps for migrant children and youth.
 
Cultural norms and social attitudes continue to challenge efforts to eliminate violence against children. Despite advocacy for positive parenting practices, corporal punishment remains a widely accepted form of discipline especially in the homes. Time constraints faced by caregivers for training, limited participation in behaviour change initiatives and lack of confidence to implement some of the positive behaviour management strategies learned remain challenges. This highlights the need for sustained community engagement including support for parents and caregivers as they implement new behaviours. 

Fragmented data systems and disconnected service delivery mechanisms have slowed progress in child protection programming. While Trinidad and Tobago has a fully functional child protection information management system (Primero/CPIMS+), the system is not yet available in the other 11 countries in the subregion. Efforts are underway to support its implementation in three additional countries, but broader investment is needed to scale up and integrate digital case management solutions across the region. 

Strengthening data governance, interoperability, and capacity for case management will be essential to improving coordination, service delivery, and accountability in child protection A lack of child-disaggregated and climate-focused data has hindered evidence-based decision-making, while tracking children receiving services remains a persistent issue.
 
Cross-sectoral collaboration is still a critical challenge, particularly in aligning child protection, social protection, and education sector efforts. While digital tools like Power BI and the Field Monitoring Module hold promise, integrating these systems across operations and ensuring staff are adequately trained requires continuous investment. Moreover, maintaining emergency preparedness in a multi-country context is resource-intensive and demands coordinated planning and funding.

Lessons Learned

Despite these challenges, 2024 provided critical lessons to enhance future programming:
    
1.Strategic Engagement with Policymakers: Targeted engagement with policymakers is vital for achieving significant policy and legislative changes. Identifying ministry champions and leveraging cross-sectoral committees appointed by cabinets have proven effective in securing buy-in and fostering cross-departmental collaboration. For example, progress in social protection readiness assessments highlighted the importance of aligning efforts with national priorities to strengthen disaster response systems.
 
2.Proactive Emergency Preparedness: The use of the Emergency Preparedness Platform and Immediate Response Team meetings demonstrated the value of early planning and cross-sectoral collaboration in mitigating disaster impacts. Investments in shock-responsive social protection readiness assessments identified implementation gaps and scalable solutions, improving disaster response mechanisms.
 
3.Optimizing Regional Partnerships: Regional partnerships with bodies such as CDEMA, CARICOM, and the OECS proved instrumental in advancing shared agendas, particularly in transformative education and disaster resilience. These partnerships present an opportunity to establish best practices that can be scaled across the Caribbean through UNICEF’s new Business Model Initiative.

4.Leveraging Digital Innovation: The initial success of digital tools like Power BI and the Field Monitoring Module highlighted their potential to enhance transparency, efficiency, and real-time monitoring. However, these tools require continuous refinement and staff training to maximize their impact.
 
5.Integrated Programming: Mid-term and mid-year reviews underscored the importance of integrated programming to reduce siloed approaches. Cross-sectoral initiatives, such as linking climate resilience to child protection and education, amplify impact and ensure that programmes address interconnected vulnerabilities holistically.
 
6.Adapting Advocacy Strategies for High- and Middle-Income Contexts: Working in high-income and middle-income countries requires adapting advocacy strategies to address unique socio-economic contexts. Emphasizing the economic and social costs of inaction, particularly in areas such as climate resilience and violence prevention, can strengthen the case for sustained investments in children’s well-being.

7.Addressing Violence Against Children: The persistence of violence against children in the region underscores the urgent need for comprehensive child protection system strengthening to prevent and respond effectively.  Challenges such as limited resources, weak enforcement of policies, and deeply rooted social norms hinder progress. Stronger evidence-based advocacy, system strengthening, integrated programming and sustained community engagement are essential. Public awareness campaigns must be paired with systemic reforms to address these barriers, enhance service delivery and expand protective services. Partnerships with regional bodies and civil society organizations are essential to scale efforts, ensuring sustained behaviour change, and reinforcing accountability within child protection systems.
 
These lessons highlight the need for adaptive, innovative, and collaborative approaches to overcome challenges and maximize the impact of UNICEF’s work in the Eastern Caribbean.

Future Outlook 
 
From 2025 to 2026, the UNICEF ECA inclusive education section will focus on transforming education systems to ensure inclusive, equitable, and high-quality learning for all children. This will involve a comprehensive approach that includes foundational learning, systems transformation, and the Caribbean Safe School Initiative. Emphasizing the development of skills and competencies, we will consolidate and expand digital transformation through initiatives like GIGA, the Ed Tech Policy, and a digital curriculum. We will also work towards the institutionalization of integrated ECD programmes, with a focus on prevention, protection, and developmental initiatives, including literacy and numeracy, early identification and intervention, responsive parenting, and creating child-friendly environments. Special attention will be given to vulnerable and marginalized children, including those on the move, those with disabilities, or those affected by dropout, alternative education needs, or emergencies. Through continued data generation, research, and the implementation of a pilot integrated ECD strategy, we aim to enhance education outcomes and build on lessons learned post-COVID, ensuring that every child has the opportunity to thrive in a supportive and inclusive educational environment. Similarly, the Social Policy Social Protection section will continue to focus on integrated systems, especially to mitigate and respond to risks as well as to increase resilience. In addition, the section will concentrate on mainstreaming gender in its activities to ensure social protection leads to transformational outcomes as well as embedding public finance analysis and advocacy in all work completed, so programming can be effective and sustainable.
 
Advancing policy initiatives for effective governance, coordination, implementation, and monitoring of inclusive and equitable ECD programmes will be a key focus. Promoting integration across sectors, fostering safe environments, and ensuring holistic development within homes and communities will be prioritized. Sustainable, long-term financial commitments are essential to ensure ongoing impact, and programming must be more flexible and resilient in the face of evolving crises.

Expanding the use of digital tools will be prioritized, with further integration and training to maximize their impact on operational efficiency and transparency. Sustaining preparedness for emergencies will also be crucial, with ongoing investment to maintain readiness and improve response strategies for future emergencies. Leveraging digital tools like RapidPro and U-Report for climate polls and youth engagement will continue, along with investing in improved data collection systems and fostering collaborative efforts with governments and partners. Establishing robust, country-level WASH coordination groups will ensure swift, harmonized emergency responses. Addressing data gaps will ensure that future interventions are more targeted, inclusive, and effective in meeting the needs of children and communities.

Belize’s GDP continues its strong trajectory, with a growth rate of 8.7% in 2022 and 4.7% in 2023 (IMF). Key sectors accelerating this growth include tourism, construction, retail, wholesale trade, transport, and business process outsourcing. The public debt ratio improved from 103% of GDP in 2020 to 66.2% in 2023, driven by strong GDP growth, better fiscal balance, and innovative debt conversion like the “Blue Loan/Bond” and restructuring the Petrocaribe debts. 
Despite the important growth, inequities remain. The Labour Force Survey (2024) reported unemployment of 3,447 persons, with females experiencing a higher unemployment rate (3.1%) compared to males (1.4%). 
Reducing poverty remains a national priority for Belize. According to the latest monetary poverty statistics, 52% of total population and 60% of children aged 0-14 years live in poor households (2018/2019). The government has been estimating the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) since 2021, which showed some drop in the incidence from 35.7 % in 2021 to 22.1% in 2024. In 2024, rural areas experienced significantly higher levels of poverty at 30.9% compared to 9.7% in urban regions. Children are consistently overrepresented in multidimensional poverty at 43.2% in 2021, 33.7% in 2023 and 30.5% in 2024. 
Despite high levels of poverty and deprivation, social protection coverage and spending are low. Only 32% of Belizeans benefit from at least one social protection program (compared to 62.1% average for the Latin America and Caribbean region) with just 2% relying on public (social assistance) benefits compared to 24.4% regional average, highlighting inequities and financial burdens on individuals. The coverage for women is lower than that of men. Only 24% of women are covered by at least one social protection benefit, compared to 37% of men. 
Belize allocates an average of 1% of GDP to social protection, far below the regional average of 4.8%, and the ILO benchmark of 3.8%. This allocation falls below the lowest cost for social protection spending floor in Belize (2.21% of GDP) leaving the country’s most vulnerable groups prone to shocks without full access to basic services.
In 2024, Belize initiated the development of an Integrated National Financing Framework to strengthen the national framework for financing Belize Medium-term Development Strategy, Nationally Determined Contributions, and social protection strategy by unlocking investment in these agendas. This is anchored on Belize's high susceptibility to climate events. 
In 2022, Belize ranked 120th on the ND-GAIN Vulnerability Index. In 2024, “El Niño” triggered record-breaking temperatures in May, leading to wildfires that disrupted agriculture, and education in 28 communities posing health risks to children. In November, the heavy rainfall from Tropical Storm Sara resulted in unprecedented levels of floods in the Cayo and Belize Districts. Although 40% of schools serve as hurricane shelters, most lack resilient infrastructure. 
The 2022 Belize Digital Government Act has facilitated national digital transformation and the partnership with GIGA aims to increase the number of public schools with internet access (currently 40%) to improve educational outcomes for children. 
According to the World Bank Public Expenditure Review 2024, Belize allocates 18.9% of public expenditures to education, one of the highest levels in the region. However, the quality of education is decreasing potentially caused by the proliferation of private religious education and the role of teacher unions.  The education system faces efficiency issues, including high dropout rates and grade repetition, as well as an increasing trend in the percentage of students performing inadequately in core subjects. 
Primary school completion rate improved from 93.4% in 2017 to 96.1% in 2022. The government has invested in increasing secondary completion rates from 60.4% through implementation of Education Upliftment Programme. 
Belize has made strides in healthcare, with a life expectancy of 74.9 years (PAHO/WHO, 2021) which is above the Global life expectancy of 73.3 years. Additionally, access to primary and preventative services through the National Health Insurance Scheme along with the removal of user fees in primary and secondary health facilities, have also enhanced access. Significant interventions are being implemented to improve the under-5 mortality rate of 19 per 1,000 live births and the immunization rate for children under one, which is at 85%. Mental health and NCDs among adolescents are a growing concern. 
UNICEF’s advocacy and action led to amendment of Marriage Act, increasing the age of marriage to 18, and abolishing parental consent at age 14. A barrier remains as it still allows for parental or judicial consent for children 16 and 17 years. However, family violence remains a concern, with 65% of crimes against children being sexual in nature.
The country's position as a transit country for irregular migrants adds strain to its child protection services. Between 40,000 and 60,000 migrants face integration barriers, and migrant children are often detained without adequate care. A comprehensive migration policy is needed to support migrant families and protect children from trafficking and exploitation. Belize has made significant strides toward inclusion, aiming to combat discrimination and advance social cohesion. 
Access to essential services such as safe drinking water remain uneven. While 96% of people in Belize have access to safe water, rural regions lag behind. Approximately 20 rural villages lack basic water systems, and only 58.3% of schools have drinking water facilities. Expanding WASH services in underserved regions remains crucial. 
In 2024, Belize conducted a VNR on its progress toward the 17 SDGs. The report reveals that data is fully collected for 47% of the indicators and 26% were partially available. It also showed that Goals 6,7 and 12 are on track and Goals 1,2 and 10 are well behind achieving the targets. The UN/KIOCA $3.46 million project is expected to close this gap. 
Partnerships and capacity-building remain priorities for Belize to achieve SDGs. The government established International Cooperation Council to optimize foreign aid and align international partnerships with national goals, participated in World Trade Organization’s Trade Facilitation Agreement to improve border efficiency and signed the Millennium Challenge Cooperation Compact for $125 million to address constraints related to low-quality education and high electricity costs.
Politically, Belize’s landscape remains stable. The People’s United Party secured a victory in the March 2024 municipal elections, suggesting strong public support for the current administration. General elections are expected to be held during the first half of 2025.

The year 2024, marking the mid-term of the 2022-2026 Country Programme, was pivotal for UNICEF Belize. Reaching the mid-point with a sharpened focus and strategic shifts to accelerate results for children, the Strategic Moment of Reflection and Mid-Term Review identified opportunities and best practices for scale up, bottlenecks for adjustments, and intentional investment in efficient and effective programme implementation. Collaborative efforts with national and international stakeholders, UNICEF Regional Office and adolescents informed transformative changes in child protection, education, health, and social protection. These achievements underscore the organization’s commitment to upholding children's rights, aligning with national priorities, and advancing the SDGs. Through strategic advocacy, capacity building, and evidence-based interventions, UNICEF addressed immediate challenges and laid the groundwork for sustainable, long-term solutions. 
Belize made significant strides in strengthening its child protection system. The landmark legislative action to revise the Marriage Act, raising the legal age of marriage to 18, has safeguarded over 80,000 adolescents from the detrimental effects of early marriage, thanks to the impactful "I am a Child, not a Bride" campaign. UNICEF added its strong advocacy voice in championing this legislative reform, supporting national consultations and providing technical assistance to National Commission for Families and Children. This initiative addressed the structural barrier of early marriage, protected girls' rights, and challenged traditional gender norms, supporting their long-term development. Going forward, strong advocacy, along with SBC initiatives are needed to ensure that parental and judicial consent for 16 and 17-year-olds is abolished. This milestone reflects Belize’s adherence to the commitments outlined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and demonstrates the effectiveness of child-centered advocacy in shaping national policy. 
 Furthermore, Belize’s acceded to two Hague Conventions related to rights of children as UNICEF commemorates the 35th Anniversary of CRC, namely on Child Protection and on Child Support. By acceding to these conventions, Belize enhances the protection of children, and also further demonstrates the government's strong commitment to social protection, non-discrimination, equity and equality amongst all individuals. These ratifications are attributable to UNICEF’s advocacy efforts and direct support to the Government of Belize (GOB) to participate at the October 2023 Eighth Meeting of the Special Commission of the Hague Conference on Private International Law on the practical operation of the 1980 Child Abduction and 1996 Child Protection Convention. 
In alignment with the National Children’s Agenda, the Belize Child Protection System Management Response, the UNCRC, the UNICEF Child Protection System Strengthening Framework, and the INSPIRE Seven Strategies for Ending Violence Against Children, Belize has pledged to improve national response and support services through legislative and policy reforms, including banning corporal punishment in all settings. Complementing these gender-transformative legislative efforts, UNICEF facilitated capacity building for social services personnel, equipping them to identify, prevent, and address child rights violations. Over 60,000 children benefited from enhanced mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) provided through community initiatives, ensuring that vulnerable children, including those affected by migration and those in conflict with the law, receive comprehensive care and support, as well as parenting for nurturing care. The revision of the hazardous work list within the Child Labour Act and the introduction of the Families Bill 2024 consolidated family-related legislation, offering more comprehensive protection for children. 
The Roving Caregiver’s Programme (RCP) was expanded and now reaches more homes in vulnerable communities in Corozal, Cayo, Belize and Toledo, and offers informal learning programmes for young children, aged 3–4 years old. National technical capacities were significantly increased, training 642 practitioners and benefiting over 7,000 children, adolescents, and caregivers. 1000 children, adolescents, mothers, fathers, and caregivers were engaged through targeted parenting and MHPSS interventions in and out of school and in residential care facilities. Through the multisectoral parenting interventions, 3,505 children and adolescents received Care for Child Development (CCD) counseling and early stimulation activities, including children with disabilities and migrant children. Additionally, 419 families, including 1,257 boys and girls were also impacted through court-mandated parenting workshops, and parenting sessions conducted by key UNICEF partners at primary and secondary schools.
UNICEF supported the establishment of innovative platforms such as the National Child Justice League, which provided opportunities for intergenerational dialogue and policy reform. Adolescents actively participated in mock trials and consultations, fostering their understanding of the justice system and amplifying their voices in legal reform. Notably, three boys were relocated from detention facilities to residential care, an intervention that underscores UNICEF’s commitment to creating safe, nurturing environments for children in conflict with the law. Furthermore, UNICEF’s advocacy ensured that child-friendly spaces were prioritized in judicial processes, reinforcing the principle of justice without barriers. 
Belize’s participation in the First Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children and the operationalization of the Women’s Parliamentary Caucus’s two-year strategic plan underscored UNICEF’s commitment to global and regional priorities. The Women’s Parliamentary Caucus hosted a landmark regional forum focused on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), bringing together over 90 political leaders and key stakeholders. This event highlighted Belize’s role in accelerating gender equality and women’s empowerment across the Caribbean, advancing inclusive governance and reinforcing the importance of women’s leadership in political spaces. 
The protection agenda also extended to migrant children, as UNICEF collaborated with local and international partners to strengthen in-transit shelters and provide psychosocial support and case management services 36 migrant children (22 males, 14 females). Birth registration campaigns in rural communities ensured that over 1,000 undocumented children gained legal identity, granting them access to essential services and protections. Another key intervention was supporting the Family Support and Gender Affairs Department in strengthening its gender-transformative approach. 
In education, UNICEF played a central role in advancing inclusive and equitable learning opportunities for children and adolescents through technical support in curriculum development and capacity building. The implementation of Belize’s competency-based curriculum across all primary and secondary schools represented a significant step toward transforming the national education system. The curriculum, aligned with international standards, emphasizes foundational literacy, numeracy, critical thinking, and digital skills, equipping students with the competencies necessary for the 21st century. This reform was supported by intensive teacher training programs, with 95 percent of teachers receiving capacity-building sessions on innovative pedagogies and assessment methodologies. 
Digital transformation was a key focus in 2024. UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology (MOECST) to establish USpaces in underserved districts, providing children with access to digital learning resources, peer support, and safe environments for creative engagement. These safe spaces for children (U Space) have been established as a key approach to reaching and providing them with key information, links to services, peer connection, and support. This significant step was taken by the government to advance digital connectivity in schools and communities, as the code.org curriculum is currently being implemented in 62 primary schools countrywide. The Girls in ICT initiative empowered over 110 girls, including out-of-school youth, with technology skills, challenging gender norms and fostering equitable access to digital education. Additionally, foundational literacy and numeracy programs in migrant communities reached thousands of children, addressing learning gaps exacerbated by displacement and socio-economic challenges. 
UNICEF’s social and behavior change campaign, MoRE, engaged over 14,500 students across primary and secondary schools. This dynamic gender-transformative initiative inspired students, teachers, and parents to strive for holistic excellence in academics, health, innovation, and environmental stewardship. Schools demonstrating exemplary progress were recognized, creating a culture of continuous improvement, and fostering leadership among educators and students alike. 
The education sector also saw the establishment of the Belize Education Alliance (BEA), formed with the support of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and a coalition of civil society organizations dedicated to strengthening strategic planning and policy implementation. Through dialogues and consultations, BEA contributed to advancing foundational learning, regional education priorities, and transformative agenda items such as digital inclusivity and gender equality. UNICEF, as the grant agent for a $1.6 million System Capacity Grant, spearheaded efforts to build resilient education systems and secure additional investments for early childhood development and quality learning. 
In health and nutrition, guided by UNICEF’s 2030 Conceptual Framework for Maternal and Child Nutrition, BCO’s contributions were instrumental in enhancing maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health outcomes. The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) and the revised national breastfeeding policy aimed to increase exclusive breastfeeding rates from 33 percent to 50 percent, recognizing breastfeeding as a cornerstone of child survival and development. UNICEF introduced Kangaroo Mother Care practices to improve neonatal care, particularly for premature infants, training health workers and providing essential equipment to hospitals nationwide. This initiative significantly reduced neonatal morbidity and mortality, reflecting UNICEF’s commitment to reducing preventable child deaths. 
UNICEF also enhanced community-based health and nutrition services, impacting over 50,000 women and children in rural areas. Community health workers were trained to deliver high-quality counseling on infant and young child feeding, while malnutrition screening and treatment protocols were strengthened. Innovative tools such as the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape were piloted to identify infants at risk of poor growth, demonstrating the effectiveness of timely interventions in improving nutritional outcomes. 
Recognizing the importance of adolescent development, UNICEF developed an Adolescent Development and Participation (ADAP) strategy. The strategy incorporates innovative and multisectoral interventions to ensure all children and adolescents are empowered to achieve their full potential. The "Healthy Habits, Healthy Schools, Healthy Belize" campaign, aligned with the national mandate banning sugary beverages in schools, reached over 7,500 adolescents through school campaigns and health fairs. Partnerships with influencers, including Miss Universe Belize, amplified messages on mental health, nutrition, and adolescent empowerment, reaching thousands of young people through innovative campaigns. 
Actions to address the growing mental health challenges among adolescents centered on increasing mental health support nationwide. UNICEF trained 27 participants from government institutions, civil society organizations, and NGOs on the "Helping Adolescents Thrive" (HAT) guide. This training is expected to reach an estimated 50,000 adolescents, providing tools to manage stress, improve emotional regulation, and foster peer support. Youth engagement in climate change integrated the voices of 200 adolescents and young people in the development of Belize’s Multi-Sectoral National Adaptation Plan and CDM Country Work Programme. 
In 2024, Belize achieved a historic milestone with the development of its first National Social Protection Policy and Strategy (2025–2035). This comprehensive framework addresses life-cycle vulnerabilities through initiatives such as universal child grants, maternity benefits, and disability allowances and aims to ensure that everyone has access to minimum social protection and income security across their lifecycle. The strategy will be implemented across 10 years with gradual expansion of proposed and existing social protection programmes reaching increased coverage of social protection. The policy and strategy were both developed through a participatory process, involving all Government of Belize ministries and agencies that have a role in the design and delivery of social protection interventions, as well as development partners, workers and employers’ associations, and civil society organizations.  
In line with the national priorities of the social protection systems strengthening, efforts were made to make the system responsive to shocks. UNICEF provided technical support in updating the manual of the government’s flagship social assistance programme - Building Opportunities for Our Social Transformation (BOOST) programme to make it responsive to shocks.  Additionally, as part of the digitalization strategy of the Ministry of Human Development, Families & Indigenous Peoples’ Affairs (MHDFIPA), UNICEF has initiated the development of a Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) to enhance the transparency, accountability, and responsiveness of the services provided by the ministry. This will also strengthen the continuity of services during shocks and disasters and improve service delivery during challenges posed by disasters and other emergencies particularly for the most vulnerable groups, including children, the elderly, and marginalized communities by providing an accessible and efficient platform for lodging complaints and seeking redress. Recognizing the need for increased funding for shock-responsive social protection (SRSP), an analysis of social protection budgets and expenditures has been supported by UNICEF generating evidence for the government to explore and advocate for opportunities for increased investment in SRSP. 
UNICEF’s advocacy extended to disaster resilience through a signed MoU with NEMO to develop Belize’s first *National Comprehensive Disaster Management Policy* and National Disaster Preparedness and Response Plan. These frameworks incorporate child-sensitive approaches, addressing the unique vulnerabilities of children and families during emergencies. By integrating disaster risk management into the social protection strategy, the government aims to ensure social protection systems can effectively respond to emergencies and natural hazards, providing timely support to affected populations. 
The CO provided crucial evidence on out-of-pocket expenses that families incur to ensure their children can access health and education services. Additionally, it produced budget briefs for the health and education sectors, offering timely policy recommendations to strengthen public finance management, improve budget allocation efficiency, and enhance service delivery. These efforts are expected to significantly influence government decision-making. The study included a nationally representative face-to-face household survey of 797 households with children aged 0-17 years, providing detailed information on the levels and factors associated with OoPE for health and education services at both private and public facilities. The survey was conducted by Genesis Analytics, supported by the University of Belize, using a sampling frame provided by the Statistical Institute of Belize. The OoPE survey was complemented by key informant interviews with stakeholders from the Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW), MOECST, Ministry of Finance (MOF), and school officials to understand the policy landscape, government programs, major cost drivers for households, and district-level differences. A workshop in November 2024 validated the findings and recommendations of the OoPE analysis, providing a platform for key stakeholders to review the analysis, provide feedback, and discuss potential policy implications. 
Moreover, Belize has initiated the development of an Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) to strengthen the national framework for financing Belize’s Plan Belize Medium-term Development Strategy (MTDS), Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and social protection strategy. This forward-looking, integrated financing strategy aims to unlock investment in these agendas. Together with  UNDP, UNICEF has been active in this engagement by becoming part of its governance mechanisms, recognizing the opportunity to secure funding for the social protection strategy and engage in climate financing as a critical investment for children. Furthermore, UNICEF continued its advocacy for child-sensitive NDCs to strengthen child-critical social services to be more climate and disaster-resilient when the government is updating NDC with ambitious targets for emission reduction and contributing to enhanced engagement with children and young people in advocating for child-friendly climate action plans, budgets and financing strategies. 
BCO continued its investment in data systems in 2023. The implementation of MICS7 (Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey) provided an opportunity to build the capacity of the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) and MOECST by linking survey data with administrative data. This pioneering initiative, known as MICSLINK, aims to create a more integrated data system, fostering a responsive, evidence-driven education system that meets children’s needs. 
UNICEF supported expanding the Belize National Statistical System to include 231 unique SDG indicators and the 44 indicators from the Children’s Agenda 2030, improving monitoring efficiency. BCO also helped complete the Voluntary National Review, ensuring children's voices were represented.
UNICEF supported the Disability Taskforce and advocated for the passing of the Belize Disabilities Bill. Introduced in 2024, this bill marks a significant step towards ensuring the rights and equal opportunities for persons with disabilities in Belize. This comprehensive legislation aims to promote, protect, and ensure the full and equal enjoyment of privileges, interests, rights, benefits, and treatment for persons with disabilities, thereby creating a more inclusive and equitable society. The bill includes provisions for a, National Commission for Persons with Disabilities, Protection from Discrimination, Access to Education and Employment, Healthcare and Accessibility. As a follow up the Government has endorsed and initiated the conduct of a situation analysis of children with disabilities, the first in almost ten years.
In response to the United Nations Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review, UNICEF strengthened collaboration with CSOs by establishing a mechanism for continuous engagement. The first Development Forum was held in the third quarter of 2024 with 50 CSOs, with additional forums planned for each subsequent quarter. Furthermore, in collaboration with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in Belize, UNICEF produced the report “Towards Complete Compliance with the Convention on the Rights of the Child.” This report guided strategic shifts for BCO’s 2022–2026 Country Programme Document and assessed Belize’s performance on six regional themes: recognizing children as rights holders, strengthening institutional frameworks, advancing civil rights, ensuring accountability, removing discriminatory barriers, and addressing emerging issues such as climate change and mental health. 
UNICEF's technical expertise provided significant support to the annual capacity building and sensitization sessions with UN Implementing Partners on PSEA/SH. At the interagency level, our contributions have been reflected in the drafting of the Standard Operating Procedures for Victims Assistance Protocols, which have been submitted to the UNCT for review and approval. Internally, UNICEF-supported partners have prioritized PSEA as a critical operational and programmatic focus, driving continuous awareness and support within their target communities.
UNICEF Belize mobilized considerable resources for its programmes for the rest of the country programme. In addition to becoming the grant agent for the $1.6 million System Capacity Grant of GEP, the health programme received $500 thousand in Set Aside Funds for Community Health & Nutrition, $570 thousand from Phase 2 of the ACT-A funding from the Republic of Korea for maintaining and strengthening essential health services, and $250 thousand from Global CEED thematic funds for the Sustainability and Climate Action Plan. Additionally, the ECHO programme for strengthening shock-responsive social systems has been extended with additional funding.

UNICEF’s partnership with the GOB, under the leadership of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade (MFA), has significantly contributed to advancing the national priorities of the Medium-Term Development Plan 2022-2026. By jointly implementing workplans for 2024-2025 with 9 Ministries, several impactful results were achieved. The partnership with the MOECST resulted in a robust Digital Transformative Agenda, leveraging technology to transform and accelerate learning and skills development. Additionally, the formation of the Belize Education Alliance, supported by the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), marked a significant milestone. Thanks to these solid partnerships, UNICEF Belize was selected as the grant agent for the System Capacity Grant of $1.6M USD. 
In 2024, UNICEF partnered with the MFA to spearhead an inter-ministerial dialogue on the impact of CRC implementation in Belize, leading to the Government signing a call-to-action framework to accelerate child rights. The partnership with the Child Justice Steering Committee continued, aligning with the thematic focus of UNCRC@35 on enhancing access to justice for children. This included a collective call to action against the detention of children under discriminatory State of Emergencies, ensuring fair treatment for children in contact with the law. 
In collaboration with UN sister agencies, UNICEF played a significant role in strategic engagements with the government, such as the development of the National Voluntary Report, Integrated National Financing Framework, and Nationally Determined Contributions. Considerable progress was made in collaboration with UNDP to leverage opportunities for synergy and complementarity in programme implementation. Joint programmes on Just Energy Transition and strengthening the data ecosystem in Belize were launched. More specifically, UNICEF, in strategic partnership with the MFA and UN agencies led by UNDP, leveraged nearly $2.6M USD from KOICA to co-create the National Strategy for Statistics and develop the accompanying monitoring tool, the Belize National Statistical System. 
The development of the National Social Protection Policy and Strategy, leveraging partnerships with UN agencies and development partners, provided a framework for reducing poverty and deprivations, especially for marginalized children and populations. The coordination of the new social protection strategy will be overseen by the International Cooperation Council, chaired by the MFA, established in September 2023 to enhance inter-ministerial collaboration for development cooperation. In partnership with the PAHO, IDB, and Salud Mesoamerica, UNICEF supported the government in scaling up access to equitable quality community-based primary health care and building a more resilient health system to reduce neonatal mortality. 
The joint work plan with UNFPA, UNHCR, and IOM was renewed for a third year running to support migrant and refugee families, ensuring that migrant and refugee children and their families received necessary protection and services, aligning with international standards. Another important partnership with UNFPA and UN Women continued in providing technical engagement with the Women’s Parliamentary Caucus to strengthen their strategic positioning to address gender equality and commitments under the CEDAW. 
UNICEF actively engaged in the Belize Development Partners Network, established in 2024, contributing effectively to the governance and discussions of its thematic groups. The thematic group on socio-economy focused on poverty reduction and social protection, as well as health and education, with UNICEF ensuring synergies and complementarities in these social sectors for greater results for children and communities. 
Considerable progress was made in partnership with academia in the reporting year. Highlights include the inaugural partnership with Galen University, a private academic institution in Belize, to integrate disaster risk management into higher learning curricula. This collaboration introduced the Post-Graduate Diploma Program in Disaster Risk Management, the first of its kind in the country. Furthermore, UNICEF joined the UN Country Team to formalize collaboration with higher education academia through a Declaration of Intent. This partnership aims to advance the Sustainable Development Goals and support the objectives of MTDS 2022-2026 and the UNMSDCF 2022-2026. UNICEF actively engaged with UNCT in expanding partnerships with higher education academia through a series of University Tours, sharing more on career and volunteering opportunities within the UN System in Belize and globally. Students benefited from engaging panel discussions with current and retired UN staff and volunteers. 
A partnership was established with academic institutions to introduce Kangaroo mother care practice, an innovative approach for managing premature births, which is the most common cause of neonatal mortality in Belize. This was complemented by the deployment of innovative newborn health products through a partnership with a private manufacturing company to improve newborn survival. UNICEF also partnered with Yale University to conduct the first-ever situation analysis on adolescent and perinatal mental health, Galen University to engage young people in climate actions, and the University of the West Indies for staff leadership training. These partnerships aimed to address critical health issues and promote sustainable development. 
UNICEF continued its partnership with CSOs through Programme Cooperation Agreements to ensure the continuity of essential services for children and communities. Partnerships with local NGOs RET, Community Development Foundations, Belize Red Cross Association, and the Belize Football Federation strengthened reporting mechanisms, supported families, and participated in national child protection responses. In the private sector, UNICEF Belize engaged with telecommunications companies like Digi and SMART to enahnce digital solutions for efficient service delivery and community outreach. These efforts promoted transparency, accountability, and efficiency, particularly in implementing Nutrition Cash Transfers for under-5 children and pregnant women. Continued partnership with these companies resulted in  600,000 free SMS which increased engagement by 3,165  increase in U-Report.  Partnership was for the first time initiated with Business Processing Outsourcing companies, on family friendly policies including breast feeding rooms and day care centers linked to joint UNICEF/ILO supported child labour policy and implementation plan (2022).
New partnerships included collaboration with Belizean media professionals to produce two Op-Eds and an established partnership with the Caribbean Broadcasting Union and UNICEF Eastern Caribbean to provide capacity-building opportunities and special Media Awards. The Miss Universe Belize formalized a partnership workplan featuring the reigning queen as a Champion for Children, advocating for mental health, nutrition, adolescent girls, and climate. A local renowned artist joined as an Art Ambassador, painting visual depictions of child rights messages.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
