NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Advocacy has served as a dynamic instrument, significantly enhancing the defense of children and adolescents' rights. Effective advocacy has catalyzed partnerships at all levels, demonstrating UNICEF convening power and strongly influencing public policies for children. By further refining our advocacy strategies, UNICEF could ensure more impactful and sustainable outcomes. Additionally, engaging stakeholders through targeted communication strategies, including Social Behavior Change interventions, would address barriers and facilitators across all levels to promote positive change focusing on specific groups to foster social transformation.
The evolving socio-political landscape and significant polarization in the Legislative and Senate required UNICEF to refine and adapt its strategies, particularly in policy advice and influencing political decisions impacting the rights of children and adolescents. A primary challenge is expanding our activities despite the recognition of the budget for children and reestablishing our presence in parliament, which is crucial for the budget cycle and public policies. By building strong relationships with key political figures, UNICEF can better influence policy decisions affecting children and adolescents. This strategic approach will enhance our ability to secure favorable outcomes and ensure the sustainability of our initiatives.
Increasing interaction with the Legislature and at the local level is essential to ensure that the needs of children and adolescents are prioritized in political decisions. This requires dedicated personnel in Congress to monitor legislative activities related to children’s rights and strategically inform UNICEF so we amplify our advocacy efforts. Effective public monitoring at the local level is also vital for our advocacy initiatives. Consequently, a dynamic advocacy strategy responsive to political changes is essential to ensure our messages remain relevant and impactful. It is also fundamental to build trust with local governments and adapt advocacy strategies to regional realities to achieve more effective results.
Understanding and leveraging UNICEF's added value is essential for strengthening partnerships at both national and local levels. Conducting a comprehensive assessment of our unique contributions and effectively communicating these to our partners will be pivotal. This approach will help UNICEF build stronger alliances with the public and private sectors, ensuring that its interventions are recognized and supported. Moreover, the quality of UNICEF' partnerships, both financial and non-financial, is crucial for strategic resource allocation and enhancing the effectiveness of our interventions. Ensuring the continuity and scalability of our actions is central to achieving long-term impact. UNICEF should focus on developing sustainable models that can be scaled up and replicated. This includes creating robust frameworks for monitoring and evaluation to track the transformation of inputs into outcomes and results for disadvantaged children. By documenting best practices and lessons learned, the replication of successful initiatives will be improved.
Ensuring that national-level partnerships resonate at the local and municipal levels has been a significant challenge. Although we generate good data, the challenge is to use it strategically to influence public policies, especially on complex issues and to understand how this data can engage key stakeholders, including ministries and local governments. Moving forward, prioritizing the collection and analysis of disaggregated data is crucial to tailoring UNICEF interventions more effectively, particularly in a context where race, ethnicity and gender determine children's outcomes. To address this, UNICEF needs to enhance its planning and monitoring systems to track the local impact of national partnerships. This involves developing tools and frameworks for real-time data collection and analysis, incorporating disaggregated data and comprehensive research. Additionally, improving project management tools and mechanisms, as recommended by the AXA-funded nutrition project evaluation[i], would be beneficial. In response, the introduction of a new monitoring tool by the Health Sector has addressed some of these challenges. This tool, comprising a questionnaire and a database spreadsheet, has enhanced data management and activity prioritization. It has proven to be a successful initiative for monitoring results and improving overall performance, demonstrating how targeted solutions can effectively tackle identified issues.
Significant progress has been made in integrating Gender, Race, and Ethnicity (GRE) into programmatic activities. However, challenges remain, particularly regarding the intentionality of actions and gaps in ensuring comprehensive GRE integration. Intersectionality is a core component of UNICEF's as outlined in the CPD 2024-2028. Merely disaggregating data is insufficient to address gender issues comprehensively. Therefore, UNICEF needs to integrate intersectional approaches into all programmes, ensuring tailored and transformative strategies on gender, race, and ethnicity. This would require training staff and partners on intersectionality and improving the monitoring of relevant indicators.
Positive experiences in integrating a gender perspective in the COMPAZ evaluation,[1] as well as the results achieved in terms of girls' empowerment and menstrual dignity, demonstrate that intentional actions can address important structural drivers affecting the rights of children and adolescents, thereby reinforcing equity and diversity. UNICEF stood out by participating at the Local Evaluation Week, as a guest from the Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), to present its Guidance on How to Integrate Gender in Evaluation. The exchange of knowledge took place showcasing the theoretical and practical approach of the COMPAZ Evaluation, launched in the previous year, along with the participation of government, academia, and other UN agencies. The open debate aimed to discuss how the principle of gender can accurately be integrated in evaluations in all its phases, showcasing the good usage of insights gained during previous years. The COMPAZ Evaluation provided a path of continuity on how UNICEF can better improve the integration of gender with intentionality within the programme. However, the challenge remains to translate the CPD into actions that yield the expected results, which must be addressed in 2025.
Understanding the complexity of quilombola and indigenous territories is essential when implementing local actions. Positive interventions from the Education sector have played a pivotal role in addressing structural inequalities and rights deprivations, especially for quilombola and indigenous children and adolescents. Programmatic interventions that strengthen community retention, preserving language, culture, and tradition, are crucial to preventing the vulnerabilities that can arise from migration to cities for education.
Several challenges exist as we move into 2025, mainly around prioritizing a small number of high impact actions that UNICEF can engage with, advocate for, and galvanize action around to promote equity in rights and well-being for Brazil’s children

Chile is a high-income country with a strong legal framework, solid centralized institutions and public services, and a strong private sector. Two major additional public policy milestones were achieved in 2024 for the protection and promotion of child rights. 1) The adoption of the National Policy and Action Plan for Children and Adolescents 2024–2032 to strengthen strategic planning, implementation and intersectoral coordination of the Child Rights Guarantee Law (2022) in areas of survival, development, protection, participation and well-being, and  2) the implementation of the Commission for Truth, Justice, Reparations and Guarantees of Non-Repetition for child victims who have been under state protection, with the aim of providing comprehensive reparations to victims and their families.


   


The promising macro social economic situation however has not reduced the persistent inequality and disparity in the country, nor does it necessarily reach the most vulnerable children, especially those residing in peri-urban and rural areas. Economic recovery post-COVID 19 has remained uneven in 2024, with inflation up from 3.9% in 2023 to 4.5% in 2024 and unemployment decreasing only slightly by 0.3% from 2023 to 8.6% [1]. National elections are planned for 2025 while the municipal elections in 2024 saw a shift towards more center-right wing parties. The 2025 national budget discussions and allocations were overshadowed by public concern over increasing violent crime and migration.  


  


Official statistics show an increase in homicides from 845 to 1,248 between 2018 and 2023 (4.5 to 6.3 victims per 100,000 inhabitants) with the highest cases in 2022. Child homicide rates increased by 23% from 54 in 2022 to 66 in 2023: rising to 1.5 per 100,000 from 1.0 in 2021[2]. Preliminary data from 2024 suggests that child homicides are likely to increase. 65% of child homicides were due to firearms in urban violence and 21% of child homicides were related to intrafamily violence. In 2024, the number of adolescents under specialized juvenile justice services increased from 4,097 in 2023 to 4,591 due to involvement in crime. National data indicates that 12% of children experienced exposure to 10 or more violent events [3] while 24.4% of households with children reported being victims of socially significant crimes in 2022 (18%) [4]. All forms of violence against children in the home and school remain high at 36-39% prevalence [5].                                                                                                                                      


In 2023, the number of non-nationals in Chile reached 1.9 million [6], representing an estimated 9,6% of the total population in Chile, of which 15,8% (302,306) are children. The nationalities with the highest presence are those from Venezuela (38.0%), Peru (13.6%) and Colombia (10.9%). The number of people awaiting regularization of their status in Chile is estimated at around 336,000.  


  


While income poverty has significantly declined to 6.5% in 2022 from 10.7% in 2022, regional disparities persist. Children experience higher income poverty (10.5%) and multidimensional poverty (18.4%). These multidimensional poverty figures rise even greater among children living in rural areas (27.5%) or coming from disadvantaged groups such as indigenous children (21.9%) and migrant children (36.6%) [7]. Data from EANNA indicates that 507,833 children between 5 and 17 years old (15.5%) are subjected to some form of child labor [8]. Of these, 139,457 are engaged in child labor for economic purposes (4.3% of total number of children and adolescents 5 to 17 years old) [9]. 


  


Learning outcomes show some recovery since COVID-19. 2023 assessments [10] indicate modest improvements in mathematics and reading. However, significant gaps persist, especially at tenth grade where performance remains below pre-pandemic levels. And although school attendance is mandatory until secondary levels, approximately 6.5% or 50,000 children drop out each year, mostly adolescents from low-income groups. While reform has been agreed towards municipal schools as a new model to support dedicated education challenges through Local Public Education Services, implementation is slower than anticipated with 24 of the 70 planned local services operational by the end of 2024. Hereby hindering the focus needed to address specific educational challenges of the most vulnerable children. The enrolment of migrant children has increased significantly. As of 2024, there are approximately 80,000 migrant students holding a special temporary identity number for education, representing an increase of 11,000 students from 2023.  


  


Chile’s vulnerability to climate change is disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable children. The Children’s Climate Risk Index (CCRI) of 2024[11] ranks Chile as number 108 out of 163 countries globally. Indicators reveal high-risk levels in areas of water scarcity, heatwaves and pollution. From 2021 to 2024, over 30,000 children were affected by extreme events including weather fronts (83%) and wildfires (16%). Housing damage was severe with 59% of families reporting moderate-to-high damage and 14% total loss. 65% of emergency shelters were schools causing disruption to education for thousands of children. In February, Chile faced devastating fires that affected six regions. The fires caused 134 deaths, 6,587 homes were destroyed and 5,387 people were affected, of which 77% were children [12]. 


  


Chile faces significant challenges in monitoring the SDGs indicators related to children and adolescents. It shows compliance with global goals mainly in ¿¿health and nutrition. Of the 44 indicators prioritized by UNICEF for children, 20% are missing from the Voluntary National Report and 86% of the reported indicators present gaps in international standards and disaggregation geographically.[13]

UNICEF has established strategies to support the government in closing the gap so that more children and adolescents are comprehensively and directly reached by public policies and services.  


  


The National Policy and Action Plan for Children and Adolescents 2024–2032 was approved in 2024. UNICEF played a significant role in evaluating the previous plan and formulating the new plan; the effective participation of girls, boys and adolescents through the councils created; and strengthening the recently established Local Offices for Children (OLNs).  


  


Following years of persistent advocacy with the Committee on the Rights of the Child and the Ombudsman for Children, the government launched a commission in 2024 to review the violation of children’s rights – both past and present – in national institutions while under protection of the state with the aim of providing comprehensive reparations to child victims and their families.  


  


UNICEF contributed to four main key national challenges impeding children's rights in Chile: 


  


1.    Positioning child rights: aiming at advancing and not regressing the rights that allow children to reach their full potential 


  


UNICEF's advocacy and communication strategy were focused on influencing high-level decision makers, communicating important child rights concepts to the public and taking a position on issues relevant to children and adolescents. Various communication actions were carried out with parliament, either through the preparation of key documents for discussion or attending high-level meetings to influence decision-making in favour of children's rights in the areas such as education, migration and justice   A significant effort was made to raise awareness of the impact of emergencies on the rights and needs of children, especially the most vulnerable.  


  


As in previous years, UNICEF was invited to participate in relevant public activities carried out by different state authorities, such as campaign launches, inaugurations, presentations and the enactment of law projects. UNICEF remained a relevant spokesperson for the media, maintaining a constant presence at national and regional levels articulating a child rights perspective for national debates on violence, crime, migration and child poverty. Teresa Paneque, astronomer and UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador, actively supported these efforts – particularly with regard to promoting girls’ participation in sciences – on social media and through the book Astronomical ABC.  


  


UNICEF also supported the monitoring and reporting of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicators, which led to adjustments in SDG reporting processes at the Statistics National Institute, to ensure the regular reporting of child-sensitive indicators. As a result, UNICEF will implement multiple indicator cluster survey modules in 2025, providing data for evidence-based policymaking in the areas of violent discipline and early childhood development, mental health and subjective well-being.  


  


  


2.    Implementation of the Integrated Protection of Child Rights Guarantee System: the comprehensive protection system for children made progress in its inter-sectoral implementation and the establishment of Local Offices for Children 


  


UNICEF supported the Undersecretariat for Children in the implementation of the Child Rights Guarantee System at the local level by providing technical assistance to the roll-out of OLNs in 200 municipalities. Guides were developed on understanding comprehensive protection, child rights promotion, case management, referral and administrative mechanisms with specific attention for the most vulnerable children. Due to the pressing needs for the protection of migrant children, UNICEF supported the development of a dedicated technical note for OLNs with the objective to ensure protection by the Public Prosecutor's Office.  


  


UNICEF supported juvenile justice reforms through technical assistance to the new Juvenile Social Reintegration Service and advocated to prevent the passing of a new law proposing harsher punishment for adolescents involved in serious crime. UNICEF also facilitated consultations with experts, public officials and children on access to justice in contribution to the new General Comment 27 on Children’s Rights to Access to Justice and Effective Remedies being developed by the Committee on the Rights of the Child.  


  


In progressing towards the guarantee of a social protection floor focused on social services and benefits for children, UNICEF developed an operational framework for its implementation in collaboration with the International Labour Organization and the Undersecretariat for Children. Operationalization was thereafter incorporated with a budget in the Policy for Children and Adolescents 2024–2032. A cost model for inclusive care in early education, focusing on children with a disability, was developed with the World Bank. UNICEF also assisted the Ministry of Finance and the Undersecretariat for Children to create a mechanism to review public spending on children for progressive monitoring in coming years.  


  


Important contributions were made for the adoption of the national Obesity Prevention Strategy and strengthening of the International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes. Through social media engagement, UNICEF focused on suicide prevention, health body-mind connection and body image disorders to tackle mental health challenges among children and adolescents.  


  


UINCEF also ensured relevant child participation in various national policy decision-making processes: 


-          A consultation took place with over 100 young people and 6 speakers during the Meeting of the Education Ministers from LAC in Santiago. An agreement to systematically include young people's participation in future Ministers' Meetings was formalized in the assembly minutes. 


-          Five youth environmental organizations reviewed the draft Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Plan for the Energy Sector during the national workshop. 


-          130 students from 3 schools in Mejillones contributed to the Socio-Ecological Just Transition Plan for the closure of the coal energy plant and a local sustainable energetic conversion in partnership with the Ministry of Environment.  


-          A focus group of students supported General Comment 27 on Children’s Rights to Access to Justice and Effective Remedies. Participants emphasized a lack of tools for peaceful conflict resolution, structural inequalities and insufficient police training on child and adolescent rights. 


-          Youth representatives engaged in dialogue with the United Nations Special Representative on Violence, COP, CRC 35 and other global events.  


UNICEF also assisted in building the capacity of over 200 local advisory councils for children and adolescents to strategically influence local policies and advocate for their rights with the aim to reach 345 councils by 2025. 


  


3.    Prevention and eradication of violence against children: Action Plan and pledge to prevent violence against children 


  


Led by the Undersecretariat for Children, UNICEF together with other relevant ministries contributed to the definition of the national strategy for preventing violence against children (VAC), which is now part of the Policy and Action Plan for Children and Adolescents 2024–2032. The actions committed to in this strategy are part of the government's pledge of the first Global Ministerial Conference on VAC held in Colombia in 2024. It includes work with communities at the territorial level on social norms, support for parenting through two programmes (Nobody is Perfect and Skills for Life), and the implementation of an intersectoral system focusing on alerts to identify children at risk of violence with the aim to prevent and protect. This system covers children in general, as well as children under state protection and adolescents in juvenile justice.  


  


UNICEF completed an anthropological study and participative consultations with the University of Frontera on Mapuche (indigenous) children in two territories affected by armed violence resulting from the conflict between the state and Mapuche communities. The consultations highlighted the psychosocial impact ongoing conflict is having on children and the inequities in access to basic services. Based on this study and the consultations, a strategic plan will be defined with communities and OLNs in 2025 to respond to the effects of VAC and limited access to inclusive education at the territorial level.  


  


UNICEF advocated for and technically supported the government to establish a Commission for Truth, Justice, Reparations and Guarantees of Non-Repetition for child victims who have been under state protection in institutions since 1978. It is the first of its kind in the region and is based on recommendations made by the Committee on the Rights of the Child. 


  


Systemic progress was made in preventing school violence and advancing mental health and psychosocial support in schools. As part of the Council for Educational Reactivation composed by 23 members from different sectors, UNICEF successfully advocated for the tracking of academic and non-academic indicators at schools. As a result, the Ministry of Education (MoE) initiated a school environment and well-being monitoring system which will allow policymakers and education administrators to track the physical and mental well-being of students as well as the school environment in order to make evidence-based decisions to prevent violence and address mental health with greater understanding and knowledge. 


  


UNICEF implemented evidence-based initiatives to prevent violence in early childhood education. The Caring for the Caregiver programme, in collaboration with the Undersecretariat of Early Childhood Education, trained a professional to regionalize this framework, equipping educators to reduce parental stress and promote nurturing care. The Child and Family Approach programme, piloted in Araucanía with Education 2020, supported 60 children and families in Perquenco through play-based methodologies, producing educational materials for broader application. A pilot project with Fundación Integra addressed violence in three high-risk communities focusing on equipping educators and families with tools to manage stress and promote socioemotional resilience. Participants reported increased knowledge and skills, laying the groundwork for scaling up these interventions in 2025. 


  


4.    Protection, inclusion and humanitarian services for children on the move: reaching over 12,000 people including 3,530 boys and 3,288 girls 


  


Due to inconsistent response by the government to protect children and their families on the move, UNICEF has exponentially increased its technical and financial assistance to address the humanitarian needs and rights of migrant children in north Chile while seeking to connectthese actions to ongoing decentralization efforts of national systems to protect children through MoE, the Ministry of Social Development and Family (MIDESOF) and the Ministry of Justice. UNICEF mobilized US$ 2 million as extra funds from ECHO, BPRM, MoE and the private sector. 


  


This has fostered a multisectoral and integrated programming approach based on the Core Commitments for Children (CCC) to connect humanitarian action and development activities at the local level to prioritize Child Protection, Education, WASH and cross-sectoral interventions. In 2024, UNICEF reached a total population of 12,867 people including 6,818 children and adolescents; 58% of the total participants were Venezuelan nationals. 9,002 people accessed mechanisms set-up as part of UNICEF Accountability to Affected Populations including 2,839 boys and 2,452 girls. These included information and access to services as well as activities with local communities to prevent xenophobia, promote intercultural dialogue and foster inclusion.  


  


In the Child Protection sector, two comprehensive support spaces (Espacio de Apoyo Integral) were established with Fundación Madre Josefa (FMJ), along with two socio-sports intervention programmes with Fútbol Más. With the technical assistance of UNICEF in the border area with Bolivia (Colchane) and in collaboration with implementing partner FMJ, the timely identification and monitoring of unaccompanied and separated children was promoted (CCC 2.3.5). This made it possible to assist 57 children and adolescents in coordination with regional and local institutions, providing comprehensive assistance including psychological first aid and migration guidance. In Education in Emergencies (EiE), three Temporary Learning Spaces and one Accelerated Education programme were set up with World Vision and the capacity of MoE teachers was expanded to deal with the diverse education needs of students. EiE response reached 1,657 children and adolescents – all beneficiaries had access to psychosocial support and 888 children received individualized case management. With support from Servicio Jesuita a Migrante, 211 humanitarian visa applications were started for children and adolescents. Gender-based violence case management was mainstreamed. 


  


In general, there has been a lack of information on the regularization processes for children and adolescents. There have also been significant difficulties such as the lack of personal documents by many to access a visa, as established by law. UNICEF generated evidence on the issue and advocated with the relevant institutions to support a more effective visa application process. This included close collaboration with the Family Courts in Iquique while implementing an advocacy strategy with national and local authorities to highlight the complexities and challenges. In 2024, the UNICEF Country Office established closer collaboration with IOM and UNHCR to transfer knowledge and gather best practices for migrant children specifically in shelters. UNICEF developed a protocol outlining guiding criteria to ensure the protection of children and adolescents, and Social and Behaviour Change interventions were also mainstreamed throughout the operation and procedures of humanitarian responses in the two government-led shelters.  


  


Gender Mainstreaming: UNICEF developed and validated its Gender Action Plan and participated in a United Nations Country Team SWAP Gender Score Card review. UNICEF also participated in many projects that boosted gender results such as: providing technical assistance to the Ministry of Gender Equality and MIDESOF to ensure a gender-responsive social protection system; supporting the incorporation of a child-sensitive and gender-sensitive Social Protection Floor; collaborating with the development of a measure of child poverty and well-being of children and adolescents; contributing to the generation and systematization of evidence on Integrated Care Systems with a focus on children and adolescents; generating new evidence of the country’s position in comprehensive sexual education through the elaboration of a Working Document that synthesizes and analyses the country’s advances on Comprehensive Sexual Education from a Child Rights Approach and proposes a Theory of Change Model for Programmatic Implementation that was formulated through a participatory process involving women and girls’ child service outcomes; and launching local humanitarian response that directly addresses gender-based violence risk factors in the population on the move through prevention, case management and psychosocial support, reaching 113 women and girls through a comprehensive programme. 


 


Private Fundraise and Partnership: With the goal to support children’s rights nationally and globally, UNICEF mobilized US$ 19,2 million. Chile´s Individual Giving channel is the biggest operation in LACRO in terms of gross income, raising more than US$ 18,9 million. UNICEF successfully acquired 35,000 new pledge donors in 2024. Fundraising campaigns also contributed to strengthening UNICEF´s positive brand recognition within the country and expanded its fundraising potential among individual donors. By the end of 2024, UNICEF Chile’s pledge donor house list reached 125,000 people. 


 


Corporate Progress: UNICEF faced numerous operational challenges in 2024. The number of recruitment processes increased from 30 in 2023 to 44 in 2024, resulting in a rise in staff from 70 to 80. This increase necessitated additional space, tools and technical support. Changes in UNICEF systems, such as the new Procurement Case Manager tool and the Fiori travel tool, have positively impacted the administration of operations, while the new Business Model Initiative is set for progressive implementation. Training for these new tools posed challenges, as did the introduction of new policies and technologies. Copilot and the Payment Card Industry (PCI) Data Security Standard were implemented, ensuring UNICEF’s compliance with the PCI standard. 


Another significant development in 2024 was the approval of the new People and Culture Division at the global level. The former Human Resources team now reports directly to the Representative, offering specialized expertise to senior managers with continued technical support from Operations. The creation of the Learning Committee and the corresponding comprehensive and inclusive internal policy generated an enabling environment for the development of the entire UNICEF Chile workforce.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
National Policy and Action Plan for -Children and Adolescents 2024–2032: Learning to close the gap between national policies and local governance, and violence against children 


  


In a centralized policy environment, a significant overarching challenge is to translate national policies into quality services at the local level equal for all children in a vast and geographically diverse country such as Chile, especially for the most disadvantaged.  


UNICEF supported the development of the National Policy and Action Plan for Children and Adolescents 2024-2032. The lesson learned from this effort is that while Chile develops sound public policies, UNICEF’s role as an external observer and advisor is crucial to ensure the continuity of the adoption and implementation of these public policies for children from one government to the next. Hereby influencing important decisions in areas such as education, health, justice, and social development in a sustainable, structural and child-centered manner. The current challenge for UNICEF is to assist the implementation of this Plan by supporting the current government to establish OLN as the territorial extension of the National Child Protection System and establish SLEP (Local Public Education Services) to ensure adequate, quality and standardized educational opportunities appropriate for children in their specific local communities. 


An increase in deaths due to violence crime in Chile has shifted the national response to increased security measures with less focus on prevention and addressing the root causes of child vulnerability such as poverty, lack of opportunities, inequality, and limited services to basic services. With more than 20,000 children requiring specialized protective intervention per month, there is a realization by the State that existing services and resources are not effective enough to stop child rights violations. After years of persistent advocacy by UNICEF, there is a better understanding by the State and society of the different types of violence faced by children and the need to develop a dedicated intersectoral strategy as part of the National Policy and Action Plan to address violence against children and protect children from being drawn into perpetrating violent crimes. A strategy that entails an intersectoral approach with private and public sector partners at both national and decentralized level with tools and approaches that provide social behavior changes, personalized advocacy and specific interventions for and with adolescents.  


  


  


Public and Private Alliance for Children 


  


Chile is recognized as a reference country for various other Latin America countries due to its strong legal and institutional framework for children. It also has robust private sector which plays a significant role in national decisions making. Unlike many other countries, the private sector in Chile provides basic services such as water and electricity whereby profit is often one of the key factors for the limited services for disadvantaged children and their families. The private sector, however, has multiple foundations dedicated to social issues with the ability to successfully mobilize resources for programs in the country and abroad. UNICEF Chile is learning to further diversify its sources of financing and establish a stronger public and private sector dialogue and alliances to influence child-sensitive decision-making processes and convene a large national movement for child rights. Through the Business Model Initiative (BMI), UNICEF Chile will be able to experiment with innovative alliance models. 




Children on the move: lessons learned for a high-income country  




Despite ongoing advocacy efforts by UNICEF and other UN agencies, the response by the government to the persistent migration from Venezuela, Colombia, Peru and other countries has been inconsistent, including for unaccompanied children.  Upon arrival in the country, immediate support mechanisms for migrants are limited and access to basic services or employment for adults is severely hampered, as regularisation of migrants is difficult. The subject forms a senstive and ongoing debate in Congress and Parliament. So, while Chile is a high-income country and UNICEF continue to advocate for the rights of all children, also migrant children and their families, the lesson learned is that UNICEF has found itself needing to provide humanitarian support services for migrant children as a last resort. As such, it has contracted five implementing partners and the establishment a humanitarian protection network for children covering two regions in northern Chile with additional funds from BPRM and ECHO. Migrant children and their families generally seek refuge in the poorest peri-urban localities (informal settlements), UNICEF hereby is  adopting and promoting a host-community approach for both the Chilean poor and migrants whereby a nexus is created between humanitarian services and the decentralized public services now starting to be implemented through the Local Offices for Children (OLN) and the Local Public Education Services (SLEP). 


  


Corporate challenges and opportunities 


  


Due to the increasing operational complexity for UNICEF related to the growth of private fundraising and partnerships (PFP) in Chile, the UNICEF Country Office is learning to work even more closely with UNICEF PFP and ICT globally to integrate corporate fundraising platforms and solutions. Long Term Agreement contracts have doubled since 2023 as PFP expanded to diversified fundraising channels. A security breach early in the year has brought dedicated attention to become Payment Card Industry compliant by early 2025. Efficiency and market tracking have been strengthened to allow for enhanced planning and the ability to adjust in a timely manner. The Business Model Initiative will seek to further strengthen the interdependency between PFP and other sections in the CO as part of a whole-office approach and build on the lessons outlined below. 


  


Some other corporate lessons include: a) the need to look at process efficiencies due to the increased number of Programme Cooperation Agreements with high volume of transactions; b) the formation of a task force to identify improvements in physical space and teleworking for an optimal working arrangement due to the significant growth in staff; c) the identification of appropriate office space with other United Nations agencies for outposted staff in north Chile; d) the development of an office strategy to manage expectations, mentor and coach UNVs and temporary appointments; and e) with the growth of office staff, a Learning and Development Committee was formed to ensure a structured and equitable approach to staff learning and development.  


  


Overall, there is an opportunity with the transition of Human Resources to People and Culture to drive a value-based office change and align office practices with evolving organizational priorities to strengthen professional growth. 


 


Lessons learned from evaluation 




The joint evaluation with the Government of Chile of strategic public policies provides key lessons in program development. In particular, the Evaluation of the National Public Education Strategy (ENEP) identifies a lag in the incorporation of new needs that emerged after the health crisis, such as the impacts on school coexistence and the impact on post-pandemic mental health. Similarly, a key lesson is the identification of discrepancies between national objectives and implementation at the territorial level. This is an element common to several programs at the national level, which in the case of ENEP is observed on the basis that plans and strategies designed at the central level did not always translate into actions aligned with local capacities and priorities, generating tensions and lack of cohesion in the interventions. 



Local ownership, although important, was not backed by clear oversight or technical support mechanisms, resulting in fragmented program implementation. These types of elements are a central part of CO's strategies in capacity building at subnational levels and advocacy for the harmonization of public policies to these challenges.

Colombia's economy continued to recover, with projected growth of 1.5% and estimated inflation of 5%. Navigating a complex political landscape, the government continued to push key reforms in health, pensions, and labour systems aimed at fostering a more equitable society. In addition to structural inequality, the country faces the complex challenges of armed conflict, migration, and climate vulnerability, which disproportionately impact children, particularly those from Indigenous, Afro-Colombian, rural, displaced, and migrant communities.
 
While the implementation of the Peace Agreement signed in 2016 between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia People's Army continued, the government suspended peace negotiations with the National Liberation Army in September of 2024. Peace negotiations with other major non-state armed groups (NSAGs) remain stalled, and over 200 of these groups operate in 589 municipalities, controlling more than half the country. The International Commitee of the Red Cross (ICRC) [1] recognizes at least five non-international armed conflicts in Colombia taking place. In 2024, more than 175,000 people were internally displaced, and 125,000 were confined. Confinements are primarily driven by confrontations and threats from NSAGs, causing enormous harm and forcing communities to restrict their livelihood activities.
 
Child recruitment has surged, with Indigenous children accounting for 51% of the victims. Since 2019, the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism established under Resolution 1612 has consistently recorded increased grave violations. According to the Victims' Unit, Colombia's protracted armed conflict has resulted in 9.8 million victims, 17% of them (1.7 million) under 18.

Colombia hosts 2.8 million Venezuelan migrants, 28% of whom are under 18. Additionally, the country serves as a transit point for migrants, with 340,500 irregular migrants in 2024 crossing the Darien Gap towards North America. Due to ongoing political instability in Venezuela, the country is preparing for a continuous flow of migrants and refugees. This precarious situation may be further aggravated by potential reductions in US funding and shifting geopolitical dynamics.
 
Colombia continues to face high levels of poverty and inequality. In 2023, monetary poverty affected 33.0% of the population (41.2% in rural areas) and 52.3% of the child and adolescent population. Poverty in Colombia is concentrated in rural areas, female-headed households, and Afro-Colombian and Indigenous populations. Multidimensional poverty affects 39% of Indigenous households, compared to the national average of 12.9%. Colombia has the third-highest Gini coefficient globally (54.8).

Economic setbacks and increasing poverty have impacted children's nutritional status. The prevalence of moderate and severe acute malnutrition in children under five reached 0.37% in 2023 (13,662 cases), a 12% increase since 2022. Acute malnutrition affected 18.5% of Indigenous children and 3.1% of migrant children under five in 2022. In 2023, children from Indigenous groups accounted for 26% of acute malnutrition cases and 60% of deaths from malnutrition. 

Mental health among children, especially in conflict-affected Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities, was identified by young people as a top concern. According to the National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, the death rate per 100,000 people by suicide increased from 6.16 in 2022 to 6.59 in 2023. Among adolescent women, suicide was the leading cause of violent death (42%).

There are challenges in terms of quality of education, with disparities between public and private schools, urban and rural areas, and marginalized groups, including Indigenous and Afro-descendant populations and students with special educational needs. Many school-aged children are not acquiring age-appropriate foundational learning, especially in vulnerable communities where learning poverty rates exceed 80%. Half of 10-year-old children cannot read or comprehend simple text. 
 
Domestic violence against children has surged, with a rate of 43.41 per 100,000 people in 2022—a 19.35% increase compared to 2021. Among reported cases, 66.98% of aggressors were parents or caregivers, and 83.57% of incidents occurred at home. Data on legal examinations for alleged sexual crimes reveals an increase in incidents since 2020. In 2022, 82.3% of such examinations involved children and adolescents. Seven in ten victims (71.9%) were girls under 18. 

UNICEF co-hosted the 2024 First Ministerial Conference to End Violence against Children in Bogotá, discussing proven prevention strategies to achieve 2030 SDG of ending violence against children. Colombia pledged to enhance capacities to prevent and address violence, empower children with resilience skills and online safety tools, and advance legal frameworks for digital child protection.
 
Colombia ranks as the fifth most vulnerable country to disasters and climate change, with 28% of the population at high risk of flooding and 31% at significant risk of mass movements. In 2024, natural disasters disrupted the livelihoods of 1.7 million people nationwide. Sixty-three percent were impacted by drought, including water shortages. At the same time, 438,000 (25%) were affected by flooding. Funding to the national disaster preparedness agency (UNGRD) has been affected as it still addressing corruption allegations. 

COP16, held in Cali, Colombia, in 2024, marked significant progress in biodiversity conservation efforts. In a landmark decision during the closing plenary, delegates approved creating a new subsidiary body under the Convention on Biological Diversity, enhancing participation of Indigenous and Afro descendant communities, and communities in biodiversity governance. Children, adolescents, and youth were actively engaged in climate and biodiversity discussions during pre-COP16 and COP16 events, and their voices were heard in various decision-making scenarios. 

Although government efforts have sought to reform the health, education, pension, and labour systems, there is uncertainty regarding the proposed reforms' feasibility and fiscal sustainability. Similarly, the sustainability of the Ministry of Equality and Equity, created in 2023, is under scrutiny following a ruling by the Constitutional Court. These ambiguities raise concerns that these evolving institutional frameworks may overshadow children's rights. 

In November 2024, the Senate approved Bill 297, abolishing child marriage and early unions involving underage partners. The law also establishes the National Comprehensive Program for Children's and Adolescents' Life Projects to increase the prevention of such unions. This legislation is vital, as a UNICEF study found that 23% of women aged 20–24 are married or in an early union, and the 2018 Census reported that 81.1% of adolescent girls aged 13–14 who had lived with a partner experienced intimate partner violence

UNICEF continued addressing the root causes of child mortality, poverty, vulnerability, and exclusion, engaging with various partners and stakeholders to advance rights-based policies and legislation, support families, and influence social behaviours and norms. This year, UNICEF programmes reached 1.5 million individuals across 12 departments, with plans for further expansion in 2025. This territorial strategy reflects UNICEF’s unwavering commitment to reaching the most underserved areas and working towards ensuring that no child is left behind.

Amid a landscape of institutional reforms and uncertainty, UNICEF has focused on ensuring that the Colombian State prioritizes children in institutional reforms. Of particular note is UNICEF's central role, in conjunction with UNWOMEN and the United Nations Population Fund, in the approval of a landmark law prohibiting child marriage and early unions.
 
UNICEF delivered life-saving services while implementing medium-term strategies to address the triple nexus of humanitarian assistance, peacebuilding, and sustainable development. These efforts included capacity building, evidence generation, risk management, community participation, communication and accountability to affected populations, and resilience-building measures to prevent future crises and protect children in humanitarian contexts.
 
A unifying theme across UNICEF’s work in 2024 was its focus on community-driven solutions, capacity building, and integrating policies to promote sustainable, long-term impact. By designing models tailored to the unique needs of local communities while ensuring scalability to other regions, UNICEF demonstrated a holistic approach to supporting vulnerable populations, reducing inequalities, and fostering resilience among marginalized groups. UNICEF trained 127 community and educational agents in Vichada, Norte de Santander, Nariño, and La Guajira, enhancing their knowledge in providing essential services for migrant children under five. The training included key practices in hygiene, health, and nutrition aligned with national guidelines. This community-focused primary health care process has potentially improved the quality and coverage of care for 1,200 children and their families.
 
UNICEF also prioritised the needs of Indigenous and Afro-descendant populations through an ethnic and gender-sensitive approach, ensuring tailored interventions for these vulnerable groups. Many of UNICEF’s models were adopted by government institutions, enabling replication and scaling to reach even more children and families. Territories inhabited by Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities, especially in border zones and areas where armed actors have strengthened their presence and control were prioritised. Implemented actions, based on psychosocial support, social behaviour change (SBC), and gender approaches benefited 13,651 children and adolescents, 4,424 young people (of whom 65 % were female and 35% were male), families, caregivers, and public officials. There were 103 initiatives led by adolescents and young people identified and supported, and 50 community routes were designed with the participation of families, leaders, and their authorities. 
 
In the humanitarian sector, UNICEF led the Water Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), education, and nutrition clusters and co-led the Child Protection Area of Responsibility, while piloting innovative approaches such as the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) Flagship Initiative and the United Nations-led Durable Solutions for Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) initiative.
 
Advocacy, communication, and social mobilisation were key pillars of UNICEF’s strategy, driving progress in critical focus areas such as mental health, child and adolescent participation, and literacy. These efforts addressed immediate needs and laid a solid foundation for sustainable improvements in children’s well-being and rights.
 
Below are some of the main achievements of 2024:
 

Ensuring no child is left behind: Acute malnutrition     identification and treatment in rural and dispersed communities
 
To adequately serve the Colombian context, UNICEF reviewed and adapted international evidence to incorporate a community-based approach for identifying and treating acute malnutrition. This approach included training community agents to use anthropometric measurement and mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) to detect acute malnutrition in rural and dispersed communities, especially among Indigenous populations in Guainía, Vichada, Guajira, and Chocó. In an area spanning 2,597 km², characterised by low population density and challenges like geographic isolation and armed conflict, UNICEF Colombia has fostered community-based approaches to prevent and treat malnutrition, training 49 community agents to reach 1,076 families through screening, nutritional treatment, and promoting breastfeeding and complementary feeding in regions with high malnutrition rates. This approach helped fill a critical service gap and prevent and treat acute malnutrition.
 
This initiative's success has sparked high-level discussions within the government about integrating innovative and effective strategies for preventing and treating malnutrition into the country’s management guidelines and pathways. Combining training, capacity building, and community participation empowers communities to take charge of their nutritional health, creating a sustainable model that can be replicated in other regions facing similar challenges.
 

 Communication and social mobilization in favor of children and adolescents’ mental health
 
The "Embrace Your Mind, Let's Talk About Mental Health" campaign aimed to increase the visibility of children's emotional challenges and exclusion in underserved communities. The campaign sought to shine a light on the gap between the perspectives of adults and the experiences of young people facing emotional challenges and psychological distress due to adverse life circumstances.  The campaign reached 16 million subscribers via traditional media and strategic digital platforms, directly engaging 1,027,000 people and significantly boosting organic communication efforts. Its primary goal was to transform the negative narrative surrounding mental health in Colombia, promoting it as a positive, everyday topic free from stigma and myths.
 
Over 30 digital influencers, including UNICEF national ambassadors and popular Colombian creator JuanDa, amplified the campaign, with nearly 7 million followers on Instagram and 26.7 million on TikTok, where he openly discusses mental health. The campaign exceeded its target audience by 2,018%, with a 227.83% interaction growth. The campaign helped simplify discussions around mental health, making the topic more accessible, especially in vulnerable regions. By leveraging social media, it achieved widespread visibility and greater acceptance among segmented audiences. Pre- and post-campaign measurements and in-depth interviews revealed a marked increase in positive perceptions about mental health. 
 
In addition, the campaign sought to strengthen stakeholders’ capacities and foster community engagement in regions strongly impacted by armed conflict and adverse socioeconomic conditions, such as Chocó and Arauca. The organization worked with adolescents and teachers using methodologies developed and transferred by UNICEF to local stakeholders. It empowered them to become providers of psychosocial well-being and mental health within schools and the community. 
 
 3. Overcoming learning loss by fostering early and basic literacy skills in vulnerable communities
 
“The Blue Teacher” multi-modality strategy has significantly advanced literacy skills by focusing on foundational reading and writing abilities. The strategy includes a chat feature enabled 51,649 interactions with over 16,000 teachers from diverse regions, addressing pedagogical challenges and refining teaching methods. Moreover, the “Blue Learning Kit” course engaged 4,411 participants, equipping them with innovative educational methodologies to further enhance literacy efforts nationwide. 
 
Seventy-seven community leaders received training in community literacy programmes using the ATAL methodology. These programmes emphasise literacy for children, particularly those excluded from formal education. This initiative has fostered educational inclusion and helped reduce learning gaps in vulnerable communities.
 
To advance early literacy, UNICEF was instrumental in creating and implementing “Colombia se escribe Leyendo,” an initiative encompassing over 30 organizations committed to improving early literacy. The initiative includes more than 10 certified education secretariats leading advocacy efforts to address the learning crisis. Over 60 participants from various organizations mobilised territorial resources to support literacy initiatives in Antioquia and Valle del Cauca as part of this initiative. At the launch, $2.2 million was announced for evidence-based literacy materials for all schools in Antioquia and $2.5 million to support literacy initiatives in schools along the Cauca River, targeting Valle del Cauca and Cauca, to be invested between 2025 and 2027.
 
4. A bold initiative to support adolescents’ transition to higher education. 
 
Through the “Life Trajectories: Opportunities for High School Students” initiative, UNICEF Colombia introduced micro-credentials to gain certified skills in technical fields such as digital technologies, arts, mathematics, climate change and the environment, human sciences and social development, and health sciences. The aim is to facilitate students' transition to higher education while equipping them with competitive skills for the workforce. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with four higher education institutions to establish an academic pathway that recognises and builds upon the knowledge gained via micro-credentials.
 
The pilot enrolled 505 adolescents in the micro-credentialing programme(70% female and 30% male), with 78% completing their courses. Seventy percent of those who completed the programme were female, and 51% pursued STEM-related courses. This initiative has provided adolescents in rural and remote areas greater access to advanced knowledge. It has been crucial in encouraging young women to strengthen their STEM skills, as initially intended, promoting autonomous learning and motivation. Implementing micro-credentials in rural and remote schools was a significant challenge due to the low internet penetration rate (around 30%) and low digital literacy. 
The pilot is Colombia´s first initiative of public schools offering micro-credentials in upper secondary education.
 
5. New legislation to abolish child marriage and early unions
 
Persistent technical leadership and inter-agency advocacy resulted in Congress passing the “Girls, Not Wives” law after nine previous failed attempts. This landmark legislation establishes the minimum age for marriage at 18 with no exceptions and eliminates early unions. The law also makes essential references to prevention programmes. This was possible through a systematic collaborative agenda with UN-Women and UNFPA to hold two high-level meetings with congressional representatives and senators. These discussions fostered a shared understanding of harmful practices, aligning legislative efforts with the Committee on the Rights of the Child and the Committee on CEDAW recommendations.  By presenting country-specific evidence, these meetings helped shape specific public policies to protect girls and adolescents at risk of CMEU. 
 
UNICEF, civil society, and other UN agencies developed two policy briefs and a joint advocacy and communication strategy. The CMEU working group produced critical evidence-based recommendations for both the Ministry of Equality and Equity and Health, emphasising the links between CMEU and children’s domestic and care work. These inputs also influenced the ongoing review of the Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) Policy.
 
6. Shaping government programmes for the reintegration of demobilised Indigenous children 
 
UNICEF provided technical and financial support to the Regional Indigenous Council of Cauca (CRIC) and the Colombian Institute of Family Welfare (ICBF) to develop a new reintegration process for Indigenous children and adolescents who have been victims of recruitment by armed groups. This initiative, called Enraizamiento, was created in response to a disturbing rise in the recruitment of Indigenous children by various armed actors. According to a 2023 study conducted by the ICBF and UNICEF, 10% of children affected by recruitment are Indigenous. The Department of Cauca reported the highest number of cases in the country, with 214 documented instances in 2014, according to the Ombudsman's Office.
 
The Enraizamiento initiative acknowledges and integrates the traditions and cultural perspectives of the Indigenous communities in Northern Cauca. This programme facilitates the demobilisation of children and adolescents from armed groups, helping them reintegrate into their families and communities. As a result of these efforts, the ICBF adapted its institutional guidelines to include Enraizamiento as an official programme for reintegrating Indigenous children and adolescents, securing funding, and beginning its implementation in Cauca.
 
The Enraizamiento process, led by Colombian civil society and institutions, has the potential to serve as a replicable model for other Indigenous and Afro-Colombian communities facing similar challenges. UNICEF's support has strengthened the ICBF's Specialized Program for Demobilized Children, emphasizing concrete actions that incorporate gender and ethnic perspectives into the reintegration process.
 
7. Fostering adolescent participation and development
 
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in promoting adolescent and youth leadership through the Seeds for Change toolkit. This toolkit includes a comprehensive collection of tools, guides, and methodologies designed to enhance meaningful participation and strengthen adolescent leadership. It emphasises perspectives on gender and ethnicity while ensuring universal accessibility. 
 
UNICEF and its partners, including the ICBF and local authorities, have used this toolkit as part of the Child-Friendly Territories programme and other initiatives that support adolescents’ participation and development. This toolkit has helped strengthen the capacities of at least 18 local governments, enhancing their roles in advancing youth centred plans and supporting adolescent participation. In 2024, ICBF’s sub-directorates for Adolescent Criminal Responsibility and Childhood and Adolescence received the transfer of the toolkit. As a result, over 4,400 adolescents receiving specialized care and 126,000 children and adolescents involved in the "Dream Catchers" empowerment programme will benefit from strengthened technical support, fostering long-term positive change. 
 
The Seeds for Change toolkit was developed through the multisectoral collaboration of UNICEF programme areas, including protection, education, social inclusion, health and nutrition, WASH, emergency response, gender equality, social and behaviour change (SBC), and communications. It leverages UNICEF’s decades of experience and lessons learned in adolescent participation and development in Colombia and globally. Its widespread implementation and adoption by the ICBF results from UNICEF’s territorial strategy and its sustained efforts in building partnerships and advancing comprehensive communication and advocacy strategies.
 
8. Influencing public policy and plans for the end of open defecation in La Guajira
 
UNICEF successfully influenced the inclusion of the end of open defecation in La Guajira's departmental development plan and Maicao and Manaure's local development plans. This milestone reflects strong support for local governance in achieving SDG 6.2, especially the target on ending open defecation. 
 
This achievement was possible through a combination of key factors. The first factor was evidence generation. UNICEF implemented the Total and Sustainable Sanitation and Hygiene (SAHTOSO) methodology, successfully certifying 56 communities in La Guajira as free from open defecation (30 communities in 2024, 22 in 2023, and 4 in 2022). By systematizing the process and developing a monitoring tool, UNICEF demonstrated the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of this approach, which focuses on self-built latrines and handwashing practices. The evidence generated contributed to achieving SDG 6.2 and played a significant role in preventing child mortality caused by sanitation-related diseases in children under five.
 
Advocacy and capacity building were critical in achieving this success. UNICEF disseminated results through training and capacity-building sessions for health, water, sanitation, and hygiene authorities. Local authorities, including the Manaure Health Secretariat and the La Guajira Departmental Water Plan, were actively involved in verifying compliance with open defecation standards. Decision-makers, such as health secretaries from Maicao and Uribia, attended certification processes, and technical meetings and political negotiations were held to build consensus and gain commitment for SAHTOSO across municipal and departmental governments.
 
The third important factor was policy integration. Once political and technical interest had been secured, UNICEF facilitated four workshops per entity to set targets, define indicators, identify funding sources, and establish legal frameworks for including the elimination of open defecation in development plans approved by municipal councils.
 
Finally, UNICEF provided technical assistance and support to strengthen the implementation of SAHTOSO, helping municipalities build technical capacity for applying the methodology and structuring investment projects tailored to each territory. Following two workshops with technical officials from municipalities and departmental authorities, initial drafts of investment plans were completed and are currently under review. In 2025, UNICEF will assist authorities in finalising the project drafts to secure funding, with implementation scheduled for 2026 and 2027.
 
9. Responding to emergencies and crises through immediate life-saving interventions and long-term solutions.
 
In 2024, UNICEF Colombia's emergency response efforts prioritised holistic and sustainable approaches to addressing complex challenges. Key areas of focus included ensuring learning continuity in regions affected by humanitarian crises, preventing risks associated with armed conflict—such as landmine accidents and the recruitment of children by illegal groups—and enhancing community preparedness for climate-related emergencies.
 
A cornerstone of UNICEF’s strategy was to provide both immediate relief and medium-term solutions by integrating humanitarian assistance, peacebuilding, and sustainable development. In 2024, UNICEF provided critical services to more than 27,300 children and adolescents as part of its response to sudden-onset emergencies. These services include safe drinking water and hygiene, socioemotional first aid, primary health care and nutrition services, and risk prevention measures. Additionally, life-saving protection pathways were activated to safeguard children and adolescents in vulnerable situations. UNICEF provided these services in response to 15 distinct emergency events, including seven linked to armed conflict, such as displacement and confinement. Additionally, UNICEF responded to three floods and two droughts exacerbated by climate change, to , to almost 31,000 people in need.
 
UNICEF's initiatives evolved from direct intervention and assistance to more systemic approaches, integrating their programmes into local government strategies, enhancing legal support, focusing on sustainable models for long-term impact on migrant children's welfare, and incorporating gender transformative content and tools.

The approach to protect migrant children from violence, particularly gender-based violence (GBV), was refined through the implementation of the "Inspira" model. “Inspira” systematises good practices and lessons learned from previous experiences, is based on the recognition of the differential impacts of migration on children, adolescents, women, and girls, and proposes psychosocial actions to strengthen their knowledge and skills to protect themselves, to access to child protection services, local integration opportunities and increase their empowerment, was adopted by the Mayor's Office of Barranquilla enhancing community prevention services in urban areas with migrant populations. Furthermore, as its migratory component, UNICEF collaborated to integrate "Inspira" into ICBF's "Atrapa Sueños" strategy. It was implemented in Nariño, Arauca, Norte de Santander, Vichada, and Atlántico, benefiting 2,569 children (1,192 boys and 1,377 girls / 6-10 years: 46%; 11-18: 54%).
 
UNICEF's "Te acompaño" strategy, aimed at identifying migrant children at high risk or survivors of violence (especially GBV), facilitating their access to protection systems, according to their special age and gender differential needs, was incorporated into ICBF's Response Mobile Teams for Migrant Children (ERAM). ERAM operates in Turbo, Necoclí, Acandí, Nariño, Arauca, Norte de Santander, and La Guajira, focusing on areas with increased migration and child protection risks. 958 children (45% girls and 55% boys / 6-10 years: 14%; 11-18: 86%) accessed protection services

In Business Engagement and Child Rights agenda, it is worth mentioning the progress made in: a) specially in Education (with 50 companies and private sector organizations contributing to Schoo-to-Work strategy "Vidas en Trayectoria" and cajas de compensación familiar receiving formal transfers of PIO methodology) and Social Inclusion (with the launch of Empresas que Cuidan Colombia and the technical assistance to government in the "Care CONPES". b) breastfeeding promotion with Banco de Bogotá and El Dorado Airport, including strong advocacy efforts.

Partnership with the private sector to advance early child development 
 
In 2024, UNICEF partnered with Jerónimo Martins, a Portuguese company operating in food distribution and specialized retail across various countries, including Colombia, to enhance child development services in Tumaco. This collaboration adopted a comprehensive approach, focusing on strengthening local coordination mechanisms, ensuring smooth transitions into school, early detection of malnutrition, promoting healthy lifestyles, and improving early childhood education (ECE) services through better pedagogical guidelines. The multisectoral model encompassed education, child protection, health, and nutrition services, engaging key local stakeholders such as the Working Group on Children, Adolescents and Families (MIAF), the Colombian Institute for Family Welfare (ICBF), and the Education Secretariat.
 
The mobilisation of private sector resources enabled reaching 2,936 children and teachers. Six educational institutions were rehabilitated and 181 professionals received training to enhance children's learning outcomes. The collaboration also improved responsiveness to complex challenges by ensuring resources were allocated to the areas of greatest need. Private sector resources enabled the implementation of innovative strategies and positioned the partnership as a catalyst for programmatic advancements in early childhood development (ECD). In summary, this partnership delivered immediate results and strengthened the sustainability of interventions, significantly improving the wellbeing of children in Tumaco. It also demonstrated the potential for scaling this framework to other regions with similar needs. As of 2023, only 51% of young children in Colombia had access to ECD services, highlighting the importance of this initiative.
 
2. Partnership with the private sector to support higher education and workforce integration for adolescents.
 
The "Life Trajectories: Opportunities for High School Students" strategy fostered partnerships between schools and the private sector to support students' career perspectives (locally termed life projects) through internships, mentoring, business visits, workshops, training programs, business fairs, and social entrepreneurship initiatives. To date, 24 partnerships have been established with private sector organisations across the construction, agribusiness, tourism, digital services, and creative industries sectors, benefiting 1,779 adolescents. These efforts have been instrumental in promoting transitions to post-secondary education and facilitating a smooth progression from school to the workforce.
 
The partnership also engaged with 27 organisations in Apartadó, Tumaco, Tibú, Belén de Bajirá, and Barranquilla to identify their key human resource needs and connect them with micro-credential programs involving adolescents. This approach equipped young people with the tools to make informed decisions about their future.
 
In Barranquilla, UNICEF established a technical working group to facilitate ongoing discussions on the school-to-work transition. The group brought together nine organisations, including the local education authority, the local social development authority, and private sector representatives. The working group seeks to align the educational needs of institutions with the demands of the productive sector, addressing regional skill gaps. A collaborative work plan has been developed, extending through 2025, to coordinate efforts among the participating institutions effectively.
 
3. Partnerships for the prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse perpetrated by humanitarian actors.
 
As co-leaders of the Protection Against Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) Task Force, members from the Country Humanitarian Team (CHT), Interagency Group on Mixed Migration Flows(GIFMM), and the PSEA Network were engaged in the national adaptation of the Sexual Exploitation and Abuse Risk Overview (SEARO). This collaboration was instrumental in identifying local risks, using locally sourced data, and enabling a more detailed geographic risk analysis. These efforts will strengthen local ownership and evidence-based decision-making for the SEARO, benefiting Local Coordination Teams, the local GIFMM, and other stakeholders.
 
The adapted SEARO will be integrated into the Response Plan for Community Priorities (RPCP), Refugee and Migrant Needs Analysis (RMNA), and Regional Refugee and Migrant Response Plan (RMRP)  planning processes, improving resource mobilisation to prevent and mitigate sexual exploitation and abuse risks and to support victims. UNICEF's key contribution was incorporating a child rights perspective into the process, informed by lessons learned and data from the country office's 2024 Child Risk Overview.
 
4. Partnerships before, during and after COP16
 
In partnership with key stakeholders, UNICEF Colombia played a central role in amplifying the voices of children, adolescents, and youth in climate and biodiversity discussions during pre-COP16 and COP16 events. Collaborations with organisations like the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), the Global Youth Biodiversity Network (GYBN), Save the Children, Fondo Acción, and Colombian government entities, including the ICBF and the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, were critical to these achievements. Additional support from UN agencies such as the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) further contributed to the success of these efforts.
 
The partnership launched in July 2024 with the development of a roadmap agreed upon during a meeting between the ICBF, the Ministry of Environment and UNICEF. This roadmap outlined a clear strategy to ensure the inclusion of children, adolescents, and youth in COP16 events and negotiations. UNICEF facilitated the involvement of LCOY and GYBN as official youth representatives for climate change and biodiversity and brought together additional partners, including Save the Children and Fondo Acción, to contribute technical expertise and resources.

As a result of this partnership, UNICEF and its partners organised ten pre-COP territorial events, engaging 544 young people and ensuring broad representation. In the week leading up to COP16, significant events such as Colombia Teaches Colombia (COL-COL) and the National and Global Youth Summits brought together 750 young people (437 women and 313 men) to discuss biodiversity conservation. These dialogues culminated in a statement presented to the President of COP16.
 
At COP16, partners coordinated ten UN Pavilion events featuring 40 panellists. The Pavilion itself was a notable symbol of successful collaboration, with eight UN agencies working together to present an intersectional perspective on biodiversity conservation and emphasize the importance of including diverse communities in decision-making. 

These partnerships transformed COP16 and pre-COP16 into powerful platforms for elevating youth perspectives in climate and biodiversity policymaking. The collaboration continues to thrive, focusing on advancing nationally determined, child-sensitive contributions and strengthening the role of youth in both global and national environmental agendas.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
1. Transitioning from a project-based approach to coalition building has proven to be a pivotal strategy in advancing foundational literacy and setting the groundwork for Colombia to effectively address the learning crisis at scale. The main challenge has been integrating collective impact planning and programme implementation to mobilize territorial resources and secure substantial funding for evidence-based literacy materials. This coalition-building model, which leverages diverse expertise and resources, offers valuable insights for other initiatives within the education sector where large-scale, impactful interventions are needed.

2. During the current Country Programme, UNICEF developed a strategy to strengthen institutional capacities for protecting children on the move. It focuses on improving services of the specialised child protection system, enabling the Colombian State to expand coverage, identify at-risk children, refine prioritisation criteria, and incorporate methodologies that address the specific impacts of violence on children based on gender, age, and migratory profile.
The strategy enabled institutions such as the Colombian Institute for Family Welfare (ICBF) and the Barranquilla Mayor's Office to adopt these methodologies, leading to more timely, qualified, and differentiated care for migrant children—both to prevent violence and to meet their specific protection needs. 

However merely improving the existing services proved insufficient address specific risk factors, such as those faced by unaccompanied adolescents nearing adulthood. In response, UNICEF designed a targeted approach to promote the socio-economic integration of migrant adolescents once they reached the age of majority. This initiative introduced innovative concepts, including autonomous living, the development and empowerment of migrant adolescents as agents of local and community development, and the promotion of deinstitutionalisation.
This new approach has been adopted by ICBF, while underlying analysis have informed the new UNICEF Country Programme, serving as a key lesson to enhance the comprehensive strengthening of local child protection services.
 
3. Based on the formative evaluation of the Child-Friendly Territories Strategy, key actions were identified to strengthen UNICEF’s territorial approach and improve results for children and adolescents. Three main lessons emerged, which should be incorporated into the design of a new business model:

Coordination of actions and institutional actors: There is a need to enhance coordination among     humanitarian and development actors, strengthen local governments, and     involve the private sector and communities in co-creating resilient     ecosystems that can address various crises and challenges. 
Public-private synergies and investment optimisation: UNICEF’s technical and financial cooperation should focus on synergies and incentives to optimise public-private investment. This involves leveraging financing instruments that increase the impact and scale of national and territorial public programmes, ensuring they also include     preparedness and humanitarian response strategies. 
Local capacity building and service expansion: It is essential to integrate local     capacity-building from across programme areas to expand the range of comprehensive services and financing flows in prioritised territories. This includes promoting active participation from both the community and the private sector.
 
4.     Lessons learned in emergency preparedness and response
As Colombia was simultaneously affected by armed conflict, migration, climate-related disasters, and volcanic eruptions, significant progress was made in strengthening preparedness mechanisms and anticipatory actions.
