UNICEF’s contributions to policy, programmes and strategies across all pillars of the country programme, positioned the CO as a partner of choice due to its technical expertise and convening role on issues affecting children.  The introduction of a multi-sectoral mechanism on data management facilitated a constructive dialogue across ministries and sectors and paved the way for the approval of a new round of MICS 7, planned for 2025.  While this mechanism was initially established to assess progress on child related SDGs indicators, weaknesses identified during these monthly meetings opened the conversation on data sources and supported the decision to conduct a new MIC survey to update the data available on key children’s related SDGs.
Evidence gathered during the year for the Common Country Analysis allowed the CO to look at potential programmatic entry points that could inform the next country programme and address some of the pressing needs affecting the most vulnerable children.  While education, child protection, health, and nutrition interventions continue to be implemented in line with the CPD, new areas emerged, such as WASH and social policy, where UNICEF has expertise that could be tested in the country, consolidating UNICEF’s future role in these goal areas. In addition, the decentralization process offered new opportunities for focusing efforts on local governance and building local capacity on child-focused programming. 
Additionally, advocacy actions promoted the participation of children and adolescents, generating opportunities for greater consultations on issues that affect them and their engagement in public events and the media. The use of the Adolescent kit for expression and innovation offered a practical tool that could be relevant in different contexts to engage adolescents to discuss relevant issues, from violence prevention to psychosocial and emotional support and their role in responding to emergencies.  Civil society partners played a key role in facilitating these consultations, promoting participatory methodologies, and documenting child-centered experiences and valuing their opinions. A forum is planned for 2025 to identify innovative and replicable participatory approaches in Cuba, prioritizing active listening and adolescent empowerment in child-focused work.
The confluence of simultaneous emergencies and the decrease in national capacities for a rapid and effective response reaffirm the relevance of strengthening emergency preparedness with a focus on shock-responsive systems. Preparedness and pre-positioning of stocks have been key to ensure UNICEF had a timely and effective emergency response to hurricanes Oscar and Rafael and two earthquakes in Granma and Santiago provinces. The CO organized a rapid response and was the first UN agency to bring health and WASH supplies to respond to hurricane Oscar and Rafael, ensuring children’s needs were effectively and timely addressed while reaching nearly 400,000 people in the first weeks after the event.  This was particularly appreciated by affected populations and government counterparts, positioning UNICEF in the sector and capturing media coverage. The ongoing energy crisis affecting the country, including children’s services, has a negative impact on the continuity of their education as well as access to basic services such as water in school, requiring a climate resilient approach in the emergency response. Ensuring an effective climate resilient humanitarian-development nexus is key to future programmatic responses. 
In 2024, UNICEF Cuba harnessed and strengthened existing partnerships, to respond to both emergency and development needs. Despite Cuba’s challenging context, new partnerships and resources for development were identified and leveraged. More efforts with regional and global support are required in 2025 to expand public partnerships in contexts like Cuba. South-to-south cooperation needs to be emphasized in 2025 to complement system strengthening efforts. Public-private partnerships for early childhood development initiated in 2024 highlighted the need to review the potential of such partnerships across programmatic areas in 2025, including the role of businesses to advance results for children.

The Dominican Republic, an upper-middle-income country, has experienced robust economic growth and is aiming to achieve high-income status by 2030. The population stands at 10.7 million, with 31 percent under the age of 18 and 72 percent residing in urban areas. To align with its economic advancement, there is a necessity for the development of institutional capacities and social policies. 
 
President Luis Abinader was re-elected with a decisive 59 percent of the votes in the 2024 first round, reflecting strong popular support. His government is expected to continue focusing on economic stability and institutional reforms. The Modern Revolutionary Party (PRM) has maintained a significant majority in Congress, facilitating the implementation of its legislative agenda. 
 
A fiscal reform proposal, aimed at modernizing the tax system, increasing revenue, and reducing tax evasion, which could translate into more resources for social programs was withdrawn from Congress. Despite intense advocacy by UNICEF and multiple civil society partners, academia, and institutions, for both, the approval of the new Penal Code Bill, and the elimination of some provisions that could worsen child rights, such as physical punishment, the revision was postponed. Progress was made on the Legal Identity Law, the draft of General Education Law, and regulations on inclusive education. 
 
Public investment in children and adolescents saw a slight increase between 2016 and 2021, rising from five percent to six percent of GDP. Preliminary data for 2023 indicate it remains the same.  The Ministry of Tourism reported that during 2024 more than 11 million tourists visited the country. Along with remittances, which the Central Bank indicates amounted to USD 11 billion in 2024, and free trade zones, these have been the three main pillars for the country's economic stability. 
 
This year, there were modest advances in the implementation of the 2023 Committee on the Rights of the Child recommendations. The suggested legal framework reforms to prevent violence against women and children is pending but the protocol for the care of migrant children was approved. 
 
Child monetary poverty was 30 percent in 2023, a significant reduction from 2022, when it was 35 percent (MEPyD, 2023), while extreme monetary poverty affects five percent of Dominican children. Multidimensional child poverty (TPMI) declined from 22.3 percent in 2022 to 21.5 percent in 2023, reaching 27 percent in rural areas. 
 
The government continued to support poor households through the cash transfer programme Alimentate and others, reaching one and a half million households. The Fund for Support to Children and Adolescents with Disabilities is projected to double its coverage to 6,582 households in 2024. 
 
The emergency cash transfer for the floods in November 2023 reached 15,200 affected vulnerable households, (around 15,960 children and adolescents). The social protection system has shown flexibility and adaptability to make vertical and horizontal expansions of its regular programme.

The global hunger index established that 2.2 percent of children under five suffer from acute malnutrition while 7 percent were at risk, with a higher impact on households facing greater social and economic vulnerability, as well as on children on the move. 

The Neonatal Mortality Rate at the national level fell by 20 percent in 2024 compared to 2023 and in the prioritized hospitals supported by UNICEF it fell by 33 percent in the last three years. However, the Maternal Mortality Ratio increased from 115 in 2023 to 120 in 2024 (data by epidemiological week forty-four). 
 
The country still faces significant challenges in coverage of essential health services (currently at 66 percent), and basic immunization rates (82 percent). Only 51 percent of children under two years receive a diet with the minimum appropriate diversity. Challenges in delivery care include the extremely high C-Section rate (63 percent) and the low percentage of newborns placed in skin-to-skin contact with their mothers at birth (23 percent). Exclusive breastfeeding while increasing from 4 percent (2014) to 16 percent (2019) also remains insufficient (MICS 2019). 
 
The mental health of children and adolescents has shown deterioration according to various qualitative consultations conducted by UNICEF and its implementing partners, without a clear policy yet ensuring provision of mental health services. 
 
Adequate knowledge about HIV/AIDS prevention has decreased to 32 percent, and only 62 percent of women received counseling on HIV/AIDS during their prenatal care visits (MICS 2019).  

The Ministry of Education reported very encouraging learning improvements between 2023 (baseline year) and 2024 in the first three grades of primary through the Building the Base of Learning (CON BASE) Programme: the worst performing students in previous assessments achieved higher growth than the rest in satisfactory learning, in reading and writing competencies jumping from 17 percent to 50 percent. The group with the worst results in Mathematics improved from 47 percent to 65 percent in the "solving calculations and counting" competency. 

Fifteen percent of girls experience their sexual initiation before the age of 15. Condom use among occasional sexual partners has decreased in recent years to 46 percent. Both trends present significant challenges for sexual and reproductive health education in the country. While adolescent fertility has decreased slightly, early motherhood remains a concern, with 20 percent of girls under 18 having given birth. Also, two percent of girls under 15 have experienced early motherhood, underscoring the need for targeted interventions. Educational attainment plays a significant role, as half of adolescents who only reach primary education have had a child before the age of 18, compared to six percent of those with tertiary education. Furthermore, 61 percent of girls and adolescents have experienced sexual violence at some point in their lives (MICS 2019). 
 
Early unions remain a common practice, even though child marriage is legally prohibited under the age of 18 without exception. There was a slight reduction from 37 percent in 2014 to 32 percent in 2019 for young women who married or were in union before the age of 18, and from 12 percent to nine percent for those who united or married before the age of 15. Among those in the poorest quintile, half of all women were in union before the age of 18, while for women from households with only primary education, this figure reaches 65 percent.  
 
Foreign children, without regular residence, especially from Haiti, can access education and basic health services, which are not denied due to their migratory status. However, the lack of birth registration (whether Dominican or foreign) prevents them from receiving study certificates after finishing school, in addition to denying them access to a legal identity and social protection services. 

Only 45 percent of households have adequate water management (free from E.coli and available when needed) for drinking at home. The effects of climate change are disproportionately affecting children in vulnerable areas.  
 
Due to its geographical location, the country is exposed to tropical storms, floods, droughts, and earthquakes. The state has a good capacity to respond immediately to disasters caused by climate shocks. Prevention and response to other disasters and crises are more limited, especially concerning earthquakes, despite the island being at risk due to its positioning on a series of geological faults.  
 
Advances in artificial intelligence and technology are beginning to impact children and adolescents, highlighting the need for inclusive digital education. Digital infrastructure is robust, with 85 percent internet penetration and 90 percent mobile coverage. However, a 60 percent gap in access to significant connectivity exists between the highest and lowest income brackets, particularly in rural areas.

General Outlook  

UNICEF is focusing its efforts to ensure that the State defines legal frameworks, develops policies and institutions, assigns sufficient resources, and has effective capacity to ensure the basic rights of all children through quality, equitable and sustainable programmes and policies that are implemented at scale. As different sectors and subsectors present diverse levels of development our emphasis varies somewhat among different issues: focus on primary education and maternal neonatal health is mostly on improving quality and effectiveness of services, inclusive education work tries to address issues of equity, in early childhood and early unions our focus is veering towards increasing coverage while on other sectors, such as protection and response to violence and abuse and social protection, we are still focusing on supporting the design of the basic structures of the system. 
   
To ensure that our strategies and internal structure are well fitted to address these challenges, UNICEF DR is engaged in the New Business Model Initiative to explore innovative strategies to enhance our impact and efficiency in this evolving context.   
   
EDUCATION  

While coverage for primary education is virtually universal in the Dominican Republic, and several efforts have been put in place to strengthen the system, low learning achievements – as compared to comparable countries in LAC – remain a major challenge for the full enjoyment of children’s right to quality education, and to the longer-term development prospects of the DR.   
  
To respond to this challenge UNICEF has been supporting the Ministry of Education (MoE), through a focused strategy to enhance foundational learning in the first cycle of primary, as the policy from which to enhance lifelong learning capacities. In 2024 we are starting to see the first encouraging fruits of these efforts, which are reaching 100% of students of the first cycle in public schools.   
  
The MoE continued the nationwide implementation of the Building the Base of Learning (CON BASE) Programme, improving the fundamental learning of Spanish Language and Mathematics, which has reached universal coverage in public schools in 2024. CON BASE has proven to be effective in improving student learning, with an equity focus, significantly reducing the gap between children with the best and those with the worst results. This has been possible due to UNICEF’s capacity development effort in the MoE to improve the ongoing training and coaching of teachers and the constant monitoring of results so that managers can generate improvement plans for the implementation based on evidence.  
 
The progress in improving learning achievements was confirmed with the results of the two learning assessments: a survey in 2024 and a census in 2023. A critical equity result was that the students who had obtained the worst results in the initial assessment achieved a higher percentage of satisfactory learning in Reading and Writing, increasing from 17% to 50% achievement in the "writing text types" competency, narrowing the gap between those with the best and worst results from 33 to 13 percentage points. The group with the worst results, in Mathematics, improved from 47% to 65% in the "solving calculations and counting" competency, reducing the gap between the groups with the best and worst results from 38 to nine percentage points. These data were validated by external researchers.  

Having reached scale and impact, the focus is now on sustainability and quality assurance, further strengthening the capacities of local and regional teams of MoE, allowing the gradual withdrawal of external support. Its represents an exemplary proof of UNICEF’s role and value add in middle income countries.    
 
Another crucial challenge shared with many countries in LAC is ensuring that education becomes a truly inclusive process, which ensures the rights of children with disabilities to reach their full potential and be integrated into their communities and society at large.  
In 2024 the Dominican Republic reached a historic milestone, with the approval of Ordinance 05-2024 by the National Education Council, establishing the Inclusive Education Guidelines for the national educational system with UNICEF support.  
 
This achievement was inspired and informed by a UNICEF-backed pilot experience in 9 educational centres for two years, which was the basis to design and validate the Inclusive Education Model of the Dominican Republic, covering initial, primary, and technical-professional education. School principals, teachers, families, students and MoE officials participated in the pilot experience, and consultations were held with civil society working with people with disabilities.   
 
The normative framework was complemented by a Progressive Scale-up Plan that defines milestones and funding requirements to ensure that inclusive education becomes a reality in the DR over time. To guarantee the national appropriation and progressive scale-up of the model, training of local universities as capacity multiplication hubs is being currently organized with the support of international UNICEF experts (fully funded by the GoDR).  
 
The DR has high quality early childhood development public services, though coverage is limited. The system has an explicit equity focus and services are currently oriented towards the most deprived. UNICEF supported the National Institute for Early Childhood Development (INAIPI) in implementing two national rounds of assessments using the Dominican Early Childhood Development Measuring System (SIMEDID), reaching over 118,000 children. For the first time there is data collected for a period of 18 months on children’s development, allowing INAIPI to create individualized follow up plans and make efficient and targeted policy decisions based on evidence. Preliminary results are promising, with 84% of children meeting their developmental milestones. In 2024, SIMEDID has been promoted as the national standard tool, seeking its gradual adoption by all sectors providing services to children under five. Furthermore, SIMEDID innovation has become a reference for other countries in the region. In addition to focusing on quality, discussions are ongoing with the Ministry of the Presidency (MP) to design strategies to expand coverage of ECD programmes.   
  
EARLY UNIONS  

With one in three young women having entered marriage or marital union before the age of 18, the DR presents one of the worst levels of this harmful practice in LAC. UNICEF has been engaging with other national and international actors to address this challenge for child rights. In the past years because of these efforts child marriage was banned in 2021, and a national Policy for the Prevention and Care of Early Unions and Adolescent Pregnancy (PPA) was put in place. The issue has become a national priority with intersectoral support.  
 
UNICEF continued to support the implementation of the PPA providing technical and financial assistance to the SUPERATE Programme to implement interventions for the empowerment of girls and adolescents through the Girls' Clubs, as well as awareness-raising among mothers, young men,  adults and community leaders in nine prioritized municipalities, reaching 3,454 girls and adolescents between the ages of 10 and 19 participating in the Girl Clubs programme at the end of 2024 (surpassing the annual goal by 14%). The girls in the programme showed improved knowledge and life skills, especially in recognizing their rights, understanding gender roles, and adopting attitudes that foster their empowerment.   
 
As part of the behaviour change strategy to prevent early unions, SUPERATE promotes the creation of an enabling environment for girls and adolescents and sensitized 3,530 mothers and fathers and community leaders. Through the MoE, 60,078 (31,778 girls) secondary school students from 4 prioritized educational regions increased their knowledge about the causes and consequences of early unions in 2024. Since 2021, 297,786 secondary school students (158,352 women) from 1,442 schools have participated in specific sessions for the prevention of early unions.  
 
Supérate partnered with five civil society organizations to implement the programme, expanding its modalities of implementation, fostering collaboration with civil society, and generating key evidence for scaling the programme to additional territories. Moreover, also in 2024, Supérate increased its investment in the programme and secured an enhanced budget for the Girls' Clubs and complementary efforts to prevent early unions in 2025. Discussions are ongoing with other institutions to explore alternative strategies for scale-up.  
  
HEALTH & NUTRITION  

Comparing epidemiological week 45 in 2023 with the same week in 2024, 611 newborns’ lives were saved thanks to interventions and strategies aimed at caring for mothers and their newborns.  
 
From January to October 2024, UNICEF supported the National Health Service (SNS) in implementing and strengthening the Kangaroo Mother Care programme, reaching 3,799 premature and low-weight babies from 18 hospitals .This raised the total number of premature and low-weight babies who have received kangaroo mother interventions since 2020 to 38,039, with only 9.5% abandoning the programme. UNICEF has provided technical assistance to improve the neurological assessment of premature and low-weight babies cared for in kangaroo units. The Retinopathy Detection Programme was also implemented in 16 of these hospitals to prevent blindness with a total of 3,706 premature infants having been screened.   
 
UNICEF's support, along with other agencies, for the Accelerated Plan to Reduce Neonatal Deaths is having an impact on the lives of newborns. Clinical practice showed a significant improvement as monitoring indicates that the number of prioritized hospitals has achieved an 80% compliance level with protocols for low-risk pregnancy, vaginal delivery, postpartum maternal care, immediate newborn care, and breastfeeding. This increased from three to 11 (of the 24 hospitals). These measures have benefited 57% of all newborns (51,015), corresponding to the 24 hospitals for the period January-October 2024.   
 
The national neonatal mortality rate decreased by 20% in 2024 compared to 2023, and in the 22 UNICEF-supported priority hospitals, the rate per 1,000 live births dropped from 30 in 2022 to 25 in 2023 and 20 in 2024, a 33% reduction. This success was made possible by the coordinated efforts of UNICEF, PAHO/WHO, UNFPA, USAID, Project Hope and DOFMI to improve the technical skills of 210 nurses in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) in six hospitals. They strengthened infection prevention and control measures, particularly reinforcing adherence to handwashing protocols as a critical intervention, the medical equipment disinfection and reuse of disposables, aiming to reduce hospital acquired infections and improve overall patient safety in neonatal care settings.  
 
In a performance evaluation of seven of the ten prioritized NICUs conducted by nurses from Miguel Servet Hospital in Zaragoza, Spain, deficiencies in actions protecting the neurodevelopment of premature babies were identified. In response, UNICEF provided technical assistance to train 50 neonatologists and NICU nurses in development-centered neonatal care (DCNC), to reduce stress and suffering of neonates, promote neurological and emotional development, the importance of skin-to-skin contact and keeping NICUs open for parents to maintain contact with their babies. The training also presented evidence on environmental factors such as lighting and noise causing toxic stress and the promotion of non-nutritive sucking and motor containment, along with active pain prevention through non-pharmacological measures.  

Some progress has been achieved in reducing the cesarean section rate in the monitored hospitals, which declined from 63% in 2023 to 51% in 2024.   
In collaboration with New York University, the annual reduction rates necessary to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were determined: The SDGs aim to achieve a rate of 70/100,000 live births for MMR and 12/100 live births for NMR in 20 prioritized hospitals. For MMR, the projected annual reduction for each hospital ranges from 3.4% to 25%, and for NMR, from 3% to 16.7%, with averages of 8.85% and 6.3%, respectively.  
 
A bottleneck analysis of WASH conditions in health centres and the effects of climate change using the WASH BAT tool was conducted, facilitated by SIWI and coordinated by the MEPYD and the CCC, with the participation of over 50 central and local health managers and technicians, water and sanitation service operators, and NGOs. Preliminary results indicate that health centres in the DR face severe vulnerabilities to climate change; an action plan is being developed with national authorities and partners to strengthen the resilience of the health system in WASH.  

CHILD PROTECTION   
  
Normative and institutional framework for child protection  

A comprehensive legal review and advocacy strategy was concluded, following the 2023 CRC Observations and the CPSS approach. The main recommendations from this study include revising laws to explicitly prohibit all forms of violence, and the importance of improving institutional responses and promoting preventive measures.   
  
Simultaneously, intra- and inter-sectoral coordination mechanisms between CONANI and other sectoral actors were designed and agreed upon in line with CRC recommendations. Strategic high-level political events were held to relaunch the strategic framework for strengthening the child protection system as the road map for the prioritized actions with all the institutions involved.  
  
UNICEF provided technical and financial assistance to CONANI to implement a special protection risk case management model, supported by the PRIMERO/CPIMS+ platform, and supported the recruitment of 12 and the training of 40 frontline staff. UNICEF also supported the creation of the Case Management Unit and a case management model within CONANI.   
  
Thanks to UNICEF's advocacy, the Protocol for Identification, Care, and Protection of Children and Adolescents on the Move was approved by CONANI to ensure that the best interests of the child are prioritized, preventing arbitrary deportations, and safeguarding the rights of vulnerable children and families affected by migration.   
  
Legal identity  

Progress was achieved in strengthening legal identity for vulnerable populations through innovative research, cross-sector collaboration, advocacy to enhance legal frameworks, and targeted interventions. UNICEF's efforts resulted in a new protection protocol, capacity-building for institutions, and benefits for over 10,000 children and families.  
  
Although progress has been made through initiatives like hospital-based birth registration, the modernization of civil registration laws and simplified late registration processes, significant gaps persist. UNICEF agreed with MoH and PAHO to revise the manual for birth and death registration, for standardizing birth certificate issuance to enhance the accuracy and accessibility of civil registration. A total of 356 public officials, 123 community leaders and 180 representative individuals from vulnerable communities were trained in birth registration procedures.  
  
Children on the Move  

UNICEF installed a safe space for children at the main migration detention centre to provide a safe and separate area for children (best interest determination, psychosocial support, nutrition, immunization, mitigation of GBV risks). UNICEF maintained personnel in 4 of 6 migration detention centres, assisting 9,743 (57% male) detained children, including 3,250 (71% male) Unaccompanied and Separated Children (UASC), including 68 pregnant or lactating adolescents. Of the total UASC, 717 (60% male) UASC were also released and reunified with their families in the DR, including 155 (57% male) minors entitled to the Dominican nationality, and 31 pregnant adolescents. 1,043 children accompanied by an adult were released and reunified in the DR. Cases assisted represented a 61% increase compared to 2023. Despite UNICEF’s advocacy, 1,856 UASC children were returned to Haiti.   
  
Psychosocial support in detention centers was provided to 5,165 (2,814 female), including 561 adults, 160 received help to obtain legal identity, 2,135 received personal hygiene and menstrual dignity kits, and 2,515 received food and water.   
  
UNICEF provided information on accessing services, particularly for migratory regularization and birth registration, and referred 10,000 children, adolescents, and their families to specialized services for access to documentation, education, health, and mental health, especially in cases of gender-based violence. More than 2,000 children and adolescents participated in community recreational and psychosocial support activities.  
  
Were established 22 new friendly spaces and 18 communities were trained to provide psychosocial support in vulnerable groups, primarily targeting populations affected by migration, bringing the total to 40 friendly spaces in the country supported by UNICEF.   
  
UNICEF trained and developed tools to strengthen the capacities of public officials, armed forces members, and civil society on the rights of children in mobility: a diploma for 34 migration agents; a specialized course for 50 inspectors and immigration control coordinators; 91 public officials completed other related courses. Support was also provided for the International Seminar "Global Flows of Human Mobility and Migration Policies," with 400 attendees.

SOCIAL INCLUSION  
 
During 2024, UNICEF supported the government's progress in including the most vulnerable children in social protection programmes. Through the National Fund for Children and Adolescents with Disabilities, the SUPERATE programme reached 6,582 households, 106% more than in 2023. UNICEF also supported the strengthening of shock-responsive social protection to respond to multiple impacts, more effectively identify affected vulnerable households, and provide a comprehensive response according to their needs. In addition to the above, UNICEF supported the government in monitoring public investment in children for the fiscal years 2022 and 2023. 
 
CLIMATE CHANGE  

The country has made significant progress in integrating a child focus in its climate change policies and is gradually adopting a regional and global leadership role on this matter.  

Several workshops and forums were held on the effects of climate change on early childhood, children and adolescence; adaptation processes; and strengthening the resilience of basic services aimed at children.  A Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC-RD) is being developed under the coordination of the Climate Change Council (CCC), with UNICEF support and the participation of CONANI, MP, INAIPI, and MoE, to identify the main climate threats and risks of early childhood, children, and adolescence and propose appropriate responses.  The Government has committed to integrating an early childhood, children, and adolescence approach in the update of the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) with UNICEF support, to be submitted to the UNFCCC in 2025.   
  
The Delegation of the DR in the expert dialogue on children and climate change, held within the framework of SB60 in Bonn in June 2024 played a vocal role in stressing the importance of climate change for young children.  The Vice-Minister of Environment and Natural Resources of the DR acted as a key speaker in the special session of the Executive Board for “Putting children at the heart of climate action and galvanizing global solutions.”  
 
EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE 

UNICEF made significant progress in emergency preparedness and resilience in the areas of education, nutrition, WASH, and operations. In education, the ECHO-funded project was completed, resulting in 80 school DRM plans, training for 525 staff and the engagement of 402 children as climate change ambassadors, in addition to various policy development initiatives. In the area of nutrition, UNICEF procured RUTF packages for distribution and worked on national guidelines for emergency nutrition. WASH activities included supporting the national coordination group, monitoring cholera cases, and improving preparedness through the purchase of hygiene kits. 
 
  
YOUTH PARTICIPATION  

In August 2024, the country joined the U-Report global network, as a tool to facilitate adolescent and youth participation. Coordination efforts were made with government institutions, civil society, and UN agencies, which facilitated the recruitment of more than 1,700 U-Reporters. Of this total, 65% correspond to adolescents between 13 and 19 years old, while 26% are young people between 20 and 24 years old.    
    
In 2024, the Adolescent and Youth Advisory Council (Altavoz), formed by UNICEF in 2022, was consolidated and consistently supported activities, initiatives and projects of UNICEF and its partners. The initiative "I recommend for my rights” included a consultation with adolescents and young people on their priorities for health, education, violence prevention, poverty and spaces for recreation and participation, which were presented to public officials and decision-makers in the framework of the celebration of the Summit of the Future.  
  
KNOWLEDGE MANAGEMENT   

Knowledge management work focused on strengthening the capacities of monitoring and evaluation of national data and statistics systems. The financial and technical support for the ENHOGAR 2024 (annual household survey) was key for obtaining critical data about children. Two evaluations were developed: a) Programme for the reduction of child marriage and early unions 2018-2023; and b) global evaluation of early childhood educational services and educational outcomes in the early years of education (ECE-ECD) with a stand-alone paper. Eleven studies were completed during the year and another fifteen are ongoing. A community of practice of researchers on children’s issues was established as well as a new initiative to promote the generation and sharing of knowledge on children in the DR.

UNICEF established and consolidated several strategic partnerships with the aim of advancing its mission to improve the lives of children and adolescents. These collaborations have yielded significant results, demonstrating the power of collective action in addressing critical issues. 

UNICEF's communication efforts have been successful in positioning child rights through 3,861 top media publications, reaching over 20 million people and increasing followers by 4.13% to 220,893. These efforts have also received support from 93 celebrity influencers and 32 children. 

UNICEF has taken the first steps in 2024 towards creating a strong, well-articulated and effective network of civil society organizations, starting with implementing partners and strategic allies in current interventions, to gradually grow into a national coalition for the rights of children and adolescents. With this purpose, the country office conducted a mapping of civil society organizations to strengthen the Country Programme partnership strategy. In 2024, UNICEF resumed its collaboration with faith-based organizations, which have proven to be valuable allies in the past. These organizations are strategically targeted to achieve current results. 

Thanks to these partnerships, the office received resources from a variety of funding sources, including private companies, individual donors, bilateral donors, national committees, regular resources, and thematic funds. 

UNICEF raised $2.1 million, an increase of 36%, with a 56% increase in individual donors, Working on Business for Results, 145 businesses were engaged: 44 were donor companies, and 60 donated in kind through their core business. 

The in-kind contribution was US$1.4M, especially in publicity and thanks to the partnerships with media, which provided important brand positioning.  
 
Advocacy efforts with different business sectors to raise awareness of the impact of climate change on early childhood, participating in the Annual Business Forum, which reached 47 companies and where UNICEF promoted responsible business practices and investment in children.   

Bilateral donors such as the Bureau Population for Refugees and Migrants of the US (BPRM), European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), the Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), and the Generalitat Valenciana through the Spanish Committee were decisive for the results with vulnerable populations, including girls and children on the move. 

The office also received regular resources and thematic funds, which were earmarked for specific purposes, including the Girl's Strategy, education, Climate Change, Water and Sanitation, and Health.  
 
These funds were used as catalytic funds to leverage public funds from the government, with the aim of achieving better results for children. In education, UNICEF has successfully made the Ministry of Education the main partner and financier of the Education component. This is because the joint actions impact the strengthening of the quality of the national educational system, aligning it with government planning. 
 
The Building the Base of Learning (CON BASE) Programme, the Inclusive Education Model and the National Strategy for a Culture of Peace are all priorities in the current Government Plan and are integrated with actions, goals, and financing in the Sector Plan of the MoE.  
 
Additionally, the National Institute for Teacher Training and Capacity Building (INAFOCAM) is a key partner of UNICEF, financing the training processes included in the CON BASE programme. UNICEF is currently preparing a university training proposal to continue building national capacity, integrated into INFOCAM's planning, guaranteeing public funding. The Latin American Faculty of Social Sciences (FLACSO) is a key partner in the process of generating information for the implementation of the CON BASE Programme, supporting us with external research.  
 
In 2024, partnerships were crucial for advancing child protection in the country. The Office of the First Lady led events to reinforce initiatives and secure political prioritization. Collaborations with IOM and UNHCR improved civil registration, child protection, and the prevention of gender-based violence in detention centres, benefiting vulnerable children and their families. 
 
The collaboration with UN agencies (PAHO/WHO and UNFPA), DOFMI, and the technical support of Miguel Servet Hospital in Zaragoza, Spain, continues to provide technical assistance, equipment, and supplies to improve neonatal survival rates and maternal morbidity and mortality. A partnership with New York University has enabled the establishment of annual reduction rates for MMR and NMR needed to meet the 2030 health SDG targets in 20 prioritized hospitals. With this information, periodic monitoring of intra-hospital MMR and NMR trends will be possible, identifying gaps and designing strategies to address them. 
 
UNICEF has led the development and validation of official guidelines for emergency feeding and nutrition. This has been in collaboration with FAO, WFP, PAHO/WHO, INCAP, and national actors such as CONANI, INAIPI, INEFI, and ASODONUD. The document's aim is clear: to ensure food security during crises and strengthen emergency responses.  
 
In October 2024, the Technical Secretariat for Food Sovereignty and Nutritional Security (SETESSAN) invited UNICEF to analyze the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). This analysis, scheduled for January 2025, will identify populations at greatest risk and develop a focused action plan. The 2024 IPC report identified 1 million people in Phase 3 (crisis), emphasizing the urgent need for action to ensure food security. 
 
The partnerships with the Office of the First Lady were instrumental in promoting child protection, organizing significant events to bolster initiatives and ensure political prioritization. Collaborations with IOM and UNHCR improved civil registration, child protection and the prevention of gender-based violence in detention centres, benefiting vulnerable children and their families. 
 
In the social protection area, UNICEF's main partners were: 

The SUPERATE Programme, for the expansion of coverage of children with disabilities in social protection programmes and interventions for the prevention of early unions. 
To support the scaling up of early union prevention interventions, UNICEF strengthened its partnerships with five civil society organizations, including feminist organizations such as CIPAF (Research Center for Women's Action) and the NAM (Women's Support Center) and community organizations such as SOS Villages, Center for Integral Development and FUNDSAZURZA.  
The SUPERATE Programme, the Unified System of Beneficiaries (SIUBEN), WFP and UNDP were strategic partners for shock-responsive social protection.  

The study of the investment aimed at children and adolescents (IpNA 2022 and 2023) was coordinated by the General Directorate of Budget (DIGEPRES) of the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Economy, Planning and Development (MEPyD) and the National Council for Children and Adolescents (CONANI). 
 
To advance the intersection between climate change, children, and adolescents, UNICEF strengthened its strategic alliance with the CNCCMDL, MoE, CONANI, INAIPI, and the Ministry of the Presidency (MP). 
 
To support the implementation of the adolescent and youth participation strategy and the U-Report platform, alliances with government institutions were strengthened and with the Ombudsman. Likewise, civil society organizations such as Red Cross Youth, Plan International, Scouts Dominicana, Globalizate Radio, University of British Columbia (UBC), among others.   
 
The new statistics law received support through the interagency Power of Data (PoD) initiative, with UNICEF as leader alongside UNFPA and the UN resident coordinator office. National evaluation capacities were strengthened with support of the UNICEF regional office. 

Key milestones in the CO's knowledge management strategy included formalizing an alliance with the University of British Columbia and partnering with the Etikos foundation for ethical review processes. Other allies were Vanderbilt University, UNIBE, CIPAF, and the University of Maine. They have also led to better evidence sharing and programmatic improvements.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

The country faced significant challenges in child protection, including delays in systemic reforms due to political transitions, increased deportations of Haitian migrants creating humanitarian gaps for unaccompanied children, and the delayed enactment of regulations under Law No. 4-23, which hindered progress in harmonizing legal identity processes.  Sustained advocacy and collaboration between stakeholders were essential to align legal frameworks with child protection goals. Furthermore, capacity-building for frontline staff enhanced case management and service delivery. Additionally, the effective use of data systems like PRIMERO demonstrated the potential to accelerate response times and improve decision-making.  
 
The observed reduction in neonatal mortality in 2023 and 2024 underscores the effectiveness of joint planning with the Acceleration Plan for Reducing Neonatal Mortality and coordinated implementation between cooperation agencies and health authorities. These best practices are expected to be applied to maternal mortality reduction efforts in 2025, generating evidence to challenge the political discourse attributing high MMR to external factors, such as the use of services by the Haitian population, and focusing on improving service quality and respectful care. 
 
To ensure quality care, the Ministry of Public Health must update obstetric care protocols, aligning them with evidence-based international standards, and strengthen its regulatory role in monitoring professional performance in this area.  Political commitment has been slow in establishing microbiology laboratories in eight of the ten prioritized facilities. Standardized cultures, such as Group B Streptococcus screening, are essential to prevent neonatal sepsis and must be consistently implemented. Frequent changes in authorities remain a significant challenge to ensuring continuity and improving service quality. Structural reforms, better hospital infrastructure, and specialized academic training are necessary to consolidate quality care aligned with user needs and improve health indicators. 
 
Innovations such as "nests" for premature infants have proven effective, replicating the womb environment to promote neurodevelopment. Additionally, promoting breastfeeding and non-pharmacological strategies to relieve pain highlights a holistic approach to neonatal care.  
The update of the NUTREMUAC App has enabled faster diagnoses and efficient follow-up for acute malnutrition. The exchange of best practices with UNICEF Mexico inspired the development of Norm 675, addressing front-of-pack food labelling, currently in the legislative approval process.  
 
The MoE's Building the Base of Learning (CON BASE) Programme, supported by UNICEF, has successfully established itself as a national scale and sustainable programme. It is promoted by the Literacy at an Opportune Age policy, which is a priority policy by the government with 100% public funding.  The lesson learnt is that thanks to UNICEF's technical assistance, the teaching methodology for national application has been developed, involving didactic sequence guides for teachers and booklets for students. Due to this national ownership, the methodology has been accepted and implemented in 100% of primary schools, making it the first national programme with its own standardized methodologies led by the MoE. 

The use of digital tools to monitor student learning has significantly strengthened the Ministry of Education's ability to track educational outcomes and improve student performance. These tools are now used more systematically by pedagogical coordinators in 85% of schools, contributing to more evidence-based implementation and documentation of learning in the CONBASE programme. 

In addressing the challenges of creating and strengthening a national mechanism for the participation of young people, UNICEF has learnt that a strategy is needed to build the capacity of government institutions and NGOs, including an understanding of what meaningful participation by young people really means. This implies promoting deep reflection on the institutional role as duty bearers of rights, challenging adult-centred attitudes or practices that limit the full exercise of the right to participation of children and adolescents. 
 
The knowledge management initiative focuses on impact and scalability by supporting management and programme teams in planning, results chains, and indicators providing immediate results as a support strategy for improving the efficiency of programme implementation.  
To advance in the integration of the intersection between early childhood and climate change, the articulation between the entities that guarantee the rights of early childhood and those of climate change has made it possible to advance this agenda.  
  
To accelerate the reach of the Girls' Clubs' educational programme, UNICEF collaborated with Supérate, forming a pioneering consortium of actors. This innovative model linked the public sector, private enterprise, civil society and the UN, enabling rapid deployment and enhancing capacities to prevent early unions. The Girls' Clubs were able to be rapidly deployed, local experiences of civil society organizations were utilized, and their capacities were increased. Drawing from this experience, UNICEF has developed a framework for designing sustainable models for expanding Girls' Clubs in rural environments and contexts where direct intervention by public institutions is challenging.   
 
Thinking about the future, the Dominican Republic CO is a participant/learning lab of the New Business Model Initiative, which is based on the following elements: technical and public advocacy, impactful policy design and midstream policy/programme implementation, amongst others. The cornerstone of this initiative is knowledge management, which involves the development of national capacities, the production of quality evidence and the enhancement of partnerships and innovations. The implementation of this initiative will engender a new modus operandi for scaling up and achieving impactful results for children.  
 
In terms of violence against children and adolescents, this remains a significant challenge. It is vital to accelerate the implementation of a system-wide advocacy plan that prioritizes the strengthening of the special protection system against violence at the highest political levels to guarantee sustainability and political commitment. UNICEF aims to reinforce advocacy for policy enforcement and cross-sector reforms to ensure that child protection remains a national priority. Expanding psychosocial support and community engagement initiatives will address vulnerabilities among migrant populations, and strengthening partnerships will mobilize resources and sustain progress. 
 
The agenda of climate change and children will demand a strong focus to support the government in defining child-sensitive climate policies, including NDC 3.0, and to position the country as a champion in the global arena regarding child rights and climate financing and policy mechanisms.   
 
To scale up the early union prevention interventions, UNICEF will focus its technical and financial assistance on improving the effectiveness of the SUPERATE Programme's operational processes, as well as on the design of an education programme to be implemented by the CSOs. The strategy includes the design of a pilot conditional cash transfer programme to complement the program, as well as the generation of evidence on its effectiveness to advocate for more public budget. 
 
Regarding education, given the strengthening of capacities in the territories, UNICEF is promoting a gradual withdrawal of its support, reducing international technical assistance to a minimum and national assistance to 60%, moving from support in the 18 regional areas to teamwork supporting the 5 axes that group the 18 educational regions. We will continue to support the actions of the program, promoting greater autonomy of the MoE actors.

The political situation in Ecuador is undergoing a significant transition with the presidential and National Assembly (Congress) elections scheduled for early 2025. In this context, a confrontation between the elected Vice President Veronica Abad and President Daniel Noboa has been a central point of political discussion. 

In the economic sphere, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) adjusted its growth forecasts for Ecuador in October 2024, projecting 0.3 per cent growth for 2024 and an improvement for 2025, with an estimated growth of 1.2 per cent. These figures are below regional projections of 2.1 per cent and 2.5 per cent for 2024 and 2025 respectively. In addition, the power crisis in the country has led to electricity rationing for several hours a day since October, which has  negatively impacted economic growth. The economic impact has grown significantly over time and, for two months of interruptions in electricity supply, the Quito Chamber of Commerce estimated that the industrial sector lost USD 4 billion, while the commercial sector experienced a decrease of USD 3.5 billion[1]. 

Limited economic growth is also reflected by stagnant adequate employment. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), between September 2023 and September 2024, the adequate employment rate remained around 36 per cent. Similarly, there has been no statistically significant change in the income poverty between June 2023 and June 2024, standing at approximately 26 per cent. As for income poverty among children and adolescents, this indicator was 33.2 per cent in 2023, compared with 23.9 per cent of the general population, which shows a greater impact on children and adolescents[2].

Child labour remains a serious problem, especially in rural areas. In 2023, child labour affected 17.7 per cent of adolescents aged 15 to 17 nationwide, rising to 40.1 per cent in rural areas and reaching a worrying 63.8 per cent among the indigenous population[3].

Violence is another major concern in the country. According to the Ministry of the Interior, 6,986 homicides were recorded in 2024, of which 582 were children and adolescents. The records show a 15% reduction compared to 2023; however, it remains one of the highest rates in the region, reaching a rate of 39 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants [4]. Violence against children begins in the early years of life, with 53.4 per cent of children between the ages of 1 and 4 experiencing psychological violent discipline and 46.1 per cent suffering physical violent discipline[5] according to the INEC National Survey of Child Malnutrition 2023-2024. Due to the increase of violence, the National Government has declared State of Emergency some territories in Ecuador.

Chronic malnutrition in children has been a priority for the last four governments. According to the National Survey of Child Malnutrition, there was a 0.8 percentage point decrease between the 2022-2023 and 2023-2024 among children under two years of age, although this reduction is not statistically significant. Inequalities persist; while chronic malnutrition nationwide was 19.3 per cent in the 2023-2024 survey, it reached 32.3 per cent among indigenous children. Children in the rural Sierra region are among the most affected, with a 26.8 per cent rate. As for overweight and obesity, in 2018, 35.4% of children between 5 and 11 years of age have overweight or obesity [6].  

In terms of mortality rates, they decreased between 2022 and 2023: from 6.7 to 5.8 per cent for neonatal, from 10.7 to 9.7 per cent in children below 1 year of age, and from 13.1 to 12.3 per cent in children under five years of age per 1,000 live births[7].  The maternal mortality ratio also decreased from 41.2 to 35.6 per 100,000 live births between 2022 and 2023.
 
The country faces additional challenges to achieve comprehensive early child development. The National Survey of Child Malnutrition 2023-2024 shows that anaemia affects 36.9 per cent of children under two years of age. In addition, 30.5 per cent of children under five consume water contaminated with E. coli, with a higher incidence in rural areas (48.9 per cent) compared to urban areas (20.7 per cent). Just six out of ten children under the age of five are engaged in four or more activities with a household member, and only 40.9 per cent have one or more books, with a marked difference based on the educational level of the mothers (25.3 per cent whose mothers have basic or no education, 64.8 per cent whose mothers have higher education). On average, children between 43 and 59 months old understand 29.5 words, with significant variations based on the educational level of their mothers (24.5 if their mothers have basic or no education, 35.8 if their mothers have higher education)[8]. In addition, there is a problem of public provision of child development services; only three out of ten children under the age of three can access such services.

In education, there remains a challenge to ensure the inclusion of approximately 265,000 children and adolescents between the ages of 5 and 17 who are outside the education system and represent 6.4% of that age group [9]. Fifty-five per cent of those outside the education system are adolescents aged 15 to 17.  Among the main reasons for dropping out of school in this group are the lack of financial resources and an educational offer that does not meet their expectations.  In the case of female adolescents, pregnancy and childcare are significant factors. In addition to access problems, there are low learning levels. The pandemic exacerbated learning difficulties at all levels of education, resulting in a decline in academic achievement, both during and after the pandemic. Currently, only three out of ten children in middle basic education (11 years old) manage to reach the minimum threshold of knowledge, skills and abilities that are essential for their level, both in Language and Literature and in Math.[10]

•       Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices, and essential supplies (supports SDGs 2 and 3; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 1; National Development Plan Objective 1; UNSDCF Area 1) 
 
UNICEF prioritized work to support the national government through the Technical Secretariat ‘Ecuador Grows Without Malnutrition’ and the MoH in updating regulations and tools to implement the strategy to reduce chronic malnutrition. UNICEF provided technical assistance to update the National Plan for Chronic Undernutrition in Children, supported capacity-building of service providers and conducted social behavioral campaigns at the local level in prioritized territories. UNICEF supported the implementation of a social and behavioural change (SBC) strategy aimed to prevent chronic undernutrition in children with the figure of “Maximo,” who played a key role with a projected reach of approximately 8 million people and who aims to generate community empowerment and SBC. 

UNICEF also provided technical assistance to health professionals to train them on best practices in breastfeeding protection, promotion and support and in the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and Chagas disease. These actions benefited pregnant women in priority communities. The country office also assisted in training adolescents as health promoters to lead prevention and community empowerment campaigns, with a special focus on teen pregnancy prevention.

In priority territories, technical assistance was provided via implementing partners to achieve cross-sectoral coordination at cantonal and parish boards with the aim of reducing the prevalence of chronic undernutrition in children by developing cross sectoral plans and nominal follow up of detected cases. It supported the administration of tools to measure and evaluate continuous quality improvement in health services and it supported community empowerment by training of community monitors. 

Finally, UNICEF empowered civil society organizations and academia to join efforts to build up strategies and policies to promote healthier food environments for children, in compliance with the agreements of the Cuenca Consensus. CO also updated the “ComeAventuras - Aquí por ti” tool, designed to promote healthy eating practices in children in the educational community.

•       Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future (supports SDG 4; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 2; National Development Plan Objective 2; UNSDCF Area 1) 

UNICEF made significant strides in promoting inclusive and quality education, early childhood development (ECD), and adolescent participation through innovative and evidence-based approaches. Collaborating with key partners, including the Ministry of Education, Institute of Evaluation of Education, Ministry of Social and Economic Inclusion in Ecuador, and international organisations. 

UNICEF prioritised inclusive ECD, benefiting over 44,801 children and strengthening the skills of 1,814 educators in marginalised areas. Key achievements included training 1,500 teachers in "growing-up with love" caregiving methodologies, positively impacting 37,542 children. A home-based early education model expanded services to 4,678 children in remote areas through tailored kits and support for itinerant educators.

The country office's education programmess impacted over 107,835 students and 10,626 of teachers. Initiatives included the implementation of a school reintegration programme and innovative evaluation systems, emphasising intercultural bilingual curricula and context-sensitive methodologies. A major milestone was the Early Warning System for school dropout prevention, piloted in 17 schools in three provinces, supporting 5,820 students and training 510 educators. In December 2024 UNICEF launched an extension of the system to include psychological risks and build a scalability plan to generalise its implementation. 

Additionally, UNICEF launched the Lahaa[1], digital platform to provide adolescents girls and women with educational and health information, focusing on gender-based violence prevention and teenage pregnancy prevention. During 2024, the platform in Ecuador received 61,937 visits. Teacher training complemented these efforts, ensuring the platform’s effective use. 
Partnerships facilitated the National Conference on Intercultural Bilingual Education, advancing bilingual intercultural curricula and ethno-educational models for Indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian communities. 

UNICEF developed intercultural bilingual pedagogies for the AiCofan[2] community, training educators and providing materials for 325 children. In Esmeraldas, a culturally adapted ethno-educational model supported Afro-Ecuadorian families, benefiting 1,256 children and 38 educators. These models focus on culturally sensitive ECD, ensuring access for the most vulnerable populations.

UNICEF’s ACCION 360 methodology strengthened transferable skills for 625 adolescents, emphasizing teamwork, critical thinking, and conflict resolution. Piloted in vulnerable areas, the program addressed adolescents’ concerns about education’s relevance, identified through the U-Report platform.

UNICEF organised podcast workshops for 283 adolescents in at-risk communities. Participants created 30 podcasts, amplifying their voices while fostering creativity and empowerment. These efforts complemented the "+Educa2"[3] competition, promoting digital technologies, 21st-century skills, and inclusive learning environments.

 •       Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment (supports SDGs 6 and 13; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 4; National Development Plan Objectives 7; UNSDCF Area 2) 
 
In Indigenous communities across the Sierra and Amazon regions, UNICEF has improved 35 rural community water boards, benefiting over 24,000 people. These systems integrate renewable energy, strengthen local governance, and promote public-community partnerships. The active participation of women and youth in the operation and maintenance of these systems has been pivotal, with a particular focus on prioritizing women's involvement in the leadership of these community water boards. The HWISE scale was applied to measure water insecurity in these households, providing essential data for designing interventions tailored to local needs.

In Chimborazo, the province with the highest prevalence of stunting, UNICEF implemented the WASH FIT methodology in 6 health care facilities and 14 child development centres, benefiting over 34,000 people. These efforts included infrastructure improvements, hygiene promotion, and staff training. In the Amazon region, nearly 25,000 children and their communities benefited from the “Smart Resilient Schools” model, which incorporates rainwater harvesting systems, solar panels, edible forests with an emphasis on ancestral knowledge, and sustainable menstrual hygiene practices.

UNICEF supported the development of the Second NDCs, incorporating intergenerational methodologies and approaches, as well as National Climate Change Mitigation Plan. Through the U-Report tool, UNICEF amplified the voices of over 6,000 children and youth, ensuring their inclusion in Ecuador´s Fifth National Communication to the UNFCCC. Additionally, UNICEF is leading the development of the National Strategy for Action for Climate Empowerment and published the booklet “Saberes ancestrales y cambio climático” (Ancestral Knowledge and Climate Change) highlighting the link between ancestral knowledge and sustainability.

Regarding the biodiversity agenda, UNICEF has promoted youth participation in shaping Ecuador´s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP). It organised the second Climate Academy for indigenous youth with a focus on biodiversity, bioeconomy and bio-entrepreneurship. UNICEF also supported the creation of the GYBN Ecuador Chapter and facilitated youth participation in COP16 on Biodiversity and COP29 on Climate Change.

For the third consecutive year, UNICEF supported the Local and Regional Conferences of Youth (LCOY and RCOY). Altogether, these actions in the climate and biodiversity agendas have enabled the meaningful participation of more than 8,500 children, adolescents, and youth (51% female and 49% male) across Ecuador.

•       Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect, and harmful practices (supports SDGs 5 and 16; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 3; National Development Plan Objective 3; UNSDCF Area 4)

UNICEF Ecuador has taken decisive steps in 2024 to prevent violence against children at the legislative and public policy levels, as well as in the implementation of projects that have directly benefited more than 100,000 people in over ten localities. UNICEF played a key role in preventing legislative reforms that go against the rights of adolescents in juvenile justice processes, ensuring that adolescents are not tried as adults, that the age of criminal liability is not lowered and that custodial sanctions against them are not increased. After several years of work and advocacy, the Standing Committee on Children and Adolescents of the National Assembly approved the draft Organic Code for the Comprehensive Protection of Children and Adolescents to be considered by the plenary of the National Assembly for final approval. This new law restores the specialised child protection system, substantially improves children´s protection services and radically changes the administration of juvenile justice, among other advances. All of this aligns with the strengthening of protective services, such as deinstitutionalization, emerging care and its link to the justice system.

In December 2024, four children aged eleven to fifteen were murdered following their detention by military personnel in Guayaquil. In response, UNICEF issued a public note on social media expressing solidarity with victims´ families and emphasising the importance of ensuring justice and comprehensive reparation for them. Previously, the United Nations Human Rights Office for South America (OHCHR) and UNICEF's Latin America and Caribbean Regional Office, with the support of Ecuador CO, issued an official statement calling for a thorough, transparent, timely, and impartial investigation, in line with international standards. In collaboration with OHCHR, UNICEF is supporting the Ecuadorian State with technical assistance to assure effective measures that uphold the rights of the victims and their families. UNICEF presented a report of the case to the CRC for its review prior to the periodic examination of the Ecuadorian State, which will take place in the third week of January.

UNICEF remains engaged with national institutions, social oversight mechanisms, and civil society organisations to reinforce the State’s capacity to fulfil its obligations to guarantee children's rights under national and international law, particularly focusing on strengthening safeguards to prevent similar violations and ensuring that adolescents in conflict with the law have access to a specialised justice system, so that such devastating incidents are not repeated.

In response to the violence crisis, UNICEF worked on and presented the National Strategy to Prevent Violence against Children and Adolescents in Ecuador in coordination with the State, civil society, international cooperation and adolescent participation. The strategy proposes a seven-axis action plan (INSPIRE) to provide specific responses. UNICEF also developed a study regarding the issue of forced recruitment of children by criminal gangs, and it has also worked with State institutions to ensure protection services for child victims.

At community level, UNICEF implements its “protective communities” strategy that includes community violence prevention interventions, adolescent empowerment, life skills, parenthood, the creation of community protection pathways, care and response in emergencies; with a strong emphasis on mental health. These interventions reached more than 5,000 people in 2024, who are now agents of change in communities most affected by criminal violence in the country. This response has been combined with that of other emergencies where UNICEF Ecuador has implemented Comprehensive Support Spaces with over 63,000 services, as well as “Friendly Spaces” where over 20,000 children received care, and more than 5,000 received legal assistance, with an emphasis on comprehensive care for unaccompanied and separated children where over 500 received emergent foster care and case management services.

On social media, UNICEF promoted key messages through the #CortaLaViolencia regional campaign and local content to prevent violence against children reaching 7,019,417 accounts.
On PSEA intervention, UNICEF provided training not only to staff but also to public institutions and civil society organizations in the regions where we operate, reaching over 450 individuals, including those involved in AAP. All our partners signed compliance clauses on PSEA policy in their PCAs and have updated their evaluations accordingly. We collaborate with various Agencies to avoid duplicating partner evaluations and improve response protocols at the local level.   

   •       Every child, including adolescents, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free from poverty (supports SDG 1; UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 5; National Development Plan Objective 1; UNSDCF Area 1) 
   
 UNICEF works to ensure that every child and adolescent in Ecuador has access to inclusive social protection and lives free of poverty, in line with SDG 1, Target Area 5 of the UNICEF Strategic Plan, Goal 5 of the National Development Plan and Area 1 of the UNSDCF.
In 2024, UNICEF strengthened local government planning and budgeting capacities with a focus on childhood. Some of its actions were: 1) Generating information to support decisions based on child welfare. 2) Measuring local investment in children to promote equitable and efficient budgets for vulnerable families.

In Quito, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Metropolitan District Municipality to create the 2024-2034 Metropolitan Early Childhood Policy, the first in the country. This policy addresses health, nutrition, protection, learning, environment and “care of caregivers” as a new gender responsive approach, and benefits 155,000 children under the age of 5, with special attention on the most vulnerable. It also supports the development of the 10-Year Action Plan, its costing and funding strategy.

At the national level, UNICEF is working with the Ministry of Economy and Finance to optimise public resources to reduce poverty and inequality in households with children. It aided the creation of the budget programme for the Strategy to Reduce Chronic Malnutrition, which prioritises evidence-based interventions to fight malnutrition in children under the age of five. In addition, it promotes public expenditure assessment and inter-agency coordination to improve results.

As part of “Childhood First” strategy, UNICEF and the Feminist Alliance for Femicide Monitoring developed the study “Waiting for Summer”, which highlights the situation of child and adolescent victims of femicide. This analysis will serve as a basis for promoting a comprehensive care and reparation programme, in accordance with the Transformative and Comprehensive Accompaniment and Reparation Act to benefit affected families.
 
Cross sectoral support

Field operations and emergencies.

In preparation for the El Niño phenomenon, UNICEF Ecuador, together with the Polytechnic School of the Coast (ESPOL), developed scenarios on the potentials impacts this phenomenon could have in Ecuador.  As part of this work, a methodology was developed that can be applied to other emergencies, and officials from the Ministry of Education, Ministry of Health, Secretariat of Risk Management, among others, were trained on it. In this framework of preparation for the El Niño phenomenon, UNICEF Ecuador updated its EPP, developed a contingency plan and sent various humanitarian supplies, including purification tablets, tents and jerry cans.

Regarding the migration crisis of Venezuelan citizens, UNICEF Ecuador continues to support the response to the crisis in the protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and education sectors.  This is done within the framework of inter-agency work coordinated by the Working Group for Refugees and Migrants (GTRM).  

During the flood emergency in the Alausí canton in May, UNICEF Ecuador contributed with WASH supplies, baby kits, and conducted community workshops for preparedness and risk management, among others, in support of national efforts. 

Emergency response and development nexus activities were implemented thanks to the strengthened UNICEF presence in the field.  UNICEF actively participated in the international Earthquake Response Exercise (ERE) 2024 led by the National Secretariat for Risk Management formed by echnical Working Groups (MTT by its Spanish acronym) MTT1, MTT4 and MTT5. In this exercise, UNICEF provided technical support to the Humanitarian Country Team for the management of MIRA, flash appeals and active coordination with MTT8 (Foreign Affairs).

Communication.  

With the #PrimeroLaInfancia (Childhood First) strategy to prioritise children, UNICEF made commitments with the private sector, civil society, academia, youth and the media. Together with the Ecuadorian Consortium for Social Responsibility (CERES) and Corporación Mucho Mejor Ecuador (Much Better Ecuador), it implemented a pilot project to promote positive parenting in companies. With the civil society, UNICEF developed research on the impact of femicide on children. With the project “Time Machine 2030”, developed with the Ecuadorian Corporation for the Development of Research and Academy (CEDIA), it trained young people in creative writing and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 

UNICEF accompanied a group of 37 young people in creating a manifesto against violence. The document “Una generación que protege a una infancia que florece” (A generation that protects a flourishing childhood) was shared with national authorities along with the presentation of the National Strategy for Violence Prevention. 

To disseminate content, UNICEF formed partnerships with Forbes Magazine, Multicines, Teleamazonas, Tinta Digital and Diario Metro. It also agreed to work for children’s rights with the Municipality of Quito and associations of local governments, CONGOPE, CONAGOPARE and AME. 
UNICEF held the #PrimeroLaInfancia Forum which included 25 panellists and 600 attendees and achieved a media impact valued at US$ 250,000, with a total reach of 42 million (it is important to consider that a person could be reached with the information through different media channels). 

The #PrimeroLaInfancia campaign reached 3,007,479 accounts. On World Children’s Day, with the support of Diario Metro, a publication reached over 220,000 people. 
The Generación MÁS community, a youth group close to UNICEF, grew from 213 to 437 members. Over 200 young people participated in activities such as workshops, content creation, consultations on relevant topics and the Climate Academy.

The U-Report tool was instrumental in gathering young people’s opinions through eight surveys on safety, health, artificial intelligence, climate change and access to justice, which reached over 55,000 responses in total. 

Monitoring and evaluation. 
 
UNICEF Ecuador shared the Laboratory of Information of Children and Adolescents in Ecuador that provides information on their situation in the areas of health and nutrition, WASH, education, protection and social inclusion.  This has made it possible to contribute to the processing, consolidation and visualisation of information. 

In the evaluation area, the results were: 1) The country office completed the real-time evaluation of its WASH in schools strategy.  The results of this evaluation were shared with implementing partners, the Ministry of Education and the National Institute of Educational Evaluation.  2) The formative evaluation of the chronic malnutrition reduction strategy began in the last quarter of the year. 3) UNICEF Ecuador has estimated the impact of the MYRP programme on the comprehensive learning of students in the educational institutions that were part of the programme.  This exercise was conducted together with the National Institute of Educational Evaluation.  4) The country office was able to share its experience at the regional level on the use of administrative records to assess the impact of the strategy to reduce chronic malnutrition in children in the Imbabura and Chimborazo provinces, and the real-time evaluation of WASH in schools strategy. 5) Strengthened the capacities of the National Planning Secretariat and the National Institute of Educational Evaluation in evaluation through the ExCel course developed by HQ and supported by LACRO.
