Chronic malnutrition in children 

Strategic partnerships are essential to advancing children's rights, as highlighted in its Strategic Plan. Some of the key partners that facilitate access to health and nutrition services for pregnant women, children, adolescents and their families, especially those in more vulnerable situations, include the National Government, with entities such as the Ministry of Public Health, the Technical Secretariat Ecuador Grows Without Child Malnutrition, the Ministry of Economic and Social Inclusion, the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Education and the Civil Registry; as well as local governments, United Nations agencies (PAHO/WHO, UNAIDS, UNFPA, WFP and FAO), International Financial Institutions (World Bank, Inter-American Development Bank and CAF), civil society, academic institutions and the private sector.
In addition, the collaboration with the Technical Secretariat ‘Ecuador Grows Without Child Malnutrition’ and the Ministry of Public Health stands out in strengthening the implementation of the National Plan for the Prevention of Chronic Malnutrition in Children. This effort has made it possible to establish cross-sector strategies, such as the expansion of prenatal control, nutrition education and child growth monitoring services.
 
Children on the Move 
 
Ecuador has become a transit and destination country for thousands of Venezuelan migrants and refugees. Many are children and adolescents who face significant barriers to accessing basic services, such as education, health and protection, as well as being exposed to risks of exploitation and abuse.

Working together with the GTRM, the Joint Needs Assessment was implemented in 2024, which serves as an input, among others, to the Refugee and Migrant Response Plan 2025 (RMRP). UNICEF, in coordination with other United Nations agencies, especially UNHCR and IOM, and their implementing partners, continues to support the implementation of programmes that contribute migrants and refugees’ access to education, protection, WASH, etc.  Some of these initiatives include Comprehensive Support Spaces (places where services are provided by the national government, local government, NGOs, among other service providers), temporary shelters for separated or unaccompanied children and adolescents, and the implementation of the Protocol for the Comprehensive Protection of Non-National Children and Adolescents, in coordination with the Ministry of Economic and Social Inclusion. The data collected and analysed will be utilised by the Humanitarian Country Team for evidence-based planning of humanitarian actions during 2025.

Alliances with the private sector and the academia

 In the framework of the #PrimeroLaInfancia strategy, which seeks to mobilise all social actors to prioritise children in their actions, UNICEF Ecuador consolidated important partnerships with the private sector, the academia, the media and civil society organisations, especially women's groups. In addition to improving our relationship with these stakeholders, these partnerships have increased UNICEF’s visibility to targeted audiences. Thanks to the agreement with Forbes Magazine, UNICEF managed to position priority issues for children in the business forums “Reinventing Ecuador” and “Sustainable Ecuador”. UNICEF also had fundraising spaces at the magazine’s events. UNICEF also formed an alliance with the Corporate Social Responsibility Consortium (CERES) and two articles were published in its communication channels. It is worth noting the partnership with Tinta Digital, a project developed on social media that targets young people, which allowed the generation of workshops for Youth Skills Week and create content together. In addition, UNICEF was part of two Tinta Fest festivals in Macas and Cuenca to expand the youth community and promote projects focused on this segment. UNICEF also partnered with Fundación Crisfé and Teleamazonas to broadcast messages on TV promoting positive parenting and healthy habits. This advertisement plan is valued at $195,000. In partnership with Multicines, spots for the #CortaLaViolencia (Stop Violence) and #PrimeroLaInfancia campaigns were screened in 80 cinemas in Quito, Guayaquil, Cuenca and Manta. 
 
Alliance with women´s organizations 

A Pilot capacity-building programme for women and adolescents' organisations for the prevention of gender-based violence against children, adolescents and women in Pichincha, Guayas, Esmeraldas, Chimborazo, Sucumbíos and Esmeraldas. This participatory process involved the collaboration of nearly 30 grassroots organisations of women and adolescents working in these territories. The objective of the programme was to provide knowledge, techniques and tools to women and adolescents to strengthen their skills in promoting and defending the rights of children, adolescents and women. Special emphasis was placed on the prevention of gender-based violence, seeking to align the agenda of the women's movement with the protection of the rights of children and adolescents.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Primero La Infancia (Childhood First)

While UNICEF has made significant strides in building partnerships with key actors in society, such as the private sector, academia, local governments, the media and women’s social organisations, it requires continuous efforts are required to maintain the proposed activities, build loyalty with existing partners, and generate new partnerships. 
In addition, in this changing landscape, it is important to achieve significant results to increase public investment, ensure the sustainability and prioritisation of children and adolescents in the decision-making processes of authorities and governments at different levels.

It is also important to develop specific advocacy strategies to increase the impact of the products developed under the #PrimeroLaInfancia initiative, such as a manifesto created by young people for the protection of children from violence and the study on the consequences of femicide on children and adolescents. 

It is also necessary to reinforce the production of communication materials and outreach campaigns to promote children’s rights in the private sector and the media. Given the positive results of public events, such as the #PrimeroLaInfancia Forum, and the actions to give the campaign a massive reach through traditional and digital media, it is essential to maintain these types of activities. 

Information Laboratory

In view of the scattering of information on children and adolescents and the outdated national information system, UNICEF Ecuador developed the Children and Adolescents Information Laboratory (https://infanciaecuador.org), in order to provide decision-makers, civil society organisations, academia and society with general with information on the situation of children and adolescents in the country.  Using administrative records, surveys and censuses carried out by the National Institute of Statistics and Census, the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Economic and Social Inclusion, among others, the laboratory processes the information and presents it in a friendly way.

Although the information laboratory has been shared through UNICEF social networks, in spaces for international cooperation and the press, among other actors, it is still necessary to promote its use.  During 2025, the laboratory will be updated with the latest available information, and activities to promote its use will include visits to universities, civil society organisations and other actors that use information on children and adolescents in the country.

Field offices strengthening

Based on the Cooperation Programme Document (CPD) 2023-2026, UNICEF Ecuador started a process of strengthening its territorial presence with permanent Field Offices in prioritised provinces: Esmeraldas, Chimborazo, and Sucumbíos, each of them located in the three broad regions of Ecuador, coastal, highlands, and Amazon, respectively; and two humanitarian satellite offices in the cities of Manta and Tulcán. Within this framework, strategic priorities have been set for the 2024-2025 period, translating them into concrete actions with clearly allocated officials, deadlines and resources.

In addition, the strengthening of the UNICEF presence in the territory allows for a more appropriate response to emergencies that may arise in these areas.  In the case of Sucumbíos Field Office, the strengthening of the territorial presence, which began in 2024, also allows testing a new model of direct implementation through UNVs to support the areas of health and nutrition, and child protection.  

Future Outlook

Ecuador continues to be a country marked by insecurity and violence that sadly affects children and adolescents. As of November 2024, the number of intentional homicides against children and adolescents reached 496[1]. This implies that, in 2025, UNICEF Ecuador must focus efforts on ensuring that the National Strategy for Violence Prevention is properly implemented. In addition, there is an urgent need to focus actions on adaptation and mitigation of the impact of climate change and its consequences on children and adolescents. As evidenced by the current energy crisis in Ecuador, it is families with children and adolescents who suffer the greatest economic impact.   In 2023, 25.2 per cent of households with children and adolescents were in income poverty, while only 9.1 per cent of households without children and adolescents were in poverty[2].

The electoral process that will take place early next year represents a challenge in terms of keeping priority issues on the political agenda, such as the national strategy to reduce chronic malnutrition among children and the prevention of violence against children and adolescents, but it also represents an opportunity for advocacy on these and other issues, such as juvenile criminal justice.

In 2025 UNICEF Ecuador will be part of the Business Model Initiative that seeks to accelerate results at scale for children and adolescents, especially those between 0 and 5 years of age.  In relation to this, the Children’s Information Laboratory in Ecuador opens the possibility of influencing sustained processes on the importance of funding for children and to also begin conversations with international financial institutions and the private sector on innovative models of financing for children in Ecuador.

In 2025, UNICEF Ecuador will develop sustained processes for the inclusion of adolescent women, especially through the STEM (Science, Telecommunications and Computer Science, Engineering and Mathematics) methodology, as part of the strategy for the empowerment of adolescent women. 
Similarly, communication, advocacy and public relations strategies should be strengthened, especially in territories where UNICEF has a presence. Efforts should be made to generate content with information on the situation of children at the local and territorial levels, and relevant stories that show the challenges and achievements of the communities where we work should be highlighted. 

UNICEF will focus on the impact it has on public investment and decision-making that advocates for the well-being of children and adolescents. Thus, sustained investment commitments will be sought from authorities and governments at different levels, in addition to working for greater interinstitutional coordination that aligns different actors and partners. Finally, efforts will be made to strengthen our partnerships and attract more private and public actors to support us and that can help us improve the well-being of children and adolescents in Ecuador.
