El Salvador, the smallest country in Central America, has seen significant shifts in its population and socio-economic landscape. According to the 2024 census, the country’s population stands at 6.03 million, with children and adolescents comprising 28.9% of the total population, about 1.75 million people. This marks a 45.7% decline in the child population since 2007, despite a 5% overall population increase. Nearly 20% of the population lives abroad, and remittances, which are critical to the Salvadoran economy, account for 25% of the GDP in 2024. 


 


The country's economic outlook includes several variables. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects a 3% GDP growth in 2024, down from 3.5% in 2023, with inflation expected to drop to 1%. Unemployment is expected to rise slightly to 5.2%. These indicators suggest some stabilisation but point to persistent challenges, which, according to the World Bank, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), include limited foreign direct investment, weak public finance transparency, and low confidence in the justice system, which hampers private investment. The country's fiscal deficit represents 3.3% of its GDP, and the public debt reached 86.3% of GDP by December 2024, a 4.45% increase since year-end 2023 (Central Reserve Bank, ONEC, and Finance Ministry, 2024). 


 


El Salvador’s national budget has reached USD 9.66 billion in 2024, a modest 2% growth, the lowest since the COVID-19 pandemic. Dollarisation and improvements in the business environment show potential for inclusive growth. In December, the Legislative Assembly approved the 2025 Budget Law, with central government expenditures reaching (26% of GDP), exceeding the Latin American average of 22% and the 20% average for Central America. Key spending priorities include social development, security, defense (37.4%) and public debt (over 28%). Despite no significant external debt maturities in 2025, debt payments remain a priority above education and health, reflecting a broader trend in Latin America, where debt servicing constrains public investment (Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC), 2024). 


 


Total government revenues are projected at 22% of GDP, with tax revenue expected to increase by 10.8% in 2025, a sharp rise compared to the 5% average growth in the last two years. Austerity measures persist, although salary increases for health and education personnel were included in the budget, addressing concerns that spurred protests. The reliance on remittances exacerbates external vulnerabilities. 


 


El Salvador also made global headlines due to Presidential re-election in February 2024 with 83% of the vote. This marks the first re-election of a president for two consecutive terms since the entry into force of the current constitution. The administration has gained popularity largely due to its success in reducing the homicide rate, which dropped from 103 per 100,000 in 2015 to a projected 1.9 per 100,000 by 2024, according to the National Civil Police. The country has been in a state of emergency since March 2022, which has suspended several constitutional rights and has resulted in the detention of over 83,600 individuals, including more than 2,800 children under 18, according to the Organisation of American States (OAS) report with official data shared by the Government of El Salvador.  


 


El Salvador faces significant challenges in its socio-economic development, particularly in health, education, and social protection. Neonatal mortality has slightly decreased from 5.2% to 5%, while overall child mortality remains steady at 8.6% (Ministry of Health -MINSAL January 2024). Vaccination coverage has improved for diseases such as DTP3 and polio, though coverage for the second dose of measles, mumps, and rubella (MCV2) has decreased (Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), 2023). Child malnutrition remains a concern, with 10.3% of children under five affected by stunting or wasting (ENS, 2021). 


 


School enrolment and retention remain a challenge. Despite the existence of 5,907 educational centres, over 350,000 children and adolescents are outside of the educational system. About 26.2% of children aged 3–6, 3.7% of children aged 7–15, and 30.3% of adolescents aged 16–18 are not enrolled (EHPM, 2023). 


 


The situation of children without parental care is a major protection concern. According to official figures , 37.9% of children and adolescents live without one or both parents, often due to abandonment, migration, or death (EHPM, 2023). Many of these children face or are at risks of violence, abuse, and exploitation, while they are also at high risk for poverty, poor nutrition, mental health issues, school dropout, utilisation by organised crime, and child labour. Gender-based violence is also a significant issue. According to the National Council for Children and Adolescents’ Observatory on Early Childhood, Childhood, and Adolescence Rights in El Salvador, over 5,430 children were victims of gender-based violence in the country in 2023, of which 90% were female, 6% were male and 4% of unidentified gender. El Salvador continues to be among the list of countries with the highest fertility rates in girls and adolescents globally, with 5.89 births per 1,000 girls (10-14 years old) and 54.44 per 1,000 adolescents (15-19 years old) (UNFPA, 2023). 


 


Limited access to adequate water and sanitation for vulnerable populations persists. According to EHPM 2023, while 96.1% of urban households have access to piped water, only 82.6% of rural households do. The proportion of urban households with piped water ownership is 87.4%, compared to just 68.9% in rural areas. Among households living in multidimensional poverty, 21.2% lack access to drinking water, and 38.2% lack adequate sanitation. According to the 2024 Census, 8.3% of households do not have water at home, and 4.7% access water through neighbours. Furthermore, 3.1% of households lack sanitation services, and 9.6% of the population shares sanitation services. Water committees supply water to over half a million households, about 28% of the population. However, 20% of the more than 2,300 water systems in the country do not disinfect the water, raising concerns about water quality. The percentage rate of under-5 mortality attributed to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene is not available in the country. 


 


Multidimensional poverty continues to affect a significant portion of the population, with 25% of households living in poverty, a 9-point decrease from 2016, when multidimensional poverty was first measured in the country (World Bank, 2024). Children are disproportionately affected, with 33.1% of households with children living in multidimensional poverty (EHPM, 2023). Additionally, 9.6% of children and adolescents have some form of disability (ibid). Data on the percentage of children with access to the social protection system is not available. 


 


El Salvador is highly vulnerable to natural disasters, including earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and the impacts of climate change. Floods, droughts, and tropical storms disproportionately affect disadvantaged communities, disrupting food security and livelihoods. The 2024 La Niña event caused severe flooding, displacing over 3,800 people in June (Ministry of Governance, 2024). In July, Civil Protection declared a national red alert due to a spike in dengue infections. Among those affected during this crisis, 60% were children under nine years old, and 40% were adolescents aged 10–19. 


 


The country is also grappling with the global migration crisis. According to the United States Customs and Border Protection, more than 53,000 Salvadorans were encountered at the Southwest land border in 2024. T By May 2024, over 90,300 people transited through El Salvador, nearly 40,000 more than during the same period in 2023 (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), 2024). The main nationalities included Ecuador, Brazil, India, and the Dominican Republic, among others.  




Between January and October 2024, 2,096 children and adolescents returned to El Salvador. Of these, 1,673 were accompanied, while 423 were unaccompanied. Between January and June 2024, 2,067 Salvadoran children and adolescents were referred by the National Institute of Migration (INM) Mexico, including 1,331 aged 0 to 11 years and 736 aged 12 to 17 years; 1,790 were accompanied, and 277 were unaccompanied. This situation highlights an ongoing migration crisis involving children on the move,  which highlights the importance of reintegration, access to social services and income-generation alternatives for returning families.

One of the most significant achievements of UNICEF in 2024 was the successful collaboration with the Government of El Salvador in the development of the National Policy for the Comprehensive Protection of Early Childhood, Childhood, and Adolescence. UNICEF's technical contributions were based on the highest standards and best practices across the Latin America and the Caribbean Region in the design of the policy. By advocating for family-centred care, UNICEF sought to ensure that children can receive emotional, social, and psychological support within their communities. This change would not only provide children with a protective environment but also help to reinforce the importance of family-based care as a child protection cornerstone. UNICEF stands ready to continue this technical assistance until the policy is finalised and for its implementation in line with standards set forth in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). 


 


UNICEF supported the rollout of a violence prevention strategy in four municipalities and six districts, focusing on creating safer communities for children. This initiative included capacity-building activities for parents and caregivers on positive parenting, emphasizing non-violent approaches, children’s autonomy, and respect for their rights. This training transformed parenting practices, creating healthier, more supportive environments for children and promoting long-term changes in how families engage with and care for their children. 


 


Children and adolescents participated in UNICEF’s violence prevention activities, fostering peace and strengthening social cohesion within their communities. By engaging in these activities, young people became active participants in transforming their communities, learning the importance of cooperation and conflict resolution. 


 


Furthermore, UNICEF provided protection services to children and adolescents on the move, focusing on mental health support, psychosocial care, and safe spaces. These services reinforced refugee, asylum-seeking, and vulnerable migrant children's well-being and facilitated their integration into communities. 


 


UNICEF contributed to the successful implementation of the "Open Arms" Plan, supporting the national framework to restore the rights of returning migrant children and families. UNICEF also joined the regional partnership on Mixed Monitoring Movement, a collaboration with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the World Food Programme (WFP), to gather and process data at border points, identify the needs of populations on the move, and forecast migration trends to adjust programs to better meet the needs of vulnerable groups. 


 


UNICEF supported the strengthening of the National Comprehensive Protection Policy in El Salvador through technical assistance and coordination to ensure the full exercise of rights and the well-being of children and adolescents. UNICEF’s support has included the coordination of a participatory assessment of the alternative care system in the country to reinforce the alternative care framework, improving protections for children without parental care across the country in line with the CRC and the Crecer Juntos Law. In addition, UNICEF established community-based protection networks, training 2,803 community members and public officials to address the specific needs of children.  


 


In collaboration with the National Judicial Council (CNJ), UNICEF provided training to 120 judicial officers on the best interests of the child, inclusive justice practices, and juvenile justice standards. Building on efforts from 2023, this training empowered the judiciary with the tools necessary to ensure that children's rights are respected in legal proceedings. By focusing on child-friendly justice and legal practices, this initiative enhances the justice system's ability to protect children from violence and exploitation, ensuring they are treated with dignity and respect. UNICEF will continue to build on this partnership to support specialized procedures for children in line with the upcoming general comment No. 27 on children’s rights to access to justice and effective remedies, considering also the country’s challenges related to juvenile justice. 


 


UNICEF, in partnership with the Attorney General’s Office, implemented a psychosocial care model to support children, adolescents, women, and other vulnerable groups impacted by violence. Through this model, UNICEF provided emotional and psychological support, helping reduce trauma and improve the mental well-being of those affected by violence. 


 


UNICEF achieved transformative results in El Salvador’s health sector through its support to institutions and communities. It focused on developing a more resilient and equitable health system, fostering long-term health improvements for the nation’s most vulnerable, and enhancing the quality, inclusivity, and accessibility of services that impact over 200,000 children, adolescents, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups. 


 


UNICEF’s support to the modernisation of the national cold chain system was a game-changer for immunisation efforts. By providing 460 tablets for real-time monitoring and 350 certified freezers, including solar-powered units, UNICEF ensured the safe storage and distribution of vaccines for the next 20 years. These advancements contributed to achieving 99.6% coverage for the first dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine and 76% for the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, protecting children and adolescents from preventable diseases and bolstering the health system's emergency readiness. The introduction of a Braille vaccination guide further emphasised inclusivity, enabling visually impaired families to access life-saving immunisation information. 


 


UNICEF’s work in maternal and neonatal health yielded remarkable results. Through technical training on quality standards of primary healthcare services, UNICEF developed the skills of 5,000 health providers across 700 Community Health Units nationwide. Additionally, 1,200 health promoters and 1,200 frontline professionals were trained in maternal and child nutrition and nutritional surveillance. UNICEF also supported health promoters and implementing partner staff on themes such as equitable access to health services and community-based interventions to increase human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, including with the participation of adolescents. These efforts enhanced the capacity of such frontline workers to provide quality care, particularly in underserved communities, directly addressing systemic inequities. 


 


UNICEF also trained over 300 prenatal educators nationwide, strengthening maternal and child nutrition and promoting the humanisation of prenatal care, childbirth, and the postnatal period. Furthermore, 215 professionals received training in Human Milk Banks and Lactation Collection Centres, enabling the implementation of the Kangaroo Strategy, which reached over 12,000 preterm infants and 1,600 newborns in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU), providing premature babies and low birth weight infants with access to life-saving and nurturing nutrition services. 


 


In border regions, UNICEF equipped four breastfeeding rooms, 49 health units, and eight Integrated Health Offices with essential resources. This ensured that emergency nutrition services reached high-need areas, providing critical support for populations facing heightened vulnerabilities. 


 


Through a Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) study conducted in three districts, UNICEF identified health promoters as key behavioural drivers. Most parents and caregivers recognised health promoters as their trusted source for information and advice regarding their children's health, including vaccination. As seen in consultations and human-interest story interviews with health promoters, community trust in their recommendations is a direct result of UNICEF’s training on better communication to enhance community immunisation services. 


 


UNICEF and the Ministry of Education, Science and Technology (MINEDUCYT) championed inclusive and innovative programmes to ensure all children in El Salvador had access to quality education, creating significant, lasting impacts across the country. For instance, UNICEF’s technical assistance to mobilise resources for the implementation of the Early Childhood Education Recovery and Coverage Expansion Strategy (2023-2030) under the "Crecer Juntos" policy will enable the expansion of preschool access for about 111,000 out-of-school children, including those with disabilities. This initiative will ensure these children acquire foundational skills and learning-readiness essential for lifelong learning, fostering equity and laying the groundwork for inclusive development. 


 


The “Reading at Home” project, implemented in partnership with the UN-India Fund, improved literacy for 6,000 children aged 0-9, supported nearly 800 teachers, and engaged 5,637 families in the poorest municipalities. By delivering inclusive reading materials, including resources tailored for children with disabilities, the project significantly reduced literacy gaps, empowered educators, and strengthened family involvement, creating a more supportive learning ecosystem. The project identifies best practices, including coordination with other countries through South-South cooperation, to inform present and future scalability of its results by the Salvadoran government in reading promotion. 


 


In partnership with the “Crecer Juntos” Institute (ICJ), UNICEF provided high-level technical assistance throughout the development of the National Parenting Practices Training Plan. By equipping families to create nurturing environments, this initiative will address critical mental health challenges, enhancing children’s physical, emotional, and cognitive development, and ensuring a more stable foundation for their growth, impacting up to 924,000 children aged 0-8 years old. 


 


UNICEF also provided non-formal education to 856 children on the move, supported 543 caregivers with training in positive parenting, and ensured educational continuity for displaced populations. Furthermore, 791 vulnerable children, including those with disabilities, gained access to education through UNICEF-supported interventions, while 548 students received psychosocial support to cope with challenges. UNICEF training for 473 teachers enhanced the social-emotional skills of 2,365 students, promoting resilience and well-being, particularly in emergencies. 


 


UNICEF’s education in emergencies strategy promoted educational continuity for children on the move through innovative digital learning materials, recognized regionally. The interactive content and games focus on developing literacy, math, and English skills, with age-specific goals. Complementing these digital tools is a kit of physical educational materials designed to foster self-care, self-protection, and fine motor skills. The initiative focuses on preparing children for future educational and life challenges, supporting their overall development in a migration context. 


 


In the Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) sector, UNICEF significantly enhanced public institutions' ability to deliver equitable, sustainable, and gender-sensitive WASH services. UNICEF directly facilitated the installation of WASH infrastructure at strategic locations, including land borders, shelters, schools, health units, and child welfare centres, reaching over 5,156 children and adolescents in mobility situations and 6,200 children from host communities. This intervention provided essential access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene amenities while empowering local institutions to design and implement inclusive programmes addressing the needs of children, especially in crises and border settings. 


 


In alignment with the Humanitarian-Development-Peace (HDP) nexus approach, UNICEF interventions integrated humanitarian aid, development strategies, and peacebuilding efforts. This comprehensive approach ensured that immediate relief efforts addressed urgent needs while laying the groundwork for sustainable development and long-term peace. 


 


UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health (MINSAL) in developing the Technical Guidelines for Climate-Resilient Water Safety Plans (PSA-RC), making these guidelines mandatory for over 2,300 community water operators. This will directly affect 28% of Salvadoran households (1.6 million people), ensuring that water systems are operated and maintained safely. By implementing these guidelines, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of the health sector to safeguard drinking water quality, resulting in long-term public health benefits for the entire population. 


 


UNICEF’s advocacy efforts were key in integrating WASH into national health and climate policies. By supporting a young activist at COP16, UNICEF underscored the importance of youth- and gender-sensitive approaches in WASH strategies. This advocacy led to a greater understanding among policymakers of the need to prioritise vulnerable populations, including women and children, in future WASH policies through consultations and incorporation of their opinions and feedback. 


 


UNICEF also contributed to the development of an action plan that integrates climate solutions into the planning of over 37 institutions and organisations. This plan promotes climate resilience in vulnerable areas, ensuring that communities are better prepared for the impacts of climate change, which in turn supports the sustainability of WASH services. 


 


UNICEF has begun coordination with the Government of El Salvador (GOES) to generate robust evidence on gaps in essential services such as health, education, and child protection in programmes and projects addressing children and adolescents, especially those affected by multidimensional poverty. With the results of the study, UNICEF will work closely with the government to improve its response to the challenges identified. 


 


All programme areas in El Salvador implemented concrete initiatives to enable accountability to affected populations and social and behavioural change. In collaboration with implementing partners and government counterparts, UNICEF undertook three significant studies focused on health (immunisation), protection (parenting practices), and migration (Accountability to Affected Populations, AAP). These studies identified the main barriers preventing children and adolescents from accessing essential services and adopting behaviours that support their well-being. By addressing social, structural, and gender-related challenges, the findings have informed better interventions and ensured that the needs of vulnerable groups are more effectively met. In immunisation, the SBC study found a strong lack of information on vaccination among male parents or caregivers, which may lead to new strategies on how to engage such a group with targeted communication. 


 


A key achievement in UNICEF’s Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) strategy was the establishment of feedback systems for distributing humanitarian kits and services, particularly for children and families on the move. These mechanisms allowed UNICEF to better tailor its interventions to the challenges faced by migrant children, improving the selection and distribution of supplies, managing inventories, and enhancing referral services. For instance, UNICEF shifted from distributing pre-packaged kits to setting up mobile units at border areas where populations on the move can select the supplies, they need most. This change addresses findings from formative research showing that migrants often left kit items behind due to limited space. Additionally, sunscreen and repellent were added to the supply list based on requests during consultations. 


 


Furthermore, in its commitment to strengthening child protection systems, UNICEF trained government officials and implementing partners on generating qualitative evidence on behaviours through the implementation of person-centred design and behavioural theories in protection programmes. This training aimed to support the government in designing programmes that consider the needs of affected populations and their feedback throughout implementation. UNICEF also designed tools to measure change intentions, assess user satisfaction, and identify improvement opportunities in government and implementing partner interventions. As a result of these efforts, the Ministry of Education (MINEDUCYT) and the First Lady’s Office expressed interest in adopting an SBC strategy to promote student participation, leadership, and well-being in their current programmes. This demonstrates the enormous replicability potential of SBC for government programming. The goal will be to measure and encourage behavioural changes that will help children become more engaged in their education and communities, fostering their growth and protection. Through the Children on the Move Initiative, UNICEF supported 2,927 government officials, CSO staff, community leaders and affected populations with training on PSEA or participation in PSEA awareness activities. 


 


In addition, UNICEF implemented highly impactful communication and advocacy strategies and initiatives to support cross-sectoral programme results. UNICEF championed health and mental well-being through digital campaigns. An immunisation campaign reached 1.6 million people, promoting vaccination for children under five and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines for adolescents aged 13–21. A mental health awareness initiative engaged 1.4 million people, addressing topics such as panic attacks, self-harm, and self-care. Articles on these topics generated significant interest, with panic attack resources reaching 21,700 views, self-harm 7,100 views, and self-care 5,200 views. This initiative reinforced UNICEF’s commitment to mental health as a cross-cutting priority, urging the organisation to improve its future communication and advocacy strategies, especially with an emphasis on rural communities, where UNICEF's campaigns had a lower reach. 


 


UNICEF also expanded its social media influence, increasing its follower base by 5.9% to 333,901 across social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram, and X). Facebook led this growth, particularly among users aged 24–32, with 672,525 interactions, reinforcing UNICEF's position as the leading organisation in social media reach in El Salvador. Additionally, UNICEF’s media presence garnered US$1.6 million in commercial and public relations value, with 196 placements across diverse platforms. 


 


UNICEF advanced significantly in planning, monitoring, and evaluation to strengthen results-based management across UNICEF and implementing partner offices and improve data reliability. To enhance the inclusion of children and adolescents with specific needs in output level monitoring, UNICEF introduced standardised monitoring and reporting matrices , ensuring that the specific needs of each group were considered. The use of standardised reporting calendars, developed in collaboration with programmatic areas and partners, improved the efficiency and consistency of data collection and processing. These efforts allowed for quicker identification of disaggregated results and facilitated the analysis of cross-cutting issues, ultimately reducing duplication and simplifying reporting. 


 


UNICEF also supported the participation of five government leaders in evaluation in the Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems’ Strengthening (IMPrESS) and the Executive Course for Evaluation Leaders (ExCel), developing their technical capacity and designing an action plan aimed at strengthening the National Evaluation Capacity Development (NECD) in the country. The country office has also begun coordination with UNICEF Headquarters and the Latin America and Caribbean Regional Office (LACRO) to participate in a global evaluation of primary healthcare and a regional evaluability assessment of Community Case Detection (CCD) best practices in Latin America.

In 2024, UNICEF El Salvador reinforced its commitment to improving the lives of children and adolescents through high-impact strategic partnerships with government institutions, United Nations (UN) agencies, international cooperation actors including International Financial Institutions (IFIs), and civil society organisations. These collaborations were critical in driving transformative results aligned with the Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and UNICEF’s country programme. By leveraging collective expertise and resources, UNICEF enhanced systemic interventions across health, education, protection, social policy, and emergency response sectors, ensuring scalable and sustainable impacts. 


 


A cornerstone of UNICEF's efforts was its partnership with the First Lady’s Office (DPD), which played a pivotal role in coordinating intersectoral policies and programmes to address the needs of children and adolescents. The collaboration prioritised strategic alignment with national priorities, fostering innovative solutions to persistent challenges. Similarly, UNICEF's partnership with the El Salvadoran Agency for International Cooperation (ESCO) streamlined programme planning, enhancing coordination and resource optimisation across sectors. 


 


In health and nutrition, the E-Health programme, developed with the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), and the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), is leveraging digital innovation to improve access to quality care for non-communicable diseases. Meanwhile, the Sustainable Food Systems programme, implemented with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), PAHO, the World Food Programme (WFP), and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), is strengthening child nutrition efforts in partnership with the Ministry of Health, ensuring a multi-sectoral approach to addressing malnutrition. Partnerships with the private sector, such as Kimberly-Clark and Amway, further supported neonatal care through human milk banks and the Kangaroo strategy, significantly improving survival rates for vulnerable newborns. 


 


In the education sector, UNICEF mobilised significant investments to advance early childhood development through improvements in educational infrastructure, teacher training, and student outcomes. Through collaborations with the World Bank (WB) and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), UNICEF managed to leverage $12 million for the national education sector via the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), tied to a $150 million IDB loan. Additionally, a GPE grant of $300,000 funded the Tech4Ed initiative, advancing digital education capabilities. 




The Agustine Project, funded by a €17.7 million investment from the European Union (EU), will enhance education by promoting conflict resolution, civic engagement, and cultural appreciation. It will prioritise students' psychological well-being, equal opportunities, and skill development. This initiative will foster supportive learning environments for long-term educational improvement, reaching 21,500 students across 860 schools over four years. Collaborative efforts with key international development stakeholders  supported the advancement of the Government of El Salvador’s National Education Policy "Mi Nueva Escuela", focusing on violence prevention and student well-being. Furthermore, UNICEF led the Interagency Group for Education Transformation, aligning UN efforts to accelerate progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in line with consultations held prior to and following up on the Transforming Education Summit. 



Child protection remained central to UNICEF’s mission in 2024. A gender-sensitive violence prevention strategy, funded by the United Kingdom National Committee and the 7 Fund (the David Beckham UNICEF Fund), addressed the root causes of violence in six districts. Additional funding from the United States Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration (PRM) supported safe spaces, psychosocial care, and education for migrant children, ensuring their safety and well-being. 


 


UNICEF also established a partnership with the Republic of Ireland to strengthen child protection systems and promote family-based care. This initiative will align the national child protection system with international standards, fostering healthier environments for vulnerable children nationwide, considering concerning official figures related to children without parental care. 


 


UNICEF formalised a $1 million partnership with the Government of Korea to address emergency needs while fostering sustainable progress, following the Humanitarian Development Peace nexus approach (HDP). This initiative will integrate child protection, education, and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) services with long-term goals such as improving mental health support, expanding economic opportunities, and building community resilience, considering a the need for community reintegration for returnees in 2025. Collaborations with local organisations and the Country Humanitarian Team enabled UNICEF to deliver prompt and effective multisectoral responses during emergencies. 


 


As part of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) @35 anniversary and World Children’s Day commemorations, UNICEF amplified the voices of children and adolescents on critical issues affecting their lives. UNICEF supported an academic visit by the Vice-President of the Committee on the Rights of the Child, in partnership with the United Nations Resident Coordinator Office (UN RCO) and Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), to raise awareness about the CRC and its Optional Protocols. Throughout the visit, the CRC vice-president and UNICEF engaged with more than 175 officials, partners, and child-focused organisations, which spurred dialogue on the state of children’s rights in El Salvador, identifying gaps and opportunities for progress, also in view of the upcoming review of El Salvador by the Committee of the Rights of the Child.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, UNICEF El Salvador tackled challenges stemming from limited public data, which hindered understanding and addressing the needs of children and adolescents. Limited data on violence further limits UNICEF’s ability to leverage child protection resources and provide system strengthening support. The data gap also affected the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, relying on outdated estimates instead of localised insights. To address these gaps, UNICEF supported evidence-generation efforts, supported the fine-tuning of government data methodologies, and collaborated with partners to enhance data systems, ensuring more informed interventions and improved outcomes for vulnerable populations. 


 


A critical lesson learned in 2024 was the urgent need for a holistic, multi-sectoral response to address mental health challenges affecting children, adolescents, their families, and communities in El Salvador. The National Survey on Mental Health (2022) highlighted significant mental health concerns among children and adolescents. Findings include behavioural issues in 35% of children, probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in 18%, bullying affecting 12%, and hyperactivity in 70% of 3–4-year-olds, with 55% overusing social media. Among adolescents, 30% experience social anxiety, 36% show obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) tendencies, and 15.6% face bullying. Alarmingly, 40% exhibit symptoms of major depression, with 30% reporting suicidal ideation, planning, or self-harm, potentially influencing violence and suicide rates. 


 


Addressing the current state of mental health care among children and adolescents, it is crucial to highlight the significant disparity between the extremely limited number of mental health professionals available in the country and the growing awareness and demand for mental health services. This gap underscores the urgent need for a forward-looking approach that prioritises community-based work and the development of institutional training programmes at scale. By supporting both national and community-based interventions in these areas, UNICEF aims to support the Government of El Salvador to bridge theshortfall of mental health professionals that the country is currently facing while simultaneously providing much-needed care at the community level. 


 


In addition, UNICEF’s communication campaigns have revealed a high demand for mental health services, further emphasising the necessity for effective referrals. UNICEF is committed to exploring and implementing alternative solutions with institutions and communities to ensure that children and adolescents receive the support they need, both from preventive as well as responsive standpoints. Through these efforts, UNICEF strives to support the strengthening of a more accessible, preventive, and responsive mental health care system for all. 


 


A multi-sectoral approach should enable UNICEF and the Government of El Salvador (GOES) to design and implement comprehensive strategies that not only address the root causes and risks of mental health issues but also consider their intersections with other developmental and social factors and sectors while optimising synergies across the board with critical child-specific social services. This ensures that interventions are integrated, impactful, and sustainable. 


 


Similarly, another area that requires a stronger multisectoral response is the situation of children living without parental care. Communities point to the significant vulnerabilities affecting these children, including school dropout, severe nutritional deficits, and mental health challenges. Furthermore, they are at heightened risk of falling victim to human trafficking, early unions, adolescent pregnancies, and being exploited by organised crime. These issues show the urgent need to ensure that the child protection system is ready to provide adequate care alternatives to prevent future social conflict dynamics. 


 


Considering these two major challenges, UNICEF has developed an advocacy strategy to be implemented starting in 2025 that prioritises addressing mental health and children without parental care, ensuring that these two issues are specifically addressed in national policies as well as through a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach. This draws on both national and international expertise to strengthen the child protection system and expand family-based care alternatives. 


 


The UNICEF implementation of the Agustine Project reflects this holistic vision, as it will promote student participation, peace building through conflict resolution, and leadership, with potential for nationwide scaling, by integrating programmes that promote a better-quality education while also preventing violence and providing psychosocial and emotional support to students. Collaborations with the private sector will focus on improving technical skills and labour market access for young people, supporting their transition to formal employment. Social and Behavioural Change (SBC) strategies will continue to underpin programme areas to encourage sustainable practices, relevance, and community involvement. 


 


One of UNICEF’s most important goals for 2025 onwards is to ensure that innovative public finance initiatives and instruments are effectively utilised to improve the lives of vulnerable populations, especially children, in the face of economic constraints. In the current context of austerity measures, UNICEF’s role becomes even more critical. UNICEF will advocate for the efficient allocation of public resources, ensuring that spending is directed toward programmes that have the highest impact, particularly in areas such as social protection. This involves prioritising investments that yield long-term benefits and address the root causes of poverty while carefully tracking expenditures to ensure that they are effective, efficient, and reaching the intended participants. 


 


Building on UNICEF’s work and expertise in social policies and Public Finance for Children at the regional level, UNICEF El Salvador will further focus on policy-level discussions to ensure that policy frameworks optimise the use of public funds to meet children’s needs. By using evidence-based approaches, UNICEF will aim to demonstrate the cost-effectiveness of investments to improve evidence-based budgeting and financial decisions. Moreover, robust monitoring systems will allow the Government of El Salvador to assess the efficiency of spending, identify gaps, and make data-driven decisions to adapt policies and improve outcomes. 


 


UNICEF’s role will consist of providing technical assistance and evidence that shows that, even in times of fiscal austerity, public resources can and should be allocated efficiently and effectively to achieve long-term, sustainable improvements in children’s and adolescents’ well-being.

The year 2024 marked the beginning of President Bernardo Arevalo’s administration, following a complex and polarized electoral process that drew significant international attention due to concerns about a potentially disrupted political transition. While political polarization remains high, and could negatively affect child rights in the short to medium term, the new government demonstrated a proactive commitment to collaborating with UNICEF. This partnership presents a promising opportunity to advance the child rights agenda despite prevailing political challenges.
The macroeconomic situation in 2024 showed signs of recovery after years of stagnation exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. Guatemala’s economy grew moderately, driven by increased remittances, which remain a significant source of income for many families. However, inflationary pressures persisted, impacting the affordability of essential goods and services, disproportionately affecting low-income households. Public investment in social sectors remained insufficient to meet the growing demand for education, health, and social protection, further straining the ability to address child rights comprehensively. Despite these challenges, fiscal stability allowed for some degree of optimism regarding targeted policy interventions under the new administration. Additionally, government’s efforts to attract foreign investment and boost export-oriented sectors showed potential for generating long-term economic benefits, although immediate impacts on marginalized communities remained limited.
In May, the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) reviewed Guatemala’s seventh periodic report (2018–2023), highlighting progress and persistent challenges in children’s rights. The CRC identified five urgent areas for action: addressing structural discrimination against indigenous and Afro-descendant populations by strengthening anti-exclusion laws; combating violence, including sexual and gang-related crimes, with prevention and reintegration programs; enhancing adolescent health through inclusive policies and services to prevent early pregnancies; integrating children’s needs into climate change policies and education; and improving juvenile justice with comprehensive models that protect rights, particularly for migrant children. These recommendations underscore the need for systemic reforms to protect Guatemala’s children.
Children in Guatemala, especially indigenous and afro-descendant, remain disproportionately affected by poverty. Official data reveal that 64.8% of children live in poverty, and 20.7% in extreme poverty. Among indigenous children, these rates escalate to 81.1% and 34.7%, respectively. This entrenched disparity perpetuates cycles of deprivation, affecting access to essential services such as education, healthcare, and nutrition. The new administration’s political commitment and its collaboration with UNICEF provides an opportunity to address these disparities through targeted policies and investments, including enhanced cash transfer programs and community-based development initiatives.
Chronic malnutrition remains a critical challenge, with 45.8% of children under five affected—the highest rate in Latin America. Progress on this front has been minimal, reflecting systemic issues in health service delivery and poverty alleviation. Acute malnutrition cases reported in 2024 (27,661) and associated deaths (70) further underscore the urgency of addressing food insecurity and malnutrition. Contributing factors include maternal malnutrition, suboptimal breastfeeding practices, and limited access to healthcare, particularly in rural/indigenous communities. Additionally, food insecurity was exacerbated by climate-induced crop failures, highlighting the need for integrated strategies that address agricultural sustainability and child nutrition.
Healthcare system faces significant resource constraints. Maternal mortality remains high at 108 deaths per 100,000 live births, while child mortality is 21 deaths per 1,000 live births, with preventable conditions as leading causes. Vaccination coverage is below targets, with 74% of children vaccinated against measles and 73% against polio. Such gaps highlight the need for strengthened healthcare infrastructure and outreach initiatives, particularly for marginalized populations. Furthermore, persistence of infectious diseases like dengue (over 38,000 reported cases in 2024) underscores the need for comprehensive public health campaigns and improved disease surveillance systems.
Educational outcomes in Guatemala are starkly inadequate. Net enrollment rates decline at higher levels of education, from 95.99% in primary education to 25.53% in upper secondary education. Learning outcomes are among the worst in the region, with 84% of sixth graders failing to meet minimum reading proficiency and 93% struggling in mathematics. The pandemic exacerbated these issues, with prolonged school closures widening existing gaps. Comprehensive reforms are needed to improve enrollment, retention and learning, with focus on girls, indigenous children, and rural adolescents. The introduction of digital learning tools and community-based programs has shown promise, though their reach remains limited by infrastructural challenges.
Violence against children remains pervasive. In 2023, the Public Ministry reported 26,767 cases, including sexual (6,261 cases) and physical violence (12,996 cases). Teenage pregnancies remain alarmingly high, with 62,306 cases among girls aged 10-19 in 2023, including 2,289 pregnancies in girls under 14. Such statistics reflect deeply ingrained societal norms and structural failures to protect children from abuse and exploitation. Addressing these issues requires robust legal frameworks, prevention programs, and access to support services for survivors. Additionally, efforts to combat gang violence, which disproportionately impacts adolescents, must be integrated into broader community safety and rehabilitation strategies.
Access to clean water and sanitation remains challenging. Nearly 23% of the population lacks access to basic water services, and 60% of schools face sanitation problems. Children in rural/indigenous areas are disproportionately affected, compounding their vulnerability to waterborne diseases. Furthermore, Guatemala’s high vulnerability to natural disasters and climate change exacerbates risks for children. Integrating children’s needs into climate adaptation policies and improving disaster preparedness are critical to safeguarding their future. Recent government initiatives to expand rural water infrastructure and promote community-led sanitation projects have been effective but require scaling-up to meet widespread needs.
Child migration remains a pressing issue. In 2024, over 135,000 children transited through Guatemala en route to North America, with 12% traveling unaccompanied. Additionally, nearly 8,000 Guatemalan children were deported from Mexico and the United States. This underscores the need for stronger protection measures for migrant children and reintegration support for returnees. The rise in unaccompanied minors highlights the urgent need for bilateral and regional cooperation to address the root causes of migration, including violence, poverty, and lack of opportunities.
These multifaceted challenges underline the importance of a coordinated and comprehensive approach to addressing systemic inequities, protecting children’s rights, and ensuring their well-being across all sectors. The political momentum and partnership opportunities in 2024 provide a critical window for transformative action to secure a brighter future for Guatemala’s children.

Health and nutrition 
UNICEF played a key advocacy role in supporting the passing of key legislation, including the Vaccination Law, which strengthened Guatemala’s immunization efforts, and the Biopsychosocial Certification of Persons with Disabilities Law, which advanced inclusion and equity. UNICEF also advocated for the Law on Comprehensive Mental Health Care, providing technical assistance, and generating evidence for its legislative review. In nutrition, UNICEF partnered with the Ministry of Health (MSPAS) and the Secretariat for Food and Nutrition Security (SESAN) to adapt the National Social and Behavior Change (SBC) strategy to the government’s “Mano a Mano” initiative, targeting poverty and malnutrition. National guidelines for managing acute malnutrition, nutrition in emergencies, and growth and development monitoring were updated, alongside the review of evidence supporting micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women and updates to the Guatemalan Food Guidelines.
 
UNICEF enhanced healthcare delivery through large-scale immunization campaigns, achieving a 91% coverage rate for children aged 2 to 5 years. The Vaccination Week of the Americas reached 259,319 children, while the MMR and OPV Vaccination Campaign covered 1,279,542 children. These efforts were supported by technical assistance, monitoring, and culturally relevant media campaigns in five Mayan languages using Máximo’s character for social and behavioral change. Maternal and newborn health services were strengthened with training for 403 health workers (65% women) in neonatal resuscitation and risk identification for maternal-to-child transmission, covering 56 health services. UNICEF also supported primary healthcare delivery for 13,218 migrants, including 11,447 individuals at the Honduras border. Emergency nutrition services screened 19,343 people, treating 1.8% of children under five with acute malnutrition and providing supplementation to 15% of underweight pregnant women.
In nutrition, UNICEF implemented along with MSPAS the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) across 100% of health services, certifying seven hospitals and benefitting 10,043 children. The Baby Friendly Spaces Initiative reached 1,669 people, with seven new companies certified, while the Breastfeeding Promoter Midwives Program certified 5,766 midwives, scaling breastfeeding promotion nationwide.
Community-based interventions were at the heart of UNICEF’s strategy. Training for 1,082 COMUSAN members facilitated the implementation of SBC plans, reaching 20,135 caregivers in 33 municipalities. The “Corazón Contento” Program delivered educational messages to 4,520 women via telephone and reached 62,850 people through 2,005 radio spots. In collaboration with local leaders, UNICEF trained 1,362 Agents of Change who conducted 2,673 counseling activities in 192 communities. Additionally, 250 traditional midwives received kits to bridge ancestral and modern medical practices, contributing to safe childbirth in remote areas.
 Youth engagement initiatives included U-Report surveys and training on human rights and assertive communication, extending outreach through Instagram live sessions and partnerships with 20 youth organizations. The "On My Mind" podcast, launched with the College of Psychologists of Guatemala, addressed adolescent mental health, reaching 155 youth and their support networks.
 As the leader of the Nutrition Cluster, UNICEF coordinated with 15 partners to develop the 2024 Humanitarian Needs Overview and Response Plan (HNRP). This included support for 71 comprehensive health and nutrition brigades, institutionalized with an annual MSPAS budget of USD 6.4 million, and delivering integrated care through capacity building and monitoring. Mobile Nutrition Teams screened and treated malnourished individuals on the move, while training and guidelines ensured the quality and consistency of emergency interventions.
 By advancing policies, strengthening services, and empowering communities, UNICEF Guatemala addressed systemic gaps in health and nutrition. Through strategic partnerships, evidence-based interventions, and community-driven approaches, UNICEF has laid the groundwork for sustainable improvements in health and nutrition for Guatemala’s most vulnerable populations.
 
Education 
UNICEF’s efforts in ECD were focused on supporting the Ministry of Education (MINEDUC) in improving access for children aged 0-4 to quality initial educational services through the "Acompáñame a Crecer" programme. A total of 276 new Comprehensive Child Development Community Centers (CECODIIs) were successfully established and ran by UNICEF in the departments of Alta Verapaz and Chiquimula. This effort impacted 6,981 children aged 0 to 4, along with 2,050 community educators, 2,867 pregnant mothers and 430 breastfeeding women. A total of 18, 076 families have benefited from this intervention in 182 communities. Technical assistance is also provided to MINEDUC staff in the implementation of "Acompáñame a Crecer", as well as in the review of technical documents and guides and in the development of an information system to adequately register participation information in the CECODIIs. Overall "Acompáñame a Crecer" coverage reached 1,500 CECODIIs, 61,178 children and 52,529 families nationwide. 
In primary education, UNICEF provided support to MINEDUC in the implementation of the Learning Recovery Strategy, specifically by printing the learning and assessment materials for students and teachers. Support was also provided to MINEDUC in the linguistic adaptation of the National Curriculum for the primary level in 3 mayan languages: kaqchiquel, tzutujil and k’iche’. Additionally, UNICEF is working with MINEDUC staff in the process of revision of the National Curriculum and actualization of key thematic areas.
UNICEF designed and implemented a teacher training program with the purpose of strengthening their competencies in digital learning and teaching. A total of 9,466 teachers from 12 prioritized departments participated in the first face-to-face session, and 8,748 continued the online training.
With the purpose of improving and promoting resilient learning environments, 275 schools in Alta Verapaz, Quiche, and Huehuetenango were benefited with improved and rehabilitated WASH services, benefitting a total of 34,236 children. Additionally, an SBC plan was implemented to promote hygiene practices within the educational community, including teachers, parents, and students.
Regarding the strengthening of MINEDUC capacities to foster a resilient primary education system with emergency response capacity, UNICEF kept its leadership and coordination role of the Education in Emergency (EiE) Cluster, made up of 48 organizations.
On Secondary Education and Adolescent Participation, UNICEF established 10 new Centers for Non-formal Education (CEEX) and supported 13 existing CEEX in the department of Alta Verapaz, benefiting 739 out-of-school adolescents (64% female and 36% male) to complete their lower and upper secondary trajectory. 
UNICEF also established 33 new Virtual Learning Environments (EVAs) in all 22 departments of the country, which provided digital skills development opportunities to 1,038 children and adolescents from the formal and non-formal education programs.
Regarding adolescent participation, UNICEF launched and implemented the “Juego Limpio” program with the support of the Ministry of Culture and Sport, with the purpose of establishing municipal football academies were children and adolescents participate in activities to promote leadership and the development of transferable skills through sport. In 2024, 1,052 adolescents enrolled and are currently participating in the program.
UNICEF also promoted spaces for adolescent participation in the decision-making processes related to education by establishing focal groups within the framework of the MINEDUC-led survey for the “National Education Agreement”. On-line and in-person consultations were also conducted with adolescents in relation to climate action and on the CRC General Comment 27 on access to justice and right to effective remedy. 
Child Protection
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Interior in the implementation of the Public Policy for the Prevention of Violence and Crime, Citizen Security and Peaceful Coexistence. Additionally, technical assistance was provided to review and update the roadmap for the formulation of Municipal Public Policies for the Prevention of Violence and Crime.
At the local level, in 2024 UNICEF targeted its support to 42 Municipal Child Protection Offices (OMPNA), enhancing the capacities of 76 municipal officers on violence prevention against children and adolescents. As of today, 190 out of the 340 municipalities of Guatemala count on an OMPNA.
In terms of prevention and response to sexual violence against children, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Secretariat against Sexual Violence, Exploitation and Human Trafficking (SVET) in the development of the implementation plan for the public policy against sexual violence in Guatemala. As part of the implementation plan, 182 officials from different public institutions benefitted from capacity building interventions focused on sexual violence prevention and comprehensive care for victims.
UNICEF supported MSPAS in the design, adoption and implementation of the Protocol for the Prevention of Suicidal Behavior in Children, Adolescents, and Youth. The participatory drafting of the protocol involved 156 officials (doctors, psychologists, social workers, nurses, epidemiologists) and 124 indigenous leaders and midwives from different departments of the country.
In terms of service provision to child victims of sexual violence, UNICEF focused on 21 municipalities of the most affected departments in the country (Alta Verapaz, Baja Verapaz, Escuintla and Guatemala City). As per primary prevention, partnering with community radio stations and local TV broadcasters allowed for reaching a total of 275,466 people in the most affected departments with violence prevention messages. As per secondary prevention. 10,161 children and adolescents at risk and 7,452 parents and caregivers participated in workshops on preventing sexual violence. Finally, in terms of tertiary prevention, psychosocial care was provided to 1,158 child and adolescent victims of sexual violence, along with 1,005 family members or primary caregivers.
UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS) in the design of a 72-hour mechanism aimed at ensuring temporary care and protection to child victim of sexual violence at the same time investigations are conducted and extended or substitute family are identified. Support to SBS also included the strengthening of the temporary family foster care program, which resulted in the certification of 72 foster families, as well as the development of guidelines on reintegration of adolescents in conflict with the law.
Over the year, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Judiciary in designing the specialized curriculum on child protection, which is now available online for staff.
The Ministry of Interior launched a hotline (1510) for the National Civil Police to receive reports of violence against children and adolescents. UNICEF trained police officers on the application of standards for emergency calls as well as on Psychological First Aid.
Continuing technical assistance was provided to the Guatemalan Institute for Migration (IGM) in the application of the National Migration Policy for the protection of children on the move. In particular, support was provided to IGM in the drafting and adoption of the National Protocol for the Reception and Care of Migrant Children and Adolescents in Guatemala, as well as in the training and deployment of Childhood Protection Officers the reception centers and shelters.
Under the umbrella of the Child Protection Programme, UNICEF supported SBS in the reception and sheltering of 2,334 unaccompanied migrant children and adolescents upon their return to Guatemala; and facilitated family reintegration of 1,110 children in 4 departments of origin. UNICEF also provided training to 2,542 psychosocial professionals from government institutions and civil society organizations providing direct care to children on the move.
WASH and Climate Resilience
Thanks to the implementation of the Total and Sustainable Sanitation and Hygiene (SAHTOSO) methodology, 8 municipalities are currently certified as Open Defecation Free (ODF) by MSPAS, benefitting 580,169 people (of which 123,535 children).
National Policy on Water and Sanitation is currently being drafted with UNICEF support, and it is expected to be adopted in 2025.
In 2024 UNICEF implemented WASH solutions at the local level to increase access to safe water and sanitation services in schools, health centers and communities. Promising market-based initiative "Baño Pro" is currently being scaled-up.
WASH in emergency efforts focused on children on the move through Guatemala and their families, ensuring access to safe water, showers and sanitary services on the route, as well as delivering age- and gender-appropriate hygiene kits and promoting hygiene habits such as hand washing and menstrual hygiene.
On climate resilience, UNICEF contributed to improving national climate governance by supporting the review of the National Climate Change Action Plan; the participatory drafting of the National Low Emissions Strategy and the launch of the updated national programs for environmental education for children (Pequeños Guardianes Ecológicos) and adolescents (Guardianes Ecológicos). Additionally, UNICEF successfully started the advocacy process to include a child-sensitive focus in Nationally Determined Contributions. At the local level, 4 municipalities benefited from the implementation of the Resilient Municipalities initiative, strengthening their capacities to invest in climate resilient local social services for children.
UNICEF established ECO Agents, a platform helping children, adolescents and young people to take part in national decision-making processes related to climate action. ECO Agents is currently made up by over 100 participants from all over the country and a leadership of 16 “representatives” (mostly female). Through ECO Agents, UNICEF created opportunities for youth participation such as the Disaster Risk Reduction Platform; the celebration of the 2024 Planet Hour activities in Guatemala City in collaboration with WWF; and the LCOY Guatemala 2024, which allowed for the participation of around 3,000 adolescents and young people (200 in-person; 800 remotely; and over 2000 through online surveys).
Social Protection
UNICEF advocated with and provided technical assistance to the new Administration on the drafting of the Public Policy on Comprehensive Early Childhood Development (Política Pública de Desarrollo Integral de la Primera Infancia 2024-2044). The Public Policy was passed in April, and Early Childhood Development was declared as a government National priority in November. UNICEF’s contribution focused on data, research, knowledge management and advocacy in the 5 phases required by Ministry of Planning (SEGEPLAN) in the Public Policy Formulation Guide (2017), as well as obtaining technical and legal endorsements, through an ongoing process that included workshops with participatory methodologies for government, civil society and the private sector. 
UNICEF proved technical assistance to the Ministry of Social Development (MIDES) on the scaling-up of the Social Household Registry (SHR), which allowed MIDES to identify 60,848 households, enabling the inclusion of 25,000 new households in the conditional cash transfer programme ‘Bono Social’ in a more timely, transparent and efficient manner. UNICEF's technical assistance supported the design and elaboration of the Ministerial Agreement that creates the SHR, the updating of the Socioeconomic Conditions Evaluation Form (FECS) and the process of technology and knowledge transfer of the information system within MIDES. UNICEF's technical assistance included support for the conceptual design of the cross-sectoral initiative to fight poverty and malnutrition (“Mano a Mano”) which promotes, under a comprehensive and human rights approach, the provision of essential goods and services to vulnerable households that have been included in the SHR. As a result, the Government has used the SHR to improve coverage of social programmes through intersectoral responses, thereby strengthening social policy and certifying the first municipality free of dirt floors.
The EU-funded municipal public finance capacity building process was completed in 2024, allowing for the elaboration and updating of 22 diagnostics and the implementation of joint capacity building and improvement plans together with the Ministry of Public Finance (MINFIN). 430 municipal officials were trained in development planning, revenue management and municipal spending. As a result, between 2023 and 2024 the budget associated with food and nutrition security increased by USD 4.8 million in 13 targeted municipalities.
UNICEF provided technical assistance to MSPAS on the implementation of the Biopsychosocial Certification System for Persons with Disabilities through the review and harmonization of normative and operational documents, the development of training workshops for 60 MSPAS health professionals who will be in charge of the disability certification units and for 20 MSPAS social communicators to strengthen their competencies in assertive communication for disability certification. In addition, 11 hospitals in the country were visited to develop a costing exercise that will be available in 2025, which has involved a process of data and research, as well as advocacy and communication actions. 
In partnership with NORCAP-CashCap and the Cash Working Group (CWG) UNICEF made progress in strengthening adaptive social protection through the publication of the Collaborative Analysis of the Normative Framework for the Delivery of Cash Transfers which includes recommendations for the inclusion of cash transfers as an instrument in emergencies and disasters. Specific recommendations were also included, such as the incorporation of adaptive social protection in the National Response Plan currently under revision, which is considered an important partnership and engagement action. UNICEF's mandate and experience in working with MIDES has been decisive in facilitating collaboration with NORCAP-CashCap and promoted channels of communication and advocacy within MIDES, in order to strengthen the Adaptive Social Protection approach, which has contributed to the creation of a specific working group on this issue and led by the authorities. 
Children on the move 
UNICEF completed its transition from sectoral to holistic, cross-sectoral interventions to address the needs of children on the move. Through mobile units and in stationary locations, UNICEF provides health, nutrition, WASH, mental health and psychological support (MHPSS) and protection services to children on the move and their families, both those in transit through Guatemala and those returned to the country. Cross-sectoral support is also provided to National Migration Authorities in the application of the Nacional Migration Policy for the protection of children in transit through and returned to Guatemala.
In 2024, UNICEF facilitated access to MHPSS services to 33,374 children on the move and adult family members, mainly in the bordering areas with Honduras and Mexico, in government shelters, and in communities of origin and return. 
101,973 people on the move had access to water, sanitation and hygiene services in facilities supported by UNICEF in protection shelters (Casas del Migrante), in Centers for the Attention of Migrants and Refugees (CAPMiR), and through mobile units. 
In collaboration with MSPAS, UNICEF provided 6,323 children and adults on the move with access to health services, as par, being mostly treated for where acute diarrheal diseases, acute respiratory infections, skin problems such as dermatitis and fungal lesions, as well as allergies. 
Finally, 9,643 children and adults had access to nutrition assessment and treatment, of whom 1,220 children under 5, 1,271 children aged 5 to 10, 1,386 adolescents aged 11 to 17. Among the benefitted adult population, 112 pregnant and 130 breastfeeding women have been attended.

UNICEF works strategically with national and subnational governments, civil society organizations, academia, private sector, international financial institutions (IFIs) and other UN Agencies to protect, promote and realize children’s rights.
  
The Office of the Resident Coordinator has been a key partner in 2024. After inter-agency consultations, UNICEF retained the leadership of the result group on social development, established as part of the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF). As part of this role, UNICEF led the elaboration of relevant sections of the new Common Country Assessment applying a child rights perspective. UNICEF, IOM and UNHCR co-chair on a six-month rotational basis the inter-agency working group on migration (GEMIG). UNICEF also leads the Clusters of Education, Nutrition, WASH, and the Area of Responsibility of Child Protection in the Humanitarian Country Team. As part of these responsibilities, the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP) 2025 was drafted in collaboration with OCHA and other humanitarian agencies. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF started the implementation of a joint programme with UNDP and UNESCO on digital transformation, after being successful in presenting a proposal to the SDG Fund. Together with FAO, PAHO and UNDP, UNICEF implements three joint programmes on WASH and nutrition funded by the Government of Sweden. An additional joint programme with UNDP is currently being negotiating with the European Union (EU). Additional collaborations with UN Agencies included OHCHR (on the CRC recommendations to Guatemala); UN Women (on violence against girls); UNFPA (on MICS), among others.
 
Achieving the expected programmatic results in 2024 was possible thanks to the establishment and cultivation of collaborations with the newly elected authorities, among others the Office of the Vice-Presidency of the Republic; the ministries of Health, Education, Social Development, Finance and Environment; the Secretariats on Sexual Violence, Social Welfare, and Food Security and Nutrition; the National Statistics Institute; the Guatemalan Migration Institute; and the National Coordinating Agency for Disaster Reduction (CONRED). Engagement with Congress and the Judiciary was instrumental for the passing of key pieces of legislations and CRC-recommendations-related advocacy efforts. 
 
Collaborations with IFIs were consolidated in 2024, namely on Early Childhood, social protection and PF4C with the World Bank, and climate action with the Inter-American Development Bank. 
 
As per the academic sector, UNICEF engaged with Universidad San Carlos and Universidad del Valle de Guatemala on WASH in School, as well as with Universidad Rafael Landivar on SBC and climate action. 
 
Being the implementing Agency of the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), together with successful engagements with public bilateral donors such as the Unites States of America, the EU, Spain and Sweden, allowed UNICEF Guatemala to maintain a yearly budget of over USD 20M in 2024. Promising engagements with traditional and non-traditional donors such us Japan, Qatar and Republic of Korea allow for optimism in terms of adequate programme funding in 2025 and beyond. 
 
Private sector engagement efforts resulted in securing funds from MSD (US$200,000) and significant efforts are ongoing in relation to CP2P. The “Empresas por la Infancia” (Businesses for Children) initiative was also launched, and is expected to produce relevant fundraising results in 2025. 
 
UNICEF Guatemala's Individual Giving operation reached 3,681 active donors in 2024, with an average donation of USD 15.34 and a cost per acquisition of USD 164. Revenues totaled USD 476,000, a 116% increase from 2023. The first digital fundraising campaign, endorsed by UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador Gaby Moreno, secured 120 new donors.
