The political transition between the outgoing Administration and the new one resulted in the need to adjust plans and strategies to the new government priorities. UNICEF unique positioning as guardian of child rights allowed for the swift establishment of a smooth collaboration with all the new authorities. 
The Mid-Term Review (MTR) offered a unique opportunity to draw lessons from the first two years of the CPD implementation cycle, to be used to improve programme delivering effectiveness at the CO level. The MTR concluded that UNICEF Guatemala CPD continues to be relevant, and no significant adjustments are required. On the other hand, the MTR process identified the need to reinforce CO capacities on ECD, ADAP, disability inclusion and gender equality, as well as on partnerships and advocacy. As the current CPD will be extended until the end of 2026, the proposed adjustments will allow Guatemala CO to be fitter to deliver results in the last couple of years of CPD implementation.
MICS piloting in the second half of 2024 allowed UNICEF and the National Statistics Institute to get insights to improve the survey questionnaires and the data capturing process, which will be used in the survey application next year. 
Two evaluations were completed in the last twelve months, focusing on child protection and non-formal education programme targeting out of school adolescents. Their conclusions, together with those of the two additional evaluations currently ongoing on nutrition and the whole CPD, will be key for the new CPD drafting process, due to start in the second semester of 2025. 
Concluding Observations on the Seventh Periodic Report of Guatemala issued by the Committee on the Rights of the Child last May are being used as a useful tool for advocacy and programming, and will guide whole-of-office work during the second phase of the CPD implementation cycle.
The passing of the Public Policy on Comprehensive Early Childhood Development, and the declaration of Early Childhood Development as a national priority by the Executive, offer UNICEF a great opportunity to build upon its current central positioning as ECD champions, reinforce its role of partner of choice of the Administration in the implementation of the policy, and mobilize resources to fund cross-sectoral, child-centered interventions, both at the national and the local levels. 
The reduction of financial engagement with Guatemala of traditional donors such as Sweden, coupled with the uncertain financial perspective of the US Government Agencies in the short- and medium-term, makes it necessary for UNICEF Guatemala to look for creative and efficient ways to deliver results for children at the same time of redoubling ongoing efforts to engage non-traditional donors such as Japan, Korea, Qatar and India, as well as to actively pursue fundraising opportunities with national and international private sector. Despite existing challenging the financial outlook for UNICEF Guatemala in 2025 and beyond is positive.

Political and socio-economic changes 
 
Guyana and Suriname face many challenges similar to other Caribbean nations and, as low-lying coastal states, are classified as Small Island Developing States (SIDS). They also share strong connections with Amazonian countries as both are part of the Amazon Basin and are largely covered by rainforest. Both countries face significant risks from climate-related hazards, including more frequent heavy rainfall, droughts, and flooding.   
  
Largely driven by the extraction of natural resources, Guyana's GDP and GNI per capita are rapidly increasing due to oil production, with Suriname anticipated to follow suit in a few years. As a result, in July 2023, Guyana’s economic status was reclassified by the World Bank from an upper middle-income to a high-income country, with a GNI per capita of USD 13,200 (World Bank 2023). The country is expected to remain one of the fastest-growing economies in the world, with double-digit growth rates in 2024 (estimated over USD 20,000 GNI per capita) and 2025. This economic achievement is, however, not accompanied by parallel social development and significant improvement in the situation of children and families or effectively addressing persistent inequities.     
  
In contrast, Suriname is classified by the World Bank as an upper-middle-income country (UMIC). The current estimated GNI per capita is USD 5,200, almost four times lower compared to Guyana´s and one of the lowest GNI per capita of UMIC countries in the region. The economy is equally driven by its abundant natural resources, including recent discoveries of offshore oil fields. Since 2021, the country entered into an agreement (Extended Fund Facility, EFF) with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to tackle fiscal imbalances, public debt, and inflation, among other issues, embarking on comprehensive economic reforms. This has resulted in a strongly reduced fiscal space availability for investing in social systems and services needed to improve the realization of children's rights and well-being. Additionally, the elimination of subsidies to fuel, electricity, as well as new taxes as part of the EFF, are also making living conditions much harder for families and children. After several years of exceptionally high inflation rates (59.12% in 2021, 52.45% in 2022, and 51.9% in 2023), inflation in 2024 is expected to drop (11% estimated). Combined with the expiration of the EFF agreement in early 2025, a more stable economic outlook, and recent investment decisions in the oil sector, these developments promise to better position the country for an economic and social recovery. Continued collaboration, social investments, and innovation will be necessary to ensure that the benefits of economic growth translate into lasting improvements in the lives of all citizens, particularly the most vulnerable children and adolescents.   
  
Both Guyana and Suriname are set to hold elections in 2025, providing a valuable opportunity to demonstrate the maturity of their democratic systems and their capacity to sustain the transformative processes that are just beginning to take shape.   
  
The current situation of child rights  
While Guyana has increased its national health budget, key challenges persist in child health. According to MOH reports, vaccine hesitancy and easy access in remote regions remains a concern, with immunization coverage for second dose measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) falling short of national targets, at just 73% in 2024. Mental health is increasingly prioritized, as evidenced by  the government launching the National Mental Health Action Plan and National Suicide Prevention Plan. However, access to mental health services, especially in rural areas, remains severely inadequate. Additionally, the healthcare system has challenges in meeting the needs of children with special health conditions, including disabilities, particularly in underserved regions, not least due to a notable lack of health care workers, including those in community health as well as health promotion and prevention.  
  
Suriname equally faces a severe shortage of healthcare professionals, especially in specialized fields like pediatrics and neonatal care. This shortage, similar to its western neighbor Guyana, combined with the country's more generalized "brain drain," severely impacts the availability of quality healthcare for children, particularly in rural areas. Essential primary health care (PHC) and Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)-nutrition services and regular immunization for children are areas of concern. The decreased level of accessibility of families to quality health systems and services, including immunization, has led to an increase in zero dose children, increased under-immune children specifically in the hinterland, and an increase in drop-out rates in immunization schedules. National immunization coverage for DTP3 declined from 91% in 2022 to 86% in 2023. Significant disparities persist across municipalities, with notably lower coverage in hard-to-reach areas. In the hinterland, specifically in district Sipaliwini, DPT3 coverage stands at 61%, compared to 109% in the capital district, Paramaribo.  
  
In Guyana, the national education budget increased by 29% in 2024, and significant investments have been made in education infrastructure. However, rural and hinterland areas continue to face major challenges in accessing quality education. The enrolment of 2,000 Venezuelan refugee children highlights the need for more culturally sensitive and adaptable educational solutions. Investments in early childhood education and foundational learning remain crucial to improving literacy and academic performance, especially for children in rural areas and marginalized communities. As mentioned in the Guyana Education Sector Plan (2021-2025), the inability to retain students to the end of a cycle and school dropouts presents a continued area of concern.  
  
Education in Suriname faces significant challenges as well, especially in rural and remote regions. While the government has made efforts to invest in quality education, including via budget adjustments, these strides were not sufficient to address the vast needs of the sector, such as shortages of (qualified and motivated) teachers, low quality of secondary education and substantial gaps in infrastructure. Government efforts aimed to bring education closer to underserved communities are commendable, yet access to quality education remains limited for many children, especially in the rainforest, marginalized communities, and children with disabilities. In addition, significant challenges remain toward attaining education SDG’s; participation, enrollment and completion rates have decreased. 
Violence against children, including abuse and exploitation remains prevalent in Guyana, with the Childcare and Protection Agency responding to 4,069 cases in 2024 – a 2.7 per cent decline in cases from the previous year. Despite legislative advancements such as the Family Violence Bill, children remain vulnerable to violence, particularly in rural areas where geographical isolation limits access to prevention and response services. The widespread nature of gender-based violence exacerbates this vulnerability coupled with a continued lack of adequate numbers of social workforce professionals, making it difficult for children, especially girls, to escape violent situations.   
Suriname also struggles with systemic gaps in child protection. Despite the establishment of the Child Ombudsbureau, vulnerable children, especially those with disabilities or living in institutional care, which remains a significant number (estimated 1000 according to the 2023 mapping of care institutions) continue to face significant barriers in accessing justice and not seeing their basic rights of protection being realized, thus leaving them at increased risk of neglect and abuse.  According to the Ministry of Justice and Police, violence among children, particularly those in conflict with the law, is rising (from 276 in 2023 to 290 in 2024), indicating the need for stronger preventive and protective measures. Gender-based violence remains pervasive, further endangering the well-being of children, particularly girls.  
While Guyana has made some progress in Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) in recent years, it remains off track in achieving the SDG target for universal access to basic WASH services. Significant disparities exist between urban and rural areas. According to the latest Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2019-2020, access to clean water was lowest in rural areas, interior locations, households with heads who had only primary or secondary education, those headed by Amerindians, and in the poorest wealth quintile. Contamination was highest in the interior Region 1 (83.4%) and lowest in coastal Region 4 (33.5%). 
These groups continue to experience limited access to safe drinking water and sanitation, which exacerbates health risks and social inequalities. The country’s focus on vulnerable rural districts has increased the demand for WASH services in these areas as well as those hosting migrants, yet progress is still slow with gaps remaining to reaching the most marginalized populations.  
Suriname, like Guyana, faces significant challenges in WASH, with equally notable disparities between urban and rural areas. The country is highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, which further exacerbates existing WASH issues. Climate change and illegal gold mining activities have led to frequent flooding, with at least two to three major floods per year, which severely affects access to clean water and sanitation, particularly in rural and interior communities, with multiple ripple-on effects for girls, boys and families. Such environmental shocks, coupled with recurrent droughts, create stagnant pools of water that worsen waterborne diseases and contribute to food insecurity. Rural and hinterland areas, where many marginalized children and women reside, are disproportionately affected, making it difficult to maintain basic WASH services. The combined impacts of these environmental events, alongside with insufficient investment and institutional capacity, further limit access to healthcare and education, compounding social inequalities and presenting significant barriers to achieving sustainable development.  
In Guyana, social protection services are more accessible in urban centers, leaving rural, Indigenous, and migrant populations facing significant barriers to accessing assistance. Public assistance programmes are insufficient to lift families out of poverty, particularly in remote and underserved areas. Vulnerable children, especially those with disabilities, remain largely uncovered by these programmes while their needs are the highest. Despite some efforts to increase the national budget for social protection, these have not yet translated into meaningful improvements for the most marginalized. The rapidly rising cost of living has further eroded the impact of any budget increases, as they do not adequately address the needs of those living in poverty. Additionally, there are no dedicated budget lines for programmes specifically targeting children, including those with special needs. As a result, children with disabilities continue to face severe challenges in accessing both financial support and services that would enhance their inclusion, well-being, and development.  
  
In Suriname, social protection programmes also face significant underfunding, and vulnerable groups, particularly children, struggle to access the assistance they need. While the government has made efforts to extend the reach of social protection services, fiscal constraints have limited their scale and impact. These limitations are particularly felt by women, especially those working in the informal sector or residing in rural areas. Children in rural areas, especially those with disabilities, are the most affected by these gaps in social protection, as they often lack the necessary services and financial support to thrive. Despite efforts to increase the overall budget for social protection, the high cost of living means these budget increases have little effect, as they fail to meet growing demands for assistance. Moreover, there are no dedicated budget lines for programmes targeting children, particularly those with special needs.  
  
In both Guyana and Suriname, progress has been made in addressing the challenges faced by vulnerable children. However, continued targeted investments and interventions are necessary to ensure that all children, especially those in rural, remote, and marginalized communities, can benefit from the countries' economic growth and have their rights realized. Strengthened social protection systems, improved access to quality education and healthcare, and more effective child protection measures are essential to ensuring the well-being of children in both countries, particularly those facing the greatest vulnerability.

Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives  
In 2024, significant strides were made in improving healthcare services for children and families in both Guyana and Suriname, driven, among others by strategic collaboration and innovative initiatives supported by UNICEF. In Guyana it’s the national health budget increased by 35%, funded by oil revenues, enabling enhanced healthcare infrastructure, and expanded access, particularly in underserved and remote areas. At this stage, 15 regional hospitals are being added to the public health infrastructure. However, the health sector continues to be plagued by a lack of adequate numbers of professionals – especially those working in remote areas. In Suriname, the increase of more than 20% in the allocation of the health was insufficient to cover and guarantee even the most basic services, especially considering the high inflation and other challenges, such as staff shortages, due to low wages and brain drain.   
In Guyana, a notable achievement was the Vaccine Boat initiative, which recently brought immunization services to riverain communities, with the purpose of improving healthcare access in hard-to-reach areas and increasing vaccination rates. UNICEF also played a critical role in strengthening the cold chain infrastructure, providing modern equipment that enhanced vaccine storage capacity and reliability, reducing wastage, and ensuring the safe delivery of vaccines. In addition, the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI), equally a UNICEF-co-led endeavor, was expanded, supporting breastfeeding practices across 27 hospitals, with 73% of newborns now receiving early initiation of breastfeeding. This initiative has positively impacted maternal and child health outcomes. Local ownership of BFHI was strengthened through the establishment of hospital committees, appointment of focal points, and the implementation of monitoring systems. Mental health has received heightened attention in Guyana through the “Hear Me Out” campaign, which reached over 160,000 people, reducing stigma, and encouraging care-seeking behaviors among adolescents, youth, and their families. Supported by UNICEF and PAHO, this campaign aimed to transform public attitudes towards mental health and increase awareness of available services. Alongside this, mental health support was expanded through UNICEF and PAHO with the training of school counselors and healthcare providers in mental health assessment and support, with a focus on adolescents. Additionally, a Mental Health Plan for Children, Adolescents, and Youth was developed with UNICEF’s technical support, laying the groundwork for future governance improvements and better service delivery. Guyana saw progress in human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, with coverage rising from 65% to 85% in targeted communities. This achievement was bolstered by a dual UNICEF-supported vaccination campaign that included both HPV and COVID-19 vaccinations, supported
 by effective communication strategies.   vaccination, with coverage rising from 65% to 85% in targeted communities. This achievement was bolstered by a dual UNICEF-supported vaccination campaign that included both HPV and COVID-19 vaccinations, supported by effective communication strategies.   
In Suriname, healthcare access for vulnerable children in remote regions was improved with the procurement of a medical boat, with the purpose of improving healthcare delivery, including school health services, vaccinations, and emergency care. Nutrition support for young children was also prioritized through the development of the digitized Baby and Toddler Booklet for Early Childhood Development (ECD). This mobile app and website provided caregivers with vital information on child development, helping them make informed decisions and improving early childhood outcomes. In Suriname, UNICEF supported community-based efforts to improve breastfeeding practices. A total of 153 community members were trained in breastfeeding support, and a draft national action plan for breastfeeding was developed and presented to the Minister of Health. This plan aims to create a comprehensive national breastfeeding policy and establish a coordination group to drive its implementation. Additionally, support was provided to revamp the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) in Suriname, working to ensure that healthcare facilities are equipped to support breastfeeding mothers and promote infant and young child feeding practices in line with global standards.  
Further, mental health services for children and adolescents in Suriname were enhanced with the launch of free psychological services for adolescents through the Medical Pedagogical Bureau. Additionally, three professional spaces were equipped to facilitate these services. To improve the mental health of children, UNICEF in partnership with the District Commissariat and the Ministry of Health, developed and piloted a comprehensive mental health strategy in Nickerie. This strategy has demonstrated a significant impact reaching over 30.000 people with raising awareness activities, more than 450 parents and caregivers with increased capacity in positive parenting, more than 200 adolescents and over 23 peer agents with increased skills to improve resilience and mental well-being, and over 80 frontline workers and 26 service providers with more capacity to provide counselling, early identification of mental health issues and other technical skills.   
 
Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills   
In 2024, significant advancements were made in education across Guyana and Suriname, with UNICEF providing vital support in early childhood development (ECD), foundational learning, and the integration of mental health into school curricula. Both countries focused on improving access, quality, and inclusivity in education, particularly for vulnerable children, including migrants and those in remote areas.  
In Guyana, notable progress was made in enhancing the quality and accessibility of ECD services for children aged 0-4. UNICEF's technical support led to the drafting of Guyana’s National Integrated Early Childhood Development Policy, which was created through an inclusive consultative process involving stakeholders at national and local levels. In addition, UNICEF supported the development of ECD training manuals, which will help improve the quality of services for parents, caregivers, and children across over 300 childcare facilities. These manuals will be finalized in 2025, followed by training for service providers and parents. The capacity of childcare providers was strengthened, with 36 providers and 20 Registration and Licensing and Child Protection Officers trained to deliver quality ECD services. As a result, 11,967 children, including 483 children from Venezuela, received critical ECD services at health facilities and childcare centers. UNICEF's efforts also supported the implementation of data-driven decision-making through Education Management Information System (EMIS) training for 92 educators, enabling real-time tracking of 4,685 students across 24 schools, especially in Region 1, an interior indigenous region.  
UNICEF also supported the Migrant Education Support Programme, increasing access to dual-language (Spanish and English) learning resources for Venezuelan children enrolled in grades 1-3. These resources, aligned with Guyana's national curriculum, aimed to ease the transition for 680 children (ages 6-9) facing language barriers, helping them integrate into the Guyanese education system. Additionally, UNICEF contributed to expanding access to early learning opportunities for children aged 2.5 to 4 years. Only 24% of children in this age group had access to early stimulation, and in 2024, efforts were made to increase this access, particularly to improve school readiness.  
In Suriname, UNICEF supported the development of the first National Early Childhood Development Policy (ECD). This critical policy aims to improve the quality of early education and intersectoral collaboration, aligning with the broader national strategy for ECD. Additionally, in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF continued supporting the "Play, Discover & Learn" curriculum, which was developed and piloted in 2022 with UNICEF’s support. This programme, which focuses on the development of children in daycare institutions, was extended to 10 additional daycare centers, benefiting 150 children annually and their families. The programme reached a broader audience through 13,500 social media views of early stimulation content.  
A major achievement in 2024, was the support to the development and launch of the National Education Policy. This was a remarkable milestone as a truly long-term education policy had not been in place for almost over fifteen years. The policy focuses on guiding curriculum reforms, teaching methods, educational modalities and to strengthening student well-being, enhancing skills, and preparing students for the future.  
 Additionally, in Suriname, UNICEF focused on improving foundational learning through a teacher professional development programme in emergent literacy. This programme, which reached 30 schools and trained 115 teachers, directly benefited over 1,000 students in grades 2 and 3, improving their reading skills. A parallel effort strengthened French language instruction in schools along the border with French Guiana, with 40 teachers receiving training, thereby increasing the pool of French-speaking educators in Suriname. UNICEF continued to integrate mental health into the education system in Suriname. In collaboration with the Ministry of Education, the mental health education programme expanded across secondary schools, training 44 student counsellors in 7 of Suriname’s 10 districts. These counsellors were equipped to use mental health video series to conduct education and awareness sessions, reaching 35,000 students across the country. A comprehensive skills development programme was implemented in the Nickerie district to address mental health challenges faced by young people. Supported by UNICEF, the Mental Health Skills Bootcamp for Adolescents, enhanced the resilience and mental well-being of 206 adolescents (129 girls and 77 boys, aged 12 to 18) from all five resorts in Nickerie. This success was driven by the increased capacity of nine local facilitators, who delivered the bootcamp to two cohorts, and 23 trained Peer Change Agents, who strengthened peer support throughout the programme.  
 
Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect, and harmful practices     
In 2024, UNICEF made notable progress in strengthening child protection and justice systems across both Guyana and Suriname, this ensured that children in contact with the law had better access to justice, protection, and effective remedies in line with their rights.   
In Guyana, UNICEF supported the passing of the Family Violence Bill, which strengthens legal protections for children against family violence, ensuring that perpetrators are held accountable. Additionally, UNICEF facilitated the creation of child-friendly spaces within the justice system, such as the Wales Children’s Court. This provided a more supportive environment for children involved in legal proceedings.  UNICEF also supported the establishment of Guyana’s first Mental Health Court, set to launch in 2025, which will ensure specialized services for children in conflict with the law. These efforts were complemented by inclusive consultations with children and adolescents that informed the development of General Comment 27 on children’s access to justice. This contributed to a broader understanding of children’s rights within legal systems. Further, UNICEF’s capacity-building initiatives, such as training 264 school principals and care coordinators on violence against children and gender-based violence, helped create safer and more supportive educational environments. As a result of UNICEF’s support, 424 migrants including children and host community members in regions 1 and 7 received psychosocial support. Through child-centered interventions and 11 community outreaches, 186 migrants and 96 host community members benefited from psychosocial support and awareness on child sexual abuse prevention and response, birth registration, school attainment and sexual and reproductive health and rights. As a result, 21 migrant children were provided with psychosocial support including transition-into-school assistance, while 17 teachers were also reached.  
In Suriname, UNICEF’s efforts mirrored these transformative initiatives. The establishment of the Child Ombudsperson Institute was approved by Parliament, and four child protection conventions were submitted for ratification. Legislation for alternative measures for children in conflict with the law was developed and is under review, aiming to reduce child detention and support reintegration into society. The establishment of a child-friendly pre-detention facility in the Nickerie district allowed children to stay in familiar surroundings during judicial processes, preserving their family connections. A data system was created to ensure efficient support and guidance for children in conflict with the law, improving and potentially expediting judicial procedures. Consultations with 124 children, including those with disabilities, provided insights into their experiences and needs, while 34 key stakeholders helped assess the state's progress in ensuring children's access to justice and remedies. UNICEF’s technical and financial support enabled the development of a qualified social workforce, including 264 care coordinators trained to address violence, mental health, and psychosocial support.   
UNICEF's initiatives in seven indigenous communities educated 250 children and 62 parents on violence prevention, resilience, and the impact of violence on child development. Awareness materials and activities on grooming laws and child pornography were also developed to enhance community understanding and protection of children’s rights.  
 
Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation, and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment  
Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions addressed critical gaps in both countries. In Guyana, over 3,000 individuals gained access to safe drinking water through upgraded facilities, while menstrual hygiene programmes benefited 860 women and girls. Community training ensured the sustainability of these initiatives. In Suriname, similar programmes improved access to WASH services in vulnerable schools and indigenous communities, reaching over 1,000 students and teachers. Solar-powered water systems and climate-resilient infrastructure were introduced to mitigate the impacts of environmental challenges.  
In Guyana, UNICEF's efforts benefited over 4,000 people, including Indigenous and migrant communities, through enhanced access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene services. Over 3,000 people gained access to clean drinking water through the upgrading of water facilities and the provision of supplies for better household water collection, treatment, and storage. Additionally, 17 Community Service Officers (CSOs) were trained to operate and maintain solar-powered water systems, ensuring the long-term sustainability of these services. In terms of hygiene promotion, UNICEF directly impacted over 3,800 individuals, with targeted support for 860 women and girls, including menstrual hygiene products and education. A key initiative was the Mobile Hygiene Corner project, which reached over 925 individuals, including 140 women and girls, in migrant settlements. To further support gender equity, UNICEF provided sanitary care packages to 720 women and girls and developed handwashing facilities, benefiting over 2,000 persons. Raised walkways were built in a migrant settlement in Region 1, benefiting 270 people and ensuring access to sanitation during floods. UNICEF, in collaboration with the Civil Defense Commission (CDC) and the Guyana Water Incorporated (GWI), also strengthened water systems in flood-prone areas to maintain essential WASH services for vulnerable communities.  
In Suriname, partnering with the Ministry of Natural Resources, WASH services in vulnerable hinterland schools in Suriname benefited over 1,000 students and teachers through improved water supply systems, handwashing sinks, and sanitary bins. Hygiene promotion campaigns reached over 1,000 students directly and over 5,000 people indirectly. Rehabilitation of sanitation facilities benefitted over 500 students. A solar-powered submersible water pump and water filters were installed in a remote indigenous community, improving water access for over 120 people. Community members were trained to maintain the system to ensure sustainability. A WASH in Emergencies training equipped 27 participants from strategic sectors with skills to address water, sanitation and hygiene needs during emergencies, focusing on challenges such as flooding and droughts. UNICEF responded to extended periods of extreme drought, which severely impacted villages in the interior. Immediate interventions to address critical water shortages, food insecurity, and potential health risks were addressed in selected villages in close collaboration with the Medical Mission.   
UNICEF reviewed and proposed options for household water treatment systems (HWTS) to Water Platform members, promoting sustainable solutions for safe water access. Furthermore, UNICEF continued to support strengthened WASH sector coordination and governance, including by building national capacity and fostering collaboration between key stakeholders, with a focus on the humanitarian context caused by a continued influx of migrants particularly from neighboring Venezuela.  
Every child, including adolescents, has an equitable chance in life  
An important step forward was the enhancement of public finance management for children across both Guyana and Suriname. In Guyana, child-focused criteria were integrated into sectoral budget evaluations, ensuring fiscal policies are more likely to prioritize children’s needs going forward, with the upcoming 2025 budget cycle now including specific criteria for assessing their impact on children.   
Suriname achieved similar advances in budgeting through national training efforts led by the government and UNICEF., Thes efforts enabled 32 organizations to apply child-friendly budgeting and Value for Money (VfM) principles in their work. Evidence generation, such as targeted analyses on children with disabilities, informed policy revisions in both nations, aiming to address systemic gaps in service delivery and improve social inclusion and resource allocation for vulnerable populations.  
In 2024, UNICEF’s collaborations with the Governments of Guyana and Suriname, alongside strategic partners such as the International Labor Organization (ILO) and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), have led to the enhancing of social protection systems with a view to ensuring greater inclusion of children, including those with disabilities. A key outcome of these partnerships was the development of a social protection strategy for each country contributing to setting a framework to improve social inclusion and protect children's rights across Guyana and Suriname.  
To improve the efficiency and impact of government spending on children’s programmes, UNICEF spearheaded Suriname’s Training of Trainers (ToT) programmes ensuring the long-term sustainability of child-friendly budgeting practices. This provides a solid foundation for more effective allocation of public funds towards improving children’s welfare.  
In both Guyana and Suriname, UNICEF-led evidence generation work led to significant advancements in understanding the impact of social protection systems on children. The situation analyses on children with disabilities, the in-depth analysis of the social protection system and the assessments of the District Commissioners' Offices in Suriname provided a clearer understanding of the challenges and gaps in the delivery of social protection services for children. By utilizing disaggregated data, UNICEF empowered the Governments of Guyana and Suriname to make more evidence-informed decisions regarding social protection policies and programmes, ensuring that children’s rights are kept in focus. Further, UNICEF’s collaboration with the Ministry of Social Affairs and Housing in Suriname led to a strengthened capacity of the Sub-Directorate of Social Work, better equipping the Ministry’s department to lead and manage future social protection initiatives.

Strategic alliances across various sectors, including government, the private sector, civil society organizations (CSOs), and international development partners, continue to be key to achieving impactful outcomes for children at scale. Given the rapid changes in the economic context, with Guyana having transitioned to a high-income country and Suriname seeing the promise of massive oil-sector related investments in the second half of the year, an ever-greater focus on exploring and expanding win-win partnerships with selected non-extractive private sector partners transpires as an ever more strategic area for mobilizing resources and know-how for the realization of child rights.  
For Guyana, there has been ongoing collaboration with the Caribbean Community, (CARICOM) in the area of Youth and in the area of Girls and ICT. UNICEF supported the finalization of the Caribbean Youth Development Action Plan (CYDAP), which led in part, to the event for International Youth Day with the theme, “From Clicks to Progress: Youth Digital Pathways for Sustainable Development” highlighting the transformative potential of digital technology in empowering youth and promoting sustainable development. UNICEF Guyana was active in the Girls and ICT Steering Committee, ensuring an impactful and visible 2024 Girls and ICT Day event.  
In Guyana, UNICEF deepened its collaboration with key government entities such as the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Education, focusing on child health, education, and social protection. Notable achievements included the engagement of the Rights of the Child Commission on promoting child health in Region 9 (Upper Takutu-Upper Essequibo) and the engagement of the Ministry of Education through the Joint Programme with PAHO on mental health, marking a significant shift towards prioritizing mental health in the education sector. Furthermore, UNICEF enhanced its partnerships with international organizations, including GAVI and PAHO, to mobilize resources and share expertise in areas such as immunization, social protection, and mental health.  
As part of UNICEF’s core advocacy strategy, the First Ladies of both Guyana and Suriname were instrumental in bridging between national governments, the media, civil society organizations, and the public, ensuring that mental health and child rights were prioritized in the national discourse. Their leadership provided visibility and credibility particularly to mental health initiatives, helping to drive policy change and ensure sustained focus on these critical issues. Indeed, in Guyana, the First Lady emerged as a critical partner in advancing UNICEF’s mental health initiatives. Her collaboration with UNICEF, the Ministry of Health, and local organizations was instrumental to the success of a mental health awareness campaign that reached a wide national audience of over 200,000 people. This partnership not only helped shed light on mental health issues affecting children and adolescents but also empowered communities to engage in conversations about mental health, reducing stigma and promoting emotional well-being.   
Similarly, in Suriname, the First Lady played an equally influential role in mental health advocacy. Through her partnership with UNICEF and the Ministry of Health, she spearheaded an integrated campaign on mental health that reached over 400,000 people, incorporating high-profile media engagements and public events. At a high-level UNGA side event attended by First Ladies of the Caribbean, the First Lady of Suriname championed increased investment in mental health across the Caribbean, driving momentum for stronger policies and funding to protect children and adolescents. Her support was crucial in building public understanding of the importance of mental health for children, and she played a central role in the launch of several youth-focused initiatives that engaged young people in advocating for mental health awareness.   
UNICEF's role as a convener between different Ministries and local authorities and organizations, including the District Commissioners' Office and community leaders, was critical in advancing the improvement of mental health services in various districts across Suriname. This partnership facilitated the implementation of localized interventions, including youth training programmes, training of health care workers, and media events focused on mental health awareness, which had a far-reaching impact at the community level.  
UNICEF’s partnership with the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) contributed to the development of a national social protection strategy, furthering Suriname’s progress toward achieving the SustainableDevelopment Goals (SDG10) and related social protection goals.   
UNICEF also leveraged private sector partnerships, such as its collaboration with the Private Sector Commission (PSC) in Guyana, to raise awareness on exclusive breastfeeding through targeted advocacy and media campaigns that reached over 10,000 people. Additionally, the partnership with TUBACEX and the Spanish National Committee for UNICEF improved water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services for children and families in schools, benefiting nearly 300 children, representing a notable seed investment that is poised to be repeated elsewhere in the country. The collaboration with TELESUR in Suriname focused on mental health and youth residency programmes, raising awareness and combating stigma, reaching over 600,000 people. In Suriname, UNICEF's collaboration with the Association of Journalists and media outlets effectively raised public awareness on critical child rights issues, including mental health, through impactful interviews, press releases, and media events.   
Additionally, UNICEF's partnerships with local civil society organizations, such as the South RUPUNI Conservation Society (SRCS) and New Zealand High Commission, helped maximize resources for child rights issues, particularly in addressing WASH and climate resilience challenges in remote areas. These collaborations ensured that UNICEF’s programmes were not only aligned with national priorities but were also sensitive to local realities and community needs.  
Both countries saw significant youth engagement in climate-resilient WASH initiatives, with young people actively contributing to the development of climate action plans and advocating for youth voices in decision-making. In Guyana, over 60 Indigenous youth participated in the Young Climate Leaders Programme, while in Suriname, 35 youth developed advocacy materials to promote climate action.  
Looking ahead, UNICEF will continue to strengthen its partnerships with local organizations, authorities, and community stakeholders in both Guyana and Suriname. These collaborations will be critical in ensuring that UNICEF’s child rights initiatives are locally owned, contextually relevant, and sustainable. Additionally, UNICEF will continue to engage with international financial institutions like the IDB, Caribbean Development Bank (CDB), Islamic Development Bank, and World Bank to scale up efforts and mobilize resources for child-focused initiatives, ensuring that no child is left behind in the development journey of both countries

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The core lessons learned during the country programme implementation in 2024 underscore the importance of strategic partnerships, efficient resource use, capacity building, and ongoing advocacy to address the complex child rights challenges and realize results at true scale in both Guyana and Suriname. The experiences and efforts of UNICEF in both countries have provided valuable insights into the strategies that drive effective programming and advocacy. The following lessons include the most critical factors for success in UNICEF’s work.  

Strategic Partnerships and Resource Maximization  
Strategic partnerships have proven essential in scaling programmes and ensuring sustainability. Collaborating with governments, civil society, academia, other development partners such as International Financial Institutions (IFI’s), and the private sector allows UNICEF to leverage additional resources and expertise to address pressing issues like climate change, child rights, and violence prevention. By fostering targeted advocacy campaigns and evidence-based policy and service development, these partnerships help mobilize resources, and drive long-term change, especially for vulnerable children and communities. The heightened visibility and reach of the national mental health campaigns serve as a powerful example.   

Youth Empowerment and Climate Resilience  
Youth engagement, particularly in climate resilience initiatives, continued to be a central focus and has led to the meaningful involvement of young people in this critical area. Building on successful youth-led initiatives such as the Youth Climate Forum, UNICEF will further engage young people in shaping climate policy, advocacy, and action at both national and global levels given this is a matter particularly affecting them and their communities. Their active participation is crucial to ensuring that the voices of youth are considered. Moving from active participation to effective participation remains a challenge when it comes to influencing meaningful content of key strategies like the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0.  

Addressing Data Gaps and Enhancing Resource Efficiency  
A major challenge remains the lack of disaggregated, quality data, which hinders evidence-based decision-making and resource allocation. Ensuring the efficient generation and use of data across sectors is vital for improving government systems and services.  Moreover, in Guyana, despite its high-income status, funding for social services, particularly for vulnerable populations, remains inadequate. This underscores the importance of resource efficiency, strategic partnerships, and maximizing the impact of available resources. Utilizing newly created child-friendly indicators in social protection with UNICEF support, efforts will be key in directing resources to areas that most positively impact children's rights. The situation is compounded by the fact that the CO has not implemented a Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) since 2018/ 2019 in Suriname, which limits the availability of standardized and internationally comparable data on child well-being and other key social indicators.   
However, UNICEF has been supporting the generation of evidence with both the Government of Guyana and Suriname on critical issues such as mental well-being, children with disabilities, and access to social protection. These efforts aim to bridge the data gap and ensure that the most marginalized children—those living with disabilities or experiencing mental health challenges—are not overlooked in social protection schemes. Through strategic investments in evidence generation and collaboration with local partners, there is potential to improve the delivery and impact of services for children and other vulnerable groups.  
  
Strengthening Coordination and Joint Program Implementation  
Effective programme coordination across UNICEF's teams—operations, programmes, and communications—has been vital to successful implementation. Engaging with government partners, UN agencies, and civil society organizations in both countries, while navigating distinct political environments, has enabled UNICEF to stay focused on joint implementation and delivering results. This collaborative approach is key to meeting shared goals despite the challenges posed by diverse languages, geographic dispersion, and differing governmental structures. However, the trends of Official Development Aid (ODA), would make it challenging to access funding to develop and implement joint programmes in the future.  
It is important to note that while Guyana and Suriname are categorized as Small Island Developing States (SIDS), they are also part of the Amazon basin. Consequently, their needs, developmental challenges, and solutions are closely aligned with those of other Amazonian countries. As a Country Office, we must prioritize understanding this unique context and leverage cooperation trends within the Amazon region to maximize impact and foster sustainable development.   

Capacity Building and Addressing Social Norms  
Developing a capable and sustainable social workforce is crucial to addressing critical child rights issues. Both Guyana and Suriname need to invest in the training and development of local professionals to deliver essential services for children and families, particularly the most vulnerable. Beyond nutrition challenges like obesity and undernutrition, there is an increasing need for social norms and interventions to address violence, abuse, exploitation, and mental health. Societal shifts and systemic changes are essential to creating a safer environment for children.

Haiti continues to face a complex, protracted, and multi-faceted crisis driven by extreme poverty, inequality, escalating armed violence, cholera outbreaks, recurring small-scale disasters, and political and economic instability. Insufficient international attention and support further exacerbate these challenges. Children are increasingly vulnerable, suffering violations of their rights amid unprecedented brutality and lawlessness. Armed groups—including non-state actors and local vigilante groups known as Bwakale—continue to perpetrate violence. Political instability, with three different governments in and out over the year, has hindered progress toward the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan, directly impacting child rights and UNICEF’s ability to deliver results at scale.

Deteriorating Security and Disrupted Basic Services: The compounded crises affect different groups and regions: urban populations trapped by armed violence, particularly in Port-au-Prince, where 85% is now controlled by non-state armed groups (NSAGs); displaced families; food-insecure communities outside of the capital; and repatriated/forcibly deported migrants. Armed violence intensified throughout 2024, further endangering children as groups expanded their control and terrorized more communities. The Kenya-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission has not met public expectations, deploying under 50% of its planned capacity by year-end.
Two major peaks of insecurity and political instability occurred in 2024. The first, from February to May, saw armed gangs storming a major prison in Port-au-Prince, killing 12 people and enabling 3,700 inmates to escape. The second, in mid-November, forced the shutdown of Haiti’s international airport after gangs shot at commercial flights, leading to widespread cancellations.
The humanitarian impact, especially on women and children, is catastrophic. Only 20% of health facilities function normally, leaving 75% of women and children in Port-au-Prince without basic health and nutrition services. The number of children unable to access education doubled to 400,000 by year-end. Nearly 35% of Haitians lack access to improved source of drinking water, while 44% of rural populations consume on unsafe sources. These inequities in accessing basic social services threaten progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and UNICEF’s mission to ensure no child is left behind.

Fragile Political Landscape: Haiti’s political instability further complicates the crisis. The Transitional Presidential Council (TPC) faced corruption allegations against three of its nine members, undermining governance. The interim Prime Minister appointed in April was dismissed in November and replaced, bringing new ministers and policy priorities. These shifts have delayed programme implementation and required continuous adaptation. The provision of basic services remains inconsistent across the country, affected by governance changes and decision-making delays.

Escalating Humanitarian Needs: In 2024, 5.5 million people, including 3 million children, required humanitarian assistance. By 2025, this number is projected to rise to six million, including 3.3 million children. As of December 2024, more than one million internally displaced persons (IDPs) - 52% of them being children - were recorded, a threefold increase from 2023. Two million people are estimated to live in areas controlled by armed groups, with 1.6 million women and children facing restricted movement and limited access to basic services.
Armed groups continue to recruit, exploit and abuse children - both boys and girls. Child recruitment surged by 70% in 2024[1], with children comprising up to 50% of their members. Over 1.6 million people are experiencing emergency levels of food insecurity, including 760,000 children at risk of wasting and malnutrition[2]. Additionally, 167,000 people were deported to Haiti in 2024, primarily from the Dominican Republic.

Economic Challenges and Widespread Poverty: Haiti’s economic outlook remains precarious, with GDP contracting for the sixth consecutive year, down 4.2% in 2024[3]. Nearly 60% of Haitians live below the poverty line, with 36.4% in extreme poverty and 41.3% facing multidimensional poverty. Inflation and rising food prices continue to strain household budgets, limiting access to nutrition, education, and healthcare. In August, the government revised the national budget, reducing it by 20.5% due to revenue shortfalls. In December, Haiti finalized a rapid crisis impact assessment (RCIA) in partnership with the UN, World Bank, and Inter-American Development Bank, creating a recovery framework and investment plan aligned with the policies on economic recovery, infrastructure, basic services and governance, including justice and public security.

Implications for UNICEF’s Programmes and Operations: The worsening humanitarian situation and volatile socio-political environment have had critical implications on UNICEF programmes and operations. Key challenges include:
-          Increased Emergency Response Focus: Escalating humanitarian needs and insecurity have compelled UNICEF to focus on life-saving interventions, diverting resources from long-term development programmes. The office had to balance its efforts across health, nutrition, child protection, education, WASH, and social protection while responding to urgent emergency interventions. The HCO prioritized nexus programming, integrating humanitarian action with long-term social services. This was achieved through a 'neighborhood approach,' which strengthened connections between emergency response and local social services in targeted communes, as well as through the Strategic Moment of Reflection (SMR) exercise, ensuring a more coordinated and sustainable impact.
-          Programme Reprioritization: UNICEF undertook a comprehensive programmatic review to realign its priorities and strategies with the government's agenda while adapting to evolving contextual and operational dynamics. This review enabled UNICEF to make informed decisions on geographic and programmatic convergence, identifying key interventions and targets to prioritize, as well as areas to scale down for the 2025–2026 period.
-          Rising Operational Costs: Security concerns and transportation challenges—such as airport and port closures as well as inaccessibility of roads —have driven up costs. Increased staff expenses, heightened security measures, and the establishment of an operational hub in Cap-Haïtien due to the prolonged inaccessibility of Port-au-Prince’s airport and port have further strained resources.
The challenges of 2024 highlight the global call to “leave no child behind” in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Through strategic collaboration with the government and donors, UNICEF remains committed to advancing the SDGs, especially SDG 1 (No Poverty), 2 (Zero Hunger), 3 (Good Health & Well-Being), 4 (Quality Education), and 6 (Clean Water & Sanitation), supporting the most vulnerable, and ensuring their rights are upheld so that no child in Haiti is left behind.
