Despite operational challenges due to a deteriorating security situation, UNICEF delivered US$40.3 million worth of development programmes in 2024, along with US$39.7 million worth of humanitarian assistance. Efforts focused on maintaining the continuity of essential health, nutrition, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), education, and child protection services, while also strengthening disaster risk reduction and emergency preparedness in response to armed group violence and the cholera outbreak.
Overall, UNICEF humanitarian work reached at least 1,411,000 people, including 862,000 children. To effectively respond, UNICEF appealed for a total of US$221.7 million to provide life-saving humanitarian support for women and children; however, by year-end, 73.5% of the appeal remained unfunded. The Corporate Level 3 Emergency Procedure, declared in April 2023, was extended in 2024, triggering organization-wide support to scale up the response in line with UNICEF Core Commitments for Children.
As sector co-lead on humanitarian WASH, education, child protection and nutrition, UNICEF maintained its support for the Civil Protection General Directorate (DGPC) and other line ministries and institutions, including the Ministry of National Education and Professional Training (MENFP), Institute of Social Welfare and Research (IBESR), Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP), and National Directorate for Water and Sanitation (DINEPA). Contingency agreements were maintained with NGOs, and stocks of key supplies were pre-positioned.

1. Health and Nutrition
Health access enhancement: In collaboration with the MSPP and civil society organizations (CSOs), UNICEF enhanced healthcare access by supporting mobile clinics to deliver an integrated package of health, immunization, and nutrition services. Additionally, UNICEF provided direct support to health facilities through rehabilitation, supply of essential health commodities, and training of health personnel. Healthcare services were provided to IDPs, host communities, and populations living in armed group-controlled areas across the West, Artibonite, and South departments. This collaboration resulted in 348,322 children and women receiving an integrated package of health interventions, including 76,000 people accessing services through mobile clinics in metropolitan Port-au-Prince. A total of 384 health professionals were deployed across 105 facilities, providing care to close to 45,000 people. Additionally, five health institutions and two pediatric neonatology units were rehabilitated, while 165 community health workers were trained in preventive care, health promotion, education, and diarrhea treatment—enhancing community-level healthcare quality.
Immunization and vaccine coverage: UNICEF maintained immunization efforts, resulting in Penta1 coverage of 81% and Penta3 coverage of 78%. To curb a cholera outbreak, 122,604 people were vaccinated. Strategic partnerships with media outlets and health officials at national and departmental levels, along with targeted communication campaigns, played a crucial role in boosting vaccine uptake and combating hesitancy.
Strengthening Nutrition information management systems and evidence generation: With UNICEF support, the MSPP developed a multisectoral nutrition plan (2024-2029) and the new protocol for the integrated management of acute malnutrition. UNICEF and WFP jointly launched a one-year plan focused on preventing and treating acute malnutrition. Additionally, UNICEF conducted the first round of the IPC AMN analysis, leveraging data from the 2023 SMART survey to inform and optimize emergency nutrition interventions across Haiti.
Reducing child malnutrition: UNICEF achieved significant strides in addressing child malnutrition, screening over 430,565 children under five (222,083 girls and 208,482 boys) for acute malnutrition. As a result, 42,138 children (21,412 girls and 20,726 boys) with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 50,664 children (27,345 girls and 23,319 boys) with moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) received lifesaving treatment. Additionally, 323,090 children (168,006 girls and 155,084 boys) benefited from Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) initiatives, including vitamin A supplementation and micronutrient powder (MNP) distribution. To strengthen prevention efforts, 310,051 child caregivers were sensitized on IYCF in Emergencies, with a focus on the prevention of wasting, sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), and gender-based violence (GBV), empowering them to play a critical role in improving child nutrition outcomes.

2. WASH
WASH sector governance improvement: Despite a complex implementation context, UNICEF remained a key player in the WASH sector, managing the WASH donors’ group secretariat and co-leading WASH in emergency coordination with the Government.  UNICEF played a critical role in fostering an enabling environment and expanding access to WASH services for the most vulnerable populations in both development and emergency settings. Under UNICEF leadership, sector coordination among donors and WASH Cluster coordination with sector partners and DINEPA remained strong throughout 2024. Regular meetings, including monthly sanitation coordination and weekly emergency meetings, helped maintain strategic discussions and operational alignment. With support of several line ministries and input of relevant civil society associations and institutions, DINEPA held a workshop to develop the Open Defecation-Free roadmap and action plan. UNICEF contributions to institutional development enabled DINEPA to advance key strategic documents, including the revision of the National Strategy for Hygiene, Toilets, Water, and Sanitation (HTWS), and the ongoing evaluation of the National Hydraulic and Sanitation Plan (PHAN) initiative. Additionally, the establishment of sanitation committees and a municipal development plan for Gros Morne municipality, in Artibonite department, further strengthened local governance and resource management.
Climate-resilient WASH services for vulnerable populations: UNICEF provided safe water access to 42,000 vulnerable individuals in marginalized and hard-to-reach areas by rehabilitating 11 drinking water networks. Additionally, new partnerships expanded the Community Approaches to Total Sanitation (CATS) approach to 15 municipalities, potentially benefiting 100,000 people. UNICEF commitment to improving WASH infrastructure in schools and healthcare facilities led to significant improvements including the rehabilitation of latrines and handwashing stations, benefiting over 15,000 children and healthcare personnel.
Emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene: UNICEF effectively mobilized WASH cluster partners and coordinated preparedness and responses to multiple crises, including displacements of populations due to violence, cholera outbreak, flooding, and specific needs of peri-urban marginalized neighborhoods under the control of armed groups. These efforts ensured emergency water supply, sanitation and hygiene services for over 600,000 affected individuals, 55.8% of whom were supported through UNICEF and its implementing partners. The cholera outbreak remains a major concern. UNICEF work on awareness-raising and response contributed to outbreak containment. The WASH cluster successfully led the mechanical cleaning of 5 km of the major drainage canals in the marginalized neighborhood of Cite Soleil preventing major flooding in this area. Through joint efforts with OPS/OMS, UNICEF supported NGOs and government agencies (MoH and DINEPA) with resources to implement integrated Health-WASH responses in hotspot areas, significantly containing the outbreak. However, cholera persists in Artibonite and Centre departments, posing an ongoing public health threat in Haiti.

3. Education
Inclusive Education Access: UNICEF education initiatives, including Back-to-School Learning (BTL) campaign, enrolled over 122,779 students, particularly girls (63,094), into formal schooling. To address the loss of over 30% of official learning time due to prolonged school closures, UNICEF provided technical and financial for the organization of catch-up classes benefiting 58,182 students, including 32,083 girls in examination classes (9th grade and NS4). These classes, taught by 1,501 teachers and school administrators, including 228 women, resulted in a 60% success rate in year-end exams. During the last quarter of 2024, approximately 46,495 children, including 24,307 girls, received education kits. UNICEF also distributed teaching materials, menstrual hygiene kits for girls, as well as early childhood development and recreational kits in schools and displacement sites.
Coordination, emergency education support and capacity building: UNICEF strengthened the Education Management Information System (SIGEE) capacity by providing technological support, including computers and satellite equipment, enhancing data management, student progress tracking, and improved decision-making for educational interventions. To support the Education in Emergencies (EiE) framework, UNICEF trained 75 education actors in the Grand South, facilitated sectoral discussions to improve coordination, and provided solar equipment and tablets to enhance education management during crises. UNICEF trained 965 teachers and school staff in pedagogical strategies, psychosocial support, and gender-based violence awareness. Additionally, 105 school board members received training in local education management.
Early childhood education and non-formal education: UNICEF continued its advocacy and collaboration with the Ministry of Education to strengthen the early childhood education sector, providing financial and technical support for the National Conference on Early Childhood Education in September 2024. The implementation of conference recommendations aims to revise the preschool curriculum, promote the subsector, and attract donor attention. To strengthen the non-formal education governance, UNICEF collaborated with inter-institutional commission for non-formal education (CIENF - COMMISSION Inter-institutionnelle pour l'éducation nonformelle), rehabilitated educational centres to meet pedagogical and infrastructure standards, and focused on life skills, basic education, and vocational training for youth.
Education in emergencies: UNICEF comprehensive crisis response focused on responding to urgent educational needs while building long-term resilience through vocational training, school rehabilitation, psychosocial support, and teacher training. Approximately 25,000 out-of-school children, 51% of whom were girls internally displaced, were identified and reintegrated into host schools across five departments (West, South, Nippes, Artibonite, and Grand’Anse). To address the psychological trauma experienced by children, UNICEF organized psychosocial support sessions for 38,194 children and adolescents, including 19,699 girls. To assist families living in extreme poverty, including IDPs, UNICEF provided humanitarian cash transfers to 3,500 parents, benefiting 11,355 children, helping them cover, in part, school-related expenses. To ensure education continuity for students living in gang-controlled areas, seven national schools were relocated to safer neighborhoods. Fourteen national schools in the West, South, and North departments were also rehabilitated and equipped with school furniture, addressing the educational needs of displaced and local students. In the Grand South, UNICEF supported the construction of new regional schools, providing as classrooms, sanitation facilities, and solar energy systems to ensure sustainable educational opportunities for affected communities.

4. Child Protection
Child protection response: A total of 115,578 children benefited from psychosocial and mental health support activities, reaching 20% of the annual target. A total of 2,253 unaccompanied and separated children were either placed in alternative care or reunited with their families, achieving 30% of the annual target. UNICEF also provided psychosocial support to 211 children associated with armed forces and groups through child-friendly spaces. Furthermore, 113 child protection actors were trained in various child protection themes.
Advocacy, partnership and information management systems: A partnership agreement and a coordination framework were established between UNICEF and IOM, focusing on information sharing and a strengthened border response for migrant children. In close collaboration with the Education cluster and Child Protection AoR, UNICEF conducted a joint needs assessment to guide evidence-based programming. UNICEF also set up a monitoring system for the protection needs of children through the U-report network.

5. Strengthened Social Protection System 
Strengthening social protection systems: Over 25,000 households benefitted from scaled-up cash transfer programmes designed to ensure access to essential services such as healthcare, education, and nutrition. These programmes bridged critical gaps exacerbated by violence, displacement, and natural disasters. In close collaboration with government counterparts, UNICEF contributed to the operationalization of the National Social Protection Policy (PNPS), ensuring its alignment with global best practices and prioritizing children and families in vulnerable situation. The policy laid the groundwork for long-term resilience and social equity, benefiting Haiti’s most disadvantaged populations. Capacity-building initiatives strengthened the technical expertise of government institutions and partners in data management, program monitoring, and evidence-based policymaking. These measures contributed to the sustainability and effectiveness of social protection programmes, enhancing their impact on vulnerable populations. UNICEF introduced incentive payments for public sector workers, ensuring service continuity during the crisis.
Contribution to reducing child poverty: UNICEF integrated multidimensional child poverty measures into national planning processes. Analyses from 2021 and 2024 provided critical insights into interconnected deprivations, including access to education, health care, and nutrition. These insights informed targeted interventions in deprived regions and influenced national budgetary and strategic frameworks, ensuring resource allocation to areas of greatest need. Through collaborations with partners, UNICEF supported the implementation of evidence-based policies aimed at breaking the cycle of poverty, particularly for children in displaced and rural communities. This holistic approach has begun to yield measurable impacts, improving the well-being of Haiti’s most vulnerable children.
 Innovations in Cash Transfers: Through UNICEF’s partnership with DIGICEL, over 80% of cash transfers were delivered digitally, enabling timely and efficient assistance to families in crisis. These transfers addressed immediate needs while supporting long-term goals such as sustaining children’s education and improving access to healthcare. To enhance program impact, UNICEF introduced robust monitoring systems, including Post-Distribution Monitoring (PDM). This adaptive approach allowed for evidence-based refinements to cash transfer mechanisms, ensuring their alignment with local needs and contexts. The integration of cash transfers with social services provided families with a comprehensive response to their challenges.
Policy development and advocacy: UNICEF prioritized policy development and advocacy, significantly contributing to the advancement of the PNPS. Advocacy efforts emphasized child-centered social protection measures, fostering equitable access to services and resilience-building strategies. Additionally, UNICEF engaged in drafting guidelines and operational frameworks to support policy implementation. By participating in platforms such as the Technical Group on Social Protection and the "Table Sectorielle sur la Protection Sociale" UNICEF strengthened collaboration among stakeholders. 

6. Emergency preparedness and response
Humanitarian response coordination: UNICEF reinforced its capacity to respond effectively to Haiti’s complex humanitarian crisis. Internally, UNICEF successfully updated its Emergency Preparedness Plan, reactivated seven emergency partnerships, and established a standing capacity across strategic regions (South, North, Artibonite, and West). The internal coordination of the L3 response has been pivotal in scaling up the humanitarian response system, enabling the expansion of emergency operations into additional departments, including Artibonite. UNICEF also successfully coordinated multisectoral responses, including support for displaced populations in IDP sites in the West, cholera response efforts, and successful negotiations to secure humanitarian access in highly challenging areas under the influence of armed groups.
Leadership and capacity building: UNICEF engaged key stakeholders, including armed actors, which facilitated critical access to affected populations, and played a key role in deploying interventions in difficult and extremely hard-to-reach areas under the control of armed groups. Risk analyses and response scenarios were updated, shared, and approved. A standing capacity plan was developed, shared, and approved. Key Minimum Preparedness Standards (supply & logistics, HR, advocacy, coordination) were updated. Furthermore, UNICEF identified contingency partners and finalized contingency program documents in readiness mode, prepositioned contingency supplies across key regions (South, North, Artibonite, and West) and provided comprehensive EPR training for staff to enhance emergency preparedness and response capabilities.

7. Social Behavior Change (SBC)
Advocacy and policy influence: UNICEF remains the leading reference for SBC expertise in a context of limited national capacities and continues to provide high-quality technical support in SBC programming across both humanitarian and development contexts. This includes strategic planning, evidence generation, and mobilization of funds for key interventions. Beyond financial support for SBC initiatives, UNICEF helped coordinate messaging on positive and healthy practices. Key achievements include the adoption of updated messages on Code of conduct in school; the back to school/learning initiative, and harmonized messages on essential family practices including cholera and nutrition for children and pregnant women. In 2024, UNICEF supported the implementation of communication strategies for routine immunization and rumour management plans, as well as the deployment of the community relays/mobilizers to strengthen community-based approaches.
Targeted campaigns and high-impact interventions: UNICEF intensified community engagement and outreach efforts, working with Government institutions and five local NGOs, including 3,500 community mobilizers and 45 local radio stations. These interventions increased service uptake, strengthened demand for essential services, and provided key insights to inform programmes and improve responses to the growing humanitarian crisis and cholera outbreak. UNICEF-supported actions engaged 1,2 million people, reached 7,5 million people with critical lifesaving messages and provided feedback tools for more than 120,000 persons, facilitating direct access to health and nutrition services and education for around 15,000 affected children and mothers.

8. PSEA/Gender 
PSEA mainstreaming: As the demand placed on UNICEF and its partners continued to increase due to the security and humanitarian situation in the country, the integration and development of activities related to the protection and prevention from sexual exploitation and abuse progressed significantly across all programmes. PSEA and gender-standard indicators were proposed and adopted by programmes for accountability.
PSEA training and awareness activities: In 2024, UNICEF started receiving complaints from affected populations, thanks to innovative activities implemented in IDP sites and the intensification of awareness-raising messages, particularly through the “espace mwen” and the discussion groups with women and adolescent girls. Approximately 237 people, including education actors, national and community police members, child protection actors, received PSEA training. A total of 362,939 people benefited from awareness-raising initiatives across programmatic sectors. Moreover, UNICEF reached 15,165 children in 35 schools with hygiene kits distribution and PSEA messages and constructed 139 disaggregated latrines in 17 communities, considering accessibility for people living with disabilities. UNICEF also supported the development of the National Immunization Strategy (NIS) 2024-2028 with recommendation to conduct a gender analysis. UNICEF funded the interagency hotline (8811) and launched a communication mechanism in RapidPro (Msg SEA8090). 

9. Planning, Monitoring and Evaluation 
Support for National Evaluation capacity Development: In 2024, UNICEF and the Ministry of Planning and External Cooperation (MPCE) agreed to strengthen the evaluation capacities of key national counterparts. The implementation of the government-validated roadmap enabled the launch of the National Evaluation Diagnostic Study. Government partners were identified to participate in the Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems’ Strengthening (IMPrESS) training in 2025. IMPrESS is part of UNICEF global Evaluation Policy Theory of Change and is framed under the General Assembly resolution for National Evaluation Capacity Development (NECD).
Support for Demographic Health Surveys: Haiti's last national census was conducted in 2003, making its results outdated. The most recent Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) surveys took place in 2012 and 2016, respectively. The two Mortality, Morbidity and Service Utilization Surveys (EMMUS) were carried out with the technical and financial support of USAID, and financial support from the Government of Canada, UNICEF, UNFPA, the World Bank, and the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria. In 2024, UNICEF and UNFPA began advocating for the MSPP to provide technical and financial support for the EMMUS VII survey, scheduled for 2025. Like other key partners, UNICEF plans to contribute financially and provide technical assistance from MICS experts at Headquarters and the regional office (LACRO). Once completed, the survey will provide up-to-date data on Haiti women and children’s health to inform programming, policy advocacy, and SDG monitoring.

The escalating crisis in Haiti has significantly increased the need for donor support to sustain life-saving interventions and restore essential services for families. The 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan for Haiti outlines a funding requirement of US$ 673.8 million for multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance. Within this plan, UNICEF’s Humanitarian Action for Children appeal requested US$ 221.7 million to address the critical needs of children and their caregivers. As of December 31, 2024, 72% of UNICEF’s appeal remained unfunded, leaving significant gaps in its ability to deliver life-saving assistance. Funds received by UNICEF throughout 2024 amounted to US$ 49.8 million out of a planned amount of US$ 145.1 million of ORR (34.3%) and received US$ 40.6 million out of a planned amount of US$ 221 million of ORE (18.4%). 

The contributions from key donors have been instrumental in sustaining critical humanitarian activities. The Bureau of Humanitarian Aid of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) has been a significant contributor, providing substantial support for various sectors. The Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (SIDA), the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (ECHO), and the Republic of Korea have also made significant contributions. These donors have played a crucial role in addressing the urgent needs of the population and supporting life-saving interventions. UNICEF Haiti also received significant support through the Global Humanitarian Funds and internal allocations via the Emergency Programme Fund (EPF) loan mechanism, which sustained critical humanitarian activities and allowed the office to respond in a flexible and timely manner as needs required to the many different crises Haiti experienced in 2024. 
Despite the generous contributions from donors and loans received, the funding gap remained a significant challenge. The shortfall in funding severely impacted the ability to provide essential services and support to those in need and limited the ability to scale up interventions in all sectors. 

In 2024, Child Protection was one of the most underfunded sectors, facing an alarming 88% funding gap, which limited the ability to provide psychosocial support and protection services for children affected by violence, exploitation, and abuse. 
In nutrition, the lack of resources has hindered efforts to provide therapeutic feeding programmes for malnourished children. These programmes are essential for saving lives and preventing long-term health complications. For the first time, a joint plan between UNICEF and WFP to accelerate the prevention and treatment of malnutrition in Haiti was developed, endorsed by the MoH and implemented. It served as a model of collaboration involving two UN agencies in Haiti. Similarly, UNICEF and WHO developed a joint essential health commodity plan. UNICEF diversified its partnerships with local implementing partners in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in other departments affected by the humanitarian situation, which ensured a strategic presence and capacity to deliver nutrition humanitarian services across the most deprived and affected communes. The health sector has also been severely impacted by the funding gap. The lack of resources has hindered efforts to provide essential healthcare services, including immunizations, maternal and child health services, and disease prevention programmes. The increase in GBV has further strained the healthcare system, as survivors require medical care, psychosocial support, and legal assistance.

In education, UNICEF intensified its efforts to mobilize resources through strategic partnerships, both public and private, to address the growing educational needs in Haiti. Regarding public partnerships, UNICEF collaborated with several institutional actors to strengthen education financing. Key partners included the Inter-American Development Bank, which mobilized funds from the Global Partnership for Education to support educational initiatives; the Government of Japan, which funded school construction and provided support for the community policing program dedicated to education; and other partners, such as Education Cannot Wait, through the Multi-Year Resilience Program and the First Emergency Response fund, as well as the European Union (EU/ECHO), Norway, Canada, France, Ireland, Cyprus, and South Korea, also contributed to enhancing access to education in emergency situations. UNICEF also leveraged partnerships with the private sector, notably with the Carlos Slim Foundation, which provided significant financial support to bolster educational responses in Haiti.

In 2024, collaboration with the World Food Programme and Ministries of Social Affairs and Labor, Humanitarian Affairs and Education facilitated the implementation of social protection programmes, particularly cash transfers, which are essential to supporting displaced populations and vulnerable households. The cash transfer programmes have proven to be effective in improving food security, access to healthcare, and overall well-being, but the shortfall in funding has constrained their potential impact.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
For UNICEF, the primary challenge in 2024 was the significant deterioration of the security situation. The country witnessed two major alarming peaks in insecurity and political instability, one from late of February to May 2024 with a devastating impact on the conditions of life for the most vulnerable as a result of violence committed by armed gangs in the capital, and the second in November 2024, with a surge of violence across many neighborhoods in the capital and the departments/areas where gangs gained ground. This situation led to reduced humanitarian access and space to implement programme interventions and deliver humanitarian assistance. Violence and insecurity on the rise throughout 2024 also resulted in a reduced UN footprint in Port-au Prince, triggering the relocation/evacuation of all non-critical PC1/PC2 staff of the country, exacerbating the already constrained on-the-ground capacity needed to deliver programmatic results.
Another major challenge was the limited funding landscape, while at the same time operational costs and programme needs significantly grew in response to the changing context and growing humanitarian needs of the population. In 2024, the significant funding gap hindered efforts to address the critical needs of children and their caregivers. Despite generous contributions from various donors, urgent needs persist, and critical gaps remain. UNICEF struggled to financially support its staffing structure due to a significant salary shortfall of over $13 million. This situation is forcing a review of all current staff costs and will lead to reductions in personnel in 2025. 

A key lesson learned in 2024 in fund management: unearmarked and flexible funding are particularly critical in a context such as Haiti because they enable UNICEF to respond swiftly and effectively to multiple crises in a more flexible and timely way, swiftly allocating resources to priority areas and ensuring timely life-saving interventions. In 2024, these funds allowed a more responsive and effective approach to addressing the humanitarian crisis. The ability to adapt to changing circumstances and address the dynamic nature of the crisis is crucial for delivering life-saving interventions and supporting vulnerable populations. The outcomes of the SMR conducted in the second semester of 2024 provided UNICEF with critical elements to adjust its programme strategies and inform future actions.

For the next biennium, major programmatic shifts/changes include, among other things: 

UNICEF     work contributing to humanitarian action/emergency response and     systems-sustaining. Interventions will be linked so that humanitarian     action also contributes to systems-sustaining and wherever possible to     nurturing peaceful conflict resolution, social cohesion, and stronger     social/community connections (nexus). This will help break down silos     between development and humanitarian programmes and ensure more coherent     and seamless approaches across both. 
In     humanitarian action, the interventions will focus on both preparedness and     response. The humanitarian response will be provided anywhere in Haiti for     crises affecting children beyond the defined threshold:    
On      new IDP sites, UNICEF will focus a rapid response on sites with more than      1,000 displaced people – the first response will focus on WASH and      Child Protection as entry point. Mobile health clinics through MSPP and/or      implementing partners will be considered following the first wave      response.   
On      sites which have been in existence for more than a year, and host more      than 2,000 displaced people, UNICEF aims to have a full      multi-sectoral emergency response – with a mix of implementing partners      and support to authorities.  
It     will consist of an integrated and multi-sectoral package of services     targeting four key groups of vulnerable children: people living in     NSAG-controlled areas in Port-au-Prince and Artibonite; IDPs and host     communities in spontaneous sites in Port-au-Prince and Artibonite;     Migrants/returnees (mostly at the border areas); and vulnerable children     in other departments of convergence (Artibonite, Centre, Ouest,     Nord-Ouest, and Sud). 
UNICEF’s     work will focus on its core areas of sectoral accountability: a) health including     immunization, nutrition and WASH as an integrated Child Survival and     Development package; b) child protection; c) education. 
With     respect to systems-sustaining, the main interventions across all sectors     will relate to capacity-building of relevant personnel (e.g. teachers,     CHWs, social workers, etc.); data and information management systems;     development and implementation of policies, strategies [we use the term     ‘systems-sustaining’ to denote the fact that with the present situation in     Haiti, UNICEF is essentially substituting for the state provision of basic     social services, i.e. attempting to prevent systems collapse.] 
As     part of systems-sustaining, UNICEF will continue to support the payment of     incentives and top-ups to social sector personnel in selected cases, where     doing so will be essential to the continuity of services or the ability of     children to access services. This is a short-term measure which will be     phased out when the situation in Haiti improves and the Government is able     to finance such payments itself. 
One     important cross-sectoral flagship will be adolescents. This is an area of     comparative advantage for UNICEF globally, and it is a space that requires     strong technical leadership and expertise in Haiti. UNICEF will build on     its existing work with adolescents across all sectors and bring it     together more coherently in a programme framework. This will include     interventions such as: non-formal education and skills building;     prevention and response to GBV amongst adolescent girls; support to CAAFAG     DDR and reintegration; adolescent reproductive health; menstrual health     and hygiene; etc.UNICEF will invest more in its data and analytic capacity, to ensure that data/evidence underpins of all its programming in Haiti. This includes stronger situation monitoring so that changes in children’s situation are known, documented and communicated to inform decisions, as well as programme monitoring so that adjustments to programmes could be made more effectively in “real-time”.

In 2024 children in Honduras continued to face multiple challenges towards the fulfillment of their rights, facing persisting high levels of poverty, widespread violence, and humanitarian situations exacerbated by the impact of climate change and migration. 
Despite these challenges, the Government of Honduras, up to its highest levels, is committed to advancing child rights. Notwithstanding the limited availability of human and financial resources (particularly at subnational levels) a new Ministry for Children, Adolescents and Family (SENAF) was established, and a comprehensive new National Policy on Children and Adolescents was approved by parliament. Honduras also demonstrated its commitment to child rights by organizing an extensive process for responding to the guiding questions of the Committee on the Rights of the Child. The dialogue between the Committee and the State of Honduras is scheduled for January 2025. During the global EVAC conference, Honduras also pledged commitments to progressively end violence against children. 
A recent census by the National Statistics Institute (INE) revealed that at least 4,000 children live in residential care institutions. Some of these children may be there due to violence and/or poverty at home and do not have the opportunity to reintegrate with their family or within their communities. Therefore, there remains a need to continue investing in integral protection mechanisms, including social protection, that aim for family reunification and community reintegration.
Limited access to quality services, especially in rural areas, is linked to insufficient investment in child-focused programmes. This is revealed by a UNICEF analysis of the 2025 budget bill, which shows a decrease in allocations for 13 out of the 23 institutions providing services to children, including a significant 18% reduction in the Ministry for Children, Adolescents and Family budget. Budgetary constraints, among others, also contribute to the modest presence of many State institutions at sub-national levels, limiting access to services.
Violence against children remains a major concern. According to the First National Survey on Violence Against Women and Girls (INE, 2024), one in two women aged 15 or older (1.8 million) have experienced violence at some point in their lives. The main perpetrators are parents (68.3%), followed by other family members (16.7%) and external individuals (9.6%). Violence occurs not only in private settings but also in schools and communities. This "continuum" of violence throughout life creates a difficult cycle to break and underscores the need for preventive and responsive interventions from an early age. As for adolescent men, they are eight times more likely to die from homicide than girls, accounting for 84.9% of the total victims recorded in 2022 between the ages of 12 and 17.
Poverty is another critical factor affecting children in Honduras. Despite some advances, 62.9% of Honduran households are living in poverty and 40.1% in extreme poverty, according to the INE (2024). This economic situation limits access to basic services and directly impacts children’s well-being.  High incidence of child labour remains a reality. According to the National Child Labour Survey (INE, 2024), 40.6% of children aged 5 to 17 are working. This not only compromises their access to education but also their physical and emotional integrity.
It is estimated that around 800,000 children are out of school, which contributes to perpetuating the cycle of poverty and limits development opportunities. In total, 60.7% of children aged 3 to 17 attend school. However, coverage is significantly lower for adolescents aged 15 to 17, with only 29.4% attending school.  Investment is required to enhance the quality and relevance of education, particularly in secondary schools. The Government of Honduras continues investing in improving school infrastructure, even though many schools still need rehabilitation, water, sanitation and hygiene facilities and electricity.
In terms of health, vaccination coverage remains low. For example, by the end of 2023, measles vaccination coverage was 77%, representing a decrease of 21% compared to 2000. And despite solid government attention to increase vaccination coverage, several bottlenecks (supply- and demand related) continue to impede quick progress. Additionally, chronic malnutrition affects 1 in 3 children in some regions and only 30% of newborn children benefit from exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months.
The humanitarian situation has also been severely affected children due to the confluence of crises such as persistent and armed violence, food insecurity, human mobility, exacerbated by the fact that Honduras is one of the countries most affected by climate change in the LAC-region. According to the 2024 Humanitarian Needs Overview, 2.8 million people need humanitarian assistance, of whom children represent a 45%.
This year Tropical Storm Sara had a severe impact, affecting 32% of the national territory in November and further worsening the situation of at least 113,000 children facing critical risks of waterborne diseases due to stagnant water, lack of hygiene and damage to sanitation systems. Drinking water systems were also severely affected, especially in two northern departments, leaving thousands of families without access to safe drinking water. The education system also suffered with 206 schools affected, disrupting the end of the school year for more than 42,000 children and adolescents. The storm increased children's vulnerability to violence, exploitation, and sexual abuse, especially in overcrowded shelters.
In 2024, Honduras recorded 358,682 irregular migrant entries up to November, a 29% reduction compared to the same period last year. It should be noted that Honduras receives approximately 25% more migrants than the number registered in Panama. Of the total migrants, 26% were children and adolescents facing multiple risks and critical needs, as shown by a protection needs assessment conducted by DRC and UNICEF in 2024. A third of the children mentioned having to sleep on the street, and a significant percentage must beg for money. Additionally, the monthly monitoring report by UNHCR, WFP, and UNICEF indicates that 85.7% of children interrupted their education and 37% of children under five have incomplete vaccination schedules.
From January until August 2024, a total of 36,658 Honduran migrant children were detained according to the United States Border Patrol. The main causes of child migration continue to be violence, climate change, poverty, and family reunification. The National Migration Institute reported the return of 9,644 migrant children to the country by November and while the State makes important efforts to reintegrate these children along with their families into their communities, more resources are required to attend all returning migrant children in a sustainable manner.

In 2024, UNICEF reached around 1.44 million people, 69% of them children, with US$ 18.6M mobilized.  In the humanitarian response alone in the context of migration and violence especially, 1.34 million people were served in 105 municipalities out of 298.
To support the important commitments of the Government towards children in 2024, extensive UNICEF technical support was provided to the start of the new Ministry for Children, Adolescents and Family (SENAF), including design of structure and definition of staff requirements and capacity building. UNICEF supported the government reinforcing the system for the Integral Protection of Children’s Rights (SIGADENAH) at national and subnational levels. In collaboration with SENAF and the Association of Honduran Municipalities (AHMON) and building on the experiences and results from previous contributions by the Government of Canada, at least 160 municipalities across the country are gradually complying with SIGADENAH as established by law. UNICEF provided training and support to these municipalities for convening all local actors related to guaranteeing child rights, conducting a local situation analysis and participatory municipal action & investment plans based on resources available by all actors, including the municipality, local NGOs, and private sector. It is foreseen that in a few years SIGADENAH will be implemented in all 298 municipalities of Honduras.
Also, UNICEF contributed to orienting national financial resources towards children, working in close collaboration with the Ministry of Finance (SEFIN) and the Committee on Budget of the National Congress. For example, UNICEF supported SENAF in key budget advocacy processes for allocation of funding, improved efficiency and quality of spending. Due to budgetary challenges, however, UNICEF supported analysis of the 2025 national budget demonstrated that less resources will be directed towards children. One exception being the UNICEF support to the Institute for Juvenile Offenders (INAMI) on its dialogue with the SEFIN, achieving a budget increase of 24% compared to the previous year (US$1.6 million).
UNICEF support was instrumental in leveraging resources for children from existing loans and influencing agendas more focused on child development from international financial institutions (IFIs). In total, more than US$ 110 million in existing loans were more oriented towards priorities for children, including for education, resilient water and sanitation facilities, and for climate adaptation of social services. Smaller, but equally important, parts of loans that were reoriented included US$700,000 towards strengthening SENAF’s institutional capacity. Additionally, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health to secure a successful proposal to the Pandemic Fund granted by the World Bank, that will enhance the country’s capacity for pandemic prevention and response.
UNICEF also provided support to the Government in responding to the questions of the International Committee on the Rights of the Child, working closely with the Committee and the State of Honduras in preparation of the dialogue to be held by the two parties in January 2025.
UNICEF contributed substantially to the preparation of the new national policy on children and adolescents, a major milestone for children in Honduras, which was approved by mid-2024. The policy, which is holistic to address all child rights, puts particular emphasis on four major challenges: 1) Early Childhood Development; 2) Children in Institutional Care; 3) Returning Child Migrants; 4) Violence Against Children. And, as part of its country programme, UNICEF support continued to address these four priorities, including through technical advice and assistance in the formulation of national plans, programmes, and initiatives, combined with tangible action for girls and boys at sub-national levels, particularly in municipalities affected by sexual exploitation of children under a Peacebuilding Fund initiative. Based on the limited presence of state institutions at sub-national levels (due to financial constraints, high rotation of civil servants and limited technical capacities for several specialized functions) UNICEF worked with a range of civil society organizations to articulate efforts and deliver tangible results for children, including through demonstrating high-impact approaches by application of a few models. For example, a) the capacity of 44% of municipal governments to deliver programs in favor of children with the local SIGADENAH model was strengthened; or b) 2.4 times more cases were managed in 2024 than in 2023 in the context of a community multisectoral reintegration model for migrant children and their families. 
In Early Childhood Development (ECD), a priority of the national policy, UNICEF worked closely with the Ministry of Social Development (SEDESOL), Ministry of Education (SEDUC), Ministry of Health (SESAL) and SENAF in the modeling of a multi-sectoral approach to children under five years old at municipal level. The testing and documenting of this model is still ongoing in the municipality of Lepaterique and once tested will be scaled-up to approximately 100 municipalities with funding from SEDESOL and additional financial support through a loan from CAF. In addition, the process for certification of all 26 public hospitals in the country as ‘mother and baby friendly hospital’, with emphasis on the promotion of exclusive breastfeeding is nearing completion and potentially benefiting the 113,000 children born in public hospitals each year (approximately 90% of all children born during the year in the country). Sustained support was also provided to SESAL for moving forward with rapidly increasing immunization levels, with at least 5% over a period of 2 years, particularly in those regions with very low vaccination rates. This support included technical assistance and capacity building to SESAL staff, provision of supplies (such as solar powered refrigerators) and the application of social and behavioural change strategies, social listening and evidence generation to address disinformation and myths about vaccination. All immunization related work was accompanied by a communication campaign, coordinated with SESAL, WHO/PAHO and USAID, and featuring the mascot ‘Maximo’, a bird figure which credits were provided by Disney Cooperation to UNICEF and initially featured in Ecuador. Based on the experiences in Ecuador and Honduras, ‘Maximo’ is now also being used in Guatemala. In addition, the program for the identification and treatment of acute malnutrition of children below five years of age was implemented in 12 health regions, helping to recover 45% of the 3,052 children 
suffering acute malnutrition.  Increased sustainability is expected in 2025 since the protocol for the use of the MUAC tape for detection and the RUTF for recovery is being institutionalized. 
On Children in Institutions, another priority of the national policy, a census on the number of children in institutional care was completed with technical support from the UNICEF Data Team (DAPM/NYHQ) and in collaboration with SENAF and INE. It was found that almost 4,000 children live in a total of 136 institutions. Many of these institutions have little or no supervision by the State and efforts are supported to strengthen the capacity of SENAF to fulfill its supervisory and normative roles. Moreover, initial steps are being made in the application of a roadmap for a responsible de-institutionalization for as many of those 4,000 children as possible, building on an integral protection system that allows them to return to their (extended) family or communities. In addition, UNICEF continued its technical support to guaranteeing the rights of children in conflict with the law by providing technical assistance to the State entity responsible for this group of highly vulnerable children (INAMI). Even though relatively limited children (some 111) are in confined specialized institutions, separated from adults, there are up to 1,342 children, mostly adolescents, with alternative measures to detention that require urgent attention, support, and follow-up. As part of such efforts, UNICEF provided technical support in strengthening INAMI's capacities for adequate responses to all children in conflict with the law despite the many capacity challenges of the State.
In 2024, nearly 10,000 migrant children were returned to Honduras and while this number is lower than previous years, it may substantially increase soon. To contribute to this priority of the national policy on children and adolescents, UNICEF, with financial support from the Government of Sweden (SIDA) and in coordination with IOM, USAID and with local NGOs and municipal authorities, developed a multi-sectoral model for reintegration of returning child migrants and their families in five out of the 10 municipalities where most migrants originate from. Initially, approximately 400 returning child migrants benefitted from this reintegration model, which was implemented in only 4 months (compared to the approximately 440 children that were reintegrated into their communities through authorities in all 2023 – hence a 140% increase in only a few months of implementation). This model is now adopted by those municipalities, even though some UNICEF support will remain, and it is anticipated that this model will also be applied in at least another 5 municipalities with high migration levels.
The final priority of the policy on children and adolescents is violence against girls and boys. Violence remains a major challenge for children in Honduras and has been highlighted up to the highest levels in the State, as a top priority for response. UNICEF, with support from the Peacebuilding Fund and in collaboration with UNODC, the Ministry of Security and a consortium of institutions and NGOs, continued a programme aimed at reducing violence and violent behaviours in Afro-descendant communities in three departments in the North of Honduras. This programme, which applies a culturally adapted and gender transformative approach, will eventually reach 15,883 direct beneficiaries (3,723 women, 3,266 men, 4,422 girls and 4,472 boys) and provides specific attention to girls empowering them and improving services to respond to the sexual violence they suffer. Moreover, with financial assistance of ECHO - EU and the Bureau of Humanitarian Affairs – and US Government/BHA, UNICEF supported violence reduction strategies in the most violent communities with gang presence in the largest cities of the country: Tegucigalpa and San Pedro Sula, reaching at least 14,000 children and providing them with alternatives, particularly through education, to being recruited into (armed) gangs. Demonstrating its commitment, the State of Honduras also pledged to eradicate violence against girls and boys during the Global EVAC Conference in November 2024, with involvement of SENAF, Ministry of Security and Ministry of the Presidency. UNICEF also contributed to improve municipal capacity to prevent and respond to child victims of violence, specifically through workshops on planning and prevention of violence in 90 municipalities and the creation of Observatories of data on violence against children in 60 more municipalities with the support of the Secretariat of Security. Within the framework of the National Plan for Response to Violence against Children, initially 5 municipalities designed
 and approved local plans to prevent violence and improve services for child survivors.
Access to quality and relevant education continues to be a de facto top priority for Honduras where still some 800,000 girls and boys (40%) of school-aged children, mostly adolescents, remain out-of-school. Throughout 2024, UNICEF worked closely with the Ministry of Education, also with technical cooperation of ECLAC and the World Bank, on the implementation of a strategy aimed at actively identifying out-of-school children and reintegrating them into school. During 2024, a partnership with the Honduran Association of Municipalities (AHMON) resulted in the launch by the President of the Country and UNICEF of the ‘Municipalities Champions for Education’ initiative, reinforcing the role of local governments in the implementation of reintegration strategies including breaking down the barriers that girls and adolescents face in accessing and continuing their educational paths. So far, nearly 50% (146) of all municipalities in the country have subscribed to the initiative. Building on these efforts, Honduras is on track to re-enroll 150,000 girls and boys into education. As part of these efforts, UNICEF supported schools in the application of digital education, developing opportunities for 47,249 students and leveraging support to connect 402,129 students and 22,144 teachers to the internet. Together with the global GIGA initiative and working closely with the Ministry of Education and the donor community, digital connectivity has increased to more than 2,000 schools in 2024, with the ambition to connect more than 6,000 schools by the end of 2025. UNICEF also supported the implementation of the MicroBit initiative, which aims at training girls into coding as part of the 21st century skills. The initiative was implemented with a gender focus to eliminate differences in girls' access to knowledge in technology, science, and engineering. 
Honduras is one of the countries in the region most at risk for adverse impacts of climate change. And given the country’s relatively young population, UNICEF worked with national authorities to renew its efforts to not only mitigate the impact of climate change on children (for example resilient water and sanitation facilities, schools, and health facilities) but also to move ahead with next steps in adaptation to the adverse effects of climate change. For this purpose, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Environment on the preparation of an application to the Green Climate Fund for scaling child-led climate action models. 
As part of its efforts in WASH, UNICEF continued supporting national authorities in increasing access to clean drinking water in remote communities, including by agreeing on technical assistance to the implementation of a IADB loan to the Honduran Fund for Social Investment (FHIS) to improve access to clean water in 22 remote communities, serving 40,000 persons. Moreover, financial resources were received from the Government of Korea (KOICA) to start working on construction or rehabilitation of gender-responsive WASH facilities in 80 schools over the next three years while a contribution of US$ 800,000 from the Government of India (through the UN Office for South-South Cooperation) was received for improving WASH facilities in the department of Gracias a Dios, one of the poorest and most remote areas of Honduras, benefitting more than 10,000 persons over the next year. Building on the pledge of Honduras during the World Water Conference, UNICEF also continued working with the various stakeholders in the water and sanitation sector to improve financing, efficiency and effectiveness of water and sanitation management in the country. 
Supporting the rights of girls, and particularly adolescent girls, remained a strong commitment of UNICEF in Honduras. In line with the global- and regional frameworks for addressing the rights of adolescent girls, UNICEF supported activities to reintegrate adolescent girls back to school, addressed violence against girls through reinforcing national policies and programmes, actively promoting action at municipal and community levels, and also advocating for adolescent (girls) friendly health services, including expanding coverage of HPV vaccination (in 2024, vaccination in 300 schools was prioritized reaching 10,000 girls in the ages between 12 and 15 years old with HPV immunization, representing 65 per cent of the goal for girls in four prioritized health regions).
Overall, UNICEF reinforced its work in addressing negative social- and cultural norms and behaviours towards child rights, particularly in addressing myths and concerns related to vaccination. UNICEF promoted evidence generation about social and behavioral barriers to immunization and that volunteers in several health regions carry out training on interpersonal communication to raise awareness among the population about the benefits and side effects of vaccines . A survey among parents and caregivers revealed that, although 85% intend to vaccinate, they face access and quality barriers that must be considered in the programming of SESAL and the plans of strategic allies such as PAHO and the World Bank. Also, a mapping was conducted of local ‘influencers’ that either promote negative attitudes towards vaccination or that could help in changing such negative cultural norms and behaviours. This has resulted in the application of tailor-made approaches and targeting of sub-populations with adequate messages for having their children vaccinated. Some SBC support was also provided to implement an integral ECD model in one municipality, with the aim of replicating a similar approach in another 100 municipalities, once proven effectively.
To reduce child labor, particularly in rural coffee-producing communities, UNICEF, in collaboration with the FAO and ILO, conducted a mapping and analysis of the coffee value chain in Honduras to understand its functioning, identify key stakeholders, and find collaboration opportunities. In four municipalities with indigenous Lenca populations, coverage and technical capacities for case management were improved, and through a partnership with the Ministry of Education and the COLOSUCA Commonwealth, 337 children were withdrawn from child labor and integrated into protection and education activities during the coffee harvest season.
 
UNICEF also continued reinforcing its responsibilities regarding child safeguarding, prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse of authority (PSEA) by orienting all partners, both governmental and non-governmental. Efforts are also ongoing to increase UNICEF’s responsibility to enhance mechanisms for accountability to affected populations (AAP) also at UN interagency level.
A significant part of the work of UNICEF in Honduras in 2024 was related to humanitarian action as the country continues facing multiple crises: 1) migration (transit and return); 2) impact of climate change on children (floods, drought, and hurricanes); 3) Armed and gang violence. In all these aspects UNICEF was a key actor within the UN System and as part of the implementation of the Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan and the work of the Humanitarian Network (consisting of Government agencies, UN Agencies, Funds and Programmes, and Civil Society organizations):
UNICEF continued fulfilling its humanitarian coordination role as cluster coordinator in WASH and Education, Sub-Cluster Coordinator in Nutrition, and co-leading the Child Protection Area of Responsibility. While the humanitarian needs have not substantially decreased, it was agreed within the UN humanitarian country team, based on instructions from OCHA and after consultation with government and members of the Humanitarian Network, to start transitioning the cluster approach to a more regular set-up with leadership by the government by early 2025. Continued support by UNICEF will be required in each of above-mentioned clusters.
Even though Honduras did not suffer from any hurricane during 2024, it suffered from the major floodings provoked by Tropical Storm Sara in November / December 2024, affecting 113,000 children and their families. As part of a coordinated response by the Humanitarian Network, UNICEF worked closely with (local) government, NGOs, and standby partners to provide immediate humanitarian assistance to those children and families most affected. Also, strong emphasis was put on influencing other humanitarian actors, and particularly (local) government to scale-up responses in the immediate-, medium- and long term.
With financial support from the US Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (BPRM), UNICEF and its partners are providing humanitarian support to children on the move (child migrants and their families), transiting the country. Currently, most of the support is concentrated at the Southern border of Honduras where UNICEF is working with a consortium of NGOs (the Life Consortium, consisting of 3 international- and 2 local NGOs) and the government to deliver such support. UNICEF also collaborated with the government in providing a human-rights and child-rights based services to the nearly 360,000 migrants (25% children) that entered Honduras.
Even though armed (gang) violence is not always seen by all international cooperation as a humanitarian issue, UNICEF provided, with funding from ECHO and the US Bureau for Humanitarian Affairs (BHA), life-saving support to children, adolescents and their families and access to basic services in communities most affected in the largest cities of the country. With a local partner, support was provided to maintaining children living in these neighborhoods in school by working with teachers and caregivers and avoiding, to the extent possible, recruitment of girls and boys into (armed) gangs. Where needed, and as a last resort, cash assistance is provided to the most vulnerable families to allow them to seek new opportunities outside of these neighborhoods. In 2024, this benefitted 5,028 children.

UNICEF in Honduras is considered as a credible partner by government, national congress, the international community, and civil society while also regular interaction occurs with multiple media outlets, academia, and child-focused foundations- and initiatives supported by the private sector. 
UNICEF contributes to the results of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) which, in turn, is in support of the ambition of Honduras to progressively achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the accompanying Sustainable Development Goals. For this purpose, UNICEF actively contributes to the work of the various UN results groups for the UNSDCF and is also involved in the implementation of multiple joint programmes (e.g. violence reduction with UNODC, child labour reduction with FAO and ILO) and closely collaborates with other Agencies, Funds and Programmes in areas of joint mandates (e.g. with WHO/PAHO in immunization and pandemic fund, with UNESCO and ESCAP in education, with UNFPA and UN Women in gender-based violence, with UNHCR and IOM in migration and forced displacement, with WFP in nutrition). Moreover, UNICEF contributed to solid coordination and cooperation for humanitarian preparedness and response, including as part of the humanitarian network.
UNICEF is an active member of the Global Movement for Children – Honduras chapter and works closely with its members. For example, in 2024, the Movement jointly advocated to promote increased allocation of national budgets to the new Ministry of Children, Adolescents and Family (SENAF). Moreover, in 2024 extensive consultations took place with civil society, including with COIPRODENH – a network of more than 20 child-focused NGOs- to better understand the situation of children in all parts of the country and to call for action for children, including through interactions with the International Committee on the Rights of the Child.
Besides close collaboration with members of the Movement, UNICEF maintains strong partnerships with a wide range of international- and national NGOs for programme implementation, particularly at the sub-national levels and for humanitarian action. This includes an innovative approach by working with consortiums of NGOs for programming rather than having partnerships with stand-alone NGOs. This approach contributes to increased efficiencies and better coordination between participating NGOs, resulting in higher programme effectiveness, visibility, and advocacy potential. Currently, UNICEF works with the LIFE Consortium (a group of in total 5 NGOs) for humanitarian action for migrants in transit, and with the CONPAZ Consortium for a programme aimed at violence prevention in indigenous- and Afro descendent communities in the North of the country.  
UNICEF continues to be a partner of choice for the international community. While funding levels for the regular programme remained somewhat below projections and relying on few donors and on inter-agency funding such as the joint SDG-fund and the Peacebuilding Fund. Contributions from global thematic funding and the modality ‘Other Resources for unfunded Regular Resources’ also contributed to having solid results for children in 2024. Some new partnerships materialized with non-traditional donors such as the Government of Korea (KOICA) and the Government of India (through the Office of UN South-South Cooperation) along with additional prospects from more traditional donors provide a relatively solid funding outlook for 2025. For humanitarian action, UNICEF benefitted from well-established partnerships with longstanding support such to the mission as the United States government (BHA, BPRM) and ECHO, CERF, GAVI and the Government of Sweden. However, many of these donors (both for the regular programme and for humanitarian action) have already indicated that funding levels may be reduced in the coming years, despite Honduras being one of the poorest countries in Latin America and suffering from multiple humanitarian situations. 
The described funding outlook demands a need for diversification of funding and new ways of working, including with much more emphasis on leveraging resources from International Financial Institutions (IFIs) such as the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and the Latin American and the Caribbean Development Bank (CAF). Moreover, UNICEF will need to reinforce its emphasis on orienting existing government resources (underutilized loans and funding available within the existing fiscal space) towards priorities for children. In addition, UNICEF already started joining efforts in application for other international funding modalities for the government, such as the Green Climate Fund, with adequate attention to the impact of climate change on children. Finally, the partnership between SESAL and UNICEF facilitated UNICEF being designated as the majority implementing partner of the Pandemic Fund ($ 13 M USD), awarded by the World Bank board. Honduras obtained a successful proposal that will increase the country's capacities for the prevention and response to future pandemics.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
