UNICEF cooperation in Honduras was characterized by abundant technical assistance to national government authorities (SENAF, SESAL, SEDUC, AMHON, SEDESOL, Ministry of Security, INE, etc.) and extensive coordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This work was combined with sub-national level action, particularly in municipalities. In 2024, UNICEF had a footprint in 60% of the 298 municipalities of the country, either in development or in humanitarian action. Due to limited State presence at the subnational level, a mix was applied of strengthening local government capacities along with support to local NGOs to deliver tangible results.
Emphasis was placed on SIGADENAH at municipal level (at least in 131 municipalities), in close collaboration with AMHON. For the coming years, it is important to further build on the partnership with AMHON and civil society since there are a lot of changes in staffing in State institutions that have a presence at the subnational level. The lack of an effectively enforced civil servant career path (irrespective of political changes) significantly hampers a systematic approach towards capacity building. For this purpose, UNICEF will continue strengthening its subnational presence, strategically positioning selected staff in municipalities across the country, working closely with UNV. These staff will primarily support action for children, convening local actors and existing resources, and for closer monitoring of UNICEF supported programme models.
The systematic approach to the application of modeling was reinforced with strategies for scaling-up such models when proved effective and including costing as a critical aspect of replication from Government and/or IFIs. Currently, UNICEF in Honduras concentrates efforts on delivering results for children through five models: 1) Local governance within the framework of SIGADENAH; 2) Schools at the center of communities; 3) Early Childhood Development; 4) Reintegration of returning child migrants; 5) Violence reduction in vulnerable urban areas. Initiatives such as Municipalities Champions of Education and the Model for the Reintegration of Returned Migrant Children show that local approaches can have a significant impact and be scaled-up by national authorities to maximize their reach. Continued efforts are required to document experiences these 5 central models as an input for the forthcoming country programme evaluation in 2025. 
During the year, UNICEF continued its efforts on leveraging funds advocating for an adequate use of funds towards child-rights, in some cases even during the negotiation of current loans and non-reimbursable aid between the State of Honduras and IFIs. It’s worth mentioning the agreement signed between UNICEF and the Honduran Social Investment Fund Ministry in the context of a $ 30 M USD loan on WASH from the IDB in vulnerable communities of the country. The cooperation will be focused for UNICEF on the provision of technical assistance, and monitoring on climate resilient and gender sensitive WASH in schools;a community centered approach to the management of safe water in communities, and the support to the production of participatory municipal safe/climate resilient water plans. Also on WASH, UNICEF managed to influence the Ministry of Finance in its negotiation with the CAF to allocate a total of $ 24 M USD loan to improve access to quality water including a child focused approach. These funds will be implemented by the national water agency from 2025.
In addition, a fruitful cooperation with the Ministry of Education and the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) took place where UNICEF provided technical support and advocated for the approval of a $12 M USD donation for Honduras from the GPE and supported the design of a $ 57 M USD loan from the IDB emphasizing rural secondary education, and a flexible learning offer in primary education.  These funds for education will be very likely endorsed by the National Congress in 2025. Worth mentioning also was the technical support that UNICEF provided to the Secretary of the Environment in the proposal submitted to the Green Climate Fund by Honduras for almost $20 MUSD.
Moreover, UNICEF continued working with the Ministry of Finance and the Budgetary Committee of National Congress in orienting existing government resources towards priorities for children. Examples of this are the additional $ 2. 3 M USD allocated from the State to SENAF and INAMI. Anticipating a possible challenge in resource mobilization from traditional partners, UNICEF will need to continue reinforcing both leveraging resources from IFIs and from the Government. For this purpose, more capacity will need to be established within the office to address Public Finance for Children.
While having a solid gender-responsive programming approach, continued attention and investment is required to address the rights of adolescent girls, particularly violence against girls, prevention of sexual abuse and exploitation, enrolment of in quality- and relevant secondary education. In 2025, UNICEF will need to consider this while developing the next UNICEFcountry programme, along with other crucial aspects such as addressing the impact of climate change on children.
By the end of 2024, the humanitarian cluster structure will transition towards more national ownership. However, strong technical assistance will remain required (given capacity challenges of the authorities at sub-national levels). Nevertheless, funding for humanitarian action is expected to be under pressure as traditional donors are gradually withdrawing support from Honduras. In this context, more emphasis could be put on addressing the humanitarian – development nexus (or the triple humanitarian – development – peace nexus). This could also be examined when developing the next UNICEF supported country programme.
The Office's emergency preparation proved effective for a prompt and adequate humanitarian response in the event of an emergency, as witnessed when responding to the severe flooding caused by Tropical Storm Sara. The office had the capacity to respond from the first 24 hours after the emergency was officially declared by the Government and it was also in coordinating assistance through humanitarian clusters. While responding and acknowledging the transition from the cluster coordination humanitarian structure to more sustained leadership by the government, continued efforts are needed to leverage resources and action from local governments and not only relying on UNICEF partners or NGOs for response and aiming for much larger scale humanitarian responses based on the responsibilities of local governments.

Jamaica is classified as an upper middle-income country with a GDP per capita of approximately $6,874 USD (2023) [1], reflecting an increase over the previous 3 years. It has an estimated population of 2.8 million, 720,000 (25%) of which are children.  Jamaica is a stable, parliamentary democracy and a member of the Commonwealth. The upcoming general elections, scheduled for 2025, present an opportunity to advocate for improvements in public policies affecting children and adolescents. Limited progress has been made towards the 2030 agenda, with only 28% of the SDG indicators on target and 32% of them worsening. As a Small Island Developing State (SIDS), Jamaica shares vulnerabilities common to other SIDS, including undiversified economies, limited social services, dependence on external markets, and susceptibility to disasters, natural hazards, and climate change. 

Despite its upper middle-income classification, around 12.3% of Jamaicans still live below the international upper-middle income poverty line. Food insecurity remains an issue, and poor eating habits contribute to challenges of obesity among children.  Although widespread access to education exists, persistent gaps in education quality hinder student learning, ultimately impacting secondary school completion rates. Jamaica’s children also experience high levels of exposure to violence. The evidence landscape on the situation of Jamaica’s children was significantly widened in 2024 with the release of the Reproductive Health Survey 2021 (RHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2022 (MICS), Jamaica Survey of Living Conditions 2022 (JSLC), Violence against Children Survey 2023 (VACS) and MICS Plus, providing key information on progress in child-related issues.


The JSLC reports an increase in poverty (16.7 %) over the previous measure in 2019 of 11.0%, with poverty being highest in rural areas (58.6%). Children (0-17) and adolescents (10-19) continue to bear a higher burden of poverty with a prevalence of 22.1% and 23.9% respectively. Income inequities are reflected in a progressively increasing Gini Coefficient, in real terms, the poorest quintile reduced consumption by 2.6 per cent, while those in the richest increased it by 9.4 per cent compared to 2019.

According to the 2022 MICS, Jamaica continues to exhibit universal birth registration at 99% however challenges remain with 16% of children under five who are not in possession of their birth certificates, with children in the poorest households being most impacted (24%). Without this legal proof of their identity, children can become "invisible" to the essential public services like healthcare, education, and social safety nets. The survey also reported that approximately 6% of children aged 2-17 years had a functional difficulty, with the most significant disparities among wealthy quintiles and mother’s education.
 
Approximately one-third (33%) of babies under 6 months are being exclusively breastfed, an increase from 24% in the 2011 MICS.  Using the FAO Food Insecurity Experience Scale, MICS PLUS estimated that 37% of households were experiencing moderate to severe food insecurity. Poor eating habits among children were reflected in 46% of children aged 1-2 years having 2 cups or more of soda or sugary drinks per day, 38% in the 3-17 age group. According to the World Health Organization, 36% of Jamaican children aged 13-15 are either overweight or obese, putting them at greater risk for non-communicable diseases.

Boys and girls in Jamaica have almost universal access to education, with 99% completion rates at the primary level and 95% at the lower secondary level. Nevertheless, the challenges lie in the quality of learning outcomes and upper secondary school completion (86%). The MICS foundational learning data revealed notable differences based on gender and socio-economic status. Girls consistently outperformed boys in reading (67% mastery compared to 58%) and in math about 50% of both genders did not demonstrate foundational numeracy skills. Students from higher income households achieved significantly better foundational reading skills (82%) compared to those from poorer households (67%). In math, both groups scored lower overall, with the wealthier students still coming out on top (66%) compared to those from lower income homes (33%). Finally, the urban/rural divide is also a factor as only 47% of rural students showed competency. Addressing these disparities is critical for improving national education outcomes.  

The Ministry of Health and Wellness reports that up to 60% of those treated at hospitals for attempted suicides, were adolescents and young people under age 24. Immunization rates decrease as the child gets older, with approximately 89% immunized (according to the schedule) at 12-23 months, falling off to 56% among those aged 24-35 months. The RHS 2021 revealed a declining fertility rate, the country is now below replacement level at 1.9 births per woman. Significant progress was made with the adolescent fertility rate, moving from the estimated 70 births per 1000 women aged 15-19 in 2008 to 32. Access to SRH services continue to be challenged by the legal age of consent (16 yrs). The survey showed a slight decline from 2008 in the use of contraception at last intercourse for both young men and women aged 15-24.

The VACS 2023 report highlights the urgent need for evidence-based interventions at scale to prevent and respond to violence against children and youth in Jamaica. More than three out of every four children and youth (ages 13-24) have experienced violence in their lifetime, which includes physical, emotional, and sexual violence. Nearly one in four females (23.7%) and over one in ten males (11.7%) experienced sexual violence during childhood. Both sexes reported high rates of physical violence, with roughly one-third of females and males experiencing it in childhood. Emotional violence from peers is also prevalent, affecting nearly one in three females and one in five males. Children and youth are often exposed to severe physical violence in their communities, witnessing violence in homes, schools, and neighborhoods. Those who have experienced violence are at a higher risk of facing health and social problems, including chronic diseases, mental health issues, substance abuse, and the perpetration of violence later in life. MICS 2022 reported a slight reduction among children aged 1-14 years who experienced violent discipline. Nevertheless, the number remains unacceptably high moving from 84% in 2011 to 76%, reflecting the pervasiveness of this practice.

Jamaica is vulnerable to several natural hazards including intense hurricanes, extreme rainfall events, droughts, sea level rise and earthquakes. The need for shock-responsive services was reinforced by the impact of Hurricane Beryl on Jamaica in July 2024. A survey of over 14,000 houses conducted by the government indicated that 779 houses were destroyed, and several thousand others suffered severe or minor damage. Social protection initiatives targeted the vulnerable groups and those most affected by the hurricane.

Focused on achieving the SDGs, national priorities, and the UNSDCF, JCO made significant contributions during 2024, including the response to Hurricane Beryl, strengthening the nexus between humanitarian and development actions, especially in the health, WASH, and social protection sectors, producing and disseminating data, and reviewing and adjusting the strategies and enablers that underlie all of the office's work.
 
Beryl Response
A Category 4 hurricane, the largest ever reported at the beginning of the hurricane season, hit Jamaica on July 5, highlighting the serious increase in sea temperatures and its effects on the most vulnerable population. Hurricane Beryl affected 328,000 people, including 93,300 children, causing severe disruptions in essential services: food and nutrition security, access to clean water, physical and mental health services, and educational continuity. 
 
Based on the Core Commitments for Children (CCC) and the emergency preparedness and response plan that had been strengthened over the past year, UNICEF provided assistance through cash transfers to 7,600 households, which included people living in poverty, children with disabilities, and adolescent mothers. UNICEF supported the Ministry of Labour and Social Security (MLSS) to enhance its direct assistance program for individuals with disabilities. This partnership focused on expanding program reach, improving accessibility and tailoring benefits to meet the unique needs of 1,500 children with disabilities.
     
UNICEF was on the ground within the first four days of the emergency, implementing its preparedness measures through partnerships with the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) and Food for the Poor (FFP). Some 6,000 10-liter water containers, which were prepositioned, were immediately distributed, alleviating the suffering of approximately 7,200 beneficiaries. More than 3,600 hygiene kits items were distributed, and 8 water points were installed to bring water closer to communities. These points were installed in coordination with local authorities to ensure their sustainability.
 
Additionally, approximately 2,000 children and their families were directly supported through social and psychosocial support activities. Further, 530 teachers from the most severely affected schools were trained in Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) and Psychological First Aid (PFA), and 150 school counselors were trained and their schools equipped with psychosocial first-aid materials to support the return to school. Specific counselling sessions were held across the 45 most affected schools, reaching some 11,000 students. Heightening public awareness of complaint and care mechanisms as well as training of implementing partners to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse were conducted.
 
Through a partnership with the Ministry of Health and Wellness, two key initiatives were implemented to address childhood malnutrition. Training and Capacity Building: 2,600 health personnel were trained to assess the nutritional status of children, enhancing their ability to identify and support those at risk. Nutrition Support: Specialized food packages were distributed to ensure children at risk of malnutrition received essential nutrients, covering their basic dietary needs.

Furthermore, public information actions and promotion of safe and healthy habits and practices through social and behavioral change strategies were developed, reaching more than 15,000 children through a special disaster preparedness and risk reduction activity guide for children - "Be Prepared: UNICEF Activity Guide on Disaster Preparedness, Prevention & Protection for Children and Youth”. Additionally, social media, television, and radio were used to promote behaviors essential to health and well-being during the crisis. The breastfeeding campaign on social media reached 3,000 individuals, focusing on exclusive breastfeeding for children from birth to six months. The television segment on breastfeeding during emergencies reached approximately 150,000 viewers, further reinforcing the importance of breastfeeding as a critical practice for infant health and nutrition.
 
Radio was used to deliver three key messages: exclusive breastfeeding, washing hands for 20 seconds, and adopting positive parenting practices by speaking to children instead of resorting to physical punishment. These messages aired daily for 30 days, reaching a total of 315,000 individuals. Additionally, arrangements have been made to expand these efforts through SMS campaigns, with breastfeeding and child protection messages targeting 100,000 individuals each, and WASH messages reaching 200,000 individuals. These SBC activities directly supported the emergency response by promoting behavior changes that safeguard health, hygiene, and family well-being during the crisis. JCO also implemented accountability actions with the affected population, whose results not only allowed for adjusting the response but also offered important lessons learned for future interventions.
 
At the coordination level, UNICEF co-led the UNETT, which in Jamaica's case was not limited to the participation of technical teams from agencies but also included the permanent presence of representatives and the Resident Coordinator. Additionally, UNICEF, in its role as technical secretary of the WASH coordination group, convened and promoted joint actions at different stages of the response.
 
Furthermore, UNICEF mobilized CERF resources by presenting a joint proposal with WFP and IOM and formed a partnership with the private sector that allowed for expanding the WASH response through a contribution of two hundred fifty thousand dollars. Some of Jamaica's main challenges in the future are the absence of national and international NGOs with experience and training in emergency response, the difficulties in pre-positioning items, the lack of intersectoral coordination, and the insufficient internal capacity to respond to emergencies.
 
Building resilience 
Throughout 2024, JCO continued working to strengthen the nexus between humanitarian and development efforts beyond the emergency response to Beryl, aiming to improve the resilience of social services for children. Notable achievements include: i) supporting the Ministry of Health and Wellness to install the country's first public oxygen plant; ii) conducting a WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) assessment in all health centers and over 70 shelters; iii)  expansion of the National Medical  Waste Management  Plant iv) continuing to enhance the vaccination system, which began at the start of this cooperation cycle with the provision of cold chain equipment nationwide. This effort has progressed during 2024 with the advancements on digitization of vaccination records and the promotion of behavioral changes to ensure vaccine adherence. Equally important were the efforts to improve the flexibility of the social protection system, through the introduction of innovative digital transformation tools such as the Benefit Level Calculation Tool and the Vulnerability Ranking Algorithm, promulgating a systematic approach to data and information management across the sector, allowing the government to better identify and target vulnerable groups, including children, for immediate assistance during emergencies. For 2025, actions to improve shock adaptation capacity will continue, including supporting the development of preparedness and response plans in 200 schools and over 50 childcare institutions and juvenile detention centers, adapting national Child Friendly Guidelines for children in emergencies, and training frontline workers to implement these guidelines effectively. 
 
Data production and promotion
UNICEF provided strong support for the development of numerous information gathering tools with MICS 6, MICS+ (6 waves, 5 disseminated), and a VAC Survey being among the most relevant. Much of this information had not been produced in the country for over 11 years. Data was obtained on more than 250 child-related indicators, and most UNICEF-custodian SDGs were updated. In many cases, this is the only source of information on various topics in the country.
 
Beyond the information production effort, the office also worked to ensure its utilization. To this end, several "Data to Action" seminars were organized, involving more than 40 stakeholders to analyze and extract policy recommendations that could be applied across different sectors. Additionally, dissemination events, face-to-face meetings with ministers and other decision-makers, and distribution through digital and traditional media accompanied the information sharing effort.
 
Special mention should be made of the fifth and sixth rounds of MICS+, which, due to its flexibility in timing and content, allowed for the capture of valuable information about the needs and response to Hurricane Beryl.
 
Advancing UNICEF Strategic Plan’s change strategies and enablers
Underlying several of these achievements was the work carried out on change strategies and enablers. During 2024, JCO made a significant effort to improve its internal operating conditions to produce better results for children. Four main processes were advanced: i) Peer review, ii) Cultural change "From Good to Great", iii) Mid-term review, and iv) Business Model Initiative.
 
Regarding the peer review conducted with LACRO, over 80% of the recommendations were implemented during 2024, which allowed for significant improvement in performance and reduction of potential risks for the office. Additionally, an ambitious internal culture review process was undertaken to respond to the Pulse Survey results and ensure all staff's adherence to CRITAS. The work plan currently underway is aimed at enhancing cross-sectoral collaboration, optimizing processes, implementing evidence-based planning, and fostering a culture of trust and accountability to maximize impact and effectiveness.
 
The mid-term review is still in progress, but the situation analysis and consultation process with external and internal stakeholders have been completed. Preliminary results point to a shift towards innovative multi-sectoral models prioritizing technical assistance, capacity development, and information dissemination. These models move away from goods procurement and provision, focusing instead on intentional, results-oriented implementation according to the country profile. The review emphasizes children and adolescent empowerment, emergency preparedness, expanding service access across health, education, and social protection sectors while enhancing partnership development, promoting the strategic use of technology and social and behavioral change strategies.
 
Finally, given the specific and common challenges faced by English-Speaking Caribbean offices, JCO is actively participating in the process of "thinking outside the box" and finding new business models to achieve results at scale for children in the region. This collaborative process between offices promises to optimize efficiency in various areas and ultimately improve outcomes for children.
 
Goal Area 1: Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies 
In 2024, the Survive and Thrive Program made significant strides in Jamaica. On one hand, Jamaica was successfully certified as having eliminated HIV vertical transmission, making it one of 19 countries worldwide to reach this achievement.  On the other hand, another key achievement was establishing the country's first public-sector PSA Oxygen Plant at St Ann's Bay Regional Hospital. It is now fully operational and serves as a primary medical oxygen source for vulnerable patients. UNICEF's support has been crucial in addressing barriers to breastfeeding, with over 50% of major hospitals now meeting international criteria for breastfeeding support.

Progress was made in developing an electronic immunization registry (EIR) software, with technical requirements finalized through extensive collaboration with various stakeholders. Adolescent health and wellbeing remained a priority, with over 53,000 young people receiving life skills education, mental health support, and sexual and reproductive health services through various platforms.
 
UNICEF advocated for policies to improve the food environment for Jamaican children and adolescents, addressing challenges such as inadequate food labeling and marketing of unhealthy foods. The National School Nutrition Policy has been submitted for Cabinet approval, and preparations for its implementation are underway. UNICEF also launched the "Fix My Food Jamaica" initiative, training young advocates to focus on strategic youth-led advocacy for Front of Package Warning Labels. 
 
The national Early Screening, Identification and Referral (ESIR) Pathway guidelines were approved and a user-friendly format intended to broaden understanding and compliance is nearing completion.  

Goal Area 2: Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future.
In 2024, UNICEF focused on enhancing quality education and school-to-work transitions through inclusive, technology-based innovations (Accessible Digital textbooks and the Learning Passport Jamaica) and system strengthening. Significant strides were made in early childhood education, implementing an early screening and referral pathway for inclusion. UNICEF also supported the evaluation of the Irie Classroom Toolbox methodology and the rolling out of the Education Management Information System in 245 schools, improving data-driven decision-making capabilities.
 
In response to Hurricane Beryl, UNICEF partnered with local organizations to provide Mental Health and Psychosocial Support training to increase the overall number of teachers trained to over 1000 island wide and established 63 volunteer-staffed Community of Care groups. These efforts supported the expansion of the school-wide positive behavior intervention and support framework, now active in over 60% of primary and secondary schools.
 
UNICEF continued to develop the FunDoo chatbot, which now has over 1,300 users, helping youth gain 21st-century life skills via WhatsApp. UNICEF also partnered with the National Vocational Training Agency to adapt School-to-Work Transition content for the chatbot and created an online STWT resource hub for the special education sector. These initiatives collectively provide a robust platform for career development and support.
 
Goal Area 3. Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices.
In 2024, UNICEF made significant progress in strengthening Jamaica's child protection system and promoting positive social and gender norms. The organization launched the Violence Against Children and Youth Survey (VACS) and released MICS and MICS+ data to inform child protection priorities. UNICEF is currently developing a costed action plan to implement recommendations from the 2022 Child Protection System Evaluation and supported Jamaica's participation in the Global Ministerial Conference on Eliminating Violence Against Children.
 
Service delivery improvements included training 70 judiciary members on child justice guidelines, digitizing child protection case management systems, and training of 40 police officers to better support children in conflict with the law.  UNICEF has also established partnerships to support children's needs in the aftermath of Hurricane Beryl and has trained 30 stakeholders and first responders to ensure prevention and response to gender-based violence in emergencies.
 
UNICEF supported the Empowered Futures Parenting Curriculum through the Women's Centre of Jamaica Foundation, empowering adolescent mothers and counselors with essential skills for child development and non-violent discipline. These comprehensive efforts demonstrate UNICEF's commitment to strengthening Jamaica's child protection system through data-driven strategies, policy enhancements, improved service delivery, and community-focused initiatives.
 
Goal Area 4. Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment. 
In 2024, UNICEF supported the response to the Beryl Hurricane, strengthened the Climate, Environment, Energy, and Disaster Risk Reduction (CEED) Framework, and improved the resilience of WASH in health sector institutions.
Hurricane Beryl, a Category 4 storm, struck Jamaica on July 5, affecting over 328,000 people, including 93,300 children. UNICEF's response was swift and comprehensive, addressing various aspects of the emergency.

UNICEF provided immediate assistance to affected families through cash transfers to 7,100 households and supplied essential items such as water containers and hygiene kits. The organization played a crucial role in coordinating Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) efforts, establishing and rehabilitating communal water points, distributing water, and promoting social and behavior change messages.
 
The organization also supported 2,000 children and families in the most affected areas with direct PFA activities and some 11,000 with school-based PFA interventions and launched public information campaigns on crucial topics such as breastfeeding, hygiene, and positive parenting. The response extended beyond immediate relief, encompassing long-term support for health and education sectors. UNICEF trained 2,600 health personnel to strengthen nutritional assessment capacity and increased the overall number of teachers trained in mental health support to more than 1000 island-wide.
 
UNICEF's commitment to long-term resilience was evident in its policy work, providing input to key national policies and incorporating a child-centered and youth engagement approach in main policy frameworks such as the Nationally Determined Contributions, the Comprehensive Disaster Risk Management Policy, and the Safe School Policy. The organization was also involved in developing and implementing WASH Climate, Energy, and Environment Division (CEED) resilient infrastructure projects for the health and education sectors.
 
Despite the comprehensive response, UNICEF identified several challenges for future disaster management, including a lack of experienced NGOs in the region and the need to improve intersectoral coordination and internal emergency response capacity. Addressing these challenges will be crucial for enhancing UNICEF's ability to respond effectively to future disasters in Jamaica.
 
Goal Area 5: Every child, including adolescents, has access to inclusive social protection and lives free of poverty.
Jamaica's social protection system has undergone significant improvements, benefiting over 400,000 people, including children, with a focus on vulnerable groups. Key achievements included strengthening institutional capacity for expansions of evidence-based emergency social protection programmes, including introduction of two new tools—the Benefit Level Calculation Tool and the Vulnerability Ranking Algorithm—designed to create a systematic approach to data management across the sector. A pilot cash transfer program reached 17,900 vulnerable individuals across 8,800 households, while four protocols on emergency social protection were developed to promote equitable access and reduce vulnerability to various risks.
 
To sustain these advancements, 199 government staff members were trained in data collection, analysis, and system integration. The effectiveness of these improvements was demonstrated during the response to Hurricane Beryl, where newly introduced Shock Responsive Social Protection protocols guided aid delivery. Approximately 7,100 households, including 10,000 children, received cash transfers, and 1,500 children with disabilities were provided with in-kind packages.
 
A feedback mechanism was implemented to assess beneficiary satisfaction with the emergency assistance. The survey revealed high satisfaction levels, with 87% of respondents rating the aid positively. However, areas for improvement were identified, particularly regarding awareness of available support services, with 68% of respondents unaware of such services. Additionally, 12% expressed dissatisfaction with service providers' behavior during distribution processes.

UUNICEF Jamaica emphasized fostering shared value partnerships with Government, UN, International Development Partners, civil societies, private sector, private foundations and other stakeholders.

Key partnerships were maintained with (i) bi-lateral donors like Global Affairs Canada, CDC/USAID, Govt of Japan; (ii) with UN - UNAIDS/UBRAF, - UN-Multi-donor Trust Funds (WFP, UNESCO, FAO), - UN Hurricane Beryl's response (WFP, IOM, UNWOMEN, UNFPA); (iii) with Multi-lateral donors and IFIs like IDB, EU; (iv) with private foundations like Bloomberg Foundation, AstraZeneca, NCB Foundation, (v) with Private sector Telecom companies like Digicel and Flow for supporting different UNICEF programs, and (vi) with academia like UWI.

Close collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Wellness yielded positive results in improving adolescent health, exemplified by the establishment of a groundbreaking Teen Hub in St Andrew and St. Thomas as well as Health, Nutrition and WASH programs. UNICEF also partnered with University of West Indies for Health, and Child Protection programmes.Collaboration was also maintained with the Ministry of Education, Youth and Information, and its agencies in particular, the CPFSA and the HEART Trust NTA for implementation of Education, Child Protection and WASH programs.

In Child Protection, UNICEF partnered with government agencies and NGOs/CSOs to combat violence against children. Major government agencies included Ministry of Justice, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, the Office of the Children's Advocate, and the Women's Centre of Jamaica Foundation. 

UNICEF effectively coordinated various partnerships to address WASH, DRR and Climate issues. Collaborations with organizations like the Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW), and the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) were strengthened. New partnerships with the National Environmental and Planning Agency, Ministry of Education and Youth (MOEY), were established.
 
UNICEF's engagement with international development agencies, including the World Bank, CDC and the IDB, facilitated improved data collection and evidence generation including MICS and VAC survey. NGOs such as Food for the Poor, Children First Agency and the United Theological College of the West Indies were also key partners.  

UNICEF's strategic use of social media and partnerships with TV producers and telecommunications companies extended its impact on education. Private sector collaborations with Flow and Digicel provided zero-rated services for youths to access chatlines while partnerships with Project STAR and the Jamaica Constabulary Force addressed unattached youth and social transformation.

These partnerships are central to UNICEF JCO’s ability to mobilize resources and implement successful programmes to influence stakeholders and support the realization of children’s rights.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges:
 
In 2024, UNICEF Jamaica faced multiple challenges that highlighted the complexities of working in upper-middle-income countries with diverse socio-economic and climatic vulnerabilities. 
 
A significant challenge was the limited availability of sustainable funding. Many donor partners perceive high and middle-income countries as less in need of development assistance, leading to reduced financial commitments. This reliance on short-term funding constrained UNICEF’s ability to scale up interventions and address emerging needs.
 
Cultural norms and social attitudes continue to challenge efforts to fulfill child rights, in particular, violence in the family context, adolescent access to friendly health services, and protection for children in conflict with the law. Despite advocacy for positive parenting practices, corporal punishment remains widely accepted. Resistance from society has prevented the government from proceeding with the corporal punishment ban. Additionally, community resistance, coupled with time constraints of caregivers, limits participation in behaviour change initiatives. The widespread conservative views around adolescent sexual and reproductive health, along with the stigma and discrimination of vulnerable populations, continue to challenge the delivery of information, life skills, and services for young people. The MOHW has reported that the rate of new HIV infections is highest among adolescents and youth; however, challenges in access to preventative information resulted in the suspension of a service designed with and for young people.  The shutdown of the Yute Chatz Chatbot for SRH information provides a valuable lesson about the importance of opening a constructive dialogue with some groups who are promoting pushback against child rights, like some faith-based organizations.

Regressive legislation to harden the punishment measure for adolescents in conflict with the law remains a permanent threat, calling, in some cases, for the death penalty and mandatory minimum sentence of more than 20 years. Even though UNICEF has been able to counteract these kinds of proposals, the social clamor and the political will are there to spread these regressive messages. Finally, some communities are resistant to the uptake of the vaccination scheme due to the profoundly rooted gender-biased distribution of the care functions. All of these highlights the need for sustained community engagement and targeted social behavior change (SBC) strategies, which the CO is undertaking.
 
The increased frequency and intensity of climate events further stressed already stretched resources. Hurricane Beryl underscored gaps in integrated emergency preparedness, risk reduction strategies and emergency response within child protection systems. As climate resilience becomes a growing priority, the need for enhanced financing mechanisms to support preparedness and emergency responses remains critical.
 
Cross-sectoral collaboration remains a critical challenge, particularly in aligning child protection, social protection, DRR, and education sector efforts. While digital tools and systems hold promise, integrating these systems across operations and ensuring staff are adequately trained requires continuous investment.
 
Slow process of policy formulation, bureaucratic bottlenecks, internal government capacity and implementation delays remained as major challenges impacting delay in utilization of funds, programmatic assurances, and meeting donor commitments.  Lack of international and local NGOs also remains as a critical challenge for effective program implementation in Jamaica. This became pertinent during the Hurricane Beryl response where the limited number of I-NGOs in Jamaica were overwhelmed with implementation requests from different development partners. 
 
Lessons Learned:
 Despite challenges, 2024 provided critical lessons to enhance future programming:
 
- Strategic Engagement with Policymakers: Targeted engagement is vital for achieving significant policy changes. Identifying ministry champions and leveraging cross-sectoral mechanisms have proven effective in securing buy-in and fostering collaboration.
 
- Evidence Generation: UNICEF's investment in evidence creation-built momentum among stakeholders. Joint studies with the government helped measure progress, review bottlenecks, and provide accurate policy advice.
 
- Integrated Programming: Mid-term reviews highlighted the importance of integrated programming to reduce siloed approaches. Cross-sectoral initiatives amplify impact and address interconnected vulnerabilities holistically.
 
- Program Reviews: UNICEF conducted reviews and consultations to finetune priorities and position itself as a partner in achieving SDGs and the government's 'Vision 2030'.
 
- Partnerships: Collaborations with local partners and UN agencies helped achieve optimal results for children. UNICEF implemented joint programs in education and social protection and partnered with the private sector for initiatives like 'FunDoo'.
 
- Digital Innovation: Initial success of digital tools highlighted their potential to enhance transparency and efficiency, though continuous refinement is needed.
 
- Emergency Preparedness: Early planning and cross-sectoral collaboration proved valuable in mitigating disaster impacts.
 
- Addressing Violence Against Children: Stronger advocacy and community engagement are needed, along with systemic reforms and expanded protective services.
 
- Youth Engagement:  The country program needs to have youth-led interventions like FunDoo and "Fix My Food Jamaica" so that the participation has a 'real' framework which makes it more meaningful and the youth innovative approaches benefit the process .
 
These lessons underscore the need for adaptive, innovative, and collaborative approaches to maximize UNICEF's impact in Jamaica.
 
Future Outlook: 
 
In the coming years, UNICEF Jamaica will implement a series of strategic initiatives to enhance its impact on children's rights and well-being. These actions are designed to address current challenges and leverage opportunities in the Jamaican context, including the pushback against children's rights, the upcoming national elections, and the evolving financial landscape.
 
The organization will focus on implementing innovative multi-sectoral models that combine interventions across different sectors to achieve scaled results for children. For example, the 'Integrated Parish Development' pilot in St. Thomas, the most disadvantaged parish in the country, utilizes comprehensive support from all UNICEF programs. This approach recognizes the interconnected nature of children's rights and aims to maximize impact by simultaneously addressing multiple deprivations. In doing so, UNICEF Jamaica will also prioritize technical assistance, capacity development, and advocacy strategies, moving away from goods procurement and provision. This shift emphasizes building Jamaica's long-term capacity to fulfill children's rights independently.
 
Other key actions include developing a partnership strategy to strengthen collaboration with the private sector and other development partners, advancing emergency preparedness, and prioritizing advocacy and social and behavior change initiatives to counteract the pushback against children's rights. The organization will leverage the upcoming 2025 general elections to advocate for child rights commitments from political parties. Additionally, the organization will strategically use technology to strengthen health, education, and social protection management systems while expanding access to services through digital platforms.
 
Recognizing challenges in partnerships with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs), particularly regarding resource and technical capacity, UNICEF Jamaica will undergo a comprehensive process to identify and onboard new CSO partners and build their capacity, including I-NGO with LACRO Support.
 
Internally, UNICEF JCO will focus on executing the "Action Plan" designed to transform the JCO team culture from "Good to Great" (G2G). This plan encompasses programmatic, operational, and culture change initiatives, with building blocks for improving processes while ensuring accountability, team cohesion, and complete adherence to CRITAS principles.

By combining local initiatives with regional cooperation and internal strengthening, UNICEF Jamaica is positioning itself to effectively fulfill its mission and achieve meaningful results for children in the years to come.

2024 was marked by the biggest electoral process ever. In June, Mexico held presidential, subnational, and legislative elections, resulting in Dr. Claudia Sheinbaum becoming the country’s first female president. Representing the MORENA party and backed by outgoing President López Obrador, Sheinbaum's victory signals a continuation of his policies. Sheinbaum's administration has announced plans to expand pro-poor policies, focusing on social protection programmes. She has committed to scaling up the child grant for all public-school students, an initiative she successfully implemented in Mexico City with UNICEF’s support, benefiting 1.2 million children. In addition, she aims to enhance early education and establish a National Care System to support working and studying women by providing quality childcare options. She is also keen to address child nutrition. Recently she announced banning sales of ultra-processed food and sugary beverages in all schools to address child obesity, an issue UNICEF has been advocating for. Overall, President Sheinbaum's agenda presents significant opportunities to reduce child poverty and improve child and adolescent wellbeing.    



It is well known that Mexico is highly susceptible to political and policy decisions of its neighboring countries, especially the United States. The triumph of Donald Trump as President of the US will pose important challenges for Mexico, particularly in areas of migration and commercial partnerships, which would have direct and indirect impacts on the wellbeing of children, adolescents, and families especially the most vulnerable. By the end of 2024, Mexico’s economic outlook was characterized by moderate growth and easing inflation. The GDP growth forecast was revised downward to 1.2% due to weakening domestic demand (with an estimated growth of 1.0% by 2025). Inflation is expected to continue its downward trend, with core inflation predicted to be below 4.0% in the fourth quarter (1). Formal employment growth is slowing, with a slower pace of job creation anticipated (1). Despite these challenges, overall, Mexico’s economy remains stable with cautious optimism for the future. 



UNICEF’s analysis (2) shows that public investment in children and adolescents decreased from 3.3% of GDP in 2018 to 2.9% in 2024. Although overall social spending has continued growing (from 50.4% of the total budget in 2018 to 54.1% in 2024), social spending for children has continued decreasing from 26.5% to 17% in the same period. The early childhood age group received the lowest public investment. Only 1.8% of total public spending in 2024 was allocated to early childhood; this represents only 19.5% of all resources directed at children and adolescents. Although important progress has been registered, poverty levels remain high, especially affecting children and adolescents. Child poverty decreased from 19.6 million (50.3%) in 2018 to 17 million (45.8%) in 2022. Still, extreme poverty currently affects 3.7 million children and adolescents (9.9%). Indigenous children and adolescents continue to be the most vulnerable of all children: 8 out of 10 are poor. 



According to the 2024 Sustainable Development Report (3), Mexico continues ranking 80 out of 166 countries. Thirty percent of the SDG related indicators have been achieved or are on track, 37% have limited progress and 33% are worsening. The most significant challenges are those related to children’s and adolescents’ rights. Areas of greatest concern remain extreme poverty among children; universal access to health and social protection; malnutrition in all its forms; maternal, neonatal and child health care; adolescent pregnancy; access to inclusive, equitable and quality education; gender equality and the empowerment of girls; inclusion and equal opportunities for the most vulnerable groups; and protection from all forms of violence, abuse and exploitation.  



Concluding observations for the sixth and seventh combined State Party Convention on the Rights of the Child report presented in December 2020 were issued in September 2024. Main areas of concern expressed by the Committee include: 


Child homicides, femicides and enforced disappearances remain alarmingly high and are often linked to organized crime and the police.  
Budget cuts in education, health and early childhood services significantly impede children's rights.  
Abuse,sexual and gang-related violence persists, and child protection is limited.  
Discrimination persists, especially among indigenous and Afro-Mexican children and     adolescents, girls and marginalized groups. 
In 2022, 15.7 million (42%) children had no access to health services (4), affecting 4.6 million children under 5. Of all children under 5, 46% do not have access to health services. Low levels of pre- and postnatal care are also concerning; only 66.2% of pregnant women reported having timely prenatal visits, and only 23% of children have attended the recommended health visits during their first year of life (5). Only 42% of two-year-old children had complete vaccination in 2023. Only one (BCG) of the six mandatory vaccines has exceeded 90% coverage (6). 



In terms of education, coverage of mandatory basic education in schools decreased 6.2 points, from 96.8% in the 2014–2015 cycle, to 91% in 2023–2024 (7). The main decline was in secondary education (8.5 points), followed by primary (5.5) and preschool (5.2).  In 2022, PISA results indicate a decline across all three assessed fields from 2018 to 2022: 5-point decrease in reading, 9-point decrease in science and 14-point decrease in mathematics. This learning crisis increased due to the extended 18-month closure of schools nationwide during COVID-19, as adding to a historical lag in learning achievement (8). 



Violence continues to be a concern. Although the overall homicide trend between 2018 and 2023 decreased from 29 to 24 per 100 thousand inhabitants (9)(10), in ten states, the rate exceeded the national average reaching between 38 and 117. Firearms were used in 7 out of 10 cases (11). Children's homicide rate decreased from 3.7 in 2018 to 3.0 per 100,000 children in 2023. (12) Meanwhile, the rate of reported sexual crimes against children almost doubled between 2018 and 2022, from 50 to 99 per 100,000 children (13) (14). As of December 2024, 14,688 children remain missing, representing 14% of all missing persons in Mexico (15). 



In terms of migration flows, 2.1 million people were apprehended at the southern border of the United States, (versus 2.4 million in 2023 - 16% less) (16). Also, in 2023 113,542 migrant children in irregular situations were detected and registered in Mexico (17), however by August 2024, 108,444 were detected (18), which will probably mean an increase by the end of the year. The percentage of unaccompanied children decreased to 4% from 11% before the pandemic. As of August 2024, Mexico sent 3,179 children (1,271 accompanied and 1,908 unaccompanied) (19) back to their countries, (33% decrease from 2023). 88% of returned children came from Guatemala and Honduras. Based on the narrative promoted by the US President, the number of deportations from the US will increase, which will put greater pressure on Mexican authorities, communities and shelters that offer support services to people on the move. 



The country is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change due to a combination of factors, such as multidimensional poverty, the fragility of ecosystems and the geographic and climate conditions. In the last 50 years, average temperatures in Mexico have risen about 0.85°C, and the winter temperatures 1.3°C, the average rainfall has diminished in the country’s southeast and multiple extreme climate events have been on the rise, such as hurricanes, severe droughts, prolonged rainfalls and floods, and fires. 2024 was a particularly challenging year in terms of a sever water shortage crisis due to lack of rain and extremely high temperatures all over the country.  These episodes have drastic effects on children, impacting their health and nutrition, school attendance, access to safe water services and their family’s economic wellbeing, among many other effects, which require further government attention and mitigation efforts.

2024 was the fifth and penultimate year of the 2020-2025 Country Programme (CP) for UNICEF in Mexico. Implementation of the CP was affected by the external context and major events such as the elections and change of government, increasing and evolving migration flow, and the emergencies derived from hurricanes Otis and John. Internally, 2024 was shaped by the consolidation and expansion of UNICEF´s field presence and a significant growth in terms of financial and human resources, as well as the beginning of the new Country Programme 2026-2031 design, starting with the development of key evidence pieces such as the CP Evaluation, a Gender Programmatic Review, SitAn, and a study on the impact of the climate change on children in Mexico. 


 


UNICEF Mexico seized the opportunity of Mexico´s presidential, legislative, and subnational elections that simultaneously took place in June 2024 to put children’s interests at the center of the new administration’s priorities, further positioning UNICEF as a reliable partner of choice to advocate for children’s rights. Prior to the elections, UNICEF launched the advocacy campaign “Good six-years for children” to influence the Government´s National Development Plan 2024-2030. Following the elections, a fully-fledged engagement strategy was used to target specific audiences and decision-makers with a clear call to action, drawing on available data, evidence and opinion pieces. UNICEF continued close dialogue with the transition team of the newly elected and first female President, Dr. Claudia Sheinbaum, before the new Government took the office in October. Once the Government was officially installed, UNICEF had a series of high-level meetings with key ministries (at minister and vice-minister levels), and concrete agreements for collaboration were made in several critical areas of interest for children. Similarly, advocacy was made at the state level where governors elections took place, such as in the states of Chiapas and Yucatan, successfully positioning children on the new government´s agenda. Building on these advocacy efforts, President Sheinbaum made commitments on top priorities for children, providing great opportunities for UNICEF to enhance its collaboration to advance the fulfilment of children’s and adolescent’s rights over the coming six years.    


 


Along with these broader advocacy efforts, important results have been achieved within the four programmatic areas, helping to move the child rights agenda forward and contributing to the goals of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF):  


 


Under Strategic Plan (SP) Goal Area 1 (Nutrition) and aligned with UNSDCF direct effect 2 (wellbeing and inclusion), UNICEF made significant strides in improving child nutrition in Mexico, both at national and sub-national levels. Key initiatives included the development and implementation of the 1,000 Days Strategy, a comprehensive national health and nutrition strategy focused on the first 1,000 days of life of a child which will now include vaccination, obstetric and neonatal health and early childhood development components, becoming a National Health and Nutrition Program for the First 1,000 Days. It also included the Eat like a Champion initiative, which inspired positive behavior change through communication and community action, reaching 179,000 followers on UNICEF’s Instagram and 829,000 on UNICEF’s Facebook, along with in-person events such as the National Polytechnic Institute-Once Race and the Children’s Day Celebration. UNICEF also contributed to legal advancements in food regulations, supporting the approval of the General Law for Healthy and Sustainable Eating and the implementation of social and behavior change tools, such as mHealth. Importantly, UNICEF support resulted in the development of Mexico’s new Legal Framework for Regulating Food Environments in Schools, which is harmonized with the food warning label policy. Set to take effect in March 2025, this regulation is expected to benefit over 30 million children and youth, contributing to SDGs 2 (zero hunger) and 3 (good health and wellbeing). Furthermore, UNICEF's advocacy efforts contributed to the approval of the General Law for Healthy and Sustainable Eating. 


 


Contributing to SP Goal Areas 2 (Education) and 4 (WASH) as well as to UNSDCF direct effects 2 (see above) and 5 (decent work and employability), UNICEF continued its efforts to prepare children to be school-ready through access to quality Early Childhood Education (ECE), to take foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN) to scale, and to equip adolescents with relevant skills for the transition to adult life through access to quality learning opportunities at secondary level. In 2024, Learning Passport, a digital solution for adolescents to access remedial education, reached an additional 45,000 upper-secondary students (adding up to almost 200,000 active users since 2021), thereby contributing to address the learning crisis that predates the prolonged school closures due to the COVID 19 pandemic. The offline model of the Learning Passport helped provide access to learning through technology for 105 schools in marginalized communities with no or limited access to the internet. Together with the Ministry of Education (MoE), UNICEF finalized a series of life skills manuals for secondary education, based on UNICEF’s Global Transferrable Skills Framework, training 1000 teachers on their use and resulting in more than 40,000 students scoring higher rates of emotional regulation after implementation. In line with SDG 5 (gender equality), UNICEF advanced an agenda for gender-transformative Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) education to dismantle barriers and promote equitable access to STEM opportunities for girls and adolescents. This resulted in the engagement of 82 multi-sectorial partners from public, private, academic and civil society sectors to cultivate enabling environments for girls' and adolescents' participation, inclusion, and access to STEM disciplines in two states, Mexico City and Nuevo León. The WASH in Schools (WinS) program focused on strengthening the enabling environment and evidence generation around WinS. A participatory research made 


in Chiapas and Chihuahua states highlighted the financial gaps in achieving universal WASH coverage, providing state governments with information to improve efficiency as well as to inform advocacy strategies on increased public financing for WinS. Other achievements in the area of menstrual health education included the development of manuals, the training of educational authorities, the launch of a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC), and the support to ongoing legislative processes.  


 


Under SP Goal Area 3 (Child Protection) and contributing to UNSDCF direct effect 10 (access to justice, protection of migrants, refugees, and asylum-seekers), UNICEF drove systemic change to create safer environments where children and adolescents in Mexico are increasingly protected from violence and exploitation. A major accomplishment was the adoption by the federal government of the first National Child Protection Case Management Model, which standardizes processes across federal and local Child Protection Authorities (CPAs). To operationalize the model, UNICEF supported the roll-out of Primero Child Protection Information Management System Plus (CPIMS+) and developed a Data Protection and Information Sharing Protocol to ensure secure implementation. In partnership with the Federal CPA, UNICEF conducted a comprehensive national needs assessment and costing study to address the financial and capacity gaps within the state level CPAs. Furthermore, UNICEF supported Mexico’s alternative care reform by developing a National Model on Deinstitutionalization, preventing unnecessary family separation, expanding family-based care alternatives, family reintegration, and other solutions to restore the right to live in a family. The first national certification and supervisory mechanism for residential care centers was operationalized. In addition, with the support of UNICEF, foster care programs were scaled up to 20 states, and 248,000 children affected by violence were reached with protection services along with 120,000 individuals through positive parenting programs. 


  


With regards to SP Goal Area 5 (Every child has an equitable chance in life) and UNSDCF direct effect 2 (see above), UNICEF´s work focused on making child poverty visible, using the latest available data (from 2022), and promoting the expansion of social protection and public investment for children during the Presidential elections and government transition. UNICEF continued its strong collaboration with CONEVAL, specifically in the development of a child poverty analysis and a study on the effects of social protection programmes in mitigating child poverty. The child poverty analysis included data at the subnational level with the development of policy briefs specifically analyzing child and adolescent poverty in priority states. UNICEF also actively participated in discussions and dialogues around the need to establish a nation-wide care system, which is a key policy priority in the country. Specifically, UNICEF highlighted the importance of expanding quality childcare, prioritizing poor and vulnerable families without social security coverage, which provided the government with first-hand evidence and concrete proposals to start building this care system, with a focus on children. Lastly, UNICEF supported various efforts to strengthen and expand public finance for children in the country by providing evidence on how the government invests in children and adolescents, pointing out the urgent need to increase the current spending (in 2012-2023 it represented around 3.3% of the GDP, while in the countries in the region this was 5% on average). 


 


To help achieve the above results, cross cutting issues were consistently mainstreamed into programmatic work in 2024. In the area of social behavior change (SBC), initiatives contributed to enriching and accelerating changes, for instance in the promotion of healthy eating habits, STEM education for girls, and the promotion of bilingual education, among others. Moreover, artistic and cultural approaches   provided children and families on the move with timely access to relevant information on health, nutrition, education, child protection and WASH. With regards to adolescent development and participation (ADAP), key strategies have been promoted to position adolescents as a new generation who are healthy, educated and protected from violence. Work on mental health, civic engagement and skills development has reached 14,295; 5,268, and 1,965 adolescents, respectively. Regarding gender and planning, monitoring and evaluation,   key pieces of evidence were developed to inform the formulation of the new Country Programme including a Gender Programmatic Review and the CP 2020-2025 evaluation. Concerning innovation, following participation at a COMPASS workshop organized by the Office of Innovation in 2024, UNICEF Mexico established a task force to lead the formulation of the innovation strategy as part of the new Country Programme Document development. 


 


Throughout the year UNICEF’s presence at the subnational level was further strengthened. The three field offices (FOs) based in Baja California, Chihuahua and Chiapas made strong efforts to enhance partnerships with the respective subnational governments. Some neighboring states were also supported by these FOs (Sonora by Baja California FO, Oaxaca and Tabasco by Chiapas FO). In Chihuahua, UNICEF continued supporting the fulfilment of migrant children’s rights while education, healthcare and child protection systems were strengthened. In addition, programmes for bilingual education and the development of socio-emotional skills for early childhood were consolidated, benefiting over 47,000 children, and the state’s response against malnutrition of indigenous children was supported in Sierra Tarahumara through donations of Ready to Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) and training of medical staff. UNICEF also contributed to significant achievements in Chiapas, Tabasco, and Oaxaca by strengthening child protection systems, improving WASH services, promoting inclusive education, and supporting children on the move. Key initiatives included the implementation of bilingual literacy programs, the development of health access routes, and the deployment of innovative SBC strategies, directly benefiting over 250,000 children and their families. In Baja California and Sonora, UNICEF support focused on strengthening services to protect the rights of children and adolescents on the move. This was achieved through actions designed and aimed at providing protection services, detecting rights violations, addressing gender-based violence, and ensuring access to health, education, safe water, culture, among others.   


 


UNICEF’s interventions to protect children on the move (CotM) and their families continued across all four programme areas. In addition to the direct work carried out by field offices in this regard, UNICEF strengthened child protection systems for CotM by implementing binational mechanisms, expanding the national registry for CotM, and reaching over 62,000 CotM and caregivers with humanitarian services. Protection pathways were rolled out in five states, while care models and tools for GBV prevention and monitoring were enhanced nationwide. Also, through the "Vamos Juntos" initiative, 143,294 children, adolescents, pregnant women, and caregivers on the move received health, nutrition, and psychosocial care. This spearheaded the development of Contigo App, an innovative mobile application aimed at creating portable electronic medical records to ensure higher-quality healthcare throughout their migratory journey, to be rolled out in 2025. As in previous years, WASH has become a key aspect of UNICEF’s interventions in the context of migration providing safe water and basic sanitation for 303,475 people on the move in shelters  and in the context of the emergency response in Acapulco (after the hurricane emergency) reaching 26,605 people with rehabilitated connection to sewage systems and 37,249 people with hygiene articles. Hygiene education initiatives reached 28,500 people on the move, while 87,963 received hygiene kits. Lastly, UNICEF continued to support education authorities at state and federal levels to improve inclusive education for CotM. High-level advocacy and collaboration with stakeholders supported system-level advancements and the dissemination of the Protocol for School Access to over 229,000 basic education schools. Two state intersectoral plans were developed in Chihuahua and Nuevo León to provide education for CotM. UNICEF’s training on inclusive education for CotM reached 6,913 individuals through a massive open online course, while 3,000 teachersparticipated in UNICEF’s blended in-service teacher training included in the National Teacher Training Catalogue. Furthermore. Furthermore, the direct provision of educational services benefitted 7,886 out-of-school CotM in Baja California, Chihuahua, Sonora, Oaxaca, and Chiapas in 2024. 


 


During 2024, UNICEF Mexico also supported the government in its response to the emergency derived from hurricane John and the recovery interventions after hurricane Otis (2023). UNICEF’s response to both hurricanes integrated emergency response with long-term recovery and resilience-building to address immediate needs while strengthening local and national systems for sustainable development. The strategy was operationalized across multiple programme sectors, ensuring that humanitarian interventions were aligned with CP objectives and tailored to the specific risks and vulnerabilities of the affected areas in the states of Guerrero for both hurricanes and in Oaxaca, and Michoacan for the hurricane John. 


 


This year, UNICEF Mexico’s gross revenue grew by 4% in comparison with 2023, reaching MXN$327.8 million. Growth was mainly driven by strong individual giving (+16.7%). Corporate and Philanthropy as the High Value channels consolidated after a very successful year 2023, which was driven by a national emergency and the International Council Symposium in Mexico. 2024 was also the year of the development of the new strategy and vision for the new CPD period until 2031: “Vision toward a Fully Funded Office” with a focus on flexible resources, and the goal to be able to fully fund Mexico’s core programmes by 2030 plus being able to contribute multi-million USD per year in regular resources globally.

Overall, UNICEF’s achievements during 2024 were possible through strong partnerships with government institutions, civil society organizations (CSOs), academic entities, private sector stakeholders, and other UN agencies. These collaborations were instrumental in ensuring impactful, sustainable results in all programme areas but also in terms of fundraising and alliances. 


 


Key government partners spanned sectors such as justice, health, nutrition, education, welfare, WASH and child protection, including the Ministries of Foreign Affairs, Wellbeing, Public Security and Civil Protection, Health, National Women’s Institute,  CONAGUA and Education among others. Some highlights in this regard are: 1) The Federal Child Protection Authority (CPA) and the Executive Secretariat of the Comprehensive Child Protection System (SE-SIPINNA) which were central to driving systemic changes in terms of legislation and policy improvements.  2) CONEVAL, with whom UNICEF has a long-standing collaboration carrying out child poverty assessments and other studies.  3) The Ministry of Health (MoH), IMSS, DIF (Welfare Agency), and INSP which partnered with UNICEF to implement a National 1,000 Days Nutrition Strategy in four states, with plans to expand to two more. 4) INSP was instrumental in advocacy and evidence generation, developing SBC materials, publishing scientific research, carrying out studies and supporting assessments on adherence to RUTF and MMS for pregnant women, as well as developing clinical guidelines for SAM. UNICEF also established strong partnerships with subnational governments, not only where UNICEF has field offices (FOs) such as Baja California, Chihuahua, and Chiapas but also in other states through remote support from the FOs and the CO.  


 


The legislative branch of government was also a critical ally. Through the partnership with the Legislative Commissions Network, UNICEF successfully positioned strategic child protection topics, resulting in five states debating draft laws to ban corporal punishment, three states presenting initiatives on femicide sentencing with aggravating factors based on age, and two states advancing discussions on criminalizing child recruitment by organized crime. UNICEF also carried out a brief analysis of the proposed public investment targeted to children in Mexico for 2025, which was presented in the Child and Adolescents Rights Commission from the House of Representatives during a discussion on inclusive budgets in the context of the budget review for 2025. 


 


Academic institutions like the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), the Autonomous University of Chiapas, and the Colegio de la Frontera Norte contributed with research, expertise, and innovative approaches to key areas such as legal reforms and migration-related initiatives.  Specialized institutes supported the scaling of methodologies, evidence generation and teacher training: MEJOREDU, Universities of Veracruz and Queretaro and Stockholm International Water Institute. 


 


CSOs were vital to extending the reach of UNICEF’s programs and mobilizing resources. Strategic partnerships with organizations like ODI A.C. helped scale up specialized courtrooms for children nationwide. Some key partners included RELAF, Save the Children, Parenthood for Lifelong Health (PLH), The Hope Effect, HIAS, Juconi, YMCA, and CAFEMIN, among many others. 


 


Collaborations with UN partners were further strengthened in 2024. For the emergency preparedness and response, UNICEF worked in close collaboration with other UN agencies under the framework of UNETE led by OCHA and the Resident Coordinator’s Office (RCO). Other partnerships with UN agencies have been established for: (i) interventions for educational inclusion of CotM and WASH in context of migration (IOM and UNHCR), (ii) STEM education for girls (UNESCO), (iii) digital transformation in education (UNESCO), and iv) UNICEF collaborated with UNHCR, IOM, UNFPA, and ILO, addressing cross-cutting issues such as migration, displacement, child marriage, commercial sexual exploitation, and child recruitment. UNICEF also supported the Resident Coordinator´s Office (RCO) to establish a Programme Management Team (PMT), that is a group of Deputy Representatives of the UN agencies, programmes and funds for joint planning and coordination purposes. A first PMT retreat was held in July 2024 where key decisions were made with regards to the UNSDCF formulation process, joint advocacy with the new government, among others.  


 


In 2024, UNICEF Mexico received the highest amount of financial contribution from the US government´s Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration (BPRM) since the partnership started in 2020. This demonstrates the trust and confidence from the previous years of collaboration and positive results achieved. It is unclear what shift the Trump administration may implement with the BPRM program, and it would be important for UNICEF Mexico to reduce reliance on the US funding to sustain our operations to meet critical needs of children on the move.  


 


Building on the successful implementation of ECHO funds for the emergency response to the Hurricane Otis in 2023, UNICEF Mexico managed to mobilize funding from ECHO to respond to the Hurricane John which hit the southern states of Guerrero, Oaxaca and Michoacan. Considering the needs to diversify funding source for protracted crisis due to migration as well as emerging internal displacement due to increasing armed violence, it is critical to further strengthen partnership with ECHO and other potential donors. 


 


In general, 2024 has seen a strong push to also leverage the potential influence of private sector partners beyond “just” fundraising, which the PFP Mexico team continues to play a key role in. To maximize impact, UNICEF strengthened alliances with key Multi-Stakeholder Partnerships, business chambers, and associations, including CCE (Consejo Coordinador Empresarial), COPARMEX (Confederación Patronal de la República Mexicana), Global Compact, ICC (International Chamber of Commerce) Mexico, and INDEX. These collaborations proved instrumental in raising awareness about family friendly politicies among 507 companies, prospecting new companies, and increasing emergency response awareness. Also, by collaborating with industry "champions" – C-level executives from organizations such as IAB, AVE, EXPOK, Expansión, Dalia Empower, and Pacto Global – the PFP team developed a comprehensive strategy to transform advertising narratives and eradicate harmful stereotypes affecting children and adolescents' development. Likewise, the Philanthropy Team leveraged influence and resources of Mexico's most affluent individuals, private foundations and FBOs/MBOs, cultivating the relations and directing their investments towards UNICEF. US$ 2,186,000 were raised from the Carlos Slim Foundation, the Gonzalo Río Arronte Foundation, Elias Sacal, Víctor González Herrera & family, among others. 


 


Partnerships with DSM, Fundacion Rio Arronte, FUNO and Liomont provided financial resources and technical expertise to support UNICEF's nutrition programs. Also, private sector contributions continued to provide important contributions for the education and WASH programme: relations were established with Essity, Akelius Foundation, Kimberley Clark, Banco Santander, Formula 1, Chery Automobile, BMW, Abertis, Fundación Televisa, Dr Simi Foundation, Fondo Unido, Elias Sacal, CENACED, C&A, Fondo Alternativa. In kind contributions were received form the WASH emergency response in Guerrero from Clorox and Rotoplas.   


 


Finally, it is worth mentioning that Regular Resources (RR) and thematic funding were pivotal in addressing challenges often underfunded by traditional donors, such as violence prevention and response, armed violence against children, and commercial sexual exploitation in the tourism sector. Flexible funds underpinned UNICEF’s ability to respond to the complex challenges of armed violence, such as child recruitment by organized crime, ensuring that no child was left behind in protection efforts.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2024 was a year of critical importance for UNICEF Mexico both given the external context (election year) and for kicking-off the formulation of the new Country Programme Document (CPD) for the 2026-2031 period. These two processes were closely interconnected: priorities that UNICEF identifies for children in Mexico were advocated to the government before and after the elections, and priorities identified by the government informed priority-setting for the new CPD.
