Fortunately, there is a high alignment between what UNICEF advocated for as issues of critical importance and the priorities defined by the government, giving UNICEF excellent opportunities to collaborate to make advances in improvement of child wellbeing in the coming years.  


 


Some examples of challenges faced by UNICEF in programme implementation can be summarized as follows: 


 


Child Protection: financial constraints and delayed funding allocations limited efforts in violence prevention and response, particularly in sensitive areas such as child recruitment, armed violence, and sexual exploitation. While the child protection system has matured in various aspects in recent years, significant challenges remain due to persistent weaknesses. For instance, although alternative care has been scaling up in the country, residential care continues to be the most frequently used option by authorities. The lack of investment in family-based care and the inadequate regulation of residential facilities have hindered sustainable change in child welfare practices. 


 


Education: The CO continued to face challenges in identifying entry points on key issues such as the learning crisis. Despite information available on concerningly low learning outcomes of Mexican students in all educational levels, and despite the availability of successful and scalable methodologies with proven positive impact on learning there is no programme or strategy at national level to address this problem, limiting opportunities for UNICEF to achieve impact at scale by supporting a strategy of national reach. Still, success factors in the implementation of the WASH and Education programmes have been the use of digital solutions - to accelerate learning, increase access and heighten students’ interest in learning – and convening and supporting strategic partnerships across sectors and with a range of partners to drive action around themes such as WASH, migration, STEM for girls and digital transformation. 


  


Social Protection: A specific situation that emerged in late November 2024 was the abolition of CONEVAL, a critical partner for UNICEF in the generation of evidence on child poverty, and in evaluating social policies in the country. The abolition responded to the Government’s intention to save resources allocated to autonomous institutions, such as CONEVAL. Still, it is not clear nor is it guaranteed yet which institution will carry out CONEVAL’s pivotal tasks. UNICEF will continue making efforts to make child poverty visible and will work with the institution (or institutions) that “inherit” the tasks of measuring poverty and evaluating social policies in Mexico. 


  


Since the emergency response to Hurricane Otis in 2023, the capacities installed at the field level have proven to be a critical factor for timely response. At the same time, due to the absence of a dedicated staff on emergency at the Country Office (CO) level, the internal emergency preparedness and response mechanisms were not well established. Establishment of the Chief of Field Operations post with emergency leadership role is expected to enhance both CO and FO level capacity for planning, implementation and monitoring of emergency-related activities, both protracted emergencies, such as migration, and rapid-onset crisis for hurricanes and earthquakes.  


 


Unpredictable funding availability for humanitarian assistance for the CoTM also posed a significant challenge for the CO. UNICEF Mexico initiated a process for a strategy development in the face of sharp reduction of the external funding to support CoTM, diverting the major interventions from direct service delivery through CSO partners to capacity building of local governments to address the crisis. In reality, instead of a reduction, UNICEF Mexico received a greater amount from the US government than in previous years. Such amount is unlikely to be sustained in the future, and modalities of delivering humanitarian assistance again will need to be reconsidered. Throughout the 2024 UNICEF emphasized the importance of transferring capacities and knowledge to local authorities, ensuring that all interventions were well accompanied by them. This strategy will be further enhanced in 2025, and UNICEF will focus on provision of technical assistance to the government both at the federal and subnational levels, especially to address possible large-scale repatriation and deportation of children and families from the US.  


 


A key finding of the CPD 2020-2025 Evaluation implemented this year was that there is limited clarity on the objectives of UNICEF field offices. All the FOs were created to respond to the migration crisis, yet their roles have evolved in the past years towards subnational level advocacy and system strengthening, so it is critical to re-define the roles and responsibilities of FO as well as field presence in other modalities. Capacities of field level staff should meet the redefined objectives.  


 


In December, UNICEF Mexico organized the Strategic Moment of Reflection workshop. With high level participation of the LACRO team, strategic discussion was held to shape the vision towards the new Country Programme. Key reflections included how the CO would make a strategic shift to reach all children in the country, while prioritizing promotion and protection of the rights of the most vulnerable children (those in extreme poverty, with indigenous background, with disabilities, children on the move, among others), and how to pave the way towards achieving self-funded status by 2031. UNICEF Mexico forms part of the Business Model Initiative in the LAC region, which provides a great opportunity to build internal capacity for reaching results for children at much greater scale through child-centered public polies and programs at federal and subnational levels through mobilization of all actors in society, through joint work among Programs, PFP and Communications, while enhancing UNICEF positioning and branding in the country for a massive increase of domestic fundraising.

In 2024, Nicaragua maintained a stable social and institutional context. As noted by the International Monetary Fund, the country demonstrated significant resilience despite recent crises, due to appropriate economic policies, substantial reserves, and multilateral support. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew at an annual rate of 3.8 percent in the first nine months of 2024, accumulating year-on-year growth of 4.2 percent. This economic growth is expected to continue in 2025. 
Nicaragua is one of the countries in the region that invests the most in the social sector relative to the total economy. The social expenditure executed in 2022 represents 50.6 percent of the total expenditure execution (56.7 percent of the initially approved budget). Of the social expenditure, 72.3 percent was invested in children and young people. This investment represented 7.5 percent of GDP and 31.8 percent of total public expenditure. A bill has recently been approved to amend the annual law on the general budget of the country, which will strengthen the allocation of resources to social spending and the financing of public investment projects (National Assembly, 2024). 
Despite being a lower-middle-income country according to the World Bank scale, this priority in social spending enables Nicaragua to make important progress in the fulfilment of children's rights, although challenges remain in coverage and specific issues, as the following data show. 
Nicaragua’s social development programmes are guided by the National Plan for Poverty Reduction and Human Development 2022-2026. This plan outlines key priorities to achieve several of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets, such as access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation, early childhood, primary and secondary education, health and well-being, and gender equality and empowerment of girls and women. 
According to the Ministry of Health (MoH), the under-five mortality rate decreased from 19.7 deaths per 1,000 live births (LBW) in 2018 to 12.3 per 1,000 LBW in 2023, and the neonatal mortality ratio decreased from 10.7 deaths per 1,000 LBW in 2018 to 8 per 1,000 LBW in 2023. The maternal mortality ratio was 30 per 100,000 live births in 2023. This decrease is due to the significant coverage of antenatal care in the first trimester of pregnancy, which reached 93 percent, the fourth antenatal care which reached more than 99 percent, and the coverage of institutional birth which reached 96 percent (2023). Exclusive six-month breastfeeding is 46 percent (2020) and 4.4 percent of children under five still suffer acute malnutrition. The third dose of pentavalent vaccines reached 100 percent by 2023. 
According to government data, safe water coverage reaches 93 percent in urban areas and 34.87 percent in rural areas (2024). Improved sanitation coverage reaches 43.57 percent of the rural population (2024). However, of the 5,559 existing rural water systems, only 458 (8.2 percent) produce safe water. 
In 2022, 1.7 million children attended school (early education 14.5 percent, primary 49.7 percent, secondary 22.9 percent). The gross completion rate was 82.2 percent in primary and 65.9 percent in lower secondary. It is estimated, however, that 7.1 percent of children of primary school age do not attend school. This figure increases to 14.6 percent for those who should be attending lower secondary school. 
The Institute for Legal Medicine (IML) dealt with 16,217 children and adolescents who were victims of violence (2023). Of these, 11,360 were victims of sexual violence and 4,911 were victims of physical or psychological violence against children and adolescents. One hundred percent of these cases were referred by institutions belonging to the National Social Welfare System. 
The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) was completed in 2024 by the National Institute of Statistics for Development (INIDE), with technical and financial support from UNICEF. It is expected to be published in early 2025. The data from the survey will provide even more accurate information on the situation of children in Nicaragua, including new data on topics where there is currently no information, such as the quality of drinking water, early unions, and the use of iodised salt. 
As noted by the World Bank, Nicaragua is classified in the highest risk group for climate-related disasters and other natural phenomena; it is in the high-risk group for earthquakes, floods and epidemics, and in the medium risk group for droughts and hurricanes. While there were no catastrophic weather events in 2024, unlike previous years, vulnerability to climate-related and natural disasters remains of the highest priority in the country. 
Nicaragua continues to be a transit country for migrants from South America and the Caribbean, who enter the country through blind spots near Peñas Blancas, San Pancho, or Bluefields, as well as through formal border crossings. This is further compounded by Nicaraguans who have also decided to migrate, mainly to the United States of America including through programmes such as the humanitarian parole.  
There is no official information on the transit of migrants through the country, but in the first nine months of 2024, 312,553 migrants of different nationalities entered Honduras through the border with Nicaragua. 
Remittances are an indicator of the country's migration situation. According to the Central Bank of Nicaragua, they represent 26.1 percent of GDP (2023). According to the same source, remittances reached $3,828.3 million in 2024, 11.5 percent more than in 2023. The main sources of remittances are the United States (83.1 percent), Costa Rica (7.4 percent) and Spain (5.8 percent). 
In 2024, UNICEF, along with other UN agencies, funds and programmes in Nicaragua continued to work in coordination to achieve the SDGs and strengthen their linkages to national priorities. UNICEF coordinated the SDG inter-agency working group and promoted the focus of UN technical assistance on five accelerators for achieving the SDGs: contributing to the achievement of universal health coverage, strengthening the technical capacity of the education system, contributing to the transformation of agri-food systems, contributing to the transformation of gender norms, and increasing the resilience to climate change.

UNICEF continued to support national efforts to ensure every child survives and thrives, within the framework of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2, 3, 4, and 5, Goal Area 1 of the Strategic Plan (SP), and Goal Area 1 of the UNICEF Gender Action Plan 2022–2025 (GAP). In 2024, UNICEF helped Nicaragua ensure child survival and improve child health and nutrition by achieving the following results:
UNICEF supported the strengthening of the Family and Community Health System of the Ministry of Health (MoH), which contributed to improving counselling skills and surveillance capacities of the Family and Community Health Team (FCHT) members in rural areas. To this end, UNICEF trained 79 percent of the FCHT’s of the Local Comprehensive Health Systems (SILAIS) of the Dry Corridor area (North) in the use of the Methodological Manual for Health Personnel and the Community Network for the Promotion of Essential Care. During the year, trained technicians identified and monitored 2,985 children with developmental disorders at the primary care level. These technicians also trained the parents of these children to provide early stimulation at home.
The quality of care for children under five years of age was improved by strengthening adherence to Protocols 146 (Manual of Procedures for the Comprehensive Management of Childhood Illnesses from 0 to 5 Years of Age in PHC) and 142 (Guide for the Implementation of the Kangaroo Family Method). With technical and financial support from UNICEF, the MoH organised 18 departmental workshops to update pediatricians and general practitioners from primary care hospitals, community child coordinators and ESAFC members on both protocols and data analysis.  
To ensure that children grow up in a protective family environment and that positive parenting practices are implemented, the use of Protocol 192 (Manual of Procedures for the Promotion of Value-Based Parenting) has been implemented at national scale. In partnership with the MOH, and the Ministry of Family (MoF), UNICEF contributed to ensuring that 16 percent of the five training sessions for parents, caregivers, and guardians conducted by technicians from the "Love for the Littlest Ones" programme, addressed the importance of play as a learning method, early stimulation during pregnancy, early stimulation for children under 3 years old, early detection and timely reference, nutrition for pregnant women, and exclusive breastfeeding.  
As part of the efforts to promote protective environment in families, especially for children with disabilities, UNICEF supported to the MoF, in the development of a toolkit for mental health and psycho-emotional support for families with children with disabilities enrolled in the Child Development Centers (CDI), as well capacity building for educators and technicians, at the national level and in the 19 departments of the country, for the provision of mental health counseling. This allowed implementation of this strategy in 65 CDI throughout the country (approximately one quarter of the total number of CDIs in the country).
To strengthen the MoH's capacity to address and improve adolescent mental health, UNICEF supported the MoH in the preparation of an adolescent and child mental health program. This programme allows the provision of counselling for adolescents on emotion management, stress management and mental health promotion in two health units that did not previously offer such services. 
UNICEF supported the MoF addressing environmental health and ECD risks. A training of trainers’ workshop was implemented with educators and technicians from the national and local level. UNICEF is also supporting the CDIs for improvement of garbage management and the importance of cleanliness. A competition for the design of solutions to address climate change in the CDIs was developed with parents and caregivers at the national level and submitted to the MoF.
To improve full immunisation coverage in remote areas, UNICEF continued to strengthen the MoH's cold chain capacity, installing two high-tech cold rooms with the capacity to store 42 percent of the vaccine doses administered annually, the development of capacity of technicians from the Expanded Immunisation Programme for the preventive maintenance of the equipment, and the installation of two smaller cold rooms in the SILAIS of Chinandega and Río San Juan. 
To ensure that every child learns and acquires skills for the future, to improve the use of technology in education and equip the Ministry of Education (MoE) with tools for the inclusion of students with disabilities in the regular education system, UNICEF has continued to support the development of the Accessible Digital Textbooks (ADT) project.  To date, a digital and accessible version of the textbook "Conociendo mi mundo" (Knowing my world), a reading book for second grade, has been completed and made available on the Ministry's digital platform for public access. UNICEF also continues to support 15 national reference schools as prototypes of inclusive education schools, which serve as a model for the Education System. The model includes training all teachers in inclusive education and disability and making physical infrastructure more inclusive.
UNICEF supported  to the MoE in a process of ownership, sensitisation and training on the gender approach, which culminated in the elaboration of a situational diagnosis and a “Gender Programme for Basic, Secondary and Teachers Training Education Subsectors”. This programme aims to permeate the entire work of the institution, from administrative processes to the learning experience in the classroom, ensuring that gender equality is respected and practiced.
The MoE prioritises socio-emotional support for students as a transversal axis in education to strengthen values such as solidarity, tolerance and peaceful coexistence. In 2024, UNICEF provided technical inputs to the creation of a socio-emotional learning programme, which proposes the mainstreaming of socio-emotional skills in all areas of knowledge. This programme is in line with a new education strategy developed in 2024 for the entire Education System.
UNICEF contributed to the training of teachers to provide socio-emotional support during emergencies in areas vulnerable to climate change, particularly the Caribbean coast. A total of 59 education leaders and municipal pedagogical advisors were trained, who in turn will train some 300 teachers from Mayangna (indigenous group) communities.
To address the issue of student achievement in key competencies, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the MOE in the development of teaching skills related to literacy and the use of technology to enhance learning. To this end, it has contributed to the development of a content package consisting of five training modules that will be validated and scaled up nationally for the development of digital and technological literacy among teachers, with the aim of better-promoting technology as a pedagogical resource in the classroom.
Through the implementation of school infrastructure projects funded by the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), in addition to completing at least 88 percent of the construction of six (6) rural schools for pre-school and primary students which will be finalized in early 2025, UNICEF has contributed to the improvement of MoE protocols in terms of contracting technical services; making construction works more comprehensive by incorporating new technologies related to the provision of water, sanitation and hygiene; and ensuring a comprehensive approach to temporary learning spaces while students wait for their new schools.
In 2024, UNICEF helped ensure that every child is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices.
UNICEF reached  9,311 adolescents with technical and financial support, increased the coverage of the School of Values for Adolescents from 420 adolescents in 2023 to 2,015 in 2024, incorporating the prevention of early unions in the contents. In addition, 6,451 parents and caregivers (30 percent male) were reached with programmes on positive parenting, violence prevention, and gender equality. UNICEF strengthened the community networks of partners Children Believe, SOS Children's Villages and university youth volunteers in gender-based violence prevention, child protection and psychosocial care, reaching 7,296 youth and adolescents, through the implementation of 12 training workshops on gender equality and prevention of sexual violence and their replication in the communities.   
UNICEF contributed to strengthening the national capacity to provide care services for child victims of sexual violence. Access to specialised care services was improved for 6,626 child victims of sexual violence by supporting the implementation of the national “Protocol for the Comprehensive Care of Children and Adolescents in Sexual Violence”, and 9,453 parents engaged and participated in psychosocial interventions through the School of Values for Parents and Caregivers, and house-to-house visits by MoF technicians, supported by UNICEF.
UNICEF supported the Ministry of the Family to update the regulations for special protection and restitution of the rights of children and adolescents, which represents an advance in public policy, as it articulates, organises, standardises, and operationalises the procedures for the special protection of children and adolescents. The Protocol for the Comprehensive Care of Child and Adolescent Victims of Sexual Violence was expanded from 10 departmental commissions (2023) to 121 municipal commissions, allowing for improved inter-institutional coordination and follow-up. As part of this intervention, UNICEF contributed directly to all 1,300 children under alternative care measures, by the MoF, who received specialised psychosocial and legal care (90 percent girls).
With UNICEF's technical support, the Minister of the Family participated in the 2024 First Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children. At this event, the Nicaraguan representative, through the government’s pledge, committed to further strengthening the legal framework and public policies and considering scalable strategies to extend the coverage of care and services to all families in the country. Within this framework, the government committed to expanding the coverage of the Schools of Values for Adolescents at the national level.
UNICEF, with the support of the MoF, reached 4,280 people with the 'My country, my safe home' campaign to raise awareness of the risks associated with irregular migration.
To achieve the goal that every child, including adolescents, have access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and live in a safe and sustainable climate and environment UNICEF, together with the National Water Authority (ANA), and with the participation of communities, contributed to improving access to safe water for 19,366 people from 29 rural communities located in the Dry Corridor and the Caribbean Coast the two most vulnerable areas of the country. This initiative supported national efforts to achieve the SDG on Water (Target 6.1) and reduce the risk of  diarrhoea and/or parasitic diseases in children, exposure to gender-based violence due to having to collect water in isolated or unsafe places, or missing school due to lack of water. 
In addition, in the first quarter of 2024, the entire sanitation infrastructure of the only formal shelter on the northern Caribbean coast, located in the community of Koom, Waspán, was rehabilitated, allowing 1,626 people (compared to 0 in 2023) from communities adjacent to the Koom shelter to use the water service when needed. By rehabilitating the water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure of two schools in the Mayagna indigenous communities of Fruta de Pan and Sakalwas, 686 children and adolescents and 18 school staff members now have access to safe water, hygiene and sanitation differentiated by gender.
UNICEF supported ANA to develop two situational analyses. The first is a climate rationale for the  WASH sector, which aims to understand how climate hazards affect WASH services and to develop actions to improve the enabling environment for sustainable and resilient management of WASH services. The second is the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), which analyses the impact of the climate crisis, environmental degradation, and unsustainable energy use on the lives of children and their families. 
UNICEF partnered with the MoH to facilitate four workshops to identify the health sector's needs and resilience to climate change and to design health sector adaptation measures to mitigate risks in children associated with climate hazards.
UNICEF provided technical assistance   to the MoH and ANA to encourage the adoption of best practices and improve the delivery of WASH services in homes, schools, and health units. To achieve this objective, 125 technical staff from the MoH, 326 technicians and community members (222 of whom are WASH service providers in 78 rural communities and 104 technicians from municipalities) participated in the generation of new knowledge and skills. 
UNICEF supported the MoF to train 60 early childhood care providers on the impact of climate change on health, child development and community hygiene reached 7,500 children and their parents or caregivers, representing 50 percent of the children enrolled in the CDIs at national level. The goal of all capacity-building and behaviour-change activities is to create a safe and healthy environment for children and adolescents to grow and thrive in dry corridor communities. 
To improve the knowledge generation for child rights in Nicaragua, the Country Programme addresses three bottlenecks  within the framework of Sustainable Development Goal 17 (Data, Monitoring and Accountability Target 17.18) to significantly increase the availability of timely, reliable and high-quality data, in alignment with Chapter V of the National Plan for Poverty Reduction and Human Development 2022-2026 . 
The first bottleneck refers to the generation of quality information for evidence-based decision-making on childhood issues. To this end, in 2024 the MICS Nicaragua 2023 Survey process was completed. The results were reviewed and validated through a set of workshops with technical levels of the different ministries involved, leading to the draft of a Survey Report document. The document is currently awaiting government approval for its publication and other actions to analyse and  disseminate the results. 
The second bottleneck is the insufficient visibility of public financial investments in children that informs national decision-making. In 2024, an agreement was reached with the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Secretariat of the Presidency to make the final adjustments to the national measurement model, specifically in the Ministry of Health, enhancing accuracy. The agreement with the Government is to institutionalise a reliable annual report, which can be published and submitted to the highest national decision-making bodies: Presidency, National Assembly, and National Budgeting Committee.
A third bottleneck is the need to strengthen institutional capacities to perform the evaluative function, so that public spending on children can be analysed based on the results of its programmatic performance. In 2024, UNICEF and the Planning Secretariat of the Presidency signed a workplan with three lines of action: i) adaptation of the national evaluation  regulatory framework, which begins with  diagnostic products  already been defined with the Secretariat; ii) training on evaluation for two  decision-makers  of the Planning Secretariat, which was completed; iii) implementing evaluations of national programmes related to childhood, starting with the evaluation of the National Programme of Child Development Centres.
To achieve greater public engagement and support for children's rights, UNICEF consistently delivered high-quality, innovative and audience-driven content to drive results, reinforce its brand and enable growth across all digital platforms.
UNICEF engaged key audiences, including children, youth, families, private sector partners and decision-makers, co-created content with media and partnered with children and youth. This involved 15,743 children, adolescents and young people in events, campaigns, and World Children's Day activations. 
UNICEF's promoted and supported the commemoration of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC)  by partnering with two television stations to promote ethical standards and awareness of children's rights through content generation and a special World Children's Day broadcast. Knowledge, among 40 journalists regarding the CRC went from low and medium level to high, through an approach focused on protecting children´s rights.
UNICEF's digital channels performed strongly in 2024. Impressions on UNICEF's digital channels reached 11,613,480. A total of 3,758,153 people were reached on others social media. Using technology to engage youth, seven podcasts were organised with children and young people as leading voices. UNICEF was mentioned in 351 articles in online and print media, remaining a credible voice and protecting its brand.
In terms of share of voice on children's issues, UNICEF maintained its leading position in the country, generating a share of voice (SOV) of 74% in online and print media, thanks to a strategic communications and advocacy plan that included digital initiatives, strategic marketing and partnership initiatives.
In 2024, UNICEF created 120 communications products on climate, health, immunisation, nutrition and WASH to cover advocacy priorities. For the 35th anniversary of the CRC and World Children's Day, UNICEF partnered with the American University (UAM) and children to relaunch Rita, an animated character created with children and youth, a process led by young volunteer students. This social innovation project aims to mainstream advocacy messages and promote behaviours that fulfil children's rights.
UNICEF also strengthened and continued to leverage U-Report, consolidating it as a key platform to amplify the voices of young people, reaching 3,600 active users in 2024, surpassing its historical record. Furthermore, 210 young volunteers from five universities across the country were trained as advocates and activists on the impact of climate change and developed innovative community projects, such as creating candles from recycled oil and environmental education activities. These initiatives promote resilience and foster sustainable practices at the local level in parts of the national territory.
Using the Human-Centred Design (HCD) methodology, in the first quarter of 2024, UNICEF led participatory processes that included community diagnostics in the Caribbean Coast and the training of a network of 125 communicators and community leaders in social listening. This enabled the design of culturally relevant messages, improving vaccine acceptance rates and developing two studies on barriers and facilitators of routine immunisation, in collaboration with faith-based organisations, who became key actors in behaviour change.
To strengthen risk-informed humanitarian and development nexus programming,  UNICEF built an automated and predictive calculation model of the affected and vulnerable population using GIS technology, which was recognized as an innovation by the Division of Analysis, Planning, and Monitoring (DAPM) and the Emergency Operations Division (EMOPS).  In addition, all risk scenarios were reviewed, updated roles and protocols were defined, the damage assessment and impact counting mechanism were adapted, staff support required in case of emergency was defined, and the indicator framework for a response plan was updated. The stock of pre-positioned emergency supplies was significantly improved.
UNICEF participated and made important contributions to the development of the UN interagency UNETE´s Emergency Preparedness and Response plan, by providing technical as well as logistical support. UNICEF hosts the UNETE´s platform which will be used by all UN agencies as a repository of all information related to emergencies.

To mobilise the resources and will to implement successful programmes to fulfill children's rights, in 2024, UNICEF fostered value-sharing partnerships with the government, United Nations agencies, funds and programmes in Nicaragua, the private sector, academia and other stakeholders. 
UNICEF partnered with the Nicaraguan public sector to implement programmes aimed at improving the survival, health and protection of children and their families. Coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), UNICEF worked with the Ministries of Health, Education and the Family. 
In addition, UNICEF maintained a strong partnership with the Central Bank of Nicaragua, with which it continued to strengthen the analysis of social spending, particularly on children. Together with the Bank and the National Institute of Information for Development, the MICS survey was completed, the results of which are expected to be published in early 2025. 
Although there were no climate- or seismic-related emergencies during the reporting period, UNICEF maintained its partnership with the National System for Disaster Prevention, Mitigation and Attention, SINAPRED, to strengthen families' resilience to climate change and other emergencies.  
Based on the Cooperation Programme in effect since March 2024, UNICEF established a partnership with the National Water Authority to support the improvement of drinking water, sanitation and hygiene services in rural communities, particularly in the Dry Corridor of Nicaragua. 
In alliance with the telecommunications companies Tigo and Claro, UNICEF reached 23,339 children to develop digital skills, address the gender digital divide and raise awareness of children's rights. 
In 2024, UNICEF mobilised $315,000 in non-financial resources from the domestic and international private sector. These collaborations supported UNICEF's mission to address children's vulnerability during the climate crisis, reaching 844,841 people affected by the torrential rains with emergency messages and 947,931 people with awareness of children's rights. 
UNICEF launched a digital literacy initiative through the Gamers in Action programme with Tigo and addressed child online safety through Safer Internet Day events. Collaborations with Tigo, the Ministry of Education, Google's Women Techmakers Programme, NicaWomanTech and UNICEF addressed the digital gender gap, reaching 1,500 female participants. 
In 2024, UNICEF expanded its partnership with some of the country's leading universities. 
Working with the National Autonomous University of Nicaragua (UNAN), the American University (UAM), the National University of Engineering (UNI), Keiser University and the Catholic University, UNICEF mobilised more than 5,000 young people in transformative initiatives for climate protection and environmental education, promoting confidence in vaccines, preventing violence and providing psychosocial support in schools. This partnership has strengthened research capacity and the application of Human Centred Design (HCD) methodology, equipping students and faculty with innovative tools to address social problems in a collaborative and evidence-based manner. These advances have solidified universities as strategic partners in advancing social and behavioural change strategies. 
The relationship with donors continues to be a strong value for UNICEF. Its positioning at the country level is reflected in donor confidence in UNICEF's performance in terms of effectiveness and efficiency. 
In 2004, UNICEF continued to actively engage with donors from both the public and private sectors. Of particular importance were the dialogues with the Delegation of the European Union in Nicaragua and with the U.S. Regional Office of the Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance , for technical support to key programmatic priorities in the Dry Corridor of Nicaragua. 
During the reporting period, $7,841,817 was received from public donors. Among them, the  European Commission / ECHO, GAVI The Vaccine Alliance, the Global Partnership for Education, the Global Vaccine Fund (World Bank), and the US Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance. UNICEF Nicaragua thanks them all for their support to the cause of Nicaragua's children. 
UNICEF has maintained ongoing dialogues with the Inter-American Development Bank, the Japan International Cooperation Agency and the embassies of Canada and Spain, among others, to seek new partnerships on programmatic priorities. 
Although the country does not have a United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework, UNICEF has worked in coordination with agencies, funds and programmes accredited in the country, is an active part of the inter-agency group on gender, emergency preparedness and response (UNETE), prevention of sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment, and leads the groups on communications and the SDG. 
These efforts contributed to the establishment of five priority accelerators for achieving the SDG (universal health coverage, transformation of sustainable and climate-adapted agri-food systems, resilience of communities exposed to climate change, gender social norms, and technical and technological capacity of the education system), which will serve as the basis for joint planning of agencies, funds and programmes to be developed in 2025. 
UNICEF supported, along with the FAO and the PAHO, the MoH in the formulation of the "Nicaragua Unida en Una Salud para Hacer Frente a Futuras Pandemias" project, a US$17 million winning proposal submitted to the Pandemic Preparedness Fund, to start  implementation in April 2025. 
The CO also partnered with UN agencies to promote early childhood development, organising inter-agency dialogues for World Children's Day and the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The year 2024 presented particular challenges for UNICEF in Nicaragua. 
The 2024-2028 CPD had a strong focus on the Caribbean Region of the country. However, the Government of Nicaragua asked the international cooperation to shift their focus from the Caribbean Coast to the Dry Corridor. UNICEF ended activities that built on the response to the emergency caused by hurricanes ETA and IOTA, which had continued as part of UNICEF's  cooperation since 2023. Terms of agreement of programme results initially committed to the Caribbean region were renegotiated. Thanks to the flexibility of these donors and the dialogue with the government, all activities have been refocused to the Dry Corridor for implementation in 2025. 
In November 2024, the Government of Nicaragua approved the Law that Regulates the Cooperation provided by  Agencies and Diplomatic Missions accredited in the country. Greater use of direct implementation modalities will be critical in 2025. To this end, the Country Office will be supported technically and administratively by the Regional Office for Latin America and the Caribbean (LACRO). 
Another important challenge has been the slow initiation of some activities established in the new CPD , in particular those related to out-of-school children and birth registration. In 2025 UNICEF Nicaragua will accelerate implementation in coordination with the MoE. 
Lastly, there has been limited work with the Justice System due to the internal reorganisation that has taken place in this institution. This situation has affected work on juvenile criminal justice and attention to victims of sexual abuse. UNICEF expects  to resume activities in the second half of 2025. 
The main lessons learned, especially those derived from the challenges already mentioned, are the following: 
UNICEF must continue to seek creative ways to implement programmes directly in the field, within the current country context and the challenges identified. To this end, it must increase its programmatic and operational flexibility, including field presence, using mechanisms such as direct implementation, outsourcing services through institutional consultancies, exploring options for strategic partners such as universities, which provide great opportunities in the current context, and deepening efforts to ensure the government ownership in all activities with the government institutions. 
UNICEF must continue to clearly demonstrate its contribution, as a United Nations agency, to the National Plan for Poverty Reduction and Human Development 2022-2026, ensuring that all its results and indicators are aligned with those of that plan. 
The proactive and innovative use of technology, for both programme development and operation, is becoming increasingly important in the context of the current work in Nicaragua. The good results in the development of geo-referenced maps using GIS technology for situation analysis and proactive calculation of the population affected by natural disasters have shown that UNICEF should continue to look for new technologies to adapt and incorporate into its programming. 
The development of the new image of "Rita", the UNICEF's animated cartoon character, in collaboration with American University’s professors and students demonstrated the potential of this alliance, which should be strengthened for  knowledge generation and support for children’s rights. 
The permanent dialogue with the donors, especially with those represented in the country, helps to face unforeseen situations and to make the requirements established in the programmes agreed with them more flexible. Programmes financed by the European Union, the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development of Canada and the Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance are good examples of it. 
The main opportunities for the coming period are related to the good relationship that UNICEF has with all its governmental partners, which will allow it to continue to implement the CPD as it has been established and to initiate new and pending activities in 2025. In particular, the good relationship with the Ministry of the Family, the Central Bank of Nicaragua, the National System for Disaster Prevention, Mitigation and Attention, the National Water Agency, the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Health stands out. 
Increased dialogue and coordination among UN agencies, funds and programmes in Nicaragua will strengthen joint projects, such as the Global Vaccine Fund, and access to other inter-agency funds for the development of joint activities, especially around the SDG accelerators mentioned above. 
Partnerships with universities have helped compensate for the reduced presence of non-governmental organisations (NGOs) in the country. Both volunteers and academic teams from universities are very important technical resources for the coming years. 
The eventual publication of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys MICS Household Survey will lead to the launch a series of specific studies that will help to improve existing information about children in Nicaragua and lay the groundwork for future policy making, investments and activities in all areas including on water quality, nutrition, early unions or gender-based violence.

While Panama became a high-income country in 2022 and poverty has significantly decreased, it remains one of the most unequal countries in the world, with a 0.49 Gini coefficient. Monetary and multi-dimensional poverty particularly affects rural and indigenous populations. Several structural factors contribute to high and persistent inequalities in Panama, including low social spending (representing 9% of the GDP compared to the regional average of 11%), centralized and inequitable public investment (the richest province receives 28% more investment per capita than the median while the poorest province receives 70% less), labour informality and lack of investment in human capital. 
Children represent one-third of Panama’s population, 26% being afro-descendant and 23% indigenous (2023 census). Poverty disproportionately affects children, with 34% experiencing multi-dimensional poverty and 39% living in monetary poverty. These figures are even more alarming in indigenous provinces (called Comarcas), where 9 out of 10 children live in poverty. While adult multi-dimensional poverty is decreasing, children’s is stagnating.
In recent years, Panama has made notable strides in advancing the rights and well-being of children. Key achievements include a law establishing a comprehensive child rights system, an increase in the education budget to 7% of the GDP, strengthened policies and services for early childhood, and significant efforts to transition children in residential care to family-based alternatives. UNICEF provided technical assistance to all these reforms.
However, recent data highlights the need for Panama to accelerate efforts to achieve several child-related targets under the SDGs. While many social services exist in the legislative framework of Panama, in reality, few are implemented due to the lack of sufficient human and financial investment. The most affected children include those living in poverty and in rural areas, indigenous children, migrant children, children with disabilities, and children without parental care—often facing multiple forms of exclusion. For instance, most rural and indigenous communities do not have health, social or early childhood development (ECD) services present at the local level. Many poor families do not access cash transfers. Additionally, social norms around corporal punishment, gender, children belonging to minorities, early care and education, and children with disabilities negatively affect children.
In preparation for the 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections, the Country Office implemented an advocacy strategy aimed at putting children on electoral programmes and positioning UNICEF as a partner of choice. As a result, key relations with future decision-makers were initiated. The arrival of a new government in July 2024 resulted in many changes at political and technical levels, requiring a significant investment in sharing evidence and ongoing policy reforms and familiarising new counterparts with UNICEF and its work.

Health and Nutrition: While Panama's infant mortality rate has steadily declined over the past 30 years, it remains twice as high in indigenous comarcas (26 per 1,000 live births), largely due to limited access to pre- and post-natal health services. Chronic malnutrition affects one in six children under five, with rates 2.5 times higher in comarcas. Additionally, two in five adolescents aged 13 to 17 are affected by overweight or obesity. Key challenges include poverty, inadequate access to nutritional services and information, and limited implementation of public policies.
Early Childhood Development (ECD):  Twenty percent of children aged 36 to 48 months in Panama do not achieve optimal development. Only 3% of children under age 3 enrolled in public early childhood centres, mostly present in urban centres. Although pre-primary education is compulsory, 44% of children aged 4 and 11% of children aged 5 are not enrolled. The main obstacle is the lack of preschool classrooms, especially in comarcas and rural areas.
Education: Access to quality education remains one of the main challenges facing children in Panama. An estimated 120,000 children and adolescents are out of school. Four out of five 15-year-old students do not achieve minimum proficiency in mathematics, and three out of five do not meet basic reading standards. The primary barriers include inequitable investment in education, the need for improvements in teachers’ training, outdated curricula, and limited access to digital learning tools. While Panama’s education budget reached an historic 7% of the GDP, only 55% of its investment sub-budget was utilised in 2023.
Child protection: Forty-five percent of children in Panama are victims of violent discipline at home, with three out of ten experiencing physical punishment. Children represent seven out of ten cases of sexual violence, and nine out of ten survivors are girls. Over 6,000 adolescents live in early unions, a rate four times higher among indigenous adolescents. While the government has been investing in the transformation of the child protection system to decrease the number of children living in institutions—achieving a 37% reduction over the past four years—there are still over 1,000 children in residential care, many for reasons not related to protection such as poverty or malnutrition.
Adolescent mothers: 14,364 adolescents in Panama are mothers. Half of them are indigenous, and 60% are out of school. Community-based preventive services, along with targeted programmes, are essential to ensure adolescent mothers have access to health care and education.
Children on the move: Despite a 40% reduction in migration flows in 2024, children still made up 21% of people on the move through the dangerous Darien Gap (63,647 children; 38% under the age of 5), including 4,579 who were travelling unaccompanied or separated from their families (mostly adolescents). The new government aims at decreasing the migration flow and signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the United States to increase repatriations. So far, children and families have not been deported. Despite the reduction in the migration flow since July, the exposure of girls and women to gender-based violence continues to increase and the humanitarian needs of children and families on the move keep putting pressure on existing social services that are already scarce or even non-existent in the Comarca Embera-Wounaan, the main territory affected by migration.

Guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the 2030 Agenda, the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022-2026, the Government Strategic Plan 2019-2024 and the 2021-2025 Country Programme Document, UNICEF in Panama focuses on generating strategic evidence, addressing social norms detrimental to children, providing technical assistance to the government for system-level transformations and supporting the implementation of innovative models for results at scale.  
UNICEF continued to support child rights monitoring in Panama to guide the planning and implementation of public policies. In partnership with the National Office of Statistics, a study on the situation of children, based on the 2023 census data, was published and launched on World Children’s Day. High-level decision-makers, including the First Lady of Panama and Ministers, attended the launch. Additionally, with UNICEF’s technical support, the Ministry of Social Development published a second measurement of the Child Multidimensional Poverty Index and committed to financing a new round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) in 2025. UNICEF also partnered with the Defensoría del Pueblo to produce the second Ombudsman’s Report on the Situation of the Human Rights of Children and Adolescents in Human Mobility. 
A standout achievement in 2024 for the Panama Country Office was receiving the prestigious UNICEF Global Staff Team Award, which recognised the team’s exceptional humanitarian support and response for children on the move in the Darien gap.
The Country Office continued to promote and invest in intersectoral strategic programming through two main office-wide initiatives:    

Government-led pilot of an integrated model to deliver basic, integrated social services in health, education, ECD, social protection and child protection at the community level: The goal of this model is to generate evidence, awareness and commitment on how Panama could     significantly expand the reach and quality of social services in the most vulnerable communities of the country at an affordable cost. The government, with UNICEF's technical and financial support, continues to lead this pilot in 13 communities in Panama Oeste and the Comarca Embera-Wounaan. In 2024, the pilot reached over 9,000 children and baseline data was collected to support future formative and impact evaluations that will inform the scale-up of the model to the rest of the country. After two years of implementation, the Government is already taking over some components to replicate them with its own budget. 
Integrated campaign on ECD: This multi-year campaign highlights the importance of the early years and mobilises support from decision-makers, families and the private sector. The four-year campaign combines programmatic efforts, advocacy, social and behaviour change (SBC), and fundraising. In 2024, the third phase of the campaign was launched in partnership with the new First Lady of Panama. This phase focuses on promoting nurturing care and positive discipline and preventing violence against children. The campaign was nominated for a national award and reached about 700,000 people and generated over 1.2 million digital impressions in 2024. 
 
1.EARLY CHILDHOOD DEVELOPMENT, HEALTH AND NUTRITION
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support the Government of Panama in implementing the national, intersectoral ECD policy for children aged 0 to 8 years. Support to the Early Childhood Intersectoral Committee led to the adoption, through a national decree, of guidelines and quality standards for community playrooms (i.e., institutional centres for learning and play in early childhood, known in Spanish as “ludotecas”). 
Within the framework of the model for basic, integrated social services, UNICEF supported the implementation of community-based ECD services that directly benefited around 500 children aged 0-3 years in 13 disadvantaged communities. This intervention is designed to promote positive care, nutrition, play and communication between young children and their caregivers. Tools, guidelines, training protocols, working modalities and a costing exercise were developed to ensure scalability. The objective is to support the government's efforts to increase coverage of ECD services in rural and indigenous communities in a cost-effective manner. After only two years of implementation, the new Minister of Social Development has committed to scaling up progressively the programme at the national level with government funding. The first milestone will be to reach an additional 2,100 children in 2025 with their own resources.
UNICEF also leveraged financial resources from the Development Bank of Latin America (CAF) to provide technical assistance to the Ministry of Social Development in scaling up ECD services. Through this partnership, UNICEF supports the government in analysing the cost of expanding access to early childhood programmes at the national level through four service modalities by running simulations of various scenarios and estimating costs to inform the scale-up. Additionally, a study is underway to identify individual, family and community factors influencing the current demand for ECD services.
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health in rolling out the Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) programme across the health sector, benefiting over 1,000 preterm and low-birth weight infants. KMC is an evidence-based approach promoting healthy development in both preterm and low-weight full-term newborns, emphasising skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breastfeeding. The Ministry of Health officially adopted KMC as a national programme through a ministerial resolution, implementing it in all neonatal care facilities at national level. Panama's largest children's hospital, “Hospital del Niño”, received a certification of excellence for its implementation by the global Kangaroo Mother Care Foundation.  In close collaboration with the children´s hospital, UNICEF piloted a new digital solution to improve caregiver adherence to care guidelines by sending targeted messages via WhatsApp, using RapidPro technology. These messages focus on nurturing care and positive parenting for children, as well as caregiver self-care.
UNICEF also provided technical assistance to the Ministry of Health to strengthen the implementation of Integrated Management of Childhood Illness and Nutrition (IMCI) by including a component on community-based healthcare in the model of social, integrated services model. The initial assessment, which identified key community health resources, was instrumental in guiding the design of the pilot programme to be initiated in 2025.
In the area of nutrition, UNICEF supported both the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Education in reviewing policies aimed at preventing obesity and overweight. This included improving regulations for kiosks that sell food to children at school to ensure that healthy meals are available. UNICEF is also supporting a study on food marketing in schools, which will provide key evidence to advocate for healthier school environments. UNICEF continued to work with the WHO/PAHO and the Ministry of Health in the development and adoption of a national Accelerated Plan to Stop Obesity, which specifically targets childhood obesity. Additionally, UNICEF contributed to the design and validation of a protocol for managing wasting in community and primary healthcare settings and provided training on nutritional screening for civil society organisations and academic partners.
 
2.EDUCATION
UNICEF supported national efforts to improve access and quality of education across Panama through technical assistance, capacity building, evidence generation and the convening of key partnerships for coordinated action and advocacy. 
Within the framework of the model for basic, integrated social services, UNICEF continued to support the Ministry of Education in piloting a school-level programme to improve foundational skills in primary and lower secondary levels, reaching over 9,000 children in 37 schools, and focusing on enhancing reading and writing skills. The programme included the development of manuals, materials, and a teacher development curriculum, supported by a robust monitoring and evaluation framework to inform future scale-up efforts.  
As part of the GIGA global initiative to promote internet connectivity in schools, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Education, UNICEF conducted a study on the cost and quality of internet access in schools. This evidence has been widely used by the government to negotiate the reduction of service rates and improve quality, particularly benefiting children in indigenous and rural areas. This dialogue between different authorities, facilitated by UNICEF, led to renewed commitments and coordination for better school connectivity.
To support the implementation of the new law on the Comprehensive Child Rights System, UNICEF worked with the Ministry of Education to design an early warning system to prevent school drop-out and address social determinants (e.g., malnutrition and domestic violence), with ongoing advocacy for its nationwide implementation in 2025.
Panama has implemented several dialogue and consensus-building processes around its educational crisis in recent years, but the lack of effective follow-up mechanisms has hindered their implementation. To address this, together with UNESCO, UNICEF initiated and coordinated the establishment of a Think Tank for education in 2024, bringing together stakeholders from various sectors, including teachers' unions, parent and student associations, the private sector, civil society, International Financial Institutions, UN agencies, and academia. The Think Tank developed a diagnostic and identified clear priorities, which were shared by all stakeholders. It aims to serve as a long-term advocacy and technical platform, fostering multi-sectoral collaboration to effectively address the ongoing educational crisis. The diagnostic and Call to Action, which identified equitable access to education, quality of education, student well-being, governance and management and partnerships as key priority areas, were presented to the new Minister of Education. Efforts will continue in 2025 to mobilise all stakeholders in the implementation of the recommendations. 
 
3. CHILD PROTECTION
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support the government’s reform of the national child protection system, focusing on strengthening community social workers, advocating for violence prevention and prohibition in all settings, promoting deinstitutionalisation, developing family-based alternative care and enhancing services and protocols for the protection of children on the move.
As part of the government-led model for basic social services, UNICEF contributed to strengthening community social workers and protocols. Inter-sectoral case management tools and training modules were developed and implemented, focusing on identifying, assessing, referring, and following up with children and families at risk. A total of 257 children (126 girls and 131 boys) benefited from case management and were referred to various social services (health, education, child protection etc.). After two years of implementing the model, a major achievement was the adoption by the Government of the case management protocol for the social service workforce for nationwide implementation through a national decree. The implementation, with technical support from UNICEF, is planned for 2025.
Strategic advocacy efforts to achieve the legal prohibition of corporal punishment in all settings were boosted by the launch of the integrated campaign on positive discipline (see above). As a result, the Government of Panama committed to scaling up their efforts to eradicate violence against children and promote positive parenting at the Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children. In 2025, advocacy and communication efforts will be strengthened with the implementation of an intersectoral strategy for gender-transformative parenting support at the community level.
UNICEF continued to support system-level transformations of existing child protection services, resulting in 376 children being deinstitutionalised and returned to safe family environments (biological families, extended families, or foster care). Compared to 2023, there has been a 92% reduction in cases of children being voluntarily institutionalised by parents without a legal reason established by a child protection authority. This progress was achieved by providing technical assistance to the National Secretariat of Children, Adolescents, and Family (SENNIAF), in partnership with the NGO RELAF. A new protocol for managing child protection cases, developed with UNICEF technical assistance, was implemented, including a standardised methodology for assessment and the development of individualised care plans. 
UNICEF also supported the implementation of Primero, a digital platform for real-time monitoring and case management of child protection cases, contributing to the delivery of services efficiently at scale while ensuring the safety and security of children´s data. In 2024, Primero was institutionalized as the only platform for managing child protection cases nationwide. With UNICEF support, all child protection case workers in the country (over 500) were trained on using Primero, preventing family separation and promoting family environments.
UNICEF also contributed to implementing the first-ever pilot foster care programme in the province of Chiriquí. In view of the positive results, the national child protection authority will expand it to the Province of Panama and the Comarca Ngäbe-Buglé in 2025, with UNICEF’s support.
Following the approval of a law that creates a comprehensive Child Rights System, UNICEF has continued to support its implementation by strengthening governance structures and community-based services. In terms of governance structures, UNICEF supported the establishment of Regional Committees in two provinces – Panama Oeste and the Comarca Embera-Wounaan. These Regional Committees will serve as intersectoral governing bodies of local protection systems. 
 
4.EMERGENCY RESPONSE FOR CHILDREN ON THE MOVE
Despite a slowdown in migration flows during the second half of the year, lifesaving services in WASH, nutrition, health, child protection, gender-based violence and psychosocial support remained critical to addressing the urgent needs of the population on the move in transit through Panama. UNICEF and its partners continued to provide vital services, ensuring that the most vulnerable children, women and families, as well as local populations affected by migration, received the assistance they needed.
Through the Child-Friendly Spaces, with its implementing partner RET, UNICEF reached 44,451 children and 9,130 caregivers with psychosocial services, offering a safe environment for children in crisis. In addition, interventions promoting safe environments were implemented in seven host communities, benefiting 2,851 indigenous children and 769 caregivers in the Comarca Embera-Wounaan. UNICEF also supported SENNIAF, the Child Protection Authority, in the case management of 4,478 children on the move, ensuring that their protection needs were addressed, and provided family-based alternative care for 274 unaccompanied and separated children.
In response to the increase in sexual violence, UNICEF supported 633 women and girl survivors and supplied Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) Kits to the Ministry of Health. At Migratory Reception Stations, UNICEF implemented Self-Care Spaces for women and adolescent girls, offering GBV mitigation and response services to 26,050 of them. 
In terms of WASH services, UNICEF’s support reached over 247,000 migrants, ensuring access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities. Partnering with the NGO Global Brigades, UNICEF expanded water production and storage capacity in both Migratory Reception Stations and host communities. In the community of Bajo Chiquito, water capacity was doubled to 50,000 litres per day, while at the Reception Station of Lajas Blancas, it increased from 85,000 to 100,000 litres per day. Additionally, UNICEF introduced new laundry services, enabling the cleaning of over 755 kilograms of clothing at the reception stations. Age- and gender-appropriate hygiene kits were distributed to 8,330 children and adults. As local communities depend on the severely contaminated river water UNICEF collaborated with local authorities to improve water infrastructure and sanitation for over 4,600 indigenous people across ten host communities, contributing to the humanitarian-development nexus.
UNICEF also supported maternal and child health initiatives, reaching 27,890 migrants, including 11,245 children under five and 834 pregnant women. Essential medicines and supplies were provided to the Ministry of Health to ensure continued health service delivery for people on the move and host communities.
Based on the findings of the evaluation of the humanitarian response, UNICEF designed an education intervention for children on the move and local children. This initiative will be launched in 2025 and is expected to reach over 18,000 children.
UNICEF strengthened its Accountability to Affected Populations processes, working closely with partners such as UNHCR. Over 500 surveys were conducted monthly to assess the needs of migrants, while regular focus groups provided valuable feedback on service satisfaction and recommendations for improvement. UNICEF also developed the first interagency protocol for the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse and implemented a feedback tool for local partners and humanitarian actors on the ground.
UNICEF continued to raise awareness at national, regional, and global levels about the alarming number of children using the dangerous jungle route and the increasing incidence of unaccompanied and separated children. The organisation’s advocacy efforts were crucial in strengthening national systems for the protection of migrant children. UNICEF contributed to the development of key decrees and protocols and played a pivotal role in advocating for enhanced response services for survivors of sexual violence.
At the local level, UNICEF led the WASH group, the Child Protection sub-group, and the Gender-Based Violence sector. It also coordinated migration flow data sharing with Central American Country Offices, bolstering regional preparedness and response efforts.
 
5.COMMUNICATION AND PRIVATE SECTOR ENGAGEMENT
UNICEF maintained its leadership as the main child rights organisation in Panama, reaching new audiences through solid partnerships with the government, the media, the private sector, the National Assembly, the Supreme Court, youth and adolescent groups, and high-profile influencers. UNICEF communication and advocacy highlighted children’s issues during the electoral process and with the newly elected government, emphasizing the situation of children and the urgent actions needed to improve conditions with a focus on equity for the most vulnerable.  
UNICEF partnered with the Latin American Centre for Journalism (CELAP) to organise the sixth annual Children’s Journalism Award, recognising excellence in reporting on children in local media. Over 90 interviews were conducted with top-tier media, ensuring child rights remained a priority on the national agenda. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with MEDCOM, one of Panama’s leading media corporations, to co-produce a monthly TV segment on early childhood, Childhood from A to Z (“Niñez de la A a la Z”), reaching nearly 100,000 viewers each month. On social media, UNICEF worked with the influencer group Super Moms (“Super Mamás”), delivering positive parenting messages to 86,000 people.
The Country Office experienced significant growth in fundraising. The number of acquired donors increased by 35% compared to 2023, and the funds raised grew by 26%. The office maintains an active donor base of 4,050 individuals and more than 90 companies are engaged with UNICEF. In response to emergencies, UNICEF launched a fundraising campaign in less than 48 hours, ensuring timely support and resources for those most in need. Based on the promising fundraising results in 2024, the Panama Country Office is on track to become self-financed by 2028.
 
6.STEWARSHIP OF RESOURCES AND OFFICE MANAGEMENT
The Country Office continued to apply the most rigorous standards to ensure the good stewardship of its financial and human resources, to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and transparency of its processes. As a result, all the organisational Key Performance Indicators were achieved. The Global Staff Survey 2024 showed very positive results on staff engagement and satisfaction, with significant improvements noted in work-life balance, adherence to standards of conduct, and performance management.

While the government remained the main partner of UNICEF in Panama, the Country Office partnered with a wide range of institutions present in the country such as the Ombudsman for Human Rights (Defensoria del Pueblo), United Nations agencies, civil society organisations, the private sector, donors and adolescents themselves. 
UNICEF leveraged support for children in Panama by actively contributing to the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNDSCF) and by working closely with several United Nations agencies to promote and protect children’s rights. UNICEF led the UNDSCF Result Group on violence and human rights and contributed to the other Result Groups (access to and quality of basic services; governance and participation; environment and climate change) through its technical assistance to improve the coverage and quality of education, health, ECD and child protection services, as well as to promote adolescent and youth participation, especially on climate change. UNICEF remained a key contributor to the UN Human Mobility Group and participated actively in coordination taskforces organised by the government at the local and national levels. 
UNICEF continued to be the leading organisation promoting child rights in the country. UNICEF partnered with key multimedia groups such as TVN Media, MEDCOM and SERTV, as well as the telecommunications company +Movil, to amplify the messages of the integrated communication campaign focusing on the prevention of violence against children. Through the promotion of positive parenting messages and tools, more than 1.5 million mobile phone users were reached, and indirectly over 300,000 children.  Forming partnerships with various stakeholders has also been crucial for accelerating fundraising efforts.  Over 90 companies and malls provided over 160 spaces and facilities for free to support events and donor recruitment in 2024. This represents a new local record for engagement with companies and networks.  
In 2024, UNICEF continued strengthening its collaboration with International Financial Institutions (IFIs) with a presence in Panama, including CAF (Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean), the World Bank, and the IDB (Inter-American Development Bank). Regular meetings were held at both technical and representative levels within the framework of new global Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with these institutions. As a result, UNICEF and CAF signed a new technical assistance agreement to support the implementation of Panama’s Early Childhood Public Policy. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with the IDB to leverage public resources towards expanding ECD services in disadvantaged areas as well as collecting updated disaggregated data on children through a new round of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS).
UNICEF is currently implementing along with UN Women, UNFPA and UNDP a joint programme for the United Nations Partnership on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities that aims to develop a more disability-inclusive and gender-transformative care and support system. This programme will contribute to strengthening basic services and support for children with disabilities and their caregivers in remote communities, building on the government-led intersectoral model for community social services supported by UNICEF. 
As mentioned above, UNICEF partnered with UNESCO to lead the development of a joint advocacy platform to mobilise support from all stakeholders in addressing the ongoing learning crisis in Panama. The “Think Tank for Education” included participation from key partners such as teachers' unions, student and parent associations, the private sector, academia, UN agencies, and IFIs. 
UNICEF actively engaged with adolescents and youth organisations to mobilise support for climate change action. Over 1,000 adolescents, primarily from indigenous communities, participated in the Local Conference for Climate Change. The conference provided a platform to foster citizenship, critical thinking, and green skills. Recognising Panama’s vulnerability to climate change—evident in internal displacement within indigenous comarcas—the event ensured the participation of adolescents from diverse provinces and regions, emphasising interculturality, local empowerment, and the indigenous worldview. Held in September 2024, the conference was organised by youth groups with UNICEF’s support and culminated in the development of a document containing adolescent proposals to inform the 2025 update of Panama’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).
UNICEF also leveraged U-Report as a tool for adolescent participation and advocacy. Additionally, the organisation established an Adolescent Consultative Committee comprising adolescents from across the country. This Committee has been instrumental in generating organic social media content, promoting peer learning, and increasing youth involvement in rights-based issues. Their efforts led to unprecedented participation by children and adolescents in the 2024 Children’s Day events organised by UNICEF.

1. Investing in innovative models to promote system-level changes at the national level: In 2024, the Country Office advanced three innovative models to achieve scalable results for children in Panama - an integrated social services model at the community level, the Kangaroo Mother Care Programme for preterm and low-weight infants, and the implementation of "Primero," a digital case management platform for child protection. From the outset, UNICEF prioritised the involvement and leadership of government institutions at political, technical, and subnational levels. Beyond financial investment, UNICEF’s primary role on these models has been to provide technical support, share regional and global innovations and best practices, and act as a broker for intersectoral and multi-sectoral collaboration. These models are designed to influence and inform government policies and budgets, leveraging "real-life" evidence, using baseline assessments, evaluations, and costing exercises, to demonstrate their effectiveness, scalability, and affordability. 
After less than two years of implementation and despite the change in government, these models are already achieving results at scale. The government, using its own budget, is replicating components on early childhood development and child protection from the integrated services model. The Ministry of Health has adopted the Kangaroo Mother Care Programme as a national initiative, while the Child Protection Authority has expanded the use of Primero as the institutional platform for child protection case management, fully assuming its costs in 2025. ICT4D (Information and Communication Technology for Development) plays a crucial role in both the Kangaroo Mother Care Programme and Primero, addressing Panama’s lagging digital transformation of social services.
2.Strengthening collaboration with International Financial Institutions (IFIs) to leverage resources to achieve results at scale: Partnering with IFIs has proven to be a critical strategy for advancing UNICEF’s programmes in Panama. By leveraging financial resources, technical expertise and policy influence, these partnerships have the potential to increase the scale and sustainability of UNICEF interventions. For instance, in 2024 the government has committed to scaling up new community-based ECD services for rural and indigenous areas developed by UNICEF, through the mobilisation of resources from an IDB loan. Additionally, thanks to UNICEF and IDB joint advocacy, conducting a new MICS survey became a condition for a budget support loan approved in 2024. UNICEF is also collaborating closely with the World Bank, CAF and IDB to generate rigorous evidence on poverty and access to early childhood development services.
3.Navigating political transitions to sustain programmatic priorities: In 2024, Panama held presidential, legislative, and local elections, resulting in a change of government at both national and subnational levels. To ensure that children remain a political priority and to maintain the continuity of programmatic priorities, UNICEF developed a pre-election advocacy strategy and a government transition plan to keep key interventions for children central to the new government’s agenda.
