This approach is aligned with the country office’s Resource Mobilization Strategy (2023-26), which aims to diversify partnerships to offset the dependence on traditional humanitarian partners, who are reducing their funding for Venezuela. Overall, UNICEF Venezuela developed proposals worth US$12 million for new and non-traditional partners, with the aim of funding the new Social Protection programme focusing on indigenous communities and disability, and the Education, Health, and Child Protection sectors, who have experienced substantial funding cuts.
Other key partnerships which UNICEF which contributed to bolstered efforts in Venezuela, included:
National Government entities: UNICEF worked closely with the Ministry of Education (MoE), the National Institute of Nutrition (INN), the Ministry of Health (MoH), the Ministry of Water (MoW), MINEC, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, IDENNA, Ombudsman’s Office, Public Ministry, Supreme Court of Justice, Public Defense, National Council for Persons with Disabilities (CONAPDIS) and the Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. As recommended by the 2023 Country Programme Evaluation, this strengthened cooperation facilitated the promotion of good practices, resource optimization, and capacity building, particularly in health, nutrition, education, child protection, WASH, and social protection sectors, reaching a greater number of vulnerable children and adolescents.
NGO partnerships: UNICEF partnered with 14 NGOs, including ASEINC, Fe y Alegría, CARITAS, World Vision, Save the Children, ASONACOP, Caritas Carúpano, CECODAP, CODHECIU, CEPIN, REHABILITARTE, Fundación Luz y Vida, FUNDANA, FUNVAPE, FUNDAINI, Intersos, Red de Casas Don Bosco, Tinta Violeta and others. These partnerships were crucial for implementing programs, especially in reaching out-of-school children, enhancing community outreach, and providing specialized support at local and community levels.
UN system: Collaborations with other agencies, funds and programmes from United Nations System such as the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the PAHO/WHO (Pan American Health Organization / World Health Organization, and the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) were vital. In 2024, these partnerships helped develop strategic work plans and promote a unified response to health, child protection, and disaster risk reduction (DRR). It is important to note that UNICEF Venezuela is implementing a joint program on DRR with UNHCR with ECHO funds. It is also promoting to international donors in Venezuela and abroad its joint programme on reproductive, maternal, neonatal, child and adolescent health with UNFPA, to address funding shortfalls in the sector. Finally, it has successfully strengthened its working relations with the WFP, and is developing two synergic, multisectoral programmes for BHA and ECHO. The 2024 RTA of UNICEF’s humanitarian response underscored the leading and coordinating role that UNICEF plays in the humanitarian architecture in Venezuela. 
Other international organizations: Furthermore, UNICEF has initiated a technical collaboration with the World Bank (WB) and the Inter-American Development Bank (BID) aiming at obtaining data on child poverty and producing a multidimensional child poverty analysis in 2025.
Local authorities and community leaders: Engagement with local authorities and community leaders was essential for programme acceptance and implementation. This local collaboration ensured smooth operations, facilitated access to communities, and promoted trust.
These partnerships were fundamental in addressing the urgent needs of the most vulnerable populations in Venezuela and enhancing the quality of services. The UNICEF contribution with these key partners facilitated:

Influence-raising: Improved relations with public and private international donors have contributed to repositioning Venezuela on the agenda, raising awareness on the numerous challenges faced by children. This has resulted in increased resource mobilization opportunities and joint advocacy efforts. 
Resource optimization: Collaborations with government bodies and NGOs help optimize  resources, ensuring that cooperation reaches the most vulnerable populations efficiently.
Enhanced service delivery: Partnerships with local and international organizations improve  the quality and reach of health, nutrition, education, child protection, and WASH services.
Capacity building: Working with the key national authorities, such as Ministry of Education and other local authorities, builds local capacities, leaving sustainable improvements in place. 
Community access: Local knowledge and presence of partners facilitate better access to communities, ensuring programmes are well-received and effectively implemented.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
UNICEF’s efforts in 2024 highlighted the importance of flexibility, resilience, and strategic partnerships in addressing the complex challenges in Venezuela. By learning from past experiences and innovating its approaches, UNICEF aims to continue improving the lives of the most vulnerable populations in the country. In 2024, UNICEF faced numerous challenges in implementing its programmes in Venezuela but also learned valuable lessons and introduced several innovations to improve its efforts. Here is an integrated summary highlighting the main challenges, lessons learned, and innovations identified by UNICEF Venezuela in 2024 (among others through a real-time assessment of UNICEF’s humanitarian response):
Challenges:

Prolonged Crisis: The ongoing economic and political crisis weakened child protection entities, programs, and services, including coordination between institutions.
Lack of Official Data: The absence of reliable data hindered effective planning and response. This also affects an effective measurement of the achievement of results and regular monitoring of the situation of children across the country.
Sensitivity in Child Protection Issues: Legal identity, mobility, and juvenile criminal justice remained sensitive areas, complicating interventions.
Electoral Context: Pre- and post- election periods produced access limitations in    communities, disrupting programmes activities.
Critical Lack of Human Resources: High turnover and low salaries affected the    implementation of programmes, particularly in education and health sectors.
Material and Financial Resource Deficiencies: Deficiencies in basic services (water, energy, gasoline, internet) and difficulties in banking intermediation led to confidentiality violations and lack of data protection within the child protection system.
International Restrictions: These hindered the flow of essential health and nutrition  supplies, causing delays and shortages that impacted the availability of critical resources.
Lessons Learned:

Technical Support: Maintaining technical support for the child protection system at national and local levels, including NGO programs, is crucial even in     critical situations.
Resilience and Flexibility: Partners demonstrated resilience and flexibility by adapting activities to access restrictions and preparing documentation to respond to regulatory changes. 
Community Planning: Effective intersectoral planning and execution with community leaders, proved essential for successful programme implementation.
Risk Mitigation: Continuous monitoring is necessary to mitigate risks of misconduct, including sexual exploitation and abuse.
GBV Concerns: Addressing the naturalization of gender-based violence (GBV) and increased risks of sexual exploitation and trafficking of children is critical.
Integrated Approaches: The integration of WASH (Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene) and nutrition interventions significantly improved recovery rates, demonstrating the benefits of a multisectoral approach.
Local Engagement: Engaging local authorities and community leaders facilitated programme  acceptance and implementation, promoting trust and smooth operations.
Communication: Complex and protracted humanitarian crises require an adaptable communication model that enables effective management of programmatic changes.
Innovations and Strategic Adjustments:

Simplified Protocols for Malnutrition: Since 2020, Venezuela has implemented simplified community-based protocols for managing acute malnutrition, accelerated by the COVID-19  pandemic. A 2024 UNICEF study validated these protocols’ effectiveness compared to standard WHO protocols, improving RUTF dosage forecasting for high-risk cases.
Family MUAC Approach: Training community health promoters and families focused on preventing and detecting acute malnutrition in children through the Family MUAC approach, supported by SBC strategies to improve child health outcomes.
Contingency Budget Lines: Including contingency budget lines in programme documents enabled prompt resource mobilization for emergencies, such as flooding in Zulia and Sucre states.
Social Protection and Social Inclusion Programme Review: The program was reviewed to adapt to the current national context, focusing on improving data and evidence generation on child poverty, adapting the child-friendly cities initiative, and enhancing social protection systems to be more inclusive of children with disabilities and indigenous children.
Training and Adaptation: Training in socio-emotional activities and adapting Sports for Development at primary and early education levels were identified as priorities for enhancing programme effectiveness.
Partnerships with Local Authorities: Strengthening partnerships with governors and mayors was necessary to support programme continuity and sustainability.
Teacher Training and Support: Investing more time in teacher training and support, as well as strengthening local teams, was essential for enhancing sustainability and ownership.
Interagency Cooperation: Promoting cooperation within the interagency education group was important for optimizing resources and ensuring comprehensive care.

With nearly half of Algeria’s population under 29 years old, more than a third under 19, and one-tenth under 4[1], children and youth remain at the center of national priorities. Continued state investments in health, education, and social protection have reinforced child rights, underpinned by policies aligned with constitutional principles. 


In 2024, more than 20% of the public budget was allocated to ministries serving children and youth, reflecting strong commitment to human capital development[2]. Social transfers accounted for 28% of total spending, with 45.2% allocated to unemployment benefits, housing assistance, school allowances, and other direct financial aid. Public spending on education represents 6.3% of GDP, and the proportion of graduates in science and engineering (29.9%) contributed to a 43-rank improvement in the Human Capital pillar of the Global Innovation Index (GII) between 2023 and 2024. These gains helped Algeria improve its overall ranking from 119th to 115th out of 133 countries.[3]


Algeria regained its pre-COVID-19 status as an upper-middle-income country, supported by a 3.9% GDP growth rate in 2024 and 4.1% in 2023, driven by non-extractive sectors and public investment. Inflation declined from 9.3% in 2022-2023 to 4.3% in 2024, reflecting macroeconomic stabilization efforts. 


Efforts to modernize education continue, with more than 11 million children enrolled in school in 2024/2025. Key reforms have focused on digitalization initiatives to reduce the burden of school materials and increased support for children with disabilities, including the recruitment of 400 school life assistants for autistic students contributing to specialized learning support. Algeria’s participation in the Nouakchott Declaration demonstrates its commitment to Agenda 2063, emphasizing equitable and quality education. The 2024 National Vocational Training Conference outlined a roadmap to strengthen workforce skills and better align training programs with labor market demands.


Child protection policies have also been reinforced. In 2024, Algeria launched a consultative process for the National Action Plan for Children (NAPC) 2025-2030, under the National Body for the Protection and Promotion of Children. This strategic framework, expected by early 2025, aims to advance child welfare policies in line with national and global commitments. At the First World Ministerial Conference on the Elimination of Violence Against Children in Bogotá, Colombia, Algeria reaffirmed its commitment to child protection and international cooperation. Additionally, Law 24-06, which revises the penal code, has introduced stricter penalties for crimes against children, including violence, neglect, exploitation, and incitement to harmful behaviors. 


The validation of Law No. 02-09 on disability by the National People's Assembly and the National Council, along with the appointment of members to the National Council for Persons with Disabilities, affirms the state's inclusive vision. This vision is aligned with international legislation, particularly the provisions of the International Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, ratified by Algeria through Presidential Decree No. 09-188 on May 12, 2009. Furthermore, the revaluation of the disability allowance strengthens this commitment. Together, these developments represent a significant asset for Algeria’s participation in the Global Disability Summit (GDS) in 2025 in Berlin.


In 2023, Algeria recorded infant, neonatal, and perinatal mortality rates of 19.9‰, 14.9‰, and 25.3‰ per 1,000 live births, respectively[4]. To strengthen maternal and child health, the Ministry of Health institutionalized Maternal and Child Protection Day on April 20th, 2024, emphasizing community-based health services. As part of national health reforms, a new national health booklet was introduced, incorporating updated vaccination schedules, new antigens, and national maternal and child health guidelines, aiming to enhance early childhood healthcare and ensure consistency with global health standards[5]. Expanded neonatal care services have also been prioritized, particularly in underserved regions. In response to regional health risks and the emergence of communicable diseases, Algeria conducted an OBRA (Outbreak Response Assessment) mission in 2024 to assess and strengthen the country’s polio response efforts. Expanded vaccination campaigns have also been launched to close immunization gaps and protect vulnerable populations[6].


To combat the rising prevalence of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) among children, including obesity, Algeria established a national multisectoral committee for school health promotion and a ministerial task force for nutrition policy development. A separate multisectoral committee, led by the Ministry of Health and including civil society, as well as the Ministries of the Interior and Education, was also created to develop a national school health plan. Furthermore, the revival of school health clubs has contributed to increasing awareness of healthy lifestyles among students. 


For nearly 50 years, Sahrawi refugees in Tindouf camps have faced food insecurity, limited access to water, housing, and social services. In response, the 2024-2025 Sahrawi Refugee Response Plan (SRRP) was developed in collaboration with 28 humanitarian partners. UNICEF leads the Education Sector, contributes substantially to Health and Nutrition, and plays an active role in the Tindouf Representatives Group (TRG) to strengthen emergency preparedness, monitor and evaluate humanitarian interventions, and ensure the continuity of education for nearly 40,000 refugee children. Despite generous contributions, a 40% funding gap persists, threatening essential services. In November 2024, a donor visit helped mobilize new commitments, reinforcing long-term funding needs for humanitarian assistance.

In 2024, the Government of Algeria strengthened national systems in health, education, child protection, social protection, and programme effectiveness, promoting evidence-based, inclusive, and sustainable approaches. UNICEF supported these efforts with technical assistance to advance child rights and well-being.


Every Child Survives and Thrives 


Led by the Ministry of Health, Algeria has advanced health and nutrition systems to improve child survival, immunization, maternal health, digital innovations, and community engagement, contributing to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being). UNICEF supported these efforts with technical expertise, capacity-building, and innovative approaches.


Strengthening Immunization Systems: The Ministry of Health, with UNICEF’s support, advanced efforts to improve immunization coverage, expand vaccine access, and enhance outbreak response. A key milestone was the cost analysis of the national immunization strategy, enabling better financial planning for sustainable vaccination efforts. Facilitating policy discussions on the HPV vaccine introduction advanced adolescent health protection. The rollout of the revised vaccination schedule, supported by training 650 vaccination personnel and updating health booklets, ensured clearer immunization guidance. To institutionalize best practices, a vaccination guide was integrated into medical and paramedical training curricula.


To enhance vaccine logistics, UNICEF provided 10 solar refrigerators, 4 refrigerated trucks, and supported a nationwide cold chain assessment in partnership with the Ministry of Health. A new digital vaccine inventory system was introduced to optimize stock management, reducing vaccine shortages, particularly in newly established Wilayas. A key achievement was the polio vaccination campaign, immunizing 557,000 children across 658 centers in 20 southern Wilayas. These efforts increased Polio campaigns coverage from 64% in 2023 to 95% in 2024, demonstrating the impact of coordinated vaccination efforts. UNICEF also contributed to vaccine procurement and social mobilization through radio campaigns, mosque-based outreach, and youth-led advocacy, addressing vaccine hesitancy.


Digital Health Systems: the Ministry of Health with UNICEF support, promoted digital transformation within Algeria’s immunization system through South-South Cooperation with China, facilitating exchanges on electronic health records, AI-driven data management, and digital governance. A key innovation was the integration of a real-time epidemiological alert platform into Algeria’s national disease surveillance system, significantly improving early detection and outbreak response capabilities. Additionally, 450 healthcare professionals were trained on digital platforms, ensuring effective disease monitoring and rapid intervention.


Maternal and Child Health & Nutrition: UNICEF supported the evaluation of Algeria’s 2015-2019 perinatal plan in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and key stakeholders, informing the development of the 2025-2030 maternal and child health strategy. This data-driven approach aims to reduce maternal, neonatal, and perinatal mortality with a focus on equitable access to high-quality care. School health was also strengthened through UNICEF’s support in developing Algeria’s first multisectoral school health plan with the Ministry of National Education, training 450 school health professionals in nutrition and obesity prevention. In 2024, nutrition was formally elevated as a national priority for the first time since 1994. UNICEF played a key role in strengthening the National Nutrition Committee and contributed to planning Algeria’s forthcoming National Nutrition Strategy (2025-2030).


Community Engagement for Health Promotion: Recognizing the importance of community-driven behavior change, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Religious Affairs, civil society organizations, and youth networks to drive health awareness at the grassroots level. A major success was training 240 Imams and Mourchidats to advocate for maternal and child health, immunization, and nutrition, leveraging their influence to promote positive health behaviors. At the same time, UNICEF established 27 health clubs in partnership with the Ministry of National Education, engaging 135,000 children and youth in promoting healthy lifestyles and vaccine confidence. UNICEF’s work on adolescent health, particularly through HPV vaccine discussions and school-based interventions, addressed gender-specific needs, contributing to the Gender Action Plan.


Strengthening Health and Nutrition Systems in Humanitarian Settings: In 2024, UNICEF strengthened essential health and nutrition services in the Sahrawi refugee camps, ensuring no child was left behind. Efforts focused on vaccination, maternal and child health, and malnutrition management, addressing critical gaps and reinforcing the health system.


To improve immunization and epidemic preparedness, UNICEF trained 229 health workers—70 percent of whom were women—and procured vaccines, including the newly introduced hexavalent vaccine. Facing funding gaps, UNICEF launched an appeal that secured in-kind vaccine donations from the Algerian Agency for International Cooperation (AICA). In response to a worsening epidemiological situation, a joint field assessment with the Algerian Ministry of Health led to two large-scale awareness campaigns and a December vaccination drive against measles and polio across all five camps. To ensure vaccine storage and distribution, UNICEF equipped regional hospitals in Laâyoune and Dakhla with generators, safeguarding cold chain functionality.


In maternal and newborn care, UNICEF trained 28 Sahrawi midwives in Algeria on high-risk pregnancy management, ultrasound use, and uterine cancer detection. To strengthen healthcare infrastructure, UNICEF provided 35 health centers with essential medical equipment, including delivery tables, infant scales, feeding tubes, and medical kits.


To combat malnutrition, UNICEF trained 196 health and nutrition workers across 29 dispensaries, enhancing their ability to detect and manage acute malnutrition. Targeted training equipped 120 professionals with specialized skills in infant nutrition and breastfeeding counseling. To sustain progress, UNICEF supported monthly nutrition workshops in all dispensaries and provided continuous technical guidance through on-site visits by nutrition consultants.


Every Child Learns 


In close collaboration with the Ministry of National Education (MEN) and the Ministry of Vocational Education and Training (MoVET), Algeria advanced efforts to strengthen foundational learning, promote data-driven education planning, embed climate resilience, and align skills development with labor market needs. UNICEF provided technical support to these national priorities, contributing to SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 13 (Climate Action).


Strengthening Learning Foundations & Preventing Dropout: Building a strong foundation for learning is essential to achieving long-term educational success. UNICEF’s support for Algeria’s National Dropout Plan has refined early intervention mechanisms, leading to an expanded strategy that now includes primary education. Analysis of 2,000 student questionnaires informed tailored solutions, while training 25 inspectors in differentiated pedagogy empowered educators to meet diverse learning needs. Additionally, 135 inspectors were trained in student evaluations, contributing to a five-point increase in student grades in the first quarter of the 2024/2025 school year.


To ensure every child gets the best start in education, the Ministry of National Education expanded efforts to enhance preschool education with curriculum improvements and targeted training for 148 inspectors and school directors in the south and west. This initiative, supported by UNICEF, builds on previous work in the north and east, with a vision to scale up nationally, ultimately benefiting 2,000 primary inspectors and 20,000 teachers through hybrid learning tools.


Data-Driven Education & Skills for the Future:In preparation for Algeria’s 2025 national educational assessment, which will evaluate 6,000 students across 300 schools in 21 Wilayas, UNICEF provided technical support for 14 training sessions on psychometrics, international assessments (e.g., PISA), and data analysis to strengthen education policy formulation.


Beyond foundational learning, Algeria is committed to preparing students for the future workforce. UNICEF contributed to efforts to integrate life skills education into curricula, supporting the training of 25 inspectors on key competencies such as communication, problem-solving, and decision-making. To enhance employability, the Ministry of Vocational Education and Training launched a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC), validated with UNICEF’s support, benefiting 220 professionals and ensuring young people acquire labor market-relevant skills. 


Advancing Inclusive & Climate-Resilient Education: As part of Algeria’s commitment to inclusive education, the government, with UNICEF’s technical assistance, advanced the implementation of the intersectoral plan for children with autism. In this framework, 18 primary education inspectors and 19 vocational training professionals received capacity-building training. Additionally, a pilot initiative in Constantine trained 55 specialized educators in innovative tools for improving learning accessibility.


To embed environmental education in schools, the World’s Largest Lesson on water scarcity was integrated into curricula. UNICEF supported this effort by developing educational materials and preparing for a 2025 national student competition on sustainability, which will further engage children in climate action. Additionally, Algeria’s participation in the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) ensured that youth perspectives were included in national climate strategies.


Aligning Education with Labor Market Needs & Youth Engagement: The Government of Algeria, through the Ministry of Vocational Education and Training (MoVET), Ministry of National Education, High Youth Council (HYC), and other partners, advanced policies to bridge the gap between education and employment. UNICEF facilitated discussions on aligning vocational training with labor market demands, contributing to a roadmap for curriculum modernization.


To strengthen intersectoral collaboration, MoVET, MEN, HYC, and multiple UN agencies (ILO, UNDP, UNFPA, UNESCO, led by UNICEF) developed a concept note on learning-to-earning pathways, prioritizing support for youth not in education, employment, or training (NEET) and persons with disabilities. This initiative aligns with Algeria’s commitments made at the High-Level Regional Conference on Learning and Youth Employment in Tunisia.


In collaboration with the High Youth Council, Algeria is advancing initiatives that promote youth participation in education, employment, entrepreneurship, and civic engagement. As part of these efforts, UNICEF provides technical support to programs such as the Youth Foresight Initiative and the Summit of the Future, ensuring that young people’s perspectives contribute to policy discussions and national development strategies.


Ensuring Quality Education in Humanitarian Settings: In the Sahrawi refugee camps in southwestern Algeria, over 44,000 children depend on quality education. For the 2024-25 school year, 36,115 children enrolled in a refugee-led education system covering preprimary, primary, and lower secondary levels, with girls slightly outnumbering boys. To enhance access and learning conditions, UNICEF provided essential learning materials, benefiting 8,590 preschoolers with play-based kits and ensuring that all students received school kits.


Supporting teachers is a priority, and in partnership with AFAD, UNICEF provided quarterly incentives to 1,193 education staff—77% of whom are women—focused on primary and lower secondary education. Additionally, a collaboration with the Autonomous University of Madrid trained 55 teachers and inspectors in hands-on science education, with top participants now leading school-based training.


A recent mathematics assessment for 4th and 8th graders revealed significant performance gaps, particularly in geometry, algebra, and fractions. These findings underscore the importance of strengthening teacher support, enhancing student engagement, and fostering parental involvement to improve learning outcomes.


To foster participation, UNICEF and CISP introduced 38 student suggestion boxes in schools, ensuring student voices are heard in decision-making. A school-based sports-for-protection initiative is also expanding, training school staff and adolescents—including youth with and without disabilities—as trainers and participants. This approach promotes inclusion, life skills development, and school-based clubs to create more supportive learning environments.


As the Education Cluster Coordinator, UNICEF plays a key role in ensuring a coordinated education response, mobilizing resources, and strengthening local capacities. A mid-term review of the 2021-25 education strategy confirmed alignment with global frameworks but highlighted the need for increased funding and better data utilization.


Every Child is Protected 


The government of Algeria advanced child protection policies, justice for children, online safety, and disability inclusion. UNICEF provided technical support to strengthen systems that contribute to SDG 16 (Peace, Justice, and Strong Institutions) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).


A National Commitment to Ending Violence Against Children:Algeria reaffirmed its dedication to child protection by actively participating in the First World Ministerial Conference on the Elimination of Violence Against Children in Bogotá. UNICEF supported the National Office for the Protection and Promotion of Childhood (ONPPE) in translating these commitments into policy actions, including finalizing the National Action Plan for Children by 2025, developing a national information system on children by 2026, and establishing a monitoring unit to prevent online child exploitation.


Strengthening Child-Friendly Judicial Systems: The Algerian government, through the General Directorate for National Security (DGSN), is enhancing child protection in the justice system. Two newly equipped hearing rooms in the High Plateaus' judicial police services provide secure, trauma-sensitive spaces for child victims to testify, reducing secondary victimization and improving evidence collection. With UNICEF's technical support, training programs for judicial police officers will integrate child-sensitive interviewing techniques, ensuring the justice system upholds children's rights and well-being.


Children with disabilities The Government of Algeria has reinforced its commitment to disability inclusion, recognizing the heightened risks of exclusion faced by children with disabilities. In preparation for the 2025 Global Disability Summit in Berlin, national consultations were conducted—led by government entities, with technical support from UNICEF, UNFPA, and the UN Resident Coordinator’s Office—to shape Algeria’s roadmap for disability rights. These discussions are guiding national efforts to enhance legal and policy frameworks, improve data collection, expand access to health services, and increase inclusivity in education and vocational training. Additional focus is being placed on enhancing digital and physical accessibility, ensuring a more inclusive environment for all children.


Child rights Awareness:In 2024, the Algerian government, through the Ministry of National Solidarity, Family, and Women's Affairs (MSNFCF) and the Ministry of National Education (MEN), led initiatives to promote child rights. A national campaign on World Children’s Day raised awareness about online child protection and safe internet use. Additionally, the National Creativity and Innovation Competition provided a platform for children, including those with disabilities, to share ideas and engage in child rights discussions. UNICEF supported these efforts with technical assistance and advocacy, ensuring alignment with global best practices.


Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life


The Government of Algeria advanced child-sensitive social protection, public finance reforms, and equity-driven policies, reinforcing efforts to reduce child poverty and promote social inclusion, in line with SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth). With technical support from UNICEF, national institutions strengthened evidence-based policymaking, enhanced social protection mechanisms, and integrated child-sensitive approaches into public finance systems.


Strengthening Data for Equity: A major milestone in Algeria’s child-sensitive policymaking was the completion of the Equity Atlas by CNESE. This comprehensive tool consolidates over 1,500 disaggregated data points, offering insights into regional and socioeconomic disparities affecting children. It equips decision-makers with the evidence needed to design targeted interventions addressing child poverty and promoting social inclusion.


To translate findings into policy, two proposals were integrated into Algeria’s social protection agenda: an operational plan to reduce multidimensional child and youth poverty and a national definition of child-sensitive poverty. UNICEF provided technical support, fostering a more structured, child-focused approach to poverty reduction.


Child-Sensitive Social Protection & Public Finance for Children: CNESE, with the Ministry of Finance and key ministries, led efforts to assess and strengthen child-sensitive social protection programs for more coherent and effective support to children and vulnerable families. UNICEF provided technical input and data analysis to inform the development of a framing law for social protection.


As part of broader UN support, Algeria advanced a joint structural project on social protection, involving ILO, UNDP, UNFPA, and led by UNICEF. This initiative supports long-term improvements in Algeria’s social protection framework, ensuring that policies effectively address the needs of children, youth, and families in vulnerable situations.


Public finance for children remained a strategic priority for Algeria, with the Ministry of Finance taking steps to integrate child-sensitive elements into the social protection system. Additionally, UNICEF initiated the development of a citizen budget with a dedicated child-focused component, ensuring that public spending decisions consider the needs of children.


In alignment with Algeria’s efforts to enhance integrated financing strategies, UNICEF worked closely with UNDP and national partners to support the development of the Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF), reinforcing the importance of sustained investments in children as part of the country’s broader economic strategy.


Institutionalizing Child-Sensitive Budgeting: To strengthen budgeting processes for child-related programs, CNESE and ONPPE advanced the development of the Programme-Based Budgeting (PBB) Manual, in collaboration with the Collaborative Africa Budget Reform Initiative (CABRI). This manual provides structured guidance on budgeting, monitoring, and evaluating child-focused initiatives under the National Plan of Action for Children (PNAD). UNICEF provided technical input and capacity-building support, ensuring that budgetary frameworks align with international best practices. Moving forward, further capacity-building efforts will be essential to ensure effective implementation.


Programme Effectiveness


The Government of Algeria strengthened its monitoring, evaluation, advocacy, partnerships, and emergency response mechanisms to enhance programme impact, contributing to SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals). UNICEF provided technical support in building national systems for evidence-based decision-making, results-driven programming, and coordinated emergency responses.


Strengthening Monitoring, Evaluation, and Evidence-Based Policymaking: UNICEF supported national efforts to enhance monitoring, evaluation, and data-driven policymaking, providing technical assistance to build capacity in evaluation methodologies. To further strengthen these capacities, UNICEF facilitated Algeria’s participation in the French-language EXCEL training, equipping representatives from CNESE, the Ministries of Finance, Education, and Health with key evaluation skills. This initiative promoted cross-country knowledge exchange and contributed to a national action plan to foster an evaluation culture within government structures. High-level meetings followed, defining concrete steps to embed evaluation practices across institutions and reinforcing a long-term commitment to data-informed governance.


Expanding Advocacy and Partnerships for Children’s Rights: UNICEF strengthened its advocacy efforts through strategic digital engagement and partnerships. A key highlight was the collaboration with Olympic champion boxer Imane Khelif, whose advocacy on the rights of children with disabilities, school sports, and Sahrawi refugee children gained global attention. A video campaign featuring her message generated over 4.2 million views, significantly amplifying UNICEF’s outreach and increasing public awareness. Media engagement also surged, with UNICEF mentions rising from 80 in 2023 to over 250 in 2024, ensuring broader dissemination of key messages and policy priorities.


Humanitarian Coordination and Emergency Response: UNICEF played a critical role in humanitarian coordination, particularly within the Sahrawi Refugee Response Plan (SRRP) 2024-2025. The establishment of the Tindouf Representative Group (TRG) in collaboration with UNHCR and WFP provided a structured platform for monthly discussions, addressing emerging challenges and aligning interventions. Additionally, the Sahrawi Refugee Partners Group in Algiers strengthened collaboration among stakeholders, ensuring coordinated efforts to support refugee needs.


A joint monitoring and evaluation mission conducted in November 2024 assessed programme implementation in Sahrawi refugee camps, leading to the establishment of management responses and the introduction of a bi-annual rotational lead system to ensure continued oversight and optimization of interventions. UNICEF also played a central role in emergency response following the September floods in Dakhla camp, which displaced 350 families and damaged key infrastructure, including five schools—three of which require urgent rehabilitation funding. Through the TRG, UNICEF coordinated rapid responses and mobilized resources to address these urgent needs.

UNICEF continued nurturing and strengthening its strategic partnerships for children while expanding engagement with new stakeholders to deliver results and mobilize resources for children. The partnership with the government was further reinforced through high-level engagement on programmatic priority areas at the national, regional and global levels. For the first time the UNICEF Middle East and North Africa Management Team meeting was held in Algeria which showcased the strong partnership between the Government of Algeria and UNICEF. It gave UNICEF’s Regional Director and Representatives from the region the opportunity to dialogue with the government around certain issues discussed at the meeting such as the child rights agenda and disability inclusion. 


UNICEF also bolstered its engagement with the Government at regional platforms for Algeria to exchange good practices as well as to reaffirm its commitments to quality education in Africa with support at the Continental Conference on Education in Mauritania, the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange in Rwanda, the High-Level Meeting Learning to Earning in Tunisia and the Pan-African Youth Forum in Oran. Moreover, UNICEF engaged closely with the government at the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Colombia to reaffirm the government’s commitments to child protection. 


Furthermore, new partnership agreements were also signed in 2024 with Ministry of Finance (MoF) and High Youth Council (HYC) to enhance child centered public financing and meaningful participation of young people. The collaboration with the HYC supported Algeria’s participation in the global UNICEF Youth Foresight Fellowship Programme which brings young people together to develop foresight skills, participate in global trends analysis, and lead their own projects, shaping a future where youth voices are heard, respected and influential. This led to the participation of the Algeria’s Youth Foresight Fellow and support to the youth delegation of Algeria at the Summit of the Future in New York City which provided a participatory platform to discuss how to address some of the issues that affect them the most.


As a flagship initiative of the MENA region, aligning with the UNICEF Executive Director’s priority, the Community Health Systems policy and implementation landscape mapping was developed in 12 countries as a vital component of the Community Health Development Partnership (CHDP) which is a collaborative effort involving UNICEF and other global, regional, and national stakeholders dedicated to increasing access to equitable, high-quality essential health services through community-based primary health care. The findings from this process were presented at a virtual regional meeting with all stakeholders involved and will be used to strengthen community-based primary health care systems in Algeria and across the region. 


UNICEF’s collaboration also brokered a first South-South Cooperation (SSC) exchange between the Algerian and Chinese MoH on the area of health system and digital management. The online seminar brought together experts from both countries to share good practices. An invitation for a follow up study visit was extended to the Algerian government. UNICEF country offices in Algeria and China will continue collaborating to promote further SSC exchanges in the areas of digital health as well as early childhood development.


UN collaboration was further enhanced through strategic engagement within the framework of the UNSDCF and area of human development in close collaboration with the office of the residence coordinator and MoFA. UNICEF led the development of two joint structural projects on supporting the strengthening of inclusive social protection system with MoF, involving UNDP, ILO and UNFPA, and “from learning to earning agenda” with MoVT and MEN, involving UNDP, UNESCO, UNFPA and ILO. UNICEF also enhanced collaboration with WHO through the support to the government’s response to the polio outbreak and work to strengthen universal primary health care with focus on community health services. In addition, important efforts to strengthening the engagement on the UN disability strategy (UNDIS) were made through the join disability programme (UNPRP) between UNICEF, UNFPA, UNESCO and the Resident Coordinator Office in support to the Ministry of National Solidarity. A stocktaking was conducted on disability inclusion in public policies and programmes, capacity building of sectors including organizations of persons with disabilities (OPDs) as well as support in the preparations of the Global Disability Summit in 2025.


Partnerships in humanitarian action were strengthened through the first-year implementation of the Sahrawi Refugee Response Plan (SRRP) 2024-2025, enhancing coordination, efficiency, and accountability among 28 partner agencies in the camps. Throughout the year two joint donor missions were conducted, four meetings with the Sahrawi Refugee Partnership Platform were organized with the host Government, Sahrawi authorities and donors on key strategic areas such as food security and nutrition, vaccination programme and sports for protection; coordination mechanisms and efforts to stretched resource mobilization and partnerships were enhanced. The advocacy with partners led to the establishment of a partnership agreement with the Algerian International Cooperation Agency (AICA), securing in-kind lifesaving vaccines and boosting public health efforts. Recognizing the protracted refugee crisis and underfunding, UNICEF and UN Agencies began exploring private sector resource mobilization, with plans to expand this approach in 2025.


The Country Office strengthened strategic partnerships and resource mobilization for key programmatic priorities and the humanitarian response in Sahrawi refugee camps through continuous dialogue with traditional partners and UNICEF National Committees engaging with the private sector. Despite challenges in mobilizing resources in an upper middle-income country and protracted humanitarian context, new partnerships were formed, including with the European Union and AICA. In 2025, the Country Office will further expand engagement with UNICEF National Committees and private sector stakeholders to diversify funding sources.
