Successful models, such as the back-to-learning initiative and its associated dashboard, have demonstrated scalability and now form the basis for a nationwide programme set to continue for the next five years with Government funding. Other programmes, like UPSHIFT and multi-purpose youth hubs, have also shown promise. However, these require further strategic scaling and enhanced capacity-building efforts to sustain their long-term impact.
 
The institutionalisation of juvenile justice capacity-building mechanisms within the Ministry of Justice is a critical lesson. Strengthening Government ownership, including the development of training curricula and the establishment of minimum standards ensures that juvenile justice frameworks are well-embedded within national systems and can operate independently over time.
 
The effectiveness of youth networks has proven essential in fostering meaningful outcomes, including meaningful youth participation at COP29. These platforms underscore the importance of inclusive decision-making and the need for youth to play an active role in shaping policies and initiatives that directly affect them. Their engagement contributes to more relevant programmes and more empowered communities and also drives innovation and the development of green skills, equipping young people to lead sustainable solutions for the future.
.
 
Forward Outlook
In 2025, UNICEF intends to commence a new country programme aligned to Iraq’s National Development Plan through the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Based on extensive consultation and analysis of the evidence, the following areas will be prioritized in the new programme:
1. Early childhood development and care;
2. Learning, skills for life and work for children who are not in school;
3. Child protection case management;
4. Climate change, with a focus on water scarcity, renewable energy for child and family services, and youth as agents of change;
5. Social protection, with a deliberate focus on working with and for adolescent girls.
 
To accelerate results in these priority areas, three key strategic shifts have been identified as part of the new programme:
 
1. To progress through the humanitarian-development-peace nexus towards development, focusing on systems strengthening;
2. To support evidence-based decision-making, model area-based approaches, and support policies and implementation for nation-wide scale-up of successful approaches;
3. To expand partnerships for advocacy and programme implementation, exploring opportunities with Iraqi private and public institutions, civil society organizations (CSOs), academia and children and young people, especially the most vulnerable.

Jordan's population is approximately 11.7 million, with a notably young demographic structure. Children under 18 years represent 40 per cent of the population, while young people aged 15-24 account for 20 per cent. Jordan ranks second globally in terms of refugees per capita, with non-Jordanians making up at least one-third of the population[1]. Approximately 1.3 million Syrians, over 611,000 of whom are registered with UNHCR[2], more than 2.4[3] million Palestinians registered with UNRWA (most holding Jordanian citizenship), and over one million individuals of other nationalities comprise the non-Jordanians. 
Jordan remains stable despite the volatile regional geopolitical situation. Its leadership engages in diplomatic efforts to maintain stability and mitigate violence, which underscores the country’s critical regional role. Jordan continues to provide substantial humanitarian aid to people affected by the conflict in Gaza. With the consolidation of a transitional government in Syria at the end of 2024, Jordanian leadership has stated its support for a peaceful, inclusive political transition supported by the UN and Arab League and for respecting the rights of Syrian refugees on decisions to return to their country.  
Economically, Jordan has shown resilience amid regional challenges. In 2024, the GDP growth rate was 2.4 per cent[4]. However, significant fiscal challenges persist, with a high debt-to-GDP ratio of 113 per cent[5], limiting the government’s ability to further invest in essential services and infrastructure. Unemployment remains a pressing issue, standing at 21.5 per cent, with rates higher for women (33.3 per cent)[6] and young people (36.6 per cent)[7]. The proportion of youth (18-24 years) not in employment, education, or training (NEET) stands at 41.1 per cent, with rates significantly higher for women, 47 per cent for Jordanian women and over 80 per cent for Syrian women[8]. Despite higher rates of female secondary and tertiary graduation, and due to several structural and social barriers, female labor force participation remains one of the lowest globally, at just 14.8 per cent.[9]
Water scarcity is a critical issue, with renewable water resources estimated at just 61 m³ per person annually—far below the threshold of 500 m³[10]. Over half the population receives water once a week or less, and non-revenue water loss is estimated at 50 per cent[11]. According to UNICEF/WHO data[12], while 98 per cent of the population has access to water services, only 86 per cent have safely managed drinking water, and 82 per cent have access to safely managed sanitation. Climate change threatens to exacerbate these vulnerabilities by reducing water availability and increasing the variability of weather events. [13]
In the absence of updated national data, the national poverty rate remains at 15.7 per cent[14] but expected to have significantly increased. UNHCR and World Bank data reveal that 67.8 per cent[15] of refugees lived below the poverty line in 2023. Despite having one of the lowest multidimensional poverty rates among middle-income countries in the region, 14 per cent of children in Jordan experience deprivation in at least two dimensions of well-being[16]. Social protection programs such as the Unified Cash Transfer Program and economic empowerment initiatives have strengthened the social safety net[17]. Key legislative advancements, including the Social Development Law No. 4 of 2024 and the Child Rights Law No. 17 of 2022, have enhanced the legal framework, professionalized the social workforce, and supported the role of community-based organizations. Despite these advancements, Jordan remains vulnerable to economic, environmental, and external shocks.
Improvements in child survival indicators are evident, with under-five mortality declining from 19 to 15 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2018 and 2023[18]. Childhood vaccination coverage has also improved, with the proportion of zero-dose children dropping from seven per cent in 2017-2018 to one per cent in 2023[19]. However, challenges persist in addressing malnutrition, obesity, and inadequate feeding practices. According to the results of the 2023 Jordan Population and Family Health Survey (JPFHS/DHS), stunting among children under five increased slightly from 7.4 percent in 2018 to 8.3 per cent among the poorest households[20]. Overweight prevalence in the same age group increased from seven per cent to 8.8 per cent, while exclusive breastfeeding declined from 26 per cent to 24 per cent[21]. 
Three-quarters of children aged 1-14 experienced violent discipline, with 72 per cent subjected to psychological aggression and 53 per cent to physical punishment[22]. Overall, 75 per cent of children aged 1–14 experienced at least one form of violent discipline, compared to 81 per cent in the 2017–18 DHS. While this represents a six per cent reduction in the use of violent discipline over the period, violence against children remains a critical concern in the country. In schools, 57 per cent of boys and 64 per cent of girls reported verbal violence, while physical violence affected 10 per cent of boys and seven per cent of girls[23]. Domestic violence cases, as reported by the Family Protection and Juvenile Department in 2023, revealed that 82 per cent of incidents involved children witnessing the violence.[24]The percentage of child marriages compared to total marriages has declined but still remains at 8.5 per cent[25].
The Government of Jordan’s efforts toward universal pre-primary education have yielded promising results, with the KG2 enrolment rate increasing from 66 per cent in 2021/2022 to 68 per cent in 2023[26]. The JPFHS/DHS report also highlighted that 84.1 per cent of children aged 2-5 years were developmentally on track[27]. 
While primary education achieved full enrolment with gender parity, challenges persisted at the secondary level.  Adolescents faced risks of dropping out due to socio-economic pressures, early marriage, or child labor. An Out of School Children Study (2020) found that 112,016 children aged six to 15 were out of school, including over 50,640 Syrian children[28]. UNICEF, UNESCO and MOE are updating this data based on the latest DHS (2023). Refugee status, poverty, barriers due to being either male or female, and disabilities remain key barriers to accessing and completing basic education. Many children are in school but not learning. An estimated 62 per cent of ten-year-olds in Jordan cannot read a simple story[29]. The PISA 2022 average results showed that the knowledge and skills of 15-year-olds in mathematics, reading and science declined compared to 2018[30].
Young people[31] in Jordan face structural and social barriers in their transition to adulthood, which has implications for economic growth and development. High unemployment among young people, exacerbated by legal restrictions for refugees, often confines young Syrians to informal sectors. On average, it takes five years for young people to secure employment due to limited job creation[32].
Empowerment of youth and ensuring they are equipped for future jobs is amongst the key national priorities as reflected in the Economic Modernization Vision[33] which will continue to guide the work of the Government, focusing on economic growth and improving the quality of life for all citizens. Additionally, it also has a strong emphasis on social protection and enhancing the country's resilience in the face of economic and social shocks. UNICEF’s programmes are well aligned with these priorities.

Goal Area 1: Every Child survives and thrives
According to the 2024 immunization administrative data, there was a notable improvement at the national level, with coverage for all antigens reaching 98 per cent compared to 92 per cent in 2023[1]. All 14 (100 per cent) Health Directorates achieved 90 per cent and above coverage in 2024, a significant increase from eight out of 14 (57 per cent) in 2023. This improvement in coverage, through mobile teams supported by UNICEF, was attributed to the focused application of the IRMMA framework (Identify – Reach – Monitor – Measure – Advocate) and micro-planning, which effectively addressed inequities and ensured no child was left behind. 
Similarly, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MOH), UNICEF implemented critical immunization efforts to protect vulnerable populations. Booster vaccine doses against oral polio virus (OPV), Tetanus, and Diphtheria (Td) were provided for 5,514 children (52 per cent female) in grades one and ten across Syrian refugee camps' schools (Za’atari and Azraq). 
To improve educational inclusivity for children with disabilities in Syrian refugee camps, UNICEF screened 1,185 children (48 per cent female) for assistive device needs. Over 700 students received support, including 585 eyeglasses, 92 hearing, and 41 mobility aids such as crutches and wheelchairs. These interventions addressed barriers to education, enhancing access and participation of vulnerable children.
UNICEF continued to tackle the complex burden of malnutrition in refugee camps by prioritizing Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) interventions. Key achievements included the delivery of 1,482 IYCF counseling sessions to caregivers and education sessions reaching 3,255 mothers with messages promoting exclusive breastfeeding and complementary feeding practices.   Additionally, 40,331 children (51 per cent girls) and 5,447 pregnant/lactating women were screened for malnutrition in 2024.  34 SAM and 138 MAM cases were identified and admitted for treatment achieving a 98 per cent cure rate. 
Goal Area 2: Every child learns
The Ministry of Education (MOE) in Jordan, supported by UNICEF, has made significant progress in transforming the education system by enhancing teaching and learning, co-designing, and implementing learning assessments, and utilizing data and evidence for planning. Key initiatives included co-designing math and reading assessments administered to over 28,000 students (51 per cent female). The results are being used to inform the MOE’s remedial gender responsive strategy and the design of the Schools Teaching for Learning Recovery (ST4LR) programme. 
An innovative Reading Recovery program targeted adolescents in refugee camps who were unable to read at a grade three level. In 2024, this program reached over 3,700 students (49 per cent female) from grade five to eight in 34 refugee camp schools and 221 adolescents and youth aged 12 to 20 (57 per cent female) in 26 non-formal education centres. Of these, 68 per cent (51 per cent female) made significant progress, scoring 70 per cent or more after completing 32 lessons. UNICEF established 73 classroom libraries in 25 camp schools, providing over 8,900 books. Syrian volunteers in partnership with Jordanian teachers developed the early grade reading skills of all 3,319 children (50 per cent female) attending KG2 centres in the refugee camps. Additionally, 840 parents (72 per cent female) attended parenting sessions to develop skills to support their children’s reading. 
Over 20,000 students from grade two to nine attended accelerated Math and Arabic sessions in 114 Makani Centres. Math assessment results from this UNICEF designed informal education program, which is aligned to the learning outcomes in the national curriculum, showed that the percentage of low performing students had significantly decreased from 68 per cent in 2023 to three per cent in 2024.  Regular quality assurance through classroom observations informed program adaptations, including facilitator training and curriculum revision.  
Teacher of the Future (TOF) is a professional development course aimed at developing skills in effective teaching and learning.  In 2024, 164 (51 per cent female) teachers and 76 supervisors (49 per cent female) from 11 Directorates completed the 80 hour-long MOE accredited course, enhancing their competencies in delivering effective and engaging learning experience to students. Teachers developed their reflective practice through a professional development journal and engaging in an online community of practice. Additionally, UNICEF provided a coaching and mentoring support to 170 school leaders and teachers (55 per cent female), focusing on strategies to improve attendance and inclusion in refugee camps. 
UNICEF advocated with the Government of Jordan, as co-chair of the Education Sector Working Group, for refugee inclusion in the national education system, with exemptions from fees and documentation grants for a further year. UNICEF also acted as joint secretariat with the MOE for the preparation of the 2024 Jordan Response Plan chapter on education. 
In refugee camps, UNICEF supported 2,043 Syrian volunteers (43 per cent female) as well as school operation costs, enabling access to education for over 36,203 Syrian refugee children and adolescents (51 per cent female). UNICEF’s support included classroom assistance, outreach, and administration, as well as maintenance, cleaning services, and security. Transportation was provided to 323 school children with disabilities in Azraq Camp (45 per cent female) and 153 children (53 per cent female) in Garden camp. In the host community, 204 Syrian volunteers (72 per cent female) supported school principals in the MOE double shift schools with tasks including monitoring attendance and assisting students with disabilities. 
UNICEF supported the Directorates of Education (DoE) to develop a class formation plan for schools in refugee camps. Based on this, 16 new classrooms were installed in Za’atari Camp, reducing overcrowding and movement between schools. UNICEF worked with all school principals in Za’atari and Azraq Camps to improve student attendance through attendance awards, recognizing 12,679 students (51 per cent female). Outreach efforts by 33 Syrian Assistant Teachers (SATs) resulted in 273 adolescents (54 per cent female) joining non-formal education.
Adolescents and Youth Development 
In 2024, UNICEF supported 87,808 adolescents and youth in Jordan (60 per cent female, 28 per cent refugees, two per cent persons with disabilities) through targeted interventions in volunteerism, skills development, employment, entrepreneurship, career counseling, and mental health support. Volunteer engagement rose from seven per cent in 2014 to 16 per cent in 2024, through the Nahno platform, benefiting 37,426 young people (59 per cent female) through experiential learning and civic engagement. 
UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MODEE) and community-based organizations to provide digital skills training for 2,031 participants (65 per cent female, 28 per cent refugees, three per cent persons with disabilities). This training led to jobs in graphic design, digital marketing, and content creation for 42 youth (80 per cent female, 11 per cent refugees). Additionally, technical and vocational training enabled 166 out of 208 youth (52 per cent female, 43 per cent refugees, two per cent persons with disabilities; 80 per cent employment rate) to secure jobs in fields such as mobile maintenance, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning, and fashion design.
In partnership with the International Labour Organization (ILO), UNICEF introduced the Job Search Clubs (JSC) methodology across Ministry of Youth (MOY) centers, providing career guidance and mentorship to 400 young people (76 per cent female, 10 per cent refugees, one per cent persons with disabilities) while addressing cultural and systemic barriers to gender equality. This initiative resulted in 100 participants securing formal employment or paid internships.
UNICEF's support in 2024 empowered youth to drive positive change and promote sustainable livelihoods. Twelve youth-led community initiatives were launched by trained Youth Climate Leaders and Climate Champions, engaging 3,000 people across Jordan in waste management, green space expansion, and sustainability efforts. UNICEF also supported the establishment of 170 Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) and Home-Based Businesses (HBBs), with a focus on young women limited by mobility restrictions due to conservative gender norms. These enterprises became a critical source of employment, engaging 1,231 young people (70 per cent females, 16 per cent refugees, one per cent persons with disabilities). This initiative not only fostered entrepreneurship and income generation, but also contributed to reducing economic disparities, increasing household economic security, promoting gender equality, and facilitating the transition of young people from learning to earning. UNICEF also collaborated with MOY, MoDEE, and VTC to deliver gender-responsive skills programs, ensuring at least 50 per cent female participation, while supporting outreach, scholarships, and staff training to influence policies and increase TVET uptake in Jordan.

UNICEF’s policy efforts for adolescents and youth targeted several key areas addressing young people’s learning, skilling, and transition to decent work. Under the Ministry of Planning and International Cooperation (MOPIC) and in collaboration with five different concerned Ministries and UN agencies, UNICEF spearheaded Jordan's participation in the High-Level Meeting in Tunisia. UNICEF supported the drafting the 2024 National Voluntary Commitments related to youth learning, skilling, and transitions to decent work, with a focus on challenges faced by girls and young women and the establishing of a national task force to streamline coordination among government entities, UN agencies, and young people. Additionally, UNICEF advanced youth engagement in climate action through Sawn[2], the Local Conference of Youth (LCOY), and participation of youth at COP29. A total of 61,950 adolescents and youth (61 per cent female, 23 per cent refugees, three per cent persons with disabilities) engaged in climate actions or volunteering initiatives, focusing on hands-on learning that cultivated leadership and community engagement. LCOY gathered 200 young advocates to propose climate solutions and six youth leaders from the 200 were given credentials to participate as members of the COP29 official national delegation.  
UNICEF also progressed on the operationalization of the Children, Youth, and Climate Action Declaration (presented at COP25)[3], promoting adolescents and youth involvement in climate adaptation and mitigation with the Ministry of Environment (MoEN) and MOY. UNICEF supported the High-Level Global Forum on Youth, Peace, and Security, launching the Arab Strategy on Youth, Peace, and Security 2023–2028 to promote youth-led peace and security initiatives. In 2024, the UPSHIFT social innovation initiative, implemented by UNICEF with the Jordan River Foundation and MOY, transitioned to MOY, equipping 12 incubation centres with harmonized visual identities, and integrating standardized procedures into the Ministry’s operational plans.
UNICEF supported MOY and the Crown Prince Foundation in recognizing significant contributions of volunteering to Jordan’s national development through Al Hussein bin Abdullah II Award for Voluntary Service.
After capacity-building, the institutionalization of Maharati programme is successfully completed and MOY is leading the programme, with UNICEF providing technical assistance and quality assurance for efficient implementation, following recent evaluation recommendations.
Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
The   Government of Jordan, in collaboration with UNICEF and UNFPA, drafted a costed, multi-sectoral and gender-responsive National Action Plan (NAP 2025-2030) to address child protection, gender-based violence, and family violence. This plan aims to improve legislative and policy framework, enhance coordination across sectors, emphasize enforcement mechanisms, ensure adequate resource allocation for child protection, strengthen the social service workforce, and empower children, parents, and communities.
The Ministry of Social Development (MOSD), with UNICEF's support, has recognized the professionalization of social work as vital to the social service. The successful mapping of the social service workforce system in Jordan has led to the design of an In-Service Accredited Training Programme to augment a new pre-service and in-service training, and the development of outlines for a five-year roadmap to strengthen the existing social service workforce capacity. 
Jordan’s Ministry of Education (MOE) incorporated the Safe to Learn programme[4] into all 3,780 schools, including those in Syrian refugee camps. In 2024, this program has empowered over 2,879 educators (52 per cent female) with the skills to identify, prevent, and refer cases of physical violence against children, fostering accountability among educational professionals. 
The National Council for Family Affairs (NCFA), with UNICEF’s support, implemented the Tracking System for Family Violence (TSFV)[5] in two locations in the country, benefiting over 6,800 vulnerable children and women. This system is now considered as a good practice by the NCFA in creating a multi-sectoral approach to address violence against children in the family setting. In 2024, UNICEF supported MOSD to increase the Early Detection and Early Intervention Units (EDEI) for children with disabilities from 15 to 19, benefiting over 615 children aged 0-6. 
Additionally, 65 children deprived of parental care have benefited from the MOSD foster care programme, with the total number of children in foster care reaching 695 by the end of 2024.
In November 2024, UNICEF supported the participation of the official Government delegation to the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Bogota. The Government of Jordan pledged to establish multi-sectoral collaboration mechanisms, institutionalize parenting programs, strengthen the social service workforce, scale up a digital case management system, and introduce child-friendly procedures in the justice and social sectors. UNICEF supported the development of these pledges in alignment with the recent recommendations of the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), setting a framework for future child protection efforts in Jordan.
In 2024, UNICEF collaborated with the MOSD, MOH, and MOE, as well as NGO partners to strengthen the capacity of 2,046 child protection personnel (42 per cent female) on different aspects of child protection. As a result, 9,027 children have benefitted from case management services out of which 1,869 are Syrian refugee children (46 per cent girls).  The case management services addressed mostly gender-based violence, emotional distress, child labour, and child marriage, contributing to safer environments for the most vulnerable children of Jordan. 
Goal Area 4: Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
In 2024, UNICEF co-lead the Humanitarian WASH Sector Working Group in Jordan, working closely with the Ministry of Water and Irrigation (MWI). UNICEF supported the MWI in monitoring progress toward SDG 6 through a situational analysis report and launched interactive water and sanitation vulnerability maps for better planning. Additional achievements included institutionalizing Climate Resilient Water and Sanitation Safety Planning (CR-WSSP) with key assessments and capacity-building initiatives, as well as conducting a WASH and Climate Social Behavior Change (SBC) Study to address behavioral barriers in refugee camps and host communities. 
UNICEF strengthened WASH and Infection Prevention Control (IPC) in healthcare facilities by supporting the MOH in developing standards, action plans, and integrating WASH data into national health systems. Collaboration with the MOE (Gender Directorate), UNICEF Headquarters (WASH and Gender sections), Water Aid, and academic institutions advanced a Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHH) monitoring assessment, laying the groundwork for coordinated efforts to improve WASH, adolescent health, and gender equality outcomes.
Despite declining groundwater resources, particularly in Za’atari, UNICEF ensured nearly 130,000 people living in Syrian refugee camps (Za’atari, Azraq and Garden) and the Rukban settlement had access to safe water. Additionally, over 121,000 people in Syrian refugee camps accessed safely managed wastewater and sanitation services. These services were complemented with community mobilization and messages on good hygiene practices, water conservation and community ownership, reaching more than 32,000 individuals in Za’atari and Garden camps.
UNICEF provided cash assistance to over 13,000 vulnerable people in 50 remote and marginalized Informal Tented Settlements (ITSs) to improve access to hygiene items and safe water. Among them, 2,626 individuals received additional cash assistance to install water storage tanks and sanitation systems. In southern Jordan, nearly 9,000 residents of Athroh and Mureigha (Ma’an Governorate) benefited from improved access to safe water through infrastructural upgrades, in collaboration with the Aqaba Water Company (AWC).  Community Water Committees were established to address local water needs in these two communities.
Additionally, over 7,200 children and adolescents in southern governorates participated in Climate Action Clubs to enhance climate awareness. In northern governorates, 20,000 students increased their awareness and knowledge of water scarcity and conservation, supported by installation of greywater treatment and reuse systems in schools and mosques.  
Goal Area 5: Every child has an equitable chance in life 
In 2024, Jordan’s social protection sector achieved significant milestones, particularly with the approval of the Social Development Law in March, the publication of the Social Worker Professionalization bylaws, and the initiation of the process to update the National Social Protection Strategy (NSPS). The Government prioritized updating the NSPS to strengthen policies for vulnerable populations, enhancing the system’s shock responsiveness, and improving social protection spending. UNICEF supported the coordination and monitoring of the current NSPS (2019-2025) and contributed to the preparation of updated strategy for 2025-2033 and its alignment with the national modernization vision.
Progress on the NSPS update was marked by completion of its first draft, after stakeholder consultations supported by UNICEF. Key contributions included the production of analytical papers, a progress monitoring report assessing the implementation of the current strategy, a reflection report analyzing strategic reforms in the sector since 2022, a report diagnosing the system’s ability to respond to shocks and a study on integrating child protection and social protection interventions. Additionally, UNICEF supported the production of a public expenditure review providing a comprehensive calculation of Jordan’s social protection spending, laying a robust evidence-based foundation for the updated strategy. 
A broader national consultation process of the draft NSPS is planned for early 2025, with the final strategy expected by Spring 2025.
In 2024, UNICEF, in collaboration with the World Bank and the World Food Programme, continued its support to the National Aid Fund (NAF) in consolidating national cash transfer programs into the Unified Cash Transfer (UCT) Programme, benefiting 235,933 vulnerable households, including 448,476 children. Key achievements in the cooperation with NAF included enhanced targeting mechanisms for the UCT and other social assistance programmes, gender-focused improvements to the Management Information System, the introduction of a household emergency module, and initial steps to transition the National Unified Registry into the Jordan Social Registry. A major milestone was the establishment of a “Cash Plus Unit” within NAF to institutionalize a model linking cash assistance with social services, building on the Takaful-Plus pilot (linking cash assistance with Makani services).
The 2023 Jordan Population and Family Health Survey (JPFHS), conducted by Jordan’s Department of Statistics with support from USAID, UNICEF, UNFPA, WFP, and WHO, launched the full results on critical socio-economic and demographic data, disaggregated by age, gender, location, wealth, and nationality, including refugee status. These findings will shape national policies, including the NSPS update and will inform the 2025 Sustainable Development Goals National Voluntary Review. The data also supported a gender correlation analysis focusing on empowerment and adolescent health themes, such as diet and pregnancy, to guide program implementation and policy advocacy in 2025.
The Makani programme, in 2024, reached over 106,000 vulnerable children (62 per cent female; two per cent persons with disabilities), adolescents, and caregivers across 114 centers in host communities, refugee camps, and informal tented settlements. The programme provided integrated services such as learning support, skills development, community-based child protection, and positive parenting sessions. Assessments showed significant improvements in children’s performance in Arabic and mathematics, as well as enhanced life and digital skills among adolescents, and young people’s understanding of gender stereotypes and gender-based norms. For example, among children attending the Makani’s accelerated learning programme, the percent of those in the highest-scoring group for Arabic increased from six per cent in the pre-test to 58 per cent after the training cycle. For mathematics, this figure increased from four per cent to 61 per cent.
UNICEF advanced efforts to institutionalize Makani within Jordan’s national social protection system. The German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development have committed financial support to integrate Makani into the government’s social protection framework starting in mid-2025. UNICEF supported this process through extensive documentation and analytical work.
Despite funding challenges, UNICEF’s child-cash assistance programme, Hajati, supported 3,284 vulnerable households, including 6,011 children (50 per cent female, nine per cent persons with disabilities), through monthly cash transfers. Due to reduced resources, coverage was adjusted mid-year, prioritizing the most vulnerable. From May onwards, 897 households, including 1,600 children, continued receiving assistance, with a focus on female-headed households and children with disabilities.
