Health & Nutrition
UNICEF continued its strong collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and key stakeholders to improve the accessibility of health and nutrition services for all individuals, including migrants and refugees (including those who recently arrived from Sudan). This was achieved through a system-strengthening approach aimed at addressing gaps in the health system, which faced several challenges across various health system components. These challenges included governance issues due to the existence of two sets of governing authorities, supply chain constraints, limited human resource capacities, difficulties in distribution, inadequate primary health care financing, and weaknesses in the health information system.
To address these challenges, UNICEF strategically deployed its technical and financial resources, with guidance from the regional office, in partnership with the Ministry of Health and organizations like the World Health Organization (WHO). As a result, UNICEF supported the operationalization of 59 health facilities in the Primary Health Care sector, providing a comprehensive essential package of health services and improving access to approximately 2 million people.
In collaboration with the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), UNICEF also played a key role in maintaining the effective operation of 712 vaccination centers and 94 national, regional, and municipal vaccine stores. This was achieved through capacity-building activities, completing the Effective Vaccine Management Assessment, and implementing a vaccine tracking system and a vaccine equipment inventory and gap analysis tool. These efforts ensured the availability and accessibility of high-quality immunization services, reaching 460,000 children under 2 years of age with routine immunization and 708,700 children under 6 years of age with Polio and Measles-Rubella supplementary immunization activities.
Additionally, UNICEF, in partnership with the Primary Health Care Institute (PHCI), scaled up nutrition programs by enhancing healthcare workers’ skills in nutritional screening, therapeutic interventions, preventive services, and caregiver education on optimal Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) practices. This initiative benefited approximately 500,000 children and their caregivers.
The 2024-2025 emergency nutrition sector response plan, was finalized with UNICEF technical support and in coordination with the Ministry of Health, PHCI, WHO, WFP,  and various Government emergency departments and units, and it plays a critical role in guiding and steering the refugee response efforts. This comprehensive plan is designed to address the nutritional needs  of approximately 446,000 people, including 375,000 refugees, 1,000 third-country nationals, and 70,000 affected host communities and internally displaced persons (IDPs) through 2025. It integrates humanitarian actions with development goals, strengthens local capacity, enhances public health systems, and builds resilience. 
Furthermore, UNICEF, in coordination with WHO and PHCI, supported the implementation of the Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) program, expanding it to 54 new health facilities and benefiting 84,600 children.
UNICEF also co-led the national Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) working group, utilizing the NCDC-run health awareness radio channel (Sahiya) to disseminate health promotion messages across the country, reaching over 2.5 million people.
Education
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in enhancing access to quality, inclusive education for children, adolescents, and youth in Libya, achieving key results across several critical areas.
At the upstream level, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education (MoE) to strengthen the education system through five main pillars: Education Management Information System (EMIS) implementation, teacher professional development, integration of life skills into the curriculum, digital learning, and inclusive education. A major achievement was the launch of the EMIS. With UNICEF’s technical support, the OpenEMIS system was piloted in 200 schools, with data entry completed by 69 schools. This led to significant system updates, including a security upgrade, enabling progress towards the Annual School Census, which will inform future policy and decisions. This work was undertaken in parallel with targeted training for MoE staff on the administration and maintenance of the system. 
In teacher development, UNICEF successfully launched the "21st Century Teacher" pedagogy program. Developed in partnership with the MoE, this 36-hour program focused on child-centered teaching and active learning. A total of 192 Core and Master Trainers were trained, who in turn trained 3,000 teachers across Libya. This program will continue to scale in 2025. In addition, 614 teachers were trained on inclusive education, helping to ensure that all children, including those with disabilities, have access to quality learning.
UNICEF also made significant progress in integrating life skills into the curriculum. The life skills program was officially launched in June 2024, and an orientation booklet for stakeholders was produced and published. Furthermore, a life skills curriculum for grade 7 was developed as a model for other grades, with UNICEF continuing to support the MoE in finalizing programs for the remaining grades.
For digital learning, UNICEF launched the Learning Passport in January 2024, providing an online learning platform aligned with the national curriculum. Although there were challenges in securing Ministry endorsement of content, UNICEF worked closely with the MoE and an EdTech company from private the sector to develop and refine the platform, improving access to education for children, especially in crisis contexts.
At the downstream level, UNICEF directly facilitated access to education for 45,118 children (18047 boys and 27071 girls), adolescents, and youth through Baity centers and five youth centers. These centers provided foundational learning, literacy, numeracy, catch-up classes, as well as life skills training to 26,503 children (13,253 girls, 13,250 boys). In 2024 UNICEF expanded its life skills programs to include a package for children aged 6-9 and extension modules on entrepreneurship, well-being, and peace-building, communication, and pathways to employment.
In response to the floods in eastern Libya, UNICEF supported recovery by providing 25 prefabricated classrooms to alleviate overcrowding, as well as 1,580 student desks and 200 whiteboards. Additionally, 1,000 school bags were distributed to children displaced by the floods. The rehabilitation of schools in the east and south continued.
UNICEF continued to lead the humanitarian education sector and is coordinating the response to the Sudanese refugee crisis. In 2024, UNICEF provided material support to Sudanese schools in Tripoli and Misrata, benefiting 1,205 refugee children. Further support, including prefabricated classrooms and teacher training, will continue into 2025.
Child Protection
In 2024, UNICEF made significant progress in strengthening the Government of Libya’s capacity to plan, coordinate, and manage child protection systems, leading to key improvements in service delivery, legal frameworks, and community engagement for the protection of children.
UNICEF supported the establishment of the first high-level National Ministerial Level Child Protection Working Group, designed to coordinate service provision, mobilize resources, and align prevention and response efforts for vulnerable children. The group’s terms of reference were drafted and shared with MOSA, with plans to ensure quarterly coordination and clarity on child protection initiatives. UNICEF also co-chaired the National Child Protection Working Group (CPWG), facilitating monthly meetings with national and international stakeholders. This forum ensured that service maps, referral pathways, and emergency child protection needs were addressed while also offering ongoing capacity-building opportunities.
A significant milestone in 2024 was the capacity-building of 2,217 frontline workers, including social workers, health staff, and volunteers from local civil society organizations (CSOs). These training sessions, held across Libya (East, South, and West), focused on core child protection concepts, case management, and mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS). Workshops also included key participants from ministry training departments to promote the institutionalization of knowledge, ensuring long-term sustainability.
UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Higher Committee for Childhood (HCC) in drafting a comprehensive child rights law, aimed at domesticating the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC). Despite the dissolution of the HCC in October 2024 and its transition to MOSA, UNICEF continued to advocate for the prioritization of a child rights law with the Minister of Social Affairs.
Further strengthening of child protection systems included the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for Family and Child Protection Units (FCPUs), which were shared with the Ministry of Interior (MOI) for feedback. These SOPs, designed to ensure harmonized structures and competencies for child protection in contact with the law, will be validated in early 2025. UNICEF also rolled out "Protecting Children in Conflict with the Law" training for MOI staff, focusing on international best practices, alternatives to detention, and MHPSS.
To enhance the protective environment for children affected by conflict, UNICEF organized workshops with the Ministry of Defense and other stakeholders, including the House of Representatives. These workshops-built awareness on grave violations against children and reinforced Libya’s commitment to handover children from military to child protection actors. A protocol for the handover of children from armed forces to MOSA is under development and expected to be validated in 2025. Revisions to increase the minimum age of recruitment into armed forces from 17 to 18 years were also finalized and are awaiting approval.
At the community level, UNICEF engaged 31,423 individuals (including 5,017 boys and 6,788 girls) in awareness-raising sessions addressing harmful social and gender norms. In response to the Sudanese refugee crisis, these efforts were scaled up in Kufra to support women and children who may have been exposed to violence. UNICEF also reached 9,076 parents and caregivers with positive parenting programs to reduce violence against children.
In terms of services, UNICEF continued to expand community-based, multi-sectoral child protection programming for both Libyan and non-Libyan children, including migrants and refugees. Through Baity centers and mobile response teams, UNICEF provided mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) to 103,197 individuals (including 48,442 boys and 44,812 girls). Additionally, 4,252 individuals received individual case management. These services, delivered through UNICEF-supported Baity centers, were essential in responding to the Sudanese conflict and ensuring that vulnerable children received comprehensive child protection support.
Efforts to enhance sustainability in child protection programming included the handover of Baity centers and child-friendly spaces in southern municipalities to Government ownership. This transition ensured that government and partners would share timetables for the continued delivery of child protection services.
WASH
 In 2024, UNICEF made transformative strides in strengthening climate resilience within Libya’s WASH sector, focusing on improving water governance, climate adaptation, and ensuring the inclusion of children’s rights in national climate policies. These efforts combined upstream system strengthening with lifesaving service delivery to address immediate needs and build long-term sustainability. UNICEF collaborated closely with the Ministry of Water Resources (MoWR) and the Ministry of Environment (MoEnv) to integrate climate change considerations into WASH planning and operations. With support from the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI), UNICEF delivered training programs on water governance and climate policy, equipping government officials and water sector actors with the knowledge and tools to manage water resources more effectively in the face of climate challenges. Geographic Information Systems (GIS) training further enabled stakeholders to map flood-prone areas, improving planning for water and sanitation services. These capacity-building initiatives laid the groundwork for more resilient and inclusive WASH systems.
UNICEF played a pivotal advocacy role, ensuring children’s needs were prioritized in key national policies, including the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), the National Adaptation Plan (NAP), and the National Water Strategy (NWS). By embedding child-sensitive considerations into these frameworks, UNICEF supported sustainable access to safe water, sanitation, and a healthy environment for Libya’s most vulnerable populations. To advance renewable energy solutions, UNICEF led studies on the solarization of desalination plants, exploring the feasibility of using solar power to operate water treatment systems. This initiative represents a vital step toward scaling up the use of renewable energy in water management, reducing reliance on fossil fuels, and enhancing climate resilience across Libya’s WASH sector.
UNICEF co-led the Water Sector Working Group (WSWG) alongside the African Development Bank (AfDB), creating a coordinated platform for government ministries, international organizations, and other stakeholders to address water shortages and build climate-resilient WASH systems. This collaboration was instrumental in aligning policies and resources to enhance sector efficiency. In January 2024, UNICEF also organized a COP28 debriefing session, facilitating discussions between youth representatives, government officials, and stakeholders on advancing climate action, particularly in the WASH sector. This effort culminated in Libya’s first Youth Climate Summit, where over  150 young advocates (94 males and 56 females including 8 of them with disability) presented innovative solutions for sustainable water management and climate resilience. 
UNICEF’s service delivery achievements in flood-affected areas were equally impactful. The organization installed 33 solar-powered water systems, providing safe drinking water to over 170,000 people (26,010 girls, 24,990 boys, 60,690 women, 58310 men).
These systems served as sustainable solutions in regions heavily impacted by floods. UNICEF supported the recovery of Derna’s water infrastructure by providing booster pumps, submersible pumps, and control panels, which restored functionality to boreholes and pumping stations, benefiting 35,000 people. To address groundwater contamination caused by flooding, UNICEF partnered with the General Company of Water and Wastewater (GCWW) to implement 49 water disinfection systems in Albayda, Shahat, Sousa, and Derna. These systems treated municipal water supplies, ensuring safe drinking water for approximately 100,000 people. Additionally, two reverse osmosis desalination plants were constructed in Almikhily and Elezziat, producing 90,000 liters of safe water per hour and benefiting 15,000 people.
Hygiene promotion and sanitation improvements remained central to UNICEF’s interventions. The "Safe Water: Healthy Lives" campaign reached 84,244 people through community sessions, school engagements, and outreach activities that promoted better hygiene practices. UNICEF rehabilitated three major sewage lines in Derna and Albayda, benefiting 36,000 people by preventing sewage flooding and improving sanitation infrastructure.
UNICEF distributed 29,200 hygiene kits across flood-affected areas, detention centers, and refugee camps, benefiting 81,297 people, including 30,000 Sudanese refugees in Kufra. Water trucking operations in refugee and migrant camps, such as those at Alassa border facilities, ensured access to clean water, delivering 1,030,000 liters to 3,000 refugees in Kufra and 120,000 liters weekly to 800 migrants at the border. By combining upstream advocacy and capacity building with targeted service delivery, UNICEF’s 2024 interventions in Libya’s WASH sector addressed critical gaps, built resilience, and ensured no one was left behind.
 Social Protection
UNICEF has made significant progress in advancing social protection in Libya, focusing on creating a child-sensitive and shock-responsive National Social Protection Strategy aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). UNICEF provided key technical support in the development of this strategy, ensuring it addresses the needs of vulnerable populations, especially children, during crises. The strategy, now including a dedicated section on shock-responsive social protection, was officially launched by the Prime Minister and is ready for national implementation.
In collaboration with the World Food Programme (WFP) and the World Bank, UNICEF assisted the Ministry of Social Affairs (MoSA) in developing a roadmap for a unified social registry. This initiative involved assessing existing data management systems, improving their interoperability, and revising vulnerability assessment criteria to reduce overlaps between social protection programs. The aim is to allocate resources efficiently, ensuring that support reaches those most in need, particularly children.
UNICEF also played a pivotal role in strengthening Libya’s social protection institutions through capacity-building efforts under the TRANSFORM program. Working with MoSA and the National Economic and Social Development Board, UNICEF trained 22 middle managers (14 female and 8 male) from seven ministries on essential social protection topics such as policy design, targeting, and cash transfer systems. Additionally, 32 frontline workers(15 female and 17 male) from 10 cities (Sabha, Brguen, Tobruk, Al Bayda, Ubari , Jebel Akhdar  Benghazi, Misrata, and Tripoli) and 20 local MoSA and SSF branches were trained on data management, beneficiary dignity, and grievance handling. Two government officers were accredited as master trainers to extend this knowledge to subnational entities.
To further enhance Libya's social protection system’s capacity to respond to shocks, UNICEF is supporting the Social Solidarity Fund (SSF) in assessing gaps and recommending reforms for programs like the National Child and Wives Grant and Basic Income Assistance. Potential adaptations include expanding programs and refining their design to make them more responsive in emergencies.
UNICEF also supported the creation of the Government Task Team on Budget Briefs, which evaluates government spending in social sectors such as health, education, and social protection. This initiative, backed by UNICEF’s technical expertise, has resulted in three budget briefs that highlight financing gaps and inform policy decisions.
In response to the devastating floods in Derna caused by Storm Daniel, UNICEF through a pilot project provided urgent assistance to 371 individuals from 51 households (45 male and 6 female headed households) through Humanitarian Cash Transfers (HCTs). This innovative approach, using certified checks, ensured targeted support for the most vulnerable. UNICEF is also working with Future Makers Society (FMS) to extend HCTs to an additional 400 households displaced by the floods.
Evidence Generation
The fragile security situation and uncertain political landscape in Libya has undermined government’s ability to strengthen its information management systems and data collection efforts.
UNICEF in collaboration with Bureau of Statistics and Census (BSC) are implementing Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) marking a significant milestone as the first ever child-focused, nationally representative household survey conducted in Libya. MICS will play a crucial role by providing data for more than 130 globally comparable indicators and enable the country to measure progress of 32 out of 80 household survey-based SDG indicators. Currently, the data collection exercise is completed in 17,800 households across all the 895 sampled clusters and the analytical phase is already initiated with an expectation of producing the preliminary findings early 2025.
 
To strengthen the BSC’s capacity in evidence generation, UNICEF provided capacity-building training for 316 BSC staff on key aspects of survey methodology, including survey design, sampling, data collection, processing, and analysis. Additionally, UNICEF continued its advocacy for evidence generation in Libya, leading to two stakeholder workshops in collaboration with BSC. These workshops brought together 67 participants from various government ministries, institutions, UN agencies, and development partners to discuss the evidence generation agenda, fostering greater coordination and collaboration in the country’s data and research efforts. 
 
In partnership with the National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB), UNICEF facilitated the establishment of the Government Task Team on Budget Briefs. This initiative aims to measure the Government’s expenditure on social sectors, including health, education, and social protection. The team, with UNICEF’s technical support produced three budget briefs in health, education, and social protection, highlighting the gaps in social sector financing.

UNICEF is co-chairing the Health and Nutrition Taskforce (as a part of Humanitarian Coordination architecture for Sudan Refugee Response Plan) alongside WHO, leading the Nutrition Sub-Working Group, where it organizes regular meetings with partners and Ministry of Health (MoH) officials. These collaborative efforts aim to strengthen coordination, address pressing health and nutrition challenges, and enhance the effectiveness of interventions in response to emergencies and ongoing health needs. This enables the creation of synergies between organizations like UNICEF, WHO, and WFP, ensuring that efforts are not duplicated and that the most urgent needs are met. 
During the recovery phase of the response to Storm Daniel in early 2024, UNICEF collaborated closely with key health sector partners, including WHO, IOM, UNHCR, UNFPA, and other international NGOs. This coordinated approach ensured synergy and complementarity among all partners, working together to build a more resilient health system. This collective effort contributed to strengthening Libya’s health infrastructure and improving service delivery in the aftermath of the storm.
UNICEF maintained strong coordination with health sector development partners through the WHO-led Health and Nutrition Taskforce and the UNSDCF-related Human Capital Development Pillar Working Group. This collaborative approach ensured inter-agency coordination, complementarity, and the effective utilization of each agency’s strengths, aiming to achieve both humanitarian and developmental objectives. UNICEF also continued its bilateral engagement with WHO and UNFPA, focusing on areas of collaboration, particularly in updating the Reproductive Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) strategy and addressing its implementation challenges. These efforts strengthened the overall health response and ensured a more integrated approach to meeting the needs of vulnerable populations in Libya.

To achieve sustainable results on water and sanitation for children in Libya, UNICEF has built strong partnerships with key stakeholders across various sectors. Collaborations with ministries such as the Ministry of Water Resources (MoWR) and the Ministry of Environment (MoEnv) have been critical in delivering essential WASH services and advancing key advocacy goals. The partnership with MoWR and the Ministry of Local Government (MoLG) enabled UNICEF to provide lifesaving WASH services to flood-affected populations in eastern Libya. Meanwhile, the collaboration with MoEnv has been instrumental in influencing climate policies, ensuring that frameworks like the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), National Adaptation Plans (NAPs), and National Communications (NCs) are child sensitive.
UNICEF also engaged non-traditional WASH sector partners, such as the Ministry of Planning (MoP) and Ministry of Youth (MoY) to leverage their existing grassroot networks including local youth councils, scout movements, and youth parliaments on climate action. These cross-ministerial collaboration has enriched UNICEF’s climate advocacy and programming, demonstrating the value of involving diverse sectors in addressing climate challenges.
A landmark partnership with the African Development Bank (AfDB), the first of its kind in the MENA region, has significantly impacted the WASH sector in Libya. Together, UNICEF and AfDB have supported MoWR in enhancing sector coordination and creating an environment for strategic reforms, paving the way for a new approach to water management and security in the country. 

In 2024, UNICEF strengthened its partnerships with IOM and UNHCR to enhance its reach to children on the move, facilitating coordinated referrals to UNICEF's Baity Centres. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with UNSMIL, UN Women, and UNDP to promote youth empowerment and female leadership in Libya. UNICEF also partnered with LECAO, a local civil society organization, to raise climate awareness, supporting education and youth initiatives, including greening activities in schools. These collaborations helped UNICEF expand its impact, addressing the needs of vulnerable children and promoting sustainable development in Libya.

To ensure child protection remains a key priority in Libya, UNICEF maintained strong partnerships with the Ministry of Social Affairs including Social Solidarity Fund, the Ministry of Interior, the Ministry of Defense, and the Highter Committee for Childhood. Partnerships with these ministries focused on the 7 domains of system strengthening, including legal and policy framework, governance and coordination structures, human resourcing, and financing.  
 
While the pilot of the UNHCR-UNICEF Blueprint for Joint Action for Refugee Children concluded in 2022, coordination established during the pilot continues, under the Letter of Understanding through child protection, education, SBC and social policy activities in Baity centers. This ensures refugee and migrant children are able to access key services including case management, MHPSS, referrals, vocational training, life skills, Arabic language classes, and cash assistance. Collaboration continues across UN Agencies including IOM, particularly in relation to children on the move. 
  
UNICEF utilized thematic humanitarian funding to enhance emergency preparedness and response, ensuring the timely deployment of lifesaving equipment, medicines, and supplies. This funding enabled rapid action within 72 hours of declaring the flood emergency and addressing the Sudanese refugee influx. Additionally, part of the thematic funding was allocated to capacity-building initiatives for healthcare staff in emergency-affected areas, strengthening the overall response efforts. Similarly Regular Resources and other Thematic funds played a crucial role in UNICEF’s efforts to provide quality education for children on the move in Libya. These funds were vital in keeping Baity centres operational across the country. They also enabled a timely response to the escalating Sudanese refugee crisis, supporting the procurement of emergency supplies and ensuring the continuation of Baity services in Kufra. Through these resources, UNICEF was able to maintain essential education services and respond effectively to the needs of vulnerable children in Libya.
