UNICEF supports programmes in 20 Middle East and North Africa (MENA) countries through 16 country offices. Despite progress, inequalities between and within countries remain substantial. MENA has diverse typologies, demographic stages and complex political economies, with persistent humanitarian challenges. In 2024, MENA faced four Level-3 emergencies in Sudan, the State of Palestine, Lebanon, and the Syrian Arab Republic. 
 
Progress towards the SDGs varies. MENA countries need high efforts to reach child-related SDG targets by 2030.  Monitoring is challenging: only half the 48 child-related SDG indicators have sufficient data. Data gaps are particularly critical for UNICEF Strategic Plan (SP) Goal Areas 2 (Learning), 3 (Protection from harm, 83 per cent missing) and 5 (Life free from poverty).
 
Extreme child poverty tripled between 2013 to 2022 from 3.4 to 10 per cent (mostly driven by Yemen). Multi-dimensional child poverty affects about a quarter of children in the six Arab middle-income countries with data, a slight reduction in recent years. Girls face particular inequities that cause poor protection, health, nutrition, education and employment prospects.  
 
Conflicts have particularly affected MENA’s economy. Counterfactual estimates suggest income per capita could have been 45 per cent higher overall, seven years after outset in conflict-affected countries, had conflicts not occurred. Economic inequalities between and within countries are substantial and widening, with MENA’s regional growth rate increasing from 1.8 per cent to an estimated 2.2 per cent in 2024 and a projected 3.8 per cent in 2025 driven by the economic growth in the Gulf countries, despite falling growth elsewhere in MENA.
 
Overall, MENA hosts 15.6 million refugees and 16.2 million internally displaced people. In all affected countries, much of the populations require mental health and psychosocial support, especially children exposed to repeated trauma, those maimed, orphaned, or with disabilities.
 
The conflict in Sudan since April 2023 has caused displacement, hunger, malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks, leaving two-thirds of the population in need. Sudan has the world’s largest child displacement crisis, with 13.6 million children needing assistance. Conflict and displacement-driven famine is present in five areas and projected in five more. Child marriage and gender-based violence rates are worsening. Over 700,000 children with severe wasting risk not surviving without treatment; 1.7 million children under age 1 risk missing vaccinations; 17 million children are out of school, lacking safety and psychosocial well-being.
 
In the State of Palestine, continued hostilities have severely affected the population in the Gaza Strip. By year-end, at least 14,500 children had been killed, an estimated 25,000 injured, and 17,000 unaccompanied and/or separated. Most children have lost access to quality health care, education (over 645,000 schoolchildren losing a full academic year), water and other vital services; and 1.9 million people were internally displaced. Women’s unemployment reached 91 per cent, while 15 per cent of households were female-headed. Additionally, the entire population of the Gaza Strip faced acute food insecurity, and in November, the FRC warned of an imminent and substantial likelihood of famine due to the rapidly deteriorating situation, with 50,400 children under five suffering acute malnutrition. There was unprecedented damage to infrastructure, including housing, and health and education facilities. By May, 60 per cent of WASH facilities were destroyed or severely damaged, exacerbating water shortages and limiting sanitation access. 
 
In Lebanon, the humanitarian situation worsened, increasing poverty and needs. Over half the Lebanese population was below the poverty line before the latest conflict. Lebanon has one of the refugee rates per capita, with 90 per cent of Syrian households in the country living in extreme poverty by 2023. Prevalence of stunting is 12 per cent, but 20 per cent among Syrian children. Only 62 per cent of displaced women and girls report access to health care, and over 40 per cent report unsafe water and sanitation. Essential services – including immunization, maternal health care, nutrition and access to medication – have been disrupted for over 10,000 people, including 4,000 children.
 
Significant military, economic, social, and political changes in the Syrian Arab Republic, culminating in government collapse on 8 December. The transition led to optimism and rebuilding efforts but also instability, disorder, and an escalating humanitarian crisis. Syria’s children require a large-scale social protection scheme to prevent extreme poverty, with more than 2.4 million children out of school, at higher risk of child labour, child marriage, trafficking, and recruitment and use in the conflict. Almost 40 per cent of hospitals and health facilities are partly or completely non-functional. Nearly 13.6 million people need water, sanitation, and hygiene services; 5.7 million require nutrition services and children are particularly vulnerable to unexploded ordnance.
 
Gulf countries experienced accelerated growth in 2024, investing in technology, green energy, health care, tourism, and finance, which positively impacted children’s social rights. Oman’s progressive social protection system, launched in 2023, is a leading effort towards SDG 1 (no poverty). 
 
he sub-region saw progress in children’s rights, with Algeria prioritizing child-centred policies and Morocco advancing in health indicators like life expectancy and maternal mortality. However, continued mixed migration within and from North Africa is expected as people flee growing economic hardship, escalating conflicts, food insecurity, and climate-related disasters, seeking safety and better opportunities.
 
Climate-induced crises in MENA, including water stress, droughts, floods, and heat waves, exacerbate humanitarian challenges, leaving children particularly vulnerable. The region contains 11 of the world’s 17 most water-stressed countries. In Djibouti, prolonged droughts left 19 per cent of the population acutely food insecure. Libya faced flash floods and infrastructure damage from Storm Daniel. Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Iraq experienced record heat waves with temperatures above 50°C.
 
Adolescent girls in MENA face significant barriers due to restrictive norms and economic inequality. Young women’s unemployment is over double that of young men and nearly three times the global average. About 17 per cent of girls marry before 18, with those having disabilities at higher risk of early and forced marriages. Nearly 50 million girls and women in five countries have undergone female genital mutilation. 
 
The economic outlook for MENA in 2024 and beyond is shaped by a mix of opportunities and challenges. Economic diversification efforts, particularly in the wealthier Gulf states, are driving growth, with investments in technology, green energy, health care, and tourism. The regional growth rate increased from 1.8 per cent to 2.2 per cent in 2024 and is projected to reach 3.8 per cent in 2025. However, MENA faces significant risks, including high youth unemployment, which stands at nearly 30 per cent for ages 15-24, inflation, and political instability. Conflicts in the region have severely affected economic performance, with GDP in Gaza contracting by 86 per cent in the second quarter of 2024. At the same time, the region's potential for technological advancement and renewable energy investments offers a path forward for sustainable growth.

Health

In 2024, MENARO provided expertise to strengthen primary healthcare in communities, improve maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health and immunization, and prepare for and respond to health emergencies throughout the region. MENARO also leveraged significant finances for child health.
 
A MENARO-led multisectoral policy and implementation landscape assessment of community health in MENA countries identified systemic gaps, set strategic directions, responded to country-specific systems-strengthening needs, and achieved better outcomes for children. Country-led processes with health ministries, communities, and key stakeholders in 13 countries increased commitments and resources.
 
On maternal and child health, MENARO conducted joint regional analysis with WHO on mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis, which will facilitate policy implementation to reduce these diseases’ burden in newborns. MENARO led capacity-building training for over 50 paediatric health-care providers and national AIDS programme leads from 11 countries. Following the workshop, Iraq, Libya, and Saudi Arabia organized in-country capacity-building training, and Tunisia began developing a national elimination strategy. 
 
MENARO supported a proposal to solarize 40 health-care facilities in the Syrian Arab Republic, supported Lebanon to secure funds to solarize two oxygen plants, and collaborated with Supply Division to procure and install 14 oxygen plants in seven MENA countries.
 
MENARO continued supporting vaccination campaigns, including in Algeria, Egypt, the Sudan, the State of Palestine (Gaza specifically), and Yemen for polio, reaching 6 million children; Iraq, Libya, the Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, and Yemen for measles, reaching 15.26 million children; and Sudan protecting 3.7 million people against cholera. In the State of Palestine and the Sudan, online insights helped counter misinformation during polio vaccination. A MENARO pilot supported Sudan to introduce vaccinations against malaria, targeting 147,432 children. MENARO also integrated gender into SBC training for the Syria Immunization Group. With L3 emergencies in four countries, MENARO provided deployment surge support, scaled up lifesaving interventions, ensured continuity of services, and supported neighbouring countries to develop health preparedness and contingency plans. 
 
MENARO led the multisectoral disease outbreak taskforce to identify actions for proactive support in MENA countries and provided technical guidance on emerging disease outbreaks such as Mpox. In Morocco and Jordan, social listening on Mpox enabled proactive communication to mitigate rumours and public anxiety.
 
MENARO supported COs to mobilize nearly $100 million for health programmes, including funds for mental health in primary health-care settings ($2.3 million for Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, and Yemen), immunization ($30.8 million for Palestine, the Sudan, and the Syrian Arab Republic), new vaccines ($15 million for Iran and Tunisia), polio ($9.5 million for Algeria, Djibouti, the State of Palestine, the Sudan, and Yemen), resilient primary health care ($2.2 million for Djibouti, Egypt, Iran, Jordan, and Lebanon), and community health ( $1.6 million for Algeria, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, and the Syrian Arab Republic). Additionally, MENARO helped COs develop Pandemic Fund proposals, securing over $38 million for Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon.
 
MENARO facilitated learning and knowledge exchanges for MENA countries, including between the health ministries of Algeria and China to strengthen primary health care. In Iraq, MENARO assisted the Ministry of Health with Digital Transformation, including drafting a Digital Health National Strategy and conducting a capacity-building workshop for ministry officers.

Preventing and treating malnutrition

MENA Nutrition Strategic Direction 2030, informed by the first MENA Regional Nutrition Situation Analysis set the narrative for programming and accelerating nutrition results, and the prevention of all forms of malnutrition has become a priority area in the MENA Regional Advocacy Strategy. An interactive dashboard was launched to provide up-to-date nutrition data. Strategic advocacy and fundraising efforts secured over $27 million for nutrition programmes, including $800,000 for MENARO and $26.5 million for COs. 
 
Through timely and high-quality technical support to all 20 MENA countries, MENARO supported multisectoral nutrition strategies to prevent malnutrition (Iraq, Morocco, Tunisia and Djibouti), breastfeeding legislation and programmes (Egypt and Tunisia), and the Baby Friendly Hospitals Initiative (Egypt and Oman). Guidelines for local complementary foods, improve counselling tools, and link with social protection programmes were developed in Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, and Yemen. UNICEF programmes reached 7.2 million children with preventive services and over 800,000 with wasting treatment in seven countries. Nine countries integrated ECD into primary health care. MENARO also supported multisectoral ECD policies in Egypt and early stimulation and care in the Sudan and the Syrian Arab Republic.
 
MENARO laid the groundwork to address overweight and obesity in middle and high-income countries. It provided Egypt, Iran, Jordan, and Lebanon with technical and strategic support in 2024, using $4 million of global thematic funds to prevent childhood overweight. MENARO supported UNICEF Gulf offices to lead technical work to advocate and plan a collaborative approach to childhood overweight prevention/.
 
The region faced significant nutritional challenges in 2024, including famine-like conditions in Sudan and the State of Palestine. MENARO was first port of call for surge and delivered comprehensive technical support, focusing on nutrition data systems, cluster coordination, and programme responses to prevent, detect, and treat malnutrition. MENARO provided technical support for a more comprehensive nutrition response for the Saharawis in Tindouf (Algeria) and facilitated progress on implementing WHO guidelines on wasting prevention and management in Yemen. 
 
Learning and skilling 

MENARO provided technical support shaped policy frameworks and supported COs to build evidence-based cases for early childhood education. This led Iraq to introduce an investment case and model for early childhood education policy, and Egypt initiated policy discussions on preschool programmes and working mothers.
 
Foundational learning (FLN) improved with support from UNICEF and the Hempel Foundation’s Foundational Learning Action Tracker. The State of Palestine led in FLN despite the ongoing conflict. The Syrian Arab Republic improved instructional efficiency, and Jordan teaching fundamentals. Life skills education became core to teaching practices, empowering youth, and MENARO field-tested a life-skills measurement tool in Tunisia, the State of Palestine, and Egypt.
 
Digital learning initiatives in Egypt, Lebanon, and the Sudan supported education in complex settings. Online and hybrid learning allowed children to access relevant opportunities, with Sudanese and Palestinian refugees using the Learning Passport while displaced in Egypt. MENARO, with the Innocenti Research Centre, led research in the Sudan and Lebanon to inform digital learning programme scaling.
 
Flexible learning pathways, including non-formal education, vocational training, and digital and employability skilling initiatives, provided opportunities for marginalized children, adolescents, and youth in Lebanon, Tunisia, Jordan, Egypt, Iraq, and Syria. To facilitate exchange of best practices, UNICEF organized a digital and green skills/jobs event, with particular attention to ensuring equal access for girls and women.
 
UNICEF partnered with ILO, UNDP, UNFPA, UNESCO, and the regional Peer Support Group (PSG) to organize the Arab States’ High-Level Meeting on Young People’s Learning, Skilling, and Transition to Decent Work (HLM24). National Voluntary Commitments made at HLM24 will improve engagement on policy discussions around learning and employment, including young people’s priorities. The MENA skills development agenda was further strengthened through strategic alignment with the Generation Unlimited global programme, resulting in a new multi-year, multi-country partnership with Education Above All (EAA) to support learning, skilling, and the transition to greener economies in Jordan, Lebanon, and Egypt.

Child protection

In 2024, MENARO engaged in advocacy, research, and systemic reform. A key event was the First Ministerial Conference on Violence Against Children (VAC) in Bogotá, where MENARO helped seven MENA countries create national pledges and engage in global dialogue. Collaborating with the United Nations Special Representative on VAC and WHO, MENARO facilitated regional consultations to align MENA priorities with global frameworks. 
 
MENARO addressed overlapping violence against children and women through a multi-country study in Jordan, Iraq, and Lebanon, which identified shared risk factors like economic stress and gender inequality, urging integrated national strategies. MENARO assisted nine countries to apply social and behavioural change (SBC) approaches to end violent disciplining of children. Another study highlighted opportunities to link child protection with social protection systems in Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia. Egypt’s Child Protection Vulnerability Index emerged as a tool to identify at-risk children, while a study in Jordan and Tunisia emphasized gaps in referral mechanisms and inter-sectoral coordination.
 
UNICEF and the International Defence Coalition mapped child detention practices across eight MENA countries, advocating non-custodial alternatives and systemic reforms. The study called for ending child detention based on migration status and prioritizing child-sensitive approaches.
 
In 2024, MENARO focused on children on the move, chairing quarterly Mediterranean Mixed Migration Calls to enhance coordination and information-sharing, and developing a ECAR-MENAR Joint Investment Case and Mediterranean Communications Matrix. Sub-regional North Africa Coordination Calls led to the creation of the MENARO Children on the Move Narrative Document, shaping advocacy messages and guiding a North Africa Investment Brief and Pitch. The MENARO Migration Working Group facilitated internal coordination and supported inter-agency efforts, contributing to ESCWA’s Situation Report on International Migration.
 
MENARO also conducted studies on child marriage drivers in conflict settings and partnered with UNFPA and ESCWA to quantify its economic costs. In North-East Syria, MENARO continued advocating for the repatriation of detained foreign children and supporting NGOs in assessing detention centres.
 
WASH and climate change

In 2024, MENARO’s WASH team responded to humanitarian crises, including armed conflicts, earthquakes, flooding, and cholera outbreaks. MENARO provided critical support to COs, through technical assistance, in-country missions, and remote guidance. The team also, reviewed Emergency Preparedness Plans, and built capacity, such as regional “WASH for Peace” training for 22 staff from 10 countries, to improve COs’ ability to respond to emergencies.
 
MENARO elevated its climate change agenda by establishing the first MENA Regional Climate Change Advisor position in support of the UNICEF Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan and the MENA region climate change accelerator. Key actions included finalizing 15 Climate Landscape Analysis for Children studies, integrating a child lens into Nationally Determined Contributions and National Action Plans, developing youth climate toolkits with UNDP. MENARO supported region-wide efforts for UNFCCC-sponsored Local Conference of Youth (LCOY) in 8 countries, as well as two Regional Conference of Youth (RCOY) for Africa (in Morocco) and MENA (in Jordan), and training programmes on youth climate leadership, (, “Youth Leadership Training on Climate Action” and the “Leadership and Advocacy for a Sustainable Environment”), supporting youth climate activists and young people in climate change processes (COP 29 on climate change and COP16 on desertification), and hosting a regional climate change network meeting in Oman. 
 
On WASH programming, MENARO partnered with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) to support upstream activities in six countries, including climate-informed WASH Bottleneck Analysis Tool (WASHBAT) studies, sanitation and water safety planning, and capacity-building initiatives like exchange visits and training. MENARO organized a regional webinar for COs on developing Climate Rationales for the WASH sector, and invested in knowledge management and evidence sharing in WASH and gender through research into menstrual health and hygiene and the adolescent girl personal care and protection package. UNICEF and WHO also collaborated on monitoring SDG 6 and the UN-Water Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water (GLAAS) survey
 
WASH in health-care facilities remained a priority, with MENARO collaborating with WHO’s Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO) to provide technical assistance and capacity building. Key initiatives included rolling out the WASH for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH-FIT), conducting regional and country-level training events in six countries, and monitoring progress on the Supply Division Call to Action on WASH in HCFs (8 Practical Steps)..
 
Social protection and social policy

As co-leader of the regional issue-based coalition on social protection, UNICEF promoted knowledge exchange and inter-agency coordination. Through the TRANSFORM Arab Region initiative, 18 training events reached over 430 government officials in eight countries (Libya, Iraq, Tunisia, Iraq, the State of Palestine, Yemen, Jordan, and Lebanon), building their capacity on integrated social protection systems. UNICEF developed a regional guide on integrating SBC approaches into social assistance programmes, alongside a joint study with the World Food Programme (WFP) on nutrition-sensitive social protection. MENARO also supported social protection initiatives that include women and persons with disabilities, assisting four COs to strengthen national frameworks. 
 
On PF4C, UNICEF conducted a landscape analysis to assess public funding trends and their impact on children’s outcomes, positioning PF4C as a top advocacy priority. MENARO engaged with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to lay the groundwork for joint advocacy in countries like Iraq, Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia. MENARO also developed a multi-year advocacy plan to influence national budget policies for child protection, and conducted assessments of nutrition supply financing.
 
UNICEF’s MENA operations maintained the largest HCT volume and coverage globally, ensuring critical support for vulnerable populations in crisis settings. To advance humanitarian cash transfer (HCT) programming, MENARO supported five large-scale emergencies (Lebanon, the State of Palestine, the Sudan, Syria, and Yemen) with surge staffing, operational design, risk management, and monitoring. It assisted COs in preparedness tasks such as contracting financial service providers, developing standard operating procedures, and training staff on HCTs. UNICEF’s MENA operations maintained the largest HCT volume and coverage globally, ensuring critical support for vulnerable populations in crisis settings. 

Humanitarian action

MENARO strengthened humanitarian preparedness, response, and coordination across Lebanon, the State of Palestine, Sudan, and the Syrian Arab Republic through cross-border operations, emergency response planning, and quality assurance for Humanitarian Action for Children appeals and Situation Reports, and CO contingency plans. MENARO managed the Global Education Cluster for the State of Palestine and Sudan. 
 
MENARO prioritized emergency supply operations, providing surge support to Lebanon, Libya, Iraq, Gaziantep (Türkiye), and Egypt, while remotely assisting the Sudan and the State of Palestine. An innovative digitized supply planning tool was introduced in the Syrian Arab Republic, Lebanon, and the State of Palestine. MENARO’s logistics hub in Jordan facilitated responses in Gaza, Lebanon and the Syrian Arab Republic; and supported in-kind donations for Gaza and Iraq.

MENARO continued providing critical assistance to northwest Syria through multi-sectoral programmes, prioritizing high-severity areas. Key achievements included delivering vaccines to 150 health facilities and 94 EPI centres, benefiting over 137,000 under-five children. Primary health-care services reached 217,297 people, and 9,737 children with severe acute malnutrition were treated. The WASH programme served 1,777,179 beneficiaries, including 131,213 with disabilities. Education initiatives reached 201,967 children, with 87,524 accessing non-formal education. MENARO also led cluster coordination in WASH, Nutrition, Education, and Child Protection, ensuring effective humanitarian response planning and implementation.
 
MENARO supported COs to establish Humanitarian Access Frameworks in Sudan, the Syrian Arab Republic, Libya, Yemen, and Lebanon, and a WASH Cluster strategy for northwest Syria. It facilitated inter-agency coordination and operationalized its Advisory Committee on Armed Non-State Actors Engagement, providing training in Sudan and the Syrian Arab Republic. MENARO was crucial in shaping the Syria Refugee Regional Refugee and Resilience Plan and supported UNRWA’s emergency response for Palestinian refugees. These efforts reinforced MENARO’s commitment to effective and localized humanitarian action.
 
Based on a MENARO-led reflection exercise conducted in 2023 on seven sudden-onset emergencies, COs strengthened Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) mechanisms (including knowledge sharing and joint guidance with SBC) and developing information provision plans for crises like the Sudan refugee influx. Localization efforts advanced through building standby partner capacity particularly in Yemen and the Sudan. 

Building capacity and closing the evidence gap in cross-cutting areas

MENARO provided significant support to build capacity across sectors, through research and knowledge management. MENARO supported countries to strengthen systems and develop partnerships for young people to participate in decisions affecting their lives, facilitating their transition to productive adulthood. Gender-responsive programming was supported through UNICEF’s Gender Action Plan and the regional framework for voice, choice and leadership, multi-country research (intersections between violence against children and women and humanitarian situations), and evidence sharing on menstrual health and hygiene and the adolescent girl personal care and protection package in Gaza, Lebanon, Egypt, and Sudan. Advocacy on women’s ability to pass nationality to their children demonstrated how equal nationality rights can promote the SDGs. Collaboration on parenting modules with Oxfam and Plan International aimed to enhance early childhood development and fathers’ engagement in immunization. Gender was integrated into MENARO-led SBC training for the Syria Immunization Group and through joint publications and support to improve immunization among zero-dose communities in Yemen, the Syrian Arab Republic, the Sudan, and Djibouti.
 
MENARO promoted integrating disability inclusion across UNICEF programmes and operations through the MENA Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy (DIPAS) Action Plan 2024-2025 officially, endorsed by UNICEF’s Executive Board in December 2023, a Regional Workshop on Improving Disability Statistics in Arab Countries organized by ESCWA, and a regional WHO-UNICEF Assistive Devices workshop in December. 
 
Steady progress was made in advancing Social and Behaviour Change and parenting agendas through increased collaborations, evidence analyses, documentation, and capacity-building. Applying a sub-regional strategy to SBC improved emergency responses and emphasized the importance of integrating SBC techniques to enhance emergency response and health plans. UNICEF led the Regional RCCE Working Group with WHO and IFRC, focusing on social cohesion and trust-building during emergencies. MENARO published a guide on integrating SBC for improving cash-plus programming and four peer-reviewed journal articles on vaccine demand, contributed to five MENA case studies in a global SBC compendium, and completed a faith-based guide for review in 2025. Mentoring on Human-Centred Design (HCD) was conducted in Iraq, Morocco, Djibouti, Jordan, and the Syrian Arab Republic. In Northwest Syria, UNICEF piloted eight HCD initiatives on immunization and nutrition through local partners, while in Morocco and Djibouti, HCD is being scaled for broader application. The Arabic “SBC Theory and Practice” online course, developed with WHO, IFRC, and IOM, was completed for launch in 2025.
 
The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) programme saw the launch of the Tunisia MICS 2023 and Qatar MICS 2023 and fieldwork completed for a survey in Libya. 

Evaluation

MENARO continued strengthening regional evidence generation and utilization, despite financial and operational constraints. MENARO and MENA COs supported the EvalMENA board to hold the EvalMENA Conference in early 2024, with key contributions on evaluation use and youth engagement, contributing to national evaluation capacity development. MENARO initiated evaluations on child protection and on AI use in Country Programme Evaluations (CPEs), both expected to be completed in 2025.These efforts reflect UNICEF’s commitment to strengthening evidence generation and utilization in the region, despite financial and operational constraints.

Resource mobilization

In a complex and shifting geopolitical landscape and ongoing regional conflicts, MENARO focused on fund-raising initiatives aimed at diversifying streams and unlocking flexible funding. While private fundraising mobilized slightly less than the exceptional year of 2023, it was still more than 300 per cent higher than in 2022. An increased proportion of fully flexible income enabled more efficient regional fund allocation.
 
MENARO developed a donor-facing investment case to address the conflict in Gaza and its impact on Palestinian refugees. This was paired with a public partner donor engagement approach, providing systematic support to L3 countries with tools and guidance on partnership management and donor relations, focusing on political discussions, donor conditionalities, and aid politicization. Additionally, MENARO launched a new platform to advocate children's priorities in the Middle East, raising awareness among key partners.
 
Another major accomplishment is the improvement of the MENA Private Sector Fundraising Cluster, which generates flexible income from private individuals. Despite lower income in 2024 than in 2023, the ratio of emergency funds to fully flexible income exceeded forecasts. A collaborative model linking the Regional Office with COs and the Headquarters Private Fundraising and Partnerships Division supported digital fundraising, brand building, and public campaigns. Meanwhile, a new regional tool was developed and tested to leverage public-private partnerships. In-country bespoke integrated engagements were created in Tunisia, Morocco, and Egypt, focusing on private sector social service delivery. This approach is helping to identify programmatic bottlenecks and initiate partnerships to advance policy and service delivery, demonstrating UNICEF's relevance and effectiveness in meeting the increasing demand for sustainable solutions from development banks and bilateral donors.

Staff well-being and development 

Staff development, well-being and security of personnel and assets remained a core focus for UNICEF in MENA. Staff benefitted from wellbeing and psychosocial safety training sessions to improve mental health literacy, prevent symptoms, and reduce risks of trauma and burnout. The training enhanced staff knowledge on mental health, emotional intelligence, supervisory skills, identifying burnout and trauma symptoms, referral mechanisms to the wellbeing team, and communication and empathy in humanitarian emergency contexts. Through training on wellbeing and psychosocial safety, staff have enhanced knowledge on mental health, referral mechanisms, and communication and empathy in humanitarian emergency contexts. 
 
People and Culture 

 In 2024, UNICEF in the MENA region enhanced its human resource management and staff development, achieving key milestones despite regional challenges. Nineteen HR practitioners successfully completed the Cornell HR Business Partner Certification Program, strengthening HR capacity in the region. MENARO expanded the recruitment hub project to an additional region, reinforcing efficiency in talent acquisition. To foster staff development and well-being, MENARO facilitated internal stretch assignments, surge missions, officer-in-charge (OIC) opportunities, and 360-degree feedback, while also mandating DIPAS training for HR practitioners by 2025.  
 
Security

In 2024, MENARO’s security team supported 18 COs, MENARO, and the Yemen outpost in Amman, ensuring the security of UNICEF personnel, premises, and assets. This enabled programme activities to be delivered within an acceptable level of risk. MENARO maintained security compliance and provided regular updates on evolving threats and regional developments. It facilitated Condition Improvement Fund funding to enable COs to enhance their security measures based on identified needs.
 
MENARO also focused on knowledge management by sending regular policy updates and reviewing CO security documents. It technically evaluated security teams, organized biweekly cross-country security meetings, and facilitated a regional network meeting. MENARO maintained a SharePoint platform for security documents and produced 40 security assessments. It developed a database for recording security incidents and conducted remote security compliance assessments, revealing acceptable overall compliance. Documents related to missions to high- and very-high-risk areas were also reviewed to ensure thorough preparedness and risk mitigation.
 
MENARO supported continuous professional development for security personnel. It also organized various security-related training events, on issues including gender considerations and emergency trauma.

Risk management

MENARO ensured programme delivery remained within acceptable risk levels through compliance assessments, coordination between countries, contribution to contingency plans, timely security analysis, capacity-building initiatives, surge deployments, and Central Investment Fund allocations, while proactive measures enhanced operational effectiveness in crisis environments.
Ongoing and new Level-3 emergencies hindered risk management activities in COs (peer reviews, HACT risk assurance efforts) and the region fell short of its target KPI of 100 per cent for the first time in three years. Nevertheless, MENARO emphasized collaboration, innovative solutions, and capacity-building. Successful digitalization roll-out included ezHACT 2.0, ePD, and eTool modules. A unified risk management approach with a harmonized risk register ensured all COs in MENA completed risk assessments. 
 
Digital Impact and ICT
 
In 2024, UNICEF MENARO made significant progress in using Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and Technology for Development (T4D) to improve children's well-being across the MENA region. The Regional Office's Digital Impact (ICT and T4D) function played a crucial role in supporting various initiatives. For example, in Iraq, MENARO T4D, in collaboration with the Health Section, assisted the Ministry of Health with Digital Transformation, including drafting a Digital Health National Strategy and conducting a capacity-building workshop for ministry officers. Additionally, reliable and responsive connectivity across the region, along with the migration of all UNICEF data centres to the Cloud, ensured a solid Business Continuity Plan (BCP) and a green ICT operation. MENARO ICT also strengthened systems for emergency data and telecommunications, facilitated several peer review missions, conducted a regional Generative Artificial Intelligence training for all ICT staff in the region, and provided technical support activities. Furthermore, the T4D function enabled digital programming across the region, including Digital Health, Vaccine Supply Chain, Digital Education, Online Protection, and GIGA School Connectivity. The COs’ satisfaction rate with the Regional ICT function (including T4D) was 92%. Finally, MENARO ICT provided end-user training and supported over 130 meetings and workshops in 2024, plus received a 96.25% satisfaction rate from the RO users. 

Supplies and logistics
 
In 2024, MENARO delivered $954 million in goods and services regionally, responding to crises in Sudan, the State of Palestine, Lebanon, and the Syrian Arab Republic through supply hubs, securing Long-Term Agreements (LTAs) for emergencies, scaling up digitization, strengthening monitoring, and strengthening supply chains.
 
Localization remained a priority, with 13 regional suppliers in Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates qualifying for LTAs to supply medicines, adolescent kits, winterization kits, hygiene kits, and more. A regional LTA was established for complementary food to support emergencies, and market assessments for assistive technologies advanced the disability agenda.
 
MENARO developed supply chain strengthening roadmaps in Yemen, Jordan, Iraq, and Lebanon. MENARO supported the $5.72 million Africa CDC Multi-Country Fund programme for Scaling Up Lifelong Learning across seven countries. Jordan signed its first Procurement Service MOU, with training provided to its Ministry of Health, while Oman CO led government awareness efforts with a visit to the Supply Division.
 
Digitization expanded with the electronic Vaccine Arrival Report (eVAR) tool in 10 countries and training on the Procurement Case Management tool in 11 countries. Two new COs adopted the Mobile Warehouse and Inventory Management System. Digital programming was supported, including Digital Health, Digital Education, Online Protection, and GIGA School Connectivity.

In 2024, MENARO forged impactful partnerships with various stakeholders, including United Nations and other international organizations, governments, donors, academia, media, and civil society organizations, to address critical issues in the MENA region. These collective efforts underscore MENARO’s commitment to improving outcomes for children across the region.
 
MENARO strengthened collaboration with United Nations agencies to advance children’s rights. With WHO Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office (EMRO), partnerships focused on community-based primary health care, including mental health integration and co-hosting the MENA Adolescent Health Conference. UNICEF’s co-leadership of the RCCE Regional Working group with WHO EMRO and IFRC MENA fostered country-level collaborative efforts. With UNFPA MENARO conducted capacity-building workshops on maternal and child health in humanitarian settings. Under the Regional UN Nutrition Collaboration Framework 2030, MENARO worked with WHO (wasting/obesity prevention), WFP (nutrition-social protection linkages), and FAO (nutrition information systems). A new partnership with UNRWA facilitated nutrition responses in Lebanon, Jordan and the State of Palestine, while collaboration with UNDP explored climate bonds to fund social sectors in MENA’s resource-constrained contexts. MENARO also worked with WHO on SDG 6 monitoring and WASH in health-care facilities, promoting guidance like the “eight practical steps.” UNFPA and ESCWA collaborated on the economic costs of child marriage. MENARO continued strengthening partnerships with the World Bank, WFP, and UNHCR for social protection, and co-led the issue-based coalition on linking cash transfers to social protection systems to improve coordination and advocacy at inter-agency level.
 
MENARO strengthened its strategic engagement with other international organizations. This included working with Africa Centres for Disease Control through co-organizing country consultation workshops, regional capacity-building training, and involvement in the high-level community health flagship. This collaboration enhanced joint advocacy for community health systems in North Africa, extending to immunization and public health emergency preparedness and response. In partnership with the African Union (AU), MENARO worked on Africa-wide nutrition strategy development, coordinating with UNICEF’s Eastern and Southern Africa Regional Office (ESARO) and West and Central Africa Regional Office (WCARO); discussions with ESCWA and Arab Forum may expand this regional engagement. UNICEF MENA, along with WCARO and ESARO, collaborated with the AU on the transform education agenda in Africa. This partnership facilitated the sharing of best practices, lessons learned, and policy innovations, including insights from North African countries on second-chance education. MENARO closely collaborated with the League of Arab States on initiatives such as the regional water scarcity initiative and climate change action, co-led by the League and FAO, and with UNFPA to highlight the economic and social gains of addressing harmful practices.
 
MENARO actively collaborated with research and academic institutions to address critical challenges. In the field of HIV, MENARO partnered with Penta, the Society for AIDS in Africa, IOM, and UNAIDS to focus on triple elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis. MENARO engaged with American University of Beirut (AUB). and other regional academic institutions to identify programmatic research needs and bridge the evidence gap in nutrition. MENARO partnered with USAID to co-fund a MENA region WASH master’s degree programme, in collaboration with the German-Jordanian University and Action Against Hunger, to build capacity and expertise in WASH. MENARO established a regional partnership with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI) to support country offices with upstream technical expertise, including workshops on WASHBAT and WASH Regulation. With Roehampton University and the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement MENARO developed and tested a life skills measurement tool for future large-scale national assessments. A multi-country study with Oxford Policy Management in Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia enhanced child protection and social protection system integration. MENARO collaborated with DIFI on parenting and launched joint research in Qatar as a model for other countries. These collaborations highlight MENARO’s commitment to leveraging research and academic partnerships to enhance health, nutrition, and education outcomes in the region.
 
MENARO expanded its partnerships with civil society organizations like ACF Canada and FHI 360 to enhance technical support for MENA countries. This included designing and implementing SMART surveys and evidence-based maternal and child nutrition interventions. In Northeast Syria (NES), MENARO supported NES Forum NGOs to prepare and train to assess eight places of detention holding Syrian and third-country national children. MENARO partnered with the International Budget Partnership to promote budget transparency in the region, starting with a regional webinar and followed by in-depth discussions in Morocco and Tunisia. A regional partnership was launched with Doha International Family Institute to support evidence-based parenting programming. MENARO partnered with Karama to establish a cohort for adolescent girls’ leadership on climate change and supported the International Day of the Girl event, focusing on girls’ rights and gender-based violence.
 
MENARO engaged the media as a strategic partner for nutrition advocacy in 2024, particularly in the context of the famine in Sudan and the famine-like situation in Gaza. These products explained the nutrition crisis, its drivers, and UNICEF’s actions in a simplified and compelling manner. UNICEF worked closely with ministries of education in Egypt and Lebanon to strengthen the implementation of digital learning initiatives, integrating technology into learning to enhance educational access and quality for vulnerable learners. MENARO worked with MENA governments to elucidate their priorities regarding violence against children, enabling countries to advance their commitments on the issue.
 
MENARO built new coalitions of partners. To boost partnership and advocate for regional priorities, MENARO initiated a group of friends for children in the Middle East to engage key public regional partners. MENARO developed and tested a new regional public-private partnership leveraging tool, and developed in-country bespoke integrated engagements with both partnership and programme leadership around private sector social service delivery in Tunisia, Morocco, and Egypt, to identify programmatic bottlenecks and initiate specific partnerships to advance both policy and service delivery. Through two flagship meetings, MENARO convened regional nutrition partners – academia, research, donors, implementing partners, United Nations agencies, and civil society – to align narratives and build synergies. A United Nations and Development Partners Roundtable strategized on promoting girls’ wellbeing, agency, and voice through national policies and initiatives.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Emergencies

In 2024, MENA faced challenges from political instability, conflict, and climate emergencies, hindering humanitarian and development responses. Political volatility restricted access to affected populations, complicating efforts to address health risks and protect communities. Climate change worsened food insecurity, nutrition vulnerabilities, and disruptions to education and social services, forcing a shift from long-term systems-building to reactive humanitarian efforts.

The crises underscored the need for adaptive strategies and preparedness. MENARO developed a methodology to evaluate community needs in fragile contexts using digital tools, leveraging existing social protection systems. Experience led teams to emphasize risk-informed programming and nexus approaches, balancing emergency response with longer-term support. Delays in strategic work due to recurring emergencies highlighted the value of integrating preparedness planning across sectors.

In 2025, MENARO will prioritize nexus programming to bridge humanitarian and development goals, using lessons from 2024 to bolster preparedness and peacebuilding. MENARO will focus on community engagement and feedback systems to support cohesion, empowerment, and resilience. MENARO also aims to strengthen resilience in fragile countries, by advancing public finance for children and disability-inclusive social protection with "plus" components to enhance multisectoral impact. 

Integration of early childhood development and nutrition with primary health care 

MENARO’s work demonstrates the impact of resilient, integrated PHC systems through collaborative models addressing HIV, AIDS, and epidemic-prone diseases, on improved health outcomes. Mobile teams have proven effective in bridging gaps in hard-to-reach areas, emphasizing the importance of multisectoral programming. 
 
While strong PHC systems are vital for addressing health crises and delivering integrated services, MENA countries face persistent gaps in fully leveraging their potential, particularly in integrating ECD with nutrition during the first 1,000 days of life. Despite proven benefits, few countries have adopted multisectoral ECD interventions (such as early stimulation and parenting support) within PHC frameworks, hindered by fragmented programming and siloed approaches.

In 2025, MENARO will prioritize scaling up ECD-nutrition integration in PHC, focusing on the first 1,000 days. Mobile health efforts will expand to balance emergency response with resilience, while cross-sector collaboration aims to break silos and align health, education, and social protection for vulnerable families. By embedding equity and innovation into PHC systems, the region can better address interconnected challenges, ensuring holistic support for children and families amid ongoing instability. 

Migration 

While media attention largely focuses on outward mixed migration from North Africa to Europe, more of the broader population movements across Africa and the Middle East occur within countries (rural-to-urban) and intra-regionally (such as West Africa to North Africa). North African countries are not only transit points but also destinations and settlement hubs for millions of migrants and refugees. Access to disaggregated data remains constrained, particularly in MENA, due to the securitization of information. Significant investment is needed in inter-regional, inter-agency, and internal coordination. 
 
MENARO has dedicated significant efforts to collaborating with country offices to develop a MENA-focused narrative that prioritizes the needs of children on the move within the region. This has proven to be beneficial toward centring the needs of children on the move in MENA, as well as toward resource mobilization and advocacy. 
 
In 2025, MENARO will work with ECARO and UNICEF HQ’s Migration and Displacement Hub to ensure the situation of children on the move in MENA and actions needed to guarantee their access to basic services and protection is at the forefront of key events, advocacy and public communication opportunities. MENARO will also work with WCARO and ESARO to build a stronger migration coordination platform with WCAR and ESAR. Finally, through Global Strategic Partnership Agreements, UNICEF will strengthen its work with IOM and UNHCR. 
 
Data 

Access to timely, disaggregated data remains a key barrier, impeding child health, nutrition, education, and migration response planning and advocacy. Fragile systems, humanitarian crises (including L3), and restricted migration data due to the framing of migration as a security threat rather than a humanitarian situation, hinder evidence-based actions. Lack of transparency and clarity about how budgets are allocated and spent also limits child-focused spending accountability. Behavioural data generation and analysis to improve the precision and relevance of service demand and behaviour change strategies is limited by capacity and resource constraints. 
 
MENARO’s work in Gaza produced innovative solutions, such as leveraging humanitarian cash transfer monitoring systems to gather nutrition data, which informed global analyses like the IPC/FRC famine alerts or conducting rapid and qualitative community assessments to understand the drivers of immunization behaviours, informing polio campaigns. This approach demonstrated the value of integrating data collection into existing programmes, even in crises. Collaborations with COs to contextualize data and partnerships with IFIs and think tanks also proved vital in addressing knowledge gaps. However, the region’s reliance on fragmented data systems revealed the need for standardized, multisectoral frameworks to capture underlying determinants of malnutrition and migration dynamics. 
 
In 2025, MENARO will prioritize digital platforms to collect real-time nutrition data, focusing on determinants like food security and health access in both humanitarian and development settings. Partnerships with IFIs and think tanks will expand to improve budgetary transparency and advocate child-focused public finance. To address migration data gaps, collaboration with DAPM/IDAC will strengthen systems for tracking vulnerable children on the move (see above). By embedding innovation in data collection and fostering cross-sector alliances, MENARO aims to transform data challenges into opportunities for targeted, equitable programming.

With the flexible funds provided by GRP, MENARO positioned UNICEF as a technical leader, thought leader, convener, and credible voice in the region through pioneering knowledge management, data, research and regional public goods. Investments in emergency preparedness through GRP, were critical for children in MENA. 
 
Community health. A MENARO-led multisectoral policy and implementation landscape assessment of community health in MENA countries contributed to identifying systemic gaps, setting strategic directions and responding to country-specific needs for strengthening systems and to achieve better outcomes for children. The country-led process with health ministries, communities and key stakeholders across 13 countries is leading to increased commitments and resources on this critical agenda. The country-specific assessment, regional report and dashboard, were launched at a high-level event in December 2024, and are being utilized for required policy actions.
 
Maternal and newborn health in humanitarian settings. With GRP funds, MENARO also supported COs with the development of a MENA-wide maternal and newborn health assessment in humanitarian settings. This contributed to generate evidence on specific challenges for maternal and newborn health quality of care and will inform preparedness and response actions as well as recovery and transition phases. 
 
Nutrition. MENARO released the MENA Nutrition Strategic Direction 2030, which set results across MENA countries and expanded strategic partnerships for nutrition across sectors and stakeholders’ communities.
 
Education. MENARO strategically promoted integration of life skills into teaching and learning practices across both formal and non-formal education settings in humanitarian and development contexts. MENARO also played a pivotal role by supporting the adaptation and implementation of tools like the Learning Passport, a digital platform, ensuring the continuation of education for displaced children and adolescents in coordination with the national partners.
 
Cross-country knowledge sharing on multisectoral primary health care components of disease outbreaks. MENARO supported the development of a 20-hour remote delivery, multisectoral training on epidemiology, preparedness and response to cholera epidemics, in English and Arabic languages. Public access to this multisectoral training package was offered, considering the increasing frequency of cholera epidemics in the MENA region. A trainer’s cholera training package was developed in English and Arabic, which compiled key information on five modules and training methodology to facilitate scenario-based exercises. The delivery of this cholera training package has reached more than 150 professionals from the region to date. 

Through GRP funds, MENARO supported the development of new regional guidance to integrate SBC evidence and approaches within cash transfer programmes for improved programme outcomes. Furthermore, translation of key global and regional SBC resources into Arabic for wider dissemination and relevant use by staff and partners in the region. 
 
In addition, GRP funds contributed to promote knowledge exchange through south-south cooperation, supported technical assistance for MICS coordination and systematic quality assurance of evidence generation in MENARO. 
 
Finally, GRP funds have been instrumental in strengthening humanitarian preparedness across the region through helping COs develop and update contingency plans to prepare for worst-case scenarios, mitigate risks to children, and ensure business continuity in high-threat environments.

Morocco's economic stability is closely tied to global trends due to its numerous free trade agreements, wheat and oil imports, foreign investments and remittances from Moroccans living abroad. Economic growth is expected to decline from 3.4% in 2023 to 2.6% in 2024[1]. Inflation is projected at 1% in 2024[2] in comparison to 6.1% in 2023 and the budget deficit remains the same (4.4%)[3]. The country experienced another year of drought with rainfall 54% lower than average. Water reserves declined by 83%, with dam reservoirs at 26% capacity, down from 34% of the previous year.[4] Agriculture, which consumes 80% of the country’s water resources, was severely affected, with irrigated crops accounting for 65% of national agricultural production. These global and domestic trends will continue to impact food security and nutrition.  

The census is a vital tool for collecting demographic, social, and economic data in Morocco. Conducted every ten years by the High Commission for Planning (HCP), it provides crucial insights into the population's structure, living conditions, and economic activities. Early findings from the 2024 Census show an aging population (13.8% aged 60 and over in 2024, up from 9.4% in 2014), rapid urbanization (62.8%) and an increase in the number of households (9,275,038 in 2024, up from 7,313,806 in 2014). The child population has largely stagnated at 11.5 million (31% of the total population). Unemployment rose from 16.2% in 2014 to 21.3% in 2024. Importantly, the activity rate for those aged 15 and over fell from 47.6% in 2014 to 41.6% in 2024, with disparities across geographical area (urban 43.8%, rural 37.6%) and gender (men 67.1%, women 16.8%) indicating a number of structural barriers.

In social protection, Morocco launched the national Direct Social Aid Programme and established the National Agency for Social Assistance (ANAS) last year to support poor and vulnerable households, children, and a significant portion of the “missing middle” who are predominantly engaged in the informal sector and remain vulnerable to shocks. As a result, in 2024, 4.8 million Moroccan children aged 0-17 representing 44% of the child population were covered (compared to 22% last year). The programme provides monthly cash transfers for children, a lump-sum birth allowance for the first two children, a yearly back-to-school allowance, and additional monthly top-ups for orphans, and disabled children.  In addition, 3.9 million children (36% of the total child population), received family allowances under the contributory social protection scheme. These children reside in families where the head of household is formally employed in the private or public sector. Collectively, these interventions bring the overall social protection coverage for children in Morocco to 80%.
In the education sector, 78.7% of children were enrolled in preschool (up from 76.2%).[5] The 2024 census shows both progress in enrollment and persistent inequalities. The enrollment rate for girls aged 6 to 11 rose from 90% in 2014 to 95.1% in 2024. However, while 94.6% of boys aged 12-14 in urban areas attend school, only 68.5% of girls in rural communities were in school.[6]  Importantly, the number of dropouts decreased by 12% from 334,664 last year to 294,458; the largest decline in recent years.

Health sector reforms were impacted by the ongoing restructuring of the Ministry of Health and Social Protection (MoHSP) and the setting up of new entities (the High Authority for Health to regulate insurance and the Agency for Medicines and Health Products tasked with the pharmaceutical policy). Frequent strikes by healthcare professionals also affected delivery of primary health care services. Persistent mistrust from the COVID-19 continued to fuel vaccine hesitancy, resulting in a resurgence of measles cases. In response, the Ministry of Health launched two catch-up vaccination campaigns in March and November 2024. Despite these efforts, the situation remains concerning with 107 deaths and 19,515 reported cases of measles.[7]

In child protection, the endorsed territorial protocol for the care of vulnerable children and children in contact with the law was adopted and signed on May 27, 2024, as part of a tri-partite agreement between the Ministry of Solidarity, Family and Social Insertion, the Public Prosecutor’s Office, and the Ministry of Youth, Culture, and Communications (MJCC). It outlines roles and responsibilities for child protection at decentralized levels. An amendment of the family code is underway with potential impact on child marriage and legal guardianship of children. Concurrently, reforms to the Penal Code and the Code of criminal procedure, addressing alternatives to detention and the age of criminal responsibility are pending parliamentary approval. Ahead of the implementation of these policies, important child protection concerns remain.  In 2023, child labor affected 110,000 children aged 7 to 17 (88,000 of which reside in rural areas).[8] In addition, 32,940 children were in conflict with the law and 11,000 children were living in residential care facilities.  Further progress is needed to accelerate implementation of the child protection protocol, increase the number of accredited social workers, improve access to integrated services, strengthen alternative care pathways, and address prevailing social norms.

Young people aged 15 to 24 make up 15.5%[9] of Morocco's population. In 2024, the Ministry of Youth rehabilitated half of all the closed youth facilities (71 of 146). These youth centers are increasingly platforms for delivering structured youth programmes, including those supported by UNICEF. In partnership with the Royal Moroccan Electronic Games Federation, the Ministry introduced electronic game clubs in its youth centers and is targeting 200 functional clubs. Furthermore, the national volunteer program Motatawi3 was launched, offering youths aged 18 to 22 opportunities for personal development and skills development in environmental stewardship, culture, and education[10].
