UNICEF Morocco completed the second year of its country programme implementation. Key results achieved contribute to the organization’s Strategic Plan (2022-2025) and its high-level goal areas.
 
Every child survives and thrives. The Health and Nutrition programme supports the Ministry of Health at central and regional levels in three strategic areas: improving access and utilization of primary health care in targeted areas; strengthening institutional capacities at decentralized levels; and promoting the adoption of positive family practices. In 2024, UNICEF Morocco collaborated with multiple departments in the MoHSP, regional health authorities, the National Initiative for Human Development (INDH), the World Health Organization and the World Bank. 
 
The National Immunization Programme, and the roll out of the WHO/UNICEF recommended Effective Vaccine Management approach, were prioritized as critical to improving access to quality primary health care.  This included technical and financial support for both “soft” programming and cold chain equipment to ensure vaccines are properly transported and stored to guarantee their potency, safety, and availability. Additional cold chain equipment, specifically 350 PQS (Performance, Quality and Safety) fridges were installed in 101 health facilities, which represent a total replacement rate of about 25 percent countrywide since 2023. Some 73 immunization health workers – a mix of trainers nationwide and select mid-level immunization managers – were oriented on best practices in programme, vaccine and cold chain management. Accompanying technical guidelines were also developed for additional trainings.  UNICEF Morocco provided procurement services for nine routine vaccines with a value of USD 9.6 million. Improvements in WASH in health facilities are ongoing. National WASH standards were developed and validated; these are essential for implementing, monitoring, and regulating services. They build on the baseline assessment conducted in 2022 and will inform the upgrading of health facilities progressively from minimum to intermediate to advanced standards.  
 
At decentralized level, two additional regional health taskforces (Souss Massa and Fès-Meknes) were accompanied to strengthen their planning, monitoring, and evaluation functions. Their draft child-centered regional health action plans by a range of stakeholders reflect context-relevant priorities.  UNICEF Morocco also contributed to the earthquake response in the office-wide target provinces (Chichaoua, Al Haouz, and Taroudant) with a focus on continuity of primary health care services through mobile health units. These mobile health units complemented the government response and focused on especially hard-to -reach communities. In 2024, over 22,000 people in remote and underserved communities benefitted from basic services with free distribution of essential drugs. Of these about 1,800 patients were referred to free specialized services in the neighboring town, and more than 3.600 children, adolescents and caregivers received mental health and psycho-social support. 
 
UNICEF worked with partners to increase positive family practices.  Vaccine misinformation has become an increasing challenge in Morocco leading to hesitancy and lowered vaccination coverage. Response measures highlighted the importance of vaccines and focused on building trust and confidence in vaccine safety and efficacy.  These included TV and radio spots in three languages, digital content campaigns with live streams, reels, and infographics, and outreach through health centers to promote the national vaccination calendar, reaching over 7 million people. Due attention was given to measles and low HPV vaccine uptake following its post-COVID-19 introduction. In addition, UNICEF contributed to a nationwide vaccination catch-up campaign, which continues to be conducted through schools. The campaign focuses on verifying and updating the vaccination status of children, working with communities to address gaps.   A "1000 Days" campaign was developed within the framework of the recently finalized nutrition SBC strategy. It covers optimal nutrition practices during a child’s first 1000 days through a multi-channel approach. Supported by MSPS, INDH, UNICEF, and the World Bank, the campaign reached 13.5 million people, including 1.2 million directly engaged in 36,000 group sessions. Survey results from a sample of 3,318 participants demonstrated strong message recall, with 95% remembering at least two key messages. The campaign’s success was driven by collaborative planning, high-quality content, and strong partner engagement.   
 
Every child learns. The education programme uses a life-cycle approach to work with partners at all levels of the ministries of education and youth, the Higher Council on Education, and NGOs to extend preschool coverage, reduce school drop-out particularly amongst girls, and support national efforts to improve quality in teaching and learning.
 
Despite government generalization of preschool education, an estimated 20% of children aged 4 to 5 years do not access services. In response, UNICEF Morocco provided technical assistance to the Ministry of National Education, Preschool, and Sports (MENPS) to develop scenarios adapted to children residing in remote settings. The resulting modelisation informed by international benchmarks, is currently being tested in the Oriental region and considers factors such as rotating educators and providing adapted transportation. Key stakeholders including foundations, associations, and preschool service providers participated in training sessions to understand and implement the approaches.    In addition, UNICEF worked with three regions (Souss-Massa, Marrakech Safi and Tangier-Tetouan-Al Hoceima) to create a "Positive Parenting for Learning" programme targeting caregivers in rural areas. The programme enhances parents' skills to foster a positive learning environment at home. Validated by the MENPS, the content is delivered through two practical guides: an overarching framework and a practical tool containing activities to organize with parents. In collaboration with the Higher Council on Education, a Measuring Early Learning and Quality Outcomes (MELQO) Study is nearing completion; it assesses school readiness by evaluating the quality of pre-primary education. For the younger cohort of children aged 0-3, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the MJCC to develop norms and standards in daycare centers. 
 
Some 294,458 learners dropped out of school in 2023-2024, of which 113,777 were girls. UNICEF continued to invest in a multi-sector model for retaining adolescent girls in school. The programme uses multidisciplinary approaches and leverages a coalition of partners at local level to identify problems and solutions for retaining girls in school. In the six target districts (with an additional two added in 2024), the programme trains front line service providers and partners on gender equality and girls’ rights, supports girl-led advocacy committees, and encourages adolescent girls and young women to engage in participatory and action research on the topics most important to them. In addition, young women are involved in skills development programmes for learning, personal empowerment, employability through UNICEF-supported programmes. Finally, given the development of a number of key policies with impact for young women and girls (family policy, review of the child protection policy and programme of action), stakeholders were trained in advocacy to influence policies that should be responsive to the situation of girls and young women. Collectively, these have resulted in a reduction of school drop out of an average of 3.2% in the 6 districts.
 
The programme also focused on young people to gain transferable life skills through formal structures such as the network of second chance schools and through extracurricular programming through the Ministry of Youth. Key activities included curriculum review for life skills education and integrating both UPSHIFT methodologies for social entrepreneurship and the use of the adolescent kit for civic engagement in national programmes.  In addition, U-Report for youth voice, participation in UNICEF's Gamechanger Coalition (gaming with girls in mind), and youth-led participatory research through national programmes are giving young people meaningful space to engage with peers in local communities, identify community-based issues and to engage effectively to propose solutions. Through these programmes, UNICEF directly reached over 44,500 adolescents and young people. 
 
UNICEF Morocco supported the MENPS strategy in two of the regions affected by the earthquake. This support was structured around three areas of intervention: 1) the rehabilitation of schools to ensure a safe and protective learning environment for children, 2) educational support to maintain educational continuity, and 3) psychosocial support to help students and educational staff overcome the trauma related to the event. As a result, 58 schools have benefited from rehabilitation or installation of modular units,(40 primary schools, 18 middle schools)to enable the start of the school year for over 19,500  children in a protective environment. In complement, 945 teachers were trained on pedagogical approaches to deliver catch-up programmes in earthquake affected areas, and over 11,000 primary school students received direct learning support. While the first semester of 2024 focused mainly on support for students in certifying years, subsequent months expanded support to all learners, regardless of their level, in the targeted communities. The educational support is based on the national adaptation of Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL).  UNICEF Morocco worked closely with the MENPS in developing a model for psychosocial support in which social workers work with teachers to manage post-traumatic stress, manage emotions in post-crisis areas and identify cases in need of further psycho-social support. This model will be included in an emergency preparedness kit that will cover lessons learned from the earthquake response, intervention plans, emergency exercises for schools and other tools.  
 
Every child is protected. UNICEF and partners in Morocco focus on four priorities in child protection: the expansion of local child protection systems, supporting the justice system to be increasingly responsive to the needs of children in contact with the law, ensuring children on the move access quality services, and that families and communities are equipped with tools and approaches to prevent violence. These are pursued in collaboration with a wide range of line ministries, foundations, CSOs, human rights entities, and UN agencies.
 
In response to the Head of Government’s instructions of 2019, which stipulated the need and standards for provincial child protection systems (DTIPE), 82 gubernatorial decisions were made to establish child protection committees, building on the 59 reported last year. To date only 23 of these are operational illustrating the gaps in child protection. These mechanisms for inter-sectoral coordination and local governance are a critical means for implementation of the national child protection policy. UNICEF Morocco provided technical assistance for the launching of a select number of committees in the regions of Tanger-Tétouan-El Hoceima, Souss-Massa, Marrakech-Safi, and Beni Mellal-Kénifra. These meetings convened child protection actors and local authorities to assume increased responsibility for consistent and predictable case management for vulnerable children. 
 
UNICEF Morocco contributed to coordination between authorities in justice, child and social protection actors. In 2024, the Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Ministry of Solidarity, Social Integration and Family, the Ministry of Youth, together with ministries of education, youth, labor, and health validated and adopted a protocol on decentralizing child protection.  The protocol clarifies roles and responsibilities of actors, formalizes the mechanisms for communication and information sharing between parties for effective case management at decentralized level. It strengthens the role of social work within case management ensuring that only as a last resort are children placed in child protection centers under the auspices of the ministry of youth. In addition, UNICEF provided technical assistance to the Office of the Public Prosecutor to develop tools such as performance indicators assisting magistrates to track children involved in proceedings, as well as modern techniques to engage with children in contact with law, and use of videoconferencing for hearings.

Together with local authorities and CSO partners facilitated 631 migrants access to basic social services, temporary accommodation, and socio-entrepreneurship activities targeting youth. In the sub-regions of Oujda, Tetouan, and Agadir over 104 local child protection actors shared information on care practices for children on the move and worked to standardize their approaches. A Letter of Understanding signed between UNICEF and UNHCR is providing a framework to jointly support youth seeking refugee status, among other actions. And, UNICEF, IOM and UNCHR, collaborated to hold the second meeting of the International Data Alliance for Children on the Move (IDAC) in Rabat which was hosted by the High Commission for Planning. Morocco’s experience in including migrant persons in the census exercise as community liaisons was highlighted in the global meeting which reviewed data challenges at country, regional and global level.
 
National partners worked to systematize the prevention of violence against children through key policy milestones. For the midterm review of the child protection policy (PNMO, 2023-2026) and the development of the next implementation plan, UNICEF facilitated consultations with stakeholders from public institutions, NGOs, children and young people. Similarly, technical support was provided to the ministry of solidarity as it developed the first ever Social Family Policy. The policy is designed to uphold the rights of each family member as they play their role in prevention and protection, while continuing to safeguarding individual rights. A training programme on promoting positive parenting was finalized, targeting CSOs partners in three regions (Béni Mellal-Khénifra, Marrakech, Safi, Tangier-Tétouan-Al Hoceima). The programme seeks to raise awareness gender equality, promoting non-violent discipline, and incorporating appropriate parenting practices in times of crisis. Through the networks of NGOs, the programme has reached 11,904 families in three regions.

In the aftermath of the earthquake, UNICEF facilitated 15 safe spaces for children in the affected provinces of Taroudant and Al Haouz, where 6,299 people including 3,677 children received community-based mental health and psychosocial support services (including services provided through mobile clinics). In addition, UNICEF worked with partners to ensure continued operations of child protection units and child protection support centers (CAPE). These facilities play an essential role in the case management system for children ahead of the establishment of the local child protection systems in those regions. UNICEF also contributed to the new National Psycho-Trauma Child Center, in partnership with the National Observatory for Child Rights, to provide specialized care to children affected by the earthquake.  Furthermore, UNICEF facilitated training sessions for professionals, including doctors and social workers, and developed a psychosocial support manual in collaboration with university partners. Training of trainers was provided to social workers, strengthening the long-term child protection system while addressing immediate emergency needs.  Some 777vulnerable children and women were identified by AMANE Foundation and the Orient-Occident Foundation and referred to support services. 
 
Every child has access to inclusive social protection. The social inclusion programme responds to priorities in evidence generation, expansion of social protection, public finance and local governance. As a cross-cutting area of work, partnerships are wide-ranging and include the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the High Commission of Planning, UN agencies, and local authorities. 
 
UNICEF Morocco invested in two flagship evidence products. For the 7th General Census, UNICEF supported the digitalization of the exercise, the participation of 102 migrants and refugees as community liaisons to improve data collection, and the inclusion of social protection questions.  The census will provide information on population distribution, demographics, current access to basic social services, and much more to guide public policy. In preparation for the 2025 Multi-Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7), UNICEF worked with partners to train local teams on the methodology and tools for data collection. The country office provided technical assistance for the survey questions and ensured the survey was translated into three Moroccan dialects. The results from the MICS7 will provide data for nearly 40% of all SDG indicators. A new partnership between with the HCP and the MoHSP will improve data sharing between the two entities, support the next Situation Analysis Report on children as well as the third measurement of multidimensional child poverty. In addition, Morocco completed and disseminated its Climate Landscape Analysis for Children report in the presence of line ministries, development partners and NGOs. The report offers recommendations on working with institutions to make social services more resilient, integrating climate chance education into school curricula and establishing partnerships in climate-related advocacy.
 
Over 80% of children in Morocco now benefit from a monthly child allowance as social protection guaranteed by law. Over the years, UNICEF contributed to this outcome through costing analysis, advocacy for universal coverage, facilitation of south-south exchange, and experience sharing between national and international stakeholders. In 2024, UNICEF together with the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the World Bank launched a study to operationalize the new agency managing social assistance focusing on procedures for beneficiaries and decentralized approaches (‘cash plus’ activities).  In parallel, UNICEF Morocco, in partnership with ESCWA, invested in significant advocacy across sectors on the integral role of social workers in an effective to the social protection system. Building on this advocacy will be a priority in 2025.
 
In response to the earthquake, UNICEF put in place a multi-year programme of response in three of the most affected provinces with a target of 50 communities and 63,000 children. The related action plans complement Government actions and focus on integrated responses for children by institutional and CSO partners. Result areas focus primarily on education continuity in addition to health, child protection, psychosocial support, and WASH services. In addition to facilitating access urgently needed services for children and their families, the programme is consolidating lessons across interventions areas for standardizing emergency preparedness and response. The emerging models are relevant to the Moroccan context and will progressively inform national programmes such as social assistance programmes linking cash to services and referrals. These efforts seek to ensure the sustainability of social protection in line with Framework Law 09-21. 
 
UNICEF Morocco continued to deepen its evaluation function. Internally, UNICEF completed the evaluation of the migration result area as stipulated in the country programme’s costed evaluation plan. The findings were debated during a stakeholder forum and shared during a partner roundtable. In a continuous effort to support the institutionalization of evaluation in public policy, a strategic roundtable co-convened with the Moroccan Association for Evaluation assessed the state of the national evaluation function by reviewing existing capacities, methodologies being used and concluding with an agenda to address gaps.

In 2024, UNICEF Morocco invested substantively in shared-value partnerships to strengthen alliances and joint action for child rights.  

The Country Office mobilized 10 million USD to address critical children’s needs through development and humanitarian interventions in line with the country programme, including UNICEF’s response to the 2023 earthquake. The top three donors to UNICEF Morocco were USAID, Japan, and the European Union; and key partners through the national committees (France, Germany, US, Spain, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, Italy, United Kingdom, and Norway) were instrumental in enabling UNICEF to contribute to the earthquake response thanks to flexible funding.  This flexibility was critical to ensuring that UNICEF’s contribution was appropriate and oriented towards sustainable approaches. Furthermore, UNICEF Morocco launched its first Friends of UNICEF strategic dialogue with the participation of over fifteen funding partners around the themes of youth development, migration, and other programme issues. The dialogue offered a platform for joint advocacy, evidence sharing, and collaboration. Through a speaker series, L’InvitE de l’UNICEF, discussions between UNICEF staff and ambassadors, ministers, and leading figures in national institutions facilitated exchange on progress for children in Morocco and the joint work required to address remaining challenges. 

UNICEF Morocco contributed to the priorities of line ministries, especially around evidence generation, policy development, and setting standards. For example, engagement with the Ministry of Youth has shifted from one focused on implementation of activities to technical support for developing norms and standards for daycares, mainstreaming U-Report for youth engagement, social entrepreneurship (UPSHIFT), and the integration of a digital youth portal (pass jeunes) offering referrals to youth-focused health services.

In 2024, UNICEF Morocco operationalized its local governance frameworks. MCO actively collaborated with decentralized authorities and community stakeholders in the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region and three provinces highly impacted by the 2023 earthquake. These efforts were guided by four multi-sector agreements, complete with detailed action plans, signed with the Ministry of Interior leadership in each sub-region. The related technical meetings and strategic annual reviews have created a common agenda for reaching the most vulnerable children and fostered trust through the collaboration across social sectors.  The localized approach to planning and implementation has given stakeholders a more complete picture of the challenges facing children and has triggered new areas of work in WASH, community engagement, and establishing effective feedback mechanisms. UNICEF Morocco also provided trainings for a wide range of participating stakeholders in child rights, results-based management, accountability to affected populations, and human-centered programme design. 

Partnerships with CSOs such as AMSED, FOO, TADAMON, AMANE Foundation extended beyond direct service delivery and offer service models that can inform system-wide approaches. This was the case for mobile health clinics and roving social behavior change teams  that provided services and information in the most remote areas of the earthquake affected zones. It also applies to the creation of child friendly spaces that have transitioned to communal recreational spaces offering linkages to longer-term care and case management for children and families. Similarly, the comprehensive services delivered by NGOs for children on the move, continue to demonstrate how holistic care for children can be transitioned to institutional arrangements.

UNICEF Morocco and partners promoted child rights through various channels. In collaboration with four regional education authorities, 50 child rights committees were trained and accompanied in advocacy. A draft advocacy guide was developed to scale this approach country wide. For World Children’s Day, a collaboration with the National Observatory for Child Rights, and the Moroccan Children’s Parliament resulted in a child-led press conference around the results of a U Report survey on how children in Morocco perceive their rights. National Youth Advocate, Meryem Amjoun championed the rights of children to quality education during key activities of the UN General Assembly and the Summit of the Future. With the National Human Rights Council (CNDH) and Bayti Association, 168 civil society organizations received training on advocating for human rights and child protection with a focus on gender equality and the prevention of gender-based violence. 

UNICEF continues to partner with sister agencies through the UN Cooperation Framework coordinated by the UN Resident Coordinator’s Office. UNICEF contributes substantively to the Operations Management Team providing technical assistance for establishing a new information database solution for UN vendors and other common services, leading the results group on social protection and the cross-cutting group on monitoring and evaluation. Similarly, the partnership between UNICEF, IOM and UNHCR is progressing around joint action plans, improving data for children on the move, and advocacy for services.  

Morocco accords great importance to south-south cooperation with a particular focus on partnership with African countries. Preparation for the second international conference on south-south cooperation and ECD in Africa to be held in January 2025, is fostering a knowledge and practice network to convene African countries around promising practice and policy as they scale access to quality early learning. In addition, strong collaboration with UNESCWA provided advocacy and capacity-building for government social sectors in social protection systems, through South-South knowledge exchange (Chile, Brazil, Tunisia and Jordan).

UNICEF expanded its partnership with young people both internally and externally. The second cohort of UNICEF’s advisory committee engages regularly with UNICEF’s programming teams to share ideas around milestone programme activities and events. The U-Report initiative, now embedded in the Ministry of Youth’s engagement strategy, registered 38,500 subscribers. The U-Reporters gathered inputs from 3,500 young people to share their feedback on the services, workshops and trainings offered by the Ministry of Youth. Similarly, 931 young people shared their insights on draft child protection policies. To mark the first anniversary of the earthquake, a select group of young people from both the affected communities and other regions of Morocco took part in an art residency programme. Their social commentary on the impact of the earthquake was shared through podcasts, art pieces, and theatre through an art festival in partnership with the Hiba Foundation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The challenges facing children are multiple. Global and regional economic volatility, political developments in the region impacting migration, and increasing climate shocks have a disproportionate impact on children, especially the most vulnerable. Where children reside (urban or rural) their socio-economic circumstances, and their access to quality social services all determine the impact of these external shocks as demonstrated by the 2023 earthquake. Across the country, pathways from quality education to meaningful employment are increasingly constrained for girls and young women. Similarly, child protection systems which are well outlined in national policies and frameworks continue to be inadequately implemented, hampered by the lack of service and coordination required at central, regional and community level. 

At the same time, access to information referring communities to existing services is varied, dependent on literacy, access to mobile phones and the proliferation of rumors on social media platforms and others. The persistent hesitancy around vaccines for children show the impact of mistrust even when information is delivered from traditionally accepted sources. And despite the ambition of ongoing national reforms – in education, primary health care and earthquake reconstruction – the pace of their implementation has the potential to impede gains that list Morocco among the 20 countries globally making progress in achieving child-related SDGs.   
Over the past year, the Country Office has reflected on several lessons learned with partners.


UNICEF’s continued presence and proximity in regions and communities is critical. It allows the Country Office to respond appropriately during external shocks with an understanding of social services available, local partners and their capacities to react at scale, and challenges of local communities. In addition, Morocco’s progress in creating social safety nets requires greater focus on those at risk of being left behind in education, child protection, health and nutrition through innovative service models (ie. ECE service models in low density areas), advocacy and partnerships. 
Secondly, continued analysis of the situation of children should be an ongoing priority to fill pressing data gaps. The 2025 MICS results combined with the completed census, present an unprecedented opportunity to review programming assumptions, and set baseline data for regional workplans. 
As outlined in UNICEF Morocco’s 2024 CLAC report, the severity of climate shocks, supporting resilient social services is an increasing priority for line ministries
Effective integrated and multisectoral programming needs to prioritize common cross-cutting strategies. In the earthquake response, progressively harmonizing referral pathways, psychosocial support approaches, community engagement, and advocacy will help improve outcomes for children. 
Finally ensuring community feedback loops and reflections around lessons learned will support improved programming.   
 
Moving forward, UNICEF will reflect on these in the following ways:

The country office will sharpen ongoing programming models that are focused on reaching children at risk of being left behind: contributing to universal coverage of preschool, wrap-around services for adolescent girls to stay in school, acceleration of local child protection systems, creating demand for primary health care services, and continued advocacy for social services to accompany the significant progress Morocco has made in ensuring an effective social protection safety net. 
Deepen the localization agenda through services and supplies. For example, identification of a local service provider for the installation, warehousing, and transportation of health refrigerators resulted in a cost-savings of 205,000 USD in comparison to an international vendor. Continuing to map and leverage local markets in a context like Morocco would yield additional resources for children.
Deepen social behavior change programming. This would primarily be anchored around regional and local actors – authorities, NGOs and community leaders to improve capacities and community engagement. This effort would focus on emergency preparedness including health security, improved feedback mechanisms for communities to strengthen community services, and access for adolescent girls to education and skills.
Expand the focus on climate resilient social services with an emphasis on WASH in schools and in health facilities against a context of growing water scarcity. In parallel UNICEF will work with partners and with the education system to integration climate awareness and civic engagement through school clubs.
Facilitating a flagship partnership around social entrepreneurship and apprenticeship programmes with the private and public sectors. With an emphasis on supporting second chance schools to provide pathways to market-friendly skills and careers, particularly for young women, this initiative will be a key pillar of UNICEF Morocco’s partnership strategy in the next two years.
Accompanying Morocco’s priority on south-south cooperation by focusing on pre-school education in partnership with African countries. This will contribute to implementing UNICEF’s Africa Strategy and provide a platform for countries to share experiences as they reach more children with quality preschool services.
Further efficiency gains in operations could also be informed by recent innovations such as the transition to a comprehensive digital banking solution and automation of invoice processing among others.
A mid-term strategic reflection of the country programme that reviews data from the census and MICS and helps to sharpen the country programme’s implementation approaches, target communities, and offers an agile structure that assures the country office is 'fit for purpose'.

In 2024, the Sultanate of Oman experienced sustained economic growth, due in large part to the enabling legal and policy frameworks. This includes ‘Oman Vision 2040’, which seeks to promote inclusive growth, enhance job creation, and develop human capital. Overall, based on the Oman’s second Voluntary National Review 2024, the Sultanate accomplished remarkable achievements vis-a-vis the Sustainable Development Goals, with an overall indicator score of 82.2 percent[1].
The government also continued monitoring progress against the 2023 Concluding Observations of the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC). In addition, in its Concluding Observations on Oman’s fourth periodic report issued in February 2024, the CEDAW Committee welcomed several legislative reforms enacted over the seven years since its previous (2017) report, including laws relating to gender equality, social protection, school education, and labour. The Committee also welcomed a number of policy reforms and programmes, including the National Women Strategy, the creation of the National Centre for Women’s and Children’s Health, Vision 2024, the 10th Five Year Development Plan and the National Digital Economy Programme. 
Oman's Gross Domestic Product is projected to grow by 0.7 per cent by the end of 2024[2]. The World Bank forecasts that Oman's economic growth will accelerate in 2025-2026, with an average projected growth of 2.4 per cent and 2.8 per cent respectively, driven by government reforms and increased investment in non-oil sectors. However, GDP per capita slightly decreased in 2023, from $23,665 to $21,549[3].
Oman's population stood at 5.2 million, with 43 per cent being expatriates, and 92.8 per cent living in urban areas[4]. In 2023, the total fertility rate reached 2.0 births per woman aged 15-49, where the Omani women recorded 2.9[5]. Young people aged 0-19 made up 31 per cent of the population, evenly distributed between males and females. However, there are significant differences in the sex ratio of Omanis (101 males per 100 females) and expatriates (344 males per 100 females), driven by inward migration servicing labour market requirements.[6]
In total, 2.7 million workers were employed in Oman by the end of 2023, of whom over two-thirds were expatriates and one-third were Omani, though it is likely this will change in light of the government’s ‘Omanisation’ policy. Gender differentials in the labour force are quite marked: fully 81.6 per cent of those employed are males, while the unemployment rate, which stands at 3.2, is only 1.7 per cent for males compared to 9.3 per cent for females. Unemployment rates are highest among holders of higher diploma degrees, at 8.9 per cent (18.3 per cent for females and 2.9 per cent for males) [7]. 
Oman has a national system whereby all the births are recorded, as evidenced by the universal birth registration rates for both male and female newborns. While government efforts to improve health services have led to sharp decreases in maternal mortality rate, reaching 17.1 per 100,000 live births in 2022 compared to 45.7 in 2021, the rate rose again to 19.9 per 100,000 in 2023. The infant mortality rate fell from 8.8 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022 to 8.5 in 2023, and under-five mortality from 11.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2022 to 10.8 deaths per 1,000 in 2023.[8]
Oman maintained universal enrolment for primary education, with gender parity. Average class size was 26 students, with 13 students per teacher in 2023/24[9]. A recent survey found that in eight out of the 11 governorates, female students had higher achievement rates than males[10]. While the 2023 Education law enshrines the right of children to be enrolled in a pre-primary school programme, enrolment in early education remained at only 57 per cent in 2022[11].
A major development in 2024 was the launch of a revised Social Protection programme that included a monthly universal child benefit, cash grants for persons with disabilities, and maternity leaves insurance. These changes are intended to enhance the social welfare framework in Oman by providing a wide range of benefits to promote families’ well-being. Additionally, the 2023 Labour Law has restructured leave provisions to increase entitlement to sick leave and maternity leave and introduce paternity leave and special leave without pay (subject to employer consent).
Currently, efforts are undergoing to strengthen the national child protection system, including case management. Child Protection Committees (CPCs) set up to prevent and address child abuse dealt with 2,281 cases during 2023. Additionally. the national child protection hotline (1100) received 1,062 calls (591 males, 471 females). More than half were cases related to neglect, with the next most frequent physical abuse, psychological abuse and sexual abuse.[12]
In conclusion, the Sultanate of Oman made significant progress in improving the status of children and women, creating a more inclusive and supportive environment for all children in the country.

In 2024, UNICEF Oman continued its efforts to enhance social services and benefits for children across various sectors, with a focus on improving social protection, early childhood development, education, child protection and nutrition. Additionally, UNICEF Oman supported the implementation of CRC recommendations through the provision of technical assistance, while also advocating for others, including the transmission of nationality from mothers married to non-Omani men and raising the minimum age of criminal responsibility.
A recent milestone in the Sultanate of Oman was the endorsement of the new Social Protection Law in 2023, which merged contributory and non-contributory systems, marking a significant milestone in providing a comprehensive social protection system. This system includes universal child benefits and cash benefits for vulnerable groups such as persons with disabilities, the elderly, and maternity benefits. The law also underpins the establishment of the ‘Social Protection Fund’. 
In 2024, UNICEF Oman focused on providing technical assistance to the Social Protection Fund (SPF) to implement the new Social Protection Law while maintaining a strong child and equity lens, by supporting the development of  the persons with disabilities eligibility criteria to ensure inclusion and to foster a cross-sectoral approach focused on disability inclusion, supporting capacity and system strengthening and showcasing Oman’s progress on the social protection programmes regionally and globally. UNICEF, in partnership with the ILO, plans to document the process of enacting the law and the successful rollout of cash benefits, providing actionable recommendations and lessons learned for future initiatives and sharing good practices regionally and globally.
Given the scale of Oman’s vision and the nascent stage of its social protection reforms, UNICEF supported SPF to hold a TRANSFORM training event, offering foundational knowledge on social protection systems and their components. The training covered essential components of a comprehensive social protection system, including legal frameworks, beneficiary identification, programme administration, governance, management information systems, financial management, and monitoring and evaluation. This training was intended to support the Social Protection Fund’s and wide range of social protection stakeholders to adopt a common understanding and help foster integration.  
In June, OCO brought its regional and global experts to engage with SPF to help identify emerging strategic priorities on social protection and disability inclusion. A regional mission from UNICEF’s Middle East and North Africa Regional Office (MENARO) visited Oman to discuss collaboration with the SPF in designing schemes for persons with disabilities, establishing a robust monitoring and evaluation system, and introducing the cash plus program for disability services. The goal is to streamline services and provide technical advice on determining eligibility. 
In recognition of a child’s early years as a critical window of opportunity for achieving the highest return in child development including nutrition and parenting, UNICEF Oman collaborated with the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD) and the Ministry of Education (MoE) to scale up early childhood development (ECD) and early childhood education (ECE) services via a series of technical studies. These studies aimed to support the scaling up of integrated ECD (IECD) services. Three analytical pieces were developed, including a costing model and financing scenarios, a roadmap for scaling up services nationwide, and a policy framework. This work involved a comprehensive analysis of the current ECD situation and provided scenarios for scaling up an IECD model. The MoSD also proposed the establishment of a center of excellence in Muscat to provide guidance to service providers and enhance their capacity at both the Muscat and Governorate levels.
The roadmap outlines the pillars and stages required for the expansion. This study should inform the establishment of 20 centers offering comprehensive ECD services across Oman to all children up to age 6, as well as children with disabilities up to age 8. These centers will offer counseling services to parents and enhance the capacities of ECD staff. The goal is to ensure that all children in Oman benefit from ECD services and to raise parental awareness of this crucial phase of child development, particularly targeting vulnerable children in low-income families and remote areas at a reasonable cost.
In addition, MENARO supported advancements in the nutrition sector through a workshop with the Ministry of Health (MoH) to discuss key issues, their causes and interventions needed, including micronutrients and complementary feeding. A field visit was also conducted to understand the sub-national context. The regional office technical mission also identified obesity as an emerging issue to be addressed. Discussions are ongoing for a planned national nutrition survey, with OCO planning to provide technical support to generate evidence on child nutrition.
Another key focus area in 2024 was the promotion of positive parenting tips and methods through a dedicated capacity-building programme with the MoH. This initiative is intended to enhance the skills of health educators and social workers in primary health-care facilities, equipping them to better support parents in their daily interactions. The programme has focused on fostering an enabling environment for parents by promoting healthy practices in child protection, nutrition, health, inclusivity, and early learning. By strengthening these capacities, the programme contributed to improving ECD outcomes and positive behavior change among families.
For ECE, in support of the 2023 Education Law that stipulates the child’s right to early education, UNICEF supported the MoE to develop a costing, financing and investment case study, which details four scenarios and policy requirements to scale up ECE. The study outlines the costs, financing strategies, investment case, and provided an implementation framework for universalizing one year of pre-primary education for children aged five to six by 2040. 
Following the completion of the ECE and IECD studies, cross-sectoral high-level meetings were held with the Minister of Social Development and Undersecretaries of the MoE to present the findings. The ECE study has been approved and is awaiting political clearance. The final IECD study is scheduled to be finalized and launched in 2025, when UNICEF will support MoSD and MoE to implement the proposed scenarios in both studies, and advocate provision of the required support and resources.
Part of the advocacy and to promote the knowledge sharing and exposure of the Omani officials, UNICEF Oman organized a study tour to Tunisia in March with the participation of representatives from the ministries of education, social development, and health to learn from Tunisia's experience in ECD reforms and programmes of, disability inclusion, and social protection. The Omani delegation has compiled a report outlining all recommended actions, which has been presented to the National Committee of Family Affairs.
Also with MOE, UNICEF Oman embarked on an evaluation study MoE to assess the Child-Friendly Education (CFE) initiative. The evaluation is intended to evaluate the initiative's alignment with the national framework, process effectiveness, inclusiveness, and develop actionable recommendations and lessons learned. The evaluation, which is expected to be completed by the end of 2025, will inform the way forward for advancing CFE.
Protecting children from violence, abuse and neglect is a key priority in Oman. UNICEF Oman has widely advocated for the importance of adopting a multi-sectoral systems approach to foster collaboration and help advance a systematic approach to respond to and prevent child protection violations. In that regard, MOSD and OCO convened a workshop in June to present the updated child protection manual in the presence of representatives from the ministries of education, health, academia, hospitals, civil society, the human rights commission, and security entities such as the Royal Oman Police and Public Prosecution among others to present the draft manual.  
The Manual is designed for establishing a unified framework to respond to child protection issues across child protection stakeholders and granting space for community engagement and promotion enabling behaviors to address relevant issues. The updated Manual will create consensus across child protection stakeholders on child protection abuses and integrate referral systems and case management procedures to create a clear and unified process for reporting and responding to abuse cases. It also outlines the legal framework governing child protection in Oman at both national and international levels, detailing the roles of various ministries. The Manual categorizes levels of abuse and provides specific mechanisms and timelines for treatment and case closure, to promptly address all cases with a focus on the well-being of children, including within the justice system. Two rounds of revision with partners were conducted and the manual is now in final draft. Once finalized, OCO will conduct a Training of Trainers to enhance the capacity of social workers in implementing the manual. Additionally, UNICEF will work closely with MoSD to introduce automation for case management and referrals.
Additionally, UNICEF has partnered with the MoSD to explore regional experiences in establishing youth participation processes in Oman through a cross-sectoral Child Parliament Committee. This initiative has facilitated a knowledge exchange between UNICEF offices and national government counterparts from Iraq and Morocco offering insights into their advanced approaches for creating sustainable dialogue mechanisms between children and policymakers.
UNICEF Oman, in collaboration with other United Nations agencies (ILO, UNDP, UNFPA, and UNESCO), facilitated the participation of the Omani delegation in a high-level meeting held in June 2024 in Tunisia. The meeting focused on supporting young people's learning, skills development, and transition to decent work, with a specific emphasis on girls and young women. The Omani delegation included representatives from the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Youth (MCSY) and the Youth Centre, along with a young Omani who represented Oman as a Youth Advisory Group member. During the meeting, Oman reaffirmed its commitments made during the 2022 high-level meeting.
Meanwhile, stakeholders were provided with support in advocacy, evidence, research initiatives, and capacity strengthening to promote evidence-based policies for children. Documenting Oman's success in eliminating mother-to-child transmission (EMTCT) of HIV and syphilis has seen deepened collaboration with WHO Oman. The final paper is awaiting endorsement from the MoH for publication and dissemination. Together with the Environment Authority (EA), UNICEF has also embarked on the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), which aims to generate evidence related to the impact of climate change on children and youth across various sectors, providing actionable recommendations to the government. A national technical working group has been established to oversee the implementation of the CLAC, with the goal of completing it by 2025.
Another key research project currently underway is with Oman's leading academic institution, Sultan Qaboos University (SQU), to generate research on child rights. An agreement was made to collaborate on a special edition of a SQU Journal focused on research on child rights encouraging researchers to contribute topics related to children in Oman to promote more research on children and strengthen collaboration with academia. This has resulted in securing over 20 quality paper proposals. Work will continue in 2025 to support researchers in conducting their research and collaborating with SQU towards the publication of the journal and organizing a scientific conference in 2025.
In terms of data, UNICEF continued its advocacy efforts related to the implementation of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7). Various high-level meetings were conducted with the National Center of Statistics and Information (NCSI) CEO to emphasize importance of the MICS in analysing social sector indicators and SDGs progress. Meetings were also held with sectoral ministries including MoH, MoE, and the Social Protection Fund to present relevant indicators and promote cross-sectoral collaboration. Unfortunately, a planned cross-sectoral workshop led by Istidama, affiliated with the Ministry of Finance, was not held due to a change in leadership. While a final decision on conducting the MICS is still pending, the NCSI demonstrated interest in a phone survey focusing on ECD and ‘Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET)’ modules. Agreement was also reached for capacity-building training on data analysis for line ministries. Other initiatives underway include a potential survey on social behaviour change, laying the groundwork for future awareness campaigns to be more tailored to the specific needs and realities of Omani families.
In response to the recent floods in the Sultanate that tragically resulted in the deaths of children, a workplan was developed in consultation with the Regional Office that include knowledge exchange activities. This plan included organizing a webinar in partnership with the MoE to share UNICEF's experience in developing school construction guidelines. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Information (MoI), the MoSD, and the MoE to raise awareness and create a public guide on protecting and guiding children during flash flooding.
As for the OCO communications, UNICEF Oman achieved significant progress in partnerships, advocacy, and awareness to promote children’s rights and well-being. With over 500 media clippings in national and international outlets, UNICEF amplified its work in Oman and beyond, showcasing its commitment to advancing children’s welfare and amplifying the UNICEF brand. UNICEF Oman’s social media platforms experienced notable growth, reaching 52,000 followers by the end of the year, an increase of 2,865. With a reach of 123,000 and over 300,000 impressions, digital platforms became instrumental in promoting children’s rights and fostering public engagement. In addition, UNICEF organized capacity-building training for media professionals and government representatives to strengthen ethical reporting on children’s issues. This initiative created a network of media advocates. Another milestone was the localization of the Parenting Campaign, in collaboration with the MoI. This initiative highlighted the importance of parenting and mental health in creating nurturing environments for children. 
World Children’s Day celebrations were a key highlight, marking the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The localized ‘Listen to the Future’ campaign featured two roundtables that empowered children to share their perspectives directly with leaders, including the head of the Omani Human Rights Commission, the Minister of Health, and regional governors. UNICEF also partnered with Virgin Radio for a child-led radio takeover and engaged community leaders in creating advocacy videos, extending the campaign’s impact.
UNICEF Oman had the honor of hosting three regional network meetings this year focusing on health and nutrition, climate change, and social protection themes. Leveraging the presence of technical experts, several side meetings were organized for the Deputy Regional Director and regional advisors to engage with high-level officials and provide their expertise on various topics.
As 2024 came to a close, OCO began developing the new Country Programme Document (CPD) for 2026-30, with a Strategic Moment of Reflection held with key government counterparts, civil society partners and sister UN agencies. Work is currently underway to finalize the CPD, which will be shared with the Government of Oman for approval before submission to the Executive Board in September 2025.

Given the importance of advancing integration and system strengthening, UNICEF continued to promote cross-sectoral working approaches and convened partners from across a wide spectrum of national stakeholders, including the ministries of health, education, and social development for all various streams of work on ECD, ECE, child protection, social protection and social behaviour change (SBC). 
In addition to on-going strong partnerships with those key ministries, a new crucial partnership that emerged in 2024 was with the newly established SPF. UNICEF forged strong collaboration and maintained a regular connection to support the swift rolling out of the Social Protection Law, offering technical assistance and advice. Of relevance to this area of work is the enhanced complementarity with ILO. Another new and strategic partnership is that with the EA on the CLAC, which is laying the foundation for cross-sectoral engagement and advocacy on climate change. UNICEF also continued to work with the NCSI, exploring opportunities related to key MICS modules and a planned knowledge, attitudes and practices survey on SBC for 2025, as well as a planned training event intended to support data use and analysis by national stakeholders.
To build alliances and foster the delivery of results for children, UNICEF engaged with a wider set of actors to raise awareness on child rights, including in academia. These efforts included holding webinars and roundtable discussions in several strategic fora, including the Royal Academy of Management and Sultan Qaboos University, Oman’s leading leadership institute and premier academic institution respectively. In addition, UNICEF also developed a new partnership with SQU to advance research on child rights and support the next generation of researchers and practitioners with guidance and opportunities to work and publish through a special journal edition on child rights. 
Additionally, UNICEF Oman deepened its engagement with a diverse range of partners to advance children’s rights and well-being, including business leaders, civil society organizations, and philanthropic stakeholders. One of the key highlights was a high-level visit to UNICEF’s Supply Division warehouse in Copenhagen, the largest humanitarian aid warehouse in the world. This visit, with the participation of members of the Business Leadership Circle and other prominent stakeholders, showcased UNICEF’s global supply chain capabilities and highlighted opportunities for the private sector to support sustainable solutions for children. This engagement not only fostered private sector interest, but also reinforced UNICEF’s position as a trusted partner in mobilizing resources and driving transformative change.
To further explore the role of philanthropy in advancing child welfare, UNICEF organized a dedicated philanthropy mission. This initiative brought a global expert to Oman to share UNICEF’s leading experiences in leveraging philanthropy to create impact in both humanitarian and development contexts through a dedicated session given to local foundations and civil society associations to support build their capacity with systematic, sustainable programming. UNICEF’s philanthropic mission also established strategic prospects for resource mobilization within the country. These efforts are designed to cultivate partnerships with local foundations to secure sustainable support for UNICEF’s programmes globally.
Moreover, UNICEF also partnered with the American Chamber of Commerce to promote implementation of family-friendly policies in Oman. Additionally, UNICEF engaged in strategic discussions with SPF to accelerate nationwide implementation of these policies, emphasizing their importance for supporting families and fostering child well-being.
Civil society partnerships also played a crucial role in UNICEF’s work. UNICEFs contributed to Oman’s Voluntary National Review for the Sustainable Development Goals in partnership with Children First Association, UNICEF facilitated child-centric discussions on the SDGs, ensuring that children’s voices were included in the VNR process. In addition, UNICEF engaged with the Omani Human Rights Commission in various dialogues, including in addressing child-related complaints, raising awareness about children's rights, and organizing a children's roundtable to celebrate World Children's Day.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The year 2024 shed light on a number of lessons learned. 
A key one is that while reforms and legislations often come at high speed, implementation requires time and persistence to invest in the technical capacity required for implementation. This underscores the importance of maintaining agility and focus on the desired impact – as well as continuous advocacy. For example, given that the ambitious vision of scaling up ECD and ECE will require substantial and sustained national investment which comes in competition with other key national priorities, UNICEF intends to use the evidence generated to support a pragmatic and gradual approach to scaling up. 
Furthermore, lessons learned from efforts on financing for children’s tools, such as costing, have provided a strong framework for advancing policy dialogue and promoting a system-strengthening approach. The adoption of a cross-sectoral inclusive strategy has enhanced national ownership and integration, creating a positive peer effect. Broadening advocacy efforts to engage academia, leadership circles, and civil society organisations has showcased UNICEF's technical expertise and increased demand for knowledge sharing and technical assistance.
Another lesson learned is that UNICEF can play a bigger role in terms of promoting a culture of evidence for children. Research on child rights in Oman remains limited, while data is drawn heavily from administrative data systems. Strengthening the connection between data providers and users is crucial for advancing data generation and analysis on children, with ongoing efforts needed to reach consensus on the most appropriate data collection tools. In addition, more work on evaluation is needed to inform the progress in achieving priorities for children as captured in national strategies and helping stakeholder to go beyond monitoring performance to evaluating outcomes and impact.  Seminars and webinars on topical issues where experiences from other countries are shared are warmly welcomed, as are study tours. Generating evidence is a key strategy to keep children's issues at the forefront of the national agenda and guide interventions towards high-impact areas. For example, ongoing efforts to enhance child protection systems will benefit from updated household-level data on child protection issues, disaggregated by governorate. 
Lastly, it is clear that there remains strong – if not increasing – demand for technical assistance from UNICEF across programming sectors as well as Social and Behaviour Change.  has exceeded UNICEF’s human and financial capacity to respond to requests in a timely fashion. UNICEF is working to innovative approaches to strengthen partnerships.
Looking forward over 2025, OCO is keen to conclude the current CPD by addressing the remaining priorities. This includes concluding on-going work on the ECD and ECE sectors by supporting the Government of Oman in expanding services and advocating for resources and partnerships. In terms of child protection, UNICEF will support MOSD in launching an updated child protection manual, training social workers, and developing an automated case management system. In the social protection sector, UNICEF will continue to offer technical assistance to enhance the system, develop a monitoring and evaluation, and integrate social protection with services, with a specific emphasis on disability inclusion through a “cash-plus” model. Regarding adolescent empowerment, UNICEF will leverage past investments to advance the future skills agenda and also increasingly work with youth groups on the climate change agenda. Lastly, UNICEF will seek to continuously collaborate with key stakeholders to enhance national capacity for evidence generation, analysis and use. UNICEF has maintained a strong capacity building component across the various areas of work and has adopted a learning-by-doing approach while implementing the various technical assistance projects, which it will apply in this last year of the CPD.

In 2024, once again, children were bearing the brunt of the conflict in the State of Palestine. In the Gaza Strip, at least 14,500 children have reportedly been killed since 7 Oct 2023, many more injured, while thousands are likely under the rubble, and an estimated 17,000 others are unaccompanied or separated from their caregivers. At least 25 percent of children who sustain injuries may experience long-term disabilities without access to rehabilitation services. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in the 15 month-period following 7 October 2023, there has been a 189 percent increase in the number of Palestinian children killed in conflict related violence compared to the preceding period (July 2022- October 2023). More than 1,200 Palestinian children have been injured, almost half by live ammunition. Over 65 percent of conflict-related fatalities and violence in the West Bank happened in the northern governorates of Jenin, Nablus, Qalqilya, Tubas and Tulkarem.

37 children were also killed in Israel on 7 October and 36 children abducted into the Gaza Strip, with 34 subsequently released and the status of two remaining Israeli children is still unknown. Three Israeli children were also killed near settlements in the West Bank in 2024.

The escalation of conflict-related violence and hostilities across the State of Palestine had an unprecedent impact on Palestinian economy reaching a record downturn in 2024 according to the latest official estimates by the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics. Real GDP in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and in the Gaza Strip plummeted by a staggering 28 percent in 2024, year-on-year (y/y) (19 percent in West Bank and 82 percent in the Gaza Strip).

Unemployment has reached 51 per cent nationwide in 2024, while it is estimated that in Gaza it stands at 80 percent. Poverty in the State of Palestine is projected to rise to 74.3 percent in 2024, affecting 4.1 million people, including 2.61 million people who are newly impoverished.

The consumer price index in the Gaza Strip surged by 238.0 percent, driven by a severe shortage of commodities resulting from the ongoing conflict and access restrictions. The situation also affected the West Bank, where the index increased by 2.5 percent. The sharp rise in prices led to a significant decline in purchasing power of 34.9 percent, with a dramatic 70.4 percent drop in the Gaza Strip and a more modest 2.4 percent decline in the West Bank.

The ESCWA/UNDP recently published policy brief estimating that by the end of 2024, the Human Development Index (HDI) may fall to 0.643, a level not seen since HDI calculations began in 2004. The HDI of the Gaza Strip is projected to drop to 0.408, erasing over 20 years of progress. The HDI of the West Bank is expected to decline to 0.676, reflecting a loss of 16 years of development.

The humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip remained catastrophic. More than 80.5 percent of the Strip was under active or previously issued displacement orders, leading to multiple displacement of 1.9 million people. Beside death, many children are facing injuries leading to multiple disabilities and becoming even more vulnerable. Children have lost access to the minimum humanitarian standard during crises for health care education, water and other vital services as outlined in UNICEF’s Core Commitments for Children, while continuously being exposed to traumatic events with almost no specialized referral services available.

Repeated attacks on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, water wells and networks have crippled the access to critical services. This coupled with overcrowded and unhygienic living conditions, open sewage and the lack of solid waste collection have created a public health catastrophe. Waterborne diseases, including diarrhea, Hepatitis A and Polio, have emerged, threatening the lives of children, especially children under two with the Poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) detected in Gaza in July 2024, after 25 years of absence. The needs for rehabilitation and assistive devices are high: by the end of May 2024, 39 physiotherapists had been killed, and all three rehabilitation centers were damaged or destroyed. Medical evacuations of critical patients with serious medical conditions and/or requiring specialized care for conflict-related injuries are taking place, however the rate has decreased by 94 percent since the Rafah crossing closure on May 6, 2024.

Persistent challenges on the entry of humanitarian aid and commercial commodities access constraints have rendered the Gaza population acutely food insecure. All 335,000 children under five are at high risk of malnutrition.

Schools serving as shelters for displaced civilians have rendered access to regular, full-time education impossible for over 658,760 school children. One year of classroom learning has already been lost, and education didn't resume in 2024/2025 academic year. As a result, education is projected to be set back by up to five years.

In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, extensive militarized operations by Israeli forces, coupled with spiking settler violence and large-scale demolitions have markedly increased children’s exposure to conflict related violence and grave violations, including displacement, casualties and injuries, as well as severe damage to basic infrastructure such as schools, health centers and water systems impeding the population to access basic services.

The Palestinian Authority (PA) embarked into a new planning cycle replacing the six years planning cycle initiated in 2023. A 'Build Palestine Vision' was developed underpinned by two national level development plans: The National Program for Development and Reform providing a strategic framework to stimulate economic revival and transform as well as enhance institutional performance; and a second one – the Gaza Reconstruction and Recovery Development Plan (GRRDP) building upon the recently updated initial damage, losses, and needs analysis prepared jointly by the European Union (EU), the World Bank (WB) and the United Nations which estimated at US$53.142 billion recovery and reconstruction needs in the short, medium and long-term across the Gaza Strip. From these two national level plans, sectoral strategies are being drafted, in parallel to the tri-partite EU/WB and UN conflict recovery framework (CRF). The CRF is expected to inform GRRDP and the sector strategies. Through its leadership on the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) Outcome two on the access to basic social services, active involvement in other outcomes related to climate and social infrastructure, UNICEF contributed to the interagency assessments and recovery plans focusing on its role as the co-lead

In 2024, UNICEF State of Palestine continued to provide lifesaving humanitarian support, access to basic supply and services and enhanced emergency preparedness in the Gaza strip, West Bank including East Jerusalem. With the aim of adjusting programmes agilely to the evolving situation and needs across the country, UNICEF managed multiple revisions of Emergency response plan, Humanitarian Action for Children appeal (HAC) and took stock through two After action reviews every six months since 7 October 2023, with a focus on improving scalability and quality of the interventions. At the interagency level, UNICEF contributed to the preparation and revision of the Interagency Flash Appeals as the leading and/or co-leading agency of three clusters and one Area of Responsibility (AoR). UNICEF also played a key role for EU-WB-UN Rapid Damage Needs Assessments (RDNA) and CRF as the co-lead of the UNSDCF outcome two on basic social services, estimating the total damage and losses incurred in Gaza for planning future recovery.

To alleviate dire humanitarian situation, UNICEF expanded its programmatic and operational capacity; Between October 2023 and the end of 2024, UNICEF increased HAC appeal funding requirement from US$23.8 million to US$526.1 million, of which 79 percent was mobilized. In the same period, UNICEF’s overall human resource has seen 80 percent of growth, from 107 to 193 staff in the main office, including 101 percent increase in the number of the staff in Gaza field office (from 34 to 79) , through which UNICEF expanded its presence in the Gaza Strip. Moreover, UNICEF tripled the value of procured supplies and services to USD$118 million compared to USD$36 million in 2023, with the concerted support from Jordan and Egypt country offices for cross-border operations and logistics.

UNICEF established robust reporting and monitoring systems, including the full deployment of UNICEF eTool’s Field Monitoring Module and Third-Party Monitoring. To better incorporate the needs and interests of affected people, UNICEF digitalized its Community Feedback Mechanism and scaled up its capacity by processing 15,000 raised cases monthly. On evaluation and research, institutional M&E capacity building of the Ministry of Education and Higher Education (MoEHE) and the Ministry of Health (MoH) progressed, and one WASH evaluation in the West Bank was completed through UNICEF’s support, while preparing the groundwork for cash transfer programme evaluation in 2025.

On cross-sectoral programming, UNICEF implemented a systematic twin-track approach to disability inclusion, creating a country-specific strategy and action plan. Other key actions were reviewing disability inclusion in emergency response plans, HAC appeals, and RDNA. Along with the mapping of organizations of persons with disabilities and rehabilitation organizations, UNICEF contributed to disability inclusion and rehabilitation strategies under capacity-building initiatives for health and nutrition clusters. Along with the normative actions, 545 wheelchairs were procured and distributed through partners in North and South Gaza for children with temporary and permanent disabilities.

UNICEF integrated gender responsiveness across its programmes. In that sense, UNICEF provided 10,000 adolescent girls in Gaza with care and protection packages, including menstrual hygiene items. It also offered awareness sessions on prenatal and postnatal care and provided cash assistance to female-headed households and pregnant and breastfeeding women. Furthermore, 7,436 adolescent girls were introduced to the Laaha platform, a virtual safe space providing access to gender-based violence (GBV) referral hotlines.

UNICEF and the Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) Network ensured safe, accessible channels for harm or misconduct related to humanitarian assistance. The Sanad campaign promoted child-sensitive and gender-inclusive pathways, while the helpline handled 113,991 calls and provided access to MHPSS, medical care, legal assistance, and referrals.

Health & Nutrition
In 2024, newborns, children and mothers continued to face significant challenges in equitable access to health and nutrition services. Health care services in Gaza suffered more than 541 attacks on facilities and medical transport crippling their capacity to provide needed care. Consequently, most hospitals are inoperable, with only one neonatal intensive care unit left functional. Moreover, the global Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) reiterated that Gaza’s acute malnutrition is at serious levels (IPC AMN Phase 3). Continued military operations and movement restrictions in the West Bank further strained the capacity of health sector.

Following the resurgence of poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) in central Gaza in July 2024, UNICEF, MoH, WHO and partners implemented a joint emergency vaccination campaign from September to November. As Poliomyelitis (polio) being a highly infectious viral disease for children, the campaign targeted all 588,000 children under ten to be vaccinated. The campaign administered 559,161 children (272,062 girls and 287,099 boys) reaching 95 percent of the target through mobilizing more than 1,200 vaccination teams. To maximize the effect of the campaign, UNICEF provided vitamin A supplementation to 448,425 children to bolster their immune system along with novel oral polio vaccines. UNICEF’s preparedness on the cold chain, building upon the routine vaccination support, significantly contributed to the campaign by promptly enhancing cold chain capacities in terms of vaccine storage, transportation, and equipment provision. A wide range of Risk communication and community engagements (RCCE) were also critical to the campaign’s success where 850 trained social mobilizers reached 90 percent of target communities during two rounds of the campaign, providing information, awareness on WASH, health and nutrition services.

UNICEF provided 585,300 people through a package of primary level critical health interventions prioritizing antenatal, post-natal, trauma care, and treatment for acute and chronic illnesses in 15 primary health care (PHC) facilities and 23 IDP shelters, along with the provision of essential medical supplies and equipment to 44 medical facilities. Additionally, seven mobile teams were deployed to serve restricted communities through UNICEF’s support, offering PHC, referrals, and vaccinations to reach more children. 4,450 health workers completed the training on maternal and newborn health with the distribution of 70,000 Maternal and child health (MCH) handbooks. On routine vaccination, UNICEF delivered 966,300 doses of vaccines protecting 134,283 children under 18 months. On disability, UNICEF is piloting 3D technology for the provision of prothesis, while also delivering 545 wheelchairs.

In an effort to relieve the worsening food and nutrition security, UNICEF and cluster partners conducted over half a million acute malnutrition screenings. Based on screenings, UNICEF provided lifesaving treatment to 33,000 children with acute malnutrition, including 7,000 severe cases. Additionally, 72,000 children under five were provided with micronutrient powder and 48,600 pregnant and breastfeeding mothers received preventative iron folate and micronutrient supplements through UNICEF’s support. Training was provided to 500 service providers on Infant and Young Child Feeding in Emergencies (IYCF-E) and Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) to inform good feeding practices and to ensure acutely malnourished children are treated timely.

At the national level, in close coordination with MoH, UNICEF provided strategic insights for Every Newborn Action Plan, Neonatal Medical Equipment Standards and CMAM guideline’s update. In the West Bank, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of 410 healthcare providers on emergency care protocols and basic life support, along with the provision of essential medical supplies and vaccine procurement service to MoH and UNRWA, serving over 129,200 children under five.

WASH
As a major actor in the water sector, UNICEF played a key role in sustaining and gradually increasing water production and quality by supporting repair and maintenance of water systems and distribution of water treatment chemicals. 6 million liters of fuel were provided for wells, desalination plants and generators for mobile desalination plants to minimize the service disruption, while UNICEF boosted the production output of one of the desalination plants by re-establishing the direct electric feeder line to mitigate 10 to 15 percent of its capacity loss due to energy cut. Additionally, to ensure the coverage of the access, emergency water trucking was provided to shelters disconnected from the water networks. These interventions enabled an average of 1.8 million people to access safe water for drinking and domestic needs each month. Vital sanitation and hygiene services including installation of mobile latrines, wastewater facilities’ rehabilitation and hygiene item distribution, benefited an average of 900,000 people monthly. As part of the integrated programme approach, 56 institutional facilities’ WASH infrastructure were supported, including 49 learning spaces and six health facilities.

UNICEF mitigated the risks of winter flooding and wastewater overflow in flood-prone areas in Gaza through providing three dewatering pumps for Gaza City, benefitting around 250,000 people, while desludging and maintenance of sewage and stormwater networks across Gaza protected around 400,000 people from flood risks. To prevent water borne diseases including acute watery diarrhea and chicken pox during winter, UNICEF’s community engagement interventions promoted partners and community’s preparedness through community volunteers, SMS messaging and setting up community action plans.
