In the West Bank, UNICEF delivered over 150 different WASH items, including pumps, generators, chlorine, fuel, pipes to the Palestinian Water Authority (PWA) facilities across regions, benefiting more than 50 percent of the West Bank population. Particularly for ensuring undisrupted operation and water quality, 18,445 litres of fuel were delivered to two water stations, and 78,312 liters of chlorine were provided to 25 water wells across the governorates. As part of its long-term strategy to address water infrastructure damage, UNICEF leveraged local resources in collaboration with partners and WASH Cluster to enhance response times, particularly during the critical first 48 hours.

At the national level, UNICEF supported PWA in conducting workshops on strengthening capacities of WASH service delivery, monitoring and coordination. Additionally, UNICEF supported the training of trainers on Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) for ten MoH staff members for enhancing a risk-based management for health care facilities, covering key aspects of WASH, environmental cleaning, and health care waste management. Finally, UNICEF promoted the mainstreaming of climate change in the national policies and advocated for the inclusion of children and youth in COP29 discussions and other youth local and regional conferences.

The WASH cluster also contributed to strategic plans such as the West Bank Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan for 2025, the Gaza Winterization Plan, Gaza North Response Plan and PWA Early Recovery Action Plan. With 73 partners across Gaza and the West Bank, the cluster enhanced governance through updated membership criteria and the reactivation of the Strategic Advisory Group.

Education
UNICEF continued the efforts for education to remain as a priority for fostering resilience of 658,760 and 806,300 school-aged children in need across the State of Palestine respectively, whose access to education has been severely disrupted due to the escalation of hostilities in the Gaza Strip and increased conflict related violence in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.

In the Gaza Strip, UNICEF provided regular face-to-face formal or non-formal education to over 70,000 children (50 percent girls) through 75 learning centers managed by implementing partners and 53 co-managed with communities and 20 managed by schools. To sustain education service in these centers, 2,500 staff received incentive payments from UNICEF while 1,082 trained adolescents and youth played a pivotal role in leading children’s return to learning. Moreover, as grade 12 students in Gaza lost their opportunity to apply for Tawjihi (national general secondary education certificate examination) in academic year 2023/24, UNICEF supported 58,527 of them to resume their learning and prepare for the exam.

In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, UNICEF facilitated inclusive and safe learning for 53,780 children (28,230 girls) through summer camp activities, integrating learning with child-friendly space initiative. Through the initiative, Science Technology Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) programme reached 11,075 students across 193 STEM clubs, fostering innovation and scientific inquiry among children while schools’ supervisors and teachers’ pedagogical capacity was strengthened for child-friendly learning with the distribution of 225 STEM kits. As part of UNICEF’s efforts to establish safe school environment, 623 teaching staff (410 women) were trained in self-care and referral mechanisms while employing 120 community social workers to bridge schools with child protection sector.

At the national level, UNICEF provided insights to plans and strategies, notably Ministry of Education and Higher Education’s (MoEHE) emergency response plan and the interagency Gaza RDNA for evidence-based infrastructure recovery and addressing learning loss. UNICEF also technically supported the ministry in reviewing the inclusive education policy, and in youth skilling and engagement, linked to the State of Palestine’s participation in 2024 Regional High-Level Meeting on Young People’s Learning, Skilling, and Transition to Decent Work.

UNICEF co-leads the Education Cluster with Save the Children and leads the Education in Emergencies (EiE) Thematic Working Group and the Life Skills Technical Working Group with MoEHE. UNICEF and the cluster contributed to the learning, and recreational activities for around 100,000 children in Gaza through the establishment of 424 learning spaces by the end of November, to mitigate learning loss and psychological impact on children and teachers. In the West Bank, UNICEF in coordination MoEHE and in cooperation with cluster partners, strived to ensure the continuity of education.

Child Protection
Conflict-related violence in the Gaza Strip and West Bank reached unprecedented levels, with 10,227 verified grave violations against children by the third quarter, tripling the 2023 figure (3,344). Parties to the conflict in Israel and in the State of Palestine were listed for grave violations by the Secretary General in his annual report on children and armed conflict (CAAC), triggering a formal Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM). UNICEF leveraged grave violations data to inform programs and advocacy, aiming to strengthen child protection, especially for the 1.1 million conflict affected children in the Gaza Strip.

UNICEF, as a leading child protection actor, scaled up activities to identify, protect and promote the rights of children, access to child protection and case management, MHPSS, and justice; 163,032 (55 per cent girls) children received Level 3 individual and group interventions (13,360) and structured and unstructured Level 2 activities (149,692), along with 90,604 caregivers (54 percent women). UNICEF co-chaired with UNRWA the Technical Working Group on Unaccompanied and separated children (UASC) under which the group developed tools and procedures for an accountable identification, documentation, tracing and reunification (IDTR) process and facilitated constructive dialogues with key stakeholders. As the provider of the last resort, UNICEF continued to provide family tracing and registration services for UASC, facilitating the reunification of 54 children with their parents and/or family members. To reduce explosive ordnance (EO) risks, UNICEF reached 200,728 children (55 percent girls) in Gaza with EO-related prevention risk education, scaling up the reach throughout 2024. Finally, UNICEF also led the provision of winter clothing for around 247,000 children for them and the families to stay dry and warm throughout the winter season.

In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, UNICEF accelerated child protection outcomes through a two-pronged approach; on one end strengthening the Ministry of Social Development’s (MoSD) institutional capacity and child protection processes. On the other end, expanding the provision of critical primary, secondary and tertiary prevention services to the affected children including those with disabilities and at risk of developing disability for rehabilitation through strategic partnerships with a wide range of actors, reinforcing comprehensive Child Protection systems. In this vein, UNICEF provided community-based MHPSS service to 14,252 children (52 percent girls) and collaborated with MoSD and CSOs to build the capacity of child protection counsellors in three West Bank governorates benefiting 292 child victims. Another 548 children with conflict-related injuries or physical disabilities (50 percent girls) received specialized care and support. The intersectoral MHPSS strategy guided the delivery of services with an emphasis on capacity building for frontline workers; Child protection diploma was institutionalized at a prominent West Bank university, building the capacity of 23 professionals and accrediting 13 case managers with Supervision Diploma.

Community-based organizations in hotspot areas received training to detect, respond to, and refer cases effectively, facilitating 348 child victim referrals.

On the Justice for Children agenda, UNICEF advanced the UN inter-agency Sawasya Programme, engaging frontline workers in specialized child protection diplomas and supporting justice institutions. Legal aid reached 704 children, offering alternatives to detention and reintegration programmes.

UNICEF continued to lead the Child Protection Area of Responsibility (CPAoR), coordinating partners, developing advocacy tools, and establishing protocols for data protection and sharing. These efforts improved the delivery and coordination of child protection services, ensuring a comprehensive response.

Social Policy
As a result of the ongoing situation, the Palestinian Authority struggled to maintain funding for programs like the national cash transfer programme (NCTP) amidst a fiscal crisis driven by reduced revenue, declining international budget support, and stagnant economic activity.
Despite these challenges, in the Gaza Strip the commercial sector continued to operate, playing a critical role in maintaining the resilience of food systems as well as other commodities complementing humanitarian assistance. UNICEF used innovative tools like the RapidPro system and in-person observations to monitor market functionality, gathering evidence that informed its programming and advocacy to restore commerce and improve nutrition for women and children.

In response to the escalating crisis, UNICEF expanded its humanitarian cash programme, leveraging national systems to support early recovery. By the end of 2024, the digital cash programme reached 1 million beneficiaries in Gaza, including 588,000 children and 172,000 families, making UNICEF’s largest cash initiative globally, with the net worth of US$45 million. On average, 120,000 people received monthly cash transfers with an average of US$248 (919 NIS) per person, accounting for 60-70 percent of all humanitarian cash provided in Gaza. UNICEF’s strategy prioritized vulnerable groups, including 23,200 families with pregnant or breastfeeding women, 6,000 families with persons with disabilities members, and 47,500 female-headed households. The programme also addressed families at risk of sexual exploitation and abuse and those caring for children without parental support. A robust grievance redress mechanism (GRM) resolved or redirected 75 percent of the 105,000 cases handled between October 2023 and October 2024, ensuring accountability and responsiveness. Cash interventions supported essential services, enabling 10,000 frontline volunteers to provide health, education, nutrition, and immunization services to vulnerable communities in Gaza and the West Bank. This included significant contributions to the Gaza polio campaign and solid waste management efforts.

Beyond the emergency response, UNICEF advanced long-term resilience by strengthening national systems and partnerships with the Palestinian Authority. Progress was made in shock-responsive social protection (SRSP), child rights, and local governance. The National Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) Action Plan was revised to incorporate government emergency response measures, monitored through a tracking database developed by OHCHR. A dedicated committee was formed to align national laws with international child rights standards, and the UN CRC National Team was reactivated. UNICEF facilitated consultations for Palestine’s first UNCRPD report, institutionalizing child rights monitoring. UNICEF’s efforts balanced immediate humanitarian needs with sustainable development, protecting vulnerable populations while laying the groundwork for systemic change in the face of unprecedented challenges.

UNICEF continued to expand partnerships with line ministries, local actors, UN agencies and civil society organizations to scale up its humanitarian response nationally. UNICEF, as the Cluster Lead Agency, continued to lead WASH and nutrition clusters, co-lead the education cluster and CPAoR. Through UNICEF’s humanitarian leadership, three clusters and one AoR coordinated the overall responses, set standards, developed tools, shared information, tracked results, and consolidated advocacy efforts and resource mobilization for the sectors. UNICEF leveraged diverse implementation modalities on the ground allowing the expansion and faster scale up, ranging from direct implementation, supporting line ministries and local actors to restore and strengthen existing services complemented by partnerships with civil society organizations.

By strengthening existing partnerships with traditional donors and diversifying the donor base with emerging ones, including global programme partnerships (GPPs), and international financial institutions (IFIs), UNICEF’s humanitarian funding reached US$415 million - 79 percent of US$526M requested in HAC appeal. UNICEF’s more rigorous risk assessment and management also contributed to better alignment with donors' strict conditionalities. In addition, the mobilization of thematic humanitarian funds played a key role in enabling UNICEF’s rapid response, allowing flexibility for adapting programmes to meet constantly changing needs.
Advocacy remains the key feature of UNICEF’s work for forging partnerships with key actors across all levels through the promotion of children’s rights with intense public and private efforts. UNICEF's advocacy raised public awareness as well as highlighted challenges and constraints faced nationally. Among the published advocacy materials, ‘Children in Gaza Need Most’ video was watched by 6.2 million viewers globally, a social media campaign on Rafah reached 40 million users, and quote cards featuring the Executive Director’s remarks were shared by 20 global influencers.

As part of the wider UN coordination efforts, UNICEF contributed to the UN interagency Early Recovery Approach and Action Plan and participated as an active member to the RDNA process being the penholder for three sectors’ RDNA and drafting of the sector strategies for education, WASH and social protection in close collaboration with the EU, the World Bank and the UN agencies.

For WASH programme, UNICEF strengthened its strategic partnerships with governmental WASH actors. PWA, MoEHE, MoH, Environmental quality agency (EQA), Costal Municipality Water Utility (CMWU), and NGOs collaborated with UNICEF on evidence generation, advocacy, WASH service provision, monitoring, and evaluation. UNICEF continued its partnership with UNOPS and UNRWA in responding to emergency needs. Also UNICEF and WFP prepared the groundwork of the e-voucher mechanism activation for efficient distribution of hygiene products. On climate change, energy and disaster risk reduction issues, UNICEF cooperated with EQA, the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority and the Stockholm International Water Institute.

For Nutrition programme, UNICEF expanded partnerships with 28 UN and NGO partners including WFP and UNRWA, which enabled the scale-up of nutrition services for children with acute malnutrition from zero to over 150 trained and equipped treatment sites for acute malnutrition screening, treatments, and provision of nutrition supplements to vulnerable groups including pregnant and breast feeding mothers. For health programme, UNICEF jointly carried out the emergency polio vaccination campaign with MoH, WHO and UNRWA throughout the planning, logistics, implementation and RCCE. For routine vaccination as per the Expanded programme for immunization (EPI), UNICEF strengthened ties with the World Bank and GAVI to ensure uninterrupted vaccine procurement, distribution and the prevention of the stockouts.

In Education, UNICEF supported MoEHE on emergency preparedness and responses through the Education sector working group, EiE and Life Skills thematic working groups to ensure access to education and well-being of school children during the crisis. UNICEF and MoEHE’s partnership advanced digital education to expand the access to formal curricula through Learning Passport, which is the education platform functioning with intermittent or no internet connectivity. For its deployment, UNICEF led the initial training of 12 ministry supervisors and the distribution plan of servers to 100 schools.

UNICEF built partnerships with actors with emergency child protection capacities, community-based child protection and psychosocial support in affected areas where social services are absent. UNICEF and IPs coordinated with child protection authorities to respond to cases of children at high risk of serious harm or death, including unaccompanied children and child survivors of violence and GBV. UNICEF maintained key partnership for the provision of UASC alternative care services: new partnerships for expanding family-type emergency care services and the integrated social protection schemes for families caring for UASC will be operational in early 2025. Despite advocacy and investments, UNICEF remains the sole provider of UASC alternative care services. As the lead agency for CPAoR, UNICEF, continued to strengthen linkages and referral pathways between communities, civil society, and state child protection authorities to prevent and respond to child protection issues.

For social protection, UNICEF maintained strong partnerships with MoSD, accelerating the growth of cash programmes and integrating them with national systems. Partnerships with key donors expanded the reach of humanitarian cash programs, while coordination with the Cash Working Group ensured smooth implementation and market monitoring. Collaboration with the Palestinian Monetary Authority and financial service providers facilitated the promotion of digital wallets for cash transfers, supporting the development of a digital ecosystem in Gaza. Institutional partnerships with ILO strengthened the national social protection system, while a new phase of the Nexus program focused on enhancing the capacity of MoSD. UNICEF also partnered with UN-Habitat and Ramallah municipality to implement the Child and Youth Friendly City Initiative, fostering local engagement in child-centered urban development.

In collaboration with communications service provider and women-led organizations, UNICEF delivered GBV prevention messages to girls and women nationally through UNICEF's Laaha platfom. Furthermore, UNICEF expanded its partnerships with organizations supporting children with disabilities tailoring child protection services with assistive devices with the aim of reaching at least five percent of beneficiaries as part of the child protection response.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, UNICEF continued to face many threats and risks in its daily operations in the Gaza Strip. Despite these, significant results were achieved in addressing the immediate needs of the population. The Two After Action Reviews after six months and after one year into the response helped reviewing strategies and business models to increase scalability and quality of interventions.

The reviews underscored the importance of geographic prioritization where weaker institutional support exists, calling for a more contextualized approach. The integrated approach was highlighted as a key programmatic element that enabled UNICEF to provide more holistic support to children. The initiatives such as the integrated approach to learning, combining learning with hygiene promotion, child protection MHPSS services as well as health/nutrition points and Cash Plus approach for vulnerable families in addition to child protection services allowed more comprehensive coverage and assistance.

Given the vast scope of needs, the analysis stressed the importance of prioritizing interventions to strengthen existing services while further addressing urgent needs. The resumption and maintenance of immunization services as part of primary health care is one of the examples. Through the first year of the crisis, UNICEF played a leading role in resuming and maintaining immunization. In November 2023, UNICEF transported available vaccines from the central cold chain warehouse in the North to the South of the Gaza Strip to adapt to the large-scale displacement of population. Thereafter regular procurement and delivery of routine vaccines, consumables as well as cold chain equipment prevented major stock out. These investments were key for the successful organization of polio vaccination campaign in September 2024.

Furthermore, the analysis revealed that the expansion and diversification of partnerships enabled UNICEF to scale up its response. This is particularly true for the direct implementation modality, though in insight this approach requires increased monitoring capacity, additional capacity building efforts and risk management. However, the review highlighted the need to continue to address logistical challenges and coordination gaps among the many partners to gain operational effectiveness.

Cross-sectoral areas, such as SBC, AAP and PSEA, were mainstreamed to raise awareness of targeted population on the different initiatives, while providing information on reporting channels. RCCE of Polio campaign in Gaza showed a successful uptake, reaching 559,000 children early September (90 percent of the target). Additionally, a social mobilization component trained and deployed more than 850 community mobilizers who engaged with parents and caregivers through face-to-face interactions and group settings to ensure dynamic two-way communication. For PSEA, ‘Kits that Fit’ approach was integrated to the procurement processes to ensure participation of communities. For that, UNICEF conducted four focus group discussions with adolescent girls which revealed high satisfaction with the care kits, but a need for more hygiene items, better water and sanitation access, and better participation in decision-making.
Accountability mechanisms were also put in place for polio vaccination campaign. Clear communication and effective CFM enabled affected populations to ask questions, raise concerns, and access timely information of the campaign. Key messages were disseminated through CFM posters, flyers and social media messages which reminded the importance of participation. A number of complaints and feedback were received regarding the vaccination centres, including from individuals with disabilities. A total of 16,602 people heard a recorded message during the hotline waiting line regarding the polio campaign.

Gender and disability inclusion were mainstreamed as within the broader programmatic framework from the onset of the response. Gender and disability inclusion strategy and action plans were developed with specific programmatic targets set. Dedicated specialists were hired for gender and disability to ensure integration across all programming milestones. Earmarked budget was allocated, and all proposals were reviewed by both specialists to ensure inclusion there where relevant. Finally, partnerships with WLOs as well as with organizations of persons with disabilities & rehabilitation organizations allowed a more targeted programmatic response.

Finally, the review highlighted the fragility of the supply chain as one of the most significant operational challenges. Despite the application of simplified procedures, the entry of supplies to Gaza and more recently to the West Bank remains extremely challenging due to the constantly changing operating environment, particularly due to the rising lack of law and order in the Gaza Strip. As a result, donor conditionalities and risk management became increasingly complex to the point UNICEF needed to adapt its implementation strategies: the increased scrutiny necessitated frequent dialogue with donors on policies pertaining to screening of IPs and contractors, and human resource management.

On the innovation side, UNICEF deployed new approaches to overcome challenges faced on the ground: the introduction of digital cash transfers through e-wallets has been significant in addressing the ongoing liquidity crisis in Gaza. With banking systems largely inoperable, UNICEF introduced e-wallets for bypassing the cash liquidity challenges. By the end of 2024, nearly 800,000 people received digital cash transfers, with many respondents using e-wallets for purchasing goods and services. This innovative solution has allowed UNICEF to sustain its humanitarian response amidst financial crisis, providing families with the flexibility to access essential supplies in a context where traditional humanitarian aid delivery has been hampered by logistical and security concerns. UNICEF's digital cash initiative is complemented by efforts to transition to a Universal Child Grant (UCG) system, aimed at providing ongoing support to the most vulnerable children across the State of Palestine. The UCG program, initially focused on children aged 0-3 years, children with disabilities, and those without parental care, is analyzed as both a life-saving humanitarian tool and an important mechanism for economic recovery in Gaza, with the potential to stimulate local demand and support broader recovery.

Overview: The UNICEF Gulf Area Office (GAO) represents UNICEF in Bahrain, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (KSA), Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is focused on advancing children’s rights domestically and globally with a focus on early childhood development, child protection, social policy, data and evidence for children. Results are achieved through strengthening partnerships and alliances with Gulf-based actors in support of children in the Gulf and around the world, especially the most vulnerable and those affected by humanitarian crises. 
Economy: Looking at the overall picture in 2024 the global economy demonstrated moderate growth, with notable regional disparities. Within the GCC countries, continued investments in economic diversification, particularly across the tourism, real estate and manufacturing sectors, drove non-oil sector growth in 2024. These gains helped offset the impact of OPEC+ oil production cuts, which significantly affected hydrocarbon output. As a result, non-oil GDP growth averaged 3.7%, outpacing the overall economic growth rate of 1.8%[2]. Looking ahead, the GCC is expected to remain economically resilient and effectively navigate the anticipated challenges of declining oil revenues and geopolitical fragmentation through balancing prudent fiscal management, achieving tax harmony, advancing urban developments to position the GCC as a leading talent hub and leading in AI with major infrastructure investments and global partnerships[3].
 
To support the GCC’s diversification investments, countries have significantly improved learning outcomes over the last decade with more efforts are underway due to its cruciality. According to the World Bank[10],the quality of education is a major factor that is holding back human capital development in the region as well as the ability of GCC countries to compete at the global level with top-performing countries. According to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index, a child born today in the GCC is expected to reach only 62% of their full potential productivity, mainly held back by low education quality.
 
Politics and Regional Dynamics: As geopolitical fragmentation intensifies in 2024, trade tensions between major trading blocs - the US, Europe, and China - are expected to escalate under the Trump administration. Amid this fragmentation, the GCC is adopting a more strategic, multipolar approach to diplomacy by diversifying alliances. KSA and the UAE have joined BRICs in 2024 as an observer and member respectively, reflecting the region’s intent to expand its influence beyond traditional partners. The GCC is also leveraging its strategic location and role as a global energy leader to deepen economic ties with emerging economies[4]
 
The relative political stability in the Gulf sub-region is in sharp contrast to the deteriorating political, security and socio-economic situation in much of the Middle East. The war in Gaza, Southern Lebanon, Sudan and Yemen are leading to deteriorating child rights, high unemployment, a massive population of refugees and forcibly displaced persons, marginalized youth, and growing poverty. The Gulf States, in particular Saudi Arabia and Qatar have committed considerable critical for UNICEF and other UN agencies, allowing them to respond to the growing needs of the most vulnerable children in the region.
 
Social and Demographic Context:  The combined population of the sub-region is estimated at 52.5 million (2023 estimates, excluding Oman[5]) disaggregated into 62.4% males and 37.6% females. Rapid population growth and urbanization (more than 80% in each of these Gulf countries) are pressing issues, resulting in environmental damage and pollution and a high demand for scarce land, water, and food. Given the climate risks facing the sub-region (including acute water scarcity, desertification, increasing temperatures, coastal erosion and flooding), the pressure of rapid population growth and urbanization is deeply concerning.
 
UNCCD COP16 in Riyadh united leaders from governments, the private sector, civil society, and global stakeholders to accelerate progress in sustainable land management. COP16 was a critical moment for governments and non-state actors to slow and reverse land degradation. Saudi Arabia’s leadership of COP16 and the successful negotiation and action taken at the Riyadh COP was critical to leverage commitment to address the loss of fertile land globally[6].  With over 40% of the world’s agricultural land already damaged and more than three-quarters of land experiencing dryer conditions[7], the conference emphasized the urgent need for innovation, investment and collaboration to restore land, safeguard food and water security, tackle climate change and combat biodiversity loss.
 
The GCC’s progress to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is mixed and varied. According to UN ESCWA[8], the GCC subregion is projected to reach the 2030 targets in five Goals: SDG 1 on no poverty, SDG 2 on zero hunger, SDG 3 on good health and wellbeing, SDG 4 on quality education, and SDG 6 on clean water and sanitation. However, the subregion has a wide data gap, which hampers efforts to effectively monitor the progress of seven of the SDG goals. Furthermore even though countries have made decent progress in SDG 7 on affordable and clean energy, SDG 9 on industry, innovation and infrastructure, and SDG 17 on partnership for the Goals; there is insufficient data in all countries for five Goals, namely SDG 10 on reduced inequalities, SDG 12 on responsible consumption and production, SDG 13 on climate action, SDG 14 on life below water and SDG 16 on peace, justice and strong institutions. Therefore, progress has not been measured by country or by subregion (ESCWA, 2024).
 
Despite progress across the Gulf countries on the SDGs, national legislations are not fully in line with international standards. The Committee on the Rights of the Child identified gaps in child rights legislation, including issues relating to the right to acquire nationality, birth registration, corporal punishments, gender-based violence and discrimination, the legal age of criminal and the definition of a child, especially regarding child marriage and juvenile justice, among others[9].
 
Looking ahead
With an anticipated increase in oil production in 2025-2026, economic growth is expected to rebound to 4.7% in 2025 (Spring 2024 Gulf Economic Update). To achieve more sustainable growth, GCC countries continue to focus on economic diversification and environmental sustainability, strategic investment in advanced telecommunications technologies, including 5G, AI and machine learning, and increase private sector-led job creation, especially for women and young people.

Early Childhood Development
 
In 2024, significant progress was made in Early Childhood Development (ECD) across the Gulf, with some noteworthy achievements in policy and legal changes, system strengthening, capacity building, advocacy, and regional collaboration.
 
In the realm of policy changes and regulatory frameworks relating to ECD, UNICEF advised the Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in their policy reforms relating to early childhood education and care. Technical advice was provided to the development of the National Framework on Early Childhood Education contributing to a key priority in the Vision 2030 goals and ensuring alignment with global standards.  The Framework provides guidance to govern the process of expansion of childcare and kindergartens with a focus on quality of education across the nation. Additionally, UNICEF has prepared a joint plan of cooperation together with the National Curricula Center for reviewing the national development standards of the age group 0-6 years which will inform the curricula development. The plan is under review for endorsement and implementation in 2025.  In UAE, UNICEF continued its involvement in the UAE’s National ECD Technical Planning Group which helped influence regulations for ECD service provider certification across early learning, health, and social protection. In Qatar, UNICEF developed and finalized a first joint national education programme of cooperation for implementation in 2025. Priorities include the development of Early Learning Standards, Inclusive Education Frameworks, and capacity building of education personnel on children’s rights, with technical support from UNICEF. In Kuwait, UNICEF provided technical advice to the advocacy efforts leading to the successful passing of legislation banning sugary and processed foods in school cafeterias, showing a commitment to healthier environments.
 
Strengthening capacities of governmental entities continued to be a key strategy for UNICEF.  In Kuwait, UNICEF continued to be a key resource and technical expert for national training workshops relating to ECD, child development and parenting, such as the parenting programmes that are being delivered by the Ministry of Health and the NGO “Birth Kuwait”. Additionally, in UAE, and following to COP28, UNICEF supported the Government in their initiative to integrate climate-focused early education  for young learners.  As a result, the Early Learning Sustainable Resource Package in partnership with the Abu Dhabi Early Childhood Authority was developed. This initiative will set the base for a nationwide climate-focused early learning in UAE. In Qatar, UNICEF has adapted and shared with the Ministry of Education child rights materials and resources. These will be used for the training of education personnel, and teachers in 2025.  UNICEF in Qatar has also provided technical guidance and orientation on the Child Friendly Cities Initiative to the Ministry of Education and Higher Education.
 
UNICEF’s advocacy for an integrated approach to early childhood development continued throughout the Gulf region by participating as a knowledge and thought leader in a number of global conferences that were convened in the Gulf countries. For example, UNICEF played an instrumental role in designing and delivering high level sessions on early childhood education, inclusive education and parenting at both the Human Capability Development Initiative organized in KSA and the World Early Childhood Development Conference in UAE.  Both forums provided the platform for UNICEF to influence the agenda in the region and globally as well as position UNICEF as a partner of choice on ECD. In Qatar, UNICEF collaborated with Education Above All in the preparation and commemoration of the 5th year Commemoration of the International Day to Protect Education from Attack held in September 2024, as part of advocacy efforts for the protection of education from attacks.
 
The achievements of 2024 are projected to have long-term impacts on children’s health, education, and overall wellbeing across the Gulf. Looking ahead, the focus will be on strengthening cross-country collaboration and implementing ECD programs consistently. Future priorities include expanding partnerships to enhance programs promoting healthy diets for young children, integrating climate and environmental awareness into preschool education, and scaling parenting programs. Continued strengthening of ECD systems in health, nutrition, responsive caregiving, early learning, and child wellbeing will be essential for sustainable progress.
 
 
 
Child Protection 
 
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support the governments of the GCC countries in advancing the child protection agenda in line with their national commitments and the global standards. 
Advancing national commitments to child protection continued to be a priority for UNICEF’s advocacy work in the Gulf countries. The first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children provided an opportunity for KSA, UAE, Qatar and Kuwait to make ambitious pledges to advance parenting, safe schools and child protection services. These pledges are anchored in policy and institutional reforms and guided and supported by UNICEF in each country.  For example, in KSA, UNICEF provided technical advice to the development of the multi-sectoral National Framework for the Prevention and Protection of Children from abuse- We Detect and Protect and the operationalization of the National Framework on Child Online Safety. 
 
In Qatar, a joint multi-year work plan was prepared with the Government to strengthen the national child protection system and the social service workforce. In the lead up to the Global Ministerial Conference on Violence Against Children, Qatar Foundation with support from UNICEF held an international conference on the family. Specifically, UNICEF facilitated the mission from the UN SRSG VAC aimed at strengthening ties with partners in Qatar and advancing its national work on strengthening child protection systems. Additionally, a review of legislation relating to children’s rights was undertaken in KSA, UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain and an advocacy strategy is under development to advocate for reforms related to banning corporal punishments and for increasing the Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility. 
 
As the digital landscape continues to evolve, protecting children online remains a critical national and global priority.  UNICEF’s collaboration with the Government of KSA at the national level has leveraged a multi country partnership with the Global Cybersecurity Forum (GCF) under HRH Prince Mohammed bin Salman global initiative to protect children in the cyberworld. Additionally, and for the first time with UNICEF’s support, the GCF launched the first Child Protection in the Cyberspace Global Summit in Riyadh. 
 
In an effort to support anti-bullying programs at scale and following UNICEF’s evaluation of the anti-bullying programme in Abu Dhabi, the programme was scaled up to 40% of the schools in the UAE providing children with better access to child protection prevention and response services.  This was achieved through UNICEF’s capacity building of 700 school committee members. Additionally, teachers and children in 50 schools were equipped with the information and skills to support children facing psychosocial distress. This was achievable through the adaptation and use of the global packages Psychological First Aid (PFA) and I Support My Friends (ISMF). UAE’s commitment to mental health nationally was further illustrated at the global level with the organization of the Fatima Bint Mubarak Motherhood and Child Forum on Mental Health in Abu Dhabi.  
 
UNICEF undertook and contributed to capacity building programmes targeting frontline workers. These included a training workshop on Child Protection and Alternatives to Detention, organized by IOM in Riyadh and a training undertaken by WHO for addressing violence against women and children in the health system in Kuwait. Other capacity building programmes with system wide implications included PRIMERO in which 50 Child Protection Specialists from the Ministry of Education in UAE were trained and have improved capacities in case management. In Qatar, UNICEF partnered with the Social Work Foundation to deliver a series of webinars on Alternative Care for Children reaching several hundred frontline workers. Another successful initiative of that contributed to the capacity building of child protection professionals is the Gulf Community of Practice on Child Protection. Three virtual meetings were convened covering topics such as parenting, technology and child rights.
 
The State of Qatar`s leadership including Her Highness Sheikha Moza with support from UNICEF and other UN agencies continued to champion at national, regional and global level, the urgent need to protect children, education and schools from attacks in conflict settings, through various high-level campaigns and events in coordination with governments, UN SG and other partners. 
 
In an effort to advance parenting, and as part of a UNICEF global benchmarking initiative on parenting programmes, a desk review of programmes was undertaken in UAE and will inform a national roundtable on parenting planned for February 2025. This initiative intends to enable UAE to move towards a coherent national approach.
 
UNICEF continued to undertake periodic campaigns on issues like mental health and online safety, which reached over 3 million people through various platforms, which included SMSs sent by the media partner Du. UNICEF participated in several milestone events through senior leadership, regional colleagues, and youth advocates. 
 
Social Policy, Data and Evaluation 
 
Considering the ambitious policy agendas of the Gulf countries, advocating for a better understanding of how the country spends on children is a key strategy to influence its socioeconomic priorities.  With a royal decree issued in KSA in 2021 to conduct a public financing analysis on children, UNICEF has launched a partnership with the Family Affairs Council (FAC) and the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and prepared a workplan to undertake the country’s first ever Child-focused Public Expenditure Measurement (C-PEM) in 2025. The C-PEM will allow the Government of KSA to analyze its spending on children, propose improvements in terms of coverage gaps and duplications, and track it over time. 
 
In an effort to improve social policies for families and children in the Gulf countries, in partnership with Innocenti Office of Research (OoR) and the Government of KSA, UNICEF has developed a series of policy briefs on childcare provision, family leave and child benefits, as well as country-specific briefs for KSA, Kuwait and Qatar. By analyzing gaps and global best practices, UNICEF intends to identify policy changes that would best serve families, particularly those with children, in the Gulf context. The policy briefs are being finalized to be presented at the second Arab Gulf Countries Policy Dialogue Series which will be held in KSA in 2025 and will focus on Family-friendly Policies in the subregion. 
 
With UAE being the host of COP28 in 2023 and KSA of COP16 in 2024, UNICEF leveraged these opportunities to advocate for child responsive policies on climate change and prevention of land degradation and to create opportunities and platforms for youth to voice their perspectives and voices. In KSA, UNICEF developed a policy brief in the lead up to COP16 focusing the impact of land degradation and desertification on child well-being. The policy brief identifies capacity gaps and advocates for child-responsive policies. Additionally, 30 young people (50% girls) living in KSA were equipped with the knowledge and skills and provided with the opportunity to participate in COP 16. The strategic partnership with UAE supporting COP28 continued in 2024 with the roll out of the trainings of the Environmental Sustainability Cross Curricular Framework (ESF) teacher toolkit, with some 700 teachers - covering approximately 20 % of the schools nationally. The roll out to all schools will continue in 2025. 
 
To assess the impact of the programme on the school system, a formative evaluation has been planned and a senior consultant is on board to conduct the study. Additionally, and through the partnership with the Ministry of Sports and Youth in Qatar and support from the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, UNICEF included youth in Qatar's official delegation as youth negotiators for the first time at COP29. Furthermore, UNICEF provided technical support for youth participation at the ECOSOC Youth Forum 2024 and supported MOSY in leading Qatar’s delegation to the Second High-Level Meeting on Young People's Learning, Skilling, and Transition to Decent Work in Tunis.
 
Leveraging commitments to address data gaps has been a priority for UNICEF in the Gulf. In 2024, UNICEF supported Governments to produce high quality, reliable data to monitor child wellbeing and the SDGs. A key milestone has been achieved in the KSA data ecosystems with the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between UNICEF and the General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT) for the implementation of a Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7). The final MICS reports will be significant in addressing existing data gaps and support the monitoring of existing policies and shape the design of new ones. 
 
In Qatar, the MICS6 survey report and the Statistical Snapshot was published on the MICS website for public access and use. This is Qatar`s 2nd MICS, which resulted in new innovations on how to undertake MICS in HIC contexts. Additionally, UNICEF supported the Qatar National Planning council to organize the International Doha Data Forum for Innovation in sustainable Development. This forum focused on innovation by using cutting edge technologies to develop new solutions and improve processes by fostering a culture of innovation in data. 
 
Key evidence products were completed and launched in 2024 which were key in informing policies and scale up of programmes. The ECD Knowledge Attitudes and Practices (KAP) study in KSA and the evaluation of the anti-bullying programme in the UAE were completed and have generated the required knowledge to inform decision-making, advocacy and contributed to significant learning within UNICEF and partners. 
 
Partnerships for Children
 
Against the 2024 revised target of US$56.2 million, the Gulf Area Office (GAO) mobilized about US$65 million, including US$3.2 million raised from digital fundraising, to support UNICEF programmes in the region and globally.

Beyond financial contribution, GAO leveraged strategic opportunities to influence long-term partnerships through key events. GAO participated in the Future Investment Initiative forum in the panel on Health and Innovation; Donors' Conference for the Sahel and Lake Chad Region saw UNICEF senior leadership engagement with KSA partners. The conference on Conjoined Twins highlighted UNICEF’s disability inclusion. To further its advocacy and capacity building goals, UNICEF developed a disability-focused webinar for Gulf partners, highlighting disability programmes in Gaza, especially in response to the ongoing crisis.
 
In Kuwait, networking and regular bilateral touch points with partners led to positive discussions and agreement to explore new areas of engagement and potential funding for 2025. 
 
In Qatar, The 2nd High-Level Strategic Dialogue between Qatar and UNICEF where the QFFD-UNICEF Global Strategic Framework Agreement and Renewed EAA Framework Agreements and 2024 RR Agreements were signed; the 2024 Doha Forum which gave a timely opportunity to tackle some of the current crisis in the MENA region; Qatar 1st ever National Consultation Meeting with local partners, such MOFA, MOE, MYS, MSF and MDS; Cop29 engagement with the State of Qatar.
 
In the UAE, in efforts to engage with high-net-worth individuals (HNWI), particularly from the Lebanese diaspora and women philanthropists, UNICEF’s Women Leadership Circle hosted two high-level briefing events (on Gaza and Lebanon crises). At the World Government Summit, UNICEF presented its education priorities for children in conflict areas. UNICEF GAO and Innocenti collaborated with the Dubai Future Foundation and launched UNICEF’s flagship report, “State of the World’s Children - The Future of Childhood in a Changing World’’ and the Future Child exhibition at the 2024 Dubai Future Forum. The event on World Children’s Day, brought together Gulf partners and supporters, including UNICEF Gulf National Ambassador Balqees Fateh and Youth Foresight Fellows.
 
GAO leveraged strategic GCC partners at key global events such as the UN General Assembly, including the Supervisor General of KSrelief Dr. Abdullah AlRabeeah, UAE Minister of State for International Cooperation Reem Al Hashimy and the participation of Al Ghurair Foundation Chairman at the GenU board meeting, and strengthened engagement with both public and private partners.

UNICEF GAO continued to work strategically with lead governmental and non-governmental partners in the Gulf to influence policies and national plans to be more child rights based, to support system strengthening and capacity building of service providers and to collaborate on social and behavioral change campaigns that promote children’s healthy development and wellbeing.  Key partners included the Family Affairs Council (FAC) in KSA, Supreme Council for Motherhood and Childhood (SCMC) and Abu Dhabi Early Childhood Authority (ECA) in UAE, Supreme Council for Family Affairs and Supreme Council for Planning and Development in Kuwait and line ministries across all the Gulf countries. These partnerships and strategic alliances were enriched through open dialogue and transparency.
 
To advance and position an integrated approach to early childhood care and education, UNICEF forged a number of partnerships that allowed greater visibility and commitment to this agenda domestically, at the gulf level and globally. In Saudi Arabia, UNICEF forged a new partnership with the Human Capability Development Programme as a key knowledge partner.  The Human Capability Development Program (HCDP) is playing a strategic role with the Ministry of Education and other partners to advance educational outcomes to the needs of the labor market, enhancing early childhood education, fostering innovation, and developing and upgrading skills.  In 2024, with the support of HCDP, a strategic plan has been development with the National Curricula Center to advance early childhood education aligning with global standards. HCDP has also facilitated a global conference Human Capability Initiative in Riyadh where UNICEF participated as knowledge partner engaging in panels and providing input to Conference reports on early childhood education. Similarly, in UAE, and building on a well-established partnership with the Early Childhood Development Authority, UNICEF played a key role in the design and convening of the World Early Childhood Development (WED) Conference where UNICEF demonstrated its leadership in parenting, early learning, and supporting children with developmental delays. 
 
Given the nature of work on child protection, partnerships expanded significantly with government ministries and related entities with local and international presence. Ongoing work and engagement in KSA on child online safety has resulted in a strategic partnership with HRH Global Initiative on Child Protection in Cyberspace with funding provided for work globally on child online safety. The partnership was announced at the Global Cybersecurity Forum of 2024 which for the first time, alongside the Forum, launched the first Global Summit on Child Protection in the Cyberspace. With UNICEF’s technical support to the planning the Summmit, together with International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and WeProtect Global Alliance, key stakeholders were brought together from across the world to position the child protection agenda at the heart of GCF and identify ways of collective action for child online safety.  
 
Beyond the above-mentioned partnership in child protection, direct work with partners such as FAC in KSA and SCMC in the UAE, collaborations with the Human Rights Council in KSA and entities like ECA in Dubai contributed to overall political buy-in and helped accelerating program work. Collaboration with UN partners like WHO, IOM and UNHCR was instrumental in advancing the overall child protection agenda, especially as they relate to the issue of migrants.  2024 was also a year, when several milestone events on child protection took place, which meant that partners at a global level were engaged. UNICEF worked with the WeProtect Global Alliance, the International Cricket Council (ICCC) and similar entities in the organization of those global events and giving them a domestic perspective.  
 
A key milestone during 2024 and where partnerships were leveraged and strengthened through continuous advocacy work is the area of generating more reliable, timely and high-quality data for the effective monitoring of child wellbeing and the SDGs in KSA and Qatar.  In KSA, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed between UNICEF and the General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT) to implement first Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS7) in KSA.  GASTAT, with UNICEF support, is in the process of identifying key stakeholders in order to establish the key governance structures to coordinate the survey it plans to execute in 2025. 
 
Similarly in Qatar and through a strategic partnership with the Qatar Statistics Authority, the MICS6 survey report was officially launched, and the Statistical Snapshot published on the MICS website for public access and use. Similar discussions for a strengthened partnership is ongoing with UAE and Bahrain national statistical authorities. In Qatar, high-level engagements with UNICEF senior leadership and Qatari partners as well as lengthy negotiations contributed to approvals on various funding envelopes from public and private partners that yielded to $48.2 Million in funding and with a $31 Million pipeline from private sector partners and $28 Million from Public, including $93 million in development concept notes with QFFD. 
 
The organization of COP 16 in the KSA in 2024 enabled UNICEF to expand its partnership landscape and build a partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment, Water and Agriculture, Arab Gulf Fund Development Programme and the Misk Foundation. Such a partnership has created an opportunity for youth living in KSA to engage at COP16, make their voices heard and contribute to UNCCD’s global strategy on youth engagement at COP.  Additionally, and through the partnership with AGFUND, a policy brief about the impact of land degradation and desertification on children’s rights was prepared with key policy asks for negotiators.  The policy brief was presented at COP16 and shared with key stakeholders. 
 
UNICEF also strengthened its collaboration with UN agencies, including WHO. Planning for a subregional meeting at the Gulf level on addressing overweight and obesity among children using a food system approach started with WHO in 2024 and will be conducted in early 2025. The meeting brings stakeholders, including the Secretariat of the GCC, working on transforming food systems in the Gulf countries to reflect on the current situation of overweight and obesity in the Gulf and identify and agree on the strategic evidence-based approaches and alliances to address this issue of concern across the Gulf.
