UNICEF’s strategic contribution in the Gulf is a combination of technical support to child rights programming and advocacy so that no one is left behind. UNICEF’s comparative advantage within High Income Countries (HICs) remains the promotion of a human rights-based approach to programming and ensuring partners continue to focus on the most vulnerable and that no one is left behind. While the gains in social development across the Gulf countries are impressive, they are not uniform and have not addressed access to social services at scale. UNICEF has demonstrated its comparative advantage in the Gulf and is well placed to support Governments as they accelerate action to address capacity gaps.
 
·         The interlinkage between domestic programming and resource mobilization offers an opportunity to leverage results across the Gulf countries. As governments of the Gulf countries are seeking UNICEF’s technical expertise in delivering best practices in their own countries in areas such as child online safety, mental health and climate change, they are keen to position as leaders in these areas regionally and globally through multi-country strategic partnership with UNICEF. In KSA and building on UNICEF’s technical support to the government in the development of the National Framework on Child Online Safety, a multi-country strategic partnership with the Global Cybersecurity Forum was launched and will allow UNICEF and KSA to advance child online safety globally.  Similarly, and in partnership with the Arab Gulf Programme for Development (AGFUND), a partnership was forged to support youth led climate action including addressing land degradation both domestically in KSA and globally in the lead up to COP16, hosted in KSA. 
 
·         The inclusion of high-income countries in a common universal development agenda and the SDGs has created opportunities to foster renewed interest in data and evidence. There is a growing appetite for filling data gaps related to the SDGs in KSA, Qatar, Bahrain and the UAE. This presented an opportunity for UNICEF to show leadership in the area of data transparency and availability. Accordingly, UNICEF has engaged with authorities and provided the technical support needed to help these countries review current data, sources and alignment with international standards and reporting processes.  There is a noticeable change in public access to data and data sharing. In KSA, for example, summary data and census and survey instruments are now shared with stakeholders. This is a new trend and if this is replicated in the other Gulf countries, it will augur well for significant improvements in the data ecosystems.
 
·         Promoting sustainable education for educators in childcare is an important part of the curricula and should be integrated.  In a pioneering initiative in UAE, UNICEF, with the support of the Abu Dhabi Early Childhood Authority and in partnership with Discovery Education, developed the Early Learning Sustainable Resource Package. Aligned with the Environmental Sustainability Cross-curricular Framework launched at COP28, it focuses on the earth’s biosphere and sustainable energy, renamed Our Earth and Our Energy for early learners. A training plan was also created to equip master trainers with practical tools to integrate environmental practices into nursery programs. This initiative will contribute significantly to all early learning centers in the UAE. 
 
·         Knowledge and experience sharing across the Gulf countries provide an opportunity to leverage action and joint collaboration.  The experience of the successful meetings of the Community of Practice on Child Protection, which was launched following the Arab Gulf Countries’ Policy Dialogues on Child Wellbeing in 2023, were well attended by policy makers and professionals from all gulf countries.  The virtual Community of Practice offered a safe space for practitioners for knowledge exchange, peer support and collaboration. It also overcame the multiple layers of approvals often required for other forms of knowledge and experience sharing. Partners are expressing the need for creating similar platforms at national level for issues like parenting. 
 
Applying a strengthened communication approach is instrumental to deliver on programme and resource mobilization results.  UNICEF GAO has adeptly utilized strategic communication to enhance visibility and support delivering both programme and resource mobilization results. Communication messages have been focusing on highlighting collaborative work as well as enhancing social and behavioral change results in the programme.  Leveraging social media, public relation efforts, media interviews, and web articles were key tools that were used to recognize the Gulf partners and their sustained support to development and humanitarian issues. Building trust with partners and being engaged with their communications teams led to extensive coverage and the running of successful campaigns.

After more than 20 months of conflict, Sudan has become one of the world’s largest and most complex humanitarian crises. Armed violence has triggered widespread displacement, food insecurity, malnutrition, disease outbreak, leaving nearly two-thirds of the population in dire need of humanitarian assistance and protection services. 
The current conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has displaced 11.5 million people within Sudan—making it the largest internal displacement crisis in the world. This includes 2.7 million people displaced before April 2023. Children account for over half of those displaced, many facing grave risks, including violence, exploitation, and loss of access to essential services. Additionally, 3.3 million people have sought refuge in neighbouring countries including Egypt, Chad, and South Sudan. 
Key border crossings, such as Adré and Tina along the Chad-Darfur border, have been vital for delivering humanitarian aid but frequently face disruptions. The extended closure of Adré, for example, restricted access to West Darfur, forcing aid convoys to take longer and more hazardous routes from Port Sudan. Seasonal flooding further complicated access, temporarily rendering the Tina crossing impassable. 
Even when crossings were operational, bureaucratic and administrative hurdles severely hampered aid delivery. Delays in obtaining travel permits and navigating registration requirements—particularly in Darfur, Kordofan, Khartoum, and Jazirah—compounded by ongoing insecurity, created a complex access environment. This prevented agencies from responding effectively to the scale of humanitarian needs. 
Sudan faces multiple, intersecting crises: mass displacement, food insecurity, malnutrition, and disease outbreaks. By late 2024, famine was confirmed in five areas (Zamzam, Abu Shouk and Al Salam camps in North Darfur, and in the Western Nuba Mountains) and projected in five more (Um Kadadah, Melit, El Fasher, At Tawisha and Al Lait in North Darfur) by mid-2025, affecting millions, including host communities and internally displaced persons.  More than 24.6 million people across Sudan are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above). This includes 8.1 million in Emergency conditions (IPC Phase 4) and 638,000 in Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5). Conflict, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access have disrupted markets and harvests, driving food prices beyond reach and worsening malnutrition. Prior to the conflict, Sudan’s global acute malnutrition (GAM) rate of 13.6 per cent among children under five was already among the world’s highest. Recent Standardized Monitoring and Assessment of Relief and Transitions (SMART) surveys indicate worsening conditions, with 43 out of 50 localities reporting GAM rates above WHO emergency threshold of 15 per cent. Three localities have recorded rates exceeding 30 per cent, crossing the famine threshold. Projections for 2025 indicate further deterioration, particularly among children under five, pregnant women, and breastfeeding mothers, with the dry season expected to exacerbate the crisis. 
The conflict has profoundly impacted Sudan’s 24 million children, leaving 17 million out of school—a generational catastrophe. Girls are particularly at risk, facing increased rates of child marriage, female genital mutilation, and sexual exploitation. These risks exacerbate gender inequalities, limiting opportunities and deepening vulnerabilities. The number of people at risk of gender-based violence has tripled since April 2023, now exceeding 12 million women, girls, men, and boys. 
Children continue to be killed, maimed, and subjected to recruitment by armed groups. Conflict-affected areas are heavily contaminated by explosive hazards, which pose long-term risks to children and communities. The destruction of schools, healthcare facilities, and water systems has left children without access to essential services, further compounding their vulnerabilities. 
Less than 25 per cent of health facilities in conflict-affected areas are functional. National vaccination coverage has dropped from 85 per cent pre-conflict to approximately 50 per cent, with coverage in active conflict zones averaging just 30 per cent. Telecommunications blackouts in Darfur, Kordofan, and Khartoum have cut millions off from information and services. 
Insecurity posed significant risks, especially in North Darfur, where attacks on aid workers and fatalities have surged. Local volunteers, essential for filling gaps left by international agencies, faced heightened vulnerability to violence, harassment, and detention, further highlighting the precarious nature of humanitarian operations. 
Looting of food aid by conflict parties and civilians has also undermined relief efforts, with major thefts reported in Gezira and Central Darfur. These incidents led to the suspension of operations in several areas, placing a growing burden on local organisations to meet urgent needs. In urban centres like Khartoum and El Fasher, community kitchens and grassroots initiatives became critical lifelines. 
Conflict dynamics have also led to a sharp rise in militarily cut-off communities, increasing from 14 to 25 locations nationwide. These areas, among the most at risk of famine according to the latest IPC report, remain inaccessible due to ongoing insecurity and administrative delays, leaving affected populations in dire need. 
In addition to the conflict, heavy rains and flooding from June to October 2024 displaced nearly 190,000 people (37,911 households) across 15 states, destroying 74,000 homes and worsening living conditions. Poor sanitation and overcrowding in displacement sites have driven disease outbreaks, including cholera (47,682 cases and 1,239 deaths, CFR 2.6 per cent), dengue fever (8,340 cases, 15 deaths), and measles (777 cases). These health emergencies have severely strained Sudan’s fragile healthcare system. 
Despite these challenges, significant progress has been made. Advocacy efforts enabled the reopening of the Adré border crossing in August 2024, facilitating scaled-up aid delivery to North Darfur. UNICEF-led breakthroughs in accessing South Kordofan and previously cut-off communities in Khartoum have also ensured that critical supplies, including ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTF), reached vulnerable populations. Local community networks and grassroots initiatives have been vital in urban centres like Khartoum and El Fasher, providing life-saving support through community kitchens and other efforts. 
Without immediate and sustained support, the situation in Sudan is likely to worsen, risking the lives of millions, particularly children. UNICEF remains committed to addressing these pressing needs, collaborating with partners to alleviate suffering and safeguard the most vulnerable populations.

Health  
In 2024, UNICEF delivered extensive health services and supplies to address the needs of millions of children and mothers across Sudan. These efforts included immuniation, emergency health responses, maternal, newborn and child health care, and outbreaks management.  
About 2.8 million children and women were reached with life-saving treatment at the primary health care (PHC) level, including 1.8 million in safe states and over one million in hard-to-reach states. UNICEF supported the functionality of health facilities in IDP hotspots, including establishing fixed and mobile clinics in IDP camps Kassala, River Nile, Gedaref and Northern states and delivering services and supplies to cover the needs of over one million people. Over 1.9 million children benefited from Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) services, with 1.1 million treated for pneumonia, diarrhoea, and malaria in safe areas. In cut-off communities, such as Jebel Aulia in Khartoum, UNICEF delivered health supplies for the first time in over six months, benefiting 200,000 children and families. Maternal and neonatal health interventions supported 17 hospitals and 517 primary healthcare facilities. UNICEF trained 740 health workers and midwives in maternal and newborn care and provided supplies that supported 772,000 mothers and newborns. Two Neonatal Intensive Care Units were rehabilitated to serve as referral centres supporting a population of 3,482,443.00, those two centres will serve as referral centres for all Sudan States. To sustain critical health services, 6,000 frontline workers and 4,400 vaccinators across 14 states received incentives, ensuring the continuity of care in both conflict-affected and stable areas. 
UNICEF’s broader health interventions reached over nine million children and mothers, addressing immunisation, emergency health responses, maternal, newborn, and child healthcare, as well as outbreak management. More than 60 million vaccine doses targeting 15 deadly diseases were delivered, benefitting 43.4 million children and adults. Major vaccination campaigns included measles-rubella for over 7.1 million children and polio vaccinations for 5.7 million children under five in eight states and partially in Khartoum and Al Jazerah states. The Big Catch-Up campaign immunised 23,000 previously unvaccinated children. 
UNICEF invested significantly in Sudan’s healthcare infrastructure by strengthening cold chain storage capacity by establishing new national supply hubs in the Red Sea, Kassala, Gedaref and White Nile and importing six refrigerated trucks. More than 500 units of cold chain equipment were installed across Sudan through the GAVI CCEOP investment. 
Targeted outbreak responses played a critical role in reducing Sudan’s cholera case fatality rate among 49,000 reported cases from 3.6 per cent at the start of the outbreak in August 2024, to 2.6  per cent the end of December 2024. Key cholera results include over 9.2 million vaccinated against cholera; 237 ORPs and five CTC established serving 798,000 children and families; 36,700+ cases treated by UNICEF delivered medicines; 422,000 reached with multisectoral response interventions. In addition, more than 1,600 health workers and community volunteers were trained in cholera management and surveillance. Emergency triage training, conducted for the first time in a decade, benefited 180 participants. 
To combat malaria, UNICEF distributed diagnostic tools, treatments, and kits to over 900,000 patients, including 65,000 children under five. A malaria vaccine was introduced in two high-burden states, and preparations for a 2025 mass campaign included placing orders for 16 million bed nets. Pre-emptive measures in flood-prone areas saw supplies prepositioned in 12 states, benefiting over 600,000 people. Following the collapse of the Arba'at Dam, healthcare and emergency supplies were delivered to 50,000 flood-affected individuals. These achievements underscore UNICEF’s dedication to delivering health services and strengthening resilience amidst one of the world’s most severe crises. 
Nutrition  
Sudan remains among the top four countries globally with the highest prevalence of acute malnutrition, a crisis exacerbated by widespread displacement, disease outbreaks, severe hunger, and restricted humanitarian access. By mid-2024, famine conditions were confirmed in Zamzam camp, while SMART surveys, conducted across 50 localities, revealed that 43 localities exceeded the WHO emergency threshold for Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) of 15 per cent, categorising them as “very high” risk. Alarmingly, GAM rates in North Darfur (Al-Lait, Al-Tawisha, Um-Keddada, and Tawila) and the Western Nuba region in Kordofan reached double the emergency threshold, corresponding to IPC Phase 5 “Catastrophe” levels. 
In response to this escalating crisis, UNICEF scaled up nutrition interventions under its comprehensive famine prevention plan, extending humanitarian support to 144 localities through 1,925 health facilities and 83 mobile teams. In 2024, admissions for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) increased by 43.8 per cent compared to 2023, with 422,170 children treated—the highest annual total in the programme’s history. This significant scale-up reflects both the growing needs and the effectiveness of UNICEF and its 31 partners in stabilising the supply chain and improving service delivery. 
UNICEF secured US$ 25.5 million worth of Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF), of which US$ 21.5 million was distributed. This included 438,000 cartons of RUTF, with 181,700 cartons delivered to Darfur via crossline and cross-border operations. Nutrition screening efforts were expanded significantly, reaching over 6.7 million children under five through health facilities, mobile teams, and community campaigns. Preventive care was also prioritised, including vitamin A supplementation for 2.9 million children, deworming treatments, and iron-folic acid supplements for 443,000 pregnant women. Additionally, over 900,000 caregivers received counselling on optimal feeding practices to enhance nutrition outcomes for young children. 
UNICEF led data collection and analysis through the Nutrition Sector Information Technical Working Group (NISTWG), conducting 31 of the 58 planned SMART surveys across 35 localities. These surveys provided critical insights to inform planning and prioritisation, ensuring resources were directed to the areas of greatest need. 
Despite these achievements, significant challenges persist. Limited access to affected populations due to ongoing conflict and displacement continues to impede service delivery in high-risk areas. Without substantial improvements in access and stability, the risk of widespread deterioration—including increased mortality and destitution—is expected to intensify in 2025. 
Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH)  
In 2024, UNICEF, in collaboration with national and international NGOs, private sector partners, and government entities, delivered improved water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services to around 10 million children and family members across 120 rural and urban localities in all 18 states. This achievement exceeded the annual target by 10 per cent, reflecting significant progress in addressing the critical needs of populations impacted by war, cholera outbreaks, flooding, and famine risks. 
Access to safe water was significantly expanded, benefiting 9.8 million people through a combination of durable and innovative solutions. UNICEF constructed or rehabilitated 467 water sources, treated water at 1,300 facilities, and provided household-level disinfection for 205,000 households. To address immediate needs, 210,000 cubic metres of water were delivered via trucking, with daily water quality monitoring ensuring safety. In urban settlements where infrastructure was severely disrupted by conflict, 4.9 million individuals in 23 targeted areas gained access to improved water services, addressing challenges stemming from displacement and resource constraints. 
Sanitation services were enhanced for 291,000 people, achieving 97 per cent of the annual target, through the construction, rehabilitation, or desludging of 14,000 latrines. Hygiene promotion campaigns reached 5.7 million individuals, emphasising the importance of handwashing with soap and preventing WASH-related diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea. Critical Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) supplies, including 792,000 bars of soap, 132,000 jerricans, and 45,000 hygiene kits, were distributed to 526,000 people. Menstrual hygiene management (MHM) interventions supported 80,000 emergency affected women and girls and 16 girl schools with essential supplies and awareness sessions. In 2025, WASH will scale up the MHM interventions to target 600,000 women and girls.
Cholera mitigation and control were central to UNICEF’s WASH response. Improved water supply reached 7.4 million people in 11 cholera-affected states, complemented by hygiene promotion campaigns targeting 3.1 million individuals. Cholera Treatment Centres (CTCs), healthcare facilities, and outpatient therapeutic programmes received comprehensive WASH packages, contributing to a significant reduction in weekly cholera cases—from 5,000 at the epidemic’s peak to just 400 by December 2024. Furthermore, 143 health facilities and 105 schools were equipped with gender-sensitive and disability-friendly WASH facilities. 
As part of its intersectoral famine prevention strategy, UNICEF provided improved water services to six million people across 79 high-priority localities. Additionally, 194,000 individuals gained access to adequate sanitation, 4.3 million participated in hygiene promotion campaigns, and 444,000 received critical supplies, including soap, jerricans, and hygiene kits. 
To enhance its WASH response capacity, UNICEF led 13 state coordination forums, achieving all annual sector coordination targets. A robust locality-level monitoring system delivered detailed, disaggregated data on beneficiaries and interventions across all 18 states. Capacity-building initiatives trained 755 sector partners and 3,750 community members, reinforcing local WASH expertise and ensuring sustainability. 
Child Protection  
In 2024, UNICEF and its partners delivered critical child protection services to over 2.8 million children, of whom 52 per cent were girls, and 168,792 caregivers. Through community mechanisms, child-friendly spaces, and learning environments, Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services were provided, fostering emotional resilience, mental well-being, and improved learning capacities. These safe spaces empowered children, particularly girls, to report Gender-Based Violence (GBV) cases, including Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) and Child Marriage (CM), facilitating timely referrals to essential services. 
UNICEF’s Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) interventions reached approximately 2.2 million individuals including 1,167,112 children and 1,089,653 adults (79 per cent of the target). These interventions empowered the vulnerable population with information on PSEA and how to safely access the reporting channels and report SEA incidents. Also, to strengthen the capacities of frontline workers on PSEA, a total of 15,460 individuals (60 percent female) from all the 18 states of Sudan, through in person and online workshops, were trained to prevent, detect, and safely, handle/refer those who disclose sexual exploitation and abuse incidents.  
Additionally, 6,473 unaccompanied and separated children received family reunification or alternative care, individualised case planning, psychosocial support, and referrals to health, nutrition, and shelter services. 
Comprehensive GBV risk mitigation, prevention, and response services were extended to 337,231 individuals, of whom 71 per cent were female. These efforts included case management, psychosocial support, medical assistance, and the distribution of GBV risk reduction materials. Post-exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) supplies were delivered to hard-to-reach areas, and Community-Based Child Protection Networks (CCPNs) were engaged to reduce risks and connect survivors to essential services. Gender-sensitive awareness campaigns educated communities on gender equality, GBV prevention, and survivor reintegration, helping to reduce stigma and foster resilience. 
UNICEF also advanced efforts to combat harmful practices by establishing 430 girls’ clubs, which reached 450,000 adolescent girls with life skills and advocacy on CM, FGM, GBV, and access to child protection services. Community engagement initiatives mobilised 386,424 individuals, while 8,797 people were trained to address harmful practices. Under the Saleema initiative, 17 communities publicly committed to abandoning FGM. UNICEF supported 70 intervention sites staffed with trained service providers and worked with the National Council for Child Welfare (NCCW) to advocate for legislative amendments, including updates to the Child Act 2020 and the draft Family Personal Law. 
Mine risk education reached 83,729 individuals, equipping children and families with life-saving knowledge about unexploded ordnance (UXO). These sessions, delivered in collaboration with the National Mine Action Center (NMAC), emphasised safe behaviour, object recognition, and reporting hazardous items to authorities. Sessions were held in schools, community centres, and child-friendly spaces, reducing risks in high-threat areas. 
To strengthen Sudan’s social service workforce, UNICEF partnered with institutions such as the NCCW, the Ministry of Social Development (MoSD), and the Combating Violence Against Women and Children Unit (CVAW). Over 150 social workers, 69 per cent of whom were women, were trained in case management, safe identification, referral practices, and monitoring, reinforcing the country’s welfare system and improving service delivery. 
UNICEF provided critical leadership on the CAAC agenda through the UN Country Task Force on Monitoring and Reporting (UNCTFMR) developing four Global Horizontal Notes (GHN) and verifying and reporting to the Security Council over 1,500 cases of grave child rights violations across the country. Negotiations with parties to the conflict to develop and implement a new action plan to end grave child rights violations as recommended by the Secretary-General are ongoing. 
Education  
The protracted conflict in Sudan has exacerbated an already critical education crisis, leaving over 17 million children out of school. The use of more than 3,000 schools as shelters for displaced families has further restricted access to education, depriving millions of children of their right to learn. Despite these immense challenges, UNICEF and its partners reached over 2.3 million children, 51 per cent of whom were girls, through formal and non-formal education initiatives in 2024. 
UNICEF supported the reopening of schools across Northern, River Nile, Red Sea, Blue Nile, Kassala, Gedaref, and White Nile states by providing essential school grants, learning materials, and launching back-to-learning campaigns. These efforts benefited over 1.5 million children, ensuring access to basic education despite the volatile environment. In addition, more than 1,500 safe learning spaces were established, delivering structured education programmes and psychosocial support to 690,000 children, including 51 per cent girls, helping address the emotional and psychological impacts of conflict. 
To improve learning outcomes and create a supportive educational environment, UNICEF trained over 7,590 teachers and facilitators from 16 states (across all states except for Khartoum and Gazirah), equipping them with the skills needed to deliver quality education. Digital learning platforms, including the Learning Passport and Let Us Learn, provided structured, self-paced education opportunities to 30,831 children, 52 per cent of whom were girls, ensuring continuity of learning for those affected by displacement and conflict. 
 In December 2024, UNICEF played a pivotal role in enabling the safe operation of the Secondary Education Certificate Exam across Sudan, supporting over 340,000 registered students. Through close collaboration with the Ministry of Education and the Education Cluster, UNICEF ensured that students could sit for their exams, safeguarding a critical step in their educational progression amidst ongoing challenges. 
 
Social Protection  
In 2024, UNICEF significantly expanded its Mother and Child Cash Transfer Plus (MCCT+)[1] programme, to support vulnerable women and children affected by Sudan’s ongoing humanitarian crisis. Building on its successes since 2021 in Kassala and Red Sea states, the programme extended its reach to an additional 27,000 women and 135,000 family members across three existing and one new locality in Kassala, as well as four existing and two new localities in Red Sea. Demonstrating its adaptability to shocks, the programme provided a US$ 60 top-up payment to 50,000 women from the initial cohort to help mitigate the effects of severe flooding in these states. 
 
In September 2024, the MCCT+ programme expanded to the River Nile state, addressing the needs of 18,500 additional women and their children, including 4,070 internally displaced women. By the end of the year, the programme had reached a total of 96,200 women and 481,000 family members across Kassala, Red Sea, and River Nile states, underscoring its critical role in supporting Sudan’s most vulnerable populations. 
The MCCT+ programme’s integration with social and behaviour change (SBC) initiatives significantly amplified its impact. Key messages on essential family practices—such as antenatal and postnatal care, child nutrition, and the prevention of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM)—were disseminated through awareness campaigns, mobile cinemas, and other communication tools. Birth registration was systematically incorporated, ensuring children’s future access to basic rights and essential services. Monitoring data revealed substantial improvements in the utilisation of health and nutrition services among pregnant and lactating women and their children, reflecting the programme’s effectiveness in promoting positive behavioural outcomes. 
 
Cross-cutting 
In 2024, UNICEF’s Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) interventions played a pivotal role in addressing critical public health challenges, famine prevention, and building community resilience. These efforts reached 4.5 million people, 60 per cent of whom were women, through participatory community engagement initiatives across health, nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection sectors. Mass media campaigns bridged information gaps and encouraged service uptake, reaching an estimated 10 million people with life-saving knowledge and preventive behaviours. To strengthen local capacities, UNICEF trained 112,135 community cadres, including health promoters. In 2024, UNICEF Sudan continued to partner with a wide range of stakeholders from the public sector, private sector, multilaterals, civil society, academia and the media to advocate and deliver results for children. UNICEF and the World Bank developed a large-scale partnership for Sudan, in consultation with key stakeholders. Total funding currently allocated towards the four programmes is around US$ 200 million. Implementation will take place in partnership with WFP and WHO, in coordination with the Government.  
Legacy investments in resilience with key partners such as German/BMZ/KfW became increasingly important throughout 2024. Flagship social protection and integrated programmes have been scaled, including MCCT+, reaching close to half a million mothers and children in the critical first 1,000 days of life and through a growing network of "Makannas”, meaning “our space” in Arabic, is a safe, integrated space designed to provide children with access to an integrated package of services, including education, protection, and WASH.  
62 international (16) international and (46) national  NGOs supported [EG1] [EG2] UNICEF in advocacy and delivery of essential services. In 2024, UNICEF's Health and Nutrition programme collaborated with 31 NGOs, comprising 16 international and 15 national organisations, through 41 active integrated programmes to implement comprehensive health and nutrition interventions across 18 states. These partnerships bring critical financial resources, technical expertise, and capacity for executing and monitoring initiatives aligned with UNICEF’s strategic objectives and priorities in Sudan. UNICEF has also fostered strong collaboration with the WFP, WHO, and various NGOs to support children with acute malnutrition through the Community-based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) programme. Additionally, UNICEF works closely with WFP, UNHCR, and WHO to deliver essential humanitarian assistance to Sudanese individuals displaced by the ongoing conflict, ensuring a coordinated and holistic response to the crisis. Furthermore, UNICEF scaled up its engagement with NGOs for WASH interventions and closely coordinated with UN agencies, mainly with UNHCR on the refugee response and with WHO on AWD/Cholera response. In education, UNICEF continued to play a leading role in the Local Education Group (LEG) in coordination with the Ministries of Education, and education partners to address the deepening learning crisis.  
UNICEF continued to expand its partnerships with community-based-organisations, including the emergency-response-rooms (ERR), to tap into local expertise and networks for offering home-grown solutions to pressing issues faced by children and families stuck in the midst of fighting.  [EG3] 
Private sector partners from the banking, telecommunications and transportation sectors supported enhancing efficiency and effectiveness of operations and programming, as well as catalysing innovation in scaling up UNICEF e-learning programming, and solarisation approaches. With support of the UNICEF Venture Fund, the office conducted a mapping of potential innovations to enhance primary healthcare in crisis settings which will inform private sector partnership work moving forward in 2025.    
International and local media supported UNICEF in advocacy and communications. Throughout the year UNICEF and partners created several moments (e.g. UNICEF-USAID-SCI “Unite with the Children of Sudan” event, World Children Day) to bring attention and help raise the voices of the children of Sudan.  
UNICEF is deeply grateful for its donor partners for their continuous and unwavering support of its three-pronged humanitarian, development, and peace nexus response. In 2024, UNICEF raised US$ 491 million (58 per cent of its US$ 840 million crisis response budget) from European Union, the governments of Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Japan, Kuwait, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Italy, United Arab Emirates, United States of America, and the United Kingdom, as well as multilateral partners such as the World Bank, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, the Global Fund, the Global Partnership for Education, Education Cannot Wait, the UN Sudan Humanitarian Fund (SHF), the UN Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF), and UNICEF National Committees, to deliver results for children.   
Despite this critical support, funding gaps continue to pose a severe challenge in reaching Sudanese children, requiring continued  urgent mobilisation of additional resources. Additional flexible funding is essential to ensure UNICEF’s agility in responding to emerging crises and sustaining critical services. Investments are also urgently needed to strengthen and stabilise social service systems, preventing their collapse and ensuring the continuation of life-saving and essential services.  
Beyond funding, intensified and coordinated advocacy efforts are imperative to call for an immediate end to grave violations of children’s rights, the establishment of a ceasefire, and steps toward lasting peace. Advocacy must also emphasise the need for safe, sustained, and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Sudan to reach the most vulnerable populations.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, UNICEF Sudan faced numerous challenges in addressing the complex needs of children in a dynamic and crisis-driven environment. Limited access to high-risk areas, delayed supply deliveries, and restricted integration with other sectors such as GBV, combined with funding shortages, hindered service delivery. Despite these obstacles, efforts to support resilience through localisation and community engagement continued. This experience reinforced the importance of the humanitarian-development-peace nexus as a foundational approach to programming, emphasising the need for risk-informed and adaptive implementation to address evolving needs effectively. 
UNICEF faced challenges in delivering health and nutrition services, particularly in high-risk areas. Limited access due to conflict and infrastructure. Gaps in maternal and newborn care, disrupted immunisation campaigns, and overreliance on cash incentives for frontline workers hindered effective service delivery. These challenges underscore the need for robust supply chains, strategic planning, and innovative solutions to ensure continuity. 
 UNICEF took several strategic measures to enhance service delivery including prepositioning critical therapeutic supplies that were used during disruptions. Additionally, a multipronged approach was used to strengthen the involvement of nontraditional partners and local networks while increasing engagement with the government. Reaching vulnerable areas through partnerships with local organisations and expansion of mobile clinics proved crucial for ensuring access to essential services. Integrated services, such as combining maternal health initiatives with outbreak response efforts, demonstrated significant effectiveness in addressing multiple needs simultaneously. Building local capacity by strengthening the health workforce was vital for ensuring the long-term sustainability of healthcare services. Additionally, supporting innovation through investments in local expertise and infrastructure was critical for the successful implementation of new and adaptive solutions in these challenging environments. For example, in areas where UN is not able to place staff members due to access restrictions, UNICEF recruited through a third-party arrangement and deployed Emergency Nutrition Officers to monitor and support in-person programme delivery on the ground. 
 In 2024, WASH programme faced numerous challenges, including insecurity, looting, and the destruction of facilities, which severely restricted access to implementation sites. High operational costs disrupted supply chains, and the destruction of urban water systems serving large local and IDP populations further compounded the difficulties. Limited human resource capacity, stemming from insecurity and disrupted civil service and NGO systems, alongside an unstable governmental management environment, hindered upstream interventions. Additionally, inadequate monitoring capacities and communication channels, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict, and donor restrictions on funding government entities further restricted programme effectiveness. 
 
Prepositioning critical supplies in at-risk states proved essential for timely support during emergencies such as conflicts and cholera outbreaks. Maintaining standby programme documents and onboarding competent partners facilitated rapid implementation in abrupt crises. Capacity building and partnerships with local governments and national NGOs accelerated interventions. Collaborating with both government and private sectors through direct payment modalities emerged as a highly effective implementation strategy. Expanded support for urban WASH facilities, critical for large populations and IDPs, remains a priority due to significant operational and maintenance challenges. Piloting innovative technologies, such as solar-powered systems, compact water treatment units, and desalination plants, showed promise in addressing gaps for underserved populations. Moreover, leveraging video-based success stories improved donor engagement and international support. Finally, UNICEF-supported community-led sanitation programmes succeeded in safer regions, largely due to collaboration with community platforms and local NGOs, underscoring the importance of localised approaches. 
 Child Protection and Education programmes faced low logistical capacity, inadequate referral systems, and heightened risks of exploitation and child recruitment. Education efforts struggled with poor e-learning connectivity, school occupation by armed groups, and restricted access in RSF-controlled areas. Child protection programmes were hindered by limited logistical capacity, weak referral systems, and increased risks of child exploitation and recruitment into armed groups. 
 Intersectional approaches between child protection, education, and other sectors enhanced programme efficiency. Integrating child-friendly spaces with safe learning areas and women’s centres increased reach and reduced intervention costs. Climate-resilient and locally sourced construction materials were identified as critical for infrastructure improvement. Collaboration with other agencies like WFP and UNHCR is crucial for standardising community initiatives. Additionally, the education system must focus on resilience, ensuring non-formal education is linked to formal academic pathways. 
 
UNICEF faced several challenges in implementing Social Protection programme, including the need for improved understanding of regional contexts and enhanced implementation readiness to adapt programmes to emergency situations, particularly in accessing hard-to-reach areas. In hard-to-reach areas, the MCCT+ programme proved unsuitable for emergencies, highlighting the need for greater flexibility in its design. Weak feedback mechanisms limited the ability to address community needs and ensure accountability, while gaps in service integration and support for issuing national IDs and birth certificates left critical child protection and social welfare needs unmet.  
The importance of refining location selection criteria to target most vulnerable areas effectively, fostering cross-sector ownership to enhance programme integration, and gaining a deeper understanding of child poverty dynamics to inform interventions. Additionally, strengthening strategies to reach inaccessible areas, improving beneficiary registration systems, and enhancing financial literacy were identified as priorities to ensure more inclusive and impactful support for vulnerable populations. 
Prioritising community engagement and Accountability to Affected People is critical to success. Communities need to be involved in decision-making to ensure UNICEF Sudan's actions are responsive to their needs. Establishing accessible feedback channels and aligning SBC initiatives with programme priorities, particularly in displacement contexts can enhance service delivery. Advocacy efforts must address child protection and programmatic intersections, while progress in Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse builds community trust and strengthens protection mechanisms. 
Integrating gender considerations into planning is critical to addressing the challenges faced by women and girls in accessing education and services. Strengthening systems and data management, bolstering local organisations, improving monitoring, and enhancing frontline workers’ capacity are key to supporting vulnerable populations. Efforts should include prepositioning supplies, improving localization, expanding adolescent health services, and exploring cross-border coordination. 
Future priorities include fostering cross-sector collaboration, advocating for sustainable government-led social protection systems, and supporting conflict resolution through community initiatives and partnerships. Flexible and adaptive programming, combined with a focus on peace advocacy and service continuity, will ensure that UNICEF Sudan effectively addresses the needs of children.

Indicator_Status3:
In Tunisia, 2024 was marked by presidential elections, economic fragility, and social disparities continued on negative trends. While the Government demonstrated commitment to addressing these challenges through expanded social protection programmes and budgets, the persistence of poverty, inflation, and regional inequalities underscored the need for reforms to break the cycle of poverty and promote social inclusion.
Presidential elections were organized in October 2024 and resulted in the re-election of President Saied with 91% of the votes. Voter turn-out was 28%, but only 6% among voters 18-35 years old, amidst a boycott of most parties. 2024 also saw significant changes within the government and numerous ministerial reshuffles in sectors critical for children. In August, the Prime Minister was replaced and a major cabinet reshuffle initiated by President Saied, replacing nineteen ministers, including those responsible for social affairs, health, education, youth, women, children, environment, and foreign affairs.
Tunisia faced notable economic challenges and stagnating growth, with the IMF projecting a GDP growth rate of 1.6% for 2024- 2025, the lowest in North Africa, following near-zero growth in 2023. Economic challenges were compounded by high inflation, which averaged 7.1%. Particularly high inflation on food prices (10.2%) presented an important challenge for lower-income households. Despite a gradual reduction in the fiscal deficit, estimated at 5.9% of GDP in 2024, public debt continued to rise to 83.7% of GDP. As of September, Fitch Ratings upgraded Tunisia’s credit rating to “CCC+”, reflecting increased confidence in the Government's ability to meet its large fiscal financing needs.
Tunisia is in the top three of countries with the highest child overweight rates in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. Despite the low rates of wasting (2%) and stunting (8%), the rapid increase in the prevalence of overweight and obesity among children represents a major public health challenge. The mid-2024 UNICEF global Child Food Poverty Report shows 36% of children living in food poverty, among which 8% in its severe form. , The Government adopted a UNICEF-supported national Child Feeding and Nutrition Strategy 2024-2030 and rolled out nation-wide sensitization and social and behaviour change activities about healthy nutrition. 
A UNICEF-supported national research agenda highlighted the negative trends and challenges faced by low-income populations and children. Simulations of inflation impacts revealed that the poverty rate increased at the end of 2023 by 1.8 percentage points, rising from 16.6% to 18.4%, while extreme poverty rose from 2.9% to 3.2%. Furthermore, 39.8% of households who, in 2021, had an income 10% above the poverty threshold had fallen below the poverty line by the end of 2023. After a decade of worsening child poverty, children account for 42% of the poor in Tunisia, while representing only 27% of the population. 
Tunisia joined the G20 Global Alliance to End Poverty and Hunger, committing to expanding social protection coverage, monthly child benefits for poor households and benefits for families with persons with disabilities, as well as school grants for 600,000 students. By 2030, the goal is to halve child poverty. The integration of the child benefits programme, introduced in Tunisia with UNICEF’s support since 2020, into the national budget, the institutionalization of doubled back-to-school grants for children aged 5–18 years, and a 22% budget increase for the Ministry of Social Affairs in 2025 reflect the commitment.
 
While Tunisia maintained an almost universal access to primary education and 89.3% of 5 years old children attend preschool, challenges remain in disparities among socio-economic groups, dropouts, system governance and learning outcomes of children. While 9 out of 10 children complete primary education, only 7 out of 10 complete junior high school, and only 46.6% of children from the poorest households. Foundational learning remains a challenge with low achievements in literacy and numeracy: just over 6 out of 10 children aged 7 to 14 master basic reading skills and only 3 out of 10 basic mathematics. Among children from the poorest families less than 5 out of 10 master basic reading, and less than 2 in 10 master basic mathematics. Poor learning achievements hampers the future transition of those children to decent jobs, possibly reinforcing the intergenerational cycle of poverty. A newly established National Education Council should support the implementation of sectoral reforms in the forthcoming years.
The fifth consecutive drought had a catastrophic impact on the harvest, including the already decimated grain harvest, negatively impacting already vulnerable agricultural households’ income. Furthermore, the cost of drinking water in Tunisia increased by 16%, exacerbating the needs of the most vulnerable. A World Bank report warned that the economy could contract by 3.4% in terms of GDP by 2030 if climate change risks are not managed and recommended Tunisia capitalise on its existing social protection system to prevent and minimise the negative impacts on the vulnerable population, for instance the national social protection system could horizontally or vertically scale up in case of shock.
In 2023, water supply dams had a filling rate of only 38%, and groundwater was overexploited to make up for the deficit, especially for agriculture. In response to the prolonged drought, the Ministry in charge of water introduced a quota system for drinking water to reduce excessive consumption and spread the deficit across all regions. Based on newly validated WASH assessments in schools, healthcare facilities and preschools, only 49% of basic health centres have access to a basic water service, 6.4% of schools are confronted with water shortages over one month, and only 61% of schools have basic sanitation service. This is posing a real threat for contagion in epidemic situations and achievement of SDGs on health and education. 
As of the third quarter 2024, the UNHCR registered 16,562 forcibly displaced individuals, mostly from Sudan, Syria, and Somalia and the number of unaccompanied minors rose sharply to 1,240. Tunisia's security-focused approach, which has included continued expulsions to the border areas with Libya and Algeria, has heightened vulnerabilities for migrants and refugees who often lack access to basic rights and services. In June 2024, the Government notified UNHCR of its intention to manage asylum and requested UNHCR to halt all new asylum applications and refugee status determinations, leading to heightened protection risks. Government policy stance and, in some cases, legal action against civil society organizations working in support of people on the move shrank operational space for assistance to people on the move.

2024 constituted the fourth and penultimate year of  the Tunisia-UNICEF programme of cooperation for 2021-2025, which is aligned  to the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF)  for the same period and the National Development Plan 2023-2025, MENA  regional Accelerators and the UNICEF Strategic Plan. Thanks to an effective  and agile response to the COVID-19 pandemic and support to government in  addressing impacts of the poly-crisis on children, UNICEF could continue  harnessing a strong positioning as trusted convener and leading partner on  advancement of child rights with the Government of Tunisia and its  development partners. Over the four years of the programme cycle, UNICEF  advocacy has had significant success in mobilizing financial support against  children’s needs reflected in the multiple raising of the funding ceiling to  more than five times the initial planned resources. 
  
Over the course of 2024, and with an expanded  programmatic scope and human resource base notably on migration, social  behaviour change and communication, partnerships and climate action, UNICEF  had an effective throughput of over 20 million USD and carried forward  ongoing commitments over 8 million to 2025, advancing towards key planned  outcomes and targets of the Country Programme in: Inclusive socio-economic  development for children; Accountable institutions for children and access to  justice; Effective education, health, and protection systems; Sustainable  management of water, sanitation and hygiene, and environmental and disaster  risks and other crises. Partnering actively with 16 line ministries and  institutions under 2024 joint workplans, diverse civil society partners, and  working from a leading position on inclusive and child-sensitive human  development among the UN system and development partner agencies, UNICEF’s  annual review with partners evidenced 12 out of 13 programme outputs as  assessed on track towards achieving ambitious planned outcome targets by end  of 2025. Slower progress was registered on SDG Focused Policies and  specifically the institutionalization of a national Multidimensional Poverty  measure which advances with the joint support of UNICEF and UNDP to the  Ministry of Economy and Planning and line ministries. 
  
Continuing with the application of a proven  combination of technical assistance and evidence-driven policy advisory with  system strengthening and capacity development for downstream social service  delivery across programmes, UNICEF could decisively support tangible positive  change in thousands of children’s lives while advancing towards sustainable  institutionalisation of supported reforms and programmes. In the fourth year  of the Country Programme, research and design or modelling and assessing of  approaches continued on emerging or under-addressed children’s issues, such  as violence in schools, water governance and climate change adaptation of  social services, while breakthroughs in policy adoption, national financing  or scale-up of coverage could be registered in a number of areas of evaluated  long-term UNICEF investment and support. Milestones of such  advocacy-to-institutionalisation cycles were reached inter alia on  child-sensitive social protection, early childhood and nutrition strategies  and the response for children out of school, providing lessons learned and  momentum to initiatives moving along these cycles. 
  
In the area of social policy and social protection, the gradual establishment of a  Universal Child benefit (UCB) since 2020 with a phased approach from  modelling through to institutionalisation of child benefits for children aged  0-5 years, then for children aged 6-18 years, was concluded. In 2024, UNICEF's  support for Tunisia's AMEN Social programme included allocation of a monthly  child benefit of approx. 10 USD for over 430,000 vulnerable children aged  6-18, including 7,350 with disabilities. Alongside child benefits, UNICEF  developed a research agenda on poverty and social protection, producing four  reports to inform policy reforms. Using data visualization strategies, key  research results were shared with national counterparts and partners and  presented at a high-level roundtable with the Minister of Social Affairs,  gaining extensive donor attention and media coverage. This  evidence-generating effort, including the evaluations for UCB programme,  combined with an advocacy strategy and training of 100 social workers under  the TRANSFORM UN Issue Based Coalition on Social Protection in MENA, was  decisive in influencing social protection policies and culminated in the  inclusion of the monthly child benefit for children from poor and vulnerable  households in the 2025 finance law and the institutionalized funding by the  Government of the doubled back-to-school allowance to the value of approx. 32  USD, – benefiting over 580,000 children aged 5-18– including children in the  last year of pre-school.
  
UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Finance to  advance child- and gender-sensitive budgeting into public policies and  national budgeting processes. As a result, child sensitive budgeting was  integrated into the 2025 national budget circular, marking the first time the  national budget framework explicitly prioritized children’s rights. Three key  ministries, namely Education, Social Affairs and Women, Family, Children and  Seniors (MFWCS) developed child-sensitive action plans annexed to the 2025  finance law and monitored with a specific budget classification to track  expenditures for children. Additionally, a child-rights budgeting guidance on  sectoral commitment was developed while promoting south-south cooperation  through a study visit of Cameroonian officials on Tunisia’s experience.
  
In Child Protection, UNICEF Tunisia focused its  efforts on strengthening the child protection system, enhancing justice for  children, supporting children on the move, and generating evidence to inform  policy and programming. UNICEF advocated with the MFWCS to recruit 40 additional  child protection delegates, effectively increasing the workforce by 50%. This  expansion was complemented by equipping all 24 governorates with the  necessary office and IT resources and further capacitating the nationwide  child helpline 1809, now operating 24/7 with a trained workforce. UNICEF  supported development and piloting of a comprehensive case management  toolkit, including revised Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and digital  tools to be integrated into the PRIMERO-based case management platform. 
  
These initiatives harmonized practices, streamlined  referrals, and enhanced data management. Over 25,000 child protection cases  were documented in 2023, underscoring the urgency of these systemic reforms.  UNICEF’s work in the justice sector prioritized child-friendly legal  frameworks and practices. By training child protection professionals and  justice officials, UNICEF promoted child-centered mediation and interviewing  techniques. These efforts helped ensure that children in contact with the law  were treated with dignity and their rights upheld. Through partnerships with  IOM, UNHCR, and the government, UNICEF provided services to 172 unaccompanied  minors who received tailored case management, psychosocial support, and  access to shelter services. Systematic referral pathways addressed gaps in  protection exacerbated by restrictive asylum policies. Community-based  initiatives further expanded protective environments for children on the  move, providing critical services and psychosocial care. An online training course  specific on dealing with children on the move for professionals working in  social protection and child protection was developed and launched on  socialprotection.org, the UN-supported knowledge sharing and capacity  building platform on social protection. Furthermore, Tunisia participated in  the regional initiative to enhance synergies between child and social  protection national systems. The assessment led to the elaboration of a capacity  building module for both social workers and child protection delegates that  will be rolled out in 2025
  
UNICEF supported groundbreaking studies to  strengthen evidence-based policy responses. A national representative study  on school violence revealed alarming rates of physical and emotional abuse,  prompting the development of a national action plan. Research on violent discipline  practices and the cost of violence against children highlighted that 86% of  Tunisians have been victims or witnesses of violence and economic burdens at  $865 million annually, driving advocacy for stronger prevention measures.  Fieldwork for the Disrupting Harm study on online exploitation was also  completed, with findings expected in 2025. Thereby, UNICEF not only addressed  immediate protection needs but also laid the groundwork for sustainable  systemic change on protection against violence, exploitation, and neglect  from strengthened institutions and an empowered social service workforce.
  
In Education UNICEF continued supporting  reform planning and system strengthening, especially in favor of the most  vulnerable children, while pushing forward advocacy on the global agendas on  foundational learning, equity, and sustainable and efficient education. The  approval, in December 2024, of the Education Sector Strategic Plan 2025-2035,  developed with UNICEF’s technical and Global Partnership for Education (GPE)  financial support, was a breakthrough for future sector reforms. The Strategy  is based on a thorough Sectoral Analysis and aims at overcoming major  systemic bottlenecks by focusing on equity and learning. The organization,  alongside UNDP, UNFPA, ILO, and UNESCO, of the second regional high-level  meeting on young people’s learning, skilling, social inclusion, and  transition to decent work in June 2024, was another major milestone  contributing to the global and regional agendas on education, employment, and  equity, and promoting sustainable solutions for adolescents and youth not in  education, employment, or training (NEET). The new voluntary national  commitments taken during the meeting reiterate the importance of the Second  Chance programme and the youth centers as strategies to respond to the needs  of the NEET. The commitments are also aligned with the new National Youth  Policy 2035, which includes a pillar dedicated to the social and economic  inclusion of youth. 
  
While contributing to improving teachers’  pre-service training and mainstreaming life skills into the education system,  UNICEF also focused on continuing to support strengthening the capacity of  the Ministry of Education (MoE) for future curriculum reforms. In this  regard, the skills of more than 390 primary school inspectors were  strengthened in curriculum design thanks to UNICEF technical assistance and  based on the National General Curriculum, which mainstreams life-skills. Based  on the training, the inspectors could already develop a framework for future  curriculum development. UNICEF continued to support the progressive expansion  of key programmes in favor of the most vulnerable children. The school  dropout prevention programme could identify more than 300 children at risk of  drop-out and accompany them with psychosocial support offered by the  counselling offices as well as with remedial education sessions. An early  warning system for detecting children at risk of dropout is now part of the  MoE’s IT solutions available to all schools in the country. The Second Chance  programme reached almost 800 adolescents (including 9 children with  disabilities) with psychosocial support, orientation, and life-skills-based  remedial education services, bringing the total number of beneficiaries since  the opening of the first center in 2020 to around 6,000. Half of the  beneficiaries have already returned to school or joined vocational training  thanks to the programme. Finally, UNICEF has strengthened its partnership with  the Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS) by launching the innovative  initiative UPSHIFT in line with the youth transition from learning to earning  agenda. Through this initiative, 1,200 youth (40% girls) from all over  Tunisia could acquire new entrepreneurial skills, strengthen their life  skills and develop innovative projects, while 84 mentors have gained  knowledge on conducting bootcamps and accompanying youth in their learning  journ
ey. In addition, 301 youth centres in vulnerable areas were provided with  recreational games and equipment to organize outdoor extracurricular  activities, benefiting 88,995 young people.
  
The Early Childhood Development (ECD) agenda continued  advancing with the support of UNICEF. A nationally-led mid-term evaluation of  the multisectoral ECD Strategy adopted in 2017 provided important insights  and direction for the future, notably the extension of the policy to 2030  with an improved governance and results framework. In addition, significant  steps towards the generalization of one year of pre-primary education were  taken with the establishment of a multisectoral committee comprising three  ministries (MOE, MFWCS, and Ministry of Religious Affairs) responsible for  the action plan for the universalization of pre-primary education. These  efforts resulted in an additional 5,000 children, particularly from rural and  deprived areas, being enrolled in the 'Classe Préparatoire', increasing the  percentage of children attending at least one year of preschool education  from 92% to 94%, thereby contributing to the attainment of SDG 4. The  Positive Parenting Programme was extended to 35 new sites and seventy-seven  frontline workers completed six months of coaching on Care for Child  Development practice, benefiting 8,000 children. Furthermore, a pool of 22  trainers in Caring for Caregivers (CFC) was established and will be  responsible for the adaptation and institutionalization of this approach,  crucial in the support to the caregivers’ mental wellbeing. 
  
The introduction of the Human Papillomavirus (HPV)  vaccine for 12-year-old girls in early 2025 represents a major achievement  following advocacy and accompaniment by UNICEF in 2024. Approximately 100,000  girls, including children on the move and out-of-school girls, will be  vaccinated. The Government signed its first agreement with the Gavi Vaccine  Alliance, and a catalytic fund was mobilized to support the introduction of  the HPV vaccine. Furthermore, UNICEF played an important role in the  digitalization of the health system, including through the modernization of  the Ministry of Health (MoH) data center, CIMS, and the integration of  routine immunization data into the national immunization repository data  system, EVAX.
  
UNICEF has been working closely with the MoH and  other partners to advocate for improved quality of nutrition services,  including the strengthening of relevant policies and regulatory frameworks.  In 2024, the Parliament approved a new Maternity Leave Law, extending paid  maternity leave for mothers from two to three months and for fathers from  seven to ten days. Additionally, the national Child Feeding and Nutrition  Strategy 2024-2030, with a significant focus on overweight prevention, was  adopted in July 2024. Furthermore, a UNICEF-supported national nutrition  communication campaign on child nutrition reached more than 6.6 million  people on social media as well as through national television and radio, and  in partnership with civil society, nineteen Social and Behaviour Change (SBC)  tools on nutrition (games, a theatre play, songs, podcasts, etc.) were  developed, and more than 7,000 children and adolescents engaged in SBC  interventions during Summer Camps of the Tunisian Scouts and the NGO Tunisian  Union for Social Solidarity.
  
WASH and WASH-led climate action programming was prioritized  in a context of five consecutive years of drought, where limited access to  water in primary health centers and prolonged water cuts in schools are  increasingly putting children in vulnerable areas at risk. UNICEF-supported  nationally representative water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) assessments  undertaken in 2021 with the Government in schools, healthcare facilities and  preschools, were validated by the Government in 2024 and highlight important  challenges in access to basic water services and basic sanitation services in  institutions hosting children: Only 49% of basic health centres have access  to a basic water service. National standards for the construction of  environmentally friendly and climate-resilient WASH infrastructures in schools  have been developed and will harmonize the construction of WASH  infrastructures that contribute to the energy transition and addressing  climate change and environmental risks. 
  
UNICEF has supported the MoH in establishing a  multisectoral interministerial committee to address the challenges related to  access to WASH services and infection prevention and control (IPC) in primary  health centers. This committee has overseen the entire process of developing  the national Plan for improving WASH/IPC services in health centers and will  be institutionalized in 2025 by a ministerial decree to ensure the effective  implementation. 
  
In view of increasing youth engagement on climate  change, UNICEF supported MoE in launching a national competition on  sustainable development and environmental education in all primary and  secondary schools, reaching at least one million pupils. In addition, UNICEF  facilitated the engagement of more than 1,200 children and youth in climate  action by not only enhancing their knowledge but also sustaining their  initiatives in awareness raising activities, local environmental projects in  schools and communities, and advocacy for child- and youth-sensitive climate  policies. 
  
The partnership between UNICEF and the Ministry of  Environment and the MoYS has been significantly strengthened with the  initiation of a youth engagement strategy in climate action and an overall  engagement and awareness raising of over 35,000 adolescents and young people.  The development of this strategy, launched in August 2024, aims to  institutionalize the participation of adolescents and young people in climate  initiatives. More than 100 adolescents and young people were consulted at the  local level, expressing their willingness to contribute to Tunisia-s efforts  to address the challenges of climate change, particularly through behaviour  change actions and green entrepreneurship. A national conference is scheduled  for early 2025 to consolidate all contributions from adolescents and young  people from various backgrounds, including NEETs, as well as actors from  various ministries, in view of the finalization of the strategy. In addition,  the recommendations from the youth consultations will feed into the update of  the Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). With regard to the NDC 3.0, the  Ministry of Environment has agreed to place greater emphasis on the education  sector, focusing on the adaptation of curricula, teaching methods and school  infrastructure. 
Programme excellence and operational effectiveness were actively pursued by UNICEF  Tunisia Country Office (TCO), aiming to propel accelerated achievement of  planned programme results with effective cross-sectoral and operational  support in a workplace culture anchored in lived UNICEF values. Alongside programmatic  and funding expansion over the course of the Country Programme, the number of  staff increased from 31 in 2020 to 51 in the structure approved during the  Mid-Term Review (+67%) with a corresponding need of adjusting and  strengthening management mechanisms. The Country Office, under a completed  new leadership, implemented an Annual Management Plan that was developed  participatorily with all staff geared towards process efficiencies and  well-being and, with the support of MENARO and Algeria offices, conducted a  peer review on governance, risk management, HACT processes and supply to  inform improvements aligned to the office modernization initiative. In  addition to fully revising the risk profile, a Business Continuity Process  exercise was conducted to ensure operational preparedness. 

In support of people and culture, visits of a MENARO  staff counselor and Ombudsman facilitated collective and individual sessions.  The office achieved the highest participation rate in the region for the  global staff survey at 94%, registering however a slight decrease in the  rating to 3.61 from 3.96 in 2022 (-0.35) in terms of Employee Experience  index. Following work during an all staff retreat and based on proposals of  an internal team representative of diverse staff categories, an action plan  on areas needing improvement such as psychological safety and personnel  empowerment, career development and internal communication. 
  
Among overall expenditures exceeding 20 million  USD, TCO processed a total of 10,801,996 in net cash transfers to  implementing partners. Conducting financial and programmatic assurance,  respectively, to 183% of the and 146% of the minimum required, UNICEF also  increased HACT Committee activity and developed a PSEA action plan. In its  portfolio approach of up- and downstream interventions, construction and  rehabilitation activities also played a critical role, with a workplan of 0.5  million USD implemented on e.g. rehabilitation and solarization of schools.  Efficient supply processes enabled the fulfilment of a procurement plan  exceeding the initial previsions by 50% and recruitment of 28 consultants  provided depth to capacity for technical assistance. In addition, UNICEF  leveraged a Swiss-funded UNV initiative, recruiting eight youth and community  UNVs, including the first two targeted recruitments of people with a  disability among the UN in Tunisia. UNOPS services were used to support the  change in modalities of the migration response with a batch recruitment of 13  child protection personnel outposted with partners.

Government: TCO collaborates with 16 out of the 25 government line ministries to implement the Tunisia-UNICEF programme of cooperation, leveraging its long-standing relationship with the government to advance the agenda for children. The annual work plans are developed collaboratively with the ministries, fostering national ownership of UNICEF’s mandate. The highly participatory annual review meetings, held with the government, development partners, civil society partners and adolescent participation earns high ratings for fostering conversations in a context of otherwise limited multi-stakeholder platforms of coordination. TCO also plays a pivotal role as convenor or co-convenor of key stakeholders. In example, TCO co-leads the national social protection platform with the EU and World Bank. Additionally, TCO co-leads with UNDP in coordinating Climate Change Action, supporting the Government’s participation in the COP and supporting the revision of the NDC. Furthermore, TCO supported the establishment of a national child protection committee in collaboration with government counterparts, UNHCR, and IOM, promoting coordination for the case management of vulnerable children, including children on the move.
The visit of the MENA Regional Director to Tunisia in June 2024 was leveraged to advance strategic discussions with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) and key ministers on critical dossiers. A visit of the UNICEF Executive Board to Tunisia is being prepared in the second quarter of 2025 with the integrated objective of further raising UNICEF’s profile with Government and development partners in the context of national an UN strategic planning for the last cycle of cooperation in the SDG era.  
UN system partnerships: TCO is closely collaborating with the Office of the Resident Coordinator and other UN agencies on the development of the upcoming UNSDCF 2026-2023, playing an active role in the Common Country Analysis to ensure that children's matters are well reflected. UNICEF has championed the creation of a UN Programme Management Team, co-chaired by UNDP and IOM, to lead to more effective and coherent support for the Tunisian Government. UNICEF continued to lead UNSDCF Result Group 3, which is divided into three groups, Health, Education, and Social Protection, and added a new sub-group on violence, co-led with UNFPA, in 2024. As Operations Management Team lead, UNICEF facilitated efficiency gains through new long term service agreements on event management and IT security. 
The co-organisation by UNICEF and sister agencies of the second regional High-Level Meeting on Learning to Earning, hosted in Tunisia in 2024, fostered interministerial convergence and renewed commitment by Tunisia to advance on the National Second Chance programme in support of out-of-school adolescents. 
To nurture increased inter-agency cooperation, UNICEF took the lead of the inter-agency working group on Youth and spearheaded engagement with the newly formed Youth Consultative Group of the MoYS. In support of children on the move, the joint workplan between UNHCR, IOM and UNICEF was updated. In 2024, several UN Agencies, including UNICEF and UNFPA supported the National Institute of Statistics in conducting the Census.
Civil Society: TCO developed eight new partnerships with Civil Society Organizations (CSO) to implement the Tunisia-UNICEF annual plan for 2024, supporting the advocacy and SBC components of the programme. The partnership with the Tunisian Scouts and ADO+ promoted healthy feeding practiceswhile the partnership with Reseau Enfants de la Terre focused on youth and children’s participation in climate change action. UNICEF invested also in the capacity building of CSO staff on the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse , as well as on HACT procedures. In cooperation with the UN Country Team, UNICEF provided a sensitization session to journalists on the convention on the rights of the child and on the support provided to the Government in the area of social protection in support of advancing on SDG 1 – No poverty. 
Private sector: In cooperation with GiZ, initial linkages were made between the Tunisian Automotive Association and the national Second Chance programme for out-of-school adolescents in view of internships and job emersion opportunities. Furthermore, the Country Office undertook a stock-taking exercise of the individual giving resource mobilisation efforts undertaken in 2022 in partnership with MoE and MoFA among Tunisians abroad in view of replicating the initiative. UNICEF also actively participated in the UN Business and Human Rights working group at country level, inter alia raising private sector awareness on the analysis on the institutional capacity to prevent violence online.. 
Development partner advocacy: TCO developed a best practice case study on the use of regular resources which was published in UNICEF’s 2023 global core resources for results report, highlighting how UNICEF Tunisia deployed Core Resources (RR) over six years to support a pioneering plan designed to strengthen the capacity and effectiveness of the country’s immunization system. To further strengthen the immunization system, the first agreement between the Gavi Vaccine Alliance and the Government of Tunisia was signed, in collaboration with WHO. Additionally, the partnership with Africa CDC was reinforced. The Representative engaged in numerous meetings with Ambassadors over the course of 2024, ensuring to have met the representatives of all the countries on the UNICEF Executive Board. The office further hosted several visits from donors in 2024, including by the Muslim World League in February 2024, by USAID in June 2024, and by KOICA in December 2024. An annual partnerships report capturing the main results achieved for children in 2023 was produced and distributed among the office’s main partners, and made available in Arabic and in English on the office’s website. 
South-South cooperation: TCO continued fostering south-south exchanges in support of its advocacy efforts on key dossiers such as the introduction of a child benefit in Tunisia.
