Among others, the Ministry of Social Affairs presented the introduction of a child benefit and the provision of financial aid to vulnerable households in support of the back-to-school period as an innovative financing mechanism in support of education during a global webinar organised by the African Union Commission, UNICEF and the GPE on innovative financing for education in Africa, with attendance of several ministers and over 500 people in total. In another example, representatives of the Government of Cameroon undertook a study mission to Tunisia to reinforce South-South Cooperation in Public Finance for Children (PF4C) between the two countries. In addition, representatives from the Government of the Sultanate of Oman embarked on a study mission in Tunisia to gain insights into the experiences of early childhood programmes.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, the penultimate year of the Country Programme, UNICEF Tunisia confirmed longer term-observations on the application of prioritised change strategies and areas for innovation, and began to assess and consolidate their implications for the Country Programme 2026-2030. 
In a context of overall increasing challenges to international cooperation and shrinking space for civil society, UNICEF continued having comparatively high access and influencing ability through technical assistance, policy advisory and tangible support on capacity and quality development. 
 
Evidence for change: The UNICEF strategic plan change strategy on data, research, evaluation, and knowledge management was one of the most productively applied approach to drive change and, in the context of Tunisia, proved itself as a relatively low-cost pathway to high returns and impact for children. A prominent example is in the progressive institutionalisation of child benefits for all children aged 0-18 years. This medium-term agenda initiated by TCO in 2017 was accompanied by a multipronged programme of complementary evidence generation activities, comprising regular surveys among beneficiary households for accountability and monitoring of results, two consecutive evaluations of the child benefits for different age groups, and an ambitious national-led, interinstitutional research agenda on children, poverty and response with social protection and realistic financing models. The highly intentional dissemination and convening efforts undertaken by UNICEF to inform and support advocacy by the Ministry of Social Affairs and other development partners on social protection played a significant role in the ultimate breakthrough of full national institutionalisation of child benefits, as well as of doubled back-to-school allowances newly targeting also pre-school children. The 2023 MICS cemented UNICEF’s position as knowledge broker on children and similar pathways and results could be registered across programme components. Evaluation played a critical role in the improvement and extension by the Government of the National Early Childhood Development Strategy, based on its 2024 Mid-Term Evaluation and the preceding Preschool Evaluation. To harness this potential, UNICEF conducted certifying training in evaluation through the International Programme for Development Evaluation Training (PIFED) for officials from 14 line ministries. 
 
Continuity in uncertainty at a critical junction: The 2024 Sustainable Development Report ranked Tunisia as number 60 out of 166 countries and first in the crisis-affected MENA region. The National Development Plan and Vision 2035 prioritise inclusive and sustainable development, reduction of poverty and inequality and human capital development and the Government, which joined the G20 Global Alliance to End Poverty and Hunger, pursues a nationally determined pathway to development and a commitment to social justice expressed in domestic policy and financing decisions. However, rising poverty and inequality along urban-rural, wealth and gender divides, sluggish economic growth further hampered by climate change impacts, and a backsliding on children learning participation and outcomes threaten further progress and make pending reforms more pressing. 
While at-scale and statistically significant progress could be achieved in areas such as social protection and pre-primary education, acceleration is required in several other areas to achieve SDGs for children. In 2024, centralization of decision making, the high turnover of ministers and key officials, and general uncertainty related to the presidential election presented challenges for the continuity of activities. Thanks to UNICEF's unassailable mandate and the good working relationship with the line ministries and officials at all levels built over years, programme activities could proceed in a responsive manner and children’s needs remained at the centre of the agenda. The systems strengthening approach has been crucial in ensuring the ownership and sustainability of the supported programme directions.
 
Power of partnerships: TCO’s integrated focus on income and influence was further strengthened during the Mid-Term Review through creation of a partnerships, advocacy and communication department to sustain [LS1] [SR2] funding levels and harness partnerships beyond bilateral donors with the private sector, international financial institutions, parliament, civil society, adolescents and youth, diaspora, and the media. Working on closely meshed advocacy strategies and messaging between less frequent leadership-level engagements and engagements at technical levels, where robust relationships can be capitalized, will be a priority to mitigate slowing cooperation with international organisations. UNICEF will continue investing strongly in coordinating programme, social policy and advocacy communications with the government, and to mobilize development and civil society partners, including the public that was engaged, in 2024, with major campaigns reaching between 4 and 5 million people.  
 
Fit for purpose and right-sized UNICEF programme scope and structure: UNICEF’s positioning as the Government’s partner for innovation and high-impact initiatives and standing with major development partners came out strengthened from the COVID-19 pandemic and economic crisis that affected Tunisia in the first years of the Country Programme. Thanks to successful collaboration on the COVID-19 response, immunization system strengthening and the progressive institutionalization of initiatives such as the child benefits and programmes for out-of-school adolescents and positive parenting, UNICEF garnered funding support far above planning levels. Throughout this expansion, UNICEF Tunisia remained structurally conservative and preserved one of the best staff to resources ratios in the organisation.  Going into the Country Programme development for 2026-2030, ex-ante analyses are conducted to ensure continued criticality and affordability of programme components. 
A high degree of continuity is envisaged, with the consolidation of shifts operated following the 2023 Mid-Term Review in relation to strengthened gender and social and behaviour change approaches as well as the response for children on the move. In addition, the mainstreaming of climate action for children into all programmes, including education and adaptive social protection, will be borne out and more strategic engagement on adolescent-focused programming and mainstreaming work for children with a disability envisaged. Positive lessons learned from results of shared multi-country positions on social policy and evaluation will be considered in ensuring the required expertise for shifts and continued effective middle-income country programming, in conjunction with MENA regional office and country offices in the Maghreb or with otherwise similar profiles.  
In going through these assessment and planning processes, UNICEF will remain centrally engaged in supporting the Government in development planning and common UN Country Team processes towards a high-quality UNSDCF for 2026-2030 which will orient finishing-line acceleration on achieving the 2030 Agenda for children in Tunisia.

Yemen remains one of the world’s largest and complex humanitarian crises. Nine years since the escalation of the conflict and over two years since the expiry of the truce between the parties, hope remains that a peaceful settlement of the conflict is in reach. However, recent regional conflict dynamics have introduced additional risks. Millions of people continue to suffer from the compounded effects of the armed conflict, ongoing economic crisis, recurrent natural hazards, and disrupted public services.
Yemen is ranked 183 out of 191 countries in the Human Development Index (HDI) with a score of 0.455 in 2021/ 2022. Over 80 per cent of the country’s population struggles to access adequate nutrition, safe drinking water and decent health services. Most public sector employees, including teachers and health care workers, have not received a regular salary in years. In 2024, an estimated 18.2 million people, approximately two thirds of the population in Yemen, including 11.2 million children, needed humanitarian assistance and protection, with 4.5 million people, including about 2.3 million children, internally displaced.
Yemen continues to face a complex protection crisis driving humanitarian needs in the country. The crisis characterized by climate related shocks, protracted large scale displacement (538 k newly displaced in 2024), marginalization, and discriminatory norms continue to have a profound impact on the people across the country, including contributing to negative coping mechanisms. In areas of reduced hostilities with improved stability and security, the effects of the prolonged crisis persist. Severe deterioration of economic conditions, extensive damaged civilian infrastructure and the collapse of basic services are key drivers of large-scale vulnerabilities and needs countrywide.
Continued weaponization of the economy, limited access to external financing, the difficulties faced by domestic banks, and global commodity prices all presented considerable obstacles. In the absence of a political agreement between the parties, these trends are expected to continue and collectively contribute to increased food and commodity prices in 2024. Given these factors, Yemen’s GDP is estimated to have contracted by 0.5 per cent in 2024, following a 1.5 per cent rebound in 2022, according to the World Bank (WB). As such, achieving peace remains crucial for economic recovery. In addition, the World Bank reported in October 2023 that Yemen has been facing extreme inflation, particularly influenced by the ongoing conflict and humanitarian challenges. While specific inflation rates can fluctuate, the World Bank indicated that inflation had reached levels around 40-50% in various contexts, especially regarding food prices and other essential goods.
A loss of livelihoods for millions of Yemenis, coupled with the ad hoc payment of civil servant salaries, continues to hold the country back. Young people under the age of 25, who account for an estimated 70 per cent of the population, are particularly affected. The current level of poverty is believed to be significantly higher than in 2014, when half (49 per cent) of Yemenis were living below the poverty line, with 2022 estimates reaching nearly 80 per cent of the population. Purchasing power is a significant food security constraint, as incomes from casual labor and livestock, the main income-generating activities for households and poor households, fluctuate.
Yemen remains highly dependent on commercial imports for access to essential items, with up to 85 per cent of food imported. This reliance exposes Yemen to international price hikes and supply disruptions. Local food production remains limited– with years of conflict, floods, drought, pests, and high farm input costs all affecting crop yields–and there were low yields in fruits, vegetables, and fisheries across 2022 and 2024.
Heightened vulnerabilities due to climate change - Yemen is among the world’s most vulnerable countries to climate change and among the least prepared for climate shocks, ranking third globally on the INFORM Climate Change Risk Index for 2022, after Somalia and South Sudan. As climate-related events and natural hazards continue to become more frequent and intense, many communities are ill-equipped to brace for their impacts. Urgent efforts are needed to support Yemen to prepare for and mitigate the worst impacts of the climate crisis.
The operating environment in Yemen continues to remain extremely complex. Insecurity, bureaucratic impediments, and dual-authority structures pose significant challenges in delivering critical life-saving services to vulnerable children and families. Development and humanitarian partners in Yemen continue to engage with institutional partners in Aden and Sana’a to address these challenges for a sustained and principled delivery of programme.
Impact on Children and Adolescents
Children in Yemen face multiple deprivations, including limited access to social services, violence, abuse, exploitation, child marriage, and increasing poverty rates. These issues have a devastating impact on their physical and psychological well-being. Adolescents (10-19 years), estimated at 6.3 million across Yemen, are particularly affected by the protracted conflict. Adolescent girls, especially those in rural areas, face multiple risks. They often have very limited access to social services such as health care, education, and vocational training.
SDG 2: Ending all Forms of Malnutrition
Food insecurity continues to be a major issue, limiting access to adequate nutrition, with pockets of the country experiencing extreme hunger. According to Yemen Multi-Indicators Cluster Survey 2022-2023 (MICS-6), slightly more than 75 per cent of the household population are experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity (MICS-6). Globally, Yemen has extremely high child malnutrition rate, driven by a weakened economy, limited financial resources, rising food prices, insufficient food consumption, protracted large-scale displacement, infectious diseases, and conflict. According to MICS-6, nearly half of the children (48.6 per cent) aged 6-59 months in Yemen has been suffering from chronic malnutrition (stunting), 16.9 per cent moderately or severely wasted, while 41 per cent are underweight. As such, 2.7 million pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and five million children under five needed life-saving humanitarian nutrition interventions, contributing to the reduction of anemia and promoting proper fetal development.
SDG 3: Ensure Healthy Lives and Well-being for All
The health situation for children in Yemen is dire, exacerbated by ongoing conflict, economic instability, and humanitarian crises. This has been the legacy of more than a decade of armed conflict and a weakened economy, despite sincere efforts by successive governments and the international donor community. The health system has been severely weakened, with 40 per cent of health facilities currently non-functional. Many healthcare workers have not been paid, and facilities lack essential medicines and supplies. Routine vaccinations and maternal health services are disrupted, increasing the risk of preventable diseases.
The most recent statistics from MICS-6reveal that Yemen’s neonatal mortality rate (the number of deaths of infants within the first 28 days of life) is estimated at 21 deaths per 1,000 live births (17 and 25 for girls and boys, respectively), the infant mortality rate (the number of deaths of infants under one year of age) is 35 per 1,000 live births (28 and 41 for girls and boys, respectively), and the under-five mortality rate is 41 per 1,000 live births (35 and 46 for girls and boys, respectively). Immunization coverage has stagnated nationally, with 28 per cent of children 0-23 month not having received any routine vaccinations. Yemen continues to suffer from regular outbreaks of cholera, measles, diphtheria, and other vaccine-preventable diseases.
SDG 4: Ensure Inclusive and Equitable Quality Education
The educational status of children in Yemen is particularly concerning, with various statistics highlighting the gravity of the situation. The education system in Yemen is facing a multi-faceted crisis that requires urgent attention. Ongoing humanitarian efforts aim to restore access to education, but the challenges are vast. Supporting education for children in Yemen is crucial for their future and for the country's long-term recovery.
The MICS-6 revealed that 23.2 per cent of children of primary school age are not attending any level of education, totaling 2.7 million children. The participation rate (net attendance) of children aged one year before the official primary entry age in organized learning is 25.1 per cent. Additionally, 870,000 children with disabilities have had their education abruptly cut due to multiple displacements. An additional 8.6 million school-aged girls and boys require support to continue their education. Some 2,783 schools are destroyed, damaged, or being used for non-educational purposes.
SDG 5: Gender
Yemen has an extremely low ranking (October 2023) on the Gender Inequality Index (178 of 189), reflecting significant disparities between genders in various areas such as reproductive health, empowerment, and labor market participation. The gender inequality index (GII) for Yemen was around 0.754, ranking it among the countries with the highest levels of gender inequality globally.
SDG 6: Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
According to MICS-6 , 81.1 per cent of household members are using improved sources of drinking water, 62.2 per cent are using improved sanitation facilities, whereas 62.2 per cent are using basic handwashing facilities where water and soap or detergent are present. As such, around 15.3 million people, including eight million children, lack access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services. Limited access to WASH facilities, services and supplies is associated with elevated risk of diseases such as cholera and dengue.
SDG 16.2: Ending abuse, exploitation, trafficking, and all forms of violence against and torture of children.
Between March 2015 and the end of September 2024, over 11,500 children have been killed or maimed due to the conflict in Yemen, according to the UN Country Taskforce on Monitoring and Reporting Grave Violations against Children, almost four per day since the escalation of the conflict in 2015. The true toll is likely to be far higher. However, there are currently limited feedback mechanisms to report child rights abuses.

In 2024, UNICEF mobilized US$412.4 million through a broad range of partnerships, in addition to US$215 million carry-forward. The total expenditure for 2024 amounted to US$489 million. The resources mobilized for the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal amounted to over US$152 million or 89 per cent of the appeal target of US$170.75 million. In 2024, UNICEF continued to operate in Sana’a and five Field Offices, covering 22 governorates.
In addition to national programs implemented throughout the 22 governorates, including Primary Health Care (PHC) programs, systems strengthening, and unconditional cash transfers (UCT), the Yemen Country Office (YCO) has focused its prevention and protection services on prioritized areas across 13 governorates and 47 districts, reaching those most in need. The services have been delivered primarily through five main channels: PHC centers, schools, social service centers, internally displaced person (IDP) camps, and community outreach.
The following highlights the key achievements during 2024, classified by UNICEF goal area:
Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives
On the Health front:
Strengthened PHC Systems: YCO significantly strengthened PHC systems and facilitated sustainable and equitable access to essential services. A total of 4,822 PHC facilities were supported, out of which 3,114 received a comprehensive support package, including provision of essential supplies, operational budget, equipment, and capacity building for 18,100 HCWs. Additional support, including capacity building and incentives, was extended to 9,000 Community Midwives (CMWs), 3,600 Community Health Workers (CHWs) and 203 Mobile Teams (MT). In addition, 17,000 outreach rounds were implemented to reinforce the integrated PHC service in hard-to-reach areas. These initiatives enabled YCO to reach 7.3 million people in need, including 3.7 million women and children who received Vaccination, Integrated Management for Child Illness (IMCI), Antenatal Care (ANC), Postnatal Care (PNC), and nutrition services.
Third-party monitoring revealed high satisfaction levels among beneficiaries and caregivers with the healthcare provided by UNICEF-supported Health Facilities. Nearly all monitored facilities (98.4 per cent were operational, offering services for an average of 8.66 hours daily. Most beneficiaries (93 per cent) were satisfied with the services, which met their healthcare needs.
Improved Quality of PHC Service Provision: Quality of PHC services provided through Healthcare Facilities was improved. Quality improvement initiatives were implemented, the number of skilled mentors increased and the capacity of 2,034 HCWs in 1,046 PHCs was enhanced. Additionally, women and newborn had increased access for 24/7 to Basic Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (BEmONC) services through the upgrade of 60 PHCs. YCO improved the technical and operational capacity of four hospitals with the procurement of oxygen stations and essential supplies. Furthermore, 52,725 newborn babies received PNC within 48 hours at the community level, thus reducing the neonatal mortality.
Safer Healthcare Environment: Safety standards were improved in 50 health facilities by the construction of incinerators, building the capacity of 600 HCWs in medical waste management, thus creating a safer healthcare environment and reducing the risk of healthcare workers' exposure to infectious agents.
Increased Immunization Coverage: YCO maintained its leadership in the immunization supply chain and delivered over 30 million vaccine doses to children aged 0-23 month and women of reproductive age. Continuous cold chain operation was maintained through the provision of diesel. Despite challenges, 759,136 children under one year of age were vaccinated with Penta-3, thus protecting them against five serious diseases: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib). Localized out-posting in five measles-affected governorates reached over 117,000 children with the MR vaccine. In IRG controlled areas, two polio vaccination campaigns achieved 100 per cent coverage, reaching 1.3 million U5 children.
Enhanced Cholera Response: YCO effectively enhanced its response to the cholera outbreak, supporting the Ministries of Health in developing a multisectoral response plan, procuring and prepositioning 1,800 AWD kits in 22 governorate health offices, operationalizing 13 Diarrhea Treatment Centers (DTCs) and 215 Oral Rehydration Centers (ORCs), and building the capacity of 528 HCWs. Additionally, 3.3 million people in thirty-four cholera-affected districts received Oral Cholera Vaccine (OCV). These efforts, along with contributions from WASH, which benefited a total of 1,224,832 individuals, who accessed safe water through light rehabilitation of WASH systems, water trucking, latrine installation, desludging, and promotion of positive hygiene behaviors. This is in addition to the Social and Behavior Change (SBC) program section which further improved the effectiveness of Cholera Response.
Strengthened Health Information Management System: The DHIS-2 system expanded to 95 per cent of PHC Centers, allowing slightly less than 80 per cent of UNICEF-supported PHC facilities to submit monthly and quarterly reports according to national standards, thus informing health and nutrition programmatic and financial decisions across Yemen.
On the Nutrition front:
Expanded Coverage and Availability of High-Impact Quality Nutrition Interventions: YCO expanded the coverage of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) treatment services in Outpatient Therapeutic Programs (OTPs) to 98 per cent of the HFs across Yemen. A total of 352,408 children aged 6-59 months with SAM were admitted for treatment, with an average cure rate of 91 per cent, defaulter rate of 7.15 per cent, and death rate at 0.26 per cent. To address the economic and access barriers to inpatient services for the SAM children and their caregivers, 6,461 SAM children with complications in 15 UNICEF-supported Therapeutic Feeding Centers (TFCs) were provided with Nutrition Vouchers.
Additionally, fixed and mobile OTPs operated by 23,209 Community Health and Nutrition Volunteers (CHNVs) and 3,000 Community Health Workers (CHWs), overcame barriers related to access, disability, and gender discrimination, ensuring children received active case findings and referrals. In 2024, Growth Monitoring reached 375,843 children under two years of age, ensuring early detection of developmental issues. Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) screening services reached 4,824,803 children under five years of age, contributing to early identification of malnutrition cases and provision of timely support.
Micronutrient powder supplementation (MNP) for children aged 6-59 months reached 1,512,120, while 2,112,095 children aged 6-59 months received two doses of Vitamin A supplements, and 1,288,922 children were provided with deworming tablets. Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation reached 1,846,095 pregnant and lactating women (PLW) and 412,518 adolescent girls, contributing to the reduction of anemia prevalence and promotion of proper fetal development.
Improved Nutrition Practices of Caregivers of Children and Improved Child Nutrition: Caregivers of children aged 0-23 months demonstrated enhanced child nutrition behavior. An aggregate of 3,927,358 Caregivers received counseling on appropriate Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) through UNICEF-supported programs.
Strengthened Nutrition System and Enhanced Capacity of Service Providers: YCO supported the revision and finalization of the Multisectoral National Action Plan (MSNAP) and continued to support HFs through DHIS-2 to timely submitte complete and accurate nutrition reports at the national level, thus informing the nutrition-related programmatic and financial decisions across Yemen.
Goal Area 2: Every child learns
In 2024, YCO bolstered Yemen's education system and improved collaboration with key stakeholders. YCO’s multipronged approach to emergency education continued to enhance access to equitable and quality primary education, ensuring meaningful learning outcomes for all children, particularly the most vulnerable, with a focus on girls.
Increased Access of Children and Adolescent, Particularly Girls, to Basic Formal/Non-Formal or Alternative Learning Opportunities in Priority Districts: UNICEF provided quality, sustainable, and equitable access to education for 33,331 children, 47 per cent of whom were girls, through alternative learning pathways. Additionally, conducive, stimulating, and engaging learning environments was created through the rehabilitation of 6,092 classrooms, benefiting 587,528 students, 47 per cent of whom were girls, thus supporting continued attendance. Moreover, YCO increased privacy and safety for girls and boys in schools by building 631 separate water and sanitation facilities. Furthermore, the distribution of school supplies and materials to 397,719 children led to continued attendance and reduced likelihood of drop-out. The Back-to-School campaigns in Yemen, for example, were highly effective, motivating 96 per cent of parents and children to return to school. Satisfaction with Back-to-School Kits (BSKs) was generally high, with 92 per cent level of satisfaction.
Continued Functioning of Schools: During the academic year 2023/ 2024 rural female teachers who are instrumental in facilitating and promoting girls’ access to education, particularly in rural areas, were supported. A total of 2,109 rural female teachers in 16 governorates were provided with cash-based incentives and salary allowance, thus impacting around 84,000 students. Additionally, in order to ensure continuity in teaching and learning in three deprived Governorates, a total of 4,709 temporary/ volunteer teachers (66 per cent females) received incentives, in addition to 34,338 government teachers and school-based staff.
YCO also empowered schools through grants and technology. The program targeted 415 schools to implement School-Based Management Model (SBM) and provided grants of a maximum of US$1,500 each to address priorities identified in the school development plans. Out of the 415 target schools, 59 received tablets to enhance data collection and management, contributing to improved programmatic decisions, better planning, and enhanced accountability. The focus remained on both access and quality, with a strong emphasis on gender equity.
Enhanced Capacity of Teachers: the capacity of teachers and school-based staff was improved through series of capacity building sessions conducted across 12 governorates, reaching 5,126 teachers on topics, including active learning, self-learning, distance and accelerated learning, safe schools, psychosocial support, school management, and environmental and social safeguarding. Additionally, the capacity of 3,721 internally displaced persons (IDP) teachers increased in Education in Emergencies (EiE) programs management.
Reduced gender disparity in Education: YCO continued to address gender-specific barriers to education and promote gender equity across all programs. UNICEF's initiatives further strengthened education systems, foster ed partnerships, and enhanced coordination with the MoE, sector stakeholders, clusters, and implementing partners, to minimize gender disparities, promote inclusive education, and ensure equal access to quality learning opportunities for both girls and boys. UNICEF's gender-responsive approach included creating safe learning environments, providing separate sanitation facilities, and supporting female teachers to encourage girls' attendance.
Goal Area 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation
In 2024, the child protection landscape continued to face significant challenges due to bureaucratic hurdles and entrenched social norms exacerbated by the ongoing conflict. To address these issues, child protection measures were incorporated into other sectoral responses wherever possible, aiming to assist the most vulnerable children. This approach also involved leveraging the partnerships with governments, civil society organizations (CSOs), and other donors operating in Yemen.
Strengthened Child Protection System to Deliver Equitable Preventive and Protection Services: In 2024, YCO significantly advanced child protection in Yemen by strengthening the child protection system, providing essential services, and mitigating the impact of conflict on children and their caregivers. The formulation of National Plan of Action (NPA) for Child Protection 2025-2030, represented a significant milestone along the child protection continuum in Yemen. It outlined strategies to strengthen child protection systems and to prevent grave violations of child rights in the context of the conflict. YCO also contributed to the establishment of Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) and advancing the Children and Armed Conflict (CAAC) agenda. Advocacy efforts led to significant advancements, including developing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for reintegrating children from armed groups and the CAAC Action Plan in IRG controlled areas.
Increased Access of Children, Adolescent, Women, and Men at risk to Equitable Protection Services in Priority Districts:
Individual cases management services provided to 14,282 children, 35 per cent of whom were girls. In addition, Community-based Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) services reached 209,774 children, adolescences, parents, and caregivers to alleviate the Psychosocial effects of the ongoing conflict. Integrating MHPSS into health and education sectors created a multidisciplinary network of skilled staff, improving emotional well-being and coping mechanisms for children and their caregivers.
In 2024, YCO prioritized birth registration as a fundamental enabling right, thus supporting birth registration of 68,163 children aged 0-17 years with the civil authorities, 40 per cent of whom were girls, despite the political challenges faced. In addition, the birth registration system was sustained with one million birth certificate materials provided by UNICEF to the Civil Registration Authority (CRA) .
Increased Protection Against Violence of All Forms: In 2024, 17,431 girls and boys affected by violence received health, social work, and justice/ law enforcement services from trained personnel. UNICEF's child-friendly justice initiatives provided legal assistance to 3,079 children, ensuring access to justice, creating reintegration opportunities, and steering vulnerable children away from incarceration. Child Protection Section within YCO collaborated with other Program Sections to reach over 1.1 million individuals through an integrated approach that addressed gender-based violence, child marriage and female genital mutilation. Additionally, 88,289 individuals received GBV prevention and mitigation services, and 84 GBV survivors received multiple assistance.
Increased Awareness of and Improved Practices Towards EORE: In 2024, through the expanded UNICEF EORE program aimed to protect children and communities from the dangers of landmines and unexploded ordnance (UXO), there has been an increased awareness of and improved behavior to the dangers of explosive ordnance and means of protection. A total of 1,769,780 those at-risks were reached through, mass media platforms, community engagement and school-based programs.
Enhanced Capacity of Social Service Workforce and Partners: The capacity of the social service workforce to support vulnerable populations, especially children and families affected by conflict was further built. A total of 1,316 social workers across 200 districts were mapped and out of which 546 were trained, with 32 per cent being female. UNICEF also supported psychosocial support and case management training for 516 teachers, social workers, and health workers. This training enhanced outreach and improved their ability to identify children in distress and refer them to specialized services
Goal Area 4: Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment.
Strengthened Systems and Enhanced Capacities of stakeholders to manage and deliver efficiently and effectively WASH services across Yemen in a sustainable environment: Building on the achievements of 2023, YCO continued to integrate humanitarian and development programming in 2024. Development initiatives focused on strengthening the resilience of local systems and communities, fostering sustainable and cost-effective outcomes. YCO intensified efforts to combat climate change and promote environmental sustainability. YCO updated the National Water Sector Strategy and Investment Program (NWSSIP II), emphasizing climate change impacts on water resources and included a dedicated sub-strategy for climate resilience and a comprehensive country investment plan.
YCO led the WASH Cluster coordination at national and sub-national levels, overseeing the WASH Development and Resilience Partners Coordination Group for Yemen, significantly contributing to the mobilization of additional humanitarian resources and enhancing response effectiveness.
To enhance the operational capacity of water and sanitation utilities, YCO implemented various capacity-building initiatives, training 541 technical staff members, six per cent of whom were females, on water and sanitation system management and consumer engagement. Additionally, YCO supplied critical equipment such as resistivity and electromagnetic meters to the Ministry of Energy and Water (MEEW), improving the capacity for groundwater resource monitoring among rural authorities.
YCO spearheaded strategic initiatives for strengthening WASH sector institutions at both national and sub-national levels. A comprehensive Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) was conducted, detailing the impact of climate change on children’s rights and access to essential services, identifying key entry points for effective climate-sensitive programming. Collaboratively with the Ministry of Water and Environment, a fuel exit strategy for 17 major cities was finalized, outlining actions for Local Water and Sanitation Corporations (LWSCs) to diminish fuel reliance by integrating renewable energy solutions and enhancing energy efficiency.
In collaboration with WHO, a national roadmap for WASH in healthcare facilities was drafted. Additionally, UNICEF rehabilitated and constructed WASH systems in 240 healthcare facilities, improving access to health care facilities and reinforcing infection prevention and control measures within these institutions.
Increased Access of Children, Adolescents, and their Families to Safe Water Supply Services at Household and Community Levels in UNICEF Priority Districts: On the humanitarian front, YCO provided resilient, equitable, and sustainable access to water services while responding to disease outbreaks such as cholera. In 2024, 1.37 million people had access to safe water through the rehabilitated and reconstructed water systems across Yemen. WASH initiatives transitioned towards climate-resilient practices by solarizing 109 water supply systems, enhancing service delivery, reducing operational costs, addressing water scarcity, and fostering a greener environment. Additionally, 1.3 million individuals in humanitarian contexts, including IDPs, benefited from emergency water supply interventions, including 195,746 people with disabilities who accessed clean drinking water through water trucking.
Monitoring information indicated that most UNICEF-supported water projects were functional and accessible to individuals and communities. Additionally, feedback from people with disabilities highlighted that establishing water points in nearby areas significantly improved their accessibility compared to the situation before the interventions.
Increased Access of Children, Adolescents, and their Families to safe/basic sanitation services and improved hygiene practices at Household and Community Levels in UNICEF Priority Districts: 607,579 individuals had access to sanitation services in humanitarian contexts with the rehabilitation of wastewater treatment facilities and sewerage networks in urban and peri-urban areas. With the support provided by UNICEF, 20 communities achieved Open Defecation Free (ODF) status. Additionally, 427,000 individuals received messages on proper hygiene practices.
Monitoring information revealed that sanitation interventions significantly improved community health by addressing cholera and AWD outbreaks. Constructed and rehabilitated latrines, for example, reduced open defecation, thereby decreasing mosquito spread. Sanitation projects were considered by beneficiaries as of high quality and sufficient for their needs, and further enhanced their families' and communities' living conditions.
Goal Area 5: Every Child has an Equitable Chance in Life.
On the Social Protection front:
Delivering life-saving cash assistance and strengthening national social protection systems, with a particular focus on children, remained a top priority for YCO in 2024. Unconditional Cash Transfers (UCT) in Yemen continued to play a vital role in addressing the acute humanitarian crisis exacerbated by the impact of the conflict, economic instability, and protracted large-scale displacement. With support from the World Bank, the YCO provided unconditional cash transfers (UCT) to 1.42 million households, benefiting 9.1 million people. UCTs allowed families to cover basic needs such as food, shelter, healthcare, and education. Payments are designed to be flexible to adapt to families' needs., significantly enhancing household resilience and access to essential services. To enhance efficiency, transparency and targeting effectiveness in UCT program implementation, the program adopted a combination of payment modalities, including for example mobile money, bank transfer, and physical cash distribution. In addition, the flexibility of cash aid empowered households to make spending decisions based on their unique circumstances, fostering dignity and agency. On a related note, the life-saving nature of the cash transfers was confirmed by post-distribution monitoring, with nearly all households spending it almost immediately to cover their basic needs on food (86 per cent), debt repayment (59 per cent) and medicines (42 per cent). Satisfaction with the UCT Project remained high with 98 per cent of respondent cash recipients highlight satisfied. The 19th payment cycle marks the final payment cycle of the current UCT Project due to concerns about the inadequacy of the benefit amount and outdated beneficiary list, both of which are still the same as defined by Social Welfare Fund before 2014. UNICEF, the World Bank and national partners are in discussions to launch a new cash transfer programme planned for fall 2025.
In addition, YCO Multidimensional Poverty Analysis (MDP), identifying key poverty drivers and informing targeted interventions. UNICEF also continued its support for the Yemen Socio-economic Update (YSEU), providing critical data for decision-making and resource allocation. Furthermore, the Social Policy programme initiated Public Finance for Children (PF4C) work, starting with primary healthcare (PHC), to address funding obstacles. Capacity building and technical assistance were provided to the Social Welfare Fund (SWF), Handicap Care and Rehabilitation Fund (HCRF), and Social Fund for Development (SFD), enhancing their roles in cash-plus programs.
On the Social and Behavior Change front:
YCO continued leading strategic interventions to address community information needs and supporting responses to outbreaks. Specifically, YCO sustained social mobilization and community engagement, supporting UNICEF programs. Approximately 9,042 community-based resources, including volunteers, religious leaders, and health workers, engaged with 6.7 million people in lifesaving practices. Additionally, 750 health education corners were established in health facilities, and various audio-visual materials reached an estimated 12 million people.
The integrated programming approach adopted in 2024 supported positive IYCF practices, hygiene promotion, back-to-school campaigns, and awareness on child protection issues. These efforts led to over 90 per cent coverage in vaccination campaigns. Youth groups motivated 15,200 caregivers to complete vaccination schedules. SBC's demand-generation activities for routine immunization addressed vaccination campaign suspensions in DFA controlled areas.
In response to the cholera/AWD outbreak, YCO adopted the implementation of multi-approach interventions., while guided by social listening. SBC collaborated with Aden University to develop curricula in Social and Behavior Change and trained 624 staff on Accountability to Affected Population (AAP) principles. A comprehensive review resulted in a multi-sectoral SBC roadmap, enhancing program delivery, and addressing critical challenges faced by Yemeni children.
On the Research front: YCO concluded a series of in-depth analyses of MICS-6 data produce statistically sound insights on some key issues, including child mortality, birth registration, child marriage, child labor, and violent discipline. The findings were employed to inform both the ongoing Situation Analysis (SitAn) of women and children in Yemen, support the programmatic and financial decisions, enable Program Sections to revise the Theory of Change (ToC), and adjust their plans accordingly. Furthermore, three studies were commissioned in 2024, including a behavioral assessment on routine immunization, a community perceptions survey to inform a system-wide humanitarian response, and a knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) study on malnutrition and the utilization of micronutrients. All these informed and improved specific programming for children, women, and men.

As previously did in 2023, YCO worked closely with the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) in implementing the extended 2022-2025 UNSDPF. It continued to partner bilaterally and multilaterally with other UN agencies in both humanitarian and development programming, to work on common goals, achieve better results, minimize duplicative efforts, ensure complementarity and integration of interventions, maximize the return for women and children, and ultimately ensure the realization of child and women rights. UNICEF continued in 2024 working very closely with government institutions both in IRG and DFA controlled areas and to ensure the alignment and responsiveness of its humanitarian response and development assistance to national strategies, priorities, plans and, strategies, and the needs of vulnerable groups, mostly women and children.
In Health Sector: UNICEF has established robust partnerships with local health authorities, including the two ministries of health, 23 Governorate Heath Offices (GHOs), and 333 District Health Offices (DHOs). These collaborations focus on developing national health policies, community-based PHC strategies, national PHC financing strategies, assessments, and capacity building.
YCO continues to leverage its partnerships with WHO and UNFPA to advance maternal, newborn, and child health initiatives. The three agencies formed the H3 coordination group to support health ministries, resulting in the development of national health strategies and the revision of training curriculums, ensuring a unified approach to improving health outcomes for mothers and children.
In immunization, UNICEF works closely with WHO to strengthen routine immunization, identify zero-dose children, and implement outbreak response strategies. Gavi is also a key ally, collaborating with UNICEF and WHO to strengthen health systems.

This project brought together WHO, United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS), and UNICEF to strengthen health service delivery, supporting PHC, secondary and tertiary care, and WASH investments.
Through the Pandemic Fund, and in partnership with the WB, WHO, and FAO, UNICEF supports community-based PHC systems. This collaboration aims to build resilient health systems capable of responding to future health emergencies. Similarly, UNICEF collaborates with the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) to achieve these goals.
In the Nutrition Sector, UNICEF closely collaborated with the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MoPHP) to deliver essential nutrition services. UNICEF also worked with NGOs such as Local Field Delivery (LFD) and “Al Tamkeen" to support areas with limited government access. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with WHO and World Food Programme (WFP) on nutrition programs, including the Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) program.

It also participated in initiatives led by the Nutrition Cluster and the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA). Furthermore, YCO partnered with the High Institute of Health Sciences to fund and run a one-year postgraduate nutrition diploma for targeting 30 health workers.
In WASH Sector: In collaboration with the Water and Environment Center at the University of Sanaa, UNICEF developed and delivered training packages to enhance the capacity of WASH staff across Yemen.
In Education Sector, UNICEF's education initiatives were executed in close collaboration with the MoE in both De Facto Authority (DFA) and Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) controlled areas, as well as with education authorities at various levels. UNICEF worked closely with the MoE in planning and implementing education activities and provided ongoing support to the Project Management Units (PMUs) of the MoEs in both IRG and DFA controlled areas.
In 2024, YCO continued its partnerships with UN organizations and international agencies, including WFP, the GPE, and Save the Children, to implement the WB-funded REAL project. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with UNESCO to strengthen the EMIS system.

In Child Protection Sector: to strengthen systems and effectively deliver child protection services, address GBV, and drive social and behavior change to end child marriage and FGM, YCO established partnerships with a broad range of stakeholders.
