Every Child Survives:
UNICEF advocates strongly for Universal Health Coverage through Primary Health Care (PHC), emphasizing that community health workers are the backbone of any system. UNICEF seized the opportunities created by the recent political transition to push for reforms to fix the fragmented health system advocating for a unified leadership structure to improve accountability. With UNICEF’s support, ten officials from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), along with four influential national health experts, visited Sri Lanka in December 2024 to learn about its Primary Health Care approach, returning with recommendations for list of recommendations for health sector reforms in Bangladesh.

Our "Reaching Every Mother and Newborn" programme continues towards its goal of achieving 90 per cent maternal and newborn health service coverage nationally by 2030. With technical support from UNICEF, the MoHFW expanded the programme to 30 sub-districts across the 10 most deprived districts in Bangladesh. As a result, 52,581 women (96 per cent of the pregnant women in these districts) completed at least one antenatal care visit with qualified providers, 43,132 women (79 per cent) received four visits; and 30,678 women (56 per cent) gave birth in healthcare institutions—a 10 per cent increase from 2023.

For newborn health, 134,155 sick newborns received services in the Special Care Newborn Units (SCANUs), with 22,028 Low Birth Weight babies benefiting from Kangaroo Mother Care. Additionally, with UNICEF’s support and advocacy, a Day Care Approach for severe pneumonia management – an alternative to hospitalization – treated 1,768 children in two districts (about 102 per cent increase from 2023) and Childhood Onset Non-Communicable Disease Protocols were developed.

In adolescent health, services from UNICEF-supported facilities reached 278,454 adolescents, and 1,557,476 adolescents were informed about health issues through digital platforms. Immunization efforts saw 97 per cent of children under one (3,729,233) vaccinated against measles, including 6,165 zero-dose and under-immunized children. The HPV (Human Papillomavirus) vaccination campaign resulted in 5,887,352 girls (93 per cent of eligible girls aged 10-14) receiving at least one dose, including marginalized girls. In the Rohingya camps, 69,880 girls received the HPV vaccine.

The urban program, six UNICEF supported Aalo clinics, registered 91,299 individuals and conducted 267,732 health consultations, including lab tests and disease screenings. UNICEF also supported the formation of a multisectoral committee to address environmental health, to address issues such as air pollution which contributes to 30 per cent of under-five mortality.
In emergency response, vaccination efforts reached 83,835 children, and essential care was provided to 34,431 pregnant women. Integrated Management of Childhood Illness services reached 228,830 children under five. In the Rohingya Refugee camps, six PHC centers provided comprehensive health consultations.

Every Child Thrives:
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) through the National Nutrition Services Operational Plan and reforms under the Fifth Health, Nutrition, and Population Sector Programme (5th HNPSP) to lay the groundwork for sustainable nationwide scale-up of nutrition services, including in underserved areas. The Community-Based Engagement (CBE) Strategy and Low Birth Weight model addressed coverage and quality bottlenecks, leading to their integration into the 5th HNPSP. Strategic advocacy and match-funding increased budgetary allocations nearly fivefold to US Dollar 31 million, enabling the Maternal and Child Nutrition Program to expand threefold, covering all 64 districts.

UNICEF helped the Directorate General of Health Services, and the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education strengthen the school-based supply of weekly Iron Folic Acid (IFA) supplements and improved real time data sharing systems for monitoring. This led to an additional 30 per cent of adolescent girls in secondary schools and colleges being reached nationwide – a step toward universal coverage.

Through the Mothers@Work initiative, UNICEF and partners scaled up workplace-based maternal and child health interventions in 160 garment factories, providing 3.5 million IFA tablets to pregnant women and piloting a community-based health package under the urban primary health care system. This addressed significant gaps in urban maternal health services, improving health outcomes for underserved populations.

In 2024 UNICEF reached over 18,000 children across 370 health facilities as part of its programme to detect and treat Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM). Admissions increased 36 per cent compared to 2023, thanks to improved program coverage, supply chain management, and facility readiness. 

Following Cyclone Remal and flash floods, UNICEF screened over 151,000 children for malnutrition and admitted 1,096 SAM cases for inpatient care. Piloting Small Quantity Lipid Supplements (SQ-LNS), which prevent malnutrition, in emergency-affected districts reached 4,000 children, while UNICEF’s collaboration with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) demonstrated the efficacy of locally produced Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food, achieving a 92 per cent recovery rate in Rohingya camps. This evidence informed the integration of community-based SAM management into the National Nutrition Services Operational Plan.

Every Child Learns: 
UNICEF’s education programme in Bangladesh continued to focus on enhancing quality learning and skilling opportunities for children, both in- and out-of-school, from childhood to adolescence. UNICEF’s technical support to the government is geared towards system strengthening, including curriculum reform, data analysis for evidence-based advocacy and programming, digital transformation, and teacher capacity development.

In 2024, UNICEF-supported alternative education programs reached 120,030 children from disadvantaged backgrounds. These included early childhood education for 4,500 children (50 per cent girls) and catch-up or remedial education programs benefiting 44,429 learners (57.7 per cent girls, 1.7 per cent children with disabilities, and 19 per cent from ethnic communities).
Through multi-grade, multi-level programs (designed to teach children from different age groups with different levels of education in the same classroom), another 71,101 out-of-school children (54 per cent girls, 3.1 per cent children with disabilities, and 3.6 per cent from ethnic communities) received non-formal primary education (NFPE). Approximately 99 per cent of these out of school children aged 10+ developed foundational literacy skills, and 95 per cent achieved foundational numeracy competencies. Furthermore, 30 per cent of NFPE learners were successfully mainstreamed into formal schools after completing their courses.

In addition, UNICEF collaborated with seven partners, including the Bureau of Non-Formal Education, to implement an Alternative Learning and Skilling Program for marginalized adolescents and young people in climate-vulnerable and hard-to-reach districts. By December 2024, 15,813 adolescents and young people (79 per cent girls, including 1,141 married) participated in skills training, including informal apprenticeships, center-based training, and entrepreneurship programs. Of these, 86 per cent completed their training successfully, and 96 per cent secured employment or started their own businesses.

In pre-primary education (PPE), UNICEF’s advocacy led to the rollout of a two-year PPE pilot in over 3,000 schools in 2023, with technical assistance in curriculum adaptation, teacher training, and quality assurance. By 2024, this pilot reached 141,117 children, and UNICEF is supporting feasibility studies for scaling up the program in the coming years.

In primary education, UNICEF continued to address last-mile challenges, such as children left behind and low learning outcomes. UNICEF is supporting the fourth Primary Education Development Program (PEDP4) and preparing for PEDP5, ensuring that interventions are evidence-based and address the most pressing challenges.

Secondary education also faces issues with equitable access and quality. National exam results show low pass rates and poor performance, prompting UNICEF’s support in enhancing the competency-based curriculum and teaching-learning materials for grades 6-7 in 2023 and grades 8-9 in 2024, benefitting 9.8 million children (54 per cent girls).

Every Child is Protected:
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support transformative progress in protecting children from violence, exploitation, and harmful practices in Bangladesh, contributing to national and global development priorities.

UNICEF supported the expansion and strengthening of Bangladesh’s juvenile justice system. Between January and October, a total of 117 children in conflict with the law benefited from diversion and probation measures, marking significant progress in restorative justice. With UNICEF’s technical and financial support, 102 Children’s Courts enhanced their capacity to implement the Children Act 2013, while 11 child-sensitive courtrooms were inaugurated across nine districts. Partnerships with legal aid services and judiciary stakeholders ensured that detained children received appropriate representation, contributing to a fairer, more child-sensitive justice system. UNICEF is currently working on promoting multi-sectoral coordination among the justice sector stakeholders (police, judges, social services and legal aid) at the decentralized level to expedite the cases pending for a long time.

In social services, the recruitment of 1,485 social workers and psychosocial counselors enabled a 190 per cent increase in case management coverage, reaching 45,919 children. The launch of the Online Case Management System transitioned case management to a digital platform, facilitating follow-up for 137,225 children and referrals for 24,828 cases. The Child Helpline (CHL-1098) addressed 331,831 calls, offering psychosocial support, rescuing children from violence, and preventing 646 child marriages, with another 236 prevented by the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs’ intervention.

UNICEF also supported the scaling of community-led child protection initiatives, with 2,091 Child Protection Community Hubs (CPCHs) delivering over 19 million child protection services to children and families, including life skills training, psychosocial support, and emergency referrals. Innovative sports-for-development programs, such as Swim-Safe and self-defense training, engaged over 155,600 children and adolescents, fostering resilience, gender equality, and inclusivity.

In humanitarian settings, UNICEF provided critical support to children affected by floods and cyclones, reaching 200,000 individuals with psychosocial services, 35,454 emergency kits, and 5000 families received cash transfers. These efforts addressed compounded vulnerabilities while strengthening systems to respond to gender-based violence and safeguarding children during crises.

Additionally, UNICEF facilitated the registration of 7,290,613million births, including 2,430,062 million children under five, strengthening Bangladesh’s civil registration system and ensuring every child’s right to identity. By supporting policy and operational reforms, including the advancement of a Department of Children Affairs, UNICEF helped mobilize national resources and reinforced the government’s commitment to child protection.

Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment:
In 2024, UNICEF continued to leverage its technical expertise, strategic partnerships with academia and the private sector, and innovation to support the Government to ensure households had access to safe water and climate-resilient sanitation, especially during climate-related disasters. 

UNICEF supported the government in developing the Sector Development Plan 2026–2040 and a sector investment plan for water and sanitation – both are aligned with national priorities and plans to ensure climate-resilient services. Additionally, UNICEF supported the revision of the WASH Policy. These are all ready for ratification and endorsement by the government. 

During the year, an estimated 580,000 people gained access to safe water, while up to 1.2 million people benefited from improved sanitation facilities through UNICEF's support. Key interventions included training caretakers of water wells, capacitating and registering local drillers in arsenic-safe drilling, and empowering communities to access safe water, resulting in 357 villages being declared arsenic-safe. In collaboration with government counterparts, 12,000 equity-based sites for safe water points were also finalized, ensuring safe water wells are close to marginalized communities. Promoting hygiene and menstrual health remained a priority, with educational initiatives reaching around 1.4 million people, especially adolescent girls and women. 

With groundwater depletion a serious challenge, groundwater monitoring was another key focus in 2024. UNICEF stepped in to facilitate a sector-wide consultation (with a focus on Gazipur city in response to its significantly depleted and polluted groundwater), initiate groundwater monitoring and mapping, and will continue to support the government in developing a comprehensive groundwater model to inform decision making and guide future groundwater extraction in selected areas. Additionally, UNICEF will continue to work with partners to develop a shared understanding of groundwater data and data-sharing protocols, in turn fostering a more coordinated approach to groundwater governance. 
 
UNICEF also collaborated with the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics to conduct a WASH in Institutions Monitoring survey to guide future actions on WASH for children in schools and health care facilities and develop a practical plan for institutional WASH programming in the country. 

Above all, innovation was at the heart of UNICEF’s efforts. UNICEF pioneered innovations with the potential to scale up, such as water quality testing in 32 health facilities, implementation of WASH Facility Improvement Tools in 16 healthcare facilities, and installation of climate-resilient sanitation technologies. 

Finally, UNICEF extended lifesaving WASH support to over 1.7 million people during devastating flood and cyclone emergencies. Through these efforts, UNICEF ensured no child was left behind, setting the stage for continued progress in addressing inequities and improving WASH outcomes in Bangladesh.

Every child has an Equitable Chance in Life:
UNICEF supported the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics and the General Economics Division to strengthen SDG monitoring. Two surveys were commissioned to address the existing data gaps: the WASH in Institutions Monitoring Survey and the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS). The results from these surveys will be available in 2025. The data will contribute updated statistics for up to 29 SDG indicators. Additionally, the national SDG Tracker was updated with improved data management and dissemination capabilities. SDG indicator metadata was updated for 50 child-focused indicators, and consultations for data validation of over 100 SDG indicators were completed.

UNICEF worked to enhance participation and accountability in social sector budgeting by supporting members of parliament and children to play stronger roles in the budgeting process. UNICEF facilitated children’s engagement with parliamentarians, presenting their budget demands and supporting parliamentary debate on the budget for children. UNICEF also provided technical support to the MoWCA’s budget submission through a costing exercise to adjust transfer value for the Mother and Child Benefit Programme (MCBP).

In collaboration with MoWCA, a cash-plus model of the MCBP was piloted in two climate-vulnerable upazilas, covering 7,880 MCBP recipients. A multi-sectoral approach was adopted to implement the cash-plus pilot using the government’s existing health and nutrition system. This allowed MoWCA to reduce targeting errors and will contribute to increased utilization of Antenatal Care and Postnatal Care services for MCBP beneficiaries.

UNICEF-supported humanitarian cash transfers reached a total of 16,683 households (67,295 people) affected by Cyclone Remal and the south-eastern flood, with a multipurpose cash (MPC) transfer of BDT6,000 (US$51). Top-up MPC was provided to 7,634 MCBP beneficiaries to demonstrate the potential of vertical expansion of existing programs. From the Post Distribution Monitoring survey, 99 per cent of recipients reported being very satisfied or satisfied. On utilization of cash, 43 per cent spent the money on medicine and 21 per cent on food items. A total of 54 per cent indicated that the spending decision was taken jointly with their husbands.

Rohingya Refugee Response and other emergencies
In 2024, UNICEF provided humanitarian assistance to 3 million people, of which 48 per cent were children, 50 per cent were females, and 2.6 per cent were persons with disabilities, achieving 95 per cent of the annual target. This assistance included Humanitarian Cash Transfers. In Health, 189,868 children aged 0 to 11 months received pentavalent 3 vaccination, exceeding the target by 10 per cent, and 469,470 children and women accessed primary healthcare services (92 per cent of the target). In Nutrition, 13,087 children aged 6-59 months with severe wasting were treated (85 per cent of the target), and 235,800 primary caregivers of children aged 0-23 months received infant and young child feeding counselling (115 per cent of the target).

In Child Protection, 1,528,139 adults and children received mental health and psychosocial support (60 per cent of target), and 818,620 women, girls, and boys accessed gender-based violence risk mitigation, prevention, and response interventions (68 per cent of the target). In Education, 269,525 children participated in formal or non-formal education, including early learning (70 per cent of the target), and 386,366 children benefited from individual learning materials (60 per cent of the target). The WASH response ensured that 3,008,911 people had access to sufficient water for drinking and domestic needs (four times of the target), and 786,759 people accessed appropriate sanitation services (166 per cent of the target).

In Social and Behaviour Change (SBC), messaging on prevention and access to critical services (368 per cent of the target) reached 6,403,085 people, and established feedback mechanisms engaged 138,451 people (67 per cent of the target). The overachievement across sectors resulted from intensified activities in disaster-prone districts affected by a cyclone and three floods in 2024.

In Cox’s Bazar and Bhasan Char, 256,063 learners, including 124,031 females and 1,538 children with disabilities, accessed education following Myanmar Curriculum. In Child Protection, 314,705 adults and children (160,961 female, 176,340 children) received mental health and psychosocial support. Approximately 330,000 people accessed sufficient water for drinking and domestic needs both in camps and the host communities. In Nutrition, 12,341 children aged 6-59 months with severe wasting were treated. In Health, 106,564 children aged 0 to 11 months received pentavalent 3 vaccination. In SBC, messaging on prevention and access to services reached 659,684 people.

Programme Effectiveness
In 2024, UNICEF focused on strengthening Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) and child safeguarding capacities. A total of 140 internal, 406 implementing partner (IP) staff, and 118 vendors were trained on these topics. UNICEF conducted PSEA capacity assessments for 32 active IPs to ensure they had robust measures in place to mitigate risks of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA). At the same time, risk mitigation measures were integrated into all project documents, and implementation was monitored by UNICEF managers. UNICEF included SEA risk mitigation in all Contract Review Committee submissions from October 2024, enhancing vendor accountability.

In 2024, UNICEF strengthened the evidence base for Social and Behavior Change (SBC) programming through various studies and initiatives. A government-led Knowledge, Attitude, Belief, and Practice study identified key drivers of 23 childcare practices, informing SBC intervention design and monitoring. Studies on Violence Against Children and Child Marriage (VAC/CM) led to increased community-based interventions, while a Community Engagement-Social and Behavior Change (CE-SBC) Monitoring and Evaluation Framework was also developed for rollout in 2025.
Local evidence on youth-led SBC activities and harmful norms improved intervention contextualization in Barishal, Khulna, Sylhet, and Rajshahi. Baseline studies on Alternative Learning Pathways in seven districts also informed SBC strategy development. A national study on pediatric non-communicable diseases will guide 2025 SBC interventions. Real-time social listening data enhanced demand generation for HPV vaccination and VAC/ECM campaigns.

In 2024, over 300 expanded programme on immunization (EPI) staff including vaccinators, immunization supervisors, community health workers, and CSO staff were trained on Community Engagement (CE) standards. Additionally, 1,200 religious leaders received Interpersonal Communication (IC) training, and over 100 media personnel and 400 journalists were oriented to mitigate misinformation on the HPV vaccine. An Accountability to Affected People (AAP) workshop in May led to an interagency AAP workplan and ongoing collaboration.

Progress was made in adhering to Global CE quality standards. Across 32 Upazilas of 17 districts, around 600,000 caregivers and community leaders were engaged in maternal and child health, nutrition, education, and child protection practices. Community-based activities on HPV vaccination, routine immunization, and VAC-ECM reached around 8 million people, while over 4.1 million received lifesaving messages during flood emergencies.

A Parenting Education Package for children aged 0-18, developed with multisector stakeholders, was approved by the government. A national multimedia campaign on VAC-ECM reached over 25 million people, and Meena content reached over 29 million. Extensive communication for the HPV campaign achieved 93 per cent coverage among 10-14-year-old girls.

By the end of 2025, all evaluations, research, and studies, including the MICS, will be critical to updating the situation analysis of women and children in Bangladesh. This will inform the new national priorities, specifically next country programme development, enhancing the strategic focus for improved results for children

In 2024, UNICEF forged and strengthened partnerships across various sectors to enhance the well-being of children and families in Bangladesh. Spanned government ministries, UN agencies, civil society organizations, academic institutions, and the private sector, to strengthen its work for children and young people, and drive impactful programming and policy advocacy.  By increasing partnerships with local businesses and international brands, UNICEF Bangladesh is paving the way for sustainable, long-term investments in children’s futures.  

Health: 
Thanks to UNICEF’s close collaboration with ministries from multiple sectors, including in health, education, social welfare, religious affairs and information, the Human Papillomavirus Virus (HPV) campaign achieved a remarkable milestone of vaccinating 93 per cent of girls aged 10 to 14 across Bangladesh. This success was underpinned by our active engagement with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) to engage with communities, religious leaders and parents. 
Multi-sectoral coordination was also pivotal in tackling environmental pollution (particularly lead pollution). A steering committee led by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change involved 19 ministries and agencies, including UNICEF, to develop a multi-sectoral strategy and action plan for a ‘Lead-Free Bangladesh’. 

UNICEF built strategic partnerships with professional and academic institutions, such as the Bangladesh Association for Child and Adolescent Mental Health (BACAMH) and the National Institute of Prevention and Social Medicine (NIPSOM), to advance evidence-based policy development. 

Other health initiatives were strengthened throughout the year, through partnering with sister UN agencies such as WHO and UNFPA, development partners including USAID, Global Affairs Canada (GAC), Asian Development Bank (ADB), Global Alliance for Vaccination and Immunization (GAVI), the Embassy of Sweden and the World Bank.

Nutrition: UNICEF collaborated with the MoHFW, Ministry of Planning, and other stakeholders to develop the fifth Health, Population, and Nutrition Sector Programme. Key partnerships included collaboration with Bangladesh National Nutrition Council (BNNC) and the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) to support nutrition governance and demonstrate a community-based engagement approach. UNICEF also collaborated with the Cabinet Division and the Ministry of Finance to develop the Financial Tracking System for Nutrition (FTS4N).

Partnerships with UN agencies, development partners, and the ready-made garment sector facilitated the implementation of nutrition programs and mainstreaming of family-friendly policies in workplaces. Finally, collaboration with academic institutions like the Institute of Nutrition and Food Science (INFS) supported knowledge generation and critical policy reforms. Alongside this, partnerships with key funders like the Bureau of Humanitarian Assistance (BHA), Foreign and Commonwealth Development Office (FCDO) and The Power of Nutrition.
  
Education: Despite political challenges, UNICEF's education section maintained strong partnerships with the Ministry of Education and other government bodies in Bangladesh. In particular, collaborations with the Directorate of Primary Education, Bureau of Non-Formal Education, and Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education supported various education programs. 

UNICEF’s partnership with the Education Local Consultative Group (ELCG) was especially pivotal in preparing the Enabling Factor Analysis (EFA) and developing the Partnership Compact (PC), which secured US$97.6 million in the Global Partnership in Education’s System Transformation Grant and US$50 million in Multiplier Grants for the country. UNICEF’s advocacy efforts also helped secure additional funding from development partners and the private sector for education programs.

Partnerships with development partners like the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank, and UNESCO under the Development Partnership Consortium (DPC) facilitated primary education programs. Bilateral donors and private sector partnerships, including those with FCDO, Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), Global Partnership for Education (GPE), Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (KfW), Embassy of Japan, Embassy of Thailand, GAC, and corporate foundations, enabled technical assistance to systems strengthening and financial resources for non-formal education programs. UNICEF also contributed to capacity building for NGOs implementing catch-up and non-formal education programs.

Child Protection: UNICEF strengthened strategic partnerships with government ministries, civil society, UN agencies, and the private sector to advance child protection. Key government partners included the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs (MoWCA) and the Ministry of Youth and Sports (MoYS). These partnerships facilitated the operationalization of the Child Protection Community Hubs, the institutionalization of Sports for Development programmes, and the nationwide rollout of the Online Case Management System. Collaboration with UN agencies and international financial institutions supported cross-sectoral challenges, while civil society partnerships scaled community-led initiatives. Private sector partnerships facilitated digital transformation and the development of tools like the Birth and Death Registration System. Bi lateral cooperation with donors like the European Commission (EC), KfW, Bureau of Population, Refugee and Migration (BPRM), FCDO and Embassy of Sweden, played a key role in mobilizing funds for child protection activities in Bangladesh. 

WASH: UNICEF's WASH programming involved close collaboration with the Local Government Division (LGD) and other government entities. Partnerships with the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) and urban WASH utilities supported water supply and sanitation services. Collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change focused on climate-resilient WASH services. UNICEF also engaged with academic institutions for capacity building and studies. Key donors, including FCDO, Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC), KfW, Embassy of Sweden and the Gates Foundation, provided generous support for WASH initiatives.

SPEAR: UNICEF worked with the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and General Economics Division (GED) to strengthen SDG monitoring and keep child poverty on the policy radar. Financial support from USAID, SDC, UNHCR, and UNFPA enabled the commissioning of MICS 2025. Partnerships with NGO partners facilitated humanitarian cash transfers and support for cyclone and flood-affected populations. The Ministry of Finance partnership under the EU-funded regional public finance for children facility was revived.

Field Services & Emergencies: UNICEF deepened its partnership with the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR) to promote child-sensitive emergency preparedness and response. Effective partnerships with donors, including Australia, Canada, and the European Union, supported government efforts to improve the lives of children and women. And collaboration with UN agencies under the Humanitarian Coordination Task Team (HCTT) and NGO partners facilitated multi-sectoral emergency responses.

Programme Effectiveness: UNICEF expanded its resource mobilization efforts in Bangladesh through partnerships with the private sector and National Committees. Significant funding was mobilized from public sector donors, private sector partnerships, and thematic funding. Core resources provided by donors enabled UNICEF to address funding gaps and deliver multisectoral interventions. Key partnerships with ODA partners, including USAID, DFAT, FCDO, KfW, Embassy of Sweden, Embassy of Japan and the European Commission were maintained, supporting UNICEF's vital work in emergencies and development.
Through these diverse and strategic partnerships, UNICEF advanced its mission to safeguard the rights and well-being of children and families in Bangladesh, driving systemic change and fostering innovation across health, nutrition, education, child protection, and WASH sectors.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Planning for Continuity Through Disruption
The political turmoil in July-August 2024 significantly disrupted program implementation, highlighting the need for UNICEF to strengthen its service continuity strategies during periods of political and economic instability and other emergencies. This includes contingency planning for a range of scenarios and developing more adaptive program designs.

Children’s Environmental Health
In 2024 an assessment of children’s environmental health, has begun to reveal that children in Bangladesh are highly exposed to a range of environmental health hazards, but a lack of government awareness, and available evidence about the burden, sources and exposure pathways has left this issue largely unaddressed. A lack of regulation of informal sectors that trade in or handle toxic goods or waste contributes to the complexity of the challenge and will need to be considered as part of future advocacy strategies. 
As an important first step, UNICEF will help address the Government’s lack of capacity for heavy metal testing. The upcoming Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS), which will include heavy metal testing in blood and identify sources, thus generating evidence and advocating for a national strategy for a lead-free Bangladesh.

Education 
The change in government has had a significant impact on Bangladesh's education sector, halting key reforms initiated by the previous administration. The decision to revert to the 2012 curriculum and delay the implementation of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2021 has created uncertainty and stalled progress toward transforming education. 
Leadership vacuums and institutional changes have disrupted critical agencies like the NCTB, DSHE, and NAEM. Schools and institutions are struggling to adjust to these abrupt policy shifts, while efforts to integrate skills courses, digitalization, and competency-based learning have been halted. This transition highlights the urgent need for renewed collaboration and strategic planning to address emerging challenges and ensure sustainable educational development.  

Unmet Protection Needs 
A critical challenge in 2024 was the limited capacity of frontline workers and social service systems to meet the growing demand for child protection services. Although recruiting 1,485 social workers and psychosocial counsellors was a significant milestone, the workforce remains insufficient for a population of 45 million children exposed to violence. Digital transformation efforts, including the Online Case Management System, were hindered by varying levels of digital literacy among social workers and limited technological infrastructure in remote areas. Additionally, entrenched gender norms and resource constraints in urban and disaster-prone regions complicated efforts to scale inclusive programming for children living on the streets and those affected by emergencies.

Protracted Rohingya Crisis 
Since the February 2021 military coup in Myanmar, violence has surged, particularly in western Myanmar, where the Arakan Army has expelled the military regime from most of Rakhine State. This instability has led to increased intercommunal tensions and an increased incidence in the forced recruitment of refugees from within the camps. This continued violence along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border, coupled with the possibility of a fresh influx of refugees, poses significant challenges to ongoing humanitarian assistance for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. The Rohingya refugee response, heavily reliant on foreign aid, is becoming increasingly tenuous due to declining international funding support.
 
Lessons learned 
The evaluation of UNICEF's gender policy, with Bangladesh as a case study, highlighted significant progress in gender-responsive initiatives like Mothers@Work and Women-Friendly Hospitals. It emphasized the shift from gender-sensitive to gender-transformative programs by addressing gender norms and engaging social influencers. The action plan to implement the recommendations includes strengthening the capacity for gender-transformative programming, generating evidence through gender indicators, fostering cross-sectoral integration, and engaging adolescents, especially girls, in planning and monitoring.
 
In 2024, UNICEF's advocacy transformed maternal and child nutrition programs by enhancing community-based models and increasing accessibility. High-level advocacy and a matching funding strategy led to a nearly fivefold increase in government budget allocations under the 5th HNPSP. This funding boost expanded the Maternal and Child Nutrition Program's coverage threefold, reaching all 64 districts. In 2025, UNICEF will build on these lessons to further strengthen and expand these programs.
 
Recent disruptions in education have highlighted the need to maintain distance learning mechanisms and develop digital and blended learning interventions to address learning losses from the reintroduction of the 2012 curriculum. UNICEF will collaborate with government agencies to build stakeholder capacity in this area. In response to climate change-induced disruptions, UNICEF will work with the government to create a resilient education system, focusing on climate-responsive curricula, resilient infrastructure, and teacher preparedness. Additionally, UNICEF will support the review of the National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2021 for the 2026 rollout and continue programs for out-of-school children, innovative interventions, and non-formal education.
 
Future Outlook
The recent establishment of 11 policy reform commissions in Bangladesh marks a significant step towards addressing systemic issues and fostering inclusive governance, but it remains to be seen what progress they will make before elections take place. These commissions, focusing on constitutional reform, police and judiciary, mass media, health and women's affairs, have the potential to create a more equitable landscape for children and young people. Yet, in a country still experiencing the aftershocks of a popular uprising and with unrest still commonplace, the urgent need for a child-sensitive and rights-respecting system of governance is glaringly evident.

The student-led mass uprising in July and August has reiterated the need for a comprehensive and coordinated policy approach for job creation for educated youth. This required a significant shift in key priorities of all stakeholders, including the Government, to invest in enhancing the quality of education at all levels to ensure young people acquire the skills needed for the job market. This involves aligning technical training programs with industry demands and improving overall educational standards.

 While the challenges remain significant, there is much hope. UNICEF will continue to partner with government, development partners, civil society and children and youth movements to create a create a safer, more equitable Bangladesh together. The future of the nation depends on the well-being and development of its youngest citizens.

Bhutan continues to uphold political stability even as it navigates various socio-economic challenges. In January 2024, Bhutan conducted the General Election of the 4th National Assembly, ushering a new Government[1]. The elections alongside ongoing development initiatives reflect Bhutan’s commitment to progress. However, issues pertaining to youth unemployment, growing mental health issues, quality of health and education services and last mile challenges persist. The long-term sustainability of development gains will require a multi-faceted approach (economic, social, governance, environmental, etc.) to ensure that Bhutan can build a resilient and sustainable foundation for continued development post graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status.

During the 2024 fiscal year, Bhutan’s real GDP Growth is projected at 5.5 per cent with an expected increase to 7 per cent for 2025[2]. Inflation rates are forecast at 4.6 per cent in 2024 and 4.2 percent in 2025[3]. As of 2022, the national poverty rate stands at 12.4 per cent with a pronounced disparity between urban (4.2 per cent) and rural (17.5 per cent) areas. The public debt accounted for 104.7 per cent of GDP in 2024 and will remain elevated in 2025[4]. Following its graduation from LDC status in December 2023, Bhutan is focused on sustaining its development trajectory and bolstering its economic outlook. 

The launch of Bhutan’s 13th Five-Year Plan (FYP) in 2024 marks a significant step towards accelerating sustainable economic growth and social development by 2029. The plan emphasizes security, governance, economic prosperity and the preservation of Bhutan’s cultural heritage, aligning with Bhutan’s international commitments, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). With an ambitious aim to double the size of the economy, the 13th FYP prioritizes investments in infrastructure, ICT, local government, and human resource development. Notably, the Royal Government of Bhutan (RGoB) allocated 34 per cent[5] of its national budget to the social sector in 2024, up from 28 per cent in 2023, benefitting children and adolescents, who constitute 34 per cent of Bhutan's estimated population of 735,553[6].  His Majesty also announced his vision of the development of the Gelephu Mindfulness City[7]. It is an innovative urban development project integrating economic growth with mindfulness, holistic living[8].

Bhutan reaffirmed its international commitments to protecting children’s rights by presenting its combined 6th and 7th periodic report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) in May 2024, outlining developments since the last concluding observations in 2017[9]. Further, at the first global ministerial conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Bogota, Colombia (November 2024), Bhutan committed to expanding child protection systems and adopting a multi-sectoral approach to safeguard children’s welfare[10]. Bhutan also presented its fourth national report to the United Nations Human Rights Council under the Universal Periodic Review (UPR) in November 2024[11],reiterating its commitment to protect and promote human rights.

The Gyalsung Programme - Bhutan's National Service Programme - was launched in September 2024[12]. This mandatory year-long training for Bhutanese youth over 18 aims to foster productive and independent citizens, with over 2,000 participants in its inaugural batch [13].
The 2023 National Health Survey report finalized in June 2024, highlighted improvements in areas including access to improved water and sanitation, immunization coverage, and institutional delivery rates[14]. However, emerging health challenges, including lifestyle-related diseases, substance abuse, and mental health issues, along with the impact of environmental factors on health, remain areas that require focused attention and action. Persistent disparities in health outcomes, especially among marginalized populations, and societal issues like violence against women and child discipline practices necessitate ongoing intervention and policy focus. 

The National Blood Lead Level Survey 2024 revealed high lead levels in 75 per cent of children in Bhutan aged 1-6[15], underscoring environmental health challenges posed to children and women.  Additionally, the Micronutrient Survey reported a declining trend in stunting but noted increases in wasting, micronutrient deficiencies, anemia, and obesity, highlighting a triple burden of malnutrition across the life course[16].  

While Bhutan has made commendable strides in advancing child rights, concerted efforts remain critical to address challenges impacting children’s well-being [17].  Priorities include reducing anemia among children and mothers, addressing neonatal mortality, enhancing adolescent health services, expanding early learning access, combating violence against children and women, and supporting the RGoB develop a comprehensive, inclusive, child-centered social protection framework. Bhutan's continued focus on these areas will ensure the country remains on a sustainable and inclusive development path.

UNICEF Bhutan Country Office (BhCO) collaborated with the Royal Government of Bhutan (RGoB) and partners to design, implement, and monitor an integrated work plan for 2024. This plan was aligned with the results of the Country Programme (2024-2028) and the outcome areas of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework. Within the respective Goal Areas, BhCO enhanced programme implementation and relevance, achieving significant milestones.

GA1: EVERY CHILD SURVIVES AND THRIVES 
The first ever National Blood Level Survey (BLL 2024) was conducted in Bhutan, giving us data on emerging trends and revealing the high prevalence of lead. The survey, Bhutan's first nationally representative household survey among children aged 1–6 years, reveals alarming findings: 75.9% of children in this age group have BLLs exceeding 3.5 µg/dL. Similarly, the survey indicates that 3 out of 5 pregnant women also have BLLs above this threshold, highlighting significant public health concerns. A high-level event featured the launch of the Blood Lead Survey Factsheet, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and WHO. The findings are expected to inform and shape policy and programmatic interventions to address lead exposure in children. 

A situational assessment on Children’s Environmental Health was conducted and launched during the International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week. The assessment unveiled key findings on the vulnerability and exposure of children to environmental hazards[1] and shall serve as a critical resource for designing impactful policies, programs, and regulations to protect children from environmental health risks. Further advancing this initiative, the BhCO and the MoH developed an innovative pre-service training module on Children’s Environmental Health. This module will be integrated into the curriculum at the Khesar Gyalpo University of Medical Sciences of Bhutan (KGUMSB), ensuring that future generations of health professionals are equipped with the expertise to tackle environmental health challenges affecting children.

Bhutan has achieved SDG targets for neonatal mortality (6.9/1000 live births), under-five child mortality (19.5/1000 live births), and maternal mortality (53/100,000 live births). In 2024, the Reproductive Maternal Newborn Child Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) Strategy 2024-2029 and Bhutan Every Newborn Action Plan (BENAP 2024-2029) were developed for policy guidance, enhancing integrated health services for children, adolescents, and women. BhCO supported the National Health Survey (NHS) report launch, trained 104 healthcare professionals in neonatal care, and completed the second phase of Medical Gas Pipeline System rehabilitation in six hospitals, ensuring uninterrupted medical gas availability for children in Samtse, Thimphu, Tsirang, Wangduephodrang, Mongar and Dewathang districts. 

To address nutritional deficiencies and associated risks, Multiple Micronutrient Supplements (MMS) were introduced in all 20 districts, targeting both pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers. With 80 per cent coverage, the MMS supplementation will enhance maternal nutritional status and reduce anemia, prematurity, and low birth weight. Additionally, Micronutrient Powder (MNP) supplementation has been implemented to address stunting and anemia in children. To further strengthen systematic evidence-based nutrition programming, the National Centre of Excellence for Nutrition was inaugurated during the year, serving as a hub for data generation and policy support.

BhCO played a pivotal role in securing uninterrupted vaccine availability for pregnant women and children, ensuring essential vaccines, including BCG, Pediatric Hepatitis B, bOPV, MMR, DTP, and Td, were consistently procured and distributed. Additionally, BhCO facilitated the procurement of HPV, DTP-HepB-Hib, PCV, and Influenza vaccines funded by the RGoB, further strengthening national immunization efforts. Beyond vaccine procurement, BhCO supported the RGoB’s transformative expansion of the country’s cold chain system – quadrupling its capacity during the Covid-19 pandemic to maintain vaccine efficacy.  Building on this achievement, BhCO provided financial support to enhance cold chain infrastructure, enabling the procurement and distribution of 320 temperature monitoring devices, 16 sets of spare parts for cold chain equipment and four combined refrigerator/freezer units across 16 health facilities. A milestone achievement was the installation of solar direct drive (SDD) refrigerator/freezer in Laya Primary Health Centre, servicing remote highland communities. As a result, 15 health facilities that previously struggled with unreliable power supply now have SDD refrigerators, ensuring safe vaccine storage.  

Recognizing that equipment is only part of the equation, BhCO also invested in building human capacity to sustain the cold chain system.  In partnership with key stakeholders, BhCO trained 23 (10 female) biomedical engineers, technicians, and electricians in basic refrigeration, installation, repair, and maintenance of cold chain equipment. This strengthened the expertise within the Bio-medical Engineering Department of National Medical Services contributing to the sustainable system for preventive maintenance and repair across the country. 

Strategic investments enabled the derivation of population-based data from the NHS Report, informing evidence-based planning for child survival programs in the 13th Five-Year Plan and UNICEF CPD 2024-2028. As part of the NHS, the first ever micronutrient survey was conducted and has provided extensive information about micronutrient deficiencies among children and women. The first ever integrated Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) strategy was developed to improve further service delivery and efficiency and resource allocation for MNCH service. High immunization coverage, along with essential health and nutrition services and efficient vaccine cold chain management, were sustained through timely procurement of vaccines, nutrition commodities, and WASH supplies, along with enhancements in cold chain supply efficiency.

GA2: EVERY CHILD LEARNS 
In 2024, BhCO, in partnership with the Ministry of Education and Skills Development (MoESD) and CSOs, reached over 28,000 children and young people, including those with disabilities, in remote areas and monastic schools. These efforts advanced Bhutan’s commitment to inclusive education following its ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and aimed to improve access to equitable quality learning opportunities and contributed to the UNSDCF Strategic Priority and CPD 2024-2028 Outcome 2, focusing on inclusive, quality, and resilient learning and education.

A significant milestone was BhCO’s advocacy and technical support in the development and Parliament approval of Bhutan’s first ever National Education Policy, aligning with the 2021 Royal Kasho on Education Reform. This policy sets the foundation for curriculum review, creating a National Training Service for teachers, and integrating technology and STEM, bridging the rural-urban education gap and preparing students for a technology-driven future.
 
BhCO also played a pivotal role in evidence-based policy development. Following a BhCO-supported Mid-Term Review of SDG4 and an innovative SDG4 costing exercise, the MoESD initiated a new funding formula for more efficient resource allocation. BhCO contributed to the MoESD's data-driven decision-making by integrating SDG indicators into Bhutan’s Annual Education Statistics and initiated several assessments and evaluations, such as the National Education Assessment (NEA) for grades III and VI and the Needs Assessment of ECCD Facilitators.

BhCO introduced several innovations in the education sector, such as digitalization, the development of Accessible Digital Textbooks for children with disabilities, and the enhancement of English and Math learning in monastic schools through digital applications. The first Education Technology Framework was developed, outlining standards and guidelines for digital content and competencies. Digital content for Grade IX Math and Science and the first ever digital skills package for UPSHIFT were also developed. The latter was implemented in 11 schools, benefiting 605 young people. These initiatives align with Bhutan’s 13th FYP to enhance digital learning access.

Overall, UNICEF's strategic positioning and innovative approaches in the education sector have contributed to improving learning opportunities and outcomes for children and young people in Bhutan, particularly the most vulnerable.

GA3: EVERY CHILD IS PROTECTED FROM VIOLENCE AND EXPLOITATION 
In 2024, BhCO in partnership with the RGoB and CSOs reached a total of 7,727 children (4,239 F) who experienced violence, exploitation, abuse, and neglect with quality child protection services, including psychosocial first aid (PFA) and child-friendly legal aid. This success was due to the enhanced capacity of 1,056 social service workers (558 F, including teachers, health workers, counselors, school well-being focal points, and lawyers).

Through the ten UNICEF-supported Women and Girls Safe Spaces (WGSS), 17,770 children and women were provided case management, psychosocial support, referrals, livelihood skills, advocacy, awareness, and community and adolescent engagement programs. Additionally, 5,530 adolescents (3,047 F) were trained in resilience and online child protection.

BhCO, in collaboration with Dratshang Lhentshog, empowered 1,694 children (305 F) in 30 monastic schools and nunneries with the knowledge and skills to protect themselves from violence and exploitation, including online threats. Additionally, 125 teachers (45 F) were trained to identify child protection concerns, including those in digital spaces, and to make safe referrals.

BhCO 's engagement with parliamentarians advanced key child rights discussions, leading to the amendment of the Marriage Act of Bhutan 1980 – raising the legal age of marriage for girls. UNICEF's advocacy was pivotal in highlighting the importance of aligning national laws with international standards. BhCO also worked with the RGoB, CSOs, and children to support Bhutan’s 6th and 7th periodic CRC reports, contributing to alternative reporting and pre-sessional working group discussions.  BhCO supported drafting the UPR and strengthened advocacy on various child rights issues. These efforts have shaped recommendations that align with national priorities, reinforcing Bhutan’s commitment to a safer, healthier future where every child can thrive.

To enhance Justice for Children (J4C) programming, BhCO supported the development of a J4C Action Plan as part of the Justice Sector Strategic Plan 2024-2028. This plan outlines concrete steps to improve access to J4C over the next five years. A landmark achievement was the establishment of the last three remaining women and child protection desk under the Royal Bhutan Police, achieving nationwide coverage and ensuring that every child in Bhutan now has access to specialized protection services.  Beyond legal frameworks, BhCO also supported the rehabilitation and reintegration efforts, collaborating with CSO Nazhoen Lamtoen to support 20 individuals transitioning back into society. The first summer school program on J4C was developed with the Jigme Singye Wangchuk School of Law (JSWSL) to build a responsive J4C workforce, ensuring long-term systemic improvements. In 2024, 204 children (20 girls) came into conflict with the law, with 39 boys receiving non-custodial measures.

GA4: EVERY CHILD LIVES IN A SAFE AND CLEAN ENVIRONMENT 
To improve the quality and coverage of WASH services in schools, monastic institutions, and health facilities, BhCO provided technical and financial support to develop the national standards on WASH in schools and monastic institutions and capacity development of WASH focal persons on WASH behavioral practices and preventive maintenance of WASH facilities. 

Coinciding with UNICEF’s 50-year partnership with the RGoB, World Water Day was celebrated with the inaugural event of an inclusive toilet at Zhemgang Lower Secondary School by the Deputy Regional Director of the South Asia Region. To ensure quality WASH services, 58 support staff from 56 schools in Tashiyangtse, Trongsa and Bumthang districts are now skilled in the operation and preventive maintenance of WASH facilities and services. As a result,10,687 children (5,499 girls) in these schools are benefiting from sustainable and quality WASH services. The support staff were provided with a WASH caretaker’s toolbox to ensure quality preventive maintenance of WASH services at schools. In addition, 5,556 children (2990 girls) in Mongar and Lhuntse districts benefitted from improved WASH services and personal hygiene behavior practices through the capacity development of 35 health coordinators in 35 schools. 

A total of 1,131 monks from four districts (Samtse, Dagana, Sarpang and Thimphu) now have functional WASH services because of the capacity development of 27 caretakers from 17 monastic schools who are provided with tools for preventive maintenance of WASH facilities. This has enabled the effective implementation of climate-resilient and environment-friendly WASH interventions in monastic institutions. As part of the integrated program in monastic institutions, eight Aqua Privy toilets and bathhouses were renovated, ensuring safety and accessibility for 252 younger children and children with disabilities, in line with the new WASH in-school standards. Additionally, to reduce PET bottle usage, 1,500 reusable tumblers were distributed across 11 monastic schools and nunneries. 

GA5: EVERY CHILD HAS AN EQUITABLE CHANCE IN LIFE 
In 2024, BhCO continued its efforts to strengthen the capacity of policymakers, including Parliamentarians. In partnership with Sherubtse College and UNDP, a social policy workshop was conducted for 23 newly elected Members of Parliament and National Assembly Secretariat staff (2 F). The workshop emphasized the importance of investing in children. As a result, the Parliamentarians committed to prioritizing child-sensitive social protection programmes in the 13th FYP, including a potential introduction of life insurance for children under eight—currently absent from government-subsidized schemes.

Years of advocacy culminated in a new partnership with the Office of the Cabinet Affairs and Strategic Coordination (OCASC) to implement a comprehensive, inclusive, and shock-responsive social protection system.  BhCO supported OCASC in conducting a situation analysis and mapping of existing social protection systems, which will serve as a baseline for developing a child-sensitive social protection framework aligned with the 13th FYP.

UNICEF also established a partnership with the European Union (EU) to strengthen public finance for children (PF4C) and social protection systems. In collaboration with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and OCASC, BhCO mobilized USD 140,428.09 under the EU Public Finance Facility Phase II. This funding will advance PF4C initiatives and enhance social protection, addressing critical funding gaps in these areas.

A critical achievement regarding partnership with local governments in 2024 was the endorsement of the integrated programming approach by the Department of Macro-Fiscal and Development Finance (DMDF), the RGoB’s focal agency for UNICEF under the MoF. Three pilot districts—Samtse, Chhukha, and Dagana—were identified to implement the integrated programme. This approach focuses on addressing last-mile challenges by reaching vulnerable communities in Bhutan’s highest Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) districts. It will promote efficiency and effectiveness by reducing duplication through improved planning and coordination among partners. It also strengthens local government and community capacities, ensuring better results for children. The RGoB’s endorsement highlights its commitment to a holistic approach to child well-being, fostering sustainable progress at the local level.

BhCO remains committed to maintaining efficiency and advancing progress across various cross-sectoral areas:
Gender
On Global Menstrual Hygiene Day, "Red Dot” Bhutan, the national advocacy platform for Menstrual Health and Hygiene (MHM) advocacy, resulted in the Government committing to make all schools period-friendly in the next five years. The day was marked with the #PeriodFriendlyWorld distribution of 10,084 sanitary pads and the launch of National Standards for WASH in Schools and Monastic Institutions. Additionally, an advocacy program for 60 Parliament members was conducted to enhance legislative frameworks and policy interventions to safeguard the well-being and rights of women and children across Bhutan.

An Adolescent Girls’ costed Action Plan (2024-2025) was developed to identify initiatives for adolescent girls across programmes. An action plan with a country brief on the prevention of adolescent pregnancy was also developed through multi-sectoral collaboration and led jointly by the UN agencies for the first time. This was presented at the South Asia Regional meeting that organized by SAARC, UNICEF, UNFPA and WHO. 

Progress has been made in Joint UN partnerships addressing gender challenges and data gaps. The 2024 UNCT SWAP Gender Equality Scorecard assessment was conducted for the first time to review the Common Country Analysis and Cooperation Framework Results Framework.  The BhCO has provided support to the national strategy to eliminate GBV and harmful practices and for the analysis of social norms related to gender, VAW/VAC, and harmful practices in partnership with UNDP and UNFPA. Both documents are currently being finalized with the NCWC who serves as the custodian of these documents. The social norms study will provide evidence-based planning for addressing VAC/W, GBV and child marriage. This marks a major area of collaboration between the three UN agencies for the first time on GBV.

PSEA
To strengthen prevention and response systems for sexual exploitation and abuse in Bhutan, BhCO worked with CSOs partners to enhance the capacities of 38 (28 F) PSEA focal points. These focal points will train their respective staff members on PSEA. For BhCO, work is underway to strengthen the internal PSEA system. The PSEA accountability framework was developed, and all staff members have signed the PSEA code of conduct. A PSEA task team is in place with representation from the operation and programmes and the PSEA action plan is in place which will be monitored regularly by the CMT. 

Humanitarian Assistance
Bhutan is highly vulnerable to natural disasters, including earthquakes, landslides, Glacial Lake Outburst Floods, flash floods, cloud bursts, and windstorms, and is at high risk to lives, livelihoods and safety of the communities, especially children. There are currently gaps in capacities to respond, especially to address the needs of children during emergencies.  BhCO collaborated with partners from RGoBs and CSOs on emergency preparedness and response planning, investing in partner’s capacity to identify, address and prevent any risks to children, especially during emergencies within their respective Cluster Plans. While BhCO and partners are mainstreaming Disaster Risk and Resilience (DRR) into development plans, BhCO will increase its efforts in 2025 to fulfill UNICEF’s commitment to localization by initiating its engagement with local actors and strengthening local capacity to identify and address the needs of children in emergencies across the country.
 
Climate
BhCO has made strides in addressing climate change. Climate change education has been successfully integrated into the curricula of Sciences, Geography, and Biology, equipping students with the knowledge and green skills necessary for a sustainable future. Additionally, an Action Plan on Climate Change and ECCD was developed in collaboration with MoESD and the Asia Pacific Regional Network for Early Childhood (ARNEC), ensuring climate resilience begins at the earliest stages of education.
 
As part of the Climate Change UPSHIFT initiative, children and youth in 70 pilot schools implemented projects focusing on carbon emissions reduction, renewable energy, waste management, and climate change awareness. Through this initiative, 15,484 adolescents and youth acquired 21st-century and employability skills, while 11,300 young people received crucial messages on mental health and psychosocial support. 
 
To adapt to the impacts of climate change, BhCO facilitated the construction of climate-resilient water supply systems, providing 1,346 (673 girls) school children in three remote schools with safe and reliable drinking water. Through the installation of safe water filtration systems, 698 child monks and 30 child nuns now have access to safe drinking water in 13 monastic schools and one nunnery. Since 2019, 2,886 monks from 42 monastic schools and 190 nuns from five nunneries have access to safe water filtration systems. Through the construction of improved and climate-resilient WASH facilities and capacity development of WASH service providers coverage and quality of WASH services in schools, healthcare facilities and monastic institutions were further enhanced.  
 
Under the Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan (SCAP), BhCO conducted the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC), gathering critical evidence on climate change and environmental conditions to inform the creation of a Climate and Environment Strategy for Children. In collaboration with the Department of Environment and Climate Change (DECC), BhCO is supporting the development of Bhutan's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 3.0 in alignment with the Paris Agreement, ensuring that social sectors and young children remain a key focus in national climate policies. 
 
BhCO facilitated a DECC official's participation in COP29, who now leads youth consultations for NDC 3.0. These consultations are creating a platform for 500 young people (250 F) to share their climate change concerns, propose solutions, and influence national climate action. Youth consultations from January to July aim to empower young people to drive change while inspiring sustainable action and influencing policy.
 
The change strategies applied by BhCO to facilitate and manage change:
    

- Programming excellence for at-scale results for children:
A pioneering integrated multi-sector child-friendly intervention has been initiated in Punakha, Zhemgang, and Mongar to enhance the wellbeing of children and youth in monastic schools. Designed in consultation with monastic authorities and children, this represents a shift towards systemic change by building stakeholder ownership and increasing investment in the holistic development of young monks and nuns.


- Winning support for the cause of children from decision makers and the wider public
In 2024, UNICEF Bhutan made significant strides in strengthening its external relations portfolio and increasing visibility in support of advocacy and resource mobilization for the children in Bhutan. Marking 50 years of UNICEF’s partnership with the RGoB, UNICEF harnessed the celebratory year and high-level visits to reinforce its position as the leading voice for children. 

The CO harnessed a high-level visit by the Deputy Regional Director for South Asia towards ensuring that the government’s priorities remained inclusive of children and young people’s issues.

The Government formally acknowledged UNICEF’s contributions to Bhutan’s development journey and for the achievements made in education, health care, water sanitation and hygiene, child protection, and nutrition services over the last 50 years. This growing recognition translated into policy advancements, including Bhutan’s renewed commitments to uphold the rights of children resulted, among others, in Bhutan committing to expanding child protection systems and adopting a multi-sectoral approach to safeguard children’s welfare, approving the National Education Policy 2024 and making climate policies more inclusive of children and young people. 
Discourses on issues impacting children and young people and, UNICEF’s support towards securing the wellbeing of mothers and children, and digitization, among others, increased awareness and visibility of UNICEF’s work in Bhutan. In 2024, UNICEF Bhutan had 188 media mentions, three times higher than that of 2023. Through Facebook and Instagram, the CO’s most used online platforms, BhCO recorded 22,330,836 impressions, maintaining UNICEF’s lead on social media and public engagement around child rights among relevant industry comparators, including UN agencies and non-profits. 
 

- Developing and leveraging resources and partnerships for children:
To sustain the gains made in the lives of children and address emerging challenges, UNICEF’s advocacy with donors and national committees resulted in BhCO mobilizing about USD 5 million to protect the rights of children, which is a 25 per cent increase from 2023. 

The European Union and UNICEF partnered to advance digitalization in education and skills and furthered its collaboration to strengthen public finance for children (PF4C) and social protection systems under the EU Public Finance Facility Phase II.  


- Harnessing the power of business and markets for children:  
 BhCO supported the biotechnology entrepreneurship training of 23 participants (10 F), including two entrepreneurs, 12 students, and nine job seekers, offering 1,200 USD seed funds to each winning team for scaling up projects using biotechnological methods.
