By leveraging flexible funding mechanisms and collaborating with the RGoB, CSOs, academia, and development partners, including UN agencies, BhCO has successfully implemented programmatic interventions across multiple sectors. These initiatives encompass health and nutrition, WASH, education (ECCD, inclusive education, digital education), child protection, ADAP, and social policy.

BhCO has collaborated with key partners such as the MoH, National Medical Services (NMS), the PEMA Secretariat, the MoESD, the Faculty of Nursing and Public Health (FNPH), and the Khesar Gyalpo University of Medical Sciences of Bhutan (KGUMSB) to strengthen maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health (MNCAH). Key areas of focus included mental health, environmental health, disability prevention and rehabilitation, and nutrition.

BhCO has deepened collaborations with government stakeholders, CSOs, development partners, and the private sector to promote child, adolescent, and women-centered WASH interventions. Partnerships with the Health and Wellbeing Division (HWD) of the MoESD, the Environmental Health Programme, the Department of Public Health of the MoH, and the Water and Sanitation Division (WSD) of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport (MoIT) were pivotal.  BhCO also engaged the Religion and Health Project (RHP) of the Central Monastic Body and the Bhutan Toilet Organization (BTO) to enhance WASH programming. Additionally, a new partnership with the Department of Climate Change under the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources enabled BhCo to play a crucial role in advancing collaborative efforts on climate action.

Through innovative and collaborative partnerships, the BhCO expanded efforts to bring education to marginalized children.  Public-private partnerships involving the MoESD, Monastic Authorities, the EU, the Global Partnership for Education, Akelius, and Eduten enhanced education outreach.   Collaborations with the Bhutan Foundation and Ability Bhutan Society advanced inclusive education, while a new partnership with Eleva Foundation enabled the development of Bhutan’s first prototype of Accessible Digital Textbooks for children with disabilities. Strengthened relations with TashiCell, a private telecom Company, resulted in free internet access for nine monastic institutions to support digital learning.  Additionally, a partnership with Eduten introduced a free digital math platform to monastic schools. Joint advocacy with the Monastic Education Council facilitated the deployment of trained English and Math teachers from the MoESD to monastic schools, further strengthening opportunities.

BhCO also extended the UPSHIFT programme in collaboration with the MoESD, Loden Foundation, and Bhutan Youth Development Fund, to integrate mentorship opportunities. A revised School-Based Parenting Manual was developed in collaboration with the PEMA Secretariat and MoESD to review enhanced parental support for child development.

The successful nationwide rollout of Eduten to approximately 30,200 fourth and fifth graders was a result of BhCO's pilot and leveraging partnership with UNICEF Global Learning Innovation Hub and the MoESD. 

BhCO, in collaboration with the Government and CSOs, expanded child protection and GBV services to the district level and engaged women, children, and community members to prevent and respond to Violence Against Children and Women (VAC/W). Partnering with UNDP and UNFPA, the NCWC and CSO RENEW led to the development of a GBV strategy and analysis of social norms on VAC/W and child marriage. This collaboration pooled resources for more impactful efforts. Thematic and RR Funding significantly supported these achievements, enhancing child protection and GBV programming through the establishment of the WGSS and evidence generation on harmful social and gender norms to design targeted interventions.  BhCO also enhanced access to justice for women and children by facilitating partnerships between the Human Dignity Clinic, JSWSL, Legal Aid Centre, and RENEW, developing an SOP to deliver legal aid to WGSS clients, thus better equipping WGSS to provide legal services.

In partnership with the Environmental Health Program of MoH, a situational assessment of child environmental health was conducted and used for advocacy during the International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week.  The situational assessment of the children’s environmental health in Bhutan was also launched during lead poisoning prevention week. The assessment will guide and design appropriate policies and programming on Children’s Environmental Health in Bhutan, including appropriate regulations. To enhance the capacity of the health system to respond to the children’s environmental health issues BhCO, in collaboration with the MoH, developed a pre-service module on Children’s Environmental Health. The module will be taught to all the pre-service health professionals at the Khesar Gyalpo University of Medical Sciences.  UNICEF also supported the Government in implementing the UN Technology Bank’s (UNTB) Hear, Listen and Speak programme where children with deafness are screened and provided with assistive technology such as hearing aids and digital hearing aids to support children's learning and development. 

As part of SCAP, the WASH program successfully forged a new partnership with the Climate Change Division, Department of Environment and Climate Change of the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources.  With support from the Health and Wellbeing Division, MoESD, BhCO also completed the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). This effort supported BhCO and partners in gathering evidence on climate change and environmental conditions, leading to the development of a Climate and Environment Strategy for Children.

BhCO has further strengthened partnerships with key government agencies and CSOs through cross-sectoral programming and upstream policy work. Strategic collaborations with the Parliament, Cabinet Office, and Ministry of Finance have deepened, recognizing their pivotal roles in budget allocation and resource distribution across sectors. A notable achievement is the establishment of a new partnership with the European Union to support public finance for children (PF4C) and social protection initiatives in Bhutan.

BhCO has also established a new partnership with the three local governments of Samtse, Chhukha, and Dagana to implement an integrated approach to programming. This collaboration is pivotal, as it aligns with UNICEF’s commitment to reaching the most deprived children and mothers who continue to face challenges in accessing essential services. In 2025, it will be a priority to build the capacity of LG authorities on the importance of prioritizing investments in children through local government budgets. Strengthening this capacity will ensure that local governments play an active role in improving outcomes for children and mothers in their communities.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
With Bhutan’s LDC graduation in 2023 and the start of the 13th FYP in 2024, BhCO continues to ensure that foundational gains made in the social sector are sustained and that critical issues pertaining to children and women continue to be prioritized by Government and civil society. This includes reflecting on challenges and lessons learned to help identify what worked well and what didn't- fostering a culture of continuous improvement.

In 2024, while most of the activities planned for health and nutrition were implemented, several challenges were faced during implementation regarding data and funding issues. The NHS 2023 report provided most data on health and nutrition, but district level data for planning targeted interventions on health and nutrition for women and children was not available. The planned MICS7 will provide sub-national data for assessing progress and planning interventions.

A Solar Direct Drive refrigerator/freezer was installed in Laya Primary Health Centre. With the installation of the solar cold chain equipment, the vaccines are stored consistently at the recommended temperature, preventing vaccine damage due to temperature excursions. Medical oxygen plants could not be installed due to lack of funding. However, BhCO will continue exploring funds for this support through the Regional Office. Capacity development of engineers and technicians of the Bio-medical Engineering Department (BMED) of National Medical Services on cold chain equipment enabled a sustainable system for preventive maintenance of cold chain supply systems across the country as health facilities in all 20 districts are supported by BMED staff.

The 13th FYP validated CPD priorities, emphasizing resource availability, pressing needs, partner capacity, and development support. Key interventions included digital solutions for secular and monastic schools, digital skills and climate change education, employability skills through youth programs, and home-based interventions for marginalized young children.
The 2024 digitalization initiative positioned BhCO as a key partner in education digitalization, collaborating with MoESD, EU, and others to create effective investment models.

The establishment of three Regional Inclusive ECCD Hubs in 2023 expanded inclusive approaches across all 20 districts in 2024. Other inclusive education activities included schoolteacher training, Rapid Neurodevelopmental Assessment (RDNA) provision to SEN schools, entrepreneurship training for young people with disabilities, and inclusion of children with disabilities in the National Education Assessment. Despite positive results, further capacity building for implementing partners is needed.

Bhutan's UPSHIFT gained recognition from the UNICEF Office of Innovation for its work focusing on employability skills for youth. The development of the Second Decade Strategy initiated in 2024 will help ensure strategic and sustainable results for adolescents and young people.
 
To advance child rights in Bhutan, it is essential to establish platforms that bring together children, decision-makers, CSOs, and service providers. These platforms will facilitate constructive dialogue- enabling children and other stakeholders to voice their concerns and engage in meaningful discussions.  BhCO worked with the Government, CSOs and children in the CRC reporting process which enabled the Committee on the Rights of the Child to get a realistic picture of the situation of the children’s rights in Bhutan leading to a targeted recommendation in improving the situation.

Strengthening the capacity of policy makers, including the Parliamentarians, is vital to ensuring they prioritize investments in children and allocate budgets effectively.  BhCO must collaborate closely with Parliamentary sub-committees, particularly the Women, Children, and Youth Committee, to address child-centered SDGs and issues related to the CRC. Parliamentarians appreciated the social policy workshop, highlighting how it deepened their understanding of the critical importance of investing in the early years of a child’s life through social protection measures. They acknowledged the long-term societal benefits of such investments and committed to prioritizing them in the 13th FYP. Continuing engagement with the parliamentarians is also critical for ensuring that the RGoB fulfills its obligations under the CRC and that legislative support can be provided to put in place legal frameworks that uphold and promote children's rights. 

Engaging government partners early in project development and resource mobilization is essential. This inclusive approach fosters ownership and ensures interventions align with national priorities and budgets under the 13th FYP.  BhCO’s upstream policy work has been instrumental in establishing and deepening partnerships with key government agencies and CSOs. Strengthened collaboration with the Parliament, Cabinet Office, and Ministry of Finance has been crucial for influencing budget allocations and ensuring children’s needs are prioritized in national planning and budgeting.

A new partnership with the European Union marks a significant milestone in securing sustainable investments for children’s well-being and development. This collaboration underscores UNICEF’s commitment to fostering a supportive environment for child-focused policies and programs in Bhutan.

Building on these achievements, BhCO is well-positioned to advocate for child-sensitive policies and leverage partnerships to drive impactful, sustainable change for children across the country.

India being is the world’s most populous country, a significant proportion of the population are children and young people[1]. This demographic structure presents significant potential for India’s future. Indeed, projections released in 2024 estimate that India will be home to 350 million children in 2050, 15 per cent of the global child population[2]. Urbanization has seen a notable rise, with an estimated 36.6 per cent of the population living in urban areas in 2024, which is projected to further increase to 43.2 per cent by 2035[3]. 
 
In 2024, India continued to grow economically. Advance estimates from the National Statistics Office (NSO) forecast a growth of 6.4 per cent in 2024-25[4].  This economic growth is driven by factors including increased industrial activity, a burgeoning services sector, solid private consumption and significant investments in infrastructure[5]. The Indian economy is expected to transition to an upper middle-income country by 2036 and is estimated to reach the $15 trillion mark by 2047[6].
 
The National Plan of Action for Children 2016 stipulates 5 per cent of the budget to be allocated to children. For the fiscal year 2024-2025, the budget allocation for children is estimated at 2.3 per cent of the total union budget, a decrease from 3.3 per cent in 2019-2020[7]. Despite this reduction, the overall children's budget has increased by 5.5 per cent compared to the previous year (2023-2024) to ¿6,130.25 crores [8]. Budgets for schemes related to Women and Children, Education, and Health have seen an increase: Mission Vatsalya (16 per cent), PM Poshan Shakti Nirman (24.6 per cent), and the flexible pool for key schemes under the Ministry of Health (23.4 per cent)[9]. The continued investment of the Government of India in these programmes highlights the commitment on key areas of child development and wellbeing.
 
2024 also witnessed the re-election of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the national elections.  The Modi 3.0 administration (as popularly referred) aims to drive India's growth, social and economic development during its third term, addressing both immediate needs and long-term goals. The BJP's manifesto titled ‘Sankalp Patra,’ focuses on four pillars: Gareeb (poor), Yuva (youth), Annadata (farmers), and Nari Shakti (women empowerment). 
 
India continues to make strides in its Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), improving its ranking from 112th place in 2023 to 109th place in 2024[10]. India's multidimensional poverty (MPI) rate decreased from 29.2 per cent in 2013-14 to 11.3 per cent in 2022-23, a decrease of 17.9 percentage points. This reduction is estimated to have lifted approximately 248.2 million people out of poverty over the ten-year period[11]. 
 
On child-related SDG targets, India is projected to be on track to meet the targets for under-5 mortality rate, reduced to 32 (both per 1,000 live births) and the maternal mortality rate, reduced to 97 (per 100,000 live births). In addition, steady improvements have been observed in birth registration (93 per cent), skilled birth attendance (91 per cent), fully immunized children (84 per cent), primary school completion rates (92 per cent), and improved source of drinking water (95.7 per cent)[12]
 
Accelerated efforts are required to achieve SDG targets in relating to nutritional status, child marriage, safety, education and learning, and women's workforce participation. For example, while there have been improvements in child nutritional outcomes, progress has been gradual over the years, and the prevalence of anemia among children aged 6-59 has risen from 58.5 per cent in 2015/16 to 68.1 per cent in 2019/21 [13]. While primary completion rate is high, India continues to face the challenge of drop out/out of school children in secondary schools, and there has been a decline in retention rate between 2023 and 2024 for both primary school (from 91 per cent to 85 per cent) and secondary school (from 65 per cent to 64 per cent)[14]. In addition, proficiency has seen a decline in both primary and secondary levels. For example, for Class 8, Language proficiency decreased from 37 per cent to 34 per cent, and Mathematics performance saw a decline from 40 per cent to 27 per cent, between 2017 and 2021[15]. Crimes against children in India also remains a concern. Latest data released in 2024 by the National Crime Records Bureau indicates an 8.7 percent increase in reported cases of crimes against children from 2021 to 2022, with a total of 162,449 cases[16]. 
Even in areas where India has made strong progress, inequities between different groups persist. There are significant geographic disparities across states and between rural and urban populations. Additionally, there are significant socio-economic disparities, rooted in gender, income levels, social groups, caste, and disability status. For example, as per NFHS-5, U-5 child mortality rates remain higher in rural compared to urban areas (46 versus 32 deaths per 1,000 live births, respectively). Neonatal mortality rates and stillbirths are highest among Scheduled Castes (22 versus 14.5 in other class), while infant mortality rates and under-five mortality rates are highest among Scheduled Tribes (32.1 and 35.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, respectively). Children from the lowest wealth quintile experience mortality rates 2.5 times higher than those from the highest wealth quintile.
 
Adverse gender social norms persist and affect children in issues such as sex selection, child marriage, gender-based violence, lower economic opportunities, and the greater burden of care on women. Although India climbed eight ranks in the global gender index (from 135 in 2020 to 127 in 2022), in 2024 India slipped back on two ranking to 129th position. Parameters such as 'Economic Participation' and 'Opportunity' saw slight improvements, but 'Educational Attainment' and 'Political Empowerment' scores have declined[17]. Child marriage rates have seen an overall declining trends; nevertheless, more than one in five girls in India are still married below the age of 18 years[18].
 
India continues to be one of the countries in the world most affected by climate change[19]. Children are particularly vulnerable to climate risks, including climate-related health impacts caused by pollution[20],[21]. Sustainable and inclusive urban development, portable social protection and disaster risk reduction remain important areas of focus. 
 
UNICEF’s State of the World Children’s Report 2024 highlights the climate and environmental crisis, alongside demographic shifts and frontier technologies, as the three critical megatrends that will shape the future for children. India will continue to house the largest number of children globally, who will increasingly be exposed to extreme weather events, and will need to navigate the promise as well as pitfalls of new, fast-paced technological developments[22]. It is imperative for India, along with the rest of the world, to implement policies and interventions now that protect and empower the next generation, to ensure equitable development, and realize the right of every child in the future.

In 2024, UNICEF India accelerated the implementation of the Country Programme, which aligned with Government of India (GoI)'s priorities, the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2023-2027, and the UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022-2025. To address equity challenges, UNICEF accelerated gender-focused programming and disability inclusion through evidence generation, analysis, advocacy, convening multi stakeholder partnerships various technical support such as developing guidelines, action plans, and training.  
 
Every child survives and thrives
In 2024, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) advanced “Every Woman, Every Newborn, Everywhere”, a global initiative to accelerate efforts toward the maternal and child health related SDG 2030 goals, reaching 19 million pregnant women and children nationwide. UNICEF supported critical Maternal Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health initiatives, including supporting the roll-out of the enhanced facility based newborn care (FBNC) across the country, promoting quality, equity, and dignity. Along with academic and professional association partners, UNICEF teams across five field offices provided technical and logistical support to the MoHFW to update the FBNC guidance, after a decade, and implement the training of trainers in all 36 states and Union Territories.  In addition, UNICEF provided technical support to strengthen systems for care beyond survival, especially of the small and vulnerable newborns, through newborn screening for birth defects, inclusive early childhood development, and initiated support in non-communicable diseases. 
UNICEF contributed to the Immunization Agenda 2030 by supporting GoI initiatives for vaccination catch-up strategies to reach dropouts, strengthening institutional capacities for human resource capacity, enhancing supply chains and systems resilience through health facility solarization. As part of the GAVI Health System Strengthening – Phase 3, UNICEF fostered partnerships with civil society organizations (CSOs) for stronger community engagement and empowerment. 
To strengthen data driven primary health care systems, UNICEF supported the development of the Reproductive and Child Health 2.0 system, aligned to the National Digital Health Mission for use of data and evidence for Universal Health Coverage, which will integrate data across all life-course programmes for 50 million pregnant women and children each year. 

Through its Anemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) programme, the MoHFW reached 55 million (45 per cent) adolescents, girls, and boys, and 28 million (95 per cent) pregnant women with Iron and Folic Acid supplements between January and November 2024[1]. UNICEF supported MoHFW to develop a standardized scorecard tool for real-time monitoring of the AMB programme, in partnership with two Centres of Excellence and other Development Partners at national and state levels. Between 2022-24, UNICEF supported the Jharkhand state government in an innovative digital approach aiming to streamline anemia cases tracking through the AMB T4 (Test-Treat-Talk-Track) mobile application. Following the pilot’s success, MoHFW plans a nationwide scale-up of the app in 2025 with UNICEF. UNICEF financially and technically supported the MoHFW to conduct data-driven annual reviews of AMB as well as the overall nutrition programme. This contributed to an 8.3 per cent increase in the Government’s allocation ($ 97.6 million) for anemia control between 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 in 12 UNICEF-supported states[2]. Furthermore, UNICEF provided financial and technical support to Government in these 12 states, including through collaboration with Centres of Excellence, to demonstrate community-based nutrition programming. In 2024, state governments monitored the growth of 55 million out of 65.6 million children under five years old (84 per cent), treated 1.15 million severely wasted children, and provided one home visit for 4.6 million children aged six to nine months out of the 4.46 million targeted (103 per cent)[3]. UNICEF contributed to these results through financial and technical support to the Government and collaboration through Centres of Excellence with demonstrative programming.
In 2024, the Ministry of Women and Child Development (MoWCD) and the National Rural Livelihood Mission widely disseminated a national resource package on healthy diets during National Nutrition Month, leading to improved reach of messages to the population, especially the most vulnerable children, through different channels such as through Anganwadi workers and radio. The resource package was developed with UNICEF technical support, based on dietary behaviour research conducted by a UNICEF partner. 
 
Early Childhood Development (ECD)
In 2024, UNICEF further strengthened its work in early childhood development. The State Government of Maharashtra, with support of UNICEF, pioneered the establishment of a Centre of Excellence at Wardha Medical College to embed ECD into its statewide policies, strategies, and budgets ($ 1.3 million 2023-2024), targeting primarily vulnerable children in the tribal areas. Recognizing Maharashtra’s efforts, and with UNICEF’s technical and financial support, the Central Government launched the “Early Childhood Development and Stimulation” guidelines, the Early Childhood Care and Education curriculum, the Poshan Bhi Padhai Bhi programme and the national protocol for children with disability, signaling the government’s move toward an inclusive ECD agenda. This positive policy environment also boosted the expansion of ECD initiatives across other states. UNICEF is supporting the development of a proof of concept on convergent and inclusive ECD to inform scale-up decisions in four states: Bihar, Jharkhand, Telangana, and Rajasthan. With UNICEF support, awareness on around ECD has also increased amongst healthcare professionals. In 2024, more than 50,000 members of the Indian Academy of Paediatrics were trained on inclusive ECD, following a large-scale awareness campaign. This initiative aimed to facilitate the MoHFW and dedicated Centres of Excellence in five states - Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Telangana - to integrate ECD into their policies and budgets and strengthen programme implementation, targeting children with birth defect and/or disability through capacity building, mentoring, and research.
 
Every child learns
UNICEF’s technical support to the Government in areas of pre-primary, primary and secondary education contributed to the release of $ 213 million in domestic financing and India’s good practices in education including mother tongue-based education and learning assessment were shared with 46 countries from Asia-Pacific and Southern African regions. 
Through providing secondary data analysis, UNICEF supported 15 states to develop quality education plans including preparation for disasters and for children with disabilities. A large-scale national learning assessment was administered by the Ministry of Education (MoE) to 2.3 million students across 75,000 schools, for which UNICEF provided technical support on drafting standards for assessments and reviewing the assessment framework. 
Government provided education access to 842,321 out-of-school children (51 per cent girls, 480 children with disabilities) in five states through UNICEF’s technical support that included providing intensive Activity for Daily Living services to children with severe and multiple disabilities to support their transition from home-based to school-based education. State Education Departments in Uttar Pradesh (UP) and Gujarat, with UNICEF support, convened consultations with 12 states on the use of early warning systems to prevent drop-out, using artificial intelligence and machine learning to predict risk for dropout. As a result, the governments of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh have prioritised the development of early warning systems in 2025. 
In 2024, UNICEF supported the GoI to improve the quality of early learning for 6.4 million children, by training 197,266 Anganwadi workers, who work in rural child centres, on play-based learning using blended approaches and in counselling parents on supporting play in the home at 250,434 ECD centres and schools. To support the implementation of India’s policy on foundational literacy and numeracy, with UNICEF technical financial support, its partner trained 93,319 teachers and supervisors (40 per cent female) on how to teach reading and numeracy, benefitting 2.1 million children.
With UNICEF support, the MoE launched 500 career information cards, covering a comprehensive overview of qualification requirements, information on education institution for degrees or diplomas, and loans/scholarships, in order to support adolescents transitioning from school to work. UNICEF further supported the Government to develop and roll out a career guidance course on its digital learning platform, Unilearn, which facilitated the training of 74,000 teachers (43per cent female), and contributed to 3.42 million students (52 per cent girls) participating in 21st century skills courses and career guidance programmes across 15 states.
 
Learning to earning 
In 2024, UNICEF continued to support key initiatives of YuWaah (Generation Unlimited India).  A Needs Gap Assessment was conducted with over 200 young people from the most marginalized communities. The consultations aimed at understanding their awareness, aspirations and access to skilling, career guidance and employment opportunities. Insights informed the development and launch of a Technical Guidance for Engaging the Most Marginalized, which carried recommendations for Governments, private sector, and development partners towards strengthening their equity and inclusion-based programming. 
The Passport to Earning initiative, which provide skilling opportunities, certified 1.6 million youth with employable skills, reaching 3.2 million young people cumulative since 2022. The Step-Up programme, which aims to provide young people with focused skills development and career preparedness training, expanded its reach in collaboration with Ministry of Labour and Employment, Punjab Skill Development Mission, Indira Ghandi National Open University  and Pratham, reaching 315,087 job seekers in 2024. YouthHub, a one-stop junction offering opportunities ranging from employment to upskilling to volunteering, connected young people, especially girls and marginalised youth, to opportunities related to advancing their futures. It secured partnerships with 13 opportunity providers to create 277,000 opportunities for children and youth, facilitating their continued learning to earning journey.
 
Every child empowered and protected 
In collaboration with the Supreme Court Juvenile Justice Committee, in 2024 UNICEF supported the GoI to convene a high-level National Stakeholder Consultation, which brought both national and state level leadership of the Judiciary and Executive together with civil society, to advance the protection of all children in India. This consultation highlighted the multifaceted challenges and the multisectoral action required to address the intersection of disabilities with other vulnerabilities, which in turn led to a national policy dialogue. This dialogue resulted in developing protocols for diversion/non-custodial approach in eight states, aiming to accelerate child-friendly approaches with law enforcement and judiciary. In addition, in partnership with the National Legal Services Authority, UNICEF drafted guidelines for the legal services scheme for children, particularly those with disabilities, which the Supreme Court notified and operationalized nationally.
With UNICEF technical support, the GoI made strides on family-based care for children and prevention of family separation through enhancing case management, building functionaries’ capacity of and supporting children's access to essential services for family integration. UNICEF supported in developing Comprehensive Care Reform Guidelines in eight states, promoting deinstitutionalization and family-based alternative care. In 2024, 309,687 children accessed social protection schemes, and 103,721 children were reunited with their families or placed in family care in UNICEF-supported states. UNICEF also supported the Government to enhance child protection systems, preventing vulnerabilities, promoting justice, mitigating violence, and improving mental health services. UNICEF collaborated with Judicial and Police Academies, Administrative training institutes and other academic institutions to train 300,000 functionaries, with the goal to institutionalize and strengthening the workforce for child protection. In support to Government programmes such as the School Health and Wellness Programme, National Adolescent Health Mission, both aim to promote health and wellbeing of children and adolescents, UNICEF supported the state governments in expanding in Mental Health and Psychosocial Support service provision capacities of frontline workers and district-level functionaries, in partnership with CSOs, academic institutions and centres of excellence.  UNICEF also provided technical support to the state governments of Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Kerala, and Telangana, on a programme designed to protect children from online risks, which reached 4.3 million children, adolescents and caregivers with psychological first aid in 2024. 
 
Adolescent development and empowerment (ADE)
In 2024, UNICEF’s technical support to the Government on adolescent development and empowerment was accelerated, based on an internal cross-sectoral framework with sharpened focus on adolescent girls. A technical brief on “Adolescent Pregnancy” was developed in consultation with MoHFW and presented at the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation Policy Dialogue on Adolescent Pregnancy (Kathmandu). This enabled broader engagement of government and stakeholders on an important issue for adolescent wellbeing, especially of adolescent girls. UNICEF facilitated new partnerships with local philanthropic foundations to support adolescent development and participation efforts, with life skills activities reaching over 261,114 adolescents in 2024. Aligning with Government’s Mission Shakti, which aims to enhance the safety, security, and empowerment of women, UNICEF supported state government platforms like Shala Adhigam (Learning programme), Advika, (Odisha girls’ empowerment programme) and Kanyashree clubs (Girls clubs), which engaged 6,481,270 adolescents in 2024. These platforms allow adolescents to raise issues around child marriage, advocate for their rights, promote positive gender norms, and address other protection risks, and enables them to participate and engage with their local panchayats and their collectives on issues affecting them, resulting in better delivery of adolescent services and the realization of their rights to participate.  
 
Every child lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment
2024 marked a decade of India’s Swachh Bharat Mission, which aims to eliminate open defecation and improve sanitation across the country. Since the inception of the Mission, 550 million people now have access to toilets in their homes, and 600,000 villages have become open defecation free[4]. With UNICEF technical support, which included the development of implementation guidelines, training of master trainers, and monitoring of progress, the Government provided safely managed water supply to an estimated 59.3 million people and sanitation services to 17.9 million people in 2024. In addition, 15,631 schools and 239 healthcare facilities received access to Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) services in 2024. Aligned with global efforts to advocate for menstrual hygiene, UNICEF provided technical support to the GoI, including developing information, education, and communication materials. An estimated 20.5 million people were reached virtually and 694,000 people were reached in-person with key messages on menstrual hygiene in 2024, aiming to address negative social norms related to menstruation.
UNICEF continues to be a partner-of-choice for the Government and other sector stakeholders on systems strengthening and capacity-building in planning, implementation, and monitoring of WASH programmes. UNICEF’s technical assistance in Social and Behavioural Change (SBC) supported a nationwide campaign that mobilized more than 300 million people and 50,500 community engagement initiatives, focusing on equity in WASH service and dignity of sanitation workers, which contributes to the safe communities and health care facilities. 
In 2024, UNICEF accelerated efforts for sustainable climate and environment in India. UNICEF completed two significant studies to strengthen evidence-based advocacy: the Climate Landscape Analysis for Children and the Vulnerability Assessment for WASH and Health systems in India. In addition, UNICEF provided technical and financial support to the Government to collaborate with grassroot youth-led networks and engage with over 12.3 million[5] young people in various climate action initiatives such as tree planting and cleaning of water bodies. UNICEF also supported the national Local Conference of the Youth which provided a platform for climate change discussions among young people and children, contributing to the United Nations Conference of Parties Global meeting on climate change. UNICEF amplified the voices of children and youth through these opportunities, enabled India’s youth to express climate concerns and way forward. Additionally, UNICEF supported youth-led advocacies in Gujarat Youth Conclave 5.0 joined with the Minister, Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, and in the 100 Climate Champions Programmes – helping bring young people at the centre of national advocacy agenda. Other milestones achieved this year include the launch of the landmark initiative the Green Rising India consortium aimed at building youth led climate action, adaptation and resilience by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in collaboration with YuWaah, supported by UNICEF. This initiative is for youth led and responsive climate programmes and policy in promoting a sustainable and environmentally conscious way of living. 
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life
In 2024, UNICEF provided technical support to the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment and MoWCD, who were able to reach 13.98 million girls, 3.07 million households, 0.21 million orphans, and 24,449 children with disability, with cash transfers and complementary services such as nutrition counselling and vocational training across 16 states. These interventions focused on reducing multi-dimensional vulnerabilities around gender, climate, child-care and disability across the life cycle. UNICEF provided analytical support towards disability inclusion, producing a social protection gap analysis, disability certification bottleneck analysis, extra-cost of care analysis and initiating of an UN-wide disability study. 
UNICEF advocated with the Ministries of Finance (MoF) and MoWCD to establish a financial intermediary to mobilise resources, including from capital markets, through a blended financing instrument (covering debt and equity), focused on care and disability but also climate/disaster, when care responsibilities of women and adolescent girls increase manifold. 
India’s Union Budget presents annual “Statement 12”, outlining details of spending on children by various Ministries. To adopt a more rigorous approach towards estimating spending on children, UNICEF developed a methodology based on experience of child budgets in 11 states to facilitate improved policy formulation targeting the children The methodology was subsequently adopted by the MoF to inform the 2024 Union Budget. 
With UNICEF technical assistance to Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR)’s Localization of SDGs initiative, 9,404[6] Gram Panchayats (grassroots governance unit) adopted resolutions on “child friendly villages” and 12,280 Gram Panchayats adopted resolutions on “women friendly villages” in 2024. UNICEF support included guideline development, documentation of good practices and training Panchayat Raj institutions. In collaboration with state governments and partners, over 350,000 elected representatives and panchayat functionaries in over 35,000 Gram Panchayats were trained on conducting children’s and women’s assemblies to ensure child participation in local governance.
UNICEF collaborated with UNESCAP to provide technical assistance to state governments in analysing its business processes to improve registering and recording of births in the Civil Registration & Vital Statistics systems in two states. In addition, in six states, UNICEF engaged with state government to promote last-mile birth registration services for 2,816,312 children aged 0-6 years in 2024. 
 
Change strategies and enablers
Several change strategies were deployed to accelerate the six programme outcomes outlined in the GOI-UNICEF County Programme Document by integrating the child rights, gender, equity, climate change and disaster risk lens in the programming, enhancing the quality and use of data and evidence, advocating child rights, and enhancing partnerships with the private sector and children and youth. 
UNICEF India marked 75 years of partnership with India, refreshing its legacy with a future-focused vision through creative digital campaigns. Stories of change on child rights included senior government leaders speaking on the transformative impact of UNICEF partnership e.g., empowering adolescents to prevent child marriage and continue learning, in reaching remote communities with mobile health services, in helping immunization coverage. Three of the six thematic advocacy priorities on youth in climate action, healthy diets and learning, were rolled out. Members of Parliament (MPs) were also engaged to have informed discussions in the national parliament on these topics. 
To advocate for child rights, UNICEF digital outreach has doubled from 2023 to 2024, achieving 4.19 billion impressions, 18.7 million engagements, and 516 million videos. UNICEF produced 438 multimedia products and 215 web articles, securing 86% positive media coverage, including 55 front-page mentions and 56 op-eds that helped set child rights issues in the media discourse. 
In the area of disaster risk reduction, UNICEF provided technical support to 10 State Governments to utilize Government Disaster Risk Management funding more effectively. This included utilization of $ 134 million for child-sensitive preparedness and risk mitigation measures in Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh and UP, resulting in continuity of access to essential social services for children during emergencies.  In addition, UNICEF provided technical support to state governments in 11 states to design and implement long-term, risk-informed and child-centred disaster risk management plans. This contributed to further strengthened capacities of various social-sectors and disaster risk management institutions and for them to access central Government funds/allocate state government funds for risk-resilience actions benefiting children. For example, the development of a 3-year $ 12 million ‘Drought Mitigation Plan’ in the state of Andhra Pradesh creates the potential for food and nutritional security of children in five drought prone districts.
In response to the impacts of natural hazards on children in 2024, UNICEF supported the government to strengthen systemic preparedness actions to prioritize women's participation and improve child-centred responses, evidenced for example by the provision of Child Friendly Spaces in relief camps in Assam, that benefited an estimated 156,861 children with ECD and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support services. UNICEF, in collaboration with partners, responded to floods and hailstorms in Assam and Northeastern India, and a cyclone in West Bengal, enabled 300,000 people including 57,200 boys and 55,705 girls to benefit from improved access to essential services such as health and WASH services in 2024. 
In 2024, UNICEF supported partners to work more effectively on SBC strategies for children to accelerate results across sectors. In six states, UNICEF supported strengthening of governments evidence-based SBC strategies through collaboration with Behavioural Insight Units and other research partners to better understand behavioural and social barriers and to identify and test innovative approaches and solutions for engagement of parents for improved nutrition and health practices. Across India, UNICEF has carried out SBC capacity building of Faith Based Organisation networks (Mind Heart Dialogue), and of more than 50 universities, as well as of government convergent partners such as National Disaster Reduction Institute and the National Rural Livelihood Mission’s Food, Health, Nutrition and WASH programme which reached around100 million women with SBC activities around parenting practices.  Aiming to further strengthen UNICEF’s gender focused programming, critical partnerships with different women’s rights organisations were initiated to conduct capacity gap assessments, gender leadership trainings, develop gender focused programming tools, and pilot a digital literacy project for girls from marginalised communities. 
To support data driven and evidence-based programming, internally, UNICEF streamlined its planning and quality assurance processes, delivered capacity workshops on systematic reviews, statistical analysis and data visualization, and organized its third Learning-from-Failure Festival, which all contributed to a stronger focus on evidence and learning within programmes. Externally, UNICEF continued to engage with NITI Aayog, Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Ministry of Women and Child Development, and other line ministries as well as select state governments, to support systems strengthening in monitoring, evaluation and data, to enable better decision-making for children based on robust evidence. UNICEF also expanded partnerships with civil society, academia and private sector, including through its second ‘Evidence for Children Roundtable’, which acted as important convening forum to discuss evidence gaps around child inequities.  
In 2024, UNICEF embarked on initiatives such as Procurement Case Manager, which combined planning and tracking of procurement activities, and enhanced the efficiency for timely delivery of goods and services for children and women in India. Efforts for Sustainable Procurement continued, with baseline assessments and a suppliers’ conference to support the future roadmap for sustainable supplies in line with the targets of the SDGs. UNICEF achieved cost savings of $ 1million for the next three years, strengthening operational efficiency and resilience through cloud migration, business automation, network modernization, and enhanced incident management. UNICEF also provided systematic capacity building to its implementing partners on Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers policy and procedures and provided technical support to strengthen the Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse capacity.

UNICEF collaborated closely with various partners including Government, civil society, the UN, private sector and other stakeholders focusing on harnessing value-based partnership to benefit children in India. It is an important programme approach for UNICEF to build and strengthen multifaceted partnerships for sustainable and equitable results for children.
 
In 2024, UNICEF continued to work directly with respective line ministries and departments but also with technical institutions and professional organizations, with the aim to contribute to broader national development results. For example, UNICEF’s partnerships with technical and training institutions such as Dr Syama Prasad Mookerjee National Institute of Water and Sanitation and Tata Institute of Social Sciences (TISS) played a pivotal role in building human resource capacity for water, sanitation, and hygiene sector in the country. Through these collaborations, professional training programmes, including the Post-Graduate Diploma in WASH, continued to empower sanitation sector professionals with essential skills for scaling interventions across India.
 
UNICEF’s partnership with Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) also continues to play an important role in advancing results for children in the country. For example, UNICEF’s collaboration with Pratham and the Language and Learning Foundation (LLF) contributed to improving Foundational Literacy and Numeracy in Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra by refining classroom practices, creating learning materials, and providing teacher training. In the area of ECD, organizations like Vikramshila, Shishu Sarothi, and LLF focused on inclusive and gender-responsive education, with the goal that all young children, regardless of background, have access to quality early education.
 
In 2024, UNICEF also contributed to further bridging public and private sector engagement in the areas of technology for development. Supporting the programme outcomes, UNICEF advocated   for responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) for child rights at national forums, scaling up Digital Public Goods like RapidPro for grassroots system strengthening, and reducing the digital divide through AI-powered multilingual tools. A Technology Landscape Mapping was initiated to leverage India’s robust digital ecosystem, guide programme innovation, and foster a digital culture to integrate cutting-edge solutions across thematic areas. U-Report India received global recognition for its impactful digital engagement and youth-focused initiatives. UNICEF forged a promising agreement with the MoPR that aims to scale U-Report subscriptions to 30 million users, empowering young voices nationwide and enhancing service delivery at the grassroots level. This has helped in better identifying the priorities of women and children in the Gram Panchayat Development Plans. Additionally, a Memorandum of Understanding with the Digital India Bhashini Division leverages AI to bridge linguistic divides, expanding equitable access to multilingual digital services, which enables a tailored approach in communicating key child rights messages to different audiences by enhancing the accessibility to the information.     
 
UNICEF engaged more than 4,000 businesses including 381 public sector undertakings and fostered collaborations with the public and private sector to drive innovative partnerships and support the responsible and sustainable business agenda. In partnership with the Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs (Ministry of corporate Affairs), Ministry of Commerce and Department of Public enterprises, Ministry of Finance, UNICEF integrated the Child Rights and business principles as well as the family friendly policies within business supply chains and provided technical knowledge to public sector undertakings to advance child rights and outcomes for children through their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).    
 
A notable milestone was establishing a partnership with the Confederation of Indian Industry to engage businesses in promoting the Inclusive Early Childhood Development agenda. A large group of businesses linked to children’s products, services came together to reflect on how they would contribute to this agenda and help give every child the best start in life through their core assets, innovative products, CSR and Employees engagement. Additionally, the IMPAct4Nutrition (I4N), a private sector platform to advance Nutrition outcomes for children an India, saw significant growth, mobilizing businesses to support nutrition initiatives in India’s aspirational districts and blocks resulting in over 617 pledged business Partners, reaching 12 million employees and their families and promoting nutrition literacy to 300 million citizens across India. With technical support from the I4N Secretariat, partners integrated nutrition-focused interventions into their CSR initiatives, catalysing INR 440 million ($ 5.2 million) to build healthier, more resilient communities helping to realise the rights of children. 
 
As knowledge partner to the Indian Institute of Corporate Affairs, UNICEF committed to growing responsible and sustainable business value chains which impact children significantly. A key achievement was the integration of family-friendly policies within the tea supply chain in Assam, including putting in place creches, breastfeeding spaces, and enabling breastfeeding breaks. The Ministry of Commerce acknowledged the work being done by UNICEF to improve lives of women and children in tea supply chains. Additionally, UNICEF has also provided technical insights by integrating Child Rights and Business Principles into the sector specific responsible business guidelines, for the ready-made garment industry and the automotive sector to ensure that children’s rights are always well covered in business value chains and industries are guided toward adopting more child-centred and child-friendly policies. This is to prevent any form of child labour and to also proactively create spaces which enable parents to care for their children and protect their rights.

Capitalizing on the learning from 2023, the UNICEF India Country Office conducted a Programme Review in 2024 reflecting the changing programme environment, the results achieved so far against the Country Programme, and areas of improvement to reposition UNICEF’s programmes toward catalysing greater impact for children in India. 
 
Capitalizing on the learning from 2023, the UNICEF India Country Office conducted a Programme Review in 2024 reflecting the changing programme environment, the results achieved so far against the Country Programme, and areas of improvement to reposition UNICEF’s programmes in India toward catalysing greater impact for children in India. 
 
Looking toward 2035, India’s trajectory suggests continued economic growth and development; however, this will likely coexist with challenges such as persistent inequities, skill gaps, protection concerns, and the triple burden of malnutrition, as well as newer challenges related to climate change, digital technologies and demographic shifts. Analysis of India’s economic and social indicators led UNICEF to sharpen its focus on the context specific equity challenges and support the government and other partners to fulfil its role as duty bearers for child rights. 
 
Through the Programme Review process, UNICEF reaffirmed that the Country Programme Document 2023-2027   remains relevant in the changing programming environment. However, the office concluded there is a need to shift the way of working, to accelerate programming focusing on equity and gender issues, enhance internal and external efforts to converge different sectoral programmes and strategies, and focus on programming at scale by strengthening partnerships, to ultimately maximize impact for children. As a result, the 2024 Programme Review refined UNICEF’s priority programme areas and further defined the need for differentiated strategies and geographic presence to address context specific equity issues to achieve results for every child.
 
As India evolves, UNICEF’s role also evolves. The review reiterated UNICEF purpose and unique role to ‘convene, catalyse, and converge’ partners and their programmes for child rights. UNICEF accelerate its work bringing different stakeholders to co-create solutions (Convene), ensure there is multisectoral action in alignment for maximum impact for children (Converge) and drive innovation and scaling up successful interventions (Catalyse). 

India’s diversity, size and political decentralized system demands a differentiated approach to programming this is driven by the difference in the government, civil society, private sector’s capacities, on the one hand, and the severity of deprivation across geographical areas in India. To enhance UNICEF programme and operational effectiveness and efficiency to better support child rights in India, UNICEF’s presence at the sub-national level, through Field Offices, continues to be essential by accelerating differentiated programming strategies and implementation modalities.

UNICEF continues to recalibrate the nature and scope of its technical support. Key lessons learned from the Review and revised strategies to address challenges identified last two years of implementation will be operationalized through rolling work plan 2025-2027. Through strategic partnerships with the government and private entities, UNICEF ensures resources are directed where they can create the most significant and sustainable impact for children. Our approach in directing finances for the protection and promotion of child rights will continue.

Furthermore, UNICEF India aims to enhance operational efficiency through cost optimization, enhanced risk management, and supply chain management. Cost-efficiency measures will focus on process optimization, strategic resource management, shared operational services, and sustainable procurement. Risk management will involve enhanced enterprise risk frameworks, data-driven decision-making, enhanced fraud prevention, crisis preparedness, and cybersecurity enhancements. Supply chain improvements will include supplier diversification, eco-friendly and sustainable procurement, and leveraging on local Indian market capacity. These strategies, integrating digital innovations and strategic partnerships, will ensure sustainable, high-impact programs for children.  

This strategic review marks a new chapter for UNICEF India, as it moved forward. By aligning resources, strategies, and partnerships with the evolving needs of India’s children, UNICEF reaffirms its commitment to children’s rights and well-being. With a focus on impact, sustainability, and equity, UNICEF is poised to lead the way in addressing the challenges and opportunities of a changing India—ensuring that no child is left behind.

The Republic of Maldives is a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) located in the Indian Ocean. The country is the most geographically dispersed in the world, and is made up of over 1,190 islands, of which 187 are inhabited. Maldives is 100 percent Muslim by Constitution and the least populous country in Asia. As per the Census 2022, Maldives has a total population of 515,132, with a child population of 119,159, i.e., 23% of the total population. The total fertility rate is 1.7 percent, which is below population replacement-level. It also showed that over a quarter of the population i.e., 132,493 out of 515,132 are resident foreigners. Most Maldivians migrate to Malé for better education and health services (20%) and to take up new jobs (19%). Others migrate to live with family or due to marriage.
Economic Overview: In 2024, the Maldives economy continued to grow, driven primarily by the tourism sector, which remains the cornerstone of the nation's economy. The country saw a growth rate of 9.8% in the first quarter of 2024, with tourist arrivals projected to reach a historic high of 2 million by the end of the year[1]. However, the decline in spending per tourist has moderated the overall economic impact[1]. 
Despite the economic growth, the Maldives faces substantial economic challenges, including a high fiscal deficit, increasing public debt, and vulnerabilities due to external economic shocks. Public debt has risen to 122.8% of GDP, driven by high levels of government spending and reliance on external non-concessional financing for infrastructure projects[1]. The government has proposed a fiscal reform agenda to address these issues, including a transition from universal to targeted subsidies and improving efficiency in health spending [2]. However, the implementation of these reforms has not been rolled out as per the timelines proposed, and the country continues to face significant fiscal and external vulnerabilities[2]. Inflation remained low at 0.5% in the first half of 2024, but food prices surged to 6.7%, affecting the cost of living, especially lower-income households[1]. In 2024, credit rating agencies have revised their assessments, increasing the country’s risk level. These adjustments reflect heightened concerns regarding economic stability, fiscal management, and external vulnerabilities.
Climate and Environmental Challenges: The Maldives, a low-lying island state, is highly vulnerable to climate change, with rising sea levels, slow onset erosion and coral reef degradation posing severe threats to its economy, environment, and livelihoods. The World Bank projects that in a worst-case scenario, these environmental challenges could reduce the Maldives' GDP by 11 percentage points by 2050[2]. Investments in climate adaptation and renewable energy are critical to mitigating these impacts and ensuring long-term sustainability.
Context for Children in the Maldives
The Maldives has made remarkable progress in advancing the rights and wellbeing of children, achieving universal access to health, primary, and lower secondary education, and maintaining low maternal and child mortality rates. However, the country faces second generation challenges related to sustainable financing of social services, child vulnerabilities, inequalities, especially for children with disability, and the impacts of climate change on children.
Malé is now one of the world’s most densely populated cities where 41% of the total population is concentrated in the Greater Malé Area. The country’s geographical dispersion and uneven population distribution poses challenges in the provision of equitable education, health, and social services for every child.
Health and Nutrition: The Maldives has a robust healthcare system with universal access to health services, with a life expectancy at birth at 82 years. The country has made significant strides in early childhood development and immunization but is experiencing a health transition associated with an increasing burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and rising rates of childhood overweight and obesity[3]. There is also a need to strengthen community engagement, health promotion and mental health support, particularly in areas where cultural stigma persists[3].
Education: While the Maldives has achieved high enrolment rates in primary and lower secondary education, the transition from lower to upper secondary remains a challenge, with over 21% of young people not in education, employment, or training[3]. The education system faces bottlenecks related to inclusion, quality of teaching, infrastructure, and the need for multiple learning pathways in formal education. The government, with support from UNICEF and other partners, is working on an education transformation agenda “THAIBA”, prioritizing inclusive education, digital learning, and the integration of mental health and wellbeing into schools.
Child Protection: Violence against children and the exploitation of children into crime are significant concerns. The Maldives has a strong legislative framework guided by the Child Rights Protection Act (CRPA) and the Juvenile Justice Act (JJA), but implementation and multi-sectoral collaboration for the protection of children and adolescents remain critical challenges[3]. UNICEF continues to advocate for the retention of the Minimum Age of Criminal Responsibility (MACR) at 15 years and works with local councils and community groups to strengthen child protection systems[3].
Social Protection: Maldives has a generous but hard to sustain social protection programme comprising 13 interventions in the benefit package. These include universal subsidies on food, fuel, electricity, water and sewage, universal health insurance (Aasandha), pensions, and allowances for disability, single parents, and foster parents. The government has progressively started an economic reform that seeks to transition the social protection package from universal subsidies to targeted subsidies. 
Climate Change and Children: The impacts of climate change pose a significant threat to the wellbeing of children in the Maldives. Extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and shoreline erosion can disrupt essential services such as healthcare, education, and protection. UNICEF is working with the government and other partners to integrate child-friendly principles into climate adaptation strategies and ensure that children's needs are prioritized in the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0) and the National Development Plan (NDP)[3].
Youth: Youth in the Maldives face several challenges, including high unemployment rates, limited access to housing and quality education, and mental health issues. Additionally, the high cost of living and housing pressures contribute to economic instability. These factors, combined with limited recreational opportunities, can lead to social vulnerabilities and increased risk of substance abuse.
Future Directions: As the Maldives approaches the 2030 deadline for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), there is a renewed focus on addressing the second-generation issues affecting children. This includes sustaining basic services, and addressing the adolescent challenge, disability inclusion, transition to upper secondary, rising NCDs burden including mental health, child protection, the challenges in parenting, and the impacts of climate change on children. The ongoing development of a long-term NDP by the Government provides an opportunity to integrate these priorities and ensure that all children, especially the most vulnerable, have a fair chance to reach their full potential[3].

UNICEF Maldives is currently in its third year of its Country Programme Document (CPD), during which it has developed and implemented in partnership with the government and other stakeholders, programmes to address the issues facing children in the changing context of the country. The following is an overview of the main achievements in 2024. 
Health System Strengthening: UNICEF Maldives prioritized immunization, sustaining high coverage levels across the Maldives. The Office supported government vaccination campaigns and prepared for the introduction of the PCV and Rotavirus vaccines in 2025. A workshop in early 2024 addressed vaccine misinformation, equipping healthcare professionals and school health officers with tools to build vaccine confidence. The “Humanly Possible” campaign during World Immunization Week, was organized in collaboration with the Health Protection Agency (HPA), to raise awareness on the importance of timely vaccinations.
UNICEF continued advocating for health sector reforms guided by Primary Health Care (PHC) principles. Technical assistance provided to the Ministry of Health (MoH) was pivotal in enacting the Food Act and amending the Health Service Act to include preventive health and a ban on vape. UNICEF also contributed to consultations on the draft Mental Health Bill, addressing gaps in mental health legislation to make it children and adolescent friendly.
A key milestone was the preparation for the establishment of an oxygen plant to improve healthcare infrastructure at the sub-national level, complemented by training sessions on integrated oxygen systems for health professionals. UNICEF’s commitment to health security included participation in outbreak response coordination, risk communication, and vaccine logistics management, including COVID-19 vaccine rollout support.
UNICEF advanced mental health awareness and stigma reduction through “Kihineh?” the Mental Health and Substance Abuse Flagship, reaching thousands of children and young people and generating demand for the National Mental Health Helpline. Wellbeing Hangouts provided safe spaces for 5,916 adolescents and young people to engage in conversation on mental health, in schools and in the communities. UNICEF trained 1,239 teachers and school counselors to deliver mental wellbeing sessions under the Helping Adolescents Thrive (HAT) programme in 31 schools. Additionally, 20 mental health professionals from the National Centre for Mental Health (NCMH) were trained in group facilitation techniques to enhance mental health services for children, adolescents, and their families. UNICEF also developed a network of 20 trained volunteers to foster community-based mental health support and promote social engagement and recovery for young adults. With NCMH, UNICEF developed and launched two resources—the "Resilient Friends" storybook and the "Parents and Carer Edition" card pack—focused on emotions and challenges faced by young children (4 - 10 years).
Food, Nutrition, and Health Promotion System: UNICEF Maldives has been promoting nutrition and healthy lifestyles, particularly for children aged 6 to 23 months, and addressing the double burden of malnutrition in children. Advocacy and training on breastfeeding and infant and young child feeding (IYCF) enhanced healthcare professionals’ capacity to provide expert support. A notable achievement was the improvement of health care providers’ skills in breastfeeding counseling through a 3-day workshop co-organized with HPA and the Reproductive Health Center of Indira Gandhi Memorial Hospital (IGMH).
UNICEF, in partnership with the MoH, HPA, and the NGO Advocating the Rights of Children (ARC), launched the “Minheyo Kaanaa” a recipe book for parents, offering practical nutrition guidance for the first 1,000 days of a child’s life. These programmes are expected to improve responsive feeding, reduce micronutrient deficiencies, and enhance dietary diversity among young children.
In 2024, UNICEF forged new partnerships to promote healthier lifestyles for children. A total of 28 swimming coaches were trained on integrating health, nutrition, and mental wellbeing messages into swim training sessions. The 3rd National Health and Nutrition Roundtable, organized with key partners, discussed policies for sustainable health practices. UNICEF also organized the World Cancer Day Run to raise awareness on healthy lifestyles and supported advocacy and communication addressing smoking and vaping, advocating for “smoke-free” spaces and increased cigarette taxes. Following the amendment to the Tobacco Control Law including a ban on vapes, UNICEF and HPA convened stakeholders to deliberate on enforcement aspects of the legislation, towards creating a tobacco free environment for children and young people.
Education System: UNICEF Maldives has been pivotal in advancing the Maldives' education transformation agenda, THAIBA, by successfully mobilizing USD 6.5 million from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to support the initiative, which emphasizes equity and inclusion. This agenda aims to reach a total of 10,000 teachers and 81,000 students across the country, including 6,600 students with disabilities. Additionally, in partnership with Google for Education and the Ministry of Education (MoE), UNICEF launched the TechPath initiative to improve access to quality education through a digitally enabled learning ecosystem. By the end of the 2025 academic year, this initiative aims to initially reach 1,500 students across 15 schools, equipping them with 808 Chromebooks, 90 Micro:bits, and enhanced teaching capacities in using Google Workspace, Chromebooks, and computational thinking and coding. 
UNICEF mobilized a total of 369 young people (197 females and 172 males) by creating impactful platforms to amplify their voices on issues like climate change, youth development, and gender equality. Through innovative programmes such as UPSHIFT and ImaGen Ventures, the office promoted design-thinking and 21st century skills, emphasizing employability and inclusive youth engagement. Central to these efforts is the Youth Reference Group (YRG), which currently comprises 23 young people (8 male, 15 female) from across the country that contribute substantively to UNICEF’s programming as well as participate in national, regional, and international programmes.
UNICEF’s experience highlights the importance of integrating innovative programmes into existing school systems. However, rapid urbanization has strained schools in the Greater Malé Area with overcrowding and teacher shortages, while smaller island schools face neglect due to declining student numbers. These disparities hinder equitable learning, particularly for vulnerable groups. Reduced domestic financing underscores the need for multi-sectoral collaboration and private sector partnerships to sustain progress and align education with industry needs for smoother school-to-work transitions.
Collaborating with local NGOs and youth-led organizations has proven effective, emphasizing the need for more approachable and youth-friendly strategies. These lessons and challenges guide UNICEF’s integrated approach to learning, protection, and participation, laying the foundation for a resilient and inclusive education system in the Maldives, where every child and young person can reach their full potential.
Child Protection System: In 2024, significant strides were made in advancing child rights and protection. A key accomplishment was the endorsement of the National Action Plan on Prevention and Response to Violence Against Children (NAP-PRVaC) in September 2024, aiming for a coordinated, multi-sectoral approach. 
UNICEF’s collaboration with the Children’s Ombudsperson’s Office (COO) advanced child rights education and participation. Key initiatives included the 2nd Child Rights Symposium – Vuna, focusing on strengthening the juvenile justice system, Kudhinge Rauyu Forum, and awareness sessions for teachers and parents across island communities. 
UNICEF, in partnership with the Maldives Police Service (MPS) and MoE, organized activities for National and World Children’s Day, engaging hundreds of children. The nationwide photo exhibition "Kudhin Bunanee: Maldives Through Children’s Eyes", showcased children’s perspectives on various issues.
Community-based protection mechanisms included strengthening existing IBAMA groups, developing a prevention programme targeting children in conflict with the law in Fuvahmulah and Hulhumalé Phase 2, and a Training of Trainers programme conducted for 16 staff of the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSFD).
Despite these achievements, the development and endorsement of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for referrals between social services, justice, and health services remain incomplete. While sectoral SOPs have been developed and aligned with CRPA and JJA, the multi-sectoral SOP is still pending, underscoring the need for stronger coordination.
Environment and Climate Response System: In 2024, UNICEF Maldives advanced the contextualization and implementation of the UNICEF Sustainability and Climate Action Plan through the Climate Resilient Actions Flagship. A key achievement was activating 282 Climate Guardians across 7 islands, enabling youth to engage in climate action and represent the Maldives at international forums like COP29. The Youth Track to COP29 introduced 26 young participants to climate diplomacy through mock COP negotiations and engagement with policymakers. It concluded with development of recommendations to national and global leaders and 3 youth representatives being supported to attend COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan.
UNICEF MCO also planted over 230 trees and organized beach clean-ups which included educating young people on waste segregation and environmental stewardship. These actions organized as part of ‘Kudhinnaa Gaathun’ missions, demonstrated a commitment to fostering climate resilience and enhancing environmental awareness.
With support from ROSA, for disaster risk reduction (DRR) and emergency preparedness, MCO prepared a contingency plan for an economic crisis, including different scenarios and sectoral responses. 
UNICEF is also partnering with the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and Maldives Red Crescent (MRC) to establish Community Emergency Response Teams (CERTs) across the 10 Kudhinnaa Gaathun islands connecting with the Climate Guardians initiative.
Social Policy and Social Protection System: UNICEF MCO, in collaboration with local island councils, developed 10 comprehensive Island Workplans for 2025, focusing on child-friendly and climate-resilient governance. This initiative addresses child rights and environmental sustainability in islands.
UNICEF MCO, with the Maldives Bureau of Statistics (MBS), completed and launched a child analysis report using Census 2022 data, providing a foundation for action plans in education, disability, employment, and child protection. This was enhanced by a Social Protection Budget Analysis, in partnership with the Ministry of Finance (MoF). With support from ROSA, a tool to identify the impacts of different scenarios of social protection subsidies was developed and presented to MoF and the World Bank. These analytical products aim to support informed decision-making in providing and protecting social services to children and families. Additionally, 187 island profiles were developed, and 16 government officials were trained in data analysis to enhance evidence-based policymaking.
UNICEF is also supporting MSFD in establishing a comprehensive Vulnerability Information Management System which is essential for tracking and supporting vulnerable populations. This system aims to ensure that no child is left behind, particularly those with disabilities and complex learning profiles. The system is currently in its pilot phase and will help identify and track vulnerable populations across the country. A disability registry with over 13,000 beneficiaries was also developed with UNICEF support to ensure coverage by social protection schemes.
UNICEF strengthened its partnership with the MoF, MSFD, and National Social Protection Agency (NSPA) to advocate for and ensure inclusive social protection reforms amid the ongoing economic reforms. This includes social protection budget analysis to inform social protection reforms.
Four policy dialogues were conducted with various stakeholders, covering child welfare, population dynamics, social protection, and the economic situation of the Maldives. UNICEF also engaged with MBS to bridge data gaps, especially in SDGs and child indicators.
The Government of Maldives (GoM) announced the development of a long-term NDP in October 2024. UNICEF MCO is working with the Ministry of Housing, Land, and Urban Development (MoHLUD) to ensure the plan is child- and youth- sensitive, accounts for their needs and includes their voices. 
Programme Convergence and Equity: UNICEF Maldives enhanced programme convergence through the Kudhinnaa Gaathun initiative, integrating child-focused priorities into workplans across 10 islands. The Kudhinnaa Gaathun Forum facilitated collaboration among city and island leaders as well as agencies at the central level. Nine islands now implement at least 3 flagship programmes, with long-term child-friendly development plans being developed in R. Meedhoo and V. Felidhoo. 
The Adolescent Girls Action Plan and the Collective Impact Platform for Adolescent Girls were launched in October 2024 to enhance coordination. Training in disability inclusion was provided to 55 participants (including UNICEF staff and government and civil society partners) through the CBM Global Disability Inclusion Group. UNICEF supported vulnerable populations through the Nikamethi Naazuku Kudhin initiative, with plans to expand Baaruveri, Climate Resilient Actions, Kihineh?, Kaigen Hin’gamaa, and Beleniveriyaa Flagship Programmes in 2025.
