Communications, Advocacy, Resource Mobilization, and Partnerships: In 2024, UNICEF Maldives implemented the annual Communications and Advocacy Plan, achieving significant milestones in digital engagement, traditional media outreach, advocacy efforts, and partnerships. Social media amplification of children and youth voices, programmatic achievements and initiatives resulted in significant improvement in engagement, reaching 250,000 people. Key content included co-creation with Climate Guardians, working with girls from different backgrounds for the International Day of the Girl (IDG), and other youth-led campaigns. Partnerships with local media and the South Asia Media Hub increased visibility of flagship programmes like Baaruveri, Beleniveriyaa, and Kihineh?. High-profile interviews with international media such as Channel News Asia (CNA) and Associated Press (AP) highlighted climate advocacy, while young people participated in regional media and advocacy trainings. 
UNICEF Maldives hosted and leveraged visits by Regional Director Sanjay Wijesekera and Deputy Executive Director Hannan Sulieman for high-level advocacy, focusing on retaining the MACR at 15 years, strengthening the juvenile justice system and child- and youth- sensitive long-term NDP. Youth-led advocacy remained a priority, with over 20 young people trained in advocacy and participation. UNICEF secured $6.5 million through GPE and additional funding for digital learning, climate resilience, and mental health initiatives. Private sector collaborations included child safeguarding training for tourism operators and the Ooredoo Maldives Fun Run, engaging over 2,200 children. World Children’s Day events also engaged children and young people in activities promoting a safe and sustainable future for every child.
Social and Behavior Change: In 2024, UNICEF Maldives prioritized Social and Behavior Change (SBC) initiatives, launching the Social and Community Listening (SCL) system to monitor public sentiment and identify awareness gaps. Monthly reports informed data-driven improvements to programming. UNICEF strategized the engagement with key influencers to promote child rights. As such, 32 healthcare workers were trained for national vaccination campaigns. An anti-bullying programme was piloted and integrated into the MoE’s 2025 workplan. Mental health initiatives included a radio drama series and demand generation for the school mental health helpline. Environmental advocacy through the CLEAN initiative engaged 55 students and reached over 10,313 people with environmental messages. The “Beleniveriyaa” Positive Parenting Flagship trained 161 facilitators, engaged with 5,589 parents through sessions and events, and had a cumulative reach of 208,572 through social media content. The “Play Power” toolkit promoted learning through play. UNICEF is also supporting the government to identify gaps in addressing early identification of disabilities.
Managing for Results: UNICEF Maldives improved its planning, monitoring, and financial management to enhance programme implementation and achieve key results. Annual and mid-year planning and reviews involved implementing partners at political and technical levels, boosting their capacity alongside the UNICEF team. Monthly planning and quarterly budget reviews (later shifted to monthly) strengthened internal processes, while regular monitoring improved KPIs, raising the scorecard average from 0.78 in 2023 to 0.93 in 2024. HACT assurance was advanced through capacity-building programmes and including orientation on global updates to the FACE Form. Engagement with CSOs was expanded through Open Calls and Direct Selections. MCO strengthened PSEA capacity for staff and CSOs, conducted timely programmatic visits using the new Field Monitoring Module (FMM) in eTools, and supported financial oversight through Spot Check Visits and the audit for implementing partners. 
Governance and Systems: UNICEF Maldives enhanced its governance and operational frameworks to ensure effective programme delivery and risk management. The 2024 Annual Management Plan (AMP) focused on quality assurance, financial management, people management, alliance building, and fostering a positive workplace culture.
Administration, Finance, and Supply: UNICEF Maldives strengthened the partnership between Operations and Programmes, maintaining an efficient financial management system that supports programme delivery. The office followed standard policies and procedures for procurement and finance, whilst ensuring proper documentation. Administrative support provided by the Operations Team includes travel management, onboarding new staff, office cleanliness, and security.
Human Resources: In 2024, UNICEF Maldives expanded its team to 31 members, including new TA positions, interns, UNVs, one JPO and consultants. Despite challenges in adhering to timelines to meet the 60-days KPI in recruitment, the office achieved 100% completion of Performance Planning for 2024. Staff development saw significant progress, with high implementation rates of the Country Office learning plan and successful completion of key training programmes. Engagement programmes, such as a staff retreats and Design Thinking workshop, and Front-Line Workers Training on Disability inclusion including all staff were organized by the office to foster a supportive learning environment.
Accessibility and Greening: The Greening Committee, formed in May 2024, has made significant progress in environmental sustainability. Initiatives include eliminating single-use plastics and implementing smart meters and smart AC and lighting systems. The Accessibility and Greening Committee’s efforts in awareness, advocacy, and practical sustainability measures have laid a strong foundation for achieving a net-zero climate footprint and promoting a culture of sustainability among staff and stakeholders.

In 2024, UNICEF Maldives strengthened its strategic partnerships across various government partners, local councils, CSOs, international development partners, and other UN agencies to advance child-focused initiatives. 
UNICEF's partnership with Google for Education and MoE contributed to the development of a comprehensive digital learning programme “TechPath” and procurement of Chromebooks for 15 schools at discounted prices. This is also part of the broader “THAIBA” education transformation agenda, supported by GPE, which exemplified the power of partnerships in driving systemic change, with UNICEF playing a pivotal technical role. Partnership with the Maldives National University (MNU) was initiated to conduct a study on Education Transition to inform implementation of THAIBA.
The partnerships with MoE facilitated the integration of mental health into schools, training teachers and counselors, and conducting Wellbeing Hangouts for the rollout of HAT in schools. Wellbeing Hangouts in the community were conducted through partnerships with NGOs such as Society for Health Education (SHE) and Mental Health Awareness Foundation (MHAF). UNICEF and WHO continued the Joint Programme on Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Psychosocial Wellbeing, and Development to hold consultations on the draft Mental Health Bill and to develop a multisectoral referral pathway. The partnership with MoH improved health systems, supported immunization programmes, and planned for the establishment of an oxygen plant, and contributed to the National Mental Health Helpline and implementing the mental health “Kihineh?” communication strategy and campaign. 
UNICEF also partnered with the telecommunications company Ooredoo for the 2024 Fun Run focusing on promoting mental health. The partnership with ARC developed the “Minheyo Kaanaa” nutrition guidebook for parents. Engagement with the Faculty of Health Sciences at MNU is being strengthened to equip future counselors and public health officers with essential knowledge and skills to prepare them to tackle potential challenges and engage effectively with the public. New partnerships included the Ministry of Sports, Fitness, and Recreation (MSFR), promoting health through physical activity as part of the implementation of “Kaigen Hin’gamaa”.
UNICEF collaborated with 12 government institutions and local councils of 10 KG islands and other islands for the Child Protection (CP) Programme, ensuring interventions reached the most vulnerable children and families. Partnerships with independent child rights and human rights institutions (COO and Human Rights Commission of the Maldives (HRCM)) promoted child rights education and monitored the rollout of CRC and related national legislation. 
Collaborations with CSOs, media, and international institutions bolstered advocacy efforts to retain the MACR at 15 years. Additionally, partnerships with Maldives Police Service, businesses, resort chains, and local guesthouses were crucial in expanding the Child Safe Tourism initiative. These partnerships were vital for reaching marginalized communities and enhancing child protection efforts.
Local partnerships were expanded through the Kudhinnaa Gaathun initiative, integrating UNICEF programmes into City/Island Councils’ workplans. Partnerships with youth-led online platform Sosal and news service The Edition were enhanced to promote positive parenting, mental health, and youth-led climate action. Key government partnerships that continued included MoE, MPS, and ARC, which co-hosted World Children’s Day events. 
The partnerships with the Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy (MoCCEE), and the Special Envoy for Climate Change at the President’s Office, and the Embassy of Japan were leveraged to co-organize the Youth Track for COP29. A new partnership with Islamic Relief Australia and UNICEF Australia also unlocked funding for climate-resilience building initiatives.
UNICEF also collaborated with MBS and NSPA to build national statistics systems and social protection, and with the Local Government Authority (LGA) and Ministry of Cities, Local Government and Public Works (MCLGPW) to create child and climate-friendly development plans. A Collective Impact Platform for Adolescent Girls was established with MSFD and other government, civil society, and private sector partners, fostering multi-sectoral support.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Lessons learned and challenges
The rollout of the Kudhinnaa Gaathun initiative demonstrated the value of actively involving island councils in UNICEF work, which led to stronger integration of child-focused priorities into local governance and workplans, ensuring children’s needs remain central to island development. A lesson learnt was that better planning and coordination within the office and with partners were essential for successful implementation of this initiative. Consistent coordination with key Government stakeholders ensured that programmes, such as immunization campaigns, mental health initiatives, education transformation efforts, parenting, and the work to strengthen child protection systems were aligned with national priorities.
The child-analysis of the Census 2022 and training of government officials in data analysis enhanced evidence-based policy making and supported informed policies and decision making across education, disability, and child protection. Developing a Vulnerability Information Management System has proven to be crucial for tracking vulnerable populations. Engaging stakeholders in policy dialogues ensured inclusive policies. 
Innovative approaches included engaging school environment clubs in the CLEAN initiative through assessments and interactive activities that informed ecosystem-focused programming. However, challenges persist in implementing climate-resilient solutions, especially for islands, schools, and health facilities. As such, delays in projects like solarizing cold storage facilities highlight capacity and resource limitations.
Strong leadership, both within UNICEF and through partnerships with government agencies, was crucial in driving reform and achieving positive outcomes. Leadership in policy advocacy, particularly in influencing the Food Act and vaping ban was vital for policy shifts and the development of health-promoting legislation. UNICEF leveraged its convening power to bring relevant stakeholders to one table to develop and rollout a targeted, multi-sectoral programme to address the issue of children in conflict with the law, in addition to its policy advocacy on retaining the minimum age of criminal responsibility. Additionally, continuing high-level advocacy to ensure the long-term NDP and the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 are child- and youth- sensitive will remain a priority in 2025. 
Successful implementation relied heavily on strong, strategic partnerships. Collaborating with MoE for mental health training and with HPA for immunization campaigns helped extend UNICEF’s reach. Internal leadership was crucial for driving initiatives across multiple sections and the integration of “Kaigen Hin’gamaa” and “Kihineh?” Flagships within Kudhinnaa Gaathun.
Robust governance and operational frameworks were essential for effective programme delivery and risk management, focusing on quality assurance, financial management, and people management to foster a positive workplace culture and strong alliances. The integration of Operations and Programmes underscored the importance of a responsive financial management system, adherence to standard procurement policies, and comprehensive documentation for transparency and accountability. 
Efficient administrative support, including travel management and office security, was crucial for maintaining operational efficiency. Human Resources development was emphasized through team expansion and achieving 100% completion of performance planning and mandatory courses, with engagement programmes fostering a supportive and growth-oriented environment. The formation of the Greening Committee and implementation of sustainability initiatives, such as eliminating single-use plastics and using smart meters, underscored the importance of environmental sustainability. These efforts laid a strong foundation for achieving a net-zero climate footprint and promoting a culture of sustainability among staff and stakeholders.
Access to specialized health services, particularly in remote and island communities, continues to be a barrier to reaching all children. The primary healthcare revitalization agenda, while recognized as important by the Government, faces challenges in implementation and stewardship, particularly in improving preventive health and community engagement. There is a need to strengthen community engagement in health promotion and mental health support initiatives, particularly in areas where cultural stigma around mental health persists. There is also a continuing challenge in addressing vaccine misinformation, particularly on social media, which can undermine public trust in immunization efforts. 
Significant staff shortages were also a major constraint to implementation. Despite the success of initiatives like the Wellbeing Hangouts, engaging young people in mental health and health promotion programmes remained challenging. There were difficulties in overcoming cultural barriers and convincing youth to actively participate in Wellbeing Hangouts. 
A lack of comprehensive data and evidence posed challenges in effectively measuring impact and tailoring interventions. Insufficient data on mental health prevalence and health outcomes made it difficult to assess programme success and identify areas for improvement. Strategizing and enhancing capacity and mutual accountability within the team is critical to keep momentum in driving the key agendas and unfinished business. 
Resource constraints in multimedia and digital content creation highlighted the need for increased capacity to meet programmatic and communication demands. Inclusivity in communication remains a priority, with adherence to disability-inclusive guidelines for video content and plans to expand the use of Dhivehi to better engage local audiences. Managing negative sentiments on social media, particularly related to global events, required strategic monitoring and proactive communication, which successfully reduced backlash. 
Challenges in partnerships and resource mobilization included complex processes, limited capacity, and perceptions of UNICEF as a donor rather than a partner. Despite these hurdles, engagement with National Committees improved, and opportunities to strengthen partnerships, especially with the private sector, were identified. Advocacy efforts faced difficulties due to policy changes and establishing new relationships with government stakeholders. 
Working with young sports personalities underscored the need for formal orientation on UNICEF’s principles, brand guidelines, and collaboration benefits. Thus, developing a structured orientation package accessible online, targeted for Friends of UNICEF is identified as being crucial for alignment when engaging with them. Additionally, a design thinking workshop for staff and partners equipped them with tools to enhance programmatic convergence and serve vulnerable populations effectively. 
Future Outlook
Looking forward, five priority areas are identified: i) addressing the adolescent challenge associated with low transition from lower to upper secondary school, youth engagement and violence and exploitation of children and adolescents; ii) positive parenting and children in preschool; iii) inclusion focusing on gender, disability, and vulnerable children and youth; iv) strengthening PHC service delivery to respond to rising NCD burden and mental health, and v) financing and sustaining social protection, education and health services in the context of the Maldives' economic reforms. UNICEF MCO will also advocate for and support the Government to develop and make the NDP and NDC 3.0 child sensitive.

In 2024, Nepal demonstrated resilience amidst a challenging global environment marred by conflicts and crises. The economy rebounded with the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth accelerating to 3.9 per cent, up from 2 per cent the previous year, driven by robust remittance inflows, revived tourism, and growing hydropower export. The fiscal deficit dropped to a seven-year low of 2.6 per cent of GDP, due to reduced public expenditure. 
 
Nepal’s third Voluntary National Review (VNR), published in June, highlighted 58.6 per cent progress toward achievement of midterm targets of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Significant strides were reported in SDG 1 (poverty reduction), SDG 4 (quality education), SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) and SDG 11 (sustainable cities and communities). Key contributors included comprehensive social security systems, school enrolment campaigns and student retention policies supported by scholarship schemes and mid-day meals, targeted support for marginalized and disadvantaged communities, as well as improved housing and enforcement of building standards.
 
Nepal intensified its climate efforts with bold steps to finalize the next set of climate commitments including the Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) 3.0 and presented its climate ambition and agenda at the 29th Conference of the Parties (COP). Importantly, the government made solid progress to incorporate more child-sensitive commitments and engage social sectors in the NDC 3.0. The government also endorsed a landmark transitional justice amendment, advancing truth, justice, and reparations for conflict victims.
 
In May, Nepal approved the 16th Five-year Periodic Plan focusing on good governance, social justice, economic prosperity, and human capital development, which impact the comprehensive wellbeing of children and women. The Green, Resilient and Inclusive Development (GRID) Strategic Action Plan (2024-2034) was also adopted, an important milestone for children, as it lays the foundation for a more sustainable and secure future for the upcoming generation. The operationalization of the GRID strategic plan requires over US$10 billion external financing over 10 years to bolster climate adaptation, resilience, and disaster risk management. 
 
Nevertheless, political instability, with frequent changes in governments and policies, continued to hinder governance. In July, the two largest parties formed a coalition with an agreement to alternate the Premiership until the 2027 elections. However, the frequent changes in leadership at federal and provincial levels disrupted policymaking for children and women. Nepal continued to grapple with several governance issues including, limited capacities at the subnational level, inefficient public finance and procurement systems, and delays in filling critical positions. To address these, the Ministry of Federal Affairs and General Administration endorsed the second phase of the Provincial and Local Governance Support Programme (PLGSP), aiming to strengthen institutional, organizational, and individual capacities.
 
Despite accelerated economic growth, Nepal continued to face significant financing gaps for development. Tax revenues declined from 20 to 16 per cent of GDP, reflecting weakened purchasing power and reduced imports. Public debt increased from 40.7 to 42.7 per cent. Accordingly, fiscal space is expected to shrink, disproportionately affecting social sectors, particularly gender equality. As Nepal approaches graduation from Least Developed Country (LDC) status in 2026, it faces stringent borrowing terms, reduced concessional financing, higher interest rates, shorter repayment periods, thereby increasing borrowing costs. 
Social sector allocations reached US$4 billion, doubling over seven years. Notably, social protection allocations increased by 14 per cent compared to last year, driven by increased social security allowances for the elderly. Education allocations increased modestly by 2.5 per cent compared to last year. However, the health sector allocation declined by 19 per cent, marking the third consecutive year of reductions. Overall, the health and education sector allocation has been consistently inadequate in recent years, with low utilization of the allocated funds. 

Social sector budget utilization remained suboptimal, with only 85 per cent of the allocated budget spent in the fiscal year 2023-24, down from 89 per cent utilization in the fiscal year 2022-23. Limited government capacity, especially at the subnational levels, continued to hinder effective fund utilization. This has had significant impact on Nepal’s progress towards achieving the SDGs, particularly those related to children, such as SDG 1 (poverty reduction), SDG 2 (zero hunger), SDG 3 (good health and well-being), SDG 4 (quality education), SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation).

Nepal’s vulnerability to climate-induced disasters remained evident with over 80 per cent of the population exposed to hazards like floods, droughts, landslides, avalanches, and extreme temperatures. The rise in the temperature led to outbreaks of vector-borne diseases like dengue to spread in higher altitudes in recent years. In 2024, Nepal reported around 35,000 dengue cases across 76 of 77 districts. The monsoon severely impacted Koshi, Madhesh and Bagmati provinces, with 250 fatalities, (including 60 children), 18 missing persons and 178 injuries. Approximately 3,000 homes, 100 kilometres of roads and 50 bridges were damaged or destroyed, resulting in economic losses exceeding US$340 million. The disaster also disrupted social sector implementation. In 2024, a total 7,933 hazard-related incidents, including floods, landslides, heavy rainfall, lightning, fire (house and forest), caused 738 deaths, of which 305 were female. 
 
Nepal’s Gender Gap Index score improved slightly from 0.659 in 2023 to 0.664 in 2024, but its global ranking dropped from 116th to 117th. Gender disparities persist, with female labour force participation at 28.7 per cent compared to 53.9 per cent for males. 
 
No major new data sources were published in 2024 for tracking impact and outcome indicators for children and women. The ongoing Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) is expected to address data gaps, with preliminary results anticipated in 2025. Administrative data showed progress in immunization with nine of 13 vaccines achieving over 90 per cent coverage. However, 34,000 children received no immunization (zero-dose) or were under-immunized, as of June 2024. The net enrolment rate in basic education rose to 95.1 per cent, while gross enrolment rate exceeded 100 per cent. However, learning outcomes stagnated, with less than 40 per cent of grade five students achieving required proficiency levels.

Despite the challenging context, in 2024, UNICEF Nepal made remarkable progress in improving the lives of children, families, and communities through transformative systemic changes. The Country Office (CO) demonstrated adaptability and operational excellence, delivering measurable outcomes across various sectors. 

The CO identified three programme and advocacy priorities: climate action, promoting the wellbeing and rights of adolescent girls, and scaling up holistic and integrated early childhood development (ECD). Clear strategies, action plans and accountability matrices have been drafted, laying a strong vision to work towards improving the early years of children while addressing issues affecting adolescent girls.

With UNICEF support, the National Planning Commission disseminated the National ECD strategy to all seven provinces and 753 municipalities reaching over 12 million social media users. In 14 ECD priority municipalities out of targeted 30, Local Integrated ECD Plan were finalized, ECD committees and ECD coordinator positions were established and teachers from 316 schools were trained to implement the Early Learning Development Standards (ELDS) tool. The Ministry of Health and Population launched the national ECD Guidelines for the health Sector. Early childhood education systems were strengthened with 21 out of 30 local governments adopting the ELDS. This resulted in 78.9 per cent of children being ready for Grade 1, compared to just 2 per cent at the beginning of the academic year. UNICEF is providing technical support for the national scale-up of this initiative that will benefit more than 30,000 schools. 

Around 35,160 adolescents were equipped with social and financial literacy skills, empowering them to prevent exploitation and violence as well as report incidents, advocate for their rights and access support services. UNICEF’s Supporting Adolescent Girls’ Education (SAGE) programme enrolled 2,918 adolescents (2,680 girls) in 17 municipalities in accredited non-formal learning, with 80 per cent expected to re-enroll in formal education next year. A total of 206 adolescent girl champions were trained and mobilized to raise awareness on health and nutrition issues.
UNICEF played a pivotal role in shaping the NDC 3.0 by joining the government-led technical committee and contributing to various thematic areas - energy, waste, forestry, adaptation, loss and damage, carbon trade, and climate finance. UNICEF engaged over 750 children and adolescents in consultations nationwide. It partnered in the Local Conference of Youth, where 200 young leaders participated and developed a Youth Statement and NDC Recommendations. The document was presented to the Minister of Forests and Environment, which has incorporated the recommendations in the NDC 3.0. 

UNICEF’s engagement and consultations with children and young people aimed at making Nepal’s NDC 3.0 truly child sensitive, aligning with Nepal’s goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2045. This supports the global target of limiting temperature rise to 1.5°C, as outlined in the Paris Agreement, thereby helping reduce climate-related risks and vulnerabilities for children, youth, and future generations. Furthermore, by integrating empowerment, resources, and active participation in climate action, the NDCs will help strengthen the resilience of children and young people.

The key results achieved with UNICEF advocacy, policy and partnership engagement, and technical assistance are outlined below by sector: 
    
Health

In 2024, UNICEF continued to make significant strides in strengthening maternal and child healthcare services. In total, 157 out of 160 Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care (EmONC) centres were made functional across Karnali, Sudurpashchim, Lumbini, and Madhesh provinces, exceeding the 2024 target of 125 facilities. These centers provided life-saving care to over 109,000 mothers and newborns, marking a 25 per cent increase from 2023. Though a partnership with the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and Nepal Paediatric Society, UNICEF’s quality improvement initiative in 12 out of 21 public hospitals in Madhesh province led to remarkable improvement in child healthcare within one year. Accurate pneumonia treatment rates soared from 40 to 65 per cent, proper diarrhoea management jumped from 45 to 85 per cent, and immediate newborn skin-to-skin contact—a critical practice for infant survival—surged from 25 to 85 per cent.  

UNICEF’s support to the national immunization programme made significant contribution to protect children from childhood diseases. The national Measles and Rubella (MR) campaign achieved 100 per cent coverage, vaccinating over 6.3 million children. Likewise, more than 1.7 million children nationwide received the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), reaching 100 per cent coverage. Following the detection of a novel mutated polio virus in Kathmandu’s sewage, 303,815 children were promptly vaccinated, preventing the spread of environmental vaccine-derived polio. Vaccine storage capacity increased by 15 per cent with the installation of 648 new cold chain equipment units across the country.

UNICEF’s commitment to strengthening a comprehensive and inclusive health system provided hope to those in need of mental health support and children with non-communicable diseases. Mental health support reached 67,358 children and adolescents in Karnali through school-based socio-emotional learning programmes and digital services, covering 25 per cent of the adolescent population in the region. Children with cancer gained access to 35 essential medicines through the Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines programme while preventive health programmes reached 43,881 young people with guidance on healthy living. Both efforts contributed to significantly improving the chances of survival and quality of life of children with cancer. 

The health system's emergency response capabilities proved robust, providing essential services to over 29,000 people during crises in 2024, including floods, earthquakes and fires. Disease surveillance improved with 43,660 cholera rapid diagnostic test kits supported by UNICEF, ensuring effective emergency response capacity while maintaining routine health services.
 
Nutrition

The third phase of the Multi Sector Nutrition Plan (MSNP) was launched with a government-approved budget of over US$1.07 billion to address maternal and child malnutrition nationwide by 2030. 

Efforts to identify and manage child wasting were strengthened through capacity-building of health workers, the establishment of outpatient therapeutic centres and increased screening. This resulted in 3.6 million children screened for wasting, a 125 per cent increase from 2023. All 17,250 severely wasted under-five children received life-saving treatment, with an 80 per cent recovery rate. Additionally, 44 per cent of children aged 6-23 months received Multiple Micronutrient Powder (MNP) together with infant and young child feeding counselling (IYCF) for their mothers and families, representing a 4 per cent increase from last year. This led to a 9-percentage point increase (56 to 63) in children exclusively breastfed and 6 percentage point increase in timely introduction of complementary foods (56 to 62).  

UNICEF’s World Breastfeeding Week social media campaign reached 9.1 million people with messages on importance of breastfeeding, with 17.6 million impressions and 3.4 million active engagements. Over 1.6 million adolescent girls received weekly Iron Folic Acid supplementation, a fourfold increase from 0.4 million in 2023. This was made possible through enhanced training of school health nurses and health coordinators in Lumbini, Gandaki, Madhesh, Bagmati, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces. The proportion of pregnant women consuming over 90 iron folic acid tablets increased from 43 per cent in 2023 to 61 in 2024.

As part of earthquake recovery efforts, 8,400 pregnant and lactating mothers received IYCF counselling. During flood and fire response and recovery in Madhesh Province, 1,233 mothers received IYCF counselling, 1,233 children aged 6-23 months received MNP and 3,061 children aged 6-59 months were screened for wasting, with an 80 per cent recovery rate for treated cases. 

Climate-resilient Water Sanitation and Hygiene 

A total of 166,348 individuals in marginalized areas were provided with safe water, representing a 76 per cent increase compared to beneficiaries reached in 2023 and 5,857 individuals now live in water-safe communities. Additionally, 55,104 people gained access to basic sanitation, reflecting a 39-fold increase from the beneficiaries reached in 2023, and 21 schools and 17 healthcare facilities were equipped with water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services. These efforts contributed to reduction of under-five diarrhoea rates from 339 to 115 per 1,000 over three years. Notably, WASH was prioritized politically, leading to the formation of the Federal WASH Parliament Forum and an 11-point consensus among 120 mayors and provincial assembly members. Advocacy efforts, along with strategic partnerships with the Municipal Association in Nepal (MuAN) and the National Association of Rural Municipalities (NARMIN), strengthened intergovernmental coordination and led to endorsement of WASH Acts in 92 municipalities, establishment of WASH Units, and implementation of water quality and open defecation free (ODF) monitoring guidelines. The WASH information system was strengthened, enabling 570 municipalities to develop WASH Plans, with 211 already endorsed. This represents a 129 per cent increase, as only 92 municipalities had endorsed their plans by the end of 2023.

Intergovernmental collaboration increased at the provincial level with MoUs signed by 62 municipalities in Gandaki, Sudurpashchim and Madhesh provinces for coordinated WASH planning. These plans will support improved access to clean water and sanitation leading to reduced morbidity and mortality. The US$198 million Green Climate Fund (GCF) project for WASH was drafted and a climate change response strategy for Water Resources Management and WASH Services was formulated. The launch of a Climate Resilient WASH (CRWASH) capacity-building package resulted in 30 national trainers, enabling integration of climate resilience into WASH plans.
Four climate-resilient WASH demonstration projects were initiated, focusing on groundwater monitoring, source protection and solarization. It also established Nepal’s first real-time groundwater monitoring station to support early warning systems for water resource management and enhanced preparedness for climate-related water challenges. Delivery of essential WASH services and supplies during disasters benefited 69,013 people. 

Education

UNICEF made significant progress in advancing inclusive, quality education for children across Nepal. The capacities of 150 local governments were strengthened to develop gender equity social inclusion (GESI)-responsive and climate resilient education plans and budgets using the School Education Sector Plan (SESP) Calibration Toolkit. This toolkit was developed with UNICEF support and was endorsed by the government for use in all 753 local governments. This was further supported through a technical facility established within the government with UNICEF’s assistance to strengthen development cooperation and coordination on SESP priorities.

Through UNICEF’s support, improved learning and safety were achieved for 104,000 children in 777 schools, and 2,383 teachers saw enhanced pedagogical skills, helping to accelerate foundational education for students. Additionally, 90 per cent of teachers reported increased confidence and knowledge in implementing mother-tongue-based multilingual education (MLE) after being trained on new standards and resources finalized by the Center for Education and Human Resource Development.

Implementation of alternative learning pathways for out-of-school children started in Madhesh, Lumbini and Bagmati provinces. Moreover, the Non-Formal Education-National Qualification Framework was finalized for accredited learning, enabling adolescents to either return to formal education or continue skills development.  

The Comprehensive School Safety Minimum Package (CSSMP) was implemented in 683 schools, resulting in 23 per cent of schools meeting CSSMP standards for safety and resilience. Preparedness and lifesaving skills were strengthened for 18,441 students, including 9,835 girls, in 264 schools through emergency drills. Local education clusters increased from 88 to 119, enhancing emergency preparedness and response. In response to the 2023 earthquake, US$9 million in partner funds was leveraged for the recovery and reconstruction of schools, benefiting 32,000 children. Also, 19,117 children were supported through learning continuity measures in emergencies, emergency supplies, mental health and psychosocial support. Additionally, UNICEF support ensured integration of climate actions in key documents like Green Schools and CSSMP as well as education being reflected in the NDC 3.0. 

Child Protection

UNICEF’s justice for children interventions led to the development of guidelines for diversion and restorative justice, enabling 29 cases involving children in conflict with the law to be resolved without formal judicial proceedings, a significant increase from six cases in 2023. Legal outreach programmes benefited 4,000 children and adolescents, educating them on their rights and promoting access to legal aid and support services. Through training of 1,959 service providers - social workers, legal professionals, and local government officials -  the frontline workers’ ability was enhanced to respond to child protection and justice issues. These efforts contributed to a child-friendly justice system prioritizing rehabilitation and reintegration. 

The expansion of case management procedures and implementation of Child Protection Information Management System+ facilitated timely service delivery, allowing 72,280 children, adolescents, and women to access psychosocial support, legal aid, birth registration and gender-based violence (GBV) assistance. Moreover, the referral pathways were strengthened in 54 municipalities, with improved multi-sectoral collaboration and response.
Community engagement and awareness-raising were central to UNICEF’s strategy with 28,605 caregivers trained to create protective environments for children and 10,731 community members empowered to prevent and respond to violence and exploitation. Awareness campaigns reached 1.7 million people, emphasizing GBV prevention and promoting help-seeking behaviours. Targeted interventions enabled 3,223 at-risk children and women in Madhesh, Lumbini, Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces to access survivor centred GBV services. 

Notably, 68 local governments integrated child protection priorities in their annual plans and budgets, while 26 local governments began implementing plans to combat child marriage. Capacity-building initiatives engaged 137,431 adolescents, caregivers, teachers, religious leaders, and community members, equipping them with knowledge and skills to prevent violence and create protective environments.

Emergency response included establishment of 26 child-friendly spaces, benefiting around 1,300 children and adolescents. Psychosocial support benefited 1,851 individuals. Around 2,394 vulnerable earthquake-affected children, identified through vulnerability assessments, received livelihood support, temporary shelter, food, clothing, and medical care.

Social Policy Governance and Evidence (SPGE)

The evaluation of Nepal's Social Security Allowances provided critical data to inform policy decisions aimed at reducing vulnerabilities. An international social protection conference, organized in partnership with the World Bank, WFP, and ILO, advanced national discussions on inclusive, child- and gender-sensitive social protection. UNICEF’s disability screening app reached 300,000 people by linking eligible individuals to social protection and disability grants. A 3D printing prosthetics lab was established to support children affected by disasters. This initiative enhanced the capacity of two clinics in Karnali and Kathmandu, benefitting 67 users with assistive technology devices.

The collaboration with the Ministry of Finance on the Economic Lab, enhanced the capacity of 55 municipalities in evidence-based planning and budgeting. Capacity-building initiatives ensured children's voices were included in local planning, and provincial Child Friendly Local Governance (CFLG) Monitoring Committees were established to ensure effective implementation of CFLG policies. 

UNICEF’s Child and Family Tracker survey provided valuable data on child poverty, advocating for the expansion of the under-five child grant. A disability-related financial burden analysis underscored the need for better social protection measures. Children participated in the VNR process and the Lumbini Province Youth Summit, ensuring their voices were included in national development plans. 

Programme Effectiveness
 
UNICEF responded to the humanitarian needs of 69,013 people, including 23,464 children, affected by floods, landslides, and other hazards. A multi-sectoral approach, including multipurpose cash, ensured comprehensive support. Capacities of 5,077 people were enhanced in disaster risk reduction, emergency preparedness and response and climate resilience. Notably, 21 municipalities developed the disability-inclusive Local Disaster and Climate Resilience Plans, integrating inclusive climate-sensitive strategies into local governance. In Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces, 11,000 households (about 20,000 children) were provided with improved cook stoves, contributing to reduced indoor air pollution and carbon trading initiatives.
 
UNICEF engaged with 126,000 people from flood-affected communities in Madhesh Province. Mobilizing 44 local volunteers and leveraging the Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) real-time community feedback dashboard ensured culturally relevant responses and strengthened trust in local governance. The use of tools like I-Hear-U, U-Report and Internet of Good Things (IoGT) enhanced real-time community engagement and response to public health issues, including human papillomavirus (HPV), breastfeeding, measles-rubella, and cholera. Over 38,000 posts were analyzed through I-Hear-U during the floods, shaping programme design and donor appeals. U-Report engaged 8,561 youth subscribers, amplifying their voices, while IoGT pages recorded 9,400 views, addressing knowledge gaps and strengthening community resilience.

Operation Effectiveness

The office maintained a 94 per cent emergency preparedness score and achieved 100 per cent compliance in the Emergency Preparedness Platform, meeting all benchmarks. All recommendations from the 2023 audit were successfully closed. A peer review conducted by the regional office identified areas for improvement across several functional processes, leading to actionable recommendations to further strengthen the governance systems and internal processes, which will continue to be implemented in 2025. Of the targeted minimum assurance activities, 100 per cent programmatic and 90 per cent financial assurance activities were completed, meeting the benchmarks. However, spot checks with some government partners were delayed due to their ongoing internal audits. One evaluation was completed, and results of the blockchain-based cash transfer pilot evaluation informed the government’s future cash transfer engagements using blockchain technology. Three other evaluations are ongoing against the two completed evaluations target. 

The CO managed a throughput of US$1.7 million for programme supplies, US$5.3 million for services contracting for both the CO and regional office, and US$32 million for procurement on behalf of the government, including lifesaving emergency commodities. Services procured through a competitive process reached 96 per cent, exceeding the target of 95 per cent.  UNICEF warehouses maintained 100 per cent of the minimum required prepositioning, ensuring emergency preparedness. However, nine per cent of the inventory in the warehouses was older than 24 months, failing to meet the benchmark of zero per cent balance for such items. Local procurement performed against long-service agreements was at 26 per cent, below the 40 per cent target.

The CO transferred around US$11.67 million to implementing partners, processing 92 per cent of cash transfer requests within the benchmark of 14 calendar days, ensuring timely disbursement of funds. A 93 per cent of regular programming partnerships were finalized within the benchmark of 45 days. All Civil Society Organization (CSO) partners were assessed for prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) risk, and 100 per cent of them were rated as low or moderate risk meeting the benchmark. 

The CO utilized 100 per cent of its regular resources and other resources, including emergency funds. The office achieved a 100 per cent on-time donor reporting rate, maintaining excellent accountability toward its supporters.

The 2024 ethnic diversity target for under-represented groups was achieved with 23 per cent representation. However, the gender ratio in staffing target was not met, with 46 per cent female staff compared to the 55 per cent target. The geographic diversity target was also not met, with 27 per cent of staff from developed countries compared to a 40 per cent target. Recruitment processes improved significantly, reducing the average duration from 87 days to 46 against a benchmark of 60 days. Performance evaluations were completed for all staff. A 98 per cent of staff completed the mandatory courses, while the learning and development plan activities achieved an 80 per cent completion rate. A total of 15 staff benefited from stretch assignments, staff exchanges, surge missions and lien on posts, ensuring career development. Ethics and Culture Champions were appointed, and all staff received ethics orientations. 

The hybrid solar power system installed on the UN premises generated approximately 125,237 kWh of electricity in 2024, contributing to a reduction of 43.6 tons of CO2, which is equivalent to planting 1,981 trees. Additionally, from December 2024, UNICEF began sharing its solar connection with UNFPA through a Letter of Understanding, under which UNFPA invested approximately US$25,000 in additional batteries and accessories.

New field offices were established in Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces, enhancing advocacy and resource leveraging at local levels. The field office in Nepalgunj was closed as per plan. The new field offices have incorporated energy-efficient LED lights alongside incandescent bulbs for lighting. Toilets are equipped with low-flow faucets to minimize water usage, and the air conditioning systems are environmentally friendly. To enhance indoor air quality, all workspaces feature IAQ monitoring devices and air purifiers. Additionally, both offices have integrated local flora, fauna, and biodiverse spaces to promote a healthier work environment.

In 2024, UNICEF expanded its network of partners to amplify the impact of strategic partnerships for transformational social change. UNICEF partnered with 147 government entities across federal, provincial, and local levels, alongside 46 national and international non-governmental organizations (NGO) and academic institutions. Government partnerships increased by 63 per cent, with 54 new collaborations with local governments and 25 with provincial/district governments. These partnerships enabled UNICEF to scale its programming, while fostering local government ownership for sustainability of its innovative delivery models. UNICEF maintained strong collaboration with key ministries - Health and Population; Education, Science and Technology; Water Supply; Finance; Federal Affairs and General Administration; Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation; as well as the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority; and the National Planning Commission. Additionally, UNICEF strengthened ties with the Ministry of Forests and Environment through its catalytic support for NDC 3.0 and preparations for COP29. To enhance governance, service delivery and system strengthening, UNICEF partnered with the Municipal Association of Nepal (MuAN) and the National Association of Rural Municipalities in Nepal (NARMIN). 

UNICEF strengthened collaboration with public donors and NatComs through tailored content, co-creation workshops, and joint field visits. Four donor visits for UNICEF USA/Zonta International, USAID HQ, UNICEF Japan/Fuji TV and UNICEF Finland were facilitated. The latter two are expected to generate US$1.7 million for UNICEF Nepal in 2025. Joint communication efforts with the World Bank at the International Social Protection Conference reached over 46,000 people through social media. Memorandums with four private sector entities included communication and advocacy efforts to help scale up the national parenting package. The partnerships reached around 7,000 individuals with parenting sessions throughout the year and other community-based advocacy events during the parenting month in June. UNICEF hosted a private sector roundtable to re-engage business sector and explore potential collaboration. A total of 32 participants from 20 businesses and associations across diverse industries participated, focusing on empowering adolescent girls, and promoting climate resilience. 

UNICEF continued its role of co-financing development partner under the education Sector Wide Approach (SWAp) arrangements. UNICEF also coordinated development partner technical assistance to help implement the Global Partnership for Education (GPE). Collaboration with the European Union (EU) in Nepal, the Embassy of Finland and GPE to strengthen the School Education Sector Plan (SESP) implementation was recognized by the EU as a model for its Global Gateway initiative. UNICEF also actively contributed to health development partners’ SWAp, advocating for child-related issues and contributing to the strengthening of health systems for universal coverage.

UNICEF, with ILO, UNFPA and UN Women, continued to support the government in advancing gender equality and women empowerment through the Government-EU-UN joint programme ‘Empowered Women, Prosperous Nepal’ (EWPN). The programme facilitated the implementation of Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI) policies in 31 local governments. It also supported the Ministry of Women, Children, and Senior Citizens to finalize a strategy to mobilize men and adolescent boys for GBV prevention. Further, it supported Madhesh Province to endorse the Girl Child Protection Act 2024, safeguarding girls’ rights to education, health, and protection from discrimination and violence, In Sudurpashchim Province, the EWPN helped endorse the province’s GESI policy. 

In earthquake-affected areas of western Nepal, UNICEF implemented the Joint Recovery Action Plan (JRAP) with WFP, UNFPA and IOM. The programme provided 25,631 people with access to safe drinking water and 27,493 people with basic sanitation services. Additionally, 33,851 people gained enhanced hygiene awareness. Further, 2,515 vulnerable children received emergency assistance, 234 children accessed child-friendly spaces, 1,851 people received psychosocial counselling and 14,721 people received mental health and psychosocial support. Also, 351 health workers and 273 female community health volunteers (FCHVs) were trained to deliver quality nutrition education and counseling.
 
UN's Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) anticipatory action programme, implemented by UNICEF with FAO, UNFPA and WFP in four municipalities of Saptari District in Madhesh Province, provided early support to 3,400 families with multipurpose cash assistance, child protection services, water, sanitation and hygiene service and supplies and social and behavior change communication.
 
The UNFPA-UNICEF Global Programme on Ending Child Marriage empowered around 26,000 vulnerable adolescent girls with social and financial skills and helped 861 girls enroll in or stay in school. Notably, as part of this programme, UNICEF also partnered with women-led cooperatives in various districts to support adolescent girls at risk of early marriage, integrating them into the networks of the cooperatives and assisting them to start small businesses and provided mentorship.
 
UNICEF initiated a partnership with UNESCO, supported by the Embassy of Norway, to build a Climate Smart, Green and Resilient Education System (CSGRES). Implemented across 70 schools in four municipalities of Bagmati Province, the programme trained 94 teachers, including 53 female teachers, on comprehensive school safety and climate change practices. Co-creation workshops with the government helped revise the Green School Implementation Guideline (GSIG) to align with global standards. 

As co-chair of the UN Operations Management Team, UNICEF contributed significantly to increasing UN efficiencies. UNICEF also co-led four humanitarian clusters - education, WASH, nutrition, and child protection - and led the Social Protection Task Team and Cash Coordination Working Group. It co-chaired the Human Capital Development Outcome of the UNSDCF, the UN Youth Group, UN Communication Group, Risk Communication and Community Engagement working groups. Active participation in UN working groups strengthened collaboration on gender in humanitarian action, procurement, prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse, and ending domestic violence.

UNICEF's strategic health partnerships in Nepal delivered transformative results in 2024, significantly improving healthcare access and quality for children. A landmark collaboration with the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health and Nepal Paediatrics Society revolutionized paediatric care standards in Madhesh province's public hospitals, leading to measurable improvements in treatment protocols and maternal-newborn care. A groundbreaking initiative with the Kathmandu Institute of Child Health established PEN Plus centers, marking Nepal's first systematic approach to providing continuous care for children with severe chronic illnesses. Through joint efforts with WHO and St. Jude Hospital, Nepal joined the Global Platform for Access to Childhood Cancer Medicines, securing sustainable access to essential cancer medications. These partnerships exemplify UNICEF's commitment to strengthening health systems through strategic collaborations, resulting in improved healthcare delivery, enhanced institutional capacity, and sustainable solutions for children's health challenges in Nepal.

Flexible funding through Regular Resources (RR) and thematic contributions enabled UNICEF to support critical interventions with transformative potential. These included implementing the Multi-Sector Nutrition Plan, improving learning outcomes, advancing social protection, and strengthening climate resilience, disaster preparedness, and humanitarian response.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The office identified three transformative programme and advocacy priorities for 2024 and beyond to further improve focus and concentration and strengthen multisectoral collaboration: climate action, promoting the wellbeing and rights of adolescent girls, and scaling up holistic and integrated early childhood development. These priorities are strategically aligned with global and regional priorities and supported by robust advocacy strategies, comprehensive programme strategies and meticulously crafted action plans with accountability matrix, to ensure impactful implementation. These guiding documents will serve as foundational references during the critical mid-term review in 2025.
 
Resource mobilization efforts were elevated and streamlined, emphasizing multi-sectoral, integrated programme proposals developed through a coordinated approach, ensuring alignment with above-mentioned priorities, and encompassing all relevant programmes. The office also initiated strategic processes to deepen donor engagements and unlock the potential of private sector collaboration for joint communication, advocacy, and fundraising. The roundtable discussion with Nepal’s private sector marked a pivotal step, paving the way for focused sessions dedicated to the three priority areas in 2025.
 
Digital solutions emerged as revolutionary tools, offering cost-effective and scalable means to deliver sustainable results for the most remote areas and marginalized communities. They offer lower operational costs by reducing the need for physical infrastructure, paperwork, and manual labour, leading to significant savings. Innovations such as tele-mental health services, the "Ma Chhu Ni" chatbot, digital case management tools, Rupantaran e-learning modules, disability screening app and community engagement tools like I-Hear-U, U-Report and IoGT were proved transformative. These tools demonstrated exceptional potential to catalyse impact change in the lives of the children, particularly during humanitarian crises.  

UN collaboration on emergency preparedness, response and recovery underscored the power of coordinated action. Initiatives such as the JRAP, Anticipatory Actions and Strengthening Urban Preparedness and Response (SUPER) showcased the UN’S collective strength in delivering timely, efficient and comprehensive support to affected populations. These efforts leveraged resources and expertise from diverse UN agencies, creating a robust framework for addressing complex challenges. 
 
Nepal’s political instability – characterized by frequent government changes, capacity deficits, especially at the subnational levels, further exacerbated by vacant posts, weak intergovernmental coordination – presented significant hurdles in timely delivery and the quality of services. To counteract these challenges, the office implemented a dynamic subnational government engagement strategy. The initiative focused on strengthening provincial and municipality governments to plan, budget, implement and monitor social sector programmes more effectively. By identifying the annual planning process at the provincial and local levels as a strategic entry point, the office ensured that children’s priorities are deeply embedded in government plans. While significant progress was achieved in education and WASH sectors, the drive for integrated planning and the delivery of comprehensive interventions through community-based service points, such as schools and health centers, remains a top priority. 
 
Programming at scale and sustainability of interventions were significant challenges across all sectors. Similarly, convergence of programme sectors and integrated programming need further improvement. Despite these complexities, the identification of three flagship results by programme sections and field offices in the beginning of the year drove integration and enabled targeted interventions in select municipalities. Engaging local governments in crafting laws, guidelines and plans nurtured ownership and commitment, laying a strong foundation for scaling interventions. However, critical gaps persist in making the plans and policies more inclusive, particularly in addressing issues such as climate change, Gender Equality, Social Inclusion, and Diversity (GESDI), and embedding these principles within the systems and services. 
 
Coordination challenges among service providers continued to hinder access to multisectoral services for children. Insufficient vertical, horizontal, and intersectional collaboration exacerbates delays and inefficiencies in delivering holistic services. Strengthening cross-sectoral collaboration through clear frameworks and leveraging service delivery points like schools and health centers are vital steps forward. Addressing capacity deficits at provincial and municipal levels requires targeted investments in capacity-building, resource allocation, and technical assistance. 

As the office gears up for the mid-term review in 2025, several high-impact strategies are set to drive future actions. Multisectoral joint programming will be pivotal for achieving synergistic outcomes and modelling integrated service delivery for children. Addressing the needs of married adolescent girls, for example, requires a coordinated blend of psychosocial services, education reintegration and economic empowerment among others.  Community engagement emerges as a cornerstone for fostering ownership and sustainability, and community-driven approaches like the Water Safe Community model, offer scalable solutions. The transformative role of social and behaviour change strategies cannot be overstated. These strategies are key to reshaping community practices and challenging entrenched social and gender norms. 

Amplifying advocacy efforts and enhancing visibility will solidify donor and stakeholder engagement, providing critical momentum for programme success. Scaling system-strengthening approaches and integrating government mechanisms will ensure enduring results at scale. Alignment with government planning processes is essential for institutionalization and long-term sustainability. While coverage targets have been met, the focus must shift to enhancing programme quality through standardized guidance and tools.

Public finance represents an untapped opportunity with the potential to unlock substantial resources for child-focused programmes. The office’s renewed focus on this area is poised to be a game-changer, paving the way for innovative financing solutions. By building on the lessons and successes of 2024, the office is well-positioned to refine its strategies, adopt adaptive approaches, and explore new frontiers of collaboration to accelerate transformative outcomes for the most marginalized children.

Pakistan is navigating a profound poly-crisis – a convergence of economic, social, political, constitutional and environmental challenges that has severely strained its social fabric and hindered its development. While Gross Domestic Product (GDP) increased from 0.29 per cent in 2021-22 to 2.38 per cent in 2023-2024, inflation, particularly food inflation, which has exceeded 50 per cent year-on-year, has intensified economic hardship for millions. Furthermore, despite an 11.5 per cent decline in indirect taxes, progress towards a fairer taxation system remains inadequate. 
Additionally, the political situation and insecurity steadily undermine government institutions' responsiveness, accountability and capacity. The limited geographic and population coverage of programmes, including emergency responses, is compounded by weak partner implementation capacities. Stark regional and economic inequalities persist in underserved provinces, such as Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP), compared to other parts of the country. These inequalities are made worse by gender-based barriers, including cultural norms and systemic biases that restrict girls' access to education, healthcare and protection services. As a result, girls face increased vulnerability to risks such as child marriage, heavy domestic responsibilities, sexual abuse and exploitation, and are more likely to drop out of school. These deprivations perpetuate cycles of disadvantage, restricting their freedom and ability to make choices and preventing them from fulfilling their potential.
Addressing these issues will become even more challenging as the country has a rapidly growing child population. Pakistan's total population is 240.5 million, of which 112 .5 million children (58.1 million boys and 54.4 million girls) aged below 18 years constitute 47 per cent, with 15.2 per cent  (36.5 million boys and 18.7 million girls) aged 0 to 4 years and 22 per cent (27.6 million boys and 25.4 million girls) aged 10 to 19 years.[6] With an annual population growth rate of 2.55 per cent – one of the highest globally – Pakistan’s population is projected to exceed 400 million by 2050.
A significant concern is the lack of proper documentation for children, with 6 in 10 under the age of 5 remaining unregistered, severely limiting their access to essential services, welfare and future employment opportunities. Violence against children, particularly girls, is a major concern and is pervasive, with over 4,213 cases reported in 2023 – an average of 11 incidents daily.[5] The real figures are probably much higher as there is systemic underreporting, weak reporting mechanisms and insufficient child protection services. 
The commitment to ‘leave no child behind’ continues to pose a significant challenge for Pakistan. Child-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) remain unmet in crucial areas. Learning poverty remains high. Although government investment in education increased by 55.9 per cent from Rs 44.71 billion in 2022-2023 to Rs 69.7 billion in 2023-2024, substantial gaps persist, with 25 million children out of school and marked gender disparities. Initiatives such as the Challenge Fund for Out-of-School Children, launched with a budget of Rs 25,000 million, aim to enhance educational access, particularly for girls. Also, complementary programmes, like the Enrolment, Retention and Progression of Out-of-School Children initiative, have promoted inclusive education, remedial programmes and free school meals. 
Health indicators are equally concerning. Approximately 40 per cent of children under the age of 5 are stunted, and 400,000 ‘zero-dose’ children lack routine immunizations. Pakistan is one of only two countries globally that has yet to eradicate polio, and more than 50 per cent of polio cases occurred in individuals who had not received any routine immunization. Reducing health expenditure to just 1 per cent of GDP in 2022-2023 and inadequate investment in water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure have hindered progress in improving maternal and child health outcomes. 
Pakistan faces severe food insecurity and high rates of acute malnutrition. Around 16 per cent of the population is food insecure and lacks access to basic services such as healthcare and nutrition. If malnutrition is left untreated during the 1,000-day window from conception, the consequences for the child are irreversible. It not only impairs the cognitive and physical development of the child but also undermines national productivity. However, Pakistan’s global acute malnutrition rate is 17.7 per cent, exceeding emergency levels, with a severe wasting rate of 6 per cent, especially among children aged 6 to 59 months. Women and girls face additional risks, as high malnutrition rates negatively impact birth outcomes. 
Key initiatives include the Pakistan Deworming Initiative, which targeted over 17 million children in high-risk districts; the Benazir Nashonuma Programme, which allocated Rs 32,268 million for maternal and child health in 2024; and the Pakistan Nutrition Initiative, which has Rs 8.5 billion in funding. 
Economic fragility, compounded by external debt burdens and critically low foreign reserves, constrains the Government’s ability to fund social programmes. Nevertheless, social protection spending, particularly through the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), increased incrementally by 16.5 per cent. The Benazir Taleemi Wazaif Programme disbursed Rs 117 billion in conditional cash transfers, enabling 14.8 million children to access education. Similarly, the Pakistan ‘Sweet Homes’ initiative allocated Rs 645.89 million for the welfare of orphaned children, and the ‘Schools for Rehabilitation of Child Labour’ initiative disbursed Rs 422.78 million to enroll former working children into non-formal education[9]. Other initiatives, such as the Interest-Free Loan Programme, provided Rs 12.2 billion of loans to 274,000 youth and women in 2023-2024, while the Benazir Undergraduate Scholarship Programme disbursed Rs 29.1 billion to support students from low-income families. While these social programmes provide essential assistance to marginalized households, particularly women, the uneven distribution of benefits, often bypassing the most disadvantaged regions and groups, erodes public trust.
Digital inequality further exacerbates societal divides, leaving marginalized youth and children at a disadvantage. With only 25 per cent of the population having internet access – largely absent in rural areas – digital inequities deepen polarization. E-learning remains underutilized, with only 11.9 per cent of internet users accessing it. [10] To bridge these gaps, initiatives like e-Rozgaar Centres aim to train one million freelancers, while Digiskills.pk 2.0 has equipped nearly 4 million individuals with marketable skills. National Incubation Centres foster entrepreneurship, supporting 1,480 startups and creating 128,000 jobs, while Universal Service Fund initiatives expand connectivity in underserved areas. 
Pakistan is becoming increasingly vulnerable to natural hazards due to its distinctive geophysical conditions and the intensifying impact of climate change. The country ranks 5th on the Global Climate Risk Index and 14th on the Child-Focused Climate Risk Index. Its water resources, agricultural productivity and ecological balance are increasingly threatened. At the same time, deep-rooted vulnerabilities such as poverty and limited access to essential services hinder the ability of affected populations to cope with and recover from disasters. Over 2.14 million children in flood-hit regions suffer from acute malnutrition. The 2022 floods caused US$ 14.9 billion in damages, displaced millions and disrupted access to education, healthcare and nutrition. 
Furthermore, the presence of approximately 3 million Afghan refugees, many of them children, strains Pakistan’s already overburdened system. Concentrated in provinces with high poverty rates, Afghan populations, particularly women and girls, face many hardships exacerbated by uncertainty over repatriation efforts.
Children with disabilities, those in informal settlements and internally displaced children face significant neglect. Recent census data identifies 1.8 million children aged 5 to 16 with disabilities or functional limitations,[11]; however, this figure likely underestimated the actual number due to stigma, gaps in methodology and limited disability categories. 
To create a cohesive and resilient society, Pakistan must focus on social services, digital inclusion, and climate resilience, especially for vulnerable groups. This approach can turn demographic challenges into opportunities for sustainable growth, building a more inclusive future.
