UNICEF's programmes are designed to support Pakistan's efforts to address the poly-crisis. The aim is for children to be born healthy, thrive with proper nutrition, and be nurtured in a safe, hygienic environment where they can learn, grow and reach their full potential while being protected from disease, violence, exploitation and abuse.
Across all programme areas, UNICEF has supported the Government—particularly the social sector—by strengthening systems to enhance capacity for planning, policy implementation, oversight and governance. This support also includes improving the delivery and coverage of quality services while increasing community demand and access.
Health
UNICEF supported the District Health Information Software2 (DHIS-2) scale-up, with 78 out of 165 districts adopting the system for evidence-based health programming to contribute to a more effective and responsive healthcare system, ultimately improving health outcomes for communities across Pakistan. Convergence programming was initiated in five districts, with joint missions in two provinces/regions in collaboration with the Nutrition and WASH sections.
To support the Lady Health Worker (LHW) Strategic Plan and the Community Health Agenda, 11,300 lady health workers were trained on pictorial counselling cards across various regions. Increasing their capacity reduces health inequalities as they operate in communities often far from health services.
UNICEF also facilitated the development of the first draft of the PC-1 for the Health Education Cell within the Ministry of National Health Services Regulation and Coordination (MoNHSR&C) and prepared a draft roadmap for addressing non-communicable diseases and preventing lead poisoning in children, all major threats to children’s survival and development. Other key actions this year that UNICEF supported included promoting renewable energy solutions. Three district-level hospitals and six hospitals in various regions now have continuous power supply and also benefit from reduced electricity costs, thereby freeing up resources for medical supplies and equipment.
To improve neonatal survival and care for every newborn, UNICEF focused on scaling up evidence-based, cost-effective interventions, such as Sick and Small Newborn Care Units, Kangaroo Mother Care Units and Home-Based Newborn Care programmes. These initiatives and Mother and Child Week campaigns extended critical services to underserved populations. UNICEF’s technical assistance and advocacy led to the endorsement of the country’s Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP) and the Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality (EPMM) initiative. 
Recognizing the role of private sector engagement, UNICEF supported the establishment of the first Kangaroo Mother Care unit in a private hospital in the Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT). A successful innovation has been using portable projectors in community health education sessions. Improving water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities has been a priority. A WASH in healthcare model was implemented in six facilities and is now ready for broader replication. 
To assess progress and challenges in maternal and child health, UNICEF, in collaboration with MoNHSRC and provincial health departments, held a national Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) review meeting. The key recommendation was to scale up IMNCI to all Universal health coverage priority districts. Over 8,790 Lady Health Workers and Lady Health Supervisors (LHWs/LHSs) were trained in IMNCI, and 10,194 healthcare providers received in-service IMNCI training, benefitting over 2 million children under the age of 5. Early Childhood Development modules based on IMNCI guidelines were rolled out in Balochistan for trainee doctors and paramedics on milestones and developmental delays. This led to the integration of ECD in ongoing IMNCI activities at health facilities. Additionally, over 5,000 service providers were trained in oxygen management and essential oxygen supplies were provided to 85 health facilities, benefiting another 2 million children.
UNICEF remained the key focal point agency during disease outbreaks and other emergencies. UNICEF’s main focus has been strengthening the capacity of government counterparts and health managers to respond to crises effectively. 
Polio eradication continued to be a national public health priority under the direct leadership of the Prime Minister. Wild poliovirus (WPV1) resurged with 73 cases in 33 districts (as of 20 January 2025), up from 6 cases in 2023. UNICEF played a leading role within the Emergency Operations Centres (EOCs) and other partners in implementing efforts to interrupt the transmission of the virus in 2025. The Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) strategy was revamped within the National Emergency Action Plan (NEAP). UNICEF also supported vaccine delivery and SBCC initiatives for eight Supplementary Immunization Activities (SIAs), including three National Immunization Days (NIDs), vaccinating an average of 44.8 million children per round. UNICEF’s Communication Network (COMNet) of 4,905 staff found ways to tackle challenges like boycotts and refusals, averting 99 potential vaccine boycotts and resolving 77 per cent of 321 reported boycotts during campaigns. As a result, 123,614 children who had missed routine immunizations were vaccinated. Community engagement and SBC strategies achieved 86.7 per cent coverage of missed children, contributing to over 95 per cent overall coverage in NIDs. Additionally, UNICEF used mass media, outdoor advertising, influencer outreach and social media campaigns to support frontline workers, dispel myths and misconceptions and counter media misinformation. Over 49 million people across provinces received educational messages on polio, routine immunization, hygiene practices and nutrition. Additionally, over 650,000 people interacted with the content, resulting in a 4 per cent increase in followers across all social media channels.
To ensure a safe working environment for polio work and protect beneficiaries, UNICEF developed and endorsed the Anti-Harassment Guidelines and created a training programme on Gender Equality and Conducive Work Environment.  To further gender-responsive efforts, a Gender Equality Strategy, Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Prevention and Mitigation Guidelines and a Referral Directory were developed.Staff from Sindh and Punjab Provincial EOCs were trained to comply with the guidelines. The guidelines and redressal practices were also integrated into frontline worker training sessions. Additionally, a three-day Training of Trainers (TOT) on UNICEF’s Safeguarding and Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) policies was conducted for third-party vendors and partners. 
In collaboration with the Pakistan Girl Guides Association, the MOHR, and the National Commission on the Rights of the Child (NCRC), UNICEF launched the 'Pakistan Girls Empowerment Forum’. This forum brought together over 500 girls from across Pakistan to develop a collective vision for their empowerment, which was presented to the Prime Minister of Pakistan on the International Day of the Girl.This forum was used for HPV-related advocacy, awareness raising, mental health and other key areas to cascade information at the grassroots level.
 
Nutrition and Child Development 
The poly-crisis has worsened child nutrition in Pakistan as food prices have hiked while families have become poorer, with many struggling to provide a balanced diet for their children. 
Although Pakistan is off-track from achieving stunting, wasting and other global nutrition targets, nutrition and child development remain amongst the humanitarian and development priorities, as evidenced by their inclusion as key pillars in some of the national documents, including the 5Es (Exports, E-Pakistan, Environment, Energy, and Equity) framework to turn around Pakistan, and manifestos of various political parties.
UNICEF enhanced nutrition responsiveness of social protection, education and health systems, policy and legal frameworks, human resources development, and private sector engagement. Notably, the Sindh Breast Milk Substitutes (BMS) Act enactment has demonstrated the Government’s strong commitment to protecting children's nutrition rights. 
To help the poorest families provide nutritious food for their children, UNICEF established a partnership with the Government/Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) on nutrition and gender-responsive social protection programmes. UNICEF also channelled global resources to match domestic funding for nutrition commodities. UNICEF spearheaded innovations, including WhatsApp ECD e-learning and integrated community-based programming. The DHIS-2 Nutrition module was rolled out in 34 districts (12 districts in Balochistan, 7 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and 15 in Punjab). 
 
In an effort to ensure children, adolescents and women in the most deprived areas access high-impact nutrition interventions, UNICEF strengthened the capacity of its partners working in these areas. The training has focused on improving interventions for infant and young child feeding (IYCF), parenting, wasting management, maternal nutrition and community engagement. In addition, 49,915 personnel were trained, 47 per cent of healthcare facilities were equipped to provide nutrition services (30 per cent in 2022), and 13 early childhood development (ECD) centres of excellence were established, contributing to a stronger, more resilient healthcare system and better health and nutritional outcomes for children and their families. Over 2.9 million mothers/caregivers received messages on parenting, infant and young child feeding and maternal nutrition; 565,049 children were treated for severe acute malnutrition; and about 1 million mothers received multiple micronutrient supplements. 
 
UNICEF supported integrated ECD services for children aged 0-8 years, ensuring a holistic approach to malnutrition, including child health, nutrition and education services. This involved UNICEF assisting with the rollout of key family care practices to 130 districts (122 districts in 2023) and the development of a costed National Multisectoral Nutrition Action Plan. Additionally, UNICEF spearheaded the delivery of the gender-responsive and climate-resilient integrated programme ‘SUCCESS’ (Scaling Up Convergence and Coverage of Essential Social Services) by promoting optimal services, healthy diets and practices, along with the integration of actions to mitigate risks of gender-based violence (GBV) and sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA). 
UNICEF sustained its advocacy and awareness efforts to ensure children remain at the heart of actions aimed at adapting to, mitigating and transforming the impacts of climate-induced shocks. Also, UNICEF continued to strengthen the humanitarian-development nexus, ensuring that humanitarian aid happens alongside long-term development efforts. For instance, PARWARISH, which began as a humanitarian response in Pakistan, has evolved into an ongoing development programme. 
A transformative approach to prevent malnutrition among children aged 5-10 years and adolescents was developed by working with the health, education, and social protection sectors. For example, working with the health sector, 794,447 adolescent girls received iron-folic acid supplementation to reduce anaemia. A national dialogue was held to prevent the advertisement of unhealthy food and beverages in and around schools. Importantly, evidence generation on the drivers of malnutrition among adolescents has been ongoing to identify other necessary interventions to reduce malnutrition among school-age children. 
 
WASH, Climate Change and Environment
Climate change in Pakistan often has the greatest impact on the most vulnerable families. Many of these families are in rural, coastal and flood-prone areas and are already dealing with poverty and limited resources.
UNICEF supported the Government in developing and revising the national and provincial water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) strategies and policies to ensure the inclusion of climate resilience considerations. UNICEF’s continued technical and financial support resulted in increased WASH budget allocations in Sindh, operational WASH Management Information Systems (MIS) in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and Punjab, successful Joint Sector Reviews (JSRs) in KP, GB and AJK, and a federal Climate Resilient WASH social and behaviour change (SBC) Plan.
UNICEF provided gender-sensitive basic water services to 1,791,489 people (877,830 men and 913,659 women), including 924,446 who were reached with climate-resilient water services. Some 417,226 people (204,441 men and 212,785 women) were reached with basic sanitation services, of whom 196,386 received climate-resilient services. Also, 2,592,606 people were reached with hygiene promotion. Climate-resilient WASH services were provided in 302 schools and 71 healthcare facilities. 
Additionally, UNICEF supported 774 villages to be certified as Open Defecation Free (ODF), benefitting 1,722,238 people. UNICEF also trained 399 government staff on water quality monitoring and climate-resilient practices in KP, Sindh and Punjab.
UNICEF led sector-wide humanitarian WASH coordination efforts at national and provincial levels to assist vulnerable populations, including refugees. UNICEF made significant progress in addressing climate risks in the WASH sector through piloting solutions such as solar-powered water systems, floating wetlands for wastewater treatment, rainwater harvesting ponds and integrated resource recovery centres. This work secured a climate finance grant from the Adaptation Fund, in partnership with ICIMOD and UN-Women, to be implemented in 2025.
UNICEF partnered with international finance institutions (IFIs) to advocate for increased investment and improved WASH services in underserved areas. For example, UNICEF partnered with the World Bank to map WASH services in low-income areas in Balochistan and with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Punjab to provide complementary social and behaviour change interventions to the ADB’s solid waste management investment. 
To address period poverty, UNICEF collaborated with Santex, GIZ, and WaterAid to engage the Tax Authority and other non-traditional government agencies to reduce tariffs on menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) products. An MHH social and behavioural campaign strategy and toolkit were developed for rollout in 2025.
UNICEF advocated for including children and their needs in the climate policy and finance, engaging over 4,000 youth in the ‘COP in My City’ initiative and supporting federal and provincial officials and five young people to attend COP 29. As a result of advocacy and engagement with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as well as the Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination (MOCC&EC), Pakistan signed the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action at COP 29, committing to protect children and young people from the impacts of climate change.
 
Education
The economic, political and environmental challenges are exacerbating the crisis in education, as rising poverty is likely to force more children to drop out of school. At the same time, extreme weather events continue to disrupt learning. 
Working with federal and provincial governments, UNICEF has been a pivotal partner in improving education quality and accessibility for children in Pakistan. Through strategic leadership as co-convenor of the Prime Minister’s Education Emergency Taskforce and co-chair of the National Education Development Partner Group (NEDPG), UNICEF has aligned stakeholders on critical initiatives, including the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), disaster response and WASH in schools. UNICEF has also co-led the Education Sector Working Group (ESWG), ensuring effective emergency responses to floods and the Afghan refugee crisis while strengthening education system resilience and continuity.
UNICEF supported the reintegration of 357,214 out-of-school children (52 per cent girls) into formal and alternative learning pathways. In flood-affected areas, 176,258 children (45 per cent of girls) continued learning through UNICEF-established Temporary Learning Centres and rehabilitated schools. These centres provided a safe, stable environment where children could continue their education, helping them maintain a sense of normalcy. UNICEF also supported the training of 1,800 teachers (50 per cent female) in ‘education in emergencies’ and psychosocial support, equipping them to deliver quality education and care in challenging conditions. 
UNICEF’s Early Childhood Education (ECE) and Foundational Learning (FL) initiatives have strengthened provincial education systems. UNICEF supported the establishment of 2,881 ECE classrooms, benefitting 262,614 children (50 per cent girls) and trained 7,307 ECE teachers (72 per cent female), providing young children with a strong educational foundation and ensuring that children, especially girls, have access to quality learning experiences from a young age. UNICEF also supported innovative approaches, including the introduction of Jolly Phonics in Gilgit Baltistan (GB), which has enhanced FL skills and enabled children to develop strong reading and writing skills early on. Additionally, 288,997 children (48 per cent girls) benefitted from FL programmes focused on literacy and numeracy across provinces, with 13,548 government teachers (52 per cent female) trained to improve learning outcomes.
 
To address skill-building and alternative learning needs, UNICEF supported 2,087 Alternative Learning Programme centres, reaching 93,986 marginalized children and adolescents (56 per cent girls), including refugees. Vocational training programmes benefitted 13,361 youth (59 per cent girls), with 70 per cent transitioning to employment.
 
As a key GPE partner, UNICEF is managing grants to enhance foundational learning, non-formal education, and capacity building, reaching over 554,789 children and setting up opportunities for future generations.
 
Child Protection
The poly-crisis has heightened child protection challenges in Pakistan, leaving them more vulnerable to exploitation and abuse, neglect and displacement. 
To help increase protection for children in these challenging circumstances, UNICEF focused its support on addressing birth registration, child marriage, child labour and response services for children at risk and survivors of violence. These efforts strengthened systems, empowered communities and enhanced service delivery, including for communities experiencing humanitarian crises.
UNICEF supported the completion of the nationwide Child Labour Survey, facilitating the development of child labour policies and costed action plans in Punjab and Gilgit Baltistan to help address and reduce child labour. 
Birth registration efforts advanced through partnerships with NADRA and local governments, with Sindh becoming the first province to waive birth registration fees. This initiative is a significant step towards ensuring that every child in Sindh, and eventually across Pakistan, is recognized, counted and protected. Integration with health services facilitated the registration of over 600,000 children.
UNICEF’s advocacy against child marriage saw the launch of the ‘Bolo’ campaign, along with groundbreaking research into cultural and religious influences, aimed at identifying and addressing the root causes and raising awareness of child marriage to contribute to reducing the prevalence. Adolescents across Pakistan were empowered through dedicated forums and life-skills training, while 25,000 caregivers benefitted from positive parenting programmes designed to create supportive and safer family environments. 
A renewed vision for response services was advanced, and national commitments were made at the Global Conference for Ending Violence Against Children. Child protection services were enhanced and reached over 3,400 children. Child Protection Units now cover 42 districts, and PRIMERO – which provides a robust digital platform for managing protection-related data, ensuring efficient and effective case handling – was rolled out to enhance case management systems. Provincial workforce strategies were introduced, engaging 539 frontline workers. UNICEF advanced Justice for Children Initiatives (JCIs) through key partnerships, finalizing a child-sensitive jail monitoring manual, a competency framework for justice system actors, and designing a diversion programme.
UNICEF supported ongoing alternative care reforms. UNICEF facilitated Pakistan's first child advisory panel to contribute to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) Committee’s preparations. UNICEF Pakistan also directly engaged with the CRC Committee as part of the 2025 review process.
Humanitarian efforts continued, including delivering mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) services to over 53,000 individuals and supporting gender-based violence (GBV) services to more than 58,000 women and children. 
Social Policy
UNICEF advanced inclusive social protection and evidence-based policymaking in collaboration with the Government and international partners. As a partner of the Ministry of Planning, Development & Special Initiatives, UNICEF supported the government to enhance poverty measurement, implement the Sustainable Developmental Goals (SDG) frameworks, and promote regional development through key publications such as the National Poverty and Inequality Report and updated Multidimensional Poverty Index. These efforts strengthened resource allocation and policy implementation. 
Advocating for equitable investments, UNICEF conducted the Public Expenditure Reviews (PER) for Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) and trained 577 high-level stakeholders in Public Finance for Children and Adaptive Social Protection. Tailored curricula for Public Finance for Nutrition (PF4N) and Early Childhood Development (ECD) were developed, bolstering financial tracking and policy optimization. Regional training in collaboration with the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics further strengthened provincial capacities.
Inclusion remained central, with the Situation Analysis of Children with Disabilities and Post-Flood Disability Assessment informing policies to enhance education, healthcare and protection access for vulnerable groups. These efforts supported 14,882 children in KP and Balochistan, providing visual and hearing aids. Over 170 stakeholders participated in consultations aligning with the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) Disability Inclusion Strategy.
Digital financial literacy initiatives trained 86,038 beneficiaries, including 510 women who were able to reach marginalized communities. Skill development programmes trained 200 individuals, including Afghan refugees, in e-commerce, mobile repair and solar panel installation, fostering economic resilience.
Over 1,500 people received hands-on training to modernize data systems and upgrade the National Socio-Economic Registry (NSER). UNICEF also facilitated data exchange among regions, improving targeting for social protection. Collaborating with BISP and GIZ, UNICEF launched a pilot integrating birth registration with social schemes in Balochistan and automated modules for the Hybrid Social Protection System.
In 2024, UNICEF led five thematic evaluations in WASH, SBC, ECD/ECE, Zawer e Taleem and Nutrition, along with five studies, including the Rapid Assessment of Returned Communities in Flood-Affected Areas, the Disability SitAn, the Post-Flood Assessment on Children with Disabilities and the Public Expenditure Review (PER) in Punjab and KP. Knowledge-sharing platforms, including the Punjab Social Protection Policy Forum and IMPrESS (Intermediate Moderated Programme for Evaluation Systems’ Strengthening) workshops, strengthened partnerships and enhanced governance frameworks. Research and evaluation efforts remained robust, with eight evaluations and nine studies. The ‘#EvidenceMatters’ event engaged over 160 stakeholders, reinforcing UNICEF's commitment to data-driven strategies. UNICEF's innovative contributions included winning the Impact Catalyst Fund for a Randomized Control Trial on the Adaptive Social Protection Initiative. The Flood Response Assessment and WASH Enabling Environment Evaluation engaged multi-stakeholders, with the latter earning a ‘satisfactory’ Global Evaluation Reports Oversight System (GEROS) rating.

In addition to the government, UNICEF has worked with other UN organizations, international financial institutions, the private sector, and other stakeholders for the rights and wellbeing of children in Pakistan. The past year witnessed a significant increase in new civil society and private sector partnerships. A total of 50 distinctive Programme Cooperation Agreements (PCAs) remained active with 80 programme documents (PDs) in the reporting year, of which 34 new PDs (including 22 regular PDs) were signed and aligned with Country Programme results. Active CSO partnerships were valued at approximately US$ 39 million, of which US$12.4 million was supplies. 
UNICEF provided technical and financial support, including capacity-building training on HACT/financial management/fraud awareness and PSEA reporting and investigations. In addition, 26 new contingency PDs were developed across programme and field offices covering multi-hazard scenarios. These are all valid until December 2027 and can be activated during an emergency.
In health, UNICEF’s main partner is the MoNHSRC, while other partners include the Federal Directorate of Immunization, the Malaria Control Programme, provincial health departments, WHO, UNFPA, GAVI, Gates Foundation, GPEI, the Pediatric Association of Pakistan, the Health Information System Pakistan, the University of Oslo, private hospitals and civil society organizations (CSOs). The CSOs have been vital in assisting in responding to emergencies and improving health service delivery, particularly in remote areas.
Multiple public and private partnerships were established to promote neutral voices in support of vaccination and combat misinformation, including with political cabinets of major parties, the provincial Scholars Task Force, the Directorate General Health, the Directorate of Education, print and electronic media and major universities. The Polio team organized Ulema Conferences at provincial and regional levels, including a Grand Ulema conference in South Waziristan and Islamabad chaired by the Prime Minister. UNICEF's advocacy efforts led to MoUs with religious leaders, institutions, Ulema, doctors, celebrities and cricketers, enhancing programme visibility and building trust. Innovative approaches like drumbeaters, bike mobilizers and partnerships with social media influencers were utilized to enhance campaign visibility in high-risk areas.
In nutrition, UNICEF built and maintained strong partnerships with the Government, UN agencies, CSOs, academic and research institutions, and multilateral and international financial institutions. The MoNHSR&C, the Ministry of Planning, Development & Special Initiatives (MoPD&SI), and the Ministry of Poverty Alleviation and Social Safety (MoPA&SS) and their respective provincial departments/sections and cells are the main government partners for nutrition and child development. UNICEF expanded partnerships with the Education Ministry for school-based programming and a healthy school environment, as well as with Provincial Food Authorities. UNICEF contributed to the partnerships by by providing technical, human resources and financial support. 
UNICEF continued convening the UN Nutrition Subgroup under the UN Cooperation Framework 2023-2027, Nutrition Sector Coordination and Nutrition Development Partners forum. In this forum, UNICEF worked with diverse partnerships during the reporting period, for example, WFP, WHO, UN Women, ILO and FAO, as well as the World Bank for joint programmes, including the BISP Nashunoma programme (BNP), emergency preparedness and response, the Joint SDG Fund mobilization, and the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) Analysis for both food insecurity and malnutrition. In addition, UNICEF partnered with UN Women and the Pakistan Business Council to initiate a Childcare Models analysis.  
To strengthen early childhood development (ECD) and expand knowledge and evidence, UNICEF partnered with academic and research institutes such as Aga Khan University, University of Child Health Sciences Lahore, Khyber Medical University, Allama Iqbal Open University and Health Services Academy. UNICEF supported capacity strengthening, human resources development, the development of ECD-related guidelines, and implementation of research and evidence generation. Additionally, UNICEF collaborated with professional associations, including the Pakistan Pediatrics Association and Pakistan ECD Alliance, for advocacy, capacity strengthening, and further mainstreaming nutrition and child development into various systems. 
UNICEF worked with government bodies, including the Commission of Afghan Refugees and with CSOs such as the ACF, Shifa Foundation, Save the Children, Care International, Muslim Hands, Qatar Charity, International Rescue Committee (IRC) and People's Primary Healthcare Initiative (PPHI). Partners, such as the Medical Emergency Resilience Foundation (MERF), were engaged in service delivery for communities in flood-affected and deprived areas. 
New partnerships were established in 2024 with the Trust for Malnutrition and Stunted Growth and the Sindh Institute of Child Health & Neonatology to support innovative approaches on promoting nutrition and child development. UNICEF worked with the Interactive Research and Development and Planning Commission for a deworming programme for school-age children and with GAIN and the National Fortification Alliance for large-scale food fortification. Meanwhile, UNICEF engaged the Pakistan Business Council to strategically involve private sector entities in promoting family-friendly policies. 
UNICEF also expanded partnerships with the Climate Change Ministry, the Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security for climate-resilient nutrition programming and food systems transformation, as well as the Ministry of Religious and Interfaith Affairs and Council of Islamic Ideology for engagement of religious and interfaith leaders in promoting nutrition and child development.
In water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), UNICEF collaborated with communities, national, provincial and territorial governments, international and national NGOs, donors (The Netherlands, Sweden, USA, ECHO, Korea, Kuwait, Ernst and Young), international financial institutions (the World Bank, the ADB and AFD), academia (the University of Engineering and Technology, KP) and the private sector (Santex) to implement its climate-resilient WASH programme. The programme improved water quality monitoring and evidence generation through partnerships with the Ministry of Climate Change and Environmental Coordination (MOCC&EC) and the Ministry of Water Resources/Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources. UNICEF worked with Health and Education ministries to enhance WASH services in schools and healthcare facilities.
At provincial level, collaborations with Public Health and Engineering and Local Government Departments and NGOs provided climate-resilient WASH services. UNICEF, in partnership with the private sector Santex, as well as GIZ and WaterAid, advocated for MHH product tax reform and innovations. UNICEF also strengthened partnerships with the World Bank, ADB and AFD to leverage WASH investments for vulnerable populations.
In education UNICEF has built strong partnerships with federal and provincial education departments, their implementing directorates, development and emergency partners such as WB, GPE, FCDO, JICA, Save the Children and UNESCO, academia, civil society and communities to implement its education agenda and tackle systemic challenges. Through partnering with Sukkur IBA University, the Aga Khan University-Institute for Educational Development, Cambridge Education, Indus Resource Centre (IRC), MHI, CARE International and the British Council, UNICEF has implemented innovative learning and skill education programmes. UNICEF also engaged with parents, adolescents and local communities to strengthen school governance and sustainability.
In child protection, UNICEF established strategic partnerships with stakeholders such as the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA), Telenor, ILO, NCRC and provincial labour departments. These collaborations facilitated efforts in child labour policy formulation, child online protection (COP) and birth registration systems. Partnerships with CSOs like IRC, DANESH, and the School of Leadership Foundation expanded mental health and parenting support initiatives. UNICEF also partnered with local governments, including the Ministry of Human Rights, provincial child protection commissions, and authorities to implement case management systems. 
In Social Policy UNICEF worked with diverse government agencies, including  MOPDSI, BISP, the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), the Social Welfare Department Punjab, the Zakat & Batul Mal Department Punjab, the Punjab Social Protection Authority, Planning & Development Department  KP, the Planning & Development Department, Balochistan, Social Welfare Department AJK, Planning & Development Department AJK and Social Welfare Department GB.  Additionally, UNICEF worked with international and local organizations: SUN (Scaling Up Nutrition), AZAT and SRSP, as well as with academic and research institutions, such as PIDE and Islamabad Bar Association(IBA).
In 2024, the SBC Think Tank was established in partnership with the Islamic Research Institute to integrate applied behavioural science into academic research, teaching and social dialogue, with the aim of shifting social norms and practices.
Overall, UNICEF partnerships have played a crucial role in improving outcomes across all stages of a child's life cycle, and  UNICEF’s donors have enabled the mobilization of resources necessary for transformative interventions.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, the UNICEF country office faced challenges in accelerating and achieving results at scale for the most marginalized children throughout every stage of the life cycle. These challenges were exacerbated by the global economic crisis, political instability, gender inequality, and climate change. 
The early stages of the life cycle presented notable threats to infant survival and development, particularly with the sharp resurgence of wild poliovirus. This was partly due to security constraints in Balochistan and Southern KP, which left more than 250,000 children unreachable during the most recent National Immunization Days (NIDS) in October. The large mobile migrant population also served as a significant vector for transmission. Additionally, the immunization campaigns faced obstacles such as vaccine boycotts, fake finger marking of children who had not received the vaccines, and the hiding of children. The health sector's poor prioritization, late planning, vertical implementation, and low health financing (1% of GDP) further compounded these challenges, making the sector heavily reliant on external funding. 
To address some of these challenges, the Social and Behavior Change Communication (SBCC) Strategy was updated, allowing for targeted, region-specific approaches. UNICEF trained 3,858 frontline workers in interpersonal communication, improving household interactions and boosting vaccination effectiveness. The ‘Campaign Facilitators Initiative’ engaged local influencers to improve access in high-risk areas, while UNICEF's Communication Network (COMNet) averted 99 potential boycotts and resolved 77 per cent of reported incidents. Creative approaches like drumbeaters and bike branding in Punjab enhanced community engagement and reduced repeated door-to-door visits.
Moving forward, the polio immunization programme will use a two-pronged approach: following the 2-4-6-month vaccination schedule and regularly assessing progress to make adjustments as needed. UNICEF will also strengthen partnerships with local influencers, media, and community leaders, expand strategies for mapping and engaging the mobile migrant population, and ensure gender-responsive programming with a gradual, systematic approach. 
Other priorities in health include strengthening provincial platforms, enhancing newborn data systems for quality care, conducting study visits for the adoption of DHIS2, engaging the private sector to bridge gaps in primary health services, scaling up the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI), solarizing health facilities to reduce costs, addressing lead poisoning, and increasing emergency contingency supplies.
In the nutrition sector, limited geographic and population coverage of nutrition programmes and weak capacity of implementing partners posed significant challenges. The widespread marketing of unhealthy ultra-processed foods and beverages, coupled with a lack of regulations and limited capacity of duty bearers, further complicated efforts. 
Strategic partnerships and engagement with professional associations and religious entities yielded positive results. For example, working with the Pakistan Pediatric Association accelerated the Sindh BMS Act enactment and the initiation of the first-ever Human Milk Bank in Pakistan. The Nutrition Matching Fund also encouraged governments, including BISP, to incentivize domestic resources for nutrition.
Strong leadership and measuring progress have been proven to be key to success in convergence programming. Also, having a dedicated team for nutrition sector coordination as well as capacity strengthening have improved nutrition outcomes. 
Moving forward, UNICEF will focus greater attention towards the 0-6-month age group and adolescent girls and young women to ensure they are well-nourished before possible pregnancies and that babies receive age-appropriate, nutritious, complementary feeding. UNICEF will also work towards strengthening capacity and programming on nutrition issues related to climate actions and gender, involving SBC and community engagement. Additionally, there will be a focus on improving public expenditure and further mainstreaming ECD interventions within the health system, including Early Identification & Intervention (EII) for disabilities or developmental delays and promoting positive parenting and early stimulation.
In the WASH sector, UNICEF faced challenges such as institutional fragmentation, lack of regulation, and rising electricity prices. Financial constraints in communities, exacerbated by inflation and insufficient government budgets, limited sanitation progress. Minimal climate finance was invested in WASH. 
UNICEF will support the development of a climate rationale and quantify sanitation emissions to increase the evidence required to mobilize climate finance, especially in sanitation services. Collaboration with the private sector, including Santex, advanced efforts related to menstrual health and hygiene (MHH). Continuous training of government staff is required to strengthen water quality monitoring and management. As International Financial Institutions (IFI) are significantly financing the WASH sector in Pakistan, UNICEF will increase efforts to influence large-scale public and IFI investments in WASH services.
Education remains vital to breaking the cycle of poverty, yet Pakistan still has 25.3 million out-of-school children, and even among those in primary schools, many are not learning. UNICEF collaborated with the Government and stakeholders to implement evidence-based strategies, emphasizing the importance of partnerships and data-driven decision-making. Persistent challenges include socio-cultural norms, weak coordination, and inadequate capacity. UNICEF's future agenda focuses on addressing learning poverty, funding gaps, and access disparities. Key priorities include expanding flexible learning pathways, integrating skill-based learning, and leveraging technology for monitoring and scaling up successful models. Community involvement and private-sector partnerships are crucial.
In the realm of child protection, securing government ownership and finalizing the Child Protection Policy in Pakistan remained a challenge. Integrating birth registration with health services, particularly through health worker support, proved to be a key issue requiring innovative approaches. Partnerships with civil society organizations played a pivotal role in scaling initiatives related to child marriage prevention, parenting and community-based structures, and enhancing government ownership. 
Challenges in child protection systems highlighted the need for case management strengthening. Moving forward, UNICEF will invest in continued advocacy, innovative solutions, and cross-sector collaboration which is key to close the gaps and scale up child protection efforts for marginalized children. 
For social policy, social protection, and evidence generation, forming high-level and strategic partnerships with various stakeholders, including academic institutions, facilitated a multi-dimensional approach to addressing child well-being. Moreover, for research and evaluation, UNICEF will commit to strengthening local evaluation skills and infrastructure as a priority to ensure better programme assessment and evidence generation. 
Given the constraints of public finances and the ongoing impact of the poly-crisis on Pakistan, UNICEF will seek to be more flexible and explore innovative programmes and financing mechanisms while strengthening and expanding partnerships with international donors, private sector stakeholders, women- and girl-led organizations, and community organizations to mobilize additional resources. Challenges in data collection highlight the need for continuous training and capacity building.

Over 659 million children call South Asia home,[1] accounting for over a quarter of the world’s children. Children, and especially girls, face severe challenges to achieving their potential – the region ranks second-lowest globally in gender parity with less than 64 per cent of its gender gap closed [2].
 
Economic growth across the region is exceeding projections, with growth now expected to exceed 6.4 per cent in 2024, and likely to remain robust at around 6.2 per cent in 2025 –2026 barring risks due to extreme weather, earthquakes, debt distress or social and political unrest [3]. Nevertheless, nearly 148.7 million people are projected to live on below US$2.15 a day, accounting for over a fifth of the world’s people living in poverty [4]. Regionally, greater-than-expected growth in India and economic recovery in Pakistan, Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka counterbalance the modest growth seen in Maldives and setbacks due to social unrest in Bangladesh [3]. Afghanistan’s slow economic recovery remains fragile and uncertain, with deep structural issues including the exclusion of women from economic activity [5].
 
In a year of elections, political instability and insecurity remained a barrier to effective operations. In Bangladesh, elections were followed by political unrest and a change of government accompanied by the ongoing Rohingya refugee issue. The security situation deteriorated in Pakistan’s northwest with humanitarian workers (especially those involved in vaccination activities) targeted, and political instability caused regular interruptions to service delivery. 
 
Social protection systems are underdeveloped and South Asia has some of the lowest coverage rates globally. The region also has the lowest levels of social spending as a share of GDP of any region in the world, partly driven by low revenue generation and exacerbated by high government debt.
 
Climate change continued to severely affect children’s lives, well-being and development. Over 6 million children were affected by severe rainfall, flooding and landslides in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, Afghanistan and Sri Lanka [6]. School closures due to climate events disrupted learning for 128 million students in South Asia, 53 per cent of all students affected globally [7]. The most marginalized children, such as girls, children with disabilities and those in rural areas, were most severely affected. Air pollution was a growing issue, accounting for 240,000 child deaths in India and Pakistan alone [8]. Despite rising demand, a regional shortfall in green skills persists.
 
While the region as a whole has improved health outcomes, progress has been uneven across countries and demographic groups. Maternal and neonatal mortality have declined significantly (by 67 and 50 per cent respectively in the last two decades) [9]. Although the COVID-19 pandemic led to a decline in immunization rates, most South Asian countries have now regained pre-pandemic levels. DTP3 stood at 90 per cent in 2023 (89 per cent in 2019), yet over 3.6 million children remain vulnerable to vaccine-preventable diseases [10]. South Asia is the only region where polio remains endemic, with 99 cases reported in Pakistan and Afghanistan in 2024 [11]. The regional disease burden is increasingly complex, with non-communicable diseases now accounting for 65.3 per cent, and increasing issues related to injury, mental health and environmental health [12].
 
South Asia has made important gains in improving maternal and child nutrition, with declining rates of stunting (2012: 41.5 per cent, 2022: 31.4 per cent) and increased exclusive breastfeeding (2012: 47 per cent, 2022: 60 per cent). However, the proportion of children under five with wasting is high and stagnant (2022: 14.8 per cent) [13]. A quarter of adolescent girls are deficient in essential micronutrients [14]. The poor nutritional status of adolescent girls and women drives intergenerational cycles of undernutrition, with poor diet quality remaining a key driver of child malnutrition and growing consumption of processed and unhealthy foods. Undernutrition is concentrated in impoverished and marginalized households.
 
South Asia’s ongoing learning crisis disproportionally affects the poorest and most vulnerable. The region is home to 93 million out-of-school children, including 78 million secondary-school-aged adolescents [15], the latter including virtually all girls in Afghanistan. The digital divide disproportionately affects girls, limiting their access to learning and skills. Six of ten children, even those in school, are in “learning poverty”, i.e. unable to read by age 10 [16].
 
Despite soaring enrolment in higher education, young people are ill-equipped for the demands of modern job markets, especially the most vulnerable, including young people with disabilities. Youth unemployment is the highest in Asia-Pacific, and 42.4 per cent of young women are not in education, employment or training: the largest gender gap globally [17]. Political tensions across the region, but especially in Afghanistan, Bangladesh and parts of Pakistan, disrupted the lives of youth and adolescents in 2024, and limited space for civic engagement, participation and skill development.
 
Demographic shifts, multi-dimensional poverty, frequent shocks fuelled by climate change, natural disasters and other humanitarian crises, and deeply ingrained harmful social norms, exacerbate child protection violations. The region accounts for nearly half of the world’s child brides and a quarter of its unregistered children under the age of five [18]. Pushback against child rights is increasing, and risks of sexual exploitation and abuse are heightened by deep-rooted patriarchal norms and humanitarian crises, particularly in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh and India.

Digital access continues to offer opportunities for civic engagement and advocacy, but digital exclusion also persists, especially for girls and young people from marginalized communities. Online safety, misinformation and disinformation, and shrinking press freedom and trust in institutions are growing concerns.

Every child survives and thrives
In 2024, UNICEF’s Regional Office for South Asia (ROSA) supported Bangladesh to introduce the potentially life-saving HPV vaccine, reaching 5.6 million girls, and facilitated preparations for HPV introduction in Pakistan and Nepal in 2025. Big Catch-Up campaigns and expanded routine immunization in Pakistan, Afghanistan, Nepal and India were crucial to close gaps in coverage since the COVID-19 pandemic, reaching 3.76 million missed children. Innovative social and behaviour change (SBC) approaches were critical to creating service demand. However, polio cases surged in Pakistan and Afghanistan, necessitating partner engagement to address bottlenecks in 2025. 

ROSA, in partnership with WHO and UNFPA, supported seven countries to implement and monitor maternal and newborn health plans, providing targeted support to Bhutan’s Every Newborn Action Plan. A regional action plan on adolescent pregnancy was launched, with country-specific plans under development with ROSA support.
 
ROSA drafted primary health-care country profiles, district systems analyses and a regional operational framework, with finalization expected in 2025. Recognizing the complexity of health system challenges in Afghanistan dedicated technical assistance was provided to conduct primary and community-based health-care reviews and start developing a UNICEF health strategy.
 
A Regional Oxygen Scale-up Strategy laid the foundation for introducing oxygen systems for maternal and newborn survival. ROSA built on COVID-19 investments, ensuring their sustainability by strengthening the capacity of Country Offices (COs) and health workers on oxygen systems. Afghanistan and Maldives were also supported with oxygen plants.
 
To advance South Asia’s digital transformation, ROSA mapped digital health solutions across all eight countries, developed a regional Digital Health Transformation Strategy, provided technical and capacity building support and launched a Digital Health National Planning Course. These strengthened CO capacities to advocate with and support governments.
 
With ROSA technical and strategic guidance, COs mobilized resources and strengthened multisectoral collaboration for community health and nutrition (CHN) systems as a key pillar of primary health care, through a regional CHN workshop, strategic partner engagements, technical support for country-specific roadmaps and action plans and a regional dashboard, alongside evidence generation.
 
ROSA developed a Model Law for Protection of Breastfeeding in South Asia to support countries in strengthening their own legal measures against infant formula marketing. The Office convened regional technical consultations which galvanized countries to improve nutritional care for at-risk infants, and advanced the UNGAP on Child Wasting by providing technical support, leveraging the Child Nutrition Fund for domestic financing in Pakistan and Bangladesh, and drafting a country operational plan in Nepal.
 
Strategic guidance and technical support to COs translated country commitments from the 2023 regional conference into Maternal Nutrition Acceleration Plans (2024–2027). With sustained advocacy and technical support by ROSA, five countries initiated antenatal multiple micronutrient supplementation. ROSA convened a regional technical meeting with governments and regional development partners, resulting in a call to action to scale up food fortification.
 
Every child learns
With ROSA support for inclusive programme design and implementation, foundational learning advanced in all eight countries. ROSA partnered with the World Bank to convene a major high-level regional event in which government officials and partners deepened knowledge and developed action points on learning assessments, teacher support, multilingual instruction and parental and community engagement.
 
All COs advanced digital learning with ROSA technical assistance and resource mobilization. Strategy and co-creation workshops in Bhutan, Pakistan, Nepal and Maldives led to the adoption of evidence-informed strategies to guide digital transformation based on local needs. With ROSA support, several countries introduced global flagship education initiatives. Nepal joined the Learning Passport; Nepal and Bhutan introduced Accessible Digital Textbooks to promote inclusive learning; Nepal and Sri Lanka introduced the Akelius initiative focusing on early grades and marginalized children respectively; and in Bangladesh, a new Learning Passport instance equipped para-workers with essential skills.
 
In Afghanistan, where girls face prohibitions on secondary education, ROSA supported the CO to design alternative learning pathways, including digital learning. These included Dana, a learning platform built on the Learning Passport, which supported out-of-school children and was also used to provide teachers with access to resources and training materials in Afghanistan.
 
Young people across South Asia strengthened rights and opportunities as COs addressed bottlenecks and reduced disparities in participation, skills development and climate action. A new Regional Strategy on Young People in Climate Action guided efforts to strengthen youth representation in climate advocacy, leading to the active participation of 20 UNICEF-supported youth delegates from six countries in COP29. 
 
Over 300 young people were empowered to lead civic actions and influence policy decisions through the regional rollout of the UNICEF Youth Advocacy Guide. The Green Rising South Asia framework, launched in collaboration with COs, fostered regional scale-up of successful youth-led climate initiatives. 
 
ROSA knowledge sessions on green skills at the Asia Pacific Youth Development Forum and Asia Pacific Youth Symposium, creating deeper trans-regional understanding of young people’s perspectives. The 32 girls from 20 Asia-Pacific countries who attended the Girls Go Green summit co-created a Joint Recommendation on inclusive and girl- and women-centred green skills development. 
 
A regional investment case for youth-inclusive local government planning targeted systemic improvements in decision-making processes in India, Nepal, Bangladesh and Bhutan, while a new partnership with UNDP led to the co-development of an online module on youth political participation and the launch of the Regional Youth Parliament on Climate Action as a platform for youth-led governance reform. These innovative partnerships and platforms are crucial for empowering young people as agents of change.
 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation
In 2024, the successful conclusion of the five-year regional programme on child labour highlighted the strengths and challenges of supporting a child protection system-strengthening approach in India and Pakistan. The launch of the third phase of the Global Programme to End Child Marriage brought renewed momentum and catalysed strategic progress through evidence generation, advocacy, gender-transformative programming, capacity building, technical support missions and resource mobilization.  In collaboration with Girls Not Brides, ROSA developed a joint guidance note on partnering with women-led organizations to address child marriage.
 
ROSA supported efforts to scale up birth registration, especially in high-burden countries (Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and Nepal) through advocacy and partnerships including the regional civil registration professionals’ network. 
 
ROSA supported participation in the Global Ministerial Conference to end Violence Against Children. Four countries attended the conference and pledged to enact laws, implement programmes and develop the capacity of the social service workforce, signing the CP Systems Strengthening Framework for Action. ROSA will follow up with support for sustained advocacy to take these commitments forward. ROSA also developed the capacity of national human and child rights institutions to bring the child rights agenda to the fore in all our work.
 
ROSA convened over 300 regional and global experts to an international conference on child and adolescent mental health which provided a space to share new research and evidence, and for practitioners and researchers to collaborate and learn.
 
Systems were strengthened at country level to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA), with capacity building and training for COs to establish PSEA governance systems. The Bhutan, Nepal and Afghanistan COs established PSEA Focal Point systems in 2024, positioning them to implement their PSEA Action Plans. CSOs were also trained to build their investigative capacity to promptly and safely investigate allegations without harming victims or complainants. In Afghanistan, ROSA supported a comprehensive capacity gap analysis of CSO partners and implemented a targeted capacity-building plan. As a result, donor compliance was enhanced, PSEA tools were adapted for effective use in South Asian contexts, and children’s vulnerabilities were reduced. 
 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment
In 2024, COs drew on ROSA technical support to implement the Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan and mobilize resources including climate finance for health facility solar electrification (GAVI-WHO-UNICEF flagship), ecosystem-based adaptation (Adaptation Fund) and climate readiness (Green Climate Fund, GCF). COs drew on GCF accreditation, achieved with ROSA support, to leverage new means of channelling climate finance to children. 
 
With ROSA support, countries improved knowledge management and developed evidence-based WASH and climate change strategies. The eight countries produced 15 WASH knowledge products, drafted work plans and performed climate landscape analyses for children. In updating their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0), countries integrated child-sensitive and sectoral commitments, with climate focal points supported by ROSA through dedicated technical working groups. ROSA support was instrumental in amplifying young people’s voices in NDC development processes.
 
With support from ROSA, Bangladesh and India scaled up inclusive city-wide sanitation, addressing wastewater treatment deficiencies. In Dhaka, the North City Corporation trialled nature-based wastewater solutions, laying the foundation for future scale-up and financing of sustainable solutions that will reduce methane emissions and antimicrobial resistance. 
 
To maintain sustainable water supply for children across the region, ROSA supported real-time monitoring of groundwater extraction from the Ganges Basin, which underpins the water supply for four South Asian countries (Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Nepal) and has historically high withdrawal rates. 
 
ROSA assisted countries to maintain and improve hand hygiene practices as crucial to preventing the spread of diseases. Bangladesh developed a strategic paper on hand hygiene, while India launched state-level roadmaps. ROSA engaged in cross-sectoral review of  WASH-FIT implementation in health-care facilities across the region, facilitating workshops and offering tailored recommendations to improve waste management and infection control for safe and hygienic health facilities for children.
 
A key innovation in 2024 was facilitating local governments in Nepal to establish a revenue model for improved cookstoves using carbon credits. This not only reduces exposure of children and women to air pollution, but it will also potentially channel US$4.3M to local government services for children. The model is now being scaled up as an innovative and sustainable means of tapping into carbon markets. ROSA also provided technical support to solar market assessments in all eight countries, with a detailed mapping of the regional solar energy landscape, identifying opportunities for expanding solarization. 
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life
UNICEF ROSA continues to strengthen inclusive and resilient social protection systems for children and their families while advancing evidence and advocacy on investing in children through public finance in South Asia.
 
ROSA is positioning social protection as a critical tool for child well-being, both in stable contexts and during crises. Through regional dialogues and knowledge-sharing events with partners, such as the ADB, FCDO, World Bank, ILO, ESCAP, UNDP, ROSA highlighted the contribution of social protection, including child benefits, in reducing child marriage, building strong care and support systems, ensuring disability inclusiveness, mitigating negative coping mechanisms, and supporting recovery from shocks. This was complemented by direct technical support to countries, including Bhutan, where social protection was integrated into the 13th Five-Year Plan, and India and Nepal, where collaboration advanced gender-responsive social protection and care systems. In Nepal, ROSA facilitated donor discussions to leverage social protection systems to expand coverage and strengthen linkages with health and nutrition services. At the same time, efforts to build shock-responsive social protection systems were reinforced through a regional convening that brought together National Disaster Management Authorities and Social Welfare Ministries to improve coordination, identify vulnerable children and families, and optimize delivery mechanisms. Humanitarian settings remained a priority, with direct support ensuring the continuity of cash transfers and the launch of the Mother and Child Cash Transfer Programme, strengthening resilience for vulnerable families. Similarly, in Pakistan, ROSA facilitated a Humanitarian Cash Transfer capacity assessment to enhance emergency response mechanisms.
 
In public finance for children, UNICEF (jointly ROSA and EAPRO) reaffirmed its strategic partnership with the EU, strengthening child-focused budgeting and social sector financing across the region. Under this collaboration, UNICEF convened governments and partners in a knowledge exchange to improve budget prioritization, efficiency, and equity, supporting Ministries of Finance in making informed investment decisions for children. A key milestone was the collection and analysis of ten years of budget and expenditure data across key social sectors in the region, enhancing evidence-based decision-making. Advocacy at the Financing for Development regional consultation further reinforced the need for an enabling fiscal environment that prioritizes social investments for human development. ROSA continued to support Country Offices engagement with the Ministries of Finance in Bhutan, the Maldives, India, and Sri Lanka, providing technical support and advocacy for child-responsive budgeting and equitable allocations across decentralized levels. In the Maldives, ROSA supported the Country Office through technical guidance on the social protection budget brief and engagement with the Ministry of Finance and the National Social Protection Agency, ensuring that children and families remained central to discussions on planned fiscal reforms.
 
This approach not only strengthened national systems but also positioned UNICEF as a trusted policy advisor and partner in advancing inclusive and sustainable social protection and public finance reforms for children in South Asia.
 
Gender
ROSA support was instrumental in the development of the action plan on adolescent pregnancy in South Asia  in collaboration between SAARC, UNICEF South Asia, UNFPA Asia Pacific and WHO, and high-level consultations involving SAARC member states, civil society organisations, academia, and young representatives. The action plan was presented in the Beijing 30+ ministerial meeting in Nov 2024 with 3 member states (Pakistan, Maldives and Nepal) declaring affirmative actions to take forward key recommendations. SAARC has instituted a technical working group for oversight of the action plan.
 
Multi-country gender barrier analysis done in 6 out of the 8 countries in South Asia has influenced the gender integration in immunization plans and immunization-related resource mobilization processes with technical support from ROSA. 
 
Humanitarian response, preparedness and disaster risk reduction (DRR)
Some 25.2 million people, including 13.2 million children, were reached with UNICEF humanitarian assistance in South Asia. Regional surge support to emergencies of exceptional scale in Bangladesh and Nepal ensured timely flash updates and situation reports, supporting funding proposals and effective response plans. 
 
Systems were strengthened for disaster preparedness and response in all eight countries through a knowledge exchange attended by national disaster authorities and ministries of social welfare, resulting in a roadmap for child-centred DRR planning, which countries committed to implement. ROSA fostered inter-agency collaboration by contributing to the revised Asia-Pacific Action Plan for the Sendai Framework, ensuring children are reflected in DRR planning.
 
Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) was institutionalized through roadmaps in Afghanistan, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. These strengthened feedback mechanisms and mainstreamed AAP into programme cycles. AAP mechanisms were instrumental in quality flood and earthquake response in Afghanistan, Bangladesh and India. A regionwide baseline study on disability inclusion in humanitarian action furthered equitable response and led to targeted interventions in Bangladesh, India, Nepal and Sri Lanka. This laid a foundation for continued partnerships with organizations for persons with disabilities in humanitarian programming.
 
Data, research, and evaluation
With ROSA support, CO staff conducted and analysed large-scale surveys such as the Household Income and Expenditure Survey and supported Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) design and implementation in Nepal, Bangladesh and two regions of Pakistan. The Office built regional skills in data analysis, providing training on the use of Small Area Estimation in daily analyses, and use of data in humanitarian action such as through profiling of populations in need, geospatial identification of populations at risk and assessment of social protection programmes. The office also built capacity on data visualization which enabled COs to visualize country information (India), review field reports (Afghanistan) and support government assessments of sub-national vulnerabilities (Maldives and Nepal). 
 
Evaluation capacity was enhanced across the region, with the launch of a National Evaluation Capacity Development road map; two COs (Sri Lanka, Bangladesh) completed their action plans and the remainder were in progress. About 170 regional government officials built their evaluation skills through participation in IMPRESS, an online training programme, and other ROSA-supported forums. With ROSA support, a high-level delegation attended ExCEL training in South Africa.
 
Nine evaluations were completed by the end of 2024, with 10 more underway. ROSA provided consistent mentoring, technical and quality assurance to all eight COs and used the South Asia region evaluation network to share lessons learned and best practices to ensure mutual learning. The Office also completed a regional meta-synthesis and meta-analysis of what works to prevent child marriage in South Asia. 
 
ROSA contributed global knowledge-sharing on evaluation by leading the establishment of a global working group for young evaluators, conducting open sessions on key topics related to evaluation, and feeding into UNICEF webinars on AI for evaluation and evidence in emergencies. The involvement of young people in evidence-generation was also advanced, with tools enabling adolescents to monitor, analyse and evaluate their reality in Pakistan, Bangladesh and India.
 
Advocacy and communication
ROSA piloted two approaches for regional support to country teams to expand advocacy capacity in the region: a slower multi-touchpoint approach for nutrition and a faster approach supporting climate advocacy goals linked to the global Sustainability and Climate Action Plan (SCAP). All COs strengthened their country strategies with support provided via the UNICEF Media Hub.  
 
A highly successful digital engagement strategy placed ROSA among the three UNICEF Offices with the highest engagement on Facebook. Strategic content produced across all programmes included 160 videos, 35 social media packs, and 16 web articles. Website engagement rose, with audiences spending 66 seconds on a page on average, compared to 16 seconds in 2023.
 
Social and behaviour change (SBC)
ROSA supported SBC programming transform norms and ensure no child is left behind in immunization, child marriage and community health and nutrition, drawing on six large-scale country studies of social and behavioural drivers, and the use of digital and offline channels to support meaningful change. 
 
SBC influenced the views and behaviours of 22 million people across South Asia, strengthening region-wide movements upholding child rights and contributing to expanded vaccination uptake. Using SBC, ROSA tackled bottlenecks such as low demand for social services, which had been exacerbated by misinformation, cultural barriers and lack of trust, and worked with Bangladesh and Pakistan COs to transform harmful norms, promote participation of women and girls in vaccination campaigns and support outreach workers to communicate effectively to increase demand. About 30,000 imams and 14,000 female faith leaders underwent training and became advocates for uptake of lifesaving vaccination. 
 
Capacity-building in SBC strengthened systems and empowered government and implementing partners. 
Regional capacity building enanced the skills of over 1,000 UNICEF staff in behavioural science, digital engagement, AAP and social and community listening, and strengthened systems in Nepal and Sri Lanka by supporting COs to develop behaviour change strategies. The I-HEAR-U platform for community listening captured real-time insights on social issues in Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Maldives.
 
Digital innovations for SBC streamlined HPV vaccination processes in Bangladesh and contributed to successful introduction. In Nepal, over 1,100 frontline health workers improved immunization outreach by building skills on interpersonal communication. This was also integrated into the Polio National Training Package in Pakistan and Afghanistan to support outreach workers in increasing vaccine demand going forward.
 
Digital transformation
Digital public infrastructure was strengthened across the region with ROSA support, including the roll-out of the Bebbo parenting programme in Bangladesh, advisory services around AI-enabled initiatives, including a chatbot providing mental health and psychosocial support in Nepal and I-HEAR-U; and digital CRVS systems and blockchain-enabled humanitarian cash transfers for efficient, transparent and secure service delivery. An innovative model to procure Chromebooks directly from the original equipment manufacturers opened access to 21-century skills for marginalized children.

Regional partnerships with governments, CSOs, private sector, multilateral organizations and young people laid the foundation for effective support to COs in achieving results for children. As UNICEF embarks on a new Regional Office Management Plan for South Asia, building on these partnerships is critical to realizing a better future for the region’s children.
 
Mobilizing resources
Private and public-sector partnerships were critical for mobilizing resources for regional and CO programming. Collaborations with GAVI, GCF and the Adaptation Fund mobilized resources for health facility solarization, climate-resilient WASH, enhancing climate-resilience of social services and demonstrating the criticality of climate finance in protecting children’s rights.
 
The private sector was a vital partner in resource mobilization and advocacy, tapping new funding streams and innovative solutions tailored to regional challenges. ROSA’s collaboration with UNICEF HQ and National Committees expanded private-sector partnerships, including with the Akelius Foundation, Vu Television and Google. ROSA also supported COs to secure funding from the EU (Afghanistan), the Global Platform for Education (Nepal, Maldives and Bangladesh) and UNGEI. A partnership with the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints supported emergency flood response in Bangladesh, a partnership with a Sri Lanka bank supported education programming, and the South Asia diaspora in the United States funded UNICEF in Pakistan.
 
Innovation in programming
Drawing on its competitive advantage as a regional and global convenor, ROSA brought together broad-based expertise for innovative programming. ROSA-led working groups enhanced vaccination coverage through zero-dose recovery, COVID-19 response and accelerated efforts under the Big Catch-up initiative in India. A collaboration with WHO led to the development of country digital health blueprints while the Asia eHealth Information Network enhanced knowledge management.
 
Regional collaboration led to approaches to achieve city-wide inclusive sanitation, with funding and expertise from the Gates Foundation. ROSA expanded on these gains through a collaboration with SAARC to revive the South Asian Conference on Sanitation (SACOSAN) as a regional platform for commitment and accountability and to advance SAARC sanitation policy guidelines aligned with SDG targets.

Academic partners generated evidence and introduced innovative approaches. A partnership with the PEN+ team at Harvard University supported strengthening paediatric non-communicable disease services. 

Substantial coverage on Afghanistan and Bangladesh emergencies and climate crisis was achieved through media engagement with AFP, CNN, BBC, Reuters, Associated Press and the Washington Post.  
 
Influencing stakeholders
Regional platforms and partnerships enabled coordinated advocacy and knowledge-sharing to influence stakeholders. ROSA strengthened its collaboration with WHO on healthy diet and nutrition and climate change, the Iodine Global Network, and a regional alliance on pre-conception nutrition. The UNICEF-led Network for Improved Nutrition was revitalized to advocate for food fortification. ROSA also convened or co-convened regional networks on digital transformation in education, adolescent skills and school health.
 
ROSA renewed the strategic collaboration with the EU through the second phase of the EU-UNICEF Public Finance Facility, deepening relationships with regional ministries of finance to promote child-focused budgeting through the development of a regional dashboard visualizing social-sector expenditure data.
 
New partnerships with WHO, ADB, SAARC, World Bank, GAVI and IFRC led to a regional coordination platform for community health and nutrition in South Asia. This was also a priority area in UNICEF’s collaboration with SAARC in 2024.
 
In collaboration with the World Bank, ROSA organized a regional workshop on scaling up foundational learning, which enabled government and CO representatives to learn from each other and from international experts, creating momentum for change and agreeing on joint priority actions at country level.
 
ROSA co-hosted a high-profile knowledge exchange event in collaboration with UN-ESCAP, OECD and IM, engaging government officials and EU representatives on child-sensitive social-sector spending, while a regional consultation with the World Bank, ADB, ILO and UN-ESCAP brought development partners together to advance the disability-inclusive social protection agenda.
 
UNICEF, UN-ESCAP and CR8 partnered to maintain momentum for birth registration and advocated with governments to digitize birth registration processes and ensure interoperability between health and CRVS systems. The partnership will play a key role in the CRVS Ministerial Conference in 2025.
 
Through partnerships with UNFPA, SAIEVAC, SAARC and civil society, ROSA led joint advocacy on preventing child marriage and developing a Regional Action Plan to End Child Marriage in collaboration with Girls Not Brides. UNICEF-supported research by CORAM International showed the wide range of partners who have engaged on this critical issue, and the potential to draw on their respective strengths to create momentum.
 
Strengthened multi-sector collaboration on adolescent skills development with EAPRO and ILO led to the revitalization of the Asia-Pacific Technical Working Group on Adolescent and Youth Education, Learning and Skills Development. This convened partners across multiple regions to set clear goals to address skills gaps and advancing equitable learning opportunities for vulnerable adolescents.
 
Youth participation
Partnerships with UN agencies, civil society organizations and youth groups through the Local Conference of Youth integrated child-sensitive perspectives into NDCs and in conversations around COP. Through consultations, advocacy, and joint initiatives, these groups enriched policy processes with grassroots insights and empowered children and young people to champion climate action. 
 
Through Green Rising South Asia, ROSA accelerated youth climate advocacy via public-private-youth partnerships. By co-convening the Fourth Asia-Pacific Youth Symposium with ADB and Plan International, ROSA spotlighted green skills, gender equity and climate resilience; the event and culminated in the Youth Agenda on Climate Change Impacts, reflecting the priorities of diverse youth. An interagency collaboration with ECARO, EAPRO, UNEP and UN Women on the Girls Go Green Summit 2024 empowered young women to lead green transitions. These partnerships were critical to accelerate the inclusion of young people in advocacy, interagency collaboration, and empowering youth to drive equitable climate action and governance reforms.
 
Flexible funding
Thematic funding catalysed progress on community health and nutrition across five countries (Maldives, Sri Lanka, Bhutan, Pakistan and Bangladesh) and created momentum to position it as a regional priority, facilitate partner engagement and collaboration.
 
Thematic funding also advanced UNICEF’s climate programme to drive SCAP areas of acceleration, and provision of technical support to develop and refine child-sensitive NDC 3.0.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
South Asia has the world’s largest child population and is prone to profound inequality, cyclical crises, insecurity and unrest and, increasingly, climate change impacts. While the region has made substantial progress in achieving its four areas for acceleration, in 2024, the Office faced significant challenges with widespread pushback against the rights of children and women; a constricted and shrinking funding environment particularly affecting many of the region’s priority areas; and a need to build capacity in key areas. The lessons learned from these challenges will inform ROSA strategies in 2025, and will shape the next ROMP.
 
Agile resource mobilization 
Growing challenges were posed by the shrinking ODA space, resource constraints, and the dynamic political and socio-economic landscape of the region, especially in areas for acceleration such as climate change.
