Approaches to resource mobilization used in 2024 showed great potential, including innovative pilots, individual giving, evidence generation to leverage climate finance and entering carbon markets. Joined-up regional and country-level engagement was critical: ROSA support contributed to US$580M received by COs from the public sector, representing 86 per cent of total contributions to South Asia. 
 
Engaging with the private sector to invest in future growth leveraged resources for under-funded areas, such as using GenU to establish sustainable, institutionalized youth engagement mechanisms. These innovative mechanisms were used to attract investment offer pathways to fill longstanding financing gaps, such as the expansion of wastewater treatment.
 
Partnerships and integrated approaches 
Local child rights issues are frequently obscured by strong country-level development indicators. Research in 2024 showed the role women-led organizations play in advocating for child rights at the local level, such as child marriage, and advancing integrated interventions such as rights-based food-systems approaches. The deep and highly localized engagement of such organizations – including those led by persons with disabilities – can help to transform social norms and ensure no child is left behind.
 
Similarly, collaborations among development partners, governments, CSOs and cross-sectoral stakeholders strengthened influence around systemic change and sustainable financing. Regional initiatives with the EU, World Bank, UN-ESCAP and UN Women demonstrated how consistent collaboration drives impactful reforms. ROSA will enhance relationships with SAARC and other influential institutions, such as the IMF, particularly on child-centred social policy.
 
4 SAR Areas for Acceleration
In a rapidly changing global and regional environment and severe climate risks, ROSA will use the lessons learned in 2024 to respond agilely and effectively to meet children’s needs, supporting COs around its four areas for acceleration. 
 
Area 1 – Community health and nutrition: In 2024, ROSA laid the foundation for response to critical emerging challenges in health, such as NCDs and mental and environmental health, by supporting regional assessments, capacity-building workshops and country profiling. These will inform policies and guide future interventions.
 
Successes in accelerating immunization in South Asia showed the value of SBC as a pillar of CHN systems. Drawing on UNICEF’s competitive advantage in SBC, ROSA will build momentum in childhood vaccination through routine immunization, Big Catch-up, targeted campaigns and enhanced outreach. A stronger focus will be placed on polio eradication, with improved surveillance, community mobilization and partner coordination, and drawing on lessons from the successful 2024 HPV introduction on effective community engagement. 
 
Area 2 – Foundational learning: In 2024, generating evidence and exposing government representatives to global and regional technical expertise and best practices strengthened their commitment to children’s right to learn, even in a shrinking resource space. For example, government officials attending a high-level regional event co-convened by ROSA and the World Bank deepened knowledge and developed action points to strengthen foundational learning. UNICEF will support generation and use of evidence at country level for improving learning in classrooms, and build on platforms such as the Learning Passport, through intersectoral collaborations and private-sector partnerships that expand access to digital learning opportunities and support training for teachers and para-teachers.
 
Area 3 – Climate: While challenges were posed by lack of capacity and human resource at CO level, where dedicated climate capacity existed it was a driver of ambitious programming and policy support to governments. Moreover, intense technical support from ROSA enabled these offices to address some resource constraints by accessing climate financing. GCF accreditation, achieved with ROSA technical support, was critical in solidifying UNICEF’s credibility with governments and enhanced the CO ability to secure climate financing from the Adaptation Fund for Pakistan and GCF readiness fund for Sri Lanka. ROSA will built on this to provide hands-on technical support to COs to identify and develop a bankable project pipeline related to SCAP, and thus leverage child-centred climate finance.
 
Piloting innovative market-based solutions, such as carbon credits through clean cooking solutions, showed ways to simultaneously achieve cross-sectoral gains in health while overcoming resource and implementation challenges. The Office will explore strategies to leverage market mechanisms to accelerate the adoption of sustainable energy solutions such as solarization of WASH, health and education facilities.  
 
Area 4 – Adolescent girls: The region faced a growing challenge with pushback against child rights, especially those of adolescent girls. Innovative approaches, including digital methods, supported secondary education of girls in Afghanistan. However, to meet the challenge of growing risks to girls posed by false narratives (already seen in Maldives, India and Nepal), the Office will seek to invest in better monitoring and response to online disinformation, and build strategic partnerships to advocate for their rights. 
 
Indeed, while digital technologies provide countless opportunities for young people, girls remain at risk of being left behind, while exposure to technology-facilitated violence and exploitation is a growing concern. Research in 2024, showed that tackling systemic barriers – unequal technology access and restrictive gender norms – is critical to inclusive engagement. Going forward, UNICEF will promote scaling up digital literacy, leverage the UN Global Digital Compact as a strategic framework to prioritize inclusion and digital equity, and advocate for the creation of safe digital spaces for girls.

GRP funds supported programme implementation and delivery of technical expertise, including support for COs in NDC 3.0 processes, the rollout of the UNICEF Youth Advocacy Guide, and scaling youth-led climate initiatives and partnerships aligned with the UNICEF Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan. Ten youth climate advocates (two from Afghanistan) also influenced development processes for ambitious, child-sensitive NDCs in their countries. 
 
The contribution supported establishment of PSEA focal point systems in four COs with capacity development to enable prompt investigation.
 
The funds facilitated ROSA support to COs to secure US$20M to design and implement innovative digital learning initiatives and supported Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Bhutan to introduce global flagship initiatives reaching the most marginalized, including the Learning Passport, Accessible Digital Textbooks and the Akelius Initiative.
 
GRP funds strengthened WASH capacity including digital monitoring technologies for groundwater management in the Ganges Basin, nature-based wastewater treatment in Bangladesh, and a hygiene roadmap in India. ROSA also supported regional intergovernmental processes and reviewed WASH FIT implementation in health-care facilities.
 
These funds supported global and regional advocacy and outreach, including through co-organizing (with HQ) events at the UN General Assembly on digital transformation, using AI in the learning crisis, and improving foundational learning outcomes.
 
Supported by these funds, UNICEF amplified youth voices in global forums, including COP29, where 20 UNICEF-supported youth delegates from six countries shaped climate discourse; and co-hosting sessions on green skills at the Asia-Pacific Youth Development Forum and the Girls Go Green Summit.
 
ROSA strengthened its communication capacity through spokesperson training, purchased essential tools to create high-quality media products, engaged interns and UNVs to manage and monitor digital platforms and supported content-gathering missions and content production on climate programming. These positioned UNICEF regionally as a trusted advocate for children.
 
ROSA built capacity and supported knowledge-sharing through regional webinars on out-of-school children, youth empowerment, disability-inclusive preparedness and gender-responsive social protection; training on child rights for independent human rights institutions; and a high-level regional event on accelerating foundational learning. Regional consultations with national human rights and child rights institutions contributed to GC-27 on children's access to justice and the right to effective remedies. In collaboration with UN Women and other partners, ROSA engaged governments at a pre-APFSD event exploring connections between social protection and climate change, highlighting the importance of adaptive systems to address emerging challenges.
 
All eight countries generated evidence and knowledge for wider learning, with 15 knowledge products produced with GRP funding and uploaded to the global WASH repository. 
 
Key evaluation products included a meta-analysis of actions against child marriage and COVID-19 documentation. Additionally, funds were used for travel to support quality evaluation, contributing to the completion of nine evaluations.
 
Based on annual digital mapping, COs rolled out targeted digital interventions including digital literacy programmes, innovative channels to inform communities during emergencies, the localized Babuni app (Bangladesh) partnerships with tech on child online protection (Pakistan) and enhanced local platforms (India). ROSA developed an in-house Social and Community Listening platform, I-HEAR-U, which automates data analysis, visualization and interpretation of social and community listening tailored to UNICEF programmatic priorities.

In 2024, conditions for human development have remained challenging as several effects of the crisis are still unwinding, despite a return to positive economic growth. After the economic crisis induced a sharp contraction in 2022 and 2023, the economy expanded across all sectors in 2024, with an average annual growth of 4 per cent. This notwithstanding, the effects on the labour market have been subdued so far, with labour force participation rates standing at a historical low. Wages have contracted significantly between 2021 and 2024, and although inflation has eased since its peak in 2022, prices remain high. As a result, it is estimated that poverty rates (at USD 3.65 per day per capita in 2017 PPP) nearly doubled from 13.1 to 25.9 per cent between 2021 and 2023. In general, this has resulted in worsening living conditions, with households resorting to adverse coping strategies, including reduced investments in health and education or taking on debt to meet daily food requirements. 

Public investments in health and education in real terms remain below pre-crisis levels and international benchmarks, although planning figures for health and education suggest a reprioritization in 2025 and 2026. Debt payments ‘squeeze’ spending on social sectors and the large and increased interest bills, amounting to 8.9 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 2023, offset some of the revenue gains. Following its mission for the Third Review under the Extended Fund Facility, the International Monetary Fund commended Sri Lanka on its progress and stressed the importance of continued revenue mobilization efforts and spending restraint. The indicative target on social spending, amounting to 0.7 per cent of GDP, only pertains to spending on four specific social assistance programmes and leaves out targets for health and education. 

Health and nutrition outcomes have further deteriorated in 2024. New data is limited, yet 2023 Government data indicates a slight worsening of neonatal, infant, and child mortality rates, as well as stillbirth rates, which may be reflective of the crisis impacts. According to the national nutrition month assessment undertaken in June, malnutrition rates remain elevated following the increases in previous years, and stunting rates for children under the age of five have even slightly increased from 10.3 per cent in 2023 to 10.5 per cent in 2024. A recent study has also shown continued high levels of low birth weight, which is a predictor of undernutrition in later years. Nonetheless, extensive crisis response measures, particularly related to addressing gaps in the identification and management of children with acute malnutrition, have led to a reduced prevalence of wasting in children under the age of five (from 10 per cent in 2023 to 9.3 per cent in 2024), and even larger declines in severe wasting rates. 

A Multisector Action Plan for Nutrition (MSAPN) has been drafted. Based on a consultative process, the MSAPN aims to integrate strategies across the health, education, and social protection sectors to address the root causes of malnutrition. National- and district-level plans and monitoring mechanisms are being set up to strengthen accountability and sustained progress towards results. Other priorities in the healthcare sector include primary healthcare reforms to address the looming challenge of non-communicable disease, as well as using digital technologies for improving health and nutrition outcomes.

Social protection reforms could not keep up with the increased demand and the needs of a significant share of the population remain unmet. The Aswesuma Welfare Benefit Payment Scheme, Sri Lanka’s new flagship social assistance programme, will be expanded by 400,000 households to 2.4 million, and transfer values for elderly persons and persons with disabilities and chronic kidney disease were increased. At the same time, fiscal reforms related to indirect taxes, notably the increased Value Added Tax and the abrupt withdrawal of electricity subsidies, have driven poverty beyond the impact of the pandemic and economic crisis; and the combined effect of these factors could not be offset by direct taxes and transfers. 

The National Social Protection Policy, launched in August, sets out the vision to provide social protection over the life cycle, starting from pregnancy and early childhood, school age and youth, over working age to old age. The Policy refers to the international human rights framework, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child. How exactly protection gaps will be closed, however, remains to be mapped out in the National Social Protection Strategy that is under development.

Persistent socioeconomic vulnerabilities continued having a negative impact on child protection outcomes, such as a high rate of placement of children in institutional care due to economic reasons. The trend of international labour migration of parents and leaving children behind without adequate care has increased. In addition, a few tragic incidents of adolescent suicide resulted in growing attention to the mental health of children and adolescents, as well as violence and corporal punishment in schools.

The legal landscape for children in Sri Lanka has significantly improved in 2024, and the Government made high-level commitments to address violence against children. Changes in the Children and Young Person’s Ordinance resulted in children between 16 to 18 being afforded protection that were previously only available to those under the age of 16. Further, these changes also repealed the provisions that condoned the infliction of corporal punishment. Changes in the Mediation Board Act resulted in greater accessibility of mediation to children in conflict with the law. In November, the Government made four formal pledges at the First Ministerial Global Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, expressing its renewed commitment to addressing the issue. 

The learning crisis in Sri Lanka continues. Only 15 per cent of grade 3 children have achieved all required literacy and numeracy skills and about a third of children miss out on preschool. In addition, increased numbers of out-of-school children have emerged as a challenge. Trends indicate that the number of school dropouts after the Ordinary Level cycle (ages 15-16) has increased between 2018/2019 and 2022/23 from 18.7 per cent to 22.4 per cent.

There has been important political momentum to strengthen Early Childhood Education (ECE) and Development (ECD). In 2024, the Cabinet officially called for a structural reform giving the Ministry of Education oversight of ECE, which creates a path towards stronger quality assurance, better alignment with primary education and formalization of the sub-sector. ECE and education, in general, are clearly expressed priorities of the incoming government.

The new government aims to improve women's and children’s nutrition and education outcomes and increase the adequacy of social assistance benefits. In September 2024, Anura Kumara Dissanayake of the National People’s Power (NPP) was elected President in the second round, constituting a major political realignment. In November 2024, parliamentary elections were held, with NPP winning 62 per cent of seats. In the government’s policy statement at the inaugural session of the parliament, the President expressed their future priorities, including addressing nutrition for pregnant women and child malnutrition through targeted transfers, quality education, and increased social assistance benefits.

As the country began stabilising this year, UNICEF in Sri Lanka entered the second year of its country programme. In 2024, UNICEF provided almost exclusively development assistance, strengthened systems and enhanced capacities in delivering quality and equitable social services for children and their families. The key achievements are presented below under the core programmatic areas of Social Policy, Health and Nutrition, Education, Child Protection, and Climate Change, as well as on operational and programmatic effectiveness that enhanced programme delivery.   
 
SOCIAL POLICY
While there have been different, partly ad-hoc, data collection efforts to shed light on the household situation, the conduct of the comprehensive Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) has been delayed. To finalise the 2025 HIES questionnaire, UNICEF provided technical support to the Department of Census and Statistics (DCS), which renewed its commitment to include child-related indicators to compute the child Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI). UNICEF will also support the implementation of the survey in 2025 to help provide an updated picture of the number of children living in poverty in all its forms. 
 
In early 2024, UNICEF concluded the nutrition-sensitive short-term cash transfer programme, which directly reached 115,729 children through a ‘cash-plus’ approach that aimed to increase purchasing power and improve diets, nutritional knowledge, and access to services. During this year, UNICEF supported an empirical study of this programme, which reported that 97 per cent of caregivers felt the transfers had improved their children’s diets, including 57 per cent who said their children’s diets were much better. UNICEF also documented lessons learnt to inform evidence-based advocacy and programmes for expanding child benefits and strengthening linkages to nutrition interventions. Encouragingly, the new National Social Protection Policy, launched in August, clearly articulates the objective of social protection over the lifecycle.  
 
Expanding child benefits, as well as access to other social services, will require more fiscal space, despite constraints. UNICEF continued advocating for safeguarding social sector spending and has started promoting a Child Rights Budget Initiative that puts children’s rights in the limelight and aims to strengthen budget and planning processes. Piggybacking on the ongoing Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) budget tagging exercise and gender budgeting, which was explicitly mentioned in the Budget Call, this initiative aims to add additional tags from a Child Rights perspective, notably Early Childhood Development and Nutrition. UNICEF has also strengthened its partnership with the European Union (EU), with Sri Lanka included in the second phase of the EU-UNICEF Public Finance Facility, to provide technical support, build capacities, and joint advocacy in this regard. At the sub-national level, UNICEF has started to promote child-friendly local governance principles and approaches by facilitating the sharing of experiences from the Eastern and Northern Provinces more widely through a workshop and study tour and working towards a Community of Practice among local authorities. 
 
HEALTH AND NUTRITION
In 2024, notable improvements in acute malnutrition indicators were observed, resulting from targeted and sustained interventions to support the health system. Treatment access for children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) increased from 32 per cent in 2021 to 85 per cent by mid-2024, contributing to a 32 per cent reduction in SAM prevalence, from 1.2 per cent in 2023 to 0.82 per cent in 2024. Wasting levels also declined from 10 per cent to 9.3 per cent. These achievements demonstrate the importance of ensuring consistent access to treatment and highlight UNICEF’s pivotal role in supporting the Ministry of Health to update SAM treatment protocols.
 
UNICEF, in collaboration with WFP, advanced sustainable solutions to malnutrition by supporting the development of locally produced Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food (RUTF) aligned with international standards. This initiative has the potential to reduce reliance on imports, improve cost efficiency, and support local economies, with rigorous, ongoing field trials ensuring its efficacy and acceptance.
 
A significant focus in 2024 was revitalizing the Multisector Action Plan for Nutrition (MSAPN) designed with UNICEF support in 2023, fostering a collaborative and comprehensive approach to combating malnutrition. Developed through extensive consultations, the MSAPN integrates strategies across sectors, such as health, education, and social protection, to address the root causes of malnutrition. District-level plans and monitoring mechanisms ensure accountability and sustained progress in implementing these initiatives.
 
To address childhood malnutrition, UNICEF emphasized early detection through growth monitoring of children under five and conducted critical research on low birth weight and growth faltering during the first 1,000 days of life. These studies provided actionable recommendations for tackling malnutrition, with the findings discussed within the Ministry of Health's Technical Advisory Committees, ensuring follow-up through established coordination mechanisms.
 
UNICEF’s commitment to maternal health was reflected in its support in revising the maternal care guidelines, introducing Multiple Micronutrient Supplements for pregnant women, and finalizing the Maternal Nutrition Acceleration Plan as part of a regional initiative. These efforts aimed to reduce low birth weight and enhance newborn outcomes. As Sri Lanka is one of 16 focus countries under the Global Maternal Nutrition Acceleration Plan, UNICEF has laid out a clear roadmap to strengthen maternal health and nutrition interventions, ensuring intensified support and resource mobilization.
 
UNICEF also strengthened public health resilience through its contributions to immunization and emergency preparedness. Enhancements to cold chain systems, equipment maintenance, and outbreak responses have bolstered the nation’s ability to sustain immunization coverage and respond effectively to future health crises. Additionally, the development of National Oxygen Guidelines and monitoring dashboards represents a significant step in improving emergency preparedness and ensuring efficient oxygen delivery during public health emergencies, pandemics, and routine care.
 
For adolescent health, UNICEF collaborated with government ministries to introduce healthy school canteen guidelines and enhance youth-focused digital health platforms. Further, UNICEF’s global ‘Caring for the Caregiver’ initiative was adapted to Sri Lanka to train caregivers to provide nurturing care with an inclusive focus on disability considerations. These initiatives address immediate health needs while fostering healthier, more inclusive future generations.
 
Efforts to integrate health promotion into preschool settings and the recent development of the National Early Childhood Development Curriculum Framework are creating long-term benefits by instilling healthy habits early. These measures enhance early childhood outcomes and contribute to lifelong well-being. UNICEF also supported the development of a digital health roadmap, improving health data quality for decision-making processes.
 
The strengthening of the health system, particularly at the community level, remained a cornerstone of UNICEF’s strategy. Trained community volunteers have conducted over 419,000 household visits covering more than 100,000 households to promote nutrition, sanitation, and home gardening. Food demonstration programmes, conducted by community volunteers in collaboration with field-level health officers and Mothers’ Support Groups (MSGs), reached nearly 10,000 mothers, while the number of MSGs increased from 4,000 to 6,272 by the end of 2024. These initiatives have strengthened community networks and created sustainable platforms for addressing nutrition and other health-related challenges at the grassroots level, making families adopt positive practices.
 
To ensure accountability and community engagement, UNICEF introduced the People’s Engagement Network and supported training on Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP). These efforts promote transparency, trust, and responsiveness of health and nutrition initiatives, ensuring that interventions align with community needs and priorities.
 
EDUCATION
UNICEF contributed to strengthening the education system to deliver better quality learning outcomes and to be more inclusive and resilient, benefitting all children nationwide; UNICEF’s direct support in the education sector benefitted almost 400,000 school-aged children (approximately 10 per cent of students in the country). 
 
In early learning, UNICEF’s advocacy, technical assistance, and convening role facilitated the drafting of three new national early childhood education policies and plans, namely the: 1) National Preschool Policy; 2) National Preschool Curriculum Framework; and 3) Integrated Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD) Action Plan. These policies and plans are helping improve coordination between the relevant actors and the coherence of the early learning system, which, once rolled out in 2025, will result in all preschool students across the country having improved access to enhanced, quality early learning. At the provincial level, UNICEF facilitated the training of preschool teachers, provided essential teaching-learning supplies and outdoor play equipment to remote preschools, and improved the infrastructure of poorly resourced preschools to increase access to quality preschool learning and school readiness for around 45,000 children in Uva, Central, and Eastern provinces, representing around 35 per cent of preschool children in these provinces and almost 10 per cent of preschool children nationwide.
 
For primary education levels, UNICEF’s technical assistance and modelling of approaches helped strengthen sustainable systems for teacher capacity building on child-centred foundational learning pedagogies. At the provincial level, UNICEF worked with provincial authorities in Uva and Central provinces to design new and innovative approaches to strengthening the system that delivers in-service training, benefitting approximately 7,190 primary school teachers, and an estimated 143,000 children through improved multi-level teaching and learning programmes. 
 
In addition, UNICEF technically and financially supported the national learning recovery programme, which directly provided remedial learning support for 158,792 struggling learners, representing 10 per cent of primary students nationwide. The programme also raised awareness of the need for remedial learning support in all schools. Leveraging these results, UNICEF advocated for national-level systemic changes that would benefit all primary school children nationwide. This contributed to national-level action, including the development of revised national guidelines on child-centred, multi-level teaching; integration of multi-level teaching in the new Grade 1 curriculum modules; and commitment to developing a national plan for improving foundational learning in primary school. 
 
UNICEF also focused on making the education system safer and more resilient, and one that promotes health and wellbeing for all girls and boys. In 2024, UNICEF enhanced the knowledge and skills of 200 school principals, 1,173 teachers, and 4,700 parents on positive disciplining approaches and increased awareness and school-level action to address issues of hate speech among 10,400 secondary school students across Uva, Central, and Eastern provinces. The best practices and lessons learned emerging from the modelling of these approaches informed UNICEF’s evidence-based advocacy for and technical support to the Government in making a high-level pledge at the first Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children. The pledge committed to scaling up the first-ever national teacher training package on positive discipline, which was developed and will be tested and rolled out in 2025.  
 
UNICEF’s technical support to the National Institute of Education led to the drafting of new curriculum content on 21st-Century Skills, including skills related to promoting health and well-being, social cohesion, and digital citizenship, which, once rolled out, will benefit secondary students nationwide. UNICEF also worked with provincial authorities in the Eastern Province to pilot an innovative initiative that uses sport as a means of promoting skills development, gender equality and social inclusion. A total of 17,092 adolescents participated in this initiative, demonstrating promising results on how sport could be used to shift gender norms and foster social cohesion among students from different backgrounds, ethnicities, and religions. 
 
To promote disaster-resilient schools, UNICEF technically supported the Ministry of Education and Provincial Departments of Education to roll out orientation training programmes on the national Comprehensive School Safety Guidelines for 2,012 education officials across all nine provinces. These sessions highlighted the need to make the system more shock-responsive by reducing the risks of disasters and promoting climate-resilient education.
 
CHILD PROTECTION
As described in the context update, the legal landscape for children in Sri Lanka improved in 2024 with important revisions to the age of criminal responsibility and condoning of corporal punishment in the Children and Young Persons Ordinance and increased mediation for children in conflict with the law through revisions in the Mediation Board Act. In support of these legislative reforms for children, UNICEF has served as the main technical partner to the Government. UNICEF also technically supported banning corporal punishment in all settings, as well as reviewing and revising legal provisions related to foster care and diversion.
 
Significant progress was seen regarding the agenda to address violence against children. After several years of relatively modest progress, towards the end of 2024, the Government of Sri Lanka, stemming from UNICEF’s sustained advocacy, made high-level commitments to tackle violence against children. At the first Ministerial Global Conference on Ending Violence Against Children, the Government made four transformative pledges for preventing and responding to violence against children through legislative measures, strengthening the workforce, and improving a continuum of services across protection and education systems. These commitments were endorsed by the Prime Minister, giving UNICEF a renewed space for offering strategic and technical support to help fulfil them.
 
Solid progress was made during the year in promoting alternative care, with more than 4,000 children reunified with their families or prevented from placement in institutional care. This year also marked a turning point in the process of implementing the alternative care reform. The government and UNICEF came to the joint conclusion that new types of services, including community-based and family-type, need to be established to reduce the unnecessary use of institutional care in response to socio-economic needs and for victims of violence. 
 
Considering that the use of violence and corporal punishment are deeply engrained in social and cultural norms, UNICEF continued its active engagement with children, parents, communities, religious leaders, and the media through key social and behavioural change communication messaging. A strong focus was placed on addressing harmful social and gender norms that condone gender-based violence and promoting social cohesion in the Northern and Eastern provinces that have known communal tensions and specific vulnerabilities for girls. UNICEF is leveraging these building blocks to create an even stronger gender-transformative child protection programme in these provinces. 
 
OPERATIONAL EFFECTIVENESS
Operational excellence was achieved by driving strategic process optimization and enhancing resource management for continued growth and efficiencies. Financial oversight and management of programmes were further strengthened with a robust risk management process and a strong quality assurance approach to financial assurance activities. Further, planning, management, governance, and oversight in the country office were strengthened through the optimal functioning of systems, structures, and tools. Strategic support was also provided to programme sections to ensure effective programme delivery. This included the procurement and delivery of goods and services worth over USD 10 million and procurement services worth USD 11.2 million, as well as technical support to 12 ongoing Technology for Development initiatives in Education, Health and Nutrition, and Child Protection. Further, the country office helped 31 female-led organizations register in the UN Global Marketplace and with UN agencies in Sri Lanka, giving them a better opportunity to participate in UN procurement activities. Staff well-being and care continue to be priorities, with the office investing in staff development and learning.
 
PROGRAMME EFFECTIVENESS AND CROSS SECTORAL
The country office continued to ensure effective programme coordination and management of the country programme, including through robust work planning and annual reviews, quality assurance of all donor reporting, effective knowledge management, and monitoring cash transfers to implementing partners in line with global standards and benchmarks. 
 
UNICEF also strengthened its cross-sectoral coordination mechanisms to ensure cross-cutting considerations, including Social Behaviour Change (SBC), disaster risk reduction, gender, and climate change adaptation, are mainstreamed across programmes for greater impact and efficiency. 
 
In 2024, UNICEF significantly strengthened its work on climate change and disaster risk reduction and developed the Sustainability Climate Action Plan (SCAP). The office is advocating with the government to ensure that the next round of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) is child-sensitive. Additionally, it is supporting youth groups to enhance their participation in climate decision-making. This includes involving youth in the process led by the Ministry of Environment to revise the NDC, ensuring that youth perspectives help shape climate policies for sustainable outcomes.
 
UNICEF collaborated with various government agencies to promote climate-resilient and innovative technologies, evidence-based advocacy, and capacity building in climate-sensitive project planning and implementation. This included the sharing of findings from assessments on the climate-resilience of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), healthcare waste, and energy services with provincial health authorities, which led to increased investments in making WASH facilities more climate-resilient and the drafting of provincial-level WASH improvement plans. UNICEF also developed relevant training manuals, evaluated facilities, trained government officers, audited water safety plans, and piloted artificial groundwater recharging and solarized rural water supplies while promoting green skills, to help integrate climate change into government policies, strategies, and development plans. 
 
UNICEF supported the development of SBC strategies to promote vaccinations among vaccine-hesitant families and for dengue control and prevention in schools; a training package for public health staff to strengthen accountability during routine and emergency services; engaging youth and religious leaders as change agents; and promoting Digital Storytelling using digital technology and tools to amplify children's voices.
 
UNICEF is dedicated to promoting gender equality and eliminating harmful gender norms. The Office has partnered with the Ministry of Health to conduct an assessment of gender-related barriers to maternal, newborn, and child health services, including immunizations, in the Western Province. This assessment has provided valuable insights and recommendations for making the health system more inclusive.  Additionally, UNICEF is implementing an initiative in the Northern and Southern provinces that empowers girls, encourages positive masculinities, and fosters social cohesion through sports. To date, 383 divisional officers (216 men and 167 women) have engaged with 2,458 children - 1,337 girls and 1,121 boys, including 52 with disabilities - as well as 1,012 parents. The insights gained from this initiative will contribute to the development of a scalable intervention model in collaboration with various partners.
 
UNICEF also created strategic visibility on key issues affecting children, as well as UNICEF’s work in the country to advance child rights. This was carried out through the production of bespoke content and strategic media relations, including capacity building of UNICEF spokespersons and young champions, and strengthening ethical reporting on children among journalists. Further, UNICEF leveraged media, mobilized young people, and pursued strategic advocacy approaches across key issues, including corporal punishment, water and climate, nutrition, and health to help achieve change for children. 
 
As a key strategy for UNICEF in Sri Lanka, private sector engagement was leveraged in innovative ways to deliver results at scale and optimize partnerships with business partners. There have been financial and non-financial wins during the year, and UNICEF continues to nurture the private sector and fundraising market to maximize results for children. UNICEF also continued to strengthen the Business Council, a strategic partnership between UNICEF and leading business figures established in June 2023, which played a vital role in fostering dialogue and collaboration across sectors to advance child rights and sustainable development in the country.

During the year, UNICEF provided leadership and cultivated strategic partnerships and collaborations across various sectors to advance child rights. Under the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), UNICEF chairs the largest Outcome Results Group related to access for all to quality social services and leads/co-leads four of the seven output groups under the Outcome. This convening role contributed to strategic joint UN planning and action on identified priority areas of work; for instance, on Social Protection, under UNICEF’s leadership, the UN agencies focused on a quality national comprehensive policy framework – with joint support provided to the launch of the National Social Protection Policy – and strengthening digital social protection, as well as exploring ways to more strongly position social protection in the revised NDCs.  
 
UNICEF has continued strengthening the collaboration with UN agencies, especially UNDP, to implement two joint programs. The first program, JURE, focuses on promoting reforms within the justice system and is funded by the European Union. The second program addresses hate speech and is supported by the Peacebuilding Fund (PBF).
 
UNICEF also continued its partnership with the European Union (EU) on strengthening public finance management for social sectors and is using joint convening power to amplify advocacy efforts. In August 2024, Phase II of the EU-UNICEF Public Finance Facility in South and Southeast Asia was launched, which is a 45-month action to contribute to the realization of children’s rights by supporting the best possible use of public budgets. This second phase of the Facility in Sri Lanka, which follows the implementation of the pilot action between 2019 and 2023, aims to ensure that children, including boys and girls, benefit from adequate and effective social sector budgets. This would be achieved through the increased utilization of evidence-based budget analysis, in tandem with strengthened evidence-based policy dialogue, advocacy, and monitoring of public finance and social sector spending. 
 
In the work on Climate Change, to bridge the gap in knowledge among children and youth, UNICEF partnered with Sri Lanka's National Youth Services Council (NYSC) to raise climate awareness and engage youth, particularly through the NYSC’s Youth Club network. The partnership aims to establish a cadre of young change agents who will lead peer education and climate mitigation/adaptation programmes in their communities, and participation of youth in climate decision-making, including NDC revisions, ensuring that youth perspectives are reflected in climate policies for sustainable outcomes. With support from HQ and the Regional Office, UNICEF Sri Lanka has established a new partnership with the Stockholm International Water Institute (SIWI), a global leading excellence centre in water governance, for the formation of a climate task force to address climate change issues in the WASH sector.  
 
In the education sector, UNICEF continued to maintain strong, strategic partnerships and collaboration with key government stakeholders, which enabled system-level and sustainable results. These include the Ministry of Education, the National Institute of Education, the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs, and Provincial Departments of Education, including their district and zonal officials, and schools. The Ministry of Education chairs a Local Education Group coordination group under the Global Partnership for Education, together with the World Bank, which is both Grant and Coordinating Agency. In 2024, UNICEF initiated thematic sub-sector coordination groups to complement LEG collaboration. UNICEF’s partnership with the World Bank was strengthened through the jointly organized South Asia Regional Meeting on Foundational Literacy and Numeracy, held in Nepal in December 2024, bringing together all South Asian countries, international organizations, and experts from around the world. This meeting helped leverage and shape Sri Lanka’s national plan for foundational learning. 
 
Further, continued collaboration and regular communication with civil society organizations working in the education sector, including ChildFund, Room to Read, Save the Children, and CERI, and academic institutions, such as the University of Peradeniya, National Education Research and Evaluation Centre, University of Colombo, and Eastern University, were important for strengthening system coordination, which remains a challenge in the education sector, across all levels of education. . New partnerships with the Private sector, including with the Commercial Bank, have offered opportunities for improving preschool learning environments. One such partnership was launched in 2024 with the Akelius Foundation, and UNICEF’s National Committee for Sweden, to help improve English Language learning outcomes using technology.
 
UNICEF led nutrition sector coordination in Sri Lanka, collaborating with the World Food Programme (WFP) as co-chair. This platform aligns priorities among 15 partner organizations, ensuring government participation, including the Nutrition Division. UNICEF also contributed to broader health and nutrition initiatives led by WHO and the World Bank and as part of the UNSDCF. 
 
UNICEF partnered with professional bodies like the Professional Colleges, Sri Lanka College of Paediatricians, and the Perinatal Society of Sri Lanka, working with the Family Health Bureau to research child growth patterns. These efforts focused on improving low birth weight and addressing acute malnutrition through equitable, high-impact services. Collaborations extended to professional colleges and the Sri Lanka Medical Association to advocate for child and women’s health, school nutrition, and oxygen system strengthening. Additionally, UNICEF supports events like the International Stillbirth Alliance’s global meeting and engages with academia to enhance programme implementation and research. 
 
UNICEF also spearheaded the Early Childhood Development Strategic Action Plan with the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs. This multisectoral initiative involved extensive consultations across government, civil society, academia, and private sectors. Through these partnerships and strategic efforts, UNICEF fostered sustainable solutions to improve child and maternal health and nutrition in Sri Lanka.  
 
For Child protection, given the increasingly prominent upstream focus of the programme, partnerships with government entities are growing in criticality. To strengthen justice for children, UNICEF continued to maintain its strong partnerships with the Ministry of Justice, Legal Aid Commission of Sri Lanka, Sri Lanka Judges’ Institute, Attorney General’s Department, and Sri Lanka Police. Strategic partnerships with the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs and the Department of Probation and Childcare Services were critical for the implementation of the National Alternative Care Policy and moving the needle on the violence-against-children agenda. 
 
Mirroring the devolved nature of the implementation of child protection interventions in Sri Lanka, UNICEF partners with child protection stakeholders at the sub-national level as well. This year, a new partnership was established with the Western Province Probation Department, expanding the rollout of UNICEF-supported alternative care programmes nationwide to all nine provinces. UNICEF maintains a strong focus on academia and universities. Four universities were supported to improve their social work education – an important element of UNICEF’s comprehensive approach to strengthening the social service workforce in the country. 
 
Partnerships with the Business Council, established in June 2023, continue as a vital platform in fostering cross-sector dialogue and collaboration with the private sector and business leaders. In 2024, three quarterly meetings of the Business Council were convened. Through these sessions, UNICEF championed critical thematic areas, including Nutrition, Corporal Punishment, and Climate Change. UNICEF also leveraged the experience of other countries, notably the UNICEF Croatia Business Council to share experiences, including best practices and lessons learned. This year, the Business Council took a step forward in funding the establishment of breastfeeding corners as part of the ‘Happy Estate Communities’ initiative in tea plantation areas.

As chair of the United Nations Communication Group (UNCG), UNICEF provided strategic technical and operational guidance to bring together the UN to identify and develop joint advocacy priorities in line with the UN Sustainable Common Development Framework and the annual priorities of the United Country Team. UNICEF leveraged the UNCG to advance key issues of children in a concerted manner. During the year, several joint initiatives were undertaken, including campaigns on gender and girl’s empowerment, countering hate speech, 16 Days of Activism Against GBV, UN Day, and social protection.

As co-chair of the United Nations Operations Management Team (OMT), UNICEF played a strategic role in contributing to the 2030 efficiency agenda to achieve cost savings that could be reallocated to development activities. This was achieved through the operationalization of the Business Operations Strategy and mutual recognition, which enables UN agencies to use each other’s policies and procedures without having to repeat the process of assessing competitiveness and legality or subject it to additional external auditing.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, the Country Office reflected on the challenges and lessons learned in implementing the country programme, as the effects of the crisis were still unfolding, particularly concerning system strengthening and the scaling up of initiatives. 
 
The country programme remains valid and relevant, emphasizing the importance of designing programmes that can quickly adapt to changing circumstances. UNICEF’s transition from humanitarian response to development work highlights the necessity of building long-term resilience and strengthening systems. This shift helps create sustainable solutions rather than temporary fixes and contributes to more robust structures that can better withstand future crises. UNICEF has also been able to effectively advocate with the new government for priorities related to children's rights. This alignment can enhance the programme’s impact and sustainability. 
 
In the context of reduced social expenditure, it is essential to prioritize interventions that offer the highest impact. Strengthening systems can lead to more cost-effective services, ensuring that limited resources are utilized both efficiently and effectively. Well-established systems are more resilient and can sustain service quality even when faced with financial constraints.
 
Effective coordination and collaboration between provincial and national levels are crucial for scaling up. The limited coordination has hindered the implementation and monitoring of interventions at scale. In instances where collaboration has been effective, regular, joint monitoring between national and provincial partners has proven to be beneficial. This good practice should be advocated for by UNICEF. Additionally, knowledge sharing and exchange visits can help recognize and replicate successful pilot initiatives, such as local child rights governance, training primary teachers on multi-level pedagogy and positive disciplining, and introducing electronic learning approaches for pre-service teacher development. 
 
Comprehensive data collection is critical for effective policymaking. The delay in the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) has led to a reliance on outdated data, which has hampered the ability to make informed decisions as well as questioning of decisions from those opposed. With the lack of recent survey data, the picture of how many children are currently covered by social protection programmes is unclear, which is particularly important in view of the ongoing social protection reforms. This situation underscores the need for continuous and updated data to accurately assess and address issues such as child poverty and malnutrition. In the education sector, gaps in data persist with an overall lack of administrative, survey, and learning outcome data at all levels, especially early childhood education and learning data.  
 
Integrating social protection and nutrition programmes is crucial to effectively combat child poverty and malnutrition. The slight reduction in wasting rates but the increase in stunting highlights the need for stronger connections between these programmes. Additionally, documenting and learning from initiatives like UNICEF’s nutrition-sensitive cash transfer programme can inform future policies and advocacy efforts to expand child benefits and ensure comprehensive social protection throughout the lifecycle.
 
Addressing deeply rooted social norms is crucial for progressing in all outcomes of the country programme. The ongoing presence of unhealthy habits, violence against children, high-stakes exams, and corporal punishment in all settings highlights the need for continuous social behaviour change initiatives. UNICEF’s efforts to engage communities, particularly in the inclusion and participation of girls, have laid a strong foundation for programmes that are gender-sensitive and address harmful social norms. 
 
UNICEF’s initiatives focused on community engagement aim to include girls and promote positive masculinities, providing a solid foundation for developing gender-sensitive interventions that tackle harmful social and gender norms. One example of this is the programme designed to empower girls and promote gender equality through sports, which actively involves fathers and boys.
 
Persistent socioeconomic vulnerabilities continued to have a negative impact on child protection outcomes, such as a high rate of placement of children in institutional care due to economic reasons. The trend of international labour migration of parents and leaving children behind without adequate care has increased. In addition, a few tragic incidents of adolescent suicide resulted in growing attention to the mental health of children and adolescents, as well as violence and corporal punishment in schools. 
 
UNICEF’s investments in the development of mental health and psychosocial services (MHPSS) in the context of the emergency, forging strong partnerships with leading local non-governmental organizations in this field, positions UNICEF well to respond to emerging needs. In a context of increased public and government attention to children’s mental health, UNICEF is well-placed to further develop MHPSS approaches. 
 
Delays in customs clearance due to un-streamlined processes and extensive follow-up requirements significantly hindered the timely delivery of essential supplies requested by the Ministry of Health. Intensive end-user monitoring was identified as critical to ensure proper utilization of supplied items.
 
Navigating the crowded social media landscape can be challenging, but UNICEF’s experience highlights the importance of strategic innovation and partnerships. By integrating community management strategies and introducing new content forms like podcasts, UNICEF was able to maintain relevance and foster deeper connections with the audience. This approach demonstrated that even with resource limitations, thoughtful content innovation and strategic partnerships can deliver measurable impact and sustain meaningful engagement. 
 
UNICEF’s efforts to involve children and youth in policy discussions on climate change empower them and ensure that their unique perspectives and needs are considered. These initiatives raise awareness among young people about climate issues and encourage them to become advocates for sustainable practices. The NDC process presents an opportunity to integrate children's voices into policy design. 
 
In 2025, UNICEF's work will continue to be guided by the country programme document, aligning with the new government's priorities. The focus will be on strengthening existing systems and scaling up initiatives piloted locally during the first two years of the country programme. Evaluating and documenting best practices and lessons learned will be crucial for developing scalable models and interventions that can be implemented nationwide. UNICEF will continue advocating for children´s rights and supporting the government in designing and implementing existing policies and national plans, particularly in nutrition, early childhood development, and social protection, elaborated with UNICEF support and following consultative processes. Additionally, UNICEF will work to enhance the government’s data and information systems, which will help monitor the situation of children and inform advocacy and policy design. The office will continue to promote coordination and cross-sector collaboration, both internally and externally, with the government, civil society organizations, the private sector, and networks of children and youth to improve the conditions for children in Sri Lanka, strengthen its work on climate change involving youth and children and continue addressing harmful practices towards boys and girls.

Avec une population de 12.910.087 habitants en 2024 (55% d’enfants et 24% d’adolescents[1]), le Bénin appartient depuis 2022 à la catégorie des pays à revenu intermédiaire de tranche inférieure (PIB/habitant de 1.303 USD). Le rapport sur le développement durable 2024 indique des avancées notables : une réduction significative des inégalités (ODD 10) et de la pauvreté, qui est passée de 36,2 % en 2022, soit une baisse de 2,3 points par rapport à 2019[2] (ODD 1). Ces progrès s’accompagnent d’une croissance économique dynamique, avec un PIB en hausse de 6,4 % en 2024[3] (ODD 8), et d’efforts encourageants pour réduire les disparités entre les hommes et les femmes (ODD 5)[4]. 
En 2024, le Bénin a renforcé ses politiques et programmes en faveur des enfants en lançant la Vision 2060, un cadre stratégique clair et structuré qui guidera les décisions à long terme. Selon les analyses de l’UNICEF, l’Etat s’est aussi illustré en 2024 par une augmentation du budget des secteurs sociaux de base, passant de 41,8% en 2022 à 46.8% en 2024, notamment de 16,1% à 18% pour l’éducation, de 4,3% à 5,3% pour la santé, et avec une légère baisse de 5,6% à 5,3% pour la protection sociale. 
Avec un budget estimatif de 1,182 millions USD, le pays a adopté la Politique Holistique de Protection Sociale qui doit renforcer la résilience des populations, notamment des enfants les plus vulnérables aux risques socio-économiques, climatiques et sécuritaires. En adoptant le Programme National d’Accélération de l’Education et du Bien-être de la Fille (PNAEBF), le gouvernement renforce sa politique volontariste en faveur des filles. Ce programme met l’accent sur l’accès aux alternatives éducatives pour les filles, leur maintien à l’école jusqu’à la fin du secondaire, leur transition vers l’emploi, et la santé sexuelle et reproductive. 
Dans cette même dynamique, le Bénin a intensifié ses réformes dans le secteur social, de la justice et de l’état civil. Il a notamment validé un programme national budgétisé de lutte contre le mariage des enfants et actualisé la politique nationale de protection de l’enfant (PNPE 2025-2034) pour éliminer les violences faites aux enfants, selon une approche systémique à l’horizon 2034.
Un autre tournant stratégique concerne la validation de la Politique Nationale d'Alimentation et de Nutrition 2024-2033 et la création de l’Agence Nationale pour l’Alimentation et la Nutrition (ANAN). Afin d’accélérer la lutte contre la malnutrition, le gouvernement a développé le programme de Supplémentation Nutritionnelle (PSN) pour les 1000 premiers jours de l’enfant (2025-2028), visant les femmes enceintes et allaitantes ainsi que les enfants de 6 à 23 mois, d’un coût estimé à 250 millions USD et financé en majorité par le gouvernement. Cet engagement renforcera l’opérationnalisation de la politique "ONE HEALTH", dont la couverture a été étendue de 6 à 75 communes (97 % du pays) en 2024.
Enfin, le Bénin a consolidé son action climatique, avec la validation du rapport Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). Le gouvernement a organisé une table ronde sur le financement de la question du climat au Bénin et a collaboré avec le FMI et la Banque Mondiale pour élaborer des approches innovantes de financement. 
En participant au Sommet du Futur en septembre 2024, le Bénin s’est engagé à aligner ses actions sur les domaines du social et de la résilience, en renforçant la coopération internationale et en repensant le multilatéralisme pour faire face aux défis actuels et futurs.
En dépit de ces progrès, les défis persistent, notamment :
•       L’indice de développement humain a baissé de 4% passant de 0,525 en 2021-2022 à 0,504 en 2023-2024 et les pertes d’indice dues aux inégalités sont passées de 36,4% à 38,7%[5];
•       4 Béninois sur 10 vivent en dessous du seuil national de pauvreté. Celle-ci constitue un facteur général de la privation des enfants[6] ;
•       9 enfants sur 10 (88%) continuent de subir une forme de violence. Une fille sur 3 (27,5%) est mariée avant l’âge de 18 ans[7] ;
•       L’application du cadre politico-légal de protection de l’enfant reste insuffisante[8] ;
•       1,9 millions d’enfants sont hors de l’école, une situation aggravée dans les zones rurales : 1 enfant sur 3 en âge d’aller à l’école primaire et 1 sur 2 en âge de fréquenter le premier cycle du secondaire ne sont pas scolarisés[9] ;
•       Plus de 90,000 enfants n’ont jamais été vaccinés[10] ;
•       36,50% des enfants souffrent de retard de croissance et seulement 4 mères sur 10 pratiquent l’allaitement maternel exclusif[11].
En 2024, près de 1,9 million[12] d'enfants du nord du Bénin ont été confrontés aux risques de la crise du Sahel, des épidémies et des inondations. Les départements de l'Alibori, de l'Atacora, de la Donga et du Borgou ont subi des attaques par des groupes armés non étatiques (GANE), qui ont déplacé 33.238 personnes (19.732 réfugiés/demandeurs d'asile[13]) et 13.506 personnes déplacées à l'intérieur du pays dont 8.219 enfants et 3.315 femmes[14]. En outre, les inondations ont touché 33.442 personnes et ont perturbé l'éducation de 6.188 élèves.[15]
Néanmoins, porté par une politique volontariste, le Bénin va poursuivre l’identification et la mise en œuvre des projets à fort impact sur l’atteinte des ODD, s’engageant notamment à poursuivre le déploiement de l’assurance maladie universelle, à atteindre l’accès universel à l’eau potable d’ici fin 2026, à renforcer davantage les filets sociaux de base ainsi qu’à une implication accrue sur les questions du climat, de l’éducation de la fille et de la digitalisation.
