Le nouveau programme pays 2024-2026 a permis, de renforcer les interventions de l’UNICEF en vue d’accélérer les résultats clés pour les enfants (KRC), en particulier la vaccination (KRC1), l’amélioration des résultats de l'apprentissage (KRC4), et la prévention des violences contre les enfants (KRC5), en définissant cinq priorités programmatiques : santé communautaire, engagement des adolescents et des jeunes, first food, éducation des filles et résilience et cohésion sociale 
 
Renforcement de l’environnement politique et stratégique et mobilisation des ressources pour la réalisation des droits des enfants à l’échelle
Depuis le début de ce nouveau cycle, l’UNICEF accompagne le gouvernement dans l’élaboration et la mise en œuvre de politiques transformatrices. En plus de l’appui technique fourni avec les Partenaires Techniques et Financiers (PTF), l’UNICEF a apporté une contribution stratégique dans la formulation la Vision 2060 du Bénin en vue de mieux inclure les droits des enfants. Ainsi plus de 800 jeunes, dont 345 adolescentes, via les U-Reporters ont été mobilisé à cet effet. 
Grâce à l’appui de l’UNICEF et de ses partenaires, le gouvernement a organisé avec succès le Forum National sur la Nutrition. Regroupant tous les acteurs et forces vives du secteur, il a reçu l’adhésion des PTF, des autorités locales et du secteur privé. En utilisant les 1000 jours comme axe d’orientation, l’initiative First Food, placera le Bénin comme un exemple dans la région. L’UNICEF a contribué au développement des directives pour sa mise en œuvre dont le pilotage dans 10 communes est prévu pour 2025 et la mise à l’échelle nationale en 2026. 
 
Avec l’appui de l’UNICEF, du bureau régional et de Supply Division, le Bénin a adhéré à l’Initiative pour l’Indépendance Vaccinale (IIV). Ce mécanisme permet d’accélérer les résultats pour les enfants dans le domaine de l’immunisation (KRC1) en couvrant 100% des besoins en vaccins Rota, PCV13, Rougeole-Rubéole et Paludisme. L’IIV garantit en outre la disponibilité continue des vaccins sûrs et efficaces, dans un contexte où le pays amorce sa sortie de l’éligibilité des financements de Gavi[1], principal bailleur pour l’achat des vaccins (88%). 
 
L’UNICEF a été désigné comme agent partenaire pour accompagner le gouvernement dans la préparation et la mise en œuvre d’un Programme sous le financement du Partenariat Mondial pour l’Education (PME). Ce programme a été approuvé par le Conseil d’Administration du PME le 2 décembre 2024 pour un montant total de 38,550,000 USD dont 25,700,000 USD pour la transformation du système éducatif et 12,850,000 USD pour l’accélération de l’éducation et du bien-être des filles (KRC4). 
L’appui technique et financier de l’UNICEF aux réformes-clés de protection de l’enfant a permis d’introduire des mesures novatrices et adaptées, notamment pour les mineurs et les filles. Ainsi des mesures non-privatives de liberté adaptées aux mineurs, un projet de politique nationale de protection de l’enfant (2025-2034) actualisée assortie d’une stratégie budgétisée (2025-2029), et un programme national de lutte contre le mariage des enfants pour le passage à l’échelle de l’approche Cash + Care-Faaba ont été adoptés en vue d’un environnement exempt de violence faites aux enfants.
 
Enfin, l’UNICEF a contribué au développement et l'adoption de la Politique holistique de protection sociale, qui intègre des dimensions essentielles telles que le genre, les personnes en situation de handicap, ainsi que les situations de crises et les changements climatiques. Elle contribue à garantir l'égalité des droits pour tous les enfants au Bénin et leurs accès aux services sociaux essentiels. Couplée au programme national pour l'accélération de l'éducation et du bien-être des filles, ces politiques transformatrices permettent d'améliorer l'accès équitable à l'éducation et de renforcer la protection des enfants, tout en s'attaquant aux inégalités structurelles et en promouvant le bien-être général des enfants et adolescentes. 
 
Renforcement des systèmes nationaux pour la délivrance de services de base de qualité et maximiser l’impact sur les enfants 
« One health »
Premier partenaire stratégique du gouvernement dans l’institutionnalisation de la santé communautaire, l’UNICEF a soutenu la conception et la mise en place l’opérationnalisation de la Politique Nationale de la Santé Communautaire. Ainsi, 48 512 cas de maladies ont été prises en charge en communauté, tandis que 11 604 cas de malnutrition modérée et 3 938 cas de malnutrition aigüe sévère ont été dépistés et référés vers les structures de prise en charge dans les 6 communes pilotes.  L’UNICEF a également accompagné le renforcement des capacités, d’une part, du groupe sectoriel Eau et Assainissement, élargi aux acteurs de la nutrition et de la santé, pour intégrer le changement climatique et les vulnérabilités des enfants dans les projets et programmes sectoriels, et d’autre part, des administrations communales sur la gouvernance dans le secteur WASH, en collaboration avec l’USAID.
L’UNICEF et l’OMS ont contribué à l’analyse et l’évaluation mondiale sur l’assainissement et l’eau potable (enquête GLASS) du Bénin ainsi qu'au démarrage du développement des comptes WASH du Bénin. En vue d’assurer une vision commune et une mise en œuvre de qualité des réformes engagées dans le secteur de l’assainissement, les acteurs de la chaine d’assainissement ont été formés sur l’assainissement géré en toute sécurité et résilient au climat. Ces actions ont été réalisées grâce à l’appui technique et financier de l’UNICEF au Ministère du Cadre de Vie et des Transports, chargé du Développement Durable. 
 
 « Zéro dose » 
En 2024, l’UNICEF a renforcé son appui au gouvernement avec des approches différenciées et pro-équité ciblant les communes à faibles performances pour améliorer l’atteinte des résultats pour les enfants (KRC1). Ainsi, 48.761 (54%) enfants zéro-dose et 56.442 (50%) enfants sous-vaccinés, sur respectivement 91.111 et 112.815 identifiés, ont été vaccinés. Pour répondre aux épidémies de rougeole et de poliomyélite, l’UNICEF a soutenu l’organisation de campagnes : 1.429.423 (102%) et 1.577.262 (113%) enfants de moins de 5 ans sur 1.396.797 enfants ciblés ont été vaccinés pour les deux tours de la riposte vaccinale contre la Polio. Durant la campagne de vaccination couplée au grand rattrapage, 3.122.614 (84%) enfants de 9 à 59 mois ont été vaccinés contre la Rougeole-Rubéole et 2.707.653 (83%) enfants de 6-59 mois supplémentés en Vitamine A. Enfin l’organisation a accompagné le pays dans l’introduction du vaccin contre le paludisme dans 16 zones sanitaires à haute transmission : 69.682 (80%) enfants de 0 à 11 mois ont reçu la 1ère dose du vaccin anti-paludisme.

Renforcement du système de protection sociale et de protection de l’enfant
L’UNICEF a appuyé la réforme de 44 guichets uniques de protection sociale (GUPS) sur 91, et déployé 7 psychologues et 192 volontaires communautaires pour répondre aux violences basées sur le genre (VBG), à la menace sécuritaire et la réadaptation communautaire des enfants vivant avec un handicap. En parallèle, 2.711 comités villageois de veille (CVV) rattachés aux 44 GUPS ont été renforcés. Au niveau national, 3.469 travailleurs sociaux de première ligne ont été outillés sur les systèmes d’information de la protection de l’enfance[2] et les processus de gestion de cas, permettant d’assister 344.455 enfants/adolescent.es (202.626 filles) selon leurs besoins. Les 29 GUPS du Nord ont coordonné l’enrôlement et le transfert monétaire pour le maintien ou la réinsertion à l’école de 100.160 filles de 9 à 15 ans. Dans les 6 communes du Couffo, l’appui à l’opérationnalisation et l’extension des CVV a fait passer la couverture de ce dispositif à 100% des villages de six départements. Reconnu par le gouvernement comme essentiel pour rapprocher les services de protection des enfants vulnérables, le rôle des CVV a été intégré dans la force du travail social à travers la nouvelle PNPE 2025-2034 ainsi que dans le programme national de lutte contre le mariage des enfants.
 
Innovations dans le système éducatif
Pour renforcer la digitalisation de l’éducation, des discussions sont en cours pour doter le pays d’une stratégie nationale en collaboration avec les ministères en charge de l’Education, du Numérique et de la digitalisation, Giga, l’UNICEF, l’Union Européenne et les compagnies de téléphonie mobile (MTN et MoovAfrica). Pour accompagner les élèves dans le développement de leurs compétences, 51 établissements de l’enseignement secondaire, dans six départements, ont été dotés de salles numériques comprenant mobilier, équipements informatiques et connexion internet. L’appui de Giga a permis d’élaborer une base de données de plus de 8.100 écoles géolocalisées pour faciliter leur connectivité. L’UNICEF a soutenu la mise en place de 526 gouvernements scolaires, permettant une meilleure implication des enfants scolarisés dans la gestion de leur établissement scolaire et l’amélioration des résultats scolaires. Les interventions de l’UNICEF en 2024 ont contribué à améliorer les résultats scolaires illustrés : le taux de réussite au CEP est passé de 81,29% en 2023 à 89,67% en 2024, et le BEPC de 69,21% en 2023 à 73,74% en 2024. Ces progrès soutiennent l’atteinte du KRC 4 en lien avec l’amélioration de la qualité de l’Education. 
 
Engagement intensifié des acteurs communautaires
Plus de 7.471 enfants, adolescents et jeunes ont été mobilisés comme partenaires actifs pour des actions inclusives de plaidoyer et de sensibilisation. Le réseau U-Report, avec ses 204.449 membres, a joué un rôle clé dans les diagnostics communautaires et les campagnes visant à transformer les normes sociales de genre et pratiques néfastes, en collaboration avec près de 150 têtes couronnées dans le Nord. Ces acteurs de première ligne ont déployé des interventions d’auto-diagnostique, de dialogue, de diffusion et de collecte d’information et de mobilisation sociale permettant ainsi d’engager plus d’un millier de femmes et jeunes dans les comportements résilients y compris dans le suivi  communautaire pour la lutte contre le mariage des enfants/les formes d’abus et d’exploitation,  le maintien des filles à l’école et l’anticipation des mesures préventives pour garantir une santé communautaire adéquate. Les efforts consentis dans le domaine ont permis d’observer des changements au niveau de près de 328 sur 1028 villages des départements du Nord, certifiés par le gouvernement comme exempts de mariage des enfants, après une évaluation du niveau d’engagement des communautés pour l’abandon de la pratique.
 
Réduction des inégalités, inclusion sociale, renforcement du genre et lutte contre le changement climatique  
Cash + Care - Faaba
100.160 filles ont reçu au moins un transfert monétaire via le programme Cash + Care-Faaba. Si l’accès à l’éducation et la prévention du mariage des enfants sont les principaux résultats attendus du transfert monétaire, la revue à mi-parcours du programme a révélé d’autres impacts positifs : l’augmentation de la consommation alimentaire et le renforcement des activités génératrices de revenus. Ces améliorations permettent aux familles de faire fructifier le transfert reçu, facilitant ainsi l’éducation et le bien-être des filles et des autres enfants du ménage. D’autres résultats stratégiques ont été atteints notamment la revue à mi-parcours (RMP) et le cas d'investissement du programme afin de réfléchir sur la durabilité et la soutenabilité. Pour atteindre ces résultat, l'UNICEF a poursuivi son appui technique et financier au ministère des Affaires Sociales et de la Microfinance (MASM) D'autres ministères ont collaboré à des degrés divers : ministère des Enseignements Maternel et Primaire, ministère des Enseignements Secondaire Technique et de la Formation Professionnelle, ministère de la Justice et de la Législation et ministère de l'Intérieur et de la Sécurité Publique. Les soutiens du Royaume des Pays-Bas et du Canada ont été critiques pour la mise à l’échelle et la durabilité de ce programme. 
  
Equité, genre et inclusion sociale
En appui au gouvernement Béninois, l’UNICEF a mis en œuvre des actions multisectorielles pour promouvoir et renforcer l’équité de genre dans l’éducation, la nutrition, WASH, protection et santé. Durant les 16 jours d’activisme contre les VBG, l’UNICEF avec le PNUD, UNFPA, les Pays bas et le Canada ont conjointement appuyé le gouvernement du Bénin dans la mobilisation de tous les acteurs aux niveaux national et départemental y compris les plateformes numériques afin de renouveler l’engagement collectif à éradiquer ces violences. Aussi, le gouvernement, appuyé par l’UNICEF, a finalisé une stratégie genre, produit de nouveaux outils et renforcé les capacités techniques de 174 acteurs sur les VBG et/ou la masculinité positive. 202.626 filles/adolescentes sur 344.455 enfants/adolescent.es ont reçu des services de prévention/réponse aux VBG/Mariage des Enfants. Une attention a été portée à l’intégration systématique du handicap, des enfants déplacés et des communautés agropastorales dans les interventions de protection de l’enfance. 2.191 enfants/adolescent.es avec un handicap ont été assistés dont 1.374 (634 filles) à travers 30 centres de réadaptation communautaire pilotés par les GUPS. 
La réduction des inégalités et inclusion du genre a été renforcée avec des initiatives ciblées pour améliorer la supplémentation en vitamine A, en particulier dans les zones à faible couverture comme Natitingou. Ces actions ont renforcé la durabilité des programmes et la capacité des acteurs locaux à fournir cette supplémentation de manière équitable. Le rôle des groupements féminins et des clubs de pères a été central dans la promotion des interventions à fort impact, notamment dans les zones de Zapkota et Gogounou. 
 
Contribution à la résilience et la paix
Au regard du contexte sécuritaire dans la zone nord du Bénin, l’UNICEF appuyé par l’Union Européenne s’est engagé dans le renforcement de la résilience des systèmes sociaux essentiels à l’enfant, notamment l’éducation. Le bureau a accompagné les efforts du gouvernement à renforcer l’employabilité et l’insertion professionnelle des jeunes dans les zones affectées, en assurant, avec ses partenaires, la formation et l’insertion professionnelle dans les métiers de l’artisanat et les activités génératrices de revenus de 1.100 jeunes (dont 653 filles). L’engagement des jeunes (notamment U-report) sur les questions de cohésion sociale a été intensifié. Un dialogue national, en partenariat avec le Haut-Commissaire à la Sédentarisation de Eleveurs, a été organisé avec les leaders agro-pastoraux sur les questions d’éducation et de cohésion sociale, posant les jalons d’une feuille de route pour soutenir l’accès des enfants agropastoraux aux services sociaux.
 
Child rights
Le gouvernement avec l’appui de l’UNICEF-Bénin et du Luxembourg, a lancé un programme 2024-2027 axé sur la réalisation des droits des enfants, dans le Zou et le Couffo, pour soutenir l’implémentation des recommandations de l’Examen périodique universel de 2023, relatives à l’élimination du travail des enfants et ses pires formes. Le pays a également adopté une feuille de route pour éliminer lesdits phénomènes, dans le cadre de l’Alliance 8.7. Ces initiatives contribuent à l’atteinte des ODD 8.7.1, 16.2 et 16.3 visant l’élimination de toutes les formes de VFE et l’égalité d’accès à la justice pour tous. La définition de mesures non-privatives de liberté pour les mineurs contribue aussi à renforcer les droits des enfants à une justice adaptée, en alignement avec l’ODD 16.3. Le plaidoyer mené en faveur du droit à l’enregistrement des naissances a abouti à un engagement de l’Agence nationale pour l’identification des personnes à accorder, en 2025, la gratuité du retrait des certificats de naissance pour les 0-5 ans. Afin d’œuvrer à l'éducation pour tous les enfants, notamment pour les enfants en dehors de l'école, le gouvernement et l'UNICEF ont entrepris une étude analysant la population des apprenants dans les écoles coraniques et les institutions éducatives communautaires qui révèle un total de près de 50.000 enfants de 5 à 14 ans inscrits[3]. Sur base de cette étude, le gouvernement et ses partenaires ont développé un cadre d'orientation et d'encadrement des écoles coraniques prenant en compte le programme officiel d'éducation de base. Cette première étape impliquant les leaders traditionnels et religieux, les organisations faîtières islamiques, les ministères de l’éducation, les partenaires techniques et financiers facilitera la création de passerelles éducatives entre l’éducation formelle et celle islamique.
 
Climat
2024 a été marqué par l'innovation technologique et le renforcement du gouvernement pour bâtir la résilience climatique avec les jeunes et les enfants. L’implication des jeunes pour le climat, accompagnés par l’UNICEF, s’est accentuée avec la mise en œuvre des projets post-COP 28, sous l’encadrement du Ministère du cadre de vie et des Transports, en charge du climat. L’UNICEF a été retenu comme l’agence partenaire pour les fonds de readiness au Green Climate Fund. D’autres partenariats notamment avec la GIZ et les agences des Nations-Unies permettent de poursuivre la mobilisation de ressources pour le Benin notamment auprès de la Banque Africaine de Developpement (BAD). Par ailleurs, les efforts du bureau pays pour baisser son empreinte carbone se sont intensifiés avec la dynamisation de son comité vert et surtout avec des choix portés pour des équipements et installations bas carbone.
 
Réponse aux urgences 
Adoptant l’approche triple nexus, l’UNICEF a renforcé son soutien au Bénin face aux crises sécuritaires, climatiques et éducatives. Plus de 18.000 personnes ont accédé à des soins de santé, et 120 074 enfants ont été vaccinés contre la rougeole. Les inondations ont conduit à des interventions WASH, dont la réhabilitation de pompes, la construction de 200 latrines et la fourniture de kits pour 25.975 personnes. En éducation, 7.050 enfants en situation d’urgence ont repris le chemin de l’école, et 30.000 élèves ont bénéficié de formations sur la cohésion sociale. 20.140 enfants malnutris ont été traités, renforçant la résilience communautaire. Enfin, 3.168 enfants ont ainsi reçu une réponse holistique contre les violences et 52.837 du soutien psychosocial à travers 56 espaces amis des enfants. 6.571 ménages PDI/réfugiés ont bénéficié d’un kit d’articles ménagers essentiels. L’UNICEF a également renforcé les capacités des partenaires gouvernementaux, mairie et de la société civile sur la préparation aux urgences, la coordination et l’évaluation rapide pour une meilleure anticipation des risques dans les zones fragiles.
 
Protection contre l’Exploitation et les Abus Sexuels (PEAS) et Redevabilité envers les Populations Affectées (AAP)
En 2024 l’UNICEF a priorisé la mise en œuvre des recommandations sur la protection contre l’exploitation et les abus sexuels et la Redevabilité envers les Populations Affectées. Le plaidoyer auprès du gouvernement a permis d'intégrer un mécanisme de signalement des allégations/cas d’EAS applicable aux partenaires gouvernementaux au mécanisme national de signalement des VBGs, d’intégrer la PEAS dans les outils de référencement des survivant(es) de VBGs et d’organiser la formation de formateurs de 82 acteurs gouvernementaux qui ont ensuite outillé 1,771 autres acteurs institutionnels. Le bureau s’est doté d’une stratégie de Redevabilité envers les Populations Affectées : 150 agents d’ONG et acteurs de la gouvernance locale ont été formés afin d’assurer leur redevabilité et de veiller à leurs droits.

Dans le cadre du renforcement de la collaboration et partenariat au sein des secteurs, l’UNICEF a continué de jouer un rôle actif dans la plupart des groupes sectoriels de partenaires techniques et financiers du Bénin. En effet, l’UNICEF est lead ou co-lead dans les groupes nutrition, WASH et protection sociale. L’UNICEF est aussi membre actif de la coordination des chefs de coopération et agences des Nations-Unies au Bénin et aussi des groupes sectoriels santé, éducation et finances publiques. 
L’UNICEF a fortement contribué à la mise en œuvre du cadre de coopération (UNSCDF) et le renforcement du One UN. Ainsi divers programmes conjoints ont été initiés en 2024 avec certaines agences onusiennes et des ressources importantes ont été mobilisées tels que : 
·       L'action conjointe de l'UNICEF et du PAM a permis de mobiliser un financement de 45 millions USD des Pays-Bas pour un projet intégré utilisant l’alimentation scolaire comme porte d’entrée pour prévenir la malnutrition dans les villages autour des écoles à cantines. Ce projet permet d’assurer la continuité des actions de promotion des pratiques nutritionnelles adéquates, notamment la diversité alimentaire, en ciblant la fenêtre d'opportunité des 1000 jours.
·       Sous le leadership de l’UNICEF, conjointement avec le PAM, l’UNHCR et l’OIM et en étroite collaboration avec le bureau régional, un programme pour la résilience et la paix a permis de mobiliser des ressources de l’Union Européenne pour les départements du Nord.
·       L’UNICEF et le PNUD se sont engagés pour ce nouveau cycle à renforcer leur collaboration pour le climat et la digitalisation en appui aux initiatives du Gouvernement. La contribution conjointe de l’UNICEF et du PNUD au Ministère du Cadre de Vie et des Transports, a permis d’assurer la participation de 6 des 8 jeunes délégués négociateurs juniors qui ont pris part à la COP 29 sur le changement climatique à Baku en Azerbaïdjan. 
·       L’UNICEF, le PNUD et L’UNFPA ont joins leur force pour le développement de la Vision 2060, permettant d’assurer l’inclusion de toutes les vulnérables dans le processus de développement de ce document stratégique.
Concernant les Institutions Financières Internationales, le Bureau a été très dynamique en 2024 en renforçant son partenariat avec le Fonds Monétaire International (FMI) et en proposant dans ses conditionnalités, la cartographie des programmes de protection sociale, la mise à jour régulière et la pleine opérationnalisation du registre social unique que le FMI a recommandé au Gouvernement. Le FMI a aussi encouragé le Bénin à poursuivre l’intégration des changements climatiques dans le projet de budget pour la gestion 2025. Des discussions importantes ont été conduites avec la Banque mondiale en vue du renforcement des synergies et du partenariat dans le domaine de la réforme des GUPS, ainsi que des programmes dans le domaine de l’éducation de la jeune fille. Enfin l’UNICEF s’est engagé plus en avant avec la Banque africaine de Developpement (BAD) autour des thèmes du changement climatique et de la nutrition. 
Dans le domaine des innovations technologiques, l'UNICEF, avec le soutien financier de l'Union Européenne, de la Coopération Suisse, de VINCI Energies, la Fondation MTN et de la Fondation Moov Africa Bénin, accompagne les efforts du gouvernement à l’initiative de promouvoir l'utilisation du numérique dans l'éducation des adolescents et des jeunes. Cette initiative prévoit une mobilisation continue des partenaires clés pour développer et déployer des contenus éducatifs adaptés au contexte local, en mettant un accent particulier sur les STEM (Sciences, Technologies, Ingénierie et Mathématiques). Cette vision à long terme contribuera à promouvoir une éducation numérique inclusive et équitable, à renforcer les compétences des jeunes, en particulier des filles, et à préparer efficacement la jeunesse béninoise à participer à l’économie numérique mondiale. 
L'UNICEF a aussi renforcé ses partenariats avec le secteur privé, notamment MTN et Moov Africa, ayant permis à 12 000 adolescents d’acquérir des compétences numériques clés. Vinci Énergies a offert à 17 écoles une meilleure connectivité et des contenus éducatifs, touchant près de 23 000 élèves. L’innovation majeure a été le partenariat avec L’Aéroport de Cotonou, passant en bleu lors de la Journée Mondiale de l’Enfance, a plaidé pour le respect des droits des enfants et facilité des dons individuels, une première au Bénin. Ces initiatives ont démontré le rôle important et l’impact durable du partenariat public-privé sur la promotion des droits des enfants.
D’autres partenariats ont été mis en place pour avancer l’agenda des enfants : 
·       Le partenariat avec Social Watch Bénin et ALCRER, pour le plaidoyer auprès du gouvernement et de l’Assemblée Nationale sur les allocations vers les secteurs sociaux sensibles aux enfants ;
·       La collaboration avec l’Ecole Nationale d’Administration de l’Université d’Abomey-Calavi pour le renforcement des capacités évaluatives des cadres des administrations publique et parlementaire de 10 pays d’Afrique francophone et la relecture de l’offre de formation de master en évaluation des politiques publiques ;
·       Le partenariat avec les OSC engagés dans la lutte contre les VBG, les ambassades des Pays Bas, de la Suisse, du Canada et du PNUD et UNFPA lors des activités durant les 16 jours d’activismes ;
·       Le renforcement de partenariat avec des organisations de la société civile locales, notamment agro-pastorales, de jeunes et de femmes (POTALMEN, PIED, Havre de paix) afin de travailler au plus près des populations.
Les fonds mobilisés sur le seuil prévu de 78.490.000USD sont 84.459.945USD, soit 108 pour cent des fonds requis pour le cycle programmatique. Les principaux donateurs sont les Pays Bas (55%), Gavi (24%), Luxembourg (10%), le Japon (6%). En 2024, le bureau pays a mobilisé 23.590.615USD, dont 22.746.278USD sous de nouveaux accords et 1.644.051USD pour les urgences. 55 pour cent (13.034.109USD) de ces fonds ont été mobilisés conjointement avec le Programme Alimentaire Mondial (PAM). Les fonds confirmés attendus s’élèvent à 51.288.160USD (GPE : 72% ; Coopération Suisse : 11% ; Canada : 8%, Japon : 3% et Bénin : 2%).  La flexibilité des fonds RR a permis de poursuivre l’appui à la réforme de l’état civil, renforcer la visibilité de UNICEF-Bénin dans les évènements stratégiques nationaux du gouvernement concernant les enfants, la réponse à la menace sécuritaire et de contribuer aux coûts transversaux et opérationnels du bureau.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook

Indicator_Status3:
Burkina Faso is a landlocked country in West Africa with a population of over 23.6 million, including 12.2 million children. It ranks 185 out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index in 2024. The country has experienced significant political changes over the past decade (2014-2024) and faces a complex development, protection, and humanitarian crisis, exacerbated by its high vulnerability to climate change, which adversely affects children.
 
Dealing with internal displacements remains a significant challenge for children. At one point, the country had over 2 million internally displaced people (IDPs), with approximately 58.5% being children. Over the year, the government reported that nearly 1 million people have returned to their homes, requiring additional support. In March 2024, over 5,000 schools were closed, affecting nearly 800,000 learners. By December 2024, the government stated that 2,500 schools had reopened over the past two years.
 
The Government of Burkina Faso claims full control over 70% of the national territory. However, several cities remain critically difficult to access as they are surrounded and are often prey to random attacks by non-state actor militias, including JNIM (affiliated with Al Qaida) and the Islamic Group in the Great Sahara.
 
Despite the challenging security crisis, Burkina Faso has made significant progress on child-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), according to the voluntary national report (VNR 2023). For instance, on SDG3 (Good Health and Well-being), maternal, infant, and neonatal mortality indicators have improved significantly. The latest household survey reveals that the under-five mortality rate has decreased from 129 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2010 to 48 in 2021. This improvement is attributed to political will and commitment to ensuring the continuity of healthcare services, even in crisis-affected regions. Burkina Faso has achieved significant improvements in immunization, with 90% of children aged 0-11 months receiving three doses of pentavalent vaccine, and 86% of health districts meeting the target of reaching more than 80% of children with three doses of DPT-containing vaccines. The transmission of polio and maternal and neonatal tetanus has been interrupted. 
 
Despite this notable progress, additional efforts are needed to achieve the SDG targets by 2030. Currently, 1 in 21 children under five dies before their fifth birthday, 1 in 56 newborns dies before completing the first four weeks of life and 1 in 505 mothers dies giving birth. Children in Burkina Faso live in a context marked by multiple crises, while social norms and practices exacerbate their vulnerability and expose them to multiple deprivations of their rights. Overall, children suffer physical violence (15.6% of children aged 12-17), psychological violence (25.7% of children aged 12-17) and sexual violence (3.1% of children aged 12-17).
 
The situation of girls remains worrying due to harmful practices such as child marriage and female genital cutting. In 2021, 7.8% of women aged 20-24 were married before age 15, and 38.2% were married before age 18. Additionally, 56.1% of women aged 15-49 and 9% of girls aged 0 to 14 have undergone female genital mutilation (FGM). Fewer adolescent girls were victims of FGM compared to older women, but efforts must be accelerated to eliminate the harmful practice by 2030. In the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector, access to safe drinking water increased from 78.3% in 2023 to 79.4% in 2024, while sanitation access remained stagnant at around 28%. This stabilization of the WASH sector performance was possible through committed efforts of the government and its partners in strengthening the system for more resilience and enforcing sector dialogue and coordination. Looking forward, a key challenge is to maintain systemic gains and adequate level of funding to ensure the sustainability of WASH services amid ongoing security concerns.
 
Burkina Faso has a strong legislative, regulatory, and institutional framework to protect and promote children’s rights, and there have been consistent and significant commitments to improving the lives of children, especially through investments in health and education. However, operationalizing of a protective environment for children in families, communities, schools, cities, is challenging due to limited access to vulnerable children and families in crisis-affected regions and insufficient funding.   The Burkina Faso government engages meaningfully to help children achieve rights including the right to survive, health, education, nutrition, protection, and vaccination, among others. The government understandably prioritizes regaining lost territory through intensified military action but has managed to maintain a balance with its response to the humanitarian and development challenges. Now, the government continues maintaining social sector budgets, but this might be challenged if the military action is prolonged.
 
UNICEF recognizes the gravity of the security situation while emphasizing the need to invest in the human capital of the Burkinabè people. The current priority is to advocate for the government to continue to see ongoing investments in health, education, nutrition, and broader child rights as both human rights and security strategic priorities. While acknowledging the emergency scenario Burkina Faso faces, there is an urgent need to strengthen the development/humanitarian nexus approach to address the challenge in the medium to long term. With 50% of the Burkinabè population under 18, investing in children’s education, health, and protection must be seen as a sustainable solution to the underlying issues that could drive the security crisis.

In support to the health system and sector, UNICEF facilitated the development of key strategic documents, including the National Strategic Plan for Community Health, the Hospital Hygiene Strategy and the Digital Health Strategic Plan. 
 
With UNICEF and other key partners’ support, the country’s Expanded Programme on Immunization continued to show a strong performance, maintaining high national routine immunization coverage rates above 90% for Penta3, despite disparities in certain security-challenged regions. Two rounds of mass polio vaccination campaigns successfully organized reached 5.6 million children each, contributing to sustaining the country’s polio-free status. The successful introduction of malaria vaccine in 27 health districts reaching 70% with the third dose, aligning with the global and regional objectives of reducing malaria-related morbidity and mortality. Key contributing factors include optimizing the country’s cold chain capacity from 70% in 2023 to 91% in 2024; strengthening vaccine management and national health infrastructure as part of UNICEF’s priorities for sustainable health systems; the extensive network of 33,000 community health workers supported by UNICEF and other partners. This performance aligns with Burkina Faso's goal of ensuring universal access to vaccination services as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, particularly Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-Being). 
 
In UNICEF’s support to direct service delivery to health systems and facilities, more than 650,000 newborns received essential neonatal care, and 5.4 million children were treated under the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness. The installation of oxygen plants in key health facilities across the country is playing a major role in improving neonatal care and reducing neonatal mortality, by increasing the availability of vital respiratory assistance.
 
To improve child nutrition outcomes, UNICEF has accelerated its advocacy efforts with Government and partners to attract more investments in nutrition programming, with a strategic focus on exclusive breastfeeding for children under six months, the Infant and young child feeding (IYCF) services including the scale-up of the use of mother-to-mother support groups (GASPA) and the nationwide Vitamin A supplementation for children under five years. UNICEF also supported strong advocacy actions for the implementation of the code for Breastmilk substitute (BMS) and the nutrition civil watch initiative for the monitoring of code violation. Additionally, UNICEF introduced the First Food agenda in nutrition programming to improve child feeding environment and access to high quality nutrition foods for children working with private sector small and medium enterprises as well as local producers.
 
Consequently, Burkina Faso is amongst the top countries in the region with highest breastfeeding prevalence. According to the 2023-24 nutrition survey, 72.5% of children under six months are exclusively breastfed (EBF), of which 54% reported early initiation at the health facility.  This was achieved by investing more in the capacity building of community-based health care workers and health providers on the Infant and young child feeding (IYCF) guidelines for the promotion and protection of breastfeeding practice in communities and health facilities. As a result, over 1.3 million mothers and caregivers received IYCF counselling services as 59,000 mother -to-mother support groups were established, including in IDP sites.   
 
At facility level, a contextualized Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative was implemented in 100 health facilities, with a track record of being certified on the 10 steps to successful EBF. 
 
At community level, with UNICEF support, over 3.7 million children under five years were reached with two annual doses of Vitamin A, coupled with deworming activities and malnutrition screening. Consequently, the management of severe acute malnutrition at the community level increased significantly from 60% in 2023 to 76% in 2024.  Through UNICEF’s action, early screening, referral and treatment of wasting were scaled-up, reaching over 146,000 severely malnourished children (73% HAC targets) with life-saving treatment meeting globally accepted standards – cure rate 92.7%, mortality 1.2% and dropout rate 6.1%.  These results were achieved thanks, among other things, to the strengthened multisectoral nutrition coordination, the Government's preparation of the nutrition investment case, as well as return on investment and budget analyses of the national contribution to nutrition. 
 
In support of the child protection systems, UNICEF acknowledges that sustain advocacy efforts have led to the finalization of the Persons and Family Code and its presentation to the National Assembly for review. A key element in the code is the proposed increase in the minimum age of marriage from 17 to 18 years of age. This will further strengthen the country’s efforts and progress made over the last five years on preventing and addressing child marriage.  
 
The percentage of women aged 20-24 years married before age 18 decreased from 46% in 2020 to 38% in 2024. UNICEF programming continued to support adolescent girls on prevention and care interventions to address child marriage.  In 2024, 104,475 adolescent girls have been reached with various services, including life skills training, family life education, schooling, vocational training, and support for professional integration.
 
To facilitate the work of case managers in caring for children in need of protection and provide up-to-date and secure data on child protection, UNICEF supported the deployment of the Child Protection Information Management System plus (CPIMS+) in two regions, with the ambition of scaling it up in all regions within the next two years. The CPIMS+ is a comprehensive inter-agency digital system for managing secure information on child protection. 
 
As part of the implementation of the "Handover Protocol" signed in 2022, and to strengthen the capacity of defense forces and VDP in human and child rights, UNICEF, with other UN agencies, in close collaboration with the Ministries of Justice, Humanitarian Action / National Solidarity and Defense, supported the training of 360 senior officers for the training of the Defense and Security Forces (FDS) and the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP), as well as the development of an illustrated guide on human rights and children's rights. Furthermore, to strengthen institutional capacity, technical and financial support was provided to the 13 regional directorates of Humanitarian Action / National Solidarity, and to some 20 NGOs and local associations, to provide care to 63,275 children, including 33,408 girls, threatened or affected by violence. UNICEF also provided psychosocial support to 207,240 children and child caretakers, including 104,326 women and girls. In total, 104,475 adolescent girls were protected from child marriage and 112,693 women, including 62,775 girls, benefited from services to prevent female genital mutilation.
 
In support of safe and clean environments for children, UNICEF’s actions directly contributed to 288,000 people gaining access to quality basic water services in 2024 especially in challenging and crisis-affected areas of Sahel, Centre Nord and Est regions. This has been achieved through a reinforced and innovative partnership with the National Water Utility Company (ONEA) and the 2iE institute (to enhance ground water knowledge) under the leadership of the Ministry of Environment, Water and Sanitation. In support of government’s sanitation sector efforts, the lives of over 560,000 people were transformed as their villages turned into open defecation-free communities. 
 
Remarkably 360,951 individuals now have access to basic sanitation facilities, surpassing the initial target of 210,000. These efforts, combined with other initiatives led by the Ministry of water, sanitation and environment, and other partners are expected to lower the percentage of people practicing open defecation from 33.6% to around 31% in 2024. 
 
UNICEF contributed to government’s push for improved education and learning outcomes in terms of access and quality. The gross enrolment rate for primary education increased from 74.5 % in 2023 to 78.2% in 2024, and completion rate from 71.5 to 82%. Girls’ education improved notably with enrolment rate rising from 75.8% to 80% and completion rate from 73% to 80.9%. UNICEF supported the efforts of the Ministry of Basic Education (MEBAPLN) in collaboration with the higher Institute of Population Sciences (ISSP) to generate evidence to inform the design of the presidential initiative for quality education (IPEQ) reference document in its "out-of-school children" component, to ensure effective care of these children in the long term.
 
As education sector lead, UNICEF played a critical role in spearheading and coordinating dialogue between technical and financial partners to mobilize, capture and direct resources to impact the transformation of education, via Special Treasury Allocation Account (CAST or the Global partnership for Education (GPE). UNICEF helped elaborate the National Strategy for Education in Emergency Situations (SN-ESU) which is the reference framework for steering education in emergency situations in a country experiencing security, humanitarian and health crises.
 
To better advocate for the centrality of children’s rights in the political agenda, UNICEF supported the network of Burkinabè parliamentarians for education and culture in 2024 with capacity building on education in emergency situations. To bring in-depth transformation of education and be more outcome-driven, UNICEF gave support and guidance to the government in the elaboration of a new curriculum more adapted to Burkinabe culture and socio-economic context.
With UNICEF’s direct support, 877,279 children (377,386 girls) have accessed quality education, through back-to-school campaign, alternative learning approaches including radio catch up initiatives, the integration of Qur’anic schools into formal and non-formal education systems, as well as construction of temporary, semi-permanent, and permanent classrooms. 
UNICEF supports the government in providing each child of school age with at least one balanced meal per day, through the Integrated School Food and Nutrition Support Program (PISANS), benefitting 108,137 children, 2,237 teachers and 476 schools in 8 municipalities. 
Thanks to government’s sustained efforts, over 2,500 schools have been reopened, facilitating the return of thousands of children to school in crisis-affected areas. 
 
Key drivers of progress for children as framed by the annual work plan (AWP) and management plan (AMP)
 
Adapting and strengthening Child-centered social protection systems. UNICEF has provided technical support to government’s National social safety nets Programme (PAMPV) to increase access to social safety nets for poor and most vulnerable households, while strengthening their resilience to shocks. UNICEF has played a central role in the strategic roll-out of the Single/unique Social Register (RSU), including its expansion into newly targeted areas and the adaptation of tools for hard-to-reach areas. This expansion has resulted in the inclusion of around 60,000 new households in the RSU in 2024; in the increased access to social protection programmes by the poorest 20% vulnerable people.  In 2024, UNICEF has started a process of the digitalization of micro-simulation of the impact of public policies for children and people of Burkina Faso. This exercise is expected to be fully completed in 2025.
 
Strengthening UNICEF’s humanitarian action and accelerating its rapid response: Building upon the existing local structures and communities, in areas classified as being at severity levels 2 and 3, UNICEF has made significant efforts to meet its core commitments for children in emergencies through the improved coordination of field presence and programming capacities in all regions.  As a result, 2,321,404 individuals were reached with multi sectoral package of humanitarian assistance, especially in most crisis-affected regions. This includes 39,809 displaced individuals assisted with multisectoral package responses under the interagency response team (ERT) with other UN agencies as UNICEF last resort provider.
 
UNICEF has also pushed for the acceleration and scalability of its localization approach to overcome the humanitarian access barriers. Through the Rapid Response and Community Resilience (3RC) approach, over 690 individuals from local organizations and structures have been trained in humanitarian early warning systems, thus, empowering them to reach 301,471 persons in areas classified at severity levels 2 and 3.
 
Furthermore, technical assistance to CONASUR has enhanced the organization's ability to manage and respond to humanitarian crisis effectively. This action included the development of contingency and humanitarian response plans, the support to capacity-building sessions of local partners, and the provision of relevant equipment and kits for rapid response.
 
UNICEF’s flexibility and adaptability have been essential in achieving remarkable results by exploring alternative strategies to ensure the continuity of health services in areas of limited access. For example, UNICEF has increased its support to the professionalization of community health workers to maintain the acceptable level of immunization services coverage in the poorest and conflict-affected zones.  This has led to an increase in measles vaccination coverage up to 80%. It appears that 30% of the vaccinated children were covered by community health workers in hard-to-reach areas.
 
Amplifying children’s voice and advocating for the centrality of child rights programming in Burkina Faso: In 2024, UNICEF has spearheaded high level advocacy towards the highest state authorities. To mark World Children’s Day, UNICEF facilitated an advocacy session at the highest level of government. 200 children from 13 regions held a parliamentary session, under the auspices of the President of the Transitional Legislative Assembly (ALT). The Ministers of Education, Health and Humanitarian Action / National Solidarity presented the progress made in the realization of children’s rights. These children then discussed with the President of Faso the status of the fulfillment of the promises he made to them in 2023.  UNICEF helped children reach millions of people with key messages on their rights such as access and quality education, on harmful practices such as child marriage. It supported the government organize major national events such as the National Culture Week (SNC), the professional media award Galian, the international craftsmanship fair SIAO and Burkina Faso’s biggest child cultural competition Fitini show, to create spaces for children to express themselves and relay their peers’ voices. 
 
Given the fact that Burkina Faso is perceived as the most neglected displacement crisis and media coverage remains low, UNICEF worked with goodwill ambassadors and digital influencers to promote children’s rights and continue amplify children’s voices. Overall, UNICEF reached 12 million people via its digital platforms and 2.7 million people viewed its advocacy videos while one of the most popular digital influencers in Burkina Faso reached his 14 million followers with child rights key messages.  
 
To boost youth’s voices and engagement, the CO launched a campaign that increased the number of u-reporters from 150,000 to 700,000 in a year, and a young artist and influencer was appointed as a U-Report ambassador. With a series of training on children’s rights and journalism, UNICEF strengthened the capacities of 120 media professionals on how to report on child rights issues and supported Galian Kids prize to award children who wrote articles or produced TV or radio programmes to speak for the voiceless. Each month, the UNICEF Burkina Faso newsletter reaches over 600 donors, potential donors and partners.
 
Improving access to PSEA referral and reporting mechanisms: To create an institutional culture to prevent and address PSEA issues timely and effectively, UNICEF continued to strengthen its institutional capacity including those of its implementing partners. All partners have been evaluated and actions taken to strengthen gaps. As at the end of 2024, no severe incidents were recorded across UNICEF and its implementing partners. UNICEF also contributed to the inter-agency work on PSEA through its support to the PSEA network and capacity building to leverage the UN accountability to affected populations.
 
Reinforcing the culture of risk informed programming: The challenging operating environment required more flexibility in operations without losing sight of compliance needs and opportunities for harmonized UN joint-operational activities at lower costs.  To this end, UNICEF has further integrated risk analysis in planning, management and implementation processes as part of the Annual Work Planning and Annual Management Plan for 2024 to ensure timely programme adaptation to mitigate possible risks, while promoting constructive dialogue with partners.  UNICEF has adapted its context-specific strategy to institute a periodic dialogue with all implementing partners on scale, impact and risk-informed programming.
 
In the same vein to mitigate the risks associated with muti-dimensional crisis, UNICEF invested more in the localization of child-centered services, especially in the crisis-affected regions to ensure that UNICEF’s programme remains flexible, agile, and fit for purpose. In each of the targeted regions, a programmatic entry point was identified, in community health, nutrition, WASH and Education to lead the delivery of a multi-sector package adapted to local realities/needs and the country context.  The bottom line is to maintain access to children and other most vulnerable populations in the fast-changing settings and to get the best value possible for UNICEF money/resources/people.
 
Advocating for the change of the legal marriage age:  UNICEF was heavily involved in advocacy for the change of legal marriage age for girls to 18 years. This was done as part of the national efforts to progressively eliminate the child marriage practice and the revised Persons and Family Code within the challenging context and its evolving cultural and social fabric in Burkina Faso.
 
Boosting Transformative Gender programming, SBC and Youth engagement: The Gender, SBC, Adolescent and Youth Engagement section worked collaboratively to implement initiatives that empowered women and adolescent girls, introduced the value of positive masculinity to drive societal change; and engaged young "future husbands" and traditional leaders to sustain gender norms change.  For example, 3,200 women were empowered through Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLA) and income-generating activities, enabling them to contribute significantly to community development and infrastructure projects in WASH. Over 2,000 women were trained in ecological charcoal production from solid organic waste and agricultural biomass.  This training has equipped them with skills to contribute to mitigate the effects of climate change and build sanitation facilities.   All these actions have been progressively contributing to reshape societal perceptions of femininity and masculinity in Burkina Faso.
 
In addition to engagement in children’s voices, the 700,000 U Reporters serve as agents of change. In the insecurity-affected Sahel region for example, U-reporters actively identified and monitored underserved children, and this action has facilitated their access to essential healthcare and social services; empowered young people to address service delivery gaps. In education, the combination of incentives and awareness programmes for girls' education has led to improved academic outcomes with an impressive result of 92.86% success rate in the high school examination compared to the national average of 52.61%.
 
In 2024, UNICEF Burkina Faso reaffirmed its commitment to disability inclusion by hiring a Disability Inclusion UN volunteer and integrating his accessibility to work environment. Targeted measures, including infrastructure adaptations, have been implemented to ensure barrier-free access. These actions reflect a strategic approach towards fostering a workplace where everyone can fully contribute in compliance with international inclusion and equity standards.

Partnerships with the National Assembly of Transition:  To strengthen advocacy for children’s rights, 200 child parliamentarians engaged in direct dialogue with decision-makers to secure commitments and action for children and to attract more public investments in education, health, and protection.  Subsequently, these parliamentarians (Children) met with the President of Faso to foster actionable plans to make children issues more visible at national level. This was part of the communication and awareness campaign that reached over 12 million people with key advocacy message for children’s wellbeing. While holding this high-level event, UNICEF strengthened partnership with the Ministry of Communication, the office of the President and that of the President of Legislative Assembly.    
 
Bringing donor countries together to leverage for children: UNICEF sustained its engagement with the group of the Friends of Faso children (GAEF) composed of ambassadors and other high-rank diplomats to continue leveraging support in favor of child rights. The group holds a meeting, or a field visit every two months to discuss efforts made to open access to social services and realization of children’s rights. 
 
Shared-value partnerships in WASH:  UNICEF has joined forces with the African Development Bank (AfDB) for climate adaption programme to tackle the adverse impacts of climate change by enhancing agricultural practices, improving water management, and reducing disaster risks.  In addition, UNICEF’s MoU with the national water and sanitation agency ONEA was an opportunity to address challenges of water scarcity in some areas, to mobilize resources and align the package of interventions with national strategic priorities.  By engaging diverse partners, UNICEF contributes to broader development SDG agenda to create favorable conditions for a brighter future for children.
 
Inter-agency collaboration to support government’s policy on school feeding: To strengthen partnership, the Country Office participated in signing an MoU with WFP, FAO, IFAD, and the Government to implement a comprehensive School Canteen Programme. This holistic initiative integrates school governance (QCFS), nutrition, WASH, and protection activities. In 2024, UNICEF reached 255 schools—over half of the 476 schools targeted. 
 
In a “One UN” approach, UNICEF works to support the host, displaced and refugees in the Sahel Region, along with FAO, UNDP, UNFPA, UNHCR and WFP, through the UN Support Programme for Integrated Development (PADI). The project aims to reach 150,000 vulnerable children and adults, (50% girls) with multi-sectoral and integrated services, including 75,000 children supported in the formal and non-formal education system. In the East Region, UNICEF also teamed up with FAO and WFP to contribute to improving women's income and strengthening child nutrition, through the integrated multisectoral support project (AMI). A total 102,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women and adolescents were supported with malnutrition prevention, vitamin A supplementation, and development of market gardening areas, rice fields and home gardens.
 
UN Joint advocacy and resource mobilization: UNICEF also worked with other UN agencies to elaborate a “One UN” resource mobilization strategy to address the acute funding needs that Burkina Faso faces year after year. To reinforce advocacy for human rights and child rights, UNICEF as co-chair of UNCG, led the elaboration of an MoU with the Ministry of communication for the UN common support to major cultural initiatives in the country. 
 
Fostering targeted and thematic collaborations with government to accelerate the delivery of results for children in different sectors: In 2024, UNICEF Burkina Faso implemented strategic initiatives that significantly enhanced programme delivery and positively impacted children’s rights. The most relevant key achievements included: (i) Strengthened Cold Chain System to expand vaccine storage capacity reinforced immunization, (ii) Rehabilitated oxygen plants to reduce child mortality and improve neonatal care. (iii) Coordinated distribution of vaccines, health kits, and nutritional supplies to high-risk regions to ensure uninterrupted access to life-saving commodities. (iv) successful "Back to School 2024" Campaign to ensure distribution of educational materials to school for thousands of children; and the continuity of education in conflict-affected areas. (v) fostered the Global eTravel Initiative to streamline Travel Authorizations, improve operational efficiency and timely programme delivery; (vi) renewed Fleet to strengthen the field missions and to support programme delivery in remote areas; (vii) Improved strategic energy efficiency and robust ICT systems to ensure continuous operational support, strengthened services delivery and monitoring in any environment. These strategic efforts have collectively created favorable conditions for UNICEF's programmes to reach the most vulnerable children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Children’s participation forums and high-level events continue to be seen as great opportunities to advocate for the centrality of child programming within national priorities.  Children’s direct involvement in advocacy initiatives such as parliamentary sessions, has demonstrated their role as key drivers of social change. They amplify messages, motivate decision-makers and raise strong commitments for progressive realization of children’s rights. 
 
In 2024, Community health engagement emerged as a cornerstone of maintaining vital services for children and families in conflict-affected and hard-to-reach areas. By collaborating with local leaders, and community health workers, UNICEF was able to sustain and continue essential services in conflict-affected areas, especially for vulnerable children in remote areas impacted by ongoing humanitarian situation. The insecurity that plagued the region led to the closure or reduced functionality of numerous health facilities, severely restricting access to essential medicines, nutrition supplies, and critical health services. 
 
Furthermore, the effectiveness of innovative strategies, such as engaging men through community groups to overcome cultural and social barriers, thereby significantly improving access to maternal and child healthcare services. The introduction of the First Food initiative was particularly useful, as it significantly enhanced young children's access to quality, affordable complementary foods, leading to better nutritional and developmental outcomes for those most at risk. UNICEF has reached 45,000 children in hard-to-reach communities through nutrition efforts, successfully incorporating micronutrient supplementation, food fortification, and novel approaches in the package of interventions to treat acute malnutrition. 
 
Despite these successes, the programme also faced challenges such as illicit sales of nutrition products, supply chain disruptions, and delays in fund accountability, which underscored systemic issues that require stronger governance, monitoring systems, and leadership. These challenges have provided valuable lessons that will guide future efforts to expand digital tools, strengthen supply chains, improve infrastructure, and address persistent gender-based barriers to healthcare access.
 
The strategic partnership with ONEA was another significant takeaway that demonstrated the effectiveness of collaborative efforts in emergency response. By reinforcing water production and distribution capacities, ONEA has significantly increased access to water for internally displaced persons (IDPs) and their host communities, particularly in urban settings. This partnership underscored the potential for UNICEF's resource mobilization, highlighting the value of strategic alliances.
 
Moreover, the collaboration between the regional Directorate of Water and Sanitation (DREA) and the Ministry of Defense Engineering teams to develop drinking water facilities in security-challenged areas offered a valuable lesson in innovation and adaptability in terms of showcasing the value of community’s involvement in quality assurance of water.   Additionally, the introduction of soap loans to Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLA) groups illustrated the pivotal role of local initiatives in improving hygiene and sanitation standards. These experiences underscore the critical importance of community participation, strategic partnerships, and innovative solutions to enhance the effectiveness and sustainability of WASH programmes.
 
Regarding Innovations and Technology for development (T4D), UNICEF has supported 3 most relevant strategic initiatives: Innovative public-private partnerships for local development plans, the digitalization of the development of public policy scenarios and digitalization of community health. Firstly, UNICEF launched an innovative public-private partnership in 20 municipalities, where mining companies operate. This partnership is built upon the UNICEF’s support to development of the Local Development Plans (LDP) in target municipalities. To this end, UNICEF has increased its support to social accountability mechanisms to facilitate Citizen control and participation social services delivery. Secondly, UNICEF has contributed to the digitization of the development of public policy scenarios through micro-simulation of their projected impact is another innovation in 2024. The great advantage of micro-simulation is that it carries out analyses at the individual level, and consequently makes it possible to monitor impact at the micro-economic level (individuals, households), or according to interest groups (women, children, the poor, etc.). It also enables to analyze the impact of shocks and to simulate the measures that best respond to these shocks (effectiveness of measures). Thirdly, UNICEF has provided support to the Ministry of Health to develop strategies for the digitalization of community health and overall digital health. The mHealth platform, built upon Rapidpro was adopted and implemented in 2024.
 
Additionally, UNICEF flagship initiative, called “UYouth” was developed to help young people achieve a sense of confidence, worthiness, and become agents of change in their communities. UYouth is an Android application integrating one of the national languages, the Mooré, aimed at enhancing youth engagement and facilitating the collection of evidence on the implementation of UNICEF programmes in the field. This initiative was designed to address the challenges faced by young people, particularly those who are illiterate by integrating a voice module that translates text into audible sound in the Mooré language. The UYouth mobile application, an extension of the U-Report platform, is designed to provide young people with access to essential information to address the misinformation issue, generate knowledge, and increase their agency.  It also serves as a channel for UNICEF to gather real-time data on programme implementation by breaking the language barrier. These efforts demonstrate UNICEF Commitments to improving public health and empower youth for a brighter future.

Cabo  Verde has made significant strides in advancing child rights, particularly in  achieving SDGs 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and 4 (Quality Education). The  country has ensured high school enrollment rates, yet challenges persist in  addressing inequities in access to education, especially for children from  lower-income households and those with disabilities. While access is nearly  universal, improving education quality remains a priority, necessitating  better data collection and enhanced teacher development programs to ensure  inclusive, high-quality education for all.
  
Cabo  Verde, through the Ministry of Family, Inclusion, and Social Development,  launched the National Strategy to Eradicate Extreme Poverty (ENEPE  2022-2026). This strategy aligns with the country’s second Strategic Plan for  Sustainable Development, aiming to eliminate extreme poverty by 2026. As of  2022, 13.1% of the population (approximately 63,335 people[1].)  lived in extreme poverty 
  
Children  are disproportionately affected by extreme poverty, with 37% of those in this  category being between 0 and 15 years old. Furthermore, 85% of households in  extreme poverty are female-headed, highlighting the intersection of gender  and economic vulnerability. The government has leveraged the Unified Social  Registry (CSU) to identify and support the most vulnerable populations,  ensuring that social protection measures effectively target at-risk children  and their families.
  
Cabo  Verde continues to strengthen its human rights framework, maintaining a  strong commitment to international conventions and regional agreements. The  country has ratified all nine-core international human rights treaties under  the United Nations system[2],  including the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC, 1992) and the  Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women  (CEDAW, 1981). Additionally, Cabo Verde adheres to key African Union and  ECOWAS human rights instruments, reinforcing its regional leadership in  upholding child rights. Recent advancements include the ratification of the  Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction,  enhancing protections against cross-border child abduction cases.
  
Cabo  Verde has achieved significant reductions in child mortality. The neonatal  mortality rate (10.6 per 1,000 live births[3])  and under-five mortality rate (13 per 1,000 live births)[4]  are among the lowest in West Africa, surpassing SDG targets. High childhood  immunization rates have been instrumental in this progress, with 98% of  children under one year fully vaccinated in 2019[5].  Furthermore, the country has made strides in eliminating mother-to-child  transmission of HIV and syphilis, reducing the transmission rate to 2.2%[6].
  
However,  malnutrition remains a challenge. In 2022, chronic malnutrition (stunting)  affected 10.2% of children under five, with higher prevalence (9.2%) among  children under 24 months. Additionally, anemia continues to be a serious  public health concern, affecting 43% of children under five[7]  and 20.6% of women aged 15-49 (22.5% among pregnant women). Strengthening  nutrition programs and improving access to diverse, nutrient-rich foods are  critical for achieving SDG 2 (Zero Hunger).
  
Cabo  Verde has made progress in expanding early childhood education. Following a  decline in pre-primary school enrollment due to the COVID-19 pandemic (from  85.6% in 2019/2020 to 72.3% in 2020/2021), rates rebounded to 95.5% in 2023[8].
  
Despite  gains in gender parity in education, disparities persist when considering  income and geographic location. Children from poor households are less likely  to complete basic education:
  

Basic education completion rates: 65.8%  for boys and 77.6% for girls from low-income households, compared to 81.5%  for boys and 88% for girls from higher-income households[9].


Dropout rates: Nationally, 5.2% of  children drop out of school, with rates as high as 11.9% in Brava and as low  as 1.4% in São Salvador do Mundo[10].
  
Children  with disabilities face significant barriers to education. Among 1,900  individuals with special educational needs[11],  26% have never attended school, and only 3.1% have completed higher education[12].  Teacher training programs must prioritize inclusive education to improve  learning outcomes for children with disabilities.
  
Cabo  Verde has strengthened its legislative framework to combat child labor,  aligning national laws with international labor standards. A 2022 child labor  survey revealed that:
  

4.2% of children engage in child labor.
  

An additional 3.5% of children  participate in legal work.
  

Child labor is more prevalent among  boys (68.5%) than girls (31.5%).
  
Efforts to eradicate child labor must focus on expanding social protection programs,  enhancing school retention strategies, and increasing awareness among communities about children’s rights.
  
Several groups remain at high risk of exclusion, requiring targeted interventions to ensure equitable development, especially:
  

Women in Vulnerable Situations[13]:  Female labor force participation (50.4%) remains significantly lower than male participation (65.5%). The poverty rate among women stood at 66% in 2022, with 85% of the most vulnerable households led by women.
  

At-Risk Children and Adolescents[14]:  37% of the most vulnerable individuals (CSU Group I) are children under 15.  Teenage pregnancy remains a critical concern, affecting 19.6% of adolescent  girls, particularly those who have dropped out of school or lack family  support.
  
Cabo Verde has demonstrated a strong commitment to upholding child rights,  aligning national policies with the SDGs and international human rights  frameworks. While progress has been made in education, health, and social  protection, challenges remain in addressing inequities, particularly among  children from low-income households, those with disabilities, and girls in  vulnerable situations.
