2024 was a momentous year for the protection of child rights in The Gambia that saw the country gain global attention. It was also the first year of the implementation of UNICEF’s Country Programme 2024-2028, which, together with the Government, establishes a five-year framework for advancing child rights, in line with The Gambia’s National Development Plan 2023-2027 (NDP) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2024-2028 (UNSDCF). This report reflects the changing situation for children, alongside the achievements of the Government, UNICEF and its partners, and the remaining challenges and way forward in realising the rights of every child.  


 


At the macro-economic level, the Gambian economy has grown by 5.8 per cent in 2024, compared to the 4.8 per cent in 2023, while inflation fell from 16.7 per cent in January to 10 per cent in September1. This positive outlook, set within a wider context of global uncertainties, demonstrates strong resilience and has been attributed to the recovery of the tourism sector, improved agricultural productivity, resilient remittance inflows and infrastructural investments. 


 


Building on this stable economic outlook, The Gambia strengthened its global engagements through the country’s hosting of 15th edition of the Organization of Islamic Conference (OIC) Summit, welcoming 57 State representatives to Banjul in May. The event also marked the commencement of The Gambia’s 3-year chairmanship of the OIC providing excellent opportunities to strengthen collaborations for the advancement of the NDP, including child rights.  


 


2024 also saw the successful completion of the country’s first digital Population and Housing Census, which confirmed that 53.6 per cent of the 2.4 million population are aged 19 years and under. The Census data will provide reliable evidence to inform better policy and programmes for children, including being used to facilitate better the implementation of the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) scheduled for 2025.  


 


At the international level, The Gambia submitted its State Report to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in April 2024, while also submitting its Universal Periodic Review report to United Nations Human Rights Council and its report on UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women’s concluding observations. These submissions are testament to the Government’s commitment to fulfilling its obligations to these global frameworks.  


 


A pivotal moment in 2024 was the high-profile attempt to repeal the law against Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), which brought global attention and threated to result in The Gambia becoming the only country to repeal a critical legal instrument protecting child rights. UNICEF and its partners, including UN agencies, development partners, CSOs, and children and adolescent groups worked collectively to establish a steadfast campaign against the repeal. In building momentum behind the protection of children and women’s rights this advocacy also sought to strengthen The Gambia’s civil society Coalition for the Prevention of Violence Against Children, whilst increasing recognition and acting as a catalyst to unlock new partnerships for UNICEF and the UN.   


 


2024 also saw The Gambia respond to the detection of a positive environmental sample for cVDPV2 (polio) in July. While Africa was declared wild polio-free in 2020, and there have since been no reported cases of wild polio, the COVID-19 pandemic, among other factors, put a strain on the health system’s resilience. UNICEF, in collaboration with WHO, supported the Ministry of Health (MoH) to respond, including facilitating vaccine procurement and the delivery of a vaccination campaign. Thanks to excellent collaboration and an effective communications campaign approximately 99 per cent of the children under five years received two doses of the lifesaving polio vaccine. UNICEF also supported the MoH to scale up preparedness in response to the regional outbreak of mpox, including strengthening the national Risk Communication and Community Engagement Plan.  


 


Beyond immunisation, the health and nutrition situation for children continued to face challenges, especially in riverine communities where the impacts of an increasingly unpredictable climate are resulting in periods of drought, flash floods and rising food insecurity. In the Central River Region (CRR) neonatal mortality rose to 17.1 per cent in the first six months of 2024, compared 14.5 per cent in 2023. While in the Upper River Region (URR) the rate more than quadrupled from 1.1 per cent in 2023 to 4.5 per cent in the first half of 2024. In CRR there was also a spike in maternal mortality up from 239.5 per 100,000 live births in 2023 to 343 in the first six months of 20242. In response, UNICEF continues to work with Government to provide life-saving nutrition supplies, while advocating for strengthened coordination in addressing persistent challenges. This includes supporting the Paediatric Association of The Gambia to host its Second Scientific Conference in November 2024, which brought together experts, healthcare professionals and key stakeholders to share learnings and discuss strengthened approaches to ensuring the survival of every mother and newborn.     


 


In February, the African Union (AU) designated 2024 as the ‘Year of Education’ and the Government, with support from UNICEF, continued to work with national and regional partners to strengthen progress towards ensuring quality education. The findings from the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education (MoBSE)’s December 2023 Assessment for Minimum Proficiency Levels indicated, however, that only 21.5 per cent of lower primary students achieved the minimum proficiency in reading and only 25.8 per cent in numeracy. Despite these challenges, good progress was made in advancing school enrolment with 656,168 children and adolescents enrolled in school. 34,346 (51.87% girls) of these children were enrolled through the Zero Out of School Programme, which is a collaboration between MoBSE, UNICEF and its partners to ensure every child can access formal education. Notwithstanding this success, it is estimated that approximately 60,000 children aged 7-12 years (19%) remain out of school3. There therefore remains a need for major acceleration and the adoption of a transformative approach to ensure the country meets its commitment to the 2022 global ‘transforming education’ agenda.

2024 saw the launch of UNICEF Gambia’s new five-year country programme (2024-2028), which outlines five priority areas in line with the NDP, UNSDCF, UNICEF’s Strategic Plan, and UNICEF’s regional Key Results for Children (KRC). In 2024, UNICEF contributed to these areas as follows:  


 


Priority 1: Every child survives and thrives (KRC1, KRC2, KRC8):  


A polio outbreak was declared on the 8th July 2024, following the detection of the vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) within an environmental sample. UNICEF responded rapidly, in collaboration with its partners including the WHO, to support the MoH to respond to the outbreak. The National Coordination Committee, comprising of key stakeholders including government, UN, the Centre for Disease Control and Prevention and CSOs, was reactivated to lead the response and manage the delivery of two rounds of a nation-wide nOPV2 vaccination campaign to ensure every child aged 5 years and under was able to receive a life-saving vaccination. The vaccination campaign was a great success with 382,768 children (90 per cent of the target) vaccinated in the first round, and 424,573 children (99.6 per cent of the target) vaccinated in the second round.   


 


The nOPV2 campaign presented an opportunity for UNICEF to trial an integrated approach to immunization and nutrition services to strengthen outcomes for children. The approach proved successful with nearly 270,000 children receiving vitamin A supplementation alongside their polio vaccination, while boosting vitamin A supplementation coverage to a record high. Over 11,200 children aged 6-23 months also received multiple micronutrient powder supplements via a targeted campaign in URR and CRR to reduce the prevalence of anaemia. 

  

UNICEF worked with the Government and its partners to strengthen both the demand for immunization services and the capacity of routine immunization systems. Responding to the rise in vaccine hesitancy noted since the Covid-19 pandemic, alongside a fall in immunization coverage in urban areas, UNICEF partnered with fifteen CSOs to engage nearly 18,000 individuals in the importance of immunization. UNICEF also procured 20 tricycles for frontline delivery partners in the URR, CRR, and Western Region 1, enabling vaccines and crucial supplies to be distributed, benefiting over 44,000 children. UNICEF further worked with the MoH to continue to strengthen the health system beyond immunisation, including supporting the development of a strategic plan for National Integrated Management of Newborn and Childhood Illnesses, alongside supporting the Paediatric Association of The Gambia to host its Second Scientific Conference that brought together national and international experts and stakeholders to share learnings and discuss strengthened approaches to preventing maternal and neonatal mortality.  



In 2024 UNICEF remained the sole provider of life-saving Ready to Use Therapeutic Food in The Gambia and continued to coordinate with the Government to provide life-saving treatment to children suffering from severe acute malnutrition, treating 3,970 children (1,945 male, 2,025 female). To prevent children becoming malnourished, UNICEF continued to collaborate with the Government and its partners to strengthen the institutionalization of exclusive breastfeeding, including supporting the monitoring of adherence to the WHO/UNICEF’s 10 steps to successful breastfeeding in five Baby Friendly Hospitals. UNICEF and its partners further trained 200 Village Support Groups in positive behavioural change approaches to support community-level breastfeeding counselling, reaching over 2,000 caregivers.   


 


Due to persistent challenges, including high-water tables in riverine communities, low investments in sanitation and persistent negative social norms and practices, 2024, unfortunately, did not see a significant reduction in open defecation (OD). UNICEF continued, however, to support continuous regional monitoring to ensure that progress previously made was maintained and continued to push towards reaching the last 1 per cent of Gambians still practicing OD, while strengthening access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services. Over 1,300 households in nearly 200 communities, in the target regions of CRR and URR, were engaged in ODF awareness raising, while UNICEF collaborated with the Government to improve access to climate resilient water supplies for over 13,500 people (6,885 girls and 6,616 boys) and to provide sanitation and hand washing facilities for over 21,200 people (10,832 girls and 10,409 boys), including integrating services with water supplies provided to schools and health facilities. In addition, over 4,000 people (2,066 female and 1,984 male), including those with disabilities, living in flood-prone communities were reached with WASH supplies, alongside the installation of 270 inclusive, climate-resilient sanitation facilities. Together these facilities will help to ensure that more children are able to thrive.   


  


Priority 2: Every child learns and develops (KRC3, KRC4):  


2024 marked the AU’s ‘Year of Education’, and throughout the year UNICEF continued to work with national and regional partners to strengthen education policy and systems to ensure no child is left behind. UNICEF continued to play a leading role in strengthening the coordination and collaboration between sectoral partners. As co-chair of the Local Education Group, in partnership with MoBSE, UNICEF led this group to coordinate effectively across the sector and to be a valuable platform for education policy advocacy and technical support. UNICEF also provided technical and financial support to the mid-term review of The Gambia’s 2016-2023 Education Sector Policy, which considered the integration of national-level commitments for transforming education, alongside the regional priorities and commitments of the AU and the NDP.  


 


2024 also saw UNICEF expand its existing partnerships and strengthen advocacy for investment in, and the transformation of, the education sector. Building on The Gambia’s successful hosting of the OIC and ongoing OIC Presidency, UNICEF expanded its existing collaboration with the Office of the First Lady of The Gambia (OFL) to initiate a tripartite partnership between UNICEF, OFL and OIC to champion the rights of children on the move and to address the vulnerabilities of children in Majalis (Koranic) institutions who account for a large percentage of out of school children. This partnership will help to shine a light on the most vulnerable children and drive forward progress in releasing every child’s right to education. 


 


In 2024, in collaboration with MoBSE, UNICEF and its partners supported the enrolment of 34,346 (51.87% girls) previously out of school children. Through the Zero Out of Schools Programme, children, families and their school communities were supported to overcome challenges linked to school absence, including through the provision of targeted cash transfers, school transportation, strengthened teacher training and increased access to learning materials, including specific resources for children with disabilities and the construction of WASH facilities in schools. At the same time, UNICEF worked with MoBSE to strengthen the Education Management Information System (EMIS) to gather greater evidence on the number of out-of-school children and quicker identification and provision of support for those who may be at a greater risk of dropping out. UNICEF also collaborated with MoBSE to strengthen access to digital learning, including leading the completion of a comprehensive analysis and publication of a ‘Roadmap for a Digital Learning Programme in The Gambia’. The learnings from this analysis will be used to inform an expansion of the digital learning programme in 2025. Finally, UNICEF has commenced a strategic collaboration with MoBSE to integrate gender-transformative policies into the education sector. This includes supporting MoBSE’s Life Skills Unit to launch an adolescent girl-centric programme targeting 2,500 adolescents, which aims to generate evidence to support the importance of investing in adolescent girls, particularly in life skills, to be rolled out in 2025.   


 


Priority 3: Every child is protected from violence, exploitation and harmful practices, and has a legal identity (KRC5, KRC6, KRC7):  


2024 was a momentous year in the protection of every child in The Gambia (KRC5, KRC6). Following the proposed amendment to Women’s Amendment Act 2015 to relegalise FGM, UNICEF, in collaboration with UNFPA and the wider UN, alongside development partners, CSOs and the Children’s National Assembly of The Gambia (CNAG), rapidly scaled up its advocacy for the protection of the rights of women and girls. This included extensive engagement with influential stakeholders, including National Assembly Members (NAMs), Government Ministers, the OIC Presidency, the AU and the UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence Against Children. At the community level, UNICEF and its partners worked with FGM survivors to amplify their voices and share their stories directly with NAMs, while strengthening advocacy and social behaviour change with religious leaders including, in collaboration with Religions for Peace, supporting the emerging Interfaith Council of The Gambia to address key issues for children. Following this momentous movement, the proposed amendment was rejected by the National Assembly in July. This was a huge achievement and important movement in the protection of children’s rights in The Gambia.   


 


Throughout 2024, UNICEF and its partners continued to work with communities to engage adolescents, mothers, men and boys through platforms including Girls’ Clubs, Community-based Child Protection Committees, Mothers’ Clubs and inter-generational dialogues to increase understanding of harmful practices and strengthen adolescent girls’ leadership in the fight against harmful practices. UNICEF also continued to support the Government in its review of the National Strategy and Action Plan for both FGM and Child Marriage, ensuring lessons learnt from the threated repeal are incorporated into national approaches, as well as facilitating the development of a roadmap for the application of gender transformative and social behavioural change approaches in strengthening child protection programming in collaboration with MoGCSW, MoBSE, Ministry of Justice, the Gambian Police and CSOs. With effective protection starting from the registration of a child’s birth, UNICEF also supported the review of The Gambia’s Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Strategic Plan 2024-2029 and the provision of IT and office equipment to ensure a robust and well-function digital birth registration system.  


 


2024 saw The Gambia take strides forward in reconfirming its commitment to advancing child rights as the Government submitted its long-awaited report to the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child. In collaboration with the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), UNICEF supported the Government to submit the State Report, as well as collaborating with the NHRC and UN partners to submit and present their reports to the Committee. UNICEF further supported preparation of The Gambia’s contributions to the first Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children held in Bogota in November, as well as supporting the Government to strengthen its obligations under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), including the integration of CRPD principles into the national budgeting processes, alongside the development of a national training manual on the inclusion of children with disabilities across all government sectors. UNICEF also worked directly with CSOs led by persons with disabilities to strengthen the implementation of The Gambia’s Persons with Disabilities Act (2021), ensuring a prioritization of the inclusion of children with disabilities.  


 


Priority 4: Every child lives free from poverty:  


In 2024 UNICEF support the Government to pass key legislation and allocate increased public financing to strengthen social protection mechanisms, invest in child-friendly policies and help to end the cycle of intergenerational poverty. In collaboration with the National Social Protection Secretariate, UNICEF provided technical expertise to support the finalization of the 2024 Social Protection Act, which outlines  provisions for the universal coverage of social protection across the county, the establishment of a social protection basket-fund to support social assistance programmes and the expansion of the family strengthening programme to ensure that it reaches the most vulnerable, including the orphans and children with disabilities.    


 


Following continuous advocacy by UNICEF and its partners, the 2024 budget review and pre-budget sessions for 2025 demonstrated a significant step forward in public financing for children. Most notably is the substantial increase in funding for immunization, which was increased from 25 million Dalasi (GMD) in 2024 to 40 million GMD in 2025 and contributes substantial to The Gambia’s fulfilment of its match funding obligations to GAVI and ensuring the right to survival for every child. This increased investment followed strategic advocacy, alongside the development of a thorough investment case for immunization to the National Assembly Select Committee on Health. Further engagement with this Committee and other stakeholders will continue in 2025 to ensure that The Gambia can meet its required 50 million Dalasi commitment.   


  


Further success was seen in the expanding of legislative and national policy protections and provisions that strengthened policies on nutrition. UNICEF, together with its partners, conducted extensive high-level advocacy, working with nutrition champions in the National Assembly, to advocate successfully for the passing of the revised Nutrition Bill with a strengthened provision for the prevention of malnutrition for children under 5 years, promotion of exclusive breastfeeding, the stockpiling and availability of life-saving nutrition supplies and reinforced governance, monitoring and coordination within the nutrition sector.  


   


2024 also saw UNICEF work with its partners to strengthen transparency and accountability within the management and allocation of public finances. This included the profiling of social sector expenditures that provided further evidence and analysis to support more equitable resource allocation, including increased allocations for children. UNICEF and its partners also provided consultation and support to the Government on the development of a strategy to update the national social registry, which will be implemented in 2025. This strengthened social registry will further provide insights and analysis, alongside evidence for the targeted and equitable allocation of resources to better meet the needs of children to ensure no one is left behind.   


 


Priority 5: Cross-cutting - Championing Children’s and Adolescent’s Voices   


In 2024, UNICEF worked directly with children and youth-led organizations to create platforms and shine a spotlight on the voices of children. Throughout 2024, in collaboration with the National Youth Council, UNICEF continued to support CNAG’s 105 elected representatives, aged 10 to 17 years, to advocates for issues that matter to children across the country and facilitated opportunities for CNAG members to engage with key decision makers and stakeholders. This includes supporting the CNAG Speaker to attend COP29 in Baku as the youngest delegate and representative of The Gambia. While at the Conference, the Speaker had the opportunity to meet with fellow youth advocates, as well as the UN Secretary General, to discuss the need to accelerate global action for climate justice and climate financing, alongside the important role young people continue to play, especially in countries like The Gambia which is increasingly experiencing the adverse impacts of climate change.  The Gambia Country Office was also delighted that a young female advocate from St John’s School for the Deaf in Banjul delivered an address to UNICEF Executive Board, on behalf of children in West and Central Africa, to mark the Board’s approval of UNICEF Gambia’s new Country Programme 2024-2028.    


 


2024 also saw UNICEF launch a new partnership with the youth-led organisation, Clean Earth Gambia. Through this partnership, in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Natural Resources (MECCNR), The Gambia hosted its first National Children and Youth Conference on Climate Change in June and trained over 500 children and adolescents to be climate champions. The Conference saw young climate activists from across the country come together to devise a adolescents and youth strategy for climate change. UNICEF is now working with Clean Earth Gambia and the MECCNR to ensure that this strategy feeds into the development of The Gambia’s Climate Change Act and in the Third Nationally Determined Contributions. UNICEF has also commissioned a national Climate Landscape Analysis for Children. This consultation and analysis, which will conclude in 2025, will provide further insights into the specific challenges being faced by children due to the changing climate and help further to inform national strategies.  


 


As part of The Gambia’s celebration of International Day of The Girl in September, UNICEF, in collaboration with UNFPA, the MoGCSW and the CSO Catch Them Young, facilitated The Gambia’s first five-day STEM and career boot camp specifically for adolescent girls. Through this boot camp, 20 adolescent girls from across the country had the opportunity to gain skills in computing and coding, as well as build connections with successful female entrepreneurs and leaders, including leading a panel discussion and dialogue with Minister of Gender, Children and Social Welfare and the Heads of the UN Agencies in The Gambia. It is hoped that the model used by, and lessons learnt from, this new initiative can be scaled up and applied to the development of a new Life Skills module for adolescent girls in collaboration with MoBSE.    


 


Finally, as part of its celebrations to mark World Children’s Day, UNICEF, in collaboration with the National Youth Council, facilitated a Storytelling and Photography Workshop for 20 adolescents from the Lower River Region. The workshop not only trained these adolescents in photojournalism and advocacy, which they are using to establish photojournalism clubs within their schools, but it also provided them with an opportunity to showcase their work and advocate for their rights to senior decision makers. Following the workshop, UNICEF hosted a photography exhibition that provided an opportunity for meaningful adolescent participation, whereby four of the photographers had the opportunity to exhibit their own, and their peers’, work and engage with the First Lady of The Gambia, senior government officials, senior UN officials and key development partners.   


 


Priority 5: Cross-cutting - Strengthening Programme Effectiveness   


2024 marked the first year of implementation of UNICEF Country Programme 2024 – 2028, as well as the UNSDCF 2024 – 2028. In line with its new strategy, the UNICEF Gambia Country Office undertook several initiatives to enhance its internal operational and programme effectiveness, including an extensive peer review, dynamic resource mobilization, alongside strengthened partnerships and collaborations with Government, development partners, and CSOs.   


 


As part of the Government’s and UNICEF’s commitment to ensure the successful implementation and monitoring of the new Country Programme, UNICEF worked with partners to establish a robust and dedicated multi-partners oversight mechanism under the leadership of the Ministry of Public Service’s Department of Strategic Policy and Delivery (DSPD). Throughout the year the relevant documentations for the steering and technical committees were developed, along with the inauguration of both committees. Furthermore, UNICEF has begun a collaboration with DSPD to spearhead the child rights agenda across government aiming to strengthen coordination and understanding of the child rights agenda within government and amongst key stakeholders, whilst also supporting the strengthening of evidence-based advocacy for child rights.

The Government of The Gambia remains UNICEF’s main partner in delivering results for children. As detailed above, 2024 saw UNICEF Gambia continue to strengthen its relationship with the Government to create an enabling environment, strengthening existing policies and structures and implement programmes to achieve sustainable results for children and their families. In addition to strengthening its relationship with Government, 2024 also saw UNICEF grow its collaboration with National Assembly Members and with civil society. The threated repeal of the law against FGM provided new avenues for UNICEF to expand its collaboration with both civil society actors, religious leaders and networks and members of the National Assembly, including fostering a new collaboration with Religion for Peace to support the established of Interfaith Council of The Gambia to address key issues for children. 


  


As an active member of the United Nations Country Management Team (UNCT), and of the Programme Coordination Group, UNICEF continues to collaborate closely with other UN agencies in The Gambia and contribute to the delivery of the UNSDCF 2024-2028. This includes coordinating the development of joint proposals, developing a memorandum of understanding with the World Food Programme to strengthen coordination and collaboration across WASH and nutrition, as well as co-chairing Result Group 3 under UNSDCF Strategic Priority 2: Human Development, Social Inclusion and People Centred Governance. UNICEF is also spearheading the UNCT’s engagement with adolescents and has led the establishment of a Youth and Adolescent Advisory Board, which will commence its activities in 2025.  


 


In 2024, UNICEF worked in particularly close collaboration with WHO is response to the polio outbreak and Mpox preparedness, and with UNFPA to implement the UN Joint Programme on the elimination of FGM and to mobilize resources and leverage key partnerships to prevent the repeal of the law against FGM. This included expanding UNICEF and UNFPA’s existing partnership with United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), alongside strengthened collaboration with the Germany Embassy, EU Delegation, Spanish Consulate, US Embassy and British High Commission in Banjul to prevent the repeal and advocate for the ending of all harmful practices and violence against children, in particular girls, in The Gambia. UNICEF continued to be an active member of the Development Partners Group in The Gambia and as highlighted above, facilitated strengthened engagement between key partners and adolescent advocates to champion the child rights’ issues that matter to adolescents and children in The Gambia.   


 


UNICEF also continued to deepen its strategic partnership with The Government of Japan who are contributing to the strengthening of community resilience in the face of climate threats and food insecurity through investment in climate-resilient WASH facilities and nutrition supplies and services. In August, in partnership with the Embassy of Japan, UNICEF formally handed over 2,500 cartons of Ready to Use Therapeutic Food, 100 cartons of F75 milk and 100 cartons of F100 milk to The Government of The Gambia and the National Nutrition Agency (NaNA) to provide lifesaving treatment to children suffering from serve acute malnutrition. UNICEF is also expanding its partnership with The Government of Japan, and a regional-based Japanese enterprises, to unlock additional resources to ensure access to digital learning and skills development for over 24,000 children. This is in addition to a continuation in the Government of Japan’s humanitarian support to The Gambia via the 2024 Supplementary Budget, which will provide lifesaving nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene, health supplies and services to vulnerable mothers and infants in CRR and URR.  


 


In 2024, UNICEF further strengthened its collaboration and partnership with the Gambia Bureau of Statistics (GBoS) and World Bank in The Gambia, including in the planning and developing of the MICS7. UNICEF also continued to deepen its longstanding partnership with GAVI and supported the Government to leverage increased investment from GAVI.  


 


UNICEF maintained its strategic partnership with the Education Above All Foundation to ensure that zero primary-aged children are out of school in The Gambia. In May, UNICEF hosted a content gathering and media visit from the Foundation, which provided an opportunity to celebrate the partnership and increase visibility and understanding of the partnership’s impact and the continuing need for collaboration to ensure every child in The Gambia can access quality education.   


  


Finally, 2024 also saw UNICEF Gambia strengthen and expand its relationship with UNICEF’s National Committees, including conducting visits to UNICEF Canada, USA, France, Norway, UK, Germany and Belgium, and hosting a visit from UNICEF Canada. These engagements provided an opportunity to meet directly with private sector partners and strengthen the profile and visibility of UNICEF’s work in The Gambia with the National Committees. Following these engagements, UNICEF Gambia has entered in a new 2–3-year partnership with UNICEF Norway focused on engagement with the Gambian-Norwegian diaspora in support of education programmes in The Gambia, as well as a new 2-year partnership with UNICEF Canada’s Women UNLimited Group focused on child protection and a 1-year partnership with the S Foundation via UNICEF France on the First Foods Nutrition initiative. Building on the success of recent years, a 2-year extension to UNICEF The Gambia’s partnership with the German National Committee’s Club 48,3 Group to end FGM and other harmful practices was also established. These collaborations include commitments to flexible thematic funding which allow UNICEF to respond adaptively and strategically in the best interest of children.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
As reflected in this report, 2024 has been a year of substantial challenge in the advancement of child rights in The Gambia. Out of this challenge, however, has come great momentum, learnings and new opportunities. This is particularly the case in two evolving areas. The first is the emergence and response to the pushback against child rights, which is being experienced across West and Central Africa, however, emerged strongly in The Gambia in 2024. Second are the mixed results experienced in driving forward ‘last mile’ progress to end open defecation, zero dose immunization and ensure every child can access formal education.   


 


Arguably, the biggest challenge faced was the high-profile push back of child rights and the legal provisions in place to uphold these. While the legal challenge was focused on repealing the Women’s Amendment Act (2015) banning FGM, supporters of the repeal declared publicly that they also wanted to remove the law against child marriage. The organized nature of the pro-FGM campaign, alongside the continued high prevalence of harmful practices, despite the existing legislation, demonstrate the challenges that exist to protect every child, especially girls. Despite these challenges, the law against FGM was upheld, and this was a huge moment of success providing vital lessons for UNICEF and its partners in how to continue to overcome this pushback and ensure lasting protection for every child.   


 


The success of the anti-FGM advocacy, and the coordination that was able to be achieved at all levels, across UNICEF, UN Agencies, government representatives, civil society, development partners and local and international media, demonstrated the strengthen and breadth of the strategic partnerships that, when effectively mobilized, exist to deliver transformative results for children. In particular, the campaign demonstrated the increasing strength of Gambian civil society (particularly women-led CSOs), especially in terms of coordination across sectors and the coming together of smaller organizations into a powerful, coordinated and influential coalition. UNICEF’s strategic partnership with USAID, which supported The Association of Non-Governmental Organizations in The Gambia, demonstrated the new opportunities that exist to work with CSOs in consortiums and more effectively pool resources. Looking ahead, this model of collective advocacy and strengthened coordination, alongside an increasingly effective and growing civil society, can be used to leverage better strategic partnerships to deliver transformative change for children. 


 


It was not just the increasing strength of civil society partnerships that emerged in 2024, but also, more specifically, the strength and impact of youth-led organizations. Adolescents and youth-led organizations not only played a critical role in the movement to uphold the ban on FGM, but they repeatedly demonstrated innovative, smart and powerful approaches to driving forward matters that are important to them, including convening Gambia’s first National Children and Youth Conference on Climate Change. The 2024 census confirmed that children and adolescents account for close to 54 per cent of The Gambia’s population; scaling up its focus on adolescent empowerment, and expanding collaborations with adolescent- and youth-, led organizations, presents a great opportunity for UNICEF drive forward transformative change. Looking forward into 2025, the upcoming establishment of The UN Gambia’s Adolescent and Youth Advisory Board and the expansion of the U-Report programme, alongside the finalization of UNICEF’s new Adolescent Programme Strategy, will help to build on this opportunity.    


  


The other area where substantial challenges continued to be faced in 2024 was in relation to the mixed results experienced in achieving ‘last mile’ results to ensure that every child has access to basic services including immunization, education, sanitation and protection. Despite long running efforts to be able to declare The Gambia ODF, <1 per cent of the population continues to practice OD, while, similarly, an estimated 14,000 children have not received any form of immunization. While efforts to target these ‘Zero Dose’ children are ongoing, recent surveys indicate that overall immunization rates are beginning to decline in urban areas. In contrast, The Gambia has experienced substantial progress in reaching the last mile in access to education through the Zero Out of School Programme, which enrolled 34,346 children in 2024 and reached the total enrolment target for the three-year programme within two years.  


 


The Zero Out of Schools project has benefited from sustained multi-year funding thanks to a strategic partnership with the Education Above All Foundation and MoBSE, which has enabled effective planning and sustained investment. The effective sector coordination and collective advocacy that has been achieved, under UNICEF’s leadership, through the Local Education Group, including the generation and presentation of effective evidence-based advocacy for increased public finance for education, has also helped to strengthen and streamline results. These approaches can be applied to the wider ‘last mile’ agenda to strengthen resource mobilisation and better inform sector coordination. 


 


Lessons can also be drawn from the success of the national nOPV2 campaign including the integration with nutrition services. The successful integration of the immunization campaign with vitamin A supplementation, presents a good opportunity to apply this integrated approach to other programmes, including routine immunization. Between the first and the second rounds of the polio campaign, UNICEF also supported a social investigation exercise which helped to identify a 25 per cent lower uptake in the Western 1 Region compared to rural regions. In response, UNICEF and partners scaled up the campaign in this region, which resulted in a nearly 100 per cent coverage rate in the second round. Looking forward, lessons can be learnt from this in applying strengthened analysis and statistical evidence to target interventions. For example, the results of the Multiple Overlapping Deprivation Analysis (MODA) report, which was finalised in 2024, highlighted the higher levels of deprivation experienced by children in riverine communities and rural regions in CRR and URR. With the upcoming MICS offering a further opportunity for data analysis, alongside the Government’s commitment to adopt the Nsa Kenno approach and drive forward this decentralised, local government, community-led strategy in 2025, UNICEF and its partners can focus on strengthening the application of integrated, geographically targeted and data driven interventions to streamline and strengthen results for children.

Despite challenges in Ghana’s macroeconomic landscape that had the potential to affect programme delivery and outcomes, UNICEF helped to drive significant positive developments in education, health, nutrition, sanitation, water, social and child protection systems and social attitudes throughout 2024, with the goal to leave no one behind and in support of advancing Ghana’s Sustainable Development Goals, national priorities, United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) for Ghana (2023–2025), the global UNICEF Strategic Plan 2022–2025, and 5 Key Results for Children (KRC) in West and Central Africa.


The economic environment in Ghana remained challenging in 2024. High inflation rates continued to impact living standards and increase the risk of food insecurity, pushing more people into poverty – the proportion of Ghanaians living in poverty (below US$2.15 per day) is projected to increase from 26.8 per cent of the population in 2022 to 33.2 per cent in 2025 (Word Bank, 2024).



In response to these challenges, Ghana continued to implement substantial macroeconomic policy adjustments, including comprehensive debt restructuring and fiscal consolidation. The Extended Credit Facility programme negotiated with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 2023 incorporated measures to protect critical social investments. The Government’s commitment to continue to invest in social protection was evident in the doubling and indexation of the Livelihoods Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP) programme value. While sector budgets for the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MoGCSP) rose in real terms between 2023 and 2024, other social sectors including Health and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) faced declines.



In recent years, Ghana has worked towards building an accessible health system that ensures universal health coverage, with a focus on improving primary health care. Life expectancy has increased steadily, while the country has made significant progress in key child health indicators. Under-five mortality has steadily declined over the past 20 years, with Ghana outperforming regional averages and other lower-middle income countries. In 2024, Ghana maintained robust vaccination coverage for some antigens; Penta 3 vaccine coverage for children aged under one year reached 101 per cent (DHIMS, 2024). However, there has been a decline in coverage for other antigens, such as Rotavirus 3, which declined from 98.6 per cent in 2021 to 64.1 per cent in 2023. Moreover, maternal mortality has not declined as rapidly as child mortality, stagnating at 263 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births (WHO Afro 2023 estimates), well above the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) target of 70 deaths per 100,000 live births. These challenges are partly due to the fragile economic situation, with delays in government co-financing leading to stockouts of vaccines, HIV, TB and malaria treatments, and family planning commodities. New customs clearance processes for tax exemptions created extended delays for donated goods, hindering the delivery of supplies. Quality of care in health services still needs to be improved.  


 


In education, Ghana has made significant progress in increasing access to kindergarten, primary and secondary education over the last two decades. The net enrolment rates in both primary and secondary education have increased substantially: from 62.5 per cent in 2000 to 79.4 per cent in 2023 for primary, and from 32.1 per cent in 2000 to 58.8 per cent in 2023 for junior high school (Education Sector Analysis, 2023). Ghana provides two years of free and compulsory Kindergarten for children aged 4 and 5 years, with a net enrolment rate of 65 per cent – the highest of all countries in the region, compared to an average of 12 per cent for West and Central Africa (Education Sector Analysis, 2023). Despite admirable access to education, Ghana faces a learning crisis, with at least half of children in primary school at Grade 4 unable to reach ‘basic’ levels of attainment in core literacy and numeracy skills (2022 National Standardized Test).  


 


Ghana has made significant progress in ending child marriage: women married or in union before the age of 18 declined from 19 to 16 per cent and before the age of 15 from 5 to 3 per cent (MICS, 2017/18; DHS, 2022). The percentage of women who have ever experienced sexual violence has declined steadily over time, from 19 per cent in 2008 to 14 per cent in 2022 (DHS, 2022). In 2024, the child protection landscape saw meaningful progress through the Integrated Social Services approach, which expanded to reach 180 districts (69 per cent of the country). A five-year Care Reform Roadmap was launched to reduce institutional care dependency. MoGCSP confirmed its commitment to strengthen the national child protection system and address violence against children. A public-private partnership was launched to address root causes of child labour through integrated interventions across child and social protection, education and youth skills development. 



As the first country in West Africa to sign the Presidential Compact on WASH, Ghana made progress in addressing the estimated US$1.7 billion annual funding gap for the sector. This renewed dedication to SDG 6 was complemented by the revision of Ghana’s National Water Policy. While this commitment signals potential improvements in children’s access to clean water and sanitation services, significant challenges remain, with 29 per cent accessing basic sanitation, 17 per cent practicing open defecation and 48 per cent having access to hand-washing facilities with soap and water (WHO-UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme, 2023). Around 25 per cent of health facilities and 30 per cent of schools lack even basic WASH facilities (WaterAid, 2023). 


UNICEF played a vital role in responding to public health emergencies, including measles and cholera outbreaks, in addition to continuing to respond to the influx of displaced persons owing to conflict in the Sahel. 


In December 2024, Ghana witnessed a peaceful transition of political power with the National Democratic Congress candidate, His Excellency John Dramani Mahama, appointed as President-elect. In his first 120 days, the President-elect has committed to a 25-point action plan, of which 19 points hold relevance for UNICEF programmes on governance, economy, health and education.

UNICEF achieved significant progress in 2024 through strategic interventions that created lasting impact for children across multiple sectors, and were aligned with national priorities, the UNSDCF (2023–2027), and UNICEF global and regional strategies including the 5 KRCs. Key achievements demonstrated UNICEF’s strong ongoing commitment to equity, voicing vulnerabilities and sustainable development. 



Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives 



In 2024, UNICEF worked towards establishing sustainable financing mechanisms to enable Ghana to maintain its immunization coverage as it transitions out of GAVI financial support. This was achieved through UNICEF’s leadership of the Health Financing Development Partners Group, which led to multi-level and coherent advocacy and technical engagements with the Ministries of Health and Finance, as well as the World Bank, GAVI, USAID and the IMF. This unlocked critical funding during a period of limited fiscal space and initiated the creation of dedicated government budget lines for vaccines. Moreover, UNICEF drove substantial improvements in cold chain infrastructure and vaccine forecasting capacity to expand vaccine storage capacity and vaccine supply management. This infrastructure enhancement is expected to benefit over 2 million children. The procurement of essential medical supplies, worth US$23.5 million for vaccines and US$650,000 for medical devices, combined with strategic partnerships with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the expanded immunization programme, also helped minimize vaccine stockouts (KRC1–Immunization).  




The implementation of point-of-care diagnostic testing for HIV and tuberculosis across 150 sites nationwide led to significant progress in early detection and treatment. This innovative approach reduced laboratory turnaround time from 90 days to 1–5 days, enabling faster treatment initiation for 790 infants diagnosed with HIV and 769 children identified with tuberculosis.  




UNICEF integrated nutrition interventions across multiple sectors to prevent and treat malnutrition among children, adolescents and pregnant women. As part of the national polio campaign, 4.5 million children aged 6–59 months received life-saving vitamin A supplements, ensuring high coverage and efficient service delivery (KRC2–Nutrition). 




UNICEF supported the expansion of the Nutrition-Friendly Schools Initiative, which promotes healthy diets, nutrition education and micronutrient supplementation of adolescent girls in schools. An additional 800 schools across 16 regions joined the initiative, bringing the total to 3,104 schools nationwide. As part of these efforts, 1.7 million adolescent girls received weekly iron supplements to improve their health and well-being (KRC2). 




Goal Area 2: Every child learns and acquires skills for the future 




UNICEF Ghana actively promoted 2024 as the African Union’s first-ever Year of Education, including by advancing educational initiatives and highlighting Ghana’s achievements on the global stage. UNICEF Ghana produced an advocacy bulletin, highlighting both Ghana’s learning crisis and innovative practices. The African Union’s Africa Skills Week, held in Accra in October 2024, featured a UNICEF event on how youth-led innovations contribute to policy change for skills and entrepreneurship. Ghana was featured in one-third of all panels at the African Foundational Learning Exchange Summit in November 2024, with a significant focus on its achievements through the Differentiated Learning model of remedial learning.  




UNICEF’s results and programming in the areas of disability screenings, community ownership of education and foundational learning improved learning outcomes for children and steered the design of over US$111 million of new Global Partnership for Education (GPE) financing to Ghana starting in 2025. UNICEF-led screening of over 15,000 early learners for health and disability issues in 2024. This will be scaled up to all public kindergarten and P1 learners in 2025, demonstrating progress toward more inclusive education systems (KRC3–Access to learning). 




The Differentiated Learning approach proved highly successful in improving learning outcomes. English proficiency increased from 34 per cent to over 50 per cent, while Mathematics proficiency rose from 19 per cent to 44 per cent among primary learners in 501 UNICEF-supported schools in 2024; this marked the first time Ghana had data on learner progression within the Differentiated Learning model (KRC4-Quality learning). Government’s Complementary Basic Education programme reached over 70,000 out-of-school children; of these, UNICEF directly supported 1,800 children, of whom 97 per cent completed the course and over 80 per cent successfully transitioned to formal education (KRC3). The successful Communities of Excellence initiative improved community ownership of education outcomes (KRC4). With strong advocacy efforts from UNICEF, a significant advancement in early childhood education was achieved with plans to provide quality in-service training at scale to all 15,000 public kindergarten teachers from 2025. 




Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices 




The national child protection system reached a higher level of integration as mechanisms for monitoring and oversight of child protection services were enhanced and the Integrated Social Services approach was scaled to 180 districts nationwide (reaching 69 per cent of the country), resulting in 76,951 children accessing individual child protection case management and multi-sectoral referrals. This included support for 3,704 children affected by climate events and the Sahel spillover crisis. At least 1,640,265 people were reached through social and behavioural change interventions on prevention of violence against children and harmful practices, including child marriage, and addressing social and gender discriminatory norms (KRC5–Violence and Exploitation).  




As part of the Gender Transformative Accelerator Roadmap for Ending Child Marriage in Ghana, UNICEF strengthened its programming by adopting an approach focused on addressing gender inequalities, supported by specific actions and timeframe from the Roadmap. The integration of this approach into programming included the development of additional content on engagement of men and boys. This will be implemented through the existing Child Protection Community Facilitation Toolkits intervention (KRC6–Child Marriage).  




A groundbreaking initiative saw the launch of the first-ever training programme, designed with a specific curriculum provided and recognized by the School of Social Work (part of MoGCSP). 120 social service workers were trained in 2024, addressing a critical gap in formal social work training among District Officers. The capacity of the social service workforce and other government front-line workers was also enhanced on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support and Protection from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation (KRC5).  




UNICEF supported the launch of the new five-year Care Reform Roadmap (2024–2028), an important step towards reducing institutional care dependency. The goal is to reduce the number of children in institutional care from 3,430 in 2023 to 2,401 by 2028. In 2024, residential institutions have decreased from 117 to 110, with 3,225 children currently in institutional care. A total of 2,522 children in residential care were supported through the development and regular review of individualized case plans. These efforts aimed to ensure that each child received tailored support, ultimately facilitating their transition to permanent family placements. A new Registry feature on alternative care services was developed in the UNICEF-supported Social Welfare Information Management System to enhance monitoring for the Care Reform Roadmap.  




The safety of children online was advanced thanks to the launching of the National Child Online Protection Framework, the submission to Parliament of the new Legislative Instrument on Cybersecurity, the development of Standard Operational Procedures for the Child Protection Digital Forensic Lab at Police Headquarters and the finalization of new training resources and information packages for child abuse victim support (KRC5). UNICEF has strengthened its strategic partnership with Meta for the child online protection campaign via social media, reaching 6,188,539 people with key messages to increase their knowledge to keep children safe online. UNICEF was also recognized by the Government of Ghana, through the Ministry of Communications and Digitalisation, and presented with an International Cooperation Award. 


 


The establishment of the Child Labour Multisectoral and Multistakeholder Public-Private Partnership, led by UNICEF, created a comprehensive framework for addressing root causes of child labour through integrated interventions across child protection, social protection, education and youth skills development. This promising partnership, a technical collaboration with International Cocoa Initiative, included the initial integration of various monitoring systems to enhance data collection and response for child labour cases. 




Goal Area 4: Every child has access to WASH and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment 




UNICEF played an instrumental role in the design of the Presidential Compact on WASH. Ghana was the first country in West Africa to sign and has committed to practical improvements in WASH infrastructure. Two major policies were developed: the national water policy, updated in 2022/2023 and launched in 2024; and the national environmental sanitation policy, drafted in line with the African Sanitation Policy Guidelines. The innovative Sanitation in Housing Integration for Scale project continued to promote new social norms around sanitation, with 2,718 households building facilities for 21,889 people. A revolving loan fund pilot scheme provided affordable finance to 309 households to build toilets, demonstrating an innovative approach to financing sanitation improvements (KRC8).  




In April 2024, UNICEF organized a high-level inter-ministerial engagement between key ministries (Ministry of Sanitation and Water Resources, MoE, MoH, Ministry of Local Government and Ministry of Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs), highlighting the importance of inter-ministerial collaboration for sustainable WASH service delivery. The successful roll-out of the WASH Sector Information System in six regions, to provide more systematic, regular updates on 16 key indicators, strengthened accountability and decision-making in the sector. 




Goal Area 5: Every child has an equitable chance in life 




In collaboration with Ghana Statistical Service, UNICEF continued to support quality data availability and analysis related to multidimensional child poverty. UNICEF provided technical and financial support to the Ghana Living Standard Survey and to the Ghana Demographic and Health Survey. Ensuring the inclusion of the equity agenda during the political transition period, evidence pieces such as the District League Table (DLT) and related Policy Brief, and budget analyses were employed in joint advocacy with civil society partners, to include child rights in major political party manifestos, the next Medium-Term Development Plan Framework guidelines and evaluation of the current Framework. The average regional DLT score of 58.21 for 2022 is indicative of the moderate level of access to basic services in Ghana. However, the sector-specific analyses reveal disparities and uneven development across the country, with an obvious north-south divide.  




UNICEF led the United Nations Country Team in preparing a comprehensive report on the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which assessed the child rights situation in Ghana, including emerging issues of polycrises, climate change, regional instability and economic crises.  




UNICEF initiated a long-term institutional partnership with the Parliament of Ghana, details for which are within Section 3 of this report. UNICEF supported the Presidency with meaningful child participation in high-level policy dialogue, facilitating 82 children’s contributions to SDG acceleration discussions with political leaders from across Africa at the Children’s Model Summit of the Future, learnings from which were included in Ghana’s official statement in Summit of the Future. 




Evidence generation, policy dialogue and partnership contributed to tangible improvements in social protection and immunization financing, including the doubling of the LEAP grant in 2024 from the 2023 increment and release of payments to approved vaccines. Government has agreed to LEAP grant indexation to inflation and gradual increment to 20 per cent of household consumption. UNICEF’s convening efforts enabled evidence-based dialogue on Ghana’s first LEAP reassessment, ensuring that vulnerable populations such as pregnant women are not negatively affected. This dialogue included South-South exchange with Zambia and Brazil and a joint media event with the embassy of Brazil aligned with Global Alliance Against Hunger and Poverty during World Poverty Day to raise awareness of child poverty and social protection as a powerful strategy to address it.  




Cross-cutting areas 




The expansion of Youth Engagement Centres from 10 to 18 locations in all 16 regions increased access to training and resources, enabling 22,950 young people to develop digital and entrepreneurial skills in 2024. Youth leadership and participation were strengthened through the establishment of Youth Advisory Boards, whose 180 members actively contributed to career development and personal growth initiatives within the centres. By engaging with their peers to identify key areas of interest, they played a vital role in shaping relevant youth programmes. UNICEF supported youth climate negotiators, ensuring that young voices have the opportunity to shape climate action at the national and global level. 




UNICEF advanced gender equality and girls’ empowerment by driving systemic change and transformative programming. Strengthening its strategic partnership with Global Affairs Canada, UNICEF and United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) secured approval for the joint Adolescent Girls Programme Phase II (2024–2030) to enhance adolescents’ sexual and reproductive health and rights. 




Capacity-building initiatives were expanded, including the Gender Transformative Accelerator Values Clarification Workshop for Ending Child Marriage. Collaboration with UN Women amplified discussions on a gender-inclusive green economy and women’s leadership, while direct consultations with adolescent girls–25 per cent of whom have disabilities – enhanced inclusive programming, contributing to the WCARO Common Framework for Girl-Intentional Programming.  




The fourth cohort of the StartUp Lab supported 25 startups from 7 regions and from diverse sectors including education, health, agriculture, assistive technologies, fintech and climate action, providing targeted support to refine business models and establish market linkages. UNICEF’s commitment to digital innovation was demonstrated through stakeholder engagement on Digital Public Goods during Ghana Digital Innovation Week, which included showcasing the DPG Innovation Contest and UNICEF Startup Lab Challenge focused on AI-powered research tools. 


Partnerships with faith-based organizations were established to address deeply rooted, negative social norms related to child marriage and open defecation as well as to promote positive behaviours relevant to immunization, birth registration and hygiene. Through a human-centred approach, content was co-designed with users to ensure faith leaders had relevant, user-friendly tools to engage their congregations in meaningful dialogue.  




Embedding behavioural insights research and human-centred design into national systems was another focus area in 2024. UNICEF worked alongside government partners to implement behavioural design approaches to understand social and behavioural drivers relevant to teenage pregnancy and co-design solutions with adolescents to improve reproductive and mental health services. The Happy Family Game, an intervention which aims to improve communication between parents and adolescents, is currently being piloted in the Ashanti region. Routine immunization was promoted through trainings in human-centred design and interpersonal communication to government staff, supporting government to implement demand generation for immunization at national and subnational level. 




Through the Cranky Uncle Vaccine Gamification App, and implementing social listening, UNICEF played a significant role in supporting the Government to collect feedback, and address misinformation and disinformation in humanitarian and non-humanitarian contexts.  




UNICEF demonstrated agility in addressing the impact of the Akosombo Dam spillage, which affected 34,000 children and closed over 300 schools. UNICEF provided temporary classrooms and learning supplies to affected communities. Some 49,931 flood-affected people, including 17,342 children, benefited from child protection and gender-based violence prevention and response services.  




Programming was expanded in border communities in Northern Ghana to support children affected by the Sahel spillover crisis, including through the construction of new school facilities for displaced children. A total of 503 children were enrolled in new facilities in affected communities in Northern Ghana. UNICEF upgraded WASH infrastructure in eight health-care facilities in the Upper East and Upper West Regions of Ghana in areas inhabited by displaced persons. A total of 9,509 people, including 2,900 children, gained enhanced access to at least basic water services through UNICEF’s support to displaced persons and their host communities. 




As part of UNICEF’s immediate cholera response, technical support was provided to enhance risk communication and community engagement activities as well as support for the training and development of emergency preparedness and response plans on cholera for 10 districts in the Greater Accra region. 




UNICEF played a vital role in advancing the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse, leading inter-agency efforts to develop the Standard Operating Procedures on common complaint and reporting mechanisms, to enhance the capacity of 310 government and NGO partners, including the Child Protection in Emergencies Working Group, and to reach 52,576 people with sensitization materials. 




UNICEF Ghana made significant strides in communications and advocacy in 2024, strengthening media engagement and amplifying children’s voices in policy discussions. The establishment of four UNICEF Ghana Media Cafés proved particularly impactful, engaging 100 journalists and generating substantial coverage of children’s issues in major media outlets. Through strategic digital engagement, UNICEF reached over 9 million children and adults with high-quality content across its website, U-Report platform and social media channels. The U-Report platform engaged 214,262 young people through 12 polls covering critical issues including menstrual hygiene, mental health, artificial intelligence and public health awareness. To strengthen internal capacity and partner engagement, UNICEF conducted training for over 120 staff members in media interaction, ethical reporting and storytelling.  




In 2024, 17 staff members benefited from external learning initiatives, including stretch assignments, staff exchanges and surge opportunities – a 60 per cent improvement from 2023. These efforts underscore UNICEF’s commitment to a people-centred approach, ensuring a competent and motivated workforce to deliver results for children. This aligns closely with the Global Staff Survey action plan for the Ghana Office, reinforcing the organization’s emphasis on staff development as a critical driver of success. 




UNICEF Ghana made strides in environmental sustainability by replacing its fleet with three zero-emission vehicles, reflecting its commitment to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and promoting a greener future for children. 




In support of Ghana’s supply chain system, UNICEF facilitated the procurement of goods and services worth US$39.2 million. A key focus was the procurement and distribution of vaccines, medical equipment, and essential commodities, ensuring that every child in Ghana received life-saving vaccinations and medical care to combat recurring diseases. Delays in clearance of shipments from the port for over 10 months disrupted programme implementation and led to financial losses due to high demurrage and storage costs. Direct intervention from the United Nations leadership and the donor community at the highest level, including engagement with the Office of the Presidency, secured the release of all supplies before the end of 2024. 


 


These accomplishments highlight UNICEF Ghana’s unwavering commitment to transformative change through strategic partnerships, advocacy, and resource optimization. By working closely with the government and partners, UNICEF continues to leverage its resources and expertise to protect and advance the rights and well-being of every child in Ghana.

In 2024, UNICEF Ghana continued to strengthen a range of strategic partnerships across government, civil society, United Nations agencies and the private sector with the objective to leverage political and financial resources for children and enhance programme delivery. 




Sector coordination: UNICEF played an important role in development partner coordination at sector level, influencing key processes through its technical leadership and effective convening capacity. For example:


    


With its partner IRC WASH, UNICEF was instrumental in advancing the Presidential Compact on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene, which required obtaining commitment at the highest level nationally towards SDG 6, including the elimination of open defecation in Ghana. Supported under the Heads of States Initiatives, the Presidential Compact commits to mobilize US$1.7 billion annually until 2030. It also establishes a National Sanitation Authority and a National Sanitation Fund, as part of systems strengthening measures aimed at expanding climate resilient WASH infrastructure and services across the country. 


Similarly, UNICEF leveraged the support of education sector development partners in the design and approval of the GPE system capacity, multiplier and system transformation grants totalling over US$111 million, incorporating several evidence-based programmes supported by UNICEF which will be taken to scale across the country. These include the DL+ and Health and Disability Screening programmes, which will be scaled to all public schools in 2025, and Communities of Excellence, which will expand to 100 communities under GALOP. Those efforts bring additional financing to improve foundational learning within a constrained fiscal space. 


The office also continued to be influential in raising the profile of vaccine financing among development partners, leading joint advocacy efforts on sustainable financing in 2024. Similarly, UNICEF continued to support joint advocacy with IMF and World Bank on protecting social protection measures during Ghana’s economic recovery. UNICEF will lead both the Health and Social Protection sector development partner working groups in 2025. The office is also a key member of the Ghana Statistical Service Development Partners group, where it fostered evidence-based dialogue and inclusive approaches to programming among partners. 
 


Leveraging resources: UNICEF continued to strengthen key partnerships focusing on leveraging national and international investment in key national programmes. For example: 

    

Under the Multisectoral and Multistakeholder Child Labour Public-Private Partnership to address the root causes of child labour in targeted cocoa-growing communities (supported by the Swiss Platform for Sustainable Cocoa and the Swiss Secretariat for Economic Affairs), UNICEF played a key role in advancing the establishment of a Multi-Donor Trust Fund with national authorities, the private sector and the World Bank. With increasing global attention on responsible business practices, including European Union (EU) regulations, there is a critical need for sustainable financing to accelerate and scale efforts in eradicating child labour in Ghana. At the same time, UNICEF, International Labour Organization (ILO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) are collaborating to leverage existing child labour initiatives by each organization and extend joint operational reach and partnerships to support MoGCSP.


Similarly, UNICEF continued to support national authorities and development partners around the establishment of a national sanitation fund, based on UNICEF learning and demonstrated cost-effectiveness. The desired existence of a national fund was incorporated into the Presidential Compact on WASH. Several development partners have indicated their support to such a fund. 
 


National institutions: UNICEF fostered partnerships with key national institutions, providing technical assistance and catalytic financial support. For example: 



To support national capacity to advance child-friendly legislation, post-legislative oversight and related advocacy, UNICEF partnered with the African Centre for Parliamentary Affairs to assess the levels of knowledge on children’s rights within Parliament on the part of both MPs, including Committees of Parliament, and Parliamentary staff. The work also reviewed the systems, mechanisms and tools available to support Parliament’s work around children and designed related capacity strengthening and sensitization activities. The work marks a significant entry point for UNICEF towards effective engagement with Parliament. 


Similarly, working with the Office of the Special Advisor on SDGs, UNICEF contributed to the national preparation for the United Nations Summit of the Future, details of which are shared in Section 2 of this report.


Academia and civil society: UNICEF expanded engagement with several academic institutions and civil society organizations (CSOs). For example:

         

An enhanced partnership with Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology will leverage its Centre of Excellence to expand capacity development in health and education sectors for WASH infrastructure management.  


Similarly, diverse partnerships with CSOs such as Theatre for Social Change, RISE-Ghana, the Light Foundation and FACTSPACE Africa are extending programmatic reach and social change across communities, religious and traditional leaders and journalists.  


From 2025, the office will further enhance its work with academic institutions, faith-based organizations and traditional leadership, focusing on leveraging their strategic influence and human, financial and technical resources. 
 


UNICEF also sustained key partnerships with various United Nations agencies, including UNFPA to continue the Global Programme to End Child Marriage, World Food Programme and International Organization for Migration through co-chairing the United Nations Migration Network, ILO for launching Child Labour initiatives, and United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) for funding SDG localization in Ghana. They also worked on harmonizing business processes across administration, human resources, ICT, finance, supply and logistics to enhance operational efficiency.



Regular Resources were vital for improving UNICEF’s technical support, including to sector coordination, social service workforce strengthening, access to justice and data analysis for public finance management in child protection. These funds also supported humanitarian responses in Northern Ghana and the Volta Region.



UNICEF is deeply grateful to its partners supporting its work in Ghana in 2024, including the governments of Canada, France, Belgium, Korea, Japan, Switzerland, Netherlands, Norway, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, as well as Gates Foundation, Zonta INTL, Swiss Platform for Sustainable Cocoa, the Swiss Secretariat for Economic Affairs, Hapag-Lloyd, Jacob Foundation, GPE, as well as United Nations joint partnerships and UNICEF National Committees. Despite progress, Ghana faces significant challenges, and continued donor support is crucial to ensure all children in Ghana reach their full potential.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Throughout 2024, UNICEF Ghana demonstrated agility in navigating complex challenges while delivering transformative results for children. The approach taken by UNICEF Ghana enabled continued progress despite a challenging economic environment. 



1. Key challenges and lessons learned




UNICEF Ghana’s experience in 2024 demonstrated how complex challenges can catalyse innovative solutions and systemic improvements. UNICEF’s response to the following challenges yielded particularly valuable insights for future programming.  




First, the challenging macroeconomic environment – characterized by declining GDP per capita from US$2,318 in 2023 to US$2,230 (IMF World Economic Outlook, April 2024), persistent high inflation that pushed more families into poverty (World Bank, 2024), and declining Overseas Development Assistance – highlighted the critical importance of evidence-based advocacy and innovative financing approaches within a limited fiscal space environment. UNICEF’s strategic engagement with international financial institutions proved transformative, helping to secure protection for critical social investments within Ghana’s Extended Credit Facility programme. This advocacy contributed to significant budget increases for education and social protection, with MoE’s budget rising by 12.1 per cent in real terms and the budget for MoGCSP increasing by 40 per cent in real terms between 2023 and 2024. 




Second, the complexity of addressing deep-rooted challenges such as child labour and inadequate WASH services revealed the power of innovative partnerships and community engagement. The launch of the Child Labour Multisectoral and Multistakeholder Public-Private Partnership created a comprehensive framework for addressing root causes through integrated interventions across child protection, social protection, education, and youth skills development. In the WASH sector, Ghana’s signature of the Presidential Compact on WASH, especially as the first country in West Africa to do so, demonstrated how high-level political commitment can initiate a change process if the political commitment can be translated into clear actions by key stakeholders. Engagement on this with the Government will be a focus area for UNICEF in 2025. 




At the community level, the Communities of Excellence initiative in education was an important example of how empowering local stakeholders can drive sustainable improvements in learning outcomes, leading the MoE to commit to expanding the initiative to an additional 100 communities from 2025. We learned that the community, school and district education directorate accountability relationship significantly improved due to functioning School Management Committees and Parent Teacher Associations, annual school performance appraisals and performance plan development for community collective action. This plan guided project engagements to improve school infrastructure such as the donation of dual desks and learning materials, construction of classrooms through manual labour, and recruitment of Community Teaching Assistants to bridge teacher gaps. 




2. Future outlook 


 


Looking ahead to 2025, UNICEF Ghana will build on the lessons described above while pursuing several strategic priorities. Key amongst these will be strengthening shock-responsive social protection systems, which will be crucial in supporting vulnerable children and families as Ghana continues to face economic challenges and climate-related stresses. Building on the successful systems strengthening work of 2024, UNICEF will continue to support the Government of Ghana in developing more resilient and integrated social protection mechanisms that can rapidly adapt to emerging needs. 




UNICEF will prioritize scaling proven interventions, including the nationwide expansion of the Differentiated Learning approach in primary schools and the implementation of health screening for all public kindergarten and Primary 1 learners. These initiatives demonstrate how successful pilot programmes can be taken to scale through strong government partnerships and evidence-based advocacy. 




UNICEF will work to accelerate innovation in financing mechanisms, particularly through the development of sustainable funding approaches for vaccines and the expansion of public-private partnerships to sustain integrated delivery of social services.
