UNICEF has also started engagement with the newly established directorate of climate financing to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to leverage and access to more funding for children. UNICEF will also continue to prioritize digital transformation, building on successful initiatives in education, child protection and social services. The integration of human-centred design and behavioural science approaches will ensure these digital solutions effectively serve their intended users, while initiatives including the Child Labour Monitoring System will enhance data-driven decision-making. 




Climate-focused interventions will be mainstreamed across programmes, recognizing the increasing impact of climate change on children’s well-being. The ongoing Climate Landscape Analysis for Children exercise will guide UNICEF’s strategy around climate, environment, energy, and disaster risk reduction. UNICEF will continue raising awareness about environmental exposure of children to heavy metals, including supporting the MoH in the development of the National Clinical Guidelines for Prevention and Management of Heavy Metal Poisoning in 2025. Other interventions will include expanding climate-resilient WASH and education infrastructure, shock responsive social protection and strengthening community resilience to climate-related shocks with a focus on health, nutrition, social and child protection outcomes. 




With an incoming new government and cohort of Parliamentarians, UNICEF will maintain its strong focus on systems strengthening while seeking opportunities to advance crucial policy reforms in the areas of inclusive education, safe schools, and early childhood education. Drawing on lessons from 2024, the office will continue to address complex challenges, including around social protection, climate change, child labour, sanitation, and youth employability, thus ensuring that every child in Ghana has the opportunity to reach their full potential. 




The complex interplay of the factors described in this report demonstrates both progress and persistent challenges in realizing children’s rights in Ghana. A sustained focus on strengthening systems, building workforce capacity, and maintaining momentum on policy reforms will continue to be crucial for advancing child rights in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

The Republic of Guinea has a population of over 14 million, with 64% residing in rural areas [1]. Women represent 52% of the population, and nearly two-thirds of Guineans are under 25. While this youthful demographic offers economic potential, it also exacerbates the demand for jobs, education and social services. Despite recent socio-economic progress, poverty remains high at 43.7%, with children disproportionately affected (49%) [2]. Additionally, 72% of children experience multidimensional poverty, meaning they lack access to at least three fundamental rights [3]. Guinea’s context is shaped by complex political, socio-economic and environmental challenges. The country has been in a political transition since the 2021 military coup, with the transitional government - supported by international partners - pledging to restore constitutional order. Under ECOWAS mediation, a transition timetable was agreed upon, , outlining three key steps: (i) adopting a new constitution, (ii) revising electoral rolls, and (iii) organising general elections. However, progress on these milestones has been slow and remains incomplete. In parallel, authorities are pursuing five post-coup priorities, including institutional reform and state reconstruction, with a focus on strengthening social cohesion, revitalising the economy, and reinforcing the rule of law through strong and credible institutions. Despite a fire at the country’s main hydrocarbon depot in late 2023, which triggered cash flow disruptions, a fuel crisis and energy shortages, Guinea's economy demonstrated resilience, growing by 6.1% in 2024, largely driven by the mining sector [4]. However, inflation surged in the first quarter, due to rising food and transport costs and challenges in securing funding. 



Looking ahead, the Government is optimistic about sustaining economic growth in 2025, with the completion of Simandou iron ore megaproject playing a pivotal role. Investments linked to this initiative are expected to stimulate growth across other productive sectors. To guide this transformation, the Government has launched the "Simandou 2040" socio-economic development plan, aiming to leverage mining revenues for long-term economic and social progress. 



In pursuit of governance reform, Guinea has overhauled its public finance management framework, focusing on efficiency and anti-corruption measures. However, ensuring transparency and budgetary oversight remains a challenge.



The year 2024 marks the beginning of the 2024-2028 Cooperation Programme between the Government of Guinea and UNICEF, approved in February. This partnership aims to accelerate progress across multiple sectors, including health, nutrition, WASH, education, child protection and social inclusion. Currently, there is limited up-to-date data available, which affects the assessment of impact across these sectors. Efforts are ongoing to address this challenge, with the Government and development partners, including UNICEF, working to strengthen data collection systems, improve data quality, and enhance data-sharing mechanisms to ensure reliable, up-to-date data for effective decision-making and monitoring.



Every Child Survives and Thrives



Guinea faces persistent public health challenges, including multiple epidemics (polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, measles and monkeypox) due to low vaccination coverage and weak immunity. These outbreaks place mothers and children heightened risk, endangering their survival and wellbeing (SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being). 



To address this, the Government has strengthened its Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI), joined the Vaccine Independence Initiative for timely and affordable vaccine procurement, and improved the cold chain infrastructure to ensure reliable nationwide vaccine availability.

 

Malnutrition remains a pressing concern, with 26% of children chronically malnourished (compared to 25.5% in 2023), despite efforts by UNICEF and partners. The most impacted regions are Nzérékoré (33%), Faranah (29.8%), and Labé (29.4%) (SDG 2: Zero Hunger). In 2024, UNICEF prioritised integrated nutrition interventions, focusing on early childhood, adolescent and maternal nutrition, as well as the early detection of severe acute malnutrition, including in emergency situations. 



Strategic discussions on early childhood development and transformative food systems are underway, initiated by UNICEF, to enhance the multi-sectoral response to malnutrition. Efforts to mobilise partners and accelerate impact are set to intensify in 2025. 



Every Child Lives in a Clean and Safe Environment



Like other countries in the region, Guinea is increasingly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, which disproportionately affects children and women (SDG 13: Climate Action). In 2024, severe floods devastated multiple prefectures, exposing weaknesses in water, hygiene, and sanitation (WASH) infrastructure. This exacerbated health risks for vulnerable households, and disruptions to food security and livelihoods, particularly due to the destruction of cultivated lands. UNICEF and partners are working to address these gaps by expanding access to clean water, strengthening sanitation services and bolstering emergency response capacity in affected areas.



In terms of access to safe drinking water (SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation), 71% of Guineans have access to a basic drinking water service, but there are major disparities between urban (92%) and rural (59%) areas [5]. About 12% of Guineans have limited access to water services, while 8% rely on unimproved sources, a figure that rises to 13% in rural areas. As for sanitation, only 31% of the population has access to basic sanitation services, with 22% in rural areas and 47% in urban areas. Another 29% have access to limited sanitation services, including 18% in rural areas and 49% in urban areas. Moreover, 32% of the population has access to unimproved sanitation services, with 50% in rural areas and 3% in urban areas. Finally, 7% of the population practices open defecation, a figure that rises to 10% in rural areas, but drops to 1% in urban areas.



Every Child Learns



Since 2023, the school population has grown from 1.1 million to 2.3 million by 2024, with primary school enrolment reaching 92.8%, and girls’ enrolment 84.2%. Pre-school enrolment rose from 17.6% in 2021 to 23.9% in 2023 (from 230,000 to 322,000 children). Despite these gains, secondary school enrolment remains low at 37.9%, with girls at 30.7%. Guinea is facing an ongoing ‘learning crisis’, with persistent gaps in foundational skills. Primary and lower secondary completion rates have improved but remain low at 83.8% and 45.6%, respectively, compared to 65.3% and 43.9% in 2022.



In 2024, the Government has taken steps to address teacher shortages and committed to increasing budget allocations for pre-university education, to reinforce capacity and provide adequate learning materials, reflecting their commitment to human capital development (SDG 4: Quality Education). 



Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation 



Violence against children remains a major concern. Female genital mutilation (FGM) affects 94.5% of women and girls aged 15-49, while 46% of girls marry before the age of 18. Additionally, 89% of children have experienced psychological or physical violence, and 38% remain unregistered in the civil registry, limiting their access to legal rights and protections.In 2024, significant progress was made in child protection.t. Advocacy efforts by children’s organisations (Parlement des Enfants de Guinée) and youth groups (Club des Jeunes Filles Leaders de Guinée), supported by UNICEF and the Ministry for the Promotion of Women, Children and Vulnerable Persons (MPFEPV), led to the inclusion of an FGM and child marriage ban in the draft constitution (Articles 9 and 25), representing a major step forward towards legal prohibitions on these harmful practices (SDG 5: Gender Equality). A referendum in early 2025 will determine the adoption of these legal prohibitions.



Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life 



Guinea revitalised its social protection system in 2024 with the resumption of cash transfer programmes, prioritising women and children (SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities). Additionally, the Government expanded contributory social protection, by extending health insurance to all active and retired civil servants and initiating a new national occupational health and safety policy, aiming to broaden coverage for informal and independent workers. Furthermore, mobile health units have been deployed and linked to referral centres to address healthcare shortages in remote areas, improving access to diagnostics and treatment. 



Investment in social services has increased significantly, with the share of the national budget allocated to social sectors rising from 15.7% in 2023 to 21% in 2024. This reflects a strengthened commitment to inclusive and sustainable development.



Looking ahead, as Guinea advances its development agenda, sustained investment in governance, health, education and social protection will be crucial in ensuring inclusive and equitable progress. Strengthening institutions, addressing structural challenges, and leveraging economic growth for social impact will be key to shaping a sustainable future for all Guineans, particularly the most vulnerable populations.

In 2024, the first year of UNICEF’s 2024-2028 programme cycle in Guinea, UNICEF’s support led to notable progress across multiple sectors. The focus remained on community-driven development through the “communes of convergence” approach, introduced by the Government in 2018. This multi-sectoral strategy addresses critical areas such as health, nutrition, child protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), education and social protection in selected communes. This approach is designed to foster transformative and sustainable change for communities in Guinea.



Every Child Survives and Thrives



Vaccination:

    

Notable achievements were made in vaccination coverage (KRC1) and the elimination of preventable diseases. In total, 96% of children aged 0-11 months received three doses of pentavalent vaccine (441,658 children), exceeding the 2023 coverage of 91%. The dropout rate between the first and third doses of the vaccine remained low at 6%, within the target of under 10%. UNICEF played a pivotal role in these results by facilitating multi-sectoral catch-up campaigns, which integrated routine immunisation, alongside vitamin A supplementation and issuance of birth certificates. These campaigns vaccinated an additional 120,551 children with Penta3, reducing under-immunisation by 23%. 



UNICEF also played a key role in Guinea’s success in eliminating maternal and neonatal tetanus, supported the Government’s validation of a plan to introduce the malaria vaccine in 2025, and its adherance to the Vaccination Independence Initiative for vaccine procurement. Further strengthening Guinea’s vaccine cold chain, UNICEF facilitated key infrastructure enhancements, including the installation of 262 solar refrigerators, bringing the total number of health faicilites with functioning refirigirators to 1,731 units (86% of the target). Enhanced vaccine management practices led to a significant improvement in the Effective Vaccine Management score, rising from 37% in 2016 to 65% in 2024 (against a target of 80%), reflecting the advancements in the efficiency and reliability of vaccine storage and distribution systems. Through its advocacy and collaboration with high-level authorities, partners and U-Reporters, UNICEF contributed to the success of vaccination campaigns, as demonstrated by the percentage of districts meeting LQAS survey standards rising from 31% in October 2023 to 92% in December 2024.



Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health:

    

UNICEF supported an increase in the number of health facilities equipped for childbirth and neonatal resuscitation, from 358 in 2023 to 370 in 2024, covering over 90% of the 410 targeted facilities. Additionally, 250 healthcare workers received training, enabling the provision of kangaroo care to 6,941 babies and the administration of 52,876 Vitamin K injections and 171,921 eye treatments. These upgrades enabled a 30% increase in the number of live births receiving quality care, from 328,045 in 2023 to 427,250 (out of 503,279 live births in 2024). Assisted deliveries also rose by 4%, reaching 431,814 out of 559,200 expected, compared to 415,521 in 2023. 



In HIV prevention and care, 4,034 pregnant women out of 4,118 targeted (98%) were screened and placed on antiretroviral treatment during prenatal consultations, a slight decrease from 5,007 in 2023. UNICEF supported the integration of prevention of mother-to-child transmission services in 60 additional health facilities, the training of 31 healthcare workers on early diagnosis using M-PIMA devices and the equipping of 8 health centres with early diagnostic equipment. Despite these efforts, early infant diagnosis for HIV remains a challenge, with 1,741 infants out of 3,741 expected (46.5%) born to HIV-positive mothers receiving testing within two months, slightly down from 1,598 out of 3,263 (49%) in 2023. Among those tested, 69 infants were diagnosed as HIV-positive in both years.



UNICEF also played a critical role in broader health system improvements, supporting the development of key policy and strategy documents, such as the National Vaccination Strategy 2024–2028 and an Action Plan for Child Survival that defined priority interventions. It also supported the expansion of community health initiatives. As a result, over 996,595 children received developmental care, compared to 805,847 in 2023 – an increase of 24%. In child illness management, 789,455 cases were treated, including 771,911 for malaria, 11,797 for pneumonia, and 5,747 for diarrhoea, representing a substantial increase from 2023 when 176,725 children under five-year-old benefited from integrated community case management. UNICEF’s collaboration in developing the National Strategic Plan for Mental Health 2024–2028 further highlighted its comprehensive approach to health system strengthening. Community health efforts mobilized 13,000 community mobilizers and reached 4,751 individuals, including adolescents, through educational sessions and village dialogues to promote health awareness and participation.



Prevention and Treatment of Malnutrition



UNICEF contributed to creating an enabling environment for malnutrition prevention (KRC 2) by revising the national protocol for managing malnutrition in children under five to incorporate updated WHO guidelines (2023). This included measures to prevent acute malnutrition, a transition plan for shifting from Vitamin A supplementation campaigns to routine delivery, and the development of a national recipe database to address low dietary diversity in children under five.



Key achievements in 2024 included:

    

1.      Vitamin A Supplementation and Deworming: 2.69 million children received two doses of Vitamin A supplementation (96% of the target), a result consistent with 2023. Deworming with Mebendazole reached 2.4 million children aged 12–59 months, representing 102% of the target and a significant increase from 75% coverage in 2023.



2.      Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) Promotion: Awareness campaigns on IYCF practices reached 871,650 mothers and caregivers, a fourfold increase from 2023, attributed to an expansion of health centres implementing growth monitoring and promotion activities.



3.      Maternal Nutrition: Iron and folic acid supplementation, coupled with nutritional counselling, was provided to 670,654 pregnant women (more than double the 300,000 target, and triple the 198,100 women reached in 2023)).



4.      Growth Monitoring and Promotion (GMP): Coverage of GMP activities in health centres increased from 47% in 2023 to 53% in 2024, benefiting 165,816 children under five.


In November 2024, 398,000 children aged 6 to 59 months were screened for malnutrition. Among them, 28,455 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) were treated, achieving 75% of the HAC 2024 target and 30% of the estimated national caseload (97,267). SAM treatment outcomes met Sphere standards, with a 92.2% recovery rate. However, resource constraints for essential supplies limited active and passive case detection, hindering further progress. UNICEF also responded to address malnutrition during the Monkeypox outbreak in Macenta, supplying critical therapeutic nutrition products to treat 1,500 children with SAM.



UNICEF’s advocacy facilitated a novel interoperability strategy, integrating vitamin A supplementation, catch-up vaccination campaigns (reaching 319,829 children), and birth registration for 16,375 children aged 0–6 months. 



Furthermore, UNICEF supported community-based interventions, including training for 123 healthcare workers in growth monitoring and promotion in Mandiana, Siguiri, and Dinguiraye, increasing the implementation of GMP activities to 53% of health facilities in 2024 (up from 47% in 2023). These efforts supported 935 women's groups across 67 communes in implementing a comprehensive malnutrition prevention package, leading to the referral of 120,928 children for various illnesses, including diarrhoea, respiratory infections, malaria, and acute malnutrition.



Every Child Lives in a Clean and Safe Environment



In 2024, UNICEF played a pivotal role in supporting the Government to improve access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services at both strategic and operational levels. Strategically, UNICEF contributed to strengthening the policy, regulatory, and strategic framework of the sector by supporting the dissemination of the National Disaster and Emergency Management Strategy and the National Sanitation Policy Document. The validation of the Strategic Plan for Water Safety Management and the completion of the Global Analysis and Assessment of Sanitation and Drinking-Water (GLAAS) 2024, in collaboration with WHO, provided critical recommendations to advocate for increased domestic resource mobilization for WASH financing and achieving national SDG commitments.



Operationally, as part of KRC 8, UNICEF enabled 129,728 people (target 300,000), including 25,946 children under five, to live in open defecation-free communities through the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach, fostering sustainable behavioural changes. Additionally, 105,846 people, including 21,162 children under five, gained access to improved sanitation facilities through a sanitation marketing approach, surpassing initial targets. Complementing these efforts, UNICEF facilitated access to sustainable safe drinking water for 81,908 beneficiaries (target 30,000), including 16,382 children under five, through the construction of new boreholes equipped with solar-powered systems and the rehabilitation of existing water systems.



In schools, UNICEF enhanced access to water and sanitation for 18,348 students, including 8,962 girls, across 41 schools (exceeding the target of 40 schools). Improved facilities, including those tailored to the needs of adolescent girls, reduced absenteeism caused by menstrual health challenges. Menstrual health and hygiene promotion directly reached 1,805 adolescent girls in 16 schools, breaking taboos and fostering an inclusive educational environment. Schools reported no absenteeism due to menstrual health challenges in 2024.



UNICEF also responded to humanitarian needs, supporting 47,784 flood-affected individuals, including 9,557 children under five, with safe drinking water and improved sanitation for 24,104 people, including 4,621 children. These rapid interventions prevented disease outbreaks, secured water sources, and rehabilitated sanitation infrastructure.



To ensure sustainability, UNICEF trained 181 local actors in monitoring and managing community WASH infrastructure. An additional 174 stakeholders were trained to oversee climate-resilient water technologies, including solar-powered systems, ensuring durable access to potable water in the face of climate challenges.



Every Child Learns



In 2024, UNICEF Guinea continued supporting the Ministry of Education in expanding equitable access to quality education (KRC 3), with a focus on girls and marginalised groups. Key initiatives included facilitating community guidance centres and piloting innovative approaches, contributing to significant progress. Since 2023, the school population has grown from 1.1 million to 2.3 million by 2024, with primary school enrolment reaching 92.8%, and girls’ enrolment 84.2%. Pre-school enrolment rose from 17.6% in 2021 to 23.9% in 2023 (from 230,000 to 322,000 children). Despite these gains, secondary school enrolment remains low at 37.9%, with girls at 30.7%, highlighting the need for targeted policies to improve transitions and access.



UNICEF Actions to Improve Access to Education



·       National advocacy campaign: Launched to challenge community resistance and socio-cultural norms that hinder school enrolment, particularly for girls. Organised jointly by UNICEF’s Education, Social and Behavioural Change, and Communication sections, the campaign reached millions through national TV broadcasts and local meetings, raising awareness about the educational rights of all children, including those with disabilities, and emphasising the crucial role of parents and communities in supporting these rights.



·       Social protection measures to address barriers to secondary education: Introduced a scholarship programme for 1,000 pupils, providing US$125 per pupil to cover school supplies and fees, aiming to reduce socio-economic obstacles to education. 



·       Girls’ Education Accelerator: In partnership with AFD, secured over $9 million for the Girls' Education Accelerator, enhancing the potential to implement and expand girls’ education initiatives.



Addressing the Learning Crisis



Despite improvements in access, Guinea is facing an ongoing ‘learning crisis’, with persistent gaps in foundational skills. Primary and lower secondary completion rates have improved but remain low at 83.8% and 45.6%, respectively, compared to 65.3% and 43.9% in 2022. In response, UNICEF intensified its efforts to improve learning outcomes (KRC 4) by: 

    

·       Facilitating teacher training: Over 15,000 elementary and pre-school teachers were trained in multigrade classroom management and pre-school teaching methodologies.

 

·       Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL): Supported the expansion of the Ministry of Education’s Programme for the Improvement of Basic Skills (PACF) through the TaRL approach. This innovative method, grouping children by learning level rather than age, reached nearly 6,000 pupils in 18 schools in underserved rural areas, up from 1,500 in 2022. Over 60 additional teachers and facilitators were trained in child-centred teaching methods, building on the 100 actors trained in 2023. These efforts were supported by technical assistance from TaRL Africa to guide programme expansion.



·       Digital Education; Supported the Learning Passport, a platform providing over 54,000 primary and lower secondary pupils access to digital resources aligned with the national curriculum – nearly doubling the reach from 2023, when 28,000 pupils benefited from digitised learning. Building on 2023 efforts to pilot digitised content and distribute digitisation kits to schools, 2024 marked a significant scale-up, with enhanced institutional support through the National Institute of Research and Pedagogic Action (INRAP), which was equipped with a UNICEF-funded multimedia room to coordinate content integration. In partnership with Plan International, 36 school administrators were trained to integrate the platform, directly benefiting 2,000 pupils and bolstering system resilience. By complementing physical textbooks amid persistent shortages, digitised learning continues to address critical gaps in educational resources.



To improve learning conditions, UNICEF partnered with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and the Agence Française de Développement (AFD) to enhance school infrastructure. Over GNF 42 billion was allocated to local authorities, resulting in the construction and equipping of 7 nursery schools, 274 classrooms, and 100 gender-segregated latrine blocks, benefiting over 11,000 pupils. Additionally, UNICEF distributed 47,000 textbooks for secondary education and 800,000 primary education materials.



Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation



In 2024, UNICEF in Guinea made significant progress in protecting the most vulnerable children from violence, exploitation and abuse. Over 383,500 children (195,400 girls) received essential care and protection services – 26% more than in 2023. Additionally, 220,200 community members (126,600 women) were educated on protective behaviours, contributing to the prevention of harmful practices. Through strengthened systems and a focus on prevention, UNICEF engaged in key interventions, including collaboration with health, civil registry, security and justice sectors, to improve protection and ensure better outcomes for children.



UNICEF intensified its efforts to reduce sexual violence against children (KRC 5) and prevent child marriage (KRC 6), focusing on community engagement, legal frameworks and capacity-building. UNICEF strengthened partnerships withsecurity and justice services to enhance the enforcement of child protection laws. The preliminary draft of the new constitution now explicitly prohibits female genital mutilation (FGM) (Article 9) and child marriage (Article 25), marking a major legal milestone. To improve access to justice for children, 32 justice professionals, including 5 women, were trained on mobile hearings for FGM cases. These hearings raise awareness on legal provisions while serving as deterrents. Additionally, 52 social workers were trained to enhance case management for violence against children. Despite resource constraints in 2024, 370 children accessed essential services, such as forensic medicine and social work. While this fell short of the 671 targeted due to funding shortages, it underscores the continued importance of UNICEF-supported community mechanisms.



The strengthening of community protection mechanisms and awareness raising were essential in reducing harmful practices. Community surveillance mechanisms played a key role in preventing or reporting 150 cases (81 FGM and 69 child marriage), surpassing the 2023 total of 114 cases and far exceeding the 2022 figure of 11 cases. UNICEF supported the creation and enhancement of 1,026 community protection structures (83% of the 1,235 targeted), focusing on urban areas. These structures disseminate messages on preventing violence against children, identifying at-risk children, and connect them with appropriate services. A total of 2,829 community members (935 women and girls) were trained in communication techniques to raise awareness on child marriage and FGM. In terms of preventing child marriage, these efforts enabled 15,456 adolescent girls (ages 10-19) to benefit from prevention and care services, surpassing the target of 11,000 – a notable increase from 8,285 girls in 2023. The progress reflects the effectiveness of community-based approaches, bolstered by support to protection structures, youth associations and women’s groups.



UNICEF also reinforced grassroots engagement by supporting 102 new women's groups and 53 new community structures for adolescent girls, bringing the total to 542 women's groups and 107 adolescent girl platforms. These groups played a pivotal role in promoting positive social norms and combating FGM, child marriage, and other forms of violence. The engagement of 1,348 male role models, 820 female mentors, and 160 model families further strengthened community-led initiatives, encouraging protective behaviours. UNICEF also supported religious leaders in advocating against harmful practices, increasing their numbers from 77 in 2023 to 124 in 2024, including 13 women – a 61% rise. Equipped with communication tools such as harmonised sermons, preaching guides, and fatwas, these leaders raised awareness, particularly among adolescents and young people, through places of worship, interfaith debates, and radio broadcasts.



In 2024, two districts in Conakry held public ceremonies declaring the abandonment of FGM, marking a significant step forward in urban areas. Additionally, UNICEF supported 124 religious leaders, including 13 women, who advocated against harmful practices, utilizing tools like harmonized sermons, preaching guides, and fatwas to spread the message, especially among adolescents and young people. Despite these successes, the number of villages declaring FGM abandonment dropped to 209 (out of a planned 500) in 2024, compared to 236 in 2023 and 261 in 2022, due to delays in launching new cooperation programmes and limited funding.



In terms of birth registration (KRC 7), 269,781 children under one (125,690 girls) were registered, achieving 65% of the national target – a significant increase from 31% in 2023. UNICEF contributed to these results by enhancing interoperability between the health and civil registry sectors by supporting 73 new health structures to integrate with the civil registry: 351 health facilities are now integrated, covering 73% of the country. In addition, UNICEF facilitated cross-sector collaboration between the health, nutrition and civil registration programme and supported the combined vaccination. vitamin A supplementation and birth registration campaign in June (during which 15,809 children without birth certificates were registered in just four days).



Regarding children in conflict with the law, UNICEF continued to provide legal and judicial support, assisting 555 children, including 60 girls, out of a targeted 770. This support enabled 189 children, including 64 girls, to avoid detention through alternative measures such as diversion programmes, vocational training, foster care and family reunification.



Every Child Has an Equitable Chance in Life



In 2024, social protection has been one of the top three public policy priorities, shaping key decisions during the budget preparation process. This has led to a significant increase in social spending, while the reach of the social protection system has expanded to better cover women and children. The government introduced reforms to its contributory social protection system, offering health insurance to 130,000 active and retired civil servants. These reforms also include a new national occupational safety and health policy designed to expand coverage to the informal sector, targeting up to 80% of this population. Additionally, mobile health units were enhanced to address remote communities' health needs, particularly through improved diagnostics and the recruitment of qualified healthcare personnel. 



The budget for children’s rights saw a notable increase, with the share for social sectors rising from 15.7% in 2023 to 21% in 2024, mainly benefiting health and education. This shift was driven by advocacy from organizations like UNICEF and civil society, which helped guide the budget towards prioritizing social services for vulnerable populations. As a result, the country made progress in reducing poverty and inequalities, expanding access to services for children and women.




UNICEF played a pivotal role in supporting the government’s efforts by enhancing public finance management, particularly through performance-based budgeting and promoting transparency. The organization encouraged participation in budgetary discussions, especially through initiatives like the Open Budget Survey, which helped increase civil society involvement in budget debates. Additionally, UNICEF supported local governments by providing capacity-building in areas such as resource mobilization, child rights-sensitive budgeting, and emergency preparedness. These efforts helped integrate children’s needs into municipal development plans, ensuring better access to services such as healthcare, education, and nutrition, particularly in remote areas.



The expansion of social protection coverage has significantly benefited vulnerable populations, particularly children. The government’s flagship cash transfer program, which was reinstated in 2024, has directly impacted over 300,000 children, with a focus on low-income households. UNICEF supported this initiative by improving healthcare access for the poorest, especially through the Social Development and Indigence Fund (FDSI), and by providing direct financial assistance to vulnerable children, including school scholarships and healthcare support. UNICEF directly facilitated access to free services for 3,309 households and provided financial support to enhance education retention and access for the most vulnerable children. UNICEF also contributed to the management of the Unified Social Registry, which helps identify and support the most vulnerable households. Through these efforts, there has been a measurable increase in the number of children benefiting from essential services, reducing barriers to education and healthcare, and enhancing overall social protection coverage.

UNICEF’s partnerships have been instrumental in mobilising resources, strengthening advocacy, and driving sustainable progress for children in Guinea. Strategic collaborations with government entities, civil society organisations (CSOs), academic institutions, the private sector and international agencies have demonstrated the power of collective action to achieve results across UNICEF’s programmatic areas. In the health sector, UNICEF’s collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), GAVI, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the World Bank led to successful advocacy efforts, securing the signing of the Vaccine Independence Initiative plan and corresponding MOU – an important step forward in strengthening Guinea’s sustainable vaccine supply and distribution. In addition, a partnership with the Red Cross significantly enhanced vaccine management, particularly in ensuring the secure handling of the novel oral polio vaccine (nOPV2), resulting in zero lost vaccine vials. Epidemic response efforts were also strengthened through the deployment of Social and Behaviour Change Communication (SBCC) strategies and Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) initiatives to counter misinformation and reduce vaccine hesitancy.



To further promote vaccine awareness, UNICEF Guinea’s National Ambassador for Immunisation, Sekouba Bambino, collaborated with UNICEF to produce the song "No More Zero Dose". This song, which raised awareness about polio vaccination, garnered approximately 1.4 million views on YouTube, significantly boosting public engagement in immunisation campaigns. UNICEF strengthened its nutrition efforts in Guinea through partnerships with key organisations such as the World Food Programme (WFP), Helen Keller International (HKI), WHO and ChildFund. Through these partnerships, UNICEF facilitated the bi-annual Vitamin A supplementation programme for children and worked to revise the national protocol for the prevention and treatment of acute malnutrition, ensuring it aligns with the latest WHO guidelines.  Additionally, the signing of an MOU with WFP in 2024 to align nutrition and food interventions has paved the way for the launch of a joint dietary diversity programme in 2025. 



In the WASH sector, UNICEF collaborated with the key government ministries (for WASH, education and health), as well as NGOs and CSOs to integrate climate-resilience into WASH services and strengthen sustainable WASH initiatives in vulnerable communities. These efforts included working closely with the National Committee on Climate Change to co-create a proposal for submission to the National Development Budget, to secure funding for climate resilient infrastructure. UNICEF also played a key role in establishing the National Sustainability Support Committee to coordinate and monitor community-based activities that ensure local ownership and sustainable impact. 



Within the education sector, UNICEF played a leadership role in coordinating technical and financial partners, collaborating with stakeholders such as AFD, the World Bank, UN agencies and national and international CSOs to support the Government. A notable achievement in 2024 was the development of the Partnership Compact, a prerequisite for the Global Partnership for Education to channel funding via the Common Education Fund (jointly implemented by AFD and UNICEF) to support the implementation of ProDEG 2020–2029 education plan. As a result, fund disbursement rates improved from 21% in 2022 to over 65% in 2024, leading to significant progress in access to education, teacher training, textbook distribution and capacity building for decentralised structures. Furthermore, UNICEF expanded its partnership with AFD, with plans for UNICEF to take on a leading role in the girls’ education acceleration component of an AFD-funded project in 2025. This collaboration represents a broader commitment to gender equity in education, focusing on creating opportunities for girls, particularly in disadvantaged regions.



UNICEF also leveraged partnerships with high-profile figures, including appointing footballer Naby Keïta as UNICEF Champion for Children's Rights and Access to Education, and amplified youth engagement, supporting their participation in global advocacy platforms such as the African Union Education Summit and the 68th UN Commission on the Status of Women. In the child protection sector, UNICEF continued to reinforce coordination frameworks at both national and decentralised levels. These efforts ensured that children, particularly girls, had access to appropriate protection services. UNICEF-supported community protection committees reported a 20% increase in identified and addressed cases of violence, reflecting enhanced capacity in public and community actors to respond to violence against children.



In partnership with the Ministry for the Promotion of Women, Children, and Vulnerable Persons (MPFEPV), UNICEF supported key initiatives, such as the International Day of Zero Tolerance to FGM, providing resources to support victims of sexual violence. These efforts helped 370 girls access consultations and treatment – an increase from 100 in 2023. UNICEF also expanded partnerships with CSOs to intensify efforts to eliminate FGM in regions with the highest prevalence. Further strengthening its efforts, UNICEF deepened its partnership with the Swiss Committee, using additional funding to enhance the reach of local partners in remote areas by supporting the distribution of motorbikes and mobile phones, allowing partners to access hard-to-reach zones and collect data on violence, with a focus on FGM and child marriage.



To promote the respect for children's rights during crises, particularly during socio-political demonstrations, and to reduce their participation in such events, UNICEF collaborated with OHCHR and UNDP to develop a proposal, which secured funding from the Peacebuilding Fund. The project is due to start in early 2025. 



In 2024, UNICEF worked with the Guinean Bar Association to formalise a partnership aimed at providing free legal assistance to children in conflict with the law. This partnership ensures better coordination and strengthens legal protections for children’s rights in the justice system. 


 


Cross-sectoral initiatives have been enabled by collaborations with the National Food Fortification Alliance, WAHO, and CRS, which strengthened the capacity of local stakeholders and facilitated innovative approaches to integrating Vitamin A supplementation, catch-up immunisation and birth registration.



To promote social inclusion and equitable access to basic services, UNICEF strengthened its partnerships with government institutions, CSOs, and NGOs. At the national level, UNICEF provided technical and financial support for public financial management reforms, including the relaunch of programme-based budgeting and the Open Budget Survey, which advocates for transparency and accountability in public spending. UNICEF also worked with key state institutions, such as the National Directorate for Vulnerable People (DNPV) and the Social Development and Indigence Fund (FDSI), to restart the cash transfer programme for poor households. To further advance children's rights, UNICEF collaborated with NGOs such as Vision Sans Frontières, the National Confederation of Albino People of Guinea (CNAG), and the Union of Albino People of Faranah (UPAAF). These efforts focused on supporting marginalised communities, particularly children with albinism, through targeted social protection and empowerment initiatives. At the local level, UNICEF engaged with members of the special delegations set up after the dissolution of municipal councils, and partnered with youth, adolescent and women’s platforms to strengthen resource mobilisation, planning and budgeting, with a focus on children’s rights and emergency preparedness.



UNICEF in Guinea leveraged flexible funding, particularly through Regular Resources, to support these various partnerships and interventions. RR funding enabled UNICEF to respond swiftly to emergencies, support ongoing initiatives and facilitate the expansion of successful programmes across sectors. Additionally, other resources (OR) were strategically directed to local governments and regional actors, particularly in the context of the Joint Programme for the Domestic Implementation of the SDGs, using a human security approach.



To strengthen resource mobilisation, UNICEF established the Communication, Advocacy, and Partnership (CAP) unit, supporting the implementation of the Resource Mobilization Strategy 2024-2028 and the Communication and Advocacy Strategy 2024-2028, developed with the support of UNICEF’s West and Central Africa Regional Office.




UNICEF successfully mobilized US$7.27 million in funding, securing contributions from government donors, National Committees (NatCom), pooled funds and private sector partners. It also developed four business cases (on immunisation, education, early childhood development, and child protection) to attract donor interest. In addition, high-level field visits engaged stakeholders, including the Australian National Committee for UNICEF and the Japanese and Spanish ambassadors to Guinea.




UNICEF’s role as chair of the UN Communication Group reinforced ONE UN activities. Joint communication efforts with key partners, including the Government of Guinea, WFP, IOM, the Governments of Japan and Spain, the World Bank, and Gavi, expanded advocacy reach and increased visibility. 




In 2024, UNICEF’s partnerships in Guinea, supported by flexible funding, made significant strides in advancing children’s rights and improving their well-being. These collaborations with the government, CSOs, international agencies, and the private sector have proven essential in tackling challenges across immunization, nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection. Looking ahead, UNICEF plans to build on these successes by expanding its partner base and further integrating climate resilience, gender equity and human rights into its programming. The continued strength of these partnerships will be crucial in achieving lasting change for children in Guinea.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges



Cross-sectoral coordination: Despite improvements in 2024, including the combined vaccination-vitamin A-birth registration campaign, a key challenge in maternal and neonatal health has been weak coordination between different health and nutrition programmes, affecting the integration of immunisation and nutrition interventions. This disjointed approach has limited cost-saving opportunities and slowed progress towards optimal health outcomes. Similarly, within the nutrition sector, inadequate cross-sector coordination has limited a unified approach to address malnutrition. Strengthening collaboration across sectors - including health, WASH, child protection, social inclusion and education - will be essential for a more sustainable and high-impact response.



Financial Constraints: Limited financial resources, both external and domestic, have posed significant barriers to advancing health, nutrition and WASH initiatives. The over-reliance on external financing and the need for dedicated local funding mechanisms highlight the importance of innovative financing solutions. UNICEF is working with the Government to enhance domestic resource mobilisation, including through partnerships with the private sector and the development of local funding strategies.



In education, coordination gaps, slow adoption of digital transformation strategies, and difficulties in scaling key initiatives like the Learning Passport and TaRL) have hindered progress. Structural challenges, such as delays in sector-wide reviews and administrative constraints in fund disbursement, have further impacted programme delivery. Additionally, human resource shortages have affected the ability to advance key education reforms effectively.



In child protection, financial and human resource limitations, combined with coordination challenges, have slowed efforts to strengthen social work, birth registration, and juvenile justice systems. The full operationalisation of critical platforms, such as CPMIS/PRIMERO and GBV Alert Guinea, remains essential to ensure timely data collection and evidence-based decision-making.



At the governance level, efforts to improve budget transparency, decentralisation and resource allocation continue. Strengthening local governance structures, enhancing financial planning, and ensuring adequate investments in social services are key priorities to improve service delivery and child well-being.



Lessons Learned



·       Integrated and Cross-Sectoral Approaches – Collaboration across sectors has demonstrated stronger and more sustainable results, particularly in addressing malnutrition and improving maternal and child health outcomes.



·       Community Engagement – Strengthening community participation, especially through women’s groups, has been critical in improving health, nutrition, and early childhood education outcomes.



·       Leveraging Partnerships – Successful initiatives, such as cross-sector collaboration in child justice, highlight the importance of engaging multiple stakeholders, including civil society and professional bodies, to enhance programme effectiveness.



·       Digital and Communication Strategies – Expanding communication efforts through diverse digital platforms has increased outreach and awareness, particularly in preventing violence against children and harmful practices like FGM.



·       Capacity-Building for Local Governance – Investing in training and skills development for local officials presents an opportunity to strengthen governance, planning, and financial management at the community level.



Future Outlook



To address these challenges and build on lessons learned, UNICEF will prioritise the following strategic actions:

    

1.      Strengthening Coordination and Integration – Improving collaboration between sectors will help create a more cohesive approach to tackling malnutrition and other priority areas.



2.      Enhancing Domestic Resource Mobilisation – Engaging government, private sector, and local authorities to increase funding for essential services, particularly for WASH infrastructure.



3.      Developing Innovative Financing Mechanisms – Exploring new funding approaches, including engagement with the diaspora and private sector, to reduce reliance on external donors. Integrating sustainable projects into national development plans will accelerate funding mobilisation.



4.      Scaling Up Education Initiatives – Strengthening sector coordination, securing funding for key education reforms, and enhancing collaboration with education authorities to improve learning outcomes.



5.      Improving Governance and Social Protection Systems – Strengthening local planning and budgeting processes to integrate child-focused services and improve access to social protection programmes.



6.      Enhancing Digital Solutions and Data Systems – Strengthening the functionality of digital platforms to improve data collection and programme monitoring in child protection and other key areas.



7.      Revitalising Advocacy and Partnerships – Expanding collaboration with government authorities, local stakeholders, and civil society to ensure continued investment in child welfare and social sector programmes.



By implementing these strategies, UNICEF aims to overcome key challenges, enhance programme effectiveness, and ensure that all children, especially the most vulnerable, have access to quality essential services that support their rights and well-being.

In 2024, Guinea-Bissau faced significant social, economic and political challenges impeding its development, leaving vulnerable children without access to essential services. Ongoing political instability slowed implementation of the development programme.

Economically, the country remains fragile and highly dependent on its cashew industry with around 76 per cent of the household's growing cashews (World Bank 2020 Poverty Assessment). Furthermore, the World Bank’s 2024 economic update revealed that the country's debt burden remains high at an estimated 77.8 per cent of GDP in 2023 despite falling from 80.4 per cent in 2022. However, the economy showed early signs of relative recovery, with the economy growing at an estimated rate of 4.7 per cent in 2024 (Guinea-Bissau Spring 2024 Economic Update), due primarily to a solid 2024 cashew harvest. 

The latest UNDP Human Development Report (2023/2024) ranks Guinea-Bissau 179 out of 193 countries. Due to its low human development index, Guinea-Bissau is classified as a Least Developed Country (LDC). Among its slightly over 2 million population, an estimated 67 per cent live below the poverty line, surviving on less than US$2 per day, with 48 per cent being children. In addition, more than one third of the population lives in extreme poverty subsisting on less than US$1 per day. 

The last Multiple Indicators Survey (MICS6 2018-2019) stated that 64 per cent of the population is multidimensionally poor, with rural areas, where majority of the population live, being affected and compounded by gender pervasive inequalities. Poor and vulnerable communities have limited access to social protection or affordable insurance policies. 

The country is extremely vulnerable to climate variability and shocks considering its classification as a Small Island Development State (SIDS). The country is ranked fourth out of 163 countries in the UNICEF 2021 Children’s Climate Risk Index (CCRI), highlighting the elevated climate risk children face. The country has suffered erratic rainfall, prolonged droughts and rising sea levels – 8.79 mm annually over the last 15 years (far exceeding the global rate of 3.1 mm per year) – leading to coastal erosion and floods. The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) underscored rising temperatures, approximately 1.5°C today higher than in the 1950s, leading to sustained exposure to extremely high temperatures.  

Climate change is also set to exacerbate the population’s limited access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). According to the MICS 2019 survey, 68 per cent of the population has access to water, but only 45 per cent of this water is from improved sources. Approximately 39 per cent of schools face poor water access, and 64 per cent have inadequate sanitation facilities, with latrines often in poor condition. 

Immunization coverage has been recovering from the disruption of COVID-19  but remains overall low; for example, DPT3 coverage increased from 67 per cent in 2021 to 80 per cent in September 2024 (a slight decline from 85 per cent in 2023), with an estimated 14,000 zero-dose children, representing 19 per cent of the target population (EPI administrative data 2024). Furthermore, health systems recovery has been slow; although the antenatal care coverage is relatively high, 87 per cent, Guinea-Bissau endures one of the highest maternal mortality rates in Western and Central Africa, estimated at 725 per 100,000 births (WHO 2020). The newborn mortality rate is estimated to be 35 per 1,000 live births, constituting 50 per cent of under-five deaths, the third highest in the West and Central Africa region. 

Malnutrition is one of the main underlying causes of newborn and child mortality. High stunting rates at 30 per cent, are mainly due to poor infant and young child feeding practices, and anemia is a concern among pregnant women, particularly adolescent girls and young women, of whom 27 per cent had a child before 18 years (MICS 2019). 

Guinea-Bissau registers the highest HIV prevalence in West and Central Africa, 2.3 per cent, with 3.8 per cent of adolescents (aged 10-19 years) living with HIV; and stark gender disparities persist (female: 4.38 per cent, male: 2.8 per cent). While HIV-related outcomes have improved for all other age groups, this is not the case for children and adolescents. The transmission rate between mothers and babies is high, 22.44 per cent. The ART coverage among pregnant women remains low at 59.42 per cent (UNAIDS 2024). 

Guinea-Bissau's school enrolment rate remains one of the lowest in the region. UNICEF generated data revealed that the primary school enrolment rate was 61 per cent (children aged 6 to 11) in 2020, which is below the 74 per cent average for the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA) zone in 2019. The secondary school enrolment rate over the same period is 29 per cent, meaning that 29 per cent of children aged 12 to 17 were enrolled in secondary education compared to 38 per cent in in the UEMOA zone. Widespread poverty contributes to school absenteeism or drop-out, particularly when children are forced to work to support their families in cashew forming. Child protection challenges persist. The birth registration rate is low, and violence against children is prevalent and includes child labour, female genital mutilation (FGM), child marriage, corporal punishment and sexual violence. 

Social & Behaviour Change (SBC) remains a critical strategy and plays a game-changing role in accelerating programme results and addressing Guinea-Bissau’s socio-economic, health, education and climate-related challenges by influencing behaviours, shifting social norms and increasing demand for essential services. For example, SBC interventions have contributed to increased immunization uptake by mobilizing youth networks and community leaders to address vaccine hesitancy through interpersonal communication, media campaigns and social mobilization. Similarly, SBC has tackled child marriage and FGM by engaging traditional communicators and religious leaders in intergenerational dialogues, leading to increased community commitments to abandon harmful practices. In education, SBC-driven school enrollment campaigns, including door-to-door sensitization and radio broadcast, have helped reduce dropout rates by addressing negative gender and social norms. Additionally, SBC has promoted WASH improvements by empowering communities to adopt safe hygiene practices through the promotion of the Key Family Practices, ensuring better sanitation in schools and households despite climate-related challenges. SBC continues to play a crucial role in improving nutrition by promoting exclusive breastfeeding, better infant and young child feeding practices, leading to increased awareness and adoption of healthier behaviors among caregivers. SBC is essential for transforming behaviors, shifting social norms, and increasing demand for life-saving services, leading to sustainable development and improved well-being.

However, there is still a long way to go to achieve the SDGs by 2030. A significant challenge in assessing this progress is the lack of up-to-date data, with the last MICs conducted in 2018-2019 and the last population census in 2009. It is estimated that 60 per cent of the population is under 25. Therefore, it is crucial to accelerate progress to address the rights and needs of all children, including the most vulnerable, throughout their life cycle.

UNICEF actions in 2024 advanced progress towards the results outlined in the Country Programme Document (CPD) and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the UNICEF strategic plan. The programmes supported national priorities and progress towards the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and the key regional results for children (KRCs), notably on immunization (KRC1), access to education (KRC3), birth Registration (KRC7) and Open Defecation (KRC8). UNICEF also leveraged its convening role and partnerships to strengthen child rights centred policies and programmes. 
 
Following the outcomes of the National Forum in Primary Health Care (PHC) held in 2023, which culminated with a Call to Action, in 2024 UNICEF continued to lead the revitalization of primary healthcare (PHC) in Guinea-Bissau. One of the strategies for strengthening health systems has been integrating immunization services into broader PHC services. By embedding immunization within routine PHC services, UNICEF is paving the way for a more sustainable and reliable system, not only for immunization, but also for nutrition and other maternal and child health issues, including birth registration. 
 
UNICEF leveraged GAVI investments in health systems strengthening to reinforce routine immunization and allocated funds for incinerators’ repair and maintenance in the central vaccine store, CECOME, and hospitals in Bafatá and Buba. UNICEF provided procurement and logistics support to the Ministry of Health and health sector partners in strengthening supply chain management. In 2024, UNICEF delivered 240 refrigerators/freezers, 287 cold boxes, 1,212 vaccine carriers, and 316 temperature monitoring devices (including 66 RTMD-Remote Temperature Monitoring Devices), with fundings from the Africa CDC, Government of Japan and the World Bank, which had been procured in the previous year. In 2024, for the first time in five years, UNICEF’s advocacy, along with that of other partners, such as the World Bank, yielded  
US$ 508,893.35 in government co-financing for the procurement of vaccines. UNICEF leadership and advocacy, and in a close partnership with GAVI and the Ministry of Health, resulted in the introduction of new vaccines. For example, UNICEF advocated and provided support to an integrated measles and rubella campaign with Vitamin A and deworming, reaching 805,768 children between 9 months and 14 years, 91 per cent of the target. It also distributed Vitamin A to 254,485 of the 325,845 targeted children aged 6-59 months (78 per cent of the target), and deworming pills to 227,237 of the target 286,055 children aged 12-59 months (79.4 per cent of the target), and more than 13,000 children received birth registration during the campaign. UNICEF also distributed Vitamin A to 254,485 of the 325,845 targeted children aged 6-59 months (78 per cent of the target), and deworming pills to 227,237 of the targeted 286,055 children aged 12-59 months (79.4 per cent of the target), and more than 13,000 children received birth registration during the campaign.
 
Community health workers (CHW) play a vital role in health promotion, including mobilizing the communities for child immunization and providing much-needed accessible and cost-effective care, particularly in underserved remote areas. In 2024, UNICEF continued to strengthen the network of community health workers, increasing retention from 500 CHWs in 2021 (out of a targeted 3,075, or 16 per cent of the total) to 2,134 CHWs (or 69 per cent of the targeted number). In 2024, preliminary data shows registered CHWs visited 85 per cent of the targeted households (116,126 out of 136,853).  This represents approximately 812,882 people.
 
A partnership with NGO VIDA, UNDP and European Union successfully established a 24/7 helpline, ‘Linha Saúde 24h’. The helpline gives communities a way to report complaints and concerns related to health services and protection issues, promoting transparency and accountability in health governance. In 2024, the helpline received 4,532 calls, including 103 referrals for gender-based violence (GBV) cases. The helpline facilitated life-saving interventions, with operators supported by the call centre team, providing critical guidance to protect individuals in danger. 

In 2024, malnutrition prevention remained a major UNICEF priority. In partnership with WFP, UNICEF supported the first round of Vitamin A supplementation for children aged 6-59 months and deworming of children aged 12-59 months, resulting in 263,398 children receiving Vitamin A (80.8 per cent of the 325,841 children targeted), and 228,638 dewormed (79.9 per cent of 286,053 target). UNICEF also supported treatment for malnourished children, assisting 52 health facilities treating children suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM). In 2024, of the 1,011 children (440 male and 571 female) admitted with SAM, 1,003 children were successfully treated. 

Evidence shows that preventing malnutrition is often linked to waterborne diseases. To address this, UNICEF promoted an intersectoral water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) strategy in nutrition services.  

With UNICEF support, Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) implementation puts the country on track to reaching Open Defecation Free (ODF) status by 2030. CLTS activities, combined with nutrition screenings, reached 5,600 children (2,744 girls) and 10,200 caregivers, ensuring improved hygiene practices and timely malnutrition interventions. Additionally, awareness campaigns on nutrition and WASH reached 55,750 individuals (33,712 women and girls) including 25,300 children and adolescents (12,397 girls), promoting behaviour change across communities. UNICEF’s efforts also contributed to improvements in water and sanitation infrastructure and services for children, enabling communities to improve their hygiene practices across the regions of Cacheu, Oio, Tombali, Biombo and Bolama/Bijagós. 

Overall, UNICEF-supported CLTS interventions in 150 communities resulted in 49,800 individuals (25,896 female) accessing basic sanitation, out of whom 15,569 (8,096 female) lived in communities declared Open Defecation Free (ODF). Improvements in WASH infrastructure also increased access to education and health services. UNICEF constructed solar-powered water systems in seven schools and built inclusive, gender-transformative latrines in 11 schools, and rehabilitated sanitation facilities in an additional 13 schools. These investments improved WASH conditions for 23,877 students (including 11,700 girls) and removed barriers to accessing education, particularly for girls. School administrative data revealed a 25 per cent increase in consistent attendance among girls in these schools, reflecting the positive impact that gender- and menstrual hygiene-friendly facilities have on increasing access for girls. Moreover, repairs and LIXIL sink installations at the Centro Nutricional de Gabu and Centro de Saúde de Sonaco reduced waterborne disease cases by 30 per cent, according to Ministry of Health records.

UNICEF piloted innovative, climate-resilient WASH solutions, installing 220 climate-adapted latrine pits in flood-prone regions. UNICEF also supported the introduction of innovative tools, like the mWater monitoring system, which covers 12,205 water points, including 163 health facilities. This system enhanced data collection and accountability, enabling prompt responses to service disruptions. 

UNICEF leveraged key strategies around data and evidence, system strengthening, innovation and community engagement to make systematic and transformative progress to foster children’s right to education, including the most vulnerable. 

UNICEF contributed to strengthened data and knowledge management for educational decision-making by providing technical and financial support to the Ministry of Education (MENSIC) to map all schools and educational infrastructure nationwide, providing official and accurate education sector administrative data for the first time since the 2015-2016 school year: 1,937 schools mapped, covering 364,127 children in basic education (178,385 girls) and 32,831 children in secondary school (15,809 girls). The findings constitute an important planning and budget allocation tool for the government, and the basis for education system strengthening. 
In 2024 UNICEF contributed to the Guinea-Bissau’s teacher management system strengthening. The National Teachers’ Policy was technically validated, creating a clear framework and interministerial cooperation to strengthen teacher management. UNICEF supported MENESIC to analyze school mapping data and subsequently led a comprehensive verification mission to validate teaching and support staff in all 11 regions. This resulted in  MENESIC identifying 2,974 ‘non-active’ staff, leading to significant cost savings of approximately US$ 3.5 million. The Ministry used the savings to hire 4,053 contract teachers from January - June 2024, providing access to education for tens of thousands of children who would have otherwise been out of school. 

In 2024, MENESIC successfully developed the National Accelerated Formal Education Programme (PEFA). PEFA provides comprehensive learning pathways for out-of-school and at-risk children and adolescents to catch up and accelerate their learning. In 2024 the programme and its piloting strategy were finalized, including the curricular programme and calendar, the illustration and layout of four illustrated student textbooks and four teachers’ guides for the first phase of the piloting, resulting in 492 children (including 256 girls) enrolled.
UNICEF also supported MENESIC to deploy innovative technologies to improve the quality of the preschool sub-sector. Building on the successful contextualization and piloting of the Brief Early Childhood Quality Inventory (BEQI), in 2024 BEQI was used to pilot the new early childhood education (ECE) curriculum for 5-year-old children in 114 ECE centres, benefitting approximately 4,000 children. The baseline data collection is also being used to strengthen the sub-sector’s quality assurance system (QAS) and ECE educator professional development. 
As part of the ‘Ka Nô Para Aprendi’ Back to Learning Strategy, 42 youth volunteers facilitated 147 Djumbais in 20 schools Gabu, Bafata and Oio. During the Djumbais, 2,802 children (1,487 girls) received essential knowledge around education, hygiene, nutrition and GBV, empowering them with essential knowledge to stay in school. In addition, 873,863 text messages were sent to MTN customers encouraging on-time enrollment for the 2024-2025 school year, and a back-to-school video clip received 67,000 views. Anecdotal evidence from discussions with stakeholders suggests that strategy led to increased on time enrollment for the 2024-2025 school year.
Child rights monitoring was reinforced in 2024. UNICEF advocated for the submission of the country report on the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC). UNICEF also facilitated CSO submissions to the human rights universal periodic review (UPR), resulting in 18 reports.
To improve the coverage and management of child protection services, UNICEF expanded the child protection national information system to the health social service workforce. Seventy-two child protection service providers, including 32 from the health social service, reported and managed 776 child protection incidents (146 related to sexual abuse). Training modules and standard of procedures (SOPs) for the new national case management system, developed with UNICEF support, were validated and UNICEF facilitated the health system strengthening to collect high quality child protection data.

UNICEF’s support significantly improved access to birth registration in 2024, where 69,262 (34,908 male and 34,354 female) children obtained their birth certificate up from 38,881 in 2023. Importantly, 25,948 children were registered in health facilities and 20,620 through decentralized, community-level services and mobilization initiatives, demonstrating the Government’s increased capacity to provide effective and sustainable birth registration services to its citizens. At upstream level, birth registration was mainstreamed, for the first time, in the new immunization action plan (2024-2028), including integration of key strategies such as increasing awareness and community engagement for birth registration. As a result, 12,268 children accessed their birth certificate during the immunization campaign in the last quarter of 2024. Also, the new National Social Protection Policy, approved in 2024, promoted BR as a key priority for vulnerable families.

Leveraging UNFPA/UNICEF female genital mutilation (FGM) joint programme, UNICEF supported the mobilization of 59,199 people to end FGM and child marriage. As a result, 123 communities declared the abandonment of these practices and promoted girls' school enrollment to school. Additionally, 8,296 adolescent girls engaged in discussions on FGM and child marriage through life skills and safe spaces, while 1,788 families accessed parental interventions. UNICEF conducted a situational analysis of Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) in Gabú (96 per cent FGM prevalence), Bafatá (87 per cent) and Quinara (59 per cent), assessing patterns, key drivers and existing interventions. The analysis identified gaps and opportunities for targeted action. Building on these findings, UNICEF collaborated with the Government and local communities to engage traditional leaders and advocate for the prevention of FGM and child marriage.
UNICEF continued to advance the social protection agenda in Guinea-Bissau, leveraging its convening power to increase collaboration and coordination amongst UN agencies and the Government. These efforts contributed to the development and technical validation of the National Social Protection Policy (NSPP) and its implementation strategy. Approved by the Council of Ministers in June 2024, the NSPP provides a legal framework for expanding both non-contributory and contributory social protection, enhancing the state's capacity to protect vulnerable populations. The aim is to reach over 15 per cent of the population (approximately 330,000 people), including children and their families living in extreme poverty, surviving on less than US$ 1 a day.

UNICEF also successfully engaged in high-level advocacy and awareness building, strengthening knowledge and understanding about the importance of social protection systems at national, regional and community levels. For example, UNICEF supported a multisectoral team, including the Ministry of Women, Family and Social Solidarity, to produce a TV documentary highlighting the SDG joint social protection programme's impact on vulnerable families which  reached 1.3 million viewers and was further promoted through radio spots and social media posts. These efforts enhanced awareness and fostered a sense of ownership of social protection programmes among government officials, communities and the public.

UNICEF strengthened the Government’s capacity to improve public finance for children (PF4C). UNICEF’s high-level advocacy and support enabled Guinea-Bissau to participate in the Open Budget Survey (OBS) for the first time in 2024. Conducted by the International Budget Partnership, this survey measures transparency and public access to budget information and public spending in 125 countries. Guinea-Bissau ranked 117 out of 125 participants countries, highlighting key areas of improvements including budget transparency and participation. As a result, Guinea-Bissau through the Ministry of Finance, has set the standard higher to ensure that crucial budget documents are timely and published in 2025, and to ensure public participation to increase budget transparency, participation and effectiveness. 

UNICEF strengthened its support to adolescents and produced its first Adolescent Development and Participation Strategy 2024-2030, which allows the country office to adopt a holistic approach to the planning and implementation of interventions for adolescents and youth, aligned with different programme priorities, namely: WASH/Health and Nutrition; Access to learning; Child Protection; Social Inclusion; Social and Behaviour Change and External Communication/Partnerships. Progress was made in strengthening adolescent and youth engagement around climate change. For example, in 2024, in close collaboration with the Ministry of Climate Change and Biodiversity, UNICEF supported the National Youth Workshop on Climate Change and led the creation of the National Youth Climate Action Network, comprising 90 members (45 girls and 45 boys) who developed climate actions to be implemented in their respective communities.

Following UNICEF’s advocacy, the Government signed the Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Change; UNICEF also participated in the first National Dialogue on Climate and accompanied the youth ambassador to COP29. These efforts underscored the impact of climate change on children, youth and families in Guinea-Bissau, strengthening the child-responsiveness of the country's climate actions.

Media engagement was a cornerstone of UNICEF's communication and visibility strategy. UNICEF supported the production and dissemination of 75 child-focused media pieces, including TV, radio and newspaper articles. These efforts empowered children and adolescents to voice their concerns and participate actively in media, fostering a culture of advocacy and awareness at the grassroots level. The programme also leveraged digital platforms to enhance its reach and impact. Social media followers increased from 30,940 in 2023 to 38,198 in 2024  across Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and YouTube. This digital presence enabled UNICEF to engage with a broader audience and disseminate critical information on children's rights and wellbeing.
Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) played an essential role in all UNICEF-supported programmes, particularly in systems strengthening. The focus was on developing key indicators, improving coordination, generating evidence to enhance service delivery and building public confidence and increasing demand for crucial services like routine vaccinations, community health, education and child protection. For example, UNICEF supported social communication during the measles and rubella vaccination campaign, training 3,531 community health workers to identify eligible children. Communication channels reached over 1.1 million people, contributing to the vaccination update. Similarly, a partnership with the Global Fund/UNDP raised awareness about malaria prevention that included the seasonal malaria chemoprevention campaign which protected 228,700 children aged 3 months to 10 years (89.3 per cent of the target) in the region of Bafatá, Gabú, Tombali and Bolama. 

The government's capacity in child protection and social behavior change (SBC) practices was enhanced by pre-testing the Child Protection-SBC playbook on Community Engagement against Female Genital Mutilation (FGM). A total of 26 coordinators and field staff (including 9 women) from the National Committee for the Abandonment of Harmful Practices received specialized training on the playbook. This training equipped them to effectively engage with local communities and implement evidence-based SBC interventions during the field-pre-testing phase.
SBC action plans developed during  workshop with 45 traditional communicators (two women) of the regions of Gabú, Bafatá, Quinara, and Oio are driving mindset shifts, fostering empathy, and strengthening community-led efforts to eliminate female genital mutilation (FGM) and child marriage. These plans leverage the influence of the traditional communicators in these regions to engage key decision-makers, such as traditional leaders, and mobilize communities against this harmful practice. 

UNICEF partnered with 38 community radio stations, disseminating key messages on health, education and gender equality. An evaluation of these partnerships stressed their critical role in reaching marginalized populations.  A total  of 466 respondents (249 women and 217 men; 85.5 per cent of respondents) participated in the evaluation. The findings showed that radio remains a trusted medium although message assimilation varies due to cultural factors and education levels.

UNICEF empowered youth by increasing their capacity to advocate for issues affecting their well-being. UNICEF trained six youth (three girls) of the Youth Network for the Acceleration of Key Results for Children (KRC) in applied journalism, enabling them to host youth-led radio programmes.
