The 45-minute programmes are broadcast twice a month, creating space for youth-led conversations on child rights and increasing their engagement and participation.

To advance children’s rights and wellbeing and to implement the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF), particularly Outcome 3: Human Development which UNICEF leads, UNICEF focused on strengthening and expanding key partnerships in 2024.
For health thematic areas, such as the cold chain, social and behaviour change, child health, nutrition and community health, UNICEF worked closely with the Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP). UNICEF contributed significantly to the Health Partners Group, co-chaired by the EU Delegation and WHO. 

To improve WASH services, the Directorate General for Human Resources (DGRH) has been one of the core partners instrumental in advocacy efforts and in the construction of boreholes and the Ministry of Education has been a crucial partner, particularly in supervising the construction of latrines in schools. Five national NGO partners played a central role in implementing the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) programme. A key strategic partner this year has been the Spanish National Committee, whose funding and engagement has been instrumental in scaling up water, sanitation and hygiene initiatives across the country. UNICEF has also focused on reinforcing climate activities through targeted collaboration with environmental and climate-focused partners. 
 
UNICEF strengthened partnerships and engagement with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) to align education sector priorities among partners. As the Coordinating Agency for the GPE in Guinea-Bissau and the ‘chef de file’(leader) for the education sector, UNICEF led the successful development and approval of the Partnership Compact between the Government of Guinea-Bissau and the GPE. The Partnership Compact, a strategic document that aligns education sector priorities among partners to achieve the priority reform of ensuring all children complete basic education, is an important result that positions the education sector in Guinea-Bissau to receive GPE funds for 2025-2028.

These efforts build on another new partnership between UNICEF and the Agence Française de Développement for the rehabilitation of school and sports infrastructure in Bissau, which will improve children and adolescents' access to recreational and sports activities spaces and updating the physical education curriculum.  

UNICEF continued partnering with Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation (FCG in Portuguese) and UMinho University to experiment the new curriculum for 5-year-old children; UMinho provided technical support for capacity building, including a mission to train 24 lead-trainers, creating capacity in MENESIC via a cadre of experts to roll-out the new ECE curriculum. FCG and UMinho also contributed significantly to the development of teaching and learning materials to pilot the National Accelerated Formal Education Programme (PEFA), aligned with the basic education curriculum reform (RECEB).

To promote child and women’s rights and prevent and respond to violence, abuse, exploitation and neglect, UNICEF worked with diverse partners, including Interpol, and children’s and young people’s organizations. To enhance the referral, assistance and care of child victims of violent abuse, exploitation and neglect, the social service workforce from the Health and Justice sector as well as the National Association of Social Workers (AGAS), collaborated with UNICEF during 2024. Also, under the joint PBF Health Governance project, UNICEF collaborated with WHO and Interpeace, to strengthen the referral and case management of violence against children, including gender-based violence (GBV), continuing working with the health social service workforce and community health workers, through new partnerships with international NGOs, AIFO and VIDA.

To advance the legal identity agenda, enhance advocacy and ensure stronger national coordination and engagement, UNICEF continued working with UN agencies and bilateral and multilateral partners in 2024. These partners included UNDP, the World Bank and the Portuguese Cooperation/EU Project on Civil Registration (Gestdoc), aiming to accelerate the digitalization of the CR system and improve vital statistics. UNICEF collaborated with the ID4Africa initiative and supported Guinea-Bissau's participation. UNICEF worked with the World Bank on an assessment of identity systems and potential areas of collaboration with the Government to accelerate legal identity and digital identity solutions. Notably, UNICEF and UNFPA collaborated on the FGM joint programme, reinforcing partnerships to eliminate FGM and child marriage through advocacy and joint programming with key international partners.
 
In social protection, the successful implementation of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) joint project involved collaboration among multiple stakeholders, including the Ministry of Women, Family and Social Solidarity, and the Ministry of Public Administration, Employment, Vocational Training and Social Security and the United Nations Country Team (UNCT). This joint effort led to the establishment of the legal framework to build an effective and resilient shock-responsive social protection system in Guinea-Bissau. A UNCT social protection working group comprised of UNICEF, UNDP, WFP, UNFPA, FAO, RCO and ILO was established, improving  coordination, effectiveness and  information sharing and collaboration among partners. These coordination and partnership efforts helped the UNCT Team and government partners to mobilize potential new funding, including a joint proposal with the African Development Bank Transition Support Facility to finance key priorities in the National Social Protection Policy (NSPP) implementation action plan.

Regular Resources (RR) have been instrumental in strengthening Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) efforts by providing UNICEF with the agility to implement cross-cutting interventions. In 2024, RR enabled SBC to establish strategic partnerships that enhanced service delivery such as with community radios, youth associations and community leaders and reinforced national SBC systems and capacities. RR and global education thematic funds also provided essential flexible funding for the development of the National Teacher Policy and the strengthening of teacher oversight in MENESIC, contributing to the identification and removal of approximately 3,000 ‘non-active’ staff and leading to large cost savings to be reinvested into the sector.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2024 presented significant challenges that impeded the fulfillment of child rights in Guinea-Bissau, including political instability and turnover, limited and outdated social sector data and systems, the worsening of climate change effects and continued low investment in Guinea-Bissau social services. These factors made it more challenging to scale up results, particularly for the most marginalized children.

Political and institutional instabilities, the dissolution of the National Assembly and turnover in senior leadership at times delayed programme implementation, making it difficult to improve outcomes for children with lifesaving services. 

A key lesson learned for UNICEF Guinea-Bissau in 2024 is the need to continue to strengthen the capacity of government partners, including at regional and community levels, particularly in programme management and technical skills development to guarantee uninterrupted access to child-friendly services in the health, education and child protection sectors. Continued capacity building in administrative processes and financial management is needed to ensure financial resources are appropriately managed. UNICEF must also more comprehensively engage with communities and civil society to strengthen community-based programming to provide strengthened social accountability and to complement government interventions. 

A continued limited availability of up-to-date official statistics and quality administrative data hampers social sector planning, the equitable allocation of resources and implementation in Guinea-Bissau. The most recent General Population and Housing Census (RGPH) data was in 2009, and the last Multiple Indicator Sampling Survey (MICS) in 2019. The Education Management Information System (EMIS) is not currently functional, with the last official education statistics published for the 2015-2016 school year. In addition, the Health Management Information System’s (HMIS) platform, DHIS2, often lacks up-to-date data. 

To address this challenge, a key lesson learned is that UNICEF should prioritize working effectively with development partners to coordinate financial and technical support for strengthening national data systems. For example, in preparations of the fourth RGPH to be undertaken in 2025, UNICEF coordinated with UNDP and other partners to target its financial and technical support on strengthening the capacity of INE in cartography and geospatial surveying. 

Moving forward in 2025, UNICEF will continue to innovate to better use data to inform programming and social sector planning. UNICEF will continue to strengthen government capacity to use the mWater database and monitoring system, and to strengthen the use of data to inform decision making. In 2025, classroom observation data using the BEQI tool will be used to reinforce the ECE sub-sector’s quality assurance system (QAS) and ECE educator professional development system.

Another significant challenge is that the worsening effects of climate change increasingly threaten the lives of children and vulnerable populations in Guinea-Bissau. Compounding this challenge, Guinea-Bissau lacks capacity to effectively adapt infrastructure and services to mitigate the negative effects of climate change on children. 

A key lesson learned is that UNICEF Guinea-Bissau should more proactively integrate climate change and resilience into its child rights programming. The Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in Guinea-Bissau (CLAC), conducted with the Ministry of Environment and Biodiversity, reviews the climate and environment hazards on children in the country and proposes key social sector recommendations. In 2024, UNICEF Guinea-Bissau displayed increased leadership in the children’s climate agenda, participating actively in COP-29 in Baku to raise awareness with the Guinea-Bissau delegation regarding the impact of climate change on children and to increase the focus on children in the development of the new set of National Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0). UNICEF also learned the importance of mobilizing civil society support to combat climate change, particularly with and for adolescents and youth. A climate youth network was established to engage young people regarding climate change; this network will be strengthened and expanded in 2025 and beyond. UNICEF will also continue to pilot innovative climate solutions, such as climate-adapted latrine pits in flood-prone regions. Preliminary evidence suggests that this technology significantly reduced infrastructure failures, ensuring continuous access to safe sanitation and improving hygiene in vulnerable communities. Appropriate climate technologies will be further piloted and scaled in 2025.

A final challenge relates to the continued underinvestment in social services for children, particularly vulnerable children, such as girls, children with disabilities and children in rural areas. Government investments for social services is severely underfunded; only 21 per cent per cent of the General State Budget (OGE) was allocated to social sectors in 2024, well below global benchmarks. Compounding this challenge, due to competing crises and global geopolitical tensions, political instability in Guinea-Bissau, it remains difficult to mobilize external financing for Guinea-Bissau. Therefore, a key priority in 2025 will be to advocate for increased investment in the social sectors. In education, a high-level forum on the education sector in Guinea-Bissau will be held in 2025, which will be an opportunity to call for the ring-fencing of funds for the education sector.

Despite the challenges faced in 2024, major results achieved were fully aligned with the UNSDCF outputs and 2024 workplan contributing to the SDGs targets, especially SDG 16.9 (legal identity and birth registration), 5.3 (FGM and child marriage). Also Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) implementation puts the country on track to reaching Open Defecation Free (ODF) status by 2030.

Moving forward in 2025, UNICEF will also focus on strengthening adolescent and youth engagement and participation. The UNICEF Guinea-Bissau Adolescent and Youth Strategy developed in 2024, provides clear programmatic guidance to better engage with adolescents and young people. UNICEF will prioritize working with and for adolescents and youth, with a focus on adolescent girls, to strengthen access to adolescent-friendly services. In addition, UNICEF will strengthen its engagement with adolescents and youth to accelerate key results for children. An adolescent girls campaign will be organized in 2025. The launch of the U-Report youth engagement platform, planned for 2025, will contribute significantly to youth engagement.

UNICEF Liberia remains steadfast in advancing child rights in alignment with the UNICEF 2022-2025 Strategic Plan and the national priorities reflected in the development agenda. While political stability provided an opportunity to scale up the efforts towards the realization of children’s rights, persistent socio-economic challenges, including financial constraints and high-risk operating conditions, significantly hindered progress. 
The 2024 Situational Analysis of children and adolescents in Liberia (SitAn), jointly conducted by UNICEF and the Government of Liberia, supported by data from the 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census, the 2019/2020 Liberia Demographic and Health Survey, and reports from the World Bank, IMF, WHO, and Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency, underscores persistent challenges. Nearly half of Liberia’s population is under 18, with 72 percent of rural residents facing multidimensional poverty due to limited access to health, education, and essential services (SDG 1). Maternal mortality remains alarmingly high at 854 per 100,000 live births, while under-five mortality stands at 92.6 per 1,000 live births[1]. Chronic malnutrition affects 35.5 percent of children under five, and stunting persists at 29.9 percent[2] (SDG 2).
In Liberia, as per the 2016 Household Income and Expenditure Survey, 50.9% of the population live below the national poverty line, with about 2.3 million people unable to meet their basic needs[3]. 
Significant headline progress has been made in multidimensional poverty which has declined from 81.4% in 2007 (63.5% in 2013) to 52% in 2019-20 (SDG 1.2), including 24.9% in severe multidimensional poverty and 23.3% “vulnerable” to slipping back into poverty. A problematic dimension is the prevalence of under-nourishment which remains as high as 38.4 % (2020-2022)[4]. This is 5% points up from the result in the 2004-2006 period and twice as high as the average prevalence in Africa.
Education access has improved, with Net Enrolment Rates rising from 46.3 percent in 2021/22 to 51 percent in 2024. To strengthen efforts further, the President of Liberia launched a campaign to get children into school, “Back to My Classroom”, which will strive to improve further the Net Enrolment Rate in the country.  However, systemic issues remain 38 percent of primary and 64 percent of junior secondary students are over-age, and girls face entrenched barriers such as child marriage 6 percent of girls married by age 15 and 25 percent of girls by age 18) and early pregnancy (SDGs 4 and 5). Violence against children is pervasive, with 71 percent experiencing physical punishment, 80 percent bearing psychological aggression, and 28 percent of children aged 5–17 engaged in child labour. Climate change exacerbates these challenges, as Liberia—ranked among the most climate-vulnerable nations—faces increased flooding, food insecurity, and displacement, disproportionately harming children (SDG 13).
In January 2024 the new government was sworn in, ushering in governance reforms, prioritizing decentralization, anti-corruption measures, and social service investments. However, fiscal constraints, global inflation, and volatile commodity prices curtailed public spending on child-focused programs. In 2023, the sector budget out of total budget was 12.03 percent for education, 9.49% for health and 2.05% for the Ministry of Gender, Children. It was encouraging to see significant percentage increases across these social sectors in the 2024 budget: an increase to 14.83 percent for education, 10.84 percent for health and 3.80 % for the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection. But the budget allocation is still below the WHO recommended for health and the African Union recommendation for education and the total allocation in figures remain very low given the overall budget available and the high level of needs for children in the country.  These financial limitations strained healthcare, education, and protection services, underscoring the urgency of adaptive strategies to safeguard children’s well-being.
Amid operational challenges, UNICEF Liberia achieved measurable progress through strategic partnerships and innovation. Immunization campaigns reached 95 percent of target populations for measles (781,124 children between 9- 59 months) and Polio (934,689) children between 0-59 months – 109% percent of the target) vaccinations, improving child survival rates, while digital birth registration systems enhanced access to legal identity and essential services.  Child protection systems were strengthened through the CPIMS+ case management platform, and community engagement advanced efforts to eliminate harmful practices such as FGM and child marriage. WASH services expanded significantly, providing clean water and sanitation to 77,254 people and 28,579 in flood affected community, with 24 healthcare facilities across three counties benefiting from the WASH Improvement Tool.
Guided by the 2030 Agenda and the principle of “leaving no child behind,” UNICEF Liberia continued to prioritize equity-driven interventions. Decentralized governance initiatives deepened to ensure services to hard-to-reach communities, while digital tools for real-time data monitoring bolstered evidence-based decision-making. Health equity efforts focused on providing integrated community-based services and combating vaccine hesitancy through community-led awareness campaigns (SDG 3), and gender-responsive programming helped dismantle barriers to education, healthcare, and safety for girls (SDG 5).
By aligning governance reforms, community-driven approaches, and targeted SDG investments, UNICEF Liberia is forging pathways to sustainable impact. Through need-based innovation, inclusive programming, and strategic partnerships, the office remains committed to overcoming systemic challenges and ensuring a brighter, more equitable future for every child in Liberia.

In 2024, UNICEF Liberia continued to play a pivotal role in advancing the well-being of children and families across the country, aligning with both national development priorities and global frameworks such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The organization’s work spanned multiple sectors, including health, nutrition, education, child protection, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), and governance, each contributing to the realization of children’s rights. Despite facing persistent financial constraints, governance challenges, and systemic bottlenecks, UNICEF made notable progress in strengthening institutional capacity, expanding access to services, and improving policy environments.
Goal Area 1: Every child survives and thrives: 
KRC 1: Immunization and KRC 2: Prevention of Stunting
One of the most notable achievements in the health sector was UNICEF’s success in supporting the government to develop the 10-year Reproductive, Maternal Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Nutrition (RMNCAHN) Policy and 5-year Child Survival Strategy and Action Plan. UNICEF contributed to reaching 85 percent of the target population with the third dose of Pentavalent vaccine, benefiting 190,360 children under 1 year across all 15 counties. These efforts contributed to a reduction in vaccine-preventable diseases and strengthened routine immunization systems. 
To advance adolescent health, UNICEF supported the integration of HPV vaccinations with nutrition services, benefitting 31,000 adolescent girls through vaccination and essential micronutrient supplementation. However, significant challenges remain in achieving national nutrition targets, with minimum dietary diversity stagnating at 9 percent (against a target of 19 percent), exclusive breastfeeding at 55.2 percent (short of the 65 percent target), and anemia among women of childbearing age persisting at 45 percent. These indicators highlight the need for continued investment and policy refinement to ensure nutrition interventions reach the most vulnerable populations effectively. Encouragingly, the Government of Liberia’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development prioritizes stunting reduction as a national goal, providing a strong policy foundation for continued progress.
In the nutrition sector, a multisectoral approach to nutrition was strengthened with the rollout of the Liberia Multisectoral Nutrition Costed Strategic Plan, providing a framework for collaboration and coordination across government ministries, civil society organizations, and academic institutions. This initiative aims to reduce stunting from 30 percent to 18 percent by 2029 and enhance the alignment of national efforts to combat malnutrition. To further strengthen Liberia’s engagement in global nutrition initiatives, a delegation of government staff, partners, and donors, led by the Vice-President whose office leads on multi-sectoral prevention and response efforts for nutrition, visited Sierra Leone to exchange knowledge on the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement and explore strategies for addressing persistent nutrition challenges. A roadmap was subsequently developed to ensure the implementation of key recommendations from the learning exchange. A major step forward was the co-development of the five-year National Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) Strategy for Nutrition in partnership with the Ministry of Health. This strategy aims to address systemic barriers to optimal child nutrition and adolescent health through evidence-based social and behavior change interventions. The rollout of the Liberia Multisectoral Nutrition Costed Strategic Plan further cemented a multisectoral approach to tackling malnutrition, setting a national target to reduce stunting from 30 percent to 18 percent by 2029.
To enhance the quality and efficiency of nutrition services, UNICEF supported the development of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) Manual to improve the management of nutrition supplies and service delivery. This manual streamlines processes within health facilities, ensuring greater accountability, efficiency, and consistency in service provision nationwide. By strengthening supply chain management and standardizing operational procedures, this initiative plays a vital role in reducing service delivery bottlenecks and improving access to essential nutrition interventions for children and vulnerable populations. This initiative will help in effectively responding to the frequent stock outs and unbalanced procurement of the RUTF and other essential items.
UNICEF’s SBC strategy stipulates cross-sectoral initiatives focused on integrating health, nutrition, education, and protection services to enhance efficiency and outcomes. These initiatives included the development of a five-year National Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) Strategy for Nutrition, which addressed barriers to optimal practices and promoted positive health behaviours. The strategy was co-created with the Ministry of Health and involved extensive community engagement and social mobilization.
Goal Area 4: Every Child lives in a safe and clean environment.
UNICEF strengthened access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in Liberia through a combination of development, emergency, and climate-resilient programming. During the reporting period, UNICEF supported the rehabilitation of WASH infrastructure in 16 schools and 17 health care facilities (HCFs), benefiting 8,844 children and community members. These improvements contributed to reducing waterborne diseases, improving school attendance, and enhancing overall public health outcomes. Additionally, UNICEF provided life-saving WASH supplies to flood-affected communities as part of an integrated emergency response strategy.
Following severe flooding in Margibi, Montserrado, and Grand Bassa counties, UNICEF delivered essential WASH supplies to 5,039 households, benefiting 28,579 people, including 41 percent children. The distribution of jerry cans, soap, and water guards helped prevent disease outbreaks and ensured access to clean drinking water in affected communities. This intervention was embedded within the Liberia Flood Emergency Response Plan, for which UNICEF provided technical assistance to strengthen coordination between WASH stakeholders, government agencies, and humanitarian actors. Regular coordination meetings facilitated joint response planning, identifying gaps, and ensuring efficient resource allocation.
To enhance long-term sustainability, UNICEF prioritized climate-resilient WASH programming, conducting a Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) to assess the impact of climate change and environmental degradation on children’s access to WASH services. The finding will directly inform Liberia’s 2025 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC), ensuring stronger integration of WASH in climate polices and national adaptations strategies.
In health care facilities (HCFs) UNICEF implemented targeted interventions to ensure WASH sustainability and improve infection prevention and control (IPC). A total of 24 HCFs were supported with the Water Sanitation and Hygiene for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH-FIT), which provides a structured approach to enhancing water and satiations services. As part of this initiative, 120 people, including 51 women, were trained and are supporting the costed action plan development for the respective HCFs. The lessons learned will inform the national scale-up of WASH-FIT, ensuring improved hygiene conditions and safer environments for patients and healthcare providers.
Many planned activities related to policy engagement in Liberia's WASH sector did not progress as expected. This includes the WASH Sector Strategic Plan, Country-Led Monitoring, Post-ODF monitoring, and the endorsement of the "Liberia Ending Open Defecation by 2025 Road Map" and WASH Compact. This shows that WASH was not only suffering because of the lack of funds but also due to WASH services being fragmented across a number of Government Ministries and agencies – something the proposed WASH Compact aims to address.
Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns
KRC 3: Equitable and Sustainable Access to Education and 
In 2024, UNICEF played a pivotal role in advancing education access, quality, and governance in Liberia, aligning efforts with national priorities and global education targets under SDG 4 (Quality Education). A flagship achievement was the “Back to My Classroom” campaign, spearheaded by the President of Liberia, which sought to enroll 37,000 out-of-school children by 2025. Through a community-centered approach that combined door-to-door mobilization, local committee involvement, and social engagement strategies, the initiative successfully increased the Net Enrolment Rate (NER) ensuring more children had access to quality education, (to be further substantiated with data).
Governance and data-driven education reforms were a central focus. To ensure long-term education system strengthening, UNICEF supported the operationalization of the Education Sector Plan (ESP), leading to the institutionalization of Technical Working Groups (TWGs) on Data and Foundational Learning. These groups played a critical role in enhancing data-driven decision-making, improving school record-keeping, and strengthening national education policies. A major achievement was the integration of UNICEF’s advocacy within the World Bank’s GPE EXCEL program, which aligned Liberia’s education investments with global best practices. This collaboration also reinforced school-based data collection, improved School Record Keeping (SRK), and streamlined Standardized Assessments (ASC). 
KRC4: Improved Learning Outcomes 
Despite these advancements, critical challenges persist in learning outcomes, teacher quality, and resource constraints. A 2023 pilot study revealed no significant improvement in foundational literacy and numeracy, highlighting the need for more targeted interventions. While over 3,000 teachers received Continuing Professional Development (CPD) training, classroom performance indicators remained below expectations. Limited school grants further restricted efforts to enhance learning environments, support adolescent girls at risk of dropping out, and address teacher shortages.
To strengthen evidence-based policymaking, UNICEF partnered with the Community of Practice on Equity (COP+E) to conduct classroom assessments and establish literacy and numeracy baselines. Technical assistance at three Teacher Training Institutions (TTIs) enhanced the effectiveness of teacher trainers, while 61 master trainers were equipped with advanced pedagogical skills to improve foundational learning and inclusive education.
A significant milestone was achieved as the program advanced towards an evidence-based policy framework to support advocacy efforts in teacher quality, recruitment, and distribution. UNICEF played a central role in strengthening service delivery by implementing national quality standards, reaching 85,000 children in 200 schools. Although outcome indicators showed limited overall improvement, a modest increase in enrolments was observed among model schools following the orientation of 600 headteachers, PTAs, and academic registrars on school quality standards.
To further enhance policy development, UNICEF supported system strengthening and evidence generation through EMIS and school-based data convergence for ASC. Key studies, including the Teacher Allocation study and the Community of Practice on Equity (COP+E) operationalization, informed strategic decision-making to improve teacher distribution and learning outcomes.
A major priority remained removing barriers for Out-of-School Children (OOSC), with a particular focus on adolescent girls. UNICEF provided financial and technical support to the Back to My Classroom Campaign (BTMCC), a three-year initiative targeting 250,000 OOSC by 2026, with 25,000 set for reintegration by mid-2025. The campaign, launched as a national priority, aimed to reintegrate 37,000 children by 2025, is designed to ensure  sustained enrollment and support children to remain in school and complete their education.
To promote equity and inclusion, UNICEF rolled out the National School Quality Standards (NSQS) in 200 model schools, incorporating safe spaces and care packages for children with disabilities. A dedicated COP+E group was established to test interventions and generate evidence on equity and inclusion, with a focus on overcoming barriers to adolescent girls’ participation. However, resource constraints hindered the provision of school grants and limited the expansion of implementation partnerships beyond the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the Ministry of Youth and Sports (MOYS).
 
Goal Area 3: Every child is protected from violence and exploitation. 
Aligned with SDG 16, UNICEF strengthened Liberia’s child protection system, ensuring that all children have a legal identity and access to essential services. A major milestone was the digitization and decentralization of birth registration, which significantly expanded access, streamlined processes, and improved service efficiency. By leveraging real-time digital reporting, tablets, and an integrated online system, birth certificates are now issued faster, more accurately, and are accessible even in remote areas. This intervention not only strengthens Liberia’s national identity system but also protects children from the risks of statelessness and exploitation. With 58 birth registration centers now fully digitized, UNICEF provided financial and logistical support to enhance interoperability between the Birth Registration Information Management System (BRIMS) and the District Health Information System (DHIS2), enabling real-time monitoring of birth registrations and ensuring universal coverage.
To further strengthen the child protection system, a comprehensive social service workforce development plan was implemented to address the critical shortage of trained social service workers. Additionally, UNICEF supported the development and implementation of a national child protection policy framework, including a social services workforce strengthening strategy and integrated curriculum materials for child protection case management. The plan included the recruitment and training of social workers, as well as the development of guidelines and standards for social work practice. 
UNICEF further contributed to policy advancements by supporting the development and implementation of the National Commitments to End Violence Against Children by 2030, a comprehensive framework aimed at strengthening laws, scaling up services, and investing in the social service workforce. A key component of this initiative was the nationwide rollout of social behaviour and norms change campaigns, engaging 22,000 children and adults through community dialogues and advocacy efforts. These interventions challenged harmful traditional practices, addressed gender inequality, and promoted safer family and school environments.
To ensure vulnerable children receive timely and effective protection services, UNICEF supported the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Protection (MOGCSP) in the launch and rollout of the CPIMS+—a transformative tool that strengthens case management and improves service coordination for vulnerable children. The system is operational in Montserrado County and has facilitated the management of 204 cases, demonstrating its immediate value in addressing the needs of vulnerable children. UNICEF also provided critical support for the training of social workers and the procurement of necessary equipment to ensure the effective use of the system.
 
UNICEF positioned 2024 as a pivotal year for evidence generation and policy influence, ensuring that child-focused interventions are backed by robust data and strategic decision -making. This contributed towards the KRC 9 of the WCARO; Evidence Generation and Knowledge Management. Through key initiatives such as the Country Programme Evaluation (CPE), the Situation Analysis of children and adolescents in Liberia (SitAn 2024), the Gender Programmatic Report, the Situation Analysis of Adolescent girls in Liberia, and Climate Landscape Analysis for Children in Liberia (CLAC), UNICEF generated critical insights to shape future programming. The Community Led Total Sanitation strategy for the water, sanitation, and hygiene sector in Liberia, the UNICEF Country Programme Evaluation 2020–2024 for Liberia and the multi country evaluation on Child friendly Communities further provided evidence on WASH, health and child protection interventions, influencing national and multi- country strategies for improved services delivered. 
UNICEF further strengthened its governance and decentralized service planning efforts by actively contributing to the National Development Plan and the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID). As a key member of the Technical Committee and the National Steering Committee, UNICEF provided both financial and technical assistance to ensure that Liberia’s development priorities align with children’s rights and well-being. The subsequent endorsement of the 15 County Development Agendas (CDAs) marked a significant step in shaping decentralized service delivery, prioritizing child-focused investments at the local level.
UNICEF collaborated and contributed to the Global U-Report pool on topics such as monkeypox and World Children's Day. This year a U-Report poll was launched nationwide to gather young people's views on key climate change and environmental degradation issues. The findings were included in the final Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) report. During the polio campaign, the CO leveraged the Open Data Kit (ODK) digital monitoring tools to identify and vaccinate missed children in real-time, significantly reducing the number of unvaccinated children.
To ensure accountability and program effectiveness, UNICEF reinforced its monitoring and evaluation systems, achieving 100 percent of its planned program monitoring visits (PMVs) across all 15 counties and successfully implementing the Field Monitoring Mechanism (FMM). These efforts enhanced real-time oversight, identified programmatic gaps, and strengthened multi-stakeholder coordination. 
The Liberia country office, in collaboration with the Liberia Institute of Statistics and Geo-Information Services (LISGIS), we developed a concept note for the Multi-Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) to be conducted in 2025. Under the data governance for children initiative, UNICEF engaged an external firm to provide ethical clearance for the consultancies involved in two evaluations. For all data collection initiatives involving children, the data collection tools were carefully reviewed to ensure ethics and data protection.

UNICEF’s partnerships with government ministries, civil society organizations (CSOs), academic institutions, UN organizations, private sector entities, international financial institutions (IFIs), and community-based organizations were instrumental in achieving program goals and enhancing the impact of initiatives.  Through these collaborative efforts, UNICEF was able to leverage the strengths and expertise of various stakeholders, ensuring that programs were effective, sustainable, and aligned with national and global priorities.
Close collaboration with the Ministry of Health, Ministry of Education, and Ministry of Internal Affairs allowed UNICEF to reinforce national system in health, education, and protection initiatives. This engagement facilitated the roll out of national immunization campaigns, co-development of the National Social and Behaviour Change (SBC) Strategy for Nutrition, and the implementation of quality education reforms. Additionally, UNICEF’s ongoing Memorandum of Understanding with the Ministry of Internal Affairs supported decentralized governance by strengthening the capacity of traditional leaders to protect children’s rights and eliminate harmful practices, such as female genital mutilation (FGM).
To address the gaps in data, UNICEF closely collaborated with the Ministry of Gender, Children, and Social Protection (MOGCSP) in launching the CPIMS+, to enhance the case management of vulnerable children. UNICEf also collaborated with the MOGCSP to develop the social service workforce development plan to be implemented in 2025.
UNICEF worked closely with CSOs to bridge the gap between national programs and local communities, ensuring the inclusion of marginalized populations. Grassroots mobilization and advocacy efforts played a pivotal role in expanding service access. For example, the “Back to My Classroom” campaign successfully re-enrolled a significant number of out-of-school children, directly advancing Liberia’s education equity goals. Additionally, CSO engagement strengthened child protection mechanisms, improving support systems for children affected by violence, abuse, and neglect.
Academic institutions contributed to evidence generation and capacity building. UNICEF partnered with universities and research organizations to conduct studies, develop training programs, and generate data to inform policy and program decisions. For example, the CoP+E and Teacher Allocation study being conducted by Innocenti are ready sources of evidence generation for policy reviews. These partnerships enhanced the knowledge base and ensured that programs were grounded in evidence and best practices.
To improve operational efficiency and service delivery, UNICEF played a leading role in strengthening inter-agency collaboration, particularly through the UN Hub in Zwedru, which served as a coordination platform for multi-sectoral interventions in southeastern Liberia. This hub streamlined resource-sharing and cross-sectoral programming among UN agencies, ensuring that interventions in health, education, and child protection were more cohesive and impactful. Key partnerships with WHO, UNFPA, and UNDP led to critical health and protection outcomes, such as the synchronized polio vaccination campaign, which reached children across multiple West and Central African countries, ensuring widespread immunization coverage.
Strategic financial partnerships played a crucial role in expanding UNICEF’s reach and sustaining program impact. Funding from Sweden (SIDA), Ireland (Irish Aid), USAID for WASH, Japan, the National Committee for Germany, GAVI, and the Peacebuilding Fund enabled UNICEF to implement child protection, health, and education initiatives at scale. The renewal of the Child Protection Thematic Fund with SIDA provided essential resources for safeguarding children from violence and exploitation, while ongoing discussions with the EU and China present opportunities for future funding. In addition, a five-year joint program with UNFPA, submitted to the Embassy of Ireland, seeks to improve outcomes for adolescent girls—one of Liberia’s most vulnerable and overlooked populations. Collaboration with WFP also resulted in the renewal of resilience-building and social protection programs, ensuring a long-term impact beyond the current program cycle.
UNICEF continues its close collaboration with UNFPA, WHO, and UNDP on a program for at-risk youth, funded by the UN Peacebuilding Fund (PBF). The synchronized polio vaccination campaign across six West and Central African countries, led by Health and SBC sections and coordinated with WHO, was successful, with Rotary International as the primary regional donor.
This year, UNICEF Liberia strengthened private sector engagement, reconnecting with National Committees (USA, Spain, France, UK, Belgium, Switzerland, Finland, and others) and exploring partnerships with non-traditional donors like Qatar and Gulf Countries. A mapping of international and local companies was completed to identify collaboration opportunities.
UNICEF developed a public-private partnership to boost medical oxygen production and distribution, ensuring sustainable healthcare services and improving patient outcomes. Partnerships with technology firms digitized birth registration, enhancing efficiency and increasing birth registrations, thereby strengthening national identity systems.
Regarding resource mobilization, the program expanded partnerships with entities like the EU, USAID, Save the Children, and the Swedish Embassy, while fostering new relationships with partners such as the Liberia Foundational Skills Activity (LFSA). This deepened UNICEF's strategic engagement across multiple counties, adopting a systems approach to support the Ministry of Education (MOE) through coordinated efforts from all sector partners
UNICEF’s engagement with international financial institutions (IFIs) such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) played a crucial role in mobilizing resources and supporting development initiatives. These partnerships facilitated access to funding for large-scale programs and enabled UNICEF to leverage financial expertise to enhance program implementation.
Collaboration with the World Bank and IMF involved joint efforts to address key development challenges in Liberia. World Bank’s support for the education sector included funding for the implementation of the Education Sector Plan (ESP) and the development of national quality standards. These partnerships ensured that programs were adequately funded and aligned with broader development goals.
As part of UNICEF’s commitment to decentralized governance, the organization collaborated with the Liberia Institute of Statistics and Geo-Information Services (LISGIS) to develop a concept note for the 2025 Multi-Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS). This initiative will generate high-quality, nationally representative data on child well-being indicators, strengthening Liberia’s ability to monitor progress toward national and global development goals.
In 2024, UNICEF worked with 18 partners, including the government and CSOs, covering sectors such as Child Survival and Development (CSD), Education, Child Protection, Planning, Monitoring and Evaluation (PME), and Social and Behaviour Change (SBC). The total value of these partnerships was approximately US$ 3.99 million, with US$ 3.8 million in cash transferred to the government and more than US$ 0.1 million to CSOs.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, UNICEF Liberia faced several critical challenges that shaped its strategic direction and programmatic adaptations. Geographic inaccessibility, particularly in southeastern Liberia, remained a significant barrier to service delivery, with poor infrastructure limiting access to health, education, and social protection services. Financial constraints and capacity gaps among frontline workers also hindered program implementation, as inadequate funding led to reliance on short-term consultants, affecting the continuity and quality of service delivery.
Misinformation and deeply rooted cultural practices contributed to vaccine hesitancy, complicating efforts to expand immunization coverage. UNICEF responded by strengthening community-based advocacy and leveraging trusted local leaders to address public concerns. However, systemic data challenges persisted, as the absence of a harmonized national data system led to inconsistencies in data collection, affecting evidence-based decision-making and program coordination.
Despite the progress made, the country continues to struggle with achieving most of the nutrition indicators. Stunting levels among children under five remain critically high according to WHO thresholds. Minimum dietary diversity among children aged 6-23 months remains static at 9 percent against a target of 19 percent, and exclusive breastfeeding is at 55.2 percent, against a target of 65 percent. The percentage of women of childbearing age with anaemia is 45 percent, higher than the target of 38 percent stablished in the current CPD. A total of 153,495 children aged 6-59 months were reached with vitamin A supplementation against a target of 627,000, accounting for 24 percent of the target.  These indicators underscore the urgent need for sustainable, government-led nutrition programs to reduce dependence on external funding and strengthen local ownership of interventions. Disruptions in governance, including frequent leadership changes and a focus on national political activities, slowed progress in key sectors, particularly in WASH, where planned policy engagements did not advance as expected. These governance challenges highlighted the need for greater investment in decentralized service delivery, local capacity-building, and long-term institutional strengthening.
 Several critical insights from 2024 will shape UNICEF’s future programming. Local participation proved vital in overcoming service delivery barriers and improving uptake of interventions. Grassroots mobilization, traditional leadership involvement, and community-led advocacy significantly enhanced access to essential services. Collaborations with government, donors, and the private sector enabled innovative solutions and improved program reach despite financial constraints. Moving forward, strengthening co-financing models will ensure longer-term sustainability. High-quality data remains a cornerstone of targeted interventions. Improved coordination across sectors and investment in harmonized, real-time data collection tools will be critical in addressing coverage gaps. The ability to rapidly adjust to evolving circumstances was essential in maintaining program continuity and alignment with emerging needs. Greater flexibility in budgeting and resource allocation will further enhance responsiveness. Integrated programming that links health, nutrition, education, and child protection services yielded more effective and sustainable outcomes, reinforcing the importance of cross-sectoral collaboration. 
Building on the lessons from 2024, UNICEF Liberia will adapt its strategies to enhance resilience, expand community-driven initiatives, and strengthen systemic capacity for long-term impact. Greater investment in regional service delivery and local governance will ensure that interventions are better tailored to community needs and remain sustainable beyond donor funding. The Country Program Evaluation clearly and rightfully recommends the need to prioritize and understand the drivers of intersectional and compounding vulnerabilities with a focus on adolescent girls.
UNICEF will work closely with community health workers, traditional leaders, and faith-based organizations to counter misinformation and build public confidence in immunization programs. Establishing a unified data platform will improve the accuracy and timeliness of program monitoring, enabling real-time course corrections and better coordination across sectors. Expanding engagement with private sector entities and international financial institutions will diversify funding sources and drive innovation in program delivery. A validated gender work plan will guide targeted interventions to address gender disparities, ensuring that women and girls have equitable access to services and opportunities.
Looking ahead, UNICEF Liberia will leverage the insights gained in 2024 to adjust its program strategies, inform future actions, and explore new opportunities for collaboration. Prioritizing decentralized governance and strengthening local capacities to deliver services is a key focus. Expanding community-driven initiatives will ensure that programs are more responsive to local needs. Addressing vaccine hesitancy through targeted campaigns involving trusted sources like community health workers (CHWs) and traditional leaders will be critical in building trust and promoting the benefits of vaccination.
Investments in harmonizing data systems and leveraging technology for real-time monitoring will enhance decision-making. A unified data platform will improve the accuracy and timeliness of data collection and analysis. UNICEF will also scale partnerships with non-traditional actors, including private sector entities, to diversify funding sources and enhance program sustainability and for better delivery of results. Strengthening existing collaborations and exploring new ones will be essential.
UNICEF will ensure that its programs reinforce Liberia’s National Development Plan, the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development closely aligned with the UN Cooperation Framework.  With forward-looking strategies for decentralization, adolescent girls, public finance for children and data, research, monitoring and evaluation UNICEF Liberia is committed, as it develops in 2025 its next Country Program Document for five years (2026 – 2030) to transforming challenges into opportunities, ensuring that every child has access to essential services and the opportunity to reach their full potential.

In 2024, Mali continued to face significant socio-political and security challenges, marked by a complex political transition and the country's announcement of its withdrawal from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). The security landscape remained precarious, with ongoing confrontations between Malian security forces (FAMa) and Non-State Armed Groups (NSAGs), particularly in the northern and central regions. The emergence of the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) in Kidal, following the dissolution of the Cadre Stratégique Permanent pour la Défense du Peuple de l'Azawad (CSP-PDA) in November 2024, underscores the shifting dynamics among armed factions. This period witnessed intensified clashes, notably the Battle of Tinzawatene in July 2024, along with blockades that disrupted trade routes, hindered humanitarian aid, and exacerbated food insecurity in regions such as Ménaka, Boni (Mopti region), and Niafunké (Timbuktu region).

The activities of NSAGs expanded into previously stable areas, with reports of violence in Sikasso and Kayes, particularly near the borders with Mauritania and Burkina Faso. These developments severely restricted humanitarian operations and heightened risks for vulnerable populations, especially children and women. According to the latest Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) published in September 2024, Mali hosts 378,363 Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), equivalent to 105,185 households. This represents a seven percent increase compared to December 2023. Alarmingly, 58 percent of the displaced population consists of children, who face heightened vulnerabilities, including limited access to education, health and nutrition, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), and child protection services. Armed conflict remained the primary driver of displacement (90 percent), with natural disasters accounting for the remaining 10 percent. While some regions, such as Koulikoro, Koutiala, Mopti, Taoudénit, and Timbuktu, experienced slight reductions in displacement, humanitarian conditions remained dire, with 7.1 million people in need of assistance in 2024, up from 6.2 million in 2023.

Throughout the year, children in Mali continued to face significant challenges. Approximately 41.3 percent of children under 18 experienced multiple deprivations, with the situation being particularly severe in rural areas, high-density peri-urban informal settlements, among girls, and children living with disabilities. The latest National Survey on Food Security (ENSAN) indicates that approximately 1.37 million Malians were food insecure, an increase from 1.26 million in 2023. Malnutrition remained a critical issue, with stunting rates among children under five rising to 25.1 percent (up from 21.9 percent in 2023), and Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) rates increasing to 5.1 percent (up from 2.1 percent in 2023). Among women and adolescent girls, malnutrition continued to be alarmingly high, with anemia affecting 82 percent of children aged 6-59 months, 65.4 percent of adolescent girls aged 15-19 years, and 60 percent of adult women.

Gender-Based Violence (GBV) continued to disproportionately affect women and girls. Approximately 72.7 percent of girls aged 0-14 have undergone Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), and 54 percent of girls aged 20-24 were married before the age of 18. These issues, compounded by school-related GBV, early pregnancies, and entrenched sociocultural norms, continued to pose significant barriers to girls’ empowerment and well-being.

The education sector in Mali remained in crisis. As of 2024, over 3.3 million school-age children were reported to be out of school. UNICEF initiated an Out-of-School Children study to further clarify the situation. More than 2,000 schools remained non-functional (up from 1,500 in the previous year) due to insecurity, affecting over 600,000 students and 12,000 teachers. The postponement of the school year due to severe flooding further exacerbated the situation, impacting nearly 4 million children. High dropout rates and learning losses persisted, particularly for girls and children from poorer households. Barriers to education included poverty, inadequate school infrastructure, and a shortage of trained teachers. Additionally, 85 percent of secondary schools lacked adequate and separate latrines for girls and boys, indirectly contributing to low completion rates for girls.

Progress in health outcomes was mixed. Between 2010 and 2018, the maternal mortality rate fell from 660 to 325 per 100,000 live births, and neonatal mortality decreased from 39 to 34 to 29 per 1,000 live births between 2013 and 2024. However, infant mortality remained stagnant at 52 per 1,000 live births, while under-five mortality declined from 95 to 87 per 1,000 live births. Malaria, pneumonia, diarrhea, and malnutrition remained the leading causes of child mortality. Health service coverage, particularly in remote and impoverished urban areas, remained low due to weak health systems, insufficient human resources, and limited funding.

Access to water and sanitation services remained a significant challenge. As of 2024, 84 percent of the population had access to basic water services (up from 83 percent in 2021), while only 22 percent of households reported access to safely managed sanitation since 2022. Among IDPs, 48 percent lacked reliable access to water. Weak institutional coordination, insufficient maintenance of WASH infrastructure, and climate-induced events continued to undermine progress in this sector.

Mali remains one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change, with a Children's Climate Risk Index (CCRI) score categorized as "high-risk" in 2024. Over 8 million children were exposed to multiple climate and environmental risks. The severe flooding recorded— the worst in over 50 years—underscored the urgent need for climate resilience. To mitigate future disasters, preventive measures such as raising awareness about flooding risks and dredging water channels were implemented. In response to the nationally declared emergency, the Government allocated 4 billion FCFA to strengthen the national food security stock and provide immediate assistance to affected households. Under the leadership of the General Directorate of Civil Protection (DGPC – "Direction Générale de la Protection Civile"), the Crisis Coordination and Management Center was activated to oversee relief efforts. These efforts included cash transfers, distribution of non-food items (NFIs), and the temporary relocation of families to public buildings, such as schools, with support from humanitarian and development partners. The flooding also resulted in the postponement of the school year by two months, affecting nearly 4 million children, in addition to the 3 million already out of school.

Despite these challenges, there were signs of economic recovery, with GDP growth estimated at 5 percent in 2024 and projected to rise to 5.5 percent in 2025. The budget deficit remained contained at 4.4 percent in 2024 and was projected to decrease to 3.5 percent in 2025, primarily due to effective public resource mobilization and increased tax revenues. However, security expenditures, salary payments, and debt interest accounted for more than three-quarters of tax revenues, leading to a crowding-out effect on spending that could have benefited the poor and supported economic growth. Investments in social protection remained inadequate, with only 2.7 percent of the total budget allocated to this sector in 2024, down from 3 percent in 2022-2023.

Mali’s diplomatic landscape continued to be marked by significant challenges, particularly due to embassy closures and increasing tensions between the Government and some traditional donors. In response, Malian authorities focused on identifying and engaging new emerging development partners, guided by key principles of national sovereignty, strategic selection of partnerships, and prioritization of the interests of the Malian people.

In 2024, UNICEF continued its collaboration with the Government of Mali to drive transformative results in safeguarding the rights of children and adolescents. Through the implementation of the 2024 Work Plan—aligned with national development priorities and contributing to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)—UNICEF Mali adopted a life-cycle approach to deliver integrated and impactful interventions. This strategy prioritized the most vulnerable children, including those in humanitarian contexts, ensuring that no child is left behind and fostering lasting, systemic change for their development and well-being.

Pillar 1: The Early Years (0–5 Years)
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in health, nutrition, and WASH interventions for children aged 0 to 5 years, despite challenges such as insecurity, socio-economic constraints, and limited resources. By adopting an integrated approach, UNICEF strengthened community systems, improved service delivery, and addressed critical bottlenecks to ensure that no child was left behind. 

Immunization efforts led to 779,801 children aged 0-11 months receiving the DPT-Hep-Hib-3 vaccination, achieving 101 percent coverage, up from 696,339 in 2023 (92.9 percent of the target). This success was largely attributed to effective community mobilization strategies and enhancements to the cold chain. Additionally, poliovirus type II cases significantly declined from 15 in 2023 to just one in 2024. UNICEF-supported health facilities provided integrated services to 1,600,476 children under five, including 701,498 newborns, while 99.8 percent of 523,102 pregnant women received HIV testing. Strengthened skilled birth attendance and postnatal care services contributed to improved maternal and newborn health outcomes. Enhanced interoperability between health and civil registration services resulted in 509,769 children (259,649 girls) being registered and receiving birth certificates, advancing UNICEF’s Key Result for Children (KRC) 7.

UNICEF's nutrition programme delivered transformative results, with 5,297,504 children aged 6-59 months receiving Vitamin A supplementation, achieving 118 percent of the target in line with KRC 2. A total of 178,313 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition (SAM) were treated, reaching 89 percent of the targeted 201,250 children. Complementary food fortification benefited 115,959 children aged 6-23 months, achieving 96 percent of the target population. Community-based approaches, including the establishment of 676 Nutrition Support Groups and income-generating activities for 168 of them, empowered caregivers, particularly mothers, and improved child nutrition and resilience. Malnutrition screening covered 5,647,170 children, ensuring early identification and treatment of cases.

UNICEF-supported WASH interventions significantly improved access to clean water and sanitation. A total of 218,486 people gained access to basic sanitation services, while 286 communities (110 percent of the target) eliminated open defecation, compared to 181 communities (70 percent of the target) in 2023. Over 144,253 individuals gained access to safe drinking water services, while emergency WASH services reached 103,327 people in humanitarian settings. These efforts were bolstered by Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) initiatives, which empowered communities to construct 9,755 gender-sensitive latrines and rehabilitate over 20,000 existing ones. 

Progress in Early Childhood Development (ECD) was limited by financial constraints, systemic challenges, and weak integration with sectors like nutrition, WASH, and child protection. Only 35,200 children (44% of the target) accessed preschool programmes, and 16,800 (21%) received ECD kits, with barriers such as poverty, poor infrastructure, and low community engagement. While UNICEF supported safe learning spaces and educator training, issues like malnutrition, inadequate sanitation, and weak child protection systems further hindered progress. With gross enrollment rates at just 7.53%, greater investment and a holistic, cross-sectoral approach are needed.

The "Child-Friendly Communities" initiative enhanced integrated service delivery across 30 communes and 300 villages, reaching millions of children with health, nutrition, education, WASH, and child protection services. Awareness campaigns on female genital mutilation (FGM) reached 27,036 girls and women, while 135 survivors received psychosocial or medical care. Additionally, income-generating activities for 168 Nutrition Support Groups, along with educational talks, cooking demonstrations, and home visits, benefited over 33,000 people, fostering sustainable improvements in child rights.

Pillar 2: The Formative Years (6–12 Years)
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in increasing quality learning opportunities for children aged 6 to 12 in Mali, despite a challenging context marked by insecurity, displacement, and climate-related disasters. By fostering a gender-responsive, protective, safe, and clean educational environment, UNICEF strengthened education systems and enhanced learning outcomes, aligning its efforts with national priorities. Through advocacy for reopening closed schools, digital transformation of education delivery, prevention of gender-based violence (GBV), and system strengthening—including improved WASH services and innovative data collection systems—UNICEF contributed to achieving a primary completion rate of 68.7 percent, reflecting a one percentage point increase from 2023.

The educational landscape in Mali faced significant disruptions in 2024 due to conflicts, insecurity, and severe flooding, which rendered more than 2,000 schools non-functional and damaged 500 others, affecting over 600,000 students and 12,000 teachers. In response, UNICEF implemented targeted interventions that enabled 97,567 children (46 percent girls) to access formal and non-formal education, surpassing the annual target of 60,000 by 162 percent. This success was achieved through reintegrating out-of-school children, supporting school reopening, and establishing alternative education opportunities, including accelerated education programmes and community learning centers. Additionally, UNICEF constructed and rehabilitated classrooms and provided 206 temporary learning spaces, ensuring educational continuity for over 11,000 children affected by severe flooding.

UNICEF significantly improved learning conditions by distributing school kits to 223,621 students (47 percent girls), far exceeding the annual target of 90,000, thereby reducing barriers to school attendance and creating a more conducive learning environment. Furthermore, 3,677 teachers (35 percent women) received training to enhance competencies in education in emergencies, learning assessments, remedial teaching techniques, and gender-responsive pedagogy. To address students' mental health needs, 86 teachers (26 percent women) were trained in Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS), equipping them to assist children affected by crises.

Strengthening school governance was another key focus, with UNICEF enhancing the capacity of 1,449 School Management Committees (SMCs) and supporting the Ministry of Education in validating key strategic documents, including the Life Skills Education module and the Teacher Policy. UNICEF also prioritized integrating WASH services in schools, equipping 60 schools with improved facilities, benefiting 21,924 children (48 percent girls), and reducing health risks.
UNICEF supported the Ministry of Education in conducting a gender audit and revitalizing the Gender Institutionalization Committee, culminating in an annual gender operational plan. These efforts contributed to increasing female teacher representation and integrating gender priorities into education policies.

UNICEF also provided crucial child protection services, including GBV prevention and response for 297 children, and case management for 2,553 children (1,409 girls), including 22 Children Associated with Armed Forces and Armed Groups (CAFAAG) and 260 Unaccompanied and Separated Children (UASC). Despite challenges such as insecurity and reduced financial resources, UNICEF and its partners remained steadfast in their commitment to protecting vulnerable children.
Overall, UNICEF’s interventions significantly contributed to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 on quality education. The primary gross enrolment rate increased from 81.2 percent (78.1 percent for girls) in 2023 to 81.3 percent (78.5 percent for girls) in 2024 (KRC 3). Similarly, the lower secondary gross enrolment rate rose from 49 percent (47.8 percent for girls) in 2023 to 50.6 percent (50 percent for girls) in 2024. In terms of learning outcomes, the primary completion rate improved to 68.7 percent (67 percent for girls) in 2024, up from 67.8 percent in 2023, surpassing the target of 65.8 percent. Additionally, the Gender Parity Index (GPI) for primary completion increased from 0.94 in 2023 to 0.95 in 2024. These results demonstrate systematic progress in reducing educational disparities and ensuring that no child is left behind.

Pillar 3: The Second Decade (13–18 Years)
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in child protection, education, gender equality, and girls' empowerment for adolescents aged 13 to 18 in Mali, despite challenges such as insecurity and funding constraints. A key achievement was strengthening the National Case Management System, benefiting 2,089 children (1,109 girls). This included reintegrating 211 CAFAAG, supporting 790 UASC in family reunification or alternative care, and providing health, social, or justice services for 1,088 survivors of conflict-related violence (KRC 5).
Capacity-building initiatives were crucial, with 68 field staff (26 women) receiving training in MHPSS and case management. Enhanced collaboration with Child Protection Committees facilitated timely case identification and referral. Additionally, UNICEF implemented Mine Risk Education (MRE), reaching 6,612 children in conflict-affected areas, reducing risks from landmines and explosive remnants of war, and contributing to SDG 16.

Furthermore, UNICEF actively addressed harmful practices such as child marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM) through community awareness and youth-led advocacy, reaching over 102,000 adolescent girls (56 percent of the target) compared to 187,429 (141 percent of the target) in 2023. This decrease in coverage was primarily due to financial constraints. Interventions engaged 220 adolescents as mentors to promote positive behaviors and protective norms. Additionally, efforts to prevent and respond to gender-based violence in emergencies (GBViE) were scaled up, particularly in the Gao region, where 4,215 individuals—including 852 girls, 607 boys, and 1,094 women—received care and services (KRC 6). These activities not only addressed immediate needs but also aimed to transform harmful social norms and advance gender equality, aligning with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 5.

In the education sector, UNICEF supported 8,199 adolescents with school materials and provided 19,687 learning opportunities, including 9,253 for girls, contributing to SDG 4. Although these efforts fell short of the annual target due to funding constraints, they still represented progress compared to the previous year. UNICEF also enhanced gender-responsive water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in 20 secondary schools, surpassing its target of 14 schools. A menstrual hygiene education initiative, conducted in partnership with the Ministry of Education (MoE), empowered girls as leaders of change by training them to produce sanitary pads from local materials, fostering entrepreneurship, and engaging boys as allies in promoting gender equality. Over 500 participants, including 264 girls and 106 boys, along with teachers and community members, took part in these sessions. Additionally, 1,500 hygiene kits were distributed to support menstrual health, with 85 percent of participants reporting increased confidence and improved school attendance. A study on menstrual health, hygiene management marketing, and taboos was underway at the end of the year to develop a sustainable economic chain involving out-of-school adolescents and women-led groups, offering employment and income-generating opportunities.

Despite security and access challenges in central and northern Mali, UNICEF, as co-chair of the Country Task Force on Monitoring and Reporting (CTFMR), supported the Children and Armed Conflict agenda. This included monitoring six grave violations, capacity development, and reintegration support for children released from armed groups, with 1,001 children successfully reintegrated into their communities. Advocacy efforts with the Ministry of Justice led to the finalization of a National Strategy on Justice for Children and the adoption of legislation establishing a National Directorate for Child Justice. Temporary care and family reunification services were provided to 1,007 children on the move, while 368 children accessed essential social, health, and justice services. Community-based GBV prevention mechanisms were strengthened through the establishment of GBV alert committees in Kayes, Koulikoro, and Bamako.

UNICEF also supported the Extended Programme of Immunization (EPI) by introducing the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine and conducting a gender barrier analysis to identify community perceptions and address access barriers. Insights from a U-Report poll of 1,457 young participants, including 430 girls, and additional surveys reaching 5,500 adolescents on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) and MPOX informed the vaccine demand generation plan. Furthermore, UNICEF trained 439 healthcare providers and 125 youth leaders on SRHR, HPV, and HIV/AIDS prevention and screening, advancing adolescent health initiatives. These comprehensive efforts highlight UNICEF's commitment to advancing national and global development priorities while ensuring no adolescent is left behind.

Pillar 4: Enabling Environment for Community Resilience
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in enhancing an enabling environment for inclusive community resilience in Mali through multisectoral interventions. Approximately 20,000 households, with a particular focus on pregnant women and children under two, benefitted from unconditional cash transfers aimed at addressing malnutrition and economic vulnerabilities. These efforts directly supported SDGs 1 and 2 by providing immediate financial relief and fostering long-term economic stability. By strengthening community resilience against economic shocks, these interventions fulfilled critical national social protection targets and informed future policy shifts towards comprehensive social safety nets. The integration of cash transfers with social behavior change (SBC) communication and child protection measures enabled vulnerable families to better withstand economic shocks and health crises, ultimately improving the well-being of children and women, with girls comprising 50 percent of the targeted population. These initiatives aligned with national priorities and global development goals, including SDGs 1, 5, and 10.

UNICEF also contributed to the empowerment of nearly 26,000 women and youth, including 2,500 GBV survivors, through income-generating activities and public works in conflict-affected northern regions such as Kidal, Gao, Timbuktu, Mopti, Douentza, and Bandiagara. These efforts not only prevented youth recruitment into armed groups and addressed drivers of unsafe migration but also reinforced social cohesion, contributing to regional stability and supporting SDG 16. For GBV survivors, the promotion of sustainable livelihoods helped break cycles of violence and advance gender equality, furthering SDG 5 objectives.

At the policy level, UNICEF provided technical support to the Government to strengthen social protection systems. Key achievements included the development of a National Social Protection Floor encompassing essential guarantees for various vulnerable groups, such as universal health coverage, social safety nets and income support for poor families with children under five, income security for working-age individuals, and assistance for the elderly and persons with disabilities. These measures are foundational for achieving SDG 10 and align with national strategies aimed at improving the well-being of vulnerable populations. UNICEF also facilitated a public expenditure review of the social protection sector and explored innovative financing mechanisms to support local development, leading to the selection of 40 municipalities to develop tailored financing strategies that strengthen local governance and resilience.

UNICEF played a pivotal role in the 2025 Humanitarian Programming Cycle (HPC) by supporting the Multi-Sectoral Needs Assessment (MSNA), which informed the 2025 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). Additionally, UNICEF assisted the Directorate of Disaster Risk Reduction and Social Emergency Services in conducting rapid needs assessments during crises to ensure timely and informed responses. In collaboration with national partners, UNICEF supported the development and updating of key humanitarian strategies, including revising the national multi-hazard contingency plan with the General Directorate of Social Protection (DGPC) and developing the National Flood Plan with the National Directorate of Social Development (DNDS). These tools unified stakeholders under a coordinated emergency management approach. Furthermore, UNICEF organized training sessions for sectoral technical services (Education, Health, WASH, Child Protection), DGPC, DNDS staff, and civil society organization (CSO) partners in Kayes and Sikasso, regions affected by spillover humanitarian crises. Technical support for flood zone mapping and the promotion of harmonized data management tools improved coordination between the DGPC and DNDS. Internally, UNICEF developed a Flood Response Plan, significantly enhancing the speed and effectiveness of flood emergency responses.

To improve humanitarian access, UNICEF continued to implement a child-centered localization strategy. This initiative aims to support 100,000 children and 80,600 internally displaced persons (IDPs) in 489 hard-to-reach villages over nine months in collaboration with local organizations. By expanding its field presence and providing training to strengthen local institutions and organizations, UNICEF contributed to more effective and sustainable crisis preparedness and response.

Additionally, UNICEF led efforts to strengthen gender-responsive humanitarian action. To support the Humanitarian Country Team’s roadmap on gender, UNICEF mapped and trained 80 women’s organizations operating in conflict-affected areas. This initiative enhanced the leadership of women-led organizations in decision-making for humanitarian preparedness and response, improving access to vulnerable and hard-to-reach areas and expanding assistance for girls from the most vulnerable groups.
