In summary, UNICEF's comprehensive approach in 2024 significantly advanced community resilience in Mali by addressing economic vulnerabilities, empowering women and youth, strengthening social protection systems, enhancing humanitarian responses, and promoting gender equality. These efforts not only aligned with national priorities but also contributed meaningfully to global sustainable development goals, ensuring that vulnerable populations are better equipped to face challenges and thrive in their communities.

Pillar 5: Programme Effectiveness
External Communication and Advocacy
In 2024, UNICEF significantly expanded its reach and influence, strategically positioning itself as a leading advocate for children's rights, with a particular emphasis on adolescent girls, education, and climate change. By implementing a strengthened media strategy, UNICEF enhanced its engagement with national and international media, increasing visibility for key advocacy themes such as education, nutrition, and the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Mali.
UNICEF's advocacy priorities were featured 871 times in online and print media, including international outlets, reinforcing its leadership in addressing children's rights. The organization solidified its status as a digital leader, reaching over 10.3 million accounts across various social media platforms—a tenfold increase from 2023. Additionally, UNICEF produced 186 high-quality multimedia pieces to support its advocacy and fundraising efforts in both humanitarian and development contexts.

In summary, UNICEF's robust external communication and advocacy efforts in 2024 amplified its voice on critical issues affecting children and solidified its position as a key player in the global dialogue on children's rights. Through strategic media engagement and a strong digital presence, UNICEF effectively raised awareness and mobilized support for its initiatives, making significant progress in improving the lives of vulnerable children in Mali.

Resource Mobilization and Partnerships
In 2024, UNICEF demonstrated strong resource mobilization efforts, particularly in development funding through Other Regular Resources (ORR), securing a total of US$331 million for the 2020–2025 Country Programme. This figure represents 110 per cent of the original OR ceiling of US$ 300 million planned for the 2020–2024 period. However, disparities in funding allocation persisted; for instance, Pillar 1 (Early Years) received 121 per cent of its planned funding, while Pillar 3 (Second Decade, 13–18 years) reached only 53 per cent. Within the pillars, outcomes such as "Quality and Inclusive Early Learning" remained underfunded at just 42 per cent. To address these gaps, UNICEF plans to refocus its efforts in 2025 by diversifying funding sources, intensifying advocacy for underfunded outcomes, and leveraging partnerships to ensure equitable resource allocation.

Conversely, emergency funding (ORE) faced significant challenges, with a notable decline in contributions for the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal. In 2024, only 25 per cent of the required funding was mobilized for HAC, a decrease from 36 per cent in 2023 and well below the average funding rate of 52 per cent received between 2020 and 2022. This decline was attributed to competing global emergencies and tensions with Malian authorities, complicating donors' ability to prioritize support for Mali. 

Overall, while UNICEF's resource mobilization in development funding remained robust, significant gaps in funding allocation and a decline in emergency funding posed challenges to its efforts. Moving forward, addressing these disparities and strengthening partnerships will be crucial to ensuring that all children, regardless of age or circumstance, receive the support they need to thrive.

Enablers
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA)
In 2024, UNICEF significantly scaled up its efforts in Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) at the national level, enhancing interventions across five field offices. UNICEF distributed over 5,000 awareness materials focused on Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) messages and reporting mechanisms, effectively reaching 121,065 individuals, including 38,622 girls and 47,092 women. To strengthen capacity, UNICEF trained 163 staff members from implementing partner organizations on SEA prevention, risk mitigation, and reporting mechanisms. Additionally, 27 implementing partners (one community-based organization, five international NGOs, and 21 national NGOs) underwent a comprehensive PSEA risk assessment to identify and address vulnerabilities.

UNICEF also facilitated three workshops for 117 practitioners on the UN Victim Assistance Protocol, further reinforcing its commitment to safeguarding vulnerable populations. The organization supported updates to the PSEA Network Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and action plan, ensuring best practices and guidelines were in place for effective implementation. UNICEF's enhanced PSEA initiatives in 2024 demonstrated a strong commitment to protecting children and vulnerable individuals in Mali through widespread awareness campaigns, targeted training, and collaborative efforts with implementing partners. These actions promote a culture of accountability and protection within UNICEF’s operations.

Humanitarian Coordination and Field Presence
In 2024, UNICEF strengthened its humanitarian coordination, ensuring that the needs of children remained at the forefront of its efforts. Internally, the organization enhanced its response speed and capacity through structured mechanisms such as the Emergency Management Team (EMT) and the Emergency Technical Team (ETT). Externally, UNICEF's leadership in coordination platforms—including UNICEF-led or co-led clusters for WASH, Nutrition, Education, and Child Protection Area of Responsibility (CP AoR)—significantly influenced the 2025 Humanitarian Planning Cycle (HPC). This leadership secured the inclusion of 480,000 malnourished children who had initially been excluded and facilitated optimal funding from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). Additionally, UNICEF’s advocacy efforts improved access to hard-to-reach areas, directly benefiting vulnerable children affected by crises.

To expand its reach, UNICEF established an outpost in Ménaka, increasing its field presence to six operational offices, including five existing field offices and one outpost, supported by seven newly recruited local staff. These offices were equipped with essential resources, security measures, and logistical support to ensure effective and sustained programme delivery while prioritizing staff well-being. UNICEF also enhanced humanitarian preparedness through comprehensive contingency plans and strengthened supply chains via local procurement, improved storage, and prepositioned supplies, ensuring rapid and adaptable emergency responses.
UNICEF’s comprehensive approach to humanitarian coordination in 2024 not only strengthened its operational capacity but also ensured that children's needs were prioritized in crisis response efforts. By enhancing internal mechanisms, expanding field presence, and fostering collaboration with the Government and partners, UNICEF effectively positioned itself to deliver timely and impactful support to vulnerable children in Mali.

Adolescents and Youth Participation
In 2024, UNICEF made significant strides in promoting adolescent and youth participation across various initiatives focused on health, nutrition, climate change, and gender-based violence (GBV). A total of 1,863,125 adolescents and youth engaged with key initiatives through U-Report chatbots and surveys, with 52 per cent actively providing feedback and accessing critical information. This engagement highlights the importance of youth voices in shaping programmes that affect their lives.

Additionally, over 120,000 youth and adolescents participated in or led offline and online civic engagement initiatives on pressing issues such as child marriage and climate change. Continued advocacy efforts with the Government, alongside partnerships with organizations like the National Center for the Promotion of Volunteering (CNPV), facilitated the mobilization of 100 U-Reporter volunteers to raise awareness among their peers.

UNICEF’s social media campaigns, community dialogue sessions, and collaborations with religious leaders played a crucial role in promoting adolescent health, education, child protection, and gender equity. These initiatives amplified the voices of young people in decision-making processes. Notably, youth-led interventions in humanitarian contexts enabled the reintegration of 13,000 children, including 8,000 girls, back into school. In summary, UNICEF’s efforts in 2024 significantly empowered adolescents and youth, fostering their participation in critical initiatives that address health, education, and social issues. By leveraging technology, community engagement, and strategic partnerships, UNICEF effectively amplified youth voices and facilitated meaningful contributions to decision-making processes. These achievements not only enhanced the well-being of young people but also strengthened community resilience and advocacy for their rights.

Programme Monitoring
In 2024, UNICEF Mali significantly enhanced its Management for Results approach, emphasizing results-based planning, budgeting, and monitoring to align with UNICEF’s mandate and Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action (CCCs). The Country Office improved evidence-based planning through the development of a national Annual Work Plan (AWP) and 20 decentralized AWPs, including those for 19 regions and the District of Bamako, employing a bottom-up approach that prioritized local needs.

Mid-year and annual reviews, alongside a Strategic Moment of Reflection related to the development of the next Country Programme Document (CPD), were instrumental in identifying bottlenecks and accelerating implementation, ensuring that challenges were promptly addressed. To monitor progress toward programme outputs and outcomes, UNICEF utilized national statistical systems such as DHIS2, the Education Management Information System (EMIS), and the Modular and Permanent Household Survey (EMOP). Additionally, UNICEF supported the National Institute of Statistics in executing the seventh Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) and prepared for the fifth Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) scheduled for 2025.

UNICEF further strengthened programme monitoring through real-time data collection via the PREMISE platform, providing timely insights across key sectors, including health, nutrition, WASH, education, and child protection. Third-party monitoring in hard-to-reach areas ensured that activities and results were effectively captured, informing programming decisions.
The Country Office achieved an impressive 108 per cent performance rate for programmatic visits and spot checks, reflecting its commitment to rigorous monitoring practices. Additionally, UNICEF conducted capacity-building initiatives, training 35 Government staff and partners on the Harmonized Approach to Cash Transfers (HACT), evaluation methodologies, and evidence generation.

By adopting a results-based management approach, leveraging national data systems, and integrating real-time monitoring, UNICEF improved programme quality, responsiveness, and accountability, ultimately leading to better outcomes for children and communities in Mali.

In 2024, UNICEF continued to align its programmes and priorities with national frameworks, including the National Development Plan (CREDD 2019-2023), the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2020-2025, and global agendas such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the African Union’s Agenda 2063. These efforts were consistent with UNICEF’s Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and regional priorities on Key Result Areas (KRAs). By leveraging partnerships with Government entities, civil society organizations (CSOs), UN agencies, and International Financial Institutions (IFIs), UNICEF advanced children's rights and delivered transformative results for vulnerable children and families.

As part of the UN Country Team (UNCT), UNICEF played a crucial role in contributing to and co-leading flagship programmes aimed at delivering high-impact results aligned with national priorities. These programmes focused on key areas such as: (i) food systems, (ii) climate action and energy transition, and (iii) education transformation. Within this framework, UNICEF was designated as the co-lead for the Education Flagship (which includes Health and Social Protection components), working alongside UNESCO and in support of the Government. This collaboration ensured that UNICEF's mandate to promote the rights and well-being of children was integrated across all initiatives. 

Together with UNDP and UNFPA, UNICEF implemented a HACT cost-sharing strategy. This strategy included sharing information on partnership risk evaluation and management, as well as PSEA measures. This collaborative approach strengthened accountability and efficiency in resource management, ensuring that funds were utilized effectively to support vulnerable populations.
To improve sectoral coordination and capacity building, UNICEF collaborated closely with the Government of Mali, particularly with the Ministry for the Promotion of Women, Children, and Families, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation. This partnership led to the establishment of a National Directorate of Justice for Children and the development of a National Strategy for Justice for Children. Additionally, UNICEF worked alongside UNFPA, UN Women, and the UN Resident Coordinator’s Office to develop the Spotlight 2.0 initiative, aimed at eliminating violence against women and girls while mobilizing resources to support the national strategy to end child marriage.

Partnerships with other UN agencies, including OCHA, WFP, UNHCR, UNFPA, and WHO, as well as international and national NGOs, enhanced the delivery of multisectoral interventions for children. These collaborations improved access to services, facilitated aid delivery in hard-to-reach areas, and strengthened monitoring and reporting mechanisms, particularly in the context of children and armed conflict through the Country Task Forces on Monitoring and Reporting (MRM).

UNICEF led key humanitarian clusters, including WASH, Nutrition, and Education (as co-lead), as well as the Child Protection Area of Responsibility (AoR), ensuring coordinated responses to crises and alignment with the 2024 HNRP. In its humanitarian efforts in Mali, UNICEF collaborated with UN agencies, primarily OCHA, WFP, and UNFPA, on cross-cutting issues such as coordination and humanitarian access. It also participated in various coordination forums (e.g., Clusters, the Humanitarian Access Working Group, etc.). Additionally, UNICEF signed a Letter of Understanding (LoU) with UNHCR to address the increasing refugee population, which has doubled in 2024. This LoU is accompanied by a joint action plan, and a joint proposal was developed in collaboration with key partners, including the DNDS and the General Directorate of Civil Protection (DGPC). UNICEF worked with 11 national NGOs and the Malian Red Cross to develop a child-centered rapid response mechanism, ensuring that children's needs were prioritized in emergency situations. It also collaborated with the World Bank on initiatives such as the "Learning Passport" pilot project, aimed at improving access to education. Additionally, UNICEF supported income-generating activities and labor-intensive public works under the "Promotion of Access to Financing, Entrepreneurship, and Employment in Mali" (PAFEEM) project, which aimed to strengthen community resilience. UNICEF also leveraged strategic alliances with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and Education Cannot Wait (ECW). GPE mobilized an impressive US$75 million to support educational initiatives in Mali, with UNICEF serving as the Grant Manager in partnership with UNESCO, while ECW committed US$22 million to address urgent educational needs, particularly in crisis-affected areas. 

As the lead agency for Nutrition and the convener of the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement UN network, UNICEF strengthened partnerships with FAO and WFP to enhance coherence and harmonization in nutrition interventions. Joint projects with WFP addressed the socio-economic impacts of COVID-19 and built resilience in national systems and communities. Collaboration with WHO focused on epidemic response and maternal, newborn, and child health, ensuring a comprehensive approach to health and nutrition.

UNICEF expanded its private sector engagement by providing technical expertise to the Azalai and Orange Foundations. Through its partnership with Orange, UNICEF advocated for in-kind support, which included SMS services, internet connectivity, and tablets. These efforts are expected to further materialize in 2025, enhancing UNICEF's capacity to deliver educational and health services to children and families.

UNICEF maintained strong partnerships with bilateral and multilateral donors, including Germany, the United States, Canada, the World Bank, the European Union, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, the United Kingdom, and the Netherlands. These partnerships enabled UNICEF to secure additional funding to support its programmes and further its mission to improve the lives of children and families in Mali.

In summary, UNICEF's comprehensive approach in 2024 demonstrated a strong commitment to advancing children's rights and well-being in Mali. By aligning its programmes with national and global frameworks, leveraging partnerships, and implementing innovative strategies, UNICEF effectively addressed the multifaceted challenges faced by vulnerable children and families. Moving forward, UNICEF's focus on strengthening partnerships, enhancing sectoral coordination, and addressing critical funding needs will be essential to ensuring that all children in Mali receive the support and opportunities they deserve.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges 
In 2024, UNICEF faced significant challenges in programme implementation, particularly in regions affected by insecurity and humanitarian crises. These conditions restricted access to vulnerable populations, impeding progress in key areas such as Child Protection and Education. For instance, while mobile Child-Friendly Spaces (CFS) provided essential Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) to over 65,000 children, the demand for these services far exceeded the availability of trained social workers and resources, creating a substantial gap in service delivery.

Insecurity further disrupted family reunification efforts for unaccompanied children and limited access to education for out-of-school children. Although innovative solutions such as mobile CFS and community-based education models showed promise, their scalability was hindered by resource shortages and insufficient local capacity. These challenges underscored the urgent need for integrated approaches that combine immediate humanitarian relief with long-term resilience-building strategies. To address both immediate needs and root causes, UNICEF initiated efforts such as cash transfers and income-generating activities. However, these interventions require stronger stakeholder coordination and additional resources to drive systemic change effectively.

Operationally, UNICEF’s supply chain was significantly impacted by insecurity and market limitations. Humanitarian access to regions like Menaka and Kidal remained a critical issue, as land and air corridors were frequently obstructed due to logistical and security constraints. As a key member of the Access Working Group, UNICEF played a pivotal role in advocating for and implementing solutions to improve access. While these efforts contributed to collective strategies for better mobility, delays in delivering essential supplies and services to remote, conflict-affected regions persisted.

Local procurement accounted for 54 percent of UNICEF’s total supply expenditure (US$10.5 million). However, the unavailability of specialized materials locally necessitated offshore procurement, leading to increased costs and extended delivery timelines. Addressing these challenges will require continued advocacy, strategic partnerships, and innovative supply chain solutions to ensure timely and efficient programme delivery in the most affected regions.

Mali’s Worsening Crisis and UNICEF’s Response
Mali’s escalating crisis has created a "perfect storm" of rising humanitarian needs, increasing operational costs, and declining global attention. The post-MINUSMA environment has exacerbated these challenges, driving up operational expenses, reducing value for money, diminishing donor interest, and restricting UNICEF’s ability to transfer funds due to donor-imposed limitations. The withdrawal of ECOWAS, delays in Mali’s electoral process, and the closure of some embassies have further complicated advocacy efforts. As a result, UNICEF’s 2024 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was only 23% funded, down from 36% in 2023, reflecting a broader trend of donor fatigue. In response, UNICEF intensified donor engagement through quarterly humanitarian group meetings and evidence-based advocacy, including cost-of-inaction analyses. The organization also prioritized life-saving interventions in the most affected areas, optimizing resource allocation to maximize impact amid significant funding constraints.

Lessons Learned
In 2024, UNICEF Mali reinforced the importance of community-based approaches in enhancing programme delivery and sustainability. Engaging communities through diverse communication channels—such as community radio, social networks, and digital platforms—proved essential in reaching remote and vulnerable populations. Strengthened community engagement across 30 communes and 300 villages led to the development of 360 action plans addressing children's well-being in the health, education, and protection sectors. These plans promoted local ownership and accountability, ensuring that interventions remained contextually relevant and aligned with the specific needs of children and families. 

For example, community-based Child Protection Committees and foster families provided temporary care for separated children while raising awareness about violence, abuse, and exploitation. The integration of child-friendly community approaches further advanced UNICEF’s localization strategy, fostering inclusive and protective environments for children. In total, 156 child-friendly spaces, including 80 mobile units in central and northern regions, delivered group psychosocial services to 65,733 children (32,055 girls), demonstrating their effectiveness in supporting vulnerable children in crisis-affected areas. These spaces provided immediate psychosocial care and encouraged community participation, with local stakeholders, including youth and child protection committee members, playing active roles in their operation and management.

Through the "Child-Friendly Communities" initiative, health and nutrition services reached over 5.6 million children. Awareness sessions on female genital mutilation (FGM) engaged 27,036 girls and women, while 135 survivors received psychosocial or medical care. Educational talks, cooking demonstrations, and home visits benefited over 33,000 people, contributing to sustainable improvements in child health, nutrition, and rights. These experiences underscore the significance of community engagement as a cornerstone of the localization strategy, ensuring that no child is left behind.

Gender Equality and Adolescent Empowerment
In 2024, UNICEF Mali made remarkable strides in promoting gender equality and adolescent empowerment. The Country Office leveraged a multidimensional ecological model to drive systemic, community, and individual transformation. This approach integrated gender considerations across all strategic pillars and operated at interconnected levels of influence, including policy shaping, system strengthening, community mobilization, and individual empowerment.

At the policy level, UNICEF collaborated with Mali’s Ministry of Health and Social Development to conduct a gender audit within the health sector, evaluating key areas such as data systems, operations, and human resources. This audit led to the establishment of gender committees and action plans that institutionalized gender mainstreaming and prioritized girls' health while strengthening institutional capacities.

To reinforce system strengthening, girls' empowerment was prioritized through targeted programmes. Training 498 teachers in gender-responsive pedagogy helped dismantle cultural barriers to girls' education and foster inclusive school environments. Menstrual health and hygiene management (MHHM) and gender equality training extended to both educators and students, creating more supportive learning spaces. Guidance on the Gender Equality Marker and gender-based violence (GBV) risk mitigation was provided to 40 implementing partners, embedding gender-transformative programming into systemic frameworks as a requirement for partnerships.
At the community level, UNICEF organized intergenerational dialogues to advocate for gender equality and positive parenting practices, addressing challenges uniquely faced by girls. Initiatives such as "Maman Yeleen" empowered women as health leaders, improving vaccination coverage and fostering trust within health systems. Communication campaigns like "The Tongue and the Teeth" challenged harmful gender norms, promoting health awareness and positive family practices.

On an individual level, UNICEF implemented transformative programmes that empowered adolescent girls with leadership development, financial literacy, and income-generating opportunities. Over 8,000 out-of-school girls accessed safe spaces designed to nurture their resilience while integrating MHHM and reproductive health education. These initiatives directly improved school retention rates, strengthened leadership capacities, and provided tools to foster girls' independence. By linking cash transfer programmes to income-generating activities for women and youth, UNICEF further enhanced girls' and women’s empowerment, promoting household resilience and increasing opportunities for meaningful contributions to their communities.

In the context of HPV vaccine introduction, UNICEF collaborated with Mali’s Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) to conduct a gender barrier analysis, mapping challenges adolescent girls faced in accessing vaccinations. These insights informed a national communication strategy designed to address barriers and ensure that girls’ health needs were met.

Even in humanitarian contexts, UNICEF maintained a strong gender lens. Guided by the Humanitarian Country Team’s Road Map on Gender and Humanitarian Action, UNICEF and UN Women conducted Gender Rapid Analyses that informed the Humanitarian Programming Cycle (HPC) for 2024. Additionally, UNICEF piloted a gender and localization initiative, engaging 80 women-led organizations from emergency-affected areas in humanitarian preparedness and response.
UNICEF Mali's comprehensive approach to gender equality and girls' empowerment demonstrates a commitment to sustainable change at multiple levels, ensuring that the voices and needs of women and girls are not only heard but actively integrated into policies, programmes, and community practices.

Looking Ahead
The Country Programme (2020–2024) has been extended by one year, now concluding in December 2025. This extension aligns with the ongoing development of Mali’s socioeconomic development vision, "Vision 2063," which remained under formulation in 2024. The additional year provides an opportunity to accelerate progress for children, particularly in addressing lagging indicators.

In 2025, UNICEF Mali will prioritize strengthening health systems to ensure equitable and quality primary healthcare, promoting optimal nutrition and child development, supporting HIV prevention through adolescent empowerment and participation, and enhancing resilient and inclusive WASH services. Efforts will also focus on ensuring quality education and skills-building for girls and boys, providing comprehensive child protection for the most vulnerable, and advancing social inclusion through social protection initiatives.
At the same time, the Country Office will continue developing its new Country Programme (2026–2030), as Vision 2063 is expected to be finalized in the first quarter of 2025.

Conclusion
In 2024, UNICEF faced considerable challenges, particularly in regions affected by insecurity and humanitarian crises. Despite these obstacles, the organization demonstrated resilience and adaptability by implementing innovative community-based approaches and prioritizing gender-sensitive strategies. The lessons learned emphasize the importance of localization, multisectoral collaboration, and integrating gender considerations into all programming efforts.

Looking ahead, UNICEF’s extended Country Programme provides a crucial opportunity to accelerate progress for children in Mali. By focusing on strengthening health systems, promoting education, and enhancing social inclusion, UNICEF aims to address the pressing needs of vulnerable populations while laying the foundation for sustainable development. Community engagement and the empowerment of women and girls will remain central to ensuring that all children can thrive, even in challenging contexts. Through continued collaboration with partners and stakeholders, UNICEF is well-positioned to drive meaningful change and improve the lives of children and families in Mali.

The status of child rights in Mauritania in 2024 reflects a complex interplay of political, socio-economic, and environmental factors. From December 25, 2023, to January 8, 2024, the Mauritanian government conducted the 5th general census, revealing a population of 4,927,532, with half under 20 years old and 51.8% women. This demographic structure underscores the critical need for child-focused and youth policies and programs.

In 2024, the re-election of President Mohamed Ould Ghazouani with 56% of the vote in the first round under peaceful conditions, reaffirmed the country's  political and security stability. Following this re-election the newly established government articulated a comprehensive general policy framework. This policy outlines strategic priorities, including the reform of the education system to ensure equitable access and quality learning, the expansion and modernization of healthcare services with a focus on underserved rural areas, and the reinforcement of social protection mechanisms targeting the most vulnerable populations.

The government emphasizes youth empowerment through employment and civic engagement, governance reforms to enhance transparency and decentralization, and a commitment to addressing social inequalities. These priorities provide a strategic opportunity for UNICEF Mauritania to align its programming and advocacy efforts, particularly in advancing education, health, social protection, and youth-focused initiatives in Mauritania.

The government's commitment to development is highlighted by the adoption of the Consolidated Investment Budget (CIB) as part of the Finance Law for an amount of 1.2 billion US dollar (65% domestic financing, 55% external). This budget demonstrates the dedication of the government and financial partners to developing infrastructure that supports growth, improves social services, creates thousands of jobs, enhances the productive potential of the national economy, and accelerates progress toward food self-sufficiency. This initiative aligns with the ongoing implementation of the "TAAHOUDATY" Program, led by the President Mohamed Ould Ghazouani, and the Five-Year Action Plan (2021–2025) of the Strategy for Accelerated Growth and Shared Prosperity (SCAPP), which outlines the priorities for public policies as stated in the Government's General Policy Declaration. 

Economically, Mauritania's growth slowed to 3.4% in 2023, but the decline in inflation to 5% and a reduced fiscal deficit to 2.5% of GDP indicate improved macroeconomic stability[1]. This economic environment, while challenging, offers a foundation for sustained investment for children. The 2024 projected growth of 5.4% [EM1] [AD2] suggests a positive outlook, but the benefits of this growth must be equitably distributed to ensure improvements in child rights.

The 2022 Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) shows that 61.9% of children in Mauritania are multidimensionally poor., This highlights the urgent need for comprehensive poverty alleviation strategies. With 69.9% of the multidimensionally poor living in rural areas, targeted rural development programs are essential.

Civil registration and the enrollment of residents, including children, have made significant progress in 2023 and 2024 as part of the Mauritanian government's efforts to modernize and secure national identification systems. In response to the difficulties faced by the population, particularly in rural areas, in gaining access to biometric civil status, the government conducted a nationwide registration campaign deploying 54 mobile teams from September 2023 to February 2024. This initiative, supported by an off-line electronic system, has enabled 700,000 people, including 343,803 children aged 0-10, to be registered in the hardest-to-reach areas.

The Mauritanian Ministry of Economy and Finance, in collaboration with UNICEF, validated the nutrition framework documents which led to the validation of the new nutrition policy horizon 2035 and the multi-sector nutrition strategic plan 2024-2030[EM3] . The integration of a budget line for nutritional inputs in the 2024 finance law for a total of 1,600,000 USD gave visibility to the program internationally and led to the mobilization of additional innovative funds for a total of 1,200,000 USD with Matching Funds. This investment of domestic resources and mobilization of additional funds demonstrate a commitment to addressing malnutrition.

The government has been implementing an ambitious education reform under the third national development program (PNDSE 3) for the past two years, with a clear focus on improving access, quality, and inclusivity, particularly for marginalized groups. While the reform demonstrates strong commitment and vision, certain challenges in its rapid implementation could impact its ability to fully reach the most vulnerable populations.

In December, under Mauritania's leadership as the chairperson of the African Union, the country successfully hosted the Continental Education Conference,  under the auspice of the African Union and support of by UNICEF. The event saw significant participation from across the continent and internationally, with four presidents, 30 ministers of education, and over 150 experts and resource persons attending. This conference focused on transformative education priorities for Africa and was organized in close collaboration with administrative authorities, the WCAR regional office,  UNICEF Mauritania  and headquarters. The follow-up on the Nouakchott Declaration will ensure Mauritania and the continent's commitments are upheld. The successful organization of the event demonstrated strategic UNICEFpositioning in the education agenda in  African.

Mauritania continues to face high levels of gender-based violence (GBV). According to the EDS 2019-2020, 6% of women aged 15-49 reported experiencing sexual violence in the 12 months before the survey, with rates higher in rural areas (8%) than in urban areas (4%). The draft "Al Karama" law against GBV has not yet been passed, but recent cases of sexual violence have sparked strong public reactions, leading to greater mobilization and louder demands for stronger legal protections. Despite deeply rooted social resistance, this growing public awareness brings new energy to ongoing advocacy efforts to push for the adoption of the law and better protect women and girls. Under the leadership of UNICEF and in close coordination with UNFPA, OHCHR, an integrated program for prevention and combating sexual violence against girls and women will be proposed to the Government.

Climate change (extreme heat, water scarcity and flooding) poses a growing threat to children's rights in Mauritania. The severe flooding in the Gorgol and Guidimakha regions in October 2024, which displaced thousands of families [EM1] [AD2] and causing major crop losses, demonstrates the vulnerability of children to environmental shocks. The coordination leadership and response by national, regional and local authorities are commendable. It included food and water delivery, and financial aid. However, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports that these exceptional floods will become more frequent in near future highlighting the need for robust disaster management and climate resilience strategies for hundreds of thousands of people living along the River Senegal.

In 2024, with the support of UNICEF, Mauritania developed and validated two major social policy strategies: the National Social Protection Strategy II (2025–2034) and the National Strategy for Inclusion and Promotion of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2025–2034). These strategies mark substantial progress towards a more inclusive social protection system, particularly for persons with disabilities. Additionally, in December 2024, with UNICEF’s support, the Mauritanian Minister of Social Action, Childhood, and Family (MASEF) launched the tenth phase of a cash transfer program in Nouakchott, benefiting 12,000 families with a person with disability This initiative aims to enhance living conditions for vulnerable groups and promote equality and inclusion.

Mauritania is grappling with a complex migration situation, heavily influenced by the ongoing instability in neighboring Mali. The security challenges and humanitarian crises in Mali, including conflict and displacement, have led to an increase of almost 40% of the influx of refugees compared to 2023. As of November 2024, Hodh El Chargui has received 262,748 Malian refugees, with 115,150 in the M’bera camp and 147,598 in Fassala and Megve. Due to Mali's political instability, more arrivals are anticipated. The M’bera camp, originally designed for 70,000, now hosts 115,150 refugees, leading to overcrowding, food insecurity, and social tensions. New refugees are being accommodated by local communities, further straining resources. In response, UNICEF has adjusted its support to assist both refugees and host communities. Additionally, Mauritania is experiencing an increase in irregular migration flows to Europe. The Defense Minister of Mauritania has warned that worsening security in the region is driving a surge in irregular migration through Mauritania to Spain. 

In 2024, the situation for children in Mauritania presents a mix of progress and ongoing challenges. While political stability and economic improvements create a favorable environment for advancing child rights, significant gaps persist in areas such as education, health, and protection from violence. The impacts of climate change, refugees and migration further complicate the landscape. To ensure that no child is left behind, it is crucial to continue implementing inclusive and equitable policies. Addressing these challenges requires a holistic approach that integrates economic, social, and environmental dimensions, aiming to create a sustainable and equitable future for all children in Mauritania.


[1] Figures are from the World Bank

This year was the first year of implementation of the Country Programme Document 2024-2027, derived from the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2024-2027 (UNSDCF) and aligned to the Strategy for Accelerated Growth and Shared Prosperity 2016–2030 (SCAPP) and its five-year action plan 2021–2025. The country programme vision is for every child in Mauritania – both boys and girls, including adolescent girls – and especially the most vulnerable children in suburban and rural areas, to have equitable access to and benefit from high-quality essential social services that ensure that their rights are upheld and that they can reach their full potential in a safe environment. It responds to the challenges and barriers to the realization of children's rights, by promoting multi-sectoral approaches that will help to reinforce progress towards the key results for children; enhancing support to community-based, participatory and risk-analysis approaches to consolidate community resilience and strengthening the humanitarian-development-peace nexus while enhancing systems resilience. The commitment to Mauritanian youth is reflected in the establishment of a specific "outcome" dedicated to youth participation. 

In 2024, UNICEF strategically supported the Mauritanian government's national policies on human capital and access to basic social services as outlined in the SCAPP 2016-2030, ensuring the realization of children's rights in alignment with UNICEF Mauritania CPD 2022-2024.

UNICEF Mauritania supported the “result based national programme budgeting process” through a capacity-development plan for key partners in two main areas: i) the evaluation of child-centered sectoral policies, and ii) results-based budget planning. This initiative, led by the Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF), was first implemented with the sectoral ministries responsible for Health, Education, Social affairs, and Childhood.

With the support of UNICEF, the validation of the National Education Sector Development Program (PNDSE III) for 2023-2030 was an important milestone. For the first time, the program integrated components related to gender-sensitive management, school inclusion, and risk and disaster management. In addition to the sectoral strategic framework, PNDSE was strengthened by developing a strategy document for promoting preschool education, aiming to extend early childhood education to initiation classes attached to primary schools and Koranic schools which led to an increase of the preschool enrollment rate from 9.2% to 15.2%. This strategy also facilitated negotiations with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE) and the World Bank for reallocating funds to the Basic Education Sector Support Project (PASEB2) to support preschool education. This reallocation increased the budget for preschool education, contributing to greater impact and acceleration in implementing the 2025-2030 strategy. Furthermore, the text establishing pathways between original and formal education was adopted, facilitating the integration of OOSC and requiring significant organizational efforts from original education units. Supporting the policy of school inclusion, the PNDSE III was backed by UNICEF through an analysis of the profile of school-age children and adolescents with disabilities.

UNICEF provided strategic support for Koranic education, fostering dialogue on the role of mahadras in basic education and validating pathways to formal education. With UNICEF's support, an agreement was reached on the application of the orientation law (023/2022) concerning the role of original education, and a corresponding strategy was developed. To enhance school retention among adolescents, particularly girls (transition rate 60% - RESEN 2023), UNICEF extended the digital teaching experience for language education to public schools. This initiative benefited 1,087 children and adolescents through a blended learning program, and the platform dirasaty.net is now being used in the initial training of teaching staff.

In the Health sector, UNICEF’s advocacy to the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Ministry of Health led to the revision and development of key nutrition strategy and plan. The new nutrition policy for 2035 was validated, and the multisectoral strategic nutrition plan for 2024-2030 was budgeted, integrating a common results framework. The integration of a budget line amounting $1,600,000 for nutritional inputs in the 2024 finance law enhanced the visibility of Mauritania’s Nutrition program internationally. This domestic investment facilitated the mobilization of additional funds through innovative approaches like the Matching Fund for a total of $1,200,000 to strengthen the health system in Mauritania. This approach also demonstrates the effectiveness of leveraging domestic investment to attract international funding. Furthermore, the technical and political validation of the National Vaccination Strategy 2024-2028 occurred during a transitional period for the financing and co-financing of vaccines, as Mauritania attained lower middle-income country status. This transition was reflected in the increased budget allocation for vaccine purchases in the 2025 finance law and preparing for the gradual withdrawal of GAVI support by 2028.

UNICEF has also strengthened WASH systems in Mauritania by establishing strategic assessment of service quality and strengthening of local initiatives. The cross-sectoral WASH System-Wide Sustainability Check (SWSC), supporting information systems such as the National Integrated WASH Information System and the Sanitation Data Platform along with the GLAAS survey and the development of the Communal Development Plan for Dar Naim, have enhanced governance, coordination, and sustainability of WASH services.

For Child Protection systems, intra- and intersectoral coordination was strengthened with the activation of regional protection tables and the operationalization of 57% of regional juvenile justice committees. These structures facilitated the identification of challenges, promotion of social services, and actor coordination. In fact, UNICEF significantly strengthened child protection governance and coordination in Mauritania by reorganizing the Technical Group for Child Protection (GTPE) into thematic sub-groups, enhancing the use of common case management and data collection tools. Strategic partnerships with local and international organizations led to the development of national strategic documents and the creation of Community Alerts Groups to enable communities in identifying and addressing child abuse and neglect. Additionally, the establishment of a new Children's Parliament provided a platform for 116 children, including those with disabilities, to participate in public policy development.

The juvenile justice system saw notable progress in 2024, with 56 staff from the Directorate of Judicial Protection of Children (DPJE) and regional juvenile justice committees receiving training. The use of alternative measures to detention has also progressed, with 97% of arrested children (6384 out of 6573) benefiting from diversion or alternatives to detention, compared to 35% in 2020. The revision of the decree on measures applicable to minors will further diversify alternatives to detention starting in 2025.

At the local level, UNICEF strengthened its collaboration with the Ministry of the Interior, the Promotion of Decentralization, and Local Development, specifically through the General Directorate of Local Authorities. This included supporting the training of local elected officials on the "Diwan" information system, designed to enhance the administrative and financial management of municipalities. Moreover, UNICEF facilitated the update of Dar Naim’s municipal development plan, ensuring that it explicitly integrated priorities for children.

UNICEF's support extended to vulnerable households, particularly those with persons with disabilities. The social assistance program was expanded to include an additional 5,000 households, increasing the total coverage to 12,000 households. Furthermore, 500 households received productive grants to enhance their economic capacities and resilience, providing opportunities to generate income and alleviate poverty. Through a strategic partnership with the Tekavoul Cash Transfer Program, nearly 4,000 households with persons with disabilities were integrated, with a goal to include all poor households with persons with disabilities by 2030.

To improve data collection and access to services, UNICEF provided essential technical assistance. This included integrating disability into data collection tools, which significantly increased the registration rate of persons with disabilities from 1.39% in 2010 to 10% in 2024. Additionally, 13,709 disability cards were issued in 2024, facilitating access to rights and services, with 30% of beneficiaries connected to the National Health Insurance Fund (CNAM). Specific training sessions were also organized for MASEF staff to enhance their skills in managing inclusive social services and information systems.

In addition to the strategic achievements in support to national policies, UNICEF strengthened the resilience of vulnerable populations to shocks caused by refugees, poverty, and climate change through an integrated and multi-sectoral approach declined by   three pre-defined windows of opportunity and will be embedded into communal and regional plans.
The first window, 1,000 days, from pregnancy to a child's second birthday, is identified as a critical window for physical, cognitive, and potential development. This period emphasizes a holistic, integrated, multi-sectoral approach to prevent and manage malnutrition and childhood diseases leveraging community platforms, prevent Female Genital Mutilations (FGM) as well as promoting Birth Registration and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (KRC1,2,7,8). This strategic focus ensures comprehensive support during this crucial developmental phase. 
The second window, 9-14 years, supports access to education and retention in a supportive and protective environment. It focuses on raising awareness on children's rights and addressing harmful practices such as violence and child marriage (KRC3, 4, 5, and 6). This approach aims to create a safe and nurturing environment for children to thrive and develop their full potential.
The third opportunity window, 15-24 years, aims to empower young people in Mauritania by providing them with the necessary tools to become agents of change within their communities. This window focuses on equipping youth with skills, knowledge, and opportunities to actively contribute to their society's development and well-being. 
This multisectoral and integrated approach has led to the following results: 

The availability and utilization of health and nutrition services for mothers, newborns, children, and adolescents, particularly the most disadvantaged, improved relatively. According to administrative data, 12,709 children under five were treated for major childhood diseases, with 9,445 cases in the three priority Wilayas, compared to 8,331 in 2023. A vitamin A supplementation campaign combined with deworming reached 499,548 children aged 6-59 months (77% of the national target) and dewormed 445,800 children aged 12-59 months (77%). However, the proportion of unvaccinated children for DTP-HepB-Hib1 was 19%, compared to 4% in 2023. The dropout rate for Penta1-Penta3 was 13%, compared to 9% in 2023; out of the 63 Moughataa, 40% have a DTP-HepB-Hib3 coverage rate of 80% or higher (compared to 59% in 2023).  This decline in performance is due to the poor implementation of advanced and mobile vaccination strategies, the electoral context in 2024 which mobilized stakeholders and communities, as well as vaccination campaigns that slowed down routine vaccination activities.
The scale up of Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) interventions through community engagement strategies, including partnerships with national and international civil society organizations. Training 1,345 community health workers on IYCF practices and promoting the use of mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) by mothers resulted in 13,540 children being screened for malnutrition in their communities. 402 GASPA (Community-Based Management of Acute Malnutrition Groups) were established and managed by community agents, benefiting 45,506 pregnant and breastfeeding women. An integrated approach to FGM and birth registration has been promoted within GASPA, a key audience, since 88% of excisions take place before a girl's first birthday. 
UNICEF has improved drinking water supply systems for 26,179 people in 25 localities, including monitoring and reinforcing the first ever fully solar-powered system for treating salty water. These efforts aim to mitigate the impacts of climate variability and enhance sustainable water production, though further progress is needed in service continuity and quality. In Dar Naim, an urban poor district in Nouakchott, eight youth community service groups now assist 1,400 households (8,400 people) with waste and fecal sludge collection. The Municipal Technical Team has been empowered to support the entire population of 186,925 people with waste collection, road works, and water transport, with the support of UNICEF in providing specialized training and equipment. Community participation has improved through participatory and multisectoral assessments involving local authorities and communities. 
In partnerships with Civil Society Organizations, UNICEF Mauritania worked on an effective mechanism for integrating out-of-school children. This initiative successfully identified and integrated 3,943 children, including 1,709 girls, into the school system. Recognizing the importance of follow-up, UNICEF established tutoring and monitoring frameworks for 6,064 children to prevent dropouts and piloted a school monitoring mechanism in 15 schools across Hodh Chargui, Assaba, and Guidimakha.
To protect children from violence and harmful practices, ensuring their access to quality protection services, UNICEF Mauritania, targeted Gorgol, Guidimakha, Assaba, Hodh Charghui, and Nouakchott regions, using a comprehensive approach that combined community engagement, capacity building for protection actors, and system strengthening in both development and humanitarian contexts. UNICEF's efforts reduced children's vulnerability to violence through coordinated actions with partners and the involvement of families, communities, and youth. In 2024, a total of 23,388 people, including 15,849 children (10,402 girls), were mobilized against female genital mutilation (FGM) and child marriage through various community engagement platforms, such as Community Protection Systems, groups of pregnant and breastfeeding women, and schools.
The active participation of children and adolescents increased, positioning them as key actors in social change during events like World Children’s Day, the 16 Days of Activism, and International Women's Day. A total of 962 youth (461 girls) were trained as change agents, leading community awareness activities on the dangers of FGM, gender-based violence (GBV), and child marriage. The availability, inclusivity, and quality of protection services were significantly improved. In 2024, 853 professionals were trained on crucial topics such as children's rights, psychological first aid, and the care of violence victims, including GBV. As a result, 11,750 children who were victims of violence, exploitation, abuse, or neglect received protection services (a 50 percent increase compared to 2023 with 6745 children supported), including 6,220 girls, 243 children with disabilities, and 196 children on the move. Additionally, 6,280 children in humanitarian situations and 539 parents and caregivers received mental health and psychosocial support services.
Significant progress was made in enhancing youth participation and civic engagement in Mauritania. The SAFIA initiative expanded with a new urban center in Nema and 35 rural hubs, training 6,000 youth in leadership, digital literacy, financial education, and climate resilience. This initiative also established communal youth councils to facilitate dialogue with local authorities.
Youth-driven digital innovation included the creation of an inclusive education platform by 50 young tech enthusiasts and the "Skills on Wheels" program, which trained 100 master trainers who then empowered 2,000 youth. Gender equality was promoted through the "Ailes pour Elles" mentorship program, and the U-Talk platform amplified youth advocacy on gender-based violence.

The new country program for 2024-2027, characterized by an increased budget and expanded staff, presents significant factors to consider, particularly given the complexity and level of risks involved. This programme includes substantial funding for the cash transfer initiative and other critical components such as resilience and emergency response efforts (refugees’ response, flood response).
 
As part of the effective implementation of the new country program, the office developed and executed its Annual Management Plan focusing on five priorities covering quality assurance, financial management, people management, alliance building and partnerships, core values and workplace culture. 
 
The office maintained an adequate level of assurance in relation to disbursements made. In addition, all active civil society organizations (CSOs) were assessed in terms of Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). Minimum required Programmatic visits and spot checks for all partners were 100% completed. Two audits and thirteen micro-evaluations were also carried out, the final report will be available in 2025. Despite these advances, UNICEF must regularly strengthen the capacities of partners, particularly regarding HACT, PSEA, and anti-fraud training and ensure follow-up of recommendations from spot-checks, audits, and micro-evaluations of partners.
 
The financial performance of the institutional (BMM) and cross-cutting (GC) budgets in 2024 was satisfactory, with an execution rate of 100% for the BMM and 100% for the RR as of December 31st, 2024. The liquidity benchmark of 25% was maintained throughout 2024, except for September 2024. 
 
For the implementation of the new CPMP aligned to the new CPD 2024-2027, the office has strengthened its field presence by opening three new field offices, including two sub-offices. In this same dynamic, 31 new positions have been created, including 25 full-time (FT) positions. In terms of diversity, the office has improved its situation compared to 2023, with 43% female staff compared to 41% previously, and 2% of staff with disabilities, reaching the organization's recommended recruitment threshold. Additionally, 40% of the international staff come from donor countries, compared to 36% in 2023. The work environment has also been improved, with a spatial distribution of staff that promotes teamwork, increased security, and better well-being for the staff. An action plan is currently under development in response to the 2024 Global Staff survey.
 
As part of the talent outreach campaign efforts, Human Resources conducted awareness and promotion activities for job opportunities in collaboration with other United Nations agencies in Mauritania. These initiatives included awareness campaigns at three universities, interactions with women's professional associations, and organizations for people with disabilities. These efforts culminated in the United Nations Open Day in Mauritania on December 5, 2024, which hosted nearly 400 participants.
 
UNICEF continues to manage the premises and common services in Bassikounou, with a memorandum of understanding signed with other agencies (WFP, IOM, ILO, UNDP, UNFPA) and a clinic managed by UNHCR. This initiative has allowed UN staff to receive quality treatment in a location where no viable medical facility exists. The offices in Kiffa and Sélibaby have been operational since the beginning of 2024, led respectively by WFP and IOM. The Nema office has been temporarily opened, pending the completion of the new premises, which will be led by UNHCR.
 
UNICEF Mauritania's accessibility project, funded by the Greening & Accessibility Fund resulted in the construction of a toilet, access ramps, and a parking area for people with disabilities at the Nouakchott office, achieving level 2 accessibility. Regulation kits were installed to automatically turn off air conditioners after 5 minutes of inactivity, reducing energy bills by 20% in Nouakchott and Bassiknou. Furthermore, the office received four vehicles from the UNFLEET program, designed to meet average consumption standards, contributing to ozone layer protection. These initiatives have significantly enhanced inclusivity and environmental sustainability at UNICEF Mauritania.

In 2024, UNICEF Mauritania achieved several key results in areas of Partnerships and Resource Mobilization. 

For achieving results, the office successfully implemented its Partnerships and Resource Mobilization Strategy and its Action Plan, which outlines common priorities with various partners, and emphasizes the importance of diversifying our donor base. 

Based on this strategy, UNICEF Mauritania engaged dialogues with key partners at the ambassador level, including traditional government partners such as Germany, the US, the EU, and Japan, as well as an emerging government partner, Qatar. The office also engaged with a regional financial institution, the African Development Bank (AfDB), and the President of the Chamber of Commerce for developing partnerships with the private sector in Mauritania. These engagements were complemented by three high-level donor visits from Spain's State Secretary for International Cooperation, and German Parliamentarians and the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), focusing on our resilience programme, social protection programme and SAFIA Youth Center. Several technical-level meetings with potential private partners took place. Foundations and companies from abroad approached UNICEF for potential collaboration in health, education and youth empowerment. 

In terms of South-South cooperation, UNICEF has initiated negotiations with China, India and Turkey. A first capacity developpement exchange plan has been engaged with Morocco.

In terms of resource mobilization, in 2024, UNICEF Mauritania received contributions of about US$24 million (source: Funding Dashboard on InSight), including from new partners such as Lind Foundation via Danish NatCom. Out of the total contribution received, 8.47% (US$2 million) was earmarked for emergency response. 96.98% (US$ 23 million) came from public partners, and 3.02% (US$ 1 million) came from private partners. The top resource partner by far was Germany, followed by UNOCHA, the United States of America and Spain. Other partners include Norway for non-thematic fund for Social Protection, French NatCom for Nutrition and Danish NatCom for Youth. 15 proposals are currently in the pipeline with donors such as AfDB for WASH and BPRM for Education and Education Above All. UNICEF continued to strengthen its strategic partnerships through proactive communication and quality reporting, 100% of donors’ reports were submitted on time.

Our collaboration with other UN agencies was also a highlight. UNICEF Mauritania closely worked with WFP mainly on two programmes: Resilience and Social Protection. The office mobilized resources jointly with WHO and UNFPA for CERF (Health and Nutrition), finalized a proposal for a joint programme of the Peace Building Fund with IOM for WASH, and developed a concept note for the Peace Building Fund with WFP and UNDP. Under the leadership and coordination of the Resident Coordinator’s office, UN agencies in Mauritania are developing a proposal on resilience, involving seven agencies and a budget of $120M, building on the existing UNICEF-WFP resilience programme.

In terms of our engagement with international financial institutions, our partnership with the AfDB was strengthened by clearly identifying our common priorities—WASH and Climate. We increased our engagement with the AfDB by holding a meeting with the General Deputy Director for North Africa and the Country Manager for Mauritania. One proposal is currently on a waiting list, and we are finalizing another proposal for emergency WASH support.

This year, UNICEF Mauritania adopted a new advocacy strategy focusing on four key priorities: education, nutrition, the fight against gender-based violence (GBV). In the education sector, strategic efforts were deployed, particularly around the Continental Education Conference and the national education reform, to ensure the inclusion of all children in the education system. These engagements reinforced government commitments and mobilized stakeholders towards policies promoting equitable and accessible education for all. In terms of gender-based violence (GBV), advocacy efforts intensified with decision-makers and civil society to push forward the adoption of the draft law on violence against women and girls, fostering political will and sustaining momentum for legal protection frameworks. 

Additionally, significant efforts were made to promote the adoption of national strategies on disability inclusion and social protection, ensuring that the most vulnerable children and families are integrated into national policies. UNICEF collaborated with the Ministry of Economy and Finance to implement the child-sensitive public finance roadmap (PF4C) and worked on revitalizing the Public Finance Working Group, including actors such as the World Bank, Expertise France, USAID, and the European Union. This strategic positioning of UNICEF aims to create a strategic exchange space to coordinate institutional support initiatives and best practices in public finance management in favor of children. 
Through these coordinated advocacy actions, UNICEF Mauritania has reinforced its influence on key policy decisions, driving long-term impacts on child rights and protection across the country.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
The increased influx of new refugees in the Hodh El Chargui Region posed significant challenges to host communities, stretching the accessibility of basic services and impacting the quality of interventions. UNICEF quickly adapted to this new trend by mobilizing additional resources and building partnerships to respond effectively. This adaptive approach demonstrated UNICEF's agility in addressing emerging challenges. However, the surge in refugee numbers has further stretched UNICEF's resources, exacerbating existing funding gaps. In 2024, only 25% of the $10 million required for Mauritania has been secured under UNICEF’s Regional Humanitarian Action for Children Appeal (HAC).

UNICEF's advocacy led to a draft roadmap for reducing maternal and neonatal mortality, highlighting the importance of continuous advocacy and coordination. However, coordination issues among ministries delayed fund disbursement for nutritional inputs. Despite efforts, additional domestic resources for measles vaccination were not mobilized, leading to reliance on the World Bank. Vaccination coverage rates declined due to limited implementation of strategies and the electoral context. Corrective measures, including the "grand rattrapage" strategy, are underway to address these challenges. Continuous advocacy and flexible funding mechanisms are essential for effective public health initiatives.

In 2024, persistent challenges with WASH infrastructure sustainability and quality were identified, for which UNICEF could play a better role in advocating with and supporting the government for addressing these issues. Additionally, the drilling of negative or salty water borehole highlighted the need for improving the quality and protocols of geophysical studies for borehole siting implemented by both the public service (CNRE) and the private consultancy companies. Moving forward, UNICEF will focus on enhancing project design, monitoring, and control, and leveraging successful community engagement efforts to strengthen WASH outcomes.

The implementation of the Education system reform faced challenges, as the public education system was not yet ready to offer quality education or meet potential demand. A strong advocacy effort is needed to support a smooth and effective transition, while ensuring the inclusion of the most vulnerable children and maintaining quality standards. Programs for out-of-school children showed impressive results in reducing non-enrollment, and UNICEF is exploring the potential of second-chance schools such as SAFIA to further improve education access. 

UNICEF Mauritania continued to strengthen the Child Protection system confirming its strategic position for Child Protection in Mauritania. However, the limited capacity of regional MASEF directorates and the absence of fully decentralized structures have posed challenges to child protection efforts, leading to a reliance on NGOs. While their support has been instrumental, it highlights the need for more sustainable and locally anchored solutions. Harmful social norms remain deeply entrenched in communities. A deeper analysis and understanding of practices and beliefs are necessary to overcome the barriers to behavior and social change. Synergy with other social sectors will help sustain interventions and reach the most vulnerable children.

The strategic mobilization of youth as agents of change demonstrated its transformative impact. During the HPV vaccination campaign in Dar Naim, the active involvement of young people led to an unprecedented result: over 1,900 girls were vaccinated in one week. This approach not only enhanced the effectiveness of public health interventions but also highlighted the role of youth in advocacy and community engagement. Additionally, the governmental change with the rehabilitation of a Ministry of Youth with an expanded portfolio opened new opportunities but also required time to align and adjust priorities. UNICEF Mauritania will continue to leverage the energy and potential of youth to drive positive change and achieve impactful results.

Funding challenges continue to impede the implementation of social protection strategies and inclusive policies. To address this, it is essential to strengthen partnerships with the Ministry of Budget and appoint a focal point for Public Finance for Children (PF4C) to improve budget planning. Additionally, enhancing the capacity of local authorities and field actors is vital for fostering inclusive and resilient governance. Regular and structured coordination with UN agencies, as well as local and regional actors, can further boost the success of social protection programs and advocacy initiatives.

For Resource Mobilization and Partnerships, the private sector plays a significant role in having impacts on children and their families’ life in the country. Although the office successfully materialized several partnerships with companies (Société Générale Mauritanie, tele-communication companies for U-report), UNICEF Mauritania aim to develop meaningful engagement with business leaders to influence their business practices and Corporate Social Responsibility policies, as elaborated in our Partnerships and Resource Mobilization Strategy and Country Report for Private Sector Engagement. 

Leveraging flexible resources is essential for reducing transactional costs and enhancing program efficiency. For instance, flexible funding, such as the Norway thematic fund, building on our previous experience with them, helped bridge the funding gap in Social Protection and reduced transactional costs for proposal writing and reporting. Another positive example was with Canadian NatCom, which helped us simplify the proposal writing procedure. Although the project has not been started yet, UNICEF Mauritania will build on these positive experiences to reduce inefficiency and transactional costs coming from heavy proposal and report writing, by developing trust-based relationships with partners. Additionally, the office will seize opportunities with new partners, such as NatCom partners and private companies, to highlight the importance of flexible resources for optimizing our programs and maximizing the impact of their contributions. This advocacy for quality funding needs to be a collaborative effort with sister agencies, international and national NGOs and like-minded governments at country, regional and HQ levels.

To ensure programme effectiveness, it is crucial to support the national statistical system in providing reliable data for effective programming and monitoring of children’s rights. The current lack of recent statistical data and evidence presents significant challenges. To address this, a Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) is planned for 2025 in collaboration with the National Statistics Office, along with the finalization of the Situation Analysis (SITAN) in collaboration with MASEF, which will serve as a child rights monitoring tool. As we embark on the second year of the new country programme cycle, it is essential for the office to document lessons learned and conduct the evaluations outlined in its evaluation costed plan to inform systematic reviews of the programme’s theory of change, allowing for timely adjustments for the realisation of child rights in Mauritania.

Le Niger est un pays fragile, sans accès littoral, à très faible revenu, dont l’économie peu diversifiée est largement dépendante de l’agriculture de subsistance, l’élevage et l’exploitation minière. 
Malgré la reprise de la croissance avec la levée des sanctions en février 2024 et de certains partenariats, le déficit budgétaire est de 4,4 % du PIB au titre de l’année 2024, au-delà du seuil de 3% fixé par l’UEMOA. On estime qu'environ 7,5 % du PIB du financement externe au développement ont été perdus en 2023 suite au coup d'État du 26 juillet 2023, perturbant ainsi l’approvisionnement en produits essentiels et limitant les ressources budgétaires allouées aux secteurs sociaux. 
D’autre part, la forte croissance démographique (3,7%) met une pression supplémentaire sur l’offre des services dans un contexte marqué par un défaut d’investissements pour saisir la fenêtre d’opportunité d’un dividende démographique.
Le pays est particulièrement exposé aux chocs climatiques, notamment la sécheresse, les inondations et la désertification, qui ont accru la volatilité de la croissance et entraîné des crises humanitaires concomitantes (insécurité alimentaire, déplacement interne). En 2024, 1,5 million de personnes ont été touchées par des pluies intenses, causant 396 décès et détruisant les cultures et les infrastructures de base (écoles, centres de santé). Ces catastrophes ont favorisé la recrudescence d’épidémies, avec 1 064 cas de choléra déclarés, ainsi que des flambées de rougeole, méningite et dengue.
Parallèlement, les besoins humanitaires ont augmenté de 20% en un an, touchant 4,3 millions de personnes. L’insécurité alimentaire aiguë affecte 3,4 millions de Nigériens, notamment en raison des crises climatiques et des perturbations économiques.
Sur le plan sécuritaire, le Niger fait face à des défis persistants, notamment dans les zones frontalières avec le Mali et le Burkina Faso, où la présence de groupes armés non étatiques complexifie la protection des populations et l'accès aux services sociaux de base malgré les efforts du gouvernement pour renforcer la résilience communautaire et améliorer la sécurisation des territoires.
Au niveau politique, le pays connaît une période de transition depuis le coup d’État de juillet 2023. La suspension des financements de plusieurs donateurs, la fermeture des frontières et l’annonce le 28 janvier 2024 du retrait "immédiat" des trois pays de l’Alliance des États du Sahel (AES) de la Communauté économique des États d'Afrique de l'Ouest (CEDEAO) ont marqué un tournant décisif. Pour l’instant, ces pays restent membres de l'UEMOA mais se sont engagés à travailler sur une nouvelle union monétaire dans le cadre de l’AES. Ces évolutions ont eu des impacts économiques directs. Les besoins en dépenses restent importants et pressants, en raison des dépenses de sécurité élevées, tandis que la mobilisation des recettes intérieures reste faible, l'insécurité et les sanctions ayant réduit les recettes fiscales. 
Des réformes clés ont été engagées, notamment dans les domaines de la protection sociale, la nutrition, la vaccination, l’éducation et l’eau et l’assainissement, avec l’appui de l’UNICEF et de ses partenaires.
L’extrême pauvreté a stagné à 48,4 % en 2024 alors que 78% souffre de la pauvreté multidimensionnelle (ODD 1). Pour atténuer les effets de la crise, un filet de sécurité sociale soutenu par l’UNICEF, a été lancé pour fournir une aide financière aux ménages les plus vulnérables.
L’UNICEF a soutenu le renforcement du système de santé (ODD 3) en assurant la vaccination de 831 734 enfants au Penta 3, atteignant 102% de la cible contre 101% et de 819 221 enfants contre la rougeole, avec une couverture de 100,17% contre 100% en 2023. Parallèlement, le taux d’abandon vaccinal a diminué, passant de 5,2% en 2023 à 4,18% en 2024."
La mortalité maternelle et néonatale a été déclarée « urgence de santé publique » après un dialogue national. En 2024, 53% des accouchements ont été assistés par du personnel qualifié, contre 43% en 2023, mais la mortalité néonatale reste préoccupante, ayant augmenté de 24% à 43 pour 1 000 naissances vivantes entre 2012 et 2021.
Le taux d’enfants hors du système éducatif (ODD 4) a légèrement baissé (de 52% en 2023 à 50% en 2024), mais les filles restent particulièrement affectées. Une note sectorielle validée par le gouvernement et ses partenaires dont l’UNICEF, intègre désormais des approches de financements innovants pour l’amélioration des acquis scolaires.
L’une des réponses pour faire face à ces défis est le développement des programmes d’apprentissage numérique à laquelle l’UNICEF a contribué facilitant ainsi l’accès à des formations professionnalisantes au profit des jeunes.
L’accès à l’eau potable (ODD 6) a légèrement progressé, passant de 49% en 2022 à 50% en 2024. La défécation à l’air libre a diminué, passant de 68,1% en 2021 à 62% en 2024, grâce à des initiatives comme l’Assainissement Total Piloté par la Communauté (ATPC) et à des investissements dans des infrastructures hydrauliques résilientes au climat.
Le gouvernement a pris des mesures significatives pour protéger les enfants (ODD 16) et améliorer la santé maternelle et néonatale. Il a lancé un plan stratégique national contre le mariage des enfants lors de la Journée internationale de la jeune fille. 
Face aux défis du pays, l’UNICEF a ajusté sa stratégie en renforçant l’approche nexus, alliant aide humanitaire, développement et résilience communautaire. L’organisation a soutenu le renforcement des capacités à travers la gouvernance locale, la mobilisation de financements innovants et l’essor des solutions numériques en éducation, vaccination et protection sociale. Elle a également intensifié sa collaboration avec les partenaires pour optimiser les ressources et maximiser l’impact.
L’alignement des interventions du Programme de Coopération avec le Programme de Résilience pour la Sauvegarde de la Patrie (PRSP) et le Cadre de coopération des Nations Unies pour le développement durable (UNSDCF) (2023-2027) a renforcé l’alignement et la cohérence avec les priorités nationales visant la réduction des inégalités et la promotion du bien-être des enfants.
