Le Niger a maintenu ses efforts visant à réduire la pauvreté multidimensionnelle des enfants et renforcer le système de protection sociale, malgré un contexte budgétaire contraignant. Une avancée majeure en 2024 a été la validation par le gouvernement d’une feuille de route pour l’élaboration et l’institutionnalisation de la Politique Nationale de Protection Sociale (PNPS), visant à consolider les acquis de la mise en place des filets sociaux et à améliorer l’inclusion économique des populations vulnérables.
L’UNICEF a joué un rôle clé dans la mobilisation des ressources au niveau central et décentralisé, garantissant un financement durable pour les secteurs sociaux prioritaires. Grâce à ces financements, le gouvernement a pu améliorer les mécanismes de transferts sociaux, facilitant une réponse plus efficace aux chocs économiques et climatiques.
Dans ce cadre, 26 926 ménages vulnérables répartis dans 344 villages de 17 communes ont bénéficié de transferts monétaires en trois cycles de paiement (décembre 2023 – octobre 2024). Cette assistance a permis d’atténuer les effets des crises économiques et climatiques, avec un accompagnement à travers les de campagnes de sensibilisation visant à renforcer la résilience communautaire et améliorer l’accès aux services sociaux.
L’inclusion des personnes en situation de handicap a également progressé avec la mise en place d’un filet de sécurité sociale pilote, en partenariat avec la Fédération Nigérienne des Personnes Handicapées (FNPH). Ce dispositif assure une assistance ciblée, incluant des allocations financières et un accès facilité aux services essentiels, avec des avancées notables vers le déploiement de la carte d’égalité des chances (CEC) pour renforcer l’accès aux services de base pour les personnes en situation de handicap.
Dans une approche intégrée, l’UNICEF a renforcé le Nexus humanitaire-développement-paix, intégrant la protection sociale dans les réponses aux crises humanitaires et climatiques. Des dispositifs de préparation et de réponse aux chocs ont été mis en place dans plusieurs communes, couvrant 25 000 personnes affectées par des catastrophes naturelles et conflits, avec un focus sur les enfants.
Grâce à ces initiatives, le Niger progresse vers un système de protection sociale plus inclusif et résilient, combinant interventions d’urgence et réformes structurelles pour mieux protéger les populations vulnérables.
6. Gestion des programmes et optimisation des ressources
En 2024, des efforts significatifs ont été déployés pour améliorer le suivi des programmes, la gestion des ressources et l'efficacité opérationnelle, permettant d’obtenir des résultats notables malgré un contexte complexe marqué par des contraintes sécuritaires et logistiques.
Toutefois, des défis persistants ont nécessité des mesures de mitigation pour garantir l’efficacité des interventions. Les restrictions de mouvement ont limité la supervision directe sur le terrain, obligeant l’UNICEF à renforcer le suivi via RapidPro et des contrôles par des tiers (ONG partenaires et autorités locales). 
Par ailleurs, la gestion financière a été optimisée grâce à une meilleure application des procédures HACT, réduisant ainsi les risques liés à la conformité et améliorant la redevabilité des partenaires.
L’optimisation des processus d’achats et de gestion des stocks a permis d’exécuter 96,7 % du plan d’achat annuel, atteignant 41,1 millions USD, soit une augmentation de 19,8 % par rapport à 2023. La gestion des stocks a également été renforcée pour limiter les risques de pénuries, notamment pour les intrants nutritionnels et les vaccins. Grâce à une surveillance accrue et une meilleure coordination logistique, les ruptures d’approvisionnement dans les centres de santé ont été réduites de 50 % en mars à 6 % en juin 2024.
L’UNICEF a également intensifié l’usage des outils numériques pour le suivi des programmes et des dépenses, renforçant ainsi la transparence et la redevabilité. L’adoption d’un tableau de bord numérique pour la gestion des performances a facilité le suivi en temps réel des interventions, améliorant ainsi la prise de décision et l’efficacité des actions sur le terrain.
Dans le cadre du renforcement institutionnel, la Stratégie de Diversité, d’Équité et d’Inclusion (DEI) a été mise en œuvre pour favoriser un environnement de travail plus inclusif. Un accent particulier a été mis sur l'équilibre géographique et la parité de genre, garantissant une meilleure représentativité du personnel et une gestion plus efficace des ressources humaines.
En parallèle, des efforts ont été déployés pour renforcer la prévention et la réponse aux abus et exploitations sexuelles dans le cadre des interventions humanitaires. En 2024, 86 650 personnes ont été sensibilisées sur les canaux de signalement des cas d’exploitation et d’abus sexuels (EAS), tandis que 124 990 personnes, dont 80 121 enfants, ont bénéficié d’interventions de prévention et de réponse aux violences basées sur le genre (VBG).
Afin de garantir un soutien adéquat aux survivantes, 4 000 victimes de VBG, dont 1 431 filles, ont reçu une prise en charge intégrée, incluant un accompagnement médical, psychosocial, juridique et un appui à la réinsertion.
Enfin, l’UNICEF a renforcé ses mécanismes de suivi et d’audit, permettant de clore 99 % des points d’action issus des vérifications et audits en 2024. Cette gestion proactive a contribué à améliorer la performance globale des programmes, assurant une meilleure utilisation des ressources et une protection accrue des bénéficiaires.

L’UNICEF a renforcé ses collaborations stratégiques avec le gouvernement, les agences des Nations Unies, les partenaires techniques et financiers, ainsi que la société civile, afin de maximiser l’impact des interventions sur le bien-être des enfants. Dans un contexte marqué par des crises politiques et humanitaires, ces partenariats ont été essentiels pour assurer la continuité des services sociaux de base, mobiliser des financements et innover dans la mise en œuvre des programmes.
L’UNICEF a maintenu un dialogue constant avec les autorités nationales et locales afin de garantir l’intégration des priorités de l’enfance dans les politiques publiques et faciliter l’accès aux enfants et leurs parents. L’organisation a soutenu le renforcement des capacités institutionnelles, notamment à travers l’appui au Programme Élargi de Vaccination, à la réforme du système éducatif et à la mise en place d’un filet de protection sociale inclusif.
Le partenariat avec le ministère de l’Intérieur a permis d’informatiser 102 communes pour la modernisation du système d’état civil, facilitant ainsi l’enregistrement des naissances et l’accès aux droits fondamentaux. De même, l’UNICEF a accompagné la révision de la stratégie nationale de nutrition, en concertation avec le ministère de la Santé, afin d’assurer une approche multisectorielle et durable pour lutter contre la malnutrition infantile.
L’UNICEF a joué un rôle clé dans la coordination humanitaire, en assurant le leadership des clusters Éducation, WASH et Nutrition, ainsi que du sous-cluster Protection de l’enfance. La collaboration avec le PAM, l’OMS, le FNUAP et la FAO a permis entre autres une approche intégrée, en combinant interventions d’urgence et renforcement des systèmes nationaux. Par exemple, le partenariat avec le PAM a facilité la prise en charge conjointe de la malnutrition, en liant les distributions alimentaires aux activités de prévention et de traitement dans les centres de santé.
La mobilisation de ressources a également été un élément central des partenariats avec les bailleurs de fonds, notamment la Banque mondiale, l’Union européenne, l’USAID et la Coopération suédoise, la Coopération allemande qui ont contribué au financement des services sociaux essentiels. Le Niger a pu mobiliser 142 millions de dollars du Partenariat Mondial pour l’Éducation (PME), un financement historique qui permettra d’accélérer l’éducation des filles et d’améliorer la gouvernance du secteur éducatif.
L’UNICEF a renforcé son engagement avec les organisations locales et la société civile afin d’ancrer ses interventions dans les réalités communautaires. Le travail avec les ONG nationales et internationales a facilité l’extension des services de protection de l’enfance et la réponse aux violences basées sur le genre, en formant des acteurs locaux et en renforçant les mécanismes de signalement.
Le partenariat avec le secteur privé a également permis de développer des solutions innovantes, notamment dans le domaine de l’accès à l’eau et de l’éducation numérique. Par exemple, la collaboration avec Airtel a soutenu la connectivité des écoles et des centres de jeunes à travers des solutions d’apprentissage en ligne, tandis que des entreprises locales ont été impliquées dans la production et la commercialisation de serviettes hygiéniques pour améliorer la gestion de l’hygiène menstruelle des filles en milieu scolaire.
L’UNICEF a continué d’amplifier la voix des jeunes à travers U-Report Muryar Matassa, une plateforme interactive qui permet aux adolescents et jeunes de s’exprimer sur des sujets de développement et de proposer des solutions adaptées à leur réalité. En 2024, U-Report a dépassé les 60 000 utilisateurs actifs, facilitant la diffusion d’informations clés sur la santé, l’éducation et la protection de l’enfance.
À travers des sondages interactifs et des campagnes de sensibilisation, U-Report a permis de mobiliser plus de 26 754 jeunes sur des enjeux communautaires, tout en servant d’outil de plaidoyer pour influencer les politiques locales et nationales. L’intégration de cette plateforme dans les initiatives éducatives et de protection sociale a renforcé l’inclusion des jeunes dans les processus de décision et amélioré l’engagement des communautés sur les questions liées aux droits de l’enfant.
Dans un contexte en évolution, l’UNICEF continue de s’appuyer sur des partenariats stratégiques pour maximiser l’impact de ses interventions. L’organisation promeut une approche multisectorielle et inclusive, en intégrant les acteurs gouvernementaux, les agences des Nations Unies, les bailleurs de fonds, la société civile et le secteur privé dans une réponse coordonnée aux défis du Niger.
En 2024, grâce à sa stratégie de plaidoyer, l’UNICEF a mobilisé 800 leaders communautaires et religieux, ainsi que la société civile, pour amplifier la sensibilisation aux droits des enfants.
Les médias et plateformes numériques ont joué un rôle clé dans la communication et la mobilisation. 16 médias nationaux et internationaux ont couvert les actions de l’UNICEF, aboutissant à 2 500 articles publiés et à un téléthon national ayant mobilisé 1,3 milliard FCFA pour lutter contre la mortalité maternelle et néonatale. 
Sur les réseaux sociaux, 150 vidéos et photos ont touché 6,5 millions de personnes, tandis que des initiatives innovantes comme Facebook Live et #227TALKS junior ont favorisé le débat public et l'engagement des jeunes.
La mobilisation sociale a également été renforcée par l’implication de 300 artistes et 50 influenceurs, qui ont sensibilisé 10 millions de personnes aux droits des enfants à travers les 8 régions du Niger.
Sur le plan de la mobilisation des ressources, l’UNICEF a organisé 3 réunions de plaidoyer avec les Ambassadeurs et Chefs de Coopération, contribuant à la requête de financement du Partenariat Mondial pour l’Éducation. L’organisation a également pris part à 6 rencontres internationales, dont un web event sur la résilience au Sahel, en partenariat avec la coopération allemande et le Bureau Régional.
Ces efforts ont permis de renforcer la visibilité des programmes de l’UNICEF, d’amplifier l’engagement des partenaires et d’optimiser les financements pour maximiser l’impact des interventions en faveur des enfants.
En renforçant la résilience des systèmes nationaux et en plaçant les communautés et les jeunes au cœur des solutions, l’UNICEF contribue à bâtir un environnement plus protecteur, équitable et durable pour chaque enfant au Niger.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
En 2024, le Niger a été confronté à une conjoncture particulièrement difficile, marquée par la crise de la trésorerie nationale des crises humanitaires, des chocs climatiques et des contraintes budgétaires. La suspension des financements de certains partenaires, la fermeture des frontières et l’instabilité régionale ont réduit la capacité du pays à fournir des services sociaux essentiels, aggravant la vulnérabilité des enfants et des populations précaires.
L’insécurité persistante, notamment dans les zones frontalières, a entravé l’accès aux services et perturbé la mise en œuvre des programmes. De nombreuses écoles ont dû fermer, laissant des milliers d’enfants sans accès à l’éducation. Bien que des alternatives aient été mises en place, notamment des espaces d’apprentissage temporaires, la sécurisation des infrastructures scolaires reste un défi majeur.
L’approvisionnement en intrants nutritionnels et médicaux a également été un enjeu critique. Les sanctions économiques et les fermetures de frontières ont provoqué des ruptures de stocks dans plusieurs centres de santé. Grâce à une meilleure gestion logistique et à la réallocation des stocks, les ruptures d’approvisionnement ont chuté de 50% en mars à seulement 6% en juin 2024.
Les chocs climatiques ont également fragilisé les infrastructures. Plus de 1,5 million de personnes ont été affectées par des inondations massives, mettant sous pression les services d’eau, d’assainissement et d’hygiène (EAH) et augmentant les risques de maladies hydriques.
Face à ces défis, plusieurs enseignements clés ont émergé en 2024.
L’adaptabilité des interventions a été cruciale. Dans un contexte marqué par des restrictions de mouvement, l’UNICEF a renforcé ses dispositifs de suivi à distance à travers RapidPro et des contrôles par des tiers, garantissant ainsi une supervision efficace malgré les contraintes d’accès.
La diversification des financements est devenue une nécessité. La suspension des aides extérieures a mis en évidence l’urgence d’explorer des mécanismes de financement flexibles et innovants. En appuyant les collectivités locales dans l’optimisation de leurs ressources fiscales, l’UNICEF a contribué à sécuriser des financements domestiques pour les services sociaux.
L’innovation a joué un rôle clé dans l’efficacité des interventions. L’accélération de la digitalisation a permis d’optimiser le suivi des services essentiels, notamment en vaccination, nutrition et éducation. L’utilisation accrue des plateformes numériques a amélioré la prise de décision et renforcé la transparence.
L’approche Nexus s’est avérée essentielle pour intégrer la protection sociale dans la réponse humanitaire. L’expansion des transferts monétaires a permis d’atténuer l’impact des chocs climatiques et économiques sur les ménages vulnérables, tout en renforçant leur résilience.
Enfin, la crise politique a mis en évidence la nécessité de partenariats solides avec les acteurs locaux. La collaboration accrue avec la société civile et les collectivités locales a été déterminante pour garantir la continuité des services essentiels.
Pour assurer la pérennité des services sociaux et renforcer la résilience des systèmes, l’UNICEF prévoit d’intensifier ses efforts dans plusieurs domaines stratégiques.
Le développement de financements innovants sera une priorité. L’UNICEF continuera à renforcer les réformes fiscales locales pour augmenter les investissements dans les secteurs sociaux. L’exploration de mécanismes de financement mixtes, combinant des contributions publiques, privées et internationales, permettra d’assurer une plus grande stabilité financière.
L’amélioration de l’accès aux services en zones d’insécurité est un autre enjeu clé. L’extension des espaces d’apprentissage alternatifs pour les enfants déplacés et la mise en place de réseaux logistiques résilients seront renforcées pour limiter les ruptures d’approvisionnement.
L’accélération de la digitalisation continuera d’être un axe central. Le renforcement des plateformes numériques facilitera un suivi plus efficace des services de santé, d’éducation et de nutrition. Par ailleurs, l’intégration de technologies solaires garantira un accès durable à l’eau potable et aux infrastructures sanitaires.
La Protection contre l’Exploitation et les Abus Sexuels (PSEA) restera une priorité, avec des actions renforcées en sensibilisation communautaire et en prise en charge des survivantes.
L’UNICEF a adapté sa stratégie de communication et de plaidoyer en développant des contenus multimédias ciblés, mettant en avant la résilience du Niger face aux défis et l’impact du soutien des partenaires. Ces supports ont non seulement sensibilisé le public, mais aussi contribué à solliciter de nouveaux financements, en démontrant l’effet direct des contributions sur la vie des enfants et des femmes.
La synergie entre médias, artistes, influenceurs digitaux et plateformes numériques a amplifié la portée des messages sur les droits des enfants. Des initiatives comme #227TALKS junior et Facebook Live ont renforcé le débat public et permis aux jeunes de s’exprimer sur des questions clés. Ces innovations seront pérennisées et élargies en 2025.
Enfin, une meilleure coordination entre les communicateurs des ministères sectoriels, sous l’autorité du ministère de la Communication, a permis une optimisation des actions de plaidoyer. Pour améliorer davantage cet impact, il est recommandé de mettre en réseau ces acteurs afin de maximiser l’efficacité des campagnes de sensibilisation et de plaidoyer.
Les défis de 2024 ont confirmé l’importance d’une approche intégrée, alliant interventions d’urgence, développement durable et renforcement des capacités locales. L’UNICEF poursuivra cette dynamique en 2025, en s’alignant sur les priorités nationales et les stratégies des Nations Unies, afin de garantir des solutions durables et adaptées aux réalités locales.

Nigeria’s President Tinubu’s administration, in its second year in office, has advanced implementation of an ambitious reform agenda, the Renewed Hope Agenda to drive the next phase of national commitment towards economic and human development, and implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The agenda also champions reforms to fulfil child rights. These include, a new education sector roadmap focused on basic education, seeking to enroll 15 million out-of-school children in school and to improve school access, learning quality and infrastructure. Further, the government developed a health ‘sector-wide approach to programming’ (SWAp) to boost coordination among health actors and improve health outcomes, and a National costed action plan for reducing child marriage.
Nigeria is the fourth-largest economy and has the largest population in Africa, which is relatively young: 49% is aged 0-17 and 42% is aged 0-14 (above the 25% world average). Endowed with natural resources such as vast oil, gas and mineral wealth and rich farmland, there is high potential for socio-economic development. However, Nigeria’s long-standing economic and social challenges persist. Human development is low: despite improvements in the latest Human Development Index, Nigeria ranked 161 of 193 countries.
While real economic growth in 2024 is expected to resemble 2023 (2.9% real GDP growth, down from 3.45% 2021-2022 average), GDP and GDP per capita are reducing (by 45-46%) due to the Naira’s devaluation and high population growth. Inflation has been rising since 2019 and is expected to have peaked in 2024. Increased cost of living is attributable to stagnant wages, low minimum wages, and increases in food and fuel prices. The deteriorating economic situation increased already high levels of poverty, leading to greater food insecurity. Moreover, sharp disparities exist: northern regions, rural areas and low-income households tend to have lower outcomes for children (according to MICS and DHS, among other sources).
Despite the ambitious new agenda, social sectors vital to child well-being received just 15.6% of the 2024 federal budget allocation (i.e. education, health and social development and poverty reduction combined), falling short of international standards and Nigeria’s own global and national commitments. The government faces growing debt service payments putting further pressures on public expenditures. However, recent introduction of legislation on financial autonomy of local governments can present an opportunity for localized key investments for children.
To improve performance on child-related goals and targets by 2030—and benefit from a demographic dividend by investing in the human capital represented by its children and youth—Nigeria needs to reach the most vulnerable children who are currently being left behind, by accelerating and scaling up its programmes and boosting social sector investment.
Nigeria ratified the Convention of the Rights of the Child and, by December 2023, all states ratified the Child Rights Act. While Nigeria submitted in 2010 its last report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC), UNICEF has supported the government-led work on the three outstanding consecutive CRC Reports which will be presented to the CRC committee in 2025.
Obstacles to realizing rights remain steep for children. A transversal challenge are the ongoing humanitarian crises mainly in northern Nigeria due to conflict (also leading to displaced populations), epidemics, flooding, severe acute malnutrition and fire outbreaks, among others. In 2024, 4.9 million children need urgent humanitarian response. Nigeria’s children face the world’s second-highest risk from climate change, but Nigeria ranks 180 of 192 countries in readiness to respond effectively.
The country has recorded significant achievements in several areas of child well-being, but challenges exist to fulfil child rights and meet many of the SDG 2030 targets. These are detailed below by goal area.

GA1-Survive and thrive
Antenatal care increased (to 79%), breastfeeding stagnated (at 29%) and child mortality reduced considering the last decades. However, child mortality worsened since 2021 and remains concerningly high (under-five mortality rate is 110 per 1,000 live births) and neonatal mortality has been stagnant for decades. Maternal mortality improved and in 2020 (latest data) was 1,047 per 100,000 live births. Nigeria’s 2.1 million unvaccinated children represent the highest number worldwide. Furthermore, stunting and wasting rates of under-five children rose to 40% and 8%, respectively. Some 11 million children under five experience severe food poverty (among the top 20 countries), while 31.8 million people are food insecure (highest number globally). Updated 2024 figures must be higher due to the rise of low-cost, healthy diets prices. Anxiety and depression continue to affect adolescents disproportionately and birth rates among girls aged 15-19 are high (75 births per 1,000).

GA2-Learning
Despite progress, still 10.2 million primary-school-age children and 8.1 million secondary-school-age children do not attend school (UBEC, 2019) and only 38% of three- and four-year olds attend pre-primary. Moreover, among children 3-5 years above the official completion age, around 3.9 million fail to complete primary school and another 4.2 million junior secondary. Moreover, many who attend are not learning: among 7-to-14-year-olds, 73% lack reading skills and 75% numeracy skills. Nearly 200,000 trained teachers are needed to address high student/teacher ratios, especially in northern states, where learning outcomes and completion rates are also lowest. Additionally, 14.4% of 15-to-24-year-olds are not in school, employment nor training.

GA3-Protection from violence and exploitation
Children without parental care, with disabilities, in rural areas and exposed to serious insecurity are disproportionately at risk for poverty and rights violations. In 2024, the births of 10.1 million children under age five were registered with a civil authority —included 2.2 million under-one and 7.9 million late registrations— (according to eCRVS, 2025), but significant gaps remain. Child marriage and female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) have reduced, but 30% of 20-to-24-year-old women still married before age 18 and 7% aged 15-19 undergo FGM/C. Gender-based violence is widespread especially in conflict zones and displacement camps. Armed groups abducted 859 schoolchildren in 2023 and, according to the United Nations General Assembly Security Council Children and Armed Conflict, 777 in 2024. Nigeria ranked 165 of 193 countries on the 2024 Gender Inequality Index.

GA4-Safe and clean environment
Access to improved water and sanitation increased, but approximately 70% of households still consume contaminated water, only half of people with disabilities have disability-accessible latrines in their households, and around 22% of households still practice open defecation, including 53% of the poorest households.
The hottest year on record was 2024 and water availability is forecast to decline from an annual 3,300 m3 per capita in 2000 to 800 m3 in 2080. Some 78% of total air pollution-related pneumonia deaths are among children under five, the highest proportion globally.

GA5-Equitable chance in life
Nearly half (47%) of children and adolescents live in households with income below the national monetary poverty line and 67.5% are multidimensionally poor (considering health, education, living standards, work and shocks, survival and development). Multidimensional poverty drops to 59% for people 18+ years, and for children varies widely by state, ranging from 31% to 92% (northern states have higher rates). This underlines the need to address sharp age, geographic and socio-economic disparities.

UNICEF deepened its collaboration with the Government of Nigeria and other partners at national and subnational level, contributing to sustainable and transformative changes promoting equity, enhancing local ownership, and accelerating the realization of children’s rights. Through system strengthening, community engagement, and integrated programming, UNICEF’s efforts in 2024 showcased scalable models to accelerate the fulfilment of child rights, leaving no child behind.
 
Goal Area 1: Survive and Thrive
UNICEF in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and other partners contributed to improvements in Nigeria's primary health care system, accelerating outcomes for women and children through support for government plans to strengthen health systems and achieve universal health coverage. UNICEF supported development of a Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp) to health and creation of annual operational plans in 20 Nigerian states.
Optimization of service delivery capacity for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (RMNCAH) was supported with partners by constructing and building capacity of nine oxygen plants, of which 2 fully solarized. Seven newborn care units were strengthened through capacity building of health workers, demand generation and improved quality of care, aiding over 600 vulnerable newborns directly during the first months of operation (more future beneficiaries expected).
UNICEF supported Nigeria’s immunization programme to accelerate routine immunization and catchup service deliveries which in 2024 reached 1.3 million of its 2.3 million zero dose children, and protected 7.4 million (target: 7.6 million) adolescent girls aged 9–14 years against Human Papilloma Virus. In all, over 59 million children under five and adolescent girls received lifesaving vaccines. UNICEF also supported response to vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks, polio and non-polio campaigns and advocacy to increase public financing.
UNICEF provided technical support to immunization coordination platforms with government and partners, for planning, review, communication and social mobilization on key national priorities such as polio, HPV vaccination, malaria vaccine introduction and zero dose children vaccination. Evidence-based social behaviour change (SBC) demand-generation activities reached nearly 9 million community members (parents, religious, traditional, political leaders and adolescents), contributing to over 9 million adolescent girls vaccinated.
Following UNICEF advocacy, high-impact, vital small quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) and multiple micronutrient supplements (MMS) were included on Nigeria’s Essential Medicine List, enabling government procurement. By leveraging the Child Nutrition Fund, UNICEF successfully unlocked US$1.45 million to procure nutrition commodities, used to deliver 3 million doses of MMS. The continued support to the local manufactures for local production of MMS, SQ-LNS has helped increase the availability of essential nutrition commodities for scaling up of nutrition programmes. Strategic engagement with the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) on market shaping for nutraceuticals will further boost local manufacturers' capacity and market opportunities in support of the government’s localization agenda.
UNICEF, FMoHSW, Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning (MBEP) and other partners launched the final Nigeria Food Consumption and Micronutrient Survey report, providing evidence to inform policies and programming. Fourteen of 20 focus states now report key nutrition data in the strengthened District Health Management Information System.
System-strengthening efforts led to scaled-up integrated preventive nutrition interventions that reached 40.6 million children aged 6–59 months (target: 30 million) with Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) in both Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (MNCH) weeks in 2024 (a 6.1 million increase from 2023). Twenty-eight states integrated VAS with deworming and iron folic acid (IFA) supplementation (none did in 2022), resulting in de-worming of 10 million children under five (target: 15 million) and IFA and MMS supplementation for 5.4 million pregnant women in both MNCH weeks (target: 6 million). Approximately 908,000 children with severe acute malnutrition (target: 835,176) received life-saving nutrition services across six humanitarian emergency states in 2024.
To accelerate optimal nutrition practices, the government launched a National SBC Strategy and domesticated across four states, enhanced by a world record-breaking UNICEF and partner/stakeholder initiative in which 31,254 women breastfed simultaneously. Other SBC campaigns focused on children’s first 1,000 days of life. In communities, maternal, infant and young child nutrition training was scaled up to include 6,003 frontline health workers across Nigeria. Two out of three Local Government Areas (LGAs) in UNICEF's 19 focus states now have the capacity to deliver essential integrated nutrition services to combat stunting. Similarly, 3,949 (target: 4,883) primary healthcare facilities prepared to deliver counselling services for improved dietary and care practices to pregnant and lactating women.
 
Goal Area 2: Education and Learning
Nigeria’s education systems were strengthened to expand access to quality, inclusive education and learning in formal and non-formal settings through increased capacity to develop and implement evidence-based, gender-responsive, disability-inclusive, crisis-responsive sector plans. The Nigeria Education Group, a multi-stakeholder sector coordination committee co-chaired by UNICEF, collaborated with the Ministry of Education, promoting informed decisions and collective action on the national education agenda. At state level, UNICEF supported data-driven education planning and management and digitalization of the Education Management Information System in 12 states, operational teacher management systems in 11 states, collection and analysis of systematized data on learning, and collection of education finance data in six states.
UNICEF supported expanded access to education and learning: 2.62 million additional children (1,22 million females; 292 children with disabilities) began formal and non-formal education, including nearly 240,000 previously out-of-school children, through widespread mobilization efforts in 2024. Twelve states developed work plans for reducing the number of out-of-school children; extensive enrolment drives engaged traditional and religious leaders; cash assistance was provided to 24,014 poor households to support 35,027 children’s schooling; and safe school plans were developed in 3,768 schools, among other initiatives.
Learning and skills development was strengthened through improved policies, developed with UNICEF support: national policies on skills development and a policy and minimum standards for early childhood care development and education were approved. UNICEF also enhanced teacher training systems, introducing the school-based teacher professional development model in six states and provided learning materials to 1,08 million children (527,466 girls; 167,716 children with disabilities). Over 626,000 children developed skills through UNICEF interventions (early learning, foundational literacy and numeracy, digital and employability/entrepreneurship) in 2024.
 
Goal Area 3: Protection from violence and exploitation
In collaboration with Federal Ministry of Women Affairs and Social Development, Nigeria Police Force, National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons and state-level governments and partners, UNICEF made significant progress in strengthening child protection systems. UNICEF supported the establishment and enhancement of 1,167 community-based structures across 18 states, managed by 1,726 trained caseworkers using improved information systems. A breakthrough was the adoption of the National Guidelines for Alternative Care by eight states, ensuring better care standards for children without parental care. These efforts provide vulnerable children with better access to care, protection and essential services.
UNICEF’s work with the Ministry of Justice and other government offices facilitated the expansion of diversion programmes to eight states, benefiting 1,022 children in conflict with the law (target: 880). With UNICEF's support, Nigeria’s National Justice Policy now includes a dedicated Justice for Children thematic area, marking a significant step in safeguarding children's rights and promoting alternatives to detention.
UNICEF championed efforts to eliminate harmful practices. Grassroots advocacy mobilized 6.5 million people against FGM (target: 7 million), while 32,445 adolescent girls were empowered to resist child marriage. Additionally, 24,000 boys and men challenged harmful gender norms. Nigeria's leadership in hosting the UN Joint Programme Annual Technical Consultation on the elimination of FGM further reinforced commitments.
UNICEF’s support to the National Population Commission, National Identity Management Commission, National Primary Health Care Development Authority (NPHCDA), and local governments was instrumental in improving integration of birth registration with health services and deploying an electronic Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (eCRVS) system nationwide, expanding access to remote areas. The birth of 10.1 million children was registered in 2024 (target: 9.3 million), while this surpassed the target significant gaps remain, highlighting the need for sustained efforts to achieve universal birth registration. Strategic partners engagement has laid strong foundation to building system decentralization, strengthen birth registration through primary healthcare platforms and innovative technology to create a coordinated, sustainable framework for nationwide coverage.
With UNICEF support to the military and Ministry of Women Affairs and Social Development, 3,118 children in conflict areas were released from military custody and armed groups (target: 4,000), and 269,974 children accessed mental health and psychosocial support services (target: 270,000). Gender-based violence prevention and response efforts reached 105,655 women and children, demonstrating UNICEF’s holistic approach to protecting children in humanitarian settings.
 
Goal Area 4: Safe and clean environment
UNICEF in collaboration with the Federal and State Ministries of Water Resources and the State Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agencies facilitated access to safely managed drinking water to over 2 million individuals (up from 788,067 in 2023) and access to basic sanitation services for over 4.6 million people (a sharp acceleration from 3.2 million in 2023). UNICEF's efforts through the Open Defecation-Free (ODF) Acceleration Initiative led 21 LGAs to achieve ODF status (taking the total to 136 out of 774 nationwide), home to over 5.7 million people.
UNICEF supported the Federal Ministry of Water Resources and Sanitation  to develop a ‘Climate Rationale’ for WASH, identifying risks and priority actions required to improve climate resilience; a revised implementation strategy for the Clean Nigeria Campaign calling for rapid acceleration and revising the target year to 2030, in line with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); and an action plan for improving WASH facilities, responding to the findings of sector-wide sustainability checks. These documents are expected to be ratified by the National Water Council in January 2025.
UNICEF advocated with private sector firms to develop WASH businesses and held a landmark regional consultation bringing together over 100 participants from banks and diverse industries to identify investment opportunities in all aspects of sanitation. In the Northwest, despite lack of revenue for engaging multi-national companies in WASH, UNICEF engaged local private sector players leading to 67 water points managed through public-private-community partnerships, and private sector invested about US$23,000 in 7 public sanitation facilities and 11 public water facilities. Nationwide, 29 public places were provided with WASH services via public-private-partnerships.
UNICEF supported creation of a multi-agency national WASH technical working group on climate and led the multi-sectoral development of a tool for assessing the climate resilience of schools and primary health care facilities, as part of the UK-supported ‘Climate Resilient Infrastructure for Basic Services’ (CRIBS) project. As a result, the Federal Ministry of Health / NPHCDA integrated a list of interventions to improve resilience into its strategy for rehabilitating all primary healthcare facilities infrastructures. Engagement of young people under the Green Rising project led to 22,908 young people in 33 states mobilized for climate action, 72,140 kg of plastic waste collected and recycled in 29 states and 16,065 trees planted in 11 states.
 
Goal Area 5: Equitable chance in life
In pursuance of children’s right to benefit from social protection, the National Social Safety Net Coordinating Office increased the number of children captured by the social register from 30% in 2023 (31.6 million) to 34% in 2024 (36.7 million). The federal government draws beneficiaries of its cash transfer programme from this register. As planned in 2024, with sustained UNICEF technical support, 19 focus states continued to integrate poor children, including Almajiri in northern states, in their social registers.
Partly triggered by UNICEF’s advocacy and policy dialogue, the federal government committed to introduce a Universal Child Benefit and to increase, before 2026, social protection public spending by 2%. Moreover, the share of public spending increased on education from 5.2% in 2023 to 8.21% in 2024, and has slightly decreased on health from 5.32% to 5.15%. As targeted, UNICEF’s 19 focus states received support to generate evidence on linkages between budgets and outcomes to improve allocations and expenditures for optimal child outcomes.
UNICEF achieved it target for instituting child-poverty measures to inform development planning. Through advocacy and technical support, 15 states included multidimensional and monetary child poverty estimates in their state development plans, compared to nine in 2023. The Oyo State Development Agenda 2040, Social Protection Bill and other social sector bills in Oyo and Zamfara states have integrated improved outcomes for poor children and youth. 
 
Cross-sectoral change strategies and enablers
To improve delivery of results for children, UNICEF Nigeria focused on enhancing programmatic and operational efficiency, fostering strategic partnerships, and driving innovative solutions. These efforts helped strengthen systems and improve access to critical services, ensuring that the most vulnerable children benefited from UNICEF’s diverse initiatives across Nigeria.
UNICEF progressed in advancing gender-transformative programming, filling gender-related evidence gaps in immunization and WASH, establishing men’s groups in several states to address vaccine non-compliance and to promote fathers’ involvement in children’s health. UNICEF supported playful parenting sessions for caregivers, including fathers, to enhance child development, and equipped around 1,200 female volunteer community mobilizers who are supporting polio programming with entrepreneurship and business skills.
UNICEF supported government in strengthening multisectoral and integrated programming with and for adolescent girls. In Katsina and Sokoto, around 3,000 girls who engaged in intergenerational community dialogues on girls’ education successfully transitioned to junior secondary school. Enhanced coordination between education and child protection structures led to over 4,380 out-of-school adolescent girls being re-enrolled in school.
Generation Unlimited (GenU) Nigeria reached over 3.2 million children, adolescents and youth: nearly 900,000 children and youth connected to digital learning; 1.3 million adolescents and youth received career guidance, entrepreneurship skills and job-related skills through YOMA and during in-person mass events; and 1.02 million adolescents and youth engaged and were empowered through volunteering opportunities and challenges in support of climate change and gender-transformative activities.
UNICEF’s social and behaviour change programme supported empowerment of 118+ million caregivers and parents and strengthened capacities of 29,000+ stakeholders to demand and receive quality maternal/child health, birth registration, nutrition services and protection during outbreaks and emergencies, guided by robust social and community listening mechanisms (including a new real-time online listening mechanism). UNICEF leveraged strategies such as community engagement, evidence-generation, and community empowerment through feedback loops to promote accountability and enhanced social listening, to understand people’s concerns about potentially mis-informed topics and strengthen the capacities of implementing partners (IPs) to deliver key results for children.
UNICEF’s technical support to government led to substantial progress in improving data collection, analysis and monitoring to enhance outcomes for children. It supported the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) in preparing for Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 7 implementation in 2025/26. Government ownership was promoted by the establishment of a Steering Committee and Technical Working Group, and the request for public budget funding for MICS7. Additionally, UNICEF supported NBS to conduct 3 rounds of the MICS Plus survey, which provides timely phone-survey data. The MBEP and UNICEF carried out an Updated Situational Analysis (SitAn) of Children, and its Summary was launched on World Children’s Day. UNICEF helped five Nigerian states to domesticate the National Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) Policy, fostering child-centred government M&E systems linked to SDGs and national policies.
To foster evaluation practices within governments and link multiple streams of evidence to policy development, UNICEF Nigeria played a catalytic role in brokering partnerships between the government, the Center for Learning on Evaluation and Results in Anglophone Africa. Efforts were made to ensure that evaluations assessed the impact of supported interventions, and two evaluations were completed in 2024: an evaluability assessment of the country programme document and an independent evaluation of Health and HIV/AIDS programme of the Nigerian government and UNICEF. The latter reported credible impacts on reducing child mortality, supported by robust state public expenditures and complementary programmes.
UNICEF’s focus on partnerships and innovations significantly expanded its impact. The office engaged over 54 civil society organizations (CSOs), including 25 local groups, ensuring that services reach vulnerable populations. UNICEF streamlined CSO-partnership processes, enhanced risk management, and supported financial management capacity in several states as well as the digitalization of financial transactions. In addition, innovative solutions were introduced in collaboration with partners, like solar-powered oxygen plants, digitization of birth registration systems and Nigeria’s first budget code in Lagos state to track child-related spending.
UNICEF substantially increased its communication and advocacy for child rights. A key highlight was the unprecedented expansion of UNICEF’s media presence, with over 6,500 mentions across TV, radio, and print, averaging nearly 20 daily mentions. Notably, the number of TV interviews with UNICEF staff surged from 140 in 2022 to 540+ in 2024, positioning UNICEF as the leading authority on child rights. Strategic collaborations with the Nigerian Guild of Editors and orientation of over 1,000 journalists on ethical reporting ensured that child rights remained central to national narratives. UNICEF also made long-term impact by integrating child rights into the journalism curriculum across universities and polytechnics, ensuring future generations of reporters can advocate effectively for children.
UNICEF achieved transformative outcomes through digital engagement and strategic partnerships. Digital campaigns, such as the No More Zero Dose song and the Shield of Love vaccination initiative, reached around 180 million viewers in Nigeria and Ghana according to NTA viewership data, demonstrating the power of compelling storytelling combined with innovative outreach. These collaborations are expected to increase public awareness, and influence policymaker commitments, resulting in increased funding for child nutrition, education and immunization. By leveraging partnerships, media engagement and digital innovation, UNICEF successfully mainstreamed the child rights agenda in the national discourse across Nigeria.
Through humanitarian programming (2024 Humanitarian Action for Children appeal), UNICEF provided integrated, multisectoral responses to 1.5 million children and 1 million adults affected by armed conflict and violence (similar to the 2.4 million people reached in 2023). UNICEF strengthened emergency preparedness and response, reaching over 1.5 million people with life-saving interventions in WASH, health and education. Contingency supplies supported responses to cholera outbreaks, school abductions, farmer-herder violence and floods. As part of its response actions, UNICEF humanitarian cash transfers benefitted 40,670 households.
UNICEF continued to coordinate the Northeast Nigeria ‘Rapid Response Mechanism’ (RRM) working group and ensured the provision of lifesaving assistance to displaced populations. UNICEF led the development of the RRM northeast strategy, governance structure, activation process flow and toolkit. Sixteen RRM activations, of which UNICEF supported 7, were conducted in 26 LGAs in response to: epidemics, flooding, severe acute malnutrition, fire outbreaks and population movements due to conflict. Some 224,785 people were reached by RRM partners (68,277 by UNICEF) with nutrition, WASH, multi-purpose cash assistance and shelter/non-food items assistance.
UNICEF contributed to mapping Nigeria’s hazard and risk analysis: 360 maps were produced using Geographic Information Systems and over 400 participants were trained across all states. This analysis informed risk-based programming and emergency preparedness planning. In the northwest, preparedness focused on strengthening coordination within state emergency management agencies (SEMAs), including a flood contingency plan in Jigawa, multisectoral meetings with Katsina SEMA and a Kano-Jigawa dam simulation exercise.
UNICEF invested in increasing effectiveness and efficiency for programme delivery. This included an internal review to assess adequacy of UNICEF’s logistics infrastructure, optimizing energy efficiency, and fleet optimization. Further, three new armoured vehicles were delivered, facilitating safe access to hard-to-reach areas. Kano Field Office was moved to refurnished rent-free premises, and construction of a new office building for Lagos Field Office was completed, significantly improving working conditions and staff well-being.

UNICEF Nigeria continued to cultivate shared value partnerships at national and subnational level with governments, CSOs, academia, public and private sector partners through technical support, advocacy and influence to place child rights at centre stage and leverage partners’ investments and capacities to deliver results for children.
 
National and subnational partnerships for results
UNICEF collaborated with key government institutions to: address child deprivation and the incorporation of a child-rights focus; leverage resources to benefit children; and improve and implement interventions that deliver tangible results for children.
UNICEF provided technical support to government shaping up key reform agendas, including the SWAp in health, and the development of national policies —on skills development and on early childhood care and development— approved by the Council for Education.
UNICEF built new and effective partnerships with Nigerian agencies responsible for addressing climate, particularly the National Council on Climate Change and the Ministry of Environment, creating an opportunity to introduce child rights and climate-resilient programming in the National Determined Contributions and National Adaptation Plans.
UNICEF also forged a robust partnership with the Office of the Vice President through its role as co-chair of the Nutrition Development Partners Group and as a member of the Nutrition Core Working Committee to strengthen government advocacy for improved coordination, increased domestic financing, and accountability in scaling high-impact nutrition interventions. Through these partnerships, UNICEF mobilized domestic financing for the Child Nutrition Fund to unlock US$1.4 million.
UNICEF supported NBS and MBEP in their national leadership role to generate and use quality evidence for data-driven decision-making, through strengthening their ownership in implementing Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 7, domesticating the national M&E policy, and producing and disseminating the Situation Analysis of Children in Nigeria. UNICEF revitalized partnerships with Nigerian universities through the Network for Behavioural Research on Child Survival in Nigeria, leveraging leading universities across multiple disciplines to foster research and innovation to inform evidence-based interventions that address children's needs and rights.
Strategic partnerships with influential organizations like the Nigerian Editors Guild and Nigerian Television Authority ensured widespread media coverage and public awareness of child rights issues. Partnership with the Nigerian Economic Summit Group mainstreamed children’s issues into national policy discussions, driving high-level commitment. A groundbreaking partnership with the National Youth Service Corps was established in 2024, and is expected to mobilize 350,000 youth volunteers nationwide to champion child rights at the grassroots level.
Subnational partnerships were key in advancing results for children. Notably, Primary Health Care (PHC) Memoranda of Understanding with eight states addressed zero dose challenges. Birth registration progress was achieved through partnerships with State Population Commissions. Open defecation-free declarations in several LGAs were enabled by working with state water resources ministries, departments and agencies.
UNICEF collaborated with multiple states to enhance programme budgeting, establish dedicated child-focused budget lines, and strengthen monitoring and evaluation systems. For example, Katsina, Kebbi and Zamfara states adopted a programme-based budgeting approach.
Strengthened partnerships with the Nigeria Governors Forum boosted coordination and accountability for health and nutrition programmes through the Leadership Challenge—a peer review initiative supported by Gates and Aliko Dangote Foundations to motivate subnational governments to enhance healthcare delivery and coordinated action for scaling high-impact nutrition interventions. Additionally, UNICEF partnered with the Governors’ Spouse Forum to extend maternity leave and establish creches in states.
UNICEF collaborated with federal and state ministries of women affairs to strengthen community-based child protection systems and partnered with the Ministry of Women’s Affairs and the Nigerian Army to address severe child rights violations in conflict-affected areas.
 
UN partnerships and other joint efforts
UNICEF’s critical role and partnership with other agencies to implement the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2023-27 in Nigeria is evident as the office continues to champion a child rights agenda focus, leading and convening outcome areas on social protection coverage, WASH and universal health coverage while contributing to other areas focused on inclusive governance and justice systems, gender equality and human rights of marginalized groups and improved access to decent jobs.
UNICEF is a co-lead in supporting the operationalization of the Power of Data High Impact Initiative in Nigeria, alongside United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs (UN DESA), World Bank, Global Partnership for Sustainable Development Data and the Chief Statisticians of the United Nations System. Moreover, UNICEF co-leads with UNFPA the Joint Programme on the elimination of Female Genital Mutilation. UNICEF co-created joint programmes with several United Nations agencies (UNFPA, International Organization for Migration-IOM, International Labour Organization-ILO) and development partners to accelerate joint results for children towards strengthening access to reproductive and adolescent health, supporting sustainable social protection systems, and supporting the reintegration and reconciliation of children associated with armed conflict.
UNICEF engaged in coordination efforts through active participation in the Humanitarian Country Team (UN agencies, NGOs, etc.) as well as development of humanitarian performance monitoring tools to improve response quality and monitoring access in northern Nigeria. 
UNICEF worked with regional and headquarter offices to leverage regional and global insights and experiences to strengthen programming quality in Nigeria and showcase Nigeria’s good practices implementing programmes to a broader audience. This included collaboration with Education headquarters (on the Learning Passport deployment), GenU HQ (implementation of girls’ skills programme), Data Analytics Planning and Monitoring (MICS secondary analysis) and with the Regional Office to present Nigeria’s work in safe schools, digital learning and foundational learning to wider audiences.
 
Public and private partnerships and UNICEF’s Core resources for results
UNICEF remained a partner of choice in implementing child rights programmes in humanitarian and development contexts. Through established bilaterial partnerships with government development aid cooperations, foundations and multilateral partnerships (USAID, Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance, United Kingdom, Germany, European Commission/ECHO, Canada, GAVI, Global Fund, Global Partnerships for Education, Gates Foundation, Rotary Foundation and others), UNICEF enhanced advocacy efforts and leveraged resources and partners’ comparative advantages to prioritize and increase investments for Nigerian children.
Partnerships with private sector are playing an increasing role to achieve programme results. GenU partnerships with IHS Nigeria Limited and Airtel Nigeria helped provide internet to 2,060 schools, benefiting over 834,000 children with enhanced digital learning. Governments of Canada and Norway and IHS Nigeria also strengthened the health system by funding the construction and infrastructure of nine oxygen plants in tertiary hospitals, supplying solar power for seven of them, and supporting UNICEF's emergency flood response in Maiduguri through the provision of boreholes and water facilities in six camps for internally displaced population, ensuring safe drinking water for over 30,000 individuals.
Private sector partners collaborated with UNICEF to advance WASH and birth registration initiatives. UNICEF engaged over 100 participants from banks and diverse industries to identify investments opportunities in sanitation and circular economy solutions to end open defecation and promote safely managed sanitation. Driving progress in national birth registration, Banks Forte Technologies Limited was instrumental in overseeing the digitization and integration of the eCRVS system with national ID systems.
UNICEF core resources for results (RR) remained critical in achieving results for children across sectors to strengthen systems and create an enabling environment for sustained investment of resources in quality service delivery. For example, NCO utilized RR to strengthen PHC systems and MNCH interventions. RR also bolstered successful implementation of both MNCH Weeks, reaching 40.6 million children with Vitamin A supplementation. Further, UNICEF continues to demonstrate effective and scalable programme interventions using RR as a catalyst to expand and leverage key partnerships towards unlocking multi-year domestic resources and other resources (ORR) from development partners to accelerate child rights’ realization.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Challenges
Increased economic insecurity in Nigeria and continued violence in part of the country, continued to pose challenges and risks to UNICEF’s programme implementation with partners to deliver results for all children.
During 2024 the nutrition situation in Nigeria became increasingly dire, as 32 million Nigerians in 26 states were estimated to be suffering from food and nutrition insecurity during the lean season, due to an ever-changing context driven by increased violence in the Northwest, flooding and disease outbreaks and the increased cost of living, particularly food prices. In this regard, UNICEF will prioritize supporting government to accelerate efforts to strengthen food systems and improve the food environment to address the barriers to healthy diets during children’s first 1,000 days of life. UNICEF will also strengthen government scale-up of the nutrition-sensitive social protection and the human capital development agenda.
Nigeria's ambitious development agenda continues to be hindered by the underfunding of social sectors vital to child well-being. This is limiting progress in improving child survival, learning outcomes and protection services. Addressing this challenge requires strengthened national and subnational public finance advocacy. UNICEF will actively engage in advocating for programme-based budgeting that prioritizes child-focused programs. Furthermore, in response to the financial autonomy granted to local governments, UNICEF will support local partners to strengthen technical capacity and evidence-based decision-making for targeted interventions for children.
Quality evidence and data on children will be key to supporting advocacy for increased subnational domestic financing for child-related services and conflict-sensitive programming. In this regard, UNICEF will prioritize government-led initiatives to improve routine data-gathering by supporting systematic digitalization and interoperability, while also supporting implementation of quality, child-centric national and subnational surveys.
 
Lessons learned
Increased efforts for convergent programming enhanced the effectiveness and sustainability of programmes for children. Programming on climate-resilience and adaptation is a cross-sectoral effort. For example, WASH, Health, Education and Operations (Supply) for the first time collaboratively developed a tool for climate risk and vulnerability assessment of 90 facilities (schools and PHCs) in Kano and Jigawa states under the UK-supported CRIBS project resulting in identified climate-resilient infrastructure solutions. Also, PHCs targeted for solarization benefitted from WASH improvements. GenU’s platform, in conjunction with the extensive WASH network, led to accelerated engagement by young people across 26 states under the Green Rising programme. These successes were driven by better planning, coordination and collaboration among government sectors, demonstrating that cross-sectoral integration leads to more comprehensive and impactful service delivery.
Building strong subnational partnerships was instrumental to leveraging existing resources and strengthening the quality of local service delivery. A newly established partnership with Nigeria’s Association of Local Governments will be instrumental to ensuring broader and more consistent birth registration coverage in 2025. Partnerships with local institutions generated essential funding for WASH and enabled context-specific solutions. Collaboration with traditional and religious leaders, community groups and the Ministry of Local Government was critical to advancing ODF campaigns and other WASH initiatives. Additionally, piloting a low-cost General Household Survey in Jigawa State (with local government funding) produced the first-ever robust LGA-level data on key social indicators, prompting increased demand from other states for similar support. Insecurity in violence-affected regions limited access to children in need of protection and other services. The removal of fuel subsidies and currency devaluation led to reduced government allocations to social services benefitting children, while inadequate budgets for evidence-generation affected the availability of granular data in states and LGAs.
Despite progress in adolescent programming, key lessons reveal the need for more intentional and integrated approaches. Current programmes often overlook adolescents’ unique needs and multisectoral collaboration addressing challenges is scarce. Moving forward, UNICEF will focus on strengthening multisectoral programming, enhancing meaningful youth engagement, expanding data-driven initiatives for younger adolescents and prioritizing emerging adolescent concerns like digital literacy, and social protection.
 
Future outlook
In 2024 UNICEF undertook a programme review, guided by evidence, integrating lessons learned from the first two years of country programme and addressing emerging priorities, to inform its 2025–27 work plans. Three strategic programmatic shifts were agreed during the review with partners, to strengthen impact, scalability and sustainability across all programmes in the remaining 3 years of country programme implementation:
1) Recalibrating downstream and upstream work: This shift focuses on balancing service delivery with policy advocacy and systems-strengthening. All UNICEF field offices will adopt a blended model to maximize impact, moving from service delivery to sustainable, scalable interventions and strengthening UNICEF's role as a technical support agency. The shift will also emphasize staff development through capacity building in public finance for children, advocacy and rights-based programming. This approach ensures more effective engagement with LGAs, enabling evidence-based decisions on resource allocation and service provision.
2) Prioritizing cross-cutting themes: UNICEF will prioritize climate change, public finance, the humanitarian/development/peace nexus, adolescent and youth engagement, gender equality and child rights across all programme areas. Key actions include establishing a dedicated climate change output within the WASH programme, integrating adolescent and youth priorities across child-centred outcomes, and strengthened partnerships with national climate authorities and public finance institutions.
3) Leveraging partnerships and scaling-up: This shift focuses on leveraging partnerships and scaling up high-impact interventions across five key results for children—stunting, out-of-school children, non-immunized children, birth registration and open defecation—through clearly outlined actions highlighted in acceleration plans. This shift aims to institutionalize scalable models that can be expanded nationally through public and private partnerships, ensuring consistency and sustainability in programme delivery. Strengthening monitoring, evaluation and adaptive learning will guide this process, promoting evidence-driven expansion of successful initiatives.
In 2025, UNICEF will also continue its flagship, integrated and multi-sectoral programme, the First 1,000 Days of Life, to positively impact children’s health and well-being at the beginning of their lives. Spanning 15 LGAs across 7 states and 3 UNICEF Field Offices in Nigeria, the First 1,000 Days targets pregnant women, children up to age two and their families. This model maximizes UNICEF's support and brings multi sectoral stakeholders from government/partners to invest in an integrated package combining health, nutrition and WASH during women’s pregnancy and the start of children’s lives.

Thirty-two years after Cameroon ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), noticeable progress has been made in reducing under-five mortality rates (142.8 in 1993 vs. 69.8 in 2022) but significant challenges remain to ensure that every child fully enjoys their rights. According to the latest data, achieving the forty-five Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for children by 2030 will require varying levels of effort: four goals need medium effort, twenty require very large effort, and eight demand considerable effort. A decade of conflicts and crises in the North-West, South-West, and Far North Regions has exacerbated child well-being concerns, which were already under strain due to persistent structural poverty.

The last few years, Cameroon has made efforts to fulfil its obligations under international human rights treaties. Cameroon submitted its State party report to the Committee on the Rights of the Child in September 2023 and is due to submit its report on the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) in 2025, following the ratification of the CRPD in 2023. Advocacy efforts have continued for the ratification of the Optional Protocol to the CRC on the sale of children, child prostitution, and child pornography. In March 2024, the Human Rights Council adopted the report of the review of Cameroon during the Universal Period Review of November 2023. 

During his visit to Cameroon in August 2024, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged all parties to pursue a peaceful resolution to the crisis in the North-West and South-West Regions ahead of the 2025-2026 elections. He also highlighted issues related to violence against women, including child marriage, and encouraged Cameroon to prioritize sustainable development by allocating budgetary resources to climate change adaptation and mitigation.
Poverty remains a major concern, with over 45% of children—approximately six million—living below the national poverty level. The latest Household Survey (ECAM5) indicates that around 37.7% of the population lives below the monetary poverty line, underscoring the urgent need to ensure no one is left behind. Children are particularly affected, with nearly one in two (47%) deprived of access to essential services such as education, healthcare, and adequate nutrition. In response, Cameroon has incorporated climate-sensitive budgeting for 2025, allocating 3.11% of the state budget to climate-related activities, representing 12.27% of the total budget for pilot ministries[1].

Despite these efforts, public debt reimbursement remains the largest government expenditure, limiting the state's ability to make substantial social investments. While the inflation rate in 2024 was maintained below 4.5%, lower than regional averages, rising staple food prices and the termination of fuel subsidies pose additional risks to the livelihoods of the poorest households.

Every Child Survives and Thrives: The government increased the national health budget by 11.88% in 2024, now at 4% of the total budget[2]. However, this remains significantly below the 15% target recommended by the Abuja Declaration. To strengthen community health services—which can address over 80% of the population’s healthcare needs—Cameroon organized a National Community Health Forum in November 2024 bringing together more than 3,576 participants. 
To combat under-five mortality, Cameroon launched the National Immunization Strategy (2024-2028) in alignment with the Global Immunization Agenda for 2030. This initiative focuses on reaching zero-dose children and underserved communities. By December 2024, the third dose of Diphtheria, Tetanus, and Pertussis (DTP3) vaccine coverage stood at 81.4%[3], slightly below the 2023 level of 83.2% and short of the 85% target. The North-West (59.5%) and South-West (60.6%) Regions recorded the lowest immunization rates. Cameroon became the first country to introduce the malaria vaccine into routine immunization, reaching 136,154 out of the 250,000 targeted children in 2024.

Additionally, Cameroon conducted two Vitamin A Supplementation (VAS) campaigns, ensuring over 90% of children aged 6-59 months receive two doses of VAS within the 2024 calendar year. Malnutrition remains a critical issue, with stunting rates ranging from 32.1% in Adamawa to 39.4% in the North. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the Far North are the most affected, with stunting rates as high as 49.2%.

Every Child Has the Right to Education: Although 85.6% of children aged 5 to 11 years attend school, disparities persist, particularly in the North Region, where 35% of children lack access to education. In 2024, Cameroon allocated 14% of its annual budget to education, covering basic, secondary, and higher education. While this marks the highest allocation for secondary education in a decade, the budget remains below UNESCO's recommended 20%. Most funding is directed toward operational costs, such as salaries and administration, leaving limited resources for improving access and quality.

UNICEF facilitated the participation of high-level government officials in key international education conferences, such as the African Union's Pan-African Conference on Girls and Women’s Education in Ethiopia, the Africa Foundational Learning Exchange in Rwanda, and the Continental Education Conference in Mauritania. These events aimed to align Cameroon’s education policies with global and regional trends.

Every Child Has the Right to Protection: Cameroon’s birth registration rate stands at only 54.3%[4]. UNICEF supported the country's first National Forum of Mayors, engaging all 374 municipal leaders to enhance birth registration services. To address challenges faced by unregistered school children to graduate from primary schools, a special operation was conducted resulting in the issuance of nearly 50,000 birth certificates to students, enabling them to take primary school final exams.

Every Child Has the Right to a Safe and Sustainable Environment: Although 83% of Cameroonians have access to improved drinking water, this rate falls to 75% among rural and impoverished populations. The situation is exacerbated by inadequate sanitation, with only 18% of rural households having access to improved sanitation solutions. According to UNICEF’s Children’s Climate Risk Index (2021), Cameroon ranks among the ten countries globally where children are the most exposed to climate and environmental hazards, shocks and stresses.

Every Child Has the Right to Fulfill Their Potential: Approximately 6 million out of 13 million children in Cameroon live in poverty. Despite its classification as a lower-middle-income country[5], 38.6% of Cameroonians live below the national poverty line (813 CFA or $1.30 per day)[6]. The urban poverty rate has increased from 8.9% to 16.5%, posing significant challenges since 60% of Cameroon’s 26.7 million[7] residents live in cities. The Far North, North-West, North, Adamawa, and East Regions report higher poverty rates than the national average. In 2024, the government has made strides in social protection, operationalizing the Unified Social Registry (RESUC). By 2024, 70,100[8] vulnerable households were registered, with a target of 250,000 by June 2025.

Humanitarian Crises and Child Welfare: In 2024, 3.4 million people—including 1.9 million children and 510,000 persons with disabilities—required humanitarian aid[9] due to armed conflict, intercommunal violence, disease outbreaks, and climate shocks. These crises have led to displacement, human rights violations, and disruptions in essential services.
Violence escalated in the North-West and South-West Regions in 2024, with an increase in kidnappings for ransom by non-state armed groups (NSAGs). Lockdowns further hindered humanitarian responses. The crisis has internally displaced 553,500 people[10], with 73,800 refugees fleeing to Nigeria[11]. In the Far North, over 800,000 people are displaced due to violence, including 475,871 IDPs, 205,098 returnees, and 121,140 refugees[12]. The Region has also experienced severe flooding, affecting 448,164 individuals, damaging 262 schools and 65 health centers[13].

Furthermore, Cameroon hosts nearly 283,000 refugees from the Central African Republic, primarily in the Adamawa, East, and North Regions[14].
Cameroon remains a country of concern under the UN Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism on grave child rights violations. Moving forward, addressing poverty, improving education and healthcare, enhancing protection mechanisms, and promoting peace and sustainable development will be crucial to ensuring that every child in Cameroon enjoys their rights fully and equitably.
