In the third year of implementing the 2022-2026 Country Programme, despite a challenging environment and limited donor attention, UNICEF remained committed to working with partners to uphold children's rights in Cameroon. The organization adapted its programs to address diverse contexts, including humanitarian crises and the impacts of climate change.
 
UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 1: Every child, including adolescents, survives and thrives, with access to nutritious diets, quality primary health care, nurturing practices and essential supplies
Key Result for Children #1: Immunization
UNICEF significantly bolstered Cameroon’s immunization efforts, addressing critical gaps and ensuring equitable vaccine access. Through innovative strategies and partnerships, vaccination coverage and outbreak response improved. The country maintained its polio-free status and eliminated maternal and newborn tetanus. By December 2024, DPT3 coverage reached 81.4%, slightly below 2023 levels (83.2%) and the 85% target. Security challenges contributed to low rates in the North-West (59.5%) and South-West (60.6%). However, the proportion of health districts with a DPT1-DPT3 dropout rate below 7% improved from 42% in 2023 to 51% in 2024.
UNICEF strengthened routine immunization by supporting decentralized health monitoring in 64 districts, focusing on zero-dose and under-immunized children. Since 2019, 530,949 such children were identified. Using GIS mapping under the Reach the Unreached initiative, UNICEF helped vaccinate 73,151 zero-dose and 100,318 under-immunized children in the 2024 Big Catch-Up campaign. Additionally, 124,490 people, including 69,232 girls, received HPV vaccines, reducing coverage disparities.

Following the GAVI Board visit in December 2023 which focused on advocating for an effective and sustainable mechanism for immunization financing and revitalizing routine vaccination, UNICEF supported Cameroon in becoming the first African country to introduce the malaria vaccine into routine immunization. The Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) set a target for the end of 2024 to vaccinate at least 50% of the 249,133 children aged six months in the 42 prioritized districts. By the end of 2024, EPI data showed coverage rates that exceeded expectations: 69.4% for the first dose, 55.9% for the second dose, and 53.8% for the third dose. However, targeted community engagement strategies are underway to address vaccine hesitancy.

UNICEF’s response to polio resurgence highlighted its public health leadership. Three immunization campaigns, supported by Social and Behavior Change (SBC) strategies, digital tools like U-Report, and community partnerships, effectively countered vaccine hesitancy. The School without Polio program empowered teachers as mobilizers, ensuring 94% of parents were informed before campaigns. Consequently, 7,017,655 children were vaccinated—exceeding the target of 6,719,586—reducing vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) cases from 12 in 2023 to three in 2024. Cross-border campaigns with Lake Chad Basin countries further expanded reach, while improved Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) investigations refined response strategies.
To enhance vaccine availability, UNICEF improved cold chain infrastructure, increasing the proportion of facilities with PQS-compliant equipment from 65% in 2023 to 70% in 2024. Advocacy for state pre-financing supported plans to acquire 1,590 solar refrigerators by 2025, aligning with climate resilience goals.

In outbreak response, UNICEF achieved 99.97% coverage in cholera vaccination campaigns targeting flood-affected areas in the Far North. Support for Mpox and yellow fever outbreaks included technical assistance, rapid response mechanisms, and public health communication. Climate-resilient solutions—such as integrated health facilities and low-emission biomedical waste incinerators—further strengthened health system sustainability.

Key Result for Children #2: Prevention of Stunting
In 2024, UNICEF enhanced nutrition services through sector collaboration, high-impact interventions, and capacity building, focusing on the critical first 1,000 days of life to reduce stunting. A minimum package of interventions reached 26% of health districts integrating both development and humanitarian approaches – this is below the 52% target due to the lack of sufficient resources, 

Through the Stronger with Breast Milk Only (SWBO) initiative, 284,867 mothers and caregivers received key messages on optimal breastfeeding. Additionally, 346 health providers, 232 community leaders, and 150 community health workers were trained in breastfeeding counseling.
UNICEF supported bi-annual Vitamin A supplementation (VAS) campaigns in 2024, reaching 6,190,462 (96% of target) children aged 6–59 with two doses of VAS in May and December. Deworming tablets were provided to 5,631,620 children aged 12–59 months. Home fortification with micronutrient powders benefited 108,895 children aged 6–23 months. A pilot project in the North Region improved diet diversity by enriching complementary foods with small fish powder, engaging 365 health personnel and community workers.
To combat anemia, UNICEF provided iron and folic acid supplements to 207,775 pregnant women and 192,079 adolescent girls.

In addressing severe wasting, UNICEF worked with government agencies, UN partners, local organizations, and international NGOs to improve early detection and treatment, particularly in hard-to-reach areas. A total of 72,543 children under five received treatment for severe wasting in UNICEF-supported facilities, achieving an 84% recovery rate—above SPHERE standards.
As the Nutrition Sector lead for humanitarian coordination, UNICEF developed guidelines for the 2025 humanitarian program cycle and supported evaluations of Scaling Up Nutrition and 2021 N4G commitments, emphasizing stunting prevention and nutrition financing.

UNICEF integrates stunting prevention within the First 1,000 Days initiative, aligning efforts across immunization (KRC#1), nutrition (KRC#2), and birth registration (KRC#7). The Big Catch-Up campaign reinforced synergies between immunization and birth registration by reaching unvaccinated children. Social and behavior change programs promoted key family health practices, including vaccine demand and the introduction of the malaria vaccine.
To strengthen evidence-based planning, UNICEF conducted a national vaccine intention study, a behavior insight study on vaccination service utilization, and a gender barrier analysis on vaccination and Vitamin A supplementation. These findings will inform the 2025–2026 workplan.
 
UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 2: Every child, including adolescents, learns and acquires skills for the future
Key Result for Children #3: Equitable and Sustainable Access to Education & Key Result for Children #4: Improved Learning Outcomes

Between 2022 and 2024, UNICEF and its partners made significant progress in expanding access to quality education in Cameroon. Under KRC#3, nearly 200,000 vulnerable children, 55% of whom were girls, were reintegrated into school through new infrastructure, accelerated education programs, and innovative technologies.

In conflict-affected Regions like the North-West and South-West, the radio education program ensured continued learning for 29,283 children, mostly girls. The construction of 130 classrooms reduced overcrowding, particularly in areas impacted by conflict and climate change. However, the lower secondary school completion rate remained at 45.59% in 2023, below the 56% target for 2026, highlighting challenges in infrastructure and student retention.
Under KRC#4, the Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL) program helped over 70% of assessed students improve in reading, benefiting more than 7,500 children by 2024. The distribution of 253,976 school kits eased financial burdens on families, and 2,264 teachers received training in inclusive teaching methods. However, high teacher turnover and limited energy access persist. To address this, UNICEF plans to strengthen teacher training, advocate against untimely redeployment, and introduce solar energy solutions to support digital education in remote schools.

UNICEF also prioritized inclusive and healthy learning environments. The I Am Music program, officially launched in November 2024, which used music to develop life skills and emotional resilience, benefited 406 children (69% girls and 31% boys). 120 children (83% girls and 17% boys) have received a scholarship to support retention in schools or to reintegrate school for those who were out of the school system. A rapid evaluation of the pilot experience has shown increased self-control in children, increased confidence and self-esteem, and improved community engagement and social bonding. Looking ahead to 2025, UNICEF aims to expand investments in educational infrastructure, scale up the TaRL initiative nationwide, and reinforce the inclusive education system to increase the number of children with disabilities in schools. Strengthening partnerships with the Ministries of Basic and Secondary Education and international donors will be key to mobilizing resources and ensuring sustainable improvements in Cameroon’s education system.

Adolescent Engagement and Participation
In 2024, UNICEF emphasized adolescent participation, working with and supporting the Ministry of Youth (MINEJEC) to develop the National Youth Policy, ensuring young people’s voices—especially on climate change—were heard. Insights from these consultations shaped UNICEF’s climate action plan and the upcoming National Youth Policy.
Supporting adolescent girls as change agents remained a priority. The Adolescent Girls Advisory Board (AGAB) expanded with four new groups in Buea, Bertoua, Maroua, and Bikok, now totaling 60 members advising UNICEF on adolescent girl’s issues. AGAB members were trained to advocate for their rights, with girl-led initiatives raising awareness on child marriage, gender-based violence, education, climate change, mental health, teenage pregnancy, HPV vaccination, and menstrual hygiene.

The relaunch of the U-Reporter digital platform (that had been frozen in 2023) was accompanied by the creation of 15 new U-Report communities gathering 390 young people across Cameroon (mostly in the Far North Region), enhancing adolescent engagement and participation. 
 
UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 3: Every child, including adolescents, is protected from violence, exploitation, abuse, neglect and harmful practices
Key Result for Children #7: Birth Registration

In April 2024, UNICEF played a key role in organizing Cameroon’s First National Forum of Mayors on universal birth registration. All 374 mayors attended alongside key stakeholders, including government officials and civil registration institutions (BUNEC). A major outcome was the Charter of Mayors on Birth Registration, committing local leaders to register every child. Discussions emphasized integrating birth registration with health services, digitalization, and creating an interoperable system.

To drive action, UNICEF launched the My Name campaign, mobilizing 366 of 374 municipalities (98%). By December 2024, 46 councils had budgeted for birth registration, 62 had civil registry posts in health facilities, 96 used online data collection (SIGEC), and 170 established communal consultation platforms. Integration of health (DHIS2) and civil registration data helped identify 37,732 unregistered children during an immunization campaign.
With UNICEF’s support, BUNEC registered 245,029 children, including 118,374 girls. A special operation, backed by the World Bank, to provide birth registration for school children, targeted 80,000 primary students needing birth certificates to sit in the national exams. In collaboration with multiple ministries and mayors, 544 mobile court hearings were held and resulted in the registration of  57,244 students and issuance of 48,232 declaratory judgments.
UNICEF’s advocacy led to a new law on Civil Registration passed in December 2024, modernizing civil registration, scaling up birth registration units in health facilities and ensuring free, permanent, and confidential registration. Key innovations included digitalization, emergency registration for displaced persons, improved coordination, and dedicated funding for civil registration.

As part of the 2025-2029 Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) Plan, UNICEF promoted birth registration through awareness campaigns led by Child Protection Networks, positive parenting monitors, and trained women champions. This resulted in the issuance of birth certificates for 639 children. The Positive Parenting program, spearheaded by the Ministry of Women’s Empowerment and the Family (MINPROFF), reached 1,703 people, including 1,265 children and 438 adults, with additional training for 100 caregivers in the Centre Region.

Child Protection and Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Prevention
Collaboration between government services and Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) enabled mental health and psychosocial support (MHPSS) for 166,959 people, including 86,397 children. Despite resource limitations, efforts to combat child marriage were strengthened in the East, Adamawa, North, and Far North Regions. Community-based protection mechanisms, parenting programs, and engagement with local leaders helped 15,707 adolescent girls access life skills programs, while 440 at-risk girls received vocational training and scholarships.
UNICEF’s GBV interventions reached 251,120 people, including 87,851 children, while 187,520 individuals accessed safe reporting channels for the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA). Case management services were provided to 7,336 children in targeted areas.

Children Affected by Armed Conflict
In 2024, 407 children formerly associated with armed groups received reintegration support, with 201 in the Far North benefiting from socio-economic assistance. Advocacy efforts led to the release of four detained boys in Maroua Central Prison, with one reunited with family.
The UN Country Team endorsed a Handover Protocol for children associated with armed groups in January 2024. UNICEF also organized a national workshop to sensitize State Security Forces on the Safe Schools Declaration and trained personnel on the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in the Far North. Two Global Horizontal Notes (GHNs) were prepared for the Lake Chad Basin and Cameroon, contributing to the UN Secretary-General’s Annual Report on Children Affected by Armed Conflict.
 
UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 4: Every child, including adolescents, has access to safe and equitable water, sanitation and hygiene services, and lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment
Key Result for Children #8: Ending open defecation

UNICEF improved water services for 36,630 individuals, totaling 145,625 over three years, aiming for 250,000 by the end of the CPD cycle. In sanitation, 152,192 people received basic services, surpassing the 2024 target of 130,000. UNICEF enhanced local access by equipping four municipalities with skills for effective water and sanitation management and led the development of a national sanitation policy, assigning leadership to MINEE.
Solar-powered water pumping solutions increased community resilience, providing clean, reliable electricity. UNICEF constructed 32 solar water pumping systems, converted 8 boreholes to solar power, installed handpumps in 89 boreholes, and rehabilitated 131 non-functional boreholes, aiding 13,100 IDPs in the Far North. These systems also addressed energy access for health and educational facilities, integrating WASH projects with Education, Nutrition, and Child Protection initiatives. Despite challenges like vandalism, UNICEF's pilot project on multiple-use solar systems aims to scale up with government and donor support. Community ownership and capacity building are crucial to prevent vandalism and provide youth with opportunities to acquire green skills.

At the institutional level, 65 schools received new water points, 16 schools had their water systems rehabilitated, and 18 schools benefited from inclusive and gender-segregated latrines surpassing our 2024 target by 25%%. Hygiene messaging and WASH kits were provided to 39 schools, promoting menstrual hygiene among adolescent girls and raising awareness among boys, reaching 19,440 studentsility and Climate Action Plan (SCAP). UNICEF also strengthened Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) in response to Mpox cases in the South-West Region, providing chlorine and hygiene kits to healthcare facilities. UNICEF led WASH sector partners in Maroua to effectively respond to a cholera outbreak through coordination, risk communication, and distribution of cleaning supplies, hygiene kits, and chlorine. The Community Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) approach reached 141,000 people in the North and Far North, resulting in the construction of 27,232 family latrines in Mokolo municipality. Additionally, UNICEF and local partners constructed 126 emergency latrines in flood-affected communities and institutional latrines in schools, health facilities, and markets. In Bertoua, UNICEF rehabilitated 4 latrines in the Nadoungue Health Facility, and in Buea, they supported the construction of 20 gender-segregated latrines in schools, benefiting 6,000 students. These efforts underscore UNICEF's commitment to improving water and sanitation services, enhancing resilience, and promoting health and hygiene across Cameroon.

In terms of climate change, UNICEF Cameroon conducted a Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC) to understand the risks children face from climate change, disasters, and environmental degradation. This analysis, based on the 2021 Child Risk and Impact Analysis (CRIA), highlights specific climate risks for children in different Regions of Cameroon, allowing UNICEF to refine its climate action priorities and influence policy making adapted to the Coastal, Congo Basin and Sahel regions. UNICEF also developed a Climate, Energy, Environment, and Children Plan for 2024-2026, focusing on three main priorities: Protect, Empower, and Reduce, in line with the UNICEF Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan (SCAP/2023-2030). As part of this plan, 40 communities, schools, and healthcare facilities received climate-resilient services through solar systems for pumping, lighting, and cold chain management. To empower youth as climate champions, UNICEF sponsored four young climate champions to participate in COP 29 and is advocating and working together with the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development for child sensitive Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC 3.0) and National Adaptation Plan (NAP). UNICEF also launched a climate mascot, "Terra," as a symbol of its engagement on climate for and with children and youth. Additionally, a study on green skills for adolescents is ongoing to tap into the potential of the growing green economy. 
 
UNICEF Strategic Plan Goal Area 5: Every child has an equitable chance in life
The country experienced a 1.8% increase in child poverty from 2014 to 2022, bringing the total to 45%, contrary to the declining trend observed over the past decade. The North-West Region has the highest rate of child poverty. Furthermore, the deprivation level has reached 47%. To address these issues, UNICEF is supporting systematic data collection and analysis to inform policy changes and support innovative programs demonstrating its commitment to making these children visible and ensuring that no child is left behind. Recent assessments on child-related SDGs have shown delays, prompting UNICEF to take urgent action to accelerate progress.
UNICEF has advocated for the protection and expansion of inclusive investments for children, ensuring that social sector funding remains secure even during economic challenges. This advocacy has led to a 5% increase in social sector spending from 2024 to 2025. Additionally, UNICEF's efforts have contributed to the expansion and institutionalization of the safety net program, securing more national resources to close gaps in social protection for children.
The Ministry of Social Affairs (MINAS) has prioritized the extension of the National Social Registry for Cameroon (RESUC), with significant support from UNICEF, the primary contributor. UNICEF successfully engaged the World Bank in developing the information system together with MINAS. In addition, UNICEF supported the registration process and implemented an on-demand method, registering 22,100 households and bringing the total number of registered households to 70,000. This registry facilitates access to essential social protection programs throughout individuals' lives, fostering connections with other services in an inclusive and transparent way. It specifically targets excluded groups and addresses structural social inequalities that perpetuate poverty. 

UNICEF has provided humanitarian cash transfers to 1,300 households (7,317 children) affected by floods in the Far North, helping to reduce barriers to vital social services. This intervention will be expanded in response to future crises.
UNICEF has also focused its efforts on the most vulnerable children in areas with high need, supporting decentralization initiatives. Through the Child-Friendly Municipality initiative, UNICEF engaged mayors and local authorities in several municipalities, including Bana (Ouest), Bikok (Center), Mandjou and Garoua Boulai (East), Djohong (Adamawa), Lagdo (North), and Mokolo (Far North). This initiative implements a multi-sectoral strategy, emphasizing data production, strategic planning, and community mechanisms that prioritize participation and accountability. To ensure sustainability, the model will be strengthened around four pillars: 1) advocacy for child rights, 2) local governance, 3) community engagement, and 4) children and youth participation. The next phase will focus on scaling up the model through collaboration with the Ministry of Decentralization (MINDDEVEL), FEICOM (Communal Investment Funds), and the CVUC association (United Cities and Municipalities of Cameroon).

In response to the nearly 450,000 people affected by floods in the Far North, UNICEF and its partners provided a multi-sectoral response. This included treating 4,423 children with Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM), providing health services to 13,340 individuals, and distributing 1,930 WASH kits, 1,900 packs of aqua tabs, and constructing 160 emergency latrines and 70 showers. Additionally, 560 WASH and dignity kits, 10 educational kits, and 19 tents were distributed. Mental health and psychosocial support reached 2,109 children, and 1,300 households received multi-purpose cash assistance.

In the North-West and South-West Regions, UNICEF also provided multisectoral support to individuals affected by violence and displacement. This included mental health and psychosocial services for 24,760 children and caregivers, individual case management for 1,950 children, and gender-based violence (GBV) risk mitigation and response for 53,235 individuals. UNICEF also helped nearly 36,000 children gain access to education, screened 16,691 children aged 6-23 months for wasting, and treated 3,271 for SAM. Furthermore, 25,343 individuals gained access to safe sanitation facilities, improving public health.

UNICEF increased collaboration with national and local NGOs, investing in building their capacity, recognizing that local partners often have better access to remote areas and in-depth knowledge of the local context. UNICEF also continued to lead the national Localization Working Group, contributing to the progress of localization in Cameroon, particularly in terms of participation and visibility.

In addition to its immediate humanitarian efforts, UNICEF's advocacy and collaboration with various stakeholders led to systemic changes that will positively impact future humanitarian responses. More specifically, UNICEF played a key role in the development of the 2023-2030 Education Sector Plan, which includes provisions for emergencies and crises, including climate shocks. Moreover, the official launch of the CPIMS+ (Child Protection Information Management System) in Cameroon marks a significant milestone in improving case management, coordination, and data-driven decision-making in child protection.

Aligned with UNICEF’s global Nexus approach, the Country office’s humanitarian efforts were integrated with development initiatives to strengthen systems and ensure the sustainability and resilience of social services.

UNICEF continued to lead the Child Protection, Education, WASH, and Nutrition sectors at both national and sub-national levels. In this leadership role, UNICEF coordinated sector responses, ensuring effective, timely, and high-quality humanitarian assistance to meet the complex needs of children. As the lead agency and provider of last resort, UNICEF played a central role in key interventions, including the treatment of SAM cases, the provision of sanitation facilities, distribution of learning materials, and the reintegration of children formerly associated with armed groups.

Partnerships remained essential for UNICEF Cameroon in 2024, with several innovative collaborations launched to advance child rights across various sectors.

In terms of institutional partnerships, a significant partnership with 11 State Universities and the National School of Local Administration (NASLA) was formalized in July 2024 to institutionalize children's rights in Cameroon’s academic systems. This collaboration focuses on three pillars: promoting children’s rights through training and advocacy, generating evidence-based knowledge to inform policies, and integrating children’s rights into curricula across sectors such as education, health, and social protection. The first Centre for Child Rights was inaugurated at the University of Yaoundé II in December 2024, with more centers planned for 2025. This partnership positions Cameroon as a regional leader in institutionalizing children’s rights in the academia.

UNICEF also partnered with the University of Bertoua to enhance evaluation capacities, involving 43 students in field data collection for a project on child deprivation in the East Region. This youth engagement not only strengthened the evaluations but also empowered young people to contribute to future advocacy efforts. UNICEF will continue engaging young people in transformative evaluations, particularly in the upcoming evaluation of the Country Programme Document (CPD).

Through collaboration with MINEPAT and the Cameroonian Development Evaluation Association, UNICEF raised awareness of evaluation in the public sector during the 2024 Cameroonian Evaluation Days, reaching over 400 students and teachers. UNICEF also supported capacity building for 50 communal actors, including Mayors and volunteers, in Results-Based Management (RBM) to better integrate children’s priorities into local programs.
Furthermore, UNICEF launched key strategic partnerships in 2024 with the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development, Ministry of Forestry and Wildlife, and the National Climate Change Observatory (ONACC), to implement its Climate, Energy, Environment, and Children Plan. Additionally, UNICEF consulted adolescents on climate change, influencing the development of the new Youth Policy.

Flexible funding, including Regular Resources, enabled the rollout of key programs such as the Child Friendly Municipality initiative and the I Am Music program. The program, rooted in Cameroonian culture, was institutionalized in the education system and expanded to youth centers, with a focus on child rights and musical pedagogy.

In collaboration with the Government and key partners, UNICEF organized Cameroon’s first National Forum on Primary Health Care (PHC) and Community Health, mobilizing 3,576 participants. This led to the adoption of the Yaoundé Declaration, committing to institutionalize community health and improve financing and coordination.
UNICEF strengthened partnerships with International Financial Institutions (IFIs) like the World Bank and the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), focusing on social protection, health, and education. These collaborations resulted in the establishment of child-friendly safety net programs and support for education initiatives, including the PASZEP project.

The Global Partnership for Education (GPE) confirmed two allocations totaling USD 72.5 million to support system transformation and girls' education in Cameroon, focusing on teacher capacity development and improving the learning environment, with UNICEF as co-agent with UNESCO.
UNICEF’s strategic partnership with FEICOM, a national development fund operating decentralization in the country, enabled municipalities to access investment funds for local development projects. FEICOM also supported participation in the Mayor’s Forum on Birth Registration, where 374 Mayors engaged in birth registration.

UNICEF prioritized accountability in humanitarian responses, providing training on Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP) for 67 people in the Far North and working with national NGOs to establish child-sensitive complaint and feedback mechanisms. The AAP and national PSEA Networks collaborated to ensure that feedback mechanisms are accessible to children, particularly those aged 6-14.

In 2024, UNICEF worked with 41 implementing partners, 93% of which were national NGOs. Capacity building for Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (SEA) prevention was a priority, with UNICEF organizing training for 21 organizations to create a pool of investigators, addressing a critical gap in SEA investigation capacity in Cameroon.

Advancing Children's Rights and Strengthening Resource Mobilization
In a context of increasing challenges to children’s rights and competition for resources, UNICEF strengthened its partnership with the Government of Cameroon, achieving key milestones in advocacy and resource mobilization.

In 2024, UNICEF and its donors committed $35.7 million for development funding and $19.3 million for humanitarian needs. Despite these increases, significant gaps remain: the 2024 Humanitarian Appeal for Children was funded at just 30%, and the 2022-2026 CPD is only 60% funded.

UNICEF’s advocacy to mobilize more resources was amplified through press releases, videos, articles, media stories, press trips, donor briefings, media cafés, and countless social media posts, significantly increasing public awareness and engagement. This comprehensive approach led to a surge in media coverage and social media interaction, furthering UNICEF’s impact in Cameroon and resulting in an increase 1) in resources mobilized by reinforcing existing partnerships with institutional donors and revitalizing relationships, developing new partnerships among institutional donors and private sector, and by using more creative communication and partnership approaches to make a difference in a context of increased competition; 2) in UNICEF's visibility in Cameroon by documenting key programmes and initiatives and UNICEF’s areas of expertise, highlighting innovative programmes and approaches that are attractive, and implementing media and digital tools: training and press trips, press files, website and social networks and; 3)in strengthening UNICEF’s advocacy on children's rights mainly on the Days of the African Child, the climate, the Summit of the Future, the 35th anniversary of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, and by relaunching U-Report by UNICEF and the commitment, voices and empowerment of adolescents and young people to the climate.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
After three years of implementing the 2022-2026 Country Programme, UNICEF Cameroon continues to find the theory of change highly relevant in addressing child rights issues within both humanitarian and development contexts. Challenges persist, particularly in measuring progress towards the set outcome indicators and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). A key reason for this is the lack of updated data. The last Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) was conducted in 2014, and while the MICS7 is currently in development, data collection is not expected to be completed until the end of 2025. This delay hinders timely analysis, which is critical for influencing policies and strategies effectively.
While some sectors, especially health, have functional information systems, real-time data is not consistently available. This complicates the regular monitoring of progress and adapting decisions in a timely manner. However, UNICEF remains committed to leveraging available data to inform its evidence-based approach to shaping policies and programmes that address child rights issues effectively.

A new alliance with universities is also underway, with the goal of establishing a national digital platform for child rights evidence in Cameroon. This will enhance UNICEF’s role as a knowledge broker by fostering the generation, dissemination, and utilization of data for decision-making. These efforts aim to ensure that child rights remain central to national development policies and sector-specific strategies. Along these lines, UNICEF has also made significant progress in facilitating collaboration between the Ministry of Health and the Civil Registration Office to map unreached children. This initiative is vital for improving birth registration and immunization efforts and strengthening interoperability between health and civil registration for long-term sustainability.

One of the major challenges for the realization of children’s rights at the decentralized level is the low technical and financial capacity of municipalities. Even though the law on decentralization requires that 15% of the national budget be allocated to municipalities, this allocation has never been fully implemented due to administrative limitations. Additionally, the latest finance law revoked municipalities’ ability to collect local taxes, further weakening their financial capacity to plan and budget effectively. Recognizing the importance of this allocation, UNICEF has assisted selected municipalities in developing child-sensitive plans. However, advocacy efforts need to continue to ensure these municipalities receive equitable subsidies and adequate support for child-focused programmes.The “Child-Friendly Municipality” initiative, which aims to create an environment conducive to child rights realization at local level is one of the key strategies to address these capacity challenges (including financial) . The initiative involves a broad range of stakeholders, including local leaders, parents, and religious figures to foster interventions and behaviors that benefit children and families. The initiative which is currently being implemented in seven municipalities is focusing on providing support for child-sensitive planning, budgeting, enhancing quality of services, and increasing demand for these services through citizen participation and social accountability.

The security situation, particularly in the North-West and South-West Regions, remains another significant challenge, as it continues to limit access to some communities, posing a direct threat to lifesaving interventions, including immunization. Vaccination coverage in these Regions fell well below the national average (North-West: 62.3%, South-West: 57%). In addition, reports such as ECAM5 indicate worsening conditions, with Community Management of Acute Malnutrition (CMAM) coverage dropping to below 20% in these Regions, compared to over 90% in other priority areas. In education, despite some improvements in terms of inclusion and quality, thousands of school-age children remain out of school, and 41% of schools are still non-functional.

To address these challenges, UNICEF has scaled up its humanitarian operations, focusing on multi-sectoral programming in hard-to-reach areas. The aim is to implement multiple interventions in a synchronized way to maximize the impact. Thanks to the Country office’s increased advocacy actions, humanitarian funding saw a significant increase in 2024, with a 33% rise in donor contributions to the Humanitarian Response Plan (HRP). The funding gap for the Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) 2024 was reduced with 35% funded, compared to 15% in 2023, reflecting UNICEF's success in building donor trust. However, much of the funding remains earmarked, which limits the flexibility needed to address broader issues such as emergency preparedness.

UNICEF has worked closely with the government and international partners to produce regular updates on the impact of the floods in the Far North. This strategy emphasizes the importance of integrated responses and the need for stakeholders to engage to secure additional resources. Looking ahead, UNICEF plans to focus more on anticipatory actions, particularly in response to flood-related emergencies in the Far North. In 2024, UNICEF launched its first humanitarian cash assistance programme in Maga, targeting 1,300 households (11,921 individuals, including 4,048 girls and 3,269 boys) in response to the Mayo-Dana floods. This initiative strengthened UNICEF’s internal capacity, allowing the setting up of the HOPE system to manage beneficiary data and payments, which will enhance preparedness in the future.
Beyond emergency response, UNICEF Cameroon continues to prioritize cross-sectoral initiatives, especially in Early Childhood Development (ECD) and adolescent programming. The initiative, which integrates nutrition, birth registration and immunization services, has been successful in ensuring that all births are registered at health centers. Future plans include strengthening the links between these services and social protection efforts in collaboration with the World Bank. Given the critical role played by community health workers in ensuring the sustainability of these initiatives, UNICEF introduced multi-purpose community health workers (MPHWs), trained in health, nutrition, birth registration and WASH, to address community-based worker shortages and improve community communication. These MPHWs have proven effective due to their ability to deploy quickly and cost-effectively.

The Protective Learning Environment strategy uses education and child protection as entry points to address multiple issues affecting adolescent girls in a holistic manner. In the coming years, UNICEF will enhance its multi-sectoral approach by incorporating social protection and skills-building programs into interventions aimed at reducing child marriage, keeping girls in secondary school, as well as by creating new opportunities in the green skills sectors. The Country office will seize the opportunity of the Girls Movement promoted by UNICEF at the regional level to amplify these efforts, reaching thousands of girls across the country. 

However, challenges remain in addressing gender inequality, particularly in tackling child marriage and menstrual hygiene management. To combat these issues, UNICEF is strengthening community child protection mechanisms and public-private partnerships to provide life skills and vocational training for girls. Furthermore, UNICEF will continue fostering youth participation through initiatives like the Adolescent Girls Advisory Board (AGAB), U-Reporters, Les Jeunes Voix du Sahel, and the Children’s Parliament. The AGAB has already proven transformative by influencing government programming and inspiring stakeholders. In 2025, UNICEF plans to expand the AGAB, as well as strengthen adolescent girls’ participation in local governance and contribution to national policies including adolescents.
UNICEF will increase its involvement in climate action by stepping up the implementation of its Climate, Energy, Environment and Children Plan for 2024-2026, which includes advocacy for child-sensitive NDCs and national climate policies and support young people’s contribution to the COP30. Furthermore, the active participation of children and young people as agents of change will be scaled up through UNICEF’s “U-Reporters- U-Responders initiative, which aims at building the capacity of U-Reporters on emergency preparedness and climate action while expanding the U-Report platform and community. However, to achieve these ambitions, UNICEF must secure sufficient funding.

In terms of disability inclusion, progress has been made, particularly in targeting children with disabilities in all sectoral interventions. UNICEF has co-led the United Nations Disability Inclusion (UNDIC) task force contributing to positioning the Organization as a champion on disability inclusion Efforts will continue in 2025 as UNICEF takes the lead of the UNDIC and focus on supporting concrete actions in partnership with other UN agencies and MINAS, and advocating and providing support for the elaboration of Cameroon’s initial State Party report on the Convention on the Rights of Person with Disabilities (CRPD), following the country’s ratification of the CRPD in 2023. 

The evaluation of the first three years of the Country Programme scheduled for 2025 will provide valuable insights for shaping the next phase of the programme and guiding the development of the 2027-2031 Country Programme.

The Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe (STP) is a Small Island Developing State (SIDS) with a population of 230,870[i]. Tourism and agriculture are the main economic sectors[ii]. The island has made notable strides in social development, with the Human Development Index rising to 0.613[iii] in 2022 (0.608 in 2019) and the gross national income per capita reaching $2,580[iv] in 2023 ($1,810 in 2019). STP graduated from the Least Developed Country category in December 2024. 

 

However, the country faces significant economic challenges, including reliance on imports and external aid, limited infrastructure and vulnerability to external shocks[v]. The economy experienced a downturn due to the pandemic and the conflict in Ukraine, but the Gross Domestic Product increased to 0.9 per cent in 2024 (0.4 per cent in 2023[vi]), amid energy shortages and diminished international reserves. In December 2024, the International Monetary Fund approved a $24 million Extended Credit Facility[vii], opening a positive outlook. 

 

Vulnerability indicators remain higher in rural areas and on the island of Principe[viii]. Gender-based inequalities persist hindering women's access to education and labour force participation. Unemployment (8.9 per cent[ix]) is significantly higher among women and youth as 61 per cent of the population is under 25[x]. In 2020, the Santomean diaspora made up 18 per cent of the population. Rising emigration over the past two years has led to workforce gaps in key sectors like health and education and increased children’s vulnerabilities[xi].

Thirty per cent of SDGs targets are achieved or on track[xii]. However, the lack of disaggregated administrative data hampers progress and measurement. 
 
Every child survives and thrives

In terms of health and well-being (SDG-3), under-five and neonatal mortality rates dropped in 2022 to 14 and 7 per 1,000 live births[xiii] respectively from 15 and 8 in 2021. STP maintained zero cases of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Mother-to-Child Transmission for the second consecutive year. Declining vaccine confidence and staffing shortage prompted United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF) to conduct supplementary immunization and boost community adherence, ensuring no-child was left behind. The completion of the accelerated country's Transition to Vaccine Autonomy, supported by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance was extended from 2027 to 2030. The National Immunization Strategy was developed and will be validated in 2025.


Progress towards zero hunger (SDG-2) saw a decrease in stunting among children under five (from 12 per cent in 2019 to 10 per cent in 2022[xiv]). However, in 2022, 51.3 per cent of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet (48.8 per cent in 2019)[xv]. Exclusive breastfeeding rate remained steady, at 63 per cent (2024).

 
 
Every child lives in a clean and safe environment

Progress towards achieving access to clean water and sanitation (SDG-6) has been slow and requires increased financing. In 2022, only 36 per cent of households have access to safely managed water services. 43 per cent of the population still practices open defecation[xvi]. UNICEF focused on improving handwashing practices and water supply to strengthen sustainable health outcomes. The creation of the WASH multisectoral coordination mechanism marked a significant achievement.

 
Every child learns

For the 2022/2023 school year, access to pre-primary education expanded (SDG-4) to 95 per cent of the 4-5 age group, while the primary completion rate increased to 97 per cent. The number of primary and secondary-age children who dropped out of school declined to seven per cent[xvii]. However, in 2024, school attendance was affected by a 6-week teacher strike and the emigration of a considerable number of students and teachers. UNICEF contributed to the development of the Partnership Compact document to guide priorities in education policies. 

 
Every child is protected from violence and exploitation 

Violence against children (VAC), including sexual violence persists, perpetuated by harmful social practices and gender inequality (SDG-5, SDG-16) and requires at-scale solutions. Almost half of Santomean children live with only one or none of their biological parents[xviii]. The migratory crisis has significantly affected family dynamics leaving many children in the care of family members or guardians, exposing them to risks of neglect, abuse and school abandonment. UNICEF’s technical effort and advocacy focused on strengthening the child protection system and improving access to protection services. 


Every child has an equitable chance in life

Due to socio-economic shocks, STP continues to grapple with persistent poverty. In 2024, 16.8 per cent of the population lives under the threshold of $2.15 a day ($17.2 in 2023)[xix], especially in rural areas, showing limited advancement towards SGD-1. Sixty-three per cent of children aged 0-17 suffer from multi-dimensional poverty.[xx] The social protection system has been strengthened (SDG-1, SDG-10), reaching about 25 per cent of the population in extreme poverty (up from 22 in 2023)[xxi]. In 2024, UNICEF supported the government in generating evidence, realizing a major advancement to improve child-centred data, with the development of the administrative data collection manual. 

 

In 2024, the country attended the 4th International Conference on SIDS, which set an agenda to address urgent climate risks and signed the Intergovernmental Declaration on Children, Youth and Climate Action demonstrating STP’s intentions to advancing youth engagement and inclusive child-centred climate action. As president of the Community of Portuguese Language Countries for the 2023-2025 biennium, STP will advance the themes of ‘youth and sustainability.’ The National Development Plan 2025-2039, currently under development, will guide priority actions, including on the climate and youth agendas.
