UNICEF contributed to the strategic Priority Areas of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF): inclusive social system (Outcome-1), climate action (Outcome-2) and transparent and accountable institutions (Outcome-4). In a context of limited funds, resources were used strategically to generate equity focused, child-centred evidence and data to inform advocacy and drive results to accelerate progress towards the SDG. UNICEF consistently included Principe in activities, engaging national partners and civil society organisations to enhance coverage and ensured no child was left behind.


In 2024, leveraging social and behaviour change (SBC) to achieve results at scale, UNICEF placed youth engagement and gender equality at the centre of its effort, successfully mobilizing 20,604 adolescents and young people (32 per cent of the 12-24 age group). Through the U-Report initiatives, UNICEF expanded its reach to 12,246 subscribers (19 per cent of the 12-24 age group) and was nominated for a case study presented at the global level. Recognizing the significant role of youth in shaping a sustainable future, the government is updating the National Youth Strategy, with active assistance from UNICEF and the contribution of 317 adolescents and young people (152 girls). UNICEF also upheld the children’s parliament to promote civic participation and decision-making.


Every child survives and thrives 

In 2024, UNICEF played a major role in enhancing integrated high-impact interventions into primary health care, with a focus on immunization, which resulted in significant progress, positioning the agency to meet its targets by the end of the cycle, advancing coverage of quality, dignified maternal and newborn health services including for adolescent girls (UNSDCF – Outcome 1 and SDG-2 and 3). 



Collaborating with global partners (GAVI, World Bank, United States Agency for International Development - USAID, World Health Organization-WHO, United Nations Development Programme - UNDP), UNICEF focused on improving vaccination rates targeting zero-dose, under-vaccinated and hard-to-reach children in underperforming districts to ensure equal coverage. This included mobile teams, national door-to-door campaigns and supplementary immunization activities to support the Ministry of Health in achieving results at scale. UNICEF’s technical and financial support drove the increase in Human Papillomavirus (HPV) coverage to 95 per cent among girls aged 10-14 (75 per cent in 2023)improving health care for adolescent girls and advancing the UNICEF Gender Action Plan. Measles and rubella vaccine achieved 90 per cent coverage (85 per cent in 2023). STP remained free of polio and eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus, thanks to the major contribution of UNICEF on immunization.


Despite significant effort, the third dose of the pentavalent vaccine rate for children aged 0-11 months, which stayed above 90 per cent for two decades, gradually fell to 87 per cent in 2024 (90 per cent in 2023), below the target for this key result. Contributing factors include workforce shortages due to emigration and vaccine resistance. 

 

To promote vaccination uptake for HPV and reverse the downward trend in pentavalent coverage, UNICEF partnered with 50 youth associations and the Youth National Council to conduct community engagement and SBC activities, focusing on adolescents and youth. In 50 communities, 9,000 adolescents (55 per cent girls) received education on vaccination and 50 community health workers were trained. As a result, 25 per cent of Santomean adolescents gained stronger knowledge on COVID-19 and HPV, while 40 per cent were encouraged to adopt preventive behaviours, driving increased demand for routine vaccines. The full impact of these efforts on pentavalent is expected in 2025. 

 

Key advocacy and technical assistance to the Ministry of Health, jointly with immunization partners (Gavi, WHO), led to significant achievements offering positive prospects for enhanced performance and sustainability of the Expanded Programme on Immunization and health system strengthening: development of the costing component of the National Immunization Strategy set for validation in 2025; extension of the country's Transition to Vaccine Autonomy; vaccine co-financing commitments of the Ministry of Health, help in budgeting vaccine needs and preparation for the implementation of the Cold Chain Equipment Optimization Platform, approved by GAVI. 

 

In 2024, UNICEF contributed to improve child health through the Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses. By directly providing essential drugs, UNICEF helped maintain the continuity of quality health services at both central and district levels contributing to the survival of 18,227 children under five (68 per cent). Additionally, 107,705 children and adolescents accessed primary health care in UNICEF supported facilities, an increase of 27,000 from 2023. UNICEF’s integrated interventions and provision of HIV tests and antiretroviral ensured that 100 per cent of pregnant women were tested for HIV during their first consultation. This led to zero cases of Mother-to-Child Transmission, in line with the UNICEF Gender Action Plan, maintaining the trend towards eliminating transmission by 2025. However, limited funds slowed the achievement of adolescent health objectives. In 2025, efforts will focus on mobilizing funds to address this gap and supporting a national strategy.

 

UNICEF has supplemented more than 23,240 doses for children at risk (18,926 in 2023) with vitamin A, reaching 85% of target children aged 6-59 months (80% in 2023), demonstrating a positive trend since 2022.

 
Every child lives in a safe and clean environment 

UNICEF’s technical support and advocacy were key to achieving an important milestone with the creation of the WASH multisectoral coordination mechanism led by the Ministry of Environment. It will reinforce partners collaboration, including for climate change and emergencies while facilitating resource mobilization to reach sustainable outcomes and SDG-6. 

 

In 2024, due to funding constraints, modest progress was made toward access to safe and resilient WASH services (SDG-6). In line with the UNSCDF targets under Outcome-1, UNICEF funded the improvement of hand washing points in 6 health facilities and 55 schools (25 per cent of total), ensuring water supply to 41,250 students. UNICEF triggered four new communities for the Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) in Principe. One community was certified as open defecation-free, benefiting 150 people (45 children), maintaining results comparable to 2023, with slow progress towards the target set for the programme cycle. Significant efforts are required to mobilize the needed resources and technical capacity to achieve targets by 2027. 


In 2024, UNICEF accelerated youth engagement to mobilize effective community response for climate change (SDG-13, UNSDCF Outcome-2) and joined forces with UNDP to establish seven district and regional youth committees for climate change, also advancing adolescents’ leadership. They will develop and implement district multisectoral action plans with start-up funds provided by UNICEF and UNDP, to be continued in 2025. The 70 members (40 girls) were trained on WASH-integrated climate action and gender equality. UNICEF mobilized efficiently youth platforms and U-Report to involve children and youth as climate champions. Supported by UNDP and UNICEF, 139 young people (75 girls) from district committees joined the Youth Action Climate Workshop to build a network of young leaders committed to climate and gender causes. UNICEF and UNDP also sponsored three youth to attend COP 29 and the SIDS-4 summits enhancing STP’s visibility. 

 

STP has set climate goals to meet the Paris Agreement, which will be revised in 2025. In this context, UNICEF is conducting a Climate Landscape Analysis for Children (CLAC). It will provide foundational evidence, identify opportunities to integrate climate issues into sectoral risk-informed programming and guide UNICEF policy dialogue on child-focused resilient climate response, in support of the government's strategic agenda. 


Every Child Learns 

In 2024, UNICEF directly improved equitable access to quality education for 78 per cent of Santomean children from pre-school to secondary, promoting gender responsive approaches, advancing progress towards UNICEF Gender Action Plan, SDG-4 and SDG-5. 


UNICEF was a major contributor in advancing an inclusive pre-school education model placing the child at the centre of the learning process. At the end of school year 2022/2023, STP had reached a high 95 per cent enrolment rate in pre-primary for children aged 4-5 (up from 94 per cent in 2021/2022), a key result for UNICEF in STP, already meeting the CDP target. In partnership with the World Bank and Global Partnership for Education (GPE), UNICEF operationalized the pedagogical supervision digital system across all 111 kindergartens and has been providing equipment and pedagogical materials to 60 per cent of them to improve learning conditions, creating child friendly environment for over 9,300 children. With technical assistance from UNICEF, gender-responsive curriculum guidelines and supervision tools for pre-schoolers were developed and will be operationalized in 2025. 

 

The last available data underlined an increase in completion rate, reaching 97 per cent in primary education, 91 per cent in lower secondary education and 57 per cent in upper secondary education, with higher completion rates among girls at all levels (SDG-4, SDG-5), showing significant progress, beyond the programme cycle targets, contributing to UNSDCF Outcome-1. 

 

To accelerate advancement towards inclusive and equitable access to quality education, in continuity with the initiative Reimagine Education, UNICEF stepped up its commitment to strengthen the National Digital Learning Programme through the Akelius and the Learning Passport platforms, enhancing blended learning in 15 pilot schools, including five digital labs across primary and secondary. SBC interventions and capacity building of school staff (168) by youth volunteers (20) trained on the digital programme, contributed to expand access and improve teaching practices. Life skills content was added. As a result, 2,339 children and adolescents (10 per cent), among whom 1,147 girls as well 88 teachers were trained. In 2024, a total of 1,222 users were registered on the Learning Passport platform. With the World Bank support, the innovative national connectivity mapping of schools under the global Giga initiative was completed and connectivity scenarios developed. In addition, Giga application enables real-time assessment of connectivity in 13 schools. STP has become a model for innovative digital education and gained visibility, showcased during the global Giga Connectivity Forum. This pilot experience will guide the scale up of the blended learning approach in 2025-2026, informed by an evaluation of the digital programme to be conducted with Innocenti. 


Overall, 1,557 adolescents and young people, including out-of-school youth, 500 more than in 2023, were reached with educational digital programme (552), life-skills training and skill development (950) and through the Youth Parliament (55) also contributing to SDG-8. To date, with major support from UNICEF, 6,000 teenagers and youth benefited from this training (10 per cent of the target group). UNICEF mapped children with disabilities in three districts and assessed 38 adolescents. Additionally, 26 children with disabilities attended digital skill sessions. This initiative will expand in 2025, capitalizing on digital labs to guarantee lifelong learning opportunities for all. 

 

In partnership with GPE, UNICEF strengthened interventions to promote safe and inclusive school environments (SDG-4, SDG-5) through the school management empowerment programme to achieve systemic capacity strengthening. UNICEF together with the Ministry of Education developed a handbook of piloting tools to enable schools’ management to produce evidence-based improvement plans. Thirty pilot schools (14 per cent) are currently developing school improvement plans, which will be operationalized in 2025 to enhance school management skills, sustainability and ownership, improving the learning environment of 13,911 children. 

 

As coordinator of the Local Education Partners Group, UNICEF significantly contributed to the development of the Partnership Compact of the Ministry of Education and the Report on the State of the National Education System which will inform the Education Policy Charter (2026-2029).


Every child is protected from violence and exploitation 

Despite limited funding, UNICEF further strengthened the system’s ability to respond to VAC, including sexual violence, a key priority for the STP Country Office, advancing the achievement of SDG-16, SDG-5, UNICEF Gender Action Plan and UNSDCF Outcome-4. In 2024, 340 children at risk or victims received assistance through UNICEF supported services (470 in 2023), surpassing the targets set for the programme cycle. Among these victims, 208 children experienced sexual and gender-based violence (112 in 2023), showing improved response coordination to this form of violence.This growth in the number of reports reflects the positive impact of the implementation of new VAC response procedures, which have fostered greater trust and encouraged more victims to report the abuse they have suffered, thereby improving the effectiveness of the response to these situations.

 

UNICEF majorly contributed to the dissemination and implementation of the new multisectoral VAC case management and referral procedures, at the national, district and community levels, ensuring greater ownership. High-level national and district launches boosted visibility. UNICEF provided technical support to the Monitoring Commission, establishing a reference network and a coordination mechanism. As a result, 108 stakeholders were trained in the new procedures and 64 technicians are receiving online training on child and adolescent protection systems through trilateral cooperation with Brazil. UNICEF financed materials to facilitate procedures implementation and partnered efficiently with youth to provide information on tools and their role in advocating for their rights. UNICEF empowered adolescent girls through intergenerational meetings on early marriage, pregnancy, girls' rights and mechanisms for reporting cases of violence, including sexual abuse with 257 women aged 12-24. 



Through financial, technical and advocacy support, UNICEF collaboratively contributed with other partners to a major advancement in justice services for child victims of violence, including the creation of a specialized room for children's testimony in court, the provision of services to victims and the approval of a law on single testimony avoiding the revictimization of children. Trainings next year will focus on implementing child-sensitive investigations and court procedures to further build a child-friendly, gender-sensitive justice system (SDG-5, SDG-16). 



UNICEF completed the qualitative component of the Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) study, analysing social norms on violence and focusing on community, family and school settings. It will provide key evidence for advocacy and inform gender-transformative programme on violence prevention and response (SDG-4, SDG-16, SDG-5). This initiative from UNICEF will guide multi-sector partnerships in 2025.


Every child has an equitable chance in life 
Despite considerable funding gaps, UNICEF achieved notable progress in 2024 and stays on track to meet the expected targets for the cycle, supporting SDG-1, SDG-8 and SDG-10. 

UNICEF used the results of the Open and Participatory Budget Index to sensitize 12 institutions and 149 stakeholders during high-level meetings on transparent and inclusive budget emphasizing children’s priorities. Recommendations and a roadmap were identified paving the way for scaling up participatory budgeting. By 2024, 9 institutions were capable of equity focused budget monitoring and planning (1 in 2023). 

 

UNICEF conducted policy-level advocacy to expand the coverage of the social protection system to reach the most at risk children (SDG-1 and SDG-10), remaining on track to reach the Country Programme and UNSDCF targets by 2027. Using regular funds, UNICEF continued to implement the Parental Education Programme (PEP), which applies to beneficiaries of the cash transfer programme for vulnerable families funded by the World Bank. The coverage increased from 2,830 to 4,070 families (15,654 children 0-17 years – 53 per cent girls) to include households with children or family members with disabilities. As a result of UNICEF’s interventions, 19,145 people benefited from sessions to adopt positive and gender-transformative parenting practices including early identification of disabilities in children, prevention of domestic and child violence, mental health and psychosocial support. Scaling up was challenging due to limited funds and emigration disrupting the programme's logistics. Expanding human resources and securing funding will be a priority for sustainability. 

UNICEF is developing a case management protocol, referral mechanisms and a pilot intervention, to enhance access and services for children with disabilities and their families, using the PEP as a platform for integrated services. The methodology is aligned with UNICEF Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy. Findings will be used to advocate for partnerships and scale up the initiative. 
 

In 2024, through a joint initiative with the National Institute of Statistics, UNICEF was a main contributor in the development of the administrative data collection manual and its operational plan which will enhance the data ecosystem. Four working sessions with 25 public services institutions promoted interoperability of the different data and systems including on CRC monitoring, climate and disability, using an equity lens. These tools will be key to improve reliable child-centred disaggregated data collection supporting the monitoring of child rights and the SDG, advancing progress towards UNSDCF Outcome-4. 


In 2024, UNICEF realized substantial advancement in child rights monitoring. Seventy-five per cent of the recommendations from the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC) are already being addressed. In partnership with the Human Rights Office, 220 national and local decision-makers, including civil society and youth participated in eight working sessions facilitated by UNICEF to promote the ownership and monitoring of the instrument. An action plan was developed under the lead of the CRC National Commission. To reflect its commitment, UNICEF embedded the Concluding Observations from the CRC Committee in its work plan, disseminated an adolescent-friendly CRC-toolkit and shared a case study with UNICEF headquarters. 


Cross-sectoral support 
Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA)

UNICEF staff together with all government and civil society partners (20) received sector-specific trainings and guidance to monitor, respond to and prevent sexual abuse and exploitation with dedicated toolkits, advancing SDG-5 and SDG-16. Additionally, 552 young people and adolescent volunteers were trained on PSEA. The dissemination of the multisectoral procedures for case management contributed to advance knowledge and awareness on PSEA. 

 
Operations excellency

In 2024, UNICEF streamlined operations, with solid internal oversight, including a new Direct Cash Transfer tracking system, improved joint planning with the programme and a strategic Antifraud Plan (2024-2025). Funds were fully utilized, supply chain management handled effectively and 105 per cent of assurance activities completed, showing progress compared to 2023. Innovations like internet banking, e-travel platform on Fiori and asset management (mAsset) were fully implemented.



UNICEF encouraged staff engagement for results, promoted staff well-being and maintained gender diversity. UNICEF carried out a disability assessment of its premises and participated in a national assessment to recommend disability-friendly meeting rooms to partners. These efforts enhanced internal efficiency and partners collaboration, optimizing overall performance. An undergoing evaluation of the operational support will identify areas for improvement in 2025 for a more responsive business model. 

Staff members attended an introductory training on the Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan.


UNICEF improved knowledge management process by enhancing SharePoint usage and conducting regular cross-sectoral knowledge-sharing practices. Insights and good practices were documented through case studies. Mutual cooperation and knowledge sharing were maintained with other UNICEF offices to improve staff capacity.

To close the SDGs gaps, the government remained the main implementing partner at national and district level, contributing to the strengthening of institutional capacities. 

 

UNICEF diversified its partnerships furthering collaboration with civil society organisations and communities' leadership, to achieve national coverage and reach the most marginalized children and adolescents. In cooperation with 50 youth-led and youth-focused organizations, through the Youth Institute and the National Youth Council, UNICEF increased youth engagement and adherence to the climate agenda, vaccination, VAC prevention and hygiene practices. This strengthened collective effort, increased the reach and coverage of interventions, resulting in key achievements for immunization (together with ADRA, MARAPA, Plivini), climate change, prevention of violence and risky behaviour, as well as mental health initiatives for young people and adolescents (together with Helpo).

 

Efficient collaboration with traditional partners was key to remaining on track towards the SDGs. Gavi, World Bank and USAID financial and technical support was determinant to consolidate the immunization programme (SDG-3). In 2025, the partnership with Gavi will efficiently drive the improvement of the supply chain and strengthen the health system. In collaboration with the Ministry of Environment, UNICEF maintained gains for WASH (SDG-6), while positioning on the climate agenda (SDG-13). Along with the Ministry of Education, efficient collaboration with the World Bank, GPE and Akelius Foundation advanced access and quality of learning (SDG-4), through digital learning and connectivity, strengthening the education system and promoting gender transformative education (SDG-5). The KAP study, funded by GPE, will inform violence prevention. 



UNICEF is collaborating with United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), UNDP, WHO, World Bank and the Portuguese Cooperation towards multisectoral procedures for dealing with cases of gender-based violence (SDG-5). This visibility has resulted in the mobilization of strategic resources for child protection, from the Portuguese Cooperation, for the first time, and from the private sector through Natcom Portugal which will enhance VAC prevention in 2025. 

 

UNICEF maintained strategic collaboration within the United Nations (UN) leading on children's rights, engaging in concerted efforts to advance the UNSDCF in support of the national transformative agenda 'Sao Tomé and Príncipe 2030’. 



UNICEF led on youth and adolescent programming, contributing with UNDP and UNFPA to the National Youth Strategy. The partnership with UNDP effectively encouraged youth-led and youth-inclusive interventions to address climate change (SDG-13) with the Youth Climate Committees, while consolidating adolescent’s agency and gender equality (SDG-5). The partnership with UNFPA supported the advancement of adolescent girls' wellbeing and responsive health system and reduced neonatal mortality with the supply of equipment (SDG-5; SDG-3). Joint advocacy and technical support with WHO fostered progress towards SDG-3, with the extension of the vaccination transition and strategic contribution to the National Immunization Strategy. UNICEF and ILO (International Labour Organization) collaborated efficiently on social protection (SDG-1), leveraging their technical expertise. The UN Resident Coordinator’s Office is promoting joint dialogue with donors on social policy. Work engaged by UNICEF complements the support provided by the World Food Programme (WFP) and Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) to the national home-grown school feeding programme (SDG-2), using schools as a platform for integrated services. Quality education is being improved (SDG-4), with a UN-to-UN agreement with United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) to collaborate on the analysis of the education sector in 2025.

 

UNICEF efficiently allocated flexible regular and set-aside funds in favour of priority key results. In view of immunization challenges, UNICEF engaged regular funds to provide traditional vaccines to prevent stockout and maintain the coverage rate. The provision of medicines and consumables contributed to the continuity of primary health care (SDG-1). UNICEF successfully engaged key enabling SBC interventions to promote exclusive breastfeeding (SDG-2) and hand washing. To address gaps, the set-aside funds were strategically used to rehabilitate water points in schools and health units, maintain gains in CLTS (SDG-6) and launch the CLAC, key to advance the climate agenda. 



To improve data and transparency, regular resources funded interventions to advance the administrative data collection manual, advocacy sessions on the Open Budget Index, the recommendations of the CRC and social protection. They were pivotal in maintaining the PEP programme and addressing poverty (SDG-1). They also led to significant results in strengthening the response capacity to VAC, with the implementation of case management procedures and the launch of the KAP study, contributing to a safer environment for children.


The continuity of the digital learning programme was maintained, with teachers training and the implementation of the young volunteers’ programme in pilot schools. The set-aside fund ensured technical support to strengthen the management leadership of 30 schools, integrated actions for children with disabilities and the foundational work on disability referral mechanisms. 


Partnerships with the private sector in STP were essential to ensure connectivity, with the Ministry of Public Works, the National Regulatory Agency (AGER) and telecommunications operators (CST and UNITEL), thereby enhancing digital learning and popularizing the U-Report platform. 

 

UNICEF West and Central Regional Office provided key technical support and high-level advocacy on social protection, immunization, advocacy for vaccine autonomy, climate and dissemination of the VAC procedures. Giga initiative in partnership with International Telecommunication Union was crucial to promote investment in connectivity for digital education. Knowledge management remains central, with continued collaboration with UNICEF Cabo Verde on digital learning.



South-South cooperation between STP, Brazil and UNICEF was instrumental, providing the country with the opportunity for training on child and adolescent protection systems and will continue in 2025.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
In 2024, UNICEF faced significant resource mobilization challenges, with a 57 per cent funding gap which limited progress towards outcome targets. The office prioritized efforts to generate evidence and advance children’s rights, focusing on high-impact interventions, leveraging advocacy and technical expertise. UNICEF partnered with other UN agencies in the country and other UNICEF offices for joint-resource mobilization to achieve greater scale. Improved synergies with civil society organizations were key to enhance programme delivery. The graduation from the LDC group may, in time, lead to the loss of specific international support measures and require collaborative efforts to mobilize alternative resources.

 

UNICEF’s interventions were also impeded by the emigration crisis, hindering programme delivery, logistics and increasing children’s vulnerability. UNICEF responded by expanding training efforts beyond the identified needs to ensure continuity of interventions. Collaboration with other agencies has been engaged to understand the broader impact of emigration on social sectors. Going forward, this will require a more integrated approach to tackle challenges and advocate for awareness of the impact on children and service delivery. 

 

Coordination for effective implementation at national and decentralized levels - The collaborative process to develop and disseminate the VAC procedures resulted in an effective implementation nationally. The Monitoring Commission and its Executive Secretariat ensured coordinated interventions to prevent and respond to situations of risk and shared best practices. This mechanism effectively strengthened the child protection system. The political engagement at both central, district and community levels (together with civil society, community leaders, families, adolescents and youth) addressed the lack of ownership by institutions. Support from the highest spheres of governance, with the Public Prosecutor's Office and the Ministry of Justice at the forefront of the process conveyed a clear message of prioritization. UNICEF successfully conducted a similar approach for advocacy sessions on CRC recommendations to ensure greater ownership of this instrument. 

 

Reinforced support from UNICEF to generate data and evidence - The Country Programme identified building capacities in data and evidence-driven approaches as a priority to improve progress towards SDGs and investments for children. In 2024, UNICEF engaged in significant interventions to enhance data collection and strengthen the national statistical system, with the administrative data collection manual. Regular funds were used to undertake foundational analysis (KAP, CLAC, disability case management, State of the Education System Report) which will generate evidence for advocacy, resource mobilization and inform the programme. In 2025, UNICEF will concentrate effort to mobilize funds for MICS-7, as the census is planned for 2025 to bridge the data gap. 

 

Integrated SBC as a critical strategy to reach results at scale - UNICEF significantly expanded its cross-sectoral SBC initiatives and community engagement strongly supported by youth and adolescents to reach results at scale. The approach combined grassroot actions with digital content dissemination, using the U-Report platform to effectively reach 17,500 young people. This strategy accelerated impactful results at scale in immunization, improved communities’ uptake of healthy practices and increased visibility of transformative changes. To accelerate results, UNICEF will develop a multisectoral SBC strategy, better integrate community feedback into programming and enhance the monitoring of SBC impacts and results.

 

Collaboration with youth to drive positive change at community and national levels –Effective engagement with youth was a critical enabling factor to advance equity, reach results at scale and improve ownership. The SBC initiatives in partnership with youth triggered accelerated results for immunization and climate engagement, while advancing gender equality, in support to several SDGs’ targets. In 2024, UNICEF ensured that youth were active partners across all sectoral interventions, in high-level meetings and workshops, studies as well as annual review. Gender equality remained at the core of UNICEF’s youth engagement, with the objective to promote girl’s wellbeing and empowerment, with a focus on adolescent girls. The Youth Committees for Climate were an innovative way to foster community engagement, empowering young people and adolescents as climate activists embedding the climate and youth agendas. This approach increased ownership and sustainability ensuring transformative impact.

 

After two years in the Country Programme, the annual review confirmed that the underlying theory of change remains valid. UNICEF will pursue its strategic approach to improve the access to, and availability of, quality social services, to promote behavioural change, and to advocate for gender and child-sensitive policies and budgets to enable children, including adolescents, to realize their rights.  



Building on current efforts, UNICEF will expand its innovations going forward. The digital learning programme broadened access to learning materials and knowledge of extracurricular subjects. It will offer opportunities to improve continuity of learning, advance inclusive education and life and employability skills, to strengthen youth socio-economic resilience. The innovative connectivity mapping and the interactive tool providing cost scenarios lay the foundation for expanding digital learning, a key governmental priority. 



Following their positive impact on results for children, UNICEF will scale-up, expand and resource youth engagement and youth-led solutions, promoted by U-Report platform to increase results at scale. This includes innovations such as the climate committees and the engagement in pilot schools, enhancing employability of the young volunteers with a gender-transformative approach. UNICEF will continue to leverage community engagement, encouraged by integrated SBC interventions, to scale up programme implementation and accelerate results, with a focus on adolescent girls. 



UNICEF played a convening role with UNDP to foster synergies, community mobilization and youth engagement around the climate agenda. Foundational data and evidence from the CLAC will guide better multisectoral programming on environmental sustainability, including on the impacts of our interventions, with clear indicators for monitoring. In partnership with the UN system in STP and other UNICEF offices, the STP Country Office will mobilize resources for climate action and youth risk-informed programming to contribute to more sustainable and inclusive growth.

Senegal, classified as a Least Developed Country (LDC) since 2000, has made significant progress in development indicators, positioning itself on a promising path toward graduation by 2029. Of the three criteria used to determine LDC status, Senegal has surpassed the graduation thresholds for the Human Assets Index and Gross National Income. However, its Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index score of 42.3 highlights ongoing challenges, particularly its dependence on agriculture and vulnerability to climate risks, as seen in the 2024 floods that affected over 70,000 people, including around 39,000 children. [1] [2]
Senegal ranks 169th out of 193 countries on the Human Development Index. Following the Human Capital Index a child born in Senegal is projected to be only 42% as productive as they could be with complete education and full health with modest improvements observed between 2010 and 2020. These data are especially concerning for Senegal's population of nearly 18 million, with almost 40% under the age of 15. [3] [4] [5]
Senegal’s macroeconomic performance remains robust, with Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth reaching 6% in 2024, below the projected 7.1%. This growth has been fueled by anticipated revenues from hydrocarbons, marking a significant fiscal opportunity. However, fiscal challenges persist: the debt-to-GDP ratio has exceeded 70%, and the fiscal deficit stands at 7.5%. To comply with ECOWAS fiscal convergence criteria, Senegal will need to narrow this deficit to 3%, requiring prudent fiscal management [6].
The country's political stability sets it apart from many of its regional counterparts. Despite pre-election violence and concerns, the 2024 presidential and parliamentary elections resulted in decisive victories for Bassirou Diomaye Faye and the PASTEF party. These victories have given President Faye a strong mandate to implement an ambitious Vision for the country through 2050, along with an even more ambitious development strategy for 2025-2029. This strategy, which requires approximately 18,5 billion CFA francs, prioritizes key areas such as human capital development and social equity—essential for advancing children's well-being. [7] [8]
Around 4 in 10 Senegalese children live in poverty, and 1 in 2 are deprived of at least one fundamental right. Poverty is more severe in rural (66%) than urban areas (28.1%), with regions like Kédougou, and Kolda reporting the highest poverty rates. In 2023, 37.5% of the population lived below the poverty line, slightly down from 37.8% in 2018. However, inequalities persist, with the Gini index marginally decreasing from 0.351 in 2018 to 0.33 in 2023. [9]
Several key indicators, including those aligned with the 8 Key Results for Children (KRCs) [10] established for the West and Central Africa Region by UNICEF, underscore the urgent need for more efficient, adequate, and transparent investments to address the needs of children. According to the Government 2024 budget allocations, only 28% is dedicated to social expenditures. More concerning is the inadequate funding for essential sectors like health, which receives only 5% of the budget, far below the international benchmark of 15% set by the Abuja Declaration. [11]
The country faces significant health and nutrition challenges, with maternal mortality high at 213 deaths per 100,000 live births, far exceeding the SDG target of 70. Neonatal mortality is 21 per 1,000 live births, with rural areas experiencing higher rates. The leading causes of child deaths are neonatal infections (37%), malaria (14%), and pneumonia (12%). Regarding KRC 2, chronic malnutrition affects 17.5% of children under five, and only 26.5% of children aged 6–23 months meet the minimum dietary diversity needed for healthy development.[12]
Senegal has made strides in providing access to clean water, with 90.9% of households using improved water sources. However, access in urban areas (98.1%) is much higher than in rural regions (83.5%). Regarding SDG target 6.2 and KRC 8, open defecation remains a significant issue in rural areas, with 12.9% of households practicing it compared to only 0.9% in urban settings. Access to basic hygiene facilities is limited, with only 28% of the population benefiting from such services. .[12]
Access to education and progresses towards SDG 4 and KRC 3 also presents challenges, with substantial regional and gender disparities. Although girls generally have higher enrollment rates than boys in primary and lower secondary, the overall enrollment rate remains low, with approximately 41.4% of school-age children not enrolled in formal education. Technical and vocational education remains limited, with only 12 technical high schools across the country.[12]
The 2023 Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) shows mixed progress in child protection. Female genital mutilation (FGM) has decreased from 25.2% in 2019 to 20.1% in 2023 among women aged 15-49, and from 16.1% to 12.9% among girls aged 0-14. However, FGM remains high in the South-East and North, with some areas exceeding 70%. While 80% of women support ending FGM, men's support has dropped from 78% to 66%. Child marriage rates remain steady, with 30.2% of women aged 20-24 married before 18. In relation to KRC 5, the 2023 DHS did not address violence, but the 2019 survey found 2.9% of girls aged 15-17 experienced sexual violence. A 2022 Ministry of Education study found that two-thirds of students experienced violence (psychological, physical, or sexual) at home, in the community, or at school, with one-third of cases occurring in schools. On a positive note, birth registration rates have improved, with 81.4% of children under 5 now registered, up from 74.6% in 2010 and 78.7% in 2019, although regional disparities remain (64% in Louga, 93% in Dakar). [13] [14]
Climate change exacerbates existing vulnerabilities, with Senegal ranking 22nd among the 163 nations most affected by its impact on children, according to UNICEF's Climate Risk Index for Children (2021). Extreme weather events, such as droughts and floods, disrupt food security and harm children's health. Urban pollution, especially in Dakar, further threatens child well-being. [12] [15]
Gender inequality continues to impede the progress of both girls and women in Senegal. Social norms and perceptions restrict girls' opportunities, particularly in education, health, and economic participation. Women and girls are disproportionately affected by climate-related disasters, harmful practices and economic instability, exacerbating their vulnerability. [12]
