In 2024, UNICEF launched its new Country Programme (2024–2028) aligned with UNICEF global Strategic Plan as well as with the United Nations Cooperation Framework, focusing on human capital development. Following the March presidential elections and the formation of a new government, UNICEF adjusted its planning to align with the government’s priorities, emphasizing child rights. Key activities included mid-year reviews and workshops to review the Country Programme’s results and Theories of Change. As the first year of implementation of the Country Programme, UNICEF's efforts focused on building the basis for achieving CPD's overall goals aligning our approaches with the vision of the new authorities established in 2024 and laying the ground to contribute to the achievements of the expected outcomes by 2028. 
UNICEF’s support prioritized a multisectoral approach, integrating gender-transformative strategies, Social and Behavior Change (SBC) interventions, advocacy, climate action, policy dialogue, social protection, and the empowerment of adolescents as key agents of change. These efforts were designed to promote sustainable progress across the components of the Country Programme, as well as to act as enablers for the KRCs. Some results achieved include strengthening community-level capacities and knowledge, particularly in nutrition (KRC 2), integrating the most disadvantaged children into the formal education system (KRC 3), and reinforcing the national child protection system (KRC 5). 
Programme implementation in 2024 was also shaped by emergency preparedness and response to multiple crises, including the most severe floods in recent years, and awareness-raising and prevention initiatives for the MPOX epidemic.
Every child survives and thrives 
UNICEF's support has driven transformative changes in child health through the strategic reinforcement of health centers to deliver high-quality care at the primary level. This included providing critical equipment, training 200 health workers and 80 Community Health Workers in maternal and newborn care, and scaling the Helping Babies Breathe approach for neonatal resuscitation. The establishment of four state-of-the-art newborn units has redefined the safety and quality of childbirth, giving countless infants a healthy start to life, reducing regional disparities in accessing health services as recommended by the CRC Committee.
To combat pneumonia, one of the deadliest threats to children under five, UNICEF led groundbreaking efforts to strengthen oxygen therapy services. By decentralizing oxygen availability, training healthcare personnel in oxygen quantification and dimensioning, and equipping health centers with six electric generators to support PSA oxygen plants, UNICEF significantly expanded access to life-saving treatment for respiratory distress. These transformative interventions not only safeguard the health and well-being of children today but also lay a robust foundation for equitable and sustainable healthcare systems that will benefit generations to come.
UNICEF also played a pivotal role in protecting children from vaccine-preventable diseases. By facilitating a tripartite Memorandum of Understanding with the government and the World Bank, UNICEF ensured the timely provision of vaccines and supported the successful implementation of a nationwide measles and rubella follow-up campaign. This effort reached 98% of the targeted population (children aged 9 months to 14 years), significantly increasing community immunity and protecting children against these life-threatening diseases. Targeting infrastructure and capacity, UNICEF revitalized the cold chain and logistics system through maintenance and capacity-building initiatives in vaccine management. The innovative "October Rose Campaign," integrating HPV vaccination, further broke down gender and equity barriers, ensuring adolescents, particularly girls, could access immunization services.
UNICEF’s support extended to transforming child nutrition through the development of key national strategies, including the Nutrition Multisectoral Plan, Food Fortification Plan, SRMNIA-Nutrition Plan, and a comprehensive salt sector analysis. By strengthening Nutrition Committees and building the capacity of 389 health actors in Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Feeding and 235 in community Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) management, UNICEF contributed to improve the nutritional outcomes for children across the country. Six regions implemented breastfeeding action plans, and 16 districts managed SAM at the community level. Over 2.5 million children were protected with essential nutrition supplies, and 22,223 SAM cases were successfully managed. Additionally, 220 community granary food centers supported complementary feeding, directly contributing to the achievement of KRC 2.
 
Every child learns
In 2024, UNICEF led education sector coordination for technical and financial partners, supporting the government to secure a US$78 million grant from the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), along with additional partner funds. A newly developed vulnerability map and index will guide equity-based fund allocations to address persistent gaps in the education sector.
UNICEF contributed to drafting an education resilience plan addressing climate change, crises, and health emergencies, developed a remediation framework using the Teaching at the Right Level approach, and supported the National Reading and Mathematics Strategy and the National Strategy for Girls' Retention to improve transitions from elementary to middle school. A teacher study with UNICEF Innocenti Research Centre will provide recommendations to address the teacher shortage in 2025, as announced by Senegal's President, which offers a unique opportunity to address CRC Committee’s recommendation on the availability of qualified teachers, especially in rural areas.
The National Bilingual Education Program improved learning through mother-tongue instruction in Kolda which is a priority of the new government, benefiting 30 schools, 2,051 students, and distributing 13,470 textbooks with UNICEF support. Additionally, 5,402 teachers (including 1,269 women) against a target of 8,000 received training in reading, mathematics, and inclusive education. Educational materials and digital resources reached 50,105 learners, meeting the target of 50,000 while digital education initiatives helped 2,167 students and 137 teachers. These efforts contribute to the CPD outcome 2 target, ensuring primary students acquire essential reading and mathematics skills.
UNICEF supported 33,188 vulnerable children and marginalized youths against a target of 34,000, providing education through community-based preschools (11,586), bridging classes (4,342), alternative learning in Koranic schools (6,721), vocational training (305), birth certificates, girls' empowerment (10,000), and youth with disabilities (234), contributing to KRC 3.
92 traditional Koranic schools received hygiene kits to enhance the learning environment for 2,760 children, while a community-based preschool model was introduced in Koranic schools in Louga and Saint Louis, equipped with learning, play, and hygiene materials. Additionally, UNICEF supported 4,548 schools and over 113,700 girls beneficiaries with gender-sensitive initiatives, including separate toilets and access to washable pads, and began scaling up a model empowering female vocational training graduates to produce washable pads locally. These efforts follow CRC Committee’s recommendation on the access of girl students to menstrual hygiene items.
Education has been the entry point to work on disability inclusion across the different sectors. UNICEF partnered with civil society organizations (CSOs) to train 80 teachers and headmasters on inclusive education, also part of the new government priorities, and sports, and 20 school life assistants to support children with disabilities. Additionally, a national collaboration was launched with ATScales, the Ministry of Health, and WHO to integrate school-based screening and provide assistive technologies for children with visual and mobility impairments.
Every child, is protected from violence and exploitation
UNICEF collaborated with ministries responsible for child protection, alongside education, health sectors, and civil society, to strengthen child protection systems, challenge harmful social norms, , and promote access to birth registration. As a contribution to KRC 5, UNICEF’s support allowed 2,624 child victims of violence (797 girls and 1,827 boys) to access services, including 164 cases of sexual violence. However, financial challenges limited achieving the full target for this indicator in UNICEF's 2024-2028 Cooperation Programme. In addition, specific efforts were made in the context of Presidential election to prevent the involvement of children in violent demonstrations and promote social cohesion. 
UNICEF strengthened the national child protection system by building partners’ capacity, supporting reporting and care services, and deploying the Rapid Pro mechanism for violence cases. Collaboration with the security sector increased, including training social workers, magistrates, and security forces on GBV. UNICEF also contributed to developing a national alternative care framework. However, due to political issues, the child protection strategy evaluation and national action plan which constitute key recommendations from the CRC Committee were delayed, though the child marriage action plan is being validated.
As part of the UNFPA-UNICEF Joint Programme on the Elimination of FGM, UNICEF supported gender-transformative approaches for community leaders, service providers, and others through the global accelerator tool. Senegal is a pathfinder country for this initiative. The tool addresses gender roles, norms, and inequalities, reinforcing positive change. Implementing partners were trained in SBC, and an orientation guide to accelerate FGM abandonment was co-created. A joint advocacy plan involving youth, women's groups, and religious leaders was developed under the Ministry of the Family's leadership. These efforts contribute to address different recommendations issued by the CRC Committee on ending harmful practices.
UNICEF supported the late birth registration (KRC 7) of 6,800 children through coordination with Child Protection Committees and the Ministry of Education. The Ministry issued a circular for all decentralized services to identify and register students without birth certificates across various school levels. An online platform was established to monitor the registration process and track progress. Regarding interoperability with health, in collaboration with the National Agency of Civil Registry and the Ministry of Health, an assessment of the civil registration desks in health centers was prepared and recommendations are expected in early 2025 prior further expansion of this mechanism, following the recommendations of the CRC Committee.
 
Every child lives in a safe and sustainable climate and environment
In the area of water, sanitation, and hygiene, UNICEF supported the implementation of high-impact, community-based approaches to reach the most vulnerable groups by providing safe drinking water and improving individual and community hygiene. This included the establishment of drinking water points, latrines, and the promotion of Expanded Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS). These efforts led to significant achievements, such as 400,706 people in 949 Open Defecation-Free (ODF) villages abandoning open defecation, which contributed significantly to KRC 8 and the overall WASH component of the CPD, following CRC Committee’s recommendations. UNICEF’s advocacy also played a crucial role in increasing government funding for the sanitation sector, particularly for the ODF program. The CLTS initiative also positively impacted adolescent and young girls by improving their participation in community life, increasing their school attendance, and enhancing their safety. This was achieved through menstrual health and hygiene interventions, including awareness-raising and the distribution of 20,000 menstrual hygiene kits. These actions helped maintain dignity, build self-confidence, and support sexual and reproductive health, particularly among adolescent girls. These cross-sectoral efforts, with CLTS as an entry point, highlight the strong collaboration across UNICEF’s program components—WASH, health, nutrition, immunization, education, and child protection. A strategy for scaling up the expanded CLTS program, will be developed in 2025 in collaboration with partners from the Ministry of Health, Hygiene, and Sanitation, as well as other stakeholders.
 
UNICEF Senegal has advanced its efforts under the protection and empowerment pillars of its Sustainability and Climate Change Action Plan 2023-2030. It conducted studies on children’s vulnerabilities to climate change, including sector-specific vulnerability assessments in health, education, WASH, and child protection. These findings shape its cross-sectoral work plan and advocacy efforts, integrating child-specific vulnerabilities into national climate documents. Public awareness was strengthened through events like COP29, where Senegal included a youth advocate in its delegation. UNICEF also launched the Green Generation platform to equip young people with climate action and advocacy skills.
In collaboration with the Education sector, UNICEF is piloting the Green Schools initiative in the Matam region, aiming to scale it nationally. This initiative addresses climate change by greening schools, improving WASH infrastructure, raising climate awareness, enhancing teacher skills, and promoting eco-citizen practices. UNICEF is also supporting Senegal’s leadership in climate education through a high-level forum launching the Regional Declaration on Strengthening Climate Education at COP29. This multi-sectoral effort involves the Ministries of Environment and Education, with ongoing advocacy to integrate environmental and climate education into the national curriculum.
 
Every child has an equitable chance in life
In line with CRC Committee’s recommendations on increasing the part of the budget allocated to social services at the central and local level, by embedding children’s rights into public financial management, UNICEF shaped critical policy discussions and influenced resource allocations, despite the complexities of an election year. Advocacy efforts were strategically aligned with key events, including engagement with the new government, the launch of joint knowledge products like the National Multi Overlapping Deprivation Analysis, the Social Protection Expenditure Review, and the DHS. These platforms helped highlight priorities and mobilize political will, resulting in a 21% increase in education funding for children since 2019. However, gaps persist, especially in health, where funding remains at 5%, well below the 15% international benchmark and the UNICEF Country Programme's 2028 target.
UNICEF prioritized enhancing budget transparency and promoting citizen and child participation in response to Senegal's low 2023 Open Budget Survey score. This effort bolstered local governance initiatives, resulting in participatory budgeting in 7 out of 11 municipalities and across all 53 Child-Friendly Municipalities. Through the involvement of Children's Municipal Councils, local budgets now better address the needs of vulnerable populations, particularly children, while ensuring their priorities are integrated into budget discussions and debates.
UNICEF strengthened local governance by providing strategic planning support to 420 stakeholders, including mayors and community leaders. Training on harmonized planning guides helped local governments adopt a more inclusive, child-sensitive approach to planning, budgeting, and monitoring progress toward child-focused development goals.
UNICEF helped adapt the national social protection system, contributing to the second top-up of digital cash transfers through the ‘Bourse Familiale’ program, reaching 22,038 children, including girls and children with disabilities. This initiative improved school attendance and study time among girls aged 6-11, promoting gender equity, transparency, and efficiency in cash transfers. With this initiative, UNICEF enabled greater transparency and efficiency while enhancing gender-sensitive distribution methods, proving a promising model for a digital payment transition at scale and indicating that digitization can help reduce cash administration costs in the medium and longer terms. It also demonstrated the potential of social protection as an enabler to accelerate the achievement of KRCs.
UNICEF supported Senegal’s national statistics system by assisting with the rollout of the 2024-2028 statistics strategy and contributing to the completion of the DHS, which provided data on over 30 SDG indicators.
Cross-sectoral and operational strategies 
UNICEF enhanced program effectiveness through intersectoral, risk-informed planning at national and local levels, involving state and non-state partners. Governors and Prefects developed decentralized plans incorporating children's priorities, gender, inclusion, and climate change, supported by strategies in SBC, communication, empowerment, and youth engagement.
As part of its commitment to accountability to affected populations, UNICEF supported the establishment of community-based mechanisms for registering citizens' concerns with a strong adolescent component. This tool acts as a vital advocacy resource, offering stakeholders and leaders ongoing feedback on the quality, availability, accessibility, and acceptability of services, while holding them accountable for their delivery.
At the municipal level, programmatic and geographic convergence has been advanced through the establishment of 11 Convergence Communities, which are Child Friendly Municipalities where child needs are prioritized in local planification with a 360 degrees approach. This initiative usually began with a child rights situation analysis, followed by community consultations to identify priorities and the development of two-year action plans.
UNICEF continued its engagement with human rights mechanisms, supporting the government and the national coalition of child rights NGOs (CONAFE) in attending dialogues with the Committee on the Rights of the Child. UNICEF also participated in discussions with the CRC Committee and the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Wellbeing of the Child, which laid the foundation for the ongoing dissemination and implementation of their recommendations. The support provided in 2023 to revise the law transforming the Senegalese Committee for Human Rights into the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) led to the law's adoption by parliament in 2024, positioning the CNDH to regain its A-status. Additionally, UNICEF helped the CNDH develop its operational action plan, outlining priority actions to advance children's rights based on human rights mechanisms' recommendations. Despite challenges in 2024, including the transition to the new government, this collaboration with the CNDH presents opportunities to advocate for Senegal's ratification of the CRC's Optional Protocol on a communications procedure.
The Emergency Preparedness Platform (EPP) was updated to address five critical scenarios: floods, drought and food insecurity, epidemics, armed conflict in Casamance, and instability in neighboring countries. The office achieved a 100% preparedness score, underscoring its robust capacity to respond effectively to emergencies.
When one of the most severe floods in recent years struck the southeastern and northern regions of Senegal, UNICEF swiftly mobilized and delivered emergency relief supplies, including hygiene kits, water purification tablets, and non-food items, mitigating the disaster's impact. UNICEF provided essential support by distributing WASH kits to 8,692 severely affected households, benefiting approximately 43,000 individuals, including around 26,000 children.
In parallel, UNICEF collaborated with the government to enhance preparedness for a potential MPOX outbreak.
UNICEF completed its Gender Programmatic Review Action Plan to guide the implementation of gender-focused initiatives across its operations and programs. Gender-transformative approaches were embedded in key sectors such as social policy and child protection.
UNICEF kept strengthening the commitment and participation of adolescents in the planning, implementation, monitoring and evaluation processes across different programs. To help maintain social cohesion, a network of more than 1,000 adolescents and youth volunteers was set up in the South-East regions. The establishment of U-Communities by teenagers and young people is also contributing to boost demand for and the quality of essential services for children and women.
UNICEF supported the evaluation of the CLTS program, which aligns with KRC 8. The evaluation highlighted the program's performance, relevance, and efficiency, but also identified areas for improvement, particularly in sustainability. It found instances where good hygiene and sanitation practices were abandoned in areas declared open defecation free. Key insights will be shared with partners in early 2025 in order to identify how to implement the recommendations, especially regarding scaling up the initiative.
Additionally, UNICEF completed a quasi-experimental impact evaluation to assess the effects of cash transfers, implemented in collaboration with the Senegalese government, to support school enrollment and attendance for children from vulnerable households, whose results were used in strategic discussions with the government and potential donors on the importance of child-sensitive social protection. Furthermore, UNICEF collaborated with the Senegalese Evaluation Association to foster a strong evaluation culture and enhance accountability in policies and programs through the organization of capacity building initiatives on evaluation concepts and techniques, and documenting best practices in involving children and adolescents in evaluative processes.
UNICEF made significant efforts to enhance operational effectiveness, ensuring the successful delivery of programme activities. Key achievements were made in supply and logistics, particularly in vaccine and health supply chain management, emergency preparedness and response, nutrition, and strengthening national supply chain systems and capacity building. Over US$ 31 million worth of vaccines, including those for routine immunization and the MR campaign, were delivered and distributed. UNICEF operations team also proactively worked to address recommendations from financial controls, audits, and micro-assessments.
A key focus for UNICEF was strengthening Senegal’s national supply chain systems. In collaboration with the Ministry of Health and WHO, UNICEF assessed the supply chain’s maturity, identifying gaps and areas of risk. Following this assessment, UNICEF supported the drafting of the Institutional Development Plan which will address critical issues such as storage, distribution, customs clearance, and monitoring, helping to enhance the overall efficiency of the national supply chain.
UNICEF has played a pivotal leadership role in advancing the UN Reform Agenda in Senegal. By hosting the Management Unit of the UN House, UNICEF has spearheaded significant progress in the quality assurance and operationalization of a shared UN building complex, which will house 28 UN organizations. This initiative fosters inter-agency collaboration and efficiency. Despite pending legal agreements, UNICEF has demonstrated a proactive approach by designing the provision of 31 services together with a customer-centric, innovative digital service provision platform for the anticipated common back-office services.  This strategic undertaking strengthens the UN's collective impact in Senegal by maximizing resources, promoting knowledge sharing, and ultimately contributing to a more coordinated and effective UN response to the needs of children and communities, in line with the goals of the UN Reform Agenda.

In 2024, following Senegal’s political transition and amid global crises, UNICEF faced limited donor support. However, the organization pursued strategic partnerships and innovative financing to diversify its network of partners and strengthen its work in climate resilience, education, health, WASH, and child protection. UNICEF secured US$2.5 million, focusing on child protection, social protection, and girls’ education – including funding from two new donors – and established a strong US$12 million pipeline for 2025, exceeding its US$10 million target. This success included joint proposals with CSOs and UN agencies, supporting the “One UN” approach.
UNICEF Senegal focused on strengthening climate resilience to help systems and communities mitigate climate change's impact on children. After two years of negotiations and previous collaborations with Save the Children and the Ministry of Health, UNICEF became part of a consortium submitting a proposal to the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to enhance resilience in health and education. If successful, UNICEF Senegal would be the first Country Office to receive GCF funding. Discussions with Luxembourg aim to support vulnerable communities through CLTS interventions in health, nutrition, education, and child protection. Additionally, and for the first time, UNICEF developed a Peacebuilding Fund proposal with the International Organization for Migration to address WASH challenges across Senegal, Mauritania, and Mali borders. UNICEF has leveraged its technical expertise and convening power to strengthen advocacy with the Government and technical and financial partners, promoting the integration of climate change adaptation strategies into national policies and budgets. Strong collaboration with the Ministry of Environment has positioned UNICEF as a strategic partner in preparing the 2025 Nationally Determined Contributions and ensuring the participation of children and young people in this process.
In continuation with progress made since 2022, the private sector remains a significant partner. A collaboration with Nokia, facilitated through UNICEF Finland, supported digital education initiatives aimed at bridging learning gaps in underserved areas through the Xam ak Jam Tech initiative. Similarly, the Salmaïtou program, part of the global “Skills4Girls” initiative, was expanded with additional support from Chloé through UNICEF France. Both initiatives were not launched in 2024 but rather piloted in the last Country Programme and put to scale through renewed support. Interest from new partners and continued support from past donors highlight the impact of these programss. 
Resource mobilization with new partners, including Safe Online, also enabled UNICEF Senegal to strengthen its programmatic response to emerging issues, including online child protection, which contributes to address CRC Committee’s recommendations related to children’s rights in the digital environment. UNICEF Senegal is also pursuing collaboration with UN agencies, including UNDP and OHCHR, to further the business and human rights agenda. Following a series of consultations across the country with private sector, local authorities and community actors, Senegal is set to become one of the first countries in West and Central Africa to develop a National Action Plan on business and human rights, addressing the issue of child right violations caused by private sector activities, including in the mining sector.  
In emergencies like flooding and political instability, UNICEF focused on immediate needs and long-term resilience. Collaborating with UNDP and youth groups, it engaged adolescents in promoting social cohesion and preventing violence. Ahead of the 2024 presidential election, UNICEF partnered with civil society for advocacy on children's rights. UNICEF, in collaboration with JOFA, a consortium of INGOs, launched a campaign urging presidential candidates to commit to five child-focused priorities. Following the presidential election, UNICEF developed an advocacy note analyzing opportunities to accelerate the realization of children’s rights. This note was shared with technical and financial partners to encourage the integration of children’s rights into policies and strategies, as well as in their engagements with the new authorities. 
As part of joint UN efforts to mobilize resources, UNICEF Senegal achieved a significant milestone by successfully securing seed funding from the Joint SDG Fund in support of the Global Accelerator for Jobs and Social Protection, along with five other countries worldwide. This funding stream, which supports the rollout of the Global Accelerator for Jobs and Social Protection, will enable joint UN action in Senegal to strengthen national capacities for integrated employment and social protection policies. By supporting well-governed institutions and fostering just transitions, this initiative underscores UNICEF’s commitment to advancing sustainable development and improving outcomes for children and families.
In the health sector, UNICEF successfully leveraged its strategic partnerships with financial institutions to advance public health priorities. Tripartite collaboration with the World Bank and the Government and support from UNICEF Supply division was key to secure and deliver 5,460,000 additional doses of Measles-Rubella vaccines, valued at more than US$ 5.6 million, and ensuring the timely availability of vaccines to cover the expanded target group of children aged 9 months to 15 years. 
UNICEF has built strong partnerships with Canada, JICA, the EU, and the French development agency to improve efficiency, equity, and resilience through innovative financing and planning in the education sector. This advocacy led to the creation of a joint budgetary support committee, fostering dialogue between the Ministries of Education and Finance. UNICEF leveraged its role as lead agency for the technical and financial partners’ education sector coordination group to support resource mobilization efforts with the Government and key stakeholders, including approval of a GPE grant to accelerate the transformation of the education system, to be implemented by the Ministry of Education in collaboration with the French development agency. Coordinated efforts with UNESCO and other donors resulted in drafting the first education sector analysis, which will inform the revision of the education sector plan in 2025.
In 2024, UNICEF Senegal demonstrated adaptability and foresight in its resource mobilization strategy. While key partnerships such as those with the Green Climate Fund and Luxembourg remain in the discussion phase, they represent important opportunities to expand UNICEF’s impact. Moving forward, UNICEF Senegal is committed to nurturing traditional donor relationships while seizing innovative financing opportunities. Recognizing the shift in donor priorities, with many traditional donors increasingly channeling funds directly to governments or reducing overall aid budgets, UNICEF Senegal undoubtedly needs to rethink its resource mobilization strategies, with a funding gap of at least US$ 31 million until 2028. 
This forward-looking approach involves exploring diversification through individual giving, philanthropy, and private sector collaborations to align with evolving donor interests and ensure sustainability. As part of this envisioned strategy, the Dakar Youth Olympics in 2026 is seen as a promising opportunity to engage non-traditional donors and attract resources to further UNICEF’s work in Senegal. Following the introduction of the government’s 2050 Vision for a National Transformation Agenda, these efforts will ensure the continued mobilization of resources to support transformative outcomes for children in Senegal.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
2024 was a challenging year for Senegal, marked by political transitions, administrative turnover, and floods that disrupted the implementation of planned activities. Despite these difficulties, the year also brought impactful innovations and valuable lessons, laying a strong foundation for future progress.
Challenge 1: Political developments, including two elections that resulted in high turnover among government officials who had been involved in the development of the 2024–2028 CPD, created delays in the implementation of some activities. Following the March 2024 presidential elections and the formation of a new government, UNICEF in consultation with the new authorities adapted its planning to align with the updated political and development agenda they recently developed, prioritizing child rights.
Challenge 2: Integrating climate change across sectors is challenging due to limited data on its impact, especially on children. A human rights-based climate approach is needed, prioritizing children's rights and sustainable development. Better coordination, capacity-building, and improved understanding of UNICEF's role are required to access climate funds and integrate climate considerations into planning.
Challenge 3: Enhanced citizen’s engagement, improved data systems, and increased financing for children, especially in health, education, and child protection, remain critical challenges to advance child wellbeing. Addressing these is essential for advancing children's well-being in both development and humanitarian settings, requiring greater support at national and local levels.
Innovation 1: The implementation of the top-up to digital cash transfer programme highlighted the potential of digital cash transfers as a mechanism to address vulnerabilities and provide timely support to households. However, it also underscored the necessity for significant refinements to ensure their long-term success and sustainability. Addressing these challenges will be essential to transitioning digital cash transfers into a regular and effective method of social protection in Senegal.
Innovation 2: Notable innovations during the year included the development of a joint advocacy plan by women’s and youth movements, as well as the co-creation of an orientation guide to accelerate the abandonment of Female Genital Mutilation. This guide was developed collaboratively with community actors, UNICEF, and an NGO partner, serving as a practical tool for outreach workers and community members.
Lesson learnt 1: Digital technology has proven to be an essential enabler of youth participation and empowerment, the continuity of social services, and child protection during periods of disruption. In the education sector, it improved classroom management and facilitated access to vital resources, presenting scalable solutions to address future challenges. Likewise, in child protection, the Rapid Protection initiative demonstrated the transformative role of technology in connecting communities to critical services and enhancing their accessibility.
Lesson learnt 2: Despite the challenges posed by the socio-political context, UNICEF Senegal successfully executed its Annual Work Plan through comprehensive decentralized and multisectoral planning. Collaborating with state partners, local authorities, and CSOs, this approach highlighted the potential for impactful intersectoral strategies and enhanced coordination between decentralized services and local governments. At the municipal level, the planning process actively engaged communities, children, and youth, fostering inclusive and grounded strategies, representing a strategic entry point for programmatic convergence to advance key results for children.
Lessons learnt 3: 
Collaboration with social sectors and regional elected officials has led to practical models for addressing challenges. Joint efforts in education have established shared funding goals, leveraged local resources for community preschools and bridging classes, and gained support from religious and community leaders. Additionally, linking cash transfer programs to initiatives preventing girls from dropping out of school has provided valuable insights. These models will help shape the targeted focus on adolescent girls in the 2025 set-aside funds.
Future outlook
The insights gained during the year will guide Senegal Country Office in refining its programmatic strategies as follows:
·        Strengthening Multisectoral Initiatives: Expand initiatives with high multisectoral potential, such as the Expanded CLTS program, while deepening their integration by incorporating additional topics and dismantling silo-based interventions. A specific focus will be put on further developing the adolescent girl agenda, using education as an entry point for a comprehensive approach and taking advantage from the organization of a regional summit on adolescent girls in Dakar in 2025.
·        Scaling Multisectoral Planning: Document and scale up the multisectoral planning approach implemented at the decentralized level across all areas covered by the UNICEF Kolda Zone Office.
·        Strategic Advocacy: Utilize UNICEF’s influential advocacy capacity and strategic positioning in collaboration with other UN agencies, donors and NGOs to drive investments in critical priorities for children. Advocate for the implementation of the CRC Committee’s recommendations, including the adoption of the remaining optional protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on a communications procedure, particularly in collaboration with the newly established National Assembly, the Senegalese Human Rights Committee and CSOs.
·        Enhancing Coordination and Engagement: Promote stronger coordination mechanisms, enhanced citizen engagement, and improved data systems to secure increased financing for children at both national and local levels. For example, at a strategic level, UNICEF’s support to the evaluation of the 2020-2024 community health strategic plan and to the development of the new 2025-2029 strategic plan offers an excellent opportunity to keep strengthening community health strategies.
·        Accelerating Social Norms and Behavior Change: Drive progress on social norms and behavior change by strengthening partnerships with academia (for SBC social data generation and their utilization for programming and planning and measuring results) women’s movements, adolescent and youth organizations, and religious leaders, especially when addressing sensitive issues.
·        Deploying Digital Tools at scale: Ensure the widespread and sustainable deployment of proven digital tools, while intensifying efforts to secure buy-in from government partners.
·        Advancing the Climate Change Agenda: UNICEF aims to strengthen its climate change agenda by advancing pilot initiatives, integrating climate change into multisectoral approaches like CLTS, and exploring new funding opportunities through its Green Climate Fund (GCF) accreditation.
·        Supporting gender transformative approaches across the sectors: Support the implementation of the Gender Action Plan emerging from the gender programmatic review, while promoting a gender-transformative approach across sectors.
These adjustments aim to reinforce UNICEF’s impact, ensuring its strategies are sustainable, inclusive, and responsive to the evolving needs of children and communities in Senegal.

The political landscape in 2024 remained calm yet cautious. Following the contested 2023 general elections, the Independent Commission for Peace and National Cohesion mediated dialogue between the major political parties, leading to a tripartite agreement[1] aimed at addressing electoral reforms, strengthening democratic institutions and promoting sustainable peace. 



Economic challenges persisted due to an average inflation rate of 30 per cent[2] and underlying fragility such as high debt-to-GDP ratio[3]; high levels of youth unemployment and underemployment, high food insecurity of 82 per cent in February 2024[4], and limited fiscal space. Consequently, public sector financing and child-friendly budgeting remained constrained, limiting capacities to deliver integrated, quality and inclusive social services. 



In January, the Government of Sierra Leone (GoSL) launched the Medium-Term National Development Plan (MTNDP) 2024-2030, prioritizing "Big Five Game Changers"; food security, human capital development, youth employment, public sector reform, technology and infrastructure, including innovation and digitalization - to transform and accelerate national development towards the achievement of the SDGs, Agenda 2063 and other global commitments. 



The United Nations Country Team (UNCT) developed and aligned the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (UNSDCF) 2025-2030 and their respective Country Programmes to the MTNDP. UNICEF worked closely with GoSL, UN agencies, development partners, civil society organizations, communities, adolescents and children, and other stakeholders to develop the Country Programme (CP) 2025-2030 based on evidence generated from the Common Country Analysis 2023, Situation Analysis of Children and Adolescents in Sierra Leone (SiTAN), and lessons learned from the Country Programme Evaluation and Gender Programme Review (CPE, GPR) 2020-2024.



Child survival has improved with a 15 per cent decrease in the under-five mortality rate from 109.1 in 2019 to 94.3 in 2023[5]. Sustained investments in health systems strengthening have improved access to equitable and quality Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent health (MNCAH) and nutrition services through increased cold chain and vaccine management; installation and operationalization of oxygen plants; and solarization of facilities to address energy challenges. Integration of EMTCT into RMNCH+ and disaggregated MNCAH data into national data systems have improved monitoring and facilitated evidence-based decision-making for policy, prevention and treatment. Improved supply management, including strengthened first and last mile distribution; expansion of community health systems and training of health workers, and integration of innovation, social behaviour change, gender equality- and equity- based dimensions into the continuum of care have increased survival rates, expanded access to immunization and treatment of childhood illnesses; reduced malnutrition and increased HIV testing towards the achievement of SDG 3.



Access to education remains high with over 1.4 million children receiving foundational numeracy and literacy skills during the CP period 2020-2024. However, learning outcomes and teachers' pedagogical skills remain low, and adolescents and young people continue to face challenges related to low levels of education, life, digital, parenting, learning, vocational and entrepreneurial skills. Preliminary data from the Annual School Census 2024 shows a 3 per cent increase in the number of qualified teachers at the pre-primary and primary education levels from 64 per cent in 2022 to 67 per cent in 2024. GoSL maintained the 22 per cent budget allocation to education. UNICEF in collaboration with the Global Partnership for Education (GPE), the Ministries of Basic and Senior Secondary and Tertiary and Higher Education, and partners continued to reshape the education landscape by enhancing governance, strengthening system capacity and resilience, and improving service delivery to increase access to quality and inclusive education for all children, particularly the most marginalized.



Access to basic water and sanitation services remain at 65 and 23 per cent respectively, with disparities between rural and urban populations. UNICEF continues to support WASH systems strengthening for evidence-based and inclusive programming, including the development of Faecal Sludge Management Guidelines, City-wide Inclusive Sanitation, and WASH Information Management. UNICEF supported to conduct WASH Bottleneck Analysis followed by the Joint Sector Review which resulted in the Presidential WASH Compact expected to be signed in 2025. Since 2020, 306,652 people (159,322 females, 147,330 males) have access to basic water services. Cumulatively, 784,841 people (422,176 females, 362,665 males) have improved access to sanitation services and live in open defecation free environments in 21 out of 190 chiefdoms in 6 districts. 


 


The protective environment for children was strengthened through improvements in the legal and policy framework for advancing child rights such as the adoption of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act in 2024, the development the National Strategy to address Child Marriage and Teenage Pregnancy 2025-2030, and advocacy to ban Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) for children through the revised Child Rights Act. The development of a national positive parenting programme equipped 18,121 caregivers of about 72,000 children[6] with improved attitudes and behaviours according to preliminary findings. Multisectoral efforts through the Global Programme to End Child Marriage reached 93,045 adolescent girls whilst the development of the Cash+ model with social protection actors builds on the social safety net to reduce adolescent poverty.



UNICEF continued to strengthen social policy with the update of the multidimensional child poverty analysis; development of the disability assessment and certification system, and a comprehensive package of support for district development planning to enhance child-friendly decision-making and budget allocations. UNICEF supported adolescent participation in district development planning processes to draw attention to children and adolescents in district development plans and strengthened social accountability. Preparations started in 2024 for the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) to generate evidence on the situation of children and for child-focused interventions. 



The country did not face any major natural disaster in 2024, except for some floodings and minor landslides.
