Dans le cadre du Plan de coopération des Nations Unies pour le développement durable et avec les partenaires techniques et financiers, ainsi que la société civile, l’UNICEF a continué à soutenir le gouvernement togolais dans sa réponse au débordement de la crise du Sahel en ligne avec la feuille de route gouvernementale Togo 2025. Notamment, les interventions en faveur des enfants vulnérables et de leurs familles déplacées par les chocs liés au débordement ont été mises en œuvre en étroite collaboration avec le Programme d'urgence pour le renforcement de la résilience et de la sécurité des communautés (PURS) et les ministères concernés.
En 2024, cinq programmes conjoints ont continué à être mis en œuvre ou initiés : i) Muskoka depuis 2011 avec l’OMS, l’UNFPA, ONU Femmes et l’UNICEF dans le domaine de la santé maternelle et infantile, ii) UBRAF depuis 2018 avec ONUSIDA et l’UNICEF sur le VIH-Sida, iii) Pandemic Fund de la Banque mondiale depuis 2023 avec l’OMS, la FAO, l’OIM et l’UNICEF concernant la réponse aux épidémies, iv) Multi-Partner Trust Fund depuis 2024 avec l’UNODC et l’UNICEF au Togo et Gabon concernant la prévention et réponse à la traite d’êtres humains, et v) Commission européenne (INTPA) depuis 2024 avec l’UNHCR, le PAM, l’OIM et l’UNICEF dans les pays côtiers (Cote d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo et Benin) sur la réponse au débordement de la crise du Sahel. L’UNICEF a également collaboré avec le HCR, le PAM et l’OIM dans le cadre du plan de réponse du golfe de Guinée. Le plaidoyer conjoint a permis l’endossement de ce plan par le gouvernement.
L’UNICEF coordonne le sous-groupe de santé communautaire composé de l’Unité de Gestion des Projets du Fonds Mondial (Gouvernement) et des partenaires techniques et financiers (agences du Système des Nations Unies, Banque Mondiale, AFD, GAVI, GIZ, Organisation Ouest Africaine de la Santé, organisations de la société civile) pour la mise en œuvre coordonné du Plan Stratégique National de Santé Communautaire 2021-2025.
Dans le domaine du WASH, la dynamique des résultats a permis d’initier un partenariat avec le pôle d’innovation de l’UNICEF et l'Institut international de l'eau de Stockholm, pour le soutien aux développements des possibilités pour la mise à l’échelle de l’initiative Togo SANDAL avec les crédits latrines.
En lien avec l’une des trois grandes tendances sur l’avenir des enfants, l’UNICEF a établi un nouveau partenariat avec le ministère de l’environnement et des ressources forestières (MERF) pour identifier les impacts du changement climatique sur l’enfance à travers l’analyse du paysage climatique pour les enfants. Un décret portant sur la coordination multisectorielle a été publié par le MERF, impliquant les ministères sectoriels, les ministères en charge des finances et de la planification, ainsi que le milieu académique.Dans le cadre de sa stratégie de mobilisation de ressources, l’UNICEF a développé ses partenariats avec les donateurs finançant les priorités climatiques, parmi lesquels GIZ pour le Fonds Vert pour le Climat, la Banque Africaine de Développement en collaboration avec le BCR, le PAM et le PNUD. Dans ces deux cas, le gouvernement et l’UNICEF ont passé la phase de validation par les donateurs pour développer des propositions détaillées.
L’UNICEF, en tant que chef de file du secteur de l’éducation, a continué à coordonner et à mobiliser les partenaires techniques et financiers, y compris la société civile et les syndicats d’enseignants, dans le cadre du suivi du plan sectoriel de l’éducation et de l’élaboration du pacte de partenariat. Ce dernier a été finalisé et endossé par le gouvernement togolais et les partenaires en 2024 afin de promouvoir une synergie d’action en faveur de l’équité et de la qualité des apprentissages pendant les premières années de scolarisation.
L’UNICEF, en tant que chef de file du sous-groupe de la protection de l’enfant, a apporté son soutien au ministère en charge de l’action sociale, de l’administration territoriale et de la justice pour assurer la prévention des violences et la prise en charges des enfants victimes. La collaboration avec le ministère chargé de l’Action Sociale et l’UNFPA a permis la validation du Programme national visant à aider les familles et les jeunes à adopter une approche éducative positive. Une collaboration Sud-Sud Togo-Gabon a été établie sur la protection des enfants en situation de traite à travers le fonds d’affection multipartenaire sur la migration (MPTF). La mise en œuvre se fait de manière conjointe avec l’Office des Nations Unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC) dans les deux pays.
En 2024, l’UNICEF a entretenu et renforcé ses partenariats, notamment dans le cadre de la redynamisation du groupe des Partenaires Techniques et Financiers de la Protection Sociale dont elle assure la présidence. Dans ce contexte deux réunions techniques regroupant les différents acteurs concernés ont permis de finaliser et valider techniquement la Politique Nationale de Protection Sociale et aussi de promouvoir la cohérence des interventions des PTFs dans l’accompagnement au renforcement du système national de protection sociale. L’UNICEF a mis une emphase particulière sur l’établissement de partenariats émergents avec l'Agence Nationale de l'Identification (ANID) sur la mise en œuvre Registre Social des Personnes et Ménages et le ministère des finances sur l’identification et l’étiquetage des finances publiques pour l’enfance (PF4C).
L'UNICEF a renforcé son partenariat avec le Programme d'urgence pour le renforcement de la résilience et de la sécurité des communautés (PURS) dans le cadre du processus d’institutionnalisation de la coordination d'urgences. Il a également apporté une contribution effective à la coordination sectorielle dans les secteurs dont il est chef de file (eau-hygiène-assainissement, éducation, protection de l'enfant) et co-chef de file (nutrition). Le pré-lancement de l’initiative Power of Data a été une opportunité pour mobiliser les acteurs des données au Togo tandis que de nouveaux partenariats avec l’université de Kara, le réseau togolais de l’évaluation et l’organisation EvalYouth ont été établis afin de stimuler le réseau de l’évaluation et offrir des perspectives de collaboration sur le renforcement du système national d’évaluation.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Dans un contexte de scolarisation en progression, mais avec des défis persistant sur l’achèvement, l’acquisition des compétences fondamentales, la fréquentation au préscolaire et des disparités importantes, le Togo s’est engagé en 2020 dans un processus d’accélération des priorités éducatives. Il s’est matérialisé par le Plan Sectoriel de l’Education 2030 (PSE) qui vise « une transformation structurelle du système éducatif national pour fournir à la nation des ressources humaines en quantité et de qualité nécessaires à la transformation de l’économie », à travers trois objectifs majeurs :

Garantir un enseignement de qualité pour tous avec des enseignants qualifiés ;
Réguler les flux et améliorer la pertinence et la qualité de l’offre de formation professionnelle et technique afin d’élever le niveau d’employabilité des sortants et de contribuer efficacement au développement économique et social du pays ; et
Réduire les disparités qui existent, en matière d’éducation, entre les régions, les sexes, le milieu urbain et rural, les riches et les pauvres et les personnes en situation de handicap.
À la suite des premières années de mise en œuvre du PSE, la revue sectorielle conduite en 2023 et évaluant les années 2021 et 2022 a rassemblé les parties prenantes du secteur éducatif, allant des quatre ministères en charge de l’éducation jusqu’aux syndicats des enseignants et parents d’élèves. Elle a mis en exergue le défi d’opérationnalisation de cette vision stratégique avec des efforts diffus dans les plans de travail budgétisés annuels du secteur. En effet, les pilotes développés avec les partenaires techniques et financiers (PTFs) restaient à une échelle restreinte avec une approche projet et étaient rarement institutionnalisés. Cette revue a reconnu la richesse de la PSE en réformes et programmes et la nécessité associée de prioriser, dans un contexte de ressources limitées, sur des réformes transformatrices. Par ailleurs, ce constat a été repris dans le cadre de l’analyse des facteurs favorables lors de la préparation du pacte de partenariat qui a été validé en 2024 en identifiant comme réforme prioritaire l’amélioration des apprentissages fondamentaux en début de scolarité.
En ligne avec les conclusions de la revue sectorielle et en tant que partenaire principal sur l’éducation inclusive et l’enseignement préscolaire, l’UNICEF a accompagné le Gouvernement dans la mise en œuvre des recommandations pour assurer l’opérationnalisation de la vision stratégique décrite dans le PSE sur ces thématiques. Ce processus visait à établir un cadre d’opérationnalisation par l’élaboration des stratégies nationales du préscolaire et de l’éducation inclusive ainsi que d’un référentiel sur les sciences, technologie, ingénierie et mathématiques (STIM). La continuité des parties prenantes aux différentes étapes, du diagnostic jusqu’aux stratégies finalisées a aussi permis d’assurer la prise en compte des recommandations dans le développement du pacte de partenariat et une cohérence entre ces approches.
Ainsi, dans le cadre d’un processus participatif, un ensemble de documents stratégiques ont été élaborés pour objectiver la théorie du changement de la PSE. Là où ce dernier avait pour objectif d’améliorer la situation au préscolaire au sens large, la stratégie du préscolaire s’est concentrée sur la fenêtre d’opportunité que représente la mise à disposition d’au moins une année de préscolarisation. Ceci à travers une approche équitée mettant l’accent sur le milieu rural. Le développement du préscolaire favorise la scolarisation des filles en offrant un environnement structuré et sécurisé dès le jeune âge, réduisant les risques de discrimination ou de tâches domestiques précoces. Il permet aux parents, en particulier aux mères, d’avoir du temps pour d’autres activités, valorisant l’éducation des enfants, y compris des filles. En développant les compétences sociales et cognitives des filles, le préscolaire leur donne un meilleur départ dans leur parcours éducatif, augmentant ainsi leurs chances de réussite.
En ce qui concerne l’éducation inclusive, la stratégie s’est concentrée sur les adaptations pédagogiques et les soutiens spécifiques qui répondent aux besoins individuels de tous les enfants, notamment les enfants handicapés, pour ne laisser personne de côté. Cette approche permet également de développer les compétences sociales et la coopération entre tous les élèves, favorisant une intégration durable et une société plus équitable.
Le cadre de référence des STIM a établi des normes pour leur enseignement au secondaire en vue d’accélérer l’équipement des établissements et la formation des enseignants pour un enseignement pratique des matières scientifiques en ligne avec les priorités nationales.
La leçon tirée de ce processus est que le succès de l’opérationnalisation d’une vision stratégique dépend de la stabilité des parties prenantes impliquées, d’une coordination multipartite, et de l’utilisation éclairée des données disponibles, en tirant profit du système d’information national, pour prendre des décisions, notamment dans la priorisation, conditions essentielles pour créer un impact durable. Ce cadre garantit une priorisation cohérente et devrait permettre d’assurer une mobilisation technique et financière des partenaires centrée sur une approche de renforcement de système plutôt que sur une somme d’interventions isolées.
Par conséquent, il est impératif de capitaliser sur ce processus de programmation adaptative dans le cadre de planification stratégique en tirant profit des synergies multisectorielles pour réaliser les droits de l’enfant. Cette leçon apprise peut-être approfondie au sein du secteur en mettant l’emphase sur les catalyseurs de résultats, mais également avec et dans d’autres secteurs pour accélérer l’atteinte des priorités nationales et des Objectifs de Développement Durable.
Il s’agira de :

Accroitre la mobilisation de nouveaux partenaires techniques et financiers, en particulier au préscolaire ;
Documenter les catalyseurs de résultats actuels et émergents dont le digital avec des approches innovantes comme l’application d’autoformation des enseignants pour faciliter leur passage à l’échelle ; et
Tirer profit du processus de décentralisation pour renforcer la coordination, notamment autour des plans de développement communaux, et l’opérationnalisation informée par les risques, ainsi que des cadres de gouvernance adaptés.

The West and Central Africa region (WCAR) has made important progress for children in recent years. Under-five mortality was nearly halved thanks to enhanced healthcare and child survival programmes. Vaccination coverage rose from 42 per cent in 2000 to 69 per cent in 2023, driven by successful immunization campaigns and logistics support by various organizations. Access to antenatal care rose to around 57 per cent, up 10 per cent from a decade earlier, representing a critical gain for child health outcomes. Stunting rates among children under five declined from around 40 per cent in 2000 to approximately 32 per cent in 2022, reflecting advances in nutrition and food security initiatives. The out-of-school rate for primary and lower-secondary age children dropped from 42 per cent in 2000 to 26 per cent in 2023, reflecting the increased commitment by countries to boost education access. Significant policy reforms on child welfare and protection were enacted in several WCAR countries, including laws against child marriage and initiatives to support vulnerable families.
However, this progress remains fragile and uneven, and the region continues to bear a disproportionate burden of child rights deprivations. The births of 48 per cent of WCAR’s children under 12 months were not registered, WCAR accounts for two in five child deaths, 30 per cent of out-of-school children, half of global maternal deaths, and has the second-highest rate of teenage pregnancy. Persistent gender inequality and entrenched social norms continue to hinder progress toward child-focused Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Structural vulnerabilities persist, while climate shocks, economic pressures and declining development assistance compound existing challenges.

The health and nutrition landscape in WCAR remains deeply concerning. Maternal and under-five mortality are unacceptably high primarily due to limited access to healthcare, including immunization. Over 6 million children are under-vaccinated, and 4.3 million have never been vaccinated (zero-dose children). The region is home to 20 per cent of pregnant women living with HIV globally but only 48 per cent are receiving treatment. Malnutrition is a looming threat: one in three children aged 6–59 months is stunted, and 21 per cent of stunting worldwide occurs in WCAR. Continually rising food insecurity puts millions more at risk of malnutrition.

Access to education poses a significant challenge, exacerbated by the fact that by September 2024 more than 13,000 schools had closed due to armed conflict. Access to quality education remains uneven, with girls, children with disabilities and those living in rural areas disproportionately excluded. WCAR’s learning crisis jeopardizes the potential of millions of children and limits the region's broader development prospects.

Ensuring child protection in WCAR remains a critical priority. Between 2019 and 2023, the region reported the highest global incidence of child recruitment by armed groups and sexual violence. Harmful practices such as child marriage persist, and birth registration remains low, with only 52 per cent of children under 12 months formally registered. Violations of child protection and other child rights halt human capital development.

About one-third of WCAR’s population (194 million people) are without basic water services, relying on precarious sources and/or often distant water points. WCAR is the only region where the number of people practicing open defecation is increasing. About 385 million people (65 per cent) lack access to basic sanitation and 436 million (74 per cent) to basic hygiene services. Both rural and urban populations are particularly underserved: 18 per cent in rural areas have access, compared to 35 per cent in urban. Significant disparities abound in access to basic water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, with stark inequalities between the richest and poorest populations, and a disproportionate burden on women and girls.

Access to social protection is constrained for many WCAR children. Despite efforts to strengthen social protection systems, coverage remains well below the need, as reflected, for example, in high rates of extreme poverty among children. Financing constraints for national governments, due to competing demands on national budgets, remain a major bottleneck to address this issue.

Economic trends - High interest rates and short reimbursement periods, along with, competing demands and limited fiscal space restrict investments in child-focused SDGs. Informal employment dominates the labour market, leaving many families exposed to economic shocks. Rising food and energy prices coupled with stagnant wages have eroded household purchasing power. Additionally, high borrowing costs and debt servicing requirements crowd out essential social spending, deepening poverty and inequality. The region's heavy reliance on agriculture and extractive industries further undermines economic resilience due to high vulnerability to climate shocks and global market fluctuations.

Humanitarian trends - Humanitarian needs in WCAR persist and grow due to ongoing conflicts, climate-related disasters and public health emergencies. Around 15 million people (of which 8 million children) have been displaced region-wide, and 46 million children require humanitarian assistance. The Sahel and Lake Chad Basin remain epicentres of instability, but conflict spills into neighbouring countries. WCAR also has the most Children and Armed Conflict (CAAC) situations (eight) and rates second highest for the total number of violations (84,000+), according to the UN Secretary-General’s 2024 CAAC report. Climate-induced disasters further exacerbate food insecurity and malnutrition and contribute to increased child marriage, underscoring the broader effects of these crises. Humanitarian response faces persistent funding gaps and logistical challenges to access hard-to-reach areas. The increasing frequency and duration of crises places additional strain on already overstretched resources and systems, reinforcing the need for stronger response mechanisms.

Demographic trends - Rapid population growth presents both challenges and opportunities for WCAR. By 2063 the region will be home to nearly 500 million children under 18 —20 per cent of the world’s children. Harnessing the demographic dividend requires investment in economic diversification, social services and infrastructure to equip young people to become central actors in human capital development strategies and protect their rights.

Environmental trends - WCAR is among the most climate-vulnerable regions globally: 17 of the 30 most at-risk countries are located in WCAR. Rising temperatures, desertification and biodiversity loss disproportionately impact children, driving food insecurity and deepening poverty. Extreme weather events disrupt livelihoods and often compel families to migrate.
In 2024 the region experienced widespread flooding affecting nearly 6 million people —a 40 per cent increase from 2023. Countries around the Lake Chad Basin were disproportionately impacted, affecting over 5 million affected individuals. The floods not only displaced communities but also disrupted the education of approximately 10 million children across the region. Flooding also exacerbated public health crises, limiting access to healthcare and contributing to the rapid spread of waterborne diseases. These events underscore WCAR's increasing vulnerability to climate change and its extreme weather patterns.

Addressing these complex challenges requires adaptive strategies that build on existing efforts while fostering innovative approaches. Strengthening national systems, expanding strategic partnerships and mobilizing and leveraging additional resources are crucial. By reinforcing community resilience and improving access to essential services, WCAR can better protect children’s rights and accelerate progress toward sustainable development.

2.1 Key achievements and results
In October 2024, the Regional Management Team (RMT) developed a strategy to advance its commitment to child rights, including establishment of a Regional Child Rights Steering Committee to provide guidance and recommendations to the Regional Director on programming and advocacy. Planning for a new Regional Office Management Plan (ROMP) for 2026–2029, in line with the new Strategic Plan, also began in 2024. UNICEF WCAR continued to focus on its eight key results for children (KRCs), aligned with UNICEF Strategic Plan (SP) 2022-2025, the SDGs and the African Union (AU) Agenda 2063. KRCs 2–6 demonstrated a strong upward trajectory, while KRCs 1, 7, and 8 require renewed focus and are prioritized in 2025.

Goal Area 1: Every Child Survives and Thrives (KRCs 1 and 2)
Health
In 2024 UNICEF WCARO delivered extraordinary results in transforming health outcomes across the region, overcoming immense challenges to save lives and strengthen systems. UNICEF’s vaccination campaigns reached 67 million children with lifesaving measles vaccines, while polio outbreak responses slashed paralytic cases by an impressive 2.8 times. Vaccination coverage improved; 11 countries surpassed the 80 per cent DTP3 target—95 per cent in Ghana—and malaria and HPV vaccines were introduced in 12 and one countries, respectively, advancing critical health solutions for the future. In addition, digital innovations, including health platforms, enhanced vaccination adherence and real-time data collection.
In maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH), eight countries crafted national operational plans with UNICEF’s guidance, while cross-regional partnerships sparked a wave of transformation, exemplified by the ‘Every Woman Every Newborn Everywhere-Child Survival Action’ consultation, which united 24 countries, UN agencies and partners in an urgent call for progress.
UNICEF’s support to the West Africa Health Organization’s community health policy and the Muskoka Partnership further strengthened community-based primary health care, including MNCH and HIV services, to accelerate progress towards the SDGs and the African Union's AU) Agenda. In addition, the multi-country evaluation of Child-Friendly Communities (CFC) in DRC, Guinea, and Liberia underscored the need for stronger multi-sectoral integration, improved data systems, and sustained coordination to enhance programme effectiveness and impact. Groundbreaking mHealth platforms in Niger and Côte d'Ivoire further empowered health workers to deliver real-time solutions, improving efficiency and tracking. In addition, by rolling out new diagnostic strategies through ‘point of care’ machines, UNICEF supported 11 countries to increase HIV testing coverage for children and pregnant women. This innovative approach provided rapid, real-time results, improving the uptake of testing and the timely placement of HIV-positive children on treatment.
Faced with multiple health emergencies, UNICEF provided rapid, expert support across the region to respond to outbreaks (e.g., mpox, cholera, dengue), underscoring its leadership in both crisis prevention and response. Through these transformative achievements, UNICEF is shaping a healthier future for West and Central Africa, offering every child, mother, and community an opportunity to thrive.

Nutrition
UNICEF sought to improve children’s overall nutritional status by advancing progress on the five KRC2 pillars: vitamin A supplementation (VAS), complementary feeding, breastfeeding, prevention and treatment of wasting, and maternal anaemia.
Over 86 million children aged 6–59 months received two doses of VAS (annual target: 89 million), prioritizing cost-efficient delivery in low-performing countries. UNICEF also developed a decision-making tool to support sustainable VAS delivery platforms across the region.
Approximately 82 per cent of WCAR’s children experience food poverty. UNICEF expanded the First Foods Africa initiative, including a focus on incentives to local private sectors to produce affordable nutritious foods, policy development and demand creation. UNICEF collaborated with regional academia and centers of excellence to assess the potential for establishing complementary food standards across the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS). Social marketing was used in seven countries to promote demand and consumption of locally available, nutrient-rich complementary foods.
The ‘Stronger with Breastmilk Only’ initiative continued driving exclusive breastfeeding efforts. Adolescents and Civil society organizations including U-Reporters monitored compliance with the Code of Marketing of Breastmilk Substitutes in 3 countries, reporting 750 violations. UNICEF collaborated with the World Health Organization (WHO) and Helen Keller International (HKI) to strengthen monitoring systems.
To prevent and treat wasting, WCARO supported 12 country offices (COs) to align national treatment protocols with the 2023 WHO revised Guidelines. A regional workshop with WHO and the World Food Programme (WFP) provided countries with technical assistance on the implementation of the revised guidelines and specialized consultants were recruited to ensure continuous and in-depth support at the country level. Programming for small-quantity, lipid-based supplements to bolster early childhood nutrition progressed in Burkina Faso, DRC, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Togo.

Goal Area 2: Every Child Learns (KRCs 3 and 4)
WCARO supported COs’ significant progress toward strengthening education systems and improving learning outcomes. During 2024 UNICEF facilitated education access for 12.8 million children, (including approximately 600,000 out-of-school children), contributing to a net increase of 10 million primary and lower-secondary students since 2021. Learning outcomes also improved; 45 per cent of Grade 2 and 6 students achieved minimum proficiency in reading and mathematics, nearly doubling the 2024 figure (PASEC 2019).
UNICEF’s multi-sectoral and multi-country approach contributed to advancing equity, inclusion, and learning. A regional education data strategy and investment case strengthened evidence-based decision-making. An evaluation of programming supported by Norway’s aid agency in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger highlighted the need to expand infrastructure, strengthen coordination and address socio-cultural barriers through advocacy, community engagement and policy integration to sustain and improve inclusive, quality education, especially for girls. A study on multilingualism in the three countries was carried out, and nine COs leveraged 'Teachers for All' research to inform policy and practice. In collaboration with UNESCO and the AU Commission, UNICEF co-drafted the Second Continental SDG 4 Report.
Key advocacy events, particularly the AU Continental Education Conference, strengthened partnerships and education prioritization. The conference, co-led by WCARO, the AU and UNICEF Mauritania, mobilized nearly 400 high-level participants and culminated in the Nouakchott Declaration, recommending a ‘Decade of Accelerated Action for Education’ from 2025–2035 and the eradication of learning poverty. UNICEF was also selected as a grant agent for Global Partnership for Education funding in 12 WCAR countries, reinforcing its lead role in the sector. A symposium on disability inclusion convened eight COs and partners to explore strategic partnerships.
To continue system strengthening efforts, WCARO provided technical assistance to 16 COs to scale up foundational learning methodologies, including ‘teaching at the right level’, structured pedagogy and early childhood education. Nine COs contributed to stronger inclusive education policies and seven advanced adolescent girls’ programming. The Green Schools initiative, integrating climate resilience into education, reinforced UNICEF’s leadership in climate-responsive education strategies.
Innovation in digital learning accelerated, including 15 COs expanding the Learning Passport to enhance school connectivity through strategic partnerships, including with Airtel.
WCARO continued to effectively chair the Transforming Education in Africa (TEiA) Taskforce, which coordinated a series of key events and advocacy efforts throughout 2024, designated as the Year of Education (YoE). These efforts culminated in the successful Continental Education Conference held in December 2024, which led to the adoption of the Nouakchott Declaration. The Declaration included a landmark recommendation for an AU Decade of Accelerated Action for Education Transformation, Youth Skills Development, and Innovation in Africa.

Goal Area 3: Every Child is Protected from Violence and Exploitation (KRCs 5, 6 and 7)
KRC 5: UNICEF reinforced government leadership on preventing violence against children, including sexual violence, by capitalizing on the momentum of the 1st Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children (Bogotá, November 2024). Nineteen WCAR governments made concrete pledges to end violence, providing a solid foundation for advancing country-level implementation, with regional and continent-wide implications. This platform facilitated the strengthening of national, regional, and global policy commitments. A community of practice on Social Service Workforce (SSW) Development was established, involving ministries from Ghana, Liberia, Mauritania, Nigeria, Senegal, and Sierra Leone with the intention of informing national workforce investment strategies across the region. These efforts reinforced a system-wide approach to child protection, ensuring stronger prevention, response, and case management services. WCARO continued to effectively chair the Transforming Education in Africa (TEiA) taskforce, which coordinated a series of key events and advocacy efforts in 2024 as the Year of Education (YoE), and eventually wrapped up with the successful Continental Education Conference in December 2024 that resulted in the Nouakchott Declaration that included the recommendation of the AU Decade of Accelerated Action for Education Transformation, Youth Skills Development and Innovation in Africa.

KRC 6: Catalytic funding and technical support (operational research) from the regional child protection and social policy teams on ‘Cash+Care’ resulted in two models for prevention of child marriage and teenage pregnancies being taken up by Ghana and Sierra Leone for testing and implementation at scale. In The Gambia, UNICEF’s strategic advocacy with other UN agencies, religious leaders, parliamentarians, CSO networks and others prevented the repeal of an anti-FGM law, setting a precedent for policy resilience in other high-prevalence countries. Building on this experience, WCARO worked with communications and advocacy teams to provide technical support to Burkina Faso, The Gambia, Guinea, Guinea Bissau, Mali, Mauritania, and Senegal COs to develop strategic advocacy incorporating a political economy and rights-based approach in the identification, outreach, and engagement with strategic allies.

KRC 7: UNICEF WCAR’s pivotal role in driving progress in birth registration was highlighted in UNICEF’s 2024 report, The Right Start to Life: Global Levels and Trends in Birth Registration, with West Africa recording the fastest progress in Sub-Saharan Africa over the past 15 years. Sustained policy engagement at the Pan-African level has led to the widespread adoption of three proven accelerator strategies: interoperability, decentralization, and digitalization. Strategic partnerships with key technical partners such as Child Identity Protection (CHIP) and government stakeholders are reinforcing these strategies in six focus countries—Cameroon, DRC, Liberia, Niger, Nigeria, and Senegal —to secure children’s legal identity and improve their access to essential services.

Goal Area 4: Every Child Lives in a Safe and Clean Environment (KRC 8)
UNICEF WCAR expanded technical assistance to countries, including for emergency response, with support around a newly developed advocacy agenda focused on three core pillars: (i) securing high-level political commitment to drive systemic change for equitable and sustainable WASH services; (ii) ensuring that the voices and needs of the most vulnerable populations are included in national WASH strategies; and (iii) positioning WASH as a central component of efforts to increase climate finance for long-term sustainability and resilience.
WCAR’s ‘WASH & CEED’ network meeting attracted over 60 stakeholders from 19 COs and major partners. The meeting catalysed high-level dialogue on climate-resilient WASH services and WASH financing, laying the groundwork for enhanced cooperation with international financial institutions— including steps to integrate climate-resilient WASH into national climate action plans.
Knowledge management initiatives provided policymakers with evidence-based insights into important WASH programming: the KRC8 compendium of four case studies from Cote d’Ivoire, Guinea, Nigeria, and Togo, ‘Ending Open Defecation: Experiences from West and Central Africa’, demonstrated scalable, community-led approaches and their impact on sanitation improvements. Similarly, the investment case on menstrual hygiene management (MHM) highlighted measurable outcomes in education, child protection and psychosocial well-being for girls and women in Benin, Niger, and Senegal, informing national planning and resource mobilization efforts to integrate MHM into broader WASH frameworks.
The Gender-Transformative WASH Landscape Analysis, launched with UNICEF HQ, built on the success of the Accelerating Water and Sanitation for All (ASWA) programme, providing actionable insights into gender disparities in WASH access and equipping governments with practical strategies to promote gender equality while enhancing community resilience.

Goal Area 5: Every child and adolescent can access inclusive social protection and live free from poverty
Despite the significant challenges to social protection and public finance posed by the region’s severely constrained fiscal environment, opportunities emerged in climate finance, redistributive policies and enhanced domestic resource mobilization. UNICEF supported training for ECOWAS Commission staff to build foundational capacity for implementing the new social protection framework. Collaborative research with the WFP and World Bank explored the role of social protection in fostering social cohesion, particularly in conflict-affected contexts across the Sahel. The UNICEF-WFP Sahel Social Protection Joint Programme (now including Chad and Burkina Faso thus covering five countries) aligned with the Sahel Resilience Partnership to deliver cash transfers to 190,000 vulnerable households across Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger, mostly (160,000) via national systems.
WCARO provided technical assistance to support ‘Cash+’ programming to address prevailing child protection concerns. Models were introduced in Benin, Ghana, and Sierra Leone, alongside investment cases and partnerships with the private sector. Pilot child grant initiatives were launched in the DRC, Mali, and Nigeria, while cash preparedness activities expanded in Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, and Senegal. To build operational capacity, the RO Cash Taskforce conducted training for 28 staff from Sahel and Cameroon COs, promoting best practices in cash-based emergency responses. A joint workshop with UNICEF HQ set the strategic direction for WCAR’s cash transfer strategy.
These achievements demonstrate UNICEF’s strategic, results-oriented approach to optimizing social protection systems, ensuring that resources reach the most vulnerable children and building resilience across the region through partnerships with key donors.
UNICEF advanced public finance for children by advocating for increased allocations and more efficient spending in key social sectors. The region expanded its evidence base, identifying spending bottlenecks and fiscal space opportunities. Collaboration with the International Monetary Fund in Ghana helped safeguard funding for vaccines and cash transfers, while the 2023 Open Budget Survey findings informed policy dialogues on budget transparency and reforms, essential for sustainable investments for children.

2.2 Cross-cutting area results
Gender: Gender equality was a strategic priority in WCAR; UNICEF integrated programmatic approaches across 21 countries to address restrictive norms and cultural barriers, improving access to health, nutrition, and social protection services for vulnerable women and adolescent girls. Efforts to strengthen gender-responsive budgeting advanced in Côte d’Ivoire, Niger, and Togo, while gender-sensitive policies were integrated into social protection programmes in the Sahel region. Immunization equity was enhanced across nine countries, alongside the expansion of Vitamin A supplementation initiatives with a gender lens. Institutional capacity was reinforced to ensure that adolescent girls’ rights remain central to regional programming, policy, and advocacy.

Adolescents and young people (AYP): Programming sought to ensure the inclusion of adolescents as a core driver of bottom-up social change by advancing partnerships with adolescent girls, evidence-generation, participatory practices, and advocacy. Launch of the ‘Girl-Intentional Approach’ (GIA) offers multisectoral strategies relevant to all sectors and KRCs, while the multi-country study on adolescent girls’ resilience in the Sahel outlined the determinants of girls’ resilience and proposed an action model for the region. The AYP Network was strengthened, enhancing regional coordination and cross-sectoral collaboration. High-impact advocacy efforts, including a youth advocacy workshop on transforming education in Africa, served to expand and strengthen girls' and youth engagement.

Climate change, energy, and environment: UNICEF advanced child-responsive climate action in WCAR at the regional and country levels through policy advocacy, resource mobilization and youth engagement. WCARO published an advocacy brief on child-responsive adaptation and guidance on climate education. UNICEF supported several climate proposals for submission to the Green Climate Fund (GCF), AfDB and other partners. In 2024 US$53 million was secured for four countries through the AfDB’s climate action window, with more expected in 2025. Other key developments included the preparation for phase II of WCAR’s Solar Hub and the activation of strategic partnerships in the Congo Basin. Youth engagement was fostered through promoting youth manifestos, supporting youth-led projects (e.g., Green Rising) and capacity-building of young climate activists. Collaboration with the African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC) contributed to positioning child rights at the core of climate action on the continent.

Disability inclusion: UNICEF advanced disability inclusion in WCA through the development of a regional disability inclusion strategic plan. In line with the key milestones of the plan, the regional office organized a technical symposium on disability-inclusive, shock-responsive strategies involving eight COs, organizations of people with disabilities (OPDs), NGOs, WFP, and German Government agencies. Nine countries gained support for national inclusive education strategies, disability-inclusive sector planning and evidence generation on barriers to children with disabilities.

Prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA): Efforts to establish a region-wide system to PSEA expanded from 54 per cent of countries in 2023 to 75 per cent in 2024. Significant incident reports submitted through the RO rose from 24 in 2023 to 35 in 2024, as did the number of countries that reported SEA allegations (six in 2023; 10 in 2024). This increase may be attributed to several factors, notably the expansion in awareness raising of SEA (in communities and with implementing partners and UN interagency networks) together with information about where and how to report allegations, increased confidence in and trust in reporting mechanisms across countries in the region. To strengthen support and assistance to SEA survivors/victims, WCARO conducted direct training in Chad and Guinea and supported training by PSEA specialists in Cameroon, CAR, and Mali, reaching a total of 807 people. Regional and interagency collaboration improved with the development of standard operating procedures in seven countries to strengthen prevention, protection, and assistance for vulnerable children.

2.3 KRC accelerators
Knowledge management (KM): Nine COs received KM planning guidance and orientation in digital knowledge-sharing and recording lessons learned. The basic course was also translated into French (available on Agora in 2025).

Social and behaviour change (SBC): UNICEF achieved transformative SBC progress in WCAR, strengthening community resilience and driving sustainable impact. In Cameroon, eight universities institutionalized SBC education, equipping future leaders with critical skills. DRC, Guinea, Ghana, Niger, and Nigeria pioneered innovative approaches to climate action, HIV care and waste management, promoting behaviours for healthier, safer environments. Capacity-building efforts across 17 countries empowered 132 participants to improve SBC delivery in development and humanitarian contexts. UNICEF also tackled vaccine hesitancy in 2024, including SBC plans for ‘first-dose’ and under-vaccinated children in seven countries.

Monitoring, data, research: Monitoring focused on child rights, supporting countries to respond to UN and African reporting mechanisms and preparing situation analyses in Cote d’Ivoire, Liberia, Mali, and Mauritania. Leadership sessions helped shape a regional child rights vision and gain commitment.
Innovations on polycrisis and KRC analysis, small area estimates, and Reach the Unreached Initiative (RtU) complemented ongoing data work and helped link data to programme and policy discussions at WCARO and COs. The ‘Africa Expert Group on Child Data’ set up in 2024 by the UN Economic Commission on Africa and UNICEF is critical to strengthening national leadership on child data. WCARO’s regional data strategy strongly supports implementation of the data elements of UNICEF’s Africa Strategy. Numerous high-quality publications were released in 2024, covering a wide range of topics, from sustainable sanitation roadmaps and menstrual health advocacy to shock-responsive social protection systems and social registries; from anaemia prevention and sustainable feeding initiatives to foundational learning and youth leadership, digital engagement, and tech-driven solutions.

Evaluation: An innovative partnership was formalized with the Regional School of Excellence (CESAG), to strengthen national government capacity in Francophone Africa for conducting high-quality evaluations of development interventions. National evaluation capacity was strengthened across the region, culminating in the participation of over 200 evaluation professionals from 17 countries in UNICEF’s flagship training on ExCEL and IMPrESS. These initiatives have enhanced technical competencies, fostered a culture of evaluation, and strengthened national evaluation systems as accelerators of results for children.

Humanitarian preparedness and response: UNICEF advanced humanitarian preparedness and response across 24 countries: 19 achieved over 90 per cent compliance with preparedness standards. Simulation exercises in Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, and Senegal improved national readiness, while localized access strategies in Mali and DRC ensured service continuity for thousands amid instability. Emergency responses to Mpox in DRC and floods in the Republic of Congo provided life-saving assistance. Eight countries adopted the Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) toolkit for real-time monitoring, enhancing decision-making. The Sahel Resilience Partnership, supported by WFP, UNICEF and German aid agencies, protected over 3.5 million people by strengthening essential social services. Inter-agency collaboration and private-sector partners mobilized critical resources, safeguarding vulnerable children and families across the region.

T4D and innovation: UNICEF intensified efforts to expand technology for development across sectors. Airtel’s School Connectivity project connected 1,350 secondary and primary schools, benefiting 1.5 million learners in five countries with digital education. AI-powered mapping identified 1.4 million zero-dose or under-immunized children, enabling more focused strategies, and boosting vaccination coverage. Burkina Faso, Chad, DRC, Liberia, and Mali adopted green energy/solarization at data centres. The Digital Health Information System improved health tracking in Benin, Congo, DRC, Liberia, Niger, and Sierra Leone. Partnerships with Airtel, the World Bank, AUDA and Africa CDC advanced digital learning, child protection and birth registration.

2.4 Influencing global/regional discourse and policy
Communication and advocacy: WCARO delivered a wide range of impactful results using traditional and non-traditional communication and advocacy strategies. The ‘No More Zero-Dose’ song reached 100 million people through radio, TV, and digital platforms, gaining 2 million online views in under two months. The ‘MyName’ campaign for birth registration, tied to the Africa Cup of Nations, engaged millions with support from Canal+. UNICEF trained 70 youth climate leaders from 22 countries who advocated at COP29 and other global and regional meetings. Social media content generated 304 million views, with 1.4 million interactions on Facebook and a 328 per cent increase in the Regional Director’s followers. Media briefings with a regional journalists’ network led to 70+ published stories and training for 150 UNICEF staff in Ghana, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. Collaboration with other major stakeholders and partners drove advocacy for stronger education systems and early childhood development, as well as increased immunization coverage and ending polio in the region.

2.5 Internal management
Financial systems were strengthened across all 24 COs, managing US$38 million for 113 grants, and enhancing cash-transfer mechanisms during emergencies. Supply chain efficiency improved; 95 million vaccine doses were deployed in 12 countries; and US$7.96 million in nutrition supplies delivered to six countries, reducing costs and lead times through regional prepositioning.
Risk management advanced with 126 implementing partner audits covering US$74 million, achieving 101 per cent of spot checks and 112 per cent of programmatic visits; four third-party monitoring agreements were signed to strengthen oversight, particularly in hard-to-reach areas. Partnerships were streamlined; 2,250 partners managed US$500 million in cash transfers; and 98 per cent of civil society partners attained medium/full PSEA capacity.
ICT efforts helped to modernize basic social infrastructure. Twenty-two per cent of COs adopted business-grade network infrastructure, leading to 99 per cent uptime and Mali’s full transition to green energy. Purpose-built tools (e.g., invoice tracker, visa request tool) automated processes, reduced manual workloads, enhanced productivity, and improved operational agility across functions.

Public-private partnerships (PPPs): During 2024 UNICEF strengthened partnerships with the private sector, UNICEF national committees, donors, and regional organizations to enhance impact across key sectors. PPPs to tackle child labour expanded in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, and discussions on mining-related PPPs, progressed in DRC and Guinea. Innovative financing models (e.g., Solar Hub and plastic brick schools) were reviewed to attract social impact investors. UNICEF also provided technical support to COs for accessing climate-related funding, including from GCF, following UNICEF’s accreditation in October 2024.
WCARO also deepened collaborations with continental and regional institutions: the AU, ECOWAS, AfDB and the West African Development Bank (BOAD). Direct partnership with ECOWAS on the First Foods initiative positioned nutrition as a regional priority. Climate action partnerships with ECOWAS’ Centre for Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency, AfDB and BOAD have strengthened the funding for the implementation of the Sustainability and Climate Action Plan; the AfDB's climate action window secured a US$53 million pipeline for Burkina Faso, Chad, Niger, and Togo.
In the Sahel, high-level advocacy secured commitments by Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) and KfW Development Bank for €83.5 million to the multi-agency ‘Building Resilience in the Sahel’ programme, involving UNICEF, WFP, and German Development Cooperation (GiZ). During 2024 this initiative reached 3.5 million people (2.7 million children) in five Sahel countries. BMZ-KfW and the World Bank also expanded their social protection partnership, providing an additional €50 million for Burkina Faso and Chad, alongside existing programmes in Mali, Mauritania, and Niger.
UNICEF and the World Bank continued to support the Francophone Community of Practice on Cash Transfers in Africa. The joint project also supported Germany’s presidency of the Sahel Alliance, contributing to the ad hoc working group on social protection.
UNICEF secured new funding from the Pandemic Fund, exceeding US$6.5 million for Chad, DRC, and Sierra Leone to bolster health resilience. France supported transformation of the Muskoka Fund into a multi-partner trust fund, furthering UNICEF’s capacity for multi-stakeholder collaboration.

United Nations reform: UNICEF engaged actively with the Regional Collaborative Platform and Opportunities and Issues-Based Coalitions to enhance national statistical capacities. Efforts focused on flagship initiatives in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger addressing food systems and climate action, energy transition, education transformation, conflict prevention and governance support. These programmes, set to launch in early 2025, aim to deliver transformative outcomes for children and adolescents.

Health: In 2024 UNICEF WCARO fostered strategic partnerships and provided critical technical support to tackle vaccine-preventable diseases, immunization, MCNH, HIV and health emergencies. Co-leading the Polio Regional Outbreak Response Group with WHO and the Gates Foundation, UNICEF played a key role in advocacy and securing resources through collaboration with the Gavi Alliance. Strong leadership from WCA countries bolstered immunization programmes, while UNICEF co-chaired the regional Immunization Working Group. Partnerships with Africa CDC and WAHO focused on strengthening community-based health, vaccine procurement and digital health integration to ensure long-term system strengthening.

Child protection: The 1st Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children (Bogotá, November 2024) marked a critical step in strengthening partnerships with WHO, the UN Secretary-General’s Special Representative on Violence Against Children and regional governments. Key actions included developing the 'African Statement' to unify African government pledges and organizing a continent-wide webinar with ministers to reinforce commitments.
UNICEF played a pivotal role in the 2024 Africa review of the Global Compact for Migration, appearing on several key panels to advocate for child rights. Collaborative and inclusive advocacy efforts with UNFPA and national stakeholders successfully prevented the repeal of The Gambia's anti-FGM law.
Strategic investments in the social service workforce (SSW) yielded significant progress. A 2024 community of practice facilitated engagement with governments, highlighting the SSW's role in empowering women and girls and contributing to the UNICEF-World Bank Strategic Dialogue.

Nutrition: WCARO’s Nutrition team played a pivotal role in advancing First Foods as a core continental strategy, now embedded in the Africa Strategy. Relying on advocacy and technical expertise, the team influenced the integration of First Foods into the regional nutrition framework, positioning it as a priority within the Child Nutrition Fund—a significant shift in policy and funding priorities. Direct partnership with ECOWAS and other strategic stakeholders was instrumental to building consensus and aligning regional priorities on infant and young child nutrition. This collaborative approach both strengthened regional commitment to First Foods and laid the groundwork for more effective, sustained interventions to combat malnutrition across the continent.

Education: In 2024 WCARO forged key partnerships to drive transformative change in education across the region, ideally increasing opportunities for all children to access quality learning. Through strategic collaboration with Airtel, 1,000 schools in six countries were connected, unlocking new possibilities for digital learning. Partnering with the Gates Foundation and Teaching at the Right Level-Africa, WCARO convened a pivotal workshop in Abuja, uniting eight COs to enhance learning outcomes. With support from the Government of Japan, UNICEF launched initiatives to expand foundational learning in Benin, Burkina Faso, Guinea, and Mali, reinforcing the power of community-led education.
WCARO’s leadership in the Transforming Education in Africa initiative reached new heights at the AU Continental Education Conference, where the call for the ‘AU Decade of Accelerated Action’ set a bold vision for Africa’s education transformation. UNICEF's selection as the Grant Agent for GPE funding in 12 countries reflects the deep trust placed in the organization by ministries of education and partners. Collaboration with global and regional partners helped drive the first Pan-African Conference on Girls' and Women's Education, prioritizing education as a powerful tool for gender equity and empowerment.

Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH): UNICEF WCARO implemented a two-year strategic engagement plan with the African Ministers' Council on Water (AMCOW) to enhance WASH governance, data quality, youth and gender inclusion and sector financing. Key activities included a regional workshop in Senegal that brought together 80 representatives from nine countries to address WASH sector challenges; outcomes informed preparations for the 2024 UN Water Conference.
Collaboration with various partners, such as the German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources, IRC-WASH, Population Services International, SIWI, Sanitation and Water for All and multiple UN agencies, supported initiatives in systems strengthening, climate-resilient WASH services and groundwater management and monitoring by communities. The ASWA III Regional Programme, in partnership with the Directorate-General for International Cooperation, was successfully launched to continue enhancing system strengthening, climate resilience shifts, gender equity, conflict prevention, nutrition outcomes and high-level engagement for WASH.

Social policy: WCARO expanded its social protection partnerships, particularly with Germany’s BMZ and KfW Development Bank, by extending the Sahel-focused joint project with WFP to include Burkina Faso and Chad. A new contract secured €50 million to sustain efforts through 2028. Enhanced cooperation with the World Bank and the Francophone Community of Practice on Cash Transfers facilitated knowledge exchange and technical capacity building. Ongoing collaboration with the International Budget Partnership led to improved budget transparency across African nations. Plans are in place to extend this collaboration through 2027.

NarrativeTitle: Challenges, Lessons Learned and Future Outlook
Indicator_Status3:
Health:
Challenges: Ensuring sustainable immunization financing and overcoming funding gaps in the humanitarian response to acute malnutrition remain critical issues. Many countries struggle to meet vaccine co-financing obligations amid new vaccine introductions and the complexities of the Gavi transition.
Lessons Learned: Strategic partner engagement through high-level joint missions to strengthen domestic financing and systemic accountability is required. Data-driven SBC approaches have proven effective in reducing vaccine hesitancy and increasing uptake. In nutrition, optimizing supply chain processes, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and enhancing enforcement mechanisms are essential to preventing stockouts and waste. Additionally, mobilizing domestic resources and engaging high-level stakeholders can bridge funding gaps and improve emergency nutrition responses. While legislative measures to protect breastfeeding and complementary food quality are vital, stronger enforcement is needed to ensure compliance and meaningful impact.

Nutrition:
Challenges: Severe supply chain inefficiencies—delays, poor stock management, and insufficient regulatory oversight—hinder the timely delivery of life-saving supplies. Weak enforcement of legislative measures (e.g., Breastmilk Substitutes Code) further exacerbates gaps in child nutrition and health protection.
Lessons learned: Optimizing supply chain processes and strengthening regulatory frameworks and enforcement mechanisms are essential to prevent stockouts and waste. Additionally, mobilizing domestic resources and engaging high-level stakeholders can bridge funding gaps and improve emergency nutrition responses. Legislation to protect breastfeeding and complementary food quality is vital, but stronger enforcement is needed to ensure compliance and meaningful impact.

Child protection
Challenges: Persistently high rates of child marriage and FGM and potential pushback against laws prohibiting harmful practices underscore the need to address the structural causes of gender inequality and undertake strategic advocacy with key allies.
Lessons learned: Collaborative partnerships have proven highly effective. The 1st Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children demonstrated that multi-stakeholder engagement can result in concrete pledges. Additionally, investing in strategies informed by data, analysis and evaluation can shape key policies (e.g. on birth registration) by providing clear, evidence-based narratives underscoring the importance of children’s rights to identity.

Education
Challenges: A pervasive lack of sufficient education resources, coupled with a sub-optimal funding outlook, hampers UNICEF’s ability to scale up educational programmes to the national level. This shortfall directly affects efforts to bring quality education to out-of-school children and address broader learning crises.
Lessons learned: The creation of multi-country platforms—fostering initiatives in Quranic education, girls’ education, inclusive education, and digital learning—demonstrated the value of collaborative networks. Through co-creation with COs and data-driven approaches, these platforms have facilitated effective knowledge exchange, bolstered regional strategies, and ultimately enhanced educational outcomes, despite financial constraints.

Water, sanitation, and hygiene
Challenges: Lack of political engagement, weak governance and institutional instability undermine the sustainability of programmes to end open defecation and accelerate access to essential services. These challenges often lead to inadequate financial support, further jeopardizing long-term progress. Equity and gender approaches are insufficiently addressed in public policies and strategies. Low human capital and regional urbanization trends further exacerbate these constraints.
Lessons learned: Recent UNICEF initiatives highlight the relevance of integrating climate resilience in WASH programming. Substantial climate finance has been mobilized to position WASH programmes in key financing mechanisms (climate action window, GCF) to enhance sustainability and climate resilience for WASH services. System strengthening, localization and capacity development of national and regional stakeholders and continued efforts to explore innovative financing are key to sustaining and scaling up results.

Social policy and public finance
Challenges: National budgets face growing pressure as significant funding is allocated to debt service and security, leaving limited resources for social protection programmes. Restrictions on external finance further constrain efforts to expand social safety nets for vulnerable populations.
Lessons learned: Recent advances in cash programming underscore the critical role of human resource investments and cross-sectoral engagement. By aligning operational efforts with broader social protection systems, WCARO has learned that investing in skilled personnel and integrated strategies can help bridge funding gaps and enhance programme coherence.

Communications and advocacy
Challenges: The rapid evolution of digital landscapes and the rise of disinformation present significant hurdles to effective communication. These issues have the potential to undermine public trust and the positive impact of our programmes while also increasing children's exposure to online risks in the absence of adequate policies and safeguards.
Lessons learned: Enhancing digital competencies and integrating AI-driven communication strategies are imperative. Through specialized training and capacity-building initiatives, we have empowered staff to craft balanced, positive narratives—aligned with the Africa Strategy—that not only counter disinformation but also elevate UNICEF advocacy across all sectors and contribute to the transition in the narrative focused more on poly-opportunities than poly-crises.

Adolescents and youth
Challenges: Social and gender norms tend to undervalue and deprioritize adolescents, in particular girls, in areas such as service delivery, opportunities for skilling and participation. Lack of coherent, disaggregated data prevents a clear picture of the status of adolescents, particularly girls. Differing age ranges across sectoral indicators and uneven sex disaggregation create a statistical silence around adolescents aged 10–14 leading to incomplete evidence for decision-making.
Lessons learned: Integrated approaches with adolescent girls that follow common standards and principles have increased impact. Supporting AYP to contribute to decision-making in their households, communities and countries requires equivalent support to parents, community leaders and governments, to translate AYP contributions into action.

Internal Management:
Challenges: High-risk operating environment and fragile contexts along with lapses in the RO oversight, created instability, disrupted operations, and increased security risks, making it difficult to implement activities effectively and efficiently.
Lessons Learned: With the RO oversight role, CO business model reviews and agile structures were promoted to enhance adaptability and efficiency. Reevaluating operating models enabled greater flexibility, quicker decision-making, and more effective resource alignment in volatile environments.

4.2 Future Outlook
In 2025, WCARO will build upon the lessons learned and achievements of 2024, with a renewed focus on transforming the narrative on poly-crisis to one of poly-opportunities. This shift will guide our efforts to optimize strategic impact in accelerating progress towards the KRC-focused ROMP 2022–2025 and the UNICEF SP (2022–2025), in alignment with the SDGs and AU Agenda 2063. WCARO will prioritize comprehensive and strategic support to COs, reinforcing UNICEF's role as the leading agency for data on child and adolescent rights, and accelerating climate action. By focusing on region-specific and continental opportunities, WCARO aims to progressively redefine its offerings and demonstrate the value it brings to national governments and regional and continental institutions. We will support governments and their partners, as they take the lead in setting national child priorities and strategies. Additionally, WCARO will leverage other strategic partnerships, particularly with African institutions like the ACERWC, and innovative financing. We will also reinforce the humanitarian-development nexus, support resilience and adaptive programming, and engage in high-level advocacy and policy dialogue with regional institutions.

During 2024 regular resources were strategically leveraged to reinforce UNICEF’s leadership in adolescent and youth programming, SBC, social policy, and programme coordination. These investments enabled transformative initiatives, including strategic framework development, capacity-building, research dissemination, cross-sectoral collaboration, and policy advocacy, ensuring sustainable progress across WCAR.

Adolescents and youth - A major milestone was the launch of the GIA, accelerating multi-sectoral action to close gender gaps and strengthen country programming. Evidence generation on girls' resilience in the Sahel informed innovative dissemination techniques and expanded engagement with non-traditional partners. In addition, three regional publications were released: ‘WCAR Girls’ Intentional Approach,’ ‘Girls' Resilience in the Sahel’ (towards a regional model for girls' programming) and ‘Youth Standards’ to guide youth programmes by putting youth at the centre.
Youth advocacy was strengthened through collaboration with Education, WASH, and CEED, training youth advocates to transform education across Africa. A Francophone climate advocacy network was established across West and Central, East, and South, and North Africa and Haiti, enhancing regional cooperation. The AMCOW ‘Gender and Youth Inclusion’ strategy advanced gender-responsive water management efforts.
Cross-regional knowledge sharing fostered best practices in adolescent programming, enabling scalable innovations, and enhanced cross-country collaboration.

Social and behaviour change - UNICEF introduced a capacity-building toolkit on ‘Social and Behaviour Change in Humanitarian Action,’ enhancing preparedness, crisis response and public health interventions. The integration of community engagement principles into humanitarian response plans and the Humanitarian Appeal for Children strengthened participatory decision-making. UNICEF strengthened SBC capacity in humanitarian settings, ensuring that staff and partners are well-equipped to implement SBC strategies during immunization and emergencies.

Social policy - Amid financial constraints and competing fiscal demands, UNICEF worked to expand national social protection programmes, to ensure that vulnerable children, particularly those in fragile settings, received support.
Integrated social protection models, such as Cash+ Nutrition, Cash+ for Adolescents and child grants, were scaled up to improve child well-being. Evidence-based technical assistance supported government budgeting and optimizing social sector investments. Strengthened policy advocacy resulted in increased funding commitments and improved resource efficiency.

Planning, monitoring, data, and research – WCARO contributed to results across the five Goal Areas through strengthened planning, monitoring, and advocacy. Key achievements included advancing child rights during high-level discussions, integrating them into regional analyses and supporting COs, (e.g., countering pushback against The Gambia’s FGM law). Additionally, planning and monitoring efforts were improved through enhanced reporting, performance dashboards and better coordination across humanitarian and development initiatives, ensuring stronger alignment with regional priorities and sustained impact for children across the region.

Programme coordination - UNICEF played a key role in high-level coordination, ensuring strategic alignment and cross-sectoral collaboration, including support to the AU Continental Education Conference in Mauritania, leading to the Declaration of Nouakchott.
